<meta>This page begins the preface to Ralph Cudworth's major work, following his dedication to the Lord Chancellor. He shifts from addressing his patron to explaining his scholarly objectives to the general reader.</meta>

## THE
# PREFACE
### TO
## THE READER.

<margin>Fiske 1926.</margin>
*Though I confess I have seldom taken any great pleasure in reading other men's apologies <note>original: "Apologies"; here meaning formal justifications or explanations for one's work</note>, I must at this time make some myself.* First, therefore, I acknowledge that when I first engaged the press, I intended only a discourse concerning *Liberty and Necessity*, or to speak more plainly, *Against the Fatal Necessity of all Actions and Events*. We conceive that this "fatal necessity," upon whatever grounds or principles it is maintained, will serve the design of atheism and undermine Christianity and all religion. It does this by taking away all guilt and blame, punishments and rewards, and plainly rendering a Day of Judgment ridiculous. *And it is evident that some have pursued this idea of late for that very purpose.*

But afterwards, we considered that this controversy—which is indeed a dispute concerning *The True Intellectual System of the Universe*—does, in its full extent, include *other things*. The necessity of all actions and events is maintained by several people upon very different grounds, according to that tripartite <note>three-part</note> fatalism mentioned by us at the beginning of the first chapter.

For *first*, the *Democritic fate* <note>Referring to the philosophy of Democritus, who argued the world was made of atoms in mechanical motion</note> is nothing but the material necessity of all things without a God. It supposes that senseless matter, necessarily moved, is the only origin and principle of all things. Therefore, this is called by *Epicurus* the *physiological* <note>original: "Physiological"; in this context, it refers to the physical laws of nature or "physics"</note> fate, and by us, the *atheistic fate*.

Besides this, the *divine fate* is also *bipartite* <note>divided into two parts</note>. Some theists <note>those who believe in God</note> suppose God both to decree and do all things in us (evil as well as good), or to determine all actions by His immediate influence, and so make them all equally necessary to us. From this, it follows that His will is in no way regulated or determined by any essential and immutable goodness and justice; it suggests that He has nothing of morality in His nature, being only an arbitrary, omnipotent <note>all-powerful</note> will. It also follows that all moral good and evil for us creatures are...

<summary>Ralph Cudworth introduces his preface by explaining that his work aims to refute "Fatal Necessity," which he argues leads to atheism and makes religious judgment meaningless. He identifies three types of fatalism: the atheistic/materialist view and two different theological views on God's will.</summary>
<keywords>Fatalism, Atheism, Free Will, Democritus, Epicurus, Divine Fate, Necessity, Morality, Intellectual System of the Universe</keywords>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues Cudworth's exploration of "Fatalism"—the belief that all events are predetermined—and how it conflicts with the "Fundamentals of True Religion." He is specifically distinguishing between those who believe in an arbitrary God and those who believe in a good God but still deny human free will.</meta>

merely theoretical <note>original: "Theticall"; referring to things established by decree or convention rather than nature</note> or positive <note>In a legal sense, "positive" refers to laws created by humans or divine command, rather than natural laws</note> things; by law <note>original: νόμῳ (nomō)</note>, and not by nature <note>original: φύσει (physei)</note>. *This, therefore, may be called The Divine Fate: Immoral and Violent. Again, there are other divine fatalists who acknowledge a Deity that allows other things besides itself to act, and has an essential goodness and justice in its nature. Consequently, they acknowledge that there are things that are naturally just and unjust to us, and not by law and arbitrary constitution alone. Nevertheless, they take away from men all such liberty as might make them capable of praise and dispraise, rewards and punishments, and objects of distributive justice <note>Justice concerned with giving each person their due based on merit</note>. They conceive necessity to be intrinsic to the nature of every thing in its actions, and find no contingency anywhere. From this, it follows that nothing could possibly have been otherwise in the whole world than it is. And this may be called The Divine Fate: Moral (as the other was immoral) and Natural (as the other was violent). It is a concatenation <note>A series of interconnected things</note>, or complex series of causes, all in themselves necessary, depending upon a "moral" Deity (if we may speak this way)—that is, one who is essentially good and naturally just—as its head, the first contriver and orderer of all. This kind of divine fate has not only been asserted by the Stoics in the past, but also recently by various modern writers. Therefore, regarding the three fatalisms, or false hypotheses of the universe mentioned at the beginning of this book: one is* Absolute Atheism; *another* Immoral Theism, *or religion without any natural justice and morality (where everything just and unjust, according to this hypothesis, are merely theoretical or artificial things, made by arbitrary will and command only). The third and last is such a* Theism *as acknowledges not only a* God, *or omnipotent understanding being, but also natural justice and morality founded in Him and derived from Him; nevertheless, it acknowledges no liberty from necessity anywhere, and therefore no distributive or retributive justice in the world. In contrast, these three things are (as we conceive) the* fundamentals *or* essentials *of* True Religion. First, *that all things in the world do not float without a head and governor, but that there is a* God, *an omnipotent understanding being, presiding over all.* Secondly, *that since this* God *is essentially good and just, there is something* naturally beautiful and just <note>original: φύσει καλὸν καὶ δίκαιον (physei kalon kai dikaion)</note>, *something in its own nature that is immutably and eternally just and unjust, and not by arbitrary will, law, and command alone.* And lastly, *that there is* something in our own power <note>original: ἐφ' ἡμῖν (eph’ hēmin)</note>, *or that we are principles or masters of our own actions to such an extent as to be accountable to justice for them, making us guilty and blameworthy for what we do wrong, and deserving of punishment accordingly.* Which three fundamentals

--- Page 15 ---
<meta>This page continues Cudworth’s definition of the "True Intellectual System of the Universe." He concludes his discussion on the fundamentals of religion and begins outlining the structure of his massive three-volume project, which aims to refute three types of fatalism: atheism, immoral divine determinism, and moral divine determinism.</meta>

->to the Reader.<-

...of religion are suggested by the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews in these words: *He who comes to God must believe that He exists, and that He is a rewarder of those who diligently seek Him.* For to "seek out God" here is nothing other than to seek to share in His image, or to recover that divine nature and life from which we have been alienated. 

And these three things—namely, that all things do not drift without a leader or governor, but that there is an omnipotent, intelligent Being presiding over everything; that this God possesses essential goodness and justice; and that the differences between moral good and evil—between what is honorable and what is dishonest—are not determined by mere will or law alone, but by nature. Consequently, the Deity cannot act upon, influence, or force men to do things that are, in their own nature, evil. And lastly, that necessity is not intrinsic <note>Inherent; belonging to the essential nature of a thing</note> to the nature of every thing, but that human beings have such liberty or power over their own actions that they are held accountable for them and are blameworthy when they do wrong. Consequently, there is a distributive justice <note>Justice concerned with giving each person their due based on merit or behavior</note> of rewards and punishments operating throughout the world. 

I say that these three principles (which are the most important subjects the human mind can consider), when taken together, constitute the wholeness and entirety of what we call ***The True Intellectual System of the Universe***—in the same sense that *Atheism* may be called a false system of the universe. The word *Intellectual* is added to distinguish it from the other commonly named "Systems of the World" (that is, the visible and physical world), such as the *Ptolemaic*, *Tychonic*, and *Copernican* <note>Respectively: the earth-centered, hybrid, and sun-centered models of the solar system</note> systems. The first two of these are now generally considered false, while the latter is considered true. 

And so, with our perspective now expanded to include a threefold *fatalism*—or false and spurious hypotheses of the Intellectual System that make all things necessary for various reasons—we have planned to refute them all in three separate books. 

**The first** is against *Atheism* (which is the "Democritic Fate" <note>The philosophy of Democritus, who argued that everything happens by the mechanical collision of atoms in a void</note>), in which all its reasoning and philosophy are refuted, the existence of God is demonstrated, and thus "material necessity" <note>original: ὑλική ἀνάγκη (hylikē anankē)</note>—the idea that all things happen by physical compulsion—is overthrown. 

**The second** argues for a God who is not merely an omnipotent, arbitrary Will who decrees and forces all actions, both evil and good. Instead, it argues for a God who is essentially moral, good, and just, and for a "natural distinction between the honorable and the base" <note>original: Discrimen Honestorum & Turpium</note>. By this, another ground for the necessity of all human actions will be removed. 

**And the third and last** book is against the idea that necessity is intrinsic and essential to all action. It argues for such liberty, or "self-power" <note>original: Sui-Potestas</note>, in rational creatures as to make them accountable, capable of receiving rewards and punishments, and thus the proper subjects of distributive or retributive justice.

<summary>Cudworth defines the "True Intellectual System" as resting on three pillars: God's existence, God's inherent goodness, and human free will. He then outlines his three-book plan to refute atheism and various forms of determinism.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the outline of the three main sections of Cudworth’s work and explains why this volume is published independently despite the original plan for a single large volume. It concludes the explanation of why the title "Intellectual System" was chosen and begins to describe the specific theological errors (fatalisms) he intends to refute.</meta>

<header>The Preface</header>

...by which the *now only remaining foundation* of the fatal necessity of *all actions and events* will be *removed*. All three of these parts fall under that *one general title*: *The True Intellectual System of the Universe*. *Each book also has its own specific title*: first, *Against* Atheism; second, *For* Natural Justice and Morality *Founded in the* Deity; and third, *For* Liberty from Necessity, and a Distributive Justice of Rewards and Punishments in the World.

We believe this will fully *satisfy* all those who are not extremely *critical* or *fault-finding*—at least *those who have ever heard of the* Astronomical Systems of the World—concerning our general title. They will not think we are obligated by this title to *treat the hierarchy of angels and all the various species of animals, vegetables, minerals, and so on*; that is, to write *concerning everything that exists* <note>original: *De Omni Ente*</note>, or whatever is *contained within the entire scope of the universe*.

However, the *whole scale of being* is also noted here, and the general ranks of substantial beings below the Deity (or Trinity of divine persons <note>original: "Divine Hypostases." In theology, a hypostasis refers to a distinct person or individual essence of the Trinity</note>) are *considered*. According to our philosophy, these are only *two*: souls of various degrees (including angels *themselves*) and body or matter. We also *prove* the immortality of those souls. Nonetheless, we *suggested these points only to satisfy some people's curiosity*.

*Nevertheless, we confess that we might have skipped this general title and presented this volume to the reader's view not as a* part or piece, but as a whole, complete, and entire work on its own, if not for two reasons. First, *we began with those three* "Fatalisms," <note>Fatalism: The belief that all events are predetermined and inevitable, leaving no room for human choice</note> *or* false hypotheses *of the* Intellectual System, *and* promised a refutation of them all when we still thought we could fit them into a single volume. Second, *every other page throughout this entire volume accordingly bears the heading* "Book the First." This is why we must first *apologize* for *publishing one part or book alone*. We were surprised by the *length of it*, whereas we had originally *intended to include two more along with it*.

*Despite this, there is no reason why this volume should be thought* imperfect or incomplete *just because it does not contain all three things we first designed*. It contains everything belonging to its own specific title and subject, and in that respect, it is not a fragment, but a whole. This must certainly create an expectation for the two following treatises (especially in those *who find any satisfaction in this* first volume) regarding those *two other Fatalisms* or *false hypotheses* mentioned, to complete our *whole Intellectual System*. The *one* is to *prove* *that God is not merely* arbitrary omnipotent will (*without any essential goodness and justice*) decreeing—

<summary>Cudworth explains the structure of his work, "The True Intellectual System of the Universe," noting that it was originally intended as one volume but was split due to its length. He outlines the three types of "fatalism" he intends to refute: atheism, the idea of a God without essential goodness, and the denial of free will.</summary>

<keywords>Ralph Cudworth, Intellectual System of the Universe, fatalism, atheism, divine hypostases, materialism, immortality of the soul, free will, theological voluntarism</keywords>

--- Page 17 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's explanation of the three main sections of his work. He clarifies the second and third parts: the defense of immutable morality against the idea that God's will is arbitrary, and the defense of free will against fatalism. He also begins an apology for the length of the fourth chapter and his motives for defending Christianity alongside the existence of God.</meta>

<header>To the Reader.</header>

...ing and doing all things in the world, both evil and good, and thereby making them equally necessary to us. From this it would follow that all moral good and evil are merely conventional <note>original: "thetical"</note>, positive, and arbitrary things—that is, based on will rather than nature. This second part is the **defense of natural, eternal, and immutable justice or morality.** The other point is that **necessity is not intrinsic to the nature of everything** (God and all creatures) or **essential to all action**. Instead, there is **something that is up to us** <note>original: "ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν" (eph' hēmin). This is a central concept in Stoic and late antique philosophy regarding human agency and free will.</note>, meaning that **we have some liberty or power over our own actions**. This is the defense of a distributive or retributive justice that gives rewards and punishments throughout the whole world. Therefore, we think it appropriate to inform the reader that although we still truly intend to complete these works, their final finishing and publication will depend on many factors. These include not only our life and health—the latter of which is very uncertain—but also our leisure or time away from other necessary work.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Next, we must also apologize for the *fourth chapter*. Although its length makes it more of a *book* than a *chapter*, it still does not address all the *contents* listed at its beginning. Since ancient *atomic physics* <note>original: "Atomick Physiology." In this period, "physiology" referred to the general study of nature or physics.</note> became so blended and complicated with *atheism*, we focus chiefly on *two* points concerning it in this *first* chapter. 

*First*, we argue that it was not an invention of *Democritus* or *Leucippus*, but is of much greater antiquity. This is supported by the tradition passed down by *Posidonius* the *Stoic*, who claimed that it originated with a *Phoenician* named *Moschus* who lived before the *Trojan Wars*. This history suggests the theory was originally *Mosaic* <note>Many scholars of this era believed "Moschus" was a reference to the biblical Moses, implying that atomic theory was originally a divinely revealed truth.</note>. We also rely on *Aristotle’s* affirmation that the majority of the *ancient philosophers* embraced this *hypothesis*. Furthermore, it is certain that various *Italian philosophers* <note>original: "Italicks," referring to the Pythagorean school in Southern Italy.</note>—specifically *Empedocles*—practiced *atomic physics* before *Democritus*. This is the reason *Empedocles* was so highly praised by the poet *Lucretius*. 

Beyond this, there is more than a mere suspicion <note>original: "Presumption"</note> that the *homoeomery* (or *similar atomology*) of *Anaxagoras* was merely a corruption <note>original: "Degeneration"</note> of the true and original *atomology* of the ancient *Italians*. Theirs was an *anomoeomery*, or a *doctrine of dissimilar and unqualified atoms* <note>A theory where the fundamental building blocks—atoms—do not possess the secondary qualities (like color, smell, or heat) of the objects they form.</note>. Therefore, the only thing that is *true* regarding *Democritus* and *Leucippus* is that these men were indeed the *first atheizers* of this ancient *atomic physics*. They were the inventors and promoters of *atomic atheism*. This is the *true* meaning of *Diogenes Laertius* (though it is not commonly understood) when he records that they were the *first* to make *unqualified atoms* the *principles* of everything in the *universe* without exception. By this, he means they applied the theory not only to *inanimate bodies* (as the religious atomic philosophers of Italy had done before) but also to the *soul* and *mind*.

We believe that this *atomic physics*, in its *essentials*, is *unquestionably true*. Specifically, we hold that the only principles of *bodies* are *magnitude, figure, site, motion, and rest*. The *qualities* and *forms* of *inanimate bodies* are actually nothing but various combinations of these, which cause different perceptions <note>original: "Phancies"</note> in us. (This excellent discovery, made so long ago, is a notable instance of the wit and wisdom of the ancients.) 

Next, we make it clear that this *atomic physics*, when rightly understood, is far from being either the *mother* or *nurse* of *atheism*. It is not in any way *favorable* to it, as is *commonly supposed*. In fact, it is the *most direct opposite* to atheism and the *greatest defense* against it. For, *first*, we have *discovered* that the *principle* upon which this *atomology* is *founded*—and from which it grew—was none other than this: *nothing comes from nothing* <note>original: "Nothing out of Nothing," or the Latin "Ex nihilo nihil fit."</note> in its *true sense*, or, *that nothing can be caused by nothing*. From this, it was concluded that in the *natural birth of things* <note>original: "Natural Generations"</note>, no new *real entity* was produced that did not exist before. # The Preface

*We demonstrate that the qualities and forms of inanimate bodies are not entities really distinct from the size, shape, position, and motion of their parts. In this section, we have shown that the Pythagorean doctrine of the pre-existence of souls was founded upon the exact same principle as atomic physics <note>original: "Atomick Physiology." Because of this alone, we are certain (even without testimony from antiquity) that Democritus and Leucippus could not possibly have been the original inventors of this philosophy. Although Plato likely did this out of a distaste and prejudice against atomic atheists—which made him fail to properly consider or understand that physics—his expectations were greatly disappointed. The atomic theory <note>original: "Atomology"</note> which he rejected <note>original: "Exploded"</note> is, when rightly understood, actually the greatest defense against atheism. On the contrary, those "forms and qualities" which he championed are the natural breeding ground for it. Besides their confusing obscurity, they imply that something can be brought out of nothing in an impossible sense—which we show to be the entry point for all atheism. Thus, in this first chapter, we have not only stripped atheism of its claim to atomic theory, showing that the latter provides no shelter or protection to the former, but we have also made it clear that it is the greatest defense against it. This is a point we will emphasize further later on.*

*As for the second chapter, we have only this to say: we have taken the liberty here to reveal the secret mysteries <note>original: "Arcane Mysteries"</note> of atheism and to expose all its alleged rational foundations that we could find suggested in any writings. We have excluded only those arguments peculiar to the **hylozoic** <note>Hylozoism is the belief that all matter is inherently alive or possesses a soul.</note> form of atheism (which is directly contrary to the atomic form). We have presented these arguments in their strongest possible light for this purpose: so that once they are all frustrated and refuted, **theism** <note>The belief in the existence of a god or gods, specifically a creator who intervenes in the universe.</note> might achieve a greater and more rightful triumph over atheism.*

...itself. This has not been done by us out of any foolish obsession with **Pythagorean** whims <note>original: "Pythagorick Whimseys." To us, it is as certain as any principle in **geometry** that **thought** and **understanding** can never possibly result from **size**, **shape**, **position**, and **local motion**—which is all that we can attribute to a physical **body**—no matter how they are combined. 

Nor, for that matter, is it any more believable that thought could emerge from "qualities" such as **hot** and **cold**, **moist** and **dry**, or **thick** and **thin**, as claimed by **Anaximandrian atheism** <note>original: "Anaximandrian Atheisme." If we accept that premise, we confess it would be impossible for us to prove the **existence of a God** from the **observable phenomena** of the world.

In the close of this fifth chapter—because **atheists** finally pretend that **theism** and **religion** are incompatible with **civil sovereignty**—we were forced to briefly untangle and disprove all **atheistic ethics** and **politics**. But on the contrary, we assert that **justice** and **moral obligation** are not merely created by **laws** and **commands**, but exist in **nature**. By proving this, along with **conscience** and **religion**, to be the only foundation of **civil authority**, we also uphold all the rights of **civil sovereigns**—giving both to **Caesar** the things that are Caesar’s and to **God** the things that are God’s <note>A reference to the biblical instruction in Matthew 22:21 regarding the separation of duties to the state and to the divine.</note>.

However, upon further consideration (as seen on page 846), we found reason to change our opinion on this matter.

### CHAPTER I

Those who hold the necessity of all human actions and events do so upon one of two grounds. Either they suppose that necessity is inwardly essential to all agents whatsoever, and that free will <term>Contingent Liberty</term> <note>The power to choose or act differently under the same circumstances; true freedom of choice.</note> is an impossible thing <note>original: "τὸ πρᾶγμα ἀνυπόστατον"</note> or a contradiction that can have no existence anywhere in nature. The sentiment of this view was expressed by the *Epicurean* poet Lucretius:

->—*Because every thing has an internal necessity in all its actions, etc.*<-
<note>original: "Quod res quæque Neceſſum Inteſtinum habeat cunctis in rebus agendis, &c."</note>

That is, that everything naturally labors under an *internal necessity* <note>original: "Intestine Necessity"</note>. Alternatively, they may admit that free will is not only possible but also actually exists in the *Deity*, yet they believe all things are so determined by the *will* and *decrees* of this *Deity* that they are thereby made *necessary* for us. 

The first of these two opinions—that free will is an impossible thing <note>original: "πρᾶγμα ἀνυπόστατον"</note> which can have no existence in nature—may be maintained on two different grounds. One is based on a hypothesis that the universe is nothing but *matter* and *local motion*; since nothing moves itself, the action of every agent is determined by some other external agent. Therefore, *material* and *mechanical necessity* <note>original: "ὑλικὴ ἀνάγκη"</note> must rule over all things. The other ground is that, even if *thinking beings* are supposed to have a certain principle of activity within themselves, there can still be no randomness or choice in their actions because all acts of will <term>Volitions</term> are determined by a *necessary*, preceding understanding.

*Plotinus* provides another classification of *fatalists*, which in the end leads to the same conclusion as the previous one. He says: *“A man will not do wrong to divide all fatalists first into these two general heads: namely, those who derive all things from one principle, and those who do not”* <note>original: "διπλῆ τις ἂν εἴη δόξα... οἱ μὲν γὰρ ἀφ᾽ ἑνός τινος πάντα ἀρτῶσιν, οἱ δ᾽ οὔ"</note>. The former may be called *Divine Fatalists*, and the latter *Atheistical*. 

These *Divine Fatalists* he again subdivides into two groups. First are those who believe that *God*, through *immediate influence*, does all things within us; just as in animals, the limbs are not determined by themselves but by the *commanding faculty* <term>Hegemonick</term> <note>From the Greek 'hegemonikon,' referring to the ruling part of the soul or mind that directs behavior.</note> in each individual. Second are those who make *Fate* an *entangled series* <note>original: "Implexed Series"</note> or chain of causes, all of which are necessary in themselves, with God as the primary cause. The former seems to be a description of that very...

# The Mathematical or Astrological Fate. Book I.

...the very fate that is maintained by some modern <note>original: "Neoterick"</note> Christians; the latter is the fate of the *Stoics*.

Therefore, *Fatalists*—those who believe in the necessity of all human actions and events—may be divided into three main groups:

First, there are those who assert the existence of a God but suppose that He decrees and determines all things regardless of any other factors. In doing so, they make all our actions necessary. Although ancient writers and philosophers occasionally mentioned this kind of fate, it has been primarily maintained by certain modern <note>original: "Neoterick"</note> Christians, contrary to the views of the early Church.

Secondly, there are those who suppose a God who acts wisely but by necessity. They believe this God designed the general structure of the world in such a way that every event that happens now is the unavoidable result of a chain of causes. This fate is a sequence <note>original: "Concatenation"</note> of causes, each necessary in itself. This was the view asserted by the ancient *Stoics*, *Zeno* and *Chrysippus*, whom the Jewish *Essenes* <note>A Jewish sect known for their asceticism and belief in destiny.</note> seemed to follow.

And lastly, there are those who hold that everything happens by material necessity without the involvement of a God. *Epicurus* calls this "the fate of the naturalists" <note>original: "τὴν τῶν φυσικῶν εἱμαρμένην"</note>; these are, in fact, the atheists. These thinkers may also be called the Democritical Fatalists <note>Followers of Democritus, who believed the world was governed by the motion of atoms.</note>.

These three opinions concerning fate represent different theories <note>original: "Hypotheses"</note> about the intellectual system of the universe. We shall present all of them here, endeavoring to show why they are false, and then provide the true system of the world in their place.

II. As for the "Mathematical" or "Astrological Fate" that is so frequently discussed, its foundations are not very substantial. Whatever it may be, it must fall under one of the two general categories mentioned in the distribution by *Plotinus* <note>Plotinus was a major Neoplatonic philosopher who categorized different types of causality.</note>: it either derives all things from a single principle or it does not.

It seems to have first emerged among the *Chaldeans* <note>Ancient Babylonians famous for their early developments in astronomy and astrology.</note> from a type of blind *polytheism* (which is really just a disguised form of atheism). However, it was later adopted and fondly nurtured by the *Stoics*, who made it subordinate to their idea of "Divine Fate." *Manilius*, *Firmicus*, and other masters of that sect were its great promoters.

Even those who were not fatalists, including both Heathen and Christian philosophers like *Plotinus*, *Origen*, *Simplicius*, and others, attributed too much importance to astrology. While they did not believe the stars *forced* human actions here below, they supposed that Divine Providence (foreknowing all things) had arranged a remarkable coincidence between the motions of heavenly bodies and events on Earth. In this view, the stars were not causes, but signs <note>original: "Prognosticks"</note> of what would happen. 

Thus, *Origen* concludes that the stars do not *cause* events but rather *signify* them. He suggests the heavens are a kind of "Divine Volume" where those who are skilled can read or decipher human events. *Plotinus* expresses the same idea:

> "The motion of the stars was intended for the physical preservation of the whole universe, but it also serves another purpose: that those who look at them as if they were letters—if they are skilled in such 'grammar'—may read what is to come from their patterns, interpreting the meaning by way of analogy. For instance, it is like someone saying that because a bird flies high, it signifies certain high and noble actions." <note>original Greek: "φέρεσθαι μὲν ταῦτα ἐπὶ σωτηρίᾳ τῶν ὅλων, παρέχεσθαι δ᾿ ἐν ἄλλῳ χρείαν τὴν τῷ εἰς αὐτὰ ὥσπερ γράμματα βλέποντας τὰς τοιαύτων γραμματικῶν εἰδότας ἀναγινώσκειν τὰ μέλλοντα ἐκ τῶν σχημάτων κατὰ τὸ ἀνάλογον μεθοδεύοντας τὸ σημαινόμενον· ὥσπερ εἴ τις λέγοι ἐπειδὴ ὑψηλὸς ὄρνις σημαίνει ὑψηλάς τινας πράξεις"</note>

the whole; but they afford also another use collaterally in order to prediction <note>original: "Prognostication"</note>, namely that they who are skilled in the "Grammar of the Heavens" may be able, from the various configurations of the stars, to spell out future events as if they were letters. They do this by making such analogical interpretations as are commonly used in augury <note>The practice of predicting the future by observing the flight of birds.</note>: as when a bird flies high, they interpret this as some high and noble exploit.

And Simplicius, in like manner, says: <note>original: "σύμφωνός ἐστιν ἡ εἱμαρμένη περιφορά τῇ προβολῇ τῶν ψυχῶν τῇ κατ᾿ αὐτὴν ἐρχομένη εἰς τὴν γένεσιν, οὐκ ἀναγκάζουσα μὲν τὰς τῶνδε ὀρέγεσθαι ἢ τῶνδε, σύμφωνος δ᾿ ἔσται ταῖς ὀρέξεσιν αὐτῶν."</note> *The fatal movement of the heavens is made to correspond with the entry of souls into birth at such and such times; it does not force them to desire this or that, but acts in harmony with their own appetites and wills.* These philosophers were more inclined to this persuasion because of a superstitious conceit they held: that the stars, being animated, were intellectual beings of a far higher rank than men. And since God did not make them, nor anything else in the world, solely for themselves alone, but also to contribute to the public good of the universe—and since their physical influence seemed insignificant—these thinkers did not know what else could be worthy of the stars, unless it were to portend human events. This indeed is the best sense that can be made of astrological prediction; but it is a business that stands upon a very weak and tottering, if not impossible, foundation.

### III. The Opinion of a Fate Superior to the Deity

There is another wild and extravagant conceit which some of the Pagans had. Though they verbally acknowledged a deity, they nonetheless supposed a certain Fate superior to it—superior not only to all their other petty gods, but also to Jupiter himself. To this purpose is that line of the Greek poet, translated into Latin by Cicero: <note>original: "Quod fore paratum est id summum exuperat Jovem"</note> *What is prepared to happen overcomes even the highest Jupiter*; and that of Herodotus: <note>original: "τὴν πεπρωμένην μοῖραν ἀδύνατά ἐστι ἀποφυγέειν καὶ τῷ θεῷ."</note> *It is impossible for God himself to avoid the destined fate*; and <note>original: "δουλὸς θεὸς ἀνάγκης"</note> *God himself is a servant of Necessity.* 

According to this conceit, Jupiter in Homer laments his condition because the Fates had determined that his beloved Sarpedon should be slain by the son of Menoetius, and he was not able to withstand it. <margin>Lactantius, Book I, Chapter II. Lucian, *Jupiter Confutatus* (Jupiter Confuted).</margin> Though all these passages may not perhaps imply much more than what the Stoic hypothesis itself imported; for that theory did also, in some sense, make God himself a servant to the necessity of matter and to his own decrees. In that view, God could not have made the smallest thing in the world otherwise than it now is, much less was he able to alter anything. 

According to that saying of Seneca: <note>original: "Eadem Necessitas & Deos alligat. Irrevocabilis Divina pariter atque Humana cursus vehit. Ille ipse omnium Conditor ac Rector scripsit quidem Fata sed sequitur. Semper paret semel jussit."</note> *One and the same necessity ties both God and men. One irrevocable and unalterable course carries on both divine and human affairs. The very Maker and Governor of all things, who wrote the Fates, nevertheless follows them. He always obeys what he once commanded.* 

But if there were this further meaning in the passages cited before—that a necessity outside of God, which was invincible by him, determined his will in all things—then this was nothing but a certain confused and contradictory jumble of Atheism and Theism mixed together; or an odd kind of intimation, that however...

-># The Moderation of this Discourse. BOOK I.<-

The name of God might be used in compliance with common speech and opinion, but in truth, it signifies nothing but "Material Necessity"; according to this view, the blind motion of matter is really the highest Divine Power <note>original: "Numen"</note> in the world. On this point, the words of Balbus the Stoic in Cicero's writings are fitting: *The Nature of God is not all-powerful and excellent if it is subject to either Necessity or Nature, by which the Heavens, Seas, and Earth are governed. But nothing is more excellent than God. Therefore, God is not obedient or subject to any Nature.* <note>original Latin: "Non est Natura Dei Præpotens & Excellens, siquidem ea subjecta est ei vel Necessitati vel Naturæ quâ Cœlum, Maria, Terraque reguntur. Nihil autem est præstantius Deo. Nulli igitur est Naturæ obediens aut subjectus Deus."</note> God would not be the most powerful and excellent Being if He were subject to either that Necessity or Nature by which the heavens, seas, and earth are governed. But the very concept of a God implies the most excellent Being. Therefore, God is not obedient or subject to any external nature.

### IV. A Balanced View of Fate and Providence

Now we think it right to suggest that, although we will oppose those three types of Fatalism mentioned before—as they are false theories of the world's system and order <note>original: "Mundane System and Oeconomy"</note>—and although we will try to exclude that "cruel tyrant" (as Epicurus calls it) of universal Necessity reigning over everything, we still want to leave some room for **Contingent Liberty** <note>Freedom that allows for different outcomes depending on choice.</note> to move around in. Without this liberty, rational creatures could not be blamed for anything they do, nor could God have any reason to show His justice, nor indeed could His Providence be justified. 

Yet, just as we give to God the glory for all good things, we do not completely banish the idea of Fate, nor do we remove all Necessity. This total removal of Fate was something for which the "Clazomenian Philosopher" <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BC), a Pre-Socratic philosopher from Clazomenae, who was accused of attributing too much to chance.</note> of old was criticized. He claimed *that nothing that happens occurs by fate, but that some things are the works of chance.* <note>original Greek: "μηδὲν τῶν γινομένων γίνεσθαι καθ̓ εἱμαρμένην, ἀλλὰ ἔιναι τινὰ ἔργα τῆς τύχης."</note> 

The Sadducees among the Jews were also noted for this: *They abolish all Fate, and will not allow it to be anything at all, nor to have any power over human affairs, but they put everything entirely into the hands of men's own free will.* <note>original Greek: "Τὴν μὲν εἱμαρμένην ἀναιροῦσιν ἔναι ταύτην ἀξιώεντες, ὅτε κατ̓ αὐτῶν τὰ ἀνθρώπινα τέλη λαμβάνεν, ἀπαντὰ δ̓ ἐφ̓ ἡμῖν αὐτοῖς τιθέντες."</note> Some of our own thinkers seem to have come too close to this extreme, attributing perhaps more to the power of Free Will than either religion or nature will allow. 

However, the theory we shall recommend as most consistent with the truth—that of a <term>ἀπρόνοια</term> <note>The Greek text provided in the OCR is "apronoia" (lack of providence), but the context suggests the author is advocating for "Pronoia" (Providence) or is contrasting his view with "apronoia."</note> merciful <note>original: "Placable"</note> Providence, overseen by a Deity who is essentially good—will avoid all extremes. This view gives God the glory for what is good, frees Him from the blame for what is evil, and leaves a balanced mixture <note>original: "Commixture"</note> of both contingency and necessity in the world. 

As nature requires a mixture of motion and rest (without which nothing could be born), so too does the world require this balance. This middle ground <note>original: "Temper"</note> was observed by several of the ancients, such as the Pharisee sect among the Jews, who decided *that some things, and not all, were the effects of Fate, but some things were left in men's own power and liberty.* <note>original Greek: "τινά ἐστιν ἐφ̓ ἑαυτοῖς ὑπάρχειν"</note> 

This was also held by Plato among the philosophers: *Plato’s view is that the soul's own inclination is the cause of its good state, while its bad state is brought on by itself. The beginning of virtue and vice in human souls starts with their union with bodies.* <note>original Greek: "πλάτωνος δέ ἐστι, τήν ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ ῥοπὴν καὶ ἀρχὴν ἀγαθὴν ἀγαθῶν, κακὴν δὲ κακῶν ἐξ αὐτοῦ ἐπαγωγήν. Ἀρχὴ δὲ ἡ τῆς ἀνθρωπίνων ψυχῶν ἐκείνω μετὰ σωμάτων ἀρετῆς καὶ κακίας ἀρχή."</note> Plato inserts a degree of Fate into human lives and actions, but he joins it with freedom of the will as well. He does indeed suppose human souls to have within themselves the causes of their own changes to a better or worse state, and everywhere declares that God...

# CHAP. I. *The Atheistical or Democritical Fate.*

...God to be blameless for their evils, and yet he somewhere makes the three Fatal Sisters—*Clotho, Lachesis,* and *Atropos* <note>The three Fates of Greek mythology: Clotho spins the thread of life, Lachesis measures it, and Atropos cuts it.</note>—to be busy about them as well. For according to the sense of the ancients, Fate is a servant of Divine Providence in the world, and takes place differently based on the different actions of free-willed beings. And however free a thing the human will may seem to be to some, I believe it is beyond question that it can bring upon itself such necessities and fatalities that it cannot suddenly rid itself of at will. But whatever is said in the following discourse by way of opposition to that fatalism of the "modern" <note>original: "Neoterick"</note> Christians is intended only to vindicate the constant doctrine of the Christian Church in its greatest purity (as shall be demonstrated), and not to introduce any new-fangled idea of our own.

V. We must now proceed to give a more full and perfect account of these three different types of Fate, or *hypotheses* of the world’s system mentioned before, together with the grounds for them. We will begin first with the one we principally intend to disprove: the *Atheistical* or *Democritical Fate* <note>Named after Democritus, the ancient Greek philosopher who proposed that the world is made of atoms moving by necessity.</note>. As this is a matter of the most dangerous consequence of all, it also seems to be the most spreading and infectious in these latter times.

Now, this *atheistical* system of the world—which makes all things materially and mechanically necessary without a God—is built upon a specific *scientific theory* <note>original: "Physiological Hypothesis"</note> that is different from what has been generally accepted for many ages. This theory is called by some *Atomic* or *Corpuscular*, and by others *Mechanical*; therefore, we must give a full and perfect account of it. We shall do this first in general terms, briefly, without descending to those minute details which are disputed among these atomists themselves, in this manner:

The Atomic science supposes that a "Body" is nothing else but *extended and resistant bulk* <note>original Greek: διαςατόν ἀντίτυπον (diastaton antitypon)</note>. It concludes, therefore, that nothing is to be attributed to matter except what is included in its nature and *idea*: namely, greater or lesser magnitude (size), divisibility into parts, figure (shape), and position, together with motion or rest—but with the condition that no part of a body can ever move itself; it is always moved by something else. Consequently, it supposes that there is no need for anything else besides these simple elements of size, shape, location, and motion (which are all clearly understandable as different modes of extended substance) to explain physical phenomena. 

Therefore, there is no need for any "substantial forms" <note>An Aristotelian concept suggesting that objects have an internal "form" or essence that directs their behavior.</note> distinct from matter, nor for any other qualities really existing in the bodies themselves other than the results or collections of those simple elements and the arrangement of the invisible parts of bodies in respect to shape, location, and motion. Nor is there a need for any "intentional species" <note>The old theory that objects "send out" little images of themselves to our senses.</note> or appearances sent from objects to our senses. Lastly, there is no need for any other kind of motion or action really distinct from local motion (such as "generation" or "alteration"), as these are neither understandable as modes of extended substance, nor in any way necessary. For as much as the forms and...

# The Atheistical Hypothesis founded Book I.

Properties of physical bodies may well be understood to be nothing but the result of those simple elements of size, shape, position, and motion, combined in various ways. This is much the same way as a great variety of syllables and words result from the different combinations and conjunctions of a few letters, the simple elements of speech. Furthermore, the physical part of sensation—and particularly that of vision—may be explained solely by the local motion of bodies. This happens either by physical *outflows* <note>original: *effluvia*</note> (called *images, membranes,* and *skins* <note>original: *simulachra, membranæ,* and *exuviæ*</note>) streaming continually from the surface of objects, or rather, as the later and more refined atomists conceived, by pressure made from the object to the eye through the medium of light. So that <term>as if by a staff, the thing seen is reported through the stretched air</term> <note>original: ὡς διὰ βακτηρίας τοῦ ταθέντος ἀέρος τὸ βλεπόμενον ἀναγγέλλεται</term>. The sense, taking notice of the object by the subtle intervening medium that is tense and stretched (pushing every way from itself upon the optic nerves), touches the object by that medium as if with a staff. 

Again, birth and decay <note>original: "generation and corruption"</note> may be sufficiently explained by the gathering together and shrinking apart of matter, or local motion, without the need for <term>Substantial Forms</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "Substantial Forms" were the internal essences that gave things their specific nature; the atomists rejected these in favor of mechanical explanations.</note> and qualities. And lastly, those sensible *ideas* of light and colors, heat and cold, sweet and bitter—as they are distinct things from the shape, position, and motion of the invisible parts of bodies—seem plainly to be nothing else but our own *fancies*, *feelings*, and *sensations*, however they may be commonly mistaken for qualities existing in the bodies outside of us.

VI. This much may suffice for a general account of Atomic Physics <note>original: "Anatomical Physiology." In this context, the author refers to "Atomical" physics—the study of the structure of matter.</note>. We shall in the next place consider its antiquity, as well as what notice *Aristotle* took of it and the account he gives of the same. For though *Epicurus* followed this path entirely, it is well known that he was not its first inventor. Instead, it is most commonly attributed to *Democritus*, who was older than both *Aristotle* and *Plato*, being reported to have been born the year after *Socrates*. *Cicero* says that *Epicurus* watered his orchards from Democritus's fountains. *Sextus Empiricus* and *Diogenes Laertius* testify that Democritus did <term>discard all qualities</term> <note>original: ἐκβάλλειν τὰς ποιότητας</term>, and *Plutarch* notes that he made the first principles of the whole universe <term>atoms devoid of all qualities and feelings</term> <note>original: ἀτόμους ἀπαθεῖς</note>. 

However, *Laertius* claims that *Leucippus*, who was somewhat older than *Democritus*, was the first inventor of this philosophy, though he did not write as many books about it as *Democritus* did. *Aristotle*, who often takes notice of this philosophy and usually ascribes it to *Leucippus* and *Democritus* jointly, gives us this description of it in his *Metaphysics*: 

<term>Leucippus and his companion Democritus claim that the elements are the "full" and the "void" (matter and space), saying that one is "Being" and the other "Non-being." They say the causes of everything else are the differences in matter, which are only three: shape, order, and position. They call these differences by these names: *Rysmus* (shape), *Diathigte* (order), and *Trope* (position).</term> <note>original Greek: Λεύκιππος δὲ καὶ ὁ ἑταῖρος αὐτοῦ Δημόκριτος στοιχεῖα μὲν τὸ πλῆρες καὶ τὸ κενὸν εἶναί φασι λέγοντες οἷον τὸ μὲν ὂν τὸ δὲ μὴ ὂν, καὶ τὰς διαφορὰς αἰτίας τῶν ἄλλων φασὶ ταύτας μέντοι τρεῖς, σχῆμά τε καὶ τάξιν καὶ θέσιν. διαφέρειν γὰρ τὸ ὂν ῥυσμῷ καὶ διαθιγῇ καὶ τροπῇ</note>

# CHAP. I. Upon the Atomical Physiology.

"Democritus says that those so-called shavings in the air that appear in the sunbeams coming through windows are a diverse collection of seeds that serve as the elements of all nature; Leucippus says the same." <note>original Greek: οἷον ἐν τῷ ἀέρι τὰ καλέμενα ξύσματα ἐν ταῖς διὰ τῶν θυρίδων ἀκτῖσιν τὴν πανσπερμίαν στοιχεῖα λέγει Δημόκριτος τῆς ὅλης φύσεως ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ Λεύκιππος.</note> They are (he says) like those *scraps* <note>original: *Ramenta*</note> or dusty particles which appear in the *sunbeams*, a *diverse collection of seeds* <note>original: *Omnifarious Seminary*</note> which *Democritus* makes to be the first *elements* of the whole *universe*, and *Leucippus* does the same. Elsewhere the same *Aristotle* tells us that these two *philosophers* explained *birth* <note>original: *Generation*</note> and *change* <note>original: *Alteration*</note> without the use of abstract "Forms" and "Qualities," but instead by *shapes* <note>original: *Figures*</note> and *local motion*.

"Democritus and Leucippus, having established shapes (or atoms of various shapes) as the first principles, explain change and birth through them; specifically, they explain birth and decay through the combining and separating of these atoms, but change through the alteration of their order and position." <note>original Greek: Δημόκριτος δὲ καὶ Λεύκιππος ποιήσαντες τὰ σχήματα τὴν ἀλλοίωσιν καὶ τὴν γένεσιν ἐκ τούτων ποιοῦσι, διακρίσει μὲν καὶ συγκρίσει γένεσιν καὶ φθοράν, τάξει δὲ καὶ θέσει ἀλλοίωσιν·</note> Again, Aristotle elsewhere takes notice of that opinion of the *Atomists*: that all *sense* was a kind of *touch*, and that the *sensible qualities* of *bodies* (like taste or color) were to be explained by *shapes*. He attributes this not only to *Democritus*, but also to the *generality* of the old *philosophers*, though he very much disliked the idea:

"Democritus and most of the natural philosophers <note>original: *Physiologers*</note> here commit a very great absurdity, in that they make all *sense* to be *touch*, and reduce *flavors* to *shapes*." <note>original Greek: Δημόκριτος καὶ οἱ πλεῖστοι τῶν φυσιολόγων ἀτοπώτατόν τι ποιοῦσι, πάντα γὰρ τὰ αἰσθητὰ ἁπτὰ ποιοῦσι καὶ εἰς σχήματα ἀνάγουσι τοὺς χύμους·</note> *Democritus* and most of the *natural philosophers* here commit a very great absurdity, in that they make all *sense* to be *touch*, and resolve *sensible qualities* into the *shapes* of invisible *parts* or *atoms*. 

And this opinion he endeavors to disprove by these arguments. First, because there is *opposition* <note>original: *Contrariety*</note> in *qualities*—as in *black* and *white*, *hot* and *cold*, *bitter* and *sweet*—but there is no *opposition* in *shapes*. For a *circular shape* is not the opposite of a *square* or a *polygon*; therefore, there must be *real qualities* in *bodies* distinct from the *shape*, *position*, and *motion* of their parts. Again, since the variety of *shapes* and *arrangements* is *infinite*, it would follow that the *types* of *colors*, *smells*, and *tastes* should be *infinite* as well, and could not be reduced to any certain number. I leave these arguments for the *professed atomists* to answer. 

Furthermore, *Aristotle* somewhere also censures that other *fundamental principle* of this *atomical physiology*: that the *sensible ideas* of *colors* and *tastes*—such as *red*, *green*, *bitter*, and *sweet*—are, when formally considered, only *passions* and *fancies* <note>original: *phansies*</note> within us, and not real *qualities* in the *object* outside of us. For as in a *rainbow* there is really nothing outside of our sight but a *dewy cloud* <note>original: *Rorid Cloud*</note> diversely bending <note>original: *refracting*</note> and reflecting the *sunbeams* at a certain *angle*; nor are there really such *qualities* in a *transparent prism* <note>original: *Diaphanous Prisme*</note> when, by bending the *light*, it shows us the same *colors* of the *rainbow*. From this, they concluded that those things are properly the *mental images* <note>original: *Phantasms*</note> of the *person sensing* <note>original: *Sentient*</note>, caused by different *motions* on the *optic nerves*. 

So they conceived the case to be the same in all other *colors*: that both the *colors* of the *prism* and *rainbow* were as real as other *colors*, and all other *colors* were as *imaginary* as they. Then, by the same *reasoning*, they extended this idea further to the other *senses*. But this opinion *Aristotle* condemns in these words: "The earlier natural philosophers were wrong in this, thinking that nothing was either white or black without sight, nor had flavor without taste." <note>original Greek: οἱ πρότερον φυσιολόγοι τοῦτο οὐ καλῶς ἔλεγον οὐδὲν οἰόμενοι οὔτε λευκὸν οὔτε μέλαν ἄνευ ὄψεως, οὔτε χύμον ἄνευ γεύσεως·</note> *The former natural philosophers were generally wrong in this, in that*

# The Records in Aristotle and Plato Book I.

They thought there was no *black* or *white* without the *sight*, nor any *bitter* or *sweet* without the *taste*. There are other passages in *Aristotle* concerning this philosophy, which I think are unnecessary to include here; I shall have occasion to cite some of them later for other purposes.

VII. But in the next place, it will not be improper to show that *Plato* also has left a very full record of this <term>Mechanical or Atomical Physiology</term> <note>original: "Mechanical or Atomical Physiology"—a theory of nature that explains physical phenomena through the movement and collision of tiny particles or atoms.</note> (which has hardly been noticed yet). However, he does not credit it to either *Democritus* (whose name *Laertius* thinks Plato purposely avoided mentioning throughout all his writings) or *Leucippus*, but to *Protagoras*. Therefore, in his *Theaetetus*, having first declared in general that the Protagorean philosophy made all things consist of a mixture of parts (or *atoms*) and *local motion*, he represents it specifically concerning colors in this way:

"First, concerning the eyes, you must understand that what you call white color is not something existing separately outside your eyes, nor is it in your eyes; rather, black and white and every other color appear to be produced by the impact of the eyes upon a corresponding motion. Thus, what we call each color is neither the thing hitting the eye nor the eye being hit, but something unique that arises between them both." <note>original Greek: ὑπόλαϐε τοίνυν οὑτωσὶ κατὰ τὰ ὄμματα πρῶτον, ὃ δὴ καλεῖς χρῶμα λευκὸν μὴ εἶναι αὐτὸ ἕτερόν τι ἔξω τῶν σῶν ὀμμάτων μηδ' ἐν τοῖς ὄμμασι ἀλλὰ μέλαν τε καὶ λευκὸν καὶ ὁτινοῦν ἄλλο χρῶμα ἐκ τῆς προσϐολῆς τῶν ὀμμάτων πρὸς τὴν προσήκουσαν φορὰν φανεῖται γεγεννημένον, καὶ ὃ δὴ ἕκαστον εἶναί φαμεν χρῶμα οὔτε τὸ προσϐάλλον οὔτε τὸ προσϐαλλόμενον ἀλλὰ μεταξύ τι ἑκάστῳ ἴδιον γεγονός</note>

Immediately following this, he asks: "Can you or any other man be confident that as every color appears to him, it appears exactly the same to every other man and animal, any more than tastes and touches, heat and cold do?" <note>original Greek: ἦ σὺ διισχυρίσαιο ἂν ὡς οἷόν σοι φαίνεται ἕκαστον χρῶμα τοιοῦτον καὶ κυνὶ καὶ ὁτῳοῦν ζώῳ</note> From this, it is plain that *Protagoras* made <term>Sensible Qualities</term> <note>original: "Sensible Qualities"—the properties of an object that we perceive through our senses, such as color, sound, or smell.</note> not absolute things existing in the bodies themselves, but *relative* to us, and *passions* <note>original: "Passions"—here meaning subjective experiences or impressions made upon the mind.</note> within us; and so they are called shortly after "certain <term>fancies</term>, <note>original: "Phansies"</note> seemings, or appearances in us." 

But there is another passage in which a fuller account is given of the whole Protagorean doctrine, beginning thus: 

"The principle upon which all these things depend is this: that the whole universe is motion (of atoms) and nothing else besides. This motion is considered in two ways, and accordingly called by two names: <term>Action and Passion</term>. <note>original: "Action and Passion"—the 'Agent' (the object acting) and the 'Patient' (the sense organ being acted upon).</note> From the mutual meeting and, as it were, friction between these two, a vast number of offspring are born, which though infinite in number, can be reduced to two general types: the object of sense and the sensation, which are always produced together. The sensations are seeing, hearing, and the like; and the corresponding objects of sense are colors, sounds, etc." <note>original Greek: Ἀρχὴ δὲ ἐξ ἧς ἃ νῦν δὴ ἐλέγομεν πάντα ἤρτηται ἥδε αὐτῶν, ὡς τὸ πᾶν κίνησις ἦν καὶ ἄλλο παρὰ τοῦτο οὐδέν, τῆς δὲ κινήσεως δύο εἴδη πλήθει μὲν ἄπειρον ἑκάτερον, δύναμιν δὲ τὸ μὲν ποιεῖν ἔχον, τὸ δὲ πάσχειν, ἐκ δὲ τῆς τούτων ὁμιλίας τε καὶ τρίψεως πρὸς ἄλληλα γίνεται ἔκγονα πλήθει μὲν ἄπειρα δίδυμα δὲ, τὸ μὲν αἰσθητόν, τὸ δὲ αἴσθησις ἀεὶ συνεκπίπτουσα καὶ γεννωμένη μετὰ τοῦ αἰσθητοῦ, &c.</note> Therefore, when the eye, or such a <meta>proportionate...</meta>

### CHAP. I. Concerning this Atomical Physiology. 11

...proportionate *object* meet together, both the *perceived object* <note>original Greek: αἰσθητὸν</note> and the *perception* <note>original Greek: αἴσθησις</note>, the *sensible idea of white and black* and the *sense of seeing* are generated together; neither of these would have been produced if one had not met with the other. *And so in the same way, we must understand cold and heat and everything else: that in itself, nothing exists on its own, but through the association with one another, all things come to be and take all forms through motion* <note>original Greek: Καὶ τ’ ἄλλα δὴ οὕτω ψυχρὸν καὶ θερμὸν καὶ πάντα ᾧ αὐτὸν τρόπον ὑποληπτέον αὐτὸ μὲν καθ’ αὑτὸ μηδὲν εἶναι, ἐν δὲ τῇ πρὸς ἄλληλα ὁμιλίᾳ πάντα γίνεσθαι, καὶ παντοῖα ἀπὸ τῆς κινήσεως</note>. The same should be understood for all other *sensory objects* <note>original: Sensibles</note>, such as *hot* and *cold*, etc.—that none of these are *absolute* things in themselves, or *real qualities* in the *objects* outside of us. Instead, they are produced by the mutual meeting <note>original: Congress</note> of the *agent* (the object) and the *patient* (the observer) with one another, and that is done through *motion*. So, neither the *agent* has any such thing in it before its meeting with the *patient*, nor the *patient* before its meeting with the *agent*. *But from both the active and the passive coming together with each other, and giving birth to both the sensations and the things sensed, certain qualities are produced on one hand, and the perceiving things on the other* <note>original Greek: ἐκ δὲ ἀμφοτέρων τοῦ ποιοῦντος καὶ τοῦ πάσχοντος πρὸς τὰ ἄλληλα συγγινομένων καὶ τὰς αἰσθήσεις καὶ τὰ αἰσθητὰ ἀποτικτόντων, τὰ μὲν ποῖα ἄττα γίγνεσθαι τὰ δ' αἰσθανόμενα</note>.

But when the *agent* and *patient* meet, producing sensation and *sensible qualities*, both the *object* and the *perceiving being* <note>original: Sentient</note> are immediately made to be qualified in a certain way. For example, when *honey* is tasted, the *sense of tasting* and the *quality of sweetness* are produced together, even though the *sense* is commonly <note>original: vulgarly</note> attributed to the *taster* and the *quality of sweetness* to the *honey*. The *conclusion* of all this is summed up thus: *nothing is anything in itself, but it is always becoming something for someone* <note>original Greek: οὐδὲν εἶναι αὐτὸ καθ’ αὑτὸ ἀλλὰ τινὶ αἰεὶ γίγνεσθαι</note>. That is, none of those *sensory things* is anything absolute in the *objects* outside us, but they are all generated or made *relatively* to the *perceiving being*.

There is more in that *dialogue* for this purpose, which I omit here; but I have set down this much of it in the *author's* own *language*, because it seems to me to be an excellent *monument* to the *wisdom* and *insight* <note>original: Sagacity</note> of the ancient *philosophers*. The main *curiosity* in this whole business of the *mechanical* or *atomical philosophy* is expressed here more fully and plainly than it is in *Lucretius* himself: namely, that *sensory things*, according to the *ideas* we have of them, are not real *qualities* existing absolutely outside of us, but are *appearances within us* <note>original Greek: ἐν ἡμῖν φάσματα</note>, *fancies* or *phantasms* in us.

So true is this that both the Latin *interpreters*, *Ficinus* and *Serranus*, could not help but understand it in the same way, even though neither was likely acquainted with this *philosophy* (as it had not yet been restored in their time). The one expressed it thus: *Color is a sort of middle result coming from sight and motion. It is a sensory experience of this kind affecting the eyes* <note>original Latin: Color ex Aspectu Motúque Medium quiddam resultans est. Talis circa Oculos Passio</note>; and the other: *From the varying disposition of the observer and the varying appearance of the sensory object, different colors are both seen and created; however, they are only mental images and do not exist except in the mind* <note>original Latin/Greek: Ex varia Aspicientis diathesi, variáque sensibilis specie colores varios & videri & fieri, ita tamen ut sint φανταστὰ nec nisi in animo subsistant</note>. However, it appears from *Plato’s* way of telling the story and the tone of the whole *dialogue* that he himself was quite prejudiced against this *philosophy*. This was likely because *Protagoras* had used it as a foundation for both *skepticism* and *atheism*.

VIII. This is true even though Protagoras is not commonly noticed for such things, being usually represented only as a *Sophist* <note>A professional teacher or philosopher in ancient Greece, often accused of using clever but fallacious arguments.</note>. Indeed, *Laertius* and others confirm that *Protagoras* was a *student* <note>original: Auditor</note> of *Democritus*; and so he might have been, despite what *Plutarch* tells us—that *Democritus* wrote against Protagoras taking away...

# The Antiquity of Atomology. BOOK I.

...way the **absolute natures** of things. However, we believe that neither **Democritus**, nor **Protagoras**, nor **Leucippus** was the first **inventor** of this **philosophy**. Our reason is that all three of them were **atheists** (though **Protagoras** alone was banished for that **crime** by the **Athenians**), and we cannot believe that any **atheists** could be its **inventors**. Much less can we think it was the **genuine byproduct** <note>original: Spawn and Brood</note> of **atheism** itself, as some imagine. For although these **atheists** adopted it for their own purposes, trying to use it to their advantage, if it is rightly understood, it is actually the most effective **weapon** <note>original: Engin</note> against **atheism** possible. We shall demonstrate later that none of those **atheists**, whether **ancient** or **modern** (no matter how much they **pretended** to understand it), truly understood it, but perpetually contradicted themselves within it. And this is the **reason** why we focus so much on this **philosophy** here: not only because we cannot challenge the **atheists** with their own **weapons** without a perfect knowledge of it, but also because we believe we can create a **powerful antidote** against **atheism** from that very **philosophy** which so many have used as a **vehicle** <note>original Latin: Vehiculum</note> to spread this **poison** of **atheism**.

**IX.** In addition to **logic** <note>original: Reason</note>, we also have strong **historical** probability for the **opinion** that this **philosophy** is much older than either **Democritus** or **Leucippus**. First, because **Posidonius**, an **ancient** and **learned philosopher**, claimed (as both **Sextus Empiricus** and **Strabo** report) that it was an old **tradition** that the first **inventor** of this **atomic philosophy** was a certain **Moschus**, a **Phoenician**, who lived before the **Trojan Wars**, as **Strabo** also notes.

**X.** Moreover, it seems quite probable that this **Moschus**, the **Phoenician philosopher** mentioned by **Posidonius**, might be the same person as **Mochus**, the **Phoenician natural philosopher** <note>original: Physiologer</note> mentioned by **Iamblichus**. Iamblichus affirms that **Pythagoras** conversed with Mochus's **successors**, **priests**, and **prophets** while he was staying at **Sidon** (which was Pythagoras's native city). This may be taken as a **suggestion** <note>original: Intimation</note> that they instructed him in that **atomic natural philosophy** which **Moschus** or **Mochus** the **Phoenician** is said to have invented. **Mochus** or **Moschus** is clearly a **Phoenician name**, and there is one **Mochus**, a **Phoenician writer**, cited by **Athenaeus**, whom the **Latin translator** calls **Moschus**. Furthermore, **Mr. Selden** <note>John Selden (1584–1654), a famous English jurist and scholar.</note> agrees with the **theory** <note>original: Conjecture</note> of **Arcerius** (the **publisher** of **Iamblichus**) that this **Mochus** was actually the celebrated **Moses** of the **Jews**, with whose **successors**—the **Jewish philosophers**, **priests**, and **prophets**—**Pythagoras** conversed at **Sidon**. Some **unrealistic atomists** <note>original: Phantastick Atomists</note> might seize upon this to claim that their **philosophy** exists by **divine right**, as if it owed its **origin** to divine revelation. However, since **philosophy** is a **matter of reason** rather than **faith**, people should not **strive** <note>original: affect</note> to trace its **ancestry** <note>original: Pedigree</note> back to **revelation**. By that very excuse, they might seek to tyrannically impose it upon the minds of men—minds which God has purposely left free to use their own faculties. And there is no lack of other good authority for **this**: that **Pythagoras** did borrow many things from the **Jews**, and translated them into his philosophy.

**XI.** But there are yet other considerable probabilities for this: that **Pythagoras** was not unacquainted with the atomic physiology. First, this is suggested by **Democritus** himself, who was part of the **Italic** line <note>The "Italic Row" refers to the school of philosophy founded by Pythagoras in southern Italy.</note> or **Pythagorean** succession. It is recorded of him in the writings of **Laertius** that he was a great emulator of the **Pythagoreans** and seemed to have taken all his philosophy from them. Indeed, if chronology had not contradicted it, it would have been concluded that he had been a student <note>original: "Auditor"</note> of **Pythagoras** himself, for whom he testified his great admiration in a book titled by his name.

Moreover, some of **his** opinions had a plain correspondence with the **Pythagorean** doctrines. For instance, **Democritus** did not only hold <gloss>that the atoms were carried round in a vortex <note>original: "φέρεσθαι ἀτόμως ἐν τῷ ὅλῳ δινοῦντας"</note></gloss>, but also, together with **Leucippus**, <gloss>that the Earth was carried about the middle or center of this vortex (which is the Sun), turning in the meantime round upon its own axis <note>original: "τῶ γῆν ὀχεῖσθαι ἐπὶ τὸ μέσον δινουμένω"</note></gloss>. And just so, the **Pythagorean** opinion is expressed by **Aristotle**: <gloss>That the Earth, being one of the stars (that is, a planet), being carried round about the middle or center (which is fire or the Sun), did in the meantime by its rotation <note>original: "Circumgyration"</note> upon its own axis make day and night <note>original: "τὼ γῆν ἐν τῶν ἄςρων εἶναι, τὼ κυκλῶ φερόμενῶ περὶ τὸ μέσον νύκτα καὶ τὼ ἡμέραν ποιεῖν"</note></gloss>. Therefore, it may reasonably be concluded from this that as **Democritus's** philosophy was **Pythagorean**, so **Pythagoras's** philosophy was likewise **Democritical** or atomic.

**XII.** But what is of even more importance is that we have the authority of **Ecphantus**, a famous **Pythagorean**, for the fact that **Pythagoras's** **monads** <note>A "monad" in Pythagorean thought is a fundamental, indivisible unit.</note>, so much talked of, were nothing else but **physical** atoms. # BOOK I.
## Proved clearly that Empedocles was an Atomist.

XIII. But to move on from **Pythagoras** himself: it can hardly be doubted that **Empedocles**, who was also a **Pythagorean**, studied nature using the atomic theory <note>original: "physiologize atomically"</note>. There is ample proof for this, starting with a passage from his own philosophical poems:

->*Nature belongs to no individual thing;*<-
->*There is only the mixing and the separation of things that have been mixed.*<-
<note>original Greek: "φύσις οὐδενός ἐστιν ἑκάστου / Ἀλλὰ μόνον μίξις τε διάλλαξίς τε μιγέντων"</note>

Or, as it might also be translated: *There is no production of any new thing, but only the mixture and separation of things already joined.* This is not only to be understood regarding animals—following the **Pythagorean** doctrine of the transmigration of souls—but also, as he explains himself, it applies universally to all bodies. Their generation and decay are nothing but mixture and separation; or as **Aristotle** expresses it, *composition and separation* <note>original: "σύγκρισις καὶ διάκρισις"</note>, meaning the gathering together and secreting of parts, along with changes in their shape and arrangement.

It might be objected that **Empedocles** held there were four elements (Earth, Air, Fire, and Water) from which all other bodies were made, and that **Aristotle** claims he believed these elements could not be changed into one another. To this we reply: he did indeed identify four elements, but only as the first general clusters <note>original: "concretions"</note> of atoms. In this, he did no more than **Democritus** himself, who—as **Laertius** writes—believed that atoms moving in a circular motion <note>original: "vortex"</note> *generated all clusters: fire, water, air, and earth; these being systems made out of certain atoms* <note>original: "πάντα συγκρίματα γεννᾶν πῦρ ὕδωρ ἀέρα γῆν, εἶναι δὲ καὶ ταῦτα ἐξ ἀτόμων τινῶν συστήματα"</note>. 

**Plato** further confirms this; for in his book *The Laws* <note>original: "De Legibus"</note> he describes (as I suppose) that very atheistical hypothesis of **Democritus**, though without mentioning his name. He represents it in this manner: that by the random motion of senseless matter, those four elements were first made, and then out of them, the Sun, Moon, Stars, and Earth were formed.

Both **Plutarch** and **Stobaeus** testify that **Empedocles** composed the four elements themselves out of atoms. *Empedocles makes the elements to be compounded of other small particles <note>original: "corpuscula"</note>, which are the smallest units, and are, as it were, the elements of the elements* <note>original: "Ἐμπεδοκλῆς δὲ ἐκ μικροτέρων ὄγκων τὰ στοιχεῖα συγκρίνει ἅπερ ἐστὶν ἐλάχιστα, καὶ οἱονεὶ στοιχεῖα στοιχείων"</note>. And the same **Stobaeus** observes again: *Empedocles makes the smallest particles and fragments of body (that is, atoms) to exist before the four elements* <note>original: "Ἐμπεδοκλῆς πρὸ τῶν τεσσάρων στοιχείων θραύσματα ἐλάχιστα"</note>. 

However, while **Aristotle** claims that **Empedocles** denied that these elements could change into one another, that must be either an error on **Aristotle's** part or a mistake in the surviving copies of his work. This is likely because **Lucretius**, who was better acquainted with that philosophy and gives a detailed account of **Empedocles'** doctrine (along with many other ancient writers), affirms the exact opposite. Furthermore, **Empedocles** himself, in the surviving fragments of his work, expressly acknowledges this change <note>original: "transmutation"</note>:

# CHAPTER I. Studied Nature Atomically.

->And they perish into each other and grow in their turn of time.<-
<note>original Greek: Καὶ φθίνειν εἰς ἄλληλα καὶ αὔξεσθαι ἐν μέρει αἰῶνος.</note>

Besides all this, an author as great as **Plato** affirms that, according to **Empedocles**, vision and other sensations were caused by the <term>outflow of shapes</term> <note>original: ἀποῤῥοαὶ σχημάτων</note>, the "defluxions of figures" or "effluvia" of atoms. (For **Democritus's** atoms are called <term>shapes</term> <note>original: σχήματα</note> in **Aristotle**, because they were bodies that had only a specific shape without any inherent qualities.) **Empedocles** supposed that some of these figures or particles corresponded with the organs of one sense, and some with the organs of another. 

<note>original Greek: οὐκοῦν λέγετε ἀποῤῥοάς τινας τῶν ὄντων κατ᾽ Ἐμπεδοκλέα, καὶ πόρους εἰς οὓς, καὶ δι᾽ ὧν αἱ ἀποῤῥοαὶ πορεύονται, καὶ τῶν ἀποῤοῶν τὰς μὲν ἁρμόττειν ἐνίοις τῶν πόρων, τὰς δ᾽ ἐλάττους ἢ μείζους εἶναι.</note>

> *You say then, according to the doctrine of **Empedocles**, that there are certain physical emissions from bodies of different sizes and shapes, and also various pores and channels in us that correspond to them in different ways. Thus, some of these physical emissions fit into certain pores, while they are either too large or too small for others.* 

By this it is evident that **Empedocles** did not believe sensations were caused by "intentional species" <note>An old philosophical term for mental images or qualities sent from an object to the mind</note> or qualities, but generally followed the atomic way. Within that framework, there are some differences among the atomists themselves. However, **Empedocles** followed the same path here as **Democritus**. **Empedocles's** <term>outflow of shaped bodies</term> <note>original: ἀποῤῥοαὶ σχημάτων</note> is clearly the same thing as **Democritus's** <term>entry of images</term> <note>original: εἰδώλων εἰσκρίσεις</note>—the "insinuation of simulacra" or the shedding of images from bodies. The same **Plato** further adds that, according to **Empedocles**, the definition of color was this: <term>an outflow of shapes commensurate with the sight and perceptible</term> <note>original: ἀποῤῥοὴ σχημάτων ὄψει σύμμετρος καὶ αἰσθητός</note>. This refers to the outflow of figures or small shaped bodies (without qualities) that are the right size for the eyes to perceive. 

Furthermore, it is clear that **Empedocles's** study of nature <note>original: "physiology"</note> was the exact same as **Democritus's** from this passage of **Aristotle's**: 

<note>original Greek: οἱ μὲν οὖν περὶ Ἐμπεδοκλέα καὶ Δημόκριτον λανθάνουσιν αὐτοὶ ἑαυτούς, οὐ γένεσιν ἐξ ἀλλήλων ποιοῦντες, ἀλλὰ φαινομένην γένεσιν· ἐνυπάρχον γὰρ ἕκαστον ἐκκρίνεσθαί φασιν ὥσπερ ἐξ ἀγγείου ἢ γενέσεως οὔσης·</note>

> ***Empedocles** and **Democritus**, deceiving themselves, unknowingly destroy the idea that things are generated out of one another, leaving only a "seeming" generation. For they say that generation is not the production of any new entity, but only the separation <note>original: "secretion"</note> of what was already existing within; as when different kinds of things mixed together in a vessel are separated from one another.* 

Lastly, we shall confirm all this by the clear testimony of **Plutarch** (or the writer of *The Opinions of the Philosophers*): 

<note>original Greek: Ἐμπεδοκλῆς καὶ Ἐπίκουρος καὶ πάντες ὅσοι κατὰ συναθροισμὸν τῶν λεπτομερῶν σωμάτων κοσμοποιοῦσι, συγκρίσεις μὲν καὶ διακρίσεις εἰσάγουσι, γενέσεις δὲ καὶ φθορὰς οὐ κυρίως, οὐ γὰρ κατὰ ποιὸν ἐξ ἀλλοιώσεως, κατὰ δὲ πόσον ἐκ συναθροισμοῦ ταύτας γίνεσθαι·</note>

> ***Empedocles**, **Epicurus**, and all those who build the world from a collection of small atoms <note>original: "leptomeric bodies"</note>, introduce combinations and separations, but no "generations" or "destructions" in the strict sense. They do not believe these changes happen through a change in quality (alteration), but only through a change in quantity (aggregation).* 

And the same writer sets down the order and method of the creation of the world <note>original: *Cosmopoeia*</note> according to **Empedocles**: 

->**Empedocles** says that the ether was first separated, and second, the fire,<-
<note>original Greek: Ἐμπεδοκλῆς τὸν μὲν αἰθέρα πρῶτον διακριθῆναι, δεύτερον δὲ τὸ πῦρ,</note>
