<meta>This page continues the discussion of Empedocles’s atomic theories, specifically how he accounts for the creation of the elements and the world, before transitioning to a critique of Anaxagoras’s "spurious" version of atomism and listing other ancient philosophers who held atomic views.</meta>

## Anaxagoras: A Spurious Atomist. BOOK I.

<note>original Greek: ἐφ᾽ ᾧ τω̃ γλω̃ ἐξ ἄζαν ὡς σφιγόμενης τῇ εὐμη̂ τῷ ὕδωρ, ἐξ ἔρ θυμαθῶαι ἤ ἀέρα, καὶ γενέσθαι τ πυρός.</note> **Empedocles** writes that <term>Ether</term> <note>The "fifth element" or the substance of the upper atmosphere and stars</note> was first of all separated out of the confused <term>Chaos</term> of atoms. Afterward came the Fire, and then the Earth, which being constrained and, as it were, squeezed by the force of agitation, sent forth water bubbling out of it; from the evaporation of this water came the air. From the ether the heavens were made, and from fire, the sun. We see, therefore, that it was not without cause that **Lucretius** so highly praised **Empedocles**, since his physics was really the same as that of **Epicurus** and **Democritus**. He differed from them only in a few specific details, such as excluding the <term>Vacuum</term> <note>Empty space</note> and denying that there were physical "minimal units" that were truly indivisible.

### XV. Anaxagoras's Counterfeit Atomism

As for **Anaxagoras**, although he also philosophized using atoms—substituting <term>concretion</term> <note>Coming together</note> and <term>secretion</term> <note>Separation</note> in the place of "generation" and "corruption"—he insisted on the same fundamental principle as **Empedocles**, **Democritus**, and the other atomists. This principle (as we shall explain more fully later) is that *nothing can be made out of nothing, nor reduced to nothing*. Therefore, he believed there were neither any new productions nor destructions of any substances or real entities. 

Yet, as his theory of <term>Homoeomeria</term> <note>original: Homœomeria; the idea that a substance is made of particles that are the same as the whole (e.g., bone is made of "bone-atoms")</note> is represented by **Aristotle**, **Lucretius**, and other authors, he believed that bone was made of bony atoms, flesh of fleshy atoms, red things of red atoms, and hot things of hot atoms. Since these atoms were supposed to be originally endowed with many different forms and qualities essential and inseparable from them, there was indeed a wide difference between his philosophy and true atomism. However, this theory seems to have arisen from nothing else but his inability to understand the true atomic hypothesis. This caused him to reject it and substitute this spurious and counterfeit atomism of his own in its place.

### XVI. Other Ancient Atomists

Lastly, I might add here that it is recorded by reliable authors concerning various other ancient philosophers—who were not addicted to the atheism of **Democritus**—that they followed this atomic way of explaining nature. In all probability, they derived it from those religious atomists who lived before **Democritus**. 

For example:
*   **Ecphantus the Syracusan Pythagorist**, who, as **Stobaeus** writes, made "indivisible bodies and the vacuum" <note>original Greek: τά ἀδιάιρετα σώματα καὶ τὸ κενὸν</note> the principles of physics. As **Theodoret** also testifies, he taught "that the corporeal world was made up of atoms" <note>original Greek: ἐκ τω̃ν ἀτόμων συνεςάναι τ κόσμον</note>.
*   **Xenocrates**, who made "indivisible magnitudes" <note>original Greek: μεγέθη ἀδιαίρετα</note> the first principles of bodies.
*   **Heraclides**, who resolved all physical things into "certain smallest fragments and splinters of bodies" <note>original Greek: τμήματα καὶ θραύσματά τινα ἐλάχισα</note>.
*   **Asclepiades**, who supposed the entire physical world to be made "not of similar parts (as **Anaxagoras** did) but of dissimilar and <term>inconcinn</term> <note>clumsily joined or disordered</note> molecules" <note>original Greek: ἐξ ἀνομοίων καί ἀνάμερον ὄγκων</note>—that is, atoms of different magnitudes and figures.
*   And **Diodorus**, that

<meta>This page continues the argument that various ancient thinkers used atomic theory to explain the natural world. # CHAPTER I. Most of the Ancient Natural Philosophers were Atomists.

...who explained the material <term>phenomena</term> <note>Observable events or facts in nature</note> by "indivisible smallest parts" <note>original Greek: ἀμερῆ τὰ ἐλάχιστα</note> of the body. And lastly, **Metrodorus of Chios** (not Metrodorus of Lampsacus the follower of Epicurus, but the earlier one), who is also reported to have made indivisible particles and atoms the first principles of bodies.

But what need do we have for any more proof that the <term>atomical physiology</term> <note>The study of nature based on the movement of atoms; "physiology" here refers to natural philosophy or physics</note> was older than **Democritus** and **Leucippus**, and was not confined only to that one sect? Even **Aristotle** himself, in the passages already cited, expressly declares that besides Democritus, the majority of all the other natural philosophers went that way. He writes: "Democritus and most of the natural philosophers" <note>original Greek: Δημόκριτος καὶ οἱ πλεῖστοι τῶν φυσιολόγων</note> "make all sense to be touch, and resolve sensible qualities, such as the tastes of bitter and sweet, into shapes." And again, he attributes this generally to all the natural philosophers who preceded him: "The earlier natural philosophers" <note>original Greek: οἱ πρότερον φυσιολόγοι</note> "(without any exception) did not speak well on this point, when they said there was no black or white without sight, nor bitter or sweet without taste." 

Therefore, I think it cannot be reasonably doubted that the majority of the old natural philosophers before Aristotle and Democritus did follow the atomic path. This method resolves physical phenomena not into "Forms," "Qualities," or "Species" <note>These were terms used in later Aristotelian philosophy to describe the essence of things</note>, but into shapes, motions, and <term>fancies</term> <note>The subjective mental perceptions of color, sound, or taste, rather than inherent properties of the atoms themselves</note>.

### XVII.

But then there will seem to be no small difficulty in reconciling Aristotle with himself, as he plainly attributes this philosophy to Democritus and Leucippus in many places as its first source and origin. We must also account for the credibility of **Diogenes Laertius** and many other ancient writers who do the same—Democritus having had, for many ages, the general reputation for inventing atoms. 

However, we have no doubt that we can give a very good account of this matter and reconcile the seemingly different testimonies of these ancient writers, so as to remove all contradiction between them. For although atomic physics was in use long before Democritus and Leucippus—meaning they did not *make* it, but *found* it—yet these two, along with their fellow atheists (of whom **Protagoras** seems to have been one), were undoubtedly the first who ever turned this physics into a complete and entire philosophy by itself. 

They did this by deriving the origin of all things in the whole universe from senseless atoms that had nothing but shape and motion, along with a <term>vacuum</term> <note>Empty space</note>. They built such a system from these parts that it would follow that there could not be any God—not even a physical one. These two things (atomism and atheism) existed separately before. For there is no doubt that atheism has been lurking in the minds of some people in every age, and perhaps some of those ancient atheists tried to philosophize in other ways as well. There was also atomic physics before them, but without atheism. 

But these two components were never joined together before as "Atomic-Atheism" or "Atheistical Atomism." Therefore, Democritus and his comrade Leucippus need not be denied the "glory" of being considered the first inventors or founders of the *Atomic Philosophy, corrupted by atheism.*

<meta>This page continues the argument that atomism was originally part of a broader philosophy that included a belief in God and the soul, before it was isolated into a purely materialistic system by later thinkers.</meta>

-> **Democritus and Leucippus: the first Atheistic Atomists. Book I.** <-

### XVIII. 

Before **Leucippus** and **Democritus**, the doctrine of atoms was not treated as a complete and independent philosophy on its own. Instead, it was viewed only as one part or member of the entire philosophical system—and the simplest and lowest part at that. It was used only to explain what was purely physical <note>original: "Corporeal"</note> in the world. In addition to atoms, these early thinkers acknowledged something else that was not merely physical size and mechanical movement: they believed in life and self-activity, which is to say, **immaterial substance** <note>original: "Incorporeal Substance"</note>. The pinnacle and highest point of this belief is a God who is distinct from the physical world. 

Thus, there have been two types of atomists in the world: the **Atheistical** and the **Religious**. The first and most ancient atomists held a belief in immaterial substance and used natural philosophy <note>original: "Physiology"</note> in a way that was subordinate to theology and metaphysics. The other group, who allowed for no substance other than the physical body, claimed that mindless atoms and their shapes—without any Mind or Understanding (that is, without any God)—were the source of all things. This latter version is what became commonly known as "Atomical Philosophy," of which Democritus and Leucippus were the primary sources.

### XIX. 

It has indeed been boldly claimed by some recently that none of the ancient philosophers ever dreamed of such a thing as **immaterial substance**. They would lead people to believe that it was nothing but a modern and fanatical invention of some narrow-minded religious people. We shall briefly show the falsehood of that claim here. 

While there have certainly been people in every age who disbelieved in the existence of anything they could not perceive with their senses, **Plato** describes them in this way: "They would insist that whatever they cannot feel or grasp with their hands is absolutely nothing at all" <note>original Greek: οἳ διατείνοιντ' ἂν πᾶν ὃ μὴ δυνατοὶ ταῖς χερσὶ συμπιέζειν εἰσὶν, ὡς ἄρα τοῦτο οὐδὲν τὸ παράπαν ἐστί</note>. Yet this opinion was openly opposed by the best of the ancient philosophers and condemned as a piece of foolishness and stupidity. 

For this reason, Plato tells us that there has always been—just as there was in his own time—a perpetual war and controversy in the world. He calls it a kind of **Gigantomachy** <note>A "War of the Giants," referring to the mythological battle between the Olympian gods and the Giants; here, a massive intellectual conflict</note> between two parties or sects of men: those who held that there was no substance in the world except the physical body, and those who asserted the existence of immaterial substance. The philosopher describes the former group as follows: 

"These people drag everything down from heaven and the invisible realm to the earth with their hands, literally grasping rocks and oaks. When they clutch all these hard and gross things, they confidently affirm that only that which provides resistance and can be touched is real substance. They define 'body' and 'substance' as one and the same thing. And if anyone happens to speak to them of something that is not a body—that is, of an **immaterial substance**—they will utterly despise him and refuse to hear another word from him" <note>original Greek: οἳ μὲν εἰς γῆν ἐξ οὐρανοῦ καὶ τοῦ ἀοράτου πάντα ἕλκουσι ταῖς χερσὶν ἀτεχνῶς πέτρας καὶ δρῦς περιλαμβάνοντες, τῶν γὰρ τοιούτων ἐφαπτόμενοι πάντων, διισχυρίζονται τοῦτο εἶναι μόνον ὃ παρέχει προσβολὴν καὶ ἐπαφήν τινα, ταὐτὸν σῶμα καὶ οὐσίαν ὁριζόμενοι τῶν δ' ἄλλων εἴτις φησὶ μὴ σῶμα ἔχον εἶναι, καταφρονοῦντες τὸ παράπαν καὶ οὐδὲν ἐθέλοντες ἄλλο ἀκούειν</note>.

# Chapter I: Incorporeal Substance Asserted by the Ancients.

He says he had met with such people. The other group he represents in this manner: "The adversaries of these materialists <note>original: 'Corporealiſts'</note> cautiously and piously attack them from the invisible region, deriving all things from above through a downward descent. By the strength of reason, they convince others that certain **intelligible and incorporeal forms** are the true or first substance, rather than physical objects <note>original: 'Senſible things'</note>. But between these two groups, there has always been (he says) a great war and contention" <note>original Greek: "οἱ πρὸς αὐτὸς ἀμφισβητοῦντες μάλα εὐλαβῶς ἄνωθεν ἐξ ἀοράτου τόπῳ ἀμυνοῦνται νοητὰ ἄττα καὶ ἀσώματα εἴδη, βιαζόμενοι τὴν ἀληθινὴν οὐσίαν εἶναι. ἐν μέσῳ δὲ περὶ ταῦτα ἄπλετος ἀμφοτέρων μάχη τὶς ἀεὶ ξυνέστηκε"</note>. And yet, in the continuation of his discourse, he adds that those materialists had then grown a little more modest and ashamed than their great champions had been in the past, such as **Democritus** and **Protagoras**. For although they still persisted in this—that the soul was a body—they did not (it seems) have the impudence to claim that **wisdom** and **virtue** were physical things or bodies, as others before and since have done. We see here that **Plato** expressly asserts a substance distinct from the body, which he sometimes calls **incorporeal substance** <note>original: "οὐσίαν ἀσώματον"</note> and sometimes **intelligible substance** <note>original: "οὐσίαν νοητὴν"</note>, in opposition to the other which he calls **perceptible** <note>original: "αἰσθητὴν"; literally "sensible"</note>. And it is plain to anyone who has had the least acquaintance with *Plato's philosophy* that the whole scope and drift of it is to raise up men's minds from the senses to a belief in incorporeal things as the most excellent: "For incorporeal things, which are the greatest and most excellent things of all, are (he says) discoverable by reason only and nothing else" <note>original: "τὰ γὰρ ἀσώματα κάλλιστα ὄντα καὶ μέγιστα λόγῳ μόνον, ἄλλῳ δὲ οὐδενὶ, σαφῶς δείκνυται"</note>, as he writes in another place.

<margin>Plato's Cave</margin>
And his famous **Subterranean Cave**, so elegantly described by him, where he imagines men tied with their backs toward the light, which is placed at a great distance from them. They could not even turn their heads toward it, and therefore could see nothing but the shadows (of certain substances behind them) projected by it. They concluded these shadows were the only substances and realities. When they heard the sounds made by those bodies between the light and them, or their echoes, they attributed those sounds to the shadows they saw. I say, all this is a description of the state of those men who believe that the **physical body** is the only real and substantial thing in the world, and that it performs everything done within it. Therefore, they often attribute sense, reason, and understanding to nothing more than the blood and brains within us.

XX. I might also show next how **Aristotle** did not disagree with **Plato** on this matter. He plainly asserted "another substance besides perceptible things" <note>original: "ἄλλην οὐσίαν παρὰ τὰ αἰσθητὰ"</note>, "a substance separable and also actually separated from perceptible things" <note>original: "οὐσίαν χωριστὴν καὶ κεχωρισμένην τῶν αἰσθητῶν"</note>, and "an immovable nature or essence" <note>original: "ἀκίνητον οὐσίαν"</note>—subject to no generation or corruption—adding that the Deity was to be sought here. Indeed, he spoke of such a substance "as can have no physical size at all, but is impartible and indivisible" <note>original: "ἣν μέγεθος οὐδὲν ἐνδέχεται ἔχειν, ἀλλὰ ἀμερὴς καὶ ἀδιαίρετός ἐστι"</note>. He also blamed **Zeno** (not the Stoic, who was younger than Aristotle, but an older philosopher of that name) for making God a body, in these words: "for he himself says it is a body" <note>original: "αὐτὸς γὰρ σῶμα λέγει εἶναι"</note>...

# Book I: Proving Incorporeal Substance

"Whether **Zeno** speaks of God as the whole universe or as something else, he asks: if God were incorporeal, how could he be spherical? Or how could he move or rest if he were not in any place? But if God is a body, then nothing prevents him from moving." <note>original Greek: "τὸν θεὸν εἴτε τὸ τόδε τὸ πᾶν εἴτε ὅτι δήποτε αὐτὸς λέγων· ἀσώματός γε ὢν πῶς ἂν σφαιροειδὴς εἴη; ὅταν οὕτως ὅτ' ἂν κινοῖτο, ὅτ' ἂν ἠρεμοῖ μηδαμοῦ τε ὤν· ἐπεὶ ἡ σῶμά ἐστι, τί ἂν αὐτὸ κωλύει κινεῖσθαι;"</note> From this, **Zeno** implicitly affirms that God is a body, whether he means God is the entire physical universe or some specific body within it. For if God were incorporeal, how could he be shaped like a sphere? Nor could he then either move or rest, since he would not properly be in any location. But if God is a body, then nothing stops him from being moved. 

From this and other passages in **Aristotle**, it is clear enough that Aristotle supposed incorporeal substance to be "unextended"—meaning it does not take up physical space—and as such, has no relation to any specific place. However, this is a point to be debated later. Indeed, some learned men believe **Aristotle** criticized **Zeno** without good cause, and that **Zeno** described God as a sphere, or spherical, in no other sense than **Parmenides** did in his well-known verse:

-> "In every way resembling the mass of a well-rounded sphere." <-
<note>original Greek: "πάντοθεν εὐκύκλου σφαίρας ἐναλίγκιον ὄγκῳ"</note>

In this verse, **Parmenides** is understood to be describing the "Divine Eternity" <note>the concept of God's perfection and completeness</note>. However, it plainly appears from this that according to **Aristotle's** understanding, God was **incorporeal** <note>original Greek: ἀσώματος</note>, an incorporeal substance distinct from the physical world.

XXI. Now, **Plato** was especially famous for asserting this doctrine: that there was **incorporeal substance** <note>original Greek: οὐσία ἀσώματος</note>, and that the souls of men were such, but principally the Deity. **Epicurus**, taking notice of this, endeavored with all his might to disprove it, arguing in this manner: *"There can be no incorporeal God (as **Plato** maintained), not only because no man can imagine an incorporeal substance, but also because whatever is incorporeal must necessarily lack sense, wisdom, and pleasure—all of which are included in the concept of God. Therefore, an incorporeal Deity is a contradiction."* 

And concerning the human soul, **Epicurus** wrote: "Those who say that the soul is incorporeal talk nonsense..." <note>original Greek: "οἱ λέγοντες ἀσώματον εἶναι τὴν ψυχὴν ματαιάζουσι"</note> and so on. *"Those who say that the soul is incorporeal—in any sense other than as a word to describe a very thin or subtle body—talk vainly and foolishly. For if it were truly incorporeal, it could neither do anything nor be acted upon <note>original: "Suffer"</note>. It could not act upon any other thing because it could touch nothing; neither could it be affected by anything because it could not be touched by anything. Instead, it would be just like a **vacuum** or empty space, which can neither do nor receive anything, but only allows bodies a passage through it."* From this, it is further evident that this opinion <note>that the soul is incorporeal</note> was openly maintained by some philosophers even before the time of **Epicurus**.

XXII. But **Plato** and **Aristotle** were not the first inventors of this idea. For it is certain that all those philosophers who held that the human soul is immortal, and that God is distinct from this visible world (and thus truly the Creator of the world and all its parts), did effectively assert the existence of **incorporeal substance**. It is plain to everyone’s understanding that a physical <note>original: "Corporeal"</note> soul cannot be immortal and indestructible by its own nature, because its parts can be separated from one another. Furthermore, whoever denies that God is incorporeal—if they believe God is anything at all—must necessarily believe God to be either the whole physical...

# Chapter I: Substance Was Asserted by the Ancients

...physical world, or else a part of it. Therefore, if God is neither of these, he must then be an incorporeal substance. **Plato** was not the first who asserted these two things, but they were both maintained by many philosophers before him. **Pherecydes of Syros** and **Thales** were two of the most ancient philosophers among the Greeks; it is said of Pherecydes that through his lectures and debates concerning the immortality of the soul, he first drew **Pythagoras** away from another course of life to the study of philosophy. **Pherecydes of Syros** (says **Cicero**) "was the first to say that human souls are eternal." <note>original Latin: "Primus dixit animos hominum esse sempiternos."</note> And **Thales**, in a letter directed to him, congratulates him on being the first who had intended to write to the Greeks concerning divine things. **Thales** (who was the head of the Ionian succession of philosophers, just as **Pythagoras** was of the Italian) is joined with **Pythagoras** and **Plato** by the writer of *The Opinions of the Philosophers* <note>original: *De Placitis Philosophorum*</note> in this manner: "All these aforementioned philosophers assume the soul to be incorporeal by nature, calling it self-moving (or self-active) and an intelligible substance—that is, not perceptible by the senses." <note>original Greek: "Οὗτοι πάντες οἱ προτεταγμένοι ἀσώματον τὴν ψυχὴν ὑποτίθενται φύσει λέγοντες αὐτοκίνητον καὶ οὐσίαν νοητήν."</note> Now, anyone who determines the soul to be incorporeal must certainly hold the Deity to be incorporeal even more so. "**Thales** said that water was the first principle of all physical things," (says **Cicero**) "but that God was that Mind which formed all things out of water." <note>original Latin: "Aquam dixit Thales esse initium rerum... Deum autem eam Mentem quæ ex aqua cuncta fingeret."</note>

**Thales** was Phoenician by descent, and accordingly seemed to have received his two principles from there: **water**, and the **Divine Spirit** moving upon the waters. The first of these is expressed by **Sanchuniathon** in his description of Phoenician theology as "a turbid and dark chaos," <note>original Greek: "χάος θολερὸν, ἐρεβῶδες"</note> and the second is suggested in these words: "the spirit was affected with love towards its own principles," <note>original Greek: "ἠράσθη τὸ πνεῦμα τῶν ἰδίων ἀρχῶν"</note> perhaps expressing the force of the Hebrew word *Merachepheth* <note>original Hebrew: מְרַחֶפֶת, meaning "hovering" or "brooding," as used in Genesis 1:2 regarding the Spirit of God</note>. Both of them imply an understanding, prolific goodness that forms and hatches the physical world into this state of perfection; or else a <term>plastic power</term> <note>a "plastic power" refers to a natural, formative force that shapes matter according to a divine plan</note> subordinate to it.

**Zeno** (who was also originally Phoenician) tells us that **Hesiod**’s "chaos" was water; and that the material heaven, as well as the earth, was made out of water is (according to the judgment of the best interpreters) the genuine sense of Scripture in 2 Peter 3:5. By this "water," some perhaps would understand a chaos of atoms moving in a confused way. But whether **Thales** was acquainted with atomist physics or not, it is plain that he asserted—besides the soul’s immortality—a Deity distinct from the physical world.

We pass now to **Pythagoras**, whom we have proved already to have been an atomist; it is well known that he was also a professed "incorporealist" <note>someone who believes in non-physical substances</note>. That he asserted the immortality of the soul, and consequently its immateriality, is evident from his doctrine of pre-existence and transmigration <note>the belief that the soul exists before the body and moves into new bodies after death</note>. That he likewise held an incorporeal Deity distinct from the world is something not questioned by anyone. But if there were any need of proving it (because there are no surviving monuments of his own writing), perhaps it might be done from this:

# Pythagoras and Parmenides Incorporealists. BOOK I.

...because he was the chief propagator of that doctrine among the Greeks concerning three <term>hypostases</term> <note>original: "Hypostases" — individual substances or persons</note> in the <term>Deity</term> <note>God</note>.

For it is very well known to everyone that **Plato** and his **followers** held "three primary substances" <note>original Greek: τρεῖς ἀρχικὰς ὑποστάσεις</note> in the Deity, which were the first principles of all things. However, we do not claim that these Platonist *hypostases* are exactly the same as those in the Christian Trinity. Now, **Plato** himself sufficiently suggests that this was not his own invention. **Plotinus** also tells us that it was an "ancient opinion" <note>original Greek: παλαιὰ δόξα</note> before **Plato**’s time, which had been passed down by some of the **Pythagoreans**. Therefore, I believe this must be one of those "Pythagorean monstrosities" for which **Xenophon** secretly criticized **Plato** for adopting and mixing with **Socratic philosophy**, as if he had thereby corrupted its purity and simplicity. Though a <term>corporealist</term> <note>one who believes only physical matter exists</note> may pretend to be a <term>theist</term>, I never heard of any of them ever asserting a Trinity in relation to the Deity—unless it was the kind I do not think appropriate to mention here.

XXIII. It is evident from **Plato** that **Parmenides**, who was likewise a **Pythagorean**, acknowledged a <term>Deity</term> distinct from the physical world. **Plotinus** also tells us that he was one of those who asserted the triad of divine *hypostases*. Moreover, there was a great controversy among the ancient philosophers before **Plato**’s time. On one side were those who held that all things were in flux (namely **Heraclitus** and **Cratylus**). On the other side were those who asserted that some things stood still, and that there was an "unchanging substance" <note>original Greek: ἀκίνητος οὐσία</note>—namely, an eternal mind, along with eternal and unchanging truths (among whom were **Parmenides** and **Melissus**). The first group were all <term>corporealists</term>; this was the very reason they thought all things were in flux, because they supposed everything to be physical body (though this does not mean they were all <term>atheists</term>). But the latter group were all both <term>incorporealists</term> and <term>theists</term>; for whoever holds that incorporeal substance exists must also (according to reason) assert the existence of a <term>Deity</term>.

And although we did not specifically mention **Parmenides** among the <term>atomic philosophers</term> earlier, we believe it is clear from this context that he belonged to that group. He was an eminent supporter of the principle that "nothing that truly exists is either born or destroyed, generated or corrupted" <note>original Greek: οὐδὲν οὔτε γίνεσθαι οὔτε φθείρεσθαι τῶν ὄντων</note>. We shall later plainly show this to be the grand fundamental principle of the <term>atomic philosophy</term>.

XXIV. However, while we clearly proved before that **Empedocles** was an <term>atomic physiologer</term> <note>a natural philosopher who studies physical causes</note>, it might still be reasonably doubted whether he was an <term>atheist</term>, or at least a <term>corporealist</term>, because **Aristotle** accuses him of the following things. First, he is accused of making knowledge the same as sense-perception, which is a plain sign of a <term>corporealist</term>. Therefore, in the next place, he is accused of composing the soul out of the four elements, making...

### CHAPTER I. Empedocles was neither an Atheist nor a Corporealist.

...making the soul understand every physical thing by something of the same nature within itself—as fire is known by fire, and earth by earth. Lastly, Aristotle accuses him of attributing too much to fortune and claiming that various parts of animals were created by chance. He mentions that at first, certain "mongrel" animals were produced by accident, such as those that were **ox-born and man-faced** <note>original Greek: βουγενῆ καὶ ἀνδρόπρωρα</note>—creatures with the bodies of oxen and the faces of men (though they could not survive for long). This seems to give a justifiable reason to suspect that **Empedocles** was an atheist in the same way **Democritus** was.

To the first of these charges, we reply that others who had also read **Empedocles’s** poems held a different opinion than **Aristotle**. They believed **Empedocles** did not make **Sense** but rather **Reason** the **standard of truth** <note>original: "Criterion of Truth"</note>. As **Sextus Empiricus** informs us: *Others say that according to Empedocles, the standard of truth is not the senses but Right Reason; and also that Right Reason is of two types: one is **divine** <note>original Greek: θει̃ος</note>, and the other is **human** <note>original Greek: ἀνθρώπινος</note>. Of these, the divine is inexpressible, but the human can be declared.* Several passages from the remaining fragments of **Empedocles’s** poems could be cited to confirm this, but we shall produce only this one:

->**Restrain your trust in the physical senses, and understand each thing clearly with your mind.**<-
<note>original Greek: τύων πίστιν ἔρυκε νόῳ θ' ἡ̃ δη̃λον ἕκαστον</note>

As for the second accusation, **Aristotle** has greatly weakened his own testimony by accusing **Plato** of the very same thing: *Plato composes the soul out of the four elements because like is known by like, and things are made from their own principles* <note>original Greek: Πλατὼν τὴν ψυχὴν ἐκ τῶ̃ν στοιχείων ποιει̃, γινώσκεται γὰρ ὁμοίῳ ὅμοιον, τὰ δὲ πράγματα ἐκ τῶ̃ν ἀρχῶ̃ν εἶναι</note>. Therefore, it is probable that **Empedocles** was no more guilty of this fault (of making the soul physical and consisting of earth, water, air, and fire) than **Plato** was. In the judgment of all men, **Plato** was as far from that error as **Aristotle** himself, if not more so.

For **Empedocles** held the **transmigration of souls** <note>the belief that souls move from one body to another after death</note> in the same manner as **Pythagoras** before him and **Plato** after him. Consequently, he believed in both their **future immortality** and their **preexistence**; therefore, he must have asserted that they are **incorporeal** <note>non-physical or spiritual in nature</note>. **Plutarch** correctly declared this to have been his opinion: *That both those who have never yet been born and those who have already died exist* <note>original Greek: εἶναι καὶ τοὺς μηδέποτε γεγονότας καὶ τοὺς ἤδη τεθνηκότας</note>. He also asserted that **human souls** are here in a **fallen state**, describing them as **"wanderers, strangers, and fugitives from God"** <note>original Greek: μετανάστας, καὶ ξένους, καὶ φυγάδας</note>. As **Plotinus** tells us, **Empedocles** declared it to be a **divine law** *that souls who sin should fall down into these earthly bodies* <note>original Greek: ἁμαρτανούσαις ται̃ς ψυχαι̃ς πεσει̃ν ἐνταῦθα</note>. But the most complete record of the **Empedoclean philosophy** concerning the soul is found in this passage by **Hierocles**: *Man descends and falls away from the blessed region, as Empedocles the Pythagorean says—a fugitive from God and a wanderer, trusting in mad Strife—but he ascends again and recovers his ancient state.* <note>original Greek: κάτεισι καὶ ἀποπίπτει τῆς εὐδαίμονος χώρας ὁ ἄνθρωπος, ὡς Ἐμπεδοκλῆς φησιν ὁ Πυθαγόρειος, —— φυγάς θεόθεν καὶ ἀλήτης Νείκεϊ μαινομένῳ πίσυνος —— Ἄνεισι δὲ καὶ τὴν ἀρχαίαν ἕξιν ἀπολαμβάνει</note>

<summary>This page defends the philosopher Empedocles against Aristotle's claims of materialism, arguing that Empedocles actually viewed reason as the standard of truth and believed in the soul's immortality and preexistence.</summary>

# Empedocles Vindicated

->Flee the things of the earth and that joyless place,<-
->Where murder, wrath, and tribes of other dooms reign.<-
<note>original Greek: Ἐκ φεύξεῖ τὰ περὶ γῆν καὶ τὸν ἀτερπέα χῶρον, Ἔνθα φόνος τε κότος τε καὶ ἄλλων ἔθνεα κηρῶν.</note>

->Into which those who fall wander<-
->Through the field of Ate and darkness.<-
<note>original Greek: Εἰς ὃν οἱ ἐκπεσόντες —— Ἄτης —— ἀνὰ λειμῶνα τε καὶ σκότος ἠλάσκουσιν. Ate (Ἄτη) is the Greek goddess of delusion, folly, and ruin.</note>

The desire of the one fleeing the field of **Ate** hastens toward the field of **Truth**. Leaving that truth behind by the impulse of "losing one’s wings," the soul enters a physical body, neglecting its blessed life.
<note>original Greek: Ἡ δὲ ἔφεσις τοῦ φεύγοντος τὸν τῆς Ἄτης λειμῶνα πρὸς τὸν τῆς ἀληθείας ἐπείγεται λειμῶνα, ὃν ἀπολιπὼν τῇ ὁρμῇ τῆς πτεροῤῥυήσεως εἰς γήϊνον ἔρχεται σῶμα, ὀλβίου —— αἰῶνος ἀμελεής.</note>

> Man falls from his happy state—as **Empedocles** the **Pythagorean** says—by being a fugitive, apostate, and wanderer from God, driven by a certain mad and irrational strife or contention. But he ascends again and recovers his former state, if he declines and avoids these earthly things, and despises this unpleasant and wretched place, where murder and wrath, and a troop of all other mischiefs reign. Into which place, those who fall wander up and down through the field of **Ate** and darkness. But the desire of him that flees from this field of **Ate** carries him on towards the field of **Truth**; which the soul at first relinquishing, and losing its wings <note>original Greek: πτεροῤῥύησις; pterorrhuesis</note>, fell down into this earthly body, deprived of its happy life. From which it appears that **Plato’s** concept of "losing one's wings" was derived from **Empedocles** and the **Pythagoreans**.

Now, from what has already been cited, it is sufficiently manifest that **Empedocles** was so far from being either an atheist or a corporealist <term>one who believes only in physical matter</term> that he was indeed a thorough **Pythagorean**, as he is called here. And we might add to this what **Clement of Alexandria** <note>original: "Clemens Alexandrinus"</note> observes: that according to **Empedocles**, *if we live holily and justly, we shall be happy here, and more happy after our departure hence; having our happiness not necessarily confined to time, but being able to rest and fix in it to all eternity; feasting with the other immortal beings, etc.*
<note>original Greek: ἣν ὁσίως καὶ δικαίως διαβιώσωμεν, μακάριοι μὲν ἐνταῦθα, μακαριώτεροι δὲ μετὰ τὴν ἐνθένδε ἀπαλλαγήν· οὐ χρόνῳ τινὶ τὴν εὐδαιμονίαν ἔχοντες, ἀλλὰ ἐν αἰῶνι ἀναπαύεσθαι δυνάμενοι, Ἀθανάτοις ἄλλοισιν ὁμέστιοι, ἐν δὲ τραπέζαις, &c.</note>

We might also take notice of how, besides the immortal souls of men, he acknowledged **Demons** or **Angels**, declaring that some of these fell from Heaven and were since prosecuted by a divine **Nemesis** <term>retributive justice</term>. In **Plutarch**, these are called *those Empedoclean demons lapsed from Heaven, and pursued with divine vengeance; whose restless torment is there described in several verses of his.* 
<note>original Greek: οἱ θεήλατοι καὶ οὐρανοπετεῖς ἐκεῖνοι τοῦ Ἐμπεδοκλέους δαίμονες</note>

And we might observe likewise how he acknowledged a natural and immutable justice, which was not topical <term>local</term> and confined to places and countries, nor relative to particular laws, but catholic <term>universal</term> and universal, and everywhere the same, through infinite light and space—as he expresses it with poetic pomp and bravery:

->But the law for all is stretched out continuously<-
->Through the wide-ruling air and through the infinite light.<-
<note>original Greek: Ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν πάντων νόμιμον διὰ τ' εὐρυμέδοντος Αἰθέρος, ἠνεκέως τέταται διὰ τ' ἀπλέτου αὐγῆς.</note>

And the asserting of **natural morality** is no small argument that he was a **theist**.

### CHAPTER I. Either an Atheist or a Corporealist.

But what then shall we say to those other things which **Empedocles** is charged with by **Aristotle**, which seem to have so strong a smell of atheism? Certainly those mongrel and biformed animals <note>original: "Biforme Animals"; referring to mythical creatures like centaurs or hybrids</note> that are said to have sprung up out of the Earth by chance look as if they were more related to **Democritus** than **Empedocles**. It is probably the fault of the manuscript copies that it is read otherwise, as there is no other philosopher I know of who could ever find any such thing in the poems of **Empedocles**. 

But for the rest, if **Aristotle** does not misrepresent **Empedocles**—as he often does **Plato**—then it must be granted that because he was a mechanical natural philosopher <note>original: "Physiologer"</note> as well as a theologian, he did indulge a bit too much in **fortuitous mechanism**. <term>Fortuitous mechanism</term> is the theory that the universe's structures arose through random physical collisions rather than by design. This seems to be an extravagance that mechanical philosophers and **atomists** have always been more or less subject to. 

However, **Aristotle** does not charge **Empedocles** with resolving all things into fortuitous mechanism, as some philosophers have done recently (who yet pretend to be theists and believers in the incorporeal soul). Instead, he only says that Empedocles would explain *some* things in that way. Indeed, Aristotle clearly puts a difference between **Empedocles** and the atheists following **Democritus** in the words he added: *“But there are some...”* <note>original Greek: Εἰσὶ δέ τινες</note> which is as if he should have said: *“Empedocles explained some things in the fabric and structure of animals through random physical chance; but there are certain other philosophers, namely **Leucippus** and **Democritus**, who would have all things whatsoever in the whole world—heaven and earth and animals—to be made by chance and the random motion of atoms, without a Deity.”* 

It seems very plain that the **"Friendship"** and **"Discord"** of **Empedocles** <note>original: "Philia and Nichos"</note>, which he makes to be the **active cause** <note>original Greek: ἀρχὴ δραστήριος</note> and principle of motion in the universe, was a certain **plastic power** <term>Plastic Power</term> (An internal, non-conscious force that shapes matter according to a divine plan) superior to random physical chance. **Aristotle** himself acknowledges as much elsewhere. And **Plutarch** tells us that according to **Empedocles**, the order and system of the world is not the result of material causes and random mechanism, but of a divine wisdom, assigning to everything **“not such a place as nature [blindly] gives it, but such as is most convenient for the good of the whole.”** <note>original Greek: οὐχ ἣν ἡ φύσις δίδωσι χώραν, ἀλλ’ ἣν ἡ πρὸς τὸ κοινὸν ἔργον ποθεῖ σύνταξις</note> 

**Simplicius**, who had read **Empedocles**, acquaints us that he made two worlds: one **intellectual** and the other **sensible**; and the former of these was the exemplar and archetype of the latter. And so the writer of *On the Opinions of the Philosophers* <note>Latin: De Placitis Philosophorum</note> observes that **Empedocles** made **“two suns: the one archetypal [the source of light in the intellectual world] and the other apparent or sensible.”** <note>original Greek: δύο ἡλίους, τὸν μὲν ἀρχέτυπον τὸν δὲ φαινόμενον</note>

But I need take no more pains to clear **Empedocles** from those two accusations of **corporealism** <note>the belief that only physical matter exists</note> and **atheism**, since he has so fully refuted them himself in those fragments of his work still in existence. First, he expresses a hearty appreciation for the excellence of piety and the wretchedness and foolishness <note>original: "Sottishness"</note> of atheism in these verses:

> Blessed is he who has gained the wealth of divine wisdom, 
> But wretched is he whose mind is occupied with a dark opinion concerning the gods.
> <note>original Greek: Ὄλβιος ὃς θείων πραπίδων ἐκτήσατο πλοῦτον, Δειλὸς δ’ ᾧ σκοτόεσσα θεῶν πέρι δόξα μέμηλεν.</note>

# Anaxagoras as an Incorporealist. Book I.

To this sense: *He is happy who has his mind richly filled and stored with the treasures of divine knowledge; but he is miserable whose mind is darkened regarding the belief in a God.* And, secondly, by denying God to have any human form or limbs,

->For he is not distinguished with a human head upon his limbs, etc.<-
<note>original: "ου μὲν γὰρ βροτέῃ κεφαλῇ κατὰ γυῖα κέκασται, &c."</note>

*Only a Holy and Ineffable Mind, that by Swift Thoughts agitates the whole World.*

XXV. And now we shall also say something of **Anaxagoras**, having shown before that he was a "spurious atomist" <note>Anaxagoras is called "spurious" here because, while he used physical principles, he did not believe the world was made of atoms alone, but required a divine Mind.</note>. For he likewise agreed with the other atomists in this: that he asserted **incorporeal substance** <note>spiritual or non-physical reality</note> in general as the active cause and principle of motion in the universe, and particularly, an incorporeal Deity distinct from the world. He affirmed that there was, besides atoms, *a Mind that orders and is the cause of all things* <note>original: "Νοῦς ὁ διακοσμῶν τε καὶ πάντων αἴτιος"</note> (as it is expressed in **Plato**). This Mind (as **Aristotle** tells us) he made to be *the only simple, unmixed, and pure thing among all beings.* <note>original: "μόνον τῶν ὄντων ἁπλοῦν καὶ ἀμιγῆ καὶ καθαρόν"</note> And he supposed this to be that which brought the confused chaos of diverse <note>original: "omnifarious"</note> atoms into that orderly structure <note>original: "compages"</note> of the world that now exists.

XXVI. And by this time we have made it evident that those atomic natural philosophers <note>original: "Physiologers"</note> who lived before **Democritus** and **Leucippus** were all of them **incorporealists**. They joined theology and **pneumatology** <term>pneumatology</term>—the study of spirits or souls—together with their atomic natural philosophy. This is a fact expressly noted concerning **Ecphantus** the Pythagorean in the writings of **Stobaeus**: *Ecphantus held the corporeal world to consist of atoms, but yet to be ordered and governed by a divine providence.* <note>original: "Ἔκφαντος ἐκ μὲν τῶν ἀτόμων συνεσάναι τὸν κόσμον, διοικεῖσθαι δὲ ἀπὸ προνοίας"</note> That is, he joined **atomology** <note>the study of atoms</note> and theology together. And the same is also observed of **Arcesilas** (or perhaps **Archelaus**) by **Sidonius Apollinaris**:

->*After these, Arcesilaus concludes that this world-mass*<-
->*was prepared by a Divine Mind, being made of those*<-
->*parts which he himself calls light atoms.*<-
<note>original: "Post hos Arcesilaus Divinâ Mente paratam / Conjicit hanc Molem, confectam Partibus illis / Quas Atomos vocat ipse leves."</note>

### Chap. I. The ancient Atomists were Theists.

They joined theology and **incorporealism** <note>the belief in reality that is not made of matter</note> with their atomic science <note>original: "physiology"</note>. They studied atoms just as he did, but they did not become atheists; rather, that atheistical atomism was a thing first set on foot afterward by Leucippus and Democritus.

XXVII. But because many seem to be so strongly possessed with this prejudice—as if atheism were a natural and necessary byproduct of atomism—and therefore conclude that the same persons could not possibly be atomists and also incorporealists or theists, we shall further make it evident that there is not only no inconsistency between atomic science and theology, but also that there is, on the contrary, a most natural kinship <note>original: "cognation"</note> between them.

And this we shall do in two ways: First, by inquiring into the origin of this philosophy and considering what grounds or principles of reason first led the ancients into this atomic or mechanical way of studying nature. And secondly, by making it appear that the internal structure of this science is such that whosoever entertains it—if he only thoroughly understands it—must of necessity acknowledge that there is something else in the world besides body <note>meaning physical matter</note>.

First, therefore, this atomic science seems to have had its rise and origin from the strength of reason exerting its own inward active power and vigor, and thereby supporting itself against the prejudices of the senses, and at length prevailing over them in this manner: The ancients, considering and revolving the ideas of their own minds, found that they had a clear and distinct conception of two things as the general heads and principles of whatever was in the universe. One of these was **passive matter**, and the other **active power, vigor, and virtue**. To the latter belongs both **cogitation** <note>the act of thinking</note> and the power of moving matter, whether by express consciousness or not. Both of these together may be called by one general name: **Life**. So they established these two general categories of being or entity: **passive matter (or bulk)** and **self-activity (or life)**. <margin>The active and moving cause. Philo. <note>original: "αἰτιον δραστήριον καὶ κινητικόν"</note></margin> The first of these was commonly called by the ancients <term>the passive recipient <note>original: "τὸ πάσχον", literally "that which suffers or receives"</note></term>, and the latter <term>the active principle <note>original: "τὸ ποιοῦν"</note></term> and <term>the source from which motion springs <note>original: "τὸ ὅθεν ἡ κίνησις"</note></term>. *In the nature of things* (says Cicero, according to the general sense of the ancients), *two things must be sought: one, the matter from which everything is made; the other, the force which makes everything.* <note>original: "In rerum Natura... Duo quærenda sunt; Unum, quæ Materia sit, ex qua quæque res efficiatur; Alterum, quæ res sit quæ quicque Efficiat"</note> To the same purpose Seneca says: *There must be something from which a thing is made, and then someone by whom it is made; the latter is the Cause, the former is the Matter.* <note>original: "Esse debet aliquid Unde fiat, deinde à Quo fiat; hoc est Causa, illud Materia"</note> There

# The near Cognation betwixt B O O K I.

There must be something *out* of which a thing is made, and then something *by* which it is made; the *latter* is properly the *cause*, and the *former* is the *matter*. This is to be understood regarding *physical* <note>original: "corporeal"</note> things and their differences: there must be both *matter* and an *active power* for the production of them. And so also says *Aristotle*:

> "Of causes, we say that one is where the principle of motion comes from, and another is the matter." <note>original: ὅσης αἰτίας μιᾶς μὲν ὅθεν τὴν ἀρχὴν εἶναί φαμεν τῆς κινήσεως, μιᾶς δὲ τῆς ὕλης</note>

Where *Aristotle* gives the name of *cause* to the *matter* also, though others reserved that name for the *active power*. And the writer of *On the Opinions of the Philosophers* <note>original: "de Placitis Philosophorum," a work historically attributed to Plutarch</note> expresses this as the *general sense* of the *ancients*:

> "It is impossible for matter to be the single principle of all things from which all things arise, but an efficient cause must also be supposed. Just as silver alone is not enough to create a cup unless there is an agent—that is, the silversmith—to make it; the same is true for bronze, wood, and all other material." <note>original: ἀδύνατον ἀρχὴν μίαν ὕλην τῶν ὄντων ἐξ ἧς τὰ πάντα ὑποστῆναι, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ ποιοῦν αἴτιον χρὴ ὑποτιθέναι, οἷον οὐκ ἄργυρος ἀρκεῖ πρὸς τὸ ἔκπωμα γενέσθαι ἂν μὴ καὶ τὸ ποιοῦν ᾖ, τουτέστιν ὁ ἀργυροκόπος, ὁμοίως καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ χαλκοῦ, καὶ τοῦ ξύλου, καὶ τῆς ἄλλης ὕλης</note>

Now, as they understood a *necessity* for these two *principles*, so they conceived them to be such that they could not be blended together into one and the same *thing* or *substance*; they have such distinct *ideas* and *essential characters* from one another. The *Stoics* <note>a school of Hellenistic philosophy</note> were the only *people* who, offering *violence* to their own logic, clumsily and unskillfully attempted to make these two distinct things one and the same *substance*. Therefore, as the *first* of these—*matter*, or *passive extended bulk* <note>matter that takes up space but cannot move itself</note>—is taken by all for *substance* and commonly called by the name of *body*; so the other, which is by far the more *noble* of the *two* (being that which acts upon the matter and has a *commanding power* over it), must also be *substance*, of a different kind from *matter* or *body*. Therefore, it is *immaterial* or *incorporeal substance*. Neither did they find any other *entity* to be conceivable besides these two: *passive bulk* or *extension*, which is *physical substance*; and *internal self-activity* or *life*, which is the *essential character* of *incorporeal substance*. To this *latter* category belongs not only *thought* <note>original: "cogitation"</note>, but also the *power of moving matter*.

Moreover, when they further considered the *first* of these—the *material* or *physical principle*—they were not able to clearly conceive of anything else in it besides *magnitude, figure, position*, and *motion* or *rest*. These are all various *modes of extended bulk*. They concluded, therefore, according to *reason*, that there was *really* nothing else existing in *bodies* outside of us besides the various *combinations* and *arrangements* of those *simple elements*; that is, nothing but *mechanism*. From this, it necessarily followed that whatever else was supposed to be in *bodies* was, indeed, nothing but our *modes of sensation*, or the *fantasies* and *passions* within us triggered by them, mistaken for things really existing outside of us. And this is so obvious that some of those *philosophers* who had taken little notice of *atomic science* <note>original: "atomical physiology"</note> had notwithstanding

> "Though the things of sense seem to have so clear a certainty, nevertheless it is doubted concerning them whether [their qualities] have any real existence at all in the things outside us, and not rather a seeming existence only in our own passions; and there is need of mind or understanding to judge in this case, and to determine the controversy, which sense alone cannot decide." <note>original: καὶ τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς αἰσθήσεως ἃ δὴ δοκεῖ πίστιν ἔχειν ἐναργεστάτω, ἀπιστεῖται μήποτε οὐκ ἐν τοῖς ὑποκειμένοις, ἀλλ᾿ ἐν τοῖς πάθεσιν ἔχῃ τὴν δοκοῦσαν ὑπόστασιν, καὶ δεῖ ἢ διανοίας τῶν κρινόντων</note>

But the ancient physiologists <note>original: "Physiologists," meaning natural philosophers who studied the physical world.</note> concluded without any hesitancy, "That the nature of honey in itself is not the same thing as my being sweetened, nor is the nature of wormwood the same as that sense of bitterness which I have from it;" <note>original: οὐ τὸ αὐτὸ ἔστι τὸ μέλι τῷ γλυκάζεσθαί με, καὶ τὸ ἀψίνθιον τῷ πικράζεσθαι</note> "but that the <term>passion</term> <note>original: "passion," here meaning the internal sensation or feeling produced by an external object.</note> of sense differed from the absolute nature of the thing itself outside us; the senses do not comprehend the objects themselves, but only their own passions resulting from them." <note>original: διαφέρειν δὲ τὸ πάθος τοῦ ἐκτὸς ὑποκειμένου, καὶ τὰς αἰσθήσεις, τὰ μὲν ἐκτὸς ὑποκείμενα οὐ καταλαμβάνειν, μόνα δὲ εἰ ἄρα τὰ ἑαυτῶν πάθη</note>

I say therefore, that the ancients concluded the absolute nature of physical things in themselves to be nothing but a certain disposition of parts, in respect of magnitude, figure, position, and motion. In tastes, these cause us to be differently affected with those *senses* of sweetness and bitterness; and in sight, they cause those fancies of colors; and accordingly in the other *senses*, they produce other fancies. They concluded that the physical world was to be explained by these two things: one is absolute in the bodies outside us—their various *mechanism*—and the other is relative only to us—the different fancies in us, caused by the respective differences of those bodies in themselves. These fancies or fantastic *ideas* are not modes of the bodies outside us, but are modes only of that in ourselves which is cogitative <note>thinking</note> or *self-active*, that is, incorporeal. For the sensible *ideas* of hot and cold, red and green, etc., cannot be clearly conceived by us as modes of the *bodies* outside us, but they may be easily apprehended as modes of cogitation—that is, of sensation, or *sympathetical perception* in us.

The result of all this was: that whatever is either in ourselves or the whole world was to be reduced to one or the other of these two principles: *passive matter* and *extended bulk*, or *self-active power and virtue*; *corporeal* or *incorporeal substance*; *mechanism* or *life*; or else to a combination of them both together.

XXVIII. From this general account, which we have now given of the origin of the atomical physiology, it appears that the doctrine of incorporeal substance sprang up together with it. But this will be further manifest from what follows. For we shall in the next place show how this philosophy did, in an especial manner, owe its origin to the improvement of one particular principle.

<header>Nothing comes from Nothing, Book. I.</header>

There is another principle of reason, above and beyond all the rest; namely, that famous axiom so much discussed among the ancients:

->*From nothing, nothing comes; into nothing, nothing can return.* <note>original: "De Nihilo Nihil, in Nihilum Nil posse reverti"</note><-

That *nothing can come from nothing, nor go to nothing.* For although *Democritus*, *Epicurus*, and *Lucretius* abused this theorem—endeavoring to carry it further than the intention of the first atomists to disprove the divine creation of anything out of nothing (stating that *no thing is ever produced from nothing by divine power* <note>original: "Nullam rem à Nihilo gigni Divinitus unquam"</note>) and consequently to disprove a *Deity*—the meaning of it was at first more limited. It originally meant that *nothing of itself could come from nothing or go to nothing*, or that according to the *ordinary course of nature* (without an extraordinary divine power), nothing could be raised from nothing nor reduced to nothing. This is not only an undoubted rule of reason in itself, but it was also the primary origin of that atomical physiology <note>original: "Physiology," here meaning natural philosophy or the study of the physical world.</note> which, discarding the idea of "forms" and "qualities," acknowledged nothing in the physical body besides mechanism.

For this reason, it was not in vain or without purpose that *Laertius*, in his *Life of Democritus*, takes notice of this as one of his *dogmas* <note>original: "Dogmata," meaning settled doctrines or beliefs.</note>: *that nothing comes into being from what is not, nor is destroyed into what is not.* <note>original: μηδὲν ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος γίνεσθαι μηδὲ εἰς τὸ μὴ ὂν φθείρεσθαι</note> This was a fundamental principle, not only of his atheism, but also of the very atomical physiology itself which he pursued. And *Epicurus*, in his epistle to *Herodotus*, plainly derives the beginning of all his philosophy from this point:

> *We derive the beginning of our philosophy from this,* (*he says*) *that nothing is made out of nothing or destroyed to nothing. For if things were made out of nothing, then every thing might be made out of every thing, and there would be no need for "seeds" <note>original: "Seeds," referring to the fundamental particles or atoms from which specific things grow.</note>. And if whatever is corrupted were destroyed to nothing, then all things would eventually be brought to nothing.* <note>original: πρῶτον μὲν ὅτι οὐδὲν γίνεται ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος, καὶ οὐδὲν φθείρεται εἰς τὸ μὴ ὄν. Εἰ μὲν γὰρ ἐγίνετο τὸ ἐκφαινόμενον ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος, πᾶν ἐκ παντὸς ἐγίνετ’ ἄν, σπερμάτων γε οὐδὲν προσδεόμενον· καὶ εἰ ἐφθείρετο δὲ τὸ ἀφανιζόμενον εἰς τὸ μὴ ὄν, πάντα ἂν ἀπολώλει τὰ πράγματα οὐκ ὄντων τῶν εἰς ἃ διελύετο</note>

*Lucretius*, in a similar manner, begins here and insists more extensively upon those grounds of reason hinted at by *Epicurus*. First, he proves that nothing can be made out of nothing in this way:

> *For if things were made from nothing, then from all things*
> *Every species could be born; nothing would need a seed:*
> *Humans could first arise from the sea, and from the earth*
> *The scaly race of fish, and so on.* <note>original: "Nam si de nihilo fierent, ex omnibus rebus / Omne Genus nasci posset: Nil Semine egeret: / E mare primùm Homines & terra posset oriri / Squamigerum Genus, &c."</note>
> *Nor would the same fruits stay constant to their trees,*
> *But they would change; all trees could bear all things.*
> *Furthermore, why do we see the rose in spring, the grain in the heat,*
> *And the vines in autumn, poured out at nature's urging? etc.* <note>original: "Nec Fructus iidem Arboribus constare solerent, / Sed mutarentur : Ferre omnes omnia possent. / Præterea cur Vere Rosam, Frumenta Calore, / Vites Autumno, fundi, suadente videmus? &c."</note>
> *But if they were made from nothing, they would spring up suddenly*
> *At uncertain times and in unsuitable parts of the year.* <note>original: "Quòd si de nihilo fierent, subitò exorerentur / Incerto spatio atq; alienis Partibus anni."</note>

In the same way, he argues to prove that nothing is destroyed into nothingness.

> To this it may be added that nature dissolves every thing back into its own constituent parts, and does not destroy things to the point of nothingness. For if anything were mortal in all its parts, then every thing would suddenly perish, snatched from our eyes. Furthermore, if time, as it passes, completely destroys all things by consuming all their matter, from where does Venus bring back the race of living creatures, kind by kind, into the light of life? Or, once brought back, from where does the creative earth nourish and increase them, providing food for each according to its kind? Therefore, things that are seen do not utterly perish, since nature restores one thing from another, nor does she allow anything to be born unless aided by the death of another. <note>original Latin: "Huc accedit utì quicque in sua Corpora rursum / Dissolvat Natura; neque ad Nihilum interimat res: / Nam si quid Mortale à cunctis Partibus esset, / Ex oculis res quæque repentè erepta periret. / Præterea quæcunque Vetustate amovet ætas, / Si penitus perimit, consumens Materiam omnem, / Unde Animale Genus generatim in Lumina Vitæ / Redducit Venus? aut redductum Dædala Tellus / Unde alit atque auget? generatim pabula præbens, &c. / Haud igitur penitus pereunt quæcunque videntur, / Quando aliud ex alio reficit Natura; nec ullam / Rem gigni patitur nisi morte adjutam alienâ."</note>

In these passages, it is plain that *Lucretius* does not immediately aim at atheism and nothing else. He primarily seeks to establish a specific kind of atomic natural philosophy <note>original: "Atomical Physiology"</note>, upon which the followers of Democritus <note>original: "Democriticks"</note> later tried to graft atheism. 

Yet to remove that suspicion, we shall next show that generally the other ancient natural philosophers who were theists <note>Theists: those who believe in a God or gods.</note> also built the structure of their philosophy upon the same foundation: that *nothing can come from nothing, nor go to nothing*. This includes, for example, *Parmenides*, *Melissus*, *Zeno*, *Xenophanes*, *Anaxagoras*, and *Empedocles*. Of *Parmenides* and *Melissus*, *Aristotle* writes: *They say that no real entity is either generated or corrupted—that is, made anew out of nothing or destroyed to nothing.* <note>original Greek: "οὐδὲν οὐδὲ γίνεσθαί φασιν οὐδὲ φθείρεσθαι τῶν ὄντων"</note> 

And *Simplicius* tells us that *Parmenides* gave a notable reason to confirm this assertion—that nothing in nature could be made out of nothing: *Parmenides added a wonderful reason why that which is made must necessarily be made out of what already exists* <note>original Greek: "αἰτίαν τοῦ δεῖν πάντως ἐξ ὄντος γίνεσθαι τὸ γινόμενον, θαυμαστῶς ὁ Παρμενίδης προσέθηκεν"</note>; *for he says, overall, if something comes from nothing, what was the necessity <note>original: "ἀποκλήρωσις" (apoklerosis), meaning a decisive cause or lot.</note> for it to be made then, and neither sooner nor later?* <note>original Greek: "ὅλως γάρ φησιν, εἰ ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος, τίς ἡ ἀποκλήρωσις τοῦ τότε γενέσθαι ὅτε ἐγένετο, ἀλλὰ μὴ πρότερον ἢ ὕστερον"</note> 

Again, *Aristotle* testifies of *Xenophanes* and *Zeno* that they made this a main principle of their philosophy: *That it is impossible for anything to be made out of nothing.* <note>original Greek: "μὴ ἐνδέχασθαι γίνεσθαι μηδὲν ἐκ μηδενὸς"</note> And regarding this *Xenophanes*, *Sextus* the philosopher tells us that he held *that there was but one God, and that he was incorporeal* <note>Incorporeal: having no physical body or substance.</note> <note>original Greek: "ὅτι εἷς καὶ ἀσώματος Θεός"</note>, speaking of him thus:

And as for Anaxagoras, it is sufficiently known to all that his *Homæomeria* <term>original Greek: ὁμοιομέρεια; the doctrine that substances are made of "similar parts" that are identical in nature to the whole</term> or *Doctrine of Similar Atoms* (which was a certain *spurious* <note>original: "Spurious"; here meaning a corrupted or false version</note> kind of *Atomism*) was nothing but a superstructure built upon this foundation. Besides all this, Aristotle pronounces universally concerning the *Ancient Natural Philosophers* <note>original: "Physiologers"</note> without any exception, that they agreed in this one thing: "All natural philosophers agree on this opinion: that it is impossible for anything to come into being from what does not exist." <note>original Greek: περὶ ταύτης ὁμογνωμονοῦσι τῆς δόξης οἱ περὶ φύσεως, ὅτι τὸ γιγνόμενον ἐκ μὴ ὄντων γίγνεσθαι ἀδύνατον.</note> The *natural philosophers* generally agree in this (laying it down as a grand foundation) that it is *impossible* that anything should be made out of *nothing*. And again he calls this "the common opinion of naturalists" <note>original Greek: κοινὴν δόξαν τῶν φυσικῶν</note>; intimating also that they concluded it was the greatest absurdity any *natural philosopher* could be guilty of to lay down such principles from which it would follow that any *real entity* in nature came from *nothing* or went to *nothing*.

Now it may well be supposed that all these *Ancient Natural Philosophers* (most of whom were also *Theists*) did not make such a fuss about this business for nothing; therefore, we are next to show what it was they were aiming at. We affirm that one thing they all aimed at, who insisted upon the aforementioned principle, was establishing some *Atomic Physiology* <note>original: "Physiology"; here meaning the study of nature or physics</note> or another. Most of them focused on a version that takes away all *forms* and *qualities* of *bodies* (as *entities* really distinct from the *matter* and *substance*) and resolves everything into *mechanism* and *appearance* <note>original: "Phancy"; the way things appear to our senses</note>. For it is plain that if the *forms* and *qualities* of *bodies* are *entities* really distinct from the *substance*—and its various *modifications* of *figure*, *position*, and *motion*—then in all the *changes* and *transformations* of nature, and all the *generations* and *alterations* of *body* (those *forms* and *qualities* being supposed to have no *real existence* anywhere before), something must of necessity be *created* or produced miraculously out of *nothing*. Likewise, they would be reduced into *nothing* during their *decay* <note>original: "Corruptions"</note>, having no *being* anywhere afterward. 

For *example*: whenever a *candle* is lighted or kindled into a flame, there must be a new *form* of *fire*, and new *qualities* of *light* and *heat*, really distinct from the *matter* and *substance*, produced out of *nothing*—that is, *created*. These same things would be *reduced* into *nothing*, or *annihilated*, when the flame is extinguished. Similarly, when *water* is *frozen* <note>original: "Congealed"</note> into *snow*, *hail*, or *ice*, and when it is again *melted*; when *wax* is by *liquefaction* made *soft* and *transparent*, and changed to most of our *senses*; when the same kind of *nourishment* taken in by *animals* is turned into *blood*, *milk*, *flesh*, *bones*, *nerves*, and all the other *similar parts*; when that which was in the *form* of bright *flame* appears in the *form* of dark *smoke*; and that which was in the *form* of *vapor* appears in the *form* of *rain* or *water*, or the like: I say, that in all these *mutations* of *bodies*, there must be something made out of *nothing*. But that in all the *ever-changing transformations* <note>original: "Protean Transformations"; referring to Proteus, the shapeshifting sea god of Greek myth</note> of nature, which happen continually, there should be *real entities* thus perpetually produced out of *nothing* and reduced to *nothing*, seemed to be so great a

If qualities like heat or color were distinct entities, their appearance and disappearance would require constant, miraculous creation and annihilation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous one, explaining why ancient natural philosophers rejected the idea of creation out of nothing and how this led them to develop the "Atomic" or "Corpuscular" theory of matter.</meta>

# CHAPTER I. Atomical Philosophy.

This was such a paradox to the Ancients that they could by no means admit it. As we have already declared, first, they concluded it was clearly impossible by Reason that any real entity <term>an object or being that exists in reality</term> should by itself rise out of nothing. Secondly, they thought it very absurd to bring God upon the stage with his miraculous, extraordinary power perpetually at every turn. They also argued that if things were miraculously made out of nothing, then anything might be made out of anything, and there would be no cause in nature for the production of one thing rather than another, or at this time rather than that. Therefore, they sagaciously apprehended that there must be some other mystery or intrigue of nature in this business than was commonly dreamed of or suspected.

They concluded that in all these transformations, there were no such real entities of *forms* and *qualities* produced and destroyed that were distinct from the matter and the various disposition of its parts in respect to figure, position, and motion (as is commonly supposed). Instead, all these feats were performed either by the joining and separating <note>original: "Concretion and Secretion"</note> of parts that actually existed, or else by the different modifications of the same pre-existing matter or its invisible parts. To this, they added that from those different modifications of the small particles of bodies (which are not distinctly perceived by our senses), there are produced in us certain confused *appearances* or *mental images* <note>original Greek/Latin: "Phasmata or Phantasmata"</note>, *apparitions*, *fancies*, and *feelings*—such as light and colors, heat and cold, and the like. These are the things that are commonly mistaken for real qualities existing in the bodies outside of us; whereas, indeed, there is nothing absolutely in the bodies themselves like those *imaginary ideas* <note>original: "Phantastick Idea’s"</note> that we have of them. Yet, they are wisely designed by the Author of Nature for the adorning and embellishing of the physical world for us.

So they conceived that bodies were to be considered in two ways: either as they are absolutely in themselves, or as they are relative to us. As they are absolutely in themselves, there never was any *entity* really distinct from the *substance* produced in them out of *nothing*, nor *corrupted* or *destroyed* into *nothing*, but only the *accidents* and *modifications* were altered. These *accidents* and *modifications* <term>non-essential properties, such as shape or position, which can change without changing the core nature of the substance</term> are not entities really distinct from their *substance*. For example, the same body may be put into several shapes and figures, and the same man may successively stand, sit, kneel, and walk without the production of any new entities really distinct from the substance of his body. Therefore, the generations, corruptions, and alterations of inanimate bodies do not end in the production or destruction of any "substantial forms" or real entities distinct from the substance, but only in different modifications of it. 

But secondly, as bodies are considered relative to us, besides their different modifications and mechanical alterations, there are also different fancies, appearances, and *apparitions* produced in us by them; these are what unwary and unskilled philosophers mistake for absolute forms and qualities in the bodies themselves. And thus they concluded that all the *phenomena* <note>original: "Phænomena"</note> of inanimate bodies and their various transformations might be...

<summary>This page explains the ancient Atomist view that change in the physical world is not the creation of new "entities" from nothing, but rather the rearrangement of pre-existing matter. It distinguishes between the objective properties of matter (size, shape, motion) and our subjective perceptions (color, heat), which exist only in the mind.</summary>

# The Origin of the Book. I.

...be clearly resolved into these two things: first, something that is real and absolute in bodies themselves, which is nothing but their different mechanism or the arrangement of their parts regarding shape, position, and motion; and second, something that is *imaginary* <note>original: "Phantastical"</note> in the person who senses it.

That the atomic theory <note>original: "Atomical Physiology"</note> emerged in this way—from the rational principle that *nothing comes from nothing, nor goes to nothing*—can be further proved by the testimony of Aristotle, who wrote the following: 

"Because opposites are generated from each other, they must have existed within each other beforehand. For if everything that comes to be must necessarily come either from what exists or from what does not exist, and the latter—that anything should be made out of nothing—is impossible (according to the general agreement of all the ancient natural philosophers), then it follows by necessity that all physical things are made or generated out of things that were truly pre-existing, though due to the smallness of their mass they were imperceptible to us." <note>original Greek: "εκ τῶ γίνεθαι εξ αλλήλων τ'αναυτία ενυπήρχεν άρα· ει γδ πᾶν τὸ γινόμλνον ανάγκη γίνεθαι ἢ εξ όντων ἢ εξ μὴ όντων· τούτων δὲ τὸ μλὺ, εκ μὴ όντων γίνεθαι αδύνατον, περὶ γδ ταύτης ομογνωμονοῦσι τ' δόξης άπαντες οἱ περὶ φύσεως· τὸ λοιπὸν ήδη συμβαίνιν εξ ανάγκης ενόμισαν· εξ όντων μλὺ καὶ ενυπαρχόντων γίνεθαι, διὰ δ' σμικρότητα τ' ὄγκων εξ αναιθήτων ημῖν."</note>

Where Aristotle plainly suggests that all the ancient philosophers who insisted upon this principle—that *nothing comes from nothing, nor goes to nothing*—were, in one way or another, atomists. They reduced all physical things into certain masses or small particles <note>original: "Moleculæ or Corpuscula"</note> which, by reason of their smallness, were imperceptible to us <note>original Greek: "όγκες τινὰς διὰ τω σμικρότητα αναιθήτες ημῖν"</note>, which is to say, into atoms. 

However, there was a difference between these atomists. For instance, Anaxagoras was an atomist who nevertheless believed in *forms* and *qualities* that were truly distinct from the mechanical arrangements of bodies. It seems he was not able to fully understand the other atomic theory of the ancients—which rejected "qualities" and explained all physical phenomena through mechanism and perception <note>original: "Mechanism and Phancy"</note>. Yet, acknowledging their principle that *nothing could of itself come from nothing nor go to nothing*, he created a new kind of atomism of his own. 

He supposed that the whole physical world or mass of matter consisted of *similar atoms* <note>This theory is often called homoeomery: the idea that the parts of a substance are the same as the whole.</note>—that is, atoms originally endowed with all those different forms and qualities that are commonly thought to be in bodies. Some atoms were bony, some fleshy, some fiery, some watery, some white, some black, some bitter, some sweet, and the like. He believed that all bodies whatsoever contained some of all these different types of atoms (which are essentially infinite in number).

"Everything was mingled in everything, because they saw that everything was made of everything. However, things seemed to differ from one another and were named this or that based on those atoms which are most predominant in the mixture of the infinite parts," <note>original Greek: "πᾶν εν παντὶ μεμίχθαι, διότι πᾶν εκ παντὸς γίνεται, φαίνεθαι δ' διαφέροντα, καὶ προσαγορεύεθαι έτερα αλλήλων εκ τῶ μάλιστα υπερέχοντ@ διὰ τὸ πλῆθ@ εν τῆ μίξει τ' απείρων, &c."</note> etc. By reason of

# CHAPTER I. Atomic Philosophy.

...their multiplicity. From this, he concluded that all the generations <note>original: "Generations"; meaning the formation or creation of things</note>, corruptions <note>original: "Corruptions"; meaning the decay or destruction of things</note>, and alterations of bodies were caused by nothing but the combining <note>original: "Concretions"</note> and separating <note>original: "Secretions"</note> of atoms that already existed within the matter—atoms of different forms and qualities—without any new form or quality being produced out of nothing, or any existing one being reduced to nothing. 

Aristotle gives this very account of the theory of Anaxagoras <note>original: "Anaxagorean Hypothesis"</note>: 

"It seems that Anaxagoras thus thought the elements were infinite, because he accepted the common opinion of natural philosophers to be true: that nothing is produced from what is not." <note>original Greek: "ἔοικε Ἀναξαγόρας οὕτως ἄπειρα οἰηθῆναι τὰ στοιχεῖα, διὰ τὸ ὑπολαμβάνειν, τὴν κοινὴν δόξαν τῶν φυσικῶν εἶναι ἀληθῆ, ὡς οὐ γινομένου οὐδενὸς ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος."</note> 

Anaxagoras seems, therefore, to make *infinite atoms endowed with various forms and qualities the elements of bodies*, because he supposed *that common opinion of natural philosophers <note>original: "Physiologers"</note> to be true: that nothing is made from nothing*. 

But all the other ancient natural philosophers who came before Anaxagoras, as well as those after him—who, by insisting upon the same principle of *nothing coming from nothing*, did not follow Anaxagoras's specific theory (such as Empedocles, Democritus, and Protagoras)—were forced to make dissimilar molecules <note>original Greek: "ὄγκους ἀνομοίους"</note> and atoms without qualities <note>original Greek: "ἀτόμους ἀποίους"</note> the principles of bodies. These atoms were defined by nothing other than their magnitude, shape, and motion. By dismissing <note>original: "cashiering"</note> "Forms" and "Qualities" as if they were real entities separate from matter, they explained all physical phenomena <note>original: "Corporeal Phænomena"</note> through mechanism and imagination <note>original: "Phancie"</note>. 

This is because, if no real entity can come from nothing or return to nothing, then one of two things is absolutely necessary: Either these physical forms and qualities—being real entities distinct from matter—must have existed before things were formed and after they decayed, as part of certain tiny, insensible atoms (according to the doctrine of Anaxagoras); or else, they are not real entities distinct from matter at all, but only different modifications and mechanical arrangements of it, combined with how our imagination perceives them. Thus, we have shown that the genuine atomic theory of nature <note>original: "Atomical Physiology"</note> originally sprang from this rational principle: *that no real entity can of itself come from nothing or return to nothing*.

XXIX. Next, we will show how this very same principle of reason—which led the ancients to reject "substantial forms" and the inherent "qualities" of bodies in favor of atomic theory—also led them unavoidably to assert the existence of incorporeal <note>meaning: spiritual or non-physical</note> substances. It led them to conclude that the souls of humans and animals were such substances, being neither created from nothing nor destroyed into nothing. 

As we have shown, they argued against substantial forms and qualities in this way: since everyone assumes that the forms and qualities of bodies are generated and corrupted—created anew from nothing and destroyed into nothing—they could not be real entities distinct from the substance of matter. Instead, they must be only different modifications of matter’s shape, position, and motion, which cause different sensations in us; thus, they were all explained by mechanism and imagination <note>original: "Fancie"</note>. 

As for the notion of Anaxagoras—that atoms already endowed with all those various forms and qualities exist before and after a body's life, being incapable of being created or destroyed—it was nothing but a corruption <note>original: "Adulteration"</note> of the genuine atomic philosophy and a mere dream of his, which very few followed.
