...really real entities <note>original: "ly Real Entities"; likely the conclusion of "really" or "truly" from the previous page.</note> distinct from the substance of matter and its modification. They believed that humans and animals <note>original: "Brutes"</note> are not mere machines, and that life and thought <note>original: "Cogitation"</note>, sense and consciousness, reason and understanding, appetite and will, can never result from size <note>original: "Magnitudes"</note>, shapes <note>original: "Figures"</note>, positions <note>original: "Sites"</note>, and motions. Therefore, they concluded that these things are not corporeally generated and corrupted—meaning they are not created and destroyed as physical things are—in the same way the forms and qualities of bodies are. 

*It is impossible for anything to be created from nothing pre-existing.* <note>original Greek: Ἀδύνατον γίνεσθαί τι ἐκ μηδενὸς προϋπάρχοντος.</note> 

Now, there is nothing of the soul and mind, reason and understanding, nor indeed of thought and life, contained in the modifications and mechanism of bodies. Therefore, to suggest that the soul and mind arise out of the body whenever a person is born <note>original: "generated"</note> would be plainly to suggest that a real entity comes out of nothing, which is impossible. 

I say, because the forms and qualities of bodies are generated and corrupted—made and unmade—in the ordinary course of nature, these philosophers concluded that they were not real entities distinct from the substance of the body and its various modifications. But because the soul and mind is plainly a real entity distinct from the substance of the body, its modification, and its mechanism, it was therefore not a thing generated and corrupted, made and unmade. Instead, it was something that had a being of its own: a substantial thing by itself. Real entities and substances are not generated and corrupted; only modifications are.

Therefore, these ancients understood that there was a great difference between the souls of humans and animals and the forms and qualities of other inanimate bodies, and consequently between their several ways of being produced. In the generation of inanimate bodies, no new real entity is acquired that is distinct from the substance of the thing itself, but only a peculiar modification of it. 

The form of stone, or of timber, of blood, flesh, and bone, and such other natural bodies being produced, is no more a distinct substance or entity from the matter than the form of a house, stool, or table is. There is no more "new entity" acquired in the generation of natural bodies than there is in the production of artificial ones. When water is turned into vapor, a candle into flame, flame into smoke, or grass into milk, blood, and bones, there is no more a miraculous production of something out of nothing than when wool is made into cloth, or flax into linen. It is the same as when a rough and unpolished stone is hewn into a beautiful statue, or when brick, timber, and mortar—which lay together before in disorder—are brought into the form of a stately palace. In neither case is there anything more than a different disposition and modification of pre-existing matter. 

This matter of the universe is always substantially the same, neither more nor less, but only transformed like Proteus <note>original: "Proteanly transformed"; referring to the Greek sea-god Proteus, who could change his shape at will.</note> into different shapes. Thus, we see that the generation of all inanimate bodies is nothing but the change of accidents <term>In philosophy, "accidents" are qualities—like color or shape—that can change without changing the essential nature of the substance itself.</term> and modifications, while the substance remains really the same both before and after. While there is no substantial difference between a grand house or palace standing upright and the same building materials once they have been ruined and demolished—other than a difference of accidents <term>accidents: properties or characteristics of a thing that can change (like shape or position) without changing its essential nature</term> and modifications—there is another substantial difference between a living man and a dead carcass. It is very notable that Anaxagoras <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BC) was a Pre-Socratic philosopher who argued that all things are composed of "like-parted" seeds or atoms.</note> himself, who theorized the existence of bony and fleshy atoms, hot and cold, red and green, and the like—which he supposed to exist before birth <note>original: "Generations"</note> and after death <note>original: "Corruptions"</note> as always immutably the same (so that nothing might come from nothing and go to nothing)—yet he did not suggest that there were any sentient <note>original: "Animalish"</note> atoms that were sensitive and rational. The reason for this could not be because he did not think sense and understanding to be as real as hot and cold, or red and green. Rather, it was because they could not be considered physical forms and qualities; they must necessarily belong to another substance that was incorporeal. Therefore, Anaxagoras could not help but acknowledge that all souls and lives existed before and after the body by themselves, just like the physical forms and qualities in his "similar atoms" <note>original: "Similar Atoms"; referring to his theory of Homoeomery, where the parts of a substance are the same as the whole.</note>.

XXX. And now it is already manifest that from the same principle of reason mentioned before—*that nothing of itself can come from nothing nor go to nothing*—the ancient philosophers were likewise induced to assert the soul’s immortality, together with its incorporeity or distinctness from the body. No substantial entity ever vanishes of its own accord into nothing; for if it did, then in the length of time, everything might eventually become nothing. 

But the soul is a substantial entity, really distinct from the body and not merely a modification of it. Therefore, when a man dies, his soul must still remain and continue to have a being somewhere else in the universe. *All the changes that occur in nature are either accidental transformations and different modifications of the same substance, or else they are conjunctions and separations, or "anagrammatic transpositions" <note>original: "Anagrammatical Transpositions"; a metaphor suggesting that the basic elements of the universe are rearranged like the letters of an anagram to form new things.</note> of things in the universe; the substance of the whole always remains entirely the same. The birth and death of inanimate bodies is like the making of a house, stool, or table, and the unmaking or ruining of them again: they are either different modifications of one and the same substance, or various mixtures and separations, thickenings and thinnings. ### Immortality of Souls Asserted Book I.

XXXI. It is also further evident that this same principle which led the ancients to hold the soul’s immortality—or its future permanence after death—must also have led them to maintain its preexistence <note>original: "Προϋπαρξις"</note>, and consequently its transmigration into bodies <note>original: "μετενσωμάτωσις"</note>. For that which preexisted before the birth <note>original: "Generation"</note> of any animal, and was then somewhere else, must necessarily transmigrate into the body of that animal where it is now. But as for that other transmigration of human souls into the bodies of animals <note>original: "Brutes"</note>, although it cannot be denied that many of these ancients accepted it, yet Timaeus Locrus <note>Timaeus of Locri (5th century BC) was a Pythagorean philosopher and a character in Plato's dialogues.</note> and several other Pythagoreans rejected it, except as an allegorical description of the beastly transformation of men's souls by vice. 

Aristotle tells us again, agreeably to what was declared before, "That the ancient philosophers were afraid of nothing more than this one thing: that anything should be made out of nothing preexistent" <note>original: "ὅτι μάλισα φοβούμενοι διετέλεσαν οἱ παλαιοὶ τὸ ἐκ μηδενὸς γίνεσθαί τι προϋπάρχοντος"</note>. And therefore they must conclude that the souls of all animals preexisted before their births. And indeed it is a well-known thing that, according to the sense of philosophers, these two things were always included together in that one opinion of the soul's immortality: namely, its preexistence as well as its post-existence. 

Neither was there ever any of the ancients before Christianity who held the soul's future permanence after death who did not likewise assert its preexistence. They clearly perceived that if it were once granted that the soul was generated <term>generated: created or brought into being</term>, it could never be proved that it might not also be destroyed <note>original: "corrupted"</note>. And therefore the defenders of the soul's immortality commonly began here: first, to prove its preexistence, proceeding from there afterward to establish its permanence after death. This is the method used in Plato: "Our soul was somewhere before it came to exist in this present human form, and from that it appears that the soul is something immortal, and such as will subsist after death" <note>original: "ἦν που ἡμῶν ἡ ψυχὴ πρὶν ἐν τῶδε τῷ ἀνθρωπίνῳ εἴδει γενέσθαι ὥστε καὶ ταύτῃ ἀθάνατόν τι ἔοικεν ἡ ψυχὴ εἶναι"</note>. 

And the chief demonstration of the soul's preexistence to the ancients before Plato was this: because it is an entity really distinct from the body or matter and its modifications; and no real, substantial entity can either spring of itself out of nothing or be made out of any other substance distinct from it, because nothing can be made "from nothing either existing within or pre-existing" <note>original: "ἐκ μηδενὸς ἐνυπάρχοντος ἢ προϋπάρχοντος"</note>. All natural births <note>original: "Generations"</note> are but the various arrangements and modifications of what was already existing in the universe. But there was nothing of soul and mind existing within and pre-existing in the body before, as there is nothing of life and thought <note>original: "Cogitation"</note> in physical size, shape, position, and motion. ### CHAPTER I. From the same Ground with Atoms.

...as has a *Being* in Nature that is neither created nor destroyed <note>original: "Ingenerably and Incorruptibly"</note>. The mechanism of the human body was a thing made and generated, as it is only a different modification of what existed before, and has no new *Entity* in it distinct from its substance. The "Whole" or "Composite structure" <note>original: "Totum or Compositum"</note> of a man or animal may be said to be generated and corrupted in terms of the union and disunion, conjunction and separation of those two parts: the soul and the body. 

But the soul itself, according to these principles, is something that can be neither created nor destroyed. It existed before birth and will exist after the deaths and corruptions of men, just like the substance of their bodies. Everyone assumes the body's matter has existed since the first creation and that no part of it is annihilated or lost after death, but only scattered and dispersed throughout the universe. Thus, the ancient atomists concluded that souls and lives, being substantial entities in themselves, were all as old as any other substance in the universe—as old as the whole mass of matter and every smallest atom within it. 

That is, those who maintained the eternity of the world consequently also asserted "the eternity of souls and minds" <note>original: "Æternitatem Animorum"</note> (as Cicero calls it). But those who believed the world had a temporary beginning or creation held that all souls were created at the same time as the world. They would by no means be persuaded to think that every atom of senseless matter and particle of dust had such a privilege and preeminence over the souls of men and animals as to be older than them. 

Synesius <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD), a philosopher and Bishop of Ptolemais who blended Neoplatonism with Christianity.</note>, though a Christian, had been educated in this philosophy. He could not be induced—even by the hope of becoming a bishop—to suppress or hide this belief. He wrote, "Indeed, I shall never be persuaded to think my soul to be younger than my body" <note>original: "ἀμέλει τὴν ψυχὴν οὐκ ἀξιώσω ποτὲ σώματὸς ὑστερογενῆ νομίζειν"</note>. But it seems the spirit of those times was such that he was not only excused <note>original: "dispensed withal"</note> regarding this view, but also for another unorthodox opinion <note>original: "Heterodoxy"</note> of his concerning the Resurrection.

XXXII. It is also clear that this doctrine of the ancient atomists—concerning the immateriality and immortality, and the pre-existence and post-existence of souls—was not limited to human souls only, but extended universally to all souls and lives whatsoever. Before Descartes <note>original: "Cartesius"</note>, hardly anyone ever questioned whether the souls of animals <note>original: "Brutes"</note> had any sense, thought, or consciousness. All life, sense, and thought were undoubtedly concluded by these ancients to be an entity really distinct from the substance of the body, and not merely its modification, motion, or mechanism. *Life* and *mechanism* are two distinct *ideas* in the mind that cannot be confused. 

Therefore, they decided that all lives and souls currently in the world have existed since the first beginning and will always exist. No new ones are produced that do not already exist and have not always been here, nor will any of those that now exist be destroyed—any more than the substance of matter can be created or annihilated. # Empedocles from the same Principle Book I.

...generations and corruptions <note>meaning cycles of birth and decay</note>, or deaths, of men and other animals were, according to them, really nothing else but one and the same thing perpetually *rearranged* <note>original: "Anagrammatized"</note>. It was like many different syllables and words being variously and successively composed out of the same pre-existing elements or letters.

XXXIII. We have now explained how the same principle of reason that led the ancient natural philosophers <note>original: "Physiologers"</note> to become Atomists also necessarily led them to believe in the incorporeal <note>meaning they believed in non-physical substances like the soul</note>. The same logic that persuaded them that physical forms were not real entities distinct from the substance of the body—but only different arrangements and mechanisms of it—convinced them likewise that all thinking beings, all souls and lives, were incapable of being created or destroyed. They believed souls existed before the birth of specific animals and continued to exist after their deaths and decay. 

Nothing now remains but to show more specifically that this was, in fact, the case: that the same people used this principle (*that nothing can come from nothing and nothing can return to nothing*) both to support Atomism in their physics—by rejecting all "substantial forms" and qualities—and to support theology or the incorporeal, by asserting that souls are a substance truly distinct from matter, immortal, and pre-existing. We shall demonstrate this using Empedocles, starting with the passage partly cited before:

> And I shall tell you another thing: there is no "nature" <note>meaning birth or creation</note> of any of those things which are mortal, 
> Nor any end in destructive death; 
> But only a mixing and a separation of what has been mixed 
> Is there; and "nature" is but a name given to these things by men. 
> <note>original Greek: 'Αλλο δέ σοι ἐρέω φύσις οὐδενός ἔστιν ἑκάστῳ θνητῶν, οὐδέ τις οὐλομένη θανάτοιο γενέθλη, 'Αλλα μόνον μίξις τε διάλλαξίς τε μιγέντων Ἔστι, φύσις δ' ἐπὶ τοῖς ὀνομάζεται ἀνθρώποισι.</note>

Which I find translated into Latin thus:

> *But I say another thing; for mortals there is no birth,*
> *Nor is there any destruction prepared by death;*
> *There is only a mixing and a union of*
> *Mixable things; this is what mortals usually call birth.*
> <note>original Latin: Ast aliud dico; nihil est Mortalibus Ortus, Est nihil Interitus, qui rebus morte paratur; Mistio sed solum est, & Conciliatio rerum Mistilium; haec dici solita est Mortalibus Ortus.</note>

The full meaning of this is plainly that there is no *nature* <note>original: "φύσις," here meaning the production of a new substance</note> or creation of anything that did not exist before. No new substance is made that did not already truly exist. Therefore, in the generation and decay of inanimate bodies, there is no "form" or "quality" really distinct from the substance produced or destroyed, but only a different composition and modification of matter. 

However, in the birth and death of humans and animals—where souls are substances truly distinct from matter—there is nothing but the joining and separating of souls and specific bodies, both of which exist both before and after. There is no production of a new soul into being that did not exist before, nor the absolute death and destruction of any soul into nothingness. This is further expressed in the following verses:

# Chapter 1. Held Pre-existence and Atoms.

"Infants! For they have no far-reaching thoughts, who expect that anything which did not exist before can come into being, or that anything can die and be completely destroyed." <note>original Greek: Νήπιοι, οὐ γάρ σφιν δολιχόφρενές εἰσι μέριμναι, οἳ δὴ γίνεσθαι πάρος οὐκ ἐὸν ἐλπίζουσιν, ἤτοι καταθνήσκειν τε καὶ ἐξόλλυσθαι ἁπάντη.</note>

To this sense: *That they are infants in understanding and short-sighted, who think anything is made which was nothing before, or anything dies so as to be destroyed into nothing.* Upon which Plutarch <note>A Greek-Roman historian and philosopher (c. 46 – 120 AD)</note> comments in this manner: "Empedocles does not here deny birth <note>original: γένεσιν (genesis)</note>, but only birth out of nothing; nor does he deny decay <note>original: φθοράν (phthoran)</note>, but only total destruction; that is, a decay that dissolves into non-existence." <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἀναιρεῖ γένεσιν, ἀλλὰ τὴν ἐκ μὴ ὄντος· οὐδὲ φθοράν, ἀλλὰ τὴν πάντη· τουτέσι τὴν εἰς τὸ μὴ ὸν ἀπολύουσαν</note> As we have already suggested, this is to be understood differently regarding inanimate and animate things. For in inanimate things, nothing is truly produced or destroyed, because their forms and qualities are not real entities <note>distinct, self-existing things</note> distinct from their substance, but only various mixtures and modifications. But in animate things—where souls are real entities distinct from the substance of the body—nothing is produced or destroyed either, because those souls both exist before their births <note>original: generations</note> and after their deaths <note>original: corruptions</note>. This concept, regarding men and souls, is expressed more fully as follows:

-> "No man who is wise in his heart would suspect such things," <-
-> "As that as long as men live—which they call life—" <-
-> "They only then exist, and experience good and evil," <-
-> "But that before they were formed as mortals, or after they are dissolved, they are nothing at all." <-
<note>original Greek: οὐκ ἂν ἀνὴρ τοιαῦτα σοφὸς φρεσὶ μαντεύσαιτο, ὡς ὄφρα μέν τε βιῶσι, τὸ δὴ βίοτον καλέουσι, τόφρα μὲν οὖν εἰσι, καί σφιν πάρα δεινὰ καὶ ἐσθλὰ, πρὶν δὲ παγέντε βροτοὶ καὶ λυθέντες οὐδὲν ἄρ᾽ εἰσί.</note>

> *That good and ill first attend us here,*
> *And not from a time before did the soul descend;*
> *That here alone we live, and when*
> *We depart from here, we then immediately*
> *Return to our old non-existence again;*
> *Certainly, this ought not to be believed by wise and learned men.*

Therefore, according to Empedocles, this is to be considered one of the common errors: the idea that men only have a being and are capable of good and evil during the time they live what we call "life," but that both before they are born and after they are dead, they are perfectly nothing.

In addition to Empedocles, the same idea is represented by a Greek Tragedian <note>likely Euripides</note> as the sense of the ancient philosophers:

-> "Nothing that is born dies," <-
-> "But being separated one from another," <-
-> "It reveals a different form." <-
<note>original Greek: θνήσκει δ᾽ οὐδὲν τῶν γινομένων, διακρινόμενον δ᾽ ἄλλο πρὸς ἄλλο μόρφην ἑτέραν ἀπέδειξεν.</note>

*That nothing dies or utterly perishes; but things being variously combined and separated, rearranged and modified, change their form and shape only, and are put into a new appearance.*

# Pythagoras's Transmigration | BOOK 1

In agreement with this, Plato also tells us that it was an ancient tradition <note>original Greek: παλαιὸς λόγος (palaios logos)</note> or doctrine before his time, "that the living were made out of the dead, just as much as the dead were made out of the living" <note>original Greek: τοὺς ζῶντας ἐκ τῶν τεθνεώτων γεγονέναι, οὐδὲν ἧττον ἢ τοὺς τεθνεώτας ἐκ τῶν ζώντων</note>, and that this was the constant circle of nature. Moreover, the same philosopher informs us that some of those ancients suspected that what is now called death was, for humans, more properly a birth into life, and what is called birth into life was, by comparison, more likely to be considered a sinking into death. 

The former [death] was seen as the soul’s ascent out of these gross terrestrial bodies to a body more thin and subtle, and the latter [birth] as its descent from a purer body to that which is more coarse <note>original: crass</note> and terrestrial. "Who knows whether that which is called living is not indeed rather dying, and that which is called dying, living?" <note>original Greek: τίς οἶδεν εἰ τὸ ζῶν μέν ἐστι κατθανεῖν, τὸ κατθανεῖν δὲ ζῶν</note>

Furthermore, that this was the doctrine of Pythagoras himself—that no real entity <note>a distinct, self-existing thing</note> perishes in destruction <note>original: corruptions</note>, nor is produced in births <note>original: generations</note>, but only that new modifications and rearrangements are made—is fully expressed by the Latin poet <note>The poet is Ovid, writing in *Metamorphoses*, Book 15.</note>, regarding both inanimate and living things. Of the first, he says:

->*Believe me, nothing in this vast world perishes,*<-
->*But it varies and renews its appearance; and to be "born" is called*<-
->*Beginning to be something other than what one was before; and to "die" is*<-
->*To cease to be that same thing. Although those things might be moved here,*<-
->*And these things moved there, yet the sum of all things remains constant.*<-
<note>original Latin: *Nec perit in tanto quicquam (mihi credite) mundo, / Sed variat, faciemque novat: Nascique vocatur / Incipere esse aliud, quàm quod fuit antè; Morique / Desinere illud idem. Cum sint Huc forsitan Illa, / Hac Translata Illuc: Summâ tamen omnia constant.*</note>

Of the second—that the souls of animals are immortal, existed before this life, and do transmigrate <note>move from one body to another</note>—he writes from the same reasoning in this manner:

->*All things change; nothing perishes. The spirit wanders and comes*<-
->*From there to here, and from here to there, and occupies whatever limbs it pleases.*<-
->*It passes from wild beasts into human bodies,*<-
->*And from ours into beasts, and never perishes at any time.*<-
->*And just as pliable wax is stamped with new figures,*<-
->*And does not remain as it was, nor keeps the same forms,*<-
->*Yet is still the very same wax: so I teach that the soul is always*<-
->*The same, but migrates into various shapes.*<-
<note>original Latin: *Omnia mutantur; Nihil interit: Errat & illinc, / Huc venit, hinc illuc, & quoslibet occupat artus, / Spiritus, éque Feris Humana in Corpora transit, / Inque Feras Noster, nec tempore deperit ullo. / Utque novis facilis signatur Cera figuris, / Nec manet ut fuerat, nec formas servat easdem, / Sed tamen ipsa eadem est: Animam sic semper eandem / Esse, sed in varias doceo migrare Figuras.*</note>

Therefore, although it is something that has not been commonly noticed lately, we believe it to be unquestionably true that all those ancient philosophers who insisted so much upon this principle—"that no real entity is either created or destroyed" <note>original Greek: οὐδὲν οὐδὲ γίνεσθαι οὐδὲ φθείρεσθαι τῶν ὄντων</note>—were aiming at two things at once. 

First, they were establishing the immortality of all souls, including their existence before and after this life; since they are entities really distinct from the body, they could neither be created nor destroyed. Second, they were arguing that physical forms and qualities are not real entities distinct from the body and its mechanism <meta>catchword: chanism</meta>

Anaxagoras was the only dissenter in this latter point; he supposed those forms and qualities were also real entities, distinct from the substance of the body. Therefore, he attributed perpetual existence to them as well—pre-existence and post-existence in "similar atoms" <note>original: Similar Atoms; referring to Anaxagoras's theory of "homeomeries," where every substance is made of tiny parts of the same substance</note>—just as he did to the souls of animals.

And now we have made it sufficiently evident that the doctrine of the incorporeal <note>not composed of matter</note> and immortal nature of souls—we might also add their pre-existence and transmigration—had the same origin and stood upon the same basis as atomic physics <note>original: Atomical Physiology</note>. Therefore, it should not be at all surprising (as we stated before) that the same philosophers and Pythagoreans asserted both those doctrines, and that the ancient atomists were both theists and believers in incorporeal substance.

**34.** But now, to declare our views freely concerning this philosophy of the ancients, which seems so incredibly paradoxical regarding the pre-existence and transmigration of souls: we conceive indeed that their reasoning from the principle *that nothing naturally, or of itself, comes from nothing, nor goes to nothing* <note>original Latin: "De nihilo nihil, in nihilum nil posse reverti"</note>, was not only firmly conclusive against "substantial forms" and qualities of bodies being really distinct from their substance, but also for substantial incorporeal souls and their inability to be generated out of matter. Specifically, it argued for the *future immortality* or *post-existence* of all human souls. For since it is plain that they are not a mere modification of body or matter, but an entity and substance really distinct from it, we have no more reason to think that they can ever vanish into nothing of their own accord than we have to think the substance of the physical world, or any part of it, can do so. For the idea that any real substance is destroyed into nothing during the consumption of bodies by fire, age, or similar means is now generally rejected as a foolish <note>original: idiotical</note> concept; and certainly, it is no less foolish to suppose that the rational soul is utterly extinguished at death.

Furthermore, we add also that this reasoning of the ancients would be just as firm and unbreakable for the *pre-existence* and *transmigration* of souls as it is for their *post-existence* and future immortality, if we did not (as indeed we do) suppose that souls are created by God immediately and infused during birth <note>original: Generations</note>. For souls being unquestionably a distinct substance from the body, and since no substance—according to the ordinary course of nature—*comes out of nothing*, they must of necessity either have pre-existed in the universe before birth and then migrated into their respective bodies, or else they must come immediately from God. God is the fountain of all things, who at first created all the substance that now exists in the world besides himself. Now, this latter option was something those ancient philosophers would by no means admit. They judged it entirely inappropriate to bring God onto the stage perpetually and make him immediately intervene everywhere in the...

# An Assessment of Book I

The creation of generations of men and all other animals by the miraculous production of souls out of nothing. However, if we consider it carefully, we will find that there may be very good reasons for the ongoing divine creation of souls. Specifically, God did not necessarily do everything at the beginning that he ever could or would do, nor did he put forth all his creative power <note>original: "Vigour"</note> at once in a single moment, remaining thereafter only a spectator of the results and allowing nature to act alone without any further intervention—as if there were no God at all in the world. Such a theory has often led people to think that there is no other God in the world but blind and dark nature. 

God might also, for other good and wise purposes unknown to us, reserve for himself the continual exercise of his creative power in the ongoing production of new souls. Even though these souls are created later <note>original: "Juniority"</note>, they will continue to exist just as firmly as the unfeeling matter created many thousands of years before, without simply vanishing into nothing.

And so, our common theory <term>vulgar hypothesis</term> <note>In the 17th century, "vulgar" meant the commonly held or popular view among the general public.</note> regarding the new creation of souls is rational in itself. It sufficiently protects the idea that souls are not made of matter <term>incorporeity</term> and confirms their future immortality (or eternal existence after death), without introducing those controversial absurdities of their pre-existence and reincarnation <term>transmigration</term>.

**35.** But there may be some who would rather deny a future immortality to all souls—including those of animals <term>brutes</term>—to avoid the conclusion that animal souls must undergo successive reincarnations. Such people might conclude that the souls of all animals, as well as the "sensitive soul" in humans <note>The "sensitive soul" was a philosophical term for the part of the soul responsible for physical senses and basic life functions, distinct from the "rational soul" responsible for higher thought.</note>, are made of matter, and only the rational soul is distinct from physical substance. 

To these people, we have only this to say: those who attribute life, sense, thought <term>cogitation</term>, consciousness, and self-awareness—which often show some traces of reason—to mere blood and brains or organized physical bodies in animals, will never be able to clearly defend the non-physical nature and immortality of human souls. In fact, they probably do not even intend to. For either all conscious and thinking beings are non-physical <term>incorporeal</term>, or else nothing can be proved to be non-physical. From this, it would also follow that there is no God distinct from the physical world. 

Although there seems to be no great reason why it should be thought absurd to grant eternal existence to the souls of animals any more than to every atom of matter or particle of dust in the whole world, we will attempt to suggest something to ease the minds of those who are so troubled by this difficulty. Specifically, they may, if they wish, suppose that the souls of animals are merely particular outpourings <term>eradiations</term> or flows <term>effluxes</term> from that supreme Source of Life. Whenever and wherever there is matter properly prepared to receive and be animated by them, they have a sense and enjoyment of themselves...

# Chapter 1: Pythagorean Doctrine

[Souls remain] themselves in it, so long as it continues to be so; but as soon as those organized bodies of theirs, because of their decay <note>original: "Indisposition"</note>, become incapable of being acted upon by the souls any longer, they are then taken back and retracted into their *Original Head and Fountain*. For it cannot be doubted that whatever creates something out of nothing, or sends it forth from itself by free and voluntary emission <note>original: "Emanation"</note>, is also able either to draw it back to its original source or to destroy <note>original: "Annihilate"</note> it at will.

And I find that there have been some among the pagan <note>original: "Gentile"</note> philosophers themselves who held this opinion, of whom *Porphyry* is one: "Every irrational power is dissolved into the life of the whole" <note>original: "λύεται ἑκάστη δύναμις ἄλογος εἰς τὴν ὅλην ζωήν τοῦ παντός"</note>.

### XXXVI.
Neither will this at all weaken the future immortality or eternal existence <note>original: "Post-eternity"</note> of human souls. For if we are indeed theists and truly believe in a *Deity* according to the true understanding of the term, we must then acknowledge that all created beings owe the continuation and permanence of their existence not to any necessity of nature outside of God or independent of him, but to the *Divine Will* alone. Therefore, even if we had the greatest rational and philosophical assurance that our souls are immaterial substances distinct from the body, we still could not have any absolute certainty of their eternal future. This certainty can only be derived from the unchanging nature and perfection of the *Divine Nature* and *Will*, which always does what is *best*. 

For the essential goodness and wisdom of the Deity is the only source of stability for all things. As far as we mortals know, there may be good reason why the grace or favor of future immortality—granted to human souls endowed with reason, morality, and freedom of will (which makes them capable of praise or blame, reward and punishment)—is given so they may be subjects for divine justice to act upon in the next life through various rewards and punishments <note>original: "Retributions"</note>. Yet, this same favor may be denied to those lower lives and more insignificant <note>original: "contemptible"</note> souls of animals <term>brutes</term>, which lack both morality and liberty.

### XXXVII.
But if anyone, despite all this, still stubbornly argues for that ancient *Pythagorean* and *Empedoclean hypothesis*—that all lives and souls are as old as the first creation and will continue to eternity, or as long as the world lasts—as being more reasonable and probable than our theory of the continual creation of new souls, we should consider their points. They argue that the theory of new souls makes them "younger" <note>original: "Juniours"</note> than the matter of the world and their own bodies. Furthermore, they claim that this makes the divine creative power a "cheap" or degraded thing, as it would make God a servant <term>famulative</term> to animalistic <note>original: "Brutish"</note> and often unlawful lusts and improper sexual unions. Most of all, they prefer their view over the idea of the continual un-creation and annihilation of the souls of animals. To those people, we are not unwilling to acknowledge this much:

# The Sensitive Soul not Physical. BOOK I.

Indeed, of the two, this opinion is more reasonable and tolerable than the other absurdity held by those who claim either that all souls are generated—and consequently physical <note>original: "Corporeal"</note>—or at least that the "sensitive soul" <note>In historical psychology, the "sensitive soul" refers to the part of the mind responsible for processing sensations and emotions, shared by humans and animals, as distinct from the "rational soul" unique to humans.</note> in both humans and animals is physical. For besides the monstrosity of this latter opinion, which creates two distinct souls and perceiving substances in every person (a claim sufficiently disproved by our own inner experience), it also makes it absolutely impossible to prove the immortality of the rational soul, the existence of any non-physical substance, and consequently the existence of any God distinct from the physical world.

As for their claim that mindless matter can become sensitive—as if it were ignited into life and thought—just as a body that lacked light and heat can be ignited into fire and flame, this seems to show too much ignorance regarding the doctrine of bodies even in men who are otherwise learned and clever. The best natural scientists <note>original: "Naturalists"</note> have already concluded that *fire* and *flame* are nothing more than the *motion* of the *microscopic* <note>original: "Insensible"</note> parts of a body. When these parts are violently agitated, and often scattered from each other, they create the sensations <note>original: "Phancies"</note> of *light* and *heat* within animals. Now, there is no difficulty at all in understanding that the microscopic particles of a body, which were previously still, can be put into motion. This motion is simply a new way they are organized <note>original: "Modification"</note> and is not a real entity distinct from the substance of the body itself—unlike *life, sensation, and thought*. There is nothing in fire and flame, or an ignited body, different from other bodies except for its *motion* or *mechanics, and the perception of it*. 

Therefore, it is a crude idea—one that the atheists and materialists <note>original: "Corporealists"</note> of the past were always so fond of—*that souls are nothing but fiery or flame-like bodies*. For although heat in the bodies of animals is a necessary tool for the soul and life to function, it is something truly distinct from life itself. A red-hot iron is no closer to being alive than it was before it was heated, and the flame of a candle is no more alive than its extinguished wick or tallow; the difference between them is only the agitation of their microscopic parts. We might also add that, according to this theory, the souls of animals could not remain the exact same individuals throughout their entire lives. Since fire requires fuel <note>original: "Pabulum"</note> to feed upon, it does not remain the exact same physical substance over time. The soul of a newborn animal would no more be the same as the soul of that animal several years later than the flame of a newly lit candle is the same as the flame that flickers out in the socket. In fact, they are no more the same than a river or stream is the same at different points in time. This reasoning can also be extended further to prove that the soul is not a body at all, since the bodies of all animals are in a constant state of change <note>original: "perpetual Flux"</note>.

We have now sufficiently performed our first task, which was to show from the origin of atomic physics <note>original: "Atomical Physiology"</note>,

### Chapter I. Atomical Philosophy leads to Incorporealism.

It is clear that the doctrine of incorporeal substance must necessarily spring up alongside the atomic philosophy. We shall next demonstrate that the inward constitution of this philosophy is such that whosoever truly adopts and rightly understands it must, of necessity, also admit the existence of incorporeal substance. 

First, the **Atomic Hypothesis** allows nothing to **Body** except what is either included in the **Idea** of a thing that is **impenetrably extended** <note>meaning: matter that occupies space and cannot be occupied by another body at the same time</note>, or what can clearly be conceived to be a **Mode** of it—such as more or less **Magnitude** with **Divisibility**, **Figure**, **Position**, **Motion**, and **Rest**, together with the results of their various combinations. This philosophy cannot possibly make **Life** and **Thought** <note>original: "Cogitation"</note> to be **Qualities of Body**, since they are neither contained in those things mentioned before, nor can they result from any *combinations* <note>original: συζυγία (syzygia)</note> or joinings of them. Therefore, it must be granted that **Life** and **Thought** are the **Attributes** of another **Substance** distinct from **Body**, which is **Incorporeal**.

Again, since according to the direction of this **Physiology** <note>here meaning: the study of nature or physics</note>, **Body** has no other **Action** belonging to it but that of **Local Motion**, and since **Local Motion** as such is essentially **movement caused by another** <note>original: Heterokinesie; the principle that matter cannot move itself</note>—that which never springs originally from the moving thing itself, but always from the **Action** of some other **Agent** upon it—it follows undeniably that there must be something else in the **World** besides **Body**. If there were not, there could never have been any **Motion** in it at all. We shall speak more of this later.

Moreover, according to this **Philosophy**, the **Physical Phenomena** <note>original: Corporeal Phænomena</note> themselves cannot be explained by **Mechanism** alone without **Imagination** <note>original: Phancie</note>. Now, **Imagination** is not a **Mode of Body**, and therefore must be a **Mode** of some other kind of **Being** within ourselves that is **Thinking** and **Incorporeal**.

Furthermore, it is evident from the **Principles** of this **Philosophy** that **Sense** itself is not a mere **Physical Passion** <note>meaning: a passive reaction or impression</note> caused by **Bodies** from the outside. This is because the philosophy supposes that there is nothing really in **Bodies** like those **imaginary Ideas** that we have of **Sensible** things—such as **Hot** and **Cold**, **Red** and **Green**, **Bitter** and **Sweet**, and the like. These qualities must, therefore, owe their **Being** to some **Activity of the Soul** itself, which is the same as saying the soul is **Incorporeal**.

Lastly, from this **Philosophy**, it is also manifest that **Sense** is not the **criterion** <note>original: κριτήριον (kriterion); a standard for judging</note> of **Truth** concerning **Bodies** themselves. The philosophy confidently pronounces that those supposed **Qualities of Bodies** represented by **Sense** are merely **imaginary** things. From this, it plainly follows that there is something in us superior to **Sense** which judges it, detects its **imaginary nature**, condemns its **deception**, and determines what really is and is not in the **Bodies** outside of us. This must be a higher **Self-active Power of the Mind**, which plainly proves it to be **Incorporeal**.

XXXIX.

### The Advantages of the [Atomic] Science, Book I.

XXXIX. Now, this atomic science <note>original: "Atomical Physiology"</note> of the ancients seems to have two advantages or points of superiority belonging to it. The first is this: it makes the physical world understandable to us. Because mechanical principles <note>original: "Mechanism"</note> are things that we can clearly understand, whereas we cannot clearly and distinctly conceive of anything else in physical bodies. To say that this or that is done by a "form" or "quality" <note>original: "Form or Quality"—in medieval and Aristotelian philosophy, these were "hidden" properties used to explain why matter behaves the way it does without explaining the physical process</note> is nothing more than saying it is done in a way we do not understand. Or, what is even more absurd, it makes our very ignorance of the cause—disguised under those terms "forms" and "qualities"—the cause of the effect itself.

Furthermore, properties like hot and cold, red and green, bitter and sweet, and so on—when considered as they actually appear to us—can be clearly understood as different mental perceptions <note>original: "Phancies"</note> and vital sensations <note>original: "Vital Passions"</note> in us. These are caused by different motions from external objects acting upon our nerves. But they can never be clearly understood as absolute qualities existing within the bodies themselves, really distinct from their mechanical arrangement. Indeed, there is no more reason why they should be thought of as such than there is to think that, when a person is pricked with a pin or wounded with a sword, the pain they feel is an "absolute quality" inside the pin or the sword. So long as our sensory **ideas** are mistaken for substantial forms or qualities in the bodies outside of us—distinct from the substance of the matter itself—they remain perfectly incomprehensible to us.

For this reason, **Timaeus of Locri**, philosophizing (it seems) in this manner, determined accordingly that physical things could not be grasped by us except "by sense and a kind of spurious or bastardly reasoning" <note>original Greek: αἰσθήσει καὶ νόθῳ λογισμῷ (aisthei kai nothō logismō)</note>. This means that we could have no clear concepts of them in our understanding. For the same reason, **Plato** himself distinguishes between things that are "comprehensible by the understanding with reason" <note>original Greek: νοήσει μετὰ λόγου περιληπτά (noēsei meta logou perilēpta)</note> and those which are "only apprehended by opinion, together with a certain irrational sense" <note>original Greek: δόξῃ μετ᾿ αἰσθήσεως ἀλόγου (doxē met’ aisthēseōs alogou)</note>, clearly meaning by the latter physical and sensory things.

Accordingly, the **Platonists** often take this opportunity to speak extensively in disparagement of physical things. They argue that because of the smallness of "being" that is in them, they are below the reach of the understanding, and possess "not so much essence as generation" <note>original: οὐσίαν (ousian) ... γένεσιν (genesin); "Essence" refers to stable, eternal reality, while "generation" refers to things that are always changing or "becoming"</note>—which is indeed a beautiful concept <note>original: "Fine Phancie"</note>. Therefore, we must either agree with these philosophers and consider sensory things to be "incomprehensible or inconceivable" <note>original Greek: ἀκατάληπτα (akatalepta) or ἀπερίληπτα (aperilepta)</note> by our human understandings (even though the mind is able, meanwhile, to clearly conceive many things of a higher nature), or else we must adopt a favorable opinion concerning the oldest of all sciences—the atomic or mechanical—which alone makes sensory things understandable.

XL. The second advantage which this atomic science seems to have is this: it prepares an easy and clear way for the demonstration of non-physical substances <note>original: "Incorporeal Substances"</note>, by settling a distinct notion...

# Chapter 1. The Atomic Philosophy

...on of Body. He who undertakes to prove that there is something else in the world besides Body must first determine what Body is; otherwise, he will attempt to prove that there is something besides *he-knows-not-what*. But now, if all Body is made to consist of two *substantial principles* <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "substantial principles" are the fundamental components (Matter and Form) that make up a thing's essence.</note>, where one is *Matter* devoid of all *Form* (and therefore devoid of quantity as well as qualities), these philosophers *themselves* conclude that it is *incorporeal*.
<margin>
*Matter is incorporeal.* <note>original: "ἀσώματόν ἐστιν ἡ ὕλη."</note> Plotinus, page 164.
</margin>
The other principle is *Form*, which, being devoid of all *Matter*, must necessarily be incorporeal as well. In this way, *Stobaeus* <note>Johannes Stobaeus, a 5th-century compiler of Greek philosophical excerpts.</note> sets down the joint doctrine of both *Plato* and *Aristotle*: *“In the same manner that Form alone, when separated from Matter, is incorporeal, so also is Matter alone—when separated from Form—not a Body.”* <note>original: "ὃν τρόπον τὸ εἶδος τῆς ὕλης ἀφαιρεθὲν ἀσώματον, οὕτως καὶ τὴν ὕλην τοῦ εἴδους χωρισθεῖσαν οὐ σῶμα εἶναι..."</note> Instead, there is a need for the joint concurrence of both of these—*Matter* and *Form* together—to make up the *substance* of a Body. Moreover, if qualities are also added to these Forms (as the *Platonists* also consistently resolved,
<margin>
*Alcinous*, chapter 11.
</margin>
*“that qualities are incorporeal”* <note>original: "ὅτι αἱ ποιότητες ἀσώματοι"</note>), it is as if they were so many spirits possessing bodies. I say that in this way of philosophizing, the notions of Body and Spirit, Corporeal and Incorporeal, are so confounded that it is impossible to prove anything at all concerning them. Body itself is made *incorporeal* (and therefore everything is incorporeal), for whatever is wholly composed and made up of incorporeals must necessarily be incorporeal itself.

Furthermore, according to this doctrine of *Matter, Forms*, and *Qualities* in Body, Life and Understanding may be supposed to be certain *Forms* or *Qualities* of Body. Then, the souls of men may be nothing else but blood or brains, endowed with the *qualities* of sense and understanding; or perhaps some other more subtle, *sensitive*, and *rational matter* within us. The same might be said of God himself: that he is nothing but a certain *rational* or *intellectual, subtle*, and *fiery body* pervading the whole universe; or else that he is the *Form* of the whole corporeal world, which, together with *Matter*, makes up only one substance. These conceits were formerly entertained by the best of those ancients who were held captive under that dark infirmity of mind: the belief that there could be no other substance besides Body.

But the ancient *atomic philosophy*, by settling a distinct notion of Body—that it is *an impenetrably extended thing* <note>original: "διαστατὸν ἀντίτυπον"—literally, a thing with dimensions that resists being pushed into the space of another.</note> which has nothing belonging to it but magnitude, figure, site, rest, and motion, without any self-moving power—takes away all confusion. It shows clearly how far Body can go and where incorporeal substance begins, as well as the necessity for such a thing to exist in the world.

Again, this philosophy discovers not only that the doctrine of Qualities originated from men mistaking their own fancies <note>original: "Phancies"—meaning internal mental perceptions or subjective experiences.</note> for absolute realities within the bodies themselves, but also that the doctrine of Matter...

# The Entire Philosophy of the Ancients Book I.

...Matter and Form <note>Continuing from the previous page's discussion on the components of physical substance.</note> sprung from another fallacy or deception of the mind: taking *logical notions* and our *modes of conceiving* for *modes of being* and real entities in things outside of us. This shows likewise that because there is nothing else clearly intelligible in a body besides magnitude, figure, site, and motion (and their various combinations), there can be no such entities as "Forms" and "Qualities" that are really distinct from the substance of the body. This makes it evident that *life*, *thought*, and *understanding* cannot be physical things, but must necessarily be the attributes of another kind of substance distinct from the body.

XLI. We have now clearly proved two things: First, that the *natural philosophy* <note>original: "Physiology"</note> of the ancients—before not only *Aristotle* and *Plato*, but also *Democritus* and *Leucippus*—was atomic or mechanical. Secondly, that as there is no inconsistency between atomic philosophy and theology—but indeed a natural connection—the ancient atomists before *Democritus* were neither atheists nor materialists <note>original: "Corporealists"</note>. Instead, they held the non-physical nature and immortality of souls, together with a God distinct from the physical world. 

Wherefore, the first and most ancient atomists did not make "atomic principles the source of all things" <note>original: "ἀτόμους ἀρχὰς τῶν ὅλων"</note>; they never endeavored to make up an entire philosophy out of atomic theory <note>original: "Atomology"</note>. To them, the doctrine of atoms was only one part or member of the whole philosophical system; they joined to it the doctrine of non-physical substance and theology to make the system complete. This is consistent with what *Aristotle* declared in his *Metaphysics*: that ancient philosophy consisted of these two parts, *natural philosophy* <note>original: "physiologia"</note> and *theology* or *the first philosophy* <note>original: "hē prōtē philosophia"</note> (metaphysics). 

Our ancient atomists never went about, as the blundering *Democritus* afterward did, to build up a world out of mere *passive bulk* and *sluggish matter* without any *active principles* <note>original: "archai drastēriai"</note> or *non-physical powers*. They understood well that, in such a system, they could not have so much as motion, mechanism, or generation. The origin of all the motion that exists in bodies springs from something that is not a body—that is, from non-physical substance. 

And yet, even if local motion could be supposed to have risen up or sprung into this dead lump and mass of matter (no one knows how, and without dependence upon any non-physical being) to have activated it by chance, these ancient atomists would still have thought it impossible for the physical world itself to be made as it is now by random mechanism, without the guidance of any higher principle. They would have concluded it was the greatest arrogance or madness for men to assert that animals also consisted of mere mechanism, or that life and sense, reason and understanding, were really nothing else but local motion—and consequently that they themselves were but machines and *automata*. 

Therefore, they joined both *active* and *passive principles* together: physical and non-physical nature, *mechanism* and *life*, atomic theory and the study of spirits <note>original: "Atomology and Pneumatology"</note>. From both of these united, they made up one entire system of philosophy,

# CHAPTER II. Mangled by Democritus.

...corresponding with and agreeable to the true and real world outside of them. And this system of philosophy, consisting of the *doctrine of incorporeal substance* (of which God is the head) together with *atomic* and *mechanical natural philosophy* <note>original: "Physiology"</note>, seems to have been the only genuine, perfect, and complete one.

---

XLII. But it did not remain this way for long; for, after a while, this entire body of philosophy was *mangled* and *dismembered*. Some took only one part of it, and some another. Some snatched away the *atomic natural philosophy* without *pneumatology* <note>The branch of philosophy or theology concerned with spirits or spiritual beings.</note> and *theology*; others, on the contrary, took the *theology* and *doctrine of incorporeals* without the *atomic* or *mechanical natural philosophy*. The former group included *Democritus*, *Leucippus*, and *Protagoras*, who took only the dead carcass or skeleton of the old *Moschical philosophy* <note>A historical theory that atomic physics originated with a Phoenician named Moschus, whom some scholars associated with the biblical Moses.</note>—namely, the *atomic natural philosophy*. The latter group included *Plato* and *Aristotle*, who indeed took the better part—the *soul*, *spirit*, and *quintessence* of it: the *theology* and *doctrine of incorporeals*. However, they left it *unbodied* and *stripped* of its most proper and convenient vehicle, the *atomic natural philosophy*, which exposed their systems to several inconveniences.

XLIII. We begin with *Leucippus* and *Democritus*. Being inclined toward atheism, they quickly perceived that they could not sufficiently protect themselves against the idea of a God, nor effectively promote atheism to others, through the ordinary way of studying nature. This was because *Heraclitus* and other philosophers—who, like themselves, held that all substance was physical—nevertheless asserted a *physical deity*. They maintained that the form of the entire physical world was God, or else that He was *matter in a certain state* <note>original: "ὕλη πῶς ἔχουσα"</note>, such as (for example) a *methodical* and *rational fire* that moved through the whole universe like a soul. According to them, the particular souls of men and animals were merely pieces cut and sliced out of the great World-Soul. Thus, according to those thinkers, the whole physical universe, or the mass of matter, was in one way or another a God—a most wise and understanding animal that formed every detail within itself in the best possible way and providently governed it. 

Therefore, these atheists recognized how unstable and uncertain their atheistic philosophy was at that time. They saw that those very *forms* and *qualities*, and the *self-moving* power of matter (which were commonly used as a sanctuary for atheism), might instead turn out to be a *hiding place* <note>original: "Latibulum"</note> and *refuge* <note>original: "Asylum"</note> for a deity. They feared that a *physical God* (no matter what they did) might lie lurking beneath those concepts, assaulting men's minds with doubts and anxieties. Furthermore, they understood that another kind of natural philosophy was being promoted which banished those *forms* and *qualities* from matter and attributed nothing to it but magnitude, shape, position, and motion, without any self-moving power. They immediately saw a great advantage for themselves and their cause in this. Therefore, they greedily embraced this *atomic* or *mechanical natural philosophy* and violently cut it off from that other part, the *doctrine of incorporeals*...

And now joining these two things together—the atomic natural philosophy, which assumes that there is nothing in a body but size <note>original: "Magnitude"</note>, shape <note>original: "Figure"</note>, position <note>original: "Site"</note>, and motion; and that prejudice or preoccupation of their own minds, that there was no other substance in the world besides body—between these two, they produced a certain mongrel and counterfeit <note>original: "Spurious"</note> philosophy: *atheistically-atomic*, or *atomically-atheistic*.

But though we have so well proved that *Leucippus* and *Democritus* were not the first inventors, but only the corrupters and adulterators of the atomic philosophy; yet if anyone nonetheless obstinately contends that its first invention ought to be attributed to them (the very principles of their atheism seeming to lead them naturally to this: to strip and divest the body of all those forms and qualities, it being otherwise impossible for them surely and safely to exclude a material <note>original: "Corporeal"</note> deity); yet, even so, as the wit of these atheists was much to be admired in managing and carrying out those principles in such a manner as to create such a complete system of philosophy out of them, where all the parts are coherent and consistent together; we shall only say this: That if those atheists were the first inventors of this philosophy, they were certainly very unhappy and unsuccessful in it. While trying to use it to protect themselves from the possibility and danger of a *material God*, they unawares laid a foundation for the clear demonstration of an *immaterial <note>original: "Incorporeal"</note> one*. And they were indeed so far from creating any such coherent framework as is claimed, that they were forced everywhere to contradict their own principles; so that nonsense lies at the bottom of all, and is interwoven throughout their whole atheistic system. And we ought to take notice of the invincible power and force of truth, prevailing irresistibly against all endeavors to oppress it; and how desperate the cause of atheism is, when that very atomic *hypothesis* of theirs, which they would erect and build up as a strong castle to garrison themselves in, proves to be a most effective engine against them, battering their entire atheistic structure down about their ears.

XLIV. *Plato's mutilation and alteration of the old Moschical philosophy <note>A historical theory that atomic physics originated with a Phoenician named Moschus, whom some scholars associated with the biblical Moses.</note> was much more excusable, as he took the theology and metaphysics of it—the entire doctrine of immaterial beings <note>original: "Incorporeals"</note>—and abandoned the atomic or mechanical way of studying nature <note>original: "Physiologizing"</note>.* In all probability, he did this partly because those aforementioned atheists had so greatly abused that philosophy, adopting it as if it were their own, that he began to feel a jealousy and suspicion of it; and partly because he was not naturally as inclined toward natural philosophy <note>original: "Physiology"</note> as toward theology—toward the study of physical things as toward divine things. Some think this is the reason why he did not pay attention to the *Pythagorean system* of the physical world until late in his old age. *His genius was such that he was naturally more attracted to ideas than to atoms, and to formal and final causes than to material*

<margin>Material Causes.</margin> To this may be added that the way of studying nature <note>original: "Physiologizing"</note> through matter, forms, and qualities is a more arrogant <note>original: "Huffie"</note> and imaginary thing than the other. Finally, the atomic study of nature is more remote from the senses and common understanding, and therefore not so easily understood. For this reason, many learned Greeks of later times—though they had read the works of *Epicurus*, and perhaps those of *Democritus* too—were still unable to conceive how physical and sensible phenomena <note>original: "Phænomena"</note> could possibly be explained <note>original: "salved"</note> without "real qualities." One instance of this can be found in *Plutarch*, writing against *Colotes* the *Epicurean*. Therefore *Plato*, who was a zealous defender of an immaterial <note>original: "Incorporeal"</note> Deity (distinct from the world) and of immortal souls, seriously studied nature only through matter, forms and qualities, generation, corruption, and alteration. He only played and toyed occasionally with atoms and mechanism, such as when he would compose the Earth out of cubical atoms and Fire out of pyramidal atoms, and the like. It is plain that he was imitating the atomic philosophy in those instances from these words of his: <note>original Greek: "πάντα οὖν δεῖ ταῦτα διανοεῖσθαι σμικρὰ οὕτως, ὡς καθ’ ἓν ἕκαστον οὐδὲν ὁρώμενον ὑφ’ ἡμῶν, συναθροισθέντων δὲ πολλῶν, τοὺς ὄγκους αὐτῶν ὁρᾶσθαι"</note> *All these cubical and pyramidal tiny particles <note>original: "Corpuscula"</note> of fire and earth are in themselves so small that, by reason of their smallness <note>original: "parvitude"</note>, none of them can be perceived singly and alone, but only when many of them are gathered together can their masses be seen.*

XLV. And *Aristotle* here trod in *Plato's* footsteps, not only in the better part—in asserting an immaterial Deity and an immovable first mover—but also in studying nature through forms and qualities, and rejecting that mechanical way of atoms which had been so generally received among the ancients. Therefore, although the intellectual character <note>original: "Genius"</note> of these two men was very different, and *Aristotle* often contradicted *Plato* and really disagreed with him in several specific details, yet I think it may be granted to those "reconcilers" (*Porphyry*, *Simplicius*, and others) that the main essentials of their two philosophies are the same.

Now, I say the whole Aristotelian system of philosophy is infinitely to be preferred over the whole Democritic system, even though the former has been so much disparaged and the other celebrated of late among us. For while it cannot be denied that the Democritic hypothesis explains <note>original: "salve"</note> physical phenomena much more elegantly and intelligibly, in all those other things which are of far the greatest importance, it is a madness rather than a philosophy. But the Aristotelian system is right and sound here regarding those greater things: it asserts immaterial substance, a Deity distinct from the world, the natural basis of morality, and the liberty of the will. Therefore, though a recent writer on politics <note>Likely a reference to Thomas Hobbes, who criticized Aristotle's ethics in "Leviathan."</note> so exceedingly disparages *Aristotle's* *Ethics*, we shall do *Aristotle* justice here by declaring that his *Ethics* were truly such and lived up to their title. But that new model of ethics which has been thrust upon the world with so much arrogance <note>original: "Fastuosity"</note>—and is indeed nothing but the old Democritic doctrine revived—is no ethics at all, but a mere cheat, the undermining...

and the subversion of all morality by substituting something like it in its place—a mere counterfeit and changeling <note>original: "Changeling"; in folklore, a fraudulent substitute for a child, here meaning a fake version of morality.</note>. The purpose of this could be nothing other than to corrupt the world.

We add further that *Aristotle’s* system of philosophy seems to be more consistent with piety than the Cartesian *hypothesis* <note>The "Cartesian hypothesis" refers to the philosophy of René Descartes (1596–1650), which explained the universe through mechanical laws and the motion of matter.</note> itself, even though the latter plainly assumes an incorporeal <note>original: "Incorporeal"; meaning non-physical or spiritual.</note> substance. This is because the Cartesian view suggests that God contributes nothing more to the construction of the world than the turning of a vortex or whirlpool of matter. From the accidental <note>original: "fortuitous"</note> motion of this matter, according to certain general laws of nature, the entire frame of things as we know it must arise—including the precise organization and successive generation of animals—without the guidance of any mind or wisdom. In contrast, *Aristotle’s* concept of Nature is not an accidental principle; rather, it does nothing in *vain*, but does everything for a *purpose*, and in every case pursues the *best*. Therefore, it can be nothing other than a subordinate instrument of divine wisdom, acting as its *manual craftsman* <note>original: "Manuary Opificer"</note> or the executor of its designs.

However, we cannot deny that *Aristotle* has been criticized <note>original: "taxed"</note> by various ancient writers—both Christians and others—for not explicitly asserting two things: the immortality of human souls and God's providence over men, as he should have done and as his master *Plato* did. Yet, to be as fair to him as possible, we shall observe here that in his *Nicomachean Ethics*, he speaks favorably of the latter: *If the gods take any care of human affairs, as it seems they do, then it is reasonable to think that they also delight in that which is best and nearest to themselves (which would be the mind or right reason), and that they reward those who most love and honor it (as those who care for the things most pleasing to the gods) by acting rightly and honestly.* <note>original Greek: "εἰ γάρ τις ἐπιμέλεια τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων ὑπὸ θεῶν γίνεται, ὥσπερ δοκεῖ, καὶ εὔλογον χαίρειν αὐτοὺς τῷ ἀρίστῳ καὶ τῷ συγγενεστάτῳ (τοῦτο γὰρ ἂν εἴη ὁ νοῦς) καὶ τοὺς ἀγαπῶντας μάλιστα καὶ τοὺς τιμᾶντας ἀντιποιεῖν, ὡς τῶν φίλων αὐτοῖς ἐπιμελομένους, ὀρθῶς τε καλῶς πράττοντας."</note> This is a very good sentiment, were it not introduced with too much skepticism. 

And as for the point of the soul’s immortality: it is true that while other philosophers before *Aristotle* asserted the preexistence, immateriality, and immortality of all souls—not only the rational soul but the sensitive one as well (which they concluded were one and the same substance in humans)—according to *Plato’s* view that *Every soul is immortal* <note>original Greek: "πᾶσα ψυχὴ ἀθάνατος"</note>, they decided that no life or thought could be physical. *Aristotle*, on the contrary, expressly denies the preexistence—that is, the separability, immateriality, and immortality—of all sensitive souls, not only in animals <note>original: "Brutes"</note> but everywhere. He gives his reason in these words: *It is clear from these facts that it is impossible for all souls to preexist; for those principles whose activity is physical cannot possibly exist without the body—just as the power of walking cannot exist without feet—and so it is impossible for them to enter from the outside. For they cannot enter by themselves, being inseparable from the body, nor can they enter inside a body.* <note>original Greek: "ὅτι μὲν οὐκ οἷόν τε πάσας προϋπάρχειν, φανερόν ἐστιν ἐκ τῶν τοιούτων, ὅσων γάρ ἐστιν ἀρχῶν η ἐνέργεια σωματική, δῆλον ὅτι ταύτας ἄνευ σώματος ἀδύνατον ὑπάρχειν, οἷον βαδίζειν ἄνευ ποδῶν· ὥστε καὶ θύραθεν εἰσιέναι ἀδύνατον. οὔτε γὰρ αὐτὰς καθ᾽ ἑαυτὰς εἰσιέναι οἷόν τε ἀχωρίστους οὔσας, οὔτ᾽ ἐν σώματι εἰσιέναι."</note>

<header>CHAPTER I. With an Impartial Censure. 55</header>

without feet. Therefore, it is impossible that these sensitive souls <note>original: "Sensitive Souls"; the part of the soul shared by humans and animals that governs sensation and movement.</note> (preexisting) should enter the body from the outside, since they can neither arrive by themselves—naked and stripped of all physical form, as they are inseparable from it—nor can they arrive within a body, namely, the seed. This is Aristotle’s argument for why all sensitive souls must be physical <note>original: "Corporeal"</note>: because there is no walking without feet, nor seeing without eyes. 

But at the same time, he declares that the mind or intellect does exist beforehand and enters from the outside—meaning it is non-physical, separable, and immortal. He gives his reason for it in this manner: "It remains that the mind or intellect, and that alone, enters from the outside and is uniquely divine; for no physical activity shares in its activity" <note>original Greek: λείπεται δὴ τὸν νοῦν μόνον θύραθεν ἐπεισιέναι, καὶ θεῖον εἶναι μόνον· οὐδὲ γὰρ αὐτοῦ τῇ ἐνεργείᾳ κοινωνεῖ σωματικὴ ἐνέργεια·</note>. That is, it acts independently upon the body. 

Notwithstanding this, Aristotle elsewhere distinguishes between two types of mind or intellect, making it twofold: the "Agent" and the "Patient" (or Passive). He concludes that only the former is immortal, but the latter is perishable: "The active intellect alone is immortal and eternal, but the passive is corruptible" <note>original Greek: τοῦτο μόνον ἀθάνατον καὶ ἀΐδιον, ὁ δὲ παθητικὸς νοῦς φθαρτὸς</note>. Here, some interpreters who wish to excuse Aristotle argue that by "passive intellect," he does not mean the receiving part of the mind, but only the imagination <note>original: "Phantasie"</note>. They argue this because Aristotle would otherwise contradict himself, having previously affirmed that the intellect is separable, unmixed, and non-organical <note>original: "Inorganical"; not requiring a physical organ to function.</note>, which they believe must refer to the "patient" or receiving mind. 

But this excuse can hardly be accepted here, where the passive intellect is directly opposed to the agent intellect. Now, what Aristotle’s "agent understanding" actually is—and whether it is something within us, such as a faculty of our human soul, or not—seems to be a very questionable matter, and has therefore caused much dispute among his interpreters. It is concluded by many of them to be the Divine Intellect, and commonly by others to be something external. Because of this, it must be left doubtful whether he acknowledged anything non-physical and immortal within us at all. This is especially true because, after establishing the principle that nothing is non-physical except what acts independently of the body, he elsewhere plainly determines that there is no thinking <note>original: "Intellection"</note> without physical mental images <note>original: "Corporeal Phantasms"</note>. 

That which led Aristotle to all of this—positively affirming the physical nature of sensitive souls and wavering so much concerning the non-physical nature of the rational soul—seems to have been his doctrine of "Forms and Qualities." Through this doctrine, physical and non-physical substances are confused together, so that the limits of each could not be discerned by him. Therefore, we cannot applaud Aristotle for this; but what we do commend him for are chiefly these four things: 

1. **First**, for making a perfect, non-physical intellect to be the head of all things.
2. **Secondly**, for concluding that Nature, as an instrument of this intellect, does not merely act according to the necessity of material motions, but for ends and purposes, though unknown to itself.
3. **Thirdly**, for maintaining that morality is natural.
4. **And lastly**, for asserting <term>Autexousie</term> <note>original Greek: τὸ ἐφ’ ἡμῖν; meaning "that which is in our power," or free will.</note>, or liberty from necessity.

<page-num>55</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER I. What an Impression of the Senses Is.</header>

...along with the rest. It is therefore sufficient that some (perceptible) forms <note>original: "species"; in Aristotelian philosophy, these are the 'forms' or images of things perceived by the senses.</note> enter into the soul, and that others come by themselves—naked and stripped of all physical form. Being unstable, fleeting, and vanishing with a motion that is [unclear], this is Aristotle's argument: why all sensitive souls <note>original: "Sensitive Souls"; the part of the soul responsible for sensation and movement, shared with animals.</note> must necessarily be physical <note>original: "Corporeal"</note>, because there is no walking without feet, nor seeing without eyes. 

But at the same time, he declares that the intellect or intellective soul does not result from these external things, but is non-physical <note>original: "Incorporeal"</note>, separate, and immortal. He gives his reason for this in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals* <note>original Latin: "de Animal."</note>, where he says: "it remains that the mind <note>original Greek: λείπεται δὲ τὸν νοῦν</note> alone enters from the outside <note>original Greek: θύραθεν ἐπεισιέναι</note>, and that it alone is divine." Its energy is not mixed with that of the body, but is impressed upon it. 

Notwithstanding this, he does elsewhere distinguish between two types of mind or intellect, making it twofold: "Active" <note>original Latin: "Agens"</note> and "Passive" <note>original Latin: "Patiens"</note>. He concludes that only the former is immortal, but the latter is perishable <note>original: "Corruptible"</note>. Thus, it is found that his active soul is alone immortal and eternal; but in practice, the reality is quite the opposite. Some commentators <note>original: "Interpreters"</note> who would willingly excuse Aristotle contend that by the "passive soul" he does not mean a substantial nature unique to the individual man. They do this lest Aristotle should otherwise contradict himself, as he had before affirmed the intellect to be inseparable, unmixed, and non-physical—which they believe must be understood as the "active" intellect, whereas the intellect itself is opposed to the "passive." 

Now, what Aristotle's true sentiments are, and whether it is possible to determine them from his writings or not, seems to be a very questionable matter that has sparked much dispute among his commentators. It is resolved by many of them to be one and the same individual intellect in all people; others see it as a passing thing which should be detached from time to time, whether or not he denied any pre-existence to the individual mind. 

Furthermore, because he lays down the principle that "nothing is in the soul that was not previously in the senses," he finds he cannot maintain that idea if there is no thinking <note>original: "Intellection"</note> without physical imagination <note>original: "Corporeal Phantasy"</note>. What seems to me most disadvantageous to Aristotle's opinion regarding the individual and immortal soul is his doctrine (and those who have been the teachers of "Forms and Qualities" <note>This refers to the Scholastic tradition of hylomorphism, which explains change in terms of matter and form.</note>), where physical and non-physical substances are confounded together in such a way that the limits of each cannot be discerned by him. 

While we cannot explain any set rule for this, what we chiefly commend him for is: 
1. That there is something superior in us, making a specific non-physical intellect the lord of all.
2. For proving that the soul, as an instrument of this intellect, does not merely act according to the speed <note>original: "Velocity"</note> of material motions, but for such ends and purposes as are unknown to itself. 
3. For maintaining the reality of morality and liberty.
4. And fourthly, for asserting that voluntary <note>original: "Arbitrary"; here meaning 'derived from the will' (Latin: arbitrium).</note> actions are the results of liberty or free will.
