## CHAPTER 2

This chapter contains all the alleged rational grounds for the *atheistic hypothesis*. 

1. That the *Democritean philosophy* <note>original: "Democritick Philosophy" - the school of thought following Democritus, who proposed that the world is made of atoms</note>, which is composed of these two principles—*corporealism* <note>the belief that only physical matter exists</note> and *atomism*—joined together, is *essentially atheistic*. 

2. Although *Epicurus*, who was an *atomic corporealist*, claimed to believe in a *democracy of gods*, he was nevertheless an *absolute atheist*. It is further argued that *atheists* commonly *equivocate* <note>use ambiguous language to hide the truth</note> and *disguise their true beliefs*. 

3. That the *Democritean philosophy* is nothing more than a *system of atheology* (the study of the non-existence of God), or *atheism swaggering under the glorious appearance of philosophy*. Although there is another form of *atheism* which we call *Stratonical* <note>original: "Stratonical" - referring to Strato of Lampsacus, who believed nature has a life of its own without a conscious God</note>, the *Democritean atheism* is the only one worth serious consideration; all its *dark mysteries* will be revealed here. 

4. Since we are dealing with the *Deity* and producing all that *profane* and *unholy material of atheists* in order to *refute* <note>original: "confutation"</note> it, we must pray for *divine assistance* and *direction*. 

5. There are *two things* to be performed here: first, to show the *atheists’* alleged *rational grounds* against the *Deity*; and second, how they try to either *reconcile* <note>original: "salve"</note> or *refute* the *evidence to the contrary* <note>original: "Phænomena"</note>. The *first* of those *grounds* is the claim that no one can have an *idea* or *conception of God*, and that He is an *incomprehensible nothing*. 

6. The *second atheistic argument* is that there can be no *creation* out of *nothing*, nor any *omnipotence*, because *nothing* can come from *nothing*. Therefore, whatever *substantially* exists has been *self-existent from eternity* and was *uncreated* by any *deity*. 

7. The *third alleged reason* against a *Deity* is that the *strictest definition of a God* implies Him to be *incorporeal* <note>not having a physical body</note>; therefore, there can be no such *incorporeal deity* because there is no other *substance but physical matter*. 

8. The *atheists’ claim* is that the *doctrine of incorporeal substances* arose from a *ridiculous mistake of treating abstract names* and *concepts as if they were real things*. They *impudently claim the deity* to be nothing but the *chief of ghosts* <note>original: "spectres"</note>, an *Oberon* <note>the King of the Fairies in medieval and Renaissance literature</note>, or a *prince of fairies* and *fantasies* <note>original: "phancies"</note>. Their *fourth argument* against a *Deity* is that to suppose an *incorporeal mind* to be the *origin of all things* is merely to make a simple *accident* <note>original: "accident" - in philosophy, a property that is not essential to the nature of a thing</note> and *abstract concept* into the *first cause of everything*. 

9. Their *fifth argument* is a *refutation of a physical deity* <note>original: "corporeal deity"</note> based on the *principles of corporealism itself*. They argue that since *matter* is the only *substance*, and all other *differences between things are nothing but accidents* (temporary properties) that are *created* <note>original: "generable"</note> and *destroyed* <note>original: "corruptible"</note>, no *living understanding*...

# The Democritical Philosophy Book I.

[...No] existing being can be essentially incapable of decay <note>original: "incorruptible"</note>. The God of the Stoics <note>The Stoics believed God was a physical, fiery soul of the world that was subject to the cycles of the universe</note> is only incorruptible by accident <note>original: "by accident" - meaning by chance or external circumstance rather than by its fundamental nature</note>.

10. Their sixth line of reasoning comes from a combination of *atomism* <note>the theory that all reality is made of tiny, indivisible particles</note>: that the first principle of all things in the universe consists of atoms or tiny bodies <note>original: "corpuscula"</note> devoid of all qualities, and consequently of sensation and understanding (which only arise later from a specific arrangement of those atoms). Therefore, Mind or a Deity was not the original source of all things.

11. In the seventh place, they argue against the idea that the world is alive <note>original: "animation"</note>, or that it is governed by a living, intelligent nature that gives life to the whole. They claim this because sensation and understanding are specific to flesh, blood, and brains, and reason is found nowhere except in human form.

12. The eighth atheistic ground is that while everyone considers God to be a most happy, eternal, and immortal living being <note>original: "animal"</note>, no such thing can exist. This is because all living beings are collections of atoms that were originally created; they are therefore subject to death and decay when their structure <note>original: "compages," meaning a complex framework</note> is dissolved. They argue that life is not a simple, fundamental nature, but an accidental variation <note>original: "diffification," likely a typo for "diversification" or "modification"</note> of complex bodies which vanishes into nothing when their parts are separated.

13. The ninth claimed atheistic proof is that by "God" is meant a first cause or mover that was not moved by anything else from the outside. However, they argue that nothing can move itself; therefore, there can be no "unmoved mover," nor any "first" in the chain of causes—which is to say, there is no God.

14. Their further proof of this principle—that nothing can move itself—leads to an atheistic logical conclusion <note>original: "corollary"</note>: that no thinking being could be a first cause, as no thought arises by itself without a prior cause. This may be counted as a tenth argument.

15. Another mystery of atheism: that all knowledge and mental concepts are merely the result of the objects themselves (which exist outside the knower) acting upon the mind <note>original: "a passion from them"</note>. Therefore, the physical world must exist before any knowledge or concept of it, and knowledge cannot be the cause of the world.

16. The twelfth argument: that things could not have been made by a God because they are so flawed and poorly made. They were not designed for the benefit of humanity, and the flood of evil that overflows everything shows they did not come from any deity.

17. The thirteenth instance used by atheists against a deity is based on the lack of divine providence <note>God's intervention or guidance in the world</note>. They claim that in human affairs, everything is "waste and void" <note>original Hebrew: "Tơhu and Bơhu," referring to the chaos before creation in Genesis 1:2</note>, chaos, and confusion.

18. The fourteenth atheistic ground: that it is impossible for any single being to perceive <note>original: "animadvert"</note> and manage everything in all the distant parts of the entire world at once. Even if it were possible, such an infinite burden of affairs <note>original: "negotioſity"</note> would be absolutely incompatible with happiness.

19. Several bold but trivial questions from atheists: Why was the world not made sooner? What was God doing before then? Why was it made at all, since it remained unmade for so long? And how could the "Architect of the World" build such a massive structure <note>original: "fabrick"</note>?

20. The atheists' claim that it is in the best interest of humanity for there to be no God. They argue it was a noble and heroic deed for the *Democriteans* <note>followers of Democritus</note> to drive that terrifying ghost <note>original: "spectre"</note> out of the world and to free people from the constant fear of a deity and of punishment after death, which poisons all the pleasures of life.

21. Another claim of theirs is that belief in God <note>original: "theism"</note> is incompatible with the absolute power of the state <note>original: "civil sovereignty"</note>,

By "matter," we mean that which is <term>impenetrably extended</term> <note>occupying space so that no other object can be in the same spot</note>. In <term>Plato’s language</term>, this is that which has <gloss>an impact or touch <note>original Greek: prosbolē ē epaphē</note></gloss>, meaning it pushes against other bodies and resists their force. # That Epicurus was an Atheist
## Book I.

things from *Senseless Matter*, whereas to assert a God is to maintain that all things sprung originally from a *Knowing* and *Understanding Nature*.

II. *Epicurus*, who was one of those "hybrid" thinkers mentioned before (an <term>Atomic-Corporealist</term> <note>Someone who believes everything consists of physical atoms</note> or <term>Corporeal-Atomist</term>), did nonetheless claim to believe in a diverse crowd and democracy of gods. He claimed that though they were human-shaped <note>original: "anthrōpomorphoi"</note>, they were so thin and subtle that, compared to our earthly bodies, they might be called *Incorporeal*. He claimed they possessed not so much flesh as a *quasi-flesh* <note>original: "quasi-carnem"</note>, and not so much blood as a *quasi-blood* <note>original: "quasi-sanguinem"</note>—a certain kind of *aerial* or *ethereal flesh and blood*. These gods of his were not supposed to exist anywhere within our world, under the pretense that there was no place in it fit to receive them:

->You also cannot believe that the holy seats<-
->Of the gods exist in any part of the world.<-
<note>original: "Illud item non est ut possis credere sedes Esse Deûm Sanctas, in Mundi partibus ullis."</note>

And therefore they must be imagined to live in certain *Intermundane Spaces* <note>The empty spaces between different universes</note> and *Utopian Regions* outside the world. The pleasantness of these regions is elegantly described by the poet <note>The Roman poet Lucretius</note>:

->Which neither the winds shake, nor the clouds sprinkle with rain,<-
->Nor does the white snow, hardened by sharp frost,<-
->Violate them with its fall; but a cloudless sky always<-
->Covers them, and they smile with widely diffused light.<-
<note>original: "Quas neque concutiunt Venti, neque Nubila nimbis Adspergunt, neque nix acri concreta pruinâ Cana cadens violat, sempérque innubilus Æther Integit, & largè diffuso lumine ridet."</note>

To this was added the idea that the chief happiness of these gods consisted in a freedom from all duties and business <note>original: "Omnium Vacatione Munerum"</note>—in doing nothing at all so that they might live a soft and delicate life. Finally, it was claimed that although they had nothing to do with us, nor we with them, we should still worship them for the sake of their own excellent nature and happy state.

But anyone with the least bit of insight could not help but perceive that this theology of *Epicurus* was merely fictional <note>original: "Romantical"</note>. It was directly contrary to his own stated principles to admit any being other than what was formed from atoms, and consequently subject to decay. He only proposed these gods for political reasons <note>original: "upon a Politick Account"</note>, to avoid public hatred <note>original: "Common Odium"</note> and those dangers and inconveniences he might have faced by a direct denial of a God. This strategy served his purposes well. Thus *Posidonius* <note>A Stoic philosopher</note> rightly declared: "It seemed to Posidonius that Epicurus believed in no gods; and that whatever he said about the immortal gods was said only to avoid hateful public resentment" <note>original: "Nullos esse Deos Epicuro videri; quæque is de Diis immortalibus dixerit, Invidiæ detestandæ gratiâ dixisse."</note>. 

However, he was also partly joking; it gave him no small amusement to delude and mock the gullible common people in this way. "Epicurus introduced gods for the sake of joking—transparent and breezy, dwelling between two worlds as if between two sacred groves, because he feared the collapse of things" <note>original: "Deos Jocandi causâ induxit Epicurus perlucidos & perflabiles, & habitantes tanquam inter duos Lucos, sic inter duos Mundos propter metum ruinarum."</note>. Nevertheless, even if *Epicurus* had been perfectly serious in all of this, we should still declare—with all due respect to the scholar *Gassendi* <note>Pierre Gassendi, a 17th-century priest who tried to reconcile Epicureanism with Christianity</note>—that he was not a jot the

<header>C H A P. II. An Absolute Atheist.</header>

...he was no less an **Atheist**, so long as he maintained that the whole world was made *without the ordering and direction of any Understanding Being that was perfectly happy and immortal* <note>original: "mēdenos diatattontos ē diataxantos tēn pasan makariotēta echontos meta aphtharsias"</note>. He derived the origin of all things in the **Universe**—even of the soul and mind—*from senseless atoms moved randomly and by chance* <note>original: "apo tōn atomōn sōmatōn apronnoēton kai tychaian echontōn tēn kinēsin"</note>. By doing this, he joined **Democritus** in making the world, in the worst sense, *an egg of the Night* <note>original: "ōon nyktos"; a reference to ancient creation myths where the world hatches from a primordial egg born of chaos</note>. That is to say, the world is not the offspring of Mind and Understanding, but of dark **Senseless Matter**, of **Tohu** and **Bohu** <note>Hebrew for "formless and empty," referring to the chaos before creation in Genesis 1:2</note>, or a **Confused Chaos**. He derived the origin of all the perfections in the universe from the most imperfect being and the lowest of all entities, which is the height of **Atheism**. 

As for those **shadowy, romantic gods** <note>original: "Romantick Monogrammous Gods"; "monogrammous" here suggests they are mere outlines or sketches of beings rather than real entities</note> of **Epicurus**, even if he had seriously believed in them, they could have been nothing more than a kind of **aerial** and **ghostly men**, living by themselves in some unknown place outside the world. As it was said: *Epicurus, according to common opinion, leaves a God, but according to the nature of things, leaves none at all* <note>original: "Epikouros men pros tous pollous apoleipei theon hōs de pros tēn physin pragmatōn oudamōs"</note>.

And just like **Epicurus**, other **Atheists** have commonly used **masks** and **disguises**; **Atheism** for the most part prudently chooses to walk abroad in **masquerade**. Although some overly gullible people have been so deceived by this that they concluded there was hardly such a thing as an **Atheist** anywhere in the world, those who are **discerning** can easily see through these thin **veils** and **disguises**. They can perceive these **Atheists** often hinting at their **Atheism** even when they most loudly profess themselves to be **Theists**. They do this by claiming it is impossible to have any **idea** or **conception** of God at all, and that since he is not **Finite**, he cannot be **Infinite**. They claim that no knowledge or understanding can be attributed to him—which is effectively the same as saying he does not exist. But whoever accepts the **Democritic principles**—that is, whoever rejects the **forms** and **qualities of bodies** and claims that everything is merely physical matter—is not to be believed, even if he pretends to hold a belief in a **Physical Deity**. Such a belief is plainly contradictory to those principles.

### III.
Therefore, this **hybrid philosophy**, founded by **Leucippus**, **Democritus**, and **Protagoras**, and later adopted by **Epicurus**, was really nothing more than a philosophical form of **Atheology**. It was a giant-like and Titanic attempt to dethrone the **Deity**. It made *senseless atoms the first principles of all things* <note>original: "archas tōn holōn atomous"</note>, as **Laertius** <note>Diogenes Laertius, a biographer of Greek philosophers</note> writes. This applies not only to all physical bodies (which was a point already accepted by **Empedocles** and other **Atomists** who were **Theists**) but also to **everything whatsoever** in the entire universe, including the soul and the mind. This philosophy sought to dethrone God not only by explaining all the **phenomena** of the world without a **God**, but also by establishing principles from which it must follow that there could be neither a **spiritual** nor even a **physical deity**. It was **Atheism** openly boasting under the glorious appearance of wisdom and philosophy.

# The Mysteries of Atheism Revealed: BOOK 1

There is indeed another form of atheism which—insisting on the common way of philosophizing by forms and qualities—we shall call **Stratonical** <note>named after Strato of Lampsacus, a Greek philosopher who proposed a godless, naturalistic universe</note> for the sake of distinction. These thinkers are too modest to claim that everything comes from the random motion of atoms. Instead, they attribute to the various parts of matter a certain kind of **natural perception** (though not animal-like awareness). This perception is devoid of **reflexive consciousness**, but includes a **plastic power** <term>a formative or creative force that shapes matter from within</term>. Through this power, they believe matter is able to **form** and **frame** itself skillfully and methodically to its own best advantage. This is similar to **Aristotle's** concept of Nature, except that it does not depend at all on any higher Mind or Deity. 

These atheists may also be called **Hylozoic** <term>from the Greek words for "matter" (*hyle*) and "life" (*zoe*); the belief that all matter is inherently alive</term>, just as the others are called **Atomic**. This is because they derive everything in the whole universe—not only sensitive souls but also rational ones, along with the complex bodies of animals—from the **life of matter**. However, this kind of atheism seems to be merely the unformed embryo of some dark and cloudy brains. It has never been developed into a complete system, nor has it been presented in such a clear form that it could be shown openly to the world. But **Democritic** and **Atomic atheism** is the boldest and most extreme of all. It not only attempts to explain all **phenomena** <note>original: "Phænomena"; observable events or facts</note> through matter moving by chance without a God, but also tries to prove that there cannot even be a **physical deity**. Because it claims to be a complete and coherent system, it is the only one that has publicly appeared on the world stage, and therefore it is the only one that truly deserves our consideration.

And now we shall provide a full view of this philosophy and uncover all its **dark mysteries** and **depths**. We are firmly persuaded that a plain and honest representation of these ideas will be a major part of their own refutation. At the very least, we do not doubt it will be shown that although this monster—swollen with a puffed-up show of wisdom—struts and stalks so gigantically with a stately philosophical grandeur, it is actually just like the giant **Orgoglio** <note>A character in Edmund Spenser’s *The Faerie Queene* who represents pride; when defeated, he is revealed to be nothing but an empty bladder filled with air</note> in the works of our English poet. It is a mere **empty bladder** blown up with vain conceit, an **Empusa** <note>original: "Empusa"; a shape-shifting phantom or specter from Greek mythology</note>, a **phantasm**, or a **spectre**—the offspring of night, darkness, nonsense, and contradiction.

Yet, despite this, we will not misrepresent it in the slightest. We will give it every possible advantage of strength and plausibility so that atheists have no reason to claim (as they usually do) that we did not understand their mysteries, failed to grasp the strength of their cause, or purposefully smothered and concealed it. Indeed, we have gone so far that we must confess we were willing to make their arguments look like something significant enough to deserve a refutation. Whether the atheists should thank us for improving their arguments rather than complaining that we have weakened them, we leave to the judgment of impartial readers.

# CHAPTER 2: First, That There Is No Idea of God.

IV. Plato tells us that even among the pagans of his time, there was generally such a religious spirit that "all those who possess even a small share of sobriety, in every undertaking, both small and great, always call upon a god for help." <note>original: πάντες ὅσοι κατὰ βραχὺ σωφροσύνης μετέχουσι, ἐπὶ πάσῃ ὁρμῇ καὶ σμικροῦ καὶ μεγάλου πράγματος, θεὸν ἀεί που ἐπικαλοῦσι</note> Plato adds, moreover, that he himself would be very at fault if in his *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s famous dialogue concerning the nature of the physical world and the cosmos</note>, when he was to treat such a grand topic as the whole world—"whether it was created or is uncreated" <note>original: εἰ γέγονεν ἢ καὶ ἀγενές ἐστι</note>—he did not begin by religiously invoking the Deity. Therefore, it would certainly be nothing less than an act of impiety for a Christian—who is about to treat the subject of the Deity itself and bring out all the profane and unholy material of the atheists from their dark corners to refute them and better confirm our faith in the truth of God’s existence—not to implore His direction and assistance. ## Chapter II. Nothing out of Nothing.

If any substance or real entity should be created out of nothing, it would be contradictory to that unquestionable axiom of reason: *From nothing, nothing comes* <note>original: "De Nihilo Nihil"</note>. The argument is presented this way by the poet *Lucretius*, following the thoughts of *Epicurus* and *Democritus*:

->Our starting point for this inquiry shall be this:<-
->that nothing is ever produced from nothing by divine power.<-
->For truly, fear holds all mortals in check in this way;<-
->because they see many things happen on earth and in the sky,<-
->the causes of which works they can perceive by no reasoning;<-
->and they believe them to be done by divine power.<-
->For which reason, once we see that nothing can be created<-
->from nothing, then we will more safely perceive our goal:<-
->both the source from which each thing can be created,<-
->and in what way all works are done without the help of the gods.<-
<note>original Latin: "Principium hinc cujus nobis Exordia sumet... Et quo quæque modo fiant opera sine Divûm." Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura*, Book 1.</note>

It is true indeed that this seems to be chiefly aimed by the poet against that third and last sort of theists mentioned before—such as *Heraclitus* and the **Stoics** (the latter being contemporaries of *Epicurus*). They held that the matter of the whole world was self-existent and uncreated from eternity, yet believed that the "forms" of worldly things in their successive generations (as entities distinct from matter) were created or made by the **Deity** out of nothing. 

But the force of the argument must necessarily be even stronger against those other theists who believe that the very substance and matter of the world itself, as well as its forms, were created by the **Deity** out of nothing. Since nothing can come out of nothing, it follows that not even the forms and qualities of bodies (conceived as entities really distinct from matter), much less the lives and souls of animals, could ever have been created by any deity. Therefore, certainly, the substance and matter itself could not have been created either. Instead, all substance and real entity—whatever exists in the world—must have existed from eternity, uncreated and self-existent. 

Nothing can be made or produced except for the different modifications of pre-existent matter. This is achieved through motions, mixtures and separations, and the clustering and dispersing <note>original: "Concretions and Secretions"</note> of atoms, without the creation of any real, distinct entity out of nothing. Thus, there is no need for a deity to bring this about, according to the saying of *Epicurus*: "The divine nature should not be brought into these matters at all" <note>original Greek: "ἡ θεία φύσις πρὸς ταῦτα μηδαμῆ προσαγέσθω"</note>, *for the purpose of explaining these phenomena*. To conclude, therefore: if no substance or real entity can be made which did not exist before—but if all that is, will be, and can be was self-existent from eternity—then creative power (and especially the attribute of omnipotence) can belong to nothing. This is the same as saying there can be no **Deity**.

VII. Thirdly, the atheists argue against the stricter and higher sort of theists—those who claim that God is the creator of the whole physical universe and all its parts out of nothing—in this manner: that which created the whole mass of matter and body cannot itself be a body. Therefore, this notion of God plainly implies...

# The Atheists' Pretences against BOOK I.

[They believe] Him to be incorporeal <term>Incorporeal: lacking a physical body or material substance; purely spiritual.</term>. But there can be no incorporeal Deity, because by that word must necessarily be understood either that which has no magnitude or extension <term>Extension: the property of taking up space or having physical dimensions.</term> at all, or else that which is indeed extended, but in a way other than a body. If the word is taken in the former sense, then nothing at all can be so incorporeal as to be altogether unextended and devoid of geometrical quantity, because extension is the very essence of all existing *entity* <note>original: "Entity"</note>, and that which is altogether unextended is perfectly nothing. There can be neither any substance, nor any mode or accident of any substance—no nature whatsoever—that is unextended. But if the word incorporeal is taken in the latter sense, for that which is indeed extended but otherwise than a body—namely, in a way that it penetrates bodies and coexists with them—this is also a thing next to nothing, since it can neither act upon any other thing, nor be acted upon by, or sensible of, anything; it can neither do nor suffer anything.

->For nothing but a body can act or be acted upon.<-
<note>original Latin: "Nam facere & fungi nisi Corpus nulla potest res." — Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura*.</note>

Therefore, to speak plainly, this can be nothing else but empty space, or *vacuum* <term>Vacuum: a space entirely devoid of matter.</term>, which runs through all things without laying hold of anything or being affected by anything. This is the only *incorporeal thing* that is or can be in nature: space or place. Therefore, to suppose an *incorporeal Deity* is to make empty space the creator of all things.

->This argument is thus proposed by the Epicurean poet <note>The "Epicurean poet" is Lucretius (c. 99–55 BC), whose poem *On the Nature of Things* is the primary source for Epicurean philosophy.</note>.<-

->Whatever exists must itself be something<-
->with a size, whether large or small.<-
->If it can be touched, however lightly or slightly,<-
->it will increase the number of bodies and join their sum.<-
->But if it is intangible, so that in no part<-
->can it prevent anything from passing through it,<-
->this surely is what we call the vacuum, or the void.<-
<note>original Latin: "Quodcunque erit esse aliquid debebit id ipsum / Augmine vel grandi vel parvo... Scilicet hoc id erit Vacuum quod Inane vocamus."</note>

*Whatever is, is extended or has geometrical quantity and measurability in it. If it is tangible, then it is a body and fills up a place in the world, being part of the whole mass; but if it is intangible, so that it cannot resist the passage of anything through it, then it is nothing else but empty space or vacuum.* There is no third thing besides these two, and therefore whatever is not a body is empty space or nothing.

->Beside the void and bodies, no third nature<-
->can be left in the list of things to be found by itself.<-
<note>original Latin: "Præter Inane & Corpora Tertia per se, Nulla potest rerum in numero Natura relinqui."</note>

Thus the ancient Epicureans and Democritics <note>Followers of Democritus, the ancient Greek philosopher who formulated an atomic theory of the universe.</note> argued: since there is nothing incorporeal but space, there can be no incorporeal Deity.

# CHAPTER II. An Incorporeal Deity.

...beyond our conception. From this, it follows that space must necessarily be either a substance itself, or else a property <note>original: "Mode"</note> of some incorporeal substance. The *modern followers of Democritus* <note>Democriticks: followers of Democritus, ancient Greek proponents of atomism and materialism.</note> are more cautious here; they claim that space is not a nature that actually exists outside of us, but is only the mental image <note>original: "Phantasm"</note> of a body—essentially its *ghost*—which has no reality outside of our imagination. Therefore, they argue there are not two distinct natures, Body and Space (which would imply two distinct substances, one of which would have to be incorporeal), but only one nature: Body. The consequence of this view is that an "incorporeal substance" is the same thing as an *incorporeal body*, and therefore nothing at all.

VIII. But because it is generally believed that an error cannot be sufficiently disproven without discovering the *source of the lie* <note>original Greek: "τὸ αἴτιον τοῦ ψεύδους" (to aition tou pseudous)</note>, or the *cause of the mistake*, the *atheists* will next attempt to show the *origin* of this *doctrine of incorporeal substances*. They will explain the misunderstanding from which it grew and take the opportunity to further disprove the existence of a *Deity*.

They argue that the *origin* of this *doctrine of incorporeal substances* proceeded chiefly from the *abuse of abstract names*. This applies to the names of substances (whereby the essences of individual bodies, such as a man or a horse, are separated from those bodies and considered as universal concepts) and also to the names of *accidents* <term>Accidents: properties or qualities of a thing, such as color or heat, that cannot exist without a physical substance to inhabit.</term> when they are considered alone without their subjects or substances. Men have been forced to use these names for the purpose of calculation or the reckoning of the properties of bodies—comparing them with one another, or adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing them. This could not be done as long as those properties are taken concretely along with the objects they belong to. Yet, while there is some use for those *abstract names*, the *abuse* of them has also been very great. Although they are really the *names of nothing*—since the "essence" of a specific man is not anything without the man himself, nor is an "accident" anything without its substance—men have been led by them into a gross mistake: imagining them to be realities existing by themselves. 

This delusion has chiefly proceeded from the *Scholastic philosophers* <note>Scholasticks: medieval university scholars who developed highly complex systems of logic and theology.</note>, who have been so excessive in their use of these words that they could not conduct a rational discourse about anything, no matter how small, without stuffing it with their *quiddities, entities, essences, haecceities* <term>Quiddities and Haecceities: technical terms for "what-ness" and "this-ness"—the philosophical essence of a thing.</term>, and the like. Therefore, these are the ones who, being first deluded themselves, have also deluded the rest of the world. They introduced the opinion into the minds of men that the essence of everything is something outside of the thing itself, and also eternal. According to this view, when anything is made or born, no new being is produced; rather, a pre-existing and eternal essence is simply clothed (as it were) with a new garment of existence. They also argued that the mere accidents of bodies may exist alone by themselves without their substances. For example, they claimed that the *life, sense*, and *understanding* of animals (commonly called by the names of *soul* and *mind*) may exist without the physical bodies or substances after the animals are dead. This view plainly turns them into incorporeal substances, functioning as *separate*

# BOOK I. Atheists dispute against...

...separate and abstract *essences* of *men*. This has been observed by a modern writer <note>The "modern writer" is Thomas Hobbes, whose materialist philosophy is being summarized here.</note> in these words:

> "There is a great use and a great abuse of abstract names, both in everyday life and in philosophy. The abuse consists in this: because some people see that the increases and decreases of *accidents* <term>original: "Accidents"; in philosophy, these are non-essential properties of a thing, like its color or speed, as opposed to its substance</term>—that is, things that can be factored into reasoning—can be considered without considering the bodies or subjects themselves (which is called 'abstracting'), they speak of accidents as if they could be separated from all bodies. It is from this that the gross errors of certain metaphysicians originate. For from the fact that *thought* <note>original: "Cogitatio"</note> can be considered without the consideration of the body, they are prone to conclude that it is not the action of a thinking body, but a substance in its own right." <note>original Latin: "Est Hominum Abstractorum tum in omni Vita, tum in Philosophia, magnus & Usus & Abusus. Abusus in eo consistit, quòd cùm videant aliqui, Considerari posse, id est, inferri in Rationes, Accidentium Incrementa & Decrementa, sine Consideratione Corporum, sive Subjectorum suorum, (id quod appellatur Abstrahere) loquuntur de Accidentibus, tanquam possent ab omni Corpore Separari: Hinc enim Originem trahunt quorundam Metaphysicorum crassi Errores. Nam ex eo, quod Considerari potest Cogitatio, sine consideratione Corporis, inferre solent non esse Opus Corporis Cogitantis."</note>

It is a great abuse that some metaphysicians make of these *abstract names*; because *thought* <note>original: "Cogitation"</note> can be considered alone without the consideration of the *body*, they conclude that it is not the *action* or *accident* of that *body* that thinks, but a *substance* by itself. And the same writer observes elsewhere that it is on this ground that when a man is dead and buried, people say his *soul* (that is, his *life*) can walk, separated from his body, and is seen by night among the graves. By this means, the common people are confirmed in their superstitious belief in ghosts, spirits, demons, devils, fairies, and hobgoblins—invisible powers and agents called by several names—and this is done by those persons whose work it ought to be to free men from such superstition.

This belief originally had another source, not entirely unlike the first: namely, from men mistaking their own *fancies* <note>original: "Phancies"; here meaning mental images or imagination</note> for *things really existing outside of themselves*. For just as in the sense of *vision*, men are commonly deceived into supposing the image behind a mirror to be a real thing existing outside themselves, whereas it is indeed nothing but their own mental image; in the same way, when the minds of men are strongly possessed with fear, especially in the dark, they raise up *mental images* <note>original: "Phantasms"</note> of *specters*, *boogeymen* <note>original: "Bug-bears"</note>, or *frightening apparitions*. They think these are objects really existing outside of them and call them ghosts and spirits, while they are actually nothing but their own imagination. 

Thus, the mental image of a *Deity* (which is indeed the chief of all *specters*) created by fear, has for no other reason been taken for a reality. To this purpose, a modern writer says: 

> "From the fear that proceeds from ignorance of what it is that has the power to do men good or harm, men are inclined to suppose and invent for themselves several kinds of invisible powers. They stand in awe of their own imaginations; in times of distress, they invoke them, and in times of expected success, they give them thanks, making the creatures of their own fancies their gods." 

Though this is prudently spoken in the plural number (so that the criticism might be redirected toward the pagan gods), anyone would be simple not to perceive that the reasoning is the same concerning that one *Deity* who is now commonly worshipped. Therefore, this too is but the creature of men’s fear and fancy—the chief of all *imaginary ghosts and specters*—functioning, as it were, like an *Oberon* or *Prince of Fairies and Fancies*. This, we say, was the first origin of that common belief in *invisible powers*, *ghosts*, and *gods*: men taking their own imaginations for things really existing outside of them. And as for the matter and substance of these ghosts, they could not, by their own natural thought, conceive of it as anything other than

# CHAP. II. Incorporeal and Corporeal Deity.

...with that which appears in a dream to one who sleeps, or in a looking-glass to one who is awake: *thin aerial bodies* which may appear and vanish when they please. But the opinion that such spirits were incorporeal and immaterial could never enter into the minds of men by nature, unless they were corrupted by doctrine. Instead, it sprang up from those deceiving and deceived *scholars*, *scholastics*, *philosophers*, and *theologians* who enchant men's understandings. They make them believe that the abstract notions of *accidents* <term>original: "Accidents"; in philosophy, these are non-essential properties of a thing, like its color or temperature, as opposed to its core substance</term> and *essences* could exist alone by themselves, without the bodies, as certain separate and incorporeal substances.

To conclude, therefore: to claim that an incorporeal mind is the cause of all things is to make our own fancy—an imaginary ghost of the world—into a reality. It is to suppose that the mere *abstract notion* of an *accident* and a *separate essence* is not only an absolute thing by itself and a real, incorporeal *substance*, but also the first origin of all substances and of everything in the universe. This may be reckoned as a fourth atheistic argument.

IX. Fifthly, the atheists further pretend to prove that there is no other substance in the world besides body. They also use the principles of corporealism <note>the belief that only physical matter exists</note> itself to show that there can be no corporeal deity, in this manner: No one can devise any other notion of substance than that it is something extended, existing outside the mind—not imaginary, but a real and solid magnitude. For whatever is not extended is nowhere and is nothing. So, *extended substance* <note>original Latin: "Res Extensa"</note> is the only substance, the solid *basis* and *foundation* of all things. Now, this is the exact same thing as "body." For *resistance* <note>original Greek: "ἀντιτυπία" (antitypia); the quality of matter that prevents two objects from occupying the same space at the same time</note> seems to be a necessary consequence and result of extension. Those who think otherwise can show no reason why bodies might not also penetrate one another, as some materialists think they do. From this, it is inferred that body or matter is the only substance of all things. And everything else in the world—that is, all the differences between bodies—is nothing but various accidents and modifications of this extended substance, body, or matter. 

Though these accidents may sometimes be called by the names of "real qualities" and "forms," and though philosophers have different views on them, they generally agree on these two properties: First, that none of them can exist alone by themselves without extended substance or matter as the *basis* and support for them. Second, that they may all be destroyed without destroying any substance. Now, just as blackness and whiteness, or heat and cold, so too are life, sense, and understanding. They are such accidents, modifications, or qualities of body that can neither exist by themselves and can be destroyed without the destruction of any substance or matter. For if the parts of the body of any living animal are disunited and separated from one another, or if the organic arrangement of the matter is altered, those accidents, forms, or qualities of life and understanding will immediately vanish into nothing, while all the substance of the matter still remains somewhere or <meta>other</meta>

### Atheists contend that the First Principle is Matter. Book I.

...any other in the entire universe, and nothing of it is lost. Therefore, the substance of <term>matter</term> and body, as distinguished from its <term>accidents</term> <note>original: "Accidents"; in philosophy, these are non-essential properties of a thing, like its color, as opposed to its core substance</note>, is the only thing in the world that is incorruptible and indestructible. This is how we should understand the phrase "nothing can be made out of nothing, or destroyed to nothing"—namely, that every complete thing that is made or generated must be made of some pre-existing <term>matter</term>. This <term>matter</term> has existed from eternity, is self-existent and uncreated, and is also indestructible; it can never be reduced to nothing. 

This principle does not apply to the <term>accidents</term> themselves, which can all be made and destroyed, generated and corrupted. Everything in the world is merely <term>matter in a certain state</term> <note>original: "hyle pos echousa" (Greek: ὕλη πῶς ἔχουσα)</note>; it is <term>matter</term> modified or qualified in various ways. All these modifications and qualities of <term>matter</term> are, by their own nature, destructible. Only the <term>matter</term> itself—acting as their foundation and not necessarily fixed to one specific <term>accident</term>—is <term>uncreated and imperishable</term> <note>original: "ageneton kai anolethron" (Greek: ἀγένητον καὶ ἀνώλεθρον)</note>, the only necessarily existing thing. The conclusion, therefore, is that no <term>animal</term>—no living, understanding body—can be absolutely and essentially incorruptible. Incorruptibility is a property unique to <term>matter</term> that cannot be shared with anything else. Consequently, there can be no *physical deity* who is the origin of all things and essentially indestructible.

Although the *Stoics* <note>an ancient Greek school of philosophy that believed God was a physical force within the universe</note> imagined the entire physical universe to be an *animal* or *deity*, this *physical God* of theirs was only incidentally incorruptible and immortal. This was because they assumed there was no other matter existing outside this world that could invade it, pull its parts apart, or disrupt its structure <note>original: "compages"; a framework or system</note>. If such external matter did exist, the life and understanding of this *Stoic God* (this great *world-animal*), would necessarily vanish into nothing, just as happens to other animals in similar cases. Thus, from the principles of *materialism* <note>original: "Corporealism"</note> itself, it plainly follows that there can be no *physical deity*. A *deity* is supposed to be <term>uncreated and imperishable</term> <note>original: "ageneton kai anolethron"</note>—something never made and essentially indestructible—and these are properties belonging to nothing but *mindless matter*.

X. Next, the *atheists* attempt to more effectively disprove the *physical God* of the *Stoics* and others by using the principles of *atomic philosophy* in the following manner. All *physical theists* who claim that a mind or understanding nature living within the matter of the whole universe was the original creator of the world-system—and that it intellectually designed it—show a great deal of ignorance regarding philosophy and the nature of physical bodies. They mistakenly assume that "real qualities" (besides *size*, *shape*, *position*, and *motion*) exist as simple and basic properties of matter. They also assume there was a quality or faculty of understanding within the matter of the whole universe, existing eternally alongside it, which was a basic thing, not made of or derived from anything else. However, to imagine such original qualities and powers—which are truly distinct from the substance of extended matter and its various states of *divisibility*, *shape*, *position*, and *motion*—is actually to imagine many distinct substances. Therefore, these qualities would necessarily have to be *incorporeal* <note>not made of physical matter; spiritual</note>.

...physical. Consequently, these philosophers unknowingly fall into the very position they find so repulsive. For if this quality or faculty of understanding exists within the matter of the universe as something original and not derived from anything else, it can really be nothing other than an **incorporeal substance** <note>original: "Incorporeal Substance"; something that exists but has no physical body</note>. **Epicurus** suggested a caution against this common mistake regarding qualities, stating to this effect: “Qualities are not to be thought of as if they were certain natures or substances existing by themselves, since that cannot be grasped by the mind; instead, they should be considered only as various states or ways of the body being.” <note>original: "Non sic cogitandæ sunt Qualitates, quasi sint quædam per se existentes Naturæ seu Substantiæ, siquidem id mente assequi non licet ; sed solummodo ut varii modi sese habendi Corporis, considerandæ sunt."</note>

Body, by its very nature, possesses nothing except what is included in the idea of <term>extended substance</term> <note>matter that takes up space</note>: divisibility, shape, position, motion or rest, and the results from their various combinations, which cause different perceptions. Therefore, just as conventional philosophers make their "prime matter" (though they cannot clearly explain what they mean by it) devoid of all quality because it receives all qualities, we conclude that **atoms** (which are really the first principles of all things) have none of those qualities in them that belong to compounded bodies. Atoms are not, in and of themselves, black or white, hot or cold, moist or dry, bitter or sweet. All these things arise afterward from the various gatherings and textures of atoms, combined with different motions. **Lucretius** confirms this by the following reason, which is consistent with the nature of <term>atomical philosophy</term>: if there were any such real qualities in the first principles, then in the various decays of nature, all things would eventually be reduced to nothing.

> For it is necessary that something immutable remains,

> Lest all things completely return to nothing for you.

# That Senseless Atoms begot Soul and Mind. BOOK I.

> "And they are carried along, void of sound and lacking in moisture, nor do they emit any scent from their own body." <note>original: *Et sonitu sterila, & Succo jejuna feruntur, Nec jaciunt ullum proprio de corpore Odorem.* This describes the properties of atoms as being devoid of sensory qualities.</note>

Lastly, he tells us in a similar way that the same should be understood regarding life, sense, and understanding: that there are no such simple qualities or natures in the first principles <note>the basic building blocks, or atoms</note> out of which animals are composed, but that these principles are themselves altogether devoid of life, sense, and understanding.

> "Now you must admit that all things we see that have sensation are nevertheless made of senseless principles; nor do manifest facts refute this, but rather they lead us by the hand and compel us to believe that, as I say, animals are born from senseless things. Indeed, one may see living worms emerge from foul dung, when the moist earth has become rotten from untimely rains." <note>original Latin: *Nunc ea, quæ Sentire videmus...* This is a famous passage from the Roman poet Lucretius, arguing for spontaneous generation from soulless matter.</note>

*All sensitive and rational animals are made of irrational and senseless principles. This is proved by experience, in that we see worms are created out of putrified dung, moistened by excessive showers.*

Some indeed, who are no greater friends to a deity than ourselves, insist that the sense and understanding found in animals and men are derived from a prior life and understanding within matter itself. But this cannot be. If matter, as such, had life and understanding in it, then every atom of matter would necessarily be a distinct perceiving, animal, and intelligent person by itself. It would be impossible for any such men and animals as now exist to be composed of them, because every man would be a *heap of various little animals* <note>original: *Variorum Animalculorum Acervus*</note>, a collection of innumerable perceiving beings.

Therefore, just like all the other qualities of bodies, life, sense, and understanding arise from the different arrangements <note>original: "contextures"</note> of atoms that are themselves devoid of all those qualities. They come from the composition of those simple elements of *magnitudes, shapes, positions,* and *motions*, in the same way that from a few letters variously combined, an infinite variety of syllables and words is made:

> "Furthermore, it matters in our very verses with which other letters they are contained and in what position; for the same letters signify sky, sea, lands, rivers, sun; and the same signify crops, trees, and living creatures. So too in things themselves, when the gaps, paths, connections, weights, blows, collisions, motions, order, position, and shapes of matter are changed, the things themselves must also change." <note>original Latin: *Quin etiam refert nostris in versibus ipsis...* also from Lucretius.</note>

# CHAPTER II. Atheists oppose the World's Animation.

But to think that there was any *Animal-like* Nature before all these *Animals*, or that there was an antecedent Mind and Understanding, Counsel and Wisdom, by which all Animals themselves, together with the whole World, were made and contrived, is either to run round in a senseless circle—making Animals and Animality to be before one another infinitely—or else to suppose an impossible beginning of an original understanding quality within Matter. The essence of this whole argument is briefly this: The first principle of all things in the whole Universe is Matter, or Atoms devoid of all qualities, and consequently of all Life, Sensation, and Understanding. Therefore, the origin of things is no Understanding Nature, or Deity.

# Atheists Reject the Idea of a Living World. Book I.

[The Atheist argues that a mind] might rule, govern, and sway the whole universe understandingly, and in a more perfect manner than our souls do our bodies; and so long as it continues, it would exercise a sovereignty and dominion over it. Although this does not amount to the full concept of a God according to the strict sense of Theists, yet it approaches very near to it and risks bringing in all the same inconveniences <note>The "inconveniences" refer to the idea of being subject to a higher power or divine judgment.</note> along with it. Therefore, they will now prove that there is no such soul or mind as this (resulting from the arrangement of atoms) that presides over the corporeal universe, so that there may not be even a shadow of a deity left.

It was observed before that life, sense, reason, and understanding are merely qualities of solid bodies—like the qualities of heat and cold—arising from certain particular arrangements of atoms. Now, just as those first principles of bodies (namely, single atoms) have none of those qualities in them, neither does the whole universe have any qualities that it can be defined by, except for its individual parts. The whole world is neither black nor white, hot nor cold, transparent nor opaque, because it contains all those qualities within its various parts. In the same way, the whole has no life, sense, nor understanding in it, but only those parts of it which are called animals. That is, life and sense are qualities that arise only from such an arrangement of atoms as produces soft flesh, blood, and brains in bodies organized with a head, heart, bowels, nerves, muscles, veins, arteries, and the like.

->All sense is joined to<-
->viscera, nerves, and veins, and whatever we see<-
->consisting of soft flesh in a mortal body.<-
<note>Original Latin: *Sensus jungitur omnis / Visceribus, Nervis, Venis, quaecunque videmus, / Mollia mortali consistere Corpore creta.* From Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura*.</note>

And reason and understanding, properly so called, are unique attachments to the human shape; "Reason can exist nowhere except in the human form" <note>Original Latin: *Ratio nusquam esse potest nisi in hominis figura.* A common Epicurean argument cited by Cicero.</note>. From this, it is concluded that there is no life, soul, nor understanding acting through the whole world, because the world has no blood nor brains, nor any animal or human form. "Those who said that the world itself is a living and wise being, in no way saw the nature of the mind, nor into what kind of figure it could fall" <note>Original Latin: *Qui Mundum ipsum Animantem sapientemque esse dixerunt, nullo modo viderunt Animi Naturam, in quam Figuram cadere posset.*</note>. Therefore, the Epicurean poet <note>Lucretius.</note> concludes upon this ground that there is no divine sense in the whole world:

->It is seen where the soul and mind are disposed<-
->to exist and grow separately; so much more must it be denied<-
->that the whole could endure outside of a body and an animal form,<-
->either in the crumbling clods of earth, or in the fire of the sun,<-
->or in the water, or in the high regions of the air.<-
->Therefore, these things are not endowed with divine sense,<-
->since they cannot be vitally animated.<-
<note>Original Latin: *Dispositum videtur ubi esse & crescere possit / Seorsim Anima atque Animus; tanto magis inficiandum, / Totum posse extra Corpus Formámque Animalem, / Putribus in glebis terrarum, aut Solis in Igni, / Aut in Aqua durare, aut altis Ætheris oris. / Haud igitur constant Divino prædita Sensu, / Quandoquidem nequeunt vitaliter esse Animata.*</note>

Now, if there is no life nor understanding above us, nor round about us, nor anywhere else in the world, but only in ourselves and our fellow-animals, and we are the highest of all beings; if neither...

<header>CHAPTER II. Atheists contend that nothing is immortal.</header>

If the whole corporeal system is not animated, nor those greater parts of it—the sun, moon, or stars—then there can be no danger of any deity.

### XII.
Eighthly, the Democritic <note>Followers of Democritus, who proposed an atomic theory of the universe.</note> atheists dispute further against a deity in this manner: The deity is generally supposed to be *a perfectly happy animal, incorruptible and immortal* <note>original Greek: ζῶον μακάριον ἢ ἀφθαρτον</note>. Now, there is no living being that is incorruptible and immortal, and therefore none that is perfectly happy either. For according to that Democritic hypothesis of atoms in a vacuum, the only incorruptible things will be these three: 

First of all, **vacuum** or **empty space**, which must necessarily be so because it cannot suffer from anything, since it is free from blows <note>original Latin: plagarum expers</note>,

->And it remains untouched, nor is it affected in the least by any stroke.<-
<note>original Latin: Et manet intactum, nec ab istu fungitur hilum.</note>

Secondly, the **single atoms**, because by reason of their smallness and solidity, they are indivisible. And lastly, the **sum of all sums** <note>original Latin: Summa Summarum</note> of all things—that is, the total collection of all atoms dispersed everywhere throughout infinite space.

->— Because there is no place available outside<-
->Where things might depart and be dissolved.<-
<note>original Latin: Quia nulla loci stat copia certum / Quò quasi res possint discedere dissoluique.</note>

But according to that other hypothesis of some modern atomists (which also was entertained of old by Empedocles <note>A Greek pre-Socratic philosopher.</note>) that supposes a fullness of matter, there is nothing at all incorruptible but the substance of matter itself. All systems and structures <note>term: compages</note> of it—all *compositions* and *assemblages* <note>original Greek: συγκείματα and ἀθροίσματα</note>, all solidifications <note>term: concretions</note> and joinings <note>term: coagmentations</note> of matter divided by motion, together with the qualities resulting from them—are corruptible and capable of being destroyed. What joining of things is not dissolvable? <note>original Latin: Quæ est Coagmentatio rerum non dissolubilis?</note> Death does not destroy the substance of any matter; for as no matter came from nothing but was self-eternal, so none of it can ever vanish into nothing; but death dissolves all the groupings of it.

->Death does not destroy things in such a way as to<-
->Consume the material bodies, but it scatters their assembly.<-
<note>original Latin: Non sic interimt Mors res ut Materia / Corpora conficiat, sed cætum dissupat ollis.</note>

Life is no **substantial** thing, nor any primitive or **simple nature**; it is only an **accident** <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that isn't essential to the nature of a thing.</note> or **quality** arising from the grouping and weaving together of atoms or **minute particles** <note>term: corpuscula</note>. When the structure of them is disunited and dissolved, though all the substance still remains scattered and dispersed, yet the life utterly perishes and vanishes into nothing. No life is immortal; there is no immortal soul, nor immortal animal, or deity. 

Even if this whole worldly <note>term: mundane</note> system were itself an animal, yet being but a grouping of matter, it would be both corruptible and mortal. Therefore, since no living being can possibly have any security of its future permanence, there is none that can be perfectly happy. And it was rightly determined by our fellow atheists, the Hedonists and Cyrenaics <note>Schools of Greek philosophy that emphasized pleasure as the supreme good.</note>, that *perfect happiness is non-existent and indifferent* <note>original Greek: ἀδιάφορον ἀνύπαρκτον</note>. Perfect happiness is a mere notion, a romantic fiction, a thing which can have no existence anywhere. This is recorded to have been one of the arguments of Democritus...

<header>Atheists impugn a First Cause or Mover. Book I.</header>

<note>The author is discussing the philosopher Velleius's critique of Democritus.</note> ...his chief arguments against a Deity: because there can be no living being *immortal*, and consequently none *perfectly happy*. "Since Democritus—because nothing remains forever in its own state—denies that anything is everlasting, does he not completely remove God, so as to leave no remaining opinion of him?" <note>original Latin: "Cum Democritus, quia nihil semper suo statu maneat, neget, esse quicquam sempiternum, nonne Deum ita tollit omnino, ut nullam Opinionem ejus reliquam faciat?"</note>

### XIII.
A ninth pretended demonstration of the Democritic <note>Followers of Democritus, who proposed an atomic, materialist universe.</note> atheists is as follows. By "God" is understood a *First Cause* or *Mover*, which, not being acted upon by anything else beforehand, but acting originally from itself, was the *beginning* of all things. Now it is an indubitable axiom, and generally received among philosophers, that *nothing can move itself*, but "whatever is moved is moved by something else" <note>original Latin: "Quicquid movetur ab alio movetur"</note>; nothing can act otherwise than it is made to act by something outside of it acting upon it. 

The necessary consequence of this is that there can be no such thing as any *First Mover* or *First Cause*—that is, no God. This argument is urged by a modern writer <note>Likely referring to Thomas Hobbes.</note> in agreement with the sense of the ancient Democritics: "From the fact that nothing can move itself, it is not inferred (as is commonly done) that there is an Eternal Immovable Mover, but on the contrary an eternal motion; for just as it is true that nothing is moved by itself, so it is also true that nothing is moved except by something already in motion." <note>original Latin: "Ex eo quòd nihil potest movere seipsum, non inferetur, id quod inferri solet, nempe Æternum Immobile, sed contrà Æternum Motum, siquidem ut verum est, nihil moveri à seipso, ita etiam verum est nihil moveri nisi à Moto."</note> 

From this—that nothing can move itself—it cannot be rightly inferred, as it commonly is, that there is an Eternal Immovable Mover (that is, a God), but only an eternal "moved mover"; or that one thing was moved by another from eternity, without any first mover. Because as it is true that nothing can be moved by itself, so it is likewise true that nothing can be moved except by that which was itself also moved by something else before; and so the progress upwards must necessarily be infinite, without any beginning or first mover. The plain drift and scope of this reasoning is nothing other than this: to show that the argument commonly taken from motion to prove a God (that is, a First Mover or Cause) is not only ineffectual and inconclusive, but also that, on the contrary, it may be demonstrated from that very topic of motion that there can be no absolutely First Mover, no first in the order of causes—that is, no God.

### XIV.
Tenthly, because the Theists conceive that though no body <note>In the sense of physical matter.</note> can move itself, yet a perfect *cogitative* <note>Capable of thought.</note> and *thinking being* might be the *beginning* of all and the first *cause* of *motion*, the atheists will endeavor to prove the contrary in this manner. No man can conceive how any thought which did not exist before should rise up at any time unless there was some cause for it outside of the *thinker*. For otherwise, no reason can be given why this *thought* rather than that, and at this time rather than another, should start up. 

Therefore, this is universally true of all motion and action whatsoever, as it was rightly urged by the Stoics, that there can be no "motion without a cause" <note>original Greek: "κίνησις ἀναιτίος"</note>—that is, no motion which does not have some cause outside the subject of it. Or, as the same thing is expressed by a modern writer: "Nothing takes its beginning from itself, but from the action of some other immediate agent outside of it." Therefore, no *thinking being* could be a *first cause* any more than an *automaton* or *machine* could. To this, it is further argued that these...

## CHAPTER II. Atheists make Knowledge Junior to the World.

These two notions—the one of a *Knowing, Understanding Being*, and the other of a *Perfectly Happy Being*—are *contradictory*. This is because all knowledge *essentially* implies *dependence* upon something else as its *cause*. "Knowledge and understanding are signs of a power dependent on another, which is not the state of the most blessed Being" <note>original Latin: *Scientia & Intellectus signum est Potentiæ ab alio Dependentis, id quod non est Beatissimum*</note>. They conclude that *thought* and all *action* whatsoever is really nothing else but *local motion*. This is *essentially heterokinesie* <term>motion caused by an external force</term>, something that can never arise by itself but is caused by some other *agent* outside of its *subject*.

XV. In the eleventh place, the *Democritic atheists* <note>Followers of Democritus, who believed the world was made of atoms in a vacuum.</note> reason in this way: If the *world* were made by any *pre-existing mind* or *understanding* (that is, by a *Deity*), then there must necessarily have been an *idea*, *blueprint*, and *model* of the whole *world* before it was made. Consequently, there would be *actual knowledge*, both in order of *time* and *nature*, before *things* existed. But all *knowledge* is the *information gathered from the things themselves*; all *conception* of the *mind* is a *passive reaction* <note>original: "passion"</note> caused by the *things conceived* and their activity upon the mind. Therefore, knowledge is *junior* <term>younger or secondary</term> to them. For this reason, the *world* and *things* existed before *knowledge* and the *conception* of any *mind*; thus, there was no *knowledge*, *mind*, or *Deity* before the *world* to serve as its *cause*. This *argument* is proposed by the *atheistic poet* <note>referring to Lucretius</note> as follows:

-> "Furthermore, how was the model for creating things, and the very" <-
-> "concept of man, first implanted in the gods?" <-
-> "How did they know what they wanted to make, or see it in their minds?" <-
-> "In what way was the power of the primary elements ever known," <-
-> "or what they could achieve by changing their order," <-
-> "if nature itself did not provide a specimen of creation?" <-
<note>original Latin: *Exemplum porro gignundis rebus, & ipsa Notities hominum Divis unde insita primùm, Quid vellent facere ut scirent, animosq; viderent? Quove modo est unquam Vis cognita Principiorum, Quidnam inter sese permutato Ordine possent, Si non ipsa dedit specimen Natura creandi?*</note>

How could the supposed *Deity* have a *pattern* or *blueprint* in his *mind* to frame the *world* by, and from where would he receive it? How could he have any *knowledge* of *men* before they were made, or know what he himself would will to do when there was nothing yet in existence? How could he understand the *force* and *possibility* of the *atoms* <note>original: "principles"</note>—what they would produce when variously combined together—before *nature* and *things* themselves, by *creating*, had given an *example*?

XVI. A *twelfth argument* of the *Democritic* and *Epicurean atheists* against a *Deity* is to this purpose: that *things* could not be made by a *Deity* who is supposed to be a *Being* every way *perfect*, because they are so *faulty* and so *badly* made. The *argument* is thus propounded by *Lucretius*:

-> "But even if I were ignorant of what the primary elements of things are," <-
-> "yet this I would venture to assert from the very logic of the heavens," <-
-> "and to demonstrate from many other things," <-
-> "that the nature of the world was by no means prepared for us" <-
-> "by a divine power; it stands endowed with such great faults." <-
<note>original Latin: *Quòd si jam rerum ignorem primordia quæ sint, Hoc tamen ex ipsis Cœli Rationibus ausim Confirmare, aliisque ex rebus reddere multis, Nequaquam nobis Divinitùs esse paratam Naturam rerum, tantâ stat prædita Culpâ.*</note>

This *argument* "from the logic of the heavens" <note>original: *à Cœli Rationibus*</note>, based on *astronomy* or the *constitution of the heavens*, is this: that the *world's sphere* is so framed in...

# Atheists contend that the World is Ill-made. BOOK I.

Regarding the arrangement of the Equator and the Ecliptic <note>The Ecliptic is the sun's apparent path; the author refers to the tilt of the Earth's axis</note>, it is argued that this makes the greatest part of the Earth uninhabitable to humans and most other animals. This is partly due to the excess of heat in the Torrid Zone (the area between the Tropics) and partly from the extreme cold in both Frigid Zones near the Poles. Furthermore, while the Stoic Theists <note>Philosophers who believed in a providential God</note> contemporary with Epicurus concluded that the whole world was made by a Deity solely for the sake of humanity,

-> "They imagine that God established all these things <-
-> for the sake of men—" <note>Original Latin: *Horum omnia causâ / Constituisse Deum fingunt*</note> <-

It is urged to the contrary that a great part of the habitable Earth is taken up by seas, lakes, and rocks, barren heaths and sands, and is thereby made useless for mankind. They argue that the remainder of the land yields no fruit to humans unless it is conquered <note>original: "expugned"</note> by stubborn labor. Even after all that, people are often disappointed of the fruits of those labors by unseasonable weather, storms, and tempests. Again, they argue that Nature has not only produced many harmful and poisonous herbs, but also destructive and predatory animals whose strength surpasses that of humans. They claim the condition of mankind is so much inferior to that of the brutes <note>Animals</note> that Nature seems to have been but a stepmother to humans, while she has been an indulgent mother to the animals. To this purpose, the manner of a human's birth into the world is thus described by the Poet <note>Lucretius, in his work *De Rerum Natura*</note>:

> Then further, the child, like a sailor cast up by the cruel waves, lies naked on the ground, speechless, lacking every help for life, as soon as nature has cast him forth by birth-pangs from his mother’s womb into the shores of light. He fills the place with mournful crying, as is natural for one who has so many evils left to pass through in life. <note>Original Latin: *Tum porro puer, ut saevis projectus ab undis / Navita, nudus humi jacet, infans, indigus omni / Vitai auxilio, cum primum in luminis oras / Nixibus ex alvo matris natura profudit: / Vagituque locum lugubri complet, ut aequum 'st, / Quoi tantum in vita restet transire malorum.*</note>

But on the contrary, the relative advantages of animals and the privileges they have over humans are described in this manner:

> But various flocks, herds, and wild beasts grow up; they need no rattles, nor must the fond nurse use broken, coaxing speech with them; they do not seek different clothes according to the season. Finally, they have no need of weapons or high walls to protect their own, since the Earth itself and Nature, the clever creator of things, produce all things in abundance for everyone. <note>Original Latin: *At variae crescunt pecudes, armenta, feraeque: / Nec crepitacula eis opu' sunt, nec quoiquam adhibenda 'st / Almae nutricis Blanda atque Infraeta loquela; / Nec varias quaerunt vestes pro tempore coeli. / Denique non armis opus est, non moenibus altis, / Queis sua tutentur, quando omnibus omnia large / Tellus ipsa parit, naturaque Daedala rerum.*</note>

And lastly, the topic of evils in general is insisted upon by them—not those which are called *Culpa*, or "Evils of Fault" <note>Moral sins or crimes</note> (for that is a concept which the Democritic atheists utterly reject in its genuine sense), but the evils of pain and trouble. They dispute concerning these in this manner: The supposed Deity and maker of the world was either willing to abolish all evils, but...

### CHAPTER II. Atheists object against Providence.

Either God was willing to abolish evil but not able; or he was able but not willing; or thirdly, he was neither willing nor able; or else lastly, he was both able and willing. This last option is the only one that fully aligns with the concept of a God. Now, it is argued that the supposed Creator of all things was not both able and willing to abolish all evils, because if he were, there would be no evils left at all. Therefore, since there is such a *deluge* <note>original: "Deluge"; a massive flood or overwhelming amount</note> of evils overflowing everything, it must follow that either he was willing and not able to remove them (in which case he was *impotent*), or else he was able and not willing (in which case he was *envious* <note>original: "Envious"; in this context, meaning malicious or begrudging of human well-being</note>), or lastly he was neither able nor willing (and then he was both *impotent* and *envious*).

XVII. In the twelfth place, the atheists further dispute in this manner: If the world were made by any deity, then it would be governed by a *providence* <note>The protective care of God or nature as a spiritual power</note>, and if there were any *providence*, it would have to appear in human affairs. But here it is plain that all is *tohu* and *bohu* <note>Hebrew: "Tohu wa-bohu"; meaning formless and empty, or utter chaos</note>, *chaos* and *confusion*. Things happen alike to everyone: to the wise and the foolish, the religious and the impious, the virtuous and the vicious. (The atheist cannot help but use these names, though by taking away natural morality, they actually destroy the things themselves.) From this, it is concluded that all things float up and down, agitated and driven by the tumbling billows of careless fortune and chance. 

The impieties of *Dionysius* <note>Dionysius I of Syracuse, a tyrant known for his cruelty and supposed lack of reverence for the gods</note>, his scoffing abuses of religion and whatever was then sacred or worshipped as a god, were notorious; and yet it is observed that he fared not a bit the worse for it. "Neither did Olympian Jupiter strike him with a thunderbolt, nor did Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of medicine and healing</note> kill him with a wretched and lingering disease; instead, he died in his own bed, was carried to the funeral pyre with the music of flutes, and that power which he had wickedly obtained, he passed on to his heirs as if it were a most just and lawful inheritance" <note>original Latin: "Hunc nec Olympius Jupiter fulmine percussit, nec Æsculapius misero diuturnoque morbo tabescentem interemit, verum in suo lectulo mortuus, in Tympanidis rogum illatus est, eámque potestatem quam ipse per scelus nactus erat, quasi justissimam, hæreditatis loco tradidit"</note>. 

And *Diogenes* the *Cynic*, though very much a believer in God, could not help but acknowledge that *Harpalus*—a famous robber or pirate of those times who committed many villainous actions yet lived prosperously—did thereby "bear testimony against the gods" <note>original Latin: "Testimonium dicere contra Deos"</note>. 

Theists have objected to this, thinking it a strong argument for *providence* that there were so many tablets hung up in temples as monuments to those who, having prayed to the gods during storms and tempests, had escaped shipwreck. Yet, as *Diagoras* <note>Diagoras of Melos, known as "the Atheist"</note> observed, "There are no pictures of those who were shipwrecked" <note>original Latin: "Nusquam picti sunt qui Naufragium fecerunt"</note>. Therefore, these theists did not consider how many of those who prayed to the gods suffered shipwreck anyway, nor how many of those who never made any devotional prayers to any deity escaped the same dangers of storms and tempests.

<header>Atheists' Objections against Book I.</header>

Moreover, it is consistent with the idea of a God to think that thunder rattling in the clouds with thunderbolts should be the immediate signs of his wrath and displeasure. However, it is plain that these are flung at random, and that their fury often falls upon the innocent, while the notoriously guilty escape untouched. Therefore, we do not understand how any Theists <note>Those who believe in the existence of a god or gods.</note> can answer this.

> Why do those who have committed some horrible, detestable crime not find themselves struck down, breathing out the flames of lightning from a pierced breast—a sharp lesson to mortals? And why, instead, does someone conscious of no foul deed roll in flames, innocent and entangled, suddenly snatched up by a heavenly whirlwind and fire? <note>original Latin: Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura*, Book 6. The poet questions why lightning strikes the innocent rather than the guilty.</note>

Now the force of this argument appears to be very powerful, because it has not only staggered and confounded Theists in all ages, but has also effectively transformed many of them into Atheists. For Diagoras of Melos <note>A 5th-century BC Greek poet and philosopher known as "the Atheist."</note> himself was once a superstitious religious man; indeed, being a Dithyrambic <note>A passionate, choral hymn usually dedicated to Dionysus.</note> poet, he began one of his poems with these words: *All things are accomplished by God and Fortune.* <note>original Greek: κ᾿ ὀλίγονα ἢ τυχλῶ πᾶντα τελεῖται</note> But after being injured by a perjured person who suffered no evil or disaster as a result, he therefore adopted the contrary persuasion: that there was no Deity.

And there have been innumerable others who have been so influenced by this consideration that, if they did not absolutely disclaim and discard a Deity, they utterly denied Providence and any care for human affairs by any invisible powers. Among these was the poet who expressed his feelings this way:

> But when I saw human affairs shrouded in such great darkness—the guilty flourishing for a long time and the pious being harassed—my religion was shaken and began to fall. Unwillingly, I followed the path of another theory, which claims that atoms run in a void with purposeless motion, and that new forms are governed through the great vacuum by Fortune, not by Art; a theory which thinks the gods are either ambiguous or non-existent, or ignorant of our affairs. <note>original Latin: Claudian, *In Rufinum*, Book 1. The poet describes how the prosperity of the wicked leads to a loss of faith in divine order.</note>

### XVIII.

A thirteenth argument of the Democritic and Epicurean <note>Followers of Democritus and Epicurus, ancient Greek philosophers who proposed that the world is made of atoms and that gods do not interfere in human life.</note> Atheists is to this purpose: that whereas the Deity is supposed to be such a being as both knows all that is done everywhere in the most distant places of the world at once, and does himself immediately order all things; this is, first, impossible for any one Being to thus observe and order all things in the whole universe.

> Who is able to rule the sum of the immense, who can hold the powerful reins of the deep in his hand with such control? Who can turn all the heavens at once? And with his fires... <note>original Latin: Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura*, Book 2. The poet argues that the vastness of the universe is too great for any single deity to manage.</note>
