<header>CHAPTER II. A Providential Deity.</header>

*To fumigate the fertile lands with heavenly fires?*
*To be present in all places at all times?*
*To create darkness with clouds, and shake the serene*
*Heavens with sound? etc.*
<note>original Latin: "Ignibus ætheriis terras suffire feraceis? / Omnibus inque locis esse omni tempore præstò? / Nubibus ut tenebras faciat, cælique serena / Concutiat sonitu? &c." from Lucretius, De Rerum Natura.</note>

And secondly, if it were supposed to be possible, yet such infinite busyness <note>original: "Negotiability"</note> would be absolutely inconsistent with a happy state. Nor could such a Deity ever have any quiet enjoyment of himself, being perpetually filled with tumult and hurly-burly. *A busy nature is not blessed, but is a sign of weakness* <note>original Greek: "ὁ συμφύσα πραγματεία μὴ μακαρία ἐστὶ, ἀλλ᾽ ἀσθένεια"</note> and *to stand in need of others; these things happen* <note>original Greek: "προσδεῖσθαι τῆς πλησίον ταῦτα γίνεται"</note>—distraction of business and solicitous cares, displeasures and favors, do not at all agree with happiness, but they proceed from weakness <note>original: "Imbecillity"</note>, poverty <note>original: "Indigency"</note>, and fear. *That which is blessed and incorruptible would neither have any business of its own to do, nor create any for others; it would have neither displeasure nor favor toward any other persons to engage it in action; for all such things proceed from weakness.* <note>original Greek: "τὸ μακάριον οὐκ ὅτε χάριν φθαρτὸν ἔστε αὐτὸ πράγματα ἔχῃ, ὅτε ἄλλα παρέχει, ὥστε ἑτέροις ὅτε χάριν συνέχεται, ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ γὰρ πᾶν τὸ τοιοῦτον"</note> That is, favor and benevolence, as well as anger and displeasure, arise only from weakness. That which is perfectly happy and lacks nothing, *being wholly possessed and held together by its own invincibility,* <note>original Greek: "ὅλον ὄν ἐν Ἀεὶ τὴν συνοχὴν τ᾽ ἰδίας ἀδαμαντίας"</note> being wholly possessed and taken up in the enjoyment of its own happiness, would be regardless of the concerns of any others; and mind nothing besides itself, either to do it good or harm. Therefore, this *curious and busy God, this busy, restless, and meddling <term>pragmatical</term> Deity,* that must needs intermeddle and have to do with everything in the whole world, is a contradictory notion, since he could not help but be the most unhappy of all things.

### XIX.
In the next place, the atheists dispute further by proposing several bold *questions* <note>original: "Quæries"</note>, which they conceive unanswerable, after this manner: If the world were made by a Deity, why was it not made by him sooner? Or since it was so long unmade, why did he make it at all? *Why did the Builder of the world suddenly appear, after sleeping for innumerable ages before?* <note>original Latin: "Cur mundi Ædificator repentè extiterit, innu- merabili antè sæcula dormierit?"</note> How came this builder and architect of the world to start up on a sudden, after he had slept for infinite ages, and bethink himself of making a world? For, certainly, if he had been awake all that while, he would either have made it sooner, or not at all; because there was either something wanting to his happiness before, or nothing. If there had been anything wanting before, then the world could not have been so long unmade; but if he were completely happy in himself without it, then *lacking nothing, he vainly attempted to perform superfluous actions.* <note>original Greek: "μηδὲν ἐλλείπων κενοὺς ἔμελλεν ἐπιχειρεῖν πράξειν"</note> All desire of change and novelty argues a weary over-fullness <note>original: "Fastidious Satiety"</note>, proceeding from defect and need.

*What new thing could entice those who were quiet before,*
*So long after, to desire to change their former life?*
*For he seems to ought to rejoice in new things*
*Whom old things annoy; but for him to whom no ill has happened*
*In time past...*
<note>original Latin: "Quidve novi potuit tantò post, antè quietos / Inlicere, ut cuperent vitam mutare priorem? / Nam gaudere novis rebus debere videtur / Quoi veteres obsunt; sed quoi nil accidit ægri / Tempore"</note>

<summary>This page outlines the Epicurean atheist argument that a truly happy and perfect God would be too self-sufficient to bother with the "tumult" of governing a world. It also questions why a Creator would suddenly decide to make a world after remaining inactive for infinite ages.</summary>
<keywords>Epicureanism, divine providence, divine happiness, arguments against creation, Lucretius, divine indifference, problem of novelty</keywords>

# Several Bold Queries of Atheists. Book I.

*In time past, when he passed his life beautifully,*
*What could have kindled the love of novelty in such a being?*
<note>original Latin: "Tempore in anteacto, cùm pulchrè degeret ævum, Quid potuit novitatis amorem accendere tali?" — Lucretius, De Rerum Natura.</note>

Did this Deity, therefore, light up the stars as so many lamps or torches in that vast abyss of infinite darkness so that he himself might have a more comfortable and cheerful habitation? Why would he then content himself from eternity to dwell in such a melancholy, horrid, and forlorn dungeon?

*Or did the Creator lie in darkness, in life and sorrow,*
*Until the birth-origin of things dawned?*
<note>original Latin: "An Credo in tenebris vitâ & mœrore jacebat, Donec diluxit rerum Genitalis Origo?" — Lucretius.</note>

Was company and that variety of things, by which heaven and earth are distinguished, desirable to him? Why then would he continue solitary for so long, lacking the pleasure of such a spectacle? Did he make the world and men in it for this end: that he himself might be worshipped and adored, feared and honored by them? But how could he be the better for that, he who was sufficiently happy alone in himself before? Or did he do it for the sake of men, to gratify and oblige them?

*But what benefit can our gratitude bestow*
*Upon the immortal and blessed beings,*
*That they should undertake to do anything for our sake?*
<note>original Latin: "At quid immortalibus atque beatis Gratia nostra queat largirier emolumenti, Vt nostrâ quicquam causâ gerere aggrediantur?" — Lucretius.</note>

Again, if this were done for the sake of men, then it must be either for wise men or for fools. If for wise men only, then all that effort was taken for only a very few; but if for fools, what reason could there be why the Deity should seek to deserve so well at their hands? Besides this, what harm would it have been to any of us (whether wise or foolish) never to have been made?

*What evil would there have been for us in not being created?*
*For whoever is born ought to want to remain*
*In life, as long as enticing pleasure holds him:*
*But he who has never tasted the love of life,*
*Nor was in the number of the living, what does it matter if he was not created?*
<note>original Latin: "Quidve mali fuerat nobis non esse creatis? Natus enim debet quicunque est, velle manere In vita, donec retinebit blanda voluptas: Qui nunquam verò vitæ gustavit amorem, Nec fuit in numero, quid obest non esse creatum?" — Lucretius.</note>

Lastly, if this Deity must necessarily go about with great effort <note>original: "moliminously"</note> to make a world, *like a workman or a carpenter handling his materials* <note>original Greek: "ἐργάτης ὕλην ἦ τέκτονος"</note>, what tools and instruments could he have to work with? What ministers and subordinate craftsmen <note>original: "Subservient Opificers"</note>? What engines and machines for the rearing up of so huge a structure? How could he make the matter understand his meaning and obey his command? How could he move it and turn it up and down? For if he were incorporeal <note>term: "incorporeal" — having no physical body or substance</note>, he could neither touch nor be touched, but would run through all things without fastening upon anything. But if he were corporeal <note>term: "corporeal" — having a physical body or material substance</note>, then the same thing was both the materials and the architect, both the timber and the carpenter; and the stones must have hewn themselves and brought themselves together, with discretion, into a structure.

### CHAPTER II. Atheists dispute from Interests against a Deity.

XX. In the last place, the atheists argue from *interest* (which often proves to be the most effective of all arguments) against a Deity. They endeavor to persuade others that it is, first, the *interest* of *private persons* and of all *mankind* in *general*; and secondly, the *particular interest* of *civil sovereigns* and *commonwealths*, that there should neither be a *God*, nor the belief in any such thing entertained by the minds of *men*—that is, no *religion*. 

First, they say it is the *interest* of *mankind* in *general* because as long as men are persuaded that there is an *understanding being* who is infinitely *powerful* and has no *law* but his own *will* (because he has no *superior*), and who may do whatever he pleases to them at any *time*, they can never *securely* enjoy themselves or anything else, nor ever be free from disquieting *fear* and *anxiety*. What the *poets fable* regarding *Tantalus* in *hell*—always having a huge *stone* hanging over his *head*, ready to tumble down upon him at any *moment*—is nothing compared to that true *fear* which men have of a *Deity* and *religion* here in this *life*, which was indeed the very thing symbolized by that myth.

> *The wretched Tantalus does not fear the great rock hanging in the air (as the story goes), paralyzed by empty dread; but rather in life, the vain fear of the Gods oppresses mortals, and they fear whatever fall Fortune may bring.*
> <note>original Latin: "Nec miser impendens magnum timet aëre Saxum Tantalus, (ut fama est) cassâ formidine torpens: Sed magis in vita, Divûm Metus urget inanis Mortales, casúmque timent, quemcumque ferat Fors." From Lucretius, De Rerum Natura.</note>

For besides the *insecurity* men feel regarding all manner of present *evils* under the supposition of a *God*, the *immortality* of *souls* can hardly be kept out, but will crowd in after it. Then the fear of *eternal punishments* after *death* will unavoidably follow, perpetually embittering all the *comforts* of *life* and never allowing men to have the least sincere *enjoyment*.

> *—If men saw that there was a fixed limit to their miseries, they might in some way find the strength to resist the superstitions and threats of the priests. But now there is no means of resisting, no power to do so, because they must fear eternal punishments in death. For it is unknown what the nature of the soul is: whether it is born, or on the contrary, is infused into those being born; and whether it perishes with us when severed by death, or visits the darkness of Orcus <note>The Roman underworld</note> and its vast pits.*
> <note>original Latin: "—Si certam finem esse viderent Erumnarum homines, aliquâ ratione valerent, Relligionibus, atque minis obsistere Vatum. Nunc ratio nulla est restandi, nulla facultas: Æternas quoniam Pænas in morte timendum. Ignoratur enim quæ sit natura Animai, Nata sit, an contrà nascentibus insinnuetur; Et simul intereat nobiscum morte dirempta, An Tenebras Orci visat vastásque Lacunas." From Lucretius.</note>

Therefore, it is plain that those who first introduced the *belief* of a *Deity* and *religion*—whatever they might have aimed at—deserved very poorly of all *mankind*. This is because they infinitely debased and depressed the *spirits* of men under a *servile fear*,

> *They make spirits humble through the fear of the Gods, and press them down, crushed, to the earth:*
> <note>original Latin: "Efficiunt animos humiles, formidine Divûm, Depressósque premunt ad Terram."</note>

as well as caused the greatest *griefs* and *calamities* that now disturb *human life*,

> *How many groans did they then create for themselves, what wounds for us, and what tears for our descendants?* <note>original: "Quantos tum gemitus ipsi sibi, quantáq; nobis Volnera, quas lachrymas peperere Minoribu' nostris?" — Lucretius, De Rerum Natura.</note>

There can be no comfortable and happy living without banishing from our mind the belief in these two things: a Deity and the soul's immortality.

> *And that fear of Acheron <note>The underworld or hell</note> must be driven out headlong, which disturbs human life from its very depths, overspreading everything with the blackness of death, and leaving no pleasure clear and pure.* <note>original: "Et metus ille foràs præceps Acheruntis agendus Funditus, humanam qui vitam turbat ab imo, Omnia suffundens Mortis Nigrore, neque ullam Esse voluptatem Liquidam, Purúmque relinquit."</note>

It was therefore a noble and heroical exploit of **Democritus** and **Epicurus**, those two good-natured men, who—seeing the world thus oppressed under the grievous yoke of religion, the fear of a Deity, and punishment after death—took pity on this sad condition of mankind. They manfully encountered that frightening spectre or *Empusa* <note>A shapeshifting mythological monster; here used to mean a terrifying phantom</note> of a **Providential Deity**; and by clear philosophical reasons, chased it away and banished it quite out of the world. They laid down such principles as would explain all the *phenomena* <note>observable events</note> of nature without a God;

> *If you hold these things well-known, nature is seen to be immediately free, deprived of proud masters, doing all things by herself of her own accord, without the involvement of the gods.* <note>original: "Quæ bene cognita si teneas, Natura videtur Libera continuò, Dominis privata Superbis, Ipsa suâ per se sponte, Omnia Dis agere expers."</note>

So that **Lucretius** does not, without just cause, erect a triumphal arch or monument to **Epicurus** for this conquest or victory of his, obtained over the Deity and religion in this manner:

> *When human life lay foully before our eyes, oppressed on earth under the weight of religion, which showed its head from the regions of heaven, lowering over mortals with a horrible aspect; a man of Greece <note>Epicurus</note> was the first who dared to lift mortal eyes against it, and the first to stand against it; whom neither the fame of the gods, nor lightning, nor the heaven with its threatening murmur, could suppress, etc.* <note>original: "Humana ante oculos fædè quum vita jaceret, In terris oppressa gravi sub Relligione, Quæ caput à Cæli regionibus ostendebat, Horribili super aspectu mortalibus instans; Primùm Graius homo mortales tendere contrà Est oculos ausus, primúsque obsistere contrà; Quem nec fama Deûm nec fulmina, nec minitanti Murmure compressit cælum, &c."</note>

### XXI.
The **Democritic atheists** would also persuade us that it is in the interest of civil sovereigns and of all commonwealths that there should be neither Deity nor religion, in this manner: A **body politic** or commonwealth is made up of parts that are all naturally dissociated from one another because of that principle of private **self-love**. Therefore, they can be held together by nothing other than fear. Now, if there is any greater fear than the fear of the **Leviathan** <note>The state or supreme civil authority, a term famously used by Thomas Hobbes</note> and the civil representative, the whole structure and machine of this great colossus must necessarily fall to pieces and tumble down. The civil sovereign reigns only through fear; therefore, unless his fear is the king and sovereign of all fears, his empire and dominion ceases.

It also introduces the idea that a sovereign's power is undermined if citizens fear a divine power more than the state.</summary>

# CHAPTER II. Inconsistent with Civil Sovereignty.

ceases. But as the Rod of *Moses* devoured the rods of the *magicians* <note>A reference to Exodus 7:12, where Aaron’s rod-turned-serpent swallows those of Pharaoh’s sorcerers.</note>, so certainly will the fear of an omnipotent *Deity*, who can punish with eternal torments after death, quite swallow up and devour that comparatively *petty fear* of *civil sovereigns*. Consequently, it would destroy the existence of *commonwealths*, which have no foundation in *nature*, but are mere *artificial things* made by the *enchantment* and *magical art* of *policy* <note>original: "Policy"; here meaning political craft or statecraft.</note>. 

Wherefore it is well observed by a *modern writer* <note>Referring to Thomas Hobbes, author of *Leviathan* (1651).</note>, *That men ought not to suffer themselves to be abused by the doctrine of separated essences and incorporeal substances (such as God and the soul), built upon the vain philosophy of Aristotle, which would frighten men from obeying the laws of their country with empty names (such as Hell, Damnation, Fire, and Brimstone), just as men frighten birds from the corn with an empty hat, a doublet, and a crooked stick.* And again: *If the fear of spirits (the chief of which is the Deity) were taken away, men would be much more fitted than they are for civil obedience.*

Moreover, the power of *civil sovereigns* is perfectly *indivisible*; it is either *all* or *nothing*. It must be *absolute* and *infinite*, or else it is none at all. Now, it cannot be so if there is any other power equal to it to share with it, much less if there is any *superior* power (such as that of the *Deity*) to check and control it. Wherefore the *Deity* must of necessity be removed and displaced to make room for the *Leviathan* <note>Hobbes's term for the absolute state or sovereign.</note> to spread himself in.

Lastly, it is perfectly inconsistent with the nature of a *body politic* that there should be any *private judgment* allowed concerning *good* or *evil*, *lawful* or *unlawful*, *just* or *unjust*. But *conscience* (which *theism* and *religion* introduce) is *private judgment* concerning *good* and *evil*; therefore, the allowance of it is contradictory to *civil sovereignty* and a *commonwealth*. There ought to be no other *conscience* (in a *kingdom* or *commonwealth*) besides the *law* of the *country*. The allowance of *private conscience* is, *by the fact itself* <note>original: "ipso facto"</note>, a *dissolution* of the *body politic* and a return to the *state of nature*. Upon all these accounts, it must be acknowledged that those *philosophers* who undermine and weaken *theism* and *religion* deserve great thanks from all *civil sovereigns* and *commonwealths*.

XXII. Now, from all the previously mentioned considerations, the *Democritics* <note>Followers of Democritus; atomists who believe the world is made of matter and void without divine intervention.</note> confidently conclude against a *Deity*: That the *system* and *structure* <note>original: "compages"</note> of the *universe* did not have its origin from any *understanding nature*. Instead, *mind* and *understanding* itself, as well as all other things in the *world*, sprang up from *senseless nature* and *chance*, or from the *unguided* and *undirected motion* of *matter*. 

This is called by the *name of nature* because whatever moves is moved by *nature* and *necessity*. The mutual *collisions* <note>original: "occursions"</note> and *encounters* of *atoms*—their *blows* <note>original: "plage"</note>, their *strokes* and *dashings* against one another, their *reflections* and *reboundings*, their *cohesions*, *intertwinings* <note>original: "implexions"</note>, and *entanglements*, as well as their *scattered dispersions* and *tearings apart* <note>original: "divulsions"</note>—are all *natural* and *necessary*. # The Atheist's Conclusion
### Book I.

They give it the name of **Chance** and **Fortune**, because it is all unguided by any **Mind**, **Counsel**, or **Design**.

Therefore, **infinite atoms** of different sizes and figures, devoid of all **life** and **sense**, moving fortuitously <note>by chance</note> from **eternity** in infinite **space**, and making successively several **encounters**, and consequently various **implexions** <note>intertwinings</note> and **entanglements** with one another, produced first a confused **chaos** of these **omnifarious** <note>of all varieties</note> **particles**. Jumbling together with an infinite variety of **motions**, which afterward—by the tugging of their different and contrary forces, whereby they all hindered and abated each other—came, as it were by joint **conspiracy**, to be conglomerated into a **vortex** or **vortices**. 

There, after many **convolutions** and **evolutions**, **molitions** <note>labors or efforts</note> and **essays** <note>attempts</note> (in which all manner of **tricks** were tried, and all **forms** imaginable experimented with), they chanced in length of time to settle here into this **form** and **system** of things which now exists: of **earth, water, air,** and **fire**; **sun, moon,** and **stars**; **plants, animals,** and **men**. So it is that **senseless atoms**, fortuitously moved, and a **material chaos** were the first **original** <note>source</note> of all things.

This account of the **cosmopoeia** <note>original: "Cosmopæia"; the creation of the world</note> and the first **original** of the **mundane system** <note>the physical universe</note> is represented by **Lucretius** according to the mind of **Epicurus**, though without any mention of those **vortices**, which yet were an essential part of the old **Democritic hypothesis**.

> But in what ways that assembly of matter established the sky and the earth, and the depths of the sea, and the courses of the sun and moon, I will set forth in order. For certainly, the first-beginnings of things did not place themselves in their stations by design or with a clever mind, nor did they bargain what motions each should produce. But because many first-beginnings of things, driven by blows in many ways throughout an infinite time, and accustomed to be carried along by their own weights, have met in every kind of way and tried everything that they could create by meeting together; therefore it happens that, having been spread abroad through a vast age, by trying every kind of union and motion, they at last meet in such a way that they suddenly become the beginnings of great things: of Earth, Sea, and Sky, and the race of living creatures. <note>original: "Sed quibus ille modis conjectus materiæ..." from Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura*</note>

But because some seem to think that **Epicurus** was the first founder and inventor of this **doctrine**, we shall here observe that this same **atheistic hypothesis** was long before described by **Plato**, when **Epicurus** was as yet unborn. Therefore, it was doubtless according to the **doctrine** of **Leucippus**, **Democritus**, and **Protagoras**, though that **philosopher** <note>Plato</note>, in a kind of disdain (as it seems), refused to mention either of their **names**:

> They say that fire and water, and earth and air, all exist by nature and chance, and none of them by art. And that the bodies which come next—those of the earth, and of the sun, and of the moon, and of the stars—have been created by means of these absolutely soulless entities. <note>original: "τῦχῃ κ᾿ ὕδωρ..." from Plato's *Laws*, Book 10</note>

# CHAPTER II. All sprung from Nature and Chance.
<page-num>99</page-num>

"Chance or the movements of each power, or by accidents, each arising spontaneously from themselves, etc. In this way and according to these things, the whole was generated by itself, or by trial and error, or by things coinciding naturally from which they first arose; they say it was not by any of the gods, nor by art; but we say, it was by nature and chance, and that art came later from these things," etc. <note>original Greek: Τύχη ἢ φερέσματα... This is a paraphrase of Plato's *Laws*, Book X, describing the materialist view of the universe's origin.</note>

The Atheists say that Fire, Water, Air, and Earth (that is, the four Elements) were all made by Nature and Chance; and none of them by Art <note>original: "Art" here refers to "techne" or deliberate design/craftsmanship.</note> or Mind (that is, they were made by the fortuitous motion of Atoms, and not by any Deity). And they claim that those other bodies—the Terrestrial Globe, the Sun, the Moon, and the Stars (which by everyone except these Atheists were, in those times, generally supposed to be animated <note>original: "Animated" meaning possessing a soul or life-force.</note> and a kind of inferior deities)—were afterwards made out of the aforementioned elements, being altogether inanimate. 

For these elements, being moved by chance, happened to collide, and so making various mixtures together, did by that means at length produce the whole Heavens and all things in them, as likewise plants and animals here upon earth. All of these were not made by Mind, nor by Art, nor by any God; but, as we said before, by Nature and Chance. Art and Mind itself arose afterwards from the same senseless principles within animals.

## CHAPTER III.

An Introduction to the Refutation of Atheistic Grounds, in which is contained a particular account of all the several forms of Atheism. 

1. That the grounds of **Hylozoic Atheism** <note>original: "Hylozoick Atheism"; the belief that all matter possesses life or soul</note> could not be addressed in the former chapter alongside those of **Atomic Atheism**, because they are directly contrary to each other; with a further account of this Hylozoic Atheism. 

2. A suggestion, by way of caution, to prevent all mistakes: that every Hylozoist must not necessarily be condemned as an Atheist, or as a mere counterfeit, theatrical Theist. 

3. That nevertheless, such Hylozoists as are also **Corporealists** <note>those who believe only physical matter exists</note> can by no means be excused from the charge of Atheism, for two reasons. 

4. That **Strato of Lampsacus**, commonly called *the Physicist* <note>original: "Physicus"</note>, seems to have been the first proponent of Hylozoic Atheism, as he held no other God but the "Life of Nature" within matter. 

5. Further proof that Strato was an Atheist, and of a different type than **Democritus**, because he attributed an active, energetic nature to all matter, yet one without consciousness or animal-like feeling. 

6. That Strato did not derive all things from a mere accidental principle, as the **Democritic Atheists** did, nor did he acknowledge any single "Plastic Nature" <note>an organizing, formative force</note> to preside over the whole universe. Instead, he deduced the origin of things from a mixture of both chance and "Plastic Nature" working together in the various parts of matter; therefore, he must be considered a Hylozoic Atheist. 

7. That the famous **Hippocrates** was neither a Hylozoic nor a Democritic Atheist, but rather a **Heraclitic Corporeal Theist** <note>one who believes God is a physical substance, like fire, following the philosophy of Heraclitus</note>. 

8. That **Plato** took no notice of Hylozoic Atheism, nor of any other kind except that which derives the origin of all things from mere accidental nature; and therefore he addressed either the Democritic or the **Anaximandrian Atheism**, the latter of which will be explained next. 

9. That it is hardly imaginable there should have been no philosophical Atheists in the world before Democritus and **Leucippus**, since in all ages, as Plato observes, there have been some or others infected with the "Atheistic disease." That **Aristotle** affirms many of the first philosophers assigned only a **Material Cause** to the system of the world, without either an **Efficient Cause** <note>the agent that brings something about</note> or an **Intending Cause** <note>a purposeful designer</note>. They supposed matter to be the only substance, and all other things to be nothing but the "passions" and "accidents" <note>temporary qualities or states</note> of that matter, capable of being created and destroyed. 

10. That the doctrine of these **Materialists** will be more fully understood from the exceptions which Aristotle makes against them; his first exception;

<summary>This chapter introduction outlines the various forms of atheism, specifically distinguishing between the "Atomic" school of Democritus and the "Hylozoic" school of Strato, while identifying early Greek philosophers who viewed matter as the sole substance of the universe.</summary>

# Book I.

10. That they assigned no cause of motion, but introduced it into the world unacceptably. 11. **Aristotle's** second exception: that these **Materialists** did assign no cause <note>original: τῶ εὖ καὶ καλῶ</note> of "the well and the fit," and give no account of the orderly regularity of things. That **Anaxagoras** was the first **Ionic Philosopher** who made Mind and Good a principle of the **Universe**. 12. Concluded, that **Aristotle's Materialists** were downright **Atheists**, not merely because they held all substance to be body—since **Heraclitus** and **Zeno** did the same, and yet are not therefore accounted **Atheists** (they supposing their fiery matter to be originally **intellectual**, and the whole world to be an animal)—but because these made stupid matter, devoid of all understanding and life, to be the only principle. 13. As also, because they supposed everything besides the substance of matter—life and understanding, and all particular beings—to be generable and corruptible <note>meaning they are born and die, rather than being eternal</note>, and consequently that there could be no other God than such as was native and mortal. That those ancient **theologians**, who were **Theogonists** <note>those who describe the genealogy or birth of the gods</note>, and generated all the gods out of Night and Chaos, were only verbal **Theists** but real **Atheists**: senseless matter being to them the highest **divinity** <note>original: Numen</note>. 14. The great difference observed between **Aristotle's Atheistical Materialists** and the **Italic Philosophers**; the former determining all things, besides the substance of matter, to be made or generated; the latter that no real entity was either generated or corrupted. Thereupon, the latter both destroyed the idea of qualities and forms of body as independent things, and asserted the uncreated nature and incorporeity of souls. 15. How **Aristotle's Atheistic Materialists** endeavored to baffle and elude that axiom of the **Italic Philosophers**, "That nothing can come from nothing nor go to nothing." And that **Anaxagoras** was the first among the **Ionics** who yielded so far to that principle as to assert, from that basis, the existence of incorporeal substance and the pre-existence of qualities and forms in "similar atoms," because he conceived them to be things really distinct from the substance of matter. 16. The error of some writers, who, because **Aristotle** affirms that the ancient **philosophers** did generally conclude the world to have been made, from there infer that they were all **Theists**, and that **Aristotle** contradicts himself in representing many of them as **Atheists**. That the ancient **Atheists** did generally <note>original: νοσμοποιεῖν</note> assert the world to have been made, or to have had a beginning; just as some **Theists** did maintain its eternity, but in a way of dependency upon the Deity. We ought here to distinguish between the *system* of the world and the *substance* of the matter; all **Atheists** asserting the matter to have been not only eternal, but also existing independently of any other being. 17. That **Plato** and others concluded this **Materialism** or **Hylopathian Atheism** <note>the belief that all things, including souls, are merely affections or qualities of matter</note> to have been at least as old as **Homer**, who made the Ocean (or fluid matter) the father of all the gods. And that this was indeed the most ancient of all **Atheisms**, which, while verbally acknowledging gods, yet derived the origin of them all from Night and Chaos. The description of this **Atheistic hypothesis** in **Aristophanes**: that Night and Chaos first laid an egg, out of which sprung forth Love, which afterwards mingling with Chaos begat Heaven and Earth, animals, and all the gods. 18. That notwithstanding this, in **Aristotle's** judgment, **Parmenides**, **Hesiod**, and others, who made Love in like manner...

It traces the origins of "Hylopathian Atheism" back to ancient poets like Homer and Aristophanes, who depicted the gods as emerging from primal matter.</summary>

## CHAP. III.

<note>This chapter continues to categorize different philosophical systems, specifically distinguishing between those who believed in a divine "Love" as a creative force and those who believed the universe arose from mindless matter.</note>

18. Whether those who held that *Love* was the oldest of all the Gods should be excluded from the list of *Atheists*; they understood this *Love* to be an *Active Principle*, or *Cause of Motion in the Universe*. Therefore, this Love could not be an *Egg of the Night* <note>A mythological concept where the world is born from darkness</note>, nor the *Offspring of Chaos*, but was *something in the Order of Nature existing before Matter*. *Simmias of Rhodes's "Wings"*, a *poem* in honor of this *Heavenly Love*. This is not the same *Love* that was the *offspring of Poverty <note>original: Penia</note> and Plenty <note>original: Porus</note> in Plato*. In what corrected sense it may pass for true *Theology*: that *Love* is the *Supreme Deity* and *Original Source* of all things. 

19. That although *Democritus* and *Leucippus* are elsewhere criticized by *Aristotle* for this very thing—that they assigned only a *Material Cause to the Universe*—yet they were not the *persons* he intended in the previously cited *accusation*. Instead, he referred to certain *Ancient Philosophers* who were not *Atomists* but *Hylopathians* <note>Those who believe that matter itself is capable of feeling or that all things arise from the "affections" of matter</note>. 

20. That *Aristotle's Atheistic Materialists* were all the first *Ionian Philosophers* before *Anaxagoras*, with *Thales* being the *head* of them. But *Thales* is cleared from this *charge of Atheism* by several reliable *authors* (with an *account* of how he came to be so differently represented). Therefore, his immediate *successor Anaximander* is rather to be considered the *leader of this Atheistic Philosophy*. 

21. A *passage from Aristotle is examined which, at first sight, seems to make Anaximander a Divine Philosopher*, and has therefore led both *modern* and *ancient writers* into that mistake. However, when this *passage* is *well considered*, it proves the contrary: that *Anaximander* was the *chief* of the old *Atheistic Philosophers*. 

22. That it is no wonder if *Anaximander* called *senseless matter* <gloss>the divine</gloss> <note>original: τὸ θεῖον</note>, or *God*, since to all *Atheists*, that must necessarily be the highest *Deity* <note>original: Numen</note>. Also, how this matter is said to be *Immortal* and to *Govern all*, according to the agreeing *judgment* of the *Greek commentators <note>original: Scholiasts</note> on this passage*. 

23. A further *account of the Anaximandrian Philosophy*, *demonstrating it to have been purely Atheistical*. 

24. What poor *judges* the *common people* have been regarding *Theists* and *Atheists*; also, that learned men have commonly assumed there were fewer *Atheists* than there actually were. *Anaximander* and *Democritus* were *Atheists* both alike, though they *philosophized* in different ways. Some *passages* in *Plato* concern the *Anaximandrian form of Atheism* rather than the *Democritic* form. 

25. Why *Democritus* and *Leucippus* remodeled *Atheism* into the *Atomic Form*. 

26. That *besides the three forms of Atheism already mentioned*, we sometimes meet *with a fourth*. This form *supposes the Universe is not an animal, yet a kind of plant or vegetable, having one Plastic Nature in it* <note>A "plastic nature" refers to an unconscious, formative power that shapes matter</note>, *devoid of understanding and sense, which disposes and orders the whole*. 

27. That this *form of Atheism, which makes one Plastic Life preside over the whole, is different from the Hylozoic* <note>The belief that all matter is alive</note>, *in that it removes all randomness <note>original: fortuitousness</note> and subjects everything to the fate of one Plastic, methodical Nature*. 

28. Though it is possible that some *in all ages might have held this Atheistical concept*—that *things are managed by one regular and methodical, but unknowing and senseless Nature*—it seems to have been chiefly asserted by certain *false followers of Heraclitus and the Stoics*. Therefore, this *form of Atheism*, which supposes one *world-forming <note>original: Cosmoplastick</note> Nature*, may be called *Pseudo-Zenonian* <note>Named after Zeno, the founder of Stoicism, but implying a corrupted version of his teachings</note>. 

29. That, besides the *Philosophical Atheists*, *there have always been enthusiastic and fanatical Atheists*, though...

<summary>This page outlines the various historical forms of atheism, specifically distinguishing between the materialist theories of Anaximander and Democritus and the "Plastic Nature" theory of the Pseudo-Zenonians. It argues that while some ancient philosophers used divine language, they were often describing senseless matter rather than a conscious God.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the classification and critique of various forms of Atheism, specifically contrasting the Atomic and Hylozoic systems.</meta>

In some sense, all atheists may also be said to be both enthusiasts and fanatics, as they are led by an <note>original: ὁρμὴ ἄλογος</note> irrational impulse.

30. There cannot easily be any other form of atheism besides those four already mentioned, because all atheists are "corporealists" <note>those who believe only physical matter exists</note>, and yet not all corporealists are atheists; only those who claim the first principle of all things is not intellectual.

31. A classification of atheisms, producing the previously mentioned "quaternio" <note>a group of four</note> and showing the difference between them.

32. Those who talk of "sensitive and rational matter" are but bunglers at atheism; and the "canting" <note>hypocritical or jargon-filled</note> astrological atheists are not worth considering at all, because they do not understand their own positions.

33. Another classification of atheisms: they either derive the origin of things from a merely fortuitous <note>accidental</note> principle—the unguided motion of matter—or else from a "plastic" <note>formative or creative</note> and methodical, but senseless, nature. Which atheists denied the eternity of the world, and which asserted it.

34. Of these four forms of atheism, the "Atomic" (or Democritical) and the "Hylozoic" <note>the belief that matter itself is alive</note> (or Stratonical) are the chief; once these two are refuted, all atheism will be refuted.

35. Since these two forms of atheism are contrary to one another, we should reasonably focus first on the Atomic; however, we shall afterwards refute the Hylozoic and prove against all corporealists that neither thought nor life belongs to matter.

36. In the meantime, we shall not neglect any form of atheism but refute them all together, as they agree on one principle; we shall also show how the old Atomic atheists sufficiently overthrew the foundation of the Hylozoists.

37. It is observed here that the Hylozoists are not condemned merely for asserting a *plastic life* <note>an unconscious, organizing force in nature</note> distinct from animal life (which, along with most other philosophers, we judge highly probable if understood correctly), but for grossly misunderstanding it and attributing it to matter.

38. Although the refutation of atheist arguments should, according to the laws of method, have been reserved for the last part of this discourse, we have reasons to violate those laws and crave the reader's pardon for this "preposterousness" <note>original: reversing the natural order</note>. There is a significant observation by Plato: it is not only moral "vitiolity" <note>corruption or vice</note> that inclines men toward atheism, but also a desire to seem wiser than the rest of mankind. Since atheists make such a pretense of wisdom, it is a timely undertaking to prove that they stumble in all their "ratiocinations" <note>logical arguments</note>. We hope to make it appear that atheists are no "conjurers" <note>experts or magicians</note>, and that all forms of atheism are nonsense and impossibility.

We have now represented the grand mysteries of atheism, which may also be called the mysteries of the kingdom of darkness. Although some of them are only briefly hinted at here, they will be more fully examined later, when we provide an account of the atheists' endeavors to "solve the phenomenon of cogitation" <note>explain how thought arises from matter</note>. We have represented the chief grounds of atheism in general, as well as that most notorious form of atheism in particular called *Atomical*; but whereas there has been already mentioned...

# CHAPTER III.

We have mentioned another form of *atheism*, which we call *hylozoical* <note>original: "Hylozoical"; from the Greek words for "matter" and "life," the belief that all matter is alive.</note>. The principles of this system could not possibly be discussed in the previous section where we were presenting the most plausible arguments for *atheism*. This is because they are directly contrary to the principles of *atomical atheism*, and the two would have mutually destroyed each other. 

For, while *atomick atheism* supposes the concept or idea of a body to be nothing but *extended resisting bulk* <note>meaning matter that takes up space and has physical resistance but no internal life</note>, and consequently includes no form of *life* or *thought* <note>original: "Cogitation"</note> in it, *hylozoism* on the contrary claims that all body as such—and therefore every tiny atom of it—has *life essentially* belonging to it. This life consists of *natural perception and appetite*, though it lacks *animal sense* or *reflective knowledge* <note>the ability to think about one's own thoughts</note>. It is as if *life* and *matter* (or *extended bulk*) were merely two incomplete ways of looking at one and the same substance called *body*. 

By reason of this *life* (which is not *animal* but only *plastic* <note>original: "Plaſtical"; meaning a formative or creative power that shapes matter from within</note>), all parts of matter are supposed to be able to form themselves *skillfully* and *methodically* to the greatest advantage of their current capabilities. They do this without any deliberation or conscious thought. Therefore, they can sometimes, through physical organization, improve themselves further into *sense* and *self-enjoyment* in all animals, and even into *universal reason* and *reflective knowledge* in men. 

It is plain that if this were true, there would be no necessity at all for either an *incorporeal soul* in men to make them rational, or for any *Deity* in the whole universe to explain its regularity. One main difference between these two forms of atheism is this: *atomical atheism* supposes all *life* of any kind to be *accidental, producible* <note>original: "Generable"</note>, and *perishable* <note>original: "Corruptible"</note>. But *hylozoism* admits a certain *natural* or *plastic life* that is *essential* and *substantial, uncreatable* <note>original: "Ingenerable"</note>, and *indestructible* <note>original: "Incorruptible"</note>. However, it attributes this life only to *matter*, as it assumes there is no other substance in the world besides it.

II. Now, to prevent any mistakes, we think it appropriate to offer a caution here: just as every *atomist* is not necessarily an *atheist*, neither must every *hylozoist* be considered one. For whoever holds that *matter has life*, but nevertheless asserts that there is another kind of substance as well—one that is *immaterial* and *incorporeal*—is in no way guilty of that foul accusation of atheism. 

However, we should not hide the fact that there is a great difference between these two systems, *atomism* and *hylozoism*, in this regard. The former, *atomism* (as has been already stated), has a *natural kinship* and *connection* with the belief in incorporeal things, even though it was violently separated from it by the *Democritick atheists* <note>followers of Democritus, who used atomism to support atheism</note>. On the other hand, *hylozoism* seems to have a very close and intimate *correspondence* with *corporealism* <note>the belief that only physical bodies exist</note>. 

This is because, as previously indicated, if all *matter* as such has its own *life, perception*, and *self-active power*—by which it can shape itself to the best advantage, making this part a sun and that part an earth or planet, and constructing the bodies of animals most *skillfully*—and if it can also improve itself into *sense* and *self-enjoyment*, it might just as easily be thought capable of advancing itself higher into all the *acts of reason* and *understanding* in men. If that were the case, there would be no need for either an *incorporeal immortal soul* in men or a *Deity* in the universe. Indeed, it is not easily conceivable how anyone would be persuaded to admit...

<summary>This page defines Hylozoism as the belief that all matter possesses an inherent, "plastic" life, contrasting it with Atomick Atheism which views matter as lifeless bulk. The author argues that while atomism can coexist with religion, hylozoism is more naturally inclined toward atheism by removing the need for a Creator or a soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of Hylozoism—the belief that matter is inherently alive—and distinguishes between those who hold this view while remaining theists and those whose version of the theory leads inevitably to atheism.</meta>

# Every Hylozoist is not to be [Accounted an Atheist] BOOK I.

Such a monstrous paradox as this—that every atom of dust or other senseless matter is wiser than the greatest politician and the most acute philosopher that ever lived, because it possesses an infallible omniscience of all its own capabilities and congruities <note>original: "congruities"; refers to the inherent fitness or tendencies of matter to form specific structures</note>—would never be believed were it not for some strong prejudice against incorporeal substance <note>spiritual or non-physical reality</note> and a Deity. There is nothing so extravagant and outrageously wild that a mind once infected with atheistical foolishness and disbelief will not greedily swallow, rather than admit a Deity, which to such people is the highest of all imaginable paradoxes and the most frightening bugbear.

Notwithstanding all this, it must be admitted that it is possible for someone who truly believes in a Deity and an immortal rational soul to be persuaded of two things: first, that the sensitive soul in humans as well as animals is merely corporeal <note>physical or bodily</note>; and second, that there is a *material plastic life* <note>a formative, organizing power inherent in matter</note> in the seeds of all plants and animals by which they artificially form themselves. From there, they might descend further into *hylozoism* <note>the doctrine that all matter possesses life</note>—the idea that all matter, as such, has a kind of *natural life*, though not an *animal life* <note>conscious or sensory life</note>, within it. In consideration of this, we ought not to censure every *hylozoist* who professes to hold a belief in a Deity and an immortal rational soul as a mere *disguised atheist* or a *counterfeit, theatrical theist*.

### III.
But though every *hylozoist* is not necessarily an *atheist*, whoever is both a *hylozoist* and a *corporealist* <note>one who believes only physical matter exists</note> together—holding both the *life of matter* in the sense previously declared and also that there is no other *substance* in the world besides *body* and *matter*—cannot be excused from the charge of *atheism* for **two reasons**.

**First**, because although he derives the origin of all *things* not from what is perfectly *dead* and *stupid* <note>lacking sensation or thought</note>, as the *atomic atheist* does, but from that which has a kind of *life* or *perception* in it—even an infallible *omniscience* of whatever it can do or suffer, or of all its own capabilities and congruities, which seems to bear some *resemblance to a Deity*—yet all of this exists only by way of *natural* and not *animal perception*. It is indeed nothing but a *dull* and *drowsy*, *plastic* and *spermatic life* <note>spermatic: relating to the formative power in seeds or origins</note>, devoid of all *consciousness* and *self-enjoyment*. The *hylozoist's nature* is a piece of very mysterious nonsense: a thing perfectly wise without any knowledge or *consciousness* of itself. Whereas a *Deity*, according to the true notion of it, is such a *perfect understanding being* that, with full *consciousness* and *self-enjoyment*, is completely happy.

**Secondly**, because the *hylozoic corporealist*, supposing all *matter* as such to have *life* in it, must necessarily create an infinite number of those *lives* (since every atom of *matter* has a *life* of its own). These would be *coordinate* and *independent* of one another, and consequently, there would be as many independent first *principles* as there are atoms, with no one *common life* or *mind* ruling over the whole. Whereas, to assert a *God* is to derive all things <gloss>from some one principle</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἀφ᾽ ἑνὸς τινος (aph' henos tinos)</note>, or to suppose one *perfect living* and *understanding being* to be the *original* of all things and the *architect* of the whole *universe*.

Thus we see that the *hylozoic corporealist* is really an *atheist*, though carrying more the *semblance* and *disguise of a theist* than other [atheists]...

<summary>The author argues that while some theists mistakenly believe matter is alive, those who combine this "hylozoism" with the belief that only matter exists are effectively atheists because they deny a conscious, singular governing Mind.</summary>

# CHAPTER III.

<margin>Plato, *The Republic*, Book 5.</margin>
...other atheists, in that he attributes a kind of life to matter. For indeed every atheist must of necessity cast some of the incommunicable properties of the Deity, more or less, upon that which is not God—namely, matter. And those who do not attribute life to it must still bestow upon it necessary self-existence and make it the first principle of all things, which are the unique characteristics of the Deity. The *numen* <note>original: *Numen*; a Latin term for a spiritual force or local divinity</note> which the hylozoic <note>term: *Hylozoic*; from the Greek words for "matter" and "life," referring to the belief that all matter is alive</note> corporealist pays all his devotions to is a certain blind *she-god or goddess* called Nature, or the "Life of Matter." This is a very great mystery: a thing that is perfectly wise and infallibly omniscient without having any knowledge or consciousness at all. It is something like that "ancient riddle" in Plato <note>original: *πάλαιον αἴνιγμα*; *palaion ainigma*</note> "that a man who was not a man, seeing and not seeing, struck a bird that was not a bird, sitting on a branch that was not a branch, with a stone that was not a stone." <note>original: *ὅτι τε ἀνδρὸς βολῆς ὄντος εὐνοῦχον...*; This refers to a famous Greek riddle about a eunuch (the man who is not a man) hitting a bat (the bird that is not a bird) with a pumice stone (the stone that is not a stone) while it sat on a reed (the branch that is not a branch).</note> The only difference is this: that the riddle was an intelligible thing expressed in a humorous way, whereas this other theory seems to be perfect nonsense, being nothing but a misunderstanding of the plastic power <note>term: *Plastic Power*; the formative or creative force in nature</note>, as shall be shown afterwards.

## IV.

<margin>Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book 1.</margin>
<margin>St. Augustine, *The City of God*, Book 6, Chapter 10.</margin>
Now, the first and chief proponent of this hylozoic atheism was, as we conceive, Strato of Lampsacus. He was commonly called "the Naturalist" <note>original: *Physicus*</note> and had once been a student of Theophrastus and a famous Peripatetic <note>term: *Peripatetic*; a follower of Aristotle's philosophy</note>. However, he afterwards degenerated from a genuine Peripatetic into a new kind of atheist. For Velleius, an Epicurean atheist in Cicero's writings, reckons up all the various types of theists who had existed in former times and gives such a character of this Strato that he makes him out to be a strange kind of *atheistical theist*, or *divine atheist*, if we may use such a contradictory expression. His words are these: "Neither is Strato, commonly called the Naturalist or Physiologist, to be heard, who places all divinity in Nature, as having within itself the causes of all generations, corruptions, and growths, but without any manner of sense." <note>original: *Nec audiendus Strato, qui Physicus appellatur, qui omnem Vim Divinam in Natura sitam esse censet, quae Causas augendi minuendive habeat, sed careat omni sensu*</note>

Strato’s deity, therefore, was a certain *living* and *active*, but *senseless nature*. He did not derive the origin of all things from a mere accidental motion of atoms, as the Democritic and Epicurean atheists did. Because of this, he bore some slight resemblance to a theist; yet he was a downright atheist for all that, since his "God" was nothing more than a life of nature within matter that was devoid of sense and consciousness, and was multiplied along with the several parts of matter. He is described in a similar way by Seneca (quoted in St. Augustine) as a kind of mongrel thing between an atheist and a theist: "Shall I endure either Plato or the Peripatetic Strato, one of whom made God to be without a body, and the other without a mind?" <note>original: *Ego feram aut Platonem, aut Peripateticum Stratonem, quorum alter Deum sine Corpore fecit, alter sine Animo?*</note> In these words, Seneca taxes these two philosophers as being guilty of two contrary extremes: Plato, because he made God to be a pure mind or a perfectly incorporeal being; and Strato, because he made him to be a body without...

<summary>This page defines "hylozoic atheism," which views matter as possessing an unconscious life-force, and identifies the philosopher Strato of Lampsacus as its primary historical proponent.</summary>
<keywords>Hylozoism, Strato of Lampsacus, Nature, Atheism, Peripatetics, Plato, Seneca, Matter, Plastic Power</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Strato of Lampsacus and his specific form of atheism, contrasting it with the atomism of Democritus.</meta>

<page-num>108</page-num>
<header>Strato the Physicist, the First Book I.</header>

without a Mind, he acknowledging no other Deity than a certain stupid and <term>plastic life</term> <note>original: "Plaſtick Life"; a formative or creative power that acts unconsciously</note>, in all the several parts of Matter, without sense. Therefore this seems to be the only reason why *Strato* was thus sometimes reckoned amongst the Theists, though he was indeed an Atheist: because he dissented from that only form of Atheism then so commonly accepted, the Democritic and Epicurean, by attributing a kind of Life to Nature and Matter.

V.
<margin>*Academic Questions, book 4*</margin>
And that *Strato* was thus an Atheist, but of a different kind from Democritus, may further appear from this passage of Cicero <note>original: *Strato Lampſacenus negat operâ Deorum ſe uti ad fabricandum Mundum, quacunque ſint docet omnia eſſe Effecta Naturæ, nec ut ille, qui aſperis, & lævibus, & hamatis uncinatiſque Corporibus Concreta hæc eſſe dicat, interjecto Inani; Somnia cenſet hæc eſſe Democriti, non docentis ſed optantis*</note>: "*Strato* of Lampsacus denies that he makes any use of a God for the fabricating of the World, or the explaining the phenomena thereof; teaching all things to have been made by *Nature*. Yet he does not do so in such a manner as that man <note>Democritus</note> who affirmed them to be all joined together out of certain rough and smooth, hooked and crooked atoms, with empty space interspersed. He judges these things to be nothing but the mere dreams and delusions of Democritus, who was not teaching but merely wishing." Here we see that *Strato* denied the World to be made by a Deity or a perfectly understanding Nature, just as Democritus did. And yet he dissented from Democritus nonetheless, holding another kind of Nature as the origin of things than he did; for Democritus gave no account of any active principle and cause of motion, nor of the regularity that is in things. Democritus's Nature was nothing but the <term>fortuitous motion of matter</term> <note>random movement of physical particles</note>, but *Strato’s* Nature was an <term>inward plastic life</term> in the several parts of matter. By this, they could artificially frame themselves to the best advantage, according to their several capabilities, without any conscious or reflective knowledge. "Whatever either exists or is made," says the same author <note>Cicero; original: *Quicquid aut fit aut fiat, Naturæ vi, aut factum eſſe docet ponderibus & motibus*</note>, "*Strato* teaches to be made by certain inward natural forces and activities."

VI.
Furthermore, it is to be observed that though *Strato* thus attributed a certain kind of life to matter, yet he did by no means allow of any one common life—whether <term>sentient and rational</term> <note>feeling and thinking</note>, or <term>plastic and spermatic</term> <note>formative and seed-like</note> only—as ruling over the whole mass of matter and the corporeal universe. This is a thing in part affirmed by Plutarch, and may in part be gathered from these words of his: <gloss>He says that the world itself is not an animal (or a living god), but that the whole exists according to nature, and that chance provides the beginning, and thus each of the natural effects is accomplished.</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἢ κόσμον αὐτὸν ἢ ζῶον ἔναι φησι, τόδε κτ᾽ φύσιν ἔχειν τὸ πᾶν, καὶ ἐνδιδόναι τὸ αὐτόματον, ἔται ἔτω περαίνειν τῆ φυσικῶν πιθανῶν ἕκατον.</note> *Strato* affirms that the World is no animal (or God) but that what is natural in everything follows something <term>fortuitous antecedent</term> <note>a random event that happened before</note>, <term>chance first beginning, and nature acting consequently thereupon</term>. The full sense of this seems to be this: that though *Strato* did not derive the origin of all worldly things from mere <term>fortuitous mechanism</term>, as Democritus before him had done, but supposed a life and natural perception in the matter that was directive of it, yet he did not acknowledge any one common life, whether animal or plastic, as governing...

<summary>This page distinguishes Strato’s "Hylozoic" atheism—which attributes an unconscious, formative life to matter—from the purely mechanical atomism of Democritus. While Strato rejected a conscious God, he argued that matter possesses its own internal power to organize itself without needing random collisions or a universal soul.</summary>

# CHAPTER III. The Hylozoic Atheist.

governing and swaying the whole, but only supposing the several parts of matter to have so many several *plastic lives* <note>original: "Plastick Lives"; refers to an innate power in matter to form and organize itself without conscious thought</note> of their own, he must necessarily attribute something to *Fortune*, and make the mundane system <note>The physical universe</note> depend upon a certain mixture of *chance* and *plastic* or *orderly nature* both together. Consequently, he must be a hylozoist <note>One who believes that matter is inherently alive</note>. Thus we see that these are two schemes of atheism, very different from one another: that which fetches the origin of all things from the mere *fortuitous* and *unguided motion* of matter, without any *vital* or *directive principle*; and that which derives it from a certain mixture of *chance* and the *life of matter* both together, by supposing a *plastic life*, not in the whole universe as one single thing, but in all the several parts of matter by themselves. The first of these is the *atomic* and *Democritic atheism*; the second is the *hylozoic* and *Stratonic atheism*.

VII. It may perhaps be suspected by some that the famous Hippocrates, who lived long before Strato, was a supporter of hylozoic *atheism* because of such passages in his writings as these: <margin>VI. *Epidemics* §. 5.</margin> "Nature is unlearned or untaught, but it learns from itself what things it ought to do." <gloss>Alternative reading: "And without being taught, it does divine things."</gloss> And again, <margin>On Nature</margin> "Nature finds out ways for itself, not by reasoning." <note>original: "ἀνδέλεια ἡ φύσις αὐτὴ ἑαυτῆ τᾶς ἐφόδους ἐκ ἐκ διανοίας"</note> But there is nothing more affirmed here concerning *nature* by Hippocrates than what might be affirmed likewise of the *Aristotelian* and *Platonic nature*, which is supposed to act for *ends* <note>Purposes or goals</note>, though without *consultation* and *reasoning*. 

And I must confess, it seems to me in no way unbecoming of a *theist* to acknowledge such a *nature* or *principle* in the universe that may act according to *rule* and *method* for the *sake of ends*, and in order to achieve the *best*, even though it does not itself understand the reason for what it does. This is still supposed to act dependently upon a higher *intellectual principle*, having been first set to work and employed by it; otherwise, the concept is nonsense. But to assert any such *plastic nature* as being *independent* of any higher *intellectual principle*—and so being itself the first and highest *principle of activity* in the universe—this indeed must necessarily be either that hylozoic *atheism* already spoken of, or else another different *form of atheism* which shall be described later. 

However, though Hippocrates was a *corporealist* <note>One who believes only physical bodies exist</note>, we conceive he ought not to fall under the suspicion of either of those two atheisms. This is because he himself plainly asserts a higher *intellectual principle* in the universe than such a *plastic nature*: namely, an *Heraclitic corporeal God*, or *understanding fire*, which is *immortal* and pervades the whole world. In his own words: <margin>On Principles or On Flesh, Section 1.</margin> "It seems to me that what we call heat or fire is immortal and omniscient; it sees, hears, and knows all things, not only those that are present, but also those in the future." <note>original: "Δοκῦσα δὲ μοι ὁ καλέομεν θεμόν, ἀθάνατόν τε ἔνου..."</note> Therefore, we conclude that Hippocrates was neither a *hylozoic* nor a *Democritic atheist*, but an *Heraclitic corporeal theist*.

<page-num>110</page-num>
<header>Plato's Observations, Book I.</header>

VIII. It might perhaps be thought that Plato, in his dialogue the *Sophist*, intends to describe <term>Hylozoic Atheism</term> <note>original: "Hylozoick Atheism"; the belief that matter itself is alive and is the cause of all things without a God</note> when he declares it to be the opinion of many "that nature generates all things from a certain spontaneous cause, without any reason or understanding" <note>original: τὴν φύσιν πάντα γενᾶν, ἀπὸ τινὸς αἰτίας αὐτομάτης, ἢ καὶ διανοίας φύσεως</note>. But here the word "spontaneous" <note>original: αὐτομάτης</note> may just as well be rendered as "fortuitous" (happening by chance); regardless, there is no necessity that this should be understood as an "artificial" or "methodical" unknowing nature. It is true indeed that Plato himself seems to acknowledge a certain <term>plastic</term> <note>meaning "formative" or "shaping"</note> or methodical nature in the universe, subordinate to the Deity—that perfect Mind which is the supreme governor of all things. This may be gathered from his words: "Nature, together with reason and mind, or according to reason, governs and arranges all things" <note>original: τὴν φύσιν μετὰ λόγε ἢ σὺν λόγῳ καὶ νῷ τὰ πάντα διακοσμεῖν</note>. 

<margin>In the *Sophist*.</margin> Here he supposes a certain regular nature to be a partial and subordinate cause of things under the Divine Intellect. It is very probable that Aristotle derived his entire doctrine concerning a "regular and artificial nature" which acts for specific ends from the Platonic school. But as for any form of atheism that would suppose a *plastic* or *regular*, but *senseless* nature—either in the whole world or in the individual parts of matter—to be the highest principle of all things, we do not believe there is any hint of it to be found anywhere in Plato. 

For in his *Laws* <note>original: *De Legibus*</note>, where he professedly argues against atheism, he describes its doctrine in this manner: "They declare that the greatest and most beautiful things were produced by nature and chance, but that the smaller things were produced by human art" <note>original: τὰ μὲν μέγιστα καὶ κάλλιστα ἀποφάζεται φύσιν ἢ τύχην, τὰ δὲ σμικρότερα τέχνην</note>. 

<margin>Book 10.</margin> The plain meaning of this is that the first origin of things, and the frame of the whole universe, proceeded from a mere fortuitous nature, or the motion of matter unguided by any art or method. This is further explained in the following words: "They say that fire, water, earth, and air all exist by nature and chance, and that art came later" <note>original: πῦρ καὶ ὕδωρ καὶ γῆν καὶ ἀέρα, φύσει πάντα εἶναι καὶ τύχῃ φασὶν τέχνην δὲ ὕστερον</note>. He explains that the first elements—fire, water, air, and earth—were all made by nature and chance, without any art or method. Then, the bodies of the sun, moon, and stars, and the entire heavens, were afterward made out of those elements; they were viewed as devoid of all life, and only moved and mingled together by chance. Lastly, the whole mundane system, together with the orderly seasons of the year, as well as plants, animals, and men, arose in the same way from the mere fortuitous motion of senseless and stupid matter. 

Plato states this controversy between Theists and Atheists in the very same manner again in his *Philebus*: 

<margin>Page 28, Serranus edition.</margin> "Shall we say, O Protarchus, that this whole universe and this so-called 'all' is ordered by a certain irrational, reckless, and fortuitous power, and just as it happens? Or on the contrary (as our forefathers have told us), that Mind and a certain wonderful wisdom did at first frame, and still govern, all things?" <note>original: πότερον ὦ πρώταρχε, τὰ σύμπαντα, καὶ τάδε τὰ καλεύμενον ὅλον, ἐπιτετάρθαι φάμεν τινὶ ἀλόγῳ καὶ εἰκῇ δύναμιν, καὶ τῷ ὅπη ἔτυχεν; ἢ τἀναντία, καθάπερ οἱ πρόσθεν ἡμῖν ἔλεγον, νῦν καὶ φρόνησιν τινὰ θαυμασίαν συντάττεσαν διακυβερνᾶν</note>

<summary>The author argues that Plato did not recognize "Hylozoic Atheism" (the idea of a self-organizing, living matter), but rather viewed atheism as the belief that the universe arose through blind chance and the fortuitous motion of senseless matter.</summary>

### CHAPTER III. Of Fortuitous Atheisms.
<page-num>III</page-num>

Therefore, we conclude that Plato took no notice of any other form of atheism then being promoted than that which derives all things from a mere *fortuitous principle*—from nature and chance. This is the unguided motion of matter, without any *plastic* <note>original: "Plastick Artificialness"; refers to a formative or creative power that shapes matter into organized forms</note> *artfulness* or *methodicalness* in either the whole universe or its parts. But because this kind of atheism, which derives all things from a mere *fortuitous nature*, had been managed in two ways—by Democritus through the theory of atoms, and by Anaximander and others through the theory of forms and qualities (which we will discuss next)—the atheism that Plato opposes was either the *Democritic* or the *Anaximandrian atheism*, or, most probably, both of them together.

IX. It is hardly imaginable that there were no philosophical atheists in the world before Democritus and Leucippus. Plato long ago concluded that there have been atheists, more or less, in every age, when he addresses his young atheist in this manner: <margin>p. 888. *Salmasius Edition*</margin> "You are not the only one, nor are you and your friends the first to have held this opinion; for there are always more or fewer people suffering from this disease." <note>original Greek: οὐ σὺ μόνον· οὐδὲ σὺ σοι φίλοι πρῶτοι ἢ πρῶτον ταύτην δόξαν ἔδει δόξαν ἔχετε, γίγνονται γὰρ ἀεὶ πλείους ἢ ἐλάττους ταύτην τὴν νόσον ἔχοντες.</note> The full sense of this seems to be: *Neither you (my son) nor your friends (Democritus, Leucippus, and Protagoras) are the first who have entertained this opinion concerning the gods, but there have always been some, more or less, sick of this atheistic disease.* Therefore, we shall now make a diligent search and inquiry to see if we can find any other philosophers who were atheists before Democritus and Leucippus, and what form of atheism they held.

Aristotle, in his *Metaphysics*, speaking of the four types of causes <note>original: "Quaternio of Causes"; Aristotle's four causes: material, formal, efficient, and final</note>, affirms that many of those who first practiced philosophy assigned only a *material cause* to the whole system of the world, without either an *intending* <note>final cause or purpose</note> or *efficient cause*. The reason for this, he suggests, was that they asserted *matter* to be the only substance. They believed that everything else in the world, besides the substance or bulk of matter, was nothing more than different *passions* <note>original: πάθη; here meaning "undergoing change" or "states of being"</note>, *affections, accidents*, and *qualities* of matter. These were all generated out of matter and could be corrupted back into it, while the substance of matter always remained the same—neither created nor destroyed, but unmade from eternity. Aristotle’s words are these: <margin>*Book 1, Chapter 3*</margin> "Of those who first philosophized, most thought that the principles of all things were only those of a material nature. That from which all things are, and from which they first come into being, and into which they are finally destroyed—the substance remaining while the qualities change—this they say is the element and the principle of all beings." <note>original Greek: τῶν πρώτων φιλοσοφησάντων, οἱ πλεῖστοι τὰς ἐν ὕλης εἴδει μόνον ᾠήθησαν ἀρχὰς εἶναι πάντων, ἐξ ἧς ἔστι πάντα τὰ ὄντα, καὶ ἐξ ἧς γίγνεται πρῶτον, καὶ εἰς ὃ φθείρεται τελευταῖον, τῆς μὲν οὐσίας ὑπομενούσης, τοῖς δὲ πάθεσι μεταβαλλούσης, τοῦτο στοιχεῖον, καὶ ταύτην τῶν ὄντων τὴν ἀρχήν φασιν εἶναι.</note> Most of those who first philosophized took notice of no other principle of things in the universe than what is referred to the *material cause*. For that out of which all things exist, out of which they are first made, and into which they are all at last corrupted and resolved—the substance always remaining the same and being changed only in its passions and qualities—this they concluded to be the first original and principle of all things.

<summary>The author argues that atheism existed long before Democritus, rooted in the belief that the universe arose by chance from matter alone. He cites Aristotle to show that early philosophers often ignored purposeful causes, viewing matter as the only eternal substance.</summary>
