# Aristotle's Critique of the Old Materialists: Book I.

X. But the meaning of these old material philosophers will be better understood by those exceptions which *Aristotle* makes against them, which are two. First, because they acknowledged no other substance besides matter that might be an active principle in the universe, it was not possible for them to give any account of the origin of motion and action. <margin>Aristotle, *Metaphysics*, Book 1, Chapter 3.</margin> <note>original: Εἰ γὰρ ὅτι μάλιστα παρά γε γένεσις ἐκ τινὸς, ὡς ἑνὸς ἢ ἐκ πλειόνων ἐστὶν, διὰ τί τ8το συμβαίνει, καὶ τί τὸ αἴτιον; ἢ γὰρ δὴ τό γε ὑποκείμενον αὐτὸ ποιεῖ μεταβάλλειν ἑαυτὸ· λέγω δ᾽ οἷον, ὅτε τὸ ξύλον, ὅτε τὸ χαλκὸς αἴτιον τ8 μεταβάλλειν ἑκάτερον αὐτὸ· ἀλλὰ ποιεῖ τὸ μὲν ξύλον κλίνην, ὁ δ᾽ χαλκὸς ἀνδριάντα, ἀλλ᾽ ἕτερον τι τὸ μεταβολῆς αἴτιον· τὸ δὲ τ8το ζητεῖν, ὅτι τὸ ἕτερον ζητεῖν ἀρχὴν, ὡς καὶ ἡμεῖς φαίημεν, ὅθεν ἡ ἀρχὴ τ8 κινήσεως.</note> *Even if all generation <note>The process of coming into being.</note> is made ever so much out of something as the matter, yet the question still is: by what means does this come to pass, and what is the active cause which produces it? This is because the subject-matter cannot change itself. As for example, neither timber nor brass is the cause that either of them is changed; for timber alone does not make a bed, nor brass a statue, but there must be something else as the cause of the change. To inquire after this is to inquire after another principle, besides matter, which we would call the source from which motion springs.* In which words *Aristotle* intimates that these old material philosophers shuffled *motion* and *action* into the world unaccountably, or without a cause; because they acknowledged no other principle of things besides passive *matter*, which could never move, change, or alter itself.

XI. And *Aristotle's* second exception against these old material philosophers is this: that since there could be no intending causality <note>Purposeful design or "final cause."</note> in senseless and stupid matter, which they made to be the only principle of all things, they were not able to assign <note>original: τ8 εὖ καὶ καλῶς αἴτιον</note> *any cause of what is well and fit*, and so could give no account of the regular and orderly frame of this mundane system. <margin>*Metaphysics*, Book 1, Chapter 3.</margin> <note>original: τὰ μὲν ἔχειν, τὰ δ᾽ γίγνεσθαι τ8 ὄντων, ἴσως ὅτε γῆ, ὅτ᾽ ἄλλο τι τῶν τοιέτων δ᾽ αἴτιον εἶναι. δῆλ᾽ αὐτὰς αὐτομάτως, ἐκ τύχης τοιέτων ὑπάρχειν πρᾶγμα καλῶς ἔχειν.</note> *That things partly are so well in the world, and partly are made so well, cannot be imputed either to earth or water, or any other senseless body; much less is it reasonable to attribute so noble and excellent an effect as this to mere chance or fortune.* 

Where *Aristotle* again suggests that as these material philosophers shuffled motion into the world without a cause, so likewise they must suppose this motion to be altogether fortuitous <note>Happening by chance.</note> and unguided. In doing so, they essentially make fortune—which is nothing but the absence or defect of an intending cause—supply the place of both the active and intending cause (that is, the efficient and final causes). 

Whereupon *Aristotle* adds a commendation of *Anaxagoras* as the first of the Ionian philosophers who introduced *Mind* or *Intellect* as a principle in the universe. He notes that in this respect, *Anaxagoras* alone seemed to be sober and in his wits compared with those others who went before him, who talked so idly and atheistically. For *Anaxagoras's* principle was such, says *Aristotle*, as was <note>original: ὡς ἅμα τ8 καλᾶς αἰτία, ἢ τ8αὕτη ὅθεν ἡ κίνησις ὑπάρχει</note> *at once a cause of motion and also of what is well and fit.*

<summary>Aristotle critiques early materialists for failing to explain the origin of motion and the presence of order in the universe, arguing that passive matter cannot move or organize itself without an intelligent "Mind."</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, Metaphysics, Materialism, Anaxagoras, Efficient Cause, Final Cause, Motion, Teleology, Ionian Philosophers</keywords>

--- Page 129 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of ancient Greek philosophical schools, specifically contrasting the views of Anaxagoras, Plato, and Aristotle against the early Materialists regarding the origin of the universe.</meta>

# CHAPTER II. Philosophers, Atheists.

XI.
Mind is the cause of all the regularity, fitness, beauty, and order that exists in the whole universe. And thus it seems Anaxagoras himself had determined: <margin>Anaxagoras, cited in Aristotle's *On the Soul*, Book 1, Chapter 2.</margin> <gloss>Anaxagoras says that Mind is the cause of doing things well or rightly</gloss> <note>original: Ἀναξαγόρας τὸ αἴτιον τῶ καλῶς ἢ ὀρθῶς νῦν λέγῃ</note>. This is because it is the nature of Mind to aim at goals and the Good, and to order one thing fitly for the sake of another. For this reason, Anaxagoras concluded that Good, as well as Mind, was a primary principle of the universe. <margin>Aristotle, *Metaphysics*, Book 4, Chapter 10.</margin> <gloss>Anaxagoras makes the ancient principle move things—or rather, that which moves things now—but everything is for the sake of something else, so that the other is the cause</gloss> <note>original: Ἀναξαγόρας μὲν κινεῖν τὸ ἀρχαῖον, ὃ δὲ νῦν κινεῖ, ἀλλὰ πανὰ ἕνεκα τινος, ὥσε ἕτερον</note>. Anaxagoras makes Good a principle, as that which initiates movement. For though Mind moves Matter, it moves it for the sake of something; Mind itself is, as it were, first moved by the Good. Therefore, Good is also a principle. We note this specifically to show how well these three philosophers—*Aristotle, Plato,* and *Anaxagoras*—agreed together in this excellent truth: *That Mind and Good are the First Principle of all things in the universe.*

XII.
And now we think it is sufficiently evident that those old Materialists mentioned in *Aristotle*, whoever they were, were downright Atheists. This is not simply because they claimed all substance was body or matter; for *Heraclitus* first, and after him *Zeno*, did the same. They derived the origin of all things from Fire, just as *Anaximenes* did from Air, and as *Thales* is supposed by *Aristotle* to have done from Water. They did this with a bit more seeming plausibility, since Fire—being a more subtle and moveable body than any other—was thought by some of those ancients to be <gloss>the most incorporeal of all bodies</gloss> <note>original: ἀσωμάτωτον</note>. For that same reason, Earth was rejected by all those corporeal philosophers as a primary principle because of the coarseness of its parts. 

However, *Heraclitus* and *Zeno* are not considered Atheists despite this. They supposed their *Fiery Matter* to possess not only Life, but also a perfect *Understanding* that belonged to it originally; they also believed the whole world to be a living animal. In contrast, the Materialists mentioned by *Aristotle* made senseless and stupid Matter, devoid of all *Understanding* and *Life*, the first principle and root of all things. When they supposed that *Life* and *Understanding* (as well as all other differences between things) were nothing but mere <term>passions</term> <note>In this context, "passions" refers to passive effects or properties rather than emotions.</note> and accidents of matter—capable of being generated from it and decaying back into it—they were saying these qualities were produced only in a secondary way. They believed life arose from the accidental mixing of those first elementary qualities: Heat and Cold, Moist and Dry, Thick and Thin. They plainly implied that the substance of Matter is, in itself, devoid of all *Life* and *Understanding*. Now, if it is not Atheism to derive the origin of all things—even of *Life* and *Mind* itself—from dead and stupid Matter moved by chance, then there can be no such thing as Atheism at all.

XIII.
Moreover, *Aristotle*’s Materialists concluded that everything besides the substance of Matter (which is in itself indifferent to all things) was <term>generable and corruptible</term> <note>Meaning they are created and will eventually be destroyed or decay.</note>. This includes all particular and distinct beings. *Plato* takes notice of this as an Atheistic principle, expressing it in these words: <gloss>For nothing ever truly is, but everything is always becoming</gloss> <note>original: Ἔτι μὲν γὰρ οὐδέποτε ἔσιν, ἀεὶ ὃ γίγνεται</note>.

<summary>The author argues that while some ancient philosophers identified matter (like fire) as the primary substance, they were not atheists if they believed that matter possessed inherent life and intelligence. True atheism, the author contends, is the belief that life and mind emerge accidentally from dead, senseless matter.</summary>

<header>The great Difference between the BOOK I.</header>

thing is made and generated. *Forasmuch* as it plainly follows from hence, that not only all *animals* and the *souls* of men, but also if there were any *gods*—which some of those *materialists* would not hesitate, at least verbally, to acknowledge (meaning by that certain *understanding beings* superior to men)—these likewise must necessarily have been all generated, and consequently be corruptible <note>subject to decay or death</note>. Now to say that there is no other *God* than such as was made and generated, and which may be again *unmade*, *corrupted*, and *die*, or that there was once no God at all until he was made out of the matter, and that there may be none again—this is all one as to deny the thing itself. For a *native* <note>original: "native," meaning born or having a beginning</note> and *mortal God* is a pure *contradiction*. Therefore, whereas *Aristotle* in his *Metaphysics* tells us of certain theologians, *who generate all things out of night and chaos* <note>original: οἱ ἐκ νυκτὸς καὶ χάους γεννῶντες</note>, (such as did generate all things, even the *gods* themselves, out of *night* and *chaos*), we must necessarily pronounce of such *theologians* as these—who were *theogonists* <note>those who describe the genealogy or birth of gods</note> and generated all the *gods* without exception out of *senseless* and *stupid matter*—that they were but a kind of *atheistical theologians* or *theological atheists*. For though they did admit of certain beings to which they attributed the *name of gods*, yet according to the true *notion of God*, they really acknowledged none at all (that is, no *understanding nature* as the *original of things*). Instead, *night* and *chaos*, *senseless* and *stupid matter*, *fortuitously moved*, was to them the highest of all *divinities* <note>original: "numens," from the Latin numen, referring to divine power or deity</note>. So that this theology of theirs was a thing wholly founded in *atheistical nonsense*.

<margin>Book 14, chapter 8.</margin>
XIV. And now we think it seasonable here to observe how vast a difference there was between these old *materialists* in *Aristotle* and those other *philosophers* mentioned before in the first chapter, who determined *that no real entity at all is generated or corrupted into nothing* <note>original: ἐν οὐδενὸς ἐκ γίγνεσθαι ἐδὲ φθείρεσθαι ἐς οὐδέν</note>. They held that no *real entity* at all was generated or corrupted for this reason: because *nothing* could be made out of *nothing*. These were chiefly the *philosophers of the Italic* or *Pythagorean succession*, and their design in it was not—as *Aristotle* was pleased somewhere to affirm—*to do away with all generation* <note>original: ἀνελῶν πᾶσαν τὼν γένεσιν</note>, or to contradict common sense and experience by denying all *natural generations* and *alterations*. Rather, they intended only to interpret nature rightly in them, and that in a way of opposition to those *atheistic materialists*, after this manner: That in all the *mutations of nature*, *generations*, and *alterations*, there was neither any new *substance* made which was not before, nor any entity really distinct from the *pre-existing substances*. Instead, there was only that *substance* which was before, diversely *modified*; and so *nothing produced* in *generations* but new *modifications*, *mixtures*, and *separations* of *pre-existing substances*.

Now this doctrine of theirs aimed at these two things: First, the taking away of such *qualities* and *forms of body* as were commonly conceived to be things really distinct from the *substance* of extended *bulk* and all its *modifications* of more or less *magnitude*, *figure*, *position* <note>original: "site"</note>, *motion*, or *rest*. Because, if there were any such things as these produced in the *natural generations* and *alterations of bodies*, there would then be some *real entity made out of nothing* <note>original: ἐκ μηδενὸς ἐν μηδεχῶν</note>.

<summary>The author argues that "generated gods" born from matter are a contradiction in terms, labeling such thinkers "theological atheists." He contrasts this with the Pythagorean view that substance is eternal and only its modifications change.</summary>

# CHAPTER II. Pythagoreans and the Old Materialists.

*Concerning nothing existing*, out of *Nothing Inexistent* or *Pre-existent* <note>original: "περὶ οὐδενὸς ὄντος" — the philosophical principle that nothing can come from nothing</note>. Therefore they concluded that these supposed *Forms* and *Qualities* of *Bodies* were really nothing else but the different *Modifications* of *Pre-existent Matter* in respect of *Magnitude, Figure, Position* <note>original: "Site"</note>, and *Motion* or *Rest*, or different *Concretions* <note>term: the thickening or gathering of particles</note> and *Secretions* <note>term: the separation or thinning of particles</note>. These are no *Entities* really distinct from the *Substance*, but only cause different *Appearances* <note>original: "Phasmata"</note>, *Fancies*, and *Apparitions* in us.

The second thing which this *Doctrine* aimed at was establishing the *Incorporeity* <note>term: the state of having no physical body or matter</note> and *Ingenerability* <note>term: the quality of being unable to be "generated" or created out of matter</note> of all *Souls*. For since *Life*, *Thought* <note>original: "Cogitation"</note>, *Sense*, and *Understanding* could not be resolved into those *Modifications* of *Matter*—*Magnitude, Figure, Position*, and *Motion*—or into *Mechanism* and *Fancy*, but must necessarily be *Entities* really distinct from *Extended Bulk* or *Dead* and *Stupid Matter*; they concluded that therefore *Souls* could not be generated out of *Matter*. This is because such a generation would be the *Production* of some *Real Entity* out of *Nothing Inexisting* or *Pre-existing*. Instead, they must be another kind of *Incorporeal Substance* which could no more be *Generated* or *Corrupted* <note>term: "Corrupted" here means destroyed or decomposed into parts</note> than the *Substance* of *Matter* itself. Therefore, they must either *Pre-exist* in *Nature* before *Generations* or else be divinely *Created* and *Infused* into them.

It has been already proved in the *First Chapter* that the *Result* of that *Pythagorean Doctrine*—*That Nothing could be Generated out of Nothing pre-existing*—amounted to those two things mentioned: namely, the *Asserting* of the *Incorporeity* and *Ingenerability* of *Souls*, and the *Rejecting* of those *Fantastic Entities* of *Forms* and *Real Qualities* of *Bodies*. It resolved all *Corporeal Phenomena* into *Figures* or *Atoms* and the different *Apparitions* or *Fancies* caused by them. This latter point may be further confirmed from a passage of *Aristotle's*, where after he had declared that *Democritus* and *Leucippus* made the *Soul* and *Fire* consist of round *Atoms* or *Figures*, like those

<margin>Aristotle, *On Physics* <note>original: "de Nat. Auscult."</note>, Book 1, Chapter 2.</margin>

*shreds in the air* <note>original: "ἐς τῶ ἀέρι ἐύσματα"</note>—those *Fragments* <note>original: "Ramenta"</note> that appear in the *Air* when *Sunbeams* are transmitted through *Crannies*—he adds: *It seems that what is said among the Pythagoreans has the same meaning; for some of them said the soul is the fragments in the air, while others said it is that which moves them* <note>original: "ἔοικε τῶ ἐκ τῆς πυρὸς ἐκπορευομένων λεγόμενον, τῆν αὐτὴν ἔχειν διάνοιαν, ἐφασαν αὐτῶ, Ψυχὴν εἶναι τὰ ἐν τῶ ἀέρι ἐύσματα, οἱ δ᾽, τὸ ταῦτα κινεῖν"</note>. And that which is said among the *Pythagoreans* seems to have the same sense; for some of them affirm that the *Soul* is those very *Fragments, Scraps*, or *Atoms*, but others of them say that it is That which *Moves* them. The latter were doubtless the genuine *Pythagoreans*. However, it is plain from this that the old *Pythagoreans* explained nature <note>original: "Physiologized"</note> by *Fragments*—that is, *Figures* and *Atoms*—and not by *Qualities* and *Forms*, just as *Democritus* did.

But *Aristotle's Materialists*, on the contrary, took it for granted that *Matter* or *Extended Bulk* is the only *Substance*. They believed that the *Qualities* and *Forms* of *Bodies* are *Entities* really distinct from those *Modifications* of *Magnitude, Figure, Position, Motion*, or *Rest*. Finding also by experience that these were continually *Generated* and *Corrupted*, and likewise that *Life, Sense*, and *Understanding* were produced in the *Bodies* of such *Animals* where they had not been before, and

Consequently, they believed that everything in the whole world, besides the *substance* of matter, was *made* or *generated*, and might be again *corrupted*.

<margin>Book 3, Chapter 1.</margin>
Of this atheistic doctrine, *Aristotle* speaks elsewhere, as in his book *On the Heavens*: <note>original Greek: εἰσὶ γάρ τινες οἱ φασιν... μετασχηματίζεσθαι</note> "There are some who affirm that *nothing* is *un-generable* <note>original: "Ingenerable"; something that cannot be created because it has always existed</note>, but that all things are *made*; as *Hesiod* especially, and also among the rest those who first *physiologized* <note>original: "Physiologized"; studied or wrote about the laws of nature</note>. Their meaning was that all other things are *made* (or *generated*) and did *flow*, none of them having any *stability*; only that there was one thing (namely *matter*) which always remained, out of which all those other things were *transformed* and *metamorphosed*."

<margin>Book 2, Chapter 1.</margin>
Though as to *Hesiod*, *Aristotle* afterwards speaks differently. So likewise in his *Physics*, after he had declared that some of the ancients made air, some water, and some other matter the principle of all things, he adds: <note>original Greek: τῦτ ἔτι ἃ τούτων φασὶν εἶναι... ἀπειρεκίς</note> "This they affirmed to be all the *substance* or *essence* that existed; but all other things were the *passions, affections,* and *dispositions* of it. Therefore, they held that this matter was *eternal*, as being capable of no change, but all other things were *infinitely generated* and *corrupted*."

XV. But these materialists were sometimes assaulted by the other Italic philosophers <note>The "Italic" school refers to the Pythagoreans and Eleatics who argued for the permanence of true being.</note> in the manner previously declared: that no *real entities*, *distinct* from the *modifications* of any *substance*, could be *generated* or *corrupted*, because *nothing* could come from *nothing* nor go to *nothing*. These materialists would not seem to plainly contradict that theorem, but only endeavored to interpret it into compliance with their own *hypothesis*. They distinguished the *sense* of it in this manner: that it ought to be understood only of the *substance* of matter and nothing else. Namely, that no *matter* could be *made* or *corrupted*, but that all other things whatsoever—not only *forms* and *qualities* of bodies, but also *souls*, life, sense, and understanding—though really different from magnitude, figure, position, and motion, yet ought to be accounted only the *passions* <note>original: "πάθη" (pathe); meaning the passive properties or accidental qualities of a substance</note> and accidents of this matter. Therefore, they could be generated out of it and corrupted again into it, and that without the production or destruction of any real entity, matter being the only thing that is such.

<margin>Metaphysics, Book 8, Chapter 3.</margin>
All this we learn from these words of *Aristotle*: <note>original Greek: ἃ διὰ τῦτο, ἃ ἔτε γίνεσθαι... σωζομένης ἐκείνης</note> "And for this reason, they say that nothing is either generated or destroyed in an absolute sense. Just as we do not say that a man is 'generated' in an absolute sense when he becomes beautiful or musical, nor 'destroyed' when he loses these habits, because the subject—*Socrates* himself—remains the same. So it is with everything else; there must be some one nature (or more than one) from which other things are generated while that original substance is preserved."

<header>CHAPTER III. Interpreted: Nothing out of Nothing.</header>

The sense of which is this: *And therefore, as to that axiom of some philosophers—that nothing is either generated or destroyed—these materialists admit it to be true only in respect to the substance of matter, which is always preserved as the same. For example, they say: we do not say that Socrates is simply or absolutely "made" when he becomes either handsome or musical, nor that he is "destroyed" when he loses those qualities, because the subject, Socrates, still remains the same person. In the same way, we should not say that anything else is absolutely either generated or corrupted, because the substance or matter of everything always continues. For there must necessarily be some certain nature from which all other things are generated, while that nature remains one and the same.*

We have noted this passage of Aristotle's specifically because this is exactly the doctrine of atheists today: that the substance of matter (or extended bulk) is the only real entity. Therefore, they claim it is the only "unmade" thing—neither able to be generated nor created, but necessarily existing from eternity. They argue that whatever else exists in the world—such as life, animal nature, soul, and mind—are all merely "accidents" <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is an attribute that does not belong to the essence of a thing.</note> and affections of this matter. By treating them as if they had no real entity of their own, they claim these things are generated out of nothing and corrupted into nothing, so long as the matter they inhabit remains the same. The result of this logic is nothing less than this: that there can be no other gods, or God, except such as were first made or generated out of senseless matter, and may be corrupted back into it again. And here indeed lies the "grand mystery" of atheism: that everything besides the *substance of matter is made or generated, and may be again unmade or corrupted.*

However, Anaxagoras—though an Ionic philosopher and therefore, as shall be explained later, a successor to those atheistic materialists—was eventually so convinced by the Pythagorean doctrine (that no entity could be naturally generated out of nothing) that he departed from his predecessors on this point. For this reason, he acknowledged mind and soul—that is, all thinking being—to be a substance really distinct from matter, neither generated out of it nor corruptible into it. He also believed that the forms and qualities of bodies must pre-exist before they are "generated" and remain after they are "corrupted." Because he could not yet conceive of these qualities as anything other than things distinct from the modifications of size, figure, position, and motion, he believed they existed in certain "similar atoms" and were merely separated or gathered together in them. By this means, he introduced a certain "spurious" <note>original: "spurious" meaning a false or illegitimate version</note> atomism of his own. For whereas the genuine atomists before his time had supposed <term>ὅλως ἀνομοεῖς</term> <note>original: "holos anomoies" — entirely dissimilar</note>, or dissimilar atoms devoid of all forms and qualities, to be the principles of all bodies, Anaxagoras substituted in their place his <term>ὅμοιομέρεια</term> <note>original: "homoiomereia" — parts similar to the whole</note>, his "similar atoms," endowed from eternity with all manner of forms and qualities incorruptibly.

XVI. We have made it manifest that those material philosophers described by Aristotle were absolute atheists, not merely because they made body to be the only substance (though that is something Aristotle himself justly rebukes them for in these...

<margin>Book 1, Chapter 10.</margin>
Now we shall take notice of an objection made by some recent writers against this Aristotelian accusation of the old philosophers. This objection is founded upon a passage of Aristotle's own, who elsewhere in his *Book On the Heavens* <note>original: De Cælo</note>, speaking of the heaven or the world, plainly affirms: <gloss>that all the philosophers before himself did assert the world to have been made, or to have had a beginning.</gloss> <note>original: γενόμενον μὲν ἐν ἅπαντες εἶναι φασιν</note> From this, these writers infer that they must therefore all be theists and hold the *Divine Creation* of the world. Consequently, they argue that Aristotle contradicts himself by representing many of them as atheists who acknowledge only one material principle of the whole universe without any intending or efficient cause <term>a purposeful creator</term>. 

But we must pronounce this to be a great error in these writers: to conclude that all those who held the world to have been "made" were therefore theists. On the contrary, it is certain that all the first and most ancient atheists did (in Aristotle's language) <gloss>make or generate the world</gloss> <note>original: κοσμοποιεῖν ἢ γεννᾶν κόσμον</note>. That is, they supposed it not to have existed from eternity, but to have had a temporary beginning; likewise, they believed it was corruptible and would, sooner or later, have an end again. The sense of these atheistic philosophers is represented by *Lucretius* <note>A Roman poet and philosopher (c. 99–55 BC) known for "On the Nature of Things."</note> in this manner:

> And since I have taught that the mortal structures of the world,
> And the heavens, consist of a body that was born,
> And that all things within it, now and in the future,
> Must necessarily be dissolved.
> <note>original Latin: Et quoniam docui, Mundi Mortalia Templa / Esse, & Nativo consistere Corpore Cælum, / Et quæcunque in eo sunt, fientque, necesse / Esse ea Dissolvi.</note>

And there seems to be indeed a necessity, in reason, that those who derive all things from a fortuitous <term>accidental/random</term> principle—and hold everything besides the substance of matter to have been generated—should suppose the world to have been generated likewise, as well as being corruptible. Therefore, it may well be reckoned as one of the common errors to believe that all atheists held the eternity of the world.

Moreover, when Aristotle adds immediately after: <gloss>that although the ancient philosophers all held the world to have been made, yet notwithstanding, they were divided in this: that some of them supposed, for all that, that it would con-</gloss> <note>original: ἀλλὰ γενόμενον, οἱ μὲν χείρον, οἱ δ᾽ φθαρτον</note>

XVII.
Aristotle tells us that some were of the opinion that this atheistic philosophy—which derives all things from *senseless* and *stupid matter* by way of *forms* and *qualities*—was of great antiquity, as old as any records of time among the Greeks. There are some who conceive that even the most ancient of all, and those most remote from this present generation, and they also who first wrote of the gods <note>original: "Theologized"</note>, did study nature <note>original: "Physiologize"</note> after this manner. Forasmuch as they made the Ocean and Tethys to have been the original of generation; and for this cause the oath of the gods is said to be by water (called by the poets Styx), as being that from which they all derived their original. For an oath ought to be by that which is most honorable, and the most ancient thing is the most honorable. 

In these words, it is very probable that Aristotle aimed his critique at Plato. However, it is certain that Plato, in his *Theaetetus*, affirms this atheistic doctrine to have been very ancient: "that all things were the offspring of flux and motion" <note>original: "ὅτι πάντα ἔκγονα ῥοῆς τε καὶ κινήσεως"</note>. This means that all things were *made* and *generated* out of *matter*. He even charges Homer with this view, for deriving the origin of the gods themselves in a similar way from the *Ocean* (or *floating matter*) in this verse of his:

->The Ocean is the father of all gods,<-
->And Tethys is their mother.<-
-><note>original: Ὠκεανόν τε θεῶν γένεσιν, καὶ μητέρα Τηθύν.</note><-

Therefore, these indeed seem to have been the ancientest of all atheists. Though they acknowledged certain beings superior to men, which they called by the name of "Gods," they nonetheless really denied a God according to the true definition of the word. They derived the origin of everything in the universe from the Ocean—that is, *fluid matter*—or, what is the same thing, from *Night* and *Chaos*. They supposed all their gods to have been made and generated, and consequently to be mortal and corruptible. 

*Aristophanes* gives us a description of this atheistic theology in his play *The Birds* <note>original: "Aves"</note> after this manner: that at first there was *nothing* but *Night* and *Chaos*. After laying an *egg*, from that egg was produced *Love*, which, mingling again with *Chaos*, fathered *Heaven*, and *Earth*, and *Animals*, and all the gods.

*Black-winged Night first produced an egg, from which no wind had fertilized.*
*From this, as the seasons revolved, sprouted Love the longed-for,*
*Glistening on his back with golden wings, like the swift whirlwinds.*
*He, mixing with winged, nocturnal Chaos in wide Tartarus,*
*Hatched our race [the birds], and first led us upward into the light.*
*Before this, the race of Immortals did not exist, until Love mingled all things together.*
<note>original: "Κάος ὦ κὴ νύξ, Ἔρεβός τε μέλαν πρῶτον, κὴ τάρταρος εὐρύς..."</note>

First all was *Chaos*, one confused heap,
Darkness enwrapped the disagreeing deep;
In a mixed crowd, the jumbled *Elements* were,
Nor *Earth*, nor *Air*, nor *Heaven* did appear;
Teeming *Night* spreading o'er her coal-black wings,
Laid the first *Egg*; whence, after time's due course,
Issued forth *Love* (the *World's Prolific Source*)
Glistering with golden wings; which fluttering o'er
Dark *Chaos*, engendered all the numerous store
Of *Animals* and *Gods*, etc.

And whereas the *Poet* <note>Aristophanes</note> there makes the *Birds* to have been begotten between *Love* and *Chaos* before all the *Gods*; though one might think this to have been done jocularly by him, merely to humor his plot; yet *Salmasius* <note>Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), a famous French classical scholar.</note> conceives, and not without some reason, that it was really a piece of the old *Atheistic Cabala* <note>term: Cabala; here meaning a secret or traditional oral doctrine.</note>, which therefore seems to have run thus: That *Chaos* or *Matter* confusedly moved, being the first original of all things, did from there rise up gradually from lesser to greater perfection. First inanimate things such as the *Elements*, *Heaven*, *Earth*, and *Seas*; then brute animals; afterwards *Men*; and last of all the *Gods*. 

It is as if not only the substance of *Matter*, and those inanimate bodies of the *Elements*—*Fire*, *Water*, *Air*, and *Earth*—were (as *Aristotle* somewhere <margin>* On Generation and Corruption, Book 2, chapter 6.</margin> speaks, according to the sense of those *Atheistic Theologians*) "nature and the first of things, and these are gods," <note>original: "φύσις πέτρα τὰ θεὸς, θεοὶ ἦ κὴ ταῦτα"</note> being first in the order of *Nature* before *God*, as being themselves also gods, but also brute animals at least, if not *men* too. And this is the *Atheistic Creation* of the *World*, *Gods* and all, out of senseless and stupid *Matter*, or *Dark Chaos*, as the only original *Numen* <note>term: Numen; a Latin word for a spiritual force or divinity.</note>; the perfectly inverted order of the *Universe*.

### XVIII.
But though this *Hypothesis* is purely *Atheistical*—making *Love*, which is supposed to be the original *Deity*, to have itself sprung at first from an *Egg of the Night*; and consequently that all *Deity* was the *Creature* or offspring of *Matter* and *Chaos*, or *Dark Fortuitous Nature*—yet *Aristotle* somewhere conceives that not only *Parmenides*, but also *Hesiod*, and some others, who did in like manner make *Love* the supreme *Deity* and derive all things from *Love* and *Chaos*, were to be exempted from the number of those *Atheistic Materialists* described before. This is because they seemed to understand by *Love* an *Active Principle* and *Cause of Motion* in the *Universe*; which there-

Therefore, it could not spring from an "Egg of the Night," nor be the creature of Matter, but must necessarily be something independent of it, and in the order of Nature existing before it. <note>original: ὑποπλάσσειε δ᾽ ἄν τις Ἡσίοδον πρῶτον... — Aristotle, Metaphysics 1.4. Aristotle suggests that Hesiod or others who placed Love or Desire as a principle among existing things did so to establish an active cause.</note> One would suspect that *Hesiod*, and if there be any other who made *Love* or *Desire* a principle of things in the *Universe*, aimed at this very thing (namely, the settling of another *Active Principle* besides *Matter*). For *Parmenides*, describing the generation of the *Universe*, says:

> First of all the gods, she devised *Love*. <note>original: Πρῶτιςον μὲν (φυσιν) ἔρωτα Θεῶν μητίσετο πάντων.</note>

And *Hesiod* writes:

> First of all, *Chaos* came to be; but then
> The broad-breasted *Earth*...
> And *Love*, who is preeminent among all the immortal gods. <note>original: Πάντων μὲν πρῶτισα χάος γένετ᾽... — Hesiod, Theogony 116-120.</note>

As if intimating by this that besides *Matter*, there ought to be another *Cause* or *Principle* that should be the origin of *Motion* and *Activity*, and also hold and conjoin all things together. But how these two *Principles* are to be ordered, and which of them was to be placed first—whether *Love* or *Chaos*—may be judged of afterwards. In these latter words, *Aristotle* seems to suggest that *Love* should not be supposed to spring from *Chaos*, but rather to be in the order of *Nature* before it; and therefore, by this *Love* of theirs, the *Deity* must necessarily be meant. 

And indeed, *Simmias* of Rhodes, in his *Wings*—a *Hymn* made in honor of this *Love* that is senior to all the *Gods* and a *Principle* in the *Universe*—tells us plainly that it is not *Cupid*, *Venus's* soft and effeminate son, but another kind of *Love*.

> *Soft magic charms*, not *iron bands*, fast tie
> *Heaven*, *Earth*, and *Seas*. The *Gods* themselves do readily
> *Stoop* to my *Laws*. The whole *World* dances to my *Harmony*.

# CHAPTER III. Supreme Deity, no Atheists.

...a divine but demonic thing (as the philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> declares there), not **God** but a **demon** <note>original: *Demon*; here meaning a spirit of intermediate nature between gods and men</note> only, or of a middle nature. For it is nothing but *philokalia* <note>original: *φιλοκαλία*; the love of beauty</note>, or the **love** of **beauty** <note>original: *Pulchritude*</note> as such. While this love, if used rightly, may perhaps wing and inspire the mind toward noble and generous attempts, and create a scornful disdain for mean, dirty, and sordid things, it is also capable of being abused; if so, it will sink downward into brutishness and sensuality. At best, it is an affection belonging only to imperfect and *parturient* <note>laboring to bring forth or give birth</note> beings, and therefore could not be the first principle of all things.

Therefore, we see no great reason why—in a *rectified* and *qualified* sense—this may not pass for true theology: that **Love** is the supreme deity and origin of all things. This is true if by "Love" one means eternal, self-originated, intellectual **Love**, or essential and substantial goodness. Such goodness, having an infinite, overflowing fullness and fertility <note>original: *Fecundity*</note>, dispenses itself without envy <note>original: *Uninvidiously*</note> according to the highest wisdom. It sweetly governs all things without any force or violence (all things being naturally subject to its authority and readily obeying its laws) and reconciles the whole world into harmony. For the Scripture, telling us that **God** is **Love**, seems to warrant this much to us: that **Love**, in some rightly qualified sense, is **God**.

XIX. But we must leave the age of fables and descend to the age of philosophy to inquire who among the professional philosophers were atheists in the manner previously described. It is true that **Aristotle** in other places accuses **Democritus** and **Leucippus** of the very same thing—that is, of assigning only a *material cause* to the universe and giving no account of the *origin of motion*. Yet it is certain that these were not the *persons* he intended here; those he speaks of were "the first of those who philosophized" <note>original: *πρῶτοι φιλοσοφισάντων*</note>, some of the first and most ancient philosophers of all.

Moreover, it appears by his description of them that they were people who did not philosophize using the theory of *atoms*. Instead, they resolved all things in the universe into *hyle* <note>original: *ὕλη*; matter</note> and "the passions of matter" <note>original: *πᾶσιν ὕλης*</note>—that is, **matter** and the **passions** or **affections**, **qualities**, and **forms of matter**. Thus, they were not *atomical* but *hylopathian* <note>from the Greek words for "matter" and "passion/quality"; those who believe matter and its qualities are the only reality</note> philosophers. These two groups—the old *materialists* and the *Democritics*—both alike derived all things from dead and stupid **matter** moved by chance <note>original: *fortuitously*</note>. The only difference between them was that the *Democritics* managed this business by way of **atoms**, while the others used the more common way of **qualities and forms**. So, in reality, this is only one and the same *atheistic hypothesis* presented in two different schemes. Just as one is called **Atomic Atheism**, the other, for the sake of distinction, may be called **Hylopathian Atheism**.

XX. Now **Aristotle** tells us plainly that these *hylopathian atheists* of his were all the first philosophers of the *Ionic Order* and succession before **Anaxagoras**. Since **Thales** was the head of that school, he is consistently identified by **Aristotle** as "the prince and leader of this philosophy" <note>original: *ἀρχὴν ἀπὸ τῆς φιλοσοφίας*</note>—that is, this kind of *atheistical philosophy*. He derived all things whatsoever (as **Homer** had done before him) from **water**, acknowledging no other principle but **fluid matter**.

Notwithstanding this accusation by *Aristotle*, *Thales* is represented far differently by reliable authors. *Cicero* tells us that besides *Water*, which he made to be the origin of all physical things, he also asserted that *Mind* was another principle which formed all things out of the *Water*. Furthermore, *Diogenes Laertius* and *Plutarch* record that he was thought to be the first of all philosophers who determined souls to be *Immortal*. ### CHAP. III.

Having declared that several of the ancient natural philosophers <note>original: "Phyſiologers"</note> made the <term>apeiron</term> <note>original: "ἀπείρον"; the Infinite or Boundless</note> or Infinite to be the principle of all things, he adds these words:
<margin>Book 3, chapter 4.</margin>
<gloss>Therefore we say there is no principle of this Infinite, but this itself seems to be the principle of other things, and to contain all things and govern all things—as those say who do not admit other causes besides the Infinite, such as Mind or Love. And they say that this is the divine, immortal, and indestructible, as Anaximander affirms, along with most of the natural philosophers.</note> Therefore there seems to be no principle of this Infinite, but this is the principle of other things, and contains all things and governs all things—unlike those who admit other causes such as Mind or Love <note>original: "Friendſhip"</note>. And they claim that this is the only real <term>Numen</term> <note>a Latin term for a deity or divine power</note> or God in the world, it being immortal and incorruptible, as Anaximander affirms, and most of the natural philosophers. 

From this passage, some recent writers have confidently concluded that Anaximander, along with those other natural philosophers mentioned there, understood "Infinite" to mean God according to the true notion of Him—that is, an Infinite Mind, the efficient cause of the universe, and not senseless and stupid matter. They argue this because matter could not be said to be immortal and to govern all things. Consequently, they suggest that Aristotle grossly contradicts himself by claiming all those Ionian philosophers before Anaxagoras were mere materialists or atheists. 

It is also possible that Clement of Alexandria, having not sufficiently considered this very passage of Aristotle's, might have been induced to rank Anaximander among the divine philosophers. He does this in his *Exhortation to the Greeks* <note>original: "Protreptick"</note>; where, after he had condemned certain of the old philosophers as atheistic materialists <note>original: "Corporealiſts"</note>, he adds these words: 
<margin>* Clement, Protrepticus, page 43.</margin>
<gloss>But of the other philosophers, who transcended the elements and sought after something higher and more excellent, some of them celebrated the Infinite; among these were Anaximander the Milesian, Anaxagoras the Clazomenian, and the Athenian Archelaus.</gloss> 
It is as if these three had all alike acknowledged an incorporeal Deity and made an *Infinite Mind*, distinct from *matter*, the first original of all things.

But that previously cited passage of Aristotle's alone, when well considered, will itself provide a sufficient refutation of this opinion. In that text, Anaximander and those other natural philosophers are plainly opposed to Anaxagoras. Anaxagoras, besides infinite senseless matter (or "similar atoms" <note>original: "Similar Atoms"; referring to the theory of homoeomery</note>), also proposed a "plastic life and nature" called Love <note>original: "Friendſhip"</note> as another principle of the corporeal world. From this it plainly follows that Anaximander and the rest supposed not an Infinite *Mind*, but Infinite *Matter*—without either *Mind* or *plastic nature*—to have been the only original of all things, and therefore their only deity or divine power.

Moreover, since *Democritus* is linked in the context with *Anaximander* as both making the <term>to apeiron</term> <note>the Infinite</note> the first principle of all, one might as well infer from this passage that *Democritus* was a genuine theist as much as *Anaximander*. But *Democritus*—

# Infinite Matter, Anaximander's Book I.

Democritus's only principle was *infinite atoms*, without any element of *mind* or *plastic nature* <note>original: "Plastick Nature"; a creative or organizing force in nature</note>; so likewise was *Anaximander's* principle an *infinity of senseless and stupid matter*. Therefore, they were both equally atheists, though Anaximander, in the cited words, had the honor (if it may be called that) of being the only one named, as he was the most ancient of all those atheistical physicists <note>original: "Physiologers"; those who study the origins of nature</note> and their leader.

## XXII.
Neither should it seem strange at all that Anaximander and those other atheistical materialists should call *infinite matter*—which is devoid of all *understanding* and *life*—the "divine" <note>original: "τὸ θεῖον"</note>, the *deity*, or the *divine power* <note>original: "Numen"</note>. For to all those who deny a God (according to the true *concept* of Him), whatever else they substitute in His place by making it the *first principle* of all things—even if it is *senseless and stupid matter*—must necessarily be accounted the *only divine power* and the *most divine* thing of all.

Nor is it to be wondered at that this *infinite*, when understood as *matter*, should be said to be not only *incorruptible* but also *immortal*, as these two are often used as synonymous and equivalent expressions. For thus in the writings of *Lucretius*, the corruption of all inanimate bodies is called "death":

->—"The death of that which was before";<-
<note>original: "Mors ejus quod fuit ante"</note>

And again:

> "Since nature repairs one thing from another, and does not allow any thing to be born unless aided by the death of another."
> <note>original: "Quando aliud ex alio reficit Natura, nec ullam Rem Gigni patitur, nisi Morte adjutam alienâ"</note>

In like manner, "mortal" is used by him to mean "corruptible":

> "For if anything were mortal in all its parts, every thing would perish, snatched suddenly from our eyes."
> <note>original: "Nam siquid Mortale à cunctis partibus esset, Ex oculis res quæque repentè erepta periret"</note>

And this kind of language was very familiar to *Heraclitus*, as appears from these passages of his: "The death of fire is the birth of air; and the death of air is the birth of water" <note>original: "πυρὸς θάνατος, ἀέρι γένεσις· κὶ ἀέρος ὕδατι γένεσις"</note>; that is, the *corruption* of them. And again: "It is death to souls <note>meaning air or vapor</note> to become water; and death to water to become earth" <note>original: "ψυχῆσιν θάνατος, ὕδωρ γενέσθαι· ὕδατι δὲ θάνατος, γῆν γενέσθαι"</note>. In this, Heraclitus was merely imitating *Orpheus*, as appears from this verse of his, cited by *Clement of Alexandria*:

> "Water is the soul, but death is the change from water."
> <note>original: "Ἔστιν ὕδωρ ψυχῆ, θάνατος δ᾽ ὕδατοσιν ἀμοιβή"</note>

Besides this, there are many examples of this use of the word "immortal" <note>original: "ἀθάνατος"</note> in other Greek writers, and some in *Aristotle* himself, who, speaking of the heavens, attributes "immortality" <note>original: "ἀθανασία"</note> and "eternity" <note>original: "ἀϊδιότης"</note> to them.

<summary>The author argues that ancient materialists like Anaximander were atheists because they identified "the divine" with senseless, infinite matter. He explains that in ancient philosophical terminology, "death" and "immortality" were often used to describe the corruption or permanence of physical elements rather than spiritual states.</summary>

# CHAPTER III. Supreme Deity.

as one and the same thing. He also affirms that the ancients therefore made Heaven to be the seat of the Deity, "as being the only immortal things" <note>original: *ὡς ὄντα μόνον ἀθάνατα*</note>, meaning they are "incorruptible" <note>unable to decay or be destroyed</note>.

Indeed, that other expression might stagger a reader more at first sight, where it is said of this *Infinite* <note>the *Apeiron*, or boundless source</note> that it does not only *contain* but also *govern* all things. However, Simplicius <note>a 6th-century commentator on Aristotle</note> tells us that this is to be understood likewise of *matter*. He explains that no more was meant by it than that all things were *derived* from it and *depended* on it as the *First Principle*.

"These philosophers spoke always of natural principles, but not always of the supernatural principle from which it was said that nothing could be governed. For while the infinite exceeds material causes, which many people pass over, 'governing' is attributed to it as a kind of suitability, because things are produced from it." <note>original Greek: *ὁ δ᾽ λόγῳ τοῖς πλείστοις ἀεὶ τῇ φυσικῇ...*</note>

These philosophers spoke only of *natural principles* and not of *supernatural* ones. Although they say that this *Infinite* of theirs both *contains* and *governs* all things, this is not at all to be wondered at; for *containing* belongs to the *material cause* as that which goes through all things, and likewise *governing* is meant only as that from which all things are made according to a certain aptitude of the matter.

Philoponus (who was a Christian) represents Aristotle’s sense in this whole passage more fully in this manner: Those of the ancient *physiologers* <note>natural philosophers</note> who had no respect for any *active efficient cause*—as Anaxagoras had for *Mind* and Empedocles for *Friendship* and *Contention*—supposed *matter* to be the only *cause* of all things. They believed it was *infinite* in *magnitude*, *ingenerable* <note>uncreated</note>, and *incorruptible*, esteeming it to be a certain *divine* thing which did *govern* all, or preside over the *compages* <note>structure or framework</note> of the *universe*, and to be *immortal*, that is, *undestroyable*. Anaximenes said this was *air*, Thales said it was *water*, but Anaximander called it a certain *middle thing* between the elements; some chose one thing, and some another.

"And no one of them approved of a nature in our sense, not looking primarily at the power presiding over the whole... whatever each one happened upon, they suspected that to be the cause of others and thus God." <note>original Greek: *Και ἐδένα δοκιμασεν φυσιν...*</note>

And Aristotle in this passage tells us that it is no wonder if they—who did not attend to the *active cause* that presides over the *universe*—looked upon some one of the *elements* (whichever each of them thought to be the cause of all other things) as *God*. But just as they, considering only the *material principle*, conceived that to be the cause of all things, so Anaxagoras later supposed *Mind* to be the principle of all things, and Empedocles supposed *Friendship* and *Contention*.

### XXIII. But to make it further appear that *Anaximander’s* philosophy was purely *atheistical*, we think it convenient to show what account is given of it by other writers. Plutarch, in his *Opinions of the Philosophers*, at once briefly represents the *Anaximandrian* philosophy and *censures* it in this manner:

<margin>Book 1, chapter 3.</margin> "Anaximander the Milesian affirms the *Infinite* to be the first principle of all things. He says that all things are generated out of it and corrupted again into it, and therefore infinite worlds are generated and many are corrupted. He says the infinite exists so that the generation of existing things might not fail. But he errs in this: while he declares what the matter is, he does away with the efficient cause. For the 'infinite' is nothing other than matter, and matter cannot have activity unless an efficient cause is underlying it." <note>original Greek: *Ἀναξίμανδρ᾽ ἐς ὄντων τω ἀρχῶ εἶναι τὸ ἀπέιρον...*</note>

Anaximander the Milesian affirms *Infinite* to be the *First Principle*, and that all things are *generated* out of it and *corrupted* again into it, and therefore...

<page-num>128</page-num>
# A Fuller Account of Anaximander's Book I.

Therefore, he argues that *Infinite Worlds* are successively generated and corrupted in this manner. He gives the reason for it being infinite: so that there might never be any failure of new generations. But he errs in this: by assigning only a *Material Cause*, he removes the *Active Principle* of things. For *Anaximander's Infinite* is nothing other than *matter*; but *matter* can produce nothing unless there is also an *Active Cause*. Here the author also shows how *Anaximenes* followed *Anaximander* in this, by assigning only a *Material Cause* to the *Universe* without any *Efficient Cause* <note>The "efficient cause" is the agent or force that actually brings something into being.</note>; though he differed from him by making the *First Matter* to be *Air* and deriving all things from it through *Rarefaction* and *Condensation*. Thus, we see it is plain that *Anaximander's Infinite* was no *Infinite Mind* (which is the true *Deity*), but only *Infinite Matter*, devoid of any *Life* or *Active Power*. *Eusebius* is more particular in giving an account of *Anaximander's Cosmopoeia* <note>original: *Cosmopœia*; the creation or formation of the world.</note>.

<margin>Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, Book 1, page 15, Stephens Edition.</margin>
<note>original Greek: τὸ ἄπειρον φάναι τῶν πάντων αἴτιον... κὴ τὰς ἀτέρας.</note>
He says that the infinite is the cause of the whole, regarding both the generation and corruption of all things, from which he says the heavens are separated, and generally all the worlds, which are infinite. He states that from eternity there was something productive of heat and cold, which was separated at the generation of this world, and that a certain sphere of flame grew around the air surrounding the earth, like bark around a tree. When this sphere was broken off and enclosed into certain circles, the sun, the moon, and the stars were established. *Anaximander* affirms *Infinite (Matter)* to be the only *Cause* of the *Generation* and *Corruption* of all things. And that the *Heavens*, and *Infinite Worlds*, were made out of it by way of *Secretion* or *Segregation*. Also, those *Generative Principles* of *Heat* and *Cold* that were contained in it from *Eternity* being *Segregated* when this *World* was made, a certain *Sphere* of *Flame* or *Fire* did first arise and encompass the *Air* which surrounds this *Earth* (as a *Bark* does a *Tree*). This being afterwards broken and divided into smaller *Spherical Bodies*, constituted the *Sun*, the *Moon*, and all the *Stars*.

<margin>Aristotle, Physics, Book 1, chapter 4.</margin>
This *Anaximandrian Cosmopoeia* was briefly hinted at by *Aristotle* in these words: <note>original Greek: οἱ δὲ ἐκ τᾶ ἑνὸς, ἐούσας τὰς ἐναντιότητας, ἀποκρίνεσθαι, ὥσπερ Ἀναξίμανδρος φησι</note> *Some philosophers generate the world by the secretion and segregation of inherent contrarieties, as Anaximander says.*

<margin>Metaphysics, Book 14, chapter 4.</margin>
And elsewhere in his *Metaphysics*, he takes notice of *Anaximander's Mixture* <note>original Greek: Ἀναξιμάνδρος τὸ μίγμα</note> of things. From this we conclude that *Anaximander's Infinite* was nothing else but an *Infinite Chaos* of *Matter* in which were either *Actually* or *Potentially* contained all manner of *Qualities*. By the *Fortuitous Secretion* and *Segregation* of these, he supposed *Infinite Worlds* to be successively *Generated* and *Corrupted*. So we may now easily guess where *Leucippus* and *Democritus* obtained their *Infinite Worlds*, and perceive how closely related these two *Atheistic Hypotheses* were. But it will not be amiss to also take notice of that *Particular Conceit* <note>In this context, "conceit" means a fanciful or specific philosophical idea.</note> which *Anaximander* had concerning the *First Original* of *Brute Animals* and *Mankind*.

<margin>Plutarch, Physics, Book 3, chapter 19.</margin>
Of the *former*, *Plutarch* gives us this account: <note>original Greek: Ἀναξίμανδρος ἐκ φλοιοῖς ἐκτραφῆναι τὰ πρῶτα ζῶα... μεταβιῶναι</note> *Anaximander says that the first animals were generated in moisture, encompassed by thorny barks; as they grew older, they came out onto the drier part, and the bark breaking off, they survived only a short time.* That the *First Animals* were generated in *Moisture* and encompassed with certain *Thorny Barks* by which they were guarded and defended; which after further *growth*, becoming more *Dry* and *Cracking*, they issued forth, but lived only a *short time* after. And as for the first *Original* of *Men*, *Eusebius* represents...

### CHAP. III. Atheistical Philosophy.

<margin>Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, Book 1.</margin>
<note>original: Ε. P. L. 1.</note>
Eusebius represents Anaximander's sense of the matter this way: "Humans were first generated within animals of a different species. This is because while other animals are quickly able to feed themselves, humans alone require a long period of nursing. Therefore, humans could not have been preserved at the beginning in any other way." <note>original Greek: Ἐξ ἀλλοειδῶν ζώων ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἐγενήθη...</note> But 
<margin>Anaximander concludes that humans were first born from fish, and after being nourished and growing strong, etc.</margin>
Plutarch expresses this somewhat more particularly: "Anaximander concludes that humans were first generated in the bellies of fishes. After being nourished there until they grew strong and were able to shift for themselves, they were afterward cast out upon dry land." Lastly, Anaximander’s theology is both represented to us and criticized by Velleius, the Epicurean philosopher, in Cicero’s writings:
<margin>On the Nature of the Gods, Book 1.</margin>
"Anaximander’s opinion is that the Gods are born, rising and vanishing again at long intervals of time, and that there are innumerable worlds. But how can we conceive of anything as a God if it is not eternal?" <note>original Latin: Anaximandri opinio est Nativos esse Deos...</note> We learn from this that Anaximander did indeed comply with popular opinion enough to retain the name "Gods," but he actually denied the existence of the divine itself, even according to the judgment of this Epicurean philosopher. This is because all his "Gods" were born and mortal—they were nothing more than those innumerable worlds which he supposed were successively generated and destroyed in certain periods of time. Therefore, it is plain that Anaximander’s only real <term>Numen</term> <note>divine power or spirit</note>—that is, his first principle that was uncreated and indestructible—was nothing but infinite matter. This matter was devoid of all understanding and life. He supposed that by the accidental separation of its internal qualities and parts, there were generated: first, the elements of earth, water, air, and fire; then the bodies of the sun, moon, and stars; then the bodies and souls of humans and other animals; and lastly, infinite worlds like these. He viewed these worlds as secondary, "born" Gods (which were also mortal), according to that atheistical hypothesis described in Plato.

XXIV. It is certain that the common people in all ages have been very poor judges of who is a Theist <note>one who believes in God</note> and who is an Atheist. They have condemned many sincere Theists as guilty of atheism merely because they disagreed with some of the people's superstitious rites and opinions. For example, Anaxagoras of Clazomenae was the first of all the <term>Ionic</term> <note>a school of Greek philosophy from Ionia</note> philosophers (unless Thales should be excepted) who established an infinite mind as a primary principle—meaning he asserted the existence of a Deity according to the true definition. Yet, he was nonetheless generally denounced as an atheist merely because he affirmed the sun to be a "red-hot mass" <note>original Greek: μύδρον διάπυρον</note> or a fiery globe, and the moon to be an earth. In other words, he was called an atheist because he denied that the sun and moon were alive and possessed intelligent souls, and consequently denied that they were Gods. 
<margin>Plato, Apology of Socrates.</margin>
In the same way, Socrates was both accused and condemned for atheistical—

And just as the common people have unjustly condemned many theists as atheists, so have they also acquitted many rank **atheists** from the guilt of that crime, merely because they externally complied with religious worship and forms of speech. Neither is it only the common people who have been deceived in this, but also the majority of learned men. They have commonly been so superficial in this matter that they have hardly noticed more than three or four atheists who ever existed in former times—namely, *Diagoras, Theodorus, Euemerus,* and *Protagoras*. 

In reality, *Democritus* and *Anaximander* were as rank atheists as any of them, though they had the wit to carry themselves externally with more caution. Indeed, it was actually one and the same form of atheism which both of these men entertained; they derived all things alike from **dead and stupid matter moved by chance.** The difference between them was only this: they managed it in two different ways. *Anaximander* used the method of **qualities and forms**, which is the more common and obvious kind of atheism; but *Democritus* used the method of **atoms and figures**, which seems to be a more learned kind of atheism.

And though we do not doubt at all that *Plato*, in his tenth book of *The Laws* <note>original: *De Legibus*</note> where he attacks atheism, intended to refute both the **Democritic** and the **Anaximandrian** atheism, yet certain facts remain. Whether it was because he had no desire to take any notice of *Democritus* (who is not mentioned by him even once anywhere), or because he was not perfectly acquainted with that way of explaining nature <note>term: *physiologizing*</note>, it is certain that he describes the **atheistic hypothesis** more according to the **Anaximandrian** than the **Democritic** form. For when he represents atheism as resulting from the **accidental mixing** of **hot and cold, hard and soft, moist and dry particles** <note>term: *corpuscula*</note>, this is clearly more consistent with the **Anaximandrian generation** of the world (by the separation of **internal opposites** <note>original: *inexistent contrarieties*</note> within matter) than with the **Democritic creation of the world** <note>term: *cosmopæia*</note> by the **accidental clashing of atoms** which are devoid of all **qualities and forms**.

Some indeed seem to call that scheme of atheism—which deduces all things from matter by way of **qualities** and **forms**—by the name of **Peripatetic** or **Aristotelian atheism**. We suppose they do this because *Aristotle* explained nature using those "forms" and "qualities," drawing them out of the power of matter. But since *Aristotle* himself...

# CHAPTER III. Why Democritus New-modeled Atheism.

Democritus himself cannot be justly accused of being an atheist; this form of atheism ought rather, as we conceive, to be named after *Anaximander* <note>Anaximander (c. 610–546 BC) was a pre-Socratic philosopher who believed the universe originated from an infinite substance called the 'Apeiron'.</note>, and called *Anaximandrian Atheism*.

XXV. Now, the reasons why *Democritus* and *Leucippus* new-modeled *atheism*—moving it from the *Anaximandrian* and *Hylopathian* <note>original: "Hylopathian" — the theory that matter itself possesses qualities or "passions" like heat or cold that produce life.</note> forms into the *Atomic form*—seem to have been chiefly these: First, because they were well-instructed in that *atomic* way of *studying nature* <note>original: "Physiologizing"</note> and were really convinced that it was not only more *ingenious*, but also more agreeable to *truth*. The other theory, based on *real qualities* and *forms*, seemed to them to be *unintelligible*. Secondly, because they foresaw, as *Lucretius* <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), a Roman poet and philosopher who championed Epicurean atomism.</note> suggests, that the production of *forms* and *qualities* out of *nothing*, and their decay back into *nothing*, would prepare an *easy* way for people to believe in a *divine creation* and *annihilation*. 

And lastly, because (as we have already suggested) they plainly perceived that these *forms* and *qualities* of *matter* were of a doubtful nature. Therefore, while they were sometimes used as a shelter for *atheism*, they might also, on the contrary, prove to be a *refuge* <note>original: "Asylum"</note> for *corporeal theism* <note>The belief that God is a physical or material being.</note>. It might possibly be supposed that either the *matter* of the whole world, or else the more *subtle* and *fiery* part of it, was originally endowed with an *understanding form* or *quality*, and consequently the whole world was an *animal* or a *god*. 

Therefore, they took another more *effective course* to secure their *atheism* and exclude all possibility of a *physical god*. They derived the origin of all things from *atoms*, which are devoid of all *forms* and *qualities* and have nothing in them but *magnitude, shape, position,* and *motion* as their *first principles*. It followed unavoidably from this that *life* and *understanding*, as well as those other *qualities*, could only be *accidental* and *secondary results* arising from certain *random clusters* <note>original: "Fortuitous Concretions"</note> and *structures of atoms*. Thus, the world could not have been made by any *prior plan* or *understanding*, and therefore by no *deity*.

XXVI. We have here represented three different *forms* of *atheism*: the *Anaximandrian*, the *Democritical*, and the *Stratonical* <note>Named after Strato of Lampsacus, who argued that nature is a self-governing force without a conscious god.</note>. But there is yet another *form* of *atheism*, different from them all, to be noticed. This form supposes one kind of *formative* <note>original: "Plastick"</note> and *generative* <note>original: "Spermatick"</note>, *methodical* and *artificial nature*—but without any *sense* or *conscious understanding*—to preside over the whole world and arrange and preserve all things in that *regular frame* in which they exist.

<margin>Seneca, *Natural Questions*, Book 3, Section 29.</margin>
Such a *form* of *atheism* as this is hinted to us in that doubtful passage of *Seneca's*: *"Whether the world is an animal"* (for so it ought to be read, and not "a soul") *"or whether it is a body governed by nature, like trees or crops"* <note>original Latin: "Sive Animal est Mundus... sive Corpus Naturâ Gubernante, ut Arbores, ut Sata"</note>. In these words, two different *hypotheses* of the *world system* are *skeptically* proposed by one who was a *materialist* <note>original: "Corporealist"</note> and took it for granted that everything was *physical body*. First, that the whole world, though having nothing but *matter* in it, was nonetheless an *animal* (just as our *human bodies* are) endowed with one *sentient*—

# The Cosmo-Plastic Atheism Book I.

ent or *Rational Life and Nature*, one *Soul* or *Mind*, governing and ordering the Whole. This Corporeal *Cosmo-zoism* <note>original: "Cosmo-zoism"; the belief that the universe is a living animal.</note> we do not reckon among the forms of Atheism, but rather account it as a kind of spurious *Theism*, or *Theism* disguised in a pagan dress, and not without a complication of many false apprehensions concerning the Deity within it. The second is that the whole world is no *animal*, but as it were, one *huge plant* or *vegetable*: a body endowed with one *plastic* <note>original: "plastic"; here meaning formative or creative power.</note> or *spermatic nature* <note>original: "spermatic nature"; the internal power of growth and organization, like a seed.</note>, branching out the whole, orderly and methodically, but without any understanding or sense. And this must needs be accounted a form of Atheism, because it does not derive the origin of things in the universe from any clearly *intellectual principle* or *conscious nature*.

XXVII. Now this form of Atheism, which supposes the whole world (there being nothing but body in it) not to be an *animal*, but only a *great plant* or *vegetable*, having one *spermatic form* or *plastic nature* which, without any conscious reason or understanding, orders the whole, though it has some closer correspondence with that *hylozoic form* <note>original: "hylozoic"; the theory that all matter possesses life.</note> of Atheism described before—in that it does not suppose Nature to be a mere *fortuitous* <note>original: "fortuitous"; happening by chance.</note> thing, but a kind of *artificial* thing—yet it differs from it in this: the *hylozoic* theory, supposing all matter as such to have life essentially belonging to it, must therefore attribute to every part of matter (or at least every particular *whole* <note>original: "Totum"</note> that is one by continuity) a distinct *plastic life* of its own, but acknowledge no one common life as ruling over the whole corporeal universe. Consequently, it imputes the origin of all things (as has been already observed) to a certain mixture of *chance* and *plastic* or *methodical nature* both together. 

Whereas the *Cosmo-plastic Atheism* quite excludes *fortune* or *chance*, subjecting all things to the regular and orderly *fate* of one *plastic* or *plant-like nature* ruling over the whole. Thus that philosopher mentioned before <note>referring to Seneca, as indicated by the marginal note.</note> concludes that whether the world were <margin>Seneca, Natural Questions, Book 3, Chapter 29.</margin> an *animal* (in the Stoic sense) or whether it were a mere *plant* or *vegetable*, "From its beginning even to its end, whatever it ought to do or whatever it ought to suffer, is already included within it. Just as in a seed, the entire logic of the future man is comprised; and the unborn infant already possesses the law of the beard and of gray hairs. For the lineaments of the entire body and of its following age are there in a small and hidden compass. In the same way, the origin of the world contained not only the sun and moon, the cycles of the stars, and the births of animals, but also the means by which terrestrial things would be changed. Among these was the Great Flood, which came by the Law of the World no differently than winter or summer does." <note>original Latin: "Ab initio ejus usque ad exitum, quicquid facere, quicquid pati debeat, inclusum est. Ut in Semine, omnis futuri ratio hominis comprehensa est. Et Legem Barbae & Canorum, nondum natus Infans habet. Totius enim Corporis, & sequentis aetatis, in parvo occultoque, Lineamenta sunt. Sic Origo Mundi, non magis Solem & Lunam, & Vices Syderum, & Animalium Ortus, quàm quibus mutarentur Terrena, continuit. In his fuit Inundatio, quae non secus quàm Hyems, quàm Aestas, Lege Mundi venit."</note> 

Whatsoever, from the beginning to the end of it, it can either do or suffer, it was all at first included in the nature of the whole. As in the seed is contained the whole delineation of the future man, and the embryo or unborn infant has already in it the law of a beard and gray hairs—the lineaments of the whole body and of its following age being there described as it were in a little and obscure compendium—in like manner, the original and first rudiments of the world contained in them not only the sun and moon, the courses of the stars, and the generations of animals, but also the vicissitudes of all terrestrial things. And every deluge or inundation of water comes to pass no less by the Law of the World (its *spermatic* or *plastic* nature) than winter and summer do.

# CHAPTER III. Asserted by Spurious Stoics.

XXVIII. We do not deny it to be possible that some people in all ages might have entertained such an atheistical concept as this: that the origin of this entire mundane system <note>original: "Mundane System"; the physical structure of the universe</note> came from one **artificial, orderly, and methodical, but senseless nature** lodged in matter. However, we cannot trace the footsteps of this doctrine anywhere as much as among the Stoics, the sect to which **Seneca** belonged—who speaks so waveringly and uncertainly on this point (whether the world was an **animal** or a **plant**). 

Indeed, several learned men have suspected that even the **Zenonian** and **Heraclitic** deity itself was nothing other than such a **plastic nature** <note>original: "Plastick Nature"; a formative or creative force that shapes matter without conscious thought</note> or **spermatic principle** in the universe, which—just as in the **seeds of vegetables** and **animals**—frames their respective bodies **orderly** and **artificially**. Nor can it be denied that there has been just cause given for such a suspicion; for even the best of the **Stoics**, sometimes confounding **God** with **Nature**, seemed to make him nothing but an **artificial fire, orderly** and **methodically** proceeding to **generation**. And it was familiar for them, as **Laertius** tells us, to call **God** the **spermatic reason** <note>original: "σπερματικὸν Λόγον"; the formative principle or "seed-logic" of the cosmos</note> or **form of the world**. 

Nevertheless, because **Zeno** and others of the chief **Stoic doctors** also many times asserted that there was a **rational and intellectual nature** <note>original: "φύσις νοερὰ ἢ λογική"</note> (and therefore not a **plastic principle** only) in the **matter of the universe**, as well as that the whole world was an **animal** and not a mere **plant**, we incline rather to excuse the generality of the first and most ancient **Stoics** from the charge of **atheism**. We account this form of **atheism** which we now speak of to be but a certain **degeneracy** from the right **Heraclitic** and **Zenonian tradition** <note>original: "Cabala"; here meaning a received tradition or secret doctrine</note>. 

That tradition seemed to contain two things: 
1. First, that there was an **animal-like, sentient, and intellectual nature**, or a **conscious soul** and **mind**, that presided over the whole world, though lodged immediately in its **fiery matter**. 
2. Secondly, that this **sentient and intellectual nature**, or **corporeal soul** and **mind of the universe**, also contained under it (or within it, as its inferior part) a certain **plastic nature** or **spermatic principle** which was properly the **fate** of all things. 

For thus **Heraclitus** defined **fate** as: **A certain reason passing through the substance of the whole world, or an ethereal body, that was the seed of the generation of the universe** <note>original: "λόγον τῷ διὰ τῆς οὐσίας καὶ σπέρμα τῷ παντὸς γενέσεως"</note>. And **Zeno’s** first **principle**, while said to be an **intellectual nature**, is also said to have contained in it **all the spermatic reasons and forms by which everything is done according to fate** <note>original: "πᾶσας τὰς σπερματικὰς λόγες καθ᾽ ἃς ἕκαστα μαρεμβλὺ γίγνεται"</note>. 

However, though this seems to have been the genuine **doctrine** of both **Heraclitus** and **Zeno**, others of their **followers** afterwards divided these two things from one another. Taking only the latter, they made the **plastic** or **spermatic nature**—devoid of all **animality** or **conscious intellectuality**—to be the highest **principle** in the **universe**. Thus **Laertius** tells us that **Boethus**, an eminent and famous **Stoic doctor**, plainly denied the **world** to be an **animal** (that is, denied it had any **sentient, conscious, or intellectual nature** presiding over it). Consequently, he must have made it to be but **a body governed by nature, like trees or crops** <note>original: "Corpus Naturâ gubernante, ut Arbores, ut Sata"</note>.

<summary>The author argues that while original Stoicism viewed the universe as a conscious, rational "animal," later "spurious" Stoics like Boethus reduced God to a mindless, "plastic" force similar to the growth process of plants.</summary>
