# Atheism: That Blind Goddess, Nature's Fanatics. BOOK I.

<page-num>134</page-num>

...governed by a *plastic* <note>original: "plastick"; here meaning a formative or creative power</note> or *vegetative nature*, such as *trees, plants*, and *herbs*. And as it is possible that other *Stoics* and followers of *Heraclitus* <note>original: "Heracliticks"</note> might have done the same before *Boethus*, so it is very probable that he had many followers after him. Among these, while *Pliny the Elder* <note>original: "Plinius Secundus"</note> may be counted as one, *Seneca* himself was not without a doubtful trace of this *atheism*, as has been already shown. Therefore, this *form of atheism*—which supposes one *plastic* or *spermatic nature* <note>original: "spermatick nature"; a life-giving or germinal force</note>, one *plant-like* or *vegetative life* in the whole world, as the *highest principle*—may, for the sake of distinction, be called the *pseudo-Stoic* or *Stoic atheism*.

XXIX. Besides these *philosophic atheists*, whose various forms we have now described, it cannot be doubted that there have been in all ages many other *atheists* who have not philosophized at all. They did not pretend to maintain any particular *atheistic system* or *hypothesis* by way of *reason*, but were only led by a certain dull and foolish, though confident, *disbelief* of whatever they could not either *see* or *feel*. This kind of *atheist* may therefore well be accounted *enthusiastic* or *fanatical atheists*. 

In the meantime, it is true that all types of *atheists* whatsoever—even those who most of all pretend to *reason* and *philosophy*—may in some sense be justly styled both *enthusiasts* and *fanatics*. This is because they are not led or carried into this way of *atheizing* by any clear *dictates* of their *reason* or *understanding*, but only by a *blind and irrational impulse* <note>original: "ἀδὴλ ἄλογ©" (adēlon alogon)</note>. They are, as it were, *inspired* to it by that lower *earthly life* and *nature* which is called in the *Scripture oracles* "the spirit of the world" <note>original: "τὸ πνεῦμα τῶ κόσμε" (to pneuma tou kosmou)</note>, or a *mundane spirit*, and is opposed to "the Spirit that is of God" <note>original: "τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἐκ τῶ θεῶ" (to pneuma to ek tou theou)</note>. 

For when the *Apostle* speaks in this manner—*We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit that is of God*—he seems to suggest to us that just as some men were *led* and *inspired* by a *Divine Spirit*, so others again are *inspired* by a *mundane spirit*, by which is meant the *earthly life*. Now, the former of these *two* are not to be accounted *enthusiasts* (as the word is now commonly taken in a *bad sense* <note>In the 17th century, an "enthusiast" was someone who claimed direct, often irrational, divine inspiration</note>), because the *Spirit of God* is no *irrational* thing. It is either the very same thing as *reason*, or else such a thing as *Aristotle* (as if *prophesying* <note>original: "vaticinating"</note> about it) somewhere calls *a certain better and diviner thing than reason* <note>original: "λόγ© τι κρεῖττον" (logou ti kreitton)</note>, and *Plotinus* calls the *root of reason* <note>original: "ῥίζαν λόγος" (rhizan logos)</note>. 

But on the contrary, the *mundane spirit*, or *earthly life*, is *irrational foolishness*. Those who are *atheistically inspired* by it (however much they may otherwise seem to dislike *enthusiasm* and *revelations*) are nonetheless really no better than a kind of *bewitched enthusiasts* and *blind spirits* <note>original: "spiritati"; those possessed by a spirit</note>. They are wholly ridden and driven by a dark, narrow, and captive *principle of life*, and—to use their own language—they *philosophize* by it. By it, they are robbed, even in theoretical matters, of all *free reason* and *understanding*. Indeed, they are *fanatics* too, even though that word seems to refer specifically to a *deity*: for all *atheists* are the *fanatics of that blind goddess, Nature*.

XXX. We have described four several forms of *atheism*; First, the...

# CHAPTER III. The Fourfold Group of Atheisms.

The **Hylopathian** <note>original: "Hylopathian"; from the Greek words for matter and passion/affection</note> or **Anaximandrian** atheism derives all things from **dead and senseless matter** through **qualities** and **forms** that can be **created** and **destroyed**. Secondly, the **Atomical** or **Democritical** atheism does the same thing through **atoms** and **geometric figures**. Thirdly, the **Cosmoplastic** or **Stoic Atheism** supposes one **plastic** <note>meaning "form-giving" or "shaping"</note> and **methodical** but **senseless nature** to preside over the whole **physical universe**. And lastly, the **Hylozoic** or **Stratonical** atheism attributes to all **matter**, as such, a certain **living** and **energetic nature**, but one devoid of all **animal life, sensation,** and **consciousness**. 

As we do not encounter any other **forms** or **schemes** of **atheism** besides these **four**, we believe that no others can easily be devised or thought up. This is based on the following two **considerations**: 

First, because all **atheists** are mere **corporealists**—that is, they acknowledge no other **substance** besides **body** or **matter**. Just as there was never anyone known who admitted an **incorporeal** <note>non-physical or spiritual</note> **substance** yet denied a **Deity**, there is no reason why someone who accepts the former should exclude the latter. Furthermore, the same **dull** and **earthly disbelief**, or confounded **stupidity** of **mind** that makes men deny a **God**, must also incline them to deny all **incorporeal substance**. Therefore, just as **physicians** speak of a certain **disease** or **madness** called **hydrophobia**—a **symptom** in those bitten by a mad **dog** which gives them a monstrous **aversion** to **water**—so all **atheists** are possessed with a kind of **madness** that may be called **pneumatophobia** <note>a fear of spirits or breath</note>. This makes them have an irrational but desperate **abhorrence** of **spirits** or **incorporeal substances**. At the same time, they are driven by an **hylomania** <note>a madness for matter</note>, by which they **madly** dote upon **matter** and **devoutly** worship it as the only **divinity** <note>original: "Numen"</note>.

The second **consideration** is this: while there are no **atheists** who are not mere **corporealists**, not all **corporealists** are to be considered **atheists**. Those among them who—despite making all things **matter**—still suppose an **intellectual nature** exists within that **matter** to preside over the **physical universe**, should in **reason** and **charity** be excluded from that number. There have always been some people so strongly captivated by the power of a gross **imagination** that an **incorporeal God** seemed to them to be nothing but a "God of words" (as some of them call it), a mere **empty sound** or **contradictory expression**—"something" and "nothing" put together. Yet, despite this, they have been possessed with a firm belief and persuasion of a **Deity**, or that the **system** of the **universe** depends upon one **perfectly understanding being** as its **head**. Consequently, they have concluded that **matter is in some way God** <note>original Greek: "ὕλη πᾶς ἔχουσαι" — literally "matter possessing all things"</note>. 

The grossest and most foolish of all these **corporeal theists** seem to be those who argue that **God** is only one particular piece of **organized matter**, possessing a **human form** and **size**, which, endowed with **perfect reason** and **understanding**, exercises an **universal dominion** over all the rest. Although this **hypothesis** has been entertained by some within the **Christian profession** in both former and later times, it has seemed very ridiculous even to many of those **heathen philosophers** who were themselves mere **corporealists**, such as the **Stoics**, who rejected it with a kind of **indignation**.

But that other Corporeal Theism <note>The belief that God is a physical substance or body.</note> seems to be of the two rather more generous and refined, which supposes the whole World to be one *Animal*, and God to be a certain subtle and ethereal, but *Intellectual Matter*, pervading it as a *Soul*; which was the doctrine of others before the Stoics. "Hippasus of Metapontus and Heraclitus the Ephesian supposed the fiery and ethereal matter of the world to be God" <note>original: τὸ πῦρ θεὸν ὑπείληφατον... Wherefore we see that *Atheists* are now reduced into a narrow compass, since none are concluded to be *Atheists* but such as are mere *Corporealists* <note>Those who believe only physical matter exists.</note>; and all *Corporealists* must not be condemned for *Atheists* neither, but only those of them who assert that there is no *Conscious Intellectual Nature* presiding over the whole Universe. For this is that which the *Experts* <note>original: Adepti</note> in *Atheism*, of what form soever, all agree in: That the first principle of the Universe is no *Animal-like, Sentient*, and *Conscious Nature*, but that all *Animality, Sense*, and *Consciousness* is a secondary, derivative, and accidental thing, capable of being generated and corrupted, arising out of particular clusters of matter organized and dissolved together with them.

XXXI. Now if the First Principle and Original of all things in the Universe be thus supposed to be Body or Matter, devoid of all *Animality, Sense*, and *Consciousness*, then it must of necessity be either perfectly dead and stupid, and without all manner of life, or else endowed with such a kind of life only as is by some called *Plastic, Spermatic*, and *Vegetative*, by others the *Life of Nature*, or *Natural Perception*. And those *Atheists* who derive all things from dead and stupid matter must also necessarily do this, either in the way of *Qualities* and *Forms*—and these are the *Anaximandrian Atheists*—or else in the way of *Atoms* and *Figures*, which are the *Democritical* <note>Followers of Democritus, who proposed an atomic theory of the universe.</note>. But those who make Matter endowed with a *Plastic Life* <note>An unconscious, formative power in nature.</note> to be the first original of all things must necessarily suppose either one such *Plastic* and *Spermatic Life* only in the whole mass of Matter or Corporeal Universe—which are the *Stoical Atheists*—or else all Matter as such to have...

# CHAPTER III. The Asserters of Sensitive and Rational Matter.

...have *Life* and an *Energetic Nature* <note>original: "Energetick Nature"; meaning a nature capable of active force or operation</note> belonging to it (though without any *Animal Sense or Self-perception*) and consequently all the particular *parts of matter*, and *every whole formed by continuity*, to have a distinct *Plastic Life* <note>A "plastic life" refers to an unconscious, formative power in nature that organizes matter, distinct from conscious "animal" life.</note> of its own; these are the *Stratonic Atheists* <note>Followers of Strato of Lampsacus, who believed nature had a life-force but no conscious God.</note>. Therefore, there does not seem to be any room now left for any other form of *Atheism*, besides *these four*, to push its way in.

And we think it appropriate here again to emphasize what has been already suggested: that one grand difference among these several forms of *Atheism* is this: some of them attribute no *Life* at all to *Matter* as such, nor indeed acknowledge any *Plastic Life of Nature* distinct from the *Animal* life. They suppose everything whatsoever in the world—besides <term>matter without qualities</term> <note>original: ὕλη ἀποιος (hyle apoios); the raw, characterless substance of the universe</note>, the bare *substance of matter* considered as devoid of all qualities (that is, mere *extended bulk*)—to be *Generated and Corrupted* <note>In this context, "generated" means brought into being and "corrupted" means decayed or destroyed.</note>. Consequently, they resolve that all manner of *Life* whatsoever is *Generable and Corruptible*, or can be drawn out of *Nothing* and return to *Nothing* again; these are the *Anaximandrian and Democritic Atheisms*. 

But the others, which are the *Stoical and Stratonical*, do on the contrary suppose some *Life* to be *Fundamental and Original, Essential and Substantial, Ingenerable and Incorruptible*, as being a *First Principle* of things. Nevertheless, they do not hold this to be any *Animal, Conscious, and Self-perceptive Life*, but a *Plastic Life of Nature* only. All *Atheists* still agree in those *two aforementioned things*: *First*, that there is no other *Substance* in the world besides *Body* (matter); *Secondly*, that all *Animal Life, Sense and Self-perception, Conscious Understanding, and Personality* are *Generated and Corrupted*, successively drawn out of *Nothing* and reduced into *Nothing* again.

XXXII. Indeed, we are not ignorant that some who seem to be well-wishers to *Atheism* have talked sometimes of *Sensitive and Rational Matter*. They wish to suppose *three several sorts of matter* in the universe, specifically different from one another, that were originally such and self-existent from *Eternity*: namely *Senseless, Sensitive, and Rational*. It is as if the *Mundane System* <note>The physical universe or world-order.</note> might be conceived to arise from a certain jumble of these *three several sorts of matter*, as it were scuffling together in the dark without a *God*, and so producing brute animals and men. 

But this is a mere *precarious hypothesis* <note>An unproven assumption that depends on the speaker's will rather than evidence.</note>, as there is no imaginable account to be given for how there should come to be such an essential difference between *matters*, or why this piece of *matter* should be *sensitive* and that *rational*, when another is altogether *senseless*. Furthermore, the suggestors of it are but mere *novices in Atheism* and a kind of bungling *well-wishers* to it. 

First, because according to this *hypothesis*, no *Life* would be produced or destroyed in the successive *generations and corruptions of animals*, but only *combined and separated* <note>original: "Concreted and Secreted"</note> in them; and consequently all human *personalities* must be *eternal and incorruptible*. This is the same as asserting the *pre-existence and post-existence of all souls* from *eternity* to *eternity*—a thing that all *genuine and thorough-paced Atheists* abhor almost as much as they do the *Deity* itself. And secondly, because they can give no imaginable reason why there might not as well be a certain *Divine Matter*.

# The Canting Astrological Atheists. BOOK I.

But all those who are *masters* of the *craft of atheism*, and thoroughly *catechized* <note>instructed in the basic principles</note> or *initiated* in the *dark mysteries* thereof (as has been already emphasized), do perfectly agree in this: that all *animal, sentient, and conscious life, all souls and minds*, and consequently all *human personalities*, are *generated out of matter* and *corrupted again into it*, or rather *brought out of nothing and reduced into nothing again*.

We understand also that there are certain *canting* <note>original: "canting" - here meaning using hypocritical or jargon-filled speech</note> *astrological atheists* who would derive all things from the *occult qualities* and *influences of the stars*, according to their different *conjunctions, oppositions, and aspects*, in a certain blind and unaccountable manner. But these being *persons* devoid of all manner of *sense*, who do not even pretend to give an *account* of these *stars*—whether they are *animals* or not, or from where they derive their *origin* (which if they did undertake to do *atheistically*, they must eventually resolve themselves into one or another of those *hypotheses* already proposed)—therefore, as we conceive, they deserve not the least *consideration*. 

But we think it fit here to observe that such *devotees* to the heavenly *bodies* who look upon all the other *stars* as petty *deities*, but the *Sun* as the *supreme deity* and *monarch* of the *universe*, while also conceiving it to be *perfectly intellectual* (which is in a manner the same as the *Cleanthean hypothesis* <note>The theory of Cleanthes, a Stoic philosopher who believed the sun was the governing power of the world</note>), are not so much to be accounted *atheists* as *spurious, pagan, and idolatrous theists*. And upon all these *considerations*, we conclude again that there is no other *philosophical form of atheism* that can easily be devised besides these *four* mentioned: the *Anaximandrian*, the *Democritical*, the *Stoical*, and the *Stratonical*.

## XXXIII.
Amongst which *forms of atheism*, there is yet another *difference* to be observed, and accordingly another *distribution* to be made of them. It being first premised that all these aforementioned *sorts of atheists* (if they will speak consistently and agreeably to their own *principles*) must suppose all things to be, one way or another, *necessary*. For though *Epicurus* introduced *contingent liberty* <note>the idea of free will or chance events</note>, yet it is well known that he therein plainly contradicted his own *principles*. 

And this indeed was the first and principal thing intended by us in this whole *undertaking*: to confute that *false hypothesis* of the *mundane system* <note>the structure of the physical world</note> which makes all *actions* and *events necessary* upon *atheistic grounds*, but especially in the *mechanical way*. Wherefore, in the next place, we must observe that though the *principles* of all *atheists* introduce *necessity*, yet the *necessity* of these *atheists* is not one and the same, but of two different kinds. Some of them suppose a *necessity* of *dead* and *stupid matter*, which is that which is commonly meant by <gloss>material necessity</gloss> <note>original Greek: ὑλικὴ ἀνάγκη (hylikē anankē)</note>, and is also called by *Aristotle* an *absolute necessity* of things. Others suppose the *necessity* of a *plastic life* <note>a formative or creative natural force</note>, which the same *Aristotle* calls a *hypothetical necessity*. For the *Anaximandrian* and *Democritic atheists* do both of them assert a *material* and *absolute necessity* of all things; one in the way of *qualities*...

### CHAPTER III. Another Distribution of Atheism.

Qualities, and the other of Motion and Mechanism: But the Stoical and Stratonical <note>referring to Strato of Lampsacus, who believed nature had a life-force but no conscious god</note> Atheists assert a Plastic <note>term: "Plastic" here means formative or creative, like a mold</note> and Hypothetical Necessity of things only.

Now one grand difference between these two sorts of Atheism and their "necessities" lies in this: that the former, though they make all things necessary, yet they suppose them also to be fortuitous <note>original: "fortuitous" meaning happening by chance</note>; there being no inconsistency between these two. And the sense of both the Anaximandrian and Democritic Atheisms seems to be as described by Plato: *All things were mingled together by necessity according to fortune* <note>original Greek: πάντα κτῆ τύχλω ἐξ ἀνάγκης συνεκεράσθαι</note>. For that Nature from which these Atheists derived all things is at once both necessary and fortuitous. But the Plastic Atheisms suppose such a necessary Nature for the first principle of things as is not merely fortuitous, but regular, orderly, and methodical. The Stoical variety excludes all chance and fortune universally because they subject all things to one Plastic Nature ruling over the whole universe; but the Stratonical variety does it only in part, because they derive things from a mixture of both chance and Plastic Nature together.

And thus we see that there is a double notion of Nature among Atheists as well as Theists, which we cannot better express than in the words of Balbus the Stoic, portrayed by Cicero: <margin>On the Nature of the Gods, Book 2</margin> *Some consider Nature to be a certain force without reason, inciting necessary motions in bodies; but others view it as a force participating in order, proceeding as if by a planned path. No art, no hand, no craftsman can equal its skill by imitation. For the power of a seed is so great that, although it is very small, if it finds matter by which it can be nourished and grow, it so produces every thing in its own kind—partly so they are nourished through their roots and stems, and partly so they can move themselves and generate others like them.* <note>original Latin: Alii Naturam censent esse Vim quandam sine Ratione... ex se similia sui generare</note>

Some by Nature mean a certain force without reason and order, exciting necessary motions in bodies; but others understand by it such a force as, participating in order, proceeds as it were methodically. No art or craftsman can reach its exquisiteness by imitation. For the force of a seed is such that, though its size is very small, yet if it gets convenient matter for its nourishment and increase, it so forms and frames things in their several kinds, that they can be nourished through their stocks and trunks, and can also move themselves and generate their like. 

And again: *There are some who call all things by the name of "Nature," such as Epicurus; but we, when we say that the world is governed by Nature, do not mean a nature like that found in a clod of earth or a fragment of stone, or anything of that sort which has no cohesive principle; but rather like a tree or an animal, in which no randomness, but order and a certain likeness to art appears.* <note>original Latin: Sunt qui omnia Naturæ Nomine appellent... sed Ordo apparet & Artis quædam Similitudo</note>

Now according to these two different notions of Nature, the four previously mentioned forms of Atheism may be again divided <note>original: "dichotomized"</note> in this manner: into those that derive all things from a mere fortuitous and rash <note>original: "temerarious"</note> Nature, devoid of all order and—

However, it is certain that some persons atheistically inclined have been always apt to run another way, and to suppose that the *frame* of things and *system* of the *world* ever was from *eternity*, and ever will be to *eternity*, such as it is now, managed by a certain *orderly* and *regular*, but yet *senseless* and *unknowing nature*. And it is prophesied in Scripture that such atheists as these should *especially* abound in these latter days of ours: *There shall come in the last days <gloss>scoffers</gloss> <note>original: ἐμπαίκται (empaiktai)</note>, atheistical scoffers, walking after their own lusts and saying, "Where is the promise of his coming? For since the fathers fell asleep all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation."* These latter words are spoken only according to the received *hypothesis* of the Jews; the meaning of these atheists being quite otherwise: that there was neither *creation* nor *beginning* of the *world*, but that things had continued, such as they are now, from all *eternity*. 

As appears also from what the Apostle there adds by way of refutation: that *they were willfully ignorant of this, that by the word of God the heavens were of old, and the earth standing out of the water and in the water; and that as the world that then was, overflowing with water perished, so the heavens and earth which now are, by the same word are kept in store, and reserved unto fire against the day of judgment and perdition of ungodly men.* And it is evident that some of these atheists at this very day march in the garb of fanatical religionists <note>original: "Enthufiastical Religionists"; refers to those claiming direct divine inspiration but lacking traditional faith.</note>, acknowledging no more a God than a Christ outside of themselves, and allegorizing the day of *judgment* and future *conflagration* <note>The destruction of the world by fire.</note> into a kind of seemingly *mystical*, but really *atheistical nonsense*. These, if they did philosophize, would resolve themselves into one or the other of those two *hypotheses* before mentioned.

# CHAPTER III. *The World's Eternity Asserted.*

...mentioned; either that of one *Plastic <note>original: "Plastick"; referring to a formative or creative power that acts unconsciously</note>, Orderly, and Methodical, but Senseless Nature* ruling over the whole *Universe*; or else that of the *Life of Matter*, making one or the other of these two *Natures* to be their only *God* or *Numen* <note>original: "Numen"; a Latin term for a divinity or divine power</note>. It is sufficiently consistent with the principles of both these *Atheistic Hypotheses* (and no others) to maintain the *World's* both *Ante-* and *Post-Eternity* <note>The world's existence from an eternal past and into an eternal future</note>; yet in such a way that the latter of them, namely the *Hylozoists* <note>Those who believe that matter itself is alive</note>, admitting a certain mixture of *Chance* together with the *Life of Matter*, would suppose that although the main strokes of things might be preserved the same, and some kind of constant regularity always kept up in the *World*, yet the whole *Mundane System* did not in all respects continue the same from *Eternity* to *Eternity* without any *Variation*. 

<margin>Strabo, Book 1.</margin>
As *Strabo* tells us that *Strato the Physicist* maintained that the *Euxine Sea* <note>The Black Sea</note> at first had no outlet to the Mediterranean, but that by the continual running of *Rivers* into it, causing it to overflow, a passage was opened in length of time by the *Propontis* <note>Sea of Marmara</note> and *Hellespont*. He also claimed that the *Mediterranean Sea* forced open that passage of the *Herculean Straits* <note>The Straits of Gibraltar</note>, which was a continuous *Isthmus* or neck of *Land* before; and that many parts of the present *Continent* were previously *Sea*, just as much of the present habitable *Land* was once underwater. So it cannot be doubted that the same *Strato* also supposed such kinds of *Alternations* and *Vicissitudes* as these in all the greater parts of the *Mundane System*.

But the *Stoical Atheists*, who believed the whole *World* was managed by one *Orderly* and *Plastic Nature*, might very well—and consistently with their own *Hypothesis*—maintain, besides the *World's Eternity*, one constant and *Invariable Course* or *Tenor* of things in it. This is what *Pliny the Elder* <note>original: "Plinius Secundus"</note> does, who, if he were anything, seems to have been one of these *Atheists*. He wrote: "The World, and that which by another name we please to call the Heavens (by whose rotation all things are ruled), ought to be believed to be a Divinity, Eternal, Immense, such as was never Created and shall never be Destroyed... It is at once the Work of Nature and Nature itself" <note>original Latin: "Mundum & hoc quod nomine alio Cœlum appellare libuit... Idem rerum Naturæ Opus, & rerum ipſa Natura"</note>. 

<margin>Natural History, Book 2, Chapter 1.</margin>
By the way, it may be observed again that those *Atheists* who denied a *God* according to the *True Notion* of him—as a *Conscious, Understanding Being* presiding over the whole *World*—nevertheless looked upon either the *World* itself, or else a mere *Senseless Plastic Nature* within it, as a kind of *Numen* or *Deity*, because they supposed it to be *Ingenerable* <note>incapable of being created</note> and *Incorruptible* <note>incapable of being destroyed</note>. This same *Pliny*, based on the grounds of *Stoical Atheism*, maintained the *World's Eternity* and *Incorruptibility* against the *Anaximandrians* and *Democritics* <note>Followers of Anaximander and Democritus</note>. He likewise, in opposition to their <term>infinity of worlds</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀπειρία κόσμων"</note>, asserted that there was but *One World*, and that it was *Finite*. 

In like manner, we read concerning that famous *Stoic Boethus*, whom *Laertius* affirms to have denied that the *World* was an *Animal* (which, according to the language and sense of those times, was the same as denying a *God*). He also maintained, contrary to the received *Doctrine* of the *Stoics*, the *World's Ante-Eternity* and *Incorruptibility*; *Philo* testifies the same of him in his *Treatise* <term>On the Incorruptibility of the World</term> <note>original Greek: "περὶ ἀφθαρσίας κόσμου"</note>.

Nevertheless...

<summary>This page discusses how different schools of ancient atheistic thought, such as the Hylozoists and Stoical Atheists, argued for the eternity of the world by replacing a conscious God with a "senseless" plastic nature or living matter.</summary>

# Atheism Quadripartite, Book I.

Nevertheless, it seems that some of these Stoic Atheists also agreed with the majority of other Stoic Theists in assuming a successive *infinity of worlds generated and corrupted* by reason of intervening *periodical conflagrations* <note>The Stoic belief that the universe is periodically destroyed by fire and then reborn.</note>. However, they believed all this was managed by such a *stupid and senseless nature* as governs *plants and trees*. We gather this much from those words of *Seneca* cited before, where, describing this *atheistical hypothesis*, he tells us that even if the world were a *plant*—that is, governed by a *vegetative or plastic nature* <note>original: "plastick nature"; a formative, non-conscious biological force</note> without any *animal consciousness*—nevertheless, *from its beginning even unto its end* <note>original: "ab initio ejus usque ad exitum"</note>, etc., it had both a beginning and will have an end. From its beginning to its end, everything was managed by a kind of *regular law*, including its *successive conflagrations* as well as those *inundations or deluges* which have sometimes happened. Yet they understood this in such a way that in these several *revolutions and successive circuits or periods of worlds*, all things should be *hidden in identical forms* <note>original: "ὁμοειδῆ λανθάνοντα"; the idea that every cycle of the universe repeats exactly the same events and people</note>, exactly alike to what had been infinitely before, and should be again infinitely afterwards. Of which more will be said elsewhere.

XXXIV. This *four-part atheism* <note>original: "Quadripartite Atheism"</note> which we have now represented is the *Kingdom of Darkness divided*, or laboring with an *internal, seditious war* in its own bowels, and thereby destroying itself. Consequently, we might well save ourselves the labor of any further refutation of *atheism* merely by setting these several *forms of atheism* against one another and dashing them together, as they oppose and contradict each other no less than they do *theism* itself. 

For first, those two *pairs of atheisms*—on the one hand the *Anaximandrian and Democritic*, and on the other the *Stoic and Stratonic*—absolutely destroy each other. The former pair supposes the *first principle* of all things to be *stupid matter devoid of life*, contending that all *life* as well as other *qualities* is *capable of being generated and corrupted* <note>original: "Generable and Corruptible"</note>, or a mere *accidental thing*. They look upon the *plastic life of nature* as a *figment or fantastic whim* <note>original: "Phantastick Capritio"</note>, a thing almost as formidable and altogether as impossible as a *deity*. The other pair, on the contrary, founds everything upon this *principle*: that there is *a life and natural perception essential to matter, which cannot be generated or corrupted*. They contend it is utterly impossible to give any account of the *phenomena of the world*, the *origin of motion*, the *orderly frame and disposition of things*, and the *nature of animals* without this *fundamental life of nature*.

Again, the *single atheisms* belonging to each of these several *pairs* quarrel just as much between themselves. For *Democritic atheism* explodes the *Anaximandrian qualities and forms*, demonstrating that the *natural production of such entities out of nothing*, and the *corruption of them again into nothing*, is of the two rather more impossible than a *divine creation and annihilation*. And on the other side, the *Anaximandrian atheist* plainly discovers that when the *Democritics and Atomists* have spent all their fury against these *qualities and forms*, and done what they can to explain the *phenomena of nature* without them in another way, they themselves do notwithstanding like...

<summary>The author argues that the four types of atheism are internally contradictory and mutually exclusive, specifically contrasting those who view matter as lifeless (Democritic) with those who see it as having an inherent "plastic" life (Stoic/Stratonic).</summary>
<keywords>Stoicism, Seneca, conflagration, plastic nature, Anaximander, Democritus, Strato, atomism, internal contradictions of atheism</keywords>

<page-num>143</page-num>
<header>Kingdom of Darkness divided.</header>

## CHAP. III. Kingdom of Darkness divided.

Like drunken men, they reel and stagger back again into their own errors, and are unavoidably forced at last to take sanctuary in them.

In like manner, the *Stoical* and *Stratonical atheists* <note>Stratonical atheism refers to the followers of Strato of Lampsacus, who believed nature had a life-force but no conscious God.</note> may as effectively undo and refute each other. The former group argues against the latter that, besides the monstrous absurdity of making every atom of senseless matter *infallibly wise* or *omniscient* <note>all-knowing</note> without any *consciousness*, the *hylozoists* <note>term: hylozoists; those who believe that all matter is alive</note> can give no reason why the matter of the whole universe might not just as well *conspire* and *unite* into *one* being, as all the single atoms do that compose the body of any animal or man. Nor can they explain why one *conscious* life might not result from the *whole* <note>original: "Totum"</note> of the former, just as it does from the latter; by which means the whole world would become an *animal* or *God*. 

Again, the latter group contends that the *Stoical* or *cosmo-plastic atheist* <note>one who believes the world is governed by a blind, formative nature</note> can offer no reason why the whole world might not have one *sentient* and *rational* soul, as well as one *plastic soul* <note>term: plastic soul; a formative, non-conscious power that organizes matter</note> within it—that is, why it should not be an *animal* as well as a *plant*. Moreover, they argue that the sensitive souls of brute animals and the rational souls of men could never possibly emerge out of one *single, plastic*, and *vegetative soul* in the whole universe. 

And lastly, they argue it is just as impossible for the whole world to have *life* in it while none of its parts have any *life* of their own, as it is for the whole world to be white or black while no part of it has any *whiteness* or *blackness* at all. Therefore, the *Stoical atheists*, as well as the *Stoical theists*, both alike deny *incorporeal substance* <note>spiritual or non-physical reality</note> in words only, while they really admit the thing itself. This is because *one* and the same *life*, ruling over all the distant parts of the physical universe, must necessarily be an *incorporeal substance*; it exists in the whole and acts upon every part, yet no part of it exists in any single part by itself—for then it would be many lives and not one. From all this, it may be concluded that atheism is a certain strange kind of *monster* with *four heads* that are all perpetually biting, tearing, and devouring one another.

Now, though these several forms of atheism mutually destroy each other, and none of them are really significant or formidable in themselves regarding any strength of reason they possess, yet when compared among themselves, some may be more significant than the rest. 

First, as the *qualities* and *forms* of the *Anaximandrian atheist* <note>referring to Anaximander, who believed the world arose from an "infinite" primary matter</note>—supposed to be really distinct from the substances—are things unintelligible in themselves, he cannot, with any color or pretense of reason, maintain that they are naturally produced out of nothing and reduced again into nothing, while simultaneously rejecting *divine creation* and *annihilation* as impossibilities. Moreover, *Anaximandrian atheism* is, as it were, swallowed up by *Democritic atheism* <note>the atomism of Democritus</note> and further improved by it. This latter school carries on the same design with more apparent skill, greater plausibility of wit, and a more pompous show of "something" where there is, in fact, nothing. On this account, for many ages past, it has beaten the Anaximandrian...

<summary>The author argues that different schools of atheism (Stoical, Stratonical, Anaximandrian, and Democritic) are logically inconsistent and mutually destructive, effectively refuting each other's premises. He characterizes atheism as a "four-headed monster" that collapses under its own internal contradictions regarding the nature of life and matter.</summary>

# Two Principal Forms of Atheism. Book I.

<page-num>144</page-num>

Anaximandrian *Atheism* <note>Anaximander was an ancient Greek philosopher who believed the universe originated from an "infinite" material substance.</note> was driven, in a manner, quite off the stage, and reigned there alone. So that *Democritic* or *Atomic Atheism* seems to be much more significant of the two than the *Anaximandrian* or *Hylopathian* <note>original: "Hylopathian" — the belief that matter and its properties/affections are the only reality.</note>.

Again, as for the two other forms of *Atheism*: if there were any *life* at all in *matter* as its first and immediate recipient, then by reason this must necessarily be supposed to be in it in the same way that all other *physical qualities* are in *bodies*. That is, it would be *divisible* along with the matter, so that some of it would be in every part of that *matter*. This follows the *hypothesis* of the *Hylozoists* <note>Those who believe that matter possesses a form of life.</note>. 

On the contrary, the *Stoic Atheists* suppose only one *life* in the whole mass of *matter*, in such a way that none of the parts by themselves have any *life* of their own. By doing this, they (no less than the *Stoic Theists*) make this *life* of theirs to be not a *physical quality* or form, but an *incorporeal substance* <note>A non-physical spirit or soul.</note>. This contradicts their own *hypothesis* that only matter exists. From this we may conclude that *Cosmoplastic* or *Stoic Atheism* is, of the two, less significant than *Hylozoic* or *Stratonic Atheism* <note>Named after Strato of Lampsacus, who argued that nature has a life-force but no conscious God.</note>.

<margin>Section 4. Chapter 3.</margin> Therefore, among these four *forms* of *atheism* that have been proposed, these two—the *Atomic* or *Democritic*, and the *Hylozoic* or *Stratonic*—are the primary ones. 

The first of these, namely *Democritic Atheism*, accepts a true *notion* of *body*: that (according to the *doctrine* of the first and most ancient *atomists*) it is nothing but *resisting bulk*, devoid of any kind of *life*. Yet, because it takes for granted that there is no other *substance* in the world besides *body*, it concludes that all *life* and *understanding* in *animals* and *human beings* is *generated* out of *dead* and *stupid matter*. They do not see life as *qualities* and *forms* (which is the *Anaximandrian way*), but as something resulting from the *weaving together* of *atoms*, or some peculiar *composition* of *magnitudes*, *figures*, *locations*, and *motions*. Consequently, they believe that life and thought are themselves really nothing else but *local motion* and *mechanics*. This is a point that was some time ago very pertinently and judiciously observed and criticized <note>original: "perstringed" — censured or touched upon critically.</note> by the learned author of the *Epistolary Exercise* <note>original: "Exercitatio Epistolica" — likely referring to Seth Ward, Bishop of Salisbury.</note>, who is now a Reverend Bishop.

But the latter form, namely *Hylozoic Atheism*, truly acknowledges on the contrary that *life*, *thought*, and *understanding* are *entities* really distinct from *local motion* and *mechanics*. Therefore, they cannot be *generated* out of *dead* and *stupid matter*, but must necessarily exist somewhere in the world *originally*, *essentially*, and *fundamentally*. Yet, because they also take it for granted that there is no other *substance* besides *matter*, they then corrupt the *notion* of *matter* or *body* by blending and confounding it with *life*. They treat them as merely two *incomplete conceptions* of the same *substance*. They conclude that all *matter* and *substance* as such has *life* and *perception* (or a *natural* and *unconscious understanding*) essentially belonging to it. They argue that *sense* and *conscious reason* or *understanding* in *animals* arises only from the *accidental modification* of this *fundamental life* of *matter* through its *organization* into a body.

<summary>The author identifies Atomic (Democritic) and Hylozoic (Stratonic) atheism as the two most significant forms, contrasting their views on whether life is a mechanical result of moving atoms or an inherent, unconscious property of matter itself.</summary>

<page-num>146</page-num>
<header>A Digression concerning the Book I.</header>

...the world anew, under a specious show of wit and profound philosophy.

Therefore, as we could not here insist upon both these forms of *Atheism* together—because that would have been to confound the language of atheists and to have made them like the "Cadmean offspring" <note>In Greek mythology, the warriors who sprang from the dragon's teeth sown by Cadmus and immediately killed one another.</note> to do immediate execution upon themselves—we were in all reason obliged to make our first and principal assault upon *Atomic Atheism*. This is the only form significant enough for this focus because it is the only one that publicly confronts the world and, like that proud *uncircumcised Philistine* <note>A reference to Goliath, the biblical giant who defied the Israelites.</note>, openly defies the *hosts of the living God*. *Nevertheless, I intend in the close of this whole discourse* (that is, the *last book*), where we are to determine the *right intellectual system of the universe* and to assert an *incorporeal <term>non-physical</term> Deity*, to demonstrate that *life*, *thought, and understanding* do not essentially belong to *matter* and all *substance* as such, but are the *peculiar attributes and characteristics of incorporeal substance*.

XXXVI. However, since we have now introduced these several forms of *Atheism*, we shall not neglect any of them in the meantime. For in the answer to the *second atheistic ground*, we shall confute them all together at once, as they agree in this one *fundamental principle: that the origin of all things in the universe is senseless matter, or matter devoid of all animality or conscious life*. In the reply to the *fourth atheistic argumentation*, we shall briefly hint at the grounds of reason from which *incorporeal substance* is demonstrated. In the examination of the *fifth*, we shall confute the *Anaximandrian Atheism* <note>The theory attributed to the philosopher Anaximander that the world arose from an infinite, indefinite substance.</note> proposed there, which is, as it were, the *first sciography <term>outline or preliminary sketch</term> and rude delineation of atheism*. And in the confutation of the *sixth*, we shall show how the ancient *atomic atheists* did preventively overthrow the foundation of *Hylozoism* <note>The belief that all matter is alive.</note>. 

Besides all this, in order to provide a fuller and more thorough confutation of both *Cosmo-plastic* <note>The belief that the universe is governed by a blind, unconscious plastic (forming) nature.</note> and *Hylozoic Atheisms*, we shall in this very place take the opportunity to insist largely upon the *plastic life of nature*. We will first give a *true account* of it and then afterwards show how grossly it is misunderstood and how the pretense of it is abused by the supporters of both these *atheistic hypotheses*. The heads of this *larger digression*, because they could not be conveniently inserted in the table of contents for the chapter, shall be presented to the reader’s view at the end of it.

XXXVII. For we think it fit here to observe that neither the *Cosmo-plastic* or *Stoical*, nor the *Hylozoic* or *Stratonical atheists* <note>Followers of Strato of Lampsacus, who argued that nature acts without divine intelligence.</note> are condemned by us simply because they suppose such a thing as a *plastic nature* or *life distinct from the animal*. This concept is not only exploded as an *absolute non-entity* by the *atomic atheists*—who might possibly be afraid of it as something that approached too near to a *Deity*, or else would risk introducing one—but it is also utterly discarded by some *professed theists* of later times, who might nonetheless have an *undiscovered tang <term>trace or hint</term> of mechanic atheism*.

# CHAPTER III. The Plastic Life of Nature.

Atheism hangs about them in their confident rejection of all *Final* and *Intending Causality* <note>original: "Final and Intending Causality"; the idea that things in nature are designed for a specific purpose or end goal.</note> in *Nature*, and in their admitting no other *Causes* of things as *Philosophical*, except for the *Material* and *Mechanical* only. This is truly to banish all *Mental*—and consequently *Divine*—*Causality* entirely out of the *World*. It makes the whole *World* nothing more than a mere *Heap of Dust*, *Fortuitously* <note>By chance or accident.</note> agitated, or a *Dead, Corpse-like* thing that has no *Signatures* of *Mind*, *Understanding*, *Counsel*, or *Wisdom* upon it at all. Indeed, it allows for no other *Vitality* acting within it than only the *Production* of a certain *Quantity* of *Local Motion* and its *Conservation* according to some *General Laws*. The *Democritic Atheists* <note>Followers of Democritus, who believed the world was made of atoms moving in a vacuum without divine purpose.</note> take it for granted that these things would all exist as they are, even if there were no *God*. And thus <margin>*On the Heavens, Book 2, Chapter 12*</margin> *Aristotle* describes this kind of *Philosophy*: that it made the whole *World* consist "only of accidents, and of units having no order, and of atomic principles" <note>original: "ἐκ συμπτώματων μόνων, ἐκ μονάδων τάξιν μὴ ἐχόντων, ἐξ ἀρχῶν ἀτόμων"</note>—that is, of nothing but *Bodies* and *Monads* (which are *Atoms* or *Small Particles of Matter*) merely arranged and disposed together in such an order, but otherwise *Dead* and *Inanimate*.

2. For unless we admit such a thing as a *Plastic Nature* <note>A term for an internal, formative power in nature that carries out divine blueprints; "plastic" here means "form-giving" or "shaping."</note> that acts *effectively* <note>original: "ἐνεράτῶς" (energetically/effectively)</note> for the sake of something and in order to *Ends*—acting *Regularly*, *Artificially*, and *Methodically*—it seems that one of these *Two Things* must be concluded: 

Either, first, that in the *Formation* and *Organization* of the *Bodies* of *Animals*, as well as all other *Phenomena*, everything happens *Fortuitously* and occurs as it is without the *Guidance* and *Direction* of any *Mind* or *Understanding*. 

Or else, second, that *God* himself does everything *Immediately* and, as it were, with his own *Hands*. This would mean He forms the *Body* of every *Gnat* and *Fly*, *Insect* and *Mite*, just as He does other *Animals* in their *Generations*. All of these have *Members* containing so much *Contrivance* that *Galen* <note>An influential ancient Greek physician and philosopher.</note> professed he could never admire enough the *Artistry* found in the *Leg of a Fly* (and yet he would have admired the *Wisdom of Nature* even more had he been acquainted with the use of *Microscopes*). 

I say, assuming there is no *Plastic Nature*, one of these *Two things* must be concluded. This is because no one conceives that the things of *Nature* are administered with such exact *Regularity* and *Constancy* everywhere merely by the *Wisdom*, *Providence*, and *Efficiency* of those *Inferior Spirits*, *Demons*, or *Angels*. Furthermore, though it is true that the *Works of Nature* are dispensed by a *Divine Law* and *Command*, this is not to be understood in a *Vulgar Sense*—as if they were all produced by the mere *Force* of a *Verbal Law* or *Outward Command*. *Inanimate* things cannot be *Commanded* or *Governed* by such a law. Therefore, besides the *Divine Will* and *Pleasure*, there must necessarily be some other *Immediate Agent* and *Executioner* provided to produce every *Effect*. Not even a *Stone* or other *Heavy Body* could fall downward at any time merely by the *Force* of a *Verbal Law* without some other *Efficient Cause*; either *God* himself must immediately push it, or there must be some other subordinate *Cause* in *Nature* for that *Motion*. Therefore, the *Divine Law* and *Command* by which the things of *Nature* are administered must be understood as the *Real Appointment* of some *Energetic*, *Effectual*, and *Operative Cause* for the *Production* of every *Effect*.

<summary>The author argues that nature is not a random collection of atoms nor a direct, manual labor of God, but is governed by a "Plastic Nature"—a subordinate, formative power that executes divine laws.</summary>

# Final Causes
## Book I.

3. Now, to assert the first of these two things—that all the effects of nature come to pass by *material* and *mechanical necessity*, or the mere *accidental motion of matter* <note>original: "fortuitous motion of matter"</note> without any guidance or direction—is a claim no less irrational than it is impious and atheistical. This is not only because it is utterly *inconceivable* and *impossible* that such *infinite regularity* and *artistry* <note>original: "artificialness"</note> as is found everywhere throughout the whole world should constantly result from the *accidental motion of matter*, but also because there are many specific *phenomena* in nature that plainly transcend the *powers of mechanism*. 

Therefore, no sufficient *mechanical reasons* can be devised for these things, such as the *action of breathing* <note>original: "motion of respiration"</note> in animals. There are also other *phenomena* that are perfectly contrary to the *laws of mechanism*; for example, the fact that the *poles* of the *equator* and the *ecliptic* <note>The ecliptic is the sun's apparent path; the author refers to the tilt of the Earth's axis which creates seasons, arguing this specific alignment cannot be accidental.</note> are distant from one another, which we shall insist upon later. Regarding both of these kinds, other instances have been proposed by my learned friend Dr. *More* in his *Manual of Metaphysics* <note>original: "Enchiridion Metaphysicum"</note> and very ingeniously improved by him for this very purpose: namely, to prove <note>original: "evince"</note> that there is something in nature besides *mechanism*, and consequently that there exists *incorporeal substance* <note>term: substance that is not made of physical matter, such as a soul or spirit</note>.

Moreover, those *theists* <note>term: those who believe in a God who created and intervenes in the world</note> who philosophize in this manner—by resolving all *physical phenomena* <note>original: "corporeal phenomena"</note> into *accidental mechanism* or the *necessary* and *unguided motion of matter*—make *God* out to be nothing more in the world than an *idle spectator* of the various *results* of the *accidental* and *necessary motions* of *bodies*. They render his *wisdom* altogether *useless* and *insignificant*, as if it were a thing wholly *enclosed* and shut up within his own breast, not acting at all upon anything outside of himself.

<margin>Aristotle, *On the Parts of Animals*, Book 1, Chapter 1.</margin>Furthermore, all such *mechanists* as these, whether *theists* or *atheists*, do—according to that judicious *criticism* passed by *Aristotle* long ago upon *Democritus*—substitute what is essentially *a carpenter's or craftsman's wooden hand* <note>original Greek: χεῖρα ξυλίνην τίστορες</note>, moved by *strings* and *wires*, in place of *a living hand*. They create a kind of dead and wooden *world*, like a *carved statue* that has nothing *vital* or *magical* <note>In this context, "magical" refers to an internal, non-mechanical power of attraction or life.</note> about it. Whereas to those who are *thoughtful*, it will plainly appear that there is a *mixture of life* or *plastic nature* <note>term: an internal, organizing force in nature that carries out divine blueprints without being conscious itself</note> together with *mechanism* which runs through the whole *physical universe*.

And while it is claimed—not only that all *physical phenomena* may be sufficiently explained <note>original: "salved"</note> *mechanically* without any *final, intending*, and *directive causality* <note>term: the concept that things exist for a specific purpose or "end"</note>, but also that all other *reasons* for things in nature besides the *material* and *mechanical* are altogether *unphilosophical*—the same *Aristotle* ingeniously exposes the *ridiculousness* of this claim in this way: He tells us that it is just as if a carpenter, joiner, or carver should give this account (as the only satisfactory one) of any artificial structure or piece of carved imagery: *that because the tools—the axes, hatchets, planes, and chisels—happened to fall* <note>original Greek: ὅτι ἐμπεσόντος τὲ ὀργάνις τὸ μὲν κοῖλον ἐγένετο, τόδε ἐπίπεδον</note> upon the wood, this part became hollow and that part became flat...

He critiques "mechanists" who view God as a passive observer and uses Aristotle's analogies to show the absurdity of ignoring purposeful design in nature.</summary>

For is it not altogether as absurd and ridiculous for men to undertake to give an account of the formation and organization of the bodies of animals by mere fortuitous mechanism <note>original: "Fortuitous Mechanism"; meaning chance-based physical processes without a designer.</note>, without any final or intending causality? For example, why there was a heart here and brains there, and why the heart had so many and such different valves in the entrance and outlet of its ventricles, and why all the other organic parts—veins and arteries, nerves and muscles, bones and cartilages, with the joints and members—were of such a form? 

They claim this happened because, forsooth, the fluid matter of the seed happened to move in such a way in several places, thereby causing all those differences (which also vary in different animals). They argue all this is the necessary result of a certain quantity of motion that was initially and indifferently impressed upon the small particles of the matter of this universe as it turned round in a *vortex* <note>A reference to Cartesian physics, which imagined the universe as a series of swirling whirlpools of matter.</note>. 

But as the same Aristotle adds, no carpenter or artisan is so simple as to give such an account as this and think it satisfactory. Instead, he will declare that he himself directed the motion of the instruments in such a manner and toward such ends: <margin>* On the Parts of Animals, Book 1, Chapter 1.</margin> <gloss>A carpenter would give a better account than that, for he would say what he himself did; it is not enough to say that when the tool struck, such and such happened, but rather that he struck it in a certain way for a specific purpose, and for a specific cause, so that a certain shape or form might be produced.</gloss> <note>original Greek: βέλτιον ὁ τέκτων... ἀπὸ τῆσ μορφῆσ γένηται.</note> A carpenter would give a better account than that, for he would not think it sufficient to say that the building came to be of such a form because the instruments happened to fall in such a way. Rather, he will tell you that it was because he himself made such strokes, and that he directed the instruments and determined their motion in such a manner to this end: that he might make the whole a building fit and useful for its purposes. 

And this is to assign the "final cause" <note>The purpose or goal for which something exists.</note>. And certainly there is scarcely any man in his right mind who will not acknowledge that the reason for the different valves in the heart—based on their apparent usefulness within those particular structures—is more satisfactory than any reason that can be brought from mere fortuitous mechanism or the unguided motion of the seminal matter.

4. This would make the belief in Providence more difficult to accept and give an advantage to atheists. Furthermore, in the judgment of the writer of *De Mundo* <note>On the Universe; a treatise formerly attributed to Aristotle.</note>, it is not fitting in respect to God either that he should <margin>* Chapter 7.</margin> <gloss>perform all tasks himself, or continue to do whatever he wishes by being personally present everywhere; it is much more unbecoming of God. It is more dignified and appropriate that his power, through the whole universe, should govern the world, move the sun, and so on.</gloss> <note>original Greek: αὐτεργεῖν ἅπαντα... ἥλιον τε κινῆσαι, &c.</note> 

If it were not suitable for the state and majesty of Xerxes, the Great King of Persia, that he should condescend to do all the meanest offices himself...

itself; much less can this be thought decorous in respect of God. But it seems far more **august** <note>original: "August"; meaning grand or noble</note>, and becoming of the Divine Majesty, that a certain power and virtue, derived from him and passing through the universe, should move the sun and moon, and be the **immediate cause** <note>The direct agent of an action</note> of those lower things done here upon Earth.

Moreover, it does not seem agreeable to reason either that Nature, as a distinct thing from the Deity, should be quite superseded or made to signify nothing, with God himself doing all things immediately and miraculously. From this, it would also follow that all things are done either **forcibly** and **violently**, or else **artificially** only, and none of them by any **inward principle** of their own.

¶ Lastly, this opinion is further confuted by that slow and gradual process found in the generation of things, which would seem to be but a vain and idle pomp, or a trifling formality, if the agent were omnipotent. It is also confuted by those **errors** <note>original: "ἀμαρτήματα" (hamartēmata)</note> (as **Aristotle** calls them)—those **errors** and **bungles** which are committed when the matter is **inept and contumacious** <note>original: "Inept and Contumacious"; meaning unsuitable and stubborn or resistant to being shaped</note>. These argue that the agent is not irresistible, and that **Nature** is the kind of thing that is not altogether incapable (just like **human art**) of being sometimes frustrated and disappointed by the **indisposition of matter**. Whereas an **omnipotent agent**, just as it could dispatch its work in a moment, would always do it **infallibly** and **irresistibly**. No **ineptitude** or **stubbornness** of matter would ever be able to hinder such an agent, or make him **bungle** or **fumble** in anything.

5. Therefore, since things are neither all produced **fortuitously** <note>By chance</note>, or by the unguided mechanism of matter, nor may God himself reasonably be thought to do all things immediately and miraculously; it may well be concluded that there is a <term>Plastic Nature</term> <note>A formative, organizing power in nature that acts according to divine patterns but is not itself conscious</note> under him. This, as an inferior and subordinate instrument, does drudgingly execute that part of his providence which consists in the regular and orderly motion of matter. Yet, there is also besides this a higher providence to be acknowledged, which, presiding over it, often supplies its defects and sometimes overrules it; for this <term>Plastic Nature</term> cannot act **electively** <note>By conscious choice</note> nor with **discretion**. And by this means, the wisdom of God will not be shut up or confined wholly within his own breast, but will display itself abroad and print its stamps and signatures everywhere throughout the world. So that God—as **Plato** (following **Orpheus**) speaks—will be not only the **beginning** and **end**, but also the **middle** of all things. They are as much to be ascribed to his causality as if he himself had done them all immediately, without the concurrent instrumentality of any subordinate natural cause. Notwithstanding this, in this way it will also appear to human reason that all things are disposed and ordered by the Deity without any solicitous care or distracting providence.

And indeed those <term>Mechanic Theists</term> <note>Thinkers who believe God created the world like a machine but does not intervene in its daily operation</note> who, rejecting a <term>Plastic Nature</term>, choose to involve the Deity as little as possible in **mundane affairs** <note>Worldly or earthly matters</note>, either for fear of debasing him and bringing him down to...

This system allows God's wisdom to be visible throughout the universe without requiring Him to manage every trivial detail personally.</summary>

### CHAPTER III. The Instrument of the Deity.

Those who think it beneath God to involve himself in lowly tasks, or else fear subjecting him to anxious burdens, would have God contribute nothing more to the world’s system and management than only the first impressing of a certain quantity of motion upon matter, and the subsequent conserving of it according to some general laws. These men, I say, do not seem to understand themselves very well in this. For they must, of necessity, either suppose these "laws of motion" execute themselves, or else be forced to perpetually involve the Deity in the immediate motion of every atom of matter throughout the universe in order to execute and observe them. 

The former of these is plainly absurd and ridiculous, and the latter is something from which these philosophers themselves are extremely recoiling. Therefore, we can make no other conclusion than this: that they unskillfully and unknowingly establish that very thing which they oppose in words. Their "laws of nature" concerning motion are really nothing else but a **Plastic Nature** <note>original: "Plastic Nature" refers to an unconscious, formative power or organizing principle in the universe that carries out God's plan, similar to an instinctual "life force."</note> acting upon the matter of the whole physical universe. This nature both maintains the same quantity of motion in it always and also distributes it (by transferring it out of one body into another) according to such laws fatally impressed upon it. Now, if there is a **Plastic Nature** that governs the motion of matter everywhere according to laws, there can be no reason given why the same might not also extend further to the regular disposal of that matter in the formation of plants and animals and other things, in order to create that fit, coherent frame and harmony of the whole universe.

6. And as this **Plastic Nature** is a concept which seems to be in itself most reasonable, so has it also had the support of the best philosophers in all ages. For first, it is well known that **Aristotle** concerns himself with nothing more zealously than this: that worldly things are not produced merely by the necessary and unguided motion of matter, or by accidental mechanics, but by such a nature as acts regularly and artificially for specific ends. Yet, this nature is not the highest principle nor the supreme God <note>original: "Supreme Numen"</note>, but is subordinate to a perfect mind or intellect. He affirms that **mind together with nature was the cause of this universe** <note>original: "νῦς αἴτιον ἢ φύσις τῆδε τῶ παντὸς"</note>, and that heaven and earth, plants and animals, were framed by them both. That is, they were framed by **Mind** as the principal and directing cause, but by **Nature** as a subservient or executive instrument. Elsewhere, he joins God and nature together in the same way, as when he concludes that **God and Nature do nothing in vain**.

Neither was **Aristotle** the first creator or inventor of this doctrine, as **Plato** before him had plainly asserted the same. For in a passage already cited, he affirms that **Nature together with Reason**, and according to it, orders all things. He thereby makes **Nature**, as a distinct thing from the Deity, a subordinate cause under God's reason and wisdom. Elsewhere he concludes that there are **certain causes of a wise and artificial nature which the Deity uses as subservient to itself** <note>original: "ἔμφρονος φύσεως αἰτιαι ὑπηρετήσεις ὁ θεὸς χρῆται"</note>, as also that there are **co-causes which God makes use of as subordinately cooperative with himself** <note>original: "συναίτιαι αἷς συνεργεῖς θεὸς χρῆται"</note>.

<summary>The author argues that the laws of physics require a "Plastic Nature"—a subordinate, organizing force—to execute God's will in the material world. He supports this by citing Aristotle and Plato, who both viewed Nature as an executive instrument of a higher Divine Mind.</summary>

# A Plastic Nature Agreeable to the Book I.

Moreover, before Plato, Empedocles also philosophized in the same manner. When supposing two worlds—the one *Archetypal* <note>original: "Archetypal" — the original model or blueprint</note> and the other *Extypal* <note>original: "Extypal" — the physical copy or manifestation</note>—he established <gloss>Friendship</gloss> <note>original: φιλία (philia)</note> and <gloss>Discord</gloss> <note>original: νεῖκος (neikos)</note> to be the <gloss>starting principle</gloss> <note>original: ἀρχὴ δ᾽ ἐστὶ (archē d' esti)</note>, the *Active Principle* and *Immediate Operator* in this lower world. He did not understand these, as Plutarch and some others have imagined, to be two substantial principles in the world—one of Good and the other of Evil—but only a <term>Plastic Nature</term> <note>A "Plastic Nature" refers to an internal, formative power that shapes matter according to a divine plan, acting unconsciously like a biological instinct.</note>, as Aristotle suggests in several places. He called it by that name partly because he perceived that the result and final outcome of nature in all births and decays amounted to nothing more than the mixing and separation, or the thickening and secretion, of pre-existing things. He also used these terms because this <term>Plastic Nature</term> is that which reconciles the *contrarieties* and *enmities* of particular things and brings them into one general harmony in the whole.

This latter idea is a notion that Plotinus—describing this very <term>Seminary Reason</term> <note>original: "Seminary Reason" — a seed-like, formative principle (Latin: ratio seminalis)</note> or <term>Plastic Nature</term> of the world (though taking it in a somewhat broader sense than we do here)—ingeniously pursues in this manner: 

<margin>Enneads 3.1.2.16.</margin> 
<gloss>By making the parts opposite to one another and leaving them mutually deficient, it produced their composition or generation through war and battle. Thus it is one, for if it were not one, it would not exist. Having become an enemy to itself in its parts, it is thus friendly to itself in the whole. It is as if there were a dramatic play; the play, having produced these battles, makes the drama a single harmony of conflicting voices. Therefore, one might rather compare it to the harmony resulting from a struggle.</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἀντιθεῖς ἀλλήλοις τὸ μέρη... ἐκμαχομένῳ εἰκάσδε.</note>

The <term>Seminary Reason</term> or <term>Plastic Nature</term> of the universe, by opposing the parts to one another and making them individually lacking, produces by that means war and contention. And therefore, though it is one, it nevertheless consists of different and contrary things. For while there is hostility in its parts, it is nevertheless friendly and agreeable in the whole; in the same way that in a dramatic poem, clashes and contentions are reconciled into one harmony. Therefore, the <term>Seminary</term> and <term>Plastic Nature</term> of the world may fitly be compared to the harmony of disagreeing things. This Plotinic doctrine may well serve as a commentary upon Empedocles, just as Simplicius briefly represents his meaning:

<margin>On Aristotle's *On the Heavens*, Book 1, Chapter 10.</margin> 
<gloss>Empedocles establishes two worlds: the one united and intelligible, the other divided and sensible; and in this lower sensible world, he takes notice of both unity and discord.</gloss> <note>original Greek: Ἐμπεδοκλῆς δύο κόσμος συνίση... ἐν τότῳ κόσμῳ</note>

It was previously observed that Heraclitus likewise asserted a regular and <term>Artificial Nature</term> <note>original: "Artificial Nature" — nature acting with the skill of an artisan or "art," but without conscious thought.</note> as the fate of things in this lower world. For his "Reason," passing through the substance of all things or the "Ethereal Body" (which was the seed of the generation of the universe), was nothing but that <term>Spermatic</term> or <term>Plastic Nature</term> of which we now speak. And whereas there is an odd passage of this philosopher recorded—<gloss>that neither any god nor man made this world</gloss> <note>original: κόσμον τόνδε ὅτε τις θεῶν ἐπ᾽ ἀνθρώπων ἐποίησε</note>—which is justly mocked by Plutarch for its simplicity and looks very atheistic at first sight, we conceive its meaning to have been this: that the world was not made by anyone in the same way that a craftsman makes a house, by...

<summary>This page argues that ancient philosophers like Empedocles, Plotinus, and Heraclitus recognized a "Plastic Nature"—an unconscious, formative force that creates harmony out of the conflict of material parts.</summary>

<margin>In the Life of Zeno</margin>
And as Hippocrates followed Heraclitus in this (as was before declared), so did Zeno and the Stoics also. They supposed that besides an *Intellectual Nature*, acting as the *Supreme Architect* and Master-builder of the world, there was another *Plastic Nature* acting as the *Immediate Workman* and operator. This *Plastic Nature* has been already described in the words of *Balbus* <note>A character in Cicero's dialogues representing Stoic philosophy.</note> as a thing which acts not *fortuitously* <note>by chance</note> but *regularly*, *orderly*, and *artificially* <note>with the skill of an artisan</note>. And *Laertius* tells us it was defined by Zeno himself after this manner: *Nature is a habit moved from itself according to generative reasons <note>original: "spermatic reasons" or "seminal principles"</note>, perfecting and containing those several things which in determinate times are produced from it, and acting agreeably to that from which it was secreted.* <note>original Greek: ἡ φύσις ἕξις ἐξ αὐτῆς κινουμένη κατὰ σπερματικοὺς λόγους, ἀποτελοῦσά τε καὶ συνέχουσα τὰ ἐξ αὐτῆς ἐν ὡρισμένοις χρόνοις, καὶ τοιαῦτα δρῶσα ἀφ' οἵων ἀπεκρίθη.</note>

Lastly, as the later Platonists and Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note> have unanimously followed their masters in this—whose *Vegetative Soul* is also nothing other than a *Plastic Nature*—so the chemists and followers of Paracelsus insist much upon the same thing. They seem rather to have carried the notion further regarding the bodies of animals, where they call it by a new name of their own: the *Archeus* <note>term: "Archeus" was a term used by Paracelsus to describe a vital force or "internal chemist" that governs the functions of an organism.</note>.

<margin>Book 1, Chapter 4</margin>
Moreover, we cannot but observe here that among the ancients, those were generally condemned as outright atheists who acknowledged no other principle besides body or matter, necessarily and fortuitously moved, such as Democritus and the first Ionics. Even Anaxagoras himself, notwithstanding that he was a professed theist and plainly asserted *Mind* to be a *Principle*, was severely censured because he attributed too much to *material necessity*. He admitted neither this *Plastic Nature* nor a *Mundane Soul* <note>World Soul</note>, and was thus judged not only by the common people (who unjustly labeled him an atheist) but also by Plato and Aristotle, as a kind of spurious and imperfect theist, and one who had given great advantage to atheism.

*Aristotle* in his *Metaphysics* thus represents his philosophy: *Anaxagoras uses Mind and Intellect (that is, God) as a machine in the creation of the world <note>original: "cosmopoeia"</note>; and when he is at a loss to give an account of things by material necessity, then and never but then does he draw in Mind or God to help him out; but otherwise he will rather assign anything else for a cause than Mind.* <note>original Greek: Ἀναξαγόρας τε γὰρ μηχανῇ χρῆται τῷ νῷ πρὸς τὴν κοσμοποιίαν, καὶ ὅταν ἀπορήσῃ διὰ τίν' αἰτίαν ἐξ ἀνάγκης ἐστί, τότε ἕλκει αὐτόν, ἐν δὲ τοῖς ἄλλοις πάντα μᾶλλον αἰτιᾶται τῶν γινομένων ἢ νοῦν.</note> Now if Aristotle censures Anaxagoras in this manner—though he was a professed theist—because he only seldom used a *mental cause* to explain the phenomena of the world, and only then when he was at a loss for other *material* and *mechanical causes* (which it seems he sometimes confessed himself to be), what would that philosopher have thought of those so confident *mechanists* of later times, who will never vouchsafe so much...

Plato likewise in his *Phaedo* and elsewhere, condemns this *Anaxagoras* <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BC) was a Pre-Socratic philosopher who introduced the concept of *Nous* (Mind) as the ordering force of the cosmos.</note> by name for this very thing: that though he acknowledged *Mind* to be a *Cause*, yet he seldom made use of it for solving the *phenomena*. From this we may observe that, according to the *natural apprehensions* of *men* in all *ages*, those who resolve the *phenomena* of *nature* into *material necessity*—allowing for no *final* nor *mental causality* (the ordering of things toward specific *ends* or purposes)—have been strongly suspected of being *friends* to *atheism*.

For he that asserts an *occult quality* as the *cause* of any *phenomenon* does indeed assign no *cause* at all for it, but only declares his own *ignorance* of the cause. But he that asserts a *Plastic Nature* assigns a *determinate* and proper *cause*—indeed, the only *intelligible cause*—of that which is the greatest of all *phenomena* in the *world*: namely, the *well and fit* <note>original: *τὸ εὖ κὴ καλῶς*</note>, the *orderly*, *regular*, and *artificial frame* of things in the *universe*.
