### CHAPTER III. No Occult Quality.

is the only true cause of orderly regularity. He that asserts a **Plastic Nature** <note>original: "Plastick Nature"; a term for a creative, organizing force in the natural world that acts according to divine patterns but without conscious thought</note> asserts **mental causality** in the world. But the **fortuitous mechanists** <note>philosophers who believe the universe is a machine governed by blind luck or chance</note>, who, by exploding **final causes** <note>the purpose or "end goal" for which a thing exists</note>, will not allow **mind and understanding** to have any influence at all upon the frame of things, can never possibly assign any cause for this grand **phenomenon**—unless **confusion** may be said to be the cause of **order**, and **fortune or chance** the cause of **constant regularity**. Therefore, they themselves must resolve it into an **occult quality** <note>a hidden or mysterious property that cannot be explained by known laws of physics</note>. Nor indeed does there appear any great reason why such men should assert an **infinite mind** in the world, since they do not allow it to act anywhere at all, and therefore must necessarily make it to be in vain.

8. Now, this **Plastic Nature** being a thing which is not without some difficulty in its conception, we shall here endeavor to do these two things concerning it: First, to set down a right representation of it; and then afterwards to show how extremely the notion of it has been **mistaken, perverted,** and **abused** by those **atheists** who would make it to be the only **God Almighty**, or **first principle** of all things.

How the **Plastic Nature** is in general to be conceived, **Aristotle** instructs us in these words: <gloss>If the ship-building art were in the wood, it would produce the same results by nature as it does by art.</gloss> <gloss>Physics, Book 2, Chapter 8</gloss> <note>original Greek: "ἐν ἔνι ἐν τῷ ξύλῳ ἡ ναυπηγικὴ ὁμοίως ἂν τῇ φύσει"</note> If the **naupegical art** <term>the art of the shipwright</term> were in the **timber** itself, operatively and effectively, it would act there just as **nature** does. And the case is the same for all other **arts**. If the **oecodomical art** <term>the art of building or architecture</term>, which is in the **mind of the architect**, were supposed to be transfused into the **stones, bricks,** and **mortar**, acting upon them in such a manner as to make them come together of themselves and range themselves into the form of a complete **edifice**—just as **Amphion** <note>In Greek mythology, Amphion played a golden lyre so beautifully that stones moved of their own accord to build the walls of Thebes</note> was said by his **harp** to have made the **stones** move and place themselves orderly of their own accord, and so to have built the **walls of Thebes**—or if the **musical art** were conceived to be immediately in the **instruments** and **strings**, animating them as a **living soul** and making them move exactly according to the **laws of harmony** without any **external impulse**; these and such like instances, in **Aristotle's** judgment, would be fit **iconisms** <term>images or representations</term> of the **Plastic Nature**. That being **art** itself acting immediately upon the **matter** as an **inward principle** in it. To which purpose the same **philosopher** adds that this thing might be further illustrated by another instance or resemblance: <gloss>But it is most apparent when a person heals himself; for nature is like that.</gloss> <note>original Greek: "μάλιστα δ᾽ δῆλον, ὅταν τις ἰατρεύῃ αὐτὸς ἑαυτόν· τούτῳ γὰρ ἔοικεν ἡ φύσις"</note> **Nature** may be yet more clearly resembled to the **medicinal art** when it is employed by the **physician** in curing himself. So the meaning of this **philosopher** is that **nature** is to be conceived as **art acting** not from without and at a distance, but immediately upon the thing itself which is formed by it. And thus we have the first **general conception** of the **Plastic Nature**: that it is **art** itself, acting immediately on the **matter** as an **inward principle**.

9. In the next place, we are to observe that though the **Plastic Nature** be a kind of **art**, yet there are some considerable **preeminences** which...

### 10. Another Preeminence of Nature above Human Art is this,
That whereas *Human Artists* are often searching for answers and at a loss, and therefore *Consult* and *Deliberate*, as also upon second thoughts mend their former *Work*; *Nature*, on the contrary, is never searching for what to do, nor at a standstill. For that reason also (besides another that will be suggested afterwards) it does never *Consult* nor *Deliberate*. Indeed *Aristotle Intimates* that this had been the Grand Objection of the old *Atheistic Philosophers* against the *Plastic Nature*: <note>The "Plastic Nature" refers to the formative power in nature that shapes organisms, not "plastic" in the modern synthetic sense.</note> That because we do not see *Natural Bodies* *Consult* or *Deliberate*, therefore there could be *Nothing* of *Art*, *Counsel*, or *Contrivance* in them, but all came to pass *Fortuitously* <note>original: "Fortuitously"; by mere chance or accident</note>. But he confutes it in this manner:
<margin>Physics, book 2, chapter 8.</margin>
<note>original: Ἄτοπον δὲ τὸ μὴ οἴεσθαι ἕνεκά τι γίνεσθαι...</note> "It is absurd for men to think nothing is done for a purpose if they do not see that which moves it deliberating; even Art itself does not deliberate." Whence he concludes that *Nature* may act *Artificially*, *Orderly*, and *Methodically*, for the sake of *Ends* <term>original: "Ends"; goals or purposes</term>, though it never *Consults* or *Deliberates*. Indeed *Human Artists* themselves do not *Consult* properly as they are *Artists*; whenever they do so, it is for want of *Art*, and because they are searching for a solution, their *Art* being *Imperfect* and *Adventitious*. But *Art* itself, or *Perfect Art*, is never searching, and therefore never *Consults* or *Deliberates*. And *Nature* is this *Art*, which never hesitates nor studies as if unresolved what to do, but is always readily prompted. Nor does it ever repent afterwards of what it has formerly done, or go about—as it were upon second thoughts—to alter and mend its former *Course*. Instead, it goes on in one *Constant*, *Unrepenting Tenor*, from *Generation* to *Generation*, because it is the *Stamp* or *Impress* of that *Infallibly Omniscient*—

# CHAPTER III. The Divine Art Embodied.

Omniscient Art, of the Divine Understanding, which is the very Law and Rule of what is simply the best in everything.

And thus we have seen the difference between Nature and human *art*: that the latter is *imperfect art*, acting upon the *matter* from without and at a distance; but the former is *art itself* or *perfect art*, acting as an *inward principle* within it. Therefore, when *art* is said to imitate *nature*, the meaning is that *imperfect human art* imitates that *perfect art* of *nature*, which is really no other than the *divine art* itself. As before *Aristotle*, *Plato* had declared in his *Sophist* in these words: <term>τὰ φύσει λεγόμενα ποιεῖσθαι θείᾳ τέχνῃ</term> <note>original Greek: "Those things which are said to be done by nature are indeed done by divine art."</note>.

II. Notwithstanding this, we must take notice in the next place that as *nature* is not the *Deity* itself, but a thing very remote from it and far below it, so neither is it the *divine art* as it is in itself—*pure* and *abstract*—but only *concrete* and *embodied*. For the *divine art*, considered in itself, is nothing but *knowledge*, *understanding*, or *wisdom* in the *mind of God*. Now *knowledge* and *understanding*, in its own *nature*, is <term>κεχωρισμένον τι</term> <note>original Greek: "a certain separate and abstract thing"</note>, and of so *subtle* and *refined* a *nature* that it is not capable of being incorporated with *matter*, or *mingled* and *blended* with it as its *soul*. 

And therefore *Aristotle's* second instance, which he proposes as most pertinent to illustrate this business of *nature*—namely, the *physician's art* curing himself—is not entirely adequate. This is because when the *medicinal art* cures the *physician* in whom it resides, it does not *act* there as *nature* (that is, as *concrete* and *embodied art*), but only as *knowledge* and *understanding*, which is *art naked*, *abstract*, and *unbodied*. It also does its work indirectly, by the *physician's willing* and *prescribing* to himself the use of such *medicines* as merely help—by removing impediments—that which is *nature* indeed, or the *inward Archeus* <note>term: a vital principle or "internal chemist" believed by early scientists to govern the body's functions</note>, to effect the *cure*. 

*Art* is defined by *Aristotle* to be <term>λόγῳ τῷ τῆς φύσεως ἔργα ἀποδιδόναι</term> <note>original Greek: "the reason of the thing without matter"</note>; and so the *divine art* or *knowledge* in the *mind of God* is *unbodied reason*. But *nature* is <term>Ratio Mersa & Confusa</term> <note>original Latin: "Reason immersed and confused"</note>, *reason immersed* and *plunged* into *matter*, and as it were *fuddled* in it and *confounded* with it. *Nature* is not the *divine art archetypal* <note>term: the original pattern or blueprint</note>, but only *ectypal* <note>term: a copy or impression made from an original</note>; it is a living *stamp* or *signature* of the *divine wisdom*. Though it acts exactly according to its *archetype*, it does not at all comprehend nor understand the *reason* of what it does. 

The difference between these two may be compared to that between the <term>λόγος ἐνδιάθετος</term> <note>original Greek: "internal reason," often called *Verbum Mentis* or "Word of the Mind"</note>, the *reason* of the *mind* and conception, and the <term>λόγος προφορικός</term> <note>original Greek: "uttered reason"</note>, the *reason* of *external speech*. The latter, though it bears a certain *stamp* and *impress* of the former upon it, is itself nothing but *articulate sound*, devoid of all *understanding* and *sense*. Or else we may illustrate this business by another similitude, comparing the *divine art* and *wisdom* to an *architect*, but *nature* to a *manual laborer* <note>original: "manuary opificer"</note>. The difference between these two is set forth by *Aristotle* pertinently to our purpose: "the master-builders in each craft..." <note>original Greek: τῆς ἀρχιτεκτονικῆς κατ' ον</note>

12. Therefore, as we previously observed the superiority of Nature over human art, so we must here also take notice of its imperfections and defects, in which respect it falls short of human art. Having admired that wisdom and art by which the bodies of animals are framed, he concludes that one or the other of these two things must necessarily be acknowledged: either the *Vegetative* or *Plastic* Power <note>original: "Plastic Power" refers to a formative or shaping force in nature that organizes matter into living forms.</note> of the soul, by which it fabricates and organizes its own body, is more excellent and divine than the rational; or else, <margin>Harvey, *On the Generation of Animals*, Exercise 49.</margin> *that there is no intellect within nature itself, but it only appears so to our own conceptions, because we judge the divine things of nature according to our own arts, faculties, and the patterns we have borrowed from ourselves; as if the active principles of nature produced their effects in the same way that we usually perform our own artificial works.* <note>original Latin: "In Naturâ O-intellectum inesse, sed ita solum videri Conceptui nostro, qui secundum Artes nostras & Facultates, seu Exemplaria à nobisipis mutuata, de rebus Naturæ divinis judicamus; Quasi Principia Naturæ Activa, effectus suos eo modo producerent, quo nos opera nostra Artificialia solemus."</note> That in the works of nature there is neither *prudence* nor *understanding*, but it only seems so to our apprehensions, who judge of these divine things of nature according to our own arts and faculties, and patterns borrowed from ourselves; as if the *active principles* of nature did produce their *effects* in the same manner as we do our artificial works. Wherefore we conclude, agreeably to the sense of the best philosophers, both ancient and modern, that nature is such a thing that, though it acts artificially and for the sake of ends, yet it does but ape and mimic the divine art and wisdom. Nature itself does not understand those ends for which it acts, nor the reason of what it does in order to achieve them; for which cause also it is not capable of consultation or deliberation, nor can it act by choice or with discretion.

13. But because this may seem strange at first sight—that nature should be said to act *for a purpose* <note>original Greek: "ἕνεκά του" (eneka tou), meaning "for the sake of something" or "for an end."</note> for the sake of ends, and regularly or artificially, and yet be itself devoid of knowledge and understanding—we shall therefore endeavor to persuade you of the possibility, and facilitate the belief of it, by some other instances. First, consider the example of habits, particularly those musical ones of singing, playing upon instruments, and dancing. These *habits* direct every motion of the hand, voice, and body, and prompt them readily, without any deliberation or studied *consideration* of what the next following note or motion should be. If you jog a sleeping musician and sing but the first words of a song to him—which he had either himself composed or learned before—he will presently take it from you, and perhaps even before he is thoroughly awake, go on with it and sing out the remainder of the whole song to the end. Thus the fingers of an experienced lutenist <note>original: "Lutonist," a player of the lute.</note> and the legs and whole body of a skillful dancer are directed to move regularly and orderly, in a long train and series of motions, by those artificial habits in them. These habits do not themselves at all comprehend those *laws and rules of music or harmony* by which they are governed. So, the same thing may be said of these habits which was said before of nature: that they do not *know*, but only *do*. And thus we see there is no reason why this *plastic nature* (which is supposed to move the body *regularly* and *artificially*) should be thought to be an absolute impossibility. Habits, in like manner, *gradually evolve* themselves in a long train or series of *regular* and *artificial motions*, readily prompting the doing of them without comprehending that *art* and *reason* by which they are directed. # CHAPTER III. Without Express Consciousness.

<margin>Plotinus, Enneads 4, Book 4, Chapter 13.</margin>
**Plastic Nature** <note>The formative force in nature that shapes organisms.</note> in the formation of plants and animals seems to have no animal fancy, no express **consciousness** or **con-sense** <note>original: *synaesthesis*; a shared internal perception or self-awareness.</note> of what it does. Thus the often-commended philosopher <note>Plotinus</note> says: *Nature has no fancy or imagination; for as intellection and knowledge are superior to fancy, so fancy is superior to the impression of nature. Nature has no apprehension nor conscious perception of anything.* In a word, Nature is a thing that has no such self-perception or self-enjoyment in it as animals have.

16. Now we are well aware that this is a concept which the narrow principles of some recent philosophers <note>Likely referring to Cartesians (followers of René Descartes).</note> will not admit: that there should be any **action** distinct from **local motion** <note>Physical movement through space.</note> besides **express conscious thought**. For they make the first general categories of all existence to be **extension** <note>Physical matter occupying space.</note> and **thought** (that is, *extended being* and *thinking being*). Then, by supposing that the essence of **thought** consists only in **express consciousness**, they must necessarily exclude such a **Plastic Life** of Nature as we speak of, which is supposed to act without **animal fancy** or **express consciousness**. 

Therefore, we conceive that the primary categories of being ought rather to be expressed this way: **resisting** or **impenetrable extension**, and **life** (that is, **internal energy** and **self-activity**). Then, again, that **life** or **internal self-activity** is to be subdivided into that which acts with **express consciousness** and **self-awareness**, and that which is without it. The latter of these is this **Plastic Life** of Nature. 

So, there may be an **action** distinct from **local motion**, or a **vital energy**, which is not accompanied by that **fancy** or **consciousness** found in the **energies** of **animal life**. That is, there may be a simple **internal energy** or **vital self-motion** <note>original: *autokinesie*</note> which is without that **duplication** <note>The "doubling" of the mind where it both acts and observes itself acting.</note> included in the nature of **con-sense** and **consciousness**. It is this consciousness that makes a being present with itself, **attentive** to its own **actions**, or **observant** of them, perceiving itself to do or suffer, and having a **fruition** or **enjoyment** of itself. 

Indeed, it must be granted that whatever moves **matter** or determines its **motion** **vitally** must do so by some other **energy** of its own; it is also reasonable to conceive that it has some **vital sympathy** with that **matter** upon which it acts. But we apprehend that both of these may exist without **clear** and **express consciousness**.

<margin>Plotinus, Enneads 3, Book 2, Chapter 15.</margin>
Thus the philosopher says: *Every life is energy, even the lowest form of life, and therefore that of Nature. Its energy is not like that of fire, but is such an energy that, though there is no sense belonging to it, it is not reckless or accidental, but orderly and regular.*

Therefore, this controversy over whether the energy of Plastic Nature is **thought** or not seems to be merely a **logomachy** <note>A dispute about words.</note> or a contention about terminology. For if **clear** and **express consciousness** is assumed to be included in the definition of **thought**, then it must be granted that **thought** does not belong to the **Plastic Life** of **Nature**. But if the definition of that **word** is enlarged to include all **action** distinct from **local motion**, and to be of equal **extent** with **life** itself, then the **energy** of **nature** is indeed **thought**.

<summary>The author argues that "Plastic Nature"—the force that organizes life—operates through an internal energy or "life" that lacks conscious self-awareness. He challenges the Cartesian view that all non-mechanical action must be conscious, suggesting instead that life can be orderly and purposeful without being "thought" in the traditional sense.</summary>

# Vital Energies
## Book I.

And since it cannot be denied that the *plastic nature* <note>The formative force in nature that organizes matter</note> has a certain *dull* and *obscure idea* of that which it *stamps* and *prints* upon *matter*, the same *philosopher* himself does not hesitate to call this *idea* of *nature* <gloss>both a spectacle and a thing contemplated</gloss> <note>original Greek: Ἅμα καὶ Θεώρημα</note>, as likewise the *energy of nature* towards it, <gloss>a silent and unwise contemplation</gloss> <note>original Greek: Θεωρία & Ἄσοφος</note>; indeed, he allows that *nature* may be said to be, in some sense, <gloss>a lover of spectacles or contemplation.</gloss> <note>original Greek: φιλοθεάμαν</note>

17. However, it seems reasonable on several accounts that there may be some *vital energy* without *clear and express* <gloss>shared-feeling and consciousness</gloss> <note>original Greek: συναίσθησις (synaisthesis)</note>, <gloss>observation, attention, or self-perception.</gloss> For first, those *philosophers* themselves who make the *essence of the soul* consist in *thought*, and again the *essence of thought* in *clear and express consciousness*, cannot make it seem at all probable that the *souls of men*—in all profound *sleeps, lethargies, and strokes* <note>original: "apoplexies"</note>, as also of *embryos* in the *womb* from their very first arrival there—are never for even one moment without *expressly conscious thoughts*. If they were without them, according to the *principles of their philosophy*, they must, <gloss>by that very fact</gloss> <note>original Latin: ipso facto</note>, cease to exist. Now, if the *souls of men and animals* are at any time without *consciousness and self-perception*, then it must be granted that *clear and express consciousness* is not *essential to life*. 

There is some appearance of *life and vital sympathy* in certain *vegetables* and *plants* which, though called *sensitive plants* and *plant-animals*, cannot well be supposed to have *animal sense* and *imagination* <note>original: "fancy"</note> or *express consciousness* in them; although we are aware, meanwhile, how some endeavor to explain all those *phenomena mechanically*. It is certain that our *human souls* themselves are not always *conscious* of whatever they have in them; for even the *sleeping mathematician* <note>original: "geometrian"</note> has at that time all his *geometrical theorems* and *knowledge* in him in some way, as also the *sleeping musician* has all his *musical skill and songs*. Therefore, why may it not be possible for the *soul* to likewise have some *actual energy* in it which it is not *expressly conscious* of? 

We all have *experience* of doing many *animal actions without paying attention*, which we reflect upon afterward; as also that we often continue a long *series of bodily motions* by a mere *virtual intention of our minds*, and as it were by *half a thought*. That *vital sympathy* by which our *soul* is united and tied fast, as if with a *knot*, to the *body*, is a thing that we have no direct *consciousness* of, but only see in its *effects*. Nor can we tell how we come to be so differently—

### CHAPTER III. Without Express Consciousness.

We are similarly affected in our souls by many different motions made upon our bodies. Likewise, we are not conscious of that energy by which we impress a variety of *motions* and *shapes* <note>original: "figurations"</note> upon the *animal spirits* <note>In early medicine, these were thought to be fluids in the nerves that carried sensation and motion.</note> of our brain during our *imaginative thoughts* <note>original: "phantastick thoughts"</note>. For though the *geometrician* perceives himself making *lines, triangles*, and *circles* in the *dust* with his finger, he is not aware of how he first makes all those same *figures* upon the *physical spirits* of his brain. From there, however, as if from a mirror, they are reflected back to him; *fancy* <note>imagination</note> being rightly concluded by *Aristotle* to be a *weak* and *obscure sense*. 

There is also another more *interior* kind of *plastic power* in the *soul* (if we may call it that) by which it is *formative* of its own *thoughts* <note>original: "cogitations"</note>, which the soul itself is not always *conscious* of. For example, when in *sleep* or *dreams*, the soul frames *conversational discourses* <note>original: "interlocutory discourses"</note> between itself and other persons in a long series, with *coherent sense* and *appropriate connections*. In these dreams, the soul often seems to be surprised by unexpected *answers* and *retorts* <note>original: "reparties"</note>, even though the soul itself was the *poet* and *inventor* of the entire *fable* the whole time. 

Not only our *blinking* <note>original: "nictations"</note> for the most part when we are awake, but also our *tossing and turning* <note>original: "nocturnal volutations"</note> in *sleep*, are performed with very little or no *consciousness*. Respiration—or that motion of the *diaphragm* and other *muscles* which causes it—may well be concluded to be always a *vital motion*, even though it is not always an *animal* one (since no mechanical explanation for it is sufficient). No man can claim that he is perpetually *conscious* of that *energy* of his *soul* which produces breathing when he is awake, much less when he is asleep. 

And lastly, the *Cartesian* <note>referring to René Descartes</note> *attempts* to explain the *motion* of the *heart mechanically* seem to be abundantly disproven by *observation* <note>original: "autopsy"</note> and *experiment*. These prove the *systole* <note>the contraction of the heart</note> of the *heart* to be a *muscular constriction* caused by some *vital principle*. To claim this is caused by nothing but a *physical plastic quality* in the *substance* of the *heart* itself is very *unphilosophical* and *absurd*. Now, just as we have no voluntary *command* <note>original: "imperium"</note> at all over the *contraction* and *dilation* <note>original: "systole and diastole"</note> of the *heart*, we are also not conscious of any *energy* of our own *soul* that causes them. Therefore, we may reasonably conclude from this as well that there is some *vital energy* that operates without *animal imagination*, *internal sensation* <note>original: "synæsthesis"</note>, express *consciousness*, or *self-perception*.

<margin>William Harvey, *On the Generation of Animals*</margin>

And thus that *curious* and *diligent inquirer* into *nature* commended before <note>William Harvey</note> resolves: *"Nature moves as if by a kind of fate or command, acting according to laws"* <note>original Latin: "Natura tanquam Fato quodam, seu Mandato secundum Leges operante, movet"</note>. *Fate* and the *laws* or *commands* of the *Deity* concerning the *world's economy* <note>the management of the universe</note> are really the same thing. They ought to be looked upon neither as mere *words* nor as simple *will* and *thought* in the *mind of God*, but as an *energetic* and *effective principle* established by the *Deity* to bring decreed things to pass. And though this plastic nature contains no small part of Divine Providence in it, yet since it is a thing that cannot act *by choice* <note>original: "Electively"</note> nor with *discretion*, it must be granted that there is a higher and diviner Providence than this, which also presides over the corporeal world itself. The same thing which outlines the veins must also form the arteries; and that which fabricates the nerves must also project the muscles and joints. It must be the same thing that designs and organizes the heart and brain, with such communications between them. One and the self-same thing must necessarily have within it the entire idea...

# The *Incorporeal Plastic Nature.* Book I.

Idea and the complete model or platform of the whole organic body. For the several parts of matter, distant from one another and acting alone by themselves without any common director, would be unable to consult together or communicate with each other. Therefore, they could never possibly conspire to make up one such uniform and orderly system or structure as the body of every animal is. The same must also be said concerning the *Plastic Nature* <note>The "Plastic Nature" refers to an unconscious but purposeful formative power that shapes living things and the universe, acting as an instrument of Divine Providence.</note> of the whole corporeal universe, in which *all things are ordered together, conspiring into one* <note>original: ἀταξία πρὸς ἐνσύνταξιν — literally "disorder toward coordination."</note>. It must be one and the same thing which forms the whole, or else it could never have fallen into such a uniform order and harmony. Now, that which is one and the same, acting upon several distant parts of matter, cannot be corporeal <note>physical or material</note>.

Indeed, *Aristotle* is severely censured by some learned men for this: that though he talks everywhere of such a *Nature* as acts *regularly*, *artificially*, and *methodically* for the sake of the best ends, yet he nowhere positively declares whether this *Nature* of his is *corporeal* or *incorporeal*, *substantial* or *accidental*. This is, however, less to be wondered at in him because he does not clearly determine these same points concerning the rational soul either, but seems to stagger uncertainly about them. In the meantime, it cannot be denied that *Aristotle's* followers for the most part conclude this *Nature* of his to be *corporeal*. Notwithstanding this, according to the principles of his own philosophy, it cannot possibly be so. For there is nothing else attributed to body in his system besides these three: *Matter*, *Form*, and *Accidents* <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities of a thing, like its color or weight, as opposed to its "substance."</note>; none of which can be the *Aristotelian Nature*. 

First, it cannot be *Matter*; because nature, according to *Aristotle*, is supposed to be the principle of *motion* and *activity*, which matter in itself lacks. Moreover, *Aristotle* concludes that those who assign only a material cause assign no cause at all *for the "well and fit," or for that regular and artificial frame of things which is ascribed to Nature* <note>original: τὸ δὲ χάος — referring here to the lack of order in mere chaos.</note>. Upon both these accounts, it is determined by that philosopher that *Nature is more a principle and cause than matter* <note>original: ἡ φύσις μᾶλλον ἀρχὴ ἢ αἰτία τ᾽ ὕλης</note>, and therefore it cannot be one and the same thing with it. 

Again, it is just as plain that *Aristotle's* Nature cannot be the *Forms* of particular *bodies* either, as common Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> seem to believe. These forms are all generated and produced by Nature, and are just as corruptible as they are capable of being created. Whereas Nature is something that is neither generated nor corrupted, being the principle and cause of all generation and corruption. To make Nature and the material *forms* of bodies the self-same thing is the same as if one should make the *seal* (along with the *stamper* too) the same thing as the *signature* <note>The impression left behind.</note> upon the *wax*. 

And lastly, *Aristotle's* Nature can least of all be the *accidents* or *qualities* of bodies; because these act only by virtue of their *substance*, and they cannot exercise any *active power* over the *substance* itself in which they exist. Whereas the *Plastic Nature* is a thing that *dominates* over the *substance* of the whole *corporeal universe*, and which, subordinate to the Deity, put both heaven and earth into this frame in which they now exist. Therefore, since *Aristotle's* Nature can be neither the—

# CHAPTER III. Aristotle's Account of Nature.

21. Now if the plastic nature <note>The "plastic nature" refers to an unconscious, formative power that organizes matter, distinct from a conscious mind.</note> be incorporeal, then it must of necessity be either an inferior power or faculty of some soul which is also conscious, sensitive, or rational; or else a lower substantial life by itself, devoid of animal consciousness. The Platonists seem to affirm both of these together: namely, that there is a plastic nature lodged in all particular souls of animals, brutes, and men, and also that there is a general plastic or "spermatic" <note>original: *spermatick*; meaning a germinal or seed-like principle of growth.</note> principle of the whole universe distinct from their higher mundane soul <note>The "mundane soul" or *Anima Mundi* is the soul of the world.</note>, though subordinate to it and dependent upon it. <gloss>That which is called Nature is the offspring of a higher soul, which has a more powerful life in it.</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἡ λεγομένη φύσις γέννημα ψυχῆς πρεσβυτέρας δυνάμεως ἔλαττον</note> And though Aristotle does not so clearly acknowledge the incorporeity and substantiality of souls, yet he concurs very much with this Platonic doctrine: that Nature is either a lower power or faculty of some conscious soul, or else an inferior kind of life by itself, depending upon a superior soul.

And this we shall make to appear from his book *On the Parts of Animals*, <margin>Book 1, Chapter 1.</margin> after we have taken notice of some considerable preliminary passages in it in order to that end. For having first declared that, besides the material cause, there are other causes also of natural generations, namely these two: <gloss>that for whose sake (or the final cause), and that from which the principle of motion comes (or the efficient cause)</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἥτε ἕνεκα οὗ, καὶ ὅθεν ἡ ἀρχὴ τῆς κινήσεως</note>, he determines that the former of these two is the principal. <gloss>The chief of these two causes seems to be the final or the intending cause; for this is reason, and reason is equally a principle in art and in natural things.</gloss> <note>original Greek: φαίνεται δὲ πρώτη, ἣν λέγομεν ἕνεκά τινος· λόγος δὲ οὗτος, ἀρχὴ δὲ ὁ λόγος, ὁμοίως ἔν τε τοῖς κατὰ τέχνην καὶ τοῖς φύσει συνεστηκόσιν</note> Nay, the philosopher adds excellently that there is more of reason and art in the things of nature than there is in those things that are artificially made by men. <gloss>There is more of final or intending causality and of the reason of good in the works of nature than in those of human art.</gloss> <note>original Greek: μᾶλλον δ’ ἐστὶ τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα καὶ τὸ καλὸν ἐν τοῖς τῆς φύσεως ἔργοις, ἢ ἐν τοῖς τῆς τέχνης</note> After which he greatly complains of the first and most ancient physiologers <note>Natural philosophers or scientists.</note>—meaning thereby Anaximander and those other Ionics before Anaxagoras—that they considered only <gloss>the material principle</gloss> <note>original Greek: τὴν ὑλικὴν ἀρχὴν</note> and cause of things, without attending to those two other causes: the principle of motion and that which aims at ends. They talked only of fire, water, air, and earth, and generated the whole world from the fortuitous concourse <note>Accidental clashing or coming together.</note> of these senseless bodies. But at length Aristotle falls upon Democritus, who, being younger than those others before mentioned, philosophized after the same atheistical manner, but in a new way of his own, by atoms. He acknowledged no other nature, neither in the universe nor in the bodies of animals, than that of fortuitous mechanism, and supposed all things to arise from the different compositions of magnitudes, figures, sites, and motions. Of which Democritic philosophy, he gives his censure.

Aristotle censures Democritus in these following words: <note>original: "εἰ μὲν ἐν τῷ σχήματι καὶ τῷ χρώματι ἑκάστῳ ζώῳ ἢ τῷ μορίῳ, ὀρθῶς ἂν Δημόκριτος λέγοι"</note> "If *Animals* and their several parts consisted of nothing but Figure and Color, then indeed *Democritus* would be right. No member of a *dead man's body* is what it was before when he was alive—neither *eye*, nor *hand*, nor *foot*. Therefore, this is but a crude way of *philosophizing*, and just as if a *carpenter* should talk of a *wooden* hand. For these *physiologists* <note>natural philosophers</note> declare only the generations and causes of figures, or the matter out of which things are made, such as *air* and *earth*. Whereas no *artisan* would think it sufficient to give such a cause for any *artificial structure*—claiming that because the *instrument* happened to fall upon the *timber* in such a way, it therefore became *hollow* here and *flat* there—but would rather say it was because *he himself* made such strokes, and for such ends," etc.

Now at the conclusion of all this, this *philosopher* finally declares that there is another *principle* of *physical* things besides the *material* one, and one that is not only the *cause* of *motion*, but also acts *artificially* for the sake of *ends*: <note>original: "ἔστι τι τοιοῦτον ὃν ἢ καλῶμεν φύσιν"</note> "there is such a thing as that which we call *Nature*." That is, not the *accidental motion* of *senseless matter*, but a *plastic, regular, and artificial nature*, such as acts for *ends* and *goods*. He declares in the same place what this *nature* is: namely, that it is <note>original: "Ψυχὴ, ἢ ψυχῆς μέρος, ἢ μὴ ἄνευ ψυχῆς"</note> "*Soul*, or a *part* of the *soul*, or not without *soul*." From this he infers that it properly belongs to a *physiologist* to treat the subject of the *soul* as well. But he concludes afterward: <note>original: "ὅδε πᾶσα ψυχὴ φύσις"</note> "the whole soul is not nature." From this it remains that, according to *Aristotle's* sense, *nature* is <note>original: "ἢ ψυχῆς μέρος, ἢ μὴ ἄνευ ψυχῆς"</note> "either part of a soul or not without soul"—that is, either a lower *part* or *faculty* of some *conscious soul*, or else an *inferior* kind of *life* by itself, which is not without *soul* but is *subordinate* to it and dependent on it.

### 22. As for the bodies of animals, *Aristotle* first resolves in general that *nature* in them is either the whole *soul* or else some *part* of it: <note>original: "φύσις ὡς ἡ κινοῦσα, ἢ ὡς τὸ τέλος τῷ ζώῳ, ἤτοι πάση ἡ ψυχὴ, ἢ μέρος τι αὐτῆς"</note> "*Nature* as the *moving principle*, or as that which acts *artificially* for *ends* (so far as concerns the *bodies* of *animals*), is either the whole *soul* or else some *part* of it." But afterward he determines more particularly that the *plastic nature* is not the whole *soul* in *animals*, but only some *part* of it: <note>original: "ἢ πᾶσα ψυχὴ φύσις, ἀλλὰ τι μέρος αὐτῆς"</note> "not every soul is nature, but some part of it." That is, *nature* in *animals*, properly so called, is some *lower power* or *faculty* lodged in their respective *souls*, whether *sensitive* or *rational*.

And that there is a *plastic nature* in the *souls* of *animals*, the same *Aristotle* elsewhere affirms and proves in this manner: 

<margin>Aristotle, *On the Soul*, Book 1, chapter 4.</margin>
<note>original: "τί τὸ συνέχον εἰς τ᾽ ἀναντία φερόμενα, τὸ πῦρ κὴ τὴν γῆν· διασπασθήσεται γὲ εἰ μητί ἔσχι τὸ κωλύσον, εἴδ᾽ ἔσι, τῦτ᾽ ἔσιν ἡ ψυχὴ, κὴ τὸ ἀλῖον τῷ ἀυξάνεσθαι κὴ τρέφεσθαι"</note> "What is it that holds together the *bodies* of *animals*, which are made of elements tending in opposite directions, like fire and earth? They would surely fly apart if there were nothing to prevent it; and if there is such a thing, it is the *soul*, which is also the cause of growth and nourishment." What is it that in the *bodies* of *animals* holds together...

<header>CHAP. III. Lodged in the Souls of Animals.</header>

# CHAP. III. Lodged in the Souls of Animals.

...together such things as of their own nature would otherwise move contrary ways and fly asunder—such as fire and earth, which would be distracted and dissipated, the one tending upwards and the other downwards, were there not something to hinder them. Now, if there be any such thing, this must be the soul, which is also the cause of nourishment and growth <note>original: "Augmentation"</note>. To this the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> adds that, although some were of the opinion that fire was the cause of nourishment and growth in animals, yet this was indeed but <gloss>rather the soul</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον ἡ ψυχὴ</note>, while fire was only the gathering-place or instrument, and not simply the cause. And to the same purpose he philosophizes elsewhere: <margin>On Respiration, 8.</margin> <gloss>For neither is the concoction by which nourishment is produced in animals done without the soul, nor without heat, for all things are performed by fire.</gloss> <note>original Greek: οὐδὲ γὰρ ἐν τέλεσι δι᾽ ὧν γίνεται τοῖς ζώοις σιτέαναι ψυχῆς, ὅτι δεσμυθτός ἐστι, περὶ γὲ ἐργάζεται.</note>

And certainly it seems very agreeable to the phenomena to acknowledge something in the bodies of animals superior to mechanism. This may well be thought to be that which keeps their more fluid parts constantly in the same form and figure, so as not to be enormously altered in their growth by disproportionate nourishment. It is that which restores lost flesh, consolidates broken connections <note>original: "dissolved Continuities"</note>, incorporates newly received nourishment, and joins it continuously with the pre-existing parts of flesh and bone. It regenerates and repairs veins that were mangled or cut off; it causes teething <note>original: "Dentition"</note> in such a regular manner, and that not only in infants but also in adults. It is that which casts off excrements and discharges superfluities, and which makes things seem unpleasant to an internal sense that were nonetheless pleasing to the taste. 

This is that "Nature" of Hippocrates which is the healer of diseases <note>original: "Curatrix of Diseases"</note>, <gloss>the natures of physicians</gloss> <note>original Greek: αἱ φύσεις τῶν ἰατρῶν</note>, and that *Archeus* <note>A term used by Paracelsus to describe a vital force that directs biological processes.</note> of the chemists or Paracelsians, to which all medicines are but subservient, being able to effect nothing of themselves without it. I say, there seems to be such a principle as this in the bodies of animals, which is not *mechanical* but *vital*. Therefore, since entities are not to be multiplied without necessity, we may with *Aristotle* conclude it to be <gloss>a greater principle</gloss> <note>original Greek: μείζις or μείζων ἀρχῆς</note>—a certain part of the soul of those animals, or a lower unconscious power lodged in them.

23. Besides this "Plastic Nature" <note>A formative, creative power in nature that acts unconsciously.</note> which is in animals, forming their several bodies artificially as so many microcosms or "little worlds," there must also be a general Plastic Nature in the macrocosm—the whole corporeal universe—which makes all things thus conspire everywhere and agree together into one harmony. Concerning this Plastic Nature of the universe, the author of *On the World* <note>original: "de Mundo"</note> writes in this manner: <gloss>One power passing through all things, which ordered the whole world.</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἡ τ᾽ ὅλον κόσμον διακόσμος μία ἡ διὰ πάντων διήκουσα δύναμις</note> Again, he calls the same <gloss>spirit</gloss> <note>original Greek: πνεῦμα</note> and <gloss>a living and generative nature</gloss> <note>original Greek: ψυχὴ, ἡ γόνιμον ζώιαν</note>, and plainly declares it to be a thing distinct from the Deity, but subordinate to it and dependent on it. But *Aristotle* himself in that genuine...

<page-num>168</page-num>
# That Aristotle held a Plastic Nature. Book I.

In his genuine work mentioned before, Aristotle speaks clearly and positively concerning this **Plastic Nature** <note>original: "Plastick Nature"; the formative or organizing power in nature</note> of the Universe, as well as that of animals, in these words:

<note>original Greek: φαινεται γαρ ὡσαύτῳ τοῖς τεχνασις ἐσιν ἡ τέχνη... (Aristotle, On the Parts of Animals, Book 1, Chapter 1)</note>
"It seems that just as there is **Art** in **artificial** things, so in the things of **Nature**, there is another similar **Principle** or **Cause**, which we ourselves partake of; in the same manner as we do of **heat** and **cold** from the **Universe**. Therefore, it is more probable that the whole **World** was at first made by such a **Cause** as this (if indeed it was made) and that it is still preserved by the same, than that **mortal animals** should be so. For there is much more **order** and determinate **regularity** in the **heavenly bodies** than in ourselves; but more of **chance** <note>original: "fortuitousness"</note> and inconstant regularity among these **mortal** things. **Notwithstanding** this, there are some who, though they cannot help but acknowledge that the **bodies** of **animals** were all framed by an **artificial Nature**, yet they insist on contending that the **system** of the **heavens** sprang merely from **fortune** and **chance**; although there is not the least appearance of chance or **recklessness** <note>original: "temerity"</note> in it."

And then he sums up everything into this **conclusion**:
<note>original Greek: ὥςε εἶναι φανερὸν ὅτι ἵα τι τοιοῦτον ὃν ἢ καλῶμεν φύσιν.</note>
"**Wherefore** it is manifest, that there is some such thing as that which we call **Nature**." 

That is, there is not only an **artificial, methodical**, and **plastic Nature** in **animals**, by which their respective **bodies** are framed and preserved; but also that there is such a **General Plastic Nature** likewise in the **Universe**, by which the **heavens** and the whole **world** are thus **artfully** ordered and disposed.
<margin>On the Parts of Animals, Book 1, Chapter 1.</margin>

24. Now, whereas **Aristotle** in the previously cited **words** tells us that we partake of **life** and **understanding** from that which is in the **Universe**, in the same way that we partake of **heat** and **cold** from the heat and cold that is in the Universe; it is observable that this was a **notion** borrowed from **Socrates** (as we understand from both **Xenophon** and **Plato**). That **philosopher** used it as an **argument** to prove the existence of a **Deity**. The **sense** of it is represented in this manner by the **Latin poet** <note>Virgil, Aeneid, Book 6</note>:

->*In the beginning, the sky, the earth, and the watery plains,<-
->*The glowing orb of the moon, and the Titan stars,<-
->*Are nourished by a spirit within; and Mind, infused through every limb,<-
->*Moves the entire mass and mingles itself with the great body.<-
->*From this source come the race of men and beasts, and the lives of birds.<-
<note>original Latin: "Principio Cœlum ac Terram, Campósque Liquentes..."</note>

From this it may be gathered that **Aristotle** supposed this **plastic Nature** of the **Universe** to be <note>original Greek: ἡ μέρες ψυχῆς, ἢ μὴ ἀνὰ ψυχῆς</note> **either a part of some Mundane Soul** <note>the soul of the world</note> **that was also conscious and intellectual**, or at least something depending upon it.

<header>CHAPTER III. A Soul of the World.</header>

Actual (as that <term>Plastic Nature</term><note>A formative or creative power in nature that acts unconsciously, like an instinct.</note> in animals is), or at least some inferior principle depending on such a soul. And indeed, whatever the doctrine of the modern <term>Peripatetics</term><note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> may be, we have no doubt at all that Aristotle himself held the world's animation, or a <term>Mundane Soul</term><note>The Soul of the World; the idea that the universe itself is a living creature.</note>. For he plainly declares himself concerning it elsewhere in his book *On the Heavens* (*De Caelo*), in this manner: <gloss>But we commonly think of the heavens as nothing else but bodies and units <note>original: μονάδων (monads)</note>, having only a certain order, but being altogether inanimate; whereas we ought, on the contrary, to conceive of them as partaking of life, and as being endowed with a rational or intellectual life.</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἀλλ᾽ ἡμεῖς ὡς μετέχοντες... δεῖ δὲ ὡς μετεχόντων ὑπολαμβάνειν προεξέως τῇ ζωῆς.</note> For so Simplicius <note>A 6th-century commentator on Aristotle.</note> there rightly expounds the passage: <gloss>We ought to conclude that the heavens are animated with a rational soul, and thereby partake of excellence and rational life. For though "to act" <note>original: ποιεῖν (poiein)</note> may be affirmed not only of irrational souls but also of inanimate bodies, yet the word "to practice" or "to conduct oneself" <note>original: πράττειν (prattein)</note> only describes rational beings.</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἐι ἐμψύχων αὐτῇ συλλογίζεσθαι... τὸ δὲ πρὸς τῇ κυρίως τῇ λογικῇ κατηγοροῦμεν.</note> But further, to take away all manner of scruple or doubt concerning this business, that philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> affirms earlier in the same book: <gloss>That the heaven is animated, and has a principle of motion within itself.</gloss> <note>original Greek: ὅτι ὁ ςερανὸς ἔμψυχος, κὴ ἀρχὴν κινήσεως ἔχει.</note> Where by "the heaven," as in many other places of Aristotle and Plato, is to be understood the whole world.

<margin>Book 2, chapter 11</margin>
There is indeed one passage in the same book *On the Heavens* which, at first glance and slightly considered, may seem to contradict this again. It is probably this passage which has led many into the contrary persuasion—that Aristotle denied the world's animation: <gloss>But it is not reasonable to think that the heavens continue to eternity moved by a soul that constrains them to remain. Nor indeed is it possible that the life of such a soul should be painless or happy. For the continual violent motion of a body (naturally inclining to move another way) must necessarily be a very unquiet thing, void of all mental repose; especially when there is no such relaxation as the souls of mortal animals have by sleep. Instead, such a soul would be held by a certain eternal and unalterable fate of dissolution.</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἀλλὰ μὲν ὅτε ὑπὸ ψυχῆς... ἀλλ᾽ ἀναλύσιον τινὸς μοίραν κατέχων αὐτῶν ἀίδιον ἢ ἀτρεπτον.</note> In these words, Aristotle does not deny the heavens to be moved by a soul of their own (which is positively affirmed by him elsewhere). He only denies they are moved by such a soul as would violently and forcibly agitate or drive them round contrary to their own natural inclination—whereby, in the meantime, they tended downwards of themselves toward the center. And his sense concerning the motion of the heavens...

<page-num>170</page-num>
<header>The Plastic Nature of the World Book I.</header>

The Heavens are truly represented by *Simplicius* <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note> in this manner: "The whole world or heaven, being both a natural and a living body, is moved by a soul through the medium of nature." <note>original: τὸ δ᾽ ὅλον φύσικον κὴ ἔμψυχον, ὑπὸ ψυχῆς κινεῖται, διὰ μέσης τῆς φύσεως.</note> The whole World or Heaven, being as much a natural body as a living animal body, is moved properly by a Soul, but yet by means of Nature also as an instrument, so that its motion is not forced or violent. 

But whereas *Aristotle* there suggested that *Plato* had held the Heavens to be moved by a soul violently, contrary to their nature; *Simplicius*, though sufficiently devoted to *Aristotle*, honestly acknowledges his error in this. Vindicating *Plato* from that accusation, he shows how Plato likewise held a <term>Plastic Nature</term> <note>An internal, unconscious formative power that carries out the divine plan in the physical world.</note> as well as a <term>Mundane Soul</term> <note>The "World Soul" (Anima Mundi); a spirit that permeates all nature.</note>. He notes that among Plato's ten instances of motion, 
<margin>*Laws, Book 10.</margin> the ninth is that of Nature: "that which always moves another, being itself changed by something else." <note>original: τὴν ἔαυτὴν κινῦσαν, κὴ μεταβαλλομένην ὑφ᾽ ἑτέρου.</note> The tenth is that of the <term>Mundane Soul</term>: "that which originally both moves itself and other things." <note>original: τὴν ἔαυτὴν κινῦσαν κὴ ἕτερα.</note> It is as if his meaning in that place were that although Nature is a life and internal energy, it acts subserviently to a higher Soul as the first original mover.

But the grand objection against *Aristotle* holding the world to be a living, animated thing is still to come; namely, from that passage in his <term>Metaphysics</term> where he determines the highest starry heaven to be moved by an <term>Immovable Mover</term>. This is commonly supposed to be the Deity itself and not a Soul of the World; and all the other spheres likewise are supposed to be moved by so many <term>Separate Intelligences</term> <note>Purely intellectual beings or spirits associated with the celestial spheres.</note> and not by souls. 

To this we reply that indeed *Aristotle's* <term>First Immovable Mover</term> is no <term>Mundane Soul</term>, but an <term>Abstract Intellect</term> separate from matter, and the very Deity itself. His manner of moving the heavens is described by him thus: "It moves only by being loved." <note>original: κινεῖ ὃ ὡς ἐρώμενον.</note> Therefore, besides this <term>Supreme Unmoved Mover</term>, that philosopher supposed another <term>Inferior Moved Mover</term> also—that is, a <term>Mundane Soul</term>—as the proper and immediate <term>Efficient Cause</term> <note>The agent that brings something into being or initiates change.</note> of the heavenly motions. Of this he speaks in this manner: "that which itself being moved (objectively, or by appetite and desire for the First Good) moves other things." <note>original: κινύμενον ὃ τάλλα κινεῖ.</note> 

And thus that safe and sure-footed interpreter, *Alexander of Aphrodisias*, explains his master's meaning: That the heaven, being <term>Animated</term> <note>Possessing a soul or life-force.</note> and therefore indeed moved by an <term>Internal Principle</term> of its own, is nonetheless originally moved by a certain <term>Immovable</term> and <term>Separate Nature</term> which is above the Soul, "both by its contemplating of it, and having an appetite and desire of assimilating itself thereunto." <note>original: τῷ νοεῖν τε αὐτὸ, κὴ ἐφεσειν κὴ ὀρεξειν ἐχὸν τὴ ὁμοιώσεως αὐτῷ.</note> 
<margin>Natural Questions, Book 1, Chapter 1.</margin> 
*Aristotle* seems to have borrowed this notion from *Plato*, who makes the <term>Constant Regular Circumgyration</term> <note>The steady, circular orbiting of the stars and planets.</note> of the heavens to be an <term>Imitation of the Motion or Energy of Intellect</term>. So that *Aristotle's* <term>First Mover</term> is not properly the <term>Efficient</term>, but only the <term>Final</term> <note>The purpose or goal for which a thing exists.</note> and <term>Objective Cause</term> of the heavenly motions; the immediate <term>Efficient Cause</term> thereof being "Soul and Nature." <note>original: ψυχὴ καὶ φύσις.</note>

Neither may this be disproved by those other <term>Aristotelian Intelligences</term> of the lesser celestial orbs; that philosopher conceived in a similar way concerning them, that they were also the <term>Abstract Minds</term> or <term>Intellects</term> of certain...

# CHAPTER III. Depends on a Perfect Intellect.
<page-num>171</page-num>

...certain other inferior Souls, which moved their several respective bodies or orbs circularly and uniformly, in a kind of imitation of them. For this plainly appears from the fact that he affirms these his *inferior intelligences*, as well as the *Supreme Mover*, "move only as the end" <note>original: κινειν ὡς τέλος; meaning they act as a final goal or purpose rather than by physical pushing</note>.

<margin>Metaphysics, Book 14, Chapter 7. Paraphrase.</margin> Where it is *evident* that though *Aristotle* did plainly suppose a *mundane intellectual soul* <note>A soul belonging to the world or universe</note>—one that also contained, either within it or under it, a *plastic nature*—yet he did not make either of these the *Supreme Deity*. Instead, he determined the *First Principle* of things to be *one absolutely perfect mind or intellect*, *separate from matter*, which was "an immovable nature" <note>original: ἀκίνητος οὐσία</note>, whose *essence* was his *operation*, and which "moved only by being loved" <note>original: κινεῖ δὲ ὡς ἐρώμενον</note>, or as the *final cause*. Regarding this, he pronounces in this manner: "That upon such a principle as this, heaven and nature depends" <note>original: ὅτι ἐν τοιαύτης ἀρχῆς ἤρτηται ὁ οὐρανὸς καὶ ἡ φύσις</note>. That is, the *animated heaven*, or *mundane soul*, together with the *plastic nature* of the *universe*, must of necessity depend upon such an *absolutely perfect* and *immovable mind or intellect*.

Having now declared the *Aristotelian doctrine* concerning the *plastic nature* of the *universe* (with which the *Platonic* view also agrees), that it is "either part of a mundane intellectual soul" <note>original: ἢ μέρος ψυχῆς</note> (that is, a *lower power* and *faculty* of it) "or else not without a soul" <note>original: ἢ μὴ ἀπὸ ψυχῆς</note>, but some inferior thing depending on it; we think it fit to add in this place, that even if there were no such *mundane soul* distinct from the *Supreme Deity* (as both *Plato* and *Aristotle* supposed), there might nonetheless be a *plastic nature* of the *universe* depending immediately upon the *Deity* itself. For the *plastic nature* essentially depends upon *mind or intellect* and could not possibly exist without it, according to those words cited before: "Nature depends upon such an intellectual principle." For this reason, that philosopher elsewhere joins "mind" and "nature" <note>original: νοῦς and φύσις</note> both together.

25. Besides this general *plastic nature* of the *universe*, and those particular *plastic powers* in the *souls of animals*, it is not impossible that there may be other *plastic natures* as well (such as certain *lower lives* or *vegetative souls*) in some greater parts of the *universe*. All of them would depend, if not upon some higher *conscious soul*, then at least upon a *perfect intellect* presiding over the whole. 

As for example: though it is not reasonable to think that every *plant*, *herb*, and *blade of grass* has a particular *plastic life* or *vegetative soul* of its own distinct from the *mechanism* of the *body*, nor that the whole *earth* is an *animal* endowed with a *conscious soul*; yet there may possibly be, for all we know, one *plastic nature* or *life* belonging to the whole *terrestrial* (or *terraqueous*) *globe*. By this nature, all *plants* and *vegetables* connected to it may be differently formed according to their different *seeds*. Likewise, *minerals* and other *bodies* may be framed, and whatever else is effected above the *power* of *accidental mechanism* <note>original: fortuitous mechanism; the idea that things happen by blind physical chance</note>, as if by the *immediate cause*, though always...

He suggests that while individual plants may not have souls, a single Plastic Nature might govern the entire Earth to organize life and minerals beyond mere mechanical chance.</summary>

# The Errors of Atheists, who make Book I.

always subordinate to other causes, the chief of which is the Deity. And this perhaps may ease the minds of those who cannot help but think it too much to impose all responsibility upon one **Plastic Nature** <note>original: "Plastick Nature"; here meaning a formative or creative force in nature that organizes matter</note> of the **Universe**.

26. And now we have finished our **First Task**, which was to give an account of the **Plastic Nature**, the sum of which briefly amounts to this: That it is a certain **Lower Life** than the **Animal** life, which acts **Regularly** and **Artificially** <note>In the 17th-century sense: with art, skill, or design</note>, according to the **Direction** of **Mind** and **Understanding, Reason** and **Wisdom**, for **Ends** (or in **Order to Good**). Although it does not itself know the **Reason** for what it does, nor is it **Master** of that **Wisdom** according to which it acts, it is only a **Servant** to it and a **Drudging Executioner** of the same. It operates **Fatally** <note>meaning: by necessity or fixed law</note> and **Sympathetically**, according to **Laws** and **Commands** prescribed to it and impressed upon it by a **Perfect Intellect**. This Plastic Nature is either a **Lower Faculty** of some **Conscious Soul**, or else an **Inferior** kind of **Life** or **Soul** by itself; but it essentially depends upon a **Higher Intellect**.

We proceed to our **Second Undertaking**, which was to show how grossly those **Two Sorts of Atheists** mentioned before—the **Stoical** (or **Cosmo-plastic**) and the **Stratonical** (or **Hylozoic** <note>Hylozoism is the belief that all matter is alive</note>)—mistake the **Notion** of it. Both of them acknowledge this **Plastic Life of Nature**, but they pervert and abuse it to make a certain spurious and counterfeit "God-Almighty" out of it (or a **First Principle** of all things). By doing so, they exclude the **True Omnipotent Deity**, which is a **Perfect Mind** or **Consciously Understanding Nature** presiding over the **Universe**; they substitute this **Stupid Plastic Nature** in its place.

Now, the chief **Errors** or **Mistakes** of these **Atheists** concerning the **Plastic Nature** are the following **Four**. **First**, they make that to be the **First Principle** of all and the **Highest** thing in the **Universe** which is actually the **Last** and **Lowest** of all **Lives**—a thing **Essentially Secondary, Derivative**, and **Dependent**. For the **Plastic Life** of **Nature** is but the mere **Shadow** <note>original: "Umbrage"</note> of **Intellectuality**, a faint and shadowy **Imitation** of **Mind** and **Understanding**. It depends as **Essentially** upon Mind as a **Shadow** does upon a **Body**, an **Image** in a **Mirror** <note>original: "Glass"</note> upon a **Face**, or an **Echo** upon the **Original Voice**. 

So, if there had been no **Perfect Mind** or **Intellect** in the world, there could no more have been any **Plastic Nature** in it than there could be an **Image** in a **Mirror** without a **Face**, or an **Echo** without an **Original Voice**. If there is **Nature** <note>original Greek: φύσις (physis)</note>, then there must be **Mind** <note>original Greek: Νοῦς (Nous)</note>. If there is a **Plastic Nature** that acts **Regularly** and **Artificially** in **Order to Ends** and according to the **Best Wisdom** (even though it does not itself comprehend the **reason** for it, nor is clearly **Conscious** of what it does), then there must of necessity be a **Perfect Mind** or **Intellect**—that is, a **Deity**—upon which it depends. Therefore, **Aristotle** acts like a **Philosopher** in joining **Nature** and **Mind** both together; but these **Atheists** act very **Absurdly** and **Unphilosophically** by trying to make a **Senseless** and **Unconscious Plastic Nature** (and therefore one without any **Mind** or **Intellect**) the **First Original** of all things.

27. **Secondly**, these **Atheists** increase their **Former Error** by supposing *those*...

### CHAPTER III. The Plastic Nature, a God-Almighty.

It is impossible for those higher lives of sense (or animality) and of reason (or understanding) to rise from that lower *senseless life of nature* as if it were the only *original and fundamental life*. This is altogether as *irrational* and *absurd* as if one should suppose the light in the air or *ether* <note>The "ether" was historically believed to be the rarefied element filling the upper regions of space.</note> to be the *only original* and *fundamental light*, and the light of the sun and stars to be merely a *secondary* and *derivative* thing—nothing but the light of the air *modified* and *improved* by *condensation*. Or, it is as if one should maintain that the sun, the moon, and all the stars were really nothing else but the mere *reflections* of those *images* that we see in rivers and ponds of water. 

But this has always been the *foolish mood* and *deceit* of *atheists*: to invert the order of the *universe* and hang the *picture of the world* (as if it were a man) with its *heels upward*. *Conscious reason* and *understanding* are a far higher degree of life and perfection than that *dull plastic nature* <note>original: "Plastick Nature"; the unconscious, formative power in the universe that shapes matter.</note> which only *acts* but does not *know*. Reason can never possibly emerge out of it. Neither can the *duplication* of *physical organs* ever advance that *simple* and *stupid life of nature* into *redoubled consciousness* or *self-perception*; nor can any *triplication*—or indeed a *thousand-fold increase*—of them improve that nature into *reason* and *understanding*.

24. Thirdly, to better disguise their former errors, the <term>Hylozoists</term> <note>Atheists who believe that matter itself is alive and possesses a form of unconscious intelligence.</note> corrupt the notion of the *plastic life of nature* by confusing it with *wisdom* and *understanding*. Even though they themselves acknowledge that no *animal-sense*, *self-perception*, or *consciousness* belongs to it, they still insist it is *perfectly wise*. Consequently, they claim every *atom* of *senseless matter* in the whole world is *infallibly omniscient* regarding its own *capacities* and *suitabilities*, or whatever it can *do* or *suffer*. This is plainly *contradictory*. 

For while there may be such a thing as the *plastic nature*—which, according to the previous description, can *act* without *knowing* and is devoid of *express consciousness* or *self-perception*—yet *perfect knowledge* and *understanding* without *consciousness* is *nonsense* and an *impossibility*. Therefore, this must be condemned as a great piece of *foolishness* in the <term>Hylozoic atheists</term>: they attribute *perfect wisdom* and *understanding* to a *stupid, unconscious nature*. In reality, such a nature is nothing but the *difficult tool of art* <note>original: "χαλεπὸν τέχνης" (chalepon technēs); here meaning a subordinate instrument that carries out a design without understanding it.</note>, the mere *drudging instrument* or *manual craftsman* of a *perfect mind*.

25. Lastly, these <term>atheists</term> err in making this *plastic life of nature* a mere *material* or *physical thing*. In truth, *matter* or *body* cannot move itself; much less, therefore, can it *artfully* order and arrange its own *motion*. And though the *plastic nature* is indeed the *lowest* of all *lives*, it is nonetheless a *life*, an *internal energy*, and a *self-activity* distinct from *local motion*. It must, therefore, be *incorporeal* (not made of matter), as all *life* is *essentially* so. 

But the <term>Hylozoists</term> conceive of both *life* and *understanding* in a gross way, spreading them all over *matter* just as *butter* is spread upon *bread* or *plaster* upon a *wall*. Accordingly, they slice them out in different *quantities* and *sizes* along with the matter, contending that they are...

### XXXVIII.
<margin>Plato, Laws, Book 10.</margin> Plato gives an account of why he judged it necessary in those times to publicly propose that *atheistic hypothesis* in order to refute it, and also to produce rational arguments for the proof of a Deity, in this manner: "If these atheistic doctrines had not been publicly spread and made known to almost all men, it would not have been necessary to have refuted them, nor to prove a Deity by reasons; but now it is necessary." <note>original Greek: εἰ μὴ κατὰς παρεμμέλοι ησαν οἱ τούτοι λόγοι ἐν τοῖς πόλεσιν, ὡς ἔπο εἶπεν, ἀνθρώποις, λόγων, ὡς εἰσι Θεοὶ, νῦν ἦ ἀνάγκη</note> And we believe that the same necessity at this time will likewise justify our present undertaking. These *atheistic doctrines* have been as boldly vented and publicly asserted in this latter age of ours as they ever could have been in Plato's time. 

In those days, the severity of the Athenian government must have been a great check to such designs. Socrates was put to death upon a mere false and groundless accusation of *atheism*. *Protagoras* (who was undoubtedly a real *atheist*) escaped the same punishment only by flight; his books were nonetheless publicly burned in the marketplace at Athens, and he himself was condemned to perpetual exile. # CHAPTER III. Lately Revived.

[This system includes] Substance and Corporeal Atoms, another *Thinking Incorporeal Substance*, and *joining Metaphysics* or *Theology* together with *Physics* <note>original: "Physiology," used here in the archaic sense of the study of nature</note> to make up one entire *System of Philosophy*. Nor can it well be doubted that this *Physics* of his, regarding its *Mechanical* part, has been developed by the ingenious author into an *exactness* at least equal with the best *Atom-theories* <note>original: "Atomologies"</note> of the ancients. 

Nevertheless, this *Cartesian Philosophy* is highly open to *criticism* for several reasons, the chief of which is this: that deviating from that *Ancient Mosaic Atom-theory* <note>original: "Primitive Moschical Atomology," referring to the theory that atomism originated with a Phoenician named Moschus, often identified with Moses</note> by rejecting all *Plastic Nature* <note>term: "Plastic Nature" refers to an unconscious but purposeful creative force in the universe that carries out God's plan</note>, it derives the whole *system* of the *Physical Universe* from the *necessary motion of matter*. It claims matter is only divided into *particles* too small to be seen <note>original: "insensibly small"</note> and turned round in a *whirlpool* <note>original: "vortex"</note> without the *guidance* or *direction* of any *understanding nature*. 

By this means, though it boasts of explaining all *physical phenomena* by mere *accidental mechanism* and without any *purposeful* or *mental cause* <note>original: "Final or Mental Causality"</note>, yet it gives no account at all of that which is the *greatest* of all *phenomena*: *the well and the beautiful* <note>original: "τὸ εὖ καὶ καλῶς"</note>, that is, the *orderly regularity* and *harmony* of the *world system*. The cause of this *failure* has been already suggested: namely, from acknowledging only *two types of being*, *Extended* (matter) and *Thinking* (mind), and making the *essence of thought* consist only in *conscious awareness*. From this it follows that there could be no *Plastic Nature*; therefore, either all things must be done by *accidental mechanism*, or else God himself must be brought immediately upon the stage to explain every *phenomenon*. 

Our philosopher [Descartes], being overly careful to avoid this latter absurdity, threw himself into the former: the banishing of all *purposeful* and *mental causes* entirely out of the world, and acknowledging no other *philosophical causes* besides *material* and *mechanical* ones. It cannot be denied that even some of the ancient *religious Atomists* were also too much infected with this *mechanical habit*; but *René Descartes* <note>original: "Renatus Cartesius"</note> has not only outdone them all in this, but even the very *atheists* themselves, as shall be shown afterward. And therefore, as much as lies in his power, he has quite disarmed the world of that great argument for a *God* <note>original: "Deity"</note> taken from the *regular structure* and *harmony* of the *universe*. 

To this *gross failure* of his, another might be added: that he seems to make *matter necessarily existent* and *essentially infinite* and *eternal*. Notwithstanding all this, we cannot hold that *uncharitable opinion* of him—that he really intended to promote *atheism*—since the *fundamental principles* of his *philosophy* are such that no *atheistic structure* can possibly be built upon them. 

But shortly after this *Cartesian restoration* of the *ancient Atom-theory* (which acknowledges *incorporeal substance*), we have had our own *Leucippus* and *Democritus* <note>ancient Greek founders of atomism</note> as well, who also revived and brought again upon the stage that other *Atheistic Atom-theory*. This version makes *senseless* and *lifeless atoms* to be the *unlucky origins of the whole* <note>original: "ἀρχὰς τῷ ὅλων ἀτύχας"</note> and the only *principles* of all things in the *universe*. This necessarily excludes, besides *immaterial substance* and the *immortality of souls*, a *God* and *natural morality*; it also makes all *actions* and *events* necessary in a *material* and *mechanical* sense.

Now, there could be no satisfactory refutation of this *Atheistic Hypothesis* without first making a fair proposal of the various *grounds* of [the argument]...

### The Atheists are no Magicians.

## The Digression concerning the Plastic Life of Nature, or an Artificial, Orderly, and Methodical Nature. Section 37, Chapter 3.

1. Neither the Hylozoic <note>original: "Hylozoick"; the belief that all matter is alive</note> nor the Cosmo-plastic <note>original: "Cosmo-plastick"; the belief in a world-organizing force without a conscious God</note> Atheists are condemned merely for asserting an orderly and artificial "Plastic Nature"—that is, a formative power distinct from animal life. This concept is often rejected not only by Atomic Atheists but also by some professed Theists, who may nonetheless have an unnoticed trace of the "mechanically-atheistic" mindset lingering about them.

2. If we do not admit the existence of a "Plastic" <note>term: "Plastic" here means "formative" or "shaping," from the Greek *plastikos*, referring to the power that gives form to matter</note> or artificial nature, then we must conclude one of two things: either that all things happen by accidental mechanism and material necessity (the unguided motion of matter), or else that God must "do all things himself" <note>original: *αὐτεργεῖν ἅπαντα* (autergein hapanta)</note> immediately and miraculously. In the latter case, God would have to frame the body of every gnat and fly as if with his own hands. This is because divine laws and commands cannot execute themselves, nor can they be the actual physical causes of things in nature.

3. To suppose that all things happen by chance, or by the unguided motion of matter, is as irrational as it is atheistical and impious. There are many phenomena in the world that are not only beyond the powers of mere mechanics but are actually contrary to the laws of mechanics. "Mechanical Theists" <note>note: those who believe God created the world like a clock and then stepped away</note> make God a mere idle spectator of the accidental motions of matter, rendering his wisdom entirely useless and insignificant. We will examine Aristotle’s wise judgment against these "fortuitous mechanists" and show the ridiculousness of the claim that material and mechanical reasons are the only "philosophical" explanations.

4. It seems neither appropriate in respect to God’s dignity, nor consistent with reason, that he should "do all things himself" <note>original: *αὐτεργεῖn ἅπαντα*</note> immediately and miraculously. If he did, "Nature" would be entirely bypassed and rendered meaningless. This is further disproved by the slow and gradual process of growth in nature, as well as by the "errors" and "bungles" <note>note: referring to birth defects or biological abnormalities</note> that occur when the underlying matter is unsuitable or stubborn. These flaws suggest that the immediate agent in nature is not an irresistible divine power, but a subordinate one.

5. Therefore, it is reasonably inferred that there is a "Plastic Nature" in the universe acting as a subordinate instrument of Divine Providence for the orderly disposal of matter. However, this nature does not act on its own; a Higher Providence presides over it, because this Plastic Nature cannot act by choice or with its own discretion. Even those laws of nature concerning motion, which the Mechanical Theists themselves assume, are in reality nothing other than this Plastic Nature.

6. We will show the agreement of this doctrine with the opinions of the best philosophers of all ages, including Aristotle, Plato, Empedocles, Heraclitus, and Hippocrates.

<summary>This page introduces the concept of "Plastic Nature"—a subordinate, formative power used by God to organize the physical world—as a middle ground between blind chance and constant divine miracles. The author argues that mechanical explanations alone are insufficient to explain the complexity of life.</summary>
