## CHAPTER III.

Hippocrates, Zeno, and the Paracelsians <note>Followers of the Swiss physician Paracelsus, known for combining chemistry and mysticism</note>. Anaxagoras, though a professed Theist, was severely censured by both Aristotle and Plato as an encourager of Atheism, merely because he used material and mechanical causes more than mental and final causes. Why "physiologers" <note>natural philosophers or scientists</note> and astronomers were commonly suspected of Atheism in Plato's time. 

7. The **Plastic Nature** <note>term: Plastic Nature; the creative or formative power in the natural world, acting as an instrument of God</note> is no "occult quality" <note>a hidden property that cannot be explained</note>, but the only intelligible cause of that which is the grandest of all phenomena: the orderly regularity and harmony of things. The "Mechanical Theists" <note>those who believe God created the world as a machine that runs itself</note>, however much they pretend to solve all phenomena, can give no account of this at all. A God, or Infinite Mind, is asserted by them in vain and to no purpose. 

8. Two things are to be performed by us here: first, to give an account of the Plastic Nature, and then to show how the notion of it has been mistaken and abused by Atheists. The first general account of this Plastic Nature, according to Aristotle, is that it is to be conceived as **Art itself acting inwardly and immediately upon matter**; as if harmony living within musical instruments should move their strings without any external touch. 

9. Two superiorities of the Plastic Nature over human art. First, whereas human art acts upon matter from the outside in a cumbersome and laborious way, with tumult and "hurliburly" <note>commotion</note>, Nature acts on it from within more commandingly and does its work easily, cleverly, and silently. Human art acts on matter mechanically, but Nature acts vitally and magically. 

10. The second superiority of Nature over human art is that, whereas human artists are often searching and at a loss, anxiously consulting and deliberating, and upon second thoughts mending their former work, Nature is never searching, nor unresolved what to do, nor does she ever repent afterwards of what she has done by changing her former course. Human artists themselves do not consult because they are artists, but only for want of art <note>i.e., perfect skill requires no deliberation</note>; and therefore Nature, though never consulting, may act artificially. It is concluded that what is called Nature is really the **Divine Art**. 

11. Nevertheless, Nature is not the Divine Art in a pure and abstract sense, but is "concreted" <note>solidified</note> and embodied in matter: *a reason immersed and confused* <note>original: Ratio Mersa & Confusa</note>. It is not the "Archetypal" <note>original model</note> Divine Art, but the "Ectypal" <note>a copy or representation</note>. Nature differs from the Divine Art as the manual laborer differs from the architect. 

12. Two imperfections of the Plastic Nature, in respect of which it falls short even of human art. First, that though it acts for specific ends in an artificial way, it does not itself intend those ends, nor understand the reason for what it does; therefore, it cannot act by choice. The difference between "spermatic reasons" <note>term: Spermatic Reasons; the formative principles or "seeds" that guide growth</note> and knowledge. Nature only apes or mimics the Divine Art or Wisdom; it is not the master of that reason according to which it acts, but only a servant to it and a drudging executioner of it. 

13. It is proved that there may be such a thing that acts artificially even though it does not comprehend the art by which its motions are governed; first, from musical habits: the dancer resembles the artificial life of Nature. 

14. The same is further evidenced from the instincts of brute animals, which direct them to act rationally and artificially for their own good and the good of the universe, without any reason of their own. The instincts in brutes are but passive impressions of the Divine Wisdom, and a kind of fate upon them. 

15. The second imperfection of the Plastic Nature, that it acts...

20. *Notwithstanding this, because the plastic nature is a life, it must necessarily be incorporeal <note>not made of matter</note>. One and the same thing, having within it an entire model and platform and acting upon several distant parts of matter at once coherently, cannot be corporeal. Although Aristotle nowhere declares whether his "nature" is corporeal or incorporeal (which he also does not clearly state concerning the rational soul), and his followers conclude it to be corporeal, yet according to the very principles of that philosophy, it must be otherwise.*

The heart and pulp of the citrons are of a cold nature, but the seed is hot and dry and has a bitter juice. The bark, however, is very hot, of a subtle substance, and has a fragrant smell. <term>Pliny</term> <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (23–79 AD), a Roman author and naturalist</note> says that the seeds, when given to a pregnant woman or at any other time to drink in wine, help the stomach, aid digestion, and act as an antidote. <term>Paolo Ægineta</term> <note>Paulus Aegineta, a 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician</note> says that it is very good against the bites of serpents, and it is an excellent remedy against the stings of bees or wasps. It is good against the bites of rabid dogs, and it is an immediate help for <term>pleurisy</term> <note>Inflammation of the membranes around the lungs</note>. It helps those who have a cough and those who have bad breath. 

The bark of the fruit is an admirable antidote against <term>poison</term>, and it is good for the stomach and helps digestion. It is effective against the bites of vipers and rabid dogs. The juice of the pulp of citrons (<term>Pliny</term> says), when drunk with wine or with honey and water (with which the mouth may also be rinsed), is good against bad breath. The pulp of the citron is a fundamental ingredient in <term>medicine</term> <note>original: "phisick"</note>; it is cold and dry. It helps with the stings of scorpions and is good against any poison. 

The juice of the fruit has this virtue in it: it is cooling and it quenches thirst. It helps those who have an <term>ague</term> <note>A fever or shivering fit, often associated with malaria</note>. It is good against the <term>plague</term>. It is good for the stomach and aids digestion. The syrup made of the juice of citrons is good against the plague and for the stomach, and it helps with digestion. It is good for those who have a fever. It helps to digest all kinds of <term>phlegm</term> <note>One of the four humors; excess phlegm was thought to cause various illnesses</note>. It is an excellent thing to cleanse the <term>kidneys</term> <note>original: "reins"</note>. It is good against all types of obstructions in the body. It is good for the stomach, and merely smelling it refreshes the heart and spirits. It is a supreme antidote against poison and is good for coughs. There is an oil made of the peel of the citrons which is very useful for many things.

### CHAPTER IV.

The idea of God explained, as an answer to the first atheistic argument. The great prejudice against the naturalness of this idea—as essentially including unity or <note>original: "onelyness"</note> uniqueness in it—arising from pagan polytheism, is removed. It is proved that intelligent pagans generally acknowledged one supreme deity. What their polytheism and idolatry were, along with some account of Christianity. 1. The either stupid insensibility or gross impudence of atheists in denying that the word "GOD" has any meaning, or that there is any other idea answering to it besides the mere <term>phantasm</term> <note>a mental image or illusion</note> of the sound. This is the disease called by the philosopher <gloss>the petrification of the mind <note>original: ἀπολίθωσις τῆ νοητικῆς (apolithosis tē noētikēs)</note></gloss>, or a state of dead insensibility. 2. That atheists themselves must necessarily have an idea of God in their minds; otherwise, when they deny his existence, they would be denying the existence of nothing. They also have the same idea of him as theists, since they deny the very same thing that theists affirm. 3. A <term>lemma</term> <note>a preliminary proposition used to prove a larger point</note> or preparatory proposition regarding the idea of God: that though some things are made or generated, it is not possible that all things should be made. Instead, something must of necessity exist of itself from eternity, unmade, and be the cause of those other things that are made. 4. The two most opposite opinions concerning that which was self-existent from eternity or unmade, and the cause of all other things made: One, that it was nothing but mindless matter, the most imperfect of all things; the Other, that it was something most perfect, and therefore conscious and truly intellectual. Those who assert this latter opinion are theists in a strict and proper sense; those who assert the former are atheists. So the general idea of God is a perfect, consciously understanding being (or Mind), self-existent from eternity, and the cause of all other things. 5. It is observed that atheists who deny a God, according to the true idea of him, often abuse the word, calling mindless matter by that name and meaning nothing else by it but a first principle or a self-existent, unmade thing. According to this notion of the word "God," there can be no such thing as an atheist, as no man is able to persuade himself that all things sprang from nothing. 6. The **atheists** also supposed **goodness** to be included in the **idea of God**. ### CHAPTER IV.

15. **Pagan Polytheism** must be understood according to another ambiguity in the word "gods," as it was used for created intellectual beings superior to humans who were thought to deserve religious worship. That the Pagans held both **Many Gods** and **One God** (as Onatus the Pythagorean declares) in different senses: many inferior deities subordinate to one supreme God.

16. Further evidence of this: that the intelligent pagan polytheists held only a plurality of inferior deities subordinate to one supreme God. First, because after the emergence of Christianity and its conflict with paganism, when the occasion arose, no pagan asserted a multiplicity of independent deities; instead, they all universally denied it and professed to acknowledge **one supreme God**.

17. This was not a later refinement or alteration of paganism, as might possibly be suspected, but the doctrine of the most ancient pagan theologians and the greatest promoters of polytheism was consistent with this. This will be proved not from questionable writings (such as those attributed to Hermes Trismegistus and the Sibyls) but from those that are beyond doubt. First, that **Zoroaster**, the primary promoter of polytheism in the East, acknowledged one supreme deity, the maker of the world; this is proved from Eubulus in the works of Porphyry, in addition to Zoroaster's own words cited by Eusebius.

18. That **Orpheus**, commonly called "the Theologian" by the Greeks and the father of Greek polytheism, clearly asserted one supreme deity, as proved by his own words from pagan records.

19. That the **Egyptians** themselves, the most polytheistic of all nations, had an acknowledgment among them of one supreme deity.

20. That the **Poets**, who were the greatest corrupters of pagan theology and made it seem more "aristocratic" <note>original: "Aristocratically" — meaning a government by many rather than a single monarch</note> through their myths about the gods, did nonetheless acknowledge a monarchy: one prince and father of the gods. The famous passage by **Sophocles** is not to be doubted, even though it is not found in any of his tragedies currently surviving.

21. That all the pagan **Philosophers** who were theists universally asserted a "worldly monarchy" <note>original: "Mundane Monarchy" — a single supreme ruler of the universe</note>. **Pythagoras**, as much a polytheist as anyone, yet held that his first principle of things (as well as numbers) was a "monad" or unity. **Anaxagoras** held his "One Mind" ordering all things for the good. **Xenophanes** held his "One and All," and his "One God" who is the greatest among the gods.

22. **Parmenides** held his supreme God as the "One Immovable." **Empedocles** held both many gods (who were younger than "Friendship" and "Strife") and his one God called *the One* <note>original: τὸ ἓν (to hen)</note> who was older than them. **Zeno of Elea** and his demonstration of one God, as found in Aristotle.

23. **Philolaus** and his prince and governor of all, God who is always one. **Euclid of Megara** and his God called *the One Good* <note>original: ἕν τὸ ἀγαθὸν (hen to agathon)</note>. **Timaeus of Locri** and his "Mind and Good," which is above the Soul of the World. **Antisthenes** and his "One Natural God." **Onatus** and his *Corypheus* <note>original: Corypheus — the leader or conductor of a choir; here meaning the head of the gods</note>.

24. It is generally believed and true that **Socrates** acknowledged one supreme God; however, it is a common error to think he rejected all the inferior gods of the pagans. **Plato** was also a polytheist, and that passage which some rely on—claiming he was serious when he began his letters with "God" but joking when he began with "Gods"—is a forgery. Yet he was, nonetheless, an undoubted monotheist in another sense: an asserter of one God over all, of a maker of the world, of a first God, and of a greatest of the gods. ...finally the **King** of all things, for whose sake all things exist; The **Father** of the **Cause** and **Prince** of the **World**, that is, of the **Eternal Intellect**, or *Logos* <note>original: Λόγος; the Divine Word or Reason</note>. 24. **Aristotle** acknowledged **Many Gods** (counting the Stars as such) and yet was an express supporter of **one ruler** <note>original: εἷς κοίρανος</note>, One Immoveable Mover. 25. **Cleanthes** and **Chrysippus**, the **Stoics**, though they filled the whole Heaven, Earth, Air, and Sea with **Gods**, nonetheless acknowledged only **One Immortal God**, **Jupiter**. This was not only the opinion of **Philosophers** and **learned men**, but also the **General Belief** of the **Pagan common people** <term>original: vulgar; the general population</term>. That there was **One Supreme God** is proved from **Maximus Tyrius**. The **Romans** called him *God, the Best and Greatest* <note>original: Deus Optimus Maximus</note>. The Pagans, when most serious, spoke of God in the singular. *Lord, have mercy* <note>original: Kyrie Eleeson</note> was part of the **Pagans' Litany** to the Supreme God. The more civilized Pagans at this very day acknowledge one Supreme Deity, the **Maker** of the **World**. 28. **Plutarch's testimony** that, despite the variety of **Pagan religions** and the different names of Gods used in them, **One Reason**, Mind, or **Providence** ordering all things, and its **Inferior Ministers**, were worshipped alike everywhere. 29. It is plain that the **Pagan Theists** must necessarily acknowledge One **Supreme Deity**, because they generally believed the whole **World** to be **One Animal** <note>meaning a living, breathing entity possessing a soul</note>, governed by **One Soul**. Some Pagans made this **Soul** of the **World** their **Supreme God**; others believed in an **Abstract Mind superior** to it. 30. The **Hebrew Doctors** <note>Jewish scholars and rabbis</note> were generally of the persuasion that the Pagans worshipped one **Supreme God**, and that all their other gods were merely **mediators** between him and men. 31. Lastly, this is confirmed by Scripture. The **Pagans knew God**. The **Jupiter** mentioned by the poet **Aratus**, and the **Athenians’ Unknown God**, were the **True God**. 32. In order to provide a fuller explanation of **Pagan Theology** and show why it is often misunderstood, **three main points** must be emphasized. First, that the Pagans **worshipped One Supreme God under Many Names**; secondly, that besides this **One God**, they also worshipped **Many Gods**, which were actually **inferior deities subordinate** to him; thirdly, that they worshipped both the **Supreme** and **inferior Gods** through **images, statues**, and **symbols**, which were sometimes loosely called "Gods." First, that the **Supreme God** among the Pagans was **many-named** <term>original: polyonymous</term> and worshipped under several **personal names**, according to his various **attributes** and how they were shown—his **gifts** and **effects** in the **world**. 33. For the same reason, **things** that were not actual substances were **personified** and **deified** by the Pagans and worshipped as so many different **names** or **concepts** of **One God**. 34. Just as the whole **physical world**, being **animated**, was supposed by some Pagans to be the **Supreme God**, he was also worshipped in the various **parts** and **members** of it (which were given **personal names**) as if in **parcels** and **piece-meal**, or by various **incomplete concepts**. <header>CHAPTER IV.</header>

Some of the **Pagans** considered the physical world to be only the **Temple** of God, while others considered it to be the **Body** of God. 35. The **Second Point** proposed: that besides the **One Supreme God** known by several names, the **Pagans** also acknowledged and worshipped **Many Gods**—"born gods" <note>original: θεοὺς γεννητοὺς (theous gennētous)</note>, or created intellectual beings superior to humans. 36. The **Pythagorean** or **Platonic Trinity** of **Divine Persons** <note>original: Hypostases; the distinct substances or individuals within the Trinity</note>. The higher of the inferior deities according to this hypothesis: **Intellect** <note>original: Nous</note>, **Soul** <note>original: Psyche</note>, and the entire **Physical World**, along with individual **Intellects** <note>original: Noes</note> and **Unities** <note>original: Henades</note>. 37. The other **Inferior Deities** acknowledged by both the common people and philosophers, consisting of three types. First: the **Sun**, **Moon**, and **Stars**, and other major parts of the universe which were believed to be alive; these were called **Sensible** <term>perceptible by the senses</term> **Gods**. 38. Second: their invisible **Inferior Deities**, which were ethereal and aerial beings called **Demons** <term>Dæmons; in the Greek sense of "spirits" or "guiding powers," not necessarily evil</term>. The Supreme Deity appointed these to preside over kingdoms, cities, places, people, and things. 39. The last type of **Pagan Inferior Deities**: **Heroes** and **God-men** <note>original: θεάνθρωποι (theanthrōpoi)</note>. **Euemerus** was criticized by **Plutarch** for claiming that all the Pagan gods were nothing more than deceased men. 40. The **Third General Point** proposed: that the **Pagans** worshipped both the supreme and inferior gods through **images**, **statues**, and **symbols**. Initially, before images and temples existed, unshaped stones and pillars without carvings were erected as religious monuments and called "sacred stones" <note>original: βαιτύλια (baitylia) or Bethels</note>. 41. Later, images, statues, and symbols were used and housed in **temples**. These were placed at the western end of the temples to face the east, so that the Pagans entering them worshipped toward the west. This was likely one reason why the **ancient Christians** prayed toward the east. The **Golden Calf** was made to serve as a symbolic presence of the **God of Israel**. 42. All aspects of the entire **Pagan religion** are presented together at once in the works of **Plato**. 43. Some recent writers, failing to understand the true meaning of the Pagans, have confused their entire theology by assuming they worshipped the **lifeless parts** of the world as gods. Therefore, we must distinguish between their **living** and their **natural gods**. No physical thing was worshipped by the Pagans except as something either **animated** by its own particular soul, as a part of the whole **living world**, or as having **demons** presiding over it to whom the worship was actually directed; or finally, as being **images** or **symbols** of divine things. 44. Although the **Egyptians** were said to worship brute animals—for which they were generally condemned by other Pagans—the wiser among them used these animals only as **hieroglyphics** and symbols. 45. The Pagans worshipped not only the **Supreme God** but also the **Inferior Deities** through physical sacrifices. **Sacrifices** or fire-offerings, in their original and general sense, were nothing more than gifts and signs of gratitude that accompanied prayer. However, a specific concept of **atonement** <note>original: expiation</note> was later attached to **animal sacrifices**, though whether this occurred by divine command or human agreement remains undecided. 46. The **Pagan defense** <term>original: apology; a formal justification of their system</term> for these three points. First: for worshipping **one Supreme God** under many personal names, based not only on his various attributes but also his various manifestations, gifts, and effects in the visible world. This includes an excuse for those **materialistic theists** who worshipped the entire living world as the Supreme God, and the seve-

47. **Their defense for worshipping many inferior deities besides the one Supreme God.** That they, by **worshipping them only as inferior**, could not therefore be guilty of giving them that **honor** which was **proper to the Supreme**. That they **honored the Supreme God incomparably above all**. That they established a **difference in their sacrifices**, and that **material sacrifices were not the proper worship of the Supreme God, but rather below him**. 

48. **Several reasons of the Pagans for giving religious worship to inferior created beings.** **First**, that this **honor** bestowed upon them ultimately returns to the **Supreme God** and aggrandizes his **state** and **majesty**, as they are all his **ministers** and **attendants**. 

49. That just as **demons** <term>original: Dæmons; here referring to intermediary spirits</term> are **mediators** between the **celestial gods** and **men**, so those **celestial gods** and all the other **inferior deities** are themselves also **mediators** between **men** and the **Supreme God**, serving as **convenient steps** by which we ought to approach him with **reverence**. 

50. That there is an **honor in justice** due to all those excellent **beings** that are **above us**, and that the Pagans do nothing more than **honor everything as they ought, in that due rank and place** in which the **Supreme God has set it**. 

51. That **demons** or **angels** being appointed to preside over **kingdoms, cities**, and **persons**, and the various parts of the **corporeal universe**, and being in many ways **benefactors** to us, **thanks** ought to be returned to them by **sacrifice**. 

52. That the **inferior gods, demons,** and **heroes**, being all of them able to do us either **good** or **hurt**, and being also **irascible** <term>prone to anger</term>, and therefore **provokable** by our **neglect** of them, it is as much our **interest** as our **duty** to **pacify** and **appease** them through **worship**. 

53. **Lastly**, that it cannot be thought that the **Supreme God** will **envy** those **inferior gods** for the **worship** or **honor** bestowed upon them; nor can it be **suspected** that any of those **inferior deities** will **rebelliously** <note>original: "Factiously"</note> attempt to set themselves up against the **Supreme God**. 

54. That many of the **Pagans worshipped none but good demons**, and that those who worshipped **evil ones** did so only in order to **appease** and **mitigate** them, so that they might do them no harm. None but **magicians** are to be properly accounted **devil-worshippers**, as they honor **evil demons** in order to gratify their own **revenge, lust,** and **ambition**. 

55. The **Pagans plead that those demons** who delivered **oracles** and performed **miracles** among them must necessarily be **good**, since there could be no greater reproach to the **Supreme God** than to suppose him to appoint **evil demons** as **presidents** and **governors** over the **world**, or to allow them to have such a great sway and share of **power** in it. The **faith of Plato in Divine Providence**: that the **good everywhere prevails over the bad**, and that the **Delphic Apollo** was therefore a **good demon**. 

56. The **Pagans' defense for worshipping the Supreme God in images, statues, and symbols.** That these are only **worshipped representationally** <term>original: "schetically"; from the Greek *schetikōs*, meaning relatively or by way of relation</term> by them, with the **honor passing from the images to the prototype**. And that since we, living in **bodies**, cannot easily have a **conception** of anything without some **corporeal image** or **mental phantom**, this much must be granted to the **infirmity of human nature** (at least among the **common people**) to **worship God corporeally** in **images** to prevent them from falling into **atheism**.

# CHAP. IV.

Even if we accept this **defense** <note>original: "Apology"</note> of the **Pagans**, suggesting that their **case** was not altogether as **bad** as is commonly supposed, they still cannot be **justified** by it in the three particulars mentioned above. The **Scripture's condemnation** of them remains **irrefutable** <note>original: "Irrefragable"</note>: that knowing **God**, they did not **glorify** him as **God**, or **sanctify** his **name**. That is, they did not **worship** him according to his **uncommon** and **incommunicable**, his **peerless** and **exclusive** <note>original: "Infociable"</note>, **transcendent** and **singular**, **incomparable** and **unresembleable nature**. Instead, they mingled **creature-worship** in some way or another with the **worship** of the **Creator**. 

**First**, the **worshipping** of **one God** through his **various gifts** and **effects** under several **personal names** is an **absurd** practice in itself. It may also provide a great opportunity for **atheism** when the things themselves—such as wine or grain—come to be called by those **names**, like **Bacchus** or **Ceres**. The **conclusion** easily follows from there: that the good things of **nature** are the only **deities**. Furthermore, to **worship** the **physical** <note>original: "Corporeal"</note> **world** itself as if it were **animated** as the **Supreme God**, and to worship its **parts** as the **members** of **God**, is plainly to **confound God** with the **creature**. This fails to **glorify** him as the **Creator**, or according to his **separate** and **spiritual nature**. 

58. To give **religious worship** to **demons** <note>original: "Dæmons"; referring to intermediary spirits</note> or **angels**, **heroes** or **saints**, or any other **intellectual creatures**, even if one does not honor them equally with the **Supreme God**, is to deny **God** the honor of his **holiness** and his **singular**, **exclusive**, and **incommunicable nature** as the only **self-originated being** and the **Creator** of all. Of Him, through Him, and to Him are all things. Since **God** is such a **being** that there is nothing **like** him, the **worship** given to him ought to be such that nothing else has anything **like** it: a **singular, separate, and unshared worship**. Those who **worship** should not themselves be **religiously worshipped**. 

59. The **religious worship** of **created spirits** proceeded chiefly from a **fear** that they would be provoked and do harm if they were not worshipped. This is both highly **injurious** to **good spirits** and shows a **distrust** of the **sufficiency** of **God's power** to protect his **worshippers**. All **good spirits**, even when **uninvoked**, are of their own accord ready to assist those who sincerely **worship** and seek the favor of <note>original: "Propitiate"</note> the **Supreme Deity**. Therefore, there is no need for the **religious worship** of them, which would also be **offensive** to them. 

60. Men's **praying** to **images** and **statues** is much more **ridiculous** than **children** talking to **dolls made of rags** <note>original: "babies made of clouts"</note>, but it is not as **innocent**. By doing so, they **debase** both themselves and **God**, failing to **glorify** him according to his **spiritual** and **unresembleable nature**. Instead, they change the **glory** of the **incorruptible God** into the **likeness** of **corruptible man** or **beast**. 

61. The **mistake** of those who think no one can be guilty of **idolatry** if they believe **one God** is the **maker** of the **world**. 

62. Based on the same **reason**—that nothing ought to be **religiously worshipped** besides the **Supreme God**, or those whom he appoints to represent himself (because he ought to be **sanctified** and dealt with according to his **singular nature** as unlike everything else)—it follows, contrary to the opinion of some **opposers** of **idolatry**, that there ought also to be a **discrimination** made between things **sacred** and **profane**, and **reverence** used in **divine worship**. **Idolatry** and **sacrilege** are closely allied. 

63. Another **Scripture-charge** against the **Pagans** was that they were **devil-worshippers**. This is not to say they intended all their **worship** for **evil demons** or **devils**...

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut drop cap 'H' containing stylized floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc>Having in the former chapter prepared the way, we shall now proceed (with **Divine Assistance**) to answer and confute all those **Atheistic Arguments** previously proposed. The first of which was this: *That there is no* **Idea of God**, *and therefore, either no such thing exists in nature, or at least there is no possible evidence of it.*

<margin>*Proclus's Commentary on the Timaeus, page 176.*</margin>
To affirm that there is no *Idea of God* is the same as affirming that there is no *conception of the mind* answering to that *word* or *name*. And the **Modern Atheists** do not hesitate to maintain this: that the **word God** has no **meaning** <note>original: "Signification"</note>, and that there is no other *idea* or *conception* in **men's minds** answering to it, besides the mere **mental image of the sound**. Now, for anyone to go about soberly to refute this—and to prove that **God** is not the **only word** without a **meaning**, and that men do not everywhere pay all their religious devotions to the mere **mental image of a fleeting sound**, expecting all **good** from it—might very well seem to all intelligent persons a most absurd and ridiculous undertaking. This is both because the thing is so evident in itself, and because the plainest things of all are the hardest to prove; for **"He who thinks that everything can be proven, destroys the very nature of proof"** <note>original: "ὁ πάντα ἀπόδεικτα νενομικὼς, αὐτὴν ἀπόδειξιν ἀναιρεῖ"</note>. Therefore, we shall here only suggest this much: since there are different words for *God* in several languages, and men have the same *notion* or *conception* in their minds answering to them all, it must be granted that they have some other *idea* or *conception* belonging to those *words* besides the *mental images of their various sounds*. And indeed, it can be nothing else but either...

It is a monstrous stupidity and foolishness of mind, or else an extraordinary *impudence*, for these atheists to deny that there is any idea of God at all in the minds of men, or that the *word* has any meaning.

<margin>Arrian, Book 1, Chapter 5.</margin> It was observed long ago by *Epictetus* that "if any man will oppose or contradict the most evident truths, it will not be easy to find arguments with which to convince him. And yet this, notwithstanding, ought neither to be attributed to any inability in the teacher, nor to any strength of wit in the denier, but only to a certain dead insensibility in him." <note>original Greek: "ἄν τις ἐνίσται πρὸς τὰ ἄγαν ἐκφανῆ, πρὸς τοῦτον οὐ ῥᾴδιόν ἐστιν εὑρεῖν λόγον, δι’ οὗ μεταπείσει τις αὐτόν· τοῦτο δ’ οὔτε παρὰ τὴν ἐκείνου δύναμιν, οὔτε παρὰ τὴν τοῦ διδάσκοντος ἀσθένειαν."</note> Upon this, he further adds that there is a double <term>mortification</term> or <term>petrification</term> <note>original: "ἀπονέκρωσις or ἀπολίθωσις"</note> of the soul: the one, when it is stupefied and made foolish in its *intellectual faculties*; the other, when it is deadened in its *morals*, as to that sense of shame <note>original: "Pudor"</note> that naturally should belong to a man. And he concludes that either of these states (though it is not commonly understood as such) is a condition little less deplorable than that of bodily death; he also states that such a person is not at all to be disputed with. "For what sword or what fire can one bring, by burning or flashing, to make such a person perceive that he is dead? But if he is aware of it and will not acknowledge it, then he is worse than dead, being castrated as to that sense of shame that belongs to a man." <note>original Greek: "ποῖον αὐτῷ πῦρ ἢ ποῖον σίδηρον προσάγω, ἵν’ αἴσθηται ὅτι νενέκρωται; αἰσθανόμενος οὐ προσποιεῖται; ἔτι χείρων ἐστὶ τοῦ νεκροῦ, ἐκτέτμηται γὰρ τὸ αἰσθητικὸν αὐτοῦ καὶ τὸ ἐντρεπτικόν."</note> Moreover, that philosopher took notice that in those times, when this denial of most evident truths proceeded rather from impudence than stupidity or foolishness, the common people would be inclined to admire it as *strength of wit and great learning*: "But if any man's sense of shame is deadened or mortified in him, we even call this power and strength." <note>original Greek: "ἂν δέ τινος τὸ αἰδῆμον ἀπονεκρωθῇ, τοῦτο ἔτι καὶ δύναμιν καλοῦμεν."</note>

Now as this was sometimes the case of the Academics <note>original: "Academicks"; a school of philosophers known for extreme skepticism, claiming that nothing could be known for certain.</note>, so it is also commonly the case of atheists. Their minds are partly *petrified* and *benumbed* into a kind of *foolish* and *stupid insensibility*, so that they are not able to discern things that are most evident; and they are partly "depudorated," or become so void of shame, that even though they do perceive the truth, they will obstinately and impudently deny the plainest things that exist—such as this: that there is *any idea answering to the word 'God' besides the mental image of the sound*. And we insist upon this *extraordinary monstrosity of atheists* in this place because we shall have occasion later, more than once, to take notice of it again in other instances, such as when they affirm that *physical motion* and *thought* <note>original: "Local Motion and Cogitation"</note> are really one and the *self-same thing*, and the like. And we conceive it to be unquestionably true that it is often nothing else but either this *shameless impudence* or *stupid insensibility* in atheists that is admired by the ignorant as *profoundness of wit and learning*. "But shall I call this power or wit, and commend it? # That there must be some Unmade Substance BOOK I.

on that account? No more than I will commend the impudence of the <term>Cinædi</term> <note>original: *Cinædi*, a Latin term for people in antiquity known for public shamelessness or wanton behavior</note>, who do not hesitate to *do* and *say* anything in public.

II. But whatever these *atheists* deny in words, it is nevertheless evident that even they have an *idea* or *concept* in their minds corresponding to the *word* *God* when they deny his existence. Otherwise, they would be denying the existence of *nothing*. Nor can it be doubted at all that they have the same *idea of God* as *theists* do, since they deny the existence of the very thing that theists assert. In all other controversies, when men dispute together—one affirming and the other denying—both parties must have the same *idea* in their minds of what they are disputing about. Otherwise, their entire dispute would be nothing but a kind of *Babel*-language and confusion. So it must also be in this present controversy between *theists* and *atheists*. Indeed, there would be no controversy at all between them if they did not both mean one and the same thing by *God*. Nor would the *atheists* be atheists anymore if they denied the existence of something else rather than that very same thing which the *theists* affirm.

III. Therefore, we shall next declare what this *idea of God* is, or what that thing is whose existence those who affirm are called *theists*, and those who deny *atheists*. To do this, we must first establish this <term>lemma</term> <note>a preparatory proposition or premise used to prove a larger point</note> or *preparatory proposition*: while it is generally acknowledged that all things did not exist from eternity just as they are now—as *unmade*—but that some things were *made* and *generated* or produced; so it is also not possible that *all* things were *made*. There must, of necessity, be something *self-existent* from eternity and *unmade*, because if there had ever been *nothing*, there could never have been anything. The reason for this is so evident and irresistible that even the *atheists* admit they are conquered by it. They readily acknowledge it as an unquestionable truth: that there must be something <term>ungenerated</term> <note>original Greek: ἀγέννητον (*agenneton*), meaning something that was never made or produced</note>, and which therefore is the *cause* of those other things that are made. There must be something <term>self-originated</term> <note>original Greek: αὐτόφυες (*autophyes*)</note> and <term>self-existing</term> <note>original Greek: αὐθυπόστατον (*authypostaton*)</note> that is as <term>indestructible</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνώλεθρον (*anolethron*)</note> and <term>incorruptible</term> <note>original Greek: ἄφθαρτον (*aphtharton*)</note> as it is ungenerated. Its existence, therefore, must be *necessary*; for if its existence from eternity were supposed to have happened by chance, then it might just as easily happen to cease to be. Therefore, the only question now is: what is this ungenerated and indestructible, self-originated and self-existing thing, which is the cause of all other things that are made?

IV. Now, there are two grand, opposing opinions concerning this. First, some argue that the only *self-existent*, *unmade*, and *incorruptible thing*, and the *first principle* of all things, is *senseless matter*. That is, matter that is either perfectly *dead* and <term>stupid</term> <note>original: "stupid," here meaning lacking sensation or consciousness rather than lacking intelligence</note>, or at least devoid of all *animal-like* and *conscious life*. ### CHAPTER IV. The Principle of Other Created Things.

Others, on the contrary, judge it reasonable that the *First Principle* and origin of all things should be that which is *most perfect*. (As Aristotle observes of Pherecydes and his followers, "they considered the first cause and principle of generation to be the best" <note>original Greek: *τὸ γεννῆσαν πρῶτον ἄριστον τιθέασι*</note>). They understand that being endowed with *conscious life* and *intelligence* is a much *greater perfection* than being devoid of both. (As Balbus in Cicero declares on this very occasion: "And there is no doubt that what is alive, and has mind, reason, and sense, is better than that which lacks these things" <note>original Latin: *Nec dubium quin quod Animans sit, habeátque Mentem & Rationem & Senſum, id ſit melius quàm id quod his careat*</note> <margin>Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book 2</margin>).

They therefore conclude that the only *unmade thing*, which was the principle, cause, and origin of all other things, was not *senseless matter*, but a *perfect conscious understanding nature*, or *mind*. These are the people who are strictly and properly called *theists*: those who affirm that a *perfectly conscious understanding being*, or *mind*, existing of itself *from eternity*, was the cause of all other things. On the other hand, those who derive all things from *senseless matter* as the *first* origin, and deny that there is any *conscious understanding being* that is *self-existent* or *unmade*, are those who are properly called *atheists*. Therefore, the true and genuine idea of God in general is this: *A perfect conscious understanding being (or mind) existing of itself from eternity, and the cause of all other things.*

V. But it is observable here that those atheists who deny God according to this true and genuine concept of him often abuse the word, calling *senseless matter* by that name. They do this partly, perhaps, to avoid the hateful and shameful name of *atheists*, and partly because they believe that whatever is the *first principle* of things—<term>ingenerable</term> <note>original: "ingenerable," meaning something that was never created or born, but has always existed</note> and incorruptible, and the cause of all things besides itself—must therefore be the *divinest thing* of all.

Therefore, by the word "God," these people mean nothing more than that which is *unmade* or *self-existent* <note>original Greek: *ἀγέννητον*</note>, and the *first principle* <note>original Greek: *ἀρχὴ*</note> of things. In this way, as was observed before, Anaximander called *infinite matter* (which lacked any kind of life) "the divine" <note>original Greek: *τὸ θεῖον*</note> or *God*. Pliny called the *physical world* (which he believed was endowed with nothing but a <term>plastic</term> <note>in this context, "plastic" refers to a natural power that can form or shape matter without conscious thought</note>, unknowing nature) a "divine power" <note>original Latin: *Numen*</note>. Similarly, others mentioned by Aristotle called the inanimate elements *gods* because they were *supposed first principles* of things; "for these are also gods" <note>original Greek: *θεοὶ ἢ καὶ ταῦτα*</note>.

Indeed, Aristotle himself seems to be guilty of this error of *abusing* the word *God* in this way <margin>Metaphysics, book 1, chapter 4</margin> when speaking of *Love* and *Chaos* as the two first principles of things. According to the rules of grammar, he must be understood as calling them both gods: "Concerning how these two [gods] should be ranked, and which of them is to be placed first, whether Love or Chaos, is to be decided later" <note>original Greek: *τούτους μὲν οὖν πῶς χρὴ διανεῖμαι, περὶ τοῦ τίς πρῶτος, ἐξέστω κρῖναι ὕστερον*</note>. This passage from Aristotle seems to agree with one from Epicharmus: "But Chaos is said to have been made the first of the gods" <note>original Greek: *Ἀλλὰ λέγεταί μὲν χάος πρῶτον γενέσθαι θεῶν*</note>; unless we should instead understand him to mean that "Chaos was said to have been made before the gods." ### The Assertors of Two Unmade Principles, Book I.

<margin>Book 1, page 19. Caution about the use of words: "He, therefore, who has even a small understanding of these things in a more noble way, will be cautious about applying different names to different things, lest he should suffer the same fate as those who erroneously apply the name 'God' to inanimate matter." <note>original Greek: ὁ τοίνυν μεγαλοφυέστερον κἂν ὀλίγον τούτων ἐννοίαν εἰληφὼς, εὐλαβηθήσεται, ἄλλα ἄλλοις ἐφαρμόζειν ὀνόματα πράγμασι, μήποτε ὅμοιον πάθῃ τοῖς τὸ θεὸς ὄνομα ἐσφαλμένως φέρουσιν, ἐπὶ ὕλην ἄψυχον</note></margin> He, therefore, who has even the slightest consideration of these things, will take a religious care that he does not give improper names to things, lest he should fall into the same error as those who attribute the name of God to inanimate and senseless matter. Now, according to this false and spurious notion of the word "God"—when it is taken to mean any supposed "First Principle" or "Self-existent Unmade Thing," whatever that may be—there neither is nor can be any such thing as an *atheist*. This is because anyone with even a grain of reason must acknowledge that something or other *existed from eternity unmade*, and was the cause of those other things that are *made*. 

But that notion or *idea of God*, according to which some are *atheists* and some are *theists*, is, in its strictest sense, what we have already declared: *A Perfect Mind, or Consciously Understanding Nature, Self-existent from Eternity, and the Cause of all other things*. Genuine *theists* are those who believe the first origin of all things *universally* to be a *consciously understanding nature (or Perfect Mind)*. On the other hand, *atheists* are properly defined as those who derive all things from *matter*, which they view as either perfectly *dead* and *stupid* <note>original: "stupid" used here in its Latin sense, meaning "senseless" or "inert"</note>, or otherwise devoid of all *conscious* and animal-like life.

VI. But so that we may more fully and precisely declare the true *idea of God*, we must here take notice of a certain opinion held by some philosophers who took a middle path between the two previously mentioned groups. They did not make *matter* alone the sole principle of all things, nor did they make God the *sole principle*; instead, they joined them both together and held that there were *Two First Principles* or *Self-existent Unmade Beings* that were independent of one another: *God* and *Matter*. 

Among these, the *Stoics* are to be included. However, because they held that there was no other substance besides "body" (physical matter), they strangely confused themselves. They were forced by this belief to make their *Two First Principles*—the *active* and the *passive*—really both one and the self-same substance. Their doctrine on this point was described by Cicero as follows:

"They divided nature into two parts: one was the efficient cause, and the other was, as it were, providing itself to the first, out of which something might be made. In that which was the efficient cause, they believed there was force; in that which was made, a certain matter. Yet in both, there was both. For neither could matter itself hold together if it were not contained by some force, nor could force exist without some matter; for there is nothing that is not forced to be somewhere." <note>original Latin: Naturam dividebant in Res Duas, ut Altera esset Efficiens, Altera autem quasi huic se præbens, ex qua Efficeretur aliquid. In eo quod Efficeret, Vim esse censebant; in eo quod Efficeretur, Materiam quandam; in Utroque tamen Utrumque. Neque enim Materiam ipsam cohærere potuisse si nullâ Vi contineretur, neque Vim sine aliqua Materia; Nihil est enim quod non Alicubi esse cogatur.</note>

The Stoics divided nature into two things as the first principles: one of which is the efficient cause, or "artisan," and the other which offers itself to him so that things can be made out of it. In the efficient principle, they recognized an *active force*; in the patient <term>patient: the thing being acted upon</term>, they recognized *matter*. But they held that in each of these, both were found together; for matter could not stick together unless it were held by some active force, nor could the active force exist by itself without matter, because nothing exists that is not located somewhere. 

But besides these *Stoics*, there were other philosophers who, while admitting the existence of incorporeal <term>incorporeal: non-physical or spiritual</term> substance, did suppose *two first principles* as substances really distinct from one another that coexisted from eternity: an *incorporeal deity* and *matter*.

<header>CHAPTER IV. God, and the Matter.</header>

<margin>See Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 7, chapter 7.</margin>
...as for example Anaxagoras, Archelaus, Atticus, and many more; so much so that Pythagoras himself was reckoned among those by Numenius, and Plato by Plutarch and Laertius.

And we find it commonly taken for granted that Aristotle also held this persuasion, though it cannot be certainly concluded from that (as some seem to suppose) simply because he asserted the eternity of the world. Plotinus, Porphyry, Iamblichus, Proclus, and Simplicius did the same, and yet they nevertheless maintained that God was the sole principle of all things, and that matter was also derived from Him. Neither will that passage of Aristotle's in his *Metaphysics* necessarily prove the contrary: <margin>Book 1, chapter 1.</margin> "God seems to be the cause of all things and a certain first principle" <note>original Greek: Θεὸς δοκεῖ τὸ αἴτιον πᾶσιν εἶναι καὶ ἀρχή τις</note>, because this might be understood as referring only to the forms of things.

But it is plain that Plutarch was a supporter of this doctrine, from his discourse upon the Platonic *Psychogonia* <note>The "generation of the soul," a commentary on Plato's *Timaeus*</note> (among other places):

> "It is therefore better for us to follow Plato (rather than Heraclitus) and loudly declare that the world was made by God. For as the world is the best of all works, so is God the best of all causes. Nevertheless, the substance or matter out of which the world was made was not itself made; but was always ready at hand and subject to the Artificer, to be ordered and organized by Him, and made to resemble Him as much as was possible to provide. For the making of the world was not the production of it out of nothing, but out of a previously bad and disorderly state—just like the making of a house, a garment, or a statue." <note>original Greek: βέλτιον οὖν πλάτωνι πειθομένους, τὸν μὲν κόσμον ὑπὸ θεοῦ γεγονέναι λέγειν καὶ ᾄδειν· ὁ μὲν γὰρ κάλλιστος τῶν γεγονότων, ὁ δ' ἄριστος τῶν αἰτιῶν· τὴν δ' οὐσίαν καὶ ὕλην ἐξ ἧς γέγονεν, οὐ γενομένην, ἀλλὰ ὑποκειμένην ἀεὶ τῷ δημιουργῷ, εἰς διάθεσιν καὶ τάξιν αὐτῆς, καὶ πρὸς αὐτὸν ἐξομοίωσιν, ὡς δυνατὸν ἦν παρασχεῖν· οὐ γὰρ ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος ἡ γένεσις, ἀλλ' ἐκ τοῦ μὴ καλῶς, μηδ' ἱκανῶς ἔχοντος, ὡς οἰκίας, καὶ ἱματίου, καὶ ἀνδριάντος.</note>

It is also well known that Hermogenes and other ancient claimants to Christianity similarly asserted the *self-existence* and *unproduced nature* of *matter*. For this reason, they were commonly called *Materiarii*, or the *Materiarian Heretics*. They claimed by this means (as the Stoics had done before them) to explain the origin of *evils* and to free God from being blamed for them. Their reasoning for this purpose is thus set down by Tertullian: <margin>*Against Hermogenes*, page 282, Royal edition.</margin>

> "God made all things either out of Himself, or out of nothing, or out of matter. He could not make all things out of Himself, because since He is always unmade, He would then really have been the maker of nothing. And He did not make all things out of nothing, because being essentially good, He would have made *nothing that was not the best* <note>original Latin: Nihil non optimum</note>—everything in the best manner—and so there could have been no evil in the world. But since there are evils, and these could not proceed from the will of God, they must necessarily arise from the fault of something else; and therefore from the matter out of which things were made."

Lastly, it is also sufficiently well known that some modern sects of the Christian profession today also assert the *uncreatedness* of matter.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on those who believe in two eternal principles, specifically focusing on the "Imperfect Theists" who believe God and Matter both existed eternally, distinguishing them from Atheists.</meta>

<header>The Materialists <note>original: "Materiarians"</note> Book 1.</header>

These suppose, in the same way as the Stoics did, that Body is the only substance.

VII. Now, regarding all those—whoever they were—who maintained **two self-existent principles**, God and Matter, we may declare universally that they were neither better nor worse than a kind of **imperfect Theists**.

They had a certain **notion** or **idea of God**, such as it was, which seems to be the very same as that expressed by Aristotle: "an eternal, best living being" <note>original Greek: ζῶον ἄριστον ἀΐδιον</note>, and also represented by Epicurus in this manner: "a living being that possesses all happiness along with incorruptibility" <note>original Greek: ζῶον πᾶσαν ἔχον μακαριότητα μετ’ ἀφθαρσίας</note>.

<margin>
Seneca, *Natural Questions*, Preface, Book 1.
</margin>
In this, they acknowledged that besides **senseless matter**, there was also a **sentient** <note>original: "Animalish"</note> and **conscious** or **perceptive nature**, self-existent from eternity. This was in opposition to **Atheists**, who claimed that **matter**—being either devoid of all life, or at least devoid of sentient and conscious life—was the **sole principle** of all things. For it has been often observed that some Atheists attributed a kind of **plastic life** or nature to that matter, which they made the **only principle of the universe**. These **two** types of atheism were long ago noted by Seneca in these words:
> "The universe, in which we ourselves also exist, is devoid of counsel; it is either carried along by a certain rashness, or by a nature that does not know what it does." <note>original Latin: *Universum in quo nos quoque sumus, expers esse Consilii, & aut ferri Temeritate quadam aut Naturâ Nesciente quid faciat.*</note>

But no Atheist ever acknowledged **conscious life** to be a **first principle** in the universe, nor that the **whole** was governed by any **living**, **sentient**, and **understanding nature** presiding over it as its head. Instead, as was previously declared, they concluded that all **animals** and **life**, all **conscious**, **sentient**, and **self-perceptive life**, were **generated** and **corrupted**—either brought out of nothing or reduced to nothing again. Therefore, those who, on the contrary, asserted that **life** and **conscious life** are a **first principle** or an **uncreated** thing in the universe, are to be considered **Theists**. Thus, Balbus in Cicero's writings declares that to be a Theist is to assert "that the world was generated or produced at first from living principles" <note>original Latin: *Ab Animantibus Principiis Mundum, esse Generatum*</note>, and that it is also still governed by such a nature, and "that all things are subject to a sentient and conscious nature, steering and guiding them." <note>original Latin: *Res omnes subjectas esse Naturæ Sentienti*</note>

<margin>
Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book 2.
</margin>
But to distinguish this **Divine Living Being** from all others, these definers added that it was the "best" <note>original Greek: ἄριστον</note> and "most happy" <note>original Greek: μακαριώτατον</note> animal. Accordingly, this distinction is added to that **general nature of living things** by Balbus the Stoic to make the **idea** or **definition of God** complete: "We anticipate such a God with a certain notion of the mind; first, that He is a living being; then, that in all nature..." <note>original Latin: *Talem esse Deum certâ Notione animi præsentimus; Primùm, ut sit Animans; Deinde, ut in omni Natura*</note>

It highlights that the defining trait of a Theist, even an imperfect one, is the belief that a conscious, sentient being is a primary, uncreated principle of the universe.</summary>

### CHAPTER IV. Imperfect Theists.

"Nothing is more excellent than He is" <note>original Latin: *nihil Illo sit Præstantius*</note>: we sense God through a certain concept in our minds. First, we understand that He is a consciously living being <note>original Latin: *Animans*</note>; and secondly, that He is such a living being that there is nothing in the whole universe, or the nature of things, more excellent than Him.

Therefore, these *Materialist Theists* <note>original: "Materialian Theists"</note> acknowledged God to be a *perfectly understanding being*, and one who also had *power over the whole matter of the universe*. This matter was utterly unable to move itself or to produce anything without Him. All of them, except the *Anaxagoreans* <note>followers of Anaxagoras, who believed Mind (Nous) ordered a pre-existing chaos</note>, concluded that He was the *creator* of all the *forms of inanimate bodies* and of the souls of animals. However, it was universally agreed upon among them that He was at least *the orderer and disposer* of all things, and that therefore He might, on that account, well be called the <term>demiurge</term> <note>original Greek: δημιουργός; a craftsman or artisan-creator of the world</note>, *the Maker or Framer of the world*.

Notwithstanding this, as long as they maintained that *matter* existed independently of *God*, and sometimes also that it was *refractory and stubborn* toward Him—and by that means was the cause of evil, contrary to the *Divine Will*—it is plain that they could not acknowledge *Divine Omnipotence* <note>all-powerfulness</note> according to its full and proper sense. This may also further appear from these questions by *Seneca* <note>a Roman Stoic philosopher</note> concerning God: 

> "How far does God's power extend? Does He create the matter for Himself, or does He use what is provided? Does God accomplish whatever He wills? Or do the materials fail Him in many things, resulting in many things being poorly formed by this Great Artificer—not because His skill fails Him, but because the material He works upon is often disobedient to His art?" <note>original Latin: *Quantum Deus possit? Materiam ipse sibi Formet, an Datâ utatur? Deus quicquid Vult efficiat? An in multis rebus illum Tractanda destituant, & à Magno Artifice Pravè formentur multa, non quia cessat Ars, sed quia id in quo exercetur, sæpe Inobsequens Arti est?*</note>

Wherefore, I think we may well conclude that those *Materialist Theists* did not have a right and genuine idea of God.

Nevertheless, it does not follow that they must be considered *absolute atheists*. There may be some flexibility allowed in the definition of *Theism*. Although in a strict and proper sense, only those are *Theists* who acknowledge *one God who is perfectly all-powerful*, the *sole origin of all things*, and the *cause of matter* as well as everything else; yet it seems reasonable that we should consider the weakness of *human understanding*. We should extend the word further, so that it may include those who assert *one intellectual principle that is self-existent from eternity*—the *Framer and Governor of the whole world*—even if they do not believe He is the *creator of matter*. No one should be condemned as an *absolute atheist* merely because they hold that *matter is eternal and uncreated*, unless they also deny that an *eternal, unmade Mind* rules over that matter, and so make *senseless matter* the *sole origin of all things*. And this is certainly most agreeable to common understanding; for *Democritus* and *Epicurus* would never...

The author argues that while these figures lack a perfect concept of God's omnipotence, they should not be classified as absolute atheists.</summary>

# That Omnipotence is included Book I.

They would never have been condemned as Atheists merely for asserting the existence of eternal, self-existent atoms—no more than Anaxagoras and Archelaus were (who maintained the same thing)—had they not also denied that other principle of theirs: a Perfect Mind. They concluded instead that the world was made, "without the ordering and disposal of any understanding being that possessed all happiness along with incorruptibility" <note>original Greek: μηδενὸς διατάττοντος ἢ διαταξαμένου τὴν πᾶσαν ἔχοντος μακαριότητα μετ᾿ ἀφθαρσίας</note>.

### VIII.
The true and proper *idea of God*, in its most concise form, is this: *A Being Absolutely Perfect*. For this is the only concept to which *necessary existence* is *essential*, and of which it can be demonstrated. Now, just as *absolute perfection* includes everything that belongs to the Deity, it encompasses not only *necessary existence* and *perfect knowledge* or understanding, but also *omni-causality* <note>the quality of being the cause of all things</note> and *omnipotence* (in its full extent), otherwise called *infinite power*. God is not only "the best living being" <note>original Greek: ζῶον ἄριστον</note> and "a living being than whom nothing in all nature is more excellent" <note>original Latin: Animans quo nihil in omni Natura præstantius</note>, as the *Materialist Theists* described him; nor merely what Zeno of Elea called him, "the most powerful of all things" <note>original Greek: κράτιστον πάντων</note>; but he is also *absolutely omnipotent* and *infinitely powerful* <note>original Greek: παγκρατὴς, παντοκράτωρ, and παντεξούσιος</note>. Therefore, neither *matter* nor anything else can exist of itself independently of God; rather, He is the sole principle and source from which all things are derived.

However, because atheists frequently challenge this concept of *infinite power*, claiming it is completely *unintelligible* and therefore *impossible*, we shall briefly declare its meaning here and render it (we believe) easily intelligible or conceivable in the following two steps. First, by *infinite power* is meant nothing else but *perfect power*—or as Simplicius <note>a 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> calls it, "a whole and entire power" <note>original Greek: ὅλη δύναμις</note>—which has no mixture of helplessness nor any defect of power within it. Second, this *perfect power* (which is the same as *infinite power*) is really nothing other than a *power of producing and doing* all things whatsoever that are *conceivable* and do not imply a *contradiction*. For *conceivability* is the *only measure of power and its extent*, as shall be shown more fully in the proper place.

At this point, we think it appropriate to observe that the pagan theists themselves also commonly acknowledged omnipotence as an attribute of the Deity, which could be proved from many passages in their writings.

<margin>Homer, *Odyssey* Book 4</margin>

-> ———————— God gives sometimes one thing, sometimes another; <-
-> Jupiter gives both good and evil, for he can do all things. <-
<note>original Greek: θεὸς ἄλλοτ’ ἐπ’ ἄλλῳ / ζεὺς ἀγαθόντε κακόντε διδιοῖ, δύναται γὰρ ἅπαντα.</note>

-> Jupiter gives both good and evil, for he is able to do all things. <-
<note>original Latin: Deus aliud post aliud / Jupiter, Bonúmque Malúmque dat, Potest enim Omnia.</note>

<meta>This page continues the argument that omnipotence is a necessary attribute of the Divine. It explores how ancient materialist philosophers like Epicurus and Lucretius attempted to dismantle religion by arguing that all power is finite, and then transitions to arguing that power and knowledge alone are insufficient for a true concept of God without the addition of goodness and virtue.</meta>

# Knowledge and Power alone Book I.

---

That infinite power is an essential attribute of the Deity appears plainly from the writings of *Lucretius*, when he tells us that *Epicurus* <note>Epicurus (341–270 BC) was a Greek philosopher who taught that the universe was composed of atoms and void, and that while gods might exist, they have no concern for human affairs.</note>, in order to do away with *religion*, set himself to disprove *infinite power*.

<margin>Book I.</margin>
->—— He traversed the whole immense universe in mind and spirit,<-
->From which he returns as a victor to tell us what can arise,<-
->And what cannot: in short, by what logic the power of each thing<-
->Is finite, and has a deeply fixed boundary stone.<-
->Therefore, religion in its turn is cast down and trampled<-
->Underfoot; this victory levels us with the heavens.<-
<note>original Latin: Omne Immensum peragravit Mente Animóque, Unde refert nobis Victor, quid possit Oriri, Quid nequeat: Finita Potestas denique quoique Quanam fit ratione, atque altè Terminus hærens. Quare Relligio pedibus subjecta vicissim Obteritur, nos exæquat Victoria Cælo.</note>

As if he were saying that *Epicurus*, by showing that all power was *finite*, effectively destroyed *religion*; he thereby removed its object, which is an omnipotent and infinitely powerful Deity. And this is a point which the same poet often repeats: that there is no *infinite power*, and consequently no Deity according to the true *concept* of it. Finally, in his sixth book, he condemns religious people as guilty of great folly for asserting omnipotence or *infinite power* (that is, a Deity) in this manner:

->Again they fall back into ancient religions,<-
->And take on harsh masters whom the wretched believe<-
->Are able to do all things, being ignorant of what can be<-
->And what cannot; in short, by what logic the power of each thing<-
->Is finite, and has a deeply fixed boundary stone:<-
->Because of this, they are carried further astray.<-
<note>original Latin: Rursus in antiquas referuntur Relligiones, Et Dominos acres asciscunt, Omnia Posse, Quos miseri credunt, ignari quid queat esse, Quid nequeat, Finita Potestas denique quoique, Quanam fit ratione, atque altè Terminus hærens: Quo magis errantes totâ regione feruntur.</note>

Though the poet, speaking carelessly according to the customs of those times, seems to attribute omnipotence and *infinite power* to *multiple gods*, it is evident by the nature of the thing itself that this can only be the attribute of *one supreme Deity*. It may also be observed that in the passages of the poets cited previously, it is accordingly always ascribed to *God in the singular*. Nevertheless, all the inferior pagan deities were supposed by them to have certain shares of this *Divine omnipotence* specifically granted and imparted to them.

IX. But we have not yet fully explained everything that belongs to the *complete concept of God*. For *knowledge* and *power* alone will not make a *God*. God is generally conceived by everyone to be a *most venerable* and *most desirable being*. However, an *all-knowing* and *all-powerful* deity who acts on a whim—having nothing of *kindness* or *morality* in its nature to *measure* and *regulate its will*—could not be truly *noble* and *venerable*, according to the maxim, *without goodness there is no majesty* <note>original Latin: sine Bonitate nulla Majestas</note>. Neither could such a being be *desirable*, as it could only be feared and dreaded, and could never inspire firm *faith* or *confidence*. *Plutarch* says in the *Life of Aristides*:

"The Divine seems to excel in three things: incorruptibility, power, and virtue. Of these, virtue is the most majestic and divine. For even the void and the elements happen to be incorruptible; and earthquakes, lightning, the rush of winds, and the onslaught of floods possess great power..."
<note>original Greek: τὸ θεῖον τρισὶ δοκεῖ διαφέρειν, ἀφθαρσίᾳ, καὶ δυνάμει, καὶ ἀρετῇ· ὧν σεμνότατον ἡ ἀρετὴ καὶ θειότατόν ἐστι· ἀφθάρτῳ μὲν γὰρ εἶναι καὶ τὰ κενὰ, καὶ τοῖς στοιχείοις συμβέβηκε· δύναμιν δὲ σεισμοὶ καὶ κεραυνοὶ, καὶ πνευμάτων ὁρμαὶ καὶ ῥυμάτων ἐπιφοραὶ μεγάλην ἔχουσι, &c.</note>

### CHAP. IV. Make not up a God.

And *Virtue*; of all these, the *most divine and venerable* is *Virtue*. For *vacuum* <note>original: Vacuum; here referring to empty space or the void in atomistic theory</note> and the *senseless elements* have *incorruptibility*. *Earthquakes* and *thunders*, *blustering winds*, and *overflowing torrents* have *much power and force*. Therefore, the common people <note>original: the Vulgar</note> are affected in three ways toward the *Deity*: they *admire* its *happiness*, they *fear* it, and they *honor* it. They esteem the Deity *happy* for its *incorruptibility*; they *fear* it and stand in awe of it for its *power*; but they *worship* it—that is, *love and honor* it—for its *justice*. 

And indeed, an *omnipotent, arbitrary Deity* <note>A god who acts solely by will or whim without being bound by moral goodness</note> may seem to be, in some sense, a *worse* and more *undesirable thing* than the *Manichean Evil God* <note>The Manicheans believed in two opposing powers: one perfectly good and one perfectly evil</note>. This is because the latter could only be *finitely evil*, whereas the former might be *infinitely* so. However, I think it can be little doubted that the whole *Manichean hypothesis*, taken all together, is to be preferred over this idea of *one omnipotent, arbitrary Deity* (devoid of goodness and morality) ruling all things. In the Manichean system, the *evil principle* is yoked with another principle that is *essentially good*, which checks and controls it. It also seems less dishonorable to God to attribute a *defect of power* to him than a defect of *goodness and justice*.

<margin>Eudemian Ethics, Book 7, Chapter 14</margin>
Neither can *power and knowledge* alone make a being in itself completely *happy*. For we all have by nature "a certain divination" <note>original Greek: μαντεύμά τι (manteuma ti)</note> (as both *Plato* and *Aristotle* call it)—a certain *divination, presage*, and *inner prophetic sense* in our minds—of some higher *good and perfection* than either *power or knowledge*. Knowledge is plainly to be preferred over *power*, as it is that which guides and directs power's blind force and impulse. But *Aristotle* himself declares that there is "something better than reason" <note>original Greek: λόγου τι κρεῖττον (logou ti kreitton)</note>, which is the "principle and origin" <note>original Greek: λόγου ἀρχὴ (logou archē)</note> of it. For, he says, "the principle of reason is not reason, but something better" <note>original Greek: λόγου ἀρχὴ οὐ λόγος, ἀλλά τι κρεῖττον (logou archē ou logos, alla ti kreitton)</note>. Here he also suggests this to be the proper and essential character of the Deity: "For what is there that can be better than knowledge, but God?" <note>original Greek: τί ἂν οὖν κρεῖττον καὶ ἐπιστήμης, πλὴν ὁ θεὸς; (ti an oun kreitton kai epistēmēs, plēn ho theos?)</note> Likewise, the same philosopher elsewhere plainly determines that there is morality in the *nature of God*, and that his *happiness* consists principally in that, and not in external things 
<margin>The Republic (Politics), Book 7, Chapter 1</margin>
or the exercise of his power: "That every man has so much happiness as he has virtue and wisdom, and of acting according to these, should be agreed upon by us, using God as our witness; who is happy and blessed, not because of any external goods, but because of himself and because of what he is by nature—that is, because he is essentially moral and virtuous" <note>original Greek: ὅτι μὲν οὖν ἑκάστῳ τῆς εὐδαιμονίας ἐπιβάλλει τοσοῦτον, ὅσονπερ ἀρετῆς καὶ φρονήσεως, καὶ τοῦ πράττειν κατὰ ταύτας, ἔστω συνωμολογημένον ἡμῖν, μάρτυρι τῷ θεῷ χρωμένοις, ὃς εὐδαίμων μέν ἐστι καὶ μακάριος, δι᾽ οὐθὲν δὲ τῶν ἐξωτερικῶν ἀγαθῶν, ἀλλὰ δι᾽ αὑτὸν αὐτὸς, καὶ τῷ ποιός τις εἶναι τὴν φύσιν.</note>.

This doctrine of Aristotle's seems to have been borrowed from *Plato*, who in his dialogues *The Republic*, while discussing moral virtue, occasionally happens upon this dispute concerning the *sum-* <note>summum bonum: the highest good</note>

# A Good Superior to Knowledge. Book I.

<margin>Book 6.</margin>
Plato discusses the *Summum Bonum* <note>original: *Summum Bonum*; Latin for "the Highest Good"</note> or *Chief Good*; in which he concludes that it consists neither in *Pleasure* as such (according to the opinion of the *common people* <note>original: Vulgar</note>), nor yet in *Mere Knowledge* and *Understanding* (according to the idea of others who were more *refined* and *intelligent*). "You know that to the common people, pleasure seems to be the highest good, but to those who are more refined and noble-minded, it is knowledge. But those who hold this latter opinion cannot demonstrate what kind of knowledge it is that constitutes that highest and chief good; they are forced at last to say, quite ridiculously, that it is the 'knowledge of the good.' In this, they simply run in a circle: while upbraiding us for being ignorant of this highest good, they talk to us at the same time as if we already knew what it was." <note>original: οἶσθα ὅτι τοῖς μὲν πολλοῖς ἡδονὴ δοκεῖ εἶναι τὸ ἀγαθὸν... (Plato, *Republic*, Book 6, 505b)</note> Thereupon he adds: "Even though knowledge and truth are both excellent things, you will be right to conclude that the Chief Good is something that transcends them both. For just as light and the sense of sight may both rightly be said to be 'sun-like' <note>original: soliform</note> or related to the sun, yet neither can be said to be the sun itself; so knowledge and truth may both be said to be 'good-like' <note>original: boniform</note> or related to the Chief Good, but neither of them is that Chief Good itself. This Good is still to be looked upon as something more magnificent and honorable." <note>original: καλῶν ἀμφοτέρων ὄντων, γνώσεώς τε καὶ ἀληθείας... (Plato, *Republic*, Book 6, 508e-509a)</note> In all of these points from Plato, there seems to be little more than what may be found through our own experience: namely, that there is a certain *life*, or *vital and moral disposition of the soul*, which is much more *inwardly* and thoroughly *satisfying* than either *sensual pleasure* or any *knowledge* and *speculation* whatsoever.

Now, whatever this *Chief Good* may be—which is a *perfection superior to knowledge and understanding*—that philosopher resolves that it must primarily and principally exist in *God*, whom he therefore calls the *very Idea or Essence of Good* <note>original: ἰδέαν τ᾽ ἀγαθοῦ</note>. In this, he followed the footsteps of the *Pythagoreans*, and particularly *Timaeus Locrus*, who, in establishing *two principles* of the *universe*—*Mind* and *Necessity*—adds concerning the former: "The first of these two is of the nature of good, and it is called God, the principle of the best things." <note>original: τουτέων δὲ μὲν τὰς τ᾽ ἀγαθῶ φύσιος εἶμεν... (Timaeus Locrus, *On the Nature of the World and the Soul*)</note> Consistent with this doctrine, the *Hebrew Kabbalists* <note>original: Cabalists</note> also identify a *Sephirah* <note>One of the ten emanations or attributes of God in Kabbalah</note> in the Deity that is superior to both *Binah* and *Chokhmah* (*Understanding* and *Wisdom*), which they call *Keter* <note>original: Chether</note> or *the Crown*. Some would suspect this *Kabbalistic learning* to have been very ancient among the Jews, and that *Parmenides* was influenced by it, as he likewise called God *the Crown* <note>original: στεφάνην</note>. For this reason, Velleius in *Cicero* (representing...

### CHAP. IV. Morality in the Nature of God.

(Presenting the various opinions of philosophers concerning God) he censures <note>original: perstringes; meaning to criticize or graze against</note> him among the rest: *Parmenides creates a certain imaginary thing in the likeness of a crown, which he calls a wreath—a circle containing the heat of light that surrounds the heavens, and he calls this God.* <note>original: Parmenides Commentitium quiddam, Coronæ ſimilitudine efficit, ſtephanem appellat, continentem ardore lucis orbem, qui cingit Cœlum, quem appellat Deum.</note>

But all this while we seem to be searching for what the Chief and Highest Good superior to knowledge is, in which the essence of the Deity principally consists. It cannot be denied that Plato sometimes talks too metaphysically and obscurely <note>original: Clowdily</note> about it. For this reason, just as he was open to the criticism <note>original: Laſh</note> of Aristotle, so he was also commonly <note>original: Vulgarly</note> ridiculed for it, as appears by these lines from the poet Amphis in the writings of Laertius <note>original: Laertius; refers to Diogenes Laertius, a biographer of Greek philosophers</note>:

->What good that is, which you expect to find,<-
->I confess, I understand it less,<-
->Than I do Plato's Good.<-
<note>original: τὸ δ' ἀγαθὸν ὅ, τι ποτ' ἐστίν, οὗ σὺ τυγχάνειν μέλλεις διὰ ταύτην, ἧττον οἶδα τοῦτ' ἐγώ, ἢ τὸ τοῦ Πλάτωνος Ἀγαθόν·</note>

*What Good that is, which you expect from here, I confess, I understand less than I do Plato's Good.* Nevertheless, he plainly suggests these two things concerning it. First, that this nature of Good—which is also the nature of God—includes *kindness* <note>original: Benignity</note> within it. He gives this account of God's making of the world, and why he made it in such a way: *Because he was Good, and that which is Good has no envy in it; therefore, he both made the world, and also made it as well and as like to himself as was possible.* <note>Referencing Plato's *Timaeus*</note> And secondly, that it eminently <note>term: Eminently; in theology, this means possessing a quality in its highest, most perfect form</note> encompasses all virtue and justice, the divine nature being the *first pattern* of these things. For this reason, virtue is defined as *an assimilation to the Deity* <note>the process of becoming like God</note>. Justice and honesty are no *artificial* <note>original: Factitious</note> things, made by the will and command of the powerful for the weak, but they are nature and perfection, and they descend down to us from the Deity.

But the Holy Scripture, without any metaphysical pomp and obscurity, tells us plainly what that highest perfection of intellectual beings is—which is *better than reason and knowledge* <note>original: κρεῖττον λόγου καὶ ἐπιστήμης</note>—and which is also the source, life, and soul of all morality: namely, that it is *Love* or *Charity*. *Though I speak with the tongues of men and angels, and have not love, I am but sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal* <note>original: χαλκὸς ἠχῶν, ἢ κύμβαλον ἀλαλάζον</note>, which only makes a noise without any inward life. *And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not love, I am nothing*—that is, I have no inward satisfaction, peace, or true happiness. *And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and give my body to be burned, and have not love, it profits me nothing.* Despite all those things, I am utterly destitute of all true morality, virtue, and grace. And accordingly, it tells us also in the next place what the nature of God is: that he is properly neither *power* nor *knowledge* (though he possesses the perfection of both), but *Love*. And certainly, whatever dark thoughts concerning the Deity some men may sit brooding on in their cells, it can never reasonably be conceived that he, who is *the most self-sufficient and independent of all* <note>original: ἱκανώτατον ἁπάντων καὶ αὐταρκέστατον</note>...
