# The Divine Idea more explicated. BOOK I.

It is unthinkable that the most self-sufficient and self-happy Being would have any narrow and selfish designs outside of Himself, much less harbor any malicious and spiteful intentions toward His creatures. Nevertheless, because so many are prone to abuse the concept of divine love and goodness, forming ideas that destroy the awe and reverential fear we ought to have for the Deity—making people presumptuous and regardless of how they live—we think it proper to add here that God is no soft, indulgent, or biased love. Rather, justice is an essential branch of this divine goodness. As the writer of *On the Universe* <note>original: De Mundo; a treatise once attributed to Aristotle</note> well expresses it, God is "an impartial law" <note>original: νόμος ἰσοκλινὴς</note>; and as Plato says, He is "the measure of all things" <note>original: μέτρον πάντων</note>. In imitation of this, Aristotle also concludes that a good man (in a lower and more imperfect sense) is "a measure" <note>original: μέτρον</note> as well—an impartial measure of things and actions.

It is evident that the atheists themselves in those ancient times of paganism took it for granted that *goodness* was an essential attribute of the Deity whose existence they opposed. (This shows it was generally acknowledged as such by the pagan theists.) We see this from their arguments mentioned earlier—the 12th and 13th—taken from the topic of *evils*, the supposed *flawed design* of things, and the *lack of providence* over human affairs. If those arguments were true, they would not at all disprove an "arbitrary" deity (as some imagine today) made up of nothing but *will* and *power*, without any essential *goodness* and *justice*. However, those arguments of the atheists are leveled directly against the Deity according to its *true concept* or *idea*; if they could be proven, they would indeed destroy it. For it cannot be denied that the natural consequence of the doctrine that there is a God *essentially good* is that the world is *well-made* and *governed*. But we shall declare later that though there is evil in the *parts* of the world, there is none in the *whole*, and that *moral evils* are not to be blamed on the Deity.

And now we have proposed the *three principal attributes* of the Deity. The first is *infinite goodness with fruitfulness* <note>original: fecundity</note>, the second is *infinite knowledge and wisdom*, and the last is *infinite active and perceptive power*. From these *three divine attributes*, the Pythagoreans and Platonists seem to have framed their *Trinity of Primordial Principles* <note>original: Archical Hypostases; the fundamental underlying realities or substances that govern the universe</note>. These they understood as several distinct substances, ranked one below the other, yet they often extended the concept of "the divine" <note>original: τὸ θεῖον</note> far enough to include them all. This *Pythagorean Trinity* seems to be suggested by *Aristotle* in these words: 

<margin>On the Heavens, Book 1, Chapter 1.</margin> 
"As the Pythagoreans also say, the universe and all things are determined and contained by three principles" <note>original: καθάπερ γάρ φασι καὶ οἱ πυθαγόρειοι τὸ πᾶν καὶ τὰ πάντα τοῖς τρισὶ διώρισται</note>. We will say more of this Pythagorean Trinity later. But now we may expand and fill in that *concise idea* <note>original: compendious idea</note> of God we introduced—of *a Being absolutely perfect*—by adding that He is *infinitely good, wise, and powerful, necessarily existing, and not only*

It also connects these three attributes to the ancient Pythagorean and Platonic concepts of a primordial Trinity.</summary>

### CHAPTER IV. The Oneness <note>original: "Onlyness"</note> contained in this Idea.

...not only the *Framer* of the *world*, but also the *Cause* of all things. This *idea* of the *Deity* is sufficient for our current purpose.

Nevertheless, if we wish not only to attend to what is strictly necessary for a dispute with *atheists*, but also to consider the satisfaction of other free and devout minds—those who are hearty and sincere lovers of this most admirable and most glorious Being—we might venture to propose a more full, free, and extensive description of the Deity for their enjoyment. It may be described in this manner: 

*God is a Being who is absolutely perfect, uncreated or self-originated, and existing by necessity. He possesses an infinite fruitfulness <note>original: "fecundity"</note> within Himself and virtually contains all things. He also possesses an infinite kindness <note>original: "benignity"</note> or overflowing love, which He displays and communicates without envy <note>original: "uninvidiously"</note>, together with an impartial uprightness <note>original: "rectitude"</note> or a nature of justice. He fully understands Himself and the extent of His own fruitfulness, and therefore He understands all the possibilities of things, their various natures and relationships, and the best design or system for the whole universe. He also possesses infinite active and perceptive power. He is the fountain of all things, who made all that could be made and was fit to be made, producing them according to His own nature (His essential goodness and wisdom). He therefore created them according to the best pattern and in the best manner possible for the good of the whole, reconciling all the variety and conflict <note>original: "contrariety"</note> of things in the universe into one most admirable and lovely harmony. Finally, He contains and upholds all things, and governs them also in the best manner, doing so without any force or violence; for they are all naturally subject to His authority and readily obey His laws.* 

Now we see that God is such a Being that, if He could be supposed not to exist, there is nothing whose existence a good person could possibly more wish for or desire.

X. From the *idea* of God declared in this way, it evidently appears that there can be but *one* such Being. <term>Oneness</term> <note>original: μόνωσις (monōsis)</note>, unity, *singularity*, or being the only one is essential to this concept. This is because there cannot possibly be more than *one supreme* being, more than *one omnipotent* or *infinitely powerful being*, and more than *one cause* of all things besides itself. 

Even though *Epicurus* tried to distort and corrupt the concept of *God*, he pretended to satisfy that *natural intuition* or *anticipation* <note>original: "prolepsis"</note> in the minds of men by a feigned and counterfeit assertion of a multitude of equal deities who were independent of one Supreme Being. He claimed these gods were also altogether unconcerned with either the design or government of the world. Yet, he himself clearly recognized this *idea* of *God* which we have proposed, which includes *unity* or *oneness* (since he professedly opposed the existence of such a Deity). This is sufficiently clear from his own argument in the words cited earlier:

<margin>Lucretius, *On the Nature of Things*, Book 2, lines 1095–1098. <note>original citation: Lib. 2. p 1, 8. Lamb.</note></margin>
> Who can rule the sum of the infinite? Who can hold the 
> powerful reins of the deep with a controlling hand? 
> Who can rotate all the heavens together, and warm all 
> the fertile earths with celestial fires?
> <note>original: *Quis regere Immensi summam, Quis habere Profundi / Indu manu validas potis est moderanter habenas? / Quis pariter cælos omnes convertere, & omnes / Ignibus ætheriis terras suffire feraces?*</note>

# The Grand Objection against this Idea, Book 1.

->And to be present in all places at all times?<-
<note>original Latin: "Omnibus inq; locis esse omni tempore præsto?" from Lucretius</note>

From this, he would conclude it to be a thing utterly impossible for the Deity to notice <note>original: "Animadvert"</note>, order, and arrange <note>original: "Dispose"</note> all things, and be present everywhere in all the distant places of the world at once. This could not be claimed of a multitude of equal <note>original: "Coordinate"</note> gods who share the government of the world among themselves; therefore, this argument must be leveled against a divine monarchy, or one single, solitary supreme Deity ruling over all. In the same way, when he pursues the same argument further in Cicero to this effect—that even if such a thing were supposed to be possible, it would nonetheless be absolutely inconsistent with the happiness of <margin>*On the Nature of the Gods, Book 1.*</margin> any being—he still proceeds based on the same hypothesis of one sole and single Deity:

> Whether you suppose the world itself to be a god, what can be less peaceful than to whirl around the axis of the heaven with such amazing speed without a moment's pause? Or whether you imagine a god in the world, distinct from it, who governs and arranges all things, maintains the courses of the stars, the changes of the seasons, and the orderly patterns <note>original: "Orderly Vicissitudes"</note> of things, and—watching over lands and seas—preserves the well-being <note>original: "Utilities"</note> and lives of men; certainly He must be involved in much anxious trouble and labor. <note>original: "Sive ipse Mundus Deus est, quid potest esse minus quietum, quam nullo puncto temporis intermisso, versari circum axem Cœli admirabili celeritate? Sive in ipso Mundo Deus inest aliquis qui regat, qui gubernet, qui cursus astrorum, mutationes temporum, hominum commoda vitásque tueatur; næ Ille est implicatus molestis negotiis & operosis."</note>

For as Epicurus here speaks in the singular, the trouble of this divine rule <note>original: "Theocracy"</note> would not be thought so very great for a multitude of equal deities if it were divided among them; rather, it would seem to be but a playful and delightful diversion to each of them. Therefore, it is manifest that such an *idea* of God as we have declared—including *Unity*, *Oneliness*, and *Singularity*—is something that the ancient atheists during the times of Paganism were not unacquainted with, but primarily directed their force against. However, this may seem to be introduced too early here, because it will be discussed more appropriately again later.

XI. For this is what stands as the *grand prejudice* and *objection* against that *idea* of God which we have proposed, which essentially includes <term>singleness <note>original: μόνωσιν</note></term>, *singularity*, or *oneliness* within it—namely, the real existence of such a Deity as the *sole monarch* of the *universe*. The objection is this: because all the nations of the world in the past (except for a small and insignificant handful of *Jews*), along with their wisest men and greatest philosophers, were generally looked upon as *polytheists*—that is, people who acknowledged and worshipped a *multiplicity* of gods. Now, *one God* and *many gods* being directly contradictory to one another, it is therefore concluded from this that this opinion of *monarchy*, or of *one supreme God* who is the *maker* and *governor* of all, has no foundation in nature, nor in the genuine *ideas* and innate concepts <note>original: "Prolepses"</note> of men's minds, but is a mere artificial thing, owing its origin wholly...

### Chapter IV: On Pagan Polytheism.

(Continuing from the previous page)...wholly to *private fancies* and *imaginations* <note>original: "Conceits"</note>, or to *explicit laws* and *institutions* amongst *Jews*, *Christians*, and *Muslims* <note>original: "Mahometans"</note>.

For the resolving <note>original: "assoilling"</note> of this difficulty (which seems so formidable at first sight), it is necessary that we should make a diligent inquiry into the true and genuine sense of this *Pagan polytheism*. Since it is impossible that any man in his right mind <note>original: "in his Wits"</note> should believe in a multiplicity of *gods* according to that *idea of God* previously declared—that is, a *multiplicity* of *supreme*, *omnipotent*, or *infinitely powerful beings*—it is certain that *Pagan polytheism* and the multiplicity of *gods* must be understood according to some other *notion* of the word *gods*, or some *ambiguity* <note>original: "Equivocation"</note> in the use of it. 

It has been already observed that there were sometimes among the Pagans those who, meaning nothing else by *gods* but *intelligent beings superior to men*, did suppose a multitude of such deities. Yet they conceived these to be all (as well as men) *generated* and *mortal*, born successively out of *matter* and decaying <note>original: "Corrupted"</note> again into it, just as the *idols* of *Democritus* <note>Democritus was an ancient Greek philosopher who believed everything was made of atoms; he thought "gods" were temporary beings composed of particularly fine atoms</note> were. But these <term>theogonists</term> (those who describe the origin and birth of the gods), who thus generated all things whatsoever—and therefore the *gods* themselves universally—out of *night* and *chaos*, the *ocean*, or *fluid matter*, are plainly condemned by both *Aristotle* and *Plato* as outright *atheists*. This is because they make *senseless matter* the *only self-existent thing* and the *source* of all things.

Therefore, there may be another *notion* of the word *gods*, taken for *intelligent beings superior to men* that are not only *immortal* but also *self-existent* and *uncreated* <note>original: "Unmade"</note>. Indeed, the supporters of a *multiplicity* of such *gods* as these, though they cannot be accounted *theists* in a strict and proper sense (according to that *idea of God* before declared), are not commonly <note>original: "vulgarly"</note> reputed to be *atheists* either. Instead, they are looked upon as a kind of middle ground between the two and are commonly called *polytheists*. 

The reason for this seems to be that it is generally understood to be essential to *atheism* to make *senseless matter* the sole source of all things, and consequently to suppose all *conscious, intellectual beings* to be *made* or *generated*. Therefore, those who, on the contrary, assert (not *one* but) *many uncreated and self-existent intelligent beings* must be looked upon as those who approach nearer to *theism* than to *atheism*, and so deserve rather to be called *polytheists* than *atheists*.

And there is no question that those who raise the aforementioned objection against that *idea of God* (which includes *singleness* <note>original: "Oneliness"</note> and *uniqueness* in it) based on *Pagan polytheism* or a multiplicity of *gods*, take it for granted that this is to be understood as *many uncreated, self-existent deities*. They assume these are *independent* of one *supreme* God and are multiple *first principles* in the universe and *partial causes* of the world. And certainly, if it could be shown that the Pagan *polytheists* did universally acknowledge such a multiplicity of *uncreated, self-existent deities*, then the argument fetched from that against the *naturalness* <note>original: "Naturality"</note> of that *idea of God* pro-

XII. But first, this opinion of *many self-existent deities* independent of *one supreme* being is both *very irrational in itself* and also plainly *contradicts the observable facts* <note>original: "Repugnant to the Phænomena"</note>. We say first, it is *irrational* in itself because *self-existence* and *necessary existence* are essential to a *perfect being* and to nothing else. It must therefore be very *irrational* and *absurd* to suppose a *multitude* of *imperfect* intelligent beings are *self-existent*, while no *perfect one* exists. Moreover, if imperfect intelligent beings were imagined to exist by themselves from eternity, there could not possibly be any reason given why exactly that many should exist, and neither more nor less—indeed, there would be no reason why any should exist at all. But if it is supposed that these *many* self-existent deities happened only to exist this way from eternity, and their existence was *contingent* rather than *necessary*, the consequence would be that they might just as easily happen to cease to exist, and thus could not be incorruptible. 

Again, if any *single imperfect* being could exist of itself from eternity, then all things might as well do so—not only *matter*, but also the *souls* of men and other *animals*. Consequently, there could be *no creation* by any deity, and those supposed deities would therefore not deserve the name. Lastly, we might also add that there could not be a multitude of self-existent intellectual beings because reason can prove that all imperfect intelligent beings or minds partake of *one perfect mind* and also presuppose *omnipotence* or *infinite power*. However, we will not emphasize this here as it is a concept too difficult for common understanding <note>original: "too remote from Vulgar Apprehension"</note>.

Again, just as this opinion of *many self-existent deities* is *irrational* in itself, it is likewise plainly *contrary to the observable facts* <note>original: "Repugnant to the Phænomena"</note> of the *world*. In the world, as *Macrobius* <note>Macrobius was a 5th-century Roman philosopher and grammarian</note> writes, *all things are interconnected* <note>original Latin: "Omnia sunt connexa"</note>. All things *work together in a single harmony* and are carried on peacefully and quietly, constantly and evenly, without any tumult, uproar, confusion, or disorder—nor the least appearance of *schism* or *faction*. Such order could not be expected if the *world were made* and *governed* by a mob of *self-existent deities* who were equal and independent of a supreme one. Therefore, this kind of *polytheism* was refuted in passing <note>original Latin: "obiter"</note> by *Origen* <note>Origen was an influential early Christian scholar and theologian from Alexandria (c. 185–253 AD)</note>;

<margin>Against Celsus, Book 1, page 18.</margin>
> How much better is it, in agreement with what we see in the harmonious system of the world, to worship only one Maker of the world? The world is one, working in harmony throughout its whole self, and therefore could not have been made by many craftsmen—just as the whole moving heavens are not held together by many souls. <note>original Greek: πόσῳ οὖν βέλτιον τὸ ἐκ τῶν ὁρωμένων πειθόμενον τοῖς κατὰ τὴν εὐταξίαν τοῦ κόσμου σέβειν τὸν δημιουργὸν αὐτοῦ ἑνὸς ὄντος ἕνα, καὶ συμπνέοντος αὐτῷ ὅλῳ ἑαυτῷ, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο μὴ δυναμένου ὑπὸ πολλῶν δημιουργῶν γεγονέναι, ὡς οὐδ᾽ ὑπὸ πολλῶν ψυχῶν συνέχεσθαι ὅλον τὸν οὐρανὸν κινοῦν;</note>

Now, since this opinion is both irrational in itself and contrary to the *observable facts*, it is highly improbable that it was accepted or entertained by the more intelligent Pagans.

### Chapter 4: Because they held a Genealogy of the Gods <note>original: "Theogonia"</note>.

XIII. It is unquestionably clear that the pagans did not universally look upon all their gods as unmade, self-existent beings. This is evident because, ever since the time of Hesiod and Homer at least, the Greek pagans generally acknowledged a *Theogony* <note>original: "Theogonia"</note>—that is, a *genealogy and temporary production of the gods*. Yet this is not to be understood as applying to every single deity, for no one is truly a theist who does not acknowledge at least one self-existent Deity. Concerning <margin>Herodotus, *Euterpe*, page 53.</margin> this genealogy of the gods, Herodotus writes in this manner: "For where each of the gods came from, or whether they had all always existed, and what their forms were like, was not known until very recently—yesterday, so to speak. For I believe Hesiod and Homer lived no more than four hundred years before my time. It was they who created a genealogy of the gods for the Greeks, gave the gods their titles, decided their honors and functions, and described their forms." <note>original: "ὅθεν γὰρ ἐγένοντο ἕκαστος τῶν θεῶν... καὶ τοῖσι θεοῖσι τὰς ἐπωνυμίας δόντες"</note> 

From where each of the gods was born, or whether they all had existed forever, and what their forms were, was something not known until very lately; for Hesiod and Homer were (as I suppose) not more than four hundred years older than I am. And these were the ones who introduced the *Theogony* <note>The birth or genealogy of the gods</note> among the Greeks and gave the gods their various names—that is, they settled pagan theology. 

Now, if before Hesiod and Homer’s time it was not known or determined among the Greeks whether their gods were *born* or if they all *existed from eternity*, then it was not universally concluded by them that all gods were unmade and self-existent. And though perhaps some in those ancient times might have believed one way and some another concerning the birth or eternity of their gods, it does not follow that those who thought them all to be *eternal* must therefore have supposed them to be *unmade or self-existent*. For Aristotle—who argued for the eternity of the world and, consequently, for the eternity of his gods, the heavenly bodies—did not, for all that, suppose them to be self-existent or "First Principles." Instead, he believed they all depended upon *one Principle or Original Deity*. 

Indeed, the true meaning of that question in Herodotus—whether the gods were born or all existed from eternity—is (as we suppose) really no different than the question posed by Plato: "Whether the world was created or is uncreated" <note>original: "εἰ γέγονεν ὁ κόσμος ἢ ἀγενής ἐστι"</note>; that is, whether it had a beginning in time or existed as it is from eternity. This will be more fully explained later. But ever since Hesiod and Homer’s time, when the *Theogony* or genealogy of the gods was settled and generally believed among the Greeks, it is certain that they could not possibly have thought all their gods were eternal, and therefore much less could they have thought them unmade and self-existent.

But although we have clearly proved that the pagans did not universally regard all their gods as unmade, self-existent deities (since they acknowledged a birth of the gods), one might still suspect that they supposed a *multitude* of them (and not just one) to be unmade and self-existent from eternity. Therefore, we add next that no such thing appears to be true; the pagans (or anyone else) never publicly or professionally asserted a multitude of unmade, self-existent deities. First, this is plain regarding the Hesiodic gods, who were all the gods of the Greek
<meta>The text continues on the next page regarding the Hesiodic gods.</meta>

# The Hesiodian Gods Book I.

Pagans believed that there was either only one of them who was *self-existent*, or else *none* at all. This is because *Hesiod’s* gods were either all derived from *Chaos* (or the *floating water*), with *Love* itself being generated out of it as well (according to the tradition of *Aristophanes* mentioned earlier); or else *Love* was supposed to be a principle distinct from *Chaos*—namely, the *active principle* of the universe—from which, along with *Chaos*, the whole *Theogony* <note>original: "Theogonia"; the genealogy or birth of the gods</note> and *Cosmogony* <note>original: "Cosmogonia"; the origin or birth of the universe</note> were derived. 

Now, if the first of these were true—that Hesiod supposed all his gods to have sprung originally from *Chaos* or the *Ocean*—then it is plain that, despite the crowd of gods he gathered, he could be nothing other than one of those *atheistic theogonists* <note>Those who believe the gods themselves were created from material elements like water or air</note> mentioned before. In reality, he would have acknowledged no God at all in the true sense, since someone who does not accept a *self-existent Deity* is not a true *theist*. 

But if the second view is true—that Hesiod believed *Love* was a principle distinct from *Chaos*, namely the *active principle* of the universe, and derived all his other gods from it—then he was a proper *pagan theist*. Such a person acknowledges *many gods* but recognizes only *one* of them as *unmade* and *self-existent*, with all the rest being generated or created by that One. 

Indeed, it appears from the passages of *Aristotle* cited earlier that the philosopher was sometimes 
<margin>Page 116. 112.</margin> 
divided in his judgment concerning *Hesiod*, specifically where he should <unclear>rank</unclear> him: whether among the *atheists* or the *theists*. For in his book *On the Heavens* <note>original: "de Cælo"</note>, he ranks Hesiod among those who believed everything was *generated and corrupted* except for the *bare substance of matter*; that is, he places him among the *absolute atheists* and looks upon him as their leader. 

However, in his *Metaphysics*, upon further thought, Aristotle suspects that many of those who made *Love* the greatest of the gods were actually *theists*. They supposed *Love* to be a *first principle* in the universe, or the *active cause* of things, and he suggests that not only *Parmenides* but also *Hesiod* was such a person. This latter opinion is far more probable and was therefore embraced by *Plutarch*, who determines in his writings that *Hesiod* asserted one "unmade Deity" <note>original: "Θεὸν ἀγέννητον"</note>. 

This is also supported by the ancient Scholiast <gloss>writing</gloss> upon him, who wrote that Hesiod’s Love was "the heavenly Love, who is also God; for the other Love born of Aphrodite <note>original: "Venus"</note> is younger" <note>original: "ὁ οὐράνιος ἔρως, ὃς καὶ Θεός· ὁ γὰρ ἐξ Ἀφροδίτης νεώτερός ἐστιν"</note>. Similarly, *Joannes Diaconus* says: "By Love here we must not understand the son of Aphrodite—for how could he be produced before his mother was born?—but another, more ancient Love, which I take to be the active cause or principle of motion naturally implanted in every existing thing" <note>original: "ἔρωτα καὶ ἐνταῦθα νοητέον, οὐ τὸν τῆς Ἀφροδίτης παῖδα... αἰτίαν ἑκάστῳ τῶν ὄντων"</note>. While Diaconus does not seem to think this Love is God himself, he conceives of it as an active principle in the universe derived from God, rather than from matter. This opinion will be further confirmed later.

The next significant appearance of a multitude of *self-existent* deities seems to be the *thirty gods* and *aeons* <note>In Gnostic thought, these are various emanations or levels of divine power</note> of the Valentinians, which some have mistaken for independent gods. However, it is certain that all of these except for one were *generated*; they being derived by that fan-

# Chapter IV: The Ditheistic Doctrine

...fantastic inventor of these systems, from one self-originated Deity called *Bythus* <note>original: "Bythus"; from the Greek word for "Depth" or "Abyss"</note>. For thus *Epiphanius* <note>A 4th-century bishop and counter-heresy writer</note> informs us, <margin>Heresies 31</margin> "For he also intends to introduce thirty gods, Aeons, and Heavens, the first of which is *Bythus*" <note>original: *τριάκοντα γὰρ καὶ οὗτος θεοὺς καὶ Αἰῶνας καὶ Οὐρανοὺς βούλεται παραεισάγειν, ὧν ὁ πρῶτος ἐστι βυθός*</note>. By this, he meant an unfathomable depth and profundity; and therefore this *Bythus* was also called by him "the highest and ineffable <note>too great or extreme to be expressed in words</note> Father" <note>original: *ὁ ἀνωτάτω καὶ ἀκατονόμαστος πατήρ*</note>.

We do indeed acknowledge that there have been some who have really asserted a *duality of gods* in the sense declared; that is, of <term>animalish</term> <note>original: "Animalish"; here meaning "perceptive" or "possessing a soul" (from the Latin 'anima')</note> or perceptive beings who are self-existent—one as the principle of good, and the other of evil. This *Ditheism* <note>the belief in two equal and competing gods</note> of theirs seems to be the nearest approach that was ever really made to polytheism. This is true unless we should here listen to *Plutarch*, who seems to claim that the ancient *Persians* (besides their two gods, the good *Oromasdes* and the evil *Arimanius*) also asserted a third middle deity called *Mithras*. Or, we could look to some ecclesiastical writers who attribute a trinity of gods to *Marcion* (though *Tertullian* is even more generous and increases that number to nine). For those who were commonly called *Tritheists* <note>believers in three gods</note> were merely mistaken Christians and Trinitarians, and so they do not fall under this consideration. 

Now, as for that previously mentioned *Ditheism*, or the opinion of *two gods* (one good and one evil), it is evident that its origin sprang from nothing else but, first, a firm persuasion of the essential goodness of the Deity, combined with the idea that the evil in the world was altogether inconsistent and irreconcilable with that goodness. Therefore, to reconcile this phenomenon, they felt it was absolutely necessary to suppose another self-existent <term>animalish</term> principle, or an evil god. Consequently, while these Ditheists held a "monarchy" (one sole principle and origin) regarding everything good in the world, it is plain that if it were not for this issue of evil—which they conceived could not be explained any other way—they would never have asserted more than one principle or God.

The most prominent and famous supporters of this Ditheistic doctrine—of two self-existent, sentient principles in the universe, a good God and an evil demon—were the *Marcionites* and the *Manicheans*. Although both groups made some slight pretenses toward Christianity, they were not recognized as Christians by the Church. But it is certain that besides these, and even before them, some of the self-proclaimed pagans also entertained the same opinion. The famous moralist *Plutarch of Chaeronea* was an undoubted patron of this view, which he represents in his book *On Isis and Osiris* <note>original: *De Iside & Osiride*</note> with a slight variation, in this manner: <margin>Page 371. Paris edition.</margin> "The generation and constitution of this world is a mixture of contrary powers or principles (one good, the other evil), yet they are not of equal force; rather, the better of them has the upper hand. Nevertheless, it is absolutely impossible for the wicked part to be totally destroyed, for much of it is ingrained in the body and much in the soul of the universe, always struggling against the better part" <note>original: *μεμιγμένη γὰρ ἡ τοῦδε τοῦ κόσμου γένεσις καὶ σύστασις ἐξ ἐναντίων, οὐ μὴν ἰσοσθενῶν δυνάμεων, ἀλλὰ τοῦ βελτίονος τὸ κράτος ἐστίν· ἀπολέσθαι δὲ τὴν φαύλην παντάπασιν ἀδύνατον, πολλὴν μὲν ἐμπεφυκυῖαν τῷ σώματι, πολλὴν δὲ τῇ ψυχῇ τοῦ παντὸς, ἀεὶ πρὸς τὴν βελτίονα δυσμαχοῦσαν*</note>.

# Plutarch as a Ditheist or Assertor [of two principles]: Book I

Notwithstanding this, it is also absolutely impossible for the *Worse Power* or *Principle* to ever be *utterly destroyed*. Much of it is always *intermingled in the Soul* and much in the *Body of the Universe*, perpetually struggling against the *Better Principle*.

Indeed, learned men of later times have mostly looked upon *Plutarch* here as either a mere *reporter* of the opinions of other *philosophers*, or as a *follower* rather than a *leader* in this thought. Despite this, it is evident that *Plutarch* himself was heartily *committed* to this opinion. He shows no small fondness for it in several of his other writings. For example, in his *Platonic Questions*, he declares himself as follows: <margin>Page 1003, Paris edition</margin> "Or else that which is often affirmed by us is true: that a mad, irrational soul and an unformed, disorderly body coexisted with one another from eternity, neither of them having any beginning or birth." <note>original Greek: ἢ τὸ πολλάκις ὑφ' ἡμῶν λεγόμενον ἀληθές ἐστιν, ἡ μὲν γὰρ ἄνους ψυχή, καὶ τὸ ἄμορφον σῶμα, συνυπῆρχον ἀλλήλοις ἀεί, καὶ τὸ οὐδέτερον αὐτῶν γένεσιν ἔχεν οὐδὲ ἀρχήν</note>

In his *Timaean Psychogonia* <note>original: *Psychogonia*; a treatise on the "generation of the soul" described in Plato's *Timaeus*</note>, he industriously maintains the same view at length. There and elsewhere, he endeavors to establish this doctrine as much as possible upon *rational foundations*. 

**First**, he argues that *nothing can be made or produced without a cause*. Therefore, there must necessarily be some *cause of evil* as well, and a *positive* one too. He describes the opinion of those who would make the nature of evil merely an *incidental addition* <note>original Greek: *ἐπεισόδιον* (epeisodion); an "episode" or non-essential part of a plot</note> to the world as ridiculous. He rejects the idea that all the evil in the world came in only "by the way" or as a byproduct, without any *positive cause*. 

**Secondly**, he argues that since God is *essentially good*, he could not possibly be the *cause of evil*. He highly applauds *Plato* for removing God to the greatest possible distance from being the cause of evil. 

**Thirdly**, he argues that just as God could not be the cause, neither could *matter in itself devoid of all form and quality* <note>original Greek: *ὕλη ἄποιος* (hyle apoios)</note> be the cause of evil. He notes that this was the excuse of the Stoics. Because of this, he often condemns them—though inconsistently—sometimes as those who assigned no cause at all for evil, and other times as those who made *God the cause* of it. In his *Psychogonia*, he concludes that unless we acknowledge a *substantial evil principle*: "The Stoical difficulties will necessarily overtake and involve us, as we would be introducing evil into the world from nothing—without cause or origin. For since neither that which is essentially good (such as God) nor that which is devoid of all quality (such as matter) could possibly give being or birth to it." <note>original Greek: αἱ Στοικαὶ καταλαμβάνουσιν ἡμᾶς ἀπορίαι, τὸ κακὸν ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος ἀναιτίως καὶ ἀγεννήτως ἐπεισάγοντες, ἐπεὶ γάρ γε ὄντων οὔτε τὸ ἀγαθόν, οὔτε τὸ ἄποιον, εἰκὸς ἦν οὐσίαν κακοῦ καὶ γένεσιν παρασχεῖν</note> 

But in his book against the Stoics, he accuses them of being those who *made God, who is essentially good, the cause of evil*: "They themselves make God, who is good, the principle and cause of evil. This is because matter does not provide evil from itself; for it is devoid of quality and receives all the differences it possesses from the one who forms and shapes it. Therefore, evil must either exist for no reason—from nothing—or, if it exists because of a moving principle, it must have come from God." <note>original Greek: αὐτοὶ τὴν κακῶν ἀρχήν, ἀγαθὸν ὄντα τὸν θεὸν ποιοῦσι, οὐ γὰρ ἡ ὕλη τὸ κακὸν ἐξ αὑτῆς παρέσχηκεν, ἄποιος γάρ ἐστι καὶ πάσας ὅσας δέχεται διαφοράς, ὑπὸ τοῦ ποιοῦντος αὐτὴν καὶ σχηματίζοντος ἔσχηκεν. ὥστε ἀνάγκη τὸ κακὸν εἰ μὲν δι᾿ οὐδέν, ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος, εἰ δὲ διὰ τὴν κινοῦσαν ἀρχὴν ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ γεγονὸς ὑπάρχειν</note> They themselves make God, being good, the principle and cause of evil, since matter (which is devoid of quality) receives all its differences from

<summary>Plutarch argues that evil cannot originate from a good God or from neutral matter, but must stem from a self-existent "Evil Principle" or irrational soul. He criticizes the Stoics for failing to explain the origin of evil without blaming God or admitting to an effect without a cause.</summary>

# CHAPTER IV. Of an Evil Principle.

Since matter is passive and lacks the power to act on its own, it could not possibly be the cause of evil. Therefore, evil must necessarily either come from nothing, or it must come from the Active and Moving Principle, which is God. Based on all these premises joined together, Plutarch concludes that the phenomenon of evil could not possibly be explained <note>original: "salved"</note> in any other way than by supposing a **Substantial Principle** for it: a certain **Irrational and Maleficent Soul or Spirit** <note>original: "Dæmon"</note>, which was uncreated and co-existed with God and Matter from eternity. 

Accordingly, he decides that just as whatever is good in the soul and body of the universe—and likewise in the souls of men and spirits—is to be credited to God as its only source, so whatever is evil, irregular, and disorderly in them ought to be blamed on this other Substantial Principle. He calls this an **irrational and evil-doing soul** <note>original Greek: ψυχὴ ἄνους καὶ κακοποιὸς (*psychē anous kai kakopoios*)</note>, which, by inserting itself everywhere throughout the world, is mixed in with the Better Principle. He argues that the soul is not entirely the work of God <note>original Greek: ἡ μὴ πᾶν εἶναι ἔργον τοῦ Θεοῦ τὴν ψυχὴν (*hē mē pan einai ergon tou Theou tēn psychēn*)</note>. Therefore, neither the soul of the universe, nor the souls of men and spirits, were wholly the workmanship of God; rather, their lower, brutish, and disorderly parts were the effect of the Evil Principle.

But besides all this, it is evident that Plutarch was also strongly convinced of the idea that nothing substantial could be created (not even by divine power) out of nothing pre-existing. He believed that all the substance of everything in the world existed from eternity, unmade, so that God was only the "Orderer," the "Methodizer," or the "Harmonizer" of it. 

Just as he concluded that the physical world was not created by God out of nothing—as far as its substance is concerned—but was instead pre-existing matter that moved disorderly until it was brought into a regular order and harmony by Him; in the same way, he decided that the **Soul of the World** (a concept he always assumes) was not made by God out of nothing either. It was not made out of anything pre-existing that was inanimate or soulless, but was instead brought into an orderly and regular frame out of a pre-existing, disorderly soul.

<margin>*On the Generation of the Soul*, page 1014, Paris edition.</margin>

> For there was disorder <note>original Greek: ἀκοσμία (*akosmia*)</note> in the state of things before the creation of the world. This disorder was not incorporeal, nor motionless, nor soulless; rather, it had a bodily part that was formless and unstable, and a moving part that was frantic and irrational. This was the disharmony of a soul that did not possess reason. For God made neither body out of that which was not body, nor soul out of that which was not soul.

But just as a musician, who creates neither the voice nor the motion, nevertheless produces harmony by organizing them; so God—though he created neither the tangible and resisting substance of the body, nor the imaginative <note>original: "Phantastick"</note> and self-moving power of the soul—took both of those pre-existing principles. One of these was dark and obscure (matter), and the other was turbulent and irrational (the evil soul). By disposing and harmonizing them in an orderly way, he produced this most beautiful and perfect **Animal of the World** <note>Plutarch, following Plato, viewed the universe as a living, breathing entity</note>. 

And further to the same purpose, God is the father and creator <note>original Greek: πατὴρ καὶ δημιουργός (*patēr kai dēmiourgos*)</note> "not of the body simply, nor of the bulk and matter, but of the symmetry, beauty, and resemblance regarding the body."

<summary>Plutarch argues that evil stems from an eternal, irrational soul and asserts that God did not create the world's substance from nothing, but rather acted as a "Harmonizer" who organized pre-existing chaos.</summary>

# Plutarch's Grounds for an Evil God, Book 1.

<note>original Greek: γός· ταῦτα δεῖ διανοεῖσθαι καὶ περὶ ψυχῆς... ("...these things must be thought also concerning the soul, that it was neither made by God nor was it the soul of the world, but a certain power of imagination and opinion, irrational and disorderly, self-moving and ever-moving...")</note> 

**God was not the cause or maker of "body" in a simple sense—that is, he created neither its physical bulk nor its matter—but only the symmetry and beauty within the body, and the likeness it has to himself. The same conclusion must be reached concerning the Soul of the World: its substance was not made by God either. It was not always the "Soul of the World," but was originally a certain self-moving substance endowed with a power of imagination that was irrational and disorderly. This substance existed by itself from eternity. By harmonizing it and introducing appropriate numbers and proportions, God made it into the soul and ruler of this created world.** 

According to this doctrine of Plutarch's, although the "Soul of the World" had a beginning in time, it was never created out of nothing. Instead, that which already existed in a state of disorder was acted upon by the Deity and brought into a regular structure. Therefore, he concludes:

<note>original Greek: ἡ ψυχὴ νοῦ μετασχοῦσα καὶ λογισμοῦ καὶ ἁρμονίας, οὐκ ἔργον ἐστὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ μέρος, οὐδ' ὑπ' αὐτοῦ, ἀλλ' ἀπ' αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἐξ αὐτοῦ γέγονεν· ("The soul, having participated in mind and reason and harmony, is not only the work of God but also a part of him; it was not made by him, but from him and out of him.")</note> 

**A soul that shares in mind, reason, and harmony is not only the work of God but also a part of him; it was not so much made *by* him as it originated *from* him and exists *out of* him.** 

He must likewise affirm the same concerning all other souls, such as those of men and spirits <note>original: "Demons"</note>. He suggests that they are either the substance of God himself combined with that of the Evil Spirit <note>original: "Demon"</note>, or else certain delibations <term>delibations: small tastes or portions taken from a larger whole</term> from both—if anyone could even understand such a thing—blended and confused together. He does not allow that any new substance at all was created by God out of nothing pre-existing. 

It was observed at the beginning of this chapter that Plutarch asserted there were two self-existent <note>original Greek: <term>αὐθυπόστατα</term> (*authupostata*)</note> principles in the universe: **God and Matter**. However, we now understand that he was an earnest advocate <note>original: "Propugnor"</note> for a third principle besides those two, which he calls a **mad, irrational, and harmful soul or spirit** <note>original Greek: <term>ψυχὴ ἄνους καὶ κακοποιός</term> (*psychē anous kai kakopoios*)</note>. Thus, Plutarch was both a **Triarchist** <term>Triarchist: a believer in three fundamental principles</term> and a **Ditheist** <term>Ditheist: a believer in two gods or opposing divine powers</term>. He asserted three principles but only two "gods," according to the previously mentioned definition of a "god" as a self-existent being that possesses life or perception.

We are well aware that Plutarch tries his hardest to persuade us that this was the constant belief of all pagan nations and of all the wisest men and philosophers who ever lived among them. 

"For this," he says in his book *On Isis and Osiris* <note>original: *De Iside & Osiride*</note>, "is a most ancient opinion that has been passed down from theologians and lawmakers to poets and philosophers. Although its first author is unknown, it has been so firmly believed everywhere that its traces have been imprinted upon the sacrifices and mysteries—or religious rites—of both non-Greeks <note>original: "Barbarians"</note> and Greeks. Namely: that the world is neither entirely ungoverned by any mind or reason, as if everything floated in the currents of chance and fortune, nor is there any single principle steering and guiding everything without resistance or control. This is because there is a confused mixture of good and evil in everything, and nothing produced by nature is pure. Therefore..."

<summary>Plutarch argues that the Soul of the World was not created from nothing but was an eternal, disorderly force that God organized into a rational soul. He asserts that this "Ditheistic" view of two opposing powers (Good and Evil) was the universal belief of ancient civilizations and philosophers.</summary>
<keywords>Plutarch, On Isis and Osiris, Ditheism, Triarchism, Soul of the World, Evil Principle, dualism, cosmogony, self-existent principles</keywords>

# CHAPTER IV. The Unmade Soul.

It is not only one *dispenser* of things who, as if out of several *vessels*, distributes those different *liquors* of *good* and *evil*, mixing them together and splashing them as he pleases. Instead, there are two *distinct* and *contrary powers* or *principles* in the *world*: *one* of them always leading, as it were, to the *right hand*, but the other pulling in a *contrary* direction. Consequently, our whole life and the entire *world* is a certain *mixture* and *confusion* of these *two*—at least this *terrestrial world* below the *moon* is so, being everywhere full of *irregularity* and *disorder*. For if nothing can be *made* without a *cause*, and that which is *good* cannot be the *cause* of *evil*, there must necessarily be a *distinct principle* in *nature* for the *production* of *evil* as well as *good*. 

And this has been the *opinion* of the *most* and *wisest men*. Some of them affirm "that there are two gods, like rival craftsmen" <note>original Greek: θεὸς εἶναι δυό καθάπερ ἀντιτέχνες</note>—one of whom is the *maker* of all *good*, and the other of all *evil*. Others, however, call the *good principle* alone a *God*, and the *evil principle* a *demon* <note>original: dæmon</note>, as did *Zoroaster* the Magician. Besides *Zoroaster* and the *Persian Magi*, *Plutarch* claims that the *traces* of this *opinion* were also to be found in the *astrology* of the *Chaldeans* and in the *mysteries* and *religious rites* of not only the *Egyptians* but also the *Greeks* themselves. Lastly, he particularly attributes this same view to all the most famous *Greek philosophers*, such as *Pythagoras*, *Empedocles*, *Heraclitus*, *Anaxagoras*, *Plato*, and *Aristotle*—though his greatest effort of all is to prove that *Plato* was an *undoubted champion* for it:

<margin>On the Procreation of the Soul, page 1015, Edition</margin>
<note>The following is a translation of the Greek text below: "But Plato did not suffer the same error as later philosophers. He did not overlook, as they did, the third principle and power situated between matter and God. He did not endure that most absurd argument which introduces—I know not how—the nature of evils as a mere incidental byproduct. For while they do not grant Epicurus even the smallest swerve of an atom, arguing that he introduces a causeless motion out of nothing, they themselves claim that all the vice and misery in the world, along with countless other bodily absurdities and difficulties, have no cause in the first principles but occurred as a consequence. But Plato did not do this; he stripped matter of all qualities to ensure it could not be the cause of evil, and placed God at the furthest distance from being the cause of it."</note>

ἀλλὰ ταυτὸ Πλάτων οὐκ ἔπαθε τοῖς ὕστερον, οὐδὲ παριδὼν, ὡς ἐκεῖνοι, τὴν μεταξὺ τῆς ὕλης καὶ τοῦ θεοῦ τρίτην ἀρχὴν καὶ δύναμιν, ὑπέμεινε τὸν λόγον τὸν ἀτοπώτατον ἐπεισόδιον οὐκ οἶδα ὅπως ποιοῦντα, τὴν κακῶν φύσιν ἀπ' αὐτομάτου καὶ συμβεβηκός. Ἐπικούρῳ μὲν γὰρ οὐδὲ ἀκαρὲς ἐκλῖναι τὴν ἄτομον συγχωροῦσιν, ὡς ἀναίτιον ἐπεισάγοντι κίνησιν ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος, αὐτοὶ δὲ κακίαν καὶ κακοδαιμονίαν τοσαύτην, ἑτέρας τε περὶ σῶμα μυρίας ἀτοπίας καὶ δυσχερείας, αἰτίαν ἐν ταῖς ἀρχαῖς οὐκ ἐχούσας, κατ' ἐπακολούθησιν γεγονέναι λέγουσιν· ὁ δὲ Πλάτων οὐχ οὕτως· ἀλλὰ τὴν ὕλην διαφορᾶς ἁπάσης ἀπαλλάξων, καὶ τοῦ θεοῦ τὴν τῶν κακῶν αἰτίαν ἀπωτάτω τιθέμενος. 

But *Plato* was not guilty of that *error* of *later philosophers* in overlooking the *third power* which is between *matter* and *God*, and thereby falling into the *grossest of all absurdities*: *that the nature of evils* was but an *accidental addition* to the *world* and came into it merely by chance, nobody knows how. So those very philosophers who will by no means allow to *Epicurus* the *smallest swerve* <note>original: declension</note> of his *atoms* from the vertical—alleging that this would be to introduce a *motion without a cause* and to bring *something out of nothing*—do nonetheless suppose all that *vice* and *misery* which is in the *world* (along with innumerable other *absurdities* and *inconveniences* regarding the *body*) to have come into it merely by *accidental consequence*, without having any *cause* in the *first principles*. But *Plato* did not do so; instead, by stripping *matter* of all *qualities* and *differences* (by which means it could not possibly be made the *cause of evils*) and then placing *God* at the greatest distance from being the *cause* of them, he consequently resolved the issue into a *third unmade principle* between *God* and the *matter*: an *irrational soul* or *demon* moving the *matter* in a disorderly way.

Now, because *Plutarch's authority* passes so unchallenged, and his—

# Plato no Assertor, Book I.

His testimony on this particular point seems recently to have been generally received as an oracle. Consequently, it is taken for an unquestionable truth that the *ditheistic doctrine* <note>original: "Ditheistick Doctrine"; the belief that there are two rival gods or principles, one good and one evil.</note> of a *good* and *evil principle* was the *catholic* <note>meaning: universal or general</note> or *universal doctrine* of the *pagan theists*. Specifically, it is believed that *Plato*, above all others, was a professed champion for this view. We shall, therefore, take the liberty to examine *Plutarch’s* grounds for this confident assertion of his, particularly concerning *Plato*. His reasons for attributing this opinion to *Plato* are only the three that follow. 

First, because that philosopher, in his *Politicus* <note>also known as *The Statesman*</note>, speaks of a *necessary* and *innate appetite that may sometimes turn the heavens in a contrary direction*, thereby causing disorder and confusion. 

Secondly, because in the *tenth book of his Laws* (*De Legibus*), he speaks of *two kinds of souls*, of which *one is beneficent, but the other is the contrary*. 

Lastly, because in his *Timaeus*, he assumes that matter was *moved disorderly* before the world was made, which implies there was a disorderly and irrational soul existing with it as its mover, since matter is unable to move itself. 

But as to the first of these allegations from *Plato's Politicus*, we shall only observe that the philosopher—as if he had intended to prevent such an interpretation of his meaning as Plutarch’s—inserts these very words: "Neither must any such thing be supposed, as if there were two gods, contrarily minded to one another, turning the heavens sometimes one way and sometimes another." <note>original Greek: μήτ' αὖ δύο τινὲ θεὼ, φρονῶντε ἑαυτοῖς ἐναντία, στρέφειν αὐτὸν</note> 

This plain declaration of *Plato's sense*, being directly contrary to *Plutarch’s* interpretation and this *ditheistic opinion*, might also serve as a sufficient refutation of his second ground from the *tenth book of the Laws*. Plutarch argues as if *Plato* had affirmed there were *two souls* moving the heavens, the *one beneficent, but the other contrary*; however, this would be the same as asserting there are two gods, contrarily minded toward one another. 

Notwithstanding this, for a fuller answer, we shall further add that the philosopher did there, first, only categorize souls in general into "good" and "evil." These *moral differences* properly belong to that rank of beings he called *souls*, and first emerge in them according to this established doctrine: "Soul is the cause of good and beauty, and of evil and ugliness, of justice and injustice." <note>original Greek: τῶν ἀγαθῶν αἰτία ἡ ψυχὴ καὶ τῶν καλῶν, καὶ κακῶν καὶ αἰσχρῶν, δικαίων τε καὶ ἀδίκων</note> 

But then afterward, when making an inquiry concerning the soul of the world or heaven—what kind of soul that was—he positively concludes that it was no other than a soul endowed with all virtue. 

<margin>Page 898. Stephanus <note>A standard reference to the 1578 edition of Plato's works used for pagination.</note></margin>
**Athenian Guest:** "Since it is the soul that moves all things, we must of necessity affirm that the rotation of the heaven or world is moved by some soul or other, caring for it and ordering it—whether it be the best soul or the contrary." 

**Clinias:** "O Guest, it is certainly not holy nor pious to conclude otherwise than that one or more souls, endowed with all virtue, move the world." <note>original Greek: ΑΘ. ἐπειδὴ ψυχὴ μὲν ἔστιν ἡ περιάγουσα ἡμῖν πάντα, τὴν δὲ οὐρανοῦ περιφορὰν ἐξ ἀνάγκης περιάγειν φατέον, ἐπιμελουμένην καὶ κοσμοῦσαν, ἤτοι τὴν ἀρίστην ψυχὴν ἤτοι τὴν ἐναντίαν. κλ. Ω ξένε, ἀλλὰ ἔκ γε τῶν εἰρημένων οὐδ' ὅσιον ἄλλως λέγειν, ἢ πᾶσαν ἀρετὴν ἔχουσαν ψυχὴν μίαν ἢ πλείους περιάγειν αὐτά.</note> 

And as for the last thing urged by *Plutarch*, that before the world was made...

# CHAP. IV. Of a Substantial Evil Principle.

When Plato says that matter was *moved disorderly*, we believe that he was only following a commonly accepted tradition—originally coming from Moses—that the first beginning of the *creation of the world* <note>original: "Cosmopœia"</note> was from a *chaos*, or matter moved in a confused way, which was afterward brought into order. It now seems clearly evident that there is no weight at all in any of Plutarch’s earlier arguments. Nor is there any such monster to be found anywhere in Plato as this *Substantial Evil Principle* or *God*—a *wicked soul* or *demon*, *uncreated* and *self-existent from eternity*, opposite and hostile <note>original: "Inimicous"</note> to the *Good God*, and sharing the empire and dominion of the world with Him. This opinion is really nothing other than turning the *Devil* (the prince of evil spirits) into a god, making him a rival to *God*, and giving him a right to receive divine honor and worship.

<margin>Psychogonia <note>Plutarch's treatise "On the Procreation of the Soul"</note>, p. 1014. P. 1014. P. 116.</margin>
It is also noteworthy that Plutarch himself confesses that this interpretation of Plato is *new* and *paradoxical*, or an invention of his own: "and because it is contrary to most Platonists, it requires some justification" <note>original: "καὶ διὰ τὸ πλείστοις τῶν ἀπὸ Πλάτωνος ὑπεναντιοῦσθαι, δεόμενον παραμυθίας"</note>. He admitted it was contrary to the generally received opinion of Platonists and thought it needed some apology and defense. To that end, he adds again: "First, then, I will set forth my own opinion concerning these matters, trusting in what is probable, and supporting as much as possible the truth and the paradoxical nature of the argument" <note>original: "πρῶτον οὖν ἣν ἔχω περὶ τούτων διάνοιαν, ἐκθήσομαι πιστευόμενος τῷ εἰκότι, καὶ παραμυθούμενος ὡς ἔνεστι, τὸ ἀληθὲς τοῦ λόγου, καὶ παράδοξον"</note>. Furthermore, in his commentary on the *Timaeus*, Proclus mentions no other philosophers who ever attributed this doctrine to Plato—or indeed maintained any such opinion of two substantial principles of *Good* and *Evil*—except for Plutarch and Atticus (though I admit Chalcidius cites Numenius to the same effect). Proclus’s words are as follows: "The followers of Plutarch of Chaeronea and Atticus claim that unformed matter existed before the creation, and that the evil-doing soul which moved it also existed; for from where, they ask, could that motion come, if not from a soul? And if the motion was disorderly, it must then come from a disorderly soul" <note>original: "οἱ μὲν περὶ Πλούταρχον τὸν Χαιρωνέα καὶ Ἀττικόν, προεῖναί φασι τὴν ἀκόσμητον ὕλην πρὸ τῆς γενέσεως, προεῖναί δὲ καὶ τὴν κακεργάτιν ψυχὴν τὴν τοῦτο κινοῦσαν, πόθεν γὰρ ἡ κίνησις ἦν, ἢ ἀπὸ ψυχῆς; εἰ δὲ ἄτακτος ἡ κίνησις, ἀπὸ ἀτάκτου ψυχῆς"</note>.

As Proclus tells us, this opinion of theirs had been previously refuted by Porphyry and Iamblichus as something both irrational and impious. He also briefly rejects it himself with these two propositions: First, that "every soul is the offspring of God" <note>original: "πᾶσα ψυχὴ γέννημά ἐστι τοῦ Θεοῦ"</note>, and there can be no soul or anything else besides God that is self-existing. Secondly, "to make evil eternal just like good is absurd, for that which is godless cannot be held in the same honor as the divine, nor can it be equally uncreated, or even entirely set in opposition to it" <note>original: "τὸ κακὸν διαιώνιον ποιεῖν ὥσπερ καὶ τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἄτοπον, οὐ γὰρ ὁμότιμον τῷ θείῳ τὸ ἄθεον, οὔτε ἐπίσης ἀγέννητον, οὔτε ὅλως ἀντιδιῃρημένον"</note>.

# BOOK 1: The True Account of the Platonic View

But because it might likely be asked here: What explanation was it then possible for Plato to give regarding the origin of evils so as not to blame God himself, if he did not derive them from *unqualified matter* <note>original: "ὕλη ἄποιος" (hyle apoios) — matter without specific properties or qualities</note> (which Plutarch has plainly proved to be absurd), nor from an *irrational and harmful soul of the world* or *demon* that was *self-existent from eternity*? To this we shall briefly reply: Although that philosopher did not derive the origin of evils from *unqualified matter* or from an *uncreated wicked soul*, he did not therefore blame God for them either. Instead, it seems he attributed them to the *necessity of imperfect beings*. 

For just as Timaeus Locrus <note>A Pythagorean philosopher whose work was traditionally thought to have influenced Plato's *Timaeus*</note> had determined before Plato that the world was made by God and *Necessity*, so does Plato himself accordingly declare in his *Timaeus*: "The birth of this world is mixed, being composed of a certain combination of Mind and Necessity together, yet in such a way that Mind also (in some sense) rules over Necessity" <note>original: "ὅτι μεμιγμένη τόδε τοῦ κόσμου γένεσις, ἐξ ἀνάγκης κὶ νοῦ συστάσεως, νοῦ δὲ ἀνάγκης ἄρχοντος"</note>. Therefore, although according to Plato, God is properly and directly the cause of nothing else but *Good*, the *necessity* inherent in these *lower, imperfect* things unavoidably gives existence and birth to *evils*. 

First, regarding *moral evils* (which are the most significant), there is a *necessity* that there should be both *higher* and *lower inclinations* in all rational beings who are vitally united to *bodies*. As *free-willed* <note>original: "Autexousious" — a Greek-derived term meaning self-governing or having the power of self-determination</note> beings, they must have a power of determining their own actions more or less in either direction. There is also a *necessity* that the same liberty of will (which is *essential* to rational creatures) which makes them capable of *praise* and *reward*, should likewise put them in a position where they might deserve *blame* and *punishment*. 

Again, as to the evils of *pain* and *hardship*: there seems to be a *necessity* that *imperfect earthly animals* which are capable of the sense of *pleasure* should, in contrary circumstances, be subject to *displeasure* and *pain*. These circumstances will occasionally happen because of the *inconsistency* and *incompatibility* <note>original: "incompossibility" — the state of two things being unable to exist together</note> of things. 

And *lastly*, regarding the evils of *decay* and *dissolution*: there is a plain *necessity* that if there are *natural births* in the world, there should also be *decay*, according to the lines by Lucretius cited earlier:

> ->*Since Nature restores one thing from another, nor does she*<-
> ->*permit anything to be born unless aided by the death of another.*<-
> <note>original: "Quando alid ex alio reficit Natura, nec ullam / Rem gigni patitur, nisi Morte adjutam alienâ"</note>

To all of this may be added, according to the opinion of many, that there is a kind of *necessity* for some *evils* in the world to serve as a *seasoning* (as it were) to give a *relish* and *richer flavor* <note>original: "Haut-goust" — a term for a strong, spicy, or refined taste</note> to *Good*. Since the nature of *imperfect animals* is such that they are prone to have only a *dull* and *sluggish sense*—a *flat* and *tasteless* experience of *Good*—unless it is quickened and stimulated, heightened and invigorated, by being compared with the opposite *Evil*. There also seems to be a *necessary use* in the world for those *involuntary evils* <note>original: "κακὰ ἀκούσια" (kaka akousia)</note> of *pain* and *suffering*, both for the *exercise of virtue*...

<summary>This page explains that Plato did not believe evil came from an eternal wicked spirit, but rather from the "Necessity" inherent in imperfect, free-willed, and physical beings. It argues that moral evil, pain, and decay are inevitable consequences of the existence of finite creatures and the natural order.</summary>

# Chapter 4: The Origin of Evils.

...and the quickening and exciting of the *activity* of the world, as well as for the repressing, chastising, and punishing of those <term>voluntary evils</term> <note>original: "κακὰ ἑκούσια" (kaka ekousia)</note>, those *voluntary evils of vice and action*. For these several reasons, Plato probably concluded that evils could not be utterly destroyed, at least in this lower world, which according to him is the region of *lapsed souls*:

<margin>In the *Theaetetus*, page 176 (Stephanus edition).</margin>
> *But it is neither possible, O Theodorus, that evils should be quite destroyed (for there must always be something contrary to good), nor yet that they should be seated among the gods; but they will of necessity infest this lower mortal region and nature. Therefore, we ought to endeavor to flee from here with all possible speed, and our flight from here is this: to make ourselves like God as much as possible. This becoming like God consists in being just and holy with wisdom.* <note>original: "ἀλλ’ οὔτ’ ἀπολέσθαι τὰ κακὰ δυνατὸν... ὁμοίωσις δὲ, δίκαιον καὶ ὅσιον μετὰ φρονήσεως γενέσθαι."</note>

Thus, according to the sense of *Plato*, though God is the origin of all things, he is not to be considered properly the *cause of evils*, at least not *moral* ones (they being only *defects*). Instead, they are to be attributed to the <term>necessity of imperfect beings</term>, which is <term>that necessity which often resists God and, as it were, shakes off his bridle</term> <note>original: "ἀνάγκη πολλὰ τῷ Θεῷ δυσμαχοῦσα καὶ ἀφηνιάζουσα"</note>. By means of this necessity, *rational creatures* are capable of acting contrary to God's *will* and *law*, as well as their own true *nature* and *good*. Other things are also hindered from reaching that perfection which the Divine Goodness would otherwise have granted them. 

Notwithstanding this, *Mind* (that is, *God*) is also said by Plato to rule over *necessity*. This is because those evils, occasioned by the *necessity of imperfect beings*, are overruled for *good* by *Divine Art, Wisdom, and Providence*. *Typhon* and *Arimanius* <note>Typhon (Egyptian) and Arimanius (the Persian Ahriman) represent principles of chaos or evil in ancient mythologies</note>—if we may use such language—are, in a sense, outwitted by *Osiris* and *Oromasdes* <note>Osiris (Egyptian) and Oromasdes (Ahura Mazda, the Persian god of light) represent the principles of order and goodness</note>. Thus, the worst of all evils are made, despite their own nature, to contribute subserviently to the *good* and *perfection of the whole*. <term>And this must be acknowledged to be the greatest art of all: to be able to make evils good, or to tincture them with good.</term> <note>original: "καὶ τοῦτο μεγίστης τέχνης ἀγαθοποιεῖν τὰ κακὰ"</note>

---

And now we have shown, as we intended, that *Plutarch* had no sufficient grounds to attribute this opinion—of *two active perceptive principles* in the world (one the *cause of good* and the other of *evil*)—to *Plato*. As for the other Greek philosophers, Plutarch's claims that they were supporters of the same doctrine seem even more slight and frivolous. For he concludes that the * *Pythagoreans* held *two such substantial principles of good and evil* merely because they sometimes spoke of the <term>contrarieties and pairings</term> <note>original: "ἐναντιότητες" (enantiotetes) and "συσοιχίαι" (systoichiai)</note> of things, such as Finite and Infinite, Right and Left, Even and Odd, and the like. 

Plutarch also claimed that *Heraclitus* held the same opinion because he spoke of a <term>back-turning harmony of the world</term> <note>original: "παλίντονος ἁρμονία κόσμου" (palintonos harmonia kosmou)</note>, by which things move back and forth, as when a bow is successively tensioned...

<margin>* The Pythagoreans nowhere admitted evil among their primary principles. <note>original: "Οἱ Πυθαγόρειοι οὐδαμοῦ τὸ κακὸν ἐν ταῖς ἀρχαῖς παρελάμβανον" — Syrianus in Aristotle's *Metaphysics*, manuscript p. 218</note></margin>

<summary>This page argues that Plato viewed evil not as a primary force created by God or an evil soul, but as a byproduct of the inherent limitations ("necessity") of imperfect beings, which God’s providence ultimately directs toward good. The author also refutes Plutarch’s claim that the Pythagoreans and Heraclitus believed in a dualism of good and evil principles.</summary>

->The Arimanius of the Persians. Book 1.<-

...extended and slackened; as likewise because he affirmed, *everything is in flux, and war is the father and lord of all* <note>original: "πάντα ῥεῖν, καὶ πόλεμον πατέρα πάντων"</note>. Moreover, he concludes that *Empedocles’* notions of *Friendship* and *Conflict* could be nothing other than a *Good* and *Evil God*; though we have shown it to be probable that nothing else was meant by them but an *Active Seminal Power* <term>original: "Spermatick Power"; the creative or life-giving forces in nature</term> in this physical world, which causes the cycles of birth and decay <note>original: "Generation and Corruption"</note>. Again, *Anaxagoras* is credited by him with the same philosophy, for no other reason than that he made *Mind* and *Infinite Matter* the two principles of the universe. And lastly, even *Aristotle* himself cannot escape him, being made an advocate for a *Good* and *Evil God* as well, merely because he concluded that *Form* and *Privation* <term>the presence or absence of a quality in matter</term> are the two principles of natural bodies.

Neither does *Plutarch* prove his point any better regarding the beliefs of whole nations. He attributes this doctrine to the *Chaldeans* because their *astrologers* supposed *two* of the *planets* to be *beneficent*, *two* to be *maleficent*, and *three* to be of a *middle nature*. He also attributes it to the ancient Greeks because they sacrificed not only to *Olympian Jupiter*, but also to *Hades* or *Pluto*, who was sometimes called the *Infernal Jupiter*. 

We admit that his interpretation of the *traditions* and *mysteries* of the ancient *Egyptians* is clever. Yet, it is not necessary that their *Typhon* should be understood as a *Substantial Evil Principle* or a *Self-existent God*, as he argues. For it was the custom of the ancient *pagans* (as shall be more fully explained later) to use nature as a basis for their *theology* <term>original: "Physiologize in their Theology"</term> and to personify all the various things in nature. It seems more likely that these Egyptians, in that manner, only *personified* <note>original: "προσωποποιεῖν"</note> that *evil* and *confusion*, *turmoil* and *disorder*, and the *constant alternation* and *cycle* of *births* and *deaths* in this *lower world* (though not without Divine Providence) through the figure of *Typhon*.

<margin>On Isis and Osiris, page 370. Paris edition.</margin> 
Therefore, the only remaining probability is that of the *Persian Magi*: that they might indeed assert two such *Active Principles* of *Good* and *Evil*, as *Plutarch* and later the *Manicheans* did. We must admit there is some probability of this, because besides *Plutarch*, *Diogenes Laertius* affirms the same of them: *that there are two principles according to the Persian Magi, a Good Spirit and an Evil one* <note>original: "δύο κατ' αὐτὸς εἶναι ἀρχὰς, ἀγαθὸν δαίμονα καὶ κακὸν"</note>. He seems to support this with the authority of *Hermippus*, *Eudoxus*, and *Theopompus*. 

Despite this, it may well be questioned whether the meaning of those *Magi* was misunderstood. Perhaps they intended nothing more by their *Evil Spirit* than the kind of *Satanic Power* that we acknowledge—that is, not a *Substantial Evil Principle*, *uncreated* and *independent* of God, but only a *community of evil spirits* in the world, united together under *one head* or *prince*. This is supported not only because *Theodorus* (cited in *Photius*) calls the Persian *Arimanius* by that very name, *Satanas*, but also because those very *traditions* of theirs recorded by *Plutarch* himself seem to strongly favor this opinion. They go as follows: *But there comes a fated time when Arimanius, bringing plague and famine, must be necessarily and utterly destroyed and disappear; and then the earth becoming level...* <note>original: "ἔπεσι δὲ χρόνος εἱμαρμένος, ἐν ᾧ τὸν Ἀρειμάνιον λοιμὸν ἐπάγοντα καὶ λιμὸν, ὑπὸ τούτων ἀνάγκη φθαρῆναι παντάπασι καὶ ἀφανισθῆναι, τῆς δὲ γῆς ἐπι-"</note>

<summary>The author critiques Plutarch for misinterpreting ancient Greek and Egyptian philosophies as dualistic, arguing instead that figures like Typhon were personifications of natural disorder. He examines the Persian belief in Arimanius, suggesting it may refer to a subordinate "Satanic" power rather than an independent evil deity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into whether ancient cultures truly believed in two equal, self-existent gods of good and evil, specifically examining the Persian Magi and the claims made by Plutarch.</meta>

<header>CHAP. IV. The Magi, considered.</header>

...<note>original Greek: πέδῳ καὶ ὁμαλῆς γενομένης, ἕνα βίον καὶ μίαν πολιτείαν ἀνθρώπων μακαρίων καὶ ὁμογλώσσων ἁπάντων γενέσθαι</note> **when the earth becomes level and smooth, there will be one way of life and one society for a race of happy people, all speaking the same language.** That there is a **destined time at hand**, in which **Arimanius** <note>Also known as Ahriman, the spirit of evil in Zoroastrianism</note>, the bringer of **plagues** and **famines**, must by necessity be utterly destroyed; and when the Earth is made flat and even, there shall be but one **life**, and one **governance** of men, all happy and speaking the same language. Or else, as **Theopompus** <note>A Greek historian of the 4th century BCE</note> himself represented their sense: <note>original Greek: τέλος ἀπολείπεσθαι τὸν Ἅιδην, καὶ τοὺς μὲν ἀνθρώπους εὐδαίμονας ἔσεσθαι, μήτε τροφῆς δεομένους, μήτε σκιὰν ποιοῦντας· τὸν δὲ ταῦτα μηχανησάμενον Θεὸν ἠρεμεῖν καὶ ἀναπαύεσθαι χρόνῳ καλῶς μὲν οὐ πολὺν τῷ Θεῷ, ὥσπερ ἀνθρώπῳ κοιμωμένῳ μέτριον</note> **That in the end, Hades shall be utterly abolished, and then men shall be perfectly happy, their bodies neither needing food nor casting any shadow. That God, who contrived this whole scene of things, rests only for a certain season, which is not long to him, but like a brief sleep is to men.** For since an uncreated and self-existent evil demon—such as that imagined by **Plutarch** and the **Manicheans** <note>Followers of Mani, who believed in a dualistic struggle between a good spiritual world of light and an evil material world of darkness</note>—could never be utterly abolished or destroyed, it seems more probable that these **Persian Magi** did, in their **Arimanius**, either <note>original Greek: προσωποποιεῖν</note> **personify** evil only (as we suppose the Egyptians did with **Typhon**), or else understood a **Satanic power** by it. Despite this, they might possibly sacrifice to it (just as the Greeks did to evil demons) to appease or restrain it; or perhaps they were worshipping the Deity itself through the ministers of its wrath and vengeance.

However, from what has been declared, we conceive it is sufficiently clear that this **ditheistic doctrine** <term>Ditheism: The belief in two equal and independent gods, one good and one evil</term> of a **good** and **evil god** (or a good god and evil demon, both self-existent) asserted by **Plutarch** and the **Manicheans**, was never as universally accepted among the Pagans as Plutarch claims. This can be further proven by the fact that the **Manicheans** themselves declared they did not inherit this opinion from the Pagans, nor were they a branch of them or a break from them, but a completely different sect on their own. Thus **Faustus** says in St. **Augustine**: <margin>Against Faustus, book 20, chapter 3.</margin> <note>original Latin: Pagani Bona & Mala, Tetra & Splendida, Perpetua & Caduca, Mutabilia & Certa, Corporalia & Divina, Unum habere Principium dogmatizant. His ego valde contraria censeo, qui Bonis omnibus Principium fateor Deum, Contrariis verò Hylen (sic enim Mali Principium & Naturam Theologus noster appellat.)</note> **The Pagans dogmatically teach that good and evil things, foul and splendid, eternal and fleeting, changeable and certain, physical and divine, all proceed from a single Principle. I hold views very contrary to these, as I confess that God is the Principle of all good things, but Hyle (for so our theologian, Manes, names the Principle and Nature of Evil) is the source of the opposite.** And later, **Faustus** determines again that there were indeed only two sects of religion in the world really distinct from one another: **Paganism** and **Manicheism**. From this it may be concluded that this doctrine of **two active principles** of good and evil was not then seen as the generally accepted doctrine of the Pagans. Therefore, it seems reasonable to think that **Plutarch's** attributing it so universally to them was either a deliberate choice to give more authority to a concept he was personally fond of, or else because he be-

And probably Saint Athanasius is referring to these men when, in his oration *Against the Heathens*, he writes the following concerning this opinion:

"Some of the Greeks, wandering from the right path and ignorant of Christ, have declared evil to be a real entity existing by itself. After this, that Father also speaks of some degenerate Christians who fell into the same error:

"Others, falling away from the Church's teaching into heresies and making shipwreck of their faith, have likewise falsely attributed a real nature and essence to evil. <note>original Greek: οἱ δὲ ἀπὸ τῶν αἱρέσεων ἐκπεσόντες τῆς ἐκκλησιαστικῆς διδασκαλίας, καὶ περὶ τὴν πίστιν ναυαγήσαντες, καὶ οὗτοι μὲν ὑπόστασιν τῷ κακῷ ἀποφαίνονται εἶναι.</note>"

There were several sects of these heretics before the Manicheans <note>Followers of Mani, who believed in a cosmic struggle between Good/Light and Evil/Darkness</note>, who were sometimes noticed and censored by Pagan philosophers themselves. Another is Plotinus, who wrote an entire book against such Christians (the ninth book of his second *Ennead*), which was titled by Porphyry "Against the Gnostics" <note>original Greek: πρὸς τοὺς γνωστικούς</note>.

But even if we were to grant what Plutarch argues—that Pagan theologians generally claimed there were **two self-existent principles** (a **good God** and an **evil soul** or **demon**) and no more—it would still follow that all the other gods they worshiped were not seen as uncreated, self-existent beings. If they were, these theologians would have had to acknowledge many "first principles" <note>term: first principles - the fundamental, uncreated sources from which all other things originate</note>. However, it is certain that if Plutarch believed his own writings, he must have assumed that none of the Pagan gods (except for those two principles of good and evil) were considered uncreated or self-existent by their theologians. 

As for Plutarch himself, it is undeniably clear that although he was a Pagan and a worshiper of all their many gods—especially the Delian Apollo (whose priest he claimed to be)—he believed they were all (except for the one Good God and...
