And the same can be said of all his *Pagan* followers, as well as the Manicheans; for although they acknowledged a *Good* and *Evil God* (the only unmade, self-existent beings they recognized), they also worshipped innumerable other deities.

Up to this point, we have not been able to find any among the Pagans who claimed there were a *multitude of unmade, self-existent deities*. On the contrary, we shall now find one who took notice of this opinion of *many principles* <note>original Greek: πολλαὶ ἀρχαὶ</note> specifically to refute it: *Aristotle*. He was not prompted to do this because it was a generally accepted doctrine, but only because he wanted to maliciously attribute such a view to the *Pythagoreans* and *Platonists*, because they made "Ideas" (sometimes also called "Numbers") the *principles* of things in a certain sense. Nevertheless, the opinion itself is well refuted by that philosopher from the *phenomena* <note>observable events or facts</note> in this manner: <margin>Aristotle, Metaphysics, Book 14, Chapter 10.</margin> *Those who say that mathematical number is the first principle, and suppose one principle for one thing and another for another, would make the whole essence of the universe a series of disconnected episodes. They would make the world like an incoherent and disagreeing poem, where things do not all mutually contribute to one another, nor conspire together to make up one sense and harmony. But the contrary (he says) is most evident in the world; and therefore there cannot be many principles, but only one.* <note>original Greek: οἱ δὲ λέγοντες τὸν ἀριθμὸν πρῶτον τὸν μαθηματικὸν, καὶ οὕτως ἀεὶ ἄλλην ἐχομένην οὐσίαν καὶ ἀρχὰς ἑκάστης ἄλλας, ἐπεισοδιώδη τὴν τοῦ παντὸς οὐσίαν ποιοῦσιν</note>

From this it is manifest that although *Aristotle* was a worshipper of *many gods*, just like the other Pagans (he writes somewhere that it is very absurd to sacrifice to no one but *Jupiter*), yet he was no *polytheist* in the sense declared before—of *many unmade, self-existent deities*. Indeed, he was not even a *ditheist* <note>one who believes in two primary gods</note> or an advocate of *two understanding principles, a Good and Evil God* (as *Plutarch* claimed he was). Aristotle not only rejected that opinion of *many principles* <note>original Greek: πολλαὶ ἀρχαὶ</note> here, but also explicitly derived all things from *One*. In that very chapter, he affirmed that *Good* is a *principle*, but *Evil* is not. 

As for the *Platonists* and *Pythagoreans* criticized <note>original: perfringed; meaning to infringe upon or disparage</note> by him: although it is true that they made "Ideas" principles in some sense, as the *paradigms* <note>models or patterns</note> of things, even Aristotle admits in that same chapter that they also declared there was *another principle more excellent or superior* <note>original Greek: ἄλλη ἀρχὴ κυριωτέρα</note>. This is what they called *the One* <note>original Greek: τὸ ἕν</note> or *Monad* <note>original Greek: μονὰς</note>—that is, *unity itself*, or the *one most simple Deity*.

Though we demonstrated before that the *Pagan gods* were not all supposed by them to be *unmade, self-existent beings*—because they acknowledged a *Theogony* <note>original: Theogonia; the study of the origin and genealogy of the gods</note>, a *generation* and *temporary production of gods*—we have now made the best inquiry we could as to whether they held a multitude of unmade deities regardless. # A General Survey Book I.

A duality of such gods (namely, *Understanding Beings who were Unmade* <note>original: "Unmade"—meaning self-existent or eternal</note>), one good and the other *evil*, but no more. On the contrary, we have found that *Aristotle* professedly opposed this opinion of *many principles* or *unmade gods*, which he certainly would never have dared to do had it been the generally accepted opinion of the Pagans at that time. And though it is true that several of the ancient Christians, in their disputes with Pagans, do refute the idea of *many unmade deities*, we do not find that any of them seriously charge the Pagans with believing this; they only address the possibility occasionally and *more than necessary* <note>original Latin: "ex abundanti"</note>. 

However, we would be better equipped to make a clear judgment concerning this controversy—whether there were a multitude of supposed *unmade beings* among the *Pagan deities*—if we briefly surveyed their religion and considered all the different kinds of gods they worshipped. These may, as we conceive, be reduced to the following categories. 

In the first place, it is certain that many of the Pagan gods were nothing more than *dead men* (or the souls of deceased men) called *Heroes* by the Greeks and *Manes* <note>spirits of the dead</note> by the Latins, such as *Hercules*, *Liber* <note>Bacchus</note>, *Aesculapius*, *Castor*, *Pollux*, *Quirinus*, and the like. This was true not only of the Greeks and Romans, but also of the Egyptians, Syrians, and Babylonians. For this reason, Pagan sacrifices are contemptuously called the *sacrifices of the dead* in Scripture—meaning not sacrifices to dead or lifeless *statues*, as some would suggest, but to *dead men*. This was why many of the religious rites and ceremonies observed by Pagan priests were *mournful* and *funereal*. This is expressed in 

<margin>Baruch, Chapter 6, Verse 31.</margin> 

*Baruch* <note>A book of the Apocrypha</note> concerning the Babylonians: *Their priests sit in their temples with their clothes torn, their heads and beards shaved, and nothing upon their heads; they roar and cry before their gods, as men do at a feast when someone has died.* (Some of these rites are therefore thought to have been forbidden to the Israelite priests.) The same thing is noted by the poet concerning the Egyptians,

->And by your mourning, you testify that Osiris is a man:<-
<note>original Latin: "Et quem tu plangens, Hominem testaris, Osirin"</note>

And it was also suggested by *Xenophanes of Colophon*, when he rebuked the Egyptians in this manner: *If they believe them to be gods, they should not mourn; if they mourn, they should not believe them to be gods.* <note>original Greek: εἰ θεοὺς νομίζουσι μὴ θρηνεῖν, εἰ δὲ θρηνοῦσι μὴ θεοὺς νομίζειν</note> 

Moreover, it is well known that this habit of deifying men was later carried even further, and that living men (such as Emperors) also had temples and altars erected to them. Indeed, human political systems and *cities* were also sometimes deified by the Pagans, with *Rome* itself being made a *goddess*. Now, no one can imagine that those *men-gods* and *city-gods* were viewed by them as *unmade, self-existent deities*; they were not even considered *gods generated or made by nature* <note>original Greek: φύσει γεννητοὶ θεοὶ</note>, but rather artificially made by human will and choice. 

Additionally, *another* sort of Pagan deity consisted of all the major parts of the *visible world system* <note>original: "Mundane System"</note> or *corporeal world*, which were believed to be *animated* [living and ensouled]...

<summary>This page argues that Pagans did not view their numerous gods as self-existent "unmade" beings, categorizing many deities instead as deified dead men or personifications of the physical world.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, Paganism, deification, Baruch, Xenophanes, Osiris, heroes, Manes, city-gods, unmade gods</keywords>

The Sun, the Moon, and the Stars, and even the Earth itself, under the names of *Vesta* and *Cybele*, the *Mother of the Gods*, and the like. Now it is also certain that none of these could be taken for *unmade, self-existent deities* either, by those who supposed the whole world itself to have been *generated* or to have had a *beginning*, which, as *Aristotle* tells us, was the *generally received opinion* before his time. There was also a *third sort of Pagan deities*: *ethereal* and *aerial invisible animals* called *Dæmons*, *Genii*, and *Lares*, superior indeed to men, but inferior to the *celestial* or *mundane gods* mentioned before. Therefore, these must also necessarily have been looked upon by them as nothing but Γεννητοὶ Θεοὶ, *generated* or *created gods*, since they were merely certain *inferior parts of the whole generated world*.

Besides all these, the Pagans had yet another *sort of gods* that were nothing but mere *accidents* or *qualities of substances*, which therefore could not be supposed by them to be *self-existent deities* because they could not so much as *exist by themselves*. Such were *Virtue*, *Piety*, *Felicity*, *Truth*, *Faith*, *Hope*, *Justice*, *Clemency*, *Love*, *Desire*, *Health*, *Peace*, *Honor*, *Fame*, *Liberty*, *Memory*, *Sleep*, *Night*, and the like; all of which had temples or altars erected to them. Now, this kind of *Pagan gods* cannot well be conceived to have been anything else but the *several and various manifestations of that one divine force, power, and providence* that runs through the *whole world* (as it relates to the *good* and *evil* of men), *fictitiously personified* and represented as so *many gods and goddesses*.

Lastly, there is still *another kind of Pagan gods* remaining, having *substantial and personal names*, which yet cannot be conceived to be so many *intelligent beings* who are *unmade* and *independent* of any *supreme being*, if for no other reason than this: because they all have their *particular places* and *provinces*, *offices* and *functions* severally (as it were) assigned to them, and to which they are confined. They are limited so as not to interfere or clash with one another, but agreeably to make up one *orderly and harmonious system of the whole*: one of those gods ruling only in the *heavens*, another in the *air*, another in the *sea*, and another in the *earth and hell*; one being the *god or goddess of learning and wisdom*, another of *speech and eloquence*, another of *justice and political order*; one the *god of war*, another the *god of pleasure*, one the *god of corn*, and another the *god of wine*, and the like. For how can it be imagined that a multitude of *self-existent* and *independent intelligent beings* could have fallen into such a *uniform order and harmony* of their own accord? And how could they, without any clashing, peaceably and quietly share the government of the whole world among themselves and carry it on with such *constant regularity*? For this reason, we conclude also that neither those *Dii Majorum Gentium*, whether the *Twenty Selecti* or the *Twelve Consentes*, nor yet that *triumvirate* of gods among whom *Homer* shares the government of the whole world, were independent. According to that passage of *Maximus Tyrius*, "All things were divided into three by Homer: Poseidon was allotted to dwell forever in the grey sea, and Hades was allotted the misty gloom—"

--- Page 246 ---
Then, whether it be Jupiter or the sky, the sea being assigned to Neptune, the dark and subterranean parts to Pluto, and the heavens to Jupiter—which three are sometimes also called the Celestial, Marine, and Terrestrial Jupiter; nor lastly, that other Roman and Samothracian Trinity of Gods, worshipped all together in the Capitol: Jupiter, Minerva, and Juno; I say, that none of all these could reasonably be thought by the Pagans themselves to be so many really distinct, uncreated, and self-existent deities.

Therefore, the truth of this whole matter seems to be this: that the ancient Pagans applied natural science to their theology. Whether they looked upon the whole animated world as the Supreme God, and consequently the several parts of it as his living members, or else perceived it at least to be a mirror or visible image of the invisible Deity—and consequently all its several parts and things of nature as so many several manifestations of divine power and providence—they claimed that all their devotion toward the Deity ought not to be huddled up in one general and confused acknowledgment of a Supreme Invisible Being, the creator and governor of all. Instead, they believed that all the several manifestations of the Deity in the world, considered singly and apart by themselves, should be made so many distinct objects of their devout veneration. Therefore, for this purpose, they personified the things in nature and the parts of the world, speaking of them as persons and consequently as so many gods and goddesses. Yet they did this in such a way that an intelligent person might easily understand the meaning: that these were all really nothing else but so many several names and concepts of that one Divine Power and Force which runs through the whole world, displaying itself therein in many forms. To this purpose Balbus says in Cicero: "Do you not see how, from the things of nature, a system has been derived for fictitious and invented gods?" And Origen seems to insist upon this very thing (where Celsus upbraids the Jews and Christians for worshipping only one God), showing that all that seeming multiplicity of Pagan gods could not be understood as so many distinct, substantial, and independent deities;

Let Celsus therefore himself show how he is able to establish a multiplicity of gods (substantial and self-existent) according to the Greeks and other barbarian Pagans; let him declare the essence and substantial personality of that Memory which by Jupiter fathered the Muses, or of that Themis which brought forth the Hours; or let him show how the Graces, always naked, exist as individual substances. But he will never be able to do this, nor to make it appear that those fictions of the Greeks (which seem to be really nothing else but the things of nature turned into persons) are so many distinct (self-existent) deities. In a recent edition, these latter words are translated thus: "But Celsus will never be able to show that the fictions of the Greeks, which seem to become more substantial from the things themselves—"

--- Page 247 ---
CHAPTER IV. Deified, but several Names of God.

*...to prove that they themselves are Gods*, which we confess we cannot understand; but we conceive the word *σωματόποιεῖσθαι*, there translated *Validiora fieri*, is used here by *Origen* in the same sense as *προσωποποιεῖσθαι*, so that his meaning is as we have declared: that those *fictions* of the Greeks and other barbarian Pagans (which are the same as *Balbus’s* *invented and fictitious gods*) are really nothing else but the *things of nature*, figuratively and fictitiously personified, and consequently not so many distinct substantial deities, but only several notions and considerations of one God, or supreme Numen, in the world.

Now this *fictitious personifying* and *deifying* of things by the Pagan theologians was done in *two ways*: one, when those things in nature were themselves, without any further ado or change of names, spoken of as *persons*, and so made *gods* and *goddesses*, as in the many instances previously proposed. Another, when there were distinct proper and personal names assigned separately to those things, such as *Minerva* to *wisdom*, *Neptune* to the *sea*, *Ceres* to *corn*, and *Bacchus* to *wine*. In which latter case, those personal names properly signify the *invisible divine powers* supposed to preside over those several things in nature, and these are therefore properly those gods and goddesses who are *δοτῆρες ἑάων*, the *givers* and *dispensers* of good things and the removers of the contrary; but they are used improperly also for the *things of nature* themselves, which therefore, as manifestations of divine power, goodness, and providence personified, are sometimes also *incorrectly* called gods and goddesses.

This *mystery of Pagan polytheism* is thus fully declared by *Moscopulus*: *We must know that whatsoever the Greeks (or Pagans) saw to have any power, virtue, or ability in it, they looked upon it as not acting according to such power without the providence, presidency, or influence of the gods; and they called both the thing itself which has the power and the deity presiding over it by one and the same name. Whence the ministerial fire used in mechanical arts, and the god presiding over those arts that work by fire, were both alike called Hephæstus or Vulcan; so the name Demetra or Ceres was given as well to corn and fruits as to that goddess who bestows them; Athena or Minerva did alike signify wisdom and the goddess who is the dispenser of it; Dionysus or Bacchus, wine and the god who gives wine (whence Plato derives the name from the giving of wine). In like manner, they called both the childbearing of women and the goddesses who superintend the same Eilithuia or Lucina; sexual union and the*

--- Page 248 ---
the Deity presiding over it, *Aphrodite* or *Venus*. And lastly, in the same manner, by the *Muses*, they signified both those *Rational Arts*—*Rhetorick*, *Astronomy*, and *Poetry*—and the *Goddesses* who assist in or promote them. Now, as the various things in nature and parts of the physical world are thus *metonymically* and *catachrestically* called gods and goddesses, it is evident that such deities as these could not be supposed to be unmade or self-existent by those who acknowledged the whole world to have been generated and to have had a beginning. But as these names were used more properly to signify invisible and intelligent powers presiding over the things in nature and dispensing them, however they have an appearance of so many several distinct deities, yet they seem to have been all really nothing else but—as *Balbus* in *Cicero* expresses it—*Deus Pertinens per Naturam cujusque Rei*, God passing through and acting in the nature of every thing. Consequently, they are but several names, or so many different notions and considerations of that one supreme *Numen*—that divine force, power, and providence which runs through the whole world, manifesting itself there in various ways.

Therefore, since there were no other kinds of gods among the *Pagans* besides those already listed—unless their images, statues, and symbols should be accounted as such (because they were also sometimes improperly called gods), which could not be supposed by them to have been unmade or without a beginning, being the workmanship of men's own hands—we conclude universally that all that *multiplicity* of *Pagan gods* which makes so great a show and noise was really either nothing but several names and notions of *one supreme Deity* personified according to its different manifestations, gifts, and effects in the world, or else *many inferior intelligent beings* generated or created by *one Supreme*. So, *one unmade self-existent Deity*, and no more, was acknowledged by the more *intelligent* of the *ancient Pagans* (for no man can pretend to give an account of the *foolish common people* in any *religion*). Consequently, *Pagan polytheism* (or *idolatry*) consisted not in worshipping a *multiplicity* of *unmade minds*, *deities*, and *creators* self-existent from eternity and independent of *one Supreme*, but in *mingling* and *blending*, in some improper way, *creature-worship* with the *worship of the Creator*.

And that the ancient *Pagan theists* thus acknowledged *one supreme God*, who was the only θεὸς ἀγένητος, *unmade* or *unproduced Deity* (I say *theists*, because those among the *Pagans* who admitted *many gods* but none at all *unmade* were absolute *atheists*), this may be undeniably concluded from what was proved before: that they acknowledged *omnipotence* or *infinite power* to be a *divine attribute*. Because, upon the *hypothesis of many unmade self-existent deities*, it is plain that there could be none *omnipotent*, and consequently no such thing as *omnipotence* in the nature of things. Therefore, *omnipotence* was rightly and properly styled by *Macrobius* as *Summi Dei Omnipotentia*, it being an *attribute essentially peculiar* to *one supreme and sole self-existent Deity*. And

--- Page 249 ---
Simplicius, who was also a Pagan, refuted the Manichean hypothesis of two self-existent deities for this reason as well: because it destroyed the concept of omnipotence. *For those who assert two principles of the universe (one good and the other evil) and call the good principle "God," are forced to admit that he is not the cause of all things; they cannot rightly praise him as omnipotent, nor can they attribute to him absolute and total power, but only half of a total power at most, if even that.* In addition to all of this, it has already been proved that the ancient atheists under Paganism directed their attacks primarily against the opinion of monarchy, or of one supreme Deity ruling over all; from this it clearly appears that such a doctrine was indeed asserted by the Pagan theists.

And we think it noteworthy here that this was so generally confessed and acknowledged that Faustus the Manichean adopted the notion that both Christians and Jews "paganized" regarding the opinion of monarchy—that is, they derived this doctrine of one Deity, the sole principle of all things, only by tradition from the Pagans, and consequently were nothing more than schisms or subdivided sects of Paganism. *You, in revolting from the Gentiles,* he says, *first took the opinion of monarchy away with you—that is, the belief that all things come from God. Therefore, you are truly a schism, as were your predecessors the Jews. Regarding the opinion of monarchy, even they do not disagree at all with the Pagans. For this reason, it is evident that both you and the Jews are a schism of Gentilism. But if you look for distinct sects of religion, there are no more than two: that of the Gentiles, and our own.* Now, although this is false and foolish regarding the claim that Christians and Jews derived the opinion of monarchy only by tradition from the Pagans—since it is a thing founded on the principles of nature—it sufficiently shows that it was the general sense of the Pagans that all their gods were derived from one sole self-existent Deity. Thus, they neither acknowledged a multitude of unmade deities, nor that duality of them for which Plutarch contended (one good and the other evil), who accordingly denied God to be the cause of all things, writing as follows in his *Defect of Oracles*: *Those who make God the cause of nothing at all, and those who make him the cause of everything alike, both miss the mark of moderation and propriety.* But this paradox was both late to appear among the Greeks and was quickly rejected by the succession of their philosophers; therefore, it does not undermine the truth of Faustus's general observation.

--- Page 250 ---
This general assertion concerning the Pagans is again fully confirmed by St. Augustine in his reply: *If one should make a distribution of those who are bound by any religion, such that some prefer to worship one God and others many, by this distinction the Pagans are separated from us, and the Manicheans are classified with the Pagans, while we are classified with the Jews. Here you might say that you claim your many gods are of one substance; as if the Pagans do not also claim their many gods are from one, even though they attribute different offices, works, and powers to them; just as among you, one god conquers the nation of darkness, another god builds a world out of it once it is captured, etc.* And again, he later writes further to the same purpose: *Let Faustus therefore learn that we Christians do not have the opinion of monarchy from the Gentiles, but that the Gentiles have not fallen so far toward false gods as to lose the opinion of the one true God, from whom is every nature of whatever kind.*

### XIV.
It follows from what we have declared that Pagan polytheism, or the multiplicity of gods, is not to be understood in the sense previously expressed—of many unproduced and self-existent deities—but according to some other notion or ambiguity of the word "gods." For "god" is one of those words that has been used in many different senses; the atheists themselves acknowledge a "god" and "gods" according to certain private senses of their own (which they do not all agree upon either), and theists do not always have the same notion of that word. For instance, angels in Scripture are called "gods" in one sense—that is, as understanding beings superior to men, immortal, holy, and happy; and the word is again sometimes brought down lower to princes and magistrates; and not only so, but also to good men as such, when they are said to be "made partakers of the divine nature." And thus that learned philosopher and Christian Boethius says, *Every good and happy man is a god; and though there is only one God by nature, yet nothing prevents there being many by participation.* But then again, all men and angels are alike denied to be gods in other respects, and particularly regarding religious worship: *You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve.* Now, this is what seems to be essentially included in the Pagan notion of the word "god" or "gods" when taken in general—namely, a respect to religious worship. Therefore, a god in general, according to the sense of the Pagan theists, may be defined as an understanding...

--- Page 251 ---
C H A P. IV. And One God, in different Senses.

An understanding Being superior to Men, not originally derived from senseless Matter, and looked upon as an object for men’s religious worship. But this general notion of the word *God* is again restrained and limited by differences in its division. For such a God as this may be either *ἀγένητος*, *Ingenerate* or *Unproduced*, and consequently self-existent; or else *γενητὸς*, *Generated* or *Produced*, and dependent on some Higher Being as its cause. In the former sense, the intelligent Pagans, as we have declared, acknowledged only One God, who was therefore called by them *ὁ Θεὸς κατ’ ἐξοχὴν* (God in the eminent sense), according to that saying of Thales in Laertius: *πρεσβύτατον τῶν ὄντων, ὁ Θεὸς, ἀγένητον γὰρ*—*God is the oldest of all things, because he is Unmade or Unproduced, and the only thing that is so*. But in the latter sense, they admitted of Many Gods, many understanding Beings, which, though generated or produced, yet were superior to men and looked upon as objects for their religious worship. And thus the Pagan theists were both polytheists and monotheists in different senses; they acknowledged both Many Gods and One God; that is, many inferior deities, subordinate to One Supreme.

Thus Onatus the Pythagorean in Stobaeus declares himself: *δοκεῖ δέ μοι, οὐ μόνον εἷς εἶμεν ὁ θεὸς, ἀλλ’ εἷς μὲν ὁ μέγιστος, καὶ καθ’ ὑπέρτερος, καὶ ὁ κρατέων τῶ παντός· οἱ δ’ ἄλλοι πολλοὶ διαφέροντες κατὰ δύναμιν, βασιλεύει δὲ πάντων αὐτῶν ὁ τῶ κράτει καὶ μεγέθει καὶ ἀρετᾷ μείζων· οὗτος δὲ κ’ εἴη ὁ περιέχων τὸν σύμπαντα κόσμον· τοὶ δ’ ἄλλοι οἱ θέοντές εἰσι κατὰ οὐρανὸν, σύν τε τῶ παντὸς περιάγησι, κατὰ λόγον ὑπαδεύοντες, τῷ πρώτῳ καὶ νοητῷ*—*It seems to me that there is not only One God, but that there is One the Greatest and Highest God, who governs the whole world, and that there are many other gods besides him differing in power; that One God reigning over them all, who surpasses them all in power, greatness, and virtue. This is that God who contains and comprehends the whole world; but the other gods are those who, together with the revolution of the universe, orderly follow that First and Intelligible God.* Where it is evident that Onatus’s *πολλοὶ θεοὶ* or Many Gods were only the heavenly bodies, or animated stars. And partly from those words cited, but chiefly from others which follow after in the same place (which will be produced elsewhere), it plainly appears that in Onatus’s time there were some who acknowledged only One God, denying all those other gods then commonly worshipped. And indeed Anaxagoras seems to have been such a one; for insofar as he asserted One Perfect Mind ruling over all (which is the True Deity), he effectively degraded all those other Pagan gods—the sun, moon, and stars—from their godships by making the sun nothing but a globe of fire, and the moon earth and stones, and the like of the other stars and planets. And some such people there were also among the ancient Egyptians, as shall be declared in the proper place.

Moreover, Proclus, in his commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, tells us that there has always been less doubt and controversy in the world concerning the One God than concerning the Many Gods. Therefore, Onatus here declares his own view as to this particular: namely, that besides the One Supreme God, there were also many other inferior deities—that is, understanding Beings that ought to be religiously worshipped.

But because it is not impossible that one might imagine One Supreme Deity even if there were many other *θεοὶ ἀγένητοι*, unmade...

<meta>This page continues the argument that intelligent Pagans recognized one supreme, unproduced Deity who was the cause of all other "gods." It transitions into explaining that the "generation of the gods" (Theogony) was considered identical to the "generation of the world" (Cosmogony).</meta>

# The Pagan Theogony, Book I.

...made and *self-existent* gods besides—as *Plutarch* previously supposed—one Supreme God, together with an <note>original: ψυχὴ ἄνους</note> *irrational soul* or *unmade demon* inferior in power to it. Therefore, we add in the next place that the more *intelligent Pagans* did not only assert *one God* who was supreme and <note>original: κρατίστης πάντων</note> *the most powerful of all the gods*, but also one who, being *omnipotent*, was the *principle* and *cause* of all the rest, and therefore the only <note>original: Θεὸς ἀγένητος καὶ αὐθυπόστατος</note> *unproduced and self-existent Deity*. <margin>Difference 1, page 5.</margin> *Maximus Tyrius* affirms this to have been the general sense of all the *Pagans*: that there was <note>original: Θεὸς εἷς πάντων βασιλεὺς καὶ πατὴρ, καὶ Θεοὶ πολλοὶ, Θεοῦ παῖδες, συνάρχοντες θεῷ</note> *one God, the King and Father of all, and many gods, the sons of God, reigning together with God*. Neither did the poets imply anything less when *Zeus* was so often called by the Greeks, and *Jupiter* by the Latins, <note>original: πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε</note> *father of both men and gods*, and <note>original: Hominum Pater atque Deorum</note> *Father of Men and Gods*, or <note>original: Hominum Satorque Deorum</note> *Sower and Father of Men and Gods*, and the like. And indeed the <term>original: Theogonia; the genealogy or birth of the gods</term> *Theogony* of the ancient *Pagans* mentioned before was commonly declared by them universally <note>original: γενητοὺς τοὺς θεοὺς εἶναι</note> *that the gods were generated*, or as *Herodotus* expresses it, <note>original: ὅτι ἔκαστος τῶν θεῶν ἐγένετο</note> *that every one of the gods was generated or produced*. This is not to be understood as if they supposed there was no God at all *unmade* or *self-existent* (which would be *absolute atheism*), but rather that "the gods," as distinguished from "God" or "the Divine," were all universally *made* or *generated*.

But in order that we may now make this matter even easier to believe—that the *intelligent Pagans* supposed all their gods except *one* to have been *made* or *generated*, and consequently acknowledged only *one* <note>original: Θεὸν ἀγένητον καὶ αὐθυπόστατον</note> *unproduced and self-existent Deity*—we shall further observe in this place that the *Theogony* of those *ancient Pagans* (their *genesis* and *generation of gods*) was really one and the same thing as the <term>original: Cosmogonia; the creation or birth of the universe</term> *Cosmogony* (the *genesis* and *generation of the world*). Indeed, both were understood as a *temporary production* of both these *gods* and the *world*. We shall first prove this from *Plato* in his *Timaeus*. There, when he is about to treat the *Cosmogony*, he establishes this distinction concerning **two heads of being**: that some things were *eternal* and *never made*, and some again were *made* or *generated*. The former he calls <note>original: οὐσία</note> *essence*, and the latter <note>original: γένεσις</note> *generation*. He also adds this difference between them: that *eternal and immutable things* were the proper objects of science and demonstration, but other *generated things* <margin>Page 29.</margin> were objects of *faith* and *opinion* only: <note>original: ὅ, τι γὰρ πρὸς γένεσιν οὐσία, τοῦτο πρὸς πίστιν ἀλήθεια</note> *For what essence is to generation, the same is the certainty of truth or knowledge to faith*. Thereupon he declares that his reader should not expect the same evidence and certainty of truth from him when he was now to treat of things *generated* (namely, the *gods* and the *visible world*) as if he had been speaking about things *immutable* and <margin>Page 29.</margin> *eternal*. He uses these words: <note>original: ἐὰν οὖν, ὦ Σώκρατες, πολλὰ πολλῶν εἰπόντων περὶ θεῶν καὶ τῆς τοῦ παντὸς γενέσεως</note> *If therefore, O Socrates, many things having been spoken by many men concerning the gods and the generation of the universe, we are not able to speak with absolute demonstration concerning the same, you ought not at all to wonder at it, or be displeased with us, but...*

<summary>The author argues that ancient Pagans viewed their many gods as generated beings produced by one supreme, self-existent Deity. He links the "birth of the gods" (Theogony) directly to the "creation of the world" (Cosmogony), using Plato's distinction between eternal essence and generated things.</summary>

# CHAPTER IV. Joining with the Cosmogony. <note>original: "Cosmogonia"; the study of the origin of the universe</note>

On the contrary, we should be well satisfied with our performance if, on this subject, we provide only probabilities. Here, the gods are plainly referred to by Plato as belonging to **generation** <note>original: γένεσις</note> and not to **eternal or immutable essence** <note>original: οὐσία</note>; they are also associated with the generation of the world as being merely a part of it. This is not at all surprising in Plato's work. To him, as to other Pagans, the entire visible world was no less than a god; he called it **a happy god** <note>original: θεὸν εὐδαίμονα</note> and, before it was yet made, **a god about to be made** <note>original: θεὸν ἐσόμενον</note>.

This does not mean Plato considered the senseless matter of this physical world—whether viewed as perfectly dead and stupid or as endowed only with a <term>plastic nature; a formative, unconscious power that shapes matter</term>—to be a god. No inanimate thing was a god to Plato. Rather, he supposed the world to be an animal, endowed with an intellectual soul; indeed, he believed it to be the best of all animals, compounded of soul and body. <margin>Page 30.</margin> <note>original: οὕτως οὖν δὴ κατὰ λόγον τὸν εἰκότα δεῖ λέγειν, τόνδε τὸν κόσμον, ζῶον ἔμψυχον ἔννουν τε τῇ ἀληθείᾳ διὰ τὴν τοῦ θεοῦ γενέσθαι πρόνοιαν</note> **"Therefore, we must say according to the likely account that this world was truly made a living being, endowed with soul and intelligence, through the providence of God."**

Consequently, we are to conclude that this world was really made an intellectual animal by the providence of God; from being an animal, it immediately became a god. So here we must take notice of two very different gods in Plato. One is a "generated god"—this entire animated world—and the other is that God by whose providence this world was created and thus made an animal and a god. This latter God must necessarily be an unmade, self-existent Deity who does not belong to "generation" but to "essence"—not to becoming, but to immutable being.

Furthermore, those greater parts of the world—the sun, the moon, and the stars (which were also supposed to be animated with their own particular souls)—were accounted gods by Plato, just as they were by other Pagans. He plainly calls them there **visible and generated gods** <note>original: ὁρατοὶ καὶ γεννητοὶ θεοὶ</note>.

Besides these celestial gods, the Earth itself is also supposed by him to be either a god or goddess, according to those ancient copies of the *Timaeus* used by both Cicero and Proclus: <note>original: γῆν δὲ, τροφὸν μὲν ἡμετέραν... πρεσβυτάτην θεῶν ὅσοι ἐντὸς οὐρανοῦ γεγόνασι</note> **"God also fashioned the Earth, our nurse, which circles around the axis that extends through the whole universe; he made it the guardian and creator of night and day, the first and oldest of all the gods that have been generated within the heavens."**

Since that philosopher seems to make the Earth an animal and a god primarily because of its daily rotation upon its own axis, we may conclude that later in his old age (as Plutarch records from Theophrastus) he also accepted that other part of the Pythagorean hypothesis and attributed to the Earth an annual planetary motion around the sun. From this it would follow—as Plotinus expresses it—that the Earth was **one of the stars** <note>original: ἓν τῶν ἄστρων</note>. He was therefore even more inclined to think the Earth was a god, just like the other planets, or at least like the moon. The moon had been formerly represented in the Orphic tradition as simply another habitable Earth. For these verses of Orpheus are recorded by Proclus for that purpose:

<note>original: μήσατο; he devised/fashioned</note>

He specifically identifies the Earth as the oldest of these generated gods, potentially due to its rotation or planetary motion.</summary>

# Plato's Cosmogony, Book I. <note>original: "Cosmogonia"; the study of the origin and development of the universe</note>

->He devised another boundless earth, which the<-
->Immortal gods call Selene, but those on earth call Mene,<-
->Which has many mountains, many cities, and many halls.<-
<note>original Greek: μήσατο δ᾽ ἄλλην γαῖαν ἀπείρατον, ἥν τε σελήνην / Ἀθάνατοι κλήζουσιν, ἐπιχθόνιοι δέ τε μήνην, / Ἢ πόλλ᾽ ὄρε᾽ ἔχῃ, πόλλ᾽ ἄστεα, πολλὰ μέλαθρα.</note>

The sense of this is: *That God, in the creation of the world, fabricated another vast earth besides our own. The immortal gods call this earth Selene, but mortal men call it Mene, or the Moon. It contains many hills and valleys, many cities and houses.* From this, the philosopher Proclus concluded that the Moon was **an ethereal earth** <note>original: γῆν αἰθερίαν</note>. Although Proclus seems to have been a stranger to the Pythagorean system, he was deeply devoted to these Orphic traditions.

<margin>See Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, Book 1, chapter 11.</margin>
After all this, Plato—wishing to show he has omitted nothing in his *Timaean* cosmogony—also speaks of the **birth, origin, or generation** <note>original: Geneſis, Ortus</note> of the **poetic gods**. He describes them as **demons** <note>original: "Demons"; here meaning "daimons," or intermediate spirits between gods and humans</note>, such as Tethys and Phorcys, Saturn and Rhea, Jupiter and Juno, and the like. These seem to be nothing more than the **inanimate parts of the world** and **things of nature** that have been **fictitiously personified and deified** <note>original: θεοποιηθέντα</note> (as is declared elsewhere). The poets decorated this entire subject with much fiction and **physical allegory** <note>original: "Phyſiological Allegory"; an explanation of myths as representing natural or physical processes</note>.

Plato pretends to believe this poetic history of the gods <note>original: "Theogonia"</note> out of a seeming compliance with the laws of his city. He presents it as a tradition delivered down from the **sons of the gods**, who should not be supposed ignorant of their own parents. However, as the historian Eusebius well observes, Plato is actually jeering at it slyly. He plainly hints that these stories are fables when he claims they were introduced not only **without necessary demonstrations** <note>original: ἄνευ ἀναγκαίων ἀποδείξεων</note>, but also **without so much as probabilities** <note>original: ἄνευ εἰκότων</note>.

Nevertheless, Proclus suspected no such irony. Taking Plato to be in very good earnest, he interprets these poetic gods or demons as being the gods **below the Moon** (despite the fact that Plato had mentioned the Earth previously). Proclus calls them **the gods that cause generation** <note>original: γενεσιουργοὺς θεοὺς</note> and seems to understand them as the **animated elements**. In this context, Jupiter is not taken as the **Supreme God** (as he often is elsewhere), but only as the **animated ether**, just as Juno represents the **animated air**. 

On this occasion, Proclus enters into a long dispute to prove that not only were the stars animated with souls, but so were all the other **sublunary bodies or elements** (those below the moon): <margin>page 287.</margin> **"For if the whole world is a happy god, then none of the parts that complete it are godless or devoid of providence. But if all things partake of God and providence, then they share in the divine nature. If this is so, there must be certain orders of gods presiding over them. For if the Heavens, by reason of particular souls and minds, partake of that one Soul and one Mind, why should we not conclude the same concerning the elements? Is it not much more likely that these also, through certain intermediate divine orders, partake of the one divinity of the world?"** <note>original Greek: εἰ γὰρ ὅλος ὁ κόσμος θεὸς εὐδαίμων ἐστὶ... τῆς μιᾶς τοῦ κόσμου θεότητος</note>

<summary>This page explores Plato's description of the Moon as a second Earth and his skeptical treatment of traditional Greek gods as allegories for natural elements, contrasted with Proclus's more literal, theological interpretation.</summary>

# CHAPTER IV. A Theogony <note>original: "Theogonia"; a story of the origin and descent of the gods</note>

Certain intermediate orders of gods partake in that one Divinity of the entire world. For this reason, a little earlier, the same Proclus strongly condemns certain ancient natural philosophers <note>original: "Physiologers"; those who studied the internal workings of nature</note>, whom he believes Aristotle followed: <margin>Page 285.</margin>

> *Many of the natural philosophers considered these elements to be inanimate, moved at random and without providence. For while they admitted that the heavenly bodies—because of the order that appears within them—partake of Mind and the gods, they left this sublunary world (the realm of change or "generation") to float up and down without providence. Aristotle later followed this view, assigning only the "immovable intelligences" to preside over the celestial spheres (whether eight or more), but leaving all the lower elements dead and inanimate.* <note>original Greek: πολλοῖς γὰρ φυσιολόγων... ταῦτα καταλείπων</note>

Lastly, besides all those other mundane gods mentioned before as being "generated" together with the world—though Proclus seems to hold a different opinion—it is clear that Plato does not entirely forget those beings properly called **demons** <note>original: "Dæmons"; here meaning "daimons," or spirits intermediate between gods and humans</note> in his *Timaeus*. He insists on them elsewhere <margin>Page 41.</margin>, but in the very next words he clearly alludes to them in this way: *the gods who appear visibly to us as often as they please, or who can appear and disappear at will* <note>original Greek: ὅσοι φαίνονται καθ’ ὅσον ἂν ἐθέλωσι θεοὶ</note>. He also speaks of their "genesis" or generation as part of the **Cosmogony** <note>original: "Cosmogonia"; the study of the origin of the universe</note>. Afterward, calling them **Junior Gods** <note>original: νέοι Θεοὶ</note>, he describes them as those whose specific office was to superintend and preside over **human affairs**, <margin>Page 42.</margin> *and to govern this mortal animal, man, as well and excellently as possible, so that he should not fail of doing well or being happy, except as he becomes a cause of evil and misery to himself by the abuse of his own liberty.* <note>original Greek: καὶ κατὰ δύναμιν... αἴτιον</note>

This much is from Plato's *Timaeus*; however, the same point could also be proven from his other writings. This is particularly clear in a passage from his tenth book of *Laws*, where he takes notice again of the **Theogony** <note>original: "Theogonia"</note> of the ancients, noting that it had been degraded and corrupted by a great mixture of impious and immoral fables. 

> *There are, he says, certain stories and traditions extant among us Athenians—some very ancient and written partly in verse and partly in prose—concerning the gods. These describe how the heavens and the other gods were first made or generated, and then, carrying on their fabulous theogony further, describe how these generated gods afterward interacted with one another and, by fathering children in the manner of men, begat other gods.* <note>original Greek: 'Εἰσὶν ἡμῖν... ὡμίλησαν</note>

In this passage, the philosopher takes off his mask <note>original: "vizard"</note> and plainly reveals his great dislike of that entire mythical theogony (even though he acknowledges elsewhere...

### Hesiod's *Theogony*, the *Cosmogony*. Book I.

...elsewhere that it did contain underlying meanings <note>original Greek: ὑπονοίας (hyponoias)</note>, that is, *physical allegories* beneath the surface), as a thing that was destructive of all piety and virtue, because it attributed all human passions and vices to the gods. However, it plainly appears from this that the *Theogony* <note>The birth or genealogy of the gods</note> and the *Cosmogony* <note>The origin or creation of the universe</note> were one and the same thing; the *origin of the gods* here being the *origin of the heavens*, and of the sun, moon, stars, and the like.

Moreover, this same point is sufficiently manifest even from *Hesiod*'s own *Theogony*. This was undoubtedly the work at which *Plato* primarily aimed his criticism, and if it were not absolutely the first, it is certainly the most ancient writing of that kind still in existence. For in the beginning of that poem, *Hesiod* invokes his Muses in this manner:

-> Hail, children of Zeus, and give me a lovely song. <-
-> Celebrate also the sacred race of the immortals who always exist, <-
-> Who were born of Earth and starry Heaven, <-
-> And of dark Night, and those whom the salty Sea nourished. <-
-> Say also how in the beginning the gods and the Earth were made, <-
-> And the rivers, and the boundless Sea surging with its swell, <-
-> And the shining stars, and the broad Heaven above, <-
-> And the gods, the givers of good things, who were born from them. <-
<note>original Greek: χαίρετε τέκνα Διὸς... and Latin: Salvete natæ Jovis... The author provides both the original Greek and a Latin translation; both are translated here into English.</note>

Where we see plainly that the *origin of the gods* is the *origin of the Earth, Heaven, stars, seas, rivers*, and other things born from them (just as, among the rest, he likely includes the spirits <note>original: "Demons"</note> and nymphs of whom the same *Hesiod* speaks elsewhere). But immediately after this invocation of the *Muses*, the poet begins with *Chaos*, *Tartarus* <note>original: "Tartara"</note>, and *Love* as the first principles. He then proceeds to the production of the *Earth*, and of *Night* out of *Chaos*; of the *Aether* and of *Day* from *Night*; and of the *starry heavens, mountains, and seas, etc.* All of this *genesis* or birth of the gods is really nothing but a poetical description of the *Cosmogony*. Throughout the rest of that entire poem, everything seems to be natural philosophy <note>original: "Physiology"; in this period, the term referred to the study of the physical world and nature</note> veiled under fiction and allegories. 

And thus the ancient *Scholia* <note>Ancient commentaries or explanatory notes written in the margins of a manuscript</note> upon that book begin: "We must know that the entire account of the theogony suggests a physical explanation of existing things" <note>original Greek: ἰσέον ὅτι ὁ περὶ τῆς θεογονίας λόγος φυσικὴν διήγησιν τῶν ὄντων ὑπαγορεύει</note>. *Hesiod*'s gods were not only the living parts of the world, but also all the other things of nature, fictitiously personified and deified, or improperly called gods and goddesses.

<meta>This page continues the argument that the ancient "Theogony" (the birth of the gods) was synonymous with "Cosmogony" (the birth of the physical universe), extending the evidence from the Greeks to the Persians and Egyptians.</meta>

# CHAPTER IV. *How the Pagan Theogony Was Mistaken.*

Neither was it only the doctrine of the Greeks that the *world* was thus *made* or *generated*, and that the *generation of the world* was a *Theogony* <note>original: *Theogonia*; the birth or genealogy of the gods</note> or a *generation of gods* (the *world* itself and its various parts being considered gods by them), but also the same was true of the other *Barbarian Pagans*. <margin>In the Preface, page 2.</margin> For *Diogenes Laertius* has recorded, concerning the *Persian Magi*, <note>original Greek: ἀποφαίνεσθαι περί τε οὐσίας θεῶν καὶ γενέσεως, οὓς καὶ πῦρ εἶναι καὶ γῆν καὶ ὕδωρ</note> *that they declared both the essence and the generation of the gods, whom they also said were fire, earth, and water.* That is, the *animated elements* were gods (as *Proclus* also declared earlier), and these, together with the *world*, were *generated* or had a *beginning*. <margin>In the Persian Sacrifices, <note>original Greek: μάγος ἀνὴρ παρεστὼς ἐπαείδει Θεογονίην</note> *one of the Magi standing by sings the Theogony* (that is, the Cosmogony). Herodotus in *Clio*, number 132.</margin> And both *Laertius* and *Diodorus* describe the opinion of the ancient *Egyptians* as being that the *world* was *generated* or had a *temporary production*; they also held that the *sun*, *moon*, and other parts of the *world* were *gods*. But while the same *Diodorus* writes of certain *Egyptian gods* <note>original Greek: οἳ γένεσιν ἀΐδιον ἐσχηκότες</note> *who had an eternal generation*, he seems to mean by this only the *celestial gods*—the *sun, moon*, and *stars*—as distinct from those other *heroes* and *men-gods*. These latter are again described by him as <note>original Greek: οἳ θνητοὶ ὑπάρξαντες, διὰ δὲ σύνεσιν καὶ κοινὴν ἀνθρώπων εὐεργεσίαν, τετυχηκότες τῆς ἀθανασίας</note> *those who, though naturally mortal, yet by reason of their wisdom, virtue, and beneficence toward mankind, had been advanced to immortality.*

And by this time we think it appears sufficiently that the *Theogony* of the ancients is not to be understood merely as their *heroes* and *men-gods*, or as all their *gods* supposedly being nothing more than *mortal men* (<note>original Latin: *Dii Mortalibus nati Matribus*</note> "*Gods born of mortal mothers*," as *Cotta* speaks in *Cicero*) who, according to the more *common* meaning of the word, had been *generated* <note>original: *Humano More*; in the human manner</note> as some otherwise *learned men* have seemed to suppose. Instead, it extends to all the *inferior Pagan gods*, some of whom were *animated parts* of the *visible world*, such as the *sun, moon, stars*, and *earth*. So their *Theogony* was the very same thing as the *Cosmogony* <note>The origin of the universe</note>, or at least a part of it. Despite this, we do not deny that there was also a certain mixture of *history* and *herology* <note>The accounts or study of heroes</note> inserted into the *Pagan fables* of the gods, and complicated all along together with *physiology* <note>The study of nature and physical causes</note>.

We are next to observe that both this *Theogony* and *Cosmogony* of the ancient Pagans—their *generation* of the *world* and *gods*—is to be understood as a *temporary production* of them, by which they were *made* <note>original Greek: ἐκ μὴ ὄντων</note> *out of things that do not exist*, or brought into *being* from a *preceding non-existence*. For it was the general tradition among the Pagans that the *world* was made out of a preceding *chaos*, as shall be further declared afterward. And *Aristotle* affirms that before his time, this *genesis* and *temporary production* of the *world* had been universally accepted by all, and specifically that *Plato* was a *supporter* of the same. Nevertheless, the majority of the later *Platonists* endeavor with all their might to force a contrary sense upon his *Timaeus*. This is something that *Plutarch* long ago observed in this manner: <note>original Greek: οἱ πλεῖστοι τῶν χρωμένων πλάτωνι, φοβούμενοι, καὶ παραλυπούμενοι</note> *Most of those who interpret Plato, being afraid and distressed...*

It clarifies that while some gods were deified humans, the primary "generated gods" were actually the elements and celestial bodies.</summary>

# That Plato really asserted, BOOK. I.

<header>That Plato really asserted, BOOK. I.</header>

<margin>Plutarch, *On the Generation of the Soul in Plato's Timaeus*, page 1013.</margin> <note>original Greek: λυπόμενοι, πάντα μηχανῶνται, καὶ παραβιάζονται καὶ στρέφουσι, ὡς τι δεινὸν καὶ ἄῤῥητον οἰόμενοι δεῖν περικαλύπτειν καὶ ἀρνεῖσθαι, τήν τε τοῦ κόσμου τήν τε τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτοῦ γένεσιν καὶ σύστασιν, οὐκ ἐξ ἀϊδίου συνεστώτων, οὐδὲ τὸν ἄπειρον χρόνον οὕτως ἐχόντων·</note> "The *most* of *Plato's followers*, being infinitely troubled and perplexed in their minds, turn *themselves* every way, using all manner of arts and offering all kinds of violence to his text. They do this because they conceive *that they ought by all means possible to hide and conceal that opinion (as if it were insane and detestable) that the world and its soul were generated, rather than having continued from eternity or through a succession of infinite time.*" Notwithstanding this, we conceive it to be undeniably evident that *Plato*, in his *Timaeus*, does assert the *genesis* <note>origin or birth</note> of the world in this sense—namely, as a *temporary production* that did not exist from *eternity* or without a *beginning*.

First, because at the start of that discourse, he opposes these two things to one another: <note>original Greek: τὸ ἀεὶ ὂν</note> "*that which always is*" and <note>original Greek: τὸ γινόμενον ἔχον</note> "*that which is generated or made*." *Therefore*, in affirming the world to have been *generated*, he must necessarily deny its *eternity*. Again, the question is so precisely stated by him afterward that there is no possibility of any excuse <note>original: "subterfuge"</note> left: <note>original Greek: πότερον ἦν ἀεὶ γενέσεως ἀρχὴν ἔχων οὐδεμίαν, ἢ γέγονεν, ἀπ' ἀρχῆς τινος ἀρξάμενος·</note> "*Whether the world always was, having no beginning or generation, or whether it was made or generated, having commenced from a certain epoch?*" To which the answer is: <note>original Greek: γέγονεν</note> "*that it was made or had a beginning.*"

Moreover, this philosopher plainly affirms there that time itself was made, or had a beginning: <note>original Greek: χρόνος δ' οὖν μετ' οὐρανοῦ γέγονεν, ἵνα ἅμα γεννηθέντες, ἅμα καὶ λυθῶσιν, ἄν ποτε λύσις τις αὐτῶν γένηται·</note> "*Time was made together with the heavens, so that being generated together, they might be dissolved together likewise—if, at least, there should ever be any dissolution of them.*" Besides this, he plainly declares that before this *orderly world* was produced, its *matter* *moved disorderly*: <note>original Greek: πᾶν ὅσον ἦν ὁρατὸν, παραλαβὼν, οὐκ ἡσυχίαν ἄγον, ἀλλὰ κινούμενον πλημμελῶς καὶ ἀτάκτως, εἰς τάξιν αὐτὸ ἤγαγεν ἐκ τῆς ἀταξίας·</note> "*God, taking all that matter which existed (not then resting, but moving confusedly and disorderly), brought it into order out of confusion.*" This is no different than if he had said God made this world out of a preceding *chaos*; which, as we said before, was the constant tradition of the ancient *Pagans*.

Now, as to authority, we may well conclude that *Aristotle* was better able to understand both *Plato's philosophy* and the Greek language than any of those *junior Platonists* who lived hundreds of years later. And yet we are not quite destitute of other supporting votes <note>original: "suffrages"</note> besides *Aristotle's*. Not only *Philo* the Jew, but also *Plutarch* and *Atticus* (who were both *Platonic Pagans*) voted on this side, as did *Alexander of Aphrodisias*, a judicious *Peripatetic* <note>a follower of Aristotle's philosophy</note>.

The only significant objection comes from what *Plato* himself writes in his *third* and *sixth book of Laws*. In the former, *Clinias* and the Athenian *Guest* <note>original: "Hospes"; often translated as the "Athenian Stranger"</note> discourse together in this manner concerning the original or first beginning of *commonwealths*: <margin>Plato's *Laws*, page 676, Stephanus edition.</margin> <note>original Greek: πολιτείας δ' ἀρχὴν τίνα ποτὲ φῶμεν γεγονέναι; ΚΛ. λέγεις δὲ πόθεν; ΑΘ. Οἶμαι μὲν ἀπὸ χρόνου μήκους τε καὶ ἀπειρίας, καὶ τῶν μεταβολῶν ἐν τῷ τοιούτῳ. ΚΛ. Πῶς λέγεις; ΑΘ. φέρε, ἀφ' οὗ πόλεις τ' εἰσὶ καὶ ἄνθρωποι πολιτευόμενοι, δοκεῖς ἄν ποτε</note> "*What shall we say was the beginning of a political constitution?* Clinias: *From what point do you mean?* Athenian: *I think from a great length and infinity of time, and the changes occurring within it.* Clinias: *How do you mean?* Athenian: *Come now, since there have been cities and men living in states, do you think that ever...*"

<summary>The author argues that Plato's "Timaeus" clearly describes the world as having a beginning in time, refuting later Platonists who attempted to interpret his work as supporting an eternal universe. He cites Aristotle, Plutarch, and others to support this literal reading of a temporary production of the world from chaos.</summary>

### CHAPTER IV. *The Newness or Beginning of the World.*

<note>original Greek: κατανοῆσαι χρόνου πλῆθος ὅσον γέγονεν ; ΚΛ. Οὐκουν ῥᾴδιόν γε οὐδαμῶς. ΑΘ. Τὸ δέ γε ὡς ἄπειρόν τι καὶ ἀμήχανον ἂν εἴη. ΚΛ. Πάνυ μὲν οὖν ἐν τούτῳ γε. ΑΘ. Μῶν γε οὖν ὦ μύριαι μηδὲ αὖ μυρίαις ἡμῖν γεγονόσι πόλεις ἐν τούτῳ τῷ χρόνῳ; κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν δὲ τοῦ πλήθους λόγον, οὐκ ἐλάττους ἐφθαρμέναι; πεπολιτευμέναι δ’ αὖ πάσας πολιτείας πολλάκις ἑκασταχοῦ; καὶ τοτὲ μὲν ἐξ ἐλαττόνων, μείζους, τοτὲ δ’ ἐκ μειζόνων, ἐλάττους· καὶ χείρους ἐκ βελτιόνων γεγονόσι, καὶ βελτίους ἐκ χειρόνων.</note>

*Athenian (Ath.): Can we understand how much time has passed since cities and governments began?*
*Cleinias (Cl.): That is not easy at all.*
*Ath.: It would seem to be a kind of infinity and something unimaginable.*
*Cl.: That is certainly true in this case.*
*Ath.: Have there not been tens of thousands—indeed, countless thousands—of cities born during this time? And by the same logic, have just as many not been destroyed? Have they not practiced every form of government many times in every place? Have they not grown from small to large, or shrunk from large to small? And have they not become worse from better, and better from worse?*

Now we argue that if **Plato** intended here to claim an absolute infinity of past time, then it must be admitted that in his old age (when he wrote his book of ***Laws***), he changed his opinion from what it was before when he wrote his ***Timaeus***. If so, he logically should have retracted his earlier view, which he does not do here. In truth, the meaning of this philosopher in these cited words seems to be this: not that there was an absolute infinity of past time (as **Proclus** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist who argued for the eternity of the world</note> argues, taking advantage of that word <term>apeiria</term> <note>original: ἀπειρία; meaning infinity or boundlessness</note>), but only that the world had lasted for such a length of time that it was essentially inestimable or uncomputable to us. During this time, as he adds, there have been several successive destructions and disappearances of humanity caused by various accidents—specifically one very remarkable deluge and flood.

<margin>Page 781.</margin>
The latter passage, in his sixth book of ***Laws***, reads as follows: <note>original Greek: ἡ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένεσις ἢ τὸ παράπαν ἀρχὴν οὐδεμίαν εἴληχεν, οὐδ' ἕξει ποτέ γε τελευτήν · ἀλλ' ἦν τε ἀεὶ καὶ ἔσται πάντως · ἢ μῆκός τι τῆς ἀρχῆς ἀφ' οὗ γέγονεν, ἀμήχανον ἂν χρόνον ὅσον γεγονὸς ἂν εἴη.</note> *Either the human race had no beginning at all and will never have an end—but always was and always will be—or else there has been an unimaginable length of time since its beginning.* This passage sheds even more light on the first one, for we may well conclude that by "something infinite and unimaginable" <note>original Greek: ἄπειρόν τι καὶ ἀμήχανον</note> there, he did not mean an *absolute infinity* of time, but only a beginning that was very remote or distant. This is because "unimaginable" <note>original Greek: ἀμήχανον</note> is clearly used in that sense <note>original: "fence," an archaic OCR error for "sense"</note> here. We believe, therefore, that this was **Plato's** opinion in his old age when he wrote the ***Laws***: that although the world had a beginning, it had continued for a very long time that we cannot calculate. Or, at least, he thought it appropriate to express himself in that manner, perhaps because of the criticisms of **Aristotle** or others against his ***Timaeus***. By doing so, he might slightly soften his theory on the **newness of the world** <note>original: "Novity of the World"</note> by pushing its starting date back to such a great distance.

Now it is very true, as we have suggested several times before, that there have been among the pagans both **Theogonists** <note>those who write about the origin or birth of the gods</note> and **Cosmogonists** <note>those who write about the origin or birth of the universe</note>...

<summary>The author examines passages from Plato's Laws to argue that Plato did not believe in an eternally existing world, but rather one with a beginning so distant it is "unimaginable" to humans. He suggests Plato phrased it this way in his later years to counter criticisms from Aristotle while still maintaining his core belief from the Timaeus.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on different types of "theogonists"—those who write about the origins of gods—distinguishing between those whose theories lead to atheism and those, like Plato, who maintain a belief in a supreme, uncreated Creator.</meta>

# BOOK I.
## That Plato was a Divine Theogonist

...theogonists, too, who were *atheists*. They abused the word *gods* in several ways. Some of them, such as **Anaximander**, understood "gods" to be *inanimate worlds* successively generated out of *senseless matter* and then corrupted back into it. Others, such as **Anaximenes** and **Democritus**, allowed that there were certain *animals* and *understanding beings* superior to humans, but only such as were *natural* and *mortal*, just like humans, and they called these by the *name of gods*. **St. Augustine** gives us this account of the first of these two philosophers: 

> "Anaximenes made infinite air the first origin and cause of all things. Yet he was not silent about the gods, nor did he deny them. Nevertheless, he did not believe the air was made by the gods, but that the gods themselves were generated out of the air." <note>original Latin: *Anaximenes omnes rerum causas Infinito Aeri dedit, nec Deos negavit aut tacuit, non tamen ab ipsis Aerem factum, sed ipsos ex Aere ortos credidit*</note>.

These were therefore the kind of *theogonists* <note>original: "Theogonists"; those who write about the genealogy or birth of the gods.</note> who supposed all the gods, without exception, to be *generable* and *corruptible*. They acknowledged no <term>unmade God</term> <note>original Greek: Θεὸν ἀγένητον</note> at all—no *uncreated and self-existent understanding being*. Instead, they concluded that *senseless matter* was the only <term>uncreated</term> <note>original Greek: ἀγένητον</note> origin of all things, which is *absolute atheism*. 

Notwithstanding this, it is certain that not all the *pagan theogonists* were *atheists* (any more than all their *cosmogonists* <note>Those who describe the origin of the cosmos or universe.</note> were *theists*). There was another sort of *theogonist* among them who supposed that while all the *inferior worldly gods* were *made* or *generated* in one sense or another, they still asserted <term>one unmade and self-existent God</term> <note>original Greek: One Θεὸν ἀγένητον κᲲ αὐθυπόστατον</note>—one *Supreme unmade self-existent Deity* who was the cause of them all. For the sake of distinction from those atheistic ones, these may be called *Divine Theogonists*.

And that **Plato** was such a *Divine Theogonist* is a matter that we consider beyond question. But if there had been any doubt concerning it, it would have been sufficiently removed by those passages cited earlier from his *Timaeus*. To those, however, for the sake of fuller satisfaction, the following two may be added. 

The first: <margin>page 34.</margin> "This then was the whole reasoning of the God who always exists, concerning the god who was at some time to be made." <note>original Greek: ὗτος δὴ πᾶς ὄντος ἀεὶ λογισμὸς θεοῦ, περὶ δὲ τὸν ποτὲ ἐσόμενον θεὸν λογισθεὶς. The author notes that "ὄντος" (being/existing) is the correct reading from the Aldine edition, rather than "ὄντως" (really/truly) found in the edition of Henri Estienne, which followed an error in the edition by Marsilio Ficino.</note> 

Accordingly, the words are rendered this way by **Cicero**: 

> "This was the reasoning or resolution of that God who always existed, thinking about a God who would exist at some time; he made him smooth and spherical, etc." <note>original Latin: *Hæc Deus is qui Semper erat, de Aliquando Futuro Deo cogitans, levem eum effecit, & undique æquabilem, &c.*</note>. 

There, it immediately follows in Cicero's version: 

> "Thus that Eternal God procreated this perfectly happy God, the world." <note>original Latin: *Sic Deus ille Æternus, Hunc Perfectè Beatum Deum procreavit*</note>. 

In this passage, mention is plainly made of *two gods*: one a *generated god* (the living world, called elsewhere in Plato a <term>generated divinity</term> <note>original Greek: θεῖον γεννητὸν</note>), and another *eternal and unmade God* <note>original Latin: *Innatus & Infectus Deus*</note>, who was the cause of the world's generation or production. Or, to stay close to Plato's own language, there is one God who belonged to *Genesis* (or that category of *being* which he calls *generation*), and who therefore must have a prior cause for his existence, since nothing can be made without a cause; and...

<summary>The author distinguishes between "atheistic theogonists" who believe gods are born from matter and "divine theogonists" like Plato, who believe in one eternal, uncreated God who created the universe as a "generated god."</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Timaeus, Anaximander, Anaximenes, theogony, atheism, Cicero, St. Augustine, generated god, unmade God</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the argument that Plato recognized a distinction between "generated gods" (the stars and the universe) and a single, uncreated Creator, thereby categorizing him as a "divine theogonist" rather than an atheist one.</meta>

# CHAPTER IV. A Divine Theogonist.

...and another God, who was truly and properly "Essence" <note>original Greek: οὐσία</note>, an *Immutable Essence*. This God was the cause of that *Generated God*—the *Universe*—and therefore the cause of all things. 

Another passage from *Plato* is on page 41 of his *Timaeus*: 

> "When, therefore, all the gods—both those who move visibly through the heavens and those who appear to us whenever they please (that is, both the stars and demons)—were generated or created, that God who made this whole universe spoke to these generated gods in this way: 'You gods of gods, of whom I myself am the maker and father, attend to these works which were made by me.'" <note>original Greek: ἐπεὶ δ᾽ οὖν πάντες ὅσοι τε περιπολοῦσι φανερῶς καὶ ὅσοι φαίνονται καθ᾽ ὅσον ἂν ἐθέλωσι θεοὶ, γένεσιν ἔσχον, λέγει πρὸς αὐτοὺς ὁ τόδε τὸ πᾶν γεννήσας, τάδε, Θεοὶ θεῶν ὧν ἐγὼ δημιουργός, πατήρ τε ἔργων, ἃ δι᾿ ἐμοῦ γενόμενα</note>

In this passage, the phrase "gods of gods" <note>original Greek: Θεοὶ θεῶν</note>—despite various other interpretations suggested by *Proclus*—seems to have been very well translated by *Cicero* as: "You gods who are the progeny or offspring of the gods" <note>original Latin: *Dii qui Deorum Satu orti estis*</note>. 

The "gods" whose offspring these *generated gods* (the *animated stars* and *demons*) are said to be must necessarily be those "eternal gods" <note>original Greek: ἀΐδιοι θεοὶ</note> mentioned elsewhere in the same *Timaeus*. For example, the philosopher calls the world a "generated or created image of the eternal gods" <note>original Greek: τῇ ἀϊδίων θεῶν γεγονὸς ἄγαλμα</note>. *Cicero* should also be understood as referring to these when he speaks of the world being *made by the gods and by the counsel of the gods*. 

These *eternal gods* of *Plato* were called by his followers "supramundane gods" <note>original Greek: Θεοὶ ὑπερκόσμιοι</note> (gods existing beyond the physical world). According to the stricter definition of "generation" <note>original Greek: γένεσις</note> used by both *Plato* and *Aristotle*—meaning a *temporary production* of things "from nothing" <note>original Greek: ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων</note>—these gods were indeed all "uncreated" <note>original Greek: ἀγέννητοι</note>. This is because they never *did not* exist; they had no beginning to their existence. 

Nevertheless, the philosopher did not suppose them all to be "self-originated" <note>original Greek: αὐτόγονοι</note> and "self-subsistent beings" <note>original Greek: αὐθυπόστατοι</note>, or first principles. Instead, only *one* of them was truly self-originated, and the rest were derived from that one. We believe it is quite true, as *Proclus* affirms <margin>In the *Timaeus*, page 116</margin>, "that Plato reduces all things to one principle, even matter itself" <note>original Greek: ὅτι ὁ Πλάτων ἐπὶ μίαν ἀρχὴν ἀνάγει πάντα</note>. It is unquestionable that he derives all his gods from *one*. 

Therefore, all those *eternal gods* of *Plato* (except for one) were not "generated" <note>original Greek: γέννητοι</note> in one sense—that is, "according to time" <note>original Greek: κατὰ χρόνον</note> or having a temporary beginning. However, as *Proclus* distinguishes, they were still "generated from a cause" <note>original Greek: γέννητοι ἀπ᾽ αἰτίας</note>, meaning they were produced from a superior cause. There is only one such "unproduced" <note>original Greek: ἀγέννητον</note> or uncreated deity. 

Thus, according to *Plato*, there were *two* types of *secondary*, inferior, and derivative gods: 

1.  **Mundane Gods** <note>original Greek: Θεοὶ ἐγκόσμιοι</note>: Those who were all created in time along with the world. *Plato's* "theogony" <note>original Greek: Θεογονία</note> and "generation of the gods" <note>original Greek: γένεσις θεῶν</note> refer properly to these. 
2.  **Supramundane and Eternal Gods** <note>original Greek: ὑπερκόσμιοι and ἀΐδιοι θεοὶ</note>: All of whom (except for one) were produced from that one and depended on it as their cause. 

We will speak again of these inferior eternal gods of the *Platonists* and *Pythagoreans* later. In the meantime, it is evident that in the passage from *Plato* cited above, there is clear mention of both "gods who are generated" <note>original Greek: θεοὶ γένεσιν ἔχοντες</note>—that is, "produced gods" <note>original Latin: *Dii Orti*</note> who were made along with the world—and "the one who made this whole universe" <note>original Greek: ὁ τόδε τὸ πᾶν γεννήσας</note>. This creator god is himself, in every way, "unmade" <note>original Greek: ἀγέννητος</note> or unproduced.

<meta>catchword: And</meta>

<summary>This page analyzes Plato's Timaeus to show that while he speaks of many "generated" gods (the stars and universe), he ultimately subordinates them to a single, uncreated, and eternal Creator who is the first principle of all existence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that Plato and other intelligent pagan thinkers were both "theists" (believers in God) and "theogonists" (those who describe the birth of gods), because they viewed the creation of the world as the birth of "generated gods" under one supreme, uncreated Creator.</meta>

# Pagan Theogonists Assertors, BOOK I.

And accordingly, he [Plato] afterwards adds: "And he who ordered all these things remained in his own characteristic nature; and while he remained, his children, having understood the father's order, obeyed it." <note>original Greek: καὶ ὁ μὲν δὴ ταῦτα πάντα διατάξας, ἔμενεν ἐν τῷ ἑαυτοῦ κατ' τρόπον ἤθει· μενόντος δὲ νοήσαντες οἱ παῖδες τὴν τοῦ πατρὸς τάξιν, ἐπείθοντο αὐτῇ</note> Cicero translates this as: "And indeed that God who composed all things remained constantly in his own state; however, those who had been created by him (the gods), when they had recognized their Parent's order, followed it, etc." <note>original Latin: *Atque is quidem (Deus) qui cuncta composuit, constanter in suo manebat statu, qui autem erant ab eo creati (Dii) cùm Parentis ordinem cognovissent, hunc sequebantur, &c.*</note> That is, the God who framed all things remained constantly in his former state, and his "sons"—or the gods created by him—observed his order and appointment.

Plato was not alone in this view; the majority of other intelligent pagan theists <note>theists: those who believe in a God or gods</note> agreed with him throughout history regarding the generation <note>generation: in this context, the birth or creation</note> of the mundane gods <note>mundane gods: gods belonging to the physical cosmos, such as the stars or the Earth</note>. Thus, they were both theists and theogonists <note>theogonists: people who write about the origins and genealogies of gods</note>. They understood their *theogony* (the generation of gods) as nothing other than a divine *cosmogony* (the creation of the world by God), because they believed the world itself was animated <note>animated: possessing a soul or life force</note> and that its various parts were gods. 

Consequently, they asserted these three things: 
1. A *cosmogony*: the generation of the world, meaning it was not eternal but had a beginning <note>original: "Novity"</note>. 
2. That this *cosmogony* was also a *theogony*: the world itself and its various animated parts were esteemed as gods. 
3. And lastly, that both these gods and the world were made and produced by one "unproduced and self-originated Deity" <note>original Greek: θεὸς ἀγένητος καὶ αὐτοφυής</note>. 

We may briefly illustrate all these points in the works of Publius Ovidius Naso (Ovid). His paganism is clearly seen in his *Fasti* and all his other writings; he also left the stage of history before Christianity appeared, and so he may be presumed to represent the generally accepted doctrine of the pagans of that time. First, regarding the generation and beginning of the world and its production out of a chaos, he fully acknowledges it in these verses:

<margin>Metamorphoses, book 1.</margin>
> "Before the sea, the land, and the sky that covers all, 
> Nature had only one face throughout the whole world, 
> Which they called Chaos: a raw, unordered mass, 
> Nothing but sluggish weight, a heap of discordant seeds 
> Of things poorly joined together in the same place. 
> No Sun <note>original: Titan</note> yet provided light to the world, 
> Nor did the Moon <note>original: Phoebe</note> renew her horns by growing; 
> The Earth did not yet hang in the surrounding air, 
> Balanced by its own weight, nor had the Sea <note>original: Amphitrite</note> 
> Stretched her arms along the long margins of the lands. 
> Wherever there was land, etc."
> <note>original Latin: *Ante Mare & Terras, &, quod tegit omnia, Cælum, / Unus erat toto Naturæ Vultus in orbe, / Quem dixere Chaos; rudis indigestaque moles, / Nec quicquam nisi pondus iners, congestaque eodem / Non benè junctarum discordia semina rerum. / Nullus adhuc mundo præbebat Lumina Titan, / Nec nova crescendo reparabat cornua Phæbe, / Nec circumfuso pendebat in äere Tellus, / Ponderibus librata suis; nec brachia longo / Margine terrarum porrexerat Amphitrite. / Quaque erat & Tellus, &c.*</note>

Which, in Mr. George Sandys' English translation (with some minor alterations), says:

> "Before the sea and earth and heaven were framed,
> One face had Nature which they Chaos named.
> No Sun <note>original: Titan</note> yet the World with Light adorns,
> Nor waxing Moon <note>original: Phoebe</note> fills her waned Horns;"

Using Ovid's "Metamorphoses" as evidence, the author argues that "theogony" (the origin of gods) was actually a form of "cosmogony" (the origin of the universe).</summary>
