# CHAP. IV. Of One Unmade Deity.

> *Nor hung the self-poised Earth in thin Air placed,*
> *Nor did the sea <note>original: "Amphitrite," a Greek sea goddess</note> the vast shore embrace;*
> *Earth, Air, and Sea confounded, etc.*

In the next place, when there was a *World* made out of this *Chaos*, that this *Cosmogonia* <note>original Greek: *cosmogony*, or the generation of the world</note> or Generation of the *World*, was also a *Theogonia* <note>original Greek: *theogony*, or the generation of gods</note> or Generation of *Gods*, is plainly indicated in these verses:

> *Lest any region should be empty of its own living creatures, the stars and the forms of gods possess the heavenly floor.* <note>original Latin: *Neu Regio foret ulla suis Animalibus orba, Astra tenent cœleste solum, Formæque Deorum.*</note>

To this sense:

> *That no living creatures might be left out,*
> *The Gods, in the form of Stars, possess the sky.*

And all this was effected, and this orderly world system produced out of a disorderly, confused *Chaos*, not by a *fortuitous* <note>random or accidental</note> *motion* of matter, or the *jumbling of atoms*, but by the *Providence* and *Command* of **One Unmade Deity**, which was also that which furnished all the several parts of the world with their respective animals: the sea with fishes, the earth with men, and the *heaven with gods*. This is also declared by the poet <note>Ovid, in his *Metamorphoses*</note>:

> *God and a better nature ended this strife, for he separated the lands from the heaven, and the waves from the lands, and separated the clear sky from the thick air, etc. Thus when whoever of the gods it was had divided the heap and reduced the parts into members; first, so the earth would not be unequal on any side, he rounded it into the shape of a great globe. Then he spread out the seas, and ordered them to swell with rapid winds, etc. Thus the Creator's care distinguished the mass into the same number of parts, etc.* <note>original Latin: *Hanc Deus & Melior litem Natura diremit, Nam Cælo Terras, & Terris abscidit Undas: Et liquidum spisso secrevit ab Aere Cælum, &c. Sic ubi dispositam, Quisquis fuit Ille Deorum, Congeriem secuit, sectámque in membra redegit; Principio terram, nè non æqualis ab omni Parte foret, magni speciem glomeravit in orbis: Tum freta diffudit, rapidísque tumescere ventis Jussit, &c. Sic onus inclusum, numero distinxit eodem Cura Dei, &c.*</note>

> *This strife (with better nature) God decides,*
> *He Earth from Heaven, the Sea from Earth divides:*
> *He pure ether extracts from grosser air.*
> *All of which, unfolded by His prudent care*
> *From that blind mass; then happily separated*
> *In peaceful order, He confined them to their places, etc.*
> *Whatever God it was that performed this division,*
> *And brought every part to its proper proportion,*
> *First, lest the Earth should appear unequal,*
> *He turned it into the shape of a sphere.*
> *Then he spread out the seas, commanding them to roar*
> *With rushing winds, and gave the land a shore.*
> *To those he added springs, ponds, and immense lakes,*
> *And rivers which their winding borders fence.*

# Pagans, both Theogonists Book I.

While that learned paraphrast <note>likely a reference to a commentator on Ovid, such as Raphael Regius or George Sandys</note> supposed (and not without some probability) that *God and the Better Nature* <note>original Latin: *Deus & Melior Natura*</note> were one and the same thing, we instead conceive them to be distinct. We see one as subordinate to the other as its instrument: *God and the Plastic Nature* <note>original: "Plastick Nature," referring to an unconscious, formative power in the universe that carries out God's plan</note>. This agrees with what Aristotle writes in his *Physics*: *Mind and nature were both together the cause of this universe* <note>original Greek: *Νοῦς καὶ φύσις αἴτιον τοῦδε τοῦ παντός*</note>.

Nevertheless, we must observe here that although the poet <note>Ovid</note> speaks more than once of *God in the singular*, calling him the *Maker of the World* <note>original Latin: *Mundi Fabricator*</note>, *That Architect of Things* <note>original Latin: *Ille Opifex Rerum*</note>, and the *Origin of a Better World* <note>original Latin: *Mundi melioris Origo*</note>, he nonetheless affirms something else when he writes of the creation of man. In a typical Pagan fashion, he claims that although man was made by God, he was made according to the *image or likeness of the Gods who govern all things.*

->*A more sacred animal, capable of higher thought,*<-
->*Was still missing; one that could rule over the rest.*<-
->*Man was born: whether that Maker of things,*<-
->*The Origin of a better world, framed him from divine seed,*<-
->*Or whether the fresh earth, recently separated from the high*<-
->*Sky, still retained the seeds of the kindred heaven—*<-
->*Which the son of Iapetus <note>Prometheus</note>, mixing it with river water,*<-
->*Shaped into the image of the Gods who rule all things.*<-
<note>original Latin: *Sanctius his Animal, mentisque capacius altæ / Deerat adhuc, & quod dominari in cetera posset: / Natus homo est: sive hunc divino semine fecit, / Ille Opifex rerum, mundi melioris Origo: / Sive recens tellus, seductaque nuper ab alto / Æthere, cognati retinebat semina cæli. / Quam satus Iapeto, mistam fluvialibus undis, / Finxit in effigiem Moderantûm cuncta Deorum.*</note>

->The nobler being, with a mind possessed,<-
->Was wanting yet, that should command the rest.<-
->That Maker, the best world's original,<-
->Either framed him from seed celestial;<-
->Or Earth, which late he did from Heaven divide,<-
->Some sacred seeds retained to Heaven allied:<-
->Which with the living stream Prometheus mixed,<-
->And in that artificial structure fixed<-
->The form of all the all-ruling deities.<-

Because some may likely be puzzled by this seeming contradiction—that *one God* is said to be the maker of the whole world and of man, yet the *government of all* is attributed to *Gods in the plural*, and *man* is said to be made in the *image and likeness of the Gods*—we shall add more here. According to the logic of Pagan theology, the inferior and minor gods were also supposed to have their own individual shares in the government of things below them. For this reason, they are called not only by Maximus Tyrius *co-rulers with God* <note>original Greek: *συνάρχοντες θεῷ*</note>, but also by Plato himself, *the co-governors and co-reigners with the Supreme God* <note>original Greek: *τῷ μεγίστῳ δαίμονι συνάρχοντες*</note>. 

So, the government of this inferior world was often attributed by the Pagans to them jointly—the supreme and inferior gods together—under the one general name of *Gods*. But the chief of those *inferior deities*, in whose image man is also said to have been made (as well as in the likeness of the supreme), were either those *celestial gods* and *animated stars* mentioned before by the poet, or else the *Eternal Gods of Plato*, who were likewise looked upon as subordinate *co-makers of the world*.

### Chapter 4. ...and Theists.

Besides Ovid, we could cite many more of the Pagan theogonists <note>theogonist: a writer or poet who describes the origin and genealogy of the gods</note> who clearly acknowledge, in a similar way, one uncreated Deity who generated both the world and all the other gods within it. For example, Strabo—affirming that the world was <margin>Book 17, page 809.</margin> *the joint work of both nature and providence* <note>original Greek: τῆς φύσεως ἅμα καὶ τῆς προνοίας ἔργον</note>, just as it was previously attributed by Ovid to *God and a Better Nature*—adds the following concerning providence or the Deity: 

*That having a multiform fertility in it, and delighting in a variety of works, it designed principally to make animals as the most excellent things; and among them, chiefly those two noblest kinds of animals: gods and men, for whose sakes all other things were established. It then assigned heaven to the gods and earth to men—the two extreme parts of the world—for their respective homes.* <note>original Greek: τὸ τῆς προνοίας, ὅτι βεβούληται καὶ αὐτὴ ποικιλωτέρα τις εἶναι; καὶ μυρίων ἔργων δημιουργὸς, ἐν τοῖς πρώτοις ζῶα γεννᾶν, ὡς πολὺ διαφέροντα τῶν ἄλλων· καὶ τούτων τὰ κράτιστα θεός τε καὶ Ἄνθρωπος, ὧν ἕνεκεν καὶ τὰ ἄλλα συνέστηκε. τοῖς μὲν οὖν θεοῖς ἀπέδειξε τὸν οὐρανὸν, τοῖς δ᾽ Ἀνθρώποις τὴν γῆν</note> 

Similarly, Seneca (as quoted in Lactantius) says concerning God: 

*When He laid the foundations of this most beautiful structure <note>original: "fabrick"</note> and began to erect that architecture—than which nature knows nothing greater or more excellent—He intended that all things should be carried out orderly under their respective governors. Though He intended to preside over everything Himself, He nevertheless generated gods as subordinate ministers of His kingdom under Him.* <note>original Latin: Hic cùm prima Fundamenta molis pulcherrimæ jaceret, & hoc ordiretur quo neque majus quicquam novit Natura nec melius ; ut omnia sub Ducibus irent, quamvis ipse per totum se corpus intenderat, tamen Ministros regni sui Deos genuit</note> 

We will refrain from mentioning the testimonies of others here, because they may be more appropriately introduced elsewhere. We will only add, regarding Hesiod and Homer, that although they seem to have been sometimes suspected (by both Plato and Aristotle) of being *atheistic theogonists*, Aristotle changed his opinion about both of them upon more mature thought. It is most probable that they were not atheists but *divine theogonists*—those who supposed there were *many generated gods*, but *one supreme uncreated Deity* who was the maker of both the world and those gods. 

This is not only based on the grounds previously alleged concerning Hesiod, and because both poets everywhere affirm even their *generated gods* to be *immortal* (which no atheists ever did), but also for several other reasons that will be mentioned elsewhere. Furthermore, it has already been suggested that the *generated gods* of Hesiod and Homer cover more than those of Plato. They are not only the *animated parts of the world*, but also all the other *things of nature personified* and loosely <note>original: "abusively," meaning using a term in a non-literal or extended sense</note> called *gods* and *goddesses*, an account of which will be given later.

Neither should it be wondered at if these *divine theogonists* among the Pagans—much like the *atheistic ones*—often made *Chaos* and the *Ocean* senior to the gods, and *Night* their mother. This was done not only by Hesiod and Homer, but also by the majority of the ancient Pagan theists in

Epichar- <note>catchword for the next page, likely referring to the philosopher Epicharmus</note>

### How the Divine Theogonists Made the World: Book 1.

The philosopher *Epicharmus* held this view, and the later poet *Orpheus* clearly stole it from him in his *Hymn of the Night*:

> I will sing of Night, the mother of gods and men.
> <note>original Greek: Νύκτα θεῶν γενέτειραν, ἀείσομαι, ἠδὲ καὶ ἀνδρῶν· Original Latin: Noctem concelebro Genetricem Hominúmque Deúmque.</note>

These writers did not apply this idea *absolutely* and *universally* to all gods without exception, as the other *atheistic theogonists* <note>theogonist: someone who writes about the origin and genealogy of gods</note> did. The atheists acted as if there were no *uncreated Deity* at all, but rather that *Chaos* and *Night* (that is, *senseless matter*, moving blindly and by chance) were the sole origin of all things. In contrast, the divine theogonists used these terms only for the "gods"—meaning those distinguished from the *Supreme Deity*. These were the inferior *worldly gods* who were *generated* at the same time as the *world*. 

The reason for this was that it was a most ancient and nearly universal tradition among the Pagans (as has been often suggested) that the *cosmogony* <note>cosmogony: the branch of science or philosophy dealing with the origin of the universe</note> or generation of the world began from a *Chaos*. On this point, the *divine cosmogonists* agreed with the *atheistic ones*. This tradition was passed down from *Orpheus* and *Linus* among the Greeks to *Hesiod*, *Homer*, and others. It was acknowledged by *Epicharmus* and embraced by *Thales*, *Anaxagoras*, *Plato*, and other philosophers who were *theists*. The antiquity of this idea was declared by *Euripides*:

> This story is not mine, but my mother’s:
> that heaven and earth were once a single form.
> But when they were separated from each other,
> they gave birth to all things and brought them into the light:
> trees, birds, beasts, the creatures of the sea,
> and the race of mortals.
> <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἐμὸς ὁ μῦθος, ἀλλ᾽ ἐμῆς μητρὸς πάρα... Original Latin: Non hic Meus, sed Matris est sermo meæ...</note>

<margin>
*Plutarch's Table Talk, Book 4, Question 5.*
</margin>
Furthermore, it cannot reasonably be doubted that this tradition was originally *Mosaical* <note>Mosaical: derived from Moses or the Book of Genesis</note> and was, in fact, initially a *Divine Revelation*. After all, no human could otherwise claim to know what happened before mankind existed. Therefore, those Pagan *cosmogonists* who were *theists*—being *polytheists* and *theogonists* as well—asserted that besides the one *Supreme Uncreated Deity*, there were other inferior *worldly gods* generated along with the *world* (the chief of which were the *living stars*). According to the logic of that tradition, they necessarily assumed these gods were younger than *Night* and *Chaos*—at least regarding their *physical bodies*—and were their offspring, because they were all created out of a prior *dark Chaos*. 

*Plutarch* says, "They say the shrew-mouse <note>original: Mus Araneus</note> was deified by the Egyptians because it is blind, for they believed that darkness was older than light."
<note>original Greek: Τὴν μυγαλήν ἐκτεθειάσθαι λέγουσιν ὑπὸ Αἰγυπτίων τυφλὴν οὖσαν, ὅτι τὸ σκότος τοῦ φώτος ἡγοῦντο πρεσβύτερον·</note>

# CHAPTER 4. Chaos and Night, Senior to the Gods.

...ans, because they thought that *Darkness* was older than *Light*. And the case was the same concerning their demons likewise, they being conceived to have their *corporeal vehicles* <note>original: "Corporeal Vehicula"; referring to the subtle bodies or physical forms that spirits or souls were thought to inhabit</note> also. For this reason, as *Porphyrius* <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher</note> writes from *Numenius*, the ancient *Egyptians* pictured them in ships or boats floating upon the water: <note>original Greek: τοὺς γὰρ Αἰγυπτίους διὰ τοῦτο τοὺς δαίμονας ἅπαντας οὐκ ἑστάναι ἐπὶ στερεῷ, ἀλλὰ πάντας ἐπὶ πλοίῳ</note> *The Egyptians therefore represented all their demons as not standing upon firm land, but in ships upon the water.*

But as for the *incorporeal part* or *souls* of those *inferior gods*, though these *divine theogonists* <note>theogonist: one who writes about the origin and genealogy of the gods</note> could not derive their *origin* from *Chaos* or *matter*, but rather from that other principle called *Love* (as being divinely created and so having *God* for their father), they might nonetheless, in another sense, imagine *Night* to have been their *mother* too, inasmuch as they were all made *from things that are not* <note>original Greek: ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων</note>—that is, brought forth into being from an *antecedent non-existence* or *nothing*. For this reason, there seems to have been in *Orpheus* a dialogue between the *Maker of the World* and *Night*. 

That this ancient *tradition* <note>original: "Cabala"</note>, which derived the *cosmogony* <note>cosmogony: the origin or generation of the universe</note> from *Chaos* and *Love*, was at first *religious* and not *atheistical*, and that *Love* was understood in it not to be the offspring of *Chaos*, may be concluded from this: because this *Love*, as well as *Chaos*, was of a *Mosaic extraction* <note>referring to the Book of Genesis by Moses</note>. It was plainly derived from that *Spirit of God* which is said in the *Scripture* *to have moved upon the waters*—that is, upon the *Chaos*—whether by this *Spirit* is meant *God Himself* acting immediately upon matter, or some other *active principle* derived from *God* and not from *matter* (such as a *world soul* or *plastic nature* <note>plastic nature: an unconscious, creative power in nature that carries out the divine plan</note>). 

From this it also came about that, as *Porphyrius* testifies, the ancient *Pagans* thought the *water to be divinely inspired*: <margin>*On the Cave of the Nymphs, page 256.*</margin> <note>original Greek: ἡγεῖντο γὰρ προσιζάνειν τῷ ὕδατι τὰς ψυχὰς θεοπνόῳ ὄντι ὥς φησιν ὁ Νουμήνιος· διὰ τοῦτο λέγων καὶ τὸν προφήτην εἰρηκέναι, ἐμφέρεσθαι ἐπάνω τοῦ ὕδατος θεοῦ πνεῦμα</note> *They thought that souls attended upon the water or resorted to it because it was divinely inspired, as Numenius writes, adding that the prophet therefore said that the Spirit of God moved upon the water.*

And that this tradition was understood in this way by some of the ancient Pagan cosmogonists themselves appears plainly, not only from *Simmias of Rhodes* and *Parmenides*, but also from these following verses of *Orpheus*—or whoever was the writer of those *Argonautics*, which are undoubtedly ancient—where *Chaos* and *Love* are brought in together:

# How some Pagan Theists, Book I.

...been an *existing* and *intellectual being*, but also the *oldest of all* <note>original Greek: πρεσβύτατος</note>, and therefore *older* than *Chaos*, as likewise *self-perfect* or *self-originated* <note>original Greek: αὐτοτελὴς</note>. From this it is manifest that, according to the *Orphic tradition* <note>original: "Orphick Tradition"; referring to the mystical teachings attributed to the legendary poet Orpheus</note>, this *Love* from which the *cosmogony* <note>original: "Cosmogonia"; the origin or creation of the universe</note> was derived was none other than the *eternal unmade Deity* (or an *active principle* depending on it) which produced this whole *orderly world*, and all the *created gods* in it, as to their *material* part, out of *Chaos* and *Night*. Accordingly, as *Aristotle* determines in his *Metaphysics*,
<margin>Book 1. c. 6. p. 849.</margin>
not only in the place cited before, but also afterward: *Others, besides the material cause of the world, assign an efficient cause, or cause of motion—namely, those who make either Mind (and Intellect) or Love a principle.* <note>original Greek: ἕτεροι δέ τινες, ὅθεν ἡ ἀρχὴ τῆς κινήσεως, ὅσοι ἢ Νοῦν ἢ Ἔρωτα ποιοῦσιν ἀρχήν</note> Therefore we conclude that the other *atheistic tradition* <note>original: "Atheistick Cabala"</note>, or *Aristophanic tradition* mentioned before—which, as *Aristotle* also elsewhere declares concerning it, did *generate all things from night* <note>original Greek: ἐκ νυκτὸς πάντα γεννᾷν</note>, creating all things whatsoever, even the gods themselves universally out of *Night* and *Chaos*, making *Love* itself likewise to have been produced from an *Egg of the Night*. I say, that this was nothing else but a mere *corruption* of the ancient *Mosaic tradition* <note>original: "Mosaick Cabala"</note>, as also an *absolutely impossible hypothesis*, as it derives all things whatsoever in the *universe* (besides the *bare substance* of *senseless matter*, in another sense than that mentioned before) out of *non-existence* or *nothing*; as shall be also further demonstrated afterwards.

We have now represented the sense and generally received *doctrine* of the ancient *pagan theologians*, that there was indeed a *multiplicity of gods*, but yet so that *only one* of them was *unmade* or *uncreated* <note>original Greek: ἀγέννητος</note>, by whom all the other gods, together with the *world*, were made, so as to have had a *newness of being* or a *temporary beginning* to their existence. *Plato* and the *Pythagoreans* here only differ from the rest in this: that though they acknowledged the *world* and all the *worldly gods* <note>original: "Mundane Gods"</note> to have been *created* together in time, they nevertheless supposed certain other *intelligible* and *supramundane gods* <note>supramundane: existing beyond the physical universe</note> as well, which, however they were produced from one *original Deity*, were nonetheless *eternal* or without *beginning*. But now we must acknowledge that there were among the *pagan theists* some of a different persuasion from the rest, who therefore did not admit of any *theogony* <note>original: "Theogonia"; the origin or genealogy of the gods</note> in the sense declared before—that is, any *temporary creation* of gods—because they acknowledged no *cosmogony*, no *temporary production* of the *world*, but concluded it to have been from *eternity*.

That *Aristotle* was one of these is sufficiently known. His *inferior gods* therefore—the *sun*, *moon*, and *stars*—must necessarily be *unmade* or *uncreated* <note>original Greek: ἀγέννητοι</note> in this sense, so as to have had no *temporary production*, because the *whole world* to him was such. And if that *philosopher* is to be believed, he was the very *first*, at least among all the Greeks, who asserted this *uncreated* or *eternal* nature of the *world*. He affirmed that everyone before him did *generate or make the world* <note>original Greek: γεννᾷν τὸν κόσμον, and κοσμοποιεῖν</note>, that is, they attributed a *temporary production* to it, and consequently to all those *gods* also which were a part of it. ## CHAPTER IV. Neither Theogonists, nor Cosmogonists.

Notwithstanding <note>original: "standing which", continuing the word "Notwithstanding" from the previous page</note> this, the writer of *The Opinions of the Philosophers* <note>original: "de Placitis Philosophorum", a work traditionally attributed to Plutarch</note> and *Stobaeus* <note>Joannes Stobaeus, a 5th-century compiler of extracts from Greek authors</note> attribute this doctrine <note>original: "Dogma"</note> of the world's eternity to certain other Greek philosophers before *Aristotle*. (This is in addition to *Ocellus Lucanus*, who is also acknowledged by *Philo* to have been a supporter of this view.) And indeed *Epicharmus*, though a theist, seems plainly to have been of the persuasion that the world was *unmade*. He also believed there was no <term>Theogonia</term> <note>Theogony: an account of the birth or origin of the gods</note>, or temporary production of the inferior gods, as seen in these verses of his, according to *Grotius's* correction:

<margin>Excerpts page 478.</margin>
> Indeed, the gods were always present, and they never fail;
> These things I describe are always shown to us in the same way, 
> always through the same elements.
> But it is said that Chaos was the first of the gods to arise:
> How so? For it is impossible for anything to first exist out of nothing.
> Therefore, nothing was truly first, nor by Zeus was there a second;
> But those things which are now called so, will later become others.
> <note>original: "Αλλ' ἀεὶ τοὶ θεοὶ παρῆσαν... / Nempe Dî semper fuerunt..."</note>

In this passage, although he acknowledges that the general tradition of the ancient theists was that *Chaos* existed before the gods, and that the inferior worldly gods had a temporary generation or production along with the world, he nevertheless concludes against it. He bases this on the principle of reason that *nothing* could proceed from *nothing*. Therefore, he argues that both the gods, and indeed whatever else is substantial in the world, were *unmade* from eternity, with only the fashion or forms of things having been altered.

<margin>Book 2. page 82.</margin>
Moreover, *Diodorus Siculus* affirms that the *Chaldeans* likewise asserted this doctrine <note>original: "Dogma"</note> of the world’s eternity: *The Chaldeans affirm that the nature of the world is eternal, and that it neither had a beginning from the start, nor will it ever suffer destruction.* <note>original: "οἱ δ' οὖν χαλδαῖοι τὴν μὲν τοῦ κόσμου φύσιν ἀΐδιόν φασιν εἶναι, καὶ μήτε ἐξ ἀρχῆς γένεσιν ἐσχηκέναι, μήθ' ὕστερον φθορὰν ἐπιδέξεσθαι."</note> That they were not atheists despite this (any more than *Aristotle*) appears from these following words of that historian: *They also believe that the order and arrangement of the world is by a certain divine providence, and that every one of those things which come to pass in the heavens happens not by chance or spontaneously, but is carried out by a certain fixed and firmly ratified judgment of the gods.* <note>original: "τὴν δὲ τῶν ὅλων τάξιν τε καὶ διακόσμησιν, θείᾳ τινὶ προνοίᾳ γεγονέναι, καὶ νῦν ἕκαστα τῶν ἐν οὐρανῷ γινομένων, οὐχ ὡς ἔτυχεν, οὐδ' αὐτομάτως, ἀλλ' ὡρισμένῃ τινὶ καὶ βεβαίως κεκυρωμένῃ θεῶν κρίσει, συντελεῖσθαι."</note> However, it is well known to all that the majority of the later *Platonists* strictly adhered to *Aristotle* in this. They did not only assert that the physical world, along with all the *inferior worldly gods* in it, was <term>ἀγέννητος</term> <note>Ingenerate: uncreated or having no beginning</note>, or had existed from eternity; they also maintained the same concerning the souls of *men* and all other *animals;*

Nevertheless, concerning these latter *Platonists* <note>The Neoplatonists, such as Plotinus and Proclus, who lived centuries after Plato and developed his ideas into a complex mystical system.</note>, it is observable here that although they asserted the *world*, and all inferior gods and souls, to have been *ungenerated* <note>original: ἀγενήτους (ageneitous)</note>—according to the stricter sense of the word already declared, meaning they had no *temporary generation* or *beginning* but had existed from *eternity*—they by no means conceived them to be *self-originated* and *self-existing* <note>original: αὐτογενεῖς καὶ αὐθυποστάτους (autogeneis kai authypostatous)</note>. Instead, they concluded them to have all been derived from *one sole self-existent Deity* as their *cause*, which therefore, though not in order of *time*, yet in order of *nature*, existed before them. To this purpose, *Plotinus* wrote: *Mind or God was before the world, not as if it existed before it in time, but because the world proceeded from it, and that was in order of nature first, as its cause, and its archetype or paradigm; the world also always subsisting by it and from it.* <note>original: νοῦν πρὸ αὐτοῦ εἶναι οὐχ ὡς χρόνῳ πρότερον αὐτοῦ ὄντα, ἀλλ' ὅτι παρὰ νῷ ἔστι καὶ φύσει πρότερον ἐκεῖνον, καὶ αἴτιον τούτῳ, ἀρχέτυπον οἷον καὶ παράδειγμα εἰκόνος· καὶ δι' ἐκεῖνον ὄντως καὶ ὑποστάντος ἀεὶ τόνδε τὸν τρόπον</note> And again

<margin>Enneads 2.1.9.c.3.</margin>
elsewhere to the same purpose: *The things which are said to have been made or generated were not so made as if they ever had a beginning to their existence, but yet they were made and will be always made (in another sense); nor will they ever be destroyed, except as they are dissolved into those simple principles out of which some of them were compounded.* <note>original: οὐ τοίνυν ἐγένετο, ἀλλ' ἐγίνετο καὶ γενήσεται, ὅσα γενητὰ λέγεται, οὐδὲ φθαρήσεται, ἀλλ' ἢ ὅσα ἔχῃ εἰς ἅ</note> While the world is said here to have never been *made* in terms of a *temporary beginning*, in another sense, it is said to be always *made*, as it depends upon God perpetually as its <term>emanative cause</term> <note>A cause that produces an effect by naturally "flowing out" from itself, like heat from a fire.</note>. Agreeably to this, the manner of the world’s production from God is thus declared by that

<margin>Enneads 5.1.8.c.12.</margin>
philosopher: *They do not act rightly who describe the world as being corrupted and generated [having a beginning and end]; for they will not understand what manner of making or production the world had—namely, by way of effulgency or eradiation from the Deity.* <note>original: οὐκ ὀρθῶς οἱ φθείρουσι καὶ γεννῶσιν αὐτόν, ὅστις γὰρ τρόπος τῆς ποιήσεως ταύτης, οὐκ ἐθέλουσι συνιέναι, οὐδ' ἴασασιν, ὅτι ὅσον ἐκεῖνα ἐλλάμπει, οὐ μήποτε τὰ ἄλλα ἐλλείπει</note> From this it follows that *the world must have existed as long as there was a God, just as light is coeval with the sun.* So likewise *Proclus* concludes that the world was *always generated or radiated from God* <note>original: ἀεὶ γινόμενος, καὶ ἐλλαμπόμενος ἀπὸ τοῦ ὄντος</note> and therefore must be eternal, because God is eternal. Therefore, these latter Platonists supposed the same thing concerning the corporeal world and the lower mundane gods that their master *Plato* did concerning his higher eternal gods: that although they had no *temporary production*, they all depended no less upon one supreme Deity than if they had been made out of nothing by Him. From this, it is manifest that none of these philosophers perceived any <term>repugnancy</term> <note>Contradiction or inconsistency.</note> at all between these two things: *existence from eternity* and *being caused or produced by another*. -># Chapter IV. Of the World and Gods.<-

...convinced of any contradictory inconsistency here, they would have readily disclaimed their so beloved hypothesis of the *world's eternity*. It is far from the truth, as some have supposed, that the proponents of the world's eternity were all atheists. In fact, these later Platonists <note>The Neoplatonists, such as Plotinus and Proclus, who developed Plato's ideas into a complex mystical system.</note> were led into this opinion by nothing other than the sole consideration of the *Deity*; namely, its "good-natured will and generative power" <note>original: ἀγαθοειδὴς βόλησις, καὶ γόνιμος δύναμις (agathoeidēs bolēsis, kai gonimos dynamis)</note>, its *essential goodness*, and *generative power*, or *emanative fertility*, <margin>Page 116.</margin> as *Proclus* plainly declares in his commentary on the *Timaeus*.

Now, although *Aristotle* was not driven by any such *divine enthusiasm* as these Platonists seem to have been, he nonetheless really maintained the same thing in his own sober manner. He argued that although the *world* and *inferior mundane gods* had no *temporary generation* <note>A beginning in time.</note>, they were nevertheless all *produced from one supreme Deity as their cause*. This is how *Simplicius* represents that philosopher’s sense: <margin>In Aristotle's Physics, Book 8.</margin> 

> *Aristotle did not think that the world was created (so as to have had a beginning), but rather that it was produced by God in another way.* <note>original: Ἀριστοτέλης οὐ γίνεσθαι ἀξιοῖ τὸν κόσμον, ἀλλὰ κατ᾿ ἄλλον τρόπον ὑπὸ θεοῦ παράγεσθαι</note>

And again afterward:

> *Aristotle, though calling God the cause of the heavens and of its eternal motion, nonetheless demonstrates it to be ungenerated or unmade—that is, without a beginning.* <note>original: Ἀριστοτέλης τὸ αἴτιον τοῦ οὐρανοῦ καὶ τῆς ἀϊδίου κινήσεως αὐτοῦ Θεὸν λέγων, ὅμως ἀγέννητον αὐτὸν ἀποδείκνυσι</note>

However, we think it appropriate to observe here that although *Aristotle* usually expresses a great deal of zeal and confidence for that opinion of the *world’s eternity*, he does sometimes seem to falter a little and speak more weakly and skeptically about it. For example, in his book *On the Parts of Animals*, where he treats the subject of an *artificial nature*: <margin>Book 1, Chapter 1.</margin> 

> *It is more likely that the heavens were created by such a cause as this (if they were created) and that they are maintained by such a cause, than that mortal animals should be so produced*; <note>original: μᾶλλον εἰκὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν γεγονέναι, ὑπὸ τοιαύτης αἰτίας, εἰ γέγονε, καὶ εἶναι διὰ τοιαύτην αἰτίαν, μᾶλλον ἢ ζῶα τὰ θνητά</note>

which is a concept more generally acknowledged. Now, it was previously declared that *Aristotle’s artificial nature* was nothing but the mere executioner or worker of a *perfect mind*—that is, of the *Deity*. Therefore, he sometimes joins these two together in the <term>cosmopœia</term> <note>original: cosmopœia; the creation or making of the world</note>, affirming that Mind and Nature—that is, *God and Nature*—were the cause of this universe.

And now we see plainly that although there was a real controversy among the *pagan theologians* (especially from *Aristotle's* time onward) concerning the <term>cosmogonia</term> <note>original: cosmogonia; the generation or birth of the world</note> and <term>theogonia</term> <note>original: theogonia; the generation or birth of the gods</note>, according to the stricter notion of those words—meaning the *temporary generation* or *production* of the *world* and *inferior gods*, or whether they had any beginning or not—there was no controversy at all concerning their *self-existence*. It was universally agreed upon among them *that the world and the inferior gods, even if supposed by some to have existed from eternity, were nevertheless all derived from one sole self-existent Deity as their cause*; 

> *being either radiated or produced from God.* <note>original: ὑπὸ θεοῦ παραγόμενοι ἢ ἐλλαμπόμενοι (hypo theou paragomenoi ē ellampomenoi)</note>

-># The Pagans' Eternal Gods *Produced*. Book I.<-

the world's eternity, distinguished between different meanings of the word *produced* <note>original: γενητὸν (geneton), which can mean arisen, born, or made</note>. They saw it as an ambiguous term. Although they denied that the world and the inferior gods were "produced" in one sense, they clearly affirmed it in another.

<margin>Simplicius on Aristotle’s Physics, folio 255.</margin>
According to them, the word "produced" <note>original: γενητὸν</note>—when used strictly and properly—refers to *that which, in a specific moment of time, passed from non-existence into being* <note>original: τὸ ἐν μέρει χρόνου τὴν εἰς τὸ εἶναι πάροδον λαχόν</note>, or *that which did not exist before but existed afterward* <note>original: ὃ τὸ πρότερον μὴ ὂν, ὕστερον δ' ὂν</note>. Nevertheless, they acknowledge that in a broader sense, this word "produced" may also refer to *whatever depends in any way upon a superior being as its cause* <note>original: τὸ ὁπωσῶν ἀπ' αἰτίας ὑφισάμενον</note>.

The same ambiguity must apply to the word "unproduced" <note>original: ἀγένητον (ageneton)</note>. It can be understood either *chronologically* <note>original: χρονικῶς</note>, as *something that is unproduced in time because it had no beginning*; or as *something unproduced by any cause* <note>original: ἀπ' αἰτίας ἀγένητον</note>. In this latter sense, the word "unproduced" or "unmade" has the same weight and meaning as *self-subsistent* <note>original: αὐθυπόστατον (autohypostaton)</note> or *self-originated* <note>original: αὐτόγενες (autogenes)</note>. This was the term used by those pagan theists who concluded *that matter was unmade* <note>original: ὅτι ὕλη ἀγένητος</note>—meaning not only that it existed from eternity without a beginning, but also that it was self-existent and independent of any superior cause.

Regarding the first of these two senses (the chronological one), the majority of ancient pagans, including **Plato**, affirmed that the world and all the inferior gods were "produced" <note>original: γενητοὺς (genetous)</note>—meaning they were made in time or had a beginning. (Regardless of what the later Platonists claim, this was undoubtedly Plato’s meaning when he concluded the world was "produced," as he explicitly contrasts it with "eternal" <note>original: ἀΐδιον (aidion)</note>.) On the other hand, **Aristotle** and the **later Platonists** determined that the world and the inferior gods were "unproduced" <note>original: ἀγενήτους (agenetous)</note> in this sense, having no beginning in time but existing from eternity. 

However, according to the second sense of those words, all pagan theologians agreed that the world and all the inferior gods—whether they had a beginning or existed from eternity—were nonetheless *produced from a cause* <note>original: γενητοὶ ἀπ' αἰτίας</note>. Thus, there was only one *unproduced and self-existent Deity* <note>original: Θεὸς ἀγένητος</note>, who is described as *superior to a cause and older than any cause* <note>original: αἰτίας κρείττων κὶ πρεσβύτερος</note>, being the cause of all things besides himself.

<margin>On the Timaeus, page 85.</margin>
Thus, **Crantor** and his followers (as cited in **Proclus**), who were zealous defenders of the world's eternity, determined that *the world (and all the inferior mundane gods within it), despite being from eternity, could be called "produced"—meaning made—because they were generated by another cause and were not self-originated or self-existing* <note>original: γενητὸν λέγεσθαι τὸν κόσμον ὡς ἀπ' αἰτίας ἄλλης παραγόμενον, κὶ οὐκ ὄντα αὐτόγονον οὐδὲ αὐθυπόστατον</note>. In the same way, **Proclus** himself, that great champion for the world's eternity, nonetheless plainly acknowledged the generation of the gods and the world in this sense, as being produced from a superior cause: *"We speak of the generations of the gods, meaning thereby their ineffable procession and the difference between these secondary beings and their causes"* <note>original: λέγομεν θεῶν γενήσεις, τὴν ἀῤῥητον αὐτῶν πρόοδον ἐνδεικνύμενοι, κὶ τὴν τῶν δευτέρων ἑτερότητα, πρὸς τὰς αἰτίας αὐτῶν</note>. By this, he did not mean any temporary production—

### Cʜᴀᴘ. IV. Derived from One Self-existent Deity.

...production of them, but their *ineffable procession* from a *superior first cause*. Similarly, Sallustius <note>original: Salustius</note>, in his book *On the Gods and the World* <note>original: de Diis & Mundo</note>—where he contends that the world has existed from eternity or without beginning—concludes that both the world and the other inferior gods were made by one Supreme Deity, whom he calls "the First God" <note>original: ὁ πρῶτος θεὸς</note>. For he says: "Since there is a greatest power <note>or "since the First Cause is omnipotent"</note>, he ought therefore to make not only humans and other animals, but also gods and demons" <note>original: μεγίστης γὰρ δυνάμεως οὔσης, οὐκ ἀνθρώπους ἔδει καὶ ζῶα μόνα ποιεῖν, ἀλλὰ Θεός τε καὶ δαίμονας</note>. Accordingly, this is the title of his 13th chapter: "How eternal things may be said to be made or generated" <note>original: πῶς τὰ ἀΐδια λέγεται γίγνεσθαι</note>. 

It is true indeed (as we have often stated) that some of the pagan theists asserted that God was not the only unmade and self-existent being <note>original: ἀγένητον καὶ αὐθυπόστατον</note>, but that matter was also such a being. Nevertheless, this opinion was not as generally accepted among them as is commonly supposed. Although some of the ancient Fathers <note>Early Christian theologians</note> confidently attribute this view to Plato, there seems to be no sufficient reason for doing so; Porphyry <note>original: Porphyrius</note>, Iamblichus, Proclus, and other Platonists not only professedly oppose this idea as false but also as something inconsistent with Plato’s principles. 

Therefore, according to that broader definition of the word "unmade" <note>original: ἀγένητον</note>—taken as synonymous with "self-begotten" <note>original: αὐτόγενες</note> and "self-subsistent" <note>original: αὐθυπόστατον</note>—there were very many pagan theologians who agreed with Christians in this: "That God is the only unbegotten or unmade being, and that his very essence is, so to speak, unbegottenness or innascibility" <note>original: ὅτι αὐτὸ Ἀγέννητον ὁ θεὸς, καὶ οὐσία αὐτοῦ ὡς ἂν εἴποι τις ἡ Ἀγεννησία</note>; all other things, even *matter* itself, being made by him. But all the rest of them (except for a few Ditheists <note>believers in two primary and opposing gods, such as a good and an evil one</note>)—even if they supposed matter to be self-existent—concluded that there was only "one unmade or unproduced God" <note>original: εἷς θεὸς ἀγένητος</note>, and that all their other gods were "generated" <note>original: γεννητοὶ</note> in one sense or another. If they were not "made in time," they were at least "produced from a superior cause."

Nothing now remains but for us to show how the pagans distinguished between the one supreme, unmade Deity and all their other inferior, generated gods. We are especially concerned to do this because it is well known that they often blurred them together, attributing the government of the whole world to "the gods" indiscriminately, without making a proper distinction between the supreme and the inferior. The true reason for this seems to be that they supposed the supreme God does not do everything immediately in the government of the world, but permits much to be done by his inferior ministers. We saw one instance of this earlier in Ovid, and countless others could be cited from their most serious writers. 

For example, Cicero, in his first book of *Laws*: "The whole of nature, or the universe, is governed by the force, reason, power, mind, and divinity of the immortal gods" <note>original: Deorum Immortalium vi, ratione, potestate, mente, numine, Natura omnis regitur</note>. And again in his second book: "That the gods are the masters and governors of all things, and that those things which are done are carried out by their judgment and divinity; and that they deserve the very best from the human race; and what sort of person everyone..."

# How the Pagans distinguished their Gods, Book 1.

"[Citizens ought to be persuaded] to observe who each person is, what he does, what he admits into his soul, with what mind and with what piety he observes religious duties; and to understand that the gods keep an account of the pious and the impious; from the very beginning, citizens ought to be persuaded of this." <note>original: quisque sit, quid agat, quid in se admittat, qua mente, qua pietate Religiones colat, intueri ; piorúmque & impiorum habere Rationem ; à Principio Civibus suasum esse debet</note> *The minds of citizens ought to be, first of all, imbued with a firm persuasion that the Gods are the Lords and Moderators of all things, and that the conduct and management of the whole world is directed and overruled by their judgment and divine power; that they deserve the best from mankind; that they behold and consider what every man is, what he does and takes upon himself, with what mind, piety, and sincerity he observes the duties of religion; and lastly, that these Gods have a very different regard for the pious and the impious.* <note>This is a quote from the Roman statesman Cicero in his work "On the Laws."</note> 

Now, since such passages as these abound everywhere in Pagan writings, it is no wonder if many—considering their theology only slightly and superficially—have been led into error. This has caused them to conclude that the Pagans did not assert a Divine Monarchy, but instead attributed both the making and governing of the world to an *Aristocracy* or *Democracy* of <term>co-ordinate gods</term> <note>Gods of equal rank and power who rule together.</note>, who were not only all eternal, but also *self-existent* and *unmade*. Although the contrary has already been sufficiently proven, it will not be out of place for us here, in conclusion, to show how the Pagans (who sometimes jumble and confound the Supreme and inferior gods together) nonetheless distinguish, in many ways, between the one Supreme God and their many other inferior gods.

First, therefore, just as the Pagans had many proper names for one and the same Supreme God—based on several particular *considerations* of Him, regarding His various manifestations and effects in the world (which are often mistaken for so many distinct deities, some supposing them independent, others subordinate)—so they also had, besides these, other proper names for God according to that more full and comprehensive notion of Him as the Maker of the whole world and its Supreme Governor, or the sole Monarch of the universe. 

For instance, the Greeks called him *Zeus* and *Zen*, and so on; the Latins *Jupiter* and *Jovis*; the Babylonians *Belus* and *Bel*; the Persians *Mithras* and *Oromasdes*; and the Egyptians and Scythians (according to Herodotus) *Ammoun* and *Pappaeus*. And Celsus, in the writings of Origen, concludes it to be a matter of pure indifference to call the Supreme God by any of these names—whether *Zeus*, *Ammoun*, *Pappaeus*, or the like.

<margin>Book 5. Against Celsus.</margin>

"Celsus thinks it makes no difference whether we call the Highest and Supreme God 'Dia' and 'Zena' <note>inflected forms of Zeus</note> as the Greeks do; or 'Adonai' and 'Sabaoth' as the Jews do; or 'Ammoun' as the Egyptians do; or 'Pappaeus' as the Scythians do." <note>original: Κέλσος οἴεται μηδὲν διαφέρειν, Δία τὸν ὕψιστον, καλεῖν ἢ Ζῆνα, ἢ Ἀδωναῖον, ἢ Σαβαὼθ ἢ (ως Αἰγύπτιοι) Ἄμμυν, ἢ (ως Σκύθαι) Παππαῖον.</note> 

Notwithstanding this, that pious and jealous <term>Father</term> <note>Origen, an influential early Christian scholar and theologian.</note> expresses a great deal of zeal against Christians then using any of those Pagan names. "But we will rather endure any torment," he says, "than confess Zeus (or Jupiter) to be God; being well assured that the Greeks often really worship, under that name, an evil demon who is an enemy both to God and men. And we will rather suffer death than call the Supreme God Ammoun, whom the Egyptian enchanters thus invoke." 

"And let the Scythians say that Pappaeus is the God over all; but we will not be convinced..." <note>original: λεγέτωσαν δὲ καὶ Σκύθαι τὸν Παππαῖον, θεὸν εἶναι τὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσιν· ἀλλ' ἡμεῖς οὐ πεισόμεθα, τιθέντες</note>

<summary>The author argues that while Pagans used many names for gods, they actually believed in a single Supreme Monarch of the universe, though early Christian Fathers like Origen rejected using Pagan names for the true God.</summary>

# CHAPTER IV. The Supreme God, distinguished from the Inferior Gods.

<margin>Against Celsus, Book 5, page 262.</margin>

[After the God who is over all, according to what is pleasing to the one who was allotted the Scythian desert, their nation, and their language, they do not name God by his proper name as "Pappæus." However, whoever uses the general name for "God" in the Scythian or Egyptian language, or in whatever dialect one has been brought up in, will not be at fault.] <note>original: μεθ᾿ ὃ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεὸν, ὡς ᾧ φίλον τῷ λαχόντι τὴν Σκυθῶν ἐρημίαν, καὶ τὸ ἔθνος αὐτῶν καὶ διάλεκτον, οὐκ ὀνομάζοντες τὸν θεὸν, ὡς κυρίῳ ὀνόματι τῷ Παππαῖον. Σκυθιστὶ δὲ τὸ προσηγορικὸν τὸν θεὸν, καὶ Αἰγυπτισὶ, καὶ πάσῃ διαλέκτῳ, ᾗ ἕκαστος ἐντέθραπται, ὀνομάζων, οὐκ ἁμαρτήσεται</note> *And though the Scythians call the Supreme God Pappæus, yet we, acknowledging a Supreme God, will never be persuaded to call him by that name which it pleased that* **demon** <term>original: dæmon; here referring to a localized spirit or deity associated with a specific region</term> (*who ruled over the Scythian desert, people, and language*) *to impose. Nevertheless, he that shall use the descriptive name for God, either in the Scythian, Egyptian, or any other language in which he has been brought up, will not offend.* Where **Origen** plainly affirms the **Scythians** to have acknowledged **One Supreme God**, called by them **Pappæus**, and intimates that the **Egyptians** did the like, calling him **Ammon**. Neither could it possibly be his intent to deny the same regarding the Greeks and their **Zeus**, regardless of how his great **suspicion** <note>original: jealousie</note> made him call him here a "demon." This is true in a certain sense, which shall be explained afterward: that the Pagans did often, in reality, worship an evil demon under those very names of **Zeus** and **Jupiter**, just as they did under those of **Hammon** and **Pappæus**.

In the meantime, we do not deny that both the Greeks used the word **Zeus**, and the Latins **Jupiter**, sometimes **physically** <note>original: φυσικῶς (physikōs); referring to natural elements like weather or the atmosphere</note> to represent the **ether**, **fire**, or **air**. Some accordingly derived the name "Zeus" from the Greek word "to boil" <note>original: ζέω (zeo)</note>, and others derived "Dis" from "to moisten" <note>original: δεύω (deuo)</note>. From this came those figures of speech, *Sub Jove* and *Sub Dio* <note>Latin phrases meaning "under Jove" or "under the sky," used to describe being out in the open air.</note>. And thus **Cicero** writes, "**Ennius** names Jove, saying,"

<margin>On the Nature of the Gods, Book 2, page 223, Lambinus edition.</margin>

->*Behold this shining high place, which all invoke as Jove.*<-
<note>original: Aspice hoc sublime candens, quem invocant omnes Jovem.</note>

*Our Augurs also mean this when they say, "Jove Lightning," or "Jove Thundering"; for they are saying "the Heaven Lightning" or "the Heaven Thundering," etc.* The reason for these expressions seems to have been that in ancient times, some had supposed the **Animated Heaven**, **Ether**, and **Air** to be the **Supreme Deity**. We grant, moreover, that the same words have been sometimes used **historically** <note>original: ἱσορικῶς (historikōs); likely a typo for ἱστορικῶς, meaning according to human history or myth</note> as well, for a **hero** or **deified man**, said by some to have been born in **Crete**, and by others in **Arcadia**. And **Callimachus**, though he was very angry with the Cretans for claiming that **Jupiter's** burial monument was with them in **Crete** (thereby making him mortal), wrote:

> Cretans are always liars, for they have even built a tomb for you, O King; but you did not die, for you exist forever. <note>original: Κρῆτες ἀεὶ ψεῦσται, καὶ γὰρ τάφον, ὦ ἄνα, σεῖο, Κρῆτες ἐτεκτήναντο· σὺ δ' οὐ θάνες, ἐσσὶ γὰρ αἰεί·</note>

# Pagans' Proper Names: BOOK I.

The more intelligent of the Greek pagans frequently understood by **Zeus** that **Supreme Unmade Deity**, who was the **Maker of the World** and of all the **inferior gods**. Porphyry, as quoted in **Eusebius**, <margin>Preparation for the Gospel, Book 3</margin> declares their meaning: "By Zeus, the Greeks understand that Mind of the World which framed all things in it, and contains the whole world." <note>original: τὸν Δία, τὸν Νῶν κόσμῳ ὑπολαμβάνουσι, ὃς τὰ ἐν αὐτῷ ἐδημιούργησεν, ἔχων τὸν κόσμον</note> Agreeable to this is the statement of **Maximus Tyrius**: "By Jupiter you are to understand that most ancient and ruling Mind, which all things follow and obey." <note>original: κάλει τὸν μὲν Δία, νοῦν πρεσβύτατον, καὶ ἀρχικώτατον, ᾧ πάντα ἔπεταί καὶ πειθαρχεῖ</note> 

And **Eusebius** himself—though not eager to grant more to the pagans than he absolutely must—concludes with this acknowledgment: <margin>Preparation for the Gospel, Book 3, chapter 13</margin> "Let Jupiter, therefore, be no longer that fiery and ethereal substance, which the ancient pagans (according to **Plutarch**) supposed him to be; but rather that Highest Mind, which was the Maker of all things." <note>original: ἔστω ὁ Ζεὺς μηκέθ᾽ ἡ πυρώδης καὶ αἰθερία οὐσία, ὥσπερ τοῖς παλαιοῖς ἐνομίζετο, κατὰ τὸν Πλούταρχον, ἀλλ᾽ αὐτὸς ὁ ἀνωτάτω Νοῦς, ὁ τῶν ὅλων δημιουργός</note> 

However, **Phornutus** <note>Also known as Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher</note> understands **Jupiter** to be the **Soul of the World**, writing this about him: "Just as we ourselves are governed by a soul, so the world in like manner has a Soul that holds it together; and this is called Zeus, being the cause of life to all living things. Therefore, Zeus (or Jupiter) is said to reign over all things." <note>original: ὥσπερ δὲ ἡμεῖς ἀπὸ ψυχῆς διοικούμεθα, οὕτω καὶ ὁ κόσμος ψυχὴν ἔχει τὴν συνέχουσαν αὐτὸν, καὶ αὕτη καλεῖται Ζεύς, αἰτία οὖσα τοῖς ζῶσι τοῦ ζῆν, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο βασιλεύειν ὁ Ζεὺς λέγεται τῶν ὅλων</note> 

Even though there were these two different conceptions among the pagans concerning God—some perceiving Him as an **abstract Mind** separate from the world and matter, while others saw Him only as a **Soul of the World**—they all nevertheless agreed that **Zeus** or **Jupiter** was the **Supreme Moderator or Governor of all.** 

Accordingly, **Plato** in his *Cratylus*, <margin>Stephanus edition, page 396</margin> taking the two Greek forms of the name, *Zena* and *Dia*, etymologizes <term>explains the linguistic origin of</term> them as one in this manner: "These two words, when joined together, reveal the nature of God. For there is no one who is more the cause of life for us and all other living beings than He who is the ruler and king of all. Therefore, He is rightly named by the fact that He is the God through whom all living things always possess life. Though it is one name, it has been split into two parts: **Dia** and **Zena**." <note>original: συντιθέμενα εἰς ἓν δηλοῖ τὴν φύσιν τοῦ Θεοῦ, οὐ γάρ ἐστιν ἡμῖν καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις πᾶσιν, ὅστις ἐστὶν αἴτιος μᾶλλον τοῦ ζῆν, ἢ ὁ ἄρχων τε καὶ βασιλεὺς τῶν πάντων... The name "Zena" was associated with the Greek word for "living" (zen)</note> 

But it was very easy to object to Plato's position by pointing out that Zeus could not be the **Prince of all things** or the **First Source of Life** according to the *Theogony* of **Hesiod** and other ancient pagans. In those stories, Zeus himself was said to be the **son of Cronos** (or **Saturn**). Therefore, Plato addressed <term>original: preoccupied</term> this objection beforehand: "Whoever hears this," he says, "will immediately conclude that it is insulting <term>original: contumelious</term> to this Zeus (as we have described him) to be considered the son of Cronos."

# CHAP. IV. for the Supreme God.

Plato attempts to bring the traditional god **Zeus** (or **Jupiter**) into alignment with the **Third Hypostasis** of his **Divine Triad**, so that he properly signifies the **Superior Soul of the World**. Plato writes: *"Nevertheless it is reasonable to suppose Zeus or Jupiter to be the offspring of some Great Mind; for Chronos (Saturn) signifies the pure and perfect Mind Eternal; who again is said to be the son of Uranus (Cœlius)."* <note>original: εὔλογον δὲ, μεγάλης τινὸς διανοίας ἔκγονον εἶναι τὸν Δία · Κρόνου γὰρ τὸ καθαρὸν αὐτοῦ καὶ ἀκήρατον τοῦ Νοῦ · ἔστι δὲ οὗτος οὐρανοῦ υἱός, ὡς λόγος</note> Here it is clear that **Plato** endeavors to adapt this poetic trinity of gods—**Uranus**, **Chronos**, and **Zeus** (or Cœlius, Saturn, and Jupiter)—to his own trinity of divine **hypostases**: <term>Hypostases: The distinct "persons" or levels of reality in the Platonic trinity.</term> **The Good** (τ’ἀγαθὸν), **Intellect** (νοῦς), and **the Highest Soul** (ψυχή). This adaptation is further pursued by **Plotinus** in several places, such as his *Enneads*. Nevertheless, these **Three Archical Hypostases** of the **Platonic Trinity**, though viewed as distinct and subordinate substances, are frequently taken together by the Platonists as the **Whole Supreme Deity**. 

However, the name **Zeus** is attributed by Plato to each of them at different times, as **Proclus** observed <margin>P. 297.</margin> in his commentary on the *Timaeus*: *"We say, therefore, that there are several orders, ranks, or degrees of Zeus or Jupiter in Plato. For sometimes he is taken for the Demiurge (the Maker of the world), as in the Cratylus; sometimes for the first of the Saturnian triad, as in the Gorgias; sometimes for the Superior Soul of the world, as in the Phaedrus; and lastly, sometimes for the lower soul of the heavens."* <note>original: λέγωμεν ὅτι πολλαὶ μέν εἰσι τάξεις καὶ παρὰ Πλάτωνι τοῦ Διός... [as translated above]</note> Though, with all due respect to Proclus, the **Zeus** mentioned in Plato’s *Cratylus*—being clearly the **Superior Soul of the World**—is not properly the **Demiurge** <term>Demiurge: From the Greek 'demiurgos,' meaning a craftsman or creator-god who fashions the physical universe.</term> according to Proclus’s own system; that title rather belongs to the **Intellect** (νοῦς), which is the **Second Hypostasis** in the Platonic trinity.

As for the common people among the **Greek pagans**, whether they understood God to be a **Mind or Intellect separate from the world** <note>original: νοῦν ἐξηρημένον τοῦ κόσμου</note> or simply the **Soul of the World**, there is no doubt that by the word **Zeus**, they commonly understood the **Supreme Deity** in one of those senses. He was the **Father and King of Gods**, as he was frequently addressed in their solemn vows: *"O Jupiter Father"* and *"O Jupiter King."* <note>original: ζεῦ πάτερ, ζεῦ ἄνα</note> He was also invoked as **King Zeus** in that excellent prayer of an ancient poet, which was rightly praised in Plato’s *Alcibiades*:

-> O King Zeus, give us good things whether we pray for them or not, <-
-> but withhold evil things from us, even if we should pray for them. <-
<note>original: Ζεῦ βασιλεῦ, τὰ μὲν ἐσθλὰ καὶ εὐχομένοις καὶ ἀνεύκτοις / Ἄμι δίδου, τὰ δὲ δεινὰ καὶ εὐχομένοις ἀπαλέξειν</note>

Because instances of this kind are innumerable, we shall refrain from mentioning more of them. We shall only observe that **Zeus Sabazius** was another name for the Supreme God, which was sometimes introduced...

## The Supreme God denoted by Appellatives. BOOK. I.

...introduced amongst the Greeks and derived, in all probability, from the Hebrew *Sabaoth*, or *Adonai Tsebaoth*, the *Lord of Hosts* (that is, of the Heavenly Hosts), or the Supreme Governor of the World. <note>original: "Sabaoth" refers to the Hebrew word for "armies" or "hosts."</note> This was therefore noticed by *Aristophanes* as a strange and foreign God, lately crept in among them, who ought to be banished out of *Greece*. These several names of God were then commonly spoken of as if they were many distinct deities, as will be more fully explained later. We shall also show elsewhere that, besides Zeus <note>original: Ζεὺς</note>, Pan <note>original: πᾶν</note> was also used by the Greeks as a name for that God who is the supreme moderator and governor of the whole world.

That the Latins, in a similar way, frequently used the names *Jupiter* and *Jovis* to denote the Supreme Deity and Monarch of the Universe is unquestionable. This is sufficiently clear from those epithets commonly given to him, such as *the Best* and *the Greatest* <note>original: "Optimus and Maximus"</note>, as well as the title *Omnipotent* frequently bestowed upon him by *Virgil* and others. Although *Cicero* explains the origin of the word *Jupiter* as "from the act of helping" <note>original: "à Juvando"</note>, or from "the Helping Father" <note>original: "Juvans Pater"</note>—not knowing how else to do it—we may rather conclude it to have a Hebrew origin <note>original: "Hebraical Extraction"</note>. It is likely derived from the *Tetragrammaton*, the name of God consisting of four consonants. <term>Tetragrammaton: The four Hebrew letters YHWH (Yahweh), the personal name of God in the Hebrew Bible.</term> While the vowels it was pronounced with are not certainly known today, it must have had a sound similar to *Jovah*, *Jahvoh*, or *Iao* <note>original: Ἰαὼ or Ἰάω</note>; and the abbreviation of this name was *Jah*. Just as the Pagan nations had their several proper names for God alongside their common titles, so too did the Hebrews have theirs—given by God himself and most expressive of his nature, signifying *Eternal and Necessary Existence*.

Next, we shall suggest that the Pagans did not only signify the *Supreme God* by these *Proper Names*, but also frequently by <term>Appellatives</term> themselves—titles like "God" or "the Divine"—when used not for *a god* in general, but for *The God*, or *God* par excellence <note>original: κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν</note>, and by way of eminence. Thus, "the God" <note>original: ὁ Θεὸς</note> and "God" <note>original: Θεὸς</note> are often used by the Greeks not to mean "one of the gods" <note>original: θεῶν τις</note>, but for *God*, or the *Supreme Deity*. We have several examples of this in passages occasionally cited previously in this very chapter. For instance, in that of *Aristotle*: *"What is there, therefore, that can be better than Knowledge, except God?"* <note>original: τί οὖν ἂν κρεῖττον ἢ ἐπιστήμης πλὴν ὁ θεὸς;</note> There is also his other statement that happiness consists principally in virtue: *"it is a thing that ought to be acknowledged by us using God as a witness"* <note>original: ἔστω συνωμολογημένον ἡμῖν μάρτυρι τῷ θεῷ χρωμένοις</note>.

So likewise in that saying of *Thales*: *"God is the oldest of all things, because he is Unmade"* <note>original: πρεσβύτατον πάντων ὁ θεὸς, ἀγέννητον γάρ</note>. And that of *Maximus Tyrius*: *"Many gods are the sons of God and co-rulers together with God"* <note>original: πολλοὶ θεοὶ παῖδες θεοῦ, συνάρχοντες θεῷ</note>. Besides these, others have been mentioned which we shall not repeat here. Innumerable more instances of this kind could be added, such as that of *Antiphanes*: *"God is like to nothing, for which cause he cannot be understood by anyone from an image"* <note>original: Θεὸς οὐδενὶ ἔοικεν, διόπερ αὐτὸν οὐδεὶς ἐκμαθεῖν ἐξ εἰκόνος δύναται</note>. Or this from *Socrates*: *"If it please God this way, let it happen this way"* <note>original: εἰ ταύτῃ φίλον τῷ θεῷ, ταύτῃ γενέσθω</note>. If God...

# Chapter 4. *Gods* <note>original: "θεοὶ"</note> interpreted as the inferior gods only.

If *God* will have it so, let it be so. And that saying of *Epictetus*: *Do you only remember these universal principles: what is mine, and what is not mine? What would God have me do now?* <note>original: "σὺ μόνον μέμνη- σο τῶν καθολικῶν, τί ἐμὸν, τί οὐκ ἐμὸν; τί θέλει με ποιεῖν ὁ θεὸς νῦν;"</note> *Do you only remember these catholic <note>meaning: universal</note> and universal principles: What is mine and what is not mine? What would God have me now do? and what would he have me not do?* But we shall mention no more of these, because they occur so frequently in all manner of *Greek writers*, both in *poetry* and *prose*.

Therefore, we shall here only add that, as the *singular* word God <note>original: "θεὸς"</note> was often used by the *Greeks* by way of excellence <note>original: "κατ' ἐξοχὴν"</note>—that is, for the *Supreme Deity*—so was the *plural* word gods <note>original: "θεοὶ"</note> frequently used by them for the *inferior gods* as a way of distinguishing them from the *Supreme*. For example, in that common form of prayer and exclamation, *O Jupiter and the gods* <note>original: "ὦ Ζεῦ καὶ θεοὶ"</note>, and that form of oath <note>original: "Obtestation"</note>, *By Jupiter and the gods* <note>original: "πρὸς Διὸς καὶ θεῶν"</note>. So also in this passage by *Euripides*:

->But it exists, it exists; even if someone laughs at the idea,<-
->Jupiter and the gods watch over the suffering of mortals.<-
<note>original Greek: "Ἀλλ' ἔστιν, ἔστι · κἄν τις ἐγγελᾷ λόγῳ, Ζευς καὶ θεοὶ, βρότεια λεύσαντες πάθη·" and Latin: "Est, (sint licèt qui rideant) est Jupiter, Superíque; Casus qui vident Mortalium."</note>

<margin>Page 106.</margin>
<margin>
*Plato* in *The Republic*: He will never be neglected by the gods who endeavors, as much as it is possible for a man, to become righteous and to practice virtue so as to become like God. Page 613. <note>original: "οὐχ ὑπὸ θεῶν ποτὲ ἀμελεῖται, ὃς ἂν προθυμεῖσθαι ἐθέλῃ δίκαιος γίνεσθαι, καὶ ἐπιτηδεύων ἀρετὴν, εἰς ὅσον δυνατὸν ἀνθρώπῳ ὁμοιοῦσθαι θεῷ."</note>
</margin>

In these passages, just as *Jupiter* is used to represent the *Supreme God*, so is "gods" <note>original: "θεοὶ"</note> used for the *inferior gods* to distinguish them from him. Similarly, both "God" and "gods" are used together in *Plato’s Phaedo*: "God" for the *Supreme, uncreated, and incorruptible Deity*, and "gods" for the *inferior gods only*. *I suppose,* said *Socrates*, *that God and the very species, essence, or idea of life would be admitted by everyone to be indestructible. Doubtless by all men,* said *Cebes*, *but much more so, I believe, by the gods.* <note>original: "ὁ δέ γε θεὸς (οἶμαι) ἔφη ὁ Σωκράτης, καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ τῆς ζωῆς εἶδος παρὰ πάντων ἂν ὁμολογηθείη, μηδέ ποτε ἀπόλλυσθαι. παρὰ πάν- των μέντοι νὴ Δί' (ἔφη) ἀνθρώπων γε; καὶ ἔτι μᾶλλον, ὡς ἐγᾦμαι, παρὰ θεῶν."</note> But a further instance will be presented later of the word "gods" <note>original: "θεοὶ"</note> used this way to distinguish the *inferior gods only*. As previously stated, the *Theogonia*—or *Generation of the Gods*—was universally understood by the *Greeks* to refer to "the gods" <note>original: "οἱ θεοὶ"</note>, meaning the *inferior gods*.

Moreover, just as the word "God" <note>original: "θεὸς"</note> was taken by way of excellence for the *Supreme God*, so was *Daimon* <note>original: "Δαίμων"</note> or "Spirit" as well. For example, in this passage by *Callimachus*, which was previously quoted incompletely:

---
->If you know God,<-
->Know also that everything is possible for a divine spirit.<-
<note>original Greek: "Εἰ θεὸν οἶσθα, Ἴσθ' ὅτι καὶ ῥέξαι δαίμονι πᾶν δυνατόν·" and Latin: "Si Deus est tibi notus, Hoc etiam noris, omnia posse Deum."</note>
---

Where "God" <note>original: "θεὸς"</note> and "Spirit" <note>original: "Δαίμων"</note> are both used specifically <note>original: "signanter"</note> for the *Supreme God*. And this is also the case in that famous passage by another poet—

# *Daimon* <note>original: "Δαίμων"</note> used for the Supreme God. Book 1.

->—— To the wicked,<-
->On sea and land, the *Daimon* <note>In Greek mythology, "Daimon" often referred to a tutelary spirit or a lesser god, but here Cudworth argues it refers to the Supreme Being.</note> has brought ten thousand evils.<-
<note>original Greek: "τοῖς γ᾽ ἀλιτροις, Εἰν ἁλὶ καὶ γαίᾳ, κακὰ μύρια θήκατο δαίμων."</note>

Homer likewise, in one and the same place, seems to use "God" <note>original: "θεὸς"</note> and "*Daimon*" <note>original: "Δαίμων"</note> both together, in the same manner, to mean the **Supreme God**:

> "Whenever a man desires to fight against a man 
> Whom God honors, against the will of the *Daimon* <note>original: "δαίμονα"</note>, soon a great calamity rolls upon him."
> <note>original Greek: "Ὁππότ᾽ ἀνὴρ ἐθέλει πρὸς δαίμονα φωτὶ μάχεσθαι, Ὅν κε θεὸς τιμᾷ, τάχα οἱ μέγα πῆμα κυλίσθη"</note>

> *whom God honors, soon a great disaster is rolled upon him.*
> <note>original Latin: "Quoties homo vult, adverso Numine, cum viro pugnare Quem Deus honorat, mox in eum magna clades devolvitur."</note>

Again, we believe that *Jupiter*, or the **Supreme God**, was sometimes signified among the Pagans by the expression "God Himself" <note>original: "θεὸς αὐτὸς"</note>, as in this passage from *Homer’s* ninth book of the *Iliad*:

->—— Not even if God Himself would promise to me,<-

->--- *Nor if God Himself promised to me,*<-

And thus St. *Cyril* of *Alexandria* interprets *Homer* here: "For he does not say, 'If any of the gods <note>original: "θεῶν τις"</note> should promise me the selling off of my old age and the recovery of my youth,' but he reserves this matter only for the God over all. For the phrase 'God Himself' <note>original: "θεὸς αὐτὸς"</note> does not refer to any of the fictitious beings in the myths, but only points to the one who is truly God." <note>original Greek: "οὐ γὰρ πού φησιν, εἰ καὶ θεῶν τις ὑπόσχοιτό μοι τῷ μὲν γήρως ἀπεμπολωὺ, παλινάγρετον δὲ τὴν νεότητα, τετήρηκε δὲ τὸ χρῆμα μόνῳ τῷ ἐπὶ πάντας θεῷ, &c. τὸ γάρ τοι θεὸς αὐτὸς, οὐκ ἐφ᾽ ἕνα τῶν ἐν μύθοις πεπλασμένων τινὰ, αὐτὸν δὲ μόνον κατασημηνύειν ἂν τὸν ἀληθῶς ὄντα θεόν"</note> *Homer does not say, "If any of the gods would promise me freedom from old age and restoration of youth," but he reserves the matter only for the Supreme God; neither does he refer it to any of the fictitious poetic gods, but to the true God alone.* 

The same language was also spoken in the **Laws of the Twelve Tables**: "Approach the gods chastely; remove wealth. If men do otherwise, God Himself <note>original: "Deus ipse"</note> will be the avenger." <note>original Latin: "Deos adeunto caste, Opes amovento: Si secus faxint, Deus ipse vindex erit"</note> Where, although the word "gods" is used generally so as to include both the *Supreme* and *inferior gods*, yet "God Himself" denotes the Supreme God only. In like manner, "the *Daimon* Himself" <note>original: "ὁ δαίμων αὐτὸς"</note> also seems to be taken for the Supreme God in this line by *Euripides*:

->The *Daimon* Himself will release me, whenever I wish,<-
<note>original Greek: "λύσῃ με ὁ δαίμων αὐτὸς, ὅταν ἐγὼ θέλω"</note>

Which was translated thus by *Horace*:

->—— *God Himself, as soon as he wishes, will set me free.*<-
<note>original Latin: "Ipse Deus, simulatque volet, me solvet."</note>

Notwithstanding this, *Daimon* and *Daimones* are often distinguished from *Theos* and *Theoi* <note>God and Gods</note>, as they are used to represent an *inferior* rank of beings below the gods, commonly called **Demons**; which word, in a large sense...

<meta>This page continues the argument that Greek philosophical and literary terms, such as "the Divine" (to theion) and "the Divine Spirit" (to daimonion), were frequently used by pagan authors to signify the one Supreme God, distinguishing Him from the many lesser deities or spirits.</meta>

# Chapter IV. *The Divine* & *The Divine Spirit*: the Supreme Deity <note>original: "τὸ θεῖον & τὸ δαιμόνιον"</note>

This sense <note>OCR error "fence" likely refers to "sense" or "definition."</note> also includes *Heroes* under it. For though these *Demons* <note>original: "δαίμονες" (daimones), referring to spirits or lesser deities</note> are sometimes called *Gods* too, they were generally considered *Demi-gods* <note>original: "Ἡμίθεοι"</note> rather than *Gods*. Thus, *Gods and Demons* are frequently joined together as distinct things. *Plato* refers to this notion of the word when he concludes that *Love* is not a *God*, but only a *Demon*. However, we will speak more of these *Demons* later.

Furthermore, pagan writers frequently refer to the Supreme *God* as "the Divine" <note>original: "τὸ θεῖον"</note> when the word is used as a noun. For example, in this passage from *Epicharmus*:

->Nothing escapes the Divine; you must know this;<-
->He is himself our overseer; and for God, nothing is impossible.<-
<note>original Greek: "οὐδὲν διαφεύγει τὸ θεῖον· τοῦτο γινώσκειν σε δεῖ· Αὐτὸς ἔσθ' ἡμῶν ἐπόπτης· ἀδυνατεῖ δ' οὐδὲν θεῷ."</note>
<note>original Latin: "Res nulla est Deum quæ lateat, scire quod te convenit; Ipse est noster Introspector, nam Deus nil non potest."</note>

So likewise in this passage from *Plato*: "The Divine is seated far from pleasure and grief" <note>original Greek: "πόῤῥω ἡδονῆς καὶ λύπης ἵδρυται τὸ θεῖον"</note>. And *Plotinus* calls the Supreme *God* "The Divinity that is in the Universe" <note>original Greek: "τὸ ἐν τῷ παντὶ θεῖον"</note>. But because instances of this are innumerable, we shall decline mentioning any more. Instead, we will only set down the judgment of that diligent and impartial observer of the force of words, *Henricus Stephanus* <note>Henri Estienne (1528–1598), a famous French classical scholar and lexicographer.</note>, concerning it:

> "The term 'the Divine' <note>original: 'τὸ θεῖον'</note> is also often translated as 'God,' but in such a way that it must be understood that even secular <note>original: 'profanis'</note> writers did not use it for just any god. Rather, they used it for the one they meant when they said 'the God,' as if by way of excellence <note>original: 'κατ' ἐξοχὴν'</note>. This was to distinguish him from those many who were included under the title of 'gods'—namely, the highest and most supreme Deity—or, as you might say, the 'highest and best of gods' <note>original: 'θεῶν ὕπατον καὶ ἄριστον'</note>, as Homer speaks of Jove."

Lastly, just as "the Divine" <note>original: "τὸ θεῖον"</note> was used, so also was "the Divine Spirit" <note>original: "τὸ δαιμόνιον"</note> used by the *Greeks* for the Supreme *Deity* <note>original: "Numen"</note>, or that Divinity which governs the whole world. Thus, while it was commonly said (according to *Herodotus*) "That the Divine was envious" <note>original Greek: "ὅτι τὸ θεῖον φθονερόν"</note>—the meaning of which was that He did not commonly suffer any great human prosperity to continue long without some check or setback—the same proverbial speech is expressed in *Aristotle* as "the Divine Spirit is envious" <note>original Greek: "φθονερόν τὸ δαιμόνιον"</note>. 

In this sense, the word seems to be used by *Isocrates* in his work *To Demonicus*: "Honor the Divine Spirit always, but especially along with the city" <note>original Greek: "τίμα τὸ δαιμόνιον ἀεὶ μὲν, μάλιστα δὲ μετὰ τῆς πόλεως"</note>, meaning in her public sacrifices. And matches this was surely the meaning of *Epictetus* in this passage: <margin>Arrian, Book 4, chapter 4, page 387.</margin> 

> "There is but one way to tranquility of mind and happiness. Let this, therefore, be always ready at hand with you, both when you wake early in the morning, all day long, and when you go late to sleep: to consider no external things as your own, but to commit all these to God <note>original: 'τῷ δαιμονίῳ' (the Divine Spirit)</note> and Fortune." 
<note>original Greek: "μία ὁδὸς ἐπὶ εὔροιαν, τοῦτο καὶ ὄρθρου, καὶ μεθ' ἡμέραν καὶ νύκτωρ, ἔστω πρόχειρον, ἀπόστασις τῶν ἀπροαιρέτων, τὸ μηδὲν ἴδιον ἡγεῖσθαι, τὸ παραδοῦναι πάντα τῷ δαιμονίῳ, καὶ τῇ τύχῃ."</note>

And there is a very remarkable passage in *Demosthenes* (observed by *Budæus* <note>Guillaume Budé (1467–1540), a French scholar and humanist.</note>) that must not be omitted here, in which we have "the gods" <note>original: "οἱ θεοὶ"</note> used plainly for the inferior or minor *gods* only, and "the Divine Spirit" <note>original: "τὸ δαιμόνιον"</note> for...

# Pagan Descriptions of the Supreme God. Book I.

...the *Supreme God* together: "The Gods and the Deity will take notice of him who does not give a righteous sentence" <note>original Greek: "ἔσονται οἱ θεοὶ καὶ τὸ δαιμόνιον, ἢ μὴ τὰ δίκαια ψηφισάμενοι"</note>; that is, both the *Lesser Gods* and the *Supreme God himself*. Therefore, we see that the word *daimonion* <note>a Greek term for "divine power" or "deity"</note>, as far as its grammatical form is concerned, is not a diminutive <note>a word form expressing smallness</note>, as some have thought, but an adjective used as a noun, just as "the Divine" <note>original: "τὸ θεῖον" (to theion)</note> is. Nevertheless, in pagan writings, *daimonion*—as well as *daimon*, from which it is derived—is often used for a *lower rank of beings* below the *Gods*, though they are sometimes called *Gods* too. Such was the "divine spirit" <note>original: "δαιμόνιον" (daimonion)</note> of Socrates, which is so well known. However, the grammar of this word and its proper meaning in pagan writers cannot be better shown than by quoting a passage of *Socrates's own* in his *Apology*,

<margin>Page 27, Stephanus edition.</margin>
as written by *Plato*. Even though Socrates was generally supposed to have had a *spirit* <note>original: "Dæmon"</note>, he was nevertheless accused of *Atheism* by *Melitus*: "Is there anyone, Melitus, who acknowledges that there are human things, yet denies that there are any men? Or anyone who acknowledges equine <note>related to horses</note> things, yet denies that there are any horses? ... If this cannot be, then no man who acknowledges divine things can deny the existence of spirits. Therefore, if I am admitted to assert divine things <note>original: "δαιμόνια" (daimonia)</note>, it must follow that I hold there are spirits <note>original: "δαίμονας" (daimones)</note> also. Now, do we not all think that spirits are either Gods or, at least, the sons of the Gods? ... Therefore, for anyone to conceive that there are spirits and yet no Gods is as absurd as if someone thought there were mules, but neither horses nor donkeys." <note>original Greek: "ἔστιν ὅστις ἀνθρώπων, ὦ Μέλιτε... ἢ ὅστις ἵππους μὲν οὐ νομίζει, ἱππικὰ δὲ πράγματα;... ἔσθ’ ὅστις δαιμόνια μὲν νομίζει πράγματα εἶναι, δαίμονας δὲ οὐ νομίζει;... τοὺς δὲ δαίμονας οὐχὶ ἤτοι θεούς γε ἡγούμεθα εἶναι, ἢ θεῶν παῖδας;"</note>

However, in the New Testament, according to the judgment of *Origen*, *Eusebius*, and other Ancient Fathers, both those words—*daimones* and *daimonia*—are always used in a *worse sense*, referring only to *evil and impure spirits*.

But beyond all this, the pagans often characterize the *Supreme God* with titles, descriptions, and epithets that belong uniquely to him, thereby plainly distinguishing him from all other *inferior gods*. He is sometimes called by them: 
* *The Demiurge* <note>original: "ὁ Δημιουργὸς"</note>, the Architect or Maker of the world; 
* *The Prince and Chief Ruler of the universe* <note>original: "ὁ Ηγεμὼν τοῦ παντὸς καὶ Αρχηγέτης"</note>; 
* *The First* and *The Most Primary God* <note>original Greek: "ὁ πρῶτος and ὁ πρώτιστος θεὸς"; original Latin: "Primus Deus"</note>; 
* *The First Mind* <note>original: "ὁ πρῶτος νοῦς"</note>; 
* *The Great God* <note>original: "ὁ μέγας θεὸς"</note>; 
* *The Greatest Spirit* and *The Greatest of the Gods* <note>original: "ὁ μέγιστος δαίμων, and ὁ μέγιστος θεῶν"</note>; 
* *The Highest* <note>original: "ὁ Υψιστος"</note>; 
* *The Supreme of the Gods* <note>original: "ὁ ὕπατος θεῶν"</note>; 
* *The Uppermost* or *Most Transcendent God* <note>original: "ὁ ἀνωτάτω θεὸς"</note>; 
* *That Chief or Principal God* <note>original: "Princeps ille Deus"</note>; 
* *The God of Gods* <note>original: "θεὸς θεῶν"</note>; 
* *The Principle of Principles* <note>original: "Αρχὴ Αρχῶν"</note>; 
* *The First Cause* <note>original: "τὸ πρῶτον αἴτιον"</note>; 
* *He who generated or created this whole universe* <note>original: "ὁ τόδε τὸ πᾶν γεννήσας"</note>; 
* *He who rules over the whole world* <note>original: "ὁ Κρατέων τοῦ παντός"</note>; 
* *The Supreme Governor and Lord of all* <note>original: "Summus Rector & Dominus"</note>; 
* *The God over all* <note>original: "ὁ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεὸς"</note>; 
* *The unbegotten, self-generated, self-produced God...* <note>original: "ὁ θεὸς ἀγέννητος, αὐτογενὴς, αὐτοφυὴς, αὐθυ-"</note>
