# Chapter IV. Champions for Paganism Assert Monarchy.

...**self-originated** <note>original Greek: αὐθυπόστατος (authypostatos) — "self-subsisting" or "self-generated"</note>, the **Ingenerate or Unmade Self-originated and Self-subsisting Deity**; a **Monad** <note>original Greek: μονὰς (monas) — a single, indivisible unit</note>; **Unity and Goodness itself** <note>original Greek: τὸ ἓν καὶ αὐτὸ ἀγαθὸν (to hen kai auto agathon)</note>; **that which is above Essence** <note>original Greek: τὸ ἐπέκεινα τῆς Οὐσίας (to epekeina tēs Ousias)</note> or **Super-essential** <note>original Greek: τὸ ὑπερούσιον (to hyperousion)</note>; **that which is above mind and Understanding** <note>original Greek: τὸ ἐπέκεινα νοῦ (to epekeina nou)</note>; **That Supreme and Eternal Being, which is Immutable and can never perish** <note>original Latin: "Summum illud & Æternum, neque mutabile neque interiturum"</note>; **The Beginning, and End, and Middle of all things** <note>original Greek: Ἀρχὴ, καὶ τέλος, καὶ μέσον ἁπάντων (Archē, kai telos, kai meson hapantōn)</note>; **One and all things** <note>original Greek: Ἓν καὶ πάντα (Hen kai panta)</note>; **One God and All Gods** <note>original Latin: "Deus Unus & Omnes"</note>; and lastly, to name no more, **Providence** <note>original Greek: ἡ πρόνοια (hē pronoia)</note>, as distinguished from **Nature** <note>original Greek: φύσις (physis)</note>, is often used by them as a name for the Supreme God. Because "Providence" is a feminine noun in Greek, the impious and atheistic Epicureans <note>a school of philosophy that believed the gods were indifferent to human affairs and that the world was made of atoms</note> took the opportunity to mockingly and jokingly call God **"Providence, the old fortune-telling woman"** <note>original Latin: "Anum fatidicam Pronœan"</note>. Now, all these and other similar expressions are found in the writings of professed pagans (as we are able to show), and some of them very frequently. Therefore, it cannot be denied that the pagans made a clear distinction between the *Supreme God* and all their other *inferior gods*.

XV. What has now been declared might, we believe, be considered sufficient for our present goal. Our goal is to prove that the more intelligent ancient *Pagans*, despite the many gods they worshipped, generally acknowledged *one Supreme, Omnipotent, and Only Unmade Deity*. 

Nevertheless, people are often biased toward the opposite view. The reason for this seems to be that the modern *definition of the word "God"* (as it is generally understood by us Christians) essentially includes the trait of *self-existence*. Therefore, people are likely to imagine that the word must have meant the same thing to the Pagans. To counter this, we will attempt to produce further evidence for the truth of *our claim*. 

First, we believe it is a strong confirmation that after the arrival of Christianity—and throughout the entire struggle and conflict between it and *Paganism*—none of the professional champions of *Paganism* or opponents of Christianity ever argued for a *multiplicity of unmade, intelligent deities* (or *Creators*). On the contrary, when given the chance, they all generally denied such a thing. They openly professed to acknowledge *one Supreme, Self-existent Deity, who is the Maker of the whole Universe*.

It is highly probable, if not certain, that *Apollonius of Tyana* <note>a Greek Neopythagorean philosopher from the 1st century AD who was often compared to Jesus</note>—shortly after the Gospel was published to the world—was a person chosen by the *strategy* and assisted by the *powers of darkness* to perform extraordinary things. This was done simply to distract from the *miracles* of our *Saviour Christ* and to allow *Paganism* to better withstand the attacks of *Christianity*. Among the many writers of this philosopher's life, some (and particularly *Philostratus*) seem to have had no other goal in their work than to dress up *Apollonius* in a way that would make him seem to...

<summary>This page argues that ancient pagan philosophers used specific titles to distinguish a single Supreme Creator from lesser deities. It asserts that even during the rise of Christianity, pagan defenders advocated for a "Monarchy" of one God rather than a collection of multiple uncreated creators.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a discussion on how pagan defenders of the 3rd and 4th centuries attempted to bolster their own religious traditions by presenting "divine men" as rivals to Jesus Christ, specifically focusing on the philosopher Apollonius of Tyana.</meta>

# Apollonius of Tyana, Book I.

...to be a suitable rival to our Savior, **Christ**, both in terms of **holiness** and **miracles**. Therefore, Eunapius tells us that the author [Philostratus] titled his book incorrectly, and that instead of *The Life of Apollonius* <note>original Greek: 'Απολλωνίου βίου (Apollōniou biou)</note>, he should have called it *The Descent and Interaction of God with Men* <note>original Greek: θεοῦ εἰς ἀνθρώπους ἐπιδημίαν (theou eis anthrōpous epidēmian)</note>. For, as he says, this **Apollonius** was not merely a philosopher or a man, *but something intermediate between the gods and men* <note>original Greek: ἀλλά τι θεῶν καὶ ἀνθρώπων μέσον (alla ti theōn kai anthrōpōn meson)</note>. It is clear in several ways that pagans commonly used this history of Apollonius to set him up as a rival and opponent to our Savior, Christ. <margin>Letter 4</margin> **Marcellinus**, in a letter to **Saint Augustine**, describes this as the primary objection of the pagans against Christianity (and asks for Augustine's answer to it): *The Pagans falsely claim that the Lord did nothing more than what other men have been able to do; they bring forward their own Apollonius and Apuleius and other men of the magical arts, whose miracles they claim were even greater.* <note>original Latin: "Nihil aliud Dominum, quàm alii homines facere potuerunt, fecisse vel egisse mentiuntur; Apollonium siquidem suum nobis, & Apuleius, aliósque Magicae artis homines, in medium proferunt, quorum majora contendunt exstitisse miracula"</note>.

It is also well known that **Hierocles**, whom **Eusebius** praises as a very learned man, wrote a book against the Christians (titled *The Lover of Truth* <note>original Greek: φιλαλήθης (Philalēthēs) or λόγοι φιλαλήθεις (logoi philalētheis)</note>). His main purpose was to compare this **Apollonius of Tyana** with our Savior Christ and to rank him higher. *The Christians (Hierocles says) make a great fuss, exalting Jesus because he supposedly restored sight to the blind and performed other such wonders.* <note>original Greek: ῎Ανω καὶ κάτω θρυλλοῦσι, σεμνύνοντες τὸν Ἰησοῦν, ὡς τυφλοῖς ἀναβλέψαι τε παρασχόντα, καὶ τίνα τοιαῦτα δράσαντα θαυμάσια</note> These are Hierocles' own words as quoted by Eusebius. After mentioning the <term>thaumaturgi</term> <note>original Greek: θαυματουργοί (thaumatourgoi) — literally "wonder-workers" or miracle-performers</note> or miracle-workers among the pagans—focusing especially on Apollonius of Tyana and dwelling at length on his miracles—he adds at the end: *To what purpose, then, have I mentioned all these things? Only so that our solid and firm judgment on each matter might be compared with the lightheadedness of the Christians. For we do not consider a man who performed such things to be a god, but only a man favored by the gods; yet they declare Jesus to be a god based on just a few miraculous tricks.* <note>original Greek: τίνος οὖν ἕνεκα τούτων ἐμνήσθην; ἵνα ἐξῇ συγκρίνειν τὴν ἡμετέραν ἀκριβῆ καὶ βεβαίαν ἐφ᾽ ἑκάστῳ κρίσιν, καὶ τὴν τῶν χριστιανῶν κουφότητα· εἴπερ ἡμεῖς μὲν τὰ τοιαῦτα πεποιηκότα, οὐ θεὸν, ἀλλὰ θεοῖς κεχαρισμένον ἄνδρα ἡγύμεθα· οἱ δὲ δι᾽ ὀλίγας τερατείας τινὰς τὸν Ἰησοῦν θεὸν ἀναγορεύουσι</note>. 

Because Eusebius is silent on this specific point, we must add an answer from **Lactantius** (which he seems to have directed against those very words of Hierocles, though he does not name him), as it is both relevant and thorough. <margin>On Justice, Book 5, Chapter 3</margin> *It appears that we are wiser, who did not immediately grant faith in His divinity because of marvelous deeds, than you, who believed someone was a god because of minor portents. — Learn, therefore, if you have any heart, that we do not believe Christ is God solely because he performed miracles, but because we saw that everything announced to us by the predictions of the Prophets was fulfilled in him. He performed miracles; we would have thought him a magician (as you now call him, and as the Jews thought then) if all the Prophets had not, with one spirit, predicted that Christ would do those very things. Therefore, we believe him to be God not only because of his marvelous deeds and works, but also because of that very Cross, which you lick like dogs; for that too was predicted at the same time. Not, therefore, by his own testimo-* <note>The text ends here at the catchword "Testimo-", likely completing the word "testimony" on the following page.</note>

### CHAPTER IV. A Rival with our Savior Christ.

By testimony—*for who can be believed when speaking of themselves?*—but by the testimony of the Prophets, who long before sang of all the things he did and suffered, he received the credit of Divinity; which can never happen to **Apollonius**, nor **Apuleius**, nor any of the Magicians. <note>original Latin: "Testimonio, (cui enim de se dicenti potest credi?) sed Prophetarum Testimonio, qui omnia quæ fecit ac passus est, multo antè cecinerunt; fidem Divinitatis accepit; quod neque Apollonio neque Apuleio, neque cuiquam Magorum potest aliquando contingere."</note>

It is clear that we Christians are wiser than you Pagans, because we do not immediately attribute Divinity to a person simply because of their wonders. In contrast, a few astonishing events or extraordinary actions are enough for you to deify the person who does them (and indeed, some did deify **Apollonius**, even though **Hierocles** denies it). Let this writer against Christianity therefore learn—if he has any understanding or sense—that **Christ** was not believed to be a God by us Christians merely because of his miracles, but because we saw all those things performed by and fulfilled in him which were predicted to us long ago by the Prophets. He performed miracles, and we should therefore have suspected him of being a <term>magician</term> <note>original: "Magician"</note>—as you now call him, and as the Jews then supposed him to be—had not all the Prophets with one voice foretold that he should do such things. 

We believe him to be God no more because of his miracles than because of that very Cross of his, which you dispute so much, because that was likewise foretold. So, our belief in Christ's divinity is not founded upon his own testimony—for who can be believed concerning himself?—but upon the testimony of the Prophets, who sang long before of all those things which he both did and suffered. This is such a unique advantage and privilege of his that neither **Apollonius** nor **Apuleius**, nor any other magician, could ever share in it. 

Now, as for the life and morals of this **Apollonius of Tyana**: it was absolutely necessary for carrying out such a diabolical plan that the person used as an instrument should have some convincing and plausible appearance of virtue. Accordingly, **Apollonius** took upon himself the profession of a **Pythagorean** <note>A follower of the philosopher Pythagoras, known for strict asceticism and vegetarianism.</note> and acted that part externally so well that even **Sidonius Apollinaris**, though a Christian, was so dazzled by the glittering show and luster of his counterfeit virtues as if he had been enchanted by this magician long after his death. 

Nevertheless, anyone who is not very shortsighted in such matters, or biased, may easily perceive that this **Apollonius** was so far from having anything of that Divine Spirit which manifested itself in our Savior **Christ** (transcending all the philosophers that ever existed) that he fell far short of the more virtuous Pagans—for example, **Socrates**. There is a clear appearance of much pride and vainglory, besides other nonsense, discoverable in both his words and actions. **Eusebius** undertakes to prove this from **Philostratus's** own history, even though it contains many falsehoods: 

"That **Apollonius** was so far from deserving to be compared with our Savior **Christ**, that he was not fit to be ranked even among moderately and passably honest men." <note>original Greek: οὐδ᾽ ἐν ἐπιεικέσι κῂ μετρίοις ἀνδράσιν ἄξιον ἐγκρίνειν, οὐχ᾽ ὅπως τῷ σωτῆρι ἡμῶν χριστῷ παρατιθέναι τὸν Ἀπολλώνιον (oud' en epieikesi kai metriois andrasin axion enkrinein, ouch' hopōs tō sōtēri hēmōn christō paratithenai ton Apollōnion)</note> 

Therefore, regarding his reputed miracles: if credit is to be given to those stories, and such things were really done by him, it must also be concluded for this reason that they were done by nothing other than <term>magick</term> and <term>necromancy</term> <note>The practice of communicating with the dead to predict the future or perform spells.</note>; and that this **Apollonius** was but an <term>Archimago</term> <note>A "great magician" or chief sorcerer.</note> or grand magician. This should not be suspected as a mere slander cast upon him by biased Christians only, since during his lifetime—

# Apollonius of Tyana: A Professed Magician? Book I.

At the time, he was generally reputed, even among the Pagans themselves, to be nothing more than an **infamous enchanter** <note>original Greek: *γόης* (goēs)</note>, and was accused of that very crime before **Emperor Domitian**. He was also represented as such by one of the Pagan writers of his life, **Moeragenes**, who lived before <margin>Against Celsus, Book 6, page 302.</margin> **Philostratus**, as we learn from **Origen**: 

"Concerning **infamous and diabolical magic**, he who would like to know whether or not a **philosopher** can be tempted by it or ensnared <note>original: "illaqueable"</note> by it, let him read the **writings** of **Moeragenes** concerning the memorable things of **Apollonius of Tyana**, the **magician** and **philosopher**. In these, Moeragenes—who was not a **Christian** but a **Pagan philosopher** himself—affirms that some quite noble philosophers were caught by the magic of Apollonius, having approached him as if he were an enchanter <note>original Greek: *γόης* (goēs)</note>. In these accounts, I believe, he also wrote about **Euphrates** and a certain **Epicurean**." <note>original Greek: *περὶ μαγείας φαμὲν, ὅτι ὁ βου-λόμενος ἐξετάσαι, πότερόν ποτε καὶ φιλόσοφοι ἁλωτοί εἰσιν αὐτῇ, ἢ μή, ἀνα-γνώτω τὰ γεγραμμένα Μοιραγενεῖ τῷ Ἀπολλωνίου τῷ Τυανέως μάγου καὶ φιλο-σόφου ἀπομνημονευμάτων· ἐν οἷς ὁ μὴ χριστιανὸς ἀλλὰ φιλόσοφος, ἔφησεν ἁ-λῶναι ὑπό τινος ἐν Ἀπολλωνίῳ μαγείας, οὐκ ἀγενεῖς τινας φιλοσόφους, ὡς πρὸς γόητα αὐτὸν εἰσελθόντας· ἐν οἷς, οἶμαι, καὶ περὶ Ἐυφράτου πάνυ διηγήσατο, καί τινος Ἐπικυρείου*.</note>

No doubt this was the reason why **Philostratus** dismisses the authority of this Moeragenes so much, claiming that he was ignorant of many things concerning Apollonius ("For we must not pay attention to Moeragenes," etc.). Philostratus did this because Moeragenes had represented Apollonius in his true colors as a **magician**, whereas Philostratus’s entire goal and design was, on the contrary, to clear him of that accusation. The truth of that accusation, however, may be sufficiently proven even from the very things recorded by Philostratus himself. 

And here, by the way, we shall observe that it is reported by good historians that miracles were also performed by **Vespasian** at **Alexandria**. <margin>Histories, Book 4, page 111.</margin> These are the words of **Tacitus**: "Many miracles happened, by which the favor of heaven and a certain inclination of the divine powers toward **Vespasian** were shown. A certain **Alexandrian** commoner, known for a wasting disease of the eyes, threw himself at Vespasian's knees, begging with a groan for a remedy for his blindness. He did this on the advice of the god **Serapis**, whom that nation, devoted to superstitions, worships above all others. He prayed the Prince that he would deign to moisten his cheeks and the circles of his eyes with his spit. Another with a diseased hand (directed by the same oracle) beseeched him only to step upon it with his foot." <note>original Latin: *multa miracula evenere, quîs cælestis favor, & quædam in Vespasianum inclinatio numinum ostenderetur. Ex plebe Alexandrinâ quidam, oculorum tabe notus, genua ejus advolvitur, remedium cæcitatis exposcens gemitu; monitu Serapidis Dei, quem dedita superstitionibus gens ante alios colit; precabaturque Principem, ut genas & oculorum orbes dignaretur respergere oris excremento. Alius manu æger, eodem Deo auctore, ut pede ac vestigio Cæsaris calcaretur orabat.*</note>

After some debate concerning this business, both these things were done by Vespasian, and "immediately the hand was restored to use, and daylight shone again for the blind man." <note>original Latin: *statim conversa ad usum manus, & cæco reluxit dies*</note> Both of these things (says the historian) are testified to this very day by those who were eyewitnesses, at a time when there can be no advantage for anyone to lie about it. ->## CHAP. IV. Assertor of Monarchy.<-

...with **Vespasian**, but also at that very time (as **Philostratus** informs us) present with him at **Alexandria**, where he also performed many miracles himself. However, we may here take notice of another stratagem and policy of the Devil in this: it was a plan both to obscure the miracles of our Savior Christ, and to weaken men's faith in the **Messiah** and dismiss the idea of it. 

Because a rumor of prophecies had spread everywhere—stating that a King was to come out of **Judea** and rule over the whole world (by which was meant none other than the Messiah)—the Devil ensured that through these miracles performed by Vespasian, this oracle or prediction might instead seem to be fulfilled in him. Vespasian was first proclaimed Emperor in Judea, and the historian **Josephus** himself basely and flatteringly applied the prophecy to him. 

Since this business was started and suggested by the god **Serapis** (that is, by the Devil, whose counsel **Apollonius** was also likely following), this makes it even more strongly suspicious that it was really a design or policy of the Devil. By imitating the miracles of our Savior Christ through both Apollonius and Vespasian, the Devil sought to counter-work God Almighty’s plan for Christianity and to maintain or preserve his own usurped tyranny over the Pagan world.

Nevertheless, we shall here show Apollonius all the favor we can. We will therefore suppose him not to have been one of those more foul and "black" magicians of the common sort—who are not only deeply sunk in debauched lives but also knowingly pay homage to evil spirits to satisfy their lusts. Instead, we may view him as one of those more refined magicians who called themselves **Theurgists** <note>original: "Theurgists"—Practitioners of a type of "high magic" intended to invoke the presence of gods or beneficial spirits to achieve spiritual purification.</note>. These people, being somewhat free from the grosser vices and believing they are dealing only with good spirits, are nevertheless proud and vainglorious. Because they are obsessed with performing wonders and transcending the rest of humanity, they are—by a **Divine Nemesis** <note>original: "Divine Nemesis"—The Greek concept of divine retribution or a balancing justice that punishes pride.</note>—justly exposed to the illusions of the Devil or evil spirits, who cunningly insert themselves and adapt to their desires.

However, concerning this Apollonius, it is undeniable that he was a zealous upholder of **Pagan Polytheism** and a stout champion for "the Gods." He professed to have been taught by the ghost of **Pythagoras** of Samos how to worship these gods (both the invisible and the visible) and how to converse with them. For this reason, he is styled by **Vopiscus** as a "True Friend of the Gods" <note>original Latin: *Amicus verus Deorum*</note>—that is, a hearty and sincere friend to that old Pagan religion then being challenged by Christianity, in which not just one true God, but a multiplicity of gods, were worshipped.

But despite all this, Apollonius himself was a clear and undoubted proponent of **One Supreme Deity**. This is evident from his defense speech <note>original: "Apologetick Oration"</note> in Philostratus, prepared for **Domitian**, in which he calls him "the God of the universe" <note>original Greek: *τὸν τῶν ὅλων*</note> and "the God who is the creator of all things" <note>original Greek: *τὸν πάντων δημιουργὸν θεὸν*</note>. He also declares elsewhere in Philostratus that both the Indians and Egyptians agreed on this theology. Even though the Egyptians condemned the Indians for many of their other opinions, they highly applauded this doctrine: "That God was the maker of both the generation and essence of all things, and that the cause of his making them was his own goodness." <note>original Greek: *τὸν μὲν ὅλων γενέσεώς τε καὶ οὐσίας θεὸν δημιουργὸν εἶναι, τόδε ἐνθυμηθῆναι ταῦτα, αἴτιον τὸ ἀγαθὸν εἶναι αὐτόν*</note>

<margin>Philostratus, Page 142.</margin> *Essential Goodness:* Philostratus himself highly praises this philosophy of *Jarchas*, the *Indian Brahmin* <note>original: Brachman</note>: namely, that the whole world was but *one great animal*, and might be compared to a *vast ship*. In this ship, there are many inferior, subordinate governors under *one supreme* ruler—the oldest and wisest. There are also expert mariners of several types: some to attend the deck, and others to climb the masts and manage the sails. <note>original: ἐν ᾗ τὴν μὲν πρώτην καὶ τελευτάτην ἕδραν ἀποδοτέον θεῷ γενέτορι τοῦδε τοῦ ζώου, τὴν δ' ὑπ' ἐκείνῃ, θεοῖς οἳ τὰ μέρη αὐτοῦ κυβερνῶσι. καὶ τὴν ποιητῶν ἀποδεχόμεθα, ἐπειδὴ πολλὸς μὲν φάσκωσιν ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ θεὺς εἶναι, πολλὸς δ' ἐν θαλάσσῃ, πολλὸς δ' ἐν πηγαῖς τε καὶ νάμασι, πολλὸς δ' καὶ περὶ γῆν, εἶναι δ' καὶ ὑπὸ γῆν τινας.</note> *In this ship, the first and highest seat is to be given to that God who is the creator of this great animal; the seats below it belong to those gods who govern its various parts respectively. Thus, the poets were to be approved of here when they affirm that there are many gods in the heavens, many in the seas, many in the rivers and fountains, many also upon the earth, and some even under the earth.* Here we have a true representation of old Pagan theology, which Indians, Egyptians, and European poets (both Greek and Latin) all agreed upon: that there is one supreme God, the maker of the universe, and under him many inferior generated gods—or intelligent beings superior to men—appointed to govern and preside over its various parts. These lesser gods were also to be religiously honored and worshipped by men. And so much for *Apollonius Tyanaeus*.

The first Pagan writer against Christianity was *Celsus*, who lived in the time of the Emperor *Hadrian* <note>original: Adrian</note>. He was such a committed polytheist that he accused the Jews of having been seduced by the deceptions of *Moses* into

The next and greatest champion for the pagan cause in books and writings was that famous Tyrian philosopher, Malchus, called by the Greeks **Porphyry** <note>Porphyry (c. 234–c. 305 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who was a significant opponent of early Christianity.</note>. ### Hierocles in his *Philalethes*, clearly. Book I.

...have been unrefined and illiterate persons. I say, though Hierocles—for one reason or another—is not named here by Lactantius <note>Lactantius (c. 250–c. 325) was an early Christian author and advisor to Constantine the Great.</note> in these cited words or in what follows, there is no doubt that he was the person intended, for two reasons. 

First, because Lactantius tells us afterward that the main business of that *Christiano-mastix* <term>original: "Christiano-mastix"; literally "scourge of Christians," a term for a harsh critic of Christianity</term> was to compare Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Tyana was a 1st-century Greek philosopher and reputed miracle-worker used by pagans as a rival figure to Jesus.</note> with our Savior Christ: 

*Since he sought to undermine the miracles of Christ without denying them, he wanted to show that Apollonius had done equal or even greater things. It is a wonder that he omitted Apuleius <note>Apuleius (c. 124–c. 170) was a Roman philosopher and author often associated with magic.</note> too, whose many wonderful deeds are also commonly recounted by the pagans. Furthermore, he intended to prove Christ's insolence for making himself a God, suggesting that Apollonius was the more modest person; for though he performed (in the author's view) greater miracles, he never claimed such divinity for himself.* <note>original: "Cùm facta Christi mirabilia destrueret, nec tamen negaret, voluit ostendere, Apollonium vel paria, vel etiam majora fecisse. Mirum quòd Apuleium prætermiserit, cujus solent & multa & mira memorari. Et ex hoc insolentiam Christi voluit arguere, quòd Deum se constituerit: ut ille verecundior fuisse videretur, qui cùm majora faceret (ut hic putat) tamen id sibi non arrogaverit"</note> 

The second reason is because Lactantius also expressly mentions the very title of Hierocles’ book, namely, *Philalethes* <note>meaning "The Lover of Truth"</note>: 

*Although he poured out such delusions of his own ignorance and strove to completely destroy the Truth, he dared to title his wicked books—which were enemies of God—"Philaletheis," or Friends of Truth.* <note>original: "Cùm talia ignorantiæ suæ deliramenta fudisset, cúmque Veritatem penitùs excidere connixus est, ausus est Libros suos nefarios, ac Dei hostes, φιλαλήθεις annotare"</note>

<margin>Dr. Pearson, Bishop of Chester.</margin> 
From these words of Lactantius and those preceding, where he affirms that this "Scourge of Christians" wrote two books, the learned writer of the preface to the recent edition of Hierocles concludes that the full title of Hierocles’ book was *Truth-loving discourses against the Christians.* <note>original: "λόγοι φιλαλήθεις πρὸς χρισιανός"</note> I suspect that the first of those two books by Hierocles focused on arguments that Porphyry had previously urged against the Christians. However, in the second book, he added a new argument of his own: comparing Apollonius with our Savior Christ, which is the only part Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339) was a historian who wrote a specific rebuttal to Hierocles.</note> takes notice of. 

Since Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century Church Father.</note> tells us that there was a Hierocles who served as a Prefect or Governor of Alexandria during the persecutions under Diocletian, we may probably conclude that this was the very person described by Lactantius. Lactantius says he was first among the ranks of the judges and a principal actor in the persecution, and then afterwards wrote this *Philalethes* against the Christians, in which, among other things, he ventured to compare Apollonius of Tyana with our Savior Christ. 

Now, if this Hierocles—who wrote the *Philalethes* in defense of the pagan gods against the Christians—was also the author of those two other philosophical books (the *Commentary upon the Golden Verses* and *On Fate and Providence*), it could easily be proven from both of them that he was, nonetheless, a supporter of **one supreme deity**. However, Photius <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and scholar.</note> tells us that the Hierocles who wrote the book concerning *Fate and Providence* mentioned Jamblichus and his student Plutarch of Athens. From this, Jonsius <note>Johannes Jonsius (1624–1659), a German scholar of the history of philosophy.</note>—taking it for granted that it was the same Hierocles who wrote against the Christians and the work *On Fate*—infers that he could not be the same person Eusebius...

### CHAPTER IV. Acknowledged a Supreme Divinity.

...who answered the *Philalethes*, but that it must have been some other Eusebius, who was much younger. But finding Hierocles’s *Philalethes* mentioned in the works of Lactantius, we must instead conclude the opposite: that Hierocles the famous <term>original: "Christiano-mastix"; literally "scourge of Christians," a term for a harsh critic of Christianity</term> Christian-scourge was not the same person as the Hierocles who wrote *On Fate* (*De Fato*). 

This is further evident from Æneas Gazaeus in his work *Theophrastus*. There, he first mentions one Hierocles, an Alexandrian who had been his teacher and whom he highly praises: <margin>P. 7.</margin> "But tell me, I pray you, are there still left among you in Egypt any such expounders of the secret mysteries of philosophy as Hierocles our master was?" <note>original: ἀλλ’ εἰπέ μοι ἔτι παρ’ ὑμῖν εἰσὶν οἵ τῆς φιλοσοφίας δεικνύντες τὰς τελετὰς, οἷος ἦν Ἱεροκλῆς ὁ διδάσκαλος;</note> We suppose this to be the Hierocles who wrote concerning Fate and Providence (and perhaps also the commentary on the *Golden Verses*). 

But later, while discussing Apollonius of Tyana (the Cappadocian), he mentions another Hierocles, distinct from the first—namely, the one who had boasted of Apollonius’s miracles: <margin>P. 24.</margin> "Thus Apollonius is convicted of falsehood; but Hierocles—not our master, but he who boasts of the miracles [of Apollonius]—adds another incredible thing." <note>original: ὁ Ἀπολλώνιος τὰ ψευδῆ λέγων ἐλέγχεται. Ἱεροκλῆς δὲ οὐκ ὁ διδάσκαλος, ἀλλ’ ὁ προβαλλόμενος τὰ θαυμάσια, ἄπιστον καὶ τοῦτο προσέθηκεν.</note> And though it is probable that one of these was the author of that commentary on the *Golden Verses* (for the idea that it was written by a Christian is merely a dream), we cannot determine with certainty which of them it was. 

However, it is clearly manifest from Lactantius that this Hierocles, who was the scourge of Christianity and a champion for the pagan gods, was nevertheless a professed supporter of one **Supreme Deity**. Lactantius writes the following: 

"What truth, finally, have you brought us, except that as an advocate for the gods, you have in the end betrayed those very gods? For in the conclusion of your book, speaking the praises of the Supreme God—whom you confessed to be the King, the Greatest, the <term>original: "Opifex"; an artisan, creator, or maker</term> Maker of all things, the Fountain of good, the Parent of all, and the Creator and Nourisher of living beings—you have by this means stripped your Jupiter of his kingdom. By casting him down from supreme power, you have reduced him to the rank of an inferior minister. Therefore, your own epilogue convicts you of folly, vanity, and error, in that you both assert that there are gods and yet subject and <term>original: "mancipas"; to deliver up or enslave</term> enslave them to that one God whose religion you endeavor to overthrow." <note>original: "Quam tandem nobis attulisti Veritatem? nisi quod Assertor Deorum, eos ipsos ad ultimum prodidisti: Prosecutus enim Summi Dei laudes, quem Regem, quem Maximum, quem Opificem rerum, quem Fontem bonorum, quem Parentem omnium, quem Factorem Altoremque viventium confessus es; ademisti Jovi tuo Regnum; eumque Summa potestate depulsum, in Ministrorum numerum redigisti. Epilogus ergo te tuus arguit Stultitiæ, Vanitatis, Erroris. Affirmas Deos esse; & illos tamen subjicis & mancipas ei Deo, cujus Religionem conaris evertere."</note>

Here we must admit that we do not entirely understand Lactantius’s logic. Hierocles’s *Zeus* or *Jupiter* was one and the same with his Supreme God (as is also hinted at here). Although he acknowledged all the other gods to be merely his inferior ministers, he nevertheless maintained that these lower gods ought to be religiously worshipped. This was the point that Lactantius should have refuted. But what we should notice here...

The point to take notice of is this: Hierocles, a major persecutor of the Christians and the author of that bitter attack against them called *Philalethes* <note>The title *Philalethes* means "The Lover of Truth."</note>, was a strong defender of polytheism and a champion for the gods. Yet, at the same time, he clearly acknowledged one Supreme Deity. He called him the King (meaning the Monarch of the Universe), the Greatest, the <term>original: "Opifex"; meaning the maker or craftsman</term> of the world, the Fountain of Good, the Parent of all things, and the Maker and Preserver of all Life.

But the greatest opponent of Christianity in every way was the Emperor Julian <note>Often called "Julian the Apostate," he was the last pagan Roman Emperor (reigned 361–363 AD) and attempted to revive traditional Roman religion.</note>. He cannot reasonably be suspected of having disguised or softened the nature of paganism. Because he was an emperor and felt such great hostility toward Christianity—and was so fanatically zealous for the *worship of the gods*—it is significant that Julian, nevertheless, was an unquestionable defender of <margin>Cyril, *Against Julian*, Book 4, p. 115.</margin> one Supreme Deity. In his book written against the Christians, he declares the general sense of the pagans in this way:

"For our theologians say that the creator of all things is a common father and king, but that the remaining nations have been distributed by him to national and city-protecting gods, each of whom manages his own portion in a way appropriate to himself. For since in the Father all things are perfect and all are one, but in the partial [deities], a different power prevails in each, etc." <note>original: οἱ γὰρ ἡμέτεροι φασὶν, τὸν δημιουργὸν ἁπάντων μὲν εἶναι κοινὸν πατέρα καὶ βασιλέα, νενεμῆσθαι δὲ τὰ λοιπὰ τῶν ἐθνῶν ὑπ' αὐτοῦ, ἐθνάρχαις καὶ πολιοῦχοις θεοῖς, ὧν ἕκαστος ἐπιτροπεύει τὴν ἑαυτοῦ λῆξιν οἰκείως αὐτῷ· ἐπειδὴ γὰρ ἐν μὲν τῷ πατρὶ πάντα τέλεια, καὶ ἓν πάντα, ἐν δὲ τοῖς μεριστοῖς, ἄλλη παρ' ἄλλῳ κρατεῖ δύναμις, &c.</note>

Afterward in the same book, he argues that the pagans held more correct opinions regarding the Supreme God than the Jews themselves: <margin>P. 146.</margin> "If that God who is so much spoken of by Moses is the immediate creator <note>original: "Opifex"</note> of the whole world, we pagans hold better opinions of him. We suppose him to be the common Lord of all, but that there are other governors of nations and countries under him, like prefects or presidents appointed by a king. We do not rank him among those partial governors of particular countries and cities, as the Jews do." <note>original: ὡς εἰ μὲν ὁ προσεχὴς εἴη τοῦ κόσμου δημιουργὸς ὁ κηρυττόμενος ὑπὸ τοῦ Μωσέως, ἡμεῖς ὑπὲρ αὐτοῦ βελτίους ἔχομεν δόξας, οἱ κοινὸν μὲν ἐκεῖνον ὑπολαμβάνοντες ἁπάντων δεσπότην, ἐθνάρχας δὲ ἄλλους, οἱ τυγχάνουσι μὲν ὑπ' ἐκεῖνον, εἰσὶ δὲ ὥσπερ ὕπαρχοι βασιλέως, ἕκαστος τὴν ἑαυτοῦ διαφερόντως ἐπανορθούμενος φροντίδα, καὶ οὐ καθίσταμεν αὐτὸν, οὐδὲ ἀπομερίτην τῶν ὑπ' αὐτοῦ θεῶν καθισταμένων·</note>

From both of these passages, it is evident that according to Julian’s theology, all those other gods whose worship he fought for so much were only the subordinate ministers of that one Supreme God, the Maker of all.

The same thing could be further demonstrated from Julian’s oration made in praise of the Sun as a great god in this visible world. In it, he plainly acknowledges another far more glorious Deity, <margin>P. 262.</margin> who was the Cause of all things: "There is one creator of all things, but many are the creative gods circulating in heaven." <note>original: εἷς μὲν ὁ τῶν ὅλων δημιουργὸς, πολλοὶ δὲ οἱ κατ' οὐρανὸν περιπολοῦντες δημιουργικοὶ θεοί·</note> There is one God the Ma-

<page-num>275</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER IV. He Derived all his Gods from One.</header>

...maker of all things, but besides him there are many other <term>original: "Demiurgical"; gods involved in the making or fashioning of the material world</term> gods moving around the Heavens, in the midst of which is the Sun. Here we have a clear acknowledgment of one Supreme God and of many inferior deities existing together. Moreover, in the same oration, he declares that the ancient poets, in saying the Sun was the offspring of Hyperion, understood by this "Hyperion" nothing else but the *Supreme Deity*, <note>original: "τὸν πάντων ὑπερέχοντα, πάντων ἐπέκεινα, περὶ ὃν πάντα, καὶ οὗ ἕνεκα πάντα ἔσιν"</note> *Him who is above all things, beyond all things, about whom all things revolve, and for whose sake all things exist.* This Supreme Deity is described even more extensively by him in the same oration <margin>Page 248.</margin> (where he calls him the *King of all things*):

"This God—whether it is proper to call him that which is beyond mind and understanding, or the Idea of all beings (which I call the entire intelligible world), or The One (since Unity seems to be the most ancient of all things), or as Plato was accustomed to call him, The Good—this uniform cause of the whole, which provides beauty, perfection, unity, and unimaginable power to all existing things, remaining in its own productive essence, revealed the Sun as the greatest god, produced from himself as a certain intelligible Sun, in every way like himself, of which the physical Sun is but an image." <note>This passage is translated from the original Greek: οὗτος τοίνυν, εἴτε τὸ ἐπέκεινα τοῦ νοῦ καλεῖν αὐτὸν θέμις... ἥλιον θεὸν μέγιστον ἀνέφηνεν, etc.</note>

For Dionysius Petavius <note>A 17th-century Jesuit scholar and theologian.</note> rightly explains Julian's meaning in this oration: 

<margin>Page 274.</margin> 
"The secret of this most empty and wordy argument is this: that from the First and Primary God, a certain intelligible and archetypal Sun was produced, which holds exactly the same place and order in the realm of intelligible things <note>Things that can only be understood by the mind.</note> that the solar sphere we see holds among sensible things <note>Things perceived by the physical senses.</note>." <note>Translated from the original Latin: "Vanissimæ hujus & loquacissimæ disputationis mysterium est; à Principe ac Primario Deo, νοητὸν quendam, & archetypum Solem editum fuisse..."</note>

So here are three things to be distinguished from one another: first, the Supreme Deity which Plato calls "The Good"; second, the "Intelligible Sun" or Eternal Intellect; and lastly, the corporeal or physical Sun (which was believed to be animated by a soul). Here, we may notice how closely this pagan philosopher and Emperor, Julian, approached Christianity—even though he opposed it so much. He also assumed an *Eternal Mind or Intellect* acted as the immediate offspring of the *First Fountain of all things*, which seems to differ very little from the Christian <term>original: "λόγος" (Logos); the Word or Divine Reason</term>. However, it is plain that this devout restorer of paganism and zealous supporter of the worship of *the gods* asserted no multiplicity of independent, self-existent deities, but derived all his gods from *One*.

As for those other philosophers and learned men who stood in opposition to Christianity during the later stages of paganism's decline (after the time of Constantine)—such as Iamblichus, Syrianus, Proclus, Simplicius, and many others—it is unquestionably evident that they all clearly acknowledged *one Supreme Deity*.

# Pagans Disclaim a Multitude, BOOK 1.

Maximus of Madaura <note>Maximus Madaurensis was a 4th-century African rhetorician and pagan who corresponded with St. Augustine.</note>, a confident and resolute Pagan in St. Augustine's <note>original: "St. Austin's"</note> time, expressed both his own and the general sense of Pagans in this manner:

> Indeed, that there is one Supreme God, without beginning, as the great and magnificent Father of Nature—who is so mad or devoid of sense as not to acknowledge this to be most certain? <note>original Latin: "Equidem Unum esse Deum Summum, sine initio, Naturæ ceu Patrem Magnum atque Magnificum, quis tam demens tam mente captus neget esse certissimum?"</note> We invoke his virtues, diffused throughout the world, under many different names, because we are all ignorant of what his proper name truly is. Thus it happens that while we honor his divided members separately through various prayers, we are clearly seen to be worshiping the whole Deity. <note>original Latin: "Hujus nos virtutes per Mundanum opus diffusas, multis vocabulis invocamus, quoniam nomen ejus cuncti proprium videlicet ignoramus. Ita fit, ut dum ejus quasi quædam Membra carptim, variis supplicationibus prosequimur, Totum colere profectò videamur."</note>

> May the gods preserve you, through whom we Pagans, dispersed over the whole world, worship the common Father of both those gods and all mortals in a thousand different ways, yet with a harmonious discord. <note>original Latin: "Dii te servent, per quos & Eorum, atque cunctorum mortalium, Communem Patrem, universi mortales quos terra sustinet, mille modis, concordi discordia venerantur."</note>

He assumed that besides a virtuous and holy life, certain religious rites and purifications were necessary to observe for that purpose. In this letter, he also styles the Supreme God as the **One, Universal, Incomprehensible, Ineffable, and Tireless Creator.** <note>original Latin: "Unus, Universus, Incomprehensibilis, Ineffabilis & Infatigabilis Creator"</note>

# CHAP. IV. Of Independent Deities.

The Omnipotent God <note>Arnobius of Sicca (c. 255–330 AD) was an Early Christian apologist who wrote *Adversus Nationes* (Against the Pagans) to defend Christianity against Roman accusations.</note>, by the unanimous mind of all and the common consent of mortals, is known to be neither begotten nor ever brought forth into a new light; nor to have begun to exist at any time or age. He himself is the Source of things, the Creator of ages and times. For these things do not exist by themselves, but proceed from his perpetual eternity and continue always in an infinite progression. But truly Jupiter (as you claim) has both father and mother, grandfathers and grandmothers, and was only recently formed in his mother's womb, etc. <note>original Latin: "Omnipotens, mente una omnium... jam nuper in utero matris suæ formatus, &c."</note> You Pagans confuse yourselves with contradictions; for the **Omnipotent God**, according to the innate understanding of all mankind, **was neither begotten nor made, nor ever had a beginning in time, he being the Fountain and Original of all things.** But **Jupiter** (**as you say**) **had both Father and Mother, Grandfathers and Grandmothers, and was but lately formed in the womb;** and therefore he cannot be the Eternal Omnipotent God. Nevertheless **Arnobius** afterwards considering (as we suppose) that these **Poetic Fables** were, by the wiser Pagans, either totally rejected or else in some way or another interpreted as allegories, he honestly sets aside this advantage which he had against them. He grants their **Jupiter** to be the true Omnipotent Deity, and consequently the same God whom the Christians worshiped; but from this he infers that the Pagans must therefore be highly guilty, because while they worship the same God as the Christians, they still hate and persecute them in that manner.

> But let it be granted that (**as you affirm**) your **Jupiter** and the **Eternal Omnipotent God** are one and the same; why then do you pursue us with such unjust hatred? Why do you shudder at the very mention of our name as if it were a terrible omen, if the same God you worship is also worshiped by us? Or if you contend that you are in the same cause, why are the Gods your friends, but our most hostile and enraged enemies? For indeed, if one religion is common to both us and you, the anger of the heavenly beings should cease. <note>original Latin: "Sed sint, ut vultis, unum... cessat ira cælestium."</note>

To this, the Pagans' defense and reply is:

> But we do not say that the Gods are displeased with you Christians because you worship the Omnipotent God, but because you claim that a man was born—and what is considered shameful even for people of low status—was killed by the punishment of the cross, yet you contend he was a God, believe him still to survive, and adore him with your daily prayers. <note>original Latin: "Sed non idcirco Dii vobis infesti sunt... quotidianis supplicationibus adoratis:"</note>

To which **Arnobius** replies in this way: "Tell us, now I pray you, who these Gods are who take it as such a great injury and indignity to themselves that Christ should be worshiped? Are they not **Janus** and **Saturn**, **Aesculapius** and **Liber** <note>original: "Liber"; another name for Bacchus or Dionysus, the god of wine.</note>, **Mercury** the son of **Maia**, and the **Theban** or **Tyrian Hercules**, **Castor** and **Pollux**, and the like?"

> Do these gods, then, hear that Christ is worshiped and accepted and esteemed as a Deity by us with offended ears? Having forgotten their own recent lot and human condition, do they refuse to grant to another what was granted to themselves? Is this the Justice of the Heavens? Is this the holy judgment of the Gods? Is this not a kind of envy and greed? Is it not a foul sort of disparagement to want only their own fortunes to be prominent, while the affairs of others are suppressed and trampled in despised humility? <note>original Latin: "Hice ergo Christum coli... aliorum res premi & in contempta humilitate calcari?"</note>

# The Judgment of the Fathers, concerning BOOK I.

"We worship a man who was born. Why, then? Do you not also worship any man who was born? Not one or another? Not countless others? Indeed, have you not taken all those you now have in your temples from the number of mortals and granted them the heavens and the stars? Let us yield for a moment, giving in to your opinions, and grant that Christ was one of us—in mind, soul, body, and in the same frailty and condition. Is he not worthy to be called God and felt to be God by us, thanks to the grace of such great gifts? For if you have placed into the heavens among the gods Liber <note>Another name for Bacchus, the god of wine.</note> because he discovered the use of wine; or Ceres because of grain; or Aesculapius because of herbs; or Minerva because of the olive; or Triptolemus because of the plow; or finally Hercules because he overcame and tamed wild beasts, thieves, and the many-headed hydra; with how much honor should he be regarded by us, who has led us from great errors by introducing the truth?" <note>original Latin: "Natum hominem colimus; Quid enim, Vos hominem nullum colitis natum? ... qui ab erroribus nos magnis insinuatâ veritate traduxit? &c."</note>

Are these the gods who are so much offended by Christ being worshipped and accounted a God by us? They who, forgetting their former condition, would not have the same status bestowed upon another which has been granted to themselves? Is this the justice of the Heavenly Powers? Is this the righteous judgment of gods? Or is it not rather base envy and greed for them to keep it all for themselves? We worship indeed one who was born a man. What then? Do you worship no such person? Not one, and another, and countless others? And are not almost all your gods such as were taken from the rank of men and placed among the stars? And will you judge that damnable in us which you yourselves practice? Let us for the present yield this much to your lack of faith <note>original: "Infidelity"</note> and grant that Christ was but an ordinary man, of the same rank and condition as other mortals; yet might we not for all that (according to your own principles) think him worthy, by reason of the great benefits we received from him, to be accounted a God? For if you have promoted into the number of your divine beings <note>original: "Divi"</note>, Bacchus (or Liber) for inventing the use of wine, Ceres for corn, Aesculapius for herbs, Minerva for the olive, Triptolemus for the plow, and Hercules for subduing beasts, thieves, and monsters; with how great honors should he be regarded by us, who by the introduction of divine truth has delivered us from such great errors of mind?

This argument by Arnobius <note>Arnobius of Sicca (c. 255–330 AD) was an Early Christian apologist.</note>, though it was effective enough *against those specific men* <note>original: "ad homines"</note> to silence the Pagans—since there is more reason that Christ should be made a God for the benefits mankind receives from him than that Bacchus, Ceres, or Hercules should be—yet as Arnobius himself seems to suggest, it is not sufficient without something else added to it for the justification of Christianity. Neither indeed was that the chief quarrel which the Pagans had with the Christians: that they had deified one who was crucified (though the cross of Christ was also a great offense to them). Rather, it was that while they condemned the Pagans for worshipping others besides the Supreme Omnipotent God and decried all those gods of theirs, they themselves nevertheless worshipped <margin>Book 8, page 385.</margin>one mortal man as a God. Celsus <note>A 2nd-century philosopher and the first recorded intellectual critic of Christianity.</note> urges this in the works of Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD) responded to Celsus in his work "Contra Celsum."</note>: "If these Christians themselves worshipped no other but one God, or the pure Divinity, then they might perhaps seem to have some just pretense for censuring us. But now they themselves give divine honor to one who lately appeared, and yet they think they do not sin against God, even if his servant is also worshipped." <note>original Greek: "εἰ μὲν δὴ μηδένα ἄλλον ἐθεράπευον οὗτοι πλὴν ἕνα θεὸν, ἦν ἄν τις αὐτοῖς ἴσως πρὸς τοὺς ἄλλους ἀτενὴς λόγος· νυνὶ δὲ τὸν ἔναγχος φανέντα τοῦτον ὑπερθεραπεύουσι, καὶ ὅμως οὐδὲν πλημμελεῖν νομίζουσι περὶ τὸν θεὸν, εἰ καὶ ὑπηρέτης αὐτοῦ θεραπευθήσεται"</note>

# CHAP. IV. The Pagan Polytheists.

They persuade themselves that they do not offend God at all by worshipping those who are supposed to be His ministers. As Origen provides a reply to this in that passage, we shall consider it further later on.

As for the judgment of the Church Fathers in this particular matter, Clement of Alexandria was not only of the opinion that the Pagans (at least the Greeks) worshipped the true God—the same God worshipped by the Christians, though not in the right manner—but he also endeavors to 
<margin>Stromata, Book 6, page 635.</margin>
confirm this from the authority of the *Preaching of Peter*: <note>The *Preaching of Peter* (Kerygma Petrou) is an early 2nd-century Christian text, now lost except for fragments quoted by authors like Clement.</note> *“That the Greeks knew God, Peter intimates in his preaching. There is One God, says he, who made the beginning of all things, and has power over their end, etc. Worship this God, not as the Greeks do.”* In this, Clement seems to assume that the Greeks worship the same God as we do, though not according to the correct tradition received by His Son. He does not forbid us from worshipping that God whom the Greeks worship; rather, he tells us to worship Him otherwise than they do—altering only the manner of worship, but not the Object, nor preaching a different God. *“And what it means to ‘not worship God as the Greeks do,’ the same Peter indicated in those words: They worship him in images of wood and stone, brass and iron, gold and silver, and they sacrifice to the dead as if they were gods.”* Here Clement adds further from the *Preaching of Peter*: *“Neither worship God as the Jews do, etc. The one and only God,”* says Clement, *“is worshipped by the Greeks in a pagan way, by the Jews in a Jewish way, but by Us in a new and spiritual way. For the same God who gave the two Testaments to the Jews and Christians gave philosophy to the Greeks, by which the Omnipotent God is glorified among the Greeks.”* <note>original Greek: δι' ἧς ὁ παντοκράτωρ παρ' Ἕλλησι δοξάζεται</note>

<margin>On False Religion, page 727.</margin>
<margin>Book 1.</margin>
<margin>Book 1, page 16.</margin>
Lactantius Firmianus also affirms in many places that the Pagans acknowledged one Supreme Deity: *“Both philosophers and poets, and finally even those who worship the gods themselves, frequently acknowledge that there is one Supreme God.”* <note>original Latin: "Summum Deum & Philosophi & Poetæ, & ipsi denique qui Deos colunt, sæpè fatentur"</note> From this he concludes that all the other pagan gods were nothing but the ministers of this one Supreme Being and were creatures made by Him. (He then only blames them for calling these ministers “gods” and giving them religious worship). After he had declared that it was just as absurd to suppose the world is governed by many independent gods as it is to suppose a human body is governed by many independent minds or souls, he adds: *“Because those who defend the existence of many gods understand this, they say that these gods preside over individual things and parts of the world in such a way that there is only one chief Ruler. Therefore, the rest cannot be gods, but are attendants and ministers, whom that One, the greatest and most powerful of all, has placed in these offices so that they may serve his command and will. If they are not all equal, then they are not all gods. For the same thing cannot be both the servant and the master. For if ‘God’ is the name of supreme power, he must be incorruptible, perfect, impassible <note>term: impassible — incapable of suffering or being affected by external forces</note>, and subject to nothing. Therefore, those whom necessity compels to obey one Greatest God are not gods.”* <note>original Latin: "Quòd quia intelligunt isti assertores Deorum... Ergo Dii non sunt quos parere Uni Maximo Deo necessitas cogit."</note> Because the defenders of many gods understand this well, they affirm that their gods preside over the various parts of the world only because there is one chief Ruler or Governor. From this it follows that all their other gods can be nothing other than ministers and officers, whom that one Great—

# The Judgment of the Fathers, concerning BOOK I.

<margin>Page 28.</margin>
...the greatest <note>original: "est"</note> God, who is Omnipotent, has variously appointed and established [the other gods], so as to serve His command and will. Now, if all the Pagan gods are not equal, then they cannot all be gods; since that which rules and that which serves cannot be the same. "God" is a name of absolute power, and it implies incorruptibility, perfection, impassibility <term>impassibility: the theological doctrine that God does not experience pain or changing emotions from external causes</term>, and subjection to nothing. Therefore, these others ought not to be called gods, whom necessity compels to obey one Greatest God. Again in the same book, <note>original: "Nunc satis est, Demonstrare, summo ingenio viros attigisse veritatem ac propè tenuisse; nisi eos retrorsum infatuata pravis opinionibus consuetudo rapuisset, qua & Deos alios esse opinabantur, & ea quæ in usum hominis Deus fecit, tanquam sensu prædita essent, pro Diis habenda & colenda credebant."</note> "It is now sufficient to have shown that the more ingenious and intelligent Pagans came very near to the truth, and would have fully reached it, had not a certain customary infatuation with evil opinions dragged them away to an acknowledgment of other gods—leading them to a belief that those things which God made for the use of men (as if they were endowed with life or animated) ought to be accounted as gods and worshipped; namely, the stars."

<margin>Page 39.</margin>
And afterward, <note>original: "Quòd si Cultores Deorum, eos ipsos se colere putant, quos summi Dei Ministros appellamus, nihil est quod nobis faciant invidiam, qui Unum Deum dicamus, Multos negemus;"</note> "If the worshippers of the gods think that they worship no other than the ministers of the one Supreme God, then there is no reason for them to make us objects of hatred for saying that there is one God and denying many gods."

<margin>Preparation for the Gospel, Book 3, chapter 13.</margin>
Eusebius of Caesarea likewise gives us this account of the Pagans' creed, or the character of their theology as it was then presented by them: <note>original: ἕνα γὰρ ὄντα θεὸν, παντοίαις δυνάμεσι, τὰ πάντα πληροῦν, καὶ διὰ πάντων διήκειν, καὶ τοῖς πᾶσιν ἐπιστατεῖν · ἀσωμάτως δὲ καὶ ἀφανῶς ἐν πᾶσιν ὄντα, καὶ διὰ πάντων διήκοντα · καὶ τοῦτον εἰκότως διὰ τῶν δεδηλωμένων σέβειν φάσι ·</note> "The Pagans declare themselves in this manner: that there is one God who, with His various powers, fills all things, passes through all things, and presides over all things. Being incorporeally and invisibly present in all things and pervading them, He is reasonably worshipped *by* or *in* those things that are manifest and visible." This passage from Eusebius will be further considered later, when we come to give a more detailed account of Paganism.

What Saint Augustine's <note>original: "St. Austin"</note> view was concerning the theology of the Pagans has already been stated: namely, that they had not degenerated so far as to lose the knowledge of one Supreme God, from whom all of Nature comes, and that they derived all their other gods from this One. We shall now, in the last place, conclude with the judgment of Paulus Orosius, who was Augustine’s contemporary: <margin>History, Book 6, chapter 1.</margin> <note>original: "Philosophi dum intento mentis studio quærunt scrutantúrque omnia, Unum Deum, Authorem omnium repererunt, ad quem Unum omnia referrentur; unde etiam nunc Pagani, quos jam declarata Veritas de contumaciâ magis quàm de ignorantiâ convincit, cùm à nobis discutiuntur, non se Plures sequi, sed sub Uno Deo Magno, Plures Ministros venerari fatentur. Restat igitur de intelligentiâ veri Dei, per multas intelligendi suspiciones, Confusa dissensio, quia de Uno Deo, omnium penè una est opinio."</note> "The philosophers of the Gentiles, while searching and scrutinizing all things with intense mental study, found one God, the Author of all, to whom all things should be referred. Therefore, even now, the Pagans—whom the truth, once declared, convicts more of stubbornness than of ignorance—when they are questioned by us, admit that they do not follow many gods, but rather venerate many ministers under one great God. There remains, then, a confused disagreement about the understanding of the true God through many various perceptions, because regarding the one God, nearly everyone holds the same opinion."

<header>### Chapter IV. The Pagan Polytheists.</header>

...that there was *One God*, the *Author* of all things, and to that *One*, all things should be referred. Because of this, even the *Pagans* at this very day—whom the declared truth convicts of *obstinacy* <note>original: "Contumacy"</note> rather than *Ignorance*—confess when they are challenged by us that they do not follow *Many Gods*, but only worship *Many Ministers* under *One God*. So, there remains only a confused disagreement concerning the manner of understanding the true *God*, because concerning *One God*, almost everyone holds the same opinion.

By this time, we think it is sufficiently evident that the *Pagans* (at least after the arrival of *Christianity*), though they asserted there were *Many Gods*—calling all *Superior Intelligent Beings* above men by that Name, according to the saying of *St. Jerome*, "The Gentiles thought that whatever was above them was God" <note>original: "Deum quicquid supra se esset, Gentiles putabant;"</note>—yet they acknowledged *One Supreme, Omnipotent, and only Unmade Deity*.

XVI. However, it is very possible that some may still suspect that all of this was nothing more than a *Refinement* and *alteration* of *Paganism* after *Christianity* had appeared upon the *Stage*. They might see it as a kind of *doctoring* <term>original: "Mangonization"; refers to the practice of furbishing or "doctoring" up old goods to make them look new and more saleable</term> of their religion to make it more marketable and plausible, the better to defend itself and withstand the assaults of *Christianity*, while in reality the *Genuine Doctrine* of the ancient *Pagans* was far different. Although the opposite has already been made sufficiently clear from what has been stated, we shall nonetheless—for the fuller satisfaction of those who are more strongly prejudiced—demonstrate through an *Historical Deduction* made from the most ancient times all the way down, that the *Doctrine* of the *Greatest Pagan Polytheists*, both before and after *Christianity*, was always the same: that *besides their Many Gods, there was One Supreme, Omnipotent, and Only Unmade Deity*.

We shall perform this task not as some have done, by placing the chief weight upon the *Sibylline Oracles* <note>A collection of oracular utterances written in Greek hexameters and ascribed to the Sibyls, prophetesses who uttered divine revelations in a frenzied state.</note> or those reputed writings of *Hermes Trismegistus* <note>original: "Hermes Trismegist"</note>, the authority of which has been so much dismissed by *Learned Men* lately. Nor shall we rely upon such *Oracles* of the *Pagan Deities* as may be suspected of being counterfeited by *Christians*, but rather upon such *Monuments* of *Pagan Antiquity* as are altogether beyond suspicion and undoubted. 

As for the *Sibylline Oracles*, we believe there may be *Two Extremes* concerning them. One is to swallow everything now extant under that *Title* as *Genuine* and *Sincere*; yet nothing can be more manifest than that there is much *Counterfeit* and *fraudulent material* <note>original: "Supposititious stuff"</note> in this *Sibylline Mixture* <term>original: "Farrago"; a confused mixture or hodgepodge</term> which we now have. From this, besides other instances of the same kind, it appears too evidently to be denied that some pretended *Christians* of former times engaged in *Pious and Religious Frauds*. They endeavored to uphold the *Truth* of *Christianity* by *fictions* and *forgeries* of their own devising. This was a thing *Ignoble* and *Unworthy* in itself, and it suggested that those very *Defenders* of *Christianity* did not trust their own *Cause*. It may well be thought that there was a *trick of the Devil* in it also, there being no other way more *Effective* than this to render all *Christianity* (at least...

### CHAPTER IV. Sibylline Oracles.

These same *verses* could be adapted sometimes to one thing and sometimes to another. But that they did not proceed from *divine madness* <note>original: "Fury"</note> or *prophetic rage*, but rather from *skill* and *artifice*, is clearly shown by the *acrostic* <note>A poem in which certain letters in each line form a word or message; Cicero noted that Sibylline verses were structured this way, suggesting conscious composition rather than spontaneous prophecy.</note> found within them. Therefore, let us shut up the *Sibyl* and keep her hidden so that, according to the *decree* of our *ancestors*, her *verses* may not be read without the express command of the *Senate*. And lastly, he adds, "Let us also deal with the priests so that they might produce anything else from those books rather than a king, whom neither the gods nor men will hereafter tolerate in Rome" <note>original Latin: "Cum Antistitibus agamus, ut quidvis potius ex illis libris, quàm Regem proferant, quem Romæ posthac nec Dii nec Homines esse patientur"</note>. Let us also deal with the *Quindecimviri* <term>the board of fifteen priests in charge of guarding and interpreting the Sibylline Books</term> and the *interpreters* of these *Sibylline Books*, so that they would rather produce anything out of them than a *king*—a title which neither the *gods* nor *men* will hereafter tolerate at *Rome*.

While *Cicero* was mistaken regarding the *outcome* of the *Roman government* <note>Cicero hoped Rome would remain a Republic, but it soon became an Empire under Augustus.</note>, and there were undoubtedly some *predictions* in these *Sibylline Books* about a *new kingdom* or *monarchy* to be established in the *world*, it is clear that the *Roman Empire* was not the intended subject. This is plainly shown in the *description* in *Virgil’s* previously mentioned *Eclogue*, where another *fulfillment* of them is expected, though it was flatteringly applied to *Saloninus* <note>Saloninus was a son of the Roman consul Pollio; Virgil's poem was often re-interpreted to refer to various Roman heirs.</note>. Therefore, we conclude that the *kingdom* and *happy state*, or *Golden Age*, predicted in the *Sibylline Oracles*, was nothing other than that of the *Messiah*, our *Savior Christ*, and the era of *Christianity*.

Lastly, in that other passage of *Cicero's* concerning the *Sibylline Oracles*, "Let them be useful for setting aside religions rather than taking them up" <note>original Latin: "Valeant ad deponendas potiùs quàm ad suscipiendas Religiones"</note>, there seems to be a *suggestion* <note>original: "intimation"</note> that the oracles themselves tended to *lessen* rather than *increase* *pagan superstitions*. Therefore, it may probably be thought that they predicted a *change* in *pagan religion* through the introduction of the *worship* of one *sole deity*. Nor should it seem any more strange that our Savior *Christ* was foretold by a *pagan Sibyl* than that he was clearly predicted by *Balaam* the *Aramaic sorcerer* <note>A non-Israelite prophet in the Bible (Numbers 24) who prophesied the coming of a "Star out of Jacob."</note>.

However, those things in the *Sibylline verses* might have been derived in some way from *Scripture prophecies*. This is quite probable, because that *Sibylline prophet* used the very same *figures* and *allegories* to describe the *future happy state* that are found in the *Scriptures*; for example:

->—"The herds shall not fear the great lions"<-
<note>original: "Nec magnos metuent Armenta Leones"</note>
->"The serpent also shall die, etc."<-
<note>original: "Occidet & Serpens, &c."</note>

Now, just as *Cicero* seems to complain that in his time these *Sibylline Oracles* were too exposed to public view, it is very probable that even though they were supposed to be kept under the *guard* of the *Quindecimviri*, many of them were copied and circulated. This likely gave an opportunity to ignorantly zealous *Christians*—who were prone to *dutiful lies* <note>original: "officious lies"; lies told with the intent to be helpful or serve a religious purpose</note> and *pious frauds*—to add much more of their own forging to the texts. He did not accuse them of counterfeiting the entire business of these *Sibylline Oracles*, but only for inserting many of their own inventions into them:
<margin>Original: Against Celsus <note>Latin: "Contra Celsum"</note> book 7. p. 368.</margin>
"You Christians might much rather have acknowledged even the Sibyl as the offspring of God; but now you can boldly insert into her verses many slanderous <note>original: "Maledicent"</note> things of your own." <note>original Greek: "ὑμεῖς δ᾽ κἂν Σίβυλλαν, ᾗ χρῶνταί τινες ὑμῶν, εἰκότως ἂν μᾶλλον προεσήσασθε, ὡς τοῦ Θεοῦ παῖδα, νῦν δὲ παρεγράφειν μὲν εἰς τὰ ἐκείνης, πολλὰ καὶ βλάσφημα εἰκῆ δύνασθε"</note> In that passage, Origen—trying to defend the honor of Christians as best he could—pleads in their defense that Celsus, despite his claims, could not show exactly what they had secretly inserted into those *Sibylline verses*. Origen argued that if Celsus had been able to produce more ancient and uncorrupted copies in which such things were not found, he certainly would have done so.

Notwithstanding this defense, it is likely that other ancient copies were available then, and that Celsus might have encountered them, which gave him the occasion to write as he did. Regardless, this would not justify the current *Sibylline Books*, in which there are forgeries plainly discoverable even without comparing them to older copies. Nevertheless, it seems that not all the ancient Christians agreed on using these *Sibylline testimonies*. This is suggested by Celsus himself in the previously cited words, "which some of you make use of." Furthermore, they did not all acknowledge the Sibyl to have been a prophetess either. When Celsus mentions a sect of Christians called *Sibyllists*, Origen tells us that these were people who, by using the *Sibylline testimonies*, were given that name as a term of disgrace by other Christians. Those other Christians would not allow the Sibyl to have been a prophetess, perhaps conceiving it to be derogatory to the Holy Scriptures. 

But although there may be some of the ancient *Sibylline verses* still left in that jumble <note>original: "Farrago"</note> which we have today, it is impossible for us to prove which ones are genuine. Therefore, we shall not rely on any testimonies from that source to prove that the ancient Pagans acknowledged *one Supreme Deity*. Nevertheless, we shall not omit one Sibylline passage which we find recorded in *Pausanias* <note>A 2nd-century AD Greek traveler and geographer.</note>. From this, by the way, it also appears that the *Sibylline verses* were not kept so strictly secret that some of them did not become public. Pausanias tells us that the defeat of the Athenians at *Aegospotami* <note>The final major battle of the Peloponnesian War (405 BC), where the Spartan fleet destroyed the Athenian navy.</note> was predicted by the Sibyl in these words (among others):

->And then the high-thundering Zeus, who holds the greatest power,<-
->Shall bring deep-groaning sorrows upon the Athenians.<-
<note>original Greek: "Καὶ τότ᾽ Ἀθηναίοισι βαρύστονα κήδεα θήσει / Ζεὺς ὑψιβρεμέτης, ᾧπερ κράτος ἐστὶ μέγιστον, &c."</note>

->And then the High-Thundering Jupiter, who holds supreme power over all things,<-
->Shall stir up grief and groans for the descendants of Cecrops.<-
<note>original Latin: "Ac tum Cecropidis luctum gemitúsque ciebit, / Jupiter Altitonans, rerum cui Summa Potestas, &c." "Cecropidis" refers to the Athenians, named after their mythical first king, Cecrops.</note>

To this might also be added a quote from another ancient *Peliadean* <note>Referring to the Peleiades, the archaic priestesses at the Oracle of Dodona.</note> prophetess, mentioned by the same writer, in which the Divine eternity and immutability are plainly declared:

->Zeus was, Zeus is, Zeus shall be; O great Zeus.<-
<note>original Greek: "Ζεὺς ἦν, Ζεὺς ἔστι, Ζεὺς ἔσσεται, ὦ μεγάλε Ζεῦ."</note>

<summary>This page discusses the debate between Celsus and Origen regarding Christian tampering with Sibylline Oracles and concludes that while many are forgeries, some ancient verses recorded by Pausanias still point toward a belief in a supreme, eternal deity.</summary>
<keywords>Celsus, Origen, Sibylline Oracles, Sibyllists, Pausanias, Aegospotami, monotheism, Zeus, Jupiter, Peleiades</keywords>

# Chapter 4. Zoroaster as a Polytheist.

->Jupiter is, was, and shall be: O good, nurturing Jupiter. <note>original Latin: "Jupiter Est, Fuit, atque Erit : O bone Jupiter alme."</note><-

Besides these Sibylline Prophecies, there are also other oracles from the pagan deities themselves that clearly acknowledge *one supreme and greatest God*. However, we will not mention any of the oracles said to have been delivered since the era of Christianity—when the *pagan oracles* began to fail—nor those that exist only in *Christian writings*. Several of these were cited from *Porphyrius's* <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher often critical of Christianity.</note> *Book of Oracles*, but because he was suspected of bias, we shall not mention any of them here.

Nevertheless, we will take notice of *one oracle* of the *Clarian Apollo* recorded by *Macrobius*, in which *one supreme deity* is not only asserted but is also called by that *Hebrew Name* (or *Tetragrammaton* <term>the four-letter biblical name of God, often rendered as YHWH</term>) *Jao*:

->Declare that Jao is the highest God of all. <note>original Greek: "Φράζεο τὸν πάντων ὕπατον Θεὸν ἔμμεν Ἰάω."</note><-

It is certainly true that the *Clarian demon* <note>original: "Devil"</note> there cunningly tried to redirect this title to the Sun, as if the Sun were the only *supreme deity* and the true *Jao*. To this might be added another ancient oracle (which comes to mind now) of the *Dodonean Jupiter*, along with the interpretation given by *Themistocles*, to whom it was delivered. In it, he was commanded "to go to him who shares the same name as God" <note>original Greek: "πρὸς τὸν ὁμώνυμον τοῦ Θεοῦ βαδίζειν"</note>. Themistocles understood this to mean the *King of Persia*, "for both are, and are called, Great Kings" <note>original Greek: "μεγάλας γὰρ ἀμφοτέρους εἶναι τε καὶ λέγεσθαι βασιλέας"</note> because both he and God were alike called (though in different ways and degrees) the *Great King* or *Monarch*.

Regarding those writings commonly attributed to *Hermes Trismegistus* <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure combining the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth, credited with a vast body of mystical literature.</note>—which have been generally condemned by the *scholars* of this *later age* as entirely *counterfeit* and *fraudulent* <note>original: "supposititious"</note>, yet are asserted by *Athanasius Kircher* <note>A 17th-century Jesuit scholar known for his wide-ranging interests in science and orientalism.</note> to be sincere and genuine—we shall have the opportunity to state our opinion on them later.

The most ancient *theologians* and most eminent *defenders* <note>original: "assertors"</note> of *polytheism* among the pagans were *Zoroaster* in the *East* and *Orpheus* among the *Greeks*. Zoroaster was of such great antiquity that writers cannot agree on his *age*. But everyone acknowledges he was a *polytheist*; some even claim this is signified by his very name (given to him after his death), which they interpret as *A Worshipper of the Stars*. It is certain that *Ster* or *Ester* meant *star* in the *Persian language*. *Learned* men have also observed that several other words now familiar in *European languages* derived their *origin* from Persian. Despite this, one might suspect that the "aster" part was merely a *Greek suffix*, as the name is written as *Zertoost* and *Zaradust* in *Oriental languages*, and as *Zarades* by the historian *Agathias*. Regardless, *Zoroaster's polytheism* is mentioned by *Plato*;

<summary>The author examines pagan oracles that acknowledge a supreme deity and introduces Zoroaster as a key figure of ancient polytheism whose name may link him to star worship.</summary>

# Zoroaster as a Witness to the One God. Book I.

<margin>
*On Abstinence, Book 4, page 165.* <note>A work by Porphyry of Tyre.</note>
</margin>
In the work where his *magic* is defined, it is described as nothing other than the *worship of the gods* <note>original Greek: θεῶν θεραπεία</note>. From this, we also learn that the word *magia* or *magic* was originally used in a positive sense. This is confirmed by *Porphyrius*: *“Among the Persians, those who were skilled in the knowledge of the Divine and were religious worshippers of the same were called Magi.”* <note>original Greek: Παρὰ μὲν τοῖς Πέρσαις, οἱ περὶ τὸ θεῖον σοφοὶ καὶ τούτου θεράποντες, μάγοι μὲν προσαγορεύονται</note>. 

Magic is commonly thought to be founded on a certain *vital sympathy* <note>The idea that all parts of the universe are interconnected and affect one another.</note> that exists within the *universe*. Similarly, these ancient *Persian Magi* and Chaldeans (as *Psellus* <note>Michael Psellos, an 11th-century Byzantine scholar.</note> tells us) supposed *that there was a sympathy between superior and inferior beings* <note>original Greek: συμπαθῆ εἶναι τὰ ἄνω τοῖς κάτω</note>. However, it seems that the only way they originally approved of *attracting the influence and assistance of those superior invisible powers* was through *piety, devotion, and religious rites*. 

Nevertheless, their devotion was not directed only toward *one omnipotent God*, but also toward *many gods*. It is also certain that this *Divine Magic* of Zoroaster shortly afterward degenerated among many of his followers into *Theurgical Magic* <note>A form of magic intended to invoke the presence of gods or spirits.</note> and, eventually, into *sorcery* <note>original: γοητεία (goeteia)</note>, which is downright *witchcraft*—the only thing commonly called *magic* today. 

But regardless of how many gods this *Zoroaster* worshipped, he nonetheless acknowledged *one supreme deity*. This appears from the *testimony of Eubulus*, cited by *Porphyrius* in his
<margin>
*On the Cave of the Nymphs, page 254.*
</margin>
*On the Cave of the Nymphs*: *“Zoroaster was the first, as Eubulus testifies, to consecrate a natural, circular cave in the mountains near Persia. It was adorned with flowers and watered by springs, dedicated to the honor of Mithras, the maker and father of all things. To him, this cave was an image or symbol of the whole world, which was created by Mithras.”* <note>original Greek: πρῶτα μὲν, ὡς ἔφη Εὔβουλος, Ζωροάστρου αὐτοφυὲς σπήλαιον ἐν τοῖς πλησίον ὄρεσι τῆς Περσίδος, ἀνθηρὸν καὶ πηγὰς ἔχον ἀνιερώσαντος, εἰς τιμὴν τοῦ πάντων ποιητοῦ καὶ πατρὸς Μίθρου, εἰκόνα φέροντος αὐτῷ τοῦ σπηλαίου τοῦ κόσμου, ὃν ὁ Μίθρας ἐδημιούργησε</note>.

This *testimony of Eubulus* is especially valuable because, as *Porphyrius* informs us elsewhere, he wrote a long *history of Mithras* spanning many *books*. From this, we can presume he had thoroughly informed himself on everything regarding the *Persian religion*. Therefore, based on the authority of *Eubulus*, we may conclude that although the *Sun* was generally worshipped by the Persians as a *god*, *Zoroaster* and the ancient *Magi*—who were best initiated in the *Mithraic Mysteries*—
<margin>
* That *Mithras*, who was called *the hidden God* <note>original Greek: ὁ κρύφιος Θεὸς</note>, was not the visible Sun.
</margin>
asserted another deity superior to the *Sun*. They believed in a *true Mithras*, who was the *maker and father of all things* <note>original Greek: πάντων ποιητὴς καὶ πατὴρ</note>, or of the *whole world*, of which the *Sun* is only a part. 

However, they also looked upon the *Sun* as the most vivid *image* of this *deity*, through which he was worshipped. They likewise worshipped the same deity symbolically in *fire*, as *Maximus Tyrius* <note>A 2nd-century Greek philosopher.</note> informs us. Consistent with this is a passage from the *Magic Oracles*:

->— *All things are the offspring of one fire.* <note>original Greek: πάντα πυρὸς ἑνὸς ἐκγεγαῶτα</note><-

This means that all things come from *one supreme deity*. *Julian the Emperor* <note>Julian the Apostate (ruled 361–363 AD), who attempted to revive traditional paganism.</note> was a devout *sun-worshipper* of this kind; he acknowledged another *incorporeal deity* beyond the *Sun* that was superior to it. Nevertheless, we do not deny that others among the...

<summary>This page discusses the Persian Magi and Zoroaster, arguing that while they practiced polytheism and "magic" (defined as the worship of gods), they ultimately recognized a supreme creator deity named Mithras, symbolized by the sun and fire.</summary>
