# Chapter 4: Of One Supreme Deity.

The Persians, who were not able to conceive of anything incorporeal <note>original: "Incorporeal"; meaning without a physical body</note>, might—just like Heraclitus, Hippocrates, and the Stoics among the Greeks—view the fiery substance of the whole world (and especially the Sun) as an animated and intellectual being. They considered this to be the Supreme Deity and the only Mithras, according to the inscription, "To the Unconquered Sun God Mithras" <note>original Latin: "Deo Soli Invicto Mithræ"</note>. However, whether Mithras was supposed to be physical or non-physical, he was unquestionably considered by the Persians to be the Supreme Deity, according to Hesychius: "Mithras, the first god among the Persians" <note>original Greek: Μίθρας, ὁ πρῶτος ἐν Πέρσαις θεός</note>. For this reason, he was called "Omnipotent" in the inscription "To the Omnipotent God Mithras" <note>original Latin: "Omnipotenti Deo Mithræ"</note>.

<margin>Plutarch, *Life of Themistocles*.</margin>
This first, supreme, and omnipotent God was acknowledged by Artabanus the Persian during his conference with Themistocles in these words: "Among those many excellent laws of ours, the most excellent is this: that the King is to be honored and worshipped religiously as the image of that God who preserves all things" <note>original Greek: ἡμῖν δὲ πολλῶν νόμων καὶ καλῶν ὄντων, κάλλιστος οὗτός ἐστι, τὸ τιμᾷν βασιλέα, καὶ προσκυνεῖν εἰκόνα θεοῦ τοῦ τὰ πάντα σώζοντος</note>.

Scaliger, along with some others (though we do not know on what certain grounds), affirms that *Mither* in the Persian language signified "Great," and *Mithra* "Greater" or "Greatest." According to this, Mithras would be the same as the "Greater" or "Greatest God" <note>original Latin: "Deus Major" or "Maximus"</note>. Therefore, we conclude that either Herodotus was mistaken in making the Persian Mithras the same as Mylitta or Venus—and perhaps such a mistake was caused because the word *Mader* or *Mether* in the Persian language signified <term>ܡܕܪ</term> <note>Syriac script for "Mader"</note> "Mother," just as *Mylitta* did in the Syrian language—or else, rather, that this "Venus" of his is to be understood as the Heavenly Venus or Love <note>original Greek: Ἀφροδίτη οὐρανία (Aphrodite Urania)</note>. Indeed, she is called "Urania" there in Herodotus. While some would understand this as nothing more than the Moon, we conceive the Supreme Deity—True Heavenly Love (the mother and nurse of all things) <margin>The Creator.</margin>—to have been the primary meaning intended.

But Zoroaster and the ancient Magi are said to have called the Supreme God by another name as well: Oromasdes or Ormisdas. However, according to Plato, Oromasdes seems to have been the father of Zoroaster. Thus, besides Plutarch and others, Porphyry writes in the *Life of Pythagoras*:

<margin>page 191.</margin>
"Pythagoras exhorted men chiefly to the love of truth, as being that alone which could make them resemble God. He had learned from the Magi that God, whom they call Oromasdes, was, regarding physical things, most like to Light, and regarding non-physical things, most like to Truth" <note>original Greek: παρήνει μάλιστα δ᾽ ἀληθεύειν, τοῦτο γὰρ μόνον δύνασθαι τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ποιεῖν θεῷ παραπλησίους, ἐπεὶ καὶ παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ, ὡς παρὰ τῶν μάγων ἐπυνθάνετο, ὃν Ὡρομάζην καλοῦσιν ἐκεῖνοι, ἐοικέναι τὸ μὲν σῶμα φωτί· τὴν δὲ ψυχὴν ἀληθείᾳ</note>. 

Perhaps some would interpret these words differently, suggesting that Oromasdes was actually composed of a soul and a body, and was therefore nothing other than the "Animated Sun," as Mithras is also commonly supposed to have been. But the contrary is plainly implied in those Zoroastrian traditions or fables concerning Oromasdes recorded in Plutarch: "that Oromasdes was as far removed from the Sun as the Sun was from the Earth" <note>original Greek: ὅτι ἀπέστησε τοῦ ἡλίου τοσοῦτον, ὅσον ὁ ἥλιος τῆς γῆς ἀφέστηκε</note>. Therefore, according to the Persians, Oromasdes was a deity superior to the Sun.

<summary>This page explores the Persian conception of a Supreme Deity, identifying him as Mithras or Oromasdes, and discusses whether he was viewed as a physical sun-god or a more transcendent, incorporeal being.</summary>
<keywords>Mithras, Oromasdes, Zoroaster, Persian religion, monotheism, solar worship, etymology, Plutarch, Herodotus, Porphyry</keywords>

# The Threefold Mithras. Book 1.

God is properly understood as the *Fountain of Light* and the *Origin of all Good*, being the same as Plato’s *The Good* <note>original Greek: τἀγαθὸν</note> or *First Good*. From this concept, as Scaliger informs us, the Persians called the *First Day* of every month *Ormasda*, probably because he was the *Beginning of all things*. Thus, Zoroaster and the ancient *Magi* acknowledged one and the same *Supreme Deity* under the different names of *Mithras* and *Oromasdes*.

But it is noteworthy here that the *Persian Mithras* was commonly called *triplasios* <note>original Greek: τριπλάσιος</note>, meaning *Threefold* or *Triple*. For instance, Dionysius the Pseudo-Areopagite wrote, "And even to this day, the Magi perform the memorial rites of the Threefold Mithras" <note>original Greek: καὶ εἰσέτι μάγοι τὰ μνημόσυνα τοῦ τριπλασίου μίθρα τελοῦσιν</note>. Something very similar to this is recorded by Plutarch concerning *Oromasdes* as well: "Oromasdes, having increased himself threefold (or triplicated himself)" <note>original Greek: ὁ μὲν ὡρομάζης τρὶς ἑαυτὸν αὐξήσας</note>. From this, it further appears that *Mithras* and *Oromasdes* were really one and the same divine being <note>original: "Numen"</note>. 

Now, the commentators <note>original: "Scholiasts"</note> on Dionysius pretend to give a reason for this title of the *Persian Mithras*—*Triplasian*, or *Threefold*—based on the miracle performed in Hezekiah’s time. They suggest that when the day was lengthened and almost tripled, the *Magi* observed it and subsequently gave the name *Threefold* <note>original Greek: τριπλάσιος</note> to their God *Mithras* (who is the *Sun*) and established an annual festival in memory of it. However, learned men have already shown the foolishness <note>original: "Foolery"</note> of this notion <note>original: "Conceit"</note>. Therefore, it cannot well be concluded otherwise than that this is a clear indication of a *Higher Mystery*: namely, a *Trinity in Persian Theology*. 

Gerardus J. Vossius would prefer to understand this according to the *Christian Hypothesis* of a *Divine Tri-unity*, or *Three Hypostases* (distinct persons) in one and the same *Deity*, whose distinguishing characteristics are *Goodness, Wisdom, and Power*. But the *Magical* or *Zoroastrian Oracles* seem to represent this *Persian Trinity* in a way more consistent with the *Pythagorean* or *Platonic hypothesis* of *three distinct substances subordinate* to one another. The first two of these are expressed in the following verses:

->For the Father perfected all things, and delivered them to the Second Mind,<-
->whom the nations of men commonly call the First.<-
<note>original Greek: πάντα γὰρ ἐξετέλησε πατὴρ, καὶ νῷ παρέδωκε / Δευτέρῳ, ὃν πρῶτον κληΐζεται ἔθνεα ἀνδρῶν.</note>

This oracle is explained by Psellus in this way: "The First Father of the Trinity, having produced this whole creation, delivered it to the Mind or Intellect. This Mind is the one whom the whole generation of mankind—being ignorant of the Paternal Transcendence—commonly call the First God" <note>original Greek: τὴν πᾶσαν κτίσιν δημιουργήσας ὁ τῆς τριάδος πρῶτος πατὴρ, παρέδωκε ταύτην τῷ νῷ· ὅντινα νῦν τὸ ξύμπαν γένος τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ἀγνοοῦντες τὴν πατρικὴν ὑπεροχήν, θεὸν πρῶτον καλοῦσι.</note>. After this, Psellus notes the difference between this Magical or Chaldean theology and that of Christians: "However, our Christian doctrine is the opposite: namely, that the First Mind or Intellect, being the Son of the Great Father, made the whole creation..." <note>original Greek: πλὴν τὸ παρ’ ἡμῖν δόγμα ἐναντίως ἔχει, ὡς αὐτὸς ὁ πρῶτος νοῦς, ὁ ὑιὸς τοῦ μεγάλου πατρὸς, τὴν κτίσιν πᾶσαν ἐδημιούργησεν, &c.</note>

<summary>This page discusses the identification of Mithras with Oromasdes and explores the "Threefold Mithras" as evidence of a Trinity in ancient Persian theology, comparing it to Platonic and Christian concepts.</summary>
<keywords>Mithras, Oromasdes, Trinity, Persian Theology, Zoroaster, Magi, Triplasian, Platonism, Chaldean Oracles, Psellus</keywords>

### CHAP. IV. The Magic and Chaldean Trinity.

*...whole Creation. For the Father in the Mosaic Writings speaks to his Son, the Idea of the Creation; but the Son is the immediate Architect <note>original: "Opifex"</note> thereof.* He means that, according to this Persian or Chaldean <note>original: "Chaldaick"</note> Theology, the First Hypostasis <term>Hypostasis: a person or distinct essence within the Trinity</term> of the Divine Triad was the Architect <note>original Greek: δημιουργὸς</note> or Immediate Architect of the World, whereas according to Christian as well as Platonic Doctrine, he is the second. For this reason, Pletho <note>George Gemistos Plethon, a 15th-century scholar who revived Neoplatonism</note> created another interpretation of that Magic Oracle to make it more consistent with both Christian and Platonic Doctrine:

"For the Father perfected all things—namely, the intelligible forms (for these are the things which are complete and perfect)—and delivered them to the Second God after him, to rule and lead them" <note>original Greek: ὁ γὰρ πατὴρ ἅπαντα ἐξετέλεσε, τὰ νοητὰ δηλαδὴ εἴδη (ταῦτα γάρ ἐστι τὰ ἐκτετελεσμένα τε καὶ τέλεια) καὶ τῷ μεθ' ἑαυτὸν δευτέρῳ θεῷ παρέδωκεν, ἄρχειν δηλαδὴ καὶ ἡγεῖσθαι αὐτῷ, &c.</note>. 

Therefore, whatever is produced by this God, according to its own pattern <note>original: "Exemplar"</note> and the Intelligible Essence, must necessarily owe its origin also to the Highest Father. This Second God is the one whom generations of men commonly mistake for the First, as they look no higher than to the Immediate Architect of the World. According to this interpretation by Pletho (the more probable of the two), the Second Hypostasis in the Magic (or Persian) Trinity—as well as in the Platonic and Christian—is the Immediate Architect of the World; and this seems to be properly what was called Mithras in the writings of Eubulus.

But besides these *Two Hypostases*, there is also a *Third* mentioned in a certain other Magic or Chaldean Oracle, cited by *Proclus*, under the name of *Psyche*, or the Mundane Soul <term>Mundane Soul: the soul of the universe, or "Anima Mundi"</term>:

---
> ->—————— after the Paternal thoughts,<-
> ->I, the Soul, dwell. <note>original Greek: μετὰ δὲ Πατρικὰς διανοίας; ψυχὴ ἐγὼ ναίω ˙</note><-
---

*After (or next below) the Paternal Mind, I, the Soul, dwell.* Now the *Paternal Mind*, as *Psellus* informs us, is the *Second Hypostasis* mentioned before: "The Paternal Mind is the Second God, and the immediate Architect <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note> of the soul" <note>original Greek: ὁ πατρικὸς νοῦς, ὁ δεύτερος δηλαδὴ θεὸς, καὶ τῆς ψυχῆς προσεχὴς δημιουργός</note>. Therefore, although both those names, *Oromasdes* and *Mithras*, were frequently used by the *Magi* for the divinity <note>original Greek: τὸ θεῖον</note>, or the whole Deity in general, this being *Threefold* according to their theology—containing *Three Hypostases* within it—the first of those three seems to have been the one most properly called *Oromasdes*, and the second *Mithras*. 

This is not only confirmed by *Pletho*, but also comes with this further addition: that the *Third Hypostasis* of that *Persian Trinity* was the one they called *Arimanius*. He gathers this much even from *Plutarch* himself: "They say concerning Zoroaster that he divided things into three parts; and in the first and highest rank he placed Oromasdes, who in the Oracles is called the Father; the lowest he assigned to Arimanius; and the middle to Mithras, who in the same Oracles is likewise called the Second Mind" <note>original Greek: φασὶ περὶ ζωροάστρου, ὡς τριχῆ τὰ ὄντα διέλοι ˙ καὶ τῇ μὲν πρώτῃ αὐτοῦ μοίρᾳ, Ὡρεμάζην ἐφιστάνη ˙ τοῦτον δ' εἶναι, τὸν ὑπὸ τῶν λογίων πατέρα καλούμενον ˙ τῇ δὲ ἐσχάτῃ Ἀρειμάνιον ˙ μίθραν δὲ τῇ μέσῃ, καὶ τοῦτον δ' ἂν εἶναι τὸν δεύτερον Νουν καλούμενον ὑπὸ τῶν λογίων</note>. # The Zoroastrian Trinity, Book I.

How great an agreement there was between the *Zoroastrian* and the *Platonic Trinity*, they differed essentially only in words. And the middle of these—namely, the *Eternal Intellect* that contains the *ideas* <term>ideas: in the Platonic sense, the perfect blueprints or eternal forms of all things</term> of all things—being, according to the *Platonic hypothesis*, the immediate Architect <note>original Greek: δημιουργὸς, Demiurge</note> and builder of the world, this was probably that *Mithras*, as we have already suggested, who is called in *Eubulus* <note>a writer mentioned by Porphyry as an authority on Mithraic mysteries</note> the *Architect of the world, and the maker and father of all things*. 

Now, if that *third hypostasis* <term>hypostasis: a person or distinct substance within the Trinity</term> of the *Magic* or *Chaldean* <note>original: Chaldaick</note> *Oracles* is the same as the one the *Persians* call *Arimanius* <note>Ahriman, the Zoroastrian spirit of darkness and evil</note>, it must be for this reason: because this *lower world* (where souls are vitally united to bodies and are liable to fall <note>original: Lapsable</note>) is the region where all manner of evil, wickedness, pain, corruption, and mortality reign. And *Hesychius* <note>a Greek grammarian and lexicographer</note> seems to agree with this: "Arimanius," he says, "is Hades among the Persians" <note>original Greek: Ἀρειμάννης ὁ Ἅιδης παρὰ Πέρσαις</note>; that is, either *Orcus* or *Pluto* <note>gods of the underworld</note>. In this, he was merely following *Theopompus*, who in *Plutarch's* writings also calls *Arimanius* "Hades" or "Pluto." It seems he was the third in the *Persian Trinity* (or *triple deity*) just as he was in the *Homeric* triad <note>referring to the three brothers: Zeus, Poseidon, and Hades</note>. 

And this was that *Arimanius* to whom the *Persian King* in *Plutarch*, upon the flight of *Themistocles*, addressed his prayers: <margin>In the Life of Themistocles</margin> "He prayed that Arimanius would always give his enemies such a mindset that they would banish and drive away their own best men" <note>original Greek: κατευξάμενος ἀεὶ τοῖς πολεμίοις, τοιαύτας φρένας διδόναι τὸν Ἀρειμάνιον, ὅπως ἐλαύνωσι τοὺς ἀρίστους τῶν ἑαυτῶν</note>. And indeed, based on what *Plutarch* affirms—"that the Persians, from their God Mithras, called any mediator, or person in the middle between two others, Mithras" <note>original Greek: διὸ καὶ Μίθρην Πέρσαι τὸν Μεσιτὴν ὀνομάζουσι</note>—it can be more reasonably concluded that *Mithras*, according to *Persian* theology, was properly the *middle hypostasis* of that *triple* or *triplicated deity* of theirs. This is more likely than the idea that he should be a middle *self-existent God*, or *mediator*, between two uncreated opposing gods—one *good* and the other *evil*—as *Plutarch* would suppose.

Nevertheless, even if what the same *Plutarch* and others so confidently claim were true—that *Zoroaster* and the ancient *Magi* made *Good* and *Evil*, *Light* and *Darkness*, the *two fundamental principles of the universe* (meaning they asserted an *evil demon* <term>demon: here, a powerful spiritual entity, not necessarily "demonic" in the modern sense</term> *co-eternal with God and independent of him*, just as *Plutarch* himself and the *Manicheans* later did)—yet even so, it is clear that in this view also, *Zoroaster* and the *Magi* acknowledged *one single fountain and origin of all good*. They believed nothing was independent of that *one good principle or God* except for that which is so contrary to his nature and perfection that it could not proceed from him: namely, *evil*. 

But we have already expressed a suspicion that the meaning of those ancient *Magi* might have been different. They may have been philosophizing only about a certain *mixture of evil and darkness combined with good and light* that exists in the *makeup of this lower world*, and then personifying those qualities. They were also perhaps taking special note of *evil demons* (who are also acknowledged in the *Magic Oracles* and called "beasts of the earth" <note>original Greek: Θῆρες χθονὸς</note> and "terrestrial dogs" <note>original Greek: χθόνιοι κύνες</note>). The leader of these might sometimes be called, with emphasis, "the evil demon of the Persians" <note>original Greek: ὁ πονηρὸς δαίμων Περσῶν</note>, being essentially the same as the *Devil*.

<summary>The author argues that the Persian "Mithras" functions as the middle person of a divine trinity, similar to the Platonic "Intellect," rather than a mediator between two equal gods of good and evil. He suggests that the "evil" third person, Arimanius, represents the flawed nature of the physical world or the leader of fallen spirits.</summary>

# Chapter IV. Oromasdes, Mithras, and Arimanes. 291

...Devil. All of this was under the immediate presidency or government of that god whom they called *Arimanius*, *Hades*, or *Pluto*, the *third hypostasis* <term>hypostasis: a person or distinct substance within a trinity</term> in the *tripartite deity* <note>original: Triplasian Deity</note> of the *Persians*. This suspicion may be further confirmed by the fact that Persian theologians, as seen in ancient inscriptions, explicitly acknowledged *divine omnipotence*. They could not possibly have done this if they had believed in a *Manichean substantial evil principle* <note>Manichaeism: a dualistic religion that posits a radical struggle between a good spiritual world of light and an evil material world of darkness</note> that was *co-eternal with God* and *independent of him*. 

Additionally, it is worth noting that the Gnostics in the time of *Plotinus* <note>a major Neoplatonist philosopher, c. 204–270 AD</note> claimed this world was made not so much from an *essentially evil and eternal principle*, but from a *fallen soul*. To counter the authority of *Plato*, who disagreed with them, they placed *Zoroaster* on the opposite side of the scale, producing a book titled *The Revelations of Zoroaster* <note>original Greek: ἀποκάλυψις Ζωροάστρου</note>. *Porphyry* <note>a student of Plotinus</note> tells us that he wrote specifically to disprove these "Zoroastrian" revelations, calling them new, counterfeit, and forged by the Gnostics themselves. This implies that the doctrine of the ancient *Zoroaster* in no way supported or favored that *Gnostic heresy*. 

Furthermore, the tenets of these ancient *Magi* regarding the "duality of principles" are presented by various writers with great inconsistency. The account given by *Theodorus* (found in the works of *Photius*) concerning *Persian magic*, as well as the account by *Eudemus* (found in *Damascius*), are both so nonsensical that we will not trouble the reader with them here. However, neither of them suggests that the Persian *Arimanius* (or *Satan*) was an uncreated, self-existing demon. 

On the other hand, Arabian writers discussing *Al-Tanawiyyah* <note>original: Altanawiah; refers to dualism or "the Two-foldists"</note> (the *Persian duality* of good and evil principles) affirm that, according to the most respected *Magi*, *Light* was *Kadiman* <note>original: Kadiman; from the Arabic/Hebrew root for "ancient" or "primordial"</note>, the *most ancient and first God*. They claim that *Darkness* was merely a *created god*, explicitly denying that the principle of evil and *darkness* was *co-equal in age* <note>original: Coeve</note> with *God* or the *principle of good and light*. 

And *Abulfeda* <note>a 14th-century Syrian historian and geographer</note> represents the *Zoroastrian doctrine* (as the *reformed doctrine of the Magi*) <margin>Pocock, *Specimen of the History of the Arabs*, pp. 146, 147, 148.</margin> in this way: *God was older than darkness and light, and the creator of both. Thus, He was a solitary being, without companion or rival. Good and evil, virtue and vice, arose from a certain mixing of light and darkness together; without this mixture, this lower world could never have been produced. This mixture will continue until, at last, Light overcomes Darkness. Then, Light and Darkness shall each have their separate and distinct worlds, apart from one another.*

<margin>Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book I.</margin> If it were necessary, we could provide even more evidence that *Zoroaster* was a proponent of *one supreme God*, despite the many gods he worshiped. This is seen in his own description of God found in *Eusebius*: "God is the first: incorruptible, eternal, uncreated, indivisible, most unlike to anything else, the leader of everything good, unable to be bribed, the best of the good, the wisest of the wise. He is also the father of law and justice, self-taught, perfect, and the sole discoverer of the sacred laws of nature." <note>original Greek: θεός ἐστιν ὁ πρῶτος ἄφθαρτος, ἀΐδιος, ἀγένητος, ἀμερής, ἀνομοιότατος, ἡνίοχος παντὸς καλοῦ, ἀδωροδόκητος, ἀγαθῶν ἀγαθώτατος, φρονίμων φρονιμώτατος, ἔστι δὲ καὶ πατὴρ εὐνομίας καὶ δικαιοσύνης, αὐτοδίδακτος, τέλειος, καὶ ἱεροῦ φυσικοῦ μόνος εὑρετής</note> *God is the First Incorruptible, Eternal, Unmade, Indivisible, Most unlike to every thing, the Head or Leader of all Good, Unbribable, the Best of the Good, the Wisest of the Wise; He is also the Father of Law and Justice, Self-taught, Perfect, and the*

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the ancient Persian conception of God, arguing that the primary inventor of "Natural Holiness" described God in terms preserved by Eusebius and other ancient sources, which point toward a monotheistic and even trinitarian understanding within the Zoroastrian and Chaldean traditions.</meta>

# Concerning Magic, BOOK I.

...the only inventor of the "Natural Holy." <note>original: Natural Holy; likely referring to the natural law or sacred philosophy of the Persians</note> *Eusebius* <note>a 4th-century Christian historian</note> tells us that this Zoroastrian description of God was contained word-for-word in a book entitled *A Holy Collection of the Persian Monuments*. He also notes that *Ostanes* (himself a famous magician and admirer of Zoroaster) had recorded the very same about him in his *Octateuchon* <note>original: Octateuchon; a work consisting of eight books</note>.

Now, having cited the Oracles in this discourse concerning Zoroaster and the *Magi* <term>Magi: the priestly caste of ancient Persia</term>—which some call "Magical" and attribute to Zoroaster, while others call "Chaldean"—we believe it is appropriate to provide some account of them here. Indeed, if we could be certain of the antiquity and authenticity of these *reputed Oracles*, no other testimony would be needed to prove that either Zoroaster and the Persian Magi, or at least the Chaldeans, asserted not only a *divine monarchy* (one supreme deity as the origin of all things), but also a *Trinity* consistent with that unity.

It is certain that these Oracles are not as "new" as some might suspect. They were cited by *Synesius* <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher and bishop, c. 373–414 AD</note> as being venerable and of great authority in his time, under the name of *Holy Oracles* <note>original: ἱερὰ λόγια</note>. Furthermore, some of the Oracles Synesius produced are not found in the copies preserved by *Psellus* or *Pletho* <note>Michael Psellos and Gemistus Pletho, Byzantine scholars who preserved fragments of these texts</note>. From this, we may conclude that we have only a few fragments of these Oracles left today. The idea that they were forged by Christians—as some of the *Sibylline Oracles* <note>a collection of oracular utterances written in Greek hexameters ascribed to the Sibyls</note> undoubtedly were—seems unlikely because so many Pagan philosophers use them as evidence and place great importance on them.

For example, *Damascius* <note>the last head of the School of Athens, c. 458–538 AD</note> provided a considerable collection of these Oracles (which *Patritius* later gathered) that are missing from the copies of Psellus and Pletho. We also learn from *Photius* <note>a 9th-century scholar and Patriarch of Constantinople</note> that while the philosopher *Hierocles’* book on fate and providence was divided into seven parts, the goal of the fourth part was to "bring the so-called oracles into harmony with the doctrines of Plato" <note>original: τὰ λεγόμενα λόγια, εἰς συμφωνίαν συνάγειν, οἷς πλάτων ἐδογμάτισε</note>. There is no doubt that the "reputed oracles" mentioned by Hierocles were the same as these Magical or Chaldean Oracles, because philosophers frequently cite them under the name *logia* (Oracles).

<margin>Page 97.</margin> *Proclus* <note>a major Neoplatonist philosopher, 412–485 AD</note>, commenting on Plato's *Timaeus*, writes: "The Maker and Father of the universe is celebrated by Plato, Orpheus, and the Oracles as the 'Father of gods and men'; he brings forth the multitudes of gods and sends down souls for the births of men" <note>original: ὑπό τε Πλάτωνος, καὶ Ὀρφέως, καὶ λογίων, ποιητὴς καὶ πατὴρ ὑμνεῖται τοῦ παντὸς, πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε Θεῶν τε • γεννῶν μὲν τὰ πλήθη τῶν Θεῶν, ψυχὰς δὲ πέμπων εἰς γενέσεις ἀνδρῶν</note>. Just as Proclus cites other fragments of these elsewhere under the name of "Oracles," he also sometimes gives them the higher title of *The Theology of Divine Tradition* or *Initiation into the Mysteries* <note>original: Θεοπαράδοτος Θεολογία and μυσταγωγία</note>.

This magnificent praise was similarly bestowed upon the philosophy of Pythagoras by *Iamblichus* <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher, c. 245–325 AD</note>, as it was thought to have been derived largely from the Chaldeans and the Magi: "This philosophy [of Pythagoras], having been first divinely delivered or revealed by the gods, ought not to be handled by us without a religious invocation of them" <note>original: ἐκ Θεῶν αὐτῆς παραδοθείσης τὸ κατ’ ἀρχάς</note>. And it is clear that *Porphyry* was not unacquainted with these...

### CHAPTER IV. Or, The Chaldean Oracles.

That these were not the only oracles of this kind may be concluded from Porphyry's book entitled *On the Philosophy of Oracles* <note>original: περὶ τῆς ἐκ λογίων φιλοσοφίας</note>. This work consisted of several parts, one of which was called *The Oracles of the Chaldeans* <note>original: τὰ τῶν χαλδαίων λόγια</note>. That these were the very same ones we are discussing now shall be further proved later. Now, although Psellus <note>Michael Psellos, an 11th-century Byzantine monk and scholar</note> affirms that the Chaldean doctrines <term>Dogmata: principles or doctrines</term> contained in those oracles were partly accepted by both Aristotle and Plato, he does not claim that these specific Greek verses are themselves that ancient. 

Instead, it seems probable from the *Suda* <note>a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> that Julian a Chaldean and "Theurgist" <term>Theurgist: a practitioner of "god-working" or divine magic</term>, the son of Julian the Philosopher (who wrote concerning demons and the arts of ritual <term>Telesturgics: the art of performing sacred rites or consecrating statues</term>), was the first to translate those Chaldean or magical oracles into Greek verse: *Julian, in the time of Emperor Marcus Antoninus, wrote the theurgic and ritual oracles in verse* <note>original: ἰουλιανὸς, ἐπὶ μάρκου Ἀντονίνου τοῦ βασιλέως, ἔγραψε θεουργικὰ, τελεστικὰ, λόγια δι᾽ ἐπῶν</note>. 

It is quite clear—from the descriptions of operations involving the "Hecatine Circle" <note>a magical tool or ritual device associated with the goddess Hecate</note> and other passages—that there is a degree of "theurgic magic" mixed with mystical theology in these oracles. This makes it even more unlikely that they were forged by Christians. Nevertheless, they carry with them (as has already been noted) a clear acknowledgment of a *Divine Monarchy*, or *One Supreme Deity* as the origin of all things. In these texts, he is called *The Father*, the *Paternal Principle*, and that *Intelligible Being* who *cannot be apprehended otherwise than by the flower of the mind* <note>original: ὃ χρή σε νοεῖν νόου ἄνθει</note>. He is also called the *One Fire from which all things spring*. 

Psellus provides this commentary <term>gloss: an explanatory note or interpretation</term> on the oracle which states: "All things were the offspring of one fire"—*All things, whether intellectual or sensory, received their existence from the person of God alone and are turned back toward God alone, etc. Therefore, this oracle is faultless and full of our own doctrine* <note>original: πάντα τὰ ὄντα τότε νοητὰ, καὶ αἰσθητὰ, ἀπὸ μόνης θεοῦ ὑποστάσεως ἔλαβον, καὶ πρὸς μόνον θεὸν ἐπέστραπται... ἄπταιστον οὖν τὸ λόγιον, καὶ πλῆρες τοῦ ἡμετέρου δόγματος</note>.

It is also very noteworthy that these same oracles expressly determined that matter was not "uncreated" <note>original: ἀγέννητος</note> or self-existent, but was likewise derived from the deity. We learn this from Proclus <note>a 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> in his commentary on Plato's *Timaeus*. There, after positively asserting that there is *one cause of all things* <note>original: ἓν πάντων αἴτιον</note> and that *the Supreme Good, being the cause of all things, is also the cause of matter* <note>original: τἀγαθὸν πάντων αἴτιον ὂν, εἶναι καὶ ὕλης αἴτιον</note>, he confirms his assertion using the authority of the oracles: 

<margin>Page 118.</margin> 
*From this order as well, the oracles derive multi-various matter: "From that source [the Supreme Deity] altogether springs the generation of multi-various matter"* <note>original: ἀπὸ ταύτης καὶ τῆς τάξεως καὶ τὰ λόγια παράγει τὴν πολυποίκιλον ὕλην, Ἔνθεν ἄρδην θρώσκει γένεσις πολυποικίλου ὕλης</note>. 

This was unquestionably one of those very magic or Chaldean oracles. This can be further proven because it was recorded among them by Porphyry <note>a 3rd-century Neoplatonist scholar</note>, as shown by Aeneas of Gaza <note>a 5th-century Christian philosopher</note> in his *Theophrastus*: 

*For matter was neither uncreated nor without a beginning; both the Chaldeans and Porphyry teach you this. Indeed, he gives this title to the whole book he presents: "The Oracles of the Chaldeans," in which he insists that matter was created* <note>original: οὐ γὰρ ἀγέννητος οὐδὲ ἄναρχος ἡ ὕλη, τοῦτό σε καὶ χαλδαῖοι διδάσκουσι, καὶ ὁ πορφύριος· ἐπιγράφει δὲ καθόλου τὸ βιβλίον ὃ εἰς μέσον προάγει, τῶν χαλδαίων τὰ λόγια, ἐν οἷς γεγονέναι τὴν ὕλην ἰσχυρίζεται</note>.

<summary>This page discusses the origin of the Chaldean Oracles, attributing their Greek translation to Julian the Theurgist and highlighting their core philosophical claim: that both the universe and matter itself originated from a single Supreme Deity.</summary>

### The History of Orpheus, Book 1.

*A book published by him, The Oracles of the Chaldeans, in which it is confirmed that Matter was created.*

Moreover, it has already been declared that there was a clear indication of a **Divine Triad** <note>The "Divine Triad" refers to a trinity of supreme principles or deities often found in Neoplatonic interpretations of ancient theology</note> in these *Magical* or *Chaldean Oracles*. But we shall also provide the testimony of **Proclus** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who heavily influenced Western medieval and Renaissance thought</note> for it as well: "Thus the divinely delivered (or inspired) theology affirms the whole world to have been completed from these three; the World Soul <note>original: *Psyche*</note> therein speaking concerning that Zeus or Jupiter who was above the creator <term>Demiurge: the artisan-like figure responsible for fashioning and maintaining the physical universe</term> of the world, in this manner," etc. <note>original: οὕτω γὰρ ἡ θεοπαράδοτος θεολογία, φησὶ συμπεπληρῶσθαι τὸν κόσμον, ἐκ τῶνδε τῶν τριῶν λέγει γοῦν ἡ ψυχὴ περὶ τοῦ Διὸς ἐπέκεινα τοῦ δημιουργήσαντος τὸ πᾶν</note>. 

For we have already stated that Proclus’s "divinely delivered theology" (or theology of divine tradition and revelation) is one and the same thing as the *Oracles*. To this testimony of Proclus, we might also add that Oracle cited out of **Damascius** <note>The last head of the School of Athens in the 6th century</note> by **Patrizi** <note>Francesco Patrizi (1529–1597), a Venetian philosopher and scientist who published a famous collection of the Chaldean Oracles</note>:

->*In the whole world shines forth a Triad, over which a Monad rules.*<-
-><note>original: παντὶ γὰρ ἐν κόσμῳ λάμπει τριὰς ἧς μονὰς ἄρχει</note><-

In this context, the "Monad" refers to a perfect unity; nothing could be clearer than this.

<margin>Gerardus Joannes Vossius, *De Arte Poetica*, chapter 13.</margin>
**XVII.** And now we pass out of *Asia* into *Europe*, moving from *Zoroaster* to **Orpheus**. It is the opinion of some eminent scholars <term>Philologers: students of history, language, and literature</term> of recent times that there never was any such man as *Orpheus* except in "fairy-land," and that the entire *history of Orpheus* was nothing but a mere romantic allegory, utterly devoid of all truth and reality. 

<margin>Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book 1, p. 211.</margin>
However, there is nothing alleged for this opinion from antiquity except this single passage from **Cicero** concerning **Aristotle**: "Aristotle teaches that there never was such a man as Orpheus the poet" <note>original: *Orpheum Poetam docet Aristoteles nunquam fuisse*</note>. In this passage, Aristotle seems to have meant nothing more than that there was no such poet as *Orpheus* who lived before **Homer**, or that the verses commonly called "Orphic" were not actually written by Orpheus. 

Nevertheless, even if it should be granted that Aristotle had denied the existence of such a man, there seems to be no reason at all why his single testimony should outweigh the **universal consent** of all antiquity. Ancient tradition is in favor of a real *Orpheus*, the son of Oeager, Thracian by birth, and the father or **chief founder** of mythical and allegorical theology among the Greeks, as well as all their most secret <term>Arcane: secret or mysterious; understood by few</term> religious rites and mysteries. He is commonly supposed to have lived before the Trojan War (that is, in the time of the **Israelite Judges**) or, at the very least, to have been senior to both **Hesiod** and **Homer**. It is also said that he died a violent death, with most sources affirming that he was torn to pieces by women.

<margin>Plato, *The Republic*, book 10. Book 4, p. 162.</margin>
For this reason, in the vision of **Er the Pamphylian** <note>original: *Herus Pamphilius*; Er is the protagonist of the concluding myth in Plato's Republic who witnesses the reincarnation of souls</note> in *Plato*, when Orpheus's soul was to come down again into another body, he is said to have chosen the body of a swan (a bird reputed for its music) rather than be born again of a woman, because of the great hatred he had conceived for all womankind after suffering such a violent death at their hands. The historical truth of Orpheus's existence was not only acknowledged by Plato, but also by **Isocrates** <note>A famous Athenian orator</note>, who was also senior to Aristotle.

<summary>The author argues for the existence of a "Divine Triad" in the Chaldean Oracles and defends the historical existence of Orpheus against those who claim he is a myth, citing universal ancient consensus over Aristotle's potential skepticism.</summary>

## CHAP. IV. Orpheus: Not a Mere Romance

(In his speech in praise of *Busiris*;) and confirmed by the reliable historian *Diodorus Siculus*, who gave this account of *Orpheus*: *That he was a man who diligently applied himself to literature, and after learning the mythological stories <note>original: τὰ μυθολογούμενα</note> (the mythical part of theology), traveled to Egypt. There, he attained further knowledge and became the greatest of all the Greeks in the mysterious rites of religion, theological skill, and poetry.* To which *Pausanias* adds that he gained <margin>Book 9, page 586.</margin> great authority, "as being believed to have discovered expiations for wicked actions, remedies for diseases, and ways to appease divine displeasure" <note>original: οἷα πιστευόμενος εὑρηκέναι ἔργων ἀνοσίων καθαρμοὺς, νόσων τε ἰάματα, καὶ τροπὰς μηνιμάτων θείων</note>. Neither was this history of *Orpheus* contradicted by *Origen* <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD)</note>, even when *Celsus* <note>A 2nd-century Greek philosopher and opponent of early Christianity</note> gave him such a perfect opportunity and strong provocation to do so by preferring *Orpheus* over our Savior Christ. 

To all this may be added, finally, that it is commonly concluded from the Greek word *threskeia* <note>original: θρησκεία; meaning "religion" or "worship"</note> that the Greeks derived their *rites* <note>original: *Teletæ*</note> and mysteries of religion from the Thracians. Therefore, it is not reasonable to agree with the learned *Gerard Vossius* <note>A 17th-century Dutch scholar and theologian</note> that *Zalmoxis* <note>original: *Xamolxis*</note> was their founder instead of *Orpheus*. This Zalmoxis was reported by most to have been the servant of *Pythagoras* and was, consequently, far too recent <term>junior: a person or event occurring much later in time</term>. And though *Herodotus* attributes more antiquity to him, he conceived him to be nothing more than a *spirit* <note>original: *daemon*</note> who appeared to the Thracians and was worshipped by them. Meanwhile, the general tradition of the Greeks derived the Thracian religious rites and mysteries from *Orpheus* and no one else, according to this passage from *Suidas* <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>: "It is commonly said that Orpheus the Thracian was the first inventor of the religious mysteries of the Greeks, and that honoring God was from then on called *threskeuein* <note>original: θρησκεύειν; to practice religion</note>, because the discovery was Thracian" <note>original: λέγεται ὡς Ὀρφεύς Θρᾷξ, πρῶτος ἐτεχνολόγησε τὰ Ἑλλήνων μυστήρια, καὶ τὸ τιμᾶν Θεὸν θρησκεύειν ἐκάλεσεν, ὡς Θρᾳκίας οὔσης τῆς εὑρέσεως</note>. Therefore, although it may be granted that many fables and romantic stories have been mixed into his history because of his great antiquity, there appears to be no reason at all to disbelieve that such a man existed.

But even if such a man as *Orpheus* existed, it may still be questioned whether any of the poems commonly attributed to him and called "Orphic" were actually so ancient or written by him. This is especially true because *Herodotus* declares his own opinion that *Hesiod* and *Homer* were the oldest of all <margin>Book 2, page 53.</margin> the Greek poets. He says, "and those other poets said to have lived before these men actually came after them" <note>original: οἱ δὲ πρότερον ποιηταὶ λεγόμενοι τούτων τῶν ἀνδρῶν γενέσθαι ὕστερον ἐγένοντο</note>, meaning in all probability *Orpheus*, *Musaeus*, and *Linus*. *Aristotle* also seems to have followed *Herodotus* in this, as he mentions the Orphic poems in his <margin>Book 1, chapter 7, section 7.</margin> book *On the Soul* as "the verses that are called Orphic" <note>original: τὰ Ὀρφικὰ καλούμενα ἔπη</note>. Furthermore, *Cicero* tells us that some attributed all the Orphic poems to *Cercops*, a Pythagorean. It is also well known that many have attributed them to another of that school, *Onomacritus*, who lived during the time of the *Pisistratids* <note>The sons of Pisistratus, who ruled Athens in the 6th century BC</note>. For this reason, we read more than once in the works of *Sextus Empiricus* <note>A 2nd-century skeptical philosopher and physician</note> about "Onomacritus in the Orphic poems" <note>original: Ὀνομάκριτος ἐν τοῖς Ὀρφικοῖς</note>.

<summary>This page argues for the historical existence of Orpheus as the founder of Greek religious mysteries while questioning the authenticity and extreme antiquity of the poems traditionally attributed to him.</summary>

# Whether Orpheus was the Author, BOOK I.

<margin>Introduction to Stobaeus’s *Florilegium* <note>original: Proleg. in Flor. Stob.</note></margin>
In the *Orphics* <note>original: Ὀρφικοῖς</note>, it is said that *Onomacritus* <note>A 6th-century BC Greek poet and priest</note> wrote the *Orphic* poems. *Suidas* <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedist and lexicographer</note> also reports that some of the *Orphic poems* were anciently ascribed to *Theognetus*, others to *Timocles*, others to *Zopyrus*, and so on. From all of this, the scholar *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian</note> seems to have reached this conclusion: *That the Pythagoreans attributed their own books to Orpheus and Linus, in exactly the same way as the ancient Christians attributed theirs—some to the Sibyls, and others to Hermes Trismegistus. This implies that both the Orphic poems and their doctrine owed their very existence and first origin only to the Pythagoreans.* 

But on the other hand, *Clement of Alexandria* <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 150–215 AD)</note> affirms that the philosopher *Heraclitus* borrowed many things from the *Orphic poems*. And it is certain that *Plato* not only highly commends the *Orphic Hymns* for their sweetness and delightfulness, but also quotes some verses from them without showing any doubt concerning

If this is true, then those *Orphic fragments* that we have now (preserved in the writings of those who did not use the Doric dialect) must have been transformed by them out of their native idiom. 

Now, concerning *Herodotus*: because he supposed *Homer* and *Hesiod* were the oldest of all the Greek poets, he therefore seemed to conclude that the *Orphic poems* were <term>pseudepigraphous</term> <note>meaning "falsely attributed" or written under a false name</note>. Yet *Aristotle* might have been more inclined to follow *Herodotus* in this because he had no great fondness for the Pythagorean or Orphic philosophy. ### Chapter IV. Of the Orphic Poems

...or at least transmitted down by oral tradition from him. Therefore, the Pythagoreans themselves constantly maintain that before the time of Pythagoras, there was not only an Orphic *Cabala* <note>original: *Cabala*; here referring to a secret oral tradition</note> in existence, but also *Orphic Poems*. The former was declared in that ancient book called the *Hieros Logos* <note>original: Ἱερὸς λόγος</note>, or *The Holy Oration*, if we may believe <margin>Page 291.</margin> Proclus in his commentary on the *Timaeus*: "Timaeus, being a Pythagorean, follows Pythagorean principles, and these are the Orphic traditions. Ἃ γὰρ ὀρφεὺς δι' ἀποῤῥήτων λόγων μυστικῶς παραδέδωκε, ταῦτα πυθαγόρας ἐξέμαθεν ὀργιασθεὶς ἐν λειβήθροις τοῖς θρακίοις, Ἀγλαοφήμῳ τελέστα μεταδιδόντος. ταῦτα γάρ φησιν ὁ Πυθαγόρας ἐν τῷ Ἱερῷ λόγῳ.</note> In this passage, Proclus, without any doubt or hesitation, attributes the book titled *Hieros Logos*, or *The Holy Oration*, to Pythagoras himself.

Indeed, several of the ancients have concluded that Pythagoras wrote nothing at all, such as Flavius Josephus, Plutarch, Lucian, and Porphyry. Furthermore, Epigenes, as cited in Clement of Alexandria, affirms that the *Hieros Logos*, or *Holy Oration*, was actually written by Cercops, a Pythagorean. Nevertheless, Diogenes Laertius thinks those who deny Pythagoras wrote anything are not being serious. He tells us that Heraclides acknowledged this *Hieros Logos* as a genuine and undisputed work <note>original: *fœtus*, literally "offspring"</note> of Pythagoras. Iamblichus is also of the same opinion, which was the most widely accepted view, though he confesses some attributed that book to Telauges, the son of Pythagoras. 

But whoever was the writer of this *Hieros Logos*—whether Pythagoras himself, Telauges, or Cercops—it must be granted to be of great antiquity. According to its testimony, Pythagoras derived much of his theology from the Orphic traditions. Moreover, Ion of Chios in his *Trigrammi* <margin>Stromata, Book I, page 333.</margin> testified (as Clement of Alexandria informs us) that Pythagoras himself referred some poems to Orpheus as their author. This is also the general sense held by Platonists as well as Pythagoreans. 

Therefore, by all accounts, it seems most probable that either Orpheus himself wrote some philosophical or theological poems—though certain other poems might also be attributed to him because they were written in the same style of mystical and allegorical theology, and as it were in the same spirit with which this Thracian prophet was inspired—or at least that the Orphic doctrine was first conveyed down by oral *Cabala* or tradition from him. For its better preservation, it was afterwards expressed in verses that were attributed to Orpheus, in the same way that the *Golden Verses* written by Lysis were attributed to Pythagoras. 

Philoponus suggests that this latter view was Aristotle's opinion regarding the Orphic verses. He offers this gloss on the words of Aristotle cited earlier: "Aristotle calls them the 'reputed' Orphic verses because they do not seem to have been written by Orpheus himself, as the same Aristotle affirms in his book *On Philosophy*. The doctrine and opinions in them were indeed his, but Onomacritus is said to have put them into verse." <note>original: καλουμένοις εἶπε, ὅτι μὴ δοκεῖ ὀρφέως τὰ ἔπη, ὡς καὶ αὐτὸς ἐν τῷ περὶ φιλοσοφίας λέγει. # Orpheus: A Complete Polytheist. Book I.

There is no doubt at all that the *Orphic Verses*, no matter who wrote them, were very ancient (being much older than *Aristotle*, *Plato*, or *Herodotus*). They were also held in great esteem among the *Pagans*; therefore, we may very well judge the theology of the ancient *Pagans* from them.

Now, it is acknowledged by all that *Orpheus*, the *Orphic Doctrine*, and the *Poems* were polytheistic. *Justin Martyr* <note>An early Christian apologist (c. 100–165 AD)</note> affirms that *Orpheus* claimed there were three hundred and sixty gods. He also grants him this "honorable" title (if it can be considered such): "the father and first teacher of polytheism among the Greeks" <note>original: πολυθεότητος πατὴρ καὶ πρῶτος διδάσκαλος</note>. He supposed that *Homer* derived his polytheism from him: "Homer, emulating the fame of Orpheus's polytheism, wrote fabulously of many gods so that he would not seem to disagree with Orpheus’s poetry, for whom he had such great veneration" <note>original: Ὅμηρος τῆ πολυθεότητι Ὀρφέως ζηλώσας δόξαν, μυθωδῶς μὲν πλειόνων θεῶν μέμνηται, ἵνα μὴ δόξη τῆ Ὀρφέως ἀπάδειν ποιήσεως</note>. The testimony of *Athenagoras* <note>Another early Christian apologist</note> agrees with this: "Orpheus first invented the very names of the gods, describing their origins and the deeds performed by each of them; and Homer, for the most part, follows him in these matters, especially regarding the gods" <note>original: Ὀρφεὺς καὶ τὰ ὀνόματα θεῶν πρῶτος ἐξεῦρεν καὶ τὰς γενέσεις διεξῆλθε, καὶ ὅσα ἑκάστοις πέπρακται εἶπε, ὧ καὶ Ὅμηρος τὰ πολλὰ καὶ περὶ θεῶν μάλιστα ἕπεται</note>.

Indeed, the entire mythical theology—the fables of the gods along with the religious rites of the Greeks—is commonly believed to have originated from no one other than *Orpheus*. In these Orphic fables, not only were the *elements of nature* and *parts of the world* turned into gods, but all manner of human *passions*, *imperfections*, and *vices* (according to the literal sense) were attributed to the *gods*. This reached such an extent that several of the Pagans themselves took great offense at <margin>In his *Praise of Busiris*.</margin> them. For example, *Isocrates* <note>An influential Athenian orator</note> concludes that a divine Nemesis (vengeance) was inflicted upon *Orpheus* for this impiety: "Orpheus, who was most guilty of such stories, died a violent death" <note>original: Ὀρφεὺς ὁ μάλιστα τῶν τοιούτων λόγων ἁψάμενος, διασπασθεὶς τὸν βίον ἐτελεύτησε</note>.

Also, for this same reason, *Diogenes Laertius* questioned whether he should even count *Orpheus* among the philosophers. Others have concluded that *Plato* ought to have banished *Orpheus* from his ideal Republic for the same reason he banished *Homer*, which is expressed as: *For not lying well concerning the gods* <note>original: "For not Lying well concerning the Gods"; referring to Plato's critique of poets who depicted gods as immoral or deceptive</note>.

Here we may also notice the bizarre and extravagant nature of *Orpheus's* imagination from what *Damascius* <note>The last head of the Neoplatonist school at Athens</note> and others tell us: he described one of his primary beings as "a dragon having the heads of a bull and a lion attached to it, and in the middle the face of a god, with golden wings upon its shoulders" <note>original: δρακόντα κεφαλὰς ἔχοντα προσπεφυκυίας ταύρου καὶ λέοντος, ἐν μέσω δὲ θεοῦ πρόσωπον, καὶ ἐπὶ ὤμων πτερά</note>. This was supposedly an *incorporeal deity* and *Hercules*, with whom Nature (called *Ananche* <note>term: Necessity</note> and *Adrastea* <note>term: Inevitability or inescapable Fate</note>) was associated.

Nevertheless, the majority of the Greek Pagans did not look upon this *Orpheus* as merely a fanciful poet and storyteller, but as a serious and profound philosopher, or "mystical theologian"—a person transcendently holy and wise. They supposed all his fables of the gods to be deep mysteries and allegories...

# CHAPTER IV. Nevertheless a Believer in a Divine Monarchy.

<margin>Celsus, *Against Celsus*, Book 7, page 367.</margin>
These were allegories that contained some *hidden* and *obscure meaning* within them. Therefore, many held Orpheus in high regard as one who (as *Athenagoras* writes) *spoke more truly about divine matters* <note>original: ἀληθέστερον θεολογεῖν</note> than the rest, and was indeed divinely *inspired*. This reached such a point that *Celsus* <note>A 2nd-century philosopher and critic of Christianity</note> would have preferred for the *Christians* to have accepted *Orpheus* as a god instead of our *Savior Christ*, describing him as *a man who was undeniably endowed with a holy spirit and who also (just like the Christians' Jesus) died a violent death* <note>original: ἄνδρα ὁμολογουμένως ὁσίῳ χρησάμενον πνεύματι, καὶ αὐτὸν βιαίως ἀποθανόντα</note>.

<margin>Manuscript in the Collection of Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, page 14.</margin>
<margin>Page 400, Stephanus edition.</margin>
However, the idea that *Orpheus*—despite all his *polytheism* or *multiplicity of gods*—acknowledged *one supreme, uncreated Deity* as the *origin of all things*, can first be presumed from this: the two most religious philosophical sects, the *Pythagoreans* and *Platonists*, not only held *Orpheus* in great esteem (commonly calling him *the theologian* <note>original: ὁ θεολόγος</note>), but were also thought to have largely owed their theology and philosophy to him, deriving them from his *principles* and *traditions*. This has already been suggested and could be proved further. *Pythagoras*, as we are informed by *Porphyry* and *Iamblichus*, learned from all four of these sources: from the *Egyptians*, from the *Persian Magi*, from the *Chaldeans*, and from *Orpheus* or his followers. Accordingly, *Syrianus* <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note> considers *the Orphic and Pythagorean principles to be one and the same* <note>original: ὀρφικαὶ καὶ πυθαγορικαὶ ἀρχαί</note>. And as we learn from *Suidas* <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>, this same *Syrianus* wrote a book titled *The Harmony of Orpheus, Pythagoras, and Plato* <note>original: συμφωνία Ὀρφέως, πυθαγόρου καὶ πλάτωνος</note>. *Proclus*, in addition to the passage cited earlier, frequently emphasizes this elsewhere, such as in his commentary on [Plato's] *Timaeus* (page 289): "*It is Pythagorean to follow the Orphic genealogies. For the knowledge of the gods came down to the Greeks from the Orphic tradition through Pythagoras*" <note>original: πυθαγόρειον ἦν καὶ τὸ ταῖς ὀρφικαῖς ἕπεσθαι γενεαλογίαις. Ἄνωθεν γὰρ ἀπὸ τῆς ὀρφικῆς παραδόσεως διὰ πυθαγόρου καὶ εἰς Ἕλληνας ἡ περὶ θεῶν ἐπιστήμη προῆλθεν</note>. The fact that *Orphic philosophy* truly agreed and shared symbols with what was later called *Pythagorean* and *Platonic* philosophy can be seen in *Plato's* *Cratylus*, where he discusses the origin of the Greek word *soma* <note>meaning "body"</note>: "*Orpheus and his followers seem to me to have provided the best explanation for the origin of this word*" (from the word *sozesthai*, meaning "to be preserved"). "*They believe the soul is here in a state of punishment, and its body is a prison where it is kept in custody until its debts or faults are paid; it is therefore called soma*" <note>original: δοκεῖ μέντοι μοι μάλιστα θέσθαι οἱ ἀμφὶ Ὀρφέα τοῦτο τὸ ὄνομα, ὡς δίκην διδούσης τῆς ψυχῆς, τοῦτον δὲ περίβολον ἔχειν ἵνα σώζηται, δεσμωτηρίου εἰκόνα· εἶναι οὖν τῆς ψυχῆς τοῦτο αὐτὸ ἕως ἂν ἐκτίσῃ τὰ ὀφειλόμενα τὸ σῶμα</note>. Since these three philosophies share so many symbols and ideas, it is probable that just as the *Platonic* and *Pythagorean* systems did, the *Orphic* system also derived all its gods from *one self-existent Deity*.

This can be further demonstrated by the *summary* of *Orphic doctrine* written long ago by *Timotheus the Chronographer* in his *Cosmopoeia* <note>A work on the creation of the world</note>. This summary still exists in the works of *Cedrenus* <note>An 11th-century Byzantine historian</note> and in *Eusebius's Chronicle* <note>A 4th-century universal history</note>, though it is recorded imperfectly

...presented by *Suidas* <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist</note> (under the entry *Orpheus*) as his own, or without mentioning the author's name: 

"First of all, the Ether <note>The upper atmosphere or celestial fire</note> was made by God, and after the Ether a Chaos; a dark and dreadful night then covering everything under the entire Ether." <note>original: ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἀνεδείχθη τῷ κόσμῳ ὁ αἰθὴρ, ὑπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ δημιουργηθείς...</note>. 

By this, Orpheus signifies (says *Timotheus* <note>An early Christian chronicler</note>) that Night existed before Day, or that the world had a beginning. He also declared in his same exposition:

"There was a certain incomprehensible Being, who was the highest and oldest of all things, and the maker of everything—even of the Ether itself and all things beneath it." <note>original: εἰρηκὼς ἐν τῇ αὐτῇ ἐκθέσει, ἀκατάληπτόν τινα καὶ πάντων ὑπέρτατον εἶναι...</note>. 

However, because the Earth was then invisible due to the darkness, a light broke out through the Ether and illuminated the whole creation. This Light is said by him to be that highest of all Beings (mentioned before) who is also called *Counsel* and *Life*. 

"These three names" (to use the words of *Suidas* here) "declare one and the same power and authority of that God who is the maker of all, and who produces everything out of nothing into being, whether visible or invisible." <note>original: ταῦτα τὰ τρία ὀνόματα... μίαν δύναμιν ἀπεφήνατο...</note>. 

To conclude with *Timotheus*: the same Orpheus declared in his book that all things were made by one Godhead under three names, and that He is all things. <note>original: ὁ δ’ αὐτὸς Ὀρφεὺς... ὅτι διὰ τῶν αὐτῶν τριῶν ὀνομάτων μιᾶς Θεότητος, τὰ πάντα ἐγένετο, καὶ Αὐτός ἐστι τὰ πάντα</note>.

But that *Orpheus* asserted one Supreme Deity as the origin of all things is unquestionably evident from the *Orphic Verses* themselves. Nevertheless, before we cite any as proof, we shall offer this observation, or rather suspicion, of our own: it seems that some *Orphic Verses* are forgeries <term>original: supposititious</term>, just as there were forged *Sibylline* oracles, having been counterfeited either by Christians or Jews. For we must freely admit that we cannot believe everything produced by the ancient Church Fathers as "Orphic" to be genuine—that is, to have been written by Orpheus himself, by *Onomacritus* <note>A 6th-century BCE poet often accused of editing or forging Orphic poems</note>, or any other pagan of that era according to the *Orphic Cabala* <term>the secret traditional teachings of Orpheus</term> or tradition.

As for example, this verse concerning *Moses*:

-> As the ancient saying goes, so the one born-of-water decreed, <-
-> having received from God the law written in two tablets. <-
<note>original Greek: ὡς λόγος ἀρχαίων, ὡς ὑδρογενὴς διέταξεν, Ἐκ θεόθεν γνώμαισι λαβὼν κατὰ δίπλακα θεσμόν</note>
<note>original Latin: Ut habet sermo antiquorum, ut Ex-aqua-ortus descripsit, Acceptâ divinitùs Lege quæ Duplicia Præcepta continet</note>

And this which is commonly understood to be about *Abraham*:

-> For no mortal could see the ruler of men, <-
-> unless it were a certain only-begotten descendant from the <-
-> Chaldean tribe, for he was skilled in the path of the star. <-
<note>original: οὐ γάρ κέν τις ἴδοι θνητῶν, μερόπων κραίνοντα, Εἰ μὴ μουνογενής τις ἀπόῤῥωξ φύλου ἄνωθεν Χαλδαίων, ἴδρις γὰρ ἔην ἄστροιο πορείης</note>

# Chapter 4: The Professed Monarchist

> "For no mortal could see him who rules over men, unless it were a certain only-begotten one proceeding from the ancient race of the Chaldeans; for he knew the path of the star." <note>original Latin: Non enim quispiam mortalium videre posset... Chaldæorum; Sciebat enim astri cursum. This refers to a passage often interpreted by early scholars as a pagan prophecy of Abraham or Moses.</note>

The manifest forgery of such passages might make one suspect other parts as well, such as this one concerning the *Divine Word* <note>original: Logos</note>:

-> "Looking toward the Divine Word, attend to it, directing the intellectual vessel of your heart." <-
<note>original Greek: Εἰς δὲ λόγον θεῖον βλέψας, τούτῳ προσεδρεύε, Ἰθύνων κραδίης νοερὸν κύτος.</note>

Therefore, as it is not honest to rely on something for proof which we ourselves do not believe to be sincere and genuine, we shall cite no *Orphic Verses* here to prove the acknowledgment of *One Supreme Deity* except for those found attested in Pagan writings. The first of these is the copy produced by Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on Orphic theology</note> in his commentary on the *Timaeus* <note>A famous dialogue by Plato</note>:

<margin>Page 95.</margin>

-> "Therefore, along with the universe, all things were created again within Zeus: the bright height of the wide ether and the heaven, the breadth of the unharvested sea and the glorious earth, the great Ocean and the lowest depths of the earth, the rivers and the boundless sea, and all other things; all the immortal blessed gods and goddesses. Whatever has been born, or whatever was to be born later, all grew together; for they were contained in the womb of Zeus." <-
<note>original Greek: τοὔνεκα σὺν τῷ παντὶ Διὸς πάλιν ἐντὸς ἐτύχθη... Ζηνὸς δ’ ἐνὶ γαστέρι σύρρα πεφύκει.</note>

> *To this sense: Therefore, together with the universe, all things were made within Jupiter <note>The author uses the Latin "Jupiter" for the Greek "Zeus"</note>, the height of the ethereal heaven, the breadth of the earth and sea, the great ocean, the profound Tartarus <note>The deep abyss of the underworld</note>, the rivers and fountains, and all other things; all the immortal gods and goddesses. Whatever has been, or shall be, was at once contained in the womb of Jupiter.*

Proclus understands this to mean that the *Ideas* <note>In Platonic philosophy, these are the eternal patterns or blueprints of all things</note> of all things were in God before the world was produced—that is, in terms of the order of nature only, as he supposes them to be coeval <note>Existing at the same time</note> in time. However, it is plain that all things are said to be contained in the *womb and fertility of one self-originated Deity*; not only all the other gods and goddesses, but every other thing whatsoever.

Again, in the same place, Proclus introduces another copy of *Orphic Verses* (which are also found in the writer of *De Mundo* <note>A treatise "On the Universe" formerly attributed to Aristotle</note>) in this manner: "The Demiurge <note>The creator or maker of the world</note>, being full of Ideas, did by these comprehend all things within himself, as that theologian also declares in these following verses:"

-> "Zeus was first, Zeus is last, the wielder of thunder; <-
-> Zeus is the head, Zeus the middle; from Zeus all things are made; <-
-> Zeus became a male, Zeus was an immortal nymph; <-
-> Zeus is the foundation of the earth and the starry heaven." <-
<note>original Greek: Ζεὺς πρῶτος γένετο, Ζεὺς ὕστατος ἀρχικέραυνος... Ζεὺς πυθμὴν γαίης τε καὶ οὐρανοῦ ἀστερόεντος.</note>

<summary>The author identifies certain Orphic verses as potential forgeries while highlighting others cited by pagan philosophers like Proclus to show that Orpheus viewed all of creation and all lesser gods as being contained within one supreme deity, Zeus.</summary>

### Proved clearly that the Orpheists. Book I.

> "Zeus is the breath of all; Zeus is the surge of tireless fire;
> Zeus is the root of the sea; Zeus is the sun and moon;
> Zeus is the King; Zeus himself is the original father of all;
> There is one power, one god, who became the great ruler over all."
> <note>original Greek: ζεὺς πνοίη πάντων· ζεὺς ἀκαμάτου πυρὸς ὁρμή· ζεὺς πόντου ῥίζα· ζεὺς ἥλιος ἠδὲ σελήνη· ζεὺς βασιλεύς· ζεὺς αὐτὸς ἁπάντων ἀρχιγένεθλος· Ἓν κράτος, εἷς δαίμων γένετο, μέγας ἀρχὸς ἁπάντων.</note>

This, written in plain prose, means: *The high-thundering Jove <note>Another name for Jupiter or Zeus</note> is both the First and the Last; Jove is both the Head and Middle of all things; All things were made out of Jupiter; Jove is both a **Man** and an **Immortal Maid**; Jove is the depth of the Earth and the Starry Heaven; Jove is the Breath of all things; Jove is the force of the untamable Fire; Jove is the bottom of the Sea; Jove is the Sun, Moon, and Stars; Jove is both the Origin and King of all things: There is one Power, and one God, and one great Ruler over all.*

Although there are many strange expressions here, the strangest of all seems to be that Jove should be called both a **Man** and an **Immortal Maid**. However, this is simply a poetic description of being "male and female together" <note>original Greek: ἀῤῥενόθηλυς (arrhenothelus)</note>. It was very common for the *mystical theologians* among the *Pagans* to call **God** "male and female together." By this, they emphatically meant the **Divine Fecundity** <note>The power to produce offspring or create life</note>, or the generative and creative power of the Deity; it signified that **God** was able, from himself alone, to produce all things. 

Damascius the philosopher <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist, known as the last head of the School of Athens</note>, writing about this very Orphic theology, explains it this way: "The Orphic theology describes the First Principle as hermaphroditic, or male and female together, thereby denoting that Essence which is generative or productive of all things." <note>original Greek: ἀῤῥενόθηλυν αὐτὸν ὑπεστήσατο, πρὸς ἔνδειξιν τῆς πάντων γεννητικῆς οὐσίας.</note> Even that learned and pious Christian Bishop, Synesius, apparently thought the expression was so harmless that he did not hesitate to use it himself in his elegant and devout hymns to Almighty God:

-> "You are the Father, and You are the Mother;" <-
-> "You are the Male, and You are the Female." <-

-> "You are the Father, You are the Mother," <-
-> "You are the Male, You are the Female." <-
<note>original Greek: Σὺ πατὴρ, Σὺ δ' ἐσσὶ μάτηρ, / Σὺ δ' ἄῤῥην, Σὺ δὲ θῆλυς. original Latin: Tu Pater, Tu es Mater, / Tu Mas, Tu Fæmina.</note>

Besides these, there are also certain other *Orphic verses* scattered throughout the works of Proclus <note>A 5th-century philosopher</note> and cited together in Eusebius <note>A 4th-century Christian historian</note> from Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century philosopher</note>. In these, the whole **World** is represented as **One Great Animal**, with God being the **Soul** of it.

> "There is one royal body in which all these things revolve:
> Fire and water, earth and ether, night and day;
> And Wisdom <note>original Greek: Metis</note>, the first creator, and delightful Love;
> For all these things lie within the great body of Zeus.
> If you wish to see his head and beautiful face,
> It is the radiant heaven, where his golden hair
> Of glittering stars hangs beautifully in the air, etc."
> <note>original Greek: Ἓν δὲ δέμας βασίλειον ἐν ᾧ τάδε πάντα κυκλεῖται, / Πῦρ καὶ ὕδωρ, καὶ γαῖα, καὶ αἰθήρ, νύξ τε καὶ ἦμαρ· / Καὶ Μῆτις, πρῶτος γενέτωρ, καὶ Ἔρως πολυτερπής· / Πάντα γὰρ ἐν μεγάλῳ Ζηνὸς τάδε σώματι κεῖται· / Τοῦ δήτοι κεφαλὴν μὲν ἰδεῖν, καὶ καλὰ πρόσωπα, / Οὐρανὸς αἰγλήεις ὃν χρύσεαι ἀμφὶς ἔθειραι / Ἄστρων μαρμαρέων περικαλλέες ἠερέθονται, &c.</note>

# CHAPTER IV: Asserted Monarchy

> *All these things are enclosed within the Royal body:*
> *Fire and Water, Earth, and Ether, with Night and Day:*
> (*Counsel, the First Begetter, with the Power of Love:*)
> *Jupiter holds all things together within his immense Body:*
> *Look at this exceptional Head and beautiful Faces,*
> *The Heaven shining on all sides, around which his hanging*
> *Golden Hair pours out the light of the Stars:*
> *His eyes are Phoebus <note>The Sun</note>, and opposite Phoebus, returning,*
> *Is Cynthia <note>The Moon</note>, etc.*
> <note>original Latin: Omnia Regali sunt hæc in corpore clausa, / Ignis & Unda, & Terra, Æther cum Nocte Dieque : / (Consilium, Primus Genitor, cum Numine Amoris :) / Juppiter immenso sub Corpore cuncta coercet : / En hujus Caput Eximium, Vultúsque decoros / Undique resplendens Cælum, cui pendula circum / Aurea Cæsaries Astrorum lumina fundit : / Sunt oculi Phœbus, Phœboque adversa recurrens / Cynthia, &c.</note>

Where probably that one verse,

->And Counsel, the first begetter, and delightful Love <note>original Greek: Καὶ μῆτις, πρῶτος γενέτωρ, καὶ Ἔρως πολυτερπής</note><-

though truly *Orphic*, and indeed *Divine* (signifying that *Mind* and *Love* were the *First Begetters* and *Original* of all things), was nonetheless inserted improperly from some other place. But from all these citations, it plainly appears that according to the *Orphic Theology*, though there were many *Gods* and *Goddesses* admitted, yet there was *One Original* and *King* of them all, *One Supreme Deity* acknowledged. 

We are not ignorant that some of the ancient and learned Fathers, finding it contradictory for *Orpheus* to assert both *Many Gods* and *One God* at the same time, thought this was a convenient explanation <term>original: "salvo"</term> for the difficulty: to suppose that *Orpheus* had, at different times, held different moods and beliefs. They thought he was first a *committed polytheist*, asserting *Three Hundred Gods* or more, and then later a *converted monotheist*. They were led into this opinion because of certain counterfeit *Orphic verses* in the writings of Aristobulus (probably made by some unlearned Jew), wherein *Orpheus* is made to sing a *Palinodia* <term>A poem or song retracting a previous statement; a recantation</term> for his former error and *polytheism*. 

But we must ask leave, with all due respect, to disagree with the reverend authors of antiquity on this point. It appears plainly from that first <margin>See *Justin Martyr* and *Clement of Alexandria, Protrepticus*</margin> *Orphic* exception in Proclus, that *Orpheus* acknowledged both *One Unmade Deity* (the *Original* of all things) and *Many Generated Gods and Goddesses* (which were all contained within it) at the same time.

Having now made it sufficiently evident from such *Orphic fragments*—which have been acknowledged and cited by Pagan writers from *Orpheus's* *Hymns* and *Rhapsodies*—that the opinion of *Monarchy* (or *One Self-existent Deity* as the *Original* of all things) was an essential part of the *Orphic Theology* or *Cabala* <term>A mystical or secret tradition</term>; we shall further observe that, besides this *opinion of Monarchy* (but consistent with it), a *Trinity* of *Divine Hypostases* <term>Distinct persons or substances within the Godhead</term> that are *subordinate* to the first, was another part of this *Orphic Cabala*. 

Proclus, in his commentary on *Plato’s Timaeus*, makes an inquiry <margin>Page 93.</margin> into *Plato’s Demiurgus* <term>The "Craftsman" or creator of the physical world</term>. He gives us an account (amongst other Platonists) of the doctrine of *Amelius*. Amelius was a contemporary of *Plotinus* and is said to have noticed that what St. *John* the Evangelist had written concerning the *Logos* <note>The "Word" or Divine Reason</note> agreed with the *Platonic* and *Pythagorean hypothesis*. Proclus describes Amelius's view in this manner: 

*Amelius makes the Creator third, and says there are three Minds, three Kings: him who is, him who has, him who sees. These differ because the first Mind is truly...* 
<note>original Greek: ’Αμέλιος δὲ τρίτον ποιεῖ, τὸν Δημιουργὸν, καὶ Νοῦς τρεῖς, βασιλεῖς τρεῖς, τὸν ὄντα, τὸν ἔχοντα, τὸν ὁρῶντα· διαφέρουσι δὲ οὗτοι, ὅτι ὁ μὲν πρῶτος Νοῦς, ὄν-</note>

It also introduces the concept of an Orphic "Trinity" and mentions the philosopher Amelius's observation of similarities between Platonic thought and the Gospel of John.</summary>

A Trinity, part Book I.

[...how he is what he is; but the second has the intelligible within himself, but also has that which is before him, and certainly participates in that, and because of this is second; but the third has that which is in himself, and is intelligible (for every mind is the same as its kindred intelligible), but also has that which is in the second, and beholds the first; for the greater the distance, the more obscure is that which possesses it.] <note>original Greek: πως ἐστὶν ὃ ἔστιν· ὁ δὲ δεύτερος, ἔχει μὲν τὸ ἐν αὐτῷ νοητόν, ἔχει δὲ καὶ τὸ πρὸ αὐτοῦ, καὶ μετέχει πάντως ἐκείνου, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο δεύτερος· ὁ δὲ τρίτος, ἔχει μὲν τὸ ἐν αὐτῷ, καὶ ἔστι νοητόν· (πᾶς γὰρ νοῦς τῷ συγγενεῖ νοητῷ ὁ αὐτός ἐστιν) ἔχει δὲ καὶ τὸ ἐν τῷ δευτέρῳ· καὶ ὁρᾷ τὸ πρῶτον· ὅσῳ γὰρ πλείω ἡ ἀπόστασις, τοσούτῳ τὸ ἔχον ἀμυδρότερον.</note> This passage being very remarkable, we thought fit to set it down at length, and shall here translate it. *Amelius makes a threefold Demiurge <note>original: "Demiurgus," the divine craftsman of the universe</note> or Maker <note>original: "Opifex"</note> of the world, Three Minds and Three Kings: Him that Is, Him that Has, and Him that Beholds. These Three Minds differ in this: the First is essentially that which he is (or all perfection); the Second is its own Intelligible <note>The object of thought or pure essence</note>, but Has the First (as something distinct from it) and indeed partakes of it, and therefore is Second. The Third is also its own Intelligible (for every Mind is the same thing as its corresponding Intelligible), but Has that which is in the Second, and Beholds the First. For however much every Being departs from the First, that much more obscure is it.* 

After this, Proclus immediately adds: [Therefore he (Amelius) supposes these three minds and demiurgic principles of his to be the same as Plato’s Three Kings, and Orpheus's trinity of Phanes, Uranus, and Cronus; but he supposes Phanes to be principally the Demiurge.] <note>original Greek: τούτους οὖν τοὺς τρεῖς νόας καὶ δημιουργοὺς ὑποτίθεται, καὶ τοὺς παρὰ τῷ Πλάτωνι τρεῖς βασιλέας, καὶ τοὺς παρ᾽ Ὀρφέῖ τρεῖς, Φάνητα, καὶ Οὐρανὸν, καὶ Κρόνον· καὶ ὁ μάλιστα παρ᾽ αὐτῷ δημιουργὸς ὁ Φάνης ἐστίν·</note> Amelius therefore supposed these three minds and demiurgic principles of his to be both the same as Plato’s Three Kings and Orpheus’s trinity of Phanes, Uranus, and Cronus <note>Phanes (Light/Manifestation), Uranus (Heaven), and Cronus (Time/Intellect)</note>; but Phanes is supposed by him to be principally the Demiurge. 

In this matter, Proclus (who had some peculiar fancies and whimsies of his own, and was indeed a confounder of Platonic theology, mingling much unintelligible stuff with it) asserts a Monad or Unity superior to this whole Trinity. Yet he seems, nonetheless, to rightly argue against Amelius that it was not the First Hypostasis <note>The first individual person or substance of the Trinity</note>—neither in the Platonic nor Orphic Trinity—that was chiefly and properly the Demiurge or Maker of the world, but the Second. 

In the same way, Proclus’s master Syrianus had previously determined that in Orphic theology, the title of Maker properly belonged to Orpheus’s "first-begotten God" <note>original Greek: πρωτόγονος θεός</note>, which was the same as Plato’s *Nous* or Divine Intellect. Agreeably to this, Proclus’s conclusion is: [Thus much may suffice to have declared who the demiurge is, namely, that it is the Divine Intellect, which is the proper and immediate cause of the whole creation; and let it be remembered from this how the same demiurgic Jupiter is praised by both Orpheus and Plato.] <note>original Greek: τίς μὲν οὖν ὁ δημιουργός ἐστι, καὶ ὅτι Νοῦς θεῖος τῷ ὅλης ποιήσεως αἴτιος, εἰρήθω διὰ τούτων· καὶ ὅπως ὑπό τε Ὀρφέως καὶ Πλάτωνος, ὁ αὐτὸς ἀνυμνεῖται δημιουργὸς Ζεὺς, ἀπὸ τούτων ὑπεμνήσθω·</note> *Thus much may suffice to have declared who is the Demiurge of the world: namely, that it is the Divine Intellect, which is the proper and immediate cause of the whole creation, and that it is one and the same demiurgic Jupiter who is praised both by Orpheus and Plato.* 

Now, besides this, it is observable that Damascius, in his book *Concerning Principles* <note>original Greek: περὶ ἀρχῶν</note> (not yet published), giving an account of Orphic theology, tells us among other things that Orpheus introduced a triform deity <note>original Greek: τρίμορφον θεὸν</note>. To all this may be added what was previously cited from Timotheus the Chronographer: that God had Three Names—Light, Counsel, and Life—and that all things were made by one Deity under these three several names. Where Cedrenus, the preserver of that excellent fragment of antiquity, concludes in this manner: [These things Timotheus the chronographer wrote, affirming that Orpheus said so long ago that a consubstantial trinity created all things.] <note>original Greek: ταῦτα Τιμόθεος συνεγράψατο ὁ χρονογράφος, λέγων τὸν Ὀρφέα πρὸ τοσούτων χρόνων εἰπόντα, τριάδα ὁμοούσιον δημιουργῆσαι τὰ πάντα</note> *These things Timotheus the Chronographer wrote, affirming Orpheus said so long*

### CHAPTER IV. Of the Orphic Kabbalah.

...declared long ago that *all things were made by a coessential or consubstantial Trinity*. Although this might otherwise be viewed with suspicion because Timotheus was a Christian (especially regarding the word *homoousion* <note>original: ὁμοούσιον; meaning "of the same substance," a key term in early Christian debates about the nature of the Trinity</note>), yet by comparing it with what we have already cited from Pagan writers, it appears that, so far as an Orphic Trinity is concerned, he did not write this entirely without reason or foundation.

But we have not yet finished with Orpheus and Orphic theology until we have reflected further to notice the strong flavor <note>original: *Haut-goust* (French); meaning a strong or pungent taste, used here to describe a pervasive or distinct quality</note> within it of making *God to be All*. For example, if we may repeat the previously cited passages and substitute the name of *God* for Zeus or *Jupiter*: *This universe, and all things belonging to it, were made within God.* <note>original: Διὸς πάλιν ἐντὸς ἐτύχθη</note> *All things were contained together in the womb of God:* <note>original: Ζηνὸς δ’ ἐνὶ γαστέρι σύῤῥα πεφύκει</note> *God is the head and God is the middle of all things:* <note>original: Ζεὺς κεφαλὴ Ζεὺς μέσσα</note> *God is the foundation of the earth and heaven; God is the depth of the sea; God is the breath of all (or the air that we breathe); God is the force of the untamable fire; God is the sun, moon, and stars.* <note>original: Ζεὺς πυθμὴν γαίης, etc.</note> *There is one royal (or divine) body; and*

->for all these things lie in the great body of God.<-
<note>original Greek: πάντα γὰρ ἐν μεγάλῳ Ζηνὸς τάδε σώματι κεῖται</note>

In this way, the Orphic theology was also represented previously by Timotheus the Chronographer: *All things were made by God, and he himself is all things.* <note>original: διὰ τῆς θεότητος πάντα ἐγένετο, καὶ αὐτός ἐστι πάντα</note>

To further prove that the ancient Greek Pagans were indeed of such a religious disposition as to *resolve all things into God* and to make *God All*, we shall here cite a remarkable testimony from Plutarch, out of his work *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*: <margin>Page 436.</margin> <note>original Greek: Δύο πάσης γενέσεως αἰτίας ἐχούσης, οἱ μὲν σφόδρα παλαιοὶ θεολόγοι καὶ ποιηταὶ, τῇ κρείττονι μόνον ἢ νῦν προσέχειν εἵλοντο, τοῦτο δὴ τὸ κοινὸν ἐπιφθεγγόμενοι πᾶσι πράγμασι, Ζεὺς ἀρχὴ, Ζεὺς μέσσα, Διὸς δ’ ἐκ πάντα πέλονται. ταῖς δ’ ἀναγκαίαις καὶ φυσικαῖς, οὐκ ἔτι προσῄεσαν αἰτίαις· οἱ δὲ νεώτεροι τούτων καὶ φυσικοὶ προσαγορευόμενοι, τοὐναντίον ἐκείνοις, τῆς καλῆς καὶ θείας ἀποπλανηθέντες ἀρχῆς, ἐν σώμασι καὶ πάθεσι σωμάτων, πληγαῖς τε καὶ μεταβολαῖς καὶ κράσεσι τίθενται τὸ σύμπαν·</note> *While there are two causes for all creation—the divine and the natural—the most ancient theologians and poets chose to attend only to the more excellent of these two (the divine cause), resolving all things into God and pronouncing this of them universally: "God is both the beginning and the middle, and all things come from God." Consequently, these thinkers had no regard at all for the other natural and necessary causes of things. But on the contrary, their successors, who were called "Physici" (or Naturalists), straying from this most excellent and divine principle, placed all causality in bodies—their properties, collisions, changes, and mixtures.* Where, by the most ancient theolo-
