# The Grand Secret <note>original: Arcanum; refers to a hidden mystery or specialized knowledge</note> of the Orphic Book. I.

When Plutarch mentioned theologians and poets, he clearly meant *Orpheus* and his followers, as it is an *Orphic verse* cited here by him, which also serves as an acknowledgment of their antiquity. However, by their "juniors," whom he calls *Physici* <note>original: Greek φυσικοί; meaning "naturalists" or "physicists" who studied the physical world</note>, he could have meant no others than those **first Ionic philosophers**: *Anaximander*, *Anaximenes*, *Hippo*, and the rest. These were the ones followed by those degenerate members of the Italian school who later developed atheistic atomic theories: *Leucippus*, *Democritus*, and *Epicurus*. Thus, we have here another confirmation of what we asserted earlier: that the Ionic philosophers after *Thales* and before *Anaxagoras* were generally *atheistical*. Indeed, because of them, the word "Naturalists" <note>original: φυσικοί</note> came to be used often as a synonym for "Atheists" <note>original: άθεοι</note>.

Now, these two groups are condemned by *Plutarch* as two contrary extremes. The first group resolved everything into *natural and necessary causes*—that is, into *matter*, *motion*, and the *qualities of bodies*—while omitting the *Divine Cause*, making them guilty of *atheism*. The other group, altogether neglecting the *natural and necessary causes* of things, resolved everything into the *Divine Cause*, effectively swallowing up everything into God, which made them guilty of a kind of *fanaticism*. Thus, we see plainly that this was one grand *secret of the Orphic Kabbalah* and ancient *Greek theology: that God is all things*.

Some fanatics of later times have made *God to be all* in a crude sense, so as to remove all *real distinction* between God and the creature. Indeed, they allow no other being besides God, as they suppose the substance of everything—even of all inanimate bodies—to be the very substance of God himself. They view all the variety of things in the world as nothing but God under several forms, appearances, and disguises. The Stoics anciently made God to be all, and all to be God, in a somewhat different way; they conceived God properly to be the *active principle* of the entire physical universe. However, because they did not admit the existence of any non-physical substance, they supposed that this active principle, together with the *passive* principle or *matter*, made up only one and the same complete *substance*. Others, who acknowledged God to be a *non-physical substance* <note>original: incorporeal</note> distinct from matter, nevertheless made *all to be God* in a certain sense; they supposed God to be nothing but a *soul of the world*, which, together with matter, formed *one entire divine living being* <note>original: animal; used here in the classical sense of "a being with a soul"</note>.

Now, the Orphic theologians cannot be charged with *making God all* in that first and *grossly fanatical sense*, as if they removed all real distinction between God and the creature. While they asserted God to be all, they nonetheless allowed other things to have distinct beings of their own. This much is apparent from that riddle proposed by the Maker of the World to "Night" in the Orphic verses:

<margin>Proclus's Commentary on Plato's *Timaeus*</margin>
->How can all things be one to me, and yet each be distinct?<-
<note>original: πῶς δέμοι ἕν τι τὰ παντ' ἔσται, καὶ χῶρις ἕκαστον;</note>

Where "all things one," or "one all things" <note>original: Ἕν τι τὰ πάντα</note>, seems to be the Supreme Deity, or *Divine Intellect*. *Proclus* also interprets it this way: "Zeus, containing the whole and all things in a unified and intellectual manner, according to..." <note>original: τὰ ὅλα περιέχων ὁ Ζεὺς καὶ πάντα μοναδικῶς καὶ νοερῶς, κατὰ</note>

<meta>catchword: ...the [original: τότες]</meta>

<summary>This page discusses the Orphic concept of "God as All," distinguishing it from the atheistic materialism of early Greek naturalists and the later "fanatical" pantheism that erases the distinction between Creator and creature. It argues that Orphic theology maintains a balance where God contains all things while allowing individual beings to remain distinct.</summary>

### CHAPTER IV. Theology: That God is All.

"After these oracles, he [Jupiter] establishes Night, and all the mundane gods, and the portions of the universe." <note>original: τούτους χρησμοὺς, μετὰ τῆς νυκτὸς ὑφίστησι, καὶ πάντα τὰ ἐγκόσμια θεῶν, καὶ τὰς μοίρας τοῦ παντός</note> Jupiter, who contains the universe and all things within himself unitively <note>meaning as a single unity</note> and intellectually, according to these Orphic oracles, also gives a particular existence of their own to all the worldly gods and other parts of the universe. And this is "each thing separately" <note>original: χωρὶς ἕκαστον</note> in that previously cited Orphic verse: *every thing apart by itself*, the whole produced or created universe, with all its variety of things in it. Yet, these are Orphically said to be God also, in a certain other sense that shall be explained later. 

Nor can the Orphic theologians be charged with making God "all" in the second Stoic sense—as if they denied all incorporeal substance—for they plainly assert, as Damascius and others particularly note, an incorporeal God <note>original: θεὸν ἀσώματον</note>. But as for the third way, it is very true that the Orphic theologians frequently called the world "the Body of God" and its various parts "his members," making the whole universe one divine animal. Notwithstanding this, they did not suppose this animated world to be the first and highest God, but either a *second god* <note>original: δεύτερον θεὸν</note>, as the Hermetic <note>original: Hermaick</note> or Trismegistic writers call it, or else—as Numenius and other Platonists say—a *third god* <note>original: τρίτον θεὸν</note>. Its soul was the third hypostasis <note>original: hypostasis; a person or distinct substance within a divine being</note> in the Orphic trinity, just as it was in the Pythagorean and Platonic trinities. They supposed two other divine hypostases superior to it, which were perfectly separate from matter. Therefore, regarding the Supreme Deity, these Orphic theologians considered him to be all things for the two following reasons. 

First, because all things come from God, they inferred that they were all contained within him and were, in a sense, himself. This much is declared in those Orphic verses cited by Proclus and others:

-> Hiding all these things, he brought them again into the joyful light; <-
-> from his heart he was about to bring them forth, performing many-wrought deeds. <note>original: Πάντα τάδε κρύψας, αὖθις φάος ἐς πολυγηθές · μέλλεν ἀπὸ κραδίης προφέρειν, πολυδαίδαλα ῥέζων.</note> <-

Which Apuleius translates as follows:

> -> *For hiding all things in his bosom, he brought them forth* <-
> -> *into the sweet borders of light, revolving cares within his sacred breast.* <note>original: Namque Sinu Occultans, dulces in luminis oras / Cuncta tulit, sacro versans sub pectore curas.</note> <-

The meaning of this is clearly that God, at first hiding or hiddenly containing all things within himself, then displayed them and brought them forth into light—as distinct beings of their own—and so created the world. 

The second reason is that the world, though produced by God and really existing outside him, is not therefore entirely cut off from him. It does not exist on its own as a "dead thing," but is still livingly united to him, essentially dependent on him, and always supported, upheld, quickened, enlivened, acted upon, and pervaded by him. This follows the Orphic passage: *God passes through and intimately pervades all things.* <note>original: Ἐν δ' αὐτοῖς αὐτὸς περινώσεται</note>

Now, it is very true that some Christian theologians have also claimed that God is all, according to these latter meanings—as when they affirm the...

# God's Being All, a Ground of Polytheism BOOK 1.

...the whole world to be nothing else but God expanded or *unfolded* <note>original: *Deum Explicatum*</note>, and when they call the creatures—as Saint Jerome and others often do—the *rays of the Deity* <note>original: *Radios Deitatis*</note>. Indeed, the Scripture itself may seem to give some support to this idea as well, when it tells us, *that of Him, and through Him, and to Him, are all things*, which in the Orphic theology was expressed this way: God is the *beginning*, and *middle*, and *end* of *all things*; <margin>Colossians 1:16</margin> That *all things were created in him* <note>original: ἐν αὐτῷ ἐκτίσθη τὰ πάντα</note>, as in the Orphic verses—*were made within Zeus* <note>original: Διὸς ἐντὸς ἐτύχθη</note>; <margin>Colossians 1:17</margin> That *all things consist in him* <note>original: τὰ πάντα ἐν αὐτῷ συνέστηκε</note>: <margin>1 Timothy 6:13</margin> That, *in him we live and move, and have our being*; That God does <margin>1 Corinthians 15:28</margin> *give life to all things* <note>original: ζωοποιεῖν πάντα</note>, and that he ought to be made, *all in all* <note>original: πάντα ἐν πᾶσιν</note>; which supposes him in some sense to be so. 

Notwithstanding this, this is a very delicate <note>original: "ticklish"</note> point, and easily liable to mistake and abuse. As we understand it, the mistake and abuse of this one concept was the chief ground and origin of both the seeming and *real polytheism*, not only of the Greek and European pagans, but also of the Egyptian and others, as will be more particularly declared later. They concluded that because *God* was *all things*, and consequently *all things were God*, that therefore *God* ought to be worshipped in *all things*—that is, in all the several *parts of the world* and *things of nature*, but especially in those animated intellectual beings which are superior to men. 

Consistent with this, they did both *deify all things* <note>original: θεολογεῖν ἅπαντα</note>, looking upon everything as having *something supernatural* <note>original: ὑπερφυές τι</note> or a kind of divinity in it, and also bestowed several names upon *God* according to all the different *parts of the world* and *elements of nature*. They called him *Jupiter* in the starry heaven and upper air <note>original: ether</note>; *Juno* in the air; *Aeolus* in the winds; *Neptune* in the sea; *Pluto* in the earth and subterranean parts; *Minerva* and the *Muses* in learning, knowledge, and invention; *Mars* in war; *Venus* in pleasure; *Ceres* in grain <note>original: corn</note>; *Bacchus* in wine, and the like.

However, it is unquestionably evident from this that *Orpheus* and his followers—that is, the majority of the Greek pagans—acknowledged one *universal* and *all-comprehending Deity*, one who was *all*; and consequently, they could not have admitted to many self-existent and independent deities.

**XVIII.** Having treated extensively the two most eminent polytheists among the ancient pagans, *Zoroaster* and *Orpheus*, and clearly proved that they asserted one supreme *Deity*, we shall next observe that the Egyptians themselves also—notwithstanding their multifaceted *polytheism* and *idolatry*—had an acknowledgment among them of one supreme and *universal divinity* <note>original: Numen</note>.

There has been some controversy among learned men as to whether *polytheism* and *idolatry* first arose from the *Egyptians* or the *Chaldeans*, because pagan writers for the most part give precedence here to the *Egyptians*. <margin>The Syrian Goddess, p. 1059 <note>original: Dea Syria</note></margin> *Lucian* himself, who was by birth a Syrian and a diligent inquirer into the antiquities of his own country,

<page-num>309</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER IV. The Polytheism of the Egyptians.</header>

...country, claiming that the Syrians and Assyrians first received their *religion* and *gods* from the Egyptians. Even before *Lucian*, *Herodotus*—the "Father of History"—similarly reported that the Egyptians were the first to erect temples and statues to the gods. Whether the Egyptians or the Chaldeans <note>Ancient people of Mesopotamia, often associated with early astronomy and magic.</note> were the very first *polytheists* and *idolaters*, there is no question that the Greeks and Europeans generally derived their *polytheism* and *idolatry* from the Egyptians. *Herodotus* claims in one place that the Greeks received their *Twelve Gods* from there, and in another that *almost all the names of the gods came first out of Egypt into Greece* <note>original: σχέδον δὲ πάντα τὰ ὀνόματα τῶν θεῶν ἐξ Αἰγύπτου ἐλήλυθεν εἰς τὴν Ἑλλάδα</note>. In what sense this might be true of *Zeus* <note>original: Ζεὺς</note> itself—though the word is originally Greek—shall be explained later. However, it is probable that *Herodotus* had a deeper meaning: that the actual names of many Greek gods were originally Egyptian. 

In order to confirm this, we shall propose a conjecture concerning one of them: <term>Athena</term> <note>original: 'Aθηνᾶ</note>, otherwise called *Pallas* by the Greeks and *Minerva* by the Latins. First, the Greek etymologies <note>The study of the origin of words.</note> for this word all seem to be either trivial and superficial, or violent and forced. *Plato*, in his *Cratylus*, observed that according to the ancient allegorical interpreters of *Homer*, *Athena* was nothing other than *mind* <note>original: νοῦς</note> or *understanding* <note>original: διάνοια</note> personified and deified. He conceived that those who first gave her that name, intending to signify "Divine Wisdom," called it *Athena* as if it meant *the understanding of God, or the knowledge of divine things* <note>original: θεοῦ νόησιν</note>. He suggested the word was originally *Theonoe* <note>original: θεονόη</note> and was later transformed into *Athena*. 

But not being fully satisfied himself with this origin, he later attempted another, deriving the word from *knowledge concerning manners or practical knowledge* <note>original: νόησις ἐν τῷ ἤθει</note>; as if it had been at first *Ethonoe* <note>original: Ἠθονόη</note> and was then changed into *Athena*. Other Greeks have deduced this word *from the act of observing* <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀθρεῖν</note>, because it is the nature of wisdom to collect all things into one, supposing it was originally *Athrena*. Others would derive it from the word for *female* <note>original: θῆλυς</note> and the prefix "A-" (meaning "not"), because *Minerva* or *Wisdom*, though she is a goddess, has nothing of "feminine imperfection" in her. Others again would explain its origin *from the fact that virtue or wisdom is of such a noble and generous temper that it scorns to subject itself to any base and unworthy servitude* <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ μὴ πεφυκέναι θήνεσθαι καὶ ὑποτάσσεσθαι τὴν ἀρετὴν</note>. Lastly, others would derive it *from being ether-minded* <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ αἰθερονόου</note>, claiming it was originally *Aitheronnoa*. 

From all this uncertainty among the Greeks concerning the origin of the word *Athena*, and from the superficial or forced nature of these guesses, we may instead conclude that the name was not originally Greek but foreign <note>original: "Exotical"</note>, and probably—as *Herodotus* suggested—Egyptian. Therefore, let us see if we can find any Egyptian word from which *Athena* might be derived. *Plato*, in his *Timaeus*, mentions *Sais*, a city in *Egypt* where *Solon* once stayed. He tells us *that the presiding or tutelar god of that city was called Neith in the Egyptian language, but in Greek—as those same Egyptians claim—she is Athena* <note>original: ὅτι τῆς πόλεως θεὸς ἀρχηγός ἐστιν, Αἰγυπτισὶ μὲν τοὔνομα Νηΐθ, Ἑλληνισὶ δὲ, ὡς ὁ ἐκείνων λόγος, 'Aθηνᾶ</note>. Now, why might not this very Egyptian word *Neith*, by an easy inversion...

...might have been at first turned into *Thien* or *Thēn* <note>original: Θὴν</note> (people commonly pronouncing foreign <note>original: Exotick</note> words awkwardly) and then, by adding "a"s at the beginning and end, transformed into *Athena*? This seems much more probable than either *Plato’s theonoē* <note>original: θεονόη—meaning "divine mind"</note> or *ēgonoē* <note>original: Ἡγονόη—meaning "leader of mind"</note>, or any of those other Greek etymologies <note>The study of the origins of words.</note> mentioned before. And just as the *Greeks* derived the names of many of their *gods* from the *Egyptians*, the *Latins* seem to have done the same, as seen in the instance of the word *Neptune*. While *Varro* <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a Roman scholar.</note> would derive it "from covering" <note>original: à nubendo</note>—as if it were *Nuptunus*, because the sea covers and hides the land—and *Scaliger* <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a prominent Renaissance scholar.</note> with others derives it "from washing" <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ νίπτειν</note>, since this is the primary use of water; yet, as the learned *Bochart* <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar.</note> has observed, it may be derived with greater probability from the *Egyptian* word *Nephthus*. *Plutarch* tells us "that the Egyptians called the furthest parts of the land, or those that border upon the sea, Nephthus" <note>original: ὅτι Νέφθυν καλοῦσι τὸ γῆς τὰ ἔσχατα καὶ παρέβρια καὶ ψαύοντα τῆς θαλάσσης</note>. This conjecture may be further confirmed from what the same *Plutarch* writes elsewhere: that just as *Isis* was the wife of *Osiris*, the wife of *Typhon* was called *Nephthus*. From this, one might conclude that while *Isis* was sometimes seen as the *earth*, or the goddess presiding over it, *Nephthus* was the goddess of the *sea*. To this may be further added, from the same writer, that *Nephthus* was sometimes called *Aphrodite* or *Venus* by the *Egyptians*, probably because *Venus* is said to have risen out of the *sea*. 

But whatever may be thought of these etymological conjectures, it is certain that no nation in the world was ever considered by the Pagans to be more devout, religious, and superstitious than the *Egyptians*; consequently, none was more polytheistic and idolatrous. *Isocrates*, in his *Praise of Busiris*, gives them high praise <note>original: Encomium</note> for their sanctity; and *Herodotus* affirms that they were "exceedingly more religious and more devout worshippers of the Deity than all other mortals" <note>original: θεοσεβέες περισσῶς μάλιστα πάντων ἀνθρώπων</note>. Therefore, they were <margin>Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, book 9, chapter 10.</margin> highly celebrated by *Apollo’s* Oracle (recorded by *Porphyrius*) and preferred above all other nations for rightly teaching "that steep and difficult path that leads to God and happiness" <note>original: αἰπεινὴν ὁδὸν μακάρων—literally "the steep path of the blessed"</note>. In the *Scripture*, however, *Egypt* is famous for her idols and for her spiritual "prostitution and unfaithfulness" <note>original: "Whoredoms and Fornications"—Biblical metaphors for the practice of idolatry.</note>; to emphasize its impurity, she is sometimes linked with *Sodom*. For the *Egyptians*, in addition to all those other gods worshipped by the *Greeks* and other foreigners—besides the stars, demons, and heroes, and those "artificial gods" which they boasted they could create (namely, statues brought to life)—had a unique obsession <note>original: Intoxication</note> of their own. This made them infamous and ridiculous even among all the other *Pagans*: they worshipped brute animals as well, in one sense or another.

<margin>Juvenal, Satire 15.</margin>
> "Who does not know, Volusius of Bithynia, what kind of monsters demented 
> Egypt worships? One part adores the crocodile, 
> another fears the ibis bloated with snakes." <note>original: Quis nescit, Volusi Bithynice, qualia demens Ægyptus portenta colat? Crocodilon adorat Pars hæc, illa pavet saturam serpentibus Ibin.</note>

<page-num>311</page-num>
<header>Cʜᴀᴘᴛᴇʀ IV. Egypt as a School of Literature, before Greece.</header>

> ...temple-walls; but to one who comes to be a spectator of Egyptian worship, there first appear most splendid and stately temples, sumptuously adorned, along with solemn groves and many grand <note>original: pompous</note> rites and mystical ceremonies. But as soon as he enters, he perceives that it was either a cat or an ape, a crocodile, a goat, or a dog that was the object of this religious worship. <note>original Greek: σκελάτιδες· ἤδη γ’ εἰσιόντι, καὶ ἐνδοτέρω γενομένῳ, θεωρεῖται προσκυνόμενος αἴλουρος· ἢ πίθηκος, ἢ κροκόδειλος, ἢ τράγος, ἢ κύων·</note>

But notwithstanding this diverse polytheism and idolatry of these Egyptians, the fact that they did nevertheless acknowledge one supreme and universal divinity <note>original: Numen</note> may first be reasonably gathered from the great fame they held anciently throughout the whole world for their wisdom. The Egyptians are called by the Eleans in Herodotus "the wisest of men" <note>original: σοφώτατοι ἀνθρώπων</note>, and it is a commendation given to one in the same writer: *That he excelled the Egyptians in wisdom, who excelled all other mortals.* Thus it is recorded in the Scripture as a eulogy <note>original: Encomium</note> for Moses, that *he was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians*; and the excellence of Solomon's wisdom is likewise expressed by the writer of the Book of Kings in this way: *that it excelled the wisdom of all the children of the East country, and all the wisdom of Egypt.* 

By the "children of the East," the writer primarily means the Persian Magi and the Chaldeans; and there seems to be a **climax** intended here: that Solomon's wisdom did not only excel the wisdom of the Magi and of the Chaldeans, but also that of the Egyptians themselves. From this it appears that in Solomon’s time, Egypt was the chief school of literature and learning in the whole world, and that the Greeks were then little or not at all noticed, nor did they have any considerable reputation for learning. For this reason, we can by no means believe the account by Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BC – 50 AD), a Jewish philosopher.</note> in his *Life of Moses*, that besides the Egyptian priests, learned men were sent for from Greece by Pharaoh’s daughter to instruct Moses. 

On the contrary, it is manifest from the Greek records themselves that for many ages after Solomon’s time, the most famous of the Greeks traveled into Egypt to receive culture and education, such as Lycurgus, Solon, Thales, and many others, including Pythagoras and Plato. Concerning Pythagoras, Isocrates writes that upon coming into Egypt and being instructed there by the priests, he was the first to bring philosophy into Greece. Plato was also criticized <note>original: perstringed</note> by Xenophon because "he became enamored with Egypt and the extraordinary <note>original: τερατώδους—literally 'monstrous' or 'prodigious'</note> wisdom of Pythagoras" <note>original: Αἰγύπτιος ηὐράσθη καὶ τῆς Πυθαγόρου τερατώδους σοφίας</note>, not being contented with the simple philosophy of Socrates (which was little else besides morality). 

Now, just as it is improbable that the Egyptians, who were so famous for wisdom and learning, should be ignorant of one supreme deity, it is also a significant argument to the contrary that they were held in such great esteem by those two divine philosophers, Pythagoras and Plato. We grant, indeed, that after the Greeks began to flourish in all types of literature, the fame of the Egyptians was not only greatly eclipsed (so that we hear no more of Greeks traveling into Egypt for that purpose), but also that their enthusiasm for the liberal sciences did by degrees wither and decline; so that Strabo, in his time,

...could find little more in Egypt, besides the empty houses and palaces in which priests formerly famous for astronomy and philosophy had dwelt. Nevertheless, their *secret <note>original: Arcane</note> theology* remained more or less unextinguished <note>original: unextinct</note> among them to the last, as appears from what Origen, Porphyry, and Iamblichus have written concerning them.

The learning of the Egyptians was either *historical*, *philosophical*, or *theological*. First, the Egyptians were famous for their *historical learning* and knowledge of *antiquity*. It was confessed in Plato that they had records of time so much older than the Greeks that the Greeks were but children or infants compared with them. They claimed <note>original: pretended</note> to have a continued and uninterrupted series of history from the beginning of the world downward, and therefore seem to have had the clearest and strongest convictions <note>original: Perswasions</note> regarding the *cosmogony* <note>original: Cosmogonia; the theory of the origin of the universe</note>. Indeed, it cannot be denied that this tradition of the world's beginning was at first nearly universal among all nations. Concerning the Greeks and Persians, we have already shown <note>original: manifested</note> the same; and as Sanchuniathon <note>original: Sancuniathon</note> testifies the same concerning the *Phoenicians*, so <margin>Strabo, Geography, Book 15, p. 715.</margin> does Strabo likewise regarding the Indian *Brahmins* <note>original: Brachmans</note>, affirming that they agreed with the Greeks in many things, and particularly in this: *That the world was both created and perishable.* <note>original Greek: ὅτι γεννητὸς ὁ κόσμος καὶ φθαρτός; literally: "that the world was born and corruptible"</note> And though Diodorus affirms the contrary of the *Chaldeans*, <margin>Eusebius, Chronicon, p. 6.</margin> yet we ought in reason to agree rather with Berosus—in respect of his greater antiquity—who represents the sense of the ancient Chaldeans in this manner: *That there was a time when all was darkness and water, but Bel (whom they interpret as Jupiter), cutting the darkness in the middle, separated the earth and heaven from one another and so framed the world; this Bel also producing the stars, the sun, the moon, and the five planets.* <note>original Greek: γενέσθαι χρόνον ἐν ᾧ τὸ πᾶν σκότος καὶ ὕδωρ—τὸν δὲ Βῆλον, ὃν Δία μεθερμηνεύουσι, μέσον τεμόντα τὸ σκότος, χωρίσαι γῆν καὶ οὐρανὸν, ἀπ᾽ ἀλλήλων, καὶ διατάξαι τὸν κόσμον—ἀποτελέσαι δὲ τὸν Βῆλον καὶ ἄστρα καὶ ἥλιον καὶ σελήνην καὶ τοὺς πέντε πλανήτας.</note> From this testimony of Berosus, according to the version by Alexander Polyhistor, it also appears by the way that the ancient Chaldeans acknowledged one supreme deity, the maker of the whole world. They are also celebrated for this in that *Oracle of Apollo* cited from Porphyry by Eusebius:

<margin>Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, Book 9, Chapter 10.</margin>
> The Chaldeans alone obtained wisdom, and also the Hebrews,
> Worshipping in a holy manner a self-begotten King and God.

Where the Chaldeans are joined with the *Hebrews* as likewise worshipping, in a holy manner, *one self-existent deity*. Therefore, if Diodorus was not altogether mistaken, it must be concluded that in later times the Chaldeans (perhaps then receiving the doctrine of Aristotle <note>Aristotle's philosophy famously argued for the eternity of the world, contradicting the idea of a beginning or creation</note>) did desert and abandon the tradition of their ancestors concerning the *cosmogony*. But the Egyptians, however much they attributed more antiquity to the world than they should have, yet seem to have had a constant belief in its beginning, and the firmest of all other nations. They (as Kircher <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), a Jesuit scholar who published extensive, if sometimes imaginative, works on Egyptian hieroglyphs and history</note> tells us) therefore pictured *Horus*, or the *world*, as a *beardless young man*, not only to signify its constant youthful and flourishing vigor, but also the youthfulness and newness

### Chapter 4: Supporters of the Theory of the Universe's Origin

It should not be suspected that, even though the Egyptians held that the world had a beginning, they believed it was made by chance without a God—as Anaximander, Democritus, and Epicurus later did. On the contrary, this was such a well-acknowledged fact that Simplicius, a passionate advocate for the world's eternity, claims that the **Mosaic History** <note>The account of creation found in the biblical book of Genesis</note> of its creation by God was nothing other than **Egyptian fables**. This passage is so significant that I shall set it down here:

<margin>Simplicius on Aristotle’s *Physics*, Book 8, folio 268, column 1.</margin>

"If the lawgiving of the Jews is spoken of purely, saying: 'In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth; and the earth was invisible and unformed; and darkness was over the abyss, and the spirit of God moved over the water.' Then, when he had made the light, and separated the light and the darkness, he added, 'And God called the light Day, and the darkness Night; and there was evening and there was morning, one day.' If at this time he thinks there was a beginning of time, let him know that this tradition is mythical, and is drawn from Egyptian fables." <note>original Greek: Εἰ ἡ ἢ τῶν Ἰουδαίων νομοθετίω εἰλικρινῦται λέγοιτο... ἀπὸ μύθων Αἰγυπτίων εἵλκυσται.</note>

If **Grammaticus** <note>original: Grammaticus; referring to John Philoponus, a 6th-century Christian philosopher and "Grammarian" who argued for the world's creation</note> means the lawgiver of the **Jews** here, writing thus: [*In the beginning God made Heaven and Earth, and the Earth was invisible and unadorned, and Darkness was upon the Deep, and the Spirit of God moved upon the Water:*] and afterward when he had made Light, and separated the Light from the Darkness, adding [*And God called the Light Day, and the Darkness Night, and the Evening and the Morning were the First Day*]—I say, if the Grammarian thinks this to have been the first generation and beginning of time, I would have him know that all this is but a fabulous tradition, and wholly drawn from Egyptian fables.

As for the philosophy of the Egyptians: besides their **natural philosophy** <note>original: Physiology</note> and the pure and applied **mathematics** (**arithmetic**, **geometry**, and **astronomy**), they also had another higher kind of philosophy concerning incorporeal **substances**. This is evident from the fact that they were the first **supporters** of the **immortality** of **souls**, as well as their **preexistence** and **transmigration** <note>reincarnation</note>, from which their **immateriality** <note>original: Incorporeity</note> is necessarily inferred.

<margin>Herodotus, *Euterpe* (Book 2), 123.</margin>

Thus **Herodotus** says: "The Egyptians were the first to state this doctrine: that the human soul is immortal; and that when the body perishes, it always enters into another living creature being born, etc." <note>original Greek: πρῶτοι τόνδε τὸν λόγον Αἰγύπτιοί εἰσι εἰπόντες, ὡς ἀνθρώπου ψυχὴ ἀθάνατός ἐστι· τοῦ σώματος δὲ καταφθίνοντος, ἐς ἄλλο ζῶον αἰεὶ γινόμενον εἰσδύεται</note>. *The Egyptians were the first supporters of the soul's immortality and of its transmigration after the death and corruption of this body into the bodies of other animals successively—namely, until it has completed the whole circuit of terrestrial, marine, and flying animals, after which (they say) it is to return again into a human body. They suppose this revolution or* **Restoration** <term>original: Apocatastasis; a restoration or return to a former state</term> *of souls to take no less than three thousand years.* 

But whether **Herodotus** was correctly instructed in the Egyptian doctrine on this particular point may well be questioned. This is because the **Pythagoreans**, whom he subtly criticizes there for claiming to be the first inventors of this idea when they had borrowed it from the Egyptians, represented it differently. Namely, they taught that the descent of human souls into these earthly bodies was first a form of punishment, and that their sinking lower afterwards into the bodies of animals was only for some a further punishment for their deeper degeneracy; but the virtuous and pious souls should, after this life, enjoy a state of happiness in heavenly or spiritual bodies.

We come finally to the theology of the Egyptians. Now it is certain that the Egyptians, besides their popular and mythical theology (which is for the most part what *Diodorus Siculus* describes), had another *secret and recondite theology* <note>original Greek: ἀπόῤῥητος Θεολογία (aporrhētos theologia)</note> that was concealed from the common people and communicated only to kings, and such priests and others as were thought capable of it. These two theologies of theirs differed as *Aristotle*'s *Exoterics* <note>teachings for the general public</note> and *Acroamatics* <note>teachings for advanced students</note>. This much is plainly declared by *Origen*, whose very name was *Egyptian*, it being interpreted as *born of Horus* <note>original: "Horo-genitus"; Horus was an Egyptian god</note>. This was said when *Celsus* boasted that he thoroughly understood all that belonged to Christianity. *Celsus,* (he says) *seems to me here to act just as if a man traveling into Egypt—where the wise men of the Egyptians philosophize much about those things they consider divine according to their native learning, while the commoners* <term>idiots</term> <note>original: "Idiots"; meaning unlearned or lay people, not a slur in this context</note> *in the meantime hear only certain myths whose meaning they do not know, yet are very much pleased by them—should boast that he knew all that belonged to Egyptian theology, despite having only conversed with those commoners and not having been instructed by any of the priests in their secret and recondite mysteries.* Where the same *Origen* also adds that it was not a thing unique to the Egyptians to have such a secret and true theology distinct from their popular and mythical one; it was also common to the Persians, Syrians, and other non-Greek <term>Barbarian</term> pagans. *What we have now affirmed,* (he says) *concerning the difference between the wise men and the common people among the Egyptians, the same may also be said of the Persians, among whom the religious rites are performed rationally by those who are intelligent,*

# The Egyptians, besides their Vulgar, Book I.

...as well as Harpocrates and the "Sigalions" <note>original: "Sigalions"; these were statues representing silence, often identified with the Egyptian god Harpocrates</note> in their temples, which are described by the poet like this:

> "Those who suppress their voice and urge silence with a finger." <note>original Latin: *Quique premunt vocem, digitóque silentia suadent*</note>

<margin>Concerning Isis and Osiris</margin> These are statues of young men pressing their lips with their fingers. The meaning of Harpocrates is explained by **Plutarch** as follows: 

"The Harpocrates of the Egyptians is not to be taken for an imperfect or infant god, but for the guardian and regulator of human speech concerning the gods—speech which is still young, imperfect, and unformed. His finger on his mouth is a symbol of silence and discretion." <note>original Greek: τὸν δ' 'Αρποκράτην, οὐ θεὸν ἀτελῆ καὶ νήπιον, ἀλλὰ τοῦ περὶ θεῶν ἐν ἀνθρώποις λόγου νεαροῦ καὶ ἀτελοῦς καὶ ἀδιαρθρώτου προστάτην καὶ σωφρονιστήν, διὸ τῷ στόματι τὸν δάκτυλον ἔχει προσκείμενον, ἐχεμυθίας καὶ σιωπῆς σύμβολον</note>

It is true that some Christians have offered a different interpretation of this Egyptian Harpocrates. They suggested that the Egyptian gods were actually nothing more than mortal men, and that this was a secret to be hidden from the common people <note>original: "the Vulgar"</note>. While this idea is clever, it is not true. Without a doubt, the meaning of these Egyptian statues of Harpocrates was simply this: either the Supreme and incomprehensible Deity should be worshipped in silence (or at least not spoken of without great caution), or the secret mysteries of theology were not to be shared with everyone, but hidden from the uninitiated public. 

This same idea seems to have been signified by the annual festival the Egyptians held in honor of **Thoth** or **Hermes**. During this festival, the priests ate honey and figs while pronouncing the words, "Truth is sweet." <note>original Greek: γλυκὺ ἡ ἀλήθεια</note> It was also represented by the amulet that **Isis** was said to have worn, which was interpreted as "True speech." <note>original Greek: φώνη ἀληθής</note>

This **secret theology** <note>original Greek: ἀπόῤῥητος θεολογία</note>—the arcane and hidden teachings of the Egyptians—was kept from the common people in two ways: through fables or allegories, and through symbols or hieroglyphs. **Eusebius** informs us that **Porphyrius** wrote a book *Concerning the Allegorical Theology of both the Greeks and Egyptians*. <note>original Greek: περὶ τῆς ἀλληγορουμένης 'Ελλήνων καὶ Αἰγυπτίων θεολογίας</note> 

We should note here that the practice of using allegory in religious matters did not originate with Christians. It was also very common among pagan theologians. In fact, **Celsus** (as quoted by **Origen**) praised some Christians because they could create clever and handsome allegories. It is well known how both **Plutarch** and **Synesius** interpreted the Egyptian fables of **Isis** and **Osiris** allegorically—one applying them to philosophy, the other to politics. 

The Egyptian hieroglyphs—symbols that did not represent sounds or words, but directly represented objects and mental concepts—were primarily used for this purpose: to express religious and theological mysteries in a way that kept them hidden from the unlearned public. Because of this, the study of Egyptian hieroglyphs is often considered the same as their **secret theology** or **metaphysics**. And

# CHAPTER IV. The Egyptians had a Secret Theology. 317

<margin>Q. 25.</margin>
The author of the *Questions and Answers to the Orthodox* tells us that this secret knowledge was anciently held in much higher regard among the Egyptians than all their other learning. He notes that, for this reason, **Moses** was just as well-instructed in this hieroglyphic learning and metaphysical theology of theirs as he was in their mathematics. For our part, we do not doubt that the *Isiac Table* <note>original: *Mensa Isiaca*; a famous bronze tablet from antiquity depicting Egyptian deities and hieroglyphs</note> recently published—containing so many strange and unusual hieroglyphics—was a part of this "secret theology" <note>original Greek: ἀπόῤῥητος θεολογία</note> of the Egyptians, rather than mere history, as some imagine. This is true even though the author of the recent, overly-confident work *Oedipus* <note>original: *Oedipus Aegyptiacus* (1652) by Athanasius Kircher, who claimed to have fully cracked the code of hieroglyphs</note> seems to grant himself too much credit by pretending to have such a certain and exact interpretation of it. 

Now, it is reasonable to think that in all those pagan nations where there was a theology separate from the "vulgar" <note>the common religion of the masses</note> beliefs, the principal part of it was the **doctrine of one Supreme and Universal Deity, the Maker of the whole world**. Therefore, it is difficult to conceive that this "unutterable," "secret," and "enigmatic" theology <note>original Greek: ἀῤῥητός and ἀπόῤῥητος and αἰνιγματώδης θεολογία</note> of the Egyptians, which is so frequently discussed, could be anything other than a kind of **metaphysics concerning God as one perfect, incorporeal being, the origin of all things**.

We know of no significant objection that can be raised against this, except for what **Porphyry**, in his *Letter to Anebo* (an Egyptian priest), writes concerning **Chaeremon**:

> "For Chaeremon and others believe there is nothing prior to this visible and physical world. In the beginning of their accounts, they place the views of those Egyptians who recognize no other gods except the so-called planets and those stars that fill up the zodiac..." <note>original Greek: χαιρήμων μὲν γὰρ, καὶ οἱ ἄλλοι, οὐδ᾽ ἄλλο τι πρὸ τῶν ὁρωμένων κόσμων ἡγοῦνται ἐν ἀρχῇ λόγων τιθέμενοι τοὺς Αἰγυπτίων, οὐδ᾽ ἄλλους θεοὺς πλὴν τῶν πλανητῶν λεγομένων, καὶ τῶν συμπληρούντων τὸν ζῳδιακόν, &c.</note>

<margin>Preparation for the Gospel, Book 3, ch. 4.</margin> 
*Chaeremon and others acknowledge nothing before this visible and physical world. To support their opinion, they cite those Egyptians who talk of no other gods but the planets and those stars that fill up the zodiac, or those that rise along with them—their decans <note>groups of stars used in ancient Egyptian astronomy to divide the night</note>, their horoscopes, and those they call "Robust Princes." The names of these are even inserted into their almanacs or astronomical tables, along with the times of their rising and setting, and the predictions or meanings of future events derived from them. For he observed that those Egyptians who made the Sun the "Demiurge" <note>original: Demiurgus; the artisan-like creator of the world</note> or Architect of the world interpreted the stories of **Isis** and **Osiris**, and all those other religious fables, as nothing but stars, planets, and the River Nile.* 

"They interpreted everything universally into natural or inanimate things, and nothing into incorporeal and living substances." <note>original Greek: καὶ ὅλως πάντα εἰς τὰ φυσικὰ καὶ οὐδὲν εἰς ἀσωμάτους καὶ ζώσας οὐσίας ἑρμηνεύουν</note>

We confess that **Eusebius** <note>a 4th-century Christian historian</note> places great emphasis on this passage by Porphyry regarding Chaeremon. He tries to use it to his advantage, first against the Egyptians, and then against the Greeks and other pagans who derived their religion and theology from them. 

"It is manifest from this," Eusebius says, "that the very secret theology of the Egyptians deified nothing but stars and planets. It acknowledged no incorporeal principle or 'creative reason' <note>original: Demiurgick Reason</note> as the cause of this universe, but only the visible Sun." 

He then concludes in this manner: "See now what has become of this secret theology of the Egyptians, which deifies nothing but senseless matter or dead, inanimate bodies." 

However, it is well known that Eusebius took every possible opportunity to represent the pagans in the worst light and to make their theology appear ridiculous and absurd. Nevertheless, what he urges here against the Egyptians is...

## An Objection from Chæremon Answered. BOOK I.

The evidence is less valuable because he plainly contradicts himself elsewhere, declaring that the Egyptians acknowledged a **Demiurgic Reason** <note>original: *Demiurgick Reason*; a "Demiurge" is a divine craftsman or creative intellect that fashions the universe</note> and an **Intellectual Architect** of the world, who consequently was the creator of the sun. He confesses the same of the other Pagans as well. 

Now, to affirm that the Egyptians acknowledged no other Deity than inanimate matter and the senseless physical world is not only to deny that they had any **secret theology** <note>original Greek: ἀπόῤῥητος θεολογία (*aporrhētos theologia*)</note> at all (which has already been sufficiently proved), but also to brand them as **absolute atheists**. For if it is not atheism to acknowledge no other Deity besides dead and senseless matter, then the word has no meaning. 

**Chæremon** indeed seems to attribute this opinion not to all the Egyptians, but to some of them; and it is very possible that there might have been some atheists among the Egyptians, just as there were among the Greeks and their philosophers. Undoubtedly, this **Chæremon** himself was a kind of **astrological atheist**; for this reason, we conclude that he was not Chæremon the Stoic (from whom **Porphyry**, in his book *On Abstinence*, cites certain other things concerning the Egyptians), but either the Chæremon whom **Strabo** <note>a Greek geographer and historian</note> met in Egypt, or someone else of that name. 

As for the idea that there ever were, or could be, any such **"Religious Atheists"**—as **Eusebius** <note>a 4th-century Christian historian</note> and some others imagine—who acknowledge no Deity besides dead and senseless matter yet still devoutly court and worship it, constantly praying to it and begging for its help as if expecting great benefit: we confess that we do not have enough faith to believe such a thing. It is a foolishness and a contradictory nonsense that does not occur in human nature. We cannot doubt that all devout Pagans acknowledged some **living** and **understanding Deities** or other; nor can we easily believe that they ever worshipped any inanimate or senseless bodies in any way other than as symbols or images referring back to those Deities. 

Regarding that passage in **Porphyry’s** epistle concerning **Chæremon**, where he only proposes doubts to **Anebo** the Egyptian priest because he desires further information, **Iamblichus** <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher</note> has given us a full answer. He writes under the persona of **Abammo**, another Egyptian priest. This answer has not been noticed until now because **Ficinus** and **Scutellius** <note>Renaissance translators of Iamblichus</note>, not realizing that "Chæremon" was a proper name, ridiculously translated it as "I would wish" and "I would rejoice," <note>original Latin: *Optarem* and *Gauderem*</note> thereby perverting the entire meaning. The words in the Greek manuscript (now held by my learned friend **Mr. Gale** <note>Thomas Gale, a 17th-century scholar and collector of manuscripts</note>) read as follows:

> "But Chæremon and those others who pretend to write about the first causes of the world, explain only the last and lowest principles. This includes those who discuss the planets, the zodiac, the **decans** <note>groups of stars used in Egyptian astronomy to divide the night</note>, the horoscopes, and the so-called 'powerful leaders'—they reveal only the divided distributions of the primary principles. The sections in the almanacs contain only a very small part of the **Hermetic arrangements** <note>original Greek: ἑρμαϊκῶν διατάξεων; refers to the teachings of Hermes Trismegistus</note>. Furthermore, matters concerning the stars—their appearances, vanishings, or the waxing and waning of the moon—held the lowest place in Egyptian theories of causation. The Egyptians do not say that all things are physical; rather, they distinguish both the life of the soul and the intellectual life from nature. They place **Mind and Reason** <note>original Greek: νοῦν τε καὶ λόγον (*noun te kai logon*)</note> as existing by themselves, not only over the whole universe but also within us, and they say that in this way, all things are created." <note>original Greek: χαιρήμων δὲ καὶ οἵτινες ἄλλοι, τῶν περὶ τὸν κόσμον ἅπτονται πρώτων αἰτίων, τὰς τελευταίας ἀρχὰς ἐξηγεῖται, ὅσοι τε τοὺς πλανήτας, καὶ τὸν ζωδιακὸν, τοὺς δὲ δεκανοὺς, καὶ ὡροσκόπους, καὶ τοὺς λεγομένους κραταιοὺς ἡγεμόνας παραδίδουσι, τὰς μεριστὰς τῶν ἀρχῶν διανομὰς ἀναφαίνουσι· τάτε ἐν τοῖς ἀλμηνιακοῖς μέρη τι βραχύτατον περιέχει τῶν ἑρμαϊκῶν διατάξεων, καὶ τὰ περὶ ἀστέρων ἢ φάσεων, ἢ κρύψεων, ἢ σελήνης αὐξήσεων, ἢ μειώσεων ἐν τοῖς ἐσχάτοις εἶχε τὴν ἐν αἰγυπτίοις αἰτιολογίαν· φυσικά τε οὐ λέγουσιν εἶναι πάντα αἰγύπτιοι, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν τῆς ψυχῆς ζωήν, καὶ τὴν νοερὰν ἀπὸ τῆς φύσεως διακεκρίνουσιν· οὐκ ἐπὶ τοῦ παντὸς μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐφ' ἡμῶν, νοῦν τε καὶ λόγον προστησάμενοι καθ' ἑαυτοὺς ὄντας, οὕτως δημιουργεῖσθαί φασι τὰ γινόμενα.</note>

But Chæremon and those others who pretend to write of the first causes of the world, declare only the last and lowest principles, as likewise they who...

### CHAPTER IV. Some Trismegistic Books are Counterfeit.

...who treat the *Planets*, the *Zodiac*, the *Decans*, the *Horoscopes*, and the *Robust Princes* <note>original: *Robust Princes*; likely referring to the *Krataioi Hegemones*, powerful astrological rulers or planetary deities mentioned in Hermetic and Egyptian texts</note>. And the contents of the *Egyptian Almanacs* (or *Ephemerides* <note>original: *Ephemerides*; tables showing the calculated positions of celestial bodies over time</note>) contain the smallest part of the *Hermetic Teachings* <note>original: *Hermaical Institutions*</note>, namely the *Phases* and *Occultations* <note>original: *Occultations*; when one celestial body is hidden by another</note> of the stars, the *waxing* and *waning* of the *moon*, and similar *astrological matters*. These things held the lowest place in the *Egyptian explanation of causes* <note>original: *Ætiology*</note>.

The *Egyptians* do not reduce all things to (*senseless*) *Nature*. Instead, they distinguish both the *Life of the Soul* and the *Intellectual Life* from the life of *Nature*, not only in *ourselves* but also in the *Universe*. They determined that *Mind* and *Reason* existed first by themselves, and that this whole *World* was made through them. Therefore, they acknowledge a *Living Power* both before and within the *Heavens*, and place pure *Mind* above the *World* as its *Demiurge* <note>original: *Demiurgus*; a divine craftsman or creator</note> and *Architect*. 

From this testimony by *Iamblichus* <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on Egyptian religion</note>—who was only slightly younger than *Porphyry* and a contemporary of *Eusebius*, and who made it his business to thoroughly inform himself regarding the theology of the Egyptians—it clearly appears that the Egyptians did not generally assume (as *Chæremon* claimed regarding some of them) that a senseless, inanimate Nature was the original source of all things. Rather, they acknowledged that in the *World*, just as in ourselves, the *Soul* is superior to *Nature*, and *Mind* or *Intellect* is superior to the *Soul*, with Mind being the *Demiurge* of the *World*. We will later have a more suitable opportunity to cite other passages from this *Iamblichus's* *Egyptian Mysteries* to the same effect.

Therefore, there is no reason at all to suspect that the *Egyptians* were universally *Atheists* and *Anarchists* <note>in this context, those who believe there is no supreme 'archē' or ruling principle</note>, who supposed there was no *living, understanding Deity* and reduced everything to *senseless matter* as the first and highest *principle*. The real question is whether they were *Polyarchists* <note>those who believe in many independent first principles or gods</note>—those who asserted a multitude of *self-existent* or *uncreated understanding deities*. 

Now, many learned men, such as *Agostino Steuco of Gubbio* <note>original: *A. Steuchus Eugubinus*; a 16th-century Italian scholar and librarian of the Vatican</note>, have thought it unquestionably evident from the *Hermetic* or *Trismegistic writings* that *Monarchy* <note>here meaning "monotheism," the rule of a single supreme God</note> was an essential part of the *secret* and *true theology* of the Egyptians. They took it for granted that these writings are all genuine and authentic. However, there is too much reason to suspect that certain *pious frauds* <note>deceptions intended to promote a religious cause</note> have been practiced upon these *Trismegistic writings*, just as they were upon the *Sibylline* oracles. Either entire books were counterfeited by people pretending to be Christians, or at least several fake and substituted passages were inserted into some of them. 

*Isaac Casaubon* <note>a renowned classical scholar (1559–1614)</note>, who was the first to discover this, noticed many such instances in the first Hermetic book entitled *Poimandres* <note>original: *Pæmander*</note>, as well as some in the fourth book titled *Crater* <note>The Mixing Bowl</note>, and some in the thirteenth called the *Sermon on the Mount*, concerning *Regeneration*. This may rightly cause those three entire books—or at least the first and the last of them—to be suspected. We will not repeat any of the passages condemned by *Casaubon* here, but we will add one more from the *Thirteenth Book* (the *Sermon on the Mount*). Although he omitted it, this passage seems more obviously *Christian* than any other: "Tell me this also: who is the creator of regeneration? The Son of God, one man, by the will of God." <note>original Greek: λέγε μοί τοῦτο, τίς ἐστὶ γενεσιουργὸς τῆς παλιγγενεσίας; ὁ τοῦ Θεοῦ παῖς, ἄνθρωπος εἷς, θελήματι Θεοῦ (*lege moi touto, tis esti genesiourgos tēs paliggenesias? ho tou Theou pais, anthrōpos heis, thelēmati Theou*)</note> *Tell me this also, Who is the Cause or Worker of Regeneration? The Son of God, One...*

<header>All the Hermetic Books, BOOK. I.</header>

One Man, by the will of God. Therefore, although Athanasius Kircher <note>a 17th-century Jesuit scholar known for his studies on Egypt</note> argues with much zeal for the authenticity of all these *Hermetic Books* <note>original: *Trismegistick Books*</note>; yet we must declare that the three previously mentioned—at least the *Poimandres* <note>original: *Pæmander*; the most famous text in the *Corpus Hermeticum*</note> properly so called, and the *Sermon on the Mountain*—were either entirely forged and counterfeited by some pretended Christians, or else had many fake passages inserted into them. For this reason, it cannot be solidly proven from the *Hermetic Books* (if they are assumed to be all alike genuine and pure) that the Egyptian Pagans acknowledged *One Supreme and Universal Deity* <note>original: *Numen*</note>. Much less can the same be proven from that pretended book of Aristotle, *On the More Secret Part of Divine Wisdom according to the Egyptians* <note>original: *De secretiore parte Divinæ Sapientiæ secundùm Ægyptios*</note>, which was also greedily accepted by Kircher, but is unquestionably *falsely attributed* <note>original: *pseudepigraphous*</note>.

Notwithstanding this, we believe that even if all the *Hermetic Books* that now exist, or have existed in the past, had been forged by some pretended Christians—just as that book on *Secret Egyptian Wisdom* was forged by some philosopher and attributed to Aristotle—they would still, for another reason, provide a significant argument to prove that the Egyptian Pagans asserted *One Supreme Deity*. This is because every cheat and imposture must have some basis or foundation of truth to stand upon. There must have been something truly Egyptian in such counterfeit Egyptian writings (at least this idea of *One Supreme Deity*), or else they could never have gained credit at first, or maintained it afterward. 

This is especially true because these *Hermetic Books* were circulated in those ancient times before Egyptian Paganism and its succession of priests were extinct. Therefore, if the ideas so heavily emphasized in them had been inconsistent with Egyptian theology, they would have been immediately rejected <note>original: *exploded*</note> as mere lies and forgeries. Therefore, we say again: if all the *Hermetic* or *Trismegistic* books that are now extant—including those mentioned by the ancient Church Fathers that have since been lost, such as *The Hermetica* <note>original: τὰ Ἑρμικὰ</note> and *The Detailed Treatises* <note>original: τὰ διεξοδικὰ</note> and the like—had been nothing but the *religious frauds and cheats* of Christians, there must still have been some truth at the bottom to give them weight. At the very least, it shows that *Hermes Trismegistus* or the Egyptian priests, in their *Secret and True Theology*, really acknowledged *One Supreme and Universal Deity*.

But it does not follow that because some of these *Hermetic* or *Trismegistic* books now in existence were counterfeit or fake, that therefore all of them must be so. This applies not only to current books but also to those mentioned in the writings of the ancient Fathers which are now lost. Therefore, the learned Isaac Casaubon <note>a prominent 16th-century classical scholar</note> seems not to have reasoned or concluded well when, from the discovery of forgery in at most two or three of those *Hermetic Books*, he pronounces universally that they were all nothing but *Christian cheats and impostures*. He was probably led into this mistake by too confidently following that common error (which had already been refuted by Francesco Patrizi <note>original: *Patricius*; an Italian philosopher who edited the Hermetic texts</note>) that all the works published by Marsilio Ficino <note>original: *Ficinus*; a Renaissance scholar who translated the *Corpus Hermeticum*</note> under

<header>CHAPTER IV. Not Christian Frauds. 321</header>

The name *Hermes Trismegistus* [original: *Hermes Trismegist*] referred to just one book, the *Poimandres* [original: *Pæmander*], made up of several chapters. In reality, they are many distinct and independent books, of which the *Poimandres* is only the first. However, there was no reason why the *Asclepius* should have been condemned in the same way, nor several other books added by Francesco Patrizi [original: *Patricius* <note>a 16th-century Italian philosopher who published a collection of Hermetic texts</note>]. These are undoubtedly distinct from the *Poimandres*, and no signs of forgery or lack of authenticity [original: *Spuriousness or Bastardy*] have been found in them. Much less should those Hermetic [original: *Trismegistick*] books cited by the Church Fathers—which are now lost—be condemned without even being seen.

Therefore, despite everything that Isaac Casaubon [original: *Casaubon* <note>a famous Swiss classical scholar who argued that the Hermetic texts were late forgeries</note>] has written, some Hermetic books may very well be genuine, even if they are not all so. That is to say—as we will explain further—there may be books that were truly Egyptian and not forged by a Christian, even if they were perhaps not written by Hermes Trismegistus himself or in the Egyptian language. Just as it is hard to imagine how there could be counterfeit Egyptian books if there were no real ones, the idea that some were real and genuine will perhaps be made probable by the following considerations.

It cannot reasonably be denied that in ancient times among the Egyptians there was a man named Thoth, *Theuth*, or *Taut*. Along with the alphabet, he was the first inventor of arts and sciences—such as arithmetic, geometry, and astronomy—and of hieroglyphic learning. For this reason, he was called *Hermes* by the Greeks and *Mercury* [original: *Mercurius*] by the Romans [original: *Latins*]. This is confirmed by general fame throughout the ages and by the testimony of Sanchuniathon (a Phoenician historian who lived around the time of the Trojan War and wrote a book on Egyptian theology) and Manetho of Sebennytos [original: *Manetho Sebennyta*] (an Egyptian priest who was a contemporary of Ptolemy Philadelphus).

It is also confirmed by the serious philosopher Plato, who is said to have lived in Egypt for thirteen years. In his dialogue *Philebus*, Plato speaks of him as the first inventor of letters—the one who distinguished between vowels and consonants and determined their count—calling him either a "God" or a "Divine Man." In his *Phaedrus*, Plato also attributes to him the invention of arithmetic, geometry, and astronomy, along with some playful pastimes [original: *ludicrous Recreations*], and refers to him as either a God or a spirit [original: *Demon* <note>Greek *daimon*, meaning a supernatural being or spirit, not necessarily evil</note>]. Plato writes:
> "I have heard that near Naucratis in Egypt, there was one of the ancient Egyptian Gods, to whom the bird Ibis was sacred, as his symbol or hieroglyphic; the name of this spirit was Theuth." <note>original: ἤκουσα περὶ Ναύκρατιν τῆς Αἰγύπτου, γενέσθαι τῶν ἐκεῖ παλαιῶν τινα Θεῶν, οὗ καὶ τὸ ὄρνεον τὸ ἱερὸν ὃ δὴ καλοῦσιν Ἴβιν, αὐτῷ δὲ ὄνομα τῷ δαίμονι εἶναι Θεύθ</note>

In that same passage, the philosopher also adds a clever debate between this Theuth and Thamus, then the King of Egypt, regarding the usefulness and drawbacks of letters. The former boasted of his invention as a "remedy for memory and a great help to wisdom" <note>original: ὡς μνήμης καὶ σοφίας φάρμακον</note>. However, the king argued that it would instead cause forgetfulness through the neglect of memory. Therefore, it was not so much a "remedy for memory" <note>original: μνήμης... φάρμακον</note> as it was a "remedy for reminding, or the recovery of things forgotten" <note>original: ὑπομνήσεως φάρμακον</note>. He added that writing would also weaken and diminish men's natural mental powers by making them lazy, and would create a "pretense of wisdom" <note>original: δόξαν σοφίας</note> rather than "truth" <note>original: ἀλήθειαν</note>—a puffy conceit and

<header>Thoth, the Egyptian Hermes. BOOK I.</header>

...an opinion of knowledge, by a multifarious rabble of undigested notions, rather than the *truth* thereof. Moreover, since it is certain that the Egyptians were famous for *literature* before the Greeks, they must of necessity have had one or more founders of learning among them, just as the Greeks had; and *Thoth* is the only or first person celebrated among them on this account, in remembrance of whom the first month of the year was called by that name. This *Thoth* is generally supposed to have lived in the times of the Patriarchs, or considerably before *Moses*; *Moses himself* being said to have been instructed in that learning which owed its origin to him.

Again, besides this *Thoth* or *Theuth*, who was called the *First Hermes*, the Egyptians also had afterward another eminent advancer or restorer of learning, who was called the Second Hermes <note>original Greek: *δ᾽ ἕτερος Ἑρμῆς*</note>. They perhaps supposed the soul of *Thoth*, or the *First Hermes*, to have come into him by transmigration; but his proper Egyptian name was *Siphoas*, as *Syncellus* <note>a 9th-century Byzantine chronicler</note> informs us from the works of *Manetho* <note>an ancient Egyptian priest and historian</note>: *Siphoas (who is also Hermes), the son of Hephaestus* <note>original Greek: *Σιφωὰς, ὁ καὶ Ἑρμῆς, υἱὸς Ἡφαίστου*; the text uses "Vulcan," the Roman equivalent of Hephaestus</note>. This is he who is said to have been the father of *Tat*, and to have been surnamed *Trismegistus*, or "Thrice-Great" <note>original: *Τρισμέγιστος*, *Ter Maximus*</note> (he being so styled by *Manetho*, *Iamblichus*, and others). He is placed by *Eusebius* in the fiftieth year after the *Israelite Exodus*, though probably somewhat too early. 

The first of these two *Hermes* was the inventor of arts and sciences; the second was the restorer and advancer of them. The *first* wrote in hieroglyphics upon pillars, in the land of the Syringes <note>original Greek: *ἐν τῇ συριγγικῇ γῇ*. The scholar Henri Valois (Valesius) conjectured it should be read this way instead of "Seiriadic land." The "Syringes" were subterranean tunnels or galleries in Egypt.</note>. *Ammianus Marcellinus* will inform us what these *Syringes* were. The *second* interpreted and translated those hieroglyphics, composing many books in several arts and sciences. The number of these books recorded by *Iamblichus* must surely be legendary <note>original: "fabulous"</note>, unless it is understood to mean paragraphs or verses. These *Trismegistic* or *Hermetic* books were said to be carefully preserved by the priests in the inner recesses of their temples.

But besides the hieroglyphics written by the *First Hermes* and the books composed by the *Second* (who was also called *Trismegistus*), it cannot be doubted that there were many other books written by the Egyptian priests successively over several ages. *Iamblichus* informs us, at the beginning of his *On the Mysteries*, that Hermes—the god of eloquence and the president or patron of all true knowledge concerning the gods—was formerly accounted common to all the priests, to such an extent that *they dedicated the inventions of their wisdom to him, entitling all their own writings the works of Hermes* <note>original Greek: *τὰ αὐτῶν τῆς σοφίας εὑρήματα αὐτῷ ἀνετίθεσαν, Ἑρμοῦ πάντα τὰ οἰκεῖα συγγράμματα ἐπονομάζοντες*</note>, entitling their own books to *Hermes Trismegistus*. Now, although one reason for this might probably have been that those books were supposed to have been written according to the tenor of the *old Hermetic* or *Trismegistic doctrine*, yet *Iamblichus* here acquaints us with the chief ground of it: namely, that although *Hermes* was once a mortal man, he was afterward deified by the Egyptians (which is testified also by

### CHAPTER IV. Hermetic Books extant after Clement of Alexandria

(Plato) and made to be the guardian god and patron <note>original: "Fautor"</note> of all arts and sciences, but especially theology; by whose inspiration, therefore, all such books were believed to have been written. Furthermore, we may observe that in some of the Hermetic <note>original: "Hermaick"</note> or *Trismegistic* books now extant, *Hermes* is sometimes used to represent Divine *Wisdom* or *Understanding* itself. And now we see the true reason why there have been many books called *Hermetic* and *Trismegistic*, some of which, nonetheless, cannot possibly be conceived to be of such great antiquity or written by *Hermes Trismegistus* himself. This is because it was customary for the Egyptian priests to attribute <note>original: "entitle"</note> their own philosophical and theological books to *Hermes*. 

Moreover, it is very probable that several of the books written by the Egyptian priests in later times were not originally written in the Egyptian language, but in Greek. From the time of the Ptolemaic kings downward, Greek had become very familiar to all the learned Egyptians and was spoken in a common <note>original: "vulgarly"</note> manner. This is evident from those very words—*Hermes*, *Trismegistus*, and the like—so commonly used by them, as well as the proper names of places. Additionally, the Coptic language to this very day contains more Greek than Egyptian words. Indeed, *Plutarch* even ventures to explain the origins <note>original: "etymologize"</note> of those old Egyptian names—*Isis, Osiris, Horus, and Typhon*—from Greek roots, as if the Egyptians had been well-acquainted with that language in ancient times.

Now, it seems unquestionable that some of those ancient Hermetic books, written by *Hermes Trismegistus* himself (or believed to be such by the Egyptians and kept in the custody of their priests), were still in being and available among them after the beginning of Christianity. This is supported by the testimony of that pious and learned Father, *Clement of Alexandria*, who gives this particular account of them after mentioning their opinion concerning the transmigration of souls.

<margin>Stromata, Book 6, page 633.</margin>

> The Egyptians follow a certain peculiar philosophy of their own, which may be best explained by describing the order of their religious procession. First, therefore, goes the **Singer** <note>original: "Precentor"</note>, carrying two of Hermes's books along with him: one of which contains the hymns of the gods, and the other directions for the kingly office. After him follows the **Astrologer** <note>original: "Horoscopus"</note>, who is particularly instructed in Hermes's astrological books, which are four. Then succeeds the **Sacred Scribe** <note>original: "Hierogrammateus"</note>, with feathers upon his head and a book and rule in his hands. It belongs to him to be thoroughly acquainted with the **hieroglyphics**, as well as with cosmography <note>the study of the universe</note>, geography, the order of the sun, moon, and five planets, the regional description <note>original: "chorography"</note> of Egypt, and the description of the Nile. In the next place comes the **Master of the Robes** <note>original: "Stolistes"</note>, who is to be thoroughly instructed in those ten books which treat the honor of the gods, the Egyptian worship, sacrifices, first-fruits, prayers, processions <note>original: "pomps"</note>, and festivals. And last of all marches the **Prophet**, who is president of the temple and sacred things, and ought to be thoroughly versed in those other ten books, called **Priestly** <note>original: "Sacerdotal"</note>, concerning laws, the gods, and the entire discipline of the priests. Therefore, among the books of Hermes, forty-two are accounted most necessary; thirty-six of these, containing all the Egyptian philosophy, were to be learned by those particular orders...

Furthermore, it seems probable that there were certain books truly Egyptian and called *Hermaic* or *Trismegistic* (whether written by the ancient *Hermes Trismegistus* himself, or by other Egyptian priests of later times following the spirit of his doctrine and only attributed to him) which began to be noticed by other nations—the Greeks and Latins—after the rise of Christianity. This is likely because such books are mentioned and acknowledged not only by Christian writers and Church Fathers, but also by Pagans and philosophers. In *Plutarch's* discourse *On Isis and Osiris* <note>original: "de Iside & Osiride"</note>, we read the following about them:

"In the books called Hermes's, or the Hermaic books, it is reported to have been written concerning sacred names: that the power appointed to preside over the motion of the sun is called Horus by the Egyptians (just as the Greeks call it Apollo); and that which presides over the air and wind is called Osiris by some, Sarapis by others, and Sothi by others, in the Egyptian language." <note>original: "Ἐν δὲ ταῖς Ἑρμοῦ λεγομέναις βίβλοις, ἱστοροῦσι γεγράφθαι, περὶ τῶν ἱερῶν ὀνομάτων, ὅτι τὴν μὲν ἐπὶ τῇ τοῦ ἡλίου περιφορᾷ τεταγμένην δύναμιν, Ὧρον, Ἕλληνες δὲ Ἀπόλλωνα καλοῦσι, τὴν δὲ ἐπὶ τοῦ πνεύματος, οἱ μὲν Ὄσιριν, οἱ δὲ Σάραπιν, οἱ δὲ Σωθὶ Αἰγυπτιστί"</note>

Now, these "sacred names" in *Plutarch* seem to be various names for God. Therefore, whether these Hermaic books were the same ones mentioned by *Clement of Alexandria*—supposed by the Egyptians to have been written by *Hermes Trismegistus* himself—or other books written by Egyptian priests according to the tenor of his doctrine, we may observe something important: according to the Hermaic or Trismegistic doctrine, one and the same Deity was worshipped under several names and concepts, according to His various powers and virtues manifested in the world. This is a point we will insist upon more later.

Moreover, it has been generally believed that *Lucius Apuleius of Madaura* <note>original: "L. Apuleius Madaurensis"</note>, an eminent Platonic philosopher and zealous defender of paganism, was the translator of the *Asclepian Dialogue* of *Hermes Trismegistus* from Greek into Latin. Consequently, it has been published alongside *Apuleius's* other works. *Barthius* <note>Caspar von Barth, a 17th-century scholar</note> affirms that *St. Augustine* <note>original: "St. Austin"</note> somewhere explicitly attributes this translation to *Apuleius*, though we confess we have not yet found that specific passage. However, there seems to be no sufficient reason why *Colvius* <note>Andreas Colvius</note> should question this attribution based on the style and the Latin used.

Again, it is certain that *Iamblichus* <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher</note> not only mentions these Hermaic books under the name of "the books circulated as those of Hermes" <note>original: "τὰ φερόμενα ὡς Ἑρμοῦ"</note>—or those commonly attributed to him—but also defends them against the charge of being forgeries. This was not because there was any suspicion then of what *Isaac Casaubon* <note>a scholar who famously argued the Hermetic texts were late forgeries</note> is so confident of today—that these Hermaic books were all forged by Christians—but because some might then have imagined them to have been forged by philosophers. "Therefore, both in the writings of others in this manner, and those..." <note>original: "Διὸ καὶ ἐν τοῖς τῶν ἑτέρων οὕτως, καὶ τῶν"</note>

# Chapter IV. By Pagans and Philosophers.

"In the writings which he says he has come across, the solution is clear: for those books that are circulated as being by Hermes contain Hermaic opinions, even if they often use the language of the philosophers. This is because they have been translated from the Egyptian language by men who were not unacquainted with philosophy. But Chaeremon <note>original: χαιρήμων; an Egyptian priest and Stoic philosopher</note>, etc." <note>original: ἐν τοῖς συγγράμμασιν οἷς λέγει ἐπιτετυχηκέναι, σαφής ἐστιν ἡ διάλυσις· τὰ μὲν γὰρ φερόμενα, ὡς Ἑρμοῦ, ἑρμαϊκὰς περιέχει δόξας, εἰ καὶ τῇ τῶν φιλοσόφων γλώττῃ πολλάκις χρῆται· μεταγέγραπται γὰρ ἀπὸ τῆς αἰγυπτίας γλώττης ὑπ’ ἀνδρῶν φιλοσοφίας οὐκ ἀπείρως ἐχόντων. χαιρήμων δὲ, &c.</note> These things being thus discussed and determined, the solution to that difficulty from those books which Porphyry <note>A prominent Neoplatonist philosopher and critic of Christianity</note> says he met with (namely the *Hermaic* books and those writings of *Chaeremon*) will be clear and easy. For the books commonly attributed to *Hermes* do really contain the *Hermaic* opinions and doctrines in them, although they often speak the language of philosophers. The reason for this is that they were translated out of the *Egyptian* language by men who were familiar with philosophy. But *Chaeremon* and those others, etc. Here it is first observable that *Iamblichus* <note>A Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher who defended traditional Egyptian and Chaldean religion</note> does not affirm that these *Hermaic* books were written by *Hermes Trismegistus* himself; he calls them only "the books that were circulated as being by Hermes" <note>original: τὰ φερόμενα ὡς Ἑρμῦ</note>. But what he does affirm of them is this: that they did really contain the *Hermaic* opinions and derive their origin from *Egypt*. Again, whereas some might then possibly suspect that these *Hermaic* books had been counterfeited by *Greek* philosophers and contained nothing but *Greek* learning because they speak so much in the language of philosophy, *Iamblichus* gives an account for this also: the reason was *because they were translated out of the Egyptian language by men skilled in Greek philosophy, who therefore added something of their own terminology and concepts to them*. It is true indeed that most of these *Hermaic* books which we have now seem to have been written originally in *Greek*. Notwithstanding this, others of them—and particularly those that are now lost, such as the *General Treatises* <note>original: τὰ γενικὰ; Ta Genika</note> and the like—might have been, as *Iamblichus* here affirms, translated out of the *Egyptian* language, but disguised by their translators with philosophical language and other *Greek* elements intermixed with them. Moreover, from the previously cited passage of *Iamblichus*, we may clearly conclude that *Porphyry* in his letter to *Anebo* the *Egyptian* priest (of which letter only some small fragments remain) also made mention of these *Hermaic* writings. Since he found the writings of *Chaeremon* to be contradictory to them, he therefore desired to be resolved by that *Egyptian* priest whether the doctrine of those *Hermaic* books was genuine and truly *Egyptian* or not. Now, *Iamblichus* in his answer here affirms that the doctrine of the ancient *Hermes*, or the *Egyptian* theology, was substantially and truly represented in those books (commonly attributed to *Hermes*), but not so in the works of *Chaeremon*. Lastly, *St. Cyril of Alexandria* informs us that

# That Nothing Perishes; BOOK 1.

Now it cannot be doubted that this edition of *Hermaic Books* at Athens was made by some philosopher or pagan and not by Christians. This also appears from the words of *St. Cyril* himself, where, having spoken of *Moses* and the agreement of *Hermes* with him, he adds: "Mention is also made of this Moses in his own writings by the one who compiled and published the fifteen Hermaic books at Athens." <note>original: πεποὶηται ἠ κὶ τοὺτου μνημὴν, ἐν ἰδὶαις συγγϱαφαὶς, ὁ συντεθεικὼς Ἀθὴνησι, τὰ ἐπὶκλὴν Ἑϱμαϊκὰ πεντεκαὶδεκα βιβλὶα</note> For we understand that passage to mean that the pagan publisher of the *Hermaic Books* himself took notice of some agreement that existed between *Moses* and *Hermes*. 

But it should be noted here that because *Hermes* and the *Hermaic Books* were in such great credit—not only among the Christians but also among the Greek and Latin pagans—there were some counterfeit writings also pushed forward under that impressive title. Examples include that ancient *Botanical Book* mentioned by *Galen*, and those Christian forgeries of later times, the *Poimandres* <note>original: Pæmander</note> and the *Sermon on the Mount*. Since these were not cited by any ancient Father or writer, both of them were undoubtedly later than *Iamblichus*, who shows no suspicion of any Christian forgeries of this kind.

But *Casaubon* <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614) was a renowned classical scholar who argued that the Hermetic corpus was actually written in the early Christian era, not ancient Egypt.</note>, who contends that all the *theological books* attributed to *Hermes Trismegistus* were counterfeited by Christians, affirms that all the philosophy, doctrine, and learning within them (except for whatever is specifically Christian) is merely *Platonic* and *Greek* but not at all *Egyptian*. From this, he concludes that these books were forged by Christians who were skilled in *Platonic* or *Greek* learning. 

However, first, it is worth considering that since *Pythagoreanism*, *Platonism*, and Greek learning in general were largely derived from the Egyptians, it cannot be concluded that whatever is Platonic or Greek was therefore not *Egyptian*. The only instance that *Casaubon* insists upon is this *dogma* <term>dogma: a settled opinion or principle</term> in the *Trismegistic Books*: *That nothing in the world perishes, and that death is not the destruction of things, but only their change and transformation.* Because he finds this among some of the Greek philosophers, he decides it must be unique to them alone and not shared by the Egyptians. 

But since the chief design and tendency of that *dogma* was plainly to maintain the *immortality, preexistence, and transmigration of souls*—a doctrine that was unquestionably derived from the Egyptians—there is little reason to doubt that this *dogma* was itself Egyptian as well. And *Pythagoras*, who was the chief promoter of this doctrine among the Greeks, taught "that no real entity (in processes of birth and decay) was made or destroyed," <note>original: οὐδὲν οὐδὲ γὶγνεσθαι οὐδὲ φθεὶϱεσθαι τῶμ᾿ ὄντων</note> according to those verses by *Ovid* cited before:

> *Nothing in the whole world perishes, believe me,*
> *But it changes its appearance and renews its face. To be born is called*
> *Beginning to be something else, etc.*
> <note>original: Nec perit in toto quicquam, mihi credite, mundo, / Sed variat faciemque novat. Nascique vocatur / Incipere esse Aliud, &c.</note>

He did, in all probability, derive it together with its superstructure,
