### Chap. IV. Old Egyptian Philosophy.

...structure <note>This likely completes the word "structure" or "doctrine" from the previous page.</note>, (the preexistence and transmigration of souls), directly from the Egyptians. But it is observable that the Egyptians also had a peculiar ground of their own for this *dogma* <note>A settled opinion or tenet.</note> (which we do not find insisted upon by the Greek philosophers), and it is expressed this way in the eighth of Ficinus's <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was a Renaissance scholar who first translated the Hermetic corpus into Latin.</note> Hermetic books or chapters: "If the world is a second God and an immortal animal, then it is impossible that any part of this immortal animal should perish or come to nothing; for all things in the world are parts of the world, and especially man, the rational animal." <note>original Greek: εἰ δ᾽ ὁ δεύτερος Θεὸς ὁ κόσμος, καὶ ζῶον ἀθάνατον, ἀδύνταόν ἐστι τοῦ ἀθανάτου ζώου μέρος τι ἀποθανεῖν· πάντα γὰρ τὰ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ μέρη ἐστὶ τοῦ κόσμου, μάλιστα δὲ ὁ ἄνθρωπος, τὸ λογικὸν ζῶον</note>

We find this same notion also emphasized in the *Asclepian Dialogue*: "Believe this to be the second God, O Asclepius, governing all things and illuminating all worldly animals. For if the world is an animal—living, and has always been, is, and shall be—nothing in the world is mortal. For regarding every living part which is in the world itself, as in one and the same ever-living animal, there is no place for mortality." <note>original Latin: Secundum Deum hunc crede, ô Aſclepi, omnia gubernantem, omniaque mundana illuſtrantem animalia. Si enim Animal, Mundus, vivens, ſemper & fuit & eſt & erit, nihil in mundo mortale eſt: viventis enim uniuſcujuſque Partis, quæ in ipſo mundo, ſicut in uno eodemque Animale ſemper vivente, nullus eſt mortalitatis locus.</note> Although the Latin here is a little imperfect, the sense is this: you are to believe the world, O Asclepius, to be a second God, governing all things and illuminating all worldly <term>mundane</term> animals. Now, if the world is a living animal and immortal, then there is nothing mortal in it, because there is no place for mortality regarding any living part or member of that worldly animal that lives forever. 

Despite this, we do not deny that although Pythagoras first derived this notion from the Egyptians, he and his followers probably improved upon it further (as Plato tells us the Greeks generally did with what they received from the "barbarians" <note>The Greeks used the term "barbarians" to refer to any non-Greek speaking peoples, including the highly respected Egyptians.</note>). Namely, they moved toward removing the "qualities" and "forms" of bodies and resolving all physical things into magnitude, figure, and motion. 

However, it shall be clearly proved later—when we speak of that grand mystery of Egyptian theology (derived from them by Orpheus) that *God is All*—that some of the old Egyptian learning is indeed contained in these Trismegistic books now in existence. To conclude, the judgment of Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who defended the antiquity of the Hermetic writings.</note> in this case ought, without controversy, to be far preferred over Casaubon's. This is because of both his great antiquity and his being much better skilled in not only Greek but also Egyptian learning. Iamblichus held that the books attributed to Hermes Trismegistus "really contained Hermaic opinions," <note>original Greek: ἑρμαϊκὰς περιέχον δόξας</note> even though they sometimes spoke the language of the Greek philosophers.

Therefore, based on all these considerations, we conceive it reasonable to conclude that although some Hermaic books have been counterfeited by Christians since Iamblichus's time—namely the *Poimandres* <note>original: Pæmander</note> and the *Sermon on the Mount* concerning regeneration, neither of which are found cited by any ancient Father—there were other Hermaic books which, though not written by Hermes Trismegistus himself nor all of them in the Egyptian language (some being in Greek), were truly Egyptian and did, in their substance, contain the Hermaic doctrine. Such were probably those mentioned by the ancient Fathers but since lost, such as the *Generica* <note>original: τὰ γενικά</note>, which seems to have been a discourse concerning the *Cosmogony* <note>The origin or creation of the world.</note>, and the

# The Asclepian Dialogue, Book 1.

...the *detailed discourses* <note>original Greek: τὰ διέξοδικά</note>, and similar works. And some of these *Hermetic Books* <note>original: Hermaick Books; referring to the legendary Egyptian sage Hermes Trismegistus</note> that are still in existence may also be of this kind—to give a specific example, the *Asclepian Dialogue*, titled in Greek *The Perfect Discourse* <note>original Greek: ὁ τέλειος λόγος</note>. It was, in all probability, translated into Latin by the philosopher *Apuleius* <note>A 2nd-century Roman writer and philosopher, best known for the novel *The Golden Ass*.</note>. It can hardly be imagined that someone who was such a devout Pagan, such a learned philosopher, and such a witty man would be so thoroughly fooled by a counterfeit "Trismegistic" book and a mere *Christian forgery* as to spend his time translating it and recommending it to the world as a genuinely Pagan work. 

However, whether Apuleius was the translator of this *Asclepian Dialogue* or not, it is evident that its spirit is not at all Christian, but purely Pagan. One instance of this is its boasting of a power that men have of *making gods* <note>This refers to the "theurgic" practice of animating statues by drawing divine spirits into them through rituals.</note>, an idea that *St. Augustine* <note>original: St. Austin</note> thought necessary to refute. Moreover, since this dialogue was already in existence and widely known before the time of *Iamblichus* <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote about Egyptian mysteries.</note>, it must have been included in his list of *works circulated as being by Hermes* <note>original Greek: τὰ φερόμενα ὡς Ἑρμοῦ</note>. Consequently, it receives his testimony that it contained not merely *Greek* ideas, but the actual *Hermetic and Egyptian doctrine*.

<margin>Page 607, Column.</margin> 
There are indeed some objections made against this. First, there is what we read in this dialogue concerning the *purging of the world*, partly by *water* and partly by *fire*: *“Then that Lord and Father, the Supreme God and the only Governor of the world, beholding the behavior and deeds of men—by his Will (which is God's goodness), always resisting vice and restoring things from their decay—will either wash away the evil of the world by a flood or consume it by fire, and restore the world to its ancient form again.”* <note>original Latin: Tunc ille Dominus & Pater Deus, Primipotens, & Unus Gubernator mundi, intuens in mores factaque hominum, voluntate sua (quae est Dei Benignitas) vitiis resistens, & corruptelae errorem revocans, malignitatem omnem vel Alluvione diluens, vel igne consumens, ad antiquam faciem mundum revocabit</note> Since we find in the writings of *Julius Firmicus* <note>A 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer who converted to Christianity.</note> that there was an Egyptian *tradition* concerning the *restoration* <note>original Greek: ἀποκατάστασις (apocatastasis)</note> of the world, occurring *partly by deluge* <note>original Greek: κατακλυσμὸν</note> and *partly by conflagration* <note>original Greek: ἐκπύρωσιν</note>, this objection is meaningless.

There is another objection that has more plausibility, based on a prophecy we find in this *Asclepius* concerning the overthrow of Egyptian Paganism (described with much lamentation): *“Then this land, formerly the most holy seat of the religious temples of the gods, shall everywhere be full of the tombs of dead men.”* <note>original Latin: Tunc Terra ista, sanctissima sedes Delubrorum, Sepulchrorum erit mortuorumque plenissima</note>

<margin>The City of God, Book 8, Chapter 26.</margin> 
The sense of this passage is expressed by *St. Augustine* as follows: *“He seems to lament that the memorials of our martyrs would succeed in the place of their temples. He wants those who read this with a hostile and distorted mind to think that while the Pagans worshipped gods in temples, we Christians worship dead men in tombs.”* <note>original Latin: Hoc videtur dolere, quod Memoriae Martyrum nostrorum, Templis eorum Delubrisque succederent; ut viz. qui haec legunt, animo a nobis averso atque perverso, putent a Paganis Deos cultos fuisse in Templis, a nobis autem coli Mortuos in Sepulchris</note> Notwithstanding this, this very prophecy seems to have had its ac-

# CHAP. IV. No Christian Forgery.

...accomplishment too soon after, as may be gathered from these passages of *Theodoret* <margin>De Cur. G. A. L. 8.</margin>: "For the Martyrs have utterly abolished and blotted out of the minds of men the memory of those who were formerly called Gods" <note>original Greek: ἡ γὰρ αὐτῶν τῶν καλουμένων θεῶν, τὴν μνήμην, ἐκ τῆς τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐξήλειψαν (οἱ μάρτυρες) διανοίας</note>. And again: "Our Lord has now brought his own dead (that is, his Martyrs) into the room and place (that is, the Temples) of the Gods; whom he has sent away empty, and bestowed their honor upon these his Martyrs" <note>original Greek: τοὺς γὰρ οἰκείους νεκροὺς ὁ δεσπότης, ἀντεισῆξε τοῖς ὑμετέροις θεοῖς, καὶ τοὺς μὲν φρούδους ἀπέφηνε τούτοις δὲ τὸ ἐκείνων ἀπένειμε γέρας, &c.</note>. For now, instead of the festivals of *Jupiter* and *Bacchus*, the festivals of *Peter* and *Paul*, *Thomas* and *Sergius*, and other holy Martyrs are celebrated. 

Therefore, since this is such a sharp and plain description in the *Asclepian Dialogue* of what actually happened in the Christian world, it may seem suspicious—as if it were a history written after the event, rather than a prophecy before it, as it claims to be. It very much resembles that complaint of *Eunapius Sardianus* in the *Life of Aedesius*, written when the Christians had demolished the Temple of *Serapis* in *Egypt* and seized its riches and treasure: "That instead of the Gods, the Monks then gave Divine honor to certain vile and flagitious <term>wicked or shameful</term> persons deceased, called by the name of Martyrs." 

Now, if this is granted, this book must necessarily be counterfeit and supposititious <term>fraudulently substituted; a forgery</term>. Nevertheless, *St. Augustine* <note>original: St. Austin</note> entertained no such suspicion concerning this passage in the *Asclepian Dialogue*, as if it had been a history written after the fact (that is, after the tombs and memorials of the martyrs began to be so frequently visited); he supposed this book to be, unquestionably, of much greater antiquity. Therefore, he concludes it to be a prophecy or prediction made "by the instinct or suggestion of a deceitful spirit" <note>original Latin: instinctu fallacis Spiritûs</note>; with the spirits sadly foretelling the ruin of their own empire. 

Not only was this *Asclepian Dialogue* older than *St. Augustine*, but it is also cited by *Lactantius Firmianus* under the name of *The Perfect Discourse* <note>original Greek: ὁ τέλειος λόγος</note>, as was said before, and it was even then considered a work of great antiquity. Therefore, in all probability, this *Asclepian* passage was written before the described event was fulfilled. Indeed, if *Antoninus the Philosopher* <note>Referring to the Roman Emperor Marcus Aurelius</note> (as the previously mentioned *Eunapius* writes) did predict the very same thing—that after his death, that magnificent Temple of *Serapis* in *Egypt*, along with the others, should be demolished, "and the temples of the gods turned into tombs" <note>original Greek: καὶ τὰ ἱερὰ τάφους γενέσθαι</note>—why might not this *Egyptian* or *Trismegistic* writer receive the same inspiration or tradition? Or at least make the same conjecture.

<margin>Lib. 4. cap. 5.</margin> But there is yet another objection made against the sincerity of this *Asclepian Dialogue* based on *Lactantius* citing a passage from it regarding the *Second Person in the Trinity, the Son of God*. "Hermes, in that book," says Lactantius, "which is titled *The Perfect Discourse*, used these words: 'The Lord and Creator of all, whom we have been accustomed to call God, since he made a second God, visible and sensible (and I call him sensible not because he himself has sensation—for it is not the question of whether he himself has sensation—but because he falls under the observation of the senses and the mind); since he made this one, the first, and only, and one, and he appeared beautiful to him, and most full of all good things, he admired him and loved him dearly as his own offspring.'" <note>original Greek and Latin: Hermes in eo Libro (saith Lactantius) qui ὁ τέλειος λόγος inscribitur, his usus est verbis, ὁ κύριος καὶ ὁ πάντων ποιητής, ὃν θεὸν καλεῖν νενομίκαμεν, ἐπεὶ δὲ δεύτερον ἐποίησε θεὸν, ὁρατὸν καὶ αἰσθητὸν (αἰσθητὸν δέ φημι οὐ διὰ τὸ αἰσθάνεσθαι αὐτόν, περὶ γὰρ τούτου οὐκ ἔστι πότερον αὐτὸς αἰσθοῖτο, ἀλλ᾽ ὅτι εἰς αἴσθησιν ὑποπέμπει καὶ εἰς νοῦν) ἐπεὶ τοῦτον ἐποίησε, πρῶτον, καὶ μόνον, καὶ ἕνα, καλὸς δὲ ἐφάνη αὐτῷ, καὶ πληρέστατος πάντων τῶν ἀγαθῶν, ἠγάσθη τε καὶ πάνυ ἐφίλησεν ὡς ἴδιον τόκον</note>

# Chapter IV. By Lactantius and St. Augustine.

...ruling over all things that were made by him; this is the **Perfect** and **genuine** Son of the first **Omniperfect Being**. Nevertheless, the author of the *Perfect Word* <note>original Greek: τέλειος λόγος (téleios lógos)</note> or *Asclepian Dialogue*, in that previously cited passage of his, meant no such thing at all by his "Second God" (the "Son of the First") as the Christian *Logos* <note>The "Word" or Second Person of the Trinity</note> or Second Person of the Trinity. Instead, he meant only the **Visible World**. This is so plain from the words themselves that it is a wonder how **Lactantius** and **St. Augustine** <note>original: St. Austin</note> could interpret them otherwise, especially since the author questions whether this Second God were actively **sensible** <note>In this context, "sensible" means capable of perception or having senses</note> or not.

But this is further manifest from other places in that dialogue, as in this example: "The Lord of Eternity is the First God, but the Second God is the World" <note>original Latin: *Æternitatis Dominus Deus Primus est, Secundus est Mundus*</note>. And again: "The Supreme God is the Governor of that Sensible God, which contains within itself all space and all the substance of things" <note>original Latin: *Summus qui dicitur Deus Rector Gubernatorque Sensibilis Dei, ejus qui in se complectitur omnem locum, omnemque rerum substantiam*</note>. 

That it was indeed a part of the <term>Hermaic</term> <note>Relating to Hermes Trismegistus</note> or **Egyptian Theology** that the **Animated Visible World** was a **Second God** and the **Son of the First God** appears also from those Hermaic books published by **Ficinus** <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), a Renaissance scholar who translated these works</note>, commonly called the *Pæmander* <note>Modern spelling: Poimandres</note>, though that is only the first of them. There has been one passage already cited out of the Eighth Book: "The World is a Second God" <note>original Greek: δεύτερος θεὸς ὁ κόσμος (deuteros theos ho kosmos)</note>. After which follows more to the same purpose: 

"The First God is that Eternal, Unmade Maker of all things; the second is he that is made according to the image of the First, which is contained, cherished or nourished, and immortalized by him, as by his own parent, by whom it is made an Immortal Animal" <note>original Greek: πρῶτος γὰρ πάντων ὄντως, ἀΐδιος καὶ ἀγένητος, καὶ δημιουργὸς τῶν ὅλων θεός· ὁ δεύτερος δὲ ὁ κατ’ εἰκόνα αὐτοῦ ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ γενόμενος, καὶ ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ συνεχόμενος καὶ τρεφόμενος καὶ ἀθανατιζόμενος, ὡς ὑπ’ ἰδίου πατρός</note>. 

So again in the Ninth Book: "God is the Father of the World, and the World is the son of God" <note>original Greek: πατὴρ ὁ θεὸς τοῦ κόσμου, καὶ ὁ μὲν κόσμος υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ</note>. And in the Twelfth: "This whole World is a Great God and the Image of a Greater" <note>original Greek: ὁ δὲ σύμπας κόσμος οὗτος ὁ μέγας θεὸς καὶ τοῦ μείζονος εἰκών</note>.

As for the other **Hermetic** or **Trismegistic** books published partly by **Ficinus** and partly by **Patricius** <note>Francesco Patrizi (1529–1597)</note>, we cannot confidently condemn any of them as **Christian frauds** or **impostures**, except for the *Pæmander* and the *Sermon on the Mount concerning Regeneration* (the first and thirteenth of Ficino's chapters or books). Neither of these books is cited by any of the **Ancient Fathers**; therefore, it may be presumed they were not in existence in the time of **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD)</note> but were forged more recently. They were probably forged by one and the same hand, since the writer of the latter (the *Sermon on the Mount*) mentions the former (the *Pæmander*) at its conclusion.

It is questionable whether the "Crater" meant anything like the **Christian Baptistery** <note>original: Baptisterion</note>. # That Other Trismegistick Books, BOOK. I.

Before **Jamblichus’s** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who defended the antiquity of the Hermetic writings</note> time, we know no reason why we should not agree with that learned philosopher in his judgment concerning these books: that though they often speak the **language of philosophers** and were not written by **Hermes Trismegistus** himself, they do really contain **Hermaic opinions** <note>original Greek: δόξας Ἑρμαϊκάς (doxas Hermaïkas)</note> or the **Egyptian doctrine**. The ninth of **Ficino's** <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the first to translate these works into Latin during the Renaissance</note> books mentions the *Asclepian Dialogue* under the Greek title of **The Perfect Oration** <note>original Greek: ὁ τέλειος λόγος (ho téleios lógos)</note>, pretending to have been written by the same hand: 

> "Yesterday, O Asclepius, I delivered the *Perfect Oration*, and now I judge it necessary to follow that by discussing the discourse on Sense." <note>original Greek: χθὲς ὦ Ἀσκληπίε, τὸν τέλεον ἀποδέδωκα λόγον, νῦν δὲ ἀναγκαῖον ἡγῆμαι ἀκόλουθον ἐκείνῳ, καὶ τὸν περὶ αἰσθήσεως λόγον διεξελθεῖν</note> 

The meaning of this passage (which was not understood by the translator) is this:

> I lately published (O Asclepius) the book entitled *The Perfect Oration* and now I judge it necessary, following the same theme, to discourse concerning Sense.

This book, as well as the *Perfect Oration*, is cited by **Lactantius** <note>An early Christian author (c. 250–325 AD) who used Hermetic texts to support Christian ideas</note>. So is the tenth of Ficino's books, called the *Clavis* <note>Latin: "The Key"</note>, which not only claims to be related to the ninth book (and consequently to the *Asclepius* as well) but also to contain a summary of that Hermaic book called the **General Discourses** <note>original Greek: τὰ γενικά (ta genika)</note>, mentioned in **Eusebius’s** *Chronicon*: 

> "I dedicated yesterday’s discourse to you, O Asclepius, but today it is right to dedicate this to Tatius, since it is a summary of those *General Discourses* that were spoken to him." <note>original Greek: τὸν χθὲς λόγον, ὦ Ἀσκληπίε, σοι ἀνέθηκα, καὶ τὸ σήμερον δίκαιόν ἐστι ταῦτα ἀναθεῖναι ἐπεὶ καὶ τῶν Γενικῶν λόγων, τῶν πρὸς αὐτὸν λελαλημένων, ἐστὶν ἐπιτομή</note>

These *General Discourses* are mentioned again later in the same book: 

> "Have you not heard in the *General Discourses* that all souls are derived from the one soul of the universe?" <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἤκουσας ἐν τοῖς γενικοῖς, ὅτι ἀπὸ μιᾶς ψυχῆς τοῦ παντὸς πᾶσαι αἱ ψυχαὶ εἰσίν;</note>

Neither of these two passages was understood by Ficino. But undoubtedly, this latter Hermaic book had something **foisted** <note>inserted or added later by another author</note> into it, because there is a manifest contradiction found there. In the first part, the **transmigration of human souls into animals** <note>original: "brutes"</note> is asserted in the Egyptian way as the **just punishment of a wicked soul** <note>original Greek: ὡς καταδίκην ψυχῆς κακῆς (hos katadikēn psychēs kakēs)</note>, yet later in the same book, this idea is criticized and condemned as the greatest error. 

The eleventh and twelfth following books seem to us to be as **Egyptian** as any of the rest, as does that long book entitled *Kore Kosmou* <note>Greek: "The Virgin of the World"</note>, which is the thirteenth in **Patricius’s** <note>Francesco Patrizi (1529–1597), who reorganized the Hermetic collection</note> edition. In fact, it is observable that even those very books that are justly suspected and condemned as **Christian forgeries** have something of the Hermaic or Egyptian **philosophy** scattered here and there in them. 

For example, when in the *Poimandres* <note>A fundamental text in the Hermetic corpus</note> God is twice called **male and female together** <note>original Greek: ἀῤῥενόθηλυς (arrenothelus)</note>, this seems to have been Egyptian (and was adopted from them by **Orpheus**), according to that elegant passage in the *Asclepian Dialogue* concerning God: 

> "Therefore, he who alone is all things, most full of the fertility of both sexes, being always pregnant with his own will, always produces whatever he has chosen to create." <note>original Latin: *Hic ergo qui Solus est Omnia, utriusque Sexûs fœcunditate plenissimus, semper Voluntatis suæ pregnans, parit semper quicquid voluerit procreare*</note>

Again, when **death** is described in that book as:

> "surrendering the body to change, and for the form you once had to become invisible" <note>original Greek: παραδιδόναι τὸ σῶμα εἰς ἀλλοίωσιν καὶ τὸ εἶδος, ὃ εἶχες, εἰς ἀφανὲς γίνεσθαι</note>

this agrees with what is found in the eleventh book or chapter: 

> "that death is nothing but a change, because the body is dissolved while life passes into the invisible" <note>original Greek: τὴν μεταβολὴν θάνατον εἶναι, διὰ τὸ τὸ μὲν σῶμα διαλύεσθαι, τὴν δὲ ζωὴν εἰς τὸ ἀφανὲς χωρεῖν</note>

as being only the *dissolution* of the *body*, and the *life* or *soul's passing into* the *invisible* or *unseen*. In which book it is also affirmed of the *world*, "that every day some part or other of it goes into the invisible, or into Hades" <note>original Greek: γίνεσθαι μέρος αὐτῶ καθ' ἑκάστην ἡμέραν ἐν τῷ ἀφανεῖ</note>; *that is, it does not utterly perish, but only disappears from our sight, being either translated into some other place or changed into another form.* And accordingly, it is said of *animals* in the *Twelfth Book*, "that they are dissolved by death, not so they might be destroyed, but made again anew" <note>original Greek: διαλύεται, οὐχ ἵνα ἀπόληται ἀλλ' ἵνα νέα γένηται</note>. As it is also affirmed there of the *world*, that it does "make all things out of itself, and again unmake them into itself" <note>original Greek: πάντα ποιεῖν καὶ εἰς ἑαυτὸν ἀποποιεῖν</note>, "and that dissolving all things, it does perpetually renew them" <note>original Greek: καὶ διαλύων πάντα ἀνανεοῖ</note>. For nothing in the whole *world* utterly perishes, as is often declared elsewhere in these *Trismegistic* writings, and particularly in this *Twelfth Book* of *Ficino's* <note>Marsilio Ficino's 1471 Latin translation of the Corpus Hermeticum</note>: "The whole world is unchangeable, only the parts of it are alterable; and this is so because none of these utterly perishes or is absolutely destroyed" <note>original Greek: σύμπας ὁ κόσμος ἀμετάβλητος, τὰ δὲ μέρη αὐτοῦ πάντα μεταβλητά, οὐδὲν δὲ φθαρτὸν ἢ ἀπολλύμενον</note>. "For how can any part of that be corrupted which is incorruptible, or anything of God perish or go to nothing?" <note>original Greek: πῶς μέρος τι δύναται φθαρῆναι τοῦ ἀφθάρτου, ἢ ἀπολέσαι τι τοῦ Θεοῦ;</note> All of which, with *Casaubon's* <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614), a scholar who correctly argued that the Hermetic texts were written in the post-Christian era, though the author here defends their older Egyptian roots</note> leave, we take to have been originally *Egyptian doctrine*, and from there in part afterwards transplanted into *Greece*. Moreover, when in the *Poimandres* <note>A foundational text of the Hermetic corpus</note>, God is styled more than once as "Light and Life" <note>original Greek: φῶς καὶ ζωὴ</note>, this seems to have been *Egyptian* also, because it was *Orphic* <note>Refers to the ancient Greek mystery religion associated with the mythical poet Orpheus</note>. In like manner, the appendix to the *Sermon on the Mount*, called the "Hidden Hymn" <note>original Greek: ὑμνῳδία κρυπτὴ</note>, has some strains of *Egyptian theology* in it, which will be mentioned later.

<margin>On the Vanity of Idols <note>original: De Idol. van.</note></margin>
<margin>St. Augustine, Book 1, page 30.</margin>
The result of our present discourse is this: that though some of the *Trismegistic books* were either wholly counterfeited or else had certain false passages inserted into them by some *Christian* hand, there are others which were originally *Egyptian* or which, as to their substance, contain *Hermetic* or *Egyptian doctrines* (in all of which *One Supreme Deity* is everywhere asserted). We may well conclude from this that the *Egyptians* acknowledged *One Supreme Deity* among them. And in this, several of the *Ancient Fathers* have preceded us; first of all *Justin Martyr*: "Ammon in his books calls God 'Most Hidden,' and Hermes plainly and clearly declares, 'That it is hard to conceive God, but impossible to express him'" <note>original Greek: Ἄμμων πάγκρυφον τὸν Θεὸν ὀνομάζει, Ἐρμῆς δὲ σαφῶς καὶ φανερῶς λέγει, θεὸν νοῆσαι μὲν ἔστι χαλεπὸν φράσαι δὲ ἀδύνατον</note>. It does not follow that this latter passage is counterfeit, as *Casaubon* concludes, simply because there is something like it in *Plato's Timaeus*; there is doubtless a very great agreement between *Platonism* and the *ancient Egyptian doctrine*. Thus again *St. Cyprian* states: "Hermes Trismegistus also speaks of one God, and confesses him to be ineffable and inestimable" <note>original Latin: Hermes quoque Trismegistus Unum Deum loquitur, eumque ineffabilem & inæstimabilem confitetur</note>; this passage is also cited by *St. Augustine*. *Lactantius* likewise writes: "Thoth, the most ancient and most learned in every kind of..." <note>original Latin: Thoth antiquissimus & instructissimus omni genere...</note>

<summary>This page argues that ancient Egyptian philosophy, as preserved in the Hermetic texts, viewed death as a transformation rather than destruction and consistently recognized a single, supreme, and "hidden" God. The author defends the Egyptian origins of these ideas against those who claimed they were merely later Greek or Christian inventions.</summary>

<note>original Latin: ...nere Doctrinæ, adeò ut ei multarum rerum & artium scientia Trismegisti cognomen imponeret; Hic scripsit Libros & quidem multos, ad cognitionem Divinarum rerum pertinentes, in quibus Majestatem Summi & Singularis Dei asserit, iisdemque nominibus appellat, quibus nos, Deum & Patrem. Ac nè quis nomen ejus requireret ἀνώνυμον esse dixit.</note> "...of doctrine, so much so that his knowledge of many things and arts earned him the surname Trismegistus <term>Thrice-Greatest</term>. He wrote many books pertaining to the knowledge of divine matters, in which he asserts the majesty of one Supreme and Singular God, calling him by the same names that we do: God and Father. And lest anyone should demand a proper name for him, he affirmed that he is anonymous." *Thoth* (that is, *Hermes*), the most ancient and most learned in all kinds of learning (for which he was called Trismegistus), wrote many books belonging to the knowledge of divine things. In these, he asserts the majesty of one Supreme Deity, calling him by the same names that we do: God and Father; but (lest anyone should require a proper name for him) affirming him to be anonymous. Lastly, *St. Cyril* <note>Cyril of Alexandria, a 5th-century Church Father</note> has much more to the same purpose as well. We must confess that we have insisted so much on these *Hermetic* or *Trismegistic* writings here so that, in this particular case, we might vindicate these ancient Church Fathers from the accusation of either fraud and imposture, or of simplicity and folly.

But the fact that the Egyptians acknowledged one *Supreme* and *All-comprehending Deity* besides their *many gods* does not need to be proved solely from these *Trismegistic writings* (concerning which we leave others to judge as they find cause). It appears otherwise, not only because *Orpheus* (who was an undoubted supporter of *monarchy* <term>the rule of a single first principle</term>, or *one first principle* of *all things*) is generally affirmed to have derived his doctrine from the Egyptians, but also from plain and express testimonies. For besides the statement of *Apollonius of Tyana* <margin>Page 269.</margin> concerning both *Indians* and *Egyptians* cited earlier, *Plutarch*—throughout his entire book *On Isis and Osiris*—supposes the Egyptians to have asserted *one Supreme Deity* in this way, commonly calling him "the First God" <note>original Greek: τὸν πρῶτον θεὸν</note>. Thus, in the beginning of that book, he tells us that the end of all the religious rites and mysteries of that Egyptian goddess *Isis* was "the knowledge of that First God, who is the Lord of all things and can only be understood by the mind, whom this goddess encourages men to seek in her communion, as he is within her and remains with her" <note>original Greek: ἡ τοῦ πρώτου, καὶ κυρίου, καὶ νοητοῦ γνῶσις, ὃν ἡ θεὸς παρακαλεῖ ζητεῖν παρ' αὐτῇ καὶ μετ' αὐτῆς ὄντα καὶ συνόντα</note>. After which he declares that this *First God* of the Egyptians was considered by them to be an *obscure* and *hidden deity*. Accordingly, he gives the reason why they made the *crocodile* a *symbol* of him: <margin>Page 381.</margin> "Because, they say, the crocodile is the only animal which, living in the water, has his eyes covered by a thin transparent membrane falling down from the forehead, by reason of which it sees and is not seen; which is a quality that belongs to the First God: to see all things, while he himself is not seen" <note>original Greek: μόνος δέ φασιν ἐν ὑγρῷ διαιτώμενος, τὰς ὄψεις ὑμένια λεῖον καὶ διαφανῆ προκαλύπτειν, ἐκ τοῦ μετώπου κατερχόμενον, ὥστε βλέπειν μὴ βλεπόμενον. ὃ τῷ πρώτῳ θεῷ συμβέβηκεν</note>. Though *Plutarch* in that place also gives another reason why the Egyptians made the crocodile a symbol of the Deity: "Neither were the Egyptians without a plausible reason for worshipping God symbolically in the crocodile; it is said to be an imitation of God in that it is the only animal without a tongue. For the divine word <note>Greek: logos, meaning both word and reason</note>—or reason—does not need a voice, and traveling along a silent path, it guides mortal affairs according to justice" <note>original Greek: οὐ μὴν οὐδὲ ὁ κροκόδειλος αἰτίας πιθανῆς ἀμοιροῦσαν ἔσχηκε τιμήν, ἀλλὰ μίμημα θεοῦ λέγεται γεγονέναι μόνος μὲν ἄγλωσσος ὤν, φωνῆς γὰρ ὁ θεῖος λόγος ἀπροσδεής ἐστι, καὶ δι' ἀψόφου βαίνων κελεύθου καὶ δίκης τὰ θνητὰ ἄγει κατὰ δίκην</note>. <header>CHAPTER IV. A First and Supreme God.</header>

...divine *logos* or *Reason*, which does not need speech and follows a silent path of justice in the world, righteously governs and manages all human affairs without noise <note>original Greek: *logos*</note>. In the same way, *Horapollo* <note>original: "Horus-Apollo," the reputed author of a 5th-century treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphics</note> in his *Hieroglyphics* tells us that the Egyptians, acknowledging an *Almighty* and *Ruler of the World* <note>original Greek: *pantokratōr* and *kosmokratōr*</note>—an omnipotent being who governed the whole world—represented him symbolically as a *serpent*. He adds that "they also pictured a great house or palace within its circumference" <note>original Greek: *en mesō autou oikon megan deiknyntes*</note>, because the world is the royal palace of the Deity.

<margin>Book I, chapter 2.</margin>
This writer also gives another reason why the serpent was used as the hieroglyph for the Deity: "The fact that it uses its own body for food signifies that all things generated in the world by divine providence are again received back into it as they diminish" <note>original Greek: *to hōs trophē chrēsthai tō heautou sōmati...*</note>. This aptly signifies that all things produced in the world by Divine Providence eventually return to Him. *Philo of Byblos*, quoting the ancient Phoenician historian *Sanchuniathon*, gives the same reason why the serpent was deified by *Thoth* <note>original: "Taut"</note> (the Egyptian *Hermes*): "because it is immortal and dissolves into itself" <note>original Greek: *hoti athanaton kai eis heauto analyetai*</note>. Sometimes the Egyptians even added a *hawk* to the serpent, combining the symbols of the Deity. According to a famous Egyptian priest quoted by *Eusebius*, "The first and most divine being of all is symbolically represented by a serpent having the head of a hawk" <note>original Greek: *to prōton on theiotaton, ophis esti hierakos echōn morphēn*</note>. The fact that a *hawk* was also sometimes used alone as a symbol for the Deity appears from a passage in *Plutarch*: in the porch of an Egyptian temple at *Sais*, three symbols were engraved—a *young man*, an *old man*, and a *hawk*. Together, they formed this sentence: *That both the beginning and end of human life depend upon God, or Providence.* We have two more remarkable passages in the previously mentioned *Horapollo* concerning Egyptian theology which must not be overlooked <note>original: "pretermitted"</note>. The first is: "According to them, there is a spirit passing through the whole world—namely, God" <note>original Greek: *par’ autois tou pantos kosmou to diēkon esti pneuma*</note>. And again: "It seems to the Egyptians that nothing at all exists without God" <note>original Greek: *dokei autois dicha theou mēden holōs synestanai*</note>.

Next, *Iamblichus* <note>a 4th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> was a person who made it his business to inform himself thoroughly about the theology of the Egyptians. He undertakes to give an account of it in his answer to *Porphyry's* letter to *Anebo*, an Egyptian priest; his testimony, therefore, deserves great credit. He first provides a summary of their theology in this way: "That God, who is the cause of generation, of all nature, and of all the powers within the elements themselves, is separate, exempt, elevated above, and expanded over all the powers and elements in the world. For being above the world and transcending it, he is immaterial, incorporeal, supernatural, uncreated <note>original: "unmade"</note>, and indivisible. Manifested wholly from himself and within himself, he precedes all these things and contains all things within himself; and because he has embraced all things, he also shares them" <note>original Greek: *chōristos, exērēmenos, meteōros...*</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on how the ancient Egyptians viewed the relationship between the supreme God, the material world, and subordinate divine powers, drawing primarily on the work of the Neoplatonist philosopher Iamblichus.</meta>

<page-num>336</page-num>
<header>Hermes Derived Matter and All Things, Book I.</header>

...self, and in himself, he rules over all things and in himself contains all things.

And because he essentially contains all things, he therefore imparts and displays them from himself. According to this excellent description of the Deity, it is plain that the Egyptians, in asserting **One God** who **Comprehends All things**, could not possibly have supposed a **multitude of self-existent deities**. In this same passage, Iamblichus <note>original: "Jamblichus," a 4th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote "On the Mysteries of the Egyptians"</note> also tells us that just as the Egyptian hieroglyphic for material and physical things was mud or floating water, they also pictured God **sitting upon the Lote-tree <note>the Egyptian lotus</note> above the watery mud** <note>original Latin: "in Loto arbore sedentem super Lutum"</note>. **This signifies the most high eminence of the Deity above matter, which ensures that he in no way touches the mud itself. It also demonstrates God’s intellectual empire over the world, because all parts of the Lote-tree—both the leaves and the fruit—are round, representing the circular motion of the intellect, etc.** <note>original Latin: "Quod innuit Dei eminentiam altiffimam, qua fit ut nullo modo attingat Lutum ipsum. Demonstratque Dei imperium intellectuale, quia Loti arboris omnia sunt rotunda tam frondes quàm fructus, &c."</note>. This circularity represents the perfection and self-contained nature of thought. Again, he adds that the Egyptians sometimes pictured God sitting at the helm of a ship.

<margin>Section 8, Chapter 1.</margin>
But afterward in the same book, he summarizes the queries that Porphyry <note>original: "Porphyrius," a Phoenician Neoplatonist philosopher</note> had proposed to the Egyptian priest to be resolved, in this manner: "Do you wish to be shown what the Egyptians consider the first cause to be? Whether it is Intellect or something above Intellect? And whether it exists alone or with others? Whether it is incorporeal or corporeal? And if the first principle is the same as the Demiurge <note>term: the "Architect" or Creator of the world</note> and Architect of the world, or exists before him? Whether all things proceed from One or from Many? Whether they recognize Matter or specific qualities of bodies as the first principle? And if they admit a First Matter, whether they assert it to be unmade or made?" <note>original Greek: βούλει σοι δηλωθῆναι... ἢ γεννητήν;</note>.

In answer to these Porphyrian queries, Iamblichus begins: "I shall first reply to what you first demand. According to the Egyptians, before all entities and universal principles, there is **One God**. He is the first, even before the first God and King <note>likely referring to the Demiurge or creator-god who acts within the world</note>; he is immovable and remains in the solitude of his own unity, there being nothing Intelligible or anything else entwined with him, etc." <note>original Greek: ὴ πρῶτον μὲν... οὔτε ἄλλο τι.</note>.

In these words of Iamblichus and those that follow, although there is some obscurity (and we may perhaps have occasion to further consider their meaning elsewhere), he plainly declares that, according to the Egyptians, the first origin of all things was a perfect **Unity** above Intellect. However, he also intimates that besides this **First Unity**, they did admit certain other divine **hypostases** <note>term: distinct substances or persons of the Godhead</note> (such as a Perfect Intellect and a World-Soul) which were subordinate to and dependent on that Unity. Regarding this, he writes: "**The Egyptians acknowledge, before the heaven and in the heaven, a living power (or Soul), and again they place a pure Mind or Intellect above the world.**" <note>original Greek: τὴν πρὸ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ... προτιθέασι·</note>

<page-num>337</page-num>
# CHAPTER IV. From One Divine Principle.

But that they did not acknowledge a plurality of equal and independent principles is further declared by Iamblichus <note>original: "Jamblichus," a 4th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> in this manner:

> *And thus the Egyptian philosophy, from first to last, starts from Unity and from there descends to multitude. The many are always governed by the One; the infinite or undetermined nature is everywhere mastered and conquered by some finite and determined measure; and all things are ultimately governed by that highest Unity which is the first Cause of all things.* <note>original Greek: καὶ οὕτως ἄνωθεν ἄχρι τῶν τελευταίων ἡ περὶ τῶν ἀρχῶν Αἰγυπτίοις πραγματεία, ἀφ' ἑνὸς ἄρχεται, καὶ πρόεισιν εἰς πλῆθος, τῶν πολλῶν αὖθις ἀφ' ἑνὸς διακυβερνωμένων, καὶ πανταχοῦ τῆς ἀορίστου φύσεως ἐπικρατουμένης ὑπό τινος ὡρισμένου μέτρου, καὶ τῆς ἀνωτάτω ἑνιαίας πάντων αἰτίας·</note>

Moreover, in answer to the last question from Porphyry <note>A critic of the Egyptian mysteries</note> concerning matter—whether the Egyptians thought it was uncreated and self-existent, or made—Iamblichus replies:

> *According to Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Egyptian wisdom</note> and the Egyptians, matter was also made or produced by God; "materiality was cut off and separated from essentiality," as Scutellius translates it.* <note>original Greek: ὕλην δὲ παρήγαγεν ὁ Θεὸς ἀπὸ οὐσιότητος ὑποσχισθείσης ὑλότητος· and Latin: "ab Essentialitate succissa ac subscissa Materialitate"</note>

This passage from Iamblichus is noted by Proclus <note>A 5th-century philosopher</note> in his commentary on the *Timaeus* <margin>Page 117.</margin> (where he asserts that God was the "ineffable cause of matter"):

> *And the tradition of the Egyptians agrees with this: that matter was not unmade or self-existent, but produced by the Deity. For the divine Iamblichus has recorded that Hermes held that materiality was produced from "essentiality" (that is, the passive principle of matter was produced from the active principle of the Deity). And it is very probable from this that Plato also held the same opinion concerning matter, because he is supposed to have followed Hermes and the Egyptians.* <note>original Greek: καὶ ἡ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων παράδοσις τὰ αὐτὰ περὶ αὐτῆς φησίν· ὁ γέ τοι θεῖος Ἰάμβλιχος ἱστόρησεν, ὅτι καὶ Ἑρμῆς ἐκ τῆς οὐσιότητος τὴν ὑλότητα παράγεσθαι βούλεται, καὶ δὴ καὶ εἰκὸς κἀκ τούτου τὸν Πλάτωνα τὴν τοιαύτην περὶ τῆς ὕλης δόξαν ἔχειν·</note>

This is indeed more likely if what Proclus affirms concerning Orpheus is true:

> *That Orpheus also, following this same reasoning, deduced or derived matter from the "first substance of things understood by the mind"—that is, from the Supreme Deity.* <note>original Greek: ὥς τε καὶ Ὀρφεὺς κατὰ τοῦτον τὸν λόγον ἀπὸ τῆς πρωτίστης τῶν νοητῶν ὑποστάσεως παράγει τὴν ὕλην</note>

We shall conclude here, finally, with the testimony of Damascius. In his *Book of Principles*, he writes the following concerning the Egyptians:

> *Eudemus has given us no exact account of the Egyptians. But the Egyptian philosophers of our own times have declared the hidden truth of their theology, having found in certain Egyptian writings that there was, according to them, one principle of all things, praised under the name of the "Unknown Darkness," which is repeated three times. This "Unknown Darkness" is a description of that Supreme Deity who is incomprehensible.* <note>original Greek: Αἰγυπτίους δὲ ὁ μὲν Εὔδημος οὐδὲν ἀκριβὲς ἱστορεῖ· οἱ δὲ Αἰγυπτίοι καθ' ἡμᾶς φιλόσοφοι γεγονότες, ἐξήνεγκαν αὐτῶν τὴν ἀλήθειαν κεκρυμμένην, εὑρόντες ἐν Αἰγυπτίοις δή τισι λόγοις· ὡς εἴη κατ' αὐτοὺς ἡ μὲν μία τῶν ὅλων ἀρχὴ σκότος ἄγνωστον ὑμνουμένη, καὶ τοῦτο τρὶς ἀναφωνούμενον οὕτως·</note>

But that the Egyptians, among their many gods, did acknowledge one supreme God may also appear clearly enough even from their popular <term>original: "vulgar"</term> religion and theology. In this religion, they had a specific and proper name for him as such. For just as the Greeks called the supreme God...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of how ancient Egyptians and other Mediterranean cultures identified their supreme deity, specifically focusing on the god Hammon (Ammon) and his identification with the Greek Zeus and Roman Jupiter.</meta>

<page-num>338</page-num>

# Hammon, the Egyptian Jupiter: Book I

The Egyptians called the god Zeus (known to the Latins as *Jupiter* or *Jovis*) by the name *Hammon* or *Ammon*. This is according to the testimony of *Herodotus*, which has already been cited and confirmed by *Origen*, who was born in Egypt. Similarly, *Plutarch* writes in his book *On Isis and Osiris*: "Most people believe that the proper name for Zeus or Jupiter (that is, the Supreme Deity) among the Egyptians is Amous, which we Greeks pronounce Hammon" <note>original Greek: των πολλων νομιζοντων, ιδιον παρ' αιγυπτιοις ονομα του Διος ειναι, ο Αμουν, ο εσαγοντες ημεις Αμμονα λεγομεν</note>. To the same purpose, *Hesychius* states: "Ammos is Zeus" <note>original Greek: Αμμος ο Ζευς</note>. *Aristotle* also notes that "Ammous, according to Aristotle, is the same as Zeus" <note>original: Ammous according to Aristotle is the same with Zeus</note>. Because of this, Latin writers commonly called him *Jupiter Hammon*. This name *Hammon* was not only used for the Supreme Deity by the Egyptians, but also by the Arabians and all the African peoples, according to the poet *Lucan*:

->*“Although for the peoples of Ethiopia and the blessed*<-
->*Arabian nations, and even the Indians, there is but one Jupiter Ammon.”*<-
<note>original Latin: Quamvis Aethiopum populis Arabumque beatis Gentibus, atque Indis, unus sit Jupiter Ammon.</note>

Therefore, not only was *Marmarica* (a region in Africa containing the most famous temple of this god) named *Ammonia* after him, but all of Africa—as *Stephanus* informs us—was sometimes called *Ammonis* after this god Ammon. He was consequently titled the *Libyan Jupiter* <note>original Greek: Ζευς λιβυκος</note>.

Indeed, it is very probable that the word *Hammon* or *Ammon* was originally derived from *Ham* or *Cham*, the son of *Noah*, whose descendants were primarily settled in these parts of Africa. From him, Egypt was called "the Land of Ham" in the Bible. The Egyptians themselves also used this name; as *Plutarch* testifies, they called it *Chemia* <note>original Greek: χημεία</note>, and *Saint Jerome* notes they called it *Ham*. Even the Coptic people <note>original: Coptites</note> call it *Chemi* to this very day. Nevertheless, this does not prevent the name *Hammon* from being used later by the Egyptians as a name for the *Supreme God*. Among the Greeks, Zeus was likewise thought to have been at first the name of a man or *Hero*, but was later applied to signify the *Supreme God*. There might have been such a mixture of *herology* <term>herology: the study or worship of deified heroes or historical figures</term> (or history) together with theology among the Egyptians, just as there was among the Greeks. 

In fact, some learned men suggest, quite plausibly, that the *Zeus* of the Greeks was actually the same person as that *Ham* or *Cham*, the son of *Noah*, whom the Egyptians first worshiped as a hero or deified man. There are several significant points of agreement and correspondence between the poetic myths of *Saturn* and *Jupiter* and the true biblical story of *Noah* and *Ham*. There is also a great similarity between the words themselves: for just as *Cham* signifies *heat* or *fervor*, the Greek grammarians derive the word *Zeus* from the Greek word for "boiling" <note>original Greek: ζεω, meaning to boil or seethe</note>. In this sense, the previously mentioned testimony of *Herodotus* would be verified: that the Greeks received the names of most of their gods, even of Zeus himself, from the Egyptians.

Perhaps it may also be granted that the Sun was sometimes worshiped...

# CHAPTER IV. Hammon: A Hidden and Indivisible Deity.

He was worshipped by the Egyptians under the name of *Hammon*; just as he was also sometimes worshipped by the Greeks under the name of *Zeus*. And the word corresponds very well with this: *hamah* <note>original Hebrew: חמה</note> in the Hebrew language signifies not only "heat" but also the "sun," from which the word *Chamanim* <note>original Hebrew: חמנים; refers to sun-images or incense altars</note> was also derived. Nevertheless, it does not follow from this that the *visible sun* was generally considered by the Egyptians to be the *supreme deity*, any more than it was among the Greeks. But as we often have occasion to observe, there was a confused jumble of *hero-worship, natural philosophy, and theology* <note>original: Hero-logy, Physiology, and Theology</note> all mixed together in the *pagan religion*. The concept of this Egyptian god *Ammon* was neither limited by them to the *sun*, nor to the entire *physical world* or the *nature of the universe* (as some have thought). This is evident because the Egyptians themselves interpreted the name, according to their own language, to mean *that which was hidden and obscure*. Both *Manetho*, an ancient Egyptian priest, and *Hecatæus* (who wrote concerning the philosophy of the Egyptians) agree on this point in the writings of *Plutarch*: 

"Manetho of Sebennytos believes the word *Amoun* signifies 'that which is hidden,' and that concealment is expressed by this sound. Hecatæus of Abdera says that the Egyptians use this word among themselves when they call to someone who is distant or absent. Therefore, because the First God is invisible and hidden, they call him *Amoun*, as if they were inviting and urging him to approach, to appear, and to make himself known to them." <note>original Greek: μανεθὼς μὲν ὁ Σεβεννύτης τὸ κεκρυμμένον οἴεται καὶ τὴν κρύψιν ὑπὸ ταύτης δηλοῦσθαι τῆς φωνῆς. Ἑκαταῖος δ' ὁ Ἀβδερίτης φησὶ τούτῳ καὶ πρὸς ἀλλήλους τῷ ῥήματι χρῆσθαι τοὺς Αἰγυπτίους, ὅταν τινὰ προσκαλῶνται, προσκλητικὴν γὰρ εἶναι τὴν φωνήν· διὸ τὸν πρῶτον Θεὸν ὡς ἀφανῆ καὶ κεκρυμμένον ὄντα, προσκαλούμενοι καὶ παρακαλοῦντες, ἐμφανῆ γενέσθαι καὶ δῆλον αὐτοῖς, Ἀμοῦν λέγουσι.</note> 

Consistently with this, *Iamblichus* gives us this account of the true meaning of this Egyptian god *Ammon*: 

"The <term>Demiurgical Intellect</term> <note>Demiurgical Intellect: The divine creative mind that shapes the universe.</note> and the master of truth, as it proceeds with wisdom toward creation and brings the secret and invisible power of hidden reasons into the light, is called *Hammon* in the Egyptian language." <note>original Greek: ὁ δημιουργικὸς νοῦς, καὶ τῆς ἀληθείας προστάτης, καὶ σοφίᾳ ἐρχόμενος μὲν ἐπὶ γένεσιν, καὶ τὴν ἀφανῆ τῶν κεκρυμμένων λόγων δύναμιν εἰς φῶς ἄγων, ἀμῶν κατὰ τὴν τῶν Αἰγυπτίων γλῶσσαν λέγεται.</note> 

Therefore, we may conclude that *Hammon* among the Egyptians was not only the name of the *Supreme Deity*, but also of a deity who was *hidden, invisible, and incorporeal* <note>incorporeal: having no physical body or form.</note>.

And here it may be worth our observing that this Egyptian *Hammon* was in all probability mentioned in Scripture, though common <note>original: vulgar</note> interpreters have not realized it. For this is how we understand that passage in *Jeremiah* 46:25: *“The Lord of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: Behold, I will punish* <note>original: visit</note> *Ammon of No* <note>original Hebrew: אמון מנא; the text argues this refers to the god Ammon of the city No (Thebes), rather than the "multitude" of No.</note> *(that is, the god Ammon of the city of No), and Pharaoh, and Egypt, with her other gods and kings, and all who trust in him; I will deliver them into the hands of those who seek their lives, and into the hands of Nebuchadnezzar, King of Babylon.”* To understand this passage, we must observe that according to the language of those ancient pagans, every country or city had its own peculiar and proper names for the gods presiding over them or worshipped by them;

# The Egyptian Hammon, BOOK I.

Among them, the various nations and places were themselves commonly denoted and signified by the names of their respective gods. The Scripture itself also complies with this kind of language; for instance, the Moabites are called *the people of Chemosh* in *Numbers 21*. Similarly, the *gods of Damascus are said to have struck Ahaz* in *2 Chronicles 28* because the Syrians defeated him. Accordingly, whatever was done or attempted against these nations or countries is said to have been done or attempted against their gods. Thus, Moab’s captivity is described in *Jeremiah 48*: *“You shall be taken, and Chemosh shall go into captivity.”* The overthrow of Babylon is predicted in the same manner in the prophecy of *Isaiah, Chapter 46*: *“Bel bows down, Nebo stoops, they themselves are gone into captivity.”* 

The same is also threatened in *Jeremiah, Chapter 51*: *“I will punish Bel in Babylon, and I will bring out of his mouth what he has swallowed up; the nations shall no longer stream to him, for the wall of Babylon shall be broken down.”* Now *Bel*, according to *Herodotus*, was a name for the supreme god among the Babylonians, just as *Ammon* was among the Egyptians—even though both nations worshipped him in an idolatrous manner. Therefore, just as the punishment of *Bel* in those latter passages refers to the punishment of the Babylonians, the punishment of *Ammon* and the gods of *Egypt* in that earlier passage from Jeremiah refers to the punishment of the Egyptians themselves, as is also stated there. 

No was, it seems, the capital <term>original: Metropolis</term> of all *Egypt*. Therefore, *Ammon*—the chief god of those ancient Egyptians and of that city—was called *Ammon* of *No*. Likewise, the city of *No* is named after this god *Ammon* in the Scripture and called both *No-Ammon* and *Ammon-No*. The former appears in the prophecy of *Nahum, Chapter 3*: *“Are you better than No-Ammon?”*—meaning that city of *No* in which the god *Ammon* is worshipped. This is not to be understood as the Oracle of Ammon in Marmarica <note>The Siwa Oasis in the Libyan Desert, famous for its temple of Ammon visited by Alexander the Great.</note>, as some have imagined (thinking that *No* was a common noun meaning "habitation"); it is unquestionably the proper name of a city in Egypt. The latter name appears in *Ezekiel, Chapter 30*: *“I will pour out my fury upon Sin, the strength of Egypt, and will destroy Hammon-No.”* In this passage, while *Sin* refers to *Pelusium* <note>An ancient city on the eastern edge of the Nile Delta.</note>, *Hammon-No* is interpreted by the Septuagint <note>original: Seventy; the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> as *Diospolis*, the "City of Jupiter"—that is, the Egyptian Jupiter, *Hammon*. This *Diospolis* was otherwise called the Egyptian *Thebes* (anciently the capital of all *Egypt*). Its proper name in the Egyptian language seems to have been *No*, which was called both *No-Ammon* and *Hammon-No* after the chief god worshipped there; just as that god was himself named after the city, *Ammon* of *No*.

# The Egyptian Hammon, BOOK I.

Judgment upon *No*, predicted by both *Jeremiah* and *Ezekiel*, describes the place as *situated among the rivers, having the sea for its wall and rampart*. Because of this, many learned men have concluded that this description refers to *Alexandria* rather than *Diospolis* <note>Diospolis is the Greek name for the Egyptian city of Thebes, also known as No.</note> (despite the fact that *Alexandria* did not exist at the time, and was not built until much later during the reign of *Alexander* the Great). We believe this description can be understood as referring to *Egypt* in general, for which this city of *No* served as the capital <term>original: Metropolis</term>. The country was situated among rivers and had the seas—the Red Sea and the Mediterranean—for its wall and rampart. This concludes our discussion of the *Egyptian Jupiter*, or their supreme deity, whom they called **Hammon**.

There is an excellent monument of Egyptian antiquity preserved by *Plutarch* and others, which provides further evidence that the Egyptians did not believe in a multitude of *uncreated, self-existent deities*, but instead acknowledged *one supreme, universal, and all-encompassing Divinity* <note>original: Numen</note>. This evidence is found in the *inscription* upon the Temple at *Sais*: *“I am all that has been, is, and shall be; and no mortal has ever yet uncovered my veil”* <note>original Greek: Ἐγώ εἰμι πᾶν τὸ γεγονός, καὶ ὄν, καὶ ἐσόμενον, καὶ τὸν ἐμὸν πέπλον οὐδείς πω θνητὸς ἀπεκάλυψεν</note>. Although some might interpret this to mean that the deity described was nothing more than the *mindless matter* of the entire physical universe (following the opinion of *Chaereomon* mentioned and refuted earlier), it is clear that this could not be the meaning of the inscription. First, the God described here is not a mere collection <note>original: Congeries</note> of disconnected matter or a grouping of divided atoms, but is *one single thing* which was *everything*. This aligns with another inscription on an altar dedicated to the goddess *Isis*, which we will also use later: *“To you, who being one, are all things”* <note>original Latin: Tibi, Una, quæ es Omnia</note>.

<margin>“Invisible yet manifest.” Proclus says of this Egyptian God that it was both invisible and manifest. *Commentary on the Timaeus*, page 30.</margin> Furthermore, in the deity described here, there is both a *veil* (an exterior appearance) and something *hidden* and *concealed*. The meaning seems to be this: *“I am all that was, is, and shall be; the entire world is nothing but myself veiled; but no mortal has ever yet been able to behold or comprehend my naked and unveiled brightness.”* This is exactly as if the sun should say, “I am all the colors of the rainbow (whose mild and gentle light is easily seen) and they are nothing but my own *simple* and *uniform radiance*, variously refracted and softened; but no mortal can look directly at my immediate splendor and the brightness of my face without being blinded or dazzled by it.” Therefore, this description of the deity seems to resemble the description God makes of himself to *Moses*: *“You shall see my back-parts, but my face shall not be seen.”* In that passage, there is also something exterior and visible in the deity, and something **hidden**, **concealed**, **invisible**, and **incomprehensible** to mortals.

# Chapter IV. That God is All Things.

The temple of *Sais* also had, in accordance with its inscription, a *peplum* <term>a large, shawl-like garment or veil</term> or veil cast over it, similar to the one that *Minerva* or *Artemis* had at *Athens*. This was intended to signify symbolically that the Deity was invisible and incomprehensible to mortals, but had veiled itself in this visible material world. This world is, as it were, the *peplum*—the exterior, variegated, or embroidered garment of the Deity. To all these considerations, we may add, finally, what *Proclus* recorded <margin>In Timaeus, page 30.</margin>—that there was something more to this Egyptian inscription than what is mentioned by *Plutarch*. Specifically, it included these words: *And the sun was the fruit or offspring which I produced* <note>original Greek: καὶ ὃν ἔτεκον κάρπον, ἥλιος ἐγένετο</note>. From this, it is manifest that according to the Egyptians, the sun was not the Supreme Deity. The God described here was, as *Proclus* also observes, a *creative Deity* <note>original Greek: δημιουργικὴ Θεὸς; a "demiurgical" or craftsman-like God</note>, the creator of the whole world and of the sun. This Supreme Incorporeal <term>having no physical body</term> Deity was, nonetheless, said in their theology to be *All Things*, because it diffused itself through *All*.

Therefore, while *Plutarch* cites a passage from *Hecataeus* concerning the Egyptians, stating *that they take the First God and the universe for one and the same thing* <note>original Greek: τὸν πρῶτον Θεὸν τῷ παντὶ τὸν αὐτὸν νομίζειν</note>, the meaning cannot be that the First or *Supreme God* of the Egyptians was the *senseless material world*. *Plutarch* himself, in the very next words, declares him to be *invisible and hidden* <note>original Greek: ἀφανῆ καὶ κεκρυμμένον</note>. Because of this, the Egyptians—as if inviting him to manifest himself to them—called him *Hammon*. As Plutarch affirms elsewhere, *the Egyptians' First God or Supreme Deity saw all things, while he himself was not seen.* Therefore, the previously mentioned passage must be understood this way: according to the Egyptians, the *First God* and the *Universe* (or *the All*) were synonymous expressions, often used to signify the exact same thing. This is because the *First Supreme Deity* is that which contains *all things* and diffuses itself through *all things*. 

This doctrine was passed from the Egyptians to the Greeks. *Orpheus* declared that *all things were one* <note>original Greek: ἓν τὰ πάντα</note>, and after him, *Parmenides* and other philosophers argued *that the universe was one* <note>original Greek: ἓν εἶναι τὸ πᾶν</note>, and that *the universe was immovable* <note>original Greek: τὸ πᾶν ... ἀκίνητον</note>. By this, they meant nothing other than that the *First Supreme Deity* was both *One and All things, and Immovable*. This much is plainly suggested by *Aristotle* in these words: <margin>Metaphysics, Book 1.</margin> *There are some who spoke concerning the whole universe as being but one nature* <note>original Greek: εἰσὶ δέ τινες οἳ περὶ τοῦ παντὸς ὡς ἂν μιᾶς οὔσης φύσεως ἀπεφήναντο</note>. That is, they called the Supreme Deity "the Universe" because it virtually contained *all* things within itself.

Nevertheless, "the Universe" was also frequently understood by the *pagan theologians* (as we have already suggested) in a more comprehensive sense. It represented the *Deity* together with the full extent of its productivity—God as he displays himself in the *world*, or God and the *world* considered together. The latter was looked upon as nothing but an *emanation* or *outflow* from the former. And thus

# Pan, God Diffused through All. Book I.

...was the word used by Empedocles in Plutarch, when he affirmed, *that the world was not the universe, but only a small part of the whole* <note>original Greek: ὁ τὸ πᾶν εἶναι τὸν κόσμον, ἀλλ᾿ ὀλίγον τι τοῦ παντὸς μέρος</note>. And in this sense <note>original: "fence"</note>, the god **Pan** was understood by both the Arcadians and other Greeks—not as the mere physical world, senseless and inanimate, nor as having only a *plastic nature* <term>original: "plastick nature"; a term for an unconscious, forming power in nature</term> (though this was partly included in the idea of Pan), but as proceeding from a rational and *intellectual principle* that diffuses itself through all things. He was seen as the whole system of things—God and the world together as one deity. 

That the *Arcadian Pan* was not the physical world alone, but primarily its *intellectual ruler* and governor, is clear from this testimony by Macrobius: *The Arcadians worship this god (calling him the lord of matter* <note>original Greek: τὸν τῆς ὕλης κύριον</note>), *not as the "Lord of the Woods," but as the ruler or dominator over all material substance.* 

Phornustus <note>likely Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher</note> likewise describes the Pan of the other Greeks in the same way: not as the mere physical world, senseless and inanimate, but as having a rational and intellectual principle as its head and presiding over it. That is, Pan represents God and the world together as one system, the world being the efflux <term>outflowing</term> and emanation of the Deity. The lower parts of Pan (he says) were *rough* and *goat-like* because of the ruggedness of the earth, but his upper parts had a *human form* because the ether, being *rational* and *intellectual*, is the *ruling principle* <note>original: "Hegemonick"</note> of the world. 

He adds to this that Pan was imagined to be *lustful* or *lascivious* because of the *multitude* of *seminal principles* <term>original: "spermatick reasons"; the underlying rational blueprints of all things</term> contained in the world and the continual mixing and generation of things. He is said to be clothed in the *skin* of a *leopard* <note>original: "Libbard"</note> because of the *starlit heavens* and the beautiful variety of things in the world; he lives in a *desert* because of the *singularity* <term>uniqueness</term> of the world; and lastly, he is a good spirit <note>original: "demon"</note> because of the *supreme mind, reason, and understanding that governs everything within it* <note>original Greek: προεστὼς αὐτοῦ λόγος</note>. 

Pan, therefore, was not the mere physical world, senseless and inanimate, but the Deity displaying itself within it and pervading all things. In agreement with this, Diodorus Siculus determines that *Pan* and *Zeus* were but two different names for one and the same deity (as it is well known that the whole universe was frequently called *Jupiter* as well as *Pan* by the Pagans). 

And Socrates himself, in Plato, directs his prayer in a most devout and serious manner to this Pan—that is, not to the physical world or senseless matter, but to an intellectual principle ruling over all, or the Supreme Deity diffusing itself through all. Distinguishing him from the lesser gods, he says: 

> *O Good (or Gracious) Pan, and you other gods who preside over this place: Grant that I may be beautiful or fair within, and that those external things which I have may be such as may best agree with a right internal disposition of mind; and may I account him to be rich who is wise and just.* <note>original Greek: Ω῏ φίλε πὰν, καὶ ἄλλοι ὅσοι τῇδε θεοὶ, δοίητέ μοι καλῷ γενέσθαι τἄνδοθεν, τὰ ἔξωθεν δ᾿ ὅσα ἔχω τοῖς ἐντὸς εἶναι μοι φίλια.</note> 

The content of this prayer, though excellent, is nonetheless *paganly* directed to both Pan (as the Supreme God) and the inferior gods together. Thus we see that as

<meta>This page continues the discussion on how ancient thinkers identified the Supreme God with the totality of the universe (Pan), transitioning into a famous historical anecdote used by both Pagans and Christians to explain the shift in spiritual eras.</meta>

### CHAPTER IV. Demons Lament the Death of Great Pan.

...well according to the Greeks, as with the Egyptians, the First or Supreme God and *the All* <note>original Greek: τὸ πᾶν</note>—the Universe—were really the same thing.

And here we cannot help but notice, in passing, that famous and remarkable story from Plutarch’s treatise *On the Cessation of Oracles* <note>original: *Defect of Oracles*</note>, concerning **demons lamenting the death of the Great Pan**. In the time of the Emperor Tiberius (he says), certain persons embarking from Asia for Italy toward the evening sailed by the Echinades islands. There, being becalmed, they heard a loud voice calling from the shore for one Thamus, an Egyptian mariner among them. After the third call, the voice commanded him that when he reached the Palodes, he must declare that **"The Great Pan is dead."**

Thamus, with the advice of his company, resolved that if they had a steady wind when they reached the Palodes, he would pass by silently; but if they found themselves becalmed there, he would then perform what the voice had commanded. When the ship arrived at that place, there was neither a gust of wind nor any movement of the water. Whereupon Thamus, looking out from the rear deck toward the Palodes, pronounced these words with a loud voice: **"The Great Pan is dead"** <note>original Greek: ὁ μέγας πὰν τέθνηκε</note>. He had no sooner finished speaking than he was answered by a choir of many voices making a great howling and lamentation, mixed with a certain sense of wonder <note>original: "Admiration"</note>. 

Plutarch, who gives much credit to this report, adds how anxious the Emperor Tiberius was, first regarding its truth, and afterward—once he had satisfied himself that it was true—regarding its interpretation. He made great inquiries among his learned men as to who this "Pan" might be. But the only use that philosopher <note>Plutarch</note> makes of this story is to prove that demons, having bodies as well as men (though of a different kind and much more long-lived), were nonetheless mortal. He endeavored to use this to resolve the phenomenon of the *Cessation of Oracles*, arguing that the demons who had formerly haunted those places were now dead. 

However, this being a groundless notion of Plutarch's, it is much more probably concluded by Christian writers that this event—occurring in the reign of Tiberius when our Savior Christ was crucified—was actually the lamentation of evil demons (not without a mixture of amazement) upon the account of our Savior’s death occurring at that very time. They did not mourn out of love for Him who was dead, but because they sadly foretold evil for themselves; they saw it as a threat to their "Kingdom of Darkness" and an end to the tyranny and dominion they had so long exercised over mankind. This aligns with passages of Scripture such as: *Now is the Prince of this world judged*; and *Having spoiled principalities and powers* (by His death upon the Cross), *He triumphed over them in it*. 

Now, our Savior Christ could not be called "Pan" if that word were taken to mean nothing but the physical world devoid of all life, or if it meant only a *plastic nature* <term>an unconscious, organizing force in nature</term>. But this title might very well apply to Him if **Pan** was understood as the **Reason and Understanding presiding over the world** <note>original Greek: λόγος προεστὼς τοῦ κόσμου</note>, by which all things were made and by which they are all governed; or as that **Divine Wisdom which diffuses itself through all** <note>original Greek: φρόνησις διὰ πάντων διήκουσα</note>...

# How the Trismegistic Books Insist, BOOK I.

...things. Moreover, **Pan** being used not so much for the naked and abstract Deity, but for the Deity as if embodied in this **visible, physical world**, might therefore better signify **God manifested in the flesh** and clothed with a specific human body (in which respect alone he was capable of dying). Indeed, there was no other name in all of Pagan theology that could so well fit our Savior Christ as this.

We have now made it manifest that according to ancient **Egyptian theology** (from which Greek and European theology derived), there was one **intellectual Deity**, one **Mind** or **Wisdom**. Just as this Mind produced all things from itself, so does it **contain and encompass the whole** <note>original Greek: περιέχεν τὸ ὅλον (*periechein to holon*)</note> and is itself, in a manner, **all things**. 

We think it appropriate next to observe how this point of **ancient Egyptian theology**—namely, that **God is all things**—is emphasized everywhere throughout the **Hermetic** <note>original: "Hermaick or Trismegistick"</note> writings. We shall begin with the *Asclepian Dialogue*, or the **Perfect Discourse** <note>original Greek: τέλειος λόγος (*teleios logos*)</note>, translated into Latin by Apuleius. At the beginning of this work, the writer declares that **all things belong to One, and One is all things** <note>original Latin: *Omnia Unius esse, & Unum esse Omnia*</note>. He afterwards adds this explanation: 

> "Have we not already declared that **all things are One, and One is all things**? For all things existed in the Creator before he created them. Nor is he improperly called 'All Things,' since all things are his members. Therefore, in this entire discussion, be sure to remember him who is 'One and All Things,' or the Creator of all." <note>original Latin: *Nonne hoc dixi... in tota hac disputatione curato meminisse*</note>

And thus, he later declares that all created things were in the Deity before they were made: 

> "Therefore, they did not properly exist before they were made, yet even then they were in him from whom they were to be produced." <note>original Latin: *Idcirco non erant quando nata non erant, sed in eo jam tunc erant unde nasci habuerunt*</note> 

Again, he writes this concerning God: 

> "I cannot hope to sufficiently express the Author of Majesty and the Father and Lord of all things by any one name, though it were composed of many names. Call him instead by every name, since he is One and All Things; so that, of necessity, either all things must be called 

<margin>Page 612, Colv.</margin>

> by his name, or he must be called by the names of all things. He alone, therefore, is All Things..." <note>original Latin: *non spero totius Majestatis Effectorem... Hic ergo Solus Omnia*</note> 

And when he had spoken of the mutability of created things, he adds: 

> "God alone—in himself, from himself, and around himself—is altogether full and perfect, and he is his own firm stability. He cannot be moved or changed by the impulse of anything, since all things are in him, and he alone is in all things." <note>original Latin: *Solus Deus ipse In se, & A se, & Circum se...*</note>

# CHAP. IV. Upon God Being All Things.

...things. Lastly, to omit other instances, <margin>page 617.</margin> *This Sensible World <note>the world perceived by the senses; original Latin: Hic Sensibilis Mundus</note> is the receptacle of all sensible forms, qualities, or bodies, none of which can be given life <note>original: vegetari</note> and vitalized without God. For God is **all things**, and **all things** are **from God**, and all things are the **effect of his will**. Without God, nothing **was**, nor **is**, nor **shall be**; but all things are **from him**, **in him**, and **through him**. If you consider things in a right manner, you shall learn by true reason that this sensible world, and all the things within it, are covered all over by that superior world (or Deity) as if with a **garment** <note>original Latin: quasi Vestimento</note>.* 

As for the other Hermetic <note>original: Trismegistick</note> books in Marsilio Ficino’s <note>original: Ficinus</note> edition, the third of them, titled the **Sacred Discourse** <term>original Greek: ἱερὸς λόγος (*hieros logos*)</term>, concludes this way: *The Divinity is the entire cosmic composition <note>original: Mundane Compages</note> or constitution, viewed according to its nature; for nature is also established within the Divinity.* <term>original Greek: τὸ γὰρ θεῖον ἡ πᾶσα κοσμικὴ σύγκρασις, φύσει ἀναθεωρουμένη· ἐν γὰρ τῷ θείῳ καὶ ἡ φύσις συγκάθεστηκεν·</term> 

In the fifth book, written upon this argument, **That the Invisible God is Most Manifest** <term>original Greek: ὅτι ἀφανὴς θεὸς φανερώτατός ἐστι</term>, we read the following: *For there is nothing in that whole universe which he is not. He is both the things that exist and the things that do not exist; for the things that exist he has manifested, but the things that do not exist he contains within himself.* <term>original Greek: οὐδὲν γάρ ἐστιν ἐν παντὶ ἐκείνῳ, ὃ οὐκ ἔστιν αὐτός... τάδε μὴ ὄντα ἔχει ἐν ἑαυτῷ·</term> 

And again: *He is both incorporeal <note>without a physical body</note> and omnicorporeal <note>possessing all bodies; original Greek: πολυσώματος</note>; for there is nothing of any body which he is not. He is all things that are, and therefore he has all names, because all things are from one Father; and therefore he has no name, because he is the Father of all things.* <term>original Greek: ἔστιν ὁ ἀσώματος καὶ ὁ πολυσώματος... ὅτι πάντων ἐστὶ πατήρ·</term> 

And at the close of the same book: *With what shall I praise you? For those things which you have made? Or for those things which you have not made? For those things which you have manifested, or for those things which you have hidden and concealed within yourself? And for what cause shall I praise you? As if I were my own, as having something of my own, or being distinct from you? For you are whatever I may be; you are whatever I may do; you are whatever I may say. For you are all things, and there is nothing else which you are not. You are all that has been made, and you are all that has not been made.* <term>original Greek: ὑπὲρ τίνος σε ὑμνήσω... σὺ πᾶν τὸ γενόμενον, σὺ τὸ μὴ γενόμενον·</term> 

Here it is noteworthy that before things were made, God is said **to hide** <term>original Greek: κρύπτειν (*kryptein*)</term> them within himself; but when they are made, he is said **to manifest** <term>original Greek: φανεροῦν (*phaneroun*)</term> and reveal them from himself. 

In the eighth book: *Understand that the whole world is from God and in God; for God is the beginning, the container <note>original: Comprehension; in the sense of encompassing or holding all things</note>, and the constitution of all things.* <term>original Greek: νόησον ὅτι ὁ μὲν κόσμος ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ ἐν τῷ θεῷ... ὁ θεός·</term>
