and the constitution of all things. Book the Ninth: <note>original Greek: μᾶλλον ἢ λέγω ὅτι οὐκ αὐτὸς αὐτὰ ἔχει, ἀλλὰ τὸ ἀληθὲς ἀποφαίνομαι, αὐτὸς ἅπαντά ἐστιν· οὐκ ἔξωθεν αὐτὰ προσλαμβάνων, ἔξω δ' ἐπιδιδός·</note> *I would not say that God **has** all things, but rather declare the truth and say that he **is** all things; not as if receiving them from the outside, but as sending them forth from himself.* Again, later in the same book: <note>original Greek: καὶ οὐκ ἔσται πότε χρόνος, ὅτε ἀπολειφθήσεταί τι τῶν ὄντων· ὅταν δὲ λέγω τῶν ὄντων, λέγω τοῦ Θεοῦ· τὰ γὰρ ὄντα ὁ Θεὸς ἔχει, καὶ οὔτε αὐτῷ οὐδὲν ἐκτός, οὔτε αὐτὸς οὐδενός·</note> *There shall never be a time when anything that exists shall cease to be; for when I speak of "anything that is," I am speaking of God. For God contains all things within himself, and there is nothing outside of God, nor is God outside of anything.* 

Book the Tenth: <note>original Greek: τί γάρ ἐστι Θεὸς, καὶ πατὴρ, καὶ τὸ ἀγαθὸν, ἢ τὸ τῶν πάντων εἶναι οὐκ ἔτι ὄντων· ἀλλὰ ὕπαρξις αὐτὴ τῶν ὄντων;</note> *What is God, the Father and the Good, but the very Being of all things that do not yet exist, and the actual existence of things that do?* And again: <note>original Greek: ὁ Θεὸς, καὶ πατὴρ καὶ τὸ ἀγαθὸν, τῷ εἶναι τὰ πάντα,</note> *God is both the Father and the Good because he is all things.* 

Book the Eleventh: <note>original Greek: αὐτουργὸς γὰρ ὢν ἀεί ἐστιν ἐν τῷ ἔργῳ, αὐτὸς ὢν ὃ ποιεῖ· εἰ γὰρ χωρισθείη αὐτοῦ, πάντα μὲν συμπεσεῖσθαι, πάντα δὲ τεθνηξέσθαι ἀνάγκη·</note> *Since God acts directly from himself, he is always present in his own work, being himself that which he creates. For if his work were even slightly separated from him, all things would necessarily collapse and die.* Again: <note>original Greek: πάντα ἐστιν ἐν τῷ Θεῷ, οὐχ ὡς ἐν τόπῳ κείμενα,</note> *All things are in God, but not as if they were situated in a physical location.* 

And further, since our own soul can—through thought <note>original: Cogitation</note> and imagination <note>original: Phancy</note>—become whatever it wishes and go wherever it wishes, taking any form or being in any place: <note>original Greek: τοῦτον οὖν τὸν τρόπον νόησον τὸν Θεὸν, ὥσπερ νοήματα πάντα ἐν ἑαυτῷ ἔχειν, τὸν κόσμον αὐτὸν ὅλον·</note> *In this same way, you may think of God as containing the entire world within himself, just as the mind holds its own thoughts and ideas.* And at the close of that chapter, a passage also cited by St. Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria, a 5th-century Church Father who often quoted the Hermetica to show parallels with Christian doctrine.</note> serves the same purpose: <note>original Greek: ἀόρατος ὁ Θεός; εὐφήμησον καὶ τίς αὐτοῦ φανερώτερος· δι’ αὐτὸ τοῦτο πάντα ἐποίησεν, ἵνα διὰ πάντων αὐτὸν βλέπῃς· τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ ἀγαθὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ· τοῦτο δὲ αὐτοῦ ἀρετὴ, τὸ αὐτὸ φαίνεσθαι διὰ πάντων·</note> *Is God invisible? Speak reverently of him; for who is more manifest than he? For this very reason, he made all things: so that you might see him through all things. This is the goodness and excellence <note>original: Vertue</note> of the Deity—to be visible through all things.* The mind is seen through the act of thinking, but God is seen through the act of working or creating. 

Book the Twelfth: <note>original Greek: ἤκουσα τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ δαίμονος λέγοντος (ἐκεῖνος γὰρ μόνος, ὦ τέκνον, ἀληθῶς ὡς πρωτόγονος θεὸς, τὰ πάντα κατιδὼν, θείος λόγος ἐφθέγξατο) ἤκουσα γοῦν αὐτοῦ ποτὲ λέγοντος, ὅτι ἕν ἐστι τὰ πάντα·</note> *I have heard the Good Spirit <note>original: good Demon (*Agathos Daimon*); in this context, a "demon" refers to a divine or benevolent spiritual being, not an evil one.</note> say (for he alone, as the first-born God who beholds all things, spoke divine words)—I have heard him say that all things are one.* Again in the same chapter: <note>original Greek: ὁ δὲ σύμπας κόσμος οὗτος ἡνωμένος ἐκείνῳ, καὶ συνσώζων τὴν τάξιν, καὶ βούλησιν τοῦ πατρὸς, πλήρωμά ἐστι τῆς ζωῆς· καὶ οὐδέν ἐστιν ἐν τούτῳ διὰ παντὸς τοῦ αἰῶνος, οὔτε τοῦ παντὸς, οὔτε τῶν κατὰ μέρος, ὃ οὐχὶ ζῆ, νεκρὸν γὰρ οὐδὲ ἕν, οὔτε γέγονεν, οὔτε ἐστίν, οὔτε ἔσται ἐν κόσμῳ·</note> *This entire world is intimately united to him, and by following the order and will of its Father, it contains the fullness of life. Nothing within it throughout eternity—whether as a whole or in part—is without life; for there neither is, nor has been, nor shall be anything dead in the world.* The meaning is that all things depend for their life upon the Deity, who is described in Scripture as the one who gives life and vitality to everything.

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Hermetic texts, specifically focusing on the Egyptian theological concept that God is "The All" (the Universe) and "The One," and how different divine names like Neith and Isis refer to this single, all-encompassing power.</meta>

<page-num>409</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER IV. With the Old Egyptian Theology.</header>

<note>original Greek: τοῦτό ἐστιν ὁ Θεὸς, τὸ πᾶν· ἐν ᾧ τῷ παντὶ, οὐδέν ἐστιν ὁ μήἐστιν· ὅθεν οὔτε μέγεθος, οὔτε τόπος, οὔτε ποιότης, οὔτε σχῆμα, οὔτε χρόνος περὶ τὸν θεόν ἐστι· πᾶν γὰρ ἐστι, τὸ δὲ πᾶν διὰ πάντων καὶ περὶ πάντα·</note> *This is God: the Universe, or the All. And in this Universe, there is nothing which he is not. Therefore, there is neither size, nor place, nor quality, nor shape, nor time regarding God, for he is All or the Whole (whereas those specific traits belong only to individual parts).* And the *Arcane Song* <note>original: *Arcane Cantion*</note>, although that thirteenth book to which it is subjoined is likely a forgery <note>original: "supposititious"</note>, still emphasizes this point of Egyptian theology: *That God is All.* <note>original Greek: ὑμνεῖν μέλλω τὸν τῆς κτίσεως κύριον, τὸ πᾶν, καὶ τὸ ἕν·</note> *I intend to praise the Lord of creation, the All and the One.* And again: *All the powers that are in me, praise the One and the All.* 

Book the Fifteenth: <note>original Greek: ἐάν τις ἐπιχειρήσῃ τὸ πᾶν καὶ ἓν χωρίσαι, τὸ πᾶν τοῦ ἑνὸς λύσας ἀπολέσει τὸ πᾶν, πάντα γὰρ ἓν εἶναι δεῖ·</note> *If anyone attempts to separate the All from the One, by breaking the All away from the One, he will destroy the All (or the Universe); for all things must be One.* 

Book the Sixteenth: <note>original Greek: ἄρξομαι δὲ λόγῳ ἔνθεν, τὸν θεὸν ἐπικαλεσάμενος, τὸν τῶν ὅλων δεσπότην, καὶ ποιητὴν, καὶ πατέρα, καὶ περίβολον, καὶ πάντα ὄντα τὸν ἕνα, καὶ ἕνα ὄντα τὰ πάντα· τὸ πάντων γὰρ τὸ πλήρωμα, ἕν ἐστι, καὶ ἐν ἑνί·</note> *I will begin with a prayer to him who is the Lord, Maker, Father, and encompassing boundary <note>original: περίβολον (*peribolon*)</note> of all things; who, being All things, is One, and being One, is All things. For the fullness of all things is One, and resides in One.* 

And again: <note>original Greek: μόρια τοῦ θεοῦ πάντα ἐσίν· εἰ δὲ πάντα μόρια, πάντα ἄρα ὁ θεός· πάντα οὖν ποιῶν, ἑαυτὸν ποιεῖ·</note> *All things are parts of God. But if all things are parts of God, then God is All things. Therefore, in making all things, he essentially makes himself.*

Now, by all this we see how well these Hermetic <note>original: *Trismegistick*</note> books agree with that ancient Egyptian inscription in the Temple of Sais: *That God is all that was, is, and shall be.* Because Egyptian theology so clearly asserts that there is **One God who was all things**, it is completely impossible that they could have acknowledged a multitude of self-existent and independent deities.

Up to this point, we have noted **two** different Egyptian names for the same supreme deity: *Hammon* and *Neith*. But we shall find that, besides these, the supreme God was sometimes worshipped by the Egyptians under other names and concepts <note>original: "notions"</note> as well, such as *Isis*, *Osiris*, and *Sarapis*. 

First, although *Isis* has been interpreted by some as the Moon, by others as the whole Earth, by others as Ceres (the goddess of corn), and by others as the land of Egypt itself—the sense in which the Egyptians deified these things will be explained elsewhere—she was undoubtedly also sometimes understood as an universal and all-comprehending deity <term>numen</term>. Plutarch affirms that Isis and Neith were actually one and the same god among the Egyptians. Therefore, the Temple of Neith (or Minerva <note>Minerva is the Roman equivalent of Neith</note>) at Sais, where the previously mentioned inscription was found, is called by him the "Temple of Isis." Thus, Isis—just like Neith or Minerva among the Egyptians—was described there as that God who is *all that was, is, and shall be,* and whose veil no mortal has ever uncovered. This indicates she was not a particular local god, but an universal and all-encompassing deity <term>numen</term>. This can be further confirmed by an ancient inscription and dedication to the goddess Isis, which still exists at Capua.

<header>Isis, One and All Things. BOOK I.</header>

->To you,<-
->The Goddess Isis,<-
->Who are<-
->One and All things.<-
<note>original Latin: TIBI. UNA. QUÆ. ES. OMNIA. DEA. ISIS.</note>

<margin>Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, Book 11</margin>Where the Goddess **Isis** is plainly declared to be <note>original Greek: ἕν καὶ πάντα</note> **One and All things**, that is, a *Universal* and *All-comprehending Deity*. This also agrees with the speech of the Goddess **Isis** in the works of Apuleius:

<note>original Latin: En adſum tuis, commota, Luci, precibus, rerum Natura Parens, elementorum omnium Domina, ſeculorum Progenies initialis: Summa numinum, Regina marium, Prima Cœlitum, Deorum Dearumque Facies uniformis; quæ cæli luminoſa culmina, maris ſalubria flamina, inferorum deplorata ſilentia, nutibus meis diſpenſo. Cujus Numen unicum multiformi ſpecie, ritu vario, nomine multijugo totus veneratur orbis</note>

> *Behold, I am here, moved by your prayers, Lucius—I, the Parent of Nature, the Mistress of all the elements, the first-born of the ages, the highest of the divine powers, the Queen of the seas, the first of the heavenly inhabitants, the uniform face of gods and goddesses. With my nods, I govern the luminous heights of the heavens, the health-giving breezes of the sea, and the mournful silences of the underworld. My single divinity is worshipped and adored by the whole world in a multiform manner, with various rites and under many different names.*

From these words, it is clear that this Goddess **Isis** was not merely the animated **Moon** (which was instead a symbol of her), but that she was a *Universal Deity* who included the entire nature of things. She was the One Supreme God worshipped by the Pagans under several names and with different rites. This is the plain meaning of those final words, <note>original Latin: Numen Unicum</note> "the unique divinity"—that the whole world worships *one and the same Supreme God in a multiform manner, with various rites, and under many different names.* For besides the several names of the other Pagans mentioned there, the Egyptians worshipped this deity under the names of **Hammon**, **Neith**, and others that shall be described later. 

Thus **Isis** was again worshipped and invoked as the "only divine power" <note>original Latin: unicum Numen</note> by Apuleius himself in these following words:

<note>original Latin: Tu ſancta & humani generis Soſpitatrix perpetua, dulcem matris affectionem miſeris tribuis, fatorum inextricabiliter contorta retractas lina, fortunæ tempeſtates mitigas, & ſtellarum noxios meatus cohibes: Te Superi colunt, obſervant Inferi. Tu rotas orbem, luminas ſolem, regis mundum, calcas Tartarum. Tibi reſpondent ſydera, gaudent numina, ſerviunt elementa: Tuo nutu ſpirant flamina, &c.</note>

> *You, holy and perpetual Savior of Mankind, who are always bountiful in cherishing mortals and show the tender affection of a mother to them in their calamities; you untangle the twisted threads of Fate, calm the storms of Fortune, and restrain the harmful movements of the stars. The gods above worship you, and the powers below obey you. You rotate the globe, light the sun, rule the world, and tread upon Tartarus (Hell). The stars answer to you, the deities rejoice, and the elements serve you. At your command, the winds blow, etc.*

In this passage, **Isis** is clearly understood to be a Universal Divine Power <note>original Latin: Numen</note> and the supreme monarch of the world. Neither may this...

# CHAP. IV. Osiris and Serapis the Supreme Divine Power <term>numen: a Latin word for a deity or divine will</term>.

This did not prevent her from being called a Goddess, just as **Neith** also was; these Pagans regarded their Deities as being indiscriminately of either sex, male or female. But **Osiris** was even more clearly taken for the Supreme Deity. His name was sometimes said to have signified in the Egyptian language, **many-eyed** <note>original Greek: πολυόφθαλμος</note>, and sometimes **an active and beneficent force** <note>original Greek: κράτος ἐνεργῶν, καὶ ἀγαθοποιόν</note>. His hieroglyph was an eye and a scepter; the former signifying Providence and Wisdom, and the latter Power and Majesty (as **Plutarch** tells us). He is also described this way by **Apuleius**: *Osiris is that God who is the chiefest of the Greater Gods, the Greatest of the Chiefest, the Mightiest of the Mightiest, and the Ruler of the Greatest* <note>original Latin: Deus Deorum magnorum potior, & majorum summus, & summorum Maximus, & Maximorum Regnator, Osiris</note>. Therefore, the same Apuleius also tells us that **Isis** and **Osiris** were really one and the same Supreme **Divine Power**, though considered under different concepts and worshipped with different rituals, in these words: *Though Isis and Osiris are really one and the same divine power, yet their rites and ceremonies are very different* <note>original Latin: Quanquam connexa imo vero unica, ratio Numinis, Religionisque esset, tamen Teletæ discrimen esse maximum</note>. The proper definition of **Osiris** was thus declared by **Plutarch** as *that First and Highest of all Beings, which is the same as Good* <note>original Greek: τὸ πρῶτον καὶ κυριώτατον πάντων, ὃ τ᾽ ἀγαθῷ ταὐτόν ἐσι</note>.

<margin>Book 5, page 257.</margin>
Agreeing with this, **Iamblichus** affirms that *God, as the cause of all good, is called Osiris by the Egyptians* <note>original Greek: ἀγαθῶν ποιητικός ὢν Ὄσιρις κέκληται</note>. Lastly, as for **Serapis**, although **Origen** tells us that this was a new, upstart deity set up by **Ptolemy** in Alexandria, this God—in his oracle to **Nicocreon**, the King of Cyprus—declares himself also to be a Universal **Divine Power**, encompassing the whole world, in these words: *The starry heaven is my head, the sea my belly, my ears are in the ether, and the bright light of the sun is my clear, piercing eye* <note>original Greek: οὐράνιος κόσμος κεφαλὴ, &c.</note>. And undoubtedly he was worshipped by many under this concept. For as **Phylarchus** wrote concerning him, *Serapis was the name of that God who orders and governs the whole world* <note>original Greek: Σάραπις ὄνομα τοῦ τὸ πᾶν κοσμοῦντος</note>; so does **Plutarch** himself conclude that **Osiris** and **Serapis** were *both names of one God and the same divine power* <note>original Greek: ἄμφω ἑνὸς θεοῦ καὶ μιᾶς δυνάμεως</note>. Accordingly, **Diodorus Siculus** determines that these three—**Hammon**, **Osiris**, and **Serapis**—were but different names for one and the same deity, or Supreme God.

<margin>Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 4, Chapter 23.</margin>
Despite this, it seems **Porphyry** had a very low opinion of the power that manifested itself in the temple of this god **Serapis**. Above all the other Pagan gods, he suspected it to be none other than the very prince of evil demons or devils: *We do not suspect or conjecture without reason that the evil demons are under Serapis as their prince and head; this appears (he says) not only from those rites of appeasement used in the worship of this god, but also from his symbol, which was a three-headed dog, signifying that evil demon which rules in those three elements: water, earth, and air* <note>original Greek: τὰς δὴ πονηρὰς δαίμονας οὐκ εἰκῆ ὑπὸ τὸν Σαράπιν ὑποπτεύομεν, ἐδ᾽ ἐκ τῶν συμβόλων μόνον ἀναπειθέντες, &c.</note>. Indeed, it cannot be doubted that it was an evil demon or devil that delivered oracles in this temple of **Serapis**, as well as elsewhere among the Pagans, regardless of how much he desired to be worshipped as the Supreme God.

<summary>This page argues that the Egyptian gods Osiris and Serapis were viewed by ancient philosophers and historians as names for the supreme, universal deity. It also notes Porphyry's dissenting view that Serapis was actually a prince of evil demons, despite being worshipped as the highest god.</summary>

# The Egyptian Trinity; Eicon, Book I.

<margin>Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 3, Chapter 11, page 115.</margin>

Besides all this, **Eusebius** himself, citing **Porphyry**, informs us that the **Egyptians** acknowledged **One Intellectual Demiurgus** <term>Demiurgus: a Greek term for a "craftsman" or creator of the universe</term>, or Maker of the World, under the name of **Cneph**. They worshipped him in a statue of human form with a dark, sky-colored complexion, holding a girdle and a scepter in his hand, wearing a princely plume upon his head, and thrusting an egg out of his mouth. The reason for this hieroglyph <term>hieroglyph: a sacred carving or symbol representing a concept</term> is given as follows: *Because Wisdom and Reason, by which the world was made, is not easy to be found out but is hidden and obscure; and because this is the fountain of life and king of all things; and because it is intellectually moved (signified by the feathers upon his head).* <note>original Greek: ὅτι λόγον δυσεύρετον καὶ κεκρυμμένον, καὶ οὐ φανὸν, καὶ ὅτι ζωοποιὸς, καὶ ὅτι βασιλεύς, καὶ ὅτι νοερῶς κινεῖται· διὸ ἡ τοῦ πτεροῦ φύσις ἐν τῇ κεφαλῇ κεῖται</note> Moreover, by the **Egg** thrust out of the mouth of this God, was meant the world, created by the Eternal **Logos** <term>Logos: the Divine Word or Reason</term>. From this **Cneph**, it was said that **another God** was generated or produced, whom the Egyptians call **Phtha** and the Greeks call **Vulcan**; we will discuss **Phtha** more later. 

That the **Egyptians** were the most eminent supporters of the **Cosmogony** <term>Cosmogonia: the theory of the origin or "birth" of the universe</term>, or the idea that the world had a temporary beginning, has already been declared. For this reason, the commentator <term>Scholiast: an ancient commentator or annotator of a text</term> on **Ptolemy** thus criticizes them: *The Egyptians were accustomed to talk perpetually of the birth or generation of the world.* <note>original Greek: ὡς ἡμᾶς εἰώθασι λέγειν φύσειν Αἰγüπτιοι κόσμος</note> And **Asclepius**, an ancient **Egyptian** writer, in his work *Myriogenesis*, affirms that according to **Egyptian** tradition, the sun was created when the constellation **Libra** was ascending.

<margin>Scaliger, *The Emendation of Time*, Book 5, on the creation of the world.</margin>

But it is evident from this testimony of **Porphyry** that the **Egyptians** did not suppose the world to have been made by chance (as **Epicurus** and other atheistic philosophers did), but by an **Intellectual Demiurgus** whom they called **Cneph**. This **Cneph** was looked upon by them as an **uncreated** and **eternal** deity. For this very reason, the inhabitants of **Thebais** <note>Thebais: the region around the ancient city of Thebes in Upper Egypt</note> refused to worship any other god besides him, as **Plutarch** informs us in these 

<margin>Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*.</margin>

words: *While the other Egyptians paid their portion of the tax imposed upon them for the nourishment of those sacred animals worshipped by them, the inhabitants of Thebais alone refused, because they would acknowledge no mortal god, and worshipped him only whom they call Cneph, an unmade and eternal deity.* <note>original Greek: εἰς δὲ τὰς γραφὰς τῶν τιμωμένων ζώων, τὰς μὲν ἄλλας συντεταμένα τελεῖν, μόνους δὲ μὴ διδόναι τὰς Θηβαΐδα κατοικοῦντας, ὡς θνητὸν θεὸν οὐδένα νομίζοντες, ἀλλὰ ὃν καλοῦσιν αὐτοὶ Κνὴφ, ἀγένητον ὄντα καὶ ἀθάνατον</note>

Having now made it undeniably manifest that the **Egyptians** had an acknowledgment among them of **One Supreme, Universal, and Uncreated Deity**, we shall conclude this entire discourse with the two following observations. First, that a great part of **Egyptian Polytheism** was really nothing else but the worshipping of **one and the same Supreme God** under many different names and concepts, such as **Hammon**, **Neith**, **Isis**, **Osiris**, **Serapis**, and **Cneph**, to which may be added **Phtha**, and those other names found in **Iamblichus**, such as **Eicton** and **Emeph**. That pagans universally throughout the whole world did the same was also affirmed by **Apuleius** in that previously cited passage of his: *A single Divine Power, in many-formed appearance, with various rituals, and under manifold names.* <note>original Latin: Numen Unicum, multiformi specie, ritu vario, nomine multijugo</note>

<summary>This page argues that Egyptian religion centered on a single, eternal creator god named Cneph, and that their various other gods were merely different names for this one supreme deity. It highlights that the inhabitants of Thebais specifically rejected animal worship in favor of this uncreated God.</summary>

# ### Chapter IV: Cneph (or Emeph) and Phtha.

"...the whole world worships <note>original Latin: *totus veneratur orbis*</note> only one Supreme Divinity <term>Numen: a divine power or spirit</term> in many forms, under different names and with different rites." These different names for one and the same Supreme God might therefore be mistaken by some of the foolish common people <note>original: "sottish Vulgar"</note> among the pagans—as well as by learned men of more recent times—for many distinct, uncreated, and self-existing deities.

Nevertheless, a question may well be raised: among those several Egyptian names for God, might some not signify distinct, subordinate divine hypostases <term>hypostases: distinct persons or substances within a single godhead</term>? Specifically, were there any footsteps of a Trinity to be found in ancient Egyptian theology? Since Orpheus, Pythagoras, and Plato—all of whom asserted a Trinity of divine hypostases—unquestionably derived much of their doctrine from the Egyptians, it may reasonably be suspected that the Egyptians did the same before them. 

Indeed, **Athanasius Kircherus** <note>a 17th-century Jesuit scholar and polymath</note> has no doubt at all about this. He tells us that on the **Pamphylian Obelisk**, the first hieroglyph of a winged globe with a serpent emerging from it was the Egyptian symbol of a threefold deity, or a Trinity of divine hypostases. He confirms this using the testimony of **Abenephius** (an Arabian writer) and a Chaldean fragment attributed to **Sanchuniathon**. The globe is said to signify the first incomprehensible Deity, without beginning or end and self-existent; the serpent signifies the Divine Wisdom and creative virtue; and lastly, the wings signify that Active Spirit which nourishes, gives life to, and animates <note>original: "cherisheth, quickneth, and enliveneth"</note> all things. 

How much credit should be given to this interpretation, we leave for others to judge. However, the clearest evidence we can find anywhere of an Egyptian Trinity is in **Iamblichus's** book written concerning their *Mysteries*. That entire passage is worth setting down here: 

<note>The following is a modernization of the Greek passage from Iamblichus, *On the Mysteries*, Section 8, Chapter 2: κατ᾽ ἄλλω ἢ τάξιν προστάττειν ἢ ἔπεσι [Ἐρμῆς] Θεὸν ἓν Ἡμεφ, θεῶν ἡγέμενον...</note> 

"According to another order or method, **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage to whom many Egyptian works were attributed</note> places the God **Emeph** <gloss>* or Cneph</gloss> as the Prince and Ruler over all the celestial gods, whom he affirms to be a Mind understanding himself and converting his thoughts or intellections into himself. Before this **Emeph**, he places one indivisible Being, whom he calls **Eikton**, in which is the first 'Intelligible' <term>Intelligible: a philosophical term for that which can be known by the mind rather than the senses</term>, and who is worshipped only by silence. After these two, **Eikton** and **Emeph**, the **Demiurgic** <gloss>* or creator</gloss> Mind and President of truth—as it proceeds to generations with wisdom and brings forth the hidden powers of secret reasons into light—is called in the Egyptian language **Ammon**. As it skillfully <note>original: "Artificially"</note> effects all things with truth, it is called **Phtha** (whom the Greeks, attending only to the skill involved, call **Hephaestus** or **Vulcan**). As it is productive of Good, it is called **Osiris**; besides other names that it has according to its other powers."

<summary>This page explores the potential for a "Trinity" in ancient Egyptian theology, citing symbols like the winged globe and the philosophical hierarchy of deities (Eikton, Emeph, and Ammon/Phtha) described by Iamblichus.</summary>

<keywords>Egyptian Trinity, Cneph, Emeph, Phtha, Eikton, Iamblichus, Athanasius Kircherus, Hermes Trismegistus, Monotheism, Hypostases, Ancient Egyptian Religion</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the Egyptian Trinity, focusing on the writings of Iamblichus and other ancient philosophers to show how Egyptian names for God correspond to the Greek concepts of Unity, Mind, and Soul.</meta>

# The Allegory of Osiris BOOK I.

**Powers and Energies.** In this passage from *Iamblichus* <note>a Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote "On the Mysteries of the Egyptians"</note>, we clearly see three **Divine Hypostases** <term>hypostases: distinct persons or substances within a single godhead</term>, or universal, subordinate principles, according to the **Hermetic Theology**. First is an **Indivisible Unity** called *Eicton*. Second is a **Perfect Mind** that directs its own thoughts inward toward itself, called *Emeph* or *Hemphta*. Third is the immediate principle of **Generation** <term>generation: the act of producing or creating life and the physical world</term>, called by several names according to its various powers, such as *Phtha*, *Ammon*, *Osiris*, and the like. So, according to *Iamblichus*, these three names (among others) signified one and the same third divine person in Egyptian theology.

I do not need to explain here how well these three divine persons of the Egyptians agree with the **Pythagorean** or **Platonic** Trinity:
1. First, "the One" or "the Good" <note>original Greek: τὸ ἕν or τἀγαθὸν</note>, which is Unity and Goodness itself.
2. Second, "Mind" <note>original Greek: νοῦς</note>.
3. Third, "Soul" <note>original Greek: ψυχὴ</note>.

We should only remember what has already been suggested: that the Reason or Wisdom which was the *Demiurgus* <term>demiurgus: the "craftsman" or creator of the visible world</term> of the world—properly the second of the mentioned persons—was also called *Cneph* by the Egyptians. From *Cneph*, the god *Phtha* (the third person of the Egyptian Trinity) was said to have been produced or fathered. Therefore, *Cneph* and *Emeph* are one and the same. Thus, we clearly have here an Egyptian Trinity of subordinate divine persons: *Eicton*, *Emeph* (or *Cneph*), and *Phtha*.

We have nothing more to add to *Iamblichus* concerning an Egyptian Trinity, unless we should emphasize those passages cited for this purpose by some of the early Church Fathers from the Hermetic or "Trismegistic" books (one of which was previously noted from **St. Cyril**). Or, we might recall the citation from *Damascius* <note>the last head of the School of Athens</note>: "There is one principle of all things, praised under the name of the Unknown Darkness, and this is cried out three times in this way" <note>original Greek: μία τῶν ὅλων ἀρχὴ σκότος ἄγνωστον ὑμνουμένη καὶ τοῦτο τρὶς ἀναφωνούμενον οὕτως</note>. 

Agreeing with this, **Augustinus Steuchus** <note>a 16th-century Italian scholar and librarian of the Vatican</note> produces another passage from the same philosophical writer: that the Egyptians made "the first principle of all to be Darkness above all knowledge and understanding (or Unknown Darkness), they thrice repeating the same" <note>original Greek: πρώτην ἀρχὴν σκότος ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν νόησιν, σκότος ἄγνωστον, τρὶς τοῦτο ἐπιφημίζοντες</note>. The aforementioned *Steuchus* takes this to be a clear acknowledgment of a Trinity of divine persons in Egyptian theology.

Our second observation is this: Egyptian theology—as well as the **Orphic** theology which was derived from it—asserted one **Incorporeal Deity** <term>incorporeal: having no physical body; purely spiritual</term> that is **All Things**. Because of this, it is evident that they could not admit a multitude of self-existent and independent deities. Instead, the apparent polytheism of these Egyptians proceeded largely from a misunderstanding of this principle. They were led by it, in a certain sense, "to personify and deify" <note>original Greek: θεοποιεῖν</note> the various **parts of the world** and **things of nature**, bestowing the names of gods and goddesses upon them. 

This does not mean they worshipped the inanimate parts of the world as such—much less things that are not substances but merely accidents <term>accidents: properties or qualities of a thing that are not essential to its nature</term>—as many real, distinct, personal deities. Rather, because they conceived that God (who was "all things") ought to be worshipped in all things—especially those most beneficial to mankind—they followed that **Asclepian** and **Hermetic** doctrine...

<summary>This page argues that Egyptian theology contained a Trinity similar to the Platonic triad of the One, Mind, and Soul, identifying specific Egyptian gods with these roles. It also suggests that Egyptian polytheism was actually a form of monism where the various gods were personifications of the one God present in all parts of nature.</summary>

# CHAPTER IV: Cut in Pieces by Typhon

<sig>LI</sig>
<meta>catchword: Nulla</meta>

The doctrine mentioned before suggests that we should call God by the **name** of **everything**, or **everything** by the **name** of **God**. The wiser among the Egyptians and Greeks well understood that it was really **one and the same Simple Deity** that was worshipped piece by piece in the various **parts** of the **world** and **things** of **nature**, under different **names**, **notions**, and **ceremonies**. This is declared by *Plutarch* <margin>On Isis and Osiris, 351.</margin> in the following way:

<note>original Greek: ἑλληνικὸν ἡ θεὰ, καὶ ὁ τυφὼν πολέμιον τῇ θεᾷ, δι᾽ ἄγνοιαν καὶ ἀπάτην τετυφωμένος, καὶ διασπῶν καὶ ἀφανίζων τὸν ἱερὸν λόγον, ὃν ἡ Ἴσις συνάγει καὶ συντίθησι, καὶ παραδίδωσι τοῖς τελουμένοις θειώσεως</note>
"**Isis** is a **Greek word** which signifies **knowledge**; and **Typhon** is the **enemy to this goddess**. Being puffed up by **ignorance** and **error**, Typhon **distracts** and **tears apart** <note>original: "discerps"</note> the **holy doctrine** (of the **Simple Deity**). **Isis collects this doctrine together again** and **makes it one**, delivering it to those who are initiated into her sacred mysteries in order to achieve **deification** <term>deification: the process of becoming god-like or being treated as a god</term>."

In these words, *Plutarch* intimates that the **Egyptian fable** of **Isis being mangled and cut into pieces by Typhon** was an **allegory**. It signified the **tearing apart** and **distraction** of the **Simple Deity** due to the **weakness** and **ignorance of common minds**, who are not able to comprehend the whole idea of God at once. Instead, they break God down into several **names** and **partial notions**. However, **true knowledge** and **understanding**—represented by **Isis**—makes the idea of God whole again and unites it into **one**.

XIX. It is well known that the **poets**, though they were the **prophets of the pagans** and claimed a kind of **Divine Inspiration**, nevertheless filled the minds of the **common people** <note>original: "vulgar"</note> with a certain **sense of religion** and **notions of morality**. Despite this, the poets were the **great depravers** and **corruptors** <note>original: "adulterators"</note> of **pagan theology**. They were guilty of this for several reasons.

**First**, they attributed to the **gods** all manner of **human imperfections**, **passions**, and **vices** within their **fables**. The **wiser pagans** in all ages were highly sensitive to this abuse and offended by it, as is seen in these **bold passages** performed on the **stage**:

<note>original Greek: Και ἦ γὰρ ὅστις κακὸς πεφύκῃ, ζημιοῦσιν οἱ θεοί. πῶς οὖν δίκαιον, τοὺς νόμους ὑμᾶς βροτοῖς γράψαντας, αὐτοὺς ἀνομίαν ὀφλισκάνειν;</note>
<margin>Euripides in *Ion*</margin>
->—If there is any mortal<-
->Who commits crimes, the gods demand punishment;<-
->But is it not unjust that you, who write the laws<-
->That mankind must follow, should yourselves live without law?<-
<note>original Latin: Si quis est mortalium / Qui scelera patrat, exigunt poenam Dei: / At nonne iniquum est, vos, suas leges quibus / Gens debet hominum, jure nullo vivere?</note>

**The meaning is this**: Since **mortal men are punished by the gods for transgressing their laws**, is it not **unjust that you gods, who write these laws, should yourselves live without law?** And again:

<note>original Greek: Οὐκέτ᾽ ἀνθρώποις κακῶς λέγειν δίκαιον, εἰ τὰ τῶν θεῶν κακὰ μιμώμεθ᾽, ἀλλὰ τῷ διδάσκοντι τάδε</note>
->—It is no longer just to speak ill of men<-
->If we merely imitate the evils of the gods;<-
->Rather, blame the one who teaches such things.<-

<summary>This page explores the allegory of Isis and Typhon as a representation of how the unified "Simple Deity" is fragmented by ignorance but restored by wisdom. It also criticizes the ancient poets for corrupting theology by portraying the gods as immoral and lawless.</summary>
<keywords>Plutarch, Isis, Typhon, Egyptian Mythology, Simple Deity, Polytheism vs Monotheism, Euripides, Pagan Theology, Allegory, Divine Unity</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the critique of how ancient religious concepts were misunderstood and fragmented. While the previous page discussed how the "Simple Deity" was broken into parts by the ignorant (symbolized by the myth of Isis and Typhon), this page focuses on how the poets further corrupted religion by confusing the names of the gods with the physical elements of nature.</meta>

### How the Poets Depraved Religion: Book I

->Let no censure hereafter mark us, if we humans ever imitate those things which are becoming to the gods. The blame returns to the authors.<-
<note>original Latin: *Nulla nos posthac notet Censura, siquando ista quæ superos decent Imitamur homines. Culpa ad auctores redit.*</note>

> *Let men no longer be blamed for imitating the **evil actions** of the gods; for those who teach men to do such things by their own example are the only ones who can be justly blamed.*

Secondly, the poets were further guilty of **corrupting** <note>original: "depraving"</note> the **religion** and **theology** of the **pagans** by so frequently **personifying** and **deifying** all the **things of nature** and **parts of the world**. They called these things by the **names** of those gods who were supposed to preside over them—that is, the various **divine powers** manifested through them. 

*Plutarch* criticizes the poets for this. When giving directions for young men reading their **writings**, he provides this timely caution against the danger of it: 

"It is very profitable and necessary, if we would receive good from the writings of the poets and not harm, that we should understand how they use the names of the gods in different senses. Therefore, the poets sometimes use the names of the gods properly, intending to signify the gods themselves; and sometimes again they use them improperly and **equivocally** <term>equivocally: using the same word to mean different things, leading to potential confusion</term> for those powers which the gods are the givers and dispensers of, or the things which they preside over." 
<note>original Greek: τοῦτο ἀναγκαῖον, καὶ χρήσιμον, εἰ μέλλοιμεν ἐκ τῶν ποιημάτων ὠφεληθήσεσθαι καὶ μὴ βλαβήσεσθαι, τὸ γινώσκειν πῶς τοῖς τῶν θεῶν ὀνόμασιν οἱ ποιηταὶ χρῶνται. —— χρῶνται δὲ τοῖς τῶν θεῶν ὀνόμασιν οἱ ποιηταὶ, ποτὲ μὲν αὐτῶν ἐκείνων ἐφαπτόμενοι τῇ ἐννοίᾳ, ποτὲ δὲ δυνάμεις τινὰς, ὧν οἱ θεοὶ δοτῆρές εἰσι καὶ καθηγεμόνες, ὁμωνύμως προσαγορεύοντες</note>

As an example, **Vulcan** is sometimes used by the poets for that god or divine power which presides over fire and the arts that operate by fire, and sometimes the word is used for fire itself. In the same way, **Mars** is sometimes used for the god who presides over military affairs, and sometimes it signifies nothing else but **war**. *Plutarch* gives an instance of this from *Sophocles*:

->Mars (O Women) is blind; he does not see, but with the face of a boar, he throws all things into a wicked mess.<-
<note>original Greek: τυφλὸς γ’ἔ, ὦ γυναῖκες, οὐδ’ ὁρᾶν Ἄρης, συὸς προσώπῳ, πάντα τυρβάζει κακά.</note>
<note>original Latin translation: *Mars (O Mulieres) cæcus hirsuto suis Velut ore frendens, cuncta commiscet mala.*</note>

And we might give this other instance of the same from *Virgil*:

->Wicked Mars rages throughout the whole world.<-
<note>original Latin: *Furit toto Mars impius orbe.*</note>

For the God of War—that is, the Divine Providence that presides over military affairs—could not be called impious or wicked; rather, it is war itself that is so described there.

# CHAPTER IV. Of the Pagan Theology.

Among the pagans, it was believed that God was **diffused** throughout the **whole world** and was himself, in a sense, **all things**. Therefore, he should be **worshiped** in **all things**. However, the **poets** were the main ones who took this idea too far. They **personified** the various inanimate parts of the **world** and **natural things** to create a multitude of distinct **gods** and **goddesses** from them. This tendency, though it was mostly indulged by them **merely for the delight and pleasure of the reader** <note>original Greek: *ψυχαγωγίας ἕνεκεν* (psychagōgias heneken)</note>, in addition to satisfying their own poetic fancies, was a matter of dangerous consequence. As the same *Plutarch* gravely and soberly advises in his book *On Isis*, it led some into gross and irrational **superstition** (which, in our Christian language, is **idolatry**) and drove others to outright **impiety** and **atheism**. But this will be discussed again later.

Therefore, we should next observe that the poets also corrupted the theology of the pagans in another way, making it appear more **aristocratically** <term>aristocratically: in this context, a system where power is shared among several high-ranking individuals rather than held by one supreme ruler</term>. This happened principally in two ways. First, they spoke so much of the gods in general and without distinction, attributing the **government of the whole world** to them collectively. It was as if the world were managed and carried on **by a common council of gods** <note>original Latin: *Communi Consilio Deorum*</note>, or a **republic of gods**, where all things were determined by a **majority of votes**. In this view, their **Jupiter**, or supreme God, was no more among them than a speaker of a **House of Lords** or **Commons**, or the chairman of a **committee**. In this, they actually attributed more power to their inferior deities than their own principles should have allowed.

Second (which is the **last corruption** of **pagan theology** by these **poets**), they took what were actually nothing else but various **names** and **concepts** of the same supreme deity—representing his various powers manifested in the world or the different **effects** produced by him—and turned them into many really distinct persons and gods. They went so far as to sometimes show these gods at odds and variance with one another, and even with **Jupiter** himself. *Saint Basil* seems to take notice of this in his oration, *How Young Men May Benefit from Greek Literature*: **"But least of all will we give credit to the poets when they discourse concerning the gods and speak of them as many distinct and independent persons, and those not even agreeing among themselves, but taking different sides and perpetually quarreling with one another."** <note>original Greek: *πάντων δ' ἥκιστα περὶ θεῶν τι διαλεγομένοις (ποιηταῖς) προσέξομεν, καὶ μάλισθ' ὅταν, ὡς περὶ πολλῶν τε αὐτῶν διεξίωσι, καὶ τούτων οὐδὲ διανοούντων*</note>

Notwithstanding all these extravagances and errors of the poets, we shall now clearly show that they actually asserted not a multitude of **self-existent and independent deities**, but **one only unmade deity**, and that all the others were generated or created gods. This has already been proven regarding **Orpheus** from such fragments of the Orphic poems as have been owned and attested by **pagan** writers; but it would be further evident, if we could

# Homer's Gods, All Generated, BOOK I.

We should give credit to any of those other Orphic verses that are found cited by Christians and Jews only (and we cannot reasonably conclude all of these to be counterfeit and fake), among which we have this one:

->*He is the one, self-begotten; and from this one, all things are born.* <note>original Greek: Εἷς ἔς' αὐτοφυὴς, ἑνὸς ἔκγονα πάντα τέτυκται (Heis est' autophuēs, henos ekgona panta tetyktai)</note><-

Moreover, when God in the same Orphic fragments is titled **mother-father** <note>original Greek: μητρο-πάτωρ (mētro-patōr)</note>—the father and mother of all things (as was observed before)—both the Orphic and Egyptian theology made the supreme deity especially **male-female** <note>original Greek: ἀρρενό-θηλυν (arrheno-thēlyn)</note>, or hermaphroditic. This, as Clemens Alexandrinus rightly interprets the meaning of it, was to signify **the production of things out of nothing** <note>original Greek: τὴν ἐκ μὴ ὄντων γένεσιν (tēn ek mē ontōn genesin)</note>, or from the deity alone, without any pre-existing or self-existent matter.

But we shall pass from Orpheus to Homer. Now, it is certain that Homer's **gods** were not all eternal, **unmade**, and **self-existent**. He plainly declares the contrary concerning the gods in general: that they had a **Genesis**, that is, a **temporary production**, as in that previously cited verse of his:

->*The Ocean, from which the gods were generated, etc.* <note>original Greek: 'Ωκεανόν τε θεῶν γένεσιν (Ōkeanon te theōn genesin)</note><-

Where "gods" refers to all the animated parts of the world superior to men, but principally (as Eustathius <note>Eustathius of Thessalonica was a 12th-century scholar and archbishop famous for his commentaries on Homer.</note> observes) the stars. **Gods** (he says) **are here used to mean stars** <note>original Greek: θεῶν ἀντὶ ἀστέρων (theōn anti asterōn)</note>. And as the same scholar further adds, the gods or stars, by a synecdoche <term>synecdoche: a figure of speech where a part is used to represent the whole</term>, signify **all things**, or the **whole world**. He uses **a part to stand for the whole** <note>original Greek: ἀντὶ τοῦ πάντων ὡς ἀπὸ μέρους (anti tou pantōn hōs apo merous)</note>, just as the same poet elsewhere declares his meaning when speaking likewise of the ocean:

->*Which was the original of all things,* <note>original Greek: Ὅς γένεσις πάντεσσι τέτυκται (Hos genesis pantessi tetyktai)</note><-

Or from whence (not only the gods but also) **all other things were generated**. Therefore, the full meaning of **Homer** was this: that the gods or stars, together with this whole visible world, had a temporary production and were at first made out of the **ocean**—that is, out of the watery chaos. So, Homer's **Theogony** <term>Theogony: the genealogy or birth of the gods</term>, as well as Hesiod's, was one and the same thing as the **Cosmogony** <term>Cosmogony: the branch of science or mythology that deals with the origin of the universe</term>. His "generation of gods" was the same as the generation or creation of the world. Both of them, in all probability, derived this from the **Mosaic Cabala** <note>Cudworth refers here to the "Mosaic tradition," suggesting that Greek myths about a watery origin of the world were echoes of the Book of Genesis.</note> or tradition. And Eustathius tells us that, according to the ancients, Homer's **making of the armor** <note>original Greek: ὁπλοποιΐα (hoplopoiia); referring to the description of the Shield of Achilles in Book 18 of the Iliad.</note> was **a riddle or obscure sign of the world's origin** <note>original Greek: αἴνιγμα τῆς κοσμογενείας (ainigma tēs kosmogeneias)</note>.

Nevertheless, although the gods <note>original Greek: οἱ θεοὶ (hoi theoi)</note> or the **gods** in general, are by Homer...

# CHAPTER IV. From Jupiter and the Ocean.

Though the gods were generated from the Ocean or **Watery Chaos**, this is to be understood only of the **Inferior Gods**. He is supposed to be distinguished from them, whom the same poet frequently calls **God by way of eminence** <note>original Greek: ὁ Θεὸς κατ’ ἐξοχὴν (ho Theos kat’ exochēn)</note>—to whom he plainly ascribes omnipotence—and **Zeus** or **Jupiter**, whom he styles **the most powerful of all** <note>original Greek: κάρτιστον ἁπάντων (kartiston hapantōn)</note>, and **the First and Chief of the Gods** <note>original Greek: πρῶτον Θεῶν (prōton Theōn)</note>, and **the Highest of Gods and Governors** <note>original Greek: ὕπατον Θεῶν καὶ κρειόντων (hypaton Theōn kai kreiontōn)</note>, and whom he affirms infinitely to transcend the other gods in the *Iliad*, book 8:

->*So far am I above both gods and men.* <note>original Greek: τόσσον ἐγὼ περὶ τ᾽ εἰμὶ Θεῶν, περὶ τ᾽ εἰμὶ ἀνθρώπων (tosson egō peri t’ eimi Theōn, peri t’ eimi anthrōpōn)</note><-

And he is said to reign over gods as well as men in the *Iliad*, book 1:

->---<-

->*Who reigns over both gods and men.* <note>original Greek: ὅς τε Θεοῖσι καὶ ἀνθρώποισιν ἀνάσσει (hos te Theoisi kai anthrōpoisin anassei)</note><-

Lastly, Homer makes him to be the **Father of the Gods as well as Men** <note>original Greek: πατὴρ Θεῶν (patēr Theōn)</note>; that is, nothing less than the Creator of them and the entire world. Therefore, he who produced the gods and stars out of the Ocean or **Watery Chaos** must necessarily be excluded from that number of gods, as he was not himself generated or made out of it. Thus, we have previously observed that "the gods" <note>original Greek: οἱ Θεοὶ (hoi Theoi)</note>, or the **Gods** in general, are frequently taken—both by Homer and other Greek writers—as a distinction from "the God" <note>original Greek: ὁ Θεὸς (ho Theos)</note> or **Jupiter**; that is, referring to the **Inferior Gods** only.

It is true indeed that other pagan gods besides Jupiter were styled **Fathers** <note>original Latin: Patres</note> by the Latins in their solemn rites and prayers. Just as "Jupiter" is nothing more than **Father Jove** <note>original Latin: Jovis Pater</note> contracted into one word, so was Mars called **Marspiter** by them. Saturn, Janus, Neptune, and Liber <note>Another name for the god Bacchus.</note> also had the same addition made to their names: **Father Saturn**, **Father Janus**, **Father Neptune**, and **Father Liber**. Not only these, but even their **Heroes** as well (for example, **Quirinus** <note>The name given to the deified Romulus, founder of Rome.</note>) had this honorable title of **Father** bestowed on them. All of this appears from those verses of Lucilius:

> *So that there is no one among us who is not called either Best Father of the Gods,*
> *Or Father Neptune, Liber, Father Saturn, Mars,*
> *Janus, or Father Quirinus—all addressed by that one name.*
> <note>original Latin: Ut nemo sit nostrum quin aut Pater Optimus Divum, / Aut Neptunus Pater, Liber, Saturnus Pater, Mars, / Janus, Quirinus Pater nomen dicatur ad unum</note>

Despite this, there is a great difference to be observed: although those other **Gods** were called **Fathers**, none of them was ever called—either by the Greeks, **Father of the Gods** <note>original Greek: πατὴρ Θεῶν (patēr Theōn)</note>, or by the Latins, **Best Father of the Gods** <note>original Latin: Pater Optimus Divum</note>—except for Zeus or **Jupiter**, the Supreme Deity.

And that Homer was generally understood by the Pagans themselves to have asserted a **Divine Monarchy**, or One Supreme Deity ruling over all, may further appear from the following citations. Plutarch, in his *Platonic Questions*, writes: *“And Xenocrates calls Jupiter the Highest, but before him Homer styled that God, who is the Prince of all princes, the Highest of Governors.”* <note>original Greek: καὶ Ξενοκράτης Δία ὕπατον καλεῖ, πρότερον δ’ Ὅμηρος καὶ τὸν τῶν ἀρχόντων ἄρχοντα θεὸν, ὕπατον κρειόντων προσείπε (kai Xenokratēs Dia hypaton kalei, proteron d’ Homēros kai ton tōn archontōn archonta theon, hypaton kreiontōn proseipe)</note>

To Plutarch may be added Proclus, who, in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*, proved that according to that philosopher, there was <note>original Greek: τὸ τοῦ κόσμου παντὸς εἷς καὶ ὅλος δημιουργὸς (to tou kosmou pantos eis kai holos dēmiourgos)</note> *“one only Maker of the whole world.”* Proclus affirms the same of that divine poet Homer (as he styles him there): <note>original Greek: ὃς καὶ διὰ πάσης ποιήσεως ὕπατον κρειόντων καὶ πατέρα ἀνδρῶν καὶ θεῶν αὐτὸν ἀνυμνεῖ, καὶ πᾶσιν εὐφημεῖ τοῖς δημιουργικοῖς νοήμασιν (hos kai dia pasēs poiēseōs hypaton kreiontōn...)</note> *“That he also throughout all his poetry praises Jupiter as the highest of all rulers and the father both of gods and men, and attributes all demiurgical <term>demiurgical: relating to a 'demiurge' or world-creator</term> concepts to him.”* Whereupon he concludes in this manner: <note>original Greek: Ἤτω τοίνυν σύμπασαν τὴν Ἑλληνικὴν θεολογίαν ἀπεφήναμεν, τῷ Διὶ τὴν ὅλην δημιουργίαν ἀπονέμουσαν (Ētō toinyn sympasan tēn Hellēnikēn theologian apephēnamen...)</note> *“And thus we have made it manifest that all Greek theology universally ascribes the making of all things to Zeus or Jupiter.”* 

Lastly, Aristotle himself confirms the same with his testimony, where he writes of paternal authority in this manner:
<margin>Aristotle, Politics, Book 1, chapter 12</margin>
<note>original Greek: ἡ γὰρ τέκνων ἀρχὴ βασιλικὴ· διὸ καλῶς Ὅμηρος τὸν Δία προσηγόρευσεν εἰπὼν (hē gar teknōn archē basilikē...)</note> *“The paternal power or authority over children is a kingly authority. Therefore, when Homer intended to set forth Jupiter’s kingly power over all, he very well called him the Father of Men and Gods:*

->—— Father of men and gods, <note>original Greek: πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε (patēr andrōn te theōn te)</note><-

*the King of them all. For he who is a King by nature ought both to differ from those he reigns over and also be of the same kind with them, just as the senior is to the junior and he who fathers a child is to his offspring.”* In this passage, Aristotle’s sense seems to be that Jupiter had a natural, rather than an acquired, kingly power over all the gods because they were all his offspring and begotten by him, as were men. In this passage, Aristotle plainly acquits and frees Homer from all suspicion of atheism.

As for Hesiod, if we had not already sufficiently proved from his *Theogony* <note>original: Theogonia</note> that all his gods (that is, his inferior deities) were *generated* and *made* just like men, it might be made unquestionably evident from this verse of his in *Works and Days*: <note>original: Opera</note>

*There is one kind of both gods and men, and we both breathe from the same mother, or spring from the same original.* In this passage, the scholiast <term>scholiast: an ancient commentator who wrote explanatory notes on classical texts</term> understands the common mother of both **gods** and **men** to be the **Earth** and **Chaos**. He suggests that Pindar is referring here only to the inferior deities, and primarily to the **stars**.

Therefore, this statement by Pindar is to be understood as applying to all the other gods: that they, like men, were made out of the Earth or Chaos. It does not apply to that Supreme Deity whom Pindar elsewhere calls "the most powerful of the gods" <note>original Greek: θεῶν κράτιστον (theōn kratiston)</note>, "the Lord of all things" <note>original Greek: τῶν πάντων κύριον (tōn pantōn kyrion)</note>, "the cause of everything" <note>original Greek: παντὶ αἴτιον (panti aition)</note>, and "the god who is the best artificer" <note>original Greek: ἀριστοτέχναν θεόν (aristotechnan theon)</note>—the one who was the Framer of the whole world and, as Clement of Alexandria <note>Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–215 AD) was a Christian theologian who sought to find common ground between Greek philosophy and Christianity</note> tells us, the universe <note>original Greek: τὸ πᾶν (to pan)</note>. According to Pindar, this is the same God whom Chiron instructed Achilles to worship principally, above all the other gods:

<margin>Pythian Ode 6.</margin>
->— To worship the son of Cronus [Jupiter] above all,<-
->the deep-voiced ruler of lightning and thunder,<-
->among the gods.<-
-><note>original Greek: μάλιστα μὲν Κρονίδαν βαρυόπαν, στεροπᾶν κεραυνῶν τε πρύτανιν, θεῶν σέβεσθαι</note><-

The meaning of these words is explained by the scholiast as follows: *That he should honor and worship the loud-sounding Jupiter, the Lord of thunder and lightning, transcendently above all the other gods.* <note>original Greek: ἐξαιρέτως τὸν μεγαλόφωνον ἀστραπῶν καὶ κεραυνῶν δεσπότην τὸν Δία, παρὰ τοὺς ἄλλους θεοὺς τιμᾶν καὶ σέβεσθαι</note> This, by the way, refutes the opinion of those who argue that the **Supreme God**, as such, was not worshiped by the **pagans** at all.

However, one thing is certain concerning these three—Homer, Hesiod, and Pindar. They must either have been absolute atheists—acknowledging no **eternal deity** at all and making senseless *Chaos*, *Night*, and the *Ocean* the source of all their gods without exception (including Jupiter himself, their king and father)—or else they must have asserted **one** only eternal, unmade, self-existent deity, such that all the other gods were generated or created by that **one**. 

The latter was undoubtedly their true meaning. The only reason why Aristotle and Plato might have occasionally suspected otherwise seems to be that they did not understand the "Mosaic tradition" <note>original: "Moſaick Cabbala," referring to the belief that Greek wisdom originated from the teachings of Moses</note> which both Hesiod and Homer followed: the idea that the world—meaning both heaven and earth—was made at first out of a watery *chaos*. This tradition is declared by St. Peter in his second epistle, chapter 3.

Several other remarkable passages to the same effect could be produced from the two tragic poets, Aeschylus and Sophocles. However, because these have already been cited by Justin Martyr <note>Justin Martyr (100–165 AD) was an early Christian apologist who argued that Greek philosophers and poets had access to "seeds" of divine truth</note> and Clement...

# CHAPTER IV. A Passage of Sophocles Defended.

To avoid unnecessary tediousness, we shall pass over the writings of Clement of Alexandria <note>Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–215 AD) was a Christian theologian who sought to find common ground between Greek philosophy and Christianity</note> and others. However, we think it appropriate to note one famous passage from **Sophocles**:

->In truth, there is one, and only one God,<-
->who created the heavens and the vast earth,<-
->the blue swell of the sea, and the force of the winds, etc.<-
-><note>original Greek: Εἷς ταῖς ἀληθείαισιν, εἷς ἐστὶν Θεὸς, ὃς οὐρανόν τ’ ἔτευξε καὶ γαῖαν μακρὰν, πόντου τε χαροπὸν οἶδμα, κἀνέμων βίαν, &c.</note><-
-><note>original Latin: Unus profectò, Unus est tantùm Deus, Cœli ſolique machinam qui condidit, Vadumque Ponti cæruleum, & vim Spiritus, &c.</note><-

There is, in truth, only one God, who made Heaven and Earth, the Sea, Air, and Winds, etc. This is followed by a passage against image-worship <note>also known as iconolatry, the practice of worshipping physical statues or images as gods</note>. Although this sentiment is so aligned with Christian thought that it can no longer be found in the surviving tragedies of this poet (many of which have been lost), its authenticity cannot reasonably be doubted. It has been cited by so many of the <term>Ancient Fathers</term> <note>early influential Christian theologians and writers</note> in their writings against the Pagans—specifically by **Justin Martyr**, **Athenagoras**, **Clement of Alexandria**, **Eusebius**, **Cyril**, and **Theodoret**. Among these, Clement tells us that it was also verified by the ancient Pagan historian **Hecataeus**.

Furthermore, there are so many passages relevant to our purpose in the works of **Euripides** that we cannot omit them all. In his play *The Suppliants* <note>original: Supplices</note>, we find this passage, in which the absolute dependence of all people upon **Jupiter** (the Supreme Deity) is fully acknowledged:

->O Zeus, why do they say that wretched mortals<-
->have wisdom? For we depend on you,<-
->and we do whatever you happen to will.<-
-><note>original Greek: Ὦ ζεῦ, τί δῆτα τοὺς ταλαιπώρους βροτοὺς φρονεῖν λέγουσι; σοῦ γὰρ ἐξηρτήμεθα, δρῶμέν τε τοιαῦτ’, ἂν σὺ τυγχάνῃς θέλων.</note><-
-><note>original Latin: Miſeros quid Homines, O Deûm Rex & Pater, Sapere arbitramur? Pendet è nutu tuo Res noſtra, facimuſque illa quæ viſum tibi.</note><-

We also have this excellent prayer to the Supreme Governor of Heaven and Earth, cited from the same tragic poet:

->To you, the ruler of all things, I bring<-
->an offering and a sacrificial cake, whether you<-
->prefer to be called Zeus or Hades.<-
->For among the gods of heaven,<-
->you wield the scepter of Zeus,<-
->and you also share in the rule of Hades over those below.<-
->Send light to the souls of men<-
->who wish to learn beforehand what struggles<-
->they sprang from, what is the root of evils,<-
->and to which of the blessed ones they must sacrifice<-
->to find rest from their labors.<-
-><note>original Greek: Σοὶ τῷ πάντων μεδέοντι χοὴν, πέλανόν τε φέρω Ζεὺς εἴτ’ Ἀΐδης ὀνομαζόμενος στέργεις• σὺ γὰρ ἔν τε θεοῖς τοῖς οὐρανίδαις, σκῆπτρον τὸ Διὸς μεταχειρίζων, χθονίων θ’ Ἅιδῃ μετέχεις ἀρχῆς• πέμψον μὲν φῶς ψυχαῖς ἀνέρων ταῖς βουλομέναις ἄθλους προμαθεῖν πόθεν ἔβλαστον, τίς ῥίζα κακῶν, τίνι δεῖ μακάρων θύσαντα μέλους εὑρεῖν μόχθων ἀνάπαυλαν•</note><-

->To you (the Lord of all things), I offer wine,<-
-><note>original Latin: Tibi ( Cunctorum Domino ) Vinum,</note><-

# Euripides and other Greek Poets, BOOK I.

->I bring the salted meal <note>original: *Salsam Molam*; a mixture of flour and salt used in ancient sacrifices</note>, whether you belong to the Underworld <note>original: *Ditis* (Dis/Pluto)</note>,<-

->**Struggles arose, and what is the cause of evil;**<-
->**To which of the heavenly beings one must rightly sacrifice**<-
->**To find rest from their labors.**<-
<note>original Latin: *Salsamque Molam fero, ſeu Ditis, Tu, ſive Jovis nomine gaudes: Tu namque Deos Superos inter, Sceptrum tractas Sublime Jovis; Idem Regnum Terreſtre tenes. Tu Lucem animis infunde Virûm, Qui ſcire volunt, quo ſata Mentis Luctâ ſit ortu, Quæ Cauſa Mali; Cui Cœlicolûm rite litando Requiem ſit habere laborum.*</note>

Here we may observe that Zeus and Hades (*Jupiter* and *Pluto*) are both supposed to be names equally belonging to one and the same Supreme God. The essence of the prayer is this: *That God would pour light into the souls of men, enabling them to know the root from which all their evils spring, and the means by which they may avoid them.*

Lastly, there is another devotional passage cited from **Euripides** which also contains a clear acknowledgment of one self-existent Being who encompasses and governs the whole world:

->To you, the Self-begotten, who in the ethereal<-
->Whirl <note>original: *Rhombos*; referring to the circular motion of the heavens</note> have entwined the nature of all things,<-
->Around whom light, and dark-shimmering<-
->Night, and the countless multitude of stars<-
->Perpetually dance in chorus.<-
<note>original Greek: *Σὲ τὸν Αὐτοφυῆ, τὸν ἐν αἰθερίῳ Ῥόμβῳ, πάντων φύσιν ἐμπλέξανθ', Ὅν πέρι μὲν φῶς, πέρι δ' ὀρφναία Νὺξ αἰολόχρως· ἄκριτος τ' ἄστρων Ὄχλος ἐνδελεχῶς ἀμφιχορεύει·*</note>

->*You, Self-sprung Being, who enfold all things,*<-
->*And in your arms hold heaven’s whirling frame!*<-
->*Who are encircled with resplendent light,*<-
->*And yet lie mantled in the shade of night!*<-
->*About whom the exultant starry fires*<-
->*Dance nimbly round in everlasting circles.*<-

We believe the words of the second and third verses support this interpretation, which agrees with the passage from the Orphic hymns <note>Orphism was a set of religious beliefs and practices originating in the ancient Greek and Hellenistic world, associated with literature ascribed to the mythical poet Orpheus</note>:

--- for a cloud is set around him <note>original Greek: *περὶ γὰρ νέφος ἐστήρικται*</note>.

This suggests that God, being in himself a most bright and dazzling light, is—relative to us and because of the weakness of our understanding—covered over with a thick cloud. This matches the passage in Scripture: *Clouds and darkness are round about him*. I chose to follow this interpretation because it is more profound and majestic than the other common one (though that one is also grammatically and poetically sound): *That successive day and night, together with a countless multitude of stars, perpetually dance around the Deity.*

# CHAPTER IV. Supporters of a Divine Monarchy.

-> How troublesome a thing it is, O Zeus and the gods, etc. <-
<note>original Greek: Ὡς ἀργαλέον πρᾶγμ' ἐστὶ ὦ Ζεῦ κὶ θεοί...</note>

And we have this clear testimony from **Terpander**, cited by **Clement of Alexandria**: *O Zeus, origin of all things; O Zeus, leader of all.* <note>original Greek: Ζεῦ πάντων ἀρχά, Ζεῦ πάντων ἁγήτωρ</note> And these following verses are attributed to **Menander**:

-> **The one who is the most noble Lord and Father of all things,** <-
-> **Him alone you should continually worship with prayer,** <-
-> **The creator and giver of such great abundance.** <-

<note>original Greek: Τὸν ὄντα πάντων κύριον γενικώτατον / Καὶ πατέρα, τοῦτον διατέλει τιμᾶν μόνον, / Ἀγαθῶν τοιούτων εὑρέτην κὶ κτίστορα. Original Latin: Rerum universarum Imperatorem & Patrem, / Solum perpetuo colere suppliciter decet, / Artificem tantæ & Largitorem copiæ.</note>

In these lines, men are urged to worship the Supreme God alone as the sole author of all good, or at least as standing transcendently above all the other gods. There are also two remarkable testimonies—one from the ancient Greek poet **Hermesianax** and another from **Aratus**—to the same effect; these will both be reserved for other sections of this work.

Therefore, we move from the Greek to the Latin poets, where **Ennius** appears first. He traced the origin of the gods in general (who were all the lower deities) from **Erebus** <note>Erebus: In Greek mythology, the personification of deep darkness or the underworld</note> and **Night**, assuming they were all made or generated out of **Chaos**. Nevertheless, he acknowledged one who was:

---
-> —— **Father and King of both gods and men,** —— <-
<note>original Latin: Divûmque Hominumque Pater, Rex</note>

...meaning the maker or creator of the whole world. He therefore made those other gods along with the world out of Chaos, while He Himself was unmade.

**Plautus**, in a similar way, sometimes distinguishes between **Jupiter** and "the gods," and plainly acknowledges one all-knowing <term>original: "omniscient"</term> deity:

<margin>
*The Captives,* Act 2, Scene 2.
</margin>
-> **There is certainly a God who hears and sees what we do.** <-
<note>original Latin: Est profectò Deus, qui quæ nos gerimus, auditque & videt.</note>

This passage strongly resembles the words of **Manlius Torquatus** in **Livy**: *There is a celestial divinity; you are Great Jupiter* <note>original Latin: Est Cœleste Numen, Es Magne Jupiter</note>—a powerful affirmation of one supreme and universal God. The same **Plautus**, in his play *Rudens* (*The Rope*), clearly asserts one supreme monarch and emperor over all, to whom the lower gods are subordinate:

-> **He who moves all nations, seas, and lands,** <-
-> **I am a citizen of his heavenly city;** <-
-> **Jupiter, who is the Emperor of gods and men,** <-
-> **Dispatches us among the nations, one here and another there,** <-
-> **To observe the deeds, character, piety, and faith of humans.** <-
<note>original Latin: Qui Gentes omnes Mariaque & Terras movet, / Ejus sum Civis civitate Cœlitum; / Qui est Imperator Divûm atque Hominum Jupiter, / Is nos per gentes alium aliâ disparat, / Hominum qui facta, mores, pietatem & fidem / Noscamus.</note>

# The Agreement of Latin Poets, Book 1.

-> Those who pursue false lawsuits with false testimonies, <-
-> And those who swear falsely regarding money in court, <-
-> We record their names and bring them to Jupiter. <-
-> Daily He knows who seeks evil here. <-
-> He judges once more that which has been judged unjustly. <-
-> He has the names of the good recorded on other tablets. <-
-> Yet those wicked people convince themselves <-
-> That they can appease Jupiter with gifts and sacrifices; <-
-> But they waste their effort and expense, because <-
-> No worship is accepted by Him from those who are perjured. <-
<note>original Latin: *Qui falsas lites falsis testimonis / Petunt, quique in jure abjurant pecuniam, / Eorum referimus nomina exscripta ad Jovem. / Cotidie Ille scit, quis hic quærat malum. / Iterum Ille eam rem judicatam judicat. / Bonos in aliis tabulis exscriptos habet. / Atque hoc scelesti illi in animum inducunt suum / Jovem se placare posse donis, hostiis ; / Sed operam & sumptum perdunt, quia / Nihil Ei acceptum est à perjuris supplicii.*</note>

In this passage, **Jupiter**, the Supreme Monarch of gods and men, is said to appoint other inferior gods under him over all parts of the earth to observe the actions, manners, and behaviors of people everywhere, and to return the names of both the bad and the good to him. This Jupiter re-judges all unjust judgments, rendering a righteous retribution to everyone. And though wicked men imagine <note>original: "conceit"</note> that he may be bribed with sacrifices, no worship is acceptable to him from the perjured <note>term: people who have broken a holy oath</note>. Notwithstanding this, the poet later mixes the supreme and inferior gods all together, following the usual custom, under the single general name of "Gods," because they are all supposed to be co-governors of the world:

-> A pious person, praying to the gods, will find pardon <-
-> More easily than one who is wicked. <-
<note>original Latin: *Facilius, siqui pius est, à Diis supplicans, / Quam qui scelestus est, inveniet veniam sibi.*</note>

<margin>*Poenulus*, Act 5, Scene 4.</margin> Again, the same poet elsewhere introduces **Hanno** the Carthaginian, who addresses himself to Jupiter (or the Supreme God) with this form of prayer:

-> Jupiter, who cares for and nourishes the race of mankind, through whom we live <-
-> This vital age; in whose power are the hopes and lives of all people, <-
-> Grant that this day may be favorable, I pray, for the conduct of my affairs. <-
<note>original Latin: *Jupiter, qui genus colis alisque Hominum, per quem vivimus / Vitale ævum; quem penes spes, vitæque sunt Hominum Omnium, / Da diem hunc sospitem, quæso, rebus meis agundis.*</note>

Next, we have these verses by **Valerius Soranus**, an ancient and eminent poet, which are fully relevant to our point and were recorded by **Varro**:

-> Omnipotent Jupiter, the King of Kings and of the Gods himself, <-
-> The Father and Mother of the Gods; One God and All Gods. <-
<note>original Latin: *Jupiter Omnipotens, Regum Rex ipse Deûmque, / Progenitor Genitrixque Deûm ; Deus UNUS & OMNIS.*</note>

The sense is this: *Omnipotent Jupiter, the King of Kings and Gods, and the Progenitor and Mother <note>original: Genitrix</note> of those gods; One God and all gods.* In this passage, the Supreme and Omnipotent Deity is titled "Father and Mother of the Gods," in the same way he was called in **Orphic Theology** "mother-father" <note>original Greek: μητροπάτωρ</note> and "male-female" <note>original Greek: ἀῤῥενόθηλυς</note>. This expression indicates that the gods and all other things were produced from him alone, without any pre-existing matter. Moreover, according to the character of this Pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> theology, that one God was "All Gods" and "Every God," the Pagans supposed that whenever any inferior deity was worshipped by them, the Supreme God was also worshipped and honored at the same time.

# CHAPTER IV. In the Monarchy of the Whole.

Though the sense of *Ovid* has been sufficiently explained before, we cannot well omit some other passages of his, such as that grateful and sensible acknowledgment:

-> *That I speak and breathe, and behold the heavens and the light of the sun* <-
-> *(can I be ungrateful and forgetful?),* <-
-> *He himself gave it.* <-
<note>original: "Quod loquor & spiro, Cælumque & lumina Solis / Aspicio (possumne ingratus & immemor esse?) / Ipse dedit."</note>

And this in the third book of his *Metamorphoses*:

-> *That Father and Ruler of the gods, whose right hand is armed with three-forked* <-
-> *fires <note>original: "trifulcis ignibus" — referring to lightning bolts</note>, who shakes the world with His nod.* <-
<note>original: "Ille Pater Rectorque Deûm, cui Dextra trifulcis / Ignibus armata est, qui Nutu concutit Orbem."</note>

*Virgil's* theology also may sufficiently appear from his frequent acknowledgment of an omnipotent deity, and from those verses of his cited before out of *Aeneid* 6. In those verses, he plainly asserts that one God is the original of all things, at least as a *Soul of the World* <note>term: Anima Mundi, the philosophical idea that a divine spirit animates all of nature</note>. *Servius Honoratus* <note>A famous 4th-century commentator on Virgil</note> paraphrases that section this way: "God is a certain Divine Spirit, which, infused through the four elements, gives birth to all things." <note>original: "Deus est quidam Divinus Spiritus, qui per quatuor fusi elementa, gignit universa"</note> Nevertheless, we shall add from him this also from *Venus's* prayer to *Jupiter* in *Aeneid* 1:

-> ——— *O you who rule the affairs of both men and gods* <-
-> *with eternal commands, and terrify them with lightning!* <-
<note>original: "O qui res Hominumque Deûmque, / Æternis regis imperiis, & fulmine terres!"</note>

To which *Venus* again, in *Aeneid* 10, addresses the same *Jupiter* in this manner:

-> *O Father, O Eternal Power of men and gods!* <-
<note>original: "O Pater, O Hominum Divûmque Æterna Potestas!"</note>

Where we have this annotation by *Servius*: "*Eternal Power of the Gods* is used here for the purpose of distinguishing him from all the other deities <note>original: "propter aliorum Numinum discretionem"</note>." Jupiter is here called the Eternal Power of the gods to distinguish him from all the other gods who were not eternal, but were made or generated from him.

Neither should *Horace* be left out, in whose work we read to the same purpose in Book 1, Ode 12:

-> *What shall I tell of before the customary praises of the Parent?* <-
-> *Who governs the affairs of men and gods,* <-
-> *Who regulates the sea and lands, and the world* <-
-> *with its changing seasons.* <-
-> *From whom nothing greater is produced than Himself,* <-
-> *nor does anything thrive that is similar or second to Him;* <-
-> *yet Pallas <note>Another name for Athena or Minerva, the goddess of wisdom</note> has occupied the honors closest to Him.* <-
<note>original: "Quid prius dicam solitis Parentis / Laudibus? Qui res Hominum & Deorum, / Qui Mare & Terras, variisque mundum / Temperat horis. / Unde nil majus generatur ipfo, / Nec viget quicquam fimile aut fecundum; / Proximos illi tamen occupavit / Pallas honores."</note>

And again, Book 3, Ode 4:

-> *Who regulates the motionless Earth, who regulates the sea* <-
<note>original: "Qui Terram inertem, qui mare Temperat"</note>

<meta>This page continues the argument that classical Roman poets, specifically Horace and Manilius, recognized one supreme deity as the governor of the universe, despite the variety of names used for different aspects of the divine.</meta>

<header>Epicurus the Only Philosopher, Book I.</header>

->*The winds, the cities, and the gloomy kingdoms;*<-
->*Both the divine and mortal throngs,*<-
->*He ALONE rules with a just command.*<-
<note>original: "Ventosum, & Urbes, Regnaque Tristia; / Divosque, Mortalesque turmas, / Imperio regit UNUS æquo." — Horace, Odes 3.4.45-48</note>

From these words of *Horace*, "with the customary praises of the Parent," it appears that the one *Supreme Deity*, the *Parent* and Maker of all things, was at that time celebrated by the pagans as such, above all the other gods. And while those pagans commonly ascribed the government of the seas particularly to *Neptune*, and of the earth and *Hades* or the Underworld (which are here called *gloomy kingdoms*) to *Pluto*, these are all attributed here by *Horace* to one and the same Supreme and Universal Deity. It may well be concluded from this that *Jupiter*, *Neptune*, and *Pluto* were but three distinct names or concepts for one Supreme Divinity <note>term: Numen, a Latin word for a spiritual power or divinity</note>, whose sovereignty was nevertheless primarily signified by the name *Jupiter*. The same should be said of *Pallas* or *Minerva* as well; since she signifies Eternal Wisdom, that was also but another name for God, though she was looked upon as inferior to *Jupiter* and next to him in dignity. This is the case unless we should conclude her to be a second divine manifestation <note>term: Hypostasis, a Greek philosophical term for an underlying reality or a "person" of the godhead</note>, according to the doctrine of the *Pythagoreans* and *Platonists* (which was probably not unknown to *Horace*) as well as to that scriptural tradition <note>term: Cabbala, here used to refer to a mystical or traditional interpretation of the Bible</note>: *I was set up from everlasting, or ever the Earth was, when there were no depths, I was brought forth, etc.* <note>Proverbs 8:23-24</note> But we will discuss more of this later.

Lastly, we shall conclude with *Manilius*, who lived in the same *Augustan* age and was a zealous opponent of that atheistic theory <note>term: Hypothesis</note> of *Epicurus* and *Lucretius*, as appears from these verses of his:

->*Who could believe that such vast structures were made without a Divinity,*<-
->*Or that the world was created from tiny particles by a blind coincidence?*<-
<note>original: "Quis credat tantas operum sine Numine Moles, / Ex Minimis cæcoque creatum fœdere mundum?"</note>

Therefore, he also plainly asserts one Supreme Deity as the Framer and Governor of the whole world in this manner, in *Book 2*:

->*For I shall sing of Nature, powerful with a silent mind,*<-
->*And of God infused through the heavens, the earth, and the sea,*<-
->*Governing the vast mass with a balanced law,*<-
->*And of the whole world living by a mutual harmony,*<-
->*And being moved by the impulse of reason; since ONE SPIRIT*<-
->*Dwells throughout all parts and sustains the world,*<-
->*Passing through all things and giving shape to the living universe, etc.*<-
