<header>CHAPTER IV. Who asserted, Many Independent Gods.</header>

> *The world is always turning, and it presses and offers itself to us;*
> *So that it may be well known, and shows by observation*
> *What kind of thing it is, and teaches us to obey its laws.*
> *The world itself calls our minds to the stars,*
> *And does not allow its laws to be hidden, because it does not hide them.*
<note>original: "semper volvendo, seq; ipsum inculcat & offert; / Ut bene cognosci possit, monstretque videndo / Qualis eat, doceatque suas attendere Leges. / Ipse vocat nostros animos ad Sydera Mundus, / Nec patitur, quia non condit, sua Jura latere." — Manilius, Astronomica 4.915–919</note>

Despite this, we admit that according to the *Stoic doctrine*, the whole *living world*—or rather its *soul*—is made by *Manilius* to be the *supreme deity* <note>original: "Supreme Numen"</note>.

XX. We now move from the *poets* of the *pagans* to their *philosophers*. A *modern author* writing about the *religion of the Gentiles* <note>term: Gentiles, a term used here for non-Christian or pagan peoples</note> claims that very eminent *philosophers* held the *opinion* that *even all the minor pagan gods existed of themselves from eternity, uncreated*, and that they gave many reasons for this view. However, we believe it will become clear from the *rest* of this *discourse* just how far from the truth this is. We can only conclude that this *learned writer* mistook the *opinion* of *Aristotle* and the later *Platonists* regarding the *eternity of the world and the gods*. He assumed that because they believed these things were eternal, they also asserted their *self-existence*; yet the opposite has already been shown. Therefore, we shall now prove beyond doubt through a *specific list* that the *majority* of the *pagan philosophers* who were *theists*—though they acknowledged a *multiplicity of gods*—still asserted there was *only one self-existent Deity*, or a *universal divine power* <note>original: "Universal Numen"</note>, by whom the *world* and all those other *gods* were *made*. There are only a few *ditheists* <note>term: Ditheists, those who believe in two primary, opposing divine principles or gods</note> to be excepted (*such as Plutarch and Atticus*). Out of a certain *softness* and *sensitivity* of nature, and in order to clear the *one good God* from the *blame* of *evils*, they felt they had to establish an *evil soul* or *demon* <note>original: "Dæmon"</note> in the *world* that was also *self-existent*, to bear all the blame for them.

Indeed, *Epicurus* is the only *person* we can find among the famous *philosophers* who, while pretending to acknowledge *gods*, openly opposed *monarchy* <note>term: Monarchy, in this context, the rule of the universe by a single supreme God</note> and verbally asserted a *multitude of eternal, uncreated, self-existent deities*. However, he claimed these gods had nothing at all to do with either the *making* or *governing* of the *world*. The reason for this was that he would not admit under any circumstances that the *world* had been made by any *mind* or *intelligence*. Therefore he concluded,

<margin>*Lucretius, Book 3.*</margin>
->*The nature of things was by no means created by a Divine Mind,*<-
<note>original: "Naturam Rerum, haud Divinâ Mente Coortam," — Lucretius, De Rerum Natura</note>

*meaning that there was no God who was the* <term>δημιουργὸς</term> <note>original Greek: "demiurgos," meaning the craftsman or architect of the universe</note> *or framer of the world*. Nevertheless, to avoid the *hatred* <note>original: "Odium"</note> of being labeled an *atheist*, he pretended to affirm a *multitude of uncreated and incorruptible gods* who were entirely uninvolved in the *construction* of the *world*. In this, it is first evident that he was not serious or sincere. Since he admitted no other *principles* of things in his *philosophy* except *atoms* and the *vacuum* <note>term: Vacuum, the empty space or void in which atoms move</note>, he could logically acknowledge no other *gods* except those compounded out of *atoms*.

<summary>This page argues that while some modern writers claim pagan philosophers believed in multiple self-existent gods, most actually held to a single supreme creator, with Epicurus being the primary exception who proposed uninvolved, self-existent gods to avoid charges of atheism.</summary>

<header>Pythagoras both a Polytheist, BOOK I.</header>

Atoms, and therefore *corruptible*. And thus does *Origen* declare the doc-
<margin>Book 4, Against Celsus, p. 169.</margin>trine of *Epicurus*—not indeed as he pretended to hold it, but as he must have held it according to the logic of his principles, had he really asserted any gods at all: *Epicurus's gods, being composed of atoms and therefore by their very nature dissolvable, work in continual labor and toil, struggling to shake off the atoms that cause decay.* <note>original: "οἱ τῷ Ἐπικύρῳ Θεοὶ, σύνθετοι ἐξ ἀτόμων τυγχάνοντες, καὶ τὸ ὅσον ἐπὶ τῇ συστάσει ἀναλυτοὶ, πραγματεύονται τὰς φθοροποιὸς ἀτόμους ἀποσείεσθαι"</note> Nevertheless, if *Epicurus* had in good earnest asserted such a commonwealth of gods who were neither made out of atoms nor corruptible, as long as he denied that the world was made by any Mind or Wisdom (as we have already declared), he ought not to be reckoned among the *theists* but the *atheists*.

*Thales the Milesian* was one of the most ancient Greek philosophers. That he admitted a plurality of gods in some sense is evident from that saying of his cited by *Aristotle*: *All things are full of gods.* <note>original: "πάντα θεῶν πλήρη"</note> But that he nonetheless asserted one supreme and only *unmade* or *self-existent deity* is also manifest from that other apothegm <note>term: apothegm, a concise saying or maxim</note> of his in *Laertius*: *God is the oldest of all things, because he is unmade.* <note>original: "πρεσβύτατον πάντων ὁ θεὸς, ἀγέννητον γάρ"</note> From this it may be concluded that all of *Thales's* other gods were generated and were the offspring of one sole unmade deity.

*Pherecydes Syrus* was *Thales's* contemporary. *Aristotle* recorded in his *Metaphysics* that Pherecydes affirmed *the first principle from which all other things were generated was the best* <note>original: "τὸ γεννῆσαν πρῶτον ἄριστον"</note>—that is, an absolutely perfect being. Thus, in the scale of nature, things did not ascend upward from the most imperfect to the more perfect beings, but on the contrary descended downward from the *most perfect* to the *less perfect*. Moreover, *Laertius* informs us that this was the beginning of one of *Pherecydes's* books: *Jupiter, and Time, and the Earth always were.* <note>original: "Ζεὺς μὲν καὶ χρόνος εἰς ἀεὶ, καὶ χθὼν ἦν"</note> Despite this, in the following words, he makes the Earth dependent upon *Jupiter*. Though some, reading *Kronos* <note>note: the titan Saturn</note> here instead of *Chronos* <note>note: time</note>, seem to understand him to mean that *Jupiter* and *Saturn*—really one and the same divine power <note>term: Numen, a Latin term for a deity or divine presence</note>—existed always *from eternity*. In any case, there is in these words an acknowledgment of one single and eternal deity.

*Pythagoras* was the most eminent of all the ancient philosophers. That he was a polytheist as well as the other pagans may be concluded from the beginning of the *Golden Verses* (though they were not written by him):

> First, honor the immortal gods as they are established by law,
> And respect your oath; then honor the noble heroes;
> And worship the spirits of the underworld by performing the required rites.
<note>original: "Ἀθανάτους μὲν πρῶτα θεοὺς νόμῳ, ὡς διάκεινται, / Τίμα καὶ σέβου ὅρκον· ἔπειθ᾿ ἥρωας ἀγαυούς· / Τούς τε καταχθονίους σέβε δαίμονας, ἔννομα ῥέζων."</note>

In these lines, men are exhorted in the first place to worship the *immortal gods* according to how they were appointed by law; after them the *heroes*; and last of all the *terrestrial demons*. And accordingly

Accordingly, Laertius gives this account of Pythagoras's piety: <note>original: "τιμὰς θεοῖς δεῖν νομίζειν καὶ ἥρωσιν, μὴ τὰς ἴσας"</note> *That he believed men ought to worship both the gods and the heroes, though not with equal honor.* And who these gods of Pythagoras were, the same writer also declares: <note>original: "ἥλιόν τε καὶ σελήνην καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους ἀστέρας, εἶναι θεούς"</note> *That they were, at least in part, the Sun, the Moon, and the Stars.*

Despite this, the fact that Pythagoras acknowledged one supreme and universal *divine power* <note>original: "Numen"</note>—who was therefore the source of all those other gods—may partly be seen in that prayer in the *Golden Verses*. These verses, whether written by Philolaus, Lysis, or some other follower of Pythagoras, were undoubtedly ancient and consistent with his teachings.

<margin>Salmasius, Preface to the Arabic *Table of Cebes*</margin>
-> Father Zeus, either deliver all men from their many evils, <-
-> Or show to all what kind of spirit they should follow. <-
<note>original Greek: "Ζεῦ πάτερ, ἢ πολλῶν τε κακῶν λύσειας ἅπαντας· Εἰ πᾶσιν δείξαις οἵῳ τῷ δαίμονι χρῶνται·"</note>

-> *Nurturing Jupiter, command that all be freed from evils:* <-
-> *Or show them what spirit they should use.* <-
<note>original Latin: "Jupiter alme, malis jubeas vel solvier omnes : Omnibus utantur vel quonam dæmone monstra."</note>

Upon this, Hierocles writes: <note>original: "τὸν ποιητὴν καὶ πατέρα τοῦδε τοῦ παντὸς ἔθει τῷ τοῖς πυθαγορείοις τῷ τοῦ Διὸς, καὶ Ζηνὸς, ὀνόματι σεμνύνειν· δι' ὃν τὸ εἶναι, καὶ τὸ ζῇν, τοῖς πᾶσιν ὑπάρχει, τοῦτον δίκαιον ἀπὸ τῆς ἐνεργείας ὀνομάζεσθαι"</note> *It was the custom of the Pythagoreans to honor the Maker and Father of this entire universe with the names of Dis and Zen. Since it is through him that existence and life belong to all things, it is right that he be named after his creative work.* And again afterward: <note>original: "τὸ τοῦ Διὸς ὄνομα σύμβολόν ἐστι, καὶ εἰκὼν ἐν φωνῇ δημιουργικῆς οὐσίας, τῷ τοὺς πρώτους θεμένους τοῖς πράγμασι τὰ ὀνόματα διὰ σοφίας ὑπερβολὴν, ὥσπερ τινὰς ἀγαλματοποιούς ἀρίστους, διὰ τῶν ὀνομάτων, ὡς δι' εἰκόνων, ἐμφανίσαι αὐτοῦ τὰς δυνάμεις"</note> *This very name Zeus is a fitting symbol or vocal image of the creative essence <note>original: "demiurgical nature"</note>. And those who first gave names to things were, through their extraordinary wisdom, like excellent sculptors; by using those various names as images, they vividly revealed the powers of the Divine.* Furthermore, Iamblichus explains in his *Protreptics* <note>term: Protreptics, an exhortational or persuasive discourse</note> that this Pythagorean prayer was directed to the supreme divine power and King of Gods: <note>original: "ἐν δὴ τούτοις μία μὲν ἀρίστη παράκλησις εἰς τὴν θείαν εὐδαιμονίαν ἡ μεμιγμένη ταῖς εὐχαῖς καὶ ἀνακλήσεσι τῶν θεῶν, καὶ μάλιστα τοῦ βασιλέως αὐτῶν Διός"</note> *In these lines, there is one excellent exhortation to pursue divine happiness, combined with prayers and the calling upon the gods, but especially upon that Jupiter who is their king.* Moreover, this could also be further seen from the Pythagorean fragments that still survive, such as those of Ocellus Lucanus and other moralists. In these writings, while "gods" are sometimes mentioned in the plural, the word "God" is also often used in the singular to refer to that supreme deity who contains the whole.

But this will be most obvious of all from what has been recorded about the Pythagorean philosophy and its identification of a Monad <note>term: Monad, from the Greek "monas" (unit), referring to the single, indivisible source of all existence</note> as the First Principle. It is true, however, that the author of *The Opinions of the Philosophers* <note>original: "de Placitis Philosophorum"</note> claims that Pythagoras asserted two sub-

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Pythagoras's theological and philosophical framework, specifically focusing on his "First Principles." It moves from his general piety toward gods and heroes to his core metaphysical concepts: the Monad (Unity) and the Dyad (Duality).</meta>

<page-num>372</page-num>
<header>Pythagoras's Monad, BOOK I.</header>

[Sub]stantial self-existent principles, a Monad and a Dyad: while the former is acknowledged to have meant God, the latter is described with some uncertainty. In one place, it is interpreted to be a *demon*, or a principle of evil: <note>original Greek: "πυθαγόρας τῶν ἀρχῶν τὴν μὲν μονάδα θεὸν, καὶ τἀγαθὸν, ἥτις ἐστὶν ἡ τοῦ ἑνὸς φύσις, αὐτὸς ὁ νοῦς· τὴν δ' ἀόριστον δυάδα δαίμονα, καὶ τὸ κακόν, &c."</note> *Pythagoras's First Principle is God and Good, which is the Nature of Unity, and a perfect Mind; but his other Principle of Duality is a demon <term>demon: here meaning a supernatural spirit or "daimon," though linked to evil in this context</term> or evil.* But in another 
<margin>Book 1, chapter 3.</margin>
place, it is explained to be Matter: <note>original Greek: "πάλιν τὴν μονάδα καὶ τὴν ἀόριστον δυάδα ἐν ταῖς ἀρχαῖς· σπεύδειν δὲ αὐτῷ τῶν ἀρχῶν ἡ μὲν ἐπὶ τὸ ποιητικὸν αἴτιον καὶ εἰδικὸν, (ὅπερ ἐστὶ νοῦς ὁ θεὸς) ἡ δὲ ἐπὶ τὸ παθητικόν τε καὶ ὑλικόν (ὅπερ ἐστὶν ὁ ὁρατὸς κόσμος·)"</note> *Pythagoras's principles were a Monad and Infinite Duality: the former of them an active principle, Mind or God; the latter passive and Matter.* 

And Plutarch, in some of his other writings, declares that the First Matter did not exist alone by itself, dead and inanimate, but acted with an irrational soul; and that both of these together made up that wicked *demon* of his. Doubtless, this book *On the Opinions of the Philosophers* <note>original: "De Placitis Philosophorum"</note> was either written by Plutarch himself, or else by some disciple and follower of his according to his principles. Therefore, this account given of the Pythagorean doctrine was probably influenced by Plutarch’s own private notion: that God and a wicked *demon*, or else Matter together with a self-existent irrational soul, were the *First Principles of the Universe*. However, we do acknowledge that others besides Plutarch have supposed Pythagoras to have made two self-existent principles, God and Matter, but not animate, nor shaped (as Plutarch supposed) by any irrational or wicked soul.

<margin>Page 203.</margin>
Despite this, it may well be questioned whether Pythagoras meant "Matter" by his *Dyad* or not. This is because Malchus (also known as Porphyry), in his *Life of Pythagoras*, interprets those two Pythagorean principles of *Unity* and *Duality* this way: <note>original Greek: "τὸ αἴτιον τῆς συμπνοίας καὶ τῆς συμπαθείας, καὶ τῆς σωτηρίας τῶν ὅλων τοῦ κατὰ ταυτὰ καὶ ὡσαύτως ἔχοντος, ὃν προσηγόρευσαν, καὶ γὰρ τὸ ἓν τοῖς κατὰ μέρος, ἐν τοῖσδε κατὰ μέρος, ἡνωμένον τοῖς μέρεσι καὶ σύμπνοιαν, κατὰ μετουσίαν τοῦ πρώτου αἰτίου· ἣ δὲ τῆς ἑτερότητος καὶ ἀνισότητος καὶ παντὸς τοῦ μεριστοῦ καὶ ἐν μεταβολῇ καὶ ἄλλοτε ἄλλως ἔχοντος δυοειδῆ λόγον καὶ δυάδα προσηγόρευσαν·"</note> *The cause of that sympathy, harmony, and agreement which is in things, and of the preservation of the Whole (which is always the same and consistent), was called by Pythagoras Unity or a Monad (that unity which is in the things themselves being but a participation in the First Cause). But the reason for otherness, inequality, and all that is divisible, changeable, and shifting, he called a dual principle or a Dyad.* 

Thus, according to Porphyry, the Pythagorean *Dyad* does not mean "matter" so much as the *infinite and indeterminate nature* and the *passive capability of things*. In this view, the *Monad* and *Dyad* of Pythagoras seem to be the same as Plato’s *limit* <note>original: "πέρας"</note> and *infinite* <note>original: "ἄπειρον"</note>—his "Finite" and "Infinite" in his dialogue *Philebus*. Of these two, only the former is substantial: that first and most simple Being, the cause of all unity and the measure of all things.

<page-num>373</page-num>
<header>CHAP. IV. The sole Principle of All Things.</header>

However, if Pythagoras’s *Dyad* is to be understood as a substantial matter, it does not necessarily follow that he supposed *matter* to be self-existent and independent of the Deity. According to the best and most ancient writers, his *Dyad* was not a primary thing but only a secondary one, derived from his *Monad*, the sole origin of all things. Thus, *Diogenes Laertius* <note>Diogenes Laertius was a 3rd-century biographer of the Greek philosophers.</note> tells us that *Alexander*, who wrote *The Successions of Philosophers*, affirmed he had found in the Pythagorean commentaries that "a Monad was the principle of all things, but from this Monad was derived infinite Duality, to serve as matter for the Monad, which is the active cause." <note>original Greek: "ἀρχὴν μὲν τῶν ἁπάντων, μονάδα· ἐκ δὲ τῆς μονάδος, ἀόριστον δυάδα, ὡς ἂν ὕλην τῇ μονάδι αἰτίῳ ὄντι ὑποστῆναι"</note> *Hermias* agrees with this, affirming it to be one of the greatest of all the Pythagorean mysteries that a *Monad* was the sole principle of all things. Accordingly, *Clement of Alexandria* <note>Clemens Alexandrinus was a Christian theologian who sought to unite Greek philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note> cites this passage from *Thearidas*, an ancient Pythagorean, in his book *Concerning Nature*: <margin>Strom. 5. p. 611.</margin> "The true principle of all things was only One; for in the beginning, it was one and alone." <note>original Greek: "Ἁ ἀρχὰ τῶν ὄντων, ἀρχὰ μὲν ὄντως ἀληθινὰ, μία. Κεῖνα γὰρ ἐν ἀρχῇ τέ ἐστιν ἓν καὶ μόνον"</note> These words also seem to imply that the world had a beginning of existence or a start to its duration. 

And indeed, regardless of what *Ocellus Lucanus* <note>A Pythagorean philosopher who argued for the eternity of the universe.</note> may have written, we can conclude that *Pythagoras* himself did not believe in the *eternity of the world* from what *Porphyry* records of him. Porphyry gives an account of Pythagoras’s superstitious abstinence from beans, explaining: "In the beginning, when the first principle and the generation of things were in turmoil—with many things being crowded together, stirred, and decaying in the earth—a gradual flowing and separation took place. Animals were formed and plants sprang up, and at that time, from the same decaying matter, both humans and beans were formed." <note>original Greek: "ὅτι τῆς πρώτης ἀρχῆς καὶ γενέσεως ταραττομένης... ἀνθρώπους συστῆναι καὶ κυάμους βλαστῆσαι"</note>

Pythagoras is generally reported to have held a *Trinity* of divine hypostases <term>hypostases: distinct persons or substances within the Godhead</term>. Therefore, when Saint Cyril affirms that Pythagoras called God "the animation of all the heavenly spheres and the motion of all things," <note>original Greek: "ψύχωσιν τῶν ὅλων κύκλων, καὶ πάντων κίνησιν"</note> and adds that God was not, as some supposed, "outside the arrangement of the world, but within it, the whole in the whole," <note>original Greek: "ἐκτὸς τῆς διακοσμήσεως, ἀλλ’ ἐν αὐτῷ ὅλος ἐν ὅλῳ"</note> this seems properly understood as referring to that *third* divine hypostasis of the Pythagorean Trinity, namely the eternal *Soul* <note>original: "Psyche"</note>. 

Again, when God is called "Mind itself" in *Plutarch* according to Pythagoras, <note>original Greek: "αὐτὸς ὁ νοῦς"</note> this seems to refer properly to his *second hypostasis*. For Pythagoras, the supreme Deity was something even above mind or *intellect*. Similarly, in *Cicero*, Pythagoras’s opinion concerning the Deity is represented this way: "God is a Mind extended through and passing through the whole nature of things, from which our own souls are plucked." <note>original Latin: "Deum esse animum, per naturam rerum omnium intentum & commeantem, ex quo Animi nostri carperentur"</note> And again: "Our souls are sampled from the universal divine Mind." <note>original Latin: "Ex universa mente Divina, delibatos esse animos nostros"</note> In all probability, this was also to be understood as either—

<summary>This page clarifies that Pythagoras viewed the "Monad" (Unity) as the sole primary cause, with the "Dyad" (Matter) being derived from it, and explores how Pythagoras's views on God align with a Trinity of divine substances (Mind and Soul).</summary>

either of the Third or Second Divine *Hypostasis* <note>term: A Greek word meaning "substance" or "person," used here to describe the distinct persons of a divine Trinity.</note>, and not of the First. This First Principle was properly called by him "the One" <note>original Greek: τὸ ἓν</note> and "the Monad" <note>original Greek: μόνας</note>, and also, as *Plutarch* tells us, "the Good" <note>original Greek: τὸ ἀγαθὸν</note>, or *Goodness* itself.

<margin>Aristotle, *Metaphysics*, Book 1, Chapter 6.</margin>
*Aristotle* plainly states that some of the ancient theologians among the Pagans made *Eros*, or *Love*, the First Principle of all things—that is, the *Supreme Deity*. We have already shown that *Orpheus* was one of these. For when "delightful Love," which is "not blind, but full of Wisdom and Counsel" <note>original Greek: ἔρως πολυτερπὴς and πολυμήτις</note>, is described by him as "self-perfect" and the "oldest" <note>original Greek: αὐτοτελὲς and πρεσβύτατον</note> of all things, it is clear that he supposed it to be nothing less than the Supreme Deity. Therefore, since it is generally affirmed that *Pythagoras* followed Orphic principles, we may presume he did so in this matter as well. 

However, it is very true that *Plato*—who, like *Pythagoras*, called the Supreme Deity "the Good"—disagreed with Orphic theology on this point. He would not acknowledge *Love* as a name for the Supreme Deity. For instance, in his *Symposium*, speaking through the character *Agathon*, he says: "Though I should readily grant many other things to Phaedrus, I cannot agree with him that Love was older than Saturn and Japet <note>Saturn (Cronus) and Japet (Iapetus) were Titans, regarded in Greek mythology as the oldest generation of gods.</note>. On the contrary, I affirm him to be the youngest of the gods, and always youthful" <note>original Greek: Φαίδρῳ πολλὰ ἄλλα ὁμολογῶν, τοῦτο οὐχ ὁμολογῶ, ὡς Ἔρως Κρόνου καὶ Ἰαπετοῦ ἀρχαιότερός ἐστιν· ἀλλὰ φημὶ νεώτατον αὐτὸν εἶναι θεῶν, καὶ ἀεὶ νέον</note>. 

Those who made *Love* older than *Saturn* and *Japhet* supposed it to be the Supreme Deity. *Plato*, on the contrary, affirms that *Love* is not the *Supreme Deity* or Creator of *all*, but a *creature*. He considers Love a certain "Junior God," or even, as he later adds, not so much a *God* as a *Daemon* <note>term: In Greek philosophy, a spirit or intermediary being between gods and mortals, not necessarily an evil "demon."</note>, because love implies a state of imperfection. "Love," he says, "is a philosopher," whereas "no god philosophizes, nor desires to be made wise, because he is wise already" <note>original Greek: θεῶν οὐδεῖς φιλοσοφεῖ, οὐδ᾽ ἐπιθυμεῖ σοφὸς γενέσθαι, ἔστι γὰρ</note>. 

Agreeing with this doctrine, *Plotinus* determines that Love belongs to that middle rank of beings called Souls. "Every soul is a Venus," he writes. "This is also hinted at by the birth of Venus and Love being born with her. Therefore, the soul, being in its right natural state, loves God and desires to be united with him, just as a beautiful maiden loves a handsome man. But when the soul enters into the world of 'generation' <note>the physical world of birth, change, and decay</note> and is deceived by amorous allurements here below—as if by false marriage proposals—it exchanges its divine and heavenly love for another, mortal love. But if it again shakes off these lustful and wanton loves, keeping itself chaste and returning to its own Father and Origin, it will be restored to its proper state" <note>original Greek: πᾶσα ψυχὴ, ἀφροδίτη· καὶ τοῦτο αἰνίττεται καὶ τὰ τῆς ἀφροδίτης γενέθλια, καὶ ὁ ἔρως ὁ μετ᾿ αὐτῆς γενόμενος· ἐρᾷ οὖν κατὰ φύσιν ἔχουσα ψυχὴ θεοῦ, ἑνωθῆναι θέλουσα, ὥσπερ παρθένος καλὴ πρὸς καλὸν ἄνδρα· ὅταν δὲ εἰς γένεσιν ἐλθοῦσα, οἷον μνηστείαις ἀπατηθῇ, ἄλλον ἀρξαμένη θνητὸν ἔρωτα, ἐρημίᾳ πατρὸς ὑβρίζεται, &c.</note>. 

The reason for this difference between the followers of Orpheus and *Plato*—that the former made *Love* the *oldest* of all the gods, while the latter made it a *Junior God* or *Daemon*—resulted only from a double meaning of the word *Love*. For *Plato's* *Love* was the daughter of *Penia* (Poverty and Lack) together with a mixture of *Poros* (Riches). Being a compound of plenty and poverty, it was, in plain language, nothing other than the *Love of Desire*,

It concludes that the disagreement arises from using the word "Love" to describe either divine perfection or the soul's longing for what it lacks.</summary>

# CHAPTER IV. Others, the Youngest God.

*Desire*, which as *Aristotle* affirms is accompanied with grief and pain <note>original Greek: μετὰ λύπης</note>. But that *Orphic* and *Pythagorean Love* was nothing else but *infinite riches and plenty* <note>original Greek: πόρος and εὐπορία</note>, a *Love of abundance and overflowing fullness*, delighting to *communicate itself*. This was therefore said to be the *oldest* of all things and most *perfect*—that is, the *Supreme Deity*. According to this notion, in the Scripture itself, God seems to be called *Love*, though the word there is not *Eros* <note>term: ἔρως; often referring to passionate or acquisitive love</note> but *Agape* <note>term: ἀγάπη; referring to selfless, divine love</note>. 

But to say the truth, the Love described by *Parmenides* (however it was made a Principle somewhere by *Aristotle*) seems to be neither exactly the same as the *Orphic* nor the *Platonic Love*. It is not the Supreme Deity, but rather the first of the *created gods*. This appears from *Simplicius* connecting these two verses of his together in this manner:

->In the midst of these is the divinity who governs all things,<-
->whom he affirms to be the cause of the gods, saying,<-
->first of all the gods, she devised Love.<-
<note>original Greek: 'Εν δὲ μέσῳ τούτων δαίμων ὃς πάντα κυβερνᾷ, ταύτην καὶ θεῶν αἰτίαν εἶναί φησι, λέγων, πρώτιστον μὲν ἔρωτα θεῶν μητίσατο πάντων.</note>

> *In the midst of these elements is that God which governs all things, and whom Parmenides affirms to be the cause of gods, writing thus: God first of all created Love, before the other gods.* Therefore, by this *Love* of *Parmenides*, nothing else is understood but the *lower soul of the world*, together with a *plastic nature* <note>term: "Plastic nature" refers to the unconscious, formative power that shapes the physical world according to divine blueprints.</note>. Although this is the original source of *motion* and *activity* in this physical world, it is nonetheless only a *secondary* or *created god*. Before its production, *Necessity* is said by those *pagan theologians* <note>original: Ethnick Theologers</note> to have reigned. The true meaning of this seems to be that before that Divine Spirit moved upon the waters and brought things into an orderly system, there was nothing but the *necessity of material motions*, unguided by any orderly wisdom or method for good (that is, by *Love*) in that confused and floating chaos.

But it seems *Pythagoras* did not only call the Supreme Deity a *Monad*, but also a *Tetrad* or *Tetractys*. It is generally affirmed that *Pythagoras himself* used to swear by this; though *Porphyry*, *Iamblichus*, and others write that the disciples of *Pythagoras* swore by *Pythagoras* himself, who had delivered to them the doctrine or *secret tradition* <note>original: Cabala</note> of this *Tetractys*. This *Tetractys* is also called in the *Golden Verses* "the fountain of the eternal nature" <note>original Greek: πηγὴ ἀεννάου φύσεως</note>, an expression that cannot properly belong to anything but the Supreme Deity. 

And thus *Hierocles* writes: "There is nothing that can be mentioned which does not depend upon the Tetractys as its root and principle. For the Tetrad is, as we have said, the creator of all things and its cause; the intelligible God, the cause of the heavenly and sensible God <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἔστιν εἰπεῖν ὃ μὴ τῇ τετράκτυϊ, ὡς ῥίζης, καὶ ἀρχῆς ἤρτηται. ἔστι γὰρ, ὡς ἔφαμεν, δημιουργὸς τῶν ὅλων, καὶ αἰτία ἡ τετρὰς, θεὸς νοητὸς, αἴτιος τοῦ οὐρανίου, καὶ αἰσθητοῦ θεοῦ</note>," that is, of the animated world or heaven. Now the later *Pythagoreans* and *Platonists* endeavor to give reasons why God should be called *Tetras* or *Tetractys* from certain mysteries within that number *four*; as for example,

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Pythagorean "Tetractys" as a symbol for the divine, transitioning from mathematical explanations to the theory that it actually refers to the Hebrew name of God, the Tetragrammaton.</meta>

# The Tetractys, The Tetragrammaton. BOOK I.

First, because the *Tetrad* <note>term: Tetrad; the number four</note> is the *power of the decade* <note>original Greek: δύναμις δεκάδος</note>, it virtually contains the whole Decade <note>term: Decade; the number ten</note> within it, which represents all numbers or *beings*. The root of this mystery is simply this: that *One*, *Two*, *Three*, and *Four*, when added together, make *Ten*. Again, because the *Tetrad* is an arithmetical middle between the *Monad* <note>term: Monad; the number one</note> and the *Hebdomad* <note>term: Hebdomad; the number seven</note>. The *Monad* and *Hebdomad* are said to agree in this: just as the *Monad* is unbegotten or unmade—being the original source and fountain of all numbers—so the *Hebdomad* is said to be not only a *virgin* <note>original Greek: παρθένος</note> but *motherless* <note>original Greek: ἀμήτωρ; a "motherless" number</note>. Therefore, they say the Tetrad, lying in the middle between the unbegotten *Monad* and the motherless virgin *Hebdomad*, and being both begotten and begetting, must be a very mysterious number that fits the *Deity*. 

However, it was actually unfit to represent the Deity because it is "begotten" by the multiplication of another number <note>meaning 2 x 2 = 4</note>; just as the Hebdomad does not very fitly symbolize God either, because it is "barren" and begets nothing else within the first ten numbers, which is why it is called a *virgin*. Again, it is further added that the *Tetrad* fitly resembles that which is *solid*. Just as a *point* corresponds to a *Monad*, a *line* to a *Dyad* <note>term: Dyad; the number two</note>, and a *surface* to a *Triad* <note>term: Triad; the number three—the first and simplest geometric figure being a triangle</note>, so the *Tetrad* properly represents the *solid*, as the first *pyramid* is found within it. But by this logic, the Tetrad could not be as fit a symbol of the incorporeal *Deity* as it is of the physical world. 

Because these mathematical explanations are so trivial, slight, and fanciful—and because it is actually absurd for *Pythagoras* to call his *Monad* a *Tetrad*—the recent conjecture of some learned men among us seems much more probable: that Pythagoras's *Tetractys* <note>term: Tetractys; a triangular figure of ten points, but here referring to the number four</note> was actually nothing else but the *Tetragrammaton*. This is the proper name of the Supreme *God* among the *Hebrews*, consisting of *four letters* or consonants <note>the name YHWH</note>. Nor should it be wondered at that *Pythagoras* was so well acquainted with the Hebrew *Tetragrammaton*. In addition to his travels into *Egypt*, *Persia*, and *Chaldea*, and his stay at *Sidon*, he is affirmed by *Josephus*, *Porphyrius*, and others to have conversed with the *Hebrews* as well. This name was not unknown to the Etruscans and Latins either, as their *Jove* <note>Jupiter</note> was certainly derived from it. 

Indeed, it is the opinion of some philologists <note>original: philologers; scholars of historical language and literature</note> that even in the *Golden Verses* <note>a collection of moral exhortations attributed to Pythagoras</note> themselves, despite the apparent grammar of the sentence, the oath is not sworn by *Pythagoras*, but by this *Tetractys* or *Tetragrammaton*. That is, *Jova* or *Jehovah*, the *name of God*, is put for God himself, according to that accepted doctrine of the Hebrews: *He is His Name, and His Name is He* <note>original Hebrew: הוא שמו ושמו הוא</note>. It is as if the meaning of those words:

->*Yes, by Him who transmitted the Tetractys to our soul,*<-
->*The fountain of eternal nature.*<-
<note>original Greek: Ναὶ μὰ τὸν ἁμετέρᾳ ψυχᾷ παραδόντα τετρακτὺν Πάγαν ἀεννάου φύσεως</note>

were this: *By the Tetragrammaton* or *Jova, who has communicated Himself (or the Fountain of the Eternal Nature) to our human souls*. For according to Pythagorean doctrine, souls were said to be *plucked and sampled from the Divine Mind* <note>original Latin: ex Mente Divina carptæ & delibatæ</note>—that is, they are nothing but derivative streams from that first fountain of the Divine Mind.

It explains the symbolic connections between numbers and the divine while suggesting Pythagoras learned this name for God during his travels among the Hebrews.</summary>

### Chap. IV. Xenophanes's "One and All"

Therefore, we shall now summarize everything concerning Pythagoras with this conclusion from St. Cyril: <margin>Against Julian, Book 1</margin> *"Behold and see clearly: he says there is one God of the whole universe, the principle and cause of all his powers, the light and animator—or quickener—of the whole, and the source of all motion. For all things have been derived from him and are seen to have received their movement from non-existence into being."* <note>original Greek: ἰδὲ δὴ σαφῶς, ἕνα τε εἶναι λέγει τὸν ὅλων θεὸν, καὶ πάντων ἀρχὴν ἐργάτιν τε τῶν αὐτοῦ δυνάμεων, φωστῆρα καὶ ψύχωσιν, ἤτοι ζωοποίησιν τῶν ὅλων καὶ κύκλων πάντων κίνησιν· παρῆκται γὰρ τὰ πάντα παρ’ αὐτοῦ καὶ τὴν ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος εἰς τὸ εἶναι κίνησιν λαχόντα φαίνεται.</note>

Next to Pythagoras in order of time was Xenophanes of Colophon, the head of the Eleatic sect of philosophers. That he asserted both "many gods" and "one God" is sufficiently clear from the verse of his cited earlier and attested to by both Clement of Alexandria and Sextus the philosopher:

->*There is one God, the greatest among both gods and men.* <note>original Greek: Εἷς θεὸς ἔν τε θεοῖσι καὶ ἀνθρώποισι μέγιστος</note><-

Concerning this greatest God, this other verse by Xenophanes is also cited:

->*He moves the whole world without any labor or toil, merely by his mind.* <note>original Greek: Καὶ ἀπάνευθε πόνοιο νόου φρενὶ πάντα κραδαίνει</note><-

Besides this, Cicero and others tell us that Xenophanes, when philosophizing about the supreme deity, used to call it **One and All** <note>original Greek: ἓν καὶ πᾶν</note>, as being one most simple being that virtually contains all things. But Xenophanes's theosophy <note>term: theosophy; here meaning "divine philosophy" or the study of God's nature</note> is most fully explained by Simplicius, quoting Theophrastus in this manner: <margin>In Aristotle's Physics, Book 5. 56.</margin> *"Theophrastus affirms that Xenophanes of Colophon, the teacher of Parmenides, proposed one principle of all things—calling it 'One and All'—and determining it to be neither finite nor infinite (in a certain sense) and neither moving nor resting. Theophrastus also declares that Xenophanes, in this matter, did not write as a natural scientist <note>original: "Physiologer"</note>, but as a metaphysician or theologian only; Xenophanes's 'One and All' being nothing else but God. He proved God to be one solitary being because God is the best and most powerful of all things; and since there are many degrees of existence, there must necessarily be something supreme to rule over all. This best and most powerful being can be only one. He also demonstrated..."* <note>original Greek: Μίαν γὰρ τὴν ἀρχὴν, ἤτοι ἓν τὸ ὂν καὶ πᾶν, καὶ οὔτε πεπερασμένον οὔτε ἄπειρον, οὔτε κινούμενον οὔτε ἠρεμοῦν, Ξενοφάνην τὸν κολοφώνιον τὸν Παρμενίδου διδάσκαλον ὑποτίθεσθαί φησιν ὁ Θεόφραστος· ὁμολογῶν ἑτέρας εἶναι μᾶλλον ἢ τῆς περὶ φύσεως ἱστορίας, τὴν μνήμην τῆς τούτου δόξης· τὸ γὰρ ἓν τοῦτο καὶ πᾶν, τὸν θεὸν ἔλεγεν ὁ Ξενοφάνης· ὃν ἕνα μὲν δείκνυσιν ἐκ τοῦ πάντων κράτιστον εἶναι· πλειόνων γάρ φησιν ὄντων, ὁμοίως ἀνάγκη ὑπάρχειν πᾶσι τὸ κρατεῖν· τὸ δὲ πάντων κράτιστον καὶ ἄριστον, θεός· ἀγένητον δὲ ἐδείκνυεν . . . καὶ οὔτε ἄπειρον οὔτε πεπερασμένον εἶναι· διότι ἄπειρον μὲν τὸ μὴ ὂν, ὡς ἄτε ἀρχὴν ἔχον μήτε μέσον μήτε τέλος· περαίνειν δὲ πρὸς ἄλληλα τὰ πλείω· παραπλησίως δὲ καὶ τὴν κίνησιν ἀφαιρεῖ καὶ τὴν ἠρεμίαν· ἀκίνητον μὲν, &c.</note>

### Heraclitus's God; His Book I.

...demonstrate it to be *unmade*, as likewise to be neither *finite* nor *infinite* (in a certain sense), just as he removed both *motion* and *rest* from *God*. Therefore, when he says that *God* always remains or rests the same, he does not mean this as the kind of *rest* which is the opposite of *motion* (which belongs to things that can be moved), but as a different kind of *rest* that is above both that motion and its contrary. From this, it is evident that *Xenophanes* supposed (as *Sextus* the philosopher also affirms) *God* to be *incorporeal*, a *being* unlike all other things, and therefore one of which no *image* could be made. 

Now we understand that *Aristotle* did not deal honestly with *Xenophanes* when he took the expression that *God* was <term>spheryform</term> <note>original Greek: σφαιροειδὴς, meaning spherical in form</note> and inferred that *Xenophanes* made *God* out to be a physical body—nothing more than the *round corporeal world animated*. This interpretation was actually inconsistent with another *physical hypothesis* of this same *Xenophanes*: *that there were infinite suns and moons* <note>original Greek: ἀπείρους ἡλίους εἶναι καὶ σελήνας</note>. By *moons*, he understood *planets*, affirming them all to be habitable Earths, as *Cicero* tells us. Therefore, as *Simplicius* concludes, *God* was called <term>spheryform</term> by *Xenophanes* only in the sense of being *everywhere alike and uniform* <note>original Greek: παντοχόθεν ὅμοιος</note>. Regardless, it is plain that *Xenophanes*, by asserting *one God* who was *all* or the *universe*, could not acknowledge a *multitude* of *partial, self-existent deities*.

*Heraclitus* was not a *clear* but a *confused philosopher* (being neither a *good naturalist* nor a *metaphysician*), and therefore it is very hard, or rather impossible, to reconcile his several opinions with one another. This is not surprising because, among his other opinions, he is said to have held this one: *that contradictories may be true*. His writings were accordingly—as *Plato* suggests—stuffed with unintelligible, mysterious nonsense. For first, he is claimed to have acknowledged no substance other than body, and to have maintained *that all things flow, and nothing stands still or remains the same*. And yet, in his letters (following the common opinion of philosophers at that time), he assumes the *pre-existence* and *post-existence* of *human souls* in these words:

> My soul seems to prophesy <note>original Greek: τάχα καὶ ψυχὴ μαντεύεται ἀπόλυσιν ἑαυτῆς ἤδη ποτὲ ἐκ τοῦ δεσμωτηρίου τούτου· καὶ σφοδρῶς τοῦ σώματος ἐκκύπτουσα, ἀναμιμνήσκεται τὰ πάτρια χωρία, ἔνθεν κατελθοῦσα περιεβάλλετο ῥέον σῶμα τεθνειὸς τοῦτο, ὃ δοκεῖ, &c.</note> and foresee its approaching release and freedom from this prison; and looking out, as it were, through the cracks and crevices of this body, it remembers its native regions or countries from which it descended and was clothed with this *flowing mortal body*, which is made up and hardened from *phlegm, bile, serum, blood, nerves, bones, and flesh*.

And not only so, but he also acknowledges the soul's immortality, which the *Stoics* (who allowed for its survival after death for some time, at least until the next *conflagration* <note>term: conflagration; in Stoic philosophy, the periodic destruction of the universe by fire</note>) denied:

> This body shall be fated to change into something else <note>original Greek: δύσεται τὸ σῶμα εἰς τὸ εἱμαρμένον, ἀλλὰ ἡ ψυχὴ οὐ δύσεται· ἀλλὰ ἀθάνατον οὖσα χρῆμα, εἰς οὐρανὸν ἀναπτήσεται μετάρσιος· δέξονται δέ με αἰθέριοι δόμοι, καὶ πολιτεύσομαι οὐκ ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἀλλ’ ἐν θεοῖς·</note>, but my soul shall not die. Instead, being an immortal thing, it shall fly away, mounting upward to heaven; those ethereal homes shall receive me, and I shall no longer...

<summary>This page argues that Xenophanes viewed God as an incorporeal, uniform being rather than a physical sphere, and contrasts this with the contradictory writings of Heraclitus, who fluctuated between materialism and a belief in the soul's immortality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the philosopher Heraclitus, moving from his abstract theories of the soul and fire to his moral character and his views on the nature of God and religious worship.</meta>

# CHAP. IV. The Temple is the whole World.

...no longer converse with *men*, but with *gods*. Again, though *Heraclitus* asserted the *fatal necessity* <note>The belief that all events are predetermined and unavoidable.</note> of all things, he was nevertheless a *strict* moralist, and for this reason was highly esteemed by the *Stoics*, who followed him in this and other matters. He makes no small claim to this character himself in his Epistle to *Hermodorus*:

> "I have also had my difficult labors and conflicts, just as Hercules did; I have conquered pleasures, I have conquered riches, I have conquered ambition; I have subdued cowardice and flattery. Neither fear nor intemperance can control me; grief and anger are afraid of me and fly away from me. These are the victories for which I am crowned—not by Eurystheus, but by being made master of myself." <note>original Greek: κ’ ἐμοίγε πολλοί κ’ δυσχερέστατοι ἄθλοι κατώρθωνται· νενίκηκα ἡδονὰς, νενίκηκα χρήματα, νενίκηκα φιλοτιμίαν, κατεπάλαισα δειλίαν, κατεπάλαισα κολακείαν· οὐκ ἀντιλέγει μοι φόβος, οὐκ ἀντιλέγει μοι μέθη· φοβεῖταί με λύπη, φοβεῖταί με ὀργή· κ’ διὰ τούτων αὐτῶν κ’ αὐτός ἐστεφάνωμαι, ἐμαυτῷ ἐπιτάττων, οὐχ ὑπ’ Εὐρυσθέως</note>

Lastly, though *Heraclitus* claimed that fire was the first principle of all things and has some strange ideas attributed to him, he was nonetheless a *devoutly religious man*. He supposed the *fiery matter* of the whole universe "to be a living being and God" <note>original Latin: *Animantem esse & Deum*</note>. And while he acknowledged many gods, as *Aristotle* records of him—stating that when some people passed by and saw him sitting in a smoky cottage, he spoke to them in this way: "*Come in, I pray, for here there are gods also*" <note>original Latin: *Introite, nam & hic Dii sunt*</note>, since he believed all places were full of gods, demons, and souls—he was also an undoubted supporter of one supreme *divinity* <note>original: *Numen*</note> that governs all things. He believed this divinity could neither be represented by images nor confined to temples. 

For after he had been accused of impiety by *Euthycles*, he wrote to *Hermodorus* in this manner:

> "But O you unwise and unlearned! Teach us first what God is, so that you may be believed in accusing me of impiety. Tell us, where is God? Is he shut up within the walls of temples? Is this your piety, to place God in the dark, or to make him a stony god? O you unskillful people! Do you not know that God is not made with hands, and has no base or support to stand upon, nor can he be enclosed within the walls of any temple? The whole world, decorated with plants, animals, and stars, is his temple." <note>original Greek: ἀλλ’ ὦ ἀμαθεῖς ἄνθρωποι διδάξατε πρῶτον ἡμᾶς τί ἐστὶν ὁ θεός, πῶ δ’ ἐστὶν ὁ θεός; ἐν τοῖς ναοῖς ἀποκεκλεισμένος; ἀσεβεῖς γε, οἳ ἐν σκότῳ τὸν θεὸν ἱδρύετε— ἀπαίδευτοι, οὐκ ἴστε ὅτι οὐκ ἐστὶ θεὸς χειρότμητος, οὐδὲ ἐξ ἀρχῆς βάσιν ἔχει οὐδὲ ἔχει ἕνα περίβολον· ἀλλ’ ὅλος ὁ κόσμος αὐτῷ ναός ἐστι, ζώοις καὶ φυτοῖς καὶ ἄστροις πεποικιλμένος</note>

And again:

> "Am I impious, O Euthycles, who alone know what God is? Is there no God without altars? Or are stones the only witnesses of him? No, his own works give testimony to him, and principally the sun. Night and day bear witness of him; the seasons are his witnesses; the whole earth bringing forth fruits declares him; the circle of the moon, which was made by him, is a heavenly testimony of him." <note>original Greek: ἆρ’ οὐκ εἰμὶ εὐσεβὴς, εὐθύκλεις, ὃς μόνος οἶδα θεὸν; ἐὰν δὲ μὴ ἱδρυσθῇ θεῷ βωμὸς, οὐκ ἔστι θεὸς; ἐὰν δὲ ἱδρυσθῇ μὴ θεῷ, θεός ἐστιν; ὥστε λίθοι θεῶν μάρτυρες· ἔργα δεῖ μαρτυρεῖν, οἷα ἥλιος· νὺξ αὐτῷ καὶ ἡμέρα μαρτυροῦσιν· ὦραι αὐτῷ μάρτυρες, γῆ ὅλη καρποφοροῦσα, μάρτυς· σελήνης ὁ κύκλος, ἐκείνου ἔργον,, οὐράνιος μαρτυρία</note>

<meta>This page transitions from the discussion of Heraclitus to Anaxagoras, focusing on how Anaxagoras introduced the concept of a divine "Mind" into the previously materialistic Ionian school of philosophy.</meta>

<page-num>380</page-num>
<header>Anaxagoras and His Concept of One Infinite Mind, Book I.</header>

...is to be considered. His predecessors of the **Ionian Order** <note>A school of Greek philosophy centered in Ionia (modern-day Turkey) during the 6th and 5th centuries BC.</note> after **Thales**—such as **Anaximander**, **Anaximenes**, and **Hippo**—were (as has been already observed) **materialists** and **atheists**. They acknowledged no other substance besides the body and reduced all things to its motions, passions, and characteristics. This led to the cautious advice given by **Iamblichus**:

<margin>Symbol 36. p. 159.</margin>

"Prefer the **Italian Philosophy** <note>The "Italian" school refers to the Pythagorean and Eleatic schools, which were more focused on metaphysical and incorporeal concepts than the Ionian materialists.</note>, which contemplates incorporeal substances by themselves, before the Ionian, which principally considers bodies." <note>original Greek: προτίμα τὴν Ἰταλικὴν φιλοσοφίαν τὴν τὰ ἀσώματα καθ᾿ αὑτὰ θεωροῦσαν, τῆς Ἰονικῆς τῆς τὰ σώματα προηγουμένως ἐπισκοπουμένης</note>

**Anaxagoras** was the first of these Ionians who departed from that path. He saw the necessity of some other cause besides the material, since matter is unable to even move itself—and much less could it, by accidental motion, bring itself into an orderly system and structure. He therefore introduced **Mind** into the **creation of the universe** <note>original: *Cosmopœia*</note> as the principal cause of everything. This "Mind" is the same thing as **God**.

<margin>Speech 15.</margin>

Thus **Themistius**, speaking of Anaxagoras, says: "He was the first (that is, among the Ionian philosophers) who brought in Mind and God to the making of the world, and did not derive all things from senseless bodies." <note>original Greek: νοῦν καὶ Θεὸν πρῶτον ἐπαγαγόμενον τῇ κοσμοποιΐᾳ, καὶ οὐ πάντα ἀνάψας τῆς φύσεως τῶν σωμάτων</note> To the same purpose, **Plutarch** wrote in the *Life of Pericles*: "The other Ionian philosophers before Anaxagoras made fortune and blind necessity—that is, the accidental and necessary motions of matter—to be the only origin of the world. But Anaxagoras was the first who affirmed a pure and unmixed Mind to preside over all." <note>original Greek: τοῖς ὅλοις πρῶτος οὐ τύχην οὐδ᾿ ἀνάγκην, διακοσμήσεως ἀρχὴν, ἀλλὰ νοῦν ἐπέστησε καθαρὸν καὶ ἄκρατον</note>

Anaxagoras, therefore, supposed **two substantial, self-existent principles of the universe**:
1. An **Infinite Mind or God**.
2. An **Infinite Homoiomery of Matter** <note>original: *Homoiomery*; Anaxagoras's theory that matter is composed of "similar parts," where every substance contains tiny seeds of all other things but is defined by the majority part.</note>, or infinite atoms. 

These were not "unqualified" atoms, like those of **Empedocles** and **Democritus** (which was the most ancient and genuine form of **atomology** <note>The study or theory of atoms.</note>), but "similar" atoms, such as were individually endowed with all kinds of qualities and forms. His physical theory, therefore, was a modified or "spurious" kind of atomism. 

Anaxagoras did not suppose that God created matter out of nothing. Instead, he believed God was the **principle of its motion** <note>original Greek: κινήσεως ἀρχὴ</note> and also the **cause of what is good and beautiful** <note>original Greek: τοῦ εὖ καὶ καλῶς αἰτία</note>. In other words, God was the regulator of this motion for the sake of "the Good," and consequently the cause of all the order, beauty, and harmony of the world. For this reason, Anaxagoras called this divine principle not only "Mind" but also "Good," as it is that which acts for the sake of what is good. 

Therefore, according to Anaxagoras:
*   **First**, the world was not eternal but had a beginning in time. Before the world was made, there existed from eternity an infinite mass <note>original: *congeries*</note> of similar and qualified atoms, self-existent but without either order or motion.
*   **Second**, the world was not afterwards made by chance, but by **Mind** or **God**, who first moved the matter and then directed that motion to bring it into this orderly system and structure. Thus, "Mind" was the **maker of the world** <note>original Greek: νοῦς... κοσμοποιϊὸς</note> and "Mind is the king of heaven and earth" <note>original Greek: νοῦς βασιλεὺς οὐρανοῦ τε καὶ γῆς</note>, still governing the same as the sovereign monarch.
*   **Third**, Anaxagoras’s "Mind" and "God" was purely **incorporeal**. 

<margin>In Aristotle's Physics, Book 1, Folder 33, c. 2.</margin>

To this purpose, his words recorded by **Simplicius** are very remarkable: "Mind is mixed with no thing; but it alone exists by itself, for if it were not by itself..." <note>original Greek: Νοῦς μέμικται οὐδενὶ χρήματι· ἀλλὰ μόνος αὐτὸς ἐφ᾿ ἑαυτῷ ἐστὶν, εἰ μὴ γὰρ ἐφ᾿ ἑαυτῷ</note>

<header>Chap. IV. The Maker of the Whole World</header>

"Mind is mingled with nothing, but is alone by itself and separate. For if it were not by itself separated from matter, but mingled with it, it would then share in all things, because there is a portion of everything in everything (as I have said before). These mingled things would hinder it, so that it could not master or conquer anything as easily as if it were alone. For Mind is the most subtle of all things and the most pure; it has all knowledge of everything and possesses the greatest power." <note>original Greek: ῆν, ἀλλὰ τέω ἐμέμικτο ἄλλω, μετεῖχεν ἂν ἁπάντων χρημάτων, εἰ ἐμέμικτο τέω· ἐν παντὶ γὰρ παντὸς μοῖρα ἔνεσιν· ὥσπερ ἐν τοῖς πρόσθεν ἐμοὶ λέλεκται· κὶ ἀνεκώλυεν αὐτὸ τὰ συμμεμιγμένα, ὥσε μηδενὸς χρήματος κρατεῖν ὁμοίως, ὡς κὶ μόνον ἐόντα ἐφ' ἑαυτῶ· ἐζὶ γὰρ λεπτότατόν τε πάντων χρημάτων, κὶ καθαρώτατον· κὶ γνώμην γε περὶ παντὸς πᾶσαν ἴχει· κὶ ἰσχύει μέγισον.</note> Lastly, **Anaxagoras** did not assume a multitude of uncreated <note>original: "Unmade"</note> minds existing together from eternity as various partial causes and governors of the world, but only **one infinite mind** or **God**, ruling over all.

Indeed, it may well be questioned whether, besides this supreme and universal Deity, Anaxagoras acknowledged any of those other inferior gods then worshipped by the pagans. It is certain that although he asserted an infinite Mind to be the maker and governor of the whole world, he was accused by the Athenians of atheism. Besides a fine <note>original: "Mulct"</note> imposed upon him, he was banished for this. The true reason for this was simply that he affirmed the **Sun** to be nothing but a mass of fire, and the **Moon** to be an earth with mountains, valleys, cities, and houses on it. He probably concluded the same about all the other **stars** and **planets**: that they were either **fires**, like the sun, or **habitable earths**, like the moon. In assuming they were not alive <note>original: "Animated"</note>, he consequently denied them to be **gods**. 

This stripping of divinity <note>original: "Ungodding"</note> from the sun, moon, and stars was looked upon by the common people <note>original: "the Vulgar"</note> as nothing less than absolute atheism. They were very prone to think that if there were not many understanding beings superior to men—and if the sun, moon, and stars were not such beings (and therefore gods in their language)—then there was no God at all. It was not only the common people who condemned Anaxagoras for this, but even those two grave philosophers **Socrates** and **Plato** did the same. The first, in his *Apology* made to the Athenians, calls this opinion of Anaxagoras "absurd." The second, in his book *The Laws*, complains that this doctrine is a major gateway into atheism, writing: 

<margin>Plato, *The Laws*, Book 10, page 886.</margin> 

"When you and I, endeavoring by arguments to prove that there are gods, speak of the sun and moon, stars and earth, as gods and divine things, our young men presently—having been convinced by these new philosophers—will reply that these are nothing but earth and stones (senseless and inanimate bodies) which therefore cannot mind or take notice of any human affairs." <note>original Greek: ἐμῶ δὲ κὶ σῶ ὅταν τεκμήρια λέγωμεν ὡς εἰσὶ θεοὶ, ταῦτα αὐτὰ προσφέροντος, ἡλιόν τε κὶ σελήνην, καὶ ἄστρα καὶ γῆν ὡς θεὸς καὶ θεῖα ὄντα, ὑπὸ τῶν σοφῶν τούτων ἀναπεπεισμένοι ἂν λέγοιεν, ὡς γῆν τε καὶ λίθους ὄντα αὐτὰ, καὶ οὐδὲν τῶν ἀνθρωπείων πραγμάτων φροντίζειν δυνάμενα.</note> 

Where we may observe two things: First, that nothing was accounted truly and properly a "god" among the pagans unless it was endowed with life and understanding. Second, that the taking away of those inferior gods of

By denying that they were *Animated* <note>meaning: possessing a soul or life force</note>, or that they had life and understanding in them, he was, according to *Plato's* judgment, taking the most direct and effective path toward introducing absolute atheism.

Furthermore, it is true that although *Anaxagoras* was a self-declared theist—asserting that an *Infinite, Self-existent Mind* was the maker of the entire world—he was also severely criticized <note>original: "taxed"</note> by *Aristotle* and *Plato*. They viewed him as someone who was not a "thorough-paced" <note>fully committed</note> theist because he did not fully adhere to his own principles as he should have. For while claiming that *Mind* is the *Maker of the World* is essentially the same as claiming that there is a *final cause* <term>the purpose or goal for which something is made</term> for things in nature—meaning they were made in the *best possible manner*—*Anaxagoras*, when he gave his specific explanation for natural phenomena, usually relied on *material causes only*. He hardly ever made use of the mental or final cause, except when he was stumped or at a loss; only then would he bring God onto the stage <note>like a "deus ex machina" in a play, brought in to solve an otherwise impossible plot point</note>.

<margin>P. 97. Steph.</margin>
Socrates' discourse on this subject in *Plato's Phaedo* is well worth our attention:

> "I once heard someone reading," he says, "from a book by Anaxagoras, which stated that 'mind is the orderer and cause of all things.' <note>original Greek: ὡς νοῦς ἐστιν ὁ διακοσμῶν τε καὶ πάντων αἴτιος</note> I was very pleased with this, concluding that it must follow that all things were ordered and arranged as they should be, in the best possible manner. Therefore, the causes of things in nature (or at least their primary features) ought to be derived from 'that which is absolutely the best.' <note>original Greek: τὸ βέλτιστον</note> But when I later took up Anaxagoras's book and read it greedily, I was deeply disappointed. I found no other causes assigned except for air, ether, water, and similar physical and material things. He seemed to me to act just like someone who claims that Socrates does everything by mind, reason, and understanding, but then, when trying to explain the causes of my actions—such as why I am sitting here right now—explains it this way: 'Because, you see, my body is made of bones and nerves.' He would say that because my bones are solid and have joints at certain intervals, and my nerves are of such a nature that they can be both tightened <note>original: "intended"</note> and relaxed <note>original: "remitted"</note>, the lifting of my bones in the joints and the tightening and relaxing of my nerves caused my body to bend and for me to sit down in this place. In doing so, he ignores the true and proper cause: that it seemed right to the Athenians to condemn me to death, and I myself thought it most just to submit to their judgment and undergo their punishment rather than escape by fleeing. For certainly, otherwise, these nerves and bones of mine would not be here in this posture; they would be among the Megarians and Boeotians, carried there 'by the opinion of the best' <note>original Greek: ὑπὸ δόξης τοῦ βελτίστου</note>—that is, my belief that it was better to flee—had I not thought it better to submit to the city's sentence. Such philosophers," he says, "do not seem to distinguish between the true and proper cause of things and the 'cause without which' <note>original Latin phrase: *sine qua non*</note>—the condition without which the effect could not have been effected. These are the people who devise many strange physical reasons for the stable position of the Earth, without any regard to that..."

<header>CHAP. IV. Related to Material, rather than to Mental Causes.</header>

...Power which orders all things for the *best*, (possessing a *divine force* <note>original: δαιμονίαν ἰσχὺν</note> within it). However, they think they have found an *Atlas* <note>In Greek mythology, the Titan who held up the heavens; here used as a metaphor for a physical support for the universe</note> far stronger and more immortal, who can better hold all things together; for, in their opinion, *the good and the necessary are not able to bind or hold anything together* <note>original: τὸ γὰρ ἀγαθὸν καὶ τὸ δέον, οὐδὲν ξυνδεῖν, καὶ ξυνέχειν</note>.

From this passage of *Plato*’s, we may conclude that although *Anaxagoras* was sufficiently convinced of *theism* to profess that *one infinite mind* was the cause of all things (matter only excepted), he nevertheless had too much of a trace <note>original: "tang"</note> of that *old materialist and atheistical philosophy* of his predecessors still lingering about him. These predecessors resolved all the *phenomena* of nature into *physical causes*, and nothing into *mental* or *final causes* <term>the purpose or "why" behind a thing's existence</term>. We have told this long story about him because it is such an exact parallel to the philosophical mood of some in this present age. These people, while pretending to assert the existence of a God, nevertheless discard all *mental* and *final causality* from having anything to do with the structure <note>original: "fabrick"</note> of the *world*. Instead, they resolve everything into *material necessity* and *mechanism*—into *vortices* <note>whirlpools of matter</note>, *globules*, and *striated particles*, and the like. Regarding these *Christian philosophers*, we must say that they are not nearly as good *theists* as *Anaxagoras* himself was, even though he was so condemned by *Plato* and *Aristotle*. For Anaxagoras did not only assert *God* to be the cause of *motion*, but also the governor, regulator, and methodizer of that motion for the production of this harmonious system of the world; he was therefore *the cause of that which is good and beautiful* <note>original: τοῦ εὖ καὶ καλῶς αἰτίαν</note>. Whereas these modern thinkers utterly reject the latter point. Admitting only the former, they insist on supposing that heaven and earth, plants and animals, and all things whatsoever in this orderly framework <note>original: *compages*</note> of the world, resulted merely from a certain *quantity of motion* or *agitation* first impressed upon *matter* and directed into a *vortex*.

XXXI. Since the chronology of the old philosophers contains some uncertainty, we shall not scrupulously concern ourselves with it. Instead, we shall next consider *Parmenides*, a student <note>original: "auditor"</note> of *Xenophanes* and likewise a philosophical poet. Because he conversed much with two Pythagoreans, *Amenias* and *Diochaetes*, he was looked upon as one who was significantly devoted to the Pythagorean sect. That this *Parmenides* acknowledged *many gods* is evident from what has already been cited from him; regardless, he also plainly asserted *one supreme* god. As *Simplicius* tells us, he made this supreme being the *cause of the gods* <note>original: αἰτίαν θεῶν</note>, of which *Love* is said to have been the first produced. This supreme *deity* was called by *Parmenides*, as well as *Xenophanes*, *the One that was All* <note>original: Ἓν τὸ πᾶν</note>, or the *universe*; but he added to this his own idea: that it was also *immovable* <note>original: ἀκίνητον</note>.

Now, it is true that because *Parmenides*’s writings are not without obscurity, some of the ancients who were less acquainted with *metaphysical speculations* understood him *physically*. They thought he asserted that the entire corporeal *universe* was only *one thing*, and that it was *immovable*, thereby destroying—along with the *diversity* of things—all *motion*, *change*, and *action*. This interpretation would plainly make Parme-

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the ancient philosopher Parmenides, specifically addressing his concept of the "One" and defending him against accusations of absurdity by distinguishing between his metaphysical and physical teachings.</meta>

<page-num>384</page-num>
<header>Parmenides' Supreme God, Book I.</header>

...Parmenides not to have been a philosopher but a madman. Yet **Simplicius**—a man well acquainted with the opinions of ancient philosophers, and who possessed a copy of **Parmenides’** poems (then scarce, but since lost)—assures us that Parmenides dreamed of no such matter. He tells us that Parmenides wrote <note>original: οὐ περὶ τοῦ φυσικοῦ στοιχείου, ἀλλὰ περὶ τοῦ ὄντως ὄντος, or περὶ τῆς θείας ὑπεροχῆς</note> *not concerning a physical element or principle, but concerning the true Being, or the divine transcendency*. Adding that though some of those ancient philosophers did not distinguish <note>original: τὰ φυσικὰ ἀπὸ τῶν ὑπὲρ φύσιν</note> *natural things from supernatural*; yet the Pythagoreans, and **Xenophanes**, and **Parmenides**, and **Empedocles**, and **Anaxagoras**, did all <note>original: διακρίνειν</note> *distinguish* and handle these two subjects separately; <note>original: καίπερ τῇ ἀσαφείᾳ λανθάνοντες τὰς πολλοὺς</note> *however, by reason of their obscurity, it was not perceived by many*. For this cause they have most of them been misrepresented, not only by Pagans, but also by Christian writers. For as the same Simplicius informs us, Parmenides propounded two several doctrines, one after another: the first concerning theological and metaphysical things, which he called <note>original: ἀλήθειαν</note> *Truth*; the second concerning physical and corporeal things, which he called <note>original: δόξαν</note> *Opinion*. The transition between these was contained in these verses of his:

-><note>original Greek: Ἐν τῷ σοι παύω πιστὸν λόγον ἠδὲ νόημα / Ἀμφὶς ἀληθείας· δόξας δ' ἀπὸ τοῦδε βροτείας / μάνθανε· κόσμον ἐμῶν ἐπέων ἀπατηλὸν ἀκούων.</note><-
->Here I end for you my reliable discourse and thought<-
->concerning the truth; from here on, learn of mortal opinions,<-
->listening to the deceptive arrangement of my words.<-

In the former of these doctrines, Parmenides asserted *one immovable principle*; but in the latter, *two movable ones, fire and earth*. He spoke of souls also as a certain *middle* or *link* <note>original: vinculum</note> between the incorporeal and the corporeal world, affirming that God did <note>original: τὰς ψυχὰς πέμπειν ποτὲ μὲν ἐκ τοῦ ἐμφανῶς εἰς τὸ ἀειδὲς, ποτὲ δ' ἀνάπαλιν</note> *sometimes send and translate souls from the visible to the invisible regions, and sometimes again, on the contrary, from the invisible to the visible*. From this it is plain that when Parmenides asserted his *One and All Immovable*, he spoke not as a <term>physiologer</term> <note>one who studies the physical laws of nature; a natural scientist</note>, but as a metaphysician and theologian only. 

This indeed was so evident that **Aristotle** himself—though he had a mind to obscure Parmenides' sense so that he might take a shot at him in his *Physics*—could not altogether hide it. For when he begins thus, *“There must of necessity be either one principle or many; and if there be but one, then must it either be immovable, as Parmenides and Melissus affirm, or else movable,”* <note>original: ὥσπερ οἱ φυσικοὶ</note> *as the naturalists or physiologers do*; he therein plainly hints that when Parmenides and **Melissus** made *one immovable the principle of all things*, they did not write this as naturalists. And afterwards he confesses that this controversy—whether there were *one immovable principle*—does not belong to *natural philosophy*, but to some other *science*. 

But this is more plainly declared by him elsewhere, writing concerning Parmenides and Melissus in this manner: <note>original: εἰ καὶ τ' ἄλλα λέγουσι καλῶς, ἀλλ' οὐ φυσικῶς γε δεῖ νομίζειν λέγειν ; τὸ γὰρ εἶναι ἄττα τῶν ὄντων ἀγένητα καὶ ὅλως ἀκίνητα, μᾶλλον, ἐστὶν ἑτέρας καὶ προτέρας, ἢ τῆς φυσικῆς ἐπισκέψεως.</note> *“Though it be granted that Parmenides and Melissus otherwise said well, yet we must not imagine them to have spoken physically. For this fact—that some of those things which exist are uncreated and entirely immovable—belongs rather to another and more primary study than to natural science.”*

<summary>This page argues that Parmenides' concept of a single "immovable principle" was a theological and metaphysical claim about "True Being," rather than a physical theory about the material world. It highlights that even Aristotle acknowledged this distinction, separating Parmenides' "Truth" (metaphysics) from his "Opinion" (physics).</summary>
