<page-num>385</page-num>

### CHAPTER IV. One and All, Immovable.

The fact that there is something uncreated and immovable does not strictly belong to the study of physics, but rather to another science that precedes it <note>This refers to metaphysics, which Aristotle and others considered the "First Philosophy" that comes before the study of the physical world.</note>.

<margin>F. 31. C. 1.</margin>
Therefore **Parmenides**, as well as his master **Xenophanes**, meant nothing else by his "One and All" than the Supreme Deity, whom he also called "Immovable." For these ancient philosophers referred to the Supreme Deity first as "The One" <note>original: τὸ ἓν</note> and a "Monad" <note>original: μονὰς</note>, because they conceived that the first and most perfect Being, and the beginning of all things, must necessarily be the most simple. Thus **Eudorus**, quoted in **Simplicius**, explains their meaning: "They said that the One was the principle of all things, since both matter and all beings were generated from it; and this is the God who is over all" <note>original: ἀρχὴν ἔφασαν εἶναι τῶν πάντων τὸ ἓν, ὡς καὶ τῆς ὕλης καὶ τῶν ὄντων πάντων, ἐξ αὐτοῦ γεγενημένων, τοῦτο δὲ εἶναι τὸν ἐπάνω θεόν</note>. And **Syrianus** says the same thing: "Those divine men called God 'the One,' as he is the cause of unity to the whole, and of all existence and all life" <note>original: οἱ θεῖοι ἐκεῖνοι ἄνδρες, τὸ ἓν θεὸν ἔλεγον, ὡς ἑνώσεως τοῖς ὅλοις αἴτιον, καὶ παντὸς τοῦ ὄντος καὶ πάσης ζωῆς</note>. And Simplicius concludes that Parmenides' "One Being" <note>original: ἓν ὄν</note> was a certain divine principle superior to the mind or intellect, and more simple: "It remains, then, that there is one Intelligible principle that is the cause of all things, through which both the Mind and the act of thinking exist, in which all things are grasped together and united in a single unity; I say that this was Parmenides’ 'One Being'" <note>original: λείπεται ἓν τὸ νοητὸν πάντων αἴτιον, δι᾿ ὃ καὶ ὁ νοῦς ἐστὶ καὶ τὸ νοεῖν, ἐν ᾧ πάντα κατὰ μίαν ἕνωσιν συνηρημένως κατείληπται, καὶ ἡνωμένως, τοῦτο εἶναι τὸ παρμενίδειον Ἓν Ὄν</note>.

<margin>In Phys. F 17: 2.</margin>
Next, Parmenides, along with other ancients, also called his "One Being" <note>original: ἓν ὄν</note> "The All" <note>original: τὸ πᾶν</note>, or the Universe. He did so because it virtually contained all things and, as Simplicius writes, "all things are displayed distinctly from it" <note>original: πάντα διακεκριμένως ἐμφαίνεται ἀπ᾽ αὐτοῦ</note>. For this reason, in **Plato’s** *Parmenides*, this "One" is said to be "distributed into all things that are many" <note>original: εἰς πάντα πολλὰ ὄντα νενεμεμένον</note>. But it is evident that Parmenides, by his "One-All" or "the Universe," did not mean the physical world. This is clear because he called it "indivisible" <note>original: ἀδιαίρετον</note> and, as Simplicius observes, supposed it to have no magnitude, because that which is perfectly "One" can have no parts.

<margin>L. 1. c. 7.</margin>
Therefore, it may be observed here that the expression "One being All" <note>original: ἓν τὸ πᾶν</note> has been used in very different senses. While Parmenides and Xenophanes understood it to mean the Supreme Deity—that one most perfect and simple Being who was the origin of all things—others used it in an atheistic sense to refer to the most imperfect and lowest of all beings: matter or body. They claimed that all things are nothing but one and the same matter, differently modified. We learn this much from a passage in **Aristotle’s** *Metaphysics*: "As many as suggest that the 'All' is one, and that there is some single nature like matter—and that this is corporeal and has magnitude—it is clear that they err in many ways" <note>original: ὅσοι μὲν ἓν ἔν τε τὸ πᾶν καὶ μίαν εἶναί τινα φύσιν ὡς ὕλην τιθέασι, καὶ ταύτην σωματικὴν καὶ μέγεθος ἔχουσαν, δῆλον ὅτι πολλαχῶς ἁμαρτάνωσι</note>. It is manifest...

<summary>This page clarifies that Parmenides' concept of the "One and All" refers to a supreme, simple, and indivisible God rather than the physical universe. It distinguishes this theological unity from atheistic materialism, which uses similar language to describe matter.</summary>
<keywords>Parmenides, Xenophanes, Simplicius, Syrianus, Aristotle, One and All, Monad, Supreme Deity, Metaphysics, Unity, Indivisible, Matter, Corporeal Magnitude</keywords>

--- Page 404 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "One and All" philosophy, distinguishing between the materialists who saw the universe as a single moving substance and the metaphysical thinkers like Parmenides who identified the "One" as an immovable, incorporeal Deity.</meta>

<page-num>386</page-num>
<header>Parmenides' Trinity, BOOK I.</header>

It is manifest that they err in various ways. But here is a great difference to be observed between these two groups: the atheistical proponents of "One and All" (whether they meant water, air, or something else by it) none of them supposed their "One and All" to be immovable, but rather movable. However, those whose principle was "One and All Immovable" (such as Parmenides, Melissus, and Zeno) could not possibly mean anything else by it but the Deity; that there was one most simple, perfect, and immutable Being, which was incorporeal <note>original: "Incorporeal"; meaning existing without a physical body</note>, which virtually contained all things and from which all things were derived. But Heraclitus—who is one of those said to have affirmed that "One was All" <note>original: ἓν εἶναι τὸ πᾶν</note>, or that the universe was but one thing—might possibly have meant both those senses together (which also aligns with the Stoic hypothesis): that all things were both from one God and from one Fire. They were both alike "corporeal theists," who supposed an intellectual Fire to be the first principle of all things.

<margin>Book 6, chapter 1 and Book 13, chapter 7.</margin>
And though Aristotle in his *Physics* quarrels very much with Parmenides and Melissus for establishing one immovable principle, yet in his *Metaphysics*, he plainly agrees with it and owns it as very good divinity: that there is one incorporeal and immovable principle of all things, and that the supreme Deity is an immovable nature. As he writes: "If there is any such substance as this—I mean one that is separate [from matter] and immovable—as I shall later try to show, then the divinity would surely be found there, and this would be the first and most supreme principle" <note>original: εἴπερ ὑπάρχει τις οὐσία τοιαύτη, λέγω δ᾽ χωριστὴ καὶ ἀκίνητος, ὅπερ πειράσομαι δεικνύναι, ἐνταῦθα ἂν εἴη που καὶ τὸ θεῖον, καὶ αὕτη ἂν εἴη πρώτη καὶ κυριωτάτη ἀρχή</note>. But lest any should suspect that Aristotle (or perhaps Parmenides also) might still hold many such immovable principles, or many eternal, uncreated, and self-existent beings as various partial causes of the world, Simplicius assures us: "There has never been an opinion that asserted many and immovable principles" <note>original: μὴ γεγονέναι δόξαν πολλὰς καὶ ἀκινήτους τὰς ἀρχὰς λέγουσαν</note>. That is, though various ancient philosophers asserted a plurality of movable principles (and some indeed an infinity), yet there was never any opinion entertained among philosophers of many, or more than one, immovable principles. From this it may be concluded that no philosopher ever asserted a multitude of unmade, self-existent minds or independent deities as equal, co-acting principles of the world.

Indeed, Plotinus seems to think that Parmenides in his writings, by his "the Being" <note>original: τὸ ὄν, or Ens</note>, frequently meant a perfect Mind or Intellect, there being no true entity (according to him) below that which understands. This Mind, though incorporeal, was likened by him to a sphere because it comprehends all within itself, and because understanding comes not from without, but from within. But when he again called his "Being" the "One," he gave occasion for some to quarrel with him, as if he were making the same thing both one and many; for the Intellect is that which contains the ideas of all things within itself. Therefore, Parmenides' whole philosophy (says Plotinus) was better organized and more exactly and distinctly set down in Plato’s *Parmenides*, where he acknowledges three subordinate Unities, or a Trinity of divine hypostases <note>term: hypostases; distinct substances or persons within the divine nature</note>.

<summary>This page argues that Parmenides and other ancient philosophers used the concept of the "Immovable One" to describe a single, incorporeal God, rather than a material universe. It also suggests that Parmenides' philosophy prefigures the concept of a Divine Trinity as later developed in Platonism.</summary>

<keywords>Parmenides, Aristotle, Plotinus, Monotheism, Immovable Principle, Metaphysics, Trinity, Hypostases, Incorporeal Being, Greek Philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 405 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Parmenides’ philosophy, moving from the concept of a single immovable Being to the specific "Trinity of Divine Hypostases" that Plotinus and other later Platonists found in his work.</meta>

<page-num>387</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER 4. Of Divine Hypostases.</header>

<margin>Ennead 5, Book 1, Chapter 8.</margin>
"Parmenides in Plato, speaking more precisely, distinguishes three subordinate Divine Unities from one another: the first of that which is more properly One; and a second One, which he calls 'One-Many'; and a third, 'One and Many.' And he himself is also in agreement with these three natures" <note>original: ὁ παρὰ Πλάτωνι Παρμενίδης, ἀκριβέστερον λέγων, διαιρεῖ ἀπ’ ἀλλήλων, τὸ πρῶτον ἓν, ὃ κυριώτερον ἓν· καὶ δεύτερον ἓν πολλὰ λέγων· καὶ τρίτον ἓν καὶ πολλά· καὶ σύμφωνος οὗτος καὶ αὐτός ἐστι ταῖς φύσεσι ταῖς τρισίν</note>. Parmenides in Plato, speaking more exactly, distinguishes **Three Divine Unities** that are subordinate to each other: the **First** consists of that which is perfectly and most properly One; the **Second** of that which he called **One-Many**; the **Third** of that which is expressed as **One and Many**. So, Parmenides also agreed in this acknowledgment of a **Trinity of Divine or Archical Hypostases** <note>Archical Hypostases: the fundamental or originating substances or persons of the Godhead</note>. This observation by Plotinus is, by the way, the best key we know for that obscure book of Plato’s *Parmenides*. Therefore, as Parmenides asserted a Trinity of Divine Hypostases, it was the first of those hypostases that he properly called **One the Universe or All** <note>original: **ἓν τὸ πᾶν**</note>: that is, one most simple Being, the fountain and origin of all. And the second of them (which is a perfect Intellect) was apparently called by him, for the sake of distinction, **One-Many** or **One-All Things** <note>original: **ἓν πολλὰ** or **πάντα**</note>. By "All Things," he meant the **Intelligible Ideas of things**, which are all contained together in **One Perfect Mind**. Parmenides should also be understood in this way when he affirmed **that all things stood and nothing flowed**. He did not mean individual and sensory things, which (as the followers of Heraclitus <note>original: Heracliticks</note> rightly affirmed) do indeed all flow; rather, he meant the immediate objects of the mind, which are eternal and immutable. Aristotle himself acknowledged that no birth <note>original: generation</note> or decay <note>original: corruption</note> belongs to them, since there could be no immutable and certain science <note>Science: here meaning systematic, certain knowledge</note> unless there were some immutable, necessary, and eternal objects for it.

<margin>Metaphysics, Book 4, Chapter 5.</margin>
Therefore, as Aristotle also declares, the true meaning of that controversy between the followers of Heraclitus and the Parmenideans—**whether all things flowed or some things stood?**—was the same as this: **whether there were any other objects of the mind besides individual sensory things that were immutable?** And consequently, **whether there was any such thing as science or knowledge which had a firmness and stability in it?** For those followers of Heraclitus who argued that the only objects of the mind were individual and sensory things reasonably denied that there was any certain and constant knowledge. This is because there can neither be any definition of individual sensory things (as Aristotle writes) nor any proof <note>original: demonstration</note> concerning them. But the Parmenideans, on the contrary, who maintained the stability of science, reasonably concluded that besides individual sensory things, there were other objects of the mind: universal, eternal, and immutable. These they called the **Intelligible Ideas**, all originally contained in **One Archetypal Mind or Understanding**, and shared from there by inferior minds and souls. However, it must be acknowledged here that Parmenides and the Pythagoreans went a step further. They did not only suppose those Intelligible Ideas to be the eternal and immutable objects of all science, but also—as they are contained in the Divine Intellect—to be the principles and causes of all other things. For this is how Aristotle explains their meaning: "The Ideas are the causes of all other things" <note>original: **αἴτια τὰ εἴδη τοῖς ἄλλοις**</note>; and again,

<margin>Metaphysics, Book 1, Chapter 6.</margin>
"The essence of each of the other things is provided by the Ideas, and the One provides it to the Ideas" <note>original: **τὸ τὶ ἦν εἶναι ἑκάστῳ τῶν ἄλλων τὰ εἴδη παρέχονται, τοῖς δ’ εἴδεσι τὸ ἕν**</note>. The Ideas are the causes of all other things; and the essence of all other things below is imparted to them from the I-

<meta>catchword: deas</meta>

<summary>This page argues that Parmenides, as interpreted by Plotinus and Aristotle, recognized a Trinity of Divine Hypostases and identified "Intelligible Ideas" within the Divine Mind as the eternal, stable causes of the sensory world.</summary>
<keywords>Parmenides, Plotinus, Aristotle, Trinity, Hypostasis, Intelligible Ideas, Heraclitus, Metaphysics, Epistemology, Archetypal Mind</keywords>

--- Page 406 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Parmenides' philosophy, specifically how his concept of "Numbers" relates to Divine Ideas and the three fundamental levels of reality (hypostases) in ancient Greek thought.</meta>

<page-num>388</page-num>
<header>How Parmenides' "One and All," Book 1.</header>

Ideas, as the *Ideas* themselves, derive their *essence* from the *First Unity*. These *Ideas* in the *Divine Understanding* were looked upon by these *philosophers* as the *paradigms* <note>paradigms: perfect patterns or models</note> and *patterns* of all *created* things. Now, because these *Ideas* were frequently called *Numbers* by the *Pythagoreans*, we can clearly understand the meaning of that seemingly monstrous *paradox* or puzzling *riddle* <term>original: griphus</term> of theirs: that *Numbers* were the *causes* and *principles* of all things, or that *all things* were made out of *Numbers*. It actually meant nothing more than this: that *all things* were made from the *Ideas* of the *Divine Intellect*, which they called *Numbers*; these Ideas were themselves derived from a *Monad* or *Unity*. *Aristotle* somewhere mentions this very explanation of that assertion, stating that "Numbers were the causes of the essence of other things" <note>original: τοὺς ἀριθμοὺς αἰτίας εἶναι τοῖς ἄλλοις τῆς οὐσίας</note>, namely, because "the Ideas were Numbers" <note>original: τὰ εἴδη ἀριθμοί</note>. Though we are aware that the *Pythagoreans* also made all the *Numbers* within the *Decad* <note>Decad: the number ten, or a group of ten</note> to be *symbols* of *things*. But besides these *two divine hypostases* <note>hypostases: distinct substances or persons within the divine nature</note> already mentioned, *Parmenides* seems to have also asserted a *third*. Because this third level had yet more *alterity* <note>alterity: difference or "otherness"</note>, for the sake of distinction he called it neither "One the Universe or All" <note>original: ἓν τὸ πᾶν</note>, nor "One-All Things" <note>original: ἓν πάντα</note>, but "One and All things" <note>original: ἓν καὶ πάντα</note>. This is understood by *Plotinus* to be the *Eternal Soul* <note>original: Psyche</note> that actively produces *all things* in this *lower world* according to those *Divine Ideas*.

But it is further unquestionably evident that *Parmenides*, by his "One-All Immovable," really meant nothing else but the *Supreme Deity*. This is clear from those *verses* of his cited by *Simplicius* <note>Simplicius: a 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher and commentator</note> (though not noticed by *Stephanus* <note>Henricus Stephanus: a famous 16th-century printer and scholar</note> in his *Philosophical Poetry*), of which we shall only set down a few here:

<margin>
In Aristotle’s *Physics*,
folios 7, 17, and
31.
</margin>

->— Since it is ungenerated and indestructible,<-
->It never was, nor shall be, since it is now altogether all at once;<-
->A continuous One. For what origin of it will you seek?<-
->Moreover, it is motionless within the bounds of mighty bonds,<-
->Remaining the same and in the same place, it lies by itself; etc.<-
<note>Original Greek: Ὡς ἀγένητον ἐὸν καὶ ἀνώλεθρόν ἐστιν, οὐδέποτ’ ἦν, οὐδ’ ἔσται, ἐπεὶ νῦν ἔστιν ὁμοῦ πᾶν· ᝬν συνεχές· Τίνα γὰρ χρείαν διζήσεαι αὐτοῦ; Αὐτὰρ ἀκίνητον μεγάλων ἐν πείρασι δεσμῶν, ταυτὸν τ’ ἐν ταυτῷ τε μένον, καθ’ ἑαυτό τε κεῖται·</note>

In these verses, together with those that follow, the *Supreme Deity* is plainly described as a *single, solitary*, and *most simple Being*. He is *unmade* or *self-existent*, and *necessarily existing*; *incorporeal* and *devoid of magnitude*; and altogether *immutable* or *unchangeable*. His *duration*, therefore, was very different from ours; it was not a matter of *flux* or *temporary succession*, but a *constant eternity* without either *past* or *future*. From this, it may be observed that this opinion of a *standing eternity* <note>standing eternity: the concept of "nunc stans," an eternal present moment that does not pass</note> (which is different from the *flowing succession of time*) is not such a *novel thing* as some would persuade us. It was not first invented by *Christian writers, Scholastics*, or *Church Fathers*; it is at least as old as *Parmenides*. From him, it was afterwards received and embraced by the best of the other *pagan philosophers*. This is true even though it has lately been so heavily criticized—not only by *atheistic writers* but also by other *arrogant* <term>original: precocious</term> and *conceited wits*—as *nonsense* and *impossibility*.

<meta>catchword: It</meta>

<summary>This page explains how the Pythagorean concept of "Numbers" corresponds to Divine Ideas and describes Parmenides' view of the Supreme Deity as an immovable, eternal Being. The author argues that the concept of a "standing eternity" (an eternal now) is a classical philosophical tradition, not a later invention by Christian theologians.</summary>

--- Page 407 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Parmenides' philosophy, transitioning from the concept of the Divine "One" to how his successor Melissus expanded upon it, specifically addressing the debate over whether the First Principle is "Finite" or "Infinite."</meta>

<page-num>389</page-num>
<header>Chapter 4. Finite; Melissus's Infinite.</header>

<margin>Simplicius, on Aristotle’s *Physics*, folio 19.</margin>
It is well known that *Melissus* held the very same doctrine as *Parmenides*: that of the *One Immovable* that was *All*. He plainly affirmed this was *incorporeal* <note>incorporeal: having no physical body or substance</note> as well, just as *Parmenides* did. Melissus also declared that "the One being must not have a body, for if it had thickness, it would have parts" <note>original: καὶ ὁ μέλισσος ἓν ἐόν φησι, δεῖ αὐτὸ σῶμα μὴ ἔχειν, εἰ δ’ ἔχοι πάχος, ἔχοι ἂν μόρια</note>. But the only difference between them was this: *Parmenides* called this *One Immovable* that was *All* "finite" <note>original: πεπερασμένον — finite or determined</note>, but *Melissus* called it "infinite" <note>original: ἄπειρον — infinite</note>. This difference, however, was in words only; there was none at all regarding the reality of their *meaning*. Each of them endeavored, in a different way, to describe the greatest *perfection* of the *Deity*. There is a double meaning in those words *finite* and *infinite*; in one sense they signify *perfection*, but in another *imperfection*. The "disagreeing agreement" of these two philosophers, *Parmenides* and *Melissus*, as well as that of *Xenophanes* with them both concerning the *Deity*, is well explained by *Simplicius* <note>Simplicius: a 6th-century philosopher and commentator on Aristotle</note> in this manner: 

<margin>Aristotle’s *Physics*, folio 7.</margin> 
"Perhaps it will not be improper for us to digress a little here, and to gratify the studious and inquisitive reader by showing how those ancient philosophers, though seeming to dissent in their opinions concerning the principles, did nonetheless harmoniously agree together. <note>original Greek: οὐδὲν δ’ ἴσως χεῖρον ὀλίγον παρεκβάντα, τοῖς φιλομαθεστέροις ἐπιδεῖξαι, πῶς καίτοι διαφέρειν δοκοῦντες οἱ πάλαιοι, περὶ τὰς τῶν ἀρχῶν δόξας, ἐναρμονίως ὅμως συμφέρονται...</note> As first of all, they who discussed the intelligible and first principle of all—*Xenophanes*, *Parmenides*, and *Melissus*—of whom *Parmenides* called it 'One Finite and Determined.' He did so because Unity must necessarily exist before multitude; therefore, that which is the cause of measure, bound, and determination for all things ought rather to be described by measure and finitude than by infinity. Likewise, that which is every way perfect and has attained its own end—or rather is the end of all things, just as it was the beginning—must be of a determinate nature; for that which is imperfect and therefore lacking has not yet attained its term or measure. 

But *Melissus*, though considering the immutability of the Deity as well, focused instead on the inexhaustible perfection of its essence and the unlimitedness and unboundedness of its power. He therefore declared it to be infinite, as well as 'ingenit' <note>original: Ingenit — ungenerated, or having no beginning</note> or unmade. Moreover, *Xenophanes*, looking upon the Deity as the cause of all things and above all things, placed it above motion and rest and all those oppositions of lower beings, just as *Plato* does in the first hypothesis of his *Parmenides*."

<sig>Pp 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: Whereas</meta>

<summary>This page explores the subtle philosophical differences between Parmenides and Melissus regarding the nature of the "One" (the Deity), explaining that while one called it "finite" and the other "infinite," they were both describing the same perfect, incorporeal reality using different terminology.</summary>
<keywords>Melissus, Parmenides, Xenophanes, Simplicius, Finite vs Infinite, Incorporeal, One Immovable, Greek Philosophy, Neoplatonism, Nature of God</keywords>

--- Page 408 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Eleatic philosophers, specifically focusing on how Parmenides and Melissus defined the divine "One" and introducing Zeno of Elea’s logical arguments for monotheism.</meta>

<page-num>390</page-num>
<header>Zeno of Elea’s Demonstration, BOOK I.</header>

---

...whereas **Parmenides** and **Melissus**, focusing on its *stability* and *constant immutability*, and its being perhaps above *activity* <note>original: Energy</note> and *power*, *praised* it as *immovable*. From the writings of **Simplicius**, it is plain that **Parmenides**, when he called God *finite and determined* <note>original: πεπερασμένον</note>, was far from meaning that God was a *physical being of finite dimensions*, as some have ignorantly supposed. Nor did he mean that God was in any way limited in *power and perfection*. Instead, he understood it in the sense in which "limit" <note>original: πέρας</note> is used by **Plato**, as the opposite of "infinity" <note>original: ἀπειρία — often meaning "indefiniteness" or "disorder" in ancient Greek thought</note>, and as a term for the *greatest perfection*. In this sense, God is said to be *the boundary and measure of all things* <note>original: πέρας καὶ μέτρον πάντων</note>. 

However, **Melissus**, by calling God *infinite* <note>original: ἄπειρον</note> in the sense previously declared, intended to signify his *inexhaustible power and perfection*, his *eternity and incorruptibility*. In this, he agrees more with our *present theology* and our current way of *speaking*. We have produced all this to show how *curious* the ancient *philosophers* were in their *enquiries after God*, and how exact they were in their *descriptions* of him. Therefore, while **Anaximander’s** "infinite" was nothing but *eternal, senseless matter* (though he called it *the divinest thing of all* <note>original: τὸ θεῖον</note>), the "infinite" of **Melissus** was the *true Deity*.

**Zeno of Elea**—the student of **Parmenides**—fully agreed with **Parmenides** and **Melissus** that *One Immovable* being was *All*, or the *original of all things*. By this, he meant nothing other than the *Supreme Deity*. It is true that this **Zeno** devised certain *arguments* against the *physical motion of bodies*, based on the *hypothesis* of the *infinite divisibility of matter*. One of these was famously known by the name of *Achilles*, because it claimed to prove that it was impossible (under that hypothesis) for the *swift-footed Achilles* ever to overtake a *creeping snail*. (Whether or not these *arguments* are well-answered by **Aristotle** is not our purpose to inquire here.) Yet all this was nothing but a *play of wit* <note>original: Lusus Ingenii</note>, a *sportful exercise of Zeno's mind*, he being a *subtle logician and debater*. Perhaps it was also an *endeavor* to show how puzzling and perplexing the most common and accepted *phenomena of nature* can be to *human understanding*. 

That **Zeno of Elea**, by his *One Immovable* that was *All*, did not mean the *physical world* (any more than **Melissus**, **Parmenides**, and **Xenophanes** did) is evident from **Aristotle**, who wrote the following concerning him: *By such a "One Being" which was neither moved nor movable, Zeno means God* <note>original: τὸ τοιοῦτον ἓν ὂν τὸν θεὸν λέγει, μήτε κινεῖσθαι, μήτε κινητὸν εἶναι</note>. Moreover, the same **Aristotle** informs us that this **Zeno** endeavored to *demonstrate* that there was but *one God*, based on the *idea* that all men have of Him: that He is the *best*, the *supreme*, and most *powerful of all*, or an *absolutely perfect being*. 

<margin>*On Melissus, Zeno, and Gorgias*</margin>

*If God is the best of all things, then he must necessarily be one* <note>original: εἰ δ᾽ ἔστιν ὁ θεὸς ἁπάντων κράτιστον, ἕνα φησὶ προσήκειν αὐτόν</note>. This *argument* was pursued by him as follows:

*This is God and the power of God: to rule and not be ruled; so that insofar as he is not superior, to that extent he is not God. Therefore, if there were many gods, and some were superior to others while others were inferior, they would not be gods; for it is the nature of God not to be ruled. But if they were equal, God would not have the necessary nature of being the most powerful; for that which is equal is neither better nor...* <note>original: τοῦτο θεὸς καὶ θεοῦ δύναμις κρατεῖν ἀλλὰ μὴ κρατεῖσθαι· ὥστε καθὸ μὴ κρεῖττον, κατὰ τοσοῦτον οὐκ εἶναι θεόν. πλειόνων οὖν ὄντων, εἰ μὲν εἶεν τὰ μὲν ἀλλήλων κρείττους, τὰ δ᾽ ἥττους, οὐκ ἂν εἶναι θεούς· πεφυκέναι γὰρ θεὸν μὴ κρατεῖσθαι· ἴσων δ᾽ ὄντων, οὐκ ἂν ἔχειν θεὸν φύσιν δεῖν εἶναι κράτιστον· τὸ γὰρ ἴσον, οὔτε βέλτιον οὔτε...</note>

<meta>catchword: worse (original: χεῖρον)</meta>

<header>C H A P. IV. Of One God; from the Idea.</header>

...[nothing can be] worse than God; so that if He exists, and is such as God [should be], there is only one God; for He would not be able to do all that He would [if there were others]. <note>original Greek: χεῖρον εἶναι τοῦ θεοῦ· ὡς εἴπερ εἴη γε, καὶ τοιοῦτον εἴη θεὸς, ἕνα μόνον εἶναι τὸν θεὸν· οὐδὲ γὰρ οὐδὲ πάντα δύνασθαι ἃ ἂν βούλοιτο</note> *This is God and the Power of God: to prevail, conquer, and rule over all. Therefore, by as much as anything falls short of being the Best, by so much does it fall short of being God. Now, if more such Beings are supposed to exist—of which some are Better and some worse—those could not all be Gods, because it is essential to God not to be surpassed by any. But if they are conceived to be many Equal Gods, then it would not be the nature of God to be the Best, since one equal being is neither better nor worse than another. Therefore, if there is a God, and this is His nature, then there can be but One. And indeed, otherwise He would not be able to do whatever He wished.*

**Empedocles** is said to have also been a follower <note>original: "emulator"</note> of **Parmenides**, which must be understood regarding his *Metaphysics*, because in his *Physics* <note>original: "Physiology," then meaning the study of nature</note> (which was based on the *atomic theory* <note>original: "Atomical"</note>) he seems to have surpassed him. Now, that **Empedocles** acknowledged one Supreme and Universal Divinity <note>original: "Numen"</note>—and an incorporeal <note>non-physical</note> one at that—may be concluded from what has been already cited out of his philosophical poems. <margin>P. 26.</margin> Besides this, the writer of the treatise *On the Universe* <note>original: "De Mundo" — a work once attributed to Aristotle, but now thought to be by a later author</note> (who, though not **Aristotle**, was a pagan of significant antiquity) clearly affirms that **Empedocles** derived all things whatsoever from one Supreme Deity: *For all things in the air, on the earth, and in the water, may truly be called the works of God, who rules over the world. From whom also, according to the naturalist Empedocles, proceed* <note>original Greek: τὰ γὰρ δι' ἀέρος ἅπαντα, καὶ ἐπὶ γῆς, καὶ τὰ ἐν ὦδατι, θεοῦ λέγοιτ' ἂν ὄντως ἔργα εἶναι, τοῦ τὸν κόσμον ἐπέχοντος· ἐξ οὗ καὶ ὁ φυσικὸς Ἐμπεδοκλέα</note>

->all things that were, and all that are, and all that shall be hereafter, etc.<-
<note>original Greek: πάνθ' ὅσα τ' ἦν, ὅσα τ' ἔστιν, ἰδ' ὅσα τε ἔσται ὀπίσω, &c.</note>

*All the things that are upon the Earth and in the Air and Water, may truly be called the works of God, who rules over the World. Out of whom, according to the naturalist Empedocles, proceed all things that were, are, and shall be—namely Plants, Men, Beasts, and even the Gods.* Nevertheless, we believe this to be more accurate to **Empedocles’s** meaning than his exact words; he seemingly affirmed in that cited passage that all these things were made, not directly out of God, but out of *Contention* <note>Strife</note> and *Friendship* <note>Love</note>. This is because **Simplicius**, who possessed a copy of **Empedocles’s** poems, twice introduces that cited passage in this context:

> In Strife, all things are distinct and separate,
> But they come together in Love, and are desired by one another;
> For from these <note>Strife and Love</note> all that was, is, and shall be, proceeds:
> Trees have grown, and men and women,
> Beasts, birds, and water-dwelling fish,
> And even the long-lived Gods, highest in honor.
> <note>original Greek: Ἐν δὲ κότῳ διάμορφα καὶ ἄνδιχα πάντα πέλονται, / Σὺν δ' ἔβη ἐν φιλότητι καὶ ἀλλήλοισι ποθεῖται, / Ἐκ τῶν γὰρ πάνθ' ὅσ' ἦν, ὅσα τέ ἔστι, καὶ ἔσται, / Δένδρεα τε βεβλάστηκε, καὶ ἀνέρες ἠδὲ γυναῖκες, / Θῆρες, τ' οἰωνοί τε, καὶ ὑδατοθρέμμονες ἰχθῦς, / Καί τε θεοὶ δολιχαίωνες τιμῇσι φέριστοι.</note>

<meta>This page continues the examination of the ancient philosopher Empedocles, moving from his concept of a universal divinity to how he reconciled the existence of multiple "gods" (such as stars and spirits) with a single, supreme "One."</meta>

<page-num>392</page-num>
<header>Empedocles and His Many Gods, BOOK I.</header>
<page-type>text</page-type>

<margin>Aristotle, Metaphysics Book 3, chapter 4.</margin>
Beasts, men, and gods were made from *Contention* and *Friendship*. Nevertheless, since according to *Empedocles*, *Contention* and *Friendship* themselves also depended upon one Supreme Deity—which he, along with *Parmenides* and *Xenophanes*, called *τὸ ἕν*, or *The Very One*—the author of the treatise *On the Universe* <note>original: "De Mundo"; a work formerly attributed to Aristotle</note> might well conclude that, according to *Empedocles*, all things whatsoever, and not only men but gods, were derived from *One Supreme Deity*. And that this was indeed *Empedocles’* meaning appears plainly from *Aristotle* in his *Metaphysics*: "Empedocles establishes a certain principle of corruption, which is Contention; yet it would seem that he also generates this Contention itself from *The One*. For all other things are from this, except for God." <note>original Greek: τίθησι μὲν γὰρ [᾿Εμπεδοκλῆς] ἀρχήν τινα τῆς φθορᾶς τὸ νεῖκος· δόξειε δ᾽ ἂν οὐθὲν ἧττον καὶ τοῦτο γεννᾶν ἐξ αὐτοῦ τοῦ ἑνός· Ἅπαντα γὰρ ἐκ τούτου τ᾽ ἄλλα ἐστὶ πλὴν ὁ Θεός·</note> He writes, at least, in this manner:

->*From which all things that were, all that are, and all that shall be hereafter, derived their origin.* <note>original Greek: ᾿Εξ ὧν πάνθ᾽ ὅσα τ᾽ ἦν, ὅσα τ᾽ ἔσθ᾽, ὅσα τ᾽ ἔσται ὀπίσω, &c.</note><-

<margin>Metaphysics Book 3, chapter 4.</margin>
*Empedocles* makes *Contention* <note>original: "νεῖκος" (neikos) meaning strife or discord</note> to be a certain *principle of corruption and generation*. Nevertheless, he seems to generate this *Contention* itself also from the *Very One* (that is, from the Supreme Deity). For all things, according to him, come from this *Contention*, with God being the only exception. He writes in this manner: *From which (that is, Contention and Friendship) all the things that have been, are, and shall be (plants, beasts, men, and gods) derived their origin*. For it seems *Empedocles* supposed that, were it not for *Discord* or *Contention*, all things would be One. So, according to him, all things whatsoever proceeded from Contention or Discord, together with a mixture of Friendship, except for the Supreme God. This God has no *Contention* at all in Him because He is essentially *Unity* itself and *Friendship*. 

From this, *Aristotle* takes the opportunity to argue with *Empedocles*, as if it would follow from his principles that the Supreme and most happy God was the *least* wise of all. Aristotle reasons that such a God would be unable to know anything besides Himself, or anything in the world outside of Him: "Therefore, it happens that, according to his principles, the most happy God is less wise than the others; for He does not know all the elements, because He possesses no Contention. And knowledge is of like by like." <note>original Greek: διὸ καὶ συμβαίνει αὐτῷ, τὸν εὐδαιμονέστατον Θεὸν ἧττον φρόνιμον εἶναι τῶν ἄλλων· οὐ γὰρ γνωρίζει τὰ στοιχεῖα πάντα· τὸ γὰρ νεῖκος οὐκ ἔχει· ἡ δὲ γνῶσις τοῦ ὁμοίου τῷ ὁμοίῳ</note> Empedocles himself wrote:

->*For we see Earth by Earth, Water by Water, Air by Air, and Fire by Fire; Friendship by Friendship, and Contention by Contention.* <note>original Greek: γαίῃ μὲν γὰρ (φησι) γαῖαν ὀπώπαμεν, ὕδατι δ᾽ ὕδωρ, &c.</note><-

But to let this objection pass; *Empedocles* here making the gods themselves to be derived from *Contention* and *Friendship*—the Supreme Deity, or most happy God, being the only exception (who has no contention in Him, and from whom Contention and Friendship themselves were derived)—plainly acknowledged both one uncreated <note>original: "unmade"</note> Deity as the origin of all things under the name of *The Very One*, and many other inferior gods generated or produced by Him. These inferior gods were "younger" <note>original: "juniors"</note> than *Contention* or *Discord*, just as Contention was younger than *Unity*, the first and supreme Deity. These gods of *Empedocles* that were begotten from *Contention* (as well as men and other things) were undoubtedly the stars and demons <note>term: "demons" here refers to *daimones*, intermediary spirits or divine beings, not necessarily evil spirits</note>.

<summary>This page discusses Empedocles' philosophy that while the physical world and inferior gods (stars and spirits) arise from the forces of Love and Strife, these forces themselves originate from a single, supreme "One." It also notes Aristotle's critique that such a supreme God, lacking internal strife, would be "less wise" because He could only know things like Himself.</summary>

<header>CHAPTER IV. The Offspring of One God.</header>

Moreover, we may observe here that according to the doctrine of *Empedocles*, the true origin of all *evil*, regarding both *human souls* and *demons* (both of which he supposed were <term>lapsable</term><note>original: "Lapsable"; meaning capable of falling from a state of perfection or grace into sin or a physical body</note>), was derived from <margin>According to that "furious and thick strife." <note>original Greek: Νείκος μαινόμενον πύκινον</note> p. 23.</margin> that <term>Strife</term><note>original Greek: Νεῖκος (Neikos); the personification of discord and division</note>, *Discord*, and *Contention*. He believed this was necessarily contained in their nature, combined with the ill use of their *liberty*, both in this *present* state and their *pre-existent* state. Thus, *Empedocles* walked in the footsteps of *Pythagoras*, whose praises he loudly sang in his poems:

<margin>Porphyry, *Life of Pythagoras*, p. 194.</margin>
> "And there was among them a man of extraordinary knowledge, who indeed possessed the greatest wealth of understanding, and was especially a master of all kinds of wise works." <note>original Greek: Ἦν δέ τις ἐν κείνοισιν ἀνὴρ περιώσια εἰδώς, ὃς δὴ μήκιστον πραπίδων ἐκτήσατο πλοῦτον, Παντοίων τε μάλιστα σοφῶν ἐπιήρανος ἔργων, &c.</note>

> "From their number, a certain man knew many outstanding things, preserving vast riches of the mind within his breast, investigating all the learned discoveries of the wise." <note>original Latin: *Horum de numero quidam præstantia norat Plurima, Mentis Opes Amplas sub pectore servans, Omnia Vestigans Sapientum Docta Reperta, &c.*</note>

XXII. Before we come to *Socrates* and *Plato*, we shall here take notice of some other *Pythagoreans* and eminent philosophers who clearly asserted *one Supreme and Universal Divinity* <note>original: "Numen"</note>, though they undoubtedly also acknowledged *other inferior gods*. <margin>P. 23.</margin> *Philo*, in his book *On the Creation of the World* <note>original: "De Mundi Opificio"</note>, writing of the <term>Hebdomad</term><note>The number seven</note> or *septenary number*, observes that according to the *Pythagoreans*, it was called both a *motherless* and *virgin* number. This was because it was the only number within the <term>Decad</term><note>The first ten numbers</note> which was neither *generated* (produced by multiplying other numbers) nor did it *generate* any other number within that group. Philo tells us that, for this reason, they made it a *symbol of the Supreme Deity*: "The Pythagoreans likened this number to the ruler and governor of all things, or the Supreme Monarch of the universe, thinking it to bear a resemblance to his immutability." <note>original Greek: οἱ πυθαγόρειοι τὸν ἄριθμον τοῦτον ἐξομοιοῦσι τῷ ἡγεμόνι τῶν συμπάντων</note> We noted this fancy of theirs earlier. However, *Philo* occasionally cites this remarkable testimony of *Philolaus* the Pythagorean: "For God (he says) is the prince and ruler over all, always One, stable, immovable, like to himself, but unlike to everything else." <note>original Greek: Ἐστὶ γὰρ, φησὶν, ἡγεμὼν καὶ ἄρχων ἁπάντων ὁ θεὸς, εἷς ἀεὶ ὦν, μόνιμος, ἀκίνητος, αὐτὸς αὑτῷ ὅμοιος, ἕτερος τῶν ἄλλων</note> To this may be added what is further recorded in *Stobaeus* from the same *Philolaus*: <margin>Stobaeus, *Physical Selections*, p. 44.</margin> "This world was from eternity and will remain for eternity; one world governed by One, who is kindred and the best." <note>original Greek: ἦν ὁδὲ ὁ κόσμος ἐξ αἰῶνος, καὶ εἰς αἰῶνα διαμένει, εἷς ὑπὸ ἑνὸς τῶ συγγένεω καὶ κρατίστω κυβερνώμενος</note> In this passage, he seems to maintain the world's pre-eternity, along with *Ocellus*. And again: "Wherefore, said Philolaus, the world might well be called the eternal energy or effect of God and of successive generation." <note>original Greek: διὸ καὶ καλῶς ἔχειν ἔλεγε, κόσμον ἦμεν ἐνέργειαν ἀΐδιον θεῶ τε καὶ γενέσεως</note>

<margin>Chapter 4, p. 20.</margin> *Iamblichus*, in his *Exhortation to Philosophy* <note>original: "Protreptics"</note>, cites a passage from *Archytas*, another Pythagorean, to the same purpose: "Whosoever is able to reduce all kinds of things under one and the same principle, this man seems to me to have found out an excellent <term>watchtower</term><note>original: "Specula"; a high vantage point for observation</note>, or high station, from which he will be able to see God clearly..." <note>original Greek: ὅτις ἀναλύσαι οἷός τε ἐστὶ, πάντα τὰ γένεα ὑπὸ μίαν τε καὶ αὐτὰν ἀρχὰν, οὗτος δοκεῖ μοι καλὰν σκοπιὰν εὑρηκέναι, ἀφ' ἧς δυνατὸς ἐσσεῖται τὸν θεὸν κατοψᾶσθαι, &c.</note>

# CHAPTER 4. The Creator of Gods.

...of the eternal and unmade **Idea**. In these words of **Timaeus**, there are three distinct **points** of **Pagan Theology** contained: 
1. First, that there is **one Supreme God**, eternal and unmade, the creator and governor of the whole world, who made it according to the best pattern or model of his own **Ideas** and eternal wisdom. 
2. Secondly, that this world created by God is composed of other **inferior gods**, men, and brute animals. 
3. Thirdly, that the Supreme God has committed the administration of our human affairs to **demons** <note>original: "Demons"; in this context, intermediary spirits or lesser deities</note> and inferior gods, who are constant inspectors over us, some of whom he also uses for the punishment of wicked men after this life. 

Moreover, in this book by **Timaeus Locrus**, the Supreme God is often called "God" <note>original: "ὁ Θεὸς" (ho Theos)</note>, and sometimes "the Divine" <note>original: "ὁ δαίμων" (ho daimōn)</note>, used as a title of supreme excellence. He is also sometimes called "Mind" <note>original: "νόος" (noos)</note>, sometimes "the Very Good" <note>original: "τ’ ἀγαθὸν" (t’ agathon)</note>, sometimes "the Principle of the Best things" <note>original: "ἀρχὰ τῶν ἀρίστων" (archa tōn aristōn)</note>, sometimes "the Maker of the Better" <note>original: "δαμιουργὸς τῶ βελτίονος" (damiourgos tō beltionos)</note> (evil being supposed not to proceed from him), sometimes "the best and most powerful cause" <note>original: "κρατίστα αἰτία" (kratista aitia)</note>, and sometimes "the Prince and Parent of all things" <note>original: "ἀρχαγὸς καὶ γενέτωρ ἁπάντων" (archagos kai genetōr hapantōn)</note>. 

According to Timaeus, this God is not the Soul of the World, but its creator. He made the world a living being <note>original: "Animal"; here meaning a living being or ensouled entity</note> and a **secondary generated god**. "God, wishing to make the world the best creation possible, made it a generated God, one that should never be destroyed by any other cause but only by that same God who framed it, if he should ever wish to dissolve it." <note>original: "δηλόμενος ὢν ἄριστον γένναμα ποιεῖν, τῦτον ἐποίει Θεὸν γεννατὸν, ἐποκα φθαρησόμενον ὑπ’ ἄλλω αἰτίω, ἔξω τῶ αὐτῶ συντεταγμένω Θεῶ, ἔποκα δήλετο αὐτῶ διαλύειν"</note> But since it is not the nature of that which is good to destroy the best of works, the world will doubtless remain indestructible <note>original: "Incorruptible"</note> and happy forever. It is the best of all generated things, made by the best cause, who looked not at models constructed outside of himself, but at the **Idea** and the essence known through the mind as the paradigms <note>original: "Paradigms"; models or patterns</note>. Whatever is made in conformity to these must necessarily be the best and will never need to be mended. 

Moreover, he plainly declares that this **generated god** of his—the **world**—was produced in time, so as to have a beginning. "Before the heaven was made, there existed in reason both the Idea and Matter, and God the Artisan <note>original: "Opifex"</note> of the Best." <note>original: "πρὶν ὠρανὸν γενέσθαι, λόῳ ἤστην ἰδέα τε καὶ ὕλα, καὶ ὁ θεὸς δαμιουργὸς τῶ βελτίονος"</note> Therefore, whatever **Ocellus** and **Philolaus** might have thought, this **Timaeus** did not believe the world was eternal. In this, he followed not only **Pythagoras** himself (as we have already shown) but also the generality of the first Pythagoreans, of whom 
<margin>Aristotle, Metaphysics, Book 1, Chapter 7</margin>
**Aristotle** pronounces without exception that they "generated the world" <note>original: "γεννῶσι γὰρ τὸν κόσμον"</note>. 

Timaeus indeed seems in this book to assert the pre-eternity of matter, as if it were a **self-existent principle** alongside 
<margin>Clement of Alexandria, Stromata, Book 5, p. 604</margin>
God. And yet **Clement of Alexandria** cites a passage from him that points in a different direction: "But would you hear of only one principle of all things from the Greeks as well? Timaeus Locrus, in his work on nature, will witness to me word for word thus: 'There is one principle of all things that is unmade; for if it were made, it would no longer be a principle, but that from which it was made would be the principle.'" <note>original: "ἀλλ’ ἀντικρὺς καὶ μίαν ἀρχὴν καὶ παρ’ Ἑλλήνων ἀκᾶσαι ποθεῖς; τίμαιος ὁ λοκρὸς ἐν τῷ φυσικῷ συγγράμματι κατὰ λέξιν ὧδέ μοι μαρτυρήσει· μία ἀρχὰ πάντων ἐστὶν ἀγέννητος, εἰ γὰρ ἐγένετο, οὐκ ἂν ἦν ἔτι ἀρχὰ, ἀλλ’ ἐκείνα ἀρχὰ, ἐξ ἧς ἐγένετο"</note> 

<summary>This page analyzes the theology of Timaeus Locrus, presenting the Pythagorean belief in a single Supreme God who created the world as a living, "generated god" based on eternal, divine Ideas. It contrasts Timaeus's view that the world had a beginning in time with other philosophers who believed in the world's eternity, while also discussing the ultimate origin of all things from a single unmade principle.</summary>

# Onatus and His Chorus Leader of the Gods. Book I.

We see that **Timaeus Locrus** asserted **one eternal and uncreated God**, the maker of the whole world, and besides this, another **generated God** <note>original: "Generated God"; a deity brought into being, specifically the physical universe itself</note>, the world itself **animated** <note>given a soul</note> with its several parts. The difference between these two Gods is declared by him as follows:

"That eternal God, who is the prince, original, and parent of all these things, is seen only by the mind. But the other generated God is visible to our eyes—namely, this world and those parts of it which are heavenly (the stars), which are like so many particular gods contained within it." <note>original: "Θεὸν τὸν μὲν αἰώνιον νόῳ ὁρᾷ μόνος, τῶν ἁπάντων ἀρχαγὸν καὶ γενέτορα τουτέων, τὸν δὲ γεννατὸν ὄψι ὁρέομες, κόσμον δὲ τόνδε, καὶ τὰ μέρεα αὐτοῦ ὁκόσα οὐράνια ἐντί"</note>

But here it should be observed that the eternal God is not only called so by Timaeus because he is without beginning, but also because he has a distinct kind of duration from that of **time**, which is properly called **Aeon** <note>original: "Æon"; a Greek term for eternity or an infinite period of time</note> or **eternity**. In this, he follows **Parmenides**:

"Time is but an image of that uncreated duration which we call eternity. Therefore, just as this perceivable world was made according to that eternal exemplar <note>model or pattern</note> of the intelligible world, so was time made together with the world as an imitation of eternity." <note>original: "εἰκὼν δέ ἐστι τῶ ἀγεννάτω χρόνω, ὃν αἰῶνα ποταγορεύομες • ὡς γὰρ ποτ᾽ ἀΐδιον παράδειγμα τὸν ἰδανικὸν κόσμον ὅδε ὠρανὸς ἐγεννάθη, οὕτως ὡς πρὸς παράδειγμα τὸν αἰῶνα ὅδε χρόνος σὺν κόσμῳ ἐδαμιεργήθη"</note>

<margin>Page 233.</margin>
It has already been observed that **Onatus**, another **Pythagorean**, took notice of the opinion of some in his time: that there was **only one God** who encompassed the **whole world**, and no other gods besides—or at least none who should be religiously worshipped. Onatus himself, meanwhile, asserted **that there was both one God and many gods**; or, besides **one supreme and universal Numen** <note>divine power or deity</note>, there were **many other inferior and particular deities** whom men ought to worship. Now, his further explanation of both these 
<margin>Stobaeus, *Physical Extracts*, page 5.</margin>
assertions is contained in the following words:

"Those who maintain that there is only one God, and not many gods, are very much mistaken, as they do not rightly consider what the dignity and majesty of divine transcendence chiefly consists of: namely, in ruling and governing those who are like himself (that is, other gods) and in excelling or surmounting others, being superior to them. But all those other gods for whom we argue are to that first and intelligible God as the dancers are to the **Coryphaeus** <note>original: "κορυφαῖος" (koryphaios); the leader of a Greek chorus</note> or **Choragus** <note>the leader or financier of a choir</note>, and as the inferior common soldiers are to the captain or general. It properly belongs to them to follow and comply with their leader and commander. The work indeed is common or the same to them both—to the ruler and those who are ruled—but those who are ruled could not orderly work and agree together..." <note>original: "τοὶ δὲ λέγοντες ἕνα θεὸν εἶμεν, ἀλλὰ μὴ πολλὰς ἁμαρτάνοντι • τὸ γὰρ μέγιστον ἀξίωμα τᾶς θείας ὑπεροχᾶς οὐ συνθεωρῆντι • λέγω δὲ τὸ ἄρχεν καὶ καθηγέεσθαι τῶν ὁμοίων, καὶ κράτιστον καὶ καθυπέρτερον εἶμεν τῶν ἄλλων • τοὶ δ᾽ ἄλλοι θεοὶ ποτὶ τὸν πρᾶτον καὶ νοητὸν οὕτως ἔχοντι ὥσπερ χορευταὶ ποτὶ κορυφαῖον, καὶ στρατιῶται ποτὶ στραταγὸν, καὶ λοχῖται, καὶ ἐντεταγμένοι ποτὶ ταξιάρχαν καὶ λοχαρχέταν, ἔχοντε φύσιν, ἕπεσθαι καὶ ἐπακολουθεῖν ταῖς καλῶς καθηγεομένῳ • κοινὸν μὲν γὰρ αὐτῶν τὸ ἔργον ἐστὶ, καὶ τοῦ ἄρχοντι, καὶ τῶν ἀρχομένων ἀλλ᾽ οὐκέτι δύναιντο συντετάχθαι τοὶ ἀρχόμενοι ποτὶ τὸ ἔργον, ἀπολειφθέντες ἀγεμόνος • ὥσπερ οὐδὲ χορευταὶ ποτὶ συναϊδᾶν, οὐδὲ στρατιῶται ποτὶ στρατηγίαν, ἀπολειφθέντες ἀγεμόνος, τοὶ μὲν στραταγῶ, τοὶ δὲ κορυφαίω"</note>

<summary>This page explores Pythagorean views on the hierarchy of the divine, specifically how Timaeus Locrus distinguishes between the eternal Creator and the created world-god, and how Onatus defends the existence of many gods as a testament to the Supreme God's majesty.</summary>

# CHAP. IV. Euclides and the Concept of the One as the Very God.

...together into one work, they would be destitute of a *Leader*, just as *Singers* and *Dancers* could not join together into one *Dance* and *Harmony* if they were destitute of a *Coryphæus* <note>original: "Coryphæus"; the leader of a Greek chorus</note>, nor could *Soldiers* make up one orderly *Army* if they were without a *Captain* or *Commander*.

And as the Supreme God is here called by *Onatus* the *Coryphæus* of the Gods, so he is in like manner styled by the writer of *De Mundo* <note>original: "De Mundo"; an ancient philosophical treatise 'On the World'</note> the *Coryphæus* of the *World*, or its *Precentor* <note>a person who leads a congregation or choir in singing</note> and *Supporter* <note>original: "Præfultor"; one who props up or supports from the front</note>, in these words: 

"Just as in a chorus, when the Leader has begun, the whole choir—composed of men, and sometimes of women too—follows, everyone singing their part, some in higher and some in lower notes, but all mingling together into one melodious harmony; so it is with the God who governs the universe. For according to the cue given from above by him who is fittingly called the Leader, the stars and the entire heaven are always in motion." <note>original: "καθάπερ ἐν χορῷ, κορυφαίου κατάρξαντος, συνεπηχεῖ πᾶς ὁ χορὸς ἀνδρῶν, ἔσθ’ ὅτι καὶ γυναικῶν, ἐν διαφόραις φωναῖς ὀξυτέραις καὶ βαρυτέραις, μίαν ἁρμονίαν ἐμμελῆ κεραννύντων· οὕτως ἔχει καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ τὸ σύμπαν διέποντος θεοῦ· κατὰ γὰρ τὸ ἄνωθεν ἐνδόσιμον ὑπὸ τοῦ φερωνύμως ἂν κορυφαίου προσαγορευθέντος, κινεῖται μὲν τὰ ἄστρα ἀεὶ καὶ ὁ σύμπας οὐρανός"</note> 

As the *Coryphæus*, the *Precentor*, and *Supporter* begins the dance and music, the stars and heavens move round after him according to those numbers and measures which he prescribes them, all together making up one most excellent harmony.

<margin>Page 26.</margin>
It was also observed before that *Ecphantus* the *Pythagorean* and *Archelaus* (the successor of *Anaxagoras*, both of whom were *Atomists* in their *Physiology* <note>natural philosophy or the study of the physical world</note>) did assert that the *World* was *made* at first, and is still governed, by *One Divine Mind*. This is more than some *Atomists* of our own present age will acknowledge, even though they pretend to be very good *Theists* <note>believers in God</note>. 

In the next place, we shall mention *Euclides of Megara* <note>original: "Euclides Megarensis"; a philosopher and student of Socrates, not to be confused with Euclid the mathematician</note>, the head of the sect called *Megaric*. He is said to have been *Plato's* master for some time after the death of *Socrates*. His doctrine is set down by *Diogenes Laertius* <note>original: "Laertius"</note> as follows: 

"He declared that the Good is One, though called by many names: sometimes Wisdom, sometimes God, and at other times Mind, and so on. But he rejected those things opposite to the Good, saying they have no real existence." <note>original: "οὗτος ἓν τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἀπεφαίνετο, πολλοῖς ὀνόμασι καλούμενον· ὁτὲ μὲν γὰρ φρόνησιν, ὁτὲ δὲ θεὸν, καὶ ἄλλοτε νοῦν, καὶ τὰ λοιπά· τὰ δὲ ἀντικείμενα τῷ ἀγαθῷ, ἀνῄρει, μὴ εἶναι φάσκων"</note> 

We understand this to mean that Euclides (who followed *Xenophanes* and *Parmenides*) made the First Principle of all things to be **The One** or **the Very Good**. This was called sometimes Wisdom, sometimes God, sometimes Mind, and sometimes by other names. However, he removed everything opposite to Good, denying it to have any real entity; that is, he maintained that there was no positive nature of evil, or that evil was not a fundamental principle. 

We also understand the words of *Cicero* in this way, when he represents the doctrine of the *Megarics* in this manner: "That alone is good which is One, and Similar, and the Same, and Always." <note>original: "Id bonum solum esse, quod esset Unum, & Simile, & Idem, & Semper"</note> To be precise, they spoke this concerning God: that Good or Goodness itself is a name properly belonging to him, who is also One, and the Same, and Eternal. They believed that the true good of man consists in a participation in, and conformity with, this First Good. *Plato* seems to have derived this doctrine from him, for he likewise called the Supreme *Deity* by those two names, **The One** and **The Good** <note>original: "τὸ ἓν and τ’ ἀγαθὸν"</note>, and concluded that true human *Happiness* <note>original: "Felicity"</note> consists in a participation in the *First Good*, or of the *Divine Nature*.

<summary>This page discusses the theological views of Euclides of Megara and other ancient philosophers who viewed God as the "Leader" of a cosmic chorus and identified the supreme deity as "The One" or "The Good." It argues that even ancient "atomists" like Ecphantus and Archelaus believed the world was governed by a single Divine Mind.</summary>

# Antisthenes’ One Natural God. BOOK I.

<margin>
Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book 1.
Seneca, *On the Anger of God*, chapter 11.
</margin>

Next, we shall take notice of *Antisthenes*, who was also the founder of another *sect*, namely the *Cynics*. In a certain *physiological treatise*, he is said to have affirmed: "There are many popular gods, but only one natural God" <note>original Latin: *Esse Populares Deos Multos, sed Naturalem Unum*</note>. Or, as it is expressed by *Lactantius*: "There is but one natural God, although nations and cities have their own several popular ones" <note>original Latin: *Unum esse Naturalem Deum, quamvis Gentes & Urbes suos habeant Populares*</note>. Therefore, *Velleius* the *Epicurean* (in *Cicero’s* writings) argues with this *Antisthenes* as one who destroyed the *nature of the gods*, because he denied a *multitude of independent deities* such as *Epicurus* claimed to exist. 

However, this statement by *Antisthenes* is not to be understood as if he intended to eliminate all the *inferior gods* of the *pagans*. If he had attempted that at all, he would undoubtedly have been considered an *atheist*, just as *Anaxagoras* was. Rather, his meaning was only to interpret the *theology of the pagans* regarding those other gods of theirs that were, or might be, seen as *absolute and independent*. He argued that these, though they were *many popular gods*, were indeed only *one and the same natural God* called by several names. 

For example, when the Greeks worshipped *Zeus*, the Latins *Jove*, the Egyptians *Ammon*, the Babylonians *Bel*, and the Scythians *Pappas*, these were indeed *many popular gods*, yet they were nevertheless all but *one and the same natural God*. Similarly, when the laws of those same pagan cities and countries mentioned several gods as supreme and absolute in their various territories—such as *Jupiter* in the heavens, *Juno* in the air, or *Neptune* in the sea—or as being chief in different roles and functions—such as *Minerva* for learning or *Bellona* for war—*Antisthenes* declared that these also were indeed *many popular or civil gods*, but all were really *one and the same natural God*. (*Aristotle* takes notice of this in his book against *Zeno*: "According to the laws of cities and countries, the gods are many, with one being best for one thing and another for another" <note>original Greek: *κατὰ τὸν νόμον, πολλὰ κρατίστους ἀλλήλων οἱ θεοὶ*</note>.)

To *Antisthenes* might be added *Diogenes of Sinope*. It is recorded of him by *Diogenes Laertius* that, observing a woman worshipping the statue or image of a *god* too superstitiously, he spoke to her to reduce her superstition: "Are you not careful, woman, that you do not behave unseemly in the sight of that God who stands behind you? For all things are full of him" <note>original Greek: *εὐλαβῇ, ὦ γύναι, μή ποτε θεοῦ ὄπισθεν ἑστῶτος (πάντα γὰρ ἔστιν αὐτοῦ πλήρη) ἀσχημονήσῃς*</note>. By this, he gave her the opportunity to think more of that supreme and universal *divine power* <term>original: "Numen"; a Latin term for a deity or divine spirit presiding over a place or thing</term> that fills the whole world and is everywhere.

XXIII. It has been frequently stated that *Socrates* died as a *martyr* for *only one God*, in opposition to those *many gods* of the *pagans*. *Tertullian*, for one, writes of him: "Socrates was therefore condemned to die because he destroyed the gods" <note>original Latin: *Propterea damnatus est Socrates, quia Deos destruebat*</note>. And indeed, that *Socrates* asserted one supreme God, the maker and governor of the whole 
<meta>catchword: World</meta>

<summary>This page explores the views of the Cynic philosophers Antisthenes and Diogenes, as well as Socrates, arguing that they believed the numerous "popular" gods of paganism were actually different names or manifestations of a single "natural" God.</summary>

# CHAPTER IV. Socrates as an Asserter of One Supreme Deity.

That the world was made by a Mind is a thing not at all to be doubted. In his discourse with Aristodemus in the first book of Xenophon's *Memoirs*, Socrates convinced him that the things of this world were not made by chance, but by mind and counsel: "Viewing it in this way, it certainly seems that these things are the workmanship of some wise Artificer, who was also a lover of living beings." <note>original Greek: οὕτω γε σκοπουμένῳ πάνυ ἔοικε ταῦτα σοφοῦ τινος δημιουργοῦ, καὶ φιλοζώου τεχνήματι</note> <note>Socrates uses a "teleological" argument here, suggesting that the complexity of life implies a purposeful designer (the Artificer) rather than random luck.</note>

And so he endeavored to persuade him that the mind and understanding within us was derived from some Mind and Understanding in the universe, just as the earth and water within our bodies are derived from the earth and water of the universe: "Do you think that you alone possess wisdom, and that there is no wisdom anywhere else in the whole world outside of you? You know that you have only a small part of the vast quantity of earth in your body, and a little of the water and fire; and since all other great elements exist, do you think you have received a small portion of each to form your frame? Do you then believe that you have somehow luckily snatched up mind alone—which exists nowhere else—for yourself, while there is no such thing anywhere else in the world, and all those infinite things are instead disposed in an orderly way by chance?" <note>original Greek: σὺ δὲ σαυτὸν φρόνιμόν τι δοκεῖς ἔχειν, ἄλλοθι δὲ οὐδαμοῦ οὐδὲν φρόνιμον εἶναι, εἰδὼς ὅτι γῆς τε μικρὸν μέρος ἐν τῷ σώματι πολλῆς οὔσης ἔχεις, καὶ ὑγροῦ βραχύ, πολλοῦ ὄντος, καὶ τῶν ἄλλων δήπου μεγάλων ὄντων ἑκάστου μικρὸν μέρος λαβόντι τὸ συνήρμοσταί σοι; νοῦν δὲ μόνον ἄρα οὐδαμοῦ ὄντα σὲ εὐτυχῶς πως δοκεῖς συναρπάσαι</note>

And when Aristodemus afterward objected that he could not see any Artificer who made the world—as he could see the craftsmen who made other human things—Socrates replied: "Neither do you see your own soul, which rules over your body; so by that same reasoning, you might conclude that you do nothing by mind and understanding, but everything by chance, just as you claim all things in the world are done by chance." <note>original Greek: οὐδὲ γὰρ τὴν σεαυτοῦ σύγε ψυχὴν ὁρᾷς, ἣ τοῦ σώματος κυρία ἐστίν· ὥστε κατάγε τοῦτο ἔξεστί σοι λέγειν, ὅτι οὐδὲ γνώμῃ ἀλλὰ τύχῃ πάντα πράττε</note>

Again, when Aristodemus further disputed the necessity of worshipping the Deity, saying: "I do not despise the divine, Socrates, but I think it is too magnificent a being to need my worship." <note>original Greek: οὐχ ὑπερορῶ τὸ δαιμόνιον, ὦ Σώκρατες, ἀλλ’ ἐκεῖνον μεγαλοπρεπέστερον ἡγοῦμαι, ἢ ὡς τῆς ἐμῆς θεραπείας προσδεῖσθαι</note> Socrates answered: "The more magnificent and illustrious the being is that deigns to care for you, the more in all reason it ought to be honored by you." <note>original Greek: ὅσῳ μεγαλοπρεπέστερον ἀξιοῖ σὲ θεραπεύειν, τοσούτῳ μᾶλλον τιμητέον αὐτό</note>

Lastly, when Aristodemus expressed his disbelief in Providence—finding it incredible, if not impossible, that one and the same Deity could mind all things at once—Socrates endeavored to cure his disbelief in this manner: "My good friend, understand that your mind, being within you, manages your body however it wishes. You should therefore believe that the wisdom which is in the universe also disposes all things as it pleases. If your eye can reach across many miles, why should the eye of God be unable to see everything at once?" <note>original Greek: ὦ ’γαθέ, κατάμαθε, ὅτι καὶ ὁ σὸς νοῦς ἐνὼν τὸ σὸν σῶμα ὅπως βούλεται μεταχειρίζεται· οἴεσθαι οὖν χρὴ καὶ τὴν ἐν παντὶ φρόνησιν τὰ πάντα ὅπως ἂν αὐτῇ ἡδὺ ᾖ οὕτω τίθεσθαι· καὶ μὴ τὸ σὸν μὲν ὄμμα δύνασθαι, ἐπὶ πολλὰ στάδια ἐξικνεῖσθαι, τὸν δὲ τοῦ θεοῦ ὀφθαλμὸν ἀδύνατον εἶναι ἅμα πάντα ὁρᾷν</note>

<meta>catchword: your</meta>

<summary>Socrates argues against Aristodemus's skepticism by comparing the human soul's control over the body to a universal Mind's control over the world, asserting the existence of a single, all-seeing Providence.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Aristodemus, Xenophon, Artificer, Providence, Teleology, Universal Mind, Greek Philosophy</keywords>

# That Socrates was a Martyr for One God — Book I.

If your eye can see things several miles away from it, why should it be thought impossible for the *Eye of God* to behold all things at once? Lastly, if your *soul* can think about things both here and in *Egypt* and in *Sicily*, why may not the *Great Mind* or *Wisdom of God* be able to take care of all things in all places? 

And then he concludes that if *Aristodemus* would diligently apply himself to the worship of God, he should at length be convinced, "that the divine is of such a nature and so great, as to see all things at once, and hear all things, and be present everywhere, and take care of all affairs." <note>original Greek: ὅτι τοιοῦτον καὶ τοιοῦτόν ἐστι τὸ θεῖον, ὥσθ’ ἅμα πάντα ὁρᾷν, καὶ πάντα ἀκούειν, καὶ πανταχοῦ παρεῖναι, καὶ ἅμα πάντων ἐπιμελεῖσθαι</note> 

Moreover, Socrates, in his discourse with *Euthydemus* in *Xenophon's Fourth Book*, speaks thus concerning that invisible Deity which governs the whole world: 

"The other gods, while giving us good things, do not do so by appearing visibly to us. And he who organizes and holds together the entire universe (in which all things are beautiful and good) and who continually supplies us with them—he, though he is seen to do the greatest things of all, nevertheless is himself invisible and unseen. This ought to be wondered at less by us because the *sun*, who seems manifest to all, yet will not suffer himself to be exactly and distinctly viewed; if anyone boldly and shamelessly tries to gaze upon him, he will be deprived of his sight. So also the soul of man, which more than anything else in him partakes of the divine, is that which manifestly rules and reigns in us, yet it is never seen. Considering these particulars, one ought not to despise invisible things, but to honor the Supreme Deity, taking notice of his power from his effects." <note>original Greek: οἱ γὰρ ἄλλοι θεοὶ ἡμῖν τὰ ἀγαθὰ διδόντες... ἃ χρὴ κατανοοῦντα μὴ καταφρονεῖν τῶν ἀοράτων, ἀλλ’ ἐκ τῶν γινομένων τὴν δύναμιν αὐτῶν, καταμανθάνοντα τιμᾶν τὸ δαιμόνιον</note>

In this passage, we have the terms *to daimonion* <note>original Greek: τὸ δαιμόνιον</note> and *to theion* <note>original Greek: τὸ θεῖον</note>—meaning "the Deity" or "the Divine"—plainly used to refer to the Supreme God. We have set down these passages of Socrates here concerning God and Providence specifically to shame those in our own modern days who are so inclined toward atheism—if they have any *pudor* <note>Latin: "shame" or "modesty"</note> left in them at all.

<margin>Against Celsus, Book 6, page 277</margin>
But despite Socrates clearly acknowledging one Supreme and Universal *Numen* <term>numen: a Latin term for divine power or a presiding spirit</term>, it does not follow that he rejected all the other "inferior gods" of the Pagans, as is commonly believed. On the contrary, the very passages just cited mention other gods besides the Supreme. 

How much Socrates conformed to Pagan religion and worship can be seen from his famous last words. Even at his most serious moment, after he had drunk the poison, he requested that his friends offer a votive cock on his behalf to *Aesculapius* <note>The Greek god of healing; Socrates' request is often interpreted as a thanks for the "cure" of death.</note>. For this, the church father *Origen* criticized him: 

"And they who had philosophized so greatly about the soul, and described the way of life of one who has lived well, having abandoned the greatness of what God revealed to them, think of cheap and small things, paying a cock to Aesculapius." <note>original Greek: καὶ τηλικαῦτα φιλοσοφήσαντες περὶ τῆς ψυχῆς... ἀλεκτρυόνα τῷ Ἀσκληπιῷ ἀποδιδόντες</note> And they who had philosophized...

### CHAP. IV. One only God; a common misconception <note>original: "Vulgar Error"</note>.

...philosophized so excellently concerning the Soul, and discoursed concerning the happiness of the future state for those who live well, yet afterward sink down from these great, high, and noble things to a superstitious regard for little, small, and trifling matters, such as the *sacrificing of a rooster to Asclepius* <note>original: "Paying of a Cock to Æsculapius." Asclepius was the god of healing; Socrates' last words requested this sacrifice, often interpreted as thanks for death "curing" the soul of the body's ailments.</note>. However, *Origen* does not charge *Socrates* with such gross and downright idolatry here as he does elsewhere for his sacrificing to the *Pythian Apollo*, who was merely a lower deity <note>original: "Inferiour Demon"</note>. And perhaps some may excuse *Socrates* here, thinking that he looked upon *Asclepius* as no other than the *Supreme Deity* called by that name, exercising his providence over the *sickness and health* or recovery of men. Therefore, he wished a sacrifice of thanksgiving <note>original: "Eucharistick Sacrifice"</note> to be offered on his behalf, as having now been cured of all diseases at once by death.

However, *Plato* informs us that *Socrates*, immediately before he drank his poison, did "pray to the gods that his migration from here to there might be fortunate" <note>original Greek: εὔχεσθαι τοῖς Θεοῖς, τὴν μετοίκησιν τὴν ἐνθένδε ἐκεῖσε εὐτυχῆ εἶναι</note>. He prayed not to "God," but to "the gods"—that is, to both the *supreme* and *lower gods* together, just as in *Plato*’s *Phaedrus* he prayed to *Pan* and the other *guardian gods* <note>original: "Tutelar Gods"</note> of that place—*that his transition from this world into the other might be happy for him.*

And *Xenophon*, in his *Memoirs*, informs us that *Socrates* did, both in his words and practice, approve of that doctrine of the *Pythian Apollo*: *that the rule of piety and religion ought to be the law of every particular city and country.* He affirmed it to be a point of vanity for any man to be eccentric <note>original: "singular"</note> in this regard. Lastly, in his own *Apology*, as written by *Plato*, he professes to acknowledge the *sun, moon*, and *stars* as *gods*, condemning the contrary doctrine of *Anaxagoras* as irrational and absurd. Therefore, we may well conclude that this opinion—that *Socrates* was condemned for denying the *many gods* of the pagans, or that he was a martyr for *one only God*—is nothing but a *common misconception* <note>original: "Vulgar Errour"</note>.

But if you ask what that accusation of impiety really was with which he was charged, *Socrates* himself in *Plato*’s *Euthyphro* will inform you: it was for his free and open condemnation of those traditions concerning the gods in which wicked, dishonest, and unjust actions were attributed to them. For when *Euthyphro*—having accused his own father of murder (merely for putting a man in prison who happened to die there)—wished to justify himself by the examples of the gods, namely *Jupiter* and *Saturn*, because *Jupiter* (the best and justest of the gods) had committed his father *Saturn* to prison for devouring his sons, just as *Saturn* himself had castrated his father *Caelius* <note>Greek: Uranus</note> for some of his misdeeds, *Socrates* addresses him this way: "Is not this the very thing, O Euthyphro, for which I am accused? Namely, because when I hear anyone affirming such matters as these concerning the gods, I am very loath to believe them, and do not hesitate publicly to declare my dislike of them?" <note>original Greek: ἆρά γε, ὦ Εὐθύφρον, τοῦτ’ ἔστιν οὗ ἕνεκα τὴν γραφὴν φεύγω, ὅτι τὰ τοιαῦτα ἐπειδάν τις περὶ τῶν Θεῶν λέγῃ, δυσχερῶς ἀποδέχομαι, &c.</note> And can you, O Euthyphro, in good earnest think that there are indeed wars and contentions among the gods, and that those other things were also done by them which poets and painters commonly attribute to them—such as the *Peplos* <note>A ceremonial robe or veil</note> of *Minerva*, which in the *Panathenaic Festival* <note>An Athenian festival in honor of the goddess Athena (Minerva)</note> is with great pomp and ceremony brought...

<meta>catchword: brought</meta>

<summary>This page argues that the belief that Socrates was a martyr for monotheism is a "common misconception," as historical records show him participating in traditional polytheistic rituals and acknowledging celestial bodies as gods. Instead, his legal troubles stemmed from his vocal rejection of myths that portrayed the gods as immoral or unjust.</summary>

# Plato also a Real Polytheist. BOOK I.

...brought into the *Acropolis*, is embroidered all over with? <note>This refers to the *Peplos*, a sacred robe embroidered with mythological scenes, presented to Athena during the Panathenaic festival.</note> Thus we see that *Socrates*, though he asserted one *Supreme Deity*, yet he acknowledged nonetheless other *inferior created gods*, together with the rest of the *pagans*, honoring and worshipping them. He only disliked those *poetic fables* concerning them (believed at that time by the common people <note>original: "the Vulgar"</note>) in which all manner of *unjust* and *immoral actions* were *attributed* <note>original: "Fathered"</note> to them. This dislike, together with the *envy* of many, was the only true reason why he was then accused of *impiety* and *atheism*.

It has also been affirmed by many that *Plato* really asserted *only one God* and no more, and that therefore whenever he speaks of *gods plurally*, he must be understood to have done this not according to his own judgment, but only as a way of *political compliance* with the *Athenians*, and for fear of being made to drink poison in the same manner as *Socrates* was. In confirmation of which opinion, there is also a passage cited out of that *Thirteenth Epistle* of *Plato's* to *Dionysius* <note>Dionysius the Younger, the tyrant of Syracuse.</note>, wherein he gives this as a *mark* by which his *serious epistles*—and such as were written according to the true sense of his own mind—might be distinguished by his friends from those which were otherwise: "When I begin my epistles with God, then you may conclude I write seriously, but not so when I begin with gods." <note>original Greek: τὸ μὲν γὰρ σπουδαίας ἐπιστολῆς Θεὸς ἄρχει, Θεοὶ δὲ τῆς ἧττον</note> And this passage seems to be therefore the more *authentic* because it was long ago produced <margin>Preparation for the Gospel, Book 11, Chapter 13. <note>original: "Præp. Ev. l. 11. c. 13." A work by the church historian Eusebius.</note></margin> by *Eusebius* for this very purpose: namely, to prove that *Plato* acknowledged *only one God*. Eusebius wrote: "It is manifest that Plato really acknowledged only one God, however much in compliance with the language of the Greeks he often spoke of gods plurally; this is clear from that epistle of his to Dionysius, wherein he gives this symbol or mark, by which he might be known to write seriously—namely, when he began his epistles with God, and not with gods." <note>original Greek: δῆλος δὲ ἐστιν ἕνα Θεὸν εἰδὼς, εἰ καὶ συνήθως Ἕλλησι τῇ τῶν πλειόνων εἴωθε χρῆσθαι προσηγορίᾳ, καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς πρὸς Διονύσιον ἐπιστολῆς, ἐν ᾗ σύμβολα δίδως, τῶν τε διὰ σπουδῆς αὐτῷ γραφομένων, καὶ τῶν ἄλλως ἀπεῤῥιμμένων·</note>

Notwithstanding this, we have already demonstrated out of *Plato's Timaeus* that he did in good earnest assert a *plurality of gods*. By these *gods* of his, we are to understand *living* <note>original: "Animated"</note> or *intellectual beings* superior to *men*, to whom honor and worship from men are due. He declares therein not only the *Sun*, and *Moon*, and *Stars*, but also the *Earth* itself (as a living being) to be a *god* or *goddess*. <margin>Page 40, Serranus edition. <note>original: "P. 40. Ser." Referring to the 1578 edition of Plato by Jean de Serres.</note></margin> For though it is now read in our *copies* as "the oldest of bodies" <note>original Greek: πρεσβυτάτην σωμάτων</note>, meaning that the *Earth* was the *oldest of all the bodies within the heavens*, yet it is certain that anciently it was read otherwise: "the oldest of the gods" <note>original Greek: πρεσβυτάτην Θεῶν</note>. This is known not only from *Proclus* and *Cicero*, but also from *Diogenes Laertius*, who wrote: "The Earth is the oldest of the gods within the heavens, created to distinguish day and night; being at the center, it moves around the center." <note>original Greek: γῆν δὲ πρεσβυτάτην μὲν εἶναι τῶν ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ Θεῶν, γενέσθαι ἢ δημιούργημα, ὡς νύκτα καὶ ἡμέραν ποιεῖν, οὖσαν δ᾽ ἐπὶ τοῦ μέσου, κινεῖσθαι περὶ τὸ μέσον</note> Though *Plato's gods* were for the most part made of fire <note>original: "Fiery"</note>, yet he supposed the *Earth* to be a *god* or *goddess* too, affirming it to be the *oldest of all the gods within the heavens, made* or *created to distinguish day and night, by its daily rotation* <note>original: "Diurnal Circumgyration"</note>—
