# CHAPTER IV. Nevertheless a Monarchist.

...rotation upon its own *axis*, in the middle or center of the world. For when *Plato* wrote his *Timaeus*, he acknowledged only the *diurnal motion* <note>The daily rotation of the Earth on its axis.</note> of the Earth, though he is said to have admitted its *annual* <note>The yearly orbit of the Earth around the sun.</note> motion later in life. This could be further proven from all his other writings, but especially his *Book of Laws* (along with his *Epinomis*) said to have been written in his old age. In these works, he strongly insists upon the *divinity* of the *Sun, Moon*, and *Stars*. He complains that the young men of *Athens* were then so infected with the *Anaxagorean doctrine* <note>Anaxagoras taught that the sun and stars were not gods but red-hot stones or earth.</note>, which claimed they were nothing but inanimate stones and earth. He also approves of the then commonly accepted custom of worshipping the *rising* and *setting Sun* and *Moon* as gods, a practice he likely followed himself. <margin>Laws, Book 10, page 887.</margin> "The prostrations and adorations used by both the Greeks and all foreigners toward the rising and setting sun and moon—occurring in all types of circumstances, whether in prosperity or adversity—declare them to be most certainly regarded as gods, without the slightest suspicion that they are not." <note>original Greek: Ἀνατέλλοντός τε ἡλίου καὶ σελήνης, καὶ πρὸς δυσμὰς ἰόντων, προσκυλίσεις ἅμα καὶ προσκυνήσεις Ἑλλήνων τε καὶ βαρβάρων πάντων, ἐν συμφοραῖς παντοíαις ἐχομένων καὶ ἐν εὐπραγíαις, ὡς ὅτι μάλιστα ὄντων, καὶ οὐδαμῆ ὑποψíαν ἐπιδιδόντων ὡς οὐκ εἰσὶ θεοí.</note> Therefore, we cannot conclude otherwise but that this *Thirteenth Epistle* of *Plato* to *Dionysius*—though it apparently existed before *Eusebius's* time—was a forgery and a counterfeit created by some zealous but ignorant Christian. Accordingly, a *nothuetai* <note>original: Νοθεύεται; a mark of spuriousness or illegitimacy.</note>, or brand of forgery, is prefixed to it in all the standard editions of *Plato's* works.

However, although *Plato* acknowledged and worshipped *many gods*, it is undeniably evident that he was no *polyarchist* <note>One who believes in many equal rulers/gods.</note>, but a *monarchist*—a defender of *one supreme God*, the only *autophyes* <note>original: αὐτοφυής; self-originated or self-existent.</note>, or *self-originated Being*, the maker of the heaven and earth, and of all those *other gods*. First, it is plain that according to *Plato*, the *Soul* of the *whole world* was not itself *eternal*, much less *self-existent*, but was *made* or produced by God in time (though indeed before its *Body*, the *world*), as seen in these words of his: <margin>Plato, Timaeus, p. 34.</margin> "God did not fabricate or make the Soul of the world in the same order that we are now discussing it—that is, after the body, as if it were younger than it. For he would not have allowed the soul, which was to rule and govern, to be joined to that which it was to rule unless the soul were older. Thus, he made the soul more excellent, first, and senior to the body." <note>original Greek: τὴν ψυχὴν οὐκ ὡς νῦν ὑστέραν ἐπιχειροῦμεν λέγειν, οὕτως ἐμηχανήσατο καὶ ὁ θεὸς νεωτέραν, οὐ γὰρ ἂν ξυνέσῃ καὶ ἀρετῇ προτέραν καὶ πρεσβυτέραν ψυχὴν σώματος, ὡς δεσπότιν καὶ ἄρξουσαν ἀρξομένου συνεστήσατο.</note> On this account, *Aristotle* argues with *Plato*, accusing him of contradicting himself by affirming that the *Soul* is a starting principle and yet claiming it is not eternal but was made along with the heavens: <margin>Aristotle, Metaphysics, Book 14, ch. 6.</margin> "Neither is it possible for Plato to explain himself here, for he sometimes declares the Soul to be a principle—as that which moves itself—and yet again affirms it not to be eternal, but made together with the heavens." <note>original Greek: ἀλλὰ μὴν οὐδὲ πλάτωνí γε οἷόν τε λέγειν, ἣν οἴεται ἀρχὴν εἶναι ἐνίοτε αὐτὸ ἑαυτὸ κινῶν, ὕστερον γὰρ καὶ ἅμα τῷ οὐρανῷ ἡ ψυχή.</note> For this reason, some Platonists conclude that *Plato* asserted a *double Psyche* <note>Soul.</note>: one being the third *hypostasis* <note>A distinct person or substance within a trinity.</note> of his *Trinity* and eternal, the other created in time along with the *world*. This seems to be a probable opinion. Therefore, since according to *Plato*, the *Soul of the world*—which is the chief of all his inferior gods—was not self-existent but made or produced...

# Plato’s One God, the Maker: Book I.

...produced by God in time, all those other *gods* of his, which were but parts of the world—such as the *sun, moon, stars, and demons*—must necessarily be so too. But lest anyone should suspect that *Plato* might, despite this, suppose the world and its gods were not made by one only unmade God, but by a multitude of coordinate, self-existent principles or conspiring deities, we shall observe that the contrary is plainly declared by him. In answer to the question of whether there were many and infinite worlds (as some philosophers had maintained) or only one, he resolved it thus:

<margin>Timaeus, page 31</margin> 
"Have we then rightly affirmed that there is only one heaven (or world), or would it be more correct to speak of many or infinite worlds? We say there is but one, if indeed it is to be created according to its intellectual paradigm <note>An "intellectual paradigm" is an ideal model or blueprint in the mind of God.</note>, containing the ideas of all animals and other things in it. For there can be but one archetypal animal <note>original: τὸ γὰρ περιέχον πάντα ὁπόσα νοητὰ ζῶα... (that which contains all intelligible living beings)</note>, which is the paradigm of all created beings; therefore, so that the world may agree with its paradigm in this respect of solitude or 'oneness,' it is neither two nor infinite, but this one-and-only-begotten heaven, having been made, exists and shall exist." <note>original: πότερον οὖν ὀρθῶς ἕνα οὐρανὸν προειρήκαμεν, ἢ πολλοὺς καὶ ἀπείρους λέγειν ἦν ὀρθότερον; ἕνα, εἴπερ κατὰ τὸ παράδειγμα δεδημιουργημένος ἔσται · τὸ γὰρ περιέχον πάντα ὁπόσα νοητὰ ζῶα, μεθ᾽ ἑτέρου δεύτερον οὐκ ἄν ποτ᾽ εἴη, &c. ἵνα οὖν τόδε κατὰ τὴν μόνωσιν, ὅμοιον ᾖ τῷ παντελεῖ ζῴῳ, διὰ ταῦτα οὔτε δύο, οὔτ᾽ ἀπείρους ἐποίησεν ὁ ποιῶν κόσμους, ἀλλ᾽ εἷς ὅδε μονογενὴς οὐρανὸς γεγονώς, ἔστι τε καὶ ἔσεται·</note> His meaning is that there is but one archetypal Mind, the Demiurge <term>Demiurge</term><note>From the Greek *demiourgos*, meaning "craftsman" or "artisan"; Plato's term for the creator of the physical universe.</note> or Maker of all things that were produced, and therefore there is but one world.

And this one God who, according to *Plato*, was the Maker of the whole world, is frequently called by him in his *Timaeus* and elsewhere:
* *God* or *The God* <note>original: ὁ Θεὸς</note> by way of excellence; 
* sometimes *the Architect* or *Artificer of the World* <note>original: ὁ δημιουργὸς</note>; 
* sometimes *the Maker and Father of this universe, whom it is hard to find out, but impossible to declare to the common people* <note>original: ὁ ποιητὴς καὶ πατὴρ τοῦδε τοῦ παντὸς</note>; 
* again, *the God over all* <note>original: ὁ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεὸς</note>; 
* *the Creator of Nature* <note>original: τῆς φύσεως κτίστης</note>; 
* *the sole Principle of the Universe* <note>original: τοῦ παντὸς ἀρχὴ</note>; 
* *the Cause of all things* <note>original: πάντων αἴτιον</note>; 
* *Mind, the King of all things* <note>original: νοῦς πάντων βασιλεύς</note>; 
* *that sovereign Mind, which orders all things and passes through all things* <note>original: νοῦς αὐτοκράτωρ πάντα κοσμῶν διὰ πάντων ἰὼν</note>; 
* *the Governor of the Whole* <note>original: τοῦ παντὸς κυβερνήτης</note>; 
* *that which always is and was never made* <note>original: τὸ ὂν ἀεὶ, γένεσιν δὲ οὐκ ἔχον</note>; 
* *the First God* <note>original: ὁ πρῶτος θεὸς</note>; 
* *the Greatest Spirit and the Greatest of the gods* <note>original: ὁ μέγιστος δαίμων, and ὁ μέγιστος θεῶν</note>; 
* *He who generated or produced the sun* <note>original: ὁ ἥλιον γεννήσας</note>; 
* and *He who makes Earth, and Heaven, and the gods; and does all things both in Heaven, and Hell, and under the Earth* <note>original: ὁ γῆν, οὐρανὸν καὶ θεοὺς, καὶ πάντα τὰ ἐν οὐρανῷ καὶ τὰ ἐν ᾅδου, καὶ ὑπὸ γῆς, ἅπαντα ἐργάζεται</note>.

<margin>The Republic, Book 10</margin>
Again, he is the one by whose efficiency the things of the world <margin>In Sophist</margin> *were afterwards made when they did not exist before*, <note>original: ὕστερον ἐγένετο, πρότερον οὐκ ὄντα</note> or were brought forth into being from an antecedent non-existence. This philosopher somewhere suggests that it was as easy for God to produce those real things—the *sun, moon, stars, and earth, etc.*—from himself, as it <margin>The Republic, Book 10</margin> is for us to produce the images of ourselves and whatever else we please, simply by positioning a looking-glass. Lastly, he is called *He who causes or produces both all other things, and*

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the nature of the Supreme Creator, moving from Plato’s argument for a single Maker to the concept of God as "self-originated" or "self-made," as explored by later Platonists like Plotinus and early Christian writers like Lactantius.</meta>

# CHAP. IV. Of Gods, and All; Self-made

even *Himself*; the meaning of which is this: He who is self-originated <note>original: αὐτοφυὴς (*autophuēs*)</note> (as the same *Plato* also calls him) is a *Self-originated Being*, coming *from no other cause besides Himself*, but being the *cause of all other things*. Neither does *Lactantius Firmianus* himself refuse to speak of God in this very manner: that *He made himself* <note>original: *Seipsum fecit*</note>, and that he was *procreated from himself, and therefore such a one as he willed himself to be* <note>original: *Ex Seipso procreatus, et propterea Talis, Qualem se esse voluit*</note>; that *He made Himself*, and that, being *procreated from Himself*, He therefore was every way such as he *willed* himself to be.

<margin>Ennead 6, Book 8, Page 749</margin>
This unusual and bold strain of *theology* is very much insisted upon by *Plotinus* in his book, *Concerning the Will of the First One, or Unity* <note>original: περὶ τοῦ θελήματος τοῦ ἑνὸς (*peri tou thelēmatos tou henos*)</note>. There he writes thus of the Supreme **God**: *He is the cause of himself, from himself, and is himself for himself* <note>original: αἴτιον ἑαυτοῦ, καὶ παρ᾽ αὑτοῦ, καὶ δι᾽ αὑτοῦ αὐτός (*aition heautou, kai par’ hautou, kai di’ hautou autos*)</note>. And again: *He is the one who makes himself, and is lord over himself; and he did not become what someone else willed, but he is as he himself wills* <note>original: αὐτὸς ἔστιν ὁ ποιῶν ἑαυτὸν, καὶ κύριος ἑαυτοῦ, καὶ οὐχ ὡς τις ἕτερος ἠθέλησε γενόμενος, ἀλλ᾽ ὡς θέλει αὐτός (*autos estin ho poiōn heauton, kai kyrios heautou, kai ouch hōs tis heteros ēthelēse genomenos, all’ hōs thelei autos*)</note>. *This is He, who is the Maker of himself; and is Lord over himself (in a certain sense); for he was not made that which another willed him to be, but he is that which he wills himself to be.* Moreover,

<margin>Page 751</margin>
*Since he is himself that which he loved, and this is his subsistence—if indeed he is a remaining energy—then he himself is an effect. But since he is the effect of no other, he must be his own effect; therefore he is not as he happened to be, but as he acts and as he himself wills* <note>original: αὐτὸς ὢν τοῦτο ὅπερ ἠγάπησε, τοῦτο δὲ ἔστιν ὑπόστασις αὐτοῦ, εἴπερ ἐνέργεια μένουσα· ὥστε ἐνέργημα αὐτὸς, ἀλλὰ ἄλλου μὲν οὐδενὸς, ἑαυτοῦ ἄρα ἐνέργημα αὐτὸς, οὐκ ἄρα ὡς συμβέβηκεν ἔστιν, ἀλλ᾽ ὡς ἐνεργεῖ αὐτὸς καὶ ὡς αὐτὸς ἐθέλει (*autos ōn touto hoper ēgapēse, touto de estin hypostasis autou, eiper energeia menousa; hōste energēma autos, alla allou men oudenos, heautou ara energēma autos, ouk ara hōs symbebēken estin, all’ hōs energei autos kai hōs autos ethelei*)</note>. The Supreme Deity, loving himself as a pure light, is himself what he loved. Thus, as it were, begetting and giving subsistence <note>Hypostasis: individual existence or substance.</note> to himself, he being a standing energy <note>Energy here refers to *energeia*, meaning "activity" or "actualized power."</note>. Therefore, since God is a work or energy, and yet he is not the work or energy of any other being, he must necessarily be (in some sense) his own work or energy; so that God is not what he happened to be, but what he wills himself to be.

<margin>Page 748</margin>
Thus also a little before: *We must trace back the will and the essence to one thing; and if willing is from itself, it is necessary that being is from itself, so that reason finds that he has made himself. For if the will is from himself and is, as it were, his own work, and this is the same as his subsistence, then he himself would be the one who gave subsistence to himself; so that he is not what he happened to be, but what he himself willed* <note>original: ἀνακτέον εἰς ἓν τὴν βούλησιν καὶ τὴν οὐσίαν· τὸ δὲ θέλειν παρ᾽ αὑτοῦ, ἀνάγκη ἄρα τὸ εἶναι παρ᾽ αὑτοῦ, ὥστε αὐτὸ πεποιηκέναι αὐτὸν, ὁ λόγος ἀνεύρεν· εἰ γὰρ ἡ βούλησις παρ᾽ αὑτοῦ, καὶ οἷον ἔργον αὐτοῦ, αὕτη ἡ ταυτὸν τῇ ὑποστάσει αὐτοῦ αὐτὸς ἂν εἴη ὑποστήσας ἂν εἴη αὐτὸν, ὥστε οὐχ ὅπερ ἔτυχέν ἔστιν, ἀλλ᾽ ὅπερ ἐβουλήθη αὐτός (*anakteon eis hen tēn boulēsin kai tēn ousian; to de thelein par’ hautou, anagkē ara to einai par’ hautou, hōste auto pepoiēkenai auton, ho logos aneuron...*)</note>. We must of necessity make Will and Essence the same in the First Being. Wherefore, since his willing is from himself, his being must needs be from himself too; the consequence of which reasoning is this: that He made himself. For if his volition be from himself, and his own work, and this be the same with his subsistence or substance, he may be then said to have given subsistence to himself. Wherefore he is not what he happened to be, but what he willed himself to be. But because this is so unusual a notion, we shall here set down yet one or two more passages from this philosopher concerning it:

<margin>Page 747</margin>
*His essence is not outside of his will, but his will is co-existent with his essence; and it is not possible to take him without his willing for himself that which he is. And he runs along with himself, willing himself to be, and being that which he wills; and the will and himself are one. And because of this, he is no less himself—not something else that he happened to be, but that which he willed to be. For what else would he have willed but that which he is? And if we were to suppose that it were chosen for him what he should will to be, and it were permitted for him to change his own nature into something else, he would neither want to become anything else, nor would he blame himself as being what he is by necessity; and he is himself that which he always willed and wills, since indeed the nature of the Good is truly his will* <note>original: οὐκ ἔξω τοῦ βουλήσεως αὐτοῦ ἡ οὐσία, ἀλλὰ σύνεσιν αὐτῷ τῇ οἷον οὐσίᾳ ἡ θέλησις· καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν αὐτὸν λαβεῖν, ἄνευ τοῦ θέλειν ἑαυτῷ ὅπερ ἐστὶ... (*ouk exō tou boulēseōs autou hē ousian...*)</note>. The essence of the Supreme God is not without his will, but his will and essence are the same; so that God concurs with himself, himself willing to be as he is, and being that which he wills; and his will and himself being one and the same. For himself is not one thing (as happening to be that which he is) and then willing to be another; for what could God will to be, but that

that

# The First Hypostasis of Plato’s Trinity. BOOK 1.

...that which he is? And if we should suppose that it were in his own choice to be what he would, and that he had the liberty to change his nature into whatever else he pleased, it is certain that he would neither will to be anything else besides what he is, nor complain of himself for being what he is out of necessity. He is, indeed, no other than that which he himself has willed and does always will to be. For his Will is his *Essential Goodness*, so that his Will does not follow his nature but concurs with it. In the very essence of this Good, there is contained his choice and the willing of himself to be as such. 

Lastly, <margin>Page 755.</margin> "Therefore, he is entirely Will, and there is no longer anything that is not willed, nor anything before Will. First, therefore, he is Will itself; he is as he willed and such as he willed, and that which follows the Will, which such a Will generated—though it generated nothing else within him." <note>original: πᾶν ἄρα βόλησις, καὶ οὐκέτι τὸ μὴ βολόμενον, οὐδὲ τὸ πρὸ βολήσεως ἄρα· πρῶτον ἄρα ἡ βόλησις αὐτὸς, καὶ τὸ ὡς ἐβόλετο ἄρα καὶ οἷον ἐβόλετο, καὶ τὸ τῇ βολήσῃ ἑπόμενον ὃ ἡ τοιαύτη βόλησις ἐγέννησε· ἐγέννησε δὲ οὐδὲν ἔτι ἐν αὐτῷ (*pan ara bolēsis, kai ouketi to mē bolomenon, oude to pro bolēseōs ara; prōton ara hē bolēsis autos, kai to hōs eboleto ara kai hoion eboleto, kai to tē bolēsē hepomenon ho hē toiautē bolēsis egennēse; egennēse de ouden eti en autō*)</note> *God is all Will, nor is there anything in him which he does not Will, nor is his Being before his Will, but his Will is Himself, or he Himself the first Will.* 

So, he is as he himself would be, and such as he would be, and yet his will did not generate or produce anything that was not there before. And now we may in all probability conclude that *Lactantius* <note>A 4th-century Christian author</note> derived this doctrine from *Plato* and *Plotinus*. How far this is to be either allowed or excused, we leave others to judge. We shall only observe that the word <term>self-begotten</term> <note>original: αὐτογενὴς (*autogenēs*)</note>, frequently attributed to God by Christians as well as Pagans, seems to imply as much. 

Furthermore, the goal and intent of *Plotinus* in all this was plainly to set forth the self-existence of the Supreme Deity in a more vivid manner. He also wanted to refute that odd idea, which some might possibly entertain of God, as if he either happened by chance to be what he is, or were such by a certain necessity of nature and had his being imposed upon him. On the contrary, he is in every way what he would *Will* and *Choose* to be, just as if he had *made himself* by his own *Will* and *Choice*. Neither have we set down all this only to explain that one expression of *Plato's*—*that God causes himself and all things*—but also to show how precisely accurate and careful some of these Pagans were in their speculations concerning the Deity.

To return, therefore, to *Plato*: though some have suspected that <term>Trinity</term> (which is commonly called <term>Platonic</term>) to have been nothing but a mere fiction and invention of some later Platonists, yet the opposite seems unquestionably evident. *Plato* himself really asserted such a <term>Trinity</term> of *universal and divine hypostases* <note>The underlying substances or distinct persons of the Godhead</note>, which have the nature of <term>Principles</term>. 

For first, in his tenth book of *Laws*, where he formally opposes <term>Atheists</term> and undertakes to prove the existence of a Deity, he does not ascend higher than the *Psyche*, or *Universal Mundane Soul* <note>The soul of the world</note>, as a self-moving principle and the immediate or proper cause of all the motion that is in the world. And this is all the God that he undertakes to prove there. But in other places of his writings, he frequently asserts that above the *self-moving Soul* there is an *immovable and standing Nous or Intellect*. This was properly the *Demiurge* <note>original: Demiurgus; the Creator or Craft-worker</note>, or <term>Master-builder</term> <note>original: Architectonick</note> who framed the whole world. And lastly, above this *multi-form Intellect*, he plainly asserts yet a higher <term>hypostasis</term>: one most simple and most absolutely perfect Being, which he calls <term>The One</term> <note>original: τὸ ἓν (*to hen*)</note>...

# CHAPTER IV. The King of All Things.

...in opposition to that Multiplicity which suggests something of imperfection within it. He is *The Good* <note>original: τ'αγαθὸν (*t'agathon*)</note>, or *Goodness itself*, being above *Mind* and *Understanding*. He is the *First Intelligible* and an *Infinite Fecundity*, together with overflowing *Benignity* <note>original: "benignity" here refers to kindness or generosity</note>. Accordingly, in his *Second Epistle to Dionysius*, Plato mentions a *Trinity of Divine Hypostases* <term>hypostasis: a term used to describe a distinct person or level of reality within the Godhead</term> all together. 

Now, the words *God* <note>original: ὁ θεὸς (*ho theos*)</note> and *the Divinity* <note>original: τὸ θεῖον (*to theion*)</note> in *Plato* sometimes seem to encompass this whole *Trinity of Divine Hypostases*. At other times, however, they are applied individually to each of them. We have already observed that *Zeus* or *Jupiter* in *Plato* is not always taken for the *First and Highest Hypostasis* in his *Trinity*. Sometimes the *Second Hypostasis* of *Mind* or *Intellect* is meant by those names, and sometimes even his *Third Hypostasis* of the *Universal and Eternal Psyche* <note>the World-Soul</note>. Nevertheless, the *First* of these *Three Hypostases* is what the Platonists properly call the *Fountain of the Godhead* <note>original: πηγὴ τῆς θεότητος (*pēgē tēs theotētos*)</note>. *Plato* himself calls this level: 

-> *The King of All things, about whom are All things, and for whose sake are All things, and the Cause of all Good and Excellent Things.* <note>original: ὁ πάντων βασιλεύς περὶ ὃν πάντα ἐστί, καὶ οὗ ἕνεκα πάντα, καὶ αἴτιον πάντων τῶν καλῶν (*ho pantōn basileus peri hon panta esti, kai hou heneka panta, kai aition pantōn tōn kalōn*)</note> <-

This *First Divine Hypostasis*, which in *Plato’s* theology is properly the *Original Deity* <note>original: αὐτόθεος (*autotheos*), or God-in-himself</note>, is discussed at length by that philosopher in the sixth book of his *Politics* <note>referring to Plato's "Republic"</note> under the name and title of *The Good*. He primarily illustrates this concept through the *Resemblance of the Sun*. The Sun is also called a *Heavenly God* by the philosopher and is said to be the *offspring of this Highest Good* and something *analogous* to it in the physical world:

> *This is the same in the Intelligible World, to Intellect (or Knowledge) and Intelligibles, as the Sun is in the Sensible World, to Sight and Visibles.* <note>original: ὅ, τι περ αὐτὸ ἐν τῷ νοητῷ τόπῳ, πρός τε νοῦν καὶ τὰ νοούμενα, τοῦτο τοῦτον ἐν τῷ ὁρατῷ πρός τε ὄψιν καὶ τὰ ὁρώμενα (*ho, ti per auto en tō noētō topō, pros te noun kai ta nooumena, touto touton en tō horatō pros te opsin kai ta horōmena*)</note>

For, just as the *Sun* is not *Sight* itself but only the *Cause* of it, and the *Light* by which we see is not the same as the *Sun* itself but only a *Sun-like thing* <note>original: ἡλιοειδές (*hēlioeides*)</note>; so neither is the *Supreme and Highest Good* properly *Knowledge*, but rather the *Cause of Knowledge*. Nor is *Intellect* (precisely considered as such) the *Best and Most Perfect Being*, but only a *Boniform thing* <term>boniform: having the form or nature of the Good; original: ἀγαθοειδές (*agathoeides*)</term>. Again, *as the Sun gives to things not only their visibility but also their generation, so does that Highest Good not only cause the knowability of things, but also their very essences and beings.* 

-> *This Highest Good is not itself properly Essence, but above Essence, transcending it in both dignity and power.* <note>original: οὐκ οὐσίας ὄντος τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ, ἀλλ' ἔτι ἐπέκεινα τῆς οὐσίας, πρεσβείᾳ καὶ δυνάμει ὑπερέχοντος (*ouk ousias ontos tou agathou, all' eti epekeina tēs ousias, presbeia kai dynamei hyperechontos*)</note> <-

Some of the *Greek Fathers* of the Church seem to have adopted this language and concept of *Plato’s*, though they applied it to the whole *Trinity* when they called God *Super-essential* <note>original: ὑπερούσιον (*hyperousion*), meaning beyond being or essence</note>. But the philosopher's meaning, as we understand it, was simply that this *Highest Good* has no *particular characteristic* upon it that limits or defines it; it is the *hidden and incomprehensible source* of all things. Finally, we should observe that this *First Divine Hypostasis* of the Platonic Trinity is called by that philosopher, *The Father of the Prince and Cause of All things* <note>original: τοῦτο ἡγεμόνος καὶ αἰτίου πάντων πατήρ (*touto hēgemonos kai aitiou pantōn patēr*)</note>. In this, we cannot help but notice an

There is an admirable correspondence between Platonic philosophy and Christianity in that the second *Hypostasis* <term>hypostasis: a distinct person or level of reality within the Godhead</term> of both their Trinities (sometimes called *Logos* <note>original: λόγος (*logos*), meaning Word or Reason</note> by the Platonists, as well as *Nous* <note>original: νοῦς (*nous*), meaning Mind</note>) is said to be the immediate cause of all things. This is the *Demiurge* <note>original: *Demiurgus*, the "Architect" or "Craftsman"</note>, the architect, maker, or artificer of the whole world.

Now, we might join *Xenophon* here with *Plato*, because he was his contemporary and a fellow student of Socrates (though it seems there was not always a good relationship between them). Although *Xenophon* acknowledges a plurality of *gods* in various places in his writings, he also gives plain testimony of *one supreme and universal Numen* <term>numen: a Latin term for a divine power or spirit presiding over the universe</term>. Specifically, he writes:

> *He that both agitates all things and establishes the frame of the whole world—though he is clearly great and powerful—is, in his form, invisible.* <note>original: ὁ πάντα σείων καὶ ἀτρεμίζων, ὡς μὲν μέγας τις, καὶ δυνατὸς φανερός, ὁποῖος δ' ἐστὶ μορφὴν ἀφανής (*ho panta seiōn...*)</note>

<margin>Book 10, chapter 8.</margin>
XXIV. Next, we come to *Aristotle*. That he acknowledged more gods than *one* (like the other Pagans) appears from his frequent use of the word in its plural form. This is particularly evident in a passage from his *Nicomachean Ethics*:

<note>original Greek: ἡ δὲ τελεία εὐδαιμονία, ὅτι θεωρητική τις ἐστὶν ἐνέργεια... (the author provides the following translation, here modernized)</note>

*That perfect happiness is a speculative or contemplative activity <note>original: θεωρητική τις ἐστὶν ἐνέργεια (*theōrētikē tis estin energeia*)</note> may be made manifest from this: we consider the gods to be the most blessed and happy of all beings. Now, what kind of moral actions should we attribute to them? Should we attribute justice to them? It would look ridiculous to imagine the gods making contracts and bargains among themselves, and the like. Or should we attribute acts of courage and magnanimity to them? As if the gods had their own fears, dangers, and difficulties to encounter! Or acts of liberality <term>liberality: the quality of being generous or giving</term>? As if the gods had something like money, and there were indigents among them to receive alms! Finally, shall we attribute to them the actions of temperance? But would it not be a disparaging form of praise to say of the gods that they conquer and master their vicious lusts and appetites? Thus, running through all the actions of moral virtue, we find them to be small, mean, and unworthy of the gods. And yet, we all believe the gods are alive, and consequently, that they act—unless we should suppose them to sleep perpetually as Endymion <note>In Greek myth, a beautiful youth granted eternal life but also eternal sleep</note> did. Therefore, if all moral actions, and especially all mechanical operations, are taken away from a being that lives and understands, what is left to it besides contemplation?*

To this, Aristotle adds a further argument for the same point: other animals, who are deprived of contemplation, do not share in happiness. For to the gods...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Aristotle's perspective on the divine, transitioning from his recognition of a "Supreme Numen" to his acknowledgment of a plurality of living, intellectual gods.</meta>

# CHAP. IV. His Polytheism.

"...all their life is happy; for men, it is happy only as much as it approaches contemplation. However, brute animals, which do not contemplate at all, do not share in happiness at all." <note>original Greek: ἡ δὲ τελεία εὐδαιμονία, ὅτι θ... (continued from previous page)</note> In this passage, Aristotle plainly acknowledges a plurality of **gods** and asserts that there is a certain higher rank of beings above humanity.

By the way, we may observe here how those words of his—"All men assume the gods are living" <note>original: ζῆν τε πάντες ὑπειλήφασι θεοὺς (*zēn te pantes hypeilēphasi theous*)</note>—and the arguments that follow him, can be used to refute the opinion of some recent writers. These writers claim that the Pagans generally worshipped the inanimate parts of the world as true and proper gods. Aristotle tells us here that they universally agreed on this: that the gods were animals—living and understanding beings—who are therefore capable of contemplation.

Moreover, in his *Politics*, <margin>Book 5, chapter 11.</margin> while writing about the means to preserve a "tyranny" (as he calls it), Aristotle lists this as one method among others:

> "Furthermore, a ruler should always appear to be exceptionally serious about the worship of the gods. For people are less afraid of suffering any injustice from such kings or princes if they believe the leader is religiously disposed and cares for the gods. Additionally, they will be less likely to plot against him, assuming that he has the gods as his allies and assistants." <note>original: ἔτι δὲ τὰ πρὸς τοὺς θεοὺς φαίνεσθαι ἀεὶ σπουδάζοντα διαφερόντως, ἧττόν τε γὰρ φοβῶνται, τὸ παθεῖν τι παράνομον ὑπὸ τῶν τοιούτων, ἐὰν δεισιδαίμονα νομίζωσιν εἶναι τὸν ἄρχοντα καὶ φροντίζειν τῶν θεῶν· καὶ ἐπιβουλεύουσιν ἧττον, ὡς συμμάχους ἔχοντι καὶ τοὺς θεούς (*eti de ta pros tous theous...*)</note>

In this passage, the word *deisidaimōn* <term>deisidaimōn: literally "fearing the spirits," usually translated as "superstitious," but here used by Aristotle to mean "religiously devout"</term> seems to be used in a positive sense, as a form of praise for a religious person. However, we must admit that Aristotle himself does not write here so much like a devout man as he does a mere politician.

Likewise, in his first book of *On the Heavens*, <margin>Chapter 3.</margin> he writes:

> "All men have a conviction or persuasion that there are gods. And all those who think so—both barbarians and Greeks—assign the highest place to that which is divine, as they suppose the immortal heavens to be the most appropriate place for immortal gods." <note>original: πάντες ἄνθρωποι περὶ θεῶν ἔχουσιν ὑπόληψιν, καὶ πάντες τὸν ἀνωτάτω τῷ θείῳ τόπον ἀποδιδόασι, καὶ βάρβαροι καὶ Ἕλληνες, ὡς τῷ ἀθανάτῳ τὸ ἀθάνατον συνηρτημένον, εἴπερ ἔν τὶ τι θεῖον, ὥσπερ καὶ ἔστι (*pantes anthrōpoi peri theōn echousin hypolēpsin...*)</note>

Therefore, if there is any divinity—as there unquestionably is—the body of the heavens must be acknowledged to be of a different kind from that of the four elements (earth, air, fire, and water).

In the following book, he tells us again that it is most agreeable "to that vaticination <term>vaticination: an instinctive, prophetic feeling or innate sense</term> which all men have in their minds concerning the gods" to suppose the heaven to be a quintessence <term>quintessence: a "fifth element" (beyond the standard four) that was believed to be pure, heavenly, and incorruptible</term>, distinct from the elements and therefore incorruptible. Here, Aristotle affirms that men generally have a "vaticination" in their minds concerning gods—namely, that they themselves are not the highest beings, but that there is a rank of intellectual beings superior to men. The chief of these is the Supreme Deity, concerning whom there is indeed the greatest "vaticination" of all.

We acknowledge it to be very true that Aristotle does not insist upon the existence of "demons" <note>original: *Demons* (daimones); in Greek thought, these were intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil</note> as much as Plato and the general Pagan population did in that age. Probably, he did not have as strong a belief in their existence, though he does mention them occasionally, such as in his *Metaphysics* when speaking of bodies compounded of the elements...

<summary>Aristotle argues that the universal human belief in living, contemplative gods proves that the divine exists and occupies the incorruptible heavens. He also discusses the political utility of a ruler appearing religious and the innate human "vaticination" or instinct regarding a supreme being.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the examination of Aristotle's theology, specifically focusing on his acknowledgment of both a plurality of celestial "Intelligences" and a single Supreme God.</meta>

# Aristotle a Plain Asserter, BOOK I.

He gives examples of **animals and demons** <note>original: ζῶα τε καὶ δαιμόνια (*zōa te kai daimonia*)</note>, and elsewhere he suggests they have airy bodies in these words: <margin>On the Soul, Book 1.</margin> "For someone might ask for what reason the soul in the air is better and more immortal than the soul in animals" <note>original: ἐπιζητήσειε γὰρ ἄν τις, καὶ διὰ τίνα αἰτίαν, ἡ ἐν τῷ ἀέρι ψυχὴ, τῆς ἐν τοῖς ζώοις βελτίων ἐστὶ, καὶ ἀθανατωτέρα</note>. However, whether *Aristotle* believed in these lower demon-gods or not, it is certain that he acknowledged a higher kind of gods: namely the **Intelligences** of all the various celestial spheres, and perhaps also the souls of the spheres and the stars themselves. Since these spheres were—according to the astronomy accepted at the time—forty-seven in number, he must necessarily acknowledge at least that many gods.

Besides these, *Aristotle* also seems to suppose another sort of **incorporeal gods** beyond the heavens where, according to him, there is neither body, nor place, nor **vacuum**, nor time. He writes: <margin>On the Heavens, Book 1. chapter 9.</margin> "Those who exist there are not naturally in a place, nor does time make them grow old, nor is there any change at all in those things positioned above the outermost revolution. Instead, being unalterable and impassive, they lead the best and most self-sufficient life throughout all eternity" <note>original: οὔτ᾿ ἐν τόπῳ τὰ ἐκεῖ πέφυκεν, οὔτε χρόνος αὐτὰ ποιεῖ γηράσκειν, οὐδ᾿ ἔστιν οὐδενὸς οὐδεμία μεταβολὴ, τῶν ὑπὲρ τὴν ἐξωτάτω τεταγμένων φοράν, ἀλλ᾿ ἀναλλοίωτα καὶ ἀπαθῆ, τὴν ἀρίστην ἔχουσα ζωὴν καὶ αὐταρκεστάτην διατελεῖ τὸν ἅπαντα αἰῶνα</note>. But this passage is not without suspicion of being **fraudulent** <note>original: "supposititious"; likely a later addition not written by Aristotle</note>.

Despite all of this, it is also unquestionable that *Aristotle* did assert **one supreme and universal deity** <note>original: "Numen"</note>. For although it is granted that he often uses the singular **God** <note>original: θεὸς (*theos*)</note>, as well as **the divine** <note>original: τὸ θεῖον (*to theion*)</note> and **the spiritual power** <note>original: τὸ δαιμόνιον (*to daimonion*)</note>, many times indefinitely to mean "a god in general" or any divine being—and though such passages have often been mistaken by Christian writers as if *Aristotle* meant the Supreme God in them—it is nevertheless certain that he also often uses those words emphatically to refer to **one only Supreme God**.

As in this passage from his *Metaphysics*: <margin>Book 1.</margin> "God seems to be the cause for all things and a certain first principle" <note>original: ὅ, τε γὰρ θεὸς δοκεῖ τὸ αἴτιον πᾶσιν εἶναι καὶ ἀρχή τις</note>. And also in his *On the Soul*, where he speaks of the soul of the heavens and its circular motion: <margin>Book 1. chapter 3.</margin> "Neither is it a good explanation for the circular motion of the heavens to say, as the Platonists do, that God made the soul of the world move the heaven in a circle because it was **better** <note>original: τὸ βέλτιον (*to beltion*)</note>—as if it were better for it to move than to stay still, or to move in this way rather than another. But since this is a speculation that properly belongs to some other science, we shall not pursue it further in this place."

He uses this language again later in the same book: "It follows from the principles of Empedocles that God must be the most unwise of all beings; for He alone would be ignorant of one of the elements—**Strife** <note>original: νεῖκος (*neikos*)</note>, or Contention—while mortal animals may know or conceive of all things, because they are compounded of all elements" <note>original: συμβαίνει δὲ Ἐμπεδοκλεῖ γε καὶ ἀφρονέστατον εἶναι τὸν θεὸν, μόνον γὰρ τῶν στοιχείων ἓν οὐ γνωρίζει, τὸ Νεῖκος, τὰ δὲ θνητὰ πάντα, ἐκ πάντων γὰρ ἕκαστον</note>. This is because Empedocles' God is composed of nothing but **Love** <note>original: φιλία (*philia*)</note>, unity, and friendship, and thus cannot know its opposite.

### CHAPTER IV. Of One Universal Divine Power <note>original: Numen</note>. 411

---

The same passage we have again in his *Metaphysics*, from which it was previously cited for another purpose. To these might be added another place from his book, *On Generation and Corruption*: "God has filled up the Whole or Universe, and constantly supplies it, having made a continual successive generation" <note>original: τὸ ὅλον συνεπλήρωσεν ὁ θεὸς, ἐντελεχῆ ποιήσας γένεσιν (*to holon syneplērōsen ho theos, entelechē poiēsas genesin*)</note>. Lastly, the term "the Divine" <note>original: τὸ δαιμόνιον (*to daimonion*)</note> is sometimes plainly used by *Aristotle* as well, not for divinity in general, or for anything that is divine, but for that **One Supreme Deity**, the Governor of the whole world. Thus, in that passage of his *Rhetoric to Alexander*: <margin>Chapter 1. page 609. P.</margin> "This is that in which we men differ from other animals, having received the greatest honor from God: that though they are endowed with appetite, anger, and other passions as well as we, yet we alone are furnished with speech and reason" <note>original: τοῦτό ἐστιν ᾧ διαφέρομεν τῶν λοιπῶν ζώων, ἡμεῖς οἱ μεγίστης τιμῆς ὑπὸ τοῦ δαιμονίου τετυχηκότες</note>.

Beyond this, *Aristotle* in his *Metaphysics* (<margin>Book 14. chapter 10. Paris edition.</margin> as has been already observed) professedly opposes that **imaginary opinion** of many independent principles of the universe—that is, of many unmade, self-existent deities. He refutes this from the "phenomena" (observable facts), because "all things are plainly ordered together toward One" <note>original: ἅπαντα πρὸς ἓν συντέτακται (*hapanta pros hen syntetaktai*)</note>, the whole world conspiring into **one agreeing harmony**. In contrast, if there were many principles or independent deities, the system of the world would necessarily have been "incoherent" <note>original: ἐπεισοδιώδης (*epeisodiōdēs*)</note> and unharmonious, like a poorly written drama patched together with many irrelevant insertions. Thereupon *Aristotle* concludes in this manner: "But things do not wish to be poorly governed" (which was then, it seems, a kind of proverbial speech);

-> "The government of many is not good; let there be one ruler." <-
<note>original: οὐκ ἀγαθὸν πολυκοιρανίη, εἷς κοίρανος (*ouk agathon polykoiraniē, heis koiranos*) — a famous line from Homer's Iliad.</note>

Therefore, there is one Prince or Monarch over all. From this passage of *Aristotle’s*, it is evident that although he asserted a **multiplicity of gods** in the popular sense <note>original: vulgar sense</note>, as has been already declared, he absolutely denied a **polyarchy** (rule by many) or a "mundane aristocracy"—that is, a multiplicity of first principles and independent deities. 

Therefore, though *Aristotle* was very fond of his whimsical theory of as many "Intelligibles" or eternal and immovable minds (now commonly called **Intelligences**) as there are movable spheres in the heavens—which he also sometimes calls "principles"—he must necessarily be interpreted to have derived all of these from **One Supreme Universal Deity**. As *Simplicius* <note>A 6th-century commentator on Aristotle.</note> expresses it, this is "the Principle of Principles" <note>original: ἀρχὴ ἀρχῶν (*archē archōn*)</note>, which comprehends and contains those inferior deities under it, in the same way that the *Primum Mobile* <note>The outermost moving sphere in ancient astronomy.</note> or highest sphere contains all the lesser spheres within it. Otherwise, there would not be "one prince or monarch over the whole," and the government of the world would be a "rule of many" <note>original: Polychærany</note> or an aristocracy of gods, which was concluded to be a bad form of government. Moreover, as <margin>*Enneads* 5. Book 1. chapter 7.</margin> *Plotinus* <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> represents *Aristotle’s* sense, it is not conceivable that so many...

### Aristotle's First Immovable Mover. Book I.

...many independent principles should thus constantly conspire *toward one work: the symphony of the whole heaven* <note>original: πρὸς ἓν ἔργον τὴν τοῦ παντὸς οὐρανοῦ συμφωνίαν (*pros hen ergon tēn tou pantos ouranou symphōnian*)</note>, into one work, that agreeable **symphony** and **harmony** of the **whole heaven**. There could also be no reason why there should be exactly as many of these **intelligences** as there are **spheres** and no more; and it is absurd to suppose *that the first principles exist by chance* <note>original: κατὰ συντυχίαν τὰς ἀρχὰς εἶναι (*kata syntychian tas archas einai*)</note>, or that the **first principles** of the **universe** happened by accident.

Now this highest principle, as it is an **immovable essence** <note>original: ἀκίνητος οὐσία (*akinētos ousia*)</note>, is by **Aristotle** in the first place supposed to be the **principle of motion** <note>original: ἀρχὴ κινήσεως (*archē kinēseōs*)</note> in the **universe**, or at least of that chief motion of the ***Primum Mobile*** <term>The "First Moved" or outermost sphere in classical astronomy, which was thought to carry all other spheres around the Earth from East to West</term> or highest sphere (which, according to the astronomy of those times, seems to have been the sphere of the fixed stars). By its rapid rotation, all the other spheres and heavens were imagined to be carried round from East to West. 

<margin>Metaphysics, Book 14, chapter 8, page 1003. Paris edition.</margin>

Accordingly, the supreme deity is called by **Aristotle** **the first immovable mover** <note>original: τὸ πρῶτον κινοῦν ἀκίνητον (*to prōton kinoun akinēton*)</note>, or the **mover of the *Primum Mobile* and the whole heaven**. Since he concluded that this **first mover** is only **one**, he infers from this the **singularity of the heaven or world**:

<margin>Metaphysics, Book 14, chapter 8.</margin>

*There is one numerically first immovable mover and no more; and therefore there is but one movable thing as well, that is, but one heaven or world* <note>original: ἓν μὲν ἄρα τῷ λόγῳ καὶ ἀριθμῷ, τὸ πρῶτον κινοῦν ἀκίνητον ὄν· καὶ τὸ κινούμενον ἄρα ἀεὶ καὶ συνεχῶς ἓν μόνον· εἷς ἄρα οὐρανὸς μόνος (*hen men ara tō logō kai arithmō, to prōton kinoun akinēton on; kai to kinoumenon ara aei kai synechōs hen monon; heis ara ouranos monos*)</note>. 

In this doctrine of Aristotle's, there seems to be a great difference between his philosophy and that of **Plato**. **Plato** makes the **principle of motion** in the heavens and the whole world to be a **self-moving soul**, while **Aristotle** supposes it to be an **immovable mind or intellect**. Nevertheless, according to **Aristotle's** own explanation, the difference between them is not great, if there is any at all. **Aristotle's immovable mover** is understood by him not to move the heavens **efficiently** <term>By physical force or direct action</term>, but only **objectively** and **finally** <term>By acting as a goal or purpose</term>, *as being loved* <note>original: ὡς ἐρώμενον (*hōs erōmenon*)</note>.

<margin>Page 167.</margin>

**Proclus**, in his commentary on **Plato's** *Timaeus*, criticizes this concept in the following manner: *Some of the ancients, turning the world toward the mind (or intellect) and giving it motion through love of that first desirable thing, said that nothing descended from the mind into the world; they placed the mind on the same level as other lovable sensory things that have nothing generative in their own nature* <note>original: τῶν παλαιῶν οἱ μὲν τὸν κόσμον ἐπιστρέψαντες ἐπὶ τὸν νοῦν, καὶ διὰ τοῦ ἔρωτος, τοῦ περὶ τὸ πρῶτον ὀρεκτὸν, δόντες αὐτῷ τὴν κίνησιν, οὐδὲν ἔφασαν ἀπὸ τοῦ νοῦ καθήκειν εἰς αὐτὸν, ἐν ἴσῳ προστάξαντες αὐτὸν τοῖς ἐρασμίοις μὲν τῶν αἰσθητῶν, μηδὲν δὲ γεννητικὸν ἔχουσιν ἐν τῇ ἑαυτῶν φύσει</note>. Here **Proclus** seems to think that **Aristotle** attributed no **efficiency** (creative power) at all to God regarding the world; however, the contrary will be clearly proven later. 

In the meantime, it is certain that **Aristotle**, besides his **immovable mover** of the heavens (which moves only **finally**, or as **being loved**), must also suppose another **immediate mover** of them, or an **efficient cause** of that motion. This could be nothing other than **a soul** which, enamored with this **supreme mind**, continually turned the heavens round as if in imitation of it. This seems to be nothing but **Plato's** doctrine in disguise; for that philosopher likewise affirmed that the **circular motions** of the heavens are caused ef- <meta>catchword: ficiently</meta>

# Chapter IV. His Cause of Well and Fit.

He is described sufficiently as a *Soul of the World* in his *Timaeus* to be **a motion that is most agreeable to that of mind or wisdom** <note>original Greek: τὼ περὶ νοῦν καὶ φρόνησιν μάλιστα ἔσαν (*tō peri noun kai phronēsin malista esan*)</note>. And again in his *Laws*, he calls it **that which of all physical motions most resembles the circular path of the intellect** <note>original Greek: τὴν τοῦ νοῦ περιόδῳ πάντως ὡς δυνατὸν; οἰκειοτάτω καὶ ὁμοίαν (*tēn tou nou periodō pantōs hōs dynaton; oikeiotatō kai homoian*)</note>. This Platonic concept found acceptance with **Boethius**, who, writing of the *Soul of the World*, represents it thus:

<margin>Consolation of Philosophy, Book 3, Meter 9.</margin>

> ->*Which, when divided, she gathered its motion into two orbs,*<-
> ->*Returning into itself it goes, and circles*<-
> ->*The deep mind, and turns the heaven with a similar image.*<-
> <note>original Latin: Quæ cum Secta Duos motum glomeravit in Orbes, / In semet reditura meat, Mentemque Profundam / Circuit, & simili convertit Imagine Cœlum.</note>

Therefore, according to both **Plato's hypothesis** and **Aristotle's**, it may be affirmed of the **Supreme Deity**, in the language of the same **Boethius**, that:

->—— *And remaining stable, he causes all things to move,*<-
<note>original Latin: Stabiliſque manens dat cuncta Moveri</note>

**Being itself immovable, it causes all other things to move.** The **immediate efficient cause** <term>The direct force or agent that produces an effect</term> of this motion also seems to have been a **Mundane Soul** <term>The "World Soul," a spirit thought to animate the entire universe</term>, no less according to **Aristotle** than **Plato**. However, **Aristotle** did not think it fit to make this **Soul** a **first principle**; in all probability, this was because he was not as certain of the **incorporeity** <term>The state of being non-physical or without a body</term> of souls as he was of minds or intellects.

<margin>Metaphysics, Book 14, chapter 7, page...</margin>
Nevertheless, turning the *Primum Mobile*—and doing so only as something that is "loved," or as the **final cause** of it, as **Proclus** supposed—is not the only thing that **Aristotle** attributed to his **first and highest immovable principle**, or the **Supreme Deity**. He, as well as **Anaxagoras**, asserted it to be also **the cause of well and fit** <note>original Greek: τοῦ εὖ καὶ καλῶς αἰτίαν (*tou eu kai kalōs aitian*)</note>, or **that without which there could be no such thing as "well"** <note>original Greek: τὸ οὗ οὐκ ἄνευ τὸ εὖ (*to hou ouk aneu to eu*)</note>. That is to say, there would be no **order, aptitude, proportion, and harmony in the universe**.

He excellently declared that **unless there were something else in the world besides physical things, there could be neither beginning nor order in it, but one thing would be the principle of another infinitely, or without end** <note>original Greek: εἰ μὴ ἔσται παρὰ τὰ αἰσθητὰ ἄλλα, οὐκ ἔσται ἀρχὴ καὶ τάξις, ἀλλ᾿ ἀεὶ τ᾿ ἀρχῆς ἀρχὴ (*ei mē estai para ta aisthēta alla, ouk estai archē kai taxis, all' aei t' archēs archē*)</note>. And again, in another place already cited: **it is not at all likely that either fire or earth or any such body should be the cause of that "well and fit" that is in the world; nor can so noble an effect as this be reasonably imputed to chance or fortune** <note>original Greek: τοῦ εὖ καὶ καλῶς, ἴσως οὔτε πῦρ οὔτε γῆν... οὐδ᾿ αὐτῷ αὐτομάτῳ καὶ τύχῃ τοσοῦτον ἐπιτρέψαι πράγμα καλῶς ἔχειν (*tou eu kai kalōs, isōs oute pyr oute gēn... oud' autō automatō kai tychē tosouton epitrepsai pragma kalōs echein*)</note>.

Therefore, agreeing with **Anaxagoras**, he concludes that it is ***Nous*** or **Mind** which is properly **the cause of well and right** <note>original Greek: αἴτιον τοῦ καλῶς καὶ ὀρθῶς (*aition tou kalōs kai orthōs*)</note>, and accordingly, he frequently calls the **Supreme Deity** by that name. He also affirms that the **order, beauty, and harmony of the whole world** depend upon that **one highest and supreme being** in it, in the same way that the **order of an army** depends upon the **General or Emperor**, who does not exist for the sake of the order, but the order exists for him. This **Highest Being of the Universe** is therefore also called by him, in conformity with **Plato**,

to **the separate good** <note>original Greek: τὸ ἀγαθὸν κεχωρισμένον (*to agathon kechōrismenon*)</note>, **the Separate Good of the World**, in a way that distinguishes it from that **intrinsic** or **inherent good** of the world, which is the **order** and **harmony** itself: **"We must also consider in what way the nature of the whole contains the good and the highest good; whether as something separate and existing by itself, or as its internal order? Or rather both of them together? For example, the good of an army consists both in its order and in its general, but primarily in the general. For the general is not there because of the order, but the order exists because of him; for all things are ordered together in some way toward God and in relation to him."** <note>original Greek: Ἐπισκεπτέον δὲ καὶ ποτέρως ἔχει ἡ τοῦ ὅλου φύσις τὸ ἀγαθὸν καὶ τὸ ἄριστον; πότερον κεχωρισμένον τι, καὶ αὐτὸ καθ' αὑτὸ; ἢ τὴν τάξιν; ἢ ἀμφοτέρως ὥσπερ στράτευμα; καὶ γὰρ ἐν τῇ τάξει τὸ εὖ καὶ ὁ στρατηγός, καὶ μᾶλλον οὗτος, οὐ γὰρ οὗτος διὰ τὴν τάξιν, ἀλλ' ἐκείνη διὰ τοῦτόν ἐστιν· πάντα γὰρ συντέτακταί πως</note> Therefore, since **Aristotle’s** Supreme Deity—by whatever name it is called, whether **Mind** or **Good**—is the proper **efficient cause** <term>The direct agent that brings something into being</term> of all that **well-being** and **fitness** found in the universe, and of all its order, beauty, and harmony, it must be granted that besides being the **final cause** <term>The ultimate purpose or goal for which something exists</term> of motion (turning the heavens by being **loved**), it was also the **efficient cause** of the whole frame of nature and the **system** of the world. And in this way, he plainly declares his meaning:

<margin>Metaphysics, Book 1, Chapter 3.</margin>
where he applauds **Anaxagoras** <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who was the first to propose "Mind" (Nous) as the organizing force of the universe</note> for maintaining **that Mind is the cause not only of all order, but also of the whole world** <note>original Greek: Νοῦν εἶναι καὶ τοῦ κόσμου καὶ τῆς τάξεως πάσης αἴτιον</note>; and when he himself positively affirms:

<margin>Metaphysics, Book 12, Chapter 7.</margin>

He also

<margin>On the Parts of Animals, Book 1.</margin>
somewhere affirms that if the heavens or the world were **generated** (that is, **made in time**, so as to have had a beginning), then it was certainly made not by **chance** or fortune, but by such an **artificial nature** as is the instrument of a **perfect mind**. And in his *Physics*:

<margin>Physics, Book 2, Chapter 6.</margin>
where he argues for the world's eternal existence in the past, he nevertheless concludes: **"That Mind together with Nature must of necessity be the cause of this whole universe."** <note>original Greek: ἀνάγκη νοῦν αἴτιον καὶ φύσιν εἶναι τοῦδε τοῦ παντός</note> For even if the world were co-eternal with the Mind, it was still, in the order of nature, subsequent to it and junior to it as its effect.

<margin>Aristotle, On the Soul, Book 1, Chapter 7.</margin>
He generously resolves this by saying: **"it is most reasonable to conclude that Mind is the oldest of all things, and senior to the world and the elements; and that according to nature, it has a princely and sovereign dominion over all."** <note>original Greek: εὐλογώτατόν εἶναι νοῦν πρεσβύτατον, καὶ κύριον κατὰ φύσιν· τὰ δὲ στοιχεῖά φασι πρῶτα τῶν ὄντων εἶναι</note> This contrasts with the view of others (namely, the atheists) who claim that the elements were the first beings. Therefore, we think it is now sufficiently evident that **Aristotle’s** Supreme Deity does not only move the heavens **as something that is loved** (acting as the final cause of motion), but was also the **efficient cause** of this whole **world system**, framed according to the **best wisdom** and in the **best** possible manner.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "Efficient Cause" of the universe, contrasting the ancient philosophical view of God as an inherently good "Mind" with the view of God as a purely arbitrary will. <header>Chap. IV. The Efficient Cause of the World.</header>

...according to the common understanding <note>original: Vulgar Sence</note> of many in our day—as if he were indeed an understanding or perceptive being, and perfectly all-knowing, but nevertheless one who acted all things arbitrarily, being not determined by any rule or nature of goodness, but only by his own random will. For according to those ancient philosophers, that which acts without regard for the good would not be considered "Mind" <note>original Latin: *Mens*</note> so much as "Madness" <note>original Latin: *Dementia*</note> or folly. To attribute the structure of nature or the system of the world, along with its government, to such a principle would have been judged by them as equivalent to attributing it to chance or fortune. 

But Aristotle and those other philosophers who called the supreme God *Nous* <note>original Greek: Νοῦς</note> or "Mind" understood by that term that which, of all things in the world, is most opposite to chance, fortune, and rashness. They meant that which is regulated by "the well and the fit" <note>original Greek: τὸ εὖ καὶ καλῶς (*to eu kai kalōs*)</note> of everything—if it is not, in fact, the very rule, measure, and essence of fitness itself; that which acts all for ends and the good, and does everything in the best manner for the sake of the whole. 

Thus Socrates, in the passage cited earlier from Plato's *Phaedo*, interprets the meaning of the opinion that "Mind made the world and was the cause of all things": "I thought that if this were so, the Mind orders all things and places each thing in the way that is best" <note>original Greek: ἡγησάμην, εἰ τοῦτο οὕτως ἔχει, τὸν νοῦν πάντα κοσμεῖν, καὶ ἕκαστον τιθέναι ταύτῃ ὅπῃ ἂν βέλτιστα ἔχῃ (*hēgēsamēn, ei touto houtōs echei, ton noun panta kosmein, kai hekaston tithenai tautē hopē an beltista echē*)</note>. Therefore, every thing might be concluded to have been disposed of in the best possible manner. And accordingly Theophrastus, Aristotle’s student and successor, describes God in this way: "The first and divinest being, who wills all the best things" <note>original Greek: τὸ πρῶτον καὶ θειότατον, πάντα τὰ ἄριστα βουλόμενον (*to prōton kai theiotaton, panta ta arista boulomenon*)</note>. 

Which of these two hypotheses concerning God is more agreeable to piety and true Christianity—one from the ancient pagan philosophers, that God is as essentially goodness as he is wisdom (or, as Plotinus calls him following Plato, "decency and fitness itself"); or the other from some recent professors of Christianity, that he is nothing but arbitrary will, all-powerful and all-knowing—we shall leave to be considered.

<margin>Metaphysics, Book 1, Chapter 3.</margin>
<margin>Book 2, Chapter 23.</margin>
<margin>Magna Moralia, Book 2, Chapter 15.</margin>
Lastly, it is not improbable that Aristotle attributed even the very substance of things themselves to divine efficiency <term>The power of an agent to produce an effect</term>, beyond just the structure of nature and the fabric of the world (nor can there be much doubt about anything except perhaps matter). This is suggested partly by his affirmation that God is a cause and principle for all things, and partly from his praise of this doctrine of Anaxagoras: "That Mind was, together with the 'well' and the 'fit,' the cause and principle of things themselves" <note>original Greek: ἅμα τῷ καλῶς, αἰτίαν καὶ ἀρχὴν εἶναι τῶν ὄντων νοῦν (*hama tō kalōs, aitian kai archēn einai tōn ontōn noun*)</note>. 

Regardless, it can be further confirmed that Aristotle’s inferior gods—and therefore his "intelligences" of the lesser spheres, which were incorporeal substances—were all produced or created by one Supreme Being. This is seen in his definition in his *Rhetoric*: "The divine is nothing other than either God or the work of God" <note>original Greek: τὸ δαιμόνιον οὐδέν ἐστιν, ἀλλ' ἢ θεός, ἢ θεοῦ ἔργον (*to daimoniōn ouden estin, all’ ē theos, ē theou ergon*)</note>. In this context, "God" <note>original Greek: θεὸς (*theos*)</note> is unquestionably used in a way that implies eminence, referring to the Supreme Deity, as in those other passages of Aristotle cited previously, to which several more might be added, such as: "God possesses all good things and is self-sufficient" <note>original Greek: πάντα ἔχει τ' ἀγαθὰ ὁ θεός, καὶ ἔστιν αὐτάρκης (*panta echei t' agatha ho theos, kai estin autarkēs*)</note>. <meta>This page continues the examination of Aristotle’s theology, following the previous discussion on God as a "Mind" that acts for the sake of the good. It moves from God's role as the "Efficient Cause" to his nature as a self-sufficient, eternal, and incorporeal substance.</meta>

# The Principal Heads Book I.

...possesses <note>original: [possess]eth</note> all good things and is *self-sufficient*. Again, where he speaks of things that are more than praiseworthy, <margin>Nicomachean Ethics, Book 1, Chapter 12</margin> he says, "Such are God and the Good, for to these are all other things referred" <note>original Greek: τοιοῦτον δὲ εἶναι τὸν Θεὸν καὶ τ’ἀγαθόν, πρὸς ταῦτα γὰρ καὶ τ’ἄλλα ἀναφέρεσθαι (*toioūton de einai ton Theon kai t’agathon, pros tauta gar kai t’alla anapheresthai*)</note>. But here Aristotle, by affirming that there is nothing divine except either God himself or the work and *effect* of God, plainly implies that there was no multitude of *self-existent* deities. He suggests that those intelligences of the lesser stars or spheres, however eternal they may be, were themselves also produced or caused by one supreme deity.

<margin>Metaphysics, Book 6, Chapter 1</margin> Furthermore, Aristotle declares that this study concerning the deity constitutes a particular science by itself. It is distinct from those other speculative sciences of *physiology* <note>original: physiology; here meaning the study of nature or physics</note> and *pure mathematics*. Thus, there are three speculative sciences in all, distinguished by their different objects: *physiology*, *pure mathematics*, and *theology* (or *metaphysics*). The first of these—*physiology*—is concerned with "things both inseparable from matter and in motion" <note>original Greek: περὶ ἀχώριστα μὲν, ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἀκίνητα (*peri achōrista men, all’ ouk akinēta*)</note>. The second (namely, geometry or *pure mathematics*) is "about things that are indeed immovable, but not really separable from matter" <note>original Greek: περὶ ἀκίνητα μὲν ἀλλ’ οὐ χωριστὰ, ἀλλ’ ὡς ἐν ὕλῃ (*peri akinēta men all’ ou chōrista, all’ hōs en hylē*)</note>, so that they do not exist alone by themselves. But the third and last, *theology*, concerns "things both immovable and separable" <note>original Greek: περὶ χωριστὰ καὶ ἀκίνητα (*peri chōrista kai akinēta*)</note> from matter—that is, incorporeal substances. 

This philosopher adds there: "For if there were no other substance besides these natural things, which are material and in motion, then physiology would be the primary science. But if there is any immovable substance, the philosophy of it must necessarily be prior in the order of nature" <note>original Greek: εἰ μὴ γάρ τις ἑτέρα οὐσία παρὰ τὰς φύσει συνεστηκυίας, ἡ φυσικὴ ἂν εἴη πρώτη ἐπιστήμη, εἰ δ’ ἔστι τις οὐσία ἀκίνητος, αὕτη προτέρα, καὶ φιλοσοφία πρώτη (*ei mē gar tis hetera ousia para tas physei synestēkyias, hē physikē an eiē prōtē epistēmē, ei d’ esti tis ousia akinētos, hautē protera, kai philosophia prōtē*)</note>. Lastly, he concludes that as the speculative sciences in general are more noble and excellent than others, so is *theology* (or *metaphysics*) the most honorable of all the speculative sciences. 

Now the chief points of *Aristotelian theology*, or his metaphysical doctrine concerning God, seem to be these *four* following. First, that although all things are not *uncreated* <note>original: Ingenit; meaning unbegotten or having no beginning</note> or unmade—according to his book against Xenophanes: "Is it necessary that all things should be unmade, or does nothing prevent some things from being generated from other things?" <note>original Greek: ἆρ’ ἀνάγκη ἀγένητα πάντα εἶναι, ἢ οὐδὲν κωλύει γεγονέναι ἕτερα ἐξ ἑτέρων; (*ara anagkē agenēta panta einai, ē ouden kōlyei gegonenai hetera ex heterōn?*)</note>—yet there must necessarily be something *eternal* <margin>Metaphysics, Book 14, Chapter 6</margin> *and unmade*. It must also be incorruptible, because "if all substances were corruptible, then all things might come to nothing" <note>original Greek: εἰ πᾶσαι οὐσίαι φθαρταὶ, πάντα φθαρτά (*ei pasai ousiai phthartai, panta phtharta*)</note>. This *eternal*, *unmade* (or self-existent), and *incorruptible* substance, according to Aristotle, is not mindless matter, but a *perfect mind*. 

Secondly, that God is also an incorporeal substance, <margin>Metaphysics, Book 14, Chapter 7</margin> "separate from sensible things" <note>original Greek: κεχωρισμένη τῶν αἰσθητῶν (*kechōrismenē tōn aisthētōn*)</note>. Not only that, but according to Aristotle’s judgment, he is also "indivisible, without parts, and without magnitude" <note>original Greek: ἀδιαίρετος, καὶ ἀμερὴς, καὶ ἀμεγέθης (*adiairetos, kai amerēs, kai amegethēs*)</note>. Nor can it be denied that, besides Aristotle, the majority of those other ancients who asserted the existence of incorporeal substance also supposed it to be *unextended*. They divided substances (as we learn from Philo) into "extended and unextended substances" <note>original Greek: διαστηματικαὶ, καὶ ἀδιάστατοι οὐσίαι (*diastēmatikai, kai adiastatoi ousiai*)</note>. Whether this doctrine...

# Chapter IV. Of Aristotle’s Theology.

Whether this is true or not is not to be discussed here. <margin>Metaphysics, Book 14, Chapters 7 and 9</margin> Thirdly, *that in God, the Intellect is essentially the same thing as the objects of its thought* <note>original Greek: ταυτὸ νῦς καὶ νοητὸν (*tauto nous kai noēton*)</note>. Because the *Divine Mind* is (at least in the order of Nature) *Senior* <note>meaning: prior or superior in rank</note> to all things and the *Architect* <note>original: architectonical</note> of the world, it could not look outward for its objects or find them anywhere outside itself; therefore, it must necessarily contain them all within itself. This conclusion of *Aristotle's* is no less agreeable to *Theism* than to *Platonism*. On the contrary, *Atheists*—who assert that the *Mind* and *Understanding* as such are, in the order of nature, *Junior* <note>meaning: secondary or appearing later</note> to *Matter* and the *World*—suppose (consistent with their own hypothesis) that all *intellection* <note>the act of thinking</note> occurs by way of a *passive response* <note>original: passion</note> to physical things outside themselves. They believe no *Mind* or *Intellect* contains its *intelligibles* (its immediate objects of thought) within itself.

<margin>Metaphysics, Book 14, Chapter 6</margin> Lastly, he argues that because God is an *Immovable Substance*, his *essence* is *activity* <note>original Greek: οὐσία (ousia) is ἐνέργεια (energeia)</note>. His *Essence* and his *Act* or Operation are the same: "There must therefore necessarily be such a principle, whose very essence is activity" <note>original Greek: δεῖ ἄρα εἶναι οὐσίαν τοιαύτην ἧς ἡ οὐσία ἐνέργεια (*dei ara einai ousian toiautēn hēs hē ousia energeia*)</note>. From this *theorem*, *Aristotle* indeed endeavors to establish the *eternity of the world*—arguing that it was not made "from night, from a chaotic heap of all things, and from non-existence" <note>original Greek: ἐκ νυκτὸς, καὶ ὁμοῦ πάντων, καὶ ἐκ μὴ ὄντος (*ek nyktos, kai homou pantōn, kai ek mē ontos*)</note>. That is, he argues it was not brought into being from a previous state of non-existence. Because God is an *Immovable Nature* whose *essence* is *activity*, he cannot be supposed to have rested or "slept" from eternity, doing nothing at all, and then, after infinite ages, to have begun to move matter or make the world. This reasoning of *Aristotle's* might not be inconsiderable if the *world*, *motion*, and *time* were capable of existing from *eternity* or without a beginning. We will discuss this more elsewhere. However, it is undeniably evident from this that *Aristotle*, though asserting the *world's eternity*, nevertheless derived that eternity from God, because he sought to prove it from the *essential activity* and *immutability* of the *Deity*.

<margin>Metaphysics, Book 14, Chapter 8</margin> We shall now conclude everything concerning *Aristotle* with this short summary that he himself gives us of his own creed and religion, in agreement with the *traditions of his pagan ancestors*:

"It has been handed down to us from very ancient times that the stars are gods also, and that the Divine encompasses the whole of nature. But the other stories were added later in the form of myths to persuade the multitude and for their usefulness to the laws and the public interest—to keep men in obedience to civil laws. For example, they say that these gods are of human form or resemble other animals, along with other things that follow from or are similar to these." <note>original Greek: παραδέδοται ὑπὸ τῶν ἀρχαίων καὶ παλαιῶν, ὅτι θεοί τέ εἰσιν οὗτοι, καὶ περιέχει τὸ θεῖον τὴν ὅλην φύσιν· τὰ δὲ λοιπὰ μυθικῶς ἤδη προσήχθαι πρὸς τὴν πειθὼ τῶν πολλῶν, καὶ τὴν εἰς τοὺς νόμους καὶ τὸ συμφέρον χρῆσιν· ἀνθρωποειδεῖς τε γὰρ τούτους καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ζώων ὁμοίους τισὶ λέγουσι, καὶ τούτοις ἕτερα ἀκόλουθα καὶ παραπλήσια (*paradedotai hypo tōn archaiōn...*)</note>

In these words of *Aristotle*, three things may be noticed. First, that it was the general persuasion of civilized pagans from all known antiquity downward that there is one *Divine Principle* <note>original Greek: τὸ θεῖον (*to theion*)</note> which comprehends the whole of nature. Here, *the Divine* is plainly used by *Aristotle* to mean the *Supreme Deity*. And his own opinion concerning this particular matter is elsewhere expressed thus...

Aristotle uses the concept of God's constant activity to argue for an eternal universe while acknowledging a single supreme "Divine" behind ancient myths.</summary>

### Speusippus and Xenocrates, Book I.

<margin>In Aristotle's *Politics*</margin>It is declared in this manner, where he speaks of Order, Harmony, and Proportion: "For this is the work of a divine power, which also holds this universe together" <note>original Greek: θείας γὰρ δὴ τοῦτο δυνάμεως ἔργον, ἥτις καὶ τόδε συνέχει τὸ πᾶν (*theias gar dē touto dynameōs ergon, hētis kai tode synechei to pan*)</note>. This Divinity, containing and comprehending the whole of Nature and the Universe, must necessarily be a single and solitary Being, according to that expression of Horace cited before:

->*Nothing flourishes that is like it or second to it.*<-
<note>original Latin: *Nec viget quicquam Simile aut Secundum*</note>

The next point is that, according to the *Pagan Tradition*, besides this *Universal Numen* <note>a divine power or spirit presiding over a place or thing</note>, there were certain other *particular* and *inferior deities* as well. These were *understanding beings superior to men*—namely, the *animated stars* or *spheres*, according to common belief. However, *Aristotle's philosophy* would interpret this chiefly as their *immovable minds* or *intelligences*. 

Lastly, all the rest of the *Pagan religion* and *theology*, with those *two things* only excepted, were *fabulous* and *fictitious*. They were invented to better persuade the common people to piety and to keep them in obedience to civil laws. Among these inventions we may count the idea that the gods are all like men or other *animals*, and therefore should be worshiped through images and statues of those various forms, along with all the other "fabulous farrago" <note>a confused mixture or hodgepodge</note> that depends on this. 

Once these fictions are separated from the rest, the *ancient tradition* <note>original Greek: πάτριος δόξα (*patrios doxa*)</note> of their *Pagan ancestors* remains comprised within those *two particulars* mentioned above: namely, that there is *one Supreme Deity that contains the whole universe*, and that besides it, the *animated stars* (or their *minds*) are certain *inferior gods* as well.

To *Aristotle* may be added *Speusippus* and *Xenocrates*, his equals and rivals, who were *Plato's* successors, along with *Theophrastus*, Aristotle's own scholar and successor. Regarding Speusippus, it is recorded in *Cicero* that, agreeing with *Plato*, he asserted: <margin>On the Nature of the Gods, Book 1.</margin> "A certain force by which all things are governed, and that a living one" <note>original Latin: *Vim quandam, quâ omnia regantur, eamque Animalem*</note>. Because of this, *Velleius* the *Epicurean* complains that Speusippus endeavors "to pluck the knowledge of the gods from the minds of men" <note>original Latin: *Evellere ex animis cognitionem Deorum*</note>. 

Indeed, both he and *Plato* did destroy those *Epicurean gods*, who were all supposed to be *independent* and to have no influence at all on the *government* of the world. However, neither of them denied a *plurality of subordinate and dependent deities*, who were *generated* or *created* by *one Supreme* God and employed by him as his ministers in the *management* <note>original: economy</note> of the *universe*. Had they denied such a thing, they would certainly have been condemned as *atheists* at that time. 

Finally, the theology of *Xenocrates* is represented by *Stobaeus* in this way: <margin>Physical Selections, Book 1, chapter 3.</margin> "The Monad and the Dyad are gods. The first, having the rank of a male father, he calls Zeus, the Odd, and Mind, which is his primary god. The second is like a mother of the gods, ruling over the realm below the heavens, which is to him..." <note>original Greek: τὴν μονάδα καὶ τὴν δυάδα θεὸς, τὴν μὲν ὡς ἀρῥένα πατρὸς ἔχουσαν τάξιν, ἥτινα προσαγορεύει καὶ Ζῆνα, καὶ Περιττὸν, καὶ Νοῦν, ὅστις ἐστὶν αὐτῷ πρῶτος θεός· τὴν δὲ θήλειαν μητρὸς θεῶν δίκην, τῆς ὑπὸ τὸν οὐρανὸν λήξεως ἡγεμένην, ἥτις ἐστὶν αὐτῷ... (*tēn monada kai tēn dyada theos...*)</note>

# CHAP. IV. and Theophrastus, Monarchists.

...the soul of the universe, etc. <note>original Greek: ψυχὴ τοῦ παντὸς (*psychē tou pantos*)</note> That both a **Monad** and **Dyad** were Gods: the one **Masculine**, having the rank of a **Father**, which he calls **Zen** <note>an ancient variant of the name Zeus</note> and **Mind**, and which is also to him the **First God**; the other **Feminine**, as it were the **Mother of the Gods**, which is to him the **Soul of the Universe**. Besides these, he acknowledges the **Heaven** to be **Divine**—that is, **animated** with a **particular soul** of its own—and the **Fiery Stars** to be **Celestial Gods**. He also asserted the existence of certain **Sublunary** <note>literally "under the moon"; referring to the earthly realm</note> **Gods**, namely the **Invisible Demons**. Where, instead of the **Platonic Trinity**, **Xenocrates** seems to have acknowledged only a **Duality** of **Divine Hypostases** <note>fundamental substances or persons of the Godhead</note>; the **First** called a **Monad** and **Mind**, the **Second** a **Dyad** and **Soul of the Universe**. And lastly, we have this testimony of **Theophrastus**, among others, cited from his *Metaphysics*: "For there is one divine principle of all things, through which everything both exists and remains." <note>original Greek: Θεία γὰρ πάντων ἀρχὴ, δι᾽ ἧς ἅπαντα καὶ ἔστι καὶ διαμένει (*Theia gar pantōn archē, di' hēs hapanta kai esti kai diamenei*)</note>

XXV. The **Stoics** and their chief **Doctors** <note>teachers or leading scholars</note>, **Zeno**, **Cleanthes**, and **Chrysippus**, were no better **Naturalists** and **Metaphysicians** than **Heraclitus**, whose footsteps they followed. In a similar way, they admitted no other **Substance** besides **Body** (matter), according to the true and proper **notion** of it—as that which is not only **Extended** <note>original Greek: διαστατὸν (*diastaton*)</note>, but also **Resisting** and **Impenetrable** <note>original Greek: ἀντίτυπον (*antitypon*)</note>. 

So, according to these **Stoics**, the **souls** not only of other **animals** but of **men** as well were properly **Corporeal**. That is, they were **substances impenetrably extended**. They differed from the other part of the person, commonly called the **Body**, only in that they were a **thinner and more subtle body** <note>original Greek: σῶμα ἀραιότερον καὶ λεπτομερέστερον (*sōma araioteron kai leptomeresteron*)</note>, and a **hot and fiery spirit** <note>original Greek: πνεῦμα ἔνθερμον (*pneuma enthermon*)</note>. These **philosophers** supposed that **thought**, **reason**, and **understanding** are located only in the **Fiery Matter** of the **Universe**. 

And though the **generality** of these **Stoics** acknowledged that **human souls** have a certain **permanency** after **death**—and some believed they lasted until the next **Conflagration** <note>the periodic destruction of the universe by fire in Stoic belief</note> (unless perhaps they should be crushed and broken all to pieces during their **passage** out of the **body** by the downfall of some **tower**, **steeple**, or the like upon them)—yet they all concluded against their **Immortality**. For they believed nothing at all was **Immortal** (as shall be declared later) except for **Jupiter**, or the **One Supreme Deity**. 

As for the **punishment** of **wicked souls** after death, some Stoics seem to have utterly rejected the idea as a mere **fiction** of **poets**. Indeed, **Epictetus** himself denies there was any **Acheron**, **Cocytus**, or **Phlegethon** <note>mythological rivers of the Greek underworld</note>. Yet others granted that while the better **souls** after **death** did mount up to the **stars**, their **first origin**, the **wicked** wandered up and down here in certain **dark** and **miry subterranean places**, until at length they were quite extinct. 

Nevertheless, they all seem to have held the persuasion that **frightening** people with punishments after **death** was not a **proper** or **suitable** means to promote **virtue**. They believed virtue ought to be pursued for its own sake, or for the **good** of **honesty**, just as **vice** is to be avoided for the **evil** of **turpitude** <note>depravity or wickedness</note> within it, and not for any other **external evil** that follows it. Therefore, **Chrysippus** reprehended **Plato** for adding such frightening <margin>Plutarch, *On Stoic Self-Contradictions*, page 1040.</margin> stories of punishments after death to his *Republic*. He says it is not right to deter people by means of the... <note>original Greek: φησὶν οὐκ ὀρθῶς ἀποτρέπειν τῷ ἀπὸ τῶν (*phēsin ouk orthōs apotrepein tō apo tōn*)</note>

<note>original catchword: θεῶν (gods)</note>
