# The Stoic Materialists; Book I.

...the fear of the gods, and of injustice, or Cephalus; that the account of punishments by God is easily misrepresented and leads many to opposite conclusions by distractions and conflicting probabilities, being no different from the stories of Akko and Alphito, which women use to stop children from being naughty. <note>original Greek: θεῶν φόβῳ, τ’ ἀδικίας, ἢ Κέφαλον · δυσδιάβλητον τ’ εἶναι καὶ πρὸς τἀναντίον ἐξάγοντα πολλοὺς περισπασμοὺς καὶ πιθανότητας ἀντιπιπτούσας, τὸν περὶ τῶν ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ κολάσεων λόγον, ὡς οὐδὲν διαφέροντα τῆς Ἀκκοῦς καὶ τῆς Ἀλφιτοῦς, δι’ ὧν τὰ παιδάρια τοῦ κακοσχολεῖν αἱ γυναῖκες ἀνέργουσι</note> *Chrysippus claims that* Plato *(speaking through the character Cephalus) does not correctly discourage men from injustice by using the fear of divine punishment and vengeance after death. He argues that this opinion (of torments after death) is open to many objections, and the opposite view is not without its own probabilities. Therefore, it seems to him like nothing more than women frightening children into behaving with those boogeymen Akko and Alphito.* <note>Akko and Alphito were nursery "bogeywomen" or spirits in Greek folklore used to scare children into obedience.</note> But how foolishly these Stoics doted upon the *hypothesis* that *everything is a body* is evident from the fact that they maintained even *accidents* <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is an attribute or quality that does not belong to the essential nature of a thing.</note> and *qualities* themselves were physical bodies. To them, *voice* and *sound*, *night* and *day*, *evening* and *morning*, *summer* and *winter*—and even *calendars*, *mid-month days*, *months*, and *years*—were all physical bodies. And not only that, but they even included the *qualities* of the mind itself, such as *virtue* and *vice*, along with its motions and feelings, like *anger*, *envy*, *grief*, and *joy*. This follows a passage in **Seneca**: "The goods of a body are themselves bodies; the mind is a body; therefore, the goods of the mind are bodies as well." <note>original Latin: *Corporis Bona sunt Corpora, Corpora ergo sunt & quæ animi, nam & hic Corpus est*</note> Using this same logic, they further inferred that all the *actions, passions*, and *qualities* of the *mind* were not only bodies but also *living animals*. "It is clear that the soul is an animal, since it is what makes us animals; now virtue is nothing other than the soul in a certain state, and therefore virtue is an animal too." <note>original Latin: *Animam constat Animal esse, cum ipsa efficiat, ut simus Animalia; Virtus autem nihil aliud est quàm Animus taliter se habens, ergo Animal est*</note> Thus we see what absurd conclusions these lovers of the body made (though they were considered great masters of logic) and how they were fooled in their reasoning and philosophy.

Nevertheless, even though these Stoics were such *foolish materialists*, they were not atheists because of it. They decided that the mind or *understanding*—though always housed in a *physical substance*—was not originally born out of *senseless matter* that had been modified in some way. Instead, they believed it was an *eternal, uncreated thing* and the creator of the entire world system. Therefore, regarding the controversy so debated among the ancients—whether the world was made by *chance*, by the *necessity of material motions*, or by *mind, reason, and understanding*—they openly maintained that it was created neither by chance nor by material necessity, but *by a divine and eternal mind that is perfect in every way*. <note>original Latin: *Divinâ Mente*</note> They also affirmed that human souls were derived from this one eternal mind, rather than from senseless matter. They held that "wisdom and mind descended to men from the gods." <note>original Latin: *Prudentiam & Mentem à Diis ad Homines pervenisse*</note> They also believed that "reason is nothing other than a part of the divine spirit immersed into a human body." <note>original Latin: *Ratio nihil aliud est, quàm in Corpus humanum Pars Divini Spiritus mersa*</note> Thus, to them, human souls were nothing other than "certain parts of God, or chips and fragments broken off from him." <note>original Greek: μόρια θεοῦ καὶ ἀποσπάσματα (*moria theou kai apospasmata*)</note> Neither were the reasons by which these...

# CHAP. IV. But not Atheists.

These Stoics would prove that the world had a **Divine Original** <note>origin</note> through arguments that are not at all contemptible, nor much inferior to those used in more recent times. Their reasoning included the following:

First, it is no more likely that this orderly system of the world was made by chance than that the *Annals* of Ennius <note>Quintus Ennius (c. 239–169 BCE) was a famous early Roman poet, often called the father of Roman poetry.</note> or Homer's *Iliad* could have resulted from the accidental projection or tumbling out of many different letters all mixed together. There is as much continued and coherent sense, and as many distinct combinations, in this **Real Poem** of the world as there is in any fanciful poem made by men. And since we see no houses or cities, no books or libraries, made anywhere by the accidental motions of matter, it is madness to think that this admirable complex structure of the whole world first resulted from such a cause.

Again, there could not possibly be such an agreeing and conspiring connection <note>original: "Cognation"</note> of things, and such a **Universal Harmony** throughout the whole world as there now is, **unless they were all contained by one and the same Divine Spirit** <note>original Latin: *nisi ea Uno Divino & Continuato Spiritu con-tinerentur*</note>. This is the most obvious argument for the unity or uniqueness of the Deity.

They also reasoned from the **Scale of Nature**, or the gradual perfection of things in the universe, ranked one above another. They argued that there must be something **Absolutely Perfect**, and that either the world itself, or something presiding over it, was **wise from the beginning** <note>original Latin: *à Principio Sapiens*</note>, or rather, wise without beginning and from eternity. For just as in the growth of plants and animals, **Nature, by its own particular path, arrives at last at the ultimate perfection** <note>original Latin: *Natura suo quodam Itinere ad Ultimum pervenit*</note> that those things are respectively capable of—and just as the arts of painting and architecture aim at perfection—**so in the nature of the whole universe, it is necessary for something to be finished and perfected.** <note>original Latin: *ita in omni Naturâ neceffe est Absolvi aliquid & Perfici*</note> **It is necessary that there be some excellent nature, than which nothing is better** <note>original Latin: *Neceffe est præstantem aliquam esse Naturam qua nihil est Melius*</note>. Since there is such a gradual ascent and scale of perfections in nature, one above another, there must necessarily be some most excellent and perfect being at the top of all, as its head, than which nothing can be better.

Moreover, they disputed in the Socratic manner as follows: **From where did man snatch life, mind, and reason?** <note>original Latin: *Unde arripuit Homo Vitam, Mentem & Rationem?*</note> Or from what was it kindled in him? For is it not plain that we derive the moisture and fluidity of our bodies from the water that is in the universe, their consistency and solidity from the earth, their heat and activity from the fire, and their airy quality <note>original: "Spirituosity"</note> from the air? **But that which far transcends all these things—reason, mind, and understanding—where did we find it? From where did we derive it? Does the universe possess all those other parts of ours in it, and in a far greater proportion, yet have nothing at all of that which is the most excellent thing in us?** <note>original Latin: *Illud autem quod vincit hæc omnia, Rationem, Mentem & Consilium, &c. Ubi invenimus? unde sustulimus? An cætera Mundus habebit omnia? Hoc unum quod plurimi est non habebit?*</note> **Nothing that is devoid of mind and reason can generate from itself living beings that possess reason; but the world generates living beings possessed of reason.** <note>original Latin: *Nihil quod Animi, quodque Rationis est expers, id generare ex se potest Animantes, compotesque Rationis, Mundus autem generat Animantes compotes Rationis*</note> Nothing that is [devoid of mind...]

living <note>original: "Animant"</note> and rational; but the world generates such beings, and therefore it itself (or that which contains it and presides over it) must necessarily be living, and rational or intellectual. This argumentation is further supported by such comparisons as these: *If musical pipes sounding harmoniously were produced from the olive tree, you would not doubt that there was some knowledge of flute-playing within the olive tree itself. What if plane trees bore lutes that played musically and in rhythm? You would surely think the same: that music existed within the plane trees. Why, therefore, should the world not be judged to be living and wise, since it produces living and wise beings from itself?* <note>original Latin: "Si ex Oliva modulatè canentes Tibiæ naſcerentur, non dubitares quin eſſet in Oliva Tibicinis quædam Scientia. Quid ſi Platani Fidiculas ferrent numeroſè ſonantes, idem ſcilicet cenſeres in Platanis ineſſe Muſicam. Cur igitur Mundus non Animans Sapienſque judicetur, cum ex ſe procreet Animantes atque Sapientes?"</note> 

And though perhaps some may think the response of Cotta <note>Gaius Aurelius Cotta, a character in Cicero’s *On the Nature of the Gods*, representing the Academic Skeptic viewpoint.</note> here to have been a smart and witty retort: *Socrates asks where we snatched our souls from, if there were none in the world? And I ask, where did we snatch speech? Where did we get numbers? Where did we get songs? Unless, of course, we think the sun talks with the moon when he approaches near her in the alignments <note>original: "Syzygiæ," referring to the straight-line configuration of three celestial bodies in a gravitational system</note>; or that the world sings harmoniously, as Pythagoras imagined.* <note>original Latin: "Quærit Socrates unde Animam arripuerimus, ſi nulla fuerit in mundo? Et ego quæro unde Orationem? unde Numeros? unde Cantus? niſi verò loqui Solem cum Luna putemus, cum propius acceſſerit: aut ad harmoniam canere Mundum ut Pythagoras exiſtimat."</note> Yet this, however smart it may seem, was really but an empty flash of Academic wit <note>The "Academic" school of philosophy was known for its skepticism and habit of arguing against all settled dogmas.</note> without any solidity at all in it, as shall be shown afterward.

Lastly, the Stoics endeavored to prove the existence of a God in this manner: *Just as there is no part of our body which is not inferior to ourselves, so the entire universe must necessarily be of greater value than any part of the universe.* <note>original Latin: "Ut nulla pars Corporis noſtri eſt quæ non ſit minor quam Noſmetipſi ſumus, ſic Mundum Univerſum pluris eſſe neceſſe eſt quam Partem aliquam Univerſi."</note> Therefore, since it is better to be endowed with life and understanding than to be devoid of them, and these are pure perfections, because they exist in some measure in the parts, they must necessarily be much more in the whole. *No part of a thing that lacks all sensation can be sentient* <note>original Latin: "Nullius ſenſu carentis Pars, poteſt eſſe Sentiens."</note>; that is, no part of that which is utterly dead and senseless can have life and understanding in it. And it is a madness for any man to suppose *that there is nothing in the whole world better than himself* <note>original Latin: "Nihil in omni Mundo Melius eſſe quam ſe"</note>, or than mankind, which is but a part of it. 

Now Cotta here again exercises his jeering Academic wit in the same manner as before: *If this pleases you, you will soon conclude that the world is very good at reading books, and so on. In that way, the world will also be eloquent, a mathematician, a musician, filled with every kind of learning, and finally, the world will be a philosopher.* <note>original Latin: "Hoc ſi placet, jam effici-es, ut Mundus optimè Librum legere videatur, &c. Iſto modo etiam Diſertus, Mathematicus, Muſicus, omni denique doctrina refertus, po-ſtremo Philoſophus erit Mundus."</note> But neither this objection of his nor that former one has any strength <note>original: "firmitude"</note> at all in them. This is because although an *effect* cannot be better or more perfect than its *cause*, nor a *part* than the *whole*; and therefore whatever there is

# CHAPTER IV. Arguments for a God.

If there is *pure perfection* in any *effect*, it must necessarily exist even more in the *cause*. Regarding those things mentioned there by *Cotta* (which all have a plain mixture of imperfection in them), although they could not exist *formally* <note>meaning: in the same outward form or structure</note> in that which is *absolutely perfect*, it is sufficient that they are all *eminently* <note>meaning: in a higher or more excellent way</note> and *virtually* <note>meaning: through its inherent power</note> contained within it.

By such arguments as these (in addition to those taken from the topic of foreknowledge and divination), the ancient *Stoics* endeavored to demonstrate the existence of a God, or a *Universal Numen* <note>original: "Numen," meaning a divine power or spirit</note>, the Maker and Governor of the whole world. They argued that such a being was not a mere *plastic* <note>meaning: a mindless formative or molding force</note> or *methodical* and *senseless* force, but a *conscious* and *perfectly intellectual nature*. So, to them, the world was neither a mere *heap* and *collection* <note>original: "congeries"</note> of dead and *stupid matter* accidentally joined together, nor was it a *huge plant* or *vegetable*—that is, something endowed only with a *spermatic principle* <note>meaning: a basic biological or reproductive force</note>. Instead, it was *an animal* shaped and enlivened by an *intellectual soul*. Although they were *corporealists* <note>philosophers who believe everything, including the soul, is made of matter</note> and sometimes called the *whole world* itself (the *mundane animal*) "*God*," and sometimes the *fiery principle* within it (the *intellectual* and *ruling part* <note>original: "Hegemonick"</note> of the *mundane soul*), the God of the *Stoics* was properly not the *matter* itself. Rather, it was that *great soul*, *mind*, and *understanding*—or, in *Seneca's* language, that *incorporeal reason* <note>original Latin: "Ratio Incorporalis"</note>—that rules the matter of the whole world. This *Stoic God* was also called "the Good" as well as "Mind" <note>original Greek: "τ'ἀγαθὸν" (t'agathon) and "νοῦς" (nous)</note>, as a being that is *most moral, benign, and beneficent*, according to this excellent description of him by *Cleanthes* found in *Clement of Alexandria*:

> ->You ask me what the Good is like? Listen then:<-
> ->Orderly, just, holy, pious,<-
> ->self-governing, useful, beautiful, proper, etc.<-
<note>original Greek: "τ'ἀγαθὸν ἐρωτᾷς μ' οἷόν ἐστι ἄκουε δή, τεταγμένον, δίκαιον, ὅσιον, εὐσεβὲς, κρατῶν ἑαυτοῦ, χρήσιμον, καλὸν, δέον, &c."</note>

<margin>Plutarch, *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*, page 425.</margin>But this Maker and Governor of the whole world was most commonly named by the Stoics *Zeus* and *Zen*, or *Jupiter*. Some of them concluded that there was only one *Zeus* or *independent deity* because the whole world was only *one animal* governed by *one soul*. Others, on the contrary, endeavored to prove the *unity* and *singularity* of the world from the oneness of this *Zeus* (the *supreme deity*), which they took for granted, and because there is *but one fate and providence*. Plutarch, however, would by no means allow this latter conclusion. He wrote the following while pleading for a plurality of worlds: "Who would fear the other arguments of the Stoics, when they ask how there can remain one fate and one providence, and why there will not be many Joves and Zeus’s if there are many worlds? <note>original Greek: "τὰ δ' ἄλλα τῶν Στωικῶν τίς ἂν φοβηθείη, πυνθανομένων πῶς εἱμαρμένη μία μένει καὶ πρόνοια, καὶ οὐ πολλοὶ Δίες καὶ Ζῆνες ἔσονται, πλειόνων ὄντων κόσμων;"</note> For what necessity is there that there must be more Zeus’s than one, if there were more worlds? And why might not that one and the same God of this..."

# The Stoics acknowledged only one God BOOK I.

"*Could the universe, which we call the Lord and Father of all, be the First Prince and Highest Governor in all those worlds? Or what hinders a multitude of worlds from being all subject to the Fate and Providence of one Jupiter or Supreme God, himself inspecting and ordering every one of them? Could he not impart principles and spermatic reasons <note>original: "spermatick reasons," the formative or reproductive principles that organize matter</note> to them, according to which all things might be governed and disposed? For if many distinct persons in an army or a chorus can be reduced into one body or polity <note>meaning: an organized society or system</note>, could not ten, or fifty, or a hundred worlds in the universe all be governed by one Reason, and be ordered together in reference to one principle?*" In this passage, these two things are plainly contained: *First*, that the *Stoics* unquestionably asserted one Supreme Deity, or *Universal Monarch*, over the whole world; and *secondly*, that *Plutarch* was so far from accepting the contrary opinion that he concluded that even if there were *ten*, or *fifty*, or a *hundred worlds*, they would all still be subject to *one supreme, solitary, and independent Deity.*

However, although these *Stoics* unquestionably asserted one sole independent and *Universal Numen* <note>meaning: a divine power or spirit</note> as the Monarch over the whole world, they nevertheless—along with other Pagans—acknowledged a *plurality of gods*. They concluded, "*That all things were full of gods and demons*" <note>original Greek: πάντα μεσὰ εἶναι θεῶν καὶ δαιμόνων</note>. And so far were they from falling short of the other Pagans regarding this polytheism or multiplicity of gods, they seem rather to have surpassed and outstripped them in it. *Plutarch* mentions their "*so great a multitude of gods*" <note>original Greek: τοσοῦτον πλῆθος θεῶν</note> and affirms that they "*filled the whole heaven, earth, air, and sea with gods*" <note>original Greek: ἐμπεπληκέναι τῷ λόγῳ θεῶν τὸν οὐρανὸν, τὴν γῆν, καὶ ἀέρα, τὴν θάλασσαν</note>. Nevertheless, they plainly declare that all this multiplicity of gods (*except for one*) was *generated* or *created* in time by that *one*, called *Zeus* or *Jupiter*. He was not only the *spermatic reason*, but also the *soul* and *mind* of the whole *universe*; he produced the world and those gods out of non-existence into being. And not only that, but they also believe that in the <term>successive conflagrations</term> <note>the periodic destruction and renewal of the universe by fire, a central Stoic doctrine</note>, these gods are all again resolved and swallowed up into that *one.*

<margin>Page 420.</margin>

Thus *Plutarch*, in his work *On the Defect of Oracles*, writing about the *mortality of demons*, states: "*We know the Stoics to maintain this opinion, not only concerning demons, but also the gods themselves, that they are mortal. For though they own such a multitude of gods, yet do they acknowledge only one of them eternal and incorruptible; affirming concerning all the rest, that as they were made in time, so they shall be again corrupted and destroyed*" <note>original Greek: τοὺς Στωικὸς γινώσκομεν, οὐ μόνον περὶ δαιμόνων τὴν αὐτὴν δόξαν ἔχοντας, ἀλλὰ καὶ θεῶν, ὄντων τοσοῦτον τὸ πλῆθος· ἑνὶ χρωμένους ἀϊδίῳ καὶ ἀφθάρτῳ, τοὺς δ' ἄλλους καὶ γεγονέναι καὶ φθαρήσεσθαι νομίζοντας</note>. *Plutarch* himself defends the mortality of demons there, but only regarding their corporeal part—meaning they die to their present bodies and migrate into others, while their souls remain immortal and incorruptible. But the *Stoics* maintained the same regarding both *gods* and *demons*, and in such a manner that their very souls, lives, and personalities would be utterly extinguished and destroyed. ### CHAPTER IV. One Eternal and Immortal God.

For this purpose, Plutarch writes again in his book *Common Notions against the Stoics* <margin>Page 1075.</margin> <note>original Greek: χρύσιππος καὶ κλεάνθης ἐμπεπληκότες... πλὴν μόνον τοῦ Διός· εἰς ὃν πάντας καταναλίσκουσι τοὺς ἄλλους, etc.</note>: "Chrysippus and Cleanthes, having filled (so to speak) the whole heaven, earth, air, and sea with gods, leave not even one of these many gods incorruptible or eternal, except for Jupiter alone. They consume all the others into him; thereby making him a *helluo* <term>helluo: a glutton or devourer</term> and devourer of gods. This is as bad as if they should affirm him to be corruptible, as it implies as much imperfection for one to be nourished and preserved by the consumption of other things into himself as for himself to die." 

Now, this is not only gathered as a consequence of other Stoic principles, but it is something they expressly assert and loudly proclaim in all their writings concerning the gods, providence, fate, and nature: <note>original Greek: ταῦτα δὲ οὐχ ὡς ἄλλα πολλὰ... διαῤῥήδην λέγουσι, τοὺς θεοὺς ἅπαντας, εἶναι γεγονότας καὶ φθαρσομένους ὑπὸ πυρὸς... ὥσπερ κηρίνους ἢ καττιτερίνους ὄντας</note> that all the gods were generated (created in time) and that they shall all be destroyed by fire. They suppose them to be "meltable," as if they were objects made of wax or tin. This indeed is essential to the Stoic doctrine and inseparable from their principles, because they held that everything is *body* <note>meaning: material or physical substance</note>. They believed that in the successive universal fires (conflagrations), all physical systems and structures <term>compages: a complex structure or framework</term> shall be dissolved by fire. Consequently, no other deity can possibly remain safe and untouched except Jupiter alone, the fiery principle of the universe, who is *animated* or *intellectual*. 

There is a significant difference to observe here between these Stoics and other Pagan theists. While others for the most part acknowledged that their gods were created in time by *one supreme universal Numen* <note>Numen: a divine power or spirit</note>, yet still believed them to be *immortal* and eternal, the Stoic Pagans maintained that all their other gods—except Jupiter alone—were not only created <note>original: γεγονότες (gegonotes)</note> but also corruptible <note>original: φθαρσόμενοι (phtharsomenoi)</note>. They believed these gods would be destroyed just as they were created, so much so that their very personalities would be utterly abolished and annihilated. In the universal fire, all the Stoic gods would be, as it were, melted and merged into *one*.

Therefore, during the intervals between the successive universal fires, the Stoics all agreed that there is no more than *one God* (*Zeus* or *Jupiter*) left alone. At that time, indeed, nothing else exists besides himself. He afterwards produces the entire *mundane system* <note>meaning: the physical world</note>, together with *all the gods*, out of himself again. Chrysippus, as quoted in Plutarch, <margin>Page 1077.</margin> <note>original Greek: ἐοικέναι τῷ μὲν ἀνθρώπῳ τὸν Δία καὶ τὸν κόσμον... διατελεῖν ἀμφοτέρους</note> affirms: "That just as Jupiter and the world may be compared to a man, so may providence be compared to the soul. When, therefore, there is a universal fire, Jupiter—the only incorruptible one among the gods—will remain and withdraw himself..."

It specifically describes the "conflagration"—a periodic fire that consumes the universe—during which all lesser gods are merged back into Jupiter, leaving him alone in self-reflection until the next cycle of creation begins.</meta>

<header>The Stoics Worshipped, Book I.</header>

...into *Providence*; *and so both together remain in that same Ethereal Substance*. However, *Jupiter* and *Providence* are really but *one* and the same thing. And *Seneca* writes as follows concerning the life of a wise man in solitude: <margin>Epistle 6.</margin> <note>original: "Qualis futura est Vita Sapientis, si sine amicis relinquatur, in custodiam conjectus, aut in desertum littus ejectus? Qualis est Jovis, cum Resoluto mundo, & DIIS IN UNUM CONFUSIS, paulisper cessante Natura, acquiescit sibi, Cogitationibus suis traditus"</note> "If you ask what the life of a wise man would be like in either a prison or a desert, I answer: it is the same as that of *Jupiter* when, after the world is dissolved and the GODS ARE ALL MERGED INTO ONE, and the course of Nature ceases for a while, he rests in himself, devoted to his own thoughts." 

Arrian’s *Epictetus* likewise, speaking of the same thing, ironically introduces *Jupiter* bemoaning himself during the universal fire as now being left quite alone, in this manner: <margin>Arrian Book 3, Chapter 13.</margin> <note>original Greek: τάλας ἐγὼ, οὔτε τὴν Ἥραν ἔχω, οὔτε τὴν Ἀθηνᾶν, οὔτε τὸν Ἀπόλλωνα, οὔτε ὅλως ἢ ἀδελφὸν, ἢ υἱὸν, ἢ ἔγγονον, ἢ συγγενῆ</note> *"Alas, I am now left all alone; I have neither Juno, nor Minerva, nor Apollo with me; neither brother nor son, nor nephew nor kinsman (neither god nor goddess) to keep me company."* He also adds, according to the thinking of the Stoics, that in all these successive universal fires, <note>original Greek: ὁ Ζεὺς αὐτὸς ἑαυτῷ σύνεσι, καὶ ἡσυχάζει ἐφ᾿ ἑαυτῷ, καὶ ἐννοεῖ τὴν διοίκησιν ἑαυτοῦ, οἵα ἐστὶ, καὶ ἐν ἐπινοίαις γίνεται πρεπούσαις ἑαυτῷ</note> "Jupiter, being left alone, converses only with himself, and rests in himself, considering his own government—what it is like—and is entertained with thoughts worthy of himself." 

Thus, we have made it unquestionably evident that the Stoics acknowledged only *one independent* and *self-existent deity*, *one universal Numen* <term>Numen: divine power or spirit</term>, who was not only the *creator* of all the other gods, but also, in certain alternating cycles of time, the *un-creator* of them. He then swallows them up and devours them all into himself, just as he had previously produced them (along with the world) out of himself.

---

It is granted that these Stoics, as well as other *pagans*, did *religiously worship more gods than one*—that is, *more intelligent beings superior to men*. For it was *Epictetus's* own exhortation: <note>original Greek: Εὐχου θεοῖς</note> "Pray to the gods." And the same philosopher describes the disposition of a rightly-minded person this way: <note>original Greek: θέλω εἰδέναι τί μοι καθῆκον πρὸς τοὺς θεούς</note> "I would willingly know what is my duty, first to the gods, and then to my parents and other relations." 

And these are *Marcus Antoninus's* <note>Known today as Marcus Aurelius</note> precepts: <note>original Greek: Αἰδοῦ θεὸς</note> "Revere the gods," and <note>original Greek: ἐν ἅπασι θεοὺς ἐπικαλοῦ</note> "In everything implore the aid and assistance of the gods." Accordingly, in the conclusion of his first book, he thankfully ascribes many particular benefits to *the gods* in common: <note>original Greek: παρὰ τῶν θεῶν τὸ ἀγαθὸς πάππος, &c.</note> "I owe to the gods that I had good ancestors and parents, etc." Among the rest, he reckons this as one: that he never was very skilled in either poetry or rhetoric. He believed these would probably have hindered him from attaining far better things had he succeeded in pursuing them. After his entire list, he concludes: <note>original Greek: πάντα γὰρ ταῦτα θεῶν βοηθῶν καὶ τύχης δεῖται</note> "For all these things need the assistance of the gods and fortune"—namely, because they are not in our own power.

Despite this underlying monotheism, the text notes that prominent Stoics like Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius still practiced and encouraged the religious worship of multiple gods as superior beings.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the Stoic conception of divinity, moving from the idea of the universal conflagration (where all gods merge into one) to how the Stoics used the terms "God" and "the Gods" interchangeably while still maintaining a belief in a single Supreme Being who governs the universe.</meta>

### CHAPTER IV: Their Inferior Gods

It also cannot be denied that they often detracted from the honor of the **Supreme God** by attributing things to the **Gods** in common (as the givers of them) which plainly belong to the **Supreme God** alone. For instance, when **Epictetus** <margin>Book 3, chapter 24</margin> describes **Reason** in men as a gift of the **Gods**: "Is Reason therefore given to us by the Gods merely to make us miserable and unhappy?" <note>original Greek: ἡμῖν ἐν λόγῳ· ἐπὶ ἀτυχίᾳ καὶ κακοδαιμονίᾳ δέδοται ὑπὸ τῶν Θεῶν;</note> And when he again attributes **Virtue** to them: "Have you overcome your lust, your intemperance, your **anger**? <margin>Book 4, chapter 3</margin> How much greater cause then do you have to offer sacrifice than if you had obtained a consulship or a governorship? For those things come only from yourself and from the Gods." <note>original Greek: πόσῳ μείζων αἰτία θυσίας, ἢ ὑπατεία ἢ ὑπαρχία, ταῦτα ἐκ τοῦ αὐτοῦ γίνεται καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν Θεῶν</note>

Though the reason for these speeches of theirs seems to be no other than this: they took it for granted that those understanding beings superior to men, whom they called **Gods**, were all instruments and ministers of the Supreme God in the government of the world. Therefore, they believed these beings had some kind of impact or influence, more or less, upon all the concerns of mankind. Because of this, they often used the words **God** and **Gods** interchangeably and without distinction. For example, the same celebrated speech of **Socrates** is sometimes expressed in the singular: "If it is pleasing to God in this way, let it be so," <note>original Greek: εἰ ταύτῃ τῷ Θεῷ φίλον</note> (*Arrian's Epictetus* Book 1, chapter 29 and Book 4, chapter 4) and sometimes again in the plural: "If it is pleasing to the Gods in this way." <note>original Greek: εἰ ταύτῃ φίλον τοῖς Θεοῖς</note>

Therefore, despite the **many gods** of those Stoics, they worshipped, for all that, **One Supreme Being**—that is, **One Universal <term>Numen</term>** <note>original: "Numen"; a Latin term for divine power or a presiding spirit</note> that contains and comprehends the whole world. He was described by them in various ways: sometimes as the nature and reason of the whole world—"The nature of the <margin>Antoninus, Book 9</margin> whole, the oldest of all the gods," <note>original Greek: ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις πρεσβυτάτη θεῶν</note> and "That nature which governs all things"; <margin>Antoninus, Book 7, section 18</margin> <note>original Greek: ἡ τὰ ὅλα διοικοῦσα φύσις</note> "that Reason which governs the substance of all"; <margin>Antoninus, Book 6, section 1</margin> <note>original Greek: ὁ τὴν τῶν ὅλων οὐσίαν διοικῶν λόγος</note> and <margin>Antoninus, Book 5, section 24</margin> "that Reason which passes through the substance of the universe and, through all eternity, orders and manages the whole according to appointed periods." <note>original Greek: ὁ διὰ τῆς οὐσίας διήκων λόγος, καὶ διὰ παντὸς τοῦ αἰῶνος κατὰ περιόδους τεταγμένας οἰκονομῶν τὸ πᾶν</note>

Sometimes he is called "the cause of all things"; <margin>Antoninus, Book 9</margin> <note>original Greek: ἡ τῶν ὅλων αἰτία</note> sometimes "the <term>Hegemonick</term> <note>original: "Hegemonick"; from the Greek "hegemonikon," referring to the "ruling part" or commanding faculty of the soul or the universe</note> and ruling principle <margin>Antoninus, Book 7, section 47</margin> of the whole world," <note>original Greek: τὸ τοῦ κόσμου ἡγεμονικόν</note> and "the Prince of the world." <note>original Greek: ὁ ἡγεμὼν τοῦ κόσμου</note> Again, he is "the Governor of the Whole," as in this passage from **Epictetus**: <margin>Book 1, chapter 12</margin> "A good man submits his mind to the Governor of the whole universe, just as good citizens submit theirs to the law of the city." <note>original Greek: ὁ καλὸς καὶ ἀγαθὸς τὴν αὑτοῦ γνώμην ὑποτέταχε τῷ διοικοῦντι τὰ ὅλα, καθάπερ οἱ ἀγαθοὶ πολῖται νόμῳ τῆς πόλεως</note> He is also called "the Orderer of all" in this other religious passage by the same philosopher: <margin>Epictetus, p. 119, Cambridge edition</margin> "To be instructed is to want things to be exactly as they happen. And how do they happen? As that Great Disposer of all has appointed them." <note>original Greek: τὸ παιδεύεσθαι, τουτέστι μανθάνειν ἕκαστα οὕτω θέλειν ὡς γίνεται· πῶς δὲ γίνεται; ὡς διέταξεν αὐτὰ ὁ διατάσσων</note> Again, the Supreme God is sometimes called by them "that intellectual principle which contains the whole," as in this instruction by Marcus Antoninus.

It provides numerous examples of how they used titles like "Nature," "Reason," and "Disposer" to describe the single divine force ruling the universe.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Stoic view of the divine, transitioning from the concept of God as a universal fire to the Stoics' more personal and philosophical descriptions of a Supreme Mind that governs and permeates the universe.</meta>

<header>The Stoics honored, Book 1.</header>

<margin>Marcus Aurelius, Book 8, Section 45.</margin> **Marcus Aurelius** <note>original: "M. Antoninus"</note> says that we should **"not only breathe with the surrounding air, but also think with the Mind that surrounds all things."** <note>original Greek: μὴ μόνον συμπνεῖν τῷ περιέχοντι ἀέρι, ἀλλὰ καὶ συμφρονεῖν τῷ περιέχοντι πάντα νοερῷ</note> He means **"that as our bodies breathe the common air, so should our souls suck and draw in vital breath from that Great Mind that encompasses the Universe, becoming, as it were, one spirit with the same."** He is also called by them <margin>Marcus Aurelius, page 125.</margin> **"the Mind and Understanding of the whole world,"** <note>original Greek: ὁ τοῦ ὅλου νοῦς καὶ διάνοια</note> <margin>Marcus Aurelius, page 257.</margin> **"the one intellectual fountain of all things,"** <note>original Greek: μία πάντων πηγὴ νοερά</note> and lastly, to name no more, <margin>Marcus Aurelius, Book 7, Section 7.</margin> **"One God through all, one substance, and one law."** <note>original Greek: Θεὸς εἷς διὰ πάντων, καὶ οὐσία μία, καὶ νόμος εἷς</note>

This Supreme God was also commonly called by the Stoics—along with the majority of other Pagans—**"God,"** <note>original Greek: ὁ Θεὸς</note> emphatically and as a title of excellence. We see this in the words of **Epictetus**: **"Want nothing but what God wants, and then who will be able to hinder you?"** <note>original Greek: μηδὲν ἄλλο θέλε, ἢ ἃ ὁ Θεὸς θέλει, καὶ τίς σε κωλύσει;</note> <margin>Book 2, chapter 18.</margin> And again: **"Strive to appear beautiful to God; desire to be pure with your pure self and with God."** <note>original Greek: Θέλησον καλὸς φανῆναι τῷ Θεῷ, ἐπιθύμησον καθαρὸς μετὰ καθαροῦ σαυτοῦ γενέσθαι καὶ μετὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ</note> Also, where he speaks of the regular course of things in Nature: **"That it proceeds orderly, everything as it were obeying the command of God; when he bids the plants to blossom, they blossom; and when he bids them to sprout, they sprout."** <note>original Greek: τεταγμένως, καθάπερ ἐκ προστάγματος Θεοῦ, ὅταν ἐκεῖνος εἴπῃ τοῖς φυτοῖς ἀνθεῖν ἀνθεῖ, ὅταν εἴπῃ βλαστάνειν βλαστάνει</note> Innumerable other instances could be added to these.

**Zeus** or **Jupiter** was the proper name of this **Supreme God** among the Stoics as well; because of this, they call the government of the whole world <margin>Epictetus, page 251.</margin> **"the government or management of Zeus."** <note>original Greek: Διὸς διοίκησις</note> Finally, this Supreme God is sometimes explicitly distinguished by them from the other **gods** <margin>Book 4, chapter 12.</margin> by name, as in this quote from **Epictetus**: **"I have someone whom I ought to be subject to, whom I must obey: God and those who come after him,"** <note>original Greek: ἐγὼ δ’ ἔχω τίνι ὑποτέταχθαι, τίνι πείθεσθαι, τῷ Θεῷ καὶ τοῖς μετ’ ἐκεῖνον</note> meaning the Supreme and the inferior gods. Likewise, where he encourages us not to desire things outside of our own power: **"But leave those things to Zeus, and hand them over to the other gods; let them govern and direct them."** <note>original Greek: ἀλλὰ τῷ Διὶ χάρισαι αὐτὰ, καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις θεοῖς, ἐκείνοις παράδος, ἐκεῖνοι κυβερνάτωσαν</note> <margin>Book 2, chapter 17.</margin> And so again, where he speaks in the character of someone who places his happiness in things outside of his control: **"I shall then sit lamenting and speaking evil of everyone, even Zeus himself and the other gods."** <note>original Greek: κάθημαι καὶ στένω, καὶ ὃν δύναμαι λοιδορῶ, τὸν Δία καὶ τοὺς θεοὺς ἄλλους</note>

It must be reasonably assumed that this **Jupiter**, or the **Universal Divine Power** <note>original: "Universal Numen"</note> of the world, was honored by these Stoics far above all their other **particular gods**. They acknowledged him as the maker or creator of those gods as well as the whole world, and as the only eternal and immortal God. All those other gods, as has already been stated, were considered by the Stoics to be perishable, mortal, and capable of being destroyed, just as they were once generated or created.

For although **Cicero's** character **Lucilius Balbus**, while pretending to represent the doctrine of <margin>On the Nature of the Gods, Book 2, page 225, Lambin edition.</margin> the Stoics, attributes the very first origin of the world to a plurality of gods in these words: **"I say therefore that by the Providence of the Gods, the World and all parts of the World were both established in the beginning and are at all times governed,"** <note>original Latin: Dico igitur Providentiâ Deorum, Mundum & omnes Mundi partes, & initio constitutas esse, & omni tempore administrari</note> yet undoubtedly Cicero forgot himself in this...

<summary>This page explores the Stoic concept of a Supreme Being, often identified as Zeus or the Universal Mind, who is the creator and governor of both the universe and the lesser, mortal gods. Through the writings of Marcus Aurelius and Epictetus, it emphasizes that while the Stoics used the term "gods" in the plural, they maintained a clear hierarchy with one eternal, supreme intellect at the top.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that Stoic philosophy, despite its mention of multiple gods, ultimately centers on a single Supreme Deity (Jupiter) who creates and reabsorbs all other entities during the periodic destruction and renewal of the universe.</meta>

<header>### CHAPTER IV. The Supreme God above all.</header>

...and he spoke the language of some other pagans, who—together with the generation of the world—held a plurality of eternal (though not independent) deities, rather than that of the Stoics. The Stoics asserted only one eternal God, and supposed that in the repeated universal fires <note>original: "reiterated conflagrations"; the Stoic belief that the universe is periodically destroyed by fire and then reborn</note>, all the gods are melted and blended into one. Thus Jupiter, being then left alone, must necessarily recreate the world again, as well as all those other gods, out of himself. 

And thus does Zeno, as recorded in Laertius <note>Diogenes Laertius, a 3rd-century biographer of Greek philosophers</note>, describe the **creation of the world** <note>original Greek: cosmopœia</note>: **"God at first, being alone by himself,"** <note>original Greek: τὸν Θεὸν κατ' ἀρχὰς, καθ' αὑτὸν ὄντα</note> **"converted the fiery substance of the world by degrees into water—that is, into a denser chaos. Out of this water, he himself afterwards—as the seminal reason of the world—formed the elements and the whole system of the universe."** <note>original: "Spermatick Reason"; the logos or organizing principle that acts like a seed to develop the universe</note> 

And **Cicero** himself elsewhere, in his *On the Laws*, cautiously attributes the first origin of mankind not to the gods in common, but to the Supreme God only: **"This provident animal... whom we call Man, was generated in a noble condition by the SUPREME GOD."** <note>original Latin: "Hoc Animal Providum, &c. quem vocamus Hominem, præclara quadam conditione Generatum esse, à SUMMO DEO"</note> This is stated more according to the sense of the Stoics than the Platonists, whose "inferior generated gods" (having been made first) were supposed to have had a hand in the **crafting** <note>original: "fabrefaction"</note> of mankind and other animals.

Thus **Epictetus** plainly ascribes the making of the whole world to **God**, or the **One Supreme Deity**, where he mentions the "Galileans" (that is, the Christians) and their contempt for death—though he attributes it only to habit in them, and not to right knowledge. <margin>Book 4, chapter 7.</margin> (Similarly, **Marcus Aurelius** <note>original: M. Antoninus</note> ascribes the same to **"mere obstinacy of mind"**) <note>original Greek: ψιλὴ παραταξις</note>. <margin>Book 11, Section 3.</margin> **"Can some be so affected out of madness, and the Galileans out of habit? And can no one learn through reason and demonstration that God made all things in the world, and the whole world itself, perfect and unhindered; but the parts thereof for the use of the whole, so that the parts ought therefore to yield and give place to the whole?"** <note>original Greek: ὑπὸ μανίας μὲν δύναταί τις οὕτω διατεθῆναι, καὶ ὑπὸ ἔθος οἱ γαλιλαῖοι, ὑπὸ λόγῳ δὲ καὶ ἀποδείξεως οὐδεὶς δύναται μαθεῖν, ὅτι ὁ Θεὸς πάντα πεποίηκε τὰ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ, καὶ αὐτὸν τὸν κόσμον</note> 

Thus does he again elsewhere ask: **"Who made the sun?"** <note>original Greek: τὸν ἥλιον τίς πεποίηκε</note> **"Who made the fruits of the earth? Who the seasons of the year? Who the agreeable fitness of things? Why, then, having received all from another—even your very self—do you murmur and complain against the giver of them if he takes away any one thing from you? Did he not bring you into the world? Show you the light? Bestow sense and reason upon you?"** Now, since the sun was the chief of the inferior Stoic gods, and he was made by another, all the rest of their gods must necessarily be so too. 

And this is plainly expressed in the following citation: <margin>Book 1, chapter 3.</margin> **"If anyone could be thoroughly sensible of this—that we are all made by God as principal parts of the world, and that God is the father both of men and gods—he would never think meanly of himself, knowing that he is the son of Jupiter also."** <note>original Greek: εἴ τις τῷ δόγματι τούτῳ συμπαθῆσαι κατ' ἀξίαν δύναιτο, ὅτι γεγόναμεν ὑπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ πάντες προηγουμένως, καὶ ὁ Θεὸς πατήρ ἐστι τῶν τ' ἀνθρώπων καὶ τῶν Θεῶν, οὐδὲν ἀγεννὲς, οὐδὲ ταπεινὸν ἐνθυμηθήσεται περὶ ἑαυτοῦ</note> Here "God" <note>original Greek: Theos</note> is clearly used for the Supreme God, and "gods" <note>original Greek: theoi</note> for the inferior gods only. Again, he attributes the making of man and the government of the whole world to God or **Jupiter** only: **"God [made] all..."**

<summary>This page discusses the Stoic belief in a single Supreme Creator (Jupiter) who periodically reabsorbs all other gods into himself and recreates the universe from his own substance. It cites Zeno, Cicero, and Epictetus to demonstrate that while the Stoics spoke of multiple gods, they viewed them as created beings subordinate to one eternal, supreme deity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that the Stoics, despite their complex theology, ultimately viewed the universe as governed by a single, benevolent Supreme God to whom they owed total devotion.</meta>

<header>The Stoics' Devotion, BOOK I.</header>

<margin>Book 3, chapter 24.</margin>
<note>original Greek: τὰς ἀνθρώπȣς ἐπὶ τὸ εὐδαιμονεῖν ἐποίησε, &c.</note> **"God made all people for this purpose: that they might be happy. As was fitting for one who had a fatherly care for us, he placed our good and evil in those things which are within our own power."** And <margin>Book 3, chapter 24.</margin> <note>original Greek: τῷ ὄντι κακῶς διοικεῖται τὰ ὅλα, εἰ μὴ ἐπιμελεῖται ὁ Ζεὺς τῶν ἑαυτῶ πολιτῶν, ἵν’ ὦσιν ὅμοιοι αὐτῷ εὐδαίμονες</note> **"The universe would be poorly governed if Jupiter took no care for his own citizens, so that they might also be happy like himself."**

That these Stoics did indeed religiously worship and honor the Supreme God above all their other gods may appear from various examples. First, from their acknowledging him to be the sovereign legislator and professing subjection and obedience to his laws, considering this to be their greatest freedom. Thus **Epictetus** says: <margin>Book 4, chapter 7.</margin> <note>original Greek: εἰς ἐμὲ ὐδεὶς ἐξωσίαν ἔχει, ἠλυθερωμαι ὑπὸ τῶ θεῶ, ἔγνωκα αὐτῶ τὰς ἐντολὰς, ἐκέτι ὐδεὶς δȣλαγωγήσαι με δύναται</note> **"No person has power over me; I have been set free by God (by becoming his subject). I know his commandments, and no person can bring me into bondage to himself."** <margin>Book 3, chapter 5.</margin> **And again:** <note>original Greek: ταῦτα ἐπιτηδύων θέλω εὑρεθῆναι, ἵν’ εἰπεῖν δύναμαι τῷ θεῷ; μήτι παρέβλὺ ζῷ τὰς ἐντολὰς; &c.</note> **"I would want to be found occupied with these things, so that I may be able to say to God: 'Have I ever broken any of your commandments? Have I used my faculties and innate ideas <term>anticipations</term> <note>original: "Anticipations (or Common Notions)"; in Stoic philosophy, these are the fundamental moral truths inherent in all human minds</note> in any way other than what you required?'"**

Again, this is seen from their acknowledging him to be the supreme governor of the whole world and the orderer of all things in it by his fate and providence, and their professing to submit their wills to his will in everything. **Epictetus** somewhere addresses the Supreme God in this way: <note>original Greek: μήτι ἐμεμψάμlω ζῷ τὴν διοίκησιν; ἐνόσησα ὅτι ἐθέλησας...</note>

> **"Did I ever complain of your government? I was sick when you wanted me to be—and so were others—but I was so willingly. I was poor also at your appointment, but rejoicing. I never held any public office <term>magistracy</term> or had any high status because you did not want me to, and I never desired it. Did you ever see me more depressed or melancholy because of this? Have I appeared before you at any time with a discontented face? Was I not always prepared and ready for whatever you commanded? Do you want me now to depart from this festival? I am ready to go; and I give you all my thanks because you honored me so far as to let me keep the feast with you, behold your works, and observe your management <term>oeconomy</term> <note>original: "Oeconomy of the world"; the divine administration or structural order of the universe</note> of the world. Let death find me occupied in no other way than this: thinking and writing about such things."**

He likewise exhorts others in this manner: <margin>Book 2, chapter 16.</margin> <note>original Greek: τόλμησον ἀναβλέψας πρὸς τὸν θεὸν εἰπεῖν, ὅτι χρῶ μοι λοιπὸν εἰς ὃ ἂν θέλῃς...</note> **"Dare to look up to God and say: 'Use me for whatever you wish from now on; I am of one mind with you; I am your equal <note>original Greek: ἴσ(o) εἰμί; likely meaning "at one" or in total agreement with the divine will</note>. I refuse nothing that seems good to you. Lead me where you will; clothe me in whatever garments you wish. Do you want me to hold office, or live as a private citizen, to stay, or to flee <note>original Greek: φεύγειν; to go into exile</note>..."**

<meta>catchword: to flee,</meta>

<summary>This page highlights the deep personal devotion of the Stoic philosopher Epictetus toward the Supreme God, emphasizing total submission to divine providence and the pursuit of happiness through obedience to God's laws.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument regarding the Stoics' devotion to a single Supreme God, illustrating how they sought to align their will with the divine and find happiness through piety and gratitude.</meta>

# CHAPTER IV. To the Supreme God.

[...to flee, to be poor, or to be rich; I will defend you before all men regarding these things, and I will show the nature of each of them as it truly is.] <note>original Greek: φεύγειν, πένεσθαι, πλουτεῖν ; ἐγώ σοι ὑπὲρ ἀπάντων τούτων πρὸς τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἀπολογήσομαι, δείξω τὴν ἑκάστου φύσιν οἵα ἐστίν·</note> **"Dare to lift up your eyes to God and say: 'Use me hereafter for whatever you please. I agree with you and am of the same mind; I am indifferent to all things. I refuse nothing that seems good to you. Lead me wherever you wish. Let me play whatever part you want, whether as a public official or a private citizen, a rich man or a beggar. I will defend you <term>apologize</term> <note>original: "apologize"; here used in the classical sense of an "apologia" or a formal defense of God's providence against human complaints.</note> regarding all these things before men. And I will also show the true nature of every one of them.'"**

The same is likewise manifest from their claims *to look toward God and refer all things to him*; expecting help and assistance from him, and placing their confidence in him. Thus also **Epictetus** says:
<margin>Book 2, chapter 19.</margin>
[And I have this purpose: to make you free, happy, and looking toward God in everything, both small and great.] <note>original Greek: Κἀγὼ μὲν ἔχω ταύτην ἐπιβολὴν ἀποτελέσαι ὑμᾶς ἐλευθέρους, εὐδαιμονοῦντας, εἰς τὸν Θεὸν ἀφορῶντας, ἐν παντὶ μικρῷ καὶ μεγάλῳ·</note> **"My design is this: to make you free and undisturbed, always looking toward God, in every matter, whether small or great."** Again, the same Stoic concludes: 
<margin>Book 2, chapter 16.</margin>
[It is not possible to cast out grief, fear, desire, etc., in any other way than by looking to God alone, being devoted to him alone, and being consecrated to his commands.] <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἔστιν ἄλλως ἐκβαλεῖν λύπην, φόβον, ἐπιθυμίαν, &c. εἰ μὴ πρὸς μόνον τὸν Θεὸν ἀποβλέποντα, ἐκείνῳ μόνῳ προπεπονθότα, τοῖς ἐκείνου προστάγμασι καθωσιωμένον·</note> **"A person will never be able to expel grief, fear, desire, envy, etc., in any other way than by looking to God alone, being devoted to him, and observing his commandments."** And he affirms of **Hercules** that this great example of piety was observed by him long ago:
<margin>Book 3, chapter 24.</margin>
[He called Zeus his father, and looking toward him, he did whatever he did.] <note>original Greek: τὸν Δία αὐτοῦ πατέρα ἐκάλει, καὶ πρὸς ἐκεῖνον ἀφορῶν ἔπραττεν ἃ ἔπραττε·</note> **"As he called Jupiter <note>original: Zeus/Jupiter; often used by Stoics as a proper name for the Supreme God or Universal Reason.</note>, or the Supreme God, his Father, so he did whatever he did while looking toward him."** Thus **Marcus Antoninus** speaks of
<margin>Book 8, section 23.</margin>
a **double relation** that we all have: one [to those who live with us] <note>original Greek: πρὸς τοὺς συμβιοῦντας</note>, and another [to that divine cause from which all things happen to everyone] <note>original Greek: πρὸς τὴν θείαν αἰτίαν ἀφ᾽ ἧς συμβαίνει πᾶσιν πάντα</note>, **to that Divine Cause from which all things happen to all.** As
<margin>Book 3, section 11.</margin>
he likewise affirms: [You will do nothing human well without referring it to the divine.] <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἀνθρωπινόν τι ἄνευ τῆς ἐπὶ τὰ θεῖα συναναφορᾶς εὖ πράξεις</note> **"No human thing is well done without a reference to God."** And he excellently exhorts men:
<margin>Book 6, section 5.</margin>
[Delight in one thing and find rest in it: in passing from one social action to another social action with the remembrance of God.] <note>original Greek: ἑνὶ τέρπου, καὶ προσαναπαύου, τῷ ἀπὸ πράξεως κοινωνικῆς μεταβαίνειν ἐπὶ πρᾶξιν κοινωνικὴν σὺν μνήμῃ τοῦ Θεοῦ·</note> **"To be delighted and satisfied with this one thing: in doing one action after another that tends toward the common good, or the good of human society, together with the remembrance of God."** Lastly, he declares 
<margin>Book 6, section 8.</margin>
his own confidence in the Supreme Deity in these words: [I trust in the one who governs.] <note>original Greek: θαρρῶ τῷ διοικοῦντι</note> **"I trust and rely upon the Governor of the whole world."**

This may be concluded also from their **thanking the one Supreme God for all things** as the author of all good, and delightfully celebrating his praises. **Epictetus** declares it to be the duty of a good man:
<margin>Book 4, chapter 7.</margin>
[To give thanks for all things to God.] <note>original Greek: χάριν ἔχειν ὑπέρ πάντων τῷ Θεῷ</note> **"To thank God for all things."** And elsewhere
<margin>Book 1, chapter 16.</margin>
he speaks thus: [If we had understanding, what else ought we to do, both publicly and privately, than to hymn the Divine, to praise Him, and to recount His favors? Should we not, while digging and plowing and eating, sing the hymn to God? 'Great is God, that He provided us these tools with which we shall work the earth; Great is God, that He gave us hands, etc... that we grow without noticing it, that we breathe while sleeping.' These things we ought to praise in every instance, and sing the greatest and most divine hymn, that He gave us the power to understand these things. What then? If I were a nightingale, I would do the things of a nightingale; if a swan, the things of a swan; but now I am a rational being, I must hymn God.] <note>original Greek: εἰ νοῦν εἴχομεν, ἄλλό τι ἔδει ἡμᾶς ποιεῖν, καὶ κοινῇ καὶ ἰδίᾳ, ἢ ὑμνεῖν τὸ θεῖον, καὶ εὐφημεῖν, καὶ ἐπεξέρχεσθαι τὰς χάριτας ; οὐκ ἔδει καὶ σκάπτοντας, καὶ ἀροῦντας, καὶ ἐσθίοντας, ᾄδειν τὸν ὕμνον τὸν εἰς τὸν Θεόν ; μέγας ὁ Θεὸς ὅτι ἡμῖν παρέχεν ὄργανα ταῦτα, δι᾽ ὧν τὴν γῆν ἐργασόμεθα· μέγας ὁ Θεὸς ὅτι χεῖρας ἔδωκεν, &c. ὅτι αὔξεσθαι λεληθότως, ὅτι καθεύδοντας ἀναπνεῖν· ταῦτα ἐφ᾽ ἑκάστου εὐφημεῖν ἔδει, καὶ τὸν μέγιστον καὶ θειότατον ὕμνον ἐφυμνεῖν, ὅτι τὴν δύναμιν ἔδωκε τὴν παρακολουθητικὴν τούτων· τί οὖν ; &c. εἰ γὰρ ἀηδὼν ἤμην, ἐποίουν τὰ τῆς ἀηδόνος, εἰ κύκνος, τὰ τοῦ κύκνου, νῦν δὲ λογικὸς εἰμί, ὑμνεῖν με δεῖ τὸν Θεόν.</note> **"If we had understanding, what else should we do, both in public and in private, but sing hymns to the Divine, praise Him, and recount His favors? Should we not, while digging, plowing, and eating, sing the hymn to God? 'Great is God, because He has provided us with these tools by which we work the earth; Great is God, because He has given us hands, and the power to swallow, and a stomach, and the ability to grow without noticing it, and to breathe while we sleep.' We should praise these things on every occasion, and sing the greatest and most divine hymn of all: that He has given us the faculty to understand and follow these things. What then? Since most of you have become blind, should there not be someone to fill this place and sing the hymn to God on behalf of everyone? For if I were a nightingale, I would do the part of a nightingale; if a swan, the part of a swan. But now, since I am a rational being, I must praise God."**

# Cleanthes's Devout Hymn: Book I

Should we not publicly and privately praise **God**, bless **him**, and return thanks to him? Ought not those who dig, plow, and eat, continually sing such a **Hymn to God** as this: "**Great is that God, who gave us these organs to cultivate the earth with; Great is that God who gave us hands, etc., who enabled us to grow imperceptibly, and to breathe in our sleep.**" But the **greatest** and **most divine hymn of all** is **this: to praise God for the faculty of understanding all these things.** What then if for the most part men are blinded? Ought there not to be some **one** person who should perform this office, and sing a hymn to **God** for everyone? If I were a **nightingale**, I would perform the office of a nightingale; or if a **swan**, that of a swan. But now, being a **rational creature**, I ought to celebrate and sing aloud the praises of **God**, that is, of the **Supreme Deity**.

<margin>Book 2, chapter 18.</margin>
Lastly, the same is evident from their **invoking** the Supreme God as such, addressing their devotions to him alone without connecting him with any other gods, and particularly imploring his **assistance** against the assaults of **temptations**, which they called **"fancies"** <note>original: "Phancies"; here referring to *phantasiai*, the mental impressions or intrusive thoughts that the Stoics believed one must test against reason.</note>. To this purpose is that of **Epictetus**: [The struggle is great, the task is divine; it is for kingship, for freedom. Remember God; call upon him as your helper and protector, just as sailors call upon Castor and Pollux in a storm.] <note>original Greek: μέγας ὁ ἀγών ἐστι, θεῖον τὸ ἔργον, ὑπὲρ βασιλείας, ὑπὲρ ἐλευθερίας, τοῦ θεοῦ μέμνησο, ἐκεῖνον ἐπικαλοῦ βοηθὸν καὶ παραστάτην, ὡς τοὺς Διοσκούρους ἐν χειμῶνι οἱ πλέοντες·</note> **"This is a great conflict or contention, a divine enterprise; it is for liberty and for a kingdom. Now remember the Supreme God; call upon him as your helper and assistant, as sailors do upon Castor and Pollux in a tempest."** He also commends this form of devotional address, or divine ejaculation <note>In this context, an "ejaculation" is a short, sudden prayer or exclamation of faith.</note>, which was part of **Cleanthes's** litany, to be used frequently as the occasion arises: [Lead me, O Zeus, and you, O Fate, wherever I am assigned by you; for I will follow without hesitation. And even if I am unwilling, I must follow nonetheless.] <note>original Greek: Ἄγου δέ με ὦ Ζεῦ, καὶ σὺ ἡ πεπρωμένη ὅποι ποθ' (ὑμῖν) εἰμὶ διατεταγμένος, ὡς ἕψομαί γε ἄοκνος· ἢν δὲ γε μὴ θέλω, οὐδὲν ἧττον ἕψομαι·</note> **"Lead me, O Jupiter, and you, Fate, wherever I am destined by you; and I will readily and cheerfully follow. Even if I were ever so reluctant, yet I must necessarily follow."** In this context, **Jupiter** and **Fate** are really only one and the same Supreme Deity under two different names. Therefore, the sense of this devotional prayer was rendered no less truly and faithfully than elegantly by **Seneca**:

<margin>Letter 106.</margin>
> ->**Lead me, Father and Ruler of the high heavens,**<-
> ->**Wherever you please; there is no delay in obeying.**<-
> ->**I am present, eager; even if I were unwilling, I would follow groaning,**<-
> ->**And I would endure as a bad man what I might have suffered as a good man.**<-
<note>original Latin: *Duc me Parens, Celsique Dominator Poli, / Quocunque placuit, nulla parendi est mora, / Assum impiger; fac nolle, comitabor Gemens, / Malusque patiar, quod pati licuit bono.*</note>

But because many are so extremely unwilling to believe that the Pagans ever made any religious address to the Supreme God as such, we shall here set down an **excellent** and **devout hymn** to him by the same **Cleanthes**. We include it especially because it has been little noticed. To further gratify the reader, we shall subjoin an elegant translation of it into **Latin verse**, which is thanks to the poetry of my learned friend, **Dr. Duport**.

<margin>Stephanus, *Philosophical Poetry*, page 49.</margin>
**Most glorious of the immortals, many-named, always almighty,**
**Zeus, author of nature, governing all things with law,**
**Greetings! For it is right for all mortals to address you.**

# CHAPTER IV: A Hymn to the Supreme God

<note>original Greek: Ἐκ σοῦ γὰρ γένος ἐσμέν... This poem by Cleanthes (c. 331–232 BC) is one of the most important surviving texts of early Stoicism. It expresses a deep religious devotion to a single, providential God who governs the universe through "Logos" (Reason).</note>

For we are your offspring, <note>This line was famously quoted by the Apostle Paul in the New Testament (Acts 17:28) to connect with his Greek audience.</note> having alone received the gift of speech, as many as live and creep as mortals upon the earth. 
Therefore, I will praise you and sing of your power forever. 
To you, all this world, as it revolves around the earth, 
is obedient; it follows wherever you lead and is willingly governed by you. 
You hold such a servant in your invincible hands—
the double-edged, fiery, ever-living lightning bolt. 
For under its stroke all nature shudders; 
by it, you direct the common reason <note>original: *logos*; the rational principle that the Stoics believed permeated and organized the entire universe.</note>, which moves through all things, 
mingling with the great and small lights. 
Being so great, you are the highest king through all eternity. 
No deed is done on earth without you, O God, 
nor in the divine ethereal sphere, nor in the sea, 
except what the wicked do in their own foolishness. 
But you know how to order what is chaotic, and things unlovely are lovely to you. 
For you have so harmonized all good things with the evil into one, 
that there becomes one eternal reason for all things. 
This reason the wicked among mortals flee and ignore—
wretched ones, who, though always desiring to possess good things, 
neither see nor hear God’s universal law, 
by obeying which they might lead a noble life with understanding. 
Instead, they rush headlong without beauty, each after different goals: 
some with a fierce ambition for fame, 
others turned toward greed with no sense of order, 
others toward indulgence and the pleasant works of the body. 
But O Zeus, giver of all, shrouded in dark clouds, lord of the lightning, 
deliver humans from their wretched ignorance; 
scatter it, O Father, from their souls, and grant them to attain 
the wisdom in which you trust to govern all things with justice. 
Thus, being honored, we may repay you with honor, 
hymning your works continuously, as is fitting 
for a mortal; since there is no greater prize for either mortals 
or gods than to forever hymn the universal law with justice.

# Cicero Not an Asserter of Atheism, Book 1

> Nothing happens in the divine ether, nor across the blue of the sea,
> driven by its own error, except what the wicked race commits.
> You direct things, confused in themselves, into a certain order;
> by your guidance, even ungrateful things have their own grace.
> With happy harmony, you indeed join all good things mixed with evil into One,
> so that a single, common, and ever-enduring Reason for all things may rise—

> If they obeyed it, they could lead a good life with reason and mind;
> instead, they are driven headlong into evil by their own will,
> and their own pleasure drags each one away.
> Ambition and an immense desire for praise drives one man;
> another is driven by greed and a mad love of possessing;
> another by enticing lust and the sweet license of Venus:
> thus, rushing into diverse paths, they tend in different directions.

XXVI. It would be endless now to cite all the testimonies of other philosophers and pagan writers of later times concerning one supreme and universal divine power <note>original: *Numen*</note>. Therefore, we shall content ourselves only to provide examples of some of the most remarkable, beginning with Marcus Tullius Cicero. Although some would suspect him to have been a skeptic regarding theism—because in his *On the Nature of the Gods* <note>original: *De Natura Deorum*</note>, he introduces Cotta the Academic to oppose both Quintus Lucilius Balbus the Stoic and Gaius Velleius the Epicurean—it appears clearly enough from various other parts of his writings that he was a committed and sincere theist. For example, in his second book *On Divination* <note>original: *De Divin.*</note>: *That there is some most excellent and eternal nature, which is to be admired and honored by mankind, the beauty <note>original: *Pulchritudo*</note> of the world and the order of the heavenly bodies compel us to confess.* And also in his oration *On the Response of the Soothsayers* <note>original: *De Haruspicum responsis*</note>: *Who is so senseless <note>original: *vecors*</note> that, when he has looked up to heaven, does not immediately sense that there are gods? # CHAPTER IV. Of Many Independent Gods.

We will cite more passages for this purpose later. However, in his philosophical writings, it is certain that Cicero chose to follow the method of the **New Academy** <note>The New Academy was a school of philosophy that practiced academic skepticism, focusing on probability rather than absolute certainty.</note> established by Carneades. That is, he wrote skeptically, partly for practical reasons and partly for other reasons he hinted at himself in these words: <margin>On the Nature of the Gods, Book 1.</margin>

> Those who wish to know what we ourselves think about every matter are more curious than they need to be. In a debate, one should seek the weight of Reason rather than the weight of Authority. Furthermore, the authority of those who claim to teach is often a hindrance to those who wish to learn; for the students stop using their own judgment and take for granted whatever is decided by the person they respect. <note>original Latin: *Qui requirunt quid quaque de re ipsi sentiamus, curiosiùs id faciunt quam necesse est. Non enim tam Authoritatis in disputando quam Rationis momenta quærenda sunt. Quinetiam obest plerumque iis qui discere volunt, Auctoritas eorum qui se docere profitentur. Desinunt enim suum judicium adhibere, idque habent ratum, quod ab eo quem probant, judicatum vident.*</note>

Nevertheless, at the end of this discourse *On the Nature of the Gods* (as St. Augustine also observes), Cicero plainly declares himself to be more inclined toward the doctrine of **Balbus** <note>Balbus is the character representing the Stoic viewpoint in Cicero's dialogue.</note> than toward that of either **Velleius** or **Cotta**. That is, although he did not agree with Stoic doctrine or theology in every point (being himself more a **Platonist** than a **Stoic**), he still much preferred it over both the Epicureanism of Velleius and the skepticism of Cotta. 

Because of this, Augustinus Steuchus <note>A 16th-century Italian scholar and librarian.</note> and other learned men argue with several of Cicero’s passages on a different ground—not as being atheistic, but as seeming to favor a multitude of **independent gods**. Cicero sometimes attributes the government of the world, the creation of mankind, and the original structure of the entire world to **Gods in the plural**. For example, he writes:

"To ensure the world would be perpetually beautiful, great care has been taken by the Providence of the Gods." <note>original Latin: *Ut perpetuus Mundi esset ornatus, magna adhibita cura est à Providentia Deorum.*</note>

And: "That the immortal gods have provided for the convenience of mankind appears from the very fabric and figure of them." <note>original Latin: *A Diis Immortalibus Hominibus provisum esse...*</note> <margin>On the Nature of the Gods, Book 2, Chapter 25.</margin>

And the place cited before: "I say, therefore, that the world and all its parts were at first established by the Providence of the Gods." <note>original Latin: *Dico igitur Providentia Deorum, Mundum & omnes Mundi partes initio constitutas esse.*</note>

And finally, where he states the central debate of that book, *On the Nature of the Gods*, this way: <margin>Page 195, Lambinus edition.</margin> "Whether the gods do nothing at all and are free from care and labor? Or, on the contrary, whether all things were made and established by them from the beginning, and are moved and governed by them for all eternity?" <note>original Latin: *Utrum Dii nihil agant, nihil moliantur? An contrà ab His, & à Principio Omnia facta, & constituta sint, & ad infinitum tempus regantur atque moveantur?*</note>

Despite this, it is evident that this learned orator and philosopher plainly acknowledged the **Monarchy of the Whole**, or **one Supreme and Universal <term>Numen</term>** <note>Numen: A Latin term for divine power or a presiding spirit.</note> over all. This is clear, first, from his frequent use of the word "God" in the singular, emphatically and as a title of excellence. For example: "Nothing can be less pleasing to God himself than that there should not be a path open to all to worship and appease him (regardless of the cost of sacrifices)." <note>original Latin: *Ipsi Deo nihil minus gratum, quàm non omnibus patere ad se Placandum & Colendum viam.*</note> <margin>On the Laws, Book 2, Page 335.</margin> 

And, "Unless God helps..." <note>original Latin: *Nisi juvante Deo...*</note> <margin>On the Nature of the Gods, Book 2.</margin>

# CHAP. IV. The Makers of the World, were.

<margin>
*The Dream of Scipio* <note>original: *Somn. Scip.*</note>
*On the Laws* <note>original: *De Leg.*</note>
*On Divination* <note>original: *De Div.*</note>
*The Dream of Scipio* <note>original: *Somn. Scip.*</note>
</margin>
...all things obey, <note>original Latin: *parent omnia*</note> *That God, whose Divine Power all things obey.* We read also in *Cicero* of the *Highest* or *Supreme God* <note>original Latin: *Summus or Supremus Deus*</note>, to whom the first making of Man is properly attributed by him; of *The Divine Power of the Supreme Lord and Governor* <note>original Latin: *Summi Rectoris & Domini Numen*</note>; of the *most powerful God* <note>original Latin: *Deus præpotens*</note>, and *Jupiter who has power over all things* <note>original Latin: *Rerum omnium præpotens Jupiter*</note>; and of *That Chief or Principal God, who governs this whole world in the same manner as a human soul governs that body over which it is placed* <note>original Latin: *Princeps ille Deus, qui omnem hunc mundum regit, ficut Animus humanus id corpus cui præpositus est*</note>. Therefore, regarding those passages mentioned earlier where the government of the world—at least concerning the affairs of mankind—is ascribed by *Cicero* to *Gods* in the plural, this was done by him and other Pagans for no other reason than this: they did not suppose the Supreme God did everything himself immediately in the government of the world. Instead, they believed he assigned certain provinces to other inferior gods as ministers under him. These gods, sharing in the stewardship <term>economy</term> <note>original: "Oeconomy," referring here to the divine administration or management of the universe.</note> of the world, were looked upon as its co-governors along with him. Thus, when *Balbus* in *Cicero* tried to excuse some seeming defects of Providence—such as the prosperity of the wicked and the misfortunes of good men—by pretending that *The gods did not attend to all things, any more than kings do* <note>original Latin: *Non animadvertere omnia Deos, nè Reges quidem*</note>, *Cotta*, among 

<margin>*On the Nature of the Gods, Book 3* <note>original: *De N.D. L. 3.*</note></margin>
other things, replied this way: *Even if it were granted that the Divine Mind (or Supreme Deity) were occupied with turning the heavens, watching the earth, and governing the seas, why does he let so many other gods do nothing at all? Or why does he not appoint some of those idle gods over human affairs, which, according to you, Balbus, and the Stoics, are innumerable?* <note>original Latin: *Fac Divinam Mentem esse distentam, Cœlum versantem, terram tuentem, maria moderantem, cur tam multos Deos nihil agere & cessare patitur? Cur non rebus humanis aliquos otiosos Deos præfecit, qui à te Balbe Innumerabiles explicati sunt?*</note> Again, when the Immortal Gods are said by *Cicero* to have provided for the convenience of mankind in their *original constitution*, this is undoubtedly to be understood according to the *Platonic Hypothesis*: that the gods and demons, being first made by the Supreme God, were afterward set to work and employed by him in the making of man and other mortal animals. 

And finally, as to the point that carries the greatest difficulty of all—when the whole world is said by *Cicero* to have been made by the providence of the *Gods*—this must also be understood as referring to those *eternal gods* of *Plato’s*, according to whose *likeness* or *image* the world and man are said to have been made. That is, it refers to the Trinity of Divine *Hypostases* <note>In theology, "hypostases" refers to the distinct persons or substances within the deity.</note>, called by *Amelius* "Plato’s Three Minds and Three Kings," and by other Platonists the *First*, *Second*, and *Third God*, and *The First Cause and the Second Cause, etc.* <note>original Greek: *τὸ πρῶτον αἴτιον, and τὸ δεύτερον αἴτιον*</note>. Here it may be observed, as we learn from *St. Cyril*, that some Pagans endeavored to justify this language and doctrine of theirs even from the Mosaic writings themselves.

<margin>*Against Julian, Book 1* <note>original: *Contra Jul. L. 1.*</note></margin>
*By making the God of all things speak to other gods, they suspect that he said, "Let us make man in our image and after our likeness"* <note>original Greek: *θεοῖς ἑτέροις ὑποποιήσαντες τ' ὅλων φᾶναι θεόν, ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον καθ' εἰκόνα ἡμετέραν & καθ' ὁμοίωσιν*</note>; *they suspected that the God of the Universe, being about to make man, did there speak to the other gods* (*those who are second after him* <note>original Greek: *τοῖς μεθ' ἑαυτ' δ' δευτέροις*</note>...

# Varro's Natural Theology, BOOK I.

...or the intermediate gods <note>original Greek: ἢ ἐν μέσον θεοὶ</note>, who were secondary and inferior to him) after this manner: *Let Us make man according to Our own Image and likeness.* This phrase St. Cyril and other Christian writers understand as referring to the Trinity. Now, those "Eternal Gods" of *Plato*, in whose image the world and man are said by him to have been made—and who (though one of them was properly called the *Demiurgus* <term>the Craftsman or Creator</term>) yet all had an influence and causality upon its creation—were (as has been already observed) not many independent and self-originated deities. Instead, they were all derived from one First Principle. Therefore, *Cicero*, following *Plato* in this, is not to be suspected of being an asserter of many independent gods or partial creators of the world, especially since in so many other places in his writings, he plainly acknowledges a Divine Monarchy.

We pass from *Marcus Tullius Cicero* to *Marcus Terentius Varro*, his contemporary, a man famous for his vast and varied knowledge <note>original: polymathy</note>. He was unquestionably reputed to be the most learned of all the Romans, at least regarding antiquity, even if not the most eloquent. He wrote forty-one books concerning the antiquities of human and divine things. In these, he surpassed even the Roman *Pontifices* <term>high priests</term> themselves and exposed their ignorance regarding many points of their own religion. In these books, he distinguished **three kinds of theology**: the first **Mythical** (or Fabulous), the second **Physical** (or Natural), and the last **Civil** (or Popular). 

1. The first is best suited for the theater or the stage. 
2. The second is for the world or the wiser men in it. 
3. The third is for cities or the general population of civilized commoners. 

This was also agreeable to the doctrine of *Scævola*, that learned *Pontifex*, concerning **three sorts of gods**: the poetical, the philosophical, and the political. As for the Mythical and Poetical theology, it was criticized by *Varro* in this manner:

<margin>Augustine, *The City of God*, Book 6, Chapter 5.</margin>
> "In it are many things invented contrary to the dignity and nature of the immortal beings <note>original Latin: *In eo sunt multa contra Dignitatem & Naturam immortalium ficta*</note>. For in this, one god is born from a head, another from a thigh, another from drops of blood. In this, the gods have stolen, committed adultery, and served mankind. Finally, in this, all things are attributed to the gods that are not only characteristic of men, but even of the most contemptible and wicked of men." 
— *Varro argues that, according to the literal sense, this theology contains many things contrary to the dignity and nature of immortal beings.*

And as for the second, the **Natural Theology**, which is the true one, *Varro* conceived this to be above the capacity of the common citizens. He believed it was therefore necessary that there should be another theology designed more for them, a middle kind between the Natural and the Fabulous, which is called **Civil Theology**. For he affirmed:

<margin>Augustine, *The City of God*, Book 4, Chapter 31.</margin>
> "There are many things which are true that it is not useful for the common people to know; and some things which, even if they are false, it is better for the people to believe otherwise <note>original Latin: *Multa esse vera quæ vulgo ſcire non ſit utile, & quædam quæ tametſi falſa ſint, aliter exiſtimare populum expediat*</note>." 

*Scævola*, the Roman *Pontifex*, likewise did not want the common people to know that...

<summary>This page discusses the transition from Cicero's monotheistic leanings to Varro's classification of theology into three types: Mythical (poetic/theatrical), Natural (philosophical/true), and Civil (political/popular). Varro and Scævola argue that while Natural theology is true, Civil theology is necessary for social order, even if it involves maintaining false beliefs among the public.</summary>
