### CHAPTER IV. Distinct from the Mythical and Civil.

that the True God had neither sex, nor age, nor bodily members.
<margin>City of God, Book 4, Chapter 27</margin>
"He therefore judges it expedient," says St. Augustine <note>original: St. Austin</note> of him, "that cities should be deceived in their religion; which Varro himself does not hesitate to affirm in his *Books of Divine Things*." <note>original Latin: *Expedire igitur existimat falli in Religione Civitates, quod dicere etiam in Libris Rerum Divinarum, ipse Varro non dubitat*</note> Scævola, therefore, judges it expedient that cities should be deceived in their religion; which also Varro himself does not hesitate to affirm in his own writings. Therefore, although Varro disapproved of Fabulous <term>mythical or fictional</term> Theology, yet out of a pious design as he conceived it, he endeavored to assert as much as he could the Civil Theology then received among the Romans, and to protect it from contempt. Yet, he did so in such a way that, 
<margin>City of God, Book 4, Chapter 31</margin>
"if he were to establish a new city *himself*, he does not hesitate to confess that he would dedicate gods and the names of gods in another manner, more agreeably to the *Form of Nature* or *Natural Theology*." <note>original Latin: *Si eam Civitatem novam constitueret, ex Naturæ potiùs Formulâ, Deos & Deorum nomina se fuisse dedicaturum, non dubitet confiteri*</note> Now, what Varro's own sense was concerning God, he freely declared in those *Books of Divine Things*: namely, that He was the Great Soul and Mind of the whole world. Thus St. Augustine notes:
<margin>City of God, Book 4, Chapter 9</margin>
"To Varro, only those seem to have understood what God is who believed Him to be a Soul, governing the whole world by motion and reason." <note>original Latin: *Hi soli Varroni videntur animadvertisse quid esset Deus, qui crediderunt eum esse Animam, Motu ac Ratione mundum gubernantem*</note> So Varro plainly asserted **one supreme** and **universal divine power** <term>original: *numen*</term>. He erred only in this (as St. Augustine conceives) that he called Him *a Soul*, and not the Creator of the soul, or a *pure* and *abstract mind*. 

But as Varro acknowledged **one universal divinity**, the whole animated world, or rather the soul of it—which he also affirmed was called by several names, such as *Tellus* in the earth, *Neptune* in the sea, and the like—so did he also admit (together with the rest of the Pagans) other particular gods. These were to him nothing but *parts* of the world *animated* with souls superior to men:
<margin>City of God, Book 7, Chapter 6</margin>
"That from the highest circuit of the heavens down to the sphere of the moon, there are ethereal souls or animals—the stars—which are not only understood to be celestial gods, but are even seen to be so. And between the sphere of the moon and the peaks of the clouds, there are aerial souls or animals; these are seen by the mind rather than the eyes, and are called Heroes, Lares, and Genii." <note>original Latin: *A summo Circuitu cæli, usque ad Circulum Lunæ, æthereas Animas esse Astra ac Stellas, eosque cælestes Deos, non modo intelligi esse sed etiam videri: Inter Lunæ verò gyrum & nimborum Cacumina Aereas esse Animas, sed eas animo non oculis videri; & vocari Heroas & Lares & Genios*</note> So, according to Varro, the only true natural gods were, as he himself determined, the *Soul of the World and its parts* <note>original Latin: *Anima Mundi, ac Partes ejus*</note>: first, the great soul and mind of the whole world which encompasses everything; and secondly, the animated parts of the world superior to men. 

Varro also affirmed that these gods were worshipped more purely <note>original Latin: *castius*</note> and chastely without images, as they were by the first Romans for one hundred and seventy years. He concluded:
<margin>City of God, Book 4, Chapter 31</margin>
"That those nations who first set up images of the gods both took away fear <term>reverence or awe</term> from their cities and added error; wisely judging," says St. Augustine, "that gods could easily be despised in the stupidity of images." <note>original Latin: *qui primi simulachra Deorum populi posuerunt, eos civitatibus suis & metum dempsisse & errorem addidisse: prudenter existimans... Deos facilè posse in Simulachrorum stoliditate contemni*</note>

# Seneca’s View of the Former of the Universe, etc. Book I.

*...error to them: he wisely judging that the foolishness of images <note>original: "foppery of images"</note> would easily make their gods appear contemptible.*

<margin>Seneca, Natural Questions, Book 2, chapter 45</margin>
Lucius Annaeus Seneca the philosopher was a contemporary of our Savior Christ and his Apostles. Although he frequently acknowledged a plurality of gods, he nevertheless plainly asserted One Supreme God. He did not only speak of Him in the singular and as an eminent being, but also plainly described Him as such; as when he calls him:

* The Framer and Former of the Universe <note>original Latin: *Formatorem Universi*</note>; 
* The Ruler, Judge, and Guardian of the World <note>original: *Rectorem & Arbitrum & Custodem Mundi*</note>; 
* Him upon whom all things depend <note>original: *Ex quo suspensa sunt omnia*</note>; 
* The Mind and Spirit of the Universe <note>original: *Animum ac Spiritum Universi*</note>; 
* The Lord and Artificer of this whole worldly work <note>original: *Mundani hujus operis Dominum & Artificem*</note>; 
* To whom every name belongs <note>original: *Cui nomen omne convenit*</note>; 
* From whom all things spring <note>original: *Ex quo nata sunt omnia*</note>; 
* By whose Spirit we live <note>original: *Cujus Spiritu vivimus*</note>; 
* Who is present in all His parts and sustains Himself by His own power <note>original: *Totum suis partibus inditum, & se sustinentem sua vi*</note>; 
* By whose Counsel the world is provided for, so that it proceeds unshaken and unfolds its own actions <note>original: *Cujus Consilio huic mundo providetur, ut inconcussus eat, & actus suos explicet*</note>; 
* By whose Decree all things are done <note>original: *Cujus Decreto omnia fiunt*</note>; 
* The Divine Spirit that is diffused through all things, both great and small, with equal intensity <note>original: *Divinum Spiritum per omnia maxima & minima æquali intentione diffusum*</note>; 
<margin>Page 442, Lipsius edition</margin>
* The God whose power extends to all things <note>original: *Deum potentem omnium*</note>; 
* That greatest and most powerful God, who Himself carries all things <note>original: *Deum illum maximum potentissimumque, qui ipse vehit omnia*</note>; 
* Who is present everywhere to all things <note>original: *Qui ubique & omnibus præsto est*</note>; 
* The God of Heaven and of all the gods, upon whom are suspended all those other divine powers <note>original: *numina*</note> which we individually worship and adore <note>original: *Cœli & Deorum omnium Deum, a quo ista Numina quæ singula adoramus & colimus, suspensa sunt*</note>.

<margin>Augustine, City of God, Book 6, chapter 10</margin>
Moreover, we may observe from St. Augustine <note>original: St. Austin</note> that this Seneca, in a book of his against superstitions (which is now lost), did not only highly praise **Natural Theology** <term>the study of God based on reason and nature</term>, but also plainly censured and condemned the **Civil Theology** <term>the official state religion and rituals</term> then received among the Romans. He did so with more freedom and vehemence than Varro had used against the Fabulous <term>myth-based</term> or theatrical and poetic theology. Concerning a great part of the state religion, Seneca pronounced that a wise man would observe such things "only as commanded by the laws, but not at all as pleasing to the gods" <note>original Latin: *tanquam Legibus jussa, non tanquam Diis grata*</note>. In this, he was exercising civil obedience rather than true worship.

<margin>Quintilian, Book 7, chapter 3</margin>
Marcus Fabius Quintilianus, though no admirer of Seneca's literary style, yet fully agreed with him in the same **Natural Theology**. He sets down this as the generally received notion or definition of God: "That God is a Spirit mingled with and diffused through all the parts of the world" <note>original Latin: *Deum esse Spiritum omnibus partibus immistum*</note>. From this definition, he inferred that Epicurus was an atheist, even though Epicurus verbally claimed there were gods. Quintilian argued this because Epicurus denied the existence of a God according to this generally received notion, instead giving his "gods" a limited human form and placing them in the empty spaces between worlds. And the younger Pliny, though...

# CHAP. IV. Symmachus; One Worshipped by All.

<margin>Epistle 97.</margin>
...although he was a persecutor of the Christians, concluding that "whatever it was that they confessed, certainly their persistence and inflexible obstinacy ought to be punished" <note>This refers to Pliny the Younger in his famous letter to Emperor Trajan regarding the early Christians; original: *quale-cunque esset quod faterentur, pervicaciam certè & inflexibilem obstinationem debere puniri*</note>. This is sufficiently clear from his *Panegyric* oration to Trajan, where God is called "that God who is manifest and present, inhabiting the whole heaven and stars" <note>original: *Deus ille, qui manifestus ac præsens Cœlum ac Sydera insidet*</note>. 

<margin>And Parent of the World, and Parent of Men and Gods. <note>original: *Mundi Parens, and Parens Hominum Deorum*</note></margin>

Lucius Apuleius <note>A 2nd-century Platonic philosopher and author</note>—whose alleged miracles the pagans used to try and support their religion, much as they did with those of Apollonius of Tyana—also plainly asserts one Supreme and Universal Divine Power in several places in his writings. We shall only provide one example here: 

<margin>On Philosophy, page 278, Colv.</margin> 
"Since the Highest of the Gods does not only consider all these things in his mind and thought, but also encompasses the beginning, middle, and end of all things; and having found them, He governs all things by the universality and constancy of the hidden order of His providence" <note>original: *Cum Summus Deorum, cuncta hæc non solùm cogitationum ratione consideret; sed Prima, Media, & Ultima obeat; compertaque intimæ Providentiæ ordinationis universitate & Constantia regat*</note>. 

Lastly, Symmachus <note>Quintus Aurelius Symmachus (c. 340–402 AD), one of the last great defenders of traditional Roman paganism</note>, who was a zealous advocate for the restoration of paganism, declared that the pagans worshiped one and the same God as the Christians, but in different ways. He believed there was no necessity for God to be worshiped by everyone in the same manner. 

<margin>Page 306.</margin>

# The Author of *De Mundo*, Book 1.

->*Searching in a different way, as if the path were multiplied by scattered tracks,*<-
->*and the wheel-rim wore down a hundred paths,*<-
->*seeking the hidden God with various explorations.*<-
<note>original: "Quæri aliter, quàm si sparsis via multiplicetur / Tramitibus, & centenos terat orbita calles, / Quæsitura Deum variata indage latentem." These lines represent the pagan argument that many paths (religions) lead to the same God.</note>

And the beginning of Prudentius's <note>A Roman Christian poet (c. 348–413 AD) known for his "Psychomachia."</note> refutation is this:

->*The truth is far different. For a great maze of roads*<-
->*contains uncertain twists and wanders quite perplexingly.*<-
->*Only the simple way is free from error; it does not know how to turn*<-
->*into a side-path, nor is it hesitant at many crossroads, etc.*<-
<note>original: "Longè aliud verum est. Nam multa ambago viarum / Anfractus dubios habet, & perplexius errat. / Sola errore caret simplex via, nescia flecti / In diverticulum, biviis nec pluribus anceps, &c."</note>

We shall now also provide examples from some of the later Greek writers. Although the author of the book *De Mundo* <note>On the Universe; a treatise formerly attributed to Aristotle but now thought to be by a later "Pseudo-Aristotle."</note> was not Aristotle, it plainly appears that he was a pagan from certain passages. For instance, he approves of **sacrificing to the gods** and **worshipping heroes and dead men**. Furthermore, Apuleius <note>The North African philosopher and author of "The Golden Ass" mentioned on the previous page.</note> would not have otherwise translated so much of that book and incorporated it into his own work, also titled *De Mundo*. 

This author does not only commend the saying of Heraclitus— <margin>Chapter 6.</margin> *“Out of all things one, and out of one all things,”* <note>original: "ἐκ πάντων ἓν, καὶ ἐξ ἑνὸς πάντα"</note> meaning that there is one harmonious system made out of all things, and that all things are derived from one—but he himself also writes excellently concerning the Supreme God. He calls Him *“the cause which holds all things together”* <note>original: "τὴν τῶν ὅλων συνεκτικὴν αἰτίαν"</note> and *“the best and most excellent part of the world.”* <note>original: "τὸ τοῦ κόσμου κυριώτατον"</note> He begins in this manner: 

*“It is an ancient opinion or tradition that has been conveyed down to all men from their ancestors: that all things are from God and consist through God; and that no nature is sufficient to preserve itself if left alone and devoid of divine assistance and influence.”* <note>original: "ἀρχαῖος μὲν οὖν τις λόγος καὶ πάτριός ἐστι πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις, ὡς ἐκ θεοῦ τὰ πάντα, καὶ διὰ θεοῦ ἡμῖν συνέστηκε· οὐδεμία δὲ φύσις, αὐτὴ καθ᾽ ἑαυτὴν αὐτάρκης, ἐρημωθεῖσα τῆς ἐκ τούτου σωτηρίας"</note>

Here we may observe that Apuleius's Latin version alters the sentence, rendering the words this way: *“It is an old opinion, and one that has deeply entered the thoughts of all men: that God exists; that He has no author of His origin; and that God is the safety and preservation of those things which He Himself has made.”* <note>original: "Vetus opinio est, atque in cogitationes omnium hominum penitus incidit, Deum esse: Originis non habere auctorem: Deumque esse salutem & perseverantiam Earum, quas effecerit, rerum."</note> 

So, while the original Greek states that it is the general opinion of all mankind **that all things are from God and depend on Him** (and that nothing at all can preserve its own existence without Him), Apuleius adjusts the words. He makes the general consensus of mankind reach no higher than this: that there is a God who was not created by anyone else, and who preserves only those things that He created. 

From this, it may be probably concluded that Apuleius—who is said to have been a descendant of Plutarch <note>A famous Greek philosopher and biographer.</note>—was also infected with Plutarch's paradoxical opinions. Consequently, Apuleius likely supposed that not all things were made by God or depended on Him (as the author of *De Mundo* affirms). Instead, he believed there was something besides God—namely, **Matter** and an **Evil Principle**—that was uncreated and self-existent. 

Afterward, the same writer of *De Mundo* elegantly illustrates with metaphors how God, by one simple motion and energy of His own, produces and governs all the variety of motions in the universe without any labor or toil. He describes how God "holds together the..."

# CHAPTER IV. And Plutarch; Their Testimonies.

...contain the harmony and preservation of the whole <note>original: "τῆς ὅλων ἁρμονίαν τε καὶ σωτηρίαν"</note>. And lastly, he concludes:

->**That what a pilot is to a ship, a charioteer to a chariot, the leader <note>original: "coryphaeus" – the conductor of a Greek chorus</note> to a choir, law to a city, and a general to an army; the same is God to the world.**<-
<note>original: "ὅπερ ἐν νηὶ κυβερνήτης, ἐν ἅρματι δὲ ἡνίοχος, ἐν χορῷ κορυφαῖος, ἐν πόλει νόμος, ἐν στρατοπέδῳ ἡγεμὼν, τοῦτο θεὸς ἐν κόσμῳ"</note>

There is only this difference: whereas the government of some of these is toilsome and anxious, the divine government and steering of the world is most easy and effortless. For as this writer adds, **God, being himself immovable, moves all things; in the same manner as law, being immovable in itself, orders and disposes all things by moving the minds of the citizens.**

Plutarch of Chaeronea <note>A famous Greek philosopher and biographer (c. 46–119 AD).</note> (as has been already declared) was unfortunately caught up in **two false opinions**. The first was that **matter is uncreated** <note>original: "ingenit"</note>, based on the pretense that **nothing could be made out of nothing**. The second was the belief in a **positive, substantial evil principle**, or an irrational soul and self-existent demon. He held this because:

->**"There is no greater absurdity imaginable than that evil should proceed from the providence of God, like a bad poem <note>original: "epigram"</note> resulting from the will of the poet."**<-
<note>original: "τὴν κακίαν γεγονέναι κατὰ τὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ πρόνοιαν, ὥσπερ τὸ φαῦλον ἐπίγραμμα κατὰ τὴν τοῦ ποιητοῦ βούλησιν, πᾶσαν ἐπίνοιαν ἀτοπίας ὑπερβάλλει"</note>

In this respect, he was previously called by us a **ditheist** <note>Someone who believes in two equal and opposing gods or principles, one good and one evil.</note>. Plutarch was also a worshiper of the many pagan gods, being himself a priest of the Pythian Apollo. Notwithstanding this, he unquestionably asserted one sole principle of all good, the cause of all things (**evil and matter only excepted**), the framer of the entire world, and the maker of all the gods within it. He is, therefore, often called "God" by Plutarch in a way of excellence. For example, Plutarch affirms that **"God always acts as a geometrician"** <note>original: "ἀεὶ γεωμετρεῖν τὸν Θεὸν"</note>, meaning he does all things with measure and proportion. Again, he states that **"all things are made by God according to harmony"** <note>original: "πάντα καθ᾿ ἁρμονίαν ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ κατασκευάζεσθαι"</note>, and that **"God is called a harmonist and musician"** <note>original: "ὁ θεὸς ἁρμονικὸς καλεῖται καὶ μουσικός"</note>.

He also gives God these titles: **the Great God** <note>original: "ὁ μέγας θεός"</note>, **the Highest or Uppermost God** <note>original: "ὁ ἀνωτάτω θεός"</note>, **the First God** <note>original: "ὁ πρῶτος θεός"</note>, and **the Uncreated, Self-existent God** <note>original: "ὁ ἀγέννητος θεός"</note>. According to Plutarch, all the other pagan gods were made in time, together with the world. He is likewise styled by Plutarch as the **"sea of beauty"** <note>original: "πέλαγος τοῦ καλοῦ"; original English: "pulchritude"</note>. His standing and permanent duration, which exists without the flow of time, is excellently described by the same writer in his book concerning the inscription at Delphi. Lastly, Plutarch affirms that people generally pray to this supreme God for whatever is not in their own power <note>original: "ὅσα μὴ παρ᾿ ἡμῖν ἐστὶν, εὐχόμεθα τὸν θεὸν διδόναι"</note>.

<margin>Pages 199, 210, 203.</margin>
Dio Chrysostom, a professional speaker <note>term: "sophist" – though here used as a title for a rhetorician/philosopher</note> and contemporary of Plutarch, also acknowledged many gods. Yet, he nevertheless asserted that **"the whole world is under a kingly power or monarchy"** <note>original: "βασιλεύεσθαι τὸ ὅλον"</note>. He sometimes calls the supreme God **"the common king of gods and men, their governor, and father"** <note>original: "τὸν κοινὸν ἀνθρώπων καὶ θεῶν βασιλέα τε καὶ ἄρχοντα, καὶ πρύτανιν καὶ πατέρα"</note>, **"the God that rules over all"** <note>original: "τὸν πάντων κρατοῦντα θεὸν"</note>, **"the First and Greatest God,"** and the leader...

<meta>catchword: innermost <note>original: "εσώτα" (esōta)</note></meta>

<summary>This page analyzes the writings of Plutarch and Dio Chrysostom to show that, despite their involvement in traditional polytheism, they both maintained the existence of a single, supreme, and uncreated God who governs the universe as a monarch. Plutarch is specifically noted for his "ditheism," believing in a secondary evil principle to explain the existence of suffering without blaming God's providence.</summary>

# Dio Chrysostom and Galen, Book I.

<margin>P. 446.</margin>
<note>original: "ἑστῶτα τῶν ὅλων, καὶ διϋθύνοντα τὰ ἅπαντα οὐρανὸν καὶ κόσμον, &c."</note> *The chief President over all things, who orders and guides the whole Heaven and World, as a wise Pilot does a Ship;* <note>original: "τὸν τοῦ ξύμπαντος ἡγεμόνα οὐρανοῦ, καὶ τῆς ὅλης δεσπότην οὐσίας"</note> *the Ruler of the whole Heaven, and Lord of the Whole Essence;* and the like.

<margin>P. 201.</margin>
And he affirming that there is a **Natural Prolepsis** <term>A "natural prolepsis" is an innate idea or a concept naturally present in the human mind from birth, rather than learned through experience.</term> in the minds of men concerning him: <note>original: "περὶ δὲ θεῶν τε καθόλου φύσεως, καὶ μάλιστα τοῦ πάντων ἡγεμόνος, πρῶτον μὲν καὶ ἐν πρώτοις δόξα τις ἐπίνοια κοινὴ τοῦ ξύμπαντος ἀνθρωπίνου γένους · ὁμοίως μὲν Ἑλλήνων ὁμοίως δὲ βαρβάρων, ἀναγκαία καὶ ἔμφυτος ἐν παντὶ τῷ λογικῷ γιγνομένη κατὰ φύσιν, ἄνευ θνητοῦ διδασκάλου καὶ μυσταγωγοῦ"</note> *Concerning the nature of the Gods in general, but especially of that Supreme Ruler over all; there is an opinion in all humankind, as well non-Greeks as Greeks; that is naturally implanted in them as rational Beings, and not derived from any mortal Teacher.* The meaning of this is that men are naturally possessed with a persuasion that there is One God, the Supreme Governor of the whole World, and that there are also below him, but above men, many other intellectual beings, which these Pagans called **Gods**.

<margin>P. 402.</margin>
That **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 210 AD), a prominent Greek physician and philosopher whose views dominated Western medical science for centuries.</note> was no atheist, and what his religion was, may plainly appear from this one passage out of his third book *On the Usefulness of Parts* <note>original: "De Usu Partium"</note>, to omit many others: <note>original: "ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἴσως εἰ ἐπὶ πλέον τοιούτων μνημονεύοιμι βοσκημάτων... δυνάμεως ἀηττήτου"</note> *Should I any longer insist upon such brutish persons as those, the wise and sober might justly condemn me as defiling this holy discourse, which I compose as a true hymn to the praise of him that made us. I conceive true piety and religion toward God to consist in this: not that I should sacrifice many Hecatombs* <term>A "hecatomb" was a grand public sacrifice of one hundred oxen in ancient Greece.</term>, *or burn much incense and cassia to him, but that I should myself first acknowledge, and then declare to others, how great his wisdom is, how great his power, and how great his goodness. For that he would adorn the whole world after this manner, begrudging nothing of that good which it was capable of receiving, I conclude to be a demonstration of most absolute goodness, and thus let him be praised by us as Good. And that he was able to find out how all things might be adorned in the best possible manner is a sign of the greatest wisdom in him. And lastly, to be able to effect and bring to pass all those things which he had thus decreed argues an insuperable power.*

**Maximus Tyrius** <note>A Greek philosopher and rhetorician of the 2nd century AD.</note>, in the close of his first Dissertation, gives us this short representation of his own theology: <note>original: "βούλομαι δέ σοι δεῖξαι τὸ λεγόμενον σαφεστέρα εἰκόνι. Ἐννόει μεγάλην ἀρχὴν καὶ βασιλείαν ἐῤῥωμένην πρὸς μίαν ψυχὴν βασιλέως τοῦ ἀρίστου καὶ πρεσβυτάτου συμπάντων νενευκότων ἑκόντων· ὁ-"</note> *I wish to show you what is meant by a clearer image. Imagine a great authority and a powerful kingdom centered on the single soul of a king—the best and oldest of all—whom everyone follows willingly; who—*

<summary>This page presents testimonies from Dio Chrysostom and the physician Galen, arguing that ancient Pagans possessed an innate belief in one supreme God despite their polytheism. Galen specifically describes his anatomical studies as a "true hymn" to the Creator's wisdom, power, and goodness.</summary>

# Chapter IV. Maximus Tyrius, Aristides

<note>original Greek: "ρον ἢ τ' ἀρχῆς ἐκ ἄλυν ποταμὸν, ἐδὲ ἑλλήσποντον, ἐδὲ τὴν μαιῶτιν, ἐδὲ τὰς ἐπὶ τῷ ὠκεανῷ ἠϊόνας· ἀλλὰ ἐρανὸν καὶ γῆν· τ μὲν ὑπὸ τῷ δ' ἔνερθεν· βασιλέα δὲ αὐτῷ δὴ τὸ μέγαν ἀτρεμοῦντα, ὥς πρ νόμον παρέχοντα τοῖς πειθομένοις, σωτηρίαν ὑπάρχου- σαν αὐτῷ, καὶ κοινωνὸς τῆς ἀρχῆς, πολλὰς μὲν ὁρατὰς θεὸς, πολλὰς δ' ἀφανεῖς· τὰς μὲν περὶ τὰ πρόθυρα αὐτὰ εἰλημμένους, οἷον εἰσαγγελέας τινὰς καὶ βασιλεῖς συγγενεστάτους, ὁμοτραπέζους αὐτοῖς καὶ συνεστίες· τὰς δὲ τόπων ὑπηρέτας, τὰς δ' ἐπὶ τᾶτων καταδεεσέρες· διαδοχὴν ὁρᾷς καὶ τάξιν ἀρχῆς καταβαίνουσαν ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ μέχρι γῆς:"</note>

*I will now more plainly declare my sense by this comparison. Imagine in your mind a great and powerful kingdom or principality, in which all the rest freely and with one consent agree to direct their actions according to the will and command of one Supreme King, the oldest and the best. And then suppose the boundaries and limits of this empire are not the River Halys <note>The Halys River (modern Kızılırmak) was a major boundary in ancient Anatolia.</note>, nor the Hellespont, nor the Maeotian Lake <note>The Sea of Azov.</note>, nor the shores of the ocean, but heaven above and the earth beneath. Here, then, let that great King sit immovable, prescribing laws to all his subjects, in which their safety and security consist. The partners of his empire are many gods, both visible and invisible; some of those nearest to him and immediately attending him are in the highest royal dignity, feasting, as it were, at the same table with him. Others, again, are their ministers and attendants, and a third sort are inferior to them both. And thus you see how the order and chain of this government descends by steps and degrees from the Supreme God to the earth and men.*

In this comparison, we have a plain acknowledgment of one Supreme God, the monarch of the whole world, and three subordinate ranks of inferior gods serving as his ministers in the government of the world. The writer also calls these <note>original: "θεοὺς θεοῦ παῖδας, καὶ φίλους"</note> *gods the sons and friends of God.*

**Aristides**, the famous orator and intellectual <term>The original calls him a "Sophist," which in this era referred to a highly respected professional public speaker and teacher of rhetoric.</term> from the time of Hadrian, is perfectly clear on this point in his first oration (or hymn) dedicated to **Jupiter** after surviving a great storm. After his introduction, he begins like this:

<note>original Greek: "Ζεὺς τὰ πάντα ἐποίησε, καὶ Διός ἐστιν ἔργα ὅσα ἐστὶ πάντα, καὶ ποταμὸς, καὶ γῆ, καὶ θάλαττα, καὶ ἐρανὸς· καὶ ὅσα τότων μεταξὺ ἄνω, καὶ ὅσα ὑπὸ ταῦτα· καὶ θεοὶ καὶ ἄνθρωποι, καὶ ὅσα ψυχὴν ἔχει, καὶ ὅσα εἰς ὄψιν ἀφικνεῖται, καὶ ὅσα δεῖ νοήσει λαβεῖν. Ἐποίησε δὲ πρῶτος αὐτὸς ἑαυτόν· ἐν Κρήτης ἐν εὐώδεσιν ἄντροις τραφείς· οὐδ' ἐμέλλησεν αὐτὸν Κρόνος καταπιεῖν· ἀντ' ἀντ' ἐκεῖνο λίθον κατέπιεν, οὐδ' ἐκινδύνευσε Ζεὺς, οὐδὲ μήποτε κινδυνεύσει· οὐδ' ἔστι πρεσβύτερόν οὐδὲν Διός· οὐ μᾶλλόν γε ἢ υἱεῖς τε πατέρων πρεσβύτεροι γέ- νοιτ' ἂν, καὶ τὰ γινόμενα τῶν ποιύντων· ἀλλ' οὗδε ἐστὶ πρῶτός τε καὶ πρεσβύ- τατος, καὶ ἀρχηγέτης τῶν πάντων· αὐτὸς ἐξ αὑτοῦ γενόμενος· ὁπότε δὲ ἐγένετο, οὐκ ἔστιν εἰπεῖν ἀλλ' ἦντε ἄρα ἐξ ἀρχῆς καὶ ἔσαι εἰσαεί, αὐτοπάτωρ τε καὶ μεί- ζων ἢ ἐξ ἄλλου γεγονέναι. Καὶ ὥσπερ τὴν Ἀθηνᾶν ἄρα ἐκ τῆς κεφαλῆς ἔφυσε, καὶ γάμου οὐδὲν προσεδεήθη εἰς αὐτὴν, ὅτως ἔτι πρότερον αὐτὸς ἑαυτὸν ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ ἐποίησε, καὶ οὐδὲν προσεδεήθη ἑτέρου εἰς τὸ εἶναι· ἀλλ' αὐτὸ τἀναντίον πάντα εἶναι ἀπ' ἐκείνου ἤρξατο, καὶ οὐκ ἔστι χρόνον εἰπεῖν· Οὔτε γὰρ χρόνος ἦν πω τότε ὅτε μηδὲ ἄλλο μηδέν· δημιουργοῦ γὰρ ἔργον οὐδέν ἐστι πρεσβύτερον· ὅτω δὴ ἀρχὴ μὲν ἁπάν- των Ζεὺς καὶ ἐκ Διὸς πάντα, ἅτε δὲ ὢν χρόνου τε κρείττων, καὶ οὐδένα ἔχων τὸν ἀν- τικόψοντα, αὐτός τε ὁμοῦ καὶ ὁ κόσμος ἦν, οὕτω ταχὺ πάντα ἐποίησε, ἐποίησε δὲ ὧδε, &c."</note>

*Jupiter made all things, and all things whatsoever exist are the works of Jupiter: rivers, and earth, and sea, and heaven; everything between them above, and everything beneath them. He made gods and men, and everything that has a soul, everything that can be seen, and everything that must be understood by the mind. He first made himself. Though the myth says he was raised in the fragrant caves of Crete, Cronus never really swallowed him; instead, Cronus swallowed a stone. Jupiter was never in danger, nor will he ever be. Nothing is older than Jupiter, no more than sons could be older than their fathers, or created things older than their creators. Rather, he is the first and the oldest, the originator of all things, having come from himself. When he came into being cannot be said; rather, he was there from the beginning and shall be forever—his own father, and greater than if he had been born from another. And just as he produced Athena from his head and needed no marriage to conceive her, even earlier he made himself from himself and needed no other for his existence. On the contrary, all things began to exist from him, and no specific time can be named for this. For there was no time yet when nothing else existed; no work of a creator is older than the creator himself. Thus, Jupiter is the beginning of all things and all things are from Jupiter. Since he is superior to time and has no opponent, he and the world existed together; he made all things so quickly...*

<sig>Yy 2</sig>

<summary>This page presents excerpts from Maximus Tyrius and Aelius Aristides to show that these Pagan thinkers viewed Jupiter (the Supreme God) as a self-created, eternal monarch who governs a hierarchy of subordinate gods and the entire universe.</summary>

## Plotinus; The Divinity Book I.

*...are between these, and gods and men and all animals—whatever is perceivable either by sense or by the mind. But Jupiter, first of all <margin>How God was said to be self-made: See pages 405 and 406.</margin> made himself; for he was not raised in the flowery and fragrant <note>original: odoriferous</note> caves of Crete, nor was Saturn ever about to devour him, nor did he swallow a stone instead of him. For Jupiter was never in danger, nor will he ever be in danger of anything. Neither is there anything older than Jupiter, any more than there are sons older than their parents or works older than their craftsmen <note>original: Opificers</note>. But he is the first and the oldest, and the prince of all things, having been made from himself. It cannot be declared when he was made, for he was from the beginning and ever will be his own father—greater than to have been begotten from another. Just as he produced Minerva from his brain and needed no marriage for that purpose, so before this did he produce himself from himself, needing the help of no other thing for his existence. But on the contrary, all things began to exist from him, and no man can tell the time; since there was then no time when there was nothing else besides him, and no work can be older than its maker. Thus was Jupiter the beginning of all things, and all things were from Jupiter, who is better than Time, which had its beginning together with the world. And again, <note>original Greek: ὡς ἡ καὶ θεῶν ὅσα φῦλα ἀποῤῥοὴ τοῦ Διὸς τοῦ πάντων πατρὸς δυνάμεως ἕκαστα ἔχει, καὶ ἀτεχνῶς κατὰ τὴν Ὁμήρου σειρὰν, ἅπαντα εἰς αὐτὸν διήρτηται, καὶ πάντα ἐξ αὐτοῦ ἐξῆπται· ἔρωτά τε καὶ ἀνάγκην δύο τούτω συναγωγότατα καὶ ἰσχυροτάτω ἐν τοῖς πρώτοις ἐγέννησεν, ὅπως αὐτὰ τὰ πάντα συνέχοιεν, &c. ἐποίει θεὸς μὲν, ἀνθρώπων ἐπιμελητὰς, ἀνθρώπους δὲ θεῶν θεραπευτὰς τε καὶ ὑπηρέτας, &c. πάντα δὲ πανταχοῦ Διὸς μεστὰ, καὶ ἁπάντων θεῶν εὐεργεσίαι, Διὸς εἰσὶν ἔργον, &c.</note> "Just as all the various races of the gods are an outflow and derivation from the power of Jupiter, the father of all, and—strictly according to Homer's Chain <note>A classical metaphor from the Iliad representing the hierarchical connection of all things to the divine.</note>—all things are suspended from him and all things are attached to him; he produced Love and Necessity among the first, these two most unifying and powerful forces, so that they might hold all things together, etc. God made the gods to be the caretakers of men, and men to be the worshippers and servants of those gods, etc. All things everywhere are full of Jupiter, and the benefits of all the other gods are Jupiter's work, etc." All the several kinds of gods are but an outflow <note>original: Defluxion</note> and derivation from Jupiter, and according to Homer’s Chain, all things are connected with him and depend upon him. He, among the first, produced Love and Necessity, the two most powerful binders of things together, so that they might make all things firmly cohere. He made gods to be the caretakers of men, and he made men to be the worshippers and servants of those gods. All things are everywhere full of Jupiter, and the benefits of all the other gods are his work and are to be attributed to him, being done in compliance with the order he had prescribed for them.*

It is certain that all the later philosophers after the rise of Christianity—whether Platonists or Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note>—though for the most part they asserted the eternity of the world, yet universally agreed in acknowledging one Supreme Deity, the cause of the whole world and of all the other gods. And as Numenius, Plotinus, Amelius, Porphyry, Proclus, Damascius, and others also held a Trinity of divine <term>Hypostases</term> <note>Hypostases refers to the three fundamental substances or persons in the Neoplatonic Trinity: The One (the Good), Intellect (Nous), and Soul (Psyche).</note>, some of those philosophers had excellent contemplations concerning <margin>Enneads, Book 2, Chapter 9, Section 9.</margin> the Deity, particularly Plotinus. Although he derived matter and all things from one divine principle, he was still an advocate for many gods. Thus, in his book written against the Gnostics: <note>original Greek: χρὴ ὡς ἄριστον μὲν αὐτὸν πειρᾶσθαι γίνεσθαι, μὴ μόνον δὲ αὐτὸν νομίζειν ἄριστον δύνασθαι γένεσθαι, οὕτω γὰρ οὔπω ἄριστος, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀνθρώπους ἄλλους ἀρίστους, ἔτι δὲ δαίμονας ἀγαθοὺς εἶναι· πολὺ δὲ μᾶλλον θεοὺς, τούς τε ἐν τῷδε ὄντας κἀκεῖ βλέποντας· πάντων δὲ μάλιστα τὸν ἡγεμόνα τοῦδε τοῦ παντὸς, ψυχὴν μακαριωτάτην· ἐντεῦθεν δὲ ἤδη καὶ τοὺς νοητοὺς ὑμνεῖν θεοὺς, ὑφ' ἅπασι δὲ ἤδη,</note> "One must strive to become as good as possible, but not to think that he alone can be good (for then he is not yet the best), but also that there are other good men, and even more, good spirits, and much more, gods—both those in this world and those who look toward the higher realm. And above all, one should praise the leader of this whole universe, the most blessed Soul; and from there, already sing hymns to the intelligible gods <note>In Neoplatonism, "intelligible gods" are divine beings existing in the realm of the Intellect, rather than the physical world.</note>, and then under them all..."

<summary>This page discusses the Neoplatonic conception of God (Jupiter) as a self-caused being from whom all other gods and the universe originate. It highlights that later philosophers like Plotinus, while acknowledging many deities, maintained the existence of one supreme source and a divine hierarchy.</summary>

### CHAP. IV. Not to be Contracted into One.

<note>original Greek: τὸν μέγαν τὸν ἐκεῖ βασιλέα · καὶ ἐν τῷ πλήθει μάλιστα τῶν Θεῶν, τὸ μέγα αὐτοῦ ἐνδείκνυσθαι. οὐ γὰρ τὸ συστεῖλαι εἰς ἕν, ἀλλὰ τὸ δεῖξαι πολὺ τὸ θεῖον ὅσον ἔδειξεν αὐτὸς, τουτέστι δύναμιν Θεοῦ εἰδότων, ὅταν μένων ὃς ἔστι, πολλοὺς ποιῇ, πάντας εἰς αὐτὸν ἀνηρτημένους, καὶ δι᾽ ἐκεῖνον καὶ παρ᾽ ἐκείνου ὄντας · καὶ ὁ κόσμος ὅδε δι᾽ ἐκεῖνον ἔστι κἀκεῖ βλέπει, καὶ πᾶς, καὶ Θεῶν ἕκαστος ·</note>

*Every man ought to strive with all his might to become as good as possible, but yet not to think himself to be the only thing that is good. He should recognize that there are also other good men in the world, and good demons <note>The word "demon" here refers to "daimons," intermediary spirits or divine beings in Greek philosophy, rather than evil spirits.</note>, but much more so gods: who, though inhabiting this inferior world, still look up to that superior world; and most of all, the Prince of this Universe, that most happy soul. From there he ought to ascend yet higher and praise those intelligible gods, but above all that great King and Monarch; declaring his greatness and majesty by the multitude of gods who are under him. For it is not the part of those who know the power of God to contract all into one, but to show forth all that divinity which he himself has displayed. Remaining one, he creates many depending on him, who exist by him and from him. For this whole world exists by him and looks up perpetually to him, as does every one of the gods within it.* 

And **Themistius** the Peripatetic <note>A follower of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note> (who was so far from being a Christian that, as **Petavius** <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), a prominent French Jesuit theologian.</note> probably conjectures, he criticizes <note>original: perstringes</note> our Savior Christ under the name of **Empedocles** for making himself a **God**) does not only affirm that one and the same **Supreme God** was worshipped by Pagans, Christians, and all nations, though in different manners; but also that God was delighted with this **Variety of Religions**: 

<margin>Orat. 12.</margin> <note>original Greek: ταύτῃ νόμιζε γάννυσθαι τῇ ποικιλίᾳ τὸν τοῦ παντὸς ἀρχηγέτην · ἄλλως Σύρος ἐθέλει πολιτεύεσθαι, ἄλλως Ἕλληνας, ἄλλως Αἰγυπτίους, καὶ οὐδ᾽ αὐτὸς Σύρος ὁμοίως, ἀλλ᾽ ἤδη κατακεκερμάτισαι εἰς μικρά ·</note>

*Believe that the Author and Prince of the Universe seems to be delighted with this variety of worship. He would have the Syrians worship him one way, the Greeks another, and the Egyptians another; neither do the Syrians (or Christians) themselves all agree, as they are subdivided into many sects.*

We shall conclude, therefore, with this full testimony of **St. Cyril**, in <margin>P. 23.</margin> his *First* Book against **Julian** <note>The Emperor Julian the Apostate, who attempted to revive Paganism.</note>: 

<note>original Greek: ἅπασιν ἐναργές, ὅτι καὶ τοῖς τὰ Ἑλλήνων φιλοσοφεῖν εἰωθόσιν, ἕνα μὲν ἐδόκει θεὸν εἶναι συνομολογεῖν, τὸν τῶν ὅλων δημιουργὸν, καὶ πάντων ἐπέκεινα κατὰ φύσιν, πεποιῆσθαι δὲ παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ, καὶ παρῆχθαι πρὸς γένεσιν ἑτέρους τινὰς θεοὺς, καθὰ φασὶν αὐτοὶ, νοητούς τε καὶ αἰσθητούς ·</note>

*It is manifest to all that among those who study Greek philosophy, it is universally acknowledged that there is one God, the maker of the universe, who is by nature above all things; but that there have been made by him, and produced into existence, certain other gods (as they call them), both intelligible and sensible <note>Meaning gods understood by the mind and those visible in the physical world, like the stars.</note>.*

XXVII. Neither was this the opinion of philosophers and learned men only among the Pagans, but even of the common people <note>original: Vulgar</note> also. We do not pretend to account for the most foolish <note>original: sottish</note> common people among them, who considered their religion very little; they probably did not understand that mystery of the Pagan theology (to be explained later) that many of their gods were nothing but different names and concepts of one Supreme Deity, according to its various manifestations and *effects*. It cites Plotinus, Themistius, and St. Cyril of Alexandria to show that polytheism was often seen as a way to express the vastness of one God's power rather than a denial of His unity.</summary>

### THE COMMON PAGANS ACKNOWLEDGED ONE SUPREME GOD, BOOK 1.

...receive this tradition of one Supreme God, which remained current among the generality of the Greek and Latin Pagans at least, whether **learned** or **unlearned**. We can best judge the opinions of the <term>common people</term> <note>original: "Vulgar"; referring to the general public or uneducated masses rather than something offensive.</note> and the general population of the ancient Pagans by looking at the poets and mythologists, who were their primary instructors. 

Thus **Aristotle**, in his *Politics*, writing <margin>Book 8, chapter 5.</margin> about music, judges men's opinions concerning the gods based on the poets: "We may learn what opinion men have concerning the gods from this: the poets never depict Jupiter singing or playing an instrument." <note>original Greek: σκοπεῖν δ' ἔξεστι τὴν ὑπόληψιν ἣν ἔχομεν περὶ τῶν θεῶν, ὅτι ὁ Ζεὺς αὐτὸς ᾄδει καὶ κιθαρίζει τοῖς ποιηταῖς</note>

Now, we have already proved through various testimonies of the poets that (even though they corrupted the Pagan religion in other ways) they maintained this tradition of one Supreme Deity, one **King** and **Father** of **Gods**. Many more testimonies could have been added—such as from Seneca the tragedian, Statius, Lucan, Silius Italicus, Persius, and Martial—but we declined them at the time to avoid being tedious. Therefore, we shall content ourselves here with this affirmation from **Dio Chrysostomus** concerning the theology of the poets: <margin>Speech 36, page 447</margin> 

"All the poets, in summary, call the first and greatest God 'the Father' of the entire rational race, and also its 'King.' Following the <insert>teachings</insert> of the poets, men build altars to King Jupiter and do not hesitate to call him 'Father' in their prayers." <note>original Greek: ὅτι δ' οὖν πάντες οἱ ποιηταὶ κατὰ ταῦτα, τὸν πρῶτον καὶ μέγιστον θεὸν πατέρα καλοῦσι συλλήβδην ἅπαντος τοῦ λογικοῦ γένους, καὶ δὴ καὶ βασιλέα· οἷς πειθόμενοι οἱ ἄνθρωποι Διὸς βασιλέως ἱδρύονται βωμούς· καὶ δὴ καὶ πατέρα αὐτὸν οὐκ ὀκνοῦσι προσαγορεύειν ταῖς εὐχαῖς</note>

Furthermore, **Aristotle** himself recorded this in his *Politics*: "All men say that the gods are ruled by a kingly power," <note>original Greek: πάντες λέγουσι θεοὺς βασιλεύεσθαι</note> or that there is one Supreme King and Monarch over the gods. And **Maximus Tyrius** declares that both the unlearned and the learned throughout the whole Pagan world universally agreed that there was one *Supreme God*, the *Father* of all the other gods: <margin>Dissertation 1, pages 4, 5.</margin>

"If you were to gather an assembly of these several trades and professions—a painter, a sculptor <note>original: "Statuary"</note>, a poet, and a philosopher—and all of them were required to declare their views concerning God, do you think that the painter would say one thing, the sculptor another, the poet another, and the philosopher another? No, by Zeus! Neither would the Scythian <note>original: "Scythes"; ancient nomadic people of Central Eurasia.</note>, nor the Greek, nor the Persian, nor the inhabitant of the far north <note>original: "Hyperborean."</note>. Rather, you would see that in some matters people vote for one thing and in others another, and that they differ from one another in almost everything. Good is not the same for everyone, nor is evil similar, nor the ugly, nor the beautiful. For law and justice are tossed up and down, torn and mangled. It is not just that one nation disagrees with another in these matters, but even city with city, household with household, man with man, and even a man with himself. Yet, in the midst of so much war, factionalism, and discord, you would see one harmonious law and reason across the entire earth: that **GOD IS THE ONE KING AND FATHER OF ALL**, and there are many gods, children of God, who rule alongside Him. This the Greek says, and the foreigner <note>original: "barbaros"; in ancient Greek, this referred to anyone who did not speak Greek.</note> says; the person from the mainland and the person from the sea; the wise and the unwise." <note>original Greek: Εἰ συναγαγὼν ἐκκλησίαν τῶν τεχνῶν τούτων, κελεύσεις ἅπαντας ἀθρόους διὰ ψηφίσματος ἑνὸς ἀποκρίνασθαι περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ, οἴει ἄλλο μὲν ἂν τὸν γραφέα εἰπεῖν, ἄλλο δὲ τὸν ἀγαλματοποιὸν, καὶ τὸν ποιητὴν ἄλλο, καὶ τὸν φιλόσοφον ἄλλο; ἀλλ' οὐδὲ μὰ Δία τὸν Σκύθην, οὐδὲ τὸν Ἕλληνα, οὐδὲ τὸν Πέρσην, ἢ τὸν Ὑπερβόρειον· ἀλλὰ ἴδοις ἂν ἐν μὲν τοῖς ἄλλα, ἐν δὲ τοῖς ἄλλα, καὶ τὰ ταῦτα ψηφιζομένους τοὺς ἀνθρώπους, πάντας δὲ πᾶσι διαφερομένους· καὶ τὸ ἀγαθὸν οὐ πᾶσι, τὸ δὲ κακὸν ὅμοιον, οὐ τὸ αἰσχρὸν, οὐ τὸ καλόν· νόμος μὲν γὰρ δὴ καὶ δίκη ἄνω καὶ κάτω φέρεται διασπώμενα καὶ σπαρασσόμενα· μὴ γὰρ ὅτι γένος γένει ὁμολογεῖ ἐν τούτοις, ἀλλ' οὐδὲ πόλις πόλει, ἀλλ' οὐδὲ οἶκος οἴκῳ, οὐδὲ ἀνὴρ ἀνδρὶ, οὐδὲ αὐτὸς αὑτῷ· ἐν τοσούτῳ δὲ πολέμῳ καὶ στάσει καὶ διαφωνίᾳ, ἕνα ἴδοις ἂν ἐν πάσῃ γῇ ὁμόφωνον νόμον καὶ λόγον, ὅτι ΘΕΟΣ ΕΙΣ ΠΑΝΤΩΝ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΥΣ ΚΑΙ ΠΑΤΗΡ, καὶ θεοὶ πολλοὶ θεοῦ παῖδες, συνάρχοντες θεῷ· ταῦτα δὲ ὁ Ἕλλην λέγει καὶ ὁ βάρβαρος λέγει, καὶ ὁ ἠπειρώτης καὶ ὁ θαλάττιος, καὶ ὁ σοφὸς καὶ ὁ ἄσοφος</note>

This consensus is supported by the writings of poets, the observations of Aristotle, and the philosophical claims of Maximus Tyrius regarding a global, harmonious understanding of divine hierarchy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that while human laws and customs vary wildly, the belief in one Supreme God is a universal intuition shared by all mankind. It specifically provides evidence of this consensus among different ancient nations and their various names for the same Supreme Deity. The catchword "Origen" at the bottom of the OCR suggests the next page will involve the writings of the church father Origen.</meta>

...nor the **Hyperborean** <note>A mythical people who lived in the far north "beyond the North Wind."</note>. In other matters, we find people speaking very inconsistently with one another, almost as if everyone disagreed with everyone else. The same things are not considered "good" or "evil" by everyone, nor are they consistently seen as "honorable" or "dishonorable." For law and justice themselves vary everywhere; not only do nations disagree with each other, but cities, households, and even individuals differ—and ultimately, a person may even disagree with their own self. 

Yet, amid all this conflict, contention, and discord, you will find one consistent law and opinion throughout the whole world: **THAT THERE IS ONE GOD, THE KING AND FATHER OF ALL**, and **many gods**, who are the **sons of God** and **reign alongside Him**. Both the Greeks and the barbarians <note>original: "Barbarian"; in antiquity, this referred to any non-Greek speaker, not necessarily someone uncivilized.</note> affirm this, as do those living on the continents and on the coasts, the wise and the unlearned alike. 

Nothing could be more complete than this testimony from **Maximus Tyrius**, showing that the majority of the Pagan world—both the common, uneducated people and the wise and learned—agreed that there was **one Supreme God**, the **Creator** and **Governor** of **all**. **Dio Chrysostomus** offered a similar testimony cited earlier: <margin>Speech 12, page 201.</margin> "Regarding the general nature of the gods, and especially regarding the ruler of all things, there is one common opinion and conception held by the entire human race, shared equally by Greeks and barbarians." <note>original Greek: Περὶ δὲ θεῶν τῆς τε καθόλου φύσεως, καὶ μάλιστα τοῦ πάντων ἡγεμόνος, δόξα καὶ ἐπίνοια κοινὴ τοῦ ξύμπαντος ἀνθρωπίνου γένους, ὁμοίως δὲ Ἑλλήνων, ὁμοίως δὲ βαρβάρων</note> In this passage, **Dio** clearly suggests that there was an even more universal agreement among nations regarding the belief in **one God** than there was regarding the belief in **many gods**.

It has already been noted that various Pagan nations commonly had their own unique names for the **one Supreme God**. Just as the Greeks called Him **Zeus** or **Zen**, and the Latins called Him **Jupiter** or **Jovis**, the Egyptians, Africans, and Arabians called Him **Hammon**. Therefore, the Greeks referred to Hammon as "the African Zeus," and the Latins called Him "the African Jupiter." This is why **Cicero** writes in *On the Nature of the Gods*: "The appearance of the Capitoline Jupiter to us is one thing, and the appearance of the African Jupiter Ammon is another." <note>original Latin: Jovis Capitolini Nobis alia species, alia Afris Ammonis Jovis</note> 

As **Herodotus** tells us, the name for the **Scythian Jupiter** was **Pappæus**, which means "**Father**." The **Persians** likewise had their **ancestral Zeus** <note>original Greek: Ζεὺς πατρῷος</note>, as **Xenophon** describes Him—their national Zeus or Jupiter (namely **Mithras** or **Oromasdes**). In the same writings of Xenophon, He is distinguished from the Sun; and in the proclamation of **Cyrus** in the Bible <note>referring to the Book of Ezra 1:2</note>, He is called "**the Lord God of Heaven, who had given him all the kingdoms of the earth**." 

Similarly, **Berosus** (a priest of his) declared that the Babylonian **Bel** was the **God** who created heaven and earth. Learned men also believe that **Baal** (which is the same as **Bel** and means "**Lord**") was originally a name for the Supreme God among the Phoenicians as well—the Creator of heaven and earth, sometimes called **Beelsamen**, or "**the Lord of Heaven**." Likewise, **Molech** (which means "**King**") was the **king of the gods** among the Ammonites. **Marnas** (the chief god of the people of Gaza, who were Philistines) means "**the Lord of men**"; it was from this deity that the Cretans derived their **Jupiter**, whom they called the "**Father of gods and men**."

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how early Christian fathers viewed Pagan monotheism, specifically focusing on whether the names of Pagan deities—specifically the Roman Jupiter—could be applied to the Supreme God of Christianity.</meta>

# The Roman and Samothracian BOOK 1.

**Origen** <note>A prominent early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 184–253 AD).</note> indeed argued that it was not lawful for Christians to call the Supreme God by any of those Pagan names. He likely did so for these reasons: because those names were then frequently given to idols, and because they were contaminated and defiled by absurd and impure myths. Nevertheless, that learned Father does acknowledge that the Pagans really meant <term>The God over all</term> <note>original Greek: Θεὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσιν</note> by those various names. 

However, **Lactantius Firmianus** <note>An early Christian author (c. 250–325 AD) who became an advisor to the first Christian Roman emperor, Constantine I.</note> would by no means allow this regarding the Roman **Jupiter** worshipped in the Capitol. He endeavored to refute it in this manner: <margin>Book 1, chapter 11.</margin> *It is a vain belief of those who give the name of Jupiter to the Supreme God. For some are accustomed to defend their errors in this way: when they have been convinced of the existence of one God and cannot deny it, they claim they worship Him, but choose to call Him Jupiter. What could be more absurd? For Jupiter is not usually worshipped without the partnership of his wife and daughter. From this it clearly appears what this Jupiter is; it is not right for that name to be transferred to a place where there is neither a Minerva nor a Juno.* 

The basis for this argument by Lactantius was that the great Capitoline Temple of Jupiter had three <term>small chapels</term> <note>original: "sacella"</note> or lesser shrines within it, all contained under one roof: Jupiter's in the middle, Minerva's on the right hand, and Juno's on the left, according to the words of the poet:

->Threefold partners shine in the Tarpeian Temple.<-
<note>original Latin: "Trina in Tarpeio fulgent consortia Templo." The Tarpeian Rock was part of the Capitoline Hill in Rome.</note>

According to poetic theology, this **Juno** is said to be the wife of Jupiter, and **Minerva** is his daughter—born not from Juno, but from his own brain. Here it is plain that there is a certain mixture of *mythical* or *poetic* theology along with *natural* theology, as there was almost everywhere else, to make up the *civil* (state) theology of the Pagans. 

But here—according to the more deep and secret doctrine of the Pagans—these three Capitoline gods (Jupiter, Minerva, and Juno), as well as some others, may be understood to have been nothing more than *different names and concepts* for **One Supreme Deity**, according to His various attributes and manifestations. In this view:
* **Jupiter** signifies the Divine Power and Sovereignty, seated and enthroned in the heavens.
* **Minerva** signifies the Divine Wisdom and Understanding.
* **Juno** signifies the same Deity acting in the lower parts of the world. 

Unless, instead, we follow **Macrobius** <note>A Roman provincial writer and philosopher (fl. early 5th century AD) known for his Neoplatonic interpretations of mythology.</note> and interpret them all three through natural physics. He would make **Minerva** the *higher heaven*, **Jupiter** the *middle ether*, and **Juno** the *lower air and earth*, all of which are animated—that is, *one God* acting differently in these three regions of the world. However, this seems less appropriate, because it would place Minerva above Jupiter.

### CHAP. IV. The Trinity; or the Cabiri.

Nevertheless, it may be reasonably suspected—as **G. J. Vossius** <note>Gerardus Johannes Vossius (1577–1649), a prominent Dutch scholar and theologian.</note> has already observed—that there was a higher and more sacred mystery intended in this Capitoline Trinity: namely, a **Trinity of Divine Hypostases** <note>The term "hypostasis" refers to the distinct "persons" or "subsistences" within the one Godhead.</note>. For these three Roman or Capitoline Gods were said to have been first brought into Italy out of Phrygia by the Trojans. Before that, they were brought into Phrygia by Dardanus from the island of Samothrace, roughly eight hundred years after the Great Flood (if we may believe **Eusebius** <note>An early Christian historian and bishop (c. 260–339 AD).</note>). 

In Latin, these were called the *Dii Penates* <note>Household or inner gods.</note>, which **Macrobius** <note>A Roman provincial of the early 5th century known for his encyclopedic writings.</note> interprets as, "The Gods through whom we deeply breathe, through whom we have our bodies, and through whom we possess the reason of our minds" <note>original Latin: *Dii Per quos Penitus spiramus, per quos habemus Corpus, per quos rationem animi possidemus*</note>. That is, "the Gods in whom we live, and move, and have our being." **Varro** (quoted in **Arnobius** <note>A Christian apologist of the 4th century.</note>) calls them "The Gods who are within, and in the most inward recesses of heaven" <note>original Latin: *Dii qui sunt Intrinsecus, atque in Intimis Penetralibus Cæli*</note>. 

Similarly, they were called by the Samothracians the *Cabiri* (Greek: Κάβειροι), which Varro rightly interprets as "Powerful Gods" or "Mighty Gods" (Greek: Θεοὶ δυνατοί; Latin: *Divi Potes*). The name *Cabiri* is clearly the Hebrew word *Kabirim* <note>original Hebrew: כבירים, meaning "mighty ones"</note>. This gives a just reason to suspect that this ancient tradition of Three Divine Hypostases—unquestionably accepted by Orpheus, Pythagoras, and Plato among the Greeks, and probably by the Egyptians and Persians—originally sprang from the Hebrews. 

The first of these Divine Hypostases, called **Jove**, is the Fountain of the Godhead. The second, called by the Latins **Minerva**, fitly expresses the Divine **Logos** <note>The "Word" or "Wisdom" of God.</note>. Varro interprets Minerva as that in which "the ideas and first patterns of things were contained" <note>original Latin: *Ideæ & Exempla rerum*</note>. <margin>*On the Theology of the Gentiles, Book 8, chapter 12.*</margin> The third is **Juno**, called "the love and delight of Jove" <note>original Latin: *Amor ac Delicium Jovis*</note>, which Vossius thinks corresponds well enough to the Divine Spirit.

<margin>*P. 63.*</margin> But **Lactantius** has yet another objection against the Roman Jupiter being the Supreme God:
> *What if we add that the nature of this name, Jupiter, does not express a Divine power, but only a human one? Cicero interprets both Jove and Juno as being named from the act of "helping" (Latin: à Juvando). And Jupiter is named as if he were a "Helping Father" (Latin: Juvans Pater). This name is not at all appropriate for God, because helping is something humans do, etc. No one prays to God merely to "help" him, but to "save" him, etc. Nor is a father said to "help" the son he fathered. Therefore, he is not only ignorant but also impious who, by using the name Jove or Jupiter, diminishes the power of the Supreme Authority.* <note>original Latin: *Quid? quod hujus nominis proprietas, non Divinam vim sed Humanam exprimit? Jovem enim Junonemque à Juvando esse dictos Cicero interpretatur. Et Jupiter quasi Juvans Pater dicitur. Quod nomen in Deum minimè convenit, quia Juvare hominis est, &c. Nemo sic Deum precatur, ut se Adjuvet, sed ut Servet, &c. Ergo non Imperitus modo, sed etiam Impius est, qui nomine Jovis Virtutem Summæ Potestatis imminuit.*</note>

But while this argument by Lactantius seems weak enough on its own, its foundation is absolutely ruinous. The true origin of the name **Jupiter** (though Cicero did not know it) is certainly not *Juvans Pater* ("Helping Father"), but *Jovis Pater*, or "Father Jove," the Father of Gods and Men. The name *Jovis* is actually the Hebrew **Tetragrammaton** <note>The four-letter holy name of God in Hebrew (YHWH), often rendered as Jehovah or Yahweh.</note> (however the Romans came by it), only altered by a Latin ending. Therefore, as there could be...

# The Capitoline Jupiter Book I

There is no impiety at all in calling the Supreme God *Jove* or *Jovis*, as it is that very name which God himself chose to be called by. <note>original: "Jove/Jovis". The author is suggesting a phonetic and etymological connection between the Latin "Jovis" and the Hebrew Tetragrammaton, "Yahweh" or "Jehovah."</note> Likewise, there is no reason why the Latins should not mean the Supreme God by that name, just as the Greeks unquestionably did by *Zeus*, which will be proved later from irrefutable authority.

This is especially clear if we consider that the common Roman people typically bestowed these two epithets upon the Capitoline *Jupiter* (meaning not the senseless statue, but the God who was worshipped through that material statue): *Optimus* and *Maximus*, or *the Best and the Greatest*. By this, they signified him to be a Being who is *infinitely good and powerful*. Thus **Cicero** writes in his *On the Nature of the Gods*: "That same Jupiter who is called by the poets 'The Father of Gods and Men' is called by our ancestors 'The Best and the Greatest'." <note>original Latin: *Jupiter à Poetis dicitur Divum atque Hominum Pater, à majoribus autem noſtris Optimus Maximus*</note> And in his *Speech for Sextus Roscius*: "Jupiter the Best and Greatest, by whose nod and command the heavens, the earth, and the seas are governed." <note>original Latin: *Jupiter Optimus Maximus, cujus nutu & arbitrio, Cælum, Terra, Mariaque reguntur*</note>

So too, the younger **Pliny**, in his *Panegyric* oration, says: "The Father of men and gods is worshipped under the name, first of the Best, and then of the Greatest." <note>original Latin: *Parens Hominum Deorumque, Optimi prius, deinde Maximi nomine colitur*</note> Moreover, **Servius Honoratus** informs us that the high priests <term>original: "Pontifices"</term> in their public sacrifices were accustomed to address Jupiter with these words: "Omnipotent Jupiter, or by whatever other name you wish to be called." <note>original Latin: *Omnipotens Jupiter, ſeu quo alio nomine appellari volueris*</note> From this, it is plain that the Romans, under the name of *Jupiter*, worshipped the Omnipotent God.

According to **Seneca**, the ancient Etruscans <note>original: "Hetrurians". An ancient civilization in Italy known for their complex religious rituals and influence on Roman religion.</note>—whom he distinguishes from philosophers as a kind of illiterate and superstitious people—held this very same notion of the word *Jupiter*: namely, that of the Supreme Monarch of the Universe. He writes: "These things are common to both the Etruscans and philosophers; they differ only in this point." <note>original Latin: *Hæc adhuc Etruſcis & Philoſophis communia ſunt, in illo diſſentiunt*</note>

<margin>Seneca, *Natural Questions*, Book 2, chapter 41.</margin> First, Seneca sets down their tradition concerning thunderbolts in this manner: "The Etruscans say that thunderbolts are sent by Jupiter, and they assign three 'hands' <note>original: *manubias*. In Roman divination, this referred to different categories or 'handfuls' of lightning bolts.</note> to him. The first, as they say, warns and is peaceful, and is sent by Jupiter's own decision. The second Jupiter sends, but only by the advice and consensus of a Council; for he calls together the twelve gods, and so on. The third Jupiter also sends, but only after calling a Council of those whom they call the 'Superior' and 'Involved' Gods <note>original: *Superiores & Involutos*. These were mysterious, high-ranking deities in Etruscan mythology who were rarely named.</note>; this bolt utterly wastes and destroys both private and public states." <note>original Latin: *Fulmina dicunt à Jove mitti, & tres illi manubias dant. Prima (ut aiunt) monet & placata eſt, & ipſius conſilio Jovis mittitur. Secundam quidem mittit Jupiter, ſed ex Conſilii ſententiâ; Duodecim enim Deos advocat, &c. Tertiam idem Jupiter mittit, ſed adhibitis in Conſilium Diis quos Superiores & Involutos vocant, quæ vaſtat, &c.*</note>

Seneca then provides a commentary on this old Etruscan doctrine, explaining that it was not to be taken literally. Instead, it was meant to impress awe upon men and to signify that Jupiter himself intended nothing but good. It suggested that he inflicts evil not by himself, but only in partnership with others and when the necessity of the case requires it. Finally, he adds: "They [the Etruscans] did not even believe that Jupiter was the kind of being we see in the Capitol and in other..." <note>original: *Ne hoc quidem crediderunt (Etruſci) Jovem qualem in Capitolio, & in cæteris*</note>

Through the analysis of titles like "Best and Greatest" and the symbolism of thunderbolts, the author demonstrates that ancient religious traditions recognized a singular, omnipotent governor of the universe.</summary>

### CHAPTER IV. The Supreme God.

"...[in his] temples, [they do not believe him] to hurl thunderbolts with his own hand; but they understand him to be the same Jupiter as we do: the guardian and ruler of the universe, the Mind and Spirit, the Lord and Artificer of this worldly work, to whom every name is appropriate." <note>original: *ædibus colimus, mittere manu sua fulmina; sed eundem quem nos, Jovem intelligunt; custodem rectoremque Universi, Animum ac Spiritum, Mundani hujus operis Dominum & Artificem, cui nomen omne convenit.* These lines, likely from Seneca, describe Etruscan (Hetrurian) theology.</note> Neither did these Etruscans believe that such a Jupiter as we worship in the Capitol and in the other temples threw thunderbolts with his own hands. Instead, they understood him to be the very same Jupiter that we now recognize: the Keeper and Governor of the *Universe*, the *Mind* and *Spirit* of the whole, the *Lord* and *Artificer* of this *worldly structure* <term>original: "Mundane Fabrick"</term>, to whom every name belongs. 

And lastly, that the common <term>original: "vulgar"</term> Romans afterward, around the beginning of Christianity, held the same notion of *Jupiter* as the Supreme God, is clearly evident from what **Tertullian** recorded in his book *To Scapula*. He notes that when **Marcus Aurelius**, during his German expedition, obtained refreshing showers from heaven during a great drought through the prayers of Christian soldiers made to God: "Then the people, crying out, 'To Jupiter, the God of Gods, who alone is powerful,' gave testimony to our God in the name of Jove." <note>original: *Tunc Populus adclamans JOVI DEO DEORUM, QUI SOLUS POTENS EST, in Jovis nomine Deo nostro testimonium reddidit*</note> Here, by the way, we also see that *Tertullian* was not as scrupulous <note>original: "nice"</note> as **Lactantius**, but freely acknowledged that the Pagans meant the True God by their name *Jupiter*.

Nothing is more frequent among Pagan writers than speaking of God in the singular, thereby signifying the *One Supreme Deity*. This same habit was also very familiar to the *common Pagans* in their ordinary discourse and everyday speech, as has been recorded by various Church Fathers. **Tertullian**, in his book *On the Testimony of the Soul* and his *Apology*, provides examples of several of these phrases then commonly used by Pagans, such as: "God sees," "I commend to God," "God will repay," "God will judge between us," "What God wills," "If God wills," "What God has given," "If God gives," <note>original: *Deus videt, Deo commendo, Deus reddet, Deus inter nos judicabit, Quod Deus vult, Si Deus voluerit, Quod Deus dederit, Si Deus dederit*</note> and the like. 

Likewise, **Minutius Felix** writes: "When they stretch out their hands to heaven, they say nothing else but 'God.' And 'He is Great,' and 'God is True,' etc. Is this the natural speech of the common people, or the prayer of a confessing Christian?" <note>original: *Cum ad Cælum manus tendunt, nihil aliud quàm Deum Dicunt. Et Magnus est, & Deus Verus est, &c. vulgi iste Naturalis sermo, an Christiani confitentis oratio?*</note> 

And finally, **Lactantius** states: "When they swear, and when they wish, and when they give thanks, they name not many gods, but God only; the Truth, by a secret force of nature, thus breaking forth from them whether they will or no." <note>original: *Cum Jurant, & cum Optant, & cum Gratias agunt, non Deos multos, sed Deum nominant; adeò ipsa veritas, cogente natura, etiam ab invitis pectoribus erumpit*</note> And again: "They fly to God, aid is sought from God, they pray that God would help them. And if anyone, reduced to the extreme necessity of begging, asks for food with prayers, he calls upon God alone, and through his divine and unique power seeks the mercy of men for himself." <note>original: *Ad Deum confugiunt, à Deo petitur auxilium, Deus ut subveniat oratur. Et si quis ad extremam mendicandi necessitatem redactus, victum precibus exposcit, Deum Solum obtestatur, & per ejus divinum atque unicum Numen hominum sibi misericordiam quærit*</note> This same point is also fully confirmed by **Proclus**...

# Lord Have Mercy; the Pagans BOOK I.

Proclus, in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*, observes that the *One Supreme God* was more *universally* believed throughout the world in all ages than the *many inferior gods*. 
<margin>Page 286.</margin>
"Perhaps you might say," Proclus writes, "that souls forget those things closer to them more quickly, but remember the higher principles more clearly. For these act more upon them because of their superiority of power, and they seem to be present to them through their activity. This also happens with our physical sight: for although we do not see many things lying on the earth, we nevertheless see the fixed sphere itself and the stars, because they illuminate our sight with their own light. In the same way, the eye of the soul suffers more forgetfulness and blindness regarding closer things than regarding the higher and more divine principles. Therefore, all religions and sects concede that there is a first principle, and all people call upon God as a helper. But not all believe that there are gods after him, or that a providence from him exists in the universe; for 'The One' (Unity) appears more clearly to them than 'The Multitude.'" <note>original Greek: τάχα δ’ ἂν εἴποις... τοῦ πλήθους</note>

*And perhaps you may affirm, that souls do sooner lose their knowledge of those things which are lower and nearer to them, but retain a stronger remembrance of those higher principles. Because these act more vigorously upon them, by reason of the transcendency of their power, and by their energy seem to be present with them. And the same thing happens as to our bodily sight; for though there be many things here upon earth which none of us see, yet every one observes that highest sphere, and takes notice of the fixed stars in it, because these strongly radiate with their light upon our eyes. In like manner does the eye of our soul sooner lose the sight and remembrance of the lower than of the higher and diviner principles. And thus all religions and sects acknowledge that one highest principle of all, and men everywhere call upon God for their helper; but that there are gods after and below that highest principle, and that there is a certain providence descending down from these upon the universe, all sects do not believe; the reason for this is because The One, or Unity, appears more clearly and plainly to them than The Many, or a multitude.*

Moreover, we learn from Arrian’s *Epictetus* that the very form of prayer which has been in use for so long in the Christian Church, *Kyrie Eleison* <note>Greek: Κύριε ἐλέησον, meaning "Lord, have mercy"</note>, was anciently part of the *pagans'* litany to the Supreme God, either among the Greeks, the
<margin>Book 2, chapter 7.</margin>
Latins, or both. "Invoking God," says *Epictetus*, "we pray to him in this manner: *Lord, have mercy upon us.*" <note>original Greek: τὸν θεὸν ἐπικαλούμενοι δεόμεθα αὐτοῦ, Κύριε ἐλέησον</note> Now, this *Epictetus* lived in the times of Hadrian the Emperor, and it is undeniably clear from the context that this passage refers to pagans and not Christians, as he is speaking there of those who used *augury* <term>original: "Auguria"; the practice of divining the future or the will of the gods by observing the flight of birds</term> or divination. 

Moreover, in the writings of the Greek pagans, the Supreme God is often called *Kyrios*, or "Lord." To prove this, we do not only have the passage of the *Perfect Discourse* <note>original: τέλειος λόγος (Teleios Logos), also known as the *Asclepian Dialogue*</note> cited by Lactantius, where we read of "the Lord and Maker of all" <note>original Greek: ὁ Κύριος καὶ πάντων ποιητής</note>. Menander, in Justin Martyr, also styles the Supreme God "the most universal Lord of all" <note>original Greek: τὸν ὄντα πάντων κύριον γενικώτατον</note>. And Osiris, in Plutarch, is called "the Lord of all things" <note>original Greek: ἁπάντων Κύριος</note>. This is also done "absolutely"—meaning the title is used on its own without any added description—and that not only by the translators of the Septuagint <note>original: "the Seventy"; the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> and Christians, but also by pagan writers. Thus, in Plutarch's *On Isis and Osiris*, we read of "the first, and Lord, and [intelligible]..."

It provides examples from philosophers like Proclus and Epictetus to show that the title "Lord" was commonly applied to the highest divine principle in paganism.</summary>

# CHAPTER IV. A Litany to the Supreme God.

...the **knowledge of the first Intelligible** and the **Lord**, that is, the **Supreme God**. And **Oromasdes** <note>original: Oromasdes; referring to Ahura Mazda, the supreme deity in Zoroastrianism</note> is called "the Lord" <note>original Greek: ὁ κύριος (ho kyrios)</note> in **Plutarch**'s *Life of Alexander*; just as "Mind" <note>original Greek: Νοῦς (Nous)</note> is also called "Lord" <note>original Greek: κύριος</note> by **Aristotle**—that is, <margin>On the Soul, Book 1.</margin> the **Supreme Ruler over all**. Likewise, **Plato**, in his *Sixth Epistle* (c. 7, addressed to Hermias and others), describes his **First Divine Hypostasis** <term>Hypostasis: a person or distinct essence of the Godhead</term>, or the **Absolutely Supreme Deity**, as "The Father of the Prince and Cause of the World" (that is, of the Eternal Intellect), "the LORD" <note>original Greek: τοῦ ἡγεμόνος καὶ αἰτίου πατέρα Κύριον</note>. Again, **Iamblichus** writes the following about the **Supreme God**: "It is agreed that every good <margin>Life of Pythagoras, page 89.</margin> thing ought to be asked of the Lord—that is, the Supreme God" <note>original Greek: δεῖν ὁμολογεῖσθαι ὑπὸ τοῦ κυρίου ἀγαθὸν ζητεῖν</note>. These words are later repeated by him on page 129, though the printed copy is corrupted to: "it is necessary to agree concerning the Lord to seek the good." Finally, **Clement of Alexandria** tells us that the **Supreme God** was called not by just one name, but by several different ones, namely: "Either the One, or the Good, or Mind, or Being itself, or the Father, or God, or the Creator, or the Lord" <note>original Greek: ἤτοι Ἓν, ἢ τ᾿ Ἀγαθὸν, ἢ Νοῦν, ἢ αὐτὸ τό Ὄν, ἢ Πατέρα, ἢ θεὸν, ἢ Δημιουργὸν, ἢ Κύριον</note>. Therefore, we conclude that this *Kyrie Eleison* <note>original: "Lord have mercy"</note>, or *Domine Miserere*, in **Arrianus**, was a **pagan litany** or prayer to the **Supreme God**. However, from the *Stratagemata* <note>A manual on military strategy</note> of the Emperor **Maurice**, it appears that in his time, a *Kyrie Eleison* was <margin>Rigaltius's Glossary.</margin> also commonly sung by Christian armies before battle.

Even the most foolishly superstitious and idolatrous of all the pagans—those who worshipped countless gods—generally acknowledged **One Supreme Deity** over them all, **One Universal Spirit**. This is positively affirmed and fully attested by **Aurelius Prudentius** in his *Apotheosis*, in these words:

> <margin>Verse 254.</margin>
> Is there anyone reclining in a temple among a thousand sacred objects,
> worshipping ridiculous gods with salt, turf, and incense,
> who does not think there is a Supreme God, and He alone is over all?
> Although he may consecrate smoking altars to Saturns, Junos, and Cythereas,
> and other monstrous figures;
> yet whenever he looks up toward heaven,
> he recognizes all authority in one God, whom a vast
> system of powers serves, equipped with various ministers.
> <note>original Latin: Ecquis in Idolio recubans... Variis instructa Ministris.</note>

We are well aware that **Plato**, in his *Cratylus* (where he attempts to provide the etymologies <term>Etymology: the study of the origin of words</term> of words, including the word "Gods" <note>original Greek: Θεοὶ (Theoi)</note>), writes about the **first and most ancient inhabitants of Greece**. He states that they seemed to him—like other foreigners at that time—to have acknowledged no other gods than those that were **visible and sensible**, such as the **Sun**, the **Moon**, the **Earth**, the **Stars**, and the **Heavens**. Because they perceived these things to be in perpetual motion, they called them "Gods" <note>original Greek: Θεὸς</note> from the word "to run" <note>original Greek: θέειν (theein)</note>. However, Plato notes that when they later became aware of **invisible gods**, they applied the same name to them as well. **Eusebius** occasionally uses this passage from Plato to try to prove that the pagans universally acknowledged no gods other than those that were **physical and inanimate**. This is clearly contrary to Plato's meaning. Plato never suggests that any nation was so barbaric as to worship **senseless and inanimate bodies** as gods for their own sake; rather, he suggests the opposite: that they...
