# The Sun, according to Macrobius, BOOK I.

Does he distinguish there between those *original inhabitants* of *Greece* and other *foreigners* <note>original: Barbarians</note>, and the later *civilized Greeks*, who also took notice of *invisible gods*. However, if this claim by *Plato* were true—that *some* of the ancient *Pagans* worshipped nothing but *visible* and *perceptible gods* (taking no notice of any *incorporeal beings*)—it still does not follow that those *Pagans* had no notion at all of *one Supreme* and *Universal Deity* <note>original: Numen</note>. On the contrary, it is manifest that some of those *corporealists* <term>Corporealists: those who believe that only physical matter exists and that God is a physical substance</term> looked upon the whole *heaven* and *ether* as an *animated* being and as the *Highest God*, according to the lines by *Euripides* cited by *Cicero*:

<margin>On the Nature of the Gods, p. 223.</margin>
> See the sublime expanse, the boundless ether,
> Which surrounds and embraces the earth in its tender grasp;
> Consider this the highest god, and call this Jove <note>original Latin: Vides Sublime fusum, immoderatum æthera, / Qui tenero terram circumvectu amplectitur, / Hunc Summum habeto Divum, hunc perhibeto Jovem.</note>.

Others of them conceived that *subtle fiery substance* which permeates and pervades the whole *world* (supposed to be intellectual or conscious) to be the *Supreme Deity* that governs all. This opinion was also held by philosophers, namely the *Heraclitics* and *Stoics*. And finally, since *Macrobius*, speaking through the character of *Vettius Praetextatus*, refers so many of the Pagan gods to the Sun, it is not improbable that some of these Pagans might adore the *Animated Sun* as the *Sovereign Deity* <note>original: Numen</note>, and perhaps invoke him in that form of prayer mentioned there: **"O Almighty Sun, the spirit of the world"** <note>original Greek: Ἥλιε παντοκράτωρ, κόσμου πνεῦμα</note>. Even *Cleanthes* himself, that learned *Stoic* and devout *religious scholar*, is suspected by some to have held this persuasion.

<margin>Book 1, chapter 17.</margin>
Nevertheless, we think it appropriate here to observe that it was not *Macrobius's* intention in his *Saturnalia* to defend the idea—either as his own opinion or the general opinion of Pagans—that the *Animated Sun* was *absolutely the highest deity* (as some have thought). Nor did he intend to reduce that multiplicity of Pagan gods into a seeming monarchy to align more closely with Christianity. Instead, he plainly limits his discourse to "only those gods who are beneath the heavens" <note>original Latin: Dii duntaxat qui sub Cœlo sunt</note>—that is, the *lower sort of worldly gods*. He undertook to show not that all of these, but only many of them, could be reduced to the Sun as "many-named" <note>original: Polyonymous</note>, being called by several names according to his various *powers* and *effects*. For what *Macrobius's* own opinion was concerning the *Supreme Deity* appears plainly from his other writings, particularly this passage from his commentary on *Scipio’s Dream*, where the *highest sphere* and *starry heaven* was called the *Supreme God*:

> "That he called this outermost sphere the Supreme God must not be understood to mean that it is the First Cause and the most Almighty God; since the sphere itself, which is the heaven, is the work of the Soul, the Soul proceeded from the Mind, and the Mind was created by God, who is truly supreme. But he called it supreme in relation to the order of other things that are beneath it; and he called it God because it is not only a divine and immortal living being, full of glorious reason from that purest Mind, but also because it..." <note>original Latin: Quod hunc Extimum Globum, Summum Deum vocavit, non ita accipiendum est, ut iste Prima Causa, & Deus ille Omnipotentissimus existimetur; cum Globus ipse, quod Cœlum est, Animæ sit Fabrica, Anima ex Mente processerit, Mens ex Deo, qui verè Summus est, procreata sit. sed Summum quidem dixit ad Cæterorum Ordinem qui subjecti sunt: Deum verò quòd non modò Immortale Animal ac Divinum sit, plenum inclytæ ex illa purissima Mente rationis, sed quod &</note>

# CHAPTER IV. Not the Supreme Deity.

...all the virtues <note>original Latin: *virtutes*—here meaning powers or moral excellencies</note> that follow that peak of First Omnipotence, he either creates or contains. Finally, the ancients called him Jupiter, and among theologians, Jupiter is the Soul of the World <note>original Latin: *Mundi Anima*</note>. 

That the **Outermost Sphere** is here called **The Supreme God** is not to be understood as if this were thought to be **The First Cause** or **The Most Omnipotent God of all**. For this **Starry Sphere**, being only a part of the Heaven, was made or produced by **Soul**. This **Soul** also proceeded from a **Perfect Mind** or **Intellect**; and again, that **Mind** was begotten from that **God** who is **Truly Supreme**. 

But the **Highest Sphere** is here called the **Supreme God** only in respect to those **Lesser Spheres** or **Gods** that are contained under it. It is styled a **God** because it is not only an **Immortal** and **Divine Living Being** <note>original: *Animal*—in the sense of an "animated" or "living" entity</note>, full of **Reason** derived from that **Purest Mind**, but also because it makes or contains within itself all those **virtues** which follow from the **Omnipotence of the First Summit**. Lastly, this was called **Jupiter** by the ancients, and to theologians, **Jupiter** is the **Soul of the World**. 

Therefore, although **Macrobius** (and generally the other **Pagans**) undoubtedly worshipped the Sun as a **Great God**, and probably would not hesitate to call him **Jupiter** or <term>pantokrator</term> <note>original Greek: *πάντωκράτωρ*—meaning "Almighty" or "Ruler of all"</note>, or even **Supreme God** (just as the **Starry Heaven** was so styled in *Scipio's Dream*), he did so because the Sun was the **Chief Moderator** in this **Lower World**. Nevertheless, it is plain that he was far from thinking the Sun was the **First Cause** <note>original Latin: *Primam Causam*</note> or the **most Omnipotent God of all**. He acknowledged that above the **Sun** and **Heaven** there existed, first, an **Eternal Psyche** (the Maker or Creator of them both); then, above this **Psyche**, a **Perfect Mind** or **Intellect**; and lastly, above that **Mind**, a **God** who was **Truly Supreme** <note>original Latin: *Verè Summus*</note>—the **First Cause and the most Omnipotent of all Gods**. In this, **Macrobius** clearly followed the philosophy of Plato, asserting a Trinity of Divine <term>Hypostases</term> <note>distinct levels of divine reality or "persons"</note>. This same doctrine is further declared by him elsewhere in this manner:

<margin>The Dream of Scipio, Book I, Chapter 14.</margin>
> God, who is and is called the First Cause, the only source of all things that exist or seem to exist, is the Principle and Origin of all. He, through the overflowing fertility of his Majesty, created **Mind** from himself. This **Mind**, which is called **Nous** <note>original Greek: *Νῶς*</note>, as it gazes toward its Father, maintains the perfect likeness of its Author; but as it looks backward, it creates **Soul** from itself. In turn, this **Soul** is clothed by the part it gazes upon [the Mind], but as its focus gradually turns back toward the construction of physical forms, it degenerates into those corporeal things <note>original Latin: *Deus qui Prima Causa est & vocatur...*</note>.

In addition to this, the same **Macrobius** tells us that: 

> Ancient times fashioned no **image** or statue <note>original Latin: *Simulachrum*</note> of the **Highest God and Prince of all things**, because he is above **Soul** and **Nature**, a realm where it is not lawful for any **myths** <note>original: *fabulosity*</note> to enter. However, regarding the other **Gods**, the **Soul of the World**, and those below...

# The Sun, not the Persian Jupiter. BOOK 1.

...below it, they thought it not inconvenient here to make use of *Images*, and *Fiction* or *Myth-making* <note>original: "Fabulosity"—the creation of myths or fables</note>. From all of this, it plainly appears that neither *Macrobius* himself, nor the majority of the ancient Pagans (according to his understanding), viewed the *Living Sun* <note>original: "Animated Sun"</note> as the *Absolutely Supreme and Highest Being*.

And perhaps it may not be out of place to suggest here what has already been observed: that the Persians themselves—who of all Pagan nations have been most accused of worshipping the Sun as the *Supreme Deity* under the name of *Mithras*—did, nonetheless, if we may believe *Eubulus* (who wrote an extensive history of *Mithras*), acknowledge another *Invisible Deity* superior to it. This deity, who was the *Maker* of the sun and of the entire *World*, was considered the *True and Proper Mithras*. This opinion is also plainly confirmed, not only by <margin>Book 1, Note 131.</margin> *Herodotus*, who distinguishes their *Jupiter* from the Sun, but also by *Xenophon* in several places. For instance, he speaks of *Cyrus* being warned in a dream of his approaching death, and thereupon offering his devotion through sacrifices and prayers: first to the ancestral Jupiter <note>original Greek: "Ζεύς πατρώος" (Zeus patrōos)</note>, the *Persian Jupiter*, and then to the Sun and the <margin>Cyrus's Education, Book 8, p. 184.</margin> other gods. *He sacrificed to their Ancestral (or Persian) Jupiter, to the Sun, and to the other gods upon the mountain tops, as the Persian custom is; praying in this manner: "You, our Ancestral Jupiter (that is, you Mithras or Oromasdes), and you Sun, and all you other gods, accept, I pray you, these my sacrifices of thanksgiving," etc.* <note>original Greek: "Ἔθυε Διΐ τε πατρώῳ καὶ ἡλίῳ καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις θεοῖς ἐπὶ τῶν ἄκρων, ὡς πέρσαι θύουσι, ὧδε ἐπευχόμενος, Ζεῦ πατρῶε καὶ ἥliε καὶ πάντες θεοὶ, δέχεσθε τάδε χαριστήρια, &c."</note> And we also find a similar prayer used by <margin>On the Fortune of Alexander, Book 2.</margin> *Darius* in *Plutarch*: *Ancestral Jupiter of the Persians* <note>original Greek: "Ζεῦ πατρῶε περσῶν"</note>, meaning the supreme God of the Persians. Moreover, *Herodotus* and *Curtius* record that in Persian ceremonies and processions, a chariot sacred to *Jupiter* was traditionally drawn, distinct from the chariot of the Sun. But *Cyrus's* proclamation in the Book of *Esdras* <note>referring to the biblical book of Ezra, often called 1 Esdras in older scholarship</note> puts the matter beyond doubt; for *That Lord God of Heaven* who is said there to have given *Cyrus* all the kingdoms of the earth and commanded him to build Him a *House at Jerusalem* cannot be understood as being the Sun.

The Ethiopians in *Strabo's* time might well be looked upon as barbarians, and yet they not only acknowledged *One Supreme Deity*, but one that was distinct from the world and therefore *Invisible*. He wrote the following concerning them: <margin>Book 17, p. 822.</margin> *They believe that there is one immortal God, and that he is the cause of all things; and another mortal one, who is unnamed; but for the most part, they consider their benefactors and kings to be gods.* <note>original Greek: "θεὸν νομίζουσι τὸν μὲν ἀθάνατον, τοῦτον δ' εἶναι τὸν αἴτιον τῶν πάντων, τὸν δὲ θνητὸν, ἀνώνυμόν τινα, ὡς δ' ἐπιτοπολὺ τοὺς εὐεργέτας καὶ βασιλικοὺς θεοὺς νομίζουσι"</note> And although *Caesar* claims of the ancient Germans, *They count as gods only those whom they can see and by whose power they are clearly helped: the Sun, Vulcan (fire), and the Moon* <note>original Latin: "Deorum numero eos solos ducunt, quos cernunt, & quorum opibus apertè juvantur, Solem, & Vulcanum, & Lunam"</note>, he is contradicted by *Tacitus*, who, coming after him, had better information. <margin>See Schedius's "On the German Gods".</margin> Others have recorded that they acknowledged *One Supreme God*, first under the name of *Thau*, and then *Thautes* and *Theutates*. Finally, the majority of the Pagans at this very day, such as the *Indians* and *Chinese*...

<summary>The author argues that ancient Persians, Ethiopians, and Germans—often mistakenly viewed as purely nature-worshippers—actually recognized a supreme, invisible Creator above the Sun and other celestial deities.</summary>

# Chapter 4. Plutarch's Agreement of Pagan Religions. 459

The Chinese, Siamese, and Guineans; the inhabitants of Peru, Mexico, Virginia, and New England (some of whom are quite primitive <note>original: "Barbarous"—in this context, meaning non-European or living in a state of nature</note>) acknowledge **One Supreme** or **Greatest God**. They have their several proper names for him, such as *Parmiscer, Fetisso, Wiracocha, Pachacamac, Vitziliputzti*, and others, though they also worship other gods and idols. We shall conclude this point with the testimony of Joseph de Acosta <note>Joseph de Acosta (1540–1600) was a Spanish Jesuit missionary and naturalist who wrote extensively about the peoples of South America.</note>:

<margin>Concerning the Procurement of Indian Salvation, Book 5, p. 479.</margin>
> *This is common to almost all the barbarians: they confess one God who is Supreme over all things and perfectly Good. They also have a clear belief in certain evil spirits, which our barbarians call "Zupay." Therefore, they ought to be first well instructed on who that Supreme and Eternal Maker of all things is, whom they ignorantly worship; and then they must be taught how great a difference there is between those wicked demons and his faithful ministers, the angels.* <note>original Latin: "Hoc commune apud omnes penè Barbaros est, ut Deum quidem Omnium rerum Supremum & summè Bonum, fateantur... gens pessima Cacodæmonum."</note>

This is common almost to all the barbarians: to confess one Supreme God over all, who is perfectly Good; as they also have a belief among them of certain evil spirits, which are called by our barbarians *Zupay*. Therefore they ought to be first well instructed in what that Supreme and Eternal Maker of all things is, whom they ignorantly worship; and then how great a difference there is between those wicked demons <note>original: "Cacodæmonum"</note> and his faithful ministers, the angels.

XXVIII. It has been already declared that, according to Themistius and Symmachus <note>Two prominent 4th-century figures who advocated for religious pluralism within the Roman Empire.</note> (two zealous Pagans), one and the same **supreme God** was worshipped in all the various Pagan religions throughout the world, though in different manners. In their opinion, this diversity of religions was not inconvenient in itself, nor was it ungrateful or unacceptable to Almighty God. They believed it was more for His honor, state, and grandeur to be worshipped with this variety, rather than in only one way. Now, that this was also the opinion of other older Pagans before them may appear from this remarkable testimony of **Plutarch** in his book *On Isis and Osiris* <note>original: "De Iside"</note>. In this work, he defends Egyptian worship (which was the main purpose of that whole book) while declaring that no inanimate thing should be looked upon or worshipped as a God:

<margin>Page 377.</margin>
> *For no inanimate thing is a god to men. Rather, we have accounted as gods those who bestow these things upon us and provide us a continual and lasting supply for our use. These gods are not different for different nations; it is not as if the barbarians and the Greeks, or the southern and northern inhabitants of the globe, had different gods. But just as the sun, the moon, the heaven, the earth, and the sea are common to all, though called by different names in different countries, so there is* **ONE REASON** <note>original Greek: "ΕΝΟΣ ΛΟΓΟΥ" (Enos Logou)—meaning a single underlying logic or Word</note> *ordering these things and* **ONE PROVIDENCE** <note>original Greek: "ΜΙΑΣ ΠΡΟΝΟΙΑΣ" (Mias Pronoias)</note> *directing all, with inferior subservient ministers appointed over everyone. These have had different honors and names bestowed upon them by different laws. Those who are initiated use symbols—some obscure, some more clear—to guide their understanding toward the divine, though not without some danger.* <note>original Greek: "οὐ γὰρ ἔνυδ’ ἄψυχα ἀνθρώποις ὁ Θεὸς... ἐπὶ τὰ θεῖα νόησιν ὁδηγοῦντες οὐκ ἀκινδύνως·"</note>

*No inanimate thing ought to be esteemed as a God; instead, those who bestow these things upon us and afford us a continual supply for our use have been therefore accounted by us as Gods. These Gods are not different for different nations; as if the barbarians and the Greeks, the Southern and the Northern inhabitants of the globe, did not have the same, but entirely different Gods. But as the Sun and the Moon, and the Heaven and the Earth, and the Sea, are common to all—though called by several names in several countries—so* **ONE REASON** *ordering these things and* **ONE PROVIDENCE** *dispensing all, along with the inferior subservient ministers, have had several names and honors bestowed upon them by the...*

### Livy; the Same God Everywhere. Book 1.

The laws of several countries have been everywhere worshiped throughout the whole world. And there have also been different symbols consecrated to them, the better to conduct and lead on men’s understandings to *divine things*; though this has not been without some hazard or danger of casting men upon one of two inconveniences: either *superstition* or *atheism*. On this point, Plutarch plainly affirms that the several religions of the *pagan nations*—whether *Greeks* or *barbarians*, including the *Egyptians* as well as others—consisted in nothing else but the worshiping of one and the same Supreme Mind, *Reason*, and *Providence* that orders all things in the world. He argues they also worshiped its subservient powers appointed over all things <note>original Greek: ὑπεργοὶ δυνάμεις ἐπὶ πάντα τεταγμένοι</note>, which were appointed by it over all the several parts of the world, though under different *names*, *rites*, and *ceremonies*, and with different *symbols*.

Moreover, Titus Livius (Livy) was of the very same opinion: that the pagan gods of several countries—though called by several names and worshiped with such a great diversity of rites and ceremonies—were not, for all that, different, but were the same gods common to all. This may be concluded from this passage of his, where he writes of <margin>Book 28. Chapter 12.</margin> *Hannibal*: "I do not know whether Hannibal was more admirable in his adversity or prosperity; he who, having a mixed collection <note>original: "colluvies"—a jumbled mass or dregs</note> of all nations under him, which had different rites, different ceremonies, and *almost* different gods from one another, did nonetheless so unite them all together in one common bond that no rebellion at all occurred among them." <note>original Latin: *Nescio an Mirabilior fuerit in adversis, quàm secundis rebus. Quippe qui mistos ex colluvione omnium gentium, quibus alius Ritus, alia sacra, alii PROPE Dii essent, ita uno vinculo copulaverit, ut nulla seditio extiterit.*</note> 

In this passage, Livy plainly suggests that though there was as great a diversity of religious rites and ceremonies among the pagans as if they had worshiped different gods, the gods of them all were really the same—namely, one Supreme God and his ministers under him. And the same Livy elsewhere declares this to have been the general opinion of the Romans and Italians likewise at that time. He tells us how they quarreled with Quintus Fulvius Flaccus because, while serving as <term>Censor</term> <note>A high-ranking Roman official responsible for public morals and overseeing public works.</note> and building a new temple in Spain, he uncovered another temple dedicated to *Juno Lacinia* among the *Bruttii* <note>An ancient people of southern Italy.</note>. Taking off the marble tiles, he sent them to Spain to adorn his newly erected temple. They accused him publicly in the Senate house in this manner: <margin>Decade 5.</margin> "That he was building temples with the ruins of other temples, as if the same immortal gods were not everywhere, but that some should be worshiped and adorned with the spoils of others." <note>original Latin: *Quod ruinis Templorum Templa ædificaret, tanquam non Iidem ubique Dii immortales essent, sed spoliis aliorum alii colendi exornandique*</note>

The Egyptians were doubtless the most unique of all the pagans, and the most oddly different from the rest in their manner of worship. Yet, nevertheless, these also agreed with the rest in those fundamentals of worshiping one Supreme and Universal <term>Numen</term> <note>original: "Numen"—a Latin term for divinity, divine power, or a presiding spirit.</note>, to-

# CHAPTER 4. Asclepiades: Symphony of Theologies.

...together with his *inferior ministers*, as *Plutarch* diligently sets himself to maintain in that previously mentioned book *On Isis*. This point was further clarified and explained (as *Damascius* <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher, c. 458–538 AD</note> informs us) by two famous Egyptian philosophers, *Asclepiades* and *Heraiscus*, in certain writings of theirs that have since been lost:

<margin>Damascius, *On Principles* (Manuscript)</margin>
"Although Eudemus has given us no certain account of the Egyptians, yet the Egyptian philosophers of more recent times have declared the hidden truth of their theology. Having found it in certain Egyptian monuments, they say that according to them there is one principle of all things, celebrated under the name of the *Unknown Darkness* <note>original Greek: σκότος ἄγνωστον</note>, and this is repeated three times, etc. Moreover, this is to be observed concerning these Egyptians: they are often prone to dividing and multiplying things that are actually one and the same. Accordingly, they have divided and multiplied the first intelligible being—the one supreme deity—into the properties of many gods, as anyone may find who chooses to consult their writings. I refer to the work of *Heraiscus* titled *The Universal Doctrine of the Egyptians* <note>original Greek: Αἰγυπτίου καθόλου λόγου</note>, written for the philosopher *Proclus*, and that *Symphony* or harmony of the Egyptians with other theologians, which was begun by *Asclepiades* but left unfinished." <note>original: translations of Damascius's Greek text</note>

Of this work by *Asclepiades* the Egyptian, *Suidas* <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> also makes mention under the entry for "Heraiscus": "But *Asclepiades*, having been more deeply immersed in ancient Egyptian books, was more thoroughly instructed and exactly skilled in his ancestral theology. He searched into its principles and all the conclusions resulting from them, as is clearly evident from those hymns he composed in praise of the Egyptian gods, and from the treatise he began to write which contains *The Symphony of All Theologies* <note>original Greek: θεολογιῶν ἁπασῶν συμφωνίαν</note>." 

Now, we argue that *Asclepiades’s Symphony* of all the *pagan theologies* (and therefore the agreement of the Egyptian religion with the rest) consisted in their shared belief in those two fundamental points expressed by *Plutarch*. Namely: the worship of *one supreme* and *universal deity* <note>original Latin: "Numen"</note>, who is *Reason* and *Providence* governing all things; and then the worship of his subservient ministers (the instruments of *Providence*) appointed by him over all the parts of the world. Because these ministers were honored under various names and with different rites and ceremonies, according to the laws of their respective countries, it caused all that *diversity of religions* that existed among them. Both of these fundamental points of *pagan theology* were likewise acknowledged by *Symmachus* <note>Quintus Aurelius Symmachus (c. 340–402 AD), a Roman statesman who sought to preserve traditional paganism</note>. The first of them was expressed this way:

> "It is reasonable that whatever all worship should be thought of as one," <note>original Latin: "Aequum est quicquid omnes colunt, Unum putari"</note>

...it is thought <note>original Latin: putari</note>, **"That all religions agreed in this: the worshipping of one and the same supreme deity"** <note>original Latin: Numen</note>. The second point is this: **"The Divine Mind distributed various guardian and tutelary spirits under him to cities and countries"** <note>original Latin: Varios Custodes Urbibus Mens Divina distribuit</note>. The author adds that **"every nation had its own peculiar customs and laws"** <note>original Latin: Suus cuique Mos est, suum cuique Jus</note>, and that these external differences in religion should not be obsessed over; rather, everyone should observe the religion of their own country. 

Alternatively, these **two fundamental points of pagan theology** may be expressed this way:
1. There is one self-originated deity who was the *Demiurge* <note>original Greek: δημιουργὸς; the Creator or Maker</note> of the whole world.
2. Besides him, there are other gods to be religiously worshipped (that is, intellectual beings superior to humans), all of whom were nonetheless made or created by that One. 

<margin>Stobaeus, *Physical Selections*, chapter 1</margin>
*Stobaeus* <note>A 5th-century compiler of Greek philosophical extracts</note> thus declares their view: **"The multitude of gods is the work of the Creator, brought into being together with the world"** <note>original Greek: τὸ πλῆθος τῶν θεῶν ἔργον ἐστὶ τοῦ δημιουργοῦ, ἅμα τῷ κόσμῳ γινόμενον</note>.

### XXIX. The World as a Living Being

That pagan theologians generally acknowledged one supreme and universal deity appears plainly from the fact that they supposed the whole world to be an **"Animal"** <note>In this context, "animal" refers to an "animated being" or a living entity possessed of a soul (anima)</note>. 

<margin>Plutarch, book 2, chapter 3; Stobaeus, *Physical Selections*, chapter 25</margin>
Thus, the writer of *On the Opinions of the Philosophers* <note>A work traditionally attributed to Plutarch</note>, and *Stobaeus* following him, wrote: **"All others assert the world to be an animated being and governed by Providence; only Leucippus, Democritus, and Epicurus—and those who introduce atoms and the vacuum as the principles of all things—dissent, acknowledging neither that the world is animated nor that it is governed by Providence, but rather by some irrational nature"** <note>original Greek: οἱ μὲν ἄλλοι πάντες ἔμψυχον τὸν κόσμον καὶ προνοίᾳ διοικούμενον· Λεύκιππος δὲ καὶ Δημόκριτος καὶ Ἐπίκουρος, καὶ ὅσοι τὰ ἄτομα εἰσηγοῦνται καὶ τὸ κενὸν, οὔτε ἔμψυχον οὔτε προνοίᾳ διοικεῖσθαι, φύσει δέ τινι ἀλόγῳ</note>.

In passing, we may observe the deception of *Gassendi* <note>Pierre Gassendi (1592–1655), a French philosopher who sought to reconcile Epicureanism with Christianity</note>, who takes this opportunity to highly praise *Epicurus* as someone who approached closer to Christianity than all other philosophers because he denied the world was an "animal." However, according to the language and notions of those times, to deny the world's animation was the same thing as being an atheist or denying God. This is because all the pagans who then asserted Providence also held the world to be animated. *Epicurus* did not deny the world's animation for any reason other than his denial of Providence.

The ground upon which this opinion of the world's animation was built was obvious even to common understanding. It is expressed by *Plotinus* <note>The founder of Neoplatonism, c. 204–270 AD</note> according to the sense of the ancients:

<margin>Plotinus, *Enneads* 4, book 3, chapter 7</margin>
**"It is absurd to affirm that the heaven or world is inanimate—devoid of life and soul—when we ourselves, who have only a part of the mundane body in us, are endowed with a soul. For how could a part have life and soul in it if the whole were dead and inanimate?"** <note>original Greek: ἄτοπον τὸν οὐρανὸν ἄψυχον λέγειν, ἡμῶν οἳ μέρος σώματος ἔχομεν τοῦ παντὸς, ψυχὴν ἐχόντων· πῶς γὰρ ἂν τὸ μέρος ἔχειν, ἀψύχου τοῦ παντὸς ὄντος</note>.

Now, if the whole world is one single living being, then it must necessarily be governed by one soul, and not by many. This one soul of the world, and the whole "mundane animal," was regarded by some of the pagan theologians as...

# CHAPTER IV. The World as One Living Being

Theologians (namely the Stoics) considered the world to be the <term>πρῶτος θεὸς</term> <note>original Greek: "protos theos"; the First God</note>, **the First and Highest God of all**.

Nevertheless, others among the pagan theologians, though likewise asserting the world's animation, would by no means allow the *World Soul* <note>original: "Mundane Soul"</note> to be the *Supreme Deity*. They conceived the *First and Highest God* to be an *abstract* and *immovable Mind*, rather than a *soul*. 

<margin>History of the Gods, page 12</margin>
Thus a panegyrist <note>A speaker or writer who delivers a formal speech of praise</note> (also cited by *Gyraldus*) invokes the Supreme Deity doubtfully and cautiously, as if not knowing well what to call him—whether *Soul* or *Mind*:

> "You, Supreme Creator of all things, who have as many names as you have willed there to be languages of nations; for we cannot know what you yourself wish to be called: whether there is in you a certain divine force and Mind which, infused throughout the whole world, is mingled with all the elements and, without any external impulse of vigor, is moved by yourself; or whether you are some power elevated above all the heavens, looking down upon the whole work of nature as if from a higher citadel: You, I say, we pray to, etc." <note>original Latin: *Te Summe rerum Sator, cujus tot nomina sunt, quot gentium linguas esse voluisti; quem enim te ipse dici velis, scire non possumus: sive in te quaedam vis Mensque Divina est, quae toto infusa mundo, omnibus miscearis elementis, & sine ullo extrinsecus accidente vigoris impulsu, per te ipse movearis; sive aliqua supra omne Coelum potestas es, quae hoc opus totum ex altiore Naturae arce despicias: Te inquam oramus, &c.*</note>

As the Supreme Deity was thus considered only as a *Perfect Mind*, superior to the *Soul*, so the World Soul and the whole animated world were frequently called by these pagans the <term>δεύτερος θεὸς</term> <note>original Greek: "deuteros theos"; the Second God</note>, **the Second God**. Thus, in the *Asclepian Dialogue* (also called the *Perfect Oration* <note>A foundational text of Hermeticism, an ancient philosophical and religious tradition</note>), the Lord and Maker of all is said to have made a *Second God, Visible and Sensible*, which is the *World*.

But for the most part, those who asserted a God superior to the Soul of the World maintained a *Trinity of Universal Principles*, or subordinate *Divine Hypostases* <note>In this context, "hypostases" refers to distinct persons or substances within the divine nature</note>. They conceived that just as there was a *Perfect Mind* or *Intellect* above the *World Soul*, so that *Mind* and *Intellect* as such was not the *First Principle* either. This is because there must be an <term>νοητὸν</term> <note>original Greek: "noeton"; an object of thought or "Intelligible"</note> in the order of nature before the <term>νοῦς</term> <note>original Greek: "nous"; the Mind or Intellect</note>—an *Intelligible* before the *Intellect*. 

This *First Intelligible* was called by them <term>τὸ ἓν</term> <note>original Greek: "to hen"; The One</note> and <term>τἀγαθὸν</term> <note>original Greek: "tagathon"; The Good</note>—*Unity and Goodness* itself in substance, the cause of *Mind* and all things. Now, as the *Tagathon* (the highest of these *three hypostases*) was sometimes called by them the <term>ὁ πρῶτος θεὸς</term> <note>the First God</note> and the *Intellect* was called the <term>ὁ δεύτερος θεὸς</term> <note>the Second God</note>, so the *World Soul* and animated world were called the <term>τρίτος θεὸς</term> <note>original Greek: "tritos theos"; the Third God</note>.

<margin>page 93.</margin>
Thus *Numenius* <note>A 2nd-century philosopher who bridged Pythagorean and Platonic thought</note> in *Proclus's* commentary on *Plato's Timaeus* says: "Numenius, praising Three Gods, calls the Father the First God, the Maker the Second, and the Work the Third. For the world, according to him, is the Third God; just as he supposes the Creator to be double—both the First and the Second God—and the thing created to be the Third." <note>original Greek: Νεμήνιος μὲν γὰρ τρεῖς ἀνυμνήσας θεὸς, πατέρα μὲν καλεῖ τὸν πρῶτον, ποιητὴν δὲ τὸν δεύτερον, ποίημα δὲ τὸν τρίτον· ὁ γὰρ κόσμος κατ’ αὐτὸν ὁ τρίτος ἐστὶ θεὸς, ὡς ὁ κατ’ αὐτὸν δημιουργὸς διττὸς, ὅτε πρῶτος καὶ ὁ δεύτερος θεὸς, τὸ δὲ δημιουργούμενον ὁ τρίτος</note>.

<margin>Enneads, Book 3, Chapter 5, Section 6.</margin>
*Plotinus* <note>The primary philosopher of Neoplatonism</note> speaks of this in a similar way, as very familiar language among those pagans: "And the world, as is commonly said, is the Third God." <note>original Greek: καὶ ὁ κόσμος θεὸς, ὥσπερ σύνηθες λέγειν, τρίτος</note>.

<summary>This page explains how pagan theologians categorized divinity into a hierarchy: the Supreme One (The Good), the Intellect (the Second God), and the World Soul or the world itself (the Third God).</summary>
<keywords>Stoics, Mundane Soul, World Soul, Second God, Third God, Trinity of Principles, Numenius, Plotinus, Neoplatonism, Intelligible vs Intellect</keywords>

# The World not Cut off, Book I.

But neither those who held the Supreme Deity to be an immovable *Mind* or *Intellect*, superior to the *World Soul* <note>original: "Mundane Soul"</note> (such as **Aristotle** and **Xenocrates**), supposed that the World Soul and the entire world depended upon *many* such self-existent immovable intellects as their *First Cause*, but only upon *one*. 

Similarly, those who admitted a <term>Trinity of Divine Hypostases</term> <note>hypostases: distinct persons or substances within the Godhead</note> and made the Supreme Deity properly a *Monad* <note>monad: a single, indivisible unit or "The One"</note> above *Mind* or *Intellect*, did not conceive that the Intellect depended upon *many* such coordinate Monads as *First Principles*, but upon *one only*. 

From this it plainly appears that the pagan theologians always reduced things under a *monarchy*. They did not acknowledge *many independent deities*, but rather *one universal Divine Power* <note>original: "Numen"</note>—whether called *Soul*, *Mind*, or *Monad*—as the head of all. It has already been stated that those pagans who were Trinitarians (especially the **Platonists**) often took those three subordinate levels—a *Monad*, *Mind*, and *Soul*—together as the <term>Divine</term> <note>original Greek: τὸ Θεῖον</note> or *One Supreme Deity*. They supposed an extraordinary kind of *unity* in that *Trinity*, and thus allowed for a certain *latitude* and *gradation* within the *Deity*.

In this context, two things may be observed concerning the *pagan theologians*. First, according to them, the entire physical system was generally not a *dead thing*, like a machine or <term>automaton</term> <note>automaton: a self-operating machine</note> artificially made by men. Instead, *life* and *soul* were mingled with and diffused throughout it all. Indeed, **Aristotle** himself criticizes those who claimed the world consisted of nothing but dead and inanimate <term>monads</term> or atoms, viewing them as a kind of *atheist*. 

Secondly, no matter how much some of them supposed the *Supreme Deity* and *First Cause* to be elevated above the heavens and the physical world, they did not therefore conceive the world to be quite *cut off* from God, nor God from the world, as if they had no commerce or influence upon one another. Rather, as all things proceeded from this *First Cause*, they supposed it to be closely and intimately united with all those emanations from itself (though without *mixture or confusion*), and that all things subsist in it and are pervaded by it.

<margin>Page 100, paragraph.</margin> **Plutarch**, in his *Platonic Questions*, proposes this among others: <note>original Greek: τί δή ποτε τὸν ἀνωτάτω Θεὸν, πατέρα πάντων καὶ ποιητὴν προσείπεν;</note> *“Why did Plato call the highest God the father and maker of all?”* To which he answers first: <note>original Greek: τῶν μὲν θεῶν γεννητῶν καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων πατήρ ἐστι, ποιητὴς δὲ τῶν ἀλόγων καὶ τῶν ἀψύχων·</note> *“Perhaps he was called the Father of all the generated gods and of men, but the Maker of the irrational and lifeless things of the world.”* 

But afterward he adds that this *Highest God* might also be styled the *Father* of the entire physical world, as well as its *Maker*, because it is no *dead and lifeless thing*, but endowed with *life*: <note>original Greek: ἐμψύχου γὰρ γέννησις ἡ γέννησίς ἐστι· καὶ ποιητῇ μὲν, οἷος οἰκοδόμος ἢ ὑφάντης, ἢ λύρας δημιουργὸς ἢ ἀνδριάντος, ἀπήλλακται τὸ γενόμενον ἔργον· ἀπὸ δὲ τοῦ γεννήσαντος ἀρχὴ καὶ δύναμις ἐγκέκραται τῷ τεκνωθέντι, καὶ συνέχει τὴν φύσιν, ἀπόσπασμα καὶ μόριον οὖσαν τοῦ τεκνώσαντος. Ἐπεὶ τοίνυν οὐ πεπλασμένοις ὁ κόσμος, οὐδὲ συνηρμοσμένοις ποιήμασιν ἔοικεν, ἀλλ’ ἔστιν αὐτῷ μοῖρα πολλὴ ζωότητος καὶ θειότητος, ἣν ὁ Θεὸς ἐγκατέσπειρεν ἀφ’ ἑαυτοῦ τῇ ὕλῃ καὶ κατέμιξεν, εἰκό-</note> *“For the birth of a living thing is a true generation. While a finished work—such as one made by a builder, a weaver, or a maker of lyres or statues—is separated from its maker, a principle and power from the father is blended into the offspring and holds its nature together, being a fragment and part of the parent. Since, therefore, the world does not resemble molded or assembled works, but possesses a great portion of life and divinity which God sowed from himself into matter and mixed with it, it is likely...”*

<summary>This page argues that pagan theologians viewed the universe as a living organism unified under a single supreme cause, rather than a collection of independent gods or a dead machine. It highlights Plutarch's distinction between God as a "maker" of objects and a "father" of a living world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that ancient pagan philosophers viewed the world not as a separate, mechanical entity, but as something intimately connected to its divine source—either as a "living animal" fathered by God or as a structure sustained by a World Soul.</meta>

# CHAPTER IV. Arguments from the Deity

<note>original Greek: ...τως ἅμα πατήρ τε τοῦ κόσμου ζώου γεγονότος, καὶ ποιητὴς ἐπονομάζεται</note> ...he is named both the Father and the Maker of the world, which has become a living creature. *Begetting <note>original: "Generation"</note> is the making or production of something living <note>original: "Animate"</note>. The work of a craftsman <note>original: "Artificer"</note>, such as an architect or sculptor <note>original: "Statuary"</note>, as soon as it is produced, departs and is removed from its maker, having no intrinsic dependence upon him. Whereas from a parent who begets, there is a principle and power infused into the offspring and mingled with it; this principle contains its whole nature, being a kind of detachment <note>original: "Avulsion"</note> from the parent. Therefore, since the world is not like those works that are artificially made and put together by men, but has a share of life and divinity which God has inserted into it and mingled with it, God is rightly styled by **Plato** not only the Maker, but also the Father of the whole world, as it is a living animal.* To the same purpose also **Plotinus** writes: <margin>Ennead 4, Book 3, Chapter 9.</margin> <note>original Greek: γενόμενος δὴ οἷον οἶκος τις καλὸς καὶ ποικίλος, οὐκ ἀπετμήθη τοῦ πεποιηκότος, οὐδ' αὖ ἐκοίνωσεν αὑτῷ· ἔχει γὰρ ψυχὴν κρατούμενος οὐ κρατῶν, καὶ ἐχόμενος ἀλλ' οὐκ ἔχων, κεῖται γὰρ ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ ἀνεχούσῃ αὐτὸν, καὶ οὐκ ἄμοιρόν ἐστιν αὐτῆς, ὡς ἂν ἐν ὕδασι δίκτυον τεγόμενον ζωῇ</note> *The world, being made like a large and stately building <note>original: "Edifice"</note>, was neither cut off and separated from its Maker, nor yet mingled and confused with him. For he still remains above, presiding over it. The world is so animated that it is possessed by a Soul, rather than possessing it; it lies in that great <term>Psyche</term> <note>Psyche: The World Soul or Mundane Soul</note> which sustains it, like a net in the waters, entirely moistened with life.* 

Thus **Plotinus**, supposing the whole physical world to be *animated*, affirms that it is neither cut off from its Maker (by which Maker he here understands the *World Soul* <note>original: "Mundane Soul"</note>), nor is that World Soul itself *immersed* into its body (the world) in the same way our human souls are into our bodies. Instead, it presides over the world and acts upon it as something elevated above it. And although, according to him, that **Second Divine <term>Hypostasis</term>** <note>hypostasis: a distinct person or substance within the Trinity of Neo-Platonism</note> of **Nous** or **Intellect** is likewise elevated above this World Soul—and again, the **First Hypostasis** or Supreme Deity (called by him **Unity** and **Goodness**) is above the Intellect—yet the physical world could not be said to be cut off from these either. All three—the **Monad**, **Mind**, and **Soul**—are closely and intimately united together.

XXX. The **Hebrews** were the only nation who, for several ages before Christianity, professedly opposed the <term>polytheism</term> <note>polytheism: the worship of many gods</note> and <term>idolatry</term> of the pagan world. Therefore, it may probably be concluded that they had the right notion of this pagan polytheism and understood what it consisted in: namely, whether it lay in worshipping many *unmade, self-originated deities* as partial creators of the world, or else in worshipping other *created beings superior to men* alongside the Supreme God. 

Now **Philo** <note>Philo of Alexandria: a Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with Jewish scripture</note> plainly understood pagan polytheism in this latter way. This appears from a passage in his book *On the Confusion of Languages*, where he speaks of the Supreme God (the Maker and Lord of the whole world) and of his <note>original Greek: δυνάμεις ἀρωγοὶ</note> *innumerable assistant powers*, both visible and invisible. <margin>Page 345.</margin> He adds: <note>original Greek: καταπλαγέντες οὖν τινὲς τὴν ἑκατέρου τῶν κόσμων φύσιν, οὐ μόνον ὅλας ἐξεθείωσαν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ κάλλιστα τῶν ἐν αὐτοῖς μερῶν, ἥλιον, καὶ σελήνην, καὶ τὸν σύμπαντα οὐρανὸν, ἅπερ οὐδὲν αἰδεσθέντες θεοὺς ἐκάλεσαν, ὧν τὴν ἐπίνοιαν κατιδὼν μωϋσῆς φησι κύριε κύριε βασιλεῦ τῶν θεῶν, ἔνδειξιν τῆς παρ' ὑπηκόοις ἀρχόντων διαφορᾶς</note> *Therefore, some men, being struck with admiration for the nature of both worlds, not only deified the whole, but also the most beautiful parts within them—the sun, the moon, and the entire heaven—which they did not hesitate to call gods. Seeing through their way of thinking, Moses says, "Lord, Lord, King of the gods," indicating the difference between the Ruler and his subjects.* Wherefore some men being struck with admiration...

# The Hebrew Notion, Book 1.

...admiration of both these worlds, the *Visible* and the *Invisible*, they have not only deified the *whole* of them, but also their *several parts*, such as the *Sun*, the *Moon*, and the whole *Heaven*. They did not hesitate to call these *gods*. Moses respected this notion and language of theirs in those words of his, *You Lord the King of Gods*; he thereby declaring the **transcendency** <note>original: "transcendency," meaning the supreme excellence or superiority</note> of the Supreme **God** above all those subjects of His called **gods**. To the same purpose **Philo** also writes in his commentary <margin>753.</margin> upon the Decalogue: <note>original Greek: πᾶσαν οὖν τὴν τοιαύτην τερθρείαν ἀπωσάμενοι, τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς φύσει μὴ προσκυνῶμεν, εἰ καὶ καθαρωτέρας καὶ ἀθανατωτέρας οὐσίας ἔλαχον, ἀδελφὰ δ᾿ ἀλλήλων τὰ γενόμενα, καθ᾿ ὃ γέγονεν, ἐπεὶ καὶ πατὴρ ἁπάντων ὁ ποιητὴς τῶν ὅλων· καὶ πρῶτον τοῦτο καὶ ἱερώτατον παράγγελμα στηλιτεύωμεν ἐν αὐτοῖς, ἕνα τὸν ἀνωτάτω νομίζειν τε καὶ τιμᾶν Θεόν</note> *Therefore, removing all such imposture, let us worship no beings that are by nature brothers and related <note>original: "Germane"</note> to us, even though they are endowed with far more pure and immortal essences than we are. For all created things, as such, have a kind of related and brotherly equality with one another, the Maker of all things being their common Father. But let us deeply imprint this first and most holy commandment in our hearts: to acknowledge and worship one only highest God.* 

And again afterward: <note>original Greek: ὅσοι μὲν ἡλίου, καὶ σελήνης, καὶ τοῦ σύμπαντος οὐρανοῦ τε καὶ κόσμου, καὶ τῶν ἐν αὐτοῖς ὁλοχερεστάτων μερῶν ὡς θεῶν πρεπολοῦτε καὶ θεραπεύονται, διαμαρτάνουσι, τοὺς ὑπηκόους τοῦ ἄρχοντος σεμνύνοντες</note> *Those who worship the sun, and the moon, and the whole heaven and world, and the principal parts of them as gods, are in error, in that they worship the subjects of the Prince; whereas the Prince alone ought to be worshipped.* Thus, according to **Philo**, pagan polytheism consisted of giving religious worship, besides to the Supreme God, to other created understanding beings and parts of the world that are more pure and immortal than humans.

**Flavius Josephus**, in his *Jewish Antiquities*, extolling **Abraham's** wisdom and piety, writes thus concerning him: <note>original Greek: πρῶτος οὖν τολμᾷ Θεὸν ἀποφήνασθαι δημιουργὸν τῶν ὅλων ἕνα</note> which some would understand in this manner: *that Abraham was the first who publicly declared that there was one God the Demiurge <note>original: "Demiurgus," a term for a divine craftsman or creator of the universe</note> or maker of the whole world.* It is as if all mankind besides at that time had supposed the world to have been made not by *one* but by *many gods*. But the true meaning of those words is this: that **Abraham** was the first who, in that degenerate age, publicly declared that the Maker of the whole world was the one only God, and alone to be religiously worshipped. Accordingly, it follows afterward in the same writer: <note>original Greek: ᾧ καλῶς ἔχει μόνῳ τὴν τιμὴν καὶ τὴν εὐχαριστίαν ἀπονέμειν</note> *to whom alone men ought to give honor and thanks.* 

And the reason for this is also set down there: <note>original Greek: τῶν δ᾿ λοιπῶν, εἰ καί τι πρὸς εὐδαιμονίαν συντελεῖ, κατὰ προσταγὴν τὴν τούτου παρέχειν ἕκαστον καὶ οὐ κατ᾿ οἰκείαν ἰσχύν</note> *Because all those other beings that were then worshipped as gods—whatever any of them contributed to the happiness of mankind—they did it not by their own power, but by his appointment and command.* He uses the examples of the Sun, Moon, Earth, and Sea, which are all made and ordered by a higher power and providence, by the force of which they contribute to our utility. It is as if he should have said that no created being ought to be religiously worshipped, but the Creator only. And this agrees

It highlights Abraham's historical role as the first to publicly declare that only the Maker of the world deserves religious worship, as all other entities act only by His command.</summary>

<header>CHAP. IV. Of the Pagan Polytheism.</header>

<margin>Genesis 21:33</margin>This agrees with what we read in Scripture concerning **Abraham**, that he *called upon the Name of the Lord*, <note>original Hebrew: אל עולם (*El Olam*)</note> *The God of the whole World*. That is, he worshipped no particular created beings, as the other Pagans at that time did, but only that Supreme *Universal Divinity* <note>original: "Numen," a Latin term for divine power or a deity</note>, who made and contains the whole world. And thus <margin>On Idolatry, chapter 1, section 7</margin> **Maimonides** <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a highly influential Sephardic Jewish philosopher and scholar</note> interprets that passage: <note>original Hebrew: התחיל להודיע לעם שאין ראוי לעבוד אלא לאלוה העולם</note> *Abraham began to teach that none ought to be religiously worshipped, save only the God of the whole world.* Moreover, the same **Josephus** afterwards in his twelfth book introduces **Aristaeus** (who seems to have been a secret Greek convert) pleading with **Ptolemy Philadelphus** <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus, the King of Egypt who famously commissioned the Septuagint translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> on behalf of the Jews and their liberty, in this manner: <note>original Greek: τὴν βασιλείαν σοῦ διέποντος, τοῦ θεμένου τὰς νόμους αὐτοῖς, ᾧ γὰρ ἅπαντα συνεστάμενον θεὸν, ᾧ οὗτοι καὶ ἡμεῖς σεβόμεθα, Ζῆνα καλοῦντες αὐτὸν, ἑτοίμως ἀπὸ τοῦ σύμπασιν ἐμφύειν τὸ ζῆν, τὴν ἐπίκλησιν αὐτοῦ νοήσαντες</note> *It would well agree with your goodness and magnanimity to free the Jews from that miserable captivity they are under, since the same God who governs your kingdom gave laws to them, as I have found out through diligent research. For both they and we alike worship the God who made all things—we calling him **Zene** <note>a form of Zeus</note> because he gives life to all, correctly understanding his title from the fact that he implants life in all things. Therefore, for the honor of that God, whom they worship in a unique manner, please indulge them the liberty of returning to their native country.* Where Aristaeus also, according to the sense of the Pagans, thus concludes: *Know, O King, that I do not intercede for these Jews because I have any kinship with them,* <note>original Greek: πάντων δὲ ἀνθρώπων δημιέργημα ὄντων τοῦ θεοῦ, καὶ γινώσκων αὐτὸν ἡδόμενον τοῖς ὑποῖσιν, ἐπί τούτῳ καὶ σὲ παρακαλῶ</note> *but because all men are the workmanship of God; and knowing that he is delighted with those who are pious, I therefore thus exhort you.*

As for the later Jewish writers and Rabbis, it is certain that the majority of them supposed the *Pagans* to have acknowledged *One Supreme and Universal Divinity*, and to have worshipped all their other gods only as his *ministers*, or as mediators between him and them. **Maimonides** in his work *Halachot Akum* <note>Laws regarding Idolatry</note> describes the rise of Pagan Polytheism in the days of **Enosh** <note>The grandson of Adam</note> in this manner: <note>original Hebrew: בימי אנוש טעו בני האדם טעות גדול ונבערה עצת חכמי אותו הדור ואנוש עצמו מן הטועים היה וזו היתה טעותם : אמרו הואיל והאל ברא כוכבים אלו וגלגלים להנהיג את העולם ונתנם במרום וחלק להם כבוד והם שמשין המשמשים לפניו ראוים: הם לשבחם ולפארם ולחלוק להם כבוד וזהו רצון האל ברוך הוא לגדל ולכבד מי שגדלו וכבדו כמו שהמלך רוצה לכבד העומדים לפניו וזהו כבודו של מלך</note> *In the days of Enosh, the sons of men erred grievously, and the wise men of that age became foolish (even Enosh himself being among those who erred). Their error was this: they said that since God had created the stars and celestial spheres to govern the world, and placing them on high, had bestowed this honor upon them so that they should be his ministers and subservient instruments; men ought therefore to praise them, honor them, and worship them. They believed this was the pleasure of the Blessed God: that men should magnify and honor those whom he himself has magnified and honored, just as a king wishes his ministers to be reverenced—this honor ultimately reflecting back on the king himself.* Again, the same Maimonides writes at the beginning of the second chapter of that book: <note>original Hebrew: עיקר הצווי העבודה זרה שלא לעבוד אחד מכל הברואים</note> *The essence of the commandment concerning idolatry is not to worship any of the created beings...*

It highlights Maimonides' theory that polytheism began when people mistakenly started worshipping God's "ministers"—the stars and celestial bodies—as a way of honoring the Creator.</summary>

<header>The Pagans' Many Gods, Book I.</header>

> <note>original Hebrew: לא מלאך ולא גלגל ולא כוכב ולא אחד מן היסודות ולא אחד מכל הנבראים מהן ואף עלפי שהעובד יודע שהשם הוא האלהים והוא עובד הנברא הזה על דרך שעבד אנוש ואנשי דורו תחלה הרי זה עבד עבודה זרה</note>
> **Neither an angel, nor a celestial sphere, nor a star, nor any of the four elements, nor any thing made out of them should be worshipped. For even though the worshiper knows that the Lord is God and is superior to them all, if he worships a created thing in the way that Enosh and the rest of his generation first did, he is nonetheless guilty of "strange worship" [idolatry].**

The foundation of that commandment against "strange worship" (now commonly called **idolatry**) is this: no one should worship any created being whatsoever—neither an angel, nor a celestial sphere, nor a star, nor any of the four elements, nor anything made out of them. For even if the person worshipping these things knows that the **Lord** is God and superior to them all, and worships those creatures only in the same way that **Enosh** <note>In Jewish tradition, the generation of Enosh, grandson of Adam, is often cited as the era when humanity first began to fall into idolatry by worshipping stars as God's ministers.</note> and the rest of that age did, he is nonetheless guilty of strange worship, or idolatry. Furthermore, even after the time of Enosh, in succeeding ages, the polytheism of the pagan nations was nothing other than this: worshipping created beings (besides the one Supreme God) as the ministers of His providence and as intermediaries or mediators between Him and humanity. This is likewise declared by **Maimonides** <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent Jewish philosopher and scholar</note> in his *Guide for the Perplexed* (original: *More Nevochim*) to have been the universal belief of all the Hebrews or Jews:

<margin>Part 1, chapter 36.</margin>
> <note>original Hebrew: ואתה יודע כי כל מי שעובד עבודה זרה לא יעבדה דעת שאין אלוה בלעדי ה' ולא דמה מעולם כלל מן העובדים ולא ידמה מן הבאים שהצורה אשר יעשה מן המתכות או מן האבנים והעצים שהצורה ההיא היא אשר בראה השמים והארץ אבל אמנם יעבדוה על צד שהוא דמיון לדבר שהוא אמצעי בינם ובין האלוה וזה ממה שלא יחלוק בו אחד מבעלי תורתנו</note>
> **You know that whoever commits idolatry does not do so because he supposes there is no other God besides the one he worships. It never entered the minds of any idolaters—nor ever will—that the statue they made of metal, stone, or wood is the very God who created heaven and earth. Rather, they worship those statues and images only as a representation of something that acts as a mediator between God and themselves. This is a point on which none of our religious scholars disagree.**

You know that whoever commits idolatry does not do so assuming that there is no other God besides what he worships. It never entered the minds of any idolaters—nor ever will—that the statue made by them from metal, stone, or wood is that very God who created heaven and earth. Instead, they worship those statues and images only as the representation of something that is a mediator between God and them. **Moses Albelda**, the author of the book entitled *The Everlasting Burnt Offering* (original: *Gnolath Tamid*), reduces all pagan polytheism and idolatry to these two principles—one which regarded God, and the other which regarded humanity itself:

<margin>Folio 147.</margin>
> <note>original Hebrew: הא' טענו לזה מצדו ית' ואומרים כי הוא גבוה מעל גבוה ואא להדבק בו רק ע"י האמצעיים כמנהג המלך בו שהרוצים לשאול שאלה מה ממנו ושלוה ע"י אמצעי ולכן עשים אותה הע"א כדי להוריד השפע האלהי על ידה: הב' טוענין מצד עצמם וזה כי היות האדם גשמי אינו יכול להתבודד מעצמו אם לא ישים נגדו דבר מה מוחש ועירוה ויעוררו להכין עצמו כדי שתדבק בו השגחתו יתברך</note>
> **First, they argued this from God's side, saying that He is "high above the high" [supremely transcendent], and it is impossible to be united to Him except through intermediaries, following the custom of an earthly king. Those who wish to petition a king do so through an intermediary. Therefore, they made idols to draw down divine influence through them. Secondly, they argued from their own side: because humans are physical, they cannot focus their minds on God alone unless they place something tangible before them to stir their devotion and prepare themselves so that His providence may attach to them.**

The idolaters first argued this in respect to God: since He was of such transcendent perfection above humanity, it was not possible for people to be united with or have communion with Him except through certain middle beings or mediators. This follows the custom of earthly kings, who receive petitions through the hands of mediators and intercessors. Secondly, they argued this in respect to themselves: being physical, they could not understand God abstractly. They felt they needed something tangible to excite and stir up their devotion and fix their imagination upon. **Joseph Albo** <note>A 15th-century Spanish Jewish philosopher</note>, in the book called *Principles* (original: *Ikkarim*), concludes that **Ahab** and the other idolatrous kings of Israel and Judah worshipped other gods based on those two reasons mentioned by Maimonides and no other. Namely, they believed the Supreme God was honored by worshipping His ministers, and that there ought to be certain middle beings and mediators between Him and humanity.

<margin>Part 3, chapter 18.</margin>
> <note>original Hebrew: אחאב וזלתו ממלכי ישראל ויהודה היו טועין אחר הכחות הגלגלויות משתי צדדין שאמרנו וגם שלמה טעה בזה עם היותם מאמינים במציאות השם ואחדותו אם כשהיו חושבים לכבד את השם בזה ואם כשהיו חושבין לעשות סרסור ואמצעיים בינם ובין השם יתב'</note>
> **Ahab and other kings of Israel and Judah erred by following the celestial powers for the two reasons we mentioned. Solomon also erred in this, despite their belief in the existence of God and His unity. They either thought to honor God through this, or they thought to create agents and intermediaries between themselves and God, may He be blessed.**

<summary>This page presents the arguments of Jewish scholars like Maimonides and Albo, who claim that pagan idolatry was not a denial of the Supreme God, but rather a misguided attempt to worship Him through created intermediaries and physical symbols.</summary>

<header>Chapter IV. Worshipped as Mediators.</header>

*Ahab and other Kings of Israel and Judah, and even Solomon himself, erred in worshipping the stars based on those two reasons already mentioned from Maimonides, despite the fact that they believed in the existence of God and His unity. They partly believed they should honor God by worshipping His ministers, and partly worshipped them as mediators between God and themselves. And the same writer determines the meaning of that First Commandment (which is to him the Second <note>In the Jewish numbering of the Ten Commandments, the first "word" is the declaration "I am the Lord your God," making the prohibition of other gods the second.</note>) "Thou shalt have no other gods before my face," to be this:*

->**"To set them up as intermediaries between Me and you, or to think you are exalting Me through their worship."** <note>original Hebrew: להכניס אותם אמצעיים ביני ובינך או שתחשוב לרומם אותי בעבודתם</note><-

*You shall not set up other inferior gods as mediators between Me and yourself, or worship them in such a way as to think you are honoring Me by doing so. Rabbi David Kimchi <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), also known as Radak, was a foundational medieval Jewish biblical commentator and grammarian.</note> (on 2 Kings 17) writes the following concerning that Israelite priest who, by the command of the King of Assyria, was sent to Samaria to teach the new inhabitants there how to worship the God of that land (of whom it is later said that they both feared the Lord and served their idols [strange worship]):*

> **"If he had told them not to practice strange worship <note>original: עבודה זרה (Avodah Zarah), the standard Hebrew term for idolatry.</note> at all, they would not have listened to him, as that was something all those Eastern people were educated in from their very infancy—to the point that it was a kind of fundamental truth to them. Therefore, he permitted them to worship all their various gods as they had done before, only he required them to direct the intention of their minds to the God of Israel (as the Supreme God). For those gods could do them neither good nor harm, except according to His will and pleasure; yet they worshipped them for this purpose: that they might be MEDIATORS between them and the Creator."** <note>original Hebrew: אם יאמר להם שלא יהיו עובדים עבודה זרה כלל לא היו מאמינים שהוא דבר שגדלו בו כל האומות מקדם והוא אצלם כמו מושכל ראשון אך אמר להם שיהיו עובדים את אלוהיהם כמו שהיו עובדים ובלבד שתהא כוונת האל בלבם כי אלא האלהים לא ירעו ולא ייטיבו כי אם ברצון האל אלא שעובדים אותם להיותם אמצעיים בינם ובין הבורא</note>

*In the Book Nitzachon <note>Sefer Nitzachon (The Book of Victory) is a medieval Jewish apologetic and polemical text.</note>, all the polytheism and idolatry of the pagans is reduced to these three categories: First,* **"They worshipped the ministers of God for His honor"** <note>original Hebrew: עבדו משרתי השם לכבודו</note> *when they worshipped God's agents thinking it would honor Him; and Second,* **"They worshipped those who were advocates for them"** <note>original Hebrew: עבדו אותם שהיו מליצים בעדם</note> *when they worshipped them as speakers and intercessors for them with God; and Lastly,* **"They worshipped wood and stone as a memorial of Him"** <note>original Hebrew: עבדו לעץ ואבן לזכרו</note> *when they worshipped statues of wood and stone as reminders of Him. And though it is true that Isaac Abrabanel <note>Isaac Abrabanel (1437–1508) was a Portuguese Jewish statesman and philosopher.</note> (on 2 Kings 17) enumerates even more types of pagan idolatry, totaling ten, they are all merely different modes of creature-worship. There is no such thing to be found among them as the worship of many uncreated, independent deities acting as partial creators of the world.*

Moreover, those Rabbinic writers commonly interpret certain passages of Scripture in this sense: that the pagan idolaters nonetheless acknowledged one Supreme Deity. For example, Jeremiah 10:7: *"Who is there that will not fear You, You King of Nations? For among all their wise men and in all their kingdoms, there is none like You; though they have all become brutish, and their worshipping of stocks [wooden idols] is a doctrine of vanity."* For Maimonides thus glosses <note>A "gloss" is an explanatory note or interpretation of a text.</note> upon those words:

Another passage is **Malachi 1:11**. Although we read this in the future tense as a prophecy of the Gentiles, the Jews understand it as referring to the present time when those words were written: *From the rising of the sun to its going down, my name is great among the Gentiles; and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure offering, for my name is great among the Gentiles, says the Lord of Hosts.* "But you profane it," etc. Upon these words, **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Also known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French commentator on the Torah and Talmud.</note> explains it this way:

-> "Whoever has understanding knows that he is the God who is over them all; and in every place, even among the nations, there are free-will offerings brought to my name." <note>original Hebrew: מי שיש לו עז יודע שהוא אלוה שהוא על כולם ובכל מקום מתנדבים לשמי אף האומות</note><-

And **Kimchi** agrees with him here:

-> "Even though the nations worship the host of heaven, they still confess that I am the **First Cause**; they only worship the stars so that they might be mediators between me and them." <note>original Hebrew: אף על פי שהגוים עובדים לצבא השמים מודים בי שאני הסבה הראשונה אלא שעובדים אותם שיהיו אמצעיים ביני ובינם</note><-

Whether either of these two scriptural passages sufficiently proves what these Jews intend or not, it is nonetheless evident from their interpretations that they themselves assumed the pagans acknowledged **one Supreme Deity**, and that their **other gods** were nothing more than his **creatures** and **ministers**. 

Nevertheless, there is another place in Scripture which seems even more relevant to this point, and has been interpreted as such by Rabbi Solomon and others: **Psalm 65:5** (verse 6 in some versions), where God is called *the confidence of all the ends of the earth, and of those who are far away in the sea* <note>original Hebrew: מבטח כל קצוי ארץ וים רחקים</note>—that is, even of all the pagan world.

Thus we see plainly that the Hebrew scholars and Rabbis have generally held this conviction: that the ancient pagan nations (at least the intelligent among them) acknowledged one Supreme God of the whole world. They believed all other gods were merely creatures and inferior ministers who were worshipped for **two reasons**: either because the pagans thought the honor shown to them benefited the Supreme God, or else so they might be <term>mediators</term> <note>original Hebrew: אמצעיים (Emtza'iyim)</note>, <term>negotiators</term> <note>original Hebrew: סרסורים (Sarsurim), referring to agents or brokers</note>, and <term>intercessors</term> <note>original Hebrew: מליצין (Melitzin), referring to advocates or orators</term> with Him. # CHAPTER 4: God, as affirmed by the Hebrews.

The gods of the pagans were thought by these Hebrew scholars to be primarily of two types: *angels*, and *stars* or *spheres*. The latter of these (the stars and spheres), both Jews and pagans concluded were *animated* and *intelligent*:
<margin>Maimonides, The Foundations of the Law (Yesodei HaTorah), Chapter 3, Section 9.</margin>
For as **Maimonides** <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and astronomer.</note> expressly states: "The stars and spheres are every one of them animated, and endowed with life, knowledge, and understanding. And they acknowledge Him who commanded and the world was made; every one of them, according to their degree and excellence, praises and honors their Creator, just as the angels do." <note>original Hebrew: כל הכוכבים והגלגלים כולן בעלי נפש ודעה והשכל הם והם חיים ועומדים ומכירין את מי שאמר והיה העולם כל אחד ואחד לפי גודלו ולפי מעלתו משבחין ומפארים ליוצרם כמו המלאכים</note> And they would confirm this from that passage of Scripture, **Nehemiah 9:6**: *You, even you, are Lord alone; You have made heaven, the heaven of heavens with all their host, the earth with all things that are therein, the seas and all that is therein, and You preserve them all; and the host of heaven worships You.* The "host of heaven" is a phrase commonly used in the Bible to refer to the stars.

---

## XXXI.
Finally, this same point is plainly confirmed by the scriptures of the New Testament as well: that the Gentiles and pagans, however much they were polytheists and idolaters, were not unacquainted with the knowledge of the *True God*—that is, of the *One only self-existent* and *omnipotent Being* who encompasses all things under Him. From this, it necessarily follows that their many other *gods* were all supposed to have been derived from this One, and to be **dependent on Him**.

For first, **St. Paul** in his letter to the Romans tells us that these Gentiles or pagans "suppressed the truth in unrighteousness" <note>original Greek: τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἐν ἀδικίᾳ κατέχειν</note>, or "unjustly detained and imprisoned the truth." This is primarily understood as the *truth* concerning *God*, as is clear from the text that follows. Therefore, it implies that the *pagans* were not without such a knowledge of God as might and should have kept them from all kinds of idolatry; however, by their own fault, it proved ineffective for that purpose, as is declared afterward:
<margin>Romans 1:28</margin>
"They did not see fit to retain God in their acknowledgement" <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἐδοκίμασαν τὸν θεὸν ἔχειν ἐν ἐπιγνώσει</note>, or their practical knowledge of Him. Here, a distinction must be observed between "knowledge" <note>original Greek: γνῶσις (gnosis)</note> and "acknowledgment" <note>original Greek: ἐπίγνωσις (epignosis)</note> of God. The former is plainly granted to the pagans in this chapter, while the latter is denied to them because they fell into polytheism and idolatry.
<margin>Romans 1:25</margin>
This is the meaning of these words: "They exchanged the truth of God for a lie" <note>original Greek: μετήλλαξαν τὴν ἀλήθειαν τοῦ θεοῦ ἐν τῷ ψεύδει</note>. Again, the same apostle affirms there that "what may be known of God is manifest among them" <note>original Greek: τὸ γνωστὸν τοῦ θεוῦ φανερόν ἐστιν ἐν αὐτοῖς</note>, because God Himself showed it to them. While there is an aspect of God that is *unknowable* and *incomprehensible* to all mortals, that which is *knowable*—His eternal power and divinity, along with the attributes belonging to them—is made manifest to all humanity through His works. *For since the creation of the world, His invisible attributes are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made.* Furthermore, this apostle explicitly declares that the pagans knew God, as seen in the criticism which—

It explains that the "host of heaven" was viewed as intelligent beings and distinguishes between having knowledge of God and truly acknowledging Him in practice.</summary>

# Pagans' Knowledge of the True God: Book 1

<margin>Romans 1:21</margin>
The Apostle Paul says of them, "Because, although they knew God, they did not glorify Him as God" <note>original Greek: διότι γνόντες τὸν Θεὸν, οὐχ ὡς Θεὸν ἐδόξασαν</note>; because they fell into **polytheism** and **idolatry**. Although the Apostle here cites only the latter of those two—their "changing the glory of the incorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and four-footed beasts, and creeping things" <note>Romans 1:23</note>—the reason for this focus is that the **idolatry** of the pagans (properly so called, meaning their worship of wood and stone formed into the likeness of man or beast) was generally considered by the Jews to be the most gross of all their 
<margin>Philo, *On the Decalogue*, page 753.</margin>
**religious errors**. Thus, **Philo Judaeus** <note>A Hellenistic Jewish philosopher from Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE).</note> plainly declares: "Whoever worships the sun, moon, the entire heaven and world, and the chief parts within them as gods, unquestionably errs (for they honor the subjects instead of the Prince). However, they are guilty of less iniquity and injustice than those who shape wood, stone, silver, gold, and similar materials into statues to worship them, etc." <note>original Greek: ὅσοι μὲν ἡλίου καὶ σελήνης, καὶ τοῦ σύμπαντος οὐρανοῦ τε καὶ κόσμου... ἧττον δὲ τῶν ἀλλων ἀδικοῦσι, τῶν ξύλα καὶ λίθους... μορφωσάντων</note>. He later gives this account for that assertion: "Because these people have cut off the most excellent support <term>original: fulcrum</term> of the soul: the proper conception of the ever-living God. By doing so, like unballasted ships, they are tossed up and down perpetually, never able to rest in any safe harbor" <note>original Greek: τὸ γὰρ κάλλιστον ἔρεισμα τῆς ψυχῆς ἐξέκοψαν, τὴν περὶ τοῦ ζῶντος ἀεὶ θεοῦ προσήκουσαν ὑπόληψιν</note>. 

From this, it came to pass that the **polytheism** of the pagans—their worship of inferior gods (such as stars and demons)—was also commonly called **idolatry** by Jews and Christians, being named "by its most famous type" <note>original Latin: *à famosiore specie*</note>. Lastly, the Apostle plainly declares that the error of pagan superstition universally consisted not in worshiping *many independent gods and creators*, but in joining **creature-worship**, as such, in some way or another with the worship of the Creator: "They worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator" <note>Romans 1:25</note>. 
<margin>Romans 1:25</margin>
These words <note>original Greek: ἐσεβάσθησαν καὶ ἐλάτρευσαν τῇ κτίσει παρὰ τὸν κτίσαντα</note> are to be rendered either as, "They [religiously] worshiped the creature **besides** the Creator," for that preposition is often used in this sense. For example, **Aristotle** affirms 
<margin>Aristotle, *Metaphysics*, Book 1, Chapter 6.</margin>
concerning **Plato** that he "made unity and numbers to be **besides** the things" <note>original Greek: τὸ ἓν καὶ τοὺς ἀριθμοὺς παρὰ τὰ πράγματα ποιῆσαι</note>. He did not make numbers to be the things themselves, as the Pythagoreans had done, but made "numbers to exist by themselves, **besides** the perceivable things" <note>original Greek: τοὺς ἀριθμοὺς παρὰ τὰ αἰσθητὰ</note>. By "numbers," as Aristotle himself explains there, he means the **Ideas** contained in the **First Intellect** (which was Plato's second **divine hypostasis** <note>Hypostasis: a term for a distinct substance or person within a divine hierarchy.</note>). Likewise, by "Unity" <note>original Greek: τὸ ἓν</note>, which gives essence <note>original Greek: τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι</note> to those Ideas, he means Plato's first **divine hypostasis**, the "One Itself" <note>original Latin: *Ipsum Unum*</note>.

Or else the words ought to be translated thus: "And worshiped the creature **above** or **more than** the Creator." The preposition "beside/beyond" <note>Greek: παρὰ (para)</note> is sometimes used comparatively to signify **excess**. For example, in **Luke 13:2**: "Think you that these Galileans were sinners **beyond** all the Galileans?" <note>original Greek: ἁμαρτωλοὶ παρὰ πάντας τοὺς Γαλιλαίους</note>. And verse 4: "Think you that those eighteen upon whom the tower of Siloam fell, were debtors **above** all the men that dwelt in Jerusalem?" <note>original Greek: ὀφειλέται παρὰ πάντας</note>. According...

It uses linguistic analysis of Greek prepositions to show that pagans "knew God" but failed to honor Him exclusively.</summary>

### Chapter IV: God, Testified in Scripture

According to either of these interpretations, it is supposed that the Pagans did worship the *True God*, the *Creator* of the whole world; though they worshipped the *creature* as well—*besides* Him, or (perhaps in some sense) *above* Him and *more* than Him. 

But as for that other interpretation of <term>more than/instead of the Creator</term> <note>original Greek: παρὰ τὸν κτίσαντα</note>, which Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605) was a major French Protestant theologian and successor to John Calvin.</note> chose to follow—that they worshipped the creature while the *Creator* was completely ignored—this is no true *literal* version. It is only a gloss or commentary made according to a certain preconceived and far-fetched opinion that the Pagans did not worship the *Supreme God* or *Creator* at all, but universally transferred all their worship only to the *creature*. 

However, we leave it to others to investigate in what sense the Pagans might be said to worship the *creatures* *above*, *beyond*, or *more* than the Creator (since it is impossible for a *creature*, as a creature, to be worshipped with more internal and mental honor than its *Creator* when viewed as such). Is it because religious worship, which properly and only belongs to the *Creator* and not at all to the *creature*, is transferred from the *Creator* to the *creature*? Such people might then be said to worship the *creature more than the Creator*. Or is it because some of these *Pagans* might more frequently address their devotions to their inferior gods (such as *stars*, *demons*, and *heroes*), thinking the Supreme God was either *above* their worship, *incomprehensible*, or *inaccessible* to them? Or lastly, is it because the *image-worshippers* and *statue-worshippers* among the Pagans (whom the Apostle Paul principally refers to there) directed all their external devotion to *physical objects* and *created forms*? 

Regardless, it cannot be thought that the Apostle Paul here only criticizes the Pagans for worshipping creatures *more* than the Creator—as if they had not offended at all if they had worshipped them as equals. Doubtless, their sin was that they gave any religious worship at all to the *creature*, though it is said in a way of *aggravating* their crime that they also worshipped the *creature more than the Creator*. Thus, we see plainly that *Pagan superstition* and *idolatry* (according to the true scriptural definition) consisted not in worshipping *many creators*, but in worshipping the *creatures* along with the *Creator*.

Besides this, we have in the Acts of the Apostles a speech that Saint *Paul* made at *Athens* in the *Areopagus* <note>The Areopagus was the high court of Athens, meeting on a hill of the same name.</note> court, beginning in this way: *“Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are more than ordinarily religious.”* For the word <term>very religious</term> <note>original Greek: δεισιδαιμονεστέρους; this word can mean "very religious" or "superstitious."</note> seems to be taken there in a positive sense. It is not only more likely that Saint *Paul* would begin his speech by trying to *win their favor* <note>original Latin: captare benevolentiam</note> with a compliment, but it is also very unlikely that he would call their worship of the *True God* "superstition." For he continues: *“For as I passed by and looked at your sacred monuments, I found an altar with this inscription: <term>TO THE UNKNOWN GOD</term> <note>original Greek: Ἀγνώστῳ θεῷ</note>.”* It is true that both *Philostratus* and *Pausanias* <note>Philostratus (c. 170–250 CE) and Pausanias (c. 110–180 CE) were Greek authors who described the monuments and customs of Greece.</note> write that there were in Athens <term>altars of unknown gods</term> <note>original Greek: Ἀγνώστων θεῶν βωμοὶ</note>; but their meaning in this might well be, not that there were altars...
