# The Athenians' Unknown God, Book I

...dedicated to "Unknown Gods" in the plural, but rather that there were several altars which had this singular inscription: **TO THE UNKNOWN GOD.** That there was at least one such altar, besides what is recorded in Scripture, is evident from the dialogue in Lucian’s works entitled *Philopatris* <note>A satirical dialogue once attributed to the Greek writer Lucian, though now thought to be by a later author. It mocks both pagan and Christian beliefs.</note>. In this work, the character Critias uses this form of oath: "No, by the Unknown God at Athens" <note>original Greek: Νὴ τὸν Ἄγνωστον ἐν Ἀθήναις</note>. Furthermore, Triephon says at the close of that dialogue:

> "But we, having found that Unknown God at Athens and worshipped him with hands stretched up to heaven, will give thanks to him, as having been thought worthy to be made subject to his power" <note>original Greek: ἡμεῖς δὲ τὸν ἐν Ἀθήναις Ἄγνωστον ἐφευρόντες, καὶ προσκυνήσαντες, χεῖρας εἰς οὐρανὸν ἐκτείναντες, τούτῳ εὐχαριστήσομεν, ὡς καταξιωθέντες, &c.</note>.

These passages unquestionably refer to that Athenian inscription on one or more altars. The latter passage plainly implies that this **Unknown God** of the Athenians was the **Supreme Governor of the World.** This is followed by Saint Paul’s oration: "Whom therefore you worship in ignorance <note>original Greek: ὃν οὖν ἀγνοοῦντες εὐσεβεῖτε</note> (under this name of the Unknown God), Him I declare to you: the God who made the world and all things in it, the Lord of heaven and earth." 

From this passage, we may conclude two things based on firm Scriptural authority: 

**First**, that by the "Unknown God" of the Athenians, Paul meant the **Only True God, He who made the world and all things in it.** In all probability, He was styled by them the "Unknown God" <note>original Greek: Ἄγνωστος Θεὸς</note> because He is not only invisible but also incomprehensible to mortals. Regarding this, Josephus writes in his work *Against Apion*: 

> "He is knowable to us only by the effects of His power, but as to His own essence, He is unknowable or incomprehensible" <note>original Greek: δυνάμει μόνον ἡμῖν γνώριμον, ὁποῖος δὲ κατ᾽ οὐσίαν ἄγνωστος</note>. 

Similarly, in the writings of Dion Cassius, the God of the Jews is said to be "ineffable and invisible" <note>original Greek: ἄῤῥητόν τε καὶ ἀειδής; "ineffable" means too great or sacred to be expressed in words</note>. When the poet Lucan calls Him an "Uncertain God" <note>original Latin: Incertus Deus</note>, the reason seems to be not only because there was no image of Him, but also because He was not then commonly known by any proper name. This is because the *Tetragrammaton* <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH, which was considered too sacred to pronounce aloud in common use.</note> was religiously avoided by the Jews in everyday speech so that it would not be profaned. 

Some learned men have mentioned that pagans sometimes sacrificed "to the proper and convenient god" <note>original Greek: προσήκοντι θεῷ</note> without using a specific name. However, this seems irrelevant here. That practice proceeded only from the superstitious fear of those pagans—who supposed several gods presided over different things—that they might be mistaken by not addressing the specific god responsible for a certain situation, thus making their devotion unsuccessful. 

However, the statement that this **Unknown God** was "ignorantly worshipped" by the Athenians is to be understood chiefly in regard to their **Polytheism** and **Idolatry**. 

**The second thing** that may be concluded is this: these Athenian pagans did "religiously worship" <note>original Greek: εὐσεβεῖν</note> the **True God, the Lord of Heaven and Earth.** Thus, we have a Scriptural refutation of the opinion that pagans did not worship the Supreme God at all.

Lastly, Saint Paul cites a passage from Aratus, a heathen poet, concerning *Zeus* or *Jupiter*:

# Chapter IV. And Aratus’s Zeus, the True God.

-> “For we are also his offspring” <note>original Greek: τοῦ γὰρ καὶ γένος εἰμέν</note> <-

By quoting the phrase, *“For we are his offspring,”* and interpreting it as a reference to the True God “in whom we live and move and have our being,” we have a clear scriptural acknowledgment that by the “Zeus” of the Greek pagans, they sometimes meant the **True God**. Indeed, it is evident from both the preceding and following verses that Aratus’s **Zeus** was neither a man born in Crete nor in Arcadia, but the **Maker** and **Supreme Governor** of the whole world. Aratus’s poem, *Phænomena*, begins this way:

-> “Let us begin with Zeus” <note>original Greek: Ἐκ Διὸς ἀρχώμεθα</note> <-

(Which in Tully’s <note>Tully is the traditional English name for the Roman statesman and writer Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> version is *“The beginning from Jove is the start for the Muses”* <note>original Latin: Ab Jove Musarum Primordia</note>), and then follows a description of this **Zeus** or **Jupiter**:

> ...of whom we men are never silent;
> and of whom all things are full,
> for all the streets and all the marketplaces of men are full of Zeus;
> the sea and the harbors are full of him;
> and in every way we all have need of Zeus:
> For we are also his offspring.
> <note>original Greek: ——— τοῦ οὐδέποτ' ἄνδρες ἐῶμεν / Ἄῤῥητον· μεσταὶ δὲ Διὸς πᾶσαι μὲν ἀγυιαí, / Πᾶσαι δ' ἀνθρώπων ἀγοραὶ· μεστὴ δὲ θάλασσα, / Καὶ λιμένες· πάντη δὲ Διὸς κεχρήμεθα πάντες· / τοῦ γὰρ καὶ γένος εἰμέν·</note>

The meaning is this: *Him of whom we men are never silent; and of whom all things are full, as he permeates and pervades all and is everywhere; and whose beneficence we all constantly use and enjoy: For we also are his offspring.* Regarding this, **Theon** the Scholiast <term>Scholiast: An ancient commentator or annotator who wrote explanatory notes on classical texts.</term> writes: "Aratus, being about to describe the positions of the stars, very appropriately invokes Zeus, their Father and Maker, first of all. For by 'Zeus' here, we must understand the Demiurge" <note>original Greek: πάνυ πρεπόντως ὁ Ἄρατος τὴν τῶν ἄστρων διεξιέναι μέλλων θέσιν, τὸν πατέρα τούτων καὶ δημιουργὸν, Δία, ἐν πρώτοις προσφωνεῖ· Δία δὲ νῦν τὸν Δημιουργὸν ἀκουστέον·</note>.

By **Zeus**, we are here to understand the **Demiurge** <term>Demiurge: A philosophical term, common in Platonism, for the "Artisan" or "Creator" of the universe.</term> of the world, or as he later expresses it, “the God who created all things” <note>original Greek: ὁ τὰ πάντα δημιουργήσας θεός</note>. Notwithstanding this, we must admit that this Scholiast adds that some of these passages by the poet—even the one cited by the Apostle, “For we are his offspring”—could also be understood in another sense: as referring to the **Physical Zeus** <note>original Greek: Ζεὺς φυσικός</note>, meaning the air. However, there is not the slightest shadow of probability for this, and we believe he mentions it for no other reason than to show off his philological skill. 

Nevertheless, the Scholiast sets down the following as the genuine and proper sense of those words: "This agrees with the title of Jupiter when he is called the Father of gods and men. For if he created us and all these other things for the benefit of human life, we may rightly be called His, and address him as our Father and Maker" <note>original Greek: πρὸς τὸν πατέρα ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε· εἰ γὰρ αὐτὸς ταῦτα ἐδημιούργησε πρὸς τὸ τοῖς ἀνθρώποις βιωφιλὲς, αὐτοῦ ἂν κληθείημεν, αὐτὸν πατέρα καὶ δημιουργὸν ἐπιγραφόμενοι</note>. That this was the only concept the poet had here of **Zeus** or **Jupiter** is undeniably clear from the following words:

-> ...and he, being kind to men, <-
-> shows favorable signs... <-
<note>original Greek: ——— ὁ δ' ἤπιος ἀνθρώποισι / Δέξια σημαίνει ————</note>

Therefore it is evident from the context of *Aratus* that by his *Zeus* or *Jupiter* he really meant the Supreme God, the Maker of the whole world. Since this is plainly confirmed by St. *Paul* and the Scripture, it ought to be a matter beyond controversy among us. Neither is it reasonable to think that *Aratus* was unique in this; rather, he spoke according to the accepted theology of the Greeks, which was held not only among philosophers and learned men, but even among the common people.

# Chapter IV. Distinct from the Fabulous, and Civil.

...this: that the generality of the world before Christianity, by their natural light and contemplation of the works of God, did not attain to such a *practical knowledge* of God as might both free them from *idolatry* and *effectively* bring them to a *holy life*.

<margin>Pages 314, 315.</margin>
XXXII. But in order to provide a fuller explanation of this *pagan theology* and give a more satisfactory account of it, there are *three main points* that must be insisted upon: *First*, that the intelligent pagans worshipped the *one supreme God* under *many different names*; *secondly*, that besides this *one God*, they also worshipped *many gods* who were actually inferior deities subordinate to him; *thirdly*, that they worshipped both the supreme and inferior gods through *images*, *statues*, and *symbols*, which were sometimes abusively <note>misleadingly or improperly</note> called "gods" as well. We begin with the first point: that the supreme God among the pagans was <term>polyonymous</term> <note>original: "Polyonimous"; meaning having many names</note> and was worshipped under several *personal names* according to various *notions* and *considerations* of him, based on his several *attributes*, *powers*, *manifestations*, and *effects* in the world.

<margin>Pages 114, 115.</margin>
It has already been observed from the writings of *Origen* <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 185–253 AD).</note> that not only the *Egyptians*, but also the *Syrians*, *Persians*, *Indians*, and other "barbarian" pagans had, besides their *vulgar <note>common or popular</note> theology*, another more *arcane* and *recondite* <note>hidden or obscure</note> one known among their priests and learned men. That the same was true concerning the Greeks and Latins is unquestionably evident from the account we have given of their *philosophical theology*. By the *vulgar theology* of the pagans, we mean not only their *mythical* or *fabulous* stories, but also their *political* or *civil theology*. Concerning both of these, *St. Austin* <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD).</note> truly affirmed: <margin>The City of God, Book 4, Chapter 8.</margin> *Both the civil and the fabulous are both fabulous and civil.* <note>original Latin: "Et Civilis & Fabulosa, ambæ Fabulosæ sunt, ambæque Civiles"</note> And by their more arcane or recondite theology, he undoubtedly means that which they conceived to be the *natural and true theology*. 

This distinction between *natural and true theology* and *civil and political theology* was acknowledged by all the ancient Greek philosophers—most expressly by *Antisthenes*, *Plato*, *Aristotle*, and the Stoics. It was also owned and much insisted upon both by *Scaevola*, that famous Roman <term>Pontifex</term> <note>a high-ranking priest in ancient Rome</note>, and by *Varro*, that most learned antiquary. They both agreed that the *civil theology* then established by Roman laws was only the theology of the common people, but not the *truth*. They held that there was another theology besides it, which they called *natural*, and which was the theology of *wise men* and of *truth*. Nevertheless, they granted that it was necessary in cities and commonwealths that, besides this natural and true theology (which the generality of the common people were incapable of understanding), there should be another *civil* or *political theology* accommodated to their understanding. This *civil theology* differed from the *natural* only by having a certain mixture of *fable* <note>original: "fabulosity"</note> in it, and was therefore looked upon by them as a middle ground between the natural and the fabulous or *poetical theology*.

Therefore, it was acknowledged that the *vulgar theology* of the *pagans*—meaning not only their *fabulous* stories but even their *civil* laws—

...was often very different from *Natural* and *True Theology*. Although wise men among them in all ages tried as much as they could to hide and disguise this difference—using allegory on the *Poetic Fables* of the gods to bring that theology into some seeming agreement with *Natural* and *Philosophic* theology—whatever they could not reconcile in this way, they excused as being necessary for the *common people* <note>original: "Vulgar"</note>.

The *Fabulous Theology* of both the Greeks and Romans not only *created* <note>original: "Generate"</note> all the other gods, but even *Jupiter* himself, their *Supreme Deity* <note>original: "Numen"</note>, by giving him a father and a mother, a grandfather and a grandmother. And though the Romans did not clearly adopt this into their *Civil Theology*, they were criticized <note>original: "taxed"</note> by *St. Augustine* <note>original: "St. Austin"</note> for allowing the statue of *Jupiter’s Nurse* to be kept in the Capitol as a *religious monument*. Even though this was no different from the *atheistic doctrine* of *Euhemerus*—namely, *that all the gods were really nothing more than mortal men*—it was nonetheless tolerated and overlooked by politicians as a necessary concession to the common people. It was extremely difficult for the public to conceive of any *living being* or *animal* that was never *created* and was *without a beginning*. To such an extent that *Callimachus*—who would by no means admit that *Jupiter* had a tomb in either *Crete* or *Arcadia* (looking upon it as a foul insult to him) for this reason:

->“You did not die, for you exist forever”<-

Because he was *immortal* and *could never die*—nevertheless attributed a *temporary birth* and origin to him, as *Origen* and others observe. Nevertheless, the majority of the more civilized and intelligent Pagans, and even the poets themselves, still constantly maintained this much of *Natural* and *True Theology*: *that Jupiter was the father of both gods and men*. That is, he was the *Maker of the whole world* and, consequently, was himself *without a father, eternal*, and *uncreated*, according to that *Peleadean Oracle* cited earlier from *Pausanias*:

->“Zeus was, Zeus is, Zeus shall be”<-
<note>original: "Ζεὺς ἦν, Ζεὺς ἔστι, Ζεὺς ἔσσεται"</note>

Furthermore, the *Civil Theology* of the Pagans, as well as their *Poetic* theology, contained not only many *imaginary* <note>original: "Phantastick"</note> gods, but also the appearance of a *plurality of independent deities*. It made several gods *supreme* in their own territories and roles: for instance, one as the chief ruler over the *heavens*, another over the *air* and *winds*, another over the *sea*, and another over the *earth* and *hell*. One was the giver of *grain* <note>original: "Corn"</note>, another of *wine*; one was the god of *learning*, another of *pleasure*, and another the god of *war*; and so on for all other things. However, the *Natural Theology* of the Pagans (as it was called)—though it did admit a *plurality of gods* in a certain sense (namely, *inferior deities subordinate* to *one supreme* god)—did not allow for more than *one independent deity*. Nor did it acknowledge any gods at all except those that were *natural*; that is, those that had a *real existence in nature and the world*

# Chapter IV. Their Real and Natural Gods.

...without, and not in *men's opinion only.* And these *Varro* <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a Roman scholar who categorized theology into three types: mythical, natural, and civil.</note> concluded to be no other than, first, the *Soul of the World*, and then the *animated parts thereof superior to men;* that is, *one supreme universal Numen* <note>original: "Numen"; a Latin term for a deity or divine power</note> *unmade,* and other *particular generated gods,* such as *stars, demons, and heroes.* Therefore all the other gods besides these are frequently exploded by Pagan writers (such as *Cicero* and others) under the name of *Dii Poetici* <note>original: "Dii Poetici"; Poetical Gods</note>, that is, not *philosophical,* but *poetical gods,* and *Dii Commentitii* and *Fictitii* <note>original: "Dii Commentitii and Fictitii"; Invented and Fictitious Gods</note>, that is, *not natural and real, but feigned and fictitious gods.* 

In the meantime, they gave this account of them: that they were indeed nothing else but so many several names and notions of *one supreme Numen,* according to his *several powers* and various *manifestations* and *effects* in the world. It was thought fit by the wisdom of the ancient Pagan theologians that all those manifold glories and perfections of the Deity should not be huddled up, and as it were crowded and crumpled together, in one general acknowledgment of an *Invisible Being* the Maker of the world, but that they should be distinctly and severally displayed, and each of them adored singly and apart. This was also done (for the greater pomp and solemnity) under so many *personal names.* Perhaps the unskillful and foolish common people <note>original: "sottish Vulgar"</note> might sometimes mistake these names, not only for so many *real and substantial,* but also *independent and self-existent deities.*

We have before proved that one and the same supreme God, in Egyptian theology, had several proper and personal names given to him, according to several notions of him and his several *powers* and *effects.* *Iamblichus* himself, in that passage already cited, plainly affirms as much: <margin>*On the Egyptian Mysteries*</margin> "The creative mind <note>original: "ὁ δημιουργικὸς νοῦς" (ho dēmiourgikos nous)</note> and president of truth, as it proceeds with wisdom to generation and brings forth the invisible power of the hidden reasons contained within itself into the light, is called in the Egyptian language *Ammon*; as it skillfully accomplishes all things with truth, it is called *Phtha*; as it is productive of good things, it is called *Osiris*; besides which it also has several other names, according to its other powers and energies: as namely *Neith* (or according to *Proclus's* copy, *Neithas*) the tutelar god of the city *Sais,* from whence probably the Greek *Athena* was derived (the Athenians being said to have been at first a colony of these *Saites*); and this is *the divine wisdom diffusing itself through all.*" 

So likewise *Serapis,* which though some would have to be the Sun, is by others plainly described as an *universal Numen.* As *Aristides* says in his eighth oration upon <margin>Page 95.</margin> this god *Serapis:* "Those who inhabit the great city in Egypt call upon this god *Serapis* as their only *Jupiter,* he being supposed to be in no way defective in power, but to pervade all things and to fill the whole universe <note>original: "οἱ μὲν δὴ τῆς μεγάλης... καὶ τὸ πᾶν πεπλήρωκε"</note>. For while the powers and honors of the other gods are divided, and men call upon different gods for different things, he, like the leader of them all, contains the beginnings and the ends."

# The Supreme God Polyonymous, Book I.

...are divided, and some of them are invoked for *one thing*, and *some for another*; This is looked upon by them as the *Coryphaeus* <note>original: "Coryphæus"; the leader or head of a group, such as the leader of a Greek chorus</note> of all the Gods, who contains the beginning and end of all things, and who is able to supply all wants. *Cneph* is also described by *Eusebius* as that *Divine Intellect*, which was the *Demiurge* <note>original: "Demiurgus"; a craftsman-like figure responsible for fashioning and maintaining the universe</note> of the world and which gives life to all things, just as he is said by *Plutarch* to be unmade <note>original: "ἀγένητος" (agenetos)</note>, so that this was also another *Egyptian Name of God*; as likewise were *Emeph* and *Eicton* in *Iamblichus*; though these may be severally distinguished into a *Trinity of Divine Hypostases* <note>original: "Trinity of Divine Hypostases"; three distinct persons or substances in one divine nature</note>. Lastly, when *Isis*, who was sometimes called *Multimammea* <note>original: "Multimammea"; many-breasted</note>, and depicted as full of *Breasts* all over to signify her *Feeding* all things, describes herself in *Apuleius* as: 

"The highest of the deities, the first of those who dwell in heaven, the uniform face of gods and goddesses, whose unique power the whole world worships in multiform shape, various ritual, and manifold name" <note>original: "Summa Numinum, Prima Caelitum, Deorum Dearumque facies Uniformis, cujus numen Unicum multiformi specie, ritu vario, nomine multijugo totus veneratur Orbis"</note>; 

As she plainly makes herself out to be the *Supreme Deity*, so does she intimate that all the Gods and Goddesses were compendiously contained in *Her Alone*, and that *she* (that is, the *Supreme God*) was worshipped under several personal *Names* and with different rites throughout the whole *Pagan World*. Moreover, this is particularly noted concerning the *Egyptians* by *Damascius* the Philosopher, that "They divided the Intelligible <note>the Supreme Deity</note> into the individualities of many gods, breaking and dividing the same into the Names and Properties of Many Gods" <note>original: "τὸ νοητὸν διῃρήκασιν εἰς πολλῶν θεῶν ἰδιότητας"</note>. Now the *Egyptian Theology* was, in a sense, the pattern for all the rest, but especially for those *European Theologies* of the Greeks and Romans.

Who likewise, that they often *Made Many Gods of One*, is evident from their bestowing so many *Proper* and *Personal Names* upon each of those inferior Gods of theirs: *The Sun*, *The Moon*, and *The Earth*. The first of these, usually called *Apollo*, therefore had this epithet of *Polyonymous* <note>the God with many names</note> commonly given to him. These many *Proper Names* of his are insisted upon by *Macrobius* in his *Saturnalia*, though he probably makes more of them than they actually were. And the *Moon* was not only called by that name, but also *Diana*, and *Lucina*, and *Hecate*, and otherwise; so much so that this Goddess also has been styled *Polyonymous* as well as her brother the Sun. And lastly, the *Earth*, besides those honorary titles of *Bona Dea*, *Magna Dea*, and *Mater Deorum*—*the Good Goddess*, *the Great Goddess*, and *the Mother of the Gods*—was multiplied by them into those *Many Goddesses* of *Vesta*, *Rhea*, *Cybele*, *Ceres*, *Proserpina*, *Ops*, and so on. And for this cause was she thus described by *Aeschylus*:

->And Earth, one form of many names.<-
<note>original Greek: "Καὶ Γαῖα πολλῶν ὀνομάτων μορφὴ μία"; original Latin: "Et Tellus Multorum Nominum Facies Una"</note>

Now if these inferior *Gods* of the Pagans each had so many *Personal Names* bestowed upon them, much more might the *Supreme God* be *Polyonymous* <note>having many names</note> among them; and so indeed he was commonly styled, as that learned Grammarian *Hesychius* suggests, upon that...

<summary>This page explores the concept of "Polyonymy," or the use of many names for the one Supreme God, particularly in Egyptian and Graeco-Roman theology. It explains that various deities (like Isis, Apollo, or the Earth) were often understood by philosophers as different names or aspects of a single divine power.</summary>

### CHAPTER IV. Amongst the Pagans.

The word *polyonymous* <note>original: "πολυώνυμον" (polyonymon); meaning "having many names"</note>—they called the Monad <note>term: The Monad represents the number one, unity, or the Supreme Being in Pythagorean philosophy</note> by this name, and it was also an epithet of Apollo. In the Pythagorean language, by the "Monad" is meant the Supreme Deity, who was thus styled by the Pagans as *polyonymous*, or **the Being that has many names**. Accordingly, Cleanthes begins his previously cited hymn to him this way:

->O most glorious of the immortals, called by many names,<-
<note>original: "Κύδιστ' ἀθανάτων, πολυώνυμε" (Kydist' athanaton, polyonyme)</note>

"You most glorious of all the immortal gods, who are called by many names." And Zeno, his master, in the writings of Laertius, expressly declares: "God is called by many different names according to his several powers and virtues." <note>original: "ὁ Θεὸς πολλαῖς προσηγορίαις ὀνομάζεται κατὰ τὰς δυνάμεις" (ho Theos pollais prosegoriais onomazetai kata tas dynameis)</note> Instances of these names shall be noted later. The writer of the treatise *On the Universe* <note>original: "De Mundo"; a work once attributed to Aristotle</note> also says: "Though he is only one, he is many-named, being named after all the effects that he himself brings about." <note>original: "Εἷς δὲ ὢν πολυώνυμός ἐστι, κατονομαζόμενος τοῖς πάθεσι πᾶσιν ἅπερ αὐτὸς νεοχμεῖ" (Heis de on polyonymos esti, katonomazomenos tois pathesi pasin haper autos neochmei)</note>

<margin>On Benefits, Book 4.</margin>
Seneca says: "You may apply to him whatever proper names you wish, provided they signify some force and effect of heavenly things. He may have as many names as he has manifestations, offices, and gifts." <note>original: "Quæcunque voles illi Propria Nomina aptabis, vim aliquam Effectumq; Cœlestium rerum continentia. Tot Appellationes ejus possunt esse quot Munera"</note> Macrobius also, on the authority of Virgil, determines: "The various effects of one God were to be considered as several deities." <note>original: "Unius Dei Effectus Varios pro Variis censendos esse" (or as Vossius corrects it, "Censeri")</note> That is, they were expressed by several personal names. As he affirms there, the various virtues of the Sun gave names to diverse gods, because they provided the occasion for the Sun to be called by several proper and personal names.

We shall conclude with the words of Maximus of Madaura, previously cited from Saint Augustine: "We invoke his virtues, which are diffused through the work of the world, by many names, because we do not know what his proper name is. Thus it happens that while we honor his various members, as it were, piece by piece through different prayers, we are clearly seen to worship the whole, leaving out nothing of him." <note>original: "Hujus Virtutes per Mundanum Opus diffusas, Nos multis vocabulis invocamus, quoniam Nomen ejus Proprium ignoramus. Ita fit ut dum ejus quasi quædam Membra carptim variis supplicationibus prosequimur, Totum colere profecto videamur"</note> With these latter words, the poet seems to agree when he has Jupiter speak to the other gods:

->O gods, inhabitants of heaven, you who are my members;<-
->whom our power has made, divided into different offices.<-
<note>original: "Cœlicolæ, Mea Membra, Dei; quos Nostra Potestas, Officiis divisa facit"</note>

Where it is plainly suggested that the **many Pagan gods** were but the several divided members of the one Supreme Deity. This was either because, according to the Stoic sense, the real and natural gods were all but **parts of the world-soul** <note>original: "Mundane soul"</note>, or else because all those other **imaginary gods** <note>original: "Phantastick Gods"</note> were nothing but several personal names given to the various powers, virtues, and offices of the one Supreme Being.

Scholars and philosophers like Seneca and Macrobius argue that these many names simply represent the various powers and effects of one God in the world.</summary>

# Several Proper Names of God, BOOK I.

Now, the various names of God that the author of *On the Universe* <note>original: *De Mundo*; a treatise once attributed to Aristotle</note> gives as examples to prove that God is *polyonymous* <note>term: "Many-named"</note> are, first of all, these: **The Thunderer** and **The Lightener** <note>original: "Βρονταῖος" (Brontaios) and "Ἀστραπαῖος" (Astrapaios)</note>, **The Giver of Rain** <note>original: "Ὑέτιος" (Huetios)</note>, **The Bestower of Fruits** <note>original: "Ἐπικάρπιος" (Epikarpios)</note>, **The Keeper of Cities** <note>original: "Πολιεύς" (Polieus)</note>, and **The Mild and Appeasable** <note>original: "Μειλίχιος" (Meilichios)</note>. Under this last concept, they sacrificed no animals to him, but only the fruits of the earth. These are joined by many other such epithets, such as **The Friendly**, **The Hospitable**, **The Military**, **The Giver of Victory**, **The Purifier**, **The Avenger**, and so on. <note>original: "Φίλιος, Ξένιος, Στράτιος, Τροπαιοῦχος, Καθάρσιος, Παλαιμναῖος"</note> Lastly, he is called **Saviour** and **Liberator** <note>original: "Σωτήρ" (Soter) and "Ἐλευθέριος" (Eleutherios)</note>.

In response to this, the Romans also gave Jupiter many such names, such as **The Victor**, **The Unconquered**, **The Helper**, and **The Stayer** <note>original: "Victor, Invictus, Opitulus, Stator"</note>. According to Seneca, the true meaning of this last name, **Stator**, was not what the historians claim—that the retreating Roman army stood their ground after a vow was made to him—but "because all things stand firm and are established by his favor." <note>original: "Sed quod stant beneficio ejus Omnia"</note> For this same reason, he was also called by them **The Hundred-footed** <note>original: "Centupeda"</note> (as Saint Augustine <note>original: "St. Austin"</note> informs us), as if he were standing firm on a hundred feet, and **The Support** <note>original: "Tigillus"</note>, meaning the beam, prop, and supporter of the world. He was also titled by the Latins, among other names, **The Nourishing** and **The Provider** <note>original: "Almus" and "Ruminus"</note>, meaning <margin>The word *ruma* means "breast."</margin> "He who nourishes all things, as if from his own breasts."

Furthermore, the author of *On the Universe* adds another set of names by which God was called:
*   **Necessity** <note>original: "Ἀνάγκη" (Ananke)</note>, because he is an unchangeable being. <margin>Cicero, *Academic Questions*, Book 1.</margin> However, Cicero gives another reason for this name: "Sometimes they call God 'Necessity' because nothing can be otherwise than he has appointed." <note>original: "Interdum Deum Necessitatem appellant, quia nihil aliter esse possit, atque ab eo constitutum sit"</note>
*   **Fate** <note>original: "Εἱμαρμένη" (Heimarmene)</note>, because all things are connected together by him and proceed from him without hindrance.
*   **The Determined** <note>original: "Πεπρωμένη" (Pepromene)</note>, because all things in the world are limited by him, and nothing is left infinite or undetermined.
*   **Portion** <note>original: "Μοῖρα" (Moira)</note>, because he makes a proper division and distribution of all things.
*   **The Inevitable** <note>original: "Ἀδράστεια" (Adrasteia)</note>, because his power is such that no one can possibly avoid or escape him.

Finally, that "ingenious fable" (as he calls it) of the three Fatal Sisters—**Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos**—meant nothing other than God himself. As the author states: "All of this is nothing else but God, as the noble and generous Plato also intimates when he affirms that God contains the beginning, middle, and end of all things." <note>original: "ταῦτα δὲ πάντα ἐστὶν οὐκ ἄλλο τι, πλὴν ὁ Θεός..."</note>

Both Cicero and Seneca tell us that among the Latins, God was not only called **Fate**, but also **Nature** and **Fortune**. Seneca asks: "What is Nature else but God and the Divine Reason, inserted into the whole world and all its several parts?" <note>original: "Quid aliud est Natura quam Deus, & Divina Ratio, toti Mundo & Partibus ejus inserta?"</note> He adds that God and Nature were no more two different things than were his own names, Annaeus and Seneca. And Cicero says: "They sometimes call God also by the name of Fortune, because he surprises us with many events and brings about things we did not expect, because of the obscurity of causes and our own ignorance." <note>original: "Nonnunquam Deum Fortunam appellant, quod efficiat multa improvisa..."</note> Seneca concludes concerning these and similar names of God: "All these are names of the same God,"

It emphasizes that philosophical traditions viewed these many names as ways to understand how God sustains, governs, and establishes the universe.</summary>

# CHAP. IV. According to his Universal Notion.

[These] are the names of one and the same God, using his power in various ways; <note>original: "sunt, variè utentis sua Potestate"</note> *These are all names of one and the same God, variously manifesting his power.*

<margin>City of God, Book 7, chapter 11 <note>original: C.D.L.7.c.11</note></margin>
But concerning most of these previously mentioned **Names** of God, and others like them, it was rightly observed by **St. Augustine** <note>original: St. Austin</note> that they did not actually suggest the existence of **many distinct gods**. He wrote: "They imposed all these surnames upon the One God because of various causes and powers; however, they did not force him to be as many gods as there were things, etc. <note>original: "Hæc omnia cognomina imposuerunt Uni Deo, propter Causas Potestatesque Diversas, non tamen propter tot res, etiam tot Deos eum esse coegerunt, &c."</note> Even if the Pagans gave all these different names to one God based on his various powers, they did not seem to make so many gods out of them—as if *Victor* were one god, *Invictus* (Unconquered) another god, *Centupeda* (Hundred-footed) another, *Tigillus* (The Beam) another, and *Ruminus* (The Nourisher) yet another."

Therefore, there are other names of God used among the Pagans which have a greater appearance of being distinct deities. This is not only because they are proper names, but also because each had its own specific temple and different rituals of worship. These are of two sorts: first, those that signify the **Deity** according to its **Universal** and **all-comprehending nature**; and second, those that denote God only according to certain **particular powers, manifestations, and effects** in the world.

Of the first kind, there are quite a few. First of all, **PAN**—as the very word implies—was understood to be a **Universal Divinity** <note>term: "Numen"</note>. He was supposed to be the **Harmonizer** <note>original: "Harmostes"</note> of the whole **world**, or the one who plays upon the world as if it were a **musical instrument**, according to the writings of **Orpheus** (or **Onomacritus**):

->Striking the harmony of the world with playful song,<-
<note>original: Ἁρμονίαν κόσμοιο κρέκων φιλοπαίγμονι μολπῇ</note>

As we have shown before, the Arcadians and Greeks did not mean the **inanimate physical world** by "Pan," nor did they mean a world driven only by a **senseless nature**. Instead, they meant a world proceeding from an **intellectual principle** or **Divine Spirit**, which framed it **harmoniously** and continues to keep it in tune, acting upon it and governing it. Therefore, he is called the **Universal Pastor** and **Shepherd** of all **mankind** and of the whole world, according to another Orphic passage:

->Nourishing the race of humans and the boundless earth.<-
<note>original: βόσκων ἀνθρώπων γενεὰν, καὶ ἀτέρμονα γαῖαν</note>

->*Nourishing the human race and the earth without limit.*<-
<note>original: Pascens Humanum Genus, ac sine limite Terram.</note>

And this **Pan**, **Socrates** in **Plato's *Phaedrus*** plainly invokes as the **Supreme Divinity**. Therefore, **Pan** is the **one and only God** (*for there cannot possibly be more than one Pan, more than one "All" or Universe*) who contained **all** within himself, displayed **all** from himself, framing the world **harmoniously**, and who is, in a sense, **all things**.

Again, **JANUS**—whom the Romans first invoked in all their sacrifices and prayers, and who was never omitted regardless of which god they were sacrificing to—was unquestionably often regarded as a **Universal Divinity**, as in this line from **Martial**:

->O most beautiful Father of the shining world.<-
<note>original: Nitidique Sator pulcherrime mundi.</note>

<margin>Ovid, *Fasti*, Book 1</margin>
And again in this passage from *Ovid*:

> Whatever you see everywhere—the Heavens, the Sea, the Clouds, the Earth—
> All are closed and opened by my Hand:
> The Guardianship of the vast World belongs to me alone.
> <note>original: "Quicquid ubique vides, Cœlum, Mare, Nubila, Terras, / Omnia sunt nostra clausa patentque Manu : / Me penes est Unum vasti Custodia Mundi."</note>

From these passages, it also appears that *Janus* was not merely the senseless and inanimate matter of the world, but a principle presiding over it. Without doubt, all the beginnings of things were referred to this *Janus* because he was considered the most ancient God and the beginning of all things. **St. Augustine** <note>original: St. Austin</note>, concluding him to be the same as *Jupiter*, therefore quarrels with the Pagans (that is, with their **Civil Theology** <note>The public, state-sanctioned religion of the Roman Empire, as opposed to the private views of philosophers.</note>) for making two gods out of one.

<margin>*City of God*, Book 7, chapter 10</margin>
*Since, therefore, Janus is the World, and Jupiter is the World, and there is but one World, why are Janus and Jupiter two Gods? Why do they have separate Temples, separate Altars, distinct Sacred rites, and statues of different forms? If it is because the power of Beginnings is one thing, and the power of Causes another—receiving the name Janus from the former and Jupiter from the latter—I ask whether or not, if one man has two different skills concerning different things (because each has a different power), he should therefore be called two Craftsmen? etc. Or is there any more reason why one and the same God, having two powers, one over the beginnings of things and another over the causes, should therefore be considered two Gods?*
<note>original: "Cum ergo Janus Mundus fit, & Jupiter Mundus fit... nunquid si unus homo in diversis rebus duas habeat potestates... ideo Duo dicuntur Artifices?"</note>

Where both *Jupiter* and *Janus* are said to be the "World," this should be understood properly as referring not to the physical matter, but to the Soul or Mind of the World, as **St. Augustine** himself declares elsewhere:

<margin>*City of God*, Book 4, chapter 11</margin>
*Let Jupiter be the Mind of this corporeal World, which both fills and moves that whole mass, compounded and made up of the four Elements.*
<note>original: "Sit Jupiter Corporei hujus Mundi Animus, qui universam istam Molem, ex quatuor Elementis constructam atque compactam, implet & movet"</note>

Nevertheless, just as the soul and body together are called "the man," the whole "Animated World" was called "God" by the Pagans. Now, the aforementioned argument by **St. Augustine**, though effective against the Pagans' **Civil Theology**, did not affect their other **Arcane** <note>original: "Arcane" — hidden or secret knowledge intended for the initiated.</note> and **Natural Theology**. That deeper theology plainly acknowledged that all these were but **one God**, who for certain reasons was worshipped under **several names** and with **different rites**. Therefore, since *Janus* and *Jupiter* were really just different names for one and the same Supreme God, the conjecture of the scholar **Salmasius** seems very probable: that the Romans derived their name *Janus* from *Zanos*, the **Aetolian Jupiter** <note>A regional Greek variation of the name Zeus/Jupiter.</note>.

**GENIUS** was also another of the twenty **Select Roman Gods**. It was likewise a **Universal Numen** <note>original: "Numen" — a divine power or spirit presiding over a place or thing.</note>, containing the entire nature of things...

### Chap. IV. Names of The Supreme Deity.

That this is the case appears from this passage by **Festus** <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a 2nd-century Roman grammarian.</note>: *They called that God Genius, who possesses the power of begetting or producing all things.* <note>original: "Genium appellabant Deum, qui vim obtineret rerum omnium genendarum."</note> <margin>St. Augustine, *City of God*, Book 7, chapter 13.</margin> And **St. Augustine** <note>original: St. Austin</note> also plainly declares *Genius* to be the same as *Jupiter*; that is, to be but another name for the One Supreme God. *When Varro elsewhere calls the rational mind of every person a "Genius," and affirms such a mind of the whole world to be God, he plainly implies that God is the Universal Genius of the world, and that Genius and Jupiter are the same. This, therefore, is the one they call Jupiter.* <note>original: "Cum alio loco [Varro] dicit, Genium esse Uniuscujusque animum rationalem; talem autem Mundi Animum Deum esse, ad hoc idem utique revocat, ut tanquam Universalis Genius, ipse Mundi Animus esse credatur. Hic est igitur quem appellant Jovem."</note> And afterwards: *It remains that they call him, uniquely and preeminently, the God Genius, whom they call the Mind of the World; and through this, Jupiter.* <note>original: "Restat ut eum Singulariter & Excellenter dicant Deum Genium, quem dicunt Mundi Animum; ac per hoc Jovem."</note> And though *Genius* is sometimes used for the mind of every man, yet the God *Genius*, spoken of in an excellent sense, can be no other than the Mind of the whole world, or *Jupiter*.

Again, that **Chronos** or **Saturn** was no *particular deity*, but the *Universal Spirit* <note>original: Numen</note> of the whole world, is plainly affirmed by **Dionysius of Halicarnassus**. <margin>Roman Antiquities, Book 1, page 24. Edition: Stephanus.</margin> Where commending the fertility of Italy, he writes thus: *Wherefore it is no wonder if the ancients thought this country to be sacred to Saturn, they supposing this God to be the giver and perfecter of all happiness to men; whether we ought to call him Chronos as the Greeks insist, or Saturn as the Romans; he being either way such a God as encompasses the whole nature of the world.* <note>original: "οὐδὲν οὖν θαυμαστὸν τοὺς παλαιοὺς ἱερὰν ὑπολαβεῖν τὴν Κρόνου τὴν χώραν ταύτην, τὸν μὲν δαίμονα τοῦτον, οἰομένους εἶναι πάσης εὐδαιμονίας δοτῆρα, καὶ πληρωτὴν ἀνθρώποις· εἴτε χρόνον αὐτὸν δεῖ καλεῖν, ὡς Ἕλληνες ἀξιοῦσιν, εἴτε Κρόνον ὡς Ῥωμαῖοι, πᾶσαν τὴν περιειληφότα τὴν τοῦ κόσμου φύσιν, ὁπότερον ἄν τις ὀνομάσοι."</note> But the word *Saturn* was **Etruscan** <note>original: Hetrurian</note> (a language which was originally **Oriental**) and being derived from the word <term>סתר</term> <note>Hebrew: *satar*, meaning "to hide" or "conceal"</note>, signifies *Hidden*. So, by *Saturn* was meant that *Hidden Principle* of the *Universe* which contains all things. He was therefore called by the Romans *Deus Latius*, the **Hidden God**; just as the wife of Saturn in the *Pontifical Books* is *Latia Saturni*, and the land itself (which in the Etruscan language was *Saturnia*) is called in Roman *Latium*. From this, the inhabitants were called *Latins*, which is as much as to say, the worshippers of the *Hidden God*. 

Moreover, that *Saturn* could not be inferior to *Jupiter*, according to **mythological theology** <note>original: Fabulous Theology</note>, is plain from this: because he is said in those stories to have been Jupiter's *father*. But then the question arises: how could *Saturn* and *Jupiter* both be one and the same *Universal Spirit*? To which there are several answers. First, **Plato**, who proposes this difficulty in his dialogue *Cratylus*, solves it this way: that by *Jupiter* here we are to understand the **Soul of the World**. According to his theology, this soul was derived from a *Perfect and Eternal Mind* or *Intellect* (which *Chronos* is interpreted to be), just as *Chronos* also depended upon *Uranus* or *Coelus*, the *Supreme Heavenly God*, or *First Original Deity*. In this way, Plato finds his **Trinity of Divine Hypostases** <note>A "hypostasis" is a foundational substance or person of the divinity.</note>—which are the governing principles of the universe—the <term>The Good</term> <note>original: τἀγαθὸν (Tagathon)</note>, the <term>Mind</term> <note>original: Νοῦς (Nous)</note>, and the <term>Soul</term> <note>original: Ψυχή (Psyche)</note>—represented in *Uranus, Chronos*, and *Zeus*; or *Coelus, Saturn*, and *Jupiter*. Others conceive that, according to the...

It connects Saturn's name to the concept of a "Hidden God" and interprets the relationship between Uranus, Saturn, and Jupiter as an early philosophical Trinity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that various mythological figures, such as Saturn, Uranus, and Minerva, were interpreted by ancient philosophers as different names or aspects of the one Supreme God rather than distinct, competing deities.</meta>

<header>Cælus, Minerva, Apollo, etc. Book 1.</header>

The plainer and more simple sense of **Hesiod's** *Theogony* <note>A poem by Hesiod (c. 700 BC) describing the origins and genealogies of the Greek gods.</note> is that **Jupiter**, who along with **Neptune** and **Pluto** is said to have been the son of **Saturn**, was not the Supreme Deity, nor even the Soul of the World. Instead, he represented only the **Ether** <note>The upper atmosphere or the "fiery" element of the heavens.</note>, just as Neptune represented the sea and Pluto represented the earth. All of these are said to have been fathered by **Chronos** (or Saturn), the son of **Uranus**. This is as much as to say they were produced by the "Hidden Virtue of the Supreme Heavenly God."

However, the writer of *De Mundo* <note>An ancient Greek treatise "On the World," once attributed to Aristotle.</note>, though considering Jupiter to be the first and Supreme God, takes **Chronos** to signify "immensity of duration" or "eternity." In this sense, Jupiter is the "son of Chronos" because he *continues from one boundless eternity to another* <note>original: διήκειν ἐξ αἰῶνος ἀτέρμονος εἰς ἕτερον αἰῶνα</note>. Thus, to that author, Chronos and Zeus (Jupiter) are essentially the same thing.

But we are inclined to think that no sincere and learned pagan, who well understood **Natural Theology** <note>The study of God based on reason and the observation of nature, rather than revelation.</note>, would deny that the best answer of all to this difficulty is this: there is no coherent sense to be made of everything in **Fabulous Theology** <note>The mythological stories of the gods, often distinguished by ancient scholars from "Natural" or "Civil" theology.</note>.

**St. Augustine** <note>original: St. Austin</note>, quoting the Roman scholar **Varro**, gives us this account of **Saturn**: he is the one who continually produces from himself the "hidden seeds" and "forms" of things, and then reduces or receives them back into himself. Some think this was the true meaning of the fable about Saturn devouring his male children; it signifies that the forms of these physical things are perpetually destroyed, while the material parts (represented by the females) remain.

In any case, it is plain that this was just another pagan **adumbration** <note>A faint sketch or imperfect representation.</note> of the Deity. <margin>St. Augustine, *City of God*, Book 4, chapter 12.</margin> The Deity was also sometimes defined by them, as St. Augustine also informs us, as *a certain bosom, or deep hollow and inward recess of Nature, which contains all things within itself* <note>original: "Sinus quidam Naturæ in seipso continens omnia"</note>. Augustine himself concludes that, according to this Varronian notion of Saturn, the pagans' Jupiter and Saturn were really one and the same **Numen** <term>A divine power or spirit; the essence of a deity.</term> (*City of God*, Book 7, chapter 13).

Therefore, we may reasonably affirm that **Saturn** was another name for the Supreme God among the pagans. It signified that secret and hidden power which comprehends, pervades, and supports the whole world, and which produces the "seeds" or seminal principles and forms of all things from itself. <margin>As seen in the old inscription: "The Best and Greatest Eternal Heaven, Jupiter" <note>original: OPTIMUS MAXIMUS CÆLUS ÆTERNUS JUPITER</note>.</margin> Likewise, **Uranus** (or **Caelus**, meaning Heaven) was clearly yet another name for the same Supreme Deity (or the "First Divine Hypostasis" <note>A technical term for a distinct person or essence within the Godhead.</note>) who encompasses everything.

Next, while it is true that **Minerva** is sometimes regarded as a particular god, or as God manifested specifically in the Ether (as will be shown later), she was also often understood as the Supreme God according to his most general definition—as a universal Numen diffusing himself through all things. It has already been proven that **Neith** (or Neithas) among the Egyptians was the same as **Athena** among the Greeks and **Minerva** among the Romans. That she was a universal Numen appears from the Egyptian inscription in the temple of this god: *I am all that was, is, and shall be.*

Accordingly, **Athenagoras** <note>A 2nd-century Christian apologist.</note> tells us that the Greeks' Athena was *wisdom passing and diffusing itself through all things* <note>original: ἡ φρόνησις διὰ πάντων διήκουσα</note>. This is similar to the biblical **Book of Wisdom**, where wisdom is called *the architect of all things* <note>original: ἡ πάντων τεχνῖτις</note> and is said *to pass and move through all things* <note>original: διήκειν καὶ χωρεῖν διὰ πάντων</note>.

<summary>This page argues that the deities Saturn, Uranus, and Minerva were not distinct gods to learned pagans, but rather different names for the Supreme Deity’s various functions, such as his eternity, his role as the source of all "seeds" of life, and his universal wisdom.</summary>

Therefore, this *Athena* or *Minerva* of the *Pagans* was either the *First Supreme Deity*—a *Perfect* and *Infinite Mind*, the *Original* source of all things—or else a *Second Divine Hypostasis* <term>Hypostasis: a person or distinct essence within the Godhead</term>, the immediate *offspring* and *first-begotten* of that *First Original Deity*. Thus *Aristides* in his *Oration upon Minerva* writes:

"Everything most excellent is in Athena and from Athena. To speak briefly, she is the only immediate offspring of the only Maker and King of all things. For he had no one of equal honor with himself with whom he might create her; instead, withdrawing into himself, he alone from himself generated and brought her forth. Thus, she is certainly the only genuine offspring of the Father, born of an equal nature with himself, etc." <note>original Greek: πάντα μὲν ἓν τὰ κάλλισα περὶ Ἀθηνᾶν... τοῦ γένους γενομένη</note>

And again:

We may observe here, by the way, that this word *Angel* came into use among the *Pagans* from *Jews* and *Christians* around the same age that *Aristides* lived; after which, we find it frequently in the writings of their *Philosophers*. Lastly, *Aristides* concludes his oration on *Minerva* this way:

"For one who says from these things that she is, in a sense, the power and virtue of Zeus himself, would not be mistaken. Therefore (not to enumerate every minor detail regarding Minerva), we conclude that all the works of Zeus are shared by Zeus and Athena." <note>original Greek: σχεδὸν γὰρ δύναμιν... καὶ τῆς Ἀθηνᾶς</note>

Therefore, the notion favored by the learned and industrious *Vossius* <note>Gerardus Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch classical scholar and theologian.</note>—that the *Pagans' Universal Deity* <note>original: Numen</note> was nothing more than a *senseless nature* or a *formative principle* <note>original: Spermatick Reason</note> of the whole world, unguided by any higher *intellectual principle* (which is actually nothing better than outright *Atheism*)—is clearly proven wrong here. They established *Wisdom* and *Understanding*, under the names of *Neith*, *Athena*, and *Minerva*, to be either the *Absolutely Supreme Deity* or its *first-begotten offspring*.

That Apollo is the maker of the Sun and of the whole world is plainly testified by Plutarch (who is a competent witness in this case, being a priest of this *Apollo*). He wrote the following concerning him in his *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*: <note>original Greek: εἴτε ἡλιός ἐστιν εἴτε κύριος ἡλίου καὶ πατὴρ, καὶ ἐπέκεινα τοῦ ὁρατοῦ παντὸς, οὐκ εἰκὸς ἀπαξιῶν φωνῆς τοὺς νῦν ἀνθρώπους, οἷς αἴτιός ἐστι γενέσεως καὶ τροφῆς, καὶ τοῦ εἶναι καὶ φρονεῖν·</note>
> *Whether* Apollo *is the* Sun, *or whether he is the* Lord *and* Father *of the sun, placed far above all* perceivable *and* physical nature, *it is not likely that he would now deny his* oracles *to those for whom he himself is the cause of* generation *and* nourishment, *of* life *and* understanding.

<margin>P. 108.</margin>
Moreover, *Urania Aphrodite*—the *Heavenly Venus* or *Love*—was also a *universal divine power* <term>Numen: a deity or divine presence</term>, or another name for God. According to this *general concept*, God is understood as *encompassing the whole world*. This is the same as the *Eros* (or *Love*) that *Orpheus* and others mentioned in *Aristotle* claimed was the *first origin* of all things. It is certain that the ancients distinguished between two versions of Venus and Love. As *Pausanias* says in *Plato's Symposium*: <note>original Greek: ἡ μὲν γέ που πρεσβυτέρα καὶ ἀμήτωρ οὐρανοῦ θυγάτηρ, ἣν δὴ καὶ οὐρανίαν ἐπονομάζομεν· ἡ δὲ νεωτέρα, Διὸς καὶ Διώνης, ἣν δὴ πάνδημον καλοῦμεν· ἀναγκαῖον δὴ καὶ Ἔρωτα, τὸν μὲν ἑτέρᾳ συνεργὸν, πάνδημον ὀρθῶς καλεῖσθαι, τὸν δὲ, οὐράνιον·</note>
> *There are surely two* Venuses *and therefore two* Loves. *One is the* older *and without a* mother, *the daughter of* Uranus *or* Heaven, *whom we call the* Heavenly Venus. *The other is younger, born from* Jupiter *and* Dione, *whom we call the* common <note>original: "Vulgar"</note> Venus. *Accordingly, there are necessarily two* Loves *corresponding to these two* Venuses: *the one* common, *and the other* heavenly.

The *elder of these Venuses* is said in *Plato* to be senior to *Iapetus* <note>original: "Japhet"</note> and *Saturn*, and by *Orpheus* she is called the *oldest of all things* and the *first parent* <note>original: πρῶτος γενέτωρ</note>, the *first begetter* of all. For this reason, perhaps, she was called *Mylitta* or *Genitrix* <term>Genitrix: she who brings forth; a mother</term> by the *oriental nations*, as she was the *fruitful mother* of all. This was also the same as *Plato's* "the first beautiful" <note>original: τὸ πρῶτον καλὸν</note>, the *first fair*; the *cause of all beauty, order, and harmony* in the world. The writer *Pausanias* tells us that temples were built specifically for each of these *Venuses* or *Loves*—the *Heavenly* and the *Common*—and that *Urania*, or the *Heavenly Venus*, was so named "because the love belonging to it was pure and free from all physical desire." <note>original: ἐπὶ ἔρωτι καθαρῷ καὶ ἀπηλλαγμένῳ πόθου σωμάτων</note> In humans, this is merely a *participation* in that *first Urania*, or *Heavenly Venus* and *Love*—which is *God himself*. Thus, *Venus* is described as the *supreme divine power* by *Euripides* (as cited in *Stobaeus*).

Now *Plutarch* and *Stobaeus* testify that the *Stoics* called not only *Nature*, but also the **Supreme Deity** itself (the Architect of the whole world) <note>original: "τεχνικὸν πῦρ"</note> *an artificial fire*, because they conceived him to be corporeal. And *Iamblichus*, making *Phtha* to be the same *Supreme God* among the *Egyptians* as *Osiris* and *Amun*—or rather, more properly, viewing all of them alike as the *Soul of the World*—tells us that *Hephaestus* in Greek theology was the same as this Egyptian *Phtha*: <note>original: "Ἕλληνες εἰς Ἥφαιστον μεταλαμβάνουσι τὸ φθὰ, τῷ τεχνικῷ μόνον προσβάλλοντες"</note> *Among the Greeks, Hephaestus (or Vulcan) corresponds to the Egyptian Phtha, regarding only his technical or artistic skill.* Therefore, just as the Egyptians understood the *Supreme God* (or at least the *Soul of the World*) through *Phtha*, so the Greeks understood him through *Hephaestus* as the one who *artistically frames all things*.

<margin>Seneca, On Benefits, Book 4, Chapter 8.</margin> Furthermore, *Seneca* gives us yet other names for the Supreme Deity, according to the sense of the Stoics: <note>original: "Hunc & Liberum Patrem, & Herculem, ac Mercurium nostri putant, Liberum Patrem, quia Omnium Parens, &c. Herculem, quod vis ejus invicta sit; Mercurium, quia Ratio penes illum est, Numerusque, & Ordo, & Scientia"</note> *Furthermore, our philosophers take this Author of all things to be Liber Pater <term>Liber Pater</term>—an ancient Italian god of fertility and wine, often identified with Bacchus—Hercules, and Mercury. They call him the first because he is the Parent of all things; the second because his force and power are unconquerable; and the third because in him and from him come Reason, Number, Order, and Knowledge.* 

We can already see that the Supreme God was sufficiently *polyonymous* <term>polyonymous</term>—having many names—among the pagans. All these—*Jupiter, Pan, Janus, Genius, Saturn, Caelus, Minerva, Apollo, Aphrodite Urania, Hephaestus, Liber Pater, Hercules*, and *Mercury*—were not so many really distinct and substantial gods, much less *self-existent and independent ones*. Rather, they were only several names for that one Supreme, Universal, and *all-comprehending Divine Spirit* <note>original: "Numen"</note>, according to different notions and considerations of him.

But besides these, there were many other pagan gods called by *Servius* <note>original: "Dii Speciales"</note> *special* or *particular gods*. These cannot be thought of as so many *really distinct* and *substantial beings* (that is, *natural gods*), much less *self-existent* and *independent*. Instead, they are only so many several *names* or *notions* of *one* and the *same Supreme Deity*, according to certain *particular powers* and *manifestations* of it. 

It is true that some recent Christian writers, arguing against pagan polytheism and idolatry, have charged them with believing in at least a trinity of independent gods—namely *Jupiter, Neptune*, and *Pluto*—who shared the government of the whole world among them and consequently acknowledged no *one universal deity*. However, it is certain that according to the more hidden doctrine and <term>Cabala</term>—here meaning a secret or oral tradition—of the pagans concerning *natural true theology*, these three were considered distinct and independent gods only as <note>original: "Dii Poetici & Commentitii"</note> *poetical and fictitious gods*. In reality, they were esteemed as nothing other than several names and notions of *one* and the same supreme *divine power*, acting variously in those different parts of the world: the *Heavens*, the *Sea*, the *Earth*, and *Hell*. # Chapter IV. One and the same Natural God.

He was also called *Orcus* and *Dis* by the Latins (the latter word seems to be a contraction of *Dives* <note>original: "rich"</note> to match the Greek *Pluto*). Just as Balbus in Cicero attributes to him "all Earthly Power," <note>original: "Omnem Vim terrenam"</note> others commonly assign him the rule of separate souls after death. Now it is certain that, according to this latter notion, **Plato** understood Pluto as nothing other than a name for that part of **Divine Providence** which acts upon the souls of men after death.

The philosopher Marsilio Ficinus observed this in his commentary on Plato’s *Cratylus*: "Pay attention above all else: Pluto here signifies primarily Divine Providence as it pertains to separate souls." <note>original: "Animadverte præ cæteris, Plutonem hic ſignificare præcipuè, Providentiam Divinam ad Separatas Animas pertinentem"</note> According to Plato, this Providence binds and keeps pure souls in that separate state with the best bond <note>original: "vinculum"</note> of all—which is not necessity, but love and desire—as they are delighted and charmed by the pure joys they experience there.

Plato is to be understood in the same way in his book *Laws*, where he writes <margin>Book 8.</margin> concerning Pluto in this manner: "Military men should not be troubled or offended by such a god, but should honor him as one who is always most beneficial to the human race. For I affirm with the greatest seriousness that the union of the soul with this earthly body is never better than their dissolution or separation." <note>original: "Καὶ οὐ δυσχεραντέον πολεμικοῖς ἀνθρώποις τὸν τοιοῦτον θεὸν, ἀλλὰ τιμητέον, ὡς ὄντα ἀεὶ τῷ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένει ἄριστον· κοινωνία γὰρ ψυχῇ καὶ σώματι, διαλύσεως οὐκ ἔστιν ἢ κρεῖττον, ὡς ἐγώ φαίην ἂν σπουδῇ λέγων"</note> Therefore, according to Plato, Pluto is nothing but a name for that part of Divine Providence exercised upon human souls during their separation from these earthly bodies.

For this reason, Pluto was called by Virgil the "**Stygian Jupiter**." However, others took Pluto and Ceres in a broader sense, representing the manifestation of the Deity throughout this entire earthly globe. This is how the author of *On the World* <note>original: "De Mundo"</note> should be understood when he tells us that God, or Jupiter, is "both celestial and terrestrial, being named after every nature and fortune, since he himself is the cause of all things." <note>original: "οὐράνιός τε καὶ χθόνιος, πάσης ἐπώνυμος ὢν φύσεως τε καὶ τύχης, ἅτε πάντων αὐτὸς αἴτιος ὤν"</note> Therefore, Pluto is the "terrestrial Jupiter" <note>original: "ζεύς χθόνιος" (Zeus chthonios)</note> or "subterranean Jupiter" <note>original: "καταχθόνιος" (katachthonios)</note>. That other Jupiter, who is distinguished from both Pluto and Neptune, is properly the "Heavenly Jupiter" <note>original: "ζεύς οὐράνιος" (Zeus ouranios)</note>—God as he manifests himself in the heavens.

This is why *Zeus* and *Hades* (Jupiter and Pluto) are described as one and the same thing in a passage cited by Julian as an oracle of Apollo, though others attribute it to Orpheus:

->**"Jupiter and Pluto are one and the same God."** <note>original: "Εἷς Ζεύς, εἷς Ἀΐδης"</note><-

# More Popular and Poetic Gods, BOOK I.

Lastly, Hermesianax the Colophonian poet, in those verses of his (which will be provided later), identifies Pluto in the first place—along with many other pagan gods—as being really one and the same with Jupiter.

That Neptune was also another name for the Supreme God, based on a different consideration of him—namely, as acting within the seas (at least according to the secret <note>original: "arcane"</note> and natural theology of the pagans)—is clearly stated by several of the ancients. Xenocrates (as quoted in Stobaeus) and Zeno (in Diogenes Laertius) affirm that *God, when acting in the water, is called Poseidon or Neptune*. To the same purpose, Balbus speaks in
<margin>*On the Nature of the Gods, Book 2*</margin> Cicero: *“But once these poetic fables are despised and rejected, it is easy for us to understand how God, passing through the nature of every thing, may be called by several names: through the Earth he is* **Ceres** *(and* **Pluto**), *through the Seas* **Neptune**, *and through other parts of the world by other names. Thus, all these titular gods were merely different*
<margin>*On the Nature of the Gods, Book 3*</margin> *denominations of one Supreme Deity.”* <note>original: "Sed tamen his Fabulis spretis ac repudiatis, Deus Pertinens per Naturam cujusque rei, per Terras Ceres, per Maria Neptunus, alii per alia, poterunt intelligi, qui qualesque sint, etc."</note> And Cotta afterward represents the sense of this theology this way: *“Your meaning is that Neptune is a Mind which, with understanding, passes through the sea; and the same applies to Ceres through the Earth.”* <note>original: "Neptunum esse dicis Animum cum Intelligentiâ per mare pergentem, idem de Cerere"</note> Lastly, to name no more, Maximus Tyrius also agrees with this in <margin>*Dissertation 30*</margin>: *“You are to call Jupiter that most ancient and princely Mind, which all things follow and obey, etc.; and Neptune that Spirit which, passing through the earth and sea, maintains their order and harmony.”* <note>original: "κάλει τὸν μὲν νῦν πρεσβύτατον... τὸν δὲ Ποσειδῶ, πνεῦμα διὰ γῆς καὶ θαλάττης ἰὸν, οἰκονομοῦν αὐτῶν τὴν στάσιν καὶ τὴν ἁρμονίαν"</note>

Finally, that these three—Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto—were not three distinct substantial beings, but only several names for *One Supreme God* (according to the *true* and *natural theology* of the pagans), is plainly declared by Pausanias in his *Description of Corinth* <note>original: "Corinthiacks"</note>. He explains the meaning of a certain statue of Jupiter with three eyes (called the "Country Jupiter" of the Trojans) in this manner: *“One might conclude that this statue was made to have three eyes for the following reason: it is a common belief among all men that Jupiter reigns in heaven. But as for him who is said to rule under the earth, there is a verse of Homer’s which also names him 'Jupiter':”*

-> *Jupiter of the Underworld, and the dread Persephone.* <-

### CHAPTER IV. The Same Natural God.

...to have three eyes, one may guess this to have been the reason: Because first, common speech among all men describes Jupiter as reigning in Heaven. Again, he who is said to rule under the Earth is also called Zeus or Jupiter in a certain verse of Homer—namely, the "Infernal" or "Subterraneous" Jupiter, together with Proserpina. And lastly, Aeschylus (the son of Euphorion) also calls that God who is the King of the Sea "Jupiter." Therefore, this sculptor made Jupiter with three eyes to signify that it is one and the same God who rules in those three separate parts of the world: the Heaven, the Sea, and the Earth. Whether Pausanias was right or not in his conjecture concerning this three-eyed statue of Jupiter, it is evident that he himself and other ancient pagans acknowledged Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto to be but three different names and partial perspectives of one and the same God who rules over the whole world. And since both Proserpina and Ceres were really the same as Pluto, and Salacia the same as Neptune, we may well conclude that all these—Jupiter, Neptune, Salacia, Pluto, Proserpina, and Ceres—though separate "Poetical" and "Political" gods <note>The author distinguishes between gods as they appear in myths (Poetical) or state religion (Political) versus the underlying reality (Natural/Philosophical).</note>, yet were really taken for one and the same Natural and Philosophical God.

Moreover, just as Neptune was a name for God as he manifested himself in the sea and ruled over it, so was Juno another name for God as he acted in the air. This is expressly affirmed by both Xenocrates (in Stobaeus) and Zeno (in Diogenes Laertius). And St. Augustine <note>original: "St. Austin"</note>, posing this question—why Juno was joined to Jupiter as his wife and sister—records the pagans’ answer as follows: "Because (they say) we understand God in the upper atmosphere <note>original: "Æther"</note> to be Jupiter, and in the lower air to be Juno." <note>original: "Quia Jovem (inquiunt) in Æthere accipimus, in Aere Junonem"</note> But the reason why Juno was feminine and a goddess is given by Cicero this way: "They made the air feminine and attributed it to Juno, a goddess, because nothing is softer than the air." <note>original: "Effæminarunt autem eum, Junonique tribuerunt, quod nihil est aere mollius"</note> Minerva was also sometimes taken for a special or particular god, and then she was nothing else (as Zeno informs us) but a name for the Supreme God as he passes through the higher atmosphere <note>original: "Æther"</note>. This gave occasion for St. Augustine to object against pagan theology in this way: 
<margin>City of God, Book 4, Chapter 10.</margin> "If Minerva is said to possess the highest part of the atmosphere, and for this reason the poets pretend she was born from Jupiter’s head, why is she not rather designated the Queen of the Gods, since she is superior to Jupiter?" <note>original: "Si ætheris partem Superiorem Minerva tenere dicitur, & hac occasione fingere Poetas, quod de Jovis Capite nata sit, cur non ergo ipsa potius Deorum Regina deputatur, quod sit Jove Superior?"</note> Furthermore, as the Supreme God was called Neptune in the sea and Juno in the air, so by the same reasoning we may conclude that he was called Vulcan in the fire. Lastly, while the Sun and Moon were themselves sometimes worshipped by the pagans as inferior deities—they being supposed to be animated with particular souls of their own—so was the Supreme God also worshipped in them both (as well as in the other parts of the world) and under those names of Apollo and Diana. Thus, by appointing a god to preside over every part of the world, the pagans merely made the Supreme God *polyonymous* <term>polyonymous: having many names</term>, all those gods of theirs being indeed nothing but several names for Him. This theology of the ancient pagans is treated by Maximus Tyrius...

494 Many other Pagan Gods, in St. Augustine; BOOK I.

<margin>Dissertation 16, page 163.</margin> Maximus Tyrius, concerning Homer’s *Philosophy* (after he had mentioned his tripartite empire of the world, shared between *Jupiter*, *Neptune*, and *Pluto*), thus declares: <note>original: "εὕροις δ' ἂν καὶ ἄλλας παρ' Ὁμήρῳ ἀρχὰς καὶ γενέσεις παντοδαπῶν ὀνομάτων· ὧν ὁ μὲν ἀνόητος ὡς μύθων ἀκούει, ὁ δὲ φιλόσοφος ὡς πραγμάτων· ἔστιν αὐταῖς καὶ ἀρετῆς ἀρχὴ, ἀλλ' Ἀθηνᾶ λέγεται, &c."</note> *You may also find in Homer other principles and the origins of various names; which the ignorant hear as fables, but a philosopher will understand as realities. For he assigns a principle of virtue and wisdom, which he calls* Minerva; *another of love and desire, which he calls* Venus; *another of craftsmanship <note>original: "artificialness"</note>, and that is* Vulcan, *who rules over the fire. And* Apollo *also with him presides over dances, the* Muses *over songs,* Mars *over war,* Aeolus *over winds, and* Ceres *over fruits. And then he concludes thus:* <note>original: "καὶ οὐδὲν μέρος Ὁμήρῳ ἄθεον, οὐδὲ δυνάστου ἄπορον, οὐδὲ ἀρχῆς ἔρημον, ἀλλὰ πάντα μεστὰ θείων ὀνομάτων, καὶ θείων λόγων, καὶ θείας τέχνης"</note> *So that no part of nature, nor of the world, is to Homer godless (or void of a God); none is destitute of a ruler, or without a superior government; but all things are full of divine names, divine reason, and divine art.* Where his "divine names" are nothing but several *names* of God, manifesting himself in various ways through the different parts of nature and the world, and presiding over them.

Therefore, besides those *special gods* of the Pagans already mentioned, who were appointed to preside over several parts of the world, there are *others* who are also but *several names of the Supreme God*, as he performs several *offices* and *functions* in the world and bestows various *gifts* upon mankind. For example, when giving corn and fruits, he is called *Ceres*; in bestowing wine, *Bacchus*; in men’s recovery of their health, *Aesculapius*; in presiding over trade <note>original: "traffick"</note> and commerce, *Mercury*; in governing military affairs, *Mars*; in ordering the winds, *Aeolus*, and the like.

That the more philosophical Pagans really interpreted the fables of the gods in this way—making their *many poetical and political gods* to be nothing more than *one and the same Supreme Natural God*—is evident from the testimonies of *Antisthenes*, *Plato*, *Xenocrates*, *Zeno*, *Cleanthes*, and *Chrysippus* (who all allegorized the fables of the gods accordingly), and of *Scaevola* the Roman *Pontifex* <term>the high priest of the Roman state religion</term>, of *Cicero*, *Varro*, *Seneca*, and many others. But even their poets sometimes ventured to reveal this *hidden theology* <note>original: "arcane theology"</note>, as is manifest from those fragments preserved of *Hermesianax* the Colophonian among the Greeks, and of *Valerius Soranus* among the Latins. The former lists the chief Pagan gods, declaring them all to be but one and the same divine power <note>original: "numen"</note>:

-> Pluto, Persephone, Ceres, and kind Venus and the Cupids, <-
-> The Tritons, Nereus, Tethys, and the dark-haired Neptune, <-
-> Hermes, and the famous Hephaestus, Pan, Zeus, and Hera, <-
-> Artemis, and far-shooting Apollo—all are but one God. <-
<note>original Greek: "Πλούτων, Περσεφόνη, Δημήτηρ, Κύπρις, Ἔρωτες, / Τρίτωνες, Νηρεὺς, Τηθὺς, καὶ Κυανοχαίτης, / Ἑρμῆς, θ' Ἥφαιστός τε κλυτὸς, Πὰν, Ζεύς τε καὶ Ἥρη, / Ἄρτεμις, ἠδ' ἑκάεργος Ἀπόλλων, εἷς θεὸς ἐστί."</note>

-> *Pluto, Persephone, Ceres, and nourishing Venus and the Loves...* <-

The latter pronouncing universally, that *Almighty Jupiter* is

One God, and All Gods. Whether by his *Jupiter* he here meant the *Soul of the World* only—as Varro would interpret him according to his own theory <note>original: "Hypothesis"</note>—or whether he meant an *Abstract Mind* superior to it; he likely made this *Jupiter* to be *All Gods* based on these two reasons: First, as he was the *Begetter* and *Creator* of all the other natural gods, which were the *pagans' inferior deities* (such as the *stars* and *spirits* <note>original: "Dæmons"</note>). Secondly, because all the other poetic and political gods were *nothing else* but *various names* and *concepts* of him.

We shall add in the last place, that *St. Augustine* <note>original: "St. Austin"</note>, making a more full and detailed list of the *Pagan Gods*, and mentioning many others besides the *Select Roman Gods* (which are not commonly noticed today), pronounces universally of them all, according to the sense of the more intelligent Pagans: that they were but *one and the same Jupiter*.

<margin>*The City of God, Book 4, chapter 11.* <note>original: "De Civ. D. L. 4. c. 11."</note></margin> 

"Let him be Jupiter in the Upper Air, Juno in the Air, Neptune in the Sea; in the lower parts of the sea, let him be Salacia; in the Earth, Pluto; in the Underworld, Proserpina; in the domestic hearths, Vesta; in the blacksmith’s furnace, Vulcan; in those who divine, Apollo; in commerce, Mercury; in Janus the Initiator; in Terminus the Ender <note>original: "Terminator"; the god of boundaries</note>; Saturn in Time; Mars and Bellona in Wars; Liber in the Vineyards; Ceres in the Grain <note>original: "Frumentis"</note>; Diana in the Woods; Minerva in the Intellect. Finally, let him also be that crowd of, as it were, plebeian <note>meaning common or minor</note> gods: let him preside over the seeds of men under the name of Liber, and over the seeds of women under the name of Libera. Let him be Diespiter, who brings the birth to the light of Day. Let him be the goddess Mena, whom they set over the menstrual cycles of women; let him be Lucina, who is invoked by those in labor; let him bring help to the newborn, receiving them into the lap of the Earth, and be called Opis. Let him open the mouth in crying, and be called the god Vagitanus. Let him lift them from the earth, and be called the goddess Levana. Let him guard the cradles and be called the goddess Cunina. Let him be present in those goddesses who sing the fates of the newborn, and are called Carmentes. Let him preside over chance events, and be called Fortune. In the goddess Rumina, let him provide the breast for infants. In the goddess Potina, let him mix the drink. In the goddess Educa, let him provide food. From the fear of infants, let him be called Paventia. From the hope that comes, Venilia; from pleasure, Volupia. From action, Agenoria. From the impulses by which a person is driven to excessive action, let him be named the goddess Stimula. Let him be the goddess Strenua, by making one vigorous. Numeria, who teaches how to count; Camena, who teaches how to sing. Let him also be the god Consus by providing counsel; and the goddess Sentia by inspiring thoughts. Let him be the goddess Juventas, who takes charge of the beginnings of youth after the childhood toga <note>original: "prætextam"; the purple-bordered toga worn by Roman children</note> is set aside. Let him be Fortune the Bearded <note>original: "Fortuna Barbata"</note>, who clothes adults with a beard when he wishes to honor them. Let him join spouses in the god Jugatinus; and when the belt is loosened for the virgin bride, let him be invoked as the goddess Virginensis. Let him be Mutinus (who is Priapus among the Greeks), if they are not ashamed. All these things which I have said, and whatever I have not said, all these Gods and Goddesses are but One Jupiter."

*...whether they are, as some wish, all those parts of him—as it seems to those who are pleased to consider him the Soul of the World—or whether they are his powers <note>original: "Virtutes"</note>, which is the opinion of many great teachers.* <note>original: "sive sint ut quidam volunt omnia ista Partes ejus, sicut eis videtur quibus eum placet esse Mundi Animum; sive Virtutes ejus, quæ sententia velut magnorum multorumque Doctorum est."</note> Let us grant, according to the Pagans, that the Supreme God is **Jupiter** in the upper air <note>original: "Æther"</note>; **Juno** in the air; **Neptune** in the sea; **Salacia** in the lower parts of the sea; **Pluto** in the Earth; **Proserpina** in its lower parts; **Vesta** in the domestic hearths; **Vulcan** in the smiths' forges; **Apollo** in divination; **Mercury** in commerce and trade; **Janus** in the beginnings of things; **Terminus** in their ends; **Saturn** in time; **Mars** and **Bellona** in wars; **Liber** in the vineyards; **Ceres** in the grain fields; **Diana** in the woods; and **Minerva** in the intellect <note>original: "Wits"</note>.
