<header>CHAPTER IV. Not the same with the Physiological.</header>

...contemplating more keenly with the edge of the mind. <note>original: "acie mentis acrius contemplantes"</note> *What is clearer here than that he [Apuleius] understood the "Consenting Gods" <term>Dii Consentes: the council of the twelve primary Roman deities who "consented" to Jupiter's decisions</term> to be not Celestial or Sub-celestial Bodies, but a certain higher Nature, visible only to minds?* <note>original: "Quid apertius hic quam ab eo, per Deos Consentes intelligi, non Corpora Cœlestia vel Subcœlestia, sed sublimiorem quandam Naturam, nec nisi animis conspicuam?"</note> According to the *Philosophical Doctrine* concerning the gods, *Venus* is either the *Moon*, or *Lucifer* <note>the morning star</note>, or *Hesperus* <note>the evening star</note>; but according to the *Poetic* and *Civil Theology* of the *Pagans*, there were certain *Eternal Minds* placed above the *Heavens*, distinct from the *Stars*. Accordingly, *Apuleius* requires us to consider *Jupiter* and *Apollo*, *Juno* and *Venus*, and all those other gods called *Consentes*; he affirms of them that, although *Nature* has denied them to our sight, we nonetheless apprehend and admire them through the diligent contemplation of our *minds*. Regarding these words, *Vossius* says: *“Nothing can be more plain than that the Consenting Gods were understood by Apuleius to be neither Celestial nor Sub-celestial Bodies, but a certain higher Nature perceptible only to our Minds.”*

Upon these words of his, we shall make the following remarks. *First*, that this learned writer seems here, as he does throughout his whole book, to mistake the *Philosophical Theology* of *Scævola*, *Varro*, and others for that which was *Physiological* <term>Physiological: here meaning "Natural Philosophy," or the study of physical nature and the elements rather than spiritual essence</term> only. (We will later explain this *Physiological Theology* of the *Pagans*.) For the *Philosophical Theology* of the *Pagans* did not deify *Natural* and *Sensible* [physical] *Bodies* only; its principal part was the assertion of *One Supreme* and *Universal Numen* [Divine Power], from which all their other gods were derived.

Neither was *Venus*, according to this *Philosophical* and *Secret* <note>original: "Arcane"</note> *Theology*, taken only for the Moon, or for *Lucifer* or *Hesperus*, as this learned writer [Vossius] conceives; rather, as we have already proved, she was taken for the *Supreme Deity* also, either in its *Universal Notion* or through some *particular consideration* of it. Therefore, the *Philosophical Theology* of both *Scævola* and *Varro* and others was called *Natural*, not because it was *Physiological* only, but (in another sense) because it was *Real* and *True*. It was the theology neither of *Cities* [Civil] nor of *Stages and Theaters* [Poetic], but of the *World* and the *Wise Men* in it; for *Philosophy* is properly that which considers the *Absolute Truth* and *Nature* of things. This *Philosophical Theology*, therefore, was opposed to both the *Civil* and *Poetical*, which consisted only in *Opinion* and *Fancy*.

Our second remark is that *Vossius* also seems to improperly suggest that both the *Civil* and *Poetical Theology*, as such, were "philosophizing." In reality, the *first* of these was properly nothing but the *Law of Cities and Commonwealths, together with common opinion and error*; and the *second* was nothing but *Fancy, Fiction, and Fable*. *Those things belong to the poets, says Cotta in Cicero; but we wish to be philosophers, authors of realities <note>original: "rerum"</note>, not of fables.* <note>original: "Poetarum ista sunt... nos autem Philosophi esse volumus, Rerum authores, non Fabularum."</note>

But the main thing we notice in these words of *Vossius* is this: they seem to imply that the *Consenting*, the *Select*, and other *Civil* and *Poetical* gods of the *Pagans* were generally considered to be so many *Substantial* and *Eternal Minds*, or *Super-celestial* and *Independent* understanding beings—with their *Jupiter* being placed only on an equal footing with *Apollo, Juno, Venus*, and the rest. Since *Vossius* offers no other proof for this than the work *On the God of Socrates* <note>original: "De Deo Socratis"</note> by *Apuleius*, who was a *Platonic Philosopher*, we shall here make it evident that he did not rightly understand him...

# Apuleius's Interpretation of the Gods

Neither should we think any less of **Vossius** <note>Gerardus Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch scholar and theologian</note>—even though we readily acknowledge the vast and diverse learning of this eminent scholar <note>original: "Philologer"</note>—simply because he was not as well-versed in all the fine details and formal points <note>original: "Niceties and Punctilios"</note> of the **Platonic School**. 

For although **Apuleius** does in that book take notice of another kind of **invisible gods** besides those **visible gods** (the stars)—such as the **Twelve Consenting Gods** <term>Dii Consentes: the twelve primary Roman deities</term> and others—he says we "may conjecture with our minds, from the various benefits in human life perceived in those things which each of them cares for." <note>original: "animis conjectare, per varias Utilitates in vita agenda, animadversas in iis rebus, quibus eorum singuli curant"</note> 

Yet, it is clear that Apuleius was no fanatic regarding this **Civil Theology** <term>the public religion of the state</term>, because in that very place, he speaks out against superstition as well as irreligious profanity. His goal there was plainly nothing other than to bring the **Civil** and **Poetical Theologies** of the Pagans into a graceful conformity and agreement with their **Philosophical, Natural, and Real Theology**. This higher theology derived all the gods from **One Supreme and Universal Deity** <note>original: "Numen"</note>. He endeavors to do this in the Platonic way, being himself much devoted to that philosophy.

"Plato thinks all these gods placed in the highest ether are true, incorporeal, living beings, without beginning or end, but eternal in both directions <note>original: "prorsus ac retro æviternos"</note>; they are by their very nature removed from the contagion of the body, and their minds are reaching toward the highest happiness... Why should I now begin to describe the Parent of these gods, who is the Lord and Author of all things? He alone is free from all bonds of suffering or acting, and is not bound by any obligation to any other thing. For Plato—who was endowed with a heavenly eloquence equal to the immortal gods—often declares that this highest God, because of an incredible and ineffable excess of majesty, cannot be even slightly comprehended by any speech, due to the poverty of human language." <note>original: "Hos Deos in sublimi ætheris vertice locatos, Plato existimat veros, incorporales, animales... Quorum Parentem, qui omnium rerum Dominator atque Auctor est... hunc solum majestatis incredibili quadam nimietate & ineffabili, non posse penuria sermonis humani, quavis oratione vel modicè comprehendi."</note>

From these words of **Apuleius**, it is plain that, according to him, the **Twelve Consenting Gods** and all the other invisible gods were derived from **One Original Deity** as their Parent and Author. 

But then, if you ask what gods of **Plato** these should be—the ones Apuleius wishes to reconcile with the civil and poetic gods contained in those two verses by **Ennius** <note>Quintus Ennius, an early Roman poet</note>:

->*Juno, Vesta, Minerva, Ceres, Diana, Venus, Mars.*<-
->*Mercury, Jove, Neptune, Vulcan, Apollo.*<-

and others of this kind (that is, all their other "Invisible" gods, properly so called)—we reply that these are none other than Plato’s **Ideas**. These are the **First Paradigms** and **Patterns** of things in the **Archetypal World**, which is the **Divine Intellect** (his second level of divine existence <note>original: "Hypostasis"</note>), derived from his first Original Deity and most Simple **Monad** <note>the "One" or first principle</note>. For as Plato writes in his *Timaeus*: "It is necessary that this sensible world be an image of something." <note>original: "ἀνάγκη τόνδε τὸν κόσμον, εἰκόνα τινὸς εἶναι"</note> This sensible world...

<summary>Apuleius attempts to reconcile popular Pagan gods with Platonic philosophy by identifying the various deities as "Ideas" or intellectual patterns existing within a single Divine Intellect. He emphasizes that while there are many named gods, they all originate from one supreme, ineffable, and incomprehensible Author.</summary>

# CHAPTER IV. Pagan Gods as Plato's Ideas

...the world must necessarily be the image of another Intelligible world. And again afterward, in the *Timaeus*:
<margin>Plato in Timaeus p. 30.</margin>
"To which of the living beings did the Creator liken the world when he framed it? <note>original: τίνι τῶν ζώων αὐτὸν εἰς ὁμοιότητα ὁ συνιστὰς συνέστησε;</note> Let us not deign to think it was any particular living thing, since nothing can be beautiful that is made according to an imperfect copy. Rather, let us conclude it to be that Living Being which contains all other living beings within it, as its parts. For that Intelligible World <term>the realm of perfect forms and ideas that exists beyond the physical senses</term> contains all Intelligible Living Beings within it, in the same manner as this Sensible <note>perceived by the senses</note> World contains us and all other visible creatures."

Therefore, since **Plato** himself here and elsewhere spoke obscurely of this **Intelligible World** and its **Ideas**, it is no wonder if many of his Pagan followers absurdly made so many distinct living beings and gods out of them. Among these, **Apuleius** <note>a 2nd-century Platonic philosopher and author</note> accordingly referred all the **Civil** and **Poetic Gods** of the Pagans (meaning their gods properly so called, the **Invisible** ones) to this Intelligible world of Plato and its various Ideas. **Apuleius** was not alone in this; other
<margin>St. Cyril, *Against Julian*, Book 2, p. 65.</margin>
Pagan theologians did the same. For example, **Julian** <note>Julian the Apostate (r. 361–363 AD), the last pagan Roman Emperor</note> in his book against the Christians wrote:

"Plato names as gods those who are visible—the sun, the moon, the stars, and the heaven—but these are all merely images of other invisible gods. <note>original: θεοὺς ὀνομάζει πλάτων τοὺς ἐμφανεῖς...</note> The sun that is visible to our eyes is but an image of another Intelligible and Invisible Sun. Likewise, the visible moon and every one of the stars are but images and resemblances of another Intelligible moon and other Intelligible stars. Therefore, Plato also acknowledged these other Invisible Gods, existing within and co-existing with the **Demiurge** <term>the Creator or 'Craftsman' of the universe in Platonic thought</term>, from whom they were generated and produced. This Demiurge, in Plato's writing, thus addresses these Invisible and Intelligible Gods: *'You Gods of gods,'* meaning: *'You Invisible Gods, who are the gods and causes of the visible gods.'* There is, therefore, one common maker of both these kinds of gods, who first of all made a heaven, earth, sea, and stars in the Intelligible World, as the **Archetypes** and **Paradigms** <term>the original patterns or models</term> of those in the Sensible World."

Where **St. Cyril** <note>Cyril of Alexandria, a 5th-century Church Father who wrote a massive refutation of Julian the Apostate</note> in his rebuttal writes the following:

"By these things, our noble Julian seems to want to point out those 'Ideas' which Plato sometimes contends are substances that exist by themselves, and at other times defines as the thoughts of God. <note>original: ἔοικε δὲ διὰ τούτων ὁ γενναῖος ἡμῖν Ἰουλιανὸς...</note> However, no matter how it may be, the experts in these matters say that this line of reasoning is unacceptable even to Plato's own disciples. For **Aristotle** says, 'Farewell to the Forms [the Ideas], for they are mere idle talk <note>original: τερετίσματα, meaning 'chirpings' or 'nonsense'</note>; and even if they do exist, they contribute nothing to the argument.'"

Regardless of the truth of the matter, those skilled in this area of learning affirm that these Ideas were rejected by Plato's own disciples; *Aristotle* discarded them as fictions, or at least as mere notions that could have no real causal effect or influence on things. But the meaning of this Pagan theology may be more fully understood from what the same St. **Cyril** further objects against it:

<margin>
St. Cyril, *Against Julian*, Book 6, p. 200.
</margin>

> Julian adds that the God of the universe who made heaven and earth is the Demiurge <term>a craftsman-like figure responsible for fashioning the universe</term> of both these sensible things and the other intelligible things. Therefore, if—as he himself clearly admits—the unbegotten <note>original: ἀγέννητος (unbegotten/unmade)</note> God is the creator of both of these, how can he claim that the things created by him co-exist with and exist within him? How, tell me, can that which is created co-exist with the unbegotten God, and in what manner can it exist within him? For we Christians indeed strongly maintain that the unmade Word of God <note>the Logos</note> necessarily co-exists with and exists within the Father who generated Him, proceeding from Him not by creation but by generation. But this defender of Platonic trifles, while acknowledging the Supreme God to be unbegotten, nevertheless claims that the things made and created by him exist within him, thus mixing and confusing everything. <note>original: προσεπάγει δ' ὃτι καὶ τῶν ἐμφανῶν καὶ τῶν νοητῶν δημιουργὸς ἐστιν ὁ τῶν ὃλων Θεὸς... (the Greek text provided in the source)</note>

The sense of this passage seems to be that Julian and the *Platonic* Pagans would likely reply that those *Ideas* of the *Intelligible* and *Archetypal World* (which is the first *nous* <note>original: νοῦς (intellect)</note> or *Intellect*) proceeding from the *Highest Hypostasis* <term>the underlying substance or person of the Divinity</term> and *Original Deity* by way of necessary and eternal emanation, are no more to be considered *creatures* than the Christian *Logos* <note>the Word of God</note>. Therefore, they might, with just as little absurdity, be said to exist *with* and *in* that *First Original Deity*.

Furthermore, the same **Julian** elsewhere in that book of his also applies this Platonic notion to the specific Pagan gods, just as **Apuleius** had done before. He writes of **Aesculapius** <note>the god of medicine</note> in this mystical way:

> For Jupiter, among the intelligible things, generated Aesculapius out of himself, and manifested him here on earth through the life-giving <note>original: "vivifick"</note> life of the sun. Coming down from heaven and appearing in a unified way in human form around Epidaurus, he extended his healing power over the whole earth. <note>original: ὁ γὰρ Ζεὺς, ἐν μὲν τοῖς νοητοῖς ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ τὸν Ἀσκληπιὸν ἐγέννησεν... (the Greek text provided in the source)</note>

In this view, *Aesculapius* is first of all the eternal *Idea* of the medicinal art or skill, generated by the Supreme God in the *intelligible world*. Afterward, through the life-giving influence of the sun, this Idea was incarnated and appeared in human form at *Epidaurus*. This is the doctrine of that **Julian**, who so strongly opposed the incarnation of the eternal *Logos* in our...

### CHAP. IV. and Others, The Divine Ideas. 501

...our Savior Jesus Christ. This doctrine of *many intelligible gods and eternal powers* (which make up the *Archetypal World* <term>the world of ideal forms or blueprints</term>) was not first invented by Platonic Pagans after the rise of Christianity, as some might suspect. That such an idea existed among them even earlier can be concluded from this passage <margin>Philo, *On the Confusion of Tongues*, p. 345, Paris edition.</margin> of **Philo's**:

> Though God is only one, He has around Himself countless auxiliary powers, all of which bring help and salvation to created things. Through these powers, the incorporeal and intelligible world was formed—the archetype of this visible world—composed of invisible ideas just as this world is composed of visible bodies. Therefore, some people, struck with wonder at the nature of both these worlds, have not only deified them in their entirety but also the most beautiful of their parts—the sun, the moon, and the whole heaven—which they did not hesitate to call gods. <note>original: εἷς ὢν ὁ θεὸς ἀμυθήτους περὶ αὑτὸν ἔχει δυνάμεις ἀρωγοὺς καὶ σωτηρίους τοῦ γενομένου πάσας· δι’ αὑτῶν τῶν δυνάμεων, ὁ ἀσώματος καὶ νοητὸς ἐπάγη κόσμος, τὸ τοῦ φαινομένου τόδε ἀρχέτυπον, ἰδέαις ἀοράτοις συσταθείς, ὥσπερ οὗτος σώμασιν ὁρατοῖς· καταπλαγέντες οὖν τινες τὴν ἑκατέρου τῶν κόσμων φύσιν, οὐ μόνον ὅλους ἐξεθείωσαν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ κάλλιστα τῶν ἐν αὐτοῖς μερῶν, ἥλιον, καὶ σελήνην, καὶ τὸν σύμπαντα οὐρανόν, ἅπερ οὐδὲν αἰδεσθέντες θεοὺς ἐκάλεσαν·</note>

In this passage, Philo seems to speak of a "double" sun, moon, and heaven, just as the Emperor **Julian** did—one being "sensible" <term>perceived by the senses</term> and the other being "intelligible" <term>grasped by the mind</term>. Furthermore, **Plotinus** himself sometimes agrees with this notion, calling the Ideas of the Divine Intellect "intelligible gods" <note>original: νοητοὺς θεοὺς</note>. For example, in the passage cited earlier, he encourages those ascending above the "Soul of the World" <term>the spiritual force animating the universe</term> "to praise the intelligible gods" <note>original: θεοὺς ὑμνεῖν νοητοὺς</note>. By this, he means the Divine Intellect, which he describes elsewhere as being both "one and many" <note>original: εἷς καὶ πολλοὶ</note>.

We have now provided a full account of **Apuleius’s** meaning in his book *On the God of Socrates* regarding the "civil" and "poetic" pagan gods. His goal was not to claim there is a multitude of independent, substantial, and eternal deities or minds. Instead, he sought to bring the "vulgar" <note>original: vulgar (common or popular)</note> theology of the pagans—found in both civic religion and poetry—into alignment with "natural," "real," and "philosophical" theology. He did this using Platonic principles. Many other pagan Platonists, both before and after the rise of Christianity, agreed with him. They claimed that the many invisible gods of paganism were actually nothing more than the eternal "Ideas" within the Divine Intellect. These were called the parts of the "intelligible" and "archetypal" world. They believed these Ideas were the "paradigms" <term>perfect models or templates</term> and patterns according to which this physical world and everything in it were created and upon which they depend, being merely participants in those Ideas.

Therefore, although this might be seen as a "monstrous extravagance" <note>original: monstrous extravagancy (an extreme or bizarre deviation)</note> on the part of these Platonic philosophers—treating Divine Ideas or archetypal patterns not just as real entities, but as distinct living beings, persons, and gods—it was simply their habit to multiply gods on any slight occasion. Nevertheless, we must acknowledge that at the same time, they declared all of these were derived from one Supreme Deity. Not only that, but they believed these Ideas existed *within* that Deity—just as they did when they were not occupied with defending pagan poly-

# The Pagans' Invisible Gods, BOOK I.

Polytheism, they freely acknowledge all these *intelligible Ideas* to be really nothing else but **thoughts in the Mind of God** <note>original: νοήματα</note>, or the **First Intellect**. These are not like the *slight, accidental*, and *vanishing* <note>original: evanid</note> thoughts found in our human souls. Consequently, they are not so many *distinct substances, persons*, and *gods*—and certainly not *independent ones*—but only various **partial ways of considering the Deity**.

It has already been shown, using the works of **St. Augustine** <note>original: St. Austin</note>, **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BCE) was a Roman scholar whose works on religion were frequently cited and critiqued by early Christian writers like Augustine.</note>, and others, what a "rabble of invisible gods and goddesses" the Pagans possessed. This was in addition to their **Noble Gods** <note>original: *Dii Nobiles*</note> and **Gods of the Greater Nations** <note>original: *Dii Majorum Gentium*</note> (which were known as the **Council of Twelve** <term>original: *Consentes*; the twelve major Roman deities</term> and the **Select Gods** <note>original: *Selecti*</note>). These minor deities included: 

*Goddess Mena, God Vagitanus, Goddess Levana, Goddess Cunina, Goddess Rumina, Goddess Potina, Goddess Educa, Goddess Paventina, Goddess Venilia, Goddess Agenoria, Goddess Stimula, Goddess Strenua, Goddess Numeria, God Consus, Goddess Sentia, God Jugatinus, Goddess Virginensis, and God Mutinus.* 

To these might be added many more from other passages by the same **St. Augustine**, such as: 

*Goddess Deverra, God Domiducus, God Domitius, Goddess Manturna, God Father Subigus, Goddess Mother Prema, Goddess Pertunda, Goddess Rufina, Goddess Collatina, Goddess Vallonia, Goddess Seia, Goddess Segetia, Goddess Tutilina, God Nodotus, Goddess Volutina, Goddess Patelena, Goddess Hostilina, Goddess Flora, Goddess Lacturtia, Goddess Matura, and Goddess Runcina.* 

Besides these, there are so many other Pagan gods and goddesses mentioned in other writings that we cannot list or name them all here. Many of them were assigned very small, mean, and even contemptible duties, as their names mostly imply. Some of these duties are of such a nature that it would not be appropriate to interpret them here <note>The author is likely referring to deities associated with bodily functions or sexual acts, which 17th-century sensibilities found "unfit" for translation.</note>. 

From this, it plainly appears that for these Pagans, **nothing at all was without a god** <note>original: μηδὲν ἄθεον</note>. They held such a strong conviction that Divine Providence extended itself to all things that they expressed it by assigning **every thing in Nature**, **every part of the world**, and **every human action** a particular god or goddess by name to preside over it. 

Now, it is **utterly incredible** that intelligent Pagans should believe in good earnest that all these *invisible gods and goddesses* were so many *separate, substantial minds*, or *eternal and unmade understanding beings* really existing in the world. For how could anyone possibly persuade themselves that there was one eternal, unmade mind or spirit which, for example, essentially presided over **the rocking of infants' cradles** and nothing else? Or another over the **sweeping of houses**? Another over **ears of corn**? Another over the **husks of grain**? And another over the **knots of straw and grass**, and the like? 

The case is exactly the same for those "Noble Gods" of theirs—the *Consentes* and *Selecti*. There is no reason why those should all be considered so many *substantial and eternal spirits* that are self-existent or unmade, if none of these minor ones were. Therefore, if these are not all separate substantial and eternal minds—so many self-existing and independent deities—then they must necessarily be either **various partial ways of considering the Deity** (specifically, the various manifestations of Divine Power and Providence personified) or else **inferior ministers** of the same. And thus have we already...

<summary>This page argues that the vast "rabble" of minor Roman deities were not viewed by intelligent Pagans as independent, eternal gods, but rather as personifications of a single Divine Providence acting in every small detail of life.</summary>

# CHAP. IV. Divine Virtues and Powers Deified,

<margin>*Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, Book 3, chapter 13, page 121.*</margin>
<margin>*Book 1, chapter 1, page 85.*</margin>
It has been showed that the more sophisticated and Platonic Pagans (such as **Julian**, **Apuleius**, and others) understood these **Council Gods** <term>original: *Consentes*; the twelve major Roman deities</term> and **Select Gods**, and all the other **invisible** ones, to be really nothing else but the **Ideas** of the **Intelligible and Archetypal World** (which is the **Divine Intellect**). This means they are indeed but **partial considerations of the Deity**, as it **virtually** and **perfectly** <note>original: "exemplarily"</note> contains all things. 

Meanwhile, others, taking a more plain and easy path, concluded that these gods of theirs were all but several **names and notions of the One Supreme Deity**, according to the **various manifestations** of its power in the world. As **Seneca** expressly affirms—not only regarding Fate, Nature, and Fortune, etc., but also **Father Liber** <note>original: *Liber Pater*; an Italian god of fertility and wine, often identified with Bacchus</note>, **Hercules**, and **Mercury** (previously mentioned by him)—that they were "all names of one and the same God, using his power in various ways" <note>original: *Omnia ejusdem Dei Nomina, variè utentis suâ potestate*</note>. **Zeno** (as recorded in **Diogenes Laertius**) concludes the same for all the rest. Or else—which amounts to the same thing—they were the **several powers and virtues of one God fictitiously personified and deified**. As the Pagans in **Eusebius** defend themselves, they "deify nothing but the invisible powers of that God who is over all" <note>original: *θεοποιεῖν τὰς ἀοράτους δυνάμεις αὐτοῦ τοῦ ἐπὶ πᾶσιν*</note>.

Nevertheless, because those several powers of the **Supreme God** were not supposed to be all executed immediately by himself, but by certain other **subservient powers** <note>original: *ὑπεργοὶ δυνάμεις*</note> or **ministering spirits** under him, appointed to preside over the several things of nature, parts of the world, and affairs of mankind (commonly called **Demons**), these gods were sometimes taken to be such subservient spirits or demons collectively. This is perhaps seen in this passage from **Epictetus**: "When will **Zephyrus** (the West Wind) blow? When it seems good to himself, my good friend, or to **Aeolus**; for God has not made you the steward of the winds, but Aeolus" <note>original: *πότε ὁ ζέφυρος πνεύσῃ ; ὅταν αὐτῷ δόξῃ, ὦ βέλτιστε, ἢ τῷ Αἰόλῳ · σὲ γὰρ οὐκ ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς ταμίαν τῶν ἀνέμων, ἀλλὰ τὸν Αἰόλον*</note>.

<margin>*Book 1, chapter 1.*</margin>
But for the fuller clearing of the whole **Pagan Theology**, and especially this one point: that their **polytheism** <note>original: *πολυθεΐα*</note> was in great part nothing else but **polyonymy** <note>original: *πολυωνυμία*; the use of many names</note>—their multiplicity of gods being nothing but the many names for one God—two things must be further noted. First, according to Pagan theology, **God was conceived to be diffused throughout the whole world, to permeate and pervade all things, to exist in all things, and to intimately act in all things.** Thus, we observed before from **Horus Apollo** that the Egyptian theologians conceived of God as "a spirit pervading the whole world" <note>original: *τοῦ παντὸς κόσμου τὸ διῆκον πνεῦμα*</note>. Likewise, they concluded that "nothing at all exists without God" <note>original: *δίχα Θεοῦ μηδὲν ὅλως συνεστάναι*</note>.

This same theology was also universally accepted among the Greeks. For thus **Diogenes the Cynic** says in **Laertius**: "All things are full of him" <note>original: *αὐτοῦ πάντα πλήρη*</note>. And **Aristotle** (or the writer of *On Plants*) makes God not only comprehend the whole world but also be an **inward principle of life** in animals: "What could be the principle in the life or soul of animals? Certainly no other than that noble living being <note>or "living creature"</note> which encompasses the heavens, or the sun, the stars, and the planets" <note>original: *τίς ἂν εἴη ἡ ἀρχὴ ἡ ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ τοῦ ζώου ; τί ἄλλο, εἰ μὴ τὸ αὐτογενὲς ζῶον, ὃ τὸν οὐρανὸν περιέληφε, ἢ ἥλιον, τὰ ἄστρα, καὶ τοὺς πλάνητας*</note>.

<summary>This page argues that Pagan polytheism was often a form of "polyonymy," where different gods represented the various powers or names of a single, omnipresent Supreme Being. It cites thinkers like Seneca, Epictetus, and Horus Apollo to show that the divine was seen as a spirit pervading and animating all of nature.</summary>

...and surrounds the whole Heaven, the Sun, the stars, and the planets.

<margin>*Against the Mathematicians*, page 331.</margin>
**Sextus Empiricus** thus represents the opinion <note>original: "fence," likely a transcription of *dokein* or "sense"</note> of **Pythagoras**, **Empedocles**, and all the Italian philosophers: "That we men have not only a connection among ourselves with one another, but also with the Gods above us, and with irrational animals <note>original: *brute animals*</note> below us; because there is one Spirit which, like a Soul, pervades the whole world and unites all its parts together" <note>original Greek: μὴ μόνον ἡμῖν πρὸς ἀλλήλους καὶ πρὸς τοὺς θεοὺς εἶναί τινὰ κοινωνίαν, ἀλλὰ καὶ πρὸς τὰ ἄλογα τῶν ζώων· ἓν γὰρ ὑπάρχειν πνεῦμα τὸ διὰ παντὸς κόσμου διῆκον, ψυχῆς τρόπον, τὸ καὶ ἑνοῦν ἡμᾶς πρὸς ἐκεῖνα</note>.

<margin>*Exhortation to the Heathen*, page 44.</margin>
**Clement of Alexandria** writes this about the **Stoics**: "They affirm that the divine pervades all the matter of the universe, and even the most lowly parts of it" <note>original Greek: διὰ πάσης ὕλης, καὶ διὰ τ’ ἀτιμοτάτης τὸ θεῖον διήκειν λέγουσι</note>. This is a view that the Church Father seems to dislike. **Tertullian** also expressed their doctrine this way: "The Stoics would have God run through matter in the same way that honey runs through the honeycomb" <note>original Latin: *Stoici volunt Deum sic per Materiam decucurrisse, quomodo Mel per Favos*</note>.

<margin>Book 15, page 730.</margin>
**Strabo** testifies concerning the ancient Indian **Brahmans** <note>original: *Brachmans*</note> that "in many things they shared the same opinions as the Greeks; for they say that the world had a beginning and that it is perishable <note>original: *corrupted*</note>, and that God, who governs and made it, pervades the whole of it" <note>original Greek: περὶ πολλῶν τοῖς Ἕλλησιν ὁμοδοξεῖν, ὅτι γὰρ γενητὸς ὁ κόσμος· καὶ φθαρτὸς λέγειν κἀκείνους, ὅ τε διοικῶν αὐτὸν καὶ ποιῶν Θεὸς, δι’ ὅλου διαπεφοίτηκεν αὐτοῦ</note>. 

The Latins also fully agreed with the Greeks in this. For though **Seneca** somewhere proposes this question—"Whether God is only externally poured around his work, the world, or whether he is inwardly implanted and pervades it all?" <note>original Latin: *Utrum Extrinsecus operi suo Circumfusus sit Deus, an toti inditus?*</note>—he elsewhere answers it himself when he calls God "a Divine Spirit, diffused through all things, greatest and smallest, with equal intensity" <note>original Latin: *Divinum Spiritum per omnia, maxima, ac minima, æquali intentione diffusum*</note>. 

In **Quintilian’s** theology, God is "a Spirit mixed into all parts" and "that Spirit poured out there through all the parts of the nature of things" <note>original Latin: *Spiritus omnibus partibus Immistus; and Illic fusus, per omnes rerum Naturæ partes Spiritus*</note>. **Apuleius** likewise affirms "that God permeates all things" <note>original Latin: *Deum omnia permeare*</note>, and that "there is nothing so excellent or powerful that, if deprived of God's help, it could be satisfied with its own nature alone" <note>original Latin: *Nulla res est tam præstantibus viribus, quæ viduata Dei auxilio, sui natura contenta sit*</note>. And again: "Not only our thoughts now, but our eyes, ears, and physical senses grasp the presence of God in all these perceptible things" <note>original Latin: *Dei Præsentiam, non jam cogitatio sola, sed Oculi, & aures, & sensibilis substantia comprehendit*</note>. 

**Servius**, in agreement with this doctrine of the ancient Pagans, determines that "no part of the elements is without God" <note>original Latin: *Nulla Pars Elementi sine Deo est*</note>. That the poets fully embraced the same theology is evident from those well-known passages of theirs: "All things are full of Jupiter" <note>original Latin: *Jovis omnia plena*</note> and "All the streets are full of Zeus" <note>original Greek: μεσταὶ δὲ Διὸς πᾶσαι μὲν ἀγυιαὶ</note>. In other words, all the things of nature and parts of the world are full of God. This is also seen in this passage from **Virgil**:

<margin>*Virgil, Georgics*, Book 4.</margin>

->— For God goes through all <-
-> lands, the reaches of the sea, and the deep heaven. <-
<note>original Latin: *— Deum namque ire per omnes / Terrasque, Tractusque Maris, Cœlumque profundum*</note>

The author argues that this "immanence" was a core tenet of ancient theology, shared by poets like Virgil and philosophers like the Stoics.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that ancient philosophers believed God to be a distinct, pure Spirit that nevertheless permeates and governs the entire physical universe.</meta>

<page-num>505</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER IV. Theology Pervades All Things.</header>

Finally, we should observe that both **Plato** and **Anaxagoras**, neither of whom confused God with the world but kept them distinct and affirmed God to be "unmingled with anything" <note>original Greek: οὐδενὶ μεμιγμένον</note>, nevertheless concluded "that he orders and governs all things, passing through and pervading all things" <note>original Greek: αὐτὸν πάντα κοσμεῖν τὰ πράγματα διὰ πάντων ἰόντα</note>. This is the very same doctrine held by Christian theologians: "That God permeates and passes through all things, without being mixed with them" <note>original Greek: τὸν θεὸν διὰ πάντων ἀμίγως διήκειν</note>. In his dialogue *Cratylus*, Plato plainly uses "Justice" <note>Greek: δίκαιον (*dikaion*)</note> as a name for God. He explains its etymology as "passing through all things" <note>Greek: διὰ ἰὸν (*dia ion*)</note> and provides the best extant account of **Heraclitus's** theosophy <term>theosophy: a system of philosophy or religion that proposes to establish direct contact with the divine</term> (if it is not actually a fragment written by Heraclitus himself) in these words:

<margin>*Cratylus*, page 413.</margin>

> Those who believe the universe is in constant motion suppose that a great part of it does nothing but move and change. But they also believe there is something that passes through and pervades this whole universe, through which all created things are made. This substance is both the swiftest and most subtle thing; for it could not otherwise pass through all things if it were not so subtle that nothing could keep it out or hinder it; and it must be the swiftest so that it may treat all other things as if they stood still, so that nothing escapes it. Since this substance presides over and orders all things by permeating and passing through them, it was correctly named "Justice" <note>Greek: δίκαιον (*dikaion*)</note>, as if it were "passing through" <note>Greek: διαϊὸν (*dia-ion*)</note>; the letter 'k' <note>original: Cappa (kappa)</note> was only added for the sake of a more pleasant pronunciation.

Here we have Heraclitus's description of **God**, namely: "That most subtle and most swift substance which permeates and passes through the whole universe, by which all things that are made, are made" <note>original Greek: τὸ λεπτότατον καὶ τὸ τάχιστον, διὰ παντὸς διεξιὸν, δι᾽ οὗ πάντα τὰ γιγνόμενα γίγνεται</note>. Now, Plato says that some of these followers of Heraclitus say this substance is fire, while others say it is heat. But Plato, mocking both these ideas, concludes with Anaxagoras that it is a **Perfect Mind**, "unmixed with anything," which yet "permeates and passes through all things, framing, ordering, and disposing of them all."

Therefore, since it was the universally accepted doctrine of the pagans that God was a Spirit or Substance spread through the whole world—which, by permeating and acting within all things, ordered them all—it is no wonder if they called him by different names in various parts of the world and in different aspects of nature. Or, to use **Cicero's** language: "it is no wonder if God, pervading the nature of every thing, was called Ceres in the earth, Neptune in the sea, Juno in the air, etc." <note>original Latin: *Deus Pertinens per Naturam cujusque rei, per Terras Ceres, per Maria Neptunus, &c.*</note> And this very same account is given by **Paulus Orosius** (in his historical work against the pagans, dedicated to St. Augustine) regarding the origin of pagan polytheism:

<margin>Book 6, chapter 1.</margin>

"Some, while they believe God to be in many things, have created many gods out of an indiscriminate fear" <note>original Latin: *Quidam dum In Multis Deum credunt, Multos Deos, indiscreto Timore, finxerunt*</note>.

<meta>catchword: In</meta>

<summary>This page explains the philosophical concept of God as a "Perfect Mind" or subtle substance that permeates the entire universe. It argues that pagan polytheism arose from giving different names to this single divine presence as it manifested in different parts of nature, such as the earth or sea.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that while some Pagans viewed God as a spirit pervading the universe, others held a "higher" view that God is essentially everything that exists.</meta>

<page-num>506</page-num>
<header>A Higher Level of the Pagan Theology, BOOK I.</header>

In *many things*, they have therefore, out of an *unwise fear* <note>original: "indiscreet fear"</note>, invented *many gods*. In these words, he suggests that the Pagans' *many gods* were really just *different names* for *one God* as he exists *in many things*, or in the *various parts* of the world; just as the same ocean is called by different names as it beats upon different shores.

Secondly, *Pagan theology* sometimes went to an even higher level. They did not only suppose that *God pervades the whole world* and is *diffused through all things* (which still maintains some difference and distinction between *God* and the *world*), but also that *He Himself is, in a sense, all things*. That ancient *Egyptian theology*—from which the theologies of other nations were derived—reached this high point is evident from that excellent monument of *Egyptian antiquity*, the *Saitic Inscription* <note>The inscription at the Temple of Neith in Sais, Egypt.</note> often mentioned: *I am all that was, is, and shall be*. 

Furthermore, the *Trismegistic books* <term>Trismegistic: referring to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure to whom a series of influential philosophical and religious texts (the Hermetica) were attributed</term> insist so much everywhere upon this notion—*That God is all things*—that it makes it more probable (as has been observed) that they were not entirely counterfeit or fake. Instead, according to the testimony of *Iamblichus*, they contained at least some *Hermetic opinions* <note>original Greek: δόξας Ἑρμαϊκὰς</note>, reflecting the *old Egyptian philosophy* <note>original: "Theutical or Hermaical Philosophy," referring to Thoth or Hermes</note>. 

In all probability, this doctrine was brought from *Egypt* into *Greece* by *Orpheus*. The *Orphic verses* themselves lean heavily on this idea, and the *Orphic theology* was summarized this way by *Timotheus the Chronographer*: *That all things were made by God*, and *That He Himself is all things*. To this purpose is this passage by the playwright *Aeschylus*:

<margin>Grotius, Excerpts page 57.</margin>
->Zeus is the ether, Zeus is the earth, Zeus is the heaven;<-
->Zeus is indeed all things, and whatever is even higher than these.<-
<note>original Greek: Ζεύς ἐστιν αἰθήρ, Ζεύς δὲ γῆ, Ζεύς δ’ οὐρανός • Ζεύς τοι τὰ πάντα, χὤ, τι τῶν δ’ ἔθ’ ὑπέρτερον •</note>

->And Earth, and Ether, and the Tower of the Sky is Jupiter,<-
->And He alone is all things, and something even more sublime.<-
<note>original Latin translation of the same: Et Terra, & Æther, & Poli Arx est Jupiter, Et Cuncta Solus, & aliquid Sublimius.</note>

And again,

<margin>Ibid. page 53.</margin>
->Sometimes he appears as unquenchable fire in his rush;<-
->Sometimes as water, sometimes as darkness;<-
->And he himself becomes like wild beasts,<-
->The wind, the cloud, the lightning, thunder, and rain.<-
<note>original Greek: Ποτὲ μὲν ὡς πῦρ φαίνεται ῎Απλαστον ὁρμῇ • ποτὲ δ’ ὕδωρ, ποτὲ δ’ γνόφῳ • Καὶ θηρσὶν αὐτὸς γίνεται παρεμφερὴς, ᾿Ανέμῳ, νέφει τε, κἀστραπῇ, βροντῇ, βροχῇ •</note>

->Now as darkness, now equal to water;<-

As also this passage by *Lucan* among the *Latin* poets:

<margin>Book 9, verse 580.</margin>

<note>original Latin: Superos quid quærimus ultra ? Jupiter est quodcunque Vides, quocunque moveris.</note>

The following passages from *Seneca* the philosopher agree with this: *What is God? He is all that you see, and all that you do not see.* And *so*

# CHAPTER IV. Theology: That God is All Things.

"He alone is all things; he holds his work both outside and inside." <note>original Latin: *Solus est Omnia; opus suum & Extrà & Intrà tenet*</note> What is God? He is all that you see, and all that you do not see. He alone is All Things, containing his own work not only outside of himself but also within. 

This was not only the doctrine of those Pagans who held God to be the "Soul of the World"—and consequently believed the entire living world to be the Supreme Deity—but also the view of others who conceived of God as an Abstract Mind superior to the World Soul. Some even saw Him as a simple "Monad" <term>Monad: a single, indivisible unit or the ultimate source of all existence</term> superior even to Mind itself. Philosophers such as Xenophanes, Parmenides, and Melissus described God as being "One and All Things." They supposed that because all things were *from* him, they must have first existed, in a sense, *in* him, and that He himself was All Things. 

The author of the *Asclepian Dialogue* <note>A famous Hermetic text attributed to Hermes Trismegistus</note> agrees with this when he makes "One is All Things" <note>original Latin: *Unus Omnia*</note> and "the Creator of All Things" <note>original Latin: *Creator Omnium*</note> equivalent expressions. He affirms that before things were made, "they existed in him then, from where they were destined to be born." <note>original Latin: *In eo jam tunc erant, unde Nasci habuerunt*</note>. 

Similarly, other *Trismegistic Books* give this account of God being both all things that *are* and all things that *are not*: "He manifested the things that are from himself" <note>original Greek: *τὰ μὴ ὄντα ἐφάνερωσε*</note> and "he still contains within himself the things that are not" <note>original Greek: *τὰ ὃ μὴ ὄντα ἔχει*</note>. Or, as it is expressed elsewhere, he "hides and conceals them in himself." <note>original Greek: *κρύπτειν*</note>. 

The *Orphic Verses* <note>Poems attributed to the mythical singer Orpheus, central to the Orphic mystery religion</note> gave this same account of God being "All Things," "having hidden all things within himself" <note>original Greek: *πάντα τὰ ἢ κρύψας*</note> before they were made, and then later displaying them from himself and bringing them forth into the light. Or, as another verse puts it:

->— "They were all grown together in the womb of Zeus," <- <note>original Greek: *Ζηνὸς ἀπὸ ἐν γασέρι σῦρρα πεφύκει*</note>

meaning that before they were produced, they were all contained together in the womb of God.

Now, this concept was not only a further basis for that apparent "Polytheism" among the Pagans—which was really nothing more than "Polyonymy" <term>Polyonymy: the practice of using many different names for one single God</term> or the personification of his various powers—but it also explains another more strange and puzzling phenomenon in their theology. This was their practice of personifying the inanimate parts of the world and things of nature, bestowing the names of gods and goddesses upon them. 

It was previously observed from the writings of *Moschopulus* <note>Manuel Moschopulus, a 13th-century Byzantine scholar</note> that the <margin>P. 229.</margin> Pagans would "call the things in nature, and the gods which presided over them, by one and the same name." <note>original Greek: *ἐν ὀνόματι τότε τῷ θεὸν ὀνομάζειν, ὃ ἢ ἐπικρατέστερα τῦτοῦ δύναμιν ἔχον...*</note> For example, they did not only call the god who presides over the arts that use fire *Hephaestus* or *Vulcan*, but they also called *Fire* itself by those names. *Demeter* or *Ceres* was not only the goddess supposed to give corn and fruits, but was also a name for *Corn* itself. So *Dionysus* or *Bacchus* did not only signify the god who gives wine, but also *Wine* itself. Mentioning *Venus*, *Minerva*, and the *Muses* as further examples, he concludes that this applies universally to all the rest. 

Thus *Arnobius* <note>An Early Christian apologist of the 4th century</note> wrote in his book against the <margin>L. 5.</margin> Pagans: "In your common speech, you call a battle 'Mars,' water 'Neptune,' wine 'Father Liber,' bread 'Ceres,' thread 'Minerva,' and obscene lusts 'Venus.'" <note>original Latin: *In usu sermonis vestri, Martem pro Pugna appellatis, pro Aqua Neptunum, Liberum Patrem pro Vino, Cererem pro Pane, Minervam pro Stamine, pro Obscœnis libidinibus Venerem*</note>. Now, we will not deny but...

<summary>This page explores the theological concept that God is "All Things," arguing that ancient Pagans viewed the natural world as manifestations of a single divine source. This belief led to "polyonymy," where different names (like Vulcan for fire or Ceres for corn) were used for both the deity and the physical element they governed.</summary>

<page-num>508</page-num>

# The Parts of the World and Things (Book I)

...but this was sometimes done **metonymically** <term>metonymy: a figure of speech in which a thing or concept is referred to by the name of something closely associated with it</term>, where the **efficient cause** <term>efficient cause: the primary agent or force that produces an effect</term> and the ruling or governing principle were substituted for the effect, or for that which was ruled and governed by it. In this way, "War" was frequently styled "Mars," and that line of **Terence** <note>Publius Terentius Afer, a Roman playwright</note> may also be understood in this sense: "Without Ceres (food) and Liber (wine), Venus (love) grows cold." <note>original Latin: *Sine Cerere & Libero friget Venus*</note> 

<margin>On Isis and Osiris, page 379.</margin>
And **Plutarch** (who declares his great dislike of this kind of language) conceives that there was originally no more to it than this: "Just as we, when someone buys the books of Plato, commonly say that he buys 'Plato'; and when one acts the plays of Menander, that he acts 'Menander'; so did the ancients not hesitate to call the gifts and effects of the gods by the names of those gods respectively, thereby honoring them also for their utility." <note>original Greek: *ὥσπερ ἡμεῖς τὸν ὠνούμενον βιβλία Πλάτωνος, ὠνεῖσθαί φαμεν Πλάτωνα, καὶ Μένανδρον τὸ ὑποκρίνεσθαι τὰ Μενάνδρου ποιήματα ὑποτιθέμενον, οὕτως ἐκεῖνοι, τοῖς τῶν θεῶν ὀνόμασι τὰ τῶν θεῶν δῶρα καὶ ποιήματα καλεῖν οὐκ ἐφείδοντο, τιμῶντες ὑπὸ χρείας καὶ σεμνύνοντες*</note>

But he grants that
<margin>Ibid.</margin>
afterward, this language was abused and taken further by ignorant persons, and not without great impiety: "Their followers, receiving these traditions without education and interpreting them ignorantly, attributed the 'passions' <note>In this context, "passions" refers to the seasonal changes or physical states of the harvest</note> of the fruits—their appearances and disappearances—to the gods themselves who preside over them. Thus, they not only called them by these names but believed them to be the actual births and deaths of the gods, thereby filling themselves with absurd, lawless, and confused opinions." <note>original Greek: *οἱ δ᾽ ὕστεροι ἀπαιδεύτως δεχόμενοι καὶ ἀμαθῶς ἀναστρέφοντες, ἐπὶ τοὺς θεοὺς τὰ πάθη τῶν καρπῶν καὶ τὰς παρουσίας τῶν ἀναγκαίων καὶ ἀποκρύψεις, θεῶν γενέσεις καὶ φθοράς, οὐ προσαγορεύοντες μόνον ἀλλὰ καὶ νομίζοντες, ἀτόπων καὶ ἀνόμων καὶ τεταραγμένων δοξῶν αὑτοὺς ἐνέπλησαν*</note>

Here, Plutarch rightly condemns the common people among both the Egyptians and Greeks for their foolishness in their mournful rituals, where they attributed the "passions" belonging to the fruits of the earth to the gods, effectively making the crops themselves into deities. Nevertheless, the inanimate parts of the world and the things of nature were frequently deified by the Pagans, not only metonymically but also in a 

<margin>On the Nature of the Gods, Book 2, page 222.</margin>
further sense, as **Cicero** plainly declares: "First, they called that which was produced by a god by the name of the god himself—as when we call grain 'Ceres' and wine 'Liber.' But also, whatever thing possesses some greater power is called such that the thing itself is named a god." <note>original Latin: *Tum illud quod erat à Deo natum, Nomine ipsius Dei nuncupabant, ut cum Fruges Cererem appellamus, Vinum autem Liberum; Tum autem Res ipsa in qua Vis inest Major, sic appellatur ut ea ipsa Res nominetur Deus.*</note> 

<margin>On the Decalogue, pages 751, 752.</margin>
**Philo** <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher</note> also represents the religion of the Pagans in this way: first deifying corporeal, inanimate things, and then bestowing those proper personal names upon them. "For some have deified the four elements: the earth, the water, the air, and the fire. Some the sun and the moon, and the planets and fixed stars; others the heaven, others the whole world. But that highest and most ancient Being—the parent of all, the ruler of the great city, the commander of the invincible army, the pilot who always governs everything for its preservation—they have concealed by bestowing false names upon those other things, each in their own way. For they call the earth 'Kore,' 'Demeter,' and 'Pluto'; and the sea 'Poseidon,' inventing sea-demons as his subordinates; and the air 'Hera,' and the fire 'Hephaestus,' and the sun 'Apollo,' and the moon 'Artemis,' etc." <note>original Greek: *ἐκτεθειώκασι γὰρ οἱ μὲν τὰς τέσσαρας ἀρχάς, γῆν, καὶ ὕδωρ, καὶ ἀέρα, καὶ πῦρ· οἱ δ᾽ ἥλιον καὶ σελήνην καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους πλανήτας, καὶ ἀπλανεῖς ἀστέρας· οἱ μὲν μόνον τὸν οὐρανόν, οἱ δὲ σύμπαντα κόσμον· τὸν δ᾽ ἀνωτάτω καὶ πρεσβύτατον, τὸν γεννητήν, τὸν ἄρχοντα τῆς μεγάλης πόλεως, τὸν στρατιάρχην τῆς ἀηττήτου στρατιᾶς, τὸν κυβερνήτην ὃς οἰκονομεῖ σωτηρίως ἀεὶ ἅπαντα, παρεκαλύψαντο, ψευδωνύμους προσηγορίας ἐκείνοις ἐπιφημίσαντες, ἑτέρας ἕτεροι· καλοῦσι γὰρ τὴν γῆν Κόρην, Δήμητρα, Πλούτωνα· τὴν δὲ θάλασσαν Ποσειδῶνα, δαίμονας ἐναλίους ὑπάρχας αὐτῷ προσαναπλάττοντες, &c. Ἥραν δὲ τὸν ἀέρα, καὶ τὸ πῦρ Ἥφαιστον, καὶ ἥλιον Ἀπόλλωνα, καὶ σελήνην Ἄρτεμιν, &c.*</note> That highest and most ancient Being, the parent of...

# CHAPTER IV. Of Nature, Personified and Deified.

...of all things, the Chief Prince of this great City, and the Emperor of this invincible Army, who governs all things beneficially <note>original: "salutiferously"</note>, Him have they covered, concealed, and obscured, by bestowing counterfeit personal names of gods upon each of these things. For the Earth they called **Proserpina**, **Pluto**, and **Ceres**; the Sea, **Neptune**, under whom they place many **demons** and **nymphs** also as his inferior ministers; the Air, **Juno**; the Fire, **Vulcan**; the Sun, **Apollo**; the Moon, **Diana**, etc. And dissecting the heavens into two hemispheres, one above the Earth and the other under it, they call these the **Dioscuri** <note>The twins Castor and Pollux</note>, feigning them to live alternately, one one day and the other another.

We do not deny here that the four elements, as well as the sun, moon, and stars, were supposed by some of the pagans to be animated with particular souls of their own (which **Ammianus Marcellinus** <note>A 4th-century Roman historian</note> seems principally to call the *Spirits of the Elements* <note>original Latin: "Spiritus Elementorum"</note>, worshipped by **Julian** <note>The Emperor Julian "the Apostate," who attempted to revive paganism</note>) and, on that account, to be so many inferior gods themselves. Notwithstanding this, it may be concluded that the inanimate parts of these elements were also deified by the pagans. This is evident because **Plato**, who in his *Cratylus* derives the name **Dionysus** from "the giving of wine" <note>original: "etymologizeth Dionyſus from Giving of Wine"</note>, and <margin>On Laws, page 783</margin> elsewhere calls the fruits of the earth "the gifts of Ceres" <note>original Greek: τὰ Δήμητρος δῶρα</note>, does himself, nevertheless, in compliance with this common speech, call wine and water—as mixed together in a glass (or cup) <margin>On Laws, Book 6.</margin> to be drunk—gods. There he affirms that a city ought to be: "tempered like a bowl, where the furious wine, being poured out, bubbles and sparkles, but being corrected by another sober god (that is, by water), both together make a good and moderate drink." <note>original Greek: δίκην κρατῆρος κεκраμένω, οὗ μαινόμενος μὲν οἶνος κεχυμένος ζεῖ, κολαζόμενος δὲ ὑπὸ νήφοντος ἑτέρου Θεοῦ, καλὴν κοινωνίαν λαβὼν, ἀγαθὸν πόμα καὶ μέτριον ἀπεργάζεται</note> **Cicero** also tells us that before the Roman admirals went to sea, they were accustomed to offer up a sacrifice to the waves. But of this, more later.

However, it is certain that mere accidents <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities or properties of a thing</note> and qualities of things in nature were commonly personified and deified by these pagans. For instance, "Time" in **Sophocles's** *Electra* is a god: "For Time is an easy god." <note>original Greek: χρόνος γὰρ εὐмаρὴς Θεός</note> And "Love" in **Plato's** *Symposium*, where it is wondered at that no poet had ever made a hymn "to Love, being such and so great a god." <note>original Greek: τῷ Ἔρωτι τηλικώτῳ ὄντι καὶ τοσώτῳ Θεῷ</note> Though the same <margin>Page 12.</margin> **Plato** in his *Philebus*, when **Protarchus** had called "Pleasure" a goddess, says: "My fear, O Protarchus, concerning the names of the gods, is extraordinarily great—beyond the greatest human fear. Therefore, as for **Venus**, I am willing to call her whatever she pleases to be called; but Pleasure, I know, is a various and multiform thing." <note>original Greek: τὸ δ' ἐμὸν δέος, ὦ Πрώταρχε, ἀεὶ πρὸς τὰ τῶν Θεῶν ὀνόματα οὐκ ἔστι κατ’ ἄνθρωπον, ἀλλὰ πέρα τοῦ μεγίστου φόβου· καὶ νῦν τὴν μὲν Ἀφροδίτην, ὅπη ἐκείνῃ φίλον, ταύτην προσαγοреύω, τὴν δ’ ἡдονὴν οἶδα ὡς ἔστι ποικίλον</note>

Therefore, it cannot be denied that the pagans did, in some sense or another, deify or theologize all the parts of the world and the things of nature. We conceive that this was done at first for no other reason than this: because they supposed God not only to permeate and pervade all things, to be diffused through all, and to act in and upon *all*, but also to be Himself, in a manner, *all* things. They expressed this by personifying the things of nature individually, and bestowing the names of gods and

<summary>This page explains how ancient pagans personified and deified physical elements (like water and fire) and abstract concepts (like time and pleasure) as a way of expressing their belief that a single God permeates all of nature.</summary>

# The Pagans Book. I.

...goddesses upon them. Only we shall here observe that this was done especially (besides the greater parts of the world) to two sorts of things: first, those in which **human utility** was most concerned. 

<margin>Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods, Book 2, page 222.</margin> 
Thus **Cicero** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), a Roman statesman and philosopher</note> writes: "Many other natures of gods have been established and named, both by the wise men of Greece and by our ancestors, for no reason other than the great benefits received from them" <note>original Latin: *Multæ aliæ Naturæ Deorum ex Magnis Beneficiis eorum, non sine causa & à Græciæ Sapientibus & à Majoribus nostris, constitutæ nominatæque sunt*</note>. The reason for this is given by him as follows: "Because they thought that whatever brought any great utility to the human race did not happen without the divine goodness toward men" <note>original Latin: *Quia quicquid magnam Utilitatem generi afferret humano, id non sine Divina Bonitate erga homines fieri arbitrabantur*</note>. Secondly, such things as were most wonderful, extraordinary, or surprising; to which 

<margin>Seneca, Letter 41.</margin> 
that passage from **Seneca** <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BCE–65 CE), a Stoic philosopher</note> seems pertinent: "We adore the rising heads and springs of great rivers. Every sudden and plentiful eruption of waters out of the hidden caverns of the earth has its altars erected to it; and some pools have been made sacred for their immense depth <note>original: "profundity"</note> and darkness" <note>original Latin: *Magnorum Fluminum Capita Veneramur. Subita & ex abdito vasti amnis eruptio Aras habet. Coluntur Aquarum Calentium Fontes; & Stagna quædam vel Opacitas vel immensa Altitudo sacravit.*</note>.

<margin>Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, Book 3, chapter 6.</margin> 
Now this is what is properly called the **physiological theology** <note>The study of the physical world and nature as a manifestation of the divine</note> of the pagans: their **personifying** and **deifying** (in a certain sense) the **things of nature**, whether they be **inanimate substances** or the **qualities** <note>original: "affections"</note> **of substances**. A great part of this physiological theology was **allegorically** contained in the **poetic fables** of the gods. **Eusebius** <note>A 4th-century Christian historian and bishop</note> indeed was of the opinion that those poetic fables were at first only **historical** and **herological** <note>The study or worship of heroes or deified humans</note>, but that afterwards some people attempted to **allegorize** them into **physiological senses** to make them seem less impious and ridiculous:

"Such was the ancient theology of the pagans (namely, historical accounts of deceased men who were worshipped as gods), which some late upstarts have altered, devising other philosophical and physiological senses for those histories of their gods, so that they might thereby render them more impressive <note>original: "specious"</note> and hide their impiety. For being neither willing to abandon those follies <note>original: "fopperies"</note> of their forefathers, nor being themselves able to bear the impiety of these fables (concerning the gods) according to their literal sense, they have attempted to cure them through physiological interpretations" <note>original Greek: τοιαύτη ἦν τὰ τῆς παλαιᾶς θεολογίας... ἐπὶ φυσικὰς διηγήσεις καὶ θεωρίας τοὺς μύθους μετεσκευάσαντο</note>. 

Neither can it be doubted that there was some mixture of herology and history in the poetic mythology; nor can it be denied that the pagans of later times, such as **Porphyry** <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> and others, did invent and devise certain new allegorical senses of their own that were never originally intended. **Origen** <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian</note>, writing before 

<margin>Origen, Against Celsus, Book 3, page 123.</margin> 
both him and Porphyry, noted this of the pagans: that when the absurdity of their fables concerning the gods was objected to and urged against them, some of them would, "apologizing for these things, take refuge in allegories" <note>original Greek: περὶ τούτων ἀπολογούμενοι ἐπ’ ἀλληγορίας καταφύγειν</note>.

<summary>This page discusses "physiological theology," the pagan practice of deifying natural phenomena and physical substances based on their usefulness to humanity or their awe-inspiring qualities. It explores the debate over whether these myths were originally historical accounts of humans (herology) that were later allegorized to hide their perceived absurdity.</summary>

### Chapter IV. Physiological Theology.

But long before the times of Christianity, those early Stoics—Zeno, Cleanthes, and Chrysippus—were famous for the great efforts they took in allegorizing these poetic fables of the gods. Regarding this, Cotta in Cicero’s writings says:

> "Zeno first, and after him Cleanthes and then Chrysippus, took on a great and quite unnecessary burden in trying to provide a rational explanation for these fabricated fables and explaining the reasons why everything was named as it was. By doing this, you surely admit that the reality is far different from common opinion; for those who are called 'gods' are actually the 'natures of things,' not physical forms of deities." <note>original Latin: "Magnam molestiam suscepit & minimè necessariam, primus Zeno, post Cleanthes, deindè Chrysippus, Commentitiarum Fabularum reddere rationem, & vocabulorum cur quidque ita appellatum sit, causas explicare. Quod cum facitis, illud profectò confitemini, longè aliter rem se habere atque hominum opinio sit; eos qui Dii appellantur, Rerum Naturas esse, non Figuras Deorum"</note>

From this it is plain that, regarding poetic theology, the Stoics took it for granted that the natures of things were personified and deified. They believed those gods were not *living animals*, nor even *philosophical* entities, but *fictitious*, and nothing more than the things of nature turned into allegory.

<margin>Book 4, page 196.</margin>
Origen also gives us a sample of Chrysippus’s method of allegorizing in his interpretation of an indecent picture or table of *Jupiter* and *Juno* in *Samos*:

> "For this solemn philosopher says in his writings that Matter, having received the 'spermatic reasons' <term>the creative principles or "seeds" of form</term> of God, contains them within itself for the beautification of the universe. For Hera (Juno) in the painting at Samos signifies Matter, and the god Zeus (Jupiter) signifies God." <note>original Greek: "λέγει γὰρ ἐν τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ συγγράμμασιν ὁ σεμνὸς φιλόσοφος, ὅτι τὰς σπερματικοὺς λόγους τοῦ θεοῦ ἡ ὕλη παραδεξαμένη, ἔχει ἐν ἑαυτῇ, εἰς κατακόσμησιν τῶν ὅλων· ὕλη γὰρ ἐν τῇ κατὰ τὴν Σάμον γραφῇ, ἡ Ἥρα, καὶ ὁ θεὸς ὁ Ζεύς"</note>

Upon this occasion, that pious Father <note>Origen, an early Christian scholar</note> adds:

> "For the sake of these, and innumerable other such fables, we will never endure calling 'the God over all' by the name of Jupiter. Instead, practicing pure piety toward the Maker of the world, we will take care not to defile divine things even with a name." <note>original Greek: "καὶ διὰ ταῦτα δὴ ἡμεῖς, καὶ διὰ τὰς τοιαύτας μύθους καὶ ἄλλας μυρίας, οὐδὲ μέχρι ὀνόματος θέλομεν Δία καλεῖν τὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεὸν, ἀλλὰ καθαρὰν εὐσέβειαν εἰς τὸν δημιουργὸν ἀσκοῦντες, οὐδὲ μέχρι ὀνόματος χραίνομεν τὰ θεῖα"</note>

And here we see again, according to Chrysippus’s interpretation, that Hera (or Juno) was not a *living* or *real god*, but only the nature of Matter personified and deified—that is, a purely fictitious and poetic god.

And we think it is unquestionably evident from Hesiod’s *Theogony* <note>A poem describing the origins and genealogies of the Greek gods</note> that many of these poetic fables, according to their original intent, were really nothing else but *physiology <term>the study of nature</term> allegorized*. Consequently, those "gods" were nothing but the natures of things personified and deified.

<margin>Page 378.</margin>
Plato himself, though no friend to these poetic fables, plainly suggests as much in his second book of *The Republic*:

> "The battles of the gods, and such other things as Homer has invented concerning them, ought not to be admitted into our commonwealth, whether they are delivered as allegories or without allegories. This is because young people are not able to judge what is an allegory and what is not." <note>original Greek: "καὶ θεομαχίας, ὅσας Ὅμηρος πεποίηκεν, οὐ παραδεκτέον εἰς τὴν πόλιν, οὔτ’ ἐν ὑπονοίαις πεποιημένας, οὔτ’ ἄνευ ὑπονοιῶν· ὁ γὰρ νέος, οὐκ οἷός τε κρίνειν ὅ, τι τε ὑπόνοια καὶ ὃ μὴ"</note>

And it appears from Dionysius of Halicarnassus <note>A Greek historian and teacher of rhetoric</note> that this was the general opinion concerning the Greek fables: that some of them...

It highlights the critique of these allegories by early Christian thinkers like Origen and the caution expressed by Plato regarding their use in education.</summary>

<page-num>512</page-num>

# This Physiological Theology, Book I.

<margin>Sallustius, *On the Gods and the World*, Book 2, page 68.</margin>
...them were *Physically*, and some *Tropologically Allegorical* <note>original: "Tropologically"—referring to a figurative or moral interpretation of scripture or myth</note>: *Let no man think me to be ignorant that some of the Greek Fables are profitable to men, partly as declaring the Works of Nature by Allegories, partly as being helpful for human life,* etc. <note>original Greek: μηδεὶς ὑπολάβοι με ἀγνοεῖν ὅτι τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν μύθων, εἰσί τινες ἀνθρώποις χρήσιμοι, οἱ μὲν ἐπιδεικνύμενοι τὰ τῆς φύσεως ἔργα δι᾿ ἀλληγορίας, οἱ δὲ παραμυθίας ἕνεκα συγκείμενοι τῶν ἀνθρωπείων συμφορῶν, &c.</note> Thus also *Cicero* writes: <margin>Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book 2, page 223.</margin> *From another line of reasoning, and indeed a physical one, a great multitude of gods has emerged who, dressed in human form, provided the poets with stories, but filled the lives of men with every kind of superstition.* <note>original Latin: "Alia quoque ex ratione, & quidem Physicâ, magna fluxit Multitudo Deorum qui induti specie humanâ, Fabulas Poetis suppeditaverunt, hominum autem vitam Superstitione omni refercerunt."</note>

*Eusebius* <note>An early Christian historian and bishop</note> indeed, seems sometimes to cast it as an accusation against the whole of Pagan Theology that it did *deify inanimate nature* <note>original Greek: θειάζειν τὴν ἄψυχον οὐσίαν</note>; but this is properly to be understood of this part of their theology only, which was *Physiological* <note>meaning the study of nature or physics</note>, and of their *Mythology* or the *Poetic Fables of the Gods Allegorized*. Otherwise, such an accusation is apparently false, and would be the same as calling them outright Atheists. For he that acknowledges no *living God* <note>original: "Animant God"</note>, as has been declared, acknowledges no God at all, according to the true notion of Him; whether he derives all things from a fortuitous *motion of matter*, as *Epicurus* and *Democritus* did, or from a *plastic* <note>forming or creative</note> and orderly but senseless Nature, as some degenerate *Stoics* and *Strato* the Peripatetic did. This form of atheism seems to be described by *Manilius*:

> *Either the Earth knows no Father, nor do Flame, Air,*
> *Or Water; but they make a God out of the four elements,*
> *And have built the globe of the world, and forbid*
> *Anything to be sought beyond themselves.*
> <note>original Latin: "Aut neque Terra Patrem novit, nec Flamma, nec Aer, / Aut Humor, faciuntque Deum per quatuor artus, / Et Mundi struxere Globum, prohibentque requiri / Ultra se quidquam."</note>

Neither should this *Physiological Theology* of the Pagans—which consisted only in *personifying* and *deifying inanimate substances* and the natures of things—be confused (as it has been by some recent writers) with that *Philosophical Theology* of *Scævola*, *Varro*, and others. That philosophical version was also called *Natural*, but in another sense: as *True* and *Real*. Physiological theology was, in fact, merely a part of the *Poetical* theology first, and afterward of the *Political* theology; it owed its origin largely to the fancies of *poets*, whose habit it was to constantly *personify things and natural forces*.

But the *Philosophical Theology* properly so called, which according to *Varro* was that *about which the philosophers have left many books* <note>original Latin: "de qua multos libros Philosophi reliquerunt"</note>, admitted only *Living Gods* <note>original: "Animal Gods"</note> that actually existed in Nature (which is why they were called *Natural*). These included one Supreme *Universal Numen* <note>original: "Numen"—a Latin term for a deity or divine presence</note>, a Perfect Soul or Mind comprehending all things, and his *ministering powers* <note>original Greek: ὑπουργοὶ δυνάμεις</note>—other inferior intelligent beings who were his ministers created by him, such as stars and demons. In this hidden, "arcane" theology, all those personified gods or "deified natures" were interpreted in a way that agreed with this belief in a single supreme mind.

*St. Augustine* <note>original: "St. Austin"</note> often notices that the Pagans mingled and, as it were, incorporated *physiology* with their theology, and he justly condemns the practice. As he writes in his 49th Epistle: *The impious do not excuse their sacrilegious rites and idols by elegantly interpreting what each one signifies. For all that interpretation refers to the creature, not to the Creator, to whom alone the service of religion is due...* <note>original Latin: "Neque illinc excusant impii, sua Sacrilega Sacra & Simulachra, quòd eleganter interpretantur quid quæque significent: Omnis quippe illa Interpretatio ad Creaturam refertur, non ad Creatorem, cui uni debetur Servitus Religionis..."</note>

<summary>This page distinguishes between "Physiological Theology," which treats gods as allegorical personifications of nature, and "Philosophical Theology," which recognizes a supreme intelligent Mind and his subordinate spirits.</summary>
<keywords>Physiological Theology, Philosophical Theology, Allegory, Cicero, Varro, St. Augustine, Numen, personification of nature, Stoicism, Atheism</keywords>

It draws on Augustine, Cicero, Plato, and Aristotle to show that even the Pagans distinguished between literal objects (like corn or wine) and the actual divine beings they believed governed them.</meta>

# Chapter 4: Not Varro’s Natural Theology

...by that name is called *Latria* in Greek <note>original: "no nomine Latria Graecè appellatur"</note>. Neither do the Pagans sufficiently excuse their sacrilegious rites and images by this argument: because they elegantly (and ingeniously) interpret what each of those things signifies. For this interpretation is referred to the creature, and not to the Creator, to whom alone belongs religious worship—that which by the Greeks is called *Latria*.

And again, in his book *The City of God* (Book 6, Chapter 8): "For they claim that those things have certain physical interpretations (as they say), that is, interpretations based on natural reasons <note>original: "Atenim habent ista Physiologicas quasdam (sicut aiunt) id est, Naturalium Rationum Interpretationes"</note>. As if in this dispute we were seeking for physics and not theology—that is, the explanation of nature and not of God <note>original: "Quasi verò nos in hac Disputatione Physiologiam quaeramus, & non Theologiam; id est, Rationem Naturae, & non Dei"</note>. For although He who is the true God is God not by opinion but by nature, yet not every nature is God <note>original: "Quamvis enim qui verus Deus est, non Opinione sed Natura sit Deus; non tamen omnis Natura Deus est."</note>."

But the Pagans pretend that these things have certain <term>Physiological</term> <note>original: "Physiological"—in this historical context, this refers to "Physics" or the "study of nature," rather than the modern biological definition</note> interpretations, or are according to natural reasons. It is as if in this discussion we sought for physics and not theology—the reason of nature and not of God. For although the true God is God not only in opinion but by His very nature, yet not every part of nature is God. But certainly the first and chief ground of this practice of theirs—to "theologize" physics and deify (in one sense or another) all the things of nature—was no other than what has been already suggested: their supposition that God is not only diffused throughout the whole world and in all things, but also, in a manner, is all things. Therefore, they believed He ought to be worshipped in all the things of nature and parts of the world.

<margin>Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book 3, page 345.</margin>
Therefore, these personified gods of the Pagans—or those things of nature deified by them and called gods and goddesses—were, for all that, by no means accounted by the intelligent among them as true and proper gods. Thus Cotta says in Cicero: "When we call grain *Ceres* and wine *Liber* [Bacchus] <note>original: "Cum Fruges Cererem, Vinum Liberum dicimus"</note>, we are using a common and familiar figure of speech. But do you think anyone is so mad as to believe that the thing he eats is actually a god?"

The Pagans really accounted as a god only that being from whom they might reasonably expect benefit by worshipping and invoking them. Therefore, nothing was truly and properly a god to them but what was both substantial and also living and intellectual. <margin>Plato, *Laws*, Book 10.</margin> For Plato writes that the atheistic wits of his time concluded the sun, moon, and stars were not gods because they were nothing but earth and stones (or a certain fiery matter) devoid of all understanding and sense. For this reason, they were "unable to take notice of any human affairs" <note>original Greek: οὐδὲν τῶν ἀνθρωπείων πραγμάτων φροντίζειν δυνάμενα</note>.

And Aristotle affirms concerning the gods in general "that all men have supposed them to live, and consequently to act" <note>original Greek: ζῆν τε πάντες ὑπειλήφασιν αὐτοὺς, καὶ ἐνεργεῖν ἄρα</note>, etc., since they cannot be supposed to sleep perpetually as Endymion <note>A figure in Greek myth granted eternal sleep</note> did. The Pagans universally conceived the gods to be <term>Happy Animals</term> <note>In ancient philosophy, "animal" simply meant a "living being" (a creature with a soul), and gods were considered the most blessed of these</note>; and Aristotle concludes that the happiness of them all consists in contemplation. Even Lucretius himself would not forbid men from using the language then commonly accepted among the Pagans—calling the sea *Neptune*, grain *Ceres*, wine *Bacchus*, and the earth the *Mother of the Gods*—provided that they did not think any of these, for all that, to be truly and really gods.

<summary>This page argues that ancient Pagans did not literally worship inanimate objects like corn or wine as gods, but used them as symbols for divine forces; true divinity required a being to be living, intellectual, and capable of action.</summary>
