# Nothing Inanimate is Really a God: Book I

<margin>
Book 2, page 165. Lambinus edition.
</margin>

> If anyone decides to call the sea Neptune, and grain Ceres, and prefers to misuse the name of Bacchus rather than use the proper name of the wine: let us grant him to declare that the globe of the Earth is the Mother of the Gods, provided that in reality it is not so. <note>original Latin: "Hic siquis Mare Neptunum, Cereremque vocare Constituit fruges, & Bacchi nomine abuti Mavolt, quam Laticis proprium proferre vocamen: Concedamus ut hic, Terrarum dictitet Orbem Esse Deum Matrem, dum non sit re tamen apse." From the Roman poet Lucretius.</note>

And the reason why the Earth was not really a Goddess is given by him thus:

-> *For indeed, the Earth at all times lacks all sense.* <note>original Latin: "Terra quidem vero caret omni tempore Sensu."</note> <-

<margin>
Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book 2, page 220.
</margin>

Because it is constantly devoid of all manner of sense. Thus Balbus, in the works of Cicero, tells us that the first thing included in the notion or **Idea** of a God is this: *That it be a living being <term>Animant</term> <note>original: "Animans"—meaning a being endowed with life, breath, or soul</note>; or endowed with Life, Sense, and Understanding.* And he, conceiving the **Stars** to be undoubtedly such, therefore concludes them to be Gods. *Because the Ether is most subtle, and in continual agitation and vigor, it is necessary that the living creature <note>original: "Animal"</note> which is born in it must also possess the sharpest sense. Therefore, since the Stars are born in the Ether, it is reasonable to think them to have Sense and Understanding; from which it follows that the Stars ought to be counted among the number of Gods.* <note>original Latin: "Quoniam tenuissimus est Æther, & semper agitatur & viget, necesse est, quod Animal in eo gignatur, idem quoque Sensu acerrimo esse. Quare cum in Æthere Astra gignantur, consentaneum est in iis Sensum inesse & Intelligentiam. Ex quo efficitur in Deorum numero Astra esse ducenda."</note> And Cotta, in the <margin>Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, page 241.</margin> Third Book, affirms that all men were so far from thinking the Stars to be Gods, that *many would not even admit them to be living beings <note>original: "Animantes"</note>:* plainly intimating that unless they were animated with life, they could not possibly be Gods.

<margin>
Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*, page 377.
</margin>

Lastly, Plutarch for this very reason absolutely condemns that whole practice of giving the names of Gods and Goddesses to inanimate things as absurd, impious, and atheistical. He writes that *they who give the names of Gods to senseless and inanimate natures and things—and such as are necessarily destroyed by men who need and use them—produce most wicked and atheistical opinions in the minds of men. For it cannot be conceived how these things themselves should be gods; for nothing that is inanimate is a god to men.* <note>original Greek: "ἀφύας κὶ ἀθέας ἐμποιεῖσι δόξας, ἀναισθήτοις, κὶ ἀψύχοις, κὶ φθειρομέναις ἀναγκαίως ὑπ’ ἀνθρώπων δεομένων κὶ χρωμένων φύσεσι κὶ πράγμασιν ὀνόματα Θεῶν ἐπιφέροντες· ταῦτα μὲν γὰρ αὐτὰ νοῆσαι θεὸς οὐκ ἔστιν· οὐ γὰρ οὖν οὐδὲ ἄψυχον ἀνθρώποις ὁ Θεός."</note> And now we have very good reason to conclude that the distinction or division of Pagan Gods (used by some) into **Living** <note>original: "Animal"</note> and **Natural** (by "Natural" meaning inanimate) is utterly to be rejected if we speak of their true and proper Gods; since nothing was a god to the Pagans except what had Life, Sense, and Understanding. Therefore, those **Personified Gods** that were nothing but the natures of things deified as such, were only **Counterfeit and Fictitious Gods** <note>original Latin: "Dii Commentitii & Fictitii"</note>; or as Origen calls them in that place cited before, *the fictions of the Greeks (and other Pagans) that were merely things turned into persons and deified.* <note>original Greek: "τὰ Ἑλλήνων ἀναπλάσματα, σωματοποιεῖσθαι δοκοῦντα ἀπὸ τῶν πραγμάτων."</note> Neither...

<summary>This page argues that ancient Pagans required their "Gods" to be living, sentient beings. Using Lucretius, Cicero, and Plutarch, the author shows that treating inanimate objects as gods was considered a poetic metaphor or a dangerous error rather than true theology.</summary>
<keywords>Paganism, Deification, Lucretius, Cicero, Plutarch, Origen, Animism, Polytheism, Natural Theology, Philosophy of Religion</keywords>

# CHAPTER IV. A God to the Pagans.

Can there be any other defense made for these *Personified* and *Deified Things of Nature* than this: that they were all really many *distinct names of one supreme God*, or *partial considerations* of him, according to the *various manifestations of himself in his works*? Thus, according to the old *Egyptian Theology* previously explained, God is said to have both *no name* and *every name*. As it is expressed in the *Asclepian Dialogue*:

> "Since he cannot be fully declared by any one name, however many names it is composed of, he is instead to be called by every name, for he is both One and All Things. Therefore, either everything must be called by his name, or he must be called by the name of everything." <note>original Latin: "Cum non possit Unus quamvis è Multis composito Nomine nuncupari, potius Omni Nomine vocandus est, siquidem sit Unus & Omnia; ut necesse sit, aut Omnia Ipsius Nomine, aut Ipsum Omnium Nomine nuncupari."</note>

Seneca also seems to fully agree with this *Egyptian doctrine* when he gives this description of God: "He to whom every name belongs." <note>original Latin: "Cui Nomen Omne convenit."</note> He further declares concerning him: "You may give him whatever names you please," and, "There may be as many names for him as there are gifts and effects of his." <note>original Latin: "Quæcunque voles illi Nomina aptabis" and "Tot Appellationes ejus possunt esse, quot Munera."</note> Finally, Seneca makes God and Nature to be really *one and the same thing*, and states that *everything we see is God*. The writer of the treatise *On the World* <term>De Mundo</term> <note>A work formerly attributed to Aristotle, now thought to be by a later author.</note> is likewise consistent with this when he affirms that God "may be named after every nature, because he is the cause of all things." <note>original Greek: πάσης ἐπώνυμος φύσεως ἅτε πάντων αὐτὸς αἴτιος ὤν.</note> We say, therefore, that when the Pagans engaged in this *theologizing of physics* <note>original: "Theologizing of Physiology." At this time, "physiology" referred to the study of natural philosophy or the laws of nature.</note> and *deifying the things of nature* and *parts of the world*, they accordingly *called everything by the name of God*, or *God by the name of everything*.

<margin>Julian, *Oration 4*</margin>
<margin>Page 286</margin>

Therefore, these *personified* and *deified things of nature* were not themselves *properly* and *directly* worshipped by intelligent Pagans (who acknowledged *no inanimate thing as a God*) in a way that their worship ended with the objects themselves. Instead, they were worshipped either *relatively* to the Supreme God, or at most in a way of *association* with him, as his *effects* and *images*. Thus, it was not so much the things themselves that were worshipped, but God who was worshipped in them. For these Pagans professed that they did "look upon the heaven (and the world) not casually, nor like grazing cattle," <note>original Greek: τὸν οὐρανὸν μὴ παρέργως, μηδὲ ὥσπερ τὰ βοσκήματα θεωρεῖν.</note> who take notice of nothing but those sensible appearances <term>Phantasms</term> that force themselves upon their senses. Or, as the same Emperor Julian more fully expresses it in that same oration, they did "not view and contemplate the heaven and world with the same eyes that oxen and horses do, or any of the irrational and ignorant animals; but from that which is visible to their outward senses, they sought to investigate the invisible nature under it." <note>original Greek: τὸν οὐρανὸν οὐχ ὥσπερ ἵππους καὶ βόας ὁρᾷν, ἤ τι τῶν ἀλόγων καὶ ἀμαθῶν ζώων· ἀλλὰ ἐξ αὐτοῦ τοῦ φανεροῦ τὴν ἀφανῆ πολυπραγμονεῖν φύσιν.</note> That is, they professed to behold all things with *religious eyes*, and to *see God in everything*, not only as *pervading all things* and *diffused through all things*, but also as *being, in a sense, all things*. Therefore, they looked upon the whole world as a *sacred thing* that possessed a kind of *divinity* within it; it being, according to their theology—

<summary>This page explains that Pagans did not worship inanimate objects as gods themselves, but rather as various names or manifestations of the one Supreme God who is present in all of nature. The author uses Egyptian, Stoic (Seneca), and Neoplatonic (Julian) sources to argue that for the "intelligent" Pagan, nature was a visible image of an invisible divine reality.</summary>

# The Pagan Theologians approving, BOOK I.

theology, nothing but *God himself Visibly Displayed*. And thus was God worshipped by the *Pagans* in the whole *Corporeal World* taken all at once together, or in the *Universe*, under the *Name of Pan* <note>The Greek god of nature, often interpreted by philosophers as a symbol for the "All" (Pan meaning "all" in Greek).</note>. They also commonly conceived of *Zeus* and *Jupiter* in the same manner. That is, they did not think of him *abstractly* only (as we usually conceive of *God* today) but *concretely*, together with everything that proceeds and emanates from him—the *Whole World*. 

As it was previously noted that an old *Egyptian monument* described God as *all that was, is, and shall be*, so it was also observed from *Plutarch* that the *Egyptians* took the *First God* and the *Universe* for *one and the same thing*. They did this not only because they supposed the *Supreme God* to contain all things within himself *virtually*, but also because they were accustomed to conceive of him together with his outflowing and the full extent of his *fecundity*—the whole world displayed from him all at once as one entire thing. Similarly, the Pagans in *Plato* conflate <note>original: "confound"</note> 
<margin>De Leg. l 7. p. 821.</margin> 
"the greatest god" <note>original Greek: *τὸν μέγιστον θεὸν*</note> and "the whole world together" <note>original Greek: *ὅλον τὸν κόσμον*</note> as being one and the same thing. This notion was so familiar
<margin>L. 16. p. 761.</margin>
with these Pagans that *Strabo* himself, writing about *Moses*, could not conceive of his God (and the God of the *Jews*) in any other way than this: "that which contains us all, and the earth, and the sea, which we call the heaven and world, and the nature of the whole" <note>original Greek: *τὸ περιέχον ἡμᾶς ἅπαντας, καὶ γῆν, καὶ θάλασσαν, ὃ καλοῦμεν οὐρανὸν καὶ κόσμον, καὶ τὴν τῶν ὅλων φύσιν*</note>. 

By this, however, *Strabo* did not mean an inanimate heaven or world, or a mindless nature, but an *intelligent being* who framed the entire world and contained it, and was conceived of together with it. Because of this, he tells us that according to *Moses*, no wise person would attempt to make any *image* or *picture* resembling anything found among us. From this we conclude that when *Strabo* writes of the *Persians* and claims they "take the heaven for Jupiter" <note>original Greek: *τὸν οὐρανὸν ἡγεῖσθαι Δία*</note>, and when *Herodotus* before him says they "call the whole circle of the heaven Jupiter" <note>original Greek: *κύκλον πάντα τοῦ οὐρανοῦ Δία καλεῖν*</note> (that is, the *Supreme God*), neither of them meant that the inanimate body of the heavens was their *highest god*. Rather, although he was an *intelligent nature*, because he framed the whole heaven or world and contained it, he was conceived of together with it. 

Moreover, God was also worshipped by the Pagans in the *various parts* of the world under *various names*. For example, he was worshipped in the higher and lower *ether* <note>term: ether: In ancient physics, the rare, pure substance of the upper atmosphere believed to be the home of the gods.</note> under the names of *Minerva* and *Jupiter*; in the *air* under the name of *Juno*; in the *fire* under the name of *Vulcan*; and in the *sea* under the name of *Neptune*, etc. It cannot be reasonably doubted that when Roman sea-captains sacrificed to the *waves*, they intended to worship that God *who acts in the waves, and whose wonders are in the deep.*

Beyond this, the Pagans seemed to feel a kind of necessity for worshipping God in this way—through his works and in the visible things of this world—because the common people <note>original: "the generality of the Vulgar"</note> were then unable to form any notion or conception at all of an *invisible deity*. Therefore, unless they were kept in a religious path by such a worship...

### CHAPTER IV. On Worshipping God through His Works.

...worship of God that was accommodated and suitable to their low level of understanding would unavoidably lead to *Atheism*. Indeed, even the most *philosophical minds* among them, admitting that God was *incomprehensible* to them, seemed to feel the need for some *tangible supports* <note>original: "Sensible Props"</note> to lean upon. This very explanation is given by the *Pagans* regarding their practices in *Eusebius*: <margin>*Preparation for the Gospel, Book 3, Chapter 13.*</margin> "That God being incorporeally and invisibly present in all things, and pervading or passing through all things, it was reasonable that men should worship him by and through those things that are visible and manifest." <note>original Greek: ἀσωμάτως καὶ ἀφανῶς ἐν πᾶσιν ὄντα θεὸν, καὶ διὰ πάντων διήκοντα, καὶ τοῦτον εἰκότως διὰ τῶν δηλωμένων σέβειν φάσιν</note> 

Plato likewise represents this as the common opinion of the Pagans in his time: <margin>*Laws, Book 7, page 821.*</margin> "that as for the Greatest God, and the Whole World, men should not busily and curiously search after the knowledge of it, nor officiously <note>original: "pragmatically"</note> inquire into the causes of things, it being not pious for them so to do." <note>original Greek: τὸν μέγιστον θεὸν καὶ ὅλον τὸν κόσμον φαμὲν οὔτε ζητεῖν δεῖν, οὔτε πολυπραγμονεῖν, τὰς αἰτίας ἐρευνῶντας· οὐ γὰρ οὐδ’ ὅσιον εἶναι</note> The meaning of this seems to be nothing other than that men ought to content themselves with worshipping God through his works and in this visible world, rather than troubling themselves with further curious speculations concerning the nature of that which is *incomprehensible* to them. Although Plato expresses his dislike for this view, he himself elsewhere plainly allows for worshipping the *First Invisible God* in those *visible images* that he has made of himself: the Sun, Moon, and Stars. 

Maximus Tyrius does indeed exhort men to ascend, in the contemplation of God, above all corporeal <term>corporeal: physical or bodily</term> things: <margin>*Dissertations, 1.*</margin> "The end of your journey," he says, "is not the heaven, nor those shining bodies in the heaven. For though those are beautiful and divine, and the genuine offspring of that Supreme Deity, framed in the best manner, you ought to transcend all of these and lift your head far above the starry heavens, to the place of truth." <note>original Greek: τέλος τῆς ὁδοῦ οὐχ ὁ οὐρανὸς... ἐπὶ τὸν ἀληθῆ τόπον, &c.</note> 

Nevertheless, he closes his discourse in this way: "But if you are too weak and unable to contemplate that Father and Maker of all things, it will be sufficient for you for the present to behold his works and to worship his progeny or offspring, which is various and manifold. For there are not only—according to the Boeotian poet <note>The "Boeotian poet" is Hesiod, who in his work *Works and Days* wrote that there are 30,000 immortal guardians of men.</note>—thirty thousand gods who are all the sons and friends of the Supreme God, but an inconceivable number. Such in the heaven are the natures of the stars, and in the ether, the demons, and so on." <note>original Greek: εἰ δὲ ἐξασθενεῖς πρὸς τὴν τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ δημιουργοῦ θέαν... τοῦτο μὲν κατ’ οὐρανὸν αἱ ἀστέρων φύσεις, &c.</note> 

Lastly, Socrates himself not only allowed this way of worshipping God (because he himself is invisible) in his works that are visible, but also recommended the same to *Euthydemus*: <margin>*Xenophon, Memorabilia, Book 4.*</margin> "You shall know that I speak the truth if you do not wait until you see the physical forms of the gods themselves, but instead consider it enough to worship and honor the gods by observing their works." <note>original Greek: ὅτι δέ γε ἀληθῆ λέγω, καὶ σὺ γνώσῃ ἂν μὴ ἀναμένῃς ἕως ἂν τὰς μορφὰς τῶν θεῶν ἴδῃς, ἀλλ’ ἐξαρκῇ σοι τὰ ἔργα αὐτῶν ὁρῶντι σέβεσθαι καὶ τιμᾶν τοὺς θεούς</note> This he afterward...

<meta>This page continues the argument that Pagan worship of the natural world was intended as a way to honor the Supreme Deity through his visible creations, moving now into the personification of abstract qualities.</meta>

<margin>P. 236, 237.</margin> This particularly applies to the Supreme God, who made and contains the whole world. Because he is invisible, he has made himself visible through his works, and consequently was to be worshipped and adored in them. Whether Socrates, Plato, and their genuine followers would extend this any further than to the *living parts* <note>original: "Animated Parts"</note> of the world—such as the sun, moon, and stars—we cannot determine for certain. 

However, we think it very probable that many of those Pagans who are accused of worshipping *inanimate things*, and particularly the elements (earth, air, fire, and water), did nevertheless direct their worship to the spirits of those elements. As the historian Ammianus Marcellinus tells us the Emperor Julian did, they worshipped primarily the souls of these elements. Many of these Pagans supposed all elements to be *alive* (as was previously observed regarding the philosopher Proclus), and partly they worshipped those demons which they believed lived in and presided over parts of them. For this reason, it was said by Plato and other ancient writers that "all things are full of gods and demons." <note>original Greek: πάντα θεῶν πλήρη</note>

XXXIII. But it further appears that these *physical gods*—that is, the *things of nature personified and deified*—were not considered by the Pagans to be *true and proper gods*, much less *independent* and *self-existent* ones. This is because they did not only personify and deify substantial things and inanimate bodies, but also mere *accidents and qualities* <note>original: "Accidents, and Affections"</note> of substances. 

For example, they first deified the *passions of the mind*. St. Gregory Nazianzen says, "They considered the passions of the mind to be gods, or at least worshipped them as gods" <note>original Greek: τὰ πάθη θεὸς ἐνόμισαν, ἢ θεὸς ἐτίμησαν</note>; that is, they built temples or altars in their names. Thus, *Hope* was not only a goddess to the poet Theognis:

-> "Hope is the only good goddess remaining among men; <-
-> the others have all left for Olympus." <-
<note>original Greek: Ἔλπις ἐν ἀνθρώποισι μόνη θεὸς ἐσθλὴ ἔνεσιν, Ἄλλοι δ᾽ Ὄλυμπονδ᾽ ἐκπρολιπόντες ἔβαν.</note>

(Here he fancifully depicts her as the *only deity left to humanity*, as if the other gods had all forsaken their heavenly mansions and the world). But Hope also had real temples dedicated to her at Rome, such as the one consecrated by Attillius in the *Forum Olitorium* (the vegetable market), and others elsewhere. In these temples, she was commonly depicted or imagined as a *woman* covered in a *green cloak* <note>original: "pall"</note> and holding a *cup in her hand*. 

In the same way, *Love* and *Desire* were gods or goddesses too, as were *Care, Memory, Opinion, Truth, Virtue, Piety, Faith, Justice, Clemency, Concord, Victory, and so on*. This *Victory*, along with *Virtue*, was listed among the gods by the playwright Plautus in the prologue of his play *Amphitruo*. Not only that, but an altar was erected to her near the entrance of the Senate House at Rome. After it was once demolished, the statesman Symmachus earnestly tried to restore it during the reign of Emperor Theodosius. Among other things, he wrote concerning it: "Let no man deny that she should be worshipped, whom he admits is desirable." <note>original Latin: Nemo Colendam neget, quam profitetur Optandam</note> 

Besides all these, *Echo* was a goddess to these Pagans as well, and so was *Night* (to whom they sacrificed a cock), and *Sleep*, and *Death* itself, and many more such *qualities of things*...

# CHAPTER IV. *And Deified by the Pagans.*

Vossius <note>Gerardus Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch scholar who wrote *De Theologia Gentili* (On Gentile Theology), a massive study of pagan religions.</note> has collected the largest catalog of these things in the eighth book of his *On Gentile Theology*. This practice of personifying and deifying <term>accidental things</term> <note>original: "Accidental Things"; in philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities or properties of a thing, like its color or a temporary emotion, as opposed to its core substance.</note> was so common among these pagans that, as St. Chrysostom observed, St. Paul was said by some of the common people of Athens to be a proclaimer of "strange gods" when he preached to them about Jesus and the *Resurrection* (Acts 17:18). This was because they supposed him not only to have made Jesus a god, but also *Anastasis* (the Greek word for Resurrection) into a goddess as well. Indeed, this habit of turning the things of nature into theology drove these pagans so far as to deify "evil things" as well—that is, things that are both harmful and immoral.

<margin>Pliny, *Natural History*, Book 2, chapter 7.</margin>
Regarding the former, Pliny wrote: "The underworld is also divided into classes, and diseases and many plagues are numbered among the gods, because in our trembling fear we desire to have these pacified. Therefore, a temple was publicly dedicated to Fever on the Palatine Hill, just as altars were erected elsewhere to Orbona <note>The goddess of orphans or parents who had lost children.</note> and to Evil Fortune." <note>original Latin: *Inferi quoque in genera describuntur, Morbique, & multæ etiam Pestes, dum esse placatas trepido metu cupimus. Ideoque etiam publicè Febri Fanum in Palatio dedicatum est, Orbonæ ad ædem Larium, & Malæ Fortunæ Exquiliis.*</note>

<margin>Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book 2.</margin>
Regarding the latter, Balbus says in the works of Cicero: "From this same practice, the names of Lust, Pleasure, and Wanton Desire <note>original: "Lubentinæ Veneris"; referring to Venus as the goddess of sexual pleasure.</note> were consecrated—things that are vicious and unnatural, yet consecrated and deified." <note>original Latin: *Quo ex genere Cupidinis & Voluptatis, & Lubentinæ Veneris, Vocabula Consecrata sunt, Vitiosarum rerum & non Naturalium.*</note> Cicero, in his book *On Laws*, informs us that in Athens there were even temples dedicated to Insolence <note>original: "Contumely"</note> and Impudence. However, he also provides this criticism of such practices:

<margin>Gruter's Edition is slightly different.</margin>
"All things of this kind are to be detested and rejected," <note>original Latin: *Quæ omnia ejusmodi detestanda & repudianda sunt*</note> and nothing should be deified except what is virtuous or good. Despite this, it is certain that such evil things were consecrated for no other reason than that they might be prayed against to be turned away. Furthermore, just as these things of nature were sometimes deified by the pagans plainly and openly under their own common names, this was also sometimes done in disguise under other "proper" names. For example, *Pleasure* was deified under the names of Volupia and *Lubentina Venus*; *Time* (according to the opinion of some) under the name of Cronos or Saturn, which, as it produces all things, also devours all things back into itself; and *Prudence* or *Wisdom* was deified under the names of Athena or Minerva.

<margin>Origen, *Against Celsus*, Book 8, page 421.</margin>
For it is plain that Origen understood it this way. When Celsus not only approved of worshipping God Almighty in the sun and in Minerva as something lawful, but also commended it as a highly pious act, Origen replied: "We speak well of the sun as a beautiful work of God... but as for that Athena or Minerva, whom Celsus here joins with the sun, this is a thing fabulously devised by the Greeks (whether according to some mystical, secret, and allegorical sense, or without it) when they say that she was born out of Jupiter’s brain fully armed." <note>original Greek: Εὐφημεῖσθαι ἥλιον ὡς καλὸν Θεοῦ δημιούργημα... Ἀθηνᾶν μέντοι μετὰ ἡλίου τασσομένην, ἐμυθοποίησαν οἱ Ἑλλήνων λόγοι, εἴτ᾽ ἐν ὑπονοίαις, εἴτε χωρὶς ὑπονοιῶν, φάσκοντες ἐκ τῆς τοῦ Διὸς γεγενῆσθαι κεφαλῆς, καθωπλισμένην.</note> And again later: "If it is granted that by Athena or Minerva, prudence is meant figuratively..." <note>original Greek: ἵνα ᾗ καὶ τροπολογῆται καὶ λέγεται φρόνησις εἶναι ἡ Ἀθηνᾶ.</note> Therefore, not only according to the poets, but also—

# 520 Those Natures of Things Deified, BOOK I.

<margin>L. 2.</margin>
According to the political and civil theology of the pagans, these <term>accidental things of nature</term> <note>original: "Accidental Things of Nature"; in philosophy, these are qualities or properties (like "bravery" or "intelligence") that belong to a person but are not independent substances in themselves.</note> and the qualities of physical substances were personified and turned into various gods and goddesses. Cicero himself, in his book *On Laws*, approved of such political gods: "It is well that Mind, Piety, Virtue, and Faith are consecrated by human hands; temples have been publicly dedicated to all of these in Rome, so that those who possess them (as all good men do) may believe they have the gods themselves placed within their own minds." <note>original Latin: *Bene verò quod Mens, Pietas, Virtus, Fides, consecratur manu: quarum omnium Romæ dedicata publicè Templa sunt, ut illa qui habeant (habent autem omnes boni) Deos ipsos in animis suis collocatos putent.*</note> He even established a law for them in his own ideal commonwealth, but with a cautionary provision that no evil or vicious things be consecrated among them: "But let those things through which a man is granted ascent to heaven—Mind, Virtue, Piety, and Faith—have shrines or temples dedicated to them. However, let no religious ceremonies be performed for vices." <note>original Latin: *Ast olla, propter quæ datur homini adscensus in Cœlum, Mentem, Virtutem, Pietatem, Fidem, earumque laudum delubra sunto. Nec ulla vitiorum Solemnia obeunto.*</note>

<margin>P. 422.</margin>
<margin>P. 285.</margin>
Despite all this, according to the theology of the pagans which was called "Natural" by Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a Roman scholar who divided theology into three parts: mythical, physical (natural), and civil.</note> (meaning not just the study of nature, but that which is true and real) and "Philosophical" by Scævola—and which is opposed by both of them to "Poetical and Fabulous" and "Political and Civil" theology—I say, according to this higher theology of theirs, these deified accidental things of nature could by no means be recognized as true and proper gods. This is because they were so far from having any life or consciousness in them that they did not even have <term>substantial essence</term> <note>original Greek: ὑπόστασιν καὶ οὐσίαν (*hypostasin kai ousian*); a technical term for real, independent existence or being.</note> of their own.

Thus Origen <note>A prominent early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD).</note> disputes against the godship of Minerva when she is <term>tropologically</term> <note>original: "Tropologically"; interpreted as a metaphor or a moral allegory rather than a literal being.</note> interpreted as Prudence: "If Athena or Minerva is interpreted metaphorically and said to be Prudence, let the pagans show what substantial essence it has, or that it really exists according to this metaphorical interpretation." <note>original Greek: ἵνα ἢ καὶ τροπολογῆται καὶ λέγηται φρόνησις εἶναι ἡ Ἀθηνᾶ, παραστησάτω τις αὐτῆς τὴν ὑπόστασιν καὶ τὴν οὐσίαν, ὡς ὑφεστηκυίας κατὰ τὴν τροπολογίαν ταύτην.</note> This is exactly the same as if he had said, "Let the pagans show how this can be a god or goddess when it has no substantial essence and does not exist by itself, but is merely a quality belonging to other substances." 

Origen argues the same point regarding other such "gods" of theirs, such as Memory (the mother of the Muses) and the naked Graces. In his first book, where Celsus argued for a multitude of gods against the Jews, Origen countered that these things, having no substantial essence or independent existence, could not possibly be considered gods. Therefore, they were nothing more than "mere figments of the Greeks; things made to have human bodies, and thus personified and deified." <note>original Greek: Ἑλλήνων ἀναπλάσματα σωματοποιηθέντα ἀπὸ τῶν πραγμάτων.</note> We believe there cannot be a truer commentary upon this passage by Origen than the following verses by Prudentius <note>A Roman Christian poet (c. 348–413 AD) who wrote against the pagan senator Symmachus.</note> in his second book against Symmachus:

# 521 Chapter 4. The Many Names of God.

->*Stop, if you have any shame, you pagan foolishness, at last,*<-
->*Representing incorporeal things with counterfeit human limbs.*<-
<note>original Latin: "Desine, si pudor est, Gentilis ineptia, tandem / Res Incorporeas, Simulatis Fingere membris." This is a quote from the Christian poet Prudentius, criticizing the practice of depicting abstract ideas as human-like gods.</note>

Let the pagans be at last ashamed, if they have any shame in them, of this folly of theirs: describing and representing *incorporeal things* with *counterfeit human members*. In this context, the *accidents* <note>original: "Accidents"; in classical philosophy, these are properties or qualities of a thing (like being healthy or victorious) that are not the thing's essential nature.</note> and *affections* of things—such as *Victory* was (whose altar Symmachus <note>Quintus Aurelius Symmachus (c. 340–402 AD) was a Roman statesman who famously petitioned for the restoration of the Altar of Victory in the Senate House.</note> argued to restore)—are called *incorporeal things* by Prudentius. This matches the conclusion of the Greek philosophers, who held that *qualities* (ποιότητες <note>original: ποιότητες (poiotētes)</note>) were *incorporeal* (ἀσώματοι <note>original: ἀσώματοι (asōmatoi)</note>). 

It is not even possible that the pagans themselves were unaware of this. <margin>On the Nature of the Gods, Book 3.</margin> Accordingly, we find that Cotta, in the writings of Cicero, utterly banishes and rejects these "gods" from philosophical and true theology for this very reason: "Do you think, then, that there is any need for a more subtle argument to refute these things? For we see that *Mind*, *Faith*, *Hope*, *Virtue*, *Honor*, *Victory*, *Health*, *Concord*, and the like, have the force of *things*, but not of *gods*. For they either exist within us, as *Mind*, *Hope*, *Faith*, *Virtue*, and *Concord* do; or they are things we hope will happen to us, such as *Honor*, *Health*, and *Victory*. I will understand why the power of the gods should be in these things only when I have learned it." <note>original Latin: "Num censes igitur subtiliore ratione opus esse ad hæc refellenda? Nam Mentem, Fidem, Spem, Virtutem, Honorem, Victoriam, Salutem, Concordiam, cæteraque ejusmodi, Rerum Vim habere videmus, non Deorum. Aut enim in nobismet insunt ipsis, ut Mens, ut Spes, ut Fides, ut Virtus, ut Concordia; aut optandæ nobis sunt, ut Honos, ut Salus, ut Victoria. Quare autem in his Vis Deorum sit, tum intelligam cum cognovero."</note>

Is there any need, do you think, for great cleverness to disprove these things? For *Mind*, *Faith*, *Hope*, *Virtue*, *Honor*, *Victory*, *Health*, *Concord*, and the like—we see them to have the power of *things*, but not of *gods*. This is because they either exist in us, as *Mind*, *Hope*, *Virtue*, and *Concord*; or they are things we desire to happen to us, such as *Honor*, *Health*, and *Victory* (that is, they are nothing but mere *accidents* or *affections* of things). Therefore, it is impossible to understand how they can have the power of *gods* in them. Later, Cicero affirms: "Those who are called gods in the allegorical mythology of the pagans are really just the *natures of things*, and not the *true figures* or *forms of gods*." <note>original Latin: "Eos qui Dii appellantur, Rerum Naturas esse, non Figuras Deorum."</note>

Therefore, since the pagans themselves acknowledged that those *personified* and *deified things of nature* were not *true* and *proper gods*, their meaning could certainly be nothing other than this: they were many *different names* and *partial ways of viewing* the *one supreme God* as he manifests himself in all the *things of nature*. For that *force* <note>original: "Vis"</note> which Cicero tells us was called "God" or "deified" in all these things is really nothing other than something of *God* in *every thing* that is good. 

We understand the following words of Balbus in Cicero in the same way: <margin>On the Nature of the Gods, Book 2.</margin> "Because the force of these things was so great that they could not be governed without God, the things themselves obtained the names of gods." <note>original Latin: "Quarum Rerum, quia Vis erat tanta, ut sine Deo regi non posset, ipsa Res Deorum Nomen obtinuit."</note> This means that God was acknowledged and worshipped in all of them; the pagans signified this by calling them "gods." 

Even Pliny, though not a particularly religious person, <margin>Natural History, Book 2, Chapter 7.</margin> yet being clever, easily understood this to be the meaning: "Frail and toilsome mortality has broken and crumbled the deity into *parts*, mindful of its own weakness, so that everyone might worship that portion which they needed most." <note>original Latin: "Fragilis & laboriosa Mortalitas, in Partes ista digessit, Infirmitatis suæ memor, ut Portionibus quisque coleret, quo maximè indigeret."</note>

### Chap. IV. Of dividing the Simple Deity into Parts.

Substantial minds (or spirits) were not considered independent and self-existent, nor even eternal. Instead, they were created by one Supreme Mind or God and appointed by him to preside over the various parts of the world and the elements of nature as his ministers. The author <term>Vossius</term> <note>Gerardus Johannes Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch scholar who wrote extensively on paganism and theology.</note> also affirms this regarding those "Deified Accidents" <note>original: "Deified Accidents and Affections"; these are qualities, states of being, or events (like Justice or Victory) that were worshipped as gods.</note> and attributes. He argues that they were understood as substantial minds or created spirits presiding over those various things or managing them. 

His words at the beginning of his eighth book—where he speaks concerning these attributes and qualities deified by the pagans—are as follows: 

> There is an almost immense abundance of such gods. In Civil Theology <term>Civil Theology</term> <note>The religion of the state and city, as practiced in public rituals, as opposed to the "Natural Theology" of philosophers.</note>, they are usually considered as certain minds who received this honor from the Supreme God: that they should preside over those qualities. Indeed, they believed that God, whom they called "Best and Greatest" <note>original Latin: "Optimum Maximum"; a standard Roman title for Jupiter as the supreme deity.</note>, did not take care of everything by himself—since, as they said, that would greatly diminish his happiness—but, like a king, has many male and female ministers, each of whom he has placed in charge of this or that duty. Thus Justice, who is also called Astraea and Themis, was put in charge of all acts where justice was required; Comus was believed to oversee feasts. It was the same for other gods of that type, who took their names from the quality they were believed to oversee. If viewed this way, they differ from spirits or good and bad angels only in this: the latter are truly created by God, while the "Minds" we speak of now are inventions of the human mind. People, noticing the great power in certain qualities, imagined specific Minds to be in charge of each. The priests could easily persuade simpler people of these inventions because it seemed plausible that the Supreme Mind, the King of all gods, should have countless other minds serving him as ministers. This would make the Supreme God’s happiness more perfect, free him from being tangled in many cares, and allow his majesty to shine more brightly through the sheer number of his servants. And such indeed was the doctrine of Civil Theology. <note>original Latin: "Hujusmodi Deorum propè immensa est copia... Ac talis quidem Opinio erat Theologiæ Civilis."</note>

Of such gods as these, there was an innumerable company among the pagans. In their Civil Theology they were usually considered as certain Minds (or spirits) appointed by the Supreme God to preside over the properties of things. They supposed that God, whom they called the Best and the Greatest, did not take care of everything immediately himself, since that would necessarily be a distraction to him and a hindrance to his happiness. Instead, they believed he had, like a king, many male and female ministers under him who had their various offices assigned to them. 

Thus Justice—who was also called Astraea and Themis—was thought by them to preside over all those actions where justice was concerned. And Comus over all reveling, and the like. If these gods are considered in this way, they differ from angels (both good and bad) only in this: the latter are beings really created by God, while the former are merely the inventions of men. People, based on the number of qualities that have any great force in them, devised and imagined certain minds to preside over each one. 

The common people might have been more easily led into this belief by their priests because it seemed reasonable to them that the Supreme Mind, who is the King of all the gods, should have many other minds as his subservient ministers under him, both to free him from anxious care and to add to his grandeur and majesty. And such was the doctrine of Civil Theology.

# The Pagans' Political Gods <note>original: "Polit. Gods"; refers to the gods of "Civil Theology," the official religion of the state.</note>, sometimes BOOK I.

No man in his right mind could possibly suppose that these were themselves *True* and *Proper Gods*, as they have no *existence* of their own. While it is true that the majority of common Pagans conceived of these as *Created Minds* or *Spirits* appointed by the *Supreme God* to preside as his *ministers* over various *qualities* or *substances* <note>original: "Affections of Substances"</note>, the author plainly implies the same regarding all the other *Political Gods* of the Pagans. They were not looked upon as *uncreated*, *self-existent*, and *independent beings*, but only as *inferior minds* or *spirits*, created by the *Supreme God* and appointed by him to preside over the *various parts* of the *world* and *things of nature*, each having their *assigned roles*. Therefore, in the main, *we* and *Vossius* <note>Gerardus Johannes Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch classical scholar.</note> are now well agreed: namely, that the ancient Pagans asserted no such thing as a *multitude* of *independent deities*. There only remain a few particular differences of smaller importance between us.

<margin>St. Augustine, City of God, Book 4, Chapter 24.</margin> We ourselves have previously observed that *Aeolus* <note>The ruler of the winds in Greek mythology.</note> was probably understood by the philosopher *Epictetus* (in the writings of *Arrianus*) not as *one* individual, but as *many created ministers* of the Supreme God, or *demons collectively*, appointed by him to preside over the *winds* in all the various parts of the world. And the Pagans mentioned in St. *Augustine* <note>original: "St. Austin"</note> seem to interpret those *Deified Accidents* <note>The worship of qualities or states of being, like "Virtue" or "Victory," as if they were gods.</note> and *things of nature* in the same way—as the names of certain *unknown gods* or *demons* (one or more) that were appointed to preside over them or to distribute them.

As St. Augustine writes: *Because our ancestors knew well that these things do not happen to anyone without the special gift and favor of some God; therefore those Gods, whose names they did not know, were named after the things themselves which they perceived were being bestowed by them. There was only a slight change made to the names, such as when the God that causes War was called Bellona rather than Bellum <note>original Latin: "Bellum" means "War."</note>; the God who presides over infants’ cradles Cunina rather than Cuna <note>original Latin: "Cuna" means "Cradle."</note>; the one who gives corn Segetia <note>original Latin: from "segetes," meaning "crops."</note>; and the one who provides apples Pomona <note>original Latin: from "poma," meaning "fruit."</note>, and so on. But at other times, this was done without any change to the word at all, calling both the thing and the God who is its giver by one and the same name. As Pecunia signifies not only money, but also the Goddess who gives money; Virtus the Goddess who gives virtue; Honor the God who bestows honor; Concordia the Goddess who causes concord; and Victory the Goddess who provides victory. So also when Felicity <note>Happiness or good fortune.</note> is called a Goddess, it does not mean the thing which is given, but that Divine Power from whom Felicity is given.* <note>original: "Quoniam sciebant Majores nostri nemini talia, nisi aliquo Deo largiente concedi, quorum Deorum nomina non inveniebant, earum rerum nominibus appellabant Deos..."</note>

### CHAPTER IV. The Ministers of One Supreme.

Pagans may seem to have understood, by those deified things of nature, certain inferior *gods* or *demons* (one or more) who were the ministers of the Supreme God, appointed by him to preside over those various things respectively, or to manage them. We also cannot deny that, given the great ignorance and diversity of opinions among the Pagans, some might possibly have understood those *political gods* <note>original: "Political Gods"; refers to the gods recognized by the laws of the state (Civil Theology).</note> and deified things in the way described by *Vossius* <note>Gerardus Johannes Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch scholar who studied how natural objects became viewed as spirits.</note>—as so many individual minds or spirits appointed to preside over those several things throughout the whole world, and nothing else. 

Nevertheless, it does not seem at all probable that the general opinion among civilized Pagans was that all their gods were merely individual created minds or spirits, each appointed to preside over one specific thing everywhere throughout the whole world. For example, it is unlikely they believed that the goddess *Victory* was one individual created female spirit, appointed to bestow victory on whoever enjoyed it in all parts of the world; or that the goddess *Justice* was another such individual mind or spirit, created to dispense justice everywhere and meddle with nothing else. The same applies to all those other accidental things or deified qualities <note>original: "Affections Deified"</note>, such as *Virtue*, *Honor*, *Concord*, *Felicity*, and so on.

<margin>On False Religion, Chapter 7.</margin>
And *Lactantius Firmianus* <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325) who wrote "The Divine Institutes."</note>, taking notice of the Pagans' claim to worship nothing but one Supreme God and his subservient ministers, who were generated or created by him, plainly denies that the popular Pagan gods are these ministers. He references *Seneca* in his *Exhortations*, who wrote that "God had generated the ministers of his kingdom under him" <note>original: *Genuisse Regni sui Ministros Deum*</note> (who were also called "gods" by the Pagans). *Lactantius* replies: "But these ministers of the Divine Kingdom, or subservient created spirits, are neither gods, nor do they wish to be called gods or honored as such... Nor indeed are they those gods who are commonly worshipped by the Pagans, whose number is small and fixed" <note>original: *Verum hi neque Dii sunt, neque Deos se vocari, aut coli volunt, &c. Nec tamen illi sunt qui vulgo coluntur, quorum & exiguus & certus est numerus*</note>. 

That is, the Pagan gods are organized into certain ranks, and their number is determined by the needs of human life; of these, their "noble and select gods" are but a few. Whereas, he says, the ministers of the Supreme God are—according to the Pagans' own opinion—not twelve, nor twenty, nor three hundred and sixty, but countless: namely, the stars and demons.

<margin>Aristotle, On Melissus, Xenophanes, and Gorgias, page 1246.</margin>

Instead, one god is supposed to be most powerful regarding one thing, and another god regarding another: "If a person takes God to be the most powerful of all things, meaning the most powerful and the best, this does not seem to match the law; instead, many gods are considered superior to one another. Therefore, he did not take this common agreement about God from what is generally believed" <note>original: εἴπερ ἅπαντα ἐπικράτιστον τὸν θεὸν λαμβάνει τοῦτο δυνατώτατον καὶ βέλτιστον λέγων, οὐ δοκεῖ τοῦτο κατὰ τὸν νόμον, ἀλλὰ πολλὰ κρείττους εἶναι ἀλλήλων οἱ θεοί· ἔκουν ἐκ τοῦ δοκεῖν ἔληφε ταύτην κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ τὴν ὁμολογίαν·</note>. <meta>This page continues the discussion on how ancient philosophers, specifically Zeno and Aristotle, reconciled the existence of many "political gods" with the concept of a single Supreme Being. It explores the distinction between "Civil Theology" (the gods of the state) and "Natural Theology" (the God of philosophy and nature).</meta>

# The Pagans' Political Gods, Generally, BOOK I.

People have an idea in their minds of God as *one being, the most excellent and most powerful of all*. This does not seem to match the Law (that is, the *Civil Theology* <note>original: "Civil Theology"; the branch of religion dealing with the official gods and rituals recognized by the state laws.</note>), for there, the *gods* are ranked as *better than one another* in relation to different things. Therefore, *Zeno* did not take this *consensus of mankind* concerning God from popular appearances. 

From this passage of *Aristotle’s*, we may well conclude that the many *political gods* of the Pagans were not all popularly viewed as the *subservient ministers* of *one Supreme God*. Yet, because they generally acknowledged (as Aristotle himself admits) a *monarchy*—and consequently not many *independent deities*—it must follow, as *Zeno* would undoubtedly reply, that these *political gods* were merely *one and the same Supreme Natural God*. They were, in a sense, *portioned out* and *multiplied*; that is, they received *several names* according to *different concepts* of him, and as he exercises *different powers* and produces *various effects*. 

We have already sufficiently proved this to have been the general view of the leading Pagan *doctors* <note>original: "Doctors"; refers to learned teachers or philosophers.</note>: that these *many political and popular gods* were but the <term>polyonymy</term> <note>original: "Polyonymy"; the practice of giving many different names to the same entity.</note> of *one Natural God*. They were either *partial considerations* of him, or his *various powers, virtues, effects, and manifestations* in the world, individually *personified and deified*.

<margin>Book 8, Chapter 1.</margin>
And so *Vossius* <note>Gerardus Johannes Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch classical scholar.</note> himself later admits as well: that according to *Natural Theology*, the *many Pagan gods* were merely *several names for one God*. However, this learned philologist <note>original: "Philologer"; a scholar of historical languages and literature.</note> plainly narrows and restricts the *notion* of this *Natural Theology* too much, improperly calling its God the *Nature of Things*. Nevertheless, he acknowledges it as such a nature that was endowed with *sense* and *understanding*. 

His words are these: 

"The opinion of the natural theologians was quite different; they recognized no divinity other than the Nature of Things, and they attributed all the gods of the nations to it, and so on. Indeed, their intention was that, as Nature was engaged with this or that quality, so the divinities and names of the gods would vary. When, therefore, they saw some greater power anywhere, they believed it to be something divine; thus they reached the point of creating a vast crowd of gods and goddesses. Meanwhile, the more wise stated that all these were one divinity: namely, the Nature of Things, which, although it was one, received various names and was worshipped in different ways according to its various effects." <note>original Latin: "Dispar verò sententia Theologorum Naturalium, qui non aliud Numen agnoscebant quàm Naturam Rerum, eóque omnia Gentium Numina referebant, &c. Nempe mens eorum fuit, sicut Natura esset occupata, circa hanc vel illam Affectionem, ita Numina Nominaque Deorum variare. Cum igitur ubicunque Vim aliquam majorem viderent, ita Divinum aliquid crederent: eò etiam devenere, ut immanem Deorum Dearumque fingerent Catervam. Sagaciores interim haec cuncta, Unum esse Numen aiebant: putà Rerum Naturam, quae licet una foret, pro variis tamen Effectis varia sortiretur nomina, vario etiam afficeretur cultu."</note> 

But the case is very different regarding the *natural theologians* who acknowledged no other God but the *Nature of Things* and referred all the *Pagan gods* to that. For they conceived that as Nature was occupied with several things, so were the divine powers and the names of gods multiplied and diversified. Wherever they saw any greater force, they immediately imagined something divine, and by that means, they eventually came to invent an innumerable company of gods and goddesses. But the more wise, in the meantime, affirmed all these to be but one and the same God—to wit, the Nature of Things—which, though really but one, yet according to its various effects, both received different names and was worshipped in different manners. 

In this passage, *Vossius* calls the Supreme God of these *natural theologians* the *Nature of Things*, as if *Natural Theology* had been named after *physics* or *natural philosophy* alone; whereas we have already shown that *Natural Theology*...

<header>Chap. IV. The Many Names of One God.</header>

The theology of Varro and Scaevola was of equal scope with *Philosophical Theology*. From the history we have already provided, it clearly appears that their only <term>Numen</term> <note>original: "Numen"; a Latin term for divine power or a deity.</note> was not some *Blind* and *Unintelligible Nature of Things*. It was also called *Natural* in another sense, meaning *Real*, as opposed to *Opinion*, *Fantasy*, and *Myth*, or anything that has no *Reality of Existence* anywhere in the world. 

Thus, *St. Augustine* <note>original: "St. Austin"</note> distinguishes between the *Nature of the Gods* <note>original: "Natura Deorum"</note> and the *Institutes of Men* <note>original: "Hominum Instituta"</note> concerning them. He also explains the difference between *Civil* and *Natural Theology*, according to the mind of *Varro*, in this manner: *It may come to pass that in a city, according to false opinions, those things are worshiped and believed which have no real existence anywhere, whether in the world or outside it.* <note>original: "Fieri potest ut in Urbe, secundum Falsas opiniones ea colantur & credantur, quorum in Mundo vel extra Mundum Natura sit nusquam."</note>

Therefore, we must move past this "Nature of Things" (which was properly the God of no one except for *atheistic philosophers* like *Epicurus* and *Strato*). If we instead substitute that *Great Mind* or *Soul of the whole World* which *pervades all things* and is *diffused through all* (which was the *True God* of the Pagan Theists), then the claim of the scholar *Vossius* becomes unquestionably true regarding their *Natural Theologians*. According to them, those *many poetical* and *political gods* mentioned before were only *one* and the *same Natural* or *Real God*. 

In respect to his different *virtues*, *powers*, and *effects*, he was called by several *names* and worshiped in different ways. Nevertheless, according to those theologians, there were also really many other *inferior ministers* of this *One Supreme God* (whether called *Minds* or *Demons*) who were supposed to be the *subservient executioners* of all those various powers of his. Accordingly, we previously saw this full and true account of the *Pagans' Natural Theology* set down by the poet *Prudentius*:

-> — — — — — — — — *In One God* <-
> -> *He placed all authority, whom a vast system* <-
> -> *Of powers serves, equipped with various ministers.* <-
<note>original: "In Uno Constituit jus omne Deo, cui serviat ingens Virtutum ratio, Variis instructa Ministris."</note>

*Namely: That it acknowledged one Supreme Omnipotent God, ruling over all, who displays and exercises his many virtues and powers in the world (all of which are individually personified and deified in the Poetical and Civil Theologies), together with the subservient ministry of other inferior created minds, understanding beings, or demons, whom they also called gods.*

It is very true, as we have already declared, that the more *high-flown Platonic Pagans* reduced those *many poetical* and *political gods*—and therefore certainly all the *personified* and *deified things* of nature as well—to the *Platonic Ideas*. These were the *First Paradigms* and *Patterns of Things* in the *Archetypal World* <note>the world of original concepts or "Forms" upon which the physical world is modeled</note>. They affirmed these were begotten from the *Supreme Deity* (that is, from the *First Hypostasis* of the *Platonic Trinity*). These were commonly called by them <term>νοητοὶ θεοὶ</term> <note>original: "noētoi theoi"</note>, or *Intelligible Gods*, as if they had indeed been many *distinct substances* and *persons*. And as we have also proved from the writings of *Philo*, this *high-flown Pagan theology* was older than...

than either Julian or Apuleius; so do we think it not unworthy of our observation here, that the very same doctrine is by Celsus also attributed to the **Egyptian theologians**. He notes that they pretend to worship brute animals only as **symbols** of those **Eternal Ideas**. <margin>Origen, *Against Celsus*, Book 3, page 120.</margin> He writes that it is wrong to laugh at the Egyptians, who "offer many significant riddles, teaching that such things are honors paid to eternal ideas, and not (as the common people think) to ephemeral animals." <note>original Greek: "τῷ μὲν Αἰγυπτίων καταγελᾶν, καί τοι πολλὰ καὶ οὐ φαῦλα παρεχόντων αἰνίγματα, ἐπὰν ἰδεῶν ἀϊδίων, καὶ οὐχ (ὡς δοκοῦσι οἱ πολλοί) ζώων ἐφημερίων τιμὰς εἶναι τὰ τοιαῦτα διδάσκωσιν"</note> Celsus also adds, *That we Christians deride the Egyptians without cause, as they have many mysteries in their religion, for they profess that perishing brute animals are not worshiped by them, but the Eternal Ideas.* According to this account by Celsus, it would seem that this doctrine of **Eternal Ideas**—acting as the <term>paradigms</term> <note>Original: "Paradigms"; these are the perfect blueprints or patterns in the divine mind from which all things in the physical world are modeled.</note> and patterns of all things here below in this sensible world—was not unique to Plato or the Greeks, but was shared by the Egyptians as well. 

These Eternal Ideas were supposed to have been generated from that *First Divine <term>Hypostasis</term>* <note>original: "Hypostasis"; in this context, it refers to a "person" or "level of reality" within a divine Trinity.</note> of the Platonist and Egyptian Trinity, and were called "Intelligible Gods." Nevertheless, they were all acknowledged to exist within one Divine Intellect, according to the teaching of Plotinus: "the objects of thought do not exist outside the mind." <note>original Greek: "οὐκ ἔξω τοῦ νοῦ τὰ νοητᾶ"</note> This Mind or Intellect is the *Second Divine Hypostasis*. Therefore, these Intelligible and Invisible Gods (though generated from God) are said by Julian in his book against the Christians to *both coexist with God and exist within him.* 

To this purpose also is another <margin>Page 347.</margin> passage from Julian’s sixth oration: "For God is All things, forasmuch as he contains within himself the causes of all things that exist in any way. Whether they are immortal causes of immortal things, or causes of corruptible and perishing things—these causes are not themselves mortal or corruptible, but are eternal and always remaining; they are the causes of the perpetual generation and new production of things." <note>original Greek: "πάντα γὰρ αὐτός ἐστιν, εἴπερ καὶ ἐν ἑαυτῷ καὶ παρ' ἑαυτῷ ἔχοι τῶν ὁπωσοῦν ὄντων τὰς αἰτίας· εἴτε ἀθανάτων ἀθάνατος· εἴτε ἐπικήρων οὐ θνητὰς οὐδὲ ἐπικήρους, ἀϊδίους δὲ καὶ μενούσας ἀεὶ, αἳ καὶ τούτοις εἰσὶν αἰτίαι τῆς ἀειγενεσίας·"</note> 

Now, these causes of all things contained in God are nothing other than the **Divine Ideas**. Therefore, it plainly appears from this that these Platonist and Egyptian pagans, who reduced their many gods to these Divine Ideas, did not consider them to be so many minds or spirits really distinct from the **Supreme God** (even if they were dependent on him). Instead, they were only so many **partial considerations of one God**, viewed as being *All things*—that is, containing within himself the causes of all things. Accordingly, we find in Origen that just as the Egyptian theologians called their religious animals "symbols of the Eternal Ideas," they also called them <margin>Origen, *Against Celsus*, page 120.</margin> "**symbols of God**." Celsus applauds the Egyptian theologians for talking so magnificently and mysteriously of those brute animals they worshiped, affirming them to be "certain symbols of God." <note>original Greek: "τὰ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων σεμνολογούντων καὶ τὰ περὶ τῶν ἀλόγων ζώων, καὶ φασκόντων εἶναί τινα αὐτὰ καὶ θεοῦ σύμβολα·"</note>

And now we have provided some account of the <term>polyonymy</term> <note>original: "Polyonymy"; the practice of giving many names to a single person or deity.</note> of the **One Supreme God** in the theologies of the pagans—or of his being called by **many proper personal names**, which carries the appearance of there being many separate gods. > O wise Creator of things! O BEGINNING OF THE GODS!

**Genius** was seen as the *Great Mind* and *Soul* of the whole *world*. **Saturn** was seen as that *hidden source* and *principle* from which all *forms* and *lives* emerge and into which they again retire, being stored there as if in a *secret warehouse*. Or else, as one of the **Egyptian** or **Hermetic** <note>original: "Hermaick"; relating to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom and magic.</note> writers expresses it, he is that which does **"make all things out of itself, and unmake them into itself again."** <note>original Greek: "πάντα ποιεῖν καὶ εἰς ἑαυτὸν ἀποποιεῖν"</note> This **Etruscan** <note>original: "Hetrurian"</note> Saturn corresponds to the **Egyptian Hammon**, which likewise signified "hidden," and is accordingly interpreted by **Iamblichus** as **"he that brings forth the invisible power of the hidden reasons of things (contained within himself) into the light."** <note>original Greek: "ὁ τὴν ἀφανῆ καὶ κεκρυμμένων λόγων δύναμιν εἰς φῶς ἄγων"</note> God was also called **Athena** or **Minerva**, representing *wisdom* diffusing itself through all things, and **Aphrodite Urania**, the *Heavenly Venus* or *Love*.

Thus **Phanes**, who was **Orpheus’s** *Supreme God* (so called, according to **Lactantius**, **"because when there was yet nothing, he first appeared out of that infinite abyss,"** <note>original Latin: "Quia cum adhuc nihil esset, Primus ex Infinito apparuerit"</note> but according to **Proclus**, because he did **"reveal and make manifest the intelligible unities (or ideas) from himself"** <note>original Greek: "ἐκφαίνειν τὰς νοητὰς ἑνάδας"</note>), was styled in **Orphic** and **Egyptian** theology as **"tender and soft love,"** <note>original Greek: "ἁβρὸς ἔρως"</note> as Proclus informs us in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*. We think the conjecture of **Athanasius Kircher** is more probable than either of these: that *Phanes* was an *Egyptian name*. **Pherecydes Syrus** likewise affirmed **"that Jupiter was turned entirely into love when he intended to create the world."** <note>original Greek: "εἰς ἔρωτα μεταβεβλῆσθαι τὸν Δία μέλλοντα δημιουργεῖν"</note>

In addition to these, there were other such names for the *Supreme God*, many more than we have mentioned; for example, **Summanus** among the ancient **Romans**, a name that afterward became obsolete.

<margin>St. Augustine, City of God, Book 4, Chapter 23</margin>
Of this, **St. Augustine** says: **"The ancient Romans worshipped some god called Summanus, to whom they attributed the lightning of the night, even more than they did Jupiter, to whom the daytime lightning belonged. But after a distinguished and grand temple was built for Jupiter, because of the dignity of that house, the crowd flocked to him so much that one can hardly find anyone who remembers having even read the name of Summanus, which can no longer be heard."** <note>original Latin: "Romani veteres nescio quem Summanum, cui Nocturna Fulmina tribuebant, coluerunt magis quam Jovem... ut vix inveniatur qui Summani nomen... se saltem legisse meminerit"</note>

[now presiding] over certain parts of the world and acting in them; or as exercising certain *special powers* and *virtues* in the world. These several *virtues* and *powers* of one God, *personified* <note>original: "Personated"</note> and *deified* by the pagans, appeared to be *many distinct gods*; yet they were really nothing but several *names* <note>original: "Denominations"</note> for the one Supreme God, who is still considered as a being distinct from the world and nature.

<margin>*Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 3, Chapter 13</margin> <note>original: "Pr. Evan. L. 3. c. 13." referring to Eusebius of Caesarea's *Praeparatio Evangelica*.</note>
But lastly, as God was supposed by these pagans not only to *pervade all things* and *to fill all things*, but also—since he is the cause of *all things*—to be himself in a manner *all things*, he was also called by the name of *everything*, or *everything* was called by *his name*. That is, the various things of nature and parts of the world were themselves *verbally deified* by these pagans and called *gods* and *goddesses*. It was not that they truly considered these things to be gods in themselves, but that they thought it appropriate to acknowledge *God in them* as the author of them all. For thus the pagans in St. *Augustine* <note>original: "Austin"</note> said: "Can you think that our pagan ancestors were so foolish <note>original: "sottish"</note> as not to know that these things are but divine gifts, and not gods themselves?" <note>original Latin: "Usque adeone, inquiunt, Majores nostros insipientes fuisse credendum est, ut haec nescirent Munera Divina esse, non Deos?"</note> And *Cicero* also tells us that the meaning of their deifying these things of nature was only to signify that they acknowledged *the force of all things to be divine* and to be governed by God; and that *whatever brought any great benefit to mankind was not such without the divine goodness.* They also conceived that the invisible and incomprehensible Deity, who was the cause of *all* things, ought to be worshiped in all his works and effects, through which he had made himself *visible*. This matches what they declare in that passage of *Eusebius* previously cited in part: "They did not deify those visible bodies of the sun, moon, and stars, nor the other perceptible <note>original: "Sensible"</note> parts of the world themselves, but those invisible powers of the God over all that were displayed in them. For they affirm that God, who is but one, yet fills all things with his various powers and passes through all things—inasmuch as he is invisibly and incorporeally present in all—is reasonably to be worshiped in and by those visible things." <note>original Greek: "μὴ τὰ ὁρώμενα σώματα ἡλίου καὶ σελήνης καὶ ἄστρων, μηδέ γε τὰ αἰσθητὰ μέρη τοῦ κόσμου φήσουσι θεοποιεῖν, ἀλλὰ τὰς ἐν τούτοις ἀοράτους δυνάμεις, αὐτοῦ δὴ τοῦ ἐπὶ πᾶσιν· ἕνα γὰρ ὄντα θεὸν, παντοίαις δυνάμεσι τὰ πάντα πληροῦν, καὶ διὰ πάντων διήκειν, καὶ τοῖς πᾶσιν ἐπιστατεῖν· ἀσωμάτως δὲ καὶ ἀφανῶς ἐν πᾶσιν ὄντα, καὶ διὰ πάντων διήκοντα, καὶ τοῦτον εἰκότως διὰ τῶν δεδηλωμένων σέβειν"</note>

*Athanasius*, Bishop of Alexandria, in his book against the Greeks, reduces all the *false gods* of the pagans under two general categories. The first consists of *poetical, fictitious, or imaginary gods*; the second consists of *creatures* or *real things of nature deified* by them. His words are as follows: "Since our reasoning has sufficiently proved that the poetical gods of the pagans are no gods at all, and has also shown that those who deify the creatures are in great error—thus refuting the whole of pagan idolatry and proving it to be mere ungodliness and impiety—there is nothing..." <note>original Greek: "εἰ γὰρ δὴ τοὺς παρὰ ποιηταῖς λεγομένους θεοὺς, οὐκ εἶναι θεοὺς ὁ λόγος ἔδειξε, καὶ τοὺς τὴν κτίσιν θεοποιοῦντας ἤλεγξε πλανωμένους, &c."</note>

<meta>This page continues the argument that early Christian authors, such as Athanasius, viewed the various pagan gods not as real, independent beings, but as poetic personifications or "fictitious names" for the different powers and manifestations of the one Supreme God.</meta>

<page-num>531</page-num>
<header>Cʜᴀᴘ. IV. Poetical and Fantastical.</header>

Now only *True Piety* remains; he who is worshipped by us *Christians* is the only *True God*, the *Lord of Nature*, and the *Maker of all substances*. From this, we may observe that according to *Athanasius*, the *pagan poetic gods* <note>original: "Poetick Gods"</note> were not *real things* in nature. Therefore, they could be nothing other than the *various notions* and *powers* of the *one Supreme God deified*, or *several names* for him. So, Athanasius's *poetic gods*, or the gods fabulously devised by the poets <note>original Greek: οἱ παρὰ ποιηταῖς μυθυόμενοι θεοὶ</note>, were chiefly those *two kinds* of *pagan gods* first mentioned by us. These are: first, the *various aspects* <note>original: "Considerations"</note> of the *one Supreme Deity* <note>original Latin: "Numen"</note> according to its general *notion*, expressed by so many *proper names*; and second, his *particular powers* diffused throughout the *world*, individually *personified* <note>original: "Personated"</note> and *deified*. When considered as so many distinct deities, these are nothing but mere *fiction* and *fancy* <note>original: "Phancy"</note> without any reality. And the *pagans* themselves in *Athanasius* acknowledge this:

<margin>P. 14.</margin>
"For perhaps, as they themselves say, even the names are fabricated, and there is no Zeus at all, nor Cronus, nor Hera, nor Ares; but the poets feign these to exist in order to deceive their listeners." <note>original Greek: ἴσως γδ ὡς αὐτοί φαϚι, κὶ τὰ ὀνόματα πέπλαϚαι, κὶ οὐκ ἔϚι μὲν ὅλως Ζεὺς, οὐδὲ Κρόνῳ, οὐδὲ Ἥρα, οὐδὲ Ἄρης· πλάτονται δὲ τότες, ὡς ὄντας οἱ ποιηταὶ πρὸς ἀπάτω τῷ ἀκόντων.</note> Despite this, that *third sort* of *pagan gods* we also mentioned—which were *inanimate substances* and the *natures of things deified*—may also be rightly called *poetical gods*. For although those things themselves are *real* and not *feigned*, their *personification* and *deification* are mere *fiction* and *fantasy* <note>original: "Phantastry"</note>. However the first occasion for this arose—from the *theological opinion* or persuasion that *God*, who is *in all things* and is the *cause of all things*, ought to be worshipped *in all things*, especially since he is himself *invisible*—making those things into so many *persons* and *gods* was nothing but *poetic fiction* and *fantasy*. Their old *mythology* and *allegorical fables* of the gods follow this same pattern.

XXXIV. So far, we have declared the general sense of the *pagans* (including those who supposed *God* to be a *being elevated above the world*) that they agreed on these *two things*. First: the *breaking* and *crumbling*, as it were, of the *simple Deity*, and the *parceling* out of that deity into *many particular notions* and *partial aspects* <note>original: "Considerations"</note>, according to the *various manifestations* of its *power* and *providence* in the world. By *personifying* and *deifying* these separately, they made, as it were, *many gods out of one*. The chief *ground* <note>meaning: basis or reason</note> for this was that they did not consider the *Deity* according to its *simple nature* and in the *abstract* only, but also *concretely* in relation to the *world*. They saw how he *displays himself* there, *pervades all*, and *diffuses his virtues* throughout all. Just as the *Sun*, reflected by thick vapors, is sometimes multiplied; and just as the same *object* viewed through a *polyhedral glass* <note>original: "Polyedrous Glass"; a prism or multi-faceted lens</note> is represented in several places at once because of those many surfaces, and is thus rendered *manifold* to the spectator; so the *one* and the same supreme *God*, considered *concretely* with the *world* as *manifesting* his *several powers* and *virtues* in it, was multiplied into *several names*, not with—

<summary>Athanasius argues that pagan gods were mere poetic fictions used to represent the various powers and manifestations of the one true God throughout the natural world. He suggests that while the physical elements deified by pagans are real, their personification as distinct deities is a product of human fancy.</summary>

<page-num>532</page-num>
# Of those Pagan Theologians, who BOOK 1.

...produced the appearance of *so many different gods*. However, for those ancient pagans, <term>Polyonymy</term> <note>original: "πολυώνυμον" - having many names</note> was the same thing as having many powers <note>original: "πολυδύναμον"</note>. To have *many names* was identical to having *many powers*. This is according to this passage by *Callimachus* concerning *Diana*:

-> "Grant me to keep my virginity forever, Father, and to have many names." <-
-> <note>original Greek: Δός μοι παρθενίην αἰώνιον, ἄππα, φυλάσσειν, Καὶ Πολυωνυμίην.</note> <-

And this passage from *Virgil* concerning *Alecto* <note>Alecto was one of the Furies in Greek and Roman mythology, representing relentless anger.</note>:

-> "You have a thousand names, a thousand ways of doing harm." <-
-> <note>original Latin: Tibi Nomina Mille, Mille nocendi Artes.</note> <-

Accordingly, the *many pagan gods* are interpreted in *Plato's Cratylus* as the *many powers* of *one God diffused* through the world. The pagan theologians seemed to feel that it was more suitable to the pomp, state, and grandeur of the Supreme God for him to be considered *diffusively* and called by *many names* signifying his *many different virtues* and *powers*. They accounted <term>polyonymy</term> to be an *honor*, rather than contracting and shrinking God down into *one general notion* of a *perfect mind*, the *maker* or *creator* of the whole *world*.

*The second thing* in which the *pagans* agreed is their *personifying* and *deifying* the *parts of the world* and the *things of nature* themselves, thereby making them into so many *gods and goddesses* as well. Their meaning in doing this was declared to be nothing other than this: that God, who not only *pervades all things* but was also the *cause of all things* (and therefore is himself, in a way, *all things*), ought to be worshipped in all the *things of nature* and *parts of the world*. They also believed that the *force* of every thing was *divine*, and that in all things beneficial to mankind, *the divine goodness* ought to be acknowledged.

We shall now observe how both those previously mentioned principles—that *God pervades all things* and that he *is all things*—were the *chief grounds* for the *seeming polytheism* of the *pagans*. These ideas were improved and carried further by those among them who had no *higher notion* of the *Supreme Deity* than as the *soul of the world*. That this *opinion* found acceptance among so many of them was probably because it was so obvious for religious people to conceive that, just as they themselves consisted of *body* and *soul*, so the *body of the whole world* was not without its *soul* either. They believed their *human souls* were derived from the *life* and *soul* of the *world*, just as the *earth* and *water* in their bodies came from the *earth* and *water* of the *world*. 

Now, while the more refined *pagans* (as previously observed) supposed God to *pervade* and *pass through all things* without mixing with them <note>original Greek: ἀμιγῶς</note>, these others concluded God to be—according to a rigid sense of the definition in *Quintilian*—"a spirit mingled with all the parts of the world" <note>original Latin: Spiritum omnibus Partibus Immixtum</note>. Or else, in the language of *Manilius*:

-> "And God infused into the heaven, the lands, and the sea," <-
-> <note>original Latin: Infusumque Deum Cælo, Terrisque Fretoque</note> <-

<sig>Z z 4</sig>

<summary>This page explains the concept of "Polyonymy," where the many names of pagan gods were understood as different powers of one Supreme God. It also discusses the "Soul of the World" philosophy, which views God as a spirit infused into every part of the physical universe.</summary>

<page-num>533</page-num>

# CHAPTER 4. God as the Soul of the World.

God was thought to be infused into the heavens, the earth, and the seas: "and by a sacred path, God breathes together [with his work]" <note>original Latin: *Sacroque meatu Conspirare Deum*</note>, intimately harmonizing with his own creation, the world, as if being almost one with it. For this reason, he was commonly called "Nature" as well. This was defined by some of the Stoics as "God mingled throughout the world" <note>original Latin: *Deus Mundo permistus*</note>, and "Divine Reason inserted into the whole world" <note>original Latin: *Divina Ratio toti Mundo insita*</note>. 

Despite this, this "Nature"—to distinguish it from the particular natures of individual things—was called the "Common Nature" <note>original Greek: *κοινὴ φύσις*; original Latin: *Communis Natura*</note>. These thinkers plainly declared that this was not a "senseless nature." This follows the view of Balbus in the writings of Cicero: "It is Nature that contains the whole world and protects it; and this is certainly a nature that is not without sense and reason" <note>original Latin: *Natura est quæ continet Mundum omnem, eumque tuetur; atque ea quidem non sine Sensu, atque Ratione*</note>. Elsewhere, it is said to be "perfect and eternal reason, the Divine Mind and Wisdom." It also contains within itself all the <term>seminal reasons</term> <note>original Greek: *λόγοι σπερματικοὶ* (logoi spermatikoi)—the active, rational principles that guide the growth and development of all living things in nature.</note> by which natural things are produced. 

Therefore, we see that such "naturalists" as these may well be considered <term>theists</term> (even Moses himself was accounted as one of them in the writings of Strabo). In contrast, those who acknowledge no higher principle in the world than a "senseless nature"—whether they believe it is governed by "chance" or is "orderly and methodical"—cannot be considered anything other than absolute atheists.

<margin>As Simplicius describes God to be "All things before all things." <note>original Greek: *πάντα πρὸ πάντων*; original Latin: *Omnia ante omnia*</note> In his commentary on Epictetus, page 234.</margin>

Furthermore, some of these pagans admitted no "incorporeal substance" (spirit) and concluded that this "Soul of the World" was itself a "body" too. However, they described it as a "most subtle and most swift body" <note>original Greek: *λεπτότατον καὶ τάχιστον*</note>, as was previously noted from Plato. Even so, they believed it was endowed with a perfect mind and understanding, as well as with "seminal reasons." By working its way into all other bodies, this soul permeated and spread through the whole universe, framing all things by inwardly mingling itself with them. Heraclitus and Hippasus thought this substance was fire, while Diogenes Apolloniates thought it was air. Simplicius, who had read some of Diogenes' works that were still available then, defends him from the charge of atheism that philosophers like Hippo and Anaximander face.

Again, while the more sophisticated pagans affirmed that the Supreme God was "All"—yet still something "Above All" because he was higher than the Soul of the World—others had a different view. (Aeschylus probably meant the former in his previously cited passage: "Jupiter is the air, Jupiter is the earth, Jupiter is the heaven; Jupiter is all things, and yet something higher than all, or above all" <note>original Greek: *Ζεύς τοι τὰ πάντα καὶ τι τ̈͂δ᾽ ὑπέρτερον*</note>). 

However, those pagans who acknowledged no higher <term>numen</term> <note>a Latin term for a deity or divine power</note> than the Soul of the World made God out to be "all things" in a more literal, physical sense. They supposed that the entire physical world, being animated, was also the Supreme Deity. To them, God was originally that eternal, unmade Soul and Mind which diffuses itself through all things. Yet they conceived that, just as the human soul and body together make up one rational animal (a human), this "Mundane Soul" and its body (the physical world) similarly made up one entire "Divine Animal," or God.

<summary>This page explores the Stoic and Pagan concept of God as the "Soul of the World," a rational principle infused into nature that makes the entire universe a "Divine Animal." It distinguishes between those who saw God as both the world and something above it, versus those who viewed the physical universe itself as the totality of the deity.</summary>
