# To these, the Parts of the World, BOOK I.

It is indeed true that, just as the human soul acts principally in one specific part of the body—which has therefore been called the <term>Hegemonicon</term> <note>original Greek: *ἡγεμονικόν* (hegemonikon)—the "ruling part" or seat of the soul</note> or the <term>Principale</term> <note>the principal or governing part</note>—some taking this to be the brain and others the heart, while Strato (according to Tertullian) ridiculously suggested it was the space between the eyebrows; so the Stoics supposed the Great Soul or Mind of the world to act principally in one part of it as its ruling part (though they did not all agree on which part that was). This part was sometimes emphatically called **God**. Nevertheless, they all acknowledged that this World-Soul, like the souls of other animals, pervades, animates, enlivens, and activates its whole body—the world—to varying degrees. This is plainly declared by Laertius in the *Life of Zeno*:

"The Stoics affirm that the world is governed by Mind and Providence, with this Mind passing through all its parts, just as the soul does in us. Yet it does not act in all parts alike, but in some more and in some less. It passes through some parts only as a <term>habit</term> <note>original Greek: *ἕξις* (hexis)—a physical state of being or cohesion, the lowest level of soul activity</note>, such as through the bones and nerves; but through others as mind or understanding, such as through that which is called the ruling part. So the whole world, being a living and rational animal, has its ruling part too. According to Antipater, this is the ether; to Posidonius, the air; to Cleanthes, the sun, and so on. They also say that this first God is, as it were, sensibly diffused through all animals and plants, but through the earth itself only as a physical state. Therefore, the whole world, being thus activated and animated by one divine soul, is itself—according to these Stoics—the supreme God." <note>original Greek: *τὸν δὴ κόσμον διοικεῖσθαι κατὰ νοῦν καὶ πρόνοιαν... διὰ δὲ τῆς γῆς αὐτῆς καθ᾿ ἕξιν*</note>

<margin>
*Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 13, chapter 25.
Book 5, page 235.
</margin>

Thus Didymus, in the writings of Eusebius, says, "The Stoics call the whole world God" <note>original Greek: *ὅλον τὸν κόσμον προσαγορεύσει θεόν*</note>; and Origen, writing against Celsus, says, "The Greeks universally affirm the world to be a god, but the Stoics say it is the first and chief God" <note>original Greek: *σαφῶς δὴ τὸν ὅλον κόσμον λέγουσιν εἶναι θεὸν, Στωϊκοὶ μὲν τὸν πρῶτον*</note>. And accordingly, the poet Manilius wrote:

->*By which it may appear that the world is governed by a Divine Power,*<-
->*And is itself God:*<-
<note>original Latin: *Quâ pateat Mundum Divino Numine verti Atque Ipsum esse Deum*</note>

By this, it may appear that the world is governed by a divine mind, and is also God itself. Similarly, Seneca the philosopher wrote, "This whole world, within which we are contained, is both one single thing and is God" <note>original Latin: *Totum hoc quo continemur, & Unum est, & Deus est*</note>. This is not to be understood as referring to the mere matter of the world—as if it were nothing but a heap of atoms or endowed only with a <term>plastic</term> <note>formative or creative but unconscious</note> and senseless nature—but rather as it is animated by such a soul that, besides sense, was originally endowed with perfect understanding, and deriving all its divinity from that source.

<margin>
*The City of God*, Book 7, chapter 6.
</margin>

For this is how Varro, in the writings of St. Augustine, declares both his own and the Stoic view concerning this point: "The same Varro says, still speaking of natural theology, that he thinks God is..." <note>original Latin: *Dicit idem Varro, adhuc de Naturali Theologia præloquens, Deum se arbitrari esse*</note>

<meta>The text cuts off here, continuing with the word "esse" (to be) on the following page.</meta>

<summary>This page explores the Stoic concept of the World-Soul, arguing that God acts as the governing mind of the universe, much like the human soul governs the body, leading the Stoics to identify the entire animated world as the supreme deity.</summary>

### CHAPTER IV. The Parts and Members of God.

*...that God is the Soul of the World <note>original Latin: "esse Animam Mundi"</note> (which the Greeks call the Cosmos) and that this World itself is also God. But this should be understood in the same way as we speak of a Wise Man: although he consists of both Body and Soul, he is called "Wise" only because of his Mind or Soul. Similarly, the World is called "God" because of its Mind or Soul, even though it consists of both Mind and Body.*

The same Varro, when discussing <term>Natural Theology</term> <note>the study of God based on reason and the observation of nature rather than revelation</note>, declares that in his own view, the same principle applies. Now, if the *entire living world* is the *Supreme God*, it plainly follows that the *various parts and members* of it must be the *parts and members of God*. This was readily acknowledged by Seneca: *We are all members of one great Body* <note>original Latin: "Membra sumus Corporis magni"</note>; and *This whole world is God, and we are not only His members, but also His fellows or companions* <note>original Latin: "Totum hoc Deus est, Socii ejus & Membra sumus"</note>. This suggests that our human souls have a certain kind of *fellowship* with that *Great Soul of the Universe*. 

Accordingly, the <term>Soul of the World</term> and the whole <term>Mundane Animal</term> <note>the concept of the universe as a single, massive living creature</note> were frequently worshipped by the Pagans through these individual *members*—the primary *parts of the world* and the most important *elements of nature*—as if worshipping God piece by piece. Nevertheless, it does not follow that they truly considered these to be many *separate* gods. If that were the case, then not only every person, but every lowly animal, every plant, every herb, every blade of grass, every river, and every hill would have to be a separate god. 

<margin>Book 5, page 234.</margin> Origen observes this when arguing against the assertion of <term>Celsus</term> <note>a 2nd-century Greek philosopher and opponent of early Christianity</note>, who claimed that if the whole world were God, then all its individual parts must also be gods or divine:

<note>original Greek: ὡς εἶναι θεῖα οὐ μόνον ἀνθρώπους, ἀλλὰ καὶ πάντα τὰ ἄλογα ζῶα, μέρη ὄντα τοῦ κόσμου, πρὸς δὲ τούτοις καὶ τὰ φυτά· εἰ δὲ μέρη τοῦ κόσμου καὶ οἱ ποταμοὶ, καὶ τὰ ὄρη, καὶ αἱ θάλασσαι· ἆρ’ ἐπεὶ ὅλος ὁ κόσμος θεός ἐστιν, ἤδη καὶ οἱ ποταμοὶ καὶ αἱ θάλασσαι θεοί εἰσιν· ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ τοῦτο φήσουσιν Ἕλληνες· τὰς δὲ ἐπιστατοῦντας (εἴ ἄρα δαίμονας, ἢ θεοὺς, ὡς ἐκεῖνοι ὀνομάζουσι) ποταμοῖς καὶ θαλάσσαις, τούτους ἂν λέγοιεν θεούς. Καὶ τὸ καθολικὸν Κέλσου γίνεται καὶ καθ’ Ἕλληνας ψεῦδος, ὅτι ἐάντι ὅλον ἦ θεὸς, πάντως τὰ μέρη τούτου ἔστι θεῖα· κατὰ τοῦτο γὰρ θεῖα ἔσται ζῶα, καὶ μυῖαι, καὶ σκνίφες, καὶ σκώληκες, καὶ πᾶν τὸ τῶν ὄφεων εἶδος, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ τῶν ὀρνέων, καὶ τὸ τῶν ἰχθύων· ἅπερ οὐδ’ οἱ λέγοντες θεὸν εἶναι τὸν κόσμον, φήσουσιν·</note>

*From this it would follow that not only humans must be divine and gods, but also all brute animals too (since they are parts of the world), and plants besides. Furthermore, if rivers, mountains, and seas are parts of the world, then (if the whole world is God) they must also be gods according to Celsus. Yet even the Greeks themselves will not claim this; rather, they would say that those spirits or <term>demons</term> <note>in this context, "daemons" refers to lesser guiding spirits, not necessarily evil beings</note> (as they call them) who preside over these rivers and seas are gods. Therefore, Celsus’s general claim is false even by Greek standards: that if the whole is God, then all the parts must be divine. For it would follow from this that flies, gnats, worms, and every kind of serpent, bird, and fish are divine animals or gods—something even those who claim the world is God will not say.*

<summary>This page discusses the ancient view that the world is a single living organism (the Mundane Animal) whose "Soul" is God. It argues that while the parts of the world were seen as members of God, the Greeks did not consider every individual object, like a fly or a river, to be a separate deity.</summary>

-> This Living Universe Worshipped, BOOK I. <-

Therefore, while it is true that the Pagans often *personified* <note>original: "Personate"</note> and *deified* the *primary parts* of the *world* and the *things* of *nature*—just as they did the *various powers* and *virtues* of the <term>World Soul</term> <note>original: "Mundane Soul"</note> spread throughout the entire *world*—the educated among them did not view these as many *separate* and *distinct gods*. Instead, they worshipped them only as *parts* and *members* of *one great living universe* <note>original: "Mundane Animal"</note>, or rather, they worshipped the *soul of the entire world (their supreme deity)* through all these various *manifestations*. 

St. Augustine <note>original: "St. Austin"</note> suggests this when writing against Faustus the Manichean <note>a follower of Manichaeism, a dualistic religion that Augustine famously converted from to Christianity</note>. He prefers even the Pagan gods to those of the Manicheans: *“Now indeed the heaven, earth, sea, and air, sun, moon, and all the other stars—these are manifest to the eyes and present to our senses. When the Pagans worship these as gods, or as PARTS OF ONE GREAT GOD (for some of them think the entire universe is the GREATEST GOD), they worship things that actually exist. But since you [Manicheans] worship things that do not exist at all, you would be closer to true piety if you were at least Pagans who worship physical bodies; for though bodies ought not to be worshipped, they are at least true and real things.”* <note>original Latin: "Jam verò Cœlum, & Terra, & Mare, & Aer, & Sol, & Luna, & cætera sydera omnia, hæc manifesta oculis apparent, atque ipsis sensibus præsto sunt. Quæ cum Pagani tanquam Deos colunt, vel tanquam PARTES UNIUS MAGNI DEI (nam universum Mundum quidam eorum putant MAXIMUM DEUM) ea colunt quæ sunt. Vos autem cum ea colatis, quæ omninò non sunt, propinquiores essetis Veræ Pietati, si saltem Pagani essetis, qui Corpora colunt, etsi non colenda, tamen vera."</note>

<margin>Book 4, chapter 11. <note>original: "L. 4. c. 11."</note></margin>

This point is further insisted upon by the same St. Augustine in his book *The City of God* <note>original Latin: "De Civitate Dei"</note>. After listing many Pagan gods, he points out the foolishness of worshipping the various divided *members, parts*, and *powers* of the *one great God* when they are *personified* in that way: 

*“All these things which I have said, and whatever I have not said (for I did not think it necessary to mention everything), let all these gods and goddesses be one and the same Jupiter. Let them be his PARTS or his POWERS and VIRTUES, according to the sense of those who think God is the soul or mind of the whole world—an opinion held by many great scholars. If this is the case (though we will not examine the nature of that claim for now), what would these people lose if they worshipped the one God by a more sensible shortcut <note>original: "prudentiori Compendio"</note>? For how could any part of him be neglected if he himself were being worshipped? If, however, they fear that his omitted or neglected parts might become angry, then it follows that the universe is not actually the life of a single living organism <note>original: "Unius Animantis"</note> containing all the gods together as its own VIRTUES, MEMBERS, or PARTS. Instead, each part must have its own life separate from the others, if one part can be angry while another is not, or one pacified while another is provoked. But if they say that the whole—that is, Jupiter himself—could be offended if his PARTS were not also worshipped individually and piece-by-piece, that is a foolish argument. For none of the parts would be left out if the one God who possesses them all were worshipped.”* <note>original Latin: "Hæc omnia quæ dixi, & quæcunq; non dixi... stultè dicitur."</note> What would these

<page-num>537</page-num>
# CHAP. IV. In its Several Parts and Members.

What would these *Pagans* lose if, in a more sensible summary, they should worship *only one God*? For what part of him could be despised when his whole self was worshipped? But if they fear that his parts, if omitted or neglected, should be angry or take offense, then it is not as they pretend: the *life of one Great Animal* which at once contains all the gods as his virtues, members, or parts. Instead, it would mean every *part* has its own *life by itself*, separate from the rest, since *one of them may be angry when another is pleased*, and vice versa. But if it should be said that all together—that is, the whole *Jupiter*—might be offended if his *parts* were not all worshipped individually and singly, this would be foolishly said; because none of the parts can be omitted when *he, who has everything, is worshipped*.

Thus do the Pagans in the writings of *Athanasius* <note>original: "Athanasius"; a 4th-century Christian theologian and church father</note> also declare that they did not worship the various *parts of the world* as truly being so many *true and proper gods*, but only as the *parts* or *members* of their *one Supreme God*—that *Great <term>Mundane Animal</term>* <note>original: "Mundane Animal"; the "World Animal" or the universe viewed as a single living organism</note> (*or the whole animated world*) taken all together as one thing: <note>original Greek: ἀλλ’ ἴσως διαιρούμενα μὲν, καὶ καθ’ ἑαυτὰ λαμβανόμενα, ἐνδεᾶ αὐτὰ καὶ αὐτοὶ συνομολογοῦσιν, ὁμοῦ δὲ πάντα συνάπτοντες, καὶ ὡς ἓν ἀποτελοῦντες μέγα σῶμα, τὸ ὅλον θεὸν εἶναι φάσιν</note> *“But the Pagans themselves will acknowledge that the divided parts of the world, taken separately, are but impoverished and imperfect things; nevertheless, they contend that as they are joined all together by them into one Great Body (enlivened by one Soul), so the whole of them is truly and properly God.”* And now we think it is sufficiently evident that though these *Pagans verbally personified and deified* not only the several *powers and virtues* of the *one Supreme God* or World Soul spread throughout the entire world, but also the several *parts of the world itself* and the *natures of things*, yet their meaning in this was not to make these, in themselves, truly so many several *true and proper gods* (*much less independent ones*). Rather, they intended to worship *one Supreme God* (*which to them was the whole animated world*) in those various *parts* and *members*—as it were, piece by piece, or under so many *incomplete conceptions*.

<margin>Against Celsus, page 260.</margin>
The Pagans, therefore, were plainly divided in their *natural theology* regarding their opinions concerning the *Supreme God*. Some of them conceived him to be nothing higher than a *World Soul*, whereas others of them—to use the language of *Origen* <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian</note>—did <note>original Greek: ὑπερβαίνειν πᾶσαν τὴν αἰσθητὴν φύσιν, καὶ μηδαμοῦ αὐτῆς νομίζειν ἱδρύσθαι τὸν θεόν, p. 260. ἄνω δὲ καὶ ὑπὲρ τὰ σώματα ζητεῖν αὐτὸν</note> *“transcend all perceptible nature, and thinking God not at all to be located there, looked for him above all physical things.”* Now the former of these *Pagans* worshipped the whole *physical world* as the *body of God*. But the latter group, though they had higher thoughts of *God* than as a mere *World Soul*, still supposed *him* to have been the *cause* of all things, and so at first to have contained all things within himself. They also believed that the world, after it was made, was not cut off from him, nor did it exist alone by itself as a *dead thing*, but was closely united to him and livingly dependent on him. These, I say, though they did not take the world to be *God*, or the *body of God*, yet they also looked upon it...

<summary>This page argues that Pagan polytheism was effectively the worship of one Supreme God (the "World Animal") through its various parts, rather than a belief in many independent deities. It cites Athanasius and Origen to show that even when Pagans deified nature, they viewed the parts as imperfect on their own and divine only when united in the whole.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on how ancient philosophers and religious groups viewed the world as either the body of God or a sacred vessel for the divine.</meta>

<page-num>538</page-num>
<header>The World to some The Body: Book I.</header>

...as *Divine* and *Sacred*; and they supposed that God was to be worshipped in *All*, or that the whole world was to be worshipped as his *Image* or *Temple*. Thus *Plutarch*, though he strongly disliked the *deifying of inanimate things*, did nevertheless approve of worshipping God in the whole physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> world; he affirmed it to be "a most holy and most God-fitting temple" <note>original Greek: ἱερὸν ἁγιώτατον καὶ θεοπρεπέστατον</note>. And the ancient *Persians* or *Magi*—who by no means would allow God to be worshipped in any *artificial temples* made by human hands—did nonetheless worship God *under the open sky* <note>original Latin: "Sub Dio"</note> and upon the tops of mountains, in the whole physical world as his *natural temple*. As *Cicero* testifies: <margin>On the Laws, Book 2, Page 335.</margin> *“Neither do I follow the Persian Magi, by whose advice and persuasion Xerxes is said to have burned all the temples of the Greeks, because they enclosed and shut up their gods within walls. To those gods, they believed all things ought to be open and free, and the entire world should be their temple and home.”* <note>original Latin: "Nec sequor Magos Persarum, quibus auctoribus Xerxes inflammasse Templa Graeciæ dicitur, quod Parietibus inkluderent Deos quibus omnia deberent esse patentia ac libera, quorumque hic Mundus Omnis Templum esset & Domicilium"</note> 

And therefore, when *Diogenes Laertius* writes of these *Magi* that they did *“declare fire, earth, and water to be gods, but condemned all statues and images,”* <note>original Greek: Θεὸς ἀποφαίνεσθαι πῦρ καὶ γῆν καὶ ὕδωρ, τῶν δὲ ξοάνων καταγινώσκειν</note> we understand his meaning to be nothing other than this: since they worshipped God in no temple except that of the whole world, they also allowed no other statues or images of him than the *things of nature* and *parts of the world*. In this sense, and no other, they called fire, earth, and water "gods." For they are clearly represented this way by *Clement of Alexandria*, according to the express testimony of *Dinon*: <margin>Exhortation to the Greeks, page 43.</margin> *“Dinon affirms that the Persian Magi sacrificed under the open heavens, considering fire and water to be the only statues and images of the gods. For I would not here conceal their ignorance either; while they think they are avoiding one error, they fall into another. They do not accept wood and stones as the images of the gods, as the Greeks do, nor ibises and mongooses <term>ichneumones</term> as the Egyptians do, but only fire and water, as philosophers.”* <note>original Greek: θύειν ἐν ὑπαίθρῳ τοὺς μάγους ὁ Δίνων λέγει, θεῶν ἀγάλματα μόνα τὸ πῦρ καὶ ὕδωρ νομίζοντας. Οὐκ ἀπεκρυψάμην οὐδὲ τὴν τούτων ἄγνοιαν. Εἰ γὰρ καὶ τὰ μάλιστα ἀποφεύγειν οἴονται τῆς πλάνης, ἀλλ᾽ εἰς ἑτέραν κατολισθαίνουσιν ἀπάτην. Ἀγάλματα μὲν θεῶν οὐ ξύλα καὶ λίθους ὑπειλήφασιν, ὥσπερ Ἕλληνες· οὐδὲ μὴν ἴβιδας καὶ ἰχνεύμονας καθάπερ Αἰγύπτιοι· ἀλλὰ πῦρ τε καὶ ὕδωρ ὡς φιλόσοφοι</note> 

This difference between the pagan theologians—that some looked upon the whole world as God (or as the *body of God*) while others saw it only as the *image* or the *temple of God*—is noted by *Macrobius* in his commentary on *Scipio’s Dream*, <margin>Book 1, Chapter 14.</margin> where the world was called a temple: *“The whole world is rightly called here the temple of God, as an opposition to those who think that God is nothing else but the heaven itself and those celestial things we see. Therefore, to show that the omnipotence of the Highest God can scarcely be understood and can never be seen, the author called whatever is visible to human eyes His temple. Thus, whoever honors these things as temples still owes the greatest worship to the Creator; and anyone brought into this temple should know that he must live with the reverence of a priest.”* <note>original Latin: "Bene autem Universus Mundus Dei Templum vocatur, propter illos qui æstimant, nihil esse aliud Deum, nisi Cælum ipsum & Cælestia ista quæ cernimus. Ideo ut Summi Omnipotentiam Dei, ostenderet posse vix intelligi, nunquam posse videri, quicquid humano subjicitur aspectui Templum ejus vocavit; ut qui hæc veneratur ut Templa, cultum tamen maximum debeat Conditori; sciatque quisquis in usum Templi hujus inducitur, ritu sibi vivendum Sacerdotis"</note>

<header>Chapter IV. To others, The Temple of God.</header>

...think God to be nothing else but the heaven itself, and those heavenly things which we see (or the whole *sensible world animated*). Therefore *Cicero*, so that he might show the omnipotence of the first and supreme God—which can scarcely be understood and not at all perceived by the senses—calls whatever falls under human sight **His Temple**. He does this so that he who worships these things as the temple of God might, in the meantime, remember that the chief worship is due to the **Maker** and **Creator** of them; and also that he himself ought to live in the world like a **priest** or **initiate** <note>original: "Mysta"</note>, holily and religiously. 

And thus we see that the Pagans were universally **World-worshippers** <note>original Latin: "Cosmolatræ"</note> in one sense or another. This does not mean they worshipped the world as a **dead** and **inanimate** thing, but either as the **body** of **God**, or at least as his **temple** or **image**. Neither of these views limited their worship to that which was merely **sensible** and **visible**, but directed it toward that great **Mind** or **Soul** which **framed** and **governed** the whole world **intelligently**. Though this was also called by them (not the "nature of things," but) **the common nature** <note>original Greek: φύσις κοινή</note> and **the nature of the universe** <note>original Greek: φύσις τοῦ παντός or τῶν ὅλων</note>, because it contained within it the **generative principles** <note>original: "spermatick Reasons"</note> or **formative principles** <note>original: "Plastick Principles"</note> of the entire world.

Furthermore, these **Pagan Theists** universally acknowledged the whole world to be an **animal** <note>meaning a living being</note>, and that **world-animal** <note>original: "Mundane Animal"</note> also to be a **god**. Those among them who did not suppose it to be the **first** and **highest God** consequently conceived it—as has been already observed—to be either a **second** or at least a **third god**. And thus *Origen* writes: 

> "The Greeks plainly say that the whole world is a god; the Stoics say it is the first god, those following Plato say it is the second, and some of them say it is the third." <note>original Greek: σαφῶς δὴ τὸν ὅλον κόσμον λέγουσιν εἶναι θεὸν, Στωϊκοὶ μὲν τὸν πρῶτον, οἱ δ' ἀπὸ Πλάτωνος τὸν δεύτερον, τινὲς δὲ αὐτῶν τὸν τρίτον</note> 

Those Platonists who called the **world-animal**, or **animated world**, the **second god**, looked upon that whole **Platonic Trinity of Divine Hypostases** (**The Good**, **Mind**, and **Soul** <note>original Greek: τἀγαθὸν, Νῦς and Ψυχή</note>) as only **one first God**. But those others who called it a **third god** supposed a greater distinction between those **three persons** <note>original: "Hypostases"</note> and made several gods of them: the first, a **Monad** or **simple goodness**; the second, **Mind** or **Intellect**; the third, **Psyche** or the **universal soul**. They concluded without further ado that this third was the **immediate soul of this physical world, existing with it from eternity.** 

Now this **second god**, which was the whole **animated world** to both the Egyptians and the Platonists, was said by both to be not only the **temple** and **image**, but also the **son of the first God**. 
<margin>Page 329, 330, 331.</margin> 
It has already been proved that the Egyptians called the **animated world** the **son of God**; and that other Pagans did the like is evident from this passage by *Celsus*. In it, he claims that the Christians called their **Jesus** the **son of God** in imitation of those ancient Pagans who 
<margin>Origen against Celsus, Book 5, Page 308.</margin> 
had styled the **world** so: 

> "I shall show where this idea came to them—to call him the son of God. Our ancestors called this world, as it was born of God, both his child and a young god. For this child of God and that one are very similar." <note>original Greek: ὁπόθεν δὲ καὶ αὐτὸ τοῦτο ἐπῆλθεν αὐτοῖς, θεοῦ υἱὸν καλεῖν, σημαίνω· Ἄνδρες παλαιοὶ, τόνδε τὸν κόσμον, ὡς ἐκ θεοῦ γενόμενον, παῖδά τε αὐτοῦ καὶ ἠίθεον προσεῖπον. Πάνυ γὰρ ὅμοιος οὗτός τε κἀκεῖνος παῖς θεοῦ</note> 

Whence these Christians came to call their *Jesus* the *son of God*, I shall now declare: namely, because our ancestors had called the *world* so...

...made by God, the *Son of God*, and *God*. Now, do you not think there is a fine *similarity* <note>original: "similitude"</note> between these two *Sons of God*—theirs and ours?
<margin>Original citation: Against Celsus, page 208.</margin> Regarding these words of his, *Origen* writes as follows: "As if we [Christians] were speaking of God, having misrepresented the things concerning the world—as it was made by God and is both His son and God." <note>original Greek: ὡς ἢ τὸν θεὸν ἡμᾶς λέγειν, ὡς παραποιήσαντας τὰ περὶ τοῦ κόσμου, ὡς ἐκ θεοῦ γενομένου, καὶ υἱὸν ὄντα αὐτοῦ καὶ θεὸν</note> *Celsus* assumed that we *Christians* had borrowed this title, "the Son of God," from the Pagans, because they called the World—as it was made by God—the *Son of God* and *God*. Therefore, these Pagans, who looked upon the entire **Animated World** only as the *Second God* and *Son of God*, undoubtedly also worshipped the *First God* within the World. They likely did this by personifying and deifying his various parts and members. This helps us understand what caused the mistake made by recent writers who claimed that the Pagans worshipped the *inanimate parts* of the world as if they were true and proper gods. These writers failed to see that the Pagans worshipped those parts only as the living members of *One Great Mundane Animal* <note>The concept that the entire universe is a single, giant living organism.</note>. To them, this world-animal was, if not the *First God*, at least the *Second God*—the temple, image, and son of the *First God*.

And now we have (as we believe) given a full account of the *seeming polytheism* of the Pagans. We have addressed not only their *Poetical* and *Fabulous* theology but also their *Political* or *Civil Theology*. The former was nothing but imagination and fiction, an attempt to make divine things resemble human things. The latter was nothing more than *popular opinion and error*, combined with the *laws* and *institutions* of *statesmen* and *politicians*. These were designed primarily to amuse the common people <note>original: "vulgar"</note> and keep them in better obedience and subjection to civil laws. Besides these, the intelligent Pagans generally acknowledged *another theology*, which was neither fiction nor mere opinion and law, but Nature and Philosophy—or *absolute truth* and *reality*. According to this *Natural* and *Philosophic Theology* of theirs, there was only *One Unmade, self-originated Deity*, and many other *Created Gods* who served as his inferior ministers. Thus, those many Poetical and Political gods could not possibly be viewed as anything other than either the *created ministers* of One Supreme God (whether considered individually or collectively), or else as the *many names* <note>original: "Polyonymy"</note> and *various titles* of Him, based on different ideas and partial concepts of Him and His various *powers* and *manifestations* in the world, which were *personified* and *deified*. We have already proved that this latter view was the most generally accepted opinion among Pagan theologians. This aligns with the philosopher *Euclides*, who said, *There is One Supreme Good (or Highest Deity) called by Many Names* <note>original Greek: ἓν τἀγαθὸν πολλοῖς ὀνόμασι καλούμενον</note>, and with *Antisthenes*, whom we cited earlier, who said *that the many popular gods were but one and the same Natural God*—or as *Lactantius* adds, *the Maker of the whole world* <note>original Latin: Summæ totius Artifex</note>.
<margin>Book 1, chapter 5.</margin>

We shall conclude by repeating what has already been suggested: although intelligent Pagans generally rejected their fabulous theology, *Saint Augustine* <note>original: "St. Austin"</note> tells us that when the absurdities of those myths were pressed against them, they would commonly reply, "Far be it; that is the chatter of fables" <note>original Latin: Absit, inquiunt, Fabularum est ista Garrulitas</note>. And again: "You are returning to fables once more" <note>original Latin: Rursus, inquiunt, ad Fabulas redis</note>. Far be it...
<margin>The City of God, Book 4, chapter 10.</margin>

# CHAPTER IV. To be Deceived in their Religion.

...from us (they say) to think such things; this is nothing but the chatter of idle fables, and they say, *You would bring us back to fables*. Although they recognized another theology besides their *Civil* <note>Theology related to state laws and public rituals.</note> one—namely, the *Natural* and *Philosophical* theology, which they saw as the only *True* one—they nonetheless acknowledged a kind of necessity. They felt that in those times, at least, there should be another theology framed and presented that would be better suited to the common people's understanding, since the *common people* <note>original: "Vulgar"</note> were not as capable of grasping the *Natural* and *Philosophical* versions. 

Thus, the *Roman High Priest Scaevola* <note>original: "Roman Pontifex scævola"</note> in the writings of *Saint Augustine* <note>original: "St. Austin"</note> declares, *He thinks it is expedient for cities to be deceived in religion*, <note>original: "Expedire existimat falli in Religione Civitates"</note> or to have something *False* or *Mythical* <note>original: "Fabulous"</note> mixed in with it. He gave this reason for it: because the *Natural* and *Philosophic Theology* contained many things which, though *True*, would be harmful for the common people to know. For example, he mentions the idea *That the true God has neither sex, nor age, nor defined body parts*, <note>original: "Quod Verus Deus nec Sexum habeat, nec Ætatem, nec definita Corporis Membra"</note> and that *Hercules* and *Aesculapius*, etc., were not *Gods* but *Men*, subject to the same weaknesses <note>original: "obnoxious to the same infirmities"</note> as others, and so on. 

The learned *Varro*, in his book on religions, publicly maintained the same doctrine. *Varro, speaking of religions, clearly says that many things are true which it is not useful for the common people to know; and many things which, even if they are false, it is expedient for the people to think otherwise. For this reason, the Greeks enclosed their <term>Teletæ</term> or mysteries within walls and kept them under a seal of secrecy.* <note>original: "Varro de Religionibus loquens, evidenter dicit, Multa esse Vera quæ vulgo scire non sit Utile; Multaque quæ tametsi Falsa sint, aliter existimare Populum expediat: & ideo Græcos Teletas & Mysteria taciturnitate parietibusque clausisse, &c." <term>Teletæ</term> refers to religious initiations or rites.</note> Regarding this statement by *Varro*, *Saint Augustine* notes: *Varro here plainly discovers and betrays the whole counsel and secrecy of statesmen and politicians, by whom cities and nations were governed.* He reveals their very *Secret of Government* <note>original: "Arcanum of Government"</note>—namely, that people were to be deceived in their *Religion* for their own good and the good of their *governors*. *Saint Augustine* adds that *Evil Demons* were much gratified by this doctrine and liked this *fraud* and *imposture* very well, as it gave them an advantage to *rule* and *tyrannize* over both the *deceivers* and the *deceived*. 

Finally, *Strabo*, though otherwise a grave and sober writer, speaks freely and bluntly to the same purpose: *It is not possible for women and the common multitude to be led toward piety, holiness, and faith merely by philosophical reason and truth; this must be done through superstition, and that cannot happen without the help of myth-making and supernatural or wonderful stories.* <note>original Greek: οὐ γὰρ ὄχλόν τε γυναικῶν καὶ παντὸς χυδαίου πλήθους ἐπαγαγεῖν λόῳ δυνατὸν φιλοσόφῳ, καὶ προσκαλέσασθαι πρὸς εὐσέβειαν καὶ οσιότητα καὶ πίσιν· ἀλλὰ δεῖ καὶ διὰ δεισιδαιμονίας, τοῦτο δ᾽ οὐκ ἄνευ μυθοποιΐας καὶ τερατείας.</note> From this, it is plain that *Strabo* did not only allow for the necessity of a *Civil Theology* alongside the *Natural* and *Philosophical*, but also for a *Mythical* <note>original: "Fabulous"</note> and *Poetical* one as well. This is less surprising in these *Pagans*, because some *Christians* also seem to acknowledge a kind of truth in this idea. *Synesius* himself, writing in this man-

Indeed, they did not think it safe to declare natural and true theology indiscriminately to everyone. Plato himself hinted at this in these words: "Just as it is hard to find the maker and father of this universe, so also, once found, it is impossible to declare him to the common people." <note>original: "τὸν ποιητὴν καὶ πατέρα τοῦδε τοῦ παντὸς, εἰς πάντας ἀδύνατον λέγειν"</note> Therefore, because God was so difficult to understand, they believed the common people should be allowed to worship him through his *works*, piece by piece, according to his various manifestations. That is, they should have at least a *civil theology* distinct from *natural* and *philosophical* theology, if not a *mythical* <note>original: "Fabulous"</note> one as well.

### XXXV.

We have now finished the first of the three points we intended to emphasize: that the Pagans worshipped one and the same Supreme God under many personal names. Thus, much of their *polytheism* was only *apparent and imaginary* <note>original: "Seeming and Phantastical"</note>, and was really nothing more than the *polyonymy* <note>term: the practice of giving many names to a single entity</note> of *one Supreme God*. They created many poetic and political *gods* out of that *one natural God*, worshipping God in parts and pieces. 

This matches the clear admission of Maximus of Madaura <note>A 4th-century rhetorician who argued that pagans and Christians essentially worshipped the same God.</note> cited earlier: "We invoke the powers of the one Supreme God, which are spread throughout the work of the world, under many different names. As we honor his various parts, as it were, piece by piece through different prayers, we are seen to worship him as a whole, leaving out nothing of him." <note>original: "Unius Summi Dei Virtutes, per Mundanum Opus Diffusas, nos multis Vocabulis invocamus; & dum Ejus quasi quædam Membra carptim variis Supplicationibus prosequimur, Totum colere videmur"</note>

We shall now proceed to the second point: besides this use of many names for one Supreme God in the poetic and civil theology of the Pagans (which was their apparent and imaginary polytheism), they also had a *real polytheism*. Even in their natural and philosophical theology, they acknowledged a multiplicity of gods—that is, substantial, intelligent beings superior to humans that really exist in the world. 

Although they called these beings "gods," they did not believe they were *unmade and self-existent* <note>original: "ἀγέννητοι and αὐτοφυεῖς"</note>, or independent beings. Instead, all of them (with only one exception) were *generated gods* <note>original: "γενητοὶ θεοὶ"</note>, according to the broader definition of that word mentioned before.

<margin>Pages 243, 254.</margin>
That is, they were not "made in time," but were "produced from a superior cause." <note>original: "ἀπ᾽ αἰτίας γεννητοὶ"</note> Plutarch, proposing this as one of his "Platonic Questions"—*why* the highest or Supreme God <note>original: "ὁ ἀνωτάτω θεὸς"</note> was called by Plato "both the Father and Maker of all things"—gives this reply in the...

### CHAPTER IV. and Many Substantial Powers.

The words previously cited state: "He is the father of the produced gods and of men (as Homer names him), but the maker of the irrational and inanimate" <note>original: "ἡ τῶν μὲν θεῶν τῶν γεννητῶν καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων πατὴρ ἐστιν ( ὡς Ὅμηρος ἐπονομάζει ) ποιητὴς δὲ τῶν ἀλόγων καὶ ἀψύχων"</note>. This suggests that he was perhaps called the Father of all the produced <note>original: "Generated"</note> gods and of men (as he is also styled in Homer), but the maker of all other irrational and inanimate beings. From this passage by Plutarch, it plainly appears that the one highest god <note>original: "ὁ ἀνωτάτω θεὸς"</note>, being in every way unmade and unproduced <note>original: "ἀγένητος"</note>, was thought to be the maker or father of all the other gods, who were therefore called "generated" <note>original: "γεννητοὶ"</note>.

<margin>Plutarch, Symposium, Book 8, Chapter 1.</margin>
This is further plainly declared elsewhere by the same Plutarch in these words: "Plato calls the one unmade and eternal God the father and maker of the world and of all other things produced" <note>original: "Πλάτωνος πατέρα καὶ ποιητὴν τοῦτε κόσμου καὶ τῶν ἄλλων γεννητῶν, τὸν Ἀγέννητον καὶ Ἀΐδιον θεὸν ἐπονομάζοντος"</note>. And though some of those "many gods" of Plato's were also called by him eternal <note>original: "Ἀΐδιοι"</note>, yet they were also "produced" <note>original: "γεννητοὶ"</note> in another sense—that is, produced and derived by way of emanation from that One, who is in every way un-derived and independent of any other cause <note>original: "Ἀγένητος"</note>.

<margin>Proclus, Platonic Theology, Book 3, Chapter 7.</margin>
And thus Proclus universally pronounces: "All the gods owe their being gods to the first God" <note>original: "Τὸ εἶναι θεοὶ, πάντες οἱ θεοὶ, διὰ τὸν πρῶτον ἔχουσι θεόν·"</note>. He adds that the first God is therefore called the fountain of the godhead <note>original: "πηγὴ τῆς θεότητος"</note>.

Therefore, the many gods of the intelligent pagans were derived from one God, and were only subservient powers <note>original: "ὑπουργοὶ δυνάμεις"</note> (as Plutarch somewhere calls them), or the ministers of the one supreme unmade deity. This supreme deity (as has been observed before) was frequently called "God" <note>original: "θεὸς"</note> by these pagans by way of eminence; while those other inferior or produced gods were called "the gods" <note>original: "θεοὶ"</note> to distinguish them from him.

<margin>Against Celsus, Book 4, page 200.</margin>
Accordingly, the view of Celsus is represented in Origen as: "That the gods were the makers of the bodies of all animals, the souls of them only being the work of God" <note>original: "θεὸς δημιουργὸς εἶναι πάντων σωμάτων, μόνης ψυχῆς ἔργον οὔσης θεοῦ·"</note>.

<margin>Ammianus Marcellinus, Book 22.</margin>
Moreover, these inferior gods are styled by Ammianus Marcellinus as **substantial powers** <note>original: "Substantiales Potestates"</note>, probably to distinguish them from those other pagan gods that were not substantial beings, but only various names and concepts of the one supreme God, or his powers personified and deified individually. These "substantial powers" mentioned by Ammianus Marcellinus (through whom divination and prophecy were shared with men) were all said to be subject to that one sovereign deity called **Themis**. He says the ancient theologians seated her "in the bedchamber and throne of Jupiter" <note>original: "In Cubili & Solio Jovis"</note>; indeed, some poets made her the wife of Jupiter, and others his sister.

<margin>Plutarch, Life of Alexander.</margin>
And Anaxarchus, in Plutarch, styles her "Jupiter's assessor" <note>original: "πάρεδρον τοῦ Διὸς"</note>, although that philosopher abused the fable and grossly corrupted its meaning, as if it signified "that whatever is done by the sovereign power is therefore lawful and right" <note>original: "πᾶν τὸ πραχθὲν ὑπὸ τοῦ κρατοῦντος θέμιτον εἶναι καὶ δίκαιον"</note>. However, the true moral of the story was this: that Justice or Righteousness sits in counsel with God, and in His mind and will, prescribes laws to nature and the whole world. **Themis**, therefore, was another name for God among the pagans, according to His universal character, besides those names mentioned before. And when Plato in his book...

# Themis; The Eternal Law, or God. Book I.

<margin>
Book 2.
</margin>
<margin>
Concerning the Goddess Themis, page 39.
</margin>
[The] Book of Laws would have men swear by the names of those three gods: *Jupiter*, *Apollo*, and *Themis*. These were but several partial notions of the one supreme deity. The meaning of this, as Pighius <note>Albert Pighius (c. 1490–1542), a Dutch theologian.</note> observes, is that oaths ought to be sanctioned by Divine fear, by Truth itself, and by Equity <note>original: "Timore Divino, Veritate ipsa, ac Æquitate sanciri debere Juramenta"</note>. For in *Jupiter* is understood the power of the supreme divinity, the punisher of falsehood and perjury; in *Apollo*, the light of Truth; and in *Themis*, what is just, right, and lawful <note>original: "In Jove enim Summi Numinis Potestatem, Falsi ac Perjurii Vindicem; in Apolline Veritatis Lumen; in Themide, Jus, Fas atque Licitum esse intelligitur"</note>. For Themis is the eternal and universal Law itself, prescribed to the world and to nature <note>original: "Est enim Themis, ipsa Lex æterna atq; Universalis, Mundo ac Naturæ præscripta"</note>; or according to Cicero, the right reason of the highest Jupiter <note>original: "Ratio recta Summi Jovis"</note>. Ficinus <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), an influential Italian humanist philosopher.</note>, in his commentary, mainly agrees with this.

So, when the pagan theologians affirmed that the divine power <note>original: "Numen"</note> of *Themis* presided over the spirits of the elements and all those other substantial powers from whom divination was shared with men, their meaning was clearly this: there was one supreme deity ruling over all the other gods, and the *Divine Mind*—which prescribes laws to nature and the whole world and contains all the *Fatal Decrees* <term>Fatal Decrees: The predetermined will of God or fate regarding the unfolding of history.</term> within it, according to the unfolding of which things come to pass in the world—was the fountain from which all divination proceeded. These secrets were more or less shared from that source with those inferior created spirits. The philosophy of pagan theology among the Greeks was plainly nothing other than this: that there is *one unmade, self-existent deity* who is the original source of all, and that there are many other substantial powers or spirits created by it to act as the *ministers* of its providence in the world. However, there was much poetry or "poetic fancy" intermingled with this philosophy, acting as a decorative flourish to create their pagan theology.

Thus, as has been declared before, the pagans held both *one God* and *many gods* in different senses: *one unmade, self-existent deity*, and *many generated* or *created gods*. Onatus the Pythagorean declared that those who asserted only one God and not many did not understand what the dignity and majesty of the divine transcendency consisted in—namely, in ruling over gods. Likewise, Plotinus <note>A major Greek-speaking philosopher of the ancient world and the founder of Neoplatonism.</note> conceived that the supreme God was most of all glorified, not by being contracted into one, but by having multitudes of gods derived from him and dependent on him, and that the honor done to them redounded <term>redounded: contributed or came back to.</term> back to him. 

In this, two things must be distinguished. First, according to the pagan theists, God was no *solitary being*; rather, there were multitudes of gods, or substantial powers and living, understanding natures superior to men. These were neither *self-existent* nor *generated out of matter*, but were all generated or created from one supreme source. Secondly, because these were all supposed to have some influence, more or less, upon the government of the world and the affairs of mankind, they were all conceived to be the proper objects of men's religious worship, adoration, and prayer. Accordingly, pagan devotion was scattered among them all. Nor were the gods of the Oriental pagans merely *dead statues* and *images*, as some would conclude from the Bible, but *living, understanding beings* superior to men (though worshipped through images). This is consistent with the reply of the Chaldeans in the Book of *Daniel* to *Nebuchadnezzar*, when he required them to tell his [dream]—

As it is written, *“Thousand thousands ministered unto him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him,”* and, *“You have come to an innumerable company of Angels.”* 

But regarding the second point—that *religious worship* and *invocation* <term>the act of calling upon a deity in prayer</term> rightly belong to these *created spirits*—this is constantly denied and condemned in the Scriptures. Such worship is a thing uniquely reserved for that one God who was the Creator of Heaven and Earth. This prophecy, which is only partially fulfilled now, will have its complete accomplishment when *“the kingdoms of this world become the kingdoms of our Lord and of his Christ.”*

### XXXVI.

We shall now show specifically what these *Many Gods* of the Pagans were. It has often been observed that the Pagans were divided in their *philosophical or natural theology* regarding their *opinions concerning the Supreme God*. Some of them thought *the Divine is elevated above the whole of nature* <note>original Greek: "τὸ θεῖον ἐξῃρημένον εἶναι τῆς ὅλης φύσεως."</note>—that the Supreme Deity was an abstract being, raised above nature and the entire world. Others, however, believed he was nothing higher than a *Soul of the World* <note>original Latin: "Anima Mundi."</note>. 

The first of these two groups were mainly the *Pythagoreans* and the *Platonists* among the Greeks. Accordingly, they had several distinctions among them concerning their gods, such as between the *supermundane and the mundane gods* <note>original Greek: "ὑπερκόσμιοι θεοὶ καὶ οἱ ἐγκόσμιοι." Supermundane gods exist beyond the physical world; mundane gods exist within it.</note>; the *eternal and the generated gods* <note>original Greek: "θεοὶ ἀΐδιοι καὶ οἱ γεννητοὶ."</note> (this latter word being used in a narrower sense for those who were made in time or had a beginning to their existence); and lastly, the *intelligible and the sensible gods* <note>original Greek: "νοητοὶ θεοὶ καὶ οἱ αἰσθητοὶ." Intelligible gods are known through the mind/intellect; sensible gods are perceived through the senses, such as the stars.</note>. 

The *supermundane, eternal, and intelligible gods* of these Pythagoreans and Platonists were, first and foremost, those *three primary hypostases* <note>original Greek: "τρεῖς ἀρχικαὶ ὑποστάσεις."</note> (as Plotinus <note>A major Greek philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) and the founder of Neoplatonism.</note> calls them). These are the *Three Divine Persons* that serve as the principles of the universe: namely *The Good* or *The One*, *Mind*, and *Soul* <note>original Greek/Latin: "Tagathon or Hen, Nous and Psyche; or Monad, Mind, and Soul."</note>. 

That this Trinity was not merely an invention of Plato's, but much older than him, is plainly stated by Plotinus in these words: <margin>Ennead 5, Book 1.</margin> *“These doctrines are not new, nor of today, but were spoken of long ago, though not openly. The discourses now extant are merely explanations of them. We confirm that these opinions are ancient by the evidence of Plato's own writings; for even Parmenides <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher.</note> touched upon such an opinion before him.”* <note>original Greek: "Καὶ εἶναι τοὺς λόγους τούσδε μὴ καινοὺς, μὴ δὲ νῦν, ἀλλὰ πάλαι μὲν εἰρῆσθαι μὴ ἀναπεπταμένως, τοὺς δὲ νῦν λόγους ἐξηγητὰς ἐκείνων γεγονέναι· μαρτυρίοις πιστωσαμένοις τὰς δόξας ταύτας παλαιὰς εἶναι, τοῖς αὐτοῦ τοῦ Πλάτωνος γράμμασιν· ἥπτετο μὲν οὖν καὶ Παρμενίδης πρότερον τῆς τοιαύτης δόξης."</note>

Now it is well known that Parmenides was a follower of the *Pythagorean sect*, and therefore it is probable that this *doctrine of a Divine Triad* was also one of the secrets <note>original: "Arcanums."</note> of that school. This is further confirmed because Numenius, a famous Pythagorean, entertained...

And we have already proved that a *Trinity* was part of that *Orphic tradition* through Amelius, who affirmed (in Proclus) that Plato’s "Three Kings" were the same as the Orphic Trinity of *Phanes*, *Uranus*, and *Cronus*.

Moreover, since all three of these—Orpheus, Pythagoras, and Plato—traveled into Egypt, they were there initiated into that *Arcane Theology* of the Egyptians (called *Hermetic*). Therefore, it seems probable (as was observed before) that this doctrine of a *Divine Triad* was also part of the *Arcane Theology* of the Egyptians.

It has also been noted that there were some traces of such a *Trinity* in the *Mithraic Mysteries* among the Persians, derived from Zoroaster. Likewise, it was expressly contained in the *Chaldean Oracles* (of whatever authority they may be). Furthermore, it has been indicated that the Samothracians very anciently had a certain *Trinity of Gods* who were the highest of all their gods. These were called by a Hebrew name as well: *Kabirim* <note>original: "Cabbarim."</note>, or the *Mighty Gods*. It was from this source that the *Roman Capitoline Trinity of Gods* was derived. The second of these was Minerva, who among the Latins (like Athena among the Greeks) was understood to signify *Divine Wisdom*.

Lastly, the *Ternary* or *Triad* was not only considered a *Sacred Number* among the Pythagoreans, but was also believed to contain some *mystery* in Nature. Therefore, it was used by other Greeks and Pagans in their religious rites, <margin>Aristotle, On the Heavens, Book 1, chapter 5.</margin> as Aristotle informs us:

> Therefore, having received this from Nature—as if observing her laws—we make use of this Number of Three in the sacrifices to the Gods and other purifications. <note>original Greek: διὸ παρὰ τῆς φύσεως εἰληφότες ὡσπερεὶ νόμους ἐκείνης, καὶ πρὸς τὰς ἁγιστείας τῶν θεῶν χρώμεθα τῷ ἀριθμῷ τούτῳ·</note>

# The Pagans' Trinity Derived; Book I.

...reason, though there be nothing in it (if rightly understood) that is repugnant to Reason. And since there are in the ancient writings of the Old Testament certain significations of a *Plurality* in the *Deity*, or of more than one *Hypostasis* <term>subsistent person or individual reality</term>, we may reasonably conclude that what *Proclus* asserts of this *Trinity* (as it was contained in the Chaldaic Oracles) is true: that it was first a *Theology of Divine Tradition* or *Revelation* <note>original Greek: Θεοδόσδοτο Θεολογίᾳ</note>, or a *Divine Cabala* <term>oral tradition</term>—namely, among the Hebrews first, and from them afterwards communicated to the Egyptians and other nations. 

It should not be considered a significant objection to the contrary that the Platonists, Pythagoreans, and other Pagan theologians did not express this, their *Trinity*, in the exact words of the *Athanasian Creed*, nor according to the form of the *Nicene Council*. This *Mystery* was gradually imparted to the world, and at first only sparingly to the Hebrews themselves, either in their *written* or *oral tradition*; but it was afterwards more fully revealed under Christianity, the whole framework of which was built upon it. 

Nevertheless, it was not so distinctly and precisely determined, nor so punctually and scrupulously stated among the Christians either, until after the rise of heresies concerning it. Nor, when all was done, did the Orthodox themselves at first universally agree in the significance of the word *Homoousios* <note>original Greek: 'ομόοσο</note>, meaning *Co-essential* or *Consubstantial*. Lastly, it is not at all to be wondered at that in such a *difficult* and *mysterious* point as this, there should be some diversity of apprehensions among the reputed Orthodox Christians themselves, and much less, therefore, among Pagans and philosophers. However, we freely acknowledge that as this *Divine Tradition* was but little understood by many of those who accepted it among the Pagans, it was also much corrupted and adulterated by many of them.

<margin>In Timaeus of Plato, p. 93. Ibid.</margin>
For first, the Pagans universally called this, their *Trinity*, a *Trinity of Gods*: either the First, the Second, and the Third God <note>original Greek: ἢ πρῶτον, ἢ Δεύτερον, καὶ ἢ τρίτον Θεὸν</note>. The more philosophical among them also called it a *Trinity of Causes*, and a *Trinity of Principles*, and sometimes a *Trinity of Creators*. Thus, this tradition of the *Trinity* is styled in *Proclus* as "the Tradition of the Three Gods" <note>original Greek: ἡ τῆς τελῶν θεῶν διδάσκαλος</note>. Accordingly, it is said of *Numenius* <note>original: "Nemenius"</note> by him that "having praised the Three Gods," he "affectedly" <note>original: "Tragically"; Greek: τριχωδῶν, likely meant as τραγῳδῶν, acting or speaking in the style of a tragedy</note> called them "the Grandfather, the Son, and the Nephew" <note>original Greek: πάππον, ἔγγονον, ἀπόγονον</note>. *Numenius* thereby suggested that as the Second of these *Gods* was the offspring of the First God, so the Third (called the *Nephew* of the First) was derived both from him and from the Second—from the First as the Grandfather, and from the Second as his Father. 

*Harpocration* likewise, along with *Atticus* and *Amelius*, are said by *Proclus* to have entertained this same tradition of the *Three Gods*, the latter of these styling them "Three Kings" and "Three Creators" <note>original Greek: βασιλέας τρεῖς and τρεῖς δημιεργὸν</note> or makers of the whole world. In like manner, *Plotinus*, speaking of the Second of these *Three Hypostases* (that is, *Nous*, the First *Mind* or *Intellect*), calls him "the Second God" <note>original Greek: δ’οὔτερον Θεὸν</note>: 

<margin>Enneads 5, Book 5, chapter 3.</margin>
> "And this nature, which is not from itself, appeared to itself before seeing that one; but it sits under it and is not separated from it, because it is as it were a foundation, or hangs from it. For while that one remains..." <note>original Greek: καὶ αὕτη ἡ φύσις, ἡ οὐκ ἀπ’αὐτοῦ, πεφάνων ἑαυτῇ, πρὶν ὀρᾶν ἐκεῖνον· ὃ δ᾽ ὕπακάθηται μὴ χωρίζευται ὅτι καλῶς ἔτως οἶον κρηπίδ᾽, ἢ ἐξ αὑτῷ ἐξήρτηται. ἔτι γὸ ἐκείνου βαινόντος</note>

[Neither] descending into any inanimate thing, nor yet onto a soul immediately, but that there should be an incredible beauty proceeding before him: <note>original Greek: βαίνοντα μηδ' ἐν ἀψύχῳ τινὸς, μὴ δ' αὖ ἐπὶ ψυχῆς εὐθὺς βεβηκέναι, ἀλλ' εἶναι αὐτῷ κάλλος ἀμήχανον πρὸ αὐτοῦ προϊόν·</note>

And so that we may also give a taste of the *mystical theology* and *spiritual fervor* <note>original: "enthusiasm"—historically, this meant a claim of direct divine inspiration</note> of these *Platonists* as well, *Porphyry* <note>original: Porphyrius</note> in his *Life of Plotinus* affirms that both *Plotinus* and *he himself* sometimes experienced a kind of *ecstatic union* with the *first* of these *three Gods*—that which is above *mind* and *understanding*:

As Plotinus often tried to raise his thoughts to the first and highest God, that God appeared to him—who has neither form nor any specific idea, but is established above intellect and all that can be understood. To him, I, Porphyry, claim to have once drawn near and been united in the sixty-eighth year of my age <note>original Greek: πολλάκις ἐνάγοντι ἑαυτὸν εἰς τὸν πρῶτον καὶ ἐπέκεινα θεὸν ταῖς ἐννοίαις, ἐφάνη ἐκεῖνος ὁ μήτε μορφήν, μήτε τινὰ ἰδέαν ἔχων, ὑπὲρ δὲ νοῦν καὶ πᾶν τὸ νοητὸν ἱδρυμένος· ᾧ δὴ καὶ ἐγὼ Πορφύριος ἅπαξ λέγω πλησιάσαι καὶ ἑνωθῆναι.</note>.

> *Plotinus often endeavored to raise up his mind to the First and Highest God; that God sometimes appeared to him—who has neither form nor idea, but is placed above intellect and all that is intelligible—to whom I, Porphyry, affirm myself to have been once united in the sixty-eighth year of my age.*

And again afterward:

His [Plotinus's] end and goal was to be united with and draw near to the God who is over all; and he achieved this goal four times while I was with him, by a certain inexpressible energy <note>original Greek: τέλος αὐτῷ καὶ σκοπὸς ἦν, τὸ ἑνωθῆναι καὶ πελάσαι τῷ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεῷ, ἔτυχε δὲ τετράκις που ὅτε συνήμην αὐτῷ τοῦ σκοποῦ τούτου</note>.

> *Plotinus's chief aim and scope was to be united to and conjoined with the Supreme God, who is above all; he attained this goal four several times while I was with him, by a certain ineffable energy.*

That is, *Plotinus* aimed at such a kind of *rapturous and ecstatic union* with *The One* <note>original Greek: τὸ ἓν</note> and *The Good* <note>original Greek: τ’ἀγαθὸν</note>—the *first* of the *three highest Gods* (called *The One* and *The Good*)—as he himself described toward the end of his *last book*. There he calls it a touch <note>original Greek: ἐπαφὴν</note>, and a presence superior to knowledge <note>original Greek: παρουσίαν ἐπιστήμης κρείττονα</note>, and the joining of our own center, as it were, with the center of the universe <note>original Greek: ἑαυτοῦ κέντρον, τῷ οἷον πάντων κέντρῳ συνάπτειν</note>.

> *A kind of union by touch, and a certain presence better than knowledge, and the joining of our own center, as it were, with the center of the universe.*

Thus we see that the *Platonic Trinity* is a *Trinity* of Gods. Therefore, of these three Gods, the second and the third must necessarily be *inferior Gods*; otherwise, they would be *three independent Gods*. However, *Pagan theology* expressly disclaims a *plurality* of *independent* and *self-originated deities*.

***

But since, according to the principles of Christianity—which was partly designed to oppose and bear down Pagan polytheism—there is *only one God* to be acknowledged, the meaning of this seems to be chiefly directed against the *deifying of created beings*, or giving *religious worship* to any besides the *uncrea-*

# The Pagans' Trinity of Gods. BOOK I.

[Crea]ted, and the Creator of all. Moreover, since the Scripture is the only true rule and measure of this *Divine Cabala* <term>original: Divine Cabala; refers to a traditional or mystical interpretation of divine secrets</term> of the *Trinity*, although the *Logos* <note>original: λόγος</note> or *Word* is said to have been *with God* (that is, *God the Father*) and also itself to *be God* (that is, not a *creature*), yet it is nowhere called *another* or *second God*. Therefore, we Christians cannot accept this pagan language of a *Trinity of Gods*, but must call it either a *Trinity* of *Divine Hypostases* <term>the underlying substances or distinct persons of the Trinity</term>, or *Subsistences*, or *Persons*, or the like. 

Nevertheless, it is observable that *Philo*—though according to his Jewish principles, he was a zealous opposer of *pagan polytheism* and *idolatry*—did not, for all that, hesitate to call the *Divine Word* <note>original: θεῖον λόγον</note>, after the *Platonic* way, a *Second God* <note>original: Δεύτερον θεὸν</note>. He did not suspect this to clash with the principles of his religion, or the *Second Commandment* of the Decalogue: *Thou shalt have no other gods before my face*. Possibly he conceived that this was to be understood of "creature-gods" only; whereas his *Second God*, the *Divine Logos* or Word, is declared by him to be *eternal* <note>original: ἀΐδιος</note>, and therefore, according to Jewish theology, *uncreated*. 

However, this language of a *second* and *third God* is not as excusable in a Jew as it might be in a pagan. The pagans, according to the principles of their religion, were so far from having any hesitation <note>original: scrupulosity</note> against a *plurality of gods* (as long as there was only one fountain of the Godhead acknowledged) that they instead accounted it an honor to the Supreme God, as has been already shown, that he should have many other gods under him—not only *titular gods*, but also those who were *religiously worshipped*. Therefore, besides this *second* and *third God*, they also indulged in their many other *creature-gods*. And indeed, St. *Augustine* <note>original: St. Austin</note> seems, on this account, to somewhat excuse the pagans 

<margin>The City of God, Book 10, Chapter 23.</margin> 

for this their *Trinity of Gods* and principles, in these words:

> *For the philosophers speak with free words, nor in these matters which are extremely difficult to be understood did they fear offending religious and scrupulous ears. But the case is otherwise with us Christians; for we are bound to specific phrases and ought to speak according to a certain rule, lest the licentious use of words should beget a wicked opinion in anyone concerning those things that are signified by them. We do not speak of two or three principles when we speak of God; just as it is not permitted for us to say "two" or "three Gods," although when we speak of each individually—whether of the Son or of the Holy Spirit—we confess each one to be God.* <note>original Latin: Liberis enim verbis loquuntur Philosophi, nec in rebus ad intelligendum difficillimis, offensionem religiosarum aurium pertimescunt. Nobis autem ad certam Regulam loqui fas est, ne Verborum licentia, etiam in rebus, quæ in his significantur, impiam gignat opinionem. Nos autem non dicimus Duo vel Tria Principia, cum de Deo loquimur: sicut nec Duos Deos vel Tres, nobis licitum est dicere, quamvis de Unoquoque loquentes, vel de Filio, vel de Spiritu Sancto, etiam singulum quemque Deum esse fateamur.</note>

That is, although this might be in a manner excusable in the pagans—because each of those three *hypostases* is God, and they therefore called them severally "gods" and collectively a "Trinity of Gods" and "principles"—they had no such rule then given to them to govern their language. They were not taught that *though the Father be God, the Son God, and the Holy Ghost God, yet they are not three Gods, but one God*. Yet this is not allowable for us Christians: to speak of a *second* or *third God* or principle, or to call the Holy Trinity a "Trinity of Gods," even though when we speak of the Father, or of the Son, or of the Holy Ghost individually, we confess each of them to be God.

It highlights that while philosophers like Philo used the term "Second God" for the Logos, St. Augustine argued that Christians must use more precise language to avoid the appearance of polytheism.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on why Pagans used the terms "First," "Second," and "Third" God, and how some philosophers mistakenly identified the physical world itself as the third member of this divine hierarchy.</meta>

-> # CHAPTER IV. The World, to some The Third God. <-

And indeed, when the Pagans spoke of a *First*, *Second*, and *Third* God, and no more—despite having innumerable other gods besides—they plainly implied by this language that these *Three Gods* of theirs were of a very different kind from all the rest of their gods. That is, they were not created gods <note>original: θεοὶ γεννητοὶ</note> but eternal <note>original: ἀΐδιοι</note>, not *created*, but *eternal* and *uncreated ones*. It will be shown later that many of them did really take this whole Trinity of Gods for the "Divine" <note>original: τὸ θεῖον</note> in general—the <term>Divine Numen</term> <note>The spiritual power or divinity presiding over a place or thing</note>—and sometimes called it the *First God* too, to distinguish it from their *generated gods*. 

So the "first God" <note>original: πρῶτος θεὸς</note> was used in different senses by these Pagans. Sometimes it was used in a larger sense to oppose all the created gods <note>original: γεννητοὶ θεοὶ</note> (the gods that were made in time along with the world). At other times, it was used more specifically to distinguish the first from those *two other eternal divine Hypostases* <term>the underlying substances or distinct persons of a Trinity</term>, which they called the *second* and *third God*. This *first* of the *three gods* is also frequently called by them "God" <note>original: Θεὸς</note> emphatically and by way of excellence, as they assumed a <term>Gradual Subordination</term> <note>The idea that the members of the Trinity exist in a hierarchy of rank or origin</note> in these *principles*.

Neither was this *Trinity of Divine Subsistences* only poorly phrased by the Pagans generally when they called it a *Trinity of Gods*; but also its <term>Cabala</term> <note>In this context, a traditional or mystical oral transmission of divine knowledge</note> was otherwise much corrupted and adulterated by several of the Platonists and Pythagoreans. For first, the *third* of these *three Hypostases*, commonly called *Psyche* <note>the Soul</note>, is made by some of them to be the "world-soul" <note>original: ψυχὴ ἐγκόσμιος; the soul of the universe</note>—the immediate soul of the physical world, inhabiting, acting upon, and enlivening it in the same way that the souls of other animals do their respective bodies. Consequently, this physical world itself, which together with its soul makes up one complete animal, was frequently called the *Third God*. 

*Proclus* affirms this of *Numenius* the Pythagorean: *“For the world, according to him, was the third God”* <note>original: ὁ γὰρ κόσμος κατ᾿ αὐτὸν ὁ τρίτος ἐστὶ θεὸς</note>. And *Plotinus*, being a great reader of this *Numenius*, seems to have been somewhat infected by him with this notion also, though it was contrary to his own principles, as seen in those words previously cited from him: *“the world, as is commonly said, is the third God”* <note>original: ὁ κόσμος θεὸς, ὥσπερ συνήθες λέγειν, τρίτος</note>.

Now, if the world is not a creature, then there is no created being at all, and everything is God. But not only *Timaeus Locrus*, but also *Plato* himself, calls it a *created divine being* <note>original: θεῖον γεννητὸν</note>. Here, the word *created* <note>original: γεννητὸν</note> refers to that which was brought into being after it once did not exist, which is the proper definition of a *creature*. So the *animated world* is identified by *Plato* as only the chief of all the *creature-gods* <note>original: γεννητοὶ θεοὶ</note>. Therefore, it is plain that in this Trinity of some Platonists and Pythagoreans—wherein the world is made to be the *Third God*—there is a confused jumble of *created* and *uncreated beings* together. For the *first* of those gods is the *father* and *fountain* of all, or the *original* of the Godhead. And the *second*, since he is called by them both the "maker" <note>original: ποιητὴς</note> and the "craftsman" <note>original: δημιουργὸς</note> of the whole world, he there-

It highlights the confusion between created and uncreated beings in certain Platonic and Pythagorean schools of thought.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that some ancient philosophers, like Numenius, incorrectly identified the physical world as the "Third God," thereby confusing created things with the uncreated Trinity.</meta>

-> ### The Cabbala of the Trinity, Book I. <-

Therefore, the third can be no creature either. In contrast, the *Third* God, which is said to be the *World*, was by *Numenius* himself also expressly called both a "work" and "the thing made" <note>original: "ποίημα and τὸ δημιουργούμενον"</note>. That is, plainly, the *creature of both the former two*. *Proclus* thus fully represents his sense: "He calls the first the Father, the second the Maker, and the third the work; so that according to him the Creator is twofold, both the first and the second God, while the thing created is the third" <note>original: "πατέρα μὲν καλεῖ τὸν πρῶτον, ποιητὴν δὲ τὸν δεύτερον, ποίημα δὲ τὸν τρίτον· ὥστε ὁ κατ᾿ αὐτὸν δημιουργὸς διττός, ὅ, τε πρῶτος καὶ ὁ δεύτερος θεός, τὸ δὲ δημιουργούμενον ὁ τρίτος"</note>. Thus, according to Numenius, there were two <term>Opificers</term> <note>Craftsmen or creators</note> or Creators of the World—the First and the Second God—and the World itself (that is, the thing made and created by them both) is said to be the Third God.

And that this *notion* of the *Trinity* is a *corrupted one* <note>original: "Adulterated One"</note> may also be further concluded from this: according to this *hypothesis*, they might as well have said there were three hundred or more gods as that there are *three*. This is because all the other "generated gods" <note>original: "γεννητοὶ θεοὶ"</note> might have been included in the count as well as the *World*, since they are parts of it and gods that differ from it not in kind, but only in degree. Therefore, these philosophers ought not to have made a *Trinity of Gods* distinguished from all the rest. Instead, they should have first categorized their gods into "eternal or uncreated" and "generated" <note>original: "θεοὶ ἀίδιοι and γεννητοὶ"</note>—that is, *eternal and created gods*—and then subdivided those *created gods* into the *whole world and its animated parts*.

However, it may be argued here in favor of this *false hypothesis* of the *Trinity* that the *World* was accounted the *Third God* only by accident, in respect to its Soul, which is properly that *Third God*. Yet *Numenius* and others plainly affirm that the World itself—as a "work" and a "thing made" <note>original: "ποίημα and δημιουργούμενον"</note>—is the *Third*. We shall therefore reply to this: even the *Soul* of the "world-animal" <note>original: "Mundane Animal"</note> itself, according to *Timaeus*, *Plato*, and others, is affirmed to be a "generated god" <note>original: "γεννητὸς θεός"</note>. This means it was produced from non-existence into being, and is therefore truly and properly a *creature*. *Aristotle*, observing this, took the opportunity to criticize *Plato* for contradicting himself by making the Soul of the World a *Principle* (that is, the *Third God*) while also supposing it to be "not eternal, but made or created together with the heavens" <note>original: "ὕστεron καὶ ἅμα τῷ οὐρανῷ"</note>, as mentioned before. Therefore, we conclude that this ancient <term>Cabala</term> <note>A traditional secret doctrine or oral tradition</note> of the *Trinity* was *depraved and corrupted* by those Platonists and Pythagoreans who made either the *World* itself, or else "an informing soul of the world" <note>original: "ψυχὴν ἐγκόσμιον"</note>, its Third <term>Hypostasis</term> <note>The underlying substance or person of the Trinity</note>. In doing so, they mingled *created* and *uncreated beings* together in what they nonetheless called a *Trinity of Causes and Principles*.

We think it highly probable that this was the true reason why *Philo* <note>A Jewish philosopher from Alexandria who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with Jewish scripture</note>, though he admitted the second *Hypostasis* of the *Platonic* and *Pythagorean* (if not *Egyptian*) *Trinity*—called by him the "Divine Word" <note>original: "θεῖος λόγος"</note> and styled the "Second God" <note>original: "δεύτερος θεός"</note>—as *Eusebius*...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how various Platonists and Pythagoreans distorted the ancient concept of the Trinity by identifying the physical world as a "Third God," a view that Christian writers like Eusebius critiqued while attempting to reconcile some philosophical terminology with their own faith.</meta>

# CHAP. IV. Adulterated by some Platonists.

Eusebius adds that even though he acknowledges a **Second Cause** <note>original: "δεύτερον αἴτιον"</note>, he would not follow the Platonists or Pythagoreans any further by accepting that **Third God** or **Cause**. Many of them supposed this third cause to be the **Soul of the whole World**, existing as a living animal. Eusebius refused this because he would have had to violate the principles of his own religion by making the entire **Created World** a **God**—a practice he condemned in the Pagans. It is true that he occasionally does not hesitate to call God the **Soul of the World** as well as its **Mind**, whether he meant **that God who is before the Word** <note>original: "τὸν πρὸ τοῦ λόγου θεόν"</note>, or perhaps the **Word** itself, the **Second God** (who, according to him, is the immediate creator and governor of the world). Nevertheless, he does not seem to mean a soul so deeply **immersed** in matter that it would make the world a living **Animal** and a **God**, but rather a more **elevated one**—that is, a **Supermundane Soul** <note>original: "ψυχὴν ὑπερκόσμιον"</note>.

To this first distortion of that **Theology of Divine Tradition** <note>original: "θεοπαράδοτος θεολογία"</note> and the ancient **Cabbala of the Trinity** by many Platonists and Pythagoreans, another may be added. Some of them declared the **Second Hypostasis** <note>A "hypostasis" refers to a distinct person or substance within the Trinity</note> of their Trinity to be the **Archetypal World**—or, as **Philo** calls it, "the world that is compounded and made up of Ideas" <note>original: "τὸν ἐκ τῶν ἰδεῶν παγέντα κόσμον"</note>. This world contains within it, in an **intelligible** way, all the kinds of things that exist in this **Lower World** in a **sensible** way <note>Things understood by the mind versus things perceived through the senses</note>. They further concluded that all these various **Ideas** within this **Archetypal and Intelligible World** are actually distinct **substances, living beings**, and **gods**. By doing this, they made that **Second Hypostasis** not **One God**, but a **collection** and **heap of gods**. These are the gods they commonly called **Intelligible Gods** <note>original: "νοητοὶ θεοὶ"</note>. This was not just to distinguish them from the **Sensible Gods** <note>original: "αἰσθητοὶ"</note> (which is a more general use of the word), but also from those other gods of theirs (which will be discussed later) called **Intellectual Gods** <note>original: "νοεροὶ θεοὶ"</note>.

<margin>P. 357.</margin>
**Proclus**, in his commentary on **Plato's Republic**, concludes that there is no **Idea of Evil**. He reasons that "if there were an Idea of Evil, that very Idea would itself be a God, because every Idea is a God, as Parmenides affirmed" <note>original: "εἰ γὰρ τῶν κακῶν ἰδέα θεὸς ἔσαι, ἐπείπερ πᾶσα ἰδέα θεὸς ὡς παρμενίδης εἴρηκεν"</note>. Even **Plotinus** himself, who was usually more sober-minded, was not entirely free from this fanciful concept that the **Ideas** were all **gods**. He wrote the following regarding the **Second God, the First Mind or Intellect**: 

<margin>En. 5. L. 1. c. 7.</margin>
"Having been begotten by the First God (that is, by way of emanation and from eternity), he generated all existing things together with himself: all the beauty of the Ideas, which are all **Intelligible Gods**" <note>original: "γεννόμενον δὲ ἤδη τὰ ὄντα σὺν αὐτῷ γεννῆσαι, πᾶν μὲν τὸ τῶν ἰδεῶν κάλλος, πάντας δὲ θεοὺς νοητούς"</note>. 

**Apuleius** also (as has been noted already) crudely and excessively attributes the same view to **Plato** in these words: "Those whom Plato considers to be the true gods: incorporeal, living beings, without any beginning or end, but eternal in both the past and the future, with their natures directed toward the highest happiness, etc." <note>original: "Quos Deos Plato existimat, Veros, Incorporales, Animales, sine ullo neque fine neque exordio, sed prorsus ac retrò æviternos, ingenio ad summam beatitudinem porrecto, &c."</note>. He, along with **Julian** and others, reduced the majority of the Pagan gods to these **Ideas** of the **Intelligible or Archetypal World**. For example, they made **Apollo** the **Intelligible Sun** (the Idea of the physical Sun) and **Diana** the **Intelligible Moon**, and so on for the rest. Finally, it has also been observed that the Egyptian theologians claimed to worship...

It critiques the philosophical move of personifying abstract concepts (like the Sun or Moon) as "Intelligible Gods" within the divine hierarchy.</summary>
