<meta>This page continues the discussion of how some Platonists expanded their theology to include "Intelligible Gods" or "Ideas" as distinct entities. It explores how Philo Judaeus integrated these concepts into a Jewish framework of creation, while warning that such philosophy could inadvertently lead back to pagan idolatry and atheism.</meta>

# Ideas, made Animals and Gods. BOOK I.

-> Worship these *Intelligible Gods*, or *Eternal Ideas*, in their *Religious Animals*, as *Symbols* of them. <-

<margin>On the Creation of the World, page 6.</margin> Philo <note>Philo Judaeus (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy.</note> indeed followed the Platonic tradition so far as to suppose that God made an *Archetypal* <note>The original model or pattern from which copies are made.</note> and *Intelligible World* <note>A world existing only in the mind or intellect, rather than in physical space.</note> before he made this *Corporeal* and *Sensible* <note>Physical and perceivable by the senses.</note> world: <note>original: "βουληθείς (ὁ Θεὸς) τὸν ὁρατὸν τουτονὶ κόσμον δημιουργῆσαι, προεξετύπου τὸν νοητὸν, ἵνα χρώμενος ἀσωμάτῳ καὶ θεοειδεστάτῳ παραδείγματι, τὸν σωματικὸν ἀπεργάσηται, πρεσβύτερον νεώτερον ἀπεικόνισμα, τοσαῦτα περιέξοντα αἰσθητὰ γένη, ὅσαπερ ἐν ἐκείνῳ νοητά· τὸ δ᾿ ἐκ τῶν ἰδεῶν συνεστῶτα κόσμον ἐν τόπῳ τινὶ ὑπονοεῖν ἀδύνατον"</note> *God, intending to make a visible world, first formed an intelligible one; so that, having an incorporeal and most god-like pattern before him, he might make the physical world according to it—this younger world being an image of that older one—containing as many sensible kinds within it as the other did intelligible ones. But it is not possible (he says) to conceive of this world of ideas as existing in any physical place.* Indeed, according to him, *Moses* himself philosophized in the same manner in his *Cosmopoeia* <note>The account of the creation of the world.</note>, describing in the first five verses of *Genesis* the creation of an intelligible heaven and earth before the *sensible* ones; <margin>page 6.</margin> <note>original: "πρῶτον οὖν παρὰ τῷ νοητῷ κόσμῳ ὁ ποιῶν ἐποίει οὐρανὸν ἀσώματον καὶ γῆν ἀόρατον, καὶ ἀέρος ἰδέαν καὶ κενοῦ, εἶθ’ ὕδατος ἀσωμάτου οὐσίαν καὶ πνεύματος, καὶ ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ἑβδόμης φωτός, ὃ πάλιν ἀσώματον ἦν καὶ νοητὸν ἡλίου παράδειγμα, &c."</note> *The Creator first of all made an incorporeal heaven and an invisible earth; the ideas of air and vacuum; incorporeal water and air; and last of all light, which was also the incorporeal and intelligible pattern of the sun and stars, and that from which their sensible light is derived.* 

But Philo does not explicitly claim that these *Ideas* of the *Intelligible* and *Archetypal World* are distinct *substances* and *living beings* <note>original: "Animals"</note>, much less *Gods*. However, he does note that some people, admiring the beauty of both these worlds, not only deified them as a whole but also their individual parts. That is, they worshipped the *various ideas* of the *intelligible world* as well as the *greater parts* of the *sensible world*, such as an *intelligible heaven* and *earth*, *sun*, and *moon*. They claimed to worship those *divine ideas* within all these *sensible things*. 

This high-flown Platonic *notion* provided a sanctuary and protection for the grossest and foulest of all *pagan superstitions* and *idolatries*. It allowed the Egyptians to worship *animals* <note>original: "Brute Animals"</note> and other pagans to worship all things in nature—even *inanimate substances* and *mere accidents* <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities like color or shape.</note>—under the pretense of worshipping the *divine ideas* within them. This directly led to absolute impiety, irreligion, and atheism. There were few who could actually comprehend those *eternal ideas*, and scarcely anyone who could fully convince themselves that these ideas had as much reality as the *physical things of nature*. Just as the *idea* of a *house* in the mind of an architect does not have as much reality as a *material house* made of stones, mortar, and timber, so their devotion inevitably sank entirely into those *sensible things*. They naturally fell, at length, into the atheistic conviction *that the good things of nature are the only deities.*

Thus, we have a multitude of pagan gods that are *supermundane* <note>Existing above or beyond the physical world.</note> and *eternal* (though all depending upon *One Supreme God*). These are the gods by...

The author warns that this philosophy was misused by Pagans to justify the worship of nature and animals, eventually leading to atheism by focusing on material things rather than divine concepts.</summary>

### Chap. IV. The Henades, and Noes, of some Platonists.

...them properly called *Intelligible* <note>original: νοητοὶ (*noētoi*)</note>, or the *Divine Ideas*. And we cannot but consider this as another corruption <note>original: "Depravation"</note> of the ancient *Mosaic Kabbalah* <note>The author refers to the "Mosaick Cabbala," a tradition believed by some Renaissance scholars to be a secret oral philosophy passed down from Moses, which they argued was the source of Greek philosophy.</note> of the *Trinity*. Specifically, the *Second Person* <note>original: "Hypostasîs"</note> of that Trinity is turned into the *Archetypal World* <note>The original blueprint or pattern of the universe.</note> and all the *Divine Ideas* are treated as so many distinct *Substances*, *Living Beings*, and *Gods*. In this view, there is not *One God*, but a whole *World of Gods*.

But beyond all this, some of these Platonists and Pythagoreans further corrupted and adulturated the ancient *Hebrew* or *Mosaic Kabbalah* of the *Trinity* (the only certain rule for which is now the New Testament Scriptures). They concluded that, just as from the *Third Person* of their *Trinity*, called *The First Soul* <note>original: ἡ πρώτη ψυχὴ (*hē prōtē psychē*)</note>, there were innumerable other *particular souls* derived—namely the souls of all lower animals that are parts of the world—so in the same way, from their *Second Person*, called *The First Mind* or *Intellect* <note>original: ὁ πρῶτος νοῦς (*ho prōtos nous*)</note>, there were derived innumerable other *particular minds* or *intellects* <note>original: μερικοὶ Νόες (*merikoi Noes*)</note>. These were thought to be substantial beings superior to the First Soul. And not only that, but they also claimed that from the First and Highest *Person* of all, called *The One* and *The Good* <note>original: τὸ Ἕν, καὶ τἀγαθὸν (*to Hen, kai tagathon*)</note>, there were likewise derived many *particular unities* <note>original: Ἑνάδες (*Henades*)</note> and *goodnesses* <note>original: Ἀγαθότητες (*Agathotetes*)</note>. These were substantial beings superior even to the First *Intellect*. <margin>N. 21.</margin> Thus Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 CE) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who systematized Platonic thought into a complex hierarchy.</note> writes in his *Theological Institutions*: *After the First One (and from it), there are many particular Unities; after the First Intellect and from it, many particular Minds or Intellects; after the First Soul, many particular and derivative souls; and lastly, after the Universal Nature, many particular natures and seminal principles.* <note>original: μετὰ γ' τὸ ἓν ἄρα τὸ πρῶτον, ἑνάδες· καὶ μετὰ νοῦν τὸν πρῶτον, νόες· καὶ μετὰ τὴν ψυχὴν τὴν πρώτην, ψυχαί· καὶ μετὰ τὴν ὅλην φύσιν, φύσεις. Also, "seminal principles" is the modernization of "Spermatick Reasons."</note> Here it may be observed in passing <note>original: "obiter"</note> that these Platonists supposed that below the *Universal Psyche*, or World Soul, there was also a *Universal nature* <note>original: φύσις (*physis*)</note>; but they believed that besides this universal nature, there were also other *particular* formative principles <note>original: λόγοι σπερματικοί (*logoi spermatikoi*), or "Plastick Principles."</note>.

Regarding these "Minds" (*Noes*), and the idea that besides the *First Universal Mind*, there are other *particular substantial minds*—a rank of beings that are not only immutably *good* and *wise*, but also entirely *immovable* <note>In Platonic thought, "immovable" refers to beings that do not change or transition between states, unlike souls which move themselves through thought or emotion.</note>, and therefore above the rank of all souls (which are *self-moving* beings)—Proclus was not alone in this view. He had the agreement of many other Platonists, among whom Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 CE), the founder of Neoplatonism.</note> seems to be one, as seen in this passage among others: *That souls are immortal, and every mind or intellect, we have elsewhere largely proved.* <note>original: ὅτι ἀθάνατοι μὲν αἱ ψυχαί, καὶ νοῦς πᾶς, ἐν ἄλλοις διὰ πλειόνων εἴρηται</note> <margin>P. 653.</margin> Upon these words, Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), an influential Italian scholar who translated Plato and Plotinus into Latin.</note> comments: *Here and in many other places, before and after, you may observe through the words of Plotinus that there are many substantial minds, distinct from souls, though there is a wonderful union between them.* <note>original: "Hic, & suprà & infrà sæpè, per verba Plotini notabis, Plures esse Mentium Animarumque Substantias inter se distinctas, quamvis inter eas Unio sit Mirabilis"</note> Moreover, they held that above these "Minds" (the immovable but multifaceted intellects), there was not only one *perfect Unity* <note>original: "Monad"</note> and *First Good*, but also a rank of *many particular unities* (*Henades*) and *goodnesses* (*Agathotetes*). This was...

<margin>In Epictetus's *Enchiridion* p. 9.</margin>
This view was asserted not only by **Proclus** and others, but also by **Simplicius**: "The Highest Good," he says <note>original: ἀφ’ ἑαυτοῦ τὸ ἀγαθὸν πάντα παράγει, τά τε πρῶτα, καὶ τὰ μέσα, καὶ τὰ ἔσχατα· ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν πρῶτα καὶ ἑαυτῷ προσεχῆ, ὅμοια ἑαυτῷ παράγει, μιὰ ἀγαθότης πολλὰς ἀγαθότητας, καὶ μία ἑνὰς ἡ ὑπὲρ πάσας, πολλὰς ἑνάδας</note>, "produces all things from himself, in several ranks and degrees: the first, the middle, and the last or lowest of all. But the first, which are closest to himself, he produces in his own likeness—one Goodness producing many Goodnesses, and one Unity (or Henade) <note>original: *henas*, a term used by Platonists to describe a fundamental unit of being</note> that is above all, producing many Unities." It is clear that by these Henades and *Autoagathotetes* <note>original: *autoagathotētes*, meaning "essential goodnesses"</note> he means **substantial beings** that are **conscious** of themselves, as seen in the following words:

<margin>P. 11.</margin>
"Those beings which are first produced from the First Good, by reason of their shared nature with him, do not fall away from being good; they are immovable and unchangeable, always fixed in the same happiness, never lacking in good nor falling from it, because they are all **essentially Goodnesses**" <note>original: τὰ μὲν οὖν πρῶτα τῶν ὑπὸ τοῦ πρώτου ἀγαθοῦ παραγομένων, διὰ τὸ πρὸς αὐτὸ ὁμόφυες, οὐκ ἐξέστη τοῦ εἶναι ἀγαθὰ, ἀκίνητα ὄντα καὶ ἀμετάβλητα, καὶ ἐν τῇ αὐτῇ ἀεὶ μακαριότητι ἱδρυμένα, οὐκ ἐνδεῆ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ, ὅτι αὐτοαγαθότητές εἰσι</note>. Afterward, he adds something regarding the *Noes* <note>original: νόες (*noes*), the plural of *nous*, meaning "minds" or "intellects"</note> as well: although these were a rank of lower beings and not "essentially Goodnesses" <note>original: αὐτοαγαθὰ (*autoagatha*)</note> but only good by **participation** <note>In Platonic philosophy, "participation" means a lower being shares in the qualities of a higher being without being its equal</note>, yet because their own nature is also **immovable**, they can never degenerate or fall away from that participation in the Good. Despite this, we must admit that some of these Platonists seem to use the word *Henades* in a different sense sometimes, understanding them as nothing more than the **Intelligible Ideas** mentioned previously. However, the ancient Platonists and Pythagoreans were not accustomed to calling these "Unities," but rather "**Numbers**."

We have now discovered more of the **pagans' inferior gods**, which they considered to be beyond this world and **eternal**. Besides those "Intelligible Gods" <note>original: νοητοὶ θεοὶ (*noētoi theoi*)</note>, there are troops of Henades and "Essential Goodnesses" (Unities and Goodnesses), and also of *Noes* (immovable **Minds** or **Intellects**). They frequently call these *Henadical* (or **Monadical**) Gods and **Intellectual Gods** <note>original: θεοὶ ἑνιαῖοι (*theoi eniaioi*) and θεοὶ νοεροὶ (*theoi noeroi*)</note>.

However, these *Noes* (Intellectual Gods) are all said to be, by their very nature, a rank of beings above **Souls**. Therefore, they are superior to that **First Soul**, which is the **Third Person** <note>original: "Hypostasis"</note> of this Trinity. Likewise, all those Henades (Monadical Gods) are a still higher rank of beings above the *Noes*, and therefore superior even to the **Second Person**, the **First Mind**. Yet all these Henades and *Noes*, although these philosophers suppose them to be **eternal**, are only **particular beings** and not **universal**. Consequently, they cannot be ranked higher than **creatures**. From this, it follows unavoidably that both the **Second** and **Third Persons** of this Trinity—the First Mind as well as the First Soul—must also be considered **creatures**, because no **created being** can be superior to anything **uncreated**. Therefore, **Proclus** and several other Platonists clearly understood this Trinity merely as a certain scale or ladder of beings in the universe. They saw it as a **gradual descent** of things from the **First** or **Highest**, moving downward step by step, lower and lower, until reaching the souls of all animals. For

<page-num>557</page-num>
### Chapter 4: A Scale or Ladder of Nature.

Because of this, Proclus, in order to complete this "Scale" of existence, adds a fourth rank to the previous three. Below the third rank of **Souls**, he adds a fourth rank of **Natures**. Below this fourth rank, there is only the passive part of the universe: **Body** and **Matter**. Consequently, their entire scale of everything above the physical body was not actually a **Trinity**, but a **Quaternity**—four ranks and degrees of beings arranged one below the other. The first rank consisted of **Henades** <note>original: *Henades*, or "Unities"</note>; the second of **Noes** <note>original: *Noes*, "Minds" or "Intellects"</note>; the third of **Souls**; and the last of **Natures**. These were like concentric orbs or spheres, one situated within and below another.

Within each of these ranks of being, they imagined there was **one first universal** and "unparticipated" <note>meaning a primary source that does not share its essence with others</note> being as the head of that rank, followed by **many particular** or "participated" ones. For example: one first universal Henade followed by many secondary, particular Henades; one first universal *Nous* <note>original: *Nous*, "Mind" or "Intellect"</note> followed by many secondary particular minds; one first universal Soul followed by many particular souls; and finally, one universal Nature followed by many particular natures.

In this scale of beings, they deified—in addition to the first "One" and "Good" <note>original: *to hen* and *tagathon*</note>—not only the first Mind and the first Soul, but also all those other particular Henades and Minds universally, and all particular souls superior to humans. They excluded from divinity only the fourth rank of "Natures" and inferior souls, because they believed that nothing should be considered a god unless it was intellectual and superior to mankind.

Although they created several degrees of gods, one below the other—calling some **eternal** <note>original: *aidios*</note> and others **generated** <note>original: *gennētos*, or "made in time"</note>—they never clearly distinguished between the "Deity" properly defined and the "Creature" (a created being). They failed to show exactly where the true Deity ended and where the created world began on this scale. Instead, by "melting" the Deity down through these degrees and bringing it lower and lower, they made the connection and joint <note>original: "juncture and commissure"</note> between God and the creature so smooth and tight that the point where they actually separated was completely impossible to see. They implied instead that they differed only in degree, and that "God" and "Creature" were not absolute opposites but comparative terms, differing only in "more" or "less." All of this was undoubtedly a major misunderstanding of the ancient **Cabbala** <note>here referring to a secret oral tradition or "received" wisdom</note> of the Trinity.

This, then, is the **Platonic Trinity** that we contrast with the **Christian Trinity**. It is not that Plato's own original concept of the Trinity was entirely different from the Christian one in its essential structure—for it was likely derived from a divine or Mosaic tradition—but rather that this tradition (as often happens with such mysterious and difficult concepts) was misunderstood, corrupted, and distorted by various later Platonists and Pythagoreans. They turned it into a Trinity that blurs the lines between God and the creature and removes all boundaries and landmarks between them. It sinks the Deity lower and lower through various ranks (multiplying the number of gods as it goes) until it eventually reaches down to the entire physical world. Even then, it does not stop, but extends divinity further to the animated parts of the world, such as the **stars** and **demons** <note>in the classical sense of guardian spirits or intermediate beings</note>. Its direct purpose or tendency is simply to lay the groundwork for infinite **polytheism**.

polytheism, **Cosmolatry** <note>original: *Cosmolatry*, or "world-worship"</note> (or **World-Idolatry**) and **Creature-Worship**. In this context, it is noteworthy that these **Platonic Pagans** were the only public and professional champions against Christianity. For though **Celsus** <note>A 2nd-century Greek philosopher and opponent of early Christianity</note> was suspected by **Origen** to have actually been an Epicurean, he at least pretended to be a Platonist as well. The reason for this might be not only because the **Platonic** and **Pythagorean sects** were the most divine of all the Pagans—approaching nearest to Christianity and the Truth (though, as the saying goes, "the corruption of the best thing is the worst," they might for that reason prove the most dangerous opponents)—and could therefore defend themselves against Christianity with the greatest confidence; but also because **Platonic principles**, as they might be understood, served more plausibly than any others to defend Pagan **Polytheism** and **Idolatry**.

Concerning the Christian Trinity, we shall observe here only **three things**. First, that it is not a **Trinity** of **mere names** or **words**, nor a Trinity of **partial notions** and **inadequate conceptions** <note>meaning incomplete ways of thinking about a single thing</note> of one and the same **thing**. For such a kind of Trinity as this might be conceived within that **First Platonic Hypostasis** <note>original: *Hypostasis*, meaning a fundamental substance or person</note> itself, called *the One* <note>original: τὸ ἕν</note> and *the Good* <note>original: τἀγαθὸν</note>, and perhaps also in that **First Person** of the **Christian Trinity**—namely, as a Trinity of **Goodness**, **Understanding** (or **Wisdom**), and **Will** (or **Active Power**), which are three inadequate conceptions of God. It is true that **Plotinus** <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher</note> was so abstract in his thinking that he maintained that the first and highest Principle of all, because of its perfect **Unity** and **Simplicity**, is above the multiplicity of knowledge and understanding. Therefore, he argued it does not even properly **understand itself** <note>original: νοεῖν ἑαυτὸ</note>. Notwithstanding this, the philosopher himself adds that it cannot therefore be said to be **ignorant** or **unwise** either, as these expressions belong only to a being that was by nature intellectual:
<margin>Enneads, Book 6, Chapter 7, Section 37.</margin>
"For an intellect that does not understand is rightly judged to be mindless." <note>original: νοῦς μὲν γὰρ μὴ νοῶν, ἀνόητος; Latin: *Intellectus nisi intelligat, demens meritò judicatur.*</note> 

And he seems to grant that it has a certain **simple clarity** and **brightness** in it, superior to that of **knowledge**—just as the body of the Sun has a certain brightness superior to that secondary light which streams from it. He suggests it may be called **knowledge itself** <note>original: νόησις αὐτὴ</note> that does not **understand**, just as motion itself does not **move**. But this can hardly be understood by ordinary mortals—that the highest and most **perfect** of all beings should not fully comprehend itself, the extent of its own fruitfulness and power, and be conscious of all that proceeds from it, even if it does so in the most simple manner. And therefore this abstract idea of **Plotinus** (and perhaps of **Plato** himself) has been rejected by later Platonists as **fanciful** and **unsafe**. For instance, **Simplicius** says:
<margin>Commentary on Epictetus, page 235.</margin>
"But it must also necessarily have the most perfect knowledge, since it cannot be ignorant of anything that is produced from itself." <note>original: ἀλλὰ καὶ γνῶσιν ἔχειν ἀνάγκη τὴν ἀκροτάτην, οὐ γὰρ ἄν τι τῶν ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ παραγομένων ἀγνοήσειεν</note>

And **St. Augustine** <note>original: *St. Austin*</note> in a similar way refutes the assertion of some Christians that the *Logos*, or Eternal Word, was that very Wisdom and Understanding by which the **Father himself was wise**; he argues that this would make the Word nothing but an **inadequate conception of God**. However, this opinion—that the **Christian Trinity** is but a **Trinity of words**, or mere logical **notions** and **inadequate conceptions of God**—has been plainly condemned by the Christian Church.

### Chapter 4. To the Pseudo-Platonic.

Church in the teachings of **Sabellius** <note>A 3rd-century priest who taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were merely different modes or "faces" of a single person, rather than three distinct persons</note> and others. Therefore, we conclude it to be a Trinity of ***Hypostases*** <note>original: *Hypostases*, referring to distinct individual existences or persons</note>, or **Subsistences**, or **Persons**.

The second thing that we observe concerning the Christian Trinity is this: although the **Second Person** <note>original: *Hypostasis*</note> was begotten from the **First**, and the **Third proceeds** from both the **First** and **Second**, yet neither this **Second** nor **Third** are **creatures**. This is for the following reasons:

First, because they were not made "out of things that do not exist" <note>original: ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων (*ex ouk onton*)</note>, as **Arius** <note>A 4th-century theologian who argued that Jesus Christ was a created being, not co-eternal with God the Father</note> maintained. That is, they were not brought into being from a previous state of non-existence. Nor can it be said of either of them, "**There was a time when they were not**" <note>original: *Erat Quando Non erant*</note>. Instead, their **going forth was from eternity**, and they were both co-eval <note>of the same age or duration</note> and co-eternal with the **Father**. 

Secondly, because they were not only **eternal emanations** (if we may call them that) but also **necessary** ones; therefore, they are both **absolutely indestructible** and **incapable of being annihilated**. According to true philosophy and theology, no **creature** could have existed from **eternity**, nor be **absolutely indestructible**. Therefore, that which is both **eternal** and **indestructible** is, *by that very fact* <note>original: *ipso facto*</note>, **uncreated**. 

Nevertheless, because some philosophers have asserted (though erroneously) both that the whole world is **eternal** and that it is a **necessary emanation** from the Deity—and consequently indestructible—we shall further add this: these **Second** and **Third Persons** of the Holy Trinity are not only **uncreated** because they were both eternal and **necessary emanations**, and are likewise unable to be annihilated, but also because they are **Universal**. Each of them comprehends the whole world and all created things within it. This **universality** of theirs is the same thing as **infinity**, whereas all other beings besides this Holy Trinity are **particular** and **finite**. Now we say that no **intellectual being** which is not only **eternal**, **necessarily existent**, and **indestructible**, but also **universal** or **infinite**, can be a creature.

Finally, we add that these **three Persons** <note>original: *Hypostases*</note> are truly and really **one God**. This is not only because they all **essentially** have one and the same **will**, according to the words of **Origen**: <margin>Against Celsus, page 386.</margin> "**Therefore we worship the Father of truth, and the Son who is the truth itself, being two distinct things in their substance, but one in agreement, harmony, and sameness of will**" <note>original: Θρησκεύομεν οὖν τὸν πατέρα τῆς ἀληθείας... (*Threskeuomen oun ton patera tes aletheias...*)</note>. 

But they are also **one God** because they are **physically** (if we may speak this way) **one** as well. They possess a **mutual interpenetration** <note>original: περιχώρησις (*perichoresis*)</note> and **mutual indwelling** <note>original: ἐνύπαρξις (*enuparxis*)</note>, according to the words of our Savior Christ: *I am in the Father, and the Father in me. And the Father that dwells in me, he does the works.* We grant, indeed, that no example of a similar unity or oneness can be found in any created beings. Nevertheless, we know certainly from our own nature that it is not impossible for two distinct substances of very different kinds—one incorporeal and the other corporeal—to be so closely united as to become **one animal** and **one person**. Much less, therefore, should it be thought impossible for these **three divine Persons** to be **one God**.

<summary>This page defines the Christian Trinity as three distinct, co-eternal, and infinite Persons who are uncreated and indestructible. It argues that their unity as one God is found in both their identical will and their mutual interpenetration of nature.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the defense of the Christian Trinity as a rational concept, specifically contrasting it with the Platonic hierarchy and refuting the idea that it is inherently contradictory to human reason.</meta>

# 560 This Platonic Trinity, not BOOK I.

We shall conclude here with confidence that the *Christian Trinity*, though there is much of *mystery* in it, contains nothing at all that is a plain *contradiction* to the undoubted principles of human reason. That is to say, there is no *impossibility* to be found within it, despite what atheists might pretend. They cry down everything as *nonsense* and absolute *impossibility* if their dull stupidity cannot reach it, or if their infatuated minds cannot easily comprehend it—and they even treat the Deity itself this way. 

It is to be wished that some religious people and *Trinitarians* <note>Those who believe in the doctrine of the Trinity: one God in three persons</note> did not align themselves too much with these atheists by choosing to represent the *mystery* of the *Christian Trinity* as something directly contradictory to all human reason and understanding. Perhaps they do this by design, to make men surrender themselves and their consciences in a blind and implicit faith wholly to their guidance. They might also do this to corrupt people's understanding, so they will swallow other opinions of theirs that are plainly contrary to human faculties. It is as if they were saying: "He who believes the *Trinity* (as we all must do if we wish to be Christians) should hesitate at nothing in religion ever after, nor scrupulously chew over or examine anything." It is as if no proposition could be more contradictory or *impossible* for the human understanding than this article of the *Christian faith*.

But for the present, we shall only endeavor to show that the *Christian Trinity* (though a mystery) is much more agreeable to reason than the *Platonic* or *Pseudo-Platonic Trinity* described before, specifically in the three particulars mentioned then. 

First, when those *Platonists* and *Pythagoreans* interpret their "Third God," or the last person <note>original: *Hypostasis*</note> of their Trinity, to be either the *world* or a worldly soul <note>original: ψυχὴ ἐγκόσμιος (*psychē egkosmios*)</note>—an *immediate soul* of the world that, together with the world as its body, makes up *one living being* and *God*—there is clearly too great a *leap* here between their *second* and *third persons*. In doing so, they debase the *Deity* too much and confound God and the creature together. This lays a foundation not only for world-worship <note>original: *Cosmo-Latry*</note> or idolatry of the world in general, but also for the grossest and most foolish of all idolatries: the worship of the inanimate parts of the world themselves, under the pretense that they are parts and members of this great *worldly living being* and *sensible God*.

<margin>Book 2, chapter 1</margin>
It is true indeed that **Origen** <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 184–253 AD)</note> and some other ancient Christian writers have supposed that God may be said in some sense to be the *soul of the world*. Thus, in his book *On First Principles* <note>original: *Peri Archon*</note>: 

"Just as our own body is made up of many members and is held together by one soul, so I believe the whole world should be thought of as a kind of immense living being, which is held together by the power and reason of God as if by one soul. I think this is even indicated by Holy Scripture, through what was said by the Prophet: 'Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord.' And 'Heaven is my throne, but the earth is my footstool.' And what the Savior says when he says that one should not swear by heaven, because it is the throne of God, nor by the earth, because it is his footstool. And also that which Paul says: 'For in him we live and move and have our being.' For how do we live and move and have our being in God, unless it is because he binds together and contains the whole world by his power?" <note>original Latin: *Sicut Corpus nostrum unum ex multis Membris aptatum est, & ab una Anima continetur, ita & Universum Mundum, velut Animal quoddam Immane opinandum puto ; quod quasi ab una Anima, Virtute Dei ac Ratione teneatur. Quod etiam à Sanctâ Scripturâ indicari arbitror, per illud quod dictum est per Prophetam ; Nonne Cœlum & Terram ego repleo, dicit Dominus ? & Cœlum mihi Sedes, Terra autem Scabellum pedum meorum ; Et quod Salvator cum ait, non esse jurandum neque per Cœlum, quia Sedes Dei est, neque per Terram quia Scabellum pedum ejus. Sed & illud quod ait Paulus, Quoniam in ipso Vivimus & Movemur & Sumus. Quomodo enim in Deo Vivimus, & Movemur, & Sumus, nisi quod in Virtute suâ Universum constringit & continet Mundum?*</note> 

As our own body is made up of many members, and contained by one...

<summary>The author argues that the Christian Trinity is more rational than the Platonic version, which risks idolatry by equating the third person of the Trinity with the physical world or its soul.</summary>

<page-num>561</page-num>
### Chap. IV. Reasonable; as the Christian.

Just as I conceive of a single human soul, so do I believe that the whole world should be viewed as *one huge, great animal*, which is held together by *one soul*—the *virtue and reason of God*. This seems to be suggested by Scripture in several places, such as in the words of the Prophet, *Do I not fill heaven and earth?* And again, *Heaven is my throne and the earth my footstool.* And in the words of our Savior, *Do not swear at all, neither by heaven, because it is the throne of God, nor by the earth because it is his footstool.* And lastly, in Paul’s speech to the Athenians, *For in him we live and move, and have our being.* For how can we be said to *live and move and have our being* in God, unless he, by his *virtue and power*, *binds* <note>original: "Constringe"</note> and *contains* the whole world? And how can *heaven be the throne of God and the earth his footstool* unless his *virtue and power* fill all things in both *heaven and earth*? 

Nevertheless, God is said here by Origen <note>An influential early Christian theologian (c. 185–253 AD)</note> to be only *as it were the soul* <note>original: "Quasi-Anima"</note> of the world. It is as if he should have said that all the perfection of a *soul* is to be attributed to God in respect to the world; he *quickens* and *enlivens* all things as much as if he were the *very soul* of it, and all its parts were his *living members*. And perhaps the whole Deity ought not to be looked upon—according to Aristotle’s notion of it—merely as an *immovable essence* <note>original: "ἀκίνητος & οὐσία"</note>. For then it is not conceivable how it could either *act* upon the *world* or be *aware* of anything in it—or for what purpose we should make any *devotional prayers* to such an *unaffected, inflexible, rocky, and diamond-hard* <note>original: "adamantine"</note> *being*. 

Therefore, all the perfection of a *worldly soul* <note>original: "Mundane Soul"</note> may perhaps be attributed to God in some sense, and he may be called *as it were the soul of the world* <note>original: "Quasi-Anima Mundi"</note>. Though St. Cyprian <note>A 3rd-century Bishop of Carthage</note> would have this properly belong to the *third person* <note>original: "Hypostasis"</note> of the Christian Trinity, namely, the *Holy Ghost*. But there is also something of imperfection plainly clinging to this notion of a *worldly soul*, besides something of paganism necessarily resulting from it, which we cannot admit. 

Therefore, *God*, or the *third divine person*, cannot be called the *soul of the world* in this sense—as if he were so *immersed* in it and so *passive* because of it, as our soul is *immersed* in and *passive* because of its *body*. Nor is it as if the *world* and this *soul* together made up one *entire animal*, where each part was incomplete on its own. 

We may learn <margin>On First Principles <note>original: "Peri Arch."</note> Book 1, chapter 6.</margin> that *God*, or the *third person* of the *Christian Trinity*, is not to be considered the *soul of the world* in this proper sense according to Origen himself, from these words of his: *It is the property only of the nature of God—that is, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—to exist without any material substance, and without being united to any physical body* <note>original: "Solius Dei, id est, Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus Sancti, Naturæ, id proprium est; ut sine Materiali Substantia, & absque ulla Corporeæ adjectionis societate intelligatur subsistere"</note>. 

By affirming that all created souls and spirits always have some body or other *vitally united* to them, and that it is the property only of the three persons of the Holy Trinity not to be *vitally united* to any body as its *soul*, Origen plainly declares his position. Whether this assertion of his is true or not (which is not to be discussed here), he clearly shows that God, or the third person of the Trinity, is not to be considered the *soul of the world* in a true and literal sense.

<summary>The author examines the concept of God as the "Soul of the World," arguing that while God animates and sustains the universe, He remains an independent, immaterial being distinct from the physical world, unlike the human soul's relationship to the body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the "Third God" or "Third Hypostasis" in Platonic thought, arguing that for the more sophisticated Platonists, this figure was an eternal Creator rather than a part of the created world.</meta>

# God, not a Mundane Soul. BOOK I.

And it is certain that the more *refined Platonists* were themselves also of this persuasion; and that their *Third God*, or *Divine Hypostasis* <note>The "hypostasis" refers to a person or distinct substance within the Trinity.</note>, was neither the whole world (as it is supposed to be animated) nor yet a *mundane soul* <note>original: "ψυχὴ ἐγκόσμιος"</note>—the *immediate soul* of this *mundane animal* <note>The "mundane animal" is the Platonic concept that the universe itself is a living being with its own soul.</note>—but only a *supermundane soul* <note>original: "ψυχὴ ὑπερκόσμιος"</note>. That is, a being that, although it presides over the whole world and takes notice of all things in it, yet is not properly an *essential part* of that *mundane animal*, but is a *being elevated* above it.

<margin>
In the *Timaeus*, pages 93, 94.
</margin>
For thus Proclus plainly affirms, not only of Amelius but also of Porphyry himself, who likewise pretended to follow Plotinus in this matter: "After Amelius, Porphyry—thinking to agree with Plotinus—calls the supermundane soul the immediate Opificer <note>original: "δημιουργὸς"; a "craftsman" or "maker" of the universe.</note> or Maker of the world, and calls that Mind or Intellect to which it is turned the 'living-being-in-itself,' so that according to him, the paradigm <note>The original pattern or blueprint.</note> of the Maker exists there." <note>original: "μετὰ δὲ Ἀμέλιον ὁ Πορφύριος οἰόμενος τῷ Πλωτίνῳ συνᾴδειν, τὴν μὲν ψυχὴν τὴν ὑπερκόσμιον ἀποκαλεῖ δημιουργὸν, τὸν δὲ νοῦν αὐτῆς, πρὸς ὃν ἀπέστραπται, τὸ αὐτοζῶον, ὡς εἶναι τὸ παράδειγμα τοῦ δημιουργοῦ κατὰ τοῦτον"</note> 

And though Proclus there asks whether or not this was Plotinus’s true meaning, Porphyry is most to be credited here, since he had such an intimate acquaintance with him. Therefore, according to these *three Platonists*—Plotinus, Amelius, and Porphyry—the *Third Hypostasis* of the *Platonic Trinity* is neither the *world* nor the *immediate soul* of the *mundane animal*. Instead, it is a certain *supermundane soul*, which was also the *Maker* and *Creator* of the *world*, and therefore *no creature*. 

Now, since the corporeal world was also supposed by these Platonists to be an *animal*, they necessarily had to acknowledge a double soul: one a *mundane soul* <note>original: "ψυχὴν ἐγκόσμιον"</note>, the *immediate soul* of this *world-animal*, and another *supermundane soul* <note>original: "ψυχὴν ὑπερκόσμιον"</note>, which was the *third* in their trinity of gods (or Divine Hypostases) and the *proper* and *immediate Maker* of the world. 

In all probability, this was *Plato’s* opinion as well. Therefore, *that soul*—which is the only deity he undertakes to prove in his *Book of Laws*—was a *supermundane soul*, and not the same as that *mundane soul* whose *genesis* or origin is described in his *Timaeus*. The former of them is a *principle* and *eternal*; the latter was made in time, together with the world (though said to be older than it, because it is before it in the order of nature). 

Thus we see plainly that although some of these Platonists and Pythagoreans either misunderstood or corrupted the *tradition of the Trinity* <note>original: "Cabbala of the Trinity"</note> so as to make its *Third Hypostasis* the *animated world*—which they themselves acknowledged to be a *thing made* <note>original: "ποίημα"</note> and a *thing created* <note>original: "δημιουργούμενον"</note>—others of the more refined thinkers among them supposed this *Third Hypostasis* of their Trinity to be not a *mundane* but a *supermundane soul* and a *Maker*, not a *creature*, but the *Creator* or *Maker* of the *whole world*.

As for the *second particular* proposed: it was also a gross absurdity in those Platonists to make the *second* person in their *trinity of gods* and hypostases not *one God* or *hypostasis*, but a *multitude of gods* and *hypostases*. It was also a monstrous extravagance of theirs to suppose that the *Ideas* were all distinct substances.

<summary>This page argues that the most sophisticated Platonists viewed the third person of their Trinity as a "supermundane soul"—an eternal Creator who exists above the world rather than as a part of it. It distinguishes this divine Creator from the "mundane soul" that animates the physical universe as a created being.</summary>

### CHAPTER IV. Ideas are neither Animals nor Gods.

<margin>p. 320. Rig.</margin> substances and animals. This is a view which, among others, <term>Tertullian</term> <note>Tertullian (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) was a prolific early Christian author from Carthage.</note> in his book *On the Soul* attributes to <term>Plato</term> in this way: "Plato intends that there are certain invisible, incorporeal, super-mundane, divine, and eternal substances, which he calls Ideas—that is, forms, patterns, and causes of these manifest natural things that are subject to bodies. He believes those Ideas are the truths, while these natural things are only their images." <note>original: "Vult Plato esse quasdam substantias Invisibiles, Incorporeales, Supermundiales, Divinas, & Æternas, quas appellat Ideas, id est, Formas & Exempla, & Causas Naturalium istorum manifestorum, & subjacentium Corporalibus : & illas quidem esse Veritates, hæc autem Imagines earum"</note>

It cannot be denied that there are some strange expressions in Plato that suggest this idea. Therefore, he might not be justified in this, nor, I think, in some of his other notions concerning these *Ideas*; for instance, when he contends that they are not only the objects of science but also the proper and physical causes of all things here below. He argues, for example, that the *Ideas* of *Similarity* and *Dissimilarity* are the actual causes of the likeness and unlikeness of all things to one another through their "participation" in them. 

Nevertheless, it cannot be doubted at all that Plato himself and most of his followers understood very well that these *Ideas* were all, in reality, nothing other than the *conceptions* <note>original: "Noemata"</note> of that one *Perfect Intellect*, which was their second *Hypostasis* <note>The second person or level of the Divine Trinity in Platonic thought.</note>. Therefore, they could not have seriously looked upon them as so many distinct substances existing separately and apart from any Mind, regardless of the extravagant expressions they sometimes used. 

Wherefore, when they called them *essences* or *substances* <note>original: "οὐσίας"</note>—as they are called in <term>Philo</term> "the most necessary essences" <note>original: "ἀναγκαιόταται οὐσίαι"</note>—their true meaning was only to signify that they were not accidental and fleeting <note>original: "evanid"</note> things like our own human conceptions. Instead, they are the *permanent objects* of all science, and perhaps even the causes of existing things. 

Again, when they sometimes called these Ideas "animals," they intended only to signify that they were not merely "dead forms," like pictures drawn on paper or carved images and statues. In this way, the philosopher <term>Amelius</term> plainly understood that passage from <term>St. John</term> the Evangelist concerning the eternal *Word* <note>original: "λόγῳ"</note>. He punctuated the words differently than our modern copies <margin>So Clement of Alexandria, St. Cyril, St. Augustine, and other Latin fathers.</margin> do: "That which was made, in him was life." <note>original: "ὃ γέγονεν ἐν αὐτῷ ζωὴ ἦν"</note> This philosopher provided a gloss on it in this manner: "In whom whatsoever was made was living, and life, and true being." <note>original: "ὃ γέγονεν ζῶν, καὶ ζωή, καὶ ὂν πεφυκέναι"</note> 

Lastly, it is no wonder if these *Ideas* immediately became "gods" to those men who took every possible occasion to multiply the number of gods. This also involved something of that Scholastic notion, "Whatever is in God, is God." <note>original: "Quicquid est in Deo, est Deus"</note> But the main reason for this was a bit of pagan poetry; these pagan theologians were generally possessed by a poetic habit of personifying things and deifying them. 

Therefore, although the *Ideas* were considered "titular gods" to many of the Platonic pagans, even <term>Julian</term> the Apostate himself (who made the most of them) supposed them all "to coexist with God and exist within him" <note>original: "συνυπάρχειν καὶ ἐνυπάρχειν"</note>—that is, within the First Mind or Second *Hypostasis* of their Trinity.

# No Created Henades. Book I.

Finally, while **Proclus** and other **Platonists** include many **particular gods** within the **three universal principles** (or **hypostases** <note>original: "Hypostases"; these are the three foundational "persons" or levels of reality in the Platonic and Christian Trinity.</note>) of their **Trinity**, such as **Noes** <note>original: "Nóes"; Greek for "minds" or "intellects."</note> (minds or intellects) superior to the **First Soul**, and **Henades** <note>original: "Henades"; Greek for "unities."</note> and **Agathotetes** <note>original: "Agathotetes"; Greek for "goodnesses."</note> (unities and goodnesses) superior even to the **First Intellect**, they effectively make these **particular beings**—which must actually be **creatures**—superior to the **hypostases** that are **universal** and **infinite**. Consequently, they treat divine principles as if they were merely created things. This **hypothesis** of theirs is entirely **absurd** and **irrational**. There are no **created beings** who are **essentially good** and **wise** by their own nature; they only possess these qualities by **participation** <note>A philosophical term meaning that a creature shares in a quality (like goodness) that belongs perfectly and essentially only to God.</note>. Nor are there any **immovable natures** among them whose *ousia* <note>original: "οὐσία"; essence or being.</note> is their *energeia* <note>original: "ἐνέργεια"; operation or activity.</note> (whose **essence** is their **operation**). Instead, all are **mutable** and **changeable**, and likely—as **Origen** and other **Church Fathers** add—**lapsable** and **peccable** <note>Subject to falling into sin.</note>.

<margin>
*On First Principles* <note>original: "Peri Archon"</note>
Book 1, Chapter 8.
page 685.
</margin>

> There is no nature which is not capable of both good and evil, except only the nature of God, who is the fountain of all good; and the wisdom of Christ, for he is the fountain of wisdom, and wisdom itself can never receive folly. He is also justice itself, which can never admit of injustice, and the reason and word itself, which can never become irrational. He is also the light itself, and it is certain that darkness cannot overcome this light. Similarly, the nature of the Holy Spirit, which is holy, does not admit pollution; for it is holy by nature and substance. But whatever other nature is holy, it is only so through participation and by the inspiration of this Holy Spirit, so that it may be sanctified. It does not possess holiness by its own nature, but only as an "accident" <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a quality that a thing has, but which is not part of its essential definition; therefore, it can be lost.</note>; for this reason, that which is accidental can fail and fall away. <note>original: "Nulla Natura est, quæ non recipiat Bonum & Malum, Exceptâ Dei Naturâ... propter quod & decidere potest, quod accidit."</note>

Therefore, since all **created beings** have only **accidental goodness** and **wisdom**, they may **degenerate** and fall into **evil** and **folly**. Origen’s point is essentially that there is no such rank of beings as **Autogaathotetes** (essential goodnesses), because there is only one **being who is essentially good**, or **goodness** itself. Nor do any such **particular created beings** exist in nature as those the **Platonists** call **Noes**—that is, **minds** or **intellects** that are **immovable**, **perfectly** and **essentially wise**, or **wisdom** itself, whose **essence** is their **operation**, and who consequently have no **flux** or **successive action** at all. Only the **Eternal Word** and **Wisdom of God** is like that. Such beings would also be absolutely **unable to be united** to any **bodies**. It is true that **Origen** did sometimes mention **Noes** (minds or intellects), but he used the term in a different sense, calling all **souls** by that name as they were first **created** by **God** and before their **fall**. This...

<meta>This page continues the argument that there are no "Immutable Intellects" among created beings, specifically contrasting the Platonist view of "Noes" (pure, unchangeable minds) with the view held by Origen and many Church Fathers that all created spirits are "Souls"—beings that are active, embodied, and capable of falling into sin.</meta>

# CHAPTER IV. Nor Immutable Intellects.

This was as much as if he should have said: although some of the **Platonists** talk much of their **Noes** <note>original: "Noes"; the plural of "Nous," meaning "minds" or "intellects" in Greek philosophy.</note>, there is actually nothing that corresponds to that name according to their definition. Instead, the only **Noes** really existing in Nature are **Unfallen but Peccable Souls** <note>Souls that have not yet sinned but are capable of doing so.</note>. **Origen** often concluded that the highest rank of created beings are, in fact, no better than those which the **Platonists** commonly call **psychai**, or **souls**. By these **souls**, he understood first of all beings that are by their own nature **self-moving** and **active**, whereas the **Noes** of the **Platonists** are considered altogether **immovable** and above **action**. 

Furthermore, he understood them to be such beings or incorporeal spirits that do not exist abstractly and separately from all matter—as the **Noes** of the **Platonists** were supposed to do—but are **vitally unitable to bodies**. Thus, together with those bodies, they compound and make up **one animal**. In this way, I say, **Origen** conceived even of the **highest angelic** and **archangelic orders**: that they were all of them **souls** united to bodies, though these bodies were pure, subtle, and ethereal. However, he supposed it was not impossible for them to sink down into bodies that were more gross and fouled <note>original: "feculent"; dregs-like or foul.</note>. It is certain that many of the ancient Christian writers agreed with **Origen** on this point: that the **highest created spirits** were not naked and **abstract minds**, but **souls** clothed with some **corporeal garment** <note>original: "indument"; a covering or robe.</note>. 

Lastly, **Origen’s** souls were also supposed to be all endowed with **Free Will** <note>original: "Liberum Arbitrium"</note>, and consequently to be **self-improvable** and **self-degradable**. No particular created spirits were absolutely **impeccable** <note>Incapable of sinning.</note> by their own nature; rather, they were **lapsable** <note>Capable of falling or sinning.</note> into **sinful habits**. In contrast, the **Platonic Noes** are supposed to be such beings as could never **fall** nor **degenerate**. The majority of Christian writers seem to have consented or agreed with **Origen** in this as well, as they supposed that he who is now the **Prince of Devils** was once an angel of the **highest order**. Thus **Saint Jerome** determines: 

> "God alone is he into whom sin does not fall; all other beings, since they have Free Will, may turn their will in either direction—that is, toward evil as well as toward good." <note>original: "Solus Deus est, in quem Peccatum non cadit; catera cùm sint Liberi Arbitrii, possunt in utramque partem suam flectere voluntatem."</note> 

It is certain that God, in the sense of perfection, is the most **free agent** of all, and **contingent liberty** <note>The freedom to choose between different possibilities.</note> is not universally denied to Him. But here, it is made the exclusive privilege of God—that is, of the Holy Trinity—to be devoid of **Free Will** <note>original: "Liberum Arbitrium"</note> insofar as it implies imperfection—namely, **peccability** and the possibility of **falling**.

It is true that some of the **Platonic philosophers** suppose that even in that rank of beings they call **souls**, although they are not **essentially unchangeable** but are all **self-moving** and **active**, there are some of so high a pitch and elevation that they can never **degenerate** nor sink down into sinful habits. **Simplicius** is one who argues this:

<margin>In his commentary on the *Enchiridion* of Epictetus, pages 12, 13.</margin>

> "But the first of the souls—since they were produced directly by those who are good in themselves—even if they possess something subordinate compared to those beings (because they are not Goodness itself, but rather desire the Good), yet because they are kindred to it, they desire it naturally and inseparably. They have their choice directed toward the Good in a single form, and they never turn aside toward the worse. And if choice consists of choosing one thing instead of another, perhaps there would be no choice for those beings? Unless one calls this choice..." <note>original Greek: "ἀλλὰ αἱ μὲν πρῶται τῶν ψυχῶν... εἰ μήτις αὐτὴν προαίρεσιν..."</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of created spirits, specifically focusing on whether higher beings like angels possess the same type of "slippery" free will as humans, or if their nature is fixed in goodness. It contrasts the views of the Neoplatonist philosopher Simplicius with the controversial Christian theologian Origen.</meta>

### Different Degrees of Souls. BOOK I.

"...as those who choose the primary goods are called noble." <note>original Greek: "ὡς τὰ πρῶτα ἀγαθὰ αἱρεομένω καλοῖ"</note> *But the first and highest of souls, which were immediately produced from what is essentially Good, although they have some decline in them—since they are not Goodness itself but merely seekers of Good—are nevertheless so closely related to that highest Good of all that they naturally and inseparably <note>original: "Indivulsively"</note> cling to it. Their wills are always uniformly directed toward it, and they never decline toward the worse.* In fact, if *Proærefis* <term>the Greek term for moral choice or deliberate decision-making</term> is defined as choosing one thing over another, perhaps there is no such thing as *Proærefis* to be attributed to them—unless one calls the act of choosing the *Primary Goods* a "choice." By these higher souls, *Simplicius* must mean either the souls of the *Sun, Moon, and Stars*, or else those of the *superior orders of demonic or angelic beings*. Although he *questions whether choice or deliberation* belongs to them, he plainly implies that they do not possess any of that *slippery free will* <note>original: "Lubricous Liberum Arbitrium"</note> which would make them capable of *vice and immorality as well as virtue*.

But whatever is to be said of this, there seems to be no necessity at all for admitting *Origen’s* assertion that all rational souls whatsoever—even those of humans and those of the highest angelic orders—are universally of one and the same nature and have no *fundamental* or *essential difference* in their makeup. Consequently, he argued that all the differences we see between them now arose only from the differences in their behavior, or the use of that *power* and *liberty* which they all alike *once* had. According to him, *Thrones, and Dominions, and Principalities, and Powers* <note>the traditional hierarchy of angels</note> were all made such by their own *merits*. Furthermore, he believed that *human souls*, though now sunk so low, are not absolutely incapable of *becoming angels* or ascending to those highest altitudes. Just as it is not impossible, according to him, that the highest angels also—the *Seraphim and Cherubim*—might in the course of time not only degenerate into devils but also sink down into human bodies.

*His* reason for this monstrous paradox is only this: that Divine Justice cannot otherwise be well resolved <note>original: "salved"</note> unless God is a "respecter of persons" <note>original Greek: "προσωπολήπτης"; one who shows unfair favoritism</note>, should he have arbitrarily made such vast differences among intellectual beings. He extends this reasoning so far as to include the *human soul* of our Savior Christ himself. He argues that this soul was not partially appointed to that transcendent dignity of its *Hypostatic Union* <note>the theological doctrine of the union of Christ's human and divine natures in one person</note>, but earned it because of its most faithful adherence to the Divine Word and Wisdom in a *pre-existent state*, beyond all other souls. He endeavors to prove this from the Scripture:

<margin>On First Principles, Book 1, Ch. 6.</margin>

*That the perfection of love and the sincerity of affection created an inseparable unity with God, so that the assumption of his soul was not accidental or based on favoritism, but was granted to him as a reward for his virtues. Hear the Prophet saying to him: "You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions." Therefore, because of the merit of its love, the soul of Christ is anointed with the oil of gladness—that is, it is made one with the Word of God. For being anointed with the oil of gladness is understood as nothing other than being filled with the Holy Spirit. He said "above your companions" because the grace of the Spirit was not given to him as it was to the prophets, but the substantial fullness of the Word of God was within him.* <note>original Latin: "Quòd dilectionis Perfectio, & affectus sinceritas, ei inseparabilem cum Deo fecerit Unitatem, ità ut non fortuita fuerit, aut cum Personæ acceptione, Animæ ejus assumptio, sed Virtutum suarum sibi merito delata; audi ad eum Prophetam dicentem, Dilexisti Justitiam & odisti iniquitatem, proptereà unxit te Deus, Deus tuus, oleo lætitiæ præ participibus tuis: Dilectionis ergo merito ungitur Oleo lætitiæ Anima Christi, id est, cum Verbo Dei Unum efficitur. Ungi namque oleo lætitiæ, non aliud intelligitur quam Spiritu Sancto repleri. Præ Participibus autem dixit; quia non Gratia Spiritus sicut Prophetis ei data est, sed ipsius Verbi Dei in ea Substantialis inerat Plenitudo."</note> That

### CHAPTER IV. Against Origen's Endless Circuits.

*The perfection of love and the sincerity of divine affection secured for this soul its inseparable union with the Godhead. Therefore, the adoption <note>original: "Assumption"</note> of this soul was neither accidental nor partial, nor based on favoritism <term>original: "Prosopolepsie," a Greek-derived term for "respect of persons" or showing unfair bias</term>; instead, it was bestowed upon it justly for the merits of its virtues. Listen (Origen says) to the Prophet declaring this to him: "You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, even your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows."* <note>Psalm 45:7</note> *The soul of Christ, therefore, was anointed with the oil of gladness—or made one with the Word of God—because of its merits of love and faithful adherence to God, and for no other reason. For to be "anointed with the oil of gladness" here properly signifies nothing else but to be replenished with the Holy Spirit. But when it is said that he was thus anointed "above his fellows," this indicates that he did not have the Holy Spirit bestowed upon him only as the prophets and other holy men had, but that the substantial fullness of the Word of God lived in him. However, Origen’s reasoning here seems to be very weak. If there is a rank of souls below the human level that is specifically different from humans (as Origen himself must confess, since he does not allow the souls of animals <note>original: "Brutes"</note> to be fallen human souls, as some Pythagoreans and Platonists believed, but instead rejects that opinion as monstrously absurd and irrational), then there is no reason why there might not also be other ranks and orders of souls superior to those of men. This could exist without the injustice of favoritism, just as Plotinus and the majority of other Platonists conceived, alongside the philosopher Simplicius.*

But we can agree with *Origen* least of all when he uses this principle—that souls, as such, are essentially endowed with *Free Will* <note>original Latin: "Liberum Arbitrium"</note> and therefore are never by their own nature incapable of sinning—to conclude that there are *endless cycles of souls moving upwards and downwards*. He thus makes them never at rest, denying them any *fixed state of holiness and happiness through divine grace*, such as a state where they might be free from the fear and danger of ever losing it. Regarding this, *St. Augustine* <note>original: "St. Austin"</note> wrote:

"The Church has deservedly rejected Origen, both for certain other opinions of his, and especially for those alternating happinesses and miseries without end, and for his infinite circuits, ascents, and descents of souls from one to the other in restless cycles after set periods of time. For by this, he has quite lost that very title of 'Pitiful' or 'Merciful' which he otherwise seemed to have deserved; he creates so many true miseries for the best of saints, in which they would successively undergo punishment and pain, and provides nothing but false happiness for them, in which they could never have any true or secure joy, free from the fear of losing the good they possess." <note>original Latin: "Illum propter alia nonnulla, & maximè propter alternantes sine cessatione beatitudines & miserias, & status miserorum intervallis ab istis ad illas, atque ab illis ad istas Itus ac Reditus Interminabiles; non immeritò reprobavit Ecclesia: quia & hoc quod Misericors videbatur, amisit, faciendo sanctis Veras Miserias, quibus pœnas luerent, & falsas Beatitudines, in quibus verum ac securum ætterni boni gaudium, non haberent."</note>

For this Origenist hypothesis seems directly contrary to the whole tenor of the Gospel, which promises eternal and everlasting life to those who believe in Christ, and per—

# The Henades and Noes, BOOK I.

Perseveringly obey him. 1 John 2:25: *This is the promise that he has promised us, even eternal life.* And Titus 1:2: *In hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, has promised.* And, *God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.* And lest all this should be taken for a *periodical eternity* <note>An "eternity" that only lasts for a specific cycle or period of time before starting over, as in the theory of reincarnation.</note> only, John 3:26 <note>The author likely intended John 11:26: "whoever lives and believes in me shall never die."</note> says, *He that believes in me shall never die.* 

Possibly this might be the meaning of Saint Paul in 2 Timothy 1:10, when he affirms of our Savior Christ, *that he has abolished death, and brought life and immortality to light through the Gospel.* This was not because he was the first who had discovered and published the soul's immortality to the world—for that was already believed not only by all the *Pharisaic Jews*, but also by the majority of *Pagans* as well. Rather, it was because these groups for the most part believed in *endless circuits* and the *transmigration of souls* <term>the movement of a soul from one body to another after death; reincarnation</term>. Therefore, Christ was the first who brought *everlasting life* to *light*, giving the world assurance through the faith of the Gospel of a *fixed* and *permanent state of happiness*, and a never-fading *crown of glory* to be obtained. *Him that overcomes, will I make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go no more out* (Revelation 3:12).

Now, the reason we mentioned <term>Origen</term> <note>A prominent early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD) who attempted to harmonize Greek philosophy, particularly Platonism, with Christian doctrine.</note> here was because he was a person not only thoroughly skilled in all *Platonic learning*, but also one who was sufficiently devoted to those *doctrines* <note>original: "Dogmata"</note>; he is commonly understood to have had too great a fondness for them. Therefore, if there had been any solid reasoning for either those particular <term>Henades</term> <note>From the Greek "henas" (unit); in Neoplatonism, these are "The Ones" or divine unities that exist at the highest level of reality.</note> or <term>Noes</term> <note>From the Greek "nous" (mind/intellect); these are pure intellectual beings or divine minds.</note> of theirs—*created beings* above the *rank* of *souls*, and consequently according to the *Platonic hypothesis*, superior even to the *Universal Soul* <note>original: "Psyche"</note> (which was the *third person* <note>original: "Hypostasis"</note> in their *trinity*, and seems to correspond to the *Holy Spirit* in the *Christian Trinity*)—Origen was as likely to have been favorable toward them as anyone else. 

But it is indeed clearly contrary to reason that there should be any such *particular* (that is, *created*) Henades and <term>essential goodnesses</term> <note>original: "αὐτοαγαθότητες" (autoagathotētes)</note> superior to the *Platonic First Mind*; or any such Noes and <term>essential wisdoms</term> <note>original: "αὐτοσοφίαι" (autosophiai)</note> superior to their *Universal Soul*. It would be just the same as if, in the *Christian Trinity*, besides the First Person or the *Father*, one should suppose a multitude of *particular fatherhoods* superior to the *Second Person*; or if besides that *Second Person*, the *Son* or *Word*, one supposed a multitude of *particular sons* or *words*, all superior to the *Third Person*, the *Holy Spirit*. To do this is plainly to create a breach in the nature of the Deity; to confound the Creator and creature together; and to suppose a group of such *creaturely gods* that they imply a manifest contradiction in the very concept of them.

Therefore, we shall observe here that it was not the *Catholic* <note>In this context, "catholic" means the universal or generally accepted doctrine of the school, not the Roman Catholic Church.</note> *doctrine* of the *Platonic school* that there were such *Henades* and *Noes*. Instead, this was only a *private opinion* of some doctors among them, and a later opinion at that. For first, as for those *Henades*, there are not the least footsteps of them to be found anywhere in *Plato's* writings; indeed, it may be plainly gathered from them that he imagined no such thing. For as much as in his *Second Epistle*—

Where he describes his *Trinity*, he does not say of the *First*, <term>about the first are the first things</term> <note>original: περὶ τὸ πρῶτον τὰ πρῶτα</note> as he does of the *Second*, <term>about the second are the second things</term> <note>original: δεύτερον περὶ τὰ δεύτερα</note>, and of the *Third*, <term>about the third are the third things</term> <note>original: τρίτον περὶ τὰ τρίτα</note>. Instead, of the *First* he says, <term>About the King of all things, are all things; and for his sake are all things; and he is the cause of all things that are good</term> <note>original: περὶ τὸν πάντων βασιλέα πάντ᾽ ἐστὶ, καὶ ἐκείνου ἕνεκα πάντα, καὶ ἐκεῖνο αἴτιον ἁπάντων τῶν καλῶν</note>. Therefore, here there are no *particular Henades* <note>original: Henades; a Neoplatonic term for "unities" or divine ones</note> and *Autoagathotetes* <note>original: Autoagathotetes; "self-goodnesses" or things that are good in their own essence</note>, *Unities* and *Goodnesses*, about the *First*—the <term>The One</term> <note>original: τὸ Ἕν</note> and <term>The Good</term> <note>original: τἀγαθὸν</note>—but all *good things* are about him, he being both the *Efficient* and *Final Cause* of all. 

Moreover, throughout all his works, *Plotinus* shows not the least suspicion of these *Henades* and *Agathotetes*. This language is scarcely to be found anywhere in the writings of any *Platonists* older than *Proclus*. *Proclus* himself, as if he were conscious that this addition <note>original: assumentum</note> to *Platonic Theology* was not a very defensible thing, sometimes avoids the issue or changes his position by being ambiguous with the word *Henades*, taking them for the *Ideas* or the *Intelligible Gods* mentioned before. 

Perhaps *Synesius* also uses the word in this way in his *First Hymn*, when God is called by him:

-><term>Pure Unity of Unities,</term> <note>original: Ἑνοτήτων ἑνὰς ἁγνὴ</note><-
-><term>And the first Monad of Monads.</term> <note>original: μονάδων μονάς τε πρώτη</note><-

That is, *The First Idea of Good, and Cause of all the Ideas*. 

As for the *Particular Noes* <note>plural of Nous; minds or intellects</note>, these indeed seem to have crept up somewhat before *Plotinus's* time. In addition to the passage cited before, he gives some hints of them elsewhere, as in *Enneads* 6, Book 4, Chapter 4: <margin>* Pages 847, 848.</margin> <term>But how can there be many souls and many minds, and not only one, but many Beings?</term> <note>original: ἀλλὰ πῶς ψυχαὶ πολλαὶ καὶ νοῖ πολλοὶ; ... Entia</note>. From this and other places in his work, *Marsilio Ficino* concluded that *Plotinus* himself really asserted a multitude of other *substantial beings* above the *rank* of *souls*, called <term>minds</term> <note>original: νόες or νοῖ</note> or *intellects*. 

Nevertheless, because *Plotinus* speaks of them so uncertainly and creates such a union between all these *minds* and their *particular respective souls*, it may well be questioned whether he really took them for anything else but the *heads* and *summits* of those *souls*. He supposed that all *souls* have a *mind* in them—the *participation* of the *First Mind*—as well as a *unity* too—the *participation* of the *First Unity*—by which they are capable of being joined with both: <margin>Enneads, Book 5, Chapter 11.</margin> <term>There must be Mind in us, as also the principle and cause of Mind, God. Not as if he were divided, but because—though remaining in himself—he is also considered to be in many, as they are capable of receiving him. Just as the center point remains in itself, yet it is also in every line drawn from the circumference; each of them, by a certain point of its own, touches it. And by some such thing in us, we are capable of touching God, being united with him, and being suspended from him; and we are firmly established there, as many of us as incline toward him.</term> <note>original: δεῖ νοῦν ἐν ἡμῖν εἶναι, καὶ νοῦ ἀρχὴν, καὶ αἰτίαν, καὶ θεὸν· ὥσπερ τὸ κέντρον ἐφ᾽ ἑαυτοῦ ἐστιν· ἔχει δὲ καὶ ἕκαστον τῶν ἐν τῷ κύκλῳ σημεῖον ἐν αὐτῷ· καὶ αἱ γραμμαὶ τὸ ἴδιον προσφέρουσι πρὸς τοῦτο· τῷ γὰρ τοιούτῳ τῶν ἐν ἡμῖν ἡμεῖς ἐφαπτόμεθα, καὶ συνεσμεν, καὶ ἀνηρτήμεθα, ἐνιδρύμεθα δὲ, οἳ ἂν συννεύωμεν ἐκεῖ·</note>

Yet those higher things are always active in their own way; the Mind, and that which is before the Mind (Unity), remain within themselves,</term> etc. <note>original: ἔχοντες τὰ τοιαῦτα οὐκ ἀντιλαμβανόμεθα, ἀλλ’ ἀργοῦμεν ταῖς τοιαύταις ἐνεργείαις τὰ πολλὰ · οἱ δ’ οὐδ’ ὅλως ἐνεργοῦσιν · ἐκεῖνα μὲν ἔστιν ἐν ταῖς ἑαυτῶν ἐνεργείαις αἰεὶ, νοῦς δὲ καὶ τὸ πρὸ νοῦ ἐν ἑαυτῷ</note>. Here, *Plotinus* seems to suggest that these *Noes* <term>original: Noes; plural of Nous, meaning "minds" or "intellectual beings"</term> or *Minds* are nothing more than something within our *Souls* by which they participate in the *First Mind*. Furthermore, it is said of *Porphyrius*—who was well acquainted with the philosophy of *Plotinus*—that he completely discarded and rejected these *Noes* or *Intellects* as *substances* actually distinct from the *First Mind* or separate from *Souls*. 

It is certain that such *Minds* as these are nowhere clearly mentioned by *Plato*; he speaks only of *Minds within Souls*, but not of any abstract and separate minds except for the one. And though some might think he hinted at them in his phrase <term>second things about the second</term> <note>original: δεύτερον περὶ τὰ δεύτερα</note> (mentioned before), these may very well be understood as the *Ideas*; just as the <term>third things about the third</term> <note>original: τρίτον περὶ τὰ τρίτα</note> refer to all *created beings*. 

Therefore, we may conclude that this *Platonic*—or rather *pseudo-Platonic*—*Trinity*, which blurs the *differences* between *God* and the *creature* (likely to favor *pagan polytheism* and *idolatry*), is not nearly as rational as the *Christian Trinity* described earlier. That Christian view distinctly declares how far the *Deity* extends and where the *creature* begins: namely, that the *Deity* encompasses this *whole Trinity of Hypostases* <term>original: Hypostases; the three distinct persons of the Trinity</term>, and that all other things whatsoever—excepting only these three *Persons*—are truly and properly their *creatures*, produced by the joint concurrence and influence of them all, as they are really but *one God*.

But it is already manifest that all the previously mentioned *distortions* and *corruptions* of that *divine Cabala* <term>original: Cabala; here referring to an ancient, received oral tradition of wisdom</term> of the Trinity, and the *spurious Trinity* described (which was called *Platonic* to distinguish it from the *Christian* one because some Platonists supported it), cannot be justly blamed on *Plato* himself, nor on all his followers *universally*. 

On the contrary, we will now show that *Plato* and some of the Platonists retained much of the *ancient, genuine Cabala* and came very close to the *true Christian Trinity*. This is because their *three Hypostases*, which they distinguished from all their other *gods*, seem not to have been considered *creatures*; rather, all other things were considered the *creatures* of these three.

First, therefore, we affirm that *Plato* himself, at the beginning of his *Timaeus*, very carefully distinguishes between *God* and the *creature* by defining the boundaries between them in this way: <term>In my opinion, we must first make this distinction: what is that which always exists and has no beginning (or becoming), and what is that which is always becoming but never truly exists?
