# Chapter IV. Partly Retained by Plato, etc.

<term>...that which is becoming and perishing, but never truly exists; and everything that becomes must of necessity become by some cause.</term> <note>original: γινόμενον καὶ ἀπολλύμενον, ὄντως δὲ οὐδέποτε ὄν· πᾶν δ' αὖ τὸ γινόμενον ὑπ' αἰτίου τινὸς ἐξ ἀνάγκης γίγνεσθαι</note> *We, intending here to discuss the Universe, judge it necessary to begin with a distinction between that which always* **Is**, *and has no* **origin** or **generation** <note>original: Ortus</note>; *and that which is* **made**, *but never truly* **is**. *The former of these, being always like itself and the same, is understood by the intellect through reason, or is the object of knowledge; the latter of them—that which is* **made** *and* **perishes**, *but never truly* **is**—*is not properly knowable, but only* **subject to opinion** <note>original: Opinable</note>, *or the object of opinion combined with irrational sense.* Now every thing that is made must of necessity be made by some cause.

The reason why *Plato*, when treating the Universe, begins here with this distinction was, as *Proclus* well observes, because <term>it is stored up in our common notions that there is something which always exists</term> <note>original: ἐν ταῖς κοιναῖς ἡμῶν ἐννοίαις ἀπόκειται, τὸ εἶναι τι ἀεὶ ὄν</note>. It is either one of our *common notions* <note>Self-evident truths recognized by all rational minds.</note>, or a thing *mathematically demonstrable*, that there must be something **eternal**, or which was **never made**, but always was and had no **beginning**. And it is evident by sense and experience that all things are not like this, but that some things are made and perish again, or are generated and corrupted. Now the later Platonists, being strongly possessed by a prejudice for the *world's eternity*—or that it had *no beginning*—have offered strange violence to *Plato’s* text in this place. They have twisted his words to a completely different sense than he intended; as if by his phrase *that which is made* <note>original: τὸ γινόμενον</note>, he did not mean something that had a beginning, but only something whose duration is *flowing and successive, or temporal*, which might nonetheless be without a beginning. It is as if he supposed the whole *physical world* to be such a thing: though it has a successive and *temporal duration*, yet it was without any beginning.

<margin>*Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book 5, Prose 6.*</margin>
And the current ran so strong in this direction that even *Boethius*, that learned Christian philosopher, was himself also carried away by its force. He also took it for granted that *Plato* held the *eternity* of the world in this sense—that is, its being without a *beginning*. <term>Some people,</term> he says, <term>when they hear that Plato believed this world had no beginning in time and would have no end, do not correctly infer from this that Plato therefore made the world co-eternal with God. For it is one thing to be led through an unending life (which Plato attributed to the world), and another thing to embrace the whole presence of an unending life all at once (which is clearly proper to the Divine Mind). Neither should God be thought of as older than created things by a quantity of time, but rather by the simplicity of His nature.</term> <note>original: Non rectè quidam... qui cum audiunt visum Platoni, Mundum hunc nec habuisse Initium Temporis, nec habiturum esse Defectum; hoc modo Conditori Conditum Mundum fieri Coæternum putant. Aliud est enim, per Interminabilem duci vitam, quod Mundo Plato tribuit; aliud Interminabilis Vitæ totam pariter complexum esse præsentiam; quod Divinæ Mentis proprium esse manifestum est. Neque Deus, Conditis rebus Antiquior videri debet, Temporis Quantitate, sed Simplicis potius proprietate Naturæ.</note> To which purpose he adds afterwards: <term>Therefore, if we wish to give things names worthy of them, following Plato, we should say that God is eternal, but the world is only perpetual.</term> <note>original: Itaque si digna rebus Nomina velimus imponere, Platonem sequentes, Deum quidem Æternum, Mundum verò dicemus esse Perpetuum</note> But as this doctrine of the later Platonists completely frustrates *Plato’s* design in this place, which was to prove or—

<header>Plato's Plurality in the Deity. BOOK I.</header>

Plato asserts that there is a **God**. Even if the world had no beginning—regardless of how long its successive duration might be—it would not necessarily follow that it was not made by some other cause. However, such a notion is directly contrary to the philosopher's own words. He himself declares that by "that which is made" <note>original: τὸ γινόμενον</note>, he did not only mean that whose duration is **successive**, but also "that which had a beginning of its generation" <note>original: τὸ γενέσεως ἀρχὴν ἔχον</note>, and "that which began from a certain epoch of time" <note>original: τὸ ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς τινὸς ἀρξάμενον</note>; or, that which once did not exist and therefore must be brought into being by some other cause. 

So, Plato plainly supposed that all <term>temporary beings</term> <note>Beings that exist within time and are subject to change.</note> once had a beginning to their duration. He declares in his *Timaeus* that **time itself was not eternal**, or without beginning, but was **made together with the heaven or world**. From this, he infers that there must of necessity be another **eternal being**—namely, one that has a <term>permanent duration</term> <note>An existence that is fixed and unchanging, unlike the flowing nature of time.</note> and was without beginning, serving as the cause of both **time** and the **world**. Since nothing can possibly be made without a cause—that is, nothing which once was not could bring itself into being—it must be produced by something else. Thus, we must eventually arrive at something that had no beginning. 

Therefore, *Plato* takes it for granted that whatever has a temporary and flowing duration was not without a beginning. He also assumes that whatever was without a beginning has a **permanent duration** or <term>standing eternity</term> <note>A state of being that exists all at once, without a past or future.</note>. He states the difference between **uncreated** and **created beings**, or between God and the **creature**, as follows: a creature is that whose duration, being temporary or successive, once had a beginning. This is his "that which is made, but never truly is" <note>original: τὸ γινόμενον μέν, ὂν δὲ οὐδέποτε</note>, and that which "must of necessity be produced by some cause" <note>original: ὑπ᾽ αἰτίας τινὸς ἐξ ἀνάγκης γίνεται</note>. But whatever is **without beginning** and has a **permanent duration** is **uncreated** or **divine**. This is his "that which always is, and has no generation, nor was ever made" <note>original: τὸ ὂν μὲν ἀεί, γένεσιν δὲ οὐκ ἔχον</note>. This is consistent with how God is styled "He who truly is" <note>original: ὁ Ὤν</note> in the Septuagint translation of the Mosaic writings.

Now, regarding this "eternal idea" <note>original: ἀΐδιος ἰδέα</note> or "nature" <note>original: φύσις</note> which always **is** and was never made, Plato speaks of it not only in the singular (as we Christians do now) but often in the plural pagan way as well. For instance, in this very *Timaeus*, he calls the world "a made or created image of the eternal gods" <note>original: τῆς ἀϊδίων θεῶν γεγονὸς ἄγαλμα</note>. By these **eternal gods**, he undoubtedly meant "that first, and second, and third" <note>original: τὸ πρῶτον, καὶ τὸ δεύτερον, καὶ τὸ τρίτον</note> which he identifies as the principles of **all things** in his second epistle to *Dionysius*. That is to say, his <term>trinity of divine hypostases</term> <note>The three distinct individualities or "persons" that make up the one divine essence in Platonic thought.</note>, by whose combined power and according to whose image and likeness the whole world was made. *Plotinus* also plainly declares this in these words cited earlier: "This world is an image always being depicted—or perpetually renewed like a reflection in a mirror—of that first, second, and third principle, which are always standing; that is, fixed in eternity and were never made" <note>original: οὗτος μὲν ὁ κόσμος εἰκὼν ἀεὶ εἰκονιζόμενος, ἑστηκότων μὲν τοῦ πρώτου καὶ τοῦ δευτέρου, καὶ τοῦ τρίτου</note>. For as *Eusebius* records, 

<summary>This page discusses Plato's distinction between created things, which have a beginning in time, and the eternal Godhead, which he describes as a Trinity of three divine principles or "hypostases."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that Plato’s philosophy includes a trinity of divine beings—the First Cause, the Mind (Intellect), and the Soul of the World—all of which are considered eternal and uncreated, serving as the architects of the universe.</meta>

<page-num>573</page-num>
<header>CHAP. IV. The Platonist Mind is Eternal. 573</header>

The ancient interpreters of *Plato* explained these first, second, and third principles in his aforementioned Epistle as a *Trinity of Gods*:

<margin>Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 11, chapter 20.</margin>

> Those who attempt to explain Plato refer these things to the First God; to the Second Cause; and to the Third, the Soul of the World; defining this third one also to be a God. <note>original: ταῦτα οἱ τὸν πλάτωνα διασαφεῖν πειρώμενοι, ἐπὶ τὸν πρῶτον θεὸν ἀνάγουσι, θείη τε τὸ δεύτερον αἴτιον, καὶ τρίτον τὴν τοῦ κόσμου ψυχὴν, θεὸν τρίτον καὶ αὐτὴν ὁριζόμενοι εἶναι.</note>

Therefore, we think there is good reason to conclude that those *eternal* or *uncreated gods* of *Plato* in his *Timaeus*—of whom he says this whole generated or created world is an *image* or *statue*—were none other than his *trinity* of *divine <term>hypostases</term>* <note>original: "Hypostases"; here meaning distinct persons or individual realities within the Godhead.</note>, who are the makers or creators of it. And it was previously (as we believe) rightly guessed that *Cicero* should also be understood as "Platonizing" when he affirmed that *all things were at first made by the gods* <note>original: "A Diis omnia à Principio facta"</note>, and that *the world and all its parts were established by the providence of the gods* <note>original: "à Providentiâ Deorum, Mundum & omnes Mundi partes constitutas esse"</note>.

But it was unquestionably acknowledged that the *second hypostasis* in *Plato's trinity*—namely, *Mind* or *Intellect*—was *eternal* or without *beginning*, even though it was said to have been "generated" or to have proceeded by way of <term>emanation</term> <note>The philosophical idea that everything flows out from a first divine source.</note> from the first, called <term>Tagathon</term> <note>The Greek term for "The Good."</note>. This could be proved by many express testimonies of the most genuine Platonists, but we shall content ourselves here with only two. One is from *Plotinus*, who writes the following concerning it:

> Let all temporal generation be completely banished from our thoughts while we treat of things eternal, or those that always exist. We attribute generation to them only in respect of causality and order, but not of time. <note>original: Enneads 5, Book 1, chapter 6. ἐκποδὼν δὲ ἡμῖν ἔστω γένεσις ἡ ἐν χρόνῳ, τὸν λόγον περὶ τῶν ἀεὶ ὄντων ποιουμένοις, &c.</note>

And although *Plotinus* speaks there specifically of the *second hypostasis* or *Mind* (*Nous*), he later extends the same principle to the third *hypostasis* of that trinity, called *Psyche*, or the *Mundane Soul*. He says that the Soul is the *Word* of the *Second*, just as the *Second* was the *Word* of the *First*:

> That which is generated from what is better than Mind can be none other than Mind, because Mind is the best of all things, and everything else is after it and secondary to it—just as the Soul <note>original: 'Psyche'</note> is in like manner the Word of Mind, and a certain energy of it, just as Mind is the Word and energy of the First Good. <note>original: Καὶ τὸ γεννώμενον ἀπὸ κρείττονος νοῦ, νοῦν εἶναι, καὶ κρείττων ἁπάντων νοῦς, ὅτι τἄλλα μετ' αὐτὸν, οἷον καὶ ἡ ψυχὴ λόγος νοῦ, καὶ ἐνέργειά τις, ὥσπερ αὐτὸς ἐκείνου.</note>

The other testimony is from *Porphyry*, cited by *St. Cyril* from the fourth book of his *Philosophical History*, where he sets down the doctrine of *Plato* in this manner:

<margin>St. Cyril, *Against Julian*, Book 1, p. 32.</margin>

> Plato spoke about the Good in this way: that from it, in a manner inconceivable to humans, a Mind was generated that is whole and self-subsisting, in which are the things that truly exist and the entire essence of all beings. This Mind is the primary beauty and Beauty itself, possessing its beauty from its own form. It proceeded before all ages, originating from God the Cause, being self-generated and its own father. For its procession did not occur because God moved toward its generation; rather, this Mind came forth self-generatively from God. It did not come forth from any beginning in time, for time did not yet exist; and even after time was created, time is nothing in relation to it, for Mind is timeless... <note>original: εἰπόντος πλάτωνος περὶ τοῦ Ἀγαθοῦ οὕτως· ἀπὸ δὲ τούτου τρόπον τινὰ ἀνθρώποις ἀνεπινόητον νοῦν γενέσθαι τε ὅλον καὶ καθ' ἑαυτὸν ὑφεστῶτα, ἐν ᾧ δὴ τὰ ὄντως ὄντα, καὶ ἡ πᾶσα οὐσία τῶν ὄντων· ὃ δὴ καὶ πρώτως καλὸν καὶ αὐτοκαλὸν, παρ' ἑαυτοῦ τὴν καλλονὴν ἔχον τὸ εἶδος· προῆλθε δὲ προαιώνιος ἀπ' αἰτίου τοῦ θεοῦ ὡρμημένος, αὐτογέννητος ὢν καὶ αὐτοπάτωρ· οὐ γὰρ ἐκείνου κινημένου πρὸς γένεσιν τὴν τούτου ἡ πρόοδος γέγονεν, ἀλλὰ τούτου παρελθόντος αὐτογόνως ἐκ θεοῦ, παρελθόντος δὲ οὐκ ἀπ' ἀρχῆς τινὸς χρονικῆς, οὔπω γὰρ χρόνος ἦν· ἀλλὰ οὐδὲ χρόνου γενομένου πρὸς αὐτὸν ἐστίν τι ὁ χρονός, ἄχρονος</note>

It emphasizes that while the Mind (Nous) and Soul (Psyche) are described as being generated from the Good (Tagathon), this generation is a matter of logical order and causality rather than a beginning in time, making all three hypostases eternal.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the eternity of the "Mind" (the second person of the Platonic Trinity) and explores the paradoxical concept of it being "self-begotten" despite originating from the First Good.</meta>

<page-num>574</page-num>
<header>The Mind or Word called Self-Parent. Book I.</header>

"For Mind is always timeless and alone eternal." <note>original: χρόνος γὰρ ἀεὶ καὶ μόνος αἰώνιος ὁ νοῦς</note> *Plato* thus declares concerning the *First Good*, *that from it was generated a certain Mind incomprehensible to mortals; in which, subsisting by itself, are contained the things that truly are, and the essences of all beings. This is the First Fair, and Beauty itself, which proceeded or sprung out of God from all eternity as its cause, but nonetheless in a peculiar manner, as "self-begotten" and as "its own parent": for it was not begotten from God as if God moved in any way toward its generation; rather, it proceeded from God as if it were self-begotten.* And this did not happen at any temporal beginning, as there was no such thing as time yet. Nor, when time was later created, did it affect him in any way; for Mind is always timeless and alone eternal. 

Here, besides the eternity of Mind or Intellect—the second divine <term>hypostasis</term> <note>original: "Hypostasis"; a distinct person or individual reality within the Godhead.</note> in the Platonic Trinity—there are other strange and unusual expressions concerning it. Although it is acknowledged to have been generated from the first original Deity, yet it is called *autopator* and *autogennetos*—*its own parent* and *its own offspring*—and is said to have sprung out *autogonos*, or *self-begottenly*. <note>original: αὐτοπάτωρ (autopator), αὐτογέννητος (autogennetos), and αὐτογόνως (autogonos).</note>

Now, because this is such a great riddle or mystery, it is worth considering its true meaning and the logic behind it, which is thus declared by *Porphyry*. Though the Mind sprung from the *First Good* or *Supreme Deity* from eternity, it is said to be *self-begotten* because it did not spring from the First as if the First "moved" toward its generation, but while the First remained still or quiet. This doctrine was previously delivered by *Plotinus* in this manner:

<margin>Ennead 5, Book 1, Chapter 6.</margin>
"Or must we say it was produced when the First was moved? For if something were produced because the First moved, the thing produced would be the third after him (following the motion), and not the second. Therefore, if there is to be a second after that First, it must arise while the First remains unmoved, without any inclination, or will, or any motion at all." <note>original: ἢ κινηθέντος φατέον γίγνεσθαι, εἰ γὰρ κινηθέντος αὐτοῦ τι γίγνοιτο, τρίτον ἀπ' ἐκείνου τὸ γιγνόμενον μετὰ τὴν κίνησιν ἂν γίγνοιτο, καὶ οὐ δεύτερον· Δεῖ οὖν ἀκινήτου ὄντος, εἴτι δεύτερον μετ' αὐτό, οὐ προσνεύσαντος, οὐδὲ βουληθέντος, οὐδὲ ὅλως κινηθέντος, ὑποστῆναι αὐτό.</note> Now this, in *Porphyry's* language, is paraphrased as being a "being produced from the First Good or original Deity self-begottenly," or in a way of *self-generation*. 

But the plain meaning seems to be no other than this: that although this second divine hypostasis did indeed proceed from the First God, it was not produced in the way a creature is made, or in a "creating way" by an arbitrary act of will or command, or by a particular *fiat* <note>An authoritative decree or command.</note> of that Supreme Deity. Instead, it was produced by way of *natural and necessary emanation*. 

*Porphyry* was not the only one to use this language. We find the very same expressions—*autopator* and *autogonos* (*self-parent* and *self-begotten*)—in *Iamblichus's* *Mysteries*, where he also applies them not to the first principle of all, but to a *second divine hypostasis*: "From this One, the self-sufficient God made himself shine forth; therefore he is called his own Father and self-begotten." <note>original: ἀπὸ γὰρ τοῦ ἑνὸς τούτου, ὁ αὐτάρκης Θεὸς ἑαυτὸν ἐξέλαμψε, διὸ καὶ αὐτοπάτωρ καὶ αὐτόγονος.</note> He is therefore called *Sui-Pater* and *Seipso-Genitus*—his own Father and begotten by himself. But we will discuss this God or divine hypostasis in *Iamblichus* more later. We cannot justify this kind of language in the Christian Trinity, because...

<page-num>575</page-num>
# CHAPTER IV. Arius no Platonist.

We have no warrant for it from the Scripture; though we are not ignorant that some recent theologians have ventured to call the Christian *Logos* <note>The "Word" or second person of the Trinity.</note> in the same manner "God-of-itself" <note>original: αὐτόθεον (autotheon)</note> and "God from himself" <note>original: ex seipso Deum</note>.

<margin>On the Trinity, Book 1, Chapter 8, Section 2.</margin>
*Dionysius Petavius*, having rightly declared the doctrine of *Arius* in this way—that the Father was the only eternal God, and that the Son or Word was a *creature* made by him in time and out of nothing (that is, produced into being after he had not existed)—adds these words: "Indeed, from that profession, as I mentioned above, it is most clearly evident that Arius was a genuine Platonist." <note>original: In ea verò professione, quod suprà memoravi, planissimè constat, Germanum Platonicum Arium extitisse.</note> But from what we have now cited out of *Plato* himself and others of his most genuine followers, it is certain that *Petavius* (though otherwise learned and industrious) was grossly mistaken here, and that *Arius* was no *Platonist* at all. And indeed, for either *Plato* or *Plotinus* to have denied the eternity of that *Second <term>Hypostasis</term>* <note>original: "Hypostasis"; a distinct person or individual reality within the Godhead.</note> of theirs—called *Nous* (Mind) or *Logos* (Word) and the *Son of the First*—would have been the same as if they had denied the eternity of *Wisdom* and *Understanding* itself. This is because, according to them, this *Second Hypostasis* is essentially nothing but "Original Wisdom itself" <note>original: αὐτοσοφία (autosophia)</note>, and consequently that very *Wisdom* by which God himself is wise. We do not dispute here how far, or in what sense, this is true.

<margin>On the Opinion of Dionysius, Volume 1, Page 567.</margin>
Nevertheless, *Athanasius* <note>The 4th-century Bishop of Alexandria and chief defender of Trinitarian orthodoxy against Arianism.</note> seems to have been fully of the same opinion with them in this, based on this passage of his: "Our Lord is both wisdom and truth, and he is not the second of another wisdom; but he alone is the one through whom the Father made all things." <note>original: Καὶ σοφία ἡ ἀλήθειά ἐστιν ὁ Κύριος, καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν ἄλλης σοφίας δεύτερος, ἀλλὰ μόνος οὗτος, δι’ οὗ τὰ πάντα πεποίηκεν ὁ πατὴρ, &c.</note> And again, "For the Father of the Word is not himself properly the Word." <note>original: οὔτε γὰρ λόγος ἐστὶν ὁ τοῦ λόγου πατήρ.</note> And, "That was not the Word which produced the Word, for the Word was with God. The Lord was begotten as Wisdom; therefore, that was not Wisdom which produced Wisdom—the one who says of herself: 'His delight was with me.'" <note>original: οὐκ ἦν λόγος ὁ τὸν λόγον προέμενος, ἦν γὰρ ὁ λόγος πρὸς τὸν Θεόν. σοφία γεγέννηται ὁ Κύριος· οὐκ ἦν οὖν σοφία ὁ τὴν σοφίαν ἀνείς· ἐγὼ γὰρ ἤμην, φησίν, ἡ προσέχαιρεν. See Proverbs 8:30.</note> But those latter words he cites with approval from *Dionysius*, Bishop of *Alexandria*. And the same *Athanasius* affirms that *Arius*, on the contrary, maintained that there was another *Word* and *Wisdom* older than that *Word* and *Wisdom* in our Savior Christ.

<margin>Page 119.</margin>
To conclude, no *Platonist* in the world ever denied the eternity of that *Nous* or *Universal Mind*, which is the *Second Hypostasis* of their *Trinity*. On the contrary, as has been already observed, some of them seemed rather to attribute too much to it by calling it "his own parent" <note>original: αὐτοπάτωρ (autopator)</note> and "his own offspring" <note>original: αὐτόγονος (autogonos)</note>—as something that was *self-begotten*. However, they meant this only in a certain mystical sense, as they did not otherwise deny that it also proceeded from the *First Good* and was the *offspring* of it. Therefore, *Plato*—who supposed the world was not *eternal* but asserted the eternity of that *Second Hypostasis* of his *Trinity*—plainly made it to be no *creature*, according to *Athanasius’s* own doctrine: "If the Son is eternal, he is not a creature; but if he happens to be a creature, he is not eternal." <note>original: εἰ ἀΐδιός ἐστιν ὁ υἱὸς, οὐκ ἔστι κτίσμα, εἰ δὲ κτίσμα τυγχάνει, οὐκ ἔστιν ἀΐδιος.</note>

<summary>The author argues that Arius was not a Platonist because Plato held the second person of the Trinity (Mind or Word) to be eternal and uncreated, whereas Arius claimed the Son was a created being. He uses the writings of Athanasius to show that the orthodox Christian view of the Word's eternity aligns more closely with Platonic philosophy than Arianism does.</summary>

--- Page 594 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument that the second and third persons of the Platonic Trinity are eternal and uncreated, refuting Dionysius Petavius's claim that Platonism was the source of Arianism.</meta>

<page-num>576</page-num>

*Eternal <note>original: ἀΐδιος (aidios)</note>. If the Son is Eternal, he was no Creature; and on the contrary, if he is a Creature, he was not Eternal.*

Neither is there any force at all in that testimony of *Macrobius* <note>A Roman philosopher of the 5th century.</note>, which *Petavius* <note>Dionysius Petavius (1583–1652), a Jesuit theologian who argued that Platonic thought led to the Arian heresy.</note> urges to the contrary; wherein the *First Cause* is said, "to have created Mind from himself" <note>original: De se Mentem Creasse</note>; and again this Mind, "to have created Soul from itself" <note>original: Animam de se Creasse</note>. This is because it is certain that these ancient Pagans did not then so strictly confine that word *create* <note>original: Creare</note> (as we Christians now do) to that narrow sense and notion of the *production of things in time*. Instead, they used it generally for all manner of *production* or *efficiency*. 

But the chief ground of *Petavius’s* mistake here—besides his prejudice against Platonism in general—was his failure to distinguish between that *spurious Trinity* of some Platonists, wherein the *Third <term>Hypostasis</term>* <note>A distinct person or individual reality within the Godhead.</note> was the *whole animated world* (which gave him occasion to write: "The third God is clearly thought to be created by the same Platonists, whom they also call a work or poem" <note>original: Tertius verò Deus manifestè Creatus ab iisdem Platonicis putatur, quem & ποίημα nominant</note>), and that other doctrine of those who made it not the world itself that is a creature, but the *Craftsman* or *Creator* of the world.

But we grant that there may be more reason to question whether *Plato* himself held the eternity of the *Mundane Soul* <note>The "Soul of the World," often considered the third person of the Platonic trinity.</note> (commonly said to be the *Third Hypostasis* of his *Trinity*) or not. In his *Timaeus*, although he acknowledged it to be *older than the world*, he does seem to attribute a *temporary generation* or *birth* to it. Nevertheless, it is in no way probable that *Plato’s third principle* of all things (mentioned in his Epistle to *Dionysius*) and that *Psyche* or *Soul* of his (which is the only God he tries to prove against the atheists in his tenth book of *The Laws* <note>original: De Legibus</note>) should ever have "not been." 

Therefore, it is most reasonable to settle this matter as *Plotinus* and others do: by supposing that *Plato* held a *Double Psyche* or *Soul*. One is <gloss>within the world</gloss> <note>original: ἐγκόσμιον (enkosmion)</note> or *Mundane*, which is, as it were, the physical form of this corporeal world, by which this world is properly made a living being <note>original: Animal</note> and a *Second* or *Created God*. The other is <gloss>above the world</gloss> <note>original: ὑπερκόσμιον (hyperkosmion)</note>, *Supramundane*, or *Separate*; and this is not so much the *form* as the *Artificer* of the *world*. 

The first of these two, which *Plotinus* calls the <margin>Enneads, Book 3, Chapter 5, Section 2.</margin> *Heavenly Venus*, he describes in this way: 

"For that which is called the Heavenly Venus, being born from Saturn—that is, from a perfect Mind or Intellect—must necessarily be that most divine Soul (the Third <term>Archical</term> <note>Supreme or principal.</note> Hypostasis). Being immediately begotten, pure from that which is pure, she always remains above, so that she neither can nor will ever descend down to these lower things, so as to be immersed in them. Being a separate substance and a nature having no share in matter, the ancients hinted at this by saying she was motherless. One might rightly call her a God, not a daemon <note>In Greek thought, a spirit lower than a god but higher than a human.</note>, as she is unmixed and pure in herself, etc. Thus, she would never fall away, being much more closely joined to the Mind than the light which shines around the sun is joined to the sun. Following Saturn—or, if you wish, Uranus, the father of Saturn—she acted toward him and was made his own, and being in love, she brought forth Love." <note>original: τὴν γὰρ οὐρανίαν λεγομένην, ἐκ Κρόνου νοῦ ὄντος ἐκείνου, ἀνάγκη ψυχὴν θειοτάτην εἶναι, εὐθὺς ἐξ αὐτοῦ ἀκήρατον ἀκηράτου, μείνασαν ἄνω ὡς μὴ ἡ εἰς τὰ τῇδε ἐλθεῖν, μήτε ἐθελήσασαν, μήτε δυναμένην, ὅτι τοῦ φύσεως μὴ κατὰ τὰ κάτω φῦσαν βαίνειν· χωριστὴν οὖσαν τινὰ ὑπόστασιν, καὶ ἀμέτοχον ὕλης οὐσίαν· ὅθεν αὐτὴν τοῦτο ᾐνίττοντο, τὰς ἀμήτορας εἶναι· ἣν δὴ καὶ θεὸν ἄντις δικαίως, οὐ δαίμονα εἴποι, ἄμικτον οὖσαν, καὶ καθαρὰν ἐφ’ ἑαυτῆς, &c. ὅθεν οὐδ’ ἂν ἐκπέσοι, νοῦ ἐξηρτημένη πολὺ μᾶλλον, ἢ ἥλιος ἂν ἔχοι ἐξ αὐτοῦ, ὅσον αὐτὸν περιλάμπει φῶς, εἰς αὐτὸν συνηρτημένον· ἐφεπομένη δὴ τῷ Κρόνῳ, ἢ εἰ βούλει τῷ πατρὶ τοῦ Κρόνου οὐρανῷ, ἐνήργησέ τε πρὸς αὐτὸν καὶ ὠκειώθη, καὶ ἐρασθεῖσα ἔρωτα ἐγέννησε.</note>

*This Heavenly Venus, which they affirm to have been begotten from Saturn, that is from a Perfect Mind or Intellect, must needs be that most Divine Soul (the Third Archical Hypostasis) which being immediately begotten, pure from that which is pure, always remains above, so that it neither can nor will ever descend down to these lower things, so as to be immersed in them: it being of*...

It refutes the idea that Platonists viewed their third principle as a created object in the Christian sense of being produced in time.</summary>

<page-num>577</page-num>

...such a nature as is not inclined to sink or fall downward. A certain separate substance, which does not participate in matter at all—as the fable hinted when it called it "Motherless"—and therefore may well be styled by us not a demon but a God. This is why this Soul can never fall; it is much more closely united and connected with that Immovable Mind or Intellect than the light surrounding the sun is connected with the sun itself. This Venus, therefore, following Chronus <note>In Neoplatonic allegory, Chronus often represents the Divine Intellect or *Nous*.</note> (or rather the father of Chronus, Uranus) and acting toward it and being enamored with it, begat Love. <note>original Greek: χωριστὴν ἢ ἐκείνω τὼ ψυχὴν λέγοντες, τῶ πρώτως ἐλλάμψασαν τῶ οὐρανῶ, χωριστὸν καὶ τὸν ἔρωτα τοῦτον θησόμεθα — "Speaking of that soul as separate, as that which first shone upon the heavens, we shall also consider this love as separate."</note> Moreover, as we call this Soul itself "separate," so is this "Love" of it (or begotten by it) a separate Love. 

After this, he speaks of another Soul of the World which is not separate from it but closely joined with it, calling it a "Lower Venus and Love"—namely, that other Venus who, in the fable, is said to have been begotten by Jupiter himself (the Superior Soul of the World) and Dione, a watery nymph. We conclude, therefore, that though this Lower Mundane Soul might, according to Plato, have a temporary production along with the world or before it, yet that other Superior and most Divine Soul—which Plotinus calls the Heavenly Venus and Love, the son of Chronus without a mother, and which was truly the Third <term>Hypostasis</term> <note>A distinct person or individual reality within the Godhead.</note> of Plato's Trinity—was eternal and without beginning. And thus, according to the aforementioned principle of Athanasius, none of these three Hypostases of Plato's Trinity were creatures, but all of them were divine and uncreated.

To make this even more evident, we shall further observe, first, that **Plato** himself in that *Second Epistle* of his to **Dionysius**, after he had mentioned his *First, Second*, and *Third*—that is, his *Trinity of Divine Hypostases*—immediately adds these words: <note>original Greek: ἡ δὲ ἀνθρωπίνη ψυχή, περὶ τὰ αὐτὰ ὀρέγεται μαθεῖν ποῖ᾽ ἄττα ἐστὶ, βλέπουσα εἰς τὰ αὑτῆς συγγενῆ, ὧν οὐδὲν ἱκανῶς ἔχει· τοῦ δὴ βασιλέως πέρι, καὶ ὧν εἶπον, οὐδὲν τοιοῦτο — "The human soul desires to learn what kind of things these are, looking at things related to itself, none of which are sufficient. But concerning the King and the things I spoke of, there is nothing of this kind."</note> "The mind of man (as if in labor) always has a great desire to know what these things are, and to that end, it looks upon things related to itself, which are all insufficient, imperfect, and of a different nature <note>original: Heterogeneous</note>. But in that King of all things, and in the other Second and Third which I spoke of, there is nothing of this kind"—that is, nothing like these created things.

Secondly, the *three Hypostases* of *Plato's Trinity* are not only all *eternal* but also *necessarily existent* and *absolutely indestructible*. For the *first* of them can no more exist without the *second*, nor the *first* and *second* without the *third*, than *original light* can exist without its *splendor, radiance*, or *brilliance*. And **Plotinus**, writing against some *Gnostics* in his time who wanted to make more than *three* of these *divine Hypostases* or *principles*, concludes that there can be neither more nor fewer of them in this manner: 

<margin>Enneads 2, Book 9, Chapter 1.</margin> 
<note>original Greek: οὐ τοίνυν δεῖ ἐφ᾽ ἑτέρας ἀρχὰς ἰέναι, ἀλλὰ τοῦτο προστησαμένους, εἶτα νοῦν μετ᾿ αὐτὸ καὶ νοεῖν πρώτως, εἶτα ψυχὴν μετὰ νοῦν· αὕτη γὰρ τάξις κατὰ φύσιν, μήτε πλείω τίθεσθαι ἐν τῷ νοητῷ, μήτε ἐλάττω· εἴτε γὰρ ἐλάττω, ἢ ψυχὴν καὶ νοῦν ταὐτὸ φήσουσιν, ἢ νοῦν καὶ τὸ πρῶτον, ἀλλ᾿ ὅτι ἕτερα ἀλλήλων, ἐδείχθη πολλαχῇ — "Therefore, one must not go to other principles, but after establishing the first, place Mind after it as the primary intellect, and then Soul after Mind. For this order is according to nature: neither to assume more than these in the intelligible world, nor fewer. For if there were fewer, they would have to say either that Soul and Mind are the same, or that Mind and the First are the same; but it has been shown in many ways that they are distinct from one another."</note>

<page-num>578</page-num>

# Plato's Trinity Co-Essential. BOOK I.

...to consider at present, if there be more than these, etc. <note>original Greek: σασθαι ἐν τῷ παρόντι, εἰ πλείω τούτων, &c.</note> Therefore, we ought not to adopt any other principles, but having placed the Simple Good first, we should set Mind (or the Supreme Intellect) next after it, and then the Universal Soul in the third place. For this is the correct order according to Nature: neither to create more Intelligibles (or Universal Principles) nor fewer than these three. For anyone who tries to reduce the number and make fewer of them must necessarily suppose either that the Soul and the Mind are the same, or else that the Mind and the First Good are the same. But we have often demonstrated that all three of these are distinct from one another. It remains now to consider that if there were more than these three principles, what sort of natures they would have to be, etc.

Thirdly, just as all three of these Platonic <term>hypostases</term> <note>Distinct persons or individual substances within the divine nature.</note> are eternal and necessarily existent, they are also clearly supposed by the Platonists to be not particular, but universal beings. That is, they are such as "contain the whole" <note>original Greek: περιέχειν τὸ ὅλον — periechein to holon</note> and comprehend the entire world under them, presiding over all things; this is the same as saying that each of them is infinite and omnipotent. For this reason, Platonic writers also call them principles, causes, and architects <note>original: "Opificers"; Greek: ἀρχαὶ (archai), αἴτια (aitia), and δημιουργοὶ (dēmiourgoi)</note> of the whole world. 

First, regarding Mind or Understanding: while the ancient philosophers before Plato (such as Anaxagoras, Archelaus, etc.) and Aristotle after him supposed Mind and Understanding to be the very first and highest principle of all—a view which the magical or Chaldean Oracles also acknowledge as the most common opinion of mankind:

->Whom the nations of men call the first.<-
<note>original Greek: Ὃν πρῶτον κληΐζεται ἔθνεα ἀνδρῶν — Hon prōton klēizetai ethnea andrōn</note>

<margin>Page 30.</margin>
While Mind is generally regarded by all men as the first and highest God, Plato—considering that unity preceded number and multiplicity in the order of nature, and that there must be an object of thought <note>original Greek: νοητὸν — noēton</note> before there is an intellect <note>original Greek: νοῦς — nous</note> to think it—realized that knowledge could not be the first principle. Finally, seeing that there is a Good transcending that of knowledge, he made one most "Simple Good" the fountain and origin of all things and the first divine hypostasis. He placed Mind or Intellect only second to it—though inseparable from it and most nearly related to it. 

For this reason, in his *Philebus*, although he agrees with those other ancient philosophers "that Mind always rules over the whole universe," <note>original Greek: ὡς ἀεὶ τοῦ παντὸς νοῦς ἄρχει</note> he adds afterward that "Mind is offspring of the cause of all things." <note>original Greek: ὅτι νοῦς ἐστὶ γενότης τοῦ πάντων αἰτίου</note> This means that Mind is not absolutely the first principle, but is akin to it; therefore, it rules over all things alongside and in a kind of subordination to that first principle, which is *Tagathon* <note>The Good.</note> or the Highest Good. When Plato affirms that Mind (his second divine hypostasis) is "offspring" <note>original Greek: γενότης — genotēs</note> with the first, it is the same as if he had said it is of the same kin, of the same nature, and of the same kind <note>original Greek: συγγενὴς (syngenes), ὁμοφυὴς (homophyēs), and ὁμογενὴς (homogenes)</note> with it. All these words are used by Athanasius <note>A 4th-century Christian theologian and defender of the Trinity.</note> as synonymous with "co-essential" or "consubstantial" <note>original Greek: ὁμοούσιος — homoousios</note>. 

Thus, Plato here plainly and expressly agrees or aligns, not with the doctrine of Arius <note>Arius taught that Jesus (the Son/Word) was a created being, subordinate to the Father, rather than being of the same substance.</note>, but with that of the Council of Nicaea and Athanasius: namely, that the second hypostasis of the Trinity—whether called Mind, Word, or Son—is not...

<page-num>579</page-num>

# CHAPTER IV. Plato's Third Person is No Creature.

...not of a different essence <note>original Greek: ἐτερούσιος — heterousios</note>, but a birth <note>original Greek: γεννήσις — gennēsis</note> or co-essential <note>original Greek: ὁμοούσιος — homoousios</note> and con-substantial with the *First*; and therefore not a *creature*.

And then, as for the *Third Hypostasis* <term>hypostasis</term> <note>A distinct person or individual substance within the Godhead.</note>, called *Psyche* or the *Superior Mundane Soul*, *Plato* in his dialogue *Cratylus* bestows the name of *Zeus*—that is, the *Supreme God*—upon it. He explains the name's origin from the Greek word "to live" <note>original Greek: ζῆν — zēn</note> and adds these words concerning it: "For there is no one who is more the cause of life to us and all other living things than this prince and king of all things" <note>original Greek: οὐ γὰρ ἔστιν ἡμῖν καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις πᾶσιν, ὅστις ἐστὶν αἴτιος μᾶλλον τοῦ ζῆν, ἢ ὁ ἄρχων τε καὶ βασιλεὺς τῶν πάντων</note>. He explains that God was called *Zeus* by the Greeks because it is through him that all animals live. 

Yet it is clear from his following words that all of this was properly meant to refer to the *Third Hypostasis* of his *Trinity*, called *Psyche* (Soul). There, he explains the poetic mythology mentioned before, which makes *Zeus* the son of *Chronos*: "It is agreeable to reason that Zeus should be the progeny or offspring of a certain great Mind" <note>original Greek: εὔλογον δὲ, μεγάλης τινὸς διανοίας ἔκγονον εἶναι τὸν Δία</note>. Now, "offspring" <note>original Greek: ἔκγονος — ekgonos</note> and "birth" <note>original Greek: γεννήσις — gennēsis</note> are equivalent terms; therefore *Plato* here also makes the *Third Hypostasis* of his *Trinity* to be *co-essential* <note>original Greek: ὁμοούσιος — homoousios</note> with the *Second*, just as he elsewhere made the *Second co-essential* with the *First*.

<margin>Ennead 5, Book 1; Proclus on Timaeus.</margin> 
It is true that by the *Demiurge* <note>original Greek: δημιουργὸς — dēmiourgos</note> or *Artificer* in *Plato*, he commonly means *Nous* or *Intellect*, his *Second Hypostasis*. (*Plotinus* affirms as much, saying, "The Demiurge for Plato is Intellect" <note>original Greek: δημιουργὸς ὁ νοῦς πλάτωνι</note>.) Nevertheless, *Amelius*, *Plotinus*, and other *Platonists* also called this *Third Hypostasis* the *Artificer* or *Creator* of the whole *world*. Some of them made him the second rank from *Mind* or *Intellect*; others made him the third rank from the *First Good*, the *Supreme Cause* of all things (whom *Atticus* and *Amelius* also styled the *Demiurge*). 

Wherefore, as was suggested before, according to the *genuine* and most ancient *Platonic doctrine*, all these *three hypostases* were the *joint-creators* of the whole *world* and of all things besides themselves. As <margin>In Plotinus's Enneads, Book 1, Chapter 2.</margin> *Marsilio Ficino* declares more than once regarding the nature of this teaching: "These three, with one common consent, produce all things" <note>original Latin: Hi Tres uno quodam consensu omnia producunt</note>. Before him, *Proclus* wrote: "All things depend upon the First One by means of Mind and Soul" <note>original Greek: πάντα ἀνήρτηται τοῦ ἑνὸς διὰ νοῦ μὲν καὶ ψυχῆς</note>. Accordingly, we shall conclude in the words of *Porphyry*: "The true and real Deity, according to Plato, extends to three divine hypostases, the last of which is Psyche or Soul."

From all this, it appears that *Arius* <note>A 4th-century priest who taught that Jesus was a created being, not co-eternal with God the Father.</note> did not follow Plato's philosophy as much as the *Nicene Fathers* and *Athanasius* did. Nevertheless, those Fathers did not make *Plato* their foundation, but rather the *Scriptures*, together with *reason* deducing natural consequences from them. We see that the *Platonic Trinity* was a certain *middle* ground between the doctrine of *Sabellius* <note>Who taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were just different "modes" or names for the same person.</note> and that of *Arius*. It was not a trinity of words only, or logical notions, or mere modes, but a *trinity of persons* (hypostases). Nor was it a jumbled confusion of *God* and *creature* (things of different essences) together, since neither the *second* nor the *third* of them were *creatures*.

<summary>This page argues that in Platonic philosophy, the Third Hypostasis (the Soul) is co-essential with the Mind and the Good, making all three persons joint-creators rather than created beings. The author concludes that the Platonic Trinity mirrors the Nicene Christian view of God more closely than the heresies of Arianism or Sabellianism.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that while the Platonic Trinity consists of eternal and uncreated beings, there remains a hierarchy and dependence among the three persons (hypostases), which the author compares to Christian doctrine.</meta>

<page-num>580</page-num>
<header>The Dependence and Subordination, Book I.</header>

...or *made in time*, but all *eternal*, *infinite*, and *creators*.

But so that it may appear even more fully how far the most *refined Platonic* and *Parmenidian* or *Pythagorean Trinity* either *agrees* or *disagrees* with the *doctrine of Scripture* and that of the *Christian Church* throughout several ages, we shall further observe *two things* concerning it. The *first* of these is that, although the *genuine Platonists* and *Pythagoreans* supposed none of their *three principal <term>archical</term> <note>original: "archical," meaning primary or ruling</note> persons <term>hypostases</term>* <note>A term for the distinct persons or individual substances within the Godhead.</note> to be actually *creatures*, but all of them *eternal*, *necessarily existent*, and *universal* or *infinite*, and consequently *creators* of the whole *world*; they nevertheless asserted an *essential dependence* of the *second person* upon the *first*, and also of the *third* upon both the *first* and *second*, along with a *gradual subordination* <note>A ranking of status or order of priority.</note> among them.

<margin>Plotinus, Enneads, Book 5, Chapter 1, Section 6.</margin>
Thus *Plotinus*, writing of the generation of the *Eternal Intellect* (which is the *second* person in the *Platonic Trinity* and corresponds to the *Son* or *Word* in the *Christian* Trinity), says: "That which is always perfect generates what is eternal, and that which it generates is always less than itself. What shall we therefore say of the most absolutely perfect Being of all? Does that produce nothing from itself? Or rather, does it not produce the greatest of all things after it? Now the greatest of all things after the most absolutely perfect Being is Mind or Intellect, and this is second to it. For Mind beholds this as its Father and stands in need of nothing else besides it; whereas that First Principle stands in need of no Mind or Intellect. What is generated from that which is better than Mind must necessarily be Mind or Intellect, because Mind is better than all other things, they being all—in the order of nature—after it and junior <note>meaning lower in rank or later in the logical order of existence</note> to it, as is the Soul <note>original Greek: Ψυχὴ — Psyche</note> itself, or the First Soul. For this is also the word or energy of Mind, just as Mind is the word and energy of the First Good." <note>original Greek: τὸ μὲν ἀεὶ τέλειον, ἀεὶ καὶ ἀΐδιον γεννᾷ, καὶ ΕΛΑΤΤΟΝ ἢ ἑαυτὸ γεννᾷ. τί οὖν χρὴ περὶ τοῦ τελεωτάτου λέγειν; μηδὲν ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ γεννᾶν, ἢ τὰ μέγιστα μετ’ αὐτόν· μέγιστον δὲ μετ’ αὐτὸν Νοῦς καὶ δεύτερον. Καὶ γὰρ ὁρᾷ ὁ Νοῦς ἐκεῖνον, καὶ δεῖται αὐτοῦ μόνου· ἐκείνῳ δὲ τούτου οὐδέν. Καὶ τὸ γεννώμενον ἀπὸ κρείττονός νοῦ, νοῦν εἶναι· καὶ κρείττων ἁπάντων ὁ Νοῦς, ὅτι τἄλλα μετ’ αὐτό. οἷον καὶ ἡ ψυχὴ λόγος νοῦ καὶ ἡ ἐνέργειά τις.</note> Again, the same is more particularly declared by him concerning that *third person* called *Psyche* (Soul): that as it *essentially depends* upon the *second*, it is also *gradually subordinate* or in some way *inferior* to it.

<margin>Page 489.</margin>
"Perfect Intellect generates Soul; and being perfect, it must necessarily generate, for so great a power could not remain sterile. But that which is begotten here also cannot be greater than its begetter, but must necessarily be inferior to it, as being its image." <note>original Greek: ψυχὴν γὰρ γεννᾷ Νοῦς, νοῦς ὢν τέλειος. Καὶ γὰρ τέλειον ὄντα, γεννᾶν ἔδει, καὶ μὴ δύναμιν οὖσαν τοσαύτην ἄγονον εἶναι· Κρεῖττον δὲ οὐκ οἷόντε ἦν εἶναι, οὐδ’ ἐνταῦθα τὸ γεννώμενον, ἀλλ’ ΕΛΑΤΤΟΝ ὂν, εἴδωλον εἶναι αὐτοῦ·</note>

<margin>Page 554.</margin>
Elsewhere the same philosopher, calling the *first person* of this Trinity *Uranus*, the *second* *Chronos*, and the *third* *Zeus* (as *Plato* had done before) and skillfully interpreting that fable as an allegory, concludes in this manner concerning *Chronos*, or the *second* of these: "That he is in a middle state or degree between his Father, who is greater, and his Son, who is less and inferior." <note>original Greek: μεταξύ ὢν πατρός τε ἀμείνονος, καὶ ἥττονος υἱοῦ</note> Again, the same thing is asserted by that philosopher in general:

<margin>Page 513.</margin>
"Among generated things..." <note>original Greek: ἐν τοῖς γεννωμένοις</note>

<summary>This page argues that the Platonic Trinity involves a hierarchy where the Second and Third Persons, though eternal and uncreated, are essentially dependent upon and subordinate to the First Person. The author uses Plotinus’s descriptions of Intellect and Soul to illustrate this gradual ranking within the divine nature.</summary>

--- Page 599 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the hierarchy of the Platonic Trinity, specifically focusing on the gradual descent and subordination of the second and third persons (hypostases) from the first.</meta>

<page-num>581</page-num>
<header>Chapter IV. In the Platonic Trinity.</header>

*“It is not possible to go upward, but only downward; in the things generated from eternity, or produced by way of natural emanation, there is no progress upward, but all downward, and always a gradual descent into greater multiplicity.”* <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἔστι πρὸς τὸ ἄνω, ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὸ κάτω χωρεῖν</note> We shall cite but only one passage more out of this philosopher, which also contains an element of reasoning: *“That which is generated or emanates immediately from the First and Highest Being is not the very same thing with it—as if it were nothing but that repeated and doubled—and as it is not the same, so neither can it be better than it.”* <note>original Greek: οὐ ταὐτὸ τὸ ἐξ ἐκείνου ἐκείνῳ, εἰ ὂν μὴ ταὐτὸ, οὐδέ γε βέλτιον</note>
<margin>Enneads, Book 5, Treatise 3, Chapter 15</margin>
From which it follows that it must necessarily be gradually subordinate and inferior to it.

This gradual subordination and *essential dependence* of the *second* and *third <term>hypostases</term>* <note>The distinct persons or individual substances of the Trinity.</note> upon the *first* is illustrated by these *Platonists* in several ways. *Ficinus* <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), an influential Italian scholar who revived Platonism in the Renaissance.</note> resembles it to the ripples in water: when some heavy body falls into it, its surface is depressed, and from there it is *circularly wrinkled* in every direction. *“One [divine person] flowed from another in almost such a way,”* he says, *“just as in water one circle depends on another circle.”* <note>original Latin: Alius sic fermè profluxit ex alio, sicut in aqua Circulus dependet à Circulo</note> Here it is also observable that the wider the circulating wave grows, the more it settles and subsides, along with a decrease in speed, until at last all becomes plain and smooth again.

But by the pagan Platonists themselves, each *following hypostasis* is many times said to be a *“print, stamp, or impression”* <note>original Greek: ἴχνος καὶ τύπος</note> made by the *former*, like the *signature* of a seal upon wax. Again, it is often called by them an *“image,”* a *“likeness,”* and an *“imitation”*; <note>original Greek: εἰκὼν, εἴδωλον, and μίμημα</note> which, if considered in terms of sound, would mean the *second hypostasis* is looked upon as the *echo* of an *original voice*, and the *third* as the *repeated echo*, or the *echo of that echo*. It is as if both the *second* and *third hypostases* were but certain replications of the *first original deity* with a reduction in intensity; which, though they are not *accidental* or *vanishing* ones, but *substantial*, yet have a similar dependence on one another and a gradual subordination. 

Or, if it is considered in terms of sight, then the *second hypostasis* would be resembled to the *image* of a face in a mirror, and the *third* to the *reflection* of that image in *another mirror*, which depend upon the *original face* and have a *gradual reduction* of its vigor. Or else the *second* and *third* may be conceived as two *<term>parelii</term>*, <note>Also known as "sun dogs"; an atmospheric phenomenon where bright spots appear on either side of the sun, creating the illusion of multiple suns.</note> or as a *second* and *third sun*. For thus does *Plotinus* call the *Universal Psyche* (the *third hypostasis*), *“the image of Mind (the second) retaining much of its splendor.”* <note>original Greek: εἰκόνα νοῦ σώζουσάν τι φῶς ἐκείνου</note> 

Despite these similarities, they would not have these analogies "squeezed" or pressed too hard, because they acknowledge that there is also some lack of similarity in them, which would then be forced out of them. Their meaning amounts to no more than this: that just as an *image in a mirror* is said *“to belong to another,”* <note>original Greek: ἑτέρου εἶναι</note> essentially belonging to and depending upon something else, so each following *hypostasis* does *essentially depend* upon the former or first, and has a subordination to it. But we meet with no expression in any of these *pagan Platonists* so unhandsome and offensive as that of *Philo’s* in his—

<summary>This page explains the Platonic concept of the Trinity as a hierarchy where the second and third persons (hypostases) are subordinate to and depend on the first, illustrated through analogies of water ripples, echoes, mirror reflections, and mock suns.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Platonic Trinity, moving from the general concept of downward emanation to specific analogies and philosophical distinctions between the three divine persons (hypostases).</meta>

<page-num>582</page-num>
<header>The Distinctive Characters, BOOK I.</header>

In his *Second Book of Allegories*, Philo writes: "The Word <note>original Greek: Logos</note> of God is his shadow, which he used as an instrument when he made the world." <note>original Greek: σκιὰ δὲ Θεοῦ ὁ λόγος αὐτοῦ ἐστιν, ᾧ καθάπερ ὀργάνῳ προσχρησάμενος ἐκοσμοποίει</note> The world is the shadow of God, which he made by using the Word as an instrument. Notwithstanding this, the same writer calls him elsewhere, more honorably, a "Second God" and "The Son of the First God." In the same place, he also declares that this shadow and image of God is itself the <term>archetype</term> <note>The original pattern or model from which copies are made.</note> of other things: "This shadow and, as it were, image (of the First God) is itself the archetype and pattern of other things below it. Just as God is the pattern of this image (which I have now called a shadow), so this image itself becomes another pattern or <term>paradigm</term> as well." <note>original Greek: αὕτη δὲ ἡ σκιὰ, καὶ ὡσανεὶ ἀπεικόνισμα, ἑτέρων ἐστὶν ἀρχέτυπον, ὥσπερ ὁ Θεὸς παράδειγμα τῆς εἰκόνος, ἣν σκιὰν νυνὶ κέκληκα, οὕτως ἡ εἰκὼν ἄλλο γίνεται παράδειγμα</note>

But this dependence and subordination of the divine <term>hypostases</term> <note>The distinct persons or individual substances of the Trinity.</note> is most frequently illustrated in Platonic writings by the radiance or <term>effulgency</term> <note>original Greek: ἔκλαμψις or ἀπαύγασμα</note>—the out-shining of light and splendor from the sun and other luminous bodies. The *Nous* (Intellect), or second hypostasis, is compared to that radiant effulgency which immediately surrounds the source and is seen together with it. As astronomers tell us, this light increases the apparent diameter of the sun, making it look larger than its true size when viewed through telescopes that cut off those lush and surrounding rays. The third hypostasis is compared to the remoter and more distant splendor, which gradually decreases as it circles further away. Thus, <margin>P. 487.</margin> Plotinus writes: "How should we consider this second hypostasis other than as the surrounding splendor which encompasses the body of the sun? From that body, which always remains the same, this splendor is perpetually generated anew." <note>original Greek: πῶς δὲ τὸ δεῖ νοῆσαι περὶ ἐκεῖνο μένον, περίλαμψιν ἐξ αὐτοῦ μὲν, ἐξ αὐτοῦ δὲ μένοντος, οἷον ἡλίου τὸ περὶ αὐτὸ λαμπρὸν, ὥσπερ περιθέον, ἐξ αὐτοῦ ἀεὶ γεννώμενον μένοντος</note>

But this essential dependence and gradual subordination of the hypostases in the Platonic Trinity will appear even more fully from the specific distinctive characters given to each of them. The first of these is often said to be "the One before all things" <note>original Greek: Ἕν πρὸ πάντων</note>—a simple unity which virtually contains all things. <margin>P. 513.</margin> As Plotinus writes: "This first principle contains all things in such a way that they are not yet separated and distinct, whereas in the second, they are discerned and distinguished by Reason." <note>original Greek: οὕτως εἶχε πάντα ὡς μὴ διακεκριμένα, τὰ δ’ ἐν δευτέρῳ διεκέκριτο τῷ λόγῳ</note> This means they are actually distinguished in their *Ideas* within the second person, whereas the First is the simple and fertile power of all things. Therefore, the second was called by Parmenides, "One actually all things" <note>original Greek: Ἕν πάντα</note>—that is, all things in their distinct Ideas. And according to the same philosopher, as Plotinus tells us, the third was "One and all things" <note>original Greek: Ἕν καὶ πάντα</note>—possessing even more multiplicity and <term>alterity</term> <note>Difference or "otherness."</note> within it. It is "One effectively all things." This third person is that which actively displays and produces into being what was virtually or potentially contained in the First, and ideally or as a model in the Second. 

Accordingly, the first of these is sometimes said to be "all things unitively" <note>original Greek: πάντα ἑνικῶς</note>; the second, "all things intellectually" <note>original Greek: πάντα νοερῶς</note>; and the third, "all things animally" <note>original Greek: πάνta ψυχικῶς; referring here to the soul (Psyche) as the source of life and movement</note>—that is, self-movably, actively, and productively. Furthermore, the first of these is commonly called "The Good" <note>original Greek: Τ’αγαθὸν</note>...

It defines the First as a simple unity, the Second as the realm of distinct ideas, and the Third as the active, life-giving power that brings things into being.</summary>

<page-num>583</page-num>
<header>Cʜᴀᴘ. IV. Of Plato's Three Hypostases.</header>

The First is the Good, or *Goodness* itself, above Mind and Understanding, and also <term>above essence</term> <note>original Greek: ὑπερούσιον</note>, ineffable and incomprehensible. And sometimes it is also called a <term>simple light</term> <note>original Greek: φῶς ἁπλᾶν</note>. The Second is <term>Mind</term>, <term>Word</term>, and <term>Wisdom</term> <note>original Greek: Νοῦς, Λόγος, Σοφία</note>, which possesses *unity and goodness only by participation*, or is <term>characterized by the Good</term> <note>original Greek: Ἀγαθοειδὴς; "boniform"</note>, but does so *essentially and formally*. This is *Mind or Understanding, Reason and Wisdom, and all-comprehending or infinite knowledge*. The Third is the <term>soul</term> <note>original Greek: Ψυχὴ</note>, the *self-movable soul*. It possesses *goodness and wisdom by participation, but is essentially and formally infinite self-activity, or effectiveness; an infinite, active, perceptive, and conscious power*. <note>original: "animadversive power"</note> Sometimes it is also styled <term>Venus and Love</term> <note>original Greek: Ἀφροδίτη and Ἔρως</note>, but in a different sense from that of the *First* Good, which is also called Love. The First is a *Love of redundancy*, or *overflowing fullness and fecundity*. <margin>Plotinus, 494.</margin> As Plotinus writes: <note>original Greek: ὃν γὰρ τέλειον, τῷ μηδὲν ζητεῖν, μηδὲ ἔχειν, μηδὲ δεῖσθαι, οἷον ὑπερεῤῥύη, καὶ τὸ ὑπερπλῆρες αὐτοῦ πεποίηκε πάντα</note> *That which, being absolutely perfect and seeking or wanting nothing, as it were overflowed; and by its exuberant redundancy, produced all things*. In contrast, this latter Soul is a *Love of infinite activity*. Of the *First*, Plotinus says that it is <term>above all action</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνενέργητος</note>; for this reason, the making of the world is not properly ascribed to him, though he is the *original fountain of all*. According to Numenius: <margin>Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 11, chapter 18.</margin> <note>original Greek: Καὶ γὰρ οὔτε δημιουργεῖν ἔστι χρεὼν τὸ πρῶτον, καὶ τοῦ δημιουργοῦντος θεοῦ (τοῦ υἱοῦ) χρὴ εἶναι, καὶ νομίζεσθαι πατέρα τὸν πρῶτον θεόν</note> *Neither is it fit to attribute the architecture of the world to the First God, but rather to account him the Father of that God who is the Artificer (the Son)*. Numenius speaks further to the same purpose: <note>original Greek: τὸν μὲν πρῶτον θεὸν ἀργὸν ἔργων ξυμπάντων καὶ Βασιλέα</note> *It is to be acknowledged that the First God is free from all manner of work or action, he being the King of all things*. Of the Second, to whom the *energy of intellection* <note>The activity of using the intellect or understanding.</note> is attributed, it is said nonetheless that his <term>essence</term> is his <term>operation</term> <note>original Greek: οὐσία is his ἐνέργεια</note>, and that he is an <term>immovable essence</term> <note>original Greek: ἀκίνητος οὐσία</note>—though a *multiform* nature, he is yet an *immovable* one. He, therefore, is properly called the Demiurge, as the *contriving architect* or *artificer*, in whom the *archetypal world* is contained, and who is the *first paradigm* or *pattern* of the whole universe. But the Third is a kind of *movable deity*, <note>original Greek: τὸ περὶ νοῦν κινούμενον καὶ νοῦ φῶς, καὶ ἴχνος ἐξηρτημένον ἐκείνου</note> *that which moves about the mind or intellect, the light or radiance thereof, and its print or signature, which always depends upon it and acts according to it*. This is that which reduces both the *fecundity* of the *First Simple Good* and the *immovable wisdom and architectural contrivance* of the *Second* into *act and energy*. This is the *immediate and manual craftsman of the whole world* <note>original: "manuary opificer"</note> and <term>that which actually governs, rules, and presides over all</term> <note>original Greek: τὸ ἡγεμονοῦν τοῦ παντὸς</note>. Amelius, in the passage previously cited from Proclus, calls these three divine hypostases *Three Minds* and *Three Kings*. He styles the First <term>Him that is</term> <note>original Greek: τὸν ὄντα</note>; the Second <term>Him that has</term> <note>original Greek: τὸν ἔχοντα</note>; and the Third <term>Him that beholds</term> <note>original Greek: τὸν ὁρῶντα</note>. In these expressions, though they are unique to him, he denotes an *essential dependence* and a *gradual subordination* among them.

Now, that which is most liable to objection in this Platonic scale or gradation of the Deity seems to be the difference between the First...

<header>Platonists make Mind and Wisdom, Book I.</header>

*First* and the *second*. Since the *Essential Character* of the *second* is said to be *Understanding*, *Reason*, and *Wisdom*, it seems to follow that either the *First* and the *Second* are really nothing more than two different names or *incomplete concepts* <note>original: "Inadequate Conceptions"</note> of *one* and the same thing; or else, if they are distinct <term>hypostases</term> <note>individual substances or persons within the divine nature</note>, the *First* of them must necessarily be without mind and without reason <note>original Greek: ἄνους καὶ ἄλογος</note>, which would be very absurd. To which our only reply is as follows:

First, this is indeed one secret mystery <note>original: "Peculiar Arcanum"</note> of the *Platonic* and *Pythagorean theology* (which yet seems to have been first derived from *Orpheus* and the *Egyptians*, or rather from the *Hebrews* themselves): that while *Pagan theologians* generally concluded that Mind is the oldest of all things <note>original Greek: νοῦν πάντων προγενέστατον</note>—the *Highest Principle* and *First Origin* of the *World*—those others placed something above it, and consequently made Mind not the *First* but the *Second*. They did this primarily for the *three* following reasons:

First, because *Understanding*, *Reason*, *Knowledge*, and *Wisdom* cannot be conceived by us mortals in any way other than containing something of *multiplicity* in them. However, it seems most reasonable to make the *First Principle* of all not *Number* or *Multitude*, but a perfect <term>Monad</term> <note>the ultimate unit or Unity</note>.

<margin>P. 518.</margin>
Thus *Plotinus* argues: "Thought, just like sight, is in its own nature an indefinite thing, and is defined by the object of thought. Therefore, it is said that Ideas, like numbers, are born from 'Infinite Duality' and 'Unity.' This is the nature of the Intellect; which, consequently, is not simple, but multiple, as it contemplates many Ideas and is composed of two things: the object understood and the mind that understands." <note>original Greek: ἀόριστον μὲν νόησις ὥσπερ ὄψις, ὁριζομένη δὲ ὑπὸ τοῦ νοητοῦ· διὸ καὶ εἴρηται ἐκ τῆς ἀορίστου δυάδος καὶ τοῦ ἑνὸς τὰ εἴδη καὶ οἱ ἀριθμοί· τοῦτο γαὸ ὁ νοῦς· διὸ οὐχ ἁπλῶς, ἀλλὰ πολλά, &c.</note>

<margin>514.</margin>
And again elsewhere: "The principle of everything is simpler than the thing itself. Therefore, the sensible world was made from the Intellect or the realm of thought; and before this, there must necessarily be something simpler still. For 'the many' did not proceed from 'the many,' but this multiform thing, the Intellect, proceeded from that which is not multiform, but simple—just as numbers proceed from Unity." <note>original Greek: τὸ πρὸ τοῦ κόσμου νοητοῦ, οὔτε νοῦς οὔτε κόσμος νοητός, ἁπλούστερον δέ· οὐ γὰρ ἐκ πολλοῦ πολύ, ἀλλὰ τὸ πολὺ τοῦτο ἐξ οὐ πολλοῦ, &c.</note>

<margin>P. 535.</margin>
To this purpose he also argues in these words: "If the act of understanding involves 'the many' or contains multiplicity within it, then that which contains no multiplicity does not, strictly speaking, understand. This non-multiple thing is the First; but thought and knowledge, properly so called, are to be placed among the things that follow after it and are Second." <note>original Greek: εἰ τὸ νοεῖν τὸ πλῆθος, δεῖ ἐν τῷ μὴ πλήθει τὸ νοεῖν μὴ εἶναι· ἦν δὲ τοῦτο τὸ πρῶτον ἐν τοῖς ὑστέροις ἄρα αὐτοῦ τὸ νοεῖν, καὶ νοῦς ἔσται</note> And he often concludes that knowledge (properly so called because of its multiplicity) belongs to the second rank of being <note>original Greek: ἐν τῇ δευτέρᾳ φύσει εἶναι τὸ γινώσκειν</note>, and not the first. 

Another ground or reason is that, in the order of nature, there must be an object of thought before there is a mind to think it <note>original: "Νοητὸν before Νοῦς"</note>. From this, *Plotinus* concludes: "To understand is not the first, neither in essence nor in value; but the second—a thing that follows in the order of nature after the First Good. Once it was brought into existence, it moved itself toward the Good..." <note>original Greek: τὸ νοεῖν οὐ πρῶτον, οὔτε τῷ εἶναι, οὔτε τῷ τίμιον εἶναι· ἀλλὰ δεύτερον, καὶ γενόμενον, ἐπειδὴ ὑπέστη τὸ ἀγαθόν· καὶ γενόμενον ἐκίνησε πρὸς αὑτό, &c.</note> and

The author argues that because thought involves multiplicity and requires an object to be thought about, it cannot be the absolute, simple First Principle.</summary>

# CHAPTER IV. *Not the First, but Second.*

...and springing up from there, as that which is moved by a desire toward it. Their third and last ground or reason is that because *intellection* <note>the act of understanding or thinking</note> and *knowledge* are not the *highest good*, there must be some substantial thing that is naturally *superior* to the *intellect*. This is a consideration that *Plato* insists upon heavily in the sixth book of his *Republic*. Now, upon these several accounts, the *Platonists* confidently conclude <margin>Plat. p. 512.</margin> "that the Supreme Deity is more excellent and better than the *Logos* <note>original Greek: λόγος; the Word or Reason</note>, the intellect, and sense; he provides these things, but he is not these things himself." <note>original Greek: ὅτι θεὸς κρείττων λόγου καὶ νοῦ καὶ αἰσθήσεως, ἀρχὴν ταῦτα ἐκ αὐτὸς ὢν ταῦτα</note> And <margin>P. 514.</margin> "That which was generated from the First Principle was the manifold and entire Word (or Reason); but clearly, the First Principle itself was not the Word. If you demand, therefore, how Word or Reason should proceed from that which is not Word or Reason? We answer: in the same way that a 'boniform' <note>good-like; having the form of the good</note> thing proceeds from Goodness itself." <note>original Greek: τὸ γινόμενον ἐξ αὐτοῦ λόγος πολὺς καὶ πᾶς· τὸ ἦν δηλονότι οὐ λόγος· πᾶς δὲ ἦν ἐξ οὐ λόγου λόγου· καὶ πᾶς τὸ ἀγαθοειδὲς ἐξ ἀγαθοῦ</note>

With this *Platonic* and *Pythagorean* doctrine, *Philo the Jew* also exactly agrees: "The God who is before the Word or Reason is better and more excellent than the entire rational nature; nor is it right that any thing which is generated should be perfectly like that which is originally from itself and above all." <note>original Greek: ὁ πρὸ τοῦ θεοῦ λόγος, κρείσσων ἐστὶν ἢ πᾶσα λογικὴ φύσις, τῷ δὲ ὑπὲρ τῶν πάντων ἐν τῇ βελτίστῃ καὶ τινι ἐξαιρέτῳ καθεστῶτι ἰδέᾳ, οὐδὲν θέμις ἦν γεννητὸν ἐξομοιοῦσθαι</note> 

Indeed, we would not have insisted upon this so much if it were not because of the devout veneration we have for all the mysteries of Scripture. The Scripture seems to give no small support to this doctrine when it similarly establishes an *Eternal Word* and *Wisdom* to be the *second hypostasis* <term>hypostasis</term> <note>a distinct person or substance within the Trinity</note> of the Divine Triad, and the *first-begotten Son* or offspring of *God the Father*. *Athanasius*, as was observed before, also complies very much with this *Platonic notion* when he denies that there was any *logos* or *sophia*—any reason or wisdom—before that Word and Son of God, who is the *second hypostasis* of the Holy Trinity. 

What then? Shall we say that the *first hypostasis* or person in the Platonic Trinity (and perhaps the Christian one as well) is "without mind and without reason" <note>original Greek: ἄνους καὶ ἄλογος</note>—senseless, irrational, and altogether devoid of mind and understanding? Would this not be to introduce a certain kind of *mysterious atheism*? Under the pretense of magnifying and advancing the Supreme Deity, would we not be monstrously degrading him? For why might we not just as easily suppose that *senseless matter* was the first original of all things as a *senseless, incorporeal being*? 

*Plotinus*, therefore, who rigidly and even superstitiously adheres to *Plato’s* text here, makes the first and highest principle of all to be a being that—by reason of its *absolute* and *transcendent perfection*—is not only above *understanding*, *knowledge*, and *reason*, but even above *essence* itself. He can find no other names for this principle but *Unity* and *Substantial Goodness*. Consequently, he views *knowledge* and *wisdom* as but a *second* or subsequent thing <note>original: "Post-Nate Thing"</note>, even though they are eternal. 

Nevertheless, *Plotinus* does seem to struggle with this *metaphysical profundity*. He sometimes endeavors to solve the difficulty by distinguishing between a *double light*: the one *simple* and *uniform*, and the other *multiform* or manifold;

<summary>This page explores the Platonic argument that the First Principle (the Good) is superior to the Intellect because knowledge implies multiplicity, whereas the source must be absolute Unity. Cudworth compares this to the Christian Trinity, where the "Word" or "Wisdom" is the second person, while cautioning that this "higher than mind" status must not be confused with irrationality or atheism.</summary>

<keywords>Platonism, Philo the Jew, Logos, Hypostasis, Divine Triad, Athanasius, Plotinus, Unity, Highest Good, Metaphysical Profundity</keywords>

--- Page 604 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of why the Platonic Trinity involves a hierarchy, focusing on the distinction between the "Simple Light" of the First Principle and the "Multiform Light" of the second.</meta>

...fold; and attributing the *former* of these to the *Supreme Deity* alone (whose *Simple Original Light* he compares to the *Luminous Body* of the *Sun* itself); and the latter of them to the *second Hypostasis* <note>original: "hypostasis"; here referring to a distinct person or level of existence within the Divine Trinity</note>, as being the *radiance* <note>original Greek: ἔκλαμψις</note> or *effulgence* <note>original Greek: ἀπαύγασμα</note>, the *surrounding brightness* or *out-shining splendor* of that *Sun*. Thus, in *Ennead* 5, Book 6, Chapter 4, Plotinus writes: "That from which this multiform light of *Mind* <note>original Greek: Νοῦς; often translated as Intellect or Divine Mind</note> or *Intellect* (the *Second Hypostasis*) is derived, is another, most simple light" <note>original Greek: τὸ παρέχον τοῦτο τὸ φῶς, φῶς ἐστιν ἁπλὃν ... φῶς ἁπλὃν</note>. As he writes elsewhere accordingly regarding the *First Principle*, or *Supreme Deity*, it exists "in a different kind of knowledge or understanding than the understanding of the Second Hypostasis, called Intellect" <note>original Greek: ἐν νοήσει ἑτέρᾳ ἢ κατὰ τὴν τοῦ νοῦ νόησιν</note>. Sometimes again, this philosopher subtly distinguishes between *intelligence itself* <note>original Greek: νόησις αὐτὴ</note> and *that which understands*, or *that which possesses intelligence* <note>original Greek: τὸ νοῦν or τὸ ἔχον τὴν νόησιν</note>; making the *First Principle* the *former* of these *two*, and the *second Hypostasis* of their Trinity the *latter*:

<margin>Page 537.</margin> "For intelligence itself does not understand, but rather that which possesses intelligence. For in that which understands, there are two elements; but this [the First Principle] is in no way two" <note>original Greek: οὐ γὰρ ἡ νόησις νοεῖ, ἀλλὰ τὸ ἔχον τὴν νόησιν · δύο οὖν πάλιν αὖ, ἐν τῷ νοοῦντι γίνονται · τοῦτο δὴ οὐδαμῆ δύο</note>. Now, that *duplicity* <note>original: "duplicity"; the state of being two-fold or having two parts</note> which he imagines to be in "that which possesses intelligence" is either the duplicity of the one who has this intelligence and the intelligence itself (as they are not the same); or else it is the subject and the *intelligible* <note>original Greek: τὸ νοητὸν</note>, the *object* of his thought. The *Intellect* requires an *intelligible* object to exist before it in the order of nature. And from this subtlety, he would infer that there is a certain kind of *imperfection* and *need* in that which *understands* or *possesses intelligence*: "That which understands is needy, just like that which sees" <note>original Greek: ἐνδεὲς τὸ νοεῖν, ὥσπερ τὸ ὁρᾷν</note>. 

But perhaps this difficulty might be more easily solved, even according to the logic of the *Platonic hypothesis*, by assuming that the lower status of their *second Hypostasis* consists only in this: that it is not *essentially* "the Good" <note>original Greek: τ'αγαθὸν</note> or *Goodness itself*, but only *good-like* <note>original Greek: ἀγαθοειδὲς; "boniform"</note>, or *good by participation*. It is *essentially* no higher than *Mind, Reason, and Wisdom* <note>original Greek: Νοῦς, Λόγος and Σοφία</note>; for which reason it is called by those names as its proper *characteristic*. It is not as if the *First* were devoid of *wisdom* under the pretense of being above it, but because this *Second* is not *essentially* anything higher. In the same way, the *Third Hypostasis* is not *essentially Wisdom* itself (standing still or at rest, without motion or action), but *Wisdom as it is in motion*, or *Wisdom moving and acting*.

# The Basis of this Platonic Doctrine

The primary basis for this Platonic doctrine—of an *essential dependence* and therefore a *gradual subordination* within their *Trinity* of *Divine Hypostases*—comes from that fundamental principle of their *theology*: that there is only *one original* source of all things, and only "one fountain of the Godhead" <note>original Greek: μία πηγὴ τῆς θεότητος</note>. From this fountain, all other things whatsoever, whether *temporal* or *eternal*, *created* or *uncreated*, were entirely derived. And therefore, this *Second Hypostasis* of their Trinity, since it must derive its whole *being* from the *First*—as the *reflection* comes from the *light* <note>original Greek: ἀπαύγασμα from the φῶς</note>—must of necessity also have an *essential dependence*...

It concludes that the hierarchy in the Platonic Trinity stems from the belief in a single original "fountain" of divinity from which all else is derived.</summary>
