# CHAPTER IV. Gradation in the Deity.

...upon the same; and consequently, a *Gradual Subordination* to it.

For though they commonly affirm their *second hypostasis* <note>original: "hypostasis"; a term used in theology to describe a distinct person or "mode of being" within the Trinity</note> to have been *begotten* from their *first*, and their *third* from their *second*; yet they do not by any means understand this to be a *generation* like that of *men*. In human generation, the *father*, *son*, and *grandson*—at least when they are *adults*—have no *essential dependence* on one another, nor any *gradual subordination* in their nature; they are all perfectly *co-equal* and equally *absolute*. 

This is because human generation is an *imperfect generation*, where that which is *begotten* does not receive its whole being *originally* from the one that did *beget* it, but from *God* and *nature*. The begetter is merely either a channel or an instrument, having been himself previously begotten or produced by someone else. Whereas the *first divine hypostasis* is altogether *unbegotten* from any other, he being the *sole principle* and *origin* of all things. Therefore, the *second* must necessarily derive its whole essence from him and be generated in another manner—namely, by a way of *natural emanation*, just as *light* is from the *sun*. Consequently, though it is *co-eternal*, it has an *essential dependence* on him and a *gradual subordination* to *him*.

Moreover, the *Platonists* would recommend this *gradation in the deity*, or *trinity of subordinate hypostases*, for this reason: because by this means, there will not be so vast a *chasm* and *gap* <note>original: "hiatus"</note> between God and the highest creatures; nor will there be so great a *leap* and *jump* in the creation as there would otherwise have to be. Nor will the whole deity be pushed up to such a disproportionate *height* and *elevation* as would render it altogether incapable of having any *intercourse* or *dealings* <note>original: "commerce"</note> with the lower world. According to this *hypothesis* of theirs, the deity is brought down by certain *steps* and *degrees*, nearer and nearer to us. 

For if the *whole deity* were nothing but *one simple monad* <note>original: "monad"; a single, indivisible unit or point of origin</note>, devoid of all manner of *multiplicity*—as God is frequently represented to be—then it could not well be conceived by us mortals how it should contain the *distinct ideas* of all things within itself, and that *multiform platform* and *pattern* <note>original: "paradigm"</note> of the *created universe* commonly called the *archetypal world* <note>the "archetypal world" refers to the divine blueprint or ideal model of the universe existing in the mind of God</note>. 

Again, were the deity only an *immovable mind*—as *Aristotle's* God is "an absolutely immovable substance" <note>original Greek: ἀκίνητος οὐσία</note>, whose *essence* and *operation* are one and the same; and as other theologians affirm that *whatsoever is in God, is God*—it would likewise be utterly inconceivable, not only how there should be any *liberty of will* at all in God (whereas the same theologians, contradicting themselves, zealously argue nonetheless that all the actions of the deity are not necessary, and but few of them are such), but also how the *deity* should have any *dealings* or *intercourse* with the *lower world*. How should it *quicken* and *actuate* the whole, be sensible of all the motions in it, and act *as the occasion arises* <note>original Latin: pro re natâ</note> accordingly? All of these the *instincts* and *common notions* of mankind urge upon them. Neither can they be denied without erasing the very foundations of all religion, since it would be to no more purpose for men to make their *devotional prayers* <note>original: "addresses"</note> to such an *immovable*, *inflexible*, and *unaffectable deity* than to a—

# Plato's Three Hypostases, BOOK I.

...senseless *adamantine rock*. But these difficulties (as the *Platonists* claim) are all removed by that *Third Hypostasis* <note>original: "hypostasis"; a term used in theology and philosophy to describe a distinct person or "mode of being" within the Trinity</note> in their *Trinity*; which is a kind of *movable deity*. And thus all the *phenomena* of the *Deity*—or the different *common notions* in the minds of men concerning it—though seemingly repugnant and clashing with one another, are (in their opinion) fairly reconciled and resolved by this *Trinity of subordinate divine hypostases*.

Lastly, they also claim that according to this *hypothesis* of theirs, a reasonable explanation can be given to the human mind as to both why there are exactly *three divine hypostases*, and why there could be no more. Whereas, according to other views, it would seem to have been a mere arbitrary matter; either there might have been only *one solitary divine hypostasis*; or only a *duality* of them; or else they might have been *countless*, numbering beyond a *trinity*.

The second thing which we shall observe concerning the most authentic *Platonic* and *Parmenidean Trinity* is this: that though these philosophers sometimes called their *three divine hypostases* not only <term>three natures</term> <note>original Greek: "treis physeis"</note>, and *three principles*, and *three causes*, and *three craftsmen* <note>original: "Opificers"; builders or creators of the universe</note>; but also *three gods*; and a *first*, and *second*, and *third God*; yet for all that, they often supposed all these *three* to be really one *divinity* <note>original Greek: "theion"</note>, one *divine power* <note>original Latin: "Numen"</note>. 

It has been already proved from *Origen* and others that the *Platonists* most commonly called the *animated world* <note>the universe viewed as a living, ensouled being</note> the *second God*, though some of them, such as *Numenius*, styled it the *third God*. Now, those who called the *world* the *second God* actually attributed less divinity to it than those who would have it be the *third God*. This is because the latter group supposed the *Soul of the World* to be the *Third Hypostasis* of their *Trinity*. However, the others, taking all these *three divine hypostases* together as *one supreme and first God*, called the *world* the *second God*; they supposed its *soul* to be a different soul, inferior to that *First Psyche* <note>Soul</note> which was properly their *Third Hypostasis*. 

Therefore, this was really the same as if they should have called the animated *world* the *fourth God*. Only by that other way of reckoning, when they called it a *second God*, they hinted that although those *three divine hypostases* were frequently called *three gods*, they were nonetheless really all but one *divinity* <note>original: "theion"</note>; or as *Plotinus* speaks, *the divinity which is in the whole world* <note>original Greek: "to en tō panti theion"</note>. Thus, when God is so often spoken of in *Plato* in the singular, the word is not always to be understood as referring to the *First Hypostasis* only, or *The Good* <note>original: "Tagathon"</note>, but many times plainly to the *first*, and *second*, and *third* <note>original: "prōton, and deuteron, and triton"</note> all together—or that whole *divinity* which consists of, or is made up of, these *three hypostases*. 

This will further appear from the fact that when the whole *world* is said in *Plato* to be the *image of the eternal gods*, and also by *Plotinus* to be the image of the *first, second, and third* (by whom it is always produced anew, as an *image in a mirror* is), this is not to be understood as if the *world* being *tripartite* <note>divided into three parts</note>, each *third* part of it was separately produced or created by one of those *three*;

It notes that while they used terms like "Three Gods," they essentially maintained a belief in one divine power expressed through three levels of being.</summary>

# CHAPTER IV. Really One Divinity.

Nor can it be conceived how there could be *three* really distinct creations of one and the same thing. Therefore, because the world has only one creation and was created by those *three divine hypostases* <note>original: "hypostases"; distinct "persons" or modes of existence within the Godhead</note>, it follows that they are all *three* really but *one Creator* and *one God*. 

Thus, in the writings of both *Plato* and *Plotinus*, the lives and souls of all animals (such as stars, demons, and men) are attributed to the third *hypostasis*—the first and great *Psyche* <note>original: "Psyche"; the World-Soul</note>—as their fountain and cause in a special way. This is similar to how, in our Creed, the Holy Spirit is called *the Lord and Giver of Life*. However, this is not to be understood as if the first and second *hypostases* were excluded from having any role in that creation <note>original: "causality"</note>. For the First is also called by *Plato* "the cause of all good things" <note>original Greek: "aition hapantōn tōn kalōn"</note>, and therefore is undoubtedly the chief cause of souls. The Second is called by him and others the "cause and architect" <note>original Greek: "aition" and "demiurgos"</note> of the whole world. 

We conclude, therefore, that because *souls* were created by the *joint concurrence* and *influence* of these *three subordinate hypostases*, they are all really but *one and the same God*. This is expressly affirmed by *Porphyry* as quoted in the works of *St. Cyril*: "The essence of the divinity proceeds or propagates itself (by way of descent downwards) unto three hypostases or subsistences. The highest God is the *Tagathon* <note>original: "Tagathon"; the Supreme Good</note> or Supreme Good; the second next after him is the *Demiurge* <note>original: "Demiurgus"; the divine craftsman</note>, the architect or artificer of the world; and the Soul of the World is the third. For the divinity extends as far as this Soul." <note>original Greek: "achri triōn hypostaseōn tēn theian proelthein ousian..."</note> 

Here we plainly see that though *Porphyry* calls the three divine *hypostases* "three gods," he simultaneously declares that the *essence of the Godhead* and *the divinity* extends itself to all these *three hypostases*. He includes the third and last also (which they call the *Mundane Soul* <note>the soul of the universe</note>) within its compass. Therefore, even according to the Porphyrian theology itself (which could not be suspected of trying to agree with Christianity), the *three hypostases* in the Platonic Trinity are *co-essential* <note>original: "homoousioi"; sharing the same substance</note>, both because each of them is *God* and because they are all together *one God*. *St. Cyril* himself acknowledged as much when he wrote the following about the Platonists: "Supposing three primary hypostases, they also insist that the essence of God extends to all three." <note>original Greek: "treis archikas hypostaseis hypotithemenoi..."</note>

Indeed, many people assume that because the Platonists made the *three hypostases* of their *Trinity* *gradually subordinate* to one another, they could not, for that very reason, acknowledge them to be *one divinity*. But the Platonists themselves declare all three to be *one divinity* for this very reason and no other: because they have an *essential dependence* and *gradual subordination* within them. The *second* is the *image* of the *first*, and the *third* is the *image* of both the *first* and *second*. If these three were instead supposed to be *perfectly co-equal* and have no *essential dependence* on one another, they could not be concluded by these Platonists to be

-># How *Plato*’s Trinity, Book I.<-

...any other than *three coordinate gods*, having only a *generic* or *specific identity* <note>original: "Generical or Specifical Identity"; meaning they share a common category, like "humanity," but are distinct individuals</note>. In such a case, they would be no more "one" than *three men* are "one man"—a concept from which *Platonic theology* is utterly recoiling. Such an idea is inconsistent with the *perfect monarchy* of the *universe* and highly *derogatory* to the honor of the *supreme God* and *First Cause*. 

For example, should *three suns* appear in the *heavens* all at once with *equal splendor*, it would be concluded that although they were *first* derived (or *lighted* and *kindled*) from one, they were now all alike *absolute* and *independent*. These *three* could not easily be thought of as *one sun*. This is unlike *three* that appear *gradually* differing in their *splendor*, where two of them are but the *parhelii* <term>parhelii: mock suns or sun dogs created by reflection or refraction</term> of the first and are *essentially* dependent on it. In that case, the *second* would be only the *reflected image* of the *first*, and the *third* only the *second refracted*. *At least those three equal suns could not be thought to be one thing as easily as the sun and its primary and secondary splendor (which can neither be seen without the sun, nor the sun without them) might be considered one and the same thing.*

The *Platonists*, therefore, *first* of all suppose such a close and near *conjunction* between the *three hypostases* <note>original: "hypostases"; the three distinct "persons" or levels of reality in the Trinity</note> of their *Trinity* as is nowhere else to be found in the whole *world*. To this purpose, *Plotinus* writes:

<margin>*Enneads* 5, Book 1, Chapter 6.</margin>

*Intellect is said to behold the First Good, not as if it were separated from it, but only because it follows after it, with nothing in between—just as there is nothing between Intellect and the Soul. Everything which is begotten desires and loves that which begot it, especially when these two (that which begot and that which is begotten) are alone, and nothing else exists besides them. Moreover, when that which begot is absolutely the best thing, that which is immediately begotten from it must necessarily cohere intimately with it, so as to be separated from it only by a sense of "otherness."* <note>original Greek: "ὁρᾷ δὲ αὐτὸ, οὐ χωρισθεὶς, ἀλλ’ ὅτι μετ’ αὐτὸ καὶ μεταξὺ οὐδὲν· ὡς οὐδὲ ψυχῆς καὶ νοῦ· ποθεῖ δὲ πᾶν τὸ γεννῆσαν καὶ τοῦτο ἀγαπᾷ, καὶ μάλιστα ὅταν ὦσι μόνοι, τὸ γεννῆσαν καὶ τὸ γεγεννημένον· ὅταν δὲ καὶ τὸ ἄριστον ᾖ τὸ γεννῆσαν, ἐξ ἀνάγκης σύνεσιν αὐταῖς, ὡς τῇ ἑτερότητι μόνον κεχωρίσθαι"</note>

This is the same as saying that these *three divine hypostases* are so *intimately joined* together and united with one another that they are *tantum non* <note>original Latin: "tantum non"; all but, or only just not</note> the *very same*. 

Again, the *Platonists* further declare that these *three hypostases* of their *Trinity* are *indivisible* <note>original Greek: "ἀδιαίρετοι"</note> and *inseparable*, just as the radiance <note>original Greek: "ἀπαύγασμα"</note> is *indivisibly joined* with the *light* <note>original Greek: "φῶς"</note> or the *sun*. *Athanasius* often makes use of this same *similitude* <note>original: "similitude"; analogy or comparison</note> for the same purpose. 

Thirdly, these *Platonists* also seem to attribute to their *three divine hypostases* a kind of *circuminfession* <term>circuminfession: also known as perichoresis; the mutual indwelling or interpenetration of the persons of the Trinity</term> or *mutual in-being*, just as *Christians* do. For since their *second* and *third hypostases* must necessarily be in the *first* (being virtually contained within it), so must the *first* likewise be in the *second* and *third*. They are, as it were, *two* other *editions* of it, or the first *itself* being *gradually displayed* and *expanded*. 

But to speak *specifically*, the *first* must necessarily be in the *second*—the *Tagathon* <term>Tagathon: The Supreme Good</term> in the *Nous* <term>Nous: The Divine Mind or Intellect</term>—and so both of them are *really one and the same God*. ### CHAP. IV. One Entire Divinity.

...giving Wisdom and Understanding to the Deity; but according to the principles of *Plato*, *Plotinus*, and others, the Deity does not properly understand anything except through the *Second Hypostasis* <note>original: "Hypostasis"; here referring to a distinct person or level of being within the divine nature</note>, which is its *Mind* and *Wisdom*. This *mutual indwelling* <note>original: "Emperichoresis"; a theological term describing the interpenetration and coexistence of the three persons of the Trinity</note> of the *second* or *third hypostases* was also suggested by *Plato*: "Wisdom and Mind could never exist without Soul. Therefore, in the nature of Zeus, you will say that a kingly soul and a kingly mind are contained" <note>original: Σοφία μὴν καὶ Νῦς ἄνευ ψυχῆς, οὐκ ἂν ποτε γενοίσθην. οὐκοῦν ἐν μὲν τῇ τοῦ Διὸς ἐρεῖς φύσει, βασιλικὴν μὲν ψυχήν, βασιλικὸν δὲ νοῦν ἐγγίγνεσθαι</note>. Where he speaks of that Divine Wisdom and Mind which orders all things in the world, he adds: *But Wisdom and Mind can never exist without Soul* (that is, they cannot act without it). *Therefore, in the nature of Jupiter, both a Kingly Mind and a Kingly Soul are contained at once.* Here he makes *Jupiter* represent both the *second* and *third hypostases* of his Trinity—*Mind* and *Soul*—and consequently, those *two* are considered to be but *one God*. This *Mind* is also said to be "of the same kind" <note>original: γενέτης (genetes)</note>, meaning it is *co-essential* <note>original: "Co-Essential"; sharing the same fundamental essence or substance</note> with the *First Cause* of all things. 

To conclude, just as that *First Platonic Hypostasis*—which is said to be above *Mind* and *Wisdom*—is properly *wise* and *understanding* through the *second*, so do both the *first* and the *second* *move* and *act* through the *third*. Lastly, all these *three hypostases*—*The Good* <note>original: Tagathon</note>, *Mind* <note>original: Nous</note>, and *Soul* <note>original: Psyche</note>—are said by the *Platonists* to be *one Divinity* <note>original: Θεῖον (Theion)</note>. This is in the exact same manner as the *center*, the *unchanging distance* (the radius), and the *moving circumference* of a *sphere* or *globe* are all essentially *one sphere*. *Plotinus* wrote explicitly regarding the *third hypostasis*, or *Soul*: 

<margin>Page 409</margin>
"For such a Soul is also something venerable and adorable; it is like a circle fitted to a center, which, expanding immediately after the center, becomes an extension without physical distance (for it is not a physical thing). For these things are arranged just as if one were to make 'The Good'—the First Good—the center of the universe; next, to make Mind or Intellect the immovable circle or distance; and lastly, to make Soul that which turns around, or the entire moving circumference, driven by love or desire" <note>original: σεμνὸν γάρ τι καὶ ἡ ψυχὴ ἡ τοιαύτη, οἷον κύκλῳ προσαρμόζων κέντρῳ, εὐθὺς μετὰ κέντρον αὐξηθείς, διάστημα ἀδιάστατον· οὕτω γὰρ ἔχει ἔκαστα, εἰ τ᾽ἀγαθόν τις καὶ τὸ κέντρον τάξειε, τὸν νοῦν κατὰ κύκλον ἀκίνητον, ψυχὴν δὲ κατὰ κύκλον κινύμενον ἂν τάξειε</note>. 

These *three Platonic hypostases* therefore seem to be, in reality, nothing other than *Infinite Goodness*, *Infinite Wisdom*, and *Infinite Active Love and Power*. These are not merely *qualities* or *accidental properties*, but *substantial* things that have a kind of *subordination* to one another. All of them concur together to make up *one Divinity*, just as the *center*, the *radius*, and the *circumference* together make up *one sphere*.

We have now given a full account of the *true* and *authentic Platonic*, *Parmenidean*, or *Pythagorean Trinity*. From this, it may clearly appear how far it either *agrees* or *disagrees* with the *Christian* Trinity. First, although some of the later Platonists partly misunderstood and partly corrupted that ancient *tradition* <note>original: "Cabala"; here used in the sense of an ancient, handed-down oral or mystical tradition</note> of the Trinity, as was stated before—confounding the differences between God and the created world and thereby laying a foundation for *infinite polytheism*—Plato himself and some of his genuine followers (though living before Christianity) approached so near to its doctrine that they corresponded with it in three fundamental ways. ## The Agreement and Disagreement, BOOK I.

...in not making a mere Trinity of *Names* and *Words*, or of *Logical Notions* and *Incomplete Conceptions* <note>original: "Inadequate Conceptions"</note> of *One* and the *Same thing*; but a *Trinity of Hypostases* <note>original: "Hypostases"; distinct persons or individual realities</note>, *Subsistences*, or *Persons*. 

Secondly, they agree in making none of their *Three Hypostases* to be *Creatures*, but all *Eternal*, *Necessarily Existent*, and *Universal*; *Infinite*, *Omnipotent*; and *Creators* of the whole *World*. This is the same, in the sense of the ancients, as if they had affirmed them to be *Homoousian* <note>original: "Homoousian"; of the same substance or essence</note>. 

Lastly, they agree in supposing these *Three Divine Hypostases*—however they were sometimes called *Three Gods* in a Pagan manner—to be *Essentially One Divinity*. From this, it may be concluded that just as *Arianism* <note>A heresy claiming that Jesus was a created being, not eternal with God</note> is commonly supposed to approach nearer to the Truth of Christianity than *Photinianism* <note>A heresy claiming that Jesus was a mere man who became divine</note>, so *Platonism* is undoubtedly more agreeable to Christianity than *Arianism*. It serves as a certain *middle* ground between *Arianism* and *Sabellianism* <note>The belief that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are merely different modes or "masks" of a single person</note>, which was generally the mark that the Council of Nicaea also aimed at.

Despite this, there is also a clear *Disagreement* between the Platonic Trinity as described and the currently accepted doctrine in the Christian Church. This consists of a different *explanation* of the *two latter points* mentioned. 

*First*, because the Platonists never imagined such a thing as *One and the Same Numerical Essence* or *Substance* shared by the *Three Divine Hypostases*. 

And *Secondly*, because although they acknowledged none of those *Hypostases* to be *Creatures*, but all to be *God*, they still asserted an *Essential Dependence* of the *second* and *third* upon the *First*, along with a certain *Gradual Subordination*; and therefore no *Absolute Equality*. 

This is the true reason why so many recent writers have claimed that *Platonism* *resembles* <note>original: "Symbolize with"</note> *Arianism*, and that Arianism was actually nothing but the *offspring* <note>original: "spawn"</note> of Platonism. This is because the Platonists did not acknowledge *One and the Same Numerical Essence* or *Substance* of all their *Three Hypostases*, and asserted a *Gradual Subordination* of them—but chiefly for this latter reason. 

On this account, some of the ancients also did the same, <margin>Page 34.</margin> particularly *St. Cyril* (in *Against Julian*, Book I), where he writes this concerning *Plato*: "Plato did not thoroughly perceive the whole Truth of the Trinity, but in the same way as those who follow Arius, he divided the Deity, or created a gradation within it, and introduced subordinate Hypostases" <note>original Greek: τεθεώρηκε μὲν οὖν οὐχ ὑγιῶς εἰσάπαν, ἀλλὰ τοῖς τὰ Ἀρείου πεφρονηκόσιν, ἐν ἴσῳ διαιρεῖ, καὶ ὑφίστησιν, ὑποκαθελμένας τε ἀλλήλαις τὰς ὑποστάσεις εἰσφέρει</note>. Elsewhere, the same Pious Father also criticizes the Platonists for not declaring the *Three Hypostases* of their Trinity to be, in his view, *Homoousian*—that is, *Absolutely Equal*. 

But though we have already proved that *Platonism* cannot be confused with *Arianism* (because it directly opposed the main essentials of Arianism, which were the claims that "there was a time when he was not" <note>original Latin: "Erat quando non Erat"</note>, or that the *Second Hypostasis* was made "from things that do not exist" <note>original Greek: ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων; meaning created out of nothing</note>, and that it was *changeable* and *capable of falling* <note>original: "Lapsible"</note>), yet, according to *Platonism*, the *Nous* <note>The Divine Mind or Intellect</note> is *Essentially* both *Eternal* and *Immutable*. Nevertheless, it is *unquestionably evident* that the most refined *Platonism* differed from the currently accepted *Doctrine* of the Christian Church regarding its *Gradual Subordination*; this fact cannot be *hidden*, *glossed over*, or *excused*.

<summary>This page analyzes the similarities and differences between the Platonic Trinity and the orthodox Christian Trinity, noting that while Platonism avoids the errors of Arianism by asserting the eternity of all three persons, it still maintains a hierarchy or subordination among them that Christian doctrine rejects.</summary>

# Chapter IV. Of Plato's and the Christian Trinity.

Beyond this, it cannot be denied that even the best of Plato’s followers were sometimes erratic <note>original: "extravagant"; wandering from the path of their own logic</note> in their doctrine of the Trinity. They occasionally spoke at random and inconsistently with their own principles, especially when they created such a vast and disproportionate distance between the *Second* and *Third Hypostases* <note>original: "Hypostases"; the distinct persons or levels of reality in the Trinity</note> of their system. Instead of descending gradually and orderly, they seem to, as it were, *tumble down* from the former to the latter. 

Thus *Plotinus* himself, after having spoken magnificently <margin>Enneads 5. Book 1. Chapter 2.</margin> of that *Soul of the World* (which is his *Third Hypostasis*), immediately adds: "Our soul is also of the same species <note>original: "ὁμοειδὴς δὲ καὶ ἡμετέρα"; having the same nature</note>, and if you consider it by itself—pure, naked, and stripped of everything added to it—you will find it to be that same venerable thing that the [World] Soul was." In agreement with this, the same philosopher elsewhere calls that *Mundane Soul* <note>The "World Soul" that animates the physical universe</note> "nothing but the elder sister of our human souls" <note>original: "πρεσβυτέραν καὶ ἀδελφήν"</note>. 

This line of thinking reeks of philosophical pride and arrogance—to think so highly of themselves as to nearly equalize *their own souls* with that *Mundane Soul*. Furthermore, it was a *monstrous degradation* of the *Third Hypostasis* of their Trinity, amounting to little more than *absolutely turning it into a creature*. For if our *human soul* is of the same kind or species as the *Third Hypostasis* of the Trinity, then it is not only of equal honor and dignity, but also (in the language of the Christian Church) *Co-essential* <note>original: "ὁμοούσιος" (Homoousios); of the same substance</note> with our human souls. This is similar to how the Savior Christ was described by the *Arians* in the writings of *Athanasius* <margin>Volume I. Page 557.</margin> as being "co-essential with us men" <note>original: "ὁμοούσιος ἡμῶν τῶν ἀνθρώπων"</note>. 

From this, it follows that either the *Third Hypostasis* must be a creature, or else our *human souls* must be divine. Therefore, unless these Platonists were to confine the *deity* entirely to their *First Hypostasis*—which would be monstrously absurd, as they supposed the *First Eternal Mind and Wisdom* by which the world was made to be a creature—they must necessarily make a vast leap or *jump* between the *Second* and *Third* of their *Hypostases*. The *former* is that *Perfect Wisdom* which was the architect or *Demiurgus* <note>The creator or "craftsman" of the physical universe</note> of the world, while the *latter* is merely the "elder sister of all human souls." 

Moreover, by bringing the *Third Hypostasis* of their Trinity so low and immersing it so deeply into the physical world (as if it were the *animating soul* of it) and making it only the *elder sister of our created souls*, these Platonists undoubtedly laid a foundation for their *polytheism* and *creature-worship* (now commonly called *idolatry*). Specifically, this led to their *Cosmo-latry* (worship of the world), *Astro-latry* (worship of the stars), and *Demono-latry* (worship of spirits). 

This is plainly stated in the following passage by *Plotinus*: <margin>Page 483.</margin> "This whole physical world is made a god by its soul. And the sun is also a god because it is animated, as likewise all the stars are gods for the same reason" <note>original: "διὰ ταύτην ὁ κόσμος ὅδε θεός· ἔτι δὲ καὶ ἥλιος θεὸς ὅτι ἔμψυχος, καὶ τὰ ἄλλα ἄστρα"</note>. He later adds: "That which is the cause of these gods or goddesses being gods must necessarily itself be an older god or goddess than they are" <note>original: "τὴν δὲ θεοῖς αἰτίαν τοῦ θεοῖς εἶναι, ἀνάγκη πρεσβυτέραν θεὸν αὐτῆς εἶναι"</note>. So that...

# The Platonic Levels <note>original: Βαθμοί (Bathmoi)</note> Censured. BOOK I.

This *Third Hypostasis* of the *Platonic Trinity*, called the *World Soul* <note>original: "Mundane Soul"</note>, is treated as merely a kind of *Sister-Goddess* to the souls of the *sun*, *moon*, and *stars*—though she is indeed older than they are, since they were all made *goddesses* by *her*. This creates a confused jumble of contradictory ideas. That *World Soul* is supposed to be a *sister* to other souls, yet she somehow also deifies <note>makes into gods</note> them. However, this sisterly relationship and shared nature <note>original: "Consanguinity"</note> between them would, of the two possibilities, rather degrade and *turn that World Soul into a creature*—even though it is their *Third God* or *Divine Hypostasis*—than it would *advance* and deify those *particular created souls*. 

Here, therefore, we see the *problem* <note>original: "Inconvenience"</note> with these *Platonic* levels <note>original: Βαθμοί (Bathmoi); steps or degrees</note>, stories, stairs, and gradations within the *Deity*. Such a system is liable to be abused for *creature-worship* and *idolatry* when the *distances* between levels are made so *wide* that the *lowest* aspect of the Deity is thought to differ only *gradually* from the *highest* of *created beings*. 

Because *Porphyry* <note>original: "Porphyrius"</note> followed in the footsteps of *Plotinus* here as elsewhere, this was likely the true reason why the *Arians* (as the historian *Socrates Scholasticus* records) were called *Porphyrianists* by the Emperor *Constantine*. It was not because their *Trinities* were exactly the same, but because *Arius* and *Porphyry* both used their *Trinity* as a *foundation* for *creature-worship* and *idolatry*, albeit for different reasons. 

Nevertheless, all *this* (like many other things) was written heedlessly and inadvertently by *Plotinus*; he was, as it were, nodding off <note>A reference to the idea that even great authors occasionally make mistakes</note> while writing it. It was also lazily <note>original: "supinely"</note> adopted by *Porphyry* after him. It is plainly inconsistent with the true spirit of both their theories <note>original: "Hypotheses"</note> to *level* the *Third Hypostasis* of the Trinity with *particular created souls*, as doing so creates such a *disproportionate distance* and *vast chasm* between it and the *Second Hypostasis*. 

For when *Plotinus* himself is in a more sober mood, he declares that the *Third Hypostasis* is not the *immediate animating soul* <note>original: "Informing Soul"</note> of the *physical world*, but rather a *higher, separate soul*, or a *Superior Venus*. This soul was also the *Demiurge* <note>original: "Demiurgus"; the divine craftsman</note>, the *maker* of both other *souls* and the entire *world*. As *Plato* had expressly affirmed before him, this figure is the *inspirer* of all *life* and the *creator* of *souls*—the *Lord* and *Giver of Life*. He likewise declared that among all those things that are *related and of the same nature as our human souls* <note>original: ἀνθρωπίνης ψυχῆς συγγενῆ (anthrōpinēs psychēs syngenē)</note>, there is *nothing anywhere to be found at all like it* <note>original: οὐδὲν τοιοῦτο (ouden toiouto)</note>. 

So, while *Plato* was also a *star-worshipper* and *idolater* for other reasons, he likely would not have approved of *Plotinus's* idea that *our souls are of the same species* <note>original: ὁμοειδὴς τῇ ἡμετέρα (homoeidēs tē hēmetera)</note> as that *Third Hypostasis* of the *Divine Triad*. Instead, he might have said, in the language of the *Psalmist*: 

> *It is he who has made us, and not we ourselves; we are his people and the sheep of his pasture.* <note>Psalm 100:3</note>

Despite all this, a *Christian Platonist* or *Platonic Christian* would likely defend <note>original: "Apologize for"</note> *Plato* himself, as well as the ancient and most genuine *Platonists* and *Pythagoreans*, in this way: First, because they had no *Scriptures*, *Councils*, or *Creeds* to guide them through the *darkness* of this *mystery* <note>the Trinity</note> and to restrict their language to a *regular uniformity*, they theologized freely and boldly, without hesitation, each according—

He concludes that Plato himself likely would have viewed the Divine as fundamentally distinct from created souls, even without Christian revelation.</summary>

# CHAP. IV. *The Platonic Christian's Apology.*

...according to his own private understandings, it is no wonder at all if they did not only speak many times carelessly and inconsistently with their own principles, but also plainly wander out of the *right path*. Indeed, it ought much rather to be wondered at that—living so long before Christianity as some of them did—they should in so *abstruse a point* and *dark a mystery* make so near an approach to the *Christian truth* afterwards revealed, than that they should anywhere stumble or fall short of its *accuracy*. 

They did not only extend the *true and real Deity* to *three hypostases* <note>A Greek term meaning "persons" or "individual substances" within the Trinity.</note>, but they also called the second of them the *Word* <note>original: λόγον (logon)</note> or *Reason*—as well as the *Mind* <note>original: νοῦν (noun)</note> or *Intellect*. They also called him *the Son* of the *first hypostasis*, the *Father*, and affirmed him to be the *Artificer* <note>original: δημιουργὸς (demiurgos)</note> and *Cause* <note>original: αἴτιον (aition)</note> *of the whole world*. Lastly, they described him as the Scripture does: to be the *Image*, the *Figure* or *Character*, and the *Splendor* or *Brightness of the First*. This, I say, our *Christian Platonist* supposes to be much more wonderful: that this so *great* and *abstruse a mystery* of *three eternal hypostases* in the *Deity* should have been asserted by *pagan philosophers* so long before Christianity as the principle and original of the whole world. This was, in fact, more than was acknowledged by the *Nicene Fathers* <note>The bishops at the Council of Nicaea in 325 AD, who formulated the Nicene Creed.</note> themselves; at that time, they did not even determine that the *Holy Ghost* was a *hypostasis*, much less that he was *God*.

But particularly regarding their *gradual subordination* of the *second hypostasis* to the *first*, and of the *third* to the *first* and *second*, our *Platonic Christian* would doubtless plead that they are more excusable because the generality of *Christian doctors*—for the *first three hundred years* after the Apostles' times—plainly asserted the same. These include *Justin Martyr*, *Athenagoras*, *Tatian*, *Irenaeus*, the author of the *Recognitions*, *Tertullian*, *Clement of Alexandria*, *Origen*, *Gregory Thaumaturgus*, *Dionysius of Alexandria*, *Lactantius*, and many others. Because it would be too tedious to set down all their testimonies here, we shall content ourselves only with one from the last mentioned: 

<margin>*Divine Institutes*, Book 4, Chapter 29.</margin>
> "Both the Father and the Son are God: but He is, as it were, an exuberant fountain, while He is like a stream flowing out from it; He is like the Sun, and He is like a ray extended from the Sun." <note>original Latin: *Et Pater & Filius Deus est: sed Ille quasi exuberans Fons, Hic tanquam defluens ex eo Rivus: Ille tanquam Sol, Hic tanquam Radius à Sole porrectus.*</note>

And though it is true that *Athanasius* <note>A 4th-century bishop and champion of Trinitarian orthodoxy against Arianism.</note>, writing against the Arians, appeals to the *tradition* of the Ancient Church and cites *Origen’s* testimony as well, this was only for the *eternity* and *divinity* of the *Son of God*. It was not at all for such an *absolute co-equality* of him with the *Father* that would exclude all *dependence*, *subordination*, and *inferiority*. Those ancients agreed so unanimously on this point that they are taxed <note>accused or criticized</note> by *Petavius* <note>Dionysius Petavius (1583–1652), a Jesuit theologian who argued that early Church Fathers held views similar to later heresies.</note> for "Platonism," and for having by that means corrupted the purity of the *Christian faith* in this article of the Trinity. How this can be reconciled with those other opinions—that *ecclesiastical tradition* is a rule of faith and that it is *impossible* for the *visible Church to err* in any *fundamental point*—cannot easily be understood. However, this general tradition or consent of the Christian Church for three hundred years together after the Apostles...

->## In what Sense, Plato's Trinity. BOOK I.<-

[Apo]stles' times; though it cannot justify the Platonists in anything that disagrees with the Scripture, yet it may certainly plead their excuse to some extent, as they had no scriptural revelation at all to guide them. This should, at least, make their error more tolerable or pardonable.

Moreover, the Platonic *Christian* would further offer a defense for these pagan Platonists in this manner: Their intention in thus *subordinating* the *hypostases* <note>The three distinct "persons" or "substances" within the Trinity.</note> of their *Trinity* was clearly nothing other than to exclude a *plurality of coordinate and independent gods*, which they supposed an absolute co-equality of the persons would imply. They established only as much *subordination* among them as was both necessary for this purpose and unavoidable. In their opinion, the connection between them was so close that there was *nothing in between* <note>original: μηδὲν μεταξὺ (meden metaxy)</note>, or nothing that could possibly be *thrust in between them*. 

But now, on the other hand, the only ground for the *co-equality* of the persons in the Holy Trinity is that it cannot well be conceived how they should otherwise all be *God*. Since the *essence of the Godhead*—being *absolute perfection*—can admit no degrees, these Platonists argue to the contrary. They contend that, despite the dependence and subordination which they commonly assume in these hypostases, none of them are to be considered *creatures*. Instead, they argue that the *general essence of the Godhead*, or the *uncreated nature*, truly and properly belongs to them all, according to the statement of Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher and student of Plotinus.</note> cited before: *the essence of the Godhead proceeds to three hypostases* <note>original: ἄχρι τριῶν ὑποστάσεων τὴν θείαν προελθεῖν οὐσίαν (achri trion hypostaseon ten theian proelthein ousian)</note>. 

Now, these Platonists conceive that the *essence of the Godhead*, as shared by all *three hypostases* of their *Trinity*, consists (besides *perfect intellectuality*) in the following things: 

*   **First:** In *being eternal*. As we have already shown, this was *Plato’s distinctive character* between *God* and the *creature*. Whatever was eternal is therefore *uncreated*, and whatever was not eternal is a *creature*. By "eternity," he meant having not only no beginning but also a *permanent duration*. 
*   **Again:** In having not a *contingent* but a *necessary existence*, and therefore being absolutely *indestructible*; which is perhaps also included in the former point. 
*   **Lastly:** In being not *particular* but *universal*—*one and all things* <note>original: ἓν καὶ πάντα (hen kai panta)</note>—or that which comprehends the whole. This is the same as to say it is *infinite* and *omnipotent*, and the *creator of the whole world*. 

Now, say these Platonists, if anything more were to be added to the general essence of the Godhead besides this, then it must be *self-existence*—to be *underived* from any other, and the *first original principle and cause of all*. But if this is made so essential to the Godhead or *uncreated nature* that whatever is not thus originally of itself is *by that very fact* <note>original: ipso facto</note> demoted and thrust down into the rank of *creatures*, then both the *second* and *third hypostases* (in the Christian as well as the Platonic Trinity) would necessarily be *creatures* and not *God*. Upon this supposition, the *second* would derive its whole being and *Godship* from the *first*, and the *third* from both the *first* and *second*; thus, neither the second nor third would be the *cause of all things*. But it is unquestionable to these Platonists that whatever is *eternal* and *necessarily existent*...

### Chapter 4: *Homoousian* and Co-equal

Existent, infinite, and omnipotent, and the creator of *all things*; they ought therefore to be religiously worshipped and adored as *God* by all *created beings*. Therefore, this *essence of the Godhead*, which belongs alike to all the *three hypostases* <note>original: ὑπόστασις; the distinct "persons" or individual realities of the Trinity.</note>, being—as all other essences are—*perfectly indivisible*, it might well be affirmed, according to *Platonic principles*, that all the *three divine hypostases* (though having some level of subordination among them) are nonetheless in this sense *co-equal*. They are all truly and alike *God* or *uncreated*. 

The Platonists, by distinguishing between *ousia* <note>original: οὐσία (essence or substance)</note> and *hypostasis*—the *essence of the Godhead* versus its *distinct personalities*—and by defining the *first* of these as *common, general, and universal*, are not without the support and approval of the *Orthodox Fathers* in this matter. These Fathers likewise determined that in the Deity, *essence* or *substance* differs from *hypostasis* as *the common* <note>original: τὸ κοινὸν (to koinon)</note> differs from *the singular and individual* <note>original: τὸ καθ᾽ ἕκαστον (to kath' hekaston)</note>. 

Thus, among many others, *St. Cyril* wrote: *The essence or substance of the Deity differs from the hypostasis in the same way that a genus or species differs from an individual* <note>original: ἣν ἔχει διαφορὰν τὸ γένος, ἢ εἶδος, ὑπὲρ τὸ ἄτομον, ταύτην ἡ οὐσία πρὸς τὴν ὑπόστασιν ἔχει</note>. So, according to both these Fathers and the Platonists, that *essence* or *substance* of the Godhead which all the *three persons* share is not *singular*, but *generic* or *universal*. Both groups suppose that each of the persons also possesses their own *numerical essence* <note>A unique, individual existence, even while sharing a general nature.</note>. 

Therefore, according to this distinction between the *essence* or *substance* of the Godhead and the *particular hypostases* (which was approved by the *Orthodox Fathers*), neither *Plato* nor any *intelligent Platonist* would hesitate to subscribe to the formula of the Council of Nicaea: that the Son or Word is *homoousios* <note>original: ὁμοούσιος (co-essential or consubstantial)</note> and *co-equal* with the *Father*. And we believe it will be proved later that this was the very meaning of the Council of Nicaea itself: that the Son was *co-essential* or *consubstantial* with the *Father* simply because he was *God* and not a *creature*.

Besides this, the *genuine Platonists* would undoubtedly also acknowledge all the *three hypostases* of their Trinity to be *homoousian*, *co-essential*, or *consubstantial* in a further sense than this: namely, as being all of them *one divinity* <note>original: θεῖον (theion)</note>. For just as with that passage of *Porphyry* cited before, these words of *St. Cyril* concerning them may also be understood: *That according to them, the essence of God extends to three hypostases, or includes three hypostases within it* <note>original: μέχρι τριῶν ὑποστάσεων τὴν οὐσίαν τοῦ Θεοῦ προήκειν ἰσχυρίζονται</note>. This means not only that each of these *three* is *God*, but also that they are not many separate and divided gods, but all of them together are *one God* or divinity. 

For though the *Platonists*, as Pagans, were not as careful with their language as we Christians are—often calling them *three gods*, or a *first, second, and third god*—they nonetheless declared them, as philosophers, to be *one divinity*. It seems they did this for several reasons. First, because they are *indivisibly* joined together, just as *brightness is indivisible from the sun*. And second, because they *exist within each other*: the *first* being in the *second*, and both *first* and *second*...

<summary>This page argues that the Platonic distinction between general divine essence (ousia) and individual persons (hypostasis) aligns with the views of Orthodox Church Fathers like St. Cyril. It suggests that Platonists would have agreed with the Nicene Council's claim that the Son is "consubstantial" with the Father, seeing the Trinity as one indivisible divinity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that the three persons of the Trinity share a single essence and act as a unified whole toward the creation, despite an internal hierarchy of origin.</meta>

**What Inequality, Book I.**

<margin>
Regarding the Opinion of Dionysius, page 556.
</margin>
...in the third. Finally, because the completeness of the entire Divinity is made up of all these three together, which all share **one and the same energy or action outwardly** <note>original: μίαν ἐνέργειαν... ad extra</note>. Therefore, just as the center, the radius, and the moving circumference can all be said to be **co-essential** <term>Co-essential: Sharing the same fundamental nature or essence; in Greek, *homoousios*.</term> to a sphere—and the root, trunk, and branches are co-essential to a whole tree—so too, but in a much more perfect sense, are the Platonic *Tagathon* <note>original: Τἀγαθόν; "The Good"</note>, *Nous* <note>original: Νόος; "Intellect"</note>, and *Psyche* <note>original: Ψυχή; "Soul"</note> co-essential to that **divinity in the whole universe** <note>original: ἐν τῷ παντὶ θεῖον</note>. Athanasius <note>A 4th-century Christian theologian and defender of the Trinity.</note> was also no stranger to this notion of the word *homoousios*; he affirmed that **the branches are co-essential with, and indivisible from, the vine** <note>original: τὰ κλήματα ὁμοούσια καὶ ἀδιαίρετα εἶναι τῆς ἀμπέλου</note>, and he illustrated the Trinity using that comparison. 

Nor should it be thought that the whole Trinity is "one" in the exact same way that each single person within it is "one" in themselves; if that were the case, there would have to be a trinity within each person as well. It is not called "undivided" as if the three were not truly three (which would make the mystery ridiculous), but because all three *hypostases* <term>Hypostases: The distinct persons or individual realities of the Trinity.</term> or persons are indivisibly and inseparably united to each other, like the sun and its brightness, and are really but one God. Therefore, though there is some subordination among the *hypostases* or persons in Plato's Trinity (as it is commonly described), this exists only **inwardly** <note>original: ad intra</note> within the Deity itself, in their relation to one another and when compared among themselves. But **outwardly** <note>original: ad extra</note> and toward us, they are all one and the same God, acting together in all the same works. In that respect, there is no inequality, because where there is identity of essence, there can be no inequality.

Furthermore, a "Platonic Christian" would argue in favor of these Platonists that, according to the principles of Christianity itself, there must necessarily be some dependence and subordination among the persons of the Trinity in their relation to one another. There is a priority and a sequence—not only **of order** <note>original: τάξεως</note> but also **of dignity** <note>original: ἀξιώματος</note>—among them. First, because that which exists originally of itself, derived from no other, must naturally have some superiority and preeminence over that which derives its entire being and divinity from it—just as the second person does from the first alone, and the third from the first and second together. 

Again, although all three *hypostases* or persons are equally omnipotent **outwardly** <note>original: ad extra</note>, they are not so **inwardly** <note>original: ad intra</note>, or within the Deity itself. The Son is not able to beget the Father, nor can the Holy Spirit produce either the Father or the Son. Therefore, neither of these latter two is absolutely the original cause of all things; only the first person is. On this account, the first of these three *hypostases* (the original fountain of all) was called by Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Latin writer and philosopher.</note> **the most omnipotent God** <note>original: Omnipotentissimus Deus</note>. In saying this, he implied that the second and third *hypostases*, *Nous* and *Psyche*, are also omnipotent, but not in a perfect equality with the first when compared within the Deity. However, **outwardly** <note>original: ad extra</note> and toward us, being all one, they are equally omnipotent. And Plotinus <note>The founder of Neoplatonism, 3rd century AD.</note> also writes to the same purpose: 
<margin>
Page 517.
</margin>
**"If the First be absolutely perfect and the first power, then it must necessarily be the most powerful of all beings"** <note>original: εἰ τέλειόν ἐστι τὸ πρῶτον, καὶ δύναμις ἡ πρώτη, δεῖ πάντων τῶν ὄντων δυνατώτατον εἶναι</note>; other powers only...

<summary>This page discusses the "co-essential" nature of the Trinity, comparing the Platonic triad of the Good, Intellect, and Soul to the Christian Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. It argues that while there is an internal hierarchy of origin (the Father as the source), the three persons are equal and unified in their external actions toward the world.</summary>

# Chapter IV. In the Christian Trinity.

...only imitating and partaking of it. Accordingly, the Platonic Christian would further argue that there are several places in Scripture that strongly favor a certain subordination and priority—both of order and of dignity—among the persons of the **Holy Trinity**. None of these is more obvious than the words of our Savior Christ: *My Father is greater than I.* To understand this as referring only to his **humanity** seems less reasonable; it was no news at all that the **Eternal God**, the Creator of the whole world, should be greater than a mortal man born of a woman. Thus, many of the Orthodox Fathers—including **Athanasius** himself, St. **Basil**, St. **Gregory Nazianzen**, and St. **Chrysostom**, along with several of the Latin Fathers—interpret this passage to have been spoken not of the **humanity**, but of the **divinity** of our Savior Christ.

<margin>On the Trinity, page 863 <note>original: De Trin. p. 863</note></margin>
In fact, **Petavius** himself, when explaining the Athanasian Creed, writes in this manner: "The Father is rightly and in a Catholic manner affirmed by most of the ancients to be Greater than the Son; and he is commonly said, without reproach, to be Prior to him in respect of his Origin" <note>original: Pater Major Filio, ritè & catholicè pronuntiatus est à plerisque Veterum; & Origine Prior sine reprehensione dici solet</note>. From this, he concludes the true meaning of that Creed to be this: that no Person of the Trinity is greater or less than another in respect to the **essence** of the Godhead common to them all—"Because the true Godhead can nowhere be either Lesser or Greater" <note>original: Quia Vera Deitas in nullo esse aut Minor aut Major potest</note>. Nevertheless, there may still be some **inequality** among them as they are "This God" and "That Person" <note>original: Hic Deus, and Hæc Persona</note>.

It is true, indeed, that many of those ancient Fathers restrict and limit this **inequality** only to the **relation** of the persons to one another—such as the **Father’s Begetting**, the **Son’s being begotten by the Father**, and the **Holy Ghost proceeding from both**. In all other respects, they seem to affirm a **perfect equality** among them. Nevertheless, several of them extend this difference further. For example, St. **Hilary**, a zealous opponent of the Arians <note>Arians: Followers of Arius, who taught that Jesus was a created being, not co-eternal with God the Father.</note>, writes in his *Book of Synods*: "If anyone says there is one God, and also confesses Christ as God—the Son of God before all ages—but does not confess that the Son was obedient to the Father in the creation of all things, let him be cursed" <note>original: Siquis Unum dicens Deum, Christum autem Deum, ante secula Filium Dei, Obsecutum Patri in Creatione omnium, non confitetur, Anathema sit</note>. And again: "We do not make the Son equal to or identical in form to the Father, but we understand him to be subject" <note>original: Non exaequamus vel conformamus Filium Patri, sed Subjectum intelligimus</note>.

<margin>Against the Arians, Oration 4, page 467 <note>original: Cont. Ar. Or. 4. p. 467</note></margin>
Even **Athanasius** himself, who is commonly considered the very standard of **orthodoxy** on this point, often compares the Father to the **Sun** or the **Original Light** <note>original: ἥλιῳ or φῶς</note> and the Son to its **Splendor** or **Brightness** <note>original: ἀπαύγασμα</note> (as do the Nicene Council and the Scripture itself). By this, he seems to imply a certain **dependence** of the **Second Person** upon the **First**, and a **subordination** to it. This is especially clear when he declares that the **Three Persons** of the Trinity are not to be looked upon as **Three Principles**, nor compared to **Three Suns**, but rather to the **Sun**, its **splendor**, and its **derived light**: "For it appears from the comparison we use that we do not introduce three principles (as the Marcionists and Manicheans did), because we do not compare the Trinity to three suns, but only to the sun and its brightness. So it is that we acknowledge only one principle" <note>original: οὐδὲ γὰρ τρεῖς ἀρχὰς εἰσάγομεν, ἐπεὶ μηδὲ τριῶν ἡλίων ὑπεθέμεθα τὴν εἰκόνα, ἀλλὰ ἥλιον καὶ ἀπαύγασμα, καὶ ἓν τὸ ἐξ ἡλίου ἐν τῷ ἀπαυγάσματι φῶς· οὕτω μίαν ἀρχὴν οἴδαμεν</note>. As also where

It explains the "Greater than I" scripture as referring to the Son's divine relationship to the Father, rather than just his human nature.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that early Christian theologians recognized a hierarchy or "subordination" within the Trinity, comparing the Son's relationship to the Father with natural phenomena like light from the sun or water from a fountain.</meta>

# Plato's Trinity, Rectified, Book I

<margin>P. 565.</margin>
He [Athanasius] approves of this statement by **Dionysius of Alexandria**: "God is an eternal light, which never began and shall never cease to be; therefore there is an eternal splendor also coexistent with him, which had no beginning either, but was **always generated** by him, shining out before him" <note>original: ὁ δέ γε Θεὸς αἰώνιόν ἐστι φῶς, οὔτε ἀρξάμενον, οὔτε λῆξόν ποτε· οὐκοῦν αἰώνιον πρόσκειται καὶ σύνεσιν αὐτῷ τὸ ἀπαύγασμα, ἄναρχον καὶ ἀείγενες προφαινόμενον αὐτοῦ</note>. For if the Son of God is like the splendor of the sun—**always generated** <note>original: ἀειγενὴς</note>—then he must necessarily have an **essential dependence** upon the Father and **subordination** to him. 

This same point appears further from other comparisons that the same **Dionysius** makes between the Father and the Son, which were likewise approved by **Athanasius**: namely, comparing them to a **fountain** and a **river**, or a **root** and a **branch**. 

<margin>P. 275.</margin>
He also compares them to **water** and **vapor**; for in that passage, it ought to be read "water" <note>original: ὕδατος</note> and not "spirit" <note>original: πνεύματος</note>. This is clear from his book on the **Nicene** Synod, where he affirms that the Son was begotten of the **essence** or **substance** of the **Father**, "as the splendor of the light, and as the vapor of the water" <note>original: ὡς τοῦ φωτὸς ἀπαύγασμα, ὡς ὕδατος ἀτμίς</note>. He adds: "For neither the splendor nor the vapor is the very sun or the very water; yet they are not alien to them, nor strangers to their nature. Instead, they are both outflows from the essence or substance of them" <note>original: οὔτε γὰρ τὸ ἀπαύγασμα, οὔτε ἡ ἀτμὶς, αὐτὸ τὸ ὕδωρ ἐστὶν, ἢ αὐτὸς ὁ ἥλιος· οὔτε ἀλλότριον, ἀλλὰ ἀπόῤῥοια τῆς τοῦ πατρὸς οὐσίας</note>. Just as the Son is an **outflow** from the **substance** of the **Father**, he is in no way diminished or lessened by it. 

Now, all these metaphors—the **fountain** and the **river**, the **root** and the **branch**, the **water** and the **vapor** (as well as the **sun** and its **splendor**)—seem plainly to imply some **dependence** and **subordination**. **Dionysius** undoubtedly intended them for that purpose. As **Photius** <note>A 9th-century Byzantine scholar and Patriarch of Constantinople.</note> informs us, Dionysius asserted an **inferiority** of **power** and **glory** in the **second person**, as did **Origen** before him. **Athanasius** uses the testimonies of both men without any criticism or correction. 

Therefore, when **Athanasius** and the other orthodox fathers, writing against **Arius**, so frequently assert the **equality** of all **three persons**, this should be understood only as an opposition to **Arius**. Arius made the Son **unequal** to the Father by claiming he was "of a different essence" <note>original: ἑτερόουσιον</note>—meaning one was God and the other was a creature. The orthodox fathers affirmed the contrary: that he was **equal** to the Father because he was "of the same essence" <note>original: ὁμοούσιος</note>; that is, he was **God** and **not a creature**. Despite this **equality**, there might still be some **subordination** among them, such as "this God and that person" <note>original: Hic Deus and Hæc Persona</note>, to use the language of **Petavius** <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), a prominent Jesuit theologian.</note>.

Thus, there does not seem to be as great a difference between the more **genuine Platonists** and the ancient **orthodox fathers** regarding the Trinity as many people believe. However, our **Platonic Christian** would further add that there is no necessity at all—based on the principles of **Platonism** itself—for the Platonists to suggest any more **subordination** in their Trinity than the most strictly orthodox fathers do. According to the common hypothesis of the Platonists, they define the **character** of the **first hypostasis** <term>hypostasis: a distinct person or substance within the Trinity</term> as **Infinite Goodness**; the **second** as **Infinite Wisdom**; and the **third** as **Infinite Active Love and Power**.

<summary>This page argues that the Son's "equality" with the Father in early Christian orthodoxy does not rule out a relationship of dependence and subordination, using metaphors like light and its splendor. It concludes that Platonic and Christian views of the Trinity are more aligned than commonly thought, as both describe three distinct infinite characteristics within the Godhead.</summary>

### CHAPTER IV. Reaching an Agreement with the Christian.

If we view these three persons not as accidents or qualities but as entirely substantial, it is easier to conceive that they are all really but **one** and the same **God**, rather than believing there is any significant inferiority among them. <margin>St. Augustine, *The City of God*, Book 10, Chapter 23: "When he says 'Middle,' he does not place it after, but places it between." <note>original: "Cum dicit Medium, non Postponit, sed Interponit."</note></margin> But besides this, there is another Platonist theory (which St. Augustine mentions from **Porphyry**, though he admits he did not well understand it) where the **Third Hypostasis** is made to be a certain middle point between the **First** and **Second**. **Proclus** also sometimes follows this, calling the third person in a similar way a <term>middle power</term> <note>original: μέσην δύναμιν</note> and the <term>relation of both the First and Second to one another</term> <note>original: σχέσιν ἀμφοῖν</note>. 

This matches exactly with the understanding of some Christians that the **Third Hypostasis** is, as it were, the **Nexus** <note>a connection or link</note> between the **Father** and the **Son**, and that **Love** with which the Father and Son love each other. According to this later Platonist theory, there would seem to be not so much a gradation or descent as a kind of circulation within the Trinity. Based on all these considerations, the **Christian Platonist** would conclude that although some later Platonists have corrupted the notion of the Trinity, either there is no great difference between the **genuine Platonist Trinity**, rightly understood, and the **Christian** one, or else that if the Platonist view were properly adjusted, there would not need to be any difference.

However, although the **genuine Platonists** do suppose the three <term>hypostases</term> <note>individual persons or substances</note> of their Trinity to be not only God, but also **one God**, or <term>one entire divinity</term> <note>original: μία θεότης</note>—on which account they might also say the whole has **one singular** or **numerical essence**—it must still be acknowledged that they never suppose each of these three persons to be numerically the very same, or to lack distinct individual essences of their own. In their view, this would be directly contradictory to their own theory, and would be the same as affirming that they were not actually three persons, but only one. 

Nevertheless, the **Christian Platonist** would defend them in this way: the ancient **Orthodox Fathers** of the Christian Church generally held the same belief—that the **essence** or **substance** of the Godhead, in which all three persons or hypostases agree as each is God, was not **one singular** and **individual** thing, but only **one common** and **universal essence** or **substance**. They used the word "substance" as a synonym for "essence" and applied it to "universals" as well, just as the **Peripatetics** <note>followers of Aristotle</note> do when they call "a human" or "animal in general" a **second substance** <note>original: "Substantiam secundam"</note>. Now, this is evident because these Orthodox Fathers, in the controversy over the Trinity, commonly distinguished between <term>ousia</term> <note>original: οὐσία; essence or substance</note> and <term>hypostasis</term> <note>original: ὑπόστασις; person</note> in this way: namely, that the **hypostasis** or **person** was **singular** and **individual**, while the **essence** or **substance** was **common** and **universal**. <margin>Dialogue 1 against the Heretics <note>original: Dial. 1. adv. Haer.</note></margin> This is how **Theodoret** describes the teaching of these Fathers in general: 

> "According to the teaching of the Fathers: as that which is common differs from that which is proper, and the genus from the species or the individual, so does **Essence** differ from **Person**." <note>original: κατάγε τὴν τῶν πατέρων διδασκαλίαν, ἣν ἔχει διαφορὰν τὸ κοινὸν ὑπὲρ τὸ ἴδιον, ἢ τὸ γένος ὑπὲρ τὸ εἶδος ἢ τὸ ἄτομον, ταύτην ἔχει Η ΟΥΣΙΑ πρὸς ΤΗΝ ΥΠΟΣΤΑΣΙΝ</note>

<summary>This page argues that the Platonist Trinity can be reconciled with Christian doctrine by viewing the Holy Spirit as a unifying "Nexus" of love and by applying the Church Fathers' distinction between universal "essence" and individual "personhood."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of the Trinity, specifically how the early Church Fathers distinguished between the "essence" or "nature" of God (shared by all three) and the "hypostasis" or "person" (unique to each). It addresses the debate over whether the Trinity consists of one individual substance or three individuals sharing a common species.</meta>

# The Essence of the Godhead, BOOK I.

<margin>Gregory of Nyssa, *Against Eunomius*, Book 12.</margin>
<margin>Epistle 369.</margin>
<margin>On the Trinity, Book 4, Chapter 7.</margin>
...does *Essence* or *Substance* differ from *Hypostases*? That is to say, the Church Fathers concluded that the *Essence* or *Substance* of the Godhead—which is common to all the *Three Hypostases*, or the means by which each of them is *God*—was not *one singular* or *individual* essence, but *one general* or *universal essence* and *substance*. Theodoret, however, acknowledges there that no such distinction was observed by other Greek writers between those two words *Usia* <note>original: ὐσία</note> and *Hypostasis* <note>original: ὑπόστασις</note> (meaning *Essence* or *Substance* and *Hypostasis*). Usually, the first word was not restricted only to *universals*—such as *generic* or *specific essences*—but this specific usage was unique to the *Christian* Fathers in their doctrine concerning the *Trinity*. 

In the meantime, they did not deny that each *Hypostasis*, *Prosopon* <note>original: Prosopon; a person or face</note>, or *Person* in the *Trinity* might be said in another sense (and in opposition to **Sabellius** <note>A 3rd-century heretic who argued that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were merely different "modes" or names for a single person</note>) to have its own *singular, individual*, or *existent essence* as well. They held that there are thus "three existent essences" <note>original: τρεῖς ὐσίαι</note> in the Deity as well as "three hypostases" <note>original: τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις</note>; for them, an *Hypostasis* was nothing other than an *existent essence*. However, for the sake of clarity, they thought it best to limit and assign the meanings of these two words this way: a *singular* and *existent essence* should not be called "Essence" but "Hypostasis"; and by *Usia* (*Essence* or *Substance*), they meant only that *general* or *universal nature* of the Godhead which is *common* to all those *three singular hypostases* or *persons*, or in which they all agree. 

We could pile up many more testimonies to confirm this further, such as that of **St. Basil**: "Whatever relation the common has to the proper, the same does essence (or substance) have to the hypostasis" <note>original: ὃν ἔχει λόγον τὸ κοινὸν πρὸς τὸ ἴδιον, τοῦτον ἔχει ἡ ὐσία πρὸς τὴν ὑπόστασιν</note>. But we shall satisfy ourselves with this full acknowledgment by **D. Petavius**: "In this one thing, the judgments of almost all the Greeks especially agree: that *Usia*—that is, Essence, Substance, or Nature (which they call *Physis* <note>original: φύσιν</note>)—is something general, common, and undetermined; but *Hypostasis* is that which is proper, singular, and circumscribed; and which is, as it were, compounded and made up of that common essence or substance and certain peculiar notes and properties, or individuating circumstances" <note>original: In hoc Uno Græcorum præsertim omnium judicia concordant, ὐσίαν, id est, Essentiam sive Substantiam, aut Naturam (quam φύσιν vocant) Generale esse aliquid & Commune, ac minimè definitum, ὑπόστασιν verò Proprium, Singulare, & Circumscriptum, quod ex illo Communi, & Peculiaribus quibusdam Notis ac Proprietatibus veluti componitur.</note>.

But besides this, it is further certain that quite a few of those Ancient Fathers—who were reputed **Orthodox** because they zealously opposed **Arianism** <note>The belief that Jesus was a created being, not co-eternal with the Father</note>—also held this opinion: that the *Three Hypostases* or *Persons of the Trinity* did not only share one general and universal essence of the Godhead, but were also *three individuals* under one and the same ultimate species, or specific essence and substance of the Godhead. This is just as three individual men (Thomas, Peter, and John) exist under that ultimate species of "Man," or that specific essence of humanity, having only a numerical difference from one another.

It notes that some orthodox Fathers viewed the Trinity as three individuals sharing a single divine species, similar to how three men share the essence of humanity.</summary>

It focuses on the idea of "specific unity"—where the three persons are seen as individuals sharing a common nature, much like three individual humans share the same humanity.</meta>

# CHAPTER IV. To the Universal Fathers.

Therefore, an *Hypostasis* or *Person* (in the Trinity) was defined by some of these Fathers (namely, *Anastasius* and *Cyril*) as: *an Essence or Substance, with its certain Properties* (or *individuating circumstances*) *differing only numerically from those of the same species as itself* <note>original: "Essentia cum suis quibusdam Proprietatibus, ab iis quæ sunt ejusdem Speciei, Numero differens"</note>. This doctrine was clearly asserted and diligently developed (among several others by both the Greeks and Latins), especially by *Gregory of Nyssa*, *Cyril of Alexandria*, *Maximus the Martyr*, and *John of Damascus* <note>original: Damascen</note>. Since *Dionysius Petavius* <note>A 17th-century Jesuit theologian famous for his work on the history of doctrine</note> has quoted their words at length, we will not include them here. 

These were the thinkers who primarily insisted upon the *absolute co-equality* and *independent coordination* of the three *hypostases* or *persons* in the Trinity when compared with one another. They argued that just as *three men*—even if one were a father, another a son, and the third a nephew—have no *essential dependence* on one another but are *naturally co-equal* and *unsubordinate*, there being only a *numerical difference* between them; so too did they conclude that the *three hypostases* or *persons* of the Deity (the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost) were likewise three individuals under the same *ultimate species* or *specific essence* of the Godhead. Differing only numerically from one another, they were *absolutely co-equal*, *unsubordinate*, and *independent*. This was what they commonly called their *homoousiotes*, their *co-essentiality* or *consubstantiality* <term>the concept that the persons of the Trinity share the same fundamental substance or essence</term>. 

Therefore, it is noteworthy that Saint Cyril, one of these theologians, finds no fault at all with the Platonic Trinity except for this: that such a *homoousiotes* (a co-essentiality or consubstantiality as described here) was not acknowledged within it. 

<margin>*Against Julian, Book 8, page 270.*</margin> 

> There would have been nothing at all lacking to the Platonic Trinity to make it agree perfectly with the Christian view, had they only applied the correct notion of co-essentiality to their three hypostases; so that there might have been only one specific nature or essence of the Godhead, not further distinguishable by any natural diversity but only numerically, and so that no one hypostasis would be seen as in any way inferior or subordinate to another. <note>original: ἐλελοίπη δ' ἂν πρὸς τοῦτο αὐτοῖς οὐδὲν, εἰ τὸ τῆς ὁμοουσιότητος λόγον ἐφαρμόζειν ἤθελον ὑποστάσεσι ταῖς τρισὶν, ἵνα καὶ μία νοοῖτο τῆς θεότητος φύσις, τὸ τριχίδες οὐκ ἔχουσα πρὸς ἑτερότητα φυσικὴν, καὶ τό γε δὴ δεῖν ἀλλήλων ἐν μείοσιν ὁρᾶσθαι ὑποστάσεις.</note> 

That is, if these Platonists had agreed with the theory of Saint Cyril and others—that the three persons of the Trinity were merely three independent and coordinated individuals under the same ultimate species or specific essence of the Godhead (just as *Peter*, *Paul*, and *John* are under the species or common nature of *Humanity*) and had adopted this version of *co-essentiality* or *consubstantiality*—then they would have been completely orthodox. However, we have already shown that this Platonic Trinity was *homoousian* <note>sharing the same substance</note> in another sense, and perhaps it will appear later that it was also so in the very sense used by the Nicene Fathers and by *Athanasius*. 

Furthermore, these theologians supposed the three persons of their Trinity to have nothing more than a *specific unity* or *identity* <term>unity belonging to a 'species' or category, rather than a single individual being</term>. Because it seems to follow clearly from this that they must be as much *three gods* as three men are three men, these learned Fathers attempted to use their logic...

It highlights St. Cyril's critique that the Platonic Trinity failed to recognize this absolute co-equality and lack of subordination between the divine persons.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the critique of the "specific unity" model of the Trinity, where the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost are viewed as three individuals of the same divine "species," much like three individual men share one common humanity.</meta>

# A Tritheistic Trinity. BOOK I.

Using logic to prove that *three men* are only called "three" in a misleading and improper <note>original: "abusively and improperly"</note> way—claiming they are really and truly only one, because there is only *one and the same specific essence* <note>original: "Specifick Essence" — an essence belonging to a common species or kind, rather than a single individual thing.</note> or *substance of human nature* in them all—and seriously persuading men to set aside that kind of language. By this same logic of theirs, they might as well prove that all the men in the world are only *one man*, and that all the gods of Epicurus were likewise only one god. 

Setting aside the fact that, according to this hypothesis, no reason can possibly be given why there should be exactly *three* such individuals within the "species" of God (who would differ only numerically from one another, being the same thing repeated thrice), and yet no more than three—not three hundred, or three thousand, or as many as there are individuals in the species of man—setting that aside, it seems plain that this *Trinity* is nothing other than a kind of *Tritheism* <term>Tritheism</term> <note>The belief that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three distinct, independent gods rather than one God.</note>, and one of independent and equal gods at that. 

Therefore, some would think that the ancient and genuine *Platonic Trinity* <note>The hierarchy of "The Good," "Intellect," and "Soul" described by Plato and his followers.</note>, even with all its faults, is preferable to this *Trinity* of St. *Cyril* and St. *Gregory of Nyssa* and several other reputed Orthodox Fathers; and that it is more agreeable to the principles of both *Christianity* and *reason*. However, it is evident from this that these *reputed Orthodox Fathers*—who were not few in number—were far from thinking that the *three hypostases* <term>hypostases</term> <note>The individual persons or "subsistences" of the Trinity.</note> of the Trinity had the same *singular existent essence*. They supposed them to have one and the same *essence* of the Godhead in no other way than three individual men have one common "specific essence" of manhood in them, and are all "one man." But as this *Trinity* eventually came to be denounced as *tritheistic*, another doctrine started up in its place: that of *persons* who are numerically the same, or who all have one and the same singular existent essence. This is a doctrine which does not seem to have been owned by any public authority in the Christian Church, except for that of the Lateran Council <note>Specifically the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215, which defined the "numerical" unity of the divine essence.</note> alone.

That no such thing was ever entertained by the Nicene Fathers and those first opponents of Arianism <term>Arianism</term> <note>The belief that Jesus Christ was a created being, subordinate to God the Father.</note> might be made probable, in the first place, from the free confession and acknowledgment of *D. Petavius* <note>Dionysius Petavius (1583–1652), a Jesuit theologian and historian of dogma.</note> (a person well acquainted with ecclesiastical antiquity), especially since many people are heavily influenced by such famous names and authorities:
