# CHAPTER 4: The Homoousians and Anti-Sabellians

## The Meaning of Unity

...concerning the **singularity** <note>original: "SINGULARITY" — here meaning the state of being one individual thing rather than a shared category.</note> of the divine essence. For those Nicene Bishops themselves, who understood the secrets of the Arian faction <note>The followers of Arius, who believed the Son was a created being and not equal to the Father.</note> better than anyone else and knew exactly how it should be opposed <note>original: "oppugned"</note>, intended nothing else in their Confession of Faith but to establish that **equality of essence**, dignity, and eternity between them. The word *Homoousios* <term>Homoousios</term> <note>A Greek term meaning "of the same substance" or "consubstantial."</note> itself declares this, as it signifies **equality** rather than a **singularity** of essence, as we have shown before. The same is true of other passages in that same decree, such as: *That there was no time when the Son was not*, and *That he was not made from nothing*, nor *From a different hypostasis or essence*. Thus, Petavius <note>Dionysius Petavius (1583–1652), a prominent Jesuit theologian and historian of dogma.</note> clearly admits that this same singularity of numerical essence <note>Numerical essence refers to one single, individual thing, as opposed to a shared type or species.</note> was not asserted by the Nicene Council or the most ancient Fathers. Instead, they asserted only an **equality** or sameness of "generic" essence; or that the Father and Son agreed only in one common essence or substance of the Godhead—that is, the eternal and uncreated nature.

But the truth of this will appear more fully from the following details. First, these orthodox, anti-Arian Fathers all zealously condemned **Sabellianism** <term>Sabellianism</term> <note>A heresy named after Sabellius (3rd century AD) which taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not distinct persons, but just three different roles or "modes" of a single person.</note>. Its doctrine is simply this: that there was only one *hypostasis* <term>hypostasis</term> <note>A Greek term often translated as "person" or "individual substance."</note> or single individual essence shared by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and consequently, that they were actually just three different names, notions, or modes of the very same thing. From this, absurdities like these would follow: that the Father's begetting of the Son was nothing but one name or mode of the deity begetting another; or else the same deity, under one name, begetting itself under another name. Furthermore, when the Son (or the Word) is said to have become incarnate and suffered death for us on the cross—and not the Father—it would mean that nothing but a mere logical concept or "mode" of the deity was incarnate and suffered; or else the entire deity suffered under only one particular name or mode. However, if someone claimed that this Trinity was not a Trinity of mere names and concepts (like that of the Sabellians) but of distinct *hypostases* or persons, then it must follow—since every individual essence is a *hypostasis*, according to the sense <note>original: "fence"</note> of the ancient Fathers—that there was not just a Trinity, but a "Quaternity" (a group of four) of *hypostases* in the Godhead. This is something none of those Fathers ever dreamed of.

<margin>In his Epistles.</margin>
Furthermore, as was previously suggested by Petavius, the word *Homoousios* was never used by Greek writers in any other way than to signify that things which are numerically different from one another agree in some common nature or universal essence; or that they have a "generic" unity or identity, for which many examples could be given. Indeed, it is unlikely that the Greek language would even have a name for something that does not exist in nature and cannot be conceived by the human mind: namely, several distinct things having one and the same individual essence. Accordingly, St. Basil <note>Basil of Caesarea (330–379 AD), one of the influential "Cappadocian Fathers" of the early church.</note> interprets the force of this word thus: "It plainly removes the identity of hypostasis; for a thing is not *homoousios* [of the same substance] with itself, but one thing is *homoousios* with another." <note>original: "ἀναιρεῖ τὴν ταυτότητα τῆς ὑποστάσεως· οὐ γὰρ αὐτός τί ἐστιν ἑ-αυτῷ ὁμοούσιον, ἀλλ᾽ ἕτερον ἑτέρῳ"</note> In other words, it plainly takes away the sameness of the *hypostasis*—that is, of the single numerical essence (this being that...

Furthermore, the true meaning of the Nicene Fathers may be more fully and thoroughly understood by considering the doctrine of *Arius* which they opposed and condemned. Now *Arius* maintained that the *Son* or *Word* was a *ktisma* <note>original: κτίσμα — a created thing</note> or creature, *made in time*, and *mutable* (subject to change) or *defectible* (capable of failing). <header>CHAPTER IV. The Word *Homoousios*.</header>

<margin>

The Son is not *allotriousios* <note>original: ἀλλοτριούσιος — of a different essence or substance</note>, but *homoousios* with the Father, which means *co-essential* or *consubstantial* with the Father. That is to say, he is not a *creature*, but *God*; he agrees with the Father in that *common nature* or *essence* of the *Godhead*. This is that *ousia* (essence or substance) of the ancient Fathers, which is said to be the same in all the *three hypostases* <term>hypostases</term> <note>Distinct individual persons or realities within the Trinity.</note> of the Trinity as they are called God. It is not a *single existing essence*, but the *common, general*, or *universal essence* of the *Godhead*, or of the *uncreated nature*. This was described by St. Hilary as *one nature, not by unity of person, but of kind* <note>original: *Natura Una, non Unitate Personae, sed Generis*</note>. This *unity* of the *common* or *general essence* of the Godhead is the same thing as the *equality* which some of the ancient Fathers insisted upon so much against *Arius* <note>Arius (c. 256–336 AD) taught that the Son was a created being, subordinate to the Father.</note>—namely, an *equality of nature*. In this view, the Son and Father are both equally God because that *essence of the Godhead* (which is *common* to all three persons) is, like all other *essences*, supposed to be *indivisible*. From this *equality* itself, it appears that they acknowledged no *identity of a single essence*, because it would be absurd to say that one and the self-same thing is *equal to itself*. Furthermore, some of these orthodox Fathers implied that a certain *inequality* of the *hypostases* (persons) in their mutual relation to one another could be consistent with this *equality of essence*.

<margin>

*An offspring from the Father* <note>original: ἐκ τοῦ πατρὸς γέννημα</note>; *meaning that Christ was the Son of God, not created from nothing, but from God. Anyone who affirms those things contradicts the Council, but whoever dissents from Arius must necessarily agree to these forms set by the Council.

In this same letter, to cite just one more passage from it: <margin>Page 272.</margin> *Brass, iron, gold, and so on... are of different natures and different substances from one another. If, therefore, the Son is also like this, let him be a creature just as we are, and not coessential; but if he is the Son, the Word, Wisdom, the Image of the Father, and his radiance, then he should rightly be considered coessential.* <note>original: χαλκὸς, σίδηρος καὶ χρυσὸς, &c. ἀλλ᾽ ἑτεροφυῆ καὶ ἑτερόυσια ἀλλήλων· εἰ μὲν οὖν καὶ υἱὸς οὕτως ἐστὶν, ἔστω κτίσμα ὥσπερ καὶ ἡμεῖς, καὶ μὴ ὁμοούσιος, εἰ δὲ υἱός ἐστι λόγος, σοφία, εἰκὼν τοῦ πατρὸς, ἀπαύγασμα, εἰκότως ὁμοούσιος ἂν εἴη</note> Thus, in his letter concerning Dionysius <note>Dionysius of Alexandria, a 3rd-century bishop whose views were debated during the Arian controversy.</note>, we have <margin>Page 561.</margin> "the Son being one of the created things" <note>original: ἕνα τῶν γενητῶν εἶναι τὸν υἱὸν</note> and "not being coessential with the Father" <note>original: μὴ ὁμοούσιον τῷ πατρὶ</note> used as synonymous expressions, meaning exactly the same thing.

Therefore, it seems to be unquestionably clear that when the ancient orthodox Fathers of the Christian Church maintained against Arius that the Son was *Homoousios*—"Coessential" or "Consubstantial"—with the Father, they universally understood it to mean a shared nature. Although that word is interpreted as "of the same essence or substance," they did not mean they were one single numerical individual, but rather that they shared a common or universal essence. That is, they shared the general or specific essence of the Godhead; that the Son was no creature, but truly and properly God. If it were necessary, even more testimonies could be cited from

# CHAPTER IV. The Meaning of Homoousios.

<margin>Page 929.</margin>
Athanasius writes to this purpose in his *Letter on the Synods of Ariminum and Seleucia* <note>original: "Epistle De Synodis Arimini &c. Seleuciæ"</note>. There, he writes the following concerning the difference between these two words: *homoiousion* <term>of like substance</term> and *homoousion* <term>of the same substance</term>.

> For even you yourselves know that similarity <note>original: "Similitude"</note> is not asserted <note>original: "Predicated"</note> of essences or substances, but only of shapes and qualities. Regarding essences or substances, identity or sameness is affirmed, not similarity. For example, a man is not said to be "like" another man in respect to the substance of humanity, but only in respect to his appearance or form; for in their substance, they are of the same kind <term>congenerous</term>—sharing the same nature with one another. Nor is a man properly said to be "unlike" a dog, but rather of a different nature or kind. Therefore, that which is of the same nature, kind, or species is also *homoousion*—that is, coessential or consubstantial (of the same essence or substance)—and that which is of a different nature, kind, or species is *heterousion* (of a different essence or substance). <note>original: οἴδατε γὰρ καὶ ὑμεῖς ὅτι τὸ ὅμοιον οὐκ ἐπὶ τῶν οὐσιῶν, ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ σχημάτων καὶ ποιοτήτων λέγεται ὅμοιον· ἐπὶ γὰρ τῶν οὐσιῶν οὐχ ὁμοιότης, ἀλλὰ ταυτότης ἂν λεχθείη· ἄνθρωπος γοῦν ἀνθρώπῳ ὅμοιος λέγεται οὐ κατὰ τὴν οὐσίαν --- τῇ γὰρ οὐσίᾳ ὁμοφυεῖς εἰσι· καὶ πάλιν ἄνθρωπος κυνὶ οὐκ ἀνόμοιος λέγεται ἀλλ’ ἑτεροφυής· οὐκοῦν τὸ ὁμοφυὲς καὶ ὁμοούσιον, τὸ δ’ ἑτεροφυὲς καὶ ἑτερούσιον·</note>

Again, Athanasius writes concerning <term>consubstantiality</term> in a fragment of his work *Against the Hypocrisy of Meletius*:

> He who denies that the Son is *homoousion* (consubstantial) with the Father, asserting that he is only "like" him, denies that he is God. Likewise, someone who uses the word *homoousion* but interprets it only as a similarity in substance is claiming the Son is of another, different substance from the Father. Such a person claims the Son is not God, but only like God. Furthermore, such a person does not rightly understand the phrase "From the substance of the Father," because he does not believe the Son to be consubstantial—meaning of the essence and substance of the Father—in the same way that a human son is of the same substance as the father who begot him. For if someone claims the Son is not "from God" in the same way a man is "from a man" (according to essence or substance), but is only "like" him—as a statue is like a man, or as a man might be like God—it is clear that such a person, even if they use the word *homoousios*, does not truly mean it. They refuse to understand the word according to its customary meaning, which signifies one and the same essence or substance. This word is used by the Greeks <note>The author refers here to Greek philosophers and secular writers</note> in no other sense than to signify that which has the same nature—as we ought to believe regarding the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Here we see plainly that although the word *homoousios* is interpreted as "That which has one and the same essence..." <note>original: ὁ τοίνυν ἀναιρῶν τὸ εἶναι τὸν υἱὸν ὁμοούσιον τῷ πατρὶ, λέγων δὲ ὅμοιον, ἀναιρεῖ τὸ εἶναι θεόν· ὡσαύτως δὲ καὶ ὁ ἐξηγούμενος τὸ ὁμοούσιον, ὡς ὅμοιον τῇ οὐσίᾳ ἑτέραν τὴν οὐσίαν λέγει, θεῷ δὲ ὁμοιωμένην· οὐ τοίνυν οὐδὲ τὸ ἐκ τῆς οὐσίας εἶναι πρεπόντως λέγει μὴ φρονῶν ὁμοούσιον, ὡς ἄνθρωπος ἐκ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τῆς οὐσίας· εἰ δὲ μὴ ὡς ἄνθρωπος ἐξ ἀνθρώπου κατ’ οὐσίαν, ἐκ θεοῦ ὁ υἱὸς, ἀλλ’ ὡς ἐν ὁμοιώματι καθάπερ ἀνδριὰς ἀνθρώπῳ ἢ ὡς ἄνθρωπος θεῷ, δῆλός ἐστιν ὁ τοιοῦτος ὁμοούσιον μὲν λέγων, ὁμοούσιον δὲ οὐ φρονῶν· οὐ γὰρ κατὰ τὴν συνήθειαν βούλεται τὸ ὁμοούσιον ἀκούεσθαι, ὅπερ ἐστὶν, περὶ μιᾶς καὶ τῆς αὐτῆς οὐσίας· ἀλλὰ παρὰ τὴν συνήθειαν, καὶ ἵνα διαβάλλῃ ταύτην, Ἑλληνικὴν ῥῆσιν εἰρηκέναι τὸ ὁμοούσιον ῥῆμα τοῦ ἐν Ἕλλησιν ἔθους ἐπ’ οὐδενὶ ἑτέρῳ κείμενον ἢ ἐπὶ τὴν αὐτὴν φύσιν παραστῆσαι, &c.</note>

<summary>Athanasius explains that "likeness" refers to external qualities, while "identity" refers to substance, arguing that the Son must be "homoousios" (of the same substance) with the Father to truly be God. He warns that treating the Son as merely "similar" to God reduces Him to the status of a statue or a creation rather than a true divine offspring.</summary>

### The Homoousian Trinity. Book I.

...essence or substance; yet this is understood to mean the same common nature, just as one man is of the same essence or substance as another. We could also add the supporting testimony of other orthodox Church Fathers here, but to avoid being tedious, we will omit them and only include some passages from St. Augustine <note>original: "St. Austin"</note> for the same purpose. In the fifteenth chapter of his first book *Against Maximianus* <note>original: "Contra Maxim."</note>, he writes: 

"Two real men, even if neither is the son of the other, are still of one and the same substance. However, a man who is the true son of another man cannot possibly be of a different substance from his father, even if he is not like his father in every respect. Therefore, the true Son of God is of one substance with the Father because he is a true Son; and he is like the Father in every respect because he is the Son of God." <note>original: "Duo veri Homines, etsi nullus eorum Filius sit Alterius, Unius tamen & Ejusdem sunt Substantiæ. Homo autem alterius Hominis Verus filius nullo modo potest nisi Ejusdem cum Patre esse Substantiæ, etiam si non sit per omnia Similis Patri. Quocirca Verus Dei Filius, & Unius cum Patre Substantiæ est, quia Verus Filius est; & per omnia est Patri similis, quia est Dei Filius."</note>

In this passage, Christ (the Son of God) is said to be of "one substance" with God the Father in the same way that a human son is of the same substance as his father, or any one man is of the same substance as another.

<margin>He makes the same point in his second book, chapter 6: "God the Father and the human mother are indeed different substances; however, God the Father and God the Son are not different substances, just as a human mother and a human son are not different substances." <note>original: "Diversa quidem Substantia est Deus Pater, & Homo Mater; non tamen diversa Substantia est Deus Pater & Deus Filius: sicut non est diversa Substantia, Homo Mater, & Homo Filius."</note></margin>

Again, the same St. Augustine, in his *Response to the Sermon of the Arians* <note>original: "Respons. ad Sermonem Arianorum"</note>, expresses himself this way: 

"The Arians call us 'Homoousians' because, in opposition to their error, we use the Greek term *homoousios* <term>sharing the same essence</term> to defend the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. That is, we say they are of one and the same substance—or to speak more clearly, essence (which is called *ousia* <note>original: "οὐσία"</note> in Greek). This is more plainly expressed as being of one and the same nature. Yet there is not one of those who call us 'Homoousians' who would not rather be disinherited by his own father than be thought of as having a different nature from him. How great is the impiety, then, that blinds these people! Though they acknowledge that there is only one Son of God, they refuse to confess that he is of the same nature as his Father. Instead, they claim he is of a different and unequal nature, and in many ways and things unlike him—as if he were not born of God, but created out of nothing by him as a creature; becoming a son by grace rather than by nature." <note>original: "Ariani nos vocitant Homoousianos, quia contra eorum errorem, Græco vocabulo ὁμοούσιον defendimus, Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum Sanctum; id est, Unius Ejusdemque Substantiæ, vel ut expressius dicamus Essentiæ (quæ οὐσία Græcè appellatur) quod planiùs dicitur Unius Ejusdemque Naturæ. Et tamen siquis istorum qui nos Homoousianos vocant, Filium suum non cujus ipse esset, sed Diversæ diceret esse Naturæ, Exhæredari ab ipso mallet Filius, quam hoc putari. Quanta igitur impietate isti cæcantur, qui cum confiteantur Unicum Dei Filium, nolunt Ejusdem Naturæ cujus Pater est confiteri; sed diversæ atque imparis, & multis modis rebusque dissimilis, tanquam non de Deo Natus, sed ab illo de Nihilo sit Creatus; Gratiâ Filius, non Naturâ."</note>

Finally (to mention no other passages), in the first book of *On the Trinity* <note>original: "De Trinitate"</note>, he has these words: 

"If the Son is not a creature, he is of the same substance as the Father. For every substance that is not God is a creature, and whatever is not a creature is God. And if the Son is not of the same substance as the Father, then he is a created substance." <note>original: "Si Filius Creatura non est, ejusdem cum Patre Substantiæ est. Omnis enim Substantia quæ Deus non est Creatura est: & quæ Creatura non est, Deus est. Et si non est Filius ejusdem Substantiæ cujus est Pater, ergo Facta Substantia est."</note> If the Son is not a creature, then he is of the same...

<summary>This page cites several works by St. Augustine to argue that the term "homoousios" (consubstantial) indicates that the Father and Son share the same divine nature, just as human parents and children share the same human nature. It contrasts this orthodox view with the Arian position, which suggests the Son is a created being of a different nature.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that the Son must be of the same substance as the Father to be truly God, rather than a created being. It specifically argues that "Homoousios" (of the same substance) was intended to mean a shared nature, not a single individual personhood.</meta>

# CHAPTER IV. Not Monoousian

...*same substance with the Father; for whatever substance is not God is a creature, and whatever is not a creature is God. And therefore, if the Son is not of the same substance with the Father, he must necessarily be a made and created substance, and not truly God.*

Finally, that the ancient Orthodox Fathers who used the word *Homoousios* <note>meaning "of the same substance" or "consubstantial"</note> against Arius <note>a priest whose teachings led to the Arian controversy, asserting that the Son was a created being</note> did not intend to assert that the Son has *one and the same singular or individual essence* with the Father, is plainly shown by their rejection and disowning of these two words: *tautoousion* <note>original: ταυτοόσιον; meaning "of the self-same or identical substance"</note> and *monoousion* <note>original: μονοόσιον; meaning "of a single substance"</note>. 

Regarding the first of these, <margin>Heresies 76, Number 7.</margin> Epiphanius <note>a 4th-century bishop and historian</note> writes: "And we do not say *tautoousion* [of the identical substance], lest this word be interpreted by some as agreeing with Sabellius; nevertheless, we do assert him to be the same in Godhead, in essence, and in power." <note>original: Καὶ οὐ λέγομεν ταυτοόσιον, ἵνα μὴ ἡ λέξις παρά τισι λεγομένη, Σαβελλίῳ ἀπεικασθῇ· ταυτὸν δὲ λέγομεν τῇ Θεότητι, καὶ τῇ Οὐσίᾳ, καὶ τῇ δυνάμει</note> Here it is plain that when Epiphanius affirmed the Son to be the same with the Father in Godhead and essence, he understood this only as a *generic* or *specific* sameness <note>meaning they share the same kind of nature, as two humans share "humanity"</note>, and not as a *singular* or *individual* sameness. Specifically, he meant that the Son is no creature, but is God just as the Father is God. He indicates this to be the true and genuine sense of the word *Homoousios*. He therefore rejected that other word, *Tautoousios*, because it was liable to misinterpretation and could be taken in the Sabellian <note>Sabellianism was the belief that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not three distinct persons, but merely three modes or names for one single person</note> sense—meaning something that has one and the same singular and individual essence—an error to which the word *Homoousios* was not subject.

As for that other word, *Monoousios*, Athanasius <note>the chief defender of Trinitarianism against Arianism</note> himself, in his <margin>Page 241.</margin> *Exposition of Faith*, expressly condemns it: "For we do not think the Son is a 'Son-Father' as the Sabellians do, calling him *monoousios* and not *homoousios*; for by doing so, they destroy the very being of the Son." <note>original: οὔτε γὰρ υἱοπάτορα φρονοῦμεν, ὡς οἱ Σαβέλλιοι μονοόσιον καὶ οὐχ ὁμοόσιον</note> In that manufactured word *Monoousios*, "Essence" or "Substance" (*Usia*) is taken to mean a singular or existing essence. Sabellius used this to say that the entire Deity has only one singular essence or *hypostasis* <note>a distinct individual person or reality</note> within it. 

In contrast, in the word *Homoousios*, a *common* or *universal* (either generic or specific) essence is understood. The Son is thus said to agree with the Father in the common essence of the Godhead, because he is not a creature. Therefore, Athanasius here disclaims a *Monoousian Trinity*, just as Epiphanius earlier disclaimed a *Tautoousian* one. Both rejected a Trinity that consists merely of names, notions, or inadequate concepts of one and the same singular essence or person. Instead, they distinguished these from the *Homoousian Trinity*, which is a Trinity of real persons who each have their own singular existence but agree in one common and universal essence of the Godhead, since none of them are creatures, but are all uncreated creators. 

From this, it is plain that the ancient Orthodox Fathers did not assert any such thing as one and the same singular or numerical essence for the several persons of the Trinity. According to them, such a thing would not be a real Trinity, but only a Trinity of mere names, notions, and imaginary concepts. This is disclaimed and declared against by Athanasius: "But there is a Trinity, not in name only, or as a phantom of speech, but a Trinity in truth and existence." <note>original: τριὰς δέ ἐστιν οὐχ ὡς ὀνόματος μόνον, καὶ φαντασία λέξεως, ἀλλὰ ἀληθείᾳ καὶ ὑπάρξει τριάς</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the Trinity, specifically arguing that the Orthodox "Homoousian" (same substance) view is a middle ground between Sabellianism (one person with three names) and Arianism (three different types of substances).</meta>

Trinity is not a *Trinity* of mere names and words only, but of *Hypostases* <term>Hypostases: individual, distinct existences or persons</term>, truly and really *existing*. But the *Homoousian <note>original: Homoouſian; meaning "of the same substance"</note> Trinity* of the *Orthodox* stood exactly in the *middle* between that *Monoousian <note>original: Monoouſian; meaning "of one single substance"</note> Trinity* of Sabellius <note>a 3rd-century priest who taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were just different "modes" or faces of one single person</note>, which was a *Trinity* of different *notions* or *conceptions* only of *one* and the *self-same thing*; and that other *Heteroousian <note>original: Heteroouſian; meaning "of different substances"</note> Trinity* of Arius <note>who taught that the Son was a created being, different in substance from the Father</note>, which was a *Trinity* of separate and heterogeneous *substances* (only one of which was *God*, while the others were *creatures*). This Orthodox view is a Trinity of *hypostases* or *persons*, numerically differing from one another, but all of them agreeing in one *common* or *general essence* of the *Godhead* or the *uncreated nature*, which is *eternal* and *infinite*. This was also particularly declared by Athanasius: <margin>To Serapion, Epistle, p. 202.</margin> "The Catholic Church neither believes less than this Homoousian Trinity, lest it should fall in with the Jews of Caiaphas's time or sink into Sabellianism; nor does it conceive more than this, lest on the other hand, it should tumble down into Arianism, which is the same as Greek [pagan] polytheism and idolatry; for it likewise introduces the worship of creatures alongside the Creator." <note>original: ὄυτε ἐλαττόν τι φρονεῖ ἡ καθολικὴ Ἐκκλησία, ἵνα μὴ εἰς τοὺς νῦν κατὰ Καϊάφαν Ἰουδαίους, καὶ εἰς Σαβέλλιον ἐμπέσῃ· ὄυτε πλεῖον ἐπινοεῖ, ἵνα μὴ εἰς τὴν Ἑλληνικὴν πολυθεότητα κατακυλισθῇ</note>

And now, based on all these considerations, our *Platonic Christian* would conclude that the *Orthodox Trinity* of the ancient *Christian Church* agreed with the *genuinely Platonic Trinity* in this: it was not *Monoousian*—*one sole, singular essence* under *three notions*, *conceptions*, or *modes* only—but *three hypostases* or *persons*. Likewise, the correct *Platonic Trinity* agrees with the *Trinity* of the ancient *Orthodox Christians* in this: it is not *Heteroousian* but *Homoousian*, *coessential* or *consubstantial*; none of their *three hypostases* are *creatures* or *particular beings* made in *time*; but all of them are *uncreated*, *eternal*, and *infinite*.

Notwithstanding all this, it must be granted that although this *Homoousiotes*, or *coessentiality* of the *three persons* in the Trinity, implies that they are all *God*, it does not necessarily follow from that alone that they are therefore *one God*. What then? Shall we conclude that Athanasius himself also entertained that previously mentioned and rejected opinion: that the *three persons* in the Trinity are only *three individuals* under the same *species* (like *Peter*, *Paul*, and *Timothy*), having no other *natural unity* or *identity* than a *specific* <note>meaning they share a "species" or category of being, but are separate individuals</note> one? Indeed, some have confidently attributed this to Athanasius because in those dialogues *On the Trinity* published among his works and credited to him, this idea is crudely embraced. In defense of it, this *absurd paradox* is maintained: that *Peter, Paul, and Timothy*, though they are *three hypostases*, are not to be accounted as *three men*, except *only* when they dissent from one another or disagree in will or opinion. But it is certain from several passages in those dialogues themselves that they could not have been written by Athanasius; another author has been found for them: *Maximus the Martyr*. Regardless, we must not deny that Athanasius, in his other reputedly *genuine writings*, does sometimes...

It also addresses the potential misconception that the Trinity consists of three separate individuals of the same "species," a view found in works wrongly attributed to Athanasius.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument for the "Homoousian" Trinity by citing Athanasius's reasoning on how three distinct persons can be one God based on a shared nature. It builds on the previous page's distinction between the Orthodox view and the views of Sabellius and Arius.</meta>

# CHAPTER IV. Making the Trinity One God.

Athanasius approaches so closely to this point that he places significant emphasis on this *Homoousiotes* <term>Homoousiotes: the theological concept that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of the same substance or essence</term>, this *Coessentiality* and *Common Nature* of the Godhead shared by all *Three Persons*, in order for them to be *One God*. For in that book entitled *Concerning the Common Essence of the Three Persons*, in the chapter titled "That there are not Three Gods" <note>original: ὅτι οὐκ εἰσὶ τρεῖς Θεοὶ</note>, Athanasius establishes his foundation here. When responding to the question, *How can it be said that the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, and yet there are not three Gods?*, the *first reply* he makes is this: 

"Where there is a shared nature, a single common name of dignity is also given. <note>original: ὅπου κοινὰ τὰ τῆς φύσεως, κοινὸν καὶ ὄνομα τῆς ἀξίας</note> And thus does God himself call things divided into multitudes from one common nature by one singular name. For when he is angry with men, he calls all those who are the objects of his anger by the name of 'One Man' <note>original: ἕνα ἄνθρωπον</note>; and when he is reconciled to the world, he is reconciled to it as to 'One Man.'" 

The first instances he gives of this are in Genesis 6:3 and 6:7: *My Spirit shall not always strive with man*, and *I will destroy man whom I have created*. Upon which Athanasius makes this reflection: 

"Though there was not then only one man, but infinite myriads of men, nevertheless, by the name of one nature, the Scripture calls all those men 'One Man' because of their shared essence or substance." <note>original: διὰ τὸ κοινὸν τῆς οὐσίας</note>

Again, he comments in a similar manner upon that other <margin>Page 213, 214.</margin> scripture passage, Exodus 15:1: *The horse and his rider has he thrown into the sea*. 

"When Pharaoh went out to the Red Sea and fell with infinite chariots into the same; and there were many men who were drowned together with him, and many horses; yet Moses, knowing that there was but one common nature among all those who were drowned, speaks thus of both the men and the horses: 'The Lord has thrown both the horse and the rider into the sea.' He calls such a multitude of men 'one singular man' and such a multitude of horses 'one horse' because of their shared nature." <note>original: διὰ τὴν κοινωνίαν τῆς φύσεως</note>

Whereupon Athanasius thus concludes: <margin>Page 214.</margin>

"If, therefore, among men—where the qualities of nature are scattered, and where there are differences of form, power, and will (since all men do not have the same disposition of mind, nor form, nor strength), as well as different languages (from which men are called by the poets *Meropes* <term>Meropes: a Greek poetic term for humans, literally meaning 'those who divide the voice' or articulate speakers</term>)—the whole world is nevertheless called 'one man' because of their common nature; then where there is undivided dignity, one kingdom, one power, one will, and one action, which distinguishes the Trinity from the created world, I call that One God."

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Athanasius's arguments regarding how the shared nature of the Trinity results in "One God." It specifically transitions from the analogy of humanity being called "One Man" to why the Trinity possesses a much stronger claim to unity.</meta>

### Co-Essentiality Necessary, Book I.

...One Man; might not that *Trinity of Persons*, where there is an *undivided dignity*, *one kingdom*, *one power*, *one will*, and *one energy*, be much more appropriately called *One God*? But although it is true that Athanasius in this place (if, at least, this were a genuine work <note>original: Fœtus; here meaning a literary offspring or treatise</note> of Athanasius) may justly be thought to attribute too much to this "common nature, essence, or substance" <note>original: κοινὸν τῆς φύσεως καὶ οὐσίας</note> of all the Three Persons as the basis for making them truly and properly *One God*, and though those Scripture passages are only weakly used for this purpose, yet it is plain that he did not rely on this alone. He adds other factors as well, such as their having not only *one will* but also *one energy* or *action*, which will be discussed more later.

<margin>Page 467.</margin>
Moreover, Athanasius elsewhere plainly implies that *this common essence or nature of the Godhead is not sufficient alone to make all the Three Hypostases One God*. <term>Hypostases: the distinct persons of the Trinity (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) as they exist in their own right, while sharing one essence.</term> As in his *Fourth Oration against the Arians* <note>The Arians were followers of Arius, who taught that the Son was a created being, distinct from and subordinate to the Father.</note>, where he tells us that his *Trinity of Divine Hypostases* cannot therefore be accounted *three gods* nor *three principles*, because he does not compare them to *three original suns*, but only to the *Sun*, and its *splendor*, and the *light* coming from both. Now *three suns*, according to the language of Athanasius, have a "common nature, essence, and substance" <note>original: κοινὸν τῆς φύσεως καὶ οὐσίας</note> and therefore are *coessential* or *consubstantial*; and since they cannot be accounted as one *Sun*, it is manifest that, according to Athanasius, this *specific identity* or *unity* is not sufficient to make the *three divine hypostases one God*.

Again, the same Athanasius, in his *Exposition of Faith*, writes thus: "Neither do we acknowledge three hypostases, divided or separate by themselves (as is to be seen physically in men), so that we may not comply with the pagan polytheism" <note>original: οὔτε τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις, μεμερισμένας καθ᾿ ἑαυτὰς, ὥσπερ σωματικῶς ἐπ᾿ ἀνθρώπων ἔστι λογίσασθαι, ἵνα μὴ πολυθεΐαν ὡς τὰ ἔθνη φρονήσωμεν</note>. From this it is evident that neither *three separate men*—though "coessential" <note>sharing the same human nature</note> to Athanasius—were accounted by him to be *one man*, nor can the *community of the specific nature and essence of the Godhead* alone by itself exclude *polytheism* from the Trinity.

Therefore, the true reason why Athanasius laid so great a stress upon this *Homoousiotes* <term>Homoousiotes: the theological concept that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are "of one substance."</term>, or *coessentiality* of the Trinity, in order to establish the *unity* of the *Godhead* in them, was not because this alone was sufficient to make them *one God*, but because they could not be so without it. This Athanasius often urges against the Arians, as in his *Fourth Oration*, where he tells them "that they must necessarily introduce a plurality of gods because of the difference in nature of their trinity" <note>original: πολλὰς ἂν εἰσάγοιεν [θεὸς] διὰ τὸ ἑτεροειδὲς αὐτῶν</note>. And again afterward, determining that there is "one species of the Godhead" <note>original: ἓν εἶδος τῆς Θεότητος</note> in Father, Son, and Spirit, he adds:

"And thus do we acknowledge only one God in the Trinity; and we maintain it much more piously than those heretics do, who introduce a multi-form deity consisting of different types; for we believe in the one Godhead in the Trinity <note>original: τὴν μίαν ἐν τριάδι Θεότητα φρονοῦμεν</note>. For if it is not so, and the Word is a work and a creature made out of nothing—however much he is called God by these Arians—they must necessarily say there are two gods: one a creator, and the other a creature" <note>original: οὕτω καὶ ἕνα διὰ τῆς τριάδος ὁμολογοῦμεν εἶναι τὸν Θεὸν· καὶ πολὺ μᾶλλον εὐσεβέστερον λέγομεν τῆς πολυειδοῦς τῶν αἱρετικῶν Θεότητος... ἀνάγκη λέγειν αὐτοὺς δύο θεοὺς, ἕνα μὲν κτίστην, τὸν δὲ ἕτερον κτιστόν</note>.

<summary>This page analyzes Athanasius's argument that while a shared "common nature" is necessary for the Trinity to be one God, it is not sufficient on its own without also having unity of will and action. Athanasius distinguishes the Christian Trinity from Arianism and pagan polytheism by emphasizing that the Persons are not separate like three individual men or three different suns.</summary>

# CHAPTER IV. On the Unity of the Godhead.

...then He and his Father must, of necessity, be *Two Gods*; one of them a Creator, the other a Creature. In like manner in his book, *On the <margin>Page 275.</margin> Nicene Council*, he affirms concerning the Arians: *That they preach, in a manner, Three Gods, by dividing the Holy Monad into three heterogeneous substances, completely separate from one another.* <note>original Greek: τρεῖς Θεὸς τρόπον τινα κηρύττουσιν εἰς τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις ξένας, ἀλλήλων παντάπασι κεχωρισμένας, διαιροῦντες τὴν ἁγίαν μονάδα</note> <term>Monad: A term used in philosophy and theology to refer to 'The One' or the absolute unity of the Godhead.</term> Whereas the right Orthodox Trinity, on the con-<margin>Letter to Serapion, page 202.</margin> trary, is elsewhere described by him thus: *The Holy and perfect Trinity as understood in theology—consisting of the Father, Son, and Spirit—has nothing alien, foreign, or extraneous intermingled with it; nor is it compounded of heterogeneous things, such as the Creator and Creature joined together, but it consists entirely of the power to create and make.* <note>original Greek: τριὰς τοίνυν ἁγία καὶ τελεία ἐστὶν, ἐν πατρὶ, καὶ υἱῷ, καὶ τῷ ἁγίῳ πνεύματι θεολογουμένη, οὐδὲν ἀλλότριον ἢ ἔξωθεν ἐπιμιγνύμενον ἔχουσα, οὐδὲ ἐκ δημιουργοῦ καὶ κτιστοῦ συνεσταμένη, ἀλλ᾿ ὅλη τοῦ κτίζειν καὶ δημιουργεῖν οὖσα</note> 

And whereas the Arians interpreted that statement of our Savior Christ, *I and my Father are One*, only in respect of consent or agreement of will, Athanasius, showing the insufficiency of this view, concludes thus: *Therefore, besides this consent of will, there must of necessity be another unity of essence or substance also acknowledged in the Father and the Son.* <note>original Greek: ἀνάγκη λοιπὸν κατὰ τὴν οὐσίαν νοεῖν τὴν υἱοῦ καὶ πατρὸς ἑνότητα</note> By *unity of essence or substance*, Athanasius did not mean a unity of a singular and individual essence, but of a general or universal essence only. This appears plainly from these following words: <margin>Letter on the Synods of Ariminum and Seleucia, page 923.</margin> *For those things which are made or created, though they may have an agreement of will with their Creator, yet they have this by participation only, and in a way of motion—like the one who, failing to maintain this agreement, was cast out of heaven. But the Son, being begotten from the essence or substance of the Father, is essentially or substantially one with him and the Father who begat him.* <note>original Greek: τὰ μὲν γὰρ γεννητὰ κἂν συμφωνίαν ἔχῃ πρὸς τὸν πεποιηκότα, ἀλλ᾿ ἐν κινήσει καὶ μετοχῇ ταύτην ἔχει, ὥσπερ ὁ μὴ φυλάξας ἐκβέβληται τῶν οὐρανῶν, ὁ δὲ υἱὸς ἐκ τῆς οὐσίας ὢν γέννημα, οὐσίᾳ καὶ ἓν ἐστιν αὐτὸς καὶ ὁ γεννήσας πατήρ</note> So the opposition here is between *unity of consent* with God in created beings (which are changeable) and *unity of essence* in that which is uncreated and immutably of the same will as the Father.

There are also many other places in Athanasius which, though some may understand them as referring to the *unity of a singular essence*, were not intended as such by him. Instead, they refer either to a generic or specific *essence* only, or else in another sense that shall be explained later. For example, in his *Fourth Oration*: <margin>Page 468.</margin> *We acknowledge only one Godhead in the Trinity*; <note>original Greek: τὴν μίαν ἐν τριάδι θεότητα φρονοῦμεν</note> where the following words plainly imply this to be understood, at least in part, as one common or general *essence* of the Godhead: *Because if it is not so, but the Word is a creature made out of nothing, he is either not truly God; or if he is called by that name, then there must be two gods: one a creator, the other a creature.* <note>original Greek: εἰ γὰρ μὴ οὕτως ἔχει, ἀλλ᾽ ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων ποίημα καὶ κτίσμα ἐστὶν ὁ λόγος, etc.</note> Again, when in the same book it is said: <margin>Page 456.</margin> *The Son and the Father are one thing in the propriety of nature, and in the sameness of one Godhead*; <note>original Greek: ἕν εἰσιν ὁ υἱὸς καὶ ὁ πατὴρ τῇ ἰδιότητι καὶ οἰκειότητι τῆς φύσεως, καὶ τῇ ταυτότητι τῆς μιᾶς θεότητος</note> it is evident from the context that this is not to be understood as a sameness of singular essence, but partly as a common and generic one, and partly as such another...

<summary>This page analyzes Athanasius’s arguments against the Arian belief that the Father and Son are united only by agreement of will. Athanasius contends that the Trinity must share a common, uncreated essence, as a unity of "consent" alone would imply the Son is merely a created being and thus lead to polytheism.</summary>

# How the Homoousian Trinity, BOOK I.

...their sameness or unity, as will be expressed hereafter. Lastly, when the three *hypostases* <term>Hypostases: The distinct persons or individual realities of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</term> are somewhere said by him to be *one essence or substance* <note>original Greek: μία οὐσία</note>, this is not to be understood in that place as if they all three had the same singular essence, but in some of those other senses mentioned before.

But though Athanasius nowhere declares the three *hypostases* of the Trinity to have only one and the same singular essence, but on the contrary denies them to be *monoousian* <term>Monoousian: The belief that the Trinity consists of one single, individual substance, as opposed to "homoousian," which means sharing the same kind of substance.</term>; and though he lays a great stress upon their *specific or generic unity* <note>original Greek: εἰδικὴ ἑνότης</note> and co-essentiality in order for them to be one God—for as much as without this, they could not be God at all—yet he does not rely wholly upon this as being sufficient alone for that purpose. Instead, he adds certain other considerations to support it, as follows. First, that this Trinity is not a Trinity of independent principles, but that there is only one principle or fountain of the Godhead in it, from which the others are derived. Thus he writes in his *Fifth Oration*:
<margin>Page 656.</margin>
> *There is but one principle, and accordingly but one God.* <note>original Greek: μία ἀρχὴ, καὶ κατὰ τοῦτο εἷς Θεὸς</note>

Again, in his book *Against the Sabellians*:
> *There are not two Gods, both because there are not two Fathers, and because that which is begotten is not of a different essence from that which begot. For he who introduces two principles preaches two Gods; which was the impiety of Marcion.* <note>original Greek: οὐκ εἰσὶ δύο Θεοὶ, ὅτι μηδὲ δύο πατέρες, μηδὲ ἑτερότης τοῦ γεννήσαντος ὁ γεγεννημένος · ὁ μὲν γὰρ ἀρχὰς εἰσάγων δύο, δύο κηρύττει θεοὺς, αὕτη Μαρκίωνος ἡ δυσέβεια</note> <note>Marcion of Sinope (c. 85 – c. 160) was an early Christian teacher who was declared a heretic for claiming there were two gods: a lesser, vengeful god of the Old Testament and a supreme, loving God of the New Testament.</note>

Accordingly, the same Athanasius declares:
<margin>On the Synods of Ariminum and Seleucia, page 920.</margin>
> *That the essence or substance of the Father is the principle, root, and fountain of the Son.* <note>original Greek: τὴν οὐσίαν τοῦ πατρὸς ἀρχὴν καὶ ῥίζαν καὶ πηγὴν εἶναι τοῦ υἱοῦ</note>

And in like manner he approves of this doctrine of Dionysius <note>Likely Dionysius of Alexandria, a 3rd-century bishop and theologian.</note>:
> *That God (the Father) is the first fountain of all good things, but the Son is a river poured out from him.* <note>original Greek: ὅτι πηγὴ τῶν ἀγαθῶν ἁπάντων ἐστὶν ὁ Θεὸς, ποταμὸς δὲ ὑπ' αὐτοῦ προχεόμενος ὁ υἱός</note>

To the same purpose is it also when he compares the Father and the Son to water and the vapor arising from it; to light and its splendor; to the prototype and the image. And he concludes the unity of the Godhead from this point in this manner:
<margin>On the Decrees of the Council of Nicaea, page 275.</margin>
> *The Divine Trinity must necessarily be collected and gathered up together under that omnipotent God of the whole world, as under one head.* <note>original Greek: τὴν θείαν τριάδα εἰς ἕνα ὥσπερ εἰς κορυφήν τινα, τὸν Θεὸν τῶν ὅλων τὸν παντοκράτορα λέγω, συγκεφαλαιουσθαι καὶ συνάγεσθαι πᾶσα ἀνάγκη</note>

But the chief force of this consideration is only to exclude the doctrine of the Marcionites, who claimed there were multiple independent and self-existent principles and gods. Despite this, it might still be objected that the Christian Trinity is a Trinity of distinct, subordinate gods. In opposition to this, the current argument seems only to prepare the way for what follows: namely, the close conjunction of these three *hypostases* into one God. For if they were three independent principles, there could not be any coalescence of them into one.

In the next place, therefore, Athanasius further adds that these three divine *hypostases* are not *divided and separate* <note>original Greek: μεμερισμέναι and κεχωρισμέναι</note> beings, but *indivisibly united* <note>original Greek: ἀδιαίρετοι</note> to...

<summary>Athanasius argues that the Trinity is unified because the Father is the single "fountain" or "root" from which the Son and Spirit derive, ensuring there is only one ultimate Principle rather than multiple independent gods.</summary>

It continues from the previous page's point that there are not two Gods because there are not two Fathers.</meta>

one another. Thus in his *Fifth Oration*:

> The Father and the Son are one in the Godhead; and because the Word is from Him, it is undivided, inseparable, and unparted from the Father. <note>original Greek: πατέρα καὶ υἱὸν ἓν ὄντας τῇ θεότητι, καὶ τῷ ἐξ αὐτοῦ, ἀμέριστον, καὶ ἀδιαίρετον, καὶ ἀχώριστον εἶναι τὸν λόγον ἀπὸ τοῦ πατρός</note>

*The Father and the Son are both one thing in the Godhead; and because the Word, being begotten from Him, is indivisibly and inseparably conjoined with Him.* When he affirms the Father and the Son to be *one in the Godhead*, it is plain that he does not mean they have *one and the same single essence* <note>numerical identity</note>, but only a *generic and universal* one; because in the following words, he supposes them to be *two, but indivisibly and inseparably united together.* Again, in his book *On the Opinion of Dionysius* <note>original Latin title: De Sent. Dionys.</note>:

> The Son is inseparable from the Father, just as the brightness is from the light. <note>original Greek: ἔστιν ἀδιαίρετος τοῦ πατρὸς ὁ υἱὸς, ὡς ἔστι τὸ ἀπαύγασμα πρὸς τὸ φῶς</note>

*The Son is indivisible from the Father, as the splendor is from the light.* And afterwards in the same book, he insists further upon this point, according to the sense of *Dionysius*, in this manner:

> Dionysius teaches that the Son is related to the Father and inseparable from Him, just as reason is to the mind and the river is to the fountain. Who is there, therefore, who could separate reason from the mind, or divide the river from the fountain by building a wall between them, or cut off the brightness from the light? <note>original Greek: ὅ τι ἴδιον καὶ ἀδιαίρετον τῆς τοῦ πατρὸς οὐσίας τὸν υἱὸν εἶναι διδάσκει, ὡς ἔστιν ὁ λόγος πρὸς τὸν νοῦν καὶ ὁ ποταμὸς πρὸς τὴν πηγήν· εἰ μὲν οὖν διαιρεῖν καὶ ἀποξενῶν τὸν λόγον καὶ τὸν νοῦν τις δύναται, ἢ τὸν ποταμὸν καὶ τὴν πηγήν μερίσαι καὶ τειχίσαι διελεῖν, ἢ τὸ ἀπαύγασμα ἅμα διελεῖν ἀπὸ τοῦ φωτός, &c.</note>

*Dionysius teaches that the Son is related to the Father and indivisible from Him, as reason is from the mind, and the river from the fountain. Who is there, therefore, that would go about to separate reason from the mind? Or to separate the river from the fountain, building a wall between them? Or to cut off the splendor from the light?* Thus also in his *Epistle to Serapion*, arguing that the Holy Spirit is not a *created being* <note>original: "Creature"</note>:

<margin>Page 194.</margin>

> Either let these men first divide the brightness from the light, or wisdom from him who is wise, or else let them not ask how these things can be. <note>original Greek: ἢ διελέτωσαν πρῶτον αὐτοὶ τοῦ ἀπαυγάσματος τὸ φῶς, ἢ τὴν σοφίαν τοῦ σοφοῦ, ἢ μὴ εἰπάτωσαν, πῶς ἔστι ταῦτα</note>

*Let these men first divide the splendor from the light, or wisdom from him that is wise, or else let them wonder no more how these things can be.* Elsewhere, *Athanasius* calls the whole Trinity *a Trinity undivided and united to itself* <note>original Greek: τριάδα ἀδιαίρετον καὶ ἡνωμένην πρὸς ἑαυτὴν</note>. This *Athanasian indivisibility of the Trinity* is not to be understood as if *there were not three in it*, but first of all that none of these could exist without the other—just as the *original light* or *sun* could not exist without the *brightness*, nor the *brightness* without the *original light*, and neither one nor the other of them without a *diffused, derivative light*. Therefore, God the Father being an *eternal sun*, must necessarily also have an *eternal brightness* and an *eternal light*. Secondly, it means that these are so nearly and intimately conjoined together that there is a kind of <term>συνέχεια</term> <note>original Greek: synecheia</note> *continuity* between them; which yet is not to be understood in the way of *physical things*, but in a way that is agreeable to the *nature of incorporeal things*.

Thirdly, *Athanasius* ascends even higher, affirming that the *hypostases of the Trinity* are not only *indivisibly conjoined* with one another, but also have a *mutual inexistence* in each other—which later *Greek Fathers* called <term>ἐμπεριχώρησιν</term> <note>original Greek: emperichoresin</note>, or their *circuminfession* <note>The theological concept that the three Persons of the Trinity dwell within one another while remaining distinct.</note>. To this purpose, he cites the words of *Dionysius*:

<margin>Page 665.</margin>

> For reason is the outflow of the mind, and from the heart it is channeled through the mouth, becoming another reason from the reason in the heart. Thus, each is in the other, being distinct from the other, and though they are two, they are one. So let the Father and the Word be one, and they are said to be in each other. <note>original Greek: ἀπόῤῥοια γὰρ νοῦ λόγος, καὶ ἀπὸ καρδίας διὰ στόματος ἐξοχετεύεται, ἕτερος χυόμενος τοῦ ἐν καρδίᾳ λόγου· καὶ οὕτως ἐστὶν ἑκάτερος ἐν ἑκατέρῳ, ἕτερος ὢν θατέρου, καὶ ἕν εἰσιν ὄντες δύο· ἔστω δὲ ὁ πατὴρ καὶ ὁ λόγος ἕν, καὶ ἐν ἀλλήλοις ἐλέχθησαν εἶναι</note>

*For reason is the efflux of the mind, which in men is derived from the heart into the tongue; where it becomes another reason*

It emphasizes that their unity is one of nature and inseparable connection rather than a single, identical personhood.</summary>

# The Perichoresis in the Trinity. BOOK I.

...Son or Word, differing from the thought in the heart; and yet both of these mutually exist in each other, as they belong to one another. Thus, though they are two, they are one thing. In this way, the Father and the Son are one thing, as they are said to exist in each other. Athanasius further illustrates this using certain metaphors <note>original: similitudes</note>, such as the comparison of the original light and its radiance. He affirms that the light is in the radiance, and the radiance in the sun <note>original: φῶς εἶναι ἐν τῷ ἀπαυγάσματι, καὶ ἀπαύγασμα ἐν τῷ ἡλίῳ</note>. He also uses the analogy of the prototype and the image, or the King and his portrait, which he explains in this way: <margin>Oration 4, page 457.</margin> In the portrait of the king, his form and figure are contained; and in the king himself, there is the same form and figure found in the portrait <note>original: ἐν τῇ εἰκόνι τοῦ βασιλέως τὸ εἶδος καὶ ἡ μορφή ἐστι, καὶ ἐν τῷ βασιλεῖ τὸ ἐν τῇ εἰκόνι εἶδος ἔστιν</note>. Therefore, if anyone who had seen the portrait should later desire to see the King himself, the portrait would (by way of personification <term>original: prosopopœia; a rhetorical device where an inanimate object or abstract concept is represented as speaking</term>) speak to him in this manner: <margin>Ibid.</margin> "I and the King are one, for I am in him and he is in me. What you notice in me, you may observe in him also; and what you see in him, you see likewise in me. Therefore, he who worships the image worships the King within it <note>original: ἐγὼ καὶ ὁ βασιλεὺς ἕν ἐσμεν, ἐγὼ γὰρ ἐν ἐκείνῳ εἰμὶ, κἀκεῖνος ἐν ἐμοί· καὶ ὃ ὁρᾷς ἐν ἐμοὶ, τοῦτο ἐν ἐκείνῳ βλέπεις, καὶ ὃ ἑώρακας ἐν ἐκείνῳ, τοῦτο βλέπεις ἐν ἐμοί· ὁ γὰρ προσκυνῶν τὴν εἰκόνα, ἐν αὐτῇ προσκυνεῖ τὸν βασιλέα</note>," because the image is nothing but the form of the King.

Elsewhere in his *Fourth Oration*, he elaborates on this point: <margin>Page 456.</margin> The Son is in the Father, which may be understood this way: because the whole being of the Son belongs specifically to the essence of the Father, being derived from it as radiance from light and a river from its source <note>original: fountain</note>. Thus, he who sees the Son sees that which is the Father's own. Conversely, the Father is in the Son because that which is the Father's own is exactly what the Son is—just as the sun is in its radiance, the mind is in the reason <note>original: Logos/Word</note> it produces, and the source is in the river <note>original: ἔστι γὰρ ὁ υἱὸς ἐν τῷ πατρὶ, ὥστε νοεῖν ἔξεστιν, ἐπειδὴ σύμπαν τὸ εἶναι τοῦ υἱοῦ, τοῦτο τῆς πατρὸς οὐσίας ἴδιόν ἐστιν, ὡς ἐκ φωτὸς ἀπαύγασμα, καὶ ἐκ πηγῆς ποταμός, ὥστε τὸν ὁρῶντα τὸν υἱὸν ὁρᾷν τὸ τοῦ πατρὸς ἴδιον. Ἔστι δὲ καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἐν τῷ υἱῷ, ἐπειδὴ τὸ ἐκ τοῦ πατρὸς ἴδιον, τοῦτο ὁ υἱὸς τυγχάνει ὤν, ὡς ἐν τῷ ἀπαυγάσματι ὁ ἥλιος, καὶ ἐν τῷ λόγῳ ὁ νοῦς, καὶ ἐν τῷ ποταμῷ ἡ πηγή</note>.

Athanasius also informs us of the objections <note>original: cavils</note> the Arians raised against this doctrine: <margin>Oration 4.</margin> The Arians began to mock the statement made by our Lord, *I am in the Father, and the Father in me.* They asked, "How is it possible that the former should be contained within the latter, and the latter within the former? Or how can the Father, being greater, be held within the Son, who is lesser?" They added, "What is so remarkable about the Son being in the Father, since it is written of us humans also, *For in him we live and move and have our being*?" <note>original: ἤρξαντο διασύρειν τὸ ὑπὸ τοῦ κυρίου λεγόμενον, Ἐγὼ ἐν τῷ πατρὶ καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἐν ἐμοί· λέγοντες, πῶς δύναται οὗτος ἐν ἐκείνῳ, κἀκεῖνος ἐν τούτῳ χωρεῖν; ἢ πῶς ὅλως δύναται ὁ πατὴρ μείζων ὢν, ἐν τῷ υἱῷ ἐλάττονι ὄντι χωρεῖν; καίτοι τί θαυμαστὸν εἰ ὁ υἱὸς ἐν τῷ πατρὶ, ὅπερ καὶ περὶ ἡμῶν γέγραπται, Ἐν αὐτῷ γὰρ ζῶμεν καὶ κινόμεθα καὶ ἐσμέν</note> 

In replying to this, Athanasius first observes that the basis for this Arian objection was the crudeness <note>original: grossness</note> of their understanding. He argued that they interpreted spiritual <note>original: incorporeal</note> things in a physical <note>original: corporeal</note> way <note>original: τὰ ἀσώματα σωματικῶς ἐκλαμβάνειν</note>. He then adds,

<summary>This page explains Athanasius's use of metaphors—such as light and radiance, or a king and his portrait—to illustrate the mutual indwelling (perichoresis) of the Father and the Son. It also addresses Arian objections that attempted to apply physical limitations to spiritual relationships.</summary>

# Cʜᴀᴘ. IV. Another Notion of *Homoousios*.

"For they are not, as those people think, transferred into one another <note>original: ἀντεμβιβαζόμενοι εἰς ἀλλήλους</note> as if they were being poured from one to another like empty vessels being filled, such that the Son fills the hollow of the Father and the Father fills the hollow of the Son, and neither of them were full and perfect in themselves." <note>original: οὐ γὰρ ὡς ἐκεῖνοι νομίζουσιν, ἀντεμβιβαζόμενοι εἰς ἀλλήλους εἰσὶν, ὥσπερ ἐν ἀγγείοις κενοῖς ἐξ ἀλλήλων πληρουμένοις, ὥστε τὸν μὲν υἱὸν πληροῦν τὸ κοῖλον τοῦ πατρός, τὸν δὲ πατέρα πληροῦν τὸ κοῖλον τοῦ υἱοῦ, καὶ ἑκάτερον αὐτῶν μὴ εἶναι πλήρη καὶ τέλειον</note> *For the Father and Son are not, as they suppose, poured from one to another <note>original: Transvasated</note> as if into an empty vessel: as if the Son filled up the hollow space <note>original: Concavity</note> of the Father, and again the Father that of the Son; and neither of them were full or perfect in themselves. For all this is proper to physical bodies; therefore, though the Father be in some sense greater than the Son, yet he may still be in him in an incorporeal <term>original: In-corporeal; without a physical body</term> manner. And he replies to their last petty objection <note>original: Cavil</note> this way: that the Son is not in the Father in the same way we ourselves are said to live and move and have our being in God.* "For he himself is life from the fountain of the Father, in whom all things are given life and held together <note>original: αὐτὸς γὰρ ὡς ἐκ πηγῆς τοῦ πατρός ἐστι ζωὴ, ἐν ᾧ τὰ πάντα ζωογονεῖται καὶ συνέστηκεν</note>; for he who is life does not live in another life <note>original: ὁ γὰρ ἡ ζωὴ ἐν ζωῇ ζῆ</note>," etc. *For he himself from the fountain of the Father is that life in whom all things are quickened and consist: neither does he who is the life live in another life, which would be to suppose him not to be the life itself. Nor (he says) must it be conceived that the Father is in the Son no other way than he is in holy men by strengthening them; for the Son himself is the power and wisdom of God, and all created beings are sanctified by participating in him in the Spirit. Therefore, this Perichoresis <term>original: Perichoresis; the mutual indwelling or interpenetration of the three persons of the Trinity</term> or mutual "in-being" of the Father and the Son is to be understood in a unique manner, so that they are really one by it; and what the Son and Holy Spirit do, the Father does in them, according to Athanasius:* "The Godhead of the Son is the Godhead of the Father, and so the Father exercises a providence over all things in the Son." <note>original: ἡ τοῦ υἱοῦ Θεότης τοῦ πατρὸς Θεότης ἐστί· καὶ οὕτως ἐν τῷ υἱῷ τὴν τῶν πάντων πρόνοιαν ποιεῖται</note>

Lastly, the same *Athanasius* in various places further suggests those three divine *hypostases* <term>original: Hypostases; the three distinct persons of the Trinity (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit)</term> make up one entire Divinity in the same manner as the *fountain* and the *stream* make up one entire *river*; or the *root*, the *trunk*, and the *branches* make up one entire *tree*. And in this sense also, the whole *Trinity* is said by him to be "one divinity, and one nature, and one essence, and one God." <note>original: μία Θεότης, μία φύσις, μία οὐσία, εἷς Θεὸς</note> And accordingly, the word *Homoousios* <term>original: Homoousios; the Greek theological term meaning "of the same substance" or "coessential"</term> seems here to be taken by *Athanasius* in a further sense besides the one mentioned before; not only for things that *agree* in one *common* and *general essence* (as three *individual* men are *coessential* with one another) but also for things that concurrently make up *one entire thing* and are therefore *jointly essential* to it. For when he affirms "that the tree is of the same nature as the root" and "the branches are coessential with the vine," <note>original: τὸ φυτὸν εἶναι ῥίζης ὁμοφυὲς, and τὰ κλήματα ὁμοούσια τῆς ἀμπέλου</note> his meaning is that the *root, trunk,* and *branches* are not only of *one kind*, but also all together make up the *entire essence of one plant or tree.* In like manner, those three *hypostases*—the *Father, Son,* and *Holy Spirit*—are not only *congenerous* <note>original: of the same genus or kind</note> and *coessential* because they have all the *essence* of the *Godhead* alike in them, but also as *concurrently making up one entire Divinity.* Following this, *Athanasius* further concludes that these three divine *hypostases* have not a *consent of will* only, but *essentially one* and the *self-same will*, and that they also jointly produce external effects <note>original: ad extra</note> by "one single action," <note>original: μίαν ἐνέργειαν</note> *one and the self-*

# The Reasons for this Platonic BOOK I.

<margin>Letter to Serapion, page 202.</margin>...self-same energy, operation, or *action*; nothing being peculiar to the Son as such, but only the economy of the Incarnation:

> <note>original: ὁμοία ἑαυτῇ καὶ ἀδιαίρετός ἐστι τῇ φύσει ἡ τριάς· καὶ μία ταύτης ἡ ἐνέργεια· ὁ γὰρ πατὴρ διὰ τοῦ λόγου, ἐν τῷ πνεύματι τῷ ἁγίῳ τὰ πάντα ποιεῖ· καὶ οὕτως ἡ ἑνότης τῆς ἁγίας τριάδος σώζεται· καὶ οὕτως εἷς θεὸς ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ κηρύττεται ὁ ἐπὶ πάντων, καὶ διὰ πάντων, καὶ ἐν πᾶσιν· ἐπὶ πάντων μὲν ὡς πατήρ, ὡς ἀρχὴ καὶ πηγή· διὰ πάντων δὲ διὰ τοῦ λόγου· ἐν πᾶσι δὲ, ἐν τῷ πνεύματι τῷ ἁγίῳ</note> *The Trinity is consistent with itself and by nature indivisible, and there is one energy or action within it. For the Father, through the Word, in the Holy Spirit, does all things. And thus is the unity of the holy Trinity preserved, and one God preached in the Church: namely, such as is above all, and through all, and in all. Above all as the Father, the principle and fountain; through all by the Word; and in all by the Holy Spirit.*

And elsewhere he writes often to the same purpose. Thus have we given a true and full account of how, according to Athanasius, the three divine persons <term>original: Hypostases</term>, though not "of one identical substance" <term>original: Monoousious</term> but only "of the same kind of substance" <term>original: Homoousious</term>, are really but one God or Divinity. In all of his doctrine, there is nothing that a true and genuine Platonist would not readily support. From this it may be concluded that the correct *Platonic Trinity* differs not so much from the doctrine of the ancient Church as some recent writers have supposed.

Up to this point, the "Platonic Christian" has endeavored partly to rectify and reform the *true* and *genuine Platonic Trinity*, and partly to reconcile it with the doctrine of the *ancient Church*. Nevertheless, to prevent all mistakes, we declare here that wherever this most *genuine Platonic Trinity* may be found to differ—not only from the Scripture itself (which is the sole *rule of faith*) but also from the creeds of the *Nicene* and *Constantinopolitan Councils*, and further from the doctrine of *Athanasius* in his genuine writings (whether regarding their inequality or anything else)—it is utterly disclaimed and rejected by us. As for that creed commonly called *Athanasian*, which was written a long time later by someone else: since it originally derived all its authority either from the name of Athanasius to whom it was attributed <term>original: Entituled</term>, or because it was supposed to be a summary and abridgement of his doctrine, we believe it should be interpreted according to the core of the doctrine found in the genuine writings of Athanasius. We view Athanasius as a person highly instrumental and useful to Divine Providence for preserving the Christian Church from falling, through *Arianism* <term>original: Arianism; the belief that Jesus was a created being rather than co-eternal with God</term>, into a kind of *pagan* and *idolatrous Christianity*. Such a state would have involved religiously worshipping those whom they themselves concluded were *creatures*. It was primarily through Athanasius that the doctrine of the Trinity (which previously fluctuated in loose uncertainty) came to be more precisely stated and settled.

Now the reason why we introduced the "Platonic Christian" here to make this defense <note>original: Apologizing</note> was, first, because we believed it was not in the interest of Christianity for the ancient *Platonic Trinity* to be made to seem more different from the *Christian* one than it actually is. ### CHAP. IV. Christian's Apology. <note>original: "Apology" here means a formal defense of a position, not an expression of regret.</note>

<margin>Socrates Scholasticus, Book 7, Chapter 6.</margin>
Secondly, because, as we have already proved, the ancient and genuine Platonic Trinity was doubtless *Anti-Arian*, or else the *Arian Trinity was Anti-Platonic*; the second and third *hypostases* <term>original: Hypostases; the distinct persons or "subsistences" of the Trinity</term> in the Platonic Trinity being both *eternal, infinite, and immutable*. And as for those Platonic *gradations* <note>original: Βαθμοὶ (Bathmoi); steps or ranks</note> so much spoken of, these (by St. *Cyril's* leave) were of a different kind from the *Arian* ones, there being no *inequality of creatures* compared to the *Creator* in them. Therefore *Socrates*, the ecclesiastical historian, wonders—not without cause—how those two presbyters, *Georgius* and *Timotheus*, could adhere to the *Arian faction*, since they were considered such great readers of *Plato* and *Origen*:

> <note>original: θαυμάσαι ἔν μοι ἔπησι, πᾶς ἤτοι οἱ ἄνδρες, τῇ Ἀρειανῶν θρησκείᾳ παρέμειναν, ὧν ὁ μὲν Πλάτωνα ἀεὶ μετὰ χεῖρας εἶχεν, ὁ δὲ τὸν Ὠριγένην ἀνέπνεεν· οὐδὲ γὰρ Πλάτων τὸ δεύτερον καὶ τὸ τρίτον αἴτιον, ὡς αὐτὸς ὀνομάζειν εἴωθεν, ἀρχὴν ὑπάρξεως, εἰληφέναι φησί· καὶ Ὠριγένης συναΐδιον πανταχοῦ ὁμολογεῖ τὸν υἱὸν τῷ πατρί</note> *It seems to me wonderful how those two persons should persist in the Arian persuasion, one of them having always* Plato *in his hands and the other continually breathing* Origen. *Since* Plato *nowhere affirms his first and second cause (as he was accustomed to call them) to have had any beginning of their existence; and* Origen *everywhere confesses the Son to be co-eternal with the Father.*

<margin>Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, Book 11, Chapter 9.</margin>

Besides which, another reason for this defense of the Christian Platonist was because, just as the Platonic *Pagans* after the rise of Christianity approved of the Christian *doctrine* concerning the *Logos* <term>the Word</term> as being exactly agreeable with their own, so did the *generality of the Christian Fathers*, before and after the *Nicene Council*, represent the *genuine Platonic Trinity* as really the same thing as the *Christian* one, or as approaching so near to it that they differed chiefly in circumstances or the manner of expression. The former of these is evident from that famous passage of *Amelius*, a contemporary of *Plotinus*, recorded by *Eusebius*, St. *Cyril*, and *Theodoret*:

> <note>original: Καὶ οὗτος ἄρα ἦν ὁ λόγος, καθ' ὃν αἰεὶ ὄντα, τὰ γινόμενα ἐγίνετο, ὡς ἂν καὶ ὁ Ἡράκλειτος ἀξιώσειε, καὶ νὴ Δί' ὃν ὁ Βάρβαρος ἀξιοῖ ἐν τῇ τῆς ἀρχῆς τάξει τε καὶ ἀξίᾳ καθεστηκότα, πρὸς τὸν θεὸν εἶναι, καὶ θεὸν εἶναι· δι' οὗ πάνθ' ἁπλῶς γεγενῆσθαι· ἐν ᾧ τὸ γενόμενον ζῶν καὶ ζωὴν καὶ ὂν πεφυκέναι· καὶ εἰς τὰ σώματα πίπτειν καὶ σάρκα ἐνδυσάμενον, φαντάζεσθαι ἄνθρωπον, μετὰ καὶ τοῦ τηνικαῦτα δεικνύειν τῆς φύσεως τὸ μεγαλεῖον ἀμέλει· καὶ ἀναλυθέντα πάλιν ἀποθεοῦσθαι, καὶ θεὸν εἶναι, οἷος ἦν πρὸ τοῦ εἰς τὸ σῶμα, καὶ τὸν ἄνθρωπον καταχθῆναι.</note> *And this was the* Logos *or* Word *by whom, existing from eternity according to* Heraclitus, *all things were made. And whom that* barbarian <note>original: Βάρβαρος (Barbaros). From a Greek perspective, the "barbarian" refers to the Apostle John, author of the Gospel.</note> *also places in the rank and dignity of a* principle, *affirming him to have been with* God *and to be* God, *and that all things were made by him, and that whatever was made was* life *and* being *in him. As also that he descended into a* body *and, being clothed in* flesh, *appeared as a* man, *though not without demonstration of the divinity of his nature. But that afterwards, being* loosed *or* separated *from the same, he was* deified <note>returned to divine status</note> *and became* God *again, such as he was before he came down into a mortal* body.

In these words, *Amelius* speaks favorably also of the incarnation of that *eternal Logos*. And the same is further manifest from what St. *Austin* <note>Augustine of Hippo</note> writes concerning a Platonist in his time: *The beginning of the Holy Gospel, which is named according to John* <note>original: Initium Sancti Evangelii, cui nomen est secundum Johannem</note>, a certain...

*<note>original: "quidem Platonicus, sicut à sancto Sene Simpliciano, qui posteà Mediolanensi Ecclesiæ præfedit Episcopus, solebamus audire, aureis Literis conscribendum, & per omnes Ecclesias in locis eminentissimis proponendum esse dicebat"</note> We have often heard from that holy man Simplicianus, afterward Bishop of Milan, that a certain Platonist affirmed that the beginning of Saint John’s Gospel deserved to be written in letters of gold and set up in all the most prominent places throughout the Christian churches.* 

The truth of this will sufficiently appear from the following testimonies: <margin>Page 93.</margin> Justin Martyr, in his *Apology*, affirms of Plato: <note>original: "δευτέραν χώραν τῷ παρὰ θεῷ λόγῳ δίδωσι · τὴν δὲ τρίτην τῷ λεχθέντι ἐπιφέρεσθαι τῷ ὕδατι πνεύματι, &c."</note> *That he gave the second place to the Word of God, and the third to that Spirit which is said to have moved upon the waters.* 

Clement of Alexandria, speaking of that passage in Plato's *Second Epistle to Dionysius* concerning the First, Second, and Third causes, <margin>*Stromata* Book 5, Page 598.</margin> writes thus: <note>original: "οὐκ ἄλλως ἔγωγε ἐξακούω, ἢ τὴν ἁγίαν τριάδα μηνύεσθαι, τρίτον μὲν γὰρ εἶναι τὸ ἄγιον πνεῦμα · ὁ υἱὸς δὲ δεύτερον, δι’ οὗ πάντα ἐγένετο κατὰ βούλησιν τοῦ πατρός"</note> *I understand this no otherwise than that the Holy Trinity is signified thereby—the third being the Holy Ghost, and the second the Son, by whom all things were made according to the will of the Father.*

Origen also affirms the Son of God to have been plainly <margin>Book 6, *Against Celsus*.</margin> spoken of by Plato in his *Epistle to Hermias and Coriscus*: <note>original: "ὁ πάντα ἐπαγγελλόμενος εἰδέναι κέλσος, καὶ πολλὰ τῷ πλάτωνος παρατιθέμενος, ἑκών, οἶμαι, σιωπᾷ τὸ περὶ υἱοῦ θεοῦ λόγον, τὸ παρὰ πλάτωνι λεγόμενον ἐν τῇ πρὸς ἑρμείαν καὶ κορίσκον ἐπιστολῇ"</note> *Celsus, who pretends to know all things and who cites so many other passages from Plato, purposefully (as I suppose) dissembles and conceals what Plato wrote concerning the Son of God in his Epistle to Hermias and Coriscus. There, Plato calls him the God of the whole universe and the Prince of all things both present and future, afterwards speaking of the Father of this Prince and Cause.* 

And again elsewhere in that book, he writes to the <margin>*Against Celsus* Book 6, Page 308.</margin> same purpose: <note>original: "ἀλλ' οὐδὲ ἐβουλήθη τὸ παρὰ πλάτωνι ἐν ταῖς ἐπιστολαῖς λελεγμένον, ᾧ ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω ἐμνήσθημεν, περὶ τοῦ διακοσμήσαντος τόδε τὸ πᾶν, ὡς ὄντος υἱοῦ θεοῦ, παραθέσθαι · ἵνα μὴ καὶ αὐτὸς ὑπὸ τοῦ πλάτωνος, ὃν πολλάκις ἐσέμνυνεν, ἀναγκασθῇ, παραδέξασθαι, ὅτι ὁ μὲν δημιουργὸς τοῦδε τοῦ παντός, υἱός ἐστι τοῦ θεοῦ, ὁ δὲ πρῶτος καὶ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεὸς πατὴρ ἔστιν αὐτοῦ"</note> *Neither would Celsus (here speaking of Christians making Christ the Son of God) take any notice of that passage in Plato’s Epistle mentioned before, concerning the Arranger and Governor of the whole world as being the Son of God; lest he should be compelled by the authority of Plato, whom he so often magnifies, to agree with this doctrine of ours: that the <term>original: "Demiurgus"</term> Maker of the whole world is the Son of God, but the First and Supreme Deity is his Father.*

Moreover, Saint Cyprian (or whoever was the author of the book titled *On the Holy Spirit* <note>original: "De Spiritu Sancto"</note>) affirms the Platonists' First and Universal *Psyche* <note>original: "Psyche"; the World-Soul</note> to be the same as the Holy Ghost in Christian theology, in these words: <note>original: "Hujus Sempiterna Virtus & Divinitas, cum in propria natura, ab Inquisitoribus Mundi antiquis Philosophis propriè investigari non posset; Subtilissimis tamen intuiti conjecturis Compositionem Mundi, & distinctis Elementorum affectibus, præsentem omnibus Animam adfuisse dixerunt; quibus, secundum genus & ordinem singulorum, vitam præberet & motum, & intransgressibiles figeret Metas, & Stabilitatem assignaret; & Univer-"</note> *Since his eternal power and divinity could not be properly investigated in its own nature by the ancient philosophers—those searchers of the world—they nevertheless, by the most subtle conjectures, observed the composition of the world and the distinct properties of the elements. They said that a present Soul was with them all, which provided life and motion to each according to its kind and order, fixed boundaries that could not be crossed, assigned stability, and Univer—*

### CHAPTER IV. The Genuine Platonic Trinity.

<note>original: "sam hanc Vitam, hunc motum, hanc rerum Essentiam, Animam Mundi vocaverunt."</note>...this same Life, this motion, this Essence of things, they called the Soul of the World. In the next place, Eusebius of Caesarea gives a full and <margin>Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 11, Chapter 20.</margin> clear testimony of the concordance and agreement of the *Platonic* system—at least in its main points—with the Christian Trinity, which he argues was the *Cabala* <note>The "Cabala" here refers to a secret oral tradition or mystical interpretation of the ancient Hebrews.</note> of the ancient *Hebrews*, as follows:

<note>original: "τῶν παρ' Ἑβραίοις λογίων μετὰ τὸν περὶ πατρὸς καὶ υἱοῦ λόγον, ἐν τρίτῃ τάξει τὸ ῞Αγιον Πνεῦμα καταλεγόντων· καὶ τὴν γε ἁγίαν καὶ μακαρίαν Τριάδα τοῦτον ὑποτιθεμένων τὸν τρόπον, ὡς ἂν τῆς τρίτης δυνάμεως πᾶσαν ὑπερβεβηκυίας γενητὴν φύσιν· οὖσαν πρώτην μὲν τῶν διὰ τοῦ υἱοῦ συστασῶν νοερῶν οὐσιῶν, τρίτην δὲ ἀπὸ τοῦ πρώτου Αἰτίου· θέα ὅπως καὶ ὁ Πλάτων τοιαῦτά τινα ᾐνίξατο διὰ τῆς πρὸς Διονύσιον ἐπιστολῆς, &c."</note> *The Oracles of the Hebrews, placing the Holy Spirit after the Father and the Son in the third rank, and acknowledging a holy and blessed Trinity in this way—so that this third power also transcends all created nature, being the first of those intellectual substances which proceed from the Son, and the third from the First Cause—see how Plato enigmatically declares the same things in his Epistle to Dionysius, in these words, etc.* 

The interpreters of *Plato* refer these things to a *First God*, a *Second Cause*, and a *third, the Soul of the World*, which they also call *The Third God*. In a similar way, the Divine Scriptures rank the Holy Trinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in the position of a Principle <term>principle: here used in the philosophical sense of an "arche" or fundamental source of all things</term>. 

But it is most remarkable what *Athanasius* <note>Athanasius was a 4th-century Bishop of Alexandria and a chief defender of the Trinity against Arianism.</note> himself affirms of the Platonists: that although they derived the *Second Hypostasis* <term>hypostasis: a distinct person or individual essence within the Trinity</term> of their Trinity from the *First*, and the *Third* from the *Second*, they nevertheless supposed both their Second and Third Hypostases to be *Uncreated*. Therefore, he sends the Arians <note>Arians were followers of Arius, who argued that Jesus Christ was a created being and not co-eternal with God the Father.</note> to school there. Because there is only one *Self-Originated Being* (the Unbegotten), the Arians would unskillfully conclude that the Word or Son of God must therefore be a creature. Thus, in his book concerning the decrees of the <margin>Page 278.</margin> Nicene Council:

<note>original: "ἐχρήσαντο παρ' Ἑλλήνων λοιπὸν τὴν λέξιν τοῦ ᾿Αγεννήτου· ἵνα προφάσει καὶ τούτου τοῦ ὀνόματος, ἐν τοῖς γενητοῖς πάλιν καὶ τοῖς κτίσμασι συναριθμῶσι τὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ λόγον· δι' οὗ αὐτὰ τὰ γενητὰ γέγονεν· εἰ μὲν οὖν ἀγνοοῦντες τὸ ὄνομα οὕτως ἀναισχυντοῦσιν, ἔδει μαθεῖν αὐτοὺς παρὰ τῶν αὐτοῖς δεδωκότων αὐτὸ, ὅτι καὶ ὃν λέγουσιν ἐκ τοῦ ᾿Αγαθοῦ Νοῦν, καὶ τὸν ἐκ τοῦ Νοῦ ψυχήν· καίτοι γινώσκοντες τὸ ἐξ ὧν εἰσιν, οὐκ ἐφοβήθησαν ὅμως· καὶ αὐτὰ εἰπεῖν ᾿Αγέννητα· εἰδότες ὅτι καὶ τοῦτο λέγοντες οὐκ ἐλαττοῦσι τὸ πρῶτον ἐξ οὗ καὶ ταῦτα πέφυκε· καὶ ἢ καὶ αὐτοὺς οὕτω λέγειν, ἢ μηδόλως λέγειν περὶ ὧν οὐκ ἴσασιν·"</note> *The Arians, borrowing the word "Unbegotten" <note>original: "Agennetos"</note> from the Pagans (who acknowledge only one such), make that a pretense to rank the Word or Son of God—who is the Creator of all—amongst creatures or things "made." Instead, they ought to have learned the right meaning of that word "Unbegotten" from those very Platonists who gave it to them. For the Platonists, although they acknowledge that their second person, "Intellect" <note>original: "Nous"</note>, is derived from the first, called "The Good" <note>original: "Tagathon"</note>, and their third person, "Soul" <note>original: "Psyche"</note>, is from the second, they do not hesitate to affirm them both to be uncreated <note>original: "Ageneta"</note>. They know well that by saying this, they detract nothing from the majesty of the First, from whom these two are derived. Therefore, the Arians ought either to speak as the Platonists do, or else say nothing at all about these things of which they are ignorant.* 

In these words of *Athanasius*, a plain distinction is made between *Unbegotten* <note>original: "᾿Αγεννήτῳ" (Agenneto)</note> and *Uncreated* <note>original: "ἀγενήτῳ" (ageneto)</note>; and the *Second Person of the Trinity*,
