# The Cabala of the Trinity. BOOK I.

...nity, the Son or Word of God. Although Athanasius acknowledged that the Son is not *unbegotten* <note>original: *Agennetos*</note>—since he is begotten of the Father, who is the only *Unbegotten*—the Son is nevertheless described here as *uncreated* <note>original: *Agennetos*. In this context, Athanasius uses the term to mean "not a created thing," even though the Son is "begotten" from the Father</note>. Athanasius declares that the Platonists likewise affirmed that the *second* and *third hypostases* <note>The distinct "persons" or "substances" of the Trinity</note> of their Trinity were not *creatures* <note>meaning: created beings</note>, but *uncreated*. This <margin>*The City of God* <note>original: *De C. D.* (De Civitate Dei)</note></margin> notable testimony from *Athanasius* concerning the Platonic Trinity is a significant vindication of that philosophy. We might also add the confession of *St. Augustine*, who stated that *God the Father* and *God the Son* were acknowledged by the Platonists in much the same way as by Christians. However, regarding the *Holy Spirit*, Augustine observes some difference between *Plotinus* and *Porphyry*. The former *placed the nature of the Soul after the Paternal Intellect* <note>original: *Postponere Animæ Naturam Paterno Intellectui*</note>, while the latter *interposed* it. That is, *Plotinus* positioned his *Psyche* (the Soul) after the Paternal Intellect, but *Porphyry* placed it between the *Father* and the *Son*, as a *middle ground between both*.

As previously noted, *St. Cyril of Alexandria* affirms that nothing is missing from the Platonic Trinity except for that *consubstantiality* <note>original: *Homousiotes*—the doctrine that the three persons of the Trinity are of the very same substance</note> held by him and other Church Fathers of that era. He believed they should not only all be *God* or *uncreated*, but also *three coequal individuals* under the *same ultimate species*, just as *three individual men* are of the same species. Cyril felt that the *gradual subordination* <note>the ranking of the persons as greater and lesser</note> found in the Platonic Trinity had a certain hint of *Arianism* <note>A 4th-century belief that the Son was a created being, subordinate to the Father, which was declared a heresy</note>. Nevertheless, he concludes: *“Plato was not altogether ignorant of the truth”* <note>original: πλὼ ἐκ ήγνόηκεν ὁλοσχερῶς τὸ ἀληθὲς</note>, but had knowledge of the only-begotten Son of God, as well as the Holy Spirit (which he called *Psyche*). Cyril suggests that Plato would have expressed himself correctly in every way if he had not been afraid of Anytus and Meletus <note>The men who brought the charges against Socrates that led to his execution</note> and the poison that *Socrates* drank.

Whether it was truly a fault in the Platonists that they did not consider their *hypostases* to be *three individuals* of the *same ultimate species*, we leave for others to judge. We might also add the testimony of *Chalcidius*, since he is undoubtedly considered to have been a Christian—though his language sounds rather pagan when he calls the three divine *hypostases* a *chief*, a *second*, and a *third God*: <margin>Page 277.</margin> 

> *The arrangement of this matter should be understood in this way: that the first origin of things is the Supreme and Ineffable God. Following his Providence is a Second God, the Lawgiver of both eternal and temporal life. The third is a substance called a Second Mind and Intellect, acting as a guardian of the eternal law. Subject to these three are rational souls that obey the law, along with ministerial powers, etc. Thus, the Sovereign or Supreme God commands, the second organizes, and the third executes—while souls live according to the law.* <note>original Latin: *Istius rei dispositio talis mente concipienda est; Originem quidem rerum esse Summum & Ineffabilem Deum...*</note>

In this passage, although *Chalcidius* seems more like a Platonist than a Christian, he acknowledges no such beings as *Henads* or *Noes* <note>Archaic Platonic terms for "unities" and "minds" or "intellects" used by later Neoplatonists to multiply the number of divine beings</note>, but only three divine *hypostases* and the *rational souls* beneath them. ### CHAPTER IV. Altered by Later Platonists.

The testimony of *Theodoret* in his book *On the First Principle* <note>original: *De Principio*</note> states:

> Plotinus and Numenius, in explaining Plato's meaning, declare that he asserted three things beyond time and eternal: the Good, Mind, and the Soul of the universe. He calls the "Good" what we call "Father"; he calls "Mind" what we refer to as the "Word"; and he calls "Soul" that power which animates and gives life to all things, which the divine Scriptures call the "Holy Spirit." And these things (he says) were stolen by Plato from the philosophy and theology of the Hebrews. <note>original Greek: τὴν πλάτωνος διάνοιαν ἀναπτύσσοντες ὁ Πλωτῖνος καὶ ὁ Νεμήνιος, τρία φασὶν αὐτὸν εἰρηκέναι ὑπέρχρονα καὶ ἀΐδια, τ’ ἀγαθόν, καὶ νοῦν, καὶ τοῦ παντὸς τὴν ψυχήν...</note>

Therefore, we must take notice here of a wonderful providence of Almighty God: that this doctrine of a Trinity of divine *hypostases* <note>The distinct "persons" or "substances" of the Trinity</note> found such acceptance and welcome in the *pagan world* and was received by the wisest of all their philosophers before the time of Christianity. This prepared an easier path for the acceptance of Christianity among the learned *pagans*. That this was successful is undeniably evident from the records of antiquity. 

And the *later Platonists* <note>original: "Junior Platonists," referring to Neoplatonists</note>, who were most opposed and hostile to Christianity, eventually became so aware of this that—besides their other corruptions of the Trinity mentioned before, used to justify their *polytheism* <note>The worship of many gods</note> and *idolatry*—they likely for this very reason completely innovated, changed, and perverted the whole *Cabala* <note>Here referring to an ancient tradition of secret wisdom</note>. They no longer acknowledged a *Trinity*, but instead a *Quaternity* (four), a *Quinary* (five), or even more divine *hypostases*. 

They first argued that before the *Trinity*, there was another supreme and *highest hypostasis*, not to be counted with the others but standing alone by himself. We believe the first innovator in this regard was *Iamblichus*, who in his *Egyptian Mysteries*—where he seems to make *Egyptian theology* agree with his own hypotheses—writes in this manner:

> "Before the things that truly exist and the principles of all, there is one God, the first, even superior to the first God and King, immovable and remaining always in the solitude of his own unity. Nothing intelligible <note>Capable of being understood by the mind</note> or anything else is mixed with him; rather, he stands as the model for that God who is truly good, who is self-begotten and his own father. For this first God is something greater, prior to him, and the fountain of all things—the foundation of all the first intelligible ideas. Therefore, from this One, the self-sufficient God caused himself to shine forth; for this reason, he is called 'his own father' <note>original: *autopator*</note> and 'self-sufficient.' For he is the principle and the God of gods, a 'monad' <note>a single unit</note> from the One, the elder and the source of all essence." <note>original Greek: πρὸ τῶν ὄντως ὄντων, καὶ τῶν ὅλων ἀρχῶν, ἔστι θεὸς εἷς πρῶτος...</note>

<summary>Theodoret argues that Plato's Trinity was derived from Hebrew theology, serving as a providential preparation for Christianity. However, later Neoplatonists like Iamblichus distorted this tradition by adding more divine layers, such as a supreme "One" above the Trinity, to distance themselves from Christian doctrine.</summary>

# Proclus's Monad before the Trinity. Book I.

This Principle, and the God of Gods, is a *Monad* <note>A single, indivisible unit or the ultimate "One"</note> from the first *One*, existing before all *Essence*. So far as we can understand, **Iamblichus**'s <note>original: *Jamblichus*</note> meaning is that there is a *Simple Unity* in the order of *Nature* before that **The Good** <note>original: *Tagathon*</note>, or *Monad*, which is the *First* of the *Three Divine Hypostases* <note>The three distinct "persons" or "substances" of the divine</note>. This *Doctrine* was afterward taken up by **Proclus**, who explained it in this manner:

<margin>In Timaeus, Book 2, page 93.</margin>
> Everywhere Plato is accustomed to return from the multitude to the Unities; or rather, even before Plato, according to the natural order of things, the One is always before the multitude, and every divine order begins from a Monad. Therefore, though the divine Number proceeds in a Trinity, the Monad must exist before this Trinity. Let there be three Demiurgic <note>The "Demiurge" is the creator or craftsman of the universe in Platonic thought</note> Hypostases; nevertheless, before these there must be One, because none of the divine orders begins from a multitude. We conclude that the Demiurgic Number does not begin from a Trinity, but from a Monad, standing alone by itself before that Trinity. <note>original Greek: πανταχοῦ ὁ Πλάτων ἀπὸ τοῦ πλήθους ἐπὶ τὰς ἑνάδας ἀνατρέχειν εἴωθεν· μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ πρὸ τοῦ Πλάτωνος κατὰ τὴν τῶν πραγμάτων τάξιν πρὸ τοῦ πλήθους ἓν ἀεί ἐστι, καὶ πᾶσα θεία τάξις ἀπὸ μονάδος ἀρχέται· δεῖ μὲν γὰρ ἐκ τριάδος προϊέναι τὸν ἀριθμὸν τὸν θεῖον, ἀλλὰ πρὸ τῆς τριάδος ἡ μονάς· ἔστω μὲν οὖν καὶ οἱ δημιουργικοὶ τρεῖς ἀλλά τις ὁ πρὸ τῶν τριῶν εἷς, οὐδεμία γὰρ τῶν θείων τάξεων ἐκ πλήθους ἀρχέται· οὐκ ἄρα ἀπὸ τριάδος ἀρχέσθαι δεῖ τὸν δημιουργικὸν ἀριθμὸν, ἀλλ᾽ ἀπὸ μονάδος·</note>

Here **Proclus**, though endeavoring to gain some support for this doctrine from **Plato**, yet fearing that might fail him, flees to the order of *Nature*. From there, he would infer that before the Trinity of Demiurgic *Hypostases*, there must be a single *Monad* or *Henad* <note>Another term for a "unit" or "the One"</note> standing alone by itself as its head. **St. Cyril of Alexandria**, who lived after **Iamblichus** but before **Proclus**, seems to take notice of this innovation in Platonic theology as a thing then newly emerged, appearing after the time of **Porphyry**:

<margin>Against Julian, Book 8, page 271.</margin>
> But those mentioned before contradict this doctrine (of Porphyry and the ancient Platonists), affirming that **The Good** <note>original: *Tagathon*</note> ought not to be counted or reckoned together with those things which proceed from it. They argue it should be exempted from all communion because it is altogether simple and incapable of any mixture or association with any other. Wherefore, these begin their Trinity with **Mind** <note>original: *Nous*</note> or **Intellect**, making that the *First*. <note>original Greek: ἀλλ᾽ οἵ γε προειρημένοι καὶ πρὸς τοῦτο ἀντιλέγουσι, φάσκοντες μὴ δεῖν Τ᾿ΑΓΑΘΟΝ συναριθμεῖν τοῖς ἀπ᾽ αὐτοῦ· ἐξῃρῆσθαι γὰρ ἀπὸ πάσης κοινωνίας διὰ τὸ εἶναι ἁπλοῦν πάντη καὶ ἀδεκτόν τινος συμβάσεως· Ἀπὸ δὲ τοῦ ΝΟΥ (ἀρχὴ γὰρ οὗτος) τὴν τριάδα μίαν σωθῆναι.</note>

The only difference here is that **Iamblichus** seems to make the first *hypostasis* of the *Trinity* after a *Monad* to be **The Good**, while **St. Cyril** says it is **Mind**. However, they both meant the same thing, as did **Proclus** after them. Therefore, it is evident that when the *Christian Doctrine* of the *Trinity* came to be precisely stated and settled from the time of the *Council of Nicaea* and **Athanasius**, it was much insisted upon by Christians. **Iamblichus** and other *Platonists*, who were great *antagonists* of Christianity, perceived the advantage Christians had from the *Platonic Trinity*. They then for the first time *innovated* this *doctrine*, introducing a *Quaternity* <note>A group of four</note> of *Divine Hypostases* instead of a *Trinity*. In this new system, the *First* was not *coordinate* with the other *three*, nor *associated* or *reckoned* with them. But *all* of them, though *subordinate*, were yet *universal*, and such as *comprehend* the whole...

### CHAPTER IV. His other Fantastic Trinities.

...that is, *Infinite* and *Omnipotent*; and therefore none of them are *Creatures*. For it is *certain* that before this time, or the age that **Iamblichus** lived in, *there was no such thing at all dreamed of by any Platonist* as a *Unity before and above the Trinity*, which would create a *Quaternity* <note>A group of four</note> of Divine *Hypostases* <note>The distinct "persons" or "substances" of the divine</note>. **Plotinus** positively determined that there could neither be *more* nor *fewer than three*. **Proclus** himself acknowledged that the *Ancient Tradition* or *Cabala* <note>In this context, an ancient oral tradition or secret knowledge</note> spoke only of *Three Gods*. And **Numenius**, who was *older* than both of them, wrote this about **Socrates**:

<margin>Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 14, Chapter 5.</margin>
"Socrates asserted three gods" <note>original Greek: τρεῖς θεὸς τιθεμένους Σωκράτης</note>. That is, he also (before **Plato**) *asserted three gods*—meaning *three divine hypostases* and no more—as *Principles*, following the **Pythagoreans** in this regard.

Furthermore, the same **Proclus**, besides his *Henads* <note>The "ones" or ultimate units</note> and *Noes* <note>Divine intellects</note> mentioned before, added certain other *Fantastic Trinities* of his own as well. For example, he proposed a trinity of the *First Essence*, the *First Life*, and the *First Intellect* (to omit others). By doing so, that ancient *Cabala* and "Theology of Divine Tradition" <note>original Greek: θεοπαράδοτος θεολογία</note> regarding *three foundational hypostases* and no more was disguised, perverted, and corrupted.

But besides this *advantage* gained from the ancient *Pagan Platonists* and *Pythagoreans* admitting a *Trinity* into their *theology* (much like *Christianity* does, which made *Christianity* more appealing to *philosophical Pagans*), there is another *advantage* of this fact extending even to the present time. This was probably not *unintended* by *Divine Providence*: namely, that while *bold* and *arrogant wits* hastily condemn the *doctrine* of the *Trinity* as *nonsense*, an absolute *contradiction* to *human faculties*, and an *impossibility*, some of them have consequently abandoned *Christianity* and all *Revealed Religion* to profess only *Theism*. Others have frustrated the *purpose* of the doctrine by *Paganizing* it into *creature-worship* or *idolatry*. This *ignorant* and *arrogant confidence* of both groups may be refuted and silenced by the fact that the most ingenious and sharp of all the *Pagan philosophers*—the *Platonists* and *Pythagoreans*—were not biased by *Scripture Revelation* that might seem to force their *faculties*. Instead, they followed the free *sentiments* and *dictates* of their own *minds*, and yet they not only accepted this *Trinity* of *Divine Hypostases* as *eternal* and *uncreated*, but were also fond of the *hypothesis* and made it a main *fundamental* of their *theology*.

It now appears from what we have declared that, according to the ancient and genuine *Platonists* and *Pythagoreans*, none of their *Trinity of Gods* or *Divine Hypostases* were *independent*; yet neither were they "creature-gods" <note>original Greek: γεννητοὶ θεοὶ</note>. They were *uncreated*, being all not only *eternal*, *necessarily existent*, and *immutable*, but also *universal*—that is, *infinite* and *omnipotent*. They were the *causes*, *principles*, and *creators* of the whole *world*. From this it follows that these *Platonists* could not justly be accused of *idolatry* for giving *religious worship* to each *hypostasis* of their *Trinity*. # Arians charged by the Fathers, BOOK I.

*Pagan Idolatry*, or *Creature-Worship* <note>The act of giving divine honor to something created rather than the Creator</note>, cannot be justly charged against Christianity because of the *Religious Worship* given to our Savior *Christ* and the *Trinity* (the *Son* and *Holy Ghost*). According to true and *Orthodox Christianity*, none of these are *Creatures*, although the *Arian Hypothesis* <note>Arianism: the 4th-century belief that Jesus Christ was a created being, subordinate to God the Father</note> made them out to be such. This was indeed the great *reason* why the ancient *Church Fathers* so zealously opposed *Arianism*: because they believed that *Christianity*—which was intended by God Almighty as a means to root out *Pagan Idolatry*—was itself being *Paganized* and turned into *Idolatry*. It was made highly guilty of the very thing it so strongly condemned in the *Pagans*: *Creature-Worship*. 

This could be proved by numerous testimonies from *Athanasius, Basil, Gregory of Nyssa, Gregory Nazianzen, Epiphanius, John Chrysostom, Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, Faustinus*, and *Cyril of Alexandria*. All of them charged the *Arians* with being guilty of the exact same *Idolatry* as the *Gentiles* or *Pagans*, because they gave *Religious Worship* to the *Word* and *Son of God himself* (and consequently to our Savior *Christ*) even while they supposed him to be nothing more than a *Creature*. We shall content ourselves here by citing only one remarkable passage from *Athanasius* in his *Fourth Oration against the Arians*:

<margin>Pages 468, 469.</margin> "Why then do these Arian-madmen <note>original Greek: Ἀρειομανῖται</note>, thinking and reasoning in this way, not count themselves among the Pagans? For they, just like the Pagans, worship the creature besides the God who created all things. Even if the Pagans worship one uncreated and many created gods, while these Arians worship only one uncreated and one created (namely, the Son or Word of God), this does not create any real difference between them. This is because the Arians' 'One Created' being is just one of those many Pagan gods; and those many gods of the Pagans or Gentiles have the same nature as this one, as they are all alike creatures. These wretched Arians are apostates from the truth; they have fallen away from the truth of Christianity. They betray Christ even more than the Jews did, and they wallow or tumble in the filth of Pagan Idolatry, worshiping creatures and different kinds of gods—men hated by God!" <note>original Greek: διὰ τί οὖν οἱ Ἀρειομανῖται τοιαῦτα λογιζόμενοι καὶ νοῦντες... οἱ θεοστυγεῖς.</note>

In passing, we may take notice that when *Athanasius* affirms of the Arians what *St. Paul* does of the Pagans—that they "worshiped the creature besides the creator" <note>original Greek: τῇ κτίσει λατρεύειν παρὰ τὸν κτίσαντα; quoting Romans 1:25</note>—his meaning could not have been that they worshiped the creature *more than* the Creator. This is because the *Arians* constantly declared that they gave *less* worship to *Christ* the *Son* or *Word* of God (whom they accounted as a *Creature*) than they did to the Father, the *Creator*. Instead, his meaning was either that they worshiped the creature *besides* the Creator, or the creature *instead of* the Creator—occupying the place of him who alone has the right to be *Religiously Worshiped*. 

Again, when this same *Athanasius* declares that the *Greeks, Gentiles*, or *Pagans* did *universally* worship "only one uncreated" <note>original Greek: ἑνὶ ἀγεννήτῳ</note>, he seems to imply that the *Platonist Trinity* of...

<meta>This page continues the argument that the Church Fathers equated Arianism with Paganism. # Chapter IV. Comparing [Christian Heresy] with Pagan Idolatry.

*The Divine Persons <note>original: Hypostases</note>, which he claimed were all uncreated, were viewed by them as only one entire Divinity.*

But the principal things we shall observe from this passage of *Athanasius*, and those many other writings of the Fathers where they parallel the *Arians* with the *Pagans*—accusing the *former* of the very same idolatry as the *latter*, even when they worshiped our *Savior Christ* himself, or the *Word* and *Son of God*, whom they supposed to be nothing but a *creature*—are the following: 

First, they plainly declare that the majority of *Pagans* did not worship a *multitude of independent gods*. Instead, they believed that only *one* of their gods was *uncreated* or *self-existent*, and all their other *many gods* were looked upon as his creatures. This is expressly stated by *Athanasius* here: that the Greeks or *Pagans* did "worship only one uncreated, and many created gods" <note>original Greek: ἑνὶ ἀγενήτῳ καὶ πολλοῖς γενητοῖς λατρεύειν</note>. This is also clearly implied by all those other previously mentioned Fathers who charge the *Arians* with the guilt of *Pagan idolatry*. If the *Pagans* had worshiped *many uncreated and independent gods*, it would not follow that the *Arians* were *idolaters* just because the *Pagans* were. 

That this was indeed the understanding of the Fathers (both before and after the *Council of Nicaea*) concerning *Pagan polytheism* and *idolatry*—that it consisted not in worshiping *many uncreated and independent gods*, but only *one uncreated* and *many created*—has already been demonstrated elsewhere. It could be further confirmed by several of their *testimonies*, such as this one from *Saint Gregory Nazianzen* in his 37th Oration: "*What then, some might say, is there not also one deity among the Pagans, as those who philosophize more deeply among them declare?*" <note>original Greek: Τί δ' ἂν ἔχοι καὶ παρ' Ἕλλησι φαῖεν ἂν μία θεότης, ὡς οἱ τὰ τελεώτερα παρ' ἐκείνοις φιλοσοφοῦντες;</note>. 

And there is that full and remarkable statement by *Irenaeus*, where he plainly affirms of the non-Christians <note>original: Gentiles</note>: 
<margin>Book 2, Chapter 9.</margin>
"They served the creature rather than the Creator, and those who are not gods; yet they attributed the first place of the Godhead to one certain Supreme God, the Maker of this universe." <note>original Latin: Ita Creaturæ potius quam Creatori serviebant, & his qui non sunt Dii, ut Primum Deitatis Locum attribuerent, Uni alicui & Summo Fabricatori hujus Universitatis Deo</note>. 

The second thing to note is that *Athanasius* and all those other Orthodox Fathers who charged the *Arians* with *Pagan idolatry* clearly implied that even those who worship *one divine power* <note>original: Numen</note> or acknowledge *one Supreme Deity* (the Maker of the whole world) are not *incapable* of *idolatry*. Not only did the *Arians* unquestionably do so, but according to these Fathers, so did the *Pagans themselves*. 

The third thing is that, in the judgment of *Athanasius* and all the Orthodox *anti-Arian* Fathers, giving religious *worship* to any *created being* whatsoever is absolutely idolatry. This holds true even if that worship is *inferior* to the worship given to the *Supreme God*—which, according to the modern distinction, is called *service* <note>original Greek: δουλεία (douleia)</note> rather than *supreme worship* <note>original Greek: λατρεία (latreia)</note>. It is certain that the *Arians* gave a much *inferior* worship to *Christ the Son* (the *Word of God*), whom they argued was a *mere creature*, made in *time*, *mutable* and *capable of failing*, than they gave to that *eternal God* who was the creator of him.

<meta>This page continues the argument that the early Church Fathers viewed any religious worship of a created being as idolatry. It specifically uses the example of Athanasius to show that the distinction between different "levels" of worship (such as Latria and Dulia) was not recognized by the early Church in their debates with the Arians.</meta>

# Orthodox Christians worshiped, BOOK I.

These Fathers imply that the Pagans themselves gave a much lower level of worship to their *many created gods* <note>original Greek: πολλοὶ γεννητοὶ Θεοὶ</note> (whom they viewed as created beings) than they gave to that *one uncreated God* <note>original Greek: ἑνὶ ἀγεννήτῳ</note>.

Now, the *Arians* strongly argued for the *unity of the Godhead*. Nevertheless, the Church Fathers condemned them as guilty of *idolatry* for giving even a "lesser" kind of *religious worship* to *Christ* (the *Son* or *Word* of God) because they believed he was a *created being* <note>original: creature</note>. If that is true, then those who give *religious worship* to other created beings—like *angels* and the *souls* of dead men—certainly cannot be excused from that same guilt. This remains true even if the worship they offer is lower than what they give to the *Supreme Omnipotent God*, the Creator of all. 

This is because the Arians viewed the *Son* or *Word of God* as the *first*, the most glorious, and the most excellent of all created beings. They believed he was the instrument through which all other *creatures*, such as angels and souls, were made. Therefore, if it was *idolatry* for them to give a lesser kind of *religious worship* to the *Son and Word of God himself* (according to their own theory), then it must be even worse to give it to those other beings *made* by him, such as angels and deceased men. 

Furthermore, although the Arians thought the *Word and Son of God* was a creature, he was not *actually* one. Scripture clearly declares him to be a *true* object of *religious worship* ("Worship him, all you gods"). So, while the Arians were *technically* <note>original: formally</note> idolaters based on their own false theory, they were not *actually* <note>original: materially</note> worshiping a creature. In contrast, those who worship angels and saints are idolaters in both theory and reality.

It is also worth noting that these ancient Fathers did not use the modern distinction of *religious worship* into *Latria* <term>the highest form of worship, reserved for God alone as the self-existent Creator</term> and *Dulia* <term>a lower level of religious worship or veneration given to created beings like saints</term>. Instead, they concluded that *religious worship*—universally and without distinction—is only for the *Creator* and not for any *creature*. 

*Athanasius* states this plainly in his *Third Oration*: "If the Son or Word of God were to be worshiped (even if he were a creature) because he transcends us in glory and dignity, then every inferior being would be required to worship whatever is superior to it. But that is not the case; for a created being does not religiously worship another created being, but only God the Creator" <note>original Greek: εἰ γὰρ ὡς τῇ δόξῃ ὑπερέχων προσκυνεῖτο, ἔδει καὶ ἕκαστον τῶν ὑπερβεβηκότων, τῶν ὑπερεχόντων προσκυνεῖν· ἀλλ᾽ οὐκ ἔστιν οὕτως, κτίσματι γὰρ κτίσμα οὐ προσκυνεῖ, ἀλλὰ κτίσμα Θεόν</note>. 

Those who distinguish *religious worship* into *Latria* and *Dulia* must assume that the general object of worship is anything "superior to us," rather than the Creator alone. *Athanasius* directly contradicts this idea. However, the *Arians* raised an objection against these *Orthodox Fathers*. They pointed out that the *humanity* of our Savior Christ is undoubtedly a *created thing*, yet it is still part of their religious worship. It is worth seeing what account *Athanasius* gives of this:

<margin>To Adelphius, p. 157.</margin>
"We do not worship a created being—God forbid! That is the error of the Pagans and the Arians. Rather, we worship the Lord of creation who became flesh, the Word of God. For even if the flesh itself, considered on its own, is a part..." <note>original Greek: οὐ κτίσμα προσκυνοῦμεν, μὴ γένοιτο· Ἐθνικῶν γὰρ καὶ Ἀρειανῶν ἡ τοιαύτη πλάνη· ἀλλὰ τὸν Κύριον τῆς κτίσεως σαρκωθέντα τὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ λόγον προσκυνοῦμεν· εἰ γὰρ καὶ ἡ σὰρξ αὐτὴ καθ᾽ ἑαυτὴν μέρος</note>

# Chapter IV. The Divinity in Christ.

He was not part of the created things, but became the body of God. We do not worship such a body by itself, separating it from the Word; nor, when we wish to worship the Word, do we distance Him from the flesh. Rather, knowing that "the Word became flesh," we recognize Him as God even when He exists in the flesh. <note>original Greek: μέρος ἦν τῶν κτισμάτων, ἀλλὰ Θεοῦ γέγονε σῶμα, καὶ οὔτε τὸ τοιοῦτον σῶμα, καθ' ἑαυτὸ διαιροῦντες ἀπὸ τοῦ λόγου, προσκυνοῦμεν, οὔτε τὸν λόγον προσκυνῆσαι θέλοντες, μακρύνομεν αὐτὸν ἀπὸ τῆς σαρκός· ἀλλ' εἰδότες, τὸ, ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο, τοῦτον καὶ ἐν σαρκὶ γενόμενον ἐπιγινώσκομεν Θεόν.</note> *We give no religious worship to any created being <note>original: creature</note>; far be it from us! For this is the error of the Pagans and of the Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who taught that Jesus Christ was a created being rather than co-eternal with God the Father</note>. Instead, we worship the Word of God, the Lord of creation, who became incarnate. For though the flesh of Christ, considered alone by itself, was only a part of the created world, it was nevertheless made the Body of God. And we neither worship this body by itself alone, divided from the Word, nor do we remove the Word to a great distance from this flesh when we intend to worship Him. But knowing the Scripture says, "The Word was made flesh," we look upon this Word, even in the flesh, as God.* And again to the same purpose:
<margin>Page 160.</margin>
"And let them know that in worshiping the Lord in the flesh, we do not worship a created being, but the Creator who has put on a created body." <note>original Greek: Καὶ γινωσκέτωσαν ὅτι τὸν Κύριον ἐν σαρκὶ προσκυνοῦντες, οὐ κτίσματι προσκυνοῦμεν, ἀλλὰ τὸν κτίστην, ἐνδυσάμενον τὸ κτιστὸν σῶμα.</note> *Let these Arians finally know that we who worship the Lord in the flesh do not worship a created being, but only the Creator clothed in a created body.* 

For this same reason, Nestorius <note>A 5th-century Archbishop of Constantinople accused of separating Christ into two distinct persons (divine and human)</note> was later branded by the Christian Church with the name "Man-Worshiper" <note>original Greek: Ανθρωπολάτρης</note> or "Idolater." This was because he divided the Word from the flesh—separating the divinity of Christ from His humanity—and failed to acknowledge the proper *hypostatic union* <note>The theological doctrine that Christ is one person with two distinct natures, divine and human</note> between them, even though he still religiously worshiped our Savior, Christ. 

To conclude, some people try to excuse themselves from the charge of idolatry by arguing that they do not give the exact same *religious worship* to saints and angels that is reserved for Almighty God—worship that consists in honoring Him as *self-existent* and the Creator of all things. Because they acknowledge that these others are merely created beings, they assume that for an act to be "idolatry," it must involve the impossible: acknowledging more than one all-powerful Creator, or viewing created beings as creators. This implies that anyone who recognizes *one Supreme God as the Creator of the whole world* is incapable of idolatry, which directly contradicts the doctrine of the ancient Church.

Up to this point, we have answered an *atheistic objection* regarding whether the *idea of God* naturally includes *uniqueness* <note>original: oneliness</note>. This objection was based on pagan *polytheism*. We have proven extensively that, at least among civilized and intelligent Pagans, there was a general acknowledgment of *one sovereign Godhead* <note>original: Numen</note>. Their *polytheism* was partly conceptual <note>original: phantastical</note>—nothing more than the practice of giving many names to one Supreme God <note>original: polyonymy</note>, or worshiping Him through various titles and concepts based on His different powers <note>original: vertues</note> and manifestations. Although they also practiced a form of natural and real *polytheism*, this only involved *many inferior or created gods* who were subordinate to *one Supreme Uncreated God* <note>original Greek: Ἀγένητος</note>.

Nevertheless, we do not confidently claim that the idea of *many independent deities* never entered any mortal mind. Human nature is so changeable and prone to corruption that despite the *innate idea* <note>original: connate idea</note> and intuitive concept <note>original: prolepsis</note> of God in the human mind, some people undoubtedly degenerate and fall into atheism. But as for **independent invisible gods**, we cannot trace the footsteps of such a polytheism anywhere. We find nothing more than a **ditheism** <note>original: "Ditheism" — the belief in two primary, equal, and opposing gods, typically one good and one evil.</note> consisting of a **good** and **evil principle**. Only Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy.</note> and others seem to have believed that among the ancient Pagans, some were so extremely foolish as to assume a plurality of **independent visible gods**, and to mistake the sun, the moon, and all the stars for such. 

However, if there were any such people, and if these writers were not mistaken (as frequently happened), it is certain that they were very few. This is because among the most primitive peoples <note>original: "Barbarian Pagans"</note> today, there is hardly any nation to be found that does not acknowledge a **Sovereign Deity**. This is evident from all the discoveries that have been made since the improvement of navigation.

Therefore, what we have declared so far might well be considered a sufficient answer to the previously mentioned **atheistic objection** against the idea of God. Nevertheless, when we wrote the table of contents for this chapter, we intended to provide a further account of the **natural** and **real polytheism** of the Pagans, and their **varied idolatry**. This was primarily intended to **defend** <note>original: "Vindication"</note> the truth of **Christianity** against **atheists**. One major purpose of Christianity was unquestionably to destroy Pagan polytheism and idolatry, which consisted in **worshiping the creature instead of the Creator**.

But we are very aware that we have been caught off guard by the length of this chapter, which has already grown to a **disproportionate size**. Because of this, we cannot fit all the **remaining contents** into this volume, along with the full and extensive **refutation** <note>original: "Confutation"</note> of **atheistic arguments** as we had intended. Therefore, we will divide the chapter here. We will reserve those remaining contents, along with a further refutation of atheism, for another volume which we intend will follow, if God grants life, health, and time. In the meantime, we are adding only a short and concise **refutation** of all the atheistic arguments that have been proposed.

# That Sense is not Knowledge. Book I.

and head of all things, is not a perfect understanding nature, but that everything sprang from *Tohu and Bohu* <note>original: "Tohu and Bohu"; Hebrew for "waste and void," referring to the primeval chaos described in Genesis 1:2</note>, or dark and senseless matter moved by chance <note>original: "fortuitously moved"</note>. Moreover, we have not only declared the idea of God in this way, but also extensively proved and made it clearly evident that the majority of mankind in all ages has had a *prolepsis* <term>prolepsis: a philosophical term for a preconceived notion or a natural "anticipation" of an idea</term> or anticipation in their minds concerning the real and actual existence of such a Being. Even the pagans themselves—besides their many other gods, who were *intelligent beings superior to men*—acknowledged one chief and sovereign *numen* <note>original: "Numen"; a Latin term for a deity or divine power</note>, the Maker of them all and of the entire world. From this it plainly appears that those few atheists who existed in the past, and those who still exist here and there throughout the world, are nothing other than the monsters and anomalies of humankind. Nevertheless, so that we do not seem to ignore <note>original: "dissemble"</note> any of the atheists' strengths, we shall specifically state all their most plausible excuses <note>original: "colourable pretences"</note> against the idea of God and then show the folly and invalidity of them. These excuses are as follows: *First*, that we have no idea or thought of anything that is not subject to physical sense <note>original: "corporeal sense"</note>, nor the least evidence of the existence of anything except from those senses. *Second*, that because theists themselves acknowledge God to be incomprehensible, it may be inferred from this that He is a non-entity <term>non-entity: something that does not exist</term>. *Third*, that the theists' idea of God, because it includes infinity, is therefore absolutely inconceivable and impossible. *Fourth*, that theology is an arbitrary collection <note>original: "complemen"; likely a misspelling of "complement" or "composition," meaning a constructed set</note> of inconsistent and contradictory notions. And *lastly*, that the idea and existence of God owes its entire existence either to the confused nonsense of terrified <note>original: "astonish'd"</note> minds or else to the fiction and deception <note>original: "imposture"</note> of politicians.

We begin with the first: that we can have no idea, conception, or thought of anything not subject to the senses, nor the least evidence of the existence of anything except from the same. Moreover, the same writer adds that the only evidence we have of the existence of anything is from the senses; the consequence of which is this: because there is no physical sense of a deity, there can be no evidence at all of his existence. Therefore, according to the direction <note>original: "tenour"</note> of atheistic philosophy, everything is reduced to the senses as the only criterion of truth. This aligns with what Protagoras concludes in Plato's *Theaetetus*: that *knowledge is sense perception* <note>original: "Knowledge to be Sense"</note>; and a recent writer of our own determines that *sense is original knowledge*.

If *sense perception* were the same as *knowledge* and *understanding*, then anyone who sees light and colors, or feels heat and cold, would understand light and colors, heat and cold, and all other sensible things. The other kind, through the senses, he calls 'dark,' denying that it is a reliable rule for discerning the truth. His own words are these: 'There are two species of knowledge: one genuine, the other dark or obscure. The dark and obscure knowledge includes sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. But the genuine knowledge is another, more hidden and recondite.'"

In truth and reality, there are only atoms and the vacuum <note>empty space</note>. What are thought to be real are sensory perceptions <note>original: "Sensibles"</note>, but in truth, these are not the reality; only atoms and the vacuum are."

### Thoughts on what is not in the Senses. BOOK 1.

The main foundation for this rational discovery by the ancient **atomists**—that physical sensations like heat and cold, bitter and sweet, or red and green are not *real qualities* in the objects themselves, but only our own *mental images* <note>original: "Phancies"</note>—was the fact that in physical matter, such things are not *intelligible*. Instead, only *magnitude*, *shape* <note>original: "Figure"</note>, *location* <note>original: "Site"</note>, *motion*, and *rest* are understandable properties of matter. Regarding these properties, we have not only *sensible ideas*—which are passively impressed upon us from the outside world—but also *intelligible notions*, which are actively produced by the mind itself. These latter notions, however, are often accompanied by *sensory images* <note>original: "Sensible Phantaſms"</note>, and so many people unskillfully confuse the two. 

Beyond these, we also have other *intelligible notions* or *ideas* that have no *genuine mental images* <note>original: "Phantaſms"</note> associated with them at all. Anyone who doubts this can easily be satisfied and convinced by reading just a sentence or two in almost any book at hand and examining themselves to see whether they have a *sensory image* belonging to *every* single word. Anyone who is honest and open-minded will quickly be forced to confess that they encounter many words which, though they have a *meaning* <note>original: "Sence"</note> or *intelligible notion*, have no *genuine mental image* belonging to them. 

We have known some people who were confidently committed to the opposite opinion, but who were immediately stumped and confused by the very first word of *Cicero's On Duties* <note>original: "Tully’s Offices"</note>, which is *Quanquam* <note>original: "Quanquam" (Latin for "although")</note>. They were neither able to deny that the word had a meaning, nor were they able to claim that they had any mental image for it, other than the *sound* or the *letters*. 

To prove that there are *thoughts* <note>original: "Cogitations"</note> not based on physical sense, we need look no further than this very *idea* or *description of God*: *A Substance, Absolutely Perfect, Infinitely Good, Wise and Powerful, Necessarily Self-existent, and the Cause of all other things*. There is not one word in that description that is unintelligible to anyone with any understanding. Yet, no thoughtful and honest person can pretend that they have a *genuine mental image* or *sensory idea* <note>original: "Sensible Idea"</note> answering to any one of those words—not to *substance*, *absolutely perfect*, *infinitely*, *good*, *wise*, *powerful*, *necessity*, *self-existence*, or *cause*; nor, indeed, to the words *all*, *other*, or *things*. 

Therefore, it is nothing but a lack of reflection, together with a *foolish and obsessive fixation* <note>original: "Fond and Sottiſh Dotage"</note> on physical senses, that has misled some into believing they cannot have the slightest *thought* of anything that is not physical. They wrongly claim that there is nothing in the *human understanding* or *conception* that was not *first* in the *bodily senses*—a doctrine that is highly favorable to **atheism**. 

But since it is certain, on the contrary, that we have many thoughts *not* subject to the senses, it is clear that whatever cannot be perceived by the external senses is not therefore *unthinkable* or *nothing*. Anyone who asserts that must also argue that *life* and *thought* <note>original: "Cogitation"</note> themselves, along with *knowledge*, *understanding*, *reason*, *memory*, *will* <note>original: "Volition"</note>, and *desire* <note>original: "Appetite"</note>—the most significant and real things—are nothing but mere *words* without any meaning. In fact, under this hypothesis, even *imagination* <note>original: "Phancy"</note> and *sensation* themselves could hardly escape being dismissed as non-existent, because neither *imagination* nor *sensation* is perceived by the senses; only their *objects* are. We do not see the act of *vision*, nor feel the act of *touching* <note>original: "Taction"</note>, nor hear the act of *hearing* <note>original: "Audition"</note>, much less...

<summary>This page argues that human understanding includes abstract concepts (like "God" or "although") that have no physical shape or sensory image. It refutes the atheist claim that all thoughts originate in the physical senses, arguing that the mind's highest functions are independent of the body.</summary>

# CHAPTER IV. Evidence of things not perceived by the senses.

...less than hearing sight, or seeing taste, or the like. Therefore, even if God were as physical <note>original: "Corporeal"</note> as some theists have imagined him to be, the **core of his essence**, and as it were his **inner nature**, must be acknowledged by these same people to consist of **Mind**, **Wisdom**, and **Understanding**. Because of this, he could not possibly fall under the perception of the **physical senses** (**sight** or **touch**) any more than a **thought** can. However, it is demonstrated elsewhere that there is also **non-physical substance** <note>original: "Substance Incorporeal"</note>, which is therefore inherently and entirely **invisible**; and that the Deity is such a substance.

We grant, indeed, that the **evidence of specific bodies** existing **here and now** <note>original: *Hic & Nunc*</note> outside of ourselves necessarily depends upon the **information of the senses**. But nevertheless, the **certainty** of this very **evidence** does not come from the **senses** alone, but from a **combination of reason and understanding together with them**. If the **senses** were the only **evidence of things**, there could be no **absolute truth or falsehood**, nor any **certainty** of anything at all. The **senses**, as such, are only **relative** to specific persons; they are **subjective** <note>original: "Seeming and Phantaſtical"</note> and liable to much **delusion**. For if our **nerves** and **brain** are moved and affected internally in the same way they would be by a physical **object** being present—even when it is actually absent—and no other motion or sensation prevails against it to wipe it out, then that **object** must necessarily seem present to us. Furthermore, those **imaginings** that spring and bubble up from the **soul** itself are commonly mistaken by us for **sensations** when we are asleep, and sometimes by melancholic and imaginative people when they are awake. 

That **atheistic principle**—that there is no evidence at all of anything's existence except through the **physical senses**—is plainly contradicted by the **Atomic Atheists** themselves when they assert that **atoms** and the **vacuum** <note>empty space</note> are the **principles** of all things, and that the **shed images** <note>original: "Exuvious Images"; referring to the Epicurean idea that objects shed thin layers of atoms that enter our eyes</note> of bodies are the **causes** of both sight and thought. For **single atoms** and those **shed images** were never **seen** nor **felt**; and the **vacuum**, or **empty space**, is so far from being **perceivable** that these **atheists** themselves allow it to be the **one and only non-physical thing**. Therefore, they must here go beyond the **reach of the senses** and appeal to **reason** alone for the **existence** of these **principles**. 

<margin>As in Plato's *Theaetetus*, page 155, Stephanus edition.</margin> 

**Protagoras**, one of them in **Plato**, professedly does this: <note>original Greek: *ἄθρει δὴ περισκοπῶν μή- τις τῶν ἀμυήτων ἐπακούῃ· εἰσὶ δὲ οὗτοι, οἱ οὐδὲν ἄλλο οἰόμενοι εἶναι, ἢ οὗ ἂν δύνωνται ἀπρὶξ ταῖν χερсὶν λαβέсθαι, πᾶν τὸ ἀόρατον οὐκ ἀποδεχόμενοι, ὡс ἐν οὐсίαс μέρει·*</note> *Take care and look around so that none of the profane and uninitiated in the mysteries overhear you. By the profane, I mean* (he says) *those who think nothing exists except what they can grasp firmly with their hands, and who exclude all that is invisible from the rank of being.* 

If existence were granted to nothing that does not fall under the physical senses, then we would have to deny the existence of the soul and mind in ourselves and others, because we can neither feel nor see any such thing. On the contrary, we are certain of the existence of our own souls, partly from an inward **consciousness** of our own **thoughts** <note>original: "Cogitations"</note>, and partly from that principle of reason: **Nothingness cannot act**. And the existence of other individual souls is revealed to us by their effects upon their respective bodies—their motions, actions, and speech. Therefore, since the **atheists** cannot deny the existence...

<summary>The author argues that human certainty relies on reason rather than just the senses, noting that even materialist atheists believe in invisible things like atoms. He asserts that the existence of the soul is proven through consciousness and its effects on the body, even though it cannot be seen or touched.</summary>

# God, though Incomprehensible, Book I.

...of the soul or mind in men, though no such thing falls under our external senses. They have just as little reason to deny the existence of a **Perfect Mind** presiding over the **universe**. Without such a Mind, it is impossible to conceive how our own imperfect minds could have originated. The existence of that God, **whom no eye has seen nor can see**, is plainly proved by **reason** from His **effects**—seen in the visible phenomena of the universe—and from what we are conscious of within ourselves.

The second excuse used by **atheists** against the idea of **God** (and consequently His **existence**) is based on the fact that **theists** themselves acknowledge God to be **incomprehensible**. From this, atheists infer that He is a **non-entity** <note>A "non-entity" is something that does not exist at all.</note>. This line of reasoning by the atheists assumes two things: first, that whatever is **incomprehensible** is altogether **unconceivable**; and second, that whatever is **unconceivable** is **nothing**. 

The second of these two points might perhaps be granted to them: that whatever is so utterly **unconceivable** that no man can form any kind of **idea** or **conception** of it is therefore—either in itself, or at least to <margin>Plato's *Theaetetus*</margin> us—**nothing**. This is because, even though the saying of **Protagoras** is not entirely true—that **man is the measure of all things: of things that are, that they are; and of things that are not, that they are not** <note>original: "πάντων χρημάτων μέτρον ἄνθρωπον εἶναι, τῶν μὲν ὄντων ὡς ἔσι, τῶν δὲ μὴ ὄντων ὡς οὐκ ἔσι"</note>—there is still some truth to be found in it. Protagoras actually meant that there was no **absolute truth** or **falsehood**, but that everything was **relative** to particular people and only **subjective** <note>original: "Phantastical"</note> or "seeming." 

Furthermore, we must not grant that whatever a man's shallow understanding cannot easily and fully grasp should be immediately erased from the catalog of **beings**. (This flawed logic is the basis for the **rationalism**—or rather, the **infidelity**—of the **Anti-Trinitarians** <note>Anti-Trinitarians were those who rejected the doctrine of the Trinity because they found it impossible to reconcile with human reason.</note>). Yet, there is nonetheless some truth in the statement by **Aristotle** that **the soul is in a way all things** <note>original: "ψυχὴ πῶς πάντα"</note>. The **rational soul** or **mind** is able to form some **idea** and **conception** of whatever exists in the **nature** of things, whether it has an **actual** or **possible existence**, from the very highest to the lowest. 

The **mind** and **understanding** are, as it were, a **transparent** <note>original: "Diaphanous"</note> and **crystalline globe**, or a kind of **world of ideas** <note>original: "Notional World"</note>. This globe contains a **reflected image**, a corresponding **ray**, or a **representation** of whatever exists in the **true** and **real world** of **being**. On this account, it may be said that whatever is in its own **nature absolutely unconceivable** is indeed a **non-entity**.

However, we absolutely deny the first point: that whatever is **incomprehensible** is **unconceivable**. Therefore, when we affirm that **God** is **incomprehensible**, our meaning is only this: that our **imperfect minds** cannot have such a **conception** of His **nature** as to **perfectly master, conquer**, and **subdue** that **vast object** within our thoughts. Our understanding is not so fully **adequate** and **equal** <note>original: "Commensurate"</note> to Him that it can match or equalize His greatness in every way. 

Now, it does not follow at all that because **God** is thus **incomprehensible** to our **finite** and **narrow understandings**, He is utterly **unconceivable** by them, or that we cannot form any **idea** of **Him** at all and must therefore conclude He is a **non-entity**. For it is certain that we cannot even fully **comprehend** our own selves. We do not even have such an **adequate** and **comprehensive knowledge** of the **essence** of any **physical** <note>original: "Substantial"</note> thing, as that...

<summary>The author argues that while God's nature is too vast for the finite human mind to fully "comprehend" or master, He is still "conceivable." He refutes the atheist claim that an incomprehensible God is a non-existent one by explaining the mind's ability to reflect the reality of things it cannot totally grasp.</summary>

### CHAPTER IV. Yet Not Unconceivable.

...that we can perfectly **master** and conquer it. It was a **truth**, though abused by the **Sceptics**, that there is **something incomprehensible** <note>original: *ἀκαταλήπτον τι*</note> in the **essence** of even the **lowest substances**. For even a physical **body** itself—which the **atheists** think they are so well acquainted with because they can feel it with their fingers, and which is the only substance they acknowledge either in themselves or the **universe**—has such puzzling **difficulties** and **entanglements** when we think deeply about it that they can never fully explain it.

We might also point to certain **accidental things** <note>In philosophy, "accidental things" are properties like time or motion that are not essential to a thing's core identity.</note>, such as **time** and **motion**. **Truth** is **bigger** than our **minds**; we are not the **same** as it, but only have a lower **participation** in the **intellectual nature**. We are **apprehenders** <note>those who can grasp or perceive a concept</note> rather than **comprehenders** <note>those who can fully and perfectly grasp every detail of a thing</note> of it. This is indeed one mark of our **state as created beings**: that we do not have a perfectly **comprehensive knowledge**, or one that is **adequate** and **equal** to the **essences** of things. From this, we ought to be led to acknowledge that there is another **perfect mind** or **understanding being** above us in the **universe**, from which our **imperfect minds** were derived and upon which they depend. 

Therefore, if we could have no **idea** or **conception** of anything that we do not have a **full** and **perfect comprehension** of, then we could not have an **idea** or **conception** of the **nature** of any **substance** at all. But even though we do not comprehend all truth as if our **mind** were **above** it or the **master** of it, and we cannot **penetrate** into and look quite through the **nature** of everything, **rational souls** may still form certain **ideas** and **conceptions** of whatever is in the **realm of being** <note>original: *Orb of Being*</note> that are suited to their own **nature** and sufficient for their purpose. 

And though we cannot fully **comprehend** the **Deity**, nor **exhaust** the **infiniteness** of His **perfection**, yet we may have an **idea** or **conception** of a **being absolutely perfect**. Such a conception is **conformed to our own measure** <note>original: *nostro modulo conformis*</note>, suited and proportionate to our **capacity** and **scale**. It is like how we may approach near to a **mountain** and touch it with our hands, even though we cannot encompass it all around or wrap our arms around it. Whatever is in its own **nature absolutely unconceivable** is **nothing**; but this is not true of whatever is simply not fully **comprehensible** by our **imperfect understandings**.

It is true indeed that the **Deity** is more **incomprehensible** to us than anything else, which proceeds from the **fullness** of His **being** and **perfection** and from the **transcendence** of His **brightness**. But for the very same reason, it may also be said in some sense that He is more **knowable** and **conceivable** than anything. Just as the **sun**, though its **excessive splendor** dazzles our weak sight, is nevertheless far more **visible** than any of the **misty stars** <note>original: *nebulosae stellae*</note>. Where there is more **light**, there is more **visibility**; so where there is more **entity**, **reality**, and **perfection**, there is more that can be **conceived** and **known** <note>original: *conceptibility and cognoscibility*</note>. Such an **object** fills up the **mind** more and **acts** more strongly upon it. Nevertheless, because our **weak** and **imperfect minds** are lost in the **vast immensity** and **abundance** of the **Deity**, and overcome with His **transcendent light** and **dazzling brightness**, He therefore has to us an **appearance** of **darkness** and **incomprehensibility**.

Thus

<summary>The author argues that while God is incomprehensible due to His infinite perfection, He is still conceivable and knowable to human reason, much like the sun is the most visible object despite its ability to dazzle and blind the eye.</summary>

# Atheists' Pretense; That there... BOOK I.

Just as the unbounded expansion of light in the clear, transparent **ether** <note>the clear sky or upper atmosphere</note> has for us the appearance of an *azure obscurity* <note>a blue darkness</note>—which is not an absolute thing in itself, but only relative to our senses and a mere *fancy* within us.

The *incomprehensibility* of the *Deity* is so far from being an argument against the *reality* of its *existence* that, on the contrary, it is most certain that if there were nothing *incomprehensible* to us (who are but insignificant pieces and small atoms of the *universe*), then there could be no *God*. If there were no other being in the world but what our *finite* and *imperfect understandings* could span, fathom, encompass, look through and through, have a commanding view of, and perfectly conquer and subdue, then there could be nothing *absolutely* and *infinitely perfect*. For though the saying of *Empedocles* <note>A Greek pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed that "like is known by like."</note> is not true in a literal sense—as it seems to have been taken by *Aristotle*—that "fire appears" <gloss>original: φαίεται μὲν πῦρ</gloss> and so on; that by *earth* we see *earth*, by *water* we see *water*, and by *fire* we see *fire*, understanding everything by something of the same within ourselves; yet it is certain that everything is apprehended by some *internal congruity* in that which perceives it. This was perhaps the sense intended by that noble *philosophic poet*. Therefore, it cannot possibly be otherwise than that the *finiteness, narrowness*, and *imperfection* of our limited *under-standings* must make them *disproportionate* <note>original: "asymmetral"</note> or *incommensurate* to that which is *absolutely* and *infinitely perfect*.

And *nature* itself plainly suggests to us that there is some such *absolutely perfect being*—which, though not *inconceivable*, is yet *incomprehensible* to our *finite understandings*. This is shown by certain *passions* <note>emotions or instincts</note> that nature has implanted in us, which would otherwise lack an *object* to display themselves upon: namely, those of *devout veneration*, *adoration*, and *admiration*, together with a kind of *ecstasy* and *pleasing horror* <note>This refers to the "sublime," an overwhelming sense of awe and dread when facing something vast.</note>. In the silent language of *nature*, these seem to say that there is some *object* in the *world* so much *bigger* and *vaster* than our *mind* and *thoughts* that it is to them what the *ocean* is to narrow *vessels*. When these vessels have taken into themselves as much as they can by *contemplation* and filled up their entire *capacity*, there is still an *immensity* left outside which cannot enter for want of room. Therefore, it must be apprehended in some other strange and more mysterious manner: namely, by our being, as it were, *plunged* into it, and *swallowed up* or *lost* in it. To conclude: the *Deity* is indeed *incomprehensible* to our *finite* and *imperfect understandings*, but not *inconceivable*. Therefore, there is no ground at all for this *atheistic pretense* that would turn God into a *non-entity* <note>something that does not exist</note>.

We come now to the *third atheistic argument*: that because *infinity* (which according to *theology* is included in the *idea* of *God* and pervades all his *attributes*) is utterly *unconceivable*, the *Deity* itself is therefore an *impossibility* and a *non-entity*. To this effect, various passages from a *modern writer* <note>This likely refers to Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), who argued that the human mind cannot conceive of the infinite because all knowledge comes from finite mental images.</note> state that *whatsoever* we *know, we learn from our phantasms* <note>mental images or perceptions</note>, but *there is no phantasms of the infinite*...

<summary>The author argues that God's incomprehensibility is not proof of His non-existence but is a necessary result of a finite mind encountering an infinite being. He suggests that human emotions like awe and veneration point toward a vast reality that transcends our ability to fully contain it within our thoughts.</summary>

# CHAPTER IV. There can be nothing infinite.

...and therefore no *knowledge* or *conception* of it. Again, *whatever we imagine is finite*, and therefore there is no *conception* or *idea* of that which we call *infinite*. No man can have in his mind an *image* of *infinite time* or of *infinite power*. Therefore, the *name of God* is used not to make us conceive of him, but only so that we may honor him. The true meaning of this (as may be plainly gathered from other passages by the same writer <note>Likely referring to Thomas Hobbes, who argued that "infinite" describes the limits of our own minds rather than God's nature.</note>) is to be interpreted as follows: that there is nothing of *philosophic truth* and *reality* in the *idea* or *attributes* of *God*; nor any other sense in those words except to signify the *veneration* and *astonishment* of men's own *confounded minds*.

Accordingly, the word *infinite* is declared to signify nothing at all in the thing so called (since no such thing really exists), but only the *inability* of men’s own minds, together with their *rustic astonishment* <note>original: "rustick"—meaning a crude, unrefined, or uneducated sense of wonder</note> and *admiration*. Therefore, when the same writer determines that *God* must not be said to be *finite*—this being considered poor *courtship* or *compliment*—and yet the word *infinite* signifies nothing in the thing itself, nor has any conception at all answering to it, he either plainly abuses his reader or leaves him to reach this conclusion: that since God is neither *finite* nor *infinite*, he is an *inconceivable nothing*.

In like manner, another learned *well-wisher* to *atheism* declares that he who calls anything *infinite* does nothing but "attribute an unintelligible name to a thing he does not grasp" <note>original: *Rei quam non capit, attribuere nomen quod non intelligit*</note>, attributing an *unintelligible name* to a *thing inconceivable*. He argues this because all *conception* is *finite*, and it is impossible to conceive of anything that has *no bounds* or *limits*. Instead, what is mistaken for *infinite* is nothing but a *confused chaos of the mind* or an *unshaped embryo of thought*. This happens when men, going further and further in a *continual progress* without seeing any *end* before them, finally become quite weary and tired out by this endless *journey*; they sit down and call the *thing* by this *hard* and *unintelligible name*: *infinite*. From this, he also infers that because we can have no *idea* of the *infinite* that signifies anything in the thing so called, we therefore cannot possibly have "any true and genuine idea or notion of God" <note>original: *Germanam Ideam Dei*</note>. Those who understand the *language* of *atheists* know very well that the meaning of this is: there is indeed *no such thing*, or that He is a *non-entity*.

Now, since this *objection* <note>original: "exception"—here meaning a formal objection or challenge</note> against the *idea of God* (and consequently his *existence*) is made by our *modern* <note>original: "neoterick"—meaning recent or modern</note> *atheists*, we shall first show how *contradictory* they are in this regard to their *predecessors*, the *ancient philosophic atheists*. Consequently, we will show how inconsistent and disagreeing atheists have been with one another across different ages. For while these *modern atheists* would have us think it a sufficient refutation of a Deity that *there can be nothing infinite*, it is certain that the ancient *philosophic atheists* were so far from this persuasion that some of them—such as *Anaximander* <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher (c. 610–546 BC) who taught that the beginning of all things was the "apeiron."</note> expressly—made "the Infinite" <note>original: *Ἄπειρον* (Apeiron)</note> the *principle of all things*. That is, they believed in *infinitely extended and eternal matter, devoid of all life and understanding*. For although the "Infinite" <note>original: *Ἄπειρον*</note> of *Melissus* <note>A Greek philosopher of the Eleatic school (5th century BC) who argued that the universe is unchangeable and infinite.</note>—which he made *the first principle*—was a *most perfect being*, eminently...

The author then contrasts this with ancient atheists like Anaximander, who actually embraced the concept of the infinite as the foundation of the material world.</summary>

# Certain; That, Never Nothing. BOOK I.

...permanently containing *all things* (as has been already shown) and therefore the *True Deity*. *Anaximander’s* "*Apeiron* <note>original: *Ἄπειρον*—the "Boundless" or "Infinite"</note> or *Infinite*, even though it was called *Theion* <note>original: *Θεῖον*</note> or *Divine* by him (it being the only *Divinity* which he acknowledged), was nothing but *senseless matter*; an *atheistic infinite*. Therefore, both *theists* and *atheists* in those former times agreed very well on this *one point*: that there was *something* or other *infinite* as the *first principle* of all things, whether it be an *infinite mind* or *infinite matter*. Although this latter *atheistic infinity* of *extended matter* is indeed contrary to rational thought (as shall be proved later), there is no *true infinite* except for a *perfect being*, or the Holy Trinity. 

Furthermore, not only *Anaximander*, but also after him *Democritus*, *Epicurus*, and many others of that atheistic group previously asserted a *numerical infinity of worlds*, and therefore much more than an *infinity of atoms* or *particles of matter*. And though this *numerical infinity* of theirs was also *unconceivable* and *impossible*, it appears clearly from this that these *ancient philosophical atheists* were so far from rejecting *infinity* as an *impossible thing* or a *non-entity* that they were, on the contrary, very fond of it. Therefore, they never attempted to disprove a deity in this manner: *Because there can be nothing infinite.*

But in the next place, we shall make it clear that these modern atheists contradict plain reason and their own arguments just as much as they do their predecessors in that impiety when they try to disprove the existence of a God *because there can be nothing infinite, neither in duration, nor in power, nor in any other regard.* 

For first, even if it were doubted whether there is a God or not, it must be acknowledged as being as certain as anything in all geometry that there was *something* or other *infinite in duration*, or *eternal, without beginning*. Because, if there had once been nothing at all, there could never have been anything; that *common notion* or principle of *reason* has an *irresistible force* here: *that nothing could ever come from nothing.* 

Now, if there was *never nothing*, but *always something*, then there must of necessity be *something infinite in duration and eternal without beginning*. Therefore, it can be considered nothing less than extreme *foolishness* <note>original: "sottishness"—meaning dull-wittedness or stupidity</note> and *stupidity* of mind in these *modern atheists* to attack the concept of a deity based on the *impossibility of infinite duration without beginning*. 

But next, we must confess it seems hardly conceivable to us that any atheist could possibly be so remarkably foolish or so monstrously deluded as to actually think that once there was *nothing* at all, but that afterwards *senseless matter* happened (nobody knows how) to come into being, from which all other things were derived. According to this *hypothesis*, it would also follow that matter might just as well happen to cease to be at some time or other, and so all things would vanish into nothing. To conclude, therefore, these atheists must necessarily be guilty of one of these two things: either extreme *foolishness* and *stupidity* in acknowledging neither God, nor matter, nor anything at all to have existed *infinitely from eternity*...

# CHAPTER 4. Neither the World, nor Time, is Eternal.

...eternity without beginning; or else, if they do acknowledge the **pre-eternity of matter**, or its **infinite past duration** without a beginning, then they are guilty of the most **notorious impudence** by making that an **argument** against the **existence** of a **God** which they themselves attribute to **matter**.

Nevertheless, we shall readily agree with these **modern atheists** on the following **two things**: **First**, that we can have no **proper** and **genuine mental image** <note>original: "phantasm" — a mental representation or image produced by the imagination</note> of anything **infinite** whatsoever. This is because we never had a **physical sensation** of one—neither of an **infinite number** nor of an **infinite magnitude**—and therefore much less of **infinite time** or **duration**, or of **infinite power**. These two **latter** things, **time** and **power**, do not fall under the category of **physical sense**. **Secondly**, just as we have no **mental image** of anything **infinite**, neither is **infinity fully comprehensible** by our human **understandings**, which are only **finite**. 

But since it is certain, even to **mathematical evidence**, that there was **something infinite** in **duration** (or **without beginning**)—so much so that no **intelligent atheist**, upon **mature consideration**, will ever venture to contradict it—we shall use this to force these **atheists** to acknowledge the **falsehood** of these **two theorems** of theirs: ***That whatever we have no mental image or sensible idea of, and whatever is not fully comprehensible by us, is therefore a pure non-entity or nothing.*** We shall force them to confess **that there is something really existing in nature which we have neither any mental image of, nor can yet fully comprehend with our imperfect understandings.**

Indeed, we will go even further to accommodate them and acknowledge as well that, regarding those **infinities** of **number**, of **physical magnitude**, and of **time** or **successive duration**, we have not only no **mental image** nor **full intellectual comprehension** of them, but also no manner of **intelligible idea**, **notion**, or **conception**. For though it is true that **number** is said somewhere by **Aristotle** to be **infinite**, his meaning there was only in a negative **sense**: that we can never possibly come to an **end** of it by **addition**, but may in our minds still add **number** to **number infinitely**. This is the same as if he had indeed affirmed that there can be no **number actually** and **positively infinite**, according to **Aristotle's** own **definition** of **infinite** given elsewhere: namely, ***that to which nothing can be added.*** No **number** is ever so great that **one** or **more** may not still be added to it. 

And just as there can be no **infinite number**, so neither can there be any **infinity** of **physical magnitude**. This is not only because, if there were, its parts would necessarily be **infinite** in **number**, but also because just as no **number** can be so great that **more** may not be added to it, neither can any **body** or **magnitude** ever be so **vast** that more **body** or **magnitude** may not be imagined further and further. This **addition** of **finite things** never results in the **infinite**. Indeed, **infinite space** beyond the **finite world** is a concept that has been much discussed; it is supposed by some to be **infinite body**, but by others to be an **incorporeal infinite**, through whose **actual distance** (which is nonetheless **measurable** by **poles** <note>A "pole" (or rod/perch) is a unit of length equal to 16.5 feet or 5.5 yards.</note> and **miles**)

<summary>The author argues that while human minds cannot imagine or fully comprehend infinity, its existence is a logical necessity. He uses Aristotle's definitions to show that mathematical concepts like number and magnitude cannot be "actually infinite" because they can always be added to, yet something must have existed eternally.</summary>

->Eternity, a Philosophical Book I.<-

This *finite world* might roll and tumble infinitely. But as we conceive it, all that can be demonstrated here is simply this: no matter how vast the *finite world* might be, it is always possible for more *magnitude* and *physical matter* to be added to it, further and further, by *divine power*, infinitely. In other words, the world could never be made so great, even by God Himself, that His own omnipotence could not make it even greater. 

This *potential infinity*—or the *indefinite ability to increase* physical size—seems to have been mistaken for an *actual infinity* of *space*. However, for this very reason—because more could always be added to the magnitude of the physical world without end—it is impossible for it to ever be positively and *actually infinite*. By "actually infinite," we mean something to which nothing more can possibly be added. 

Therefore, we conclude regarding *physical magnitude*, just as we did previously regarding *number*, that there can be no absolute and *actual infinity* of it. Even if the world is much vaster than common astronomers <note>original: "vulgar astronomers" — the mainstream scientific consensus of the era, which often placed the stars in a fixed outer sphere.</note> suppose (those who believe the *starry sphere* is the *outermost wall* of the universe), it is still not absolutely infinite. It does not truly have *no bounds* or *limits* at all, nor is it something to which *nothing* more could be added by *divine power*. 

Finally, we also affirm concerning *time* or *successive duration* <term>successive duration: the passing of time moment-by-moment, like a sequence of events.</term> that there can be no infinity of that either—no *temporal eternity* without a *beginning*. This is not only because such an eternity would result in an *actual infinity* (and more than an infinity) of *numbers*, but also because, under this theory, there would always have been an *infinity of past time*—and consequently, an *infinity of past time* which was never actually *present*. However, every moment of *past time* must have been *present* at some point; and if so, then every moment (at least all but one) must have once been *future* as well. From this, it follows that there was a *first moment* or a *beginning of time*. Thus, reason concludes that neither the *world* nor *time itself* has been *infinite* in its *past duration*, nor *eternal without a beginning*.

At this point, the *atheist* will likely think he has gained a great advantage in disproving the existence of God, asking: "*Do not those who thus destroy the eternity of the world, by the same logic, also destroy the eternity of the world’s Creator?*" <note>original Latin: "Nonne qui Æternitatem Mundi sic tollunt, eâdem operâ etiam Mundi Conditori Æternitatem tollunt?"</note> For if *time itself* were not *eternal*, then how could the *Deity* or anything else be so? The *atheist* confidently takes it for granted that God Himself could not be eternal in any other way than through a *successive flux of infinite time*. 

But we argue, on the contrary, that this provides a clear *demonstration* of the *existence* of a *Deity*. Since the *world* and *time itself* were not *infinite* in their *past duration* but had a *beginning*, they must both have been made together by some other Being. This Being is, by the order of *nature, senior* to time, and exists without time and before time. He is above that *successive flux*, encompassing His *yesterday*, *today*, and *forever* within the *stability* and *unchanging perfection* of His own Being. 

To put it another way: *something* was necessarily *infinite* in *duration* and without a *beginning*. But neither the *world*, nor *motion*, nor *time*—that is, no *successive being*—was such a thing. Therefore, there is something else whose *being* and *duration* is not successive...
