# C H A P. IV. *Attributes of the Deity.*

...cessive and *flowing*, but *permanent*; to whom this *infinity* belongs.
*Atheists* can only sneer or mock at this point, showing their limited wit by quibbling over the *Standing Now* <note>original: *Nunc-stans* — a Latin philosophical term for an eternal present that does not pass away.</note> or a *Standing Now of Eternity*. They act as if that *standing eternity* of the *Deity* (which has been argued for with such *reason* by the ancient, genuine *Theists*) were nothing but a *pathetic little moment of time frozen in place*. They speak as if the *duration* of all *beings* whatsoever must necessarily be like our own. However, the *duration* of every thing must of necessity agree with its *nature*. Therefore, just as something with an *imperfect nature* is always *flowing* like a *river*—consisting of *continual motion* and *changes* one after another—it must also have a *successive* and *flowing duration*. It slides perpetually from the *present* into the *past* and is always rushing toward the *future*, waiting for *something* of itself which is *not yet* in existence, but is still to come. In the same way, that being whose *perfect nature* is *essentially unchangeable*, always the *same*, and *necessarily existent*, must have a *permanent duration*. It never loses any part of itself that was once *present* (as if it slid away), nor does it run forward to meet *something* of itself that does not yet exist. It is as *contradictory* for such a being to have ever begun as it is for it to ever *cease* to be.

Now, the *modern atheists* pretend to have proved that *nothing is infinite*—neither in *duration* nor in any other way—and consequently that there is *no Deity*. They claim this merely because we have no *physical sense* or *mental image* of the *infinite*, nor can we *fully comprehend* it. Therefore, they conclude that the *words* *infinite* and *eternal* signify nothing in the thing itself. Instead, they claim these words only represent men's own *ignorance* and *inability* to conceive *when* or *if* that which is called *eternal* began. They suggest these terms are born from the *confused nonsense* of *astonished minds* and a *mindless veneration* of a *bogeyman* raised up by their own *fears* and *fancies*. Or, they claim it is merely the *progress* of their *thoughts* moving further and further backward *indefinitely*. (Though they plainly contradict themselves in all this by sometimes acknowledging that *matter* and *motion* are *infinite* and *eternal*, which proves either their *extreme foolishness* or their *nerve*.) 

We have shown with *mathematical evidence* and *certainty* that there is really something *infinite in duration* or *eternal*. By this, we do not mean men's own *ignorance*, the *confused nonsense* of their *devotion*, nor the *pointless progress* of their *minds* moving further and further *indefinitely* (which never actually reaches the *infinite*). Rather, it refers to a *reality* in the thing itself: namely, that it *never was non-existent* and had no *beginning*. Moreover, having *demonstrated* regarding this *infinity* and *eternity* without a *beginning* that it cannot possibly belong to any *successive being* <term>successive being: a being that exists moment-to-moment through time, like humans or the physical world.</term>, we confidently conclude against these *atheists* as well. It was not *matter* and *motion*, or this *physical universe*, but a *perfect, unchangeable nature* of a *permanent duration* (that is, a *God*) to whom eternity belonged. 

To sum up everything, therefore, we say that *infinite* and *eternal* are not *words* that signify nothing in the thing itself. Nor are they merely *titles of honor*, *compliments*, or *flattery*—that is, *devout* and *religious nonsense*, *error*, and *falsehood*. Rather, they are *attributes* belonging to the *Deity*, and to Him alone, in the most *philosophical* sense.

<header>646 Omnipotence, not to be Extended B O O K I.</header>

Truth and Reality. And though we, being *finite*, have no *full comprehension* or *complete understanding* of this *Infinity* and *Eternity* (just as we do not of the *Deity*), yet we cannot be without some *notion, conception*, and *apprehension* of it. We can demonstrate that it belongs to something, and yet to nothing except a *Perfect, Unchangeable Nature*. But the notion of this *Infinite Eternity* will be further clarified in the following *explanation and defense of Infinite Power.*

For the *atheists* primarily quarrel with *Infinite Power*, or *Omnipotence*. In the same way, they pretend that this is *utterly inconceivable*, *impossible*, and *attached to nothing*. Thus, a *modern atheistic writer* <note>The author likely refers to Thomas Hobbes, who argued that terms like "infinite" were merely expressions of our own limitations or titles of respect rather than descriptions of reality.</note> concludes that since *no man can conceive Infinite Power*, this is also nothing but an *attribute of honor* which the *confused nonsense of astonished minds* bestows upon the *object* of their *devotion*, without any *philosophical truth or reality*. Here, our *modern atheists* indeed have the *support* and *agreement* of the ancient *philosophical atheists* as well. As appears from the *verses* previously cited from *Lucretius* <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), a Roman poet and philosopher who argued for atomism and against divine intervention.</note>, they concerned themselves with nothing more than asserting that *all power is finite*, and that *Omnipotence*, or *Infinite Power, belongs to nothing.*

First, therefore, it is observable here that this *Omnipotence* or *Infinite Power* asserted by *theists* has been commonly either ignorantly mistaken or willfully misrepresented by these *atheists*. They do this by design to make it seem *impossible* and *ridiculous*, as if it meant a *power of producing and doing anything whatsoever without exception*, even if it were *contradictory*. For instance, a recent *atheistic person*, while appearing to assert this *Divine Omnipotence* and *Infinite Power*, really and intentionally abused the concept with this *mocking irony*: *That God, by His Omnipotence or Infinite Power, could turn this tree into a syllogism.* <note>original: "scoptick irony" — a syllogism is a formal logical argument (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal). The atheist is mocking the idea that God could turn a physical object into a logical structure.</note> Children, indeed, sometimes have such *childish apprehensions* of the *Divine Omnipotence*. Even *René Descartes* <note>original: "Ren. Cartesius" — the Latinized name of the French philosopher (1596–1650).</note> (though otherwise a *sharp philosopher*) was no less *childish* here. He affirmed that all things whatsoever—even the *natures of good and evil*, and all *truth* and *falsehood*—depend so much on the *arbitrary will and power of God* that *if He had pleased, two times two would not have been four, nor would the three angles of a plane triangle have been equal to two right angles*, and the like. He only added that, despite this, once these things were settled by the *Divine Decree*, they became *unchangeable*—meaning, I suppose, not in themselves or to God, but to us. No *paradox* of any old *philosopher* was ever more *absurd* and *irrational* than this. Certainly, if anyone desired to persuade the world that *Descartes*, despite all his pretenses of *demonstrating a Deity*, was actually a *hypocritical theist* or a *disguised atheist*, he could find no better evidence in all his writings than this point. This is plainly to destroy the *Deity* by making one *attribute* of God *devour and swallow up another*: making *Infinite Will and Power* consume *Infinite Understanding and Wisdom.* For to suppose God to *understand* and to be *wise* only because of His *will* is the same as to suppose Him...

<header>Chapter IV. Relating to Contradictory Things.</header>

him to have really no *understanding* at all. Therefore, we do not affirm God to be so *omnipotent* or *infinitely powerful* that he is able to destroy or change the *intelligible natures* <note>The essential qualities of things that can be understood by the mind.</note> of things at his pleasure; for this would be the same as saying that God is so *omnipotent* and *infinitely powerful* that he is able to destroy, or to baffle and make a fool of his own *wisdom* and *understanding*—which is the very rule and measure of his *power*. We do not say, therefore, that God, by his *omnipotence* or *infinite power*, could make *two times two* not equal *four*, or turn a tree into a *syllogism* <note>A formal logical argument consisting of two premises and a conclusion.</note>; but we say that *omnipotence* or *infinite power* is that which can *produce* and *do* all whatever is *possible*—that is, whatever is *conceivable* and implies no manner of *contradiction*. The very *essence* of *possibility* is nothing other than *conceivability*. And this is how the point has been stated all along, not only by *Christian theists*, but even by the *ancient pagan theologians* themselves: that *omnipotence* or *infinite power* is that which can do all things that do not imply a *contradiction*, or which are not *unconceivable*. This is evident from the words of *Agatho* <note>A Greek tragic poet (c. 448–400 BC).</note>, cited previously from *Aristotle*, that *nothing is exempted from the divine power* except the ability to make "what has been done to be undone" <note>original Greek: πεπραγμένα ἀγένητα</note>, or other things similar to this. Now, since *infinite power* is nothing else but a power of doing whatever is *conceivable*, it is plainly absurd to say that a *power* of doing nothing but what is *conceivable* is itself *unconceivable*.

<margin>*What infinity means.*</margin>
But because the atheists view *infinity* as such a *desperate* and *frightening* thing, we shall here make it somewhat easier to understand. We will take off that frightening mask from it, which makes it seem like such a *mormo* <note>A Greek "bogeyman" or female spirit used to frighten children.</note> or bugbear to them, by declaring in the next place that *infinity* is really nothing else but *perfection*. For *infinite understanding* and *knowledge* is nothing other than *perfect knowledge*—that which has no *defect* or mixture of ignorance in it, or the *knowledge* of whatever is *knowable*. In the same way, *infinite power* is nothing other than *perfect power*—that which has no *defect* or mixture of weakness in it; a *power* of producing and doing all whatever is *possible*, which is to say, whatever is *conceivable*. *Infinite power* can do whatever *infinite understanding* can *conceive*, and nothing else. Conception is the measure of power and its extent, and whatever is in itself *unconceivable* is therefore *impossible*. Lastly, *infinity* of duration, or *eternity*, is really nothing else but *perfection*, as it includes necessary existence and immutability <note>The state of being unchangeable.</note> within it. So it is not only contradictory for such a being to cease to be or exist, but also to have had a "newness" or beginning of being, or to have any flux or change within it by *dying* to the *present* and acquiring something new to itself which it did not have before. Despite this, this being comprehends the differences of *past*, *present*, and *future*, or the *successive order* of all *temporary things*. And because *infinity* is *perfection*, nothing that includes any element of imperfection in its very *idea* and *essence* can ever be truly and properly *infinite*—such as *number*, *physical magnitude*, and *successive duration*. All of these can only *counterfeit and imitate infinity* <note>original Latin: Mentiri Infinitatem</note> by having more and more added to them *infinitely*, whereby

...even though they never reach it or overtake it. There is nothing truly *infinite*—neither in *knowledge*, nor in *power*, nor in *duration*—except for *one absolutely perfect being*, or *the Holy Trinity*.

Now, it is evident that we have an *idea* or *conception* of *perfection*, or a *perfect being*, based on the notion of *imperfection* that is so familiar to us. *Perfection* is the rule and *measure* of *imperfection*, not the other way around; just as a *straight line* is the *rule* and *measure* of a *crooked line*, and not a *crooked line* the measure of a *straight* one. Thus, *perfection* is *first conceivable* in the order of nature before *imperfection*, just as *light* comes before *darkness*, and a *positive* state comes before a *privative* <note>original: "Privative"; a term in philosophy for the absence or lack of a quality that should normally be present (like blindness being the privative of sight).</note> state or a defect. For *perfection* is not properly the lack of *imperfection*, but rather *imperfection* is the lack of *perfection*. 

Moreover, we perceive different degrees of *perfection* in the essences of things, and consequently, a *scale* or *ladder* of *perfections* in nature, one above another: such as *living* and *animated things* being above *senseless* and *inanimate* things, and *rational things* being above those that are merely *sensitive* <note>Having the ability to perceive through senses, but lacking higher reasoning.</note>. This perception exists because of that notion or *idea* which we first have of that which is *absolutely perfect* as the standard. By comparing things with this standard and measuring them against it, we notice their approach toward it to a greater or lesser degree. Indeed, these *gradual ascents* could not be *infinite* or *without end*; they must eventually arrive at that which is *absolutely perfect* as the summit of them all. 

Lastly, we could not perceive *imperfection* in even the most *perfect* of all those things we have ever experienced in our lives if we did not have a *notion* or *idea* of that which is *absolutely perfect*, against which we secretly compare them and perceive them to fall short. We might also add that it is not conceivable how any *lesser perfection* could exist in any category unless there were *first* something *perfect* in that category from which it was derived. 

The following words from *Boethius* <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher; this quote is from his "Consolation of Philosophy," Book 4.</note> express the very sense and language of nature in rational beings: "Everything that is said to be imperfect is held to be imperfect because of a lessening of that which is perfect. From this it follows that if in any kind of thing something appears to be imperfect, there must necessarily be something perfect in that same kind. For if perfection were removed, one could not even imagine where that which is considered imperfect could have come from. For the nature of things did not take its beginning from unfinished and imperfect things; but proceeding from things whole and absolute, it descends into these lower, worn-out, and exhausted states." <note>original Latin: "Omne quod Imperfectum esse dicitur, id deminutione Perfecti Imperfectum esse perhibetur. Quò fit, ut si in quolibet genere Imperfectum quid esse videatur, in eo Perfectum quoque aliquid esse, necesse sit. Etenim sublata Perfectione, unde illud, quod Imperfectum perhibetur, exstiterit, ne fingi quidem potest. Neque enim à Diminutis Inconsummatisque, Natura Rerum cepit exordium; sed ab Integris Absolutisque procedens, in hæc extrema, atque effæta dilabitur."</note> But of this, more will be said elsewhere.

Therefore, since *infinite* is the same as *absolutely perfect*, because we have a notion or *idea* of the latter, we must necessarily have one of the former.

# Chapter IV. Theology is Not Contradictory

...measure. From this, we also learn that although the word *infinite* is negative in its form, its *meaning*—in those things that are truly capable of it—is *positive*. It is the same as being *absolutely perfect*. Similarly, the *meaning* of the word *finite* is *negative*, as it is the same as being *imperfect*. Thus, *finite* is properly the *negation* of *infinite*, as the infinite comes before it in the order of nature; *infinite* is not merely the negation of the *finite*. However, in things that are incapable of true *infinity* because they are *essentially finite*—such as *numbers*, *physical size*, and *time*—*infinity* is a merely *imaginary thing* and a *non-entity*. In those cases, it can only be conceived by the *negation* of the *finite*, just as we conceive of *nothing* by the *negation* of *something*; that is, we can have no *positive conception* of it at all.

We conclude that to assert an *infinite being* is nothing other than to assert a being that is *absolutely perfect*—one who *never was not* (had no *beginning*), who could produce all things *possible* and *conceivable*, and upon whom all other things must depend. This is to assert the existence of a *God*: one *absolutely perfect being* who is the *origin of all things*. *God*, *infinite*, and *absolutely perfect* are simply different *names* for *one and the same thing*.

We come now to the *fourth atheistic objection*: that *theology is nothing but an arbitrary compilation of inconsistent and contradictory notions*. First, we do not deny that some *theologians* (or *bigoted religious thinkers*) of recent times extend *divine omnipotence* to things that are *contradictory* and *impossible*, such as *making one and the same body exist entirely in several different places at once*. <note>This is likely a reference to debates over the Real Presence in the Eucharist, where some argued a physical body could be in multiple locations simultaneously.</note> Likewise, others may sometimes unskillfully attribute *inconsistent* or *contradictory* things to the *Deity* because they seem to be *perfections*. 

For example, although it is generally concluded by *theologians* that there is a *natural justice* and *holiness* in the *Deity*, some nevertheless argue that the *will of God* is not determined by any *prior rule* or *nature of justice*. Instead, they believe that whatever he might be supposed to *will arbitrarily* would therefore be *just by that very fact*. They call this *divine sovereignty* and view it as a *great perfection*. However, it is certain that these *two things* are directly *contradictory* to one another: namely, *that there is something just and unjust by nature* <note>original: φύσει (*physei*)</note> (meaning there is a *natural holiness in God*), and *that the arbitrary will and command of the Deity is the only rule of justice and injustice*. 

Furthermore, some *theologians* determine that *whatever is in God is God*, or *essential to the Deity*. Because they conceive such *immutability* <note>The quality of being unchanging.</note> to be a *necessary perfection*, they seem to not only *contradict* the idea of *freedom of will* in the *Deity* (which they themselves nevertheless argue for to a high degree, claiming all things are *arbitrarily determined* by *divine decree*), but they also take away from God all *power of acting outwardly* <note>original: "ad Extra"; acting upon things outside of Himself, such as creating or interacting with the universe.</note>, and of *perceiving* or *noticing things done sequentially here in the world*. But it does not follow from these and similar *contradictions* made by mistaken *theologians* that *theology* itself is *contradictory* or has no *philosophical truth* in it at all; no...

<header>God's Understanding, without BOOK I.</header>

...any more than the fact that *philosophers* hold *contradictory opinions* means that *philosophy* itself is *contradictory*, or that there is *nothing absolutely true or false*, but (according to the *Protagorean doctrine* <note>The belief attributed to Protagoras that "man is the measure of all things," implying truth is relative and subjective.</note>) that all truth is merely *seeming and imaginary*.

But next, we add that although it is true that the *nature of things* admits nothing *contradictory*, and that whatever plainly implies a *contradiction* must necessarily be a *non-entity* <term>something that does not exist</term>, this rule is still prone to being much abused. This happens when men conclude that whatever their *shallow and coarse understandings* cannot grasp must immediately be *contradictory* and *impossible*. 

For example, *atheists and materialists* cannot conceive of any *substance* other than *body* <note>original: "Body"; in this context, it refers to physical, three-dimensional matter.</note>. Therefore, they immediately decide that an *incorporeal substance* is a contradiction in terms—as if one were saying "incorporeal body." Consequently, when *theologians* say *God* is an *incorporeal substance*, to these men, it is an *absolute impossibility*. 

As a *modern writer* <note>Referring to Thomas Hobbes, whose materialist philosophy argued that only physical matter exists.</note> puts it: 
> *The universe—that is, the whole mass of all things—is corporeal, which is to say, it is body. Now, every part of a body is a body, and consequently, every part of the universe is a body; and that which is not body is no part of it. And because the universe is everything, that which is no part of it is nothing. Therefore, when spirits are called incorporeal, this is only a title of honor; it may be attributed with more piety to God himself, in whom we consider not which attribute best expresses his nature (which is incomprehensible), but which best expresses our desire to honor him.* 

In this view, the word *incorporeal* is said to be merely an *attribute of honor*—that is, an attribute that expresses only the *reverence* in men’s minds but signifies nothing in nature and has no *philosophical truth or reality* behind it. To them, an *incorporeal substance* is as *contradictory* as saying something is "both something and nothing." 

Despite this, the contradiction exists only in the *weakness and childishness* of these men’s *understandings*, not in the thing itself. It can be demonstrated that there is another *substance* besides *body*, according to the *true and genuine definition* of it. However, because this mistake is not limited to *atheists*—since some *theists* also suffer from this same *mental weakness* of being unable to conceive of any *substance* other than *body*, and therefore argue for a *corporeal God*—we shall next show, from a passage by a *modern writer*, what kind of *contradictions* these *atheists* attribute to all *theology*. 

Specifically, they claim theology supposes *God* to *perceive physical things* without any *organs of sense*, and to *understand and be wise without any brains*. 
> *Pious men (he says) attribute to God Almighty, for the sake of honor, whatever they see as honorable in the world, such as seeing, hearing, willing, knowing, justice, wisdom, and so on. But they deny him such lowly things as eyes, ears, and brains—organs without which we worms neither have, nor can imagine, such faculties to exist. So far, they do well. But when they dispute God’s actions philosophically, they then consider them again as if He did indeed have such faculties.* 

This is a mistake, and that is why they fall into so many difficulties. We ought not to dispute *God’s nature*; He is not a fit subject for our *philosophy*.

# Chapter IV. Brains, no Contradiction.

True religion consists of obedience to Christ's representatives <note>original: "Lieutenants"; referring to the "Erastian" view that the sovereign or civil ruler holds authority over the church.</note>, and in giving God such honor, both in attributes and actions, as they, in their various positions of authority, shall ordain. Here, the plain and undisguised meaning of the author seems to be this: that God is not a subject of philosophy, as all real things are. (As he declares elsewhere, "Religion is not a matter of philosophy, but only of law and arbitrary constitution." <note>original: "Religio non est Philosophia sed Lex"</note>). According to this view, God has no real nature of His own, nor is He a true inhabitant of the world or heaven. Instead, He is—like all other ghosts and spirits—only an inhabitant of men's brains; that is, a figment of their fear and fancy, or a mere political scarecrow.

Therefore, such attributes are to be given to Him without any hesitation <term>original: "scrupulosity"</term>, exactly as the civil law of every country appoints, and no other. The wise and clever <term>original: "nasute"; literally meaning having a keen sense of smell, used here to mean perceptive or shrewd</term> very well understand that this whole business of religion is nothing but mere pageantry. They believe the attributes of the Deity actually signify nothing true or false, nor anything in nature; they represent only men’s *reverence* and *devotion* toward the object of their *fear*, the expression of which is determined by civil law. 

Therefore, it is acceptable enough—so long as they are only *attributes of honor* signifying *devotion*—to say that God sees all things and yet has no eyes; that He hears all things and yet has no ears; and that He understands and is wise and yet has no brains (or whatever else you please to say of Him). But when men who do not understand the true secret <term>original: "cabal"; here meaning the hidden logic of the materialist position</term> try to go further, they mistake *attributes of honor* for *attributes of nature* and philosophical truth. They use them as premises to infer absolute truth, to refute falsehood, or as matters to dispute and reason upon. That is, when they insist on supposing that such a thing as a God *really* exists in the world, they involve themselves in all manner of *contradiction*, *nonsense*, and *absurdity*.

For example, they seriously affirm that this God *really* sees everything in the world and yet has no eyes; that He indeed hears all things and yet has no ears; and finally, that He understands and is wise and yet has no brains. To the atheist, these things are all absolutely contradictory, inconceivable, and impossible. The sum of it all is this: when religion and theology (which are really nothing but *law* and *fantasy* <note>original: "Phantastry"</note>) are turned into *philosophy*, they become mere jargon and meaningless nonsense.

Now we see the nature of those *contradictions* that the atheists charge against theology. These contradictions only exist because of the *coarseness*, *stupidity*, and *brutishness* of these men’s own understandings. This is also where the following definition of knowledge and understanding comes from: *that it is nothing but a disturbance <note>original: "tumult"</note> of the mind, caused by external things pressing against the physical organs of a man's body.* 

"O you brutish people, when will you understand? And you fools, when will you be wise? He who planted the ear (and gave man's soul the power of hearing through it), shall He not hear—even though He Himself has no ears? He who formed the eye (and gave the human soul the power of seeing, using the eye as an instrument), shall He not see—even though He Himself has no eyes? Finally, He who teaches man knowledge (or gave him an understanding mind, in addition to brains), shall He not know and understand—even though He Himself is without brains?" <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 94:8–10, used here to argue that the Creator must possess the faculties He gives to His creatures, even if He does not possess their physical organs.</note>

# The Attributes of God. Book 1.

It is certain that no *simple idea*, such as that of a *triangle*, a *square*, a *cube*, or a *sphere*, can possibly be *contradictory* <note>original: "contradictious"</note> to itself. Therefore, it is even less possible for the *idea* of a *Perfect Being* (which is the *comprehensive* <note>original: "compendious"</note> *idea of God*) to be so, since it is even *simpler* than any of the others. Indeed, this *simple idea* of a *Perfect Being* is *full of* <note>original: "pregnant of"</note> many *attributes*. Therefore, the *idea* of *God*, when fully explained by all of them, might seem in this respect to be a *composite* <note>original: "compounded"</note> *idea*—one *conception consisting* of *many* parts. If these parts were truly *contradictory*, they would make the whole thing a *non-entity* <term>something that cannot exist in reality because it is logically impossible</term>. 

For example, a *flat triangle whose three angles are greater than two right angles* is *contradictory* and *unconceivable*; therefore, it is not a *true idea* but a *non-entity*. However, all the *genuine attributes of the Deity* that make up its *entire idea* are as *demonstrable* for a *Perfect Being* as the *properties* of a *triangle* or a *square* are for those respective ideas. Therefore, they cannot *possibly* be *contradictory*—neither to the idea of God nor to one another—because things that agree with a *third thing* must also agree with each other.

Furthermore, the *genuine attributes of the Deity*—specifically those that can be *proven* to belong to an *absolutely Perfect Being*—are not only not *contradictory*, but are also *necessarily connected* and *inseparable from one another*. It would be impossible for there to be *one thing infinite in wisdom only, another thing infinite only in power*, and *another thing infinite only in duration (or eternal)*. Instead, the very same thing that is *infinite in wisdom* must also be *infinite in power* and *infinite in duration*, and *the other way around* <note>original: "vice versâ"</note>. Whatever is *infinite* in any one *perfection* must, of necessity, possess all *perfections*. In this way, all the *genuine attributes of the Deity* are not only consistent but are also *inseparably linked* <note>original: "concatenate"</note>. The *idea* of *God* is not a *collection* <note>original: "congeries"</note> of *conflicting* things, nor of things that are only loosely *connected* to one another.

In truth, all the various *attributes* of the *Deity* are nothing more than *partial* and *incomplete* <note>original: "inadequate"</note> *conceptions* of *one and the same, simple, Perfect Being*. We view it, as it were, piece by piece, because of the *imperfection* of our *human understandings*, which cannot fully *grasp* it all at once. Therefore, they are *really* all but *one thing*, though they have the *appearance of many* to us. Just as the *one simple light of the sun*, when *refracted* and *reflected* differently from a *dewy* <term>original: "rorid"</term> *cloud*, appears to us as the various *colors* of the *rainbow*.

Therefore, the *attributes of God* are not a *bundle of inconceivable* and *impossible* ideas *jumbled* <note>original: "huddled"</note> together. Nor are they *attributes* given merely for *honor* and *compliment*—the *religious nonsense* of *awed* <note>original: "astonish'd"</note> *minds* expressing *devotion* toward something they *fear*. Instead, they are all *attributes of nature* and of *most rigorous* <note>original: "severe"</note> *philosophical truth*. Nor is the *idea* of *God* an *arbitrary* <note>original: "arbitrarious"</note> *compilation* of things *unnecessarily connected* and separable from one another:

### CHAP. IV. Devout Religious Nonsense.

...another: it is no *manufactured* <note>original: "Factitious"</note> nor *fake* thing, made up by any *inventive power* of the soul. Instead, it is a *natural* and most *simple, non-composite idea*. It is the kind of idea to which nothing can be *arbitrarily* added, and from which nothing can be taken away. 

Despite this, because of the imperfection of human minds, there can be—and are—different understandings concerning it. For just as everyone who has a concept of a *plain triangle* in general does not necessarily know that it includes the property of having *three angles equal to two right angles* (180 degrees); nor does everyone who has an *idea* of a *right-angled triangle* <note>original: "Rectangular Triangle"</note> immediately understand that the *square of the hypotenuse* <note>original: "Subtense"</note> is *equal to the squares of both the sides*; so neither does everyone who has a conception of a *Perfect Being* immediately know everything that is included in that *idea*. Furthermore, people may easily mistake things for *absolute perfections* which are not actually so, as has already been partially shown.

And now, whereas the atheists claim next to give an account of that *supposed contradictoriness* in the *idea and attributes of God*—namely, that it proceeded principally from *fear*, or the *confused nonsense of people’s terrified minds*, huddling together every imaginable *attribute of honor, courtliness, and flattery* <note>original: "Complement"</note> without any *philosophical truth, sense, or meaning*—as well as in part from the *fiction and trickery of politicians*: all of this has been already anticipated. Its foundation has been quite taken away by our showing that there is nothing in the *genuine idea of God* and His *attributes* but what is *demonstrable of a Perfect Being*. Nothing can be the least bit *added* to that *idea*, or *taken* from it, any more than anything can be *added* to or *taken from the idea of a triangle or of a square*.

From this it follows unavoidably that there cannot possibly be anything either *contradictory or arbitrary in the Divine Idea*. The genuine attributes of it are *attributes of necessary philosophical truth*. That is to say, they are attributes that do not only express the *piety, devotion, and reverence* of people's own minds, but declare the *real nature* of the thing itself. 

Therefore, when a *modern atheist writer* <note>This is a reference to Thomas Hobbes and his critique of scholastic theology.</note> claims of all those who reason and conclude concerning *God’s nature* from His *attributes*: *That losing their understanding in the very first attempt, they fall from one absurdity to another without end, in the same way as someone ignorant of royal court ceremonies, coming into the presence of a greater person than he was used to speaking to, and stumbling at his entrance, lets slip his cloak to save himself from falling, then drops his hat to recover his cloak, and so with one disorder after another, reveals his rural ignorance and shock*—we say that although there is some *wit and imagination* <note>original: "Phancy"</note> in this, yet as it is applied to theology and the *genuine attributes of the Deity*, there is not the slightest *philosophical truth* in it.

# Fear and Ignorance of Causes; BOOK I.

...most highly dishonor him, by representing him as a being who is in no way *lovable* <note>original: "Amiable"</note> or *desirable*.

But the *atheists* are most of all concerned with explaining that *undeniable phenomenon*: the *general belief* <note>original: "Persuasion"</note> in the *existence* of a *God* within the minds of men, and their *inclination* <note>original: "Propensity"</note> toward *religion* in all ages and places of the world. They wonder where this comes from if no such thing actually exists in nature. They think they can explain this, finally, *partly* from people's *own fear* combined with their *ignorance of causes*, and *partly* from the *inventions of lawmakers* and *politicians* who try to keep people in civil obedience. First, we shall plainly and simply state the *atheists’* meaning, and then demonstrate the *invalidity* and *foolishness* of these excuses for explaining the aforementioned *phenomenon*.

First, then, these atheists claim that because of their *natural weakness* <note>original: "Imbecillity"</note>, mankind lives in perpetual *worry*, *anxiety*, and *fear* concerning *future events* or their *good* and *bad fortune* to come. This *passion of fear* inclines people to *imagine* things that are *formidable* and *frightening*, and to *suspect* or *believe* in the *existence* of things that do not actually exist. I say that this *distrustful fear* and *jealousy* in the minds of men concerning their *future condition* creates for them the *phantom* <note>original: "Phantasm"</note> of a most *terrifying specter*: an *invisible, intelligent being* who *arbitrarily governs* and *influences* the affairs of the whole world, *tyrannizing over mankind* at will. 

And when people’s *excessive fear* and *imagination* have thus created such a *mormo* <note>original: "Mormo"; a Greek term for a biting female spirit or bugbear used to frighten children</note> or *bugbear*—a terrifying specter that is not truly an *inhabitant of the world* or of *heaven*, but only of people’s *brains*—they afterward stand in awe of their *own imagination*. They tremblingly worship this *creation* and *figment* of their own *fear* and *fancy* as something *really existing* outside of themselves, or as a *God*. They devise all manner of expressions of *honor* and *reverence* toward it, anxiously trying, by every conceivable way, to appease <note>original: "Propitiate"</note> and make amends to it. Thus, they have brought upon themselves a most heavy *yoke of bondage* and filled their *lives* with all kinds of bitterness and misery.

Furthermore, to this *fear of future events*, the atheists also add *ignorance of causes* as a further *explanation for this phenomenon of religion* which is so generally accepted in the world. For mankind (they say) are *naturally inquisitive* about the *causes* of things—not only the *events* of their *own good* and *bad fortune*, but also the *phenomena of the world* and the *effects* of *nature*. And such is their *curiosity* that wherever they cannot discover *visible* and *natural causes*, they are prone to *invent* and *imagine* other *invisible* and *supernatural causes*. 

It was observed of the *tragic playwrights* that whenever they could not easily resolve a plot, they were wont to bring a god onto the stage <note>original: "Deus ex machina"</note>. Similarly, *Aristotle* records of *Anaxagoras* <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BC) was a philosopher who argued that "Mind" (Nous) was the primary cause of the universe's order.</note> that he never resorted to *Mind* or *Understanding* (that is, to *God*) as a *cause*, except when he was at a loss for other *natural* and *necessary causes*. ### CHAP. IV. The Atheists' Seeds of Religion

...Anaxagoras to assert a *Deity*. They turn to this as a kind of *refuge*, *asylum*, or *sanctuary* for their *ignorance*.

They are so superstitiously addicted to *signs*, *portents*, *oracles*, *divinations*, and *prophecies* because of the same delusional <note>original: "Phantastick"</note> supposition: that the things of the *world* are managed not by *nature*, but by some *intelligent* and *purposeful agent* or *person*.

Therefore, they have skillfully exploited *people's fear and ignorance* and nurtured those *seeds of religion* in them (which they view as weaknesses of human nature). They further confirmed the public belief in *ghosts and spirits, miracles and wonders, oracles and divinations* through stories or fables that are publicly permitted and promoted. According to that *definition of religion* given by a *modern writer*:

> *Fear of an invisible power, feigned by the mind or imagined from stories publicly allowed, is religion; when not allowed, it is superstition.*

And so that religion, nurtured by politicians, might be entirely compliant with and obedient to their designs—and in no way resistant <note>original: "Refractory"</note> to them—it has been their great care to persuade the people that their laws were not merely their own...

### Chapter IV. The Old Atheist Clique <note>original: "Cabal"; refers to a secret group or traditional school of thought</note>

**Religion:** As also that this *opinion* proceeds from the *ignorance* of how to distinguish *dreams* and other strong *mental images* <note>original: "Phancies"</note> from *vision* and *sensation*; he seems herein to have also followed in the *footsteps* of *Lucretius*, who gives the same account of *religion* in his *Fifth Book*:

-> *Now, what cause has spread the divinity of the Gods throughout great nations,* <-
-> *And filled cities with altars, and so forth,* <-
-> *It is not so difficult to explain in words.* <-
-> *For indeed, even then, the mortal generations of men* <-
-> *Saw the noble faces of the Gods with waking minds,* <-
-> *And even more so in sleep, with wonderful bodily size.* <-
-> *To these, therefore, they attributed sensation, and so forth.* <note>original: "Nunc quæ cauſa Deûm per magnas Numina gentes... His igitur Senſum tribuebant, &c." from Lucretius's *De Rerum Natura*</note> <-

**That is,** *How the noise of the Gods came to ring over the whole world and to fill all places with temples and altars is not a very difficult thing to account for. It proceeded first from men’s fearful dreams and their illusions <note>original: "Phantasms"</note> while awake, which they mistook for visions and sensations. Based on this, they attributed not only sensation to these things as if they were real, but also immortality and great power.* For although this was properly an account only of those *inferior* and *common gods* called *demons* and *spirits* <note>original: "Genii"</note>, yet it was supposed that the belief in these things easily disposed the minds of men to be persuaded of *one supreme, omnipotent Deity over all*.

Lastly, that the *ancient atheists*, as well as the *modern* ones, claimed that the *concept of a God* and *religion* was a **political invention**, is frequently declared in the writings of the *Pagans*. We see this in the work of *Cicero*: *Those who said that the entire opinion concerning the immortal Gods was invented <note>original: "fictam"</note> by wise men for the sake of the commonwealth—so that religion might lead those to their duty whom reason could not—did they not utterly destroy all religion?* <note>original: "Ii qui dixerunt totam de Diis Immortalibus Opinionem... nonne omnem Religionem funditus ſuſtulerunt?" from Cicero's *De Natura Deorum*</note> And the sense of the *ancient atheists* is represented by *Plato* in this way:
<margin>*On the Laws, Book 10*</margin>
*They first of all affirm, my dear friend, that the Gods exist not by nature, but by artifice <note>original: "τέχνη" (techne)</note> and laws only; and that from this it happens that they are different for different nations and countries, just as the various temperaments of their lawmakers happened to determine.* <note>original: "θεὸς, ὦ μακάριε, εἶναι πρῶτόν φασιν ὗτοι τέχνη, ὐ φύσει, ἀλλὰ τισὶ νόμοις..."</note> And before *Plato*, *Critias*—one of the *Thirty Tyrants* of *Athens*—plainly declared *religion* to have been at first a **political intrigue** in those verses of his recorded by *Sextus* the *Philosopher*. They begin to this effect: *That there was a time at first when men’s lives were disorderly and brutish, and the will of the stronger was the only law. After this, they consented and agreed together to make civil laws, so that the disorderly might be punished.* Notwithstanding this, it was still found that men were only hindered from open injustices, but not from secret ones. At that point, some sagacious and witty person was the author of a further invention to deter men from secret injuries as well as open ones;

Namely, by *introducing* or *inventing* an *Immortal* and *Incorruptible God*, *who hears and sees and takes notice of all things*. *Critias* <note>An ancient Greek author and politician who famously argued that gods were a "noble lie" created to enforce laws through divine fear.</note> then concluding his poem in these words:

-> In this way, I think, someone first persuaded <-

Thus have we fully declared the sense of the atheists in their account of the *phenomenon* of religion and the *belief* in a *God*. Namely, they derive it principally from these *three* springs or origins: *First*, from men’s own *fear* and *anxiety* concerning *future events*, or their *good* and *bad fortune*. *Secondly*, from their *ignorance* of the *causes* of both those *events* and the *phenomena* of *nature*, together with their *curiosity*. And *lastly*, from the *fiction* of *government rulers*, *lawmakers*, and *politicians*. 

We shall now briefly demonstrate the *weakness* and *folly* of all these claims. *First*, therefore, it is certain that such an *excess* of *fear*—which makes anyone constantly and stubbornly believe in the *existence* of something for which there is no ground in either *senses* or *reason*, and which tends toward the great *unrest* of people's own lives and the *terror* of *their minds*—cannot be considered anything other than a kind of *insanity* or *distraction*. Therefore, when the atheists themselves acknowledge that the *generality* of mankind is possessed by such a *belief* in a *Deity*, yet resolve this into such an *excess of fear*, it is the same as if they were to claim that the majority of mankind is frightened out of their wits, or *crazed* and *disturbed* in their brains. They imply that none but a few atheists, who being undaunted and undismayed have escaped this *panic terror*, remain *sober* and in their *right senses*. 

But whereas the atheists thus attribute to the majority of mankind not only *light-minded gullibility* and *fantasy*, but also such an *excess of fear* as differs not at all from *insanity* and *distraction* or *madness*; we affirm on the contrary that their supposed *courage*, *steadiness*, and *sobriety* is really nothing else but the *dull* and *foolish stupidity* of their minds. It is a *dead* and *heavy disbelief* and *earthly distrust*; because of this, they will believe nothing but what they can *feel* or *see*.

Theists indeed have a *religious fear* of God, which follows from him or their belief in him (*of which we will say more later*); but the Deity itself, or the belief in it, was not *created* by any *prior fear*—that is, by *fear concerning men’s good and bad fortune*—it being

<header>Chapter 4. Not a Monster or a Source of Terror.</header>

It is certain that no one is less *anxious* <note>original: "solicitous"</note> concerning such *events* than those who are most truly *religious*. The reason for this is that religious people place their *chief good* in nothing that is foreign <note>original: ἀλλότριον (allotrion)</note>, *alien*, or in *another's power* and exposed to the *strokes of fortune*. Instead, they place it in what is most truly their *own*: namely, the *right use of their own will*. 

Atheists, on the contrary, must necessarily be liable to great *fears* and *anxieties* concerning *external events* for this very reason: they place their *good* and *evil* in the passions of pleasure and pain <note>original: πάθη ἡδονῆς καὶ λύπης (pathē hēdonēs kai lypēs)</note>. Or, at the very least, by denying *natural honesty*, they acknowledge no other *good* but what belongs to the *animal life only* <note>the life of physical senses and instincts</note>, and which is therefore under the *empire of fortune*. It seems plainly apparent that atheists are indeed generally *timorous* and *fearful*, *suspicious* and *distrustful* creatures; this is seen in how they build all their *politics*, *civil societies*, and *justice* (improperly so called) upon the sole *foundation of fear and distrust*.

But the *grand error* of the *atheists* here is this: they suppose the *deity*, according to the sense of the majority of mankind, to be nothing but a *monster* <note>original: "Mormo," a Greek bugbear or specter</note>, *bug-bear*, or *object of terror* <note>original: "Terriculum"</note>—a *frightful*, *harmful*, and most *undesirable thing*. On the contrary, people everywhere invoke the deity for aid and assistance in their straits and difficulties; they look upon God as *appeasable* <note>original: "Exorable and Placable"</note> and, by their *trust* and *confidence* in him, acknowledge his *goodness* and *benevolence*. <margin>Synesius, *On Kingship*, page 9.</margin> *Synesius* affirms that, though men were otherwise much divided in their opinions, yet "all people everywhere, both the wise and the unwise, agree in this: that God is to be praised as one who is good and kind." <note>original: ἀγαθὸν τὸν θεὸν ὑμνοῦσιν ἅπαντες ἅπανταχοῦ καὶ σοφοὶ καὶ ἄσοφοι (agathon ton theon hymnousin hapantes hapantachou kai sophoi kai asophoi)</note>

If among the pagans there were any who understood that *proverbial speech*, "the deity is envious" <note>original: φθονερὸν τὸ δαιμόνιον (phthoneron to daimonion)</note>, in the worst sense—as if *God Almighty* were of an *envious* and *spiteful nature*—these were certainly but a few *ill-natured men* who drew a picture of the deity according to their own *likeness*. For that proverb, in that sense, was disclaimed and cried down by all the wiser pagans. One such was *Aristotle*, who affirmed that the *poets* lied in this, just as they did in many other things. <margin>Metaphysics, Book 1, Chapter 2: "Furthermore, it is possible for the deity to be envious, but poets tell many lies." <note>original: ἔτι τὸ θεῖον φθονερὸν ἐνδέχεται εἶναι, ἀλλὰ πολλὰ ψεύδονται ἀοιδοί</note> On the Malignity of Herodotus.</margin> Another was *Plutarch*, who criticized *Herodotus* for insinuating that "the deity is entirely envious and troublesome or spiteful" <note>original: τὸ θεῖον πᾶν φθονερόν τε καὶ ταραχῶδες (to theion pan phthoneron te kai tarachōdes)</note> (meaning all the gods). 

*Plutarch himself* attributed this envious trait only to that *evil demon* or *principle* he asserted; this appears from his *Life of Paulus Æmilius*, where he affirms not that "the deity is universally of an envious nature," but "that there is a certain deity or demon whose proper task it is to bring down all great and overwhelming human prosperity, and so to temper every man's life that none may be happy in this world purely and without mixture, without a check of adversity." This is essentially how a Christian would describe the actions of the *Devil*. And *Plato* plainly declares the reason for God making the world in the first place was no other than this: "He was good, and in one who is good, no envy ever arises toward anything." <note>original: ἀγαθὸς ἦν, ἀγαθῷ δὲ οὐδεὶς περὶ οὐδενὸς οὐδέποτε ἐγγίγνεται φθόνος (agathos ēn, agathō de oudeis peri oudenos oudepote engignetai phthonos)</note> From this he also concluded that "He willed that all things should be made as much like himself as possible." <note>original: πάντα ὅτι μάλιστα ἐβουλήθη γενέσθαι παραπλήσια αὑτῷ (panta hoti malista eboulēthē genesthai paraplēsia hautō)</note> That God—

<header>The Sense of: *The divine is envious* <note>original: τὸ θεῖον φθονερὸν (to theion phthoneron)</note>. Book I.</header>

...therefore [he] willed that all things should be made as much like himself as possible—that is, in the best manner. But the true meaning of that *ill-spoken proverb* seems at first to have been nothing other than what (besides the poet *Hesiod*) the Scripture itself also attributes to Almighty God: that he affects to humble and abase the *pride of men*, and to pull down all *high, towering, and lofty things*. He does this either because they are harmful and injurious to the men themselves, or because they are in some sense *enviable* <note>original: "invidious"; here meaning something that provokes a challenge to God's unique status</note> to him and derogatory to his honor—for he alone ought to be exalted, and no flesh should glory before him. There has been so much experience of this very thing in the world that even the Epicurean poet <note>The Roman poet Lucretius</note> himself could not help but confess that there was some hidden force or *power* which seemed to have a spite against all *over-swelling greatness*, and takes pleasure in casting contempt and scorn upon the pride of men:

<margin>Lambinus's edition of Lucretius, page 503.</margin>

> ->*So much does some hidden force*<-
> ->*Crush human affairs, and seems to trample upon*<-
> ->*The beautiful rods and cruel axes <note>symbols of Roman political power</note>, holding them in derision.*<-
> <note>original: "Usque adeo res humanas Vis Abdita quaedam / Obterit, & pulchros fasces, saevasque secures, / Proculcare, ac ludibrio sibi habere videtur."</note>

In saying this, he plainly reeled and staggered in his *atheism*, or else was indeed a *theist* but did not know it. It is certain that there can be no such force as this *in the kingdom of atoms* <note>original: "in Regno Atomorum"</note>—that is, in a universe governed by *senseless atoms*. 

As for those among Christians who create such a horrid representation of Almighty God—as one who created the far greatest part of mankind for no other end or design but that he might recreate and delight himself in their *eternal torments*—these people also do nothing but transcribe or copy out their own *ill nature* <note>their own malicious character</note> and then project it onto the *Deity*. On the contrary, the Scripture declares *that God is love*. Nevertheless, these very persons meanwhile dearly hug and embrace Almighty God in their own imagination as one who is *indulgently good, kind, and gracious* to themselves; they believe he has fastened his affections upon their very *persons* without any consideration for their *dispositions* or *qualities*.

It is true indeed that *religion* is often expressed in the Scripture as the *fear of God*. It has been said that *fear* is the *first measure of the Divinity in us* <note>original: "Prima Mensura Deitatis"</note>, or the *first impression* that religion makes upon men in this *vulnerable* <note>original: "obnoxious"; meaning liable to judgment or punishment</note> and guilty state, before they have arrived at the *true love of God and righteousness*. But this *religious fear* is not a *fear of God* as a merely *arbitrary, omnipotent being*, much less as *harmful and mischievous* (which could not be separated from *hatred*). Rather, it is an awesome regard for him as one who is *essentially just*, and who is as much a *punisher of vice and wickedness* as he is a *rewarder of virtue*. Lucretius himself, when he describes this *religious fear* in men, confesses it to be joined with a conscience of their duty, or to include duty within itself:

<margin>Page 503.</margin>

> ->*Then peoples and nations tremble, etc.,*<-
> ->*Lest for some foul deed committed or proud word spoken,*<-
> ->*The heavy time for paying the penalty has arrived.*<-
> <note>original: "Tunc Populi Gentesque tremunt, &c. / Ne quod ob admissum foede dictumve superbe, / Poenarum grave sit solvendi tempus adactum."</note>

<page-num>661</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER IV. How God is the Object of Fear.</header>

And this is the sense of the generality of mankind: that there being a *natural difference between moral good and evil*, there is an impartial *justice* in the *Deity* which presides over it, and inclines God to *punish the wicked* as well as to *reward the virtuous*. *Epicurus* himself acknowledged this much: "From this source, they believe the greatest harms are brought upon the wicked by the gods, and benefits upon the good" <note>original Greek: ἔνθεν καὶ μεγίστὰς βλάβας οἴονται, τοῖς κακοῖς ἐκ θεῶν ἐπάγεσθαι, καὶ ὠφελείας τοῖς ἀγαθοῖς</note>.
<margin>Epicurus, *Letter to Menoeceus*, page 46 in Gassendi's edition.</margin>
And this fear of God is not only beneficial to mankind in general by repressing the growth of wickedness, but also wholesome and beneficial to those very persons themselves who are thus *religiously affected*. It serves as a preservative for them, protecting them both from *moral evils* and from the *punishments* that follow them. 

This is the *true and genuine fear of religion*. When this fear degenerates into a *dark kind of jealous and suspicious fear of God Almighty*—viewing Him either as a *harmful* being or as a merely *arbitrary and tyrannical being*—then it is looked upon as the *vice or extreme of religion* and distinguished from it by the name <term>superstition</term> <note>original Greek: δεισιδαιμονία (deisidaimonia)</note>. Thus, the *character of a superstitious man* is given by *Plutarch*: "He thinks there are gods, but that they are distressing and harmful" <note>original: οἴεται θεὸς εἶναι, λυπηρὸς δὲ καὶ βλαβερός</note>; and "a superstitious man must necessarily hate God, as well as fear Him" <note>original: ἀνάγκη καὶ μισεῖν τὸν δεισιδαίμονα καὶ φοβεῖσθαι τοὺς θεούς</note>. 
<margin>Plutarch, *On Superstition*.</margin>
The *true fear of God* (as the *Son of Sirach* speaks) "is the beginning of His love, and faith is the beginning of cleaving to Him" <note>Sirach 25:12, from the Biblical Apocrypha</note>.
<margin>Sirach, Chapter 25, verse 12.</margin>
It is as if he should have said: *The first entrance into religion is an awful regard for God as the punisher of vice; the second step forward is faith or confidence in God, by which men rely upon Him for good and cleave to Him; and the top and perfection of all religion is the love of God above all, as the most lovable being.* 

Christianity, the best of religions, recommends *faith* to us as the inlet or introduction into all *true and noble piety*. For *he who comes to God must not only believe that He is, but also that He is a rewarder of those who seek Him*. 
<margin>Hebrews, Chapter 11, verse 1.</margin>
This *faith* is better defined in the Scripture than by any *scholastic theologian* <note>original: "Scholastick"; referring to the medieval academic philosophers</note> as the *substance of things hoped for, and the evidence of things not seen*. That is, a *confident persuasion of things that do not fall under our sight (because they are either invisible or in the future) and which are also to be hoped for*. So, *religious fear* is quite consistent with *faith*, and *faith* is closely related to *hope*, and the result of both *faith* and *hope* is *love*. These three—*faith, hope, and love*—all suppose an *essential goodness in the Deity*. 

God is such a being that if He did not exist, He would be, of all things, the most to be *wished* for. Indeed, it is in no way desirable (as that noble *Emperor* <note>Marcus Aurelius</note> concluded) for a man to live in a world void of a *God* and *providence*. He who believes in a *God* believes in all the *good* and *perfection* in the *universe* that his heart can possibly wish or desire. It is in the interest of no one that there should be no God, except for those wretched persons who have abandoned their first and only true interest—being good and being friends to God—and are desperately resolved upon paths of wickedness.

God, and to conceive of him differently from the majority of mankind—as a being who is only to be feared, and must consequently be hated—stems from nothing but their own *vice* and *ill nature*. Because they cannot help but truly *hate* that which *hinders* them from their *true liberty* and *chief good*, they inevitably interpret the *severity* of the *Deity* (which is so often spoken of as being against *wickedness*) to be nothing else but *cruelty* and *arbitrary tyranny*. That is, it comes from either being vulnerable to another’s power or standing in need of their help. So, according to these thinkers, all that is now called *love* and *friendship* among men is really nothing but either a *crouching under another's power, whom they cannot resist*, or else *a certain kind of trading for utilities* <note>original: "mercatura quædam utilitatum"</note>. <header>CHAPTER IV. No Faith or Hope in Atheism.</header>

...then it is obvious that men's obligation to obey him lies upon them only because of their **weakness** <note>original: "Imbeccillity"</note>. Or, as it is further explained by him: **"Men are therefore only subject to God because they are not omnipotent, or because they do not have enough power to resist him"** <note>original Latin: "Homines ideò Deo subjectos esse, quia Omnipotentes non sunt, aut quia ad Resistendum satis Virium non habent"</note>. Thus we see plainly how the atheists—by reason of their **vice** and **ill nature** (which makes them deny all **natural justice and honesty**, and all **natural charity and benevolence**)—transform the Deity into a monstrous shape. They imagine such an **omnipotent being** who, if he existed, would possess neither **justice** nor **benevolence** toward his **creatures**. His only **right** and **authority** to command them would be his **irresistible power**. His **creatures** could not place any **hope, trust, or confidence** in him, nor have any other **obligation** to obey him than that of **fear** and **necessity**, resulting from their **weakness** or **inability** to resist him. Such a deity as this is indeed a **boogeyman** <note>original: "Mormo"; a Greek name for a terrifying spirit used to frighten children</note> or **bugbear**—a most **formidable** and **frightful** thing.

But all of this is nothing but the **atheist’s false imagination**. **True religion** represents a most comfortable prospect of things coming from the **Deity**. On the contrary, the **atheistic view of things** is **dismal, hopeless, and forlorn**. It suggests that there is no other "good" than that which depends on things wholly outside our own power: the momentary gratification of our **insatiable appetites**, which is like perpetually pouring water into a **leaking vessel** <note>original: "Dolium Pertusum"; a reference to the Danaids of Greek myth, condemned in Hades to pour water into a perforated jar</note>. It suggests that we ourselves are but a **heap** <note>original: "Congeries"</note> of **atoms**, and upon the dissolution of our **structure** <note>original: "Compages"</note>, our life will vanish into nothing and all our **hope** will perish. It claims there is no **providence** over us, nor any **kind and good-natured being** above to take care of us, there being nothing outside of ourselves but **dead** and **senseless matter**. It is true, indeed, that there could be no spiteful designs in **sensless atoms** or a **dark, unconscious nature**.

<margin>
Plutarch, *On Superstition*.
</margin>

On this account, **Plutarch** would grant that even this **atheistic hypothesis** itself, as bad as it is, was nevertheless to be preferred over the idea of an **omnipotent, spiteful, and malicious being** (if such a theory could even exist). Such a being would be a **monarchy** of the **Manichean evil principle** <note>A reference to the followers of Mani, who believed the universe was a struggle between two equal powers of Good and Evil</note>, reigning all alone over the whole world without any **rival** and having an undisturbed **empire**. Nevertheless, it is also certain that there could be no **faith** or **hope** in these **senseless atoms**, which are moved both **necessarily** and **randomly** <note>original: "Fortuitously"</note>. There can be no more **faith** and **hope** in them than there could be in a **whirlwind** or in a **tempestuous sea**, whose merciless waves are **unrelenting** <note>original: "Inexorable"</note> and deaf to all **cries and supplications**.

<margin>
Epicurus, *Letter to Menoeceus*, page 49, Gassendi edition.
</margin>

For this reason, **Epicurus** himself confessed that it was better to give credit to the **"fable of the gods"** (as he calls it) than to serve **atheistic fate** or that **material necessity** of all things introduced by those **atheistic natural philosophers** <note>original: "Physiologers"</note> **Leucippus** and **Democritus**. He wrote: **"It would be better to follow the myth concerning the gods than the fate of the naturalists; for the one suggests a hope of winning over the gods through worship, while the other holds an unavoidable necessity"** <note>original Greek: "κρεῖττον ἦν τῷ περὶ θεῶν μύθῳ κατακολουθεῖν, ἢ τῇ τῶν φυσικῶν εἱμαρμένῃ· ὁ μὲν γὰρ ἐλπίδα παραιτήσεως ὑπογράφει θεῶν διὰ τιμῆς· ἡ δὲ ἀπαραίτητον ἔχει τὴν ἀνάγκην"</note>. And though **Epicurus** thought to improve the matter and make the **atheistic hypothesis** more tolerable by introducing into it (contrary to the **tenor** of those **principles**) **liberty**...

It highlights that even Epicurus found the myths of the gods preferable to a world of cold, mechanical fate where prayer and hope are useless.</summary>

And what **comfort** could his **freedom of will** provide him then, since he placed all his happiness in **security from external evils**? The goal of not believing in gods is not to fear them, (**said Plutarch**). <note>original Greek: "Τέλο ͂ τ ͂  μὴ νομίζειν Θεὸς, μὴ φοβεῖσθαι"</note> The **atheistic plan** in **shaking off the belief in a God was to be without fear**; but by doing so, they designed such a system for themselves that they could not have the least **hope, faith, or confidence**. Thus, in running from **fear**, they plunged themselves into **fear**; for those who are without **hope** can never be free from **fear**. The fears and anxieties of those men must necessarily be endless, who shake off that **one fear of God**—which would only preserve them from **evil**—and yet have no **faith** or **hope** in him. 

Therefore, we might conclude on better grounds than the atheists do regarding **theism**, that **atheism** (which has no foundation at all in nature or reason) springs first from the **deception of fear** <note>original: "Imposture of Fear"</note>. For the **faith of religion** is the **substance** or **confidence** of things **not seen** which are **hoped for**. On the contrary, **atheistic infidelity** must necessarily be a certain heavy **distrust, despondency, and misgiving of mind**, or a **timorous distrust and disbelief in good** that is to be hoped for beyond the reach of the senses. Namely, a disbelief in an **invisible, omnipotent being** who exercises a **just, kind, and gracious providence** over all those who commit their ways to him and endeavor to please him, both in this life and after death. 

But **vice**, or the **love of lawless liberty**, prevailing over such disbelieving persons, makes them gradually more and more desirous that there should be no God. That is, they wish for no such **hinderer of their liberty**, and consider it a happiness to be freed from the fear of him whose **justice** (if he existed) they would certainly be liable to.

And now we have made it evident that these atheists—who claim that religion and the **belief in a God** proceed from the **deception of fear**—do first of all disguise the **Deity**. They put a **monstrous, horrid, and frightening mask** <note>original: "Vizard"</note> upon it, transforming it into something that can only be feared and hated. Then they conclude (as they well might) that there is no such thing as this really existing in nature, but that it is only a **boogeyman** <note>original: "Mormo"</note> or **bugbear** <note>term: an imaginary creature used to inspire fear</note> raised up by men's fear and imagination. Of the two, it might be better said that the **opinion of a God** sprang from men's **hope for good** than from their **fear of evil**. But really, it springs from neither **hope** nor **fear** (though in different circumstances it raises both those passions in our minds). # CHAPTER IV. Theism does not come from Ignorance of Causes.

The belief in God is supported by the strongest and clearest **reason**, as will be demonstrated in the proper place. However, because the sense of a **deity** often **precedes our logical reasoning** <note>original: "Preventing Ratiocination" - in this context, 'preventing' means to come before or anticipate</note> and strikes us more **immediately**, it is certain that besides a **rational belief**, there is also a **natural intuition** <note>original: "Prolepsis"</note> or anticipation in the minds of men concerning it. Aristotle calls this *vaticination* <note>original Greek: μαντεία (manteia) - an instinctive or prophetic sense</note>.

Thus have we sufficiently refuted the **first atheistic claim**, which attempts to explain the phenomenon of religion and the **belief in a God**—so generally accepted—as a mere **deception of fear**. We come now to the **second claim**: that it proceeded from the **ignorance of causes** as well, or men's lack of **science** <note>original: "Philosophy" - specifically natural philosophy or the study of physical causes</note>. The atheists argue that people are prone, because of their **innate curiosity**, to invent or imagine **causes** where they find none. <margin>Lucretius, page 500.</margin> They claim that in the **absence** of **natural** and **necessary causes**, men's **fear** leads them to imagine **supernatural** and **divine** ones; this also provides them with a convenient **cover** and **pretext** for their **ignorance**. For this reason, these atheists do not hesitate to say of **Almighty** God what some philosophers say of "hidden qualities": that he is nothing but a **refuge and sanctuary for ignorance** <note>original Latin: "Perfugium & Asylum Ignorantiæ"</note>—or, in plain and blunt language, **the mere sanctuary of fools**.

Atheists commonly join these two things together—both **fear** and the **ignorance of causes**—as factors that work together to **produce theism**. They believe that just as the **fear of children** creates **monsters** <note>original: "Bugbears"</note> especially in the **dark**, so the **fear of men** in the **darkness** of their **ignorance of causes** creates the **bogeyman** <note>original: "Mormo" - a spirit from Greek folklore used to frighten children</note>, **specter**, or **phantom** of a **God**. This is suggested by the Epicurean poet Lucretius:

---

-> *They fear everything* <-
-> *In the blind darkness.* <-
<note>original Latin: "Omnia Cæcis / In tenebris Metuunt."</note>

<margin>Stephanus, Philosophical Poetry, p. 158, etc. Sextus Empiricus.</margin>
Accordingly, **Democritus** gave this account of the **origin of theism** or **religion**: *When in ancient times, men observed strange and terrifying events in the atmosphere and the heavens, such as thunder, lightning, thunderbolts, and eclipses of the sun and moon, they did not know the causes. Being terrified by them, they immediately attributed these things to the gods.* <note>original Greek: ὁρῶντες τὰ ἐν τοῖς μετεώροις παθήματα οἱ παλαιοὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων, καθάπερ βροντὰς καὶ ἀστραπάς, καὶ κεραυνούς, ἡλίου τε καὶ σελήνης ἐκλείψεις, ἐφοβοῦντο θεοὺς οἰόμενοι τούτων αἰτίους</note> And **Epicurus** declares this to have been the reason why he took such great pains in the study of **physics** <note>original: "Physiology" - the study of the laws of nature</note>: so that by finding out the **natural** and **necessary causes** of things, he might be able to free both himself and others from the **terror of a God** which would otherwise **invade** and **assault** them. He believed the **restlessness of men's minds**—whenever they are at a loss for **natural causes**—drives them toward **fear, suspicion, and anxiety regarding a deity**.

Therefore, when atheists dabble in **physics** and find—or think they find—**material and mechanical causes** for some of the **phenomena of nature** (especially those that the uneducated **masses** <note>original: "Vulgar"</note> sometimes attribute to God himself), they believe they can prove...

Eclipses

<page-num>666</page-num>
# Atheists, Ignorant of Causes. Book I.

---

Eclipses, for example, are shown to be no miracles; this makes it probable that thunder is not the "Voice of God Almighty" himself—as if he were roaring above in the heavens merely to frighten and amaze poor mortals, making them quake and tremble. It also suggests that thunderbolts are not thrown by his own hands as the terrible messengers of his anger and displeasure. Upon discovering these natural causes, atheists immediately conclude triumphantly regarding Nature or Matter that it does:

> ->*Nature itself, by itself, of its own accord, performs all things without the gods.*<- <note>original Latin: "Ipsa suâ per se, sponte, omnia, Diis agere expers"</note>

> ->Do all things alone of itself without a God.<-

But we shall show here in a few instances, as briefly as we can, that philosophy and the true knowledge of causes lead to God; and that atheism is nothing but an ignorance of causes and of philosophy.

For first, no atheist who derives everything from senseless atoms or matter is able to assign any cause at all for himself, or give any true account of the origin of his own soul or mind. It is utterly inconceivable and impossible that soul and mind—sense, reason, and understanding—should ever arise from irrational and senseless matter, however it is modified. Nor could they result from atoms that lack all manner of qualities; that is, from mere size, shape, position, and the motion of parts. For though it is indeed absurd to say (as these atheists allege) that "laughing and crying things" are made out of "laughing and crying principles"—

> ->*And he can laugh who is not made of laughing elements;*<- <note>original Latin: "Et Ridere potest non ex Ridentibu' factus"</note>

Yet it does not therefore follow that sensitive and rational beings might result from a combination of irrational and senseless atoms. According to the Democritic hypothesis <note>original: "Democritick Hypothesis" — the theory of Democritus that the world is composed of tiny, indivisible units of matter called atoms</note>, these atoms have nothing in them but magnitude, shape, position, and motion or rest. This is because laughing and crying are motions that result from the mechanism of human bodies organized in a certain way; however, sense and understanding are neither local motion nor mechanism. 

The case remains exactly the same in both the Anaximandrian or Hylopathian <note>The belief that everything arises from "prime matter" and its qualities, such as heat and cold</note> and in the Stratonic or Hylozoic <note>The belief that matter itself possesses a primitive form of life or "life-force"</note> forms of atheism. This is because sense and conscious understanding could no more result from those qualities of heat and cold, or moist and dry mixed <note>original: "contempered"</note> together—or from the mere organization of inanimate and senseless matter—than it could from the:

> ->*Collisions, motions, order, positions, and shapes*<- <note>original Latin: "Concursus, Motus, Ordo, Positura, Figuræ"</note>

of atoms devoid of all manner of qualities. Had there once been nothing but senseless matter, moved by chance <note>original: "Fortuitously Moved"</note>, no soul or mind, sense or understanding, could ever have emerged into being. This is because no effect can possibly transcend the perfection of its cause. Therefore, atheists are wrong to suppose that they themselves, and all souls and minds, have sprung from stupid and senseless matter; and that all the wisdom which is found anywhere in the world, both political and philosophical, [comes from such a source].

<summary>Cudworth argues that atheism is rooted in an ignorance of causes, asserting that senseless matter or atoms can never produce conscious mind, reason, or soul. He contends that an effect cannot be more "perfect" than its cause, meaning intelligence must come from a pre-existing intelligence (God) rather than random matter.</summary>
