# Chapter IV. Of the Cause of Themselves.

...to be the result of mere *fortune* and *chance*, they must be concluded to be *grossly ignorant of causes*. Had they not been so, they could never have been *atheists*. Thus, *ignorance of causes* is the *seed* not of *theism* but of *atheism*; true *philosophy* and the *knowledge of our own cause* lead necessarily to a *Deity*.

Furthermore, *atheists* are *ignorant of the cause of motion in bodies* as well, despite the fact that they suppose all things are done by it. That is, they are never able to *solve this phenomenon* <note>original: "salve this phænomenon"; in this context, "salve" means to explain or account for</note> as long as they remain *atheists* and acknowledge no substance other than *matter* or *body*. For *first*, it is undeniably certain that *motion* is not *essential* to all *body* as such, because if it were, no particles of matter could ever *rest*. Consequently, there could have been no creation or production of a *worldly system* <note>original: "Mundane System"</note> such as this, which requires a specific, proportional mixture of *motion* and *rest*. There would be no Sun, Moon, Earth, or animal bodies, since there could be no coherent stability in anything while all things fluttered and were in continual *separation* and *tearing apart* <note>original: "divulsion"</note> from one another. 

Similarly, it is certain that matter or body as such has no power to *move* itself *freely* or *spontaneously* through *will* or *desire* <note>original: "appetite"</note>. This is both because the same problems mentioned before would follow and because the *phenomena*—or what we actually observe—plainly prove the contrary. As for that remarkably absurd paradox of a few *hylozoic atheists* <note>original: "Hylozoick Atheists"; from the Greek words for "matter" and "life," referring to those who believe all matter is inherently alive</note>—the idea that all *matter* as such, and therefore every *tiny particle* of it, possesses not only *essential life* but also *perfect wisdom*, *knowledge*, *desire*, and *self-moving power* (even without animal senses or consciousness)—I will refute this elsewhere in its proper place. However, the *majority* of ancient *atheists*—namely the followers of *Anaximander* and *Democritus*—attributed no kind of *life* to *matter* itself. Therefore, they could not ascribe any *voluntary* or *spontaneous motion* to it, but only *accidental* <note>original: "fortuitous"</note> motion, according to the *Epicurean poet* <note>Lucretius</note> cited earlier:

> *For surely, the first beginnings of things did not place themselves* 
> *in their order by design or by a clever mind;*
> *nor did they bargain together on what motions each should produce.*
> <note>original Latin: "Nam certè neque Consilio, Primordia rerum, / Ordine se quæque, atque sagaci mente locârunt; / Nec quos quæque darent Motus pepigere profectò."</note>

<margin>*Alexander of Aphrodisias, Book on Fate, page...* <note>original: "Alex. Aph. Lib. de Fato, P."</note></margin>
Therefore these *Democritics*, as *Aristotle* suggests in one place, could assign no other *cause of motion* than this: *that one body moved another from eternity infinitely*. Thus, no *first unmoved mover* <note>original Greek: "proton kinoun"</note> could ever be found, because there is no *beginning* or *first* within *eternity*. From this probably came the *doctrine* of some *atheistic Stoics* mentioned by *Alexander of Aphrodisias*: *that there is no "first" in the rank and order of causes*. A *modern writer* <note>likely Thomas Hobbes</note> seems to have followed in the footsteps of these philosophers when he declared: *If anyone shall ascend by reasoning from any effect to its immediate cause, and from there to a more remote one, and so on perpetually, he will nonetheless not be able to proceed forever, but being weary, he will eventually fail.* <note>original Latin: "Si quis ab Effectu quocunque, ad Causam ejus Immediatam, atque inde and Remotiorem, ac sic perpetuò ratiocinatione ascenderit, non tamen in æternum procedere poterit, sed defatigatus aliquando deficiet."</note>

# Atheists; No Cause of Motion. BOOK I.

...from there to a more remote one, and so onwards perpetually in his reasoning <note>original: "Ratiocination"</note>; yet he will never be able to keep going through all eternity, but at length, being quite tired out by his journey, he will be forced to stop or give up. This seems to be the same as if he should have said: one thing moved or caused another infinitely from eternity; since there is no beginning in this, there is consequently no **First Mover** or **Cause** to be reached. 

But this **Infinite Progress** of these **followers of Democritus** <note>original: "Democriticks"</note> in the **Order of Causes**—and their shifting the **Cause** of **Motion** from one thing to another without end or beginning—was rightly understood by **Aristotle** to be, in fact, the assigning of **no cause of motion** at all. "They proceed to infinity," <note>original: εἰς ἄπειρον εἶσιν, εἰ μήτι ἔσται κατὰ φύσιν κινῶν πρῶτον</note> he says, "unless there is something that is a first mover according to nature." Those who acknowledge **no First Mover according to Nature** (**he says**) **must necessarily make a useless, infinite progress**; that is, in the language of this philosopher, they assign no cause at all for **motion**. 

**Epicurus**, therefore, to fix the matter, discarded all other **qualities** according to the principles of **atomic physics** <note>original: "Atomick Physiology"</note>; yet he nonetheless admitted this **one quality of gravity** or **weight** <note>original: "Ponderosity"</note> in atoms, pressing them continually downward in **infinite space**. In this, nothing could be more absurd or **unphilosophical** than to create **upward** and **downward** in **infinite space**, or a **gravity** tending toward **no center** or **place of rest**. Furthermore, he did not assign any **cause of motion** either, but only effectively affirmed that atoms tend downward because they simply did so. A **quality of gravity** signifies only an **effort to move downward**, but why or for what reason, nobody knows. 

It is exactly as if **Epicurus** had said that atoms moved downward by a **hidden quality** <term>occult quality: a property that is observed but whose cause is unknown</term>. He either used this as a **sanctuary** or **refuge** for his **ignorance**, or else, even more absurdly, he made his very ignorance itself (disguised under the name of a **quality**) into the **cause of motion**. 

Thus, all atheists either assigned **no cause** at all for **motion** (as did the **followers of Anaximander** and **Democritus**) or else no **true** one (as did the **hylozoists** <term>hylozoists: those who believe that all matter, in every form, is alive or possesses a soul</term>). To avoid admitting to the existence of **non-physical substance** <note>original: "Incorporeal Substance"</note>, these latter thinkers would venture to attribute **perfect understanding**, **desire** or **will**, and **self-moving power** to all mindless **matter** whatsoever. 

But since it appears plainly that **matter** or **body** cannot **move itself**, then either the **motion** of all **bodies** must have no cause at all, or there must necessarily be some other **substance** besides **body**—one that is **self-active** and **hylarchical** <term>hylarchical: having the power to rule over or organize matter</term>, possessing a **natural power** of ruling over **matter**. On this latter account, **Plato** rightly determined that **thought** <note>original: "Cogitation"</note>—which is **self-activity** or **autokinesis** <note>original: "Autochinesie"; from the Greek for self-motion</note>—was, in the order of **nature**, prior to the **physical movement** of bodies, which is **heterokinesis** <note>original: "Heterochinesie"; from the Greek for being moved by something else</note>. 

Although **motion** considered **passively** in bodies—as their **transfer** or **change of distance and place**—is indeed a physical thing or a **state** of those moving bodies themselves, it is different when considered **actively**. As the **moving force** <note>original: "Vis Movens"</note>—the **active force** which causes this **transfer** or **change of place**—it is a **non-physical thing**. It is the **energy** of a **self-active substance** acting upon that sluggish **matter** or **body**, which cannot move itself at all. Therefore, in the bodies of **animals**, the **true** and **proper cause of motion** (or at least the **direction** of it) is not the **matter** itself **organized**. Rather, it is the **soul**—either as a **thinking entity** or a **formative, self-active one** <note>original: "Plastickly Self-Active"; the 'plastic' power refers to the soul's ability to shape and organize the physical body</note>—which is vitally united to the body and **naturally rules** over it. But in the world as a whole, it is either **God** himself, who originally impressed—

The author concludes that motion must originate from a non-physical, self-active substance, such as the soul in animals or God in the universe.</summary>

# Chapter IV: Nor of the Worldly Order

<margin>In Acts 17:28.</margin>
...bestowing a certain *quantity of motion* upon the matter of the universe and constantly preserving it, according to the Scripture: *In him we live and move.* (This also seems to have been the meaning of that noble Agrigentine poet and philosopher <note>Empedocles of Akragas (c. 494–434 BCE), who proposed that Love and Strife move the elements</note> when he described God as being only "a pure or holy mind that agitates the whole world with swift thoughts.") Alternatively, God acts through an instrument—an inferior created spirit, soul, or "life of nature." This is a subordinate <term>hylarchical principle</term> <note>original: "Hylarchical Principle"; a governing principle over matter, from the Greek "hyle" (matter) and "arche" (rule)</note> which has the power to *move matter regularly* according to the direction of a superior *perfect mind.* And so we see again that *ignorance of causes is the seed of atheism, and not of theism.* No atheists are able to assign a true cause of *motion*; the knowledge of which plainly leads to a **God**.

Furthermore, those atheists who acknowledge no other principle of things but *senseless matter moved by chance* must also be *ignorant* of the cause of that *grand phenomenon* called by *Aristotle* "the well and fit in nature" <note>original: τὸ εῦ ἢ καλῶς; referring to the inherent order, goodness, and beauty of the natural world</note>. That is, they cannot explain the most skillful frame of the whole worldly system in general, and the bodies of animals in particular, together with the *harmonious cooperation* of it all. For those who boasted themselves able to give *natural causes* for all things whatsoever without a **God** can give no other cause at all for this phenomenon except that the *world happened by chance to be made as it is.* 

Now, those who make **fortune** and **chance** the only cause of this so admirable phenomenon—the most regular and skillful frame and *harmony* of the *universe*—either make the mere *absence* and *lack* of a *cause* to be a cause (since fortune and chance are nothing other than the *absence or lack of an intending cause*); or else they make their own *ignorance of a cause* (saying "they know not how") to be a **cause**. As the *author of the Leviathan* <note>Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), whose materialistic philosophy the author is critiquing</note> interprets the meaning of this: "Many times," *he says*, "men substitute their own ignorance as the cause of natural events, but disguise it in other words, as when they say that fortune is the cause of contingent things—that is, of things for which they know no cause." 

Alternatively, they affirm—against all reason—that one thing is the cause of its opposite: such as *confusion* being the cause of *order, beauty,* and *harmony*; *chance* and *fortune* being the cause of *art* and *skill*; or *folly* and *nonsense* being the cause of the most *wise* and *regular contrivance.* Or lastly, they deny it has any cause at all, since they deny an *intending cause*; and there cannot possibly be any other cause of *skillfulness* and *harmonious cooperation* than **mind** and **wisdom**, **counsel** and **contrivance**.

But because the *atheists* here offer some *excuses* for this ignorance, we shall not hide any of them but bring them all to light, so that we may reveal their weakness and folly. First, therefore, they *pretend that the world is not so skillfully and well made* but that it could have been made much *better*, and that there are many *faults* and *flaws* to be found in it. From this, they would infer that it was not made by a **God**, since He is supposed by *theists* to be no *clumsy worker* but a *perfect mind* or a *being infinitely good and wise* who, therefore, should have made all things for the *best.*

# God and Nature, all for The Best. BOOK I.

<meta>catchword: came</meta>

But since this is already set down by itself as a *twelfth atheistic objection* against a Deity, we must reserve the refutation of it for its proper place. We shall only observe this much here in passing: there are certain *theists* of later times who—either because they imagine a purely *arbitrary Deity*, because their *faith* in the *Divine Goodness* is weak, or because they judge things according to their own *private appetites* and *selfish passions* rather than with a *free, unbiased universality* of mind and an *impartial regard* for the *good* of the *whole*—claim the world could have been made much *better* than it is. These people may also look only at the *present scene* of things and ignore the *future*, or they may lack a comprehensive view of the entire *plot* of *Divine Providence*. Lastly, we mortals all stand on such *low* ground that we cannot take a commanding view and *prospect* of the whole frame of things; our shallow understandings are unable to fathom the depths of Divine Wisdom or trace all the methods and designs of Providence. 

To grant that the world might have been made much *better* than it now is, is indeed the same as saying that it is *not well* made. These <term>modern Christians</term> <note>original: "Neo-terick Christians"; "neoteric" means new or contemporary, referring to 17th-century thinkers who emphasized God's absolute will over His wisdom</note> seem to give a much greater advantage to atheists than the pagan theists of the past did. Those pagans stood their ground and generously maintained that since *Mind—not fortune, chance, arbitrary self-will, or irrational, omnipotent whim—is the maker of all things, <term>the absolute best</term> <note>original: τὸ βέλτιστον (to beltiston)</note> in every case was the measure and rule of both nature and providence.* This was upheld as far as the necessity of things would admit and in compliance with the good of the whole.

Again, the *atomic atheists* further allege that although there are many things in the world which serve well for certain *uses*, it does not follow that they were made *intentionally* and *designedly* for those *uses*. They argue that even if things happen to be made a certain way by chance, they may still serve some purpose afterward, with their various *uses* being a *consequence* of their form. Therefore, they say all the things of nature happened by *chance* to be made as they are, and their various uses were merely *consequent* or *following* upon that. Thus, the <term>Epicurean poet</term> <note>Lucretius (c. 99–55 BCE), whose poem "On the Nature of Things" argued that the world was formed by the random collision of atoms</note> wrote:

<margin>
Lucretius, Book 4, 
p. 367, Lambin edition.
</margin>

-> ——— *Nothing in the body was born so that we might* <-
-> *use it, but what was born creates its own use.* <-
<note>original: "Nil ideo natum est in Corpore, ut Uti / Possemus, sed quod Natum est id procreat Usum."</note>

Nothing in a man's body was made out of a design for any *use*, but all the several parts, having happened to be made as they are, found their *uses* as a *consequence*. In a similar way, the old *atheistic philosophers* mentioned in *Aristotle* concluded: <margin>Physics, Book 2, chapter 8.</margin> *that the front teeth rose up by necessity, being thin and sharp and thus fit for cutting, while the molars became thick and broad and thus useful for grinding food. They claimed this did not happen for that purpose, but by coincidence; and they said the same of all other parts that seem to exist for a purpose.* <note>original: τοὺς ὀδόντας ἐξ ἀνάγκης ἀνατεῖλαι, τοὺς μὲν ἐμπροσθίους ὀξεῖς, ἐπιτηδείους πρὸς τὸ διαιρεῖν, τοὺς δὲ γομφίους πλατεῖς, καὶ χρησίμους πρὸς τὸ λεαίνειν τὴν τροφήν· ἐπεὶ οὐ τούτου ἕνεκα γενέσθαι, ἀλλὰ συμπεσεῖν· ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ περὶ τῶν ἄλλων μερῶν, ἐν ὅσοις δοκεῖ ὑπάρχειν τὸ ἕνεκά του</note> That is, the *front teeth* were made by *material* or *mechanical necessity* to be thin and sharp, which made them fit for cutting, while the jaw teeth were made thick and broad, whereby they became...

# Cʜᴀᴘ. IV. Things Made for Ends and Uses.

[These teeth] became *useful* for the *grinding* of *food*. But neither of them were *intended* to be so for the sake of these *uses*; rather, they *happened* by *chance* alone. The same applies to all the other *parts* of the *body* which seem to be made for specific *ends*. Similarly, *Aristotle* represents the views of those ancient *atheists* regarding the other *parts* of the *universe* or the *things* of *nature*. They claimed these were all created by the *necessity* of *undirected material* (or *mechanical*) *motions*, and yet they nonetheless had various *consequent uses* resulting from this *accidental structure*. "What prevents Nature from acting without respect to ends, or because something is better? For instance, Zeus (the sky) does not rain intentionally to make the corn grow, but out of necessity." <note>original: "τί κωλύει τὴὺ φύσιν μὴ ἕνεκά τᵾ ποιεῖν, μηδ’ ὅτι βέλτιον, ἀλλ’ ὥσπερ ὕει ὁ Ζεὺς, οὐχ ὅπως τ̃ σῖτον αὐξήσῃ, ἀλλ’ ἐξ ἀνάγκης, &c."</note> This is because the vapors, being raised up into the middle region and there cooled and condensed, must descend again in the form of water. But it is a matter of mere chance, without any intention, that the grain is made to grow because of it; just as the opposite sometimes happens when an excess of rain ruins the crop.

But to this we *reply*: although a thing that *happens accidentally* to be made a certain way may sometimes prove useful for some purpose later, we must look closer when a thing consists of many *parts* that are all *artfully proportioned* together and *meticulously* <note>original: "with much Curiosity"; "curiosity" here means careful detail or craftsmanship</note> accommodated to one another. If even one of these *parts* were missing, or were placed and disposed of differently in the slightest way, the whole would have been rendered entirely *unfit* <note>original: "Inept"</note> for that *use*. In such cases, we may well conclude that it was not made by *chance*, but by *deliberate counsel* and *design* for those specific *uses*. Take *the eye*, for example. Its *structure* and *fabric*, consisting of many *parts* (liquids and tissues), is so *artfully* composed. No reasonable person who considers its entire *anatomy* and the *meticulous detail* of its *structure* could think otherwise: it was designed for the *use of seeing*. It did not *happen accidentally* to be made that way, with the *use of seeing* merely following its creation, as the *Epicurean poet* <note>Referring to the Roman poet Lucretius in his work "On the Nature of Things"</note> would try to persuade us:

<margin>Page 367, Lambinus edition</margin>
> "Do not imagine that the bright lights of the eyes were created so that we might be able to see." <note>original: "Lumina ne facias Oculorum clara Creata, Proſpicere ut poſſimus."</note>

You must be very careful to avoid entertaining that opinion—so dangerous to theism—that eyes were made for the sake of seeing and ears for the sake of hearing. But consider what a person must believe to think that not only did *eyes* happen to be made that way (with the *unintended use of seeing* following), but also that in all the same animals, *ears* also *happened* to be made that way, and the *use of hearing* followed them. And that a *mouth* and *tongue* likewise *happened* to be made, and the *use of eating* and (in humans) *speaking* was also an *accidental consequence*. And that *feet* were made by *chance* in those same animals, followed by the *use of walking*; and *hands* were made by *chance* also, upon which so many necessary *uses* depend—along with *innumerable* other *parts* of the *body*, both *simple* and *complex* <note>original: "Similar and Organical"; in early anatomy, "similar" parts were uniform tissues like bone or skin, while "organical" parts were complex structures like the heart or liver</note>, none of which could...

The author contends that the intricate, interconnected design of these organs proves they were created with specific purposes (teleology) in mind.</summary>

# Nature, both Mechanical and Vital. BOOK I.

...could have been missing without making the whole thing **ineffective** or **useless**. I say, to think that all these things happened to be made this way by **chance** in every single animal, and were not **designed** by a **mind** or **wisdom** <note>original: "Councel"</note> so that they might jointly **act together** and **contribute** to the **good of the whole**—this argues for the greatest imaginable **dullness of mind**. However, this absurd and ridiculous idea was long ago so thoroughly refuted—and its folly so fully revealed—by that learned pagan philosopher and physician, **Galen**, in his book *On the Use of Parts*, that it would be completely redundant to insist any further upon it.

Therefore, the idea that the **front teeth** are made **thin** and **sharp**, and the **molars** <note>original: "Jaw-Teeth"</note> **thick** and **broad**, by **chance** alone and not for a specific **use**, was one of the **foolish ideas of Democritus** <note>original: "Democritick Dotages"; Democritus was an ancient Greek philosopher who proposed that the world was made of atoms moving in a vacuum.</note>. Another such idea was that nothing in the clouds and weather was intended for the **good** of this **habitable Earth**, within whose **atmosphere** they are contained, but that all of it proceeded from **material** and **mechanical necessity**. 

Although **Descartes** <note>original: "Cartesius"</note> seems to have written his entire book on *Meteors* in favor of this view, he begins it by mocking those who **place God in the clouds and imagine his hands to be employed in opening and shutting the chambers of the winds, in sprinkling the flowers with dew, and striking the tops of mountains with thunder.** He closes his discourse with the boast that he had now made it clear there was no need to resort to miracles (that is, to **bring a God upon the stage**) to explain those **phenomena**. Yet it would be easy enough to demonstrate the flaws in his **mechanical explanations** in several particulars. It is easy to prove that all those things could not be carried out with such constant regularity by **random mechanism** <note>original: "Fortuitous Mechanism"</note> alone, without any superior principle to guide and steer them. 

Nevertheless, we acknowledge that **God** and **Nature** do everything in the most **frugal** and **efficient way**, with the least amount of **unnecessary labor** <note>original: "Operoseness"</note>. Therefore, **mechanical powers** are not rejected but are utilized as far as they can helpfully comply with the **intellectual model** and **plan**. But even so, everything is supervised by **one understanding** and **intending cause**, and nothing happens without **His approval**. When either those **mechanical powers** fall short, or the stubborn **necessity of matter** proves uncooperative, He overrules them and supplies the defects through that which is **vital**. He does this without setting His own hands immediately to every task; there is a **subservient minister** under Him, an **artificial nature**, which—as a <term>Archeus</term> <note>original: "Archeus"; in early modern science, this was a vital force or "master-workman" that governed the growth and functions of a living body or the world.</note> of the whole world—governs its **fluctuating mechanism** and does all things faithfully for the **ends** and **purposes intended** by its **director**.

But our **atomic atheists** still further argue that, although it might seem strange that matter moved by chance should fall into such a **regular frame** as this is at the very first attempt—having so many **aptitudes** for **uses**, so many **connections** between different things, and such an agreeing **harmony** in the whole—yet it should not seem the least bit strange if **atoms** in **motion**, making all possible combinations and structures, and trying all manner of **outcomes** and **experiments**,

# CHAPTER IV. The Atheists' Once-Inept World.

...elements, should, after producing innumerable other **strange anomalies** <note>original: "Freaks"</note> and **incongruous forms**, eventually fall into a system such as this one. Therefore they claim that our Earth at first brought forth various **monstrous and irregular shapes of animals**,

<margin>Lucretius, Book 5, Page 476. Lambinus edition.</margin>
->Some were found partly deprived of feet, others widowed of hands;<-
->many even without a mouth, or blind without a face.<-
<note>original: "Orba pedum partim, manuum viduata vicissim; / Multa sine ore etiam, sine Voltu cæca reperta."</note>

Some were born without feet, some without hands, some lacking a mouth and face, and others wanting the necessary muscles and nerves for the motion of their limbs. The ancient philosophical atheists were so bold and extravagant in this regard that they did not hesitate to claim that among those monstrous shapes of animals, there were once produced **Centaurs**, **Scyllas**, and **Chimeras**; **ox-born and human-faced** <note>original: "βουγενῆ καὶ ἀνδρόπρωρα"</note>, mixed **ox-shaped** and **human-shaped**, **two-formed** and **three-formed animals**. However, **Epicurus**, feeling a little ashamed of this—as it must inevitably look odd and ridiculous—and appearing more cautious and disciplined, tries to correct the extravagance of this fantasy:

<margin>Lucretius, Book 5, Page 479.</margin>
->Nevertheless, there were not then any Centaurs, nor at any time<-
->can there be a creature of double nature and twin body,<-
->a power joined together from limbs of different kinds.<-
<note>original: "Sed neque Centauri fuerunt, neque tempore in ullo, / Esse queat Duplici Naturâ, & Corpore Bino, / Ex alienigenis Membris compacta potestas."</note>

He added that those who imagined such things might as well fancy **rivers flowing with golden streams**, **trees growing sparkling diamonds**, and **such vastly giant men that they could stride over seas, take up mountains in their grip, and turn the heavens around with the strength of their arms**. Yet against all this, he gravely offers a reason that plainly overthrows his own principles:

<margin>Page 480.</margin>
->Thus each thing proceeds in its own manner, and all<-
->maintain their distinctions by a certain covenant of nature.<-
<note>original: "Res sic quæque suo ritu procedit, & omnes, / Fœdere Naturæ certo discrimina servant."</note>

He argues this is because things, by a certain **covenant of nature** <note>term: A phrase used by Lucretius to describe the fixed laws or boundaries of the natural world.</note>, always maintain their **specific differences** without being mixed together. But what **covenant of nature** can exist in **infinite chance**? Or what **law** can be set to the **absolutely random motions of atoms** to restrict them? Therefore, it must be acknowledged that according to the genuine **hypothesis of atomic atheism**, every imaginable form of inanimate bodies, plants, and animals—such as **Centaurs**, **Scyllas**, and **Chimeras**—should be producible by the **random motions of matter**. There would be nothing to hinder it, while matter continues:

->To come together in every way, and to try everything<-
->that they might create by meeting one another,<-
<note>original: "Omnimodis coire, atque omnia pertentare / Quæcunque inter se possint congressa creare,"</note>

...putting itself into all kinds of combinations, playing all manner of **strange tricks** <note>original: "Freaks"</note>, and attempting every possible outcome and experiment.

Now, it cannot be thought strange (as they suppose) if, among infinite worlds, one or two should chance to fall into some regularity. The same **wheel of Fortune**, which moving upward has brought into view this scene of things that now exists, will, by turning round, sometime or other carry it all away again, introducing a new one in its place. Then we shall have Centaurs, Scyllas, and Chimeras again—all manner of unfit forms of animals, as before.

# Chapter IV. There was never an unfit system.

...conclusions and **experiments**, were at length (they know not how) **taught**, and by the **necessity** of things **themselves**, as it were, **driven** to a certain kind of pattern of **artistry** and **systematic order**. They argue that although their **motions** were at first all **random** and **accidental**, yet over a long period of time, they became **orderly** and **skilful**, and governed by a certain **law**. They supposedly developed a kind of **habit** of moving **regularly** through long **practice** and **experience**; or else they were forced by the mere **necessity** of things to move as they should have done, had **art** and **wisdom** directed them. Thus **Epicurus** says in his *Letter to Herodotus*: <margin>Page 28. Gassendi edition.</margin> "Moreover, it must be supposed that nature was taught and compelled to many things of all kinds by the things themselves." <note>original Greek: "ἀλλὰ μὴν ὑποληπτέον καὶ τὴν φύσιν πολλὰ καὶ παντοῖα ὑπὸ τῶν αὐτῶν τῶν πραγμάτων διδαχθῆναί τε καὶ ἀναγκασθῆναι"</note> Or else, as **Gassendi** <note>Pierre Gassendi (1592–1655), a French philosopher who revived Epicurean atomism.</note> interprets the words, "imbued by degrees with a certain kind of natural and necessary doctrine." <note>original Latin: "quadam veluti Naturali Necessariaque Doctrina sensim imbuta"</note>

To these **atheistic excuses**, we shall briefly reply: **First**, that it is but an **idle dream**, or rather an **impudent forgery** of these **atheists**, to claim that in the past there were all manner of **monstrous** and **irregular shapes** of **animals** produced in our world—such as **centaurs**, **Scyllas**, and **chimeras**, etc.—and indeed that at first, none but such monsters existed. There is not the slightest trace of any such thing appearing in all the **records** of **history** or **traditions** of **former times**. Furthermore, these **atheists** are not able to give any reason why such things are not produced at this **present time**, even if the individuals themselves could not survive long or reproduce. At the very least, they cannot explain why it should not **happen** that in some ages or countries, there were either all **androgynous** <term>hermaphrodites</term> (having both sexes), or else no animals but of one sex (male or female only), or lastly, none of any sex at all. 

Neither is there any more reason to believe these **atheists** when (though they are enemies to **divination**) they would **prophesy** concerning **future** times, claiming that in our world, everything shall eventually fall into **confusion** and **nonsense** again. And as their theory of an **infinity of worlds** is an **absolute impossibility**, we turn to their **bold** and **confident assertion** concerning those **supposed** other **worlds**. They speak as if they had traveled over them all, claiming that among ten thousand of them, there is hardly **one** that has as much regularity in it as our own world. To this, one might reply with equal confidence and much more logical probability: that were every **planet** around our **sun** a **habitable earth**, and every **fixed star** a **sun** having its own several other **planets** or **habitable earths** moving around it—and not any one of these **deserted** or **uninhabited**, but all peopled with **animals**—we say, even if this extravagant supposition were true, there would not be found a single **ridiculous** or **unfit system** <note>original: "Inept System"</note> among them all. Rather, the **Divine Art** and **Wisdom** (which, being infinite, can never be defective nor anywhere idle) would exercise its dominion over all, and everywhere **imprint** the **sculptures** and **signatures** of itself.

In the next place, we affirm that the **random motions** of **mindless atoms**, no matter how many **experiments** and conclusions they tried...

# Chance, not Artistry. BOOK I.

No matter how many **combinations** and **aggregate forms** of things were created, they could never produce even the **form** or **system** of one complete animal, with all its **organic** parts so **skilfully** <note>original: "Artificially"; in this period, "artificial" meant "created with skill or art," the opposite of "natural" or "random."</note> arranged (each animal being, as it were, a **little world**). Much less could it produce the **system** of this **great world**, with its variety of animals; and least of all could chance **constantly** maintain such **regularity** and **artistry** everywhere. For the idea that the **random motions** of **irrational, senseless**, and **inert** <note>original: "Stupid"</note> **matter** should, over time, become **skilful** and develop a **habit** of acting as **regularly** and **methodically** as if **perfect art** or **wisdom** had directed them—this is the most **immense nonsense imaginable**. It can be considered nothing other than **atheistic fanaticism**.

It is no more possible for the **random motion of dead and senseless matter** to ever, by itself, be **taught** and **forced** to produce such an **orderly** and **regular system** as the **framework** of this entire **world** is (together with the **bodies** of **animals**) and to constantly maintain it, than it is possible for a man who is perfectly **illiterate**—unable to read or write—to take a pen in his hand and make all sorts of scrawls with ink on paper, and eventually be **taught** and **forced** by the **process** itself to write a whole quire <note>A quire is a set of 24 sheets of paper.</note> of paper with **characters** that, when **deciphered** by a key, would prove to be coherent **philosophical sense**. 

Or it is no more possible than if we ourselves, writing down the mere **letters** of the **alphabet** in a transposed way, randomly, without the least **thought** of **words** or **meaning**, should at length (after scribbling a long time together what was altogether **meaningless**) have been **taught** and **forced** by the **process** itself—without the least **study** or **consideration** of our own—to write this entire volume. 

Or to use another **example**: this is no more possible than if ten or twelve **people**, altogether unskilled in **music**, were given several instruments and struck the **strings** or **keys** randomly; and that after some time of **discord** and **jarring**, they should at length be **taught** and **forced** to fall into the most **exquisite harmony** and continue it uninterruptedly for several hours.

Therefore, it would be ridiculous for someone who has read the works of **Plato** or **Aristotle**, or those six books by **T. Lucretius Carus**, *On the Nature of Things* <note>original Latin: "De Natura Rerum"</note>, to argue that the letters of those books might have been put together by **chance**, or scribbled at random without the least **thought** or **study** by the writer, who also lacked any **philosophical skill**. 

Likewise, it would be ridiculous for someone who hears ten or twelve people playing in **harmony** <note>original: "Consort"</note> on musical instruments and creating delightful harmony to persuade himself that none of those players had the least **musical art** or **skill**, but struck the strings by chance. 

In the same way, it must be much more ridiculous and absurd to suppose that this **skilful system** of the whole world resulted from the **random motion of senseless atoms** without the direction of any **art** or **wisdom**. There is much more **sense, art**, and **philosophy** in the world than in any **philosophical volume** or **poem** ever written by men, and more **harmony** and...

<header>CHAPTER 4. Nature’s Intending Cause.</header>

We conclude, therefore, with *Aristotle*, <margin>*Physics, Book 2, Chapter 8*</margin> <note>original Greek: ἀδύνατον δ' ταῦτα τοῦτον ἔχειν τὸν τρόπον</note> *that it is absolutely impossible for things to have happened in this way*; that is, by mere **fortune** and **chance**, and without the **direction** of any **mind** or **God**. The Divine Mind and *Wisdom* has so printed its seal or signature upon the matter of the whole physical world that **fortune** and **chance** could never possibly have counterfeited it.

Despite all this, the ancient atheists attempted to demonstrate, using their impressive skill in logic, that *the framework of nature* could not possibly have been made by any *intending cause* <note>An "intending cause" refers to a creator who acts with a specific purpose or goal in mind.</note> for the sake of *ends* and *uses*. For example, they argued that *eyes* could not have been made intentionally for the *use* of *seeing*, nor *ears* intentionally for the *use* of *hearing*, and so on for the rest. Their reason was that these things—the organs themselves—existed in both *time* and *nature* before their various *uses*. This argument is seriously proposed by the poet *Lucretius* in this way:

> <margin>*Lambinus edition, page 367.*</margin> *The power of sight did not exist before the eyes were born, nor was there speaking with words before the tongue was created. Rather, the origin of the tongue occurred long before speech, and ears were created long before sound was ever heard. In short, all the limbs and organs existed, I believe, before their use began. Therefore, they could not have been created for the purpose of being used.* <note>original Latin: *Nec fuit ante, Videre, Oculorum lumina nata, / Nec Dictis Orare, prius, quam Lingua Creata est; / Sed potius longè Linguæ præcessit Origo / Sermonem, multoque Creatæ sunt prius Aures, / Quam Sonus est Auditus; & omnia denique membra, / Antè fuere, ut opinor, eorum quam fuit usus. / Haud igitur potuere Utendi crescere causâ.*</note>

To this effect: *There was no such thing as seeing before eyes were made, nor hearing before ears, nor speaking before the tongue. Instead, the origin of the tongue far preceded speech; likewise, eyes and ears were made before there was any seeing of colors or hearing of sounds. In the same way, all the other members of the body were produced before their respective uses. Therefore, they could not have been made intentionally for the sake of those uses.* The force of this argument lies in this proposition: *Whatever is made for the sake of something else must exist in time after the thing for which it was made. Or, that for which a thing is made must come first—not only in the order of nature, but also in time—before the thing that is made for it.* The *Epicurean* poet [Lucretius] endeavors to prove this with several examples:

> <margin>*Ibid.*</margin> *On the contrary, engaging in hand-to-hand combat in battle existed long before bright weapons flew, etc.* <note>original Latin: *At Contra conferre Manu certamina pugnæ, / Antè fuit multò quàm lucida tela volarent, &c.*</note>

*Darts were made for the sake of fighting, but fighting existed before darts, otherwise they would never have been invented. Bucklers <note>A buckler is a small, round shield.</note> were thought up and devised for the purpose of keeping off blows and strikes, but the act of dodging strikes existed before bucklers. Similarly, beds were contrived for the sake of resting and sleeping, but resting and sleeping are older than beds and provided the occasion for their invention. Cups were intended and designed for the sake of drinking, which they would not have been, had*

<header>The Logic of Atheists. BOOK I.</header>

...had there not been drinking before. Based on the strength of these examples, the poet [Lucretius] would imply that whoever claims **eyes** were made for the sake of **seeing** must likewise suppose there was some kind of **seeing** before **eyes** existed. But since there was no **seeing** at all before **eyes**, then **eyes** could not have been made for the sake of **seeing**. This is the **atheistic demonstration**: that the parts of human bodies, and other things in nature, could not have been made by any **purposeful cause** <note>original: "Intending Cause," meaning a creator who acts with a specific goal.</note> for the sake of **purposes** and **uses**.

However, it is evident that this **logic of atheists** differs from that of all other **humans**. According to standard logic, **the goal** (the purpose for which a thing is made) exists in the **intention** before the **means** (the thing made for it); yet, in terms of **time** and **execution**, the goal comes after the means. Thus, the more **effective** way of fighting and killing—for whose sake **javelins** <note>original: "Darts"</note> were invented—happened in **time** after javelins were made, even though it was in the **intention** before them. It is true, indeed, that **fighting** in general existed before **javelins**, **sleeping** before **beds**, and **drinking** before **cups**. These activities gave people the occasion to think of **means** for more **effective fighting** and more **comfortable** <note>original: "Commodious"</note> **sleeping** and **drinking**. Humans are commonly motivated by their **experience of things** and the sense of their **needs** and **wants** to **think up** <note>original: "excogitate"</note> and provide fit **means** and **remedies**. 

But it does not follow that the **Creator of the world** <note>original: "Maker of the World"</note> could not have had, all at once and beforehand, a **prior knowledge** <note>original: "Preventive Knowledge"</note> of whatever would be useful and for the **good of animals**, and so made them **intentionally** for those **uses**. Therefore, the argument should have been framed this way: whatever anything is made for as its goal, that goal must be in the **knowledge** and **intention** of the maker before the existence of the thing made for it. And therefore, if **eyes** were made for the sake or **goal of seeing**, then **seeing** must necessarily be in the **knowledge** and **intention** of the maker of **eyes** before there were any **eyes** actually existing. But [the atheists argue] there could be no **knowledge of seeing** before there were any **eyes**. Therefore, **eyes** could not be made for the sake of **seeing**.

<margin>Book 3, page 368.</margin>
This is indeed the **true intent** and **direction** of the previously stated **atheistic argument**, however they disguised it in their way of proposing it. The reason for this was that they took it for granted that all knowledge, as such, is derived from the **senses**, coming from **pre-existing things that are known**. From this, it follows that there could be no **knowledge of vision** or **seeing** before there was **actual seeing** and **eyes**. Thus, they think it is demonstrated that **eyes** could not be made by any deity for the sake of **seeing** before seeing existed—any more than **spectacles** could be made by men for the sake of **eyes** before there were **eyes**. Thus does the **Epicurean** poet conclude triumphantly:

> All these things are actually distinct; they were born first and only afterwards gave us a sense of their usefulness. In this category, we especially see the senses and the limbs. Therefore, again and again, it is far from the truth that you could believe... <note>original Latin: *Illa quidem seorsum sunt omnia, quæ prius ipsa Nata, dedere suæ post Notitiam Utilitatis. <header>CHAPTER IV. Knowledge is Older than Things.</header>

->*Could have been created for the sake of utility.* <note>original: "Utilitatis ob officium potuisse creari."</note><-

*That is: the members of human bodies and the organs of sense were first made by themselves, and only afterward did they provide notice or knowledge of their various uses; none of which could have existed beforehand. Therefore, we affirm again and again that it is impossible these things should have been designed specifically for their uses.*

So the controversy is finally reduced entirely to this: whether or not all **knowledge** and **understanding** universally arises from **things that existed before** the one who knows them. Since this is asserted by atheists, they conclude that the **things of the world** could not have been made by the **previous counsel, contrivance, and intention** of any **understanding Deity**. Instead, they believe everything **stumbled** into existence, one after another, following the **series** or **sequence** of the **random motions of matter**. They argue that from this process, **knowledge** and **understanding**, **counsel** and **intention**, sprouted up afterward as something **younger than things** and the **world**. 

But this has already been identified as the **eleventh atheistic argument** against a **Deity**: namely, *that all knowledge and mental concepts are simply the information provided by the known things themselves (which existed before and outside the knower) and a passive impression received from them; therefore, the world must exist before any knowledge or concept of it, and no knowledge or concept can exist before the world as its cause.* We shall save the answer to this and the refutation of it for its proper place. There, we shall plainly demonstrate that **knowledge** or **understanding** is not, in its own nature, <term>ectypal</term> <note>original: "Ectypal," meaning a copy or derivative of something else</note>, but <term>archetypal</term> <note>original: "Archetypal," meaning the original pattern or source</note>; and that it is **older** than the **world** and is the **maker** of all things.

However, the **atheists** argue further against **proving** a **God** from **the goodness and beauty** <note>original: "τὸ εὖ καὶ καλῶς"</note> of the **regular frame of the whole world** in general, and the **artificial structure** of the **bodies of animals**. They argue that it is altogether unreasonable to suppose there is no **cause** in nature for these **phenomena**, especially for things that are produced every day, such as the **bodies of animals**. They think it is wrong (as done by **tragic poets**) to introduce a **God**, as if **from a machine** <note>original: "from a Machin," referring to the *Deus ex machina* device where a god is lowered onto a stage to resolve a plot</note>, to forcibly explain them. 

Indeed, they think that even if there were a **God**, He should not be lowered to such humble tasks as making the body of every lowly animal, as if with His **own hands by a miracle**. Nor should **nature** or the world be supposed to be so **imperfect** that it must be clumsily patched together everywhere in this manner. It is **nature**, therefore, which is the **cause** of these **natural productions** and **generations**. They argue that **nature** does not **intend** or act **designedly** for **ends** and **uses**. This appears to be true, they say, not only because nature never **consults** or **deliberates** (which **Aristotle** noted was the reason some people in ancient times denied that natural things were made for specific **purposes**), but also because nature has no **animal-like awareness** or **consciousness**, and no **understanding** or **desire**. 

Therefore, they claim this opinion—that there is **intention** and **final causality** <note>the idea that things are made for a specific purpose or "end goal"</note> in **nature**—is nothing more than an **Idol of the Cave** <note>original: "Idolum specus," a term from Francis Bacon referring to the personal prejudices and biases of an individual's mind</note> or a **prejudice** of men's minds.

<page-num>680</page-num>
<header>God, *not* doing all things Himself <note>original: "αὐτουργεῖν ἅπαντα" (autourgein hapanta)</note>. Book I.</header>

Human minds often project their own **properties** onto things outside of themselves. They think that because they themselves **intend** and act for specific **ends** (purposes), **Nature** must do the same. They might as well claim that **Nature laughs** and **cries**, **speaks** and **walks**, **reasons**, and **philosophizes**, just because they do so themselves. But as a modern philosopher concludes: *The universe, as a collection of natural things, has no intention belonging to it.* Accordingly, all **final causes** <note>Final Causes: The purpose or "end" for which something is created or exists.</note> were rightly banished by **Democritus** out of **physics** <note>original: "Physiology," which in this era referred to the study of the laws of nature and the physical world.</note>, as **Aristotle** records of him: <note>original: "τὸ δ᾽ ἕνεκα ἀφεὶς λέγειν, πάντα ἀνάγει οἷς χρῆται ἡ φύσις"</note> *Leaving aside the "for what purpose," he reduced all things to natural and necessary causes used by nature.*

To all of this, we briefly reply: there are indeed two **extremes** to be avoided here. **One** is the view of those who derive all things from the **random motions** of **senseless matter**, which is the **extreme** position of the **Atomic Atheists**. The **other** is the view of overly zealous religious people, who insist that God <note>original: "αὐτουργεῖν ἅπαντα" (autourgein hapanta)</note> *must do all things Himself immediately*, as if everything in Nature were a **miracle**.

But there is a **middle ground** between these two **extremes**. Namely, to assume that, besides God and in subordination to Him, there is a **Nature**. This Nature is **not random**, but **artificial** (skillfully designed) and **methodical**. By governing the **motion** of matter and bringing it into **regularity**, it serves as a **secondary** or **inferior cause** of all that is created. Now, this **Artificial Nature** <note>original: "Natura Artificiosa"</note>, though it does not understand the reason for what it does, nor properly **intend** its own **ends**, can still be understood to act **regularly** for the sake of **ends understood** and **intended** by that **Perfect Mind** (God) upon which it depends. 

Consider this analogy: **manual laborers** <note>original: "Manuary Opificers"</note> do not understand the overall designs of the **architect**, but only perform the specific tasks he assigns them. Or consider how the **printing types** or **forms of letters**, when put together, **print coherent philosophical sense**, even though the letters themselves understand nothing. (We have already discussed this **Artificial** or **Formative Nature** <note>original: "Spermatick Nature"</note> at length in the appendix to the third chapter.) And thus, things are neither performed **immediately** and **miraculously** by God Himself, nor are they done **randomly** and **recklessly**. Instead, they are done **regularly** and **methodically** for the sake of **ends**. These ends are not **understood** by Nature itself, but by that **Higher Mind** which is the **cause** of Nature and, in a sense, continually **inspires** it. 

Some people have, indeed, clumsily attributed their **own properties** or **animal feelings** <note>original: "Idiopathies"</note> to **inanimate bodies**. For example, when they say that **matter desires forms** as a **female** desires a **male**, or that **heavy bodies** fall by an **appetite** toward the **center** so they can rest there, or that they sometimes **ascend** by **discretion** (choice) to avoid a **vacuum** (a void). 

<margin>Lord Bacon.</margin>

If the **Advancer of Learning** <note>A reference to Francis Bacon and his work *The Advancement of Learning*.</note> is understood to be speaking of these fanciful extravagances, then there is nothing to object to in the following passage of his: <note>original: "Incredibile est quantum agmen Idolorum Philosophiæ immiserit, Naturalium Operationum ad Similitudinem Actionum Humanarum Reductio"</note> *It is incredible how many errors have been spread through philosophy from this one delusion: reducing natural actions to the mode of human actions, or thinking that Nature acts as a man does.* But if his point is extended further—to remove all **final causes** from the things of Nature—as if nothing...

# Chapter IV. Final Causality is no "Idol of the Cave."

If nothing were done in the world for **purposes intended by a Higher Mind**, then that is the very **spirit of atheism and infidelity**. It is no **"Idol of the Cave"** or **"Den"** <note>original: "Idolum Specus"; a term from Francis Bacon referring to personal biases or fallacies arising from an individual's specific nature or education</note> (to use that fashionable language)—that is, no **prejudice** or **fallacy** imposed upon ourselves from attributing our own **animal-like properties** to things outside of us—to think that the **frame** and **system** of this entire world was contrived by a **Perfectly Understanding Being** or **Mind** (which even now presides over it) which has everywhere **imprinted** the **signatures** of its own **wisdom** upon **matter**. 

Furthermore, although Nature itself does not strictly **intend**, it acts according to an **intellectual blueprint prescribed to it**, as it is the **manual craftsman** <note>original: "Manuary Opificer"</note> of the **divine master-building art** <note>original: "Architectonick Art"</note>, or like this **art** itself **infused into and embodied within matter**. Thus, **Cicero’s character Balbus** long ago declared concerning it: *it is not a force without reason, inciting necessary motions in bodies blindly; but a force that shares in order, proceeding as if on a path; whose skill no art, no craftsman, can achieve by imitation.* <note>original: "Vis quædam ſine Ratione, ciens Motus in Corporibus Neceſſarios ; ſed Vis particeps Ordinis, tanquam via progrediens ; cujus Solertiam nulla Ars, nemo Artifex conſequi poteſt imitando"</note> For it is altogether inconceivable how we ourselves should have mind and intention within us if there were none in the universe, or in that **Highest Principle** from which all things proceed. 

Moreover, it was truly affirmed by **Aristotle** that there is much more **art** in some of the things of **Nature** than there is in anything artificially made by humans. Therefore, **intention**, or **final** and **mental causality**, can no more be excluded from the consideration of **natural** things than it can from the consideration of **artificial things**. Now, it is plain that **artificial things**, such as a house or a clock, can neither be understood nor can any true cause for them be assigned without considering **design** or **intention for ends and benefit**. For to say that a **house** is merely **stones, timber, mortar, iron, glass, lead, etc.** all put together is not to give a definition of it, nor to explain what it truly is. A house is such an **appropriate arrangement** of all these **materials** as to make the whole fit for **habitation** and the **uses** of men. Therefore, it is not enough to assign the cause of a house simply by declaring from which quarry the stones were dug, or in which woods or forests the timber was cut, and so forth.

<margin>Natural Philosophy <note>original: "Nat. Auſc." (Physica)</note>, Book 2, chapter 9.</margin>
Nor, as **Aristotle** adds: *If anyone should think that a wall was made by necessity, because heavy things naturally tend to fall downward and light things to rise to the top; therefore the stones and foundations are at the bottom, the earth for the walls being lighter is higher, and the wood, being the lightest, is higher still.* <note>original Greek: "εἴτις τὸν τοῖχον γεγονῆσθαι ἐξ ἀνάγκης νομίζοι, ὅτι τὰ μὲν βαρέα κάτω πέφυκε φέρεσθαι, τὰ δὲ κοῦφα ἐπιπολῆς· διὸ οἱ λίθοι μὲν κάτω καὶ θεμέλια, ἡ δὲ γῆ ἄνω διὰ τὴν κουφότητα, ἐπιπολῆς· μάλιστα δὲ ξύλα· κουφότατα γάρ·"</note> This is how the atheistic philosophers of that time explained the world and the bodies of animals through **material necessity**. Nor, finally, can we explain a house, as the same **Aristotle** elsewhere suggests, *merely because the tool happened to fall* <note>original Greek: "ἐμπέσοντος τοῦ ὀργάνου"</note> in a certain way—meaning, because the hands of the laborers and the axes, hammers, trowels, and other instruments all happened by chance to move in such a way. We say that...

<page-num>682</page-num>
# Final Causes, Philosophy Book I.

...that to list all of these materials would be to fail to assign the true cause of a house, without declaring that the architect first framed in his mind a model or plan of such a thing to be made out of those materials. These materials are so aptly arranged into a **foundation, walls, roof, doors, rooms, stairs, chimneys, windows, and so on**, as to make the whole structure fit for **habitation and other human uses.** In the same way, the **things of nature** (in whose very essence <term>Final Causality</term> <note>the principle that things exist for a specific purpose or "end"</note> is just as much included) can neither be rightly understood, nor can their causes be assigned, merely from **matter** and **mechanism**, or from the **necessary and unguided motion** of matter, without **design** or **intention** for **ends and the good.** 

Therefore, to say that the bodies of animals became what they are merely because the <term>fluid seed</term> <note>original: "Fluid Seed"; referring to embryonic fluids or semen</note> happened by motion to make such **tracks** and produce such **fibers and outlines** from which that **structure** <note>original: "Compages"</note> of the whole resulted, is not to assign a **cause** for them. Instead, it is to pretend, smother, and conceal their **true efficient cause**, which is the **wisdom and design** of that **Divine Architect and Geometer.** He makes them in every way fit for the habitation and uses of their respective souls. Indeed, we cannot banish all **final**—that is, all **mental causality**—from **philosophy** or the consideration of **nature** without at the same time banishing **reason and understanding** from ourselves, looking upon the things of nature with no other eyes than **animals** <note>original: "Brutes"</note> do. 

However, none of the ancient atheists would ever undertake to assign **necessary causes** for all the **parts of the bodies of animals** and their **formation** <note>original: "Efformation"</note> from mere **matter, motion, and mechanism.** Those small and pitiful attempts that have been made by some of them in a **few instances**—such as that the **spine** <note>original: "Spina Dorsi"</note> came from the **bending** of the bodies of animals when they first sprung out of the earth; the **intestines** from the **flow of humors** carving out a crooked and winding channel for itself; and that the **nostrils** were broken open by the **bursting out of breath**—these, I say, only show the **unfeasibility** and **impossibility** of such an explanation. 

And therefore **Democritus** was so wise as to never pretend to give an account in this way of the **formation of the fetus**, looking upon it as an absolutely hopeless task. Nor would he venture to say any more concerning it (as **Aristotle** informs us) than **"that it always happens thus by necessity"** <note>original: "ὅτι οὕτως ἀεὶ ἐξ ἀνάγκης γίνεται"</note>. He stopped all further inquiry concerning it in this manner: **"That to ask 'why' about any of these things—for what cause it was so—was to seek a beginning for the infinite."** <note>original: "τὸ ἐρωτᾶν τὸ διὰ τί, περὶ τῶν τοιούτων τινὸς, τὸ ζητεῖν εἶναι τοῦ ἀπείρου ἀρχὴν"</note> As if all the motions from **eternity** had an influence upon, and contribution to, whatever physical thing was now produced. And **Lucretius**, despite all his swaggering and boasting that he and **Epicurus** were able to assign natural and necessary causes for everything without a God, has nowhere so much as one word concerning it. We conclude, therefore, that **Aristotle’s** judgment concerning **final causes in philosophy** is much to be preferred over that of **Democritus**:

<margin>

# CHAP. IV. The Mechanical Theists Censured.

...does not address the cause of the **purpose** <note>original: "End"</note>. Thus we see plainly that the **Atomic Atheists** are utterly ignorant of the cause of the **good and beautiful order** <note>original: τοῦ εὖ καὶ καλῶς; the Greek phrase refers to the moral and aesthetic excellence of the universe's design</note> of the regular and artificial structure of things in nature, and consequently of the whole **world system** <note>original: "Mundane System"</note>. The true knowledge of this necessarily leads to a God.

<margin>Descartes</margin>
But it is remarkably strange that these **atheists** should, in their ignorance and **foolishness** <note>original: "Sottishness"</note>, be justified by any **professed theists and Christians** of recent times. These people, by also using atomic theory in their **physics** <note>original: "Physiology"; here referring to the study of natural philosophy and the laws of matter</note>, would try to persuade us in a similar way that this whole **world system**, along with plants and animals, was derived merely from the **necessary and unguided motion** of **small particles of matter**. They claim matter was first turned in a **whirlpool** <note>original: "Vortex"; a reference to René Descartes' theory of planetary motion</note> or else jumbled together in a **chaos**, without any intention for **purpose** <note>original: "Ends"</note> or **goodness**—that is, without the direction of any **mind**. Meanwhile, they describe God as standing by merely as an **idle spectator** of this **play of atoms** <note>original: *Lusus Atomorum*</note>, this **playful dance of atoms**, and the various results that come from it. 

Indeed, these **mechanical theists** have quite outstripped and outdone the **atomic atheists** themselves; they are much more **shameless** <note>original: "Immodest"</note> and extreme than the atheists ever were. For the **professed atheists** never dared to claim that this **regular system** of things resulted from the **accidental motions of atoms** at the very beginning—at least not before those atoms had, for a long time, produced many other **unfit combinations**, or **cluttered forms** of particular things, and **nonsensical systems** of the whole. The atheists also supposed that the **regularity** of things here in this world would not always continue, but that sooner or later, **confusion and disorder** would break in again. 

Moreover, the atheists believed that besides our world, there are at this very instant countless other **irregular** worlds, and that there is only one in a thousand or ten thousand among the **infinite worlds** that possesses such regularity. The reason for all this is that it was generally taken for granted and seen as a **common idea** that **"nothing that comes from fortune or chance happens constantly and always in the same way"** <note>original: τῷ ἀπὸ τύχης καὶ τοῦ αὐτομάτου, οὐδὲν ἀεὶ οὕτω γίνεται</note>, as **Aristotle** expresses it. 

But our **mechanical or atomic theists** claim that their atoms never fumbled even once in these accidental motions, nor produced any **unfit system** or **mismatched forms** at all. Instead, from the very beginning, they claim the atoms took their places and arranged themselves so orderly, methodically, and wisely that they could not have done it better if they had been **directed by the most perfect wisdom**. 

Therefore, these **atomic theists** completely **undermine** <note>original: "Evacuate"</note> that great argument for a God taken from the **evidence** <note>original: "Phænomenon"</note> of the **artificial structure** of things. This argument has been emphasized in all ages and commonly makes the strongest impression on the **human mind**. By doing this, they leave only certain **abstract arguments** <note>original: "Metaphysical Arguments"</note> for a **deity**. Though these may be good, because of their **complexity** <note>original: "Subtilty"</note>, they have little impact on the **general public**; even among the **learned**, they often produce more **doubtful debate** and **skepticism** than **clear conviction and satisfaction**.

# A Confutation of BOOK I.

In the meantime, these atheists are laughing secretly and triumphing not a little to see the *cause of theism* thus betrayed by its professed *friends* and *defenders*. They see the *grand argument* for God’s existence totally undermined <note>original: "slurred"</note> by them, so that their work is effectively done for them.

Now, as this argues the greatest *insensibility of mind*, or *foolishness* <note>original: "Sottishness"</note> and *stupidity* in these *pretended theists*—to not take the slightest notice of the *regular and designed* <note>original: "Artificial"</note> *frame* of things, or the *signs* <note>original: "Signatures"</note> of *divine art* and *wisdom* within them, nor to look upon the world and things of nature with any *other eyes* than *oxen* and *horses* do—so are there many *phenomena* in nature that cannot be explained this way. Because these things are partly *above* the force of these *mechanical powers* and partly *contrary* to them, they can never be *resolved* <note>original: "Salved"</note> by mechanics alone, nor without *final causes* <note>term: "Final Causes" refers to the purpose or end goal for which something exists, implying intentional design</note> and some *vital principle* <note>term: "Vital Principle" refers to a non-mechanical force or soul that gives life and organization to matter</note>. 

Take, for example, the phenomenon of *gravity* (the *tendency of bodies downward*), the *motion of the diaphragm in breathing* <note>original: "Respiration"</note>, or the *beating of the heart* <note>original: "Systole and Diastole"</note>. As previously stated, the heart's movement is a *muscular contraction* and *relaxation*, and therefore *vital* <note>original: "Vital" here means biological or life-driven rather than purely physical</note> rather than *mechanical*. 

We might also add, among many others, the *intersection of the planes of the Equator and the Ecliptic*, or the *Earth's daily motion* upon an *axis* that is neither *parallel* with the axis of the *ecliptic* nor *perpendicular* to its *plane*. For although *Descartes* <note>original: "Cartesius"</note> felt he had to imagine that this *Earth* of ours was once a *sun*, and thus the center of a smaller *vortex* <note>original: "Vortex"; in Cartesian physics, a whirlpool of particles that carries planets along</note> whose *axis* was directed in this way—and which therefore still kept the same position because *striated particles* <note>original: "Striate Particles"; Descartes' theory of screw-shaped magnetic particles that maintained the Earth's orientation</note> found no fit pores or paths through it except in this *direction*—yet he himself confesses a problem. He admits that because these *two motions* of the *Earth* (the *annual* and *daily*) would be much more conveniently made upon *parallel axes*, then according to the *laws* of *mechanism*, they should perpetually be brought closer and closer together until finally the *Equator* and the *Ecliptic* come to have their axes *parallel* to each other.

This has not yet happened. Nor has there been any closer approach made between them for these last two thousand years, according to the best observations and judgments of *astronomers*. Therefore, the continuation of these *two motions of the Earth* (the *annual* and *daily*) upon *axes that are different or not parallel* can be attributed to nothing but a *final and mental cause*, or "the best" <note>original: τὸ βέλτισον; "to beltiston"</note>. It continues this way because it was *best* that it should be so, as the *variety of the seasons* of the year depends upon this tilt.

But the greatest of all the particular *phenomena* is the *organization and formation* of the bodies of *animals*, which consist of such variety and complexity <note>original: "Curiosity"</note>. These *mechanical philosophers* are in no way able to give an account of this based on the *necessary motion of matter unguided by a mind for specific ends*. They therefore prudently break off their scientific system before they reach the subject of animals, leaving it altogether untouched. We acknowledge, indeed, that there is a posthumous work attributed to *Descartes* titled *On the Formation of the Fetus* <note>original: *De la Formation du Fœtus*</note>, in which he attempts to explain all this through *accidental mechanism*. But the theory in that book is built entirely upon a *false supposition*...

# Chap. IV. The Mechanick Theists

...sufficiently refuted by the learned *Harvey* <note>William Harvey (1578–1657), the English physician who first described the systemic circulation of blood.</note>, in his *Book of Generation* <note>original: "De Generatione Animalium"</note>, where he shows *that the seed does not materially enter into the composition of the egg*. His theory is precarious and open to objection throughout; nor does it explain the differences between various animals, or offer the slightest reason why an animal of one species or kind might not be formed out of the seed of another.

It is indeed claimed here by these *Mechanical Theists* that *Final Causes* <note>term: "Final Causes" refers to the purpose or "end" for which something exists, such as the eye being designed for the purpose of seeing.</note> should therefore be of no concern to a philosopher. They argue that we should not presume to be as wise as Almighty God, or to be privy to his secrets. Thus, in the *Metaphysical Meditations*: *“And for this sole reason, I consider that entire class of causes usually sought from a purpose to have no use in physical matters; for I do not think I can investigate the purposes of God without rashness.”* <note>original Latin: "Atq; ob hanc Unicam Rationem totum illud Causarum genus, quod à Fine peti solet, in Rebus Physicis nullum Usum habere existimo; non enim absque Temeritate me puto, investigare posse Fines Dei."</note> And again, likewise in the *Principles of Philosophy*: *“We admit no reasons regarding natural things based on the end which God or Nature proposed in making them, because we ought not to presume so much of ourselves as to think we can be participants in his plans.”* <note>original Latin: "Nullas unquam Rationes circa Res Naturales, à Fine quem Deus aut Natura in iis faciendis sibi proposuit, admittimus, quia non tantum nobis debemus arrogare, ut ejus Consiliorum participes esse possimus."</note> 

But the question is not whether we can always understand the goals of Almighty God and know what is *absolutely best* in every case—and accordingly conclude that the thing is or ought to be so. Rather, the question is whether anything at all was made by God for a purpose or for the sake of goodness, other than what would have resulted on its own from the *accidental motion of matter*. 

Nevertheless, we see no reason at all why it should be thought a *presumption* or an *intrusion* into the secrets of Almighty God to affirm that eyes were made by him for the *purpose of seeing* (and accordingly so designed as to best achieve that) and ears for the *purpose of hearing*, and the like. This is so plain that nothing but *senseless stupidity* <note>original: "Sottish Stupidity"</note> or *atheistic disbelief* (masked perhaps under a hypocritical veil of *humility*) can cause anyone to doubt it. 

Therefore, *Aristotle* justly rebuked *Anaxagoras* for that absurd aphorism of his: *“That man was the wisest (or most skillful) of all animals because he happened to have hands.”* <note>original Greek: "διὰ τὸ χεῖρας ἔχειν, φρονιμώτατον εἶναι τῶν ζώων, τὸν ἄνθρωπον"</note> Aristotle did not hesitate to affirm the contrary: *“That it was far more reasonable to think that because man was the wisest (or most skillful and active) of all animals, he was therefore given hands. For Nature (he says) distributes, just as a wise man does, what is suitable to each; and it is more proper to give flutes to one who has musical skill, than to bestow musical skill upon someone who happens to have flutes.”* <note>original Greek: "εὔλογον διὰ τὸ φρονιμώτατον εἶναι τῶν ζώων χεῖρας ἔχειν· ἡ γὰρ φύσις ἀεὶ διανέμει καθάπερ ἄνθρωπος φρόνιμος, τῷ δυναμένῳ χρῆσθαι ἕκαστον· προσήκει γὰρ τῷ ὄντι αὐλητῇ δῦναι μᾶλλον αὐλὸς, ἢ τῷ αὐλὸς έχοντι προσθεῖναι αὐλητικήν·"</note>

Wherefore these *Mechanical Theists* would further allege, with some greater appearance of reason: that it is below the *dignity of Almighty God* to condescend to all those lowly and trivial *tasks*, and to do the things of *nature* himself immediately; and also that it would be a mere flaw <note>original: "Botch"</note> in *nature* if its *defects* had to be supplied everywhere by *miracles*. But to this also the reply is easy: that although *Divine Wisdom* itself designed the system of the whole world for specific ends and for the sake of goodness, yet *Nature*, as an *inferior minister*...

# These Mechanick Theists Smitten, BOOK I.

[the Master], immediately executes it; I say, not a dead, accidental <note>original: "Fortuitous"</note>, and merely *mechanical* nature; but a *vital*, *orderly*, and *skillfully-designed* <note>original: "Artificial"</note> *nature*. This *nature*, asserted by most of the ancient philosophers who <margin>Stephanus, *Philosophical Poetry* <note>original: "Steph. Poes. Philos."</note></margin> were theists, is described by *Proclus* <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher who specialized in the works of Plato.</note> as follows: 

"Nature is the last of all those causes that fabricate this corporeal and sensible world, and the furthest boundary of incorporeal substances. Being full of rational principles <note>original: "λόγων" (logon)</note> and powers through which it directs worldly affairs, it proceeds from the life-giving goddess [Divine Wisdom]..." <note>original Greek: "ἡ φύσις ἐσχάτη μέν ἐστι τῶν τὸ σωματοειδὲς τοῦτο καὶ αἰσθητὸν δημιουργούντων αἰτίων, καὶ τὸ πέρας τοῦ τῶν ἀσωμάτων οὐσιῶν πλάτους· πλήρης δὲ λόγων καὶ δυνάμεων δι' ὧν κατευθύνει τὰ ἐγκόσμια· τοιαύτη δὲ οὖσα προελήλυθεν ἀπὸ τῆς ζωογόνου θεᾶς"</note>

->And about the back of the goddess, boundless nature is suspended,<-
<note>original Greek: "Νώτοις δ' ἀμφὶ, θεᾶς φύσις ἄπλετος ἠώρηται"</note>

"...from whom all life proceeds, both the intellectual kind and that which is inseparable from the things it governs. Being hung and suspended from that source, nature passes through all things without hindrance and breathes life into everything. Because of nature, even inanimate things partake of a kind of life, and corruptible things remain eternal in their species, being held together by the causes of the forms within it." <note>original Greek: "ἀφ' ἧς πᾶσα ζωὴ πρόεισιν, ἥ τε νοερὰ καὶ ἡ ἀχώριστος τῶν διοικουμένων· ἐξηρτημένη δὲ ἐκεῖθεν καὶ ἀπηωρημένη, φοιτᾷ διὰ πάντα ἀκωλύτως, καὶ πάντα ἐμπνεῖ, δι' ἣν τὰ ἄψυχα ψυχῆς μετέχει τινὸς, καὶ τὰ φθειρόμενα μένει διαιωνίως ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ, ταῖς ἐν αὐτῇ τῶν εἰδῶν αἰτίαις συνεχόμενα·"</note>

->Untiring nature rules over the worlds and their works,<-
->says the oracle,<-
->so that the heavens may run their eternal course, dragging all else along;<-
->And so forth.<-
<note>original Greek: "Ἄρχει δ' αὖ φύσις ἀκαμάτη κόσμων τε καὶ ἔργων / φησὶ τὸ λόγιον, / Οὐρανὸς ὄφρα θέῃ δρόμον αἴδιον κατασύρων· / Καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς."</note>

*Nature is the last of all those causes that fabricate this corporeal and sensible world, and the utmost bound of incorporeal substances. Which being full of reasons and powers, orders and presides over all mundane affairs. It proceeds (according to the Magic Oracles) from that supreme goddess, the Divine Wisdom, which is the fountain of all life, as well intellectual as that which is bound up <note>original: "Concrete"</note> with matter. Which Wisdom this nature always essentially depends upon, passing through all things without hindrance; by means of which even inanimate things partake of a kind of life; and things corruptible remain eternal in their species, they being contained by its standing forms or ideas as their causes. And thus does the oracle describe nature as presiding over the whole corporeal world and perpetually turning round the heavens.* 

Here we have a description of *one universal substantial life, soul, or spirit of nature*, subordinate to the Deity. Besides this, the same *Proclus* elsewhere supposes other "particular natures" or "generative principles" <note>original: "Spermatick Reasons"</note> in his words: "After the first soul, there are particular souls; and after the universal nature, there are particular natures." <note>original Greek: "μετὰ τὴν ψυχὴν τὴν πρώτην, ψυχαί· καὶ μετὰ τὴν ὅλην φύσιν, φύσεις"</note> It may be observed here that this *Proclus*, though he was a superstitious pagan much addicted to multiplying gods (subordinate to one supreme) or a bigoted polytheist who had a habit of deifying almost everything—and therefore wanted this nature to be called a goddess too—yet he declares it not to be properly such, but only improperly <note>original: "Abusively"</note> called so (namely, because it was not an intellectual or thinking thing). He says the bodies of the sun, moon, and stars, which were supposed to be animated, were called gods too, as they were the "statues of the gods." This is the meaning of those words: "Nature is a god or goddess, not as having godship properly belonging to it, but as the divine bodies are called gods because they are statues of the gods." <note>original Greek: "ἡ θεὸς μὲν τῷ ἐκθεοῦσθαι, καὶ οὐκ αὐτόθεν ἔχουσα τὸ εἶναι θεός· καὶ γὰρ τὰ θεῖα σώματα, θεοὺς καλοῦμεν, ὡς ἀγάλματα τῶν θεῶν"</note>
