# CHAP. IV. With an Atheistic Blast. 687

Therefore, we cannot reach any other conclusion regarding these **Mechanistic Theists** of ours. They insist on deriving all **physical** <note>original: "Corporeal"</note> things from a **dead** and **unthinking nature**, or from the **necessary motions** of **senseless matter**, without the **direction** of any **mind** or **intention** for **purpose** and **goodness**. Because of this, they are indeed **close relatives** <note>original: "Cousin-Germans"</note> to **atheists**, or are possessed to some degree by a kind of **atheistic fanaticism** <note>original: "Enthusiasm"</note>. They are, to that extent, **inspired** by a **spirit** of **disbelief**, which is the very **spirit** of **atheism**.

But these **Mechanistic Theists** are, in turn, balanced by another group of **atheists** who are neither **mechanical** nor **accidental** <note>original: "Fortuitous"</note>: namely, the **Hylozoists** <term>Hylozoism: the belief that all matter possesses inherent life and soul.</term>. These people are unquestionably convinced that **the works of nature are the works of intelligence** <note>original Latin: "Opera Naturae sunt Opera Intelligentiae"</note>, and that the **origin** of these **physical** things was not **dead** and **unthinking matter** moved **by chance**. For this reason, **Strato** <note>Strato of Lampsacus (c. 335 – c. 269 BC), a Greek Peripatetic philosopher.</note> mocked the **rough** and **smooth**, **crooked** and **hooked atoms** of **Democritus** as mere **dreams** and **nonsense** <note>original: "Dotages"</note>. Nevertheless, because these Hylozoists refuse to admit any **substance** other than **matter**, they assume that **life** and **perception** **essentially** belong to all **matter** as such. By this, they mean matter has a **perfect knowledge** of whatever it can do or undergo—though without **conscious awareness** <note>original: "Animal-consciousness"</note>—and can shape itself to its best advantage. They believe matter sometimes improves itself through **biological organization** <note>original: "Organization"</note> into **sensation** in **animals** <note>original: "Brutes"</note> and into **reason** and **reflective understanding** in **human beings**. 

Therefore, according to the principles of these **Hylozoists**, there is no need for a **God** at all—that is, for a single **perfect mind** or **understanding being** presiding over the whole world. Consequently, they conclude that the **belief** in a **God** is only a mistake. They argue it is a **faulty concept** <note>original: "Inadequate Conception"</note> of **matter** in general, where its **life** and **energetic nature** are viewed in **abstract isolation** as if they were a complete **substance** on their own. Nevertheless, these **Hylozoistic atheists** are also unable to explain that **phenomenon** of the **regularity** and **harmony** of the entire **universe** through this **hypothesis** of theirs. This is because every **part of matter** is, according to them, a **distinct perceiving thing** by itself, whose knowledge extends only to its own concerns. Since there is no single entity presiding over everything, the elements of the entire world (**in which all things are co-ordered together** <note>original Greek: "ἐν ᾧ πάντα συντέτακται"</note>) could never have fallen into one such **agreeing** and **unified harmony**.

And as for those other **Cosmo-Plastic Atheists** <term>Cosmo-Plastic Atheism: The theory that the world is a self-organizing organism, like a giant plant, that functions without a conscious creator.</term>, who imagine the whole world to be like **one huge plant**, **tree**, or **vegetable**, or to have only **one seed-like** <note>original: "Spermatick"</note>, **formative** <note>original: "Plastick"</note>, and **artful nature** that **orderly** and **methodically** arranges the whole but without **sensation** or **understanding**—these people cannot solve the problem either. That is, they cannot explain the aforementioned **phenomenon**, as it is utterly **impossible** for there to be any such **organized** and **regular nature** unless it is derived from and dependent upon a **perfect mind** or **wisdom**.

And thus we see plainly that no **atheists** whatsoever can explain the **phenomena** of **nature**, and particularly this one: the **regular**...

# The Phenomenon of the World. BOOK I. 688

...singular frame and harmony of the universe; and that true **Philosophy**, or the **knowledge of causes**, **necessarily** leads to a **God**.

But besides these **phenomena** of **thinking** <note>original: "Cogitation"</note> or the **soul** and **mind** in **animals**, the **physical motion** in **bodies**, and the **designed structure** <note>original: "Artificial Frame"</note> of things for **purposes** and **uses**, together with the **unified harmony** of the **whole**—none of which can be **explained** <note>original: "Salved"</note> without a **Deity**—we might also add another point. The **accidental** <note>original: "Fortuitous"</note> atheists (the followers of **Anaximander** and **Democritus**), who universally claimed the **recent origin** <note>original: "Novity"</note> of this **worldly system**, were unable to give any believable account of the **first beginning** of humans and those **larger animals**, which are only produced through reproduction by the mixing of male and female.

<margin>Book 3, last chapter.</margin>
**Aristotle**, in his book *The Generation of Animals*, writes the following: "Regarding the origin of humans and four-footed animals, if they were ever born from the earth <note>original Greek: "γηγενεῖς"</note>, as some claim, one might suppose it happened in one of two ways: either by forming first as worms through decay <note>original: "Putrefaction"</note>, or else being formed in certain eggs growing out of the earth." <note>original Greek: "περὶ δὲ τῆς ἀνθρώπων καὶ τετραπόδων γενέσεως, ὑπολάβοι τις ἂν, εἴπερ ἐγίγοντό ποτε γηγενεῖς, ὥσπερ φασί τινες, δύο τρόπων γίνεσθαι τὸν ἕτερον· ἢ γὰρ ὡς σκώληκος συνισταμένου τὸ πρῶτον, ἢ ἐξ ᾠῶν"</note> And then, after a short while, he concludes again: "If there were indeed some beginning of birth for all animals, it is reasonable to think it was one of these two aforementioned ways." <note>original Greek: "εἴπερ οὖν τις ἀρχὴ τῆς γενέσεως πᾶσι τοῖς ζῴοις, εὔλογον δυεῖν τούτων εἶναι τὴν ἑτέραν"</note> It is well known that **Aristotle**, though a **Theist**, elsewhere asserts the **world's eternity**. According to that hypothesis of his, there was never a **first male** nor **female** in any species of animal; instead, one begat another **infinitely** without any **beginning**. This idea is utterly repulsive to our **human faculties**, which are never able to form a **conception** of such an **infinity** of **number** and **time**, or of a **successive generation** from **eternity**. But here **Aristotle** himself seems **hesitant** <note>original: "staggering"</note> or **skeptical** about it, saying: "*If* humans were ever generated out of the earth," and "*If* there were any beginning to the generation of animals." He also proposes it in his *Topics* as an example of a **disputable** matter: <margin>Book 1, chapter 9.</margin> "**Whether the world is eternal or not?**" <note>original Greek: "πότερον ὁ Κόσμος ἀΐδιος ἢ οὔ"</note> He ranks it among **those great things for which we can give no certain reason, one way or the other**. <note>original Greek: "περὶ ὧν λόγον μὴ ἔχομεν, ὄντων μεγάλων"</note> Now (he says), if the **world had a beginning**, and if humans were once **earth-born** or **indigenous** <note>original Greek: "γηγενεῖς or αὐτόχθονες"</note>, then they must have been, in all probability, either generated as **worms** out of **decay**, or else out of **eggs**—he supposedly thought those **eggs** grew out of the earth. But the **majority** of **atheists** in **Aristotle’s** time, as well as **theists**, denied this **eternity** of the **worldly system**. They felt it did not fit their **hypothesis**, because such a **constant** and **invariable order** in the **world** from **eternity** does not look like the result of **chance**. Nor can it easily be supposed to have existed without the **providence** of a **perfect mind** presiding over it and being **older** than it <note>original: "Senior to it"</note> in **nature** (as **Aristotle** conceived), even if not in **time**. They, therefore, in all probability, also concluded that **humans at first**...

# CHAP. IV. The Beginning of Animals.

They were first thought to have been generated in one of these **two** ways: either out of **decay** <note>original: "Putrefaction"</note> or from **eggs**. This was supposedly caused by the **random motion** <note>original: "Fortuitous Motion"</note> of **matter**, without the providence or **direction** of any **deity**. But following **Aristotle**, **Epicurus** imagined those **first** humans and other **animals** to have been **formed** in certain **wombs** or **pouches** <note>original: "Bags"</note> growing out of the **earth**:

->*Wombs grew, attached to the earth by roots* <note>original Latin: "Crescebant Uteri terræ radicibus apti"</note><-

And this was supposedly achieved by nothing other than the **random motion** of **atoms** as well.

<margin>In Philo, *On the Incorruptibility of the World*.</margin>
But if humans had been formed at first in this manner—either in **wombs** or **eggs** (growing out of the earth) or generated out of **decay** by **chance**—then there would be no imaginable reason why it should not occasionally happen now. The motions of **atoms** are as brisk and vigorous as they ever were, and will continue to be so for all **eternity**. Therefore, there is not the least ground at all for that **flimsy fantasy** <note>original: "Precarious Phancy"</note> and **pretense** of **Epicurus**: that the Earth, like a **child-bearing woman** growing old, finally became **sterile** <note>original: "Effete"</note> and barren. 

Moreover, the **humans** thus at first released out of **pouches**, **wombs**, or **egg-shells** (or generated out of **decay**) were supposed by these **atheists** themselves to have been produced not in a **mature** and **adult** state, but in an **infant-like**, weak, and tender state—just as they are born into the world now. Because of this, they would have been unable to **feed** and **nourish** themselves, or defend themselves from harm and injury. 

But when the same **Epicurus** tries to pretend that the **Earth** (which had been such a **fruitful mother**) also became by **chance** a tender and indulgent **nurse** to her own offspring—sending forth streams or rivers of milk for them out of those gaps in her **damaged surface** <note>original: "Wounded Surface"</note> from which they had previously burst—he might as well have claimed (as **Critolaus** <note>A Peripatetic philosopher who argued for the eternity of the world.</note> observed long ago) that the **Earth** had **breasts** and **nipples** as well as **wombs** and **milk**. And if so, what should hinder her from having **arms** and **hands** also, and **swaddling clothes** <note>original: "Swaddling-bands"</note> to boot? 

Neither is it any less **unfounded** <note>original: "Precarious"</note> when the same **atheistic philosopher** adds that in this imaginary state of the **newborn** world, there was for a long time neither any extreme heat nor cold, nor any harsh and rough blasts of wind to annoy or injure those tender **earth-born infants** and **nurslings**. 

Considering all these things, **Anaximander** seems of the **two** to have concluded more wisely: that humans—because they require a longer time than other **animals** to be raised—were at first generated in the **bellies** of **fishes** and nourished there for a good while, until they were at length able to defend and shift for themselves, and then were **vomited up** <note>original: "Disgorged"</note> and cast onto dry land. Thus we see that there is nothing in the world so monstrous or prodigiously absurd that men with **atheistic** leanings will not rather imagine and swallow down, than entertain the notion of a **God**.

Therefore, we have here **a knot that requires a champion to untie** <note>original Latin: "Dignus Vindice Nodus"; a reference to the poet Horace, suggesting a problem so difficult it requires divine intervention</note>, and this **phenomenon** of the **first beginning** of mankind and other greater **animals** cannot **be**

# Other Phenomena, not BOOK I.

[The origin of life cannot] be explained <note>original: "salved"</note> otherwise than according to the Biblical History of Moses <note>original: "Mosaick History"</note>, by admitting a *God from a machine* <note>original Greek: "theos apo mechanes"; a term referring to a divine intervention that resolves a complex plot</note>—that is, an extraordinary manifestation of the Deity in forming man and other animals, both male and female, at once out of the earth. Furthermore, they were created not in a *crude, tender, and infant-like state*, but as mature *adults*, so that they might be able immediately to care for themselves, multiply, and propagate their kind through biological reproduction. Once this was done and there was no longer any necessity for such an extraordinary method of proceeding, God put a stop to it immediately so that no more *earth-born humans* <note>original Latin: "Terrigenae" or Greek: "Autochthones"</note> should be produced. 

For when all these circumstances are considered together, it plainly appears that this entire *phenomenon* surpasses not only *mechanical* forces but also *plastic powers* <note>original: "Plastick Powers"; the formative, unconscious forces of nature</note>. There is a great deal of *discretion* <note>i.e., conscious choice and judgment</note> involved in it, which the latter cannot achieve, as they always act by fate and necessity. Nevertheless, we shall not decide here whether God Almighty might have used the subordinate ministry of angels or superior spirits (created before man) in this first extraordinary formation of the bodies of animals out of the earth in a mature and *adult state*. Similarly, Plato in his *Timaeus* introduces the supreme God (whom he supposes to be the immediate Creator of all *immortal souls*) addressing the *lesser gods* <note>original: "Junior Gods"</note> and setting them to work on the manufacturing of *mortal bodies*: *"Now it is your task to weave the mortal to the immortal, creating animals and bringing them to life"* <note>original Greek: "to de loipon hymeis, athanatō thnēton prosyphainontes, apergazesthe zōa kai gennate"</note>. He later adds, *"After the sowing of immortal souls, [the Supreme God] committed the task of forming mortal bodies to these lesser gods"* <note>original Greek: "meta ton sporon, toos neoios paredōke theois, sōmata plattein thnēta"</note>. Some conceive this idea of Plato’s to have been derived from the words of Moses: *“Let us make man in our image.”*

Moreover, these atheists are no more able to explain <note>original: "Salve"</note> that other common and ordinary *phenomenon* either: the *conservation of animal species* by constantly maintaining a proper *numerical proportion* between the *male and female sexes* in the world. For if this depended only upon *random mechanics* <note>original: "Fortuitous Mechanism"</note>, it is hard to imagine how, in some age or another, it would not happen that either all *males* or all *females* were born, leading to the failure of the species. Indeed, it can hardly be thought of as anything other than a *Providence* superior to that of *plastic* or *spermatic nature* <note>referring to the unconscious biological forces of growth and reproduction</note>, which does not have enough knowledge or *discretion* allowed to it to be able to manage this affair alone.

Lastly, there are other *phenomena*, no less real though not *biological* <note>original: "Physiological"</note>, which atheists cannot explain in any way. These include *natural justice*, honesty, duty, and obligation (the true foundation of both *ethics* and *politics*), and the *“what is up to us”* <note>original Greek: "to eph' hēmin"</note> or *freedom of the will* properly so called. This is not the *random determination* that occurs when there is a *perfect equality* or *indifference* in the desirability of objects; rather, it is that by which people deserve *praise* and *blame*, *rewards* and *punishments*, thus becoming appropriate subjects for *compensatory justice* <note>original: "Remunerative Justice"</note> to act upon,

<meta>catchword: upon,</meta>

It also asserts that moral realities like justice and free will are inexplicable under an atheistic worldview.</summary>

# CHAPTER IV. Explainable <note>original: "salvable"</note> by Atheists.

...upon a *Main Hinge* upon which Religion turns (though these two concepts are not commonly as well distinguished as they ought to be). For when *Epicurus* (an *absolute atheist*), departing here from the views of *Democritus*, pretended to explain <note>original: "salve"</note> this by his *slight swerve of first principles* <note>original Latin: "Exiguum Clinamen Principiorum"; Epicurus’s theory that atoms randomly swerve to allow for free will in a materialist universe</note>, this attempt of his was nothing other than a plain delirium <note>original: "Delirancy"</note> or *atheistic frenzy* in him.

And now we have already *refuted in advance* <note>original: "Preventively Confuted"</note> the *third atheistic excuse* as well, which tries to explain the *phenomenon* of religion and the *belief in a God* that is so generally accepted. Namely, the claim that religion arises from the *fiction and trickery of politicians*. We have not only demonstrated that there is a *natural preconception* <note>original: "Natural Prolepsis"</note> and *anticipation of a God* in the minds of men—acting as the *object of their fear* even *before reason*—but also that the *belief in God* is sustained and upheld by the strongest reason. The *phenomena of nature* are in no way *explainable*, nor are the *causes of things assignable*, without a Deity. Therefore, since religion is founded both upon the *instincts of nature* and upon *solid reason*, it cannot possibly be a *fiction* or *trickery of politicians*. 

Nevertheless, we shall speak specifically to this point as well. The atheists conceive that, although those *infirmities of human nature*—*men's fear and ignorant gullibility*—dispose and incline them toward the *belief in a God* (or a rank of beings superior to men, whether visible or invisible, commonly called *gods* by the Pagans), this belief would not be so universally accepted as it is, especially that of *one Supreme Deity*, the *first origin* of all things and *Monarch of the Universe*, were it not for the *fraud and fiction of lawmakers* and *civil sovereigns*. These rulers, to better keep men in peace and subjection under them, and in a kind of religious and superstitious observation of their laws and *devotion* to the same, devised this *notion of a God* and then filled the minds of men with a belief in his existence and an *awe* of him.

Now, we do not deny that *politicians* may sometimes abuse *religion* and make it serve the promotion of their own private interests and designs. Yet they could not do this effectively if the thing itself were a mere *cheat and invention* <note>original: "Figment"</note> of their own, with no reality at all in *nature* nor anything *solid* at the bottom of it. But since religion prevails so universally everywhere, it is not conceivable how *civil sovereigns* throughout the whole world—some of whom are so distant and have so little contact with one another—should nonetheless all agree so well in this *one cheating mystery of government* or *piece of state-deception* <note>original: "State-Coozenage"</note>. Nor, if they could agree, is it conceivable how they would be able so effectively to possess the general population of mankind (the wise as well as the unwise) with such a constant *fear, awe, and dread* of a mere *counterfeit thing* and an *invisible nothing*. This "nothing" not only has no foundation in sense or reason, but also (as the atheists suppose) leads to their own great terror and unease, bringing them at once under a miserable enslavement <note>original: "Vassallage"</note> of both mind and body. This is especially true since men are not generally so quick to think that the more someone has of *power and dignity*, they therefore have so much the more of—

# God and Religion, Book I

Knowledge and skill in philosophy and the things of nature above others. And is it not strange that the world should not all this while have suspected or discovered this *cheat* and *trickery* <note>original: "Juggle"</note> of *politicians*, and have *sensed* <note>original: "Smelt out"</note> a *plot* against themselves in the *fiction of religion* to take away their liberty and enslave them under bondage? And is it not strange that so many of these *politicians* and *civil sovereigns* themselves also should have been unacquainted with this, and as simply awed by the fear of this *invisible nothing* as any others? 

All other *cheats* and *trickeries*, once they are detected even a little, are immediately thereafter quite shamed and never again have the confidence to impose themselves upon the world. But though the *atheists* have, for these *two thousand years past*, been continually buzzing into men’s ears that *religion is nothing but a mere state-trick and political imposture*, yet its credit has not been in the least impaired by this, nor its power and dominion over the minds of men abated. From this it may be concluded that it is no *counterfeit and fictitious thing*, but something deeply rooted in the *intellectual nature of man*, a thing solid at the bottom and *supported by its own strength*. 

This may appear even more fully from *Christianity*, a religion founded on no *human policy*, nor tending to promote any *worldly interest or design*. Yet by its *own* or the *Divine force*, it has prevailed over the *power* and *policy*, the *rage* and *madness* of all *civil states, Jewish and Pagan*, and has conquered so great a part of the persecuting world under it. It did this not by *resisting or opposing force*, but by suffering deaths and martyrdoms in adherence to that principle: *That it is better to obey God than men*. This very thing was foretold in the *prophetic Scripture*:

> *Why do the nations <note>original: "Heathen"</note> rage, and the people imagine a vain thing? The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the Lord, and against his Christ, etc. He that sits in the heavens shall laugh; the Lord shall have them in derision. Then shall he speak unto them in his wrath, etc. Yet have I set my king upon my holy hill of Zion. I will give thee the nations for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession. Be wise now therefore, O ye kings, etc.*

---

But that *theism, or religion*, is no *trickery or imposture* <note>original: "Gullery or Imposture"</note> will be yet further made unquestionably evident. That the generality of mankind have agreed in the acknowledgment of one *Supreme Deity*—as a Being *eternal and necessarily existent, absolutely perfect, and omnipotent*, and the *maker of the whole world*—has been already largely proved in the foregoing *discourse*. To this purpose is this quote from *Sextus the philosopher*: 

<margin>Against the Mathematicians 314</margin>
<note>original Greek: Κοινὴν γὰρ πρόληψιν ἔχουσι πάντες ἄνθρωποι περὶ θεοῦ, καθ᾽ ἣν μακάριόν τι ἔστι ζῶον καὶ ἄφθαρτον καὶ τέλειον ἐν εὐδαιμονίᾳ, καὶ παντὸς κακοῦ ἀνεπίδεκτον</note>
*For all men have this common preconception <note>original: "Prolepsis"</note> concerning God: that he is a living being, incorruptible, perfectly happy, and incapable of any manner of evil.* 

And the notion of that God which *Epicurus* opposed was no other than this: *An understanding being, having all happiness, with incorruptibility, that framed the whole world.* Now, I say, that if there be no such thing as...

# Chapter IV. Political Figments

<margin>Against the Mathematicians, 314.</margin>
If this *existence* and this *idea of God* were a mere *fictitious thing*, then it would have been altogether *arbitrary* <note>original: "arbitrarious"</note>. But it is inconceivable how the *generality* of mankind (except for only a few *atheists*) should universally agree on one and the same *arbitrary invention*. This line of reasoning has been used previously by some *theists*, as appears from the previously mentioned *Sextus*: "It is altogether irrational to think that all men should by chance hit upon the same properties (in the idea of God) without being naturally moved to do so." <note>original: "τελέως δὲ ἐστιν ἄλογον, τὸ τύχῃ πάντας τοῖς αὐτοῖς ἐπιβάλλειν ἰδιώμασιν, ἀλλὰ μὴ φυσικῶς οὕτως 314. ἐκκινεῖσθαι."</note> Neither is the explanation that the *atheists* offer here sufficient—that *statesmen* and *politicians* everywhere possessed the minds of men with one and the same *idea*. The difficulty remains: how could *civil sovereigns* and *lawmakers* in all the distant parts of the world, even those who had no communication or interaction with one another, universally arrive at <note>original: "jump in"</note> one and the same *fictitious* and *arbitrary idea*?

Moreover, if there were no *God*, it is *not conceivable* how that previously mentioned *idea* could ever have entered into the minds of men, or how it could have been formed within them. Here the *atheists* again think it is enough to say that this *notion* or *idea* was *placed* into the minds of the *generality* of mankind by *lawmakers* and *politicians* telling them of such a being and persuading them to believe in his *existence*; or that it was propagated and passed down by *oral tradition* from the very first *inventor* of it. But this demonstrates their great ignorance of *philosophy*, to think that any *notion* or *idea* is put into men's minds from the outside merely by *telling* or by *words*. We are passive to nothing from words except their sounds and the mental images <note>original: "phantasms"</note> they create; they only prompt the soul to stir up such notions as it already had within itself (whether *innate* or *acquired* <note>original: "adventitious"</note>) which those words, by the agreement of men, were made to represent. Or, they prompt the soul to reflect further upon its own *ideas*, considering them more distinctly and comparing them with one another. And although all learning is not the *remembrance* of what the *soul* once actually understood in a *pre-existent state*, as *Plato* suggests somewhere (and as *Boethius* wrote):

> *But if the Muse of Plato sounds the truth,* <note>original: "Quod si Platonis Musa personat Verum"</note>
> *Whatever someone learns, he remembers what he had forgotten;* <note>original: "Quod quisque Discit, Immemor Recordatur"</note>

Yet all *human teaching* is only *maieutical* <term>the Socratic method of bringing latent ideas into consciousness; literally, "midwifery"</term>, or *obstetrical* <note>original: "obstetricious"</note>. It is not the *filling* of the soul like a *vessel*, merely by *pouring* into it from the *outside*, but the *kindling* of it from *within*. It is a process of helping the soul to stir and awaken, compare, and combine its own *notions* so as to arrive at the *knowledge* of that which it was previously ignorant of. This concept was better expressed by the aforementioned *philosophical* poet in these words:

> *Truly, the seed of truth stays within,* <note>original: "Hæret profecto Semen introrsum Veri"</note>
> *Which is stirred up by the fanning of instruction.* <note>original: "Quod excitatur Ventilante Doctrina"</note>

# The Idea of God, from Book I.

Therefore, the mere *telling* of people, "*There is a God*," could not instill any *idea* of him into their minds; nor could providing this *definition* of him—that he is a *Being Absolutely Perfect*, *Eternal*, and *Self-Existent*—make them understand anything of his nature if they were not able to *evoke notions* or *ideas* from within themselves that corresponded to those various words. 

However, the difficulty still remains: how could those *civil rulers* and *lawmakers*, or how could *Critias* <note>A leading member of the Thirty Tyrants of Athens, often cited by ancient atheists as the one who claimed gods were invented to frighten people into obeying the law.</note>, the very first inventor of that deception of a God, form that *idea* within themselves? If we suppose that God does not exist, then it is the *idea of nothing*, or of a *non-entity*. This point was also wisely suggested by the same *Sextus*: 

<margin>Against the Mathematicians, 313, 314.</margin>

"But those who dispute this say that certain lawmakers instilled the opinion of God into men, not knowing that the original absurdity still awaits them. For if someone were to ask, from where did the lawmakers—since no one had previously handed it down—arrive at the conception of God?" <note>original: "οἱ δ' διαμφισβητοῦντές, φασὶν ὅτι νομοθέται τινες ἐνεποίησαν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, τὴν περὶ θεοῦ δόξαν, μὴ εἰδότες ὅτι τὸ ἀρχῆθεν ἄτοπον αὐτοῖς περιμένει, ζητήσαντος ἄν τινος, πόθεν δ' οἱ νομοθέται, μηδενὸς πρότερον παραδόντος, ἦλθον εἰς ἐπίνοιαν θεοῦ;"</note> 

Regarding this, the *atheists* who claim that certain lawmakers first put this notion of a God into the minds of men do not consider that they remain entangled in the same difficulty if anyone further asks them: "How could those lawmakers themselves first form that idea?" From which it is afterward concluded: 

"Therefore, it was not by law, nor by any legislation, that the people of old accepted that God exists." <note>original: "οὐ τοίνυν νομῷ, οὐδὲ κατά τινα νομοθεσίαν, παρεδέξαντο οἱ πάλαιοι τῶν ἀνθρώπων εἶναι θεόν."</note> That is, the notion of a God did not spring from the arbitrary <note>original: "arbitrarious"</note> fiction of lawmakers and politicians.

But some *atheists* will still reply further *that there is a power of invention* <note>original: "feigning power"</note> *in the human soul by which it can frame ideas or conceptions of things that never actually were nor ever will be—such as a centaur or a golden mountain—and that by such an inventive power as this, the idea of God might be framed even though no such thing exists.* 

To this we respond that we do not deny that the *human soul* has a power of *combining* <note>original: "compounding"</note> *ideas and things* together which exist separately and apart in nature, but never were (nor ever will be) in that specific combination. Indeed, this is the only *inventive power* that the soul possesses. For the mind cannot create any *new thought* <note>original: "cogitation"</note> which did not exist before, but can only *combine* that which *is*. 

Just as a *painter* cannot *invent colors* <note>original: "feign colours"</note> but must use those that exist in nature—though he can combine them in various ways and, with his brush, draw the figures and outlines <note>original: "lineaments"</note> of things that exist nowhere—he can add the neck, shoulders, and body of a horse to the head and face of a man. In the same way, that more subtle *painter* or *illustrator* <note>original: "limner"</note>, the *mind* and *imagination* of man, can frame *combined ideas* of things that exist nowhere. 

Nonetheless, his "simple colors" must be real. He cannot invent any thought which was not already in nature, nor create a *positive conception* of that which is *absolutely nothing*. To do so would be no less than to make *nothing be something*, or to create *something out of nothing*. And though the whole of these *fictional ideas* (such as a *golden mountain*) does not actually exist anywhere, because it does not absolutely imply a *contradiction* for it to exist, it therefore has a *possible existence* <note>original: "possible entity"</note>; otherwise, it could not even be conceived. By contrast, a *triangular square*, for example, being a *contradictory thing*, does not have even a *possible existence* and therefore is not *conceivable* as such (though both a triangle and a square are individually conceivable). It is mere nonsense, nothing, and no idea at all.

<summary>This page argues that the concept of God could not have been a mere political invention because the human mind is incapable of inventing entirely new concepts; it can only combine existing realities into new arrangements.</summary>

### CHAP. IV. Feigning Power of the Soul.

Indeed, we conceive that a Theist might reverently say that Almighty God himself—though he can create more or fewer really existing things as he pleases, and could make a whole world out of *nothing*—yet he cannot create more *thought* or *conception* than *is*, or than was already contained in his own *Infinite Mind* and *Eternal Wisdom*. Nor can he have a *positive idea* of anything that has neither *actual* nor *possible existence*.

But the Idea of God is not a *compilation* or *aggregation* of things that exist separately and apart in the world. If it were, it would be a purely *arbitrary* thing, and it could be whatever anyone pleased: one person adding more things together and another fewer, but each of them writing the *name* or *title* of "*God*" under these various *fancies*, much like clumsy painters used to do. On the contrary, we have already proved that the *Idea of God* is one most *simple idea* of an *Absolutely Perfect Being*, although it involves several *partial* and *incomplete conceptions*. Thus, nothing can be added to it or taken away from it, as nothing is included within it except what is *provable* of a *Perfect Being*; therefore, it is not arbitrary at all.

Moreover, many of those *partial conceptions* contained in the entire Idea of God are nowhere else to be found in the whole world, existing individually and apart. Therefore, if there is no God, they must be *absolute non-entities*—such as *immutability*, *necessary existence*, *infinity*, and *perfection*, etc. Consequently, any painter who creates this *idea* must, according to the atheist's supposition, *invent the colors* themselves or create *new thought* and *conception* out of *nothing*.

Lastly, if there is no God existing now, it is impossible that there ever should be one. Thus, the whole *Idea of God* would be the idea of something that has no *possible existence* either. In contrast, those other *fictitious ideas* created by the human mind—though they may represent things that do not have *actual existence*—nonetheless all have a *possible existence*, as was said before.

But so that we may hide nothing of the atheist's strength, we must acknowledge that some of them have further claimed that, besides this *power of combining* things, the human soul also has another *expanding*, or *increasing* and *improving power*. They argue that by using both powers together, even if no God exists or is even *possible*, the *idea* of him can still be *fictitiously* created. Those *partial ideas* which are found nowhere else arise, as they say, from a *transition from men* <note>original: *μετάβασις ἀπὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων*</note>—a gradual process of *amplification*, *augmentation*, and *improvement*.

<margin>*Against the Mathematicians*, p. 317.</margin>

Thus we read in *Sextus* <note>Sextus Empiricus, a Skeptic philosopher who recorded many atheist arguments.</note>: "The idea that God is eternal, incorruptible, and perfect in happiness arose by a transition from men. For just as we have a conception of a Cyclops by magnifying the common man in our imagination, so by conceiving of a happy and blessed man who is complete with all good things, and then intensifying these qualities, we conceive of God as the ultimate peak of those very traits. And again, when the ancients imagined a long-lived man, they increased that time to infinity, and from there arrived at the concept of eternity." <note>original: "τὸ ἀΐδιον εἶναι τὸν θεὸν, καὶ ἄφθαρτον, καὶ τέλειον ἐν εὐδαιμονίᾳ, παρῆλθε κατὰ τὴν ἀπὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων μετάβασιν· ὡς γὰρ τὸν κοινὸν ἄνθρωπον αὐξήσαντες τῇ φαντασίᾳ, νόησιν ἔχομεν Κύκλωπος, οὕτως ἄνθρωπον εὐδαίμονα νοήσαντες καὶ μακάριον καὶ συμπεπληρωμένον πᾶσι τοῖς ἀγαθοῖς, εἶτα ταῦτα ἐπιτείναντες, τὸν ἐν αὐτοῖς ἐκείνοις ἄκρον ἐνοήσαμεν θεόν· καὶ πάλιν πολυχρόνιόν τινα φαντασιωθέντες ἄνθρωπον οἱ παλαιοὶ, ἐπηύξησαν τὸν χρόνον εἰς ἄπειρον, εἶτα ἐντεῦθεν εἰς ἔννοιαν ἀϊδίου παραγενόμενοι"</note>

# The Idea of God is not from Amplification: Book 1.

...reasoning, they said that God is also eternal. <note>original: "...νοι, ἔφασαν καὶ ἀϊδιον εἶναι τὸν θεόν"</note> The ideas of the eternity, incorruptibility, and perfect happiness of the Deity were imaginary constructions, created by transitioning from human traits. For just as we create the phantom of a **Cyclops** in our imagination by increasing the size of an ordinary man, so when we see a **happy man** who has all good things, we **amplify**, **intensify**, and, as it were, **expand** <note>original: swell</note> that same image in our minds higher and higher until we finally reach the idea of a **Being who is absolutely happy**, which is **God**. In the same way, the ancients noticed a very **long-lived** <note>original: longeve</note> man and, by increasing this lifespan further and further toward infinity, they framed the notion or idea of **eternity** and attributed it to **God**.

But to this we reply: First, according to the principles of the atheists themselves, the soul could not possibly have any such **amplifying** and **inventive power** by which it could **create more than what exists**. This is because they assume the soul has no **active power** at all; instead, they believe all our **conceptions** are nothing but mere **passive impressions** <note>original: passions</note> received from external **objects**. This follows the view of **Protagoras** in **Plato’s** *Theaetetus*:

<margin>Page 167. Serranus edition.</margin>
"It is not possible for a man to conceive of that which does not exist, nor to experience anything more or different than what he passively suffers." <note>original: "τὰ μὴ ὄντα δυνατὸν δοξάσαι, οὔτε ἄλλα παρ᾽ ἃ ἂν πάσχῃ"</note> Furthermore, as **Sextus the Philosopher** <note>Sextus Empiricus, a skeptical philosopher often cited in debates about the origins of ideas</note> also suggests, the atheists here are clearly guilty of that fallacy or error in **reasoning** <note>original: ratiocination</note> commonly called a **circular argument**, or "reasoning through one another." <note>original: δι᾽ ἀλλήλων</note> For they could not judge the greatest perfection and happiness they have experienced in men to be **imperfect** except by having a **prior idea** of **perfection** and **happiness** with which to compare it. By virtue of this idea, they are able to **amplify** those lesser perfections of men further and further, using **imperfect things** as an occasion to think of that which is **absolutely perfect**. In other words, while these atheists themselves first derive the **idea of imperfection** from their concept of **perfection**, they fail to notice this and instead try to construct the **notion** or **idea** of that which is **absolutely perfect** (by way of **amplification**) from that which is **imperfect**. 

But the fact that humans possess a notion of **absolute perfection**—which acts as the **rule** or **measure** by which they judge other things (comparing them to it) to be **imperfect**—shows that this idea is first in the order of nature. This is evident because all **theologians**, both **Pagan** and **Christian**, give this instruction for conceiving of God: it should primarily be done **by way of removal** <note>original: Per Viam Remotionis; this refers to "apophatic theology," or defining God by what He is not (e.g., not finite, not mortal).</note>—that is, by removing all **imperfection from him**. Thus, **Alcinous** <note>A Middle Platonist philosopher whose handbook on Platonism was influential in the Renaissance.</note> says, "The first way of conceiving of God is by removal or abstraction." <note>original: πρώτη μὲν αὐτοῦ νόησις ἡ κατ᾽ ἀφαίρεσιν</note> 

Finally, we add that **finite** things, even when put together, can never equal the **infinite**. This is clear from the example of **human longevity** mentioned before: even if one were to **amplify** a lifespan as much as possible by adding more and more **past time** or years to it, they would never be able to reach an **eternity** that has no beginning. **God** does not differ from these **imperfect created things** merely in **degree**, but in his **entire nature**. And though **infinite space** might be raised as an objection here—as something taken for granted that, being nothing but **extension** or **magnitude**, must be made up of **finite parts**—nevertheless, as was stated before, we

### CHAPTER 4. Of Imperfect Things.

...we have no certainty of anything more than this: that the **Finite World** might have been made **bigger and bigger infinitely**, or **without end**. However, this infinity of magnitude is only like that of **number**, which is **potential** <note>Potential infinity refers to something that can be increased without end, as opposed to an "actual" infinity which is complete and whole.</note>. From this, it may be inferred that one, just like the other, can never be **actually infinite**. Therefore, if there were no **infinitely perfect being** in **nature**, the **idea** of such a being could never be created by any **amplifying power** of the **soul**, or by the **addition** of **finites**.

Nor is the objection that **Gassendi** <note>original: "Gassendus"; referring to Pierre Gassendi (1592–1655), a French philosopher and scientist.</note> argues so strongly here of any importance: that even if there were no God or **infinite being**, the **idea** of him might still be **invented** <note>original: "feigned"</note> by the mind, just as the idea of **infinite worlds** or **infinite matter** was invented by some **philosophers**. For **infinite worlds** and **infinite matter** are merely words **poorly put together**. Infinity is a real thing in **nature** (and no **fiction** of the **mind**) just like the **world** or **matter**; however, it is proper to the **Deity** alone. It is no wonder if those who denied a God—yet retained this notion of infinity—misapplied it to **matter**, just as they also misapplied other properties of the **Deity**.

To conclude this: our human soul cannot **invent** or **create** any new thought or conception that did not exist before; it can only variously combine that which already **is**. Nor can it ever make a **positive idea** of an **absolute non-entity**—that is, something that has neither **actual** nor **possible existence**. Much less could our **imperfect beings** create the **entity** of so **vast a thought** as that of an **infinitely perfect being** out of **nothing**. This would, in fact, be a greater feat than for **God Almighty**, or a **perfect being**, to create a **real world** out of **nothing**, because there is no logical contradiction in the latter, while there is in the former. We affirm, therefore, that if there were no God, the **idea** of an **absolutely** or **infinitely perfect being** could never have been made or invented, neither by politicians, nor by poets, nor philosophers, nor any other. This may be considered another argument for the existence of a **Deity**.

Furthermore, it will appear beyond question from what follows that **religion** is no fiction of politicians. Just as the **sanctity** <note>original: "religion"</note> of an **oath** is a **necessary bond of civil society**, so **obligation** in **conscience**—recognizing the Deity as its origin and as the punisher of those who violate it—is the very foundation of all civil sovereignty. For **pacts** and **covenants** (to which some would reduce all **civil power**) are nothing but mere words and breath without this obligation in conscience. The **laws** and **commands** of civil sovereigns do not create obligation; rather, they presuppose it as something that exists in the order of nature before them, and without which they would be **invalid**. 

This is a truth so evident that the author of *The Citizen* <note>original: "De Cive"; a work by Thomas Hobbes published in 1642.</note> could not hide it, even though he did not rightly understand this **natural obligation**. He acknowledges it in these words: <margin>On Empire, chapter 14, section 21.</margin> "The obligation to civil obedience, by whose power civil laws are valid, is prior to all civil law. For if any supreme prince were to frame a civil law in this form, 'You shall not rebel,' he would achieve nothing. For unless the citizens are first obligated to obey—that is, not to rebel—every law is invalid; and if they are already obligated, the law is unnecessary." <note>original: "Obligatio ad Obedientiam Civilem, cujus vi Leges Civiles Validæ sunt, Omni Lege Civili prior est. — Quod si quis Princeps Summus, Legem Civilem in hanc Formulam conciperet, Non Rebellabis, nihil efficeret. Nam nisi prius Obligentur Cives ad Obediendum, hoc est, ad Non Rebellandum, Omnis Lex Invalida est ; & si prius Obligentur est superflua."</note> The obligation to **civil**...

# Religion: The Foundation of Civil Power. Book 1.

**Civil obedience**, the force that makes all **civil laws valid**, exists before those **civil laws**. If any ruler <note>original: "Prince"</note> were to make a **law** for **this purpose**—stating that no one should rebel against him—it would mean nothing. This is because unless the people to whom the law is made were already obligated to **obey**, or not to **rebel**, the **law** is **invalid**; and if they already were obligated, **then the law is unnecessary** <note>original: "superfluous"</note>. 

Now, this **previous obligation** to **civil obedience** cannot be derived solely from people's **personal benefit** <note>original: "Private Utility"</note>, as the aforementioned author of *On the Citizen* <note>original: "De Cive"; a 1642 work by Thomas Hobbes</note> and of the *Leviathan* <note>Hobbes's 1651 work arguing for absolute sovereignty</note> supposes. This is because if every person were the **judge** of their own benefit, it would then be lawful for any subject to rebel against their sovereign ruler, and to poison or stab him, whenever they could reasonably persuade themselves that it would serve their own advantage, or that they might gain the throne <note>original: "Sovereignty"</note> for themselves. Were the **obligation** to **civil obedience** based only on people's **personal benefit**, it would be just as easily **dissolved** by that same benefit. 

It remains, therefore, that **conscience** and a **religious obligation to duty** are the only **basis** and **essential foundation** of a **state** <note>original: "Polity or Common-Wealth"</note>. Without this, there could be no **right** or **authority** of **commanding** in any sovereign, nor any **validity** in any laws. Therefore, **religious obligation** cannot be thought of as a **fiction** or **deception** <note>original: "Imposture"</note> created by **civil rulers**, unless **civil sovereignty** itself is considered a **fiction and deception**, or something that has no **foundation in nature** but is entirely **artificial** or based on **force** <note>original: "Violent"</note>.

Furthermore, had a **religious regard** for the **Deity** been a mere **figment** or **invention** of **politicians** to promote their own ends and keep people in obedience and subjection, they would undoubtedly have designed and contrived it to be **flexible** and **compliant** in every way. Specifically, they would have persuaded the world that whatever they commanded was agreeable to the **divine will**, and whatever was forbidden by their **laws** was displeasing to **God Almighty** and would be **punished** by Him. They would claim that God rules over the world in no other way than through these **civil rulers** as His **representatives** <term>original: "Vicegerents"; officials acting on behalf of a ruler or God</term>, and as the only **prophets** and **interpreters** of His will to humanity. In this way, the **civil law** of every **country** and the **arbitrary will** of rulers would be acknowledged as the only **measure** of **just** and **unjust** (there being nothing that is **naturally** so), and the only **rule of conscience and religion**. Rulers might think that from a religion modeled this way, they would have an **absolute power** or an **infinite right** to do or command whatever they pleased without exception. Nothing would be unlawful for them, and their subjects would always be obligated in **conscience**, without the slightest hesitation, to obey.

But this is merely a **mask** <note>original: "Larva"; in Latin, this refers to a ghost or a mask, implying a hollow imitation</note> of **religion** and would be a mockery of God Almighty. Indeed, this is the only kind of religion that can truly be called a **political fiction**. Mankind in general could never be persuaded that the **arbitrary will of civil rulers** was the only **rule of justice and conscience**, or that God Almighty could command nothing or reveal His will concerning religion to humanity in any other way than through these rulers as His **prophets** and **interpreters**. True **religion and conscience** are no such **waxen things**, **slavishly devoted** <note>original: "Servilely Addicted"</note> to...

# Chapter 4: But Disowned by Politicians.

...the arbitrary wills of men; but they are **stubbornly disobedient** <note>original: "Immorigerous"</note>, **stiff**, and **inflexible**. They respect the Deity only, his **eternal** or **everlasting laws**, and his **revealed will**. Whenever human laws clash with these (which is not impossible), they conclude that **God ought to be obeyed, and not men**. For this reason, **godless politicians** declare open war against **religion**, viewing it as something utterly **inconsistent** with **civil sovereignty**. They believe it introduces a **fear** greater than the **fear of the Leviathan** <note>In Thomas Hobbes's philosophy, the "Leviathan" represents the absolute power of the state</note>—namely, the fear of **Him** who can inflict **eternal punishments** after death. They also see it as clashing with that monstrous, **infinite**, and **unlimited power** of theirs. This is a kind of power that **genuine theists** do not even attribute to **God Almighty himself**: a power to make their mere arbitrary **will** the **rule of justice**, rather than **justice** the **rule of their will**. Thus, a **modern writer of politics** <note>Referring to Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), author of the "Leviathan"</note> condemns as **seditious doctrine**—tending toward the dissolution of a **commonwealth**—the idea **that subjects may judge what is good and evil, just and unjust**, or have any other **conscience** besides the **law of the land**.

### Extraordinary Phenomena; Book I.

...disclaimed by these politicians as being altogether inconsistent with their designs, they cannot be supposed to have been the **fictions** <note>original: "Figments"</note> of **secular rulers** <note>original: "Civil Sovereigns"</note>, or the mere **creations of political strategy**. And thus have we abundantly refuted those three **atheistic excuses** <note>original: "Pretences"</note> used to explain away the **phenomenon of religion**: that it arises from **fear**, from the **ignorance of causes**, or from the **invention of politicians**.

But besides those **ordinary phenomena** mentioned before, which atheists cannot explain away <note>original: "no way Salvable"</note>, there are certain other **extraordinary phenomena** that either immediately prove a **God** and **Providence**, or else prove that there is a **rank of invisible, intelligent beings** superior to men, from which a **Deity** may afterwards be inferred. These are especially these **three**: **apparitions**, **miracles**, and **prophecies**. Regarding these, atheists—stubbornly denying **historical facts**—insist on attributing such things either to **deceptive fraud** and knavery, or else to men’s own **fear and imagination**. They claim people are ignorant of how to distinguish **dreams** and other strong **fantasies** <note>original: "Imaginations"</note> from actual **vision and the senses**. Or, lastly, they attribute them to certain **religious tales or legends** allowed by the **official authority of secular rulers** for **political ends**. Therefore, we shall briefly suggest something here to defend the **historical truth** of those phenomena against atheists.

First, regarding **apparitions**: though there is much of the **mythical** <note>original: "Fabulosity"</note> in these accounts, it cannot reasonably be concluded that there is no **truth** in them at all. Something of this kind has been asserted in all ages and many times attested to by persons of **unquestionable wisdom** and **undoubted truthfulness**. And while atheists attribute the **origin** of these things to men mistaking both their **dreams** and their **waking fantasies** for **real visions and sensations**, they plainly contradict a **main fundamental principle** of their own **philosophy**: that **sense is the only ground of certainty** and the **standard** <note>original: "Criterion"</note> of all **truth**. For if wise and intelligent persons can be so frequently mistaken by confusing their own **dreams and fantasies** with **physical sensations**, how can there be any certainty of knowledge at all from the **senses**? Furthermore, they discredit both the **senses** and **human testimony** so much that if the same were done in other cases, it would plainly overthrow the foundations of all **human life**.

Therefore, other atheists, being aware of the problem <note>original: "Inconvenience"</note> with denying so many **physical appearances** and **testimonies** or **historical accounts**, have chosen instead to acknowledge the **reality of apparitions**. Nevertheless, they conclude them to be things caused and **created by the power of the imagination alone**. They argue as if the strength of the **imagination** were such that it could not only **create fantasies** but also **real, physical objects**—and at a distance from the person imagining them, too—such that the senses of others shall be affected by them for a time, though they quickly vanish again. From this **monstrous paradox**, we may observe the **fanaticism** of some **atheists**. It shows that there is nothing so monstrously absurd that men infected with **atheistic disbelief** will not rather accept into their

For if "invisible ghosts" or "spirits" are once acknowledged as **permanent beings** <note>original: "Things Permanent"</note>, it will not be easy for anyone to explain why there might not also be one **Supreme Spirit** <note>original: "Supreme Ghost"</note> presiding over all of them and the whole world.

Finally, we shall observe that **Democritus** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher (c. 460 – c. 370 BC) known for his "atomic" theory of the universe; usually considered a materialist.</note> was further convinced by these accounts of **apparitions**. He granted that there was a certain kind of **permanent being**, independent of the imagination and **superior to men**, which could appear in different forms and disappear at will. He called these "**idols**" or "**images**," supposing them to be of the same nature as those **shedded emissions** <note>original: "Exuvious Effluxes"; in ancient physics, these were thin films of atoms that were thought to constantly peel off the surface of objects, allowing them to be seen.</note> that stream continually from the surface of bodies. However, he would not allow them to have anything immortal in them. Instead, he believed their **physical structures** <note>original: "Concretions"</note> would eventually dissolve, and their personalities would then vanish into nothingness. Thus the philosopher **Sextus** <margin>Against the Mathematicians <note>original: *Adv. Math.*</note>, p. 311.</margin> writes: 

"Democritus asserts that certain idols or specters often approach men, some of which are beneficial and some harmful. Because of this, he prays that he might have the good fortune to meet with favorable idols. He adds that these are of a vast size and very long-lived, though not incorruptible. They sometimes foretell future events to men, appearing visibly and speaking with audible voices." <note>original: *δημόκριτος εἴδωλά τινα φησὶν ἐμπελάζειν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, καὶ τούτων τὰ μὲν εἶναι ἀγαθοποιά, τὰ δὲ κακοποιά· ἔνθεν καὶ εὔχεται εὐλόγων τυχεῖν εἰδώλων· εἶναι δὲ ταῦτα μεγάλα τε καὶ ὑπερμεγέθη, καὶ δύσφθαρτα μὲν, οὐκ ἄφθαρτα δὲ, προσημαίνειν τε τὰ μέλλοντα τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, θεωρούμενα καὶ φωνὰς ἀφιέντα.*</note> 

Now, although **Democritus** was criticized by his fellow atheists for this concession—since they felt he gave too much ground to theists—he believed he had sufficiently protected himself against the "danger" of admitting a God. He did this by assuming all these **idols** of his were **corruptible** <note>meaning they can decay and die</note>. He thought they were nothing but finer **clusters of atoms** <note>original: "Concretions of Atoms"</note>, a kind of aerial or **heavenly** <note>original: "Æthereal"</note> animal that was entirely physical and lacked an immortal soul, just as he believed men were. Thus, he thought a God could no more be proven by their existence than by the existence of humans. For he adds in Sextus: 

"Ancient people, having perceived these apparitions or idols, developed the idea of a God from them; however, besides these idols, there is no other God who possesses an incorruptible nature." <note>original: *ὅθεν τούτων αὐτῶν φαντασίαν λαβόντες οἱ παλαιοὶ, ὑπενόησαν εἶναι θεὸν, μηδενὸς ἄλλου παρὰ ταῦτα ὄντος θεοῦ, τοῦ ἀφθάρτου φύσιν ἔχοντος.*</note> 

However, even though Democritus remained crudely atheistic, he was more convinced than our modern atheists are that stories of **apparitions** were not all fables. He believed that there are not only land-dwelling animals, but also **aerial** and **heavenly** <note>original: "Ætherial"</note> animals, and that our Earth is not the only inhabited place while the vast regions above lie empty, solitary, and wasted. Here it may be observed again that several of the ancient Church Fathers—though they did not go as far as Democritus in making **angelic beings** entirely physical—nevertheless supposed them to have certain subtle heavenly or aerial bodies. In this regard, **St. Augustine** <note>original: "St. Austin"</note>, in his 115th Epistle, calls angels "**heavenly**" <note>original: *Æthereos*</note> and **devils**,

# Of Apparitions and Spirits, Book I.

This is the view Michael Psellus <note>An 11th-century Byzantine monk and philosopher known for his work on demonology.</note> presents in his dialogue, *On the Operation of Demons* <note>original: *περὶ ἐνεργείας δαιμόνων*</note>: 

"But you must know, noble friend, that the race of demons is not entirely without bodies; they are joined to a body and live within one. This can also be learned from the venerable Church Fathers. Even the divine Basil <note>St. Basil the Great (c. 330–379), an influential Greek bishop and theologian.</note> contends that bodies exist not only in demons, but even in the pure angels themselves—describing them as certain subtle, airy, and purified spirits," and so forth. 

Afterward, Psellus shows how the body that is natural to angels <note>original: *σύμφυες ἀγγέλοις σῶμα*</note> differs from the body to which demons are united. He explains this by the **radiant splendor** of the angelic body compared to the **dark, smoky obscurity** <note>original: "fuliginous"</note> of the demonic one. 

Furthermore, he tries to confirm that demons are not without bodies by citing the words of our Savior, who said they shall be **punished with fire**. Psellus argues that this would be impossible if they were all entirely without bodies. Some might even try to prove the same regarding angels based on other words of our Savior regarding the state of the resurrection. He affirmed that those who are worthy of it shall neither marry nor be given in marriage, but will be **equal to the angels** <note>original: *ἰσάγγελοι*</note>. This comparison of humans (who have bodies) to angels would seem less appropriate if angels were completely devoid of any physical form. However, we do not make a final determination on this point.

To this evidence of **apparitions**, we might add two others: **magicians** or **wizards**, and **those possessed by spirits** <note>original: *Demoniacks* or *Energumeni*</note>. Both of these cases also prove the real existence of spirits. They show that spirits are not merely fantasies or imaginary inhabitants of the human brain, but real inhabitants of the world. Furthermore, they show that among these spirits, there are some foul, unclean, and wicked ones (though God did not make them so; they became so through their own rebellion). 

This provides some confirmation of the **truth of Christianity**, as the Scriptures insist so much on these **evil demons** or **devils**. The Bible declares that one primary reason Jesus Christ came into the world was to oppose these allied powers of the kingdom of darkness and to rescue mankind from their slavery and bondage. 

As for wizards and magicians—people who associate and ally themselves in a specific way with these evil spirits to satisfy their own revenge, lust, ambition, and other passions—we have more than just the Scriptures as proof. There has been such extensive testimony given by disinterested people in all ages that those who so confidently dismiss <note>original: "Exploders"</note> them in our present age can hardly avoid the suspicion of being inclined toward atheism. 

But as for the **demoniacs** <note>those possessed by demons</note> and **those possessed by spirits** <note>original: *Energumeni*</note>, many have wondered why there were so many of them in our Savior's time, and yet hardly any or none in our own age. It is certain from the writings of Josephus <note>A 1st-century Jewish historian.</note> in several places that the Pharisaic Jews of that time generally believed in these **people possessed by demons** <note>original: *δαιμονιζόμενοι*</note>. They believed these were men possessed by devils or infested by them. It is clear that this was not merely a phrase or figure of speech used among them to describe people who were very **ill-affected**—

### CHAPTER IV. Witches and Demoniacs

That they were affected in their bodies may be seen from this: Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a famous Jewish-Roman historian.</note> declares his opinion concerning **demons** or **devils** that they were **the spirits or souls of wicked men who had died, which then entered into the bodies of the living** <note>original: *πονηρῶν ἀνθρώπων πνεύματα τοῖς ζῶσιν εἰσδυόμενα*</note>. Because of this belief, the Jews in our Savior’s time were not at all surprised when he cast out devils, as it was common for them to practice exorcism as well—an art they claimed to have learned from **Solomon**. Regarding this, Josephus writes:

<margin>Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 8, Chapter 2.</margin>

**God also granted Solomon the ability to learn the art used against demons for the benefit and healing of people. He composed certain incantations by which diseases are relieved, and he left behind methods of exorcism by which demons are bound so that they never return, driving them away. This method of healing remains very powerful among us even to this day.** <note>original: *παρέσχε δ' αὐτῷ μαθεῖν ὁ θεὸς, καὶ τὴν κατὰ τῶν δαιμόνων τέχνην, εἰς ὠφέλειαν καὶ θεραπείαν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις· ἐπωδάς τε συνταξάμενος οἷς παρηγορεῖται τὰ νόσματα, καὶ τρόπους ἐξορκώσεων κατέλιπεν, οἷς ἐνδούμενα τὰ δαιμόνια ὡς μηκέτ' ἐπανελθεῖν, ἐκδιώκουσι. Καὶ αὕτη μέχρι νῦν ἡ θεραπεία πλεῖστον ἰσχύει.*</note>

Despite this, we do not think it is at all probable what a recent **atheistic writer** <note>Likely a reference to Thomas Hobbes, who argued that "possession" in the Bible was simply a term for natural diseases or madness.</note> has asserted: that the minds of the Jews back then were so full of demons and devils that they generally mistook all kinds of physical illnesses—such as fevers, agues <note>A fever marked by regular fits of shivering.</note>, muteness, and deafness—for devils.

We do grant, however, that this very thing was later attributed by **Plotinus** <note>A major Greek-speaking philosopher (c. 204–270 AD), the founder of Neoplatonism.</note> to the **Gnostics** <note>A diverse group of early religious movements that emphasized secret knowledge (*gnosis*) for salvation.</note>: that they supposed all diseases to be devils and therefore believed they should not be cured by medicine <note>original: *physick*</note>, but expelled by words or charms.

As Plotinus writes in *Enneads*, Book 2, Chapter 9, Section 14:

**Now when they claim that diseases are demons, and assert they can remove them with words, making great promises, they may seem more impressive to the common people—who admire the powers of magicians—but they would not convince sensible people that diseases do not have natural causes, such as from over-eating, lack of nutrition, decay, and so forth. This is clearly shown by their cures; for when the bowels are purged or medicine is given, the disease passes out below. It is also healed by bloodletting and fasting—unless these men would say that the demon is starved by this, causing it to waste away.** <note>original: *νῦν δ' ὑποστησάμενοι τὰς νόσους δαιμόνια εἶναι, καὶ ταῦτα ἐξαιρεῖν λόγῳ φάσκοντες δύνασθαι, καὶ ἐπαγγελλόμενοι, σεμνότεροι μὲν ἂν εἶναι δόξαιεν παρὰ τοῖς πολλοῖς, οἳ τὰς παρὰ τοῖς μάγοις δυνάμεις θαυμάζουσι, τοὺς μέντοι σωφρονοῦντας οὐκ ἂν πείθοιεν, ὡς οὐκ αἱ νόσοι τὰς αἰτίας ἔχουσι, ἢ πλησμοναῖς, ἢ ἐνδείαις &c. δηλοῦσι δὲ αἱ θεραπεῖαι αὐτῶν, γαστρὸς γὰρ ῥυείσης ἢ φαρμάκου δοθέντος, διεχώρησε κάτω τὸ νόσημα· καὶ αἵματος ἀφηρημένου καὶ ἐνδείᾳ ἠιάσατο· ἢ πεινήσαντος τοῦ δαιμονίου, καὶ τοῦ φαρμάκου ποιήσαντος τήκεσθαι.*</note>

Nor can we think that the Jews in our Savior's time either supposed all madmen to be **demoniacs** <note>Individuals believed to be possessed by demons.</note>, or all demoniacs to be madmen (though this latter view seems to be asserted by an eminent writer of our own). We read of devils being cast out from people other than madmen, such as the woman who had a "spirit of infirmity" only—she was bent over and could not lift herself up, and our Savior Christ said she had been **bound by Satan**.

Therefore, the understanding of the Jews in the past seems to have been this: when there were any unusual and extraordinary symptoms in a physical sickness—but especially in the case of **madness**—this was looked upon as something more than natural and was attributed by them to the possession or infestation...

<header>Energumeni or Demoniacs; BOOK I.</header>

...of some Devil. This belief was not unique to the Jews of that time—supposing that evil demons were the causes of bodily diseases with extraordinary symptoms, especially **madness**. The Greeks and other Gentiles were also convinced of this, as shown by the story of **Apollonius of Tyana** <note>original: *Apollonius Tyanaeus*; a famous 1st-century philosopher and reputed miracle-worker.</note> curing a "laughing demoniac" in Athens. Apollonius reportedly drove out the evil spirit through threats and menaces; as the spirit departed, it is said to have knocked down a Royal Porch <note>The *Stoa Basileios* in Athens.</note> in the city with a great noise. Another example is when he freed the city of Ephesus from the plague by ordering the stoning of an old, ragged beggar. Apollonius claimed this man was the personification of the **plague**, which was revealed to be a demon when it transformed into the shape of a **shaggy dog**.

However, the idea that there is some truth in this opinion—and that even today, evil spirits or **demons** do sometimes truly act upon the bodies of men to either cause or worsen physical ailments—has been the judgment of two very experienced physicians, **Sennert** and **Fernel**.

The former, Daniel Sennert, in his book *On Madness* <note>original: *De Mania. Lib. 1. cap. 15.*</note>, wrote:

"Although the Devil may, by Divine permission, possess and occupy men without any existing morbid disposition of the body, he usually mingles himself with bodily diseases, especially those involving **melancholy** <note>In historical medicine, "melancholy" was a physical disease caused by an excess of black bile, often linked to depression or insanity.</note>; and perhaps this happens more often than is commonly believed or suspected." <note>original: *Etſi ſine ulla Corporis Morboſa Diſpoſitione, Deo permittente, hominem Obſidere & Occupare Dæmon poſſit, tamen quandoque Morbis, & præcipuè Melancholicis, ſeſe immiſcet Dæmon; & forſan frequentius hoc accidit, quam ſæpè creditur.*</note>

The other physician, Jean Fernel, in his work *On the Hidden Causes of Things* <note>original: *De Abditis rerum Cauſis*</note>, after attributing real physical effects to witchcraft and enchantment, adds:

"Not only do these wicked magicians inflict diseases upon men's bodies, but they also send devils into them. By this means, the victims appear distorted by a kind of fury and madness. Yet this differs from **Simple Madness** (the natural disease) in one specific way: they speak about very high and difficult matters, reveal secrets from the past or things hidden, and disclose the private thoughts of those sitting nearby." <note>original: *Neque ſolum morbos, verum etiam Dæmonas, ſcelerati homines in corpora immittunt. Hi quidem viſuntur Furoris quadam ſpecie diſtorti; hoc uno tamen à Simplici Furore diſtant, quod ſummè ardua obloquantur, præterita & occulta renuntient, aſſidentiúmque arcana referent.*</note>

Fernel then provides two notable instances of people he knew personally who were clearly <term>demoniacal</term> <gloss>possessed or acted upon by an evil spirit</gloss>; one of these will be mentioned later.

When people suffering from madness do more than just reveal secrets or past events, but also predict the future and speak in languages they never learned, it proves beyond all doubt that they are not merely "maniacs" (sufferers of natural madness), but <term>Energumeni</term> <gloss>demoniacs</gloss>. That such cases have occurred often since the time of our Savior Christ can be proven by the records of credible writers. **Psellus**, in his book *On the Operation of Demons* <note>original: *Περὶ Ἐνεργείας Δαιμόνων* / *De Operat. Dæm.*</note>, swears this was true of a certain madwoman. Though she knew nothing but her own mother tongue, when a stranger from Armenia was brought into the room, she immediately spoke to him in the **Armenian language**.

<margin>Page 69.</margin>

"We all stood amazed," <note>original: *ἡμεῖς δὲ τεθηπότες ἧμεν, ὅτι κατ’ Ἀρμενίων ἐφθέγγετο, γυνὴ μηδέποτε μηδ' εἰς ὄψιν ἀφιγμένη τούτοις, μηδὲ κεφαλὴν εἰδυῖα πλέον οὐδέν* / "We all stood amazed because she spoke in the Armenian tongue—a woman who had never even seen these people, nor knew anything more [of the language] than she knew of her own head."</note>

But because this instance is more distant from our present time, we shall set down another remarkable one of a more recent date from the aforementioned **Fernel**, who was an eyewitness to it. A young man of a noble family was strangely convulsed in his body; first one limb and then another was so violently agitated that four different people could hardly hold him down. At first, this happened without any disorder in his head or mental illness. Fernel, along with other skillful physicians, was called to him and applied all manner of remedies: blisters, purgations, cupping glasses, treatments with heat, ointments, plasters, and strengthening medicines—but all in vain. The reason for this is given by Fernel himself:

"Because we were all far from the knowledge of the truth. For in the third month, it was first plainly discovered to us that a certain demon was the author of all this mischief. He revealed himself through his speech and by using unusual words and sentences in both Greek and Latin (although the patient was completely ignorant of the Greek language). He also revealed many of the secrets of those standing by, especially of the physicians, whom he mocked for tormenting the patient in that manner with their useless <note>original: "frustraneous"</note> remedies." <note>original Latin: Quoniam omnes longe aberamus à cognitione veri. Nam Menſe Tertio, primum deprehenſus Dæmon quidam totius Mali Author: Voce, inſuetisque verbis ac ſententiis tum Latinis tum Græcis, (quanquam ignarus Linguæ Græcæ Laborans eſſet) ſe prodens. Is multa aſſidentium maximáque medicorum Secreta detegebat, ridens quòd irritis Pharmacis corpus hoc penè jugulaſſent.</note>

Here, therefore, we have an unquestionable instance of a **demoniac** <note>A person believed to be possessed by an evil spirit.</note> in these recent times of ours. He was someone who at first, for two months together, showed no sign of madness or *mania* at all, though afterward the *demon* possessed his entire body and used his tongue to speak through it. Fernel concludes his entire discourse in this manner: "These things I produce to make it clear..."

# Of Miracles. And How BOOK I.

...manifest, that *evil demons* (or *devils*) do sometimes enter into the very bodies of men, afflicting and tormenting them in an unheard-of manner. At other times, though they do not enter into and possess the whole body, they cause innumerable diseases. They do this partly by agitating and disturbing the healthy humours <term>The four "humours" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) were anciently believed to regulate health and personality.</term> of the body, and partly by diverting harmful fluids into the vital organs, obstructing the veins and other passages, or disordering the structure of the limbs. There are many other instances of this kind recorded by reliable modern writers concerning persons who were either wholly *demoniacal* and *possessed* by *evil demons* (as shown by their discovering secrets and speaking languages they had never learned) or otherwise so *affected* and *infested* by them that they exhibited *unusual* and *supernatural symptoms*. For the sake of brevity, we shall omit those cases here.

However, we thought it necessary to insist on this argument of *demoniacs* as much for the *vindication of Christianity* as for the *conviction of atheists*. We find some people so wavering in their religion that, because of this one issue of *demoniacs* (they being strongly convinced that there neither is, nor ever was, any such thing), they are ready to suspect the whole Gospel or New Testament itself of being a *fable* <note>original: "fabulosity"</note> and an imposture.

We come now to the *second head* proposed: *miracles and supernatural effects*. That there has been something *miraculous* or *above nature* done even among the *pagans* (whether by *good* or *evil spirits*) appears not only from their own records but also from the *Scripture* itself. It is well known that the pagans claimed to have *miracles* as well as *oracles*, even after the time of Christianity. These were attributed not only to *Apollonius of Tyana* <note>A Greek philosopher and reputed miracle-worker from the 1st century AD.</note> and *Apuleius*, but also to the Roman Emperors themselves, such as *Vespasian* and *Hadrian*. Such events were especially reported in the Temple of *Aesculapius* <note>The Greek god of medicine and healing.</note>. This is evident from a Greek tablet hung up in Rome, in which, among other things, this is recorded:

-> *That a blind man, being commanded by the oracle to kneel before the altar, then passing from the right side of it to the left, was to lay five fingers upon the altar; afterwards, lifting up his hand, he was to touch his eyes with them. All this being done accordingly, he recovered his sight, while the people all cheered that great miracles were performed under the Emperor Antoninus, etc.* <-

But we have in the Scripture an account of *miracles* that are both greater in number and of a higher nature, performed especially by *Moses*, our *Savior Christ*, and his *Apostles*.

Therefore, it seems there are two sorts of miracles or *supernatural effects*. First, there are those which—though they could not be done by any ordinary and natural causes here among us, and in that respect may be called *supernatural*—might nonetheless be performed (by God’s permission only) by the *ordinary and natural power* of other *invisible created spirits*, such as angels or *demons*. For example, if a stone or other heavy body should first fly upward and then hang in the air without any visible mover or support, this would be a *miracle* or *supernatural effect* to us.
