### CHAPTER IV. How Miracles Confirm a Prophet.

These are created invisible beings, such as *angels* or *demons*. They act only with God's permission, and it is understood that without His special providence <term>divine guidance and care</term>, they cannot interfere in our human affairs in this way. Furthermore, if a completely illiterate person should suddenly speak Greek or Latin, this would also be considered a *miracle* or *supernatural effect* by us, just as the Apostles' speaking in tongues is regarded. And yet, among *demoniacs* <term>those possessed by demons</term>, this is sometimes done by *evil demons*, with God only permitting it. Another such example among the *pagans* was the *Miracle of the Whetstone* <note>original: *Miraculum Cotis*</note> (as Apuleius calls it) performed by Accius Navius <note>a famous legendary augur of early Rome</note>, when at his command a whetstone was cut in two with a razor.

But secondly, there is another sort of *miracles* or *supernatural effects* that are above the power of all *secondary causes* <term>natural forces or created beings acting as intermediaries</term>, or any *natural created being* whatsoever. Such effects can be attributed to none but God Almighty Himself, the Author of Nature, who can therefore control it at His pleasure.

As for that recent *theological politician* <note>a reference to Baruch Spinoza, whose *Tractatus Theologico-Politicus* argued against the possibility of miracles</note> who, writing against *miracles*, denies both those of the *former* and of this *latter kind*, contending that a *miracle* is nothing but a *name* which the ignorant masses give to an *unusual work of nature* <note>original: *Opus Naturae Insolitum*</note>, or to anything for which they cannot assign a cause. He also argues that if anything were done *contrary to nature or above it*, it would weaken rather than confirm our belief in the *divine existence*. We find his discourse so weak, groundless, and insignificant in every respect that we do not think it deserves a detailed rebuttal here.

But the *former sort* of those *miracles* is what should be understood from 
<margin>Deuteronomy 13</margin>
*“If there arises among you a prophet or a dreamer of dreams, and gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or wonder comes to pass, of which he spoke to you, saying: 'Let us go after other gods and serve them'; you shall not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer of dreams. For the Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul.”* For it cannot be supposed that God Almighty would Himself purposely inspire any man to exhort others to idolatry, and then immediately assist such a person with His own *supernatural power* of doing miracles to confirm such a doctrine. Rather, the meaning is that by the suggestion of evil spirits, some *false prophets* might be raised up to tempt the *Jews* toward idolatry; or at least, that with the assistance of these spirits, such miracles might be performed to confirm it, similar to those sometimes done by the *Egyptian sorcerers* or *magicians*. In such cases, God Himself does not interpose to hinder them, for the reason that He might thereby *prove* and *try* the people's faithfulness toward Him. This is because both by the *pure light of nature* and God's *revealed will* (previously confirmed by miracles), idolatry—or the religious worship of any being but God Almighty—had already been sufficiently condemned. From this, it is evident that *miracles* alone (at least such *miracles* as these) are not sufficient confirmation of a *true prophet* without considering the *doctrine* he teaches. For even if a man had performed many true and real miracles among the *Jews*, if he then persuaded them toward idolatry, he was to be confidently condemned to death as a *false prophet*.

# Miracles in what Case, Book I.

Accordingly, in the New Testament, we read that our Savior Christ forewarned his disciples that ***False Prophets*** and ***False Christs*** should arise and show great ***signs*** or ***wonders***, so much so that, if it were possible, they would seduce the very ***Elect*** <term>those chosen by God for salvation</term>. And St. Paul foretells, concerning the ***Man of Sin***, or ***Antichrist***, that his coming should be ***after the working of Satan, with all power, and signs, and wonders (or miracles) of a lie***. 

For we conceive that by "wonders" <note>original Greek: Τέ̀ρατα (*terata*), often referring to omens or portents</note> are meant not only feigned and counterfeit miracles—that is, mere cheating and juggling tricks—but also true wonders and real miracles (of the first sort previously mentioned <note>supernatural acts performed by created spirits rather than God directly</note>) done for the confirmation of a lie, as the doctrine of this "Man of Sin" is called later in that passage. Otherwise, how could his coming be said to be "according to the ***working of Satan, with all power***"? 

In the same way, in St. John's *Apocalypse* <note>the Book of Revelation</note>, where the coming of the same ***Man of Sin*** and the ***mystery of iniquity*** is described again, we read in Chapter 13 of a ***two-horned beast like a lamb***, that ***he shall do great wonders and deceive those that dwell on the earth, by means of those miracles which he has power to do in the sight of the beast***. And again in Chapter 16, of certain ***unclean spirits like frogs*** coming out of the mouth of the ***dragon***, the ***beast***, and the ***false prophet***, which are the ***spirits of devils working miracles that go forth to the kings of the earth***. And lastly, in Chapter 19, of the ***false prophet that wrought miracles before the beast***. 

All of these seem to be understood as not only feigned and counterfeit miracles, but also true and real ones, effected by the ***working of Satan*** in confirmation of a ***lie***—that is, of ***idolatry, false religion, and imposture***. God Almighty permits this, partly as a way of ***probation*** or ***trial*** of the faithfulness of his own servants, and partly as a ***just judgment*** and ***punishment*** upon those who do not receive the ***love of the truth*** so that they might be saved, as the Apostle declares. 

Therefore, those miracles claimed for many ages past to have been performed before the ***relics of saints*** and ***images***, etc.—even if they were all true—could by no means justify or warrant the ***religious worship*** given to them by many. This is because true and real miracles done for the purpose of promoting ***idolatry*** are so far from justifying that idolatry that they are themselves condemned as ***wonders of a lie*** <note>original Greek: Τέ̀ρατα ψεῦδος (*terata pseudos*)</note>, performed by the working of Satan.

But as for the miracles of our Savior Christ: even if they had all been only of the ***former kind***—such as might have been done, with God's permission, by the ***natural power of created spirits*** and their assistance—they still ought to have been received. Because he came in the ***name of the Lord***, teaching neither ***idolatry*** nor anything contrary to the clear ***light*** and ***law of nature***, he should have been accepted by the ***Jews*** themselves and owned as a ***true prophet***, according to the ***doctrine of Moses*** himself. Moses, in both the 13th and 18th chapters of *Deuteronomy*, plainly assumes that God would in no other case permit any ***false prophet*** to perform ***miracles*** by the assistance of ***evil spirits***, except in the case of ***idolatry*** and that which is always understood to be plainly discoverable by the ***light of nature*** to...

It distinguishes Christ's miracles as valid because they align with the law of nature and the worship of God, unlike those used to promote idolatry.</summary>

None shall be rejected under the **notion** of **false prophets** except those who either do not perform **real miracles** or, if they do, come in the name of **other gods** or **exhort** people to **idolatry**. 

Nevertheless, our **Savior Christ** performed other **miracles** of a higher **nature** by the **immediate power** of **God Almighty** himself. For example, he raised **Lazarus**—who had been dead for four days—back to **life**. It cannot be imagined that it is within the **power** of **created spirits** (whether **bad** or **good**) to bring the **souls** of deceased men back to their **bodies** whenever they please, or to change the **laws** of **nature** and **fate**. However, one must not think that God will ever set this **seal** of his to a **lie**, or to anything that is plainly contrary to the **light** and **law of nature**.

The conclusion is that though all **miracles** collectively <note>original: "promiscuously," meaning without distinction</note> do not immediately prove the **existence** of a **God**, nor **confirm** a **prophet** or any specific **doctrine**, they all demonstrate that there is a **rank of invisible, intelligent beings superior to humans**, which **atheists** commonly deny. 

We also read of some such **miracles** that could not be performed except by a **power perfectly supernatural**, or by **God Almighty** himself. To deny and disbelieve all **miracles** is either to deny all **certainty of sense** (which would indeed make **sensation** itself **miraculous**) or else to monstrously and unreasonably dismiss **human testimony** and **history**. The **Jews** would never have so stubbornly and persistently adhered to the **ceremonial law** of **Moses** had they not always believed it to have been unquestionably confirmed by **miracles**. And if the **Gentiles** had initially accepted the **faith of Christ** without **miracles**, that itself would have been **the greatest of miracles**.

### Miracles and Oracles, Book 1:

The last **extraordinary phenomenon** proposed was that of **divination**, **oracles**, **prophecies**, or **predictions** of **future events** that are otherwise **unknowable** to men. These either **prove a God exists**, or at least that there are **intelligent beings superior** to humans. For if there is **prescience** <note>original: "presension," meaning foreknowledge</note> or **foreknowledge** of future events that are completely **unknowable** to human understanding alone, then it is certain that there is some more **perfect understanding** or **knowledge** in the **world** than that of humans. And thus, that **maxim** of the **ancient pagan theists** is **unquestionably true** in its original and proper sense: <note>original Latin: "Si Divinatio est Diij sunt"</note> *If there is divination, or a foreknowledge of future events (undiscoverable by men), then there are gods.* In their **language**, this meant nothing more than saying there are **intelligent beings superior** to humans.

<margin>On Divination, Book 1</margin> <note>Cicero’s *De Divinatione*</note>

Therefore, we must distinguish between **oracles** and **predictions** here in the same way we did before with **miracles**: they may be of two **kinds**. First, those that might proceed only from the **natural predictive power** of **created spirits superior** to humans, whether they are called **angels or demons**. For these are supposed to have not only clearer understandings than humans and a greater insight into **nature**, but also—because of their **agility** and **invisibility**—the opportunity to know things at a great distance and to be privy to human **secret plots** and **consultations**. It is easily conceivable that many **future events** near at hand, which cannot be foreknown by humans, may be foreseen (at least probably) by them, and that without any **miraculous divine revelation**, since their **causes** are already in **existence**. 

Just as people learned in **astronomy** can foretell **eclipses** of the **sun** and **moon**, which are completely **unknowable** to the **common people** <note>original: "vulgar"</note>. And just as **princes** or **statesmen** who are provided with great **intelligence**—both **foreign** <note>original: "foresign"</note> and **domestic**—can predict more about **war** and **peace**, or the **fate** of **kingdoms**, than **ignorant commoners** <note>original: "plebeians"</note>. 

And such were those **predictions** that **Democritus**, though otherwise very inclined toward **atheism**, allowed for. **Cicero** wrote of him: <note>original Latin: "Plurimis Locis, gravis author Democritus, Præ-sensionem rerum futurarum comprobat"</note> *"In many places, that serious author Democritus approves of the foreknowledge of future events."* The reason for this was that he supposed there were certain **intelligent beings superior** to humans, which he called **idols** <note>original: "eidola," images or spirits that Democritus believed flowed from objects and could communicate information</note>. Because they had a larger **comprehension** of things and other advantages of **knowledge**, they could therefore foretell many **future events** that humans were ignorant of. 

And although it might be thought that **Democritus** would not have held this **opinion** about the **foreknowledge** of **human events** if he had not also asserted the **necessity** of all human **actions** and **choices** <note>original: "volitions"</note>, but instead held the **freedom of the will**, as **Epicurus** did later (as if this were **inconsistent** with all kinds of **prediction** and **probable** or **conjectural foreknowledge**); yet it is certain that there is not as much **randomness** <note>original: "contingency"</note> in all **human actions** due to this **freedom of the will** as was previously supposed by **Epicurus**, and still is by many. It is plain that humans act according to what **appears to be good**, and that in many cases and circumstances, this may be **foreknown** without any...

### Chapter 4: Proof of Invisible Beings

...any **divine revelation**, what such or such persons would do. For example, that a **pleasure-seeking person** <note>original: "voluptuous Person"</note>, having a strong temptation to satisfy his sensual appetite—and that without incurring any inconvenience of shame or punishment—would readily agree to it. Besides this, such **invisible spirits**, as **angels** or **demons**, may sometimes predict what they themselves **cause** and **bring about**.

Secondly, there is another sort of **prediction of future events** which cannot be attributed to the **natural predictive faculty** of any such **created spirits**, but only to the **supernatural foreknowledge** <note>original: "Prescience"</note> **of God Almighty**, or **a Being Infinitely Perfect**. This includes events far off in time, for which there are not yet any immediate **causes** actually in existence; events which also depend upon many circumstances and a long series of things, where if any one of them were different, the outcome would change. This also applies to the **uncertainty of human acts of will** <note>original: "Humane Volitions"</note>, which are not always necessarily linked and chained to what comes before, but are often loose and free; and to that **contingency** <note>uncertainty</note> that arises from the **indifference or the equal appeal of different choices** <note>original: "Indifferency or Equality of Eligibility in Objects"</note>. 

Lastly, there are things that do not depend upon **external circumstances** at all, nor are caused by **natural preceding** things, but by some **supernatural power**. I say, when such **future events** as these are foretold and accordingly come to pass, this can be attributed to no other being but one who **comprehends, sways**, and **governs** all, and is, by a peculiar **privilege** or **prerogative** of its own **nature**, **omniscient** <note>all-knowing</note>. 

**Epicurus**, although he really rejected **divination** and the **prediction of future events** because he denied **divine providence**, still pretended another reason against it: that it was absolutely **inconsistent with the liberty of the will** and **destructive of it**. <margin>Diogenes Laertius, Life of Epicurus</margin> "Divination is non-existent; and if it were existent, things happening would be nothing to us" <note>original Greek: ἡ μαντικὴ ἀνύπαρκτον· εἰ δὲ καὶ ὑπαρκτική, οὐδὲν πρὸς ἡμᾶς τὰ γινόμενα</note>. Divination is a thing which has no **existence** nor **possibility in nature**; and if there were such a thing, it would take away all **liberty of the will** and leave nothing in **men's own power**. 

In the same way, **Carneades** (as recorded in **Cicero**) maintained: "That not even Apollo could tell future things, unless they were those whose causes nature so contained that it was necessary for them to happen." <note>original Latin: Ne Apollinem quidem futura posse dicere, nisi ea quorum Causas Natura ita contineret, ut ea fieri necesse esset</note> That is, **Apollo himself** was not able to foretell any **future events** other than such as had **necessary causes in nature** already existing. 

And some **Christian theists** of later times have, in like manner, denied to **God Almighty** all **foreknowledge of human actions** based on the same **presumption**—that it is both **inconsistent with men's liberty of will** and **destructive to it**. For, they say, if men's actions are **free**, then they are **unforeknowable** because they have no **necessary causes**. And again, if there is any **foreknowledge** of them, then they cannot be **free**, as they are **automatically necessitated** <note>original: "ipso facto Necessitated"</note> by that foreknowledge. 

But it is certain that **foreknowledge** does not destroy the **liberty of man’s will** or impose any **necessity** upon it. Men’s actions are not **future** because they are **foreknown**; rather, they are **foreknown** because they are **future**. Even if a thing were completely **contingent** <note>happening by chance or free choice</note>, if we assume it *will* be done, it must have been **destined to be future from all eternity**. Therefore, it is extreme **arrogance** for men to presume to measure the knowledge of **God Almighty** by their own, simply because they themselves can **naturally foreknow** nothing except through some **preceding causes**, such as an **eclipse of the sun or moon**.

Multa cernunt Arufpices, multa Augures provident, multa Oraculis providentur, multa Vaticinationibus, multa Somniis, multa portentis."</note>.

Indeed, it seems undeniable from history that even among the pagans, there were predictions of future events—undiscoverable by any human wisdom <note>original: "Sagacity"</note>—which eventually came true. ### Chapter IV: Triumphing Over Pagan Oracles

The King wanted to know from him whether it could be done or not. After Navius had performed his augural ceremonies <term>rituals used by an "augur" to interpret the will of the gods through signs like bird flight</term>, he replied that the thing could indeed be done. Whereupon Priscus declared what his thought was: namely, that a whetstone might be cut in two with a razor. Navius insisted they make a trial; therefore, a whetstone was immediately brought into the court. In the sight of the King and all the people, it was divided with a razor. 

But the predictions among those pagans were for the most part only of the former kind—those which proceeded merely from the natural presaging <term>foretelling or predicting</term> faculty of these demons. This is apparent because their oracles were often expressed ambiguously, so that they might be taken either way; it seems those demons themselves were not confident of the outcome. It is also shown by the fact that they were sometimes plainly mistaken about events. Because of this, they seldom ventured to foretell any events in the remote distance, but only those which were near at hand and shortly to come to pass, which might be probably conjectured from the state of things then in being. 

Notwithstanding this, we acknowledge that there are some few instances of predictions among the pagans of the other kind <note>meaning long-term, specific prophecies that seem beyond mere guessing</note>. One such instance was mentioned by **Cicero** in his book *On Divination*, where he declares the <term>doctrine of Diodorus concerning Necessity and Contingency</term>: "it was not necessary that Cypselus the tyrant should reign at Corinth, even though that had been predicted by Apollo’s oracle a thousand years before" <note>original: "non neceſse fuiſse Cypſelum regnare Corinthi, quanquam id Milleſimo ante anno, Apollinis Oraculo editum eſſet"</note>. 

There is also the record by **Varro** concerning <term>Vectius Valens</term>, an augur in the time of Romulus. When Rome was being built, he predicted from the flight of twelve vultures that the city would continue for twelve hundred years. This seems to have been fulfilled accordingly in the year of our Lord 455, immediately after the death of <term>Valentinian III</term> (whom some consider to be the last real Emperor of the West or Rome), when <term>Genseric</term> the Vandal took the city a second time and set it on fire. 

But above all are the <term>Sibyls</term> <note>female prophets in the ancient world believed to possess divine knowledge</note>. Pagan writers record such things about their prophecies that it makes one very suspicious that they did foretell the coming of our Savior Christ and the era of Christianity. If these and similar pagan prophecies were real, then they must have had some higher origin than the natural presaging faculty of their demons—especially those of the Sibyls. For all we know, they might have been supernaturally assisted to predict our Savior Christ among the pagans in the West, just as <term>Balaam</term> <note>a non-Israelite prophet in the Bible (Numbers 22-24) who was nevertheless compelled by God to give true prophecies</note> was in the East.

But here the Scripture triumphs over paganism and all its oracles and divinations. The Bible contains so many unquestionable predictions of events to follow a long time afterward—events that can be attributed to nothing but the supernatural foreknowledge and omniscience of Almighty God. For example, there are those concerning the Messiah, or our Savior Christ, delivered by **Jacob**, **Moses**, **David**, **Isaiah**, **Jeremiah**, **Daniel**, and most of the prophets. They foretold various particular circumstances of his coming and that grand event which followed: the general reception and entertainment <note>meaning the acceptance and welcoming of the faith</note> of the gospel by the Gentiles <note>non-Jewish nations</note>...

# Scripture Prophecies Evince a God. Book I.

The acceptance of *Christianity*—that is, the belief in the *Messiah* promised to the *Jews*, together with the shaking off of their *gods* and *idols*—must be considered. Among these *Scripture prophecies* concerning our *Saviour Christ*, we must certainly include one of the most significant: that of *Daniel's Weeks* <note>Referring to the "Seventy Weeks" prophecy in Daniel 9:24-27, traditionally interpreted as 490 years.</note>, or four hundred and ninety years. This was to begin from the *issuing of the command, or the decree made by Artaxerxes the son of Xerxes* in the seventh year of his reign, for the return of the people of *Israel*, *priests*, and *Levites* to *Jerusalem*. It was to end with the *death* of the *Messiah* and the preaching of the *Gospel* to the *Jews* alone. We are not unaware that some learned men, both in the past and more recently, have strained their intellects—sometimes using no small amount of force—to redirect this *prophecy* in another way. However, it is evident from the nature of the prophecy itself that these predictions concerning our *Saviour Christ* could have no other origin than the immediate *supernatural revelation of God Almighty*. Such events depended on no *natural causes*, much less upon those *constellations* favored by *astrological atheists*, but only upon His own *secret will and counsel*.

But besides these *prophecies* concerning our *Saviour Christ*, there are others contained in the *Scripture* concerning the *fates* and *successions* of the chief *kingdoms, empires*, and *political systems* of the *world*. These include the *rise of the Persian Monarchy*; its *fall* and *conquest* by the *Macedonian Alexander*; and the *four-part division* of this *Greek empire* after *Alexander’s* death. It also includes the *succession* of the *Seleucids* and *Ptolemies* <note>original: *Seleucidae* and *Lagidae* (the dynasty founded by Ptolemy I, son of Lagus)</note>, a *prophetic history* so consistent with the actual events that it was claimed by *Porphyry* <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher and critic of Christianity who argued Daniel was written after the fact.</note> to have been written after they occurred. Finally, it includes the *rise* and *continuance* of the *Roman Empire*. 

Despite the efforts of some to distort all those *Scripture prophecies* that extend to the present times, it is clearly demonstrable that the *Roman Empire* was *Daniel's fourth*, *ten-horned beast*. It represents the *legs* and *toes* of *Nebuchadnezzar's statue*: that *fourth empire* as strong as *iron*, which eventually came to be broken or divided into *ten* or many *principalities* (called in *prophetic language* and according to the *image* <note>original: *Eichon* (from the Greek *eikon*)</note>, *horns*). Among these was to start up another *horn with eyes, speaking great words against the Most High*, and *making war with the saints and prevailing against them for a time, times, and half a time*. This *prophecy of Daniel* is the *foundation* of *St. John's Apocalypse* <note>The Book of Revelation</note>, where it is further developed, filled in, and enlarged with the addition of several particulars. Thus, both *Daniel* and *John* have, from their respective eras, set down a *prophetic calendar of times* in a continuous *series*—the former more *concisely* and *generally*, the latter more *comprehensively* and *specifically*—leading to the very end of the *world*.

And thus we see plainly that the *Scripture prophecies* demonstrate the existence of a *Deity*. These cannot possibly be dismissed by *atheists* as resulting from men's *fear* and *imagination*, nor as the *inventions* of *politicians*. They not only prove a *Deity* but also confirm *Christianity*. This is partly because Christianity was predicted by them in its various circumstances—a major one being the *Gentiles' acceptance* of it—and partly as it predicted itself...

# CHAPTER IV. Whether God is Demonstrable.

Both of these *Scripture prophecies*—those *of Christ* in the *Old Testament* and those *from him* in the *New*—are of equal, if not greater, force to us in this present age for the confirmation of our faith than the *miracles* themselves recorded in the Scripture. This is because we now have certain knowledge of many of those events ourselves and have no reason to suspect anything other than that the *prophecies* were written long before they occurred.

To conclude, all these *extraordinary phenomena*—such as *apparitions*, *witchcraft*, *possessions*, *miracles*, and *prophecies*—prove that *spirits*, *angels*, or *demons*, though *invisible* to us, are no *fancies* <note>original: "Phancies"</note> but *real and substantial inhabitants of the world*. This does not support the *atheistic hypothesis*. Some of these phenomena, specifically the higher kind of miracles and predictions, also immediately force the acknowledgment of a *Deity*: a Being superior to *nature* who can therefore check and control it, and who, comprehending the whole, foreknows the most remotely distant and *contingent events*.

And now, we have not only fully answered and refuted all the *atheistic pretenses* against the *idea of God* (which tend to disprove His *existence*) but also occasionally proposed several *solid and substantial arguments for a Deity*. These include: 
* That all *successive things*—the *world*, *motion*, and *time*—are by their own nature absolutely incapable of an *eternal past* <note>original: "Ante-Eternity"</note>, and therefore there must of necessity be something else of a *permanent duration* that was eternal without beginning. 
* That no atheist, according to his own principles, can possibly give any account of the origin of his own *soul* or *mind*. 
* That the *phenomenon of motion* cannot be explained <note>original: "Saved"</note> without an *incorporeal principle* <note>A non-physical or spiritual source.</note> presiding over the whole. 
* That the *good and the beautiful* <note>original: "τὸ εὖ καὶ καλῶς"</note>, the *artificial, regular, and orderly frame of things*, together with the *harmony* of the whole, demonstrate an *understanding and intending cause of the world* that ordered things for *ends and good*. 

Besides these, there are several other *phenomena*, both *ordinary* and *extraordinary*, which atheists—being unable to explain—are forced to deny.

<margin>Book 1, Chapter 1.</margin>
It is true that some of the ancient *theists* themselves affirmed that there could be no *demonstration of a God*. This assertion has been misunderstood by others to mean that there is no certainty at all to be had of *God’s existence*, but only a *conjectural probability*—no *knowledge* or *science*, but only *faith* and *opinion*. However, the true meaning of those ancient *theists* who denied that there could be a *demonstration of a God* was only this: that the *existence of a God* could not be demonstrated *a priori* <note>From the earlier; a logical argument that moves from cause to effect.</note>, since He is the *First Cause* of all things. 

Thus does *Alexander Aphrodisias* <note>A celebrated Aristotelian commentator (c. 200 AD).</note>, in his *Physical Doubts and Solutions*, declare himself after he had proposed an argument for a God based on *Aristotelian principles* regarding *motion*: "This demonstration is by way of analysis; for it is not possible for there to be a demonstration of the first principle. Instead, one must begin from things that are subsequent and visible, and by using analysis to show how they agree with these, establish the nature of that first principle" <note>original: "ἡ δεῖξις κατ᾽ ἀνάλυσιν, οὐ γὰρ οἷόν τε τῆς πρώτης ἀρχῆς ἀπόδειξιν εἶναι, ἀλλὰ δεῖ ἀπὸ τῶν ὑστέρων τε καὶ φανερῶν ἀρξαμένους, κατὰ τὴν πρὸς ταῦτα συμφωνίαν ἀναλύσει χρωμένους συστῆσαι τὴν ἐκείνου φύσιν."</note>. That this argument or proof of his was by way of analysis only, it being not possible...

_Cartesian Skepticism; Book I._

<margin>Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, Book 5, page 388.</margin>

Therefore (he says) we must begin here with things that come *after* it <note>original: "things that are After it"</note>, and manifest it by way of *analysis* <note>In philosophy, "analysis" refers to the process of reasoning backward from effects to their causes.</note>, ascending to the proof of that *first nature* which existed before them. To the same purpose, *Clement of Alexandria* <note>Titus Flavius Clemens (c. 150 – c. 215 AD), a Christian theologian and philosopher.</note>, having first affirmed: 

"That God is the most difficult thing of all to be discussed <note>original: ὡς δυσμεταχείριστος ὁ περὶ Θεοῦ λόγος (as the discourse concerning God is difficult to handle)</note>. Because the principle of every thing is hard to find out, the first and most ancient principle of all—which was the cause of all other things being made—must necessarily be the hardest of all to declare or manifest."

He afterwards adds: 

"But neither can God be apprehended by any demonstrative science <note>original: ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐπιστήμη λαμβάνεται τῇ ἀποδεικτικῇ (but neither is knowledge received by demonstration)</note>. For such science is based on things that come *before* in the order of nature, and are *more knowable*; whereas nothing can exist *before* that which is altogether unmade <note>original: τῷ δὲ ἀγεννήτῳ προσγινομένου οὐδεὶς ἂν ἐπεὶ ἑαυτῷ (nothing can be prior to the unbegotten/unmade)</note>." 

And it is certain that it implies a contradiction for God, or a *perfect being*, to be demonstrated in this way—by anything coming before Him as His cause. Nevertheless, it does not follow that there can be no certainty at all of the existence of a God, but only "conjectural probability"; or that there is no "knowledge," but only faith and opinion. 

For we may have certain knowledge of things whose *reason why* <note>original: διότι (dioti) — the cause or explanation for why something is as it is.</note> cannot be demonstrated *a priori* <note>term: a priori — reasoning from causes to effects, or from universal principles to particular instances.</note>, or from antecedent necessary causes. For example, the fact that there was something *eternal in itself*, without a beginning, is not at all demonstrable by any prior cause, since it is a contradiction for such a thing to *have* a cause. Nevertheless, based only on the fact that *something exists*—which no one can possibly doubt—we may have not only an opinion, but also certain knowledge from the necessity of "irrefragable reason" <note>Unquestionable or undeniable logic.</note>, that there was never "nothing." Rather, something or other has always existed from eternity, without a beginning. 

In the same way, though the existence of a God or *perfect being* cannot be demonstrated *a priori*, we may nonetheless necessarily infer His existence from *our very selves* (whose existence we cannot doubt) and from what is contained in our own minds, or otherwise follows from Him, by undeniable principles of reason. Whenever anything is thus necessarily inferred from what is undeniable and indubitable, this is a *demonstration*. Though it is not a demonstration of the "why" <note>original: διότι (dioti)</note>, it is a demonstration of the "fact" <note>original: ὅτι (hoti) — the proof that a thing exists, even if the underlying cause remains unproven.</note>; it proves *that* the thing is, though not *why* it is. Many geometrical demonstrations are of this very kind.

It has been asserted by a late eminent philosopher <note>Referring to René Descartes (1596–1650), whose "Cartesian" philosophy famously wrestled with radical doubt.</note> that there is no possible certainty to be had of anything until we are certain of the existence of a God who is essentially good. He argues this because we can never otherwise free our minds from the nagging suspicion—which might assault us with irresistible force—that we might possibly have been made by chance, or fate, or by the pleasure of some *evil demon*, or even an arbitrary omnipotent deity, such that we would be deceived in all our most clear and evident perceptions. Therefore, we could even be deceived in geometrical theorems themselves, and even in our

# CHAPTER IV. Our Faculties Might Be False.

<sig>Kkkk 2</sig>

<margin>*Common Notions.*</margin> But once we are assured of the existence of such a God as is *essentially good*—who therefore neither will nor can deceive—then, and not before, will this suspicion utterly vanish. We ourselves will become *certain* that our *faculties of reason and understanding* are not false and *deceptive* <note>original: "imposturous"</note>, but *rightly made*. From which *hypothesis* it plainly follows that all those *theists* who suppose God to be a mere arbitrary being—whose will is not determined by any nature of goodness or rule of justice, but whose will itself is the first rule of both (they thinking this to be the *highest perfection, liberty, and power*)—can never be reasonably certain of the truth of anything, not even that two and two are four. This is because, so long as they hold to that persuasion, they can never be assured that such an *arbitrary, omnipotent Deity* might not have designedly made them such that they would be deceived in all their *clearest perceptions*.

Now, although there is a *plausibility of piety* in this doctrine—as it makes the knowledge of a *God essentially good* so necessary a *precondition* <note>original Latin: "precognitum" (something known beforehand)</note> to all other *science* that there can be no *certainty of truth* at all without it—yet that very *supposition* renders it utterly impossible ever to arrive at any certainty concerning the existence of a *God essentially good*. The supposition is that our *understanding faculties* might possibly be made to deceive us in all our *clearest perceptions*. If we admit this, we can never prove God's goodness, because this cannot be proved in any other way than by the use of our *faculties of understanding, reason, and discourse*. 

To say that the *truth of our understanding faculties* is put beyond all doubt as soon as we are assured of the existence of a *God essentially good* (who therefore cannot deceive), while this existence of God is meanwhile only proved by our *understanding faculties*, is a contradiction. That is to say, it is at once to prove the *truth of God’s existence* from our *faculties of reason and understanding*, and then again to prove the *truth of those faculties* from the *existence of a God essentially good*. This, I say, is plainly to move round in a *circle* <note>This is famously known as the "Cartesian Circle," a critique of René Descartes's philosophy.</note> and to prove nothing at all. This is a gross oversight which the aforementioned philosopher <note>Referring to René Descartes.</note> seems plainly guilty of.

Therefore, according to this *hypothesis*, we are necessarily condemned to *eternal skepticism*. This applies first to the *existence of a God*; after all our *arguments* and *demonstrations* for it, we must at length gratify the atheists with this *confession* in the conclusion: that it is *possible, notwithstanding, that there may be no God*. But it also applies to all other things, the *certainty* of which is supposed to depend upon the certainty of the existence of such a God who cannot deceive.

So, if we intend to claim any certainty at all concerning the *existence of a God*, we must of necessity reject <note>original: "explode," meaning to drive out or discredit</note> this *new skeptical hypothesis*—the idea that it is *possible our understandings were made* to deceive us in all our *clearest perceptions*. By means of that hypothesis, we can be certain of the truth of nothing; therefore, we must use our utmost endeavor to remove it. In the first place, therefore, we affirm that no power, however great, and therefore not *Omnipotence* itself,

# No False Knowledge or Understanding. BOOK I.

To suggest otherwise would plainly take away the *nature* of both *truth* and *falsehood*, or make them nothing but *words* without any meaning. *Truth* is not *artificial* <note>original: "factitious"</note>; it is a thing which cannot be arbitrarily *made*, but simply *is*. The *divine will* and *omnipotence* itself (as we are now considering them) have no authority <note>original: "imperium"</note> over the *divine understanding*. For if God understood only by his *will*, he would not understand at all. 

In the next place, we add that although the truth of *individual contingent propositions* <note>Statements about specific, non-necessary facts, like "it is raining."</note> depends upon the *things* themselves existing outside the mind as their *measure* and original pattern <note>original: "archetype"</note>, the case is different for the *universal* and *abstract theorems of science*. The terms of these theorems are the *reasons of things* which exist nowhere but in the mind itself (whose *mental concepts* <note>original Greek: "noemata"</note> and *ideas* they are). Therefore, the measure and rule of truth concerning them can be no foreign or external thing outside the mind; it must be *native* and *domestic* to the mind, or contained within the mind itself. Consequently, this measure can be nothing other than the mind's *clear and distinct perception*. 

In these *intelligible ideas* of the mind, whatever is *clearly perceived to be, is*; or, what is the same thing, it is *true*. Every *clear and distinct perception* is an *entity* (a real thing) or a *truth*, just as that which is incompatible with *conception* is a *non-entity* or *falsehood*. Indeed, the very *essence* of truth here is this *clear perceptibility* or *intelligibility*. Therefore, there cannot be any clear or distinct perception of *falsehood*. This must be acknowledged by everyone who, while granting that *false opinions* exist, agrees that there can be no such thing as *false knowledge*. For the *knowledge* of these *universal abstract truths* is nothing but the *clear and distinct perception* of the various *ideas* of the mind and their necessary relations to one another. Therefore, to say that there can be no *false knowledge* is the same as saying that there can be no *false clear and distinct perceptions* of the ideas of the mind. 

In *false opinions*, the *perception of the understanding power* itself is not *false*, but only *obscure*. It is not the *understanding power* or nature within us that *errs*; rather, it is *we ourselves* who *err* when we rashly and unwarily give our assent to things that are not *clearly perceived* by that power. 

The conclusion of all this is that since no *power*, however great, can make anything indifferently *true*, and since the *essence* of truth in *universal abstract things* is nothing but *clear perceptibility*, it follows that Omnipotence cannot make anything that is *false* be clearly perceived to exist. Nor can God create such *minds and understanding faculties* as would have clear conceptions of *falsehoods* (that is, of *non-entities*) in the same way they have of *truths* or *entities*. 

For example, no rational, understanding being who knows what a "part" is and what a "whole" is, or what a "cause" and an "effect" are, could possibly be made to clearly conceive the *part* to be greater than the *whole*, or the *effect* to be before the *cause*, or similar absurdities. Therefore, we may presume with reverence to say that God could not possibly have made a world of *rational creatures*—whether in the *moon*, or on some other planet, or anywhere else—who would *clearly and distinctly conceive* everything to be contrary to what we clearly perceive. Nor could our *human faculties* have been made so that we would have as clear conceptions of *falsehoods* as we do of *truths*. *Mind or understanding faculties* in *creatures* may be made greater or

# CHAPTER IV. Sense Phantasmal and Relative.

...less, weak, imperfect, and obscure, but they could not be made false, or such as should have clear and distinct conceptions of that which *is not*. This is because every *clear perception* is an *entity* <note>original: "Entity"; here meaning a real, existing thing</note>, and though Omnipotence can make *something* out of *nothing*, it cannot make something be nothing, nor *nothing be something*. 

All of this is no more than what is generally acknowledged by theologians when they affirm that God Almighty himself cannot do things that are *contradictory* <note>original: "Contradictious"</note>. There is no other reason for this assertion but this: because *contradiction is incompatible with conception*. So that *conception* and *knowledge* are hereby made the *measure* of all *power*; even omnipotence or *infinite power* itself is determined by them. From this it follows that *power has no dominion over understanding, truth, and knowledge*, nor can infinite power make anything whatsoever clearly conceivable if it is not so by nature. For if it could make *contradictory* things clearly conceivable, then it would itself be able to do them; because whatever can be *clearly conceived* by anyone can unquestionably be done by *infinite power*.

It is true indeed that *sense*, considered alone by itself, does not reach the *absolute* nature or existence of things outside of us. By itself, sense is nothing but *seeming, appearance, and fantasy* <note>original: "Phancy"; the faculty of the mind that receives sensory images</note>. And this is how the saying of some ancient philosophers should be understood: *every fantasy is true* <note>original Greek: "πᾶσα φαντασία ἀληθής"</note>. This is because *sense* and *fantasy* do not reach the *absolute truth and falsehood* of things, but keep themselves only within *seeming and appearance*; and every *appearance* must necessarily be a true *appearance*. 

Nevertheless, it is certain that *sense* often represents physical things to us differently than they actually are. Although this is not a *formal* falsehood, it is a *material falsehood* <term>material falsehood</term> <note>A "material falsehood" occurs when the sensory data itself is misleading—like an oar appearing bent in water—even if the mind has not yet made a formal error in judgment about it.</note>. Therefore, the nature of sense is not *absolute*, but *relative to the perceivers* <note>original Greek: "πρὸς τὶ, or τινὶ" (pros ti, or tini)</note>. By sense alone, without any mixture of reason or understanding, we can be certain of nothing more regarding the things outside of us than this: that they *so seem to us*.

<margin>Plato's *Theaetetus*, page 154.</margin> 

Hence came the saying of the ancient *atomic philosophers* in Plato: *“Neither you nor any other person can be certain that every other man and animal has the very same mental images of colors that he himself has”* <note>original Greek: "ἢ οὐ διισχυρίζοιο ἂν ὡς οἷόν σοι φαίνεται ἑκάστῳ χρῶμα, τοιοῦτον καὶ κυνὶ καὶ ὁτῳοῦν ζώῳ"</note>. Now, if there were no other perception in us but that of *sense* (as the old *atheistic philosophers* concluded when they claimed *knowledge* is nothing but *sense*), then all our human perceptions would be merely *seeming, phantasmal, and relative*; none of them would reach the *absolute truth of things*. 

In the language of Protagoras, everyone would then *“think or opine only his own things”* <note>original Greek: "τὰ αὑτοῦ μόνον δοξάζειν"</note>; all his *truths* being *private and relative* to himself. That *Protagorean aphorism* would also have to be accepted in the sense that philosopher intended: *“man is the measure of all things”* <note>original Greek: "πάντων χρημάτων μέτρον ἄνθρωπος"</note> to himself. This would mean that no one man’s opinion was more correct than another’s, but *“that which seemed to each person was true to the person to whom it seemed”* <note>original Greek: "τὸ φαινόμενον ἑκάστῳ"</note>. In this view, all truth and perception would be nothing but *seeming and relative*. 

But here lies one main difference between *understanding or knowledge and sense*; whereas the latter is...

# Mind reaches Absolute Truth. Book I.

While sense is only phantasmal <note>original: "Phantastical"; based on appearances rather than objective reality</note> and relative, the former <note>referring to the understanding or the rational mind</note> reaches beyond fancy and appearance to the **absoluteness of truth**. For as it has been already declared, whatever is clearly and distinctly perceived in things **abstract and universal** by any one **rational being** in the whole world is not a **private** thing, true only to himself who perceived it. Rather, it is—as some Stoics have called it—a **public, catholic, and universal truth** <note>original Greek: "ἀληθὲς καθολικόν"</note>. It holds true everywhere; and as **Empedocles** sang of **natural justice**:

->---<-
->”It is extended throughout the vast ether, and through infinite light or space.”<-
-><note>original Greek: "ΑἰθέρΘ ἡμεκέως τέταται διὰ τ᾽ ἀπερμόνΘ ΛύγΘ, διὰ τ᾽ ἀπλέτε ἀυζῆς"</note><-
->---<-

Even if there were indeed **infinite worlds**, all thickly peopled with **rational animals**, this truth would be alike **true** to every one of them. Nor is it conceivable that **Omnipotence** itself could create any such **understanding beings** who could have **clear and distinct perceptions** of the opposite of everything we perceive, any more than God could do things that are **contradictory**. 

In all **probability**, because **sense** is indeed nothing but **seeming, phantasmal, and relative**, this is the reason that some people have been so prone and inclined to suspect the same of **understanding and all mental perception** too—that this also is but **seeming and relative**. They suspect that men’s **minds** or **understandings** might have been so made by an **arbitrary, omnipotent deity** as to clearly and distinctly perceive everything that is **false**. 

But if, notwithstanding all that has been said, any will still sing the **old song** <note>referring to a repetitive or tired skeptical argument</note> again—*“That all this which we have declared is indeed true, if our human faculties be true or rightly made; but we can go no further than our faculties, and whether these be true or not, no man can ever be certain”*—we have no other reply to make but that this is an overly stiff and heavy adherence to a prejudice of their own minds. They believe that not only **sense**, but also **reason** and **understanding** and all **human perception**, is merely **seeming or phantasmal**, and **relative** to our **faculties** only, without reaching the **absoluteness** of any **truth**; they believe that the **human mind has no criterion of truth at all within itself**.

Nevertheless, it will probably be further **objected** here that it is too great an **arrogance** for **created beings** to pretend to an **absolute certainty** of anything, since it is the **sole privilege** and **prerogative** of **God Almighty** to be **infallible**, who is therefore **styled** in **scripture** as **the only wise one** <note>original Greek: "ὁ μόνος σοφός"</note>. To which we briefly answer: that the **Deity** is the first **original fountain** of **truth and wisdom**, which is said to be *“the brightness of the everlasting light, the unspotted mirror of the power of God, and the image of his goodness.”* <note>A reference to the Book of Wisdom 7:26</note>

**The Divine Word is the archetypal pattern** <note>original: "Archetypal Pattern"; the original model or blueprint</note> **of all truth**; it is **ignorant** of **nothing** and knows all things **infallibly**. But **created beings** have only a **derivative participation** in this, their **understandings** being **obscure**, and they **erring** in many things and being **ignorant** of more. And it seems to be no **derogation** <note>original: "Derogation"; a lessening or detraction</note> from **Almighty God** to suppose that **created minds**, by a **participation** of the **Divine Mind**, [attain certain truths]...

# CHAP. IV. A Certainty of Something.

The **mind** should be able to know **certainty**—that two and two make four; that equals added to equals will make equals; that a whole is greater than its part; that the cause comes before the effect; that nothing can be made without a cause; and other such **common notions** <note>original: "Common Notions"; fundamental self-evident principles or axioms</note>, which are the principles from which all their knowledge is derived. Indeed, were **rational creatures** never able to be **certain** of any such thing as this at all, what would their life be but a mere **dream** or **shadow**? And would they not be themselves but a **ridiculous and pompous piece of fantastic vanity**? 

Besides, it is in no way **congruous** <note>original: "Congruous"; fitting or suitable</note> to think that God Almighty should make **rational creatures** in such a way as to be in an utter **impossibility** of ever attaining to any **certainty** of His own **existence**, or of having more than a **hypothetical assurance** of it. Such a person might say, "If our **faculties** are **true** (which possibly may be otherwise), then there is a God." We shall conclude this **discourse** against **Cartesian skepticism** <note>the method of doubting everything until a clear and distinct idea is found, associated with René Descartes</note> with that of **Origen's**: "**Knowledge** is the only thing in the world which **creatures** have that is in its own **nature firm** <note>original Greek: "Μόνον ἐκ τῆ ὄντῶν βέβαιον ὕφισιμαν"</note>;" they have **something of certainty** here, but nowhere else.

Therefore, since we now have that which **Archimedes** <note>a Greek mathematician who famously said "Give me a place to stand, and I will move the earth"</note> required—some **firm ground** and **footing** to stand upon, such a **certainty of truth** in our **common notions** that they cannot **possibly be false**—without which nothing at all could be proved by **reason**, we shall in the next place endeavor not to shake or unsettle anything (which was the **undertaking** of that **geometrician**), but to confirm and establish the **truth of God’s existence**. We will do this from the very **idea** of Him, which has hitherto been made good and defended against all the assaults of **atheists**.

It is well known that **Descartes** <note>original: "Carteſius"</note> has lately claimed to do this with **mathematical evidence and certainty**, and he dispatches the business briefly in this manner: **God, or a Perfect Being**, includes **necessary existence** in His very **idea**; and therefore He Is. But though the **inventor** of this **argument** (or rather the **reviver** of that which had been used before by some **Scholastics** <note>medieval theologians who used logic and philosophy to explain Christian doctrine</note>) affirms it to be as good a **demonstration** for the **existence of a God** from **His idea** as the proof in **geometry** that a **triangle** has **three angles** equal to two right angles is from the **idea of a triangle**, it is nevertheless certain that, by one means or another, this **argument** has not so far proved so **fortunate** and **successful**. There are many who cannot be made sensible of any **efficacy** in it, and not a few who condemn it as a mere **sophism** <note>a clever but false argument intended to deceive</note>. 

As for ourselves, we have no desire to quarrel with other men’s **arguments for God** <note>original Latin: "Pro Deo"</note>, nor yet would we be thought to rely on anything in this cause which is not in every way **solid and substantial**. Therefore, we shall here endeavor to set down the utmost that we **possibly** can, both **against** this argument and **for it**, **impartially** and **candidly**. Then, when we have done, we will leave the **intelligent readers** to make their own **judgment** concerning the same.

Against it in this manner: **First**, because we can **frame** an **idea** in...

# Against the Cartesian, Book I.

...in our own minds, of an *Absolutely Perfect Being*, including *Necessary Existence* in it, it will not at all follow from that, that there is therefore such a *Perfect Being Really Existing* outside of our minds. We are able to form in our minds the *Ideas* of many other things that never were, nor will be. All that can be certainly inferred from the *Idea* of a *Perfect Being* seems to be this: that if it contains nothing which is *contradictory* <note>original: "Contradictious"; self-contradictory or logically impossible</note> to itself, then it is *not impossible* that there might be such a *Being* actually *existing*. 

However, the strength of this *argument* does not lie merely in the fact that we have an *Idea* of a *Perfect Being* and therefore it must exist. Instead, it relies on the fact that our *Idea* of it includes *Necessary Existence*, which the *Idea* of *nothing* else includes. Therefore, a further objection may be raised in this manner: 

It is very true that the concept of a *Perfect Being* must include *Necessary Existence*, because a being cannot be "perfect" in every way if its *existence* is merely *contingent* <note>original: "Contingent"; dependent on circumstances or not existing by its own nature</note> rather than *necessary*. Yet, it does not follow from this that there is actually such a *Perfect Being existing*. All that can be deduced from it is no more than this: first, that whatever does not have *Necessary* and *Eternal Existence* is not an *Absolutely Perfect Being*; and second, that if there is any *Absolutely Perfect Being*, then its *existence* was always *necessary* and will always be so. That is, it must have *existed* of itself from all *eternity incorruptibly* without a *beginning*, and must *needs exist* for all *eternity incorruptibly*, being never able to cease to be. 

It seems, indeed, no more to follow that because a *Perfect Being* includes *necessary existence* in its *Idea*, there is therefore such a *Perfect Being actually existing*, than to say that because a *Perfect Being* includes *Necessary Omniscience* <note>original: "Omniscience"; all-knowing</note> and *Omnipotence* <note>original: "Omnipotence"; all-powerful</note> in it, there is therefore such a *Perfect Omniscient* and *Omnipotent Being*. In both cases, all that follows is only this: that if there is any *Being absolutely perfect*, then it is both *omniscient* and *omnipotent*, and it *existed* of *itself necessarily* and can never *cease* to be. 

Therefore, a *fallacy* <note>a failure in reasoning or a flaw in an argument</note> lies in this *argumentation* when a *conclusion* is made *absolutely* based on a *necessity* of *existence* that was only affirmed *hypothetically* (upon the *supposition* that a *Perfect Being* exists). 

As some would try to prove the *necessity* of all *human events*—for example, the story of *Adam's sinning*—in this manner: they argue it was always *true* beforehand that either *Adam* would eat the *forbidden fruit* or he would not eat it. If he was going to eat it, he would *certainly* eat it, and not *contingently*; and again, if he was not going to eat it, then he would *certainly* and *necessarily* not eat it. Therefore, they claim, whether he eats it or not, he does so *necessarily* and not *contingently*. In this case, it is plain that an *absolute necessity* is wrongly inferred in the *conclusion* from a *hypothetical* one in the *premises*. 

In the same way, when we suppose an *Absolutely Perfect Being* exists and affirm that its *existence* must be *necessary* rather than *contingent*, and then conclude *absolutely* that there *is* such a *Perfect Being*, it seems to be the very same *fallacy*. From the *Idea* of a *Perfect Being* including *Necessary Existence*, it follows undeniably that if there is any *thing absolutely perfect*, it *must exist necessarily* and not *contingently*. But it does not follow that there *must*, of *necessity*, be such a *Perfect Being existing*. These two *propositions* carry a very different sense from one...

### Chapter 4. Demonstration; and For it.

...one another. And the latter of them—that there must of necessity be a God or *Perfect Being* existing—seems to be a thing altogether undemonstrable. This is because it implies that the existence of God or a *Perfect Being* may be proved *a priori* <note>original: "A Priori"; reasoning from theoretical deduction or causes rather than from observation or effects</note>, or from some *antecedent necessary cause*. As was declared before, this is considered contradictory and impossible.

And now, in the interest of fairness <note>original: "Justice"</note>, we are obliged to plead the best we can for the defensive side as well. The argument is as follows: Since the idea of God, or an *Absolutely Perfect Being*, includes within it a *necessary relation* <note>original: "Necessary Scheſis"; from the Greek *scheis*, meaning a state, disposition, or relationship</note> to existence—and not an *impossible* or *contingent* one—it follows from this, absolutely and without any "ifs" or "ands," that he does exist. 

For just as we can confidently conclude that *contradictory* <note>original: "Contradictious"</note> things never were nor will be (because their very idea contains an *impossible relation* to existence); and just as we can pronounce that other things which are not *contradictory* but only *imperfect* (which therefore have a *contingent relation* to existence) *possibly* might be or might not be; in the same way, we may conclude by *parity of reason* <note>by the same logic</note> regarding a *Perfect Being*. Because its idea includes a *necessary relation* to existence (or an *impossible* one to *non-existence*), or because it contains *existence* in its very *essence*, we may conclude that it is neither *impossible to be*, nor merely *contingent to be* or not to *be*. Instead, it *certainly is*, and *cannot but be*; or, it is *impossible it should not be*. 

And indeed, when we say of *imperfect beings* (implying no contradiction in them) that they may *possibly* either be or not be, we are secretly assuming the *existence* of a *perfect being*. This is because nothing which is *not* currently in existence could ever be *possible* to be, unless there were something actually in *being* that has sufficient *power* to *cause* or *produce* it. It is true that we have the ideas of many things in our minds that never were and never will be; but these are only those that include a *contingent*, not a *necessary*, existence in their *nature*. Therefore, it does not follow that a *Perfect Being*, which includes *necessity of existence* in its idea, might still fail to exist. 

Therefore, this *necessity of existence* (or *impossibility of non-existence*) contained in the idea of a *Perfect Being* must not be taken merely *hypothetically* or *consequently* in this manner: "if there is any thing absolutely perfect, then its existence both was and will be necessary." Instead, it must be taken *absolutely*. While *contradictory* things cannot *possibly be*, and *imperfect* things may *possibly* either be or not *be*, a *Perfect Being* cannot but be; it is *impossible* that it should not be. 

Otherwise, if the force of the *argumentation* were merely *hypothetical*—as in, "If there is a Perfect Being, then its existence both was and will be necessary"—this would plainly imply that a *Perfect Being* might either be or not be, despite that *necessity of existence* included in its *nature*. In other words, its existence would be *contingent*, which is a *manifest contradiction*: that the same thing should exist both *contingently* and *necessarily*. 

This *hypothetical absurdity* will appear more plainly if the *argument* is expressed in other words: that *necessity of existence*, the *impossibility of non-existence*, and *actual existence* belong to the very *essence* of a *Perfect Being*. It would then be ridiculous to try to evade the point by saying, "If there is a Perfect Being, then it is, and cannot but be." This *identical proposition* <note>a statement that is true by its own terms, like "A is A"</note> is true of every thing else, but...

## Other Demonstrations Book I.

...but absurd. Therefore, something more must be inferred from the <term>necessity of existence</term> included in the idea of a *perfect being* than that; it can be nothing else but this: that he *absolutely* and *actually exists*. Furthermore, no <term>theists</term> <note>those who believe in a personal God</note> would be able to prove that <term>God</term> or a *perfect being* (whom they suppose to *exist*) might not have *happened* to exist by *chance* alone, if it cannot be inferred from the <term>necessity of existence</term> included in *the idea of God* that he *could not but exist*. 

Despite this, there is no attempt here (as some claim) to prove the <term>existence of a God</term> or *perfect being* *a priori* <note>original: "A Priori"; reasoning from theoretical deduction rather than from observation or effects</note>, or from any *prior necessary cause*. Instead, the proof comes only from that *necessity* which is included within itself, or which is *concomitant* <note>original: "Concomitant"; naturally accompanying</note> and *concurrent* with it: the *necessity* of its own *perfect nature*. 

We shall now leave the intelligent and impartial reader to make their own judgment concerning the previously mentioned <term>Cartesian argument</term> <note>The argument popularized by René Descartes that the idea of a perfect being must include the attribute of existence</note> for a <term>Deity</term>. This argument is drawn from God's *idea* as including the <term>necessity of existence</term>, concluding that *he exists*. The reader must decide whether it is merely *sophistical* <note>original: "Sophistical"; a plausible but fallacious or deceptive argument</note> or has some *solidity* and *reality* in it. However, it is not very likely that many *atheists* will be convinced by it. They will probably say that this is no *proof* <note>original: "Probation"</note> of a Deity at all, but only an *affirmation* of the very thing in <term>dispute</term> and a mere <term>begging of the question</term> <note>a logical fallacy where the conclusion is assumed in the premises</note>—stating that <term>God exists</term> because he *exists* or *cannot but exist*.

Therefore, we will attempt to construct an *argument* or *demonstration* for the <term>existence of a God</term> from his *idea* (as including <term>necessary existence</term>) in other ways. And first, we shall make an *attempt* at it in this manner: 

It does not follow that because we can *form an idea of something in our minds*, that thing *really exists*. Nevertheless, whatever we can *form an idea of that implies no contradiction* in its *conception*, we can certainly conclude this much: that such a *thing was not impossible to be*. To us, nothing is *impossible* except what is *contradictory* <note>original: "Contradictious"</note> and *repugnant* to *conception*. Now, the *idea of God* or a *perfect being* can *imply* no contradiction, because it is only the *idea* of something that has all *possible* and *conceivable perfections* within it—that is, all *perfections* which are not contradictions in themselves or to one another. 

Even those who will not accept the *conclusion*—that because the *idea of a perfect being* includes *necessity of existence*, it must therefore *actually exist*—cannot deny this: since the idea *implies* no contradiction, it is therefore a *possible* thing, or not *impossible* to exist. For since it is true of all other <term>contingent</term> <note>things that may or may not exist, depending on circumstances</note> things that they are *possible* if their *idea* implies no *contradiction*, the same must be granted for that whose very *idea* and *essence* contains a *necessity of existence*—which is true of the *essence* of nothing but a *perfect being*. 

And this is the first step we now take in our *argumentation* from the *idea of God* or a *perfect being* (having nothing *contradictory* in it): that <term>God</term> is at least *possible*, or in no way *impossible* to have existed. Next, as this particular *idea* of that which is *possible* includes *necessity of existence* within it; from these *two* things put together—the *possibility* of such a *being* and its *necessary existence*...

### Chapter IV: Of a God from His Idea

...existence (if not from the latter alone), it will follow according to reason that He *Actually Is*. If *God* or a *Perfect Being*, in whose *essence* is contained *necessary existence*, is *possible* (meaning it is in no way *impossible* for Him to have been), then *He is*. This is because, upon the supposition of His *non-existence*, it would be *absolutely impossible* for Him ever to have been. It does not follow in this way concerning *imperfect beings*, which are *contingently possible* <note>original: "Contingently Possible"; existing only if certain conditions are met, rather than existing by necessity</note>. Even if they do *not* exist, it was still *possible* for them to have been. But a *perfect, necessarily existent being*, based on the mere supposition of its *non-existence*, could no more *possibly have been* than it could *possibly exist in the future*. This is because if it *could have been* while not actually existing, then it would not be a *necessary existent being*. The sum of all is this: *a necessary existent being*, if it is *possible*, it *is*; because upon the supposition of its *non-existence*, it would be *impossible* for it ever to have been. Therefore, *God* is either *impossible* to have been, or else *He is*. For if *God* were *possible* and yet is *not*, then He is not a *necessary* but a *contingent being*, which is contrary to the <term>hypothesis</term> <note>original: "Hypothesis"; the initial definition or proposition being tested</note>.

But because this *argumentation* may perhaps suffer the same fate as the former, and because of its *subtlety*, achieve little effect—or even be considered <term>sophistical</term> <note>original: "Sophistical"; a clever but fallacious or misleading argument</note>—men are generally prone to distrust the *firmness* and *solidity* of such *thin* and *subtle cobwebs* (as these and the like may seem to be). They doubt their ability to support the weight of so great a truth and suspect themselves to be <term>ensnared</term> <note>original: "Illaqueated"; trapped or entangled as if in a net</note> and circumvented by them. Therefore, we shall place no stress upon this either, but proceed to something which is yet more *plain* and *straightforward*, in this manner: Whatever we can form an *idea* of in our minds that implies no manner of *contradiction*, this either *Actually Is*, or else *if it is not*, it is *possible* for it to *be*. But *if God is not*, *He is not possible* hereafter to *be*; therefore *He Is*. The reason and necessity of the <term>minor premise</term> <note>original: "Minor"; the second part of a logical argument or syllogism</note> is evident: because *if God is not*, and yet is *possible* hereafter to be, then He would not be an *eternal* and *necessarily existent being*, which is <term>contradictory</term> <note>original: "Contradictious"</note> to His *idea*. And the ground of the <term>major premise</term> <note>original: "Major"; the first part of a logical argument or syllogism</note>, upon which all the weight lies, has been already declared where we proved before: *that if there were no God* or *perfect being*, we could never have had any *conception* or *idea* of Him in our minds. This is because there can be no *positive conception* of an *absolute nothing*—that which has neither *actual* nor *possible existence*. Here the structure of the argument is only inverted: Because we have an *idea* of *God*, or a *perfect being*, implying no manner of contradiction in it, it must therefore have some kind of *entity* <note>original: "Entity"; a thing with distinct and independent existence</note> or another, either an *actual* or *possible* one. But *God*, if He is *not*, is not *possible* to *be*; therefore He does *actually exist*.

But perhaps this argumentation also, however firm and solid it may be, may prove less convincing of the *existence* of a *God* to the <term>generality</term> <note>original: "Generality"; the majority of people</note>. This is because whatever is *received* is *received* according to the *capacity* of the *recipient*. # A Necessary Being, Certain. BOOK I.

Here is yet a plainer demonstration for the existence of God based on the very idea of Him, which includes *necessary existence*. First, it is established as a premise that, beyond question, *something or other* has existed from all eternity without a beginning. It is certain that everything could not have been created, because nothing can come from nothing, nor can anything be created by itself. Therefore, if there had ever been a time when there was absolutely nothing, there could never have been anything at all. From this, it is undeniable that there was always *something*, and consequently, there was *something uncreated* that *existed by itself from all eternity*.

Now the entire question—and indeed, this is the only real debate between *theists* and *atheists*—is this: since *something* certainly *existed by itself from all eternity*, what is that thing? Is it a *perfect* or an *imperfect being*? We argue, therefore, that whatever *existed by itself* from eternity and without a beginning did so *naturally and necessarily*, or by the necessity of its own nature. 

Nothing could exist by itself from eternity, *naturally and necessarily*, except that which contains *necessary and eternal self-existence* within its own nature. But there is nothing that contains *necessary eternal existence* in its own nature or <term>essence</term> <note>original: "Essence"; the fundamental nature or core identity of a thing</note> except an *absolutely perfect being*. All other *imperfect* things are, by their nature, *contingently possible* <note>original: "Contingently Possible"; existing only if certain conditions are met, rather than existing by necessity</note>—that is, they might either exist or not exist. 

Therefore, since *something or other* must and does *exist by itself naturally and necessarily from eternity uncreated*, and since nothing could do this except that which includes *necessary self-existence* in its nature or essence, it is certain that this was a *perfect being*, or *God*. Nothing else could exist this way; all other *imperfect* things, which have no *necessary self-existence* in their nature, derive their being from Him. 

In this regard, *atheists* are infinitely *absurd* and unreasonable. They refuse to acknowledge that a *perfect being* exists at all—even though such a being contains *independent self-existence* or *necessity of existence* (which is the same as an *impossibility of non-existence*) in its nature and essence. Yet, at the same time, they claim that the most *imperfect* of all beings—*inanimate body and matter*—has *existed by itself necessarily from all eternity*, even though matter has no *necessity of existence* in its nature.

We might add, as a further confirmation of this argument, what has already been proven: no *temporary, successive being* could possibly have existed from eternity and independent of anything else. These are beings whose *duration* is in a *continual flux*, as if they were being created anew every moment. This includes our *own souls*, the *world*, and *moving matter*. All these must have had a *beginning* and been *caused by something else*—namely, by an *absolutely perfect being* whose duration is *permanent* and exists without any *successive generation* or *flux*.

Besides all these arguments, the *idea of God* (which we have already defined) allows us to state the controversy between *theists* and *atheists* exactly and to resolve it satisfactorily. To do this, we must first establish another premise: just as it is certain that not everything was created, but rather that *something existed by itself from eternity uncreated*, so it is...

## CHAP. IV. The Controversy Stated.
