<margin>Aristotle, *Metaphysics*, Book 14, Chapter 3. Edited by Du Vall.</margin>
It is likewise certain that every thing was not *unmade* <note>original: "Unmade"; uncreated or self-existent</note> neither, nor *existed by itself from eternity*, but something was *made* and had a *beginning*. On this one point, there is full agreement between *theists* and *atheists*: no *atheist* asserts that every thing has been *unmade*, but they all acknowledge themselves to have been *generated* <note>original: "Generated"; brought into being or born</note> and to have had a *beginning*—that is, their own *souls* and *personalities*, as well as the *lives* and *souls* of all other *men* and *animals*. 

Therefore, since something certainly *existed by itself from eternity*, but other things were *made* and had a *beginning* (which must therefore necessarily derive their being from that which *existed by itself unmade*), here is the *state of the controversy* between *theists* and *atheists*: whether that which *existed by itself from all eternity*, and was the *cause* of all other things, was a *perfect being* and *God*, or the most *imperfect of all things whatsoever*, namely *inanimate* and *senseless matter*. 

The *former* is the *doctrine of theists*, as *Aristotle* affirms of those *ancients* who did not write *fabulously* <note>original: "Fabulously"; in the manner of myths or fables</note> *concerning* the *first principles*. He mentions, <note>original: "οἷον Φερεκύδης, & ἱερεῖς τινες, τὸ γεννήσαν πρώτον τὸ Ἀριστον πᾶσι, κὶ οἱ μάγοι τὸ θεῖον ἢ σοφόν, οἷον Ἐμπεδοκλῆς τὸ φιλίαν πρώτην, Ἀναξαγόρας νοῦν"</note> "such as Pherecydes and certain priests, who held the first generator to be the best of all; and the Magi, who held the divine or wise principle; such as Empedocles, who made 'friendship' the first, and Anaxagoras, who made 'Mind' the first." As namely, *Pherecydes*, and the *Magi*, and *Empedocles*, and *Anaxagoras*, and many others; they agreed in this: that the *first original* of all things was the *best* and *most perfect*. 

By the way, we may also observe that, according to *Aristotle*, the *ancient Magi* did not acknowledge a *substantial evil principle* <note>This refers to the idea of "Dualism," where a good god and an evil god are equally eternal and powerful.</note>; they made that which is the *best and most perfect being*, alone by itself, to be the *first begetter* of all. This, I say, is the *hypothesis of theists*: that there is one *absolutely perfect being*, *existing by itself from all eternity*, from whom all other lesser *perfections* or *imperfect beings* did gradually *descend*, until at last they end in *senseless matter* or *inanimate body*. 

But the *atheistic hypothesis*, on the contrary, makes *senseless matter*—the most *imperfect thing*—to be the *first principle* or the only *self-existent being*, and the *cause* of all other things. Consequently, it holds that *all higher degrees of perfections* in the world have *climbed up* or *emerged by way of ascent from there*; such as *life*, *sense*, *understanding*, and *reason* arising from that which is altogether *dead* and *senseless*. 

Nay, as was observed before, there has been among the ancient *pagans* a certain kind of *religious atheists*. These people, while *verbally acknowledging a God* or *soul of the world* presiding over the whole, nevertheless supposed this God to have first *emerged* out of *senseless matter*, *night*, and *chaos*; and therefore, he would doubtless be *dissolvable* again into the same. It is of these people that the following passage in *Aristotle* should be understood: <note>original: "βαιπάλδν ἢ ἀρχὴν φασὶν ὃ τές πρώτος οἷον Νύκτα, ἢ Οὐρανόν, ἢ χάος, ἢ Ὠκεανόν, ἀλλὰ τὲ δια"</note> "They suppose that the first things—such as Night, and Heaven, and Chaos, and the Ocean—do not rule, but rather Jupiter (or God) rules and governs all." 

Here it is implied that *Heaven*, *Night*, *Chaos*, and the *Ocean*, according to these thinkers, were *older than Jupiter*, or existed in the *order of nature* before him. They believed that things *ascended* upward from that which was most *imperfect*, like *night* and *chaos*, to the more *perfect*, and at length to *Jupiter* himself: the *mundane soul* <note>original: "Mundane Soul"; the "World-Soul" or spirit that animates the physical universe</note> who governs the whole world just as our *soul* governs our *body*. This same *opinion* is afterwards again noted and criticized by *Aristotle* in these words: "But if someone should hold that..."

# Not All from the Most Imperfect. Book I.

[Aristotle says that he does not think rightly who compares] "the principles of the universe to those of animals or plants; claiming that the more perfect things always arise from the imperfect; for a man generates a man, and the seed is not first." <note>original Greek: ὅλα ἀρχὰς, τῇ ζώων ἢ φυτῶν· ὅτι ἐκ τῶν ἀτελῶν ἀεὶ τὰ τελειότερα· ἄνθρωπος δὲ ἄνθρωπον γεννᾶ, ἢ οὐκ ἔστι σπέρμα πρῶτον. This is a paraphrase from Aristotle's *Metaphysics*, arguing that the "perfect" must precede the "imperfect" in the chain of causality.</note> Nor would he think correctly who should compare the principles of the universe to those of animals and plants, where more perfect things (like mature organisms) always seem to arise from indeterminate and imperfect things (like seeds). For even in those cases, the situation is different than they suppose; for it is a man who generates a man, and the seed is not the first thing in existence.

The <term>controversy</term> being thus clearly stated between <term>theists</term> and <term>atheists</term>, it may now—with great ease and to the full conviction of all minds that are unbiased and not already filled with false principles—be decided. On the one hand, it is undeniably evident that <term>lesser perfections</term> may naturally descend from <term>greater</term> ones, or at least from that which is *absolutely perfect* and which virtually contains everything. But on the other hand, it is utterly impossible that <term>greater perfections</term> and <term>higher degrees of being</term> should rise and ascend out of <term>lesser</term> and <term>lower</term> ones. If that were possible, then that which is the most *absolutely imperfect* of all things would be the first fountain and origin of all. Since no effect can possibly exceed the power of its cause, it is certain that in the universe, things did not *ascend and mount*, or *climb up from lower perfection to higher*. On the contrary, they *descend and slide down from higher to lower*, so that the first origin of all things was not the most <term>imperfect</term>, but the most *perfect being*. 

To speak more specifically, it is certain—despite all the empty claims of <term>Lucretius</term> and other <term>atheists</term> or <term>semi-atheists</term> to the contrary—that <term>life and sense</term> could never possibly spring out of <term>dead and senseless matter</term> as its only <term>original</term> source. This is true whether one argues by way of <term>atoms</term> (since no arrangement of <term>magnitudes</term>, <term>shapes</term>, <term>positions</term>, and <term>motions</term> is ever able to produce <term>thought</term> <note>original: "Cogitation"</note>) or by way of <term>qualities</term>. <term>Life</term> and <term>perception</term> can no more result from a mixture of <term>elements</term> or <term>combinations of qualities</term> like <term>heat and cold</term>, <term>moist and dry</term>, etc., than they can from <term>unqualified atoms</term>. This is undeniably demonstrable from that very <term>principle of reason</term> which the <term>atheists</term> are so fond of but misuse because they misunderstand it (as will be shown later): that *nothing can come from nothing*. Much less could <term>understanding and reason</term> in humans ever have emerged out of <term>stupid matter</term> <note>original: "Stupid"; meaning dull, inanimate, or lacking sensation</note> that is devoid of all manner of <term>life</term>.

Therefore, we must freely declare here against the darkness of that <term>philosophy</term> which has sometimes been carelessly accepted even by those who were not <term>atheists</term>: the idea that <term>sense</term> may rise from a certain <term>modification</term>, <term>mixture</term>, or <term>organization</term> of <term>dead and senseless matter</term>, and that <term>understanding</term> and <term>reason</term> may result from <term>sense</term>. The plain consequence of both these ideas is that <term>senseless matter</term> may prove to be the <term>origin</term> of all things and the only <term>divinity</term> <note>original: "Numen"</note>. This <term>doctrine</term>, therefore, is undoubtedly a major part of the <term>philosophy of the kingdom of darkness</term>. But this <term>darkness</term> has recently been largely dispelled by the light of the <term>atomic philosophy</term> restored to its first <term>genuine</term> and <term>pure state</term> <note>original: "Virgin State"</note>, as yet <term>unspoiled</term> <note>original: "Undeflowred"</note> by <term>atheists</term>. This clearly shows how far <term>physical bodies and mechanism</term> can go and proves that <term>life and thought</term> can never <term>emerge</term> from them. It is built upon that <term>fundamental principle</term>—as we made evident in the first chapter—that *nothing can come from nothing*. And <term>Strato</term> and

<header>CHAP. IV. Mind Eternal and Unmade.</header>
<meta>catchword: could</meta>

The **Hylozoic Atheists** <note>original: "Hylozoick Atheists"; from the Greek words for "matter" and "life," referring to the belief that all matter is inherently alive.</note> were so well aware and so sensible of this—that all *Life* and *Understanding* could not possibly be *Generated* or *Made* from nothing—that they therefore thought it necessary to attribute *Life* and *Perception* (or *Understanding*), along with *Appetite* and *Self-moving Power*, to all *Matter* as such. They did this so that matter might be fitly qualified to be the *Original* of all things. Nothing could be more monstrous than this opinion, and we shall demonstrate its *impossibility* elsewhere. In the meantime, we do not hesitate to assert that the *argument proposed* is a *sufficient demonstration* of the *impossibility of Atheism*. This will be further shown in our answer to the *second atheist objection* against a *Divine Creation*: the claim that *nothing can come from nothing*.

But this *controversy* between *Theists* and *Atheists* may be yet more particularly stated based on the *Idea of God*, which includes *Mind* or *Understanding* as an *essential* part of it. Namely: Is *Mind* *Eternal* and *Unmade*, acting as the *Maker* of all; or else was all *Mind* itself *Made* or *Generated*, and that out of *Senseless Matter*? For according to the doctrine of the pagan *Theists*, *Mind* was "the oldest of all things, the lord of nature, senior to the world and elements" <note>original Greek: πρεσβυτάτη, καὶ κύριος τῆς φύσεως</note>; and by *Nature* it has a *princely* and *lordly dominion over all*. But according to those *Atheists* who make *Matter* or *Body* (devoid of all *Life* and *Understanding*) the *First Principle*, *Mind* must be "something born later" <note>original Greek: ὑστερογενὴς</note>, a thing *younger than the world*; a *weak, shadowy, and evanid image* <note>original: "evanid"; meaning vanishing or fading away.</note>, and *next to nothing*.

And the *controversy* as thus stated may be also clearly and satisfactorily decided. For *first*, we say that as it is certainly *true* that *if there had once been nothing at all, there could never have been anything*; so it is true likewise that *if once there had been no life in the whole universe, but all had been dead, then could there never have been any life or motion in it*. And *if once there had been no mind, understanding, or knowledge, then could there never have been any mind or understanding produced*. This is because to suppose *Life* and *Understanding* to rise and spring up out of that which is altogether *dead* and *senseless* as its only *original* is plainly to suppose *something to come out of nothing*. It cannot be said of other things, such as the *physical world* and *matter*, that *if once they had not been, they could never possibly have been*. This is because even if there had been no *world* nor *matter*, these could have been produced from a *perfect, omnipotent, incorporeal being*, which in itself *eminently* contains all things. *Dead* and *senseless matter could never have created or generated Mind and understanding, but a perfect, omnipotent Mind could create matter*. Therefore, because *Mind* exists, we are certain that there was some *Mind* or other from *Eternity* without *beginning*; though it does not follow that because *Body* exists, there was *Body* or *Matter* from *Eternity unmade*. Now, these *imperfect minds* of ours were by no means *themselves eternal* or without *beginning*, but were brought forth into *being* from a previous *non-existence*. # Knowledge, Not Fanciful: Book I
<page-num>730</page-num>

...could not possibly be made, nor could one be produced from another infinitely; there must necessarily be an **Eternal Unmade Mind** from which our own **imperfect minds** were derived. This **Perfect, Omnipotent Mind** was the **cause** of all other things as well as of human **souls**.

But before we proceed with any further arguments, we must note here that the atheists believe a large part of their strength lies in this very point: namely, their attempt to disprove God's existence based on the nature of **understanding** and **knowledge**. Indeed, they boast about this more than anything else. We have already categorized this as the **eleventh atheist argument**: *that since **knowledge** is the processing of information from the **things themselves that are known**, and all **conception** is an action of the thing conceived and a passive reaction of the person conceiving, then the **world** and all **perceivable things** <note>original: "sensible things"; things perceived by the senses</note> must have existed before there could be any knowledge or conception of them. Therefore, no knowledge or conception could have existed before the world as its cause.*

Or to put it more briefly: the world could not have been made by knowledge and understanding, because no knowledge or understanding of the world (or anything in it) could exist until after it was made. According to these atheists, **things made knowledge**, and not **knowledge made things**. By "things," they mean only those that are **perceivable** and **physical** <note>original: "sensible and corporeal"</note>. Thus, mind and understanding could not be the creator of the world and these physical things because they are merely a **product** <note>original: "creature"</note> of them—a secondary, derived result, or a **fanciful image** <note>original: "phantastick image"</note> of them. In this view, mind is the **youngest** and most dependent thing in the whole world. From this, it follows that to suppose mind and understanding to be the maker of all things makes no more sense than if one should suppose that the **reflections** <note>original: "images"</note> in **ponds** and **rivers** are the **makers** of the **sun**, **moon**, and **stars**, and the other things they represent.

On these grounds, a modern writer <note>referring to Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679)</note> presumes to determine that knowledge and understanding are not to be attributed to **God Almighty**, because they imply **imperfection** and a dependence on external physical things.

<margin>*On the Citizen*, Religion, chapter 15, section 14.</margin>
"Since knowledge and understanding in us are nothing else but a mental disturbance <note>original: *tumultus*</note> raised by external things pressing against our organs, we must not think that any such thing happens to God. For it is a sign of a power that **depends** on another."
<margin>*Leviathan*, chapter 31.</margin>
This is also translated into English as: "**Knowledge and understanding in us are nothing but a tumult in the mind, raised by external things that press the organic parts of a man's body; there is no such thing in God, nor can they be attributed to Him, as they are things that depend on natural causes.**"

By denying knowledge and understanding to God on the pretext that they indicate imperfection and dependence on external physical things (being nothing more than a "tumult" raised by their motions and pressures), this writer must absolutely deny that the **first principle** of all things has any knowing or understanding nature—unless he had identified some other kind of knowledge, distinct from that of humans, and clearly attributed it to God Almighty. This concludes the perspective of the atheists.

# Chapter IV: The Image of Sensibles

For the demonstration of the contrary—namely, the **existence** of a **God, or a Mind before the world**, based on the **nature of knowledge** and **understanding**. First, therefore, it is a **foolish notion of these atheists** <note>original: "sottish conceit"; foolish or senseless idea</note>, proceeding from their failure to pay attention to their own **thoughts**, to claim that not only **sensory perception** but also **knowledge** and **understanding** in **humans** is nothing but a **commotion** <note>original: "tumult"</note> raised by **physical** <note>original: "corporeal"</note> things from the outside pressing upon the **organs** of their **body**. Or, as they explain themselves more clearly: it is nothing but the **activity of perceivable objects** upon **them**, and their **passive reaction** to those objects. 

For if this were true, then everything that **suffered** and **received motion**—especially **passive bodies**, such as **mirrors**—would have something of both **sensory perception** and **understanding** within them. It is plain that nothing comes to us from **bodies** outside of us except **physical motion** and **pressure**. Neither is **sensory perception** itself the mere **perception of those motions**, but rather the **perception** of how we are **affected by them**, processed through **imagination** <note>original: "phancy"</note>. 

But **perceivable** <note>original: "sensible"</note> things themselves (as, for example, **light** and **colors**) are not **known** or **understood** either by the **passive reaction** or the **imagination of the senses**—not by anything merely **foreign** and **added from the outside**—but by **intellectual ideas produced by the mind** itself. That is, by something **native** and **internal** to it. Nothing is truer than this statement by **Boethius**: 

> **Everything that is known is known not by its own force and power, but by the force, power, vigor, and activity of the one who knows or comprehends it.** <note>original: "Omne quod Scitur, non ex Sua, sed ex Comprehendentium Naturâ, Vi, & Facultate Cognoscitur." From Boethius’s "The Consolation of Philosophy."</note> 

Therefore, besides the **mental images** <note>original: "phantasms"</note> of **individual bodies**, or of **perceivable** things **existing** outside of us (which are not mere passive reactions either), it is plain that our **human mind has** other **thoughts or conceptions** in it. Namely, the **ideas of the intellectual natures and essences** of things, which are **universal**, and by and under which the mind **understands individual things**. 

It is a **ridiculous notion** of a **modern atheist writer** <note>This likely refers to Thomas Hobbes, who argued for "nominalism"—the idea that universal categories are just names, not realities.</note> that **universals are nothing else but names** attributed to many **individual bodies**, because whatever **exists** is **individual**. For though whatever **exists** outside the **mind** is **individual**, yet it is plain that there are **conceptions** in our **minds** that are **objectively universal**. Although these **universal objects** of our **mind** do not **exist** as such anywhere outside of it, they are not therefore **nothing**. Rather, they have an **intellectual reality** <note>original: "intelligible entity"</note> for this very reason: because they are **conceivable**. For since **non-existence** is not **conceivable**, whatever is **conceivable** and an **object of the mind** is therefore **something**. 

And as for **self-evident truths** <note>original: "axiomatical truths"</note> in which something is affirmed or denied: **these are not all passive reactions from bodies outside us**. (For what **physical motion** could **impress** this **common notion** upon our **minds**: that *things which agree with a third thing, agree with each other*, or any other such rule?) **Neither** are these things gathered only by **induction** from repeated and reiterated **sensory experiences**, as we clearly understand all at once that it is **impossible** they should be otherwise. Thus **Aristotle** insightfully wrote:

> **It is evident that one cannot gain knowledge of the universal theorems of geometry through sense perception. For even if we could perceive by sense that the three angles of a triangle were equal to two right angles, we would still seek a demonstration of it; for we sense only individual things, but knowledge consists in recognizing the universal.** <note>original Greek: "ὅδε θήσασθαι δι αισθήσεως ἔσιν..." from Aristotle's "Posterior Analytics." The text argues that seeing one triangle isn't the same as proving a mathematical law for all triangles.</note>

<summary>This page argues that human knowledge is not a passive byproduct of physical matter but arises from universal, intellectual ideas inherent to the mind itself. It refutes the materialist view that "universals" are just names, asserting they have a real existence in the intellect.</summary>

# Knowledge and Intellection, BOOK I.

We should not rest satisfied in this, as if we had sufficient knowledge of it, but would seek further for a demonstration. Sensory perception reaches only to **Singulars** <note>original: "Singulars"; individual, specific things or objects</note>, but Knowledge reaches to **Universals** <note>original: "Universals"; general concepts, categories, or abstract principles</note>. When from the **Universal Idea** of a Triangle—which is neither here, nor there, nor anywhere outside of our **Mind**, but yet has an **Intelligible Entity** <note>original: "Intelligible Entity"; a thing that exists as an object of thought or understanding</note>—we see a plain necessity that its **Three Angles** must be equal to two right angles, then do we **know** the truth of this **Universal Theorem**, and not before. We also understand that every singular triangle (as far as it is a true triangle) has this property within it. Therefore, the **knowledge** of this and similar truths is not derived from **Singulars**. We do not arrive at these truths by way of **ascent**, moving from **Singulars** to **Universals**. On the contrary, having first found them in the **Universals**, we afterwards descend and apply them to **Singulars**. Thus, our knowledge here is not **after singular bodies**, nor secondary or derivative **from** them; but in the order of nature, it is **before** them and **proleptical** <term>proleptical</term> <note>original: "proleptical"; existing beforehand or anticipatory; knowledge that is prior to experience</note> to them.

Now these **Universal Conceptions**—some of which are also **abstract** (such as life, sense, reason, knowledge, and the like)—are often about things whose singular instances do not fall under **sense** at all. Therefore, these concepts could never possibly be impressed upon us from **singular bodies** by physical motion. Furthermore, some concepts belong to corporeal and **sensible things**, yet their accuracy cannot be reached by **sense**. Neither did they ever exist in the matter of this lower world which surrounds us here, and therefore they could not be stamped upon us from the outside. Examples include the ideas of a **perfect straight line**, and a **plain surface** <note>original: "superficies"</note>, or of an **exact triangle**, **circle**, **sphere**, or **cube**. No material thing here among us is bounded by such **straight lines** that even by microscopes there may not be discovered much irregularity and deformity in them. It is very probable that there are no **perfectly straight lines**, no such **triangles**, **circles**, **spheres**, or **cubes** that answer to the **exactness** of our **conceptions** in any part of the whole material universe, nor ever will be. 

Notwithstanding this, they are not **absolute non-entities** <note>original: "Non-Entities"; things that do not exist</note>, since we can demonstrate things concerning them. Even though they never were nor will be, they are **possible** to exist, since nothing can be **conceived** unless it either **is**, or else is **possible** to be. The human mind, therefore, has a **power** of framing **ideas** and **conceptions** not only of what **actually is**, but also of things which never were, nor perhaps ever will be, because they are only **possible** to be. But when from our **conceptions** we conclude of some things that, though they are not, yet they are **possible** to be; since nothing that **is not** can be **possible** to be unless there is something **actually** in being which has sufficient power to produce it, we do implicitly suppose the existence of a **God** or **Omnipotent Being** thereby. Such a being can make whatever is **conceivable**—though it does not yet exist—to actually exist; and therefore make material triangles, circles, spheres, and cubes that are **mathematically exact**.

The result of what we have said so far is this: since **singular bodies** are not the only **objects** of our **mind** and **thought** <note>original: "cogitation"</note>, the mind also has **universal** and **abstract ideas** of the **intelligible natures** or **essences** of things. Some of these are such that their singulars do not at...

# CHAPTER IV. Suppose Infinite Power.

...at all fall under the senses; others, though they belong to bodies, yet sense can never reach them, nor were they ever in matter. Moreover, since our mind can conceive of things which nowhere *actually exist*, but are only *possible*, and can have such a *demonstrative science* of *universal truths* as the senses can never ascend to; it follows that *human knowledge* and *understanding* itself is not the mere *image* and *creation* <note>original: "Creature"</note> of *individual bodies* <note>original: "Singular Bodies"</note> alone. It is not *derivative* or *ectypal* <term>ectypal</term> <note>original: "Ectypal"; a copy or reproduction of an original pattern</note> from them and, in the order of nature, *secondary* <note>original: "junior"</note> to them. Instead, as if *hovering* aloft over the entire *physical universe*, it is something *independent* of *individual bodies*, or *prior* <note>original: "Proleptical"</note> to them, and in the *order* of *nature*, *before* them.

But what explanation can we then *possibly* give for *knowledge* and *understanding*, their *nature* and *origin*? For there must be something that is *intelligible* [understandable] which, in the order of *nature*, exists before *Nous* <note>original: "Νοῦς"; Mind or Intellect</note> or *intellection* [the act of understanding]? Certainly, no other explanation than this: the *first original knowledge* is that of a *Perfect Being*, *infinitely good* and *powerful*, *comprehending* itself and the utmost *extent* of its own *productivity* <note>original: "Fecundity"</note> and *power*—that is, the *possibilities* of all things, their *ideas*, with their several *relations* to one another, and all *necessary* and *immutable truths*. Here, therefore, is a *knowledge* existing before the world and all *sensory* <note>original: "Sensible"</note> things, which was *archetypal* <term>archetypal</term> <note>original: "Archetypal"; the original pattern or model</note> and *paradigmatic* to them. From this one *Perfect Mind* and *knowledge*, all other *imperfect minds* (being *derived* from it) have a certain *participation*. By this, they are enabled to *frame intelligible ideas* not only of whatever actually *exists*, but also of such things as never *were* nor *will be*, but are only *possible*, or *objects* of *Divine Power*.

Wherefore, since it is certain that even *human knowledge* and *understanding* itself is not a mere *passive reaction* <note>original: "Passion"</note> caused by *sensory things* and *individual bodies* existing outside of us (which is the only *foundation* of that previously mentioned *atheistic argument* that *things made knowledge* and *not knowledge things*), it must therefore have some other *origin*. Moreover, since *knowledge* and *understanding* apprehend things *prior* to their *existence* (*Mind* being able to frame *conceptions* of all *possible entities* and *modifications*), they plainly *suppose* the *actual existence* of a *Perfect Being* in their very nature. This Being is *infinitely productive* and *powerful*, and could *produce* all things *possible* or *conceivable*. The *first original knowledge* or *Mind*, from which all other *knowledges* and *minds* are *derived*, belongs to an *absolutely perfect* and *omnipotent Being*. This Being *comprehends itself* and the *extent* of its own *power* or its *communicability*—that is, the *ideas* of all *possibilities* of things that may be *produced* by it, together with their *relations* to one another and their *necessary, immutable truths*. This is consistent with how *Wisdom* and *Understanding* are described as:

> *the breath of the power of God, an efflux of the glory of the Almighty, the activity of the energy of God, or the image of his goodness* <note>original Greek: "ἄτμις τῆς τῶ Θεῶ δυνάμεως, ἀπόρροια τῆς τῶ παντο-κράτορος δόξης, ἐνέργεια τῶ τῶ Θεῶ ἐνεργείας, ἢ εἰκών τῶ ἀγαθῶ αὐτῶ"</note>. <margin>Wisdom 7</margin>

These are: the *breath* (or *vapor*) of the *power* of *God*, and an *efflux* (or *emanation*) from the *glory* of the *Almighty*; a clear *mirror* (or *looking glass*) of his *active energy* or *virtue*, and the *image* of his *goodness*. I say, the result of all this is that the *nature* of *knowledge*...

### Eternal Truths; Book I.

Now, the existence of **Understanding** is so far from being a reason to disprove a **Deity** (as **atheists** ignorantly claim) that it actually provides a firm **demonstration** to the contrary. It proves the **existence** of a **God**, a **perfect, omnipotent Being** who **comprehends** itself and the full **extent** of its own **power**, including all the **possibilities** of **things**. This is a **Mind that existed before the world** and is **prior** to **all things**. It is not an <term>ectypal</term> <note>original: "Ecctypal"; a copy or reproduction of an original</note> thing, but an <term>archetypal</term> <note>original: "Archetypal"; a primary model or blueprint</note> thing, which contained within itself—as a kind of **intellectual world**—the **paradigm** or **platform** according to which this **perceptible world** <note>original: "Sensible World"</note> was made.

This can be further confirmed by what is generally acknowledged and cannot reasonably be denied by anyone: that there are **eternal truths** <note>original: "Eternal Verities"</note>. These are truths that were never **made**, had no **beginning**, and can never be **destroyed** or **cease** to be. For example, consider **fundamental principles** <note>original: "Common Notions"</note> such as: *that equals added to equals make equals*; or that the **cause** is, in the order of **nature**, prior to the **effect**, and so on. This also includes all **geometrical theorems**, as **Aristotle** himself declared in his *Ethics*:

> "Regarding **immutable** <note>original: "Immutable"; unchanging</note> **things**, no man consults or deliberates; for example, regarding the **diameter** or **diagonal** of a **square**, whether it should be **incommensurable** <note>original: "Incommensurable"; having no common measure, such as the relationship between a square's side and its diagonal</note> to the **sides** or not." <note>original: "οἷον ὦει τ' ἡ διάμετρος ἢ τ' ἡ πλευρὰς ὅτι ἀσύμμετροι"</note>

Here, Aristotle plainly affirms that this **geometrical theorem**—that the **diameter** of a **square** is **incommensurable** to its **sides**—is an **eternal truth**. 

Such **eternal truths** are found not only in **mathematics** concerning **quantity**, but also in **ethics** concerning **morality**. There exist **eternally just things** <note>original: "αἰώνια δίκαια"</note>, as **Justin Martyr** calls them. These were not **made** just at a certain **time** by a **law** or an **arbitrary command**, but are **immutably** so in their own **nature**. They were from **everlasting** to **everlasting**, and (as it is said of that **Eternal Word** which comprehends all **truth**) are the same **yesterday**, **today**, and **forever**. Regarding these, there is a famous passage by **Sophocles** in his play *Antigone*:

> For these things do not live only today or yesterday, but forever,
> And no one knows from when they first appeared.
> <note>original: "Ὄυ γάρ τι νῦν γε κἀχθὲς, ἀλλ᾽ ἀεὶ / Ζῇ ταῦτα, κὐδεὶς οἶδεν ἐξ ὅτου φάνη."</note>

These are not matters of **today** or **yesterday**; they **live** forever, and no man knows their **date** or where they originated. No one can name the time when **fundamental principles** and **geometrical truths** were first **made** or **generated** out of **nothing**, or brought into **being** from a state of **non-existence**. 

It is certain that truths such as these—that the **diameter** and **sides** of a **square** are **incommensurable**, or that the **square** <note>original: "Power"</note> of the **hypotenuse** in a **right-angled triangle** is **equal** to the **squares** of both the **sides**—were not created by any **human's thinking** or by those first **geometricians** who **discovered** or **demonstrated** them. They were only **discovering** and **demonstrating** that which already **was**. Therefore, these **truths** existed before there was any human to **think** of them, and they would continue to exist even if all the people in the **world** were **annihilated**. Indeed, they would remain even if there were no **physical squares** or **triangles** anywhere in the whole **world**, nor any **matter** at all. They existed without beginning before the **world** began, and they would, by **necessity**, exist forever after, should the world cease to be.

# CHAPTER IV. and Intelligibles.

Now, if *eternal truths* exist—which were never created and could not help but exist—then the <term>rationes rerum</term> <note>original: "Rationes Rerum"; the fundamental reasons or principles of things</note>, the *simple reasons* of things, or their *intelligible natures* and *essences* from which those truths are composed, must of *necessity be eternal* as well. 

For how can it be an *eternal truth* that the *diameter* of a *square* is <term>incommensurable</term> <note>original: "Incommenſurable"; having no common measure; in geometry, it means the ratio cannot be expressed as a whole number</note> with its *sides*, if the *reasons* of a *square*, *diameter*, and *sides*—or their *intelligible essences*—were not themselves *eternal*? These are therefore called by **Plato** (a man of much <term>meditation</term> <note>original: "Meditation"; deep, focused thought</note> and a highly respected philosopher) not only "things which are always the same and unchangeable" <note>original: ἃ ταῦτα ἀεὶ ἔχοντα</note>, but also "things which were never made, but always are" <note>original: τὰ μὴ γιγνόμενα, ἀλλ᾽ ἀεὶ ὄντα</note>. Sometimes he calls them "things that were neither made nor can be destroyed" <note>original: μήτε γινόμενα, μήτε ἀπολλύμενα</note> and "things unborn and undying" <note>original: τὰ ἀγένεται ὴ ἀνώλεθρα</note>. 

Concerning this, **Cicero** wrote: "Plato affirms these things to have been never made, but always to be, and to be contained in reason and understanding" <note>original: "Hæc Plato negat Gigni, sed Semper Eſſe, & Ratione Intelligentiâ Contineri."</note>. And though it may seem strange, even **Aristotle** himself—despite his frequent disagreements with Plato’s theory of *Ideas*—actually agrees in the main point here: that the *forms* and *species*, or the *universal intelligible essences* of things (which are the proper and immediate *objects of science*), were *eternal* and never made. 

Thus, in his *Metaphysics*, Aristotle says: "No man makes the form, or species of a thing, nor was it ever generated" <note>original: τὸ εἶδ© ἀεὶ καὶ ὁδεις ποιεί γιγνῶται</note>. Again, he writes: "There is no generation of the essence of a sphere" <note>original: ἔτι δὴ ὅτι ἐκ ἔτιν ἐπὶ γίνεσις</note>; and, "The forms or species of things exist without any generation or corruption" <note>original: ἄνευ γενέσεως ὴ φθορᾶς τὰ ἔδη</note>. He sometimes calls these *objects of science* an "immutable essence or nature" <note>original: ἀκίνητον ἐσιάν or φύσιν</note>. 

Finally, when he writes against the <term>Heraclitics</term> <note>original: "Heracliticks"; followers of Heraclitus, who believed everything is in a state of constant flux</note> and other <term>Scepticks</term> <note>original: "Scepticks"; those who doubt the possibility of certain knowledge</note> who denied all *certainty of science*, he first identifies the root of their error. He explains that they wrongly assumed that *individual bodies*, or <term>sensibles</term> <note>original: "Senſibles"; things that can be perceived by the physical senses</note> existing *outside* of us, were the *only things* or *objects* of the *mind* or *knowledge*:

> "The origin of these men’s mistake was this: they sought for truth in things, and they conceived the only existing things to be sensibles, in which it is certain there is much of the indeterminate nature. Therefore, perceiving that the entire nature of sensibles is movable—or in a state of perpetual flux and mutation—and since nothing can possibly be verified or constantly affirmed concerning that which is not the same but always changing, they concluded there could be no truth at all, nor certainty of science. They believed that the things which are the only objects of knowledge never remain the same." <note>Aristotle, Metaphysics, Book 4, Chapter 5. Original Greek: αἴτιον δὲ τῆς τοις, ὅτι οἷ ἐφ ὅλων τῶ ἀληθῶν ἠδόκεν, τὰ ὴ ὄντα ὑπέλαβον εἶναι τὰ αἰσθητὰ μόνον...</note>

Then Aristotle adds, in opposition to this skeptical doctrine and its flawed foundation:

> "We would have these men know, therefore, that there is another kind of essence of things besides that of sensibles, to which belongs neither [change, nor destruction, nor generation...]" <note>original: ἀξιόωμεν αὐτοῖς ὑπολαμάον ἢ ἀλλην ἐσίαν εἶναι ἐκ ὄντων, ὴ ὅτι κίνησις ὑπέρχετ ὴ ὅτι φθόρα ὴ ἄνετ© ὴ γένεσις</note>

...neither motion, nor decay, nor any <term>generation</term> <note>original: "Generation"; the process of coming into being or being born</note> at all. By these *essences of things*, which have no beginning or ending, **Aristotle** could understand nothing else but those intelligible natures, *species*, and *ideas* which are the *permanent* and *unchangeable objects of science*.

And it is certain that there could be no constant and unchangeable science at all if there were no other objects of the mind besides individual and sensory things, because these are all changeable. Therefore, the *proper* and *immediate objects of geometry* are not individual and material triangles, squares, spheres, and cubes, etc. This is not only because none of these physical shapes are found to be mathematically exact, and because mathematicians in all the various distant ages and places of the world could not have the same individual bodies before them, but also because none of them continue unchangeably the same. All physical things are more or less in perpetual *motion* and *mutation*. In contrast, that which any geometrical theorem verifies and demonstrates must be *immutably* and *unalterably* the same.

The *triangles* and *circles*, *spheres* and *cubes* of **Euclid**, **Archimedes**, **Pappus**, **Apollonius**, and all other ancient and modern mathematicians, in all the distant places and times of the world, were both indivisibly *one and the same*, and also perfectly *unchangeable* and *indestructible*, for the science of geometry is itself like that. For this reason, it is also stated of these mathematical things by the aforementioned **Aristotle** <margin>Metaphysics, Book 12, Chapter 5.</margin> that they are *nowhere as in a specific place*, as all individual bodies are: "It is absurd to make mathematical objects exist in a place as solid bodies do, for place belongs only to individual things, which are therefore separated from one another by place; but mathematical things are not anywhere." <note>original: "ἄτοπον γὰρ καὶ τὸ τόπον ἅμα τοῖς στερεοῖς τοῖς μαθηματικοῖς ποιῆσαι, ὁ μὲν γὰρ τόπος τῶν καθ' ἕκαστον ἴδιος · διὸ χωριστὰ τόπῳ · τὰ δὲ μαθηματικά, οὐ ποῦ."</note> Because they are universal and abstract, they exist only in minds; nevertheless, for the same reason, they are also everywhere, as they are in every mind that understands them.

Lastly, these intelligible essences and *ideas* of things are also called by **Philo** *the most necessary essences* <note>original: "ἀναγκαιόταται οὐσίαι"</note>, as they are not only eternal but also have necessary existence belonging to them. For though there is no absolute necessity that matter or bodies should exist, there is an *absolute necessity that truth should exist*.

If, therefore, there are eternal "intelligibles" or ideas, and eternal truths, and if necessary existence belongs to them, then there must be an Eternal Mind necessarily existing. This is because these truths and the intelligible essences of things cannot possibly be anywhere but in a mind. By the "essences of things," when they are said to be eternal, we do not mean their actual physical substances (as if everything were in itself eternal and uncreated). Nor do we mean that God, in the act of creation, did only as a modern writer misleadingly puts it, "like a tailor, clothe the prior essences of things with a new garment of existence" <note>original: "Sartoris instar, vestire Essentias rerum novâ Existentiâ"</note>. Instead, we mean only their *known state of being* <note>original: "Eſſe Cognitum"; a philosophical term referring to things as they exist as objects of thought or understanding</note>—their possible and intelligible natures—as they were objects of infinite power and understanding before they were physically made. There must be a Mind older than the world and all sensory things, which simultaneously contains within it the ideas of all intelligible things, their necessary <term>scheses</term> <note>original: "Scheſes"; the Greek term for the logical relations or connections between different concepts</note> and relationships to one another,

# Chapter 4: All Minds Partake of One

...and all their **immutable truths**: a Mind which does not <note>original: *ὁτὲ μὲν νοεῖν, ὁτὲ δ’ οὐ νοεῖν*</note> "sometimes think and sometimes not think" (as **Aristotle** writes of it), as if it were sometimes awake and sometimes asleep, or like an eye sometimes open and sometimes shut. Instead, it is <note>original: *οὐσία ἐνέργεια*</note> "an essence that is activity" and energy; it has no defect in it. As we have already declared, this can be no other than the **Mind** of an **omnipotent** and **infinitely perfect Being**. This Being comprehends **itself** and the **extent** of its own **power**, or how far it is communicable—that is, all the possibilities of things that may be made by it and their **respective truths**. **Mind** and **knowledge**, in their very nature, suppose the **actual existence** of an **omnipotent** or **infinitely powerful Being** as its <term>intelligible object</term> <note>original: *Νοητὸν* (noeton); the thing that is known or understood</note>. Knowledge is nothing but the comprehension and measurement of the extent of **infinite** or **divine power**.

From this, it is also evident that there can be only **one original Mind**, or no more than **one self-existent understanding Being**. All other **minds** whatsoever **partake** of this one **original Mind**, being stamped, as it were, with the impression or signature of one and the same seal. This is why all minds, in different places and ages of the world, have **ideas** or **notions** of things that are **exactly alike**, and **truths** that are **indivisibly the same**. Truths are not multiplied by the diversity of **minds** that apprehend them, because they are all but <term>ectypal</term> <note>original: "Ectypal"; a copy or secondary representation of a pattern</note> participations of one and the same **original** or <term>archetypal</term> <note>original: "Archetypal"; the original model or primary pattern</note> **Mind** and **Truth**. Just as the same face may be reflected in several mirrors, or the image of the same sun may be in a thousand eyes at once, or one and the same voice may be in a thousand ears listening to it; so when innumerable **created minds** have the same **ideas** of things and understand the **same truths**, it is but **one** and the same **eternal light** reflected in them all ("that light which enlightens every man that comes into the world" <note>A reference to John 1:9</note>), or the same voice of that **one everlasting Word** that is never silent, re-echoed by them. 

Thus, **Themistius** <note>A 4th-century Greek philosopher and rhetorician</note> concluded that it would be impossible for one person, by teaching, to produce in the **mind** of another the very same notions, conceptions, and knowledge that he had in his own mind <note>original: *εἰ μὴ ταὐτὸν ἦν τὸ νόημα τοῦ διδάσκοντος καὶ τοῦ μανθάνοντος*</note> "if the thought of the teacher and the learner were not the same"—if the minds of both the teacher and the learner were not, as it were, printed and stamped alike. He also argued that people could not possibly confer together as they do, instantly apprehending one another’s meaning and raising up the very same senses in their minds merely by the occasion of words and sounds, <note>original: *εἰ μήτις ἦν Εἷς Νοῦς οὗ πάντες ἐκοινωνοῦμεν*</note> "if there were not some one Mind which all men shared." 

As for that **anti-monarchical opinion** <note>Here referring to the belief in multiple independent first causes or gods</note> of **many understanding beings** or **minds** that are **self-originated** and **independent** (none of which, therefore, could be omnipotent), it is inconceivable. Such minds could not all agree on the same **truths**, as there would be no **common measure** of **truth** between them, any more than a **common rule** for their **wills**. Indeed, they could not have any knowledge or **understanding** at all in the proper sense. Understanding is the comprehension of the **possibilities** of things, or of the **extent** of **infinite power**; however, according to this hypothesis, there is no **infinite power** at all, since the power of each of those many supposed principles...

We have now, more extensively than we initially planned, refuted the *first atheistic argument*. 2. Secondly, we shall make it evident that in the sense used in this *atheistic objection*, it is *absolutely false* *that nothing can come from nothing* or be *made out of nothing*. We will show that a divine *creation* and *omnipotence* cannot be attacked in any way by that principle, if it is rightly understood. 
3. Thirdly and lastly, we shall prove that just as this principle or *common notion*, *nothing out of nothing*, cannot be used to defeat *theism* or a divine creation, the very same principle—rightly understood—can *demonstrably prove* the *impossibility* of all atheism. This is because atheism implies bringing something out of nothing in an *impossible sense*. We will also show how this principle proves the existence of a God.

We grant, therefore, in the first place, that in some sense it is an *undoubted principle of reason*, or an *undeniable common notion*, that *nothing can come from nothing*. 
* First, it is unquestionably true that *nothing which once did not exist could ever come into being of its own accord*; or *that nothing could bring itself out of non-existence into being*. 
* *Nothing can begin to exist from itself*, and *nothing can be made or produced without an efficient cause* <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The primary source of change or the agent that brings something into existence.</note>.

# CHAPTER IV. Nothing out of Nothing.

If anything has been made, then something must necessarily have been made out of nothing by itself, which is impossible.

Again, just as **nothing** which was **not** could ever **by itself** come into **being**, or be **made**, without an **efficient cause** <note>The "efficient cause" is the primary agent or force that brings something into existence or initiates a change.</note>, it is also certain that **nothing** can be **efficiently caused** or **produced** by something that does not have at least **equal** (if not **greater**) **perfection**, as well as **sufficient power** to **produce** it. We say **nothing** which **was not** could **ever be brought into being** by that which does not have **formally equal perfection** in it; this is because **nothing** can **give** what it does not have. Therefore, if the **perfection** or **entity** of the **effect** is greater than that of the supposed **cause**, that extra portion must necessarily come from **nothing** or be made without a **cause**.

Moreover, whatever has **equal perfection** to another thing could not necessarily **cause** or **produce** that other thing because it might either have no **active power** at all (as **matter** does not, being merely **passive**) or else lack **sufficient active** and **productive power**. For **example**, though it is not **impossible** that **motion**, which once did not exist, should be **produced**, it is **impossible** that it should ever be **produced** without a **sufficient cause**. 

Therefore, if there were once no **motion** at all in the whole world, nor any **life** or **self-active power** in anything, but all things were **dead**, then it is certain that no **motion** or **mutation** <note>original: "mutation"; change or alteration</note> could ever possibly arise in it for all **eternity**. There would be no **sufficient cause** to **produce** it, since nothing can produce **motion** except that which has **life** or **self-activity** in it. If **motion** or anything else should begin to exist without a **sufficient cause**, then it must necessarily be **caused by itself**, or **of itself** come into **being**, which is **impossible**. 

Now, no **imperfect being** whatsoever has a **sufficient emanative power** <note>Emanative power refers to the ability to produce something by "flowing forth" from one's own essence.</note> to **create** any other **substance** or **produce** it out of **nothing**. The most that can be done by **imperfect beings** is only to **produce** new **accidents** <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are properties or qualities (like color, shape, or thought) that exist in a substance but are not the substance itself.</note> and **modifications**. For instance, **human souls** can **produce** new **thoughts** <note>original: "cogitations"</note> in themselves and new **local motion** in **bodies**. No **imperfect being** is **substantially emanative**, or can **produce** another **substance** out of **non-existence**. 

Therefore, for any **substance** to be brought into **being** by an **imperfect substance**—which lacks **sufficient emanative** or **creative power**—is plainly **impossible**. It is the same as saying that a **substance** might, **of itself**, come out of **nothing** into **being**. And thus it is granted that no **substance** could be **created** or brought out of **non-existence** into **being** except by the sole **efficiency** of an **absolutely perfect being**, which has both **greater perfection** (**it eminently containing all things in it**) and also a **sufficient emanative** or **creative power**.

And now we have given an account of **two senses** in which it is **impossible for anything** to come from **nothing**: 
1. **One**: For a thing which was **not** to bring **itself** into **being**, or to be **made** without an **efficient cause**. 
2. **Another**: For a thing to be **efficiently caused** by that which does not have at least **equal perfection** in it, or a **sufficient emanative** or **productive power**. 

Both of these **senses** of this axiom respect the **efficient cause**, and thus it was frequently

->Nothing from Nothing; not BOOK I.<-

We shall now propose a third sense in which this axiom is also verified—that ***nothing can be made out of nothing***—specifically regarding the **material cause** <note>The "material cause" refers to the physical substance or matter from which something is made.</note>. For since no **imperfect**, **natural being** has any **creative power**, or can efficiently produce any **new substance** or **real entity** (which did not exist before) into being, but can only act upon **pre-existing matter** through motion and modify it; and since **matter**, being merely **passive**, cannot cause anything that did not exist before or that does not result from its **composition** or **modification**, it follows undeniably that in all **natural generations** and **productions** out of **pre-existing matter** (without a **divine creation**), no **new substance** or **real entity** can ever be brought out of **non-existence** into **being**. 

And this was precisely what the ancient **natural philosophers** <note>original: "Physiologers"—early scientists or philosophers who studied the natural world (physike).</note> meant when (as **Aristotle** tells us) they insisted so much upon this principle: *that it was impossible that any real entity should be* (naturally) *made or generated out of nothing* <note>original Greek: τὸ γινόμενον ἐκ μὴ ὄντων γίνεσθαι ἀδύνατον</note>. Or, as it is also expressed: *that no real entity was either generated or corrupted* <note>original Greek: οὐδὲν οὐδὲ γίνεσθαι οὐδὲ φθείρεσθαι τῶν ὄντων</note>. That is, in **natural generations**, **corruptions**, and **alterations** (where **God** is assumed not to **miraculously** intervene), there is no **creation** of any **new substance** or **real entity** out of **nothing**, nor **annihilation** or **destruction** of anything into **nothing**.

We are well aware that most **modern writers** have interpreted this **doctrine** of the old **natural philosophers** in **Aristotle** in a completely different sense. They claim it was intended to deny all **divine creation** out of **nothing** (or **non-existence**); they suggest that everything sprang from **matter** (which existed of itself from eternity) either **without** a **God**, or—since **Parmenides**, **Empedocles**, and other supporters of this **doctrine** were undoubtedly **theists**—**with Him**. In this view, God could not **create** any **new entity** out of **nothing**, but could only make things out of **pre-existing, unmade matter**, just as a carpenter builds a house or a weaver makes a piece of cloth. 

Thus, it is commonly taken for granted that no **pagan philosopher** ever went so far as to acknowledge a **divine creation** of anything out of **nothing** in the sense used by **Christian theologians**. We grant that besides the **Stoics**, there have been other **philosophical theists** among the **pagans** of this persuasion: that **nothing** was or could be made by **God** except out of **something pre-existing**. **Plutarch of Chaeronea** is one such example, who in a place already cited positively affirms *that although the world was indeed made by God, the substance or matter out of which it was made was not made, but always lay ready for the Creator* <note>original Greek: τὸν μὲν κόσμον ὑπὸ Θεοῦ γεγονέναι, τὴν δὲ οὐσίαν καὶ ὕλην ἐξ ἧς γέγονεν, οὐ γενομένην, ἀλλὰ ὑποκειμένην ἀεὶ τῷ δημιουργῷ</note>. And then he adds this very reason for it: *because there can be no creation of anything out of nothing, but only out of something pre-existing that is not rightly ordered or sufficiently prepared, such as in a house, garment, or statue* <note>original Greek: οὐ γὰρ ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος γένεσις, ἀλλ’ ἐκ τοῦ μὴ καλῶς, μηδ’ ἱκανῶς ἔχοντος, ὡς οἰκίας καὶ ἱματίου καὶ ἀνδριάντος</note>. ### CHAPTER IV. Against Divine Creation.

However, in our view, neither **Plutarch** nor the **Stoics** should be considered **absolute** and **outright atheists** because of this, but rather only **imperfect, mongrel, and false atheists**. Therefore, even if atheists were able to prove that there could be no **creation out of nothing pre-existing** (which they cannot do at all), this still would not overthrow **theism** in general, as there is a range of belief within it. 

Nevertheless, it will appear undeniably from what follows that those ancient **Italians** <note>Italicks: Refers to the "Italian school" of philosophy, primarily the Pythagoreans who lived in Southern Italy.</note> and **Pythagoreans** were far from intending to derive all things from matter, whether **without** or **with** a **God**. On the contrary, they plainly intended the opposite: namely, to prove that no **new real entity** could be **made out of matter**, and particularly that **souls** could not be **generated out of the same**. Therefore, according to them, souls must necessarily have another **divine origin** and be **made by God**, not out of **matter**, but out of **nothing pre-existing**—since no one could suppose that all **souls existed of themselves from eternity without being made**. 

Indeed, all those **pagan philosophers** who asserted the **incorporeity of souls** <term>incorporeity: the state of having no physical body or material substance</term> must, in the same way, necessarily suppose that they were not **made** out of **pre-existing matter**, but by **God** out of **nothing**. **Plutarch** is the only exception here, because of a certain odd **hypothesis** that was uniquely his own: a **third principle**, besides **God** and **matter**, which was a **disordered soul** or a **self-existent evil demon**. He seems to have supposed that all **individual human souls** were made neither out of **nothing**, nor out of **pre-existing matter** or **body**, but out of a strange **mixture** of the **substance of that evil soul** and **God** blended together. For this reason, he claims that souls are not so much God's work as a part of Him <note>original Greek: ἔργον as μέρος Θεοῦ (ergon as meros Theou)</note>. And now, let anyone **judge** whether Plutarch’s account provides even further reason to complain about that **Boeotian air**. 

Therefore, we conclude that those old **natural philosophers** <note>original: "physiologers"—early scientists or philosophers who studied the nature of the physical world (physike).</note> mentioned in **Aristotle**, who insisted so much on that **principle**—that **no real entity could be made or generated out of nothing**—were acting only as **natural philosophers**. They were not acting as **theologians** or **metaphysicians**, for they were not opposing a **divine creation out of nothing pre-existing**. Instead, they were only contending that no **new entity** could be made out of **matter**, and that in **natural births and decays** <note>original: "generations and corruptions"</note> there was no **creation** or **annihilation** of anything.

But the true scope and meaning of these **natural philosophers** will appear more plainly from the **use** or **improvement** they made of this **philosophical principle**, which was **twofold**. 

**First**, it is certain that on this **foundation**, they all endeavored to establish a peculiar kind of **natural science** and some form of "**atomology**" (atomic theory)—either a **homoeomery** <term>homoeomery: Anaxagoras's theory that substances are made of infinitely small parts that are the same as the whole (e.g., bone is made of tiny bits of bone)</term> or an **anomoeomery** (a **similar or dissimilar atomology**). For **Anaxagoras** looked upon this **maxim** of the **Italian philosophers**—that **nothing could be physically made out of nothing**, or **no real entity generated or destroyed**—as an **undisputed principle of reason**. Also, because he could not conceive of the **forms and qualities of bodies** as anything other than **real entities** distinct from the **substance of matter** or its **modifications**;

# Atomology, and Incorporeity Book I.

They concluded that therefore in the processes of **birth**, **decay**, and **change**, things were not created out of **nothing** or **destroyed** into **nothing**. Instead, everything was naturally made "out of pre-existing and in-existing things" <note>original Greek: *ek proyparchontōn kai enyparchontōn*</note>. Consequently, they believed that in all things there were **dissimilar atoms** and **particles** of every kind. However, because of their extreme **smallness** <term>parvitude: smallness or insignificance in size</term>, they are **imperceptible** to us, and everything seemed to consist only of whatever was most **dominant** and **noticeable** within it. 

To wit, they believed that **bone** was made out of **bony atoms**, and **flesh** out of **fleshy** ones; **hot** things out of **hot atoms**, and **cold** things out of **cold** ones; **black** out of **black**, and **white** out of **white**, and so on. They held that **nothing** comes from **nothing**, but everything comes out of **pre-existing similar atoms**. This was the view of **Anaxagoras**, as plainly stated by **Aristotle**: because **opposites** were made out of one another, they must have **already existed within** each other. Since every thing must necessarily be made either out of **something** or out of **nothing**, and all **natural philosophers** <note>original: "physiologers"</note> agree that it is **impossible** for anything to be made out of **nothing**, it follows unavoidably that whatever is **generated** must be **produced** out of things **pre-existing** and **residing within**, though they are **imperceptible** to us because of their **smallness**. That is, they are made out of **similar** or **homogeneous atoms**, of which some of every kind exist in **every** thing—everything being mixed into everything. Here, therefore, we have the **Anaxagorean Homoeomery** <term>homoeomery: the theory that the tiny parts of a substance are the same as the whole substance (for example, a piece of gold is made of gold-particles)</term>, or **similar atomology**, built upon this principle of **reason** as its **foundation**: that **nothing can naturally be made or generated out of nothing**.

But the **Italians** or **Pythagoreans**, both before and after **Anaxagoras** (with whom **Leucippus**, **Democritus**, and **Epicurus**—those **atheistic followers** of the **Italian natural philosophy**—also agreed), used much better **reasoning**. From the same fundamental principle, they concluded that since these **forms** and **qualities** of bodies were undoubtedly **produced** and **destroyed**, they were not **real entities distinct** from the **substance of matter** or its **modifications**. Instead, they were only different **arrangements** or **modifications** of its **imperceptible parts**, which cause different **mental perceptions** <note>original: "phantasms"</note> in us. This was the **first** origin of **dissimilar atomology**. 

To these **philosophers**, therefore, nothing else was conceivable in **matter** or **body** except for the **size of its parts**, their **shape**, **position**, and **motion** or **rest**. These were those few **elements** which, by existing within and being combined in various ways, they supposed resulted in all those (commonly so-called) **forms** and **qualities** of bodies during **generation**, without producing any **new real entity** out of **nothing**. For just as from a few **letters** in the **alphabet** of every **language**, placed and combined differently, there **result** innumerable **syllables**, **words**, and **sounds** that signify all the various things in heaven and earth—and sometimes from the exact same **letters**, neither more nor fewer, but only **rearranged**, very different **sounds** are produced in **us** without creating any **new real entity** out of **nothing**—in the very same way, from those **fewer letters** in the **alphabet** of **physical nature** (the various **modifications** of **matter** regarding **size**, **shape**, **position**, and **motion**), all those **syllables** of **things** in the whole World,

This causes very different **phantasms** <note>original: "Phantasms" — mental images or perceptions</note> in us, which are therefore commonly supposed to be **forms** and **qualities** inherent in the things themselves; just as the same water is successively changed and transformed into vapor, snow, hail, and ice. For if those supposed **forms** and **qualities**—produced during **generations** <term>generations: the process of coming into being or birth</term> and **alterations**—were **entities** really **distinct** from the **substance** of **matter** or its different **modifications** (such as the **size**, **shape**, **position**, and **motion** of its parts), then they would materially proceed from **nothing**, which is impossible. (There were no such things already **in-existing** as **Anaxagoras** supposed.)

This **dissimilar atomology** of the ancient **Italics** <note>Italics: referring to the Pythagorean and early Greek philosophers based in Southern Italy</note>, as far as it concerns these material **forms** and **qualities**, seems undoubtedly to be the only true **physiology** <term>physiology: the study of the physical laws of nature</term>. It is built upon this sure principle of reason: because **nothing** can give what it does not have, no new **substance** or **real entity** can be materially produced in the **generations** and **alterations** of nature as such; only **modifications** can be produced. Just as when an **architect** builds a house or a **weaver** makes a piece of cloth, there is only a different **modification** of the **pre-existing matter**.

This is the first **improvement** that the ancient **Italic philosophers** made on this **principle**: that **nothing** can be (**physically** and **materially**) **generated** out of **nothing**, or that **no real entity** is **naturally generated** or **corrupted** <term>corrupted: destroyed or decomposed</term>. Therefore, the **forms** and **qualities** of **bodies** were not **real entities**, but only **different modifications**. 

But besides this, there was another thing which these **philosophers** primarily **aimed at** here as a **corollary** <term>corollary: a natural consequence or logical conclusion</term> deducible from the same **principle** concerning **souls**. Since the **souls** of **animals**, and especially **humans**, are unquestionably **entities** really **distinct** from **matter** and all its **modifications** (as no **size**, **shapes**, **positions**, or **motions** are ever able to beget **thought** or **consciousness**, much less the **power** of **understanding eternal truths**), it follows that these could not be **generated** out of **matter**, nor **corrupted** into it. 

Because **forms** and **qualities** are continually **generated** and **corrupted**—made out of **nothing** and **reduced** to **nothing** again—they are not **entities** really **distinct** from **matter** and its different **modifications**. But because **souls** (at least **human** ones) are unquestionably **entities** really **distinct** from **matter** and its **modifications**, they cannot possibly be **generated** out of **matter**...

# Generation and Corruption of Animals; BOOK I.

...matter, nor decayed into it. For if *human souls* were *generated* out of *matter*, then some *real entity* would have to be *materially produced* out of *nothing*, since there is *nothing* of *life* and *thought* <term>cogitation: the action of thinking</term> in *matter*; which is a *thing absolutely impossible*. Therefore, these *philosophers* concluded concerning *souls* that, not being *generated* out of *matter*, they were *introduced* <note>original: "Insinuated"</note> into *bodies* during the process of *birth* <term>generations: the act of coming into being or birth</term>. And this was always a *great controversy* between *theists* and *atheists* concerning the *human soul*, as the poet *Lucretius* expresses it:

->*Whether it was born, or on the contrary is introduced into those being born,*<-
<note>original Latin: "Nata sit, an contrà Nafcentibus Infinuetur"</note>

Whether *it was made or generated out of matter* (which is indeed *out of nothing*), or else *was from without* <note>original Greek: θύραθεν</note>, *introduced into bodies during birth?* This latter opinion of theirs supposes *souls* to have *existed before the births* of all *animals*, just as they *exist after their deaths and decays*; there being properly *nothing* of them *generated* except their *union* with those particular *bodies*. 

So that the *births* and *deaths* <note>original: "Generations, and Corruptions or Deaths"</note> of *animals*, according to this *hypothesis*, are nothing but an *anagrammatic rearrangement* <note>original: "Anagrammatical Transposition"</note> of *things in the universe*. *Pre- and post-existent souls* are sometimes united to one *body* and sometimes to another. But it does not therefore follow—simply because these *ancient philosophers* held *souls* to be thus *ingenerable* <term>ingenerable: incapable of being generated or produced from matter</term> and to have *pre-existed* before the *birth* of *animals*—that they supposed all *souls* to have *existed of themselves from eternity unmade*. This is a *thing* which was never asserted by either *theist* or *atheist*; since even those *philosophical theists* who maintained *the eternity of human minds* <note>original Latin: "Æternitatem Animorum"</note> and souls along with the *world's* existence, nevertheless asserted their *essential dependence* upon the *Deity*, like that of *light* upon the *Sun*; as if they were a kind of *eternal radiance, emanation, or radiation* from an *eternal Sun*. 

Even *Proclus* himself—that *great champion* for the *eternity of the world* and *souls*—expressly declared in this very case, when he wrote against *Plutarch’s self-existent evil soul*, that *there is no self-existent soul; but every soul whatsoever is the work, effect, and production of God* <note>original Greek: πᾶσα ψυχὴ γέννημα ἐστι τοῦ θεοῦ</note>. Therefore, when they affirmed *souls* to be *ingenerable*, their meaning was no more than this: that they were not merely *accidental things* (as *forms* and *qualities* are), nor any more *generated* out of *matter* than *matter itself* is *generated* out of *something else*. On this account, as *Aristotle* informs us, *souls* were also called by them *principles* <note>original Greek: ἀρχαί</note> as well as *matter*, they being both *substances* in the *universe* that are equally *original*; that is, neither of them was *made* out of the other. 

But they did not suppose them to be *unmade* <note>original Greek: ἀγενήτες</note> or *ingenerate* in the other *sense*—as if they had been *self-originated* and *independent*, as *Plutarch's second and third principles* (his *evil soul* and *matter*) were *imagined* by him to be. Instead, they undoubtedly believed that if the *world* had had any beginning, they would then have been all *created together* with it, out of *nothing pre-existing*. But as for the perpetual *creation* of *new souls* in the *successive births of animals*, this indeed is a thing

### CHAPTER IV. Anagrammatic Transposition

...a thing which those <term>philosophers</term> were extremely repelled by. They thought it inconsistent that <term>souls</term>, which are superior in the <term>order of nature</term> to <term>bodies</term>, should be younger than them in the <term>order of time</term>. They also felt it was not <term>reasonable</term> that <term>divine creation</term> (treated as if it were <term>prostituted</term> <note>original: "Prostituted," meaning debased or made to serve a common, lower purpose</note>) should endlessly and perpetually wait upon <term>natural births</term> <note>original: "Generations"</note> and be <term>intermingled with them</term>.

But regarding this <term>pre-existence of souls</term>, we have already stated our own view in the first chapter. Although we cannot deny that, besides <term>Origen</term> <note>an early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD) who taught that souls existed before their bodies</note>, several other <term>ancient fathers</term> of the Church before the <term>Fifth Council</term> <note>The Second Council of Constantinople in 553 AD, which condemned certain teachings on the pre-existence of souls</note> seem either to have <term>embraced</term> <note>original: "Espoused"</note> it or at least favored it. Even Saint <term>Augustine</term> himself sometimes <term>wavers</term> <note>original: "Staggering"</note> on this point and thinks it a <term>great secret</term> whether <term>men’s souls existed before their births</term> or not. Elsewhere, he concludes it is a matter of <term>indifference</term>, where everyone may have the <term>freedom to hold an opinion</term> either way without causing offense. Therefore, all that can be certainly affirmed in this <term>case</term> is that <term>human souls</term> could not possibly be <term>produced</term> <note>original: "Generated"</note> out of <term>matter</term>. Instead, they were created at some point by God Almighty out of <term>nothing previously existing</term>, either <term>at the time of birth</term> <note>original: "In Generations"</note> or <term>before them</term>.

Finally, regarding <term>brute animals</term>, we must admit that if they are not merely <term>machines</term> or <term>automata</term> (as some seem inclined to believe), but are <term>conscious</term> and <term>thinking beings</term>, then the same <term>principle of reason</term> implies that they cannot be <term>produced</term> out of <term>matter</term> either. Therefore, they must be <term>derived from the fountain of all life</term> and <term>created out of nothing</term> by Him. Since He can <term>annihilate</term> as easily as He can <term>create</term>, and does everything for the <term>best</term>, no one needs to worry about their <term>permanence</term> or <term>immortality</term>.

We have now provided a <term>full and specific account</term> of the <term>various ways</term> <note>original: "Several Senses"</note> in which this <term>axiom</term> <note>a self-evident truth</note> must be acknowledged as <term>undeniably true</term>: that <term>nothing can possibly be made out of nothing</term> or <term>come from nothing</term>. These are the three ways:

1.  First, that <term>nothing which did not exist</term> could ever bring itself into <term>being</term> or <term>produce itself effectively</term> <note>original: "Efficiently Produce it self"</note>. In other words, <term>nothing can possibly be made</term> without an <term>efficient cause</term> <note>the primary source of change or creation</note>.
2.  Second, that <term>nothing which did not exist</term> could be <term>produced or brought into being</term> by any other <term>efficient cause</term> except one that has at least <term>equal perfection</term> and <term>sufficient active or productive power</term> within it. For if anything were made by something that does not have <term>equal perfection</term>, then the part of the <term>effect</term> that <term>exceeds</term> <note>original: "Transcendeth"</note> the <term>cause</term> must have been <term>made without a cause</term> (since <term>nothing can give what it does not have</term>), or else it was <term>caused by itself</term> or by <term>nothing</term>. Furthermore, <term>to suppose a thing to be produced by something that has no sufficient productive power</term> is <term>really to suppose</term> that it was <term>produced from itself</term> without a <term>cause</term>, or <term>from nothing</term>. Here we acknowledge that no <term>natural</term>, <term>imperfect</term>, or <term>created being</term> can <term>create</term> or <term>produce from itself</term> <note>original: "Emanatively Produce"</note> a <term>new substance</term> that did not exist <term>before</term>, giving it its <term>entire being</term>. Thus far, the <term>axiom is verified in respect of the efficient cause</term>.
3.  But in the <term>third place</term>, it is also <term>true</term> in <term>respect of the material</term> cause as well.
