# Nothing from Nothing, Causally BOOK I.

Matter itself could never be made, but was **self-existent**. The falsity of this is sufficiently evident from what has already been declared concerning human souls—their being undoubtedly **incorporeal substances** <note>substances that do not have a physical body, like souls or spirits</note>, which therefore could never be **generated out of matter**—and it will be further demonstrated afterward. But the **third and last sense is this**: that **nothing which is materially made out of pre-existing things (as some things are) can have any other real entity than what was either contained in or results from the things themselves when so modified**. Or, **that there can be no new entities or substances naturally generated out of matter**; and therefore that all **natural generations** <note>original: "Generations," meaning the process of something coming into being or birth</note> are really nothing else but mixtures or new modifications of **pre-existing things**.

These, I say, are all the **senses** in which it is **impossible** that anything should be made out of **nothing**, or **"come from nothing"**; and they may all be reduced to this **one general sense: that nothing can be made out of nothing, causally; or, that nothing cannot cause anything, either efficiently or materially**. While this is undeniably true, it is so far from arguing against a **divine creation** or the **existence of a God** that the same may be **demonstratively proved** and shown from it later.

<margin>out of nothing <note>original Greek: ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων (ex ouk ontōn)</note></margin>
But there is another sense in which things may be said to be made **out of nothing**, when those words are not taken **causally**, but only to signify the **point of departure** <note>original Latin: Terminus A quo</note>, or the term from which they are made—specifically, an **antecedent non-existence**. In this case, the meaning of this **proposition**—that **nothing can possibly be made out of nothing**—is that **nothing which once was not could, by any power whatsoever, be afterwards brought into being**. This is the sense emphasized in this second **atheistic argument**, framed according to the principles of **Democritic** or **Epicurean atheism** <note>ancient Greek philosophies that claimed the world consists only of atoms and empty space, denying divine creation</note>: that no **real entity** which once was not could by any power whatsoever **be made** or brought out of **non-existence** into **being**. Consequently, they argue that no **creative power** to produce something out of nothing can possibly belong to anything, no matter how perfect it is supposed to be.

In response to this, we shall accomplish these **two things**. First, we shall make it appear that **"nothing out of nothing,"** when taken in the sense just declared, is so far from being a **common notion** <note>a self-evident truth accepted by all</note> that it is not **true** at all. Secondly, we shall prove that **if** it were true, it would actually weigh more against **atheism** than it does against **theism**, and therefore should by no means be used by **atheists** as an **argument against a deity**. **First**, therefore, it is unquestionably certain that this cannot be **universally true**—that **nothing which once was not could possibly be made or brought out of non-existence into being**—because **if** it were, then there could be no such thing as **making** or **causing** at all. There would be no **action** or **motion**, and consequently no **generation** or **change** in the **physical universe**; instead, the whole world would be like a **rigid, immovable rock of adamant** <note>a legendary, unbreakable stone</note>. This would undoubtedly be a better argument against **motion** than any of **Zeno's** <note>Zeno of Elea, a Greek philosopher famous for paradoxes that seemed to prove motion is impossible</note> were. But we all have experience within ourselves of a power of producing **new thoughts**,

# CHAPTER 4: How "Nothing out of Nothing" is False

**Thoughts** in our own minds, new **intellectual** and **moral habits**, as also **new physical movement** <note>original: "Local Motion"</note> in our bodies—or at least **new directions** of that movement—cause **new forms** <note>original: "Modifications"</note> in the **bodies** around us. Therefore, **atheists** are forced to restrict the meaning of the proposition "nothing comes from nothing" to **substantial things only**. They claim that although **new attributes** <note>original: "Accidents"</note> and **modifications** may be produced out of **nothing**, no **new substances** can be **made**. However, they are unable to give any reason why one of these should be inherently more impossible than the other, or why no substance should be **capable of being made** <note>original: "Makeable"</note>.

Some people are staggered by the seeming plausibility of the atheist argument chiefly for the following reasons:

First, because of the **confusion** of their own **conceptions**. It is certain that **nothing can possibly be made out of nothing** in one sense—namely, **causally** (nothing cannot be its own cause). But because they do not distinguish between different meanings, and are unaware of the double meaning in the phrase **out of things that do not exist** <note>original Greek: ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων (ex ouk ontōn)</note>, they inadvertently agree to those words in the wrong sense: the sense that no **substance** (such as **matter**) could possibly be brought out of **non-existence** into **being**.

Secondly, they engage in unskillful **arguing** from **artificial things**. Because nothing can be **made by art** except out of **pre-existing matter**—such as a house, a garment, and the like—there is nothing done in the production of these things but only a **new modification** of what already substantially existed. From this, they over-hastily conclude that no power whatsoever could produce anything in any other way than out of **pre-existing matter**, and that matter itself therefore could not possibly be made.

In this conceit, they are further confirmed because the **ancient natural philosophers** <note>original: "Old Physiologers," referring to early Greek scientists like Democritus or Epicurus</note> maintained the same thing regarding **natural generations** <note>the process of things being born or produced in nature</note> as well: that nothing in them was produced **out of things that do not exist** <note>original Greek: ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων</note>. They believed there was no **new substance** or **entity made** in nature that was really distinct from the **pre-existing matter** and its **modifications**. Atheists unwarily extend this principle beyond the bounds of **physics** into **metaphysics**, and improperly measure or limit **infinite power** by it.

Lastly, because it is undeniably certain regarding **ourselves** and all **imperfect created beings** that none of us can **create** any **new substance** which did not exist before, people are apt to measure all things by their own **limited standard** <note>original: "scantling"</note>. They suppose it is universally impossible, according to **human reason**, for any power whatsoever to **create** in this way. From this, they conclude that **theology** must be acknowledged as **contradictory** to the principles of **natural light** and **understanding** <note>natural reason or common sense</note>.

But since it is certain that **imperfect created beings** can themselves produce **some things** out of **nothing pre-existing**—such as **new thoughts**, **new physical movements**, and **new modifications and transformations of physical things**—it is very reasonable to think that an **absolutely perfect being** could do something more. That is, God could **create new substances out of nothing**, or give them their entire being. It may well be thought just as easy for God, or an omnipotent being, to make a whole world, matter and all, **out of things that do not exist** <note>original Greek: ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων</note>, as it is for us to **create a thought**, or to **move a finger**, or for the **sun** to send out **rays**, or a **candle** to give **light**, or lastly, for any **opaque body** to produce an image of itself in **mirrors** or **water**, or to project a shadow. All these **imperfect** things are but the...

Energies, rays, images, or shadows of the Deity. For a substance which once did not exist to be made by God—a being of **infinite perfection**—is not for it to be made **out of nothing** in the **impossible sense**, since it comes from Him who is **everything**. Nor can it be called **impossible** for any thing whatsoever to be made by that which has not only **infinitely greater perfection**, but also a **sufficient active power** to produce it, as He is **substantially emanative** <note>original: "Substantially Emanative"; the idea that God’s substance can overflow or produce effects outside itself</note>. It is true that **infinite power** itself cannot do things that are in their **own nature impossible**. Therefore, the only thing atheists need to prove is that it is **absolutely impossible** for a substance (though not for an **attribute** <note>original: "Accident"</note> or **form** <note>original: "Modification"</note>) to be brought from **non-existence** into **being**. In reality, nothing is **absolutely impossible** in itself except for that which implies a **contradiction**. While it is **contradictory** for a thing to **exist** and **not exist** at the same time, there is no **contradiction** at all in an **imperfect, contingent being** <note>term: a "contingent being" is something that does not have to exist, but depends on something else for its existence</note> which did not exist before coming into being afterward. Therefore, since this is in no way **impossible**, it must be recognized as a **proper object** of **infinite power**—something that can be achieved by a **perfect, all-powerful being**.

<margin>See *Enchiridion Metaphysicum*, chapter 10 <note>original: "Enchir. Met."; a philosophical work by Henry More</note>.</margin>
If nothing could be made **out of things that do not exist** <note>original: ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων (ex ouk ontōn)</note>—meaning **nothing which did not exist before could afterward be brought into being**—then the reason must be that no **substance** or **real entity** can be **caused** by any other **substance** in a way that allows it to receive its **entire being** from it. Consequently, every **substance** or **real entity** in the whole world would not only have existed from **eternity without a beginning**, but would also have existed **of itself necessarily** and **independently** of anything else.

But **first**, it has already been stated that it is contrary to **human reason** <note>original: "Humane Faculties"</note> for any **temporary, successive being**—or even **time** itself—to be **eternal** without a beginning. Under that **hypothesis**, there would have always been an **infinity of past time**, which would mean there was necessarily a **past time that was never present**. Furthermore, to claim that every **substantial thing** has not only existed **from eternity** without a beginning (as some **mistaken theists** have done) but has also existed **independently** of any other **cause** or **origin**—and therefore **by its own necessity**—is actually to **make something come from nothing in the impossible sense** (namely, **causally**). For just as some **atheists claim** that **nothing could ever move itself**, yet nonetheless suppose that **motion** has existed from all eternity, they are clearly making this **motion** (however **eternal** they imagine it) **come from nothing** in the impossible sense. In the same way, those who suppose that things exist **necessarily of themselves**—even though they have no **self-existence** or **necessary existence** in their nature (which **only a perfect being has**) —are making this **necessary existence** come from **nothing**. Therefore, while it is certain that something has **existed necessarily of itself** from all eternity—namely a **perfect being** (whose **necessary existence** does not come from nothing because it is essentially included in its own nature)—it is equally certain that there can be only **one such thing**. **Necessity** of existence being **natural**

# CHAP. IV. Souls Substantial, etc.

...and essential to no more. But as for all other things, which are in their own nature contingently possible <term>contingently possible: things that do not have to exist by necessity, but can be brought into being or cease to be</term> to be or not to be, reason pronounces that they could not exist of **themselves** necessarily, but were caused by something else and derived their origin from that one absolutely perfect and necessarily existent Being. 

So it is that Plato's distinction must be allowed here, between two kinds of beings: *that which always is, and was never made, nor had a beginning* <note>original Greek: "τὸ μὲν ἀεὶ ὂν, γένεσιν δὲ οὐκ ἔχον"</note>; and *that which was made, or had a beginning, but never truly is* <note>original Greek: "τὸ γινόμενον μὲν ὂν δὲ οὐδέποτε"</note>. The latter does not have a permanent duration, but a successive or flowing one. Accordingly, Aristotle also affirms that there is no necessity for all things to be unmade or self-originated; rather, some things might be made from others that were themselves unmade.

Lastly, we shall disprove the truth of this assertion—*that whatever substantially and really is, existed of itself from all eternity unmade*—in the following way. It would follow from that claim that not only **matter** and **unqualified atoms** (as the **Democritic** atheists <note>referring to followers of Democritus, who believed the world was made of nothing but atoms and empty space</note> suppose), but also **souls**, especially **human** souls, must have **existed** of **themselves** from **eternity unmade**. For no one can be so foolish <note>original: "sottish"</note> as to imagine that he himself—or that which thinks within him, his own soul or mind and personality—is not a real entity, while every clod of earth is considered one. 

It is certain that the mind can never be generated out of dead and senseless matter or body, nor result as a modification of it from **magnitudes**, **figures**, **locations**, and **motions**. Therefore, the soul must be a thing really distinct from matter: an **incorporeal substance** <term>incorporeal substance: a reality that exists but does not have a physical body</term>. The **Democritic atheists** are grossly deceived here, thinking that because the **forms** and **qualities** of **bodies** can be reduced to those aforementioned elements of matter—and therefore concluded to be no entities really distinct from the substance of matter, but only different modifications of it—that the same can be said of souls, including the **rational** soul. 

Therefore, if no substance or real entity could ever be brought out of non-existence into being, or be caused by anything else, then all human souls and personalities (as well as matter and atoms) must have existed not only from eternity without beginning, but also of themselves, independent of any other thing. 

But atheists are so repulsed by this eternity of human souls that they will not even admit their post-existence or immortality. They fear that if any living, understanding being should prove to be immortal, they could not sufficiently protect themselves against the possibility and danger of a God. Some theists, indeed, have asserted the *eternity of souls* <note>original Latin: "Æternitatem Animorum"</note>—not only the pre-existence, but also the eternity of all human minds along with the world. **Cicero** does this more than once; in his *Book of Divination*, he further declares: "*Our mind, because it has lived from all eternity and has associated with innumerable minds, sees all things that are in the nature of things*" <note>original Latin: "Animus quià vixit ab omni Æternitate, Versatusque est cum innumerabilibus Animis, omnia quæ in naturâ rerum sunt videt"</note>. And again: "*Since the minds of men ever were, and ever will be*" <note>original Latin: "Cum Animi hominum semper fuerint futurique sint"</note>. Nevertheless, none of these...

<header>Creation Out of Nothing Pre-Existing. Book I.</header>

These thinkers always maintained that **human minds** and their distinct **personalities** were all **self-originated**, existing independently of anything else as their **cause** or **origin**. However, it was demonstrated earlier from the **nature of knowledge and understanding**—which encompasses the **possibilities of all things** and therefore assumes **infinite power**—that there can be only **one mind, or understanding being, that is self-existent**. All other **minds** merely partake in that **one mind**. 

Therefore, it is hardly possible for anyone to seriously entertain the idea that their **own particular soul, mind, and personality**—and consequently all **human souls**—did not only **pre-exist** before their **respective bodies** and were from **eternity** without **beginning**, but also **existed by their own power**, **necessarily** and **independently** of anything else, even though they are now subject to the **laws of fate**. 

Therefore, if **human souls, minds, and personalities** are unquestionably **substantial things** and **truly distinct from matter** (which means they could not possibly be **generated out of it**), and if they did not **all exist from eternity** by **their own power, necessarily and independently**, it is certain that they must derive their whole being from **God**, or be **created** out of nothing <note>original Greek: "ἐκ μὴ ὄντων" (ek mē ontōn), meaning "out of things that do not exist"</note>, or out of **non-existence** by Him. And if **human souls** were unquestionably **created** in this way, it cannot reasonably be doubted that **matter** or **body** itself was **created** likewise out of **nothing**, or **caused** by **God**. For whatever power could **create one** thing **out of nothing** could **create** everything. Indeed, there is **really more substance**—that is, a **higher degree of being**—in **minds and souls** (which are **conscious, self-moving, and understanding beings**) than in **senseless matter or inactive mass**.

But because this **doctrine of a divine creation out of nothing pre-existing** faces significant prejudice, mainly because it is generally taken for granted that none of the **pagan theists** (who are supposed to have relied only on the simple **light of nature**) ever acknowledged such a **creative power** in **God**, or believed that **God** was the **cause** of any **substance**, we must of **necessity** declare here that this is a great **mistake**, however common it may be. 

For instance, in his dialogue *The Sophist*, **Plato** defined **efficient** or **effective power** in general as: "a power or causality whereby that which was not before was afterwards made to be" <note>original Greek: "Ποιητικὸν πᾶσαν ἔφαμεν εἶναι δύναμιν, ἥτις ἂν αἰτία γίγνηται τοῖς μὴ πρότερον οὖσιν ὕστερον γίγνεσθαι"</note>. After dividing this **efficiency** into **divine** and **human**, he immediately adds concerning the former: "Shall we not then say that all animals and other things were, by the divine craftsmanship alone, made to be after they had not been?" <note>original Greek: "Ζῶα δὴ πάντα, &c. μῶν ἄλλις τιτὸς ἢ Θεὸς δημιουγὸν φήσομεν ἔχειν ὕστερον γίγνεσθαι..."</note>. 

From this, at least, it is certain that **Plato** did not at all question the **possibility of a thing being made out of nothing** in this **sense**—that is, brought into **being after it had not been by a divine power**. Some might think he meant this only regarding the **first physical structure of animals**, where everything (including **souls**) might still have been **made out of pre-existing matter**. However, we shall further add what he declares in his *Timaeus* concerning the **soul**:

->as for the soul, which we are now mentioning later...<-

<header>CHAPTER IV. Acknowledged by Philosophers.</header>

<note>The text begins with a quote from Plato's *Timaeus* (34c), discussing how we mistakenly speak of the soul as if it were created after the body.</note>
"Let us attempt to say how God devised the soul; he did not leave the elder to be ruled by the younger, but he established the soul as prior to and older than the body in both its origin and its excellence, to be a mistress and ruler over that which is to be ruled." <note>original Greek: ἐπιχειρῶμεν λέγειν, ὅπως ἐμηχανήσατο καὶ ὁ θεὸς νεωτέραν, ᾗ γῆν ἂν ἄρξασθαι πρεσβύτερον ὑπὸ νεωτέρας εἴασεν, ὁ δὲ δὴ γενέσει καὶ ἀρετῇ προτέραν καὶ πρεσβυτέραν ψυχὴν σώματος, ὡς δεσπότιν καὶ ἄρξουσαν ἀρξομένῳ συνεστήσατο</note> *That God did not make it after the body, and younger than it, since it was not fit that the elder should be ruled or governed by the younger; but he made the soul before the body, older than it, and superior to it, in respect of both time and dignity.* This notion is further pursued by him in his **Tenth** book *Of Laws*: "Therefore we would have spoken most rightly, properly, truly, and perfectly if we said that the soul was created for us before the body; and that the body is second and later, being ruled by the soul, which rules by its nature." <note>original Greek: ὀρθῶς ἄρα καὶ κυρίως ἀληθεστάτα τε καὶ τελεώτατα εἰρηκότες ἂν ἦμεν, ψυχὴν μὲν προτέραν γεγονέναι σώματος ἡμῖν· σῶμα δὲ δεύτερόν τε καὶ ὕστερον ψυχῆς ἀρχούσης ἀρχόμενον καὶ φύσιν</note> From this, he also draws this corollary: "If the soul appears older than the body, then the things belonging to the soul must also be older than those of the body. Therefore, character, habits, wills, reasonings, true opinions, cares, and memories must have existed before the length, breadth, and depth of bodies, if indeed the soul is older than the body." <note>original Greek: ὡς εἰ ἡ ψυχὴ φανείη πρεσβύτερα σώματος· ὅσα δὲ τὰ ψυχῆς τῶν τε σώματος ἔσοιτο πρεσβύτερα· τρόποι καὶ ἤθη καὶ βουλήσεις καὶ λογισμοὶ καὶ δόξαι ἀληθεῖς, ἐπιμέλειάι τε καὶ μνῆμαι, πρότερα μήκους σωμάτων καὶ πλάτους καὶ βάθους, εἴη γεγονότα ἄν, εἴπερ καὶ ψυχὴ σώματος</note> 

From this, it is plain that *Plato's* first *production of souls by God* could not have come out of any *pre-existing body or matter*. He affirms them to be before not only this or that particular body, but before all matter whatsoever—before *length, breadth,* and *depth*. This may be further confirmed because in his ***Sophist***, he plainly condemns the opinion of some "that the soul itself possessed some kind of body," <note>original Greek: τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτὴν σῶμά τι κεκτῆσθαι</note> and he often elsewhere declares the soul to be incorporeal. 

It is also certain that not only *Plato*, but all those pagan philosophers who asserted the incorporeal nature and immortality of human souls, could not possibly conceive of souls being made out of *pre-existent matter*. Instead, they must have been made "out of nothing," <note>original Greek: ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων (ex ouk ontōn)</note> because they were not *eternal* but had a *newness of being* (as *Plato* himself seemed to suppose). Or, if they were conceived to be *eternal* (which was the opinion of most of the *later Platonists* <note>Often referred to as Neoplatonists, who believed the soul's existence was an eternal emanation from the divine.</note>), they were still thought to have derived their whole *substance* from the *Deity* and always to depend upon it, just as *eternal light* would depend upon an *eternal sun*. 

*Plutarch* and his followers are the only exceptions here. They would not have *souls made out of nothing by God*, nor yet out of *pre-existing corporeal matter* (since souls are incorporeal). Instead, they believed souls were made out of a strange *mixture of the substance of God himself* with the *substance of a certain disorderly soul, which was self-existent and uncreated*. We have already spoken of this. 

But it is undeniably evident that the *genuine Platonists* universally supposed that one *substance* might be *caused* by another and derive its whole being from it. This is clear because their *second divine <term>hypostasis</term>* <note>original: "Hypostasis"; in this context, it refers to a distinct substance or person within the divine hierarchy.</note> or substance (though *eternal*) was, according to them, *derived from* or *begotten by their first*. Likewise, their *third hypostasis* or substance was *produced from both the first and second*. All other inferior levels of being, such as the *particular souls of demons and men*, were derived from that whole trinity of divine hypostases.

He explains that while most Platonists believed souls were created by God (either in time or as an eternal emanation), Plutarch held a unique view that souls were mixed from God's substance and a pre-existing "disorderly soul."</summary>

<header>Matter is not considered "unmade" by all. Book I.</header>

<margin>
*Thus Hierocles in Photius:* <note>original Greek: δημιουργὸν Θεὸν προϋφίσησιν ὁ Πλάτων πάσης ἐμφανές τε καὶ ἀφανοῦς διακοσμήσεως, ἐκ μηδενὸς προϋποκειμένης γεγονυμένης</note> "Plato posits God as the creator of all visible and invisible order, produced from no pre-existing matter." <note>original Latin: Plato censuit Mundum à Deo, ex nullâ priùs existente Materiâ, productum, &c.</note> *Plato believed the world was produced by God from no previously existing matter, etc.*
</margin>

[hy]postases jointly concurring. And as for matter or body itself, it is also certain that Plotinus, Porphyry, Iamblichus, Hierocles, and other Platonists expressly denied it to have been <term>unmade</term> <note>original: ἀγέννητον</note> or self-existent. They conceived it to have derived its whole *being* from the Deity, who accordingly is styled by Proclus "the ineffable cause of matter" <note>original: ἀῤῥήτῳ αἰτίᾳ τῆς ὕλης</note>. In the same way, we have already shown that according to the Chaldean Oracles, matter itself was also *caused* or *produced* by the Deity. To this purpose, Proclus cites this verse: <note>original: Ἔνθεν ἄδην θρώσκει γένεσις πολυποικίλης ὕλης</note> "From there (that is, *from the Deity*) the generation of multiform matter leaps forth abundantly." The meter here requires that it should be read as "abundantly" <note>original Greek: ἄδην (aden)</note> and not "invisibly" <note>original Greek: ἀέδην (aeden)</note>, as it is in Proclus's copy. 

Furthermore, Iamblichus has recorded in his *Mysteries* that Hermes and the old Egyptian theologians likewise held that matter was not <term>unmade</term> <note>original: ἀγέννητον</note>—that is, self-existent or underived from the Deity—but was instead *caused* by it. From this, Proclus concludes it is probable that Plato held the same persuasion, as Orpheus had done before him; Orpheus is supposed to have derived this, along with other things, from the Egyptians. 

It is true that many of these philosophers asserted that matter, souls, and the whole *world* were *eternal* without a beginning. Consequently, they believed they were not *created* "out of nothing" <note>original: ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων</note> in that stricter sense—meaning out of a state of not existing at a specific point in time. Nevertheless, they still supposed that these things received their whole being from the Deity and depended on it just as much as if they had once not existed and were afterward *made* by it. For if a power gives any substance its *whole being*—even from *eternity*, so that it never *was not*—that same power could unquestionably have produced it "out of nothing" <note>original: ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων</note> (or out of a prior non-existence) if we were to suppose that it once had not existed.

We have now sufficiently disproved the truth of that assertion, "Nothing can be made out of nothing," in its atheistic sense. That sense claims that *nothing which previously was* not *could afterwards possibly be made to be.* This atheist argument is not usually extended to "accidental things" <note>properties or characteristics, like color or shape</note> and modifications, but is restricted only to "substantials." They claim that no substance whatsoever could have a newness of being or be caused by any other substance. Instead, they argue that whatever substantial thing exists anywhere in the world has *existed of itself* from eternity, independent of anything else, and that only different modifications are ever *made* or *produced*. 

This same assertion has also sometimes been expressed another way: *Nothing can be made except out of pre-existing substance.* The meaning here is that nothing can be made except for new accidental modifications of what was already substantially there. In this view, no *substance* itself is "makeable" or "producible" by any other substance, neither in *time* (so as to have a beginning of being) nor even from *eternity*. Because atheists and some others take it for granted that there is no other substance besides *body* or *matter*, they further limit the meaning of that proposition in this way: *Nothing can be made except out of pre-existing matter*; that is, *nothing can be made, but out...*

<summary>Cudworth argues that many ancient philosophers, including Platonists and Egyptians, believed matter was created by God rather than being self-existent. He challenges the atheistic maxim that "nothing comes from nothing" by distinguishing between the creation of substance and the mere modification of existing matter.</summary>

# CHAP. IV. Plutarch’s Spurious Theism.

...of corporeal substance pre-existing. This is an **Idol of the Cave** <note>original: *Idolum Specus* — a term coined by Francis Bacon to describe errors of judgment arising from an individual's particular biases or limited experiences</note> (if I may use that language), which in all probability had its first origin chiefly from men measuring the extent of all power by their own production of artificial things. 

Because, forsooth, a carpenter or architect cannot make a house except out of pre-existing timber, bricks, and stones; nor a tailor a garment except out of pre-existing cloth; nor a cook puddings or pies except out of pre-existing materials or ingredients; they assume that no power whatsoever—not even that of Almighty God—can extend any further than to the new modifying of pre-existent matter, but not to the production or causing of any substance itself. 

We shall in the next place make it appear that, were this assertion true—that no substance or real entity which once was not could be caused or produced—it would nonetheless, of the two, challenge Atheism more than Theism. (It is possible for falsehoods, though not for truths, to disagree with one another.) This is because the Atheists actually bring more "out of nothing," or non-existence, than the Theists do; therefore, they ought not to make this an objection against Theism. 

For although according to true and genuine theology, God (or a perfect being) is supposed to be the only necessary self-existent thing and the cause of all other substance, and consequently to have produced all imperfect things—not only souls, but also matter itself—**out of nothing** <note>original Greek: ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων</note> or a preceding non-existence, yet there is a "latitude" or range of belief within Theism due to the weakness of human understandings. 

Wherefore, there are some who, though influenced by that **Idol of the Cave** or imprisoned in it—the idea that nothing can possibly be made except out of pre-existing matter by modifying it—do nonetheless devoutly worship a Deity according to their notion of it. They see Him as a perfectly understanding being who was not "made." Though He is not the creator of matter, He is the maker of the whole world out of it and the supreme governor of the same. They thus suppose two principles in the universe: an active one and a passive one, God and matter. 

Besides this, it is not impossible for others to think that although matter or body is not the only substance and human souls are **incorporeal**, the substance of these souls was not created out of nothing any more than that of body. Instead, they believe souls were made either out of some pre-existing common soul (serving as their "intelligible matter") or out of the substance of the Deity itself; or else they existed of themselves from eternity, unmade. Yet, these people may nevertheless acknowledge one supreme, self-existent understanding being who, though neither the creator of matter nor of souls, is the supreme governor and orderer of all. 

It is certain that Plutarch’s God was no better than this; yet that pagan was notwithstanding a devoutly religious man in his own way, as well as a sincere moralist. Such a version of Theism or theology—though not genuine and pure, but rather imperfect and **mongrel** <note>meaning a hybrid or impure form</note> things—would perhaps be little less troublesome and uneasy to the Atheists than the true kind. 

Thus we have shown that this principle—that nothing can come out of nothing, or be made otherwise than out of pre-existing substance or matter—is indeed contradictory to true and genuine theology. However, it is not absolutely inconsistent with all manners of religion, as there are certain spurious or imperfect forms of Theism built upon this foundation. But now on the...

On the contrary, we shall make it manifest that this very principle used by atheists is, in truth and reality, contradictory to all forms of atheism and destructive to it. This is because atheists **universally claim that real entities and substantial things are generated and corrupted**—that is, produced out of nothing or non-existence and reduced to nothing again. For they claim that everything in existence, except for the bare substance of matter (which to them is either no specific thing at all, or else nothing but mere bulk or a divisible magnitude that occupies space), comes out of nothing and goes to nothing. 

Thus does Aristotle, in a passage cited earlier, describe the atheist view: "For there are some who say that nothing is uncreated, but that all things are generated" <note>original Greek: εἰσὶ γάρ τινες, οἳ φασιν οὐδὲν ἀγέννητον εἶναι τῶν πραγμάτων, ἀλλὰ πάντα γίνεσθαι</note>. He later explains their meaning more distinctly: "That all other things are generated and in flux, and nothing is stable; but that there is only one thing which remains, from which all these other things are naturally transformed" <note>original Greek: τὰ μὲν ἄλλα γίνεσθαί τε καὶ ῥεῖν, εἶναι δὲ παγίως οὐδέν· ἓν δέ τι μόνον ὑπομένειν, ἐξ οὗ ταῦτα πάντα μετασχηματίζεσθαι πέφυκεν</note>. This implies that these things are perpetually brought out of nothing and reduced to nothing.

Aristotle further adds that they affirmed this "one thing" (namely, matter) to be the only substance and uncreated from eternity. However, they believed all other things whatsoever were merely "passions, states, and dispositions of it" <note>original Greek: πάθη καὶ ἕξεις καὶ διαθέσεις</note> and were "generated and corrupted infinitely" <note>original Greek: γίνεσθαι καὶ φθείρεσθαι ἀπειράκις</note>. In other words, they believed these things are produced out of nothing or non-existence and reduced back to nothing without end.

This is undoubtedly the true meaning of a passage in the tenth book of Plato’s *Laws* <note>original: *De Legibus*</note>, which was misunderstood by Latin translators. In presenting the atheist hypothesis of the system of the universe, Plato reveals their "grand secret" <note>original Latin: *Grand Arcanum*</note> and what they considered "the wisest and most mysterious of all doctrines" <note>original Greek: σοφώτατον ἁπάντων λόγων</note>: "Certain men say that all things are being made, have been made, and will be made; some by nature, some by art, and some by fortune or chance" <note>original Greek: λέγουσί που τινὲς ὡς πάντα ἐστὶ τὰ πράγματα γινόμενα καὶ γενόμενα, καὶ γενησόμενα· τὰ μὲν φύσει, τὰ δὲ τέχνῃ, τὰ δὲ διὰ τύχης</note>. 

Unquestionably, Plato's phrase "certain men affirm that all things are generated or made, etc." is the very same as Aristotle’s statement: "there are some who say that nothing is unmade, but that all things are generated." Perhaps Aristotle's comment was even taken from Plato's. Nevertheless, it must be understood in the way Aristotle later explains: that this applies to everything except for the bare substance of matter. 

Therefore, it is certain that one of two things must be true:
1. Either there is no real entity in the whole world besides the bare substance of matter—meaning there is nothing but divisible and separable physical extension, or magnitude that occupies space. Consequently, this would mean that life, thought <note>original: *cogitation*</note>, sense, consciousness, reason, understanding, and all our own minds and personalities are not real entities.
2. Or else, according to the atheist hypothesis, real entities are produced out of nothing and reduced to nothing again.

### CHAPTER 4: Their Argument Retorted <note>original: Retorted; in this context, it means turning an opponent's argument back against them.</note>

Theists suppose all the *greatest perfections* in the universe, such as *life* and *understanding*, to have been *eternal* and *unmade* within a *perfect being*—the *Deity*. These were neither brought out of *nothing* or *non-existence*, nor can they be *reduced* to *nothing*. Only *imperfect beings* were *made out of nothing* or *produced out of non-existence* by this one *perfect being* or *Deity*. 

The *atheists*, on the contrary, suppose the *lowest* and most *imperfect* of all beings—*matter*, *bulk*, or *divisible* and *resisting extension*—to be the *only self-existent* and *unmade thing*. They conclude that all the *greatest perfections* in the universe—*life, thought <note>original: cogitation</note>*, and *understanding*—are *made out of nothing* or *non-existence*, and are also reduced to *nothing* again. 

Indeed, the *Hylozoic <note>original: Hylozoick; referring to the belief that all matter possesses life</note> atheists*, being somewhat aware of this *inconvenience* of making all *life* and *understanding* come *out of nothing*, argued that there must necessarily be some *fundamental life* and *perception* that is not *accidental* but *substantial*, and which was never *generated* and cannot be *destroyed <note>original: corrupted</note>*. They have therefore attributed a kind of *life* and *perception* to all *matter* as such. 

Despite this, even these thinkers—insofar as they deny that *matter* has *animal sense* and *consciousness*—suppose that all *animal life* or *sense*, and *conscious understanding*, are *generated* and *destroyed*, *produced out of nothing* and *reduced to nothing* again. 

Neither can *life, thought*, and *understanding* be considered among the *modes* <note>In philosophy, a "mode" is a temporary state or quality of a substance, like its shape or position, rather than the substance itself.</note> of *matter* (that is, of *magnitude* or *divisible* and <term>antitypous</term> <note>original: antitypous; meaning "impenetrable" or "resisting," the property of matter that prevents two bodies from occupying the same space</note> *extension*), since they can be *conceived* without matter. Conversely, *modes* cannot be conceived without their *substance*. Standing, sitting, and walking cannot be *conceived* without a *body*, and one that is properly *organized* too; therefore, they are *nothing* but different *modes* of such a *body*. 

When a *human body* that was *standing* later *sits* or *walks*, no one thinks this is a *miraculous production* of some *new real entity out of nothing*. Nor is it when the same *matter* that was *square* or *cubic* is made *spherical* or *cylindrical*. But when there is *life* and *understanding* where there was none before, then unquestionably a new *real entity* has been *produced*. 

But the *Democritic* and *Epicurean atheists* themselves, following the *tenor* of the *atomic physics <note>original: atomick physiology</note>*, acknowledge no other *modes* of *matter* or *body* except more or less *magnitude* of *parts, shape <note>original: figure</note>, position <note>original: site</note>, motion*, or *rest*. And on this very basis, they reject *qualities* <note>This refers to "secondary qualities" like color or heat, which atomists argued weren't real things in themselves.</note> when considered as *entities* really distinct from these *modes*. They do this because if these qualities were generated or altered, they would be *real entities made out of nothing*, or without a *cause*. Therefore, they *resolve* these *qualities* into mechanism and fancy. 

However, *life, thought*, and *understanding* are things that have more *real entity* in them and can in no way be *explained <note>original: salved</note>* by *mechanism* and *fancy*. Therefore, they are undoubtedly not *modes* of *matter* or *body*, but *attributes* of another kind of *substance* that is *incorporeal <note>not consisting of matter; spiritual or non-physical</note>*. All *thinking <note>original: cogitative</note> beings*, especially *human souls* and *personalities*, are unquestionably *substantial things*. Yet, the *atheists* bring these—and consequently *themselves*—out of *nothing* or *non-existence*, and *reduce* them to *nothing* again. 

The *conclusion* is that these very *atheists*, who argue against *theists* that *nothing can be made out of nothing*, do themselves bring *all* things out of *nothing* or *non-existence* and perpetually *reduce* them to *nothing* again. According to their *principles*, since once there was

no life, nor *understanding* at all in the universe, so may there be none again. Those who deny a God—because they believe no *creative power* can belong to *anything*—nevertheless attribute to *matter* (though it is a merely *passive*, *sluggish*, and *inactive* thing) a creative power to produce substantial things (such as *human souls* and *personalities*) out of *nothing*. In this way, that formidable argument of the *atheists*—that there can be no God because *nothing* can be made out of *nothing*—is not only proved to be false, but is also turned back <note>original: Retorted</note> against these atheists themselves. They are the ones bringing all things, except for *senseless* and featureless <note>original: unqualified</note> *matter*, out of *nothing*.

We have now declared, first, in what sense this proposition is unquestionably true: that *nothing can be made out of nothing, or come from nothing*—namely, *causally*. This means that *nothing which did not exist before could afterward be made without a cause, and a sufficient cause*. Or, more particularly, in these three ways:

1. First, that *nothing which did not exist before could afterward be brought into being by itself, or without an efficient cause*. 
2. Secondly, that *nothing which once was not could be made or produced efficiently by anything which did not have at least equal perfection within it, and a sufficient active or productive power*. Consequently, no *new substance* can be *made* except by a *perfect being*, which alone is capable of producing substance from itself <term>substantially emanative</term>. 
3. Thirdly and lastly, that when things are *made* out of *pre-existing matter*—as in artificial productions and natural births—*there can be no new real entity produced, but only different modifications* of what already *substantially* existed. The *material cause* itself *efficiently produces nothing*. 

This was how this axiom was understood by *Cicero*: that *nothing* could be *made* out of *nothing*—namely, *causally*. In his book *On Fate* <note>original: De Fato</note>, he rebukes *Epicurus* for trying to avoid *fate* and establish *freedom of the will* by that absurd fiction of *atoms swerving uncertainly from the perpendicular*.

> "Nor even as things stand is there any reason why Epicurus should dread Fate and seek protection from atoms, leading them out of their path; and at one time take on two insoluble problems: one, that something might happen without a cause, from which it would follow that something is made out of nothing; which neither he, nor any natural philosopher <term>physiologer</term>, would approve." <note>original Latin: "Nec cum haec ita sint, est causa, cur Epicurus Fatum extimescat, & ab Atomis petat praesidium, easque De Via deducat; & uno tempore suscipiat res duas inenodabiles, Unam ut fine Causâ fiat aliquid, ex quo existat, ut De Nihilo quippiam fiat; quod nec ipse, nec cuiquam Physico placet."</note>

There is, for all that, no reason why *Epicurus* should be so afraid of *fate* and seek refuge in *atoms* (supposing them in their *infinite descents* to *swerve uncertainly from the perpendicular* and laying this as a foundation for *freedom of the will*). By doing so, he plunged himself at once into two inextricable difficulties. The first was the supposition of *something being made without a cause*—or, what is the same thing, out of *nothing*—a thing that will neither be allowed by any *natural philosopher* <term>physiologer</term>, nor could *Epicurus* himself be pleased or satisfied with it. The reason for this is that it was a fundamental principle of the *atomist philosophy* that *nothing* (in this sense) could be *made out of nothing*. 

Furthermore, we have in the next place declared in what other sense this proposition—that *nothing can be made out of nothing*—is false. This occurs when "out of nothing" is not taken *causally*, but as signifying the *starting point* <note>original: Terminus From which</note>. In this false sense, the claim is that *nothing* can be *made* out of a previous state of non-existence; that no *real entity* or *substance* which did not exist before could, by *any power whatsoever*, be afterwards brought into being. Or that *nothing*...

### CHAP. IV. From Nothing out of Nothing.

...thing can possibly be **made**, except out of **something pre-existing**, by the new **modification** of that thing. And it appears from the writings of **Cicero** that the **true** and **genuine sense** of this proposition, *From nothing, nothing is made* <note>original: De Nihilo nihil fit</note> (according to the minds of those **ancient natural philosophers** <note>original: Physiologers</note> who laid so much stress upon it), was not that **nothing** could, by any power whatsoever, be brought out of **non-existence** into **being**. Rather, it meant only that **nothing could be made without a cause**. Nor did they mean by **cause** the **material** cause only; in this sense, as if **nothing** could possibly be **made** except out of **pre-existing matter**. **Epicurus** was criticized <note>original: taxed</note> by **Cicero** for introducing his **third motion of atoms**, or **the swerve of the principles** <note>original: Clinamen Principiorum</note>, **out of nothing**, or **without an efficient cause**. Indeed, all motion was also considered by those **atomic atheists** to be, in this sense, **from nothing**. 

Nevertheless, we have also shown that if this proposition, **nothing out of nothing**, were true in that **atheistic sense** (as directed against a **Deity**), it would challenge **atheism** itself more than it does **theism**. This is because atheists claim to generate and corrupt all things (except for the substance of matter)—including all **life**, **sense**, **understanding**, **human souls**, **minds**, and **personalities**. They produce these things, and consequently themselves, out of **nothing**, and resolve them all back into **nothing** again. We shall now, in the third and last place, make it manifest that the **atheists** do not only bring **real entities** and **substantial things** out of **nothing** in the second sense—that is, out of an **antecedent non-existence** (which is a thing possible only to **God**, or a **perfect being**)—but also that they bring them out of **nothing** in the **absolutely impossible sense**: that is, they suppose them to be **made without a cause**, or **nothing to be the cause of something**.

But we must prepare the way for this by setting down, first, a brief and concise summary of the whole **atheistic hypothesis**. Those atheists who contend that **nothing can be made** except **new accidents** or **modifications** of **pre-existing substance**, take it for granted that there is no other substance besides **body** or **matter**. They conclude, accordingly, that **nothing can be made** except out of **pre-existing matter** or **body**. And then they add to this that **matter** being the only **substance**, the only **unmade self-existent thing**, whatever else is in the world besides the bare **substance of this matter** was **made out of it** or **produced by it**. 

So, there are these three things contained in the **atheistic hypothesis**: 
1. First, that **no substance can be made** or **caused** by anything else, but only new **modifications**. 
2. Secondly, that **matter** or **body is the only substance**, and therefore whatever is made is **made** out of **pre-existing matter**. 
3. Thirdly and lastly, that whatever else there is in the whole world besides the substance of matter is **made** or **generated out of matter**. 

And now we shall demonstrate the **absolute impossibility** of this **atheistic hypothesis** from that very principle of the **ancient natural philosophers**: that **nothing can be made out of nothing** in its **true sense**. This hypothesis not only brings **real entities** and **substantial things** out of an **antecedent non-existence** (though nothing but an **infinitely perfect being** can create in this way), but it also **produces** them without **a cause**.

First, therefore, when they affirm **Matter** to be the **Only Substance**, and all things else whatsoever to be **Made** out of **that** alone, they hereby plainly **suppose** all things to be **made without an efficient cause** <term>Efficient Cause: the active agent or force that brings something into being, as opposed to the material it is made from.</term>. This is to bring them out of **nothing** in an **impossible sense**. For although it is not **true** that **nothing** can be **made** except out of **pre-existing matter** (meaning that **God** himself, if he is assumed to exist, could in this respect do no more than a carpenter or tailor does)—I say, although it is not **universally true** that everything which is **made** must have a **material cause** (so that the **four types of causes** <note>original: "Quaternio of Causes"; the material, formal, efficient, and final causes in Aristotelian logic</note> in **Logic** are not to be applied to all things caused whatsoever)—yet it is certain that **nothing** which once was not could **possibly** be **made without an efficient cause**. 

Therefore, if there is anything **made** which did not exist before, there must of **necessity** be some other **substance existing** besides **matter** as the **efficient cause** of it. This is because **matter** alone could not **make** anything; just as **marble** cannot make a **statue**, nor **timber** and **stones** a **house**, nor **cloth** a **garment**. This is our first **demonstration** of the **impossibility** of the **atheistic hypothesis**: it supposes all things besides the bare substance of **matter** to be **made** out of **matter** alone, without any other **active principle or Deity**—or to be **made without an efficient cause**, which is to bring them from **nothing** in an **impossible sense**. To this may be added as an appendix: whereas the **Democritic** and **Epicurean atheists** admit no other **efficient causality** in **nature** than only **local motion** <note>original: "Local Motion"; movement from one place to another in space</note>, and allow no **self-moving power** to **matter** or **body** (their only substance), they thereby make all the **motion** in the whole world to be without a **cause**. It would be **action from nothing** without any **subject** or **agent**, and the **efficiency** of all things without an **efficient [cause]**.

In the next place, even if we were so generous as to grant the **atomic atheists** **motion without a cause**, or permit **Strato** and the **hylozoic atheists** <term>Hylozoic: from the Greek 'hyle' (matter) and 'zoe' (life); those who believe that matter is inherently alive or possesses a soul.</term> to attribute a **self-moving power** to **matter**, we still affirm that this **matter** and **motion** together could not **possibly produce** any new **real entity** which did not exist before. **Matter**, as such, **efficiently causes nothing**, and **motion** only changes the **modifications** of **matter**, such as its **shape**, **location**, **position**, and the **arrangement of parts**. 

Therefore, if **matter** as such has no **animal sense** and **conscious understanding** essentially belonging to it (which no **atheists** have yet had the impudence to assert), then no **motion** or **modification** of **matter**, and no **structure of atoms**, can **possibly** produce **sense** and **understanding**, **soul** and **mind**. This would be to bring **something** out of **nothing** in that **impossible sense**, or to suppose **something** to be **made** by itself without a **cause**. This may serve also as a **refutation** of those **imperfect** and **false** <note>original: "spurious"</note> **theists** who will not allow **Almighty God** (whether they suppose Him to be **corporeal** <note>possessing a physical body</note> or **incorporeal**) the **power of making** anything except out of **pre-existing matter** by newly **modifying** it—just as a **carpenter** makes a **house** out of **pre-existing timber** and **stone**, or a **tailor** a **garment** out of **pre-existing cloth**. ### CHAP. IV. and Mind, without a Cause.

If they cannot result from any **modifications** or **contextures** <note>original: "contextures"; the way things are woven or joined together</note> of matter, it would plainly follow from this that God could not **possibly** make **animals**, or **produce sense** and **understanding**, **souls** and **minds**. Yet, these **theists** <note>believers in a God who created the world</note> suppose him to have done exactly that. Therefore, they ought in reason to acknowledge him not only to be the maker of new **modifications** of **matter** (as a carpenter who merely builds a house out of pre-existing wood), but also the creator of **real entities** distinct from matter itself.

And this was the very doctrine (as we have already declared) of the most ancient **atomic physiologers** <term>Atomic Physiologers: early Greek philosophers, like Democritus or Epicurus, who studied nature through the theory of atoms.</term>. Their view was not that everything whatsoever might be **made** out of **pre-existing matter**. On the contrary, they held that in all **natural generations**, there is no **real entity** produced out of the **matter** which was not already in it, but only new **modifications**. Consequently, because **souls** and **minds** are not mere **modifications** of **matter** in respect to magnitude, figure, position, and motion, they could never be produced out of it. If they were, they would necessarily have to come from **nothing**—that is, be made either by **themselves** without a **cause**, or without a **sufficient cause**. 

It has also been noted previously from **Aristotle** how the old **atheistic materialists** were challenged by those **Italic philosophers** <note>the "Italic" school refers to Pythagoras and his followers</note>. The challenge was this: nothing which was not already in **matter** (aside from its **modifications**) could **possibly** be produced out of it, because **nothing can come out of nothing**. Consequently, in all **natural generations** and **corruptions** <note>the process of things being born or decaying</note>, there is no **real entity** made or **destroyed**. 

The atheists endeavored to evade this argument without denying the words of that proposition, in this manner: "wherefore they think that nothing is either generated or destroyed, since this sort of nature is always preserved, just as we do not say Socrates is generated when he becomes musical or handsome" <note>original Greek: διὰ τίθετο ἔτε γίγνεσθαι ἔτε ἀπόλλυσθαι, ὡς τῆς τοιαύτης φύσεως ἀεὶ οὔσης, ὥσπερ ἔ ὴ ἔ σωφροσύνην</note>. Their point was that there is indeed **nothing generated** or **corrupted** (in a certain **sense**), because the same **substance** of **matter** always remains, being never made nor **destroyed**. Just as men do not say that **Socrates** is "made" when he becomes **musical** or **handsome**, nor "**destroyed**" when he loses these **dispositions**—because the **subject Socrates** existed before and still remains—so too is no **substantial thing** or **real entity** in the world **made** or **destroyed** in this sense. This is because **matter**, which is the **substance** of all, perpetually remains. 

All other things whatsoever are but "passions, habits, and dispositions" <note>original Greek: πάθη ἔ ἕξεις ἔ διαθέσεις</note> of that matter, just as "musicality" or "unmusicality" are in respect to **Socrates**. This is the same as saying that all things besides **matter**, being merely **accidents** of it, are **generated** out of it and **corruptible** back into it, without the production of any **real entity** out of **nothing**, or the reduction of any into **nothing**, so long as the **substance** of **matter** (which is the only **real entity**) remains always the same. 

Therefore, though **life, sense,** and **understanding**, and all **souls** and **minds**, are **generated** out of **matter**, it does not follow (in their view) that any **real entity** is made or **produced**, because these are **nothing** but **accidents** and **modifications** of **matter**. This was the **subterfuge** of the old **Hylopathian atheists** <term>Hylopathian Atheists: those who believe that matter (hyle) itself has the capacity for qualities or "passions" like life and thought.</term>.

# Life and Understanding, Book I.

[Things are] generated and corrupted without the producing of any *real entity* out of *nothing*, and without the reducing of any into *nothing*; because the *substance* still remains entirely the same. But the atheists, taking it for granted that there is no other *substance* besides *body* or *matter*, therefore falsely suppose that what is really *incorporeal substance* <note>original: "incorporeal"; not composed of matter; spiritual</note>—or else its *attributes*, *properties*, and *modes* <term>Modes: the specific ways or states in which a substance exists, such as a particular shape, position, or arrangement.</term>—are merely the *accidents of matter* <term>Accidents: in philosophy, these are non-essential properties or characteristics that can change without changing the nature of the substance itself.</term>. Consequently, they conclude that these can be generated out of matter without the production of any *real entity* out of *nothing*. 

We say, therefore, that it does not follow simply because the same *numerical matter* (for example, a *piece of wax*) may be successively made spherical, cubical, cylindrical, pyramidal, or any other *figure*; or because the same man may successively *stand*, *sit*, *kneel*, and *walk*—both without the production of anything out of *nothing*. Nor does it follow because a heap of stones, bricks, mortar, and timber, lying together in a disorganized and confused mess, may be made into a stately palace without the *miraculous creation* of any *real entity* out of *nothing*. It does not follow that the same can be affirmed of everything else besides the bare *substance* of *matter*—namely *life* and *understanding*, *soul* and *mind*. Atheists claim that even though there is no such thing in *matter* itself, the production of them out of *matter* would not be the production of *something* out of *nothing*. 

One ground for this mistake has been that men do not rightly consider what the *accidents of a substance* are, and that they are indeed *nothing* but its *modes*. Now, a *mode* is something that cannot possibly be conceived without that of which it is a mode. For example, *standing*, *sitting*, *kneeling*, and *walking* cannot be conceived without an *organized body*, and therefore they are only *modes* of it. But *life* and *thought* <note>original: "cogitation"</note> may be clearly understood without a *body* or anything regarding *extension* <term>Extension: the physical property of taking up space (having length, breadth, and thickness).</term>. Indeed, a *thought* cannot be conceived as having a certain *length*, *breadth*, and *thickness*, nor can it be *hewn* and *sliced* into many *pieces*—which, if laid together like *small chips*, would reconstruct the entirety of that whole *thought*. 

From this, it ought to be concluded that *thought* is not an *accident* or *mode* of *matter* or *bulky extension*, but a *mode* or *attribute* of another *substance* that is *really* distinct from *matter*, or *incorporeal*. Indeed, there is *nothing* else clearly conceivable by us in *body* or *bulky extension* except for more or less *magnitude of parts*, *figures*, *position* <note>original: "site"</note>, *motion*, or *rest*. All the *different bodies* in the whole *world* are only various *combinations* or *syllables* made up of these few *letters*. But no amount of *magnitudes*, *figures*, *positions*, and *motions* can possibly spell or compose *life* and *sense*, *thought* and *understanding*, as if they were its *syllables*. Therefore, to suppose these are generated out of *matter* is plainly to suppose some *real entity* to be brought out of *nothing*, or *something* to be made without a *cause*—which is *impossible*.

But what has principally confirmed men in this error is the matter of *sensible qualities* and *forms*, as they are commonly <note>original: "vulgarly"</note> conceived to be distinct *entities* from those previously mentioned *modifications of matter* (in respect to magnitude of parts, figure, position, motion, or rest). # CHAP. IV. No Accidents of Matter.

[...things are] generated and corrupted, there seems to be no reason why the same might not also be acknowledged concerning *life, sense, thought* <note>original: "cogitation"</note>, and *understanding*—that these are but *qualities* or *accidents of matter* as well (though of a different kind) and consequently may be generated out of it without the *making of any real thing out of nothing*. 

But the *Democritic* and *Epicurean atheists* themselves have, based on the principles of *atomic philosophy*, sufficiently refuted and corrected this mistake concerning *sensible qualities* <term>Sensible qualities: properties like color, heat, or smell that we perceive through our senses, which the atomists argued were not in the objects themselves but in the mind.</term>. They rejected and banished them all, as being conceived to be *entities really distinct* from the previously mentioned *modifications of matter*—and for this very reason: because the *generation* of them would, upon this supposition, be the *production of something out of nothing*, or without a *cause*. They concluded, therefore, that these qualities are really nothing else but *mechanism*, or different *modifications of matter* in respect to the *size* <note>original: "magnitude"</note> *of parts, shape* <note>original: "figure"</note>, *position* <note>original: "site"</note>, and *motion* or *rest*. They only cause different *fancies* <note>original: "phancies"; mental perceptions or appearances</note> and *apparitions* within us. 

And in truth, this common opinion of the *real qualities* of bodies seems to have no other origin than people mistaking their own *fancies, passions*, and *feelings* <note>original: "affections"</note> for things really existing in the objects outside of them. For just as *sensible qualities* are thought to be things distinct from the aforementioned *modifications of matter*, so they are in reality nothing but our own *fancies, passions*, and *feelings*; consequently, they are not *accidents* or *modifications of matter*, but *accidents* and *modifications* of our *own souls*, which are *incorporeal substances* <term>Incorporeal substances: entities that do not have a physical body, such as the mind or soul.</term>. 

Now, if these *Democritic* and *Epicurean atheists* themselves concluded that *real qualities* (considered as distinct from the modifications of matter) could not possibly be *generated* out of it—because this would be the *production of something out of nothing*—they certainly should have acknowledged the same concerning *life* and *thought*, *sense* and *understanding*. They should have seen that the *generation* of these out of *senseless matter* would be an *impossible production of something out of nothing*. Consequently, these are not *corporeal things*, but the *attributes, properties*, or *modes* of *incorporeal substance*; since they can in no way be resolved into *mechanism* and *fancy* (or the modifications of matter), as the *common sensible qualities* can and should be. 

For though the *Democritics* and *Epicureans* did indeed suppose all *human thoughts* to be *caused* or *produced* by the *impact* <note>original: "incursion"</note> *of physical atoms* upon the *thinker*, yet none of them ever reached such a degree of either *stupidity* <note>original: "sottishness"</note> or *shamelessness* <note>original: "impudence"</note> as a *modern writer* <note>The author is referring here to Thomas Hobbes.</note> has done: to maintain that *thought, intelligence* <note>original: "intellection"</note>, and *will* <note>original: "volition"</note> are themselves really nothing else but *local motion* or *mechanism* in the internal *parts of the brain* and *heart*. He claims that "*the mind itself is nothing but motion in certain parts of the organized body*" <note>original: "Mens nihil aliud præterquam Motus, in partibus quibusdam Corporis Organici"</note>. This writer, as if *Descartes* <note>original: "Cartesius"</note> had not been paradoxical enough in making *brute animals* (though supposed by him to be devoid of all *thought*) nothing but mere *machines*, was not content with that. He has advanced much further in making this *monstrous* <note>original: "prodigious"</note> *conclusion*: that all *thinking beings* and *men* themselves are really nothing else but *machines* and *automata*. Whereas he might as well have affirmed *heaven* to be *earth*, *color* to be *sound*, *number* to be *shape*, or anything...

# Theism Proved, from Nothing out of Nothing. BOOK I.

Soul in human beings, or to attribute a **creative power** to all **matter**, (which is only a **passive thing**) while this power is meanwhile denied by the atheist to a **perfect being**. Both of these assertions, just like the former one, result in **producing real entities out of nothing by way of causation**. Thus, we have demonstrated the impossibility and nonsense of all **atheism** from this very principle—the same one by which the atheists try to attack theism in its true sense—that **nothing can be made without a cause, or that nothing cannot be the cause of anything.**

Now, if there is no middle ground between **atheism** and **theism**, and all things must of necessity either spring from **senseless matter** or else from a **perfect understanding being**, then this **demonstration** of the impossibility of **atheism** is a sufficient establishment of the truth of **theism**. This is what geometricians call a **proof by impossibility** <note>original: "Deduction Ad Impossibile"; also known as "reductio ad absurdum," where a premise is proven true because its opposite leads to a logical contradiction.</note>, which they accept as valid and frequently use. Thus: Either there is a **God**, or else **matter** must be acknowledged to be the only **self-existent thing**, and all other things whatsoever must be **made out of it**. But it is impossible that all things should be made out of **senseless matter**; therefore, there is a **God**. Nevertheless, for further satisfaction, we shall show here how the existence of a **God** may also be **directly** demonstrated from this very **principle** in which the atheists try to take sanctuary and from which they attempt to attack theism: **From nothing, nothing comes** <note>original: "De Nihilo Nihil"</note>, meaning that **nothing can be made out of nothing by way of causation, or that nothing cannot be the cause of anything.**

In the first place, we shall take our beginning from what has already been frequently declared: that it is **mathematically certain that something or other existed of itself from all eternity, or without beginning, and unmade by anything else**. The certainty of this proposition depends upon this very **principle** as its foundation: **That nothing can come from nothing, or be made out of nothing, or that nothing which once was not can of itself come into being without a cause.** It follows **unavoidably** from this that if there had once been **nothing**, there could **never** have been **anything**. 

Having thus laid the foundation, we shall in the next place build this further structure: because something certainly existed of itself from eternity **unmade**, there is also **actually** a **necessarily existent being**. To suppose that anything existed "of itself" from eternity by its own **free will and choice**, and therefore not necessarily but **contingently** <note>In philosophy, something is "contingent" if it could have been otherwise or might not have happened; "necessary" means it must exist and cannot be otherwise.</note> (since it might have willed otherwise), is to suppose it to have existed before it **was**, and so positively to have been the **cause of itself**, which is impossible, as has already been declared. Therefore, when a thing is said to be **of itself**, or the **cause of itself**, this is to be understood in no other way than either in a **negative sense** (as having nothing else for its cause) or because its **necessary eternal existence** is **essential** to the perfection of its own nature. Therefore, that which existed **of itself** from eternity, **independently** of anything else, did not exist **contingently but necessarily**. So there is undoubtedly something **actually in being** whose existence is, and always was, **necessary**. In the next place...

<header>CHAPTER IV. Matter is not Necessarily Existent.</header>

It is also certain that **nothing** could **exist necessarily of itself** unless it included the **necessity of existence** in its own **nature**. To suppose that anything exists **necessarily of itself** when it has no **necessity of existence** in its own **nature** is clearly to suppose that its **necessary existence** **comes from nothing**, since it could neither proceed from that **thing** itself, nor from anything else. Finally, there is **nothing** which includes the **necessity of existence** in its very **nature** and **essence** except for an **absolutely perfect being**. The result of all this is that **God**, or a **perfect being**, certainly **exists**, and that there is **nothing** else which **existed of itself from eternity**, **necessarily** and **independently**. Instead, all other things whatsoever derived their **being** from him or were **caused by him**, including **matter** or **body** itself.

What has caused some **theists** to hesitate here, and made them so inclined to believe that **matter** also **existed** from **eternity unmade**, is partly (as has already been suggested) a foolish notion <note>original: "idiotical conceit"</note> that because **nothing can be artificially made by humans** except out of **pre-existing matter**—such as **houses**, **clothes**, **puddings**, and **pies**—therefore there could be no other way of making anything by any power whatsoever. This is assumed even though humans themselves can produce something out of no pre-existing **matter**, such as **thoughts** <note>original: "cogitations"</note> and **physical movement** <note>original: "local motion"</note>. This also stems partly from certain **false opinions** held concerning **matter**. 

First, some **theists** have supposed an **incorporeal first matter** <note>original Greek: "hylen asomaton"; "hyle" is the Greek term for the fundamental substance or "stuff" of the universe</note>. From this **incorporeal matter**, together with an **incorporeal form** joined to it, they believed the **essence** of a physical body was **composed** and **made up**. It is no wonder if these same **imaginative philosophers** further added that from this **incorporeal matter**, by way of an **incorporeal form**, the **incorporeal qualities** of the **body** were also produced. Now, it is difficult to imagine what else could be meant by this **incorporeal matter** other than a **metaphysical concept** of the **potentiality** or **possibility** of things in relation to the **Deity**. Because this potentiality is indeed **eternal** and as **unmade** as **God himself**—being **nothing** but the **divine power considered passively**, or the **reverse** of it—these **philosophers** were, in all probability, prone to think that the **physical matter** of this **corporeal universe** was **eternal** and **unmade**. This **incorporeal matter** was not a **new opinion** held only by some **later Platonists**, but was older than **Aristotle** himself, as appears plainly from these 

<margin>
*Physics, Book 1, Chapter 6.*
</margin>

<header>Atheistic Arguments Against, Book I.</header>

...according to the opinion of some, would it not follow from that premise that matter was *infinite*, *eternal*, and *necessarily existent*? This is not because *space* or *distance* could exist alone by itself—as an *accident* <note>original: "accident" — in philosophy, a property or quality that cannot exist without a substance to belong to</note> without a *substance*—it being plainly *impossible* that *nothing* should have any *accidents*, *modifications*, and *attributes*, or be *measurable* by *yards* and *poles*. Rather, it is because this *space* is supposed by them not to be the *extension* of *body* <note>original: "body" — physical matter</note>, but the *infinite* and *unbounded extension* of the *Deity*. 

But in the next place: if *space* is concluded to be certainly *nothing* else but the *extension* and *distance* of *body* or *matter* considered in *general* (without respect to this or that *particular body*) and *abstractly*, in order to allow for the *conception* of *motion* and the *measurement* of *things*. For *space* considered this way is *necessarily immovable* in regard to its respective parts; just as the *two extremes* of a *yard distance* can never possibly come closer to one another. If so, then we say that there appears to be no sufficient ground for this *positive infinity* of *space*. We are certain of no more than this: that however *great* the *world* or any *shaped body* <note>original: "figurate body"</note> might be, it is not *impossible* for it to be still *greater* and *greater* without *end*. 

This *indefinite increasability* of *body* and *space* seems to be mistaken for a *positive infinity*. In fact, for this very *reason*—because it can never be so *great* that more *magnitude* could not still be added to it—it can never be *positively infinite*. Nor is there perhaps so great an *absurdity* in the idea *that another world* could not *possibly* be made a *mile distant* from this one; for since there would be *nothing* between them, they would necessarily *touch*. Nor is it absurd to say *that this finite world* could have no *mountains* and *valleys* on its *exterior surface*, since it might be *spherical*, *cubical*, or *cylindrical*, or formed in any other *regular figure* that the *Maker* pleased. 

To conclude, therefore: by "space" outside the *finite world*, we should *understand* *nothing* but the *possibility* of *body* existing further and further without *end*, yet never actually reaching *infinity*. Such a *space* as this also existed before this *world* was *created*—a *possibility* for that much *body* to be *produced*. But *space* and *actual distance*, as something really *measurable* by *yards* and *poles*, though it may be *greater* and *greater* without *end*, yet it cannot be *positively infinite* such that no more could be added to it. Therefore, there can be no *argument* from this to prove the *necessary existence* of *matter*.

Moreover, the *existence* of a *Deity* might be further *demonstrated* from this *common notion*: *that nothing can come from nothing causally*. If there were no *God*, just as we could not have had any *idea* of him or of a *perfect being* (since it must have *come* from *nothing* and been the *idea* or *conception* of *nothing*), so neither could there have been any *knowledge* or *understanding* at all. For *individual bodies existing* outside of us cannot enter into us and put *understanding* in us; there is nothing but *local motions* <note>original: "local motions" — the physical movement of matter or particles</note> transmitted from them to our *organs of sense*. The *mind* must have its *immediate intelligibles* <note>original: "immediate intelligibles" — innate ideas or truths that the mind understands directly without external physical input</note> within itself; otherwise, it could not possibly *understand* any *thing*. These *intelligibles* and their relations to one another, or *truths* <note>original: "verities"</note>, are (as was said before) *eternal*. Moreover, the *mind* can frame *ideas* or *conceptions* not only of *things actually existing*...
