# CHAPTER IV. Incorporeal Deity, Confuted.

[...ex]isting, but also of all *possibilities*; which plainly implies and supposes the *actual existence* of a *being infinitely powerful* that could produce them. So, the proper *object* of the *mind* and *understanding* is a *perfect being* and the full extent of its power. This *perfect being*, comprehending itself and the extent of its own *power* (or the *possibilities* of all things), is the *first original mind*, from which all other minds originate. Therefore, if there were no *perfect omnipotent being* comprehending itself and its own power—that is, all the *possibilities* of things—then the *intelligible objects* of the mind and *ideas* must have come from *nothing*.

However, it has already been proved from this principle, *nothing comes from nothing*, that the powers of *sensation* <note>original: "sense"</note> and *understanding*, or the entities of *soul* and *mind*, could never have *resulted* from any modifications of *senseless matter* whatsoever. Therefore, since it is *mathematically* certain that our *human souls* and *persons* could not possibly have been generated out of *matter*, one of these two things will undeniably follow: either they must all have existed of themselves from an *unmade eternity*, or else they must have been created "out of nothing" <note>original: ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων</note>—that is, out of an antecedent *non-existence*—by a *perfect understanding being* that was itself unmade, or at least they must have derived their whole substance from it. So, it is just as certain that there is a God as it is that our *human souls* and *persons* did not all exist from *eternity by themselves*. And that there must be some *eternal unmade mind* has also already been demonstrated from the same principle: *nothing out of nothing*. Thus, we have abundantly disproved <note>original: "confuted"</note> the *second atheistic argument*—the claim that there can be no *omnipotence* or *divine creation* because *nothing can be made out of nothing*. We have plainly shown that this very principle, when understood in its *true sense*, actually provides a *demonstration* for the contrary.

(The atheists believe it necessarily follows from both of these that there can be no God at all.) Secondly, we shall show that from the very principles of *atheistic materialism* <note>original: "corporealism"</note> (as represented in the *fifth* and *sixth* sections), *incorporeal substance is demonstrable*. And lastly, since there is undeniably *incorporeal substance*, the two following *atheistic arguments* against a *corporeal deity* (in the *seventh* and *eighth* sections) will be proved altogether *insignificant*.

# Body, the Atheist's Only Substance. BOOK I.

I have already observed that although not all *corporealists* <note>original: "Corporealists"; those who believe that only physical matter (body) exists</note> are necessarily *atheists*, yet *atheists* have universally been *corporealists*. This has always been their *first* and *greatest postulate* <note>original: "Postulatum"; a fundamental assumption</note>: *that there is no other substance besides body*. Thus *Plato* declared long ago concerning them: 

<margin>Sophist p. 172. Ficinus</margin> *They contend strongly that only that which is tangible or can resist their touch really exists, concluding that "body" and "substance" are one and the same thing. And if anyone should affirm that there is anything incorporeal, they will immediately cry him down and not hear a word more from him.* <note>original: "διϊσχυρίζονται τοῦτο εἶναι μόνον... οὐδὲν ἐθέλοντες ἄλλο ἀκούειν"</note> 

For there can be no doubt that the people Plato intended here were those very *atheists* whom he spoke of afterward in the same *dialogue*: 

*Whether shall we assent to that opinion nowadays entertained by so many: that nature generates all things from a certain accidental cause, without the direction of any mind or understanding? Or rather, that it produces them according to reason and knowledge, proceeding from God?* <note>original: "μῶν τὰ τῶν πολλῶν δόγματι... ἀπὸ θεοῦ γινομένης;"</note> 

Indeed, the philosopher tells us there that some of these *atheistic* people began then to be somewhat ashamed of making *prudence*, *justice*, and other *moral virtues* into *corporeal things* or *bodies*: 

*Although they affirm concerning the soul itself that it seems to them to be corporeal, yet concerning prudence and those other virtues mentioned, some now scarcely have the confidence to maintain that these are either bodies or nothing.* <note>original: "ἀποκρίνονται τὴν μὲν ψυχὴν... διϊσχυρίζεσθαι"</note> 

But this (he says) was indeed nothing less than completely *giving up* the *cause* of *atheism*. *Because if it is once granted that there is even the slightest thing that is incorporeal, this will be sufficient to overthrow the atheistic foundation.* <note>original: "εἰ γάρ τι καὶ σμικρὸν... ἐξαρκεῖ"</note> 

Therefore, he concludes that people like these were but *mongrel* and *imperfect atheists*. *For those who are thorough-paced and genuine atheists indeed will hesitate at neither of those previously mentioned things, but will contend that whatever they cannot grasp with their hands is altogether nothing.* <note>original: "ἐπεὶ αὐτῶν γ’ ἂν ἓν ἐπαισχυνθεῖεν... οὐδὲν τὸ παράπαν ἐστί"</note> 

That is, that there is no other *substance* or *entity* in the *world* but only *body*—that which is *tangible* or *resists* the *touch*. *Aristotle* also represents the *atheistic hypothesis* in the same way: *They affirm that matter or body is all the substance there is, and that all other things are but the passions and affections of it.* <note>original: "τοῦτο καὶ τοσαύτην φασὶν εἶναι... πάθη τούτων"</note> And again in his *Metaphysics*:

<margin>Metaphysics Book I, chapter 7</margin> *These men maintain that all is one, and that there is but one only nature as the matter of all things, and this is corporeal, or endowed with magnitude.* <note>original: "ἓν τὸ πᾶν, καὶ μίαν εἶναί τινα φύσιν... μέγεθος ἔχουσαν"</note> 

And now we see plainly that the ancient *atheists* were of the very same mind with these

### CHAPTER 4. Atheist Incorporeal Space, Non-Sense.

There are those in our days who argue that *body*—or that which is *tangible* and *divisible*—is the *only substantial thing*. From this, it follows that an *incorporeal substance* would be the same as an *incorporeal body*—that is, an *impossibility*—and that there can be no *incorporeal Deity*.

But in the management of this *cause*, there has been some disagreement among the *atheists* themselves. First, the *Democriteans* <note>original: "Democriticks"</note> and *Epicureans*, while agreeing with all other *atheists* that whatever was *unextended* and devoid of *magnitude* was therefore *nothing* (so that there could be no *substance*, *accident*, or *mode* of any substance that was *unextended*), nonetheless distinguished between a *double nature*. 

*First*, that which is so *extended* as to be *impenetrable* and *tangible* (or *resists touch*), which is *body*. And *secondly*, that which is also *extended*, but *penetrably* and *intangibly*, which is *space* or *vacuum*. This is a nature, according to them, really distinct from *body*, and the only *incorporeal thing* there is. Now, since this *space* (which is the only *incorporeal*) can neither *do* nor *suffer* anything, but only provide *place* or *room* for *bodies* to *subsist* in or *pass* through, they argue that there cannot be any *active*, *understanding*, *incorporeal Deity*. This is the *argumentation* of the *Democritean atheists*.

To this we reply: if *space* is indeed a *nature* distinct from *body* and a *thing truly incorporeal* as they claim, then it undeniably follows from this very principle of theirs that there must be an *incorporeal substance*. Furthermore, since this *space* is also supposed by them to be *infinite*, there must be an *infinite incorporeal Deity*. This is because if *space* is not the *extension* of *body*, nor a property <note>original: "Affection"; in this context, it refers to a quality or attribute of a substance</note> of it, then it must necessarily be either an *accident existing* alone by itself without a *substance* (which is *impossible*), or else the *extension* or property of some other *incorporeal substance* that is *infinite*. 

But here *Gassendi* <note>original: "Gassendus"; Pierre Gassendi (1592–1655), a French philosopher who sought to reconcile Epicurean atomism with Christian thought</note> will step in to help his good friends, the *Democriteans* and *Epicureans*, in a difficult situation <note>original: "at a dead Lift"</note>. He undertakes to maintain that although *space* is indeed an *incorporeal thing*, it would not necessarily follow that it is an *incorporeal substance* or a property of one, nor yet that it is an *accident existing* alone by itself without a *substance*. He claims this because this *space* is really neither *accident* nor *substance*, but a certain *middle nature* or *essence* between the two. 

To this subterfuge of his—so that we do not quarrel about words—we shall make this reply: undoubtedly, *whatever exists*, or has any kind of *entity*, either *subsists* by itself or else is an *attribute*, property <note>original: "Affection"</note>, or *mode* of something that does *subsist* by itself. For it is certain that there can be no *mode*, *accident*, or property of *nothing*; and consequently, *nothing* cannot be *extended* nor *measurable*. But if *space* is neither the *extension* of *body* nor of an *incorporeal substance*, then it must necessarily be the *extension* of *nothing* and the property of *nothing*; and *nothing* must be *measurable* by *yards* and *rods* <note>original: "Poles"; a unit of measurement equal to 16.5 feet</note>. We conclude, therefore, that from this very *hypothesis* of the *Democritean* and *Epicurean atheists*—that *space* is a *nature* distinct from *body* and *positively infinite*—it follows undeniably that there must be some [incorporeal substance].

<summary>This page critiques the Epicurean view that space is a "middle nature" between substance and accident, arguing that if infinite space is a real entity, it must be an attribute of an infinite incorporeal substance (God).</summary>

some *incorporeal substance*, of which *extension* is a *property* <note>original: "affection"</note>; and because nothing can be *infinite* except the *Deity*, it follows that this is the *infinite extension* of an *incorporeal Deity*, just as some learned *theists* and *incorporealists* have asserted. And thus, the *argument* of these *Democritus-following* and *Epicurean atheists* against an *incorporeal Deity* is abundantly proven wrong. We have shown that from the very *principle* of their own—by which they would try to disprove God—an incorporeal Deity is actually *demonstrable* against them.

To this it might be further added that *Epicurus*, who openly opposed *Plato’s incorporeal God* as an impossibility, nevertheless clearly *contradicted* himself when he asserted the existence of a *democracy of monogrammous gods* <note>Epicurus imagined gods as thin, faint outlines or "monograms" that lived in the spaces between worlds, rather than solid beings.</note>. These gods were not *compounded* of *atoms* and *vacuum* (which were, according to him, the only *principles of body*) so that they might be *incorruptible*. Nor could they *touch* or be *touched*, but were *penetrable*, as is declared in these *verses* of *Lucretius*:

Quæ quoniam manuum Tactum, suffugit & Ictum, Tactile nil nobis quod sit, contingere debet. Tangere enim non quit, quod Tangi non licet ipsum."</note>

(Even though *tangibility* and *impenetrability* were elsewhere defined by him as the very *essence of body*.) And lastly, he claimed these gods did not have a *body*, but a *quasi-body* <note>original: "Quasi-Corpus"; meaning "as if it were a body."</note>, and therefore they must truly be *incorporeal*. Though there is no doubt that *Epicurus* was being deceptive in all this; he did not believe a bit of it himself, nor in any such gods at all.

But there were other *atheists* who also concluded that whatever was *unextended was nothing*. They were aware of the inconvenience of making *space* a thing really distinct from *body* (from which it would unavoidably follow that space was a *property* of an *incorporeal substance*). Therefore, they acknowledged not *two natures of extended things*, but as we saw earlier in *Aristotle*, "one single nature, and that a bodily one" <note>original: "μίαν τινὰ φύσιν καὶ ταύτην σωματικήν"</note>. To them, *space* was either a merely *imaginary thing* that has no reality outside our minds but is only a *phantasm* <note>A mental image or illusion.</note> of our own—and in their modern language, a kind of *ghost*, *apparition*, or *spectre* of a body—or else it was indeed the very *extension* of *body* itself, considered in *general* and *abstractly* from this or that *individual movable body*. These men, therefore, framed their *argumentation* against an *incorporeal Deity* in this manner: *Nothing truly exists but what is extended*, or has a *certain magnitude* (because that which is *unextended and has no magnitude is nowhere*, and consequently *nothing*). *But whatever is extended and in a place is body.* Therefore, there is no other *substance* besides *body*, and consequently, there can be no *incorporeal Deity*. Or else, to put the argument into a more approved *logical form* <note>original: "Syllogistick Form"</note>: *Whatever is extended is body, or corporeal; but whatever exists is extended. Therefore—*

# Chapter V. Whether anything is Unextended.

Therefore, *whatever exists is a body, or is corporeal. And consequently, there can be no incorporeal God.*

To this *argument*, those who *assert the existence of incorporeal substance* <note>Incorporeal substance: a reality that is not made of matter, such as a spirit or soul.</note> have replied in *two ways*. 

*First*, the majority of the ancient *incorporealists* took it for granted that whatever was *extended* <note>Extended: having physical dimensions like length or width.</note> in *magnitude* and had *parts* separate from one another was *divisible*. They also believed such things were *impenetrable* by anything else that was extended, because there can be no *penetration of dimensions* (meaning two physical sizes cannot occupy the same space). Therefore, *no single magnitude* can be *absorbed or swallowed up* into another; it must necessarily stand outside of it, adding to the total quantity. 

Because of this, they readily agreed to the *proposition* that *whatever is extended into length, width, and depth is a body.* However, being strongly persuaded that some other *substance* exists besides *body*, they denied the other proposition: *that whatever exists is extended, or that what is unextended is nothing.* They maintained that besides *body*, or *extended substance*, there was another *incorporeal* substance. This substance was therefore unextended, devoid of magnitude, without quantity, without parts, and indivisible. <note>original Greek: "ἀδιάστατον, καὶ ἀμεγέθες, καὶ ἄποσον, καὶ ἀμερὲς, καὶ ἀδιαίρετον"</note>

That *Plato* himself *philosophized* in this manner can be proved from several passages in his writings. For example, in his *Tenth Book of Laws*, he affirms that the *soul* itself, and those things which belong to it (such as *thought*), are *in the order of nature, prior to the length, depth, and width of bodies.* <note>original Greek: "πρότερα μήκος σωμάτων καὶ βάθος καὶ πλάτος"</note> Doubtless, his meaning was not that there is a different kind of *length, width, and depth* in *souls* that existed before those of *bodies*. Rather, his point was that *length, width, and depth* are *essential properties of body only*. Therefore, the *soul and thought*, being *devoid of these*, were in the order of nature *before them*. 

Again, in his *Timaeus*, when speaking of *place, space, and matter*, Plato condemns as a *vulgar error* the idea *that whatever exists must necessarily be in some place or other, and what is in no place is nothing.* He writes:

> *The third kind is that of space, which provides a home for all things that are created. And when we look upon this, we say in a dreamlike way that it is necessary for everything that exists to be in some place and occupy a certain room and space; and that whatever is not somewhere, either on earth or in heaven, is nothing.* <note>original Greek: "τρίτον δὲ αὖ γένος τὸ τῆς χώρας, ἕδραν παρέχον ὅσα ἔχει γένεσιν πᾶσιν— πρὸς ὃ δὴ καὶ ὀνειροπολοῦμεν βλέποντες, καὶ φαμὲν ἀναγκαῖον εἶναί που, τὸ ὂν ἅπαν ἔν τινι τόπῳ, καὶ κατέχον χώραν τινά· τὸ δὲ μήτε ἐν γῇ, μήτε που κατ’ οὐρανόν, οὐδὲν εἶναι"</note>

This *drowsy* or *dreaming imagination* (which, he says, haunts and possesses men like a ghost) persists even when they think about the *true and awakened nature of the Deity.* Elsewhere, this philosopher discourses on *God* under the title of *the vast sea of beauty* <note>original: "πολὺ πέλαγος τοῦ καλοῦ"</note> and describes Him in this way:

> *As that which is not anywhere, either on earth or in heaven, but is itself alone by itself, and with itself, always uniform; while all other beautiful things partake of it.* <note>original Greek: "οὐδέπη ὄν, ἢ ἐν γῇ, ἢ ἐν οὐρανῷ, ἀλλ’ αὐτὸ, μεθ’ αὑτοῦ, μονοειδὲς ἀεὶ ὄν, τὰ δὲ ἄλλα πάντα καλὰ ἐκείνου μετέχοντα"</note>

And as for *Aristotle's*—

# Plato and Aristotle as Defenders, Book I.
## Aristotle's Views on the Divine Nature

...Aristotle's perspective in this particular; that he did not depart here, as he did in some other matters, from his master Plato, may appear from that entire chapter or section at the end of his *Physics* <note>original: "Physicks"</note>, dedicated to this very subject: to prove <note>original: ὅτι τὸ ἀμερὲς ἀναγκαῖον εἶναι, καὶ μηδὲν ἔχον μέγεθος</note> "that the First Immovable Mover (which is God Almighty) must of necessity be devoid of parts, or indivisible, and have no magnitude at all." The conclusion of that section, and his whole book of *Physics*, is this: 

"Since these things have been determined, it is clearly impossible that the first mover, which is itself immovable, should have any magnitude. For if it has magnitude, that magnitude must necessarily be either finite or infinite. However, it was demonstrated earlier in the *Physics* that there can be no infinite magnitude; and it has now been proved that nothing with a finite magnitude can have infinite power. Therefore, it is plain that the First Mover is indivisible, devoid of parts, and has no magnitude at all." <note>original: διωρισμένων δὲ τούτων, φανερὸν ὅτι ἀδύνατον τὸ πρῶτον κινοῦν καὶ ἀκίνητον ἔχειν τι μέγεθος· εἰ γὰρ μέγεθος ἔχει, ἀνάγκη ἤτοι πεπερασμένον αὐτὸ εἶναι, ἢ ἄπειρον· ἄπειρον μὲν οὖν ὅτι οὐκ ἐνδέχεται μέγεθος εἶναι, δέδεικται πρότερον ἐν τοῖς φυσικοῖς· ὅτι δὲ τὸ πεπερασμένον ἀδύνατον ἔχειν ἄπειρον δύναμιν, δέδεικται νῦν· φανερὸν τοίνυν, ὅτι ἀδιαίρετόν ἐστι, καὶ ἀμερὲς, καὶ οὐδὲν ἔχον μέγεθος.</note>

This same doctrine is again taught and asserted by Aristotle in his *Metaphysics*:

<margin>Book 14, chapter 7 <note>In modern editions, this is typically found in Book 12 (Lambda).</note></margin>

"From what has been declared, it is manifest that there is an eternal and immovable substance, separate from sensible things <note>Sensible things: objects that can be perceived by the five senses.</note>. It has also been shown that this substance cannot possibly have any magnitude, but is devoid of parts and indivisible. This is because no finite thing can have infinite power, and there is no such thing possible as infinite magnitude." <note>original: ὅτι μὲν οὖν ἔστιν οὐσία τις ἀΐδιος καὶ ἀκίνητος, καὶ κεχωρισμένη τῶν αἰσθητῶν, φανερὸν ἐκ τῶν εἰρημένων· δέδεικται δὲ καὶ ὅτι μέγεθος οὐδὲν ἐνδέχεται ἔχειν ταύτην τὴν οὐσίαν, ἀλλὰ ἀμερὴς καὶ ἀδιαίρετός ἐστι· οὐδὲν γὰρ ἔχει δύναμιν ἄπειρον πεπερασμένον, καὶ ὅλως οὐκ ἔστιν οὐδὲν ἄπειρον.</note>

Neither does Aristotle limit this quality solely to the Supreme Deity—to be thus devoid of magnitude and parts, and consequently indivisible. He elsewhere attributes the same to all other immaterial or incorporeal things, and particularly to the human mind: <note>original: ἀδιαίρετον πᾶν τὸ μὴ ὕλην ἔχον, ὥσπερ ὁ ἀνθρώπινος νοῦς</note> "Everything that is devoid of matter is indivisible, such as the human mind." 

And he asserts the same regarding both the world soul <note>original: "Mundane Soul"</note> and the rational soul: that they are not magnitudes, though he (rather mockingly, in his usual style) attributes the opposite opinion to Plato.

<margin>*On the Soul*, Book 1, chapter 3</margin>

"It is not correct to say that either the soul of the world or the rational soul are magnitudes. For the intellect is one and continuous, just as the act of thinking <note>original: "intellection"</note> is, which is the same as the objects of thought <note>original: "intelligibles"</note>. But these are 'one' in the way numbers are, not as physical magnitudes are. Therefore, the intellect is not continuous in that physical way; rather, it is either devoid of parts or not continuous like a magnitude. For if it were a magnitude, how could it think with any of its parts? Would those parts be divided by size or by points? If by points, and points are infinite, it is clear it could never finish a thought. If it were divided by size, it would think the same thing many times, or even an infinite number of times. Furthermore, how can something with parts think of something that is indivisible?" <note>original: οὐ καλῶς τὸ λέγειν τὴν ψυχὴν μέγεθος εἶναι. ὁ δὲ νοῦς εἷς καὶ συνεχὴς, ὥσπερ καὶ ἡ νόησις· ἡ δὲ νόησις τὰ νοήματα· ταῦτα δὲ τῷ ἐφεξῆς ἓν, ὡς ὁ ἀριθμὸς, ἀλλ' οὐχ ὡς τὸ μέγεθος· διόπερ οὐδὲ νοῦς οὕτω συνεχής· ἀλλ' ἤτοι ἀμερὴς, ἢ οὐχ ὡς τὸ μέγεθός τι συνεχές· πῶς γὰρ δὴ καὶ νοήσει μέγεθος ὢν, ὁτῳοῦν τῶν μορίων τῶν αὑτοῦ; μορίων δ' ἤτοι κατὰ μέγεθος, ἢ κατὰ στιγμήν· εἰ μὲν οὖν κατὰ στιγμήν, αὗται δ' ἄπειροι, δῆλον ὡς οὐδέποτε διέξεισιν· εἰ δὲ κατὰ μέγεθος, πολλάκις ἢ ἀπειράκις νοήσει τὸ αὐτό· ἔτι δὲ πῶς νοήσει τὸ ἀμερὲς μεριστῷ.</note>

Aristotle argues that since no finite physical body can possess infinite power, the source of infinite power must be indivisible and non-material.</summary>

### CHAPTER V. Of Unextended Incorporeals. 773

Can the soul understand with any of its parts, whether we imagine them as points or as smaller <term>magnitudes</term> <note>physical sizes or dimensions</note>? In either case, would there not be an innumerable company of separate acts of understanding? Moreover, how can the soul conceive of anything that is indivisible if it were itself composed of divisible parts? Furthermore, in this same book, *On the Soul* <note>original: *De Anima*</note>, Aristotle stiffly denies that souls in general are either in a place or are moved locally, except by "accident"—meaning they are only said to be moved because they are within a body that moves. Thus, Simplicius writes: "See how Aristotle everywhere denies or excludes corporeal (or local) motions from the soul." <note>original: ὅρᾳ ὡς πανταχοῦ τὰς σωματικὰς ἀποφάσκει τῆς ψυχῆς κινήσεις</note> <margin>Fol. 6.</margin> And again: "Aristotle will by no means allow any incorporeal things whatsoever—whether they are of the first, second, or lowest rank—themselves to be moved, as they are all the causes of motion." <note>original: ἀπαγορεύει μὴ κινεῖσθαι τὰ ἀσώματα τῆς κινήσεως αἴτια κἂν πρῶτα κἂν μέσᾳ κἂν ἔσχατα ᾖ</note> Philoponus likewise states: "You see how Aristotle, regarding corporeal motions, declares the soul to be immovable. For whatever is in a place (and is movable) is a body." <note>original: ὁρᾷς ὡς πρὸς τὰς σωματικὰς κινήσεις ἀποβλέπων, οὕτως αὐτὴν ἀκίνητον εἶναί φησι· πᾶν γὰρ τὸ ἐν τόπῳ σῶμά ἐστιν</note> Lastly, in the passage cited previously, Aristotle plainly states that the essence of corporeal substance (as opposed to incorporeal) consists in **Magnitude**.

Besides Plato and Aristotle, we might here list many other ancient "Incorporealists" <note>philosophers who believe in non-physical reality</note> who clearly maintained the same doctrine. Philo Judaeus does not only assert a general "double essence" or substance—one <term>indistant</term> <note>original: ἀδιάστατον; without spatial extension</note> and one <term>distant</term> <note>original: διαστηματικὴν; having physical extension</note>—but somewhere he writes this concerning the **Deity**: <margin>On the Confusion of Tongues, p. 339 <note>original: *De Confus. Ling. p. 339*</note></margin> "All things are filled with God, as He contains them, but is not contained by them or in them. To Him alone it belongs to be both everywhere and nowhere. He is nowhere because He Himself created space and place along with bodies, and it is not lawful to say the Creator is included within any of His creatures. And He is everywhere because He extends His virtues and powers throughout earth and water, air and heaven, leaving no part of the world destitute of them. By collecting all things together under Himself, He has bound them fast with invisible bonds." <note>original: ὑπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ πεπλήρωται τὰ πάντα, περιέχοντος οὐ περιεχομένου... &c.</note> 

But no one has more industriously pursued this topic than Plotinus, who everywhere asserts that **Body** and **Magnitude** are one and the same thing. He argues that besides this, there is another **Incorporeal Substance** which is consequently "without quantity, without magnitude, and without parts that are locally distant from one another." <note>original: ἄποσος καὶ ἀμεγέθης καὶ ἀμερὴς</note> He describes it as "having, in its own nature, transcended the imperfection of quantity." <note>original: ὃ ἐν τῇ αὐτοῦ οὐσίᾳ τὸ ποσὸν εἶναι ὑπερβέβηκεν</note> Plotinus also wrote two whole books on this very subject: "That one and the self-same numerical thing may be entirely everywhere as a whole." <note>original: τὸ ὂν ἓν καὶ ταυτὸν ἀριθμῷ ἅμα πανταχοῦ εἶναι ὅλον</note> His principal design was to prove that the **Deity** is not just a part of itself...

<meta>catchword: here,</meta>

<summary>This page explores the arguments of Aristotle, Simplicius, Philo, and Plotinus regarding the nature of incorporeal substances, arguing that the soul and God are "unextended"—meaning they exist without physical size or spatial parts.</summary>

...here, and *part of it there*; and so much of it in one place, and so much in another (as if the very *substance* of it were *measurable* by *yards* and *poles*), but the whole *undivided Deity* is everywhere. <margin>P. 667.</margin> As Plotinus <note>The author is quoting the Neoplatonist philosopher Plotinus.</note> says, "God is before all things that are in a place." <note>original: πρὸ τῶν ἐν τόπῳ ἁπάντων</note> And, "It is not at all to be wondered at that God, not being in a place, should be present to everything that is in a place, wholly and entirely. For reason pronounces that as a necessity: since He occupies no place, He must therefore of necessity be [wholly] <note>original: ὅλως</note>—all of Him indivisibly present—to whatsoever He is present." <note>original: θαυμαστὸν δ᾽ οὐ, εἰ αὐτὸ μὴ ὂν ἐν τόπῳ, παντὶ τῷ ἐν τόπῳ ὄντι, ὅλως πάρεστι. φησὶ γὰρ ὁ λόγος, ὡς ἀνάγκη· αὐτῷ τόπον οὐκ εἰληχότι, ᾧ πάρεστι, τούτῳ ὅλον παρεῖναι.</note> Neither is this, he says, a thing only deduced by reason, but something suggested by the *instincts* of *mankind* even before reasoning: "That one and the same numerical substance (namely, of the Deity) is at once entirely everywhere, is agreeable to the common notions and sentiments of mankind, when we often, by the instincts of nature, speak of that God who is in every one of us as being one and the same in all." <note>original: τὸ ἓν καὶ ταυτὸν ἀριθμῷ, πανταχοῦ ἅμα ὅλον εἶναι, κοινὴ ἔννοια φησὶν εἶναι, ὅταν πάντες κινύμενοι αὐτοφυῶς λέγωσι, τὸν ἐν ἑκάστῳ ἡμῶν Θεὸν, ὡς ἕνα καὶ τὸν αὐτόν</note> To which the philosopher adds: "And this is the firmest of all principles, that which our souls do, as it were, naturally and of themselves speak; and which is not collected by reason, but comes forth from them before reasoning." <note>original: καὶ ἔστι πάντων βεβαιοτάτη ἀρχὴ, ἣν ὥσπερ αἱ ψυχαὶ ἡμῶν φθέγγονται, &c.</note>

Moreover, he often affirms of the human *soul*—or rather takes it as a thing for granted—that it is, in its whole or all, <margin>P. 644.</margin> in every part of the body; that is, it is undivided. "As for the human soul, it is one and the same numerically in the hand and in the foot." <note>original: ἐπὶ δὲ τῆς ψυχῆς, τὸ αὐτὸ ἀριθμῷ, τὸ ἐν τῷ ποδὶ, καὶ τῇ χειρὶ ὑπάρχει</note> And again: "Since we commonly suppose our own soul to be the same, both in our foot and in our hand; why should we not in like manner acknowledge that the World Soul <note>original: Mundane Soul; the soul of the universe</note> or Deity, which is in one part of the universe, is the same as that in another?" <note>original: εἶτα πῶς ἐν ποδὶ καὶ χειρὶ τὴν αὐτην, τὴν δὲ ἐν τῷ ἑτέρῳ μέρει τοῦ παντὸς, οὐ τὴν αὐτὴν τὴν ἐν τῷδε</note> In like manner, *Simplicius*, proving that a body is not the first principle because there must of necessity be something *self-moving*, and what is so must needs be *incorporeal*, writes this: <margin>P. 649.</margin> "Because what is such must of necessity be indivisible and non-extended <note>original: indistant; not occupying spatial distance or extension</note>; for were it divisible and extended, it could not all be joined with its whole self, so that the whole should both actively move and be moved." <note>original: τὸ δὲ τοιοῦτον ἀμερὲς εὐθὺς ἀνάγκη εἶναι καὶ ἀδιάστατον, μεριστὸν γὰρ καὶ διαστατὸν ὑπάρχον, οὐ δύναται ὅλον ὅλῳ ἑαυτῷ ἐφαρμόζειν, ὡς τὸ ὅλον εἶναι κινοῦν, καὶ ὅλον τὸ αὐτὸ κινούμενον.</note>

This same thing seems further *evident* in the soul's being *all conscious of itself* and *reflexive* upon its whole *self*, which could not be if one part of it were distant from another. Again, the same philosopher expressly denies that the *soul*, though it is a *self-moving substance*, is at all *locally moved*, except by accident in respect of the *body* which is moved by it. "The soul is not moved by corporeal or local motions (for in respect of these it is immovable), but by cognitive ones only, which are called deliberating, thinking, and opining; it moves bodies according to corporeal motions..." <note>original: οὐ τὰς σωματικὰς κινύμενον κινήσεις (κατὰ γὰρ ἐκείνας ἀκίνητόν ἐστι) ἀλλὰ τὰς ψυχικὰς, αἷς ὀνόματά ἐστι βουλεύεσθαι, διανοεῖν, δοξάζειν, κινεῖ τὰ σώματα κατὰ τὰς σωματικὰς κινήσεις</note>

Drawing on Plotinus and Simplicius, it asserts that the soul's ability to be conscious of itself and move the body stems from its indivisible nature.</summary>

### Chapter V. Unextended Substance

(the names of which are *Consultation* and *Deliberation*, etc.) it *moves bodies locally*. This was *Plato’s real meaning* when he defined the soul as a *self-moving substance* and the *cause of all bodily motion*. He meant that by moving itself through *thought* <note>original: Cogitation</note>, it moved bodies through space (even though *Aristotle* refused to acknowledge this). This clearly appears from his own words and is acknowledged by the Greek commentators themselves in their notes on *Aristotle’s* *On the Soul* <note>original: De Anima</note>. Thus, *Simplicius* says elsewhere: "Since the soul is not in a place, it is not capable of any local motion." <note>original: ἐπεὶ δ' οὐκ ἐν τόπῳ ψυχή, οὐδ' ἂν κινοῖτο, τὰς τῶν ἐν τόπῳ ὄντων κινήσεις</note>

We would omit the testimonies of any more philosophers if we did not find *Porphyry* <note>Porphyry (c. 234 – c. 305 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus.</note> so thorough and clear on this point. He makes this the very beginning of his *Introduction to Intelligibles* <note>original: ἀφορμαὶ πρὸς τὰ νοητὰ (Sententiae)</note>: "Though every body is in a place, nothing that is properly incorporeal is in a place." <note>original: πᾶν σῶμα ἐν τόπῳ, οὐδὲν δὲ τῶν καθ' ἑαυτὸ ἀσωμάτων ἐν τόπῳ</note> He later pursues the point in this manner:

<margin>P. 229, 230</margin>
"Neither does that which is incorporeal move through space by its will. Place relates only to physical size and bulk. But that which is devoid of bulk and size is likewise devoid of local motion. Therefore, it is only present by a certain disposition and inclination toward one thing more than another; its presence there cannot be detected except by its operations and effects." <note>original: οὐδὲ τυπικῶς διέρχεται τὸ ἀσώματον· ὅπου βούλεται· ὄγκῳ γὰρ συνυφίσταται τόπος· τὸ δ' ἄοικον παντελῶς καὶ ἀμέγεθες, ὑπὸ τῶν ἐν τόπῳ ἀκρατήτων, τυπικῆς τε κινήσεως ἄμοιρον, διαθεῖσα τοίνυν ποία ἔχει εὑρίσκεται, ὅπου καὶ διάκειται· καὶ ἐκ τῶν ἔργων αὐτοῦ φανερὰ ἡ παρουσία αὐτοῦ γίνεται</note>

Again, concerning the three *Divine Hypostases* <note>The three fundamental levels of reality in Neoplatonism: The One (God), Intellect (Nous), and Soul (Psyche).</note>, he writes:

<margin>P. 231</margin>
"The Supreme God is everywhere because he is nowhere; and the same is true of the second and third divine hypostases, *Intellect* <note>original: Nous</note> and *Soul* <note>original: Psyche</note>." <note>original: ὁ Θεὸς πανταχοῦ ὅτι οὐδαμοῦ, καὶ ὁ νοῦς πανταχοῦ ὅτι οὐδαμοῦ, καὶ ψυχὴ πανταχοῦ ὅτι οὐδαμοῦ</note>

The Supreme God is everywhere and nowhere in respect to the things that come after him, existing only as his own and in himself. *Intellect* is in the Supreme God, yet everywhere and nowhere to those things that come after it. *Soul* (the Mundane or World Soul) is both in the Intellect and the Supreme God, yet everywhere and nowhere in relation to bodies. Lastly, *Body* is both in the Soul of the world and in God. Here, Porphyry denies that God is locally within the physical world. He thinks it more proper to say that the physical world is in God, rather than God being in the world; this is because the world is held and contained within the Divine Power, but the Deity is not confined within the physical locations of the world.

Furthermore, he declares his meaning in this way: "Even if an incorporeal space or vacuum were imagined (as Democritus and Epicurus supposed), Mind or God could not possibly exist in this empty space as if spread out with it. For such a vacuum would only be able to receive bodies; it could not receive the activity of Mind or Intellect, nor provide any 'place' or room for it, since that is not a bulky thing." <note>original: οὐδ' εἰ κενὸν ἄν τι ἐπινοηθείη ἀσώματον, ἐν κενῷ οἷόν τε εἶναι νοῦν, σώματος μὲν γὰρ δεκτικὸν ἂν εἴη τὸ κενόν. νοῦ δὲ ἐνέργειαν χωρῆσαι ἀμήχανον, καὶ τόπον δοῦναι ἐνεργείᾳ</note> And again: "The world is present in the Mind in a spread-out <term>distensively</term> <note>original: διαστατικῶς; meaning occupying space or having extension</note> manner, but the Incorporeal is present to the world in an indivisible and non-extended way. That which is indivisible becomes whole in every part of the extended thing, being the same and..." <note>original: ὁ μὲν κόσμος ἐν τῷ νῷ διαστατικῶς πάρεστι, τὸ δὲ ἀσώματον τῷ κόσμῳ ἀμερῶς καὶ ἀδιαστάτως· τὸ δὲ ἀμερὲς ἐν διαστατῷ ὅλον γίνεται κατὰ πᾶν μέρος, ταὐτὸν ν καὶ</note>

<note>original: καὶ ἐν ἀριθμῷ· αὐτὸ ἀμερῶς πάρεστι καὶ ἀπληθύντως καὶ ἀτόπως, κατὰ τὴν αὑτοῦ φύσιν, ταῖς μεριστῶς, καὶ πεπληθυσμένως, καὶ ὅτι ἐν τόπῳ</note> "And in number: it is impartibly present, and without being multiplied, and without occupying space—according to its own nature—to those things that are divided, multiplied, and exist in a place." *The physical <note>original: Corporeal</note> world is distantly present to the intelligible realm (or the Deity); and that intelligible realm is indivisibly and non-distantly present with the world. But when that which is non-distant and unextended is present with that which is distant and extended, then the whole of the former is one and the same numerically in every part of the latter. That is, it is indivisibly, unmultipliedly, and non-locally present there (according to its own nature) with that which is naturally divisible, multipliable, and located in a place. Lastly, he affirms the same likewise of the human soul: that this is also* <note>original: οὐσία ἀμεγέθης</note> *a substance devoid of magnitude, which is not locally present to this or that body, but is present by disposition and energy; therefore, the whole of it is in every part of the body without being divided.*

As for Christian writers, besides Origen—who was such a famous defender <note>original: Asserter</note> of *incorporeal substance* that (as Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus (c. 380 – after 439), a Christian church historian.</note> records) the Egyptian monks and Anthropomorphites <note>term: Anthropomorphites: A sect that believed God has a physical human form and body.</note> threatened death to Theophilus, the Bishop of Alexandria, unless he would simultaneously denounce <note>original: execrate</note> the writings of Origen and profess a belief in a *physical God of human form*—and who also maintained that *incorporeal substance* was *unextended*, as might be proved from various passages in both his book *Against Celsus* and his *On First Principles* <note>original: Peri Archon</note>; we say (besides Origen and other Greeks) that St. Augustine among the Latins clearly asserted the same. In his book *On the Magnitude of the Soul* <note>original: De Quantitate Animæ</note> and elsewhere, he maintained concerning the *human soul* that, being *incorporeal*, it has no *dimensions of length, breadth, or depth*, and is <note>original: Illocabilis</note> *impossible to locate as if in a place*. 

We shall conclude with the testimony of Boethius, who was both a philosopher and a Christian. <note>original: Quædam sunt Communes Animi Conceptiones, per se notæ, apud Sapientes tantum; Ut Incorporealia non esse In Loco</note> "There are certain common conceptions," he says, "or notions of the mind, which are known by themselves among wise men only; such as this, for example: that incorporeal things are in no place." From this, it is manifest that the majority of those regarded as *wise men* were not formerly of the opinion <note>original: Quod Nusquam est nihil est</note> "that what is nowhere, or in no certain place, is nothing." They did not look upon that idea as a *common notion*, but only as a *common error* <note>original: Vulgar Errour</note>.

By this time, we have made it unquestionably evident that this opinion—that *incorporeal substance* is *unextended, non-distant, and devoid of magnitude*—is no *novel* or *recent* thing, nor was it first started in the Scholastic Age <note>term: Scholastic Age: The period of Medieval philosophy (c. 1100–1500) associated with university "Schoolmen" like Thomas Aquinas.</note>. Rather, it was the general belief <note>original: Perswasion</note> of the most ancient and learned defenders of incorporeal substance. Specifically, they believed that the *Deity* was not *partly here and partly there*, nor was His *substance* *measurable by yards and rods* <note>original: Poles</note>, as if a certain amount of Him were contained in one room and a specific amount and no more in another, according to their various dimensions. Instead, they held that the whole *undivided Deity* was at once in *every part* of the world, and consequently *not in any place* <note>original: No where Locally</note> in the same manner as physical bodies. ### Chap. V. Unextended Deity, Answered.

Having addressed these prejudices, we shall in the next place show how these ancient **Incorporealists** endeavored to acquit themselves in repelling the several efforts and plausible arguments made against their view. The first of these is this:—That to suppose incorporeal substances are unextended and indivisible is to make them **Absolute Parvitudes** <note>term: Parvitudes: A philosophical term for things that are infinitely small or "littlenesses."</note>, and by doing so, to render them all (even the Deity itself!) contemptible. They argue that such substances must of necessity be either **Physical Minimums** <note>term: Physical Minimums: The smallest possible physical particles that cannot be divided further.</note>, which cannot actually be divided further because of their smallness (if there be any such thing), or else mere **Mathematical Points**, which are not even mentally divisible. If this were true, then thousands of these incorporeal substances, or spirits, might dance together at once upon a needle's point.

<margin>P. 656.</margin>
To which it was long since replied by Plotinus: <note>original: ὥς μικρόν · οὕτω γὰρ οὐδὲν ἧττον καὶ μεριστὸν ἔσται· καὶ οὐ παντὶ αὑτὸ ἐφαρ- μόζει· οὐδ' ἂν αὐξομένῳ τὸ αὐτὸ συνέσται· ἀλλ' οὐδ' οὕτως ὡς σημεῖον, οὐ γὰρ ἓν σημεῖον ὁ ὄγκος, ἀλλ' ἄπειρα ἐν αὐτῷ, οὐδ' ὡς ἐφαρμόζει</note> "As if it were a little thing; for in that case it would still be no less divisible, and it would not adapt itself to the whole, nor would it coexist with that which increases. Nor is it like a point; for a physical mass is not one point, but contains infinite points within it, and it does not adapt itself in that way either." *God and all other incorporeal substances are not so indivisible as if they were parvitudes, or little things, such as physical points; for if they were, they would still be mathematically divisible. Nor are they like mathematical points, which indeed are not bodies or substances at all, but only the boundaries of a line. In neither of these ways could the Deity* coincide <note>original: Congruere</note> *with the world, nor souls with their respective bodies, so as to be present with the whole of them.*

<margin>P. 764.</margin>
Again, he writes particularly concerning the Deity thus: <note>original: οὔτε οὕτως ἀμερὲς, ὡς τὸ σμι- κρότατον, μέγιστον γὰρ ἁπάντων, οὐ μεγέθει ἀλλὰ δυνάμει· ——— ληπτέον δὲ καὶ ἄπειρον αὐτὸν, οὐ τῷ ἀδιεξιτήτῳ, ἢ τοῦ μεγέθους, ἢ τοῦ ἀριθμοῦ, ἀλλὰ τῷ ἀπεριλήπτῳ τῆς δυνάμεως.</note> "God is not indivisible in the sense of being the smallest thing, for he is the greatest of all—not in magnitude, but in power. Furthermore, he is to be acknowledged as infinite, not as if he were a magnitude or a number that could never be fully traversed, but because his power is incomprehensible." *God is not so indivisible as if he were the smallest or least of things, for he is the greatest of all, not in respect of magnitude, but of power. Moreover, as he is indivisible, so is he also to be acknowledged infinite, not as if he were either a magnitude or a number which could never be passed through, but because his power is incomprehensible.*

Moreover, the same philosopher condemns it as a vulgar error—proceeding from the senses and imagination—to think that whatever is unextended and lacks distance must therefore necessarily be "little." He affirms, on the contrary, that the common people are much mistaken regarding true greatness and littleness.

<margin>P. 645.</margin>
<note>original: μέγα νομίζοντες τὸ αἰσθητὸν, ἀπορῶμεν πῶς ἐν μεγάλῳ καὶ τοσούτῳ ἐκείνη ἡ φύσις ἐκτείνεται · τὸ δ' ἐστὶ τοῦτο τὸ λεγόμενον μέγα μικρόν · ὃ δὲ νομί- ζεται μικρὸν εἶναι, μέγα · εἴτε ὅλον ἐπὶ παντὸ τοῦ μέρους φθάνει, μᾶλλον δὲ τοῦτο πανταχόθεν τοῖς αὑτοῦ μέρεσιν ἐπ' ἐκεῖνο ἰὸν, εὑρίσκει αὐτὸ πανταχοῦ πᾶν καὶ μεῖζον ἑαυτοῦ</note> "Because we look upon this sensible world as great, we wonder how that indivisible and unextended nature of the Deity can be present everywhere within it. However, that which is commonly called 'great' is actually small, and that which is imagined to be 'little' is actually great. For the whole of the divine nature reaches every part of the world; or rather, this physical world, approaching that nature from all sides with its own parts, finds it to be everywhere whole and greater than itself." *We commonly looking upon this sensible world as great, wonder how that (indivisible and unextended) nature of the Deity can everywhere comply and be present with it. Whereas that which is vulgarly called great is indeed little, and that which is thus imagined to be little is indeed great. Inasmuch as the whole of this diffuses itself through every part of the other; or rather this whole*

<margin>Sent. p. 243.</margin>
*corporeal universe, in every one of its parts, finds that whole and entire; and therefore greater than itself.* To the same purpose also Porphyry writes: <note>original: τὸ ὄντως ὂν οὔτε μέγα, οὔτε μικρόν ἐστι· (τὸ γὰρ μέγα καὶ μικρὸν κυρίως ὄγκου ἴδια) ἐκβεβηκὸς δὲ τὸ μέγα καὶ μικρόν· καὶ ὑπὲρ τὸ μέγιστον καὶ ὑπὲρ τὸ ἐλάχιστον, ταὐτὸ καὶ ἓν ἀριθμῷ ὄν· εἰ καὶ εὑρίσκεται ἅμα ὑπὸ παντὸς μεγίστου, καὶ ὑπὸ παντὸς ἐλαχίστου εὑρισκόμενον· μήτε ἆρα ὡς μέγι- στον αὐτὸ ὑπονοήσεις· εἰ δὲ μὴ, ἀπορήσεις πῶς μέγιστον ὂν τοῖς ἐλαχίστοις ὄγκοις</note> "That which truly exists is neither great nor small (for 'great' and 'small' are properly properties of physical bulk); rather, it transcends both greatness and smallness. It is above the greatest and above the least, being the same and numerically one, even though it is found simultaneously by every greatest thing and every least thing. Therefore, you should not imagine it as the greatest thing; otherwise, you will be at a loss to explain how, being so great, it is present in the smallest physical masses..."

<header>Incorporeal, not Points or Littleness. BOOK I.</header>

[The Deity] is present, neither diminished nor contracted; nor as something very small, otherwise you will again be at a loss to explain how, being the smallest thing, it is present in the greatest houses, without being multiplied or increased. <note>original: πάρεστι, μὴ μειωθὲν, ἢ συσταλέν· μήτε ὡς ἐλάχιστον, εἰ ὴ μὴ, πάλιν ἀπορήσεις, πῶς ἐλάχιστον ὂν τοῖς μεγίστοις οἴκοις πάρεστι, μὴ πολλαπλασιαθὲν, ἢ ἀυξηθὲν</note> *The Deity, who is the only true Being, is neither Great nor Little (since Great and Little properly belong to physical size or magnitude). Instead, He exceeds both the greatness of every thing that is great, and the littleness of whatever is little. He is indivisible and more at one with Himself than any thing that is little, and more powerful than any thing that is great. Thus, He is above both the greatest and the least, being found—all one and the same—by every greatest and every smallest thing that participates in Him. Therefore, you must not look upon God as the "Greatest thing" (in terms of physical quantity), for then you might well doubt how, being the Greatest, He can be fully present within every smallest thing, neither diminished nor contracted. Nor must you look upon Him as the "Least thing" either; for if you do so, you will again be at a loss as to how, being the Least thing, He can be present within all the greatest physical masses, neither multiplied nor increased.* In a word, the sum of their answer amounts to this: an incorporeal, unextended Deity is neither a **physical point**, because a physical point has distance within it and is mentally divisible; nor is He a **mathematical one**. This is because a mathematical point, though having no size or substance in it, still has a location and position—a point being, according to **Aristotle**, a "unit having location and position." God is not to be conceived as a **parvitude** <note>term: parvitude: an archaic term for "littleness" or a tiny physical thing.</note> or a very **little thing**, because then He could not coincide <note>original: congruere</note> with all the greatest things. Nor is He a **great thing** in terms of physical quantity and extension, because then He could not be fully present within every tiny thing. Nor does true greatness consist of physical mass or size, for all magnitude is ultimately small, since there can be no infinite magnitude, and no finite magnitude can have infinite power, as **Aristotle** previously argued. 

And to conclude: although some people (who are far from being atheists) may joke about that idea of thousands of spirits dancing at once upon a needle’s point, and although atheists may try to mock and ridicule all incorporeal substance in that way, this is based on a clear misunderstanding of the hypothesis and proves nothing at all against it. This is because an unextended substance is not a **parvitude** (as is assumed here), since it has no size at all; nor does it have any place, position, or local motion properly belonging to it. Therefore, it can neither dance upon a needle’s point, nor anywhere else.

<margin>☞</margin>
But in the next place, it is further **objected** that whatever is neither great nor little, whatever occupies no space, and has no place or location among physical bodies, must therefore be an absolute **non-entity** <note>term: non-entity: something that does not exist at all.</note>. This is because magnitude (size) or extension are the very essence of being or existence itself; they argue that there can be neither substance nor quality that is unextended. Since whatever is **extended** is **bodily**, there can be no other substance besides **body**, nor anything **incorporeal**, except in the sense that the word may be used for a **thin** and **subtle body**. In this sense, fire was said by some in Aristotle’s works to be "the most incorporeal of all the elements" and "the most bodiless" <note>original: μάλιστα τῶν στοιχείων ἀσώματον, καὶ ἀσωματώτατον</note>. Aristotle himself used the word in the same manner,

# Chapter 5. Extension and Entity are Not the Same.

When he affirms that all *philosophers* defined the *soul* by three things—*motion*, *sense*, and *incorporeity*—several of those he mentions understood the *soul* to be "incorporeal" only in the sense of being a *thin and subtle body* <note>original: σῶμα λεπτόμερες</note>. In answer to this objection, we may remember that *Plato*, in the passage cited earlier, declares it to be a *common error* <note>original: vulgar error</note> to think that whatever does not take up space, and is in no place, is nothing. He suggests that the origin of this error springs from people adhering too much to those *lower faculties* of *sense* and *imagination*, which are able to conceive of nothing but what is *corporeal* (physical). Accordingly:

<margin>Page 656.</margin>
*Plotinus* says: *Sense indeed—which we rely on when we disbelieve these ideas—tells us of "here" and "there." But Reason dictates that "here" and "there" should be understood in relation to the Deity, not as if He were physically extended across "here" and "there," but because every extended thing, and the various parts of the world, partake everywhere of Him, who remains without distance and unextended.* <note>original: ἡ μὲν αἴσθησις, ᾗ προσέχοντες ἀπιστοῦμεν τοῖς λεγομένοις, λέγουσα ὧδε καὶ ὧδε· ὁ δὲ λόγος τὸ ὧδε καὶ ὧδε φησὶν, οὐκ ἐκταθεῖσαν ὧδε καὶ ὧδε γεγονέναι, ἀλλὰ τὸ ἐκταθὲν πᾶν αὐτῆς μεταληφέναι, ὄντος ἀδιαστάτου αὐτοῦ.</note> To the same purpose:

<margin>Aphorisms, page 242.</margin>
*Porphyry* writes: *We ought therefore, in our inquiries concerning corporeal and incorporeal beings, to preserve the distinct properties of each and not confuse their natures. Especially, we must take care that our fancy and imagination do not impose upon our judgments, leading us to attribute to incorporeal things what properly belongs only to bodies. For we are all accustomed to bodies, but as for incorporeals, scarcely anyone reaches a knowledge of them; people are always wavering and distrusting them as long as they are held under the power of their imagination.* <note>original: δεῖ τοίνυν ἐν ταῖς σκέψεσι κατακρατοῦντας τῆς ἑκατέρου ἰδιότητος, μὴ ἐπαλλάττειν τὰς φύσεις· μᾶλλον δὲ τὰ προσόντα τοῖς σώμασιν, ἢ τοιαῦτα, μὴ φαντάζεσθαι καὶ δοξάζειν περὶ τὸ ἀσώματον· τῶν μὲν γὰρ σωμάτων, ἐν συνηθείᾳ πᾶς· ἐκείνων δὲ μόλις ἐν γνώσει γίνεται, ἀοριστῶν περὶ αὐτά, ἕως ἂν ὑπὸ φαντασίας κρατῆται</note> Later on, he proposes a framework for this: *How we should think of incorporeals, so as not to confuse their natures with physical bodies:* *That the unextended and non-distant Deity is present as a whole in infinite parts of the extended world. He is neither divided—as if applying part to part—nor multiplied into many wholes according to the number of things that partake of Him. Instead, the whole of Him (being numerically one and the same) is present to all parts of the bulky world, and to every individual thing in it, without being divided or multiplied; meanwhile, the world partakes of Him in a divided and partial way.* <note>original: ἐν ἀπείροις μέρεσι τοῦ διαστατοῦ παρὸν ὅλον τὸ ἀδιάστατον, οὔτε μερισθὲν μέρεσι, τῷ μέρει διδὸν μέρος, οὔτε πληθυνθὲν τῷ πλήθει παρέχειν ἑαυτὸ πόλλα πλασιασθέν· ἀλλ’ ὅλον πᾶσί τε τοῖς μέρεσι τοῦ διωγκωμένου, ἑνί τε ἑκάστῳ τοῦ πλήθους, ἀμερῶς καὶ ἀπληθύντως καὶ ὡς ἓν ἀριθμῷ· τὸ δὲ μερικῶς καὶ διῃρημένως ἀπολαύειν αὐτοῦ.</note>

It was granted, therefore, by these *ancients*, that this *unextended and non-distant nature* of *incorporeals* is *unimaginable* <note>original: ἀφάνταστον; literally: "impossible to represent as a mental image"</note>. They concluded that this was the only reason why so many have pronounced it to be *impossible*: because they attended only to *sense* and *imagination*, making them the only measure of *things* and *truth*. Accordingly, it was maintained by several of them (as *Porphyry* tells us) that *imagination* and *intellectual understanding* <note>term: intellection</note> are...

...but **two different names** for one and the same thing. <note>original: ὀνόματος διαφορᾶς προσθέσεως τῇ τοῦ νοῦ ὑποστάσει, καὶ τῇ φαντασίας, ἡ γὰρ ἐν λογικῷ ζώῳ φαντασία δέδοκτο αὐτοῖς νόησις</note> *There is only a difference of names, and no more, between the Mind and Fancy. Fancy and Imagination in rational animals seem to be the same thing as understanding.* But there are many things that no one can have any *phantasm* <note>mental image</note> or *imagination* of, and yet they are nonetheless unquestionably acknowledged by everyone as *entities* or *realities*. From this, it is plain that we must have other *faculties* within us that extend beyond *fancy* and *imagination*. Reason indeed dictates that whatever can either *act* or *be acted upon* must therefore undoubtedly be *something*. However, the idea that whatever is *unextended*—meaning it has no *distinct parts* separated from one another—must therefore be *nothing*, is no *common notion* <note>self-evident truth</note>. Instead, it is the *false suggestion* of *imagination alone* and a *common error*. There is no need to fear at all that a Being *infinitely wise* and *powerful*—which acts upon the whole world and all its parts, *shaping* and *governing* it—should prove to be a *non-entity* merely for want of *bulk* and *extension*. We should not think it *vanishes into nothing* because it does not *swell* out into *space* and *distance* as *bodies* [physical objects] do. Nor does *active force* and *power* itself depend upon *bulk* and *extension*; if it did, then whatever had the greater *bulk* would have the greater *activity*. 

Therefore, there are *two kinds of substances in the universe*. The *first is corporeal* [physical], which are nothing but masses <note>original: ὄγκοι, bulks or tumors</note> devoid of all *self-active power*. The *second is incorporeal* [spiritual], which are *substantial powers, strengths, and activities* <note>original: ἄογκοι δυνάμεις</note>. Though these act upon *bulk* and *extension*, they are themselves *without bulk* and devoid of *physical quantity* and *dimensions*. However, they have a certain "depth" within them in another sense: an *essential profundity*. 

<margin>In Aristotle's Physics, page 3.</margin>
According to this passage from *Simplicius*: <note>original: μεριστὴ μὲν ἁπλῶς ἡ σωματικὴ οὐσία πᾶσα, ἄλλων ἀλλαχοῦ τῶν μορίων κειμένων· ἀμέριστος δὲ εἰλικρινῶς ἡ νοερὰ, πολὺ δὲ βάθος ἔχουσα</note> *All physical substance is simply divisible, as some of its parts lie in one place and some in another. But intellectual substance is purely indivisible and without dimensions, though it has much depth and profundity in another sense.* 

It is evident that there is something *unimaginable* <note>original: ἀφάνταστον</note> even in *matter* itself, whether you suppose it to be *infinitely divisible* or *not*—as you must of necessity suppose one or the other. It is manifest from this that we ought not always to judge *physical things* themselves according to *imagination*. For instance, although *astronomical reasoning* assures us that the *Sun* is really more than a *hundred times* larger than the whole *Earth*, we still cannot possibly *imagine* the *Sun* to be of such a *size*, nor indeed even the *Earth* itself as half as big as we know it to be. The reason for this is partly because we never had a *sense* or *sight* of such *vast size* all at *once*. Furthermore, because our *senses* always represent the *Sun* to us <note>original: ὡς πεδιαῖον</note> *as being a foot in diameter*, and because we are accustomed to always *imagining* it according to the *appearance of our senses*, we are not able to form any *imagination* of it as being much *larger*. Therefore, if *imagination* is not to be *trusted*, nor made the *criterion* or *measure of truth* regarding *sensible things* [objects we can perceive] themselves, much less should it be used for *insensible things* [objects beyond physical perception]. <page-num>781</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER V. Not the Measures of Things.</header>

Ancient **Incorporealists** <note>Those who believe in the existence of non-physical substances, such as the soul or God.</note> argued in this manner: that it is as difficult for us to conceive of a **Substance** whose **Duration** is **Unextended** or **Unstretched** out in **Time** (into **Past**, **Present**, and **Future**, and therefore without **Beginning**) as it is to conceive of that which is **Unextended** in terms of **Parts**, **Place**, or **Space** (in **Length**, **Breadth**, and **Thickness**). Yet **Reason** pronounces that there must necessarily be not only a **Duration** without **Beginning**, but also a **timeless eternity** <note>original: ἄχρονος αἰών</note>, or a **Permanent Duration**, which differs from that **Successive Flux** of **Time** (which is one of **Plato's** **generated things** <note>original: γεννητὰ</note>, or things that had a beginning).

<margin>Page 669.</margin> This parity of **Reason** is insisted upon by **Plotinus** in this way: *“For the same reason that we deny Local Extension to the Deity, we must also deny Temporal Distance to him. We must affirm that God is not in Time, but above Time, in Eternity. For while Time is always scattered and stretched out in length and distance, with one moment following after another, Eternity remains the same, without any flow. Nevertheless, it outlasts Time and transcends its flow, even though Time seems to be stretched and spun out further in length.”* <note>original: διὸ οὐδ' ἐν χρόνῳ, ἀλλὰ παντὸς χρόνου ἔξω, τοῦ μὲν χρόνου σκιδναμένου αἰεὶ πρὸς διάστασιν, τοῦ δ' αἰῶνος ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ μένοντος καὶ κρατοῦντος, καὶ πλείονος ὄντος δυνάμει ἀϊδίῳ, τοῦ ἐπὶ πολλὰ δοκοῦντος ἰέναι χρόνου</note> Now, the reason why we cannot form a **Conception** of such a **Timeless Eternity** is only because we ourselves are **Essentially Involved** in **Time**. Accordingly, our **Conceptions** are **Chained**, **Fettered**, and **Confined** to that narrow and dark dungeon in which we ourselves are imprisoned. Notwithstanding this, our **Freer Faculties** assure us of the **Existence** of a **Being** which far transcends ourselves—namely, one that is **Infinitely Perfect**. By this means, we have a **certain prophetic inkling** <note>original: μαντείαν τινὰ; often translated as "vaticination" or "divination," meaning an intuitive grasp of a higher truth.</note> of such a **Standing Timeless Eternity** as its **Duration**.

But as for that idea of **Immaterial** or **Incorporeal Bodies**, or the notion that God and Human Souls are "incorporeal" only in the sense of being a **thin-parted body** <note>original: σῶμα λεπτόμερες; a "subtle body" made of very fine matter.</note> (such as **Wind** or **Vapor**, **Air**, or **Ether**), it is certain that this is false according to the principles of the most ancient **Atomic Philosophy** (before it was corrupted by atheism). There is no such **Real Quality** as **subtlety** or **thinness** <note>original: tenuity</note> in a fundamental sense (because this is altogether **Unintelligible**). Instead, this **Difference** arises entirely from **Motion** dividing the **invisible parts** and agitating them in every way, together with a certain **Structure** <note>original: contexture</note> of those **Parts**. It is not impossible that the **Finest** and most **Subtle Body** that **exists** might become as **Gross**, **Hard**, **Heavy**, and **Opaque** as **Flesh**, **Earth**, **Stones**, **Lead**, or **Iron**. Conversely, the **Grossest** of these **Bodies**, through **Motion** and a **Different Structure** of **Parts**, might not only be **Crystallized**, but also become as **Thin**, **Soft**, and **Fluid** as the Finest **Ether**. 

So, there is no **Essential Difference** between a **Thick** and **Thin**, a **Gross** and **Fine**, an **Opaque** and **Transparent** <note>original: Pellucide</note>, or a **Hard** and **Soft Body**—these are **Accidental** qualities only. Therefore, there is no reason why **Life** and **Understanding** should be thought to belong to one type of body rather than the other. Besides this, the **Reasons** of the ancient **Incorporealists** (which will be produced later) will **Prove** <note>original: Evince</note> that the **Human Soul** and **Mind** cannot possibly be any **Body** whatsoever, no matter how **Fine**, **Thin**, and **Subtle**, because the **Parts** of a body are always **Divisible** and **Separable** from one another by **Motion**.

<sig>Sfff 2</sig>

<summary>This page argues that God exists in a "timeless eternity" that transcends the successive flow of time, a concept our reason can grasp even if our time-bound imagination cannot. It also refutes the idea that the soul is merely a "subtle body" (like air or ether), arguing that matter is essentially the same whether it is thick or thin, and thus life cannot arise from physical parts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of unextended substances (entities without physical size or spatial parts), specifically responding to the logical objections raised against the idea that an incorporeal being can be present entirely in every part of a body.</meta>

<page-num>782</page-num>
<header>What Unextended, must be, BOOK I.</header>
<sig>S g g g</sig>

But it is further objected against this **unextended nature** of **incorporeal substances** (as they are said to be **all in the whole**, and all in **every part** of that body which they are united to, or act upon) that this is an **absolute contradiction** and **impossibility**. The objection is that if the **whole of God** be in this one point of matter, then there can be nothing at all of Him in the next adjoining point; for that must necessarily be another "whole," and not the same as the former. In the same way, if the whole **human soul** is in this one part of the organized body, then there can be none of it in any other part; and so the **whole is not in the whole**. To this objection, the ancient **incorporealists** <note>Those who believe in the existence of non-physical substances.</note> made this **twofold reply**.

First, by way of **concession**: they admit that it is indeed an **absolute contradiction** for an **extended substance** or **body** to be **all of itself in every part or point of that space** which the whole occupies. Thus **Plotinus** says: <note>original: σώματι ἀδύνατον ἐν πλείοσι τὸ αὐτὸ ὅλον εἶναι, καὶ τὸ μέρος ὅπερ τὸ ὅλον ὑπάρχειν</note> *“It is impossible for a body, or extended substance, to be one and the same—all of it in every part of that space which it possesses—and for every part thereof to be the same with the whole.”* 
<margin>Enneads, Book 4, Chapter 7, page 460.</margin>

But secondly, as for an **unextended and non-distant substance** <note>original: Indistant; meaning a substance that lacks spatial spread or "distance" between parts</note>, which has no parts separate from one another, it is so far from being a **contradiction** that it should be **all of it in every part of that body** which it **acts** upon, that it is **impossible** it should be otherwise—such as only a part being in a part of the body. If an equal quantity of both were to coexist together, it would mean that an **unextended substance** is actually **extended**. We say it is contradictory to the nature of that substance—which is supposed to be <note>original: ἀμεγέθης, ἄποσος, ἀδιάστατος, ἀμερὴς, ἀδιαίρετος</note> **devoid of magnitude, quantity, and parts; non-distant and indivisible**—that it should be joined with an **extended body** in any way other than this, which is looked upon as such "conjuring"; namely, that the **whole of it should be present with, and act upon, every part thereof.**

<margin>Page 662.</margin>
Thus **Plotinus** states: <note>original: οὗτος ὁ λόγος ἐξ αὐτοῦ τοῦ πράγματος, καὶ τῆς οὐσίας ἀλλότριον οὐδὲν, οὐδ' ἐκ τῆς ἑτέρας φύσεως ἑλκύσας</note> *“This form of doctrine concerning incorporeals is necessarily taken from the thing itself (namely, their nature as unextended) and has nothing in it foreign to that essence, as if it were confusing the corporeal nature with it.”* **Whatever is unextended and non-distant** cannot possibly **coexist** with an **extended substance** point-by-point and part-by-part. Instead, it must of necessity be <note>original: ὅλον ἓν καὶ ταὐτὸν ἀριθμῷ</note> **all of it, one and the same numerically**; that is (like itself), **undividedly, in every part of that** which it acts upon. Therefore the word "whole" in this context—when it is said that **the whole of God** is in **every part of the world**, and the **whole soul in every part of the body**—is not to be taken in a **positive sense** (meaning a whole consisting of parts laid out next to each other), but in a **negative sense only**, for <note>original: μὴ μεμερισμένον</note> **a whole undivided**. So the meaning is no more than this: that **God is not divided** in the world, nor the **soul divided** in the body, with a **part here and a part there**; but the **Divine** <note>original: Τὸ θεῖον</note> is **everywhere, all of it, undividedly**.
<margin>Page 662.</margin>

Thus again **Plotinus** says: <note>original: εἰ ἦν πανταχοῦ Θεὸς, οὐχ οἷόν τε μεμερισμένον· οὐ γὰρ ἂν ἔτι πανταχοῦ αὐτὸς εἴη, ἀλλ' ἕκαστον αὐτοῦ μέρος, τὸ μὲν ὧ...</note> *“If God were everywhere, He could not be divided; for if He were, He would no longer be everywhere Himself, but each part of Him would be in one place...”*

<summary>This page defends the concept that incorporeal beings like God or the soul are "all in every part" of a body by explaining that, since they lack physical size and parts (unextended), they cannot be spread out point-by-point like matter.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Incorporealists, unextended substance, soul and body, omnipresence, indivisibility, magnitude, metaphysics</keywords>

--- Page 801 ---
<meta>This page continues the philosophical defense of "unextended substances"—beings that exist without physical size or parts. The author is addressing the logical puzzle of how God or a soul can be "all in every part" of a physical space without being divided like matter.</meta>

<page-num>783</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER V. All in Every Part.</header>

<note>original: ὅτι, τὸ ὃ ὡδὶ ἔσται, αὐτὸς οὐχ εἷς ἔτι ἔσται...</note> Because, if he were here in this specific way, he would no longer be one; just as if a **magnitude** <note>A physical size or dimension.</note> were cut into many pieces, all those parts would no longer be that original whole. Furthermore, he would be a **body**. If these things are impossible, then that previously disbelieved idea would reappear: to think that in a whole human being, God is simultaneously everywhere, and yet remains the same whole in every place.

*If, therefore, God is everywhere, it cannot possibly be that he is so **dividedly**. Because then he himself would not be everywhere, but only a **part** of him here and a **part** of him there throughout the whole world, as he would not be one undivided thing. Moreover, this would be the same as if a **magnitude** were cut and divided into many parts, where none of those parts could be that whole magnitude. Lastly, this would be the very same as making God a **body**.* 

Now, if these things are **impossible**, then that much-disbelieved concept (often looked upon as a puzzling **riddle** <note>original: Griphus; a complex puzzle or enigma.</note> or rather as **contradictory nonsense**) must be an **undoubted truth** according to the **common notions of mankind**: that God is everywhere. That is to say, He is all of himself—the same whole, undivided—everywhere. The sum of all this is that although it is an **absolute contradiction** for a **body** or a **physical quantity** <note>original: Quantum.</note> to be **all in every part** <note>original: ὁμοῦ πᾶν</note> of the space it occupies, it is no contradiction at all for an **unextended and "indistant" being** <note>A being that lacks spatial spread or "distance" between internal parts.</note> to be all of itself **undividedly** in every part of the body it **acts** upon. On the contrary, it would be flatly contradictory to say that it is only **part of it in a part** of the body, as that would mean dividing an **indivisible thing** into parts.

### The Fourth and Last Objection

The **fourth and last objection** against **incorporeal and unextended substance** concerns the **lack of location** <note>original: Illocality.</note> and **immobility** that would follow for **human souls** and other **finite particular spirits**, such as **daemons** or **angels**. 

The objection argues that it is not only **absurd** in itself to suppose these **finite and particular beings** are "nowhere and everywhere" (from which it would seem to follow that they might **act** upon the entire **corporeal universe** or know everything happening everywhere). It also argues that this **concept** contradicts the **very principles of religious people** themselves and is clearly proven wrong by them. They universally acknowledge that **human souls**, upon departing the **body** at death, **locally move** from there into a certain other **place** called **Hades**, **Hell**, or the **Underworld** <note>original: Inferi.</note>. 

Now, the latter part of this objection must be answered **first**. This is indeed something that the ancient **defenders of incorporeal substance** (as unextended) were aware of—that the **commonly received tradition of human souls** going into **Hades** after death might be used as an objection against them. To satisfy this, **Plotinus** suggests these **two things**:

First, <note>original: τὸ μὲν εἰς Ἅδου γίνεσθαι, εἰ μὲν ἐν τῷ Ἀϊδῇ τὸ χωρὶς λέγεται;</note> *that if by **Hades** is meant nothing but* <note>original: τὸ ἀιδὲς</note> *the **invisible** (as it often is), then "going into Hades" signifies nothing more than the soul no longer being vitally united to this earthly body, but acting independently by itself; thus, it has no necessary "place" included in the concept.* 
<margin>Enneads, Book 6, Book 4, Chapter 16.</margin>

Secondly, <note>original: Εἰ δέ τινα χείρω τόπον· τί θαυμαστόν; ἐπεὶ καὶ νῦν ὃ τὸ σῶμα ἡμῶν ἐν τῷ τόπῳ κἀκείνη λέγεται ἐκεῖ· ἀλλ᾽ οὐ χ᾽ ὅτι ἔτι σώματι; ἢ τὸ εἴδωλον εἰ μὴ ἀποσπασθείη, πῶς οὐκ ἐκεῖ ὃ τὸ εἴδωλον;</note> *But if by Hades is understood a **certain worse place** (as it sometimes is), what is the wonder? For even now, while our body is in a place, the soul is also said to be "there"—but not because it is itself a body. Or, if the soul's image <note>The "eidolon" or lower aspect of the soul that stays connected to the physical realm.</note> is not torn away from the body, how can that image not be in that place?*

<summary>This page argues that God must be present "all in every part" of the universe because He is indivisible and non-physical. It also addresses the objection that if souls are non-spatial, they could not "move" to Hades after death, suggesting Hades may simply refer to an invisible state rather than a physical location.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the relationship between the soul and the physical world. Specifically, it addresses the Neoplatonic debate over whether a soul can ever exist without some form of body, even after death.</meta>

<page-num>784</page-num>
<header>Souls always United to some BOOK I.</header>

What wonder is this? Since even now, wherever our body is, our soul is said to reside in that same place? But you will reply: how can this be, when there is no longer any body left? We answer that if the "idol" <note>original: *eidolon*; in this context, an image, shadow, or "ghost-body" that reflects the soul.</note> of the soul is not quite separated from it, why should the soul itself not be said to be there as well, where its idol is? By the "idol of the soul," *Plotinus* seems to mean an airy or spirit-like body, energized and brought to life by the soul, which clings to it after death. 

But when the same philosopher supposes that this very idol of the soul is also separable from it—and that it can even exist on its own, going alone into *Hades* (or the "worse place") while the soul itself lives only in the *Intelligible World* (where there is no place or distance), lodged in the **Naked Deity**—having nothing at all of a body hanging about it, and being now not a part but the whole, situated neither here nor there; in this "high flight" of his, he <margin>Enneads Book 4, Chapter 3, Section 4.</margin> is simultaneously absurdly paradoxical by dividing the life of the soul into two, and he forgot the doctrine of his own school. As he himself mentions elsewhere, the school's doctrine was this: <note>original: τὴν ἡμετέραν ψυχὴν τὸ δὲ μὲν σῶμα καταλείψειν, οὐ πάντη δὲ ἔξω σώματός ἔσεσθαι</note> *that our soul, though it shall quit this body, yet shall it never be entirely disunited from every kind of body.* 

Therefore, *Porphyrius* <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD), a student of Plotinus and a major Neoplatonist philosopher.</note>, when answering the same objection—though he was otherwise very devoted to *Plotinus* and uses his language here—departs from him on this point. He adheres instead to the ancient *Pythagorean tradition*, which (as will appear later) was this: *that human souls are always united to some body or other.*

<margin>Aphorisms, p. 232.</margin> <note>original: Ὥσπερ τὸ ἐπὶ γῆς εἶναι ψυχῇ ἐστιν, οὐ τὸ γῆς ἐπιβαίνειν, ὡς τὰ σώματα· τὸ δὲ προεστάναι σώματος, ὃ γῆς ἐπιβαίνει· οὕτω καὶ ἐν ᾍδου εἶναι ἐστι ψυχῇ, ὅταν προεστήκῃ εἰδώλῳ, φύσιν μὲν ἔχοντος εἶναι ἐν τόπῳ, σκότος δὲ τὴν ὑπόστασιν κεκτημένῳ· ὥστε εἰ ὁ ᾍδης ὑπόγειός ἐστι τόπος σκοτεινός, ἡ ψυχὴ ἐν ᾍδου γίνεται ἐφελκομένη τὸ εἴδωλον· ἐξελθούσῃ γὰρ αὐτῇ τοῦ στερεοῦ σώματος, τὸ πνεῦμα συνομαρτεῖ, ὃ ἐκ τῶν σφαιρῶν συνελέξατο· ἐπεὶ δὲ διήκει τὸ βαρὺ πνεῦμα, καὶ ἔνυγρον, ἄχρι τῶν ὑπογείων τόπων, οὕτω καὶ αὐτὴ λέγεται χωρεῖν ὑπὸ γῆν· οὐχ ὅτι ἡ αὐτὴ οὐσία μεταβαίνῃ τόπους, καὶ ἐν τόποις γίνεται· ἀλλ' ὅτι τῶν πεφυκότων σωμάτων, τόπους μεταβαίνειν, σχέσεις ἀναδέχεται.</note>

> *Just as the soul's being here upon Earth,* (he says) *is not its moving up and down upon it in the manner of physical bodies, but rather its presiding over a body which moves upon the Earth; so its being in Hades is nothing but its presiding over that "idol"—that enlivened vaporous body whose nature it is to be in a physical place and which has a dark substance. Therefore, if Hades is understood as an underground and dark place, the soul may nevertheless be said to go into Hades because, when it quits this gross earthy body, a more spirit-like and subtle body—collected from the planetary spheres (or elements)—still accompanies it. Since this spirit-body is moist and heavy, and naturally descends to underground places, the soul itself may be said in this sense to go "under the Earth" with it. This is not because the substance of the soul itself passed from one place to another, but because of its relationship and vital union to a body that does so.* 

In this passage, *Porphyrius* adds—contrary to the view of *Plotinus*—that the soul is never completely naked of all body. Instead, it always has some body or other joined with it that is suitable and agreeable to its own present disposition (either a purer or an impurer one). But upon first quitting this gross earthy body, the spirit-like body which accompanies it (as its "vehicle") must necessarily go away fouled and thickened with gross va-
