...vapors and steams of the body; until the soul afterwards, by degrees purging itself, this body becomes at length *a dry splendor, which has no misty obscurity, nor casts any shadow.*

<margin>Introduction to Aristotle’s *On the Soul* (*De Anima*)</margin>
But because this doctrine of the **Ancient Incorporealists** <note>Those who believe the soul is a non-physical substance distinct from the body.</note>, concerning the human soul being always (after death) united to some body or other, is more fully declared by **Philoponus** <note>John Philoponus (c. 490 – c. 570), a Christian philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note> than by any other that we have yet met with, we shall here excerpt some passages out of him about it. First, therefore, he declares this as his own opinion, agreeable to the sense of the best philosophers:

*The rational soul, as to its energy, is separable from all body; but the irrational part or life of it is separable only from this gross body, and not from all body whatsoever. Instead, it has (after death) a spirituous or airy body in which it acts. This, I say, is a true opinion, as shall be proved by us afterward.* <note>original: τὴν μὲν λογικὴν χωριστὴν, τὴν δ' ἄλογον, τότε μὲν χωριστὴν, ἄλλῳ μέντοι τινὸς σώματι ἀχώριστον, λέγω δὴ τῷ πνευματικῷ, ὅπερ ἀληθὴς δόξα, ὡς δείξομεν.</note>

And again:

*The irrational life of the soul does not have its entire being in this gross, earthy body, but remains even after the soul's departure from it, having for its vehicle and subject the spirituous body. This body itself is also compounded out of the four elements, but receives its name from the predominant part—namely, air—just as this gross body of ours is called "earthy" from what is most predominant in it.* <note>original: ἡ δὲ ἄλογος οὐκ ἔτι ἐν τούτῳ ἔχει τὸ εἶναι, ἐπιδιαμένει γὰρ καὶ μετὰ ἔξοδον τὴν ἐκ τούτου τῆς ψυχῆς, ὄχημα καὶ ὑποκείμενον ἔχουσα τὸ πνευματικὸν σῶμα· ὃ καὶ αὐτό ἐστι μὲν ἐκ τῶν τεσσάρων, λέγεται δὲ ἐκ τοῦ πλεονάζοντος τοῦ ἀέρος· ὥσπερ καὶ τοῦτο γήϊνον, λέγεται ἐκ τοῦ πλεονάζοντος.</note>

Thus we see that, according to Philoponus, the human soul after death does not merely exercise its rational powers and think only of metaphysical and mathematical notions or abstract things (which are in neither time nor place). It also exercises its lower sensitive and irrational faculties, which it could not possibly do were it not then **vitally united** to some body. This body accompanying the soul he calls **pneumatical**—that is (not "spiritual" in the sense used in Scripture, but) **spirituous**, vaporous, or airy.

Let us, therefore, in the next place, see what rational account Philoponus can give of this doctrine of the ancients, and of his own opinion agreeably thereunto.

<margin>Ibid.</margin>
*It is agreed—or rather, demonstrated—that our human soul (in those who are not purged) arrives in Hades after its exit from the body, to suffer punishment there for a life not well lived. For Providence does not only care for our existence, but also for our well-being. Therefore, the soul is not neglected when it has slipped into an unnatural state, but receives the appropriate care. And since its sinning occurred because of a love of pleasure, it follows of necessity that its purification must occur through pain; for in this case, as in medicine, opposites are the cures for opposites. For this reason, the soul being purified in the subterranean places of judgment suffers through punishment. But if the soul were entirely incorporeal, it would be impossible for it to suffer. How, then, is it punished? It is absolutely necessary, then, that some body be attached to it, which—by being excessively divided or compressed, or by being subjected to extreme cold or heat—causes the soul to feel pain through its sympathy with that body. What kind of body, then, is it that is attached to the soul? Certainly not this physical one, for that has been dissolved into the elements from which it was composed. Rather, it is this "spirituous body" we are talking about. Therefore, in this body, as in a subject, reside anger, desire, and the rest.* <note>original: ἡ ψυχὴ ἡ ἡμετέρα... καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς.</note>

<summary>This page explores the philosophical argument that the soul remains attached to a subtle "spirituous" or "pneumatical" body after death. According to Philoponus, this airy vehicle allows the soul to experience sensory purification and punishment in the afterlife, which would be impossible for a purely incorporeal entity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "spirituous body" or "airy vehicle" of the soul, focusing on its role in the afterlife and the physical manifestation of ghosts.</meta>

# The Soul’s Spirituous or Airy [Body] Book I.

(If the soul is not purified and cleansed in this life), after its departure out of this body, it is acknowledged, or rather *demonstrated*, to go into *Hades* <note>original: *Hades*; here referring to the underworld or a state of post-mortem existence</note>, there to receive *punishment* for its past evil *actions*. For *Providence* does not only take care of our being, but also of our *well-being*. Therefore, though the *soul* has lapsed into a *preternatural state* <term>original: *Preter-Natural State*; a condition contrary to its original, divine nature</term>, it is not neglected by *Providence*, but has *appropriate care* taken of it in order to its *recovery*. And since sinning had its *origin* from the *desire of pleasure*, it *must of necessity be cured by pain*. For here also *contraries are the cures of contraries*. Therefore the *soul*, needing to be purified, is *punished and pained* in those *subterranean courtrooms and prisons* in order to its *amendment*. 

But if the *soul* be *incorporeal* <note>bodiless or non-physical</note>, it is *impossible* for it to *suffer*. How then can it be *punished*? There must of *necessity be some body joined with it* which—being immoderately *constricted* or *agitated, solidified, or dissolved, and discordantly moved* by *heat and cold* or the like—may make the *soul feel pain* by reason of *sympathy* <note>the philosophical concept that the soul feels what happens to its connected body</note>, as it is here in this life. What *body*, therefore, *is it* that is then *conjoined with the soul* after the dissolution of that *earthy body* into its *elements*? Certainly it can be no other than this *pneumatical* <term>spiritual or airy</term> or *spirituous body which we now speak of*. For in this are *seated*, as their *subject*, the *irascible and concupiscible passions* <note>original: *Iraſcible and Concupiſcible Paſſions*; the classical division of emotions into "anger/spirit" and "desire/appetite"</note>, and they are inseparable from *it*; nor could they be in the *soul* if it were *disunited from all body*. And that *soul* which is freed from *these* would be immediately *freed from the cycle of birth*; nor would it be involved in those *subterranean courtrooms and prisons*, but would be carried up aloft to the *higher celestial regions*, and so on. 

After which he endeavors further to confirm *this opinion from common phenomena*: 

*Furthermore, it is even more evident what the spirituous body is, and that anger and desire are inseparable from it, by the very activity of things. For why do shadowy phantoms appear at graves? For certainly the soul itself is not shaped, nor is it visible at all. But they say that impure souls, after the departure from this body, wander for some time with the spirit, and this spirit is shown around graves. Therefore, one must care for a good life; for they say by this spirit, thickened from a wicked diet, the soul is dragged down toward the passions in this life as well.* <note>original: δῆλον δ' ἔτι μᾶλλον ὅτι τί ἐστι τὸ πνευματικὸν σῶμα, καὶ τούτου ἀχώριστα θυμὸς καὶ ἐπιθυμία, ἐξ αὐτῆς τῶν πραγμάτων ἐνεργείας· πόθεν γὰρ ἐν τοῖς τάφοις τὰ σκιοειδῆ φαίνονται φαντάσματα; οὐ γὰρ δήγε ἡ ψυχὴ ἐσχημάτισται, ἢ ὅλως ἐστὶν ὁρατή· ἀλλὰ φασὶ τὰς ἀκαθάρτους ψυχὰς, μετὰ τὴν ἔξοδον τούτου τοῦ σώματος πλανᾶσθαι ἐπὶ τινα χρόνον μετὰ τοῦ πνεύματος, καὶ τοῦτο παραδεικνύναι περὶ τοὺς τάφους· διὸ φροντιστέον εὐζωΐας· ὑπὸ τούτου γάρ φασι τοῦ πνεύματος, παχυνθέντος ἐκ μοχθηρᾶς διαίτης, κατασπᾶσθαι περὶ τὰ πάθη τὴν ψυχήν</note> 

*Furthermore, that there is such a pneumatical (spirituous, vaporous, or airy) body, which accompanies unpurified souls after death, is evident also from the phenomena themselves. For what other account can be given of those specters or phantasms which appear shadow-like about graves or sepulchers? Since the soul itself is neither of any figure, nor yet at all visible. Wherefore these ancients say that impure souls, after their departure out of this body, wander here up and down for a certain time in their spirituous, vaporous, and airy body, appearing about sepulchers and haunting their former habitations. For which cause there is great reason that we should take care of living well, as also of abstaining from a fouler and grosser diet; these ancients telling us likewise that this spirituous body of ours, being fouled and thickened by evil diet, is apt to render the soul, in this life also, more vulnerable to the disturbances of passions.* 

And here *Philoponus* goes on to gratify us with a further *account* of some other of the opinions of these *ancients* concerning this *spirituous or airy body* accompanying the soul after death: 

*For they say it also has something of the vegetative life, for it is even nourished. It is nourished, however, not like this body, but through vapors; not through specific organs, but the whole absorbing through the whole, so to speak, as sponges do...* <note>original: ἔχει γάρ τι καὶ αὐτό φασι τῆς φυτικῆς ζωῆς, καὶ γὰρ τρέφεσθαι. τρέφεσθαι δ' οὐχ οὕτως ὡς τοῦτο τὸ σῶμα, ἀλλὰ δι᾿ ἀτμῶν οὐ διὰ μορίων, ἀλλ᾿ ὅλον δι᾿ ὅλου, φέρε εἰπεῖν, ὡς οἱ σπόγγοι</note>

<meta>catchword: ...receive [δέχονται]</meta>

It uses the appearance of ghosts near graves as evidence for this subtle body and suggests that a poor diet can "thicken" this spirit, making the soul more prone to earthly passions.</summary>

# CHAP. V. Body (Supposed) after Death.

They receive the vapors; for this reason, serious people take care to maintain a thinner and drier diet, so that the spirit may not be thickened but rather refined. They say they also use purifications for this purpose; for while this earthy body is washed with water, that spirit-body is cleansed by purifications through vapors; for it is nourished by some vapors and cleansed by others. They say it is not organized into parts, but acts as a whole throughout, both in its senses and in its perception of sensible things. Because of this, Aristotle also says in his *Metaphysics* that there is properly only one sense and only one sensory organ. <note>original Greek: δέχονται τὰς ἀτμὸς· διὰ τοῦτο φροντίζουσιν οἱ σπουδαῖοι τῆς λεπτοτέρας διαίτης καὶ ξηροτέρας, διὰ τὸ μὴ παχύνεσθαι τὸ πνεῦμα ἀλλὰ λεπτύνασθαι... καὶ τὸ κυρίως αἰσθητήριον ἕν.</note> They further add *that the soul also exercises something of a plant-like and formative life* <term>original: Plantal and Plastick Life; referring to basic biological functions like growth and the shaping of the body</term> *within those spiritual or airy bodies after death. These bodies are also nourished, though not in the same way as our gross, earthy bodies are here, but rather by vapors. This nourishment does not occur through specific parts or organs, but throughout their entire being (like sponges), as they soak up these vapors everywhere. For this reason, those who are wise will also take care in this life to maintain a thinner and drier diet, so that the spiritual body (which we possess even now within our grosser body) may not be clogged and thickened, but instead refined.* 

Over and above this, *those ancients also made use of purifications* <term>original: Catharms</term> *for the same purpose. For just as this earthy body is washed by water, so is that spiritual body cleansed by purifying vapors; some of these vapors are nutritious, while others are purgative.* Moreover, these ancients further declared *concerning this spiritual body: that it was not organized into distinct organs, but instead exercised all functions of sense throughout its entire form. The soul hears, sees, and perceives all sensible things through every part of it. For this reason, Aristotle himself affirms in his Metaphysics that there is properly only one sense and only one sensory organ.* <note>original: *Metaphysicks*</note> By this *one sensory organ*, he means the *spirit*, or *subtle airy body*, in which the *sensitive power* immediately perceives all variety of sensible things through the whole of itself. 

And if it is asked, *“How does it happen, then, that this spirit appears to have organs in tombs, and most commonly in human form, but sometimes in the form of other animals?”* To this, those ancients replied *that their frequent appearance in human form results from being thickened by a poor diet. They are then, as it were, stamped with the form of this external surrounding body in which they reside—just as crystal is shaped and colored like the things it is fastened to or reflects. Their occasional appearance in other forms comes from the imaginative power* <term>original: Phantastick Power</term> *of the soul itself, which can transform this spiritual body into any shape at will. For being airy, when it is condensed and fixed, it becomes visible; and again, it becomes invisible and vanishes from sight when it is expanded and thinned.*

Now, from these passages cited from *Philoponus* <note>John Philoponus (c. 490–570 AD), an Alexandrian philosopher and commentator on Aristotle</note>, it further appears that the ancient defenders of the soul’s immortality did not believe human souls were completely stripped "stark naked" from all bodies after death. Instead, they believed that most souls possessed a certain spiritual, vaporous, or airy body that accompanied them, though with varying degrees of purity or impurity. They also conceived that this spiritual body (or at least some part of it) clings to the soul even during this life, before death, as its internal garment or clothing, which then remains with it...

# The Luciform Body, etc. Third, Book I.

...when that other *gross, earthly part* of the body is shed at death like an *outer garment*. Some have even been inclined to think (based on certain *historical phenomena* <note>The author is likely referring to accounts of ghosts or out-of-body experiences.</note>) that these two are so distinct that it is not impossible for this *spirit-body*, together with the *soul*, to be *locally separated* from the other *grosser body* for some time before death, and even without death occurring. Indeed, this much cannot be denied: our *soul* acts not only immediately upon *bones, flesh, and brains*, and other such *gross parts* of this body, but first and chiefly upon the *animal spirits* <term>In early modern medicine, "animal spirits" were a subtle fluid believed to act as the intermediary between the soul and the physical body, carrying signals through the nerves.</term> as the immediate instruments of *sense and imagination*. It is by their vigor and activity that the other heavy and unwieldy bulk of the body is so nimbly moved. Therefore, we know of no reason why we may not agree here with *Porphyry* <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher.</note>, who said: *The blood is the food and nourishment of the spirit (that is, that subtle body called the animal spirits), and this spirit is the vehicle of the soul, or the more immediate seat of life.* <note>original: τὸ αἷμα νομὴ καὶ τροφὴ ἐστι τοῦ πνεύματος, τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα ὄχημα τῆς ψυχῆς</note>

Nevertheless, the same *Philoponus* <note>John Philoponus (c. 490–570 AD) was an Alexandrian philosopher and theologian.</note> adds there that, according to these ancients, besides the *terrestrial body* and this *spiritual and airy body*, there is yet a *third kind of body* of a higher rank than either of the former. This body belongs specifically to such *souls* after death that are purged and cleansed from *corporeal affections, lusts, and passions*. It was called by them the *luciform, celestial, and eternal body*. <note>original: σῶμα αὐγοειδὲς, and οὐράνιον, and ἀΐδιον</note> The soul (he says) continues in either the *terrestrial* or the *airy body* only so long:

> *...until, having purified itself, it is carried upward, freed from the cycle of rebirth. Then it puts away both anger and desire at once, together with this second vehicle or body which we call "spirituous." For these ancients say there is another heavenly body, always joined with the soul and eternal, which they call "luciform" or "star-like." For the soul, being a thing of this universe, must necessarily have some part of the world as a province assigned to it which it may govern. And since the soul is always in motion and ought always to act, it must have a body eternally joined with it which it may always bring to life. For these reasons, they affirm that the soul always has a luciform body.* <note>original: ἕως ἑαυτὴν καθάρασα ἀνενεχθῇ, τῆς γενέσεως ἀπαλλαγεῖσα... διὰ ταῦτα οὖν τὸ αὐγοειδές φασι σῶμα αὐτὴν ἀεὶ ἔχειν</note>

This *lucid and ethereal body of the soul* is a thing often mentioned by other writers as well, such as *Proclus* in his commentary upon the *Timaeus*: <margin>P. 290.</margin> *The human soul also has (he says) such an ethereal vehicle belonging to it, as Plato himself suggests; for Plato says that the Creator placed the soul into a vehicle. For every soul must, before inhabiting mortal bodies, use eternal and easily moved bodies, since it possesses the power of movement as part of its essence.* <note>original: καὶ τῆς ἀνθρωπίνης ψυχῆς ἐξήρτηται τι τοιοῦτον ὄχημα αἰθέριον, ὡς αὐτός φησιν· ἐμβιβάζαι γοῦν εἰς ὄχημα καὶ αὐτήν φησι τὸν δημιουργόν· καὶ γὰρ πᾶσαν ψυχὴν ἀνάγκη πρὸ τῶν θνητῶν σωμάτων, ἀϊδίοις καὶ εὐκινήτοις χρῆσθαι σώμασιν, ὡς κατ’ οὐσίαν ἔχουσαν τὸ κινεῖν</note>

It cites ancient authorities like Porphyry, Philoponus, and Proclus to argue that the soul always requires a body of some level of refinement to act within the world.</summary>

### CHAPTER V. The Luciform and Heavenly Body.

The philosopher Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher who summarized much of the ancient Greek philosophical tradition.</note> suggests this when he affirms that the *Demiurge* <term>original: Demiurgus; the "Architect" or Creator of the universe in Platonic philosophy</term> at first placed the soul in a *Chariot*. He argues that of necessity, every soul, before inhabiting this *mortal body*, must have an *eternal* and easily *movable body*, because it is *essential* for the soul to move. Elsewhere, the same *Proclus* writes: <margin>P. 164.</margin> "While we remain above, we have no need of these divided organs which are attached to us as we descend into this world of generation <note>original: ἄνω μένοντες οὐδὲν δεόμεθα... αἰσθήσεις</note>; but the uniform lucid or splendid vehicle is sufficient, since it has all the senses united within it." This doctrine of the *unorganized luciform* and *spirituous vehicles* seems to have been derived from *Plato*. In his *Epinomis*, Plato writes the following concerning a *good* and *wise* man after *death*: "Of whom, whether I be in jest or earnest, I constantly affirm that when he fulfills his destiny in death, he shall no longer possess this variety of senses which we have now; instead, having received only a single portion and having become one instead of many, he will be happy." <note>original: ὃν καὶ διϊσχυρίζομαι... εὐδαίμονα ἔσεσθαι</note>

Furthermore, *Hierocles* <note>Hierocles of Alexandria was a 5th-century Neoplatonist.</note> insists much upon this *luciform and ethereal body*, "which the oracles also call the thin and subtle vehicle, or chariot of the soul." <note>original: ὃ καὶ ψυχῆς λεπτὸν ὄχημα οἱ χρησμοὶ καλοῦσι</note> By these "oracles," he undoubtedly means the *Magical* or *Chaldean Oracles* mentioned before. Among those still surviving under that title, there seems to be a clear acknowledgment of these *two vehicles of the soul*, or its *internal garments*: the *spirituous* body and the *luciform* body. The latter is enigmatically called the *Plain Superficies* <term>An "extreme surface" or a flat, two-dimensional-like state of being, used here to describe something incredibly thin and subtle.</term> in these words: "Take care not to defile or contaminate the spirit, nor to make the plain surface deep." <note>original: μὴ πνεῦμα μολύνῃς, μηδὲ βαθύνῃς τὸ Ἐπίπεδον</note>

For this is how *Psellus* <note>Michael Psellus (c. 1017–1078) was a Byzantine philosopher and historian.</note> explains that oracle: "The Chaldean philosophers bestow upon the soul two internal tunics or vestments. One they called the 'pneumatical' or spirituous body, which is woven for the soul out of the gross, sensible body (being its thinner and more subtle part). The other is the luciform vestment of the soul, pure and translucent, and this is what is here called the 'plain surface'." <note>original: δύο χιτῶνας ἐπενδύουσι... Ἐπίπεδον</note> This, says *Pletho* <note>Gemistus Pletho (c. 1355–1452) was a Greek scholar and Neoplatonist.</note>, is not to be understood as if it lacked *three dimensions* (for it is still a *body*), but only to emphasize its *subtlety* and *thinness*. 

Therefore, when the aforementioned *Hierocles* also calls this *luciform* and *ethereal body* the "spiritual vehicle of the rational soul," <note>original: τὸ πνευματικὸν ὄχημα τῆς λογικῆς ψυχῆς</note> he does not use the word "spiritual" in the same sense as *Philoponus* and others. He does not intend to confuse this *ethereal body* with that other *spirituous* or *airy body* and make them one and the same. Instead, he styles it "spiritual" in a higher sense (one that comes close to the language of *Scripture*), as being a body more *suitable* and *naturally related* to that *highest and most divine part of the soul*—the mind or reason—than the other *terrestrial body* is. For that reason, the physical body is also called by the same *Hierocles* (as well as by *St. Paul*) the "animal or natural bo-..." <note>original: σῶμα ψυχικόν; Hierocles and Paul both use this term to describe the physical, biological body as opposed to the "spiritual body."</note>

It explores how ancient philosophers like Proclus, Plato, and Hierocles viewed these subtle bodies as the soul's true garments once it is purified of earthly matter.</summary>

It cites Virgil's Aeneid and Neoplatonic philosophers to show that these concepts were rooted in ancient tradition.</meta>

body.) Thus, this *Spiritual Body* mentioned by *Hierocles* is not the *Airy Body*, but the *Ethereal Body*. It is the same as the "divine body" <note>original: θεσπέσιον σῶμα (*thespesion sōma*)</note> described by *Synesius*. This distinction of *two interior vehicles* or *coverings of the soul*, in addition to the *outer vestment* of the *terrestrial body* (which *Plato* called "the shell-like body" <note>original: τὸ ὀστρεῶδες (*to ostreōdes*); a metaphor comparing the physical body to an oyster shell.</note>), is not a mere invention of the later *Platonists* after the rise of *Christianity*. Instead, it is a *tradition* passed down from *antiquity*. This appears plainly from *Virgil* in the sixth book of his *Aeneid*. Though not commonly understood this way, he first writes about the *spirit-like* or *Airy Body* in which unpurified souls receive *punishment* after death:

> "Even when life leaves them with the final light, all evils do not completely depart from the wretched souls, nor do all bodily plagues vanish. It is unavoidable that many stains, long ingrained, should grow deep into their being in strange ways. Therefore, they are disciplined with punishments and pay the price for their former sins. Some are stretched out, empty, hanging in the winds; for others, the stain of crime is washed away under a vast whirlpool or burned out with fire." <note>original: *Quin & Supremo cum Lumine Vita reliquit... Infectum eluitur Scelus, aut exuritur Igni.*</note>

And then he writes again of the other *Pure, Ethereal, and Fiery Body* in this manner:

> "Until a long day, when the cycle of time is complete, has removed the hardened stain and left pure the ethereal sense and the fire of simple air." <note>original: *Donec Longa dies perfecto temporis Orbe... Æthereum Sensum, atque Aurai Simplicis Ignem.*</note>

As observed before, the *ancient defenders* of the *soul's immortality* believed that, besides this *terrestrial body*, the soul possessed another *spirit-like* or *Airy Body*. They conceived that this body not only accompanied the soul after death but also clung to it during this life as its *interior vest* or *inner layer*. (By this, they probably meant what is commonly called the *animal spirits* <note>In early medicine, "animal spirits" were thought to be a subtle fluid that carried instructions from the brain through the nerves.</note>, which spread from the *brain* through the *nerves* throughout the whole *body*). In the same way, it is certain that many of them—supposing the soul to have a *third Luciform* or *Ethereal Body* in addition to the two mentioned—conceived that this also adhered to the soul even in this *mortal life* as its *innermost clothing*. However, they acknowledged that its *force* was greatly weakened and its *splendor* entirely obscured by the *heavy weight* and *gross vapors* of the *terrestrial body*. 

Thus, *Suidas* <note>A 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia.</note> tells us under the word *Augoeides* (Luciform), quoting *Isidore*: "According to some philosophers, the soul has a certain Luciform vehicle, also called star-like or sun-like, and eternal. This Luciform body is now shut up within this terrestrial body (like a light in a dark lantern), with some believing it is contained within the head, etc." <note>original: ὡς ἔχοι ἡ ψυχὴ Αὐγοειδὲς ὄχημα... εἴσω τῆς κεφαλῆς</note> <margin>P. 293.</margin> *Hierocles* agrees with this: "The splendid or Luciform body lies within this mortal body of ours, continually breathing life into the soulless body and maintaining its harmony." <note>original: ἐν τῷ θνητῷ ἡμῶν σώματι, τὸ Αὐγοειδὲς ἔγκειται... τὴν ἁρμονίαν αὐτοῦ συνέχον.</note>

<page-num>791</page-num>
<header>Chap. V. With Ethereal Bodies.</header>

continually inspiring it with life and containing its harmony. The basis for this opinion was that these philosophers generally conceived the human soul to have *pre-existed* before it came into this *earthly body*. They believed it existed either from eternity or from the first beginning of the world's creation. Being never without a body, and then in a perfect state, it was thought to have had a *lucid* and *ethereal body*—either *co-eternal* or *co-existent* <note>original: co-eve</note> with it (though second to it in the order of nature)—serving as its *chariot* or *vehicle* <note>original: *ochēma*</note>. This vehicle, being incorruptible, always inseparably adhered to the soul during its *later lapses* and *descents* first into an *aerial* body, and then into a *terrestrial* one. This ethereal body acted as the *link* <note>original: *vinculum*</note> of union between the soul and those other bodies. 

Thus *Pletho* <note>George Gemistos Plethon (c. 1355–1452), a Neoplatonist scholar who reintroduced Greek philosophy to the West.</note> declares their view: "It is by means of such a body that the human soul is joined to its mortal frame; the whole soul being interwoven with the whole vital spirit of the embryo, since the soul itself is a spirit as well." <note>original: διὰ δὴ τοιοῦτο σώματος τῷ δή ποτε τῷ θνητῷ τόνγε ἀνθρωπίνην ψυχὴν συγγίνεσθαι, ὅλῃ ὅλῳ τῷ τ’ ἐμβρύῳ ζωτικῷ πνεύματι διὰ συγγένειαν ἐπιπλεκομένην ἅτε πνεύματός τινος καὶ αὐτῆς οὔσης (*dia dē toiouto sōmatos...*)</note> 

But long before *Pletho*, this doctrine was declared and asserted by *Galen* <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire.</note> as being in agreement with both <margin>Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato, Book 7.</margin> *Plato’s* views and his own. He first premised that the *immediate organ* or *instrument* of *sight* was a *luciform* <note>original: αὐγοειδὲς (*augoeides*), meaning "light-like" or "radiant."</note> and ethereal spirit. "Wherefore we may reasonably affirm that the organ of sight is a luciform or ethereal body, just as that of hearing is aerial; that of smelling is vaporous; that of taste is moist or watery; and that of touch is earthy." <note>original: δέοντας οὖν ἐροῦμεν αὐγοειδὲς μὲν εἶναι τὸ τῆς ὄψεως ὄργανον... (*deontas oun eroumen augoeides men einai...*)</note> This follows the principle that "like is perceived by like." 

Accordingly, he understood those famous verses of *Empedocles* <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed the theory of the four elements.</note>—which, if interpreted as *Aristotle* does, seem like nonsense—in this way: "And this was what Empedocles meant to signify in those famous verses of his: it is certain that by the most earthy of our senses, touch, we perceive the earthy nature of sensible things; and by the most luciform sense, namely sight, we perceive the properties of light; by that which is aerial, we perceive sounds; by that which is moist and sponge-like, we perceive tastes; and lastly, by the organ of smelling (which is the extremity of the cavities of the brain replenished with vapors), we perceive odors." <note>original: καὶ τοῦτ’ ἄρ’ ἦν ὃ βούλεται δηλοῦν ὁ Ἐμπεδοκλῆς ἐν οἷς φησί, γαίῃ μὲν γὰρ γαῖαν... (*kai tout’ ar’ ēn ho bouletai dēloun ho Empedoklēs...*)</note> 

After this, he writes concerning the *essence* or *substance* of the soul in this manner: "And if we should now declare anything concerning the essence or substance of the soul, we must affirm one of these two things: either that the soul itself is this luciform and ethereal body (a conclusion which the Stoics, whether they like it or not, will be brought to by consequence, as will Aristotle himself); or else that the soul is itself an incorporeal substance, but that this luciform ethereal body is its primary vehicle, through which, as a medium, it communicates with other bodies. We must say that this vehicle is extended throughout the brain; and by its connection to it, the spirit used for sight becomes light-like." <note>original: εἰ δὲ καὶ περὶ ψυχῆς οὐσίας ἀποφήνασθαι χρή, δυοῖν θάτερον ἀναγκαῖον εἰπεῖν... (*ei de kai peri psychēs ousias apophēnasthai chrē...*)</note>

middle <note>original: Middle (a bridge or connecting element)</note>, by which it communicates with *other bodies*. Therefore, we must say that *this ethereal, lucid body* is *extended throughout the whole brain*. From this is derived that *luciform spirit* <note>original: *Luciform* (light-like)</note> *that is the immediate instrument of sight*. Now, it was for this reason that these *philosophers*, in addition to the *moral purification* of the soul and the *intellectual* or *philosophical* purification, highly recommended a *mystical* or *telestic* <note>original: *telestick* (relating to religious rites or initiations)</note> way of *purifying* this *ethereal body* within us through diet and *purifications* <note>original: *catharms* (ceremonial or medicinal cleansings)</note>.

Thus, the previously mentioned *Hierocles* <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a commentary on the Golden Verses of Pythagoras.</note> writes: "Since this mortal body has attached itself to our *lucid* or *splendid body* as an addition, we ought to *purify the former also, and free it from sympathy with the latter*." <note>original: ἐπειδὴ καὶ τῷ Ἀυγοειδεῖ ἡμῶν σώματι προσέφυ σῶμα θνητὸν ὄν, καθαρεύεσθαι δεῖ καὶ τοῦτο (*epeidē kai tō Augoeidei hēmōn sōmati prosephy sōma thnēton on, kathareuesthai dei kai touto*)</note> And again afterward: "Together with the purifications of the rational soul, the purification of the *luciform* or *ethereal vehicle* is also to be considered, so that this being made light and *winged* <note>original: *alate*</note>, might in no way hinder the soul's ascent upward." <note>original: αἱ τῆς λογικῆς ψυχῆς καθάρσεις καὶ τοῦ Ἀυγοειδοῦς ὀχήματος προμηθεῖσθαι, ὅπως ἂν αὐταῖς ὑπόπτερον καὶ τοῦτο γενόμενον μὴ ἐμποδὼν ἵστηται πρὸς τὴν ἄνω πορείαν (*hai tēs logikēs psychēs katharseis kai tou Augoeidous ochēmatos promētheisthai...*)</note> But he who endeavors to *purify the mind only*, neglecting the body, does not apply himself to the whole man. Whereupon he concludes: "I therefore call this the *telestic* or *mystic operation*, which is concerned with the *purification of the lucid or ethereal vehicle*." <note>original: τὴν Τελεστικὴν ἐνέργειαν λέγω, τὴν τοῦ Ἀυγοειδοῦς καθαρτικὴν δύναμιν (*tēn Telestikēn energeian legō, tēn tou Augoeidous kathartikēn dynamin*)</note> 

And whereas philosophy was defined by *Plato* and *Socrates* to be a *continual exercise of dying*—which *Pliny* <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), a Roman author and naturalist.</note> nevertheless thought to be nothing but a *hypochondriacal* or *melancholic* <note>original: *atrabilarian* (caused by "black bile")</note> ailment in them, using these words which *Salmasius* <note>Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), a renowned French classical scholar.</note> and other critics can by no means understand: "*There is even a certain disease, to die through wisdom*," <note>original: *Est etiam quidam Morbus, Per Sapientiam Mori*</note> meaning that *dying by wisdom or philosophy is but a certain kind of bodily disease or overgrown melancholy*—though they supposed this principally to consist in a *moral dying to bodily lusts and passions*, yet the design of it was also partly *mystical* and *telestic*. It aimed at this further goal: that when they should put off *this terrestrial body*, they might at once *die also to the spirit-like or aerial body*. Then their soul would have nothing left hanging about it but only the *pure ethereal body*, its *light-winged chariot*, which in the language of *Virgil* <note>Publius Vergilius Maro (70–19 BC), the Roman epic poet.</note> is:

->—*And that there be left pure*<-
->*The ethereal sense and the fire of simple air.*<-
<note>original: *Purumque relinqui Æthereum Sensum, atque Aurai Simplicis Ignem*</note>

Notwithstanding this, the *Pythagoreans* and *Platonists* do not seem to have all been of the persuasion that the same *identical* <note>original: *numerical* (meaning the specific same entity)</note> *ethereal body* which the soul was first created with continues to surround it and adheres to it *inseparably* for all eternity during its *descents* into other *grosser bodies*. Rather, they seem to have supposed that, according to the *moral disposition of the soul*, it always finds or creates a *kindred and suitable body* that is correspondingly *pure* or *impure*. Consequently, by *moral virtue* and *philosophy*, it might again recover that *celestial body* which was lost by its *fall* and *descent* to this world. This seems to have been the sense of *Porphyry* <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–c. 305 AD) who was a student of Plotinus.</note> in these words of his: "In whatever state the soul is disposed, it finds a body defined by its rank and its own characteristics. Therefore, for a soul in a purer state, its natural body is that which is near..." <note>original: ὡς ἂν διετέθη ἡ ψυχὴ, εὑρίσκει σῶμα τάξει καὶ τοῖς οἰκείοις διωρισμένον· διὸ καθαρώτερον μὲν διακειμένῃ σύμφυτον τὸ ἐγγύς (*hōs an dietethē hē psychē, heuriskei sōma taxei kai tois oikeiois diōrismenon...*)</note>

# CHAPTER 5. Demons, Soul and Body.

... the immaterial body, which is the ethereal one <note>original: τὸ ἄϋλο̅ σῶμα, ὅπερ ἐστὶ τὸ αἰθέριον (*to aylo sōma, hoper esti to aitherion*)</note>. *However the soul is affected in itself, it always finds a body suitable and agreeable to its present disposition. Therefore, for purified souls, a body naturally accrues that is nearly immaterial—that is, an ethereal one. And probably Plato was of the same mind when he affirmed that the soul is always in a body, but sometimes of one kind and sometimes of another.*

Now, from what has been declared, it already appears that the *most ancient proponents* of the *incorporeity* <note>The state of being immaterial or without a physical body.</note> and *immortality* of the *human soul* *supposed it, nonetheless, to be always joined with a body.* Thus *Hierocles* <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> states plainly: <margin>P. 289.</margin> "The rational nature, having an innate body, so proceeded from the Creator <note>original: *Demiurgus* (the craftsman of the universe in Platonic philosophy)</note> into being, that neither is the body itself the soul, nor can the soul exist without a body. Though the soul itself is incorporeal, its whole form nonetheless is bounded within a body." <note>original: ἡ λογικὴ οὐσία σύμφυες ἔχουσα σῶμα... (*hē logikē ousia symphyes echousa sōma...*)</note> Accordingly, the definition which he gives of a human being is this: "A rational soul, together with an innate immortal body" <note>original: ψυχὴ λογικὴ μετὰ συμφυῦς ἀθανάτου σώματος (*psychē logikē meta symphyous athanatou sōmatos*)</note>. <margin>P. 290.</margin> He concludes afterward that this *enlivened terrestrial body*, or *mortal man*, is nothing but "the image of the true man" <note>original: εἴδωλον ἀνθρώπου (*eidōlon anthrōpou*)</note>, or an *addition* to him, which is therefore *separable* from the soul.

He does not affirm this only of *human souls*, but also of all other *rational beings* whatsoever *below the supreme Deity and above men*—that they *always naturally inhabit a body*. Therefore, a *demon* or *angel* (words used as *synonyms* by *Hierocles*) is also defined by him in the same manner: "A rational soul together with a radiant body" <note>original: ψυχὴ λογικὴ μετὰ φωτεινοῦ σώματος (*psychē logikē meta phōteinou sōmatos*)</note>.

And accordingly, *Proclus* <note>A later Neoplatonist philosopher who influenced medieval theology.</note> in his commentary on *Plato’s Timaeus* affirms: "That every demon superior to our human souls has both an intellectual soul and an ethereal vehicle, the entirety of its being made up or compounded of these two things" <note>original: πάντα δαίμονα τῶν ἡμετέρων κρείττονα ψυχῶν... (*panta daimona tōn hēmeterōn kreittona psychōn...*)</note>. So there is hardly any other difference left between *demons* or *angels* and *men*, according to these *philosophers*, except this: the *former* can fall only as far as *aerial bodies* and no further, while the *latter* can fall into *terrestrial bodies* as well.

Now, *Hierocles* positively affirms that this was the *true tradition* <note>original: *Cabala* (here referring to a received oral or secret tradition)</note> and *genuine doctrine of the ancient Pythagoreans*, which was later adopted by *Plato*: "And this was the doctrine of the Pythagoreans, which Plato afterward revealed, likening every divine and human soul (that is, in our modern language, every created rational being) to the innate power of a winged pair of horses and a driver or charioteer together. By the chariot, he meant an enlivened body, and by the charioteer, the incorporeal soul itself acting upon it." <note>original: καὶ τοῦτο τῶν Πυθαγορείων ἦν δόγμα... (*kai touto tōn Pythagoreiōn ēn dogma...*)</note>

And now we have given a full account of how the ancient *proponents of incorporeal substance as unextended* answered that *objection*...

# The Soul's Happiness, not in Book I.

One **objection** against the **illocality** <note>The state of not being restricted to a specific location.</note> and **immobility** of **particular, finite spirits** (such as **demons** or **angels**, and **human souls**) is as follows: though these spirits are in **themselves** and **directly immovable**, they might still be **moved**, in a certain sense, **by accident** <note>original: *per accidens*; meaning they move because the body they are attached to moves, rather than moving of their own power through space.</note> along with those **bodies** to which they are **vitally united**. Regarding the **pretense** <note>claim or argument</note> that these **finite spirits** or **incorporeal substances**, being **unextended** (having no physical dimensions) and thus having no inherent **relation** to any **place**, might therefore **actuate** and **inform** the **whole corporeal world at once** and take **cognizance** <note>awareness or knowledge</note> of all things within it; the reply was this: because these are **essentially** only **parts** of the **universe**, and therefore do not **comprehend** the **whole**—being **finite** or **particular** and not **universal beings** (unlike the **three hypostases** <note>The three fundamental substances or persons: The One, Intellect, and Soul.</note> of the **Platonic Trinity**) — the **sphere** of their **activity** could not possibly **extend** any further than to the **quickening** <note>giving life to</note> and **enlivening** of certain **parts of matter** and the **world** allotted to them. Through this, they become **particular animals**; it is **peculiar** to the **Deity**, or that **incorporeal substance** which is **infinite**, to **quicken** and **actuate all things**.

But it would be no **irrelevant digression** here (considering the main **scope** of our **present undertaking**) if we briefly compared the aforementioned **doctrine** and **cabbala** <note>Used here to mean a traditional or secret philosophical transmission.</note> of the **ancient incorporealists** (the **Pythagoreans** and **Platonists**) with that of **Christianity**, and considered the **agreement** or **disagreement** between them. **First**, there is a plain **agreement** of these **best** and most **religious philosophers** with **Christianity** in this: that the most **consummate happiness** and **highest perfection** that **human nature** is capable of does not consist in a **separate state of souls**, stripped **naked** from all **body** and having no manner of **commerce** with **matter**—as some **high-flown persons** in all **ages** have been apt to **conceive**. For among the **philosophers** (and **Platonists** too), **Plotinus** was such a person. The **unevenness** and **unsafeness** of his **temper** may sufficiently appear from this: just as he conceived that **human souls** might possibly ascend to such a high **pitch** as to quite shake off **commerce** with all **body**, so did he on the other hand **imagine** that they might also **descend** and **sink down** so low as to **animate** not only the **bodies of beasts**, but even of **trees** and **plants** too. These are two **inconsistent paradoxes**; the **latter** is a most **monstrous extravagance**, which even **Empedocles** (though otherwise a **great wit**) seems to have been guilty of as well, from those **verses** of his in **Athenaeus**:

> For I have already been a boy and a girl, 
> a bush, a bird, and a mute fish in the sea.
> <note>original: Ἤδη γὰρ ποτ' ἐγὼ γενόμην κοῦρός τε κόρη τε, θάμνος, τ' οἰωνός τε καὶ ἐὶν ἁλὶ ἔλλοπος ἰχθύς (*Ēdē gar pot' egō genomen kouros te korē te, thamnos, t' oiōnos te kai ein hali ellopos ichthys*)</note>

And among the **Jews**, the famous **Maimonides** <note>A preeminent 12th-century Jewish philosopher and Torah scholar.</note> was also of this **persuasion**, it being a **known aphorism** of his in his **great work**: **"That in the world to come (or state of consummate happiness) there shall be nothing at all of body, but pure incorporeity."** <note>original: שבעולם הבא אין גוף או גוויה (*she-ba-olam ha-ba ein guf o geviyah*)</note> Upon which **account**, being accused as a **denier** of the **resurrection** (an **article** of the **Jewish** as well as the **Christian faith**), he wrote that **book** entitled **The Letter to Yemen** <note>original: *Iggereth Teman*; Maimonides' defense of the Resurrection is primarily found in his *Treatise on Resurrection* (*Ma'amar Tehiyath ha-Metim*), though he also addresses Jewish faith in the *Letter to Yemen*.</note> purposely to purge

# CHAPTER V. Separation from all Body.

...clear <note>original: "purge"</note> himself, and to reconcile those two assertions together, which he does in such a manner that there should indeed be a resurrection, at the first coming of the **Jewish Messiahs**, of certain persons to live here for a while upon the earth—to eat and drink, marry and be given in marriage, and then die again. After this, in the **world to come**, they should forever continue as **pure souls**, unattached to any body. In this, it may be well suspected that the design **Maimonides** <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a highly influential Sephardic Jewish philosopher.</note> aimed at was directed against **Christianity**. Nevertheless, regarding this particular point, Christianity has the unanimous agreement <note>original: "concurrent suffrages"</note> of the best **philosophers**: that the most genuine and perfect state of the **human soul**, which is immortal by its own nature, is to continue forever **not without, but with a body**. 

And yet our extremist enthusiasts <note>original: "high-flown enthusiasts"; in the 17th century, "enthusiasts" referred to those who claimed direct, private divine inspiration, often rejecting traditional church structures.</note> generally (though calling themselves Christians) are such great **spiritualists**, and so much in favor of the **inward resurrection**—which we do not deny is also a scriptural concept, as in the words of St. Paul, *If you be risen with Christ, etc.* and again, *If by any means I might attain to the resurrection of the dead*—that they completely allegorize away, along with other **parts of Christianity**, the **outward resurrection of the body**. Indeed, they will scarcely acknowledge any **future immortality or life to come after death**. Their **spirituality** thus ends in **Sadduceeism** <note>original: "Sadducism"; the belief of the Sadducees, a Jewish sect that denied the resurrection of the dead and the existence of spirits.</note> and **infidelity**, if not eventually in **downright atheism and sensuality**.

But besides this, there is yet a further **correspondence of Christianity** with the previously mentioned **philosophical tradition** <note>original: "philosophick Cabbala"; here referring to the ancient tradition of wisdom shared by Plato and Pythagoras.</note>. This is because Christianity also supposes that the **highest perfection** of our **human souls** does not consist in being **eternally joined** with such **gross bodies** as these we now have, **unchanged and unaltered**. For just as the **Pythagoreans** and **Platonists** have always complained of these **terrestrial bodies** as **prisons or living sepulchers of the soul**, so does **Christianity** seem to follow the same theme in these **scriptural expressions**: *In this we groan earnestly, desiring to be clothed upon with our house which is from heaven*; and again, *We that are in this tabernacle do groan, being burdened, not because we would be unclothed* (that is, stripped quite naked of all body), *but so clothed upon that mortality might be swallowed up by life*; and lastly, *Ourselves also, who have the first fruits of the Spirit, groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption (sonship or inheritance), namely, the redemption of our bodies*. 

That is, the freedom of the soul from all those **evils and maladies** of the body which we lie oppressed under here. Therefore, we cannot think that the same **heavy load and luggage**, which the **souls** of good men are burdened with here and groan to be delivered from, shall be laid upon them again at the **general resurrection** and bound fast to them for all **eternity**. For of such a **resurrection** as this, **Plotinus** <note>A major Greek-speaking philosopher of the 3rd century and founder of Neoplatonism.</note> (though perhaps mistaking it for the **true Christian resurrection**) might have had some cause to affirm that it would be but a resurrection to another sleep <note>original: ἀνάςασις εἰς ἄλλον ὕπνον (*anastasis eis allon hypnon*)</note>. In such a state, the **soul** seems not to be thoroughly awake here, but as if it were lulled into a stupor <note>original: "soporated"</note> by the **dull steams and opiate-like vapors** of this **gross body**. For as the author of the **Book of Wisdom** says: *The corruptible body presses down the soul, and the earthly tabernacle weighs down the mind*...

...upon many things. This will become even clearer from the account that the Bible itself gives us regarding the *Resurrection*. First, in general terms, when St. Paul answers the question <note>original: "Querie"</note> of the skeptical philosopher <note>original: "Philosophick Infidel"</note>—*How are the dead raised, or with what body do they come?*—he replies in this manner: *You fool* (meaning, you who think you can puzzle or defeat the Christian doctrine of the resurrection, which you do not understand), *what you sow does not come to life <note>original: "Quickened"</note> unless it first dies to what it was. And you do not sow the body that shall be, but a bare grain—like wheat, or barley, or something similar. But God (in the ordinary course of nature) gives it a body as it has pleased him* (that is, a stalk and an ear, containing many grains within husks, and therefore neither in size nor quality the same as that which was sown underground). *Nor does he give every seed the same kind of body; rather, he gives to every seed its own corresponding body—one kind of ear to wheat, and another to barley.*

It is as if he were saying: Understand that our present body is to be viewed merely as a kind of seed for the *resurrection body*. Therefore, it is in some sense the *same*, and in some sense *not the same* as the original. Besides this general account, the specific contrasts that the Bible makes between the present and future body seem very consistent with those found in the *philosophic tradition* <note>original: "Philosophick Cabala"; here referring to a body of esoteric philosophical tradition, often Platonic or Pythagorean, thought to align with spiritual truths.</note>. First, the *present body* is said to be "sown in corruption," while the *future body* is "raised in incorruption." For the "children of the resurrection" cannot die anymore, and "mortality shall be swallowed up by life." Therefore, the Christian resurrection body, as well as that of the philosophic tradition, is an **immortal body** <note>original: "σῶμα ἀθάνατον"</note> and **eternal** <note>original: "ἀΐδιον"</note> as well (2 Corinthians 5:1).

Again, the body that is "sown" is described as a dishonorable, shameful, and inglorious body. For this reason, St. Paul also calls it **the body of our humble state** <note>original: "τὸ σῶμα τῆς ταπεινώσεως ἡμῶν"; usually translated as "our lowly body"</note>, a body suited to the fallen state of the soul. But the body that shall be raised will be a *glorious body*, **conformed to his glorious body** <note>original: "σύμμορφον τῷ σώματι τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ"</note>—the body of Christ. When Christ was transfigured <note>The Transfiguration is an event in the Gospels where Jesus becomes radiant in glory upon a mountain.</note>, his face shone like the sun and his clothing was white as light. The "glory" of a body consists only in its beautiful proportions and its brilliance. Thus, there is one glory of the sun, another of the moon, and another of the stars—meaning they each have a different level of brilliance.

Therefore, according to the Bible as well as the philosophic tradition, the future body of the righteous will be a **luminous body** <note>original: "σῶμα φωτεινὸν"</note>, a **radiant body** <note>original: "σῶμα αὐγοειδὲς"</note>, and a **star-like body** <note>original: "σῶμα ἀστεροειδὲς"</note>—a glorious, splendid, light-filled, and starlike body. As it says in Wisdom 3:7, **"In the time of their visitation they shall shine forth"** <note>original: "ἐν καιρῷ ἐπισκοπῆς αὐτῶν ἐκλάμψουσι"</note>. In Daniel 12:2–3, it says, "Those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky <note>original: "Firmament"</note>, and those who lead many to righteousness like the stars forever and ever." And Matthew 13:43 states, "Then shall the righteous shine forth like the sun in the kingdom of their Father." It is likely, therefore, that this future glorious resurrection body is that "inheritance of the saints in light" mentioned in Colossians 1:12. Furthermore, there is another difference between the present and the future body of the righteous...

# CHAPTER IV. With the Pythagorean Tradition <note>original: "Pythagorick Cabbala"</note>.

*Righteous*, in which St. Paul and Hierocles <note>Hierocles of Alexandria (5th century AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a commentary on the Golden Verses of Pythagoras.</note> agree quite well. The first kind of body is called by both of them a **natural body** <note>original Greek: "Σῶμα ψυχικὸν" (Sōma psychikon); literally, a "soulish" or "animal" body.</note>, and the second is called a **spiritual body** <note>original Greek: "Σῶμα πνευματικὸν" (Sōma pneumatikon)</note>. This latter expression in Scripture does not only indicate its **subtlety** and **refinement** <note>original: "Tenuity"</note>, but also—just as this present body is called an "animal body" because it is suitable for that animal life which men share with brute animals—so is that future body called "spiritual," as it bears a fit proportion and correspondence to souls renewed in the spirit of their mind, or those in whom the **Divine Spirit dwells and acts**, exercising its dominion. *There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body. And the first Adam was made a living soul, the last Adam a life-giving spirit.* And thus are those called **natural** <note>original: "ψυχικοὶ" (psychikoi)</note> in the Scripture described as **those who do not have the Spirit** <note>original: "οἱ πνεῦμα μὴ ἔχοντες"</note>. And **the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God** <note>original: "ψυχικὸς ἄνθρωπος οὐ δέχεται τὰ τοῦ πνεύματος τοῦ Θεοῦ"</note>. This Spirit is also said in Scripture to be the **guarantee** <note>original: "Earnest"</note> of our **future inheritance** (*Ephesians 1:14*), and the guarantee of this spiritual and heavenly body (*2 Corinthians 5:5*). It is also said to be that by which (as the efficient cause) these **mortal bodies** shall be **given life** <note>original: "Quickened"</note> (*Romans 8:11*): *If the Spirit of him who raised up Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he that raised up Christ from the dead shall also give life to your mortal bodies by his Spirit that dwells in you.*

Hierocles does not fall much short of this Scriptural notion of a "spiritual body" when he describes it as that <margin>Page 297</margin> **which is joined to the intellectual perfection of the soul** <note>original Greek: "ὃ τῇ νοερᾷ τελειότητι τῆς ψυχῆς συνάπτεται"</note>. This spiritual body is what the ancient **Hebrews** called **Eagles' Wings** <note>original Hebrew: "כנפי נשרים" (Kanfei Nesharim)</note>. We read this in the **Gemara** of the **Sanhedrin** (*Chapter 11, folio 92, column 2*):

> *If you ask what shall become of the righteous when God shall renew the world, the answer is: God shall make them wings like eagles, by which they shall fly upon the face of the waters.*

Again, as this **present body** is called in Scripture an **earthly body**, so is the **future body** of the righteous styled by St. Paul, as well as the Pythagoreans, a **heavenly body**; and those who shall then possess it are called **heavenly men** (*1 Corinthians 15*): *As is the heavenly, such are they that are heavenly.* Besides this, just as philosophers supposed both **demons** (or **angels**) and **men** to have one and the same **shining, heavenly, and etherial body** <note>original Greek: "Σῶμα αὐγοειδὲς, οὐράνιον, and αἰθέριον" (Sōma augoeides, ouranion, and aitherion)</note>, we may also look to the words of our Savior. He affirms that *those who shall be accounted worthy to obtain that world and the resurrection from the dead will neither marry nor be given in marriage, nor can they die anymore; for they are **equal to the angels*** <note>original Greek: "ἰσάγγελοι" (isangeloi)</note>.

From this, I say, we may venture to call this **resurrection body** of the **just** an **angelic** or **angel-like** body. This is especially true because the ancient Hebrews (as we learn from Nachmanides <note>A leading medieval Jewish scholar (1194–1270), also known as Ramban.</note> in *The Gate of Reward* <note>original: "Shaar Haggemul"</note>) styled it **the angelic clothing of the soul** <note>original Hebrew: "לבושת הנפש המלאכותי" (Levushat ha-Nefesh ha-Malakuti)</note>. <margin>Thus St. Augustine calls them "Angelic bodies" (Corpora Angelica) and says they are "such as those of the angels" (Qualia sunt Angelorum).</margin> Even **Tertullian** himself called it **angelified flesh** <note>original Latin: "Angelicatam Carnem"</note>. But lastly, St. Paul is not only **positive** in his doctrine here, but also **negative**: *Now this I say, brethren, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, neither does corruption inherit incorruption.* This passage undoubtedly should not be treated as a mere allegory...

<summary>This page correlates the Christian concept of the "spiritual body" with Neoplatonic and Jewish traditions, arguing that the resurrected body is a refined, angelic, and heavenly form rather than one made of "flesh and blood."</summary>

# The Mystery of the Resurrection; Book I.

It may be inferred from this that the **happy resurrection body** shall not be this foul and gross body of ours merely **varnished** and **gilded** on the outside while remaining **dirty, slovenly, and ruinous** within. It will not retain the same seeds of **corruption** and **mortality** in its **nature** that it had before, though kept away by a perpetual **miracle** as if by **violence** defended from being seized and devoured by the **jaws** of **Death**. Rather, it shall be so inwardly changed in its **nature** that its possessors **cannot die anymore**. 

However, all that has been said about the **resurrection body** should not be understood as if it belonged **universally** to all who shall be raised up on the last day, or made to appear upon the Earth in their own persons at that **Great and General Assizes** <note>original: "Assizes"; refers to the final judicial judgment of all souls, like a supreme court session.</note>. It is not the case that they shall all alike (**wicked** as well as **good**) have such **glorious**, **spiritual**, and **celestial bodies**. Instead, this is only a description of the <term>resurrection of life</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀνάστασις τῆς ζωῆς" (anastasis tēs zōēs)</note>, which is also emphatically called by our Savior Christ the <term>resurrection from the dead</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀνάστασις ἡ ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν" (anastasis hē ek tōn nekrōn)</note>, or the resurrection to a **happy immortality**. Those who are thought worthy of it are likewise styled by him as the <term>children of the resurrection</term> <note>original Greek: "υἱοὶ ἀναστάσεως" (huioi anastaseōs)</note>. It is only of this resurrection that **St. Paul** treats in that 15th chapter of his first letter to the **Corinthians**. We say that this **Christian resurrection of life** is the **vesting** and **settling** of the souls of good men in their **glorious**, **spiritual**, **heavenly**, and **immortal bodies**. 

The complete happiness of a man, and all the good that he can desire, was summed up by the heathen poet <note>The Roman poet Juvenal.</note> as: *That there be a sound mind in a sound body* <note>original Latin: "Ut sit Mens Sana in Corpore Sano"</note>. **Christian happiness** seems to be entirely comprised of these **two things**: 
1. Being **inwardly regenerated** and **renewed** in the **spirit** of their **mind**, cleansed from all **pollution** of **flesh** and **spirit**, and made partakers of the **divine life** and **nature**.
2. Being **outwardly clothed** with **glorious**, **spiritual**, **celestial**, and **incorruptible bodies**. 

The Scripture plainly declares that our souls are not at home here in this **terrestrial body** and these **earthly mansions**, but that they are **strangers** and **pilgrims** within it. The Patriarchs also confessed this, plainly declaring that they **sought a country**—not the one they came from, but a **heavenly** one. From these passages of Scripture, some would indeed infer that souls, being first created **pure** by God, **pre-existed** in **celestial bodies** before this **earthly birth** <note>original: "terrene nativity"</note>, but afterwards straggled and wandered down here. **Philo** for one says: <term>For our soul, having left its heavenly mansion, came down into this earthly body as if into a strange land</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀπολιποῦσα μὲν γὰρ ἡ ψυχὴ τὸν οὐράνιον τόπον, καθάπερ εἰς ξένην χώραν ἦλθε, τὸ σῶμα"</note>. 

However, this much is certain: our **human souls** were at first intended and designed by God Almighty, their maker, for other **bodies** and other **regions** as their proper home and country, and their eternal resting place. Nevertheless, for us, that which is **spiritual** is not first, but that which is **natural**, and afterwards **that which is spiritual**. Now, although some would infer from St. Paul's words—where he calls this **happy resurrection body** <term>our dwelling which is from heaven</term> <note>original Greek: "οἰκητήριον ἡμῶν τὸ ἐξ οὐρανοῦ" (oikētērion hēmōn to ex ouranou)</note>, or which comes out of **heaven**—that it will not be taken out of **graves** and **charnel houses**, they also conceive that the **individuation** and **sameness**...

<summary>This page discusses the nature of the resurrection body, distinguishing the "resurrection of life" for the righteous from a general resurrection, and explores the idea that human souls are destined for a heavenly, spiritual body rather than their current corruptible ones.</summary>

#### CHAP. V. A Spiritual and Heavenly Body.

The sameness of men’s persons does not necessarily depend upon the **exact physical identity** <note>original: "Numerical Identity"; the state of being comprised of the exact same atoms or particles.</note> of all the parts of **matter**. We never continue to be composed of the same matter anyway, because our bodies are always flowing like a **river** and passing away by **invisible evaporation** <note>original: "Insensible Transpiration"; the process of losing moisture and matter through the skin without noticing it.</note>. It is certain that we do not have all the exact same matter—neither more nor less—in infancy as we do in old age, even though we are still the self-same persons. 

Nevertheless, according to the best philosophy (which acknowledges no **essential** or **specific difference** in types of matter), the foulest and heaviest body that exists may, merely by motion, not only be **crystallized**, but also brought into the **purity** and **thinness** of the **finest ether**. Undoubtedly, that same physical body of our **Savior Christ** which lay in the tomb was, after his resurrection, thus **transformed** into a **spiritual** and **heavenly body**. Its **subtlety** and **fineness** appeared when he entered the room where the **doors were shut** and when he **vanished out of sight**. However, its **glory** was suspended for a time, partly to better convince his disciples of the truth of his resurrection, and partly because they were not then able to bear the splendor of it. We conclude, therefore, that the **Christian mystery** of the **resurrection of life** consists not in the soul’s being reunited to these **vile rags** of mortality—these **heavy bodies** of ours (**as they are now**)—but in having them **changed into the likeness of Christ’s glorious body**, and in this **mortal putting on immortality**.

Hitherto we have seen the agreement that exists between **Christianity** and the old philosophical **Cabbala** <note>original: "Cabbala"; here referring to an ancient, secret tradition of divine wisdom or philosophy.</note> concerning the soul in these two things: 
1. First, that the highest **happiness** and **perfection** of the **human soul** does not consist in a **state of pure separation** from all **body**.
2. Secondly, that it does not consist in an **eternal union** with such **heavy terrestrial bodies** as these, when **unchanged**. The soul is not **at home** but is a **stranger** and **pilgrim** in them, oppressed by their weight. 

Instead, the souls of good men shall at last arrive at **glorious, spiritual, heavenly, and immortal bodies**. 

But now we come to this **point**: are **human souls** always **united** to some **body** or other? Consequently, when they put off this **heavy terrestrial body** at death, are they not thereby quite **divested** and **stripped naked** of all body, but instead have a **certain, subtle, and spirit-like body** still adhering to them and accompanying them? Or, have all souls that have departed out of this life from the very beginning of the world continued in a **state of separation** from all body, and shall they continue so until the **Day of Judgment** or the **General Resurrection**? 

We must confess that this is a matter not so explicitly determined or expressly decided in **Christianity** either way. Nevertheless, it is first of all certain from Scripture— 
<margin>Death is called "sleep" in Scripture only as a **euphemism** <note>original Greek: "κατ' εὐφημισμόν" (kat' euphemismon), a mild or indirect word used to substitute for a harsh or blunt one.</note>.</margin> 
—that souls departed out of these **terrestrial bodies** are neither dead nor **asleep** until the last trumpet and **General Resurrection**, but are still **alive** and **awake**. Our Savior Christ affirmed that they **all live unto God**. The meaning of this seems to be that those who are said to be dead are dead only to **men** here upon Earth; they are neither dead to themselves, nor yet to God. Their life is not extinct, but only disappearing to us and withdrawn from our view.

<summary>The author argues that personal identity remains constant even as physical matter changes, comparing the believer's future "spiritual body" to the transformed body of Christ. He also explores the "intermediate state" of the soul, noting that while Scripture says souls remain alive and awake after death, it is debated whether they possess a subtle body before the final resurrection.</summary>

<header>Of the State of the Soul BOOK I.</header>

...from our sight; for as much as they have left this stage which we still continue to act upon. And thus it is also said of our Savior Christ himself, even after his resurrection, that *he lives unto God* (Romans 6:10). From this, it is evident that those who are said to *live to God* are not supposed to be any less *alive* than they were when they *lived among men*. 

Now it seems to be a privilege or prerogative proper to the **Deity** alone to *live* and *act* alone, without a **vital union** <note>original: "Vital Union"; a living connection between soul and body.</note> or conjunction with any body. 

<margin>About First Principles (*Peri Archon*), Book 2.</margin> "It is worth our inquiry," said Origen, "whether it is possible for rational creatures to remain entirely bodiless <note>original: "penitus Incorporeas"</note> once they have reached the highest degree of holiness and happiness? Or is it necessary that they are always joined to some kind of body?" <note>original: "Quærendum, Si Poſſibile eſt, penitus Incorporeas remanere Rationabiles Creaturas, cum ad Summum Sanctitatis ac Beatudinis venerint ? An neceſſe eſt eas ſemper Conjunctas eſſe Corporibus ?"</note> 

Afterwards, he plainly affirms it to be impossible "for any other nature, besides the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, to live entirely without a body." <note>original: "Vivere præter Corpus, Ullam aliam Naturam, præter Patrem, & Filium, & Spiritum Sanctum."</note> Indeed, if it were most natural to the human soul and most perfect for it to continue separate from all bodies, then (as Origen implied) the souls of good men would surely remain in such a state of separation for all eternity after the Day of Judgment. 

But on the contrary, if it is natural for souls to **enliven** and **form** some body or other—even if it is not always an **earthly** one—as our **inward sense** inclines us to think, then it does not seem probable that they should be kept for so long in an **unnatural** or **extraordinary** <note>original: "Preter-Natural"; something outside the normal course of nature.</note> state of **nakedness** and separation from all bodies by a kind of violence; some of them even from the time of **Adam** until the Day of Judgment.

Again, the Scripture also suggests that souls departed from this life have a knowledge of one another and are also capable of the **punishment of sense** or pain. "Fear him," says our Savior, "who after he has killed, has power to cast into hell" (Luke 12). And the soul of the **rich man** is said to be in **torments** immediately after death, before the **Day of Judgment**, and he is also said to have **known Abraham and Lazarus**. 

It seems neither agreeable to our **common notions** nor to piety to conclude that the souls of wicked men—departing from this life throughout the various ages from the beginning of the world until the Day of Judgment—have no manner of punishment inflicted on them except for **remorse of conscience** and the expectation of future judgment. Now, it is not conceivable how souls after death should **know** others and be **knowable** themselves, and **converse** with one another, and have any punishment of **sense** or **pain** inflicted on them, were they not **vitally united** to some bodies. 

And thus did **Tertullian** reason long ago: 

<margin>On the Soul (*De Anima*), p. 309. Rigal edition.</margin> "The soul of a certain man suffers in the underworld <note>original: "apud Inferos"</note>, and is punished in flame, and is tortured in his tongue, and begs for the comfort of a drop of water from the finger of a happier soul. You might think that account of the rejoicing poor man and the mourning rich man is just a metaphor. But why is Lazarus named there if the story is not true? Even if it is a metaphor, it serves as evidence of the truth. For if the soul did not have a body, it could not take on the appearance <note>original: "Imaginem"</note> of a body. Nor..." <note>original: "Dolet apud Inferos Anima cujuſdam, & Punitur in Flamma, & Cruciatur in Linguâ, & de digito animæ fœlicioris implorat Solatium Roris. Imaginem exiſtimas, exitum illum Pauperis Lætantis, & Divitis mœrentis. Et quid illic Lazari nomen, ſi non in veritate res eſt ? Sed etſi Imago credenda eſt, Teſtimonium erit veritatis. Si enim non habet Anima Corpus, non caperet Imaginem Corporis. Nec..."</note>

<page-num>801</page-num>
# Chapter 5. After Death: Tertullian

*Scripture would lie about bodily members if they did not exist <note>original: "mentiretur de Corporalibus Membris Scriptura, si non erant"</note>. What is it that is carried down to the underworld after the separation of the body? What is held there and reserved until the Day of Judgment? To what place did Christ also descend by dying? I believe it was to the souls of the Patriarchs. The incorporeality of the soul is free from every kind of custody or imprisonment; it is immune to punishment and to comfort. For that by which it is punished or comforted must be a body. Therefore, if the soul receives any torment or solace in the prison or lodging-place of the underworld—whether in fire or in Abraham's bosom—the corporeality of the soul will be proven. For incorporeality suffers nothing, having nothing through which it could suffer; or if it does have something, that thing must be a body. Insofar as everything corporeal is capable of suffering, so whatever is capable of suffering is corporeal <note>original: "In quantum enim Omne Corporale Passibile est; in tantum quod Passibile est Corporale est."</note>.* 

We read in Scripture of a soul tormented in Hell, punished with flames, and desirous of a drop of water to cool his tongue. You will say, perhaps, that this is a parable and fictitious. What, then, does the name of Lazarus signify there if it were not a real thing? But even if it is a parable, it must nonetheless, in its main points, speak in agreement with the truth. For if the soul (after death) has no body at all, then it cannot have any corporeal image, shape, or figure. Nor can it be thought that the Scripture would lie concerning bodily members if there were none. 

But what is that which, after its separation from this body, is carried down into Hell, and there detained prisoner and reserved until the Day of Judgment? And what is that which Christ, while dying, descended down unto? I suppose it was to the souls of the Patriarchs. But incorporeality is free from all custody or imprisonment, as it is also devoid of pain and pleasure. Therefore, if souls are sensible of pain after death and tormented with fire, then they must necessarily have some corporeity; for incorporeality suffers nothing. And as every corporeal thing is passive or <term>patible</term> <note>capable of feeling or suffering</note>, so again, whatever is passive is corporeal. 

Tertullian would also further confirm this from a vision or revelation of a certain "sister-prophet"—as he claimed that miracles and prophecy were not yet altogether extinct in his time. *Among other things,* she said, *a soul was shown to me in bodily form; it appeared as a spirit, tender and bright, of an airy color, and in every way of human form <note>original: "Inter cætera ostensa est mihi Anima Corporaliter, & Spiritus videbatur, Tenera & Lucida, & Aerii Coloris, Et Formæ per omnia Humanæ"</note>.* 

Agreeing with this, Tertullian himself adds: *No other shape is to be assigned to a human soul except the human shape; and indeed, it is the shape of that body which each soul previously carried about <note>original: "Effigiem non aliam Animæ Humanæ deputandam præter Humanam, & quidem ejus Corporis quod unaquæque circuntulit."</note>.* 

It is true indeed that Tertullian here pushes the matter so far as to make the soul itself corporeal, shaped, and colored, and—after death—possessing the very same shape that its respective body had before in this life. He was one of those who were unable to conceive of anything existing that was truly incorporeal; therefore, being a religious man, he concluded that God himself must be a certain kind of body as well. But the reasons he insists upon here will actually extend no further than to prove that the soul has, after death, some body vitally united to it. By means of this body, it is both capable of conversation and sensible of pain—for body alone can have no sense of anything.

And this is what Irenæus gathers from the same Scripture:
