# St. Irenaeus and Origen, BOOK I.

<margin>Book 2, chapter 62.</margin>...not that the Soul *is a body*, but that it *has a body* joined with it after death, and that this body is of the same *form and figure* as the *body* which it had before in this life. "Our Lord has most fully taught us that souls do not merely survive by moving from one body into another, but also that they keep the same character of the body to which they are then adapted; and that they remember the actions and omissions of their past life." <note>original Latin: "Plenissimè autem Dominus docuit, non solùm perseverare, non de corpore in corpus transgredientes animas, sed & Characterem corporis, in quo etiam adaptantur, custodire eundem; Et meminisse eas Operum quæ egerunt hic, & à quibus cessaverunt"</note> This is found in the narrative <note>original: "Enarration"</note> which is written concerning the *Rich Man* and *Lazarus*, who was *refreshed* in *Abraham’s bosom*; in which he affirms that the Rich Man knew both Lazarus and Abraham after death, and that each of them remained in their own rank <note>original: "order"</note>.

<margin>Chapter 63.</margin>And so again in the following chapter: "By these things it is most clearly shown that souls both persist after death and do not pass from one body to another; that they have a human figure or shape (so that they may be recognized); that they remember the things here upon the Earth and their own actions; and lastly, that each kind—both good and bad—has their distinct and suitable habitations assigned them, even before the Judgment." <note>original Latin: "Per hæc manifestissimè declaratum est, & Perseverare Animas; & non de corpore in corpus Exire; & habere Hominis Figuram; (ut etiam cognoscantur) & meminisse eorum quæ hic sint; & Dignam Habitationem Unamquamque Gentem percipere, etiam antè Judicium."</note> 

Now, Irenaeus did not mean here that souls are themselves *bodily substances*, and consequently have a certain *character, form*, and *figure* of their own. Rather, he meant only that they have certain *bodies* joined with them which are shaped. This is evident, first of all, from the words themselves: "To keep the same character of the body in which they are also then adapted." <note>original Latin: "Characterem corporis, in quo etiam adaptantur, custodire Eundem"</note> The natural sense of this is that they keep the *character of the body* (the one they are adapted to after death) which is the same as the one their *bodies* had previously in this *life*. This is further proven because elsewhere he plainly declares that *souls themselves are incorporeal*; as in his Fifth Book and Seventh Chapter: "But the breath of life is incorporeal." <note>original Latin: "Flatus autem Vitæ Incorporalis est"</note>

Furthermore, Origen was of the same persuasion—that souls after death had certain *subtle bodies* <note>Early theologians often described post-death bodies as "subtle," meaning refined, ethereal, or made of a higher form of matter than the physical body.</note> united to them. He believed those bodies of theirs had the same <term>characterizing form</term> <note>original Greek: εἶδος χαρακτηρίζον (eidos charaktērizon)</note> which their earthly bodies had before. He also thinks that this, together with the soul's immortality, can be sufficiently proved from the frequent apparitions of *ghosts* or *departed souls*. He argues this in opposition to *Celsus* <note>An early critic of Christianity who argued that stories of the resurrection were mere hallucinations or magic.</note>, who endeavored to invalidate the Scripture testimonies concerning the apparitions of our Savior Christ by attributing them either to *magical deception*, *fanatical frenzy*, or the disciples mistaking their own dreams and fancies for reality.

<summary>This page examines the writings of Irenaeus and Origen to argue that the soul is incorporeal but is joined to a "subtle" body after death that retains the person's recognizable human shape and memory. Irenaeus uses the biblical story of Lazarus and the Rich Man as evidence that souls recognize one another and maintain their identities before the final judgment.</summary>
<keywords>Irenaeus, Origen, Celsus, incorporeality of the soul, subtle body, afterlife, Lazarus and the Rich Man, apparitions, ghosts, Church Fathers</keywords>

<page-num>803</page-num>
<header>Chapter V. Concerning Souls after Death.</header>

For *visions* and *sensations*, according to the *Epicurean* way; <note>original Greek: "τοῦτο δ' οὐδὲν ἧττον κατασκευαστικόν ἐστιν ἀναγκαίου δόγματος, ὡς ἄρα ἡ ψυχὴ ὑφέστηκε τῶν ἀποθανόντων· καὶ οὐ μάτην πεπίστευκε περὶ τῆς ἀθανασίας αὐτῆς, ὁ τοῦτο τὸ δόγμα ἀνιληφώς"</note> "this is nonetheless proof of a necessary doctrine: that the soul of the deceased continues to exist. Therefore, whoever has accepted this doctrine has not believed in its immortality in vain." As *Plato* also says in his work on the soul, <note>original Greek: "σκιωιδῆ φαντάσματα περὶ μνημεῖα τινα γεγονέναι τῶν ἤδη τεθνηκότων"</note> "shadowy phantoms of those already dead have appeared around certain monuments." *Though this might seem to have been smartly opposed by* Celsus, *yet those very apparitions of ghosts are nonetheless a sufficient argument or proof of a certain necessary opinion: that souls do continue to exist after death. Neither did* Plato *vainly conclude the immortality and permanence of the soul (among other things) from those shadow-like phantoms of the dead that have appeared to many around graves and monuments.* Whereupon Origen gives this further account of these *apparitions*: <note>original Greek: "τὰ μὲν οὖν γινόμενα περὶ ψυχῆς τεθνηκότων φαντάσματα ἀπό τινος ὑποκειμένου γίνεται, τοῦ κατὰ τὴν ὑφεστηκυῖαν ἐν τῷ καλουμένῳ αὐγοειδεῖ σώματι ψυχήν"</note> *For these apparitions of the dead are not mere groundless imaginations; rather, they proceed from the souls themselves, which really remain and survive after death, and exist in that which is called a luciform body.* <term>luciform body</term> <note>From the Greek "augoeides soma," meaning a body made of light or radiance; a spiritual vehicle for the soul.</note> Here, *Origen* takes this *luciform body* in a larger sense than the *Greek philosophers* usually did; namely, he includes within the term that *airy* or *vaporous body* which belongs to *unpurged souls* <note>souls that have not yet been cleansed of worldly attachments</note> who most frequently appear in it after death. In contrast, it is thought appropriate for *purged souls* to be clothed with the *luciform body* only. 

Besides this, the same *Origen* tells us that the thing which Saint *Thomas* the Apostle disbelieved was not our Savior's appearing after death (as if he had thought it impossible for *ghosts* or *departed souls* to *visibly appear*), but only his *rising and appearing* in that same *solid body* which had been crucified and laid in the sepulcher. <note>original Greek: "συγκατετέθετο μὲν γὰρ ἐκεῖνος τῇ φασκούσῃ αὐτὸν ἑωρακέναι, ὡς οὐκ ἀδύνατον ὂν, τὸ τὴν ψυχὴν τοῦ τεθνηκότος ὀφθῆναι· οὐκέτι δ' ἐνόμιζεν εἶναι τὸ ἐν σώματι αὐτὸν ἀντιτύπῳ ἐγηγέρθαι"</note> *Thomas also, as well as the other Apostles, agreed with the woman who claimed she had seen Jesus; he did not think it at all impossible for the soul of a dead man to be seen. However, he did not believe that Jesus had risen and appeared in that self-same solid body in which he lived before.* <note>The Greek "antitypos" here refers to a body that is solid or resistant to the touch.</note> *For this reason he said not only, "Unless I see him," but added also, "And unless I shall put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe."* 

Where again *Origen* adds: <note>original Greek: "ταῦτα δ' ἐλέγετο ὑπὸ τοῦ Θωμᾶ, κρίνοντος ὅτι δύναται ὀφθαλμοῖς αἰσθητοῖς φανῆναι ψυχῆς σῶμα πάντα τῷ προτέρῳ εἴδει, —μεγεθός τε, καὶ ὄμματα καλ’ ἐοικυίης, καὶ φωνήν"</note> *These things were said by* Thomas, *who judged that the body of a departed soul (which had become condensed) might be seen with the eyes of sense, resembling in every way the form it had before in this life—in respect of size, figure, color, and voice;*

->And often wearing the same clothes as it wore upon its body.<-
<note>original: "Πολλάκι δ' ἢ τοῖα περὶ χροῒ εἵματ' ἐχούσης." This is a quote from Homer's Iliad, describing the ghost of Patroclus.</note>

Therefore, according to *Origen*, the *Jews* at that time were generally possessed with the opinion that *souls after death had certain bodies united to them,*

It specifically interprets Saint Thomas's doubt not as a disbelief in ghosts, but as skepticism that Jesus had risen in his physical, solid body rather than an ethereal one.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that departed souls possess subtle, ethereal bodies that can occasionally become visible to the living, referencing the views of Origen and biblical accounts of Christ's resurrection.</meta>

<page-num>804</page-num>
<header>What Countenance, for the BOOK I.</header>

in which they might *visibly appear*. It is not a significant counter-argument that a learned critic objects that *Josephus*, when writing about their opinions, makes no mention of this; especially since he also omitted other significant *doctrines* <note>original: "dogmata"</note> of theirs, such as that of the *resurrection*. However, it is at least certain from this that *Origen* himself took it for granted that *departed human souls* were not entirely naked or unclothed. Instead, they were clothed with a certain *subtle body* <note>In this context, "subtle" means refined, thin, or ethereal, rather than physical and solid.</note> in which they could also *visibly appear*, and that they did so in their *original form*.

Moreover, it might also be observed here that when our Savior first *appeared* to his *disciples*, and it is said that they were frightened, supposing they had seen a *spirit*, our Savior does not tell them that a *spirit* or *ghost* had no body at all in which it could *visibly appear*. Rather, as if taking that for granted, he says *that a spirit has no flesh and bones*—that is, no *solid body* <note>original Greek: "σῶμα ἀντίτυπον" (sōma antitypon), referring to a body that offers resistance or is "counter-striking."</note>—no such *solid body* as they would find him to have. He therefore told them to *handle him* to remove their doubts. It is as if he said, "Though *spirits*, or *ghosts*, and *departed souls* have *bodies* (or *vehicles*) which they can *condense* enough to sometimes make a *visible appearance* to the eyes of men, they do not have any such *solid bodies* as those made of *flesh and bone*. Therefore, by *feeling* and *handling*, you may satisfy yourselves that I am not a mere *appearing spirit, ghost, or soul*, as others have frequently done without a *miracle*. Instead, I appear in that very same *solid body* in which I was *crucified* by the *Jews*, which was raised out of the *tomb* <note>original: "sepulchre"</note> by miraculous *divine power*, and is now to be found there no longer." Consistent with this statement from our Savior Christ is that of *Apollonius* in the writings of *Philostratus*: <note>original Greek: "λάβέ μοι, ἔφη, κἂν μὲν διαφύγω σε, εἴδωλον εἰμί · εἰ δὲ ὑπομείναιμι ἁπτόμενος, πεῖθε καὶ ζῇν τε με, καὶ μὴ ἀποβεβληκέναι τὸ σῶμα"</note> *"Touch me and handle me," he said, "and if you find me to avoid the touch, then you may conclude me to be a spirit or ghost (that is, a departed soul); but if I firmly resist your touch, then believe me really to be alive and not yet to have cast off the body."*

And indeed, though *spirits* or *ghosts* had certain *subtle bodies* which they could *condense* enough to make them sometimes *visible to men*, it is reasonable to think they could not *compress* <note>original: "constipate," meaning to pack together tightly or thicken</note> or *fix* them into the *firmness, density*, and *solidity* of *flesh and bone* to remain in that state—or at least, not without such difficulty and pain as would discourage them from attempting it. Despite this, it is not denied that they may possibly sometimes make use of other *solid bodies*, moving and acting through them, as in that famous story of *Phlegon* <note>Phlegon of Tralles recorded a famous ghost story about a girl named Philinnion who returned from the dead to visit a young man.</note> where the *body did not vanish* as other *ghosts* usually do, but was left behind as a *dead corpse*. Now, as for our Savior Christ's body after his *resurrection* and before his *ascension*: despite its solidity when *handled*, it also sometimes *vanished* out of his disciples' sight. This was probably, as *Origen* conceived, intentionally preserved for a time in a certain *middle state* between the *density* <note>original: "crassities"</note> of a *mortal body* and the *spirituality* of a *perfectly glorified, heavenly, and ethereal body*.

<page-num>805</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER V. Bodies of Ghosts, in Scripture.</header>
<sig>Xxxx 2</sig>

<margin>1 Peter 3:18, 19.</margin>
<margin>Of this St. Augustine, in his 12th Book, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis* <note>original: *De Gen. ad Lit.*</note>, chapter 33: "And indeed it is not without merit believed that Christ's soul came even to those places where sinners are tortured, so that he might release those whom his justice, hidden from us, judged should be released" <note>original Latin: *Et Christi quidem Animam venisse usque ad ea loca in quibus peccatores cruciantur, ut eos solvent, quos esse solvendos, occulta nobis sua justitia judicabat, non immerito creditur.*</note></margin>
This passage, as interpreted by the majority of the Ancient Church Fathers, would naturally imply that even the soul of our Savior Christ himself—after his death and before his Resurrection—was not entirely naked of all body, but instead had a certain subtle or spiritual clothing. This comes from the words of St. Peter: "being put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit, in which he also went and preached to the spirits in prison" <note>original Greek: θανατωθεὶς μὲν σαρκὶ, ζωοποιηθεὶς δὲ τῷ πνεύματι, ἐν ᾧ καὶ τοῖς ἐν φυλακῇ πνεύμασι πορευθεὶς ἐκήρυξε</note>. Because the Ancients understood this as our Savior Christ descending into Hades or Hell, it is rendered this way in the Latin Vulgate: "Put to death in the flesh, but quickened in the Spirit. In which (Spirit) also, he went and preached to those spirits that were in prison, etc."

Thus, the word *spirit* <note>original: *πνεύματι* (pneumati)</note> here, according to this interpretation, should be understood as a *spirit-body* or spiritual body. The meaning would be this: when our Savior Christ was put to death in the flesh (the physical, fleshy body), he was "quickened" or made alive in the *spirit* (a spiritual body). In this spiritual body, he also went and preached to those spirits that were in prison. 

Those who support this interpretation would undoubtedly argue that the word *spirit* here could not refer to Christ's soul itself. Since the soul is naturally immortal, it could not properly be said to be "quickened" or "made alive" after death. Nor could he (meaning Christ's soul) be said to go "in this spirit"—which would mean "the soul within the soul"—to preach to the spirits in prison. They would also add that *spirit* here could not mean the Divine Holy Spirit either, which was the primary cause <note>original: "Efficient Cause"</note> of the resurrection of Christ's body. If it did, there would be no direct contrast between "being put to death in the flesh" and "made alive in the spirit," unless both are understood as types of matter. 

Furthermore, the following verse would be understood this way: that our Savior Christ went in that *spirit* (the spiritual body) in which he was made alive when he was put to death in the flesh, and in that form preached to the spirits in prison. By these "spirits in prison," the text would mean not pure, incorporeal substances or "naked" souls, but souls clothed with subtle, spirit-like bodies—as the word "spirit" is often understood elsewhere in Scripture.

But we are unquestionably certain from the Scripture of this: not only Elijah <note>original: "Elias"</note> (whose earthly body seems to have been at least partially spiritualized during his ascent in that fiery chariot), but also Moses appeared visibly to our Savior Christ and his disciples on the Mount of Transfiguration. Therefore, since our faith will not allow us to think this was a mere illusion <note>original: "prestigious thing"</note>, they must have appeared in real bodies. These bodies also seem to have been "bright-form" <note>original Greek: Αυγοειδῆ (Augoeidē)</note>, luciform, or glowing, much like our Savior's own transfigured body at that time.

<margin>Irenaeus, Book 5, chapter 8.</margin>
Again, there are several places in Scripture which affirm that those who are reborn and renewed have, even here in this life, a certain "earnest" <note>original: "earnest" - meaning a down payment or pledge</note> of their future inheritance, which is their spiritual or heavenly body. Similarly, the "quickening" or bringing to life of their mortal bodies is attributed to the power of the Spirit dwelling within them. This has been noted by some of the ancients, such as Irenaeus: "But now we receive a certain portion of his Spirit, for the perfecting and preparation of incorruptibility, gradually becoming accustomed to receive and carry God. Which the Apostle also called a pledge; that is, a portion of that honor which is promised to us by God" <note>original Latin: *Nunc autem Partem aliquam Spiritus ejus sumimus, ad Perfectionem & Præparationem Incorruptelæ, paulatim assuescentes Capere & Portare Deum. Quod & Pignus dixit Apostolus; hoc est, Partem ejus Honoris, qui à Deo nobis promissus est*</note> —— If therefore this pledge dwelling in us now...

The author uses the biblical appearances of Moses and Elijah and the writings of Irenaeus to support the idea that spiritual beings possess refined, "luciform" bodies.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that the soul is not entirely disembodied after death, citing early Church Fathers who believed that the "spiritual body" begins to form even before the final resurrection.</meta>

<page-num>806</page-num>

<header>Whether any Created Spirit, BOOK I.</header>

"[He] made them spiritual, and the mortal is swallowed up by immortality" <note>original Latin: *Spirituales effecit, & absorbetur Mortale ab Immortalitate.* This is likely a quote from Irenaeus.</note>. Now we have a part of that Spirit for the preparation and perfection of incorruption; we are becoming accustomed, bit by bit, to receive and bear God. The Apostle also called this an "earnest" <note>original: "earnest" (a pledge or down payment); see 2 Corinthians 1:22</note>; that is, a part of that honor which is promised to us by God. Therefore, if this earnest (or pledge) dwelling in us has already made us spiritual, then the mortal is also swallowed up by immortality. And Novatian writes, "The Holy Spirit works in us to lead our bodies toward eternity and the resurrection of immortality, while it accustoms them within itself to be mingled with heavenly virtue" <note>original Latin: *Spiritus Sanctus id agit in nobis, ut ad Æternitatem & ad Resurrectionem Immortalitatis, corpora nostra perducat, dum illa in se assuefacit cum Cælesti Virtute misceri.*</note>. This is what the Holy Spirit does in us: namely, to lead our bodies toward eternity and the resurrection of immortality, while it accustoms us to be mingled with heavenly virtue. 

Moreover, there are some passages which seem to imply that good people shall, after death, have a further beginning <term>original: inchoation</term> of their heavenly body, the full completion of which is not to be expected before the resurrection or Day of Judgment. "We know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens." For "in this we groan earnestly" <note>2 Corinthians 5:1-2</note>. And verse 5 says, "Now he who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who also has given us the earnest of the Spirit." Now, how these preludes and foretastes <term>original: prelibations</term> of an immortal body can be consistent with the soul's survival after death in a state of perfect separation from any kind of body until the Day of Judgment is not easily understood.

Lastly, there is no doubt that Irenaeus, Origen, and those other ancient writers who held the opinion that souls are clothed after death with a certain thin and subtle body, did not think this was at all inconsistent with the future resurrection. It is no more inconsistent than for someone who is wearing only a shirt or waistcoat to put on a suit of clothes or an outer garment. This will seem even less strange if one considers that even here in this life, our body is, in a sense, twofold: exterior and interior. Besides the tangible mass of our outward body, we have another interior spiritual body, which is the soul's immediate instrument for both sensation and motion. This latter body is not put into the grave with the other, nor is it imprisoned under the cold sod. Despite everything suggested here, we will not venture to decide anything on such a significant point, but will leave it skeptically undecided.

The third and final point in the previously mentioned philosophical or Pythagorean tradition <term>original: cabbala</term> concerns those beings superior to humans, commonly called "demons" by the Greeks. Philo tells us these are the same as "angels" among the Jews; accordingly, the words "demons" and "angels" are sometimes used interchangeably as synonyms by Hierocles, Simplicius, and other later Pagan writers. The theory is that these demons or angels are not pure, abstract, incorporeal substances lacking a vital union with any matter. Instead, they consist of something incorporeal and something corporeal joined together. As Hierocles writes of them, "the upper part of them is incorporeal..." <note>original Greek: τὸ μὲν ἄνω αὐτῶν ἀσώμα-</note>

<summary>This page explores the idea that the "spiritual body" begins to develop before the final Resurrection, acting as a "pledge" of immortality. It also introduces the Pythagorean view that angels and demons are not purely spirit but consist of both incorporeal and corporeal elements.</summary>

<page-num>807</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER V. Without a Corporeal Clothing.</header>

<note>original Greek: τῇ οὐσίᾳ, τὸ δὲ κάτω σωματική</note> "...in their essence, but the lower part is corporeal." They have a superior and an inferior part in them; and their *superior part* is an *incorporeal substance*, while their *inferior part* is *corporeal*. In a word, they all, as well as *humans*, consist of *soul* and *body* united together. There is only this difference between them: the *souls* of these *demons* or *angels* *never descend* down to such *gross* and *terrestrial bodies* as *human souls* do, but are always *clothed* with either *aerial* or *ethereal* ones. 

Indeed, this *Pythagorean Cabbala* <note>In this context, "Cabbala" refers to a traditional or oral philosophical doctrine rather than Jewish mysticism.</note> was universal concerning all *understanding beings* except the *Supreme Deity*, or the *Trinity of Divine Hypostases* <term>the three persons or "substances" of the Godhead</term>. This applied to all the *inferior pagan gods*: they are nothing other than *souls* vitally united to some *bodies*, and thus made up of *incorporeal* and *corporeal substance* joined together. For thus *Hierocles* <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> plainly expresses himself in the previously cited passage: 

<note>original Greek: ἡ λογικὴ οὐσία παρὰ τοῦ δημιουργοῦ εἰς τὸ εἶναι οὕτω παρῆλθεν, ὡς μήτε τὸ σῶμα εἶναι αὐτὴν μήτε ἄνευ σώματὸς, &c.</note> *The rational nature* (in general) *was so produced by God that it is neither body itself, nor yet without body; but an incorporeal substance having a related or congenital body*. 

He also declared the same thing elsewhere:
<margin>Page 176</margin>
<note>original Greek: ἔστι γὰρ πᾶς μὲν ὁ λογικὸς διάκοσμος, μετὰ τοῦ συμπεφυκότος αὐτῷ ἀφθάρτου σώματος, εἰκὼν ὅλου τοῦ δημιουργοῦ</note> *The whole rational order, or rank of being, with its congenital immortal body, is the image of the whole Deity, its maker*. 

By Hierocles’s *rational nature or essence*, and by the *whole rational order*, he plainly means all *created understanding beings*. He acknowledges only these *three kinds and degrees*: *first*, the *immortal gods*, which to him are the *animated stars*; *secondly*, *demons*, *angels*, or *heroes*; and *thirdly*, *humans*, whom he also calls <note>original Greek: καταχθόνιοι δαίμονες</note> *terrestrial demons*. He pronounces of them all that they are alike: *incorporeal substances* together with a *congenital immortal body*. He argues there is no other *understanding nature* than these, besides the *Supreme Deity*, who is *complete in himself* without the *conjunction* of any *body*. 

So, according to Hierocles, the *ancient Pythagorean Cabbala* acknowledged no such *entities* at all as the *intelligences* of *Aristotle* or the *Noes* <note>From the Greek 'nous' (mind/intellect); refers to purely intellectual beings in Platonism.</note> of some *high-flown Platonists* (that is, perfectly *unbodied minds*). Much less did it acknowledge any *rank of Henades or Unities* superior to these *Noes*. 

Indeed, such *particular created beings* as these could have neither *sense* nor *cognizance* of any *corporeal thing* existing outside of them. (Sense, as *Aristotle* observed, results from a *combination of soul and body*, just as *weaving* results from a *combination of the weaver and the weaving instruments*). Nor could they *act* upon any *part of the corporeal universe*. Thus, these *immovable beings* would be like *adamantine statues*—things *unconnected* with the rest of the *world*, having no *commerce* with anything at all but the *Deity*. They would be a kind of *insignificant metaphysical gazers* or *contemplators*. 

However, the *Deity*, although it is not properly <note>original Greek: ψυχὴ ἐγκόσμιος</note> a *mundane soul* <note>A soul that is part of the world, like a human soul is part of a body.</note> (which, together with the *corporeal world* as its *body*, makes up one *complete* and *entire animal*), must still take *cognizance* of all and *act* upon all in the world, because the whole world proceeded from it and perpetually depends upon it. For this reason, it has been styled by these *Pythagoreans* as <note>original Greek: ψυχὴ ὑπερκόσμιος</note> a *supramundane soul* (not a *mundane* soul)...

<summary>This page argues, via the Neoplatonist Hierocles, that all created rational beings—angels, demons, and humans—are composed of an incorporeal soul and a congenital body. Only the Supreme Deity is entirely without a body, as a purely unbodied created mind would be unable to sense or interact with the physical world.</summary>
<keywords>Hierocles, Pythagoras, Aristotle, Neoplatonism, mundane soul, supramundane soul, demons, angels, incorporeal substance, Noes, Henades, dualism</keywords>

--- Page 826 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of whether created spirits can exist without bodies, specifically focusing on the views of the 3rd-century theologian Origen and his alignment with the Pythagorean tradition (referred to as the "Pythagorick Cabbala").</meta>

<page-num>808</page-num>
<header>Origen's full Agreement, with Book I.</header>

...mundane, but) a *supra-mundane soul*. Therefore, this ancient *Pythagorean tradition* <note>original: "Pythagorick Cabbala." Here, "Cabbala" refers to a traditional or oral philosophical doctrine rather than Jewish mysticism.</note> seems to be reasonable as well: that God should be the only *incorporeal being* in this sense—one whose *essence* is complete and whose life is entire within itself, without the *conjunction* or *addition* of any *body*. However, it holds that all other *created incorporeal substances* should be *completed* and *formed* by a *vital union* with *matter*. Thus, as a whole, they are neither purely *corporeal* nor purely *incorporeal*, but a *combination* of both; and all the *highest* and *most divine* things in the universe, next to the *Supreme Deity*, are *living beings* <note>original: "Animals." In this context, the author uses the term in its Latin sense, *animalis*, meaning any creature possessed of a soul (*anima*).</note> consisting of *soul* and *body* united together. In this way, the ancient defenders of incorporeal substance (viewed as *unextended*) avoided the *absurdity* often *objected* against them—the idea that all finite created spirits have no location. Because these *incorporeal substances* are vitally clothed with some *body*, they can—by reason of the *locality* and *mobility* of their respective bodies—truly be said to <note>A printer's duplication error in the original text has been corrected here.</note> be here and there, and to *move* from place to place.

Therefore, we must also show here what *agreement* or *disagreement* exists between this part of the *Pythagorean tradition* and *Christian philosophy*. First, it has already been suggested that the very same *doctrine* held by the ancient *Pythagoreans* was plainly asserted by *Origen*. Thus, in his first book of *On First Principles* <note>original: "Peri Archon." This is Origen's most famous theological work.</note>, chapter 6, he says:

"It is unique to the nature of God alone—that is, of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—to be understood as existing without material substance, and without the companionship of any corporeal addition." <note>original: "Solius Dei, id est Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus Sancti, Naturæ id proprium est, ut sine Materiali Substantiâ, & absque Ullâ Corporeæ Adjectionis Societate, intelligatur subsistere."</note>

Again, in Book 2, chapter 2:

"Material substance in rational natures is only separable from them in thought and understanding; it seems to be made for them, or to exist after them; but they have never lived, nor do they live, without it. For a life that is perfectly incorporeal is rightly thought to belong to the Trinity alone." <note>original: "Materialem Substantiam Opinione quidem & Intellectu solum Separari, à Naturis Rationalibus... solius namque Trinitatis Incorporea Vita existere rectè putabitur."</note>

So also in his fourth book and his *Summary* <note>original: "Anacephalæosis." A Greek term for a summary or recap.</note>:

"There will always be rational natures that need a corporeal garment. Therefore, there will always be a corporeal nature, whose garments rational creatures must necessarily use. Unless someone thinks they can show that a rational nature can lead a life without any body. But we have shown above how difficult and almost impossible that is for our understanding." <note>original: "Semper erunt Rationabiles Naturæ, quæ indigent Indumento Corporeo... in Superioribus ostendimus."</note>

*Aquinas* <note>Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century philosopher and theologian.</note> claims that *Origen*, in this doctrine of his, followed the opinion of certain ancient philosophers; and undoubtedly it was the old *Pythagorean tradition* which the learned *Origen* followed here: that *the rational essence* <note>original Greek: ἡ λογικὴ οὐσία</note>, as it is in Hierocles...

<meta>This page continues the discussion regarding the nature of created spirits and whether they possess bodies. It specifically focuses on the interpretations of Origen and Hierocles, arguing that they viewed created rational beings as incorporeal souls united with subtle bodies, rather than as purely material or purely immaterial entities.</meta>

<page-num>809</page-num>
# Chap. V. The Old Pythagorean Tradition <note>original: "Pythagor. Cabbala"</note>

*Hierocles* says that "the entire rational order" <note>original: *πᾶς ὁ λογικὸς διάκοσμος*</note>—that is, the rational nature made by God, consisting of all created intelligent beings—is neither just a body nor entirely without a body. Instead, these beings always have a naturally related or congenital <note>original: "congenite"</note> body that serves as their vehicle or clothing <note>original: "indument"</note>. Thus, according to both *Origen* and *Hierocles*, all *angels* or *demons* are *incorporeal substances*. They are not "naked" or abstract, but *clothed with certain subtle bodies*. They are living beings <note>original: "animals"</note> composed and made up of *soul* and *body together*.

Therefore, *Huetius* <note>Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French scholar and bishop who critiqued Origen.</note> and other learned men do not seem to have understood *Origen* well here. They have confused *two* different *opinions* by assuming that he claimed *angels* and all *intelligent creatures* do not *have bodies*, but *are bodies* and nothing else. This would lead to the conclusion that there is no *incorporeal substance* at all except for the *Deity*. In contrast, *Origen* only affirms that nothing besides the *Trinity* could exist and live alone "without the partnership of any corporeal addition" <note>original: *absque ulla corporeæ adjectionis Societate*</note>, and that the *material nature* is merely a *necessary clothing* or garment <note>original: "indument"</note> for all *rational or intelligent creatures*.

In this sense, he says that an *incorporeal life* belongs *only to the Trinity*, because all other *intelligent beings* are living creatures <note>original: "animals"</note> composed of *soul* and *body together*. However, it can be proven from various passages in his writings that *Origen* acknowledged even our *human soul* itself to be *incorporeal*, and also that there is *something incorporeal in angels*. This is seen particularly in his sixth book against *Celsus*: "We do not believe an incorporeal substance can be consumed by fire; nor can the soul of man be dissolved into fire, nor the substance of angels, thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers" <note>original: *ἡμεῖς ἀσώματον οὐσίαν οὐκ ἴσμεν ἐκπυρουμένην, οὐδ' εἰς πῦρ ἀναλυομένην τὴν ἀνθρώπου ψυχήν, ἢ τὴν ἀγγέλων ἢ θρόνων, &c. ὑπόστασιν*</note>.

By the *substance* of angels, he undoubtedly meant their *souls*. *Origen’s* meaning was described this way by *Saint Jerome*: "In his books *On First Principles* <note>original: *Peri Archon* or *περὶ ἀρχῶν*</note>, he states that angels, thrones, dominions, powers, the governors of the darkness of this world, and every name that is named (as mentioned by Saint Paul) are all of them the souls of those bodies which they have received either by their own desire and inclination, or by divine assignment" <note>original: *In Libris περὶ ἀρχῶν, Angelos, & Thronos, & Dominationes, & Potestates, & Rectores Mundi & Tenebrarum, & omne Nomen quod nominatur, dicit, Animas esse eorum Corporum, quæ vel Desiderio vel ministerio susceperint*</note>.

Now there can be no doubt that a person who believed human souls were incorporeal in a *strict philosophical sense*—meaning they could not be affected by *fire*—also acknowledged *something incorporeal in angels*. He declares this somewhere in that book *On First Principles*: "When Paul affirms that all things, visible and invisible, were created by Christ (or the *Word* <note>original: *Logos*</note>), he suggests that even among created beings, there are some that are properly invisible substances by their own nature. Although these are not themselves corporeal, they nevertheless use bodies, even though they are superior to corporeal substance. But the substance of the Trinity must be believed to be neither a body nor inside a body, but entirely incorporeal" <note>original: *Per Christum creata dixit (Paulus) omnia Visibilia & Invisibilia, per quod declaratur, esse etiam in Creaturis quasdam Invisibiles, secundum proprietatem suam, Substantias; Sed hæ quamvis ipsæ non sunt Corporeæ, utuntur tamen Corporibus, licet ipsæ sunt Corporeâ Substantiâ meliores. Illa vero Substantia Trinitatis neque Corpus, neque In Corpore, esse credenda est: sed in toto Incorporea.*</note>. This implies that even among creatures, there are some properly

<meta>catchword: Invisible</meta>

It refutes the claim that Origen believed these beings were purely material, emphasizing that only the Trinity is entirely without a body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that Origen did not believe spirits were material substances, but rather that they were incorporeal souls bound to subtle bodies. It contrasts this with the "extremes" held by other Church Fathers.</meta>

<page-num>810</page-num>
<header>To the Majority of Fathers; BOOK I.</header>

*Created invisible substances, though they are not bodies, do use bodies; they themselves are better than physical substance. However, the substance of the Trinity is neither a body nor located in a body, but is altogether incorporeal. Therefore, angelic and human souls are not—as Huetius <note>Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a scholar who critiqued Origen’s theology.</note> supposes—called "incorporeal" by Origen only in the way that subtle bodies sometimes are by the more simple and uneducated. Rather, he uses the term in a strict philosophical sense. Origen only supposed them to differ from the Deity in this: although they are not bodies, they are always *in* bodies, or clothed with bodies. In contrast, the Deity is incorporeal in both senses, having no physical garment <note>original: "indument"</note> at all. So, there is no contradiction to be found in Origen; he constantly asserts that angels have something incorporeal in them as their superior part—and not in the common sense of a "subtle body," but in the philosophical sense—yet they also have a physical garment or clothing as their outside or lower part. In that regard only, he calls them "corporeal."*

It is true indeed that there were some among the *Ancient Fathers* who were so far from supposing *angels* to be altogether *incorporeal* that they ran into the other *extreme*. They concluded that angels had *nothing* at all incorporeal in them but were *mere bodies*. These thinkers either asserted that there was no such thing as *incorporeal substance* at all, and that not only *angels* and *human souls* but also *God himself* was a *body*; or, at least, they concluded that nothing *created* was *incorporeal*. They believed that *God*, though *himself incorporeal*, could *create* nothing but *bodies*.

These are the *two extremes*: *one*, that *angels* have nothing *corporeal* belonging to them at all; the *other*, that they are *altogether corporeal* or have *nothing incorporeal* in them. A *middle* path between both is the *Origenist hypothesis* (the same as the *Pythagorean*): that in *angels* there is a *combination* of *incorporeal* and *corporeal substance* together, or that they are *living beings* <note>original: "animals"</note> consisting of *soul* and *body*. 

We shall now show that the *greater part* of the *Ancient Fathers* supported neither of the *two aforementioned extremes* (either *that angels were wholly incorporeal* or that they were *wholly corporeal*). Rather, they favored the *middle hypothesis*: *that they had bodies* and yet *were not bodies*. Like other *earthly animals*, they were *spirits* or *souls* *clothed with ethereal* or *airy bodies*. 

That the *generality* of the *ancient* and *most learned Fathers* did not conceive *angels* to be mere *unbodied spirits* is unquestionably evident from this: they agreed with the *Greek philosophers* in the *concept* that *evil demons* or *devils* took delight in the *blood* and *savors* <term>original: "nidours" — the smell of burning fat or meat</term> of *sacrifices*. They believed the demons' more *gross, airy, and vaporous bodies* were nourished and refreshed by those *vapors*, in which they did, as it were, *luxuriate* and *gluttonize*. 

For this is what *Porphyry* <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD).</note> writes concerning them in his book *On Abstinence* <note>original: *De Abstinentia*</note>: "These are they who take pleasure in the incense, fumes, and smells of sacrifices, by which their corporeal and spirit-like part is, as it were, fattened <note>original: "pinguified"; from the Latin *pinguis* meaning fat</note>; for this lives and is nourished by vapors and fumigations." <note>original Greek: οὗτοι οἱ χαίροντες λοιβῇ τε, κνίσῃ τε, δι’ ὧν αὐτῶν, τὸ σωματικὸν καὶ πνευματικὸν πιαίνεται: ζῇ γὰρ τοῦτο ἀτμοῖς καὶ ἀναθυμιάμασι.</note> And that—

<summary>This page argues that Origen and many Church Fathers held a "middle" view of angels: they are incorporeal souls possessing "airy" or "ethereal" bodies. This explains the ancient belief that demons were physically nourished by the smoke of animal sacrifices.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous page that while some Church Fathers believed angels and demons were purely physical, others (like Origen) believed they possessed both an incorporeal soul and a physical body of varying density.</meta>

# Chapter 5: Demons and Angels, Bodied.

Before Porphyry, many other Pagan philosophers had held the same opinion, as appears from this passage by Celsus: <margin>Origen, Book 8</margin> <note>original Greek: "χρὴ γὰρ ἴσως οὐκ ἀπιστεῖν ἀνδράσι σοφοῖς, οἳ δή φασι, διότι τῶν μὲν ἐπιγείων δαιμόνων τὸ πλεῖστον γενέσει συντετηκὸς, καὶ προσηλωμένον αἵματι καὶ κνίσῃ, &c."</note> *“We ought perhaps to give credit to wise men who affirm that most of these lower demons who live around the earth are bonded to procreation and are pinned to blood and the smell of roasting meat <note>original: "nidours"</note>, and such things, being much gratified by them—though they are not able to do anything more by way of recompense than perhaps sometimes to cure the body, or to foretell good and evil fortunes to men and cities.”* Because of this, Celsus himself—though a zealous Pagan—persuaded men to be moderate in the use of these sacrifices, as they principally gratified only the inferior and worse demons. 

In the same way, Origen frequently insists upon the same thing, affirming that devils were not only delighted with the idolatry of the Pagans in their sacrifices, but also, <margin>Against Celsus, Book 7, Page 334</margin> <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ τῶν θυσιῶν ἀναθυμιάσεσι καὶ ταῖς ἀπὸ τῶν αἱμάτων καὶ ὁλοκαυτωμάτων ἀποφοραῖς τρέφεσθαι τὰ σώματα φιληδονούντων τοῖς τοιούτοις"</note> *“that their very bodies were nourished by the vapors and fumes arising from them; and that these evil demons therefore did, as it were, feast and live luxuriously <note>original: "Epicurize"</note> upon them.”* And before Origen, most of the ancient Fathers—such as Justin Martyr, Athenagoras, Tatian, Tertullian, etc., as well as many others after him—endeavored to disparage those material and bloody sacrifices for the same reason: as things by which evil demons were principally gratified. 

We shall here only cite one passage to this purpose out of Saint Basil (or whoever was the author of that commentary upon Isaiah), because there is <margin>Chapter 1</margin> something philosophical in it: <note>original Greek: "δαίμοσι διὰ τὸ φιλήδονον καὶ ἐμπαθὲς, αἱ θυσίαι φέρουσί τινα ἡδονὴν καὶ χρείαν ἐκθυμώμεναι, διὰ τῆς καύσεως ἐξατμιζομένης τοῦ αἵματος, καὶ οὕτω διὰ τῆς τοιαύτης λεπτοποιήσεως, εἰς τὴν σύστασιν αὐτῶν ἀναλαμβανομένης· ὅλοι γὰρ δι᾿ ὅλων τρέφονται τοῖς ἀτμοῖς, οὐ διὰ μασήσεως καὶ κοιλίας, ἀλλ᾿ ὡς αἱ τρίχες πάντων ζώων καὶ ὄνυχες, καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα εἰς ὅλων ἑαυτῶν τὴν οὐσίαν, τὴν τροφὴν καταδέχεται"</note> *“Sacrifices are things of no small pleasure and advantage to demons; because the blood, being evaporated by fire and so thinned, is taken into the structure <note>original: "Compages"</note> and substances of their bodies. Their whole being is nourished throughout with vapors—not by eating and stomachs or similar organs—but as the hair and nails of all animals, and whatever other such things receive nourishment into their whole substance.”* 

And thus we see it undeniably manifest that many of the ancient Fathers supposed devils to have bodies. Nor can it be doubted that they concluded the same of angels too, as these are both of the same kind and differ only as good and evil men do. And though they do not affirm this of good angels—but of devils only—that they were thus delighted and nourished with the fumes and vapors of sacrifices and that they feasted on them, the reason for this was not because they conceived the good angels to be altogether incorporeal. Rather, they believed the good angels had pure ethereal or heavenly bodies, while it was characteristic only of those gross and vaporous bodies of demons to be nourished and refreshed in that manner. 

And now, the fact that all these ancient Fathers did not suppose either angels or devils to be altogether corporeal, or to have nothing but body in them, may be concluded from this: many of them plainly declared the souls of men to be incorporeal...

<summary>This page explores the belief held by many ancient philosophers and Church Fathers that demons possess physical bodies which are nourished by the fumes and blood of animal sacrifices. It argues that while demons have gross, vaporous bodies, angels are thought to have pure ethereal bodies, yet both possess an underlying incorporeal soul.</summary>

# St. Augustine and Others; That BOOK I.

And therefore it cannot be imagined that they would so far degrade angels below humans as to refuse to acknowledge that they have any incorporeal nature at all.

But we shall now provide examples of a few among the many *ancients* who plainly asserted that both *devils* and *angels* are incorporeal spirits, and that they are not merely bodies, but rather that they *have* bodies; that is, they consist of a soul and a body, or an incorporeal and corporeal substance joined together. That angels themselves *have* bodies is declared everywhere by *St. Augustine* <note>original: St. Austin</note> in his writings. He affirms <margin>Commentary on Psalm 85</margin> that the bodies of good men after the Resurrection shall be *just like the bodies of angels* <note>original Latin: Qualia sunt Angelorum Corpora</note>, and that they <margin>Commentary on Psalm 145</margin> shall be *angelic bodies, fit for the society and conversation of angels* <note>original Latin: Corpora Angelica in Societate Angelorum</note>. He also explains the difference <margin>On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, Book 3, Chapter 10</margin> between the bodies of *angels* and *devils* in this way: *“Before they transgressed, demons possessed celestial bodies; these were converted as a punishment into an aerial quality, so that they can now suffer from fire”* <note>original Latin: Dæmones antequam transgrederentur, Cælestia Corpora gerebant, quæ conversa sint ex pæna in Aeream Qualitatem, ut jam possint ab Igne Pati</note>. This implies that although devils possessed celestial bodies like angels before their fall, these were later changed into an "aerial" form as a punishment, making them susceptible to the pain of fire.

Moreover, the same *St. Augustine* elsewhere calls good angels by the name of *blessed and holy souls* <note>original Latin: Animæ Beatæ atque Sanctæ</note>. Although it is true that in his <margin>Book 2, Chapter 11</margin> *Retractions* <note>Augustine’s late-life work where he reviewed and corrected his earlier writings</note> he recalls and corrects this, it was only a point of caution <note>original: "scrupulosity"</note> for that pious Father regarding the specific word, because he could not find angels called by the name "souls" anywhere in Scripture. Even there, he was far from denying that they are incorporeal spirits joined with bodies. And certainly, since he everywhere concludes that human souls are incorporeal, he cannot be thought to have supposed that angels have no incorporeal element <note>original: "nothing at all Body"; the context and the author's argument suggest "nothing at all incorporeal," meaning Augustine did not believe angels were purely material</note> in them. 

Again, *Claudianus Mamertus* <note>a 5th-century Gallo-Roman theologian</note>, writing against *Faustus* <note>Faustus of Riez, a bishop who argued that only God is truly incorporeal and that angels have material bodies</note>—who claimed that angels were merely bodies without souls or anything incorporeal—maintains the opposite view. He argues not that they are merely incorporeal spirits without bodies (which is the other extreme), but that they consist of both the corporeal and the incorporeal—soul and body joined together. He writes this regarding the devils: *“The devil consists of a double and different substance; he is both corporeal and incorporeal”* <note>original Latin: Diabolus ex Duplici diversaque Substantia constat: & Corporeus est & Incorporeus</note>. 

And again <margin>Book 3</margin> concerning angels: *“It is manifest that the blessed angels are of a two-fold substance; they are incorporeal in that part of them through which God is visible to them, and likewise corporeal in that part through which they are visible to men”* <note>original Latin: Patet Beatos Angelos, Utriusque Substantiæ, & Incorporeos esse in ea sui parte, qua ipsis Visibilis Deus; & in ea itidem Parte Corporeos, qua hominibus sunt ipsi Visibiles</note>. 

<margin>Book 3, On the Trinity</margin> Moreover, *Fulgentius* <note>Fulgentius of Ruspe, a 6th-century North African bishop</note> writes concerning angels in this manner: *“Great and learned men plainly affirm that they consist of a double substance. That is, of an incorporeal spirit, by which they never cease to contemplate God, and of a body through which they occasionally appear to men. Indeed, they say that angels have ethereal—that is, fiery—bodies, while demons have aerial bodies”* <note>original Latin: Planè ex Duplici eos esse Substantia asserunt Magni & Docti Viri. Id est, Ex Spiritu Incorporeo, quo à Dei contemplatione nunquam recedunt; & ex Corpore per quod ex tempore hominibus apparent. Corpora vero Ætherea, id est, Ignea, eos dicunt habere, Dæmones vero Corpus Aereum</note>. Great and learned men affirm that angels consist of a double substance—that is, of an incorporeal spirit, by which they contemplate God, and of a body by which they are sometimes visible to men—and also that they have *ethereal*

### CHAP. V. Angels, Embodied Spirits.

*Ethereal* or *fiery bodies*, but *devils* have *airy bodies*. And perhaps this was the meaning of *John of Thessalonica* <note>original: Joannes Thessalonicensis</note> in that dialogue of his, which was read and approved in the Seventh Council <note>The Second Council of Nicaea, 787 AD</note>. Therefore, it was also the meaning of that council itself when it was declared: "The Catholic Church knows them to be intellectual beings, but not altogether incorporeal and invisible; rather, they have certain subtle bodies, either airy or fiery." <note>original Greek: νοεροὺς μὲν αὐτοὺς ἡ καθολικὴ ἐκκλησία γινώσκει, οὐ μὴν ἀσωμάτους πάντη καὶ ἀοράτους, λεπτοσωμάτους δὲ, καὶ ἀερώδεις, ἢ πυρώδεις, &c.</note> Since it was only denied there that they were *altogether incorporeal*, one would think the meaning was not that they were *altogether corporeal*—nor indeed could such an opinion be attributed to the *Catholic Church*. Rather, the meaning is that they were partly *incorporeal* and partly *corporeal*. This distinction was sufficient for the goals pursued by that council.

However, *Psellus* <note>Michael Psellus, an 11th-century Byzantine philosopher and scholar of the supernatural</note>, who was a dedicated researcher into the nature of *spirits*, declares it not only as his own opinion but also as agreeable to the views of the *ancient Fathers*: "That the demonic or angelic kind of beings is not altogether incorporeal or bodiless, but that they are joined with bodies, or have natural bodies belonging to them." <note>original Greek: ὡς οὐκ ἀσώματόν τι τὸ δαιμόνιόν ἐστι φῦλον, μετὰ σώματος δέ γε</note> He further explains the difference between the *bodies of good angels* and those of *evil demons* in this manner: 

<margin>Page 33.</margin> 

"The angelic body sends forth certain strange rays and splendors that are unbearable and overwhelming to mortal eyes. But the demonic body—though it seems to have once been like that too (since Isaiah called the one who fell from heaven 'Lucifer' <note>The 'Morning Star'</note>)—is now dark and obscure, foul and squalid, and painful to behold, having been deprived of its natural light and beauty. 

Again, the angelic body is so entirely free of gross matter that it can pass through any solid thing; it is indeed more impassible <note>term: impassible; incapable of being affected or harmed by physical force</note> than sunbeams. For although sunbeams can pass through transparent bodies, they are blocked by earthy and opaque objects and are reflected by them. In contrast, the angelic body is such that nothing is so solid or lacking in pores that it can resist or shut it out. 

But the demonic bodies, though they usually escape our sight because of their thinness, nonetheless have gross matter in them. They are patible <note>term: patible; capable of feeling or suffering</note>, especially those that inhabit subterranean places. For these have such a gross consistency and solidity that they can sometimes be felt by touch; and when struck, they feel pain and are capable of being burnt with fire." <note>original Greek: τὸ μὲν γὰρ ἀγγελικὸν, αὐγάς τινας ἐξανθίζον ξένας... τὰ δὲ δαιμόνια σώματα... ἔνυλά πη, καὶ ἐμπαθῆ...</note>

To this point, the *Thracian* <note>likely referring to a character in Psellus’s dialogue "De Operatione Daemonum"</note> adds more afterward from the...

<header>Angels called Incorporeal, BOOK I.</header>

<margin>P. 94.</margin>
According to the information provided by *Marcus the Monk*—a person formerly initiated into the *demonic mysteries* <note>original: "Diabolick Mysteries"</note> and possessor of great curiosity: "The demonic spirit or subtle body, being in every part of it capable of sensation, immediately sees and hears, and is also subject to the sensations of touch. Consequently, if it is suddenly divided or cut in two, it feels pain just as the solid bodies of other animals do. It differs from them only in this: while those other bodies, once separated, are not easily joined back together, the demonic body, when divided, is quickly restored by merging back together, like air or water. Nevertheless, it is not without a sense of pain at the moment when it is thus divided, etc." <note>original Greek: τὸ δαιμόνιον ἄρα πνεῦμα διόλου ὂν κατὰ φύσιν αἰσθητικὸν κατὰ πᾶν ἑαυτοῦ μέρος, ἀμέσως ὁρᾷ τε καὶ ἀκούει, καὶ τὰ τῆς ἁφῆς ὑπομένει πάθη, διαιρεμένον ὀδυνᾶται κατὰ τῶν σωμάτων τὰ στερεά· ταύτῃ τούτων διενεγκόν, ὅτι τὰ μὲν ἄλλα τῶν διαιρεθέντων, μόλις ἢ οὐδαμῶς ἑνοῦται τὸ δὲ διαιρούμενον εὐθὺς συμφύεται, καθάπερ ἀέρος ἢ καὶ ὕδατος μόρια μεταξύ τινος ἐμπίπτοντα στερεοῦ· ἀλλ᾿ εἰ καὶ θᾶττον ἢ λόος τοτὶ τὸ πνεῦμα συμφύεται, πλὴν ἀνιᾶται κατ᾿ αὐτὸ τὸ γίνεσθαι τὴν διαίρεσιν</note> 

Moreover, the same *Marcus* affirms that the bodies of these demons are also nourished, though in a different manner from our own: "Some of them are nourished by inhalation <note>original: "Inspiration," meaning the drawing in of air</note>, like the spirit contained in the nerves and arteries; others by sucking in the surrounding moisture, not through mouths as we do, but like sponges and shellfish <note>original: "Testaceous Fishes"</note>, drawing in the moisture from the outside." <note>original Greek: τρέφονται οἱ μὲν δι᾿ εἰσπνοῆς, ὡς τὸ ἐν ἀρτηρίαις καὶ ἐν νεύροις πνεῦμα· οἱ δὲ δι᾿ ὑγρότητος, ἀλλ᾿ οὐ στόματι καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς, ἀλλ᾿ ὥσπερ σπόγγοι καὶ ὀστρακόδερμα, σπῶντες μὲν τῆς παρακειμένης ὑγρότητος ἔξωθεν</note> 

And now we may venture to conclude that this opinion—that angels are not merely *abstract incorporeal substances* and *bodiless minds*, but consist of *something incorporeal* and *something corporeal* (that is, of a soul or spirit and a body joined together)—is not only more agreeable to *reason*, but has also had more support <note>original: "suffrages"</note> among the ancient Fathers. Their weight of authority is greater than either of the two other extremes: namely, that angels are purely bodies and have nothing incorporeal in them, or else that they are altogether incorporeal without any bodily *garment* <note>original: "Indument"</note> or *clothing*.

Despite this, the latter opinion has indeed prevailed most in these recent centuries. *Time* is rightly compared to a *river*, which quickly sinks the more weighty and *solid things* and carries along only the *lighter* and more *superficial*. However, there may be other reasons given for this as well. One is that *Aristotelian philosophy*, when generally introduced into *Christianity*, brought its *abstract intelligences* <note>In Aristotle's system, these are the immaterial beings that move the celestial spheres</note> along with it. Another reason is that some counterfeit *Platonists* spoke so much of their *Henades* <note>the "Ones," or primary unities</note> and *Noes* <note>pure intellects or minds</note>, their *simple monads* and *immovable unbodied minds*, as the highest of their *generated* and *created gods*; likely some Christians wanted their *angels* to compete with them. And lastly, it is because *angels* are not only called *spirits* in Scripture, but several of the ancients also said they were *incorporeal*. In those cases, however, they meant this either in regard to that *incorporeal part* (the *soul* or *mind*) which they supposed was within them, or else in regard to the *thinness* and *subtlety* of their bodies or *vehicles*. 

*Psellus* gives this account <margin>P. 30. 33.</margin> of the matter: "It is customary for both our own writers and those from outside the faith to call the thicker types of bodies..." <note>original Greek: καὶ τοῖς ἡμετέροις καὶ τοῖς θύραθεν, εἰωθός ἐστι, τὰ παχύτερα τῶν σωμάτων</note>

<summary>The author concludes that angels and demons are likely composed of both spirit and a subtle body, citing Marcus the Monk's descriptions of demonic sensation and nourishment as evidence. He argues that the modern preference for viewing angels as purely incorporeal stems from the influence of Aristotelian philosophy rather than the original views of the Church Fathers.</summary>

# Chapter IV. *as having Subtle Bodies.*

...it is common to call grosser bodies "corporeal"; but that which is composed of fine parts and escapes both sight and touch, not only our own writers but also many of the pagans are accustomed to call "incorporeal." <note>original Greek: σωμάτων σωματώδη λέγειν· ὁ δὲ λεπτομερές ἐστι καὶ τὴν ὄψιν διαφυγάνον, καὶ τὴν ἁφὴν ἀσώματον, οὐ μόνον οἱ καθ’ ἡμᾶς, ἀλλὰ καὶ πολλοὶ τῶν ἐκτὸς ἀξιοῦσι λέγειν.</note> And before Psellus, *Johannes Thessalonicensis*, in his Dialogue approved at the *Seventh Council* <note>The Second Council of Nicaea, 787 AD, which dealt with the use of icons and the nature of angels.</note>, wrote: "If you find angels, or demons, or separate souls called sometimes 'incorporeal,' you must understand this only in respect to the thinness <note>original: "tenuity"</note> of their bodies; as they do not consist of the grosser elements, nor are they as solid and resistant <note>original: "antitypous," meaning something that resists touch or occupies space in a way that prevents another body from being there</note> as these bodies in which we are now imprisoned." <note>original Greek: εἰ δὲ που εὕροις ἀσωμάτους καλουμένους τὰς ἀγγέλους, ἢ δαίμονας, ἢ ψυχὰς, ὡς μὴ ὄντας ἐκ συμμίξεως τῶν ὑλικῶν τεσσάρων στοιχείων, καὶ τοιαῦτα σώματα παχέα καὶ ἀντίτυπα, οἷα ἡμεῖς περικείμεθα, οὕτως αὐτὸς προσηγόρευσαν.</note>

And before both of them, *Origen* wrote in the introduction to his *On First Principles* <note>original Latin: "Peri Archon"</note>, citing a passage from an ancient book titled *The Doctrine of Peter*. In that book, our Savior Christ is said to have told his disciples that *he was not an incorporeal demon* <note>original Greek: δαιμόνιον ἀσώματον</note>. Though Origen rejected the authority of that book, he interpreted those words as follows:

"The word 'incorporeal' in that statement does not have the same meaning as it does when used by Greek and pagan authors when philosophers discuss an 'incorporeal nature.' In this little book, he called a demon 'incorporeal' because whatever the form or boundary of a demonic body may be, it is not similar to this thicker and visible body of ours. Instead, according to the sense of the person who wrote that scripture, we should understand it to mean that he [Christ] does not have the kind of body that demons have—which is naturally subtle, and thin like a breeze, and for that reason is either assumed by many to be, or at least called, 'incorporeal'—but rather that he possesses a solid and palpable body." <note>original Latin: non idem Sensus ex isto sermone ἀσωμάτου indicatur, qui Græcis vel Gentilibus auctoribus ostenditur, quum de Incorporeâ Naturâ à Philosophis disputatur. In hoc enim Libello, Incorporeum Dæmonium dixit, pro eo quod ipse ille quicunque est habitus vel circumscriptio Dæmonici Corporis, non est similis huic nostro Crassiori, vel Visibili Corpori: sed secundum sensum ejus qui composuit illam Scripturam, intelligendum est quod dixit; non esse tale Corpus quale habent Dæmones, quod est naturaliter Subtile, & velut Aura Tenue; & propter hoc vel imputatur à multis vel dicitur Incorporeum; sed habere se Corpus Solidum & Palpabile.</note>

Here we see plainly that angels, even though they are supposed to have bodies, may nevertheless be called *incorporeal*. This is because of the thinness and subtlety of their bodies compared with the grossness and solidity of our own earthly bodies. 

However, what currently most inclines some to the belief that angels have nothing corporeal about them at all is a religious regard for the authority of the *Third Lateran Council* <note>A council held in 1179 AD</note>, which approved this doctrine. They act as if the *Seventh Ecumenical Council* (also called the *Second Nicene Council*), in which the contrary view was previously owned and allowed, were not of equal force, or at least enough to counterbalance the other.

But although this *doctrine of angels*—the idea that all created intelligent beings superior to humans have a corporeal clothing or garment—agrees so exactly with the *old Pythagorean tradition* <note>original: "Pythagorick Cabbala"</note>, we have reason to think that it was not merely borrowed or derived from it...

<summary>This page argues that historical terms like "incorporeal" were often used relatively to describe the "thin" or "breezy" bodies of angels and demons, rather than to mean they lacked physical substance entirely. It cites Origen and various church councils to show that early Christian thought often viewed spiritual beings as having subtle bodies.</summary>

# In Scripture: Angels Sinning, BOOK I.

...from there, by the **Ancient Fathers**; but rather that they were led to this conclusion by the Scripture itself. For first, the **historical phenomena** <note>original: "Historick Phænomena," referring to the recorded physical appearances and actions of angels</note> of angels in the Scripture are such that they cannot easily be explained <note>original: "Salved"</note> without supposing them to have bodies. Furthermore, even if we do not place too much weight on the words of the Psalmist—*Who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire* (though the Ancient Fathers interpreted this in the sense of bodily substance with good reason)—because they may possibly be understood differently, as they sometimes are by **Rabbinical commentators**. Nor do we need to insist upon those passages from St. Paul where he speaks of the **tongues of angels**, and of the **voice of an archangel**, and similar things; for there are several other places in Scripture which seem plainly to confirm this opinion.

First, there is the statement of our Savior mentioned before for this purpose, in **Luke 20:35**: *Those who shall be accounted worthy to obtain that world, and the resurrection from the dead, neither marry nor are given in marriage, neither can they die anymore; for they are equal unto the angels.* If angels were utterly devoid of any bodies, then the **souls of good people**—while in a state of separation from the body and before any **resurrection**—would be "equal to angels" more so than they would be after their bodies are resurrected.

<margin>Augustine, *On the Literal Interpretation of Genesis*, Book 3.</margin>
Therefore, the **natural** meaning of these words (as **St. Augustine** interpreted them) seems to be that the **souls of good people**, after the **resurrection**, shall have *Angelical bodies* <note>original Latin: "Corpora Angelica"</note>, and *such bodies as those of angels are* <note>original Latin: "Qualia sunt Angelorum Corpora"</note>. In this, it is assumed that **angels** also have bodies, but of a very different kind from ours here on earth. Again, there is the passage from **St. Jude**, where he writes of the devils: *The angels which kept not their first estate* (or rather, according to the Latin Vulgate, *their own principality* <note>original Latin: "Suum Principatum"</note>) *but left their proper habitation* (or *dwelling house*), *he has reserved in everlasting chains, under darkness, unto the judgment of the great day.* These words first imply that the devils were created by God **pure**, just like the other angels, but that they did not keep *their own principality* <note>original Greek: "τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἀρχὴν" (tēn heautōn archēn)</note>. That is, they lost their **lordly power and dominion** over their **worse** and **inferior** part. This suggests they possessed a certain "duplicity" <note>meaning a twofold nature</note> in their nature, consisting of a **better** and **higher principle** which ought to **rule**, and an **inferior** part which ought to be **governed**. Indeed, it is not otherwise easy to conceive how they would be capable of **sinning**. And this **inferior part** in angels seems to refer to something **corporeal** or **bodily** within them, just as it does in humans.

In the next place, **St. Jude** adds—as the **immediate result and natural consequence** of these angels **sinning**—that they thereby **left** or **lost** *their own proper dwelling* <note>original Greek: "τὸ ἴδιον οἰκητήριον" (to idion oikētērion); Latin: "Suum Proprium Domicilium"</note>. This refers not only to their general dwelling place—those **ethereal countries** and **heavenly regions** above—but also to their **proper dwelling house** or **immediate mansion**; namely, their **heavenly body**. This is because the **heavenly body**, which good people expect after the **resurrection**, is called by **St. Paul** *our dwelling place which is from heaven* <note>original Greek: "τὸ οἰκητήριον ἡμῶν τὸ ἐξ οὐρανοῦ" (to oikētērion hēmōn to ex ouranou)</note>. The **heavenly body** is the **proper house** or **dwelling**, **clothing**, or **covering** <note>original: "Indument"</note> of both **angelic** and **human souls**; it is what makes them fit **inhabitants** for the heavenly regions. This, I say, was the **natural effect** and **consequence** of these angels **sinning**: the **leaving** or **losing** of their **pure, heavenly**...

# CHAP. V. Lost their Heavenly Body.

Heavenly Body, which became immediately thereafter **obscured** and **thickened** <note>original: "Incrassated"</note>; the bodies of **spirits incorporate** <note>spirits possessing a physical form</note> always maintain a **corresponding purity** or **impurity** based on the different disposition of their **mind** or **soul**. 

But then again, in the last place, that which was partly the **natural result of their sin** was also, by the just judgment of God, converted into their **punishment**. Because their **ethereal bodies** were thus changed into **gross**, **aerial**, **foul** <note>original: "Feculent"</note>, and **vaporous** ones, they were immediately thereupon—as St. **Peter** expresses it in a similar passage—**cast down into Tartarus** <note>original Greek: ταρταρωθέντες (*tartarōthentes*)</note>, and there **imprisoned**, or **reserved in chains under darkness**, until the judgment of the Great Day. 

It is notable here that the word **to cast into Tartarus** <note>original Greek: ταρταροῦν (*tartaroun*)</note>, used by St. Peter, is the very same word that **Apollodorus** <note>an ancient Greek scholar and mythographer</note> and other Greek writers frequently use in similar cases when they speak of the **Titans** being **cast down from heaven**. This seems to have been, in reality, nothing other than this **Fall of Angels** described through poetic myth. 

By **Tartarus** here, in all probability, is meant this **lower misty** <note>original: "Caliginous"</note> **air**, or the **atmosphere** of the **Earth**. This matches the words of **St. Austin** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo</note> concerning these angels: <margin>De Gen. ad Lit. L. 3. c. 10.</margin> **"After their sin, they were thrust down into this misty darkness, where the air is also present"** <note>original Latin: *Post Peccatum in hanc sunt detrusi Caliginem, ubi tamen & Aer*</note>. 

And here they are, as it were, **chained** and **fettered** by that same weight of their **gross** and **heavy bodies** which first sank them down here. This weight prevents them from re-ascending or returning back to those **bright ethereal regions** above. Being thus for the present **imprisoned** in this **lower Tartarus**, or **misty air** and atmosphere, they are indeed **kept** and **reserved in custody** until the **Judgment of the Great Day** and the **General Assizes** <note>a historical term for a periodic court session; here, the Final Judgment</note>. However, in the meantime, they may still seem to **dominate** and **lord it** for a while here. 

Lastly, our Savior’s command, *"Go, you cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the Devil and his angels,"* seems to be a clear **confirmation** of **devils having bodies**. First, to interpret this fire as nothing but "remorse of conscience" would risk making other **points** of our **religion uncertain** as well. Furthermore, to say that **incorporeal substances** <note>beings without any physical form</note> that are **not united to bodies** can be tormented with **fire** is—as much as is in our power—to expose **Christianity** and the Scripture to the scorn and contempt of all **philosophers** and **philosophic minds**. 

For this reason, **Psellus** <note>Michael Psellos, an 11th-century Byzantine monk and scholar</note> places great emphasis on this passage: <margin>P. 37.</margin> **"I am also convinced of this—as one persuaded by the words of our Savior—that demons shall be punished with fire. How could this be possible if they were altogether incorporeal? For it is impossible for that which is itself incorporeal, and not vitally united to any body, to suffer from a physical body. Therefore, we Christians must necessarily grant that devils shall receive punishment of sense and pain hereafter in bodies capable of suffering"** <note>original Greek: ἐμοὶ μὲν ὡς διὰ τῶν τοῦ σωτῆρος λόγων πεπεισμένῳ ταῦτα, πυρὶ κολασθήσεσθαι φασκόντων τοὺς δαίμονας· ὃ πῶς οἷον παθεῖν ἀσωμάτους ὄντας; τὸ γὰρ ἀσώματον ἀμήχανον παθεῖν ὑπὸ σωμάτων· ἀνάγκη γοῦν σώμασιν αὐτοὺς τὴν κόλασιν ὑποδέχεσθαι πεφυκόσι πάσχειν.</note>.

Now, if angels in general—that is, all **created beings superior to men**—are **incorporeal substances** (or **souls vitally united to bodies**), though not always the same kind, but sometimes of one kind and sometimes...

# More concerning Bodies, or Book I.

At various times; and the soul is never quite separate from all **body**. From this, it may seem probable that although there are other **incorporeal substances** <note>substances that do not have a physical body</note> besides the **Deity**, yet an **incorporeal life** <note>original Latin: *Vita Incorporea*</note>—a life *perfectly* without a body in the sense described by **Origen** <note>an early Christian scholar, c. 184–253 AD</note>, or **to live altogether without the companionship of any added body** <note>original Latin: *Sine Corporeæ Adjectionis Societate Vivere*</note>—is a privilege belonging properly to the **Holy Trinity** only. 

Consequently, when human souls are **divested** <note>original: "Devested"</note> of these heavy, earthly bodies by death, they do not then live and act completely without the **union** <note>original: "Conjunction"</note> of any body at all, continuing in that state until the **Resurrection** or **Day of Judgment**. This state of being purely bodiless is a privilege that not even the angels themselves—and therefore no **created, finite being**—is capable of. The imperfection of their nature necessarily requires them to be joined to some kind of body to be "complete." Without this, it is inconceivable how they could possess either **senses** or **imagination**.

<margin>Against Celsus, Book 7, page 353.</margin>
And so **Origen**, consistently with his own principles, concludes: <note>original Greek: ἡ τῇ ἑαυτῆς φύσει ἀσώματός καὶ ἀόρατος ψυχὴ, ἐν παντὶ σωματικῷ τόπῳ τυγχάνουσα, δέεται σώματος οἰκείου τῇ φύσει τοῦ τόπου ἐκείνου · ὅπερ ὅπου μὲν φορεῖ, ἀπεκδυσαμένη πρότερον ἀναγκαῖον μὲν, περίσσον δὲ ὡς πρὸς τὰ δεύτερα· ὅπου δ᾽ ἐπενδυσαμένη ᾧ πρότερον εἶχε, δεομένῳ κρείττονος ἐνδύματος εἰς τοὺς καθαρωτέρους καὶ αἰθερίους καὶ οὐρανίους τόπους ·</note> *Our soul, which in its own nature is incorporeal and invisible, always stands in need of a body suitable to the nature of whatever physical place it exists in. It sometimes carries a body after having first stripped off one that was previously necessary but is now redundant for its next state of existence. At other times, it puts on a new covering over what it already had, because it needs better clothing to fit it for those purer, ethereal, and heavenly places.*

However, in the passage that follows, we believe that Origen's meaning has been misunderstood, and his words altered and perverted. The whole passage should be read as follows: <note>original Greek: Καὶ ἐνεδύσατο μὲν ἐπὶ τὴν τῇδε γένεσιν ἐρχομένη, τὸ χρήσιμον πρὸς τὴν ἐν τῇ ὑστέρᾳ τοῦ κυούσης, ἕως ἦν ἐν αὐτῇ· ἐνεδύσατο δ᾽ ὑπ᾽ ἐκεῖνο, ὃ ἦν ἀναγκαῖον τῷ ἐπὶ γῆς μέλλοντι διαζῆν· εἶτα πάλιν ὄντος τινὸς Σκήνους, καὶ ἐπιγείου οἰκίας ἀναγκαίας πω τῷ Σκήνει, καταλύεσθαί μέν φασιν οἱ λόγοι τὴν ἐπίγειον οἰκίαν τοῦ Σκήνους, τὸ δὲ Σκῆνος ἐπενδύσασθαι οἰκίαν ἀχειροποίητον, αἰώνιον ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς· λέξουσι δ᾽ οἱ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἄνθρωποι, τὸ μὲν φθαρτὸν ἐνδύσασθαι αὐτὸ ἀφθαρσίαν ·</note> *The sense of which is this: The soul, descending here into physical birth, first put on that body which was useful while it remained in the womb; and then afterward, it put on such a body as was necessary for it to live here upon the earth. Furthermore, having here a twofold kind of body—one of which is called a* **tabernacle** <note>original Greek: Σκῆνος (*skenos*); often used by St. Paul to refer to the physical body as a temporary dwelling</note> *by St. Paul (referring to a more subtle, inner body which it had before), and the other being the "added earthly house" that is necessarily servant to this* **tabernacle** *here—the scriptures affirm that the "earthly house" of this* **tabernacle** *shall be destroyed or dissolved. However, the* **tabernacle** *itself shall then put on a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. The same scriptures declare that the corruptible must put on incorruption, and the mortal must put on immortality.* 

In this passage, it is plain that Origen interprets that **tabernacle** mentioned by **St. Paul** (2 Corinthians 5:1) as a **subtle body** <note>a non-physical or "spirit" body</note> which the soul possessed even before its **earthly birth** <note>original: "Terrene Nativity"</note>.

<summary>This page argues that only the Holy Trinity is purely incorporeal, while all created beings, including angels and human souls, require some form of body to function. Using Origen's interpretations of St. Paul, the author suggests the soul transitions through various "coverings" or bodies suited to its environment, from the womb to heaven.</summary>
