### CHAPTER IV. Vehicles of Souls, from Origen.

Birth <note>original: "Nativity"</note>, and which continues with it after death; but in good men, it will at last cover or *put on* (without death) the clothing of *immortality*. There cannot be a better *commentary* upon this passage from *Origen* than those *excerpts* <note>original Latin: "Excerpta"</note> from *Methodius* the Martyr found in *Photius*, though they also seem to be corrupted. In these, as we understand it, the meaning of *Origen* and his followers is first contained in these words:

<margin>Thus *Origen* states plainly in his *Fifth Book* (p. 244) that there is a difference between the *earthly house* in which the *tent* <note>original Greek: Σκῆνος (skēnos); a term used by St. Paul to describe the physical body as a temporary dwelling</note> resides, and the *tent* itself, in which good men groan while being burdened—not because they want to take it off, but because they want to put *immortality* on over it.</margin>
"The tent is one thing, the house of the tent is another, and we—that is, our souls—are a third thing distinct from both." <note>original Greek: ἕτερον τὸ Σκῆνος, καὶ τὸ Σκῆνος ἡ οἰκία, καὶ ἕτερον ἡμεῖς ἔνθεν τὸ Σκῆνος</note> And then it is further declared in the following passage (p. 244): "When this short-lived life of our earthly body is destroyed, our soul shall then have, before the Resurrection, a dwelling from God; until we shall at last receive it renewed, restored, and so made an incorruptible house. Therefore, in this state we groan, desiring not to put off *every kind of body*, but to put on life or immortality upon the body which we shall then have. For *that house which is from heaven, which we desire to put on, is immortality*." <note>original Greek: τῆς ζωῆς καταλυθείσης τὸ ὠκυμόρον τὴν πρὸ τῆς ἀναστάσεως ἔχουσαν οἴκησιν αἱ ψυχαὶ παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ... τὸ γὰρ οἰκητήριον τὸ ἐξ οὐρανοῦ, ὃ ἐπενδύσασθαι ἐπιθυμοῦμεν ἡ ἀθανασία</note>

<margin>as in which the tent is</margin>
<margin>being destroyed, in which those who are righteous groan, being burdened, not to be unclothed, but for the tent to be clothed upon.</margin>

Moreover, the same *Origen* endeavors to further confirm that the soul is not altogether naked after death from the words of our Savior concerning the *rich man* and *Lazarus*: "But also the man being punished, and the poor man resting in Abraham’s bosom before the coming of the Savior and before the end of the world—and therefore before the Resurrection—plainly show that even now, after death, the soul uses a body." <note>original Greek: ἀλλὰ καὶ ὁ κολαζόμενος πλάσας, καὶ ὁ ἐν κόλποις Ἀβραὰμ πένης ἀναπαυόμενος... δείκνυσιν ὅτι καὶ νῦν ἐν τῇ ἀπαλλαγῇ σώματι χρῆται ἡ ψυχή</note>

He thinks the same is further proved from the *visible appearance of Samuel’s ghost*: "Samuel also visibly appearing makes it manifest that his soul was then clothed with a body." <note>original Greek: ἀλλὰ καὶ ὁ σαμουὴλ φαινόμενος, ὡς δῆλόν ἐστιν ὁρατὸς ὤν, παρέστησιν ὅτι σῶμα περιεκέκλητο</note> To which he adds in *Photius*: "The exterior form and figure of the soul's body after death resembles that of the gross terrestrial <term>terrestrial</term><note>earthly or physical</note> body here in this life. All the histories of apparitions describe ghosts, or the souls of the dead, as appearing in the same form which their bodies had before." <note>original Greek: τὸ τῆς ψυχῆς ἅμα τῇ ἀπαλλαγῇ σχῆμα, ὁμοειδὲς τῷ παχεῖ καὶ γηΐνῳ σώματι</note> This, therefore, as was observed, is what *Origen* understands by the *tent* <note>original Greek: τὸ σκῆνος</note> in St. Paul; not this gross *earthly* body, but a certain *middle body* between it and the heavenly body, which the soul carries away with it after death. 

Now, this opinion of the learned *Origen* was never included by the ancient Fathers, or even his greatest adversaries, in the list of his errors. Nor does *Methodius* the Martyr (who was a great opponent of Origen), when he mentions this Origenist opinion in *Photius*, seem to criticize it, except for the Platonic implication that the soul is incorporeal. *Methodius* himself, on the contrary, argued not that the *soul has a body* joined with it after death as a distinct thing, but that the soul *is itself a body*: "God alone is celebrated as being truly incorporeal; but souls, created by the maker and father of all things, exist as intellectual bodies, organized into parts discernible by reason..." <note>original Greek: ὁ Θεὸς μόνος ᾄδεται ἀσώματος ὤν, αἱ δὲ ψυχαὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ δημιουργοῦ καὶ πατρὸς τῶν ὅλων, σώματα νοερὰ ὑπάρχουσαι, εἰς λόγῳ θεωρητὰ μέλη διακεκόσμηται</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of whether souls possess a "subtle body" or "vehicle" after death, focusing on the views of Joannes Thessalonicensis (John of Thessalonica) and Michael Psellus, contrasting them with Origen, Tertullian, and St. Augustine.</meta>

# John of Thessalonica and Psellus. BOOK I.

[The soul is] adorned, to receive this form; hence also in Hades <note>original Greek: ᾅδῃ (hadēi); the realm of the dead</note>, it is recorded to have both a tongue, a finger, and other members; not as if another body coexisted with these souls being there; but because these souls themselves, being stripped of every covering, are by nature such according to their essence. *God alone is praised as Incorporeal and Invisible: but Souls are made by him (who is the Father of all things) to be Intellectual Bodies, ornamentally branched out (as it were) into members distinguishable by Reason, and having the same Form and Signature as the outward Body. Why is it that in Hades (or Hell) we read of a tongue, and a finger, and other members? It is not as if there were another invisible body coexisting with these souls, but because the souls themselves are in their own nature (when stripped naked of all clothing) according to their very essence such.* <note>original Greek: κεκόσμηται, ταύτην λαβέσθαι τὴν διατύπωσιν... (this passage argues that the soul has a natural shape or "signature" resembling the human body even without a physical shell)</note> 

We say, therefore, that if one of these two opinions must necessarily be accepted—either that the soul itself **is** a body, or else that it **has** a body after death—the latter of them, which was **Origen's** view, ought certainly to be much preferred over the former. This is true whether the former is held in **Tertullian's** sense (that all *substance*, and consequently God himself, is a body) or in that of **Methodius** (that all created *substance* is such, and God alone is incorporeal).

But we have already shown that **Origen** was not alone in this opinion. **Irenaeus** before him asserted the same thing: that souls after death are *adapted to certain bodies* <note>the original Greek word was likely περιπλέκονται (periplekontai), meaning "intertwined" or "enfolded"</note> which have the same character as these terrestrial ones. **Philoponus** <note>John Philoponus (c. 490–570), a Byzantine Alexandria-based philologist and Christian philosopher</note> after him, who was not a pagan but a Christian philosopher, taught the same doctrine. We might also add that **Joannes Thessalonicensis** <note>John of Thessalonica, a 7th-century bishop</note>, in that dialogue of his read in the Seventh Synod <note>The Second Council of Nicaea, 787 AD</note>, seems to have been of the same persuasion. He affirms of souls, as well as angels and demons, that they were *often seen by many sensibly, in the form of their own bodies.* <note>original Greek: ὁραθέντες παρὰ πλειόνων αἰσθητῶς πλεονάκις, τῷ εἴδει τῶν οἰκείων αὐτῶν σωμάτων</note> 

However, it is a thing which **Psellus** <note>Michael Psellus (c. 1017–1078), a Byzantine monk and scholar</note> took for granted. When speaking of how devils insinuate their temptations into men's souls by affecting the *phantastic spirit* <note>term: phantastic spirit; a "spirit" or subtle medium through which the imagination and senses operate</note> directly, he writes <margin>Page 94.</margin> **after this manner**: 

*When one man speaks to another from afar, he must (if he would be heard) make a loud cry or noise, whereas if he stood near to him, he might softly whisper into his ear. But could he immediately approach the spirit (or subtle body) of the soul, he would not then need so much as to make a whisper; instead, he might silently and without noise communicate whatever thoughts of his own to him by the motions made upon it. And this is said to be the way that souls, leaving these bodies, converse together; they communicate their thoughts to one another without any noise.* <note>original Greek: ὁ λέγων, πόῤῥωθεν μὲν ὢν ἰχυροτέρας δεῖται κραυγῆς... (Psellus suggests that spirits communicate through direct impression on the "spirit" of another, rather than through air vibrations)</note> 

For Psellus here plainly supposes that souls after death have a *pneuma* <note>term: pneuma; here used as a "spirituous" or subtle body</note>—that is, a certain subtle body adhering to them—by motions upon which they may silently converse with each other. 

<margin>St. Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book 12, Chapter 32.</margin> It is true indeed that **St. Augustine** <note>original: "St. Austin"</note>, in his twelfth book *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, does not himself agree with this opinion...

### Chapter V. Saint Augustine’s Judgment in the Case.

...on whether the **soul has a body after death**, and even less whether it **is a body**. Nevertheless, he seems to leave every person to their own liberty in this matter, saying: <note>original Latin: "Si autem Quæritur, dum Anima de Corpore exierit, Utrum ad aliqua loca Corporalia feratur, an ad Incorporalia Corporalibus similia; an verò nec ad ipsa, sed ad illud quod & Corporibus & Similitudinibus Corporum est Excellentius; Citò quidem responderim; ad Corporalia loca eam vel non ferri nisi cum aliquo Corpore, vel non localiter ferri. Jam utrum habeat aliquod Corpus, Ostendat qui Potest; Ego autem non puto. Spiritalem enim arbitror esse non Corporalem, ad spiritalia vero pro meritis fertur, aut ad Loca Pœnalia similia Corporibus."</note> "But if it is asked, when the soul leaves this body, whether it is carried into any physical places, or to incorporeal things similar to physical ones, or else to neither, but to that which is more excellent than both bodies and the likenesses of bodies; the answer is ready: that it cannot be carried to physical places, or be moved locally anywhere at all, without a body. Now, whether the soul has some body when it leaves this body, let those who can show it; for my part, I think otherwise. For I suppose the soul to be spiritual and not physical, and that after death it is either carried to spiritual things, or else to places of punishment similar to bodies, such as have been represented to some in ecstasies, etc."

Where Saint Augustine himself seems to think the punishment of souls after death and before the **resurrection** is **fantastical** <note>In this context, "fantastical" means existing as mental images or "phantasms," rather than physical reality.</note>, or exists only in the **imagination**. However, there could not be even **fantastical punishments**, nor any imagination at all in souls without a body, if **Aristotle's** doctrine is true: that fancy or **imagination** is nothing else but a weaker sense—that is, something resulting from a combination of both soul and body together.

But it is observable that in the previously cited passage, what Saint Augustine chiefly opposed was the soul **being a body**, as **Tertullian**, **Methodius**, and others had asserted. But as for its **having a body**, he says only this: "Let him who can, show it." In the meantime, he grants that the soul cannot be **locally** moved anywhere at all after death, nor indeed be in any place, without a body.

<margin>*The City of God, Book 21, chapter 26.*</margin>
However, the same Saint Augustine—just as he elsewhere condemns the opinion of those who would take the **fire of hell** metaphorically, acknowledging it to be **real** and **physical**—also thinks it not improbable that after death and before the **resurrection**, the souls of men may suffer from a certain **fire** for the consuming and burning up of their dross: <note>original Latin: "Post istius sanè Corporis Mortem, donec ad illum Veniatur, qui post Resurrectionem Corporum futurus est Damnationis & Remunerationis Ultimus Dies; Si hoc temporis Intervallo, Ejusmodi Ignem dicuntur perpeti quem non sentiant illi, qui non habuerint tales mores & amores in hujus Corporis Vitâ, ut Eorum Ligna, & Fænum, & Stipula Consumantur: alii vero sentiunt qui ejusmodi secum ædificia portaverunt, &c. non redarguo, quia forsitan Verum est."</note> "If in this interval of time between the death of the body and the resurrection or Day of Judgment, the souls of the dead are said to suffer such a fire as can do no execution upon those who have no wood, hay, or stubble <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 3:12-15, where "wood, hay, and stubble" represent poor works or worldly attachments that are burned away in judgment.</note> to burn up; but shall be felt by those who have built such structures, etc., I do not criticize it, because perhaps it is true."

<header>Reasons of the Ancients, Book I.</header>

<margin>Against Celsus, Book 5, page 240.</margin> In his book against *Celsus*—a passage which *Saint Augustine* <note>original: "St. Austin"</note> seems to have respected—Origen writes: <note>original Greek: "ὁ συνιδὼν ὅτι ὥσπερ Ἑλλήνων τισὶν ἔδοξε, τὸ πῦρ καθάρσιον ἐπάγεται τῷ κόσμῳ· εἰκὸς δ' ὅτι καὶ ἑκάστῳ τῶν δεομένων τοῦ διὰ τοῦ πυρὸς δίκης καίοντος μὲν καὶ κατακαίοντος τοὺς μὴ ἔχοντας ὕλην δεομένην ἀναλύεσθαι ὑπ' ἐκείνου τοῦ πυρός· καίοντος δὲ καὶ κατακαίοντος τοὺς ἐν τῇ διὰ τῶν πράξεων καὶ λόγων καὶ νοημάτων τροπικῶς λεγομένῃ οἰκοδομῇ ξύλα, χόρτον, ἢ καλάμην οἰκοδομήσαντας."</note> *He perceived that, according to the Hebrews and Christians as well as some of the Greeks, a purifying fire will be brought upon the world. It is likely that this fire will also apply to every person who stands in need of such punishment and remedy. This fire can do no harm to those who have no combustible matter in them, but it will be felt by those who, in the moral structure of their thoughts, words, and actions, have metaphorically built with wood, hay, and stubble.* Now, since souls cannot suffer from fire or anything else through the senses or pain without being *vitally united* to some body, we may conclude that *Saint Augustine*, when he wrote this, was not altogether opposed to the idea of *souls having bodies after death*.

Up to this point, we have explained how the *ancient proponents of incorporeal substance* <term>Incorporeal substance: A reality that is not made of matter or physical body, such as a soul or spirit.</term> as *unextended* <note>original: "Unextended" - meaning something that does not take up physical space or have dimensions.</note> pushed back against the attacks made against it by *atheists* and *materialists* <note>original: "Corporealists"</note>. Specifically, we have shown how they freed themselves from the perceived absurdity of *finite created spirits* having no location or motion. They did this by supposing these spirits are always *vitally united* to some body; consequently, by the *location* of those respective bodies, the spirits are determined to be *here* or *there*. This follows the reasoning of <margin>Against Celsus, Book 5, page 244.</margin> *Origen*: <note>original Greek: "ἡ ψυχὴ ἡμῶν δεῖται σώματος, διὰ τὰς τοπικὰς μεταβάσεις."</note> *Our soul stands in need of a body for the purpose of moving from place to place.*

Next, we shall explain what logical grounds induced those ancients to assert and maintain a concept so contrary to the senses and imagination—and consequently to all *common understanding*—as *a substance that is in itself unextended, without distance, and indivisible, or devoid of magnitude and parts.* In this, we shall represent the views of these *ancient believers in the incorporeal* to their best advantage, in order to defend them against *atheists* and *materialists*. In the meantime, we are not asserting anything as fact ourselves, but leaving every reader to make their own judgment. You may choose to agree with this view or with the following *hypothesis* of *extended incorporeals* <note>The idea that spirits are non-material but still take up a specific amount of space.</note>.

It is observable here that it was formerly taken for granted by both sides—those who argued for and those who denied incorporeal substance—that there is only *one kind of extension*. Consequently, they believed that whatever has magnitude and parts (where one part is outside of another) is not only *intellectually* and *logically* divisible, but also *really* and *physically separable* <note>original: "discerpible"</note>. They also believed such a thing must be *resistant* <term>original: "Antitypous" - a philosophical term for the quality of matter that prevents two objects from occupying the same space.</term> and *impenetrable*, so that it cannot coexist with another body in the same place. From this, it follows that any argument proving there is some substance other than body also demonstrates—according to the logic of these ancients (both *materialists* and *spiritualists* alike)—that there is *something unextended*. # CHAPTER V. For Unextended Substance.

What is *Extended* is *Body*. Nevertheless, we shall here primarily present those arguments that aim directly to *prove* that there is *something unextendedly incorporeal* <term>Unextendedly incorporeal: A reality that has no physical dimensions or size and does not take up space, such as a thought or a soul.</term>. We also aim to show that an *Unextended Deity* is not an *impossible idea*. This is demonstrated by the fact that there is something *unextended* even within our own selves. 

Without repeating the previously mentioned reasoning of *Simplicius*—that *whatever can act upon and reflect upon its whole self cannot possibly be extended, nor have parts distant from one another*—*Plotinus* first argues in this <margin>Page 460.</margin> manner: <note>original Greek: "τί τοίνυν φήσουσι, οἱ τὴν ψυχὴν σῶμα εἶναι λέγοντες, πρῶτον μὲν περὶ ἑκάστου μέρους τῆς ψυχῆς τῆς ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ σώματι, πότερον ἕκαστον ψυχὴν, οἵα ἐστὶ καὶ ἡ ὅλη; καὶ πάλιν τοῦ μέρους τὸ μέρος; οὐδὲν ἄρα τὸ μέγεθος συνεβάλλετο τῇ οὐσίᾳ αὐτῆς· καίτοι ἔδει γε ποσοῦ τινος ὄντος· ἀλλὰ καὶ ὅλον πολλαχῆ, ὅπερ σώμασι παρεῖναι ἀδύνατον, ἐν πλείοσι τὸ αὐτὸ ὅλον εἶναι, καὶ τὸ μέρος ὅπερ τὸ ὅλον ὑπάρχειν· εἰ δὲ ἕκαστον τῶν μερῶν οὐ ψυχὴν φήσουσιν, ἐξ ἀψύχων ψυχὴ αὐτοῖς ὑπάρξει·"</note> *“What then will they say, who contend that the Soul is a Body (or extended)? Will they grant, concerning every part of the soul in the same body—such as the part in the foot, the part in the hand, and the part in the brain—and again every part of those parts, that each of them is a soul, just like the whole? If they agree to this, then it is plain that magnitude (or physical size) contributes nothing at all to the essence of the soul, as it would if the soul were an extended thing. Instead, the 'whole' would exist in many parts or places at once. This is something that cannot possibly belong to a body: that the same 'whole' should be in multiple places, and that a part should be identical to the whole. But if they will not grant that every part of their extended soul is a soul, then according to them, the soul must be made up and compounded of soulless things.”*

<margin>Ennead 4. Book 7. Chapter 2.</margin> This argument is proposed by him elsewhere in this way: <note>original Greek: "εἰ δὲ ἕκαστον ζωὴν ἔχοι, καὶ ἓν ἀρκεῖ· εἰ δὲ μηδενὸς αὐτῶν ζωὴν ἔχοντος ἡ σύνοδος πεποίηκε ζωὴν, ἄτοπον· μᾶλλον δὲ ἀδύνατον συμφόρησιν σωμάτων ζωὴν ἐργάζεσθαι, καὶ νοῦν γεννᾶν τὰ ἀνόητα."</note> *“If every one of the parts of this extended soul, or mind, has life in it, then any one of them alone would be sufficient. But to say that although none of the parts alone have life in them, yet the conjunction of them all together makes life, is absurd. It is impossible that life and soul should result from a mass of lifeless and soulless things, or that mindless things put together should beget a mind.”* 

The summary of this argument is this: either every part of an extended soul is a soul (and every part of an extended mind is a mind), or it is not. Now, if no part of a soul—assuming it is extended—is a soul or has life and mind in it when taken alone, then it is certain that the whole resulting from all those parts could have no life or mind. This is because nothing can (causally) come from nothing. It is true, of course, that corporeal *qualities* and *forms*, according to *Atomic Physics* <term>Atomick Physiology: The early scientific theory that all physical matter is made of tiny, indivisible particles (atoms) and that complex properties emerge from their arrangement.</term>, result from a composition and texture of atoms or parts, none of which possess that *quality* or *form* when taken alone. As the poet Lucretius wrote:

— — — *Lest you think that white things are made of white principles;* —
— *Or that those things which are black are born from black seeds.* —
<note>original Latin: "Ne ex Albis Alba rearis; / Aut ea quæ Nigrant, nigro de Semine nata." from Lucretius, De Rerum Natura.</note>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument that the soul and mind are "unextended" substances—meaning they exist but do not occupy physical space or have material parts—drawing specifically on the reasoning of the Neoplatonist philosopher Plotinus.</meta>

824 Reasons for Something BOOK I.

This is clear because these qualities and forms are not entities really distinct from the **magnitude** (size), **figure** (shape), **site** (position), and **motion** of parts, but are only a specific arrangement of them that causes different **fancies** <note>original: "Phancies"; here meaning subjective mental perceptions or sensory impressions</note> in us. However, **life** and **understanding**, **soul** and **mind**, are entities really distinct from the size, shape, position, and motion of parts. They are neither mere mental impressions nor "syllables of things" <note>original: "syllables of things"; a metaphor suggesting that things are just a collection of material parts, like a word is a collection of letters</note>, but are **simple** and **uncompounded realities**. Furthermore, if every supposed part of a soul were itself a soul, and every part of a mind were a mind, then every part of it besides any single part would be superfluous. Indeed, every supposed part would be the **same as the whole**. From this, it follows that the soul could not be extended or have any **real parts** at all, since no part of a physically extended thing can possibly be the same as the whole.

The same philosopher <note>Plotinus</note> also endeavors to further prove that the human soul itself is unextended and indivisible based on its energies and operations, regarding both **sensation** and **intellection** (intellectual thought). First, concerning external sensations, he reasons in this manner:

<margin>Page 461.</margin> <note>original Greek: "ὅτι μέλλει αἰσθάνεσθαί τινος ἓν αὐτὸ δεῖ εἶναι, καὶ τῷ αὐτῷ παντὸς ἀντιλαμβάνεσθαι· καὶ εἰ διὰ πολλῶν αἰσθητηρίων πλείω τὰ εἰσιόντα, ἢ πολλαὶ περὶ ἓν ποιότητες, κἂν δι' ἑνὸς ποικίλον, οἷον πρόσωπον· οὐ γὰρ ἄλλο μὲν ἑνὸς ἄλλο δ' ὀφθαλμῶν, ἀλλὰ ταὐτὸν ὁμοῦ πάντων· καὶ εἰ τὸ μὲν δι' ὀμμάτων τὸ δ' δι' ἀκοῆς, ἕν τι δεῖ εἶναι εἰς ὃ ἄμφω· ἢ πῶς ἂν εἴποι ὅτι ἕτερα ταῦτα, μὴ εἰς τὸ αὐτὸ ὁμοῦ τῶν αἰσθήσεων ἐλθόντων."</note> *“That which perceives in us must of necessity be one thing, and by one and the same indivisible point, perceive all. This is true whether there are many things entering through several organs of sense (such as the many qualities of one substance) or one complex and multiform thing entering through the same organ (such as the face or picture of a man). For it is not one thing in us that perceives the nose, another thing the eyes, and another thing the mouth; rather, it is one and the self-same thing that perceives all of them. And when one thing enters through the eye and another through the ear, these also must of necessity come at last to one indivisible point, otherwise they could not be compared together, nor could one of them be declared different from another—for their several sensations would meet nowhere together in one.”* He concludes, therefore, that this one thing in us which sensibly perceives all things may be compared to the **center of a circle**, and the several senses to lines drawn from the circumference, which all meet in that one center. Therefore, that which perceives and apprehends all things in us must truly be one and the very same; that is, unextended and indivisible.

This argument is pursued even further by him, more specifically as follows: *“If that which sensibly perceives in us were extended so as to have distant parts, one outside another, then one of these three things must be claimed: Either every part of this extended substance of the soul perceives only a part of the object; or every part of it perceives the whole object; or else everything comes to a single point which alone perceives both the several parts of the object and the whole—with all the other parts acting only as lines from the circumference leading to this center.”* Regarding the first of these three options, **Plotinus** says: <note>original Greek: "μεγέθει ὄντι τούτῳ, συμμερίζοιτο ἂν· ὥστε ἄλλο ἄλλου μέρος, καὶ μηδένα ἡμῶν ὅλου τοῦ αἰσθητοῦ ἀντίληψιν ἔχειν· ὥσπερ ἂν εἰ ἐγὼ μὲν ἄλλου· σὺ δ' ἄλλου αἴσθοιο."</note> *“If the soul were a physical magnitude, then it would have to be divided along with the sensory object; so that one part of the soul would*

#### Chap. V. Unextended, In Us.

[the soul] must perceive one part of the **object**, and **another part, another**; and **nothing within it would perceive the whole perceived thing**. It would be just as if I should have the sense of one thing, and you of another. Whereas it is plain by our internal sense that it is one and the same thing in us which perceives both the **parts** and the **whole**.

And concerning the second possibility, he writes in this manner: "But if every part of the extended soul perceives the whole sensible object, since magnitude is by nature infinitely divisible, then for every single object perceived, there would be infinite sensations and images of that same object within our ruling faculty." <note>original Greek: "εἰ δ' ὁτιῶν παντὸς αἰσθήσεται. εἰς ἄπειρα διαιρεῖσθαι τοῦ μεγέθους πεφυκότος, ἀπείρους καὶ αἰσθήσεις καθ' ἕκαστον αἰσθητὸν συμβήσεται γίνεσθαι ἑκάστῳ οἷον τοῦ αὐτοῦ ἀπείρους ἐν τῷ ἡγεμονεῦντι ἡμῶν εἰκόνας." The "ruling faculty" or *hegemonikon* was a Stoic and Neoplatonic term for the seat of the mind.</note> However, we are intimately conscious to ourselves that we have only **one sensation** of **one object** at the same time.

And as for the third and last part of the **disjunction** <note>a logical choice between several options</note>—that what sensibly perceives in every person is but **one single point**, either **mathematical** or **physical**. First, it is certain that a **mathematical point**, having neither length, width, nor depth, is not a body or a substance, but only a notion of our own mind, or a way we conceive things. And then, as for a **physical point** or **minimum**—a body so little that there cannot possibly be any smaller—**Plotinus**, asserting the **infinite divisibility** of body, here explodes the idea itself.

However, he further suggests that if there were any such **physical minimum**, or absolutely smallest body or **extended thing**, this could not possibly receive a distinct representation and sketch of all the several parts of a whole visible object at once—such as the eyes, nose, and mouth in a man’s face or **picture**, or the specific details of a building. Nor could such a **smallness** <note>original: "Parvitude"</note> or **atom** as this be the cause of all **animal motions**.

And this was one of **Aristotle's** arguments, by which he would prove **unextended incorporeals**: "How can the indivisible perceive the divisible?" <note>original Greek: "πῶς τῷ ἀμερεῖ τὸ μεριστόν ·"</note> That is: if the **soul** were **indivisible** like a **point**, how could it **perceive** that which is **divisible**? How could it take notice of all the distinct parts of any extended **object**, and have a description of the whole of them at once upon itself?

The sum of the whole argument is this: that if the soul be an extended substance, then it must of necessity be either a **physical point** or **minimum** (the smallest extended thing that can possibly exist—if there be any such thing and body is not infinitely divisible), or else it must consist of more such **physical points** joined together.

As for the first of these, it has been already declared to be impossible that one single **atom**, or the smallest point of **extension**, should be able to distinctly perceive all the variety of things. To this might be added that to suppose every soul to be but one **physical minimum**, or **smallest extended thing**, is to imply such an essential difference in matter or extension that some of its points would be naturally devoid of all life, sense, and understanding, while others would be naturally **sensitive** and **rational**. Even if this absurdity were admitted, it would still be utterly inconceivable how there should come to be exactly one such **sensitive** and **rational atom** in every man and no more, and how this should constantly remain the same from infancy to old age, while other parts of matter **perpetually pass away** <note>original: "Transpire"; referring to the constant flux and replacement of material atoms in the living body</note>.

But as for the latter: if souls be extended substances consisting of **more points**, one outside another, all concurring in every **sensation**,

<summary>Plotinus and Aristotle argue that the soul must be an indivisible, unextended substance because a physical body made of parts could not produce a single, unified perception of a complex object. They also reject the idea of the soul being a single physical atom, as it would be too small to hold complex data or remain stable as the body's matter changes.</summary>

### In Animals; One Thing, Book 1.

—sensation, then every one of those points must either perceive only a single point and part of the object, or else the whole object. Now if every point of the **extended soul** perceives only a point of the object, then there is no **one thing** in us that perceives the whole, or which can compare one part with another. But if every point of the extended soul perceives the whole object at once, consisting of many parts, then there would be innumerable perceptions of the same object in every sensation—as many as there are points in the extended soul. And from both those suppositions, it would similarly follow that no man is **one single percipient** <note>original: "Percipient" — one who perceives or senses something.</note> or person, but that there are innumerable distinct percipients and persons in every man. 

Neither can there be any other supposition made, besides those three mentioned earlier; such as that the whole extended soul should perceive both the whole sensible object and all its several parts, while no part of this soul in the meantime has any perception at all by itself. This is because the "whole" of an extended being is nothing but all the parts taken together; and if none of those parts have any life, sense, or perception in them, it is impossible that there should be any in the whole. But in very truth, to say that the whole soul perceives all, and no part of it perceives anything, is to acknowledge it not to be extended, but to be **indivisible**—which is the very thing that *Plotinus* contends for.

And that philosopher here further insists upon *internal sensations* also, and that *sympathy* or *homopathy* <note>original Greek: Συμπάθεια (Sympatheia) and Ὁμοιοπάθεια (Homoiopatheia). These terms refer to "shared feeling" or "similar feeling," describing how different parts of a living body react together as a unified whole.</note> which exists in all *animals*, for the same purpose: it being *one and the same* thing in them which perceives *pain* in the most distant extremities of the body—such as in the *sole of the foot* and in the *crown of the head*—and which moves one part to help and relieve another part suffering under it. This could not possibly happen by *traduction* <term>the physical transmission or "carrying over" of a signal</term> of all signals to one *physical point* as the *center*, for various reasons. 

<margin>P. 462.</margin> "Since, therefore, these *sympathetic senses* cannot possibly be made by *transmission* finally to *one thing*; and because *body* is *bulky* or *out-swelling extension* <note>In philosophy, "extension" refers to the quality of taking up physical space.</note> where *one part* of it *suffering*, *another* cannot *perceive* it (*for in all physical magnitude, this part is one thing and that part is another*), it follows that what perceives within us must be *everywhere*, and in all the parts of the body, *one and the same thing with itself*." <note>original Greek: Εἰ τοίνυν κατὰ διάθεσιν οὐχ οἷόν τε τὴν αἴσθησιν τοῦ τοιούτου γίνεσθαι, μὴ δὲ σώματός τινος ὄντος, ἄλλου παθόντος, ἄλλο γνῶσιν ἔχειν (παντὸς γὰρ μεγέθους τὸ μὲν ἄλλο, τὸ δὲ ἄλλο ἐστὶ) δεῖ τοιοῦτον τίθεσθαι τὸ αἰσθανόμενον, οἷον πανταχοῦ αὑτοῦ ἑαυτῷ τὸ αὐτὸ εἶναι · τοῦτο δὲ ἄλλῳ τινι τῶν ὄντων ἢ σώματι ποιεῖν προσήκει.</note> Which therefore cannot be a body itself, but must of necessity be some other entity or substance that is *incorporeal*. 

The conclusion is, that in *men and animals*, there is *one thing indivisibly the same* that encompasses their *whole exterior*, perceives both the *parts* and the *whole* of *sensible objects* (all transmitted through several senses), sympathizes with all the distant parts of the body, and acts entirely upon all of them. And this is properly called, ***I myself***—not the *extended bulk* of the *body* (which is not one but *many substances*), but an *unextended and indivisible unity* wherein all lines meet and concentrate. This is not like a *mathematical point* or the *smallest physical unit* <note>original: "Least Extensum"</note>, but like one *self-active, living, substantial power*, or ***inside-being***, that contains, holds, and connects everything together.

# CHAPTER V. Comprehending the Whole.

Lastly, the previously mentioned philosopher <note>referring to Plotinus</note> endeavors to further prove the **Human Soul** to be **unextended** [not taking up space], devoid of **magnitude** [size], and **indivisible**, based on its rational energies or operations. These include its *understandings of pure concepts* <note>original: "νοητῶν νοήσεις" (noēton noēseis)</note> and its *perceptions of things devoid of size* <note>original: "ἀμεγέθων ἀντιλήψεις" (amegethōn antilēpseis)</note>. As he asks: *For how could the soul (he says), if it were a physical size, understand that which has no size? And with that which is divisible, how could it conceive what is indivisible?* <note>original: "πῶς γὰρ μέγεθος ὂν τὸ μὴ μέγεθος νοήσει; καὶ τῷ μεριστῷ τὸ μὴ μεριστόν;"</note>

Now, it is certain that we have notions of many things that are **unimaginable** <note>Meaning they cannot be pictured as physical objects.</note>, and which therefore have nothing of **length**, **breadth**, and **thickness** in them—such as **virtue**, **vice**, and so on. <margin>Plotinus, page 463.</margin> *Justice and honesty, and the like, are things devoid of magnitude, and therefore the understanding of them must necessarily be so too. So the soul must receive these by what is indivisible, and lodge them in that which is indivisible.* <note>original: "ἀμεγέθες ᾗ οἶμαι καὶ τὸ καλὸν καὶ τὸ δίκαιον... καὶ ἐν αὐτῇ ἐν ἀμερεῖ κείσεται"</note>

We also have a notion not only of mere **latitude** [breadth] (which is indivisible as to thickness) and of **longitude** [a line] (which is indivisible as to both breadth and thickness), but also of a **mathematical point**, which is in every way indivisible as to length, breadth, and thickness. We have a conception of the **intensity** of powers and virtues, in which there is nothing of extension or physical size. Indeed, all the **abstract essences** of things (or the *things-in-themselves* <note>original: "αὐτοέκαστα" (autoekasta)</note>), which are the first objects of the understanding, are indivisible. *And though we also perceive forms that are found in matter, we perceive them as separated and abstracted from that matter; for there is nothing of flesh in our mental concept of a "man," etc.* <note>original: "εἰ δὲ τῶν ἐν ὕλῃ εἰδῶν τὰς νοήσεις φήσειεν εἶναι... οὐ γὰρ μετὰ σαρκῶν, &c."</note>

Furthermore, the **soul conceives extended** things themselves in an **unextended** and **indivisible** way. Just as the distance of an entire **hemisphere** is contracted into a narrow space in the pupil of the eye, so are all distances even more contracted within the soul itself, where they are understood without any physical distance. For the thought of a **mile's distance**, or of **ten thousand miles**, or the **radius** of the **earth**, takes up no more room in the soul, nor stretches it any more, than does the thought of a **foot** or an **inch**, or even of a **mathematical point**.

If that which perceives within us were a physical **magnitude**, it could not be *equal to every sensible object* <note>original: "ἴσον παντί αἰσθητῷ" (ison panti aisthētō)</note> and perceive both smaller and larger magnitudes alike. But least of all could it perceive things that have no magnitude at all. This was the other part of **Aristotle's argument** to prove the **soul** and **mind** to be unextended and indivisible: *For how could it perceive that which is indivisible by using something that is divisible?* <note>original: "πῶς γὰρ νοήσει τὸ ἄμερες μεριστῷ;"</note>

He had previously asked how the soul could grasp things that are divisible and of great extension if the soul were merely a point or a tiny physical speck. According to Aristotle, the soul (or that which perceives and understands) is neither **divisible** like a continuous quantity, nor yet **indivisible** in the way a mathematical or physical point is (an "absolute parvitude" or tiny speck). Rather, it is something that has in itself no **physical bulk** <note>original: "Out-Swelling Distance"</note> nor any relation to a physical **place**, except as—

# Whether Thoughts are Extended, Book I.

...as it is vitally united to a body, which (wherever it is) it always *sympathizes* with and *acts* upon.

Besides this, these *ancient proponents of non-physical substances without physical size* <note>original: "Ancient Asserters of Unextended Incorporeals"</note> would, in all probability, confirm that opinion for this reason: because we can not only conceive of *physical size* <note>original: "Extension"</note> without *thought* <note>original: "Cogitation"</note>, and again *thought* without *physical size*; from which it may be inferred that they are *truly distinct entities* and separable from one another (since we have no other *rule* to judge the *true distinction* and *separability* of things other than our own *conceptions*). But we are also unable to conceive of *thought* having *physical size*. 

We cannot conceive of a *thought* having a specific *length, breadth*, and *thickness*, *measurable* by *inches* and *feet*, or by *units of volume* <note>original: "Solid Measures"</note>. We cannot conceive of a *half*, or a *third part*, or a *twentieth part* of a *thought*—much less the *thought of an indivisible thing*. Neither can we conceive of every *thought* having a certain specific *shape* <note>original: "Figure"</note>, whether *round* or *angular*, *spherical, cubical*, *cylindrical*, or the like. 

On the contrary, if whatever lacks *physical size* is *nothing*, then thoughts must either be mere *non-entities*, or else they must be *extended* into *length, breadth*, and *thickness*; *divisible* into *parts*; and *measurable*; and also (where they are *limited* <note>original: "Finite"</note>) they must have a certain *shape*. Consequently, all the *truths* <note>original: "Verities"</note> within us (they being merely *complex, self-evident thoughts*) must necessarily be *long, broad*, and *thick*, and shaped either like a *sphere* or a *polygon* <note>original: "Angularly Figurate"</note>. 

The same must be said of *acts of will* <note>original: "Volitions"</note> as well, and of *desires* or *passions* such as *fear* and *hope, love* and *hatred, grief* and *joy*. This applies to all other things belonging to *thinking beings* (*souls* and *minds*), such as *knowledge* and *ignorance, wisdom* and *folly, virtue* and *vice, justice* and *injustice*, etc. These must either all be *absolute non-entities*, or *else extended* into *three dimensions* of *length, breadth*, and *depth* <note>original: "Profundity"</note>. They would be *measurable* not only by *inches* and *feet*, but also by *liquid measures* such as *pints* and *quarts*; and last of all (where they are *limited*, as in humans) they would have a *shape*. 

But if this is *absurd*, and if these things belonging to the *soul* and *mind* (though they are undoubtedly at least as real as the things which belong to *bodies*) are *unextended* [lacking physical size], then the *substances* of souls and minds themselves must be *unextended* also. Thus *Plotinus* says of the *mind*: "Mind is not distant from itself" <note>original: "νοῦς οὐ διαστὰς ἀφ' ἑαυτοῦ" (nous ou diastas aph' heautou)</note>. Indeed, were it so, it could not be *one thing* (as it is) but *many*; for every conceivable *part* of a *distant* and *extended substance* is a *substance* unto itself. 

The same is to be said of the *human soul*: although it *acts* upon *distant parts* of that body to which it is united, the soul itself, nonetheless, is not *scattered* out across that *distance*, nor *dispersed* into *multiplicity*, nor *infinitely divisible*. If it were, it would not be *one single substance*, or a *monad* <note>original: "Monade"; a term for a fundamental, indivisible unit of being</note>, but rather a *heap of substances*. *Soul* is no more *divisible* than *life*; regarding which the aforementioned philosopher <note>Plotinus</note> says: "Will you divide a life into two? If the whole was a life, the part will not be a life" <note>original: "ἆρα γε τὴν ζωὴν μεριεῖς; ἀλλ' εἰ τὸ πᾶν ἦν ζωὴ, τὸ μέρος ζωὴ οὐκ ἔσται" (ara ge tēn zōēn merieis? all' ei to pan ēn zōē, to meros zōē ouk estai)</note>. 

Lastly, if the *soul* and *mind*, and the things belonging to them—such as *life* and *thought, understanding* and *wisdom*, etc.—are spread out across a *distance*, having one part external to another, then no good reason can be given why they should not be just as...

### Chapter 5: Divisible and Shaped <note>original: "Figurate"</note>

*Really* and *physically*, as well as *intellectually*, thoughts would be *divisible*; and *one part* of them would be *separable* from another. As *Plotinus* wrote, "In all magnitude or extension, this is one thing, and that is another" <note>original Greek: παντὸς μεγέθους τὸ μὲν ἄλλο, τὸ δὲ ἄλλο</note>. At least no *believer in God* <note>original: "Theist"</note> ought to deny that the *Divine Power* could *split* or *divide* a *thought*—together with the *soul* in which it exists—into *many pieces*, and remove them to the *greatest distances* from one another. This must be possible because it implies no *contradiction*, and whatever we can *conceive* of may be done by *infinite power*. In such a case, neither of those pieces alone would be the *soul* or *mind*, *life* or *thought*; only all of them put together would make up one *entire mind, soul, life, and thought*.

Therefore, the *meaning* of the ancient *believers in non-physical substance* <note>original: "Incorporealists"</note> seems to have been as follows: that there are in *nature* *two kinds* of *substances* that differ specifically from one another. The *first* are *masses* <note>original Greek: ὄγκοι</note> or *bulks*, which are purely *passive things*. The *second* are *powers* <note>original Greek: Δυνάμεις</note> or *virtues*, or the *working nature* <note>original Greek: φύσις ἐργαστική</note>. The *former* of these is nothing else but *magnitude* or *extension*—not as an *abstract notion* of the *mind*, but as a *thing really existing* outside of it. For when it is called an *extended thing* <note>original Latin: "Res Extensa"</note>, the meaning is not as if the *thing* were *one thing* and the *extension* of it were *another*, but that it is *extension* or *distance* *really existing* (outside the *mind*) and not just the *concept* of it. Now, in its very *nature*, this is nothing but *one thing outside another* <note>original Latin: "Aliud Extra Aliud"</note>, and therefore it represents perfect *alterity* <note>the state of being "other" or separate</note>, *disunity*, and *divisibility*. So, no *extension* whatsoever, of any *perceivable size*, is *truly* and *really* *one substance*; rather, it is a *multitude* or *heap* of *substances*, as *many* as there are *parts* into which it is *divisible*. Moreover, because one *part* of this *magnitude* *always stands outside another*, it is an *essential property* of it to be *impenetrable* <note>original: "Antitypous," meaning resistant to being in the same space</note>—that is, to *jostle* or *shoulder out* all other *extended substance* from *penetrating* into it and *co-existing* with it, so as to *occupy* and take up the same *room* or *space*. *One yard of distance* (or of *length, breadth, and thickness*) cannot possibly be added to another without making the *whole extension double* what it was before, since one of them must of necessity stand outside the other. One *magnitude* cannot *absorb* or *swallow up* another, nor can there be any *overlapping of dimensions* <note>original: "Penetration of Dimensions"</note>. Moreover, *magnitude* or *extension* as such is pure *outside* or *outwardness*; it has nothing *within*, no *self-active power* or *virtue*. All its *activity* consists of either *keeping out* or *hindering* any other *extended thing* from *penetrating* into it (which it does merely by being *extended*, and therefore not so much by any *physical efficiency* as by a *logical necessity*) or else *local motion*, toward which it is also only *passive*. No *body* or *extension* as such is able to *move itself* or *act* upon itself.

Wherefore, if there were no other *substance* in the *world* besides this *magnitude* or *extension*, there could be no *motion* or *action* at all in it; no *life*, *thought* <note>original: "cogitation"</note>, *consciousness*, no *understanding* <note>original: "intellection"</note>, *desire*, or *will* <note>original: "volition"</note> (which are the things that make up the *greatest part* of the *universe*). Instead, all would be a dead *heap* or *lump*; nor could any one *sub-*

# Substance, that has Life BOOK I.

[Sub]stance, penetrate another, and co-exist in the same place with it. From this, it follows of necessity that, besides this **external bulky extension** and **swollen magnitude**, there must be another kind of **entity**, whose **essential attribute** or **character** is **life, self-activity**, or **thought** <note>original: "cogitation"</note>. 

First, it is plain that this is not a mere **mode** or **accidental property** <note>original: "accident"</note> of **magnitude** and **extension**. This is because **thought** can be **conceived** just as well without **extension** as **extension** can be without **thought**; whereas no **mode** of anything can be **conceived** without the thing it belongs to. And since there is unquestionably much more **entity** in **life** and **thought** than there is in mere **extension** or **magnitude**—which is the **lowest** of all **being**, and next to **nothing**—it must be attributed to the mere **delusion** and **deception** of the **imagination** that men are so prone to think that **extension** or **magnitude** is the only **substance**, and all other things are merely **accidental properties** of it, **generated** out of it and **corruptible** back into it. 

For though that **secondary** and **derived life** <note>original: "participated life"</note> in the bodies of **animals** is indeed a mere **accident**, and something that may be **present** or **absent** without destroying the subject; yet there is no reason why **primary** and **original life** itself should not be as much a **substantial thing** as mere **extension** and **magnitude**. 

Again, **extension** and **life** (or **thought**) are not **two incomplete concepts** <note>original: "inadequate conceptions"</note> of one and the same **substance** considered in pieces. It is not as if all **extension** had **life** and **thought essentially** belonging to it (as the **Hylozoists** <note>Hylozoists: philosophers who believe that all matter, in every form, possesses life or is inherently alive</note> conclude), or at least that all **life** and **thought** had **extension**. If that were true, all **souls** and **minds**, and even the **Deity** <note>God</note> itself, would be either **extended life and thought** or **living and thinking extension**. Under that view, there would be nothing in nature that is unextended; extension would be the only **entity**, so that whatever lacks it would be, by that very fact, **absolutely nothing**. 

This, I say, will also appear false because—as has been already declared—we cannot **conceive** of a **life**, **mind**, or **thought**, nor anything at all belonging to a **thinking being** as such (like **wisdom, folly, virtue, vice, etc.**), to be **extended into length, breadth, and thickness**, or to be **measurable** by **inches, feet, and yards**. From this, it may be concluded that **extension** and **life** (or **thought**) are not **incomplete concepts** of one and the same thing, since they cannot be **blended** <note>original: "complicated"</note> together into one. Rather, they are distinct **substances** from each other. 

**Lives** and **minds** are such **tight** and **compact things** in themselves, and have such a **self-unity** in their nature, that they cannot be lodged in something that is wholly **scattered** out from itself into **distance**, and **dispersed** into **infinite multiplicity**; nor can they be spread all over extension as if they were the same size as it. Nor is it conceivable how all the different **parts** of an **extended magnitude** should **jointly** concur and contribute to the **production** of **one** and the same **single** and **indivisible thought**; or how that whole **heap** or **bundle** of things should be **one thinker**. 

A **thinker** is a **monad** <note>monad: a single, indivisible unit or simple substance</note>, or one **single substance**, and not a **heap** of **substances**. In contrast, no **body** or **extended thing** is **one**, but **many substances**, because every **conceivable** or **smallest part** of it is a **real substance** by itself.

# Chapter V. An Internal Energy.

...on what *thought* <note>original: "cogitation"</note> is. The *action* of an *extended thing* <note>an object with physical dimensions</note> as such is nothing but *local motion*, *change of distance*, or *translation* from place to place—a mere *outside* and *superficial thing*. But it is certain that *thought* (imagination, understanding, and will) are not *local motions*, nor the mere moving back and forth <note>original: "fridging up and down"</note> of the parts of a physical substance as they change their place and distance. Instead, thought is **unquestionably** an *internal energy*. That is, it is an activity that exists *within* the very *substance* or *essence* of that which *thinks*—within the very *inside* of it. 

From these two kinds of *energies*, we may now conclude that there are also two kinds of *entity* or *substance* in nature. The *one* is mere *outside* and has *nothing within* it. The *other* is a kind of *entity* that has an *internal energy*; it acts *from itself*, *within itself*, and *upon itself*. It is an *inside thing*, whose action is *within* its very *essence* or *substance*. It is plain that the nature of a thinking being is such that it has an *essential inside* or *depth* <note>original: "profundity"</note>. 

Now, this *inside* of thinking beings, wherein they act or think internally within themselves, cannot have any *length, breadth, or thickness* in it. If it did, it would simply be another *outside thing*. Therefore, even if all thinking beings (souls and minds) had as much *extension* and *magnitude* belonging to them as some people suppose, this would still be nothing but the mere *outside* of their being. Besides this, they must of necessity also have an *unextended inside* that has no *outward-swelling mass* <note>original: "out-swelling tumour"</note>, and is not *scattered* into *distance* or *dispersed* into *multiplicity*. 

Consequently, this "inside" could not possibly exist *part by part* within that supposed *extension*—as if one *half* of a *mind* or *thought* were in *one half* of that space, and the other half in another. Instead, it must of necessity be *all undividedly* present, both in the *whole of it* and in *every part*. For if every *twentieth* or *hundredth part* of this extended space did not contain the *whole* of a *life* or *mind*, but only a *twentieth* or *hundredth part* of it, then none of those parts could have any true *life* or *mind* at all; consequently, the whole could not have *any*. 

Indeed, it is otherwise inconceivable how a whole quantity of extended substance could be *one thing* and have *one personality*—one "*I myself*" in it all—if there were not *one indivisible thing* presiding over it, which *held it* all together and *diffused itself* throughout the whole. Thus we see how this concept of the *whole in the whole and in every part* <note>a philosophical principle suggesting the soul is fully present in every part of the body</note> will, like a *ghost*, still haunt and follow men everywhere, no matter what they do to avoid it. 

But it is impossible for one and the same *substance* to be both *extended* and *unextended*. Therefore, in this *hypothesis* of *extended understanding spirits* (which have one part outside another), there is a *hidden entanglement* <note>original: "undiscernd complication"</note> of *two distinct substances*—extended and unextended, or *corporeal* and *incorporeal*—joined together and confused into *one*. 

Nevertheless, we must acknowledge that there is some truth aimed at here: all *finite incorporeal substances* are always naturally united to *some bodies*. Thus, the whole of these *created animals* <note>meaning any living being with a soul</note> is completed and made up of both these together: an *extended outside* and an *unextended inside* <note>The original text reverses these as "extended inside and unextended outside," likely a printer's error given the preceding argument.</note>. Both of them are indeed really distinct substances, yet they are *vitally united* to each other.

# Another Hypothesis, BOOK I.

The sum of all is: that there are *two kinds of substances* in nature. The *first* is *extension* or *magnitude*, *really existing* outside the mind. This is a thing that has no *self-unity* at all but is *infinite alterity* <note>original: "alterity"; meaning otherness or the state of being composed of different, divisible parts</note> and *divisibility*. It is also mere *outside* and *outwardness*, having nothing *within* it, nor any other *action* belonging to it except *to move locally* when it is moved. The *second* kind is *life* and *mind*, or the *self-active thinking <note>original: "cogitative"</note> nature*. This is an *inside being* whose *action* is not *local motion* but an *internal energy* *within* the substance or *essence* of the thinker himself—in the *inside* of him. Therefore, though it is *unextended*, it has a certain *inward recess* or *essential depth* <note>original: "βάθος" (bathos)</note>. 

This is a thing which can *act* entirely upon either a greater or lesser quantity of *extended substance* or *body* and its several parts, penetrating into it and coexisting in the same place with it. Therefore, it is not to be looked upon either as a *mathematical point* or a *physical point*—as an *absolute smallness* <note>original: "parvitude"</note> or the *smallest possible extension* <note>original: "extensum"</note>. This is because it has not only such an *essential inside* or *depth* <note>original: "βάθος" (bathos"</note> in which it *acts* and *thinks* within itself, but also a certain *amplitude* of *active power* *outwardly* <note>original: "ad Extra"</note>, or a sphere of *activity* upon *body*. 

On this account, it was previously affirmed by *Plotinus* <note>a major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD)</note> that an *unextended incorporeal* thing is *bigger than body*. This is because body cannot exist except as one *point* of it in one *point of space*, whereas *this one and the same indivisible* thing can simultaneously comprehend a whole *extended thing* <note>original: "extensum"</note> within it and be entirely present in every part of it. And lastly, all *finite incorporeals* <note>souls or spirits</note> are always naturally united to some body or other. From both of these together, in every *created understanding being*, one entire *animal* is completed and made, consisting of *soul* and *body*. It has something *incorporeal* and something *corporeal* in it: an *unextended inside* and an *extended outside*. By this means, it is limited to *here* and *there* and is *capable of moving locally or changing place*.

Thus we have represented the sense of the *ancient unextended incorporealists* to the best advantage we could, as an *answer* to the previously mentioned *atheistic argument* against *incorporeal substance*, and to vindicate them from the contempt of *atheists*. We affirm that their arguments prove there is some other *substance* besides *body*. Therefore, according to the principles of these atheists themselves, this must be acknowledged as *unextended*, since they conclude that whatever is *extended* is *body*. 

But whether they also absolutely prove that there is *an immaterial substance, without magnitude, without extension, without parts, and indivisible* <note>original: "ἄϋλα ἀμεγέθης, ἀδιάστατα, ἀμερὴς, and ἀδιαίρετα"</note>, we shall leave others to judge. However, it is certain that atheists who maintain the opposite must necessarily assert that every thought, and whatever belongs to the soul or mind (such as *knowledge*, *virtue*, etc.), is not only *mentally* and *mathematically divisible*—so that one might imagine a *half*, a *third*, or a *quarter of a thought*—but also *physically separable* or *divisible* <note>original: "discerpible"</note>, to-

By this extension, they are fixed to a place, yet they remain "all in every part" of that space. This *Outward Extension* is therefore not to be considered *Body* because it is *Penetrable*, *Contractible*, and *Expandable*, and because no one part of it is *Separable* from the rest by the collision or entry of any *Physical* thing upon them. The **Atheist’s Argument** against **Incorporeal Substance** is **answered in two ways**. **First**, that there is **something unextended**; and **secondly**, that **if there were nothing unextended**, yet there must necessarily be a **substance** extended in a different way than a **body** is—one that is neither **resistant** <term>original: "antitypous"; the property of matter that prevents two things from occupying the same space</term> nor **separable into parts** <term>original: "discerpible"</term>. We do not wish to be understood here as dogmatically asserting any specific theory on this point, except for what all **incorporealists** <note>philosophers who believe in substances that are not physical bodies</note> agree upon: that besides **body**, which is **extended in a way that is impenetrable and divisible**, there is in **nature** another **substance** that can **penetrate body** and is **indivisible** (or which does not consist of **parts that can be separated from one another**). That there is at least such a substance as this is unquestionably clear from what has already been declared.

But the **Atheist** will, in the next place, give an account of the **origin** of this **error** (as he calls it) regarding **incorporeal substance**. He **undertakes** to show the **mistake** from which it proceeded, which is yet another **pretended refutation** of the concept. Namely, he claims it sprang partly from the **abuse of abstract names and notions**—men making **substances** out of them—and partly from the **scholastic essences**, which were said to be **distinct** from the things themselves and **eternal**. 

From both of these **delusions and follies** combined, the **Atheist** believes that men were first confirmed in the **belief in ghosts and spirits, demons and devils, and invisible beings** called by several names. This belief also had another **origin**: men mistaking their own **fantasies** for **realities**. According to these **Atheists**, the chief of all these frightening **ghosts and specters** is the **Deity**, whom they call the **Oberon** <note>the King of the Fairies in medieval and Renaissance literature</note>, or **Prince of Fairies and Fantasies**. 

The Atheist further argues that while men, using their **natural reason**, could not conceive of these **ghosts and spirits** as anything other than a kind of **thin, airy body**, their understandings have been so **enchanted** by these **abstract names** (which are indeed the **names of nothing**) and those **separate essences and quiddities** <term>the inherent nature or "whatness" of an object</term> of the **scholastics**, that they have turned them into **incorporeal substances**. The **atheistic conclusion** is this: those who assert an **incorporeal Deity** are **really** only turning a **scholastic separate essence** (or the mere **abstract notion of an accident** <note>in philosophy, an "accident" is a property that is not essential to a thing's nature</note>) into a **substantial thing**, and making a **ghost or spirit** preside over the whole world.

In that section, we also showed that there is not only a **natural anticipation** <term>original: "prolepsis"; an innate or preconceived idea</term> **of a God** in the minds of men, but also that the **belief** in Him is **supported** by the strongest and most **substantial reason**. Indeed, His **existence** is **demonstrable with mathematical evidence** to those who are capable and not blinded by **prejudice**, nor **enchanted** by the **witchcraft of vice and wickedness**, which **corrupts their understandings**. # Chapter 5. Abstract Names and Essences.

It has also been shown that the belief in other ghosts and spirits besides the **Deity** did not merely spring from **fear** and **fancy** either, like **children's scary stories** <note>original: "bugbears"</note>, but from **real phenomena**—true, sensible apparitions documented throughout history. Without these, the belief in such things could never have persisted so generally and constantly in the world. Likewise, there is no contradiction at all to reason in the idea that there may be **aerial** and **ethereal** animals just as there are **terrestrial** animals. It is only the dull and **earthy stupidity** of men’s minds that makes them so prone to think that there is no **understanding nature** superior to mankind, that everything in the world around us is **dead**, and to disbelieve in the existence of anything which they themselves cannot either **see** or **feel**. Assuredly, the **Deity** is no **fancy**; He is the **greatest reality** in the world, and that without which nothing at all could be **real**, as He is the only **necessarily existing being**. Consequently, **atheism** is either mere **foolishness** <note>original: "sottishness"</note> or else a strange kind of **irreligious fanaticism**.

We now further add that the belief in **ghosts** and **incorporeal spirits**, and consequently of an **incorporeal Deity**, did not arise from any ridiculous mistake of treating the **abstract names** and **notions** of mere **accidents** <term>properties or qualities (like "redness" or "wisdom") that cannot exist on their own without a substance</term> as if they were **substances**. Nor did it come from the **scholastic essences** <note>formal definitions of things used by medieval and early modern university philosophers</note> that are said to be **eternal**. 

Regarding the latter, none of those **scholastics** ever dreamed that there was any **universal man** or **universal horse** existing alone by itself and separate from all **individuals**. Nor did they believe that the **abstract metaphysical essences** of men walked up and down among graves in **airy bodies** after they were dead. It is absolutely impossible for the **real essence** of anything to be separable from the thing itself, or for it to be **eternal** when the thing itself is not. If these **scholastics** viewed the **essences** of all things as **incorporeal substances**, then they would have had to make everything (even **matter** itself) into **ghosts**, **spirits**, and **incorporeal beings**; they would have even had to make **accidents** (which also have their own **essences**) into **substances**. 

But in truth, these **scholastic essences** said to be **eternal** are nothing but the **intelligible essences** of things—the natures of things as they are **conceivable** and as they are **objects** of the **mind**. In this sense, it is an acknowledged **truth** that the **essences** of things (as, for example, of a **sphere** or a **triangle**) are **eternal** and such as were never **made**, because otherwise there could be no **eternal truths** <note>original: "eternal verities"</note> concerning them. 

So the **true** meaning of these **eternal essences** is indeed nothing other than this: **that knowledge is eternal**, or that there is an **eternal mind** that understands the **intelligible natures** and **ideas** of all things—whether they **actually** exist or are only **possible**. This mind understands their **necessary** relations to one another and all the **unchangeable truths** <note>original: "immutable verities"</note> belonging to them. Therefore, although these **eternal essences** themselves are not **ghosts**, **spirits**, or **incorporeal substances** (since they are nothing but **mental objects** <note>original: "Noemata"; Greek for objects of thought or understanding</note> and **ideas**), it plainly follows from the **necessary requirement** of their existence that there is **one eternal, uncreated mind and a perfect, incorporeal Deity—a real and substantial spirit**. This Deity understands Himself, the full extent of His own power, the possibilities of things, and their **intelligible natures**, together with a **model** <note>original: "exemplar"</note>...

Incorpor. Substance Proved, BOOK I.

...exemplar or blueprint <note>original: "Platform"</note> of the whole world, and produced the same accordingly.

But our **atheistic debater** <note>original: "Atheistick Argumentator"</note> further argues that those **Scholastics** and **metaphysicians**—who conclude that life or **thought** <note>original: "cogitation"</note> is an independent substance because it can be considered abstractly without considering the body—greatly misuse those **abstract names** and notions of mere **qualities** <term>accident: a property (like color or temperature) that cannot exist on its own without a substance</term> by turning them into **incorporeal substances** (which they then imagine can walk among graves after men are dead). 

To this we reply that if these philosophers had turned the abstract notions of qualities in general into incorporeal substances, they would have had to suppose that all the qualities or attributes of bodies—such as **whiteness**, **blackness**, **heat**, and **cold**—were also incorporeal substances. This is something that has never been heard of or even imagined. But the case is quite different regarding **conscious life** or **thought**, even though it is also an abstract concept. This is because thought is not a mere quality of the body—as the atheist conveniently assumes to serve his own theory <note>original: "Hypothesis"</note>—nor is it a quality of anything else. Instead, it is an **essential attribute** of another substance distinct from the body (an incorporeal one), in the same way that **extension** or **physical size** <note>original: "magnitude"</note> is the essential attribute of a body, rather than just a temporary quality.

Having now so extensively refuted all the most significant atheistic grounds, we are compelled to address those that follow—which are of less importance—with as much brevity and conciseness as possible. The next four arguments (the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth) pretend to do nothing more than disprove a **physical God** <note>original: "Corporeal Deity"</note>. They assume that there is no other substance in the world besides **matter** <note>original: "Body"</note> to conclude that God is an impossibility—that is, the impossibility of an **eternal, uncreated Mind**, the maker and governor of the whole world. Therefore, all these arguments mean nothing to those who believe in an **incorporeal God**, who are the only **true theists**. Nevertheless, although only the **Stoics** and other "corporealists" (who are nonetheless theists) are directly affected by these arguments, we shall still consider the principles of **atheistic materialism** <note>original: "Atheistick Corporalism"</note> contained in the fifth and sixth points. We will show that because these theories are absolutely impossible, there is a **necessity for incorporeal substance**, from which the existence of God will also follow.

Here, then, are two atheistic theories based on the assumption that **everything is body**. The first focuses on **qualities** that can be created and destroyed, which we call the **hylopathian** <term>Hylopathian: The ancient belief that all things, including life and mind, are produced by the changing states or "affections" of matter</term>. The second is based on **unqualified atoms**, which is **atomic materialism and atheism**. The former of these was the most ancient, and the first **outline** or **rough sketch** <note>original: "Sciography, or Rude Delineation"</note> of atheism. For **Aristotle** tells us that the most ancient atheists were those who supposed that **matter** or **body**—that is, **bulky extension**—was the only substance and the only uncreated thing, out of which all things...

### Chapter V. From the Atheistic Grounds.

...things were made, and into which all things are again resolved. Whatever else exists in the world is nothing but the **passions**, **qualities**, and **accidents** <term>accidents: properties or characteristics that are not essential to a substance's nature</term> of matter. These are **generable** and **corruptible**—meaning they can be produced out of **nothing** and reduced to **nothing** again. From this, the necessary consequence is **that there is no eternal, unmade life or understanding**. In this view, **Mind** is not a God or a primary principle in the universe, but is essentially a **creature** <note>original: "Creature"; here meaning something created or produced rather than a self-existent being</note>.

This **Hylopathian Atheism** <term>Hylopathian: From the Greek roots for "matter" and "passion/quality"; the belief that everything is produced by the qualities of matter</term>—which supposes that everything in the universe is either the substance of **matter** and **bulk**, or else its **qualities** and **accidents**—has also been called **Anaximandrian** by us <note>Referring to Anaximander (c. 610–546 BC), a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher</note>. We do not deny that there might have been some differences among atheists of this kind in the past. Nor are we ignorant that **Simplicius** <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist commentator</note> and others believe **Anaximander** asserted that, besides matter, there were also **qualities** that were **eternal** and **unmade**. They suggest he held a theory of **Homoeomery** <term>Homoeomery: A theory that substances are made of tiny parts that have the same nature as the whole</term> or a **similar atomology**, much like **Anaxagoras** did later, except that Anaximander would not acknowledge any **unmade mind** or **life**. 

Anaximander supposed that all **life** and **understanding**, all **soul** and **mind**, rose up and were generated from a **fortuitous commixture** <note>original: "Fortuitous Commixture"; an accidental or random mixing</note> of those **similar atoms**, or from the qualities of **heat** and **cold**, **moist** and **dry**, and the like, blended together. We confess that there is some probability for this **opinion**. However, because there is no absolute certainty regarding it, and because all these ancient atheists agreed that **life** and **understanding** are either **primary** or **secondary qualities** of the **body**—and are therefore **generable** and **corruptible**—we did not think it fit to **multiply forms of atheism**. Instead, we categorize all of this as one kind of atheism, calling it indifferently **Hylopathian** or **Anaximandrian**.

The **second atheistic hypothesis** is the form of atheism described under the **sixth head**. It likewise supposes the body to be the only substance and the principles of the body to be devoid of life and understanding. However, it rejects all **real qualities** (according to the common understanding of them). It suggests that all things besides matter are generated merely from the **combinations** of **magnitudes**, **figures**, **sites**, and **motions**, or the **textures** of **unqualified atoms**—including **life** and **understanding**. Therefore, according to these thinkers, life is not a **simple**, **primitive**, or **original** thing, but is **secondary**, **compounded**, and **derivative**. As a mere **creature** of **matter** and **motion**, it could not possibly be a **God** or the **first principle** in the universe. 

This is the **Atomic Atheism** called **Democritical**, as **Leucippus** and **Democritus** were its first founders. Before them, there was another **atomology** which claimed that **unqualified atoms** were the principles of all bodies, but it still allowed for **incorporeal substance**. However, as **Laertius** declares, these two were the first who ever made "senseless atoms the principles of all things" <note>original: "ἀρχὰς τῶν ὅλων ἀτόμους"</note>, including **life**, **understanding**, **soul**, and **mind**.

Indeed, it cannot be denied that from these **two things** granted—**that all is body**, and **that the principles of body** are devoid of...
