# Life Substantial; and Book I.

If all *Life and Understanding* must come from a source, it follows unavoidably that there can be no *Corporeal Deity* <term>Corporeal Deity: a god that possesses a physical body or is composed of matter</term>. Therefore, the *Stoics*—who claimed to acknowledge no other *substance* besides Body, yet nevertheless strongly believed in the existence of a God, or an *Eternal Unmade Mind* who was the *Maker of the whole World*—denied the other *proposition* of the *Atheistic Corporealists*. The Stoics denied that the principles of all *bodies* were devoid of *Life and Understanding*. Instead, they asserted the existence of an *Intellectual Fire*, *Eternal and Unmade*, which was the *Maker of the whole Mundane System* <note>mundane system: the physical universe or world order</note>. 

Even if this *postulate* <note>original: "Postulatum"</note> of an *Eternal Living Intellectual Body* were granted to these *Stoics*, their Corporeal God could not, nonetheless, be *Absolutely Incorruptible*. As *Origen* <note>a prominent early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 185–253 AD)</note> often points out: 

<margin>Origen, *Against Celsus*, Book 1, p. 17.</margin> 
"God to the Stoics is a Body, and they are not ashamed to say he is mutable, alterable, and changeable throughout; and, quite simply, he would be capable of being destroyed, were it not that there is nothing else to destroy him." <note>original Greek: ὁ θεὸς τοῖς Στωικοῖς ἐστὶ σῶμα, οὐκ αἰδούμενοι λέγειν αὐτὸν τρεπτὸν, καὶ δι᾿ ὅλων ἀλλοιωτὸν καὶ μεταβλητὸν, καὶ ἁπαξαπλῶς δυνάμενον φθαρῆναι, παρὰ τὸ μηδὲν εἶναι τὸ φθεῖρον αὐτόν.</note> 

*God to the Stoics is a Body, and therefore Mutable, Alterable, and Changeable; he would indeed be perfectly Corruptible if there were any other Body to act upon him. Therefore, he is only Happy in this: that he lacks a Corrupter or Destroyer.* 

This point was rightly urged by the Atheistic debaters: that no *Corporeal Deity* could be absolutely *Incorruptible* by its own nature, nor could it be *Immortal* except by *accident* <note>by accident: by chance or circumstance, rather than by its essential nature</note>, because of its *Divisibility* <note>The argument that anything made of parts can be taken apart or destroyed</note>. For if there were any other matter outside of this *World* to invade it, or to disunite its parts, the *Life and Unity* of the Stoic *Corporeal God* would necessarily be scattered and destroyed. 

<margin>P. 169.</margin> 
Regarding this Stoic God, the same *Origen* further writes: 

"The God of the Stoics, being a body, sometimes has the whole of matter as his commanding part <term>commanding part: translation of the Greek 'Hegemonikon,' the ruling essence of the soul or universe</term> during the cosmic conflagration; at other times, he exists only in a part of it, during the formation of the world. For these men were not able to reach a clear notion of the Deity as a Being that is in every way Incorruptible, Simple, Uncompounded, and Indivisible." <note>original Greek: ὁ τῶν Στωικῶν Θεὸς, ἅτε σῶμα τυγχάνων, ὁτὲ μὲν ἡγεμονικὸν ἔχει τὴν ὅλην οὐσίαν, ὅταν ἡ ἐκπύρωσις ᾖ· ὁτὲ δὲ ἐπὶ μέρους γίνεται αὐτῆς, ὅταν ἡ διακόσμησις· οὐδὲ γὰρ δεδύνηνται οὗτοι τρανῶσαι τὴν φυσικὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ ἔννοιαν, ὡς πάντῃ ἀφθάρτου καὶ ἁπλοῦ, καὶ ἀσυνθέτου, καὶ ἀδιαιρέτου.</note> 

Despite this, these *Stoics* were not to be ranked among the Atheists; they were to be preferred far above them and accounted as a kind of *Imperfect Theists*.

But we shall now make it evident that in both types of *Atheistic Corporealism*—which agree on *two* things: that *Body is the only Substance*, and that *the Principles of Body are not Vital*—there is an absolute *impossibility*. This is not only because, as *Aristotle* objects, they supposed no *Active Principle* <note>active principle: a source of motion or change, as opposed to passive matter</note>, but also because their attempt to bring Life and Understanding (which are *Real Entities*) out of dead and *senseless* matter is essentially trying to bring *Something out of Nothing*. 

Indeed, the *Atomic Atheist* is the more absurd and unreasonable of the two. For even as he discards all "Real Qualities" <term>Real Qualities: inherent properties like color or heat, which atomists argued were just perceptions</term>—specifically for the reason that *Nothing can come out of Nothing*—he nevertheless produces *Life, Sense, and Understanding* (*unquestionable realities*) out of mere *Magnitudes, Figures, Sites*, and *Motions*. That is, he produces them *out of nothing*. Therefore, since there is an *absolute impossibility* in both of these *Atheistic Hypotheses* (neither...

# CHAP. V. Some Unmade.

(None of which is able to solve the *phenomenon* of *life* and *understanding*) from that confessed principle of theirs—that *matter* as such has no *life* or *understanding* belonging to it—it follows unavoidably that there must be some other *substance* besides *body* or *matter* which is *essentially vital* and *intellectual*. For "it is not possible for all things to possess a borrowed life" <note>original Greek: οὐ γὰρ πάντα χρῆται ἐπακτῷ ζωῇ</note>, because all things cannot possibly have a *foreign*, *incidental*, and *borrowed life*. Instead, something in the universe must necessarily have *life naturally* and *originally*. All *life* cannot be merely *accidental*, *generated*, and *corruptible* <note>corruptible: capable of decaying or ending</note>, produced out of nothing and *reducible* to *nothing* again; rather, there must of necessity be some *substantial life*. 

This point—*that all life is not a mere accident, but that there is substantial life*—has been of late, with much reason and judgment, insisted upon and urged by the writer of *The Life of Nature* <note>A reference to Francis Glisson (1597–1677), a physician who argued that matter possessed a "vital" force</note>. Neither must there only be such a *substantial life* that is *naturally immortal* for the future, but also one that is *eternal* and was never *made*. All other *lives* and *minds* whatsoever (none of which could possibly be generated out of *matter*) are derived from this *eternal unmade fountain* of *life* and *understanding*.

The *Hylozoic Atheists* <term>Hylozoic Atheists: those who believe that matter itself is alive and self-organizing without a separate God</term>, being well aware of this—namely, that there must necessarily be both *substantial* and *eternal unmade life*—but also supposing *matter* to be the only *substance*, thought themselves forced to attribute to all *matter* as such *life* and *understanding*. However, they viewed this life not as *animal-like* and *conscious*, but *natural* only. They conceived that from the *modification* of this life alone through *organization*, all other *animal-like life*—not only the *sensory* in *animals* <note>original: "Brutes"</note> but also the *rational* in *humans*—was derived. 

But this *Hylozoic Atheism*, by bringing all *conscious* and *reflective life* or *animality* out of a *supposedly senseless, stupid, and unconscious life* of *nature* in *matter*, and doing so merely from a different *accidental modification* or *arrangement* <note>original: "Contexture"</note> of parts, once again plainly brings *something* out of *nothing*, which is an *absolute impossibility*. 

Moreover, this *Hylozoic Atheism* was long ago, at its first *emergence* <note>original: "Emersion"</note>, *solidly refuted* by the *Atomic Atheists* <term>Atomic Atheists: materialists (like Epicurus) who believe the world is made of dead, mindless atoms</term> in this manner: If *matter* as such had *life*, *perception*, and *understanding* belonging to it, then every *atom* or *smallest particle* of it would necessarily be a *distinct perceiver* <note>original: "Percipient"</note> by itself. From this, it would follow that there could not possibly be any such *humans* and *animals* as now exist *compounded* out of them. Instead, every *human* and *animal* would be a *heap* of *innumerable perceivers*, and would have *innumerable perceptions* and *acts of thinking* <note>original: "Intellections"</note>; whereas it is plain that there is but one *life* and *understanding*, one *soul* or *mind*, one *perceiver* or *thinker* in every one. 

To say that these innumerable *particles* of *matter* *all cooperate together*—that is, to make every *human* and *animal* a *multitude* or *commonwealth* of *perceivers* and *persons*, as it were joining together <note>original: "clubbing together"</note>—is something so *absurd* and *ridiculous* that one would wonder why the *Hylozoists* did not choose instead to recant their *fundamental error* (the *life of matter*) rather than seek *shelter* and *sanctuary* for it under such a pretense. For although many *voluntary agents* and *persons* may resign their wills to *one*, and by that means have all but as it were *one*

<header>CHAP. V. Flesh, Blood, and Brains.</header>

The animation of the world is also considered in a stricter sense, as if the world were truly and properly a living creature <note>original: "Animal"</note>, and therefore a *God*, completed and made up of *soul* and *body* together, just as other animals are. To some, the *soul* of this great *world-animal* was the *highest* or *supreme deity*, while to others it was only a secondary *god*, as they assumed an *abstract mind* existed *superior* to it. However, the idea of God being the *soul of the world* in this latter *pagan* sense, and the world being an *animal* or a *god*, are concepts we absolutely disclaim and renounce. 

Nevertheless, this *seventh atheistic argument* is not directed against the soul of the world in the sense used by *pagan theists* either—since they believe that has already been refuted—but rather in the sense used by *atheistic theogonists* <term>theogonist: one who theorizes about the birth or origin of the gods from material causes</term>. These thinkers do not believe in an *eternal, uncreated soul* or *mind*, but only a *native* and *generated* one, which resulted from the *arrangement* of *matter* and the *interweaving* <note>original: "Contexture"</note> of *atoms*—the *offspring of Night and Chaos*. 

Here, the atheists—after supposedly refuting true and genuine *theism*—pretend to remove all *shadows* of it as well. Their goal is to free people from any *fear* of being subject <note>original: "obnoxious"</note> to any conscious being superior to themselves. Therefore, we could omit the refutation of this *argument* without any harm to the *cause of theism*. However, because the general *atheistic assertion* is that there is no life or *understanding* presiding over the entire world, we will briefly examine its supposed grounds, which will be enough to refute it. 

The *first* ground is that there is no other *substance* in the world except *body* (matter). The *second* is that the basic principles of bodies (atoms) are devoid of all *life* and *understanding*. The *last* is that *life* and *understanding* are merely *accidents* <term>accident: a non-essential property or quality of a thing that can change without the thing's essence being destroyed</term> of matter, resulting from a composition or arrangement of *atoms* that produces soft *flesh, blood, and brains* in organized bodies of *human form*. 

From all this, they conclude that there can be no life or *understanding* in the world as a whole because it does not have a *human form*, is not organized in that way, and has no *blood* or *brains*. But matter is not the only substance, nor are *life* and *understanding* merely properties resulting from the modification of *dead* and *lifeless matter*. Furthermore, it is not *blood* or *brains* that *understand* within us, but an *incorporeal soul* or *mind* vitally united to an *earthly organized body*. This soul will understand with even greater clarity when it is eventually clothed with a *pure*, *spiritual*, and *heavenly one*. 

There is also a higher kind of *intellectual being* <note>original: "Animals"</note> in the universe which, although consisting of *soul* and *body*, has no *flesh*, *blood*, *brains*, or organs structured like ours. And the most perfect mind and intellect of all is not the *soul* of any *body* but is complete in itself, without such a *vital union* or *sympathy* with *matter*. We conclude, therefore, that the following passage from a modern writer—"*We worms cannot conceive how God can understand without brains*"—is the *voice of a beast* <note>original: "Vox Pecudis"</note>, the *language* and *philosophy* of worms or brute animals rather than of men.

# The Atheists' Argument, BOOK I.

...there can be no such thing as an **immortal living being**, and consequently, no one can be perfectly happy. This is because all **living beings whatsoever** are merely **combinations of atoms** <note>original: "Concretions of Atoms"</note>. Just as they were first created, they are also liable to death and corruption. Life is not a **simple, primary nature** or a **substantial thing**, but merely an **accidental modification of compound bodies**. When their parts are separated or their structure is disordered, life vanishes back into nothingness. 

Because there is no immortal life, **happiness** must be a mere **insignificant word** and nothing but a **romantic fiction** <note>In this period, "romantic" referred to something belonging to the world of fictional "romances" or fables, meaning it was imaginary or unrealistic.</note>. 

Regarding this, we first note that it is telling that atheists admit that, according to their own principles, there can be no such thing as **happiness**. They believe this because there is no security of **future permanence**. To them, all **life** is perpetually coming **out of nothing** and whirling back into nothing again. 

However, this **atheistic argument** is also founded upon a **previous error**: the idea that **body is the only substance**, and that the **first principles** of body are **devoid of all life and understanding**. On the contrary, it is certain that **life** cannot possibly result from any combination of dead and lifeless things. Therefore, life must be a **simple and primary nature**. 

It is true that the **participated life** <note>Life that is derived from or shared with another source.</note> in the bodies of **animals**—which is improperly called "life," since it is really just their being **enlivened** <note>original: "Actuated"</note> by a **living soul**—is a mere **accidental thing** that can be **created** <note>original: "Generable"</note> and **destroyed** <note>original: "Corruptible"</note>. A body that is now vitally united to a living soul may be separated from it again, thereby becoming a **dead and lifeless carcass**. 

However, the **primary or original life** itself is **substantial**. There can be no such thing as a **dead carcass of a human soul**. That which has **life essentially** belonging to its **substance** must be **naturally immortal**, because no **substance** can of itself **perish** or **vanish into nothing**. 

Besides this, there must also be some life that is not only **substantial** but also **eternal and unmade**. Its existence is **necessary**, and it is **absolutely impossible for anything else to annihilate it**. Such a being must have **perfect security** regarding its own future **happiness**. This is what is meant by an **incorporeal deity**. This concludes a **brief refutation** of the **eighth atheistic argument**.

But the **Democritic atheist** <term>Democritic atheist: a follower of the philosophy of Democritus, who argued that everything in the universe is made of atoms and empty space, excluding any divine creator.</term> proceeds, attempting to further disprove the existence of a **God** using the **phenomena of motion and thought** <note>original: "Cogitation"</note> in the three following arguments. 

**First**, while **theists** commonly use an argument from **motion** to prove the existence of **God** (the **first unmoved mover**), the **atheists** contend the opposite. They claim that from the very nature of **motion**, the impossibility of any such **first unmoved mover** is clearly demonstrable. 

They use an axiom of undisputed truth regarding motion: **Whatever is moved is moved by something else**, or **nothing can move itself**. From this, they conclude it follows unavoidably that there is no **eternal unmoved being** <note>original: *Æternum Immobile*</note>. On the contrary, they argue there was an **eternal moved being** <note>original: *Æternum Motum*</note>—meaning one thing was moved by another in an infinite chain from eternity, **without any first mover or cause**,

### CHAPTER V. Refuting the Argument from Motion

The atheists argue that because **nothing could move itself**, nothing could ever **move another thing** unless it was itself first **moved** by something else.

To this we reply: The axiom that **"whatever is moved, is moved by another, and not by itself,"** was restricted by Aristotle and the other philosophers who used it to the **physical motion** <note>original: "Local Motion"</note> of bodies only. They meant that **no physical body ever moves itself originally, but is moved by something else.** 

It does not follow from this that **"nothing is moved except by something else that was already moved"** <note>original: "Nihil Movetur nisi à Moto"</note>. It also does not follow that, by necessity, **one body was moved by another body, and that by another, and so on backwards infinitely**, without any **first unmoved** or **self-moving and self-active mover**, as the **Democritic atheist** <note>A follower of Democritus, an ancient Greek philosopher who believed the world was made entirely of atoms in motion, leaving no room for a divine creator.</note> foolishly imagines. 

The motion of bodies might proceed (as it unquestionably did) from something else that is not a body and was not **previously moved**. Furthermore, the Democritic atheist groundlessly imagines that there was only **one push** given to the world at the beginning, and no more, and that this motion would continue forever, with one body constantly moving another for all eternity. 

While it is indeed a part of the **Cartesian hypothesis** <note>Referring to the physics of René Descartes, who proposed that the total amount of motion in the universe remains constant.</note> that, according to the laws of nature, a body in motion will continue to move just as a body at rest will continue to rest until that motion is transferred to another body, the case here is different. In this context, it is supposed not only that one push was given to the world at first, but also that the same **quantity of motion** or **agitation** is constantly preserved and maintained. 

But we will let this pass, as it is a rather subtle point and not correctly understood by many of the **Cartesians** themselves. We say that it is **utterly impossible** for **one body to be moved by another infinitely** without any first cause or **mover** that was **self-active**. This is not just based on the authority of Aristotle, who stated **"that it is not possible for the origin of motion to extend to infinity"** <note>original Greek: "ὅτε δυνατὸν ὅθεν ἡ ἀρχὴ τῆς κινήσεως ἰέναι εἰς ἄπειρον"</note>, but from the reason Aristotle added: **"If there were no first unmoved mover, there could be no cause of motion at all"** <note>original Greek: "εἴπερ μηδέν ἐστι τὸ πρῶτον, ὅλως αἴτιον οὐδέν ἐστι"</note>. 

If all the motion in the world were a **passive effect** <note>original: "Passion"</note> caused by something else, and yet there were no **first unmoved active mover**, then motion would be an effect without an **agent**, or a result without an **action**. Consequently, it would proceed from nothing, and either cause itself or be created without any cause. 

The root of the atheist's error here is simply this: he takes it for granted that there is no other **substance** besides body, and no other action but **physical motion**. Because of this, to him, the proposition **"no body can move itself"** is exactly the same as saying **"nothing can act from itself"** or be **self-active**.

And thus, the atheists' pretended demonstration against a God, or **first cause**, based on **motion**, is abundantly refuted. We have shown that there is no logical consistency at all in their argument.

# A First Mover Demonstrated. BOOK I.

Because no body can move **itself**, and therefore there can be no **First Unmoved Mover**; and having discovered the ground of the **atheist's error** here—their taking it for granted that there is **nothing but body**—and lastly, having plainly shown that it implies a contradiction for there to be **action** and **motion** in the world without **anything self-moving** or **self-active**: it is demonstratively certain from the existence of **motion** that there is a **First Cause** or **Unmoved Mover**. 

We shall now further add that from the principle acknowledged by the **Democritic atheists** themselves—that **no body can move itself**—it follows undeniably that there is **some other substance besides body**. This must be something **incorporeal** <note>Incorporeal: Lacking a physical body; spiritual or mental in nature.</note> which is **self-moving** and **self-active**, and was the **First Unmoved Mover of the heavens** or the world. For if no body was ever able to move itself from eternity, and yet there must of necessity be some **active cause** of the **motion** that exists in the world (since it could not cause itself), then there is unquestionably some **other substance besides body**. This substance, having the **power to move matter**, was the **First Cause of motion**, while **itself** remained **unmoved**.

Moreover, it is also certain from this that there is another **species of action**, distinct from **physical motion** <note>original: "Local Motion"</note>, which is not <term>heterochinesie</term> <note>original: "Heterochineſie"; motion caused by an external force.</note> but <term>autochinesie</term> <note>original: "Autochineſie"; self-originated motion or activity.</note> or **self-activity**. For since the physical motion of a body is essentially **heterochinesie**—caused not by the moving substance itself, but by something else acting upon it—that **action** by which physical motion is first caused cannot itself be physical motion. Instead, it must be **autochinesie** or **self-activity**: **that which is not an effect received from any other agent** <note>original: "a Passion from any other Agent"</note>, but springs from the immediate agent itself. 

This **species of action** is called **cogitation** <note>Cogitation: The process of thinking or mental activity.</note>. All the physical motion in the world was first caused by some **cogitative** or **thinking being** which was not **acted** upon by anything outside of it, nor was it **physically moved** at all, but only **mentally**. This being is the **Immovable Mover of the heavens**, or the **cosmic whirlpools** <note>original: "Vortices"; in 17th-century physics, these were large circular currents of matter believed to carry the planets.</note>. Thus, **cogitation** is, in the **order of nature**, prior to **physical motion**, and **incorporeal substance** is prior to **corporeal substance**, the former having a **natural authority** over the latter. We have now not only refuted the **ninth atheistic argument** concerning **motion**, but also demonstrated against the **Democritic atheists**—using their own principle—that there is an **incorporeal and thinking substance**, the **First Immovable Mover of the heavens and whirlpools**; that is, an **incorporeal Deity**.

But the **Democritic atheist** will yet make a further attempt to prove that there can be **nothing self-moving** or **self-active**, and that **no thinking being** could be a **First Cause**. He lays his foundation in this principle: that **nothing takes its beginning from itself, but from the action of some other agent outside of it**. From this, he would infer that **cogitation itself is heterochinesie**—the **passive reaction of the thinker** <note>original: "the Passion of the Thinker"</note> and the **action of something outside of it**. He claims that no **cogitation** ever rises up of itself without an external cause, and that **cogitation** is indeed nothing but **physical motion** or **mechanism**. He views all **living, understanding beings as machines** that are **moved from without**, and then reaches this conclusion: that therefore **no understanding being** could possibly be a **First Cause**. ### Chapter V. Something Self-Active.

...understanding Being as such, can be *perfectly happy* neither, as the *Deity* is supposed to be, because it is *dependent upon something outside of it*; and this is the *tenth atheist argument*.

Here we shall first consider that which the *Democritic atheist* <note>original: "Democritick Atheiſt"; a follower of the philosophy of Democritus, which holds that the universe consists of atoms and a void, and that all phenomena are the result of mechanical interactions.</note> makes his *fundamental principle*, or *common notion*, to disprove all <term>self-activity</term> <note>original: "Autochineſie"; the capacity for a thing to move or act by its own internal power.</note> by: *that nothing takes its beginning from itself, but from the action of some other thing outside of it.* 

If this *axiom* is understood to refer to *substantial things*, then we acknowledge it to be unquestionably true; it is the same as saying *that no substance which once was not could ever possibly cause itself or bring itself into being, but must take its beginning from the action of something else.* However, in that sense, it argues nothing at all against *Theism*. 

It is likewise true *that no action whatsoever (and therefore no thought) takes its beginning from itself or causes itself to be, but is always produced by some substantial agent.* But this will not benefit the atheist either. Therefore, if he wishes to direct his force against *Theism*, he must understand this *proposition* as follows: *that no action whatsoever takes its beginning from the immediate agent (which is the subject of it), but from the action of some other thing outside of it*; or, *that nothing can move or act except as it is moved and acted upon by something else.* 

But this is only to *beg the question*—to prove the point in dispute by simply restating it: *that nothing is self-active because nothing can act of its own accord.* Meanwhile, it is undeniably certain that there could not possibly be any *motion* or *action* at all in the universe if there were not something *self-moving* or *self-active*. Otherwise, all that *motion* or *action* would be an effect without a cause <note>original: "Paſſion from Nothing"</note> and be *made without a cause*.

And whereas the atheists would further prove that *no thought* <note>original: "Cogitation"</note> *takes its beginning from the thinker, but always from the action of some other thing outside of it*, they do so in this manner: *because it is not conceivable why this thought, rather than that, should start up at any time if there were not some cause for it outside the thinker.* 

Here, in the first place, we freely grant that our *human thoughts* are indeed commonly *occasioned* by the *encounters with sensible objects* around us. We also grant that the *connections* <note>original: "Concatenations"</note> of those *thoughts* and *mental images* <note>original: "Phantaſms"</note> in us (which are distinguished from *sensations*, whether we are asleep or awake) often depend upon *physical and mechanical causes* in the brain. 

Notwithstanding this, the claim *that all our thoughts are forced and imposed upon us from the outside, and that there is no transition in our thoughts at any time except those that were previously in the senses* (which the *Democritic atheist* asserts) is something we absolutely deny. For, if we had no *mastery* at all over our thoughts, but they were all like tennis balls, batted and struck upon us as if by rackets from the outside, then we could not steadily and constantly carry out any *designs* and *purposes* in life. 

On the contrary, that statement of *Aristotle’s* is most true (as will be further proved elsewhere): that man and all *rational beings* are, in some sense, a *principle of actions* <note>original: "ἀρχὴ πράξεων" (archē praxeōn)</note>, subordinate to the *Deity*.

# A Shocking Paradox of Atheists; BOOK I.

...which they could not possibly be, if they were not also a **source of thoughts** <note>original: "Principle of Cogitations"</note> and had some command over them. Otherwise, these thoughts would all be as much determined by external causes as the **movements of a weather vane** are. The **Rational Soul** is itself an **active and bubbling fountain of thoughts**. That perpetual and restless desire, which is as natural and essential to us as our very life, is continually raising up and pushing forward new thoughts within us, which are, as it were, offered to us. Besides this, we also have a further **power of self-reflection**, and a power of determining and fixing our mind and intention upon certain objects and arranging our thoughts accordingly. 

But the atheist must also be taught a further **lesson**: that an absolutely perfect mind (such as the Deity is supposed to be) does not—as **Aristotle** writes of it—**sometimes think and sometimes not think** <note>original: "ὁτὲ μὲν νοεῖν ὁτὲ δὲ οὐ νοεῖν"</note>. It is ignorant of nothing, nor does it need to **reason through logical steps** <term>syllogizing</term> about anything. But as for that **shocking paradox of atheists**—that **thought** itself is nothing but **physical motion** <term>local motion</term> or **mechanical action**—we could not have believed it possible that any man would ever entertain such an idea. We would have thought it was merely a slander invented against atheists, were it not certain from the records of antiquity. 

The old **religious atomists** <note>These were early philosophers who believed the world was made of atoms but still maintained the existence of God and the soul.</note> rightly reduced all **physical action** (such as birth, growth, and change) to **physical motion**, or the movement from place to place, because no other motion is conceivable in physical bodies. However, the ancient **atheistic proponents** of that philosophy (**Leucippus** and **Democritus**), not content with this, actually carried the matter even further. They made **thought** itself nothing but **physical motion**. 

It is also certain that a modern atheistic claimant to wit <note>Likely referring to the philosopher Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), who argued for a purely materialistic view of the mind.</note> has publicly owned this same conclusion: **that the mind is nothing else but physical motion in the organic parts of a man's body**. These men have sometimes been a little troubled by the "fancy," **appearance**, or **seeming** of thought—that is, the **consciousness** of it—not knowing quite what to make of it. But then they dismiss it again and satisfy themselves smugly with the idea that "fancy" is just "fancy," but the **reality of thought** is nothing but **physical motion**. They act as if there were not as much reality in fancy and consciousness as there is in physical motion! 

What inclined these men so much toward this opinion was simply that they were aware of this: if any action other than **physical motion** were admitted, they would have to acknowledge some **substance** other than **matter** <note>original: "Body"</note>. **Descartes** <note>original: "Cartesius"</note> indeed attempted to argue that non-human animals are nothing but **machines**, but he assumed there was no **thought** at all in them, and consequently nothing of true **animal life**, any more than there is in an artificial **automaton** <term>self-moving machine</term>, like a wooden eagle or the like. Nevertheless, even this was justly considered quite a paradox.

### CHAP. V. No Syllable of things. 849

[...they cannot survive] death and walk up and down in *airy bodies*, any more than the *form* of a *house* or *tree*, after its *dissolution*, can exist by itself separately or appear in some other body. But all this *foolery of atheists* has already been *refuted*. We have previously shown that *life and understanding* are *active powers*, *vital forces* <note>original: "vigours"</note>, and *perfections* that could never possibly result from mere *passive mass* <note>original: "bulk"</note> or *dead and senseless matter*, no matter how it is *modified* or *compounded*, because *nothing* can *effectively* come from *nothing*.

Nor does it follow that because *flesh* is not made out of "fleshy" components, nor *bone* out of "bony" ones, nor *red* out of red things, nor *green* out of green, that *life and understanding* may just as well be *compounded* out of things *dead and senseless*. This is because life and understanding are not *syllables* or *combinations* <note>original: "complexions"; in this context, it refers to a composite or collection of elements</note> like those physical properties. Neither the *qualities* of *heat* and *cold*, *moist* and *dry*, nor *sizes*, *shapes*, *positions*, and *motions*—no matter how they are *combined* together like *letters* spelling out words—can create life. Rather, life and mind are *simple* and *primitive things*.

Accordingly, it has been proved that there must necessarily be some *eternal, uncreated* <note>original: "unmade"</note> *life* and *mind*. For although there is no necessity for an *eternal uncreated red* or *green*—since red and green may be made out of things that are neither red nor green (these and all other so-called *physical qualities* being only various *textures of matter* or *combinations* of *size*, *shape*, *position*, and *motion* that cause those various *mental impressions* <note>original: "phancies"</note> in us)—and though there is no necessity for *eternal motion* (because if there were once no *motion* at all in *matter*, but all *bodies were at rest*, *motion* could still have been *produced* by a *self-moving* or *self-active principle*); and lastly, though there is no necessity for *eternal uncreated matter* or *bodies* either (because if there were once no *body* at all, it could still be *made* or *produced* by a *perfect, omnipotent, incorporeal being*); nevertheless, there is an *absolute necessity* that there be *eternal uncreated life* and *mind*. This is because if there were once no *life* or *mind* at all, these could never have been produced out of *matter that is altogether lifeless and mindless*.

And although the *form of a house* cannot possibly exist separately from its *matter* and *substance*—it being a *mere accidental thing* resulting from such a *structure* <note>original: "compages"; a framework or joining together of parts</note> *of stone, timber, and mortar*—nevertheless *human souls and minds* are no such *accidental forms of compounded matter*. Instead, they are *active, substantial things* that may therefore exist separately from these *bodies* and *give life* to other bodies of a different *structure*.

Even if some who are not *atheists* are too inclined to believe that *life, sensation, thought, and consciousness in animals* <note>original: "brutes"</note> are *generated* out of *dead, senseless, and unthinking matter* (being led to that view by certain *mistaken principles* and poor *philosophical methods*), this is nevertheless unquestionably a seed of *atheism*. This is because if any *life, thought, or consciousness* can be *produced* out of *dead and senseless matter*, then no *philosophy* can prevent the conclusion that all life and mind might have been produced the same way.

But the *Democritic atheists* <note>followers of Democritus, who believed the world was made only of atoms and void</note> will venture even further to deny that there is anything in nature that is *self-moving* or *self-active*, claiming instead that

# Thoughts, Not Action of Objects, Book I.
### Page 850

Whatever *moves* and *acts* was previously *moved* by something else and *made to act* by it; and that, in turn, was moved by another thing, and so on backward infinitely. From this, it would follow that there is no *first* in the order of *causes*, but only an *endless backward infinity*. But since this is the same as claiming that there is no such thing as *life* in the *world*—and that the *universe* is merely a *structure* <note>original: "compages"; a structure or framework of parts joined together</note> of *dead* and *senseless* <note>original: "stupid"; in this context, meaning lacking sensation or consciousness</note> *matter*—this idea of an *infinite chain of causes* has already been rejected as an *absolute impossibility*.

Nevertheless, the *atheists* will propose an even *greater paradox*: that all *action* of any kind—and therefore *thought* <note>original: "cogitation"</note>, *imagination* <note>original: "phancy"</note>, and *consciousness* itself—is really nothing more than *local motion* <note>physical movement from one place to another</note>. Consequently, they claim that not only *animals* but also *humans* themselves are mere *machines*. This is as much an act of *foolishness* <note>original: "sottishness"</note> or *shamelessness* as asserting that a *triangle* is a *square*, or a *sphere* is a *cube*, or that a *number* is a *shape* <note>original: "figure"</note>, or that anything is something else entirely. It is essentially the same as claiming that there is no such thing as *thought* within us, as if there were no other *action* in nature besides *physical movement* and *mechanics*.

Furthermore, the *Democritean* and *Epicurean atheists* universally agree that not only *sensations* but all the *thoughts* of the *mind* are merely the *passive experiences* <note>original: "passions"; things acted upon the thinker rather than initiated by them</note> of the thinker, caused by the *actions* of external *bodies* upon them. However, they do not all explain this in the same way. First, the *followers of Democritus* conclude that *sensation* is caused by certain *coarser physical emissions* <note>original: "grosser corporeal effluvia"</note> streaming continually from the surfaces of bodies and entering through the *nerves*. But they believe that all other *thoughts* of the *mind*—and our *imaginations*, whether sleeping or waking—proceed from another sort of *likenesses*, *images*, or *shadowy forms* <note>original: "simulachra, idols and images"</note> of a *finer* and more *subtle structure*. These enter the brain not through the open tubes or channels of the *nerves*, but directly through the smaller pores of the body. Thus, just as we never have a sensation of *anything* except by means of those *coarser physical images* forcing themselves upon the *nerves*, we also never have even the slightest *thought* in our *mind* that was not caused by those *finer physical images* and *shed skins* <note>original: "exuvious membranes"; referring to the theory that objects shed thin layers of themselves like skins</note> or *emissions* rushing upon the *brain* or the structure of the *soul*. *Leucippus and Democritus determined that both thought and sensation* <note>original: "noesis as aisthesis"</note> *are caused by certain physical "idols" coming from bodies outside; since neither sensation nor thought could otherwise possibly be produced.* <note>original Greek: "Λεύκιππος καὶ Δημόκριτος τὴν Αἴσθησιν καὶ τὴν Νόησιν Εἰδώλων ἔξωθεν προσίοντων· μηδενὶ γὰρ ἐπιβάλλειν μηδετέραν χωρὶς τοῦ προσπίπτοντος"</note> And thus Diogenes Laertius also represents the view of these *atheistic philosophers*: that the *emissions* from bodies called *idols* were the only causes *of all the motions, passions, affections, and even the very acts of will* <note>original: "volitions"</note> *of the soul.* <note>original Greek: "τῶν κατὰ ψυχὴν κινημάτων καὶ βουλημάτων ἑκάστων καὶ ἡδονῶν καὶ παθῶν"</note> So, just as we could not have the least *sensation, imagination*, or *conception* of anything except through those *physical emissions* rushing upon us from external bodies and creating those effects in us at that moment, so also we could not have

# Chapter 5: The Passion of the Thinker
### Page 851

...possess any *passion, appetite, or volition* to which we were not likewise *physically passive* <note>original: "Corporeally Passive"; the state of being acted upon by a physical body or external force</note>. This was the basis for "Democritean Fate" <note>The deterministic philosophy of Democritus, who believed all events are determined by the movement of atoms</note>, or the *necessity* of all *human actions*, maintained by them in opposition to *that which is in our power* <note>original Greek: τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν</note>, or the *liberty of the will*. This liberty cannot be understood without *self-activity* and some degree of *contingency* <note>The possibility of things happening otherwise; the opposite of absolute necessity</note>. They supposed *human volitions* <note>acts of willing or choosing</note>, as well as all other *thoughts* <note>original: "Cogitations"</note>, to be *mechanically caused* and *necessitated* by those *streaming images* <note>original: "Effluvious Images"; the ancient theory that objects shed thin layers or "films" of atoms that enter the senses</note> of bodies flowing into the minds of those who will. And although *Epicurus* sometimes pretended to *assert the liberty of the will* against *Democritus*, he nevertheless forgot himself and proceeded to *philosophize* here in the exact same way:

But there were others among the *ancient atomists* who could not believe that *sensations* themselves were *caused* by *physical emissions* <note>original: "Corporeal Effluvia"</note> or *shed layers* <note>original: "Exuvious Membranes"</note> streaming continually from bodies, for *various reasons* they provided. Instead, they believed sensations were caused only by a *pressure* from those bodies upon the *optic nerve*, resulting from a *tension* in the intervening air or ether (which is what we call *light*). By this means, a distant object is *touched* and *felt* *as if by means of a staff* <note>original Greek: οἷον διὰ βακτηρίας</note>. This *hypothesis* concerning the *physical part* of *sensation* is indeed much more *ingenious* and *reasonable* than the *former* one. 

But the *atheistic followers* of this *atomology* <note>The study of atoms and their motions</note> supposed that *sensation* was nothing more than this *pressure* from external bodies. Consequently, they concluded that *imagination* and *mental thought* <note>original: "Cogitation"</note> were merely the *relics* and *remnants* of those *sensations* previously made, which are then *preserved* in the brain—much like the *trembling vibrations* of a clock or bell after the hammer has struck, or the rolling of waves after the wind has stopped—gradually melting, fading, and decaying imperceptibly. So, according to these thinkers, *knowledge* and *understanding* are *nothing* but *fading* and *decaying sensation*, and all our *wills* <note>original: "Volitions"</note> are merely *mechanical motions* caused by the *actions* or *thrusting* <note>original: "Trusions"</note> of external bodies upon us. 

Now, while it is true that in *sensation* there is always a *prior passive state* <note>original: "Passion Antecedent"</note> produced upon the body of the *observer* <note>original: "Sentient"</note> from the outside, *sensation* itself is not this very *passive state*, but rather a *perception* of it. Much less can *mental concepts* be called the *action* of external bodies and the mere *passivity of the thinker*. Least of all can *volitions* be described this way, since there is plainly something *in our own power* <note>original Greek: ἐφ' ἡμῖν</note>—by which we become the *source* <note>original: "Principle"</note> of our *actions* and therefore deserve *praise* or *blame*—that is, something of *self-activity*.

Furthermore, according to the *Democritean* and *Epicurean atheists*, all *knowledge* and *understanding* are *really* the same thing as *sensation*. To some of them, the only difference between the *two* is that what we commonly call *sensation* is *primary* and *original knowledge*, while *knowledge* is merely *secondary*, or *fading* and *decaying sensation*. Others argue that *sensation* is *caused* by those more *vigorous images* <note>original: "Idols"; from the Greek 'eidola,' meaning the thin films of atoms supposed to radiate from objects</note>, or *emissions*—

# All Knowledge to Atheists, BOOK I.
### Page 852

...via from bodies, introduced through the nerves; but *understanding* and *knowledge* are brought in by those more *weak* and *thin*, *shadowy* and *fleeting* <note>original: "Umbratile and Evanid"</note> images that penetrate the other *smaller pores of the body*. Thus, in both ways, *understanding* and *knowledge* would be nothing but a *weaker sense*. 

Now, from this *doctrine* of the *atheistic atomists*—that all *conception* and *thought* <note>original: "Cogitation"</note> of the *mind* is *nothing else but sense and passive experience from external bodies*—this absurdity follows unavoidably: there cannot possibly be any *error* or *false judgment*. This is because it is certain that all *passive experience* <note>original: "Passion"; the state of being acted upon by an external force</note> is *true experience*, and all *sense*, *seeming*, and *appearance* are *true seeming and appearance*. Therefore, though some *sense* and *passive experience* may be more *obscure* than others, none can be *false*, as it is the very *essence of truth* itself. 

Thus *Protagoras*, one of these *atheistic atomists*, having first asserted *that knowledge is nothing else but sense*, admitted this as a *necessary consequence*: "Every opinion is true" <note>original Greek: πᾶσα δόξα ἀληθής</note>. He believed this because opinion is nothing but *seeming* and *appearance*, and every *seeming* and *appearance is truly what it is*. He argued that it is *not possible for anyone to hold an opinion of that which does not exist, or to think otherwise than he experiences*. 

*Epicurus*, being sensible of this inconvenience, endeavored to resolve this *phenomenon* of *error* and *false opinion* or *judgment* consistently with his own *principles*. He argued that although all knowledge is *sense* and all *sense is true*, *error* may nonetheless arise "from the mind's own opinion" <note>original Latin: *Ex Animi Opinatu*</note>, *by adding something of its own, over and above, to the passive experience and mental image of sense*. 

But in this, he shamefully contradicts himself. For if the mind, in *judging* and *forming an opinion*, can add anything of its own *over and above* what it *passively experiences*, then it is not a merely *passive thing*. It must have a *self-active power* of its own, and consequently will prove to be *incorporeal* <note>spiritual or non-physical</note>, because no *body* can *act* in any way other than how it *passively receives* action, or is made to *act* by something else outside of it. We conclude, therefore, that since there is such a thing as *error* or *false judgment*, all *thoughts* of the mind cannot be mere *passions*; rather, there must be something of *self-activity* in the soul itself. By means of this activity, the soul can give its *assent* to things not clearly *perceived*, and thus *err*.

Again, from this *atheistic opinion*—that all *knowledge* is *nothing else but sense*, whether *primary* or *secondary*—it also follows that there is no *absolute truth* or *falsehood*. It implies that *knowledge* is of a *private nature*, *relative*, and *imaginary* <note>original: "Phantastical"</note> only, or mere *seeming*; that is, *nothing but opinion*. This is because *sense* is plainly *seeming*, *fancy*, and *appearance*—a *private thing* that is *relative only to the one perceiving it*. 

Here also, *Protagoras*, according to his usual freedom, admitted this consequence: that since *knowledge* is *sense*, there was no *absoluteness* in it at all. He claimed *that nothing was true otherwise* than "to this or that man who thinks it so" <note>original Greek: τούτῳ καὶ τινὶ</note>; that every man did "opine only his own things" <note>original Greek: τὰ ἑαυτοῦ μόνον δοξάζειν</note>; that "man is the measure of all things" <note>original Greek: πάντων χρημάτων μέτρον ἄνθρωπος</note> and is the truth to himself; and lastly, "that whatsoever seemed to every one, was true to him to whom it seemed" <note>original Greek: τὸ φαινόμενον ἑκάστῳ τούτῳ καὶ εἶναι ᾧ φαίνεται</note>. Neither could *Democritus* himself, though a man of more discretion than *Protagoras*, hide this consequence

# Chapter V: Phantastical and Relative Knowledge

From the same principle asserted by him—that *understanding* is *phantastical* <note>original: "Phantastical"; meaning here that it is based on subjective "phantasms" or mental images rather than objective reality</note> and *knowledge* is nothing but *opinion*—Democritus occasionally admitted this before he was even aware of it. For example, he wrote: "A person ought to know by this rule: that he is removed from reality" <note>original Greek: γινώσκειν χρὴ ἄνθρωπον τῷδε τῷ κανόνι, ὅτι αἰτίης ἀπήλλακται</note>. This means we should understand that man is the kind of creature who has nothing to do with absolute truth. Again, he says: "In reality, we know nothing about anything, but for each person, knowledge is merely an influx of opinions" <note>original Greek: αἰτίη (or ἐτεῇ) οὐδὲν ἴδμεν περὶ οὐδενὸς, ἀλλ’ ἐπιρυσμίη ἑκάστοισιν ἡ δόξις</note>. This suggests we know nothing absolutely about any subject, and all our knowledge is merely opinion. Consistent with this, he determined that human knowledge was varied according to the physical temperament of people's bodies and the external things acting upon them. 

*Aristotle*, judiciously observing both these doctrines—first, that there is no error or false judgment because every opinion is true to the person holding it; and second, that nothing is absolutely true but only relatively true—realized they are fundamentally one and the same. He attributed both together to *Democritus* in these words: "Democritus held that there was nothing absolutely true; but because he thought knowledge or understanding was merely sense-perception, he therefore concluded that whatever seemed to be true according to the senses must necessarily be true (not absolutely, but relatively) to the person to whom it so seemed" <note>original Greek: οὐδὲν εἶναι ἀληθές· ὅλως ἢ διὰ τὸ ὑπολαμβάνειν φρόνησιν μὲν τὴν αἴσθησιν, τὸ φαινόμενον κατὰ τὴν αἴσθησιν ἐξ ἀνάγκης ἀληθὲς εἶναι</note>. 

The *atheistic atomists* plunged themselves into these gross absurdities while they endeavored to explain the *phenomenon* of *thought* <note>original: "Cogitation"</note>, *mind*, or *understanding* in a way that agreed with their own *hypothesis*. It is certain that all of them, including *Democritus* himself, were merely blunderers in that *atomic physiology* <note>original: "Atomick Phyſiology"; here referring to the physical study of atoms and matter</note> which they claimed to champion, for they never truly understood it. For that same science teaches two things clearly at once: first, that sense-perception is indeed *phantastical* and *relative* to the person sensing; but second, that there is a higher faculty of *understanding* and *reason* in us. This higher faculty discovers the subjective nature of the senses and reaches toward the *absoluteness* of *truth*, serving as the standard or *criterion* for it.

But the *Democritic* and *Epicurean atheists* will further conclude that the only *things* or *objects* of the *mind* are *singular sensibles* <term>sensibles: objects perceived by the senses</term>, or *bodies existing* outside the mind. Therefore, in the order of nature, these bodies must exist before all *knowledge*, *mind*, and *understanding*, since the mind is nothing but a *phantastical image* or *representation* of them. From this, they infer that the *corporeal world* and these *sensible things* could not possibly be made by any *mind* or *understanding*, because the mind is *essentially junior* to them—it is the very *image* and *creature* of matter. 

Thus, *Aristotle* observes regarding both *Democritus* and *Protagoras* that they "supposed the only things or objects of the mind to be sensibles" <note>original Greek: ὑπολαμβάνειν τὰ ὄντα μόνον εἶναι τὰ αἰσθητὰ</note>. He notes that this was the reason they made knowledge identical to sense, and therefore relative and phantastical. But we have already proved that *mind* and *understanding* are not the phantastical images of *sensibles* or *bodies*. In its own nature, the mind is not *ectypal* <term>ectypal: a copy or reproduction of an original</term>, but *archetypal* <term>archetypal: the original pattern or model</term> and *architectonical* <term>architectonical: the master design or governing principle</term> over everything. The mind is senior to the *world* and all *sensible things*. It does not look abroad for its objects anywhere outside of itself but contains them within itself. The first *original mind* is an absolutely perfect being, comprehending itself and the extent of its...

However, since it is obvious that there are objects of the *Universal Mind* besides *individual things* <note>original: "Singulars"</note>—from which it seems to follow that *sensible objects* <note>original: "Sensibles"</note> are not the only things—certain *modern atheistic thinkers* <note>Cudworth is likely referring to Thomas Hobbes and his philosophy of Nominalism</note> have invented this further device to support their cause: they claim that *universals* are nothing more than *names* or *words* used to label *individual bodies*. Consequently, they argue that in all axioms and propositions, or formal *affirmations* and negations (in which the predicate at least is *universal*), we are doing nothing more than adding or subtracting, affirming or denying, the *names of individual bodies*. They claim that *reason or logic* <note>original: "Syllogism"</note> is nothing but the *reckoning or computing* of the consequences of these *names* or *words*. They even have the *audacity* <note>original: "Impudence"</note> to claim that we know nothing at all besides those *feelings* <note>original: "Passions"</note> or *fantasies* we receive from things through the senses, except for the *names* by which things are called. 

There could not be a greater *stupidity* or *madness* than this. For if geometry were nothing but the knowledge of *names* for individual bodies, it would not deserve to be called a science. Furthermore, its truths would not be the same in *Greek* and in *Latin*. We would have to assume that geometricians, in all the different ages and places of the world, had the exact same individual bodies before them when they affirmed or denied those *universal names*.

Finally, the *Epicurean* and *Anaximandrian atheists*—consistent with their earlier principles and the nature of their *hypothesis*—both attempt to depreciate and undervalue *knowledge or understanding*. They treat it as something that has no higher degree of *perfection* or *being* <note>original: "Entity"</note> than what is found in *dead and senseless matter*. According to them, knowledge is merely a *reaction* <note>original: "Passion"</note> caused by individual bodies existing outside of us; therefore, it is both *younger* <note>original: "Junior"; meaning it appeared later in time</note> and inferior to those bodies. They see it as a tumult raised in the brain by motions acting upon it from the objects of sense. It is something that essentially depends on something else—at best, only a thin and *fading* <note>original: "Evanid"</note> image of sensible things, or rather an *image of those images of sense*; a mere *whistling and imaginary thing*. 

Because of this, they conclude that knowledge is not fit to be attributed to the *first root and source* of all things. To them, that source is nothing other than *heavy and solid, senseless matter*—the only *substantial, self-existent, independent* thing, and consequently the most *perfect and divine*. To them, life and *understanding*, *soul and mind* are not *simple and original natures* <note>original: "Primitive Natures"</note>. Instead, they are *secondary and derivative*—mere *syllables and combinations* <note>original: "Complexions"</note> of things that emerged later from certain *combinations of size, shape, position, and motion*, or *blends of qualities* <note>original: "Contemperations of Qualities"</note>; structures made of either *similar or dissimilar atoms*. And just as these thinkers consider themselves *younger* than *senseless matter and motion*—and younger than those *inanimate elements* of fire, water, air, and earth, which they see as the *first* and most *real productions of nature and chance*—so too are the *effects* and things belonging to the mind. <margin>Plato, *The Laws*, Book 10, Page 889.</margin>

*They say that the greatest and most excellent things of all were made by senseless nature and chance, but all the smaller and more inconsiderable things were made by art, mind, and understanding. They claim that art, taking those first and greater things from nature as its groundwork to act upon, frames and fabricates all the other lesser things, which are therefore commonly called "artificial."* <note>original Greek: φασὶ τὰ μὲν μέγιστα καὶ κάλλιστα ἀπεργάζεσθαι φύσιν καὶ τύχην, τὰ δὲ σμικρότερα τέχνην· ἣν δὴ παρὰ φύσεως λαμβάνουσαν, τὴν τῶν μεγάλων καὶ πρώτων γένεσιν ἔργων, πλάττειν καὶ τεκταίνεσθαι πάντα τὰ σμικρότερα, ἃ δὴ τεχνικὰ προσαγορεύομεν</note> 

The mind of these atheists is further declared by that philosopher in this manner: *The first, most real, solid, and substantial things in the whole world are those elements—fire, water, air, and earth—made by senseless nature and chance, without any art, mind, or understanding. Next to these are the bodies of the sun, moon, and stars, and this terrestrial globe, produced out of the aforementioned inanimate elements by unthinking nature or chance likewise, without any art, mind, or God. They believe the accidental meeting of similar or dissimilar atoms produced this whole system and structure* <term>original: "Compages" (a complex structure or framework of joined parts)</term> *of heaven and earth.* 

*But they argue that afterwards, art—or mind and understanding—was generated last out of those same senseless and inanimate bodies or elements. They believe it rose up only in certain smaller pieces of the universe and particular clusters of matter called animals. Being mortal things produced from mortal things, they produced certain other playful things which partake little of truth and reality, but are mere images, shadows, and imitations, such as pictures and landscapes, and so on.* <note>original Greek: τέχνην δὲ ὕστερον ἐκ τούτων ὑστέραν γενομένην, αὐτὴν θνητὴν ἐκ θνητῶν, ὕστερα γεγεννηκέναι παιδιὰς τινὰς ἀληθείας οὐ σφόδρα μετεχούσας, ἀλλ' εἴδωλ' ἄττα ξυγγενῆ ἑαυτῶν, οἷον ἡ γραφική, καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς</note> 

*But above all, they claim those moral differences of "just" and "unjust," "honest" and "dishonest," are the mere inventions of political art and slight, shadowy* <term>original: "Umbratil" (shadowy, unreal, or existing in the shade)</term> *things, compared with natural "good" and "evil," which consist in nothing but agreement or disagreement with one's senses and appetite.* 

*For, as for things good and honest, those that are such by nature differ from those which are such by law; but as for just and unjust, there is by nature no such thing at all.* <note>original Greek: τὰ γὰρ καλὰ φύσει μὲν ἄλλα νόμῳ δὲ ἕτερα, τὰ δὲ δίκαια οὐδὲ τὸ παράπαν φύσει</note> 

The result and conclusion of all this is that there is no such "scale" or "ladder" in nature as theists and metaphysicians suppose—no degrees of real perfection and existence <note>original: "Entity"</note> stacked one above another, such as life and sense being above inanimate matter, or reason and understanding being above sense. From such a ladder, it would be inferred that the order of things in nature moved downward, from higher and greater perfection to lesser and lower, which is indeed to introduce a God. 

The atheists further endeavor to prove that there is no such scale of perfection and existence because, according to that hypothesis, it would follow that even the smallest and most contemptible animal that could see the sun had a higher degree of existence and perfection...

# A Scale of Entity Asserted; BOOK I.

[...contains more perfection] in it than the sun itself; a thing ridiculously absurd. Or else, according to the instance given by Cotta: *Therefore, an ant should be preferred over this most beautiful city <note>The city of Rome.</note>, because in the city there is no sensation, while in the ant there is not only sense, but also mind, reason, and memory.* <note>original Latin: "Idcirco Formicam anteponendam esse huic Pulcherrimæ Urbi, quòd in Urbe sensus sit nullus, in Formica non modo Sensus, sed etiam Mens, Ratio, Memoria." This is a reference to Cotta, a character in Cicero’s "On the Nature of the Gods."</note> This suggests that every ant or pismire would be far superior to the most beautiful city of Rome. This is because in the city, there is no sense; whereas an ant has not only sense, but also a mind, reason, and memory—that is, a certain sagacity superior to mere sense. 

Therefore, these atheists conclude that there is no such "Scale" or "Ladder" in nature, no such climbing stairs of being and perfection where one thing is ranked above another. Instead, they believe the whole universe is one flat level. In their view, everything is actually nothing but the same uniform matter appearing under several forms, dresses, and disguises, or varied by a diversity of accidental modifications. One of these modifications is found in beings that have "fancy" <note>original: "Phancy," meaning the power of imagination or mental representation.</note> in them, commonly called **animals**. To the atheist, these are merely some of nature’s playful or whimsical creations—more neatly artificial and finer "curiosities" <note>original: "Gamaieus," likely referring to "gamahes," which were naturally figured stones or charms; here used to mean "pretty toys."</note> or **pretty toys**. But because of this fancy, they have no higher degree of **entity** <note>Essential being or existence.</note> and **perfection** in them than what is found in senseless matter. Just as they were formed, they will all also be quickly transformed again into other seemingly dull, unthinking, and inanimate shapes. This is the perspective of the atheists.

<margin>Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, Book 5, Prose 4.</margin>
But the pretended grounds of this atheistic doctrine (or rather, madness) have already been refuted over and over again. Knowledge and understanding are not a mere **passion** <note>In philosophy, "passion" refers to the state of being acted upon by an external force, rather than the modern meaning of strong emotion.</note> received from the thing being known which exists outside of the **knower**. This is because to **know** and **understand**, as Anaxagoras <note>An ancient Greek philosopher (c. 500–428 BC) who argued that Mind (Nous) was the primary cause of the universe.</note> determined long ago, is "to master" <note>original Greek: κρατεῖν</note>—to master and conquer the thing known. Consequently, it is not merely to suffer from it, or passively to lie under it, for that would be "to be mastered" <note>original Greek: κρατεῖσθαι</note> and conquered by it. 

The knowledge of **universal theorems in the sciences** does not come from the force of the thing known existing outside the **knower**, but from the **active power** and exerted vigor or strength of that which knows. As Severinus Boethius wrote: *Do you see how, in the act of knowing, all things use their own power and faculty rather than that of the things being known? And this is not without reason; for since every judgment is the action of the one who judges, it is necessary that everyone performs their own task by their own power, strength, and faculty, and not by the power of another.* <note>original Latin: "Videsne ut in cognoscendo, cuncta Suâ potius Facultate, quàm Eorum quæ Cognoscuntur Utantur ? Neque id injuriâ, nam cum omne Judicium Judicantis Actus existat, necesse est ut suam quisque Operam, non ex Alienâ, sed ex propriâ Potestate perficiat."</note> 

Sense itself is not a mere "passion" or the reception of motion from bodies outside the **sensing being**. If it were, then a looking-glass and other dead things would be able to see. Rather, sense is a **perception** of a "passion" made upon the **body** of the sensing being; therefore, it has something of the soul's own self-activity in it. However, **understanding** and the **knowledge** of **abstract sciences** is neither primary sense, nor the fading and decaying remains of sensory motions. It is a perception of another kind, and more **inward** than that of sense. It is not **sympathetic** but **unpassionate**. The <term>Noemata</term> <note>Intellectual concepts or thoughts of the mind.</note> of the mind are things distinct from the <term>Phantasmata</term> <note>Mental images or sensory "pictures" produced by the imagination.</note> of sense and imagination, which are merely a kind of **confused cogitations**. And though the objects of sense are only singular bodies existing outside the sensing being, yet...

# CHAPTER V. and the Descent of Things.

Therefore, these **sensible things** <note>original: "Sensibles," meaning objects perceived through the five senses.</note> are not the only things that exist or can be thought of. There are other objects of knowledge, or **intelligibles** <note>original: "Intelligibles," meaning things that can only be understood by the intellect, such as mathematical truths or moral concepts.</note>, which the mind contains within itself. That "dark philosophy" held by some—which tends directly toward atheism—claims that there is nothing in the mind or understanding that was not first in the physical senses and derived from the impact of matter. This view was both elegantly and solidly refuted by the philosophical Muse of Boethius in this manner:

<margin>Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, Book 5, Poem 4.</margin>

> Once the "Porch" <note>original: "Porticus." This refers to the Stoic philosophers, who met in the *Stoa Poikile* or "Painted Porch" in Athens.</note> brought forth 
> Obscure old men, 
> Who believe that sensations and images 
> Are imprinted on the mind from external bodies; 
> As it is the custom to fix 
> Pressed letters upon the surface of a page 
> Which has no marks of its own. 
> But if the mind, thriving with its own powers, 
> Explains nothing by its own motions, 
> But merely lies passive, 
> Subject to the marks of bodies, 
> And like a mirror reflects 
> Empty images of things: 
> From where does this strength thrive in our minds, 
> Which sees individual things? 
> What power looks forth on everything? 
> Or what power divides the things it knows? 
> And choosing an alternating path, 
> Now it reaches into the highest things, 
> Then returning to itself, 
> It refutes false things with the truth? 
> This is a cause far more powerful, 
> And more efficient, than that which 
> Merely suffers marks to be impressed 
> In the manner of matter. 
> Yet a sensation in the living body 
> Precedes this, exciting 
> And moving the powers of the soul, 
> When either light strikes the eyes, 
> Or a voice sounds in the ears: 
> Then the excited vigor of the mind, 
> Calling upon similar motions within, 
> Applies the forms it holds inside 
> To the external marks it receives.
<note>This poem is a translation of the Latin text provided in the original document. Boethius argues against the "blank slate" theory of the mind, suggesting the mind is active, not just a passive receiver of sensory data.</note>

It is true indeed that the **intelligible** <note>original Greek: Νοητὸν (*Noeton*), meaning the "thing understood."</note> exists in the order of nature before the intellection and conception of it. Because of this, the Pythagoreans and Platonists concluded that **Mind** or **Intellect** <note>original Greek: Νᾶς (*Nous*).</note> was not the very first and highest thing in the hierarchy of the universe. Instead, they believed there was another "Divine Hypostasis" <note>A "hypostasis" is a fundamental reality or underlying substance; here it refers to the levels of the Divine.</note> that existed before it in the order of nature. They called this **The One** and **The Good** <note>original Greek: Ἕν (*Hen*) and Τ' ἀγαθὸν (*To Agathon*).</note>, acting as the "intelligible" source for the Mind. 

However, those three primary substances of the Platonists and Pythagoreans are all really just one **Divinity** <note>original Greek: Θείον (*Theion*).</note>. Furthermore, the first of those three (which is superior to what they properly call "Mind" or "Intellect") is not supposed to be ignorant of itself. Thus, the First Mind or Understanding is nothing other than that of a perfect Being—infinitely good, productive, and powerful—who virtually contains all things. This Being comprehends itself and the extent of its own goodness, virtue, and power; that is, it understands all possibilities of things, their relations to one another, and their truths. This is a Mind that existed before the senses and before sensible things. An omnipotent, understanding Being, which is its own object of thought, is the first original of all things. 

Again, it is necessary that some other substance must exist besides body or matter, and this substance is superior to matter in the scale of nature. This is evident because, otherwise, there could be no motion at all in the universe, since no body is ever able to move itself. There must be something **self-active** and **hylarchical** <term>hylarchical</term> <note>From the Greek *hyle* (matter) and *arche* (rule). It refers to a principle that governs or rules over matter.</note>—something that can act both...

# Mind Oldest; and Lord over all. BOOK I.

---

...from itself, and upon matter, as having a *natural sovereignty* <note>original: "Natural Imperium"</note>, or command over it. *Thought* <note>original: "Cogitation"</note> is, by its very nature, prior to *physical movement* <note>original: "Local Motion"</note>. *Life* and *understanding*, *soul* and *mind*, are not mere "syllables" or "combinations" <note>original: "Complexions," referring to something composed of simpler parts</note> of things—secondary and derived—which might therefore be produced from things devoid of life and understanding. Instead, they are *simple, primitive, and uncompounded natures*. They are not "qualities" or "accidental modifications" of matter, but *substantial things*. 

For this reason, *souls* or *minds* can no more be generated out of *matter* than *matter* itself can be generated out of something else. Therefore, they are both alike (in some sense) fundamental principles, *naturally un-creatable and indestructible*; though both *matter* and *all imperfect souls and minds* were at first created by one *Perfect, Omnipotent, Understanding Being*. 

Moreover, nothing can be more evident than this: that *mind* and *understanding* possess a higher degree of *existence* <note>original: "Entity"</note> or perfection, and are a *greater reality* in nature, than mere *senseless matter* or *physical bulk* <note>original: "Bulkie Extension"</note>. Consequently, the things which belong to *souls* and *minds*—to *rational* and *intellectual beings* as such—must not have less reality, but *more reality* in them than the things which belong to *lifeless bodies*. 

Therefore, the differences between *just* and *unjust*, *honest* and *dishonest*, are greater realities in nature than the differences between *hard* and *soft*, *hot* and *cold*, or *moist* and *dry*. He who does not perceive any higher degree of perfection in a *man* than in an *oyster*—or even in a *clod of earth*, a *lump of ice*, a *piece of paste*, or a *pie crust*—does not have the *reason* or *understanding* of a man within him. 

There is unquestionably a *scale* or *ladder of nature*, with degrees of *perfection* and *existence* stacked one above another: such as *life*, *sense*, and *thought* being above *dead, senseless, and unthinking matter*; and *reason* and *understanding* being above *sense*, and so on. And if the *Sun* is nothing but a *mass of fire*, or *lifeless, subtle matter in motion* <note>original: "Agitated"</note>, then the most insignificant animal that can see the Sun—and possesses *consciousness* and *self-awareness* <note>original: "self-enjoyment," meaning the internal experience of one's own existence</note>—has a higher degree of *existence* and *perfection* within it than that entire fiery globe. It also has more perfection than the materials—*stone, timber, brick, and mortar*—of the most grand building or city. 

Notwithstanding this, the Sun, in other regards—as its vastly extended light and heat have so great an influence upon the good of the whole world, plants, and animals—may be said to be a far more noble and *useful* thing in the universe than any one particular animal whatsoever. 

Therefore, since there is plainly a *scale* or *ladder of existence*, the *order of things* was unquestionably a *descent* from higher perfection downward to lower. It is as impossible for a *greater perfection* to be produced from a *lesser* one as it is for *something to be caused by nothing*. Neither are the *steps* or *degrees* of this ladder (either upward or downward) *infinite*. Just as the *foot, bottom, or lowest rung* of it is *stupid and senseless matter*, devoid of all *life* and *understanding*, so is the *head, top, and summit* of it a *Perfect, Omnipotent Being*, who understands Himself and all the possibilities of things. 

A *Perfect, Understanding Being* is the *beginning* and *head* of the scale of existence, from which things *gradually descend* downward, lower and lower, until they end in *senseless matter*. "Mind is the oldest of all things" <note>original Greek: "Νῦς πάντων προγενέστατος" (*Nous pantōn progenestatos*)</note>, existing before the el-

# Mind Oldest; and Lord over all. BOOK I.

...elements, and the whole physical <note>original: "Corporeal"</note> world. Likewise, according to the same ancient theists, the soul is *lord by nature* <note>original: <term>κύριος κατὰ φύσιν</term></note>; it has a natural command <note>original: "Imperium"</note> and dominion over all things, being the most dominant <note>original: "Hegemonical"</note> principle. This was also affirmed by Anaxagoras: "*Mind is the sovereign king of heaven and earth*" <note>original: <term>Νοῦς βασιλεὺς οὐρανοῦ τε καὶ γῆς</term></note>.

We have now demonstrated that the Epicurean and Anaximandrian atheists—who trace the origin of all things to *senseless matter* that lacks any kind of *life*—cannot explain the *phenomenon* of *thought* <note>original: "Cogitation"</note> (*life*, *understanding*, *soul*, and *mind*) any better than they can explain *physical motion* <note>original: "Local Motion"</note>. The reason we have focused so much on this point is because these atheists do not only pretend to explain the *phenomenon* of *thought* without a *God* (thereby dismissing the argument for a *Deity*); they also try to *demonstrate* that God's existence is *impossible* based on the very nature of *knowledge*, *mind*, and *understanding*. For if *knowledge* is, by its own nature, nothing but a *passive reaction* <note>original: "Passion"</note> triggered by *individual bodies* existing outside of the *knower*; and if *life*, *understanding*, *soul*, and *mind* are *secondary* <note>original: "Junior"</note> to the body and generated out of *senseless matter*, then no *mind* or *understanding being* could possibly be a *God*—that is, a *First Principle* and the *Maker* of all things. 

And though modern writers take little or no notice of this, Plato anciently established that the very core of the *controversy* between theists and atheists consists in this very thing: namely, whether *life*, *understanding*, *soul*, and *mind* were *secondary* <note>original: "Juniors"</note> to the *body* and sprouted out of *senseless matter* as *accidental modifications* of it; or else were *substantial* things and, in the order of *nature, existed before it*. For after the passages cited before, he concludes: <margin>Plato, Laws, Book 10</margin> "*These men seem to suppose that fire, water, air, and earth are the very first things in the universe and the principles of all, calling them only* Nature; *but they believe the soul and mind sprang up afterwards out of them. Indeed, they do not only seem to suppose this, but they declare it in express words. And thus (by Jupiter) have we discovered the very fountain of that atheistic madness of the ancient natural philosophers <note>original: "Physiologers"</note>; namely, their claim that inanimate bodies are older than <note>original: "senior to"</note> the soul and mind.*" <note>original Greek: <term>κινδυνεύει ὁ λέγων ταῦτα... ζητημάτων·</term></note> 

Accordingly, that philosopher addresses the refutation of *atheism* solely by proving that the *soul* is not *secondary* <note>original: "Junior"</note> to the *senseless body* or *inanimate matter*, nor generated out of it: "*That which is the first cause of the generation and corruption of all things, the atheistic doctrine claims is not first, but came later; while that which came later, they claim is first. Because of this, they have erred concerning the true nature of the gods... they are ignorant of the nature and power of the soul—that it is among the first of things, existing before all bodies, and is the beginning of all change.*" <note>original Greek: <term>ὃ πρῶτον γενέσεως... ἀρχή·</term></note> The atheistic doctrine supposes that the first cause is not—
