# The Generation of Souls, from BOOK I.

...first made; but they take what is indeed the *last* thing to be the *first*. And this is why they err concerning the *essence of the gods*. For they are ignorant of *what kind of thing the soul is* and *what power it has*, especially concerning its *generation and production*. They do not realize that it was *first of all* made before the body, being that which *governs the motions, changes, and transformations of the body*. But if the *soul is first* in the order of nature before the body, then those things which are *related to the soul* must also exist before the *things which belong to the body*. Thus, *mind and understanding, art and law* must exist before *hard and soft, heavy and light*. Furthermore, that which these *atheists* call *nature* (the *motion of lifeless bodies*) is secondary <note>original: "Junior"</note> to *art and mind*, being *governed by them*.

Now, this *philosopher* <note>Referring to Plato</note> demonstrates that the *soul* is, by the order of *nature, before the body* using only the topic of *motion*. He argues it is *impossible* for one body to *move* another *infinitely* without any *first cause or mover*. There must necessarily be something *self-moving* and *self-active*—something with the power of *changing itself*—that was the first cause of all *physical motion* <note>original: "Local Motion"</note> in bodies. And since the very definition of the *soul* is that it is a thing which can *move or change itself* (which is also what the *essence of life* consists of), he concludes: "It has therefore been sufficiently demonstrated that the soul is the oldest of all things in the physical world, being the principle of all motion and generation within it." <note>original: ἱκανώτατα δέδειχται ψυχὴ τῶν πάντων πρεσβυτάτη γενομένη τε ἀρχὴ κινήσεως</note>

His conclusion is: "We have therefore rightly affirmed that the soul existed before our bodies, and the body is secondary and comes after the soul; the soul being that which rules, and the body being that which is ruled according to nature." <note>original: ὀρθῶς ἄρα εἰρηκότες ἂν ἦμεν ψυχὴν μὲν προτέραν γεγονέναι σωμάτων ἡμῶν, σῶμα δὲ δεύτερόν, τε καὶ ὕστερον, ψυχῆς ἀρχούσης, ἀρχόμενον κατὰ φύσιν</note> From this it follows that the *things of the soul* are also *older than the things of the body*. Therefore, *thinking, understanding, willing, and desiring* <note>original: "Cogitation, Intellection, Volition, and Appetite"</note> are, in the order of nature, prior to *length, breadth, and depth*.

It is evident that *Plato*, in all of this, meant not only the *Mundane Soul* <note>The "Soul of the World," a concept in Platonism where the universe itself has a guiding soul</note>, or his *Third Divine Hypostasis* <note>The third level of reality in the Platonic trinity (Good, Mind, and Soul)</note>—which is the source of motion in the heavens and the whole physical universe—but also all other *particular lives and souls* whatsoever. He refers to that whole *rank of beings* called "Soul." He supposed all of it to have been made first, before the *physical system*, or at least to have been *senior* to it in the order of nature as its superior (since that which rules is superior to that which is ruled). He believed no *soul or life* whatsoever could be generated out of *senseless matter*.

Therefore, we must condemn the doctrine of certain self-proclaimed theists and Christians of recent times who claim all souls—not only the *sensitive* souls of animals but also the *rational* souls of men—are generated out of *matter*. By doing so, they not only destroy the *argument for the existence of God* based on the existence of *souls* (since nothing could then prevent *senseless matter* from being the *origin of all things* if *life, understanding, soul, and mind* could spring from it), but they also give the *atheist* an advantage. The atheist could then prove the *impossibility of God* from this premise: for if *life and understanding* are, by their own nature, *factitious* <note>term: factitious | meaning: produced artificially or generated from something else</note> and able to be generated out of *matter*, then...

# Chapter V. Matter: *A Seed of Atheism.*

...are they not *substantial things*, but *accidental* <note>original: "Accidental" — here meaning a secondary property or byproduct that does not exist on its own</note> only. From this, it will plainly follow that no mind could possibly be a *God*, or *first cause* of all things, because it would not even be able to exist by *itself*. Moreover, if the mind as such is *generable* (capable of being created) and *derived from nothing*, then it must also necessarily be in its own nature *corruptible* (capable of being destroyed) and *reducible to nothing* again; whereas the Deity is a being that is both *unmade* and *incorruptible*. So, according to this *hypothesis*, there could not possibly be any other God than a *Jupiter*, or a *soul of the world*, such as the *atheistic theogonists* <note>theogonists: those who wrote myths about the birth and genealogy of the gods</note> acknowledged, who sprang out of *night*, *chaos*, and *non-existence*, and may be swallowed up again into that *dark abyss*. *Senseless matter*, therefore, being the only *unmade and incorruptible thing* and the fountain of all things—even of *life and understanding*—it must necessarily be acknowledged as the *only real deity* <note>original: "Numen" — a Latin term for divine power or divinity</note>.

Neither will the case be much different for certain others who, though they do not openly claim to *generate* the *rational soul*, but only the *sensitive soul* <note>The "sensitive soul" refers to basic animal instincts and sensory perception, as opposed to "rational" human thought</note> in both men and animals; yet they nevertheless maintain that the *human soul* itself is but a mere *blank* or *white sheet of paper*. They claim it has nothing at all in it except what was *written* upon it by the *objects of sense*, and that knowledge or *understanding* is nothing but the *result of sensory perception* and a *passive reaction* <note>original: "Passion"</note> from *physical bodies* existing outside the *knower*. For by this, they plainly make *knowledge and understanding* to be, in its own nature, *secondary to sense* <note>original: "Junior to Sense"</note> and the very *creation of physical objects*. So do they also imply that the *rational soul and mind* itself is as much *generated* as the *sensitive soul* in which it is *virtually contained*. In this view, the mind is nothing but a *higher modification of matter*, agreeing with that *Leviathan-doctrine* <note>A reference to the philosophy of Thomas Hobbes in his book "Leviathan," which argued that all human thought is a result of physical motion</note> that men differ in no other way from *brute animals* than in their *physical organization* and the *use of speech* or *words*.

In very truth, whoever maintains that any *life or soul*, any *thought or consciousness*, *self-perception, and self-activity* can spring out of *dead, senseless, and inactive matter*, can never possibly have any *rational assurance* that his own *soul* did not have a similar *origin*, and is consequently *mortal and corruptible*. For if any *life and thought* can be *generated* this way, then there is no *reason* why all *lives* should not be so; they are merely *higher degrees* of the same *kind*. Neither *life* nor anything else can be *indifferent* in its own nature—it cannot be a *substance* one moment and an *accident* (a byproduct) the next. Either all *life, thought, and consciousness* is *accidental, generable, and corruptible*, or none of it is.

That which has inclined so many to think that the *sensitive life*, at least, is nothing but a *quality or accident of matter*—capable of being *generated* out of it and *decaying* back into it—is that strange, *ever-changing transformation of matter* <note>original: "Protean Transformation"</note> into so many seemingly *unaccountable forms and shapes*. This, combined with the *Scholastic opinion* <note>Referring to the formal philosophy taught in medieval universities</note> of *real qualities*—that is, *entities distinct* from the *substance of the body* and its *modifications*, yet still *generated* out of it and *corruptible* into its...

<summary>This page argues that if consciousness and life are merely byproducts of matter, then the soul must be mortal and a self-existent God cannot exist. It specifically critiques the materialist view (like that of Thomas Hobbes) that treats the human mind as a blank slate shaped entirely by sensory input.</summary>

# The Grand Object against the BOOK I.

They concluded that just as *light* and *colors*, *heat* and *cold*, etc.—according to those *notions* <note>original: "Phancies" — the subjective mental images or perceptions we have of physical properties</note> we have of them—are *real qualities* of matter, distinct from its *substance* and *modifications*, so might *life*, *sense*, and *thought* likewise be *qualities* of matter that can be *generated* and *destroyed*. 

But these *real qualities* of the body, in the sense described, were long ago rightly exploded by the ancient Atomists and removed from the catalogue of existing things. *Laertius* recorded that they did "banish all qualities" <note>original Greek: ἐκβάλειν τὰς ποιότητας (ekbalein tas poiotētas) — to cast out or reject qualities</note>, completely dismissing and removing *qualities* from their *philosophy*. They explained all *physical phenomena*—and therefore things like *heat* and *cold*, *light* and *colors*, *fire* and *flame*, etc.—intelligibly as nothing more than the different *modifications* of *extended substance*. These include the greater or lesser *size* of *parts*, *shape*, *position*, *motion*, or *rest* (or combinations of these), and the various *notions* caused in us by them. Indeed, there is no other *entity* except *substance* and its *modifications*. Therefore, the *Democritians* <note>Followers of Democritus, an ancient Greek philosopher who proposed an atomic theory of the universe</note> and *Epicureans* shamefully contradicted themselves: while pretending to reject and dismiss all those entities called *real qualities*, they nonetheless made *life* and *understanding* into *real qualities* of matter—things that could be *generated* out of it and *destroyed* back into it.

There is nothing in a body or in matter but size, shape, position, and motion or rest. Now, it is mathematically certain that these things, however they are combined, can never possibly form or create *life* or *thought*. Therefore, life and thought cannot be an *accident of matter* <note>accident: a non-essential property or characteristic that depends on a substance for its existence</note>, but must necessarily be a *substantial thing*. 

We are not speaking here of that *life* (improperly so-called) which is commonly attributed to the bodies of humans and animals; for it is clearly *accidental* whether a body is *vitally united* to a *soul* or not. Therefore, this *life* of the *compound* <note>compound: the living being formed by the union of soul and body</note> is *corruptible* and *destructible* without the *destruction* of any *real entity*. Nothing is *destroyed* or *lost* to the *universe* in the *deaths* of humans and animals as such; there is only a *disunion* or *separation* of those two substances—the *soul* and the *body*—from one another. 

But we are speaking here of the *original life* of the *soul* itself: that this is *substantial*, neither *generated* nor *destroyed*, but only *creatable* and *annihilable* by the *Deity*. It is strange that anyone should persuade themselves that something which *rules* and *commands* animal bodies, moving them around, and which possesses sense or perception, should not be just as substantial as that *stupid* and *senseless matter* that is *ruled* by it. Furthermore, *matter* (which is merely a *passive thing*) can no more *efficiently* produce a *soul* than a *soul* can produce *matter*. No *finite, imperfect substance* is able to produce another substance out of *nothing*. Much less can a substance that has a *lower degree* of entity and *perfection* *create* that which has a *higher* degree. 

There is a *scale* or *ladder of entities* and *perfections* in the *universe*, one above another. The production of things cannot possibly occur in an *ascent* from *lower* to *higher*; it must, by necessity, be a *descent* from *higher* to *lower*. Now, to produce any one *higher rank* of being from the *lower*—such as *thought* from *size* and *physical matter*—is clearly to invert this *order* in the *scale* of the *universe*, from...

<meta>catchword: Downward</meta>

### CHAP. V. Substantiality of all Souls.

It moves from the bottom up, and therefore it is *atheistical*. By the same reasoning, if one higher rank or degree in this *scale* is produced unnaturally from a lower one, then all the rest could be produced that way as well. Therefore, we have great reason to stay on our guard and to defend this *position* <note>original: "Post"</note> against the *atheists*: that no *life* or *thought* <note>original: "Cogitation"</note> can result, either *materially* or *efficiently*, from *dead* and *senseless matter* <note>original: "Body"</note>. Since souls are all *substantial* and *immaterial* things, they can neither be *generated* out of matter nor *decomposed* <note>original: "Corrupted"</note> back into it; they can only be *created* or *annihilated* by the *Deity*.

The major objection against this *substantiality* of *sensitive souls* <note>the souls of animals capable of feeling but not higher reasoning</note>, as well as *rational souls*, is the consequence that would follow: their *permanent existence* after death, their *perpetuity*, or immortality. It seems very absurd that the souls of brutes <note>animals</note> should also be immortal or continue to exist after the deaths of the individual *animals*. This is especially true for two types of people: first, those who do not truly believe in the immortality of their own souls; and second, those *religious people* who conclude that if irrational or sensitive souls exist after death, they must immediately go to either heaven or hell. 

*René Descartes* <note>original: "R. Cartesius"</note> was so aware of how *offensive* this opinion was that he faced a strict choice: either *animals* have no sense or thought at all, or they must contain some other *substance* besides *matter*. He chose to describe them as mere *senseless machines* <note>original: "Sensless Machins"</note> rather than allow them to have *substantial souls*. In trying to avoid a *lesser absurdity* or *paradox*, he clearly plunged himself into a greater one, since almost nothing is more widely accepted than the fact that *animals have senses*. 

In truth, everyone who denies that *sensitive souls* are *substantial* and insists that *animals* are made of nothing but *matter* should logically follow *Descartes* and strip them of all feeling. On the contrary, if it is evident from *observed phenomena* that animals are not mere *senseless machines* or *automatons*—like *clocks* or *watches*—then we should not let *popular opinion* and *common prejudice* stop us from agreeing with what sound reason and philosophy clearly dictate: they must have something more than *matter* in them. 

Furthermore, when we clearly understand something to be true—such as the fact that *life* and *thought* cannot possibly arise from *dead* and *senseless matter*—we should not abandon that truth or deny it just because it comes with a difficulty we cannot easily solve. We should not reject it simply because we cannot explain away every inconvenient or seemingly absurd consequence, such as the *continued existence* of *animal souls*.

To provide an explanation for this, *Plato* and the ancient *Pythagoreans* proposed the following *hypothesis*: that all *souls*, whether *sensitive* or *rational*, are *substantial* but not *self-existent* (because there is only one source and principle of all things). Therefore, they were produced or caused by the *Deity*. But this did not happen during the birth of the individual animals; for it would be improper <note>original: "indecorous"</note> for this divine, miraculous, creative power to constantly lacquey

# The Pythagorean Cabala; for Book I.

...wait upon and attend to *natural births* <note>original: "Generations"</note>; it is also inconsistent that *souls* should be so much *younger* <note>original: "Juniors"</note> than every atom of dust in the whole *world*. Instead, either all of *them* have existed from *eternity*—according to those who denied that the *world* had a beginning <note>original: "Novity of the World"</note>—or rather, according to others who asserted the *cosmogony* <note>the origin or creation of the universe</note> occurred at the very first beginning of the *world's creation*. 

Therefore, since it is *natural* for souls as such to *activate* and *enliven* some body, or to be, as it were, *clothed* with one, these souls were immediately *invested* with certain *thin* and *subtle bodies* as soon as they were created. They were placed into *light ethereal* or *aerial chariots* and *vehicles* <note>In ancient philosophy, a "vehicle" (ochēma) was a subtle, spirit-like body that carried the soul between incarnations</note>, in which they exist both before their entrance into other *gross terrestrial bodies* and after their *departure* <note>original: "Egress"</note> from them. So, the *souls* not only of men, but also of other *animals*, have sometimes a thicker and sometimes a thinner *covering* or *clothing* <note>original: "Indument"</note>. And this is how we understand *Boethius*, referring not only to the *rational* soul but also to other inferior *sensitive souls*, in these verses of his:

->You bring forth souls and lesser lives from similar causes,<-
->and fitting them on high to light chariots,<-
->you scatter them into the heaven and earth.<-
<note>original: "Tu Causis Animas paribus Vitasque Minores, / Provehis, & Levibus sublimes Curribus aptans, / In Cœlum Terramque feris." From *The Consolation of Philosophy*.</note>

<margin>Book 5, page 290.</margin>
These *light chariots*—in which God places all *lives* or *souls* at their very first creation, and in which they are carried as they are "sown" into *gross terrestrial matter*—are *thin, aerial*, and *ethereal bodies*. But this is plainly declared by *Proclus* in his commentary on the *Timaeus*, after he had spoken of the souls of demons and men in this manner: "Every soul must of necessity have, before these mortal bodies, certain eternal and easily movable bodies, it being essential to them to move" <note>original: ἡ γὲ πᾶσαν ψυχὴν ἀνάγκη πρὸ τῶν θνητῶν σωμάτων, ἀϊδίοις καὶ εὐκινήτοις τισι χρῆσθαι σώμασιν, ὡς κατ᾽ οὐσίαν ἔχουσαν τὸ κινεῖν</note>. 

There is indeed mention made by the same *Proclus* and others of an opinion concerning *irrational* or *brutish demons* <note>original: ἄλογοι δαίμονες</note>, or *demonic aerial animals*; of which he sometimes speaks doubtfully, saying, "If there be any irrational demons, as the theurgists <note>priests or magicians who performed rituals to communicate with the divine</note> affirm" <note>original: εἴπερ γέ εἰσιν ἄλογοι δαίμονες, ὡς οἱ Θεουργοί</note>.

<margin>Book 4, page 288.</margin>
But the dispute, doubt, or controversy here was only whether there were any such *irrational demons* that were *immortal* or not. For we learn this from these words of *Ammonius* in his commentary on *Porphyry's Introduction* <note>original: "Porphyrian Isagoge"</note>: "Some affirm that there is a certain kind of irrational demons that is immortal; but others say that all these irrational or brutish demons are mortal" <note>original: οἱ μὲν γάρ φασιν εἶναί τι δαιμονίων ἀλόγων γένος ἀθάνατον, οἱ δέ φασι καὶ τὸ τοιοῦτον γένος θνητὸν εἶναι</note>. By *immortal irrational demons*, they seem to mean those that never descend into *terrestrial bodies* (and these are rejected by *Ammonius*). The *mortal* ones are those that also act upon *gross terrestrial bodies*, which are liable <note>original: "obnoxious"</note> to death and corruption. 

It is as if *Ammonius* had said: "There are no other *brutish* or *irrational demons* than the souls of the *brute animals* we have here among us, which sometimes inhabit only *aerial bodies*." Thus, according to the ancient *Pythagorean hypothesis*, there is neither any new *substantial* thing made now which did not exist before, nor is any real entity destroyed into nothing. This applies not only to matter, but also to *soul* and *life*.

# CHAP. V. Vehicles of Animal Souls.

God, after the first creation, neither makes any new *substance* nor *annihilates* anything he made. At that time, he created nothing that was not fit to be *preserved in existence* and which could not be well *used* and *placed* in the *universe*; and he never afterward *repented* of what he had previously done. Thus, *natural births* <note>original: "Generations"</note> and *deaths* <note>original: "Corruptions"</note> are nothing but *accidental changes, combinations, and separations*, or *rearrangements* <note>original: "Anagrammatical Transpositions"</note> of things that already exist. The same *souls* and *lives* are sometimes *united* to one *body* and sometimes to another; *sometimes* in *thicker* and sometimes in *thinner clothing*; sometimes in the *visible* world and sometimes in the *invisible*. They possess *aerial* as well as *earthly* <note>original: "Terrestrial"</note> *vehicles*, and no soul is ever quite naked, without any *body* at all. Because of this, *Proclus* complains about certain people he calls *spurious Platonists*: <margin>In Timaeus p. 330.</margin> *Those who destroy the thinner vehicles of souls were therefore forced, at times, to leave them in a state of separation from every body—that is, without any physical covering.* <note>original: "οἱ φθείροντες τὸ ὄχημα ἀναγκάζονται ποτε παντὸς σώματ@ ἔξω ποιεῖν τὴν ψυχὴν"</note>

This *tradition* <note>original: "Cabbala"</note>, likely derived from the *Egyptians* by *Pythagoras*, was previously fully described by us through the works of *Ovid*, although the *transmigration of human souls into the bodies of wild animals* <note>original: "Ferine Bodies"</note> has not been accepted by everyone as a *genuine part* of that doctrine. The same point was emphasized by *Virgil* in his *Georgics* (Book 4), and was also accepted and confirmed as a great truth by *Macrobius*: <margin>Commentary on the Dream of Scipio, Book 2, Ch. 12.</margin>

->There is no place for death;<-
<note>original: "Nec Morti esse Locum"</note>

> *It is established according to the assertion of true reason—which neither Cicero nor Virgil was ignorant of—I say, it is established that nothing within the living world perishes; instead, only the appearance of those things that seem to die is changed.* <note>original: "Constat inquam, Nihil intra Vivum Mundum perire, sed eorum quæ interire videntur, solam mutari Speciem."</note>

Now, however extravagant this *hypothesis* may seem, there is no doubt that a *Pythagorean* would try to find support and refuge for it in the Scriptures—especially that passage which has so puzzled and *baffled* <note>original: "non-plus'd"</note> interpreters, *Romans* 8:19: *For the earnest expectation of the creation waits for the revealing of the sons of God. For the creation was subjected to futility <note>original: "Vanity"</note>, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope; because the creation itself also will be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God. For we know that the whole creation groans and suffers the pains of childbirth <note>original: "Travelleth in pain"</note> together until now. And not only they, but we ourselves also, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption, the redemption of our body.* In this passage, it is first of all evident that the <term>creation</term> <note>original: "κτίσις" (ktisis)</note> spoken of is not the very same <insert>as</insert> the <term>children</term> <note>original: "τέκνα" (tekna)</note> or <term>sons of God</term> <note>original: "υἱοὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ" (huioi tou theou)</note>, but something distinct from them. Therefore, the Pythagorean would further argue that this "creation" must necessarily be understood as either the inanimate world, the lower animal kingdom, or both of them together.

# Brutish Souls, out of Bodies, BOOK I.

Now, although it is readily acknowledged that there is a *personification* <term>original: "Prosopopœia"; a figure of speech in which an abstract thing or inanimate object is represented as a person</term> here, all these expressions cannot, without difficulty and force, be understood as referring only to the *inanimate creation* or *senseless matter*. Namely, that this matter has an *earnest expectation* <note>original: "ἀποκαραδοκίαν"</note> of some future good for itself; that it is now made subject to *vanity* <note>original: "ματαιότητι"</note>—to frustration and the disappointment of desire—and to *corruption* <note>original: "φθορᾷ"</note> and death; and that it does so *unwillingly* <note>original: "οὐχ ἑκοῦσα"</note>, rather than by choice, yet *in hope* <note>original: "ἐπ’ ἐλπίδι"</note> of some further good to follow afterward; and that, in the meantime, it *groans* <note>original: "συστενάζειν"</note> and *suffers birth pains* <note>original: "συνωδίνειν"</note> together until it is finally delivered from the *bondage of corruption* into the *glorious liberty of the children of God*. 

Furthermore, in the *creation* <note>original: "Generations"</note> and *destruction* <note>original: "Corruptions"</note> of *senseless bodies*, such as *minerals* and *vegetables*, or when, for example, *oil* is turned into *flame*, *flame* into *smoke*, *water* into *vapor*, *vapor* into *snow* or *hail*, *grass* into *milk*, or *milk* into *blood* and *bones*, and the like—I say that in all this, no *harm* is done to anything, nor is any *real entity* destroyed. All the *substance* of *matter* remains entirely the same, without the least reduction, and only undergoes *accidental transformations*. All of this is *really nothing* but *local motion* <term>local motion: Physical movement from one place to another</term>. There is no more toil or labor for an *inanimate body* in *motion* than in *rest*, since it is just as *natural* for a *body* to be *moved* by something else as it is for it to *rest* by itself. It is nothing but a *change* of *shape*, *distance*, *position*, and the *size* of its *parts*, which causes various *sensations*, *fancies*, and *appearances* in us. 

And those who would claim the meaning of this passage is that all such *mutations* and *alternating changes* in *inanimate bodies* shall eventually cease entirely—believing these things *groan* in the meantime and suffer pain to be delivered from the *tiresome labor* of such *restless motion* so they may be at *ease* and *quiet*—by removing all *motion* this way, out of a foolish concern for the *ease* and *quiet* of *senseless matter*, they would by that very act <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> *petrify* the entire *physical universe*. Consequently, they would also petrify the *bodies* of *good men* after the *resurrection*, congealing everything into *rocky marble* or *diamond-hard stone* <note>original: "Adamant"</note>. 

Just as foolish is the idea of some that the entire *terrestrial globe* shall finally be *vitrified* <term>vitrified: Turned into glass</term> or changed into *transparent crystal*, as if it also *groaned* for this in the meantime. For whatever *change* is made to the world in the *new heaven* and the *new earth* to come, it is *reasonable* to think it will not be made for the sake of *senseless matter* or the *inanimate bodies* themselves—to which all states are the same—but only for the sake of *humans* and *animals*, the *living spectators* and inhabitants, so that it may be better suited for their *use* and *delight*. 

Indeed, those words—*“for the creature itself shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God”*—cannot be understood to refer to anything other than *animals*. This is because the *liberty of the children of God* mentioned here refers to being *clothed* in *immortal bodies* instead of *mortal* ones, which no other *creatures* are *capable* of except those consisting of *soul* and *body*. # CHAP. V. In a State of Inactivity.

Therefore, a follower of Pythagoras would interpret this passage as referring only to the *lower animal creation*, which is capable of feeling good and evil. They would argue that just as these creatures were made subject to *futility* <note>original: "Vanity"</note> and the *bondage of decay* <note>original: "Corruption"</note>, pain, misery, and death—against their own will or inclination (following the fall of man or the descent of souls)—within these *dense earthly bodies* <note>original: "Gross Terrestrial Bodies" </note>; so too, when the *Sons of God* are revealed and clothed in *heavenly and immortal bodies* instead of these *mortal ones*, then these *creatures* shall also have their specific share in the happiness of that glorious time. They would partake in a measure of that *liberty* by being freed in the same way from their *dense earthly bodies* and living instead in *refined, airy, and immortal ones*. Thus, a period would be put to all their miseries and calamities by Him who *did not create death, nor takes pleasure in the destruction of the living, but created all that lives so that it might exist and enjoy itself.* <note>A reference to the deuterocanonical Wisdom of Solomon 1:13–14.</note>

However, this much is certain: brute animals cannot be entirely excluded from this passage, because the phrase <term>pasa ktisis</term> <note>original Greek: πᾶσα κτίσις</note>, meaning *the whole creation*, will not allow it. Therefore, a Pythagorean would conclude it is a valid inference from this scriptural text that the entire rank of *irrational and animal life* below humanity shall not be utterly annihilated at the *final end* <note>original: "Consummation"</note> of things or the *future renewal of the world*. The world will not be quite stripped of all this "furniture," leaving humans alone in it; rather, there shall be a continuation of this species or rank of being. 

And it is not only that; it is not as if there should simply be a constant succession of *birth and death* <note>original: "Alternate Generations and Corruptions"</note> of animals for all eternity. Instead, the *individuals* themselves shall remain the same, because otherwise, none would actually be delivered from the *bondage of decay*. Finally, those very *souls of animals* <note>original: "Brutes"</note>, which currently groan and suffer birth pains <note>original: "Travel in Pain," referring to the archaic "travail"</note>, shall themselves share in the *liberty* of the children of God. Otherwise, they would be *laboring to give birth to nothing*—groaning not for themselves, but for others. 

But enough of this *Pythagorean hypothesis*, which—supposing all kinds of souls (the *sentient* as well as the *rational*) to be *substantial things* that persist after death in their distinct natures—grants them certain *refined, airy <term>vehicles</term>* <note>original Greek: "Ochemata"</note> to live in once these *dense earthly ones* fail them.

But even if we dismiss these *airy vehicles* of animal souls as a *whim* <note>original: "Whimsey"</note> or mere fiction, and do not allow them to animate anything other than *earthly bodies* (meaning they must be entirely without a body immediately after death), they would nonetheless continue to exist and not vanish into nothing, because they are not mere *accidental qualities* but *substantial things*. We say that in this case, although their *substances* remain, they must necessarily continue in a state of *insensibility* and *inactivity*, unless perhaps they are later reunited with some other *earthly bodies*. This is because, although *pure thought* <note>original: "Intellection"</note> is the *activity* <note>original: "Energie"</note> of the *rational soul* alone without the requirement of a *body*, the *activity* of the *sentient soul* is always linked to a body. For sensation is, as *Aristotle* rightly determined,

...determined, a *complex union of Soul and Body* together, much like *weaving* consists of both the *weaver and the weaving tools*. Therefore, we say that if the *irrational and sensory souls in animals* <note>original: "Brutes"</note>—which are also *substantial* things—are completely deprived of any *body* after death, then they can neither perceive anything nor *act* upon anything. Instead, they must remain for a long time in a state of *insensibility* and *inactivity*.

This should be considered quite possible, because no one can be certain that their own soul always maintains an uninterrupted consciousness during sleep, lethargy, or strokes <note>original: "Apoplexies"</note>, or that it was never without thoughts even while in the mother’s womb. However, there is little reason to doubt that the sensory *souls of animals* that lie dead or asleep all winter and *revive* or awake again at the approach of summer's warmth continue for that time in a state of *inactivity* and *insensibility*. For this reason, although these *animal souls* may be called *immortal* in one sense—because their *substance* and the *root of life* within them still remains—they might also be called *mortal* in another sense, because the exercise of that *life* is, at least for a time, completely suspended.

From this, it appears there is no reason at all for the *fear* and *suspicion* held by some that if animal souls are *substantial* and continue to exist after death, they must necessarily go to either *Heaven* or *Hell*. As for the suggested possibility of them awakening later in other *earthly bodies*, this seems to be nothing more than what we find through daily experience in the course of nature, such as when the *silkworm* and other caterpillars <note>original: "Worms"</note> die and are transformed into butterflies. There is little reason to doubt that the same *soul* which previously animated the body of the silkworm later *animates* <note>original: "Act"</note> that of the *butterfly*. Because of this, Christian theologians have used this as an *emblem of the Resurrection*.

Up to this point, we have presented two different *opinions* concerning the *substantial souls of animals*, which are assumed to have a *permanent existence* after death. The first is that of *Plato* and the *Pythagoreans*: that when they are stripped of these *dense earthly bodies*, they live and have an awareness of themselves in *thin, airy bodies* <note>original: "Aerial Vehicles"</note>. The other opinion—held by those who reject <note>original: "Exploding"</note> these *airy vehicles for animals* and allow them only *earthly bodies*—affirms that their substances survive death but continue in a state of *inactivity* and *insensibility*, *sleep*, *silence*, or *stupor*. 

But to tell the truth, there is no absolute necessity that these animal souls, simply because they are substantial, must therefore have a permanent existence after death for all eternity. While it is true that no substance created by God will ever vanish into nothingness on its own, it is also true that whatever God created out of nothing can possibly be annihilated and reduced to nothing by Him again. Therefore, when it is said that the *immortality of the human soul* is *demonstrable* by *natural reason*, it simply means that its *substantiality* is demonstrable. From this, it follows that it will naturally no more perish or vanish into nothing than the substance of *matter* itself. It does not mean that it is impossible for either the soul or matter...

#### CHAP. V. Absolutely Unannihilable.

...matter, by Divine Power to be annihilated. Therefore, the assurance we have regarding the immortality of our own souls must depend on something else besides their *substantial nature* <note>original: "Substantiality"</note>. Specifically, it depends on a faith in the *Divine Goodness*—that God will preserve in existence, and not annihilate, all those *created substances* whose *continued existence* <note>original: "Permanent Subsistence"</note> is consistent with His own *attributes* and the good of the *universe*. Rational souls certainly fit this description: because they possess both *morality* and *free will* <note>original: "Liberty of Will"</note>, they are capable of *rewards* and *punishments*. Consequently, they are *suitable subjects* for *Divine Justice* to be exercised upon. 

But for all we know, the situation might be different regarding the *souls of animals* <note>original: "Souls of Brute Animals"</note>, which lack both *morality* and *free will* and are therefore *incapable of reward and punishment*. While these souls will not naturally vanish into nothing on their own, God—having created them during the generation of these *animals* and allowed them some period of self-awareness—might just as easily annihilate them upon their death and decay. If this is absolutely for the best, then it is undoubtedly what happens. 

The opinion of the philosopher *Porphyry* <note>original: "Porphyrius"</note> seems to agree with this. He stated that *every irrational power or soul is resolved into the life of the whole*—meaning it is pulled back and reabsorbed into the Deity, and thus annihilated in terms of its *created nature*. However, there might be another interpretation of that philosopher's meaning here: namely, that all the *sensory souls of animals* are actually just one and the same *World Soul* <note>original: "Mundane Soul"</note>. This soul flows out and displays itself in various ways, acting upon all the different parts of matter capable of receiving it, but at their deaths, it retires back into itself. 

But we have sufficiently refuted <note>original: "retunded"</note> the force of that *objection* against the idea that all *souls* are *incapable of being generated* <note>original: "Ingenerability"</note>. We have also addressed the *substantial nature* of animal souls and the concern that they must continue after death. We have shown that, despite their *substantiality*, there is no *absolute necessity* for them to last forever or remain permanent for all eternity. Alternatively, if they do continue to exist (assuming God annihilates no substance), they must remain in a state of *inactivity*, *insensibility*, *silence*, or *sleep*, unless they possess *airy bodies* <note>original: "Aerial Vehicles"</note> through which to act.

Now, therefore, if no *souls*—no life and no *thought* <note>original: "Cogitation"</note>—could ever be generated out of *dead* and *senseless matter*, since they are not merely *accidental properties* <note>original: "Accidents"</note> but *substantial things* which would have to come from *nothing* in that case, then one of two things must be true. Either all souls have existed of themselves from eternity, or there must necessarily be some *eternal, uncreated Life and Mind* from which all other lives and minds are derived. 

That this was the *doctrine* of the ancient *theists*—that no *soul* or *mind*, and no *life* or *understanding*, was ever generated out of *matter*, but all were produced by the Deity, the sole fountain of life and understanding—could be proved here at length with many testimonies if it were necessary. However, it is clearly seen in those verses by *Virgil*. First, in his sixth *Aeneid*, after he had spoken of God as a spirit and mind diffused throughout the whole world, he adds,

*And from this source, not only men, but also all manner of brute animals and beasts, when produced into this world, do every one derive their lives or souls; as also at their deaths they render the same back again to Him, in whose hand or custody they remain undestroyed; so that there is no place anywhere in the world left for death.* This was, therefore, undoubtedly the genuine doctrine of the *ancient theists*, however some in recent times have deviated and swerved from it: that no *life* was generated out of matter, but all was created by the Deity, or derived from Him, the sole fountain of lives and souls.

And it is a *truth* so evident—that life being a substance, and not a mere *accidental* thing generated and *destroyed* <note>original: "Corrupted"</note>, there must therefore of necessity be some *eternal, unmade Life* and *Mind* from which all other *lives* and *minds* are derived—that the Hylozoic atheists <note>Hylozoic atheists (from the Greek words for "matter" and "life") believed that all matter is inherently alive and intelligent.</note> themselves (in this far wiser than the *Atomists* <note>original: "Atomicks"; those who believe the universe is made of lifeless, moving atoms.</note>) were fully convinced of it. Nevertheless, being strongly possessed by that atheistic prejudice that there is no other substance besides the body, they attribute this first, original, *unmade life* and *understanding* to all matter as such (though without animal *consciousness*) as an essential part of it, or an inherent concept of it. From this fundamental "life of nature" in matter, modified by *physical organization*, they imagine the lives of *animals* and *men* to have proceeded. So that, although the *modified lives of animals and men* as such are, according to them, *accidental* things—generated and *destroyed*, produced out of *nothing* and reduced to *nothing* again—yet this fundamental life of *matter*, which is the *basis* upon which they stand, being a substance, is also eternal and incorruptible. These *Hylozoists*, therefore, to avoid admitting a Deity, suppose every atom of *senseless matter* to have been from all eternity infallibly *omniscient*—that is, to know all things without either *error* or *ignorance*, and to have a knowledge that exists before *senses* and is *underived* from sensible objects. # CHAP. V. Deity Crumbled into Matter.

...or the product of it, though without any animal consciousness and self-perception.

But just as nothing can be more *prodigiously absurd* than to attribute *infallible omniscience* to every *atom of matter*, it is also directly contradictory to suppose *perfect knowledge, wisdom*, or *understanding* exists without any *consciousness* or *self-perception*. *Consciousness* is essential to *cogitation* <note>original: "cogitation"; thought or the act of thinking</note>. Furthermore, it is contradictory to suggest that the *substantial* and *fundamental life* in humans and other animals should never *perish*, yet their *souls and personalities* should utterly vanish into *nothing* at *death*. 

Moreover, this *hypothesis* can never explain the *phenomenon of humans and animals* either. This is not only because no *organization or modification of matter* could ever produce *consciousness* and *self-perception* in something that was previously *unconscious*, but also because if every *smallest atom* is supposed to be a *percipient* <note>original: "percipient"; one who perceives or senses</note> by itself—having its own *perfect life and understanding*—then in every single human and animal, there would be not one individual, but a *heap or commonwealth of innumerable perceivers*. 

Finally, these *hylozoic atheists* <note>original: "Hylozoick Atheists"; from the Greek 'hyle' (matter) and 'zoe' (life), these thinkers believed that matter is inherently alive</note> make every *atom of matter omniscient* but not at all *omnipotent*. They assert *perfect knowledge* without any *perfect power*, and a knowledge without *sense* that is not derived from *sensibles* <note>original: "sensibles"; things that can be perceived by the five senses</note>. We ask them: where are the *intelligibles* <note>original: "intelligibles"; objects of pure thought or abstract intellectual concepts</note> or the *objects of this knowledge*? From where are its *ideas* derived? Since these ideas do not come through *passive reception from external sensory objects*, nor could they result from those *atoms* understanding *themselves*, they must necessarily come from *nothing*. Many of them, at least, would be the *conceptions of nothing*. 

No other origin for knowledge and understanding can be devised by human wit than from an *absolutely perfect and omnipotent Being* who *comprehends* itself and the extent of its own *infinite power*—that is, *all the possibilities of things*, or all *intelligibles*. But there can be only *one such omnipotent Being*. Therefore, there is no more than *one original and eternal unmade Mind* from which all other minds are derived. This *hylozoic atheism* is nothing but the breaking and crumbling of the *single Deity*—the *one perfect understanding Being*—into *matter* and all its various *atoms*.

We have now made it manifest that these *atheists* are so far from being able to disprove *God* using the *topics of cogitation, knowledge, or understanding* that they cannot possibly explain these *phenomena* without a *God*. Indeed, these topics provide *invincible arguments for His existence*. 

First: if no *life, thought, soul, or mind* can possibly *spring out of matter or body* that is devoid of life and understanding (which is nothing but a *thing extended into length, breadth, and thickness*), then it is far from being *true* that all life and understanding are *junior* <note>original: "junior"; secondary to or occurring after</note> to *senseless matter* and its offspring. Instead, of necessity, either all lives and souls were *self-existent from eternity*, or else there must be *one perfect unmade life and mind* from which all other imperfect ones were derived. There must be an *eternal knowledge* that existed before *sense and*

# 872
## Atheists' Arguments against BOOK I.

*Sensible objects* <note>original: "Sensibles"; things that can be perceived by the five senses</note> have printed the *stamps* and *signatures* of themselves upon the *matter* of the whole world. Indeed, nothing can be more certain than this: all knowledge and understanding in *ourselves* is not a mere *reaction* <note>original: "passion"; in this context, it refers to the mind being passively acted upon by external things</note> from *individual physical objects* or *bodies existing* outside of us. The aforementioned *atheists* conclude this to be the case, and from there they would further *infer* that *knowledge*, as such, is in its own nature *secondary to physical objects* <note>original: "Junior to Sensibles"</note> and the mere *creature* of them—and consequently not their *creator*. However, nothing comes to us from the *objects of sense* outside of us except *only local motion and pressure*. Furthermore, there are other *objects of the mind* besides *individual physical things*—not only all *universals* but also such *intelligible concepts* as never were nor can be found in *the senses*. 

Now, if our *human knowledge and understanding* are not a *reaction* from things *existing* outside of us, then they can have no other *origin* than by way of *participation* from a *Perfect Mind*. This is the mind of an *infinitely productive and powerful being* who comprehends *itself* and, within *itself*, all things. This includes all the *possibilities* of things before they were made, their *relationships*, and the *truths* belonging to them. So, a *perfect, omnipotent being*, together with the *possibilities* of things contained within it, is the *first* "intelligible object" <note>original: "Νοητὸν"; Greek *Noeton*, something that can be understood by the mind rather than sensed by the body</note> or *object of mind and understanding* by which all other *individuals* are understood. If there were no such *perfect, infinitely productive, and powerful being*, there could have been no *mind or understanding* at all. Likewise, were there no *Perfect Mind*—namely, that of an *omnipotent being comprehending itself* and all *possibilities* of things virtually contained in it—all the *knowledge and intelligible ideas* of our *imperfect minds* must necessarily have *sprung from nothing*. Thus, the *existence of a God* is demonstrated once again from the *phenomenon of knowledge or understanding*.

Having quite routed and vanquished the *atheists' main body* of arguments, we shall now blow away the *remainder* of their weaker and scattered *forces* (namely, *their objections against Providence, their questions, and their arguments from self-interest*) with just a breath or two. 

Their *first objection* is against *Providence* regarding the *fabric of the world*. They argue from the *faultiness of the world system*, *intellectually considered* and in *relation to its purposes*. They say, "because it is endowed with such great fault" <note>original: "Quia tantâ stat Prædita Culpâ"; a quote from the Roman poet Lucretius (De Rerum Natura) arguing that the flaws in nature prove it was not created by a god</note>. They claim that *because* the world is so *badly made*, it could not have been made by a *God*. In this, the *atheist* takes it for granted that whoever asserts a *God* or a *Perfect Mind* to be the *origin of all things* does therefore *by that very fact* <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> suppose *all things* to be *well made* and as they should be. This, without doubt, was the view of all the ancient *theologians*. However, some *modern theists* deviate from this; they conclude that the *perfection* of the *Deity* does not consist in *goodness* at all, but in *power* and *arbitrary will only*. It is as if having a *will* determined by a *rule* or *reason* of *good* were the virtue only of *weak*, *impotent*, and *vulnerable* <note>original: "obnoxious"; here meaning subject to external influence or rules</note> *beings*, or of those who have a *superior* over them to give *laws* to them (that is, of *creatures*). Instead, they claim it is the *prerogative* of a...

## CHAP. V. Providence, Confuted.

Being irresistibly powerful, [the idea that God would] have a **will** absolutely **indifferent** to all things, and **undetermined** by anything but itself; or to will nothing because it is **good**, but to make its own **arbitrary** or **accidental** <note>original: "Contingent and Fortuitous"</note> **determination** the **sole reason** for all its **actions**—indeed, the very **rule** or **measure** of **goodness, justice**, and **wisdom** itself. These people suppose this to be the **liberty, sovereignty**, and **dominion** of the **Deity**.

Therefore, these kinds of **theists** would think themselves completely **unconcerned** with these **atheistic objections** against **providence**, or with defending the structure of the world as **faultless**. They are as ready as the atheists themselves to acknowledge that the world might really have been made much better than it is now—except they claim it must be said to be "well made" simply because it was made that way. They pretend, nevertheless, that this is no challenge at all to the existence of a **God**, <note>original: "Quia Deus non tenetur ad Optimum"</note> **because God is in no way bound or obliged to do the best**. According to them, He is indeed nothing but **omnipotent arbitrary will**.

But what else are these **theists** doing here but denying that the **accidental motion** of **senseless matter** is the **first origin** of all things, while they themselves, in the meantime, enthrone **accidental chance** and **contingency** in the **will** of an **omnipotent being**? There, they give it absolute **sovereignty** and **dominion** over everything. So, the **controversy** between the **atheists** and these **theists** seems to be nothing more than this: whether **senseless matter moving by chance**, or an **omnipotent will of chance**—one that is altogether undetermined by **goodness, justice**, and **wisdom**—is the sovereign **divine power** <note>original: "Numen"</note> and the **origin** of all things.

Certainly, we mortals could have little better reason for our **faith** and **hope** in such an omnipotent **arbitrary will** as this, than we could have in the motions of **senseless atoms** violently agitated, or in a **rapid whirlwind**. In fact, one would think that of the **two**, it should be more **desirable** to be under the empire of **senseless atoms moving by chance**, than under a will altogether undetermined by **goodness, justice**, and **wisdom**, armed with omnipotence. This is because the former could harbor no **hurtful** or **mischievous designs** against anyone, while the latter might.

But this **irrational will**, altogether undetermined by goodness, justice, and wisdom, is so far from being the **highest liberty, sovereignty**, and **dominion**, the **greatest perfection**, and the **most divine** thing of all, that it is indeed nothing else but **weakness** and **impotence** itself, or **brutish folly** and **madness**. And therefore, those **ancients** who affirmed that **Mind** was **Lord over all**, and the **supreme king of heaven and earth**, held at the same time that **Good** was the **sovereign monarch** of the **universe**. **Good reigns** in **Mind** and together with it, because **Mind** is that which orders all things for the sake of **Good**. According to them, whatever does otherwise was not <note>original: "Νῦς"</note> **Mind**, but <note>original: "Ἄνοια"</note> **Folly**—not <note>original: "Mens"</note> **Reason**, but <note>original: "Dementia"</note> **Madness**—and consequently, no **God**.

And thus does **Celsus** (quoted in the works of **Origen**) declare the nature of **God**:

<margin>P. 240.</margin> <note>original: "οὐ γὰρ τῆς πλημμελοῦς ὀρέξεως, οὐδὲ τῆς πεπλανημένης ἀκοσμίας, ἀλλὰ τῆς ὀρθῆς ἢ δικαίας φύσεως θεός ἐστιν ἀρχηγέτης"</note> **For God is not the leader of faulty desire, nor of wandering disorder, but is the ruler of a right and just nature.**

In other words, **God is not the president or head of irregular and irrational lust or appetite, and of loose, erratic disorderliness, but of the just and righteous nature**. This view was highly approved by Origen; he added further in confirmation of it—and as the general sense of Christians as well—that <note>original: "φαμὲν ὅτι οὐ δύναται αἰσχρά ὁ θεός..."</note> "We Christians (who believe in the Resurrection) say, as well as you, that **God can do nothing which is in itself evil, unsuitable, or absurd—no more than he is able to not be God.** For if God does any evil, he is no God." 

And again, <note>original: "οὐδὲν μὴ πρέπον ἑαυτῷ ὁ θεὸς βούλεται..."</note> "**God wills nothing unbecoming to himself, or what is truly inappropriate** <note>original: "indecorous"</note>; **for this would be inconsistent with his being God.**" 

To the same purpose, Plotinus wrote: <note>original: "ποιεῖ τὸ θεῖον ὡς πέφυκε..."</note> "**The Deity acts according to its own nature and essence; and its nature and essence display goodness and justice. For if these things were not found there, where else could they be found?**" 

And again elsewhere: <note>original: "θεὸς ὅπερ ἔχρην εἶναι..."</note> "**God is essentially That which Ought to be; therefore, he did not happen by chance to be such as he is; and this 'First Ought' is the source of all things whatsoever that 'Ought to be.'**"

Therefore, the Deity is not to be understood as mere **arbitrariness**, **mood**, or an **irrational, all-powerful will and appetite** (which would really be nothing more than **all-powerful chance**). Instead, God is an **overflowing fountain of love and goodness, justly and wisely distributing itself, and reaching all things with almighty power.** 

**The Will of God is goodness, justice, and wisdom; or decency, fitness, and "That Which Ought to Be" in the act of willing. So that** <note>original: "τὸ βέλτιστον"</note> **that which is absolutely the best, is** <note>original: "νόμος ἀπαράβατος"</note> **an unbreakable law to Him, because it is His very essence.** 

**God is** <note>original: "μέτρον πάντων"</note> **the impartial measure of all things, an even balance that stays level and fair to everything. He weighs out heaven and earth, and everything within them, in the most just and exact proportions—not a grain too much or too little of anything.** 

Nor is the Deity **bound** or **obliged** to do the **best** in a way that suggests **slavery** (as some people foolishly imagine this to be contrary to his **liberty**), and certainly not by the law or command of any superior (which is a contradiction). He is bound only by the **perfection of his own nature**, which he cannot possibly deviate from, any more than he can **cease to be God**. 

In **conclusion**, therefore, we acknowledge that the **atheists'** argument is valid to this extent: if there is a God, then of necessity all things must be **well-made** and as they should be; and vice versa. However, no **atheist** will ever be able to **prove** that either the **entire system of the world could have been better made**, or that **even one single thing within it is made foolishly.**

There are indeed many things in the **framework of nature** whose reasons we cannot grasp. They were made by a knowledge far superior and more transcendent than our own. Our **experience** and **reasoning** only slowly discover the complexities and designs of Providence within them. Witness the **circulation of the blood**, the **milky and lymphatic vessels** <note>Early terms for the systems that carry nutrients and fluids through the body</note>, and other things (without which the mechanical structure of animal bodies cannot be understood)—all of which were only recently discovered. Therefore, we must not conclude that what-

<summary>The author argues that God is not a being of arbitrary whim but is defined by inherent goodness and reason, meaning the world is necessarily created as well as it possibly could be. He challenges atheists to prove any flaw in the natural design, noting that many seemingly "inept" things are simply parts of nature we do not yet understand.</summary>

<page-num>875</page-num>
<header>Chapter 5: Inclination of the Earth's Axis.</header>

...whatever we cannot find the reason for, or the use it serves, is therefore *ineptly made*. We shall give one instance of this: The *Intestinum Caecum* <note>The cecum: the pouch at the beginning of the large intestine, including the appendix.</note> in the bodies of men and other animals seems, at first sight, to be merely a *botch* or *bungle* of nature, and an *odd, irrelevant appendix*. Nor do we know of any *anatomist* or *physiologist* <note>original: "physiologer"</note> who has given a rational account of it or discovered its use. And yet, because there is a *valve* at its entrance, these two together are a most clever contrivance of nature and of great benefit for animals, as they prevent the *regurgitation* of *feces* upward toward the *stomach* <note>original: "ventricle"</note>.

The first *atheistic* instance of the *faultiness* of things in the *frame of nature* concerns the *structure of the heavens* and the arrangement of the *equator* and the *ecliptic*. These intersect each other at an *angle* of twenty-three degrees and more, by which—as the atheists claim—the terrestrial globe is rendered much more *uninhabitable* than it might otherwise be. But this is built upon a *false supposition* of the ancients: that the "Torrid Zone" (all the land between the *tropics*) was utterly uninhabitable because of extreme heat. In reality, it is certain that nothing demonstrates *Providence* more than this very thing. It is the most convenient placement or arrangement that could be devised, as will appear if the inconveniences of other arrangements are considered—especially these three:

1. *First*, if the axes of those circles were *parallel* and their planes coincided;
2. *Secondly*, if they intersected each other at *right angles*;
3. *Thirdly* (which is a middle ground between both), if they cut one another at an angle of *forty-five degrees*.

For it is evident that each of these *arrangements* would result in far greater *inconveniences* to the Earth's inhabitants regarding the length of days and nights, and the distribution of heat and cold. Furthermore, the fact that these two circles continue to maintain the same *angular intersection*—even when *physical* and *mechanical causes* would naturally bring them closer together—is a further proof of *Providence*.

In the next place, the *atheist* supposes that, according to the general persuasion of *theists*, the world and all things in it were created only for the sake of *man*. He thinks he can use this point to his advantage. But this seems, at first, to have been an opinion held only by some narrow-minded *Stoics*, though it was afterward recommended to others by their own *self-love*, their *excessive vanity*, and their *puffed-up conceit* of themselves. Following that logic, *fleas* and *lice*, if they had understanding, might conclude that the bodies of other larger animals and men were made only for them. 

<margin>
As Plato said, "The part was made for the sake of the whole, and not the whole for the sake of the part." <note>original Greek: μέρος μὲν ἕνεκα ὅλου, καὶ οὐχ ὅλον μέρους ἕνεκα. From "Laws," page 903.</note>
</margin>

But the *whole* was not properly made for any *part*; rather, the *parts* were made for the *whole*, and the *whole* was made for its *Creator*. And yet, the things of this *lower world* may well be said to have been made principally (though not *only*) for man. For we ought not to monopolize divine goodness for ourselves; there are other animals superior to us <note>Likely referring to angels or other spiritual beings in the "Chain of Being."</note> that are also concerned with this *visible creation*. And it is reasonable to think that even the *low—*

<header>Evils, from the Necessity | Book I.</header>

...other animals likewise, and whatever has conscious life, was made partly also to *enjoy itself*. But *atheists* cannot be *fit judges* of whether the world was made *well* or *ill*, either in general or in relation to mankind, because they have no objective standard for *well* and *ill* without *a God and morality*, nor any true knowledge of themselves and what their own good or evil consists of. That was at first only the *perverse speech* <note>original: "froward speech"</note> of some sullen, discontented people who, when things did not turn out according to their own *private, selfish, and partial appetites*, would revenge themselves by railing against *nature* (that is, *Providence*) and calling her a *stepmother* only to mankind, while she was a *fond, partial, and indulgent mother* to other animals. Although this is elegantly expressed by *Lucretius* <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), a Roman poet and Epicurean philosopher who argued that the world was not created by gods because it is too flawed.</note>, it is all nothing but *poetic flourish* without any *philosophical truth*. The advantages of mankind are so notoriously conspicuous above those of *animals* <note>original: "brutes"</note>.

But as for *evils* in general, from which the *atheist* would conclude that the *God* of the *theist* is either *impotent* or *envious*, it has been already declared that the *true origin* of them is from the *necessity of imperfect beings* and the *impossibility of things*. However, the *divine art* and *skill* appears most clearly in *turning these evils to good* <note>original: "bonifying"</note> and making them, like *discords in music*, contribute to the *harmony of the whole* and the *good of individual persons*.

Moreover, a great part of those *evils* that men are afflicted with is not from the *reality of things*, but only from their own *imagination* <note>original: "phancy"</note> and *opinions*. As the *moralist* <note>Epictetus, a Stoic philosopher.</note> said: *“It is not things themselves that disturb men, but only their own opinions concerning things”* <note>original Greek: "ταράσσει τοὺς ἀνθρώπους οὐ τὰ πράγματα, ἀλλὰ τὰ περὶ τῶν πραγμάτων δόγματα"</note>. Therefore, since it is very much in our own power to be freed from these, *Providence* is not to be blamed on their account. *Pain* is many times nearly linked with *pleasure*, according to that *Socratic fable*: that when God could not reconcile their *contrary natures* (as he wished), he *tied them head and tail together*. And good men know that *pain* is not the *evil of the man*, but only of the *part* affected. As *Socrates* also said: *“The pain stays in the leg”* <note>original Greek: "τὸ ἀλγεῖν ἐν τῷ σκέλει μένει"</note>; it goes no further than the limb where it is. But this is often very useful to free us from the *greater evils of the mind*, upon which all our happiness depends. To the *atheists*, who acknowledge no *evil of wrongdoing* <note>original Latin: "malum culpae"; refers to moral evil, sin, or vice as opposed to physical suffering.</note> (dishonesty or moral foulness), *death* is the greatest and most tragic of all evils. But although this—according to their forlorn *hypothesis*—is nothing less than an *absolute extinction* of life, yet according to the *doctrine of the genuine theists* (which considers all souls to be *substantial* <note>Meaning souls are distinct substances that exist independently and do not simply disappear.</note>), no life will ever quite *vanish into nothing* of its own accord (without *divine annihilation*), any more than the *substance of matter* does. The *ancient Pythagoreans* and *Platonists* were so kind even to the *souls of animals* also, that—so they might not be left in a *state of inactivity and insensibility* after death—they provided them with certain *subtle bodies* <note>Often referred to as "astral" or "aetherial" bodies that the soul inhabits after the physical body dies.</note> in which they may then continue to *act*. Nor can we think otherwise but that *Aristotle* derived from this fountain that doctrine of his in his...

<page-num>877</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER V. Of Imperfect Beings.</header>

In his second book, *On the Generation of Animals, chapter 3*, after Aristotle had declared the **sensitive soul** <note>The "sensitive soul" refers to the part of the soul responsible for sensation and movement, shared by humans and animals.</note> to be **inseparable from the body**, he adds: "Every power of the soul seems to have shared in another body, more divine than the so-called elements; and as souls differ in dignity and nobility from each other, so also does this nature differ" <note>original: πάσης ἐν ψυχῆς δύναμις ἑτέρῳ σώματος ἔοικε κεκοινωνηκέναι καὶ θειοτέρῳ τῶν καλουμένων στοιχείων· ὡς δὲ διαφέρουσι τιμότητι αἱ ψυχαὶ καὶ ἀτιμίᾳ ἀλλήλων, οὕτω καὶ ἡ τοιαύτη διαφέρει φύσις·</note>. Afterward, calling this **subtle body** *pneuma* <note>original: πνεῦμα</note> or a **spirit**, he affirms it to be "analogous to the element of the stars" <note>original: ἀνάλογον τῷ τῶν ἄστρων στοιχείῳ</note>. 

However, as Galen, St. Augustine, and others have believed, Aristotle deviated here from the followers of Pythagoras. He supposed the **sensitive soul** itself to be nothing more than this **very subtle and star-like body**, rather than a distinct substance that only uses that body as a **vehicle**. Nevertheless, he plainly affirms there that the **mind** or **rational soul** is truly distinct from the **body** and comes into it "from the outside, pre-existing" <note>The idea that the human intellect exists before birth and enters the body from a divine source.</note>. Consequently, he should also acknowledge its immortality after death. 

But whatever Aristotle’s judgment was (which is not very important), it is certain that for the **rational** or **human soul**, **dying** is nothing but withdrawing into the **dressing room** <note>original: "Tyring-house," the area in a theater where actors change clothes; the author uses this as a metaphor for the soul leaving the "stage" of the physical world.</note> and putting off the **clothing of this terrestrial body**. Thus, the soul will continue to live to **God** after death, whether in a **body** or without one.

<margin>On the Laws, Book 10, page 903.</margin>
According to Plato's explicit doctrine, the soul is never quite stripped of all body. He wrote: "The soul is always joined with a body, but sometimes of one kind, and sometimes of another" <note>original: ἀεὶ ψυχὴ ἐπιτεταγμένη σώματι, τοτὲ μὲν ἄλλῳ τοτὲ δὲ ἄλλῳ·</note>. Many Christian doctors, as previously mentioned, have also thought this highly probable. In any case, our **Christian faith** assures us that the souls of good men shall eventually be clothed with **spiritual and heavenly bodies**. In Aristotle’s language, these are "analogous to the element of the stars" <note>original: ἀνάλογα τῷ τῶν ἄστρων στοιχείῳ</note>. Therefore, the **Christian resurrection** to **life and immortality** is far from being what Celsus <note>A 2nd-century Greek philosopher and opponent of early Christianity.</note> mocked as "the mere hope of worms" <note>original: σκωλήκων ἐλπίς</note>. This shall suffice as a refutation of the **first atheistic objection** against **Providence**, which was the **twelfth argument** proposed in the **second chapter**.

The **thirteenth atheistic argument**, or **second objection** against **Providence**, arises from the **seeming confusion of human affairs**. It claims that all things happen the same way to everyone: the **innocent** and the **guilty** <note>original: "nocent"</note>, the **pious** and the **impious**, the **religious** and the **profane**. In fact, it argues that many times the **worse** causes and men prevail against the **better**. This is hinted at in the passage by the poet Lucan, though spoken in the persona of a **theist**:

->“The victorious cause pleased the gods, but the defeated cause pleased Cato;”<-
<note>original Latin: *Victrix Causa Deo placuit, sed Victa Catoni;* This famous line refers to the Roman Civil War; while the gods (Providence) allowed Caesar to win, the virtuous Cato chose the losing side of the Republic.</note>

The objection continues that the **unjust** and **ungodly** often **live in total prosperity**, while the **innocent** and **devout worshippers of the deity** struggle with **adversity** all their lives. Atheists argue that if there were a **God** and **Providence**, **profane** and **irreligious persons** would be immediately **struck by lightning from heaven** or otherwise made into obvious **objects of divine vengeance**. Likewise, they expect the **pious** to be miraculously—

<page-num>878</page-num>
<header>Providence in the Oeconomy Book I.</header>

...piously protected and rescued from evil and harms.

Now, we grant indeed that this consideration has greatly puzzled and unsettled weak minds in all ages. Because *sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the hearts of the sons of men are fully set in them to do evil* <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 8:11.</note>. And the *Psalmist* himself was at one time much perplexed by this *phenomenon*—the *prosperity of the ungodly*, who *set their mouths against heaven, and whose tongues walk through the earth; so that he was tempted to think he had cleansed his heart in vain and washed his hands in innocence* (until at length, entering into the sanctuary of God, his mind became illuminated and his soul fixed in a firm trust and confidence in divine Providence: *Whom have I in heaven but you, etc. My flesh and my heart fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever* <note>References to Psalm 73.</note>). 

For as some will be inclined to infer from this that there is no God at all, but that blind *chance* and *fortune* steer everything (the *fool has said in his heart, "There is no God"*), so others will conclude that though there is a God, he either does not know what is done here below (*"How does God know? And is there knowledge in the Most High?"*), or else will not so far humble himself, or disturb his own *ease* and *quiet*, as to concern himself with our *lowly human affairs*.

<margin>
Thus did some in *Plato* conclude from this: "That gods exist, but they neglect human affairs." <note>original: εἶναι μὲν Θεὸς, τὰ δ' ἀνθρωπίνων ἀμελεῖν πραγμάτων</note>. *Laws*, Book 10.
</margin>

First of all, therefore, we say here that it is altogether unreasonable to demand that divine Providence should miraculously intervene at every turn to *punish the ungodly* and *preserve the pious*, thereby perpetually interrupting the course of nature. Such a thing would look like a "botch" or a "bungle"—a forced and violent business. Instead, Providence carries things forward in a *silent path* <note>original: ἀψόφῳ κελεύθῳ</note>, showing its art and skill in making things naturally unwind and clear up at last into a satisfactory conclusion. 

*Passion* and *self-interest* are blind or short-sighted; but that which steers the whole world is no foolish, irritable, impatient, or passionate thing, but an *impartial, disinterested, and unburdened nature*. Nevertheless, it is certain that we have sometimes seen instances in extraordinary cases of a *God from the machine* <note>original: θεὸς ἀπὸ μηχανῆς; a reference to the theatrical device where a god appears to resolve a hopeless plot</note>—God appearing, as it were, miraculously upon the stage of life and manifesting himself by taking immediate vengeance upon *notorious criminals*, or delivering his faithful servants from imminent dangers or threatened evils. This is also often done by a secret and unseen overruling of the laws of nature. 

But it must be granted that it is not always thus; the *periods* of divine Providence here in this world are commonly *longer*, and its *unfolding* is *slower*. This follows the thought of *Euripides*, which yet has a touch of *profanity* in its expression:

-> "The Deity is slow or dilatory, and this is its nature." <-
<note>original: μέλλει τὸ θεῖον δ᾽ ἔστι τοιοῦτον φύσει</note>

For this does not come from slackness or neglect in the Deity, but either from his *patience* and *long-suffering*—as he wills that men should repent—or else to teach us *patience* by his example (as *Plutarch* suggests), or...

<page-num>879</page-num>
<header>Cʜᴀᴘ. V. Of Human Affairs; Defended.</header>

...that all things may be carried out with greater pomp and solemnity; or lastly, for other particular reasons—as *Plutarch* ventures to suggest one—why it might not have been expedient for *Dionysius* the Tyrant <note>Dionysius I, the ruler of Syracuse known for his cruelty and his philosophical interests.</note>, though such a profane and irreligious person, to have been cut off suddenly. But wicked and ungodly persons often do not fail to be met with at last, and in the long run, here in this life; they are notoriously branded with the marks of divine displeasure either in themselves or their descendants. As the poet says, *Rarely does punishment fail to overtake the criminal who flees before it, even if it follows with a slow foot* <note>original: *Rarò antecedentem Scelestum, &c.* — a quote from Horace, *Odes* 3.2.31–32.</note>. It is rare that wickedness altogether escapes punishment, even if it comes slowly afterward, limping with a lame foot. As the pagan proverbs say:

->*The mills of the gods grind slowly, but they grind exceedingly fine.* <note>original: ὀψὲ θεῶν ἀλεῦσι μύλοι, ἀλέουσι δὲ λεπτά</note><-

And: *Divine justice steals on softly with woolen feet, but strikes at last with iron hands.*

Nevertheless, we cannot say that it is always this way. Wicked persons may possibly sometimes have uninterrupted prosperity here in this life, with no visible marks of divine displeasure upon them. But just as the truly virtuous will not envy them for this reason, nor complain about their own condition—knowing that *there is nothing truly evil for the good person, nor anything truly good for the wicked* <note>original: οὐδὲν κακὸν τῷ ἀγαθῷ οὐδ᾽ αὖ τῷ φαύλῳ ἀγαθόν</note>—they are so far from being shaken by this in their belief in God and providence that they are instead even more confirmed in their conviction of a *future immortality* and *judgment after death*, when all things shall be set straight and right, and *rewards* and *punishments* shall be impartially dispensed. Therefore, that saying of *Plutarch* is most true here: *There is a necessary connection between these two things—divine providence and the permanence or immortality of human souls—one and the same reason confirming them both; neither can one of these be accepted if the other is removed* <note>original: ὡς ἓν ὁ λόγος ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ τὴν πρόνοιαν ἅμα καὶ τὴν διαμονὴν τῆς ἀνθρωπίνης ψυχῆς βεβαιοῖ, καὶ θάτερον οὐκ ἔστιν ἀπολιπεῖν ἀναιροῦντα θάτερον</note>. 

But those who blame the management of things as faulty and providence as defective because judgment is not immediately executed upon the *ungodly* are like spectators of a *play*. When wicked and injurious persons are brought onto the stage, swaggering and triumphing for a while, these viewers impatiently cry out against the playwright and immediately condemn the plot. However, if they would only wait for the resolution of events and stay until the final curtain, they would see those characters leave the stage with shame and sufficient punishment. The unfolding of the world, as *Plotinus* calls it, is a *truer poem* <note>original: ἀληθέστερον ποίημα</note>, and we humans are like actors upon the stage who nevertheless insert something of our *own* into the poem as well. But God Almighty is that skillful *dramatist* who always connects what we have done before with what he brings after, creating a good, *coherent story*; and he will...
