<meta>This page continues the defense of divine providence, explaining that the apparent injustices of the world serve as a necessary trial for faith and virtue. It moves from refuting atheistic objections to addressing religious people who question God's goodness because the world seems imperfect.</meta>

<page-num>880</page-num>
<header>Not Parts of the World alone, BOOK I.</header>

...at last make it appear that a thread of exact justice ran through everything, and that rewards and punishments are measured out in "geometrical proportion" <note>original: *Geometrical Proportion* — a mathematical analogy meaning that rewards and punishments are distributed according to merit rather than simple equality.</note>.

Finally, it is inherently appropriate that there should be, somewhere, a doubtful and cloudy state of affairs to better exercise virtue and faith. For just as there could have been no Hercules if there were no monsters to subdue, so if there were no such difficulties to encounter—no puzzles or entanglements, no temptations or trials to assault us—virtue would grow sluggish. That excellent grace of faith would lack the proper occasions and objects to exercise itself upon. This is the state of things we find here; this world is like a stage erected for the more difficult parts of virtue to perform. Here we must live by faith and not by sight—that faith which is "the substance of things hoped for, and the evidence of things not seen" <note>A quotation from Hebrews 11:1.</note>. It is a belief in the goodness, power, and wisdom of God even when everything around us is dark and cloudy. "The just shall live by his faith" <note>A quotation from Habakkuk 2:4 and Romans 1:17.</note>.

We have now sufficiently refuted the second atheistic objection against Providence regarding the conduct and "economy" <note>original: *Oeconomy* — the divine management or administration of the world.</note> of human affairs. Nevertheless, this is a vast field, and much more could be said in defense of Providence regarding these and other examples if we had more room to elaborate. Therefore, to supplement what remains, we refer the reader to the writings of others who have professionally undertaken "apologies" <note>original: *Apology’s* — formal defenses or justifications.</note> for Providence, concerning both the "fabric" <note>The physical structure of the universe.</note> and the management of the world—especially the learned and clever author of the *Divine Dialogues* <note>Henry More (1614–1687), a philosopher and contemporary of the author.</note>. 

We will only add a few considerations here—not so much to refute atheists, but for the better satisfaction of those religious people who, by too easily concluding that everything could have been much better than it is, are prone to question the divine attribute of goodness in its full extent. Yet that goodness is the only foundation of our Christian faith.

First, we say that when judging the works of God, we should not consider the parts of the world only by themselves and then blame the Maker of the whole because we can imagine much finer things. It is as if someone focused only on this Earth—which is the lowest and most "dreggy" <note>original: *Dreggy* — like the sediment or coarsest part of a liquid; here meaning the most material and least pure part of the universe.</note> part of the universe—or blamed plants because they lack senses, animals because they lack reason, humans because they are not "demons" <note>original: *Demons* — in the classical sense, these are intermediary spirits or lesser deities, not necessarily evil beings.</note> or angels, and angels because they are not gods or lack divine perfection. On that basis, God should either have made nothing at all (since nothing besides himself can be absolutely perfect), or else he should have made nothing but the higher rank of angelic beings who are free from mortality and all the other evils that affect mankind. Or perhaps he should have made such fine things as the gods of Epicurus were imagined to be—living in certain delightful regions where there were no blustering winds, lowering clouds, nipping frosts, or scorching heat, nor any night or shadow; but only the calm and unclouded "ether" <note>original: *Æther* — the clear sky or the upper regions of air beyond the clouds.</note> always smiling with gentle serenity.

# Chapter V. The Whole Must Be Considered

If there were only one kind of thing (the *Best*) made in this way, there could have been no *Music* or *Harmony* at all in the world for lack of *Variety*. But we ought, in the first place, to consider the *Whole*—whether that is not the *Best* that could be made, having all that belongs to it—and then the *Parts* in reference to the *Whole*, to see whether they are not, in their several degrees and ranks, *fitting* and *agreeable* to it. This is a point that has been so well argued by **Plotinus** <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was a major Greek-speaking philosopher and the founder of Neoplatonism.</note> that we cannot speak better on it than in **his words**.

<margin>Page 256.</margin> <note>original Greek: Ὅλον γάρ τι ἐποίησε πάγκαλον, καὶ αὔταρκες, καὶ φίλον αὑτῷ, καὶ τοῖς μέρεσι τοῖς αὑτοῦ, τοῖς τε κυριωτέροις καὶ τοῖς ἐλάττοσιν ὡσαύτως προσφόροις· ὁ τοίνυν ἐκ τῶν μερῶν τὸ ὅλον αἰτιώμενος, ἄτοπος ἂν εἴη τῆς αἰτίας· τά τε γὰρ μέρη πρὸς αὐτὸ τὸ ὅλον δεῖ σκοπεῖν εἰ σύμφωνα καὶ ἁρμόττοντα ἐκείνῳ, καὶ τὸ ὅλον σκοπόμενον, μὴ πρὸς μέρη ἄττα μικρὰ βλέπειν· τοῦτο γὰρ οὐ τὸν κόσμον αἰτιωμένου ἀλλά τινα τῶν αὐτοῦ χωρὶς λαβόντα, οἷον εἰ, καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς.</note> *God made the Whole most beautiful, entire, complete, and sufficient; everything agreeing in a friendly way with itself and its parts; both the nobler and the lesser parts being alike fitting to it.*

Whoever, therefore, blames the whole because of its *parts* is an *absurd and unjust critic. For we ought to consider the parts, not alone by themselves, but in reference to the whole, to see whether they are harmonious and agreeable to the same. Otherwise, we shall not be blaming the universe, but only some of its parts taken by themselves; as if one should blame the hair or toes of a man, taking no notice at all of his divine face and appearance; or, ignoring all other animals, one should focus only on the most contemptible of them; or lastly, overlooking all other men, consider only the most deformed Thersites* <note>Thersites was a character in Homer's Iliad described as the ugliest and most foul-mouthed of the Greek soldiers.</note>. But that which God made was the Whole as one single thing; and he who pays attention to it may hear it speaking to him in this manner:

> *God Almighty has made me, and from Him I came, perfect and complete, standing in need of nothing because within me all things are contained: plants and animals, good souls, and men happy with virtue; and innumerable spirits <note>original: *Demons* — in Greek philosophy, *daimones* were intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil.</note>, and many gods. Nor is the Earth alone adorned within me with all kinds of plants and a variety of animals; nor does the power of the soul extend at most no further than to the seas—as if the whole Air, Ether <note>original: *Æther* — the material that fills the region of the universe above the terrestrial sphere.</note>, and Heaven were, in the meantime, quite empty of soul and altogether unadorned with living inhabitants. Moreover, all things within me desire the Good, and everything reaches for it according to its own power and nature. For the whole world depends upon that First and Highest Good—the gods themselves who reign in my various parts, and all animals and plants, and whatever seems to be inanimate within me. For some things within me partake only of Being; some of Life also; some of Sensation; some of Reason; and some of Intellect <note>original: *Intellect* — referring to higher spiritual intuition or pure mind.</note> above Reason. But no man ought to require equal things from unequal ones; nor that the finger should see instead of the eye; it is enough for the finger to be a finger and to perform its own duty.*

And again afterward: <note>original Greek: Ὥσπερ τεχνίτης οὐ πάντα τὰ ἐν τῷ ζώῳ ὀφθαλμοὺς ποιεῖ, οὕτως οὐδ' ὁ λόγος πάντα θεὸς εἰργάζετο· ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν θεὸς, τὰ δὲ δαίμονας δευτέραν φύσιν, εἶτα ἀνθρώπους, καὶ ζῶα ἐφεξῆς, οὐ φθόνῳ, ἀλλὰ λόγῳ ποικιλίαν νοερὰν ἔχοντι· ἡμεῖς δὲ ὥσπερ οἱ ἄπειροι γραφικῆς τέχνης αἰτιῶνται, ὡς οὐ καλὰ τὰ χρώματα πανταχοῦ, ὁ δ' ἄρα τὰ προσήκοντα ἀπέδωκεν ἑκάστῳ τόπῳ· ἢ εἴτις δρᾶμα μέμφοιτο, ὅτι μὴ πάντες ἥρωες ἐν αὐτῷ, καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς·</note> *Just as a crafts-*

# The Vastness of the Universe Book I.

<page-num>882</page-num>

...[An arti]ficer would be like a man who, seeing a great building constructed as an hospital, should find fault that the **Divine Logos** <note>original: *ΝόγOς* (Logos); the Divine Word or Reason</note> or the **generative reason** <note>original: *Spermatick Reason*; in Neoplatonic philosophy, these are the life-giving principles that organize the natural world</note> of the **World** made all things **Gods**; but instead made some **Gods**, some **spirits** <note>original: *Demons*; here referring to *daimones*, intermediary beings between gods and humans, not necessarily evil spirits</note>, some **Men**, and some **Lower Animals**. This was not done out of **envy**, but to display its own **variety** and **fertility**. 

We are like **unskilled spectators** of a **picture** who condemn the **painter** <note>original: *Limner*</note> because he has not put **bright colors** everywhere; whereas he has suited his **colors** to every part respectively, giving to each what belonged to it. Or else we are like those who would blame a **comedy** or **tragedy** because the actors were not all **kings** or **heroes**, but included some **servants** and **peasant characters** <note>original: *Rustick Clowns*</note> who talk in their **rude fashion**. Yet the **dramatic poem** would be neither **complete**, nor **elegant** and **delightful**, if those **lesser parts** <note>original: *Worser Parts*</note> were taken out of it.

Again, we cannot certainly conclude that the **works of God** and his **creation** do not transcend those narrow **limits** which **common opinion** and **imagination** set for them. People commonly think the **universe** ends just a little above the **clouds**, or at most suppose the **fixed stars**—all fastened in **one solid sphere**—to be the **outermost wall**, the **arched roof**, and the **rolling circumference** of it. Much less should we, based on such **groundless suppositions**, infer that the **world** might have been made much **better** than it is simply because it might have been much more **roomy** and **spacious**. 

We reject the **atheistic infinity** of **distant worlds**; nor can we admit that **Cartesian** <note>Referring to the philosophy of René Descartes</note>—seemingly more modest—**indefinite extension** of one **corporeal universe**. That view, according to that philosopher’s meaning, really has **no bounds** <note>original Latin: *Nullos Fines*</note> or limits at all. For we persuade ourselves that the **corporeal world** is as **incapable** of a **positive infinity** of **size** as it is of **time**; there is no **magnitude** so **great** that more could not still be **added** to it. 

Nevertheless, just as we cannot possibly **imagine** the **Sun** to be even a **quarter** or a **hundredth part** as big as we know it actually is, the whole **corporeal universe** may far transcend those narrow **bounds** in which our **imagination** would confine it. The **new celestial phenomena** and the late **improvements** of **astronomy** and **philosophy** make it seem very probable that even this **dull Earth** of ours is a **planet**, and the **Sun** is a **fixed star** at the **center** of that **vortex** <note>In Cartesian physics, a "vortex" was a large circling band of matter that carried planets around a star</note> in which it moves. Because of this, many have strongly suspected that there are other **habitable globes** besides this **Earth** of ours (which may be **sailed** around in a year or two), as well as more **Suns** with their respective **planets** than just **one**. 

Furthermore, the **distance** of all the **fixed stars** from us is so **vast** that the **diameter** of the **Earth's orbit** <note>original: *Great Orb*</note> creates no noticeable **parallax** <note>The apparent displacement of an object when viewed from different perspectives; its absence suggested the stars were much further away than previously thought</note> in their position. From this, it is also probable that the other **fixed stars** are likewise vastly distant from one another. **This**, I say, widens the **corporeal universe** for us, and makes those **flaming walls of the world** <note>original Latin: *Flammantia Moenia Mundi*</note>, as **Lucretius** <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), a Roman poet and philosopher</note> calls them, fly away before us. Now, it is not reasonable to think that all this **immense vastness** should lie **waste**, **desert**, and **uninhabited**, having nothing in it that could **praise** its **Creator** except for this **one small spot** of **Earth**. "**In my Father’s house**," (**says our Savior**), "**are many mansions**." And **Baruch**,

# Chapter V. Future and Past, with Present.

...Baruch <note>original: "ruch"; referring to the Book of Baruch 3:24–25 from the biblical Apocrypha</note> (Chapter 3, appointed by our Church to be read publicly): *O Israel, how great is the house of God, and how large is the place of his possession? <margin>Page 264.</margin>
We shall add but one thing more: that to make a right judgment of the **ways of Providence** <note>the protective care of God or nature as a spiritual power</note>, and the **justice** thereof, regarding the **economy of mankind** <note>original: "Oeconomy"; the management or divine arrangement of human affairs</note>, we must look both **forwards** and **backwards**; or **besides** the **present**, look not only upon the **future**, but also the **past time**. This rule is likewise set down by Plotinus <note>a major Greek-speaking philosopher of the 3rd century</note>: "Neither is that doctrine of the ancients to be neglected, which says that to give an account of Providence, we ought to look back upon former periods, as well as forward to what is future." <note>original Greek: οὐδ᾿ ἐκεῖνον ἀποβλητέον τὸν λόγον, ὃς οὐ πρὸς τὸ παρὸν ἑκάστῳ φησὶ βλέπειν· ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὰς πρόσθεν περιόδους, καὶ αὖ τὸ μέλλον</note> Indeed, he and those other **philosophers** who were **religious** understood this so as to conclude that a **pre-existent state** of all **particular souls**—wherein they were at first created by God **pure**, but by the abuse of their own **liberty degenerated**—was a **necessary hypothesis** for resolving that phenomenon of the **depraved state** of mankind in general here in this life. And not only so, but they endeavored in like manner to give an account also of those different conditions of particular persons regarding **morality** from their infancy, and their other different fates here, deriving them all "from things done in a former life" <note>original Greek: ἐκ τῶν προβεβιωμένων</note>, that is, from their several behaviors heretofore in a **pre-existent state**. And there have not lacked **Christian doctors** <note>teachers or theologians</note> who have complied with these **philosophers** in both views. But our **common Christianity** only agrees thus far: as to suppose a kind of **imputative pre-existence** in **Adam**, in whom all were created **pure**, and so consequently involved in his later miscarriage, to explain the **depravity** <note>original: "Pravity"</note> of **human nature**; upon which account we are all said to be, "by nature children of wrath." <note>original Greek: φύσει τέκνα ὀργῆς</note>

<meta>This page continues the defense of Divine Providence against the objection that managing the entire universe would be a distracting and laborious burden for God. It moves from discussing the vastness of the universe to the mechanism by which God governs it without being overwhelmed.</meta>

# BOOK I. Providence is not Laborious

*Even if this were possible, such an infinite amount of busyness <note>original: "negotiosity"</note> would be very uneasy and distracting to God, and altogether inconsistent with happiness. Nor would a being of irresistible power concern itself with the good or welfare of anything else; it stands in need of nothing, and all benevolence and goodwill arise from need and weakness <note>original: "indigency and imbecillity"</note>. Therefore, such a being would be entirely taken up in the enjoyment of itself and its own happiness, utterly regardless of all other things.*

To which the *reply* is, first: that although we ourselves and all created beings have only a finite power of attention <note>original: "animadversion"</note> and a narrow sphere of activity, it does not follow that the case must be the same with the Deity, who is supposed to be a being infinitely perfect, <term>lacking nothing <note>original Greek: ἀνελλιπής (anellipēs)</note></term>, having no defect of either knowledge or power. This objection is merely an *Idol of the Cave* <note>original Latin: "Idolum Specus"; a term from Francis Bacon referring to errors of judgment based on an individual's limited perspective</note>, where men measure the Deity by their own small scale and narrowness. Indeed, if there were nothing at all except what we ourselves could fully comprehend, there could be no God. If the Sun were a living creature and had life extending as far as its rays and light, it would see and perceive every atom of matter that its outstretched beams reached and touched. Now, all created beings are themselves, in some sense, but the *rays of the Deity*; therefore, God cannot help but feel and sensibly perceive all these outpourings and emanations of his own. Humans themselves can order and manage affairs in several distant places at once without any disturbance, and we have innumerable *notions* of things in our minds that lie there easily together without crowding one another or causing any *distraction* to us.

Nevertheless, the minds of weak mortals may be somewhat eased and helped here by considering what has been suggested before: that *there is no necessity for God Almighty to* <term>do all things himself <note>original Greek: αὐτουργεῖν ἅπαντα (autourgein hapanta)</note></term> immediately and through manual labor. Instead, he may have his inferior ministers and executors under him to relieve him of that supposed burden. First of all, there is an *artificial plastic nature* <note>a formative, unconscious force that shapes the physical world according to divine design</note> which, without knowledge or *animal consciousness*, organizes the matter of the universe according to the *platform* or *idea* of a *perfect mind* and forms the bodies of all animals. This was the reason why we previously insisted so much upon this *artificial, regular, and methodical nature*: namely, so that Divine Providence might neither be excluded from having an influence upon all things in this lower world (as if they resulted only from the *accidental motions of mindless matter* unguided by any mind), nor should the Deity be supposed to do everything himself *immediately* and *miraculously* without the *subservient ministry* of any *natural causes*. To us mortals, that would seem to be not only a violent process, but also a *laborious, cumbersome, and heavy business*. Thus, Plato acknowledged that there were <term>certain causes of a prudent—that is, artificial and orderly—nature, which God uses as servants in the management of the world <note>original Greek: ἔμφρονος φύσεως αἰτίαι αἷς ὑπηρετούσαις χρῆται ὁ θεός (emphronos physeōs aitiai hais hypēretousais chrētai ho theos)</note></term>. In addition to these are those *instincts* impressed upon animals, which they follow *passively*, directing them to act for ends that they either do not understand or do not notice, for the sake of their own good.

# CHAP. V. and Distractions to the Deity.

...and the good of the universe are another part of that *Divine Fate* which, being embedded into things themselves, acts as the *servant and executor of Providence*. Above all these, there are yet other conscious and intelligent ministers of the *Deity*, serving as its *eyes and hands*. These are *demonic or angelic beings* <note>The author uses "Demoniack" in the classical sense of 'daimones'—guardian spirits or intermediate beings—rather than evil spirits.</note> appointed to preside over mankind, all worldly affairs, and the things of nature, having their several distinct offices and provinces assigned to them. Regarding this, *Plato* also writes: <margin>Page 903.</margin> *“There are certain rulers or presidents appointed by that supreme God, who governs the whole world, over all the several things and parts within it, even down to the smallest detail of every action.”* <note>original Greek: τούτοις εἰσὶν ἄρχοντες προστεταγμένοι ἑκάστοις, ἐπὶ τὸ σμικρώτατον ἀεὶ πάσης τῆς πράξεως</note> All of these *inferior causes* are constantly overseen and supervised by the *watchful eye of God Almighty* himself, who may also occasionally intervene in extraordinary ways.

We do not, therefore, need to restrict and confine *Divine Providence* to only a few major things, as some do to suggest the *Deity* requires ease and *freedom from distraction*. Instead, we can and should extend it to all things whatsoever, *small* as well as *great*. Indeed, the *great* things of the world cannot be properly ordered without regard for the *small* and *little*. *As architects say, large stones cannot be well-placed in a building without small ones.* <note>original Greek: οὐδὲ γὰρ ἄνευ σμικρῶν τοὺς μεγάλους φασὶν οἱ λιθολόγοι λίθους εὖ κεῖσθαι</note> Generals of armies, governors of families, captains of ships, and skilled craftsmen cannot perform their functions or do their work as they should if they do not attend to the *small* things as well as the *great*.

The aforementioned philosopher says: *“Let us not, therefore, consider God Almighty inferior to mortal craftsmen <term>opificers <note>original: "Opificers"</note></term> who, being better at their work, use a single art to manage both small and great things with more accuracy and perfection. Let us not suppose him to be indifferent <note>original: "supine"</note> and negligent.”* <note>original Greek: Μὴ τοίνυν... σμικρά τε καὶ μεγάλα ἀπεργάζονται</note> Nevertheless, the *chief concern and employment of Divine Providence* in the world is the *stewardship <term>economy <note>original: "Oeconomy"</note></term> of souls*, or the government of rational beings. This is summarized by *Plato* in this way: <margin>Page 903.</margin> *“There is no other work left for the supreme governor <note>The Greek "petteutē" refers to a player of a board game, suggesting God moves souls like pieces on a board.</note> but to move the character that has become better into a better place and condition, and the worse into a worse.”* <note>original Greek: οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἔργον τῷ πεττευτῇ λείπεται πλὴν μετατιθέναι τὸ μὲν ἄμεινον γινόμενον ἦθος εἰς βελτίω τόπον χεῖρον δὲ εἰς τὸν χείρονα, &c.</note> Or, as he adds later, to dispose of everyone in the world in a way that best results in *“virtue being victorious and vice defeated.”* <note>original Greek: νικῶσαν ἀρετήν, ἡττωμένην δὲ κακίαν</note> In this way, the slow and *imperfect minds of mortals* may be satisfied that *Providence is not a burdensome <term>moliminous <note>original: "Moliminous"</note></term>, laborious, or distracting thing for the Deity*.

But [the opponents argue] that there is no higher source of life in *rational animals* than *narrow self-love*, and that all *goodwill and benevolence* arises only from *need and weakness <term>indigency and imbecility <note>original: "Indigency and Imbecillity"</note></term>*. They claim that no *being* whatsoever is concerned with the welfare of any other thing except for what it needs itself. And lastly, they claim that what is *irresistibly powerful*...

<meta>This page continues the refutation of atheistic arguments regarding the nature of God. Specifically, it addresses the idea that a self-sufficient being would have no reason to care for or create other beings, following the previous discussion on how Divine Providence manages the universe without being burdened by it.</meta>

885 Atheist Queries Answered. BOOK. I.

...powerful and needs nothing; it would have no benevolence or concern for the good and welfare of anything whatsoever. This is merely another **"Idol of the Atheist’s Den"** <note>This is a reference to Francis Bacon's "Idols of the Den," which are false beliefs arising from an individual's specific nature or education.</note> and only proves their bad nature, low minds, and gross immorality. The same applies to their other maxim: **that a perfectly happy being would have nothing at all to do** except enjoy its own ease and quiet. However, nothing is more troublesome to us than this <term>ataraxia</term> <note>original Greek: ἀταραξία; a state of complete calm or idleness</note>, this state of **having nothing to do**. The **activity of the Deity**, or a perfect being, is just as much a state of ease for him as is his very existence.

The **atheistic questions** are next to be answered. Since there are only three, they are naturally arranged in this order: First, **if there were a God or a perfect being who was already perfectly happy in himself, why would he bother to create a world?** Second, **if he had to make a world, why did he not make it sooner?** This **late production** makes it look as if he had only just woken up from a long sleep throughout infinite past ages, or had eventually grown tired of his solitude. Third and last, **what tools or instruments, machines or engines did he have? Or how could he move the matter of the whole world, especially if he is incorporeal?** If he were purely spirit, he would pass through all things and could not grasp or take hold of anything.

Regarding the first question, we say that the reason God made the world was out of his own **overflowing and communicative goodness**, so that there might be other beings who could also be **happy** and enjoy existence alongside him. This does not conflict with the idea that God made the world for his own **glory** and **honor**, although the philosopher **Plotinus** was cautious about that phrase: <term>It is ridiculous to say that God made the world so that he might be honored; this would be to project the motivations of human craftsmen and sculptors onto him.</term> <note>original Greek: γελοῖον ἵνα τιμᾶται, καὶ μεταφερόντων ἀπὸ τῶν ἀγαλματοποιῶν τῶν ἐνταῦθα</note> But the main reason Plotinus said this was because he believed the world proceeded not so much from the **will** of the Deity as from the **necessity** of his nature. It is also true that God did not make the world merely to show off his **skill** and **power**, but to share his goodness. This goodness is primarily and properly his **glory**, just as the **light** and **radiance of the sun** is its glory. But the atheist asks: **"What harm would it have done us never to have been created?"** The answer is easy: we would then never have enjoyed any **good** or been capable of **happiness**. If no rational creatures had been made at all, it would have been due to either a **powerless sterility** in the Deity, or a **jealous, narrow, and restricted selfishness**—a lack of kindness and shared goodness. Both of these are inconsistent with a **perfect being**. The argument can be turned back against these atheists: **what harm would it be for us to cease to exist or become nothing?** If existence is of no value, why then are these atheists, just like everyone else, so unwilling to die?

Then they argue further: why was the world not made...

# Chapter V: The World is Incapable of Eternity

...made sooner, since this *goodness* of God was without date, and from *everlasting*? But this *question* may be taken in two different *senses*: either, *Why was not the world from eternity, as God and his goodness are eternal?* or else secondly, *If the world could not be from eternity, yet why was it not made sooner, rather than so lately?* In both of these *queries*, the *atomic atheists* <note>original: "Atomick Atheists"; those who followed the ancient philosophy that the world is composed of atoms and happened by chance, rather than divine design.</note> take it for granted that the system of the world was not from eternity, but had a beginning. 

Now we say that the *reason* why the world was not *made from eternity* was not from any *defect* of *goodness* in the *divine will*, but because there is an *absolute impossibility* in the thing itself; or because the *necessity* and *incapacity* of such an *imperfect being* hindered it. For we must confess, that for our part, we are prone to believe that could the world have been from eternity, it should certainly have been so. And just so does *Philoponus* <note>John Philoponus (c. 490–570 AD), an Alexandrian Christian philosopher and scientist.</note>, in his *confutation of Proclus's arguments for the world's eternity* <note>Proclus was a Neoplatonist philosopher who argued the world must be eternal if its cause (God) is eternal.</note>, declare himself:

<margin>Page 4</margin>

-> "And we also, supposing the world not to be eternal, neither take away the fact that God is always good, nor do we accuse his creative power of weakness; but we suppose that the world cannot always exist because of the very nature of that which is created." <note>original Greek: Καὶ ἡμεῖς ἄρα μὴ εἶναι τὸν κόσμον ἀΐδιον ὑποτιθέμενοι, οὔτε τὸ εἶναι τὸν Θεὸν ἀεὶ ἀγαθὸν ἀφαιρούμεθα, οὔτε ἀσθένειαν τῇ δημιουργικῇ αὐτοῦ κατηγοροῦμεν δυνάμεως· ἀλλὰ μὴ δύνασθαι ἀεὶ εἶναι τὸν κόσμον δι᾿ αὐτὴν τὴν τοῦ γινομένου φύσιν ὑπετιθέμεθα.</note> <-

In the following words, he gives a twofold account of this *impossibility* of the world's eternity:

-> "First, because it was impossible for an actual infinity to exist, or to be traversed [run through]; and secondly, because that which is made or brought into being by another, as a distinct thing from it, cannot be co-eternal with its maker." <note>original Greek: ὅτι τε τὸ ἄπειρον κατ᾿ ἐνέργειαν ὑποστῆναι, ἢ διεξίτητον εἶναι, ἀδύνατον ἦν· καὶ ὅτι συναΐδιον εἶναι τῷ ποιοῦντι τὸ γινόμενον φύσιν οὐκ ἔχοι.</note> <-

Here it is probable that *Philoponus*, being a Christian, did not intend to oppose the *eternal generation* of the *Son of God*, but only to assert that nothing which was properly *made* or *created by God*, and nothing which was not itself *God*, could be from eternity or without a beginning. And now we see how those *atheistic exceptions* against the *newness* <note>original: "Novity"</note> of the *divine creation*—as if God must therefore either have slept from eternity, or else eventually grew tired <note>original: "contracted a Satiety"</note> of his former *solitude*, and the like—do of themselves quite vanish into *nothing*.

But then as to the *second sense* of the *question*: *Why the world, though it could not possibly be from eternity, was nonetheless made no sooner, but so lately?* We say that this is an *absurd question*, both because *time* was made together with the world, and there was no *sooner or later before time*; and also because *whatsoever had a beginning must of necessity be once but a day old.* Therefore, the world could not possibly have been so made by God in time as not to be, at some point, only *five or six thousand years old and no more, as it is now.*

And as for the *third and last query: How God could move and command the matter of the whole world, especially if he is incorporeal?* We reply: first, that all other things are derived from God as their only *fountain* and *original*, and *essentially* depend on him, who by his *absolute power* also could annihilate whatsoever he crea-

# No Interest in Atheism. BOOK I.

...Since God created all things, he must necessarily have **absolute power** over everything; and every thing whatsoever must be **naturally subject** and **compliant** to him. And since no body <note>meaning: a physical object or matter</note> can possibly **move itself**, that which first moved **matter** must of necessity be **incorporeal** <note>non-physical or spiritual</note>. Nor could it move matter by **local motion** <note>movement from one place to another</note>, as one body moves another, or as **engines** and **machines** move by **thrusting** or **pushing** (they being moved themselves beforehand). Instead, it must move matter by another kind of **action**—one that is not **local motion** or **movement caused by another** <note>original: *Heterocinesie*</note>, but **self-movement** <note>original: *Autocinesie*</note>; that is, by **thought**.

Therefore, that **notion** held by **atheists**—that a **non-physical deity** could not possibly move the **matter** of the **world** because he would pass right through it and could not fasten or lay hold of it—is **absurd**. This is because God moves matter not **mechanically**, but **vitally**, and by **thought** alone. That a **thinking being** as such has a **natural sovereignty** <note>original: *Imperium*</note> over **matter** and the **power** to **move** it without any **engines** or **machines** is unquestionably certain, even from the example of our own **souls**. Our souls move our **bodies** and **command** them in every way, merely by **will** and **thought**. A **perfect mind**, presiding over the **matter** of the whole world, could move the whole **physical universe** much more irresistibly and with infinitely more ease, merely by **will** and **thought**, than we can move our own **bodies**.

The **last head of atheist argumentation** is from **interest** <note>meaning: self-interest or what is beneficial for a person</note>. **First**, the **atheists** would persuade us that it is in the **interest** of mankind in **general**, and of **every particular person**, that there **should be no God**. By this, they mean **no being who is infinitely powerful and has no law but his own will**, and who therefore may punish whom he pleases **eternally** after death.

To this, our **first reply** is: if there is a God and souls are immortal, then a person's thinking otherwise will not change the situation, nor afford the **atheists** any relief against those two imagined evils of theirs. For **things are stubborn** <note>original: "Things are Sullen"</note> and will be as they are, whatever we think of them or wish them to be. Men will at last discover their error when perhaps it may be too late. **Wishing** is no **proving**; therefore, this **atheist argument** from **interest** is no argument at all against the **existence** of a **God**. It is nothing but the ignorant wish and vain desire of **foolish atheists**.

In the next place, this **wish of atheists** is founded entirely upon a **mistaken notion** of **Almighty God** as well—the idea that he is nothing but **arbitrary, all-powerful will**, which indeed is not a desirable thing. But as has been often declared, the **will of God** is the **will of goodness, justice**, and **wisdom** itself, all-powerful. His will is not mere **will**—the kind that has no other **reason** besides itself—but it is **law, equity**, and **fairness** <note>original: "Chancery"; refers to a court of equity that provided remedies where the strict common law failed</note>. It is **that which ought to be** <note>original: *τὸ δέον*</note> itself, decreeing, willing, and acting.

Neither does God punish anyone out of a delight in punishment, or in the evil and suffering of the persons punished. Rather, for those who are not **incurable** <note>original: *ἀνίατοι*</note>, his **punishment is medicine** <note>original: *δίκη ἰατρεία*</note>; it is **remedy** <note>original: "Physick"</note> intended for their recovery and amendment. So, the source and fountain of punishment is actually **goodness** to the...

### CHAPTER V. Infinite Hopes from the Deity.

...the **people** themselves **punished**. But for those who are **incurable**, the **punishment** inflicted on them is **intended** for the **good** of the **whole**. Therefore, this **attribute of justice** in **God** does not at all **conflict** with the **attribute of goodness**; it is simply a **branch** or a **particular expression** of it. **Goodness** and **justice** in **God** are always **intertwined** <note>original: "complicated"</note>; His **goodness** is not a foolish indulgence <note>original: "fondness"</note>, nor is His **justice cruelty**. Instead, He is both **good** in **punishing** and **just** in **rewarding** and **giving benefits**. Therefore, it can be in no one’s **interest** that there should be no **God** or **immortality**, unless perhaps for those **desperately** and **incurably** wicked people who, having abandoned their true **interest** of being **good**, now have no other **interest** left but **not to exist** or to become **nothing**.

To be without a **God** is to be without **hope** in the **world**, for **atheists** can have neither **faith** nor **hope** in **mindless matter** and its **accidental** <note>original: "fortuitous"</note> **motions**. And even if a **thinking being** had a great deal of **enjoyment** in the **present**, it could not possibly be **happy** without **immortality** and the **security** of its **future continuance**. But the **atheists** conclude that there is **nothing immortal** and that all **life perishes** and **vanishes** into **nothing**. Consequently, they also believe that <gloss>happiness is non-existent</gloss> <note>original: *eudaimonia anyparkton*</note>—that it is a thing that has no **existence** in **nature**, but is a mere **figment** and **illusion** <note>original: "chimæra"</note>, or an **idle wish** and **vain dream** of **mortals**. Therefore, it cannot be in the **interest** of **mankind** for this **hypothesis** to be **true**, as it plainly cuts off all **hope** from **men** and leaves them with an **utter impossibility** of ever being **happy**.

**God** is such a **being** that, if we could suppose Him not to exist, there is nothing that anyone who is not desperately committed to **wickedness**—including the **atheists** themselves—could possibly **wish** for or **desire** more. **To believe** in a **God** is **to believe** in the **existence** of all **possible good** and **perfection** in the **universe**. **It is to believe** that things are as they **should be**, and that the **world** is so well **framed** and **governed** that the **whole system** could not **possibly** have been **better**. For the ability to sin <term>peccability</term> arises from the **necessity** of **imperfect beings with free will** being left to themselves; therefore, it could not have been excluded even by **omnipotence** itself. And though **actual sin** might perhaps have been kept out by **force** and **violence**, yet when everything is **considered**, it was undoubtedly best for the **good** of the **whole** that it should not be **forcibly hindered** in that way. There is **nothing** that a **good** man cannot **hope** for from the **Deity**—whatever **happiness** his **being** is **capable** of, and **such things as eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor can now enter into the heart of man to conceive** <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 2:9</note>. **Infinite hopes** lie before us because of the **existence** of a **being infinitely good** and **powerful** and the **immortality of our own souls**. Nothing can **hinder** or **obstruct these hopes** except our own **wickedness** of **life**. **To believe** in a **God** and to **do** well are the **two** most **hopeful**, **cheerful**, and **comfortable** things that can possibly be. And to this purpose is that saying of **Linus** <note>A legendary figure in Greek mythology, often cited as a poet and musician</note>:

->To Hope<- <note>original: *Elpesthai*</note>

We now come to the **final atheistic argument**. In this section, they attempt to recommend their **doctrine** to **civil sovereigns** <note>kings and rulers</note> and to persuade them that **theism** (belief in God) or **religion** is absolutely **incompatible** with their **interests**. Their reasons for this are the following three. 

First, because the **civil sovereign rules** only through **fear**. Therefore, if there is any **power** or **fear** greater than the **power** and **fear** of the **Leviathan** <note>A term popularized by Thomas Hobbes to describe the all-powerful state</note>, civil authority can accomplish very little. 

Second, because **sovereignty** is by its very nature absolutely **indivisible**. It must be either **infinite** or **nothing** at all. Consequently, divine laws (both **natural** and **revealed**) that are superior to the sovereign and limit his power would effectively **destroy** it. Therefore, religion and **theism** must be pushed aside to make room for the **Leviathan** to **maneuver** as it pleases. 

Third and last, the **private judgment** of **good** and **evil**, or **just** and **unjust**, contradicts the very **existence** of a **body politic**. A state is like **one artificial man** made up of many **natural men united under one head**. It must have one **common reason**, **judgment**, and **will** ruling over the whole. However, **conscience**—which **religion** introduces—is a **private judgment** of **good** and **evil**. Therefore, it is entirely **inconsistent** with true **politics**, which can permit no **private consciences**, but only **one public conscience** based on the **law**.

In order to **answer** the first of these points, we must briefly **unravel** the **atheistic ethics** and **politics**. The foundation of their theory is first laid by **depicting human nature as villainous**. They claim that humanity does not have even the smallest **seeds** of **political** or **ethical** nature within it. They believe there is no such thing as **equity** or **philanthropy** <note>love of mankind</note>. According to them, there is no charity or benevolence except what results from **fear**, **weakness** <note>original: "Imbecillity"</note>, and **poverty** <note>original: "Indigency"</note>. There is no concern for the **public** or **common good**, but only for **private** and **selfish** interests. 

In this view, **appetite** and **utility**—the desires for sensual pleasure, honor, dominion, and **superiority** <note>original: "Precellency"</note> over others—are the only **measures** of **good** in **nature**. Therefore, nothing is **naturally just** or **unjust**, and nothing is inherently **sinful** or **unlawful**. Instead, every person by **nature** has a **right to everything** <note>original: "Jus ad omnia"</note>, whatever their **appetite** inclines them toward or whatever they judge to be **profitable**—even a right to other people's **bodies** and **lives**. **If you desire to kill, you have a natural right to do so** <note>original: "Si occidere Cupis, Jus habes"</note>. That is, you have the **liberty** to **kill** without it being a **sin** or an **injustice**. For "Right" <note>original: "Jus"</note> and "Law" or "Justice" <note>original: "Lex" or "Justitia"</note> are directly opposite to one another in the language of these **atheistic politicians**. ### Chapter 5. Atheists Vilify Human Nature.

**Beast-like <term>Belluine</term> liberty** <note>original: "Belluine," meaning characteristic of a wild beast</note> is not something created or permitted by **justice**; rather, it is founded on the assumption that justice absolutely does not exist. Therefore, if a son were not only to murder his own parents—who had tenderly raised him—but also to **exquisitely** torture them, taking pleasure in watching their sorrowful looks and hearing their lamentable **shrieks** and **outcries**, there would be **nothing** of **sin** or **injustice** in this at all, nor in anything else. This is because, according to these thinkers, **justice** is not part of **nature**, but is a merely **artificial** <note>original: "Factitious"</note> thing, **made** only by **men** and **civil laws**. 

According to the **apprehensions** of these men, **nature** has been very kind and indulgent to mankind in this regard: it has brought us into the **world** without any **fetters** or **shackles** upon us, **free** from all **duty** and **obligation**, **justice**, and **morality**. To them, these are nothing but **restraints** and **hindrances** to **true liberty**. From all of this, it follows that **nature** absolutely **dissociates** and **separates** men from one another, because their **appetites**—which are all directed only toward **private good**—are **inconsistent** with one another. Consequently, every man is by **nature** in a **state of war** and **hostility** against every other man.

In the next place, therefore, these **atheistic politicians** further argue that although this **state of nature**—which is a **liberty** from all **justice** and **obligation**, and a **lawless**, **loose**, or **beast-like right** to everything—is in itself **absolutely the best**, it nevertheless proves by **accident** to be the **worst**, due to men's **weakness** <note>original: "Imbecillity"</note>, the **equality** of their strength, and the **inconsistency** of their desires. This **war** with everyone makes a person's **right** or **liberty** to everything, in reality, a **right** or **liberty to nothing**, as they have no security for their lives, much less for the **comfortable** enjoyment of them. 

Since it is not possible for all men to have **dominion** (which would indeed be the most desirable thing according to these **principles**), the **generality** of people must necessarily feel more **evil** in such a **state of liberty** with a **universal war** against all, than they feel **good**. Therefore, after men had spent a long time **hacking**, **slashing**, and **jostling** against one another, they eventually grew weary of it. They realized it was necessary to use **art** to compensate for the **defect** of their own **power**, and to choose a **lesser evil** to avoid a **greater one**. That is, they decided to make a **voluntary reduction** of this **infinite right** and to **submit** to **terms of equality** with one another for the sake of a **sociable** and **peaceable cohabitation**. And not only **that**, but also for the **security** of **all**—to ensure that others would observe such **rules** as well as themselves—they decided to put their **necks** under the **yoke** of a **common coercive power**. The **will** of this power, being the **will** of them all, would be the very **rule**, **law**, and **measure of justice** for them.

Here, therefore, these **atheistic politicians** first of all **slander human nature** and make a **villain** of it. In the next place, they also reproach **justice** and **civil sovereignty**, making them nothing but an **ignoble** and **bastardly brat of fear**, or else a **lesser evil** submitted to merely out of **necessity** to avoid a **greater evil**—that of **war** with everyone, caused by men's **natural weakness**. So, according to this **hypothesis**, **justice** and **civil**...

# Justice to Atheists as a Necessary Evil

Government is clearly something not **good** in itself, nor **desirable** (since it is a **hindrance** to **liberty** and nothing but **shackles** and **fetters**), but it is used only by **circumstance** <note>original: "by Accident"</note> as a **necessary evil**. Thus, these politicians sometimes distinguish between **good** and **just**, saying that *good is loved for its own sake, but justice is loved only by circumstance.* <note>original Latin: "Bonum Amatur Per Se, Justum Per Accidens"</note> From this, it follows unavoidably that all men must necessarily be **unwillingly just**, <note>original Greek: "ἄκοντες δίκαιoι" (akontes dikaioi)</note> or just only with a partial rather than a full and perfect will. To them, **justice** is a thing that is not **genuinely good**, but rather has a large **amount** or **dose** of **evil** blended with it. 

This was the **old atheistic explanation for the origin** <note>original: "Generation"</note> of **justice**, and of the **body politic, civil society**, and **sovereignty**. For although a modern writer <note>This refers to Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679)</note> claims this **hypothesis** (which he looks upon as the only true **scheme of politics**) to be a **new invention**—like the **circulation of the blood** and no older than his book *On the Citizen* <note>original Latin title: "De Cive"</note>—it is actually **certain** that it was the commonly received doctrine of atheistic politicians and philosophers before **Plato's** time. Plato represents their views concerning the **origin of justice** and **civil society** in this manner:

<margin>Plato, *The Republic*, Book 2, pages 358–359.</margin> 

> First, listen to what justice is and where it came from. They say that by nature, to commit injustice is good, but to suffer it is evil. However, there is more evil in suffering it than there is good in doing it. Therefore, when men have clashed for a long time, both doing and suffering injury, those who were not strong enough to avoid the latter while achieving the former finally decided it was profitable to make a bargain with one another. They agreed through pacts and covenants neither to do nor suffer injury, but to submit to rules of equality and make laws by compact in order to live together in peace. They called the requirements of those laws "just." <note>This is a modernization of the Greek passage starting "ὃ πρῶτον ἔφην..."</note>

And then it is added:

> This, according to these philosophers, is the origin and essence of justice—a middle ground between the best and the worst. The best would be to exercise a lawless liberty to do whatever one pleases to others without suffering any consequences. The worst would be to suffer evil from others without being able to take revenge. Justice, therefore, being a middle ground between these two, is loved not as something good in itself, but only because of men's **weakness** <note>original: "Imbecillity," meaning lack of power</note> and their inability to commit injustice with impunity. For anyone who had sufficient power would never enter into such compacts or submit to equality and subjection. For example, if a man had the **magical ring** of **Gyges**, <note>In Greek legend, Gyges of Lydia found a ring that made him invisible, which he used to seize the throne.</note> which allowed him to do whatever he wanted without being seen or noticed...

# CHAPTER V. Their Authority, Created by Words.

If anyone thought this way, they would certainly never enter into covenants or submit to laws of equality and subjection. Accordingly, some of those old **atheistic philosophers** also concluded that **justice** was **another person's good** <note>original Greek: ἀλλότριον ἀγαθόν (allotrion agathon)</note>. They argued it is not properly and directly one's own good—that is, the good of the person who is just—but the good of another, partly of fellow citizens but mainly of the ruler, whose servant <note>original: "Vassal"</note> he is. It is well known that after **Plato's** time, this hypothesis concerning justice—that it was a mere manufactured <note>original: "Factitious"</note> thing arising only from human fear and weakness <note>original: "Imbecillity"</note> as a lesser evil—was also emphasized by **Epicurus**.

But let us next see how our modern atheistic philosophers and politicians handle this hypothesis to unite men by artifice <note>original: "Art"</note> into a **body politic** when they are naturally separated from one another. They also attempt to create **artificial justice** and obligation where none exists in nature. First, these makers of artificial justice, cities, and authority tell us that although men have an **infinite right by nature**, they may **alienate** <note>The original text says "Alietate," likely a printer's error for "Alienate." To alienate a right means to give it up or transfer it.</note> this right, or part of it, from themselves. They may either simply **renounce** it or **transfer** it to another person; by doing so, it becomes unlawful for them to use that right afterward. 

Thus, a recent writer <note>This refers to Thomas Hobbes</note> explains that men may declare by signs **that it is their will that it shall no longer be lawful for them to do a certain thing which they previously had a right to do** <note>original Latin: "Velle se non Licitum sibi amplius fore, certum aliquid facere quòd Jure antèa fecisse poterant"</note>. He calls this a **simple renunciation of right**. Furthermore, he says they may declare **that it is their will that it shall no longer be lawful for them to resist a specific person whom they previously could have lawfully resisted** <note>original Latin: "Velle se non Licitum sibi amplius fore alicui Resistere"</note>. This is called a **transfer** <note>original: "Translation"</note> **of right**. 

But if nothing is unlawful by its own nature, then it cannot be unlawful for a person later to use the same liberty they previously renounced or abandoned in words. No one can make something unlawful to themselves by their mere will if it was not so inherently; they can only suspend the exercise of as much of their liberty as they see fit. Even if a person could obligate <note>original: "Oblige"</note> themselves or make something unlawful by their will, nothing would be gained. This is because they could then release themselves from that obligation by their will, making the action lawful again. For what is made merely by the will can be destroyed by the will. 

Therefore, these politicians push the argument further. They tell us that no one can be obligated except by their own act, and that the **essence of injustice** is nothing other than **taking back what was previously given** <note>original Latin: "Dati Repetitio"</note>. To this we reply: if a person were naturally unobligated to anything, then they could not be obligated to stick to their own act. It would not be truly unjust or unlawful for them—upon second thought—to voluntarily undo what they had previously voluntarily done. The atheists here clearly make **injustice** a ridiculous thing. They claim it is nothing but an absurdity in life, similar to an absurdity in a debate when a person denies a proposition they had previously granted. This is not a real evil...

**Obligation; Book 1.**

In him as a **Man**, injustice is nothing more than what is called an **Absurdity** <note>In formal logic, an "absurdity" is a contradiction in an argument. The author is saying these thinkers view injustice as a logical error rather than a moral sin.</note> in a **Disputant**. That is, **Injustice** is not an **Absolute Evil** of the **Man**, but only a **Relative Incongruity** in him as a **Citizen**. 

Just as when a man speaking **Latin** fails to follow the **laws of grammar**, it is a kind of **injustice** in him as a **Latinist** or **grammarian**; so when one who lives in **civil society** fails to observe its **laws** and **conditions**, this is, as it were, the **False Latin** of a **citizen**, and nothing more. According to this **notion** of **injustice**, there is no such **real evil** or **harm** in it that could in any way withstand the **force** of **appetite** and **private utility**, or **oblige** men to **civil obedience** when it is **contrary** to their own interests. 

But these **political jugglers** and **enchanters** will here cast yet a further **mist** before men's **eyes** with their **pacts** and **covenants**. For men, they say, may **unquestionably oblige** themselves by their **covenants**, and make things **unjust** and **unlawful** to them that were not so before. Therefore, they **define injustice** again—and with more **plausibility** <note>original: "speciousness"</note>—to be the **breach of covenants**. 

But though it is true that if there is **natural justice**, then **covenants** will **oblige** us; yet if we follow the **contrary supposition**—that **nothing is naturally unjust**—then it cannot be **unjust** to **break covenants** either. **Covenants** without **natural justice** are nothing but mere **words** and **breath** (as indeed these **atheistic politicians** themselves call them, in agreement with their own **hypothesis**), and therefore they can have no **force** to **oblige** anyone. 

Consequently, these **justice-makers** are eventually forced to flee to the **laws of nature** and to **pretend** that this is a **law of nature**: *that men should stand by their pacts and covenants*. This plainly **contradicts** their main **fundamental principle** that by **nature** nothing is **unjust** or **unlawful**. For if that is so, then there can be no **laws of nature**; and if there are **laws of nature**, then there must be something **naturally unjust** and **unlawful**. 

So, this is not to **make justice**, but clearly to **unmake** their own **hypothesis** and to suppose **justice** to have been already **made by nature**, or to exist in **nature**. This is a **gross absurdity in disputation**: to **affirm** what one had previously **denied**. 

Furthermore, their **laws of nature** are indeed nothing but **juggling equivocation** <note>Deceptive wordplay or using words with double meanings.</note> and a mere **mockery**. They themselves acknowledge them to be no **laws**—because a **law** is nothing but the **word** of **him** who has **command over others**—but only **conclusions** or **theorems** concerning what leads to their own **preservation** and **defense** based on the **principle of fear**. That is, they are really the **laws** of their own **fearful** and **cowardly temperament** <note>original: "complexion"</note>. 

For those who have **courage** and **generosity** in them, according to this **hypothesis**, would never **submit** to such sneaking **terms of equality** and **subjection**. Instead, they would venture for **dominion** and resolve either to **win the saddle or lose the horse** <note>A proverbial expression meaning to risk everything to gain total control or fail completely.</note>. 

Here, therefore, our **atheistic politicians** plainly dance round in a **circle**. They first derive the **obligation** of **civil laws** from that of **covenants**, and then that of **covenants** from the **laws of nature**. And **lastly**, they derive the **obligation** of both these **laws of nature** and of **covenants** themselves from the **law**, **command**, and **sanction** of the **civil sovereign**, without which neither of them would **oblige** at all. 

Thus, it is manifest how vain the **attempts** of these **politicians** are to **make justice artificially** when there is no such thing **naturally** (which is indeed no less than trying to make **something out of nothing**); and

# CHAP. V. Artificial, nor Violent. 895

By *art* to *join* <note>original: "Consociate"</note> into *political bodies* those whom *nature* had *separated* from one another is a thing as impossible as to *tie knots* in the *wind* or *water*, or to build up a *stately palace* or *castle* out of *sand*. Indeed, the *ligaments* by which these *politicians* would tie the *members* of their huge *Leviathan* <note>A reference to Thomas Hobbes’s famous work "Leviathan" (1651), which describes the state as an artificial giant or "Artificial Man."</note> or *artificial man* together are not as good as *cobwebs*. They are really nothing but mere *will* and *words*. For if *authority* and *sovereignty* are made only by *will* and *words*, then it is plain that by *will* and *words* they may be *unmade* again at pleasure.

Neither, indeed, are these *atheistic politicians* themselves altogether unaware that this *artificial justice* and *obligation* cannot be a firm *bond* <note>original: "Vinculum"</note> of a *political body* to *join* those together and *unite* them into *one* who are *naturally separated* and *divided* from one another. They acknowledge that *contracts without the sword, being but words and breath, have no strength* to hold the *members* of their *Leviathan* or *political body* together. Therefore, they plainly resort at length from *art* to *force* and *power*, making their *civil sovereign* really *reign* only through *fear*. 

This must be their meaning when they constantly declare *all obligation, whether just* or *unjust*, to be derived only from *law*. By *law*, they understand *a command directed toward those who, because of their weakness <note>original: "Imbecillity"</note>, are not able to resist*. So, the *will* and *command* of the more *powerful* *obliges* through the *fear* of *threatened punishment*. Now, if the only *real obligation* to obey *civil laws* comes from the *fear* of *punishment*, then no man could be *obliged* to hazard his *life* for the *safety* of his prince and country. Furthermore, those who could reasonably expect to go *unpunished* would be altogether *released from obligation* and, consequently, might *justly* break any *laws* for their *own advantage*. 

This is an *assertion* so extreme <note>original: "extravagant"</note> that these *confused politicians* themselves are ashamed to plainly own it. Therefore, they *disguise* it as much as they can through *equivocation* <note>The use of ambiguous language to hide the truth.</note>. Sometimes they even confess the *truth*: *punishment does not create an obligation, but only holds those to their duty who were already obligated* <note>original: "Pœna non Obligat, sed Obligatum tenet"</note>. 

Furthermore, what is *made* by *power* and *force* alone may be *unmade* by *power* and *force* again. If *civil sovereigns reign* only through the *fear* of their own *sword*, then that *right* of theirs—so often talked about—is indeed nothing else but *might*, and their *authority* is merely *force*. Consequently, *successful* and *prosperous rebellion*, and whatever can be done by *power*, will be *by that very fact* <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> *justified*. 

Lastly, were *civil sovereigns* and *political bodies* merely *violent* and *unnatural* things, then they would all quickly *vanish* into nothing because *nature* will prevail against *force* and *violence*. Instead, we see that men everywhere constantly fall into *political order*, and the *decay* <note>original: "Corruption"</note> of one *form* of *government* is merely the *birth* <note>original: "Generation"</note> of another.

Therefore, since it is plain that *sovereignty* and *political bodies* can be neither merely *artificial* nor *violent* things, there must of necessity be some *natural bond* <note>original: "Vinculum"</note> to hold them together. This bond must be one that can really *obliges subjects* to *obey* the *lawful commands* of *sovereigns*, and *sovereigns*, in *commanding*, to seek the *good* and

<header>Sovereignty, no Creation of the People. Book I.</header>

...the welfare of their **subjects**; whom these **atheistic politicians**, (by their **infinite** and **brutal right** <note>original: "Belluine Right," from the Latin *bellua* meaning beast</note>) completely release from any such concern. This bond <note>original: "Vinculum"</note> can be nothing other than **natural justice**, and something of a **common** and **public**, a **cementing** and **binding nature** in all rational beings. The source of both of these is the **Deity**. The **right** and **authority** of God Himself is founded in **justice**, and **civil sovereignty** is a certain **participation** in this divine authority. It is not the mere **creation** of the people or of human **wills**, and therefore it is not **abolishable** by their **wills** whenever they please. Instead, it has a **stamp of divinity** upon it, as may be seen in part by this: the **right of life and death** <note>original: *Jus Vitæ & Necis*</note>, which **civil sovereigns** possess, was never held by **individuals** before the existence of **civil society**. Therefore, it could not have been **granted** by them to the ruler.

If God and nature had not created the concept of a "city" (society)—if there were not a **natural harmony** among all rational creatures and a **subjection** of them to the **Deity** as their head (which is Cicero's "**one city of gods and men**" <note>original: *Una Civitas Deorum atque Hominum*</note>)—and if God had not established the principles of **ruling and being ruled** <note>original Greek: *ἄρχειν καὶ ἄρχεσθαι*</note>, **superiority** and **subjection**, along with their respective **duty** and **obligation**, then men could never have created any firm **cities** or **political systems** through **art**, **political trickery**, or even **force**. The **civil sovereign** is no **Leviathan**, no **beast**, but a **god** (*I have said, you are gods:*). He reigns not through mere **brutal force** and **fear**, but through **natural justice** and **conscience**, and by the **right** and **authority** of God Himself. 

Nevertheless, we do not deny that there is also a need for **force** and **fear** to compel obedience from those for whom a **sense of duty** proves ineffective. Nor is the **fear** of the **civil sovereign’s** own sword enough on its own, **unassisted** by **religion** and the **fear of an invisible, omnipotent Being** who sees all things and can punish **secret**, as well as **open lawbreakers**, both in this life and after death. This is so obviously true that **atheists** have even claimed **religion** was originally nothing more than a **political invention** <note>original: "Figment"</note>. We conclude, therefore, that the **civil sovereign** does not reign merely through the **fear** of his own **power and sword**, but first through the **justice** and **authority**, and then through the **power and fear** also, of **God Almighty**. This concludes our response to the **first atheistic claim** regarding the **self-interest** of **civil sovereigns**.

Regarding their **second** claim—that **sovereignty** is **essentially infinite** and therefore completely **incompatible** with **religion**, which would **limit** and **restrict** it—we reply that the **right** and **authority** of **civil sovereigns** is not a mere **brutal liberty**, as these our **atheistic politicians** ignorantly suppose. Instead, it is a **right essentially founded** on the existence of **natural justice**, as has been stated. For the **authority** to **command** is a **right** that assumes an **obligation** in others to **obey**; without that obligation, authority would be nothing but sheer **will** and **force**. But no one can be duty-bound to obey except through **natural justice**. **Commands** do not **create an obligation** themselves; they **presuppose** that an obligation already exists. For if people were not already **obligated** to obey, no **commands** would mean anything to them. Therefore, the **original obligation** comes from **nature**, not from someone's **will**. Even if the obligation to follow the rules of **natural justice** arose from the **will** and **specific command** <note>original: "Positive Command"</note> of God, as many suppose...

<header>CHAP. V. Infinite Right, a Non-Entity.</header>

If people were good only because of threatened punishments and promised rewards, the consequence would be that no man was *good* and *just* except *by accident*, and for the *sake of something else*. In contrast, the *goodness* of *justice* or *righteousness* is *intrinsic* to the thing itself. This is what *obliges* us, rather than anything *foreign* to it. It is a different *type* <note>original: "Species"</note> of *good* from that of *appetite* and *private utility* <note>original: "Utility," meaning personal benefit or usefulness</note>, which every man may set aside. Now, there can no more be *infinite justice* than there can be an *infinite rule* or an *infinite measure*. *Justice* is essentially a *fixed* and *defined* thing <note>original: "Determinate"</note>; therefore, there cannot be any *infinite law* <note>original: "Jus"</note>, *right*, or *authority*.

If anything is in its own nature *just* and binding—something that *ought* to be done—then there must necessarily be something *unjust* or *unlawful*. Therefore, such things cannot be commanded as a matter of obligation by any *authority* whatsoever. This should not be thought of as an *attack* <note>original: "Impeachment"</note> on civil authority, as this principle extends universally to all, even to the *Deity* Himself. The *right* and *authority* of God Himself, who is the *Supreme Sovereign of the Universe*, is likewise *bounded* and *limited* by *justice*. God's will is *ruled* by His *justice*, and not His *justice* ruled by His *will*. Therefore, God Himself cannot command what is in its own nature *unjust*.

Thus we have made it evident that *infinite right and authority*—to do or command anything without exception, such that the commander's arbitrary will becomes the very rule of *justice* for others and obliges them to anything—is an *absolute contradiction* and a *non-existence* <note>original: "Non-Entity"</note>. This is because it assumes that nothing is in its own nature *just* or *unjust*. If that were true, there could be no *obligation* or *authority* at all.

Therefore, those *atheists* who would flatter civil sovereigns with this claim of *infinite right*—as if the ruler's *will* should be the very *rule of justice and conscience*—and use that excuse to bias them against *religion*, do as much harm to rulers as they do to religion. In doing so, they absolutely strip rulers of all *right* and *authority*, leaving them with nothing but mere *brutish force* and *beastly liberty* <note>original: "Belluine Liberty," from the Latin *bellua* for beast</note>. And if civil sovereigns could utterly demolish and destroy conscience and religion in the *minds* of *men* (which is an *absolute impossibility*), thinking they were making *room* for their own power, they would certainly *bury* themselves in the resulting *ruins*.

Nevertheless, this much is true: those in whom the sovereign *legislative power* of every *state* <note>original: "Polity"</note> is lodged—whether *individuals* or *assemblies*—who *make civil laws* and can reverse them at will, may unquestionably *sin* against God by making *unjust laws*. However, they cannot sin *politically* or *civilly* as violators or *transgressors* of those laws they have canceled or reversed, since they are superior to them. Nor is this all; these sovereign *legislative powers* may also be said to be *absolute* in another sense, as being <term>not accountable to others</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνυπεύθυνοι (anyperthynoi)</note>, meaning they are *not subject to judgment* or *censure* by any *human court*. This is because if they were so liable to such judgment <note>original: "obnoxious," in the archaic sense of being liable to a power or penalty</note>, then the court or power that had the *right* to *judge and censure* them would be superior to them, which contradicts the *premise* <note>original: "Hypothesis"</note>. And if this second power were again *subject to judgment* by some other, there must be either an *infinite progression* or an *endless circle*—a thing that is not only *absurd*, but also

<header>Atheism and Private Judgment. BOOK I.</header>

[This would be] also utterly inconsistent with government and *property*. Because if there were no *ultimate judgment from which there is no appeal*, there could never be any *final determination of controversies*. Otherwise, in the end, everything would be left to the *multitude of individuals* <note>original: "Multitude of Singulars"</note>, which would lead to a *dissolution of the body politic* and a *state of anarchy*. And so, we have *fully refuted* <note>original: "Confuted"</note> the *second atheistic claim* as well—the idea that religion is inconsistent with civil sovereignty.

Their *third and last* argument follows: *that private judgment of good and evil contradicts civil sovereignty and the body politic*. They argue that the state is *one "artificial man" that must be entirely governed by a single reason and will.* In their view, conscience is merely a *private judgment of good and evil, what is lawful and unlawful, and so on.* 

To this we reply that it is not religion but, on the contrary, the principles of these atheistic politicians that unavoidably introduce a *private judgment of good and evil* which is absolutely inconsistent with *civil sovereignty*. According to them, there is nothing in nature that constitutes a *public or common good*, and nothing such as *duty or obligation*. Instead, everything is based on *private appetite* and *personal benefit* <note>original: "Utility"</note>, of which every man is the *judge for himself*. For if this were the case, then whenever any man judged it to be in his own *private interest* to disobey laws, rebel against sovereigns, or even to poison or stab them, he would be unquestionably bound by *nature* and the *reason* of his own *benefit*—as the *highest law*—to do those things. 

These *atheistic politicians* will never be able to lead men out of this state of *private benefit, judgment, and will* (which is *natural* to them under these theories) through any artificial tricks, devices, or mere wordplay <note>original: "Enchantments of Words"</note> like *artificial justice*, an *artificial man*, a *common person and will*, a *public conscience*, and the like. In fact, it is notable that they themselves are forced by the logic of their own principles to permit—through complex legal reasoning <note>original: "Casuistically"</note>—the kind of *private judgment and will* that is completely inconsistent with *civil sovereignty*. For example, they argue *that any man may lawfully resist in defense of his own life* and *that those who have once rebelled may afterwards justly defend themselves by force.* 

Furthermore, this *private judgment of men*—based on their own appetites and personal benefit—cannot possibly be removed except by *natural justice*. Natural justice is not a *private* thing, but is *public and common* in nature. It is also removed by conscience, which obliges people to obey all the lawful commands of *civil sovereigns*, even when those commands go against their *appetites* and *private interest*. 

Therefore, conscience itself is not of a private and biased nature, but of a public and common one. It respects divine laws, impartial justice, equity, and the good of the *whole* when these conflict with our own *selfish good* and *private benefit*. This is the only thing that can naturally unite <note>original: "Consociate"</note> mankind, lay a foundation for *political bodies*, and remove that *private will* and *judgment* (based on appetite and personal benefit) which is inconsistent with society. This aligns with the saying of *Plato*: "That which is of a common and public nature unites, but that which is of a private nature separates and divides" <note>original: "τὸ κοινὸν συνδεῖ, τὸ ἴδιον διασπᾷ"</note>. It is true, indeed, that individual people must make a judgment in conscience for themselves (for a "public conscience" would be *nonsense* and *ridiculous*) and that they may also err in doing so. # Chapter 5. One Perfect Being: The Root of All.

...[judgment] which *conscience* judges to be *private*; nor is it *unaccountable*, except in the case of those mistaken *fanatics* <note>original: "Fanaticks"</note> who professedly follow *private impulses*. Rather, it follows either the *natural* and *eternal laws of God*, or else his revealed *will*—matters that are more *public* than the *civil laws* of any country, and of which others may also judge. Nevertheless, we do not deny that *evil persons* may and sometimes do make a *pretense* of *conscience* and *religion* in order to incite *sedition* and *rebellion*, just as the *best* things may be *abused*. But this is not the fault of *religion*, but only of the *men*. Conscience obliges one, though first to obey God, yet in subordination to him, to obey the laws of civil sovereigns as well. 

To conclude, *conscience* and *religion* oblige subjects *actively* to obey all the *lawful commands* of civil sovereigns or *legislative powers*, even when they are contrary to their own *private appetite*, *interest*, and *utility* <note>original: "Utility," meaning personal benefit or advantage</note>. But when these same sovereign legislative powers *command unlawful things*, though conscience here obliges one to obey God rather than *men*, it nonetheless obliges one *not to resist*. *Romans 13: Whosoever resists the power, resists the ordinance of God, and they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation.* And *Matthew 26: All they that take the sword, shall perish with the sword.* Here is the *patience* and the *faith of the saints*. And thus does religion give unto *Caesar* the things that are *Caesar’s*, as well as unto *God* the things that are God's.

And now, having fully *refuted* <note>original: "Confuted"</note> all the *atheistic arguments* <note>original: "Atheistick Grounds"</note>, we confidently conclude that the *original source* <note>original: "First Original"</note> of all things was neither *stupid* and *senseless matter* moved *by chance* <note>original: "Fortuitously"</note>, nor a *blind* and *ignorant* <note>original: "Nescient"</note>, though orderly and methodical, *plastic nature* <term>plastic nature</term> <note>original: "Plastick Nature"; the internal, formative power within the natural world that executes God's plan without being conscious itself</note>. Nor was it a *living matter* possessing *natural* perception or understanding without *animal sense* or *consciousness*. Nor did everything exist of itself *necessarily* from *eternity* without a *cause*. 

Instead, there is only one *Necessary Existent*, the cause of all other things; and this is an absolutely *perfect being*, infinitely *good*, *wise*, and *powerful*. He has made all that was fit to be made according to the *highest wisdom*, and exercises an exact *providence* over everything. His name ought to be hallowed and set apart from all other things. *To whom be all honor, and glory, and worship, forever and ever. Amen.*
