### Chapter 8. One Perfect Rule of All.

...which conscience judges, remaining not in itself but in those principles that uniquely follow nature's impulse. However, either the matter and manner are natural, or else the revealed will of God is more public than the changing whims of any individual conscience, and thus others may also judge it. 

Nevertheless, we do not deny that evil persons may, and sometimes do, make a pretense of conscience and religion to incite sedition and rebellion, just as the best things may be abused. But this is not the fault of religion, but only of that person's conscience. Although they are still obligated to obey God, they must also obey the laws of civil sovereigns in subordination to him. 

To conclude, conscience and religion oblige subjects to obey all the lawful commands of their sovereigns or legislators, even when those commands are contrary to their own private understanding and interests. But when those same sovereigns or legislators command and enjoin things [that conflict with divine law], though one is obligated to obey God rather than man, conscience nonetheless obliges one not to resist or wage war against them, but rather to suffer for God's sake; those who suffer in this way are the true martyrs. 

Furthermore, conscience is the final rule of our actions. Just as the law is the rule for the deed <note>original: "Fact," here meaning an action or deed</note>, and the will is the rule for the law, and the will of the lawgiver is the ultimate rule for the law itself, so conscience is the final rule for the deed. In this way, all of them are linked together.

---

And now, having fully collected all the specific observations concerning the established eternal origin of all things, we shall, in this final and excellent chapter, recommend it to everyone for use and practice. If order and method are exactly observed—for living in the presence and enjoyment of that eternal nature is essential, and without it no state can be happy—every existence is, in a sense, separated from the eternal and becomes evil without it. But this eternal origin exists in one nature: God, who is infinite goodness and bounty. He is as absolute and uncontrolled as can be, acting according to his own will and pleasure, as he has a prerogative <note>original: "Prerogative," meaning an exclusive right or power</note> over all. Therefore, man ought to be sanctified and set apart from all other things, to submit to all His laws and to His glory forever.

->THE END.<-

It ends with a summary of God as the infinite, sovereign source of all happiness.</summary>

## CHAP. II.

->Wherein are contained all the supposed rational grounds for the atheistic hypothesis.<-

I. **T**hat the *Democritic philosophy, composed of materialism <note>original: "Corporealism"</note> and atomism joined together, is essentially atheistic.* Page 59

II. *Though Epicurus, who was an atomic materialist, pretended to claim there was a "democracy of gods," he was nevertheless an absolute atheist. It is shown that atheists commonly use ambiguous language <note>original: "equivocate"</note> and disguise their true views.* 60

III. *The Democritic philosophy—which makes mindless atoms the first principles not only of physical bodies (as ancient atomism <note>original: "Atomology"</note> did) but of everything in the universe, including the soul and mind—is nothing but a system of atheism masquerading as wisdom and philosophy. Although there is another opposing form of atheism called "Stratonical" <note>Named for Strato of Lampsacus; it suggests nature itself has a non-conscious life force.</note>, Democritic atheism is the most significant; its dark mysteries will be revealed here.* 61

<column-break/>

IV. *Since we are to treat the subject of God <note>original: "the Deity"</note> and bring these profane and unholy mysteries of atheism to light in order to refute them, we ought to pray for Divine assistance and direction—as even the Pagans commonly did in such cases.* 63

V. *We must both uncover the atheists' supposed rational grounds against the existence of God and their attempts to explain all natural events <note>original: "Phænomena"</note> without a God. Their first ground: that no one can have an idea or conception of God, and therefore He is nothing but an incomprehensible non-entity.* in the same place <note>original: "ibid."</note>

VI. *A second atheistic argument: that there can be no creation out of nothing, nor any such thing as omnipotence, because nothing can come from nothing. Therefore, whatever substantially exists has existed from all eternity, by itself, uncreated by any God.* 64

VII. *A third supposed rational ground against God: that because the strict definition of a God implies that He is non-physical <note>original: "Incorporeal"</note>, there can be no such God, as there is no substance other than physical body. This is based on the claim that whatever exists has "extension" <note>takes up space</note>, and whatever has extension is either empty space or matter.* 65

VIII. *The atheists' claim that the doctrine of non-physical <note>original: "Incorporeal"</note> substance arose from a ridiculous mistake of treating abstract names and notions as real things. Their boldness in calling God merely the "chief of ghosts," an "Oberon," or a "Prince of Fairies and fantasies." This is the fourth atheist argument: that to imagine a non-physical mind as the source of all things is simply to treat the abstract concept of a mere quality <note>original: "Accident"; in philosophy, an accident is a property that is not essential to a thing's nature, like color or a specific thought.</note> as the First Cause.* 67

IX. *A fifth supposed ground of atheism: that since a non-physical God has already been "refuted," a physical one can be disproved as well using the general principles of materialism. Since matter is the only substance and all other differences are merely temporary qualities <note>original: "Accidents"</note> that can be created or destroyed, no living, understanding being can be inherently immortal <note>original: "Essentially Incorruptible"</note>. ### CHAPTER III.

An introduction to the refutation <note>original: "Confutation"</note> of atheistic grounds; wherein is contained a particular account of all the several forms of atheism, together with a necessary digression concerning a "Plastic" or "Artificial" Nature <note>term: "Plastic Nature" refers to an unconscious, formative power in the universe that organizes matter, acting like a natural instinct rather than a conscious creator.</note>.

---

<margin>104</margin>
I. Why the grounds of Hylozoic atheism <note>term: "Hylozoic atheism" is the belief that matter itself is alive and self-organizing, requiring no external God.</note> could not be discussed in the previous chapter alongside those of Atomic atheism, as they are directly opposite to each other; with a further account of this Hylozoic atheism.

<margin>105</margin>
II. A suggestion by way of caution to prevent any mistakes: every "Hylozoist" must not be immediately condemned as an atheist or as a mere insincere <note>original: "Histrionical"</note> or fake believer in God.

<margin>106</margin>
III. Nevertheless, such Hylozoists who are also "Corporealists" (meaning they acknowledge no substance other than matter) cannot be excused from the charge of atheism, for two reasons.

<margin>107</margin>
IV. That Strato of Lampsacus (commonly called "the Physicist") was probably the first to assert Hylozoic atheism, as he acknowledged no God other than the life of nature within matter.

<margin>108</margin>
V. Further proof that this Strato was an atheist, and of a different type than Democritus, because he attributed an active <note>original: "Energetick"</note> nature—but one without sense or animal-like consciousness—to all matter.

<column-break/>

<margin>108</margin>
VI. Because Strato did not derive all things from a mere accidental principle (as the Democritic atheists did), nor did he acknowledge a single Plastic Nature to preside over the whole, but instead deduced the origin of things from a mixture of chance and Plastic Nature working together in the various parts of matter, he must therefore be considered a Hylozoic atheist.

<margin>109</margin>
VII. That the famous Hippocrates was neither a Hylozoic nor a Democritic atheist, but rather a "Heraclitic Corporeal Theist" <note>This refers to a follower of Heraclitus who believed God was a material substance, like a divine fire.</note>.

<margin>110</margin>
VIII. That Plato took no notice of Hylozoic atheism, nor of any other kind except that which derives the origin of all things from a mere accidental nature; and therefore he addressed either the Democritical or the Anaximandrian atheism (the latter of which will be declared next).

<margin>111</margin>
IX. That it is hardly imaginable that there were no philosophical atheists in the world before Democritus and Leucippus. Plato also observed that there have been some people in every age suffering from the "atheistic disease." Furthermore, Aristotle affirmed that many of the first philosophers assigned only a material cause to the system of the world, without any planning or active cause. They assumed matter was the only substance, and all other things were nothing but its properties and changes, which are born and then die.

<margin>112</margin>
X. The doctrine of these materialists may be more fully understood from the objections Aristotle made against them. His first objection: that they assigned no cause for motion but introduced it into the world without explanation.

<margin>112</margin>
XI. Aristotle’s second objection: that these materialists assigned no cause for "the Well and the Fit" <note>original Greek: "τõ Εὖ καὶ Καλῶς," meaning the goodness and beauty of design</note>; that is, they gave no account of the orderly regularity of things. Anaxagoras is said to be the first "Ionic" <note>term: Philosophers from the Greek region of Ionia.</note> philosopher who made Mind and Goodness a principle of the universe.

XII. *A conclusion drawn from this: that the Materialists mentioned in* Aristotle *were outright atheists. This was not simply because they held all substance to be physical body—since* Heraclitus *and* Zeno <note>Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism.</note> *held the same view and yet are not numbered among the atheists, as they supposed the whole world to be a living animal and their "fiery matter" to be naturally intelligent—but because these Materialists made mindless matter, devoid of all understanding and life, the only primary principle.* Page 113

XIII. *They supposed everything, besides the bare substance of matter, to be capable of being created and destroyed. Consequently, they believed there could be no other God than one who was born and destined to die. Those ancient theologians and poets who claimed all the gods were generated out of Night and Chaos without exception were only "verbal" theists, but "real" atheists; to them, senseless matter was the highest divinity <note>original: "Numen"</note>.* ibid.

XIV. *The difference observed between* Aristotle’s *atheistic Materialists and the Italian philosophers <note>The "Italick" philosophers usually refers to the school of Pythagoras.</note>; the former determined that everything except the bare substance of matter was made or generated. The latter, however, held that no real entity was either created or destroyed. Consequently, the Italians rejected the idea that the "qualities" and "forms" of bodies were separate things, while asserting that souls are uncreated and non-physical.* 114

XV. *How* Aristotle’s *atheistic Materialists endeavored to bypass and evade that axiom of the Italian philosophers: "Nothing can come from nothing, nor return to nothing." *Anaxagoras* was the first among the Ionians who accepted that principle enough to assert the existence of non-physical substance and the pre-existence of qualities and forms; he conceived them to be things truly distinct from the substance of matter.* 116

XVI. *The error of some writers who, because* Aristotle *affirms that ancient philosophers generally concluded the world was "made," infer from this that they were all theists. They claim* Aristotle *contradicts himself by re-*

<column-break/>

*presenting many of them as atheists. However, the ancient atheists did generally "create the world" <note>original: Κοσμοποιεῖν</note>, asserting that the world was made or had a beginning. On the other hand, some theists maintained the world's eternal existence, but in a way that made it dependent upon the Deity. Therefore, we must distinguish between the "system" of the world and the "bare substance" of matter. All atheists contended that matter was not only eternal, but also existed independently of any other being.* Page 117

XVII. *Some of the ancients concluded that this materialism, or <term>Hylopathian Atheism</term> <note>From the Greek words for "matter" and "passive/emotion"; the belief that all things, including life and mind, arise from the accidental states or "affections" of matter.</note>, was at least as old as* Homer, *who made the Ocean (or fluid matter) the father of all the gods. This was indeed the oldest form of atheism, which acknowledges "gods" in name but derives the origin of them all from Night and Chaos. A description of this atheistic hypothesis is found in* Aristophanes: *Night and Chaos first laid an egg, out of which sprang forth Love; Love then mingled again with Chaos and fathered Heaven, Earth, animals, and all the gods.* 120

XVIII. *Despite this, in* Aristotle’s *judgment, not only* Parmenides *but also* Hesiod *and other ancients who made Love older than the gods were to be excluded from the rank of atheists. They understood "Love" to be an active principle or the cause of motion in the universe. Therefore, this Love could not result from an "egg of the Night," nor be the offspring of Chaos, but must exist in the order of nature before matter. Mention of* Simmias Rhodius’s *poem "The Wings," written in honor of this divine or heavenly Love. This is not the same Love that was the offspring of Poverty <note>original: "Penia"</note> and Plenty <note>original: "Porus"</note> in* Plato. *In what corrected and refined sense it may be accepted as true theology: that Love is the Supreme Deity and the origin of all things.* 121

XX. That Aristotle's atheistic materialists were actually all the first Ionian philosophers before Anaxagoras, with Thales being their leader. But since several good authors have cleared Thales of this charge of atheism, his successor, Anaximander, should instead be considered the founder <note>original: "αρχηγὸς"</note> or prince of this atheistic philosophy. Page 123

XXI. A passage from Aristotle is raised as an objection, which at first seems to make Anaximander a philosopher of the divine, and has therefore misled both modern and ancient writers. But when well considered, this passage proves the opposite: that Anaximander was the leader of the old atheistic philosophers. 124

XXII. It is no wonder if Anaximander called mindless matter "The Divinity" <note>original: "Τὸ Θεῖον"</note>, since for all atheists, matter must be the highest god <note>original: "Numen"</note>. How this matter may be said to be immortal and to govern all things, along with the matching opinions of the Greek commentators <note>original: "Scholiasts"</note> on this passage. 126

XXIII. A further account of the Anaximandrian philosophy, which shows it to have been purely atheistic. 127

XXIV. Just as common people have always been poor judges of who is a theist or an atheist, learned men have also commonly assumed there were fewer atheists than there actually were. Anaximander and Democritus were both equally atheists, though they theorized in different ways; some passages in Plato refer to the Anaximandrian form of atheism rather than the Democritic form. 129

XXV. The reason why Democritus and Leucippus redesigned atheism into this atomic form. 131

XXVI. Besides the three forms of atheism already mentioned, we sometimes meet with a fourth. This view assumes the universe is like a kind of plant or vegetable rather than a living animal; it possesses a single, orderly, formative nature <note>original: "Plastick Nature"</note>

<column-break/>

within it, but it is devoid of understanding and sensation, yet it still arranges and orders the whole. Page 131

XXVII. This form of atheism, which makes one mindless, formative, and plant-like nature preside over the whole, is different from "hylozoism" <note>The belief that all matter possesses life.</note> because it removes all randomness. It subjects all things universally to the fate of this one methodical but unknowing nature. 132

XXVIII. It is possible that some people in every age might have held this atheistic conceit: that all things are managed by one regular and methodical mindless nature. Nevertheless, it seems to have been mainly asserted by certain false followers of Heraclitus and the Stoics. For this reason, this world-forming <note>original: "Cosmo-plastick"</note> atheism may be called "Pseudo-Zenonian" <note>Referring to the false followers of Zeno, the founder of Stoicism.</note>. 133

XXIX. Besides the philosophical atheists, there have always been "enthusiastic" and fanatical atheists in the world. Indeed, all atheists may in some sense be said to be both enthusiasts and fanatics, as they are merely led by an irrational impulse <note>original: "Ὁρμὴ Ἄλογος"</note>. 134

XXX. There cannot easily be any other form of atheism besides these four already mentioned. This is because all atheists are materialists <note>original: "Corporealists"</note>, yet not all materialists are atheists—only those who claim the first principle of the universe is not an intelligent mind. ibid.

XXXI. A classification of atheisms that produces the aforementioned group of four and shows the differences between them. 136

XXXII. Those who talk about "sensitive" and "rational" matter as being fundamentally different are merely bunglers at atheism. Furthermore, the rambling astrological atheists are not worth considering because they do not understand their own arguments. 137

XXXIII. Another classification of atheisms: they either derive the origin of all things from a purely accidental principle and the unguided motion of matter, or from a formative <note>original: "Plastick"</note>, regular, and methodical—yet mindless—nature.

XXXIV. That of these four forms of atheism, the Atomic (or Democritic) and the Hylozoic <note>original: "Hylozoick"; the belief that all matter is inherently alive</note> (or Stratonic) are the primary ones. Once these two are refuted, all forms of atheism will be refuted. 142

XXXV. Since these two forms of atheism contradict each other, we should reasonably focus more on the Atomic form. Nevertheless, we shall also refute the Hylozoic form elsewhere, and further prove against all materialists <note>original: "Corporealists"</note> that no thought <note>original: "Cogitation"</note> or life can belong to matter. 145

XXXVI. In the meantime, we shall not neglect the other forms of atheism, but refute them all together, as they agree on one principle. We will also, as a digression here, focus extensively on the plastic life of nature <note>original: "Plastick Life of Nature"; a "plastic" nature refers to a formative, creative force in the universe that organizes matter according to a divine plan</note> in order to more fully refute both Hylozoic and Cosmo-plastic atheism. 146

1. These two forms of atheism are not condemned by us simply because they assume a "life of nature" distinct from animal life. Indeed, this concept is completely rejected by some professed theists, who in doing so resemble the Democritic atheists too closely. ibid.

2. If no "plastic" or formative nature is admitted, then one of two things must be concluded: either that all things happen by random mechanism or material necessity (the unguided motion of matter), or else that God "does all things personally" <note>original: "Αὐτουργεῖν ἅπαντα"</note>—acting directly and miraculously to frame the body of every gnat and fly, as it were, with His own hands. For divine laws and commands cannot execute themselves, nor can they alone be the actual causes of things in nature. 147

3. To suppose the first option—that all things happen by chance through the unguided motion of matter without the direction of any mind—is as irrational as it is impious.

<column-break/>

There are many phenomena that are both beyond mechanical powers and contrary to mechanical laws. The "mechanical theists" <note>those who believe God created the world like a clock and then stepped back</note> make God merely an idle spectator of the random motions of matter, rendering His wisdom completely useless and insignificant. Aristotle’s wise critique of this random mechanism, and his mockery of the idea that material and mechanical reasons are the only valid philosophical ones. Page 148

4. It seems neither fitting toward God nor consistent with reason that He should "do all things personally" <note>original: "Αὐτουργεῖν ἅπαντα"</note>—performing everything Himself directly and miraculously without the help of any natural causes. This is further disproved by the slow and gradual process of things in nature, as well as by those "errors" and failures that occur when the matter proves unsuitable and stubborn <note>original: "Inept and Contumacious"</note>, which suggest that the acting force is not irresistible. 149

5. From this, we reasonably infer that there is an "artificial" or plastic nature in the universe acting as a subordinate instrument of Divine Providence in the orderly arrangement of matter. However, this occurs with a higher Providence presiding over it, since this plastic nature cannot act by its own choice or discretion. Those "laws of nature" concerning motion, which the mechanical theists themselves assume, are really nothing other than a plastic nature or "formative principles" <note>original: "Spermatick Reasons"</note>. 150

6. The agreement of this doctrine with the feelings of the best philosophers of all ages. Anaxagoras, though a professed theist, was severely criticized by both Plato and Aristotle as an encourager of atheism simply because he used material and mechanical causes more than mental and final ones. For the same reason, natural philosophers <note>original: "Physiologers"</note> and astronomers were commonly suspected of atheism in Plato’s time. 151

10. *The second way* nature *is superior: whereas* human artists *are often searching for answers or at a loss—anxiously consulting, deliberating, and correcting their previous work upon second thought—*nature *is never searching or unresolved about what to do. 11. *Nevertheless, that* nature *is not the* divine art *in a pure and abstract form, but is solidified and embodied in* matter. *In this sense, it is not the* original model <note>original: "Archetypal"</note> *but the* derived copy <note>original: "Ectypal"</note> *of divine art.* Nature *differs from the* divine art *or* wisdom *in the same way a* manual craftsman <note>original: "Manuary Opificer"</note> *differs from an* architect. 155

19. *That nature, though it is the Divine Art or Fate, is nevertheless neither a God nor a Goddess, but a low and imperfect creature <note>original: "Creature"; here meaning a created thing or entity</note>. 20. *Despite this, because plastic nature is a form of life, it must be incorporeal <note>original: "Incorporeal"; not composed of matter; spiritual or non-physical</note>. Although Aristotle himself never declares whether this nature is corporeal or incorporeal (which he also fails to do clearly regarding the rational soul), and his followers commonly assume it to be corporeal, according to the genuine principles of his philosophy, it must be otherwise.* 165

21. *Plastic nature, being incorporeal, must either be a lower power lodged in souls (which are also conscious, sensitive, or rational) or else a distinct substantial life by itself—an inferior soul. The Platonists affirm both, which agrees with Aristotle’s determination: that nature is either part of a soul or cannot exist without a soul.* ibid.

22. *Plastic nature, regarding the bodies of animals, is a part or lower power of their respective souls. According to this definition of the word "God," there could be no such thing as an atheist, since no one can convince themselves that everything sprang from nothing.* 195

VI. *To provide a more precise explanation of this divine idea, we consider the opinion of those who assume there are two self-existent, uncreated principles: God and Matter. In this view, God is not the source of all things, nor the sole principle, but only the primary one.* 196, 197.

VII. *These "Materiarians" <note>original: "Materiarians"; those who believe matter is eternal and co-existent with God</note> are imperfect and mistaken theists. They are not atheists, because they assume the world was made and is governed by a conscious <note>original: "Animalish"</note>, feeling, and understanding nature; whereas no atheists admit that conscious life <note>original: "Animality"</note> is a first principle, but instead conclude it is entirely capable of being created and destroyed. Yet they are not genuine theists, because they do not acknowledge omnipotence in its full extent.* There is, therefore, a range of belief within theism; no one should be condemned as an absolute atheist except *those who deny that an eternal, uncreated Mind is the creator and ruler of the whole world.* 198, 199.

VIII. *An absolutely perfect Being is the most concise idea of God. This includes not only necessary existence and conscious intellect, but also omni-causality <note>The quality of being the cause of all things</note>, omnipotence, or infinite power. Therefore, God is the sole source of all things and the cause of matter itself. The true definition of infinite power. And that pagans commonly acknowledged that omnipotence, or infinite*

<column-break/>

*power, was included in the idea of God.* Page 200, 201.

IX. *Absolute perfection implies something more than just knowledge and power. There is an inner premonition <note>original: "Vaticination"</note> in the human mind of a higher Good than either. According to Aristotle, God is better than knowledge; He possesses morality in His nature, which is also where His chief happiness consists. This idea was borrowed from Plato, for whom the highest perfection and supreme Deity is substantial Goodness itself, which stands above knowledge and intellect. Agreeing with this, the Scriptures identify God and the supreme Good as Love. This is not to be understood as a weak, foolish, or biased love; for God is also rightly called an impartial Law and the measure of all things. Atheists also assume that goodness is included in the idea of the God whose existence they deny. This idea is explained here more extensively.* 202, 203, etc.

X. *This aforementioned idea of God essentially includes unity, uniqueness <note>original: "Oneliness"</note>, or solitude within it: since there cannot possibly be more than one absolutely supreme being, one cause of all things, one omnipotent being, and one who is infinitely perfect. Epicurus and his followers explicitly denied a God according to this definition.* 207

XI. *The major objection against the idea of God—specifically that it essentially includes uniqueness and singularity—comes from the historical polytheism of all ancient nations (except the Jews) and of all the wisest men and philosophers. From this, it is inferred that the idea of God is not natural but artificial, and owes its origin only to laws and arbitrary human institutions.* An inquiry is therefore made here concerning the true meaning of pagan polytheism; *the objectors confidently take it for granted that pagan polytheists universally claimed there were many uncreated, self-existent, intellectual beings and independent deities acting as partial causes of the world.* 208, 209.

**XIII.** The fact that pagan deities were not all universally looked upon as uncreated, self-existent beings is unquestionably evident from this: they generally held to *Theogonia* <note>original: "Theogonia"; the generation or birth of the gods</note>. This point of pagan theology was insisted upon by Herodotus, the most ancient Greek prose writer. In his work, the meaning of the question—whether the gods were generated or existed from eternity—seems to be the same as Plato’s question: whether the world was "made" or "unmade." 211

It is also certain that among the gods described by Hesiod, there was either only one self-existent being or none at all. Hesiod’s "Love" is supposed to be the eternal God, or the active principle of the universe. 212

The "Thirty Gods" or "Aeons" <note>original: "Æons"; in Gnostic thought, these are various emanations or powers of God</note> of the Valentinians (which have the greatest appearance of being independent deities) were all derived from one self-originated being called *Bythus*, or an "unfathomable depth." 213

Besides the Manichaeans <note>a religious movement that taught a dualistic struggle between good and evil</note>, some pagans did indeed acknowledge a "ditheism," or a duality of unmade gods: one the principle of good, the other of evil. (This is the closest approach that can be found to the supposed belief in many independent gods.) Plutarch of Chaeronea was one of the chief supporters of this; though this is not commonly noticed by learned men. His reasons for this opinion are proposed. 213, &c.

Plutarch’s claim—that this was the general persuasion of all ancient philosophers and pagan nations—is examined. His grounds for attributing this view to Plato are scrutinized and refuted. 218, &c.

The true account of the Platonic origin of evils, which arises from the necessity of imperfect things. 220

Pythagoras and other philosophers are likewise cleared from this accusation of believing in two gods. 221

The Egyptians probably only personified "evil" (the confusion and alternating changes of things in this lower

<column-break/>

world) through the figure of Typhon. The only question concerns the *Arimanius* <note>Ahriman</note> of the Persian Magi. Whether this was a self-existent principle or not is disputed. Page 222

Plutarch and Atticus were the only professed defenders of this doctrine among the Greek philosophers (along with Numenius, as mentioned in Chalcidius). They were likely the ones the Persians were criticized for by Athanasius. 223, 224

Aristotle’s rejection and refutation of "many principles" <note>original: "πωλαι αρχαι" (polai archai)</note>. 225

So that a better judgment may be made of the pagan deities, a general survey of them is provided. They are all reduced to five categories: the souls of deceased men or heroes; the animated stars and elements; "daemons" <note>intermediary spirits</note>; accidents and things of nature personified; and lastly, several personal names given to one supreme God according to the various manifestations of his power and providence in the world (which were mistaken for many substantial deities or self-existent minds). 226, &c.

Pagans who acknowledge omnipotence must necessarily assume one sovereign *Numen* <note>Divine Power</note>. Faustus the Manichaean’s notion—that the Jews and Christians "paganized" by believing in a single divine monarchy—is addressed, along with Saint Augustine’s judgment of the pagans on that matter. 231, 232

**XIV.** It is concluded that pagan polytheism must be understood as the religious worship of created intellectual beings superior to humans. Thus, the pagans held both "many gods" and "one God" in different senses: many inferior deities subordinate to one supreme God. This was the view of Onatus the Pythagorean in Stobaeus. The "Pagan’s Creed" in Maximus Tyrius: one God who is the King and Father of all, and many gods who are the sons of God. The pagan *Theogonia* <note>generation of gods</note> is thus to be understood as many gods produced by one God. 233, 234

This pagan *Theogonia* is really one and the same thing as the *Cosmogonia* <note>the creation or origin of the world</note>. Plato’s *Cosmogonia* is a *Theogonia*. 234, &c.

Hesiod’s *Theogonia* is his *Cosmogonia*. 238

The Persians and Egyptians held similar views.

**XV.** Further evidence of this: that the intelligent Pagan polytheists held only a plurality of inferior deities subordinate to one Supreme. First, because after the emergence of Christianity

<column-break/>

and its contest with Paganism, no Pagan ever asserted many independent deities, but all professed to acknowledge one Sovereign or Supreme Being. Page 265

Apollonius of Tyana <note>a Greek philosopher often compared to Jesus in late antiquity</note> was set up among the Pagans as a rival to our Savior Christ. 266, etc.

He, though styled by Vopiscus as a "true friend of the gods" and though a stout champion for Pagan polytheism, was nonetheless a professed acknowledger of one Supreme Deity. 269, 270

Celsus <note>a 2nd-century Greek philosopher and the first major intellectual opponent of Christianity</note>, the first public writer against Christianity and a zealous polytheist, nevertheless freely declares his belief in one first and greatest omnipotent God. ibid.

The next and most eminent champion for the Pagan cause, Porphyry <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote against Christianity</note>, was an undoubted supporter of one Supreme Deity. Hierocles <note>a 5th-century Neoplatonist</note>, the next eminent antagonist of Christianity and champion for the Pagan gods, did, in the conclusion of his *Philalethes* (as we learn from Lactantius), highly celebrate the praises of the one Supreme God, the parent of all things. 271, etc.

Julian the Emperor <note>reigned 361–363; known as "Julian the Apostate" for attempting to restore Paganism</note>, a zealous contender for the restitution of Paganism, plainly derived all his gods from One. 274, 275

This is true of all the other opponents of Christianity, such as Iamblichus, Syrianus, Proclus, Simplicius, etc. Maximus of Madaura, a Pagan philosopher mentioned in the writings of St. Augustine, professed his belief in one "Sovereign Divine Power" <note>original: "Sovereign Numen"</note> above all the gods. This was also the view of Longinianus. 275, 276

The Pagans mentioned in the works of Arnobius universally disclaim the opinion of many unmade deities and profess a belief in an omnipotent God. 276, 277

These Pagans were acknowledged by other Church Fathers as well to have held to one Sovereign Divine Power. 279, etc.

But more will be said on this later when we speak of the Arians <note>a group in early Christianity who held that Jesus was created by God the Father and was not co-eternal</note>.

[The Deity] was but one *Simple Deity*, worshipped *piecemeal* <note>original: "Piece-Meale"</note>. This was allegorically signified by *Osiris* being dismembered and cut in pieces by *Typhon*, and then made into *One* again by *Isis*. Page 354, 355

XIX. That the poets in many ways corrupted <note>original: "deprav'd"</note> pagan theology and made it appear more like an aristocracy <note>i.e., a council of many gods rather than a single absolute monarch</note>. 355, etc.

Despite this, they did not actually claim there were many self-existent and independent gods, but only one "unmade" God; all the others were generated or created. Homer's gods were not all eternal and unmade, but were generated out of the ocean—that is, a watery chaos. Homer's *Theogony* <note>original: "Theogonia"; the genealogy or birth of the gods</note>, like Hesiod's, is also a *Cosmogony* <note>original: "Cosmogonia"; an account of the origin of the universe</note>; his "generation of gods" is the same thing as the production or creation of the world. 357, 358

Nevertheless, Homer distinguished one unmade God—the Father or Creator of them and of the world—from all those generated gods. 359

Homer was understood this way by the pagans themselves, such as Plutarch, Proclus, and Aristotle. 359, 360

Although Hesiod's gods, properly speaking, were all generated, he also assumed there was one unmade God, the maker of them and of the world. 360, 361

Pindar likewise—a divine writer on the birth of the gods—asserted there was one unmade Deity (and no more) who was the cause of all things. Yet he still held that there were many generated gods besides his "One God," who was to be worshipped far above all the others. 361, 362

The suspicion that Aristotle sometimes had of Hesiod, and Plato had of Homer, seems to have come from them not understanding the "Mosaic Cabala" <note>The author suggests these poets followed a tradition similar to the Mosaic account in Genesis</note> followed by both poets: that the world was made out of a watery chaos. 362

That famous passage by Sophocles concerning one God, the maker of heaven, earth, and seas (cited by so many ancient Church Fathers), is defended here as genuine. 363

Clear passages in the surviving <note>original: "extant"</note> tragedies of Euripides serve the same purpose, along with other remarkable passages cited from his now lost <note>original: "inextant"</note> tragedies, in addition to the testimonies of other Greek poets. 363, etc.

<column-break/>

*The agreement of the Latin poets also* regarding the monarchy <note>The rule of a single supreme God</note> of the whole universe. Page 365

XX. After the pagan poets, their philosophers are considered. Epicurus was the only reputable philosopher who, while pretending to acknowledge gods, openly opposed "monarchy" and claimed there were a multitude of eternal, unmade deities. However, these deities had nothing to do with either the making or the governing of the world. He is therefore clearly to be counted among the atheists. All pagan philosophers who were theists (except for a few "ditheists" <note>Those who believe in two opposing primary forces, such as Good and Evil</note>) universally asserted a "mundane monarchy" <note>A single supreme ruler of the world</note>. 369, 370.

Pythagoras, though as much a polytheist as other pagans, was nevertheless a clear acknowledger of one supreme God, the maker of the universe. 371

Pythagoras's "Dyad" <note>The principle of duality or "two"</note> was not a self-existent evil god or demon, as Plutarch supposed. 372

But this "Dyad" of his—whether it was matter or not—was derived from a "Monad" <note>The principle of unity or "one"</note>, a single simple unity that is the cause of all things. 372, 373

Since Pythagoras acknowledged a trinity of divine "hypostases" <note>Distinct persons or substances within the Godhead</note>, he therefore sometimes described God as a Monad, sometimes as a Mind, and sometimes as the Soul of the World. 373

The Pythagorean Monad and First God is the same as the "Orphic Love"—older than Iapetus <note>original: "Japhet"</note> and Saturn, and the oldest of all the gods, a substantial being. In contrast, that "Love" which Plato claimed to be the youngest of the gods—the daughter of *Penia* <note>original: "Penia"; Poverty or Indigency</note> and a "parturient" <note>productive or laboring</note> thing—is nothing but a created affection in souls, personified and turned into a god. Parmenides’s "Love" is the first created god, or the lower Soul of the World; before its production, "Necessity" is said to have reigned—that is, the necessity of material motions that were not directed toward any purpose or good. 374, 375.

That Pythagoras called the supreme Deity not only a "Monad," but also a "Tetrad" or "Tetractys" also. The reasons for this are given based on the mysteries found in the number four.

Four is trifling. There is more probability in a recent *conjecture* that the Pythagorean *Tetractys* <note>original: "Tetractys"; a triangular figure of four rows of dots totaling ten, sacred to the Pythagoreans</note> was the Hebrew *Tetragrammaton* <note>original: "Tetragrammaton"; the four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH</note>, which was not entirely unknown to the *Etruscans* <note>original: "Hetrurians"</note> and *Latins*. *Page* 375, 376

*Xenophanes* was a clear *asserter* of both *many gods* and of *one God*, whom he called *One and All*. *Simplicius's* <note>original: "Simplicius his"</note> clear *testimony* for this *theosophy* of *Xenophanes*, taken from *Theophrastus*. *Xenophanes* was misrepresented by *Aristotle* as an *asserter* of a *spherical, corporeal God*. 377, 378

*Heraclitus*, though a *cloudy* <note>i.e., obscure</note> and *confusing philosopher*, and one who could not conceive of anything *incorporeal* <note>original: "Incorporeal"; lacking a physical body</note>, was nevertheless both a sincere *moralist* and a zealous *asserter* of one *supreme Deity*. 378, 379

The *Ionian philosophers* before *Anaxagoras* were all *corporealists* <note>believers that only matter exists</note>, and *some of them were atheists*. *Anaxagoras* was the *first* who asserted that an *incorporeal mind* was a *principle* <note>original: "Principle"; a fundamental source or cause</note>; though not the *cause* of *matter*, he was the cause of *motion* and of the *regularity* of things. The *world*, according to him, was not *eternal* but *made*, and formed out of *pre-existing similar atoms*; this was done not by *chance*, but by *Mind* or *God*. *This Mind* of his was purely *incorporeal*, as appears from *his own words*, cited by *Simplicius*. 380

It is *probable* that *Anaxagoras* admitted none of the *inferior pagan gods*. He was *condemned* by the *common people* <note>original: "Vulgar"</note> as an *atheist* because he *stripped the stars of their divinity* <note>original: "Ungodded the Stars"</note> by denying they were alive, and by affirming the *Sun* to be only a *mass* of *fire* and the *Moon* an *earth*. *This was also disliked* by *Plato*, as a view that would *predispose men to atheism* in those times. 381

*Anaxagoras* was further *censured* <note>original: "Censured"; criticized</note> by both *Plato* and *Aristotle* because, although he *asserted Mind* to be a *principle*, he made *much more use* of *material causes* than of *mental* and *final causes*; they looked upon this as an *atheistic trace* <note>original: "Atheistick Tang"</note> in him. *Nevertheless, Anaxagoras* was a better *theist* than *those Christian philosophers* of later times who completely banish all *mental causality* from the *world*. 382, 383

XXI. *Parmenides’s* <note>original: "Parmenides his"</note> acknowledgment of *one God* as the *cause* of all other *gods*. Which

<column-break/>

*supreme Deity* was styled by *Parmenides* as the *One-All-Immovable*. It is *proved at length* that this is *not to be taken physically*, but *metaphysically* and *theologically*. To these *ancients*, the *first principle of all* was *One: a simple unity* or *monad*. *This was said to be All* because it *virtually contains all* and is *distributed into all*, or because *all things are distinctly displayed from it*. *Lastly, the same principle was said to be immovable, indivisible, and without magnitude* to distinguish it from the *corporeal universe*. *Page* 383, etc.

"*One All*" <note>original: "Εν το πᾶν"</note> was taken in *different senses*. By *Parmenides* and *Xenophanes*, etc., it was used *divinely* to mean the *supreme Deity* (*one most simple Being who is the original of all things*). But by others mentioned in *Aristotle*, it was used *atheistically*, as if *all things* were but *one* and the same *matter in various forms* <note>original: "diversly Modified"</note>. However, the *One-All* of these *latter* thinkers was *not immovable but movable*, being nothing more than *matter* <note>original: "Body"</note>; whereas the *One-All-Immovable* is an *incorporeal Deity*. *Aristotle* agrees with <note>original: "close with"</note> this in his *Metaphysics* as *good divinity*: *that there is one incorporeal, immovable principle of all things*. *Simplicius's observation* that, although *various philosophers maintained a plurality or infinity of movable principles, none ever asserted more than one immovable principle*. 385, 386

*Parmenides*, in *Plato*, distinguishes three *divine hypostases* <note>original: "Hypostases"; distinct substances or persons within the Deity</note>. The *first* he calls the "*One All*" <note>original: "Εν το πᾶν"</note>; the *second*, the "*One All-things*" <note>original: "Εν παντα"</note>; and the *third*, the "*One and All-things*" <note>original: "Εν και παντα"</note>. 386, etc.

But it is *further unquestionably evident* that *Parmenides* really understood the *supreme Deity* by his *One-All-Immovable* from the *verses cited from him* by *Simplicius*. *In these verses, there is also attributed to the Deity a standing eternity or duration that is different from the duration of time.* 388

*The only difference between Parmenides* and *Melissus* was that the *former* called his *One-All-Immovable* "*finite*," while the *latter* called it "*infinite*." This was a difference *in words rather than reality*. The disagreeing a-

The agreement of these two philosophers is fully declared by Simplicius. Melissus's language is more agreeable with our present theology. Though Anaximander’s "Infinite" was nothing but senseless matter, Melissus's "Infinite" was the true Deity. Page 389

That Zeno of Elea, by his "One-All-Immovable," did not mean the physical world either, any more than Melissus, Parmenides, and Xenophanes did; but rather the Deity. This is evident from Aristotle. Zeno's demonstration of one God, based on the idea of a most powerful and perfect Being, is found in the same Aristotle. 390

Empedocles's first principle of all things, *the One* <note>original: "Τὸ ῞Εν"</note>, or a unity likewise, besides which he supposed "Strife" and "Friendship" to be the principles of all created beings; not only plants, brutes, and men, but gods also. 391, etc.

Empedocles's origin of all the evil in both the human soul and demons, from this *Strife* <note>original: "Νεῖκος"; discord or contention</note>, together with the ill use of their liberty. 393

XXII. The doctrine of various other Pythagoreans also the same; such as Philolaus, Archytas, Ocellus, Aristaeus, etc. Timaeus Locrus's God as the creator of gods. Onatus's "many gods," and his "one God," the *leader* <note>original: "Coryphaeus"; the conductor or leader of a chorus</note> of the gods. Euclides Megarensis's "One" as the Very Good. Antisthenes's many popular gods, but one natural God. Diogenes of Sinope's God that fills all things. 393, etc.

XXIII. That Socrates asserted one supreme God is undeniable from Xenophon. 398, 399

But that he disclaimed all the other inferior gods of the Pagans, and died as a martyr for one only God in this sense, is a *common error* <note>original: "Vulgar Errour"; a widely held but incorrect belief</note>. 400

What the impiety was that his adversaries imputed to him appears from Plato's *Euthyphro*: namely, that he freely and openly condemned those fables of the gods where wicked and unjust actions were attributed to them. 401

That Plato really asserted one only God and no more is also a *common error* <note>original: "Vulgar Errour"</note>; 

<column-break/>

and that Thirteenth Epistle to Dionysius—where he declared himself to be serious only when he began his letters with "God" and not with "gods" (though extant in Eusebius's time)—is spurious and *counterfeit* <note>original: "Supposititious"</note>. He worshipped the Sun and other stars also (supposed to be alive) as inferior gods. Page 402

Nevertheless, it is undeniably evident that Plato was no *polyarchist* <note>a believer in many independent rulers</note>, but a monarchist; no asserter of many independent gods or principles, but of one original source of all things: one first God, one greatest God, one maker of the world and of the gods. 403, 404

In what sense the supreme God is, to Plato, the cause and producer of Himself (according to Plotinus); and this notion was not only entertained by Seneca and Plotinus, but also by Lactantius. That Plato really asserted a Trinity of universal divine *hypostases* <note>original: "Hypostases"; distinct persons or substances of the Godhead</note> that have the nature of principles. The first *hypostasis* in Plato's Trinity is properly *God-in-himself* <note>original: "Αὐτόθεος"; the self-existent God</note>, the original Deity, the cause and king of all things; which he also said to be *beyond essence* <note>original: "᾿Επέκεινα τῆς οὐσίας"</note> or *supra-essential* <note>original: "Ὑπερούσιος"; above all being</note>. 407

Xenophon, though like other Pagans he acknowledged a plurality of gods, was yet a plain asserter also of one supreme and universal *divine power* <note>original: "Numen"</note>. 408

XXIV. Aristotle frequently acknowledged many gods. And whether he believed in any demons or not—which he sometimes mentions (though sparingly) and suggests they are a kind of aerial animals, more immortal than men—he did unquestionably look upon the stars, or their intelligences, as gods. 408, etc.

Notwithstanding this, Aristotle does not only often speak of "God" in the singular, and of "the Divinity" emphatically, but also professedly opposes that imaginary opinion of many independent principles or unmade deities. He refutes this from the phenomena or the *structure* <note>original: "Compages"</note> of the world, which is not *episodic* <note>original: "ἐπεισοδιώδης"; like a poorly written play with disconnected scenes</note> but all uniform, and agreeably conspiring into one harmony. 410, 411

*Immovable Mover*. The difference here between *Plato* and *Aristotle*; *Plato's* source of motion is a *Self-moving Soul*; *Aristotle's* is an *Immovable Mind*. But this difference is not as great as it seems at first glance, because *Aristotle's* Immovable Mind does not move the heavens *efficiently* <note>original: "Efficiently"; acting as the direct cause of change</note>, but *only finally* <note>original: "Finally"; acting as the ultimate goal or purpose</note>, or *as being loved*. Besides which, he must necessarily suppose another immediate mover, which could be nothing other than a *soul* within them. Page 412

*Aristotle's Immovable Mind* is not only the cause of motion, but also of *well-being and fitness*; all the *order, beauty <note>original: "Pulchritude"</note>, and harmony* that is in the world. It is called, therefore, by *Aristotle*, the *Separate Good* of the world. This, together with *Nature* (its *subordinate instrument*), is the *efficient cause* of the entire physical world system <note>original: "Mundane System"</note>. Although the world is co-eternal with the Mind, it is, in the order of nature, *secondary* <note>original: "Junior"</note> to it. 413, 414

*Aristotle* and other ancients, when they affirm *Mind* to have been the *cause* of all things, understood it this way: that all things were made by an *Absolute Wisdom* and in the *best manner*. The *Divine Will*, according to them, is *not a mere arbitrary, moody <note>original: "Humoursome"</note>, and accidental <note>original: "Fortuitous"</note> thing, but decency and fitness itself*. 415

From this passage of *Aristotle's*—that the *Divinity* is either *God* or the *work of God*—it is evident that he supposed *all the gods* to have been derived from *One*, and therefore his "intelligences" of the *spheres* were likewise derived. 415

That according to *Aristotle*, this *particular science* (metaphysics) is distinct from *physiology* <note>original: "Physiology"; here meaning the study of physical nature</note> and *geometry*. The first of these (*physiology*) is *concerned* with what is *inseparable* from matter and *movable*; the second (*geometry*) is about things that are *immovable* but not *really separable* from matter; but the *third and last* (which is *theology*) is about that which is both *immovable* and *separable*—an *incorporeal Deity*. 416

*Four Chief Points* of *Aristotle's* theology or metaphysics concerning *God*:

<column-break/>

*First, that though all things are not eternal and unmade, yet something must necessarily be so, as well as incorruptible; otherwise, everything might come to nothing. Secondly, that God is an incorporeal substance, separate from sensory things <note>original: "Sensibles"</note>, indivisible, and devoid of parts and size <note>original: "Magnitude"</note>. Thirdly, that the Divine Intellect is the same as its objects of thought <note>original: "Intelligibles"</note>, or contains them all within itself; because the Divine Mind, being prior to all things and the master designer <note>original: "Architectonical"</note> of the world, could not then look outward for its objects. The contrary is supposed by atheists. Lastly, that God being an immovable substance, His act and energy is His essence; from which Aristotle would infer the eternity of the world.* Page 416, 417

*Aristotle's creed and religion* are contained in these *two articles*: first, *that there is a Divinity which encompasses the whole of Nature, or the Universe*. And *secondly, that besides this, there are other particular, inferior gods*. But *that all other things in the religion of the pagans were added as fables <note>original: "Fabulously superadded"</note> for political purposes*. 417

*Speusippus*, *Xenocrates*, and *Theophrastus* were monarchists <note>original: "Monarchists"; meaning they believed in a single supreme ruler or God</note>. 418

XXV. The *Stoics* were no better at metaphysics than *Heraclitus*, in whose footsteps they walked, admitting no *incorporeal substance*. To these *Stoics*, even the *qualities* of the mind were *physical bodies*. 419, 420

But the *Stoics* were not, therefore, atheists; they supposed an *eternal, unmade Mind* (though lodged in matter) to be the maker of the entire physical world system. 420

The *Stoic arguments* for a God are *not insignificant*, and what those arguments were. 421, 422

The *Stoic God* is *not a mere formative <note>original: "Plastick"</note> and methodical fire, but an intellectual fire. The world, according to them, is not a plant, but an animal; and Jupiter is the soul of it. From the supposed uniqueness of this Jupiter, they would sometimes infer the singularity of the world (Plutarch, on the contrary, affirming that though there were fifty, or...)*

(Even if there were) a hundred worlds, there would still be, for all that, only one *Zeus* or *Jupiter*. 423

*Nevertheless*, the Stoics were as *polytheistic* as any *sect*. But they did so in a way that *supposed all their gods except for One to be not only born but also mortal*; made out of that *One* and *dissolved* back into that *One* again. These *gods* are all *merged into Jupiter during the universal fire* <note>original: "Conflagration"</note>. 424, 425

*Therefore*, during the *periods between successive worlds*, the Stoics acknowledged only *one lone deity* and no more; *Jupiter* was then left all alone, and the other *gods were absorbed into him*. He is, therefore, not only the *Creator* of all the other *gods* but also their *Destroyer* <note>original: "Decreatour"</note>. 425, 426

*Despite this*, the Stoics were *devout worshippers* of their *many gods*; in doing so, they sometimes *detracted* from the *honor of the Supreme Being* by *sharing his authority among them.* 426, 427

*Nevertheless*, the *Supreme God* was *praised and extolled* by them far above all the other *gods* and acknowledged to be the *only Maker of the world.* 427, etc.

Their *declaring obedience to his laws as their greatest liberty.* 430

And to *submit their wills to his will in everything, so as to know no other will but the will of Jupiter. Ibid.*

*Their aim <note>original: "Pretending"; in this context meaning to aim or claim a purpose</note> to look to God and to do nothing without referring to him*; as well as to *trust in him and rely upon him.* 431

*Their praising him as the source of all good. Ibid.*

*Their directing their prayers to him alone, without including any other god*; and particularly *begging for his help against temptations.* 432

*Cleanthes's excellent and devout hymn to the Supreme God.* 433

XXVI. *Cicero*, though *tending to write in the style of the New Academy* <note>The New Academy was a school of Greek philosophy known for skepticism</note>, was yet *no skeptic regarding the existence of God*. Nor *was he a proponent of many independent deities*. *Cicero's gods* (the *makers of the world*) are the *same as Plato's eternal gods, or the trinity of divine substances* <note>original: "Hypostases"</note>

<column-break/>

subordinate. *This language, the pagans in Saint Cyril's time would justify from the scripture, "Let us make Man."* Page 434, 435, etc.

*Varro’s threefold theology*: the *fabulous, the natural, and the civil or popular*; following *Scaevola the High Priest* <note>original: "Pontifex"</note> and his *three types of gods: poetical, philosophical, and political*. The *former* was condemned by him as *false*; the *second*, though *true*, was said to be beyond the *understanding of the common people* <note>original: "Vulgar"</note>. Therefore, there was a *necessity* for a *third* or *middle* way between both, *because many things true in religion are not fit for the common people to know.* *Varro's Supreme Divine Power* <note>original: "Numen"</note> is the *great soul or mind of the whole world; his inferior gods are parts of the world endowed with life.* *Image worship was condemned by him as inconsistent with natural theology.* 438, 439

*Seneca* was a *pagan polytheist* but a clear *supporter of one Supreme Divine Power*, which he *described excellently*. *In his book on superstition (now lost), he criticized the civil theology of the Romans as freely as Varro had criticized the fabulous or theatrical.* 440

*Quintilian, Pliny, and Apuleius* and their clear acknowledgments of *one sovereign universal deity*. *Symmachus* (a great *advocate for paganism*) and his *assertion that it was one and the same thing that was worshipped in all religions, though in different ways.* 440, 441

The writer of *On the Universe* <note>original: "De Mundo"</note>, though not *Aristotle*, was still a *pagan*. He writes of a *Cause* that *contains all things and God from whom all things come. Because this passage was left out in Apuleius's Latin translation, it gives cause for suspicion that he was infected with Plutarch's belief in two gods* <note>original: "Ditheism"; the belief in two opposing ultimate powers, usually good and evil</note>, *or at least held that matter was never created.* 442

*Plutarch* was a *priest of Apollo*; however, though he was unluckily involved in those *two false opinions of an evil principle and matter being uncreated*, he was still a *defender of one sole principle of all good.* 443

*Dio Chrysostom*, a *sophist* <note>An ancient Greek teacher of rhetoric and philosophy</note>, and his clear *testimony: "the whole world is ruled as a kingdom"* <note>original: "βασιλεύεσθαι τὸ ὅλον"</note>, *meaning that the whole world was under a kingly government or monarchy.* Ibid.

Galen’s *True Hymn in praise of his Creator, in his book* On the Use of the Parts <note>original: *De usu Partium*</note>. Page 444

Maximus Tyrius's short account of his own religion: one supreme God, the monarch of the whole world, and three subordinate ranks of inferior gods, who are the sons and friends of God, and his ministers in the government of the world. Page 444, 445

A very full and excellent description of the supreme God in Aristides' first oration or hymn to Jupiter, where he claims all the various kinds of gods are but a flowing out and derivation from Jupiter. 445, 446

All the later philosophers after the rise of Christianity (though they maintained the world's eternity) agreed on one supreme deity, the cause of this world and of the other gods. Excellent reflections in their works concerning the deity, especially Plotinus; who, though deriving matter and everything from one divine principle, was still a defender of many gods; he supposed the grandeur and majesty of the supreme God was shown by the multitude of gods under him. Themistius argued that the same supreme God was worshipped by Pagans, Christians, and all nations, though in different forms; and that God was delighted with this variety of religions. 446, 447

The full testimony of Saint Cyril, that the Greek philosophers universally acknowledged one God, the maker of the universe, from whom certain other gods—both intellectual and physical <note>original: "Intelligible and Sensible"</note>—were brought into being. ibid.

XXVII. This was not only the opinion of philosophers and learned men, but also the general belief of the common people <note>original: "the Vulgar"</note> among the Pagans. A judgment of the common people and the general public can be made from the poets. Dio Chrysostom's statement that all the poets acknowledged one first and greatest God, the father and king of all rational beings. 447

Aristotle’s testimony that all men acknowledged kingship or monar-

<column-break/>

-chy among the gods. Maximus Tyrius’s claim that, despite such a great difference of opinion in other things, yet throughout all the Gentile world, both the unlearned and the learned universally agreed in this: that there was one God, the King and Father of all, and many gods who were the sons of that one God. Dio Chrysostom also spoke to the same purpose, suggesting that the acknowledgment of the one supreme God was more general than that of the many inferior gods. 448, Page 449

That the understanding of the common Pagans in this matter is further evident because all nations had their own proper names for the one supreme God: such as Jupiter for the Romans, Zeus for the Greeks, Hammon for the Africans and Arabians, Pappaeus for the Scythians, Bel for the Babylonians, etc. 449

It is true that Origen, though allowing Christians to use descriptive titles <note>original: "Appellative Names"</note> for God in the languages of various nations, still considered it unlawful for them to call him by those proper names; because they were not only given to idols, but also tainted with wicked rituals and myths. According to this view, they should be judged as the names of a demon <note>original: "Dæmon"</note> rather than a God. Despite this, he does not deny that those Pagans always meant the supreme God by those names, but often acknowledges it. However, Lactantius denies that the Jupiter of the Capitoline hill was the supreme God, for two reasons. First, because he was not worshipped alone, but in partnership with Minerva and Juno, his daughter and wife. It is granted here that there was a mixture of mythical or poetic theology with natural theology to create the state religion <note>original: "Civil"</note>. But wise men understood these to be only three different names or concepts of one supreme God. This is confirmed by Macrobius. Page 450

Vossius’s conjecture that in this Capitoline Trinity there was a further mystery intended: the three divine persons <note>original: "Hypostases"</note>. This Roman Trinity was derived from the Samothracian *Cabiri* <note>The *Cabiri* were a group of enigmatic deities worshipped in mystery cults across the ancient Greek world, often associated with protection and the underworld.</note>.

*That just as learned Pagans did in their writings, the common people <note>original: the Vulgar</note> in their everyday speech—when being most serious—often used the word "God" in the singular and with emphasis to refer to the supreme being. This is proved from Tertullian, Minucius Felix, and Lactantius, along with Proclus’s testimony that the one supreme God was more universally believed throughout the world than the "many gods." 453, 454*

*That "Lord have mercy" <note>original: Kyrie Eleeson</note> was anciently a Pagan prayer <note>original: litany</note> to the supreme God, proved from Arrian <note>original: Arianus</note>. The supreme God was also often called "Lord" <note>original: Κύριε/Kyrie</note> by the Pagans. 454, 455*

Page 455*

*Even though some of the ancient Pagans were said to have acknowledged only visible and physical <note>original: Corporeal</note> gods, they still conceived of these as being endowed with life and understanding; thus, they supposed one supreme being among them, such as the whole heavens or the living upper atmosphere <note>original: Æther Animated</note>,*

<column-break/>

*or the subtle, fiery substance that pervades all things (the God of the followers of Heraclitus <note>original: Heracliticks</note> and the Stoics), or the Sun, which was the god of Cleanthes <note>original: Cleanthæan God</note>. Page 455, 456*

*Though Macrobius relates so many of the Pagan gods to the Sun, and certainly looked upon it as a great god himself, he still denies that it is the "most omnipotent God" <note>original: Omnipotentissimum Deum</note> of all; he asserts a Trinity of divine persons <note>original: Hypostases</note> superior to the Sun, following the Platonic tradition. 456, 457*

*That the Persians themselves, the most notorious Sun-worshippers, nevertheless acknowledged a deity superior to the Sun and its creator, as proved from Eubulus. Cyrus’s "Lord God of Heaven," who commanded him to build him a house at Jerusalem, is the same as the God of the Jews. 458*

XXVIII. *In addition to Themistius and Symmachus—who asserted that one and the same Being is worshipped in all religions, though in different ways, and that God Almighty was not displeased with this variety of worship—there is Plutarch’s memorable testimony: that just as the same sun, moon, and stars are common to all people, so were the same gods. He argued that not only the Egyptians, but all other Pagan nations worshipped one Reason and Providence that orders everything, along with its inferior, subservient powers and ministers, though they used different rituals and symbols. 459, 460*

Egyptians, but also other Pagan nations. The latter of them, Asclepiades, wrote a book entitled *The Symphony or Harmony of all Theologies* <note>original: "Theologies or Religions"</note>. He argued for these two foundational principles: that there is one Supreme God and, besides him, other inferior gods who serve as his helping ministers and are to be worshipped. From this, Symmachus and other Pagans concluded that religious differences should not be obsessively debated; instead, every person should worship God according to the laws and religion of their own country. The Pagan viewpoint is thus declared by Stobæus: that the multitude of gods is the work of the Creator <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note>, made by him along with the world. Page 461

XXIX. *That Pagan theists must necessarily acknowledge one supreme deity is further evident from this: they generally believed the whole world to be one single living being <note>original: "One Animal"</note>, animated and governed by one soul. In the view of the ancient Pagans, to deny that the world is alive was the same as being an atheist. Against the philosopher Gassendi, it is argued that Epicurus denied the world was alive only because he denied the existence of a God who provides for us. This entire living world, or the soul of it, was to the Stoics and others the First God <note>original: Πρῶτος Θεὸς</note>, the highest of all.* 462

*Other Pagan theologians also asserted that the world was alive and had a "Mundane Soul," yet they would not allow this soul to be the supreme deity. They conceived the first and highest God to be not a soul, but an abstract and unchanging Mind superior to it. To these thinkers, the living world and its soul were only a Second God <note>original: Δεύτερος Θεὸς</note>.* 463

*However, the majority of those who looked higher than the Soul of the World also acknowledged a principle superior even to Mind or Intellect, called The One <note>original: Τὸ Ἓν</note> and The Good <note>original: Τὸ Ἀγαθὸν</note>. Thus, they asserted a Trinity of subordinate divine persons <note>original: "Hypostases"</note>: the Monad, Mind, and Soul. Consequently, the living world or*

<column-break/>

*its soul was, to some of these thinkers, only the Third God <note>original: Τρίτος Θεὸς</note>.* ibid.

*The Pagans—whether they held the Soul, the Mind, or the Monad to be the highest—acknowledged only one of each kind as the head of all. They always reduced the multiplicity of things to a unity, or under a single monarchy.* 464

*It is observed that for Pagan theologians universally, the world was not a dead thing, or a mere machine and automaton. Rather, it had life or soul diffused throughout it all. Aristotle criticized those as atheists who made the world consist of nothing but dead and soulless units <note>original: "Monads"</note> or atoms. Nor was the world quite cut off from the supreme deity, regardless of how far he was elevated above it. The previously mentioned Trinity of Monad, Mind, and Soul was supposed to be most intimately united—indeed, all were but one entire Divinity, displayed in the world and supporting it.* 464, 465

XXX. *The view of the Hebrews in this controversy. According to Philo, Pagan polytheism did not consist of worshipping many independent gods and partial creators of the world, but of worshipping created beings superior to men alongside the one supreme God.* 465, 466

*This was also the view of Flavius Josephus, according to whom this was the doctrine of Abraham: that the supreme God alone was to be religiously worshipped, and no created thing along with him. Aristæus’s assertion in Josephus is that the Jews and Greeks worshipped the same supreme God, called by the Greeks Zene <note>A variation of Zeus, from the Greek "to live"</note>, as the one who gives life to all.* 466, 467

This was condemned by the Rabbis as strange worship or idolatry <note>original: עבודה זרה, Avodah Zarah</note>. The First Commandment was thus interpreted by Maimonides and Baal Ikkarim: "You shall not set up besides me any inferior gods as* media-

XXXI. *This same point is plainly confirmed by the New Testament: that the Gentiles or Pagans, however much they were polytheists and idolaters, were not unacquainted with the true God. XXXII. *To provide a fuller explanation of Pagan theology and to make it more apparent that their polytheism did not contradict their acknowledgment of one supreme, omnipotent Divine Power <note>original: "Numen"</note>, three things must be considered. First, that much of their polytheism was only apparent or imaginary <note>original: "Seeming and Phantasticall"</note>, and was really nothing but the use of many names for one God <note>original: "Polyonymy"</note>. Secondly, that their real and natural polytheism consisted only in religiously worshipping many other particular and inferior created beings—such as living <note>original: "Animated"</note> stars, demons, and heroes—alongside this one supreme, universal Divine Power. Thirdly, that because they worshipped both the supreme and inferior gods through statues, images, and symbols, these objects were also sometimes improperly <note>original: "Abusively"</note> called "gods." All Pagan polytheism can be categorized under one of these three headings.* 477

*Besides both their mythical <note>original: "Fabulous"</note> and poetic theology, and their political and civil theology, they had another natural and philosophical one. This distinction between common <note>original: "Vulgar"</note> and civil theology, and the natural and real theology, was recognized by the Greeks generally; and among the Latins by Scævola the High Priest <note>original: "Pontifex"</note>, Varro, Cicero, Seneca, and others. (Ibid.)*

*That the civil theology of the Pagans differed from the natural and real theology by a certain mixture of mythology <note>original: "Fabulosity"</note> in it. Regarding the Romans allowing the statue of Jupiter's nurse to be kept in the very Capitol as a religious monument. Jupiter's birth—or his having a father and a mother—is atheistically mythical; the poets themselves acknowledged enough of the natural and true theology to say that Jupiter, being the father of gods and men and the maker of the whole world, was himself eternal and unmade. 478*

*That the civil as well as poetic theology had some appearance of many independent deities also; they established several supreme gods in their various territories and functions: one chief for one thing, and another for another. But according to the natural and philosophical theology—the theology of wise men and of truth—all these were but poetic, invented <note>original: "Commentitious"</note>, fictitious, and imaginary gods; such as had no distinct substantial essences of their own, and therefore were really to be accounted as nothing else but several names or notions of one Supreme God. 478, 479*

*It is certain that the Egyptians had several proper and personal names for that one Supreme Universal Divine Power <note>original: "Numen"</note> that comprehends the whole world, according to several notions of it or its several powers: such as Ammon, Phtha, Osiris, Neith, and Cneph; to which may be added Serapis and Isis too. Besides Iamblichus, we have Damascius’s testimony <note>original: "Damascius his Testimony"</note> also to this purpose concerning Egyptian theology. This was the pattern for the other theologies, especially European ones like the Greek and Roman. 479, 480*

*That the Greeks and Romans also often made more gods out of one, or preferred a <term>polyonymy</term> <note>the use of many names for one thing; original: "Polyonymy"</note> of the same gods. This is evident from those many proper and personal names bestowed, first upon the Sun (of which Macrobius writes), who therefore had the epithet "many-named" <note>original Greek: πολυώνυμος (*polyonymos*)</note> given to him; and then upon the Moon, styled "many-named" as well as her brother the Sun; and lastly upon the Earth, famous likewise for her many names, such as Vesta, Cybele, Ceres, Proserpina, Ops, etc. Therefore, it is not at all to be doubted that the Supreme God, or Sovereign Power <note>original: "Numen"</note> of the whole world, was even more "many-named." This title was given to him also, as well as to Apollo in Hesychius. He was thus invoked by Cleanthes. Zeno, the writer of "On the World" <note>original: "De Mundo"</note>, Seneca, and Macrobius clearly confirm the same. Maximus of Madaura in St. Augustine fully acknowledged this. Page 480, 481*

*The first instances of the many names <note>original: "Polyonymy"</note> of the Supreme God among the Pagans are found in such names as these: The Thunderer, The God of Rain, Protector of the City, The Gracious, The God of Friendship, The God of Hospitality, The Savior <note>original Greek: Βρονταῖος, Ὑέτιος Πολιεύς, Μειλίχιος, Φίλιος, Ξένιος, Σωτήρ</note>, etc. And among the Latins: Victor (The Conqueror), Invictus (The Unconquered), Opitulus (The Helper), Stator (The Stayer), Tigillus (The Beam/Support), Centupeda (Hundred-footed), Almus (Nourishing), Ruminus (Nurturing), etc. Again: Necessity, Destiny, Fate, Fortune, and The Inevitable <note>original Greek: Ἀνάγκη, Εἱμαρμένη, Πεπρωμένη, Μοῖρα, Ἀδράστεια</note> were all several names of the one Supreme God, as likewise were Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos <note>The three Fates</note> in the writer of "On the World." And among the Latins, not only Fate, but also Nature and Fortune too, as Cicero and Seneca affirm. 482*

*But besides these, there were other proper names of the Supreme God which had a greater show and appearance of being several different gods, as they had their own peculiar temples and various specific rites of worship. And first, such as signify the Deity according to its more universal nature. As for example, Pan; which is not the inanimate physical world or a nature endowed only with senselessness, but a rational or intellectual principle displaying itself in matter, framing the world harmoniously, and being in a manner all things. This is also the universal Pastor and Shepherd of all mankind. 483*
