Janus was invoked first by the Romans in their *Sacrifices* and was never omitted. He was described as *the most Ancient God and the First Beginning of all things*. He was depicted by Ovid, Martial, *and others* as a universal deity <note>original: "Numen"</note>. St. Augustine <note>original: "S. Austin"</note> concluded that Janus was the same as Jupiter, representing the Soul or Mind of the whole world. The name Janus is probably derived from *Zanos* <note>original: "Ζανὸς"</note>, the Aeotolian name for Jupiter. Pages 483, 484

Genius was also one of the twenty "select" Roman gods; according to Festus, he was a universal deity: *that God who is the Begetter of all things.* And according to Varro (cited in St. Augustine), he is the same as Jupiter. 484, 485

Chronos or Saturn was *no particular deity* but also a universal deity who comprehends the whole nature of the world, as *affirmed by Dionysius of Halicarnassus*. The word "Saturn" is Etrurian (and originally derived from the Hebrew *Seter* <note>original: "סתר"</note>), meaning "Hidden." He was called by the Latins *Deus Latius*, the Hidden God; from this comes the name of the region Italy *Latium* and the *Latins*, *as worshippers of this Hidden God, or the secret <note>original: "Occult"</note> principle of all things.* According to Varro, he is the one who produces the hidden seeds and forms of all things out of himself and swallows them up into himself again; this explains the myth of him devouring his male children. This is *a certain inward and deep recess of nature* <note>original: "Sinus quiddam Naturae, &c."</note> containing all things within itself, which is how the Pagans sometimes defined God. To St. Augustine, he was the same as Jupiter, as was *Coelus* or *Uranus* in old inscriptions; therefore, these were also just other names for God. The poetic theology—where Jupiter is the son of Saturn and Saturn is the son of Uranus—is a hint (according to Plato) of a Trinity of universal divine persons <note>original: "Hypostases"</note>. 485, 486

Though Minerva or Athena *was sometimes restricted to a narrower meaning*, she was often taken as a name for God in his universal sense; to Athenagoras, she represented the Divine Wisdom displaying itself through all things. This is excellently described by Aristides as the first-begotten offspring of the original Deity, or the second divine person <note>term: "Hypostasis" refers to a distinct person or essence within the Godhead</note>,

<column-break/>

*by which all things were made*, in agreement with Christian theology.
Pages 486, 487

Aphrodite Urania, or the Heavenly Venus, was another name for God according to his universal sense. She is the same as that "Love" which Orpheus and other philosophers mentioned in Aristotle identified as the first origin of all things. Plato made a distinction between an elder and a younger Venus. *The former*, the daughter of Uranus (Heaven) born without a mother, is the Heavenly Venus, *said to be older than Japheth and Saturn*. *The latter*, later begotten from Jupiter and the nymph Dione, is the vulgar or common Venus. Urania, or the Heavenly Venus, was called *Mylitta* by Eastern nations, *meaning* "the Mother of all things." Pausanias mentions temples dedicated to this Heavenly Venus. *She is described by Aeschylus, Euripides, and Ovid* as the Supreme Deity and the creator of all the gods. God Almighty is also described as a Heavenly Venus or Love by Boethius. Closely related to this Urania in the writings of Pausanias is another Venus called *Apostrophia* <note>original: "Ἀποστροφία"</note> or *Verticordia* ("The Turner of Hearts"), *as she turns men's minds upward, away from unchaste love or unclean lust.* 488, 489

Though Vulcan is a specific god according to the common view, he sometimes had a more universal meaning. Zeno (as recorded in Laertius) stated that the Supreme God is called Vulcan when acting through the "artful fire" of nature. Similarly, the Soul of the World was called *Phtha* by the Egyptians; *as Iamblichus tells us, this was the same as the Greek Hephaestus or Vulcan.* 489, 490

In addition to all these names for the Supreme God, Seneca informs us that he was sometimes also called *Liber Pater* ("Father Liber") because he is the parent of all things; sometimes *Hercules* because his force is unconquerable; and sometimes *Mercury* because he is Reason, Number, Order, and Knowledge. 490

But besides this practice of using many names for God <note>term: "Polyonymy" means the use of multiple names for a single entity</note> according to his universal nature, there were also other "special gods" <note>original: "Dii Speciales"</note> among the Pagans, which likewise were...

It highlights the overlap between Pagan "natural theology" and Christian concepts, such as Divine Wisdom and the Trinity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Table of Contents, explaining how the various gods of the Greek and Roman pantheons—such as Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto—were understood by ancient philosophers as different names for a single, supreme Divine Power acting in different parts of the universe.</meta>

<page-type>toc</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>The Contents.</header>

...were really but several names of one and the same Supreme Deity, *who uses his power in various ways* <note>original: "variè utentis sua Potestate"</note> (as Seneca writes), diversely using his power in particular cases and in the several parts of the world. Thus Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto (mistaken by some Christians for a trinity of independent gods) were three political <note>original: "Civil"</note> gods, yet they were really but one and the same natural and philosophical God, acting in those three parts of the world: the heaven, the sea, the earth, and the underworld <note>original: "Hell"</note>. Pluto, in Plato’s *Cratylus*, is a name for that part of Divine Providence which is exercised in the government of departed souls after death. This is styled by Virgil as the "Stygian Jupiter." But to others, Pluto, together with Ceres, is the manifestation of the Deity in this whole terrestrial globe. The celestial and terrestrial Jupiter are but one God. Zeus and Hades are one and the same according to Orpheus. Euripides was doubtful whether God should be invoked by the name of Zeus or Hades. Hermesianax, the Colophonian poet, makes Pluto the first of those many names of God that are synonymous with Zeus. Page 490, 491

Neptune is also another specific god, a name of the Supreme Deity as acting in the seas only. This was affirmed by Xenocrates in Stobaeus, Zeno in Laertius, Balbus and Cotta in Cicero, and also by Maximus Tyrius. 492

The statue of Jupiter with three eyes in Pausanias signifies that, according to natural theology, it was one and the same God ruling in those three several parts of the world—the heaven, the sea, and the earth—who was called by three names: Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto. Therefore, since Proserpina and Ceres are the same as Pluto, and Salacia is the same as Neptune, it is concluded that all these, though several poetic and political gods, were yet but one and the same natural and philosophical God. 492, 493

Juno is also another specific god, a name of the Supreme Deity as acting in the *air*. Thus thought Xenocrates and Zeno. The Pagans in St. Augustine <note>original: "S. Austin"</note> say that God in

<column-break/>

the ether <note>original: "Æther"</note> is called Jupiter, and in the air, Juno. So Minerva is likewise, when taken as a specific god, a name of the Supreme God according to that particular consideration of him as acting in the higher ether. From this, St. Augustine argues against the Pagans. Maximus Tyrius says of these and many other gods of the Pagans that they were but *Divine names* <note>original: "Θείᾳ ὀνόματα"</note>. Page 493, 494

Yet many other specific gods among the Pagans were also really nothing but *Divine Names*, or names of God as he variously exercises his power or bestows several gifts: such as Ceres in corn and fruit, Bacchus in wine, Aesculapius <note>original: "Æsculapius"</note> in medicine, Mercury in trade <note>original: "Traffick"</note>, Mars in war, Aeolus <note>original: "Æolus"</note> in governing the winds, and so on. 494

Not only did philosophers interpret the many poetic and political gods as one and the same natural God, but the poets themselves also sometimes openly revealed this more secret <note>original: "Arcane"</note>, free, and true theology; such as Hermesianax among the Greeks and Valerius Soranus among the Latins. 494, 495

St. Augustine, making a large list <note>original: "Enumeration"</note> of the other specific gods among the Pagans, affirms of them universally that, according to the sense of the Pagan doctors, they were but one natural God and all really the same with Jupiter. 495, 496

Apuleius, in his book *On the God of Socrates* <note>original: "De Deo Socratis"</note>, was either not rightly understood by that learned and industrious philologist G.J. Vossius, or else not sufficiently attended to. His design there was plainly to reduce the Pagans' political theology into a conformity with natural and philosophical theology. As a Platonist, he did this by making the "Council of Twelve Gods" <note>original: "Dii Consentes"</note> of the Romans and their other invisible gods to be nothing but the *Divine Ideas*, and thus the offspring of one highest God. An occasion for this fancy was given by Plato, where he calls his Ideas "Animals." Nor was Apuleius alone in this; Julian, in his book against the Christians, went the very same way, and was no otherwise understood—

<meta>This page continues the Table of Contents, elaborating on how pagan philosophers and later Neoplatonists interpreted their many gods as various aspects, ideas, or names of a single Supreme Deity.</meta>

...understood by St. **Cyril**, other than as to make the **Invisible Gods** worshipped by the pagans **to be the Divine Ideas**. This was a fancy <note>original: "Phancy"; here meaning a philosophical notion or theory</note> of the same **Julian** (the Emperor who opposed the incarnation of the Eternal Word), who argued that **Aesculapius** was first of all the Idea of the Medicinal Art, generated by the Supreme God in the intelligible world <note>the realm of pure thought or concepts, as opposed to the physical world</note>. He claimed this Idea afterwards, through the life-giving influence of the Sun, was incarnated and appeared in human form around Epidaurus. This pagan doctrine is older than Christianity, as proved through the works of **Philo**, who wrote of an "Intelligible" Sun and Moon (the ideal versions) as well as "Sensible" ones (the physical versions), which were religiously worshipped by the pagans—that is, as the Ideas of the Archetypal World <note>the original model or pattern of the universe</note>. Thus, these Ideas of the Divine Intellect were also considered **intelligible gods** <note>original: "νοητοὶ Θεοί"</note> by **Plotinus**. Page 496, etc., 501.

Therefore Julian, **Apuleius**, and others who thus made all the pagan invisible gods to be nothing else but the Divine Ideas (the patterns of things in the archetypal world), supposed them not to be so many independent deities, nor really distinct substances separate from one another, but only so many partial considerations of one God. **Julian** previously affirmed that **they were born from him, coexist with him, and exist in him** <note>original: "ἐξ αὐτοῦ γεγενῆσθαι αὐτοὺς, συνυπάρχειν τε καὶ ἐνυπάρχειν αὐτῷ"</note>. 501, 502.

The fact that the pagans appointed some particular god or goddess by name to preside over everything (since **nothing at all was without a god** <note>original: "μηδὲν ἄθεον"</note> to them) appears from that catalogue of their lowly or petty gods, collected by **St. Augustine** out of **Varro**. Now, it is incredible that they should think all of these were so many single, substantial spirits of each sex, really existing apart in the world. They must, therefore, have taken them to be so many partial considerations of the Deity: either in the way of the more high-minded Platonists (as his Ideas, containing all things as examples and in essence); or else in that more common and easy way of the general public (as so many several denominations of him, according to the several manifestations of his pow-

<column-break/>

er and providence). Or, as the pagans in **Eusebius** declare themselves: **those several virtues and powers of the Supreme God were themselves personified and deified**. Yet, because these were not executed without the subservient ministry of created spirits—angels or demons—appointed to preside over such things, these spirits might also be included under those names when taken collectively. Page 502, 503.

For the fuller clearing of this point—that pagan polytheism was in great part nothing but the "polyonymy" <note>the use of many names for one thing</note> of one God—two things should be noted here. First, that pagan theology universally supposed God to be diffused through all, to permeate and pervade all, and to intimately act in all. This was the view of **Horus Apollo** of the Egyptians. Thus it was among the Greeks: **Diogenes the Cynic**, **Aristotle**, and the **Italian** and **Stoic** philosophers. Thus thought the Indian **Brahmans** <note>original: "Brachmans"</note> mentioned by Strabo. Thus also the Latin poets, and **Seneca, Quintilian, Apuleius,** and **Servius,** among others. 503, 504.

**Anaxagoras** and **Plato** also—though neither of them confused God with the physical world, but affirmed him to be unmixed with anything—concluded in a similar way that he permeates and pervades all things. Plato’s etymology of **the just** <note>original: "δίκαιον"; Plato puns on this as "dia-ion" or "that which goes through"</note> as a name for God serves this purpose in his *Cratylus*. In that work, a fragment of **Heraclitus** and his description of God agree with this: a most subtle and swift substance that permeates and passes through everything, by which all things are made. However, **Plato**, disclaiming this physical nature of the Deity, will have it be neither fire nor heat, but a perfect Mind that passes through all things without being mixed with them. 505.

Therefore, it is no wonder if the pagans, supposing God to be diffused through all things, called him by several names in the several parts of the world and things of nature: such as **Ceres** in the earth, **Neptune** in the sea, etc. This account of pagan polytheism was given by **Paulus Orosius**: **"That while they believed God to be in many things, they indiscreetly made many gods of him."** 505, 506.

It cites philosophers like Julian, Plato, and Plotinus to show that many "gods" were actually viewed as "Divine Ideas" or personified virtues of one supreme Intellect.</summary>

*It is further to be observed that many of the pagan theologians seemed to go even a step higher, supposing that God not only permeates all things but is also himself all things. That ancient Egyptian theology reached this height is evident from the inscription at Sais <note>The Temple of Neith in Sais, Egypt, reportedly bore the inscription: "I am all that has been, and is, and shall be."</note>. A strong hint of this is found in Æschylus, as well as in Lucan. This was not only the view of those who held God to be the Soul of the World, but was also the language of those other more refined philosophers like Xenophanes, Parmenides, and others; they affirmed God to be "One and All." With this agrees the author of the Asclepian Dialogue, stating that God is "One is all things" <note>original: "Unus omnia"</note>; and that before things were made, he did then "hide" <note>original Greek: κρύπτειν (kryptein)</note> them, or secretly contain them all within himself. Orpheus spoke in a similar manner. Page 506, 507*

*This served not only as a further basis for the many names <term>polyonymy</term> of the one God, according to the various ways he manifests himself in the world, but also for another strange phenomenon in pagan theology: their personification of the inanimate parts of the world and the forces of nature, and their bestowing the names of gods and goddesses upon them. This is noted by Moschopulus, cited earlier, and Arnobius. Plutarch thinks this was originally done only through metonymy <note>a figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it</note>, where the effects of the gods were called "gods"—just as the books of Plato might be called "Plato." Plutarch does not dislike the practice to that extent. However, he complains that it was later taken further by superstitious people, resulting in great impiety. Nevertheless, it is proved from Cicero, Philo, and Plato that inanimate substances and the forces of nature were formerly deified by the ancient pagans in ways other than just metonymy. Because they supposed God to permeate all things and to be all things, they looked upon everything as sacred or divine. They turned the parts of the world and the forces of nature into theology, giving them the titles of gods and goddesses—especially those things most useful to humans or those that inspired the most wonder. 507, 510*

*This is properly called the "physical" <term>physiological</term> the-*

<column-break/>

*ology of the pagans: their personification and deification of the forces of nature and inanimate substances. It is argued against Eusebius that many of the ancient poetic fables of the gods were, in their first and true meaning, allegories of physics and not merely stories about human heroes <term>herology</term>. Zeno, Cleanthes, and Chrysippus were famous for thus interpreting the fables of the gods as allegories. Chrysippus gave an allegorical meaning even to an indecent picture of Jupiter and Juno in Samos. Although Plato was no friend to these poetic fables, he nonetheless confesses that some of them contained allegories; Dionysius of Halicarnassus says the same, as does Cicero, who affirms that this personification and deification of the forces of nature filled the world with superstition. Page 510, 512*

*Arguing again against Eusebius: the entire theology of the pagans did not consist solely of deifying the forces of nature and inanimate bodies. This is because anyone who acknowledges no living <term>animant</term> God acknowledges no God at all, but is a complete atheist. 512*

*Nor should this physical <term>physiological</term> theology of the pagans—which consisted in personifying and deifying nature—be confused with the "natural" and "philosophical" theology of Varro, Scaevola, and others. Their system admitted only living gods who really existed in nature; for this reason, it was called "natural," in opposition to the fictional and imaginary gods of the poets. 512*

*Saint Augustine's <note>original: "S. Austin," a common shortening of Augustine</note> just criticism and condemnation of the pagans for thus turning physics into theology, or fictionally personifying and deifying the forces of nature. 512, 513*

*But although the pagans did thus verbally personify and deify the things of nature, the intelligent among them did not actually consider these to be true and proper gods. As Cotta says in Cicero: "Though we call grain Ceres and wine Bacchus, no one was ever so mad as to believe that what he eats and drinks is actually a god." The pagans really accounted...*

They counted as a God only those things through the invocation of which they might expect some benefit for themselves; and therefore, nothing inanimate was truly considered a God. This is proved from the writings of *Plato*, *Aristotle*, *Lucretius*, *Cicero*, and *Plutarch*. Therefore, these "deified natures" of things were merely fictitious and fantastical gods. No other sense can be made of them than this: they were really just many different names for one Supreme God, as he manifested in his various works. This follows the *Egyptian Theology*, which held that God may be called by the name of everything, or everything by the name of God. *Seneca* agrees with this, stating that there may be as many names for God as there are gifts and effects of his; as does the writer of *On the World* <note>original: "De Mundo," a treatise once attributed to Aristotle</note>, who says that God may be named after every part of nature, as he is the cause of all things.
Page 513, 515

Therefore, these deified forces of nature were not directly worshiped by intelligent pagans, but only in relation to the Supreme God, or as they were intertwined with him. Thus, it was not the things themselves that were worshiped, but God worshiped through them. The pagans' defense was that they did not look upon the world with the same eyes as oxen and horses do, but with religious eyes, so as to see God in everything. They therefore worshiped the invisible Deity in the visible manifestations of himself—God and the world together. This was sometimes called *Pan* <note>The Greek god of nature, whose name also means "All"</note> and *Jupiter*. In this way, the whole world was said to be the "Greatest God," and the circle of the heavens was worshiped by the *Persians*; not as inanimate matter, but as the visible manifestation of the Deity, flowing from him and filled by him. When the *Roman* sea captains sacrificed to the waves, their worship was intended for that God who stills the waves and quiets the billows.
515, 516

These pagans also perceived a necessity in allowing men to worship the invisible God through his visible works. This account is given by them in the works of *Eusebius*. *Plato* himself approved of worshiping the invisible God in the Sun, Moon, and

<column-break/>

Stars, viewing them as his visible images. And though *Maximus Tyrius* would have men endeavor to rise above the starry heavens and all visible things, he still allows the weaker sort of people to worship God in his progeny <note>referring to the lesser gods or celestial bodies born from the Supreme God</note>. *Socrates* also persuades *Euthydemus* to be contented with this. In addition to this, some pagans who worshiped the elements directed their intention to the spirits of those elements, as *Julian* mentions in *Ammianus* (these elements being supposed to be alive or "animated"), or else to those demons <term>dæmons</term> <note>In Greek philosophy, "daimons" were intermediate spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil</note> whom they conceived to inhabit or preside over them.
Page 516, 518

XXXIII. It is further to be observed that among those "natures of things," some were merely accidental <note>In philosophy, "accidental" refers to qualities or properties that are not essential to a thing's core existence</note>, such as Hope, Love, Desire, Memory, Truth, Virtue, Piety, Faith, Justice, Concord, Clemency, Victory, Echo, and Night. Because of this practice, the common *Athenians* supposed that *Saint Paul* had deified *Resurrection* <note>original Greek: "Anastasis"</note>, making a goddess of the Resurrection just as he made a God of *Jesus*. Vices were also sometimes deified by them, such as Contumely <term>insult</term> and Impudence (to whom temples were dedicated at *Athens*), though this was done so that these things might be deprecated <note>To "deprecate" here means to pray against something or attempt to ward it off</note>. 518, 520

Thus, *Origen* again disputes against the godhood of *Minerva* when she is interpreted allegorically as Prudence. He does the same elsewhere, on the same grounds, against the godhood of Memory (the mother of the *Muses*) and that of the *Graces*. In reality, natural theology was the true, real, and philosophical kind, opposed both to the fictions of the poets and the institutions of lawmakers and politicians. The God of the Pagans was not the "nature of things" (which could be the divine spirit <note>original: "Numen"</note> of none but atheists), but an understanding Being: the Great Mind or Soul of the whole world, pervading all things. ...of his Providence, and religiously worshiped also. A brief but full account of the Pagans' Natural Theology, set down by *Prudentius*. Page 526, 527

And when the more sophisticated <note>original: "high-flown"</note> Pagans referred these Poetical and Political Gods to the Divine Ideas or patterns of things in the Archetypal World—which, besides the Platonists, the Egyptians in *Celsus* are said to have done, making the brute animals they worshiped but symbols of the Eternal Ideas—they thereby made these gods to be but so many partial considerations of the One God. This is because He is either all things or contains within himself the causes of all things, as *Julian* himself declares in his *Sixth Oration*. 527, 528

A summary <note>original: "Anacephalæosis"</note> showing that much of Pagan Polytheism was but the many-naming <note>original: "Polyonymy"</note> of One God; he being worshiped under several names. First, according to several general concepts of him, such as *Janus*, *Genius*, *Saturn*, *Minerva*, *Urania*, or the Heavenly *Venus* (or Love), and others previously declared. This also applies to *Summanus*, according to St. Augustine <note>original: "S. Austin"</note>, and *Themis*, who is mentioned later. 528, 529

And secondly, according to other more specific concepts of him (in their "Special Gods") as acting in only some parts of the world, or exercising some particular powers. 529, 530

And lastly, as pervading all things, and being all things, or the cause of all things, he was thereupon called by the name of everything, or everything was called by his name. The Pagans in St. Augustine's writings argued that their ancestors were not so foolish <note>original: "sottish"</note> as not to understand that those things of nature were but divine gifts and not gods themselves. And the Pagans in *Eusebius* argued that the invisible God, the cause of all things, ought to be worshiped in his visible effects, in which he has displayed himself. 530

Though only the two former kinds of these gods were called "poetical" and "fictitious" by *Athanasius* (who contrasted them with those of the third sort, which were natural and real things), yet these may also be well-

<column-break/>

called poetical, fictitious, and fantastical gods too. This is because although they were real things existing in nature, their personification and deification was mere fiction, fancy, and poetry. Accordingly, they were previously called by *Origen* "Greek figments" <note>original: "Ἑλλήνων ἀναπλάσματα"</note>. Page 530, 531

XXXIV. Of those Pagans who supposed the Supreme God to be the whole living <note>original: "Animated"</note> world. It has been shown so far that even the most refined of the Pagans agreed in these two things: First, in breaking and crumbling the One Simple Deity and multiplying it into many gods, or parcelling it out into several particular concepts according to its several powers and virtues. (To these Pagans, being "many-named" <note>original: "Πολυώνυμον"</note> was the same thing as being "many-powered" <note>original: "Πολυδύναμον"</note>.) And then, in turning the whole world into theology by personifying and deifying the natures of things, accidents, and lifeless bodies. They supposed God to pervade all things and himself to be, in a manner, all things. Therefore, to the religious, everything was sacred and divine, and God was to be worshiped in all things. 531, 532

We shall now add that both those previously mentioned principles—that God pervades all things and that he is all things—were taken further by those Pagan theologians who had no higher concept of the Supreme Deity than as the Soul of the World. For first, while the more refined Pagans supposed God to pervade all things without being mixed with them, these thinkers mixed and confused him with the whole world. Some of them even supposed him to be a subtle body. 532, 533

Again, while the other more elevated <note>original: "Sublimated"</note> Pagans affirmed God to be all things yet still something above all things, these thinkers concluded him to be nothing higher than the living <note>original: "Animated"</note> world. 533

And though they supposed that in this world-animal <note>original: "Mundane Animal"</note>, as in other animals, there was something governing and authoritative <note>original: "Principal and Hegemonical"</note> (whether the Sun, or the upper air <note>original: "Æther"</note>, or Fire), which therefore was emphatically called God, yet they did conceive the whole matter of it to be alive...

...and so to be *All God*. Not simply as *Matter*, but by reason of the *Soul within it*.
Page 534, 535

Now, if the *Whole Animated World* <note>original: "Whole World Animated"</note> is the Supreme God, *then all the parts and members of the world must be the parts and members of one God*; but they are not, therefore, properly *many gods* themselves. This was affirmed by *Origen* as the true sense of these Pagans, against the careless assertion of *Celsus* that *if the whole were God, then the various parts of it must necessarily be gods*. 535

Therefore, although these *Pagans deified* the parts of the *world* and the natures of things, as well as the powers of the *Mundane Soul* <note>the "World Soul," a concept where the universe itself has a soul</note>; yet the *intelligent* among them did not *worship* them *separately* as so many *true and proper gods*, but only as the parts and members of *one great animal or God*; or rather, they *worshiped* the great *Mundane Soul* (*the life of the whole world*) in them all. This is proved from *St. Augustine* <note>original: "S. Austin"</note>. 536, 537

The same is also plainly declared by the Pagans in *Athanasius*: *that they did not account the divided parts of the world as many separate gods, but the whole, made up of them all, as one God; which could nevertheless be worshiped in its various parts.* 537

The Pagans being thus divided in their opinions concerning natural and *true theology*; some of them *worshiped the world as the body of God*, but others only *as his image or temple*. Thus *Plutarch*, though disliking the deifying of inanimate things, nonetheless approved of *worshiping God in the whole world* as his most sacred temple. And the *Persian Magi*, allowing for no *man-made temples built by human hands*, *worshiped God under the open sky* <note>original: "sub Dio"</note> and upon the tops of mountains, conceiving the whole world to be his natural temple. For the same reason, they also condemned man-made statues and images, concluding that *fire, earth, and water, and similar parts of the world* were the natural images of the deity. Thus says *Dino* in *Clement of Alexandria* <note>original: "Clemens Alexandrinus"</note>. This difference among the Pagan theologians was

<column-break/>

noted by *Macrobius*. Thus, all the Pagans were *world-worshipers in different senses: but not worshiping it as a dead and inanimate thing, but either as the body of God, or else as his temple or image.* Page 537, 539

Furthermore, as the *Pagans universally* acknowledged the *world to be a living creature* <note>original: "animal"</note>, those who did not suppose it to be the first and highest God conceived it to be either a second or a third God; and so they *worshiped it not only as a temple or image, but also as the son of the first God*. *Celsus* claimed that the Christians called their *Jesus the "Son of God" in imitation of these Pagans, who gave the world that title*. 539, 540

Thus we have made it fully appear that, according to the saying of *Antisthenes*, the *many popular gods* of the Pagans were but one and the same natural God; or, according to *Euclides*, their *many gods were but many names* <note>original: "polyonymy"</note>. So that they viewed neither their *poetical* nor their *political theology* as true and natural. 540

Nevertheless, the *wiser Pagans* generally concluded that there ought to be another theology besides the *natural* one, specifically designed for the *common people* <note>original: "Vulgar"</note>, which contained a mixture of *falsehood* and *fable*. *Varro* and *Scaevola* agreed that since the *common people* were incapable of *true and natural theology*, it was practical for them to be deceived in their religion. *Strabo* also argued that the *common people cannot be led toward piety by philosophical reason and truth, but this must be done by superstition and the help of fables and extraordinary stories*. The same was partly acknowledged as true by *Synesius*. *Plato* also stated that it is hard to find out God, but impossible to describe him to the common people; therefore, there is a necessity for a "civil theology" distinct from the natural and philosophical. 540, 542

XXXV. We come now to the next point proposed: that besides this seeming and imaginary <note>original: "phantastick"</note> *polytheism* of the Pagans—which was nothing but the *many-naming* <note>original: "polyonymy"</note> of one God—they had another *real polytheism*, even in their natural and philosophical...

...philosophical theology itself. *But this does not refer to self-existent gods, but only to those who were generated or created.* Thus, according to Plutarch, one highest "unmade" God is the Maker and Father of all the other gods, *who are generated or derived from him.* And Proclus concludes that *all the gods derive their divinity from the First God, who is therefore the fountain of the Godhead.* Page 542, 543

These inferior Pagan gods were called "substantial powers" by Ammianus Marcellinus. This was *meant to contrast them with those other* poetical and political gods *who were not substantial or real, but were only various names or concepts for the one Supreme God.* These "substantial powers" (through whom *divination and prophecy were imparted to men*) were said to be *all subject to that one sovereign deity called* Themis, whom Pagan theologians placed on the throne of Jupiter. *This* Themis *is also another name or concept for the Supreme God, in addition to those mentioned before.* Poetry and imagination <note>original: "Phantaſtry"</note> were intermingled by the Pagans with their natural or philosophical theology. 543, 544

Thus the Pagans *held there were both one God and many gods, in different senses.* Onatus and Plotinus argued *that the majesty of the Supreme God consists in having multitudes of gods dependent on him and ruled by him, and that the honor given to them reflects back upon him.* The gods of the Eastern Pagans *were not merely dead statues and images, but living, intelligent beings represented by those images.* Christians *did not assert a "solitary deity," as Pagans claimed, but agreed with* Seneca *that God has generated or created innumerable intelligent beings superior to men who serve as ministers of his kingdom. The only difference was that Christians gave these beings no religious worship.* Derived from Lactantius. 544, 546

XXXVI. *In addition to the inferior gods generally accepted by all Pagans (namely, the living stars, demons, and heroes), the more refined thinkers—who did not consider the living world itself to be the Supreme Deity—acknowledged*

<column-break/>

*a Trinity of Divine Hypostases* <note>original: "Hypoſtaſes"; distinct persons or substances within the Godhead</note> *that was superior to all of them. This doctrine was claimed by* Plotinus *to be very ancient, and not an invention of* Plato. Page 546

Parmenides *was an upholder of a* Trinity long before Plato. *This belief was attributed to the* Pythagoreans *by* Moderatus (as cited in Simplicius) *and* Iamblichus (as cited in Proclus). *Before* Pythagoras, Orpheus *had his own* Trinity: Phanes, Uranus, and Chronus, *who are the same as* Plato’s "Three Kings" or Principles. *It is probable that* Pythagoras and Orpheus *derived this from the theology of the Egyptian* Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note>. *There are some traces of such a* Trinity *in the* Mithraic mysteries *of the* Persians *and the* Zoroastrian Cabala. *The same is explicitly declared in the Magical or Chaldean Oracles.* A Trinity of gods was worshipped anciently by the Samothracians and called by the Hebrew name Cabiri, the Mighty Gods. *The Roman* Capitoline Trinity *was derived from this; the second member of which was* Minerva, or Divine Wisdom. *The "Ternary" (the number three) was used by the Pagans in their religious rites as a mysterious number.* 546, 547

*Since it is not at all probable that such a* Trinity of Divine Hypostases *could have originated from human wit, we may reasonably agree with what* Proclus *affirms: that it was originally* a theology of divine tradition or revelation <note>original: "Θεοπαράδοτος Θεολογία"</note>. *It was first imparted to the Hebrews and then communicated from them to other nations. Nevertheless, because this "Divine Cabala" was poorly understood by these Pagans, it was corrupted and distorted by many of them.* 547, 548

*This was universally called by them a* Trinity of Gods, *or a First, Second, and Third God. Some called it a* Trinity of Causes, *of* Principles, *and of* Craftsmen <note>original: "Opificers"</note>. *The tradition of the "Three Gods" mentioned in* Proclus *is ancient and famous.* Numenius *called his three gods the* Father, the Son, and the Grandson <note>original: "Nephew"</note>. *To* Plotinus, *the "Nous" or Intellect was a second God, and the world was an image of all three Gods.*

# The Contents.

The ancient tradition <note>original: "Cabbala"</note> of the Trinity. Page 556, 557

This is that Platonic, or rather **False-Platonic Trinity**, which we oppose to the Christian version; namely, a Trinity that confuses the differences between God and the created being. It brings the Deity down lower and lower by degrees, and at length scatters it into all the living parts of the world. This serves as a foundation for infinite polytheism, "world-worship" <note>original: "Cosmolatry"</note>, and the worship of created things. Hence, the Platonists and Pythagoreans were the most suitable men to be defenders of Paganism against Christianity. 557, 558

Concerning the **Christian Trinity**, three things are to be observed. First, it is not a Trinity of mere names and words, nor logical notions, or incomplete conceptions of God. This doctrine was condemned by the Christian Church in the case of Sabellius <note>a 3rd-century priest who taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were merely different "modes" or roles of one person</note> and others. Instead, it is a Trinity of individual existences <note>original: "Hypostases"</note>, subsistences, or persons. 558, 559

The second thing to observe in the Christian Trinity is that although the second person <note>original: "Hypostasis"</note> was begotten from the first, and the third proceeds from both the first and second, yet neither of them are created beings. First, because they were not made "out of nothing" <note>original: "ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων"</note>, or brought into being from a prior state of non-existence, but are both co-eternal with the Father. Secondly, because all are necessarily existent and cannot be destroyed. Thirdly, because all of them are universal, or infinite, and are the creators of all other specific beings. 559

The third thing to observe regarding the Christian Trinity is that its three persons are all truly and really one God. This is not only by reason of their agreement of will, but also because of a mutual interpenetration <note>original: "περιχώρησις" (perichoresis)</note> and indwelling <note>original: "ἐνύπαρξις" (enuparxis)</note>—a permeating and existing within each other. Though no instance of a similar unity can be found elsewhere in nature, yet since two distinct substances (the corporeal body and the incorporeal soul) make one man and person in ourselves, much more may three divine persons be one God. ibid. <note>meaning "in the same place/page"</note>

Though there is much mystery in the Christian

<column-break/>

Trinity, yet there is nothing of plain contradiction to reason within it; that is, no nonsense or impossibility. The malicious intent of those who represent the Christian Trinity as absolutely contrary to reason is to corrupt men’s understandings, and make them swallow down other things which are unquestionably nonsensical. Page 560

The Christian Trinity is much more agreeable to reason than the False-Platonic version in the three particulars mentioned before. First, the False-Platonists make their third person the "living world" or the Soul of the World. This is not only too great a leap between the second and third persons, but also a gross debasement of the Deity, confusing it with the creature. It is a foundation for world-idolatry and the worship of inanimate things as parts and members of God. ibid.

To Origen <note>an influential early Christian scholar</note>, God was only "as it were the Soul of the World" <note>original: "Quasi Anima Mundi"</note>, and not truly and properly so. All the perfection of this notion should be attributed to God, but not its imperfections. 560, 561

It is certain that according to the more refined Platonists, their third divine person was not a worldly soul, but a soul above the world, and the "craftsman" <note>original: "δημιουργὸς" (demiurge)</note> or maker of the entire world. This was the view of Amelius, Porphyry, and Plotinus. Plato likewise held there was a "double soul" of the world. To these thinkers, the third person was no creature, but a creator. 562

So in their second particular (which shows why the aforementioned False-Platonic Trinity is no true Trinity), they make all the "ideas" and original patterns <note>original: "Archetypal Paradigms"</note> of things into so many individual persons, living beings, and gods. This is a monstrous excess. It is not to be doubted that Plato well understood these "ideas" to be nothing but "thoughts" <note>original: "Noemata"</note> or conceptions of the Divine Mind, existing nowhere apart by themselves. However, they were called "essences" or "substances" <note>original: "οὐσίαι"</note> because they are not such accidental and fleeting <note>original: "Evanid"</note> things as our human thoughts are, for they are the permanent and eternal objects of all science. They were also called "living beings" <note>original: "ζῶα"</note> to signify that they...

Therefore, this Pseudo-Platonic Trinity should be rejected [original: "exploded"], as it confuses the differences between God and the creature. In contrast, the Christian Trinity is homogeneous—entirely Deity or Creator. All other things are supposed to be the creatures of those three persons <note>original: "Hypostases"</note> and produced by their joint concurrence and influence; they are all, in reality, but one God. ->Page 568, 570<-

Nevertheless, these previously mentioned corruptions and adulterations of that divine tradition [original: "Cabbala"] of the Trinity are not to be charged to Plato himself, nor to all the other ancient Platonists and Pythagoreans. Some of these approached so near to the Christian Trinity as to make their three persons [original: "Hypostases"] all truly divine and creators, with all other things being their creatures. ->in the same place [original: "ibid."]<-

First, therefore, Plato himself, in his *Timaeus*, carefully distinguishes between God and the creature and determines the bounds of each in this manner: the first is that which "always is" and was never made; the second is that which is "made" and had a beginning, but truly "is not." His meaning here was perverted by later [original: "junior"] Platonists, whom Boethius <note>a 6th-century philosopher and statesman</note> also followed. In this work, Plato takes it for granted that whatever has a temporary and successive duration had a beginning; and whatever had no beginning has no successive, but rather a permanent duration. Thus, he concludes that whatever is eternal is God, but whatever exists in time and has a beginning is a creature. ->570, 572<-

Now, according to Plato, there are more eternal gods than one. These are not just ideas or mental concepts <note>original: "Noemata"</note>, but true substantial things: his First, Second, and Third, mentioned in his *Epistle to Dionysius*, or his trinity of divine persons [original: "Hypostases"], who are the makers or creators of the whole world.

<column-break/>

Cicero's gods, by whose providence the world and all its parts were framed. ->Page 572, 573<-

The second person [original: "Hypostasis"] in Plato's Trinity, namely Mind or Intellect, is unquestionably eternal and without beginning. Plotinus affirmed the same of the third person [original: "Hypostasis"], or *Psyche* (the Soul), which is called the Word of the Second, just as the Second is the Word of the First. Porphyry's testimony to this effect is found in Saint Cyril; where Mind, or the second divine person [original: "Hypostasis"] (though said to have been begotten from the First), is nevertheless called "his own father" <note>original: αὐτοπάτωρ</note> and "self-begotten" <note>original: αὐτογέννητος</note>, and is said to have sprung forth "by self-generation" <note>original: αὐτογόνως</note>. ->Page 573, 574.<-

This mysterious riddle is explained by Plotinus. Its plain meaning is nothing more than this: that although this second person [original: "Hypostasis"] proceeded from the First, it was not produced by it in the manner of a creature, nor arbitrarily by will and choice, but by way of natural and necessary emanation. Thus, some Christians have ventured to call the *Logos* (the Word) "God of himself" <note>original: αὐτόθεον</note> and "God from himself" <note>original: "Ex seipso Deum"</note>. ->574, 575<-

Dionysius Petavius <note>a 17th-century Jesuit theologian</note>, having explained the doctrine of Arius—that the Father was the only eternal God, and the Son, or Word, was a creature made in time and out of nothing—concludes it is undeniably clear from this that Arius was a thorough [original: "German"], true, and genuine Platonist. However, it is most certain from this that Arius was no Platonist at all, and that Petavius himself did not well understand the Platonic doctrine. Had Plato denied the eternity of his second person [original: "Hypostasis"], called *Nous* (Mind), he would have had to deny the eternity of Wisdom and Understanding itself, as this was to him the very Wisdom by which God himself is wise and by which he made the world. Athanasius <note>a 4th-century champion of Trinitarian orthodoxy</note> also agrees with this: "Our Lord is Wisdom, and not secondary to any other wisdom"; and, "The Father of the Word is not himself the Word"; and, "That which produced Word and Wisdom was not itself Word and Wisdom." This was in opposition to

<header>The Contents.</header>

Arius, who maintained *another Word* and *Wisdom* that was *prior* <note>original: "Senior"</note> to the *Word* and *Wisdom* in Christ. These Platonists were so far from denying the eternity of the *Word* that they instead attributed *too much* to it by making it self-begotten. Therefore, *Plato*, by asserting the eternity of his *second person* <note>original: "Hypostasis"</note>, the *Mind* <note>original: "Nous"</note> or *Word* <note>original: "Logos"</note>, and *not* of the *world*, did thereby—according to the doctrine of *Athanasius* himself—make it to be no creature. Page 575

Nor is there any force at all in the testimony of *Macrobius*, cited by *Petavius* to the contrary, wherein the *first person* is said to have created *Mind* from itself, and the *second* to have created the *Soul*. This is because these ancient *Pagans* did not confine the word *create* <note>original: "Creare"</note> to such a narrow sense as *Christians* commonly do, but used it generally for all manners of production. *Petavius's* mistake comes chiefly from the "spurious Trinity" of the later Platonists, whose "third God" is called by themselves a *created thing* <note>original: "poiēma"</note>. *But this was not the doctrine of the ancients.* 576

Nevertheless, there is some reason to doubt whether *Plato's* third person was eternal, because in his *Timaeus*, he generates the *Soul of the World* <note>original: "Mundane Soul"</note>. This controversy is decided by supposing a double *Soul* <note>original: "Psyche"</note>: one that is *within the world* <note>original: "egkosmion"</note> and one that is *beyond the world* <note>original: "huperkosmion"</note>. The first of these is called by *Plotinus* a "heavenly Venus" and a "separate Soul." Therefore, although the lower Venus (or World Soul) was, according to *Plato*, made in time along with the *world*, the higher Divine Soul (or Heavenly Venus)—the son of *Chronos* without a mother and Plato's third person—is eternal and without beginning. 576, 577

*This is further evident from this fact: in his Epistle to Dionysius, Plato affirms that regarding the second and third persons, as well as the first, there is* **nothing of the sort** <note>original: "ouden toiouto"</note> *to be found in those things that are related to our human soul (or are creaturely).* 577

Secondly, the three persons of *Plato's* Trinity are not only all eternal, but also necessarily existent and absolutely impossible to annihilate. The *first* could no more exist without the *second* and *third* than the *sun* could exist without its primary light and secondary splendor. According to *Plotinus*, these are the three principles of the universe, so there could be neither more nor fewer of them. Those who called the second person the *Self-Father* <note>original: "Autopator"</note> signified by that title the necessity of its existence. 577, 578

Thirdly, these three Platonic persons are eternal, necessary, and likewise universal, or encompassing the whole world; that is, they are infinite and omnipotent. Therefore, they are called principles, causes, and

<column-break/>

Architects <note>original: "Opificers"</note>. Although *Mind* <note>original: "Nous"</note> is commonly looked upon as the highest principle of all things, *Plato* set before it **One Most Simple Good**. When *Plato* says that *Mind* is *of the same kind* <note>original: "genetes"</note> with the First Cause of all things, it is the same as if he had affirmed it to be *consubstantial* <note>original: "homoousion"</note> or of the same essence with it. Page 578, 579

*Plato's* third person, the *Soul* <note>original: "Psyche"</note> or the superior World Soul, is called by him *Zeus* (from the Greek word *Zēn*, meaning **to live**), and is also called the cause and fountain of life and the prince and king of all things. When it is said to be the *offspring* <note>original: "ekgonon"</note> of the Highest Mind, it is thereby made consubstantial with it as well. So, *Plato's* entire Trinity is "Homoousian" <note>of one and the same substance</note>. 579

*Though by the "Demiurge" or Architect, Plato commonly meant the second person (the Mind or Intellect), yet Atticus, Amelius, Plotinus, and others called the third person (the higher Soul) by that name as well. Therefore, according to the genuine Platonic and Parmenidean Trinity, all three persons are joint creators of the whole world. Ficinus and Proclus often say this. It was Porphyry's affirmation that the Deity, according to Plato, extends to three persons.* Ibid. <note>in the same place</note>

It is certain, therefore, that *Arius* did not follow Plato, but rather *Athanasius* and the *Nicene Fathers* did; though they did not make *Plato*, but the *Scriptures*, their foundation. The genuine Trinity of *Plato* and *Parmenides* is a middle ground between that of *Sabellius* and that of *Arius*. It is neither a Trinity of words and names, like the former, nor a "Heteroousian" <note>of different substances</note> Trinity (a confused jumble of God and creature together), but is "Homoousian" and of the same kind: all eternal, necessarily existent, infinite or omnipotent, and the Creator. 579, 580

*But so that it may appear even more fully how far the most refined Platonic and Parmenidean Trinity either agrees or disagrees with Scripture and Christian doctrine, two further things should be observed. First, the Platonists universally asserted an essential dependence of their second and third persons upon the first, as well as a gradual subordination among them. Thus Plotinus says: "Chronos" (the second person) is in a middle state between his father, who is greater, and his son, who is inferior. In this eternal generation or emanation, there is no progress upward, but all is downward in a gradual descent.* 580, 581

More on the dependence and gradual subordination of the second and third persons of the Platonic Trinity to the first. Each following person is called a *trace* <note>original: "ichnos"</note> or a *form* <note>original: "tupos"</note>, and

...and image <note>original: "εἰκὼν"</note>, and representation <note>original: "εἴδωλον"</note>, and imitation <note>original: "μίμημα"</note> of that which came before it. Philo’s controversial expression that the *Word* <note>original: "Logos"</note> is the "shadow of God." This hierarchy is commonly illustrated by the out-shining <note>original: "ἔκλαμψις"</note> or radiance <note>original: "ἀπαύγασμα"</note>—the effulgence or out-shining splendor of the sun. Page 581, 582

The same is further demonstrated from the several distinctive characters given to each Person <note>original: "Hypostasis"</note> in the true Platonic or Parmenidean Trinity. The First: One before all things <note>original: "ἓν πρὸ πάντων"</note>; The Second: One that is all things <note>original: "ἓν πάντα"</note>, regarding their distinct Ideas; The Third: One and all things <note>original: "ἓν καὶ πάντα"</note>, as really producing all things. The First is essential Unity and Goodness; the Second is Understanding and Wisdom; the Third is Self-Active Love and Power. The First, or Father, exists in an unbegotten manner <note>original: "ἀγεννήτως"</note>, above action; the Second, or Son, is the *Creator* <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note>, the maker or contriving architect of the world, but an immovable nature; the Third is a moveable Deity and the immediate governor of the whole world. Amelius’s distinction of them into "him who is," "him who has," and "him who sees" <note>original: "τὸν ὄντα, τὸν ἔχοντα, τὸν ὁρῶντα"</note>. 582, 583

The greatest difficulty in the distinctive characters of these three Platonic Persons <note>original: "Hypostases"</note>: that understanding, reason, and wisdom should be made specific to the Second, as if the First were therefore devoid of mind, reason, and wisdom. This is a secret <note>original: "Arcanum"</note> of the Platonic and Pythagorean theology: that whereas Anaxagoras, Aristotle, and the common people make Mind and Understanding the oldest of all things and the highest principle in the universe, this system supposes Mind, Knowledge, and Wisdom to be not the first, but the second. This is partly because there is multiplicity in knowledge, but there must be unity before multiplicity. It is also because there must be an object of thought <note>original: "Νοητὸν"</note> before there is an Intellect <note>original: "Νοῦς"</note>. Furthermore, the act of understanding <note>original: "Intellection"</note> or knowledge is not the highest Good or Happiness, and therefore there must be some substantial thing that is, by its nature, superior to Mind. Hence it is concluded that the Supreme Deity is better than the *Logos* (Reason, Word, or Intellect). That which is not the Word <note>original: "Logos"</note> is the source from which the Word is derived. Thus Philo says: The God who exists before Reason or the Word is better than all of rational nature. But this difficulty is common to both Platonism and Christianity, which likewise makes the Word (or Reason and Wisdom) the second, not the first, Person. Thus Athanasius denies that there is any Word, Reason, or Wisdom before the Son of God. What then? Is the First Person therefore mindless <note>original: "ἄνους"</note> and reasonless <note>original: "ἄλογος"</note>, devoid of reason and mind? Plotinus attempts to answer this by saying that the First has a simple light <note>original: "Φῶς ἁπλοῦν"</note>, different from that multiform light of knowledge. Again, he argues that the First

<column-break/>

is Intelligence itself <note>original: "Νόησις αὐτὴ"</note>, and therefore superior to the Intellect, or to that which possesses the act of understanding. (For intelligence itself does not understand/think <note>original: "ἡ νόησις οὐ νοεῖ"</note>.) Besides this, there is another attempt to resolve this difficulty. Page 583, 586

The ground of this Platonic dependence and subordination in the Divine Persons <note>original: "Hypostases"</note>: because there is but one fountain of the Godhead, so that the Second must necessarily differ from the First, as the radiance <note>original: "ἀπαύγασμα"</note> differs from the light <note>original: "Φῶς"</note>, or the splendor from the sun. 586, 587

Though the Second Person is said to have been begotten from the First, this is not to be understood as a human generation, where three men (Father, Son, and Grandson), all adults, have no essential dependence upon one another nor gradual subordination. That is merely an imperfect generation. 587

Furthermore, the Platonists would recommend this hierarchy in the Deity, or subordination of Persons, because by this means there is not so great a "leap" in the creation as there otherwise must be. Nor is the whole Deity elevated to such a disproportionate height as would render it incapable of having any intercourse with the lower world. Were the whole Deity either one simple Monad or else an immovable Mind, it could have no such liberty of will as is commonly attributed to it, nor be capable of being affected by anything here below; indeed, it would be no fitter an object for human devotion than a diamond-hard <note>original: "Adamantine"</note> rock. However, all the phenomena of the Deity can be explained <note>original: "salvable"</note> by this Platonic gradation. 587, 588

Also, according to this hypothesis, a reasonable explanation can be given as to why there are exactly three Divine Persons, and neither fewer nor more. 588

The second thing to be observed concerning the genuine Platonic or Parmenidean Trinity: that though its Persons are called "three natures," "three principles," "three creators" <note>original: "Opificers"</note>, and "three gods," they all really make up but one Divinity. For the world, being created by all three and yet having but one creation, they must necessarily be all one Creator. Porphyry, quoted in St. Cyril, states explicitly that, according to Plato, the essence of the Deity extends to three Persons <note>original: "Hypostases"</note>. 588, 589

Platonists further add that were it not for this essential dependence and subordination, the three Divine Persons would necessarily be three equal <note>original: "Co-ordinate"</note> gods; they would be no more "one God" than three men are one man, or three suns are one sun. Whereas the sun, its splendor, and its derived light may all be rightly accounted one and the same thing. 589, 590

# The Contents.

*Union, and such a close connection between their three persons <term>hypostases: distinct individualities or persons within the Godhead</term> that nothing like it is found elsewhere in nature. Plotinus says that there is nothing between them, and that they are only not the exact same thing. They also acknowledge their mutual indwelling <term>perichoresis: the mutual interpenetration of the persons of the Trinity</term>. To the Platonists, the three persons are one divinity in the same way as the center, the immovable radius, and the movable circumference of a sphere are all one sphere. The first is infinite goodness, the second is infinite wisdom, and the third is infinite active love and substantial power.* Page 590, 591

*From this full account of the true and genuine Platonic Trinity, both its agreement and disagreement with the Christian version clearly appear. First, its agreement in the three fundamental points mentioned before, and consequently its difference from Arianism <note>original: "Arianism": the belief that Jesus was a created being, not co-eternal with God the Father</note>.* 591, 592

*Secondly, despite this, its disagreement with the currently accepted doctrine lies in its assumption that the three persons do not have one and the same unique essence, nor an absolute equality, but a gradual hierarchy <note>original: "subordination"</note> and essential dependence. Because of this, some say it resembles Arianism, however different it may be in the main point.* 592

*Besides this, even the best Platonists are sometimes guilty of extravagant expressions. Plotinus’s claim that "it is of the same species as ours" <note>original: "ὁμοειδὴς δὲ καὶ ἡμετέρα"</note>, meaning that our human soul is of the same kind as the World Soul, or Third Person—the World Soul being merely the "elder sister." This would actually make it of the same essence or substance <term>consubstantial: of the same substance or essence</term> as we humans, as Saint Augustine understood it. This provides a foundation for creature-worship or idolatry. This is why the Arians were called "Porphyrianists" by Constantine <note>Porphyry was a neo-Platonic philosopher who opposed Christianity; the label was intended to brand Arians as heathens</note>. But this doctrine, being contrary to Plato, is also contradicted elsewhere by Plotinus himself.* 593, 594

*Nevertheless, a Platonic Christian would defend <note>original: "Apologize"</note> Plato and the genuine Pythagoreans in this way: First, that having no Scriptures, councils, nor creeds to direct them in the darkness of this mystery and to guide their language, they are the more excusable if they were not always uniform and were sometimes extravagant. It is more to be wondered at that they should approach so near to Christian truth.* 594, 595

*And as for their gradual hierarchy of persons and the dependence of the second and third upon the first, these Platonists are the more excusable because the majority of Christian doctors for the first three centuries seem to have asserted the same.* 595, 596

The Platonic Christian's further defense;

<column-break/>

*That the Platonists' intention in ranking their three persons was only to exclude a plurality of independent gods of equal rank. That none of Plato's three persons are creatures, but rather the essence of the Godhead belongs to them all, as they are all eternal, necessarily existing, infinite or omnipotent, and creators. Therefore, in the sense of the Council of Nicaea, they are of the same substance <term>consubstantial</term> and co-equal. The essence of the Godhead, in which all three persons agree, is considered general and universal by both the Church Fathers and the Platonists.* Page 596, 597

*In addition, the genuine Platonists would also acknowledge all three of their persons to be of the same substance <note>original: "Homoousian"</note>, co-essential, or of the same substance—yet in a further sense, as making up one entire divinity, just as the root, trunk, and branches are all part of the same vine. The Trinity is not so undivided as to mean the three are not three within it. The inequality and ranking in the Platonic Trinity exist only within the Deity itself and in the relationship of the persons to one another; toward the outside world <note>original: "ad extrà"</note>, they are all one and the same God, jointly working together in the same actions, and in that respect, they lack any inequality.* 597, 598

*Furthermore, the Platonic Christian would argue that according to the principles of Christianity itself, there must necessarily be some dependence and ranking in these persons in their relation to one another—a priority and secondary order of dignity. That which is originally "of itself" has a kind of priority and superiority over that which is wholly derived from it. The second and third persons are not as "all-powerful" as the first, because they cannot beget or produce the first. Hence the first person is styled by Macrobius as "the most omnipotent of all." Several passages in Scripture favor this hypothesis, as do the Orthodox Fathers. Consider Athanasius's comparisons: to the original light and the secondary brightness; to the fountain and the stream; the root and the branch; the water and the vapor. The equality asserted by the Orthodox was meant to oppose the Arian inequality between God and a creature—asserting that they are equally God, or uncreated. Despite this, some inequality among them is allowed by Petavius and others, regarding the relationship between "This God" and "That Person."* 599, 600

*However, there is no need for any more inequality and ranking in the Platonic Trinity than in the Christian Trinity; they are simply infinite goodness, infinite wisdom, and infinite active love and substantial power. Another hypothesis of some Platonists, hinted at by Saint Augustine from Porphyry, makes the third person a middle ground between the first*

<meta>This page continues the table of contents, focusing on the complex theological debates surrounding the nature of the Trinity. It examines how early Church Fathers and Platonic philosophers defined the "essence" of the Godhead, contrasting the idea of three distinct individuals sharing a common nature with the idea of three persons sharing a single, unique substance.</meta>

# The Contents.

...and Second; and it implies not so much a *gradation <note>original: "Gradation": a series of successive stages or degrees</note>, as a circulation <note>original: "Circulation": referring to the theological concept of perichoresis, the mutual indwelling of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit</note> within the Trinity*. Page 600, 601

*Regarding the Platonists*, they assumed their *three persons* <term>hypostases</term> (though forming *one entire divinity*) had their own *distinct, individual essences*. Without these, they believed the persons could be nothing but *three names*. The Platonic Christian would argue in defense that *the Orthodox Church Fathers themselves generally held this view: that the essence of the Godhead, in which all three persons agree, is not one single individual essence, but rather one common or universal essence*. Their distinction for this purpose was between *essence* <term>ousia</term> and *person* <term>hypostasis</term>—the former being *common* or general, the latter being *individual* or *singular*. This was the view of *Theodoret, Basil*, and many others. *Petavius* acknowledges that the *Greek Fathers* universally agreed on this point. 601, 602

*The opinion of Gregory of Nyssa, Cyril, John of Damascus*, and others was *that the persons of the Trinity are "one" only in the same way that three individuals belong to the same species, or as three men share the same common humanity*. *These were the primary supporters of an absolute, independent, and equal status among the persons* <note>original: "Un-subordinate Co-equality"</note>. *This is the only fault that Saint Cyril finds with the Platonists: that they did not insist on such a shared substance* <note>original: "Consubstantiality"</note>. *However, this view of the Trinity could be seen as tritheism <note>original: "Tritheism": the belief that there are three distinct gods</note>, as its three persons would be no more "one God" than three men are "one man." Nevertheless, it is certain that these Fathers did not believe the three persons <term>hypostases</term> of the Trinity shared the exact same individual essence*. Another *extreme view arose later to replace this tritheism, supported only by the authority of a Lateran Council*. 603, 604

*The fact that this "sameness of individual essence" was not claimed by the Nicene Fathers or the first opponents of Arius* is first clearly acknowledged by *Petavius*. 604, 605

But this is further evident because *the same Orthodox Fathers who opposed Arianism also condemned Sabellianism <note>original: "Sabellianism": the belief that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three different modes or aspects of one God, rather than three distinct persons</note>. Sabellianism claimed that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were only one person <term>hypostasis</term>—that is, they had one and the same individual essence—and therefore recognized no Trinity other than a Trinity of names or words*. 605

It also appears from the fact that *the word "consubstantial"* <term>Homoousios</term> *never had any other meaning than to signify that things which are numerically distinct agree in some common and general nature or essence*. Saint *Basil stated that a thing is not "consubstantial"* <term>Homoousios</term>, *co-essential, or of the same substance with itself, but is always consubstantial with something else*. *The term "consubstantial"* <term>To homoousion</term> means the same as *kinship* <term>syngeneia</term> in the writings of *Plotinus*. Athanasius uses it similarly, asserting that the branches are *consubstantial* <term>Homoousios</term> and of the same kind...

<column-break/>

...as the root. Additionally, terms like *of the same kind* <term>homogenes</term>, *of the same species* <term>homoeides</term>, and *of the same nature* <term>homophyes</term> were used by *Athanasius* and others as synonyms for *consubstantial* <term>homoousios</term>. *None of these words signify an identical individual essence, but only a general or universal one. The Council of Chalcedon stated that our Savior Christ, regarding his humanity, was "consubstantial"* <term>Homoousios</term> *with us humans. Thus, Athanasius denies that the Son or the Word is consubstantial with created beings; he also affirms that men are consubstantial with one another, and every son is consubstantial and shares the same essence with his father*. Page 605, 606

*Moreover, the meaning the Nicene Fathers gave to their "consubstantiality" may be more fully understood from the doctrine of Arius which they opposed. Arius made the Son a created being and therefore—as Athanasius writes—"of a different essence"* <term>heteroousios</term> *or "of a foreign substance"* <term>allotrioousios</term> *from the Father. It is clearly proved from Athanasius that by the "consubstantiality" of the Word, nothing more was meant than its being uncreated rather than a creature*. 606, 608

*Further proof from Athanasius shows that "consubstantiality" does not mean a shared individual essence, but only a shared general essence. This is also found in the writings of Saint Augustine*. 608, 611

*Finally, it is evident that the "consubstantial" <note>original: "Homoousian"</note> Fathers did not claim a shared individual essence against Arius because they rejected two other words, "identical in essence"* <term>tautoousios</term> *and "single in essence"* <term>monoousios</term>, (*believing they had a Sabellian meaning*). The former was rejected by *Epiphanius* and the latter by *Athanasius*. *Thus, those who asserted the Son was "consubstantial"* <term>homoousios</term> *with the Father denied he was "of a single essence"* <term>monoousios</term> *or "identical in essence"* <term>tautoousios</term>, *meaning they denied he had the exact same individual essence*. 612, 613

*From all these considerations, the Platonic Christian concludes that just as the genuine Trinity of Plato agreed with that of the Orthodox Christians in being "consubstantial"* <term>homoousian</term> *rather than "of a different essence"* <term>heteroousian</term>—*not made of a mix of God and creature, but entirely of the same uncreated or Creator nature—so too did the Trinity of the first Orthodox anti-Arians agree with the Platonic Trinity. It was not "of a single essence"* <term>monoousian</term> *or "identical in essence"* <term>tautoousian</term> (*one and the same individual essence under three names or concepts only*), *but was instead truly three persons* <term>hypostases</term>. 612

*Nevertheless, there remains a question to be answered: Did Athanasius, the Nicene Fathers, and all the first anti-Arians therefore assert the same thing as Gregory of Nyssa, Cyril, and others—that the three persons in the Trinity were merely three equal individuals of the same species, having only a specific unity or identity (along with a shared will)—or did they all agree in the*

*Uncreated Nature only. This is bluntly asserted in the* Dialogues on the Trinity, *commonly attributed* <note>original: "Vulgarly Imputed"</note> *to* Athanasius, *and to that purpose also, that* Three Men *are not* Three Men, *except when they* disagree *from one another in* will *and* opinion. *But these* dialogues are falsely attributed <note>original: "pseudepigraphous"</note>. *Nevertheless, it must be granted that* Athanasius *himself, in that book titled* On the Common Essence of the Persons, *seems to place somewhat too much* emphasis *upon this* common nature, essence, *or* substance *of the* Three Persons *to make them all but* One God. *However, it is certain he does not rely upon that alone; and elsewhere he acknowledges it to be insufficient. The true reason why* Athanasius *placed such great* emphasis *upon* consubstantiality <note>original: "Homoousiotes"</note> *was not because this alone would make them* One God, *but because they could not possibly be* One God *without it. For if the* Father *is* uncreated, *and the* Son *is a* creature, *then they cannot both be* One God. *Several passages from* Athanasius *are cited for this purpose. Those expressions in his work regarding* One Godhead, *the* sameness of the Godhead, *and* One Essence *or* Substance *in the* Trinity *are not to be understood as if the* Three Persons *were merely different* names, concepts, *or* modes *of* one thing. Page 612, 616

*Therefore, although* Athanasius *lays his foundation in this* <term>specific unity</term> <note>original: "εἰδικὴ ἑνότης" (eidike henotes)</note> *of the persons (which is their* consubstantiality), *in order for them to be* One God, *he also adds other considerations to it. First of all, he argues that they are not* three sources of origin <note>original: "Principles"</note>, *but only* one; *the* essence of the Father *being the* root and fountain *of the* Son and Spirit, *and the* three persons <term>hypostases</term> *gathered together under* One Head. *Here* Athanasius *implies that if they were perfectly* equal and independent, *they would not be* one, *but* three gods. 616

*In the next place, he further adds that these* three <term>hypostases</term> *are not* three separate or disjointed things, *but are* indivisibly united; *just as* brightness *is* inseparable *from the* sun, *and* wisdom *is inseparable from the one who is* wise. *Neither of these* persons *could exist without the other, nor could anything come between them; they are so immediately* joined *together that there is a kind of* <term>continuity</term> <note>original: "συνέχεια" (synecheia)</note> *between them.* 616, 617

*Thirdly,* Athanasius *goes even further, affirming that these* three <term>hypostases</term> *are not only* indivisibly joined, *but also have a* mutual indwelling <note>original: "Inexistence"</note> *in each other. This was later called* <term>perichoresis</term> <note>original: "Emperichoresis"</note>. *That statement of our Saviour,* "I am in the Father, and the Father in me," *was therefore* disputed *by the* Arians <note>Followers of Arius who believed Jesus was a created being, not fully God</note> *because they conceived of* incorporeal things *in a* physical *manner. He argues that the* Godhead of the Son *is the* Godhead of the Father, *and the* Fa-

*Lastly,* Athanasius *also in* various places *supposes the* three divine <term>hypostases</term> *to make up* one entire Divinity; *just as the* fountain *and the* stream *make up* one entire river, *or the* root, trunk, *and* branches *make up* one entire tree. *Accordingly, the word* <term>consubstantial</term> <note>original: "Homoousios"</note> *is used by* Athanasius *in a broader* sense: *not only to signify things* sharing one common and general essence, *but also those that* essentially work together *to form* one entire *thing. Nevertheless, that* tritheistic Trinity <note>The belief that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three separate gods</note> *of* St. Gregory of Nyssa, Cyril, *and others—regarding* three equal individuals *under the same* species (like three men)—*seems to have been a* deviation. 619, 620

*The* reason *for this* defense *of the* true Platonic Trinity *is that it is against the* interest *of* Christianity *for this philosophy to be made more* different *from* Christian doctrine *than it actually is. Moreover, it is certain that this* true Platonic Trinity *was* anti-Arian; *or rather, the* Arian *view was* anti-Platonic. *For this reason,* Socrates <note>A 5th-century Christian church historian</note> *wondered why* George *and* Timothy, *two priests,* should join the Arian faction, *when one of them was considered a great* Platonist *and the other a follower of* Origen. 620, 621

*Furthermore,* Platonic pagans *after the rise of* Christianity *highly approved of the* beginning *of* St. John's Gospel *concerning the* Word <note>original: "Logos"</note>, *as it exactly agreed with their* Platonic doctrine. *This is seen in* Amelius *(as cited in* Eusebius) *and others.
