# The Contents.

The most significant point to justify this apology is that the majority of Christian Fathers, both before and after the Council of Nicaea, viewed the Platonic Trinity as being very close to the Christian one. If they did not see it as exactly the same thing, they believed it approached it so nearly that it differed chiefly in circumstances or wording. This was the view of Justin Martyr, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Saint Cyprian (or the author of the book *On the Holy Spirit* <note>original: "De Spiritu Sancto"</note>), and Eusebius of Caesarea. Most importantly, Athanasius himself gave an outstanding testimony to this fact. To these may be added Saint Augustine and Theodoret. Although Saint Cyril criticized the Platonic idea of subordination (since he believed the Trinity consisted of three co-equal individuals under the same specific nature of the Godhead), he still acknowledged that Plato was not entirely ignorant of the truth, etc. It has already been made unquestionably evident that Plato’s subordination of his second person <term>hypostasis</term> to the first was not like the Arian view of a creature to the Creator. Page 621, 625.

A wonderful Providence of Almighty God is to be noted here: this doctrine of a Trinity of Divine Persons <term>hypostases</term> was accepted in the pagan world before Christianity, as if to prepare a way for learned men to receive it. The later <note>original: "Junior"</note> Platonists were so aware of this that they eventually changed the whole ancient tradition <note>original: "Cabbala"</note>, besides the corruptions of the Platonic Trinity mentioned earlier (intended to support their polytheism and idolatry). They no longer acknowledged a Trinity, but at least a Quaternity of Divine Persons—specifically, they added another person above and separate from the Trinity. This was first started by Iamblichus, continued by Proclus, and noted by Saint Cyril. Proclus also added other fantastical trinities of his own. 625, 627.

Another advantage of this Platonic Trinity extends to the present day; perhaps it was also intended by Divine Providence to humble those arrogant intellectuals who so boldly dismiss the Trinity as nonsense, an absolute contradiction to reason, and an impossibility. They will find that the best and most independent minds among the pagans—who had no scripture to force the idea upon them—were nonetheless fond of this hypothesis. 627.

It now appears clearly that the ancient Platonists and Pythagoreans should not be accused of being polytheists and idolaters for offering religious worship to their three Divine Persons. One major goal of Christianity was to free the world from idolatry and

<column-break/>

creature-worship. This is why the ancient Fathers so zealously opposed Arianism: because it undermined that goal. It turned back toward paganism and idolatry the very thing intended to rid the world of paganism. One remarkable passage from Athanasius addresses this point. Page 627, 629.

First, it is observable that Athanasius expressly states that the pagans worshipped only one uncreated God and many created gods. Similarly, Gregory of Nazianzus noted that there was only one divinity recognized among the pagans as well. Irenaeus also stated that they attributed the highest place in the deity to one supreme God, the maker of this universe. Secondly, for Athanasius and all those other Fathers who charged the Arians with idolatry, the crime was not worshiping many independent and self-existent gods. Rather, they believed idolatry consisted in giving religious worship to creatures—just as the Arians gave religious worship to the Son (the Word), whom they themselves believed to be merely a creature. 629, 630.

If the Arians were guilty of polytheism or idolatry for worshipping the Son (the Word) as a creature—even though he was the greatest of creatures and the one through whom all others were made—then those who worshipped other inferior beings were even more guilty. Athanasius argued that no creature should be an object of religious worship, and that the Orthodox worshipped the divinity within the humanity of our Savior, Christ. Nestorius was branded with the name "man-worshipper." Some suppose that for something to truly be idolatry, it must involve the impossible: worshipping more than one being as omnipotent, or with the highest form of mental worship <note>original: "Latria"</note>. 630, 632.

We have now sufficiently answered the objection against the idea of God being natural to humanity (which includes the idea of oneness) despite pagan polytheism. Further discussion on this topic (as a foundation for our defense of Christianity) is postponed to make room for a refutation of all atheistic arguments.

The first atheistic argument: that there is no idea of God. In answer to this, the idea of God has already been declared: namely, a perfect understanding Being, unmade or self-existent from eternity, and the cause of all other things. In this definition, there is nothing inconceivable or contradictory. Even these confused atheists themselves, who deny that

# The Contents.

*Even those who deny that there is any Idea of God at all must, nonetheless, of necessity suppose the opposite; because otherwise, by denying His existence, they would be denying the existence of "nothing." They also agree with Theists on this same Idea: while one denies the existence of that which the other asserts—namely, that an "Understanding Nature" is the origin of all things. This Idea of God, as containing uniqueness and singularity, is not only defended at length and validated against the objection of Pagan Polytheism, but it is also proven that mankind has a natural <term>prolepsis</term> <note>original: "prolepsis" - a Greek term for an innate "anticipation" or preconception</note> in their minds regarding the real and actual existence of such a Being. Atheists are regarded as monsters and anomalies of mankind. This serves as a sufficient refutation of the First Atheistic Argument.* Page 633, 634

*Nevertheless, so that Atheists may not claim any of their strengths are being hidden, all five of their specific exceptions against the Idea of God are declared here. Their first exception: that we can have no idea or thought of anything not subject to the senses, much less any evidence of its existence. The Answer: First, although Atheists assume that sense perception is the only knowledge, or at least the original source of knowledge, sense as such is not knowledge or understanding. If it were, then everyone who sees light and colors, or feels heat and cold, would understand light, colors, heat, and cold. It is also clearly proved from Atomic Philosophy (which Epicurean Atheists rely on so heavily) that there is a higher faculty of the soul which judges the senses, detects their illusions <note>original: "phantastry"</note>, and resolves sensible things into intelligible principles, etc. No mere feeling or passion is able to make a judgment of itself or of other things. Even the confused Democritus himself sometimes acknowledged that sense perception was merely appearance and imagination <note>original: "phantasy"</note>, and did not reach the absolute truth and reality of things. He therefore removed "qualities" <note>Refers to "secondary qualities" like color, smell, or taste, which are subjective rather than inherent in atoms.</note> from the rank of real entities because they are unintelligible, concluding them to be nothing but our own mental images. It is undeniably evident that we have ideas, notions, and thoughts of many things that never entered the senses, and of which we have no genuine mental images <note>original: "phantasms"</note>. Atheists do not pay attention to their own thoughts. The opinion that "there is nothing in the understanding which was not previously in the senses" is false and atheistical. Although people have a notion of a Perfectly Understanding Being—the cause of all things—as the object of their devotion, Atheists nonetheless try to persuade them that they have no such notion, and that the Being is a non-entity, merely because they have no sensory idea or mental image of Him. And so they might*

<column-break/>

as well prove that not only Reason and Understanding, desire <note>original: "Appetite"</note>, and will <note>original: "Volition"</note> are non-entities, but also imagination and sense itself; for none of these are perceived by the senses, only their objects are. If God were indeed physical <note>original: "Corporeal"</note>, as some mistaken Theists suppose, His essence would still consist chiefly in Mind and Understanding, which could not possibly be subject to the senses. However, it will be demonstrated elsewhere that there is also non-physical <note>original: "Incorporeal"</note> substance, which is therefore naturally imperceptible to the senses, and that the Deity is such a substance. Page 634, 637

*Though the evidence of individual physical bodies existing depends on information from the senses, the certainty of this very evidence comes not from sense alone, but from a combination of Reason and Understanding. Sense perception is illusory <note>original: "phantastical"</note>, fails to reach the absolute truth of things, and is prone to delusion. Our own imaginations are mistaken for sensations and realities during sleep, and by people suffering from mental distress <note>original: "Melancholized"</note> when awake. Even Atomic Atheists themselves assert the existence of things they cannot perceive, such as atoms, membranes, or the shed images <note>original: "Exuvious Images" - in Epicurean physics, these were thin films believed to peel off objects to create vision</note> of bodies—even non-physical space. If we must acknowledge the existence of nothing that does not fall under the senses, then we cannot acknowledge the existence of the soul or mind. God is the Great Mind that rules the entire universe, from which our imperfect minds are derived. The existence of that God, whom no eye can see, is demonstrated by Reason from His effects.* 637, 638

The second atheistic claim against the Idea of God and His existence: based on the Theists' own acknowledgement that He is "Incomprehensible," from which they infer He is a non-entity. Here it may perhaps be granted, in a correct sense, that whatever is altogether inconceivable is—either in itself, or at least to us—nothing. But the saying of Protagoras, "that every man is the measure of all things to himself," is false in the sense he intended. Just because a man’s shallow understanding cannot clearly comprehend something, it should not be immediately erased from the catalog of beings. Nevertheless, according to Aristotle, the soul and mind are in a way "all things." This is a "Crystalline Globe" or "Notional World" that contains an image of whatever is found in the real world of existence. 638

*But it is absolutely false that whatever cannot be fully comprehended by us is therefore utterly inconceivable, and consequently nothing. For we cannot even fully comprehend ourselves, nor do we have such an adequate conception of any substance as to perfectly master and understand it. The claim of the Sceptics is true to this extent: that there is something incomprehensible in the essence of everything, even of physical matter <note>original: "Body"</note> itself.*

itself. *Truth is larger than our minds. It is the exclusive property of Almighty God (who alone is wise) to perfectly comprehend the essences of all things. But it does not follow from this that we have no idea or conception of anything at all. We may have a notion or idea of a Perfect Being even if we cannot fully comprehend Him with our imperfect minds; just as we may see and touch a mountain, even if we cannot wrap our arms all the way around it. Therefore, the atheists' claim that whatever cannot be fully comprehended by human's imperfect understandings is an absolute non-entity <note>original: "Non-Entity" - something that does not exist</note> is a false theorem.* Page 638, 639

*Although God is more incomprehensible than other things because of His transcendent perfection, He also possesses more "conceivability." Just as the sun, though it dazzles our sight, is also more visible than any other object. The dark incomprehensibility of the Deity is like the blue obscurity of the clear sky; it is not something absolute in itself, but only relative to our perspective.* 639, 640

*This incomprehensibility of the Deity is so far from being an argument against His existence that it is certain, on the contrary, that if nothing were incomprehensible to our imperfect minds, there could be no God. Everything is understood through some internal consistency. The smallness and imperfection of our narrow understandings must necessarily make them asymmetrical or <term>incommensurate</term> <note>original: "incommensurate" - lacking a common measure; impossible to compare or fit together</note> with that which is absolutely perfect.* 640

*Nature itself suggests that there is something vastly larger than our minds and thoughts through the passions implanted within us: devout veneration, adoration, and wonder, accompanied by ecstasy and "pleasing horror" <note>This refers to the "sublime"—a sense of awe where something is so great it is both terrifying and beautiful.</note>. Those aspects of the Deity that cannot fit into the narrow vessels of our minds must be understood in another way—by our minds being plunged into Him, or swallowed up and lost within Him. We have a notion or conception of a Perfect Being even though we cannot fully comprehend Him; because we ourselves are imperfect, we must necessarily be unable to measure up to Him. Thus, there is no logic at all in the second atheistic claim against the idea of God and His existence based on His admitted incomprehensibility.* ibid.

*The third claim follows: that infinity, which is supposed to be essential to the Deity, is perfectly inconceivable and therefore an impossibility and a non-entity. Some passages from a modern writer <note>This likely refers to Thomas Hobbes, a contemporary critic of the author.</note> are cited for this purpose. Their meaning is that there is no philosophical truth in the idea or attributes of God, and that these words have no meaning other than to signify the veneration and astonishment of men's own minds. They claim the word "infinite" signifies nothing about the thing itself, but only describes*

<column-break/>

*the inability of our understandings and our sense of wonder. And since theists deny that God is finite, but atheists argue He cannot be infinite, they conclude He is an inconceivable nothing. Thus, another learned supporter of atheism claims that we have no idea of the infinite, and therefore no idea of God. In the language of atheists, this is the same as saying He does not exist.* Page 640, 641

*Answer: This argument—that there can be nothing infinite and therefore no God—belongs only to modern and <term>neoteric</term> <note>original: "neoterick" - modern or recent</note> atheists; it is contrary to the views of the ancients. Anaximander's <term>Apeiron</term> <note>original: "Ἄπειρον" - the Boundless or Infinite</note> referred to infinite matter, while Melissus used <term>Apeiron</term> to refer to the true Deity. Formerly, both theists and atheists agreed that there must be something or other that is infinite—either an infinite Mind or infinite Matter. The ancient atheists also asserted a numerical infinity of worlds. Thus, modern atheists refute or contradict the ancient ones.* 641, 642

*Modern atheists contradict plain reason and themselves just as much as they contradict their predecessors when they try to disprove God's existence by claiming that nothing can be infinite. For first, it is certain that something or other was infinite in duration, or eternal without a beginning. This is because if there had ever been a time when there was "nothing," then nothing could ever have come into existence. But hardly any atheist could be so <term>sottish</term> <note>original: "sottish" - foolish or dull-witted</note> as to seriously think there was once nothing at all, and then later, senseless matter just happened to exist. It is notorious impudence for those who assert that matter is eternal to use the impossibility of "infinite duration without a beginning" as an argument against the existence of God.* 642, 643

*We concede two things to the atheists: that we do not have a <term>phantasm</term> <note>original: "phantasm" - a mental image or sensory representation</note> of anything infinite, because we have never experienced infinity through our senses; and that infinity is not fully comprehensible by finite understandings. However, since it is mathematically certain that there was something infinite in duration, it is demonstrated against the atheists that there is something that truly exists of which we have no mental image and which we cannot fully comprehend.* ibid.

*Furthermore, it is granted that as for infinity in number, size, and time without a beginning, we have no mental image or full comprehension of them, nor do we have any intelligible idea or conception. From this, it might be concluded that they do not exist. In Aristotle, an "infinite number" is understood only in a negative sense, because we can never reach the end of it by adding more. For that very reason, there cannot possibly be a "positively infinite" number, since one or more may*

By *infinite space*, we should understand *nothing but the possibility of more and more matter, further and further infinitely, by divine power; or that the world could never be made so great that God was not able to make it even larger.* This *potential infinity*, or the *indefiniteness of matter* <note>original: "Indefinity of Body"</note>, seems to be mistaken for an *actual infinity of space*. They are not merely honorary titles and compliments, but attributes belonging to the Deity (and to Him alone) of the most philosophical truth. And although we have no adequate comprehension of them, we must still have some notion of that which we can demonstrate belongs to something.* 645, 646

<margin>(</margin>But the *thing* that the atheists principally quarrel with is *infinite power*, or *omnipotence*; which they also pretend is utterly *inconceivable*, *impossible*, and a *name for nothing*. This *omnipotence* is either willfully or ignorantly misrepresented by atheists, as if it were a *power to do contradictory things*. *An ironic remark by a modern atheist <note>likely Thomas Hobbes</note>: "That God could turn a tree into a syllogism." The absurd doctrine of Descartes <note>original: "Cartesius"</note>: "That God could have made two times two not equal to four; or the...*

*...three angles of a triangle not equal to two right angles." This makes one attribute of the Deity devour and destroy another: infinite will and power destroying infinite understanding and wisdom. To suppose God understands and is wise only by His will is really to give Him no understanding at all. God is not so omnipotent that He can destroy the intelligible natures of things, which would be to baffle and make a fool of His own wisdom. Infinite power is that which can do all that is possible; that is, whatever is conceivable or implies no contradiction. The very essence of possibility is conceivability. And so held all the ancient theists. It is absurd for atheists to say that a power to do nothing but what is conceivable is itself inconceivable.* *ibid.* 646

But because atheists look upon *infinity* as such a *<term>Mormo</term>* <note>Greek: a bugbear or monster used to frighten children</note>, we shall take off the *mask* <note>original: "Vizard"</note> from it by declaring that it is *really nothing else but perfection*. *Infinite understanding and knowledge is perfect understanding without any defect, and the knowledge of all things knowable. Infinite power is perfect power, or a power to do all things possible. Infinite duration is perfection of essence.* Because *infinity is perfection*, *nothing which includes any element of imperfection in its essence can be truly and properly infinite—such as number, magnitude, and time, all of which can only counterfeit infinity. Nothing can be infinite in one way if it is not infinite in every way, or a Perfect Being.* 647, 648

Now, *that we have an idea of perfection is plain from our idea of imperfection. Perfection is first in the order of nature, acting as the rule and measure. It is not the absence of imperfection, but rather imperfection is the lack of perfection. There is a scale or ladder of perfections in nature, perceived by means of that idea which we have of an absolutely perfect Being, which is their measure. Without this, we could not notice imperfection in even the most perfect of all those things we have ever experienced through our senses.* *Boethius <note>original: "Boëtius"</note> said: "That whatever is imperfect in any kind implies something in that kind which is perfect, from which it was derived. And that the nature of things did not begin from anything incomplete and imperfect, but descended downward from what was absolutely perfect, by steps and degrees, lower and lower."* 648

Therefore, since *infinite is the same as perfect*, because we have a notion of the latter, we must necessarily have one of the former. And though the word *infinite* is *negative* in form, its sense is *positive*. *The finite is the negation of the infinite, which in the order of nature comes before it; the infinite is not merely the negation of the finite. However, in things incapable of true infinity, "infinity" is here a mere...*

*Imaginary things and non-entities can only be conceived by the negation of the finite, just as "nothing" is conceived by the negation of "something." An infinite being is nothing but a perfect being—one that never "was not" and could produce all things possible or conceivable.* Pages 648, 649

The fourth atheistic pretense <note>original: "Pretence" — a claim or an argument put forward</note> against the idea of God: *That it is an arbitrary compilation of contradictory notions. Here, we first do not deny that just as some religious people extend divine power to contradictory things, so might others combine contradictions within the nature of the Deity. But it does not follow from this that theology itself is therefore contradictory, any more than philosophy is, simply because some philosophers also hold contradictory views. Nor does it follow that nothing is absolutely true in either divinity or philosophy, and that everything is merely appearance and fantasy, according to the Protagorean doctrine.* <note>Protagorean doctrine: the belief attributed to the Greek philosopher Protagoras that "man is the measure of all things," implying that truth is relative and subjective rather than objective.</note> 649, 650

*But though it is true that whatever actually implies a contradiction is a non-entity, this rule is subject to much abuse when men cry out that anything their shallow understandings cannot reach is an impossibility or nothing. This is seen when atheists and materialists reject the idea of an <term>incorporeal</term> <note>original: "Incorporeal" — existing without a physical body or matter</note> substance on this pretense, or claim it is only a title of honor expressing human respect but signifying nothing in nature and having no philosophical truth. But the true meaning of the atheists' objection—and the kind of contradictions they attribute to all theology—may be seen in a passage by a modern writer <note>This likely refers to Thomas Hobbes, who argued that God's attributes were expressions of piety rather than literal descriptions.</note>: namely, such as these; when God is said to perceive physical things despite having no organs of sense, or to understand despite having no brains. The undisguised meaning of the writer is that religion is not philosophy but law—a mere arbitrary social construction. He implies that God is not a subject of philosophy as all real things are; he is not a true inhabitant of the world or heaven, but only of human brains and fancies. According to him, God's attributes signify neither truth nor falsehood nor anything in nature, but only human reverence and devotion toward what they fear. Thus, anything may be said of God, no matter what, as long as it agrees with civil law. But when people mistake attributes of honor for attributes of philosophical truth—that is, when they suppose such a thing as a God really exists—then they claim it is all absurd nonsense and contradiction.* God's understanding without brains is no contradiction. 650, 651

*It is certain that no simple idea, such as that of a triangle or a square, can be contradictory to*

<column-break/>

*itself; much less can the idea of a Perfect Being, the most simple of all. This idea is indeed pregnant with many attributes, which, if they were contradictory, would make the whole concept a non-entity. But all the genuine attributes of the Deity are as demonstrable of a Perfect Being as the properties of a triangle or a square are of those shapes; therefore, they can be contradictory neither to the concept of God nor to one another.* Page 652

*Indeed, the genuine attributes of the Deity are not only not contradictory, but are also all necessarily connected together.* *ibid.* <note>Latin: "ibidem" — in the same place (referring to the same page mentioned above)</note>

*In truth, all the attributes of the Deity are but many partial and inadequate conceptions of one and the same Perfect Being, taken into our minds piece by piece, as it were.* *ibid.*

*The idea of God is neither fictitious nor manufactured. There is nothing arbitrary in it; it is a most natural and simple idea, to which not the least part can be added, nor anything taken away. Nevertheless, there may be different understandings of God; everyone who has a notion of a Perfect Being does not necessarily understand everything that belongs to it, any more than they would with a triangle or a sphere.* *ibid.* 653

It is concluded, therefore, that the attributes of God are *not the confused nonsense of religiously terrified minds, piling up every imaginable title of honor, courtship, and compliment. Instead, they are the attributes of necessary philosophical truth. They do not only speak of the devotion of human hearts but also declare the real nature of the thing.* Here, the wit of a modern atheistic writer is ill-placed. *(Though it is certain that some, out of superstition or ignorance, may attribute things to the Deity that are inconsistent with its nature.)* Thus, the fourth atheistic pretense against the idea of God is refuted. 653, 654

*In the next place,* the atheists feel obligated to explain this *unquestionable phenomenon: the general persuasion in the minds of men that God exists,* and *their inclination toward religion. They must explain where this comes from if there is no real object for it in nature.* And they would do this by attributing it partly to the confused nonsense of terrified minds and partly to the deception of politicians. Or else they blame these three things: human fear, ignorance of causes, and the inventions of lawmakers and civil rulers. 654

The first of these atheistic origins of religion: *That mankind, because of their natural weakness <note>original: "Imbecillity"</note>, lives in continual anxiety and fear concerning future events and their good or bad fortune. And this passion of fear*

*The second atheistic theory on the origin of theism and religion: that humans have a natural curiosity to inquire into the causes of things. Wherever they cannot discover visible and natural causes, they are prone to invent invisible and supernatural ones. As Anaxagoras said, he never turned to a God except when he was at a loss for necessary material causes. Therefore, it is no wonder if the majority of mankind, being ignorant of the causes of most things, have turned to a God as a refuge and sanctuary for their ignorance.* 654, 655

*These two explanations for the phenomenon of religion—human fear and anxiety combined with ignorance of causes and curiosity—are joined together by a modern writer. It is as if the Deity were but a bogeyman <note>original: "Mormo or Bugbear" — a Mormo was a spirit in Greek folklore used to frighten children</note> raised up by human fear in the darkness of their ignorance of causes. The belief in other ghosts and spirits is also deduced from the same origin. This theory suggests people mistake random events for omens, and are addicted to signs, portents, and prophecies, based on a fantastic and fearful supposition that the world is not governed by nature, but by some intelligent person.* 655

*But lest these two accounts of the phenomenon of religion should prove insufficient, the atheists add a third: attributing it to the fiction and deception of civil rulers. These rulers, perceiving an advantage in religion for keeping people in subjection, have dexterously exploited human fear and ignorance. They have cherished these "seeds of religion" arising from human weaknesses, confirming the belief in ghosts, spirits, miracles, and oracles through officially sanctioned tales. To make religion entirely subservient to their designs, they persuaded the people that the rulers themselves were merely the interpreters of the gods, from whom they received their laws. In this view, religion is an "engine of state" designed to keep people busy, occupy their minds, and render them tame, gentle, and fit for subjection and society.* 655, 656

*None of this is the invention of modern atheists. It is an old atheistic tradition <note>original: "Cabbal" — here meaning a secret or oral tradition of thought</note> that the gods were created by fear. Lucretius argued that the causes of religion are terror of mind and darkness, and that the empire of the gods owes all its*

<column-break/>

*existence to human ignorance of causes. He also claimed that the belief in ghosts arose because people did not know how to distinguish their dreams and other frightening fantasies from actual sensations.* 656, 657

*There is also an ancient atheistic suspicion that religion is a political invention. Cicero mentions this. The atheists in Plato's writings claim that the gods do not exist by nature, but only through human art and laws. Critias, one of the "Thirty Tyrants" of Athens, even wrote a poem to this effect.* 657, 658

*The folly and falsehood of these three atheistic claims regarding the origin of religion will be fully revealed. First, regarding fear and imagination: any fear so excessive that it makes someone constantly believe in something for which there is no basis in sense or reason—and which causes them great distress—is nothing less than madness <note>original: "Distraction"</note>. Therefore, the majority of mankind is here described by atheists as being frightened out of their wits and mentally disturbed, while only a few atheists, who have escaped this panic, remain sober and in their right senses. In reality, the "sobriety" of atheists is nothing but dull stupidity and dead disbelief, as they believe only what they can see or feel.* 658

*It is true that there is a religious fear that follows from a belief in God, and the sense of a deity is often awakened in the mind by fear and danger. However, religion is not a "creature of fear." No one is less anxious about good or bad fortune than the pious and virtuous, who do not place their chief happiness in external things <note>original: "things Aliene"</note>, but only in the right use of their own will. By contrast, the "good" sought by atheists lies entirely in things vulnerable to luck. The fearful nature of atheists is shown by their building all their politics and justice upon the foundation of fear.* 658, 659

*The atheists' great error here is the assumption that the Deity, according to the general sense of mankind, is nothing but a "terror" <note>original: "Terriculum" — a cause of fear or a scarecrow</note>, a formidable, hurtful, and undesirable thing. On the contrary, people everywhere agree on the divine attributes of goodness and kindness.* ibid.

*The phrase "The Deity is envious" <note>original: "Φθονερόν το Δαιμόνιον" (Phthoneron to Daimonion)</note>, in its worst sense, is accepted only by a few ill-natured men who portray the Deity in their own image. This idea was condemned by Aristotle in the works of poets (calling them liars for it) and by Plutarch in the writings of Herodotus. Plutarch himself restricted the meaning of this "envy" to his "evil principle" rather than God. Plato attributed the creation of the world to divine goodness, stating that God made all things as much like Himself as possible. The true meaning of this proverb is that the Deity chooses to humble and bring down the pride of men. Even Lucretius's "hidden force" that seems to spite all overbearing greatness could be nothing other than the Deity. Those*

It is true that religion is often expressed as the "fear of God." Fear is the *first measure of the Deity* <note>original: "Prima Mensura Deitatis"</note>—the first impression that religion makes upon humans in our fallen <note>original: "Lapsed"</note> state. But this is not a fear of God as someone malicious or harmful, nor as a merely arbitrary being, but as a just and impartial punisher of wickedness. Lucretius acknowledged that the human fear of God is joined with a conscience of duty. There is a natural discrimination between good and evil, accompanied by a sense of an impartial justice presiding over the world, which both rewards and punishes. The fear of God as either a harmful or an arbitrary and tyrannical being (which must inevitably be joined with a sense of hatred) is not religion, but superstition. Fear, faith, and love are the three steps and degrees of religion, according to the *Son of Sirach* <note>A reference to the Book of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, in the Apocrypha</note>. Faith is better defined in the Scriptures than by any of the Scholastic philosophers. God is such a being that if He did not exist, nothing would be more wished for than His existence. ->660, 661<-

The reason why atheists mistake the concept of God as something only to be feared, and consequently hated, stems from their own ill-nature and vice. Their vices lead them to think there is no natural difference between good and evil, but only a legal one; they see law as contrary to nature, acting as a restraint on liberty. Hence, they deny all natural charity and acknowledge no benevolence or good will except what arises from weakness, need, and fear. Their friendship is, at best, nothing more than a *trade of self-interest* <note>original: "Mercatura Utilitatum"</note>. Therefore, if an omnipotent Deity existed, this being (according to the atheist hypothesis) could not have even that fake love or benevolence toward anything, because He would stand in need of nothing and be devoid of fear. This was asserted by Cotta in Cicero's writings. It is also asserted by a recent pretender to politics <note>A reference to Thomas Hobbes, whose *Leviathan* argued that power is the basis of right</note>; he adds that God has no other right of commanding than His irresistible power, and that men have no obligation to obey Him except from their own weakness and fear, or because they cannot resist Him. Thus do atheists transform the Deity into a monstrous shape: an omnipotent being that has neither benevolence nor justice. This is indeed a *Mormo* <note>A "Mormo" was a Greek spirit or bogeyman used to frighten children</note> or bogeyman. ->661, 662<-

But while this is a false representation of theism, the atheistic view of things is actually the most uncomfortable, hopeless, and dismal for several reasons. It is true that there are no spiteful designs

<column-break/>

in senseless atoms; in this regard, Plutarch even preferred this atheistic hypothesis over the idea of an omnipotent, malicious being. However, there is no faith or hope in senseless atoms either. Epicurus confessed that it was better to believe the "fable of the gods" than the "material necessity" of all things asserted by the other atheistic natural philosophers <note>original: "Physiologers"</note> before him. But he did not improve the matter at all with his supposed "free will." The Epicureans suffered from a "panic fear" that the frame of the heavens might crack and this collection of atoms would dissolve back into a chaos. Atheists, in running from fear, plunge themselves into fear. *Atheism*, rather than *theism*, arises from the deception of fear, distrust, and a disbelief in goodness. However, once vice prevails in them, it makes them desire that there should be no God. ->Page 663, 664<-

Thus the atheists, who derive the origin of religion from fear, first put a frightening mask upon the Deity and then conclude that He is but a bogeyman <note>original: "Mormo"</note>, a creature of fear and imagination. It is more likely of the two that the belief in a God sprang from a hope for good rather than a fear of evil; but neither of these is true, as religion owes its existence to no passion, but is supported by the strongest and clearest reason. Nevertheless, there is also a natural *prolepsis* <note>A Greek term for a "preconception" or an innate idea that precedes formal reasoning</note>, or anticipation of a God in the human mind that comes before reason. This was called a *vaticination* <note>An intuitive foretelling or prophetic instinct</note> by Plato and Aristotle. ->664, 665<-

The second atheistic pretense—to explain away the phenomenon of religion as resulting from the ignorance of causes and human curiosity—is to be refuted next. (On this account, the atheists say the Deity is nothing but a "refuge of ignorance" <note>original: *asylum ignorantiae*</note> or the "sanctuary of fools.") ->665<-

Atheists, both modern and ancient, commonly combine these two together: fear and the ignorance of causes, making *theism* the offspring of both. They argue it is like children’s fear of the dark, which creates bogeymen and ghosts. This was Epicurus's reason for taking such great pains in the study of natural philosophy <note>original: "Physiology"</note>: he believed that by finding out the natural causes of things, he might free men from the terror of a God who would otherwise assault their minds. ->ibid.<-

Matter supposedly does all things alone without a God. But *we shall make it clear that philosophy and the true knowledge of causes lead to a Deity; and that atheism arises from an ignorance of causes and a lack of philosophy.* Page 665, 666

*For first, no atheist—who derives everything from senseless matter—can possibly identify a cause for himself, his own soul, or his mind. It is impossible for life and sensation to be naturally produced from something dead and senseless, or from physical properties like size, shape, position, and motion. An atheistic objection—which is irrelevant—claims that things that can laugh or cry are made from principles that cannot laugh or cry, because these behaviors result from the mechanism of the body. The **Hylozoists** <note>original: "Hylozoists"; philosophers who believe that all matter possesses a form of life or soul</note> are also unable to produce animal sensation and consciousness from something senseless and unconscious. Atheists, who suppose their own life and understanding, and all the wisdom in the world, sprang merely from senseless matter and accidental motion, are grossly ignorant of causes. The philosophy of ourselves, and the true knowledge of the cause of our own soul and mind, leads us to God.* Page 666, 667

*Again, atheists are ignorant of the cause of **motion**, by which they suppose everything is done; this phenomenon cannot be explained according to their principles. First, it is undeniably certain that motion is not essential to all body or matter as such, because if it were, there could have been no worldly system—no sun, moon, earth, etc.—as everything would be continually torn to pieces and nothing would hold together. It is also certain that dead and senseless matter—such as that described by Anaximander, Democritus, and Epicurus—cannot move itself spontaneously by will or desire. The Hylozoists are further considered elsewhere. Democritus could assign no other cause of motion than this: that one body moved another infinitely from eternity, without any first cause or mover. A modern writer <note>Likely a reference to Thomas Hobbes</note> says the same. To assert an infinite chain of causes for motion is, according to Aristotle, to assign no cause for it at all. Epicurus, though he rejected the idea of innate "qualities" in matter, was forced here to resort to a hidden quality of gravity. This is absurd in infinite space without a center of rest, and is essentially making his own ignorance—or "he knows not why"—the cause. The motion of physical bodies comes from the activity of something incorporeal <note>non-physical or spiritual</note>. Although motion understood as "translation" (moving from place to place) is a property of matter, when it is understood as the **moving force** <note>original Latin: *vis movens*</note>, it is a property or energy of something that is incorporeal and self-active. The motion of the entire physical universe originally comes from the Deity. Thus, the ignorance of the cause of*

<column-break/>

*motion is another ground for atheism.* Page 667–669

*Thirdly, atheists are also ignorant of the cause of that grand phenomenon, **the good and the beautiful** <note>original Greek: *τὸ εὖ καὶ καλῶς* (to eu kai kalōs)</note>—the regular and artificial structure of the worldly system and the bodies of animals, together with the harmony of it all. They who boast they can explain the causes of all things without a God can give no cause for this, other than that it happened by chance. This is either to make the absence of a cause into a cause (since "chance" is only the absence of an intending cause), or to make their own ignorance of the cause ("they know not why") into a cause, or to make one thing the cause of its opposite (confusion the cause of order, chance the cause of skill), or lastly, to deny it has any cause at all, since they deny an intending cause.* Page 669

*But here atheists make several excuses for this ignorance. First, they claim the world is not so well-made that it couldn't have been much better, and that many flaws are found within it; whereas a God, or perfect being, would not have bungled anything, but would have made all things in the best possible way. This is a twelfth atheistic argument, and its refutation will follow later. There are reasons why some modern theists give atheists an advantage here by acknowledging things are poorly made; meanwhile, ancient pagan theists stood their ground and generously maintained that Mind is the maker of all things—not blind fortune, chance, or an arbitrary and irrational power. They held that **the best** <note>original Greek: *τὸ βέλτιστον* (to beltiston)</note>—that which is absolutely the best for the good of the whole (as far as the necessity of things allows)—is the measure and rule of nature and Providence.* Page 669, 670

*Again, the **atomic** <note>original: "Atomick"; referring to the philosophy that the world is made of indivisible atoms</note> and Epicurean atheists pretend that although many things serve a purpose, it does not follow that they were made intentionally for those purposes; because things that happen by chance may have useful consequences. This was the view of Lucretius and the old atheistic philosophers before Aristotle regarding the parts of animal bodies and all other things. The answer is that when things consist of many parts, all skillfully proportioned together with great intricacy—such as the eye—no one who considers its anatomy and structure can reasonably conclude it was made by chance and the use of seeing followed; rather, it was made intentionally for the use of seeing. But to maintain that not only eyes happened to be so made and the use of seeing followed, but also ears, a mouth, feet, and hands...*

*Democritus's foolishness* <note>original: "Dotages"</note>; also supported by *Descartes' Book of Meteors* (first written with the design to explain all those *phenomena* without a *God*), but *unsuccessfully*. Nevertheless, we acknowledge that *God* and *Nature* do all things in the most *frugal* and *concise* way, and that the *mechanical powers* are utilized so far as they will serviceably comply with the *intellectual design* <note>original: "Platform"</note>. Again, *atheists* further pretend that although it may well seem strange that *matter moved by chance* should, at the very first, fall into such a *regularity* and *harmony* as is now in the *world*, it is not at all strange that *atoms*—moving from all eternity and making all manner of *combinations* and *textures*, and trying all experiments—should, after innumerable other *unfit* and *mismatched forms*, at length fall into such a *system* as *this*. They say, therefore, that the *Earth*, at first, brought forth various *monstrous* and *irregular shapes* of *animals*: some lacking *feet*, some *hands*, some without a *mouth*, etc., to which the ancients added *Centaurs*, *Scyllas*, and *Chimeras*; creatures that were part *bull* and part *human*. Although *Epicurus*, ashamed to admit to these, would seem to exclude them, he did so without reason. But because we now have no such *irregular shapes produced* from the *Earth*, they say that the *reason* is because none could *continue* and *propagate* their kind by reproduction except those that *happened* to be fitly made. Thus argued *Epicurus* and the *atheists* before *Aristotle*. They also add to this their *infinite worlds*, among which they pretend not one in a thousand, or of ten thousand, has as much *regularity* in it as *this* world of ours. Lastly, they predict likewise that *this world of ours* shall not always continue as such, but after a while fall into *confusion* and *disorder* again; and then we may have *Centaurs*, *Scyllas*, and *Chimeras* as before. 672, 674

Nevertheless, because this *universal* and *constant regularity* of *things* for so many ages together is so *puzzling*, they would persuade us that the *senseless atoms*, *playing* and *toying* up and down from eternity without any care or thought, were at length *taught* by the *necessity* of things and driven to a kind of *trade* or *habit* of *artistry* and *methodicalness*. 674, 675

To all which *atheistic pretenses*, we reply.

<column-break/>

First, that it is an *idle dream* or *impudent forgery* that there was once an *unfit world system* <note>original: "Inept Mundane System"</note> and, in this *world* of ours, all manner of *irregular shapes* of *animals*. This is not only because there is no tradition of any such thing, but also because no reason can possibly be given why *such* should not be produced from the Earth still, even though they could not continue long. Also, it is *another atheistic dream* that in this *world* of ours, all will quickly fall into *confusion* and *nonsense* again. And as for their *infinite worlds* being an impossibility, so their assertion of the *irregularity* of the *supposed other worlds* is well enough answered by a contrary assertion: that were every *planet* a habitable *Earth*, and every *fixed star* a *sun* having more or fewer such *habitable planets* moving round about them—and none of them *deserted* or *uninhabited*—there would not be found even one *ridiculous* or *unfit system* among them all, the *divine act* being infinite. Page 675

Again, the idea that the *accidental motions* of *senseless atoms* should, in the length of time, grow *artistic* and contract a *habit* or *trade* of *acting* as *regularly* as if directed by perfect *art* and *wisdom*—this is *atheistic fanaticism*. 675, 676

It is no more possible that *dead* and *senseless matter*, *moved by chance*, should at length be taught and necessitated by itself to produce this *artistic system* of the *world*, than that a dozen or more persons unskilled in *music*, and striking the strings as it happened, should at length be taught and necessitated to fall into *exquisite harmony*; or that the *letters* in the writings of *Plato* and *Aristotle*, though having so much *philosophical sense*, should have been all scribbled at random. There is more philosophy in the *Great Volume of the World* than in all *Aristotle’s* and *Plato’s works*, and more *harmony* than in any *artistic composition* of *vocal music*. The *divine art* and *wisdom* has printed such a *signature* of itself upon the *matter* of the *whole world* as *fortune* and *chance* could never *counterfeit*. 676, 677

But in the next place, the *atheists* will, despite all this, undertake to *demonstrate* that things could not possibly be made by any *intending cause* for *ends* and *uses* (as *eyes* for *seeing* or *ears* for *hearing*) from this argument: because *things* were all, in the *order* of *time* as well as *nature*, existing before their *uses*. This *argument* was seriously proposed by *Lucretius* in *this* manner: "If *eyes* were made for the *use* of *seeing*, then, of *necessity*, must *seeing* have existed before *eyes*; but there was no *seeing* before *eyes*; therefore, *eyes* could not be made for the *sake* of *seeing*." 677, 678

It is evident that the logic of these atheists differs from that of all other mortals. According to standard logic, the end for which anything is purposefully made is first in *intention*, but last in *execution*. It is true that men are commonly motivated by their experience of things and the sense of their needs to devise <note>original: "Excogitate"</note> means and remedies; but it does not follow from this that the Maker of the world could not have a prior knowledge of whatever would be useful for animals, and so purposefully make bodies for those uses. That argument ought to be framed this way: Whatever is made intentionally for any end—such as the eye for the purpose of seeing—that end must necessarily exist in the knowledge and intention of the Maker before the actual existence of the thing made for it. But (the atheists argue) there could be no knowledge of seeing before there were eyes; therefore, eyes could not be made intentionally for the sake of seeing. Page 678

This is the true scope of the aforementioned atheist argument, however they may disguise it when first proposing it. The ground of it is that they take it for granted that all knowledge is derived from the senses, or from known things that already exist outside of the knower. And here Lucretius triumphs. The controversy, therefore, is at last resolved into this: whether all knowledge is, in its own nature, *junior* <note>original: "Junior to Things"; meaning secondary or occurring after the physical things themselves</note> to things. For if so, it must be granted that the world could not be made by any prior knowledge. But this is afterwards fully refuted, and it is proved that knowledge is not, in its own nature, <term>ectypal</term> <note>original: "Ectypall"; a copy or representation of something else</note>, but <term>archetypal</term> <note>original: "Archetypall"; an original model or the primary source of an idea</note>; and that knowledge was older than the world and its Maker. 679

But atheists will object to proving a God from the regular and artistic <note>original: "Artificiall"</note> frame of things. They claim it is unreasonable to think there should be no cause in Nature for common phenomena, and that a God must be introduced to "save" them <note>original: "salve them"; to explain or provide a solution for observed facts</note>. They also claim this suggests the world was bungled and patched together. They argue that Nature is the cause of natural things, but that Nature does not intend or act for specific ends. Therefore, they claim the opinion that there are final causes for things in nature is nothing but an <term>Idol of the Cave</term> <note>original: "Idolum Specûs"; a term from Francis Bacon referring to personal biases or errors in human perception</note>. Therefore, it was rightly banished by Democritus out of <term>physiology</term> <note>original: "Physiology"; in this period, the term referred to the general study of nature or physics</note>. 679, 680

The Answer: Two extremes are to be avoided here. One is that of the Atomic Atheists, who derive all things from the accidental motion of senseless matter. Another is that of bigoted religionists, who insist that God does everything himself immediately, without any intermediary nature. The middle path between both is that there is not only a mechanical and accidental nature, but also an

<column-break/>

artistic nature, which serves the Deity as his manual craftsman <note>original: "Manuary Opificer"</note> and hardworking executor. It is true that some philosophers have absurdly attributed their own human properties or animal-like traits <note>original: "Idiopathies"</note> to inanimate bodies. Nevertheless, it is no "Idol of the Cave" to suppose the system of the world was framed by an understanding Being, according to whose direction Nature acts, even though Nature itself does not "intend." Balbus’s description of this "Artistic Nature" in Cicero. That there could be no mind in us if there were none in the universe. Aristotle's statement is true: that there is more "art" in some things of Nature than in anything made by men. Now, the causes of man-made things, such as a house or a clock, cannot be explained without an intention for certain ends. This is excellently pursued by Aristotle. In the same way, the things of Nature cannot be rightly understood, nor their causes fully assigned, merely from matter and motion without intention or Mind. Those who banish final or mental causality from philosophy look upon the things of Nature with no better eyes than oxen and horses. Some pitiful attempts of the ancient atheists to explain the phenomena of animals without mental causality. Democritus and Epicurus were so cautious that they never even pretended to give an account of how an embryo <note>original: "Foetus"</note> is formed. Aristotle’s judgment here is to be preferred over that of Democritus. Page 680, 683

But nothing is stranger than that these atheists should be justified in their ignorance by professed theists and Christians. These people, also using atomic theories in their natural science <note>original: "Physiology"</note>, contend that this whole worldly system resulted only from the necessary and unguided motion of matter—either turned round in a <term>vortex</term> <note>original: "Vortex"; a reference to Cartesian physics where matter moves in circular whirlpools</note> or jumbled in a <term>chaos</term>—without the direction of any mind. These "mechanical theists" are more immodest than the atomic atheists themselves. They suppose that their atoms, though moved by chance, never produced any unfit system or mismatched forms; but from the very beginning, all along, they arranged themselves so orderly that they could not have done it better had they been directed by a perfect Mind. They completely take away the argument for a God based on phenomena and the artistic frame of things, leaving only some metaphysical arguments; which, however good they may be, cannot do as much "execution" <note>meaning: they are less effective or persuasive to the general public</note> because of their subtlety. The atheists are gratified to see the cause of Theism thus betrayed by its professed friends, and the grand argument for God totally obscured <note>original: "Slurred"</note> by them. 683, 684

Indeed, it is a great insensibility of mind to look upon the things of Nature with no other eyes than...

Atheists attribute supernatural phenomena—namely **apparitions, miracles,** and **prophecies**—partly to human fear and ignorance, and partly to the fiction and deception of civil governors. The reality of these is briefly defended here. Page 700

First, regarding **apparitions**: although there is much myth-making in these accounts, there is unquestionably some truth. Atheists, by attributing these things to people mistaking their dreams and fantasies for actual sensations, contradict their own fundamental principle—that the senses are the only criterion of truth. They also dismiss human testimony more than they should. ibid.

Some atheists, realizing this, have acknowledged the reality of apparitions while still concluding they are merely products of the imagination—as if a strong fantasy could produce real substances or objects of sense. This shows the fanaticism of atheists, who would rather believe the greatest impossibilities than risk admitting the existence of a God. Persistent invisible ghosts easily suggest the existence of one supreme Spirit <note>original: "Ghost"</note> of the whole world. 700, 701

**Democritus** was further convinced that there were invisible beings superior to humans, which were independent of the imagination and permanent (he called them **"idols"**); however, he believed they had nothing immortal in them, and therefore a God could no more be proved from their existence than from the existence of humans. He granted that there were not only terrestrial animals, but also aerial and ethereal animals, and that all those vast upper regions of the universe were not desert and uninhabited. Here, there is some mention of the Church Fathers asserting that **angels** have bodies, with more on this later. 701, 702

To this phenomenon of apparitions may be added two others: **witches** and **the possessed** <term>Demoniacks: Individuals believed to be inhabited or controlled by demons</term>. Both of these prove that spirits are not mere fantasies or inhabitants of the human brain alone, but exist in the world. They also prove there are some impure spirits, which confirms the truth of Christianity. Those who confidently dismiss witchcraft are suspected of atheism. Regarding the possessed—or *energoumenoi* <note>original: *Energumeni*; a Greek term for those "worked upon" by a spirit</note>—it is certain from **Josephus** that the Jews did not take these demons or devils for bodily diseases, but for real substances possessing human bodies. Nor is it probable that they supposed (as the **Gnostics** later did) that all diseases were the infestation of evil spirits; nor yet (as some think) that all the possessed were merely insane. Rather, when there were unusual and extraordinary symptoms in any bodily ailment, especially madness, they supposed it to be supernatural and attributed it to the infestation of a devil. The **Greeks** felt the same. 702, 704

<column-break/>

That the possessed and *energoumenoi* are a real phenomenon, even in our own times, is asserted by **Jean Fernel** <note>original: *Fernelius*; a 16th-century French physician</note> and **Daniel Sennert** <note>original: *Sennertus*; a prominent 17th-century German physician and chemist</note>. Such manic persons—who not only discover secrets but also speak languages they never learned—are unquestionably possessed or *energoumenoi*. That there have been such cases since the time of our Savior is proved by **Michael Psellos** <note>original: *Pſellus*; an 11th-century Byzantine monk and philosopher</note> and by Fernel. This serves to defend **Christianity** against those who suspect the demonic possessions in Scripture are mere fictions. Page 704, 706

The second extraordinary phenomenon proposed: that of **miracles** and supernatural effects. It is evident from their own records that such things have happened among the pagans and since the beginning of Christianity. However, more instances of these are found in **Scripture**. 706

Two sorts of miracles. First, those that cannot be done by ordinary causes but can be performed by the natural power of invisible **spirits, angels,** or **demons**—such as uneducated possessed persons speaking Greek, or that miracle among the pagans of a whetstone cut in two with a razor. Second, those that transcend the natural power of all **secondary causes** <term>Second Causes: The laws of nature and the actions of created beings, as opposed to the "First Cause," which is God</term> and created beings. 706, 707

That recent *Theologico-Political Treatise* <note>original: *Politico-Theological Treatiſe*; likely a reference to Baruch Spinoza's *Tractatus Theologico-Politicus* (1670), which argued against miracles</note>, which denies both types of miracles, is insignificant and does not deserve a refutation here. 707

It is assumed in **Deuteronomy** that miracles of the first sort might be performed by **false prophets** to confirm **idolatry**. Therefore, miracles alone are not enough to confirm every doctrine. ibid.

Accordingly, in the **New Testament** we read of **lying wonders** <note>original: *Τέρατα Ψεύδους* (*Terata Pseudous*)</note>—that is, miracles performed by the power of **Satan** to confirm a lie. **God** permits this as a way of testing some and punishing others. Miracles performed to promote the worship of created things or idolatry, instead of justifying those practices, are themselves condemned by them. 708

Had the miracles of our Savior been only of the first kind, the Jews still ought to have acknowledged him as a true prophet according to the **Law of Moses**, since he came in the name of the **Lord** and did not encourage idolatry. It is assumed in Deuteronomy that God would not permit false prophets to perform miracles except in the case of idolatry, or when the doctrine is clearly false by the light of nature; otherwise, it would be an irresistible temptation. Our Savior was that **distinguished prophet** <note>original: *Eximious Prophet*</note> who was foretold, through whom God would again reveal his will to the world—and no longer out of a flaming fire. Nevertheless, some miracles of our Savior...

<columns>

*Christ’s* miracles were also of such a nature that they could be performed only by the power of Almighty God. Page 708, 709

All miracles prove the existence of spirits; to disbelieve this is to disbelieve one's own senses, or to unreasonably dismiss human testimony. *If the Gentiles had accepted the faith of Christ without miracles, this in itself would have been a great miracle.* 709

The last extraordinary phenomenon: divination or prophecy. *This also proves the existence of spirits (called "gods" by the Pagans): and thus their proverb is true; "If there is divination, then there are gods."* 710

There are two types of predictions, just as there are two types of miracles. First, those that might proceed from the natural predicting power of created spirits. *Such predictions were acknowledged by Democritus, based on his theory of "idols." There is not as much randomness <note>original: "contingency"</note> in human actions due to the liberty of the will as some people suppose.* 710, 711

Another sort of prediction of future events can be attributed only to the supernatural foreknowledge <note>original: "prescience"</note> of Almighty God. *Epicurus's claim that divination took away the freedom of the will, either by assuming or creating a necessity. Some theists also deny the foreknowledge of Almighty God for the same reason. It is certain that no created being can foreknow future events except through their causes. Therefore, predictions of such events that had no necessary preceding causes prove the existence of a God.* 711, 712

The belief that there is foreknowledge of future events that are unknowable to humans was formerly the general conviction of mankind. *Oracles and predictions among the Pagans, such as that of Aëtius Navius <note>A legendary Roman augur said to have cut a whetstone with a razor</note>, prove the existence of spirits.* Most of the Pagan oracles came from the natural predicting power of demons. *Nevertheless, there are some instances of predictions of a higher kind among them, such as those of Vēctius Valens and the Sibyls. Likewise, Balaam was divinely assisted to predict our Savior.* 712, 713

*Scripture triumphs over Pagan oracles. Predictions concerning our Savior Christ and the conversion of the Gentiles. Among these is the remarkable prophecy of the "Seventy Weeks" <note>A prophecy in Daniel 9 traditionally used to calculate the time of the Messiah's arrival</note>.* 713, 714

Other predictions concerning the fates of kingdoms and of the Church. *Daniel’s "Fourth Ten-Horned Beast" represents the Roman Empire. This prophecy of Daniel is expanded further in the Book of Revelation <note>original: "Apocalyps"</note>. Both are prophetic calendars of time until the end of the world.* 714

Atheists cannot possibly dismiss this phenomenon of Scripture prophecies—as they do others—as being caused by fear, ignorance of causes, or the fabrications of politicians. They not only...

<column-break/>

...prove a Deity, but also the truth of Christianity. *For this purpose, they are more useful to us who live now than the miracles themselves recorded in Scripture.* Page 714, 715

These five extraordinary phenomena all prove that spirits are not mere fancies, but substantial inhabitants of the world; from this, a God may be inferred. *Some of them immediately prove a Deity.* 715

Here we have not only fully refuted all the atheistic excuses regarding the "idea" of God, but have also, along the way, proposed several substantial arguments for a Deity. *God's existence will now be further proved from the very idea of God itself.* 715

It is true *that some of the ancient theists themselves—such as Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>A celebrated Aristotelian commentator</note> and Clement of Alexandria—declare God not to be "demonstrable." But their meaning was only that God cannot be demonstrated "a priori" <note>demonstrated from a preceding cause to an effect</note> from any prior necessary cause.* It does not follow from this *that there is therefore no certainty or knowledge of the existence of a God, but only guesswork, faith, and opinion. We may have a certain knowledge of things even when the **reason why** <note>original Greek: "διότι" (dioti)</note> cannot be demonstrated from a prior cause; for example, that there was something or other eternal, without a beginning. Whenever a thing is necessarily inferred from what is altogether undeniable, this may be called a demonstration. Many geometric demonstrations are like this, or prove only **the fact that it is so** <note>original Greek: "ὅτι" (hoti)</note>.* 715, 716

A skeptical position held by **Descartes** <note>original: "Cartesius"</note>: *that there can be no certainty of anything—not even of geometric theorems or common sense—until we are certain of the existence of a God who is essentially good and therefore cannot deceive us. From this, it would follow that neither atheists, nor those theists who claim God is arbitrary, can ever be certain of anything—not even that two plus two equals four.* 716, 717

However *much there is an appearance of piety in this claim, it is actually a foundation for eternal skepticism, both toward all other things and the existence of a God. Descartes here went in a circle, proving the existence of a God from our mental faculties, and then the truth of our faculties from the existence of a God; consequently, he proved nothing. If it is possible that our faculties might be false, then we must admit it is possible that there may be no God, and consequently remain forever skeptical about it.* 717

Therefore, it is necessary to explode and refute *this new skeptical hypothesis: the possibility that our faculties were made in such a way as to deceive us in our clearest perceptions. Omnipotence itself cannot make anything to be indifferently true or false. Truth is not **manufactured** <note>original: "factitious," meaning created or arbitrary</note>.*

<columns>

Regarding the universal theorems of abstract science, the measure of truth is not something foreign or external to us, but only our own clear and distinct perception. In this context, whatever is clearly perceived actually *is*. The very essence of truth is its perceptibility. It is granted by all that there can be no such thing as "false knowledge" or "false understanding." The perception of the understanding is never false, but only obscure. It is not Nature that errs in us, but we ourselves who err by giving our assent to things that are not clearly perceived. **Conclusion:** That Omnipotence <note>Almighty power</note> cannot create any understanding faculties that could have as clear and distinct a conception of falsehoods and non-existent things as they do of truths. This is because whatever is clearly and distinctly perceived must, therefore, have some existence; and even Omnipotence itself (to speak with reverence) cannot make "nothing" into "something," or "something" into "nothing." This is no more possible than doing things that are inherently contradictory. Conception is the measure of power. Page 717, 719

It is true that the senses, as such, are merely fantastical <note>original: "phantastical"; based on imagination or subjective appearance</note> and relative. If there were no other form of perception, all truth would be private, relative, and merely an appearance; nothing would be absolute. This is probably the reason why some people have suspected the same to be true of knowledge. However, the mind and understanding reach beyond fancy and appearance to the absolute nature of things. The mind has the criterion of truth within itself. 719, 720

**Objection:** It is an act of arrogance for created beings to pretend to have absolute certainty of anything. **Answer:** God alone is ignorant of nothing and infallible in all things. However, it is no insult to the Deity to suppose that he should make created minds capable of having certainty about *something*—such as the fact that the "whole" is greater than a "part," and other similar truths. Otherwise, such minds would be a mere mockery. It is reasonable to think that God has made humans so that they may possibly attain some certainty of his own existence. Origen <note>An early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD)</note> stated that knowledge is the only thing that possesses certainty. 720, 721

Having now found some firm ground or footing to stand upon—namely, a certainty of "common notions," <term>common notions</term> <note>Self-evident truths or basic principles that all rational people agree upon</note> without which nothing could be proved by reason—we shall endeavor, by means of these, to demonstrate the existence of a God from the idea of him. Ibid.

Descartes <note>original: "Cartesius"</note> undertook to do this with mathematical evidence, based on the fact that the idea of God includes "necessary existence." This argument has not been very successful so far, as many have concluded it is a sophism <note>A clever but false argument</note>. We shall impartially present everything we can, both *for* and *against* it, leaving others to make a judgment. 721

First, **Against** the Cartesian demonstration of

<column-break/>

a God: The argument states that just because we can form an idea of a "necessarily existent being," it does not follow at all that such a being *is*. This is because we can form ideas of things that never were and never will be. Nothing can be gathered from this idea except that a God is not impossible. Furthermore, from this idea (which includes necessary existence), nothing else can be inferred except that whatever lacks necessary existence is not perfect; and that if there *is* a perfect being, its existence always was and always will be necessary. However, it does not follow absolutely that it *does* exist. It is a fallacy when a conclusion is made "absolutely" from a necessity of existence that was only stated "hypothetically." Though a perfect being *must* exist necessarily, it does not follow that it *must and does* exist. The latter is impossible to demonstrate. Page 721, 723

**For** the Cartesian demonstration of a God: Just as we conclude from the notion of an "impossible thing" that it never was nor will be, and from a thing that has a contingent relation <note>original: "Schesis"; the state or relation of a thing</note> to existence that it *might* be or *might not* be; so we conclude from that which has "necessary existence" in its nature that it actually *is*. The force of this reasoning is not merely hypothetical (i.e., "If there is a perfect being, then its existence is necessary"). Such a hypothetical stance would suggest that a "necessarily existent being" might or might not exist, which is a contradiction. The absurdity of this will appear more clearly if, instead of "necessary existence," we use the term "actual existence." No theist can otherwise prove that a God (even if supposed to exist) might not have happened to exist by chance. Nevertheless, God, or a perfect being, is not demonstrated here "from the cause" <note>original: "à Priori"</note> when it is proven from its own idea. The reader is left to make a judgment. 723, 724

A preliminary exercise <note>original: "Progymnasma"; a preparatory attempt or logical drill</note>, or a trial attempt toward proving God from his idea as including necessary existence: First, because we have an idea of a perfect being that implies no contradiction, it follows that such a thing is *possible*. And from the "necessary existence" included in this idea, added to its possibility, it further follows that it *actually is*. A "necessarily existent being," if it is possible, *must be*; because if we suppose it does not exist, it would be impossible for it ever to have existed. This is not the case with contingent things. A perfect being is either "impossible to have been," or else it "is." If God were possible but did not exist, he would not be a "necessary" being, but a "contingent" one. However, no great stress is laid upon this particular argument. 724, 725

**Another Plainer Argument** for the existence of a God from his idea: Whatever we can form an idea of in our minds that implies no contradiction, this either actually is, or else...
