A further reasoning from the idea of God as including necessary existence, through certain steps. *First: it is certain that something or other existed of itself from eternity, without a beginning. Again: whatever existed of itself from eternity did so naturally and necessarily, and therefore there is a necessarily existent being. Thirdly: nothing could exist of itself from eternity naturally and necessarily except what contained necessary self-existence in its nature. Lastly: a perfect being, and nothing else, contains necessary existence in its nature. Therefore, He exists. An appendix to this argument: that no temporary, successive being could have existed from eternity without a beginning. This was proved before. 725, 726*

Again, the controversy between atheists and theists is first clearly stated based on the idea of God, and then satisfactorily decided. It is premised *that as not everything was made, so neither was everything unmade.* Atheists agree on both. The state of the controversy between theists and atheists: whether that which was itself unmade (the cause of all other made things) was the most perfect or the most imperfect being. A certain kind of atheist-leaning theism, or *theogonism* <note>The belief that gods are generated or born from natural forces</note>, which acknowledges a God or "Soul of the World" presiding over the whole, *supposed him, notwithstanding, to have emerged out of night and chaos; that is, to have been generated out of senseless matter. 726, 728*

The controversy *thus* stated is easily decided. *It is certain that lesser perfection may be derived from greater perfection, or from that which is absolutely perfect; but it is impossible that greater perfection and higher degrees of being should rise out of the lesser and lower. Things did not ascend, but descend. The idea that life and sense may naturally rise from the mere modification of dead and senseless matter—as also reason and understanding from sense—is the philosophy of the "Kingdom of Darkness." The Hylozoists <note>Those who believe that all matter possesses life or a soul</note> were so aware of this—that there must be some substantial, unmade life and understanding—that while leaning toward atheism, they thought it necessary to attribute life and understanding to all matter as such. This argument is a demonstration of the impossibility of atheism. 728, 729*

The controversy again more particularly stated, based on the idea of God as including mind and understanding. Namely: whether

<column-break/>

all mind was made or generated out of senseless matter, or whether there was an eternal, unmade mind that is the maker of all. *This is the doctrine of theists: that mind is the oldest of all things. The doctrine of atheists: that mind is a postnate <note>born later; secondary</note> thing, younger than the world, and a shadowy image of real beings. Page 729*

The controversy *thus* stated is again decided. *Although it does not follow that if there had once been no physical world or matter, there could never have been any; yet it is certain that if there had once been no life or mind, there could never have been any life or mind. Our imperfect minds are not of themselves from eternity, and are therefore derived from a perfect, unmade mind. 729, 730*

That atheists think their chief strength lies here: in disproving God based on the nature of understanding and knowledge. *According to them, things made knowledge, and knowledge did not make things. All mind and understanding is the creature of sensory things and a fantastic <note>original: "phantastick"; based on mental appearance rather than reality</note> image of them; and therefore no mind is their creator. Thus does a modern writer conclude that knowledge and understanding are not to be attributed to God, because they imply dependence upon things outside oneself; which is the same as saying that senseless matter is the most perfect of all things and the highest divinity <note>original: "numen"</note>. 730*

A concise refutation of the aforementioned atheist principles. *Knowledge is not the activity of sensory things upon the knower and his reactions. Sensory things themselves are not known by the reaction or imagination of the senses. Knowledge comes not from the force of the thing known, but from the knower. Besides the mental images of individual bodies, there are universal intelligible ideas. A late atheist paradox: that universals are nothing but names. Axiomatic truths in abstract sciences are not reactions from bodies through the senses, nor are they gathered by induction from many individual instances; instead, we perceive at once that it is impossible for them to be otherwise. An ingenious observation of Aristotle's: that even if it could be perceived by sense that the three angles of a triangle are equal to two right angles, yet this would not be science—or knowledge properly so called—which deals with universals first and from there descends to individual instances. 730, 732*

Again, we have conceptions of things incorporeal <note>non-physical</note>, as well as of physical things that never actually existed and whose accuracy the senses could not reach—such as a perfectly straight line, a flat surface, or an exact triangle, circle, or sphere. *That we have a power of framing ideas of things that never were nor will be, but are only possible. 732*

Inferred from this, *that human science*

...knowledge itself is not the mere image or product of individual sensory objects <note>original: "Singular Sensibles"</note>, but precedes them <note>original: "proleptical to them"</note> and exists before them in the order of nature. But since there must be an object of thought <note>original: "Noητὸν"</note> before there is a mind <note>original: "Νοῦς"</note>—that is, things to be understood before the act of understanding—the only true account of knowledge and its origin is that it comes from a perfect, all-powerful Being. This Being understands itself and the full extent of its own power, including the possibilities of all things, their relationships, and unchanging truths. All imperfect minds participate in this one perfect Mind. *Pages 732, 733*

Therefore, the nature of knowledge itself assumes the existence of a perfect, all-powerful Being as its object of thought <note>original: "Noητὸν"</note>. This Being, by understanding itself, is the first original knowledge—a Mind that existed before the world and all sensory objects. It is not a copy <note>original: "Ectypeal"</note>, but the original model <note>original: "Archetypal"</note> and the creator of all things. Therefore, knowledge and understanding demonstrate theism, not atheism. *733, 734*

This is further confirmed because there are eternal truths <note>original: "Eternal Verities"</note> that were never created and had no beginning. For example, Aristotle held the eternal truth that the diagonal of a square cannot be measured by the same units as its sides. Similarly, Justin Martyr spoke of "eternal laws of justice" <note>original: "αἰώνια δίκαια"</note> or eternal morals. Geometric truths are not "made" by any person's thinking but existed before all humans, and even before the world and matter itself. *734*

Now, if there are eternal truths, then the simple rational principles and understandable essences of things must also be eternal. Plato called these "things that always are" but were never made—incapable of being created or destroyed <note>original: "Ingenerable and Incorruptible"</note>. Although Aristotle disagreed with Plato’s theory of "Ideas," he agreed that the forms or species of things were eternal and never made, and that they are not "generated" or born. He also agreed that there are things other than sensory objects that are the unchanging objects of science. It is certain that there could be no unchanging science if the mind had no objects to study other than sensory things <note>original: "Sensibles"</note>. The objects of geometric science are not material triangles or squares; Aristotle said these exist "nowhere" physically. To Philo, these understandable natures of things are the most necessary essences. *735, 736*

Now, if there are eternal truths and understandable things whose existence is necessary, and since these can only exist in a mind, there must be an eternal, necessarily existing Mind that understands all these ideas and truths at once—or rather, *is* them. This can be nothing other than the mind of a perfect, all-powerful Being, who understands itself and all the possibilities of things through the extent of its own power. *736, 737*

Therefore, there can be only one original Mind, in which all other minds participate.

<column-break/>

Because of this, ideas or notions are exactly alike in different people, and truths are indivisibly the same; it is because all their minds are stamped with the same original seal. Themistius argued that one person could not teach another unless the same notion existed in both the learner and the teacher. Nor could people communicate as they do if there were not one Mind that all participated in. The "anti-monarchical" opinion—that there are many eternal and independent understanding beings—is refuted. We have now not only defended the idea of God and refuted all atheist excuses against it, but we have also demonstrated His existence from this very idea. *Pages 737, 738*

A refutation of the second atheist argument against all-powerfulness and divine creation: the claim that nothing can be made out of nothing by any power whatsoever. In response to this, three things must be emphasized. First, that "out of nothing, nothing comes" <note>original: "De Nihilo Nihil"</note> is, in one sense, an unquestionable truth, but it does not count against theism or divine creation. Second, that "nothing out of nothing" in the sense used by atheists—that nothing which once did not exist could ever be brought into being—is absolutely false. If it were true, it would count against atheism just as much as against theism. Finally, from the true sense of this very axiom ("nothing from nothing"), the absolute impossibility of atheism can be demonstrated. *738*

"Out of nothing, nothing comes" <note>original: "De Nihilo Nihil"</note> is, in some sense, a common notion of unquestionable truth. First, it is certain that nothing which once did not exist could ever come into being on its own, or that nothing can start existing by itself, or that nothing can be made or produced without an efficient cause. From this, it is demonstrated that there was never a time when "nothing" existed; or, that not everything was "made," but that something has existed of itself from eternity, uncreated and not derived from anything else. *738, 739*

Again, it is also certain that nothing could be produced by a cause that does not have at least equal perfection and sufficient active or productive power. Anything in an effect that exceeds the perfection of its supposed cause must "come from nothing" or be made without a cause. Furthermore, nothing can be produced by another thing (even if it has equal perfection) unless that cause also has a sufficient active or productive...

This page specifically addresses the ancient philosophical principle that "nothing comes from nothing."</meta>

[pro]ductive power. From this, it is certain that if there were once no motion at all in the world, and no other substance besides body (which has no self-moving power), there could never possibly be any motion or change to all eternity, for want of a sufficient cause or productive power. No imperfect being has a productive power to create any new substance which did not exist before, but only to create new accidents and modifications; that is, no creature can create. These two aforementioned senses respect the efficient cause <note>The "efficient cause" is the primary source of change or rest; the "agent" that makes something happen.</note>.
->Page 739<-

Thirdly, *nothing can be materially produced out of nothing that is pre-existing or already within a thing. Therefore, in all natural births and growth (where the supernatural power of the Deity does not intervene), no new real entity or substance is produced that was not there before; instead, there are only new modifications of what substantially pre-existed.*
->740<-

The principle *nothing comes from nothing* was heavily insisted upon by the old natural philosophers <note>original: "Physiologers"</note> before Aristotle. This concept is commonly misunderstood by modern writers, as if those ancients intended to deny that God could create the world out of nothing. It is granted that this was the view of the Stoics and of Plutarch; Plutarch affirmed that the world was made by God no differently than a house is made by a carpenter, or a garment by a tailor <note>meaning God only shaped pre-existing matter rather than creating the matter itself</note>. Plutarch and the Stoics were, therefore, imperfect theists, though they were still zealous in their religion. However, the ancient Italian philosophers <note>The "Italick" school refers to Pythagoras and his followers in Southern Italy.</note> here acted only as natural philosophers, and not as theologians or mathematicians. They were not arguing against a divine creation out of nothing; they were only contending that in the natural world, no new real entity was created, nor was anything totally destroyed in death <note>original: "Corruptions, Annihilated"</note>. Instead, they argued that only the modifications of what already existed were changed—or, that no new real entity could be made out of matter.
->740, 741<-

That this was the true meaning of those ancient natural philosophers is evident from the two ways they used this principle, *nothing comes from nothing*. First, upon this foundation, they endeavored to establish a particular kind of physics and a theory of atoms, whether similar or dissimilar: <term>Homoeomery</term> <note>the theory that substances are made of particles that are the same as the whole (e.g., gold is made of tiny gold specks)</note> or <term>Anomoeomery</term> <note>the theory that substances are made of atoms that do not share the qualities of the whole (e.g., round, colorless atoms forming a solid, red object)</note>. From this, Anaxagoras concluded that because nothing could be made out of nothing, there must be "similar atoms" of all kinds in every body. He believed that through combinations and separations, all natural things were made; so that bone was made out of pre-existing bony atoms, flesh out of fleshy atoms, and so on. This is the Anaxagorean <term>Homoeomery</term>, or "similar atomology,"

<column-break/>

built upon this principle, *nothing comes from nothing.*
->Page 741, 742<-

But the ancient Italians, both before and after Anaxagoras (whom Leucippus, Democritus, and Epicurus followed here), concluded with greater wisdom from the same principle—*nothing comes from nothing*—that those qualities and forms of bodies that are naturally generated and destroyed were not real entities distinct from the substance of matter. Instead, they were only different modifications of matter that cause different perceptions <note>original: "Phancies"</note> in us. This is an <term>Anomoeomery</term>, or "dissimilar atomology," where the atoms themselves have no qualities like color or smell. These philosophers viewed atoms as *simple elements* or *letters* in nature's alphabet; by combining them in different ways, they spelled out or compounded all the *syllables* and *words* (the complex structures) of physical things. These consist of nothing but **figure, position, motion, rest,** and the **size of parts.** If "qualities" and "forms" were real entities distinct from these and did not already exist (as Anaxagoras dreamed), they would have to come from *nothing* during natural birth; which is impossible.
->742, 743<-

Another improvement of this principle, *nothing comes from nothing*, was made by the Italian philosophers: they argued that the souls of animals, and especially human souls, could not possibly result from the mere modification of matter (figure, position, motion, etc.). Therefore, souls were not produced during birth, nor were they annihilated in death; instead, being substantial things, they existed both before and after the body <note>original: "Præ and Post Exist"</note>. Lucretius describes this as the main controversy between atheists and theists: *whether souls were born with the body, or introduced into it from the outside* <note>original: "Whether Souls were Generated, or Insinuated into Bodies"</note>. To these Pythagoreans, the birth and death of animals were merely "anagrammatical transpositions" <note>like rearranging the letters of a word to form a new one without adding or losing any letters</note>. Those philosophers who asserted that souls were un-generable and existed before the body did not necessarily believe they were self-existent or uncreated; rather, they believed all souls were derived from the Deity. Thus Proclus argued, even while maintaining that souls were as eternal as the world itself. In Plato's *Timaeus*, the idea that souls are "un-generable" means only that they were not generated out of matter; for this reason, they were called "principles" in the same way that matter was. Therefore, to Plato, souls were created by God, but *before the birth of the animal*, not during it.
->743, 745<-

Saint Augustine himself was sometimes wavering and skeptical regarding the point of pre-existence. He held that we have philosophical certainty of only this: that souls were created by God out of nothing that previously existed, at some time or other—either during birth or before. Unless animals <note>original: "Brutes"</note> are merely machines, the same reasoning applies to their souls: that they are not generated out of matter, but [created]...

*That* all three of the previously mentioned points—which establish the truth that *nothing* can *possibly* come from *nothing*—can be reduced to this *one general proposition*: *That nothing can be caused by nothing*. This will in no way conflict with the *Divine Omnipotence* or *creative power*, as shall be shown later, but will actually *confirm* it. However, those same words, *nothing out of nothing*, may carry another meaning when that phrase "out of nothing" <note>original: "ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων"</note> is not taken *causally*, but only to signify the *starting point* <note>original: "Terminus A Quo," the point from which something begins</note>, or a *prior state of non-existence*. In that case, the meaning would be that *nothing* which previously *was not* could afterwards, by any power whatsoever, be brought into *being*. This is the sense intended by the *Democritic* and *Epicurean objectors* <note>Followers of Democritus and Epicurus, ancient Greek philosophers who argued for a purely material world</note>; namely, *that no real entity can be made or brought out of non-existence into being*. Therefore, they argue that the *creative power* of *theists* is an impossibility. In the same place <note>original: "ibid."</note>.

*Our Second Undertaking*, as a way of answering this: To show *that "nothing out of nothing,"* in this sense, is *false*; and also *that*, were it *true*, it would count no more against *theism* than it does against *atheism*. Therefore, it should not be used by atheists as an argument against God. *If it were universally true* that nothing at all which once did not exist could ever be brought into being, then there could be no *making* or *causing* at all—no *motion*, *action*, *change*, or *generation*. But *we ourselves* have a *power to produce new thoughts in our minds* and *new motion in our bodies*. Therefore, atheists are forced to limit this proposition to *substances only*. Here, some are deceived by the ambiguity of this phrase "out of nothing" <note>original: "ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων"</note>, which can be taken either *causally* or to signify the *starting point*—that is, *from a prior non-existence*. They confuse these two together, even though the *first is true* but the *latter is false*. Again, others are staggered by the *plausibility* of this proposition. This is partly because no *artificial* thing (such as a *house* or *garment*) can be made by men except out of *pre-existing matter*. It is also partly because ancient *natural philosophers* <note>original: "Physiologers"</note> maintained the same regarding *natural generation*: *that no new real entity or substance* could be *produced* there. Finally, it is because it is certain that no *imperfect created being* can *create* any *new substance*. Being inclined to measure all power by these *limited examples* <note>original: "scantlings"</note>, they assume it applies to all. But it is as easy for a *perfect being* to *create* a *world* (both *matter* and everything else) *out of nothing*—in the sense of bringing it out of a prior non-

<column-break/>

existence—as it is for us to *create a thought*, or to *move a finger*, or for the *sun to send out rays*. *For an imperfect substance which once did not exist to be brought into being by God is not impossible* in any of the senses mentioned before. He has not only *infinitely greater perfection*, but also *sufficient productive* or *emanating power*. It is *true* *that infinite power cannot do things that are by their own nature impossible*; however, *nothing* is *impossible* in this way except what is *self-contradictory*. And though it is a *contradiction* for anything to *be* and *not be* at the same time, it is no contradiction at all for an *imperfect being* (which is by its nature *only potentially existent* <note>original: "contingent to existence"</note>) to *exist* after it had *not* existed. Therefore, since making a *substance* to *be* which was not *before* is in no way *self-contradictory*, and consequently not impossible in its own nature, it must be an object of *perfect power*. Page 746, 748

*Furthermore, if no real entity or substance could possibly be brought from non-existence into being, then the reason for this must be that no substance can derive its entire being from another substance. But from this, it would follow that whatever is substantial not only existed from eternity, but also existed of itself, independently of anything else. However, first, the eternal pre-existence of temporary beings is not agreeable to reason. Second, to suppose that imperfect substances have existed of themselves and by necessity is to suppose that something comes from nothing in the impossible sense, because they do not have necessary self-existence in their nature. Just as those who claim that all substance is body, and that no body is able to move itself—yet still assume motion has been from eternity—actually make this motion come from nothing or be caused by nothing. What is in its nature only possible by chance (existing or not existing) could not exist of itself; it must derive its being from something else which necessarily exists. Plato's* distinction between *two kinds of substances* must therefore be admitted: *that which always is and was never made, and that which is made or had a beginning.* 748, 749

*Lastly, if it were true that no substance can be made or produced, it would follow from that* (as the *Epicurean atheist* supposes) *that matter—and also all souls* (at least human ones)—*existed of themselves from eternity, independently of anything else. It is impossible that the mind or soul should be a modification of mindless matter, or result from shapes, positions, motions, and sizes. Human souls are substantial; therefore, according to this doctrine, they must never have been made. Yet atheists firmly deny both their pre-existence and their existence after death.* Those pagan theists who...

*Those who held the eternity of human minds nonetheless supposed them to have depended upon the Deity as their cause.* Previously proved: *that there can be only one self-existent understanding being. If human souls depend upon the Deity as their cause, then matter undoubtedly does as well.* Page 749, 750

*A common but significant mistake: the belief that no pagan theist ever acknowledged any creative power out of nothing, or that God was the cause of any substance.* Plato’s definition of *effective power* in general, and his *affirmation* that divine efficiency is the process by which things are made after they previously did not exist. *It is certain that he did not understand this as the production of souls out of matter, since he supposed souls to exist before matter and therefore to be made by God out of nothing pre-existing. All philosophers who held the immortality and incorporeity <note>the state of being without a physical body</note> of the soul asserted that it was caused by God, either in time or from eternity.* Plutarch’s unique position on this matter. *It is unquestionable that the Platonists supposed one substance could receive its entire being from another; they derived their second hypostasis <note>original: "Hypostasis," meaning substance or essential nature</note> or substance, though eternal, from the first, and their third from both, and all lower ranks of being from all three.* Plotinus, Porphyrius, Iamblichus, Hierocles, Proclus, and *others derived matter from the Deity.* This was also the view of the *Chaldean Oracles* and the ancient *Egyptian* or *Hermetic theology* according to Iamblichus. *Those Platonists who believed the world and souls to be eternal conceived them to have received their being from the Deity just as much as if they had been made in time.* 750, 752

Having now *disproved* the *proposition "nothing out of nothing" in the atheistic sense*—namely, *that no substance was caused by or derived its being from another, but that whatever is substantial existed of itself from eternity, independently*—we will next show *that even if it were true, it would no more oppose theism than it does atheism.* Falsehoods (unlike truths) may disagree with each other. Plutarch, the Stoics, and *others, who did not believe God created any substance, were nonetheless zealous theists, even if not strictly orthodox ones.* But the *ancient atheists mentioned by both Plato and Aristotle "generated" and "corrupted" all things—meaning they produced all things out of nothing, or non-existence, and reduced them to nothing again, with the exception of the raw substance of matter.* The same was done by the Democritic and Epicurean atheists themselves, the makers of this objection; though, according to the principles of their own atomic physiology <note>the study of the physical functions of matter</note>, *it is impossible that life and understanding, soul and mind, should be mere modifications of*

matter. *Just as theists attribute a creative power over all things from nothing to the Deity, so do atheists attribute it to passive and dead matter. Therefore, this cannot be an argument against theism, as it opposes atheism equally.* Page 752, 756

A summary <note>original: "Anacephalæosis," a Greek term for a recapitulation or summary</note>; in which it is *observable that Cicero considers* "to be made out of nothing" <note>original: "De Nihilo fieri"</note> and "without a cause" <note>original: "Sine Causa"</note> *to be one and the same thing. *A brief synopsis of atheism: that matter, being the only substance, is therefore the only uncreated thing; and that everything else in the world, besides the raw substance of matter, was made out of matter or produced from it alone.* 757

*The first argument: when atheists affirm that matter is the only substance and all things are made from it, they suppose everything to be made without an efficient cause <note>the primary source of change or action</note>; this is to bring them from nothing in an impossible sense. Though something may be made without a pre-existing material cause, nothing can possibly be made without an efficient cause. Therefore, if anything is made that did not exist before, there must necessarily be some substance other than matter to serve as its active, efficient cause.* The atheistic hypothesis supposes *things to be made without any active or effective principle.* Meanwhile, the Epicurean atheists *attribute the efficiency of everything to local motion <note>physical movement from place to place</note>, yet they deny that matter or body (their only substance) has a self-moving power. By this, they make all the motion in the world to have existed without a cause, or to come from nothing; all action without an agent, and all efficiency without an efficient cause.* 758

Furthermore; *even if we were to grant these atheists the existence of motion without a cause, dead and senseless matter combined with motion could never produce life, sense, and understanding. This would be getting something out of nothing in terms of causality, since local motion only changes the modifications of matter, such as its shape, place, position, and the arrangement of its parts. This also refutes those false theists who conclude that God did no more in the making of the world than a carpenter does in building a house (using the excuse that "nothing can be made out of nothing"), yet still suppose Him to make souls out of dead and senseless matter. This is essentially bringing souls out of nothing in terms of causality.* 758, 759

It was declared previously that the ancient Italians <note>original: "Italicks," referring to the pre-Socratic philosophers of southern Italy, like Pythagoras</note> and the followers of Pythagoras proved that souls could not possibly be generated out of matter, because nothing can come from nothing through cause and effect. The excuse of the atheistic Ionians <note>original: "Ionicks," early Greek physical philosophers</note>, based on Aristotle, is that matter is the only substance, and that life, sense, and understanding are nothing but the "passions," properties, and arrangements of that matter; therefore, producing them out of matter is not the production of any new real entity. Page 759

**Answer:** Atheists, taking it for granted that there is no other substance besides body or matter, falsely conclude that life, sense, and understanding are merely accidental properties or "modes" of matter. In reality, these are the modes or attributes of a non-physical <note>original: "Incorporeal"</note> and self-active substance. A "mode" is something that cannot be conceived of without the thing it belongs to; however, life and thought can be conceived of without physical extension <note>the quality of taking up space</note>, and indeed, they cannot be conceived with it. 759, 760

The chief occasion of this error comes from a misunderstanding of "qualities" and "forms." For example, because the quality of heat and the form of fire may be generated out of matter, people assume that life, thought, and understanding can be as well. But the "atomic atheists" <note>philosophers like Democritus or Epicurus who believed the world was only atoms and void</note> themselves reject the idea of qualities as things really distinct from the shape, position, and motion of parts, for this very reason: because nothing can be made out of nothing by a cause. The common opinion that such "real qualities" exist in bodies comes only from people mistaking their own imaginations, appearances, feelings, states, and perceptions for things really existing outside of them. In these qualities, whatever is distinct from the shape, position, and motion of parts is not a modification of matter, but of our own souls. These atomic atheists are infinitely absurd; while they reject qualities because "nothing can come out of nothing," they themselves try to bring life, sense, and understanding out of nothing through cause and effect. The opinion that thought is nothing but local motion, and that men themselves are mere machines, is a sign of profound foolishness <note>original: "Sottishness"</note> or intolerable impudence. 760, 762

It is very observable here that **Epicurus** himself, wishing to assert the existence of "contingent liberty" <note>free will</note>, confesses that he could not do this unless there were some such principle in the atoms themselves; this is because nothing can be made out of nothing or caused by nothing. Therefore, he ridiculously invents a "third motion" of atoms <note>the "swerve" or *clinamen*</note> to explain the phenomenon of free will. Consequently, he must be guilty of the impossible production of something out of nothing when he derives the soul and mind from dead and

<column-break/>

senseless atoms. If there were no substantial and eternal life and understanding in the universe, none could have ever been produced, because it would have had to come from nothing or be made without a cause. That "dark philosophy" <note>likely referring to the Scholastic or Aristotelian view of "substantial forms"</note> which draws forth <note>original: "Educes"</note> not only real qualities and substantial forms, but also souls themselves (at least sensitive souls) out of the power of matter, actually draws them out of nothing or makes them without a cause; thus, it prepares a direct path to atheism. Page 762, 763

Those who suppose that matter—by some means other than motion, and by a kind of miraculous efficiency—can produce souls and minds, are attributing a creative power to senseless and inactive matter. Ironically, they deny this same power to a **Perfect Being**, calling it an absolute impossibility. Thus, we have demonstrated the impossibility and nonsense of all atheism from this very principle: that nothing can be made from nothing or without a sufficient cause. 763, 764

Therefore, if there is no middle ground between these two options—that all things must spring either from a God or from matter—then this is also a demonstration of the truth of **Theism** by proving the alternative is impossible. Either there is a God, or else all things are derived from dead and senseless matter; but the latter is impossible; therefore, there is a God. Nevertheless, the existence of a God may also be directly proved from the same principle, rightly understood: that nothing comes from nothing, being caused by nothing, whether in terms of its efficiency or its material. 764

The proof follows these steps: First, it is mathematically certain from the principle of "nothing from nothing" that there was never a time when nothing existed; rather, something or other has existed of itself from eternity, un-made and independent of anything else. Had there ever been nothing, there could never have been anything. Again, whatever has existed of itself from eternity must have existed **necessarily**, and not by any free will or choice. It is certain, therefore, that there is something actually in being whose existence is, and always was, necessary. Now, that which exists necessarily of itself must have "necessity of existence" in its very nature—which nothing but a **Perfect Being** has. Therefore, there is a Perfect Being; and nothing else besides this existed of itself from eternity, but all other things (whether souls or matter) were made by it. To suppose anything exists of itself necessarily when it has no necessary existence in its nature is to suppose that "necessary existence" came from nothing. 764, 765

*Three reasons why some theists have been so hesitant and skeptical about the necessary self-existence of matter. Secondly, because some of them have supposed an "incorporeal matter" <note>original: ὕλην ἀσώματον (hylēn asōmaton)</note>, or a first matter that was unmade; an opinion older than Aristotle. Nor is there perhaps any such great absurdity in the finiteness of actual space and distance (according to this hypothesis) as some imagine. Page 765, 766*

*Moreover, the existence of a God may be further proved from this common principle: nothing comes from nothing in terms of cause. This is true not only because, if there were no God, the idea we have of a Perfect Being must have come from nothing and be a concept of nothing, but also because all the other intelligible ideas of our minds must have come from nothing as well, since they are not derived from the senses. All minds and their intelligible ideas come, by way of participation, from one Perfect Omnipotent Being who understands Himself. 766, 767*

*However, it is certain from this principle—nothing comes from nothing, or nothing is caused by nothing—that souls and minds could never have emerged out of dead and senseless matter, or from shapes, positions, and motions. Therefore, they must either have all existed by their own necessity from eternity, or else be created by the Deity out of nothing pre-existing. It is concluded that the existence of a God is altogether as certain as that our*

*human souls did not all exist from eternity by their own necessity. Thus, the second atheistic argument against omnipotence or divine creation is abundantly refuted. This argument was based on that false principle, "nothing comes from nothing," in the atheistic sense (which claims that nothing could be brought out of non-existence into being, and no substance can derive its whole being from another substance, but all was self-existent from eternity). It has been demonstrated that unless there is a God, or a perfect omnipotent Being and Creator, something must have come from nothing in the impossible sense; that is, it must have been caused by nothing, or made without a cause. ### SECTION III.

The following six atheistic arguments, which aim at two things (first disproving a non-physical <note>original: "Incorporeal"</note> Deity, and then a physical <note>original: "Corporeal"</note> one), are next taken all together. In answer to these, *three things* are done. *First*, to refute the atheistic arguments against a non-physical Deity (the third and fourth arguments). *Secondly*, to show that from the very principles of atheistic materialism <note>original: "Corporealism"</note> used in their fifth and sixth arguments, a non-physical substance is actually demonstrable. *And lastly*, that therefore the two following atheistic arguments (built upon the contrary supposition) are also insignificant. 767

Before we come to the atheistic arguments against a non-physical Deity, it is first stated: that although not all materialists <note>original: "Corporealists"</note> are atheists, all atheists are universally mere materialists. Thus Plato, in his dialogue *The Sophist*, writing of those who maintained that Nature produced all things without the direction of any mind, affirms that they held "body" and "substance" to be one and the same thing. From this, it follows that a "non-physical substance" is, to them, a "non-physical body"—which is a contradiction and nonsense—and that whatever is not a body is nothing. He likewise adds that those who asserted the soul was a body, but did not have the confidence to make prudence and other virtues into bodies (or physical things), quite overthrew the cause of atheism. Aristotle also represents the atheistic hypothesis this way: that there is but one nature, matter; and this matter is physical (or endowed with magnitude) and is the only substance, while all other things are merely the passions and properties of it. 767, 769

# The Contents.

First, *those who believed in a vacuum (such as Epicurus and Democritus, etc.), while taking it for granted that whatever is unextended or lacks magnitude is nothing, nevertheless acknowledged a double nature of extension. The first is impenetrable and tangible, which is Body; the second is penetrable and intangible, which is Space or a Vacuum. To them, this was the only incorporeal thing. Their argument was this: since nothing is incorporeal besides space (which can neither act nor be acted upon), there can be no incorporeal Deity. The Answer: If space is a real nature and yet not physical, then it must either be a property <note>original: "affection"</note> of an incorporeal substance, or else an accident without a substance.* Pierre Gassendi's <note>original: "Gassendus"</note> *helpfulness here in aiding the atheists: his claim that space is neither an accident nor a substance, but a middle nature or essence between both. But whatever exists must either subsist by itself or else be an attribute, property, or mode of something that subsists by itself. Space is either the extension of body, or of an incorporeal substance, or of nothing. But "nothing" cannot be extended; therefore space (assuming it is not the extension of body) must be the extension of an infinite incorporeal substance, which is the Deity, as some theists assert.*
Page 769, 770

*Epicurus's pretended gods, who could neither touch nor be touched, and did not have a body <note>original: "corpus"</note> but only a "sort of body" <note>original: "quasi corpus"</note>; they were therefore incorporeal things distinct from space. But it is granted that he was being deceptive or "juggling" <note>original: "colluded or juggled"</note> in this. 770*

*Other atheists who denied a vacuum and did not allow space to be a real nature, but a mere imaginary thing—the mental image <note>original: "phantasm"</note> of a body or extension considered abstractly—argued this way: "Whatever is extended is body or physical; but whatever exists is extended; therefore, whatever exists is body." 770, 771*

This argument against incorporeal substance is *answered in two ways: some defenders of incorporeal substance deny the minor premise ("whatever exists is extended"), while others deny the major premise ("whatever is extended is body"). First, most ancient incorporealists <note>philosophers who believe in non-physical reality</note> maintained that there was something unextended, "indistant" <note>meaning: without spatial dimensions or separation</note>, devoid of quantity and magnitude, without parts, and indivisible. Plato argued that the soul exists before length, breadth, and depth <note>original: "longitude, latitude, and profundity"</note>. He also denies that whatever is in no place is nothing. Aristotle’s "First Immovable Mover" is also devoid of magnitude.* For him, so is *the Mind, or that which understands.* He also denies *that the soul has a location or local motion, except "by accident" <note>meaning: moving only because the body it occupies moves</note> along with the body. 771, 773*

*Philo’s concept of a double substance: distant and in-*

<column-break/>

*distant <note>lacking spatial extension</note>. To him, God is both everywhere (because his powers extend to all things) and yet nowhere in terms of being in a specific place; for place was created by him along with physical bodies. Plotinus was very concerned with this doctrine. He wrote two books on this subject: that one and the same numerical thing (namely, the Deity) may be the whole of itself everywhere. To him, God exists before all things that are in a place; therefore, he is wholly present to whatever is present. This he would also prove from natural instinct. He likewise affirms that the human soul is numerically the same both in the hand and in the foot. Simplicius’s argument for unextended substance: that whatever is self-moving must be indivisible and "indistant" <note>lacking spatial dimensions</note>. His affirmation that souls, which do not move locally themselves, move the body through thought <note>original: "cogitation"</note>.*
Page 773, 775

No one is more thorough and explicit on this than *Porphyry <note>original: "Porphyrius"</note>. His assertion that even if such an incorporeal space existed (as Democritus and Epicurus supposed), the Mind, or God, could not be spread out <note>original: "co-extended"</note> within it; only a body could. The whole Deity is indivisibly and "indistantly" present to every part of divisible and extended things. 775, 776*

Thus *Origen* says the same in his *Against Celsus. Saint Augustine <note>original: "Saint Austine"</note> says that the human soul has no dimensions of length, breadth, and thickness, and is in itself unplaceable <note>original: "illocabilis"</note>. Boethius <note>original: "Boëtius"</note> reckons this among the common notions known only to wise men: that incorporeal things are in no place.* 776

*Therefore, this is no new or recent opinion: that the Deity is not partly here and partly there, nor measurable by yards and poles, but the undivided whole is present to every part of the world. But because there are many objections against this, we shall further show how these ancient believers in incorporeal substance <note>original: "incorporealists"</note> endeavored to free themselves from them. The first objection: that to suppose the Deity and other incorporeal substances are unextended is to make them <term>absolute parvitudes</term> <note>meaning: minute or tiny things</note>, and thus contemptible things. Plotinus's answer: that what is incorporeal is not "indivisible" in the sense of being a "little thing" (either a physical minimum or a mathematical point). If it were, God could not correspond <note>original: "congruere"</note> with the whole world, nor the soul with the whole body. Again, God is not "indivisible" in the sense of being the smallest thing; he is the greatest of all, not in magnitude, but in power. He is so indivisible that he is also infinite. It is an error proceeding from the senses and imagination to think that whatever is unextended must therefore be small. Incorporeal substance, the whole of which is present to every part of a body, is therefore greater than the body. Porphyry <note>original: "Porphyrius"</note> says the same thing: that God is neither to...*

## The Contents.

[The soul] should not be looked upon as the smallest thing, nor as the greatest, in terms of size <note>original: "Magnitude"</note>. Page 776, 778

**The Second Objection:** That whatever is neither great nor small, and possesses no location, is a non-entity (does not exist). According to Plato, Plotinus, and Porphyry <note>original: "Porphyrius"</note>, this is a mistake resulting from people relying too much on their senses and imagination. They grant that an un-extended being is <gloss>impassive <note>original: "ἀπαθὲς" (apathes) — incapable of being affected or changed</note></gloss> and unimaginable. Porphyry argues that the Mind and the imagination <note>original: "Phancy"</note> are not the same thing. Some maintain that whatever can either act or be acted upon is not "nothing," even if it does not swell out into a physical distance. Plotinus identifies two kinds of substance: bulky masses <note>original: "Tumours"</note> and un-bulky active powers. The latter are said by Simplicius to nevertheless have a certain "depth" or "profundity" within them. There is something <gloss>unimaginable <note>original: "ἀφάνταστον" (aphantaston)</note></gloss> even in physical bodies themselves. For example, we cannot possibly imagine the sun to be as large as reason proves it actually is. It is also urged by Plotinus that an un-stretched-out duration (or timeless eternity) is just as difficult to conceive as an un-extended substance; and yet eternity must certainly be attributed to the Deity. 778, 781

The idea that God and human souls are "incorporeal" only in the sense of being a <gloss>subtle body <note>original: "σῶμα λεπτομερὲς" (soma leptomeres) — a body made of thin or fine parts</note></gloss> is false. This is because the difference between "grossness" and "subtlety" in bodies, according to true philosophy, arises only from motion. The most subtle body can potentially be made as thick as lead or iron, and the thickest can be made as subtle as ether. There is no specific difference in the nature of matter itself. 781

**The Third Argument** against un-extended substance: That to be "all in the whole, and all in every part" is a contradiction and an impossibility. Plotinus grants this is true of bodies or anything that is extended. It is impossible for something that has no parts to be "a part here and a part there." Therefore, the phrase <gloss>the whole in everything <note>original: "ὅλον ἐν παντὶ" (holon en panti)</note></gloss> (meaning the whole is in the whole and the whole is in every part) should be taken only in a negative sense, meaning <gloss>undivided <note>original: "μὴ μεμερισμένον" (me memerismenon)</note></gloss>. The whole, undivided Deity is everywhere, rather than a part of Him being here only and a part of Him being there. 782, 783

**The Last Objection** is against the lack of location <note>original: "Illocality"</note> and immobility of finite created spirits and human souls. It is argued that this is not only absurd but also contrary to the generally received tradition among theists that souls move locally after death into another place called Hades. Plotinus offers two answers to this. First, that by "Hades" we may simply mean "the invisible," or the soul acting without the body. Secondly, that if "Hades" means a worse place, the soul may be said to be there where its image <note>original: "Idol" or "eidolon"</note> is. But when this same philosopher supposes the soul (in good men)

<column-break/>

to be separable even from this image, he departs from the genuine tradition <note>original: "Cabbala"</note> of his own school. The school holds that souls are always united to some body or another. This is also asserted here by Porphyry: that the soul is never entirely naked of all body, and therefore may be said to be wherever its body is. Page 784, 785

Some excerpts from Philoponus, in which the question of the ancients concerning the soul's "spirit-like" or "airy" body (after death) is extensively explained. 785, 787

Philoponus suggests here that, according to some of these ancients, the soul has such a spirit-like body even in this life as its internal instrument; this body remains with the soul when its "outer garment" (the physical body) is stripped off by death. Some held the opinion that the soul may, in this spirit-like body, leave its thicker physical body for a time without dying. It is true that our soul does not act directly upon bones and flesh, but rather upon certain thin and subtle "spirits" which are the instruments of sensation and motion. Of this, Porphyry says: "The blood is the food of the spirit, and the spirit is the vehicle of the soul." 787, 788

The same Philoponus further adds that, according to the ancients, besides the earthly body and this spirit-like or airy body, there is a third kind of body. This is unique to souls that are thoroughly purified after death; they called it a "light-form" <note>original: "Luciform"</note>, heavenly, ethereal, and star-like body. Proclus also writes of this in his commentary on the *Timaeus* (affirming it is not organized like a physical body), as does Hierocles. This is called the "thin vehicle of the soul" in the *Chaldean Oracles*, according to Psellus and Pletho. Hierocles calls it a "spiritual body" in a sense that agrees with the Scriptures; Synesius calls it the "divine body." This distinction of two internal "vehicles" or "tunics" of the soul—besides the earthly body (called <term>ostreaceous</term> <note>original: "Ostreaceous" — literally "oyster-like," referring to the physical body as a shell</note> by Plato)—was not an invention of the later Platonists after the start of Christianity; it was clearly mentioned by Virgil, though commonly misunderstood. 788, 790

Many of these Platonists and Pythagoreans supposed that the soul, in its first creation when made pure by God, was clothed with this "light-form" and heavenly body. They believed this body always remained inseparably attached to the soul during its later descents into the airy and earthly realms, though it became fouled and obscured. This was stated by Pletho and suggested by Galen when he calls this the "first vehicle of the soul." Because of this, besides the moral and intellectual purification of the soul, they also recommended a mystical or <term>telestic</term> <note>telestic: related to religious rites or initiations</note> way of purifying the ethereal vehicle through specific diets and <term>catharms</term> <note>catharms: ritual cleansings or purgations</note>. This was much emphasized by Hierocles. What Pliny's... [sentence ends mid-word]

## The Contents.

Dying by Wisdom, or the *Philosophic Death* <note>original: "Philosophick Death" — a Platonic concept where the soul separates itself from bodily passions while still alive</note>. Page 790, 792

However, it is not everyone's opinion that the same exact *ethereal body* <note>original: "Numerical Ætherial Body"</note> always sticks to the soul; rather, some believe the soul either finds or creates a body suitable for itself wherever it goes. This was the view of Porphyry <note>original: "Porphyrius"</note>, and Plato also seems to have been of that persuasion. 792, 793

Hierocles affirmed this to be the genuine tradition <note>original: "Cabbala"</note> of the ancient Pythagoreans, which Plato later followed. Hierocles defined a human being as a rational soul together with a naturally linked <note>original: "Cognate"</note> immortal body; he declared *this physical terrestrial body to be merely the idol or image of the true human, or an addition to them.* This was the answer provided by the ancient "Incorporealists" (those who believe in non-physical substances) to the objection against the idea that created spirits lack a specific location or movement. Since these spirits are naturally united to some kind of body, they can be said to be in a place and to move locally. Furthermore, it does not follow that because created spirits are not physically extended, they would therefore fill the entire physical universe. 793, 794

It is a relevant digression <note>original: "no Impertinent Digression"</note> here to compare the previously mentioned Pythagorean tradition with Christian doctrine and to consider their agreement or disagreement. First, these highly religious philosophers clearly agree with Christianity that the highest happiness and perfection of human nature does not consist in a state where souls are completely separate and un-united to *any* body, as some overly idealistic people have imagined. Plotinus held this view, though he sometimes went to the opposite extreme by suggesting human souls could animate not only the bodies of animals, but even of plants. Maimonides held a similar view among the Jews and was therefore suspected of denying the resurrection. He wrote his *Letter to the South* <note>original: "Iggereth Teman" — also known as the Letter to Yemen</note> specifically to clear himself of this suspicion. This section also discusses those who interpret the resurrection and the afterlife purely as allegories. 794, 795

Again, Christianity corresponds with the *philosophic* tradition concerning human souls in this: their happiness does not consist in being joined with gross terrestrial bodies like the ones we have now. Scripture, as well as philosophy, complains about these bodies being a heavy load and a burden to the soul; therefore, they are not to be taken up again at the resurrection. Plotinus called such a resurrection "a resurrection to another sleep." Scripture describes the difference between the resurrection body and our present body. The resurrection body of the righteous (like that of the philosophic tradition) is immortal and eter-

<column-break/>

nal; glorious and shining <note>original: "Lucid"</note>; star-like and spiritual; heavenly and angelic. *It is not this gross, fleshly body merely gilded and varnished on the outside, but changed throughout.* This is the "resurrection of life" in Scripture, emphatically called *The Resurrection*. Our souls are strangers and pilgrims in these earthly bodies; their proper home and country is the heavenly body. According to philosophy, even the coarsest body can be refined through motion into the purity and thinness <note>original: "Tenuity"</note> of the finest ether. Page 795, 799

However, Christianity does not explicitly determine whether human souls are always united to some body after death, or if they are entirely stripped of any body until the resurrection. After death, souls "live unto God." According to Origen, it is a privilege unique to the Deity to live and act alone without being vitally united to any body. If it is natural for the soul to give life to a body, then it is unlikely that it would be kept for so long in an unnatural state of separation. 799, 800

Furthermore, it is probable from Scripture *that wicked souls suffer sensory punishment or pain after death, in addition to the remorse of conscience*; it is difficult to conceive how they could experience this without bodies. This was the view of Tertullian. He added that people have the same shape or image <note>original: "Effigies"</note> after this life that they had here, though he pushed this idea too far by claiming the soul itself is a body with a specific shape and color. 800, 801

But Irenaeus clearly supposed that after death, the soul (being non-physical) is fitted to a body *that has the same character and shape as its body in this life.* 801, 802

Origen was also of this persuasion: that after death, souls have certain subtle bodies that retain the same defining form that their earthly bodies had. His opinion was that ghosts or apparitions of the dead are the souls themselves surviving in what is called a *luciform* <note>original: "Luciform Body" — a body made of light or star-like substance</note> body. He also noted that Saint Thomas did not doubt that the body of a departed soul might appear exactly like the previous one; he only disbelieved our Savior’s appearance *in the same solid body that He had before death.* 802, 804

When our Savior told his disciples *that a spirit has no flesh and bones—that is, no solid body—as he then had*, he seemed to imply that spirits have thinner bodies in which they may visibly appear. Thus, in the stories of Apollonius, touch is used as the sign to distinguish a ghost appearing from a living man. According to Origen, our Savior's body after his resurrection...

*That the "regenerate" (those spiritually reborn) here in this life have a certain "earnest" <note>original: "Earnest" — a down payment or deposit guaranteeing a future possession</note> of their future inheritance (which is their spiritual or heavenly body). This is gathered from Scripture by Irenaeus and Novatian. These "tastes" <note>original: "Prælibations"</note> of the spiritual body suggest that the soul is not perfectly separated from all forms of body after death before the Day of Judgment.*
->805, 806<-

*The opinion of Irenaeus, Origen, and others on this matter is supposed by them not to conflict at all with the Christian doctrine of the Resurrection. We make no final determination on this point ourselves.*

*The last point in the Pythagorean tradition <note>original: "Pythagorick Cabbala"</note>: That demons or angels—and indeed all created intelligent beings—consist of both soul and body (incorporeal and corporeal substance) united together, just as humans do. Hierocles held this to be true for all rational natures; he argued that no incorporeal substance, except for the Supreme Deity, is complete without being joined to a body. In this sense, God is the only truly incorporeal being; He is not a "world-soul" but a "soul above the world" <note>original: "Supra-Mundane Soul"</note>.*
->806, 808<-

*Origen’s full agreement with this ancient Pythagorean tradition: that rational creatures are neither merely bodies nor entirely without bodies, but are incorporeal substances possessing a corporeal covering <note>original: "Indument"</note>.*
->808, 809<-

*Origen was misrepresented by Huetius as claiming that angels do not have bodies but are bodies. In reality, Origen plainly acknowledged the human soul to be incorporeal and that angels also possess souls. He proves from Scripture that incorporeal creatures, though not bodies themselves, always use bodies. In contrast, the Deity is neither a body nor clothed with a body as its proper soul.*
->809, 810<-

*Some of the Church Fathers were so far from thinking angels were entirely incorporeal that they went to the opposite extreme, concluding they were entirely corporeal—that they were all body and nothing else. The middle ground between these extremes is the Origenist and Pythagorean hypothesis: that they consist of incorporeal and corporeal substance, soul and body joined together. Most ancient Fathers did not hold either extreme view. That they did not suppose angels to be perfectly un-*

<column-break/>

bodied spirits is evident from their claim that devils (just as the Greek philosophers claimed for demons) are delighted with the "smells" <note>original: "Nidours" — the smell or steam of cooking or sacrifices</note> of sacrifices, as their vaporous bodies or "airy vehicles" are refreshed by them. This was the view of Porphyry and, before him, Celsus. Among Christians (besides Origen), Justin Martyr, Athenagoras, Tatian, and others held this. Saint Basil wrote that the bodies of demons or devils are nourished by vapors, not through specific organs, but through their entire substance.
->Page 810, 812<-

*Several Fathers plainly asserted that both devils and angels consist of soul and body—incorporeal and corporeal substance joined together. These include Saint Augustine, Claudianus Mamertus, Fulgentius, John of Thessalonica, and Psellus, who offers much philosophical reasoning on this.*
->812, 814<-

*That some of the ancients, when they called angels "incorporeal," meant nothing more than that they did not have thick, heavy bodies, but rather subtle ones.*
->814, 815<-

*Though the Fathers happened to agree with the philosophical tradition on this, they seem to have been led there by Scripture. For example, our Savior said that those who obtain the resurrection of the dead shall be *equal to the angels* <note>original: "ἰσάγγελοι"</note>; according to Saint Augustine, this means they shall have angelic bodies. Also, from the Epistle of Saint Jude, it is said that the angels who sinned lost their "own proper dwelling-house"—that is, their heavenly body (called a *dwelling place* <note>original: "οἰκητήριον"</note> by Saint Paul), which made them fit to inhabit the heavenly regions. They were then cast down into the lower "Tartarus," which Saint Augustine interpreted as this dark, foggy <note>original: "Caliginous"</note> air or atmosphere of the Earth. Furthermore, the fire said to be prepared for the devils is not to be taken only metaphorically; therefore (as Psellus concludes), this implies they have bodies, because a purely incorporeal substance that is not vitally united to a body cannot be tormented by fire.*
->815, 817<-

*If all created incorporeal beings superior to humans are souls vitally united to bodies and never entirely separate from all body, then it is probable that human souls after death are not completely "naked" of all body, as if they could live and act perfectly without it—a privilege higher than that of angels and belonging only to God. Nor is it conceivable how imperfect beings could have senses or imagination without bodies. Origen, in *Against Celsus*, argues: "Our soul, though incorporeal in its own nature, always stands in need of a body suitable to the place where it is. <header>The Contents.</header>

The meaning is restored. It is evident that Origen distinguishes the "tent" <note>original: *to skenos*</note> in Saint Paul (translated as "Tabernacle") from the "Earthly House." He understands the former to be a thin, spirit-like body, which is a middle ground between the earthly and the heavenly, and which the soul remains clothed with after death. This opinion of Origen's—that the soul after death is not entirely separated from all bodies—was never listed in the official catalogue of his errors. Origen was not criticized by Methodius for asserting that souls have bodies, but for not asserting that they *are* bodies; according to Methodius, there is no truly incorporeal substance except for the Deity. This is one of the extreme views mentioned. The Origenist hypothesis is to be preferred over that of Methodius.
->Page 817, 820<-

It has already been observed that Origen was not alone in this opinion concerning human souls; Irenaeus, Philoponus, John of Thessalonica, Psellus, and others asserted the same. Saint Augustine, in his work *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis* <note>original: *De Genesi ad Litteram*</note>, grants that souls after death cannot be carried to any physical places, nor move locally, without a body. He himself seems to think that the punishment of souls before the Resurrection is mental or imaginary <note>original: "Phantasticall" — relating to the faculty of imagination or appearance rather than physical reality</note>. However, he allows for the freedom to think otherwise. In his book *The City of God* <note>original: *De Civitate Dei*</note>, he conceives that the Origenist opinion is not improbable: that some souls after death, and before the Resurrection, may suffer from a certain fire for the consuming and burning up of their impurities <note>original: "Dross"</note>. This could not happen without bodies.
->820, 822<-

So far, we have shown how the ancient defenders of "unextended incorporeals" (substances with no physical size) answered all the objections made against them. This is especially true regarding the objection about the lack of location and mobility of created incorporeal beings. Specifically, they argued that these beings are localized and made capable of motion by the bodies they are always vitally united to, according to that saying of Origen: "The soul stands in need of a body for local motions." Next to be considered are their reasons for this assertion of an unextended and non-distant substance, which is so contrary to the imagination.
->822<-

Any arguments that prove there is another substance besides physical body also demonstrate to atheists that there is something "unextended" (lacking physical dimensions), since atheists themselves take it for granted that whatever is extended is a body. Nevertheless, other arguments were proposed by these ancients to prove directly the existence of unextended substance. Plotinus's first argument aims to prove the human soul and mind are such: either every part of an "extended" soul is soul (and of a mind, mind), or it is not. If the latter—that no part of a soul or mind is by itself soul or mind—then the whole, made up of all those parts, cannot be

<column-break/>

soul or mind. But if every supposed part of a soul is soul, and of a mind, mind, then all but one would be unnecessary, or every one would be the whole—which cannot happen in physical, extended things.
->Page 822, 824<-

Again, Plotinus endeavors to prove from the "energies" (activities) of the soul that it is unextended. This is because it is one and the same indivisible thing that perceives the whole sensory object. This is further pursued: if the soul were extended, then it must either be a single physical point or more. It is impossible for it to be but one physical point. If it is more than one, then every one of those points must either perceive only one point of the object and no more, or else perceive the whole. If the former, then nothing can perceive the whole, nor compare one part of it with another. If the latter, then every person would have innumerable perceptions of the whole object at once. A fourth supposition—that the whole extended soul perceives both the whole object and all its parts (with no part of this soul having any perception by itself)—is not to be made. This is because the whole of an extended substance is nothing but the sum of all its parts; thus, if no part has any perception, the whole can have none. Moreover, to say the whole soul perceives everything and no part of it perceives anything is indeed to acknowledge it as unextended and having no separate parts.
->824, 826<-

Again, this philosopher would prove the same thing from the sympathy or "shared feeling" <note>original: "Homopathy" — from the Greek *homopathia*, meaning responding to the same stimulus or feeling</note> which is in animals; it is one and the same thing that perceives pain in the head and in the foot, and understands the whole bulk of the body.
->826<-

Lastly, he argues further from rational activities. A physical magnitude could not understand what has no magnitude and what is indivisible. However, we have a notion not only of "width" (indivisible as to thickness) and of "length" (as to breadth), but also of a mathematical point, which is indivisible in every way. We also have notions of things that have neither magnitude nor location, etc. Again, all the abstract essences of things are indivisible. We conceive of extended things themselves in an unextended way; the thought of a mile, or a distance of a thousand miles, takes up no more room in the soul than the thought of an inch, or of a mathematical point. Moreover, if that which perceives within us were a physical magnitude, it could not be equal to every sensory object and likewise perceive things both greater and smaller than itself.
->827, 828<-

Besides which, they might argue this: that we can conceive of extension (physical space) without "cogitation" (thought), and again thought without extension—from which their distinction and separability...

[Incorporeali]ty is inferrible: so can we not conceive cogitation <note>original: "cogitation" — the faculty or act of thinking</note> with extension; not the length, breadth, and thickness of a thought; nor the half, or a third, or twentieth part thereof; nor that it is shaped, round, or angular. Thoughts therefore must be non-entities, if whatsoever is unextended be nothing; as also metaphysical truths, they having neither dimensions nor figure. So too with volitions and passions, knowledge and wisdom itself, justice and temperance. If the things belonging to the soul and mind are unextended, then the soul and mind themselves must be so. Again, if the mind and soul have distant parts <note>original: "distant parts" — parts separated in space</note>, then could none of them be one substance, but many substances. If life were divided, then a half of it would not be life. Lastly, no reason could be given why they might not be as well really as intellectually divisible. Nor could a theist deny that divine power might cleave a thought, together with the soul wherein it is, into many pieces. 
->Page 828, 829<-

The sense of the ancient incorporealists <note>original: "incorporealists" — those who believe in the existence of non-physical substances</note> is therefore this: that in nature, there are two kinds of substances. The first of them is passive bulk, or distant and extended substance, which is entirely one thing outside of another; and therefore consists of as many substances as there are parts into which it can be divided. It is essentially resistant <term>original: "antitypous" — from the Greek *antitypos*, meaning solid or resistant to touch</term>; one magnitude joined to another always stands outside of it, making the whole so much bigger. Body is all outside, having nothing within, no internal energy, nor any action besides local motion <note>original: "local motion" — movement from one place to another</note>, to which it is also passive. 
->829<-

Were there no other substance besides this, there could be no motion, action, life, cogitation, intellection, or volition; but all would be a dead lump; nor could any one thing penetrate another. Therefore, there is another substance, whose character is not resistant <note>original: *ouk antitypos*</note>, the active nature: life, self-activity, and cogitation. This is no mere mode or accident of extension; it has more "entity" or being in it. Nor are these two, extension and life, merely different ways of conceiving one and the same substance. A thinker is a monad <term>original: "monad" — a single, indivisible unit or substance</term>, or one single substance. It is not conceivable how the several parts of an extended substance could jointly concur to produce one and the same thought. 
->829, 830<-

The energies of these two substances are very different. The one is nothing but local motion, or translation from place to place—a mere "outside" thing. The other is cogitation, an internal energy, or something within the "inside" of that which thinks. This inside of the thinking nature has no length, breadth, or depth, no outward-swelling tumor; because then it would be "outside" again. Were a cogitative 

<column-break/>

being extended, yet it must have, besides this extended outside, an unextended inside. But one and the same substance cannot be both extended and unextended. Therefore, in this opinion of "extended incorporeals," there is a complication of two substances and a confusion of them together into one. It is true, nevertheless, that all finite incorporeal substance is always naturally united with some extended body as its outside. 
->Page 831<-

All summed up together. 
->832<-

Hitherto the sense of the ancient asserters of unextended incorporeals has been represented to the best advantage. Nothing is asserted by us; except that these and other arguments do demonstrate, against the atheists, that there is some other substance besides body. But whether or not they prove this substance to be indistant and unextended is left to others to judge. The atheists who deny this must acknowledge every thought to be not only mentally, but also physically divisible and separable, together with the soul. They must also deny internal energy and consequently make cogitation nothing but local motion. Lastly, they must hold that no substance can co-exist with another substance more inwardly than by being placed side-by-side <note>original: "juxta-position"</note>. 
->832, 833<-

This is the first answer to the aforementioned atheistic argument against incorporeal substance, made by the ancients by denying the minor premise: that though whatsoever is extended be body, yet every thing is not extended. But the argument is otherwise answered by some learned asserters of incorporeal substance by denying the major premise: that though everything be extended, or that which is unextended is nothing, yet whatever is extended is not necessarily body. They assert another kind of extension that is incorporeal, which is both penetrable and not made up of parts that are physically separable from one another; to this belongs life, self-activity, and cogitation. It is probable that some would compound both the aforementioned hypotheses together by supposing the Deity to be altogether unextended and indivisibly present everywhere, but souls (or created incorporeals) to have an unextended inside diffused, as it were, into an extended outside. We ourselves only aim here to oppose atheists, and we dogmatize no further than to assert what all incorporealists agree in: that besides body, there is another substance which does not consist of parts really separable from one another, which is penetrable by body, is self-active, and has an internal energy distinct from local motion. All of this is demonstratively certain. This is the full answer to the first atheistic argument against incorporeal substance: that either there is something unextended, or at least extended in a different way.
