The second atheistic assault against incorporeal substance: By claiming that the origin of this mistake arose from the Scholastic essences (which are distinct from the things themselves) and the abuse of abstract names and notions, turning them into substances existing by themselves. For, although the belief in ghosts and spirits (of which God is the chief) first arose from fear, the idea that these should be incorporeal could never have entered the minds of men had they not been enchanted by these abstract names and separate essences. Page 834

The first general reply to this: That it is nothing but romantic fiction. It has already been sufficiently proved that the idea of the Deity did not arise from fear, and that all invisible ghosts are not mere fantasies; the existence of a God has also been demonstrated by reason. Apparitions are real phenomena; it is reasonable to think that there may be invisible aerial and ethereal animals, just as there are visible terrestrial ones. It is foolishness <note>original: "Sottishness" — extreme stupidity or lack of sense</note> to conclude that there is no understanding in nature superior to man. Page 834, 835

The second particular reply: That the belief in incorporeal spirits did not arise from Scholastic essences, whether considered concretely as universals only, or abstractly. No one supposes these to be things really and substantially existing outside the mind—whether a "universal man" and "universal horse," or else "humanity" and "horseness" <note>original: "Equinity" — the essential quality of being a horse</note>—and that these walk up and down in airy bodies. They are only <term>Noemata</term> <note>original: "Noemata" — Greek for "objects of thought" or mental concepts</note>, or the intelligible essences of things as objects of the mind. These essences of things are said to be eternal, as are their truths. The meaning of these eternal essences is not that they are so many eternal incorporeal substances, but that knowledge is eternal, and that there is an eternal, uncreated Mind that comprehends them, which all other minds participate in. Page 835, 836

Again, another atheistic dream is addressed: That the abstract names and notions of the mere "accidents" <note>original: "Accidents" — in philosophy, properties that are not essential to the nature of a thing</note> of bodies were turned into incorporeal substances, such as souls, minds, and ghosts. Conscious life is not an accident of bodies, as atheists suppose, but the essential attribute of another substance which is incorporeal—just as magnitude or extension is the essential attribute of a body. Page 836

The following atheistic arguments are to be dealt with more briefly. The next four—the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth—proceed only upon the supposition that there is

<column-break/>

no other substance in the world besides body or matter; therefore, they signify nothing to those who assert an incorporeal Deity. Only the Stoics and their like are concerned with answering them. Nevertheless, from the impossibility of these atheistic "corporealisms" <note>materialistic philosophies</note> contained in the fifth and sixth arguments, the necessity of an incorporeal substance will be proved. Page 836

Here are two atheistic "corporealisms" founded upon these suppositions: first, that everything is body or matter; and second, that matter as such is devoid of life and understanding. The first theory operates by way of qualities and forms that can be created and destroyed, called the <term>Hylopathian</term> <note>original: "Hylopathian" — from the Greek for "matter" and "suffering/affection," referring to the theory that all things are merely modifications of matter</note>. This is the most ancient form of atheism, as we learn from Aristotle: namely, that bulky extension is the only substantial and uncreated thing, and all other things are but the passions, qualities, and accidents of it, created out of it and destroyed back into it. The consequence of this is that there is no substantial, uncreated life and understanding, and that no mind could be a God or Creator, as mind would be entirely accidental, manufactured, and a created thing. Page 836, 837

This Hylopathian atheism is also called "Anaximandrian" by us. We are aware that Simplicius <note>a 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> believes Anaximander held a theory of <term>Homoeomery</term> <note>original: "Homœomery" — the doctrine that the parts of a substance are the same as the whole</note>, or a similar atomology of eternal uncreated qualities, as Anaxagoras did later. The only difference is that Anaximander acknowledged no uncreated life or mind but generated it all from the chance mixing of those qualified atoms. (This is a probable opinion, though not certain.) Regardless, Anaximander supposed life and understanding to be, at least, secondary qualities and accidents of the body, capable of being created and destroyed. It is not necessary to multiply the forms of atheism. Page 837

The second atheistic corporealism works by way of unqualified atoms, producing all things—even life and understanding—from the shapes, positions, motions, and sizes of parts. From this, it also follows that the mind is not a primary thing but secondary, compounded, and derivative; a creature, and no creator. This is called "Democritic"—not because Democritus was the first inventor of the "dissimilar atomology" <note>the theory of atoms having different shapes</note>, but because he was the first to use it for atheism, or the first who made dissimilar atoms the principles of all things whatsoever, even of life and understanding. [in the same place]

It cannot be denied that if these two points are granted—that everything is body, and that the first principles of body are devoid of life and understanding—it would unavoidably follow that there is no God. Therefore, the Stoics, who were corporeal theists <note>those who believe God is a physical substance</note>, denied the latter; they...

...they supposing an understanding fire, eternal and unmade, to be the maker of the whole mundane <note>original: "Mundane" — relating to the physical world or universe</note> system. It was truly observed by Origen that this corporeal God of the Stoics was only incorruptible and happy by accident—and only because he lacked a destroyer. This is not genuine theism. Page 837, 838

But there is an absolute impossibility in both these forms of atheistic corporealism; not only because they suppose no active principle, but also because they bring life and understanding—that is, "something"—out of "nothing," or create them without a cause. Here the atomic atheists are the more to be condemned of the two because they so grossly contradict themselves. From the true principle that matter, as such, is devoid of life and understanding, there arises an absolute necessity for another substance that is incorporeal, which is essentially vital and intellectual. All life cannot possibly be factitious <note>original: "Factitious" — artificial or manufactured</note> and accidental, or capable of being generated and corrupted; there must be a substantial life, and also some life that is eternal. 838, 839

The truth of this was understood and acknowledged by the Hylozoists <note>original: "Hylozoists" — those who believe that all matter possesses life</note>: that there must of necessity be both substantial and unmade life and understanding. They therefore attribute these qualities to all matter as such, but without "animality" (conscious life); which, according to them, is entirely artificial and accidental. Therefore, this hylozoic atheism also brings conscious life and animality out of nothing, or creates them without a cause. The argument of the Epicurean atheists against Stratonism <note>original: "Stratonism" — the atheistic philosophy of Strato of Lampsacus, similar to hylozoism</note> or hylozoism is unanswerable: that according to this supposition, there must be in every man and animal a heap of innumerable percipients [beings that perceive], as many as there are atoms of matter; and therefore, no single thinker. The pretense of the Hylozoists—that all the particles of matter in every animal join together—is ridiculous and impossible. 839, 840

Thus the fifth and sixth atheistic arguments are fully confuted; and from the true supposition within them—that matter, as such, is devoid of life and understanding—incorporeal substance is plainly demonstrated. This was our second undertaking. 840

The third and last undertaking: that since there is undeniably an incorporeal substance, the two following atheistic arguments (built upon the opposite supposition) are altogether insignificant. The seventh is not properly directed against theism, but against a religious kind of atheism or "theogonism" <note>original: "Theogonism" — the belief that gods are born or generated from material origins</note>; this supposed a God or soul of the world generated out of senseless matter as the offspring of Night and Chaos. A serious and true sense of the world’s animation: that there is a li-

<column-break/>

ving, sentient, and understanding nature presiding over the whole world. However, the view of pagan theists—that the whole corporeal world, being animated, is a God—is exploded [disproven] by us. This argument, therefore, being directed not against theism but against theogonism, its refutation might well be omitted here without any detriment to our cause. But because the denial of a living, understanding nature presiding over the world is atheistical, the ground of this assertion is briefly declared: that life and understanding are merely "accidents" [properties] of bodies, resulting only from such a contexture <note>original: "Contexture" — arrangement or structure</note> of atoms as produce flesh, blood, and brains in organized bodies; and that there is no reason to be found anywhere except in the human form—which is also confuted. A brutish passage from a modern writer <note>Likely referring to Thomas Hobbes</note> claims that it is inconceivable to men how God can understand without brains. Page 840, 841

The next argument (which is the eighth atheistic argument) claims that there can be no living being who is immortal or perfectly happy. This is also built upon the false supposition that all life and understanding result from a cluster of dead and senseless atoms, and therefore can be dissolved and annihilated. But there is life that is essential and substantial, which is naturally immortal; just as there is a necessity for an eternal life and a mind that is unmade and unannihilatable, which is perfectly happy. 841, 842

### SECTION IV.

The Epicurean atheists further endeavor to disprove a God from the phenomena of motion and cogitation [thought] in the three following arguments: the ninth, tenth, and eleventh. Regarding motion: from the principle that nothing can move itself, but whatever is moved is moved by another, it would follow that there can be no first cause and unmoved mover. Instead, one thing would have moved another from eternity infinitely, because nothing could move another thing if it were not itself first moved by something else. 842, 843

Answer: The meaning of this axiom is not that nothing can act from itself, as the atheist supposes (he taking it for granted that everything is a body and that all action is local motion); rather, it means that no body at rest could ever move itself locally. It is a false supposition of the atheists and some Cartesians <note>original: "Cartesians" — followers of the philosophy of René Descartes</note> that if there were but once motion in matter, it would continue of itself for all eternity. That saying of Aristotle is true: that to make an infinite...

*To claim an infinite chain of causes for motion without a First Mover is the same as saying there is no cause at all. It implies that all the motion in the world is a passion <note>original: "Passion" — in this context, an effect or something acted upon, rather than the initiator of action</note> without an agent <note>original: "Agent" — the being or force that performs an action</note>, or that it comes from nothing. It is clearly impossible that there should be any motion at all if there were nothing self-moving or self-active.* Page 843

*Therefore, from this principle—that no body <note>original: "Body" — physical matter</note> can move itself—it follows undeniably that there is some other substance in the world besides matter that has an active power of moving matter.* 843, 844

*Another conclusion from the same principle: there is another species of action distinct from local motion <note>original: "Locall Motion" — physical movement from one place to another</note>, which is not <term>heterokinesy</term> <note>original: "Heterokinesy" — movement caused by an external force</note>, but <term>autokinesy</term> <note>original: "Autokinesy" — self-originated movement</note>. The action by which local motion is first caused could not itself be local motion. All local motion is caused originally by cogitation <note>original: "Cogitation" — the act of thinking or mental activity</note>.* Thus the ninth atheistic argument regarding motion is refuted; and from the fact that no body can move itself, it is demonstrated *that there is something incorporeal <note>original: "Incorporeal" — not composed of matter; spiritual</note> which is the first cause of local motion through thought.* (In the same place)

*But the atheists further pretend to prove that thought itself is a form of movement caused by an external force, being the effect on the thinker caused by some other external agent. They argue that nothing begins from itself, and no thought can rise on its own without a cause. Therefore, they claim that thinking beings themselves are machines and that thought is merely physical motion. They argue that no understanding being can be a first cause or be perfectly happy, because it would be dependent upon something else.* 844, 845

*Answer.* It is true *that no substance begins from itself, and also that no action causes itself. But it is false to say that no action begins from the immediate agent, or that nothing can act unless it is first acted upon by something else.* Here, atheists merely *assert* what they ought to *prove*, and so they *beg the question* <note>original: "Beg the Question" — a logical fallacy where the conclusion is assumed in the premise</note>. If nothing is self-active, then all the motion and action in the universe must come from nothing or be made without a cause. 845

*It is also true that our human thoughts are frequently prompted by external objects, and that the chain of thoughts and mental images often depends upon mechanical causes. But it is false to say that all thoughts are forced upon us from the outside, or that there is no transition in our thoughts that was not previously in our senses. The human soul is a principle of actions, and therefore also of thoughts. It is a bubbling fountain of thoughts. However, there is a perfect mind that understands all truth at once and existed before physical things.* 845, 846

<column-break/>

*This is an enormous paradox and a falsehood of the atheists: that thought is physical motion and thinking beings are machines.* Here is a *correction* of what we wrote before on page 761, and a change of our opinion *upon further consideration. We now acknowledge that not only a modern writer, but also the ancient atheistic atomists, concluded that thought is really nothing other than physical motion. Nevertheless, these men are troubled by the idea of thought; because they cannot turn it into physical motion, they would persuade us that it has no reality or is nothing at all. Atheists are aware that if there is any action besides physical motion, then some other substance besides matter must be acknowledged. Those who turn thought into physical motion and men into machines are no more to be argued with than senseless machines.* Page 846, 847

*To claim that no understanding being can be happy, nor be a God, because it depends upon something outside of itself, is the same as claiming that senseless matter is the most perfect of all things. It implies that knowledge, because it suggests imperfection, is but a trivial and imaginary thing. But more on this later. Thus the tenth atheistic argument is refuted.* 847

*Another atheistic argument based on the nature of knowledge and understanding: They claim the world could not be made by an understanding being because there was no knowledge before the existence of things, which are the objects of knowledge. They say the only things that exist are physical objects, and knowledge is merely an effect caused by them. Therefore, every mind is a creature <note>original: "Creature" — a created thing</note>, and none can be a creator.* (In the same place)

This has already been fully *answered* on page 729 and the following pages. *There it was proved that individual bodies are not the only things that exist or the only objects of the mind, but that the mind contains its own truths <note>original: "Intelligibles" — things that can be understood by the intellect rather than the senses</note> within itself. And that knowledge is the <term>archetypal</term> <note>original: "Archetypal" — the original model or blueprint</note> pattern for the world and the maker of all things. So the existence of a God is demonstrable from the nature of knowledge and understanding.* 847, 848

*The atheists can no more explain the phenomenon of thought than they can explain physical motion; this is evident from their many delusions concerning it, a list of which is added here. First, they claim that all life and understanding is a mere accidental thing that can be created and destroyed, and that no life or mind is substantial or essential. This was previously refuted.* 848

*Again, they claim that life and mind are not simple or primary natures, but are merely components made of other things, and therefore neither is immortal nor incorruptible. Answer: life and—*

Understanding is an active power and could never result from mere passive matter <note>original: "Bulk"</note>; nor can any combination of dead and senseless matter possibly create life and understanding. While it is not *necessary* for an eternal, uncreated "Red" or "Green" to exist (since these colors might be made from things that aren't red or green), and it is not strictly necessary for motion to be eternal (since it could be produced by a self-active principle), and it is not necessary for matter to be eternal (since it could be created by a perfect incorporeal being), there is an absolute necessity for eternal, uncreated Life and Mind. If there had ever been a time without them, they could never have come into existence. Page 848, 849

Another atheistic hallucination: the idea that there is no "self-activity" in thought <note>original: "Cogitation"</note>, and that nothing could act except when it is forced to act by something else. This is the same as claiming all action comes from nothing, or supposing an effect without a cause. 849, 850

Another madness of theirs already mentioned: that thought is merely physical movement <note>original: "Locall Motion"</note>, and that thinking beings are just machines. This is as foolish <note>original: "Sottishness"</note> and arrogant as claiming that a number is a shape, etc. 850

A paradox of the Epicurean and Democritic atheists: that mental thought as well as sensation are merely passive reactions <note>original: "Passions"</note> of the thinker, caused by external bodies acting upon him. Some of them suppose thoughts are caused by "finer images" than those that cause sensations; others claim that thoughts are the "leftovers" of previous sensory motions. Answer: sensation itself is not a mere physical reaction, but the mind’s perception of a physical change through the imagination <note>original: "Phancy"</note>; much less is mental thought a mere reaction, and least of all is the will <note>original: "Volitions"</note>. 850, 851

Following this logic, these atheists decide that all knowledge and understanding are really the same thing as sensory perception. From this, two absurdities follow. First: there could be no such thing as "error," because every passive reaction is a real reaction, and every sensation is a real sensation—that is, it really appears that way to the person. This absurdity was accepted by Protagoras <note>a Greek philosopher known for his relativism</note>. Epicurus tried to avoid this conclusion but failed, as it contradicted his own principles. 851, 852

A second absurdity follows: that there is no absolute truth or falsehood, but all knowledge is private and relative—nothing but opinion. This was also freely accepted by Protagoras and sometimes by Democritus. However, Democritus was a blunderer in his own atomic philosophy, which clearly requires a higher faculty of reason and un-

<column-break/>

derstanding to judge the senses and reveal their illusory nature <note>original: "Phantastry"</note> by reaching absolute truth. Page 852, 853

Another atheistic error: that individual <note>original: "Singular"</note> physical objects are the only things the mind can conceive of or sense. Aristotle attributed this view to Democritus and Protagoras, but it has already been sufficiently disproven. 853, 854

To maintain this paradox, a modern atheistic writer <note>likely a reference to Thomas Hobbes</note> added his own invention: that "universals" <note>general concepts like "humanity" or "circle"</note> are nothing more than names used to group many individual objects. He claims that axioms or propositions are just the "addition and subtraction of names," and that logical reasoning <note>original: "Syllogistick Reasoning"</note> is just calculating the consequences of those names. Therefore, he argues that beyond sensory experience, we know nothing at all about anything except the names we give them. If this were true, geometric truths would not be the same in Greek as they are in Latin, etc. 854

Based on these principles, the atheists try to degrade knowledge and understanding, claiming they represent no higher perfection than what exists in senseless matter. Thus, the atheists in Plato's writings describe the mind as a playful, shadowy <note>original: "Umbratile"</note>, and fleeting <note>original: "Evanid"</note> thing—a mere image of physical bodies, which they believe are the only realities. Their goal in this is to tear down the "Scale" or "Ladder of Entities" <note>the hierarchical order of existence from lower matter to higher spirit</note>. 855, 856

All these grounds are briefly disproven again. Specifically, the opinion that so strongly favors atheism—that "nothing is in the understanding that was not first in the senses"—is refuted using the arguments of Boethius. Concepts like "Just" and "Unjust" are greater realities in nature than "Hard" and "Soft." There is unquestionably a "Ladder of Entities," and therefore it is certain that the order of things must descend from higher perfection to lower, not ascend from lower to higher. The steps of this ladder are not infinite: the bottom is inanimate matter; the top is a perfect, all-powerful Being who contains all possibilities within Himself. Mind is, by nature, Lord over all and the sovereign King of Heaven and Earth. 856, 859

The reason we insist on this so much is that atheists claim they can explain the phenomenon of thought without a God, and even use it to prove God's existence is impossible. Though modern writers may not realize it, the controversy between theists and atheists was stated this way by Plato: is the soul and mind secondary <note>original: "Juniors"</note> to senseless matter and a product of it, or are they substantial things that existed before matter in the order of nature? Accordingly, Plato refutes atheism simply by proving the soul is not "younger" than inanimate matter.

and generated out of the same. It is evident that *Plato* understood "Soul" here to mean not only the World Soul <note>original: "Mundane Soul"</note>, but also that whole rank of beings called "Soul." He argued *that no life was generated out of matter.* Page 859, 860

Those professing Christians who claim that rational souls are generated out of senseless matter are plain betrayers of the cause of *Theism*. 860, 861

Nor is the case much different for others who, though they claim to generate sensitive souls, make the rational soul a mere "blank slate" <note>original: "meer Blanks"</note>. They suggest the mind has nothing in it except what was scribbled upon it by the senses. This makes knowledge, by its very nature, junior to sensation and physical objects, which highly gratifies the *Atheists*. 861

Life is not partly accidental and partly substantial. Either all conscious life is accidental, capable of being generated and corrupted, or none of it is.* ibid.

*The doctrine of "real qualities" being generable and corruptible is also favorable to atheism. Although the atheistic Atomists reject all other qualities because "nothing can come from nothing," they contradict themselves by claiming that life and understanding are real qualities generated out of matter or caused by nothing.* 861, 862

Since there is a scale or ladder of entities in nature, producing a higher rank of beings out of a lower one—such as life and thought out of matter and physical size <note>original: "Magnitude"</note>—is to invert the order of this scale from downward to upward. Doing so lays a foundation for *Atheism*. Therefore, there is great reason to maintain this position against the *Atheists*: *that no souls can be generated out of matter.* 862, 863

The grand objection against the substantiality <note>substantiality: the state of being a real, independent substance rather than a temporary quality</note> of sensitive souls arises from the consequence of their permanent existence after death. *Descartes* <note>original: "Cartesius"</note> was so aware of this that he preferred to make animals <note>original: "Brutes"</note> into senseless machines rather than allow them to have substantial souls, which he granted they must have if they are thinking beings. What is clearly demonstrable by reason should not be abandoned just because it is attended by some difficulties or seemingly offensive consequences. 863

The <term>Pythagorean Hypothesis</term>: That all souls were created by God, not during the birth of animals, but during the <term>Creation of the World</term> <note>original: "Cosmogonia"</note>. These souls were therefore first clothed with thin and subtle bodies—aerial or ethereal <term>vehicles</term> <note>original: "Ochemata"</note>—in which they exist both before they enter terrestrial bodies and after they depart from

<column-break/>

them. This was the view of *Boethius* and *Proclus*. *Ammonius* held that his "irrational demons" were mortal—brutish souls living in aerial bodies. Since the first creation, no new substantial thing has been made or destroyed, and therefore no new life has been created. *Macrobius* looked upon this as a great truth. Page 863, 865

The Pythagoreans would endeavor to find support for this hypothesis in the Scriptures. 865, 867.

But if these aerial vehicles of brutish souls are rejected as a whim, and they are allowed only terrestrial bodies, they still will not vanish into nothing after death. Instead, they must remain in a state of insensibility and inactivity until they are reunited to other terrestrial bodies. Therefore, these are mortal in one sense, though immortal in another. Christian theologians have used the example of silkworms dying and reviving in the form of butterflies as an emblem of the Resurrection. 867, 868

However, there is no absolute necessity that the souls of animals, though they are "substances," must have a permanent existence after death in either an active or inactive state. This is because anything created by God can possibly be annihilated by Him. Only the substantiality of the rational soul is demonstrable by reason—meaning it will not vanish into nothing on its own—but it is not absolutely impossible for God to annihilate it. Our assurance of its survival depends upon faith in the Divine Goodness. *Porphyry* <note>original: "Porphyrius"</note> asserted that brutish souls are dissolved back into the life of the universe. The full answer to this objection against the substantiality of animal souls is that they may possibly be annihilated at the death of the animal, just as they were created at its birth; but if they do survive (without aerial vehicles), they must remain in a state of inactivity and insensibility. 868, 869

The doctrine of the ancient pagan theologians was that *no life or soul is generated out of dead and senseless matter*, but all are produced by the Deity just as matter is. This is proved from the writings of *Virgil*, though many other testimonies could be added. 869, 870

The <term>Hylozoic Atheists</term> <note>hylozoic: the belief that all matter possesses life</note> themselves are so aware that there must be some substantial and uncreated life (from which the lives and minds of all animals are derived) that they attribute this life to matter itself. They conclude that although the specific lives of animals and men are accidental—generated and destroyed—their fundamental life is substantial and incorruptible. These thinkers also asserted that knowledge exists before sense and is not derived from physical objects. 870, 871

This <term>Hylozoic Atheism</term> is here refuted again.

It examines the Pythagorean view of pre-existing souls and explores the potential immortality or annihilation of animal souls after death.</summary>

<header>The Contents.</header>

It is absurd to suppose that *Knowledge* and *Understanding* can exist without *Consciousness*. It is also absurd to claim that the *Substantial* and *Fundamental Life* of *Men* and other *Animals* should never *Perish*, yet their *Souls* and *Personalities* should *Vanish* into *Nothing*. No *Physical Organization* of matter can produce *Consciousness*. These *Atheists* are completely unable to give an *Account* of where the *Intelligible Objects* and *Ideas*—which form the basis of their own *Knowledge* of *Matter*—actually come from. This *Hylozoic Atheism* <note>The belief that all matter possesses life and that God is simply the sum of material life.</note> is *Nothing* but the *Crumbling* of the *Deity* into *Matter*. Page 871

It is Concluded that the *Phenomenon* of *Mind* and *Understanding* cannot possibly be *Explained* <note>original: "Salved"</note> by *Atheists* without a *God*; rather, it provides a *Solid Demonstration* of his *Existence*. 871, 872

### SECT. V.

There now remain only the *Atheistic Objections* against *Providence*, their *Questions*, and *Arguments* based on human *Interests*. *Their First Objection: From the Design of the World, which they claim is Faulty.* Or, *Because Things are Poorly Made, they argue they were not made by a God.* *This objection is directed against the View of the Ancient Theologians*, who held that *God*, being a *Perfect Mind*, therefore made the *World* in the *Best possible manner*. *Some Modern Theologians deviate from this*, as if the *Perfection of the Deity* consisted not at all in *Goodness*, but only in *Power* and *Arbitrary Will*. *The Controversy between these theologians and Atheists* is whether *Matter Moving by Chance* <note>original: "Fortuitously"</note>, or a *Random, Omnipotent Will*, is the *Origin* of all things. *There is no Ground for Faith in a merely Arbitrary Deity.* To have a *Will* that is *Undetermined* toward *Good* is not *Liberty* or *Sovereignty*, but *Weakness* <note>original: "Impotency"</note>. To *Celsus* <note>A 2nd-century critic of Christianity.</note>, *God* is the *Head* or *President* of *Righteous Nature*. *This was not only the view of Origen, but of the Ancient Christians in General.* *Plotinus* <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> said: *The Will of God is Essentially "That which Ought to be."* *God is an Impartial Balance, Weighing out Heaven and Earth.* *The Deity is not Slavishly Bound to do the Best; rather, doing the best is the Perfection of its Nature. No Atheist is able to prove the World to be Poorly Made.* 872, 874

We should not *Conclude* that *whatever we cannot find the Reason or Use for is therefore Poorly Made*. For example: The *Appendix* <note>original: "Intestinum Cæcum"</note>, though seemingly an *Odd Attachment* that *Most Anatomists* give little *Account* of, is—along with the *Valve* at its *Entrance*—an *Artistic Contrivance of Nature* to *prevent the Backflow of Waste*. 874, 875

The *First Atheistic Example of the Faultiness*

<column-break/>

of things: *The Arrangement of the Equator and the Ecliptic <note>The path of the sun as seen from Earth.</note>, which Intersect each other at an Angle that supposedly makes the Earth less Habitable than it could have been. This Objection is Founded upon a False Supposition: That the Torrid Zone <note>The hot regions near the equator.</note> is Uninhabitable. But this is actually the Best Arrangement; since it is Contrary to mechanical causes, its Persistence—along with the Constant Parallelism of the Earth's Axis—is a manifest Proof of Providence; it shows that* the Best <note>original Greek: τὸ Βέλτιστον</note> *is a Cause in Nature.* Page 875

In the next place: *Atheists try to prove against some Theists that All things were Not Made for the Sake of Mankind. This was originally only the Doctrine of narrow-minded Stoics, later recommended by human Self-Love. Whereas Plato's Doctrine was that the Whole was not made for any Part, but the Parts for the Whole. Nevertheless, Things in the Lower World were made Principally (though not Only) for Man.* Atheists are no *Judges* of whether *Worlds* are *Well* or *Ill-Made*, as they have no *Constant Measure* of *Good. To say that Nature is a Step-Mother to Man is but the bitter speech of some discontented persons, seeking to Revenge themselves by Railing against Nature—that is, Providence.* 875, 876

*Evils in General arise from the Necessity of Imperfect Beings, and the fact that some things cannot exist together at once.* 876

*Men Suffer more from their own Imaginations than from the Reality of things. Pain (which is a Real Evil of Sensation) is often Linked with Pleasure, as in the Socratic Fable. This is not the Evil of the Whole Man, but only of the Outer Self. It is Useful to free men from the Greater Evils of the Mind. Death, according to the Atheistic Hypothesis, is an Absolute Extinction of all Life; but according to Genuine Theism, it is only a Withdrawing into the Dressing Room <note>original: "Tiring-House," referring to the area behind a theater stage.</note> and putting off one's Earthly Clothing. The Dead Live to God. Christian Faith gives assurance of a Heavenly Body hereafter. The Christian Resurrection is not the "Hope of Worms" <note>A derogatory phrase used by Celsus to mock the idea of physical resurrection.</note>.* This is the Refutation of the Twelfth *Atheistic Argument*. 876, 877

The *Thirteenth* argument (which is the *Second Objection* against *Providence*) concerns *Human Affairs: Because all things happen the same way to everyone; and sometimes Vicious and Irreligious Persons are the most Prosperous.* 877, 878

*It is Granted that this Consideration has too often Shaken weak Minds in all Ages. Some conclude from this that there is no God, and that blind Chance Steers everything. Others believe that even if there is a God, he Knows nothing of what is done here below. Others believe that even if he does know, he Neglects Human Affairs.* 878

# The Contents.

It is unreasonable to require that God should miraculously intervene at every turn, or to think that every wicked person should be immediately struck by lightning. What steers the whole world is an impartial nature, not a fickle or passionate one. Yet, there is no lack of examples of an extraordinary Providence. There are good reasons for the slowness of divine vengeance. The notoriously wicked are usually caught in the long run. Page 878, 879

The occasional lack of punishment for wicked persons, far from shaking the faith of good men in Providence, actually confirms their belief in future immortality and judgment after death. The unfolding of human affairs is a kind of dramatic poem, and God Almighty is the skillful dramatist who always connects our past actions with His following response into a coherent sense. A mathematical <note>original: "Geometrical"</note> distribution of rewards and punishments. 879, 880

There should be a state of doubt and uncertainty for the exercise of faith and the more difficult aspects of virtue. Had there been no monsters to subdue, there could have been no Hercules. Here, we are to live by faith and not by sight. 880

To make a full defense of Providence would require a large volume. The reader is therefore referred to other works for more information. Only a few considerations are proposed here, not so much to refute atheists as to satisfy believers <note>original: "Theists"</note> who are sometimes inclined to question Divine Goodness, even though it is the very foundation of our Christian faith. Ibid.

First: when judging the works of God, we should not consider the parts of the world in isolation, but in relation to the whole. If only the "best" things were made, there could be no harmony because there would be no variety. As Plotinus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) who argued that the world's imperfections contribute to the beauty of the whole.</note> says, a painter <note>original: "Limner"</note> does not make the whole painting an eye, nor does he place bright colors everywhere; and a playwright does not introduce only kings and heroes upon the stage. 880, 882

Second: we should not confine God’s creation to the narrowness of common opinion, which extends the universe only a little beyond the clouds and walls it in with a sphere of fixed stars. The world is incapable of having infinite size or time. Nevertheless, just as the sun is much larger than we can imagine, so the world may be much larger still. New astronomical discoveries <note>original: "Celestial Phænomena"</note> widen the physical universe and make those imagined "flaming walls" fly away before us. It is not reasonable to think that all this immense vastness should be empty and uninhabited. 882, 883

<column-break/>

Third: we cannot make a right judgment of the ways of Providence without looking forward to the future and backward to the past, as well as at the present. The Platonists and Pythagoreans explained many phenomena through *the things done in a pre-existent state* <note>original: "τὰ προβιβιωμένα"</note>. Our common Christianity assumes only a kind of "imputative" pre-existence to explain the corruption of mankind and the evils of this state. The different fates and conditions of men in this life are to be resolved into a just, though hidden <note>original: "Occult"</note> Providence. Page 883

The third objection against Providence, or the fourteenth atheistic argument: that it is impossible for any one being to observe and order all things. Even if it were possible, it would be distracting and inconsistent with happiness. Moreover, they claim that an irresistibly powerful and happy being would not concern itself with the welfare of others, arguing that benevolence arises only from weakness. 883, 884

The reply: Because we ourselves have only a finite awareness and a narrow sphere of activity, to measure the Deity accordingly is merely an "Idol of the Cave" <note>A term used by Francis Bacon to describe the personal biases and limitations of individual human perspective.</note>. It is certain that if there were nothing beyond what we could fully comprehend, there could be no God. If the sun had life coextensive with its rays, it would perceive everything touched by them. Creatures are but the rays of the Deity. Men are able to manage affairs in many distant places without distraction, and innumerable thoughts lie together in our minds without crowding one another or causing us any disturbance. 884

To ease the minds of weak mortals, it has already been suggested that there is no necessity for God to do everything directly Himself. He has ministers under Him who execute His Providence: such as a formative "Plastic Nature" <note>A term for an unconscious, organizing life-force in nature that carries out God's plan.</note> (a reason partly insisted on before); and instincts in animals, which are a part of that Divine Fate that serves Providence. Above these are other knowing and understanding ministers of the Deity appointed to preside over human affairs. But all is overlooked by the watchful eye of God Almighty, who may Himself extraordinarily intervene. 884, 885

Therefore, there is no need to limit Providence only to a few great things to free the Deity from distraction. Small things (upon which greater things often depend) are not neglected. Nevertheless, the chief employment of Divine Providence in the governance of souls <note>original: "Oeconomy of Souls"</note> was reduced by Plato to this summary: the moving of them into better or worse states according to their behavior. Thus may the slow wits of mortals,

# The Contents.

...understand more easily that Providence is not burdensome or distracting to the Deity. Page 885

But the idea that all benevolence arises from weakness <note>original: "Imbecillity"</note>, and that a perfectly happy being would not trouble itself with any business but only enjoy its own ease, are "idols of the atheist’s den." These other views arise from the narrow-mindedness of their spirits, caused by vice and immorality. 885, 886

**The Atheistic Queries, to be answered next. The First Query:** *If there were a God who was perfectly happy in Himself, why would He go about making a world?* **Answer:** The reason for God making the world was His overflowing and communicative goodness, so that there might be other happy beings besides Himself. *This is consistent with God making the world for His own glory.* The reason why Plotinus <note>a major Neoplatonist philosopher</note> would reject that idea. It is true that God did not make the world merely to show off <note>original: "Ostentate"</note> His skill and power, but to display His goodness, which is chiefly His glory. **The Atheist’s further demand:** *What harm would it have been for us never to have been made?* **Answer:** No other harm than this: that we could never have enjoyed good, nor been capable of happiness. If there is no harm in not being made, then there is no harm in being annihilated; the distance is just as great from "nothing to something" as it is from "something to nothing." 886

**The Second Atheistic Query:** *If God's goodness was the cause of His making the world, why then was it not made sooner?* **This question is capable of two meanings. First:** *Why was the world not from eternity?* **The Reply:** This is not from any defect in Divine goodness, but because the thing itself is impossible; the necessity and incapacity of such an imperfect being <note>the world</note> prevents it. We ourselves are prone to think that if the world could have existed from eternity, it should have been so. This was the view of Philoponus in his refutation of Proclus’s arguments for the world's eternity. And now no place is left for those atheistic quibbles against the *novelty of creation* <note>the idea that the world has a beginning</note>, as if God must have slept through eternity or had grown tired of His former solitude. **Another sense of the question:** *Why, even if the world could not be from eternity, was it not made sooner?* **Answer:** The world could not possibly have been made in time without it once having been only a day old, and also once being no more than five or six thousand years old. 886, 887

**The Third Atheistic Query:** *How could God move the matter of the whole world, especially if He is non-physical?* <note>original: "Incorporeal"</note> **Answer:** Since all things are derived from the Deity and essentially depend on Him, they must necessarily be under His command and obedient to Him.

<column-break/>

And since no physical body can move itself, that which first moved matter must be non-physical <note>original: "Incorporeal"</note>, and it does not move it by machines and engines, but by thought <note>original: "Cogitation"</note> or will alone. The notion that a non-physical Deity could not move matter because He would "run through it" <note>like a ghost through a wall</note> is absurd; He moves it not mechanically, but through life <note>original: "Vitally"</note>. That thinking beings have a natural power to move matter is evident from our own souls moving our bodies, not by machines or engines, but merely by thought. It is easier for the Deity to move the whole world by will and thought than it is for us to move our own bodies. Page 887, 888

**The Last Category of Atheistic Argumentation, From Self-Interest.** **First:** That it is in the interest of individuals that there should be no infinitely powerful being who follows no law but his own will. **The First Reply:** Wishing is not proving. Nor will any man’s thinking make things different than they actually are. 888

**But Secondly:** This wish of atheists is founded upon a mistaken notion of God Almighty—that He is nothing but arbitrary, all-powerful will. God’s will is not mere whim, but law and fairness <note>original: "Equity"</note>; it is the "Right" itself choosing to act. Nor does justice in God clash with goodness; it is a branch or specific form of it. It is in the interest of no one that there should be no God, except perhaps for those who are hopelessly wicked and willfully abandon their own true good. 888, 889

To be without God is to be without hope. There is no faith or hope in senseless matter. According to the atheistic hypothesis, there is no possibility of happiness and no security of any good. 889

God is such a being that, if He did not exist, nothing would be more worth wishing for. To believe in a God is to believe in the existence of all good and perfection, and that all things are made and governed as they should be. The capacity to sin <note>original: "Peccability"</note> arises from the necessity of imperfect beings having free will. There are infinite hopes to be found in a being who is infinitely good and powerful. Democritus and Epicurus, however much they have been praised lately, were only deluded sophists <note>deceptive philosophers</note>, or clever fools and corruptors of mankind. 889, 890

**The Last Atheistic Argumentation:** That theism or religion is inconsistent with the interest of political rulers <note>original: "Civil Sovereigns"</note>. **Their first pretense for this:** That the political ruler reigns only through fear, and therefore there must be no power or fear greater than that of the *Leviathan* <note>referring to Thomas Hobbes's theory of the absolute state</note>. 890

In answer to this, **the atheistic ethics and politics must be unraveled.** Their foundation is laid in the vilifying of human nature—the claim that there is no natural justice, fairness, or charity. No public or common nature...

...in *Men*, but all private and selfish. *That every man by nature has a right to everything, even to other men's bodies and lives. That an appetite to kill and torment, by nature, gives a right. That nature has brought men into the world without any fetters or shackles of duty and obligation, which they see as the hindrances of liberty. *But in the next place, they add that though this state of nature—which is a beast-like <note>original: "Belluine"</note> liberty and lawless freedom to do anything—is in itself the best, yet by accident and because of human weakness <note>original: "Imbecillity"</note>, it proves to be the worst. *In this, these atheists first slander human nature and then debase justice and civil authority, making it the ignoble and bastardly child of fear, or a lesser evil submitted to out of necessity to avoid a greater one. According to this atheistic hypothesis, no man is willingly just. This is no new invention of the writer of* On the Citizen <note>original: *De Cive*, a work by Thomas Hobbes</note>, *but the old atheistic theory of the origin of justice, the body politic, civil society, and sovereignty (existing even before Plato's time). It is fully described in the second book of Plato's* Republic. *There, the philosopher concludes that justice, according to these thinkers, is but a middle ground between the best and the worst; loved not as a good in itself, but only because of men's weakness. Or, that justice is indeed another man's good, and the evil of the man who is just. The same hypothesis concerning justice—as an artificial <note>original: "Factitious"</note> thing that sprang only from fear and weakness and was chosen only as a lesser evil—was also insisted upon by Epicurus.*
->891, 893<-

*The vain attempts of our modern atheistic politicians to make justice by art when there is none by nature. First, by renouncing and transferring men’s rights through will and words. For if nothing is naturally unlawful, then no man, by will and words, can make anything unlawful to himself. What is made by will may be destroyed by will. The ridiculous conceit of these atheistic politicians is that injustice is nothing but a "retraction of a grant"* <note>original: *Dati Repetitio*</note>, *and such an absurdity in*

<column-break/>

*life as occurs in a debate when a man denies a proposition he had previously granted. They claim there is no real evil in the man, but only a relative inconsistency in him as a citizen.* Again, these *justice-makers* and *authority-makers* *pretend to derive their artificial justice from pacts and covenants.* But *pacts and covenants, without natural justice (as they themselves confess), are nothing but words and breath, and therefore can have no force to obligate. Therefore, they make another pretense based on certain counterfeit laws of nature of their own devising, which are nothing but mere juggling and double-talk; they are simply the laws of fear, or a product of their own timid and cowardly character <note>original: "Complexion"</note>. They ridiculously dance round in a circle when they derive the obligation of civil laws from covenants; of covenants from laws of nature; and of laws of nature again from civil laws. Their vain attempt is to join by art what nature has separated, which is like tying knots in the wind or water. Their artificial obligations, or the ligaments by which the members of their Leviathan <note>A reference to Thomas Hobbes’s famous metaphor for the state</note> are held together, are thinner than cobwebs.*
->Page 893, 895<-

*These artificial justice-makers and obligation-makers, sensible of the weakness of these attempts to join by art what nature has separated, fly at last from art to force and power, making their sovereign reign only through fear. This is the true meaning of the opinion that all obligation is derived from law—that is, the command of him who has power to compel. If the obligation to obey civil laws comes only from fear of punishment, then no man is obliged to hazard his life for the safety of his prince; and whoever can promise themselves freedom from punishment <note>original: "Impunity"</note> may justly disobey. If civil sovereigns reign only through fear, then their authority is nothing but force, and power would justify rebellion. Lastly, if civil right or authority is nothing but force and violence, then it could not last long; for that which is natural will always prevail against that which is violent.*
->895<-

*Therefore, since civil authority and bodies politic can neither be merely artificial nor violent things, there must be some natural bond <note>original: *Vinculum*</note> to hold them together; such as will both obligate subjects to obey the commands of sovereigns and obligate sovereigns, in commanding, to seek the good of their subjects. There must be something of a common, public, and binding <note>original: "Conglutinating"</note> nature, which is none other than natural justice. The authority of God Himself is founded in justice, and civil authority is a participation in that. Sovereignty is no creature of the people or of men's wills, but has a stamp...*

...a stamp of divine nature <note>original: "Divinity"</note> upon it. Had not God made a City, men—neither by art, nor political enchantment, nor by mere force—could have made any. The whole world is one city of God and rational beings. The civil sovereign is no *Leviathan*; that is, no beast, but a god. He reigns not through mere brutish force and fear, but through natural justice and conscience, and the authority of God himself. Nevertheless, there is a need for force and fear too, to compel some to their duty; nor is the sovereign's sword alone sufficient here, but he must also reign in the fear of Almighty God.
->Page 895, 896<-

The second atheistic pretense for making religion inconsistent with civil sovereignty: because it limits and confines that which, in its own nature, is and ought to be infinite. The reply: that the atheist's "infinite right and authority" of civil sovereigns is nothing but beast-like <note>original: "Belluine"</note> liberty. But true right and authority is essentially founded in natural justice; there is no authority to command where there is not an obligation to obey. Commands do not create obligation, but presuppose it, without which they would signify nothing. The first original obligation comes not from *will*, but nature. The error of those theists <note>believers in God</note> who derive all obligation to moral things from the will and positive command of God, as threatening punishments and promising rewards. From this, it would follow that no man is good and just except by accident only, and for the sake of something else. Justice is a different species of good from that of private utility. Infinite justice is as absurd as an infinite rule or measure. If there is no infinite justice, then there is no infinite right and authority. God's own authority is bounded by justice: His will is ruled by justice, and justice is not ruled by His will. Atheists, under a pretense of giving civil so-

<column-break/>

vereigns infinite right, really divest them of all right and authority, leaving them nothing but brutish force. It is proved here that the supreme powers <note>original: "Summæ Poteſtates"</note> must of necessity be unaccountable <note>original: ἀνυπεύθυνοι</note>.
->Page 896, 898<-

The last atheistic pretense for the inconsistency of religion with civil power: because conscience is a private judgment of good and evil. Answer: That not religion, but atheism, introduces such private judgment as is absolutely inconsistent with civil sovereignty. Atheism acknowledges nothing in nature that tends to the public and common good, but makes private appetite the only rule or measure of good, and utility the measure of justice. The desperate consequence of this is that private utility may justify rebellion and the murder of a parent or ruler <note>original: "Parricide"</note>. The atheists' professed assertion: that those who have once rebelled may justly defend themselves afterward by force. Though private persons must make a judgment in conscience for themselves (the atheists' "public conscience" being nonsense and a contradiction), yet the rule of conscience is not private, but public—except only to mistaken fanatics, who therefore sometimes make a pretense of conscience and religion to incite sedition and rebellion. Religion and conscience oblige subjects, in all lawful things, to actively obey the sovereign powers; in unlawful things, not to resist.
->898, 899<-

The conclusion of the whole book: That all the atheistic grounds having been fully confuted, and the impossibility of atheism demonstrated, it is certain that the origin and head of all things is no blind and unconscious nature, but a perfect understanding being, self-existent; who has made all that was fit to be made, and after the best manner, and exercises a just providence over all. To whom be all honor and glory, etc.
->ibid.<-

->The End of the Contents.<-

<summary>This page concludes the Table of Contents by refuting the idea that religion undermines the state, arguing instead that justice and divine law are the true foundations of a sovereign's authority. The book ends by asserting that the universe is governed by a perfect, conscious Being rather than blind nature.</summary>
